## Volume front matter

### Series title page

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, complete, uniform, convenient, economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully corrected by comparison with one another and with several manuscript codices; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the ample editions owed to the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indices following each individual volume or each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority and influence with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indices: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers have commented on the several books of Scripture, and in which places of their works they have done so.*

*The most accurate edition, and one easily preferred to all others, if the following are duly considered: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.*

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

The Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. Two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; one thousand three hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for eight hundred francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in this edition only in Latin translation.

# Preliminary Commentary

## § I. Which Life or Acts should be published; the various sources from which these were composed or by which they will be elucidated; and the aids or documents, one of which is also to be published at the end of the Acts

[Column 0009A]

Although before the beginning of the sixteenth century no one had expressly committed to writing the entire course of the Life, character, and deeds of St. Bruno, who, as will be shown, died in the year 1101, there nevertheless existed men from the most celebrated Order founded by this most holy patriarch—men distinguished alike in learning and piety—who, at a much earlier time, had most diligently committed to documents what they knew about the beginnings and founders of the Carthusian house and of certain other houses, if not for public publication (for perhaps their extreme modesty would not have permitted that), at least to be privately communicated within the retreats of their houses as an example to the future followers of their institution. In these writings they had at least touched upon the principal features of the life led by their holy Founder.

How consistent this is with the truth is demonstrated by the *Brief History of the Carthusian Order* inserted by Martène in volume VI of the *Veterum Scriptorum*. Its Prologue contains these words:

“Although the first five priors of the Grande Chartreuse, described below, are found in several chronicles, nevertheless their successors, I do not know for what reason, have been handed over to oblivion in such a way that absolutely no memory of them is preserved in any written record.”

2. Since the anonymous author who records this wrote, as I shall show in no. 17, near the beginning of the fifteenth century, the chronicles to which he refers in the words just quoted were certainly composed long before the sixteenth century. Since they undoubtedly treated in some fashion the deeds of the first five priors of the Grande Chartreuse, it is clear that they at least touched upon the principal matters concerning Bruno. It also appears beyond doubt that they were written by Carthusians, especially since they were found almost exclusively in Carthusian houses and for a long time remained almost entirely unpublished there.

Furthermore, of chronicles of this kind—which could rightly be called chronicles because they present events arranged according to their times, although they are also found under other names—two in particular have come to my knowledge: one more condensed, the other more extensive. Since in both of them many things related about St. Bruno have their foundation, it will be useful to inform the reader at once, at the very beginning of this Commentary, about their age and authority. In this Commentary all the deeds of the Saint are to be examined and elucidated.

3. I begin with the more condensed chronicle. In volume I of the *New Library of Manuscripts*, pp. 638 and following, Labbe lists among the *Historical Opuscula*, from a manuscript of St. Remigius at Rheims, five different eulogies. The first contains in summary the principal deeds of St. Bruno; the others contain, likewise in summary, matters relating to the four men who immediately succeeded him in the priorship of the Grande Chartreuse.

The following title is prefixed to the eulogies:

“On the institutions of the Carthusian Order.”

But in the catalogue of books prefixed to the aforesaid volume of manuscripts, after the words “On the institutions of the Carthusian Order,” there immediately follows: “or, on St. Bruno, Landuinus, Peter Francis, John the Tuscan, and Guigo of Saint-Romano, the first priors of the Chartreuse.” I do not know whether “institutions” should instead be read “institutors.” Whether this is so or not matters little; having briefly noted it, let us return to the matter itself and now investigate the time when the said eulogies were written.

In his *Dissertation on the True Cause of St. Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Desert*, chapter 1, § V, Launoy also produces from a manuscript of the statutes and customs written by Guigo, the fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, that very eulogy of St. Bruno which Labbe presents in the place just cited. He says that this manuscript, in which the eulogies of the next four successors of our Saint in the priorship of the Chartreuse also appear, is preserved among the Carthusians at Paris.

4. The anonymous Carthusian author who composed the fourth book of the *Annals of his Order*—a work that has until now been made public, though not printed, and which the Carthusian Fathers nevertheless, with their customary great courtesy, shared with me—therefore conjectures in no. 101 that the manuscript preserved by the Parisian Chartreuse was written only after the year 1257, around which time that Chartreuse was first founded and the Statutes of Riffierius, called the ancient statutes, had not yet been prescribed.

But he immediately asserts, and rightly so, that what is found in the same manuscript concerning St. Bruno and the three first priors of the Chartreuse after him was committed to writing in the time of Guigo, the fifth prior of the Chartreuse. This is established by another manuscript codex of the same customs of the Carthusian Order, sent to him in the Chartreuse by the venerable father prior of the Chartreuse of Mont-Dieu. That codex likewise contains what occurs in the Parisian manuscript concerning our Saint and his next four successors in the priorship of the Grande Chartreuse, and it is the oldest of all those now found in the Order. It was copied at the Grande Chartreuse and carried to the house of Mont-Dieu by Gaufredus, its first prior, in the year in which that house was founded, namely 1136, as is clear from the manuscript itself. At its end are written these words:

“From the hermitage of the Chartreuse, now the hermitage of Mont-Dieu, from the year 1136.”

And below:

“Gaufredus, Prior of Mont-Dieu, received this as a gift from Lord Guigo.”

5. The anonymous Carthusian annalist praised above states substantially the following. He says that the eulogy of St. Bruno copied in his oldest manuscript, and thoroughly corresponding—as is apparent from the statements of the same writer—to the eulogy presented by Labbe in the place cited above, is one and the same, with a few words added, as the eulogy of the same Saint which Launoy excerpted from the Parisian manuscript. He then transcribes in full from his oldest manuscript the eulogies of the next three priors, namely Landuinus, Peter Francus or Franciscus, and John the Tuscan, who governed the Chartreuse immediately after St. Bruno. These too agree exactly with the eulogies of the same men found in Labbe in the place cited above.

Then, lest anyone deny the antiquity established for this manuscript on the ground that it also contains the eulogy composed for Guigo, together with a note of his death, which occurred in 1137, he continues as follows:

“Thus far it speaks there of the first four priors of the Chartreuse. Immediately afterward, on the same folio—namely, on the verso—at the end of the other page, that is, the second page, in the same hand in which the entire codex was written, and with no intervening space between the lines, there followed a table of the chapters of Guigo’s customs. This continued through the next three pages.”

6. “But afterward the opening lines of this table, which immediately filled the remainder of the other page of the first folio, directly after the brief eulogy of John the Tuscan, the fourth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, as we have just said, were erased by a later hand, though one that nevertheless appears extremely old. In their place the beginning of Guigo’s Brief Life was written above the text. This Life was continued by the same later hand on another half-sheet, which can easily be detected as having been inserted between the preceding folio, on which the eulogies of the aforesaid four priors are found, and the following one, on which the said table of chapters had been continued. Hence it is evident that the eulogy of Guigo was inserted, or introduced, into the aforesaid codex after his death.”

Thus far the anonymous annalist of the Carthusian Order praised above, except for a few things which, using different characters, I added for the sake of clarity.

From these facts, and from the other matters brought forward above, it follows that the Mont-Dieu manuscript, mentioned so often, although it also contains the eulogy of Guigo, the fifth prior of the Chartreuse, and the eulogies of the first four priors of the Chartreuse supplied here by Labbe, were written while Guigo himself was still alive, that is, before the year 1138, when he had ceased to live.

Now, since this is so, these materials—which I shall henceforth call, following the example of the anonymous Carthusian annalist praised above more than once, the “Chronicle of the First Four Priors of the Chartreuse,” and which I have already distinguished above simply by the name “Chronicle”—deserve the trust of everyone. They were committed to writing by an author who, although not certainly known, was nevertheless contemporary with the events narrated in them, and most probably was Guigo himself, the writer of the primitive customs of the Chartreuse prefixed to them. Even if he did not write the things reported in that Chronicle about the first four priors of the Chartreuse, and especially about St. Bruno, he most probably at least saw and approved them.

7. Therefore, so that at the very threshold of this Commentary I may present the diligent reader with a certain summary of the Life of our Saint which can safely be trusted, I transcribe here the eulogy of St. Bruno contained in that Chronicle, including what is related there about him, exactly as it appears in Labbe in the place cited so often above. It reads as follows:

“Master Bruno, a German by nationality, from the distinguished city of Cologne, born of parents of no obscure standing [another reading adds: ‘born’], very well equipped in both secular and divine letters, canon and master of the schools of the church of Rheims, which is second to none among the churches of Gaul, abandoned the world, founded the hermitage of the Chartreuse, and governed it for six years.

“When compelled by Pope Urban, whose teacher he had once been, he went to the Roman Curia to assist that same Pope with comfort and counsel in ecclesiastical affairs. But since he could not endure the disturbances and customs of the Curia, burning with love for the solitude and quiet he had left, he abandoned the Curia and also rejected the archbishopric of the church of Rheims, to which he had been elected at the Pope’s wish. He withdrew to the hermitage in Calabria called La Torre, and there, after many laymen and clerics had gathered around him, he practiced the resolve of the solitary life for as long as he lived. There he died and was buried, approximately eleven years after his departure from the Chartreuse.”

[Column 0013A] 8. This eulogy will often be useful in the course of this Commentary. It should nevertheless be noted that its final four words, although they are not found in the manuscript of the Parisian Chartreuse from which Launoy introduced it into his dissertation praised above, are nevertheless to be retained. They were found both by Labbe in the Rheims manuscript of St. Remigius and by the anonymous author of the hitherto unpublished fourth book of the *Annals of the Carthusians*, both in the manuscript mentioned above, older than all the others, and also in others, as that author himself testifies. They also appear necessary for completeness of sense.

I now proceed to the other of the two chronicles, which supplies still more about St. Bruno and whose character and date must likewise be examined here. This is nothing other than a Carthusian work or treatise, about which John Columbi, a priest of our Society, discusses at length in his *Dissertation on the Beginnings of the Carthusians*, no. 57 and several others. In no. 61 he rightly proves that the treatise was not composed by William of Elbura or Yporegia, or, if one prefers, by the author of the treatise *On the Origin and Truth of Perfect Religion*—whether that author really was, as Columbi thought, William of Elbura, or Boso, the seventeenth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, as the often-mentioned anonymous annalist who wrote the fourth, hitherto unpublished, book of the *Annals of the Carthusians* contends in no. 55 and promises later to prove.

[Column 0013C] 9. In the meantime, I have been unable by any means to discover who that other Carthusian was, or what name he bore, who composed the treatise or Chronicle mentioned by Columbi. He prefixed no title at all to his work. Hence some have called it the *Chronicle of the Origin of the Carthusian Order*, while others have called it the *Treatise on the Narrative History of the Beginning and Advancement of the Carthusian Order*.

It could appropriately be designated by either title. For, as the aforesaid Columbi teaches in no. 49 of his work on the beginnings of the Carthusians (for I do not have the complete work at hand), it is divided into two distinct parts. One contains the beginning of the Carthusian Order; the other contains St. Bruno and the four priors of the Grande Chartreuse who immediately followed him, each placed in his proper order and further adorned with eulogies.

As to this latter point, I understand it from a letter sent to me from Cologne by Augustine Aldenbruck, a priest of our Society, after he had examined the same work, preserved there among the Carthusians, at my request.

I shall henceforth call its principal section, which presents the first five priors of the Chartreuse while preserving the chronological order in which they governed it, the *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Grande Chartreuse*. I see that the same has already been done before me in a manuscript *Chronological-Diplomatic Dissertation on St. Bruno* which F. Michael Morckens, a member of the Carthusian Order of Cologne, composed and sent to my predecessors in 1727.

10. This religious man, distinguished no less for learning—as this single work abundantly proves—than for piety, inserted in it the complete eulogy of St. Bruno. He copied it from the aforesaid *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Grande Chartreuse*, as he calls it, although others, as I have already shown, call it differently; or rather, he copied it from its most ancient exemplar. He judged this exemplar, from its characters, to have been written easily four hundred years earlier. It is preserved in the library of the Carthusians of Cologne, to whom it was once given by Peter Rinck, a distinguished benefactor of the Cologne Charterhouse. Comparison with the most ancient exemplar of the Grande Chartreuse showed it to be complete and genuine.

I shall append this eulogy of our Saint to this Commentary, marking it with the title *The Earlier Life* and distinguishing it by numbers according to our custom, adding notes at the end wherever appropriate. I do so because I have found no other older writing in which more matters about Bruno are recorded.

The reader will easily discover, by reading it through, how much this eulogy supplies concerning the holy Founder of the Carthusian Order. Its antiquity, however, will become clear from what I am now about to say concerning the antiquity of the Chronicle from which it was taken.

11. John Columbi, often praised above, contends in his *Dissertation on the Beginnings of the Carthusians*, no. 57 and the following three numbers, that this Chronicle was written from about the year 1151, or under Basil, who governed the Chartreuse from that year until 1173.

He attempts to prove this opinion from the fact that the anonymous author of the Chronicle, after announcing that he would treat “of the ancient wise men and holy founders and promoters of the Carthusian Order,” includes among these only Bruno, Landuinus, Peter, John, and Guigo, while passing over in silence Anthelm, the seventh, and Basil, the eighth prior of the Chartreuse. Yet, as Columbi clearly demonstrates, these men too ought rightly to be counted among the ancient founders and promoters of the Carthusian Order.

Accordingly, since he thinks the author omitted them because, when he wrote, they were not yet ancient, Columbi concludes that the work must have been written from about the year 1151, or under Basil, the eighth prior of the Chartreuse.

But what if the anonymous author of the Chronicle, after already listing Bruno and the other four just named, was prevented by death or by other serious intervening causes from listing Anthelm and Basil as well? What if the book of the ancient or primitive customs written by Guigo—which this anonymous writer cites near the end of the Life of St. Bruno to establish the year of his death—placed only the first five priors of the Chartreuse at its head, after the manner of the oldest Mont-Dieu codex and many others mentioned in nos. 4 and 5, which contain those same customs of Guigo?

In that case, he may have regarded only those five as the ancient founders and promoters of the Carthusian Order. Or, at least, because he did not find Anthelm and Basil mentioned there and perhaps did not know them sufficiently from another source, he may have judged that they should be passed over in silence.

12. Whatever the case may be, it appears to me highly probable, if not certain, that the Chronicle in question was written later than about the year 1151.

For in no. 2 of the eulogy or Earlier Life of our Saint, its author calls the academy of Paris the “University.” Although from about the year 1151 it had begun to form a certain association and was flourishing with teachers trained in every branch of knowledge and with a great multitude of students flocking to their lectures, it was not nevertheless adorned with the name “University” before the beginning of the thirteenth century, whatever Bulaeus argues against this in his *History of the University of Paris*. This is taught by the writers of the *Literary History of France*, vol. IX, p. 80, and is now generally acknowledged among nearly all scholars.

Moreover, the same author, a member—as I have said—of the Grande Chartreuse, mentions in no. 20 of the Life of the Saint to be published a cartulary which existed at the Grande Chartreuse when he wrote. It appears hardly credible that the Grande Chartreuse had already been supplied, from about the year 1151, with as many documents as would have been sufficient to compile a cartulary.

13. Indeed, since the houses near the principal Chartreuse—such as Portes, Maureve, Durbon, Aillon, and Vallon-Saint-Hugues—did not begin to take care to gather their documents into cartularies, which still exist intact today, until shortly before the year 1250, as the manuscript *Treatise on the Life of St. Bruno*, supplied to me by the Carthusian Fathers of this place, reports in no. 24, it becomes probable that the same concern was first undertaken at that time by the Grande Chartreuse as well.

It follows from this that the anonymous author of the Chronicle whose age we are investigating, since he mentions a cartulary existing at the Grande Chartreuse when he wrote, probably did not write before about the year 1250, contrary to Columbi’s view.

But how much later did that chronologist put his hand to writing?

14. Since William of Yporegia, to whom John Columbi attributes the *Treatise on the Origin and Truth of Perfect Religion* in no. 55 of his *Dissertation on the Beginnings of the Carthusians*, wrote it in 1313, according to Columbi’s view, while Boso, to whom the said treatise may in reality have to be attributed, died in 1313, the work must certainly have been composed before the year 1314.

Therefore, since its author, whoever he may finally have been, inserted in his work the complete *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Chartreuse* discussed here—see John Columbi’s Dissertation, already cited several times, nos. 55 and 61—it follows altogether that he wrote this Chronicle before the year 1314.

Although this appears sufficiently certain, there is nevertheless no further evidence by which I can safely determine how many years before that date he wrote it.

15. In the meantime, nothing seems to prevent our believing that this was done about fifty or even sixty years before the said year 1314. Indeed, if someone were to contend that the writing, or composition, of the Chronicle in question should be placed before about 1250, or even before about 1230, I could not prove him certainly wrong, since it is by no means absolutely certain that no cartulary then existed at the Grande Chartreuse.

Nevertheless, in order to establish that the work should be placed before either of those dates, all the other arguments by which the matter could be decisively proved would be required; and, so far as I judge, these are altogether lacking.

These, then, are the considerations which arise in attempting to determine, however approximately, the age of the Chronicle that records in order the first five priors of the Grande Chartreuse and some of their deeds. From all that has been said, it appears certain that it was written neither before the thirteenth century nor after the year 1314. How much earlier than that year it was composed, however, remains entirely uncertain, and nothing presents itself by which the age of that monument can be more precisely determined.

16. Nevertheless, although this is so, in the succeeding periods it was so well established among the Carthusians that, whenever they happened to have occasion in the books they were writing to record anything about the origin of their Order, or about St. Bruno and the four priors of the Chartreuse who followed him, they usually excerpted what they actually recorded from this same source, often using nearly the same words as its author.

The first to be mentioned among them is the author praised above more than once, whether he was William of Yporegia or Boso, who inserted that monument into his *Treatise on the Origin and Truth of Perfect Religion*.

To him may be added the chronologist of the priors of the Carthusian Order, mentioned by Columbi in no. 54 of his *Dissertation on the Beginnings of the Carthusians*. As this writer indicates there, he recounts in precisely the same words the dreadful miracle in which a man who had returned to life publicly proclaimed from his bier at Paris that he had been condemned—the same miracle that is related in the *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Chartreuse*, or in the Earlier Life of our Saint to be published here, no. 1 and following.

In another place of his work, different from that in which this account occurs, he also records the following:

“In a short time the prayer of John Birellus, Prior of the Chartreuse, and of the community was heard, and Amadeus the Green, count of Savoy, received a son by a wife who was thought to be barren. He too was called Amadeus and has now become count of Savoy.”

17. From these words it follows that the aforesaid chronologist wrote within the period extending from the year 1383 to the year 1391. For in the first of these two years Amadeus the Green died, while in the second his son, likewise called Amadeus, passed from life, as Columbi teaches in the place cited.

These same words, just quoted, are also found in the *Brief History of the Carthusian Order* in Martène’s sixth volume of *Ancient Writers*, column 189. Nevertheless, that work is continued by its author down to the year 1409.

Since it also presents the deeds of the priors of the Chartreuse in chronological order, it necessarily follows either that it is itself the work of the Carthusian prior-chronologist just cited from Columbi, and that this writer enlarged it in the year 1409 or later by additions containing deeds from the time when he had previously written, without changing anything in what he had written earlier; or that it was compiled in the year 1409 or later by another writer from the work of the Carthusian prior-chronologist praised by Columbi, preserving that author’s very words intact, and also from notices or writings obtained elsewhere.

18. Whatever the case may be, the anonymous author of this work—which I have wished to note here because it will be praised below—copied almost word for word from the *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Chartreuse*, which he clearly indicates in the Prologue had preceded him, the complete eulogy of our Saint, which I have already said will be published under the name of the Earlier Life, making only a few alterations. I understand that he did the same with the eulogies he presents of the four priors of the Chartreuse immediately following St. Bruno, from the letter sent to me from Cologne by Augustine Aldenbruck, which I cited in no. 11.

Not without reason could several others be listed in this place, among them Henry Kalkar, an learned writer of the Carthusian Order who died in 1408. Whenever they treated our Saint only incidentally, they excerpted certain things from that older monument, although they did not all use its exact words.

But since I do not think this worth pursuing, I proceed to those who, finally, near the beginning of the sixteenth century, undertook to treat all the deeds of St. Bruno systematically. They learned the material for their writings—which they too expressed not in the words of others but in their own—from the two ancient Chronicles whose age has already been discussed, and, as there is no reason to doubt, from other monuments, both older and more recent.

19. Four men in particular must be mentioned here. The first places are occupied by an anonymous Carthusian and Zacharias Benedictus, a member of the Charterhouse of St. Andrew of the Lido at Venice. The former embraced the deeds of his holy Father in prose; the latter in verse.

The work of the former was published in 1508, when Bertoldus Remboldus, a Parisian printer, prefixed it to the commentary on the Epistles of St. Paul the Apostle by St. Bruno, which he was then printing.

The work of the latter, although it did not appear before the year 1524, when Jodocus Badius appended it to the end of the works of St. Bruno that he was then publishing in Paris, had nevertheless already been composed by its author as early as the year 1508. This is clearly demonstrated by the dedicatory letter prefixed to it, addressed to Francis du Puits, Prior General of the Carthusian Order, and dated “5 Kalends of May 1508.”

Not very long after these two biographers of the Saint, that same Francis du Puits, Prior General of the Carthusian Order—whose name in Latin is rendered *a Puteo* or *de Puteo*, or, as I find it written by others (for this French surname can be rendered in Latin in various and not inappropriate ways), Puteanus—composed the Life of his holy Father in a plain and flowing style, as the anonymous Carthusian just mentioned had done.

Theodore Petraeus in the *Carthusian Library*, Morotius in the *Chronological Theatre*, and others report this. From it, as they likewise testify, Peter Blomenvenna, a member of the Cologne Charterhouse and its superior for many years, later made a fuller work by adding material obtained elsewhere, and published it from his own house at Cologne.

[Column 0018B] 20. Puteanus’s work, which is nowhere found bearing its author’s name, appears to be the very Life of St. Bruno that was printed at Basle, about the year 1515, in Gothic letters, without the author’s name. It was subsequently reprinted at Paris and appended, together with the metrical work of Zacharias Benedictus mentioned above, to the end of the works of St. Bruno by Jodocus Badius, likewise without the author’s name.

It has a Prologue prefixed to it, beginning as follows: “Not only the Lord in the Saints,” etc.; and it begins in this manner: “In the time of Gregory VII, Roman pontiff,” etc.

But a difficulty that arises here compels me to interrupt the sequence of my discussion.

Possevinus states in the *Sacred Apparatus* that the Life which has Puteanus as its author was printed at Paris by Jean Petit. Accordingly, since Launoy, in his *Dissertation on the Cause of St. Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Desert*, chapter 5, approximately midway through, further asserts that in the Life written by Puteanus the withdrawal of our Saint into the desert is placed in the year 1082, whereas in the Life of the Saint printed at Basle this withdrawal is nevertheless explicitly connected with the year 1084, someone may perhaps suspect that the latter work is not Puteanus’s production.

21. Yet the same Life, which was printed at Basle and afterward at Paris by Jodocus Badius, may perhaps have been reprinted there by Jean Petit. Or, if the matter is otherwise, Possevinus may perhaps have made an error in assigning the printer of the Life composed by Puteanus.

This last possibility certainly seems to me highly probable, because after a most diligent investigation in the public and private libraries of Paris, no Life of St. Bruno printed by Jean Petit could be found at all, as I learn from a letter received from a friend there.

As for Launoy, he may easily have mistakenly taken the Life which was not written by Puteanus for the work of that biographer, because, as I have already noted, the Life composed by Puteanus is not found bearing its author’s name.

Whatever the case may be, many considerations persuade us that the Life of our Saint printed at Basle about the year 1515 is Puteanus’s work.

First, a panel depicting the miraculous raising of the man who publicly declared at Paris that he had been condemned, Bruno’s subsequent conversion, his withdrawal into the solitude of the Chartreuse, and several other events preceding this, is prefixed to the *Statutes and Privileges of the Carthusian Order* of Francis of the Well, or, more briefly, Puteanus, printed at Basle in 1510 by Johann Amerbach. That same panel is likewise prefixed to the Basle Life of our Saint.

22. Secondly, it seems highly probable that Puteanus, who had worked very hard—probably in 1514 or even somewhat earlier—to have Bruno entered in the catalogue of the saints, then committed this Life to writing, and, once honors proper to the heavenly saints had begun to be accorded to him in that year, 1514, with the approval of Leo X, the supreme pontiff, arranged for it to be printed not long afterward. Thirdly, whenever the Basel Life of Saint Bruno is mentioned, the Carthusian tradition understands the Puteanian Life; this is shown by information supplied to me by Joseph Phily, secretary of the most reverend father and the general chapter of the Carthusian Order. It is also made certain by Theodore Petraeus, the Carthusian writer praised above, who, in his *Elucidations on Dorlandus’s Chronicle*, p. 12, calls the Life of Saint Bruno a work of Puteanus. At its end more than one hundred and sixty funeral titles, about which I shall speak shortly, or, as he calls them, epitaphs, are appended; and these are found in such numbers only in the Life of the saint printed at Basel.

Fourth and finally, the Life which Blomenvenna, as I have already shown, composed partly from the Life written by Puteanus has so great a resemblance to the Life printed at Basel—as becomes clear from a collation of the two—that one of them must necessarily have been composed in part from the other. Therefore, after considering all these points, I have no doubt that the Life whose author is Puteanus is precisely the one that appeared in print at Basel around 1515.

23. I shall now continue the discussion, already begun, of the Lives of the saint composed at the beginning of the sixteenth century. Of the four recently listed, only the one prepared by an anonymous Carthusian and printed in Paris by Berthold Rembold is unavailable to me. Of the remaining three—none of which, considering the long interval between the saint’s death and the time when their authors wrote, can be commended for its antiquity—I shall reprint only the Puteanian Life, divided, as usual, into chapters and numbered sections, from a copy of the first Basel edition. I shall omit the other two, partly for this reason: one of them has merely the appearance of a poetic jeu d’esprit, rather than of a Life written historically and sincerely; while the other, with its superfluous digressions and excessively long and frequent excursions, would bring the reader much weariness and almost no pleasure.

To make it easier, however, for anyone who may happen to desire the Life composed by Blomenvenna, I shall append another Life, composed by Surius toward the end of the sixteenth century from both the Puteanian Life and Blomenvenna’s fuller work; it therefore undoubtedly contains whatever in the latter is worthy of remembrance. At the same time, I shall weave into this commentary, whenever appropriate, excerpts from Blomenvenna and also passages from the works of Zacharias Benedictus, so that the parts belonging to the Puteanian and Surian Lives may need to be cited less often. Or, if these authors supply anything absent from the Lives being printed that deserves notice, I shall certainly not pass it over in the Notes that I shall place after them.

24. I shall therefore reprint only three different Lives of our saint: two more recent ones and one of the earlier Life mentioned above, although even that one was written more than a hundred years after his death. In addition, I shall append various Funeral Titles, which will finally be followed by posthumous glory—or rather, by a kind of supplement to it—collected from different written notices and documents. I shall arrange these titles in separate sections, each containing several of them, for the convenience of the notes to be added from time to time, and distinguish each by its own number. They will be taken from the Basel Life of the saint in the order in which they occur at its end. The reader should nevertheless first be informed of the reason for this plan and of what is meant by these titles.

It was formerly customary—even in Saint Bruno’s time—for monks, when one of the more distinguished men of their monastery had died, to send through one of their own number, who was therefore called a *Rotularius* or *Rolliger*, to monasteries, churches, or persons with whom they were connected by fellowship, friendship, or some other special bond, a document or encyclical letter announcing his death. This usually consisted of parchment strips extended lengthwise and was distinguished by the name *Rotulus* or *Rollus*, because it was not folded but rolled up like the books of the Romans. In it they requested the customary, ordinary, or prescribed prayers for the soul of the deceased. The replies to such letters, which were generally composed in verse and sometimes also in prose by the persons to whom the letters had been sent, and which were written either on the roll that had been brought or on a separate sheet, as circumstances required, were called *Funeral Titles*. Nearly all this, or at least matters closely resembling it, may be gathered from what Cangius, citing various writers, discusses in his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin* under the entries *Rotulus*, *Titulus*, and *Brevia mortuorum*.

25. In accordance with the custom just described, when Saint Bruno died in the Calabrian hermitage, the religious inhabitants of that place sent an encyclical letter announcing his death throughout the monasteries and churches of Italy, Gaul, and England. Contrary to the custom then generally observed, they sent it also to several others with whom they were not bound by a formal association, as the letter itself—soon to be printed immediately before the Funeral Titles in its proper place—makes clear. Through one of their members they dispatched it in every direction and received a great many replies, thereafter distinguished here under the name *Funeral Titles*.

I understand that these were discovered by the Carthusians at the Calabrian hermitage of Saint Stephen, after it had returned to the Carthusians in 1514. The Cistercians, who had obtained it about sixty years after Saint Bruno’s death and had held it for a very long time, had finally surrendered it to them. This is evident from the manuscript *Life of Saint Bruno*, composed anonymously by a Carthusian of Liget and chiefly drawn from the funeral titles discussed here, which was sent to our predecessors by Father Federico Flouet, a priest of our Society. The Carthusians judged the titles worthy of the press and in fact appended them to the end of the Life of the saint, which was printed at Basel not long afterward—and rightly so.

For, as will become clear in the course of this commentary, they contribute considerably to the elucidation of the saint’s deeds. Although most of them consist of inept and poorly fashioned verses, many nevertheless teach us something specifically concerning the saint. Or, if—as also frequently happens—they are formulated too generally, they at least commend Bruno, with only a few exceptions, for his exceptional learning, humility, or some other virtue. They also generally show how highly he was esteemed by everyone at that time.

I shall therefore reprint not merely the principal titles, as Surius did in the Life of the saint composed by him, but every one of them, as precious monuments of antiquity written immediately after the blessed departure of Saint Bruno from this life. I do so especially because, as I understand, many people eagerly desire them, while the Basel—or Puteanian—Life of the saint, at whose end alone they are found, is in the hands of very few.

26. Furthermore, since the Lives of Saint Bruno that are to be printed—including the very one that is to be excerpted from the Chronicle of the first five priors of the Carthusian house—do not possess such antiquity as, rightly considered in light of what has already been said, would enable them to establish their own credibility, and since, indeed, because they were not written by contemporary or nearly contemporary authors, it may reasonably be doubted whether each of their assertions agrees certainly with the truth, considerable labor will be required in this commentary to distinguish what among them is true from what is false, what is certain from what is doubtful, what is probable from what is improbable, and what is plausible from what lacks plausibility.

To accomplish this, I shall frequently use not only the eulogy of the saint copied above from the chronicle of the first four priors of the Carthusian house, and the Funeral Titles already mentioned, but also certain other ancient writings composed by authors who preserved at least some memory of Saint Bruno in passing, as well as charters, documents, or public instruments. I shall discuss the authority and reliability of all these materials when they are introduced or cited.

This entire undertaking will also be greatly lightened by several more recent writers who have treated Saint Bruno either as their principal subject or, if only incidentally, at least in more extended discussions, adducing not only ancient documents but also arguments that they were able to derive from them. Among these, an important place will be occupied by the Surianus in his Notes on the Surian Life of Saint Bruno; Mabillon, both elsewhere and especially in his *Ecclesiastical Annals*; and Hercules Zanotti in his *History of Saint Bruno*, written in Italian and printed at Bologna in 1741, which the most reverend lord, abbot of the Carthusian house of Mauerbach in Austria, sent to us in 1761.

27. The anonymous Carthusian will be no less useful: he composed the fourth book of the *Carthusian Annals*, recently printed but, as I noted above, not yet made public. So too will the writers of the *Literary History of France*, especially volume IX, in the Life of Saint Bruno; Camillus Tutinus in his *Overview of the Carthusian Order*, although I presently possess this work only in mutilated form; Morotius in the chronological *Theater of the Sacred Carthusian Order*; John Columbius in his *Dissertation on the Beginnings of the Carthusians*; Innocent le Masson in book I of the *Carthusian Annals*; and many others whom I shall name in the course of this work.

In the meantime, however, let the studious reader not expect me to cite Severus of Naples, or Severus de Trafaglionibus, as though I had seen or inspected him. Besides other material that I suspect he could contribute to our subject, he brought many monuments and charters concerning Saint Bruno and the Carthusian cause out of darkness into light, as the Surianus explains in his Notes on the Life of Saint Bruno, pp. 197ff. This writer is not held by us; nor could he be found in the other libraries that I arranged to have searched here. I did not think it necessary to seek him in distant regions, especially since I believe that his absence can at least largely be supplied by three different manuscript treatises on Saint Bruno mentioned above.

One of these, entitled *Chronological-Diplomatic Dissertation on Saint Bruno*, contains many ancient documents and charters. It was sent to my predecessors in 1727 by Michael Morkens, a member of the Cologne Carthusian house. Another, which supplies a number of materials also found in the fourth book of the *Carthusian Annals*—a book not yet published and praised again shortly—was shared with us by the Carthusians of that house. Finally, the third was composed chiefly, as I have already noted, from the saint’s Funeral Titles by an anonymous Carthusian of Liget; it was sent as a gift to our predecessors by Father Federico Flouet in 1658, as I likewise already mentioned.

28. To these may also be added the *Historico-Chronological-Critical Compendium of the Life of Saint Bruno*, filled with considerable learning, which was recently communicated to me by a member of the Parisian Carthusian house who wishes his name to be entirely concealed.

And so, studious reader, you now have the principal aids mentioned in the present section, which I shall use in this commentary to elucidate and examine the Acts of Saint Bruno.

It should further be understood that I write the words *Carthusia* and *Carthusian* indiscriminately, both with and without the aspirate, because I find most of the writers who preceded me doing so, and I would not dare accuse them of error. For even if the word *Cartus*, as Puteanus maintains in his exhortatory discourse appended to the Life of the saint composed by him—a discourse that I shall discuss in the final Note to that Life—were truly a Hebrew word meaning “perfectly called,” and even if Jerome, in *On Hebrew Names* (see the Paris edition of the works of this holy Father, 1699, vol. II, col. 27), correctly interpreted the Hebrew word *Cartham* into Latin as “vocation perfected,” it nevertheless does not follow that the names *Carthusia* and *Carthusian* received their nomenclature from the Hebrew words *Cartus* or *Cartham*. Let us now turn to the matter itself.

§ II. The Saint’s Noble Birth, Homeland, and Time of Birth

All the Lives of the saint that are to be published unanimously state that Saint Bruno was born of noble stock, and this appears beyond doubt. For the brief eulogy of him that I quoted from the Chronicle of the first four Carthusian priors, no. 7, reads as follows:

“Master Bruno, a Teuton by nation, from the illustrious city of Cologne, born of parents of no obscure standing” —that is, as is added elsewhere, born of such parents—“. . . founded the wilderness of the Chartreuse.”

Moreover, the nobility of the stock from which Bruno was born is also attested by the church of Saint Mary of Rouen. In its Funeral Title, sent to the Calabrian Carthusians in 1102 and holding place 146 among the titles of this kind that, as I said, are to be printed at the end of the Lives, it speaks of the saint as follows:

“He himself was a wise man, noble, radiant in character.”

Nor can the nobility of the family from which the saint sprang rightly be challenged on the basis of Manasses the Simoniac, archbishop of Reims, who died after Gervasius, in 1067. In his *Apology*, which will be cited several times below, he speaks of Bruno as follows (see Mabillon, *Museum Italicum*, vol. I, part II, p. 121):

“We do not greatly desire his company, since we are entirely ignorant of his life and his freedom.”

Although by these words Manasses indicates that he doubts whether the saint was freeborn, he does so only because of the vehement hatred he bore toward Bruno, whose exceedingly bad conduct was opposed to his own.

Nevertheless, some have attempted to investigate thoroughly the nobility of the family from which Bruno sprang and have written that he originated from that most noble Cologne family which the inhabitants call “de Hartenfaust,” or “of the Hard Fist,” as well as from other equally noble families, which they name below.

30. Although the matter, as you will understand from what follows, is extremely uncertain, I shall nevertheless present to the reader who and what sources transmit it, since I think this will not be unwelcome.

Erhard Winheim, a member of the Carthusian house of Würzburg, writes the following on p. 212 of his work entitled *Sacrarium Agrippinense*, which he published at Cologne in 1607:

“As for the founder of the Carthusian Order, Saint Bruno, he originated from the noble lineage of Hartenfaust, one of the fifteen Roman families brought by Saint Maternus and the emperor Trajan to the defense of the city”—namely Cologne—“as the four coats of arms of his kinsmen testify from the Cologne Chronicle.”

Theodore Petraeus, a member of the Cologne Carthusian house, observes the following in his *Elucidations on the Carthusian Chronicle of Peter Dorlandus*, which he brought out of obscurity and published in print in 1608:

“He”—namely Saint Bruno—“had parents especially distinguished among the Ubii both by birth and by virtue, descended, that is, from that most noble Roman lineage which led a new colony to Agrippina, and which the inhabitants still call ‘of the Hard Fist.’”

So much for them. The latter writer, since he asserts that both of Saint Bruno’s parents came from the most noble family called “of the Hard Fist,” makes the saint a descendant of the family of the Hard Fist, or Hartenfaust, on both his father’s and his mother’s side. The former, however, merely states that the saint originated from the family of Hartenfaust, or of the Hard Fist, without mentioning his parents; he does not determine whether this was on his father’s side, his mother’s side, or both simultaneously.

31. Those who flourished before Petraeus and Winheim—Peter Blomenvenna and Stephen Brolmannus, an antiquarian of the Ubii who flourished around the middle of the sixteenth century and is frequently praised by Gelenius from the very beginning and elsewhere in his work on the greatness of Cologne—spoke more distinctly. One of them makes the saint Hartenfaustian on his father’s side, the other on his mother’s.

Here are Blomenvenna’s words. They follow immediately upon the Prologue to the Life of the saint that he himself had printed at Cologne not long after 1515 and that, as I noted above, we shall not reprint here:

“Blessed Bruno, founder of the sacred Carthusian Order, a Teuton by nation, from the distinguished city of Cologne, which in ancient times was called Agrippina after Marcus Agrippa, son-in-law of Octavian, traced his origin to parents distinguished both by birth and by virtue. For the emperor Trajan and the Roman Senate once sent noble Romans there as settlers and guardians of the city and territory; noble neighbors were joined to them in marriage. One of these tribes was called ‘Of the Wise,’ while one of the Roman families was called ‘Of the Hard Fist.’ From the latter blessed Bruno was descended on his father’s side. On his mother’s side, however, he derived his blood from a noble Roman tribe called ‘Of Little Thought,’ from the family later called ‘Of Red Stessen.’”

32. Brolmannus, when questioned about the saint’s noble birth—as Morkens reports—gave the following account:

“Aemilius, or ‘the Wise,’ was the surname of Saint Bruno, who originated from Cologne Agrippina through his father, from the Roman-Frankish patrician family of Aemilia and of the Wise (*Vonden Weisen*), which supplied both the lineage and the reason for his surname. He had as his mother a patrician woman from the family of the Catos, which in the native Frankish language was called ‘Of the Hard Fist’ (*Vonder Hartenfaust*), or ‘of the Hard Fist,’ since it belonged to the Catos among the Ubian Romans. His maternal grandmother came from the patrician Frankish Aemilian family ‘Of Little Thoughts’ (*Vonden Cleingedancken*); his great-grandmother descended from a branch of that family called ‘Of Red Stessa’ (*Vonder Roder-Stessen*). As the line descended further, marriages were contracted, and from it came a certain knight who, for outstanding deeds in the Crusade, had his shield enlarged by a gift from kings, bearing the crowned head of an Ethiopian.”

Such are Blomenvenna and Brolmannus. The former makes the saint a Stessen on his mother’s side; the latter, an Aemilian on his father’s side. I do not wish here to examine whether all and every one of the assertions of Brolmannus, Petraeus, Blomenvenna, and Winheim, contained in the words just quoted, agree with the truth—far be it from me to suppose that they do. I shall examine only whether it is correctly asserted that the saint came from the most noble families named in the passages quoted, and especially whether he came from the Hartenfaust family, to which all four of the writers mentioned unanimously assign him.

33. Petraeus and Winheim cite or produce no ancient monument whatsoever by which they might prove the saint’s Hartenfaustian origin. Blomenvenna provides no stronger support, since he records that the saint was descended from the Hartenfaust family on his father’s side and from the Stessen family on his mother’s side.

As for Brolmannus, Morkens asserts in the manuscript *Chronological-Diplomatic Dissertation on Saint Bruno*, which I praised above, that he derived what he reports concerning the saint’s family from the ancient monuments of the house mentioned by Gelenius in book III, section 19 of *On the Greatness of Cologne Agrippina*, called “Of the Red Stessa.” Because the saint is said to have been born in that house, it displayed his sacred image affixed to its gate. Yet Brolmannus does not say what these monuments were, or of what kind.

Moreover, Brolmannus himself writes to Morkens as follows in order to prove the family that he attributes to the saint:

“In accordance with the custom of German nobles, he”—namely Saint Bruno—“had four insignia by which he displayed and defended his illustrious lineage and family:

“1. Of the Wise (*Von den Weisen*), who had a blue lion leaping in a white field.

“2. Of the Hard Fist (*Von der Hartefaust*), who adorned a white shield with two red and checkered arms, the hand clenched like a fist, as if for wrestling.

“3. Of Little Thought (*Von den Kleingedancken*), whose shield was red with a snow-white bend winding in curves.

“4. Of the Red Stessa (*Von der Roder-Stessen*), whose shield in a red field had two twisted bends and, on either side, two crowned Ethiopian heads.”

34. Yet there is no reason to regard as probable that the heraldic insignia mentioned here by Brolmannus, and displayed together with the saint’s image at the end of the Life composed by Blomenvenna and in my possession, belonged to Saint Bruno himself or were appropriate to him on account of the family from which he descended.

For heraldic insignia of the kind mentioned by Brolmannus and now in use first arose when Christians undertook the holy war in the East against the infidels—an event that occurred only toward the end of the eleventh and the beginning of the twelfth century—as Muratori correctly demonstrates from various authors in volume IV of his *Antiquities of Italy*, cols. 689ff. Bruno, however, as will become clear from what follows, was unquestionably born before the year 1050. Such insignia therefore could have belonged neither to his parents nor to Bruno himself.

I also find, however, that Morkens praises the *Commentaries on Civic Affairs* composed by Brolmannus in order to illuminate the affairs of Cologne. Since I thought that these might perhaps contain material useful for proving the lineage that he attributes to the saint, and since I had no way of knowing either those *Commentaries* or the ancient monuments—mentioned above—of the house called “Of the Red Stessa,” from which Brolmannus might have derived his account of the saint’s family, I wrote to Cologne. I asked Father Augustine Aldenbruck, a priest of our Society, to communicate to me everything he knew or could discover concerning those monuments, Brolmannus and his writings, or the family or families from which this writer asserted that the saint descended, if any such information might help establish the saint’s Hartenfaustian or another lineage.

35. The man, who deserved very well of our Museum, fulfilled this request most satisfactorily by sending us two letters. In the first he writes of Brolmannus and his *Commentaries* as follows:

“He devoted great effort to collecting the ancient monuments of the city”—namely Cologne—“but nothing from them has been made public except the *Epideigma*, containing various tablets engraved on copper, with a preface or dedication inscribed on the reverse. Where the manuscript *Commentaries on Civic Affairs* of the same author may lie, Heaven knows. I should think that, after his death, they were divided among his friends and heirs. Twenty-two years ago I saw his first book, on the origin and ancient settlements of the Ubii, in the possession of Father Hartzheim.”

Concerning the family or families from which the saint is said to have descended, he writes:

“As for what might establish the splendor of Saint Bruno’s lineage, nothing remains except constant tradition and public report. It is certainly true that those families”—the ones mentioned above by Brolmannus—“flourished here in Cologne, as is shown by numerous monuments that can still be seen in various sacred and secular buildings, together with the same shields and heraldic devices that Morkens, Brolmannus, and Gelenius produce. Yet so far I can demonstrate by no sufficiently firm evidence beyond the aforementioned tradition that Saint Bruno sprang from those same families.”

36. As for the ancient monuments of the house in which the saint is said to have been born at Cologne Agrippina, and from which Brolmannus drew what he reports about Bruno’s lineage, Aldenbruck writes:

“A few days ago I again visited the house that first received him”—namely Saint Bruno—“in its earliest cradle. The old structure, of extremely ancient workmanship, which as a young man I had often examined and which I later surveyed again when I was a teacher of more refined letters in this place, I sought in vain within the modern building constructed several years ago according to the taste of our own age.”

Then, after inserting several matters that will more appropriately be described when I discuss the saint’s posthumous glory, he continues as follows:

“The present owners and occupants of the house in which the saint is said to have been born have replaced the ancient windows with new ones, paying little attention to the shields and inscriptions that, as I have no doubt, could have been found on the old windows. Saint Bruno can be seen above the gate, and on the upper panel of the room”—the room, that is, which they claim Bruno inhabited—the same saint appears surrounded by four shields, namely those mentioned above by Brolmannus. Yet I believe that this work scarcely exceeds two hundred and fifty years in age.”

I would indeed have displayed those four shields here, engraved on copper from Blomenvenna or Morkens, in whose works they are found, if it were in any way certain that Saint Bruno derived his lineage from the families to which they belong. But the contrary will become increasingly clear from what follows.

37. In the words just quoted, the aforementioned Augustine Aldenbruck had also added that, in order to send me more certain information, he would arrange for his friends—whom he hoped to have the opportunity to ask to open and examine them—to inform him whether anything suitable for determining Saint Bruno’s noble lineage might perhaps be found in the public archives, which at Cologne are called *die Schrein*, “the chests.”

Once this had been done, he wrote the second of the two letters mentioned above, composed for the most part in the following words:

“Through the assistance of friends I succeeded in having all the older documents concerning the family ‘Of the Red Stessa’ carefully examined and scrutinized in the principal archives of that kind”—those called *die Schrein*, “the chests,” at Cologne—“but nothing else could be extracted from them except that more than six hundred years ago there were two coats of arms of the city’s principal nobility, one designated by the name of the Whites, the other by that of the Reds. Yet it is useless to seek family relationships and children in these documents, since in the oldest ones only the names of the Whites, or *de Albis*, and the Reds are found. In a later age the name of one son or another is occasionally added, in approximately this form: above, ‘Of the Whites’; below, ‘Hilliger, etc., son.’ From this I conclude only that Saint Bruno derived from his father rather the name ‘of the Whites,’ *Von den Weisen*, than Aemilius or ‘the Wise,’ as Brolmannus judged—or rather guessed—from Morkens’s recension.”

38. Such is what the aforementioned Augustine Aldenbruck wrote in response to the questions that we had put to him and set out above. Nothing whatsoever can be extracted from his report for determining the saint’s Hartenfaustian or Aemilian origin.

First, since he admits in no. 35 that he does not know where the *Commentaries on Civic Affairs* written by Brolmannus are now located, it remains just as uncertain as before whether they contain anything by which this author might prove the lineage he asserts for the saint. As for the shields and inscriptions represented on the old windows of the Stessen house, which is said to have been Saint Bruno’s birthplace, there is no evidence, so far as I know, that these were older than the fifteenth century. Nor can it be proved that the image representing Saint Bruno surrounded by the four heraldic shields listed above by Brolmannus, on the upper panel of the room that the saint was said to have inhabited, was older than the age indicated; indeed, it appears to be only about two hundred and fifty years old (see no. 36).

Therefore, even if these objects—although this is by no means established—clearly represented the saint’s Hartenfaustian or Aemilian origin, that origin would nevertheless not thereby become certain, as anyone who considers the matter will see.

Since his origin is in no way confirmed either by the public archives of the city of Cologne, as Aldenbruck indicates in the preceding paragraph, or by any other accessible monuments of recognized authority and antiquity, it remains founded solely on the public report and constant tradition cited in no. 35. It is therefore entirely uncertain. For a tradition supported only by testimonies separated by at least three centuries from the matter to which they relate cannot, as is self-evident, establish indubitable credibility. Such is, as the foregoing makes clear, the Cologne tradition concerning the saint’s Hartenfaustian or Aemilian origin.

39. Nor is there any reason to oppose to this the statements of Gelenius in book III, section 19 of *On the Greatness of Cologne Agrippina*, and of Brolmannus as reported by Morkens: namely, that the house still called “Of the Red Stessa” belonged to Saint Bruno’s parents, and that the saint himself was born there; consequently, that at least one of his parents belonged to the Hartenfaust family, already related to the Stessen family.

Apart from the fact that this rests solely on the tradition just mentioned, which does not appear capable of establishing the point, how, I ask, will you prove that the house—something required if any conclusion is to be drawn from it—was either possessed by the Stessens, from whom it then received its name, before it came into Saint Bruno’s parents’ possession, or, if it was already possessed by them, passed to the saint’s parents because of some relationship between those parents and the Stessens?

Moreover, the authority of Gelenius, who may have believed such things, is wholly insufficient to make me believe them as well. For this writer, as I now understand is also generally true of Brolmannus, is known to have gathered indiscriminately, without distinction or selection, whatever could contribute to the grandeur of the Ubii.

After carefully weighing everything, therefore, it is plainly doubtful whether the saint belonged to the Hartenfaust family—or, to speak more generally, from what particular illustrious lineage he was born, since the ancient and sufficiently suitable monuments by which this could safely be assigned are lacking.

Surius therefore acted prudently in refraining from defining the saint’s noble origin, contrary to what he could see Blomenvenna doing, from whom he partly composed his Life. He wrote only that Bruno had parents distinguished both by birth and by virtue, in no. 1.

Nevertheless, Ferdinand, prince-elector of Cologne—or rather those who composed in his name the encyclical letter sent in 1624 to the clergy of Cologne concerning the celebration of Saint Bruno’s feast, which I shall incorporate in its entirety into the *Posthumous Glory*—preferred to follow Blomenvenna rather than Surius, using these words:

“Saint Bruno, a great glory and adornment of the Church, a citizen of Cologne, was born and brought up at Cologne in the noble Hartenfaust family.”

Yet these writers cannot possess such authority, as is obvious in itself, that they should be heeded here.

40. The same must also be said of the bishop of Hierace—who was undoubtedly Octavianus, as I gather from Ughellus, volume IX of *Sacred Italy*, in his treatment of the bishops of Hierace—who, as Severus of Naples testifies in Surius’s expanded Life of our saint, p. 86, records in a catalogue of the archbishops of Reggio in Calabria compiled by him that Saint Bruno, inserted after Arnulf as the elected prelate of that church, was born of the Alcuina or Alchanirina family.

From what monuments did Octavianus compile that catalogue? From ancient ones? I would believe that much, together with Surius in the place cited. But were they also so ancient that they were capable by themselves of establishing unquestionable credibility? That neither does Surius affirm, nor could I readily persuade myself of it without testimony of wholly unimpeachable reliability.

In any event, Ughellus, who likewise lists Saint Bruno after Arnulf in the catalogue of the archbishops of Reggio as the elected successor to that see and adorns him with a notable eulogy, makes no mention whatsoever of the saint’s Alcuina or Alchanirina origin.

Let these remarks about Bruno’s lineage, which no one can easily determine, suffice. I now turn exclusively to the question of his birthplace.

All the biographers of the saint who unanimously assert that he was born of noble stock also state that he was born in Cologne Agrippina, in Germany. Their assertion is indeed entirely consistent with the truth, as is sufficiently clear from the Chronicle of the first four priors of the Greater Carthusian house alone. That chronicle was composed, as I have already shown, before 1137 and is highly trustworthy; in the eulogy of Saint Bruno, no. 7, which I copied above, it appropriately states for the present purpose:

“Master Bruno, a Teuton by nation, born in the illustrious city of Cologne of parents of no obscure standing . . . founded the wilderness of the Chartreuse.”

### 41

There is also the *Chronographia* of Sigebert of Gembloux, who died in 1113, which, in nearly the same words, places the saint’s birthplace only at Cologne; likewise Peter the Venerable, who died in 1156, calls Master Bruno “Colognian” in Book II, chapter 28, of his *Miracles*. Yet our saint is also called Remense by two writers contemporary with him: one of them composed the *Chronicle of Malleac*, published by Labbe in volume II of the *New Library of Manuscripts* [Col. 0029D]; the other composed the *Fragment of the History of France from the Time of King Robert to the Death of King Philip I*, inserted by Chesne in volume IV of the *Writers of France*. I transcribe the words of both.

The former, in the cited volume of Labbe, folio 205, reads:

> “Fulbert taught Berengarius, a canon of Saint Martin. He in turn left Bruno of Reims and many others as heirs of philosophy.”

The latter, likewise in the cited volume of Chesne, folio 89, says:

> “At this time Lanfranc, bishop of Canterbury; Guido the Lombard; Maingaud the German; and Bruno of Reims, who later led the life of a hermit, flourished in both divine and human philosophy.”

In addition, among the saint’s funeral titles there occur two in which he is explicitly called French, or at least very clearly indicated to have been French. The first, which belongs to the scholars of the church of Saint Mary of Chartres and is numbered thirty-two among those to be reprinted, reads:

> As Phoebe is to Phoebus, as the other stars are to the moon,  
> so may the whole world attend you, Bruno the Frenchman.

The second, which belongs to Saint Gervasius of Falaise in Normandy and holds place 114 among those to be reprinted, reads:

> Gaul, mother and nurse of many men,  
> when will you have men equal to this one?  
> This man once offered your peoples and clergy  
> the fountain of doctrine, etc.

### 42

Consequently, since other funeral titles of his, which it is not worthwhile to list here, also seem to indicate that Saint Bruno was French, someone might perhaps conclude that he came from Gaul and was born not at Cologne but at Reims. Yet since ancient records should not be set against one another but, if possible, reconciled, and since the saint could have been called French for a reason other than his origin, and Remense for a reason other than his birth, we must believe that this is in fact what occurred in the *Chronicle of Malleac*, the aforesaid historical *Fragment*, and the funeral titles. Otherwise, these ancient records would have to be said to conflict with the most ancient *Chronicle of the First Four Priors of the Grande Chartreuse*, or with the excerpt from it containing the saint’s eulogy. That chronicle, explicitly teaching that Bruno was German by nationality and born at Cologne, can in no way be understood as consistent with the truth unless he was in fact born at Cologne.

Thus Saint Bruno may indeed have been called Remense by the writers of the *Chronicle of Malleac* and of the aforesaid historical *Fragment*, because he was known to them less by his homeland than by the studies through which he had remained at Reims for a very long time, both as a student and as a teacher, and by the dignities he had held there. In the funeral titles he may have been regarded as French either for much the same reason, or because he had been educated chiefly in Gaul. The latter possibility should be rejected all the less because in Funeral Title 115, belonging to Saint Mary of Tournai, he is said to have been born at Cologne and educated in Gaul. Here is the poem:

> Cologne claims to have begotten him; France wishes to have reared him;  
> Bruno, Father, glory shared by both peoples,  
> by an easy ascent is joined to the ranks of heaven.

### 43

Having therefore weighed everything properly, I regard it as beyond all controversy that Saint Bruno was born at Cologne. Yet his year of birth cannot be determined with anything like the same certainty. For the present, Baillet places it after the year 1050, under 6 October, column 83; but the writers of the *Literary History of France*, volume IX, page 233, and several others observe that this date must be advanced by at least ten years—and rightly so, as the sequence of the saint’s life demonstrates.

For Saint Bruno, as I shall show below, on the occasion of the disturbances that Archbishop Manasses stirred up in the Church of Reims, resigned in 1076 or the following year the direction of the schools that he held there [Col. 0031A]. Therefore, if he was born only after 1050, as Baillet maintains, he would have done this in the twenty-fifth or certainly the twenty-sixth year of his age. Since, moreover, before doing so he had already governed the Reims schools for many years, and therefore for at least twelve or fifteen years, it would follow that he had been appointed head of these celebrated schools at the age of twelve, or at most fifteen—something no sane person will admit.

That Bruno had directed the schools of Reims for many years before resigning them follows clearly from what Marlottus writes in Book I, page 115, of his *History of the Metropolis of Reims*, and at the same time from what has already been said about the year in which the saint resigned that office. For the cited author reports that Bruno had already been appointed head or rector of the schools of Reims by Archbishop Gervasius in 1056; and it will become clear from what is said below concerning the time when Bruno first began teaching at Reims that this writer is not far from the truth [Col. 0031B].

I shall now establish from another source that the saint long presided over the Reims schools. This is fittingly confirmed here by Funeral Title 173. In it, the Regular Canons of the monastery of Saint Vincent at Noyon, who “groaned when they saw the sheet that revealed the death of Bruno, the incomparable philosopher,” explicitly affirm that he had long directed the Reims schools, speaking as follows:

> Bruno … possessed and preserved true knowledge and prudence in the liberal arts, as well as the other cardinal virtues, which he brought to completion in a good end. For a long time he had been the supreme teacher of the Church of the see of Reims, most brilliant in the Psalter and in the other sciences, and for a long time he had stood as the pillar of the entire metropolitan church.

### 44

Furthermore, when the saint resigned the direction of the Reims schools, he was not merely twenty-five or twenty-six years old—as follows, as noted, from Baillet’s opinion—but of more advanced age. In the *Life of Pope Urban II*, inserted in volume III of the posthumous works of Mabillon and Ruinart, pages 6–7, the latter of these two writers proves this most effectively from various of the saint’s funeral titles. I therefore transcribe his words, indicating beside each title the number assigned to it from which part of the evidence was drawn. He writes:

> “They call him ‘the Gem of Wisdom’ (Title 74),” namely, Saint Bruno, “the canons of Saint Mary of Blois; ‘the Light of the Churches’ (Title 82), the monks of Saint Lucian of Beauvais; ‘the Most Illustrious Sophist’ (Title 107), the monks of Saint Maximin of Micy; ‘the Teacher of Teachers’ (Title 77), the canons of Bernay; ‘the Glory of Masters, the Oar of the Reims Crowd’ (Title 109), the canons of Saint Mary Major in Paris; and they say that he ‘offered the fountain of doctrine to peoples and clergy’ (Title 114), the canons of Saint Gervasius of Falaise; ‘surpassed all masters throughout the world’ (Title 64), the canons of Saint Timothy of Reims; and that ‘as many became wise through his teaching as the mind cannot count’ (Title 131), the canons of Saint Mary of Spilings. The monks of Saint Nicholas of Angers say that “his doctrine shines throughout the world”; accordingly, the canons of the cathedral church of Saint-Croix at Orléans desire to be his “followers” (Title 78).

> “I would be excessive if I listed all his other praises. Yet one testimony cannot be omitted: that of the canons of the cathedral church of Angers, Saint Maurice. They assert that Bruno was a teacher not of boys or lesser clerics, but of serious and already learned men who studied the divine science—that is, theology—under him. This plainly indicates that he was already of mature age when he taught at Reims before his withdrawal.”

### 45

Thus far Ruinartus. He then presents to the reader, from the title of the canons of the cathedral church of Angers, which holds place 166 among those to be reprinted, several verses that read:

> His extraordinary wisdom too is celebrated everywhere;  
> Bruno’s tongue is praised more highly than Maro’s;  
> Plato’s glory grows pale beside Bruno’s praise.  
> Here he excelled the teachers; here he made  
> the greatest doctors, not by training lesser men.  
> Here was the teacher of teachers, not of clerics.  
> For no one took on Bruno’s grace of expression or gravity  
> unless he was a man of great intelligence.  
> By teaching divine things, he proclaims  
> outstanding wisdom to the reader.

After a few remarks that are less relevant here, he continues:

> “Who, then, would say that such a man, whom almost all the churches of Gaul, England, and Italy eagerly commended as the most renowned teacher of the sciences, earned these praises when he was twenty years old, or a little more or less? Who, I ask, could persuade himself that Bruno at that age had long governed schools so famous, with such a reputation for learning and teaching, that after approximately twenty years of withdrawal his death was mourned by most of the more celebrated churches of the Christian world as the death of the master of all teachers?”

Thus far Ruinartus. Indeed, since the saint is adorned in all the funeral titles cited by him with such varied and lavish praises—praises not easily earned within a brief period and at a youthful age—whether while teaching in the Reims schools or while directing them, this is an exceedingly strong argument that when he resigned that office in 1076 or the following year, as stated, he was more than twenty-five or twenty-six years old. Consequently, he must have been born before the eleventh century had passed its midpoint, that is, before the year 1050 [Col. 0032D].

### 46

But how much earlier did this occur? Zanotti (see no. 26), in the *Life of the Saint* that he composed, page 3, cites two different testimonies from monuments of Calabria that he praises, both of which report that Saint Bruno died more than ninety years old. One, which he calls an epigram and which was inscribed on the cave in which the saint lived in Calabria, consists of these two lines:

> He had already completed ninety-two years of life  
> when, released from fragile flesh, he went to the heavenly powers.

The other, which he says was taken from a very ancient manuscript, has the following concerning Bruno: He died “on the day before the Nones of October, in the year 1102 from the redemption of the world, in the eighth month; but in the ninety-second year of his age.”

Since the saint, as will be proved in its proper place below, unquestionably died in 1101, he must have been born around 1008 if we are to accept the two testimonies cited—one of which says that he died after completing ninety-two years of life, while the other says that he died while already in his ninety-second year. Yet these testimonies do not seem to me to have come from sources sufficiently ancient to deserve unquestioned confidence. Although Zanotti indicates that one of them was taken from a very ancient manuscript, he does not state how ancient it was, and thus leaves it doubtful whether it may have existed no earlier than the fourteenth or even the fifteenth century. Both dates are more remote from the saint’s own age than to allow writings composed then about him to possess assured credibility [Col. 0033B].

### 47

Indeed, Zanotti himself, although he regards that manuscript as very ancient, did not attach great weight to it. For although he says that, in order to free it from chronological error regarding the year 1102 of Christ, to which it assigns the saint’s death, the years of Christ are counted in it from the Incarnation, with the years preceding the Nativity included, nevertheless, after quoting the two testimonies that I have just transcribed, he immediately adds that it is not probable that the saint reached the advanced age asserted in them.
