He further says that this seems so to him because it is not apparent how a man of such advanced age could have led the austere mode of life that he maintained first in the Grande Chartreuse and later in Calabria, or could have endured the labors, hardships, and difficulties of the journeys to which he devoted himself. For according to the chronology derived from what follows, in 1084, when he first entered the wilderness of the Chartreuse, he would already have completed his seventy-sixth year.

This, in substance, is Zanotti’s position, and rightly so. That is why I am also dissatisfied with the opinion of those who place the saint’s birth in 1020. On that reckoning, when he withdrew into the wilderness of the Chartreuse in 1084, he would have been sixty-four years old; and it appears no more credible that at such an age he could have undertaken the exceedingly harsh life, exposed to the gravest hardships, which he then first embraced [Col. 0033D].

### 48

Therefore, since the saint, as shown above, was undoubtedly more than twenty-five or twenty-six years old when he resigned the direction of the Reims schools in 1076 or the following year, his birth seems to be placed around 1030, or somewhat later, between that year and 1040. On this reckoning, when he withdrew to the Chartreuse, he would have been only about fifty years old. Experience has shown that many men have existed, and still exist, who at that age remain vigorous and robust and fit to endure the harshest labors.

This also explains how it happened that when Bruno resigned the direction of the Reims schools in 1076 or the following year, he had already held it for a long time—about fifteen years, as stated above, or at least twelve, indeed from 1056 onward if Marlottus is correct in the passage cited above—and had already acquired the fame of his name, which Guibert of Nogent, a contemporary author whom I shall frequently cite below, explicitly asserts that he possessed at that time and which is implied by the various funeral titles cited above.

Indeed, that the saint was about fifty, or even somewhat older, when he entered the wilderness of the Chartreuse, and therefore was born at the time just assigned, is also suggested to some extent by the manner in which he is described as a man of the highest seriousness and fully mature age, both in the various funeral titles quoted above and in the *Life of Saint Hugh*, bishop of Grenoble, inserted in our April volume I. There the contemporary author Guigo, fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, speaks in chapter 11 of Saint Bruno, who came to that holy bishop a few days before entering the Chartreuse:

> “Master Bruno is here, a man renowned for religion and learning, almost a living image of uprightness, gravity, and complete maturity.”

### 49

It may also be added that, at the time when the saint withdrew into the wilderness in 1084, celebrated men were already flourishing in various churches, and that he had had these men as pupils. Among them was Odo of Châtillon, who in 1088 was raised to the supreme pontificate and took the name Urban II.

Nor can I pass over an ancient codex of the Chartreuse of Mont-Dieu in Picardy, in which Saint Bruno is said to have died at the age of seventy, as James Martini, a member of that Charterhouse, testifies in Morkens’s manuscript *Chronological-Diplomatic Dissertation on Saint Bruno*, section 1. If that codex gives the correct date, the saint, having died in 1101, must have been born around 1030. Yet since I find no statement by either Martini or Morkens concerning the age of the codex, it will be useful to strengthen the matter by another argument, which appears to me the strongest of all.

The saint probably, as I shall prove below, had Berengarius as his teacher in philosophy before 1050. Since he most probably did not take up that study before he was about seventeen, counting backward from 1050 leads to approximately 1030. It follows that the saint was born around that very year [Col. 0034D].

From this consideration especially, together with the other evidence brought forward above, it appears exceedingly probable that the saint was born around 1030, or somewhat later, between that year and 1040. Since I regard this as now sufficiently established, I proceed to other matters.

## § III. What the Saint Was Like in Childhood; Whether He Was a Canon of Saint Cunibert; At What Age He Went to Gaul to Study; and Whether He Had Berengarius as His Teacher in Philosophy

Blomenvenna speaks as follows of the saint while he was still a boy:

> “From the cradle, his mother Wisdom nursed his infancy and always taught him to advance toward better things as his age progressed. Even while he was a boy, he did nothing childish in his conduct; rather, displaying something of the religious life he would one day embrace, he was being prepared by the Lord as an instructor of many monks. The Lord granted him a good soul, a praiseworthy disposition, a teachable intellect, a tenacious memory, and a will affectionately inclined toward what is best.”

Surius says the same in his published *Life of the Saint*, differing from Blomenvenna, whom he follows exactly in substance, only in the wording he uses. Although none of these details can be explicitly confirmed by the testimony of the author or of an ancient record, taken as a whole they appear exceedingly probable. As for the saint’s exceptional qualities of mind, which shone forth in him while still a boy, the deeds that followed throughout his life do not permit us to doubt that this account agrees with the truth; and this will become abundantly clear from what follows.

Yet these are minor matters. Matters far more serious and entangled in almost insuperable difficulties now follow. After the words of Blomenvenna just quoted, he adds:

> “Then, entrusted to the schools of Paris to be imbued with the liberal arts, advancing beyond his contemporaries and regarded among the foremost philosophers, he became a master of the schools.”

According to Blomenvenna, therefore, to whom Surius also agrees, the saint was instructed in letters and the liberal arts at Paris, the most celebrated city of Gaul [Col. 0035B].

### 51

Everyone admits that Saint Bruno went from Cologne to Gaul to devote himself to letters, and this cannot in any way be called into doubt, as anyone will readily understand from what follows. Yet it may be asked at what age he went to Gaul; whether he had pursued literary studies in his homeland beforehand; whether he had previously been a canon of Saint Cunibert; and finally whether he truly went to Paris and devoted himself to study there.

First, it appears exceedingly probable that before departing for Gaul Bruno had been instructed in the rudiments of letters and grammar in his homeland. But had he also studied the higher sciences? The writers of the *Literary History of France*, volume IX, page 233, seem to imply this when they identify the place where Bruno studied there. For they write that the saint had been not only educated with great care in the collegiate church of Saint Cunibert and thoroughly instructed in both divine and human letters, but also cite in the margin Labbe’s *New Library*, volume I, page 638—that is, the eulogy of our saint, transcribed above from no. 7 of that passage. Yet nothing appears there relevant to their purpose except the statement that “Bruno had been strongly equipped with both secular and divine letters.”

As consideration makes clear, these words of the eulogy should chiefly be understood of the higher sciences, philosophy and theology, which the saint later mastered. That he did not meanwhile learn them at Cologne, before going to Gaul, is certain from the fact—proved below—that he was then of less advanced age. As for the place where they say the saint was educated and instructed in letters at Cologne, this eulogy of the saint in Labbe does not express it at all [Col. 0036A].

The writers, therefore, must have drawn what they wrote in the cited passage solely from the lengthy letter of Manasses, archbishop of Reims, to Hugh of Die, papal legate in Gaul, which they cite there together with the saint’s eulogy, and which Mabillon reproduces in *Museum Italicum*, volume I, part II, pages 119 and following. In that letter Manasses says:

> “Bruno is neither our cleric nor our native-born or reborn man, but he is a canon of Saint Cunibert of Cologne, situated in the kingdom of the Germans.”

Indeed, from these words of Manasses it is clear that the saint had been a canon in the collegiate church of Saint Cunibert at Cologne. It is also exceedingly probable that he was educated there, at least in part, and cultivated his learning there, provided that he had been enrolled among the canons of Cunibert from the time when he had not yet gone to Gaul and was still living as a youth at Cologne.

Yet some maintain that he was not given a canonry in the collegiate church of Saint Cunibert until he had been forced, around 1076 or the following year, to leave Reims because of the wicked conduct of Archbishop Manasses. Their reason is that in 1079, when Manasses wrote the aforesaid letter, the saint could not have been called a canon of the Cunibertine church by virtue of a canonry obtained there in adolescence, since by then he had undoubtedly renounced such a benefice, having for many years already become a canon of the Church of Reims. This view appears to me quite plausible [Col. 0036C].

### 53

Nevertheless, Manasses may have spoken of the saint as a canon of the Cunibertine church because, although he was no longer a canon there at that time, he had once held a canonry in it, and because Manasses, opposed to him on account of his evil conduct, refused out of hatred to regard him as a canon of Reims. This becomes easier to believe in light of the words that Manasses adds immediately after those already quoted:

> “We are not particularly eager for his companionship, since we are wholly ignorant of his life and liberty; and because, when he was with us, we were treated badly and wickedly despite the many benefices that we had conferred upon him.”

Thus Manasses speaks in order to stir up hatred against the saint in the eyes of the legate of the Apostolic See [Col. 0036D].

Moreover, the saint may perhaps still have been called a Cunibertine canon because he came from the Cunibertine college of canons, in which he had first devoted himself to a life regulated according to the canons, even though he had already transferred to another college of canons. During the period of his residence at Reims, he may merely have renounced the revenues of the canonry that he held in the Cunibertine church, while retaining the canonry itself and the title of Cunibertine canon, so that he could return to it if he ever lost his position at Reims. Certainly, in these circumstances—and especially if legitimate authority had intervened, as it could have—there is no reason to think that the saint would have sinned against the canons by possessing two distinct benefices in this way.

After these considerations, therefore, the opinion of those who maintain that Bruno was a canon of the collegiate church of Saint Cunibert at Cologne before going to Gaul does not appear entirely improbable. Accordingly, I would not dare to accuse the writers of the *Literary History of France* of unquestionable error when they make the saint a canon of the Cunibertine church before he went to Gaul and affirm that he was educated there, although the contrary opinion appears more probable [Col. 0037A].

### 54

This latter opinion will be much more probable if, in order for the saint to have been a canon of the Cunibertine church, he had to be older than fourteen or fifteen years. For when the saint was approximately that age, or perhaps still younger, he seems already to have departed from Cologne for Gaul to study letters and to have studied at Reims.

Funeral Title 56 among those to be reprinted, with which the canons of the metropolitan church of Saint Mary of Reims honored the saint, reads:

> His mother Reims taught him, a tender pupil,  
> and rejoiced that Bruno kept faith with his purpose;  
> now, migrating to the Lord, she greets him with tears and prayers.

By “tender pupil” an adolescent of fourteen or fifteen years, or perhaps somewhat younger, seems to be intended. I reach this conclusion both because the adjective *tender*, when applied to age, naturally restricts it to a small number of years, and because the saint studied the humanities at Reims and, around 1047, began to hear philosophy at Tours, when he was probably only about seventeen years old [Col. 0037C].

I shall prove the latter point below. That the saint studied the humanities at Reims is attested by Baldric, abbot of Bourgueil, a contemporary author, in Mabillon’s preface to Part II of the sixth century of the Benedictine *Annals*, no. 85. In a poem to Godfrey of Reims, not yet published, he sings of Saint Bruno:

> And then Bruno was at Reims; at Reims Bruno also studied,  
> Bruno, then the mirror of Latin studies.

By “the Latin study of that time,” he most probably means not philosophy or other higher sciences, but the humanities, which include the study of the Latin language and grammar.

### 55

Indeed, since the saint, as stated, studied at Reims when he was still very young, it is exceedingly probable that before doing so he had studied neither at Paris nor in any other city of Gaul, but had refined himself at Reims in more polished literature, that is, in the humanities. The writers of the *Literary History of France*, in the passage cited above, themselves teach this with some clarity when they assert that he devoted himself there to poetry no less than to the other sciences, in accordance with the custom of the age in which he lived.

Thus, when they praise, in the passage cited above, the eulogy of Bruno preserved in Labbe, on the sciences that Bruno had acquired at Cologne, they may have intended to infer less from that eulogy than their own words indicate, or at least may not have fully understood what followed from it.

Furthermore, the saint devoted himself entirely to the humanities, or to the study of the Latin language, at the celebrated school of Reims with such ardor and such success that he was held up as an example to others. This seems to be inferred from the last of the two verses of Baldric, abbot of Bourgueil, transcribed immediately above:

> “Bruno, then the mirror of Latin studies.”

In addition, the degree of the saint’s achievement specifically in poetry is sufficiently demonstrated by the *Paraenetic Epigram for Attaining Heavenly Things*, composed by him and printed repeatedly elsewhere, including at Paris by Josse Bade in 1524 together with the other works of the holy man. In its verses—although they are not wholly exact according to the rules of the art—there shines a grace and elegance that one seeks in vain in almost all other poets of the eleventh century, the age in which the saint flourished.

### 56

I transcribe the whole poem here as a specimen. It reads:

> The Lord created all mortals in the light,  
> that by their merits they might gain the highest joys of heaven.  
> Truly happy is the one who constantly directs his mind there  
> and vigilantly avoids every harmful thing!  
> Yet not unhappy is the one who repents of the crime he has committed  
> and often laments his wrongdoing.  
> But human beings live as though no death would follow,  
> and as though hell were merely an empty tale,  
> although experience teaches that the living are dissolved by death  
> and sacred Scripture proves the punishments of Erebus.  
> Whoever does not fear them lives wholly wretched and mad  
> and, once dead, will feel that pyre.  
> Therefore let all mortals take care to live  
> so that no infernal marsh need be feared.

It will also be easy to infer from what follows that the saint made a point of instructing himself in the higher branches of learning, no less than in the art of poetry. But where did he learn these sciences, and specifically philosophy?

In favor of Paris stand not only the words of Blomenvenna transcribed above in no. 50, Surius in the *Life of the Saint*, and quite a few other Carthusian writers, but also several others whom there is no time to name individually. Among them is Caesar Egassius Bulaeus, in the *History of the University of Paris*, published by him in 1665, volume I, pages 467 and following. Although he does not explicitly say there that the saint studied philosophy at Paris, he indicates it sufficiently; and, unlike the others, he also attempts to prove his opinion that the saint taught at Paris [Col. 0038D].

### 57

For this purpose he employs three different conjectures. I omit the last of them, since it aims only to prove that the saint taught at Paris—a matter to be discussed below—and examine only the other two.

The second of these, in Bulaeus’s words, “is drawn from an anonymous author who carried his history from Robert to the death of Philip I, and who knew Bruno or could have known him. He counts him among those who almost certainly studied and taught at Paris. ‘At this time,’ he says, namely around the year 1060, ‘Lanfranc, bishop of Canterbury; Guido the Lombard; Manigaudus the German; and Bruno of Reims, who later led an eremitical life, flourished in both divine and human philosophy.’ No one, however, will say that those men taught at Reims.”

Thus he writes. Although he does not explicitly say that the saint studied philosophy at Paris, he sufficiently implies it by wishing it to be almost certain that Bruno studied there and by adducing the anonymous author’s text, which asserts that the saint flourished in philosophy. But, I ask, how can it be certain that Bruno studied philosophy nowhere except at Paris, or even that he taught that science there?

### 58

Indeed, it appears more probable from what will be said below, and especially from the historical *Fragment* itself cited by Bulaeus, that Bruno taught philosophy at Reims. Consequently, the contrary is uncertain, and for this reason alone Bulaeus’s conjecture that Bruno received his philosophical instruction at Paris must be regarded as highly uncertain. Whether Bulaeus is more reliable concerning the other men praised by the anonymous author I leave to others to examine, and I now turn to the writer’s other conjecture.

“This,” Bulaeus writes, “is drawn from a manuscript of the *Chronicle of Malleac*, said to be preserved in Paris in the Putean Library. The author composed it around 1160, and it was published by Philip Labbe. In it the following words are found under the year 996:

> ‘Gerbert taught Fulbert, bishop of Chartres. Fulbert in turn taught Berengarius, a canon of Saint Martin. He likewise left Bruno of Reims and many others as heirs of philosophy. Bruno, a perfect philosopher and hermit, died in Christ at Calabria as the father of many monks.’

> “But where did Berengarius leave him as an heir of philosophy? Certainly, where Berengarius himself taught. Yet he is not recorded as having taught at Reims, but at Tours; and he is presumed to have taught at Paris after the death of his teacher Fulbert of Chartres. It is therefore probable that Bruno heard him at Paris—that is, in philosophy.”

### 59

Thus far Bulaeus, maintaining not only that our saint received his philosophical instruction at Paris, but also that he had there as his teacher in this discipline Berengarius, a canon of Saint Martin of Tours—the man whose widely disseminated poison of heresy, by which he denied the real presence of Christ’s Body and Blood in the sacrament of the Eucharist, anticipated Calvin and his followers, and became notorious throughout Europe.

But since Berengarius (see the writers of the *Literary History of France*, volume IX, page 140) is nowhere recorded as having taught at Paris, and since it is therefore, as Bulaeus himself sufficiently indicates in the words quoted, extremely doubtful whether he ever taught there, why did Bulaeus not rather infer from the quoted words of the *Chronicle of Malleac* that the saint heard Berengarius in philosophy at Tours, where he certainly did teach?

Indeed, since Berengarius, defeated by Lanfranc in various disputations and consequently abandoned by his pupils, was, according to Bulaeus’s own opinion, forced around 1038 to leave Paris and its schools and return to Tours, he certainly could not have had the saint as his pupil in philosophy there. Bruno, as I have shown, was born around 1030 and had not yet reached his tenth year at that time [Col. 0040A].

Bulaeus’s second conjecture, therefore—the conjecture offered to prove that Bruno received his philosophical education at Paris—also collapses. It must be said, then, that the saint studied philosophy not at Paris but either at Reims or at Tours: at Reims if Berengarius did not become his teacher in that science; at Tours if he did.

60. The former of these alternatives is attractive because it is altogether certain, both from what has already been said and from what will be said further, that Bruno studied and taught for a long time at Rheims; the latter, however, because, if Bruno really heard Berengar in philosophy, as the Chronicle of Maillezais seems to report, it appears most probable that this happened where Berengar was teaching. Therefore, in order that it may in some way be determined whether Bruno received the principles of philosophy at Rheims or at Tours, it must be investigated whether Berengar was his teacher in philosophy.

I am of the opinion that Bruno did use Berengar as his teacher in philosophy. To establish this, I shall first address those who oppose that view or at least do not favor it. After Marloth had said in *Historia metropolis Remensis*, vol. II, p. 135, that Bruno had found as his teacher—specifically in philosophy—Berengar, canon of Saint Martin of Tours, he immediately added: “if the Maillezais chronicler, Bruno’s contemporary, is to be believed.” Mabillon prefixed the following note to the profession of faith of Saint Bruno, which he published in vol. IV of the *Vetera Analecta*, p. 400:

> “Because of the affinity of their subject matter, it seemed appropriate to append Deoduin’s letter to the profession of faith of Saint Bruno, which he issued shortly before his death, condemning the heresy of Berengar, whose disciple he had been, if the Chronicle of Maillezais is to be trusted.”

Thus those two learned men, Marloth and Mabillon, whatever the author of the Chronicle of Maillezais may have written in the words cited by Bulaeus in section 58, did not regard it as certain that Bruno had ever used Berengar as his teacher in philosophy. Mabillon even asserted that the matter was not merely doubtful but contrary to the truth.

61. For in the Preface to the Benedictine *Saeculum VI*, no. 7, near the middle, he writes as follows:

> “In discussing this transmission of doctrine and learning, the chronicler of Saint-Maixent traces it back, as though to its source, to Girbert or Gerbert, a monk of Aurillac, who is said to have taught Fulbert of Chartres. Fulbert, he says, ‘taught Berengar, canon of Saint Martin, who in turn left Bruno of Rheims and many others as heirs of philosophy.’ From this passage some conclude that Bruno, founder of the holy Carthusian Order, was a disciple of Berengar. Yet, apart from the fact that the authority of that chronicler of Saint-Maixent is not so great that it can establish this, the chronicler’s actual words seem clearly to require a different interpretation. For the words ‘who in turn Bruno of Rheims,’ etc., should not be referred to Berengar but to Fulbert, who taught Berengar, who in turn [taught] Bruno of Rheims. Furthermore, the words themselves do not prove that Fulbert, much less Berengar, had Bruno as a pupil; they merely state that Bruno and many others were left as heirs of philosophy, whether by Fulbert or by Berengar, regardless of which teacher instructed them—that is, Bruno and the other heirs of philosophy.”

It is certainly known that Bruno, already a cleric and canon of Cologne, and therefore educated in letters, came from the city of Cologne to the territory of Rheims. Yet it is far more probable that he was instructed by Notger, bishop of Liège, and by Notger’s pupils. The most authoritative witness to this is Manasses, archbishop of Rheims, in his *Apologia*, where, speaking of Bruno, who opposed his conduct, he says:

> “Bruno is neither our cleric nor our native-born or reborn son, but he is a canon of Saint Cunibert, situated in the kingdom of the Teutons,” etc.

I thought this worth observing here concerning that most holy man, who, even if he had been Berengar’s disciple, was utterly remote from Berengar’s error, as is proved by Bruno’s confession concerning the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist, which we have reported elsewhere. Yet it is important to distinguish truth from falsehood and to remove that little cloud, if any existed, from so great a light.”

62. In a second Preface to the Benedictine *Saeculum VI*, Mabillon next attempts to confirm his opinion. In no. 85 he writes:

> “This Godefrid of Rheims, who was appointed by Manasses, archbishop of Rheims, as Saint Bruno’s successor in the direction of the schools at Rheims, was praised both in life and after death by Baldric, abbot of Bourgueil. Baldric says that Godefrid was born at Rheims and educated in letters together with Bruno. Thus he sings in an as-yet unpublished poem addressed to Godefrid of Rheims:
>
> Noble city, Rome’s sister—I call you a second Rome—  
> Bore you, gave you birth, and won you for herself.  
>
> She adopted you, strengthened by all the nectar of learning,  
> And placed you over her studies.  
>
> Gaul then too flourished in rich studies,  
> And through your learning Gaul flourished even more.  
>
> Swarms of pupils ran to you,  
> And, as bees, were refreshed by the honey of their parent.  
>
> At that time Bruno too was at Rheims, and at Rheims he studied;  
> Bruno was then the mirror of Latin learning.  
>
> In those same times the elder Herman studied,  
> And was a bright lamp of learning to the world.  
>
> You were young, and you were sharper than they.  
> You came third, and already you were first.  
>
> Manasses, that prince of yours, succeeded Gervasius,  
> And advanced you in learning.
>
> From this it is understood that what we demonstrated in the preceding Preface—that is, in the passage immediately before this one, transcribed above—is true: Bruno devoted himself to letters at Rheims, specifically to philosophy, and not at Tours under Berengar as teacher, as some seek to persuade us on the basis of a mistaken understanding of the Chronicle of Maillezais. And he did so not only with the aforementioned Godefrid but also with the elder Herman, whom the scholar Gozechin praises first among the wise and authoritative men of that age who, having abandoned the lower studies, withdrew into the leisure of theology.”

63. Thus far Mabillon. But the words of Baldric, abbot of Bourgueil—“At that time Bruno too was at Rheims, and at Rheims he studied; Bruno was then the mirror of Latin learning”—which, according to Mabillon, ought chiefly to establish his case, seem, when taken in their natural and more obvious sense, to signify only that Bruno devoted himself at Rheims to the humanities. If, however, one obstinately insists that by “Latin learning” Baldric did not mean the humanities, there seems to be no reason why this author should be understood as referring to philosophical studies rather than to theological studies, by which Bruno cultivated his mind at Rheims.

If, therefore, in the entire text transcribed above Baldric the abbot is in fact speaking only of theology, in which the saint applied himself at Rheims together with Godefrid of Rheims and the elder Herman, what support, I ask, can this provide for Mabillon’s opinion that the saint received philosophy not at Tours from Berengar but at Rheims?

Nevertheless, the authors of the *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. IX, p. 233, subsequently agreed with this writer, making the following marginal note at the bottom of the page:

> “It was through error and a mistaken understanding of the sense of the Chronicle of Maillezais that some authors wrote that Bruno studied at Tours under Berengar. That this happened at Rheims is expressly affirmed by Baldric, abbot of Bourgueil—namely, in the passage cited above by Mabillon.”

So they write. But let us now examine whether those who wrote that the saint studied at Tours under Berengar, or received the principles of philosophy there, were unquestionably mistaken and misunderstood the Chronicle of Maillezais, or rather whether Mabillon interprets it with sufficient success in the words given in section 61.

First, Mabillon says:

> “These words of the Chronicle of Maillezais—‘who in turn [left] Bruno of Rheims,’ etc.—are not to be referred to Berengar but to Fulbert, who taught Berengar, who in turn [taught] Bruno of Rheims.”

According to Mabillon’s interpretation, then, Fulbert, not Berengar, was the saint’s teacher in philosophy. Yet this cannot be accepted unless we are simultaneously willing to accuse the author of the Chronicle of Maillezais of error.

64. For the Fulbert of whom he speaks was bishop of Chartres. But, as the authors of the *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. VII, p. 265, clearly demonstrate, Fulbert died in 1029. At that time the saint was either not yet born or, at any rate, still too immature by reason of his age to be capable of receiving and understanding philosophical instruction, as can readily be inferred from what was said above concerning Bruno’s year of birth.

Indeed, Mabillon himself may have noticed that Fulbert of Chartres could not have been the saint’s teacher in philosophy. I suspect this because, immediately after the interpretation of the Chronicle of Maillezais just discussed, he adds another:

> “Furthermore, the very words quoted from the Chronicle of Maillezais do not prove that Fulbert, much less Berengar, had Bruno as a pupil; they merely state that Bruno and many others were left as ‘heirs of philosophy,’ whether by Fulbert or by Berengar, regardless of which teacher instructed them—that is, Bruno and the other heirs of philosophy.”

All learned men will readily abandon the opinion that the saint studied at Tours under Berengar if this second method of interpreting the Chronicle of Maillezais, employed by Mabillon, is to stand. Yet the matter, as it appears to me, is most probably otherwise. To demonstrate this, I shall quote the actual words of the Chronicle of Maillezais—not only those transcribed by Mabillon in the passage cited above, but also several others that precede them, forming a somewhat longer text. It reads:

> “Girbert, an Aquitanian by birth, a monk of Aurillac in the church of Saint Gerald, . . . . was raised by the emperor to be pope of the Romans on account of his distinction in philosophy. His former name was changed, and he was called Sylvester. For Girbert taught Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, who became bishop after Leobinus. Many writings about him remained either in written form or in the chant of the holy Church. This Fulbert in turn taught Berengar, canon of Saint Martin. He in turn left Bruno of Rheims and many others as heirs of philosophy.”

65. Here several teachers or masters of philosophy are listed in the order in which they flourished, as will be clear to anyone who considers the passage; some transmitted this science to others. Since Berengar, as everyone acknowledges, was himself a teacher or master of philosophy, the words of the chronicler of Maillezais—“He in turn left Bruno of Rheims and many others as heirs of philosophy”—must be referred not to Fulbert, as Mabillon wishes, but to Berengar. They must therefore be understood to signify that Berengar himself transmitted the knowledge of philosophy to Saint Bruno.

Indeed, the natural and most obvious sense of the words requires this interpretation, as, I believe, anyone free from prejudice will readily admit.

To prove that the saint was not taught philosophy by Berengar, and consequently that the words “He in turn [left] Bruno of Rheims,” etc., must be explained in the manner he proposes, Mabillon further adduces the following argument:

> “Bruno, already a cleric and canon of Cologne, and therefore educated in letters, came from the city of Cologne to the territory of Rheims.”

He says that this is evident from the words of Manasses, archbishop of Rheims, concerning Saint Bruno:

> “Bruno is neither our cleric nor our native-born or reborn son, but is a canon of Saint Cunibert, situated in the kingdom of the Teutons,” etc.

But we have already demonstrated above that, when the saint came from Cologne to Rheims, he had not yet been educated in letters of the higher order, such as philosophy. Nor can this be established from the words of the archbishop Manasses cited by Mabillon, since, as was said above, they rather indicate that our saint was not a canon of Saint Cunibert before he went from his homeland to Rheims in order to study letters, but only became one later, when he was compelled to leave Rheims in 1076 or the following year.

66. None of the arguments by which Mabillon seeks to prove that the words of the Chronicle of Maillezais, now discussed at length, must be explained in one or the other of the ways he proposes conclusively establishes the matter. Therefore, adhering to the natural and more obvious sense offered by those words, I continue to understand them as signifying that Berengar transmitted the principles of philosophy to Saint Bruno. On the authority of the Chronicle of Maillezais, whose author was nearly contemporary with our saint, I regard this as in fact most probable.

Mabillon does add—see section 61—that the authority of the Chronicle is not so great that it can give unquestionable credibility to its assertions, and that some of the matters it records have actually been discovered to be contrary to the truth, both by Labbe, who first published it, and afterward by the authors of the *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. XII, pp. 79–80.

But even if this is so, what it says about the philosophy transmitted to Saint Bruno by Berengar still appears most probable. For the matters in which the author of that Chronicle is accused of deviating from the truth lay far removed from his own age. In matters that occurred either in his own time or not long before it, however, he is scarcely ever reported to have erred by Labbe, who nevertheless carefully recorded his errors. Since the chronicler was contemporary with, or at least almost contemporary with, our saint, he should therefore not be thought to have erred in what he reports concerning the philosophy heard by Bruno under Berengar. Nor does Labbe accuse him of error in this matter.

Accordingly, although it is not altogether certain, it is, all things considered, exceedingly probable that our saint was taught philosophy by Berengar.

67. It further follows from this that he most probably received it not at Paris—as must also be proved here—but at Tours, since Berengar taught in that city and not, as recent critics now generally agree, elsewhere.

“But,” you will object, “Berengar was notorious and dangerous because of his impious heresy, by which he also tried to infect others. It therefore does not seem plausible that either the saint’s parents or those responsible for the care of the still-young man would have entrusted him to such a teacher, exposing him to the danger of imbibing poisonous and impious doctrines.”

Yet Berengar did not fall into heresy immediately when he began to direct the schools at Tours, nor, when he began to spread the poison of his heresy, was he immediately regarded everywhere by everyone as a heretic.

Hugh, bishop of Langres, once Berengar’s fellow student, was the first to discover—see the authors of the *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. VIII, p. 202—that Berengar denied both the reality and the transubstantiation of the Eucharistic sacrament. Not long afterward Hugh wrote him a fine letter in an effort to bring him back from his error.

Since this letter was not written earlier than shortly before October of the year 1049, it follows that Berengar’s corrupt doctrine was most probably discovered by Hugh, bishop of Langres, only in the year immediately preceding that date. It also appears that in that year, or only slightly earlier, the doctrine first caused disturbances in the Church.

Since this is so, nothing prevented the saint’s parents or guardians from sending him to Tours in 1047, when, according to what was said above, he may already have been about seventeen years old, to be instructed by Berengar in the principles of philosophy. Indeed, I do not see why he could not have been sent even in 1048 or the following year, since Berengar’s errors were not condemned until 1050, by Pope Leo IX in the council held at Rome.

68. Nor should it be considered a disgrace to Bruno or to his children that he heard in philosophy a man whose views concerning the faith were incorrect but who had not yet been condemned as a heretic. For even if this appears to follow from what has already been said, there can nevertheless be no doubt that Bruno withdrew from Berengar at least when Berengar was first condemned at the Roman council.

I infer this from the fact that Bruno abhorred Berengar’s impious heresy above all else. This is shown both by the commentaries he composed—mentioned below—on Psalm 21 and on chapter 11 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, and by the profession of faith that he issued shortly before his death, reported by Mabillon in vol. IV of the *Analecta*, pp. 400 and following, and to be transcribed below.

But since the discussion has reached the profession of faith issued by the saint near the end of his life, one further point must be brought to the reader’s attention. In that profession Bruno immediately says:

> “I believe the sacraments that the Catholic Church believes and venerates.”

He then adds:

> “And specifically, that what is consecrated on the altar is the true body, the true flesh, and the true blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, which we also receive for the remission of our sins and in hope of eternal salvation.”

Someone may perhaps wish to argue that, since these words contain a doctrine diametrically opposed to Berengarian teaching, they also prove that the saint studied philosophy at Tours under Berengar. For Bruno included those words in the profession of faith he issued, it might be argued, in order to remove from himself any suspicion of Berengarian heresy to which he might otherwise have been liable.

69. Indeed, there was a time when I too thought that one might argue from this that the saint had heard philosophy under Berengar. But after examining the matter more closely, I discovered that, after the rise of the Berengarian heresy, a custom was long observed by which learned and distinguished men, when near death, issued a profession of faith. In it they professed various doctrines of the faith, and especially those concerning the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist.

As a first example, consider Gervasius, archbishop of Rheims, who died in 1067. When he was about to die, he issued a profession of faith differing little from Bruno’s with respect to the hidden doctrine concerning the Eucharist, as may be seen in the series of the archbishops of Rheims presented by the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX.

There is also Matthew, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, whose profession of faith, issued near the end of his life and not greatly different from Bruno’s, is preserved in Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, *Book II, chapter 22 of the Miracles*. Likewise there is Louis VI, king of the Franks, whose profession of faith, also not greatly different from Bruno’s and issued when he was dying, is quoted by Baronius in the *Annals* under the year 1131.

Therefore, Saint Bruno’s having been a disciple of Berengar in philosophy cannot be inferred from the profession of faith he issued near his death.

Nor can this be argued more forcefully from the one hundred sixty-sixth funeral title, in which the cathedral church of Angers, dedicated to Saint Maurice, celebrates Bruno magnificently. Although it contains these two verses:

> The guide of error first showed the way to what was better;  
> Afterwards, [he showed] the teaching that grants joys without end,

someone might perhaps suspect from them that the saint had fallen into error against the faith, from which he later withdrew, and therefore not only had Berengar as his teacher but at some point also became a follower of Berengar’s perverse position concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist.

Yet anyone who considers these two verses together with the other verses preceding and following them in the same title will readily see that there is no legitimate basis for such a sinister suspicion concerning the saint.

70. For it will become clear that by “error” in these verses we should understand not an error against the faith to which the saint had once adhered, but the secular sciences that he had first cultivated and taught diligently and with great praise. By “better teaching,” on the other hand, we should understand not some doctrine of the sincere and true faith to which he had once been opposed, but the divine teaching of the Gospel. Afterward, when he had abandoned the world and withdrawn into the wilderness, he taught others by his example to despise earthly things and pursue heavenly ones.

To make this easier to recognize, I shall transcribe here both the verses that follow and those that precede the two already quoted. The preceding verses are:

> Bruno’s tongue is praised more than Maro’s;  
> The glory of Plato grows pale before Bruno’s praise.  
>
> Here he excelled the teachers; here he made  
> The highest teachers, not by making lesser ones.  
>
> He was the teacher of teachers, not of little clerks.  
> For no one took up Bruno’s proprieties of speech or his dignity of expression unless he was a man of great discernment.  
>
> The judgment of the prudent surpassed the sharpness of the mind;  
> As a teacher of learning, he proved fully sufficient in these matters.  
>
> He wished to set before them a more perfect way;  
> By teaching divine wisdom, he proclaimed what was excellent,  
> And he first destroyed and regarded as frivolous [the former things].

71. The following verses are:

> But worldly wisdom gives nothing except vain things;  
> This makes men proud, while that makes them blessed.  
>
> He fulfilled [his teaching] by his deeds, practicing what he taught with his mouth;  
> He delivered many sermons throughout the regions.  
>
> He passed through the city of Rome and sought out the Calabrians.

The anonymous author who composed the *Treatise on Saint Bruno*, which the Carthusians of this region shared with me, interprets the funeral title dedicated to Bruno by the church of Angers somewhat differently, in order to free the saint from any suspicion of error in the faith.

Concerning its author, he states in section 7:

> “The writer first praises Bruno because he surpassed the more celebrated teachers in every secular science, such as grammar, dialectic, and other studies of this kind. Then he shows him to be worthy of greater praise because ‘he wished to set before them a more perfect way,’ that is, knowledge—namely theology, as he explains in the following verse: ‘He proclaims excellent divine wisdom by teaching.’
>
> “Therefore, the man who had previously been a guide of error—not of false doctrine, but of perishable and worldly learning, or philosophy, as he later says, which many saints despised as contributing little or nothing to salvation—afterward ‘showed the way to better teaching,’ either by preaching, for ‘he delivered many sermons throughout the regions,’ or by teaching and interpreting Sacred Scripture for his disciples, as we saw the canons of Neuilly declare above when they called him formerly the supreme teacher of the church of Rheims, since he was highly accomplished in the Psalter and the other sciences.”

72. Thus he writes. Indeed, this interpretation, or another similar one—if the interpretation I proposed above, which nevertheless seems preferable, should perhaps be displeasing—must necessarily be accepted, since it is certain from various other funeral titles of the saint that he never departed from the faith. In those titles it is expressly stated, or at least clearly indicated, that he always preserved the faith sound and complete.

To pass over the others for the sake of brevity, I shall cite only the one hundred twentieth, in which this is declared most explicitly. In it the monks of Saint-Omer address the saint as follows:

> Therefore, may the true faith, which you always cherished,  
> Lead you to the rest of Christ, which you, Bruno, sought.

For the rest, I have wished to pursue at somewhat greater length both the question of the error in the faith of which Bruno might appear suspect and the profession of faith he issued at the end of his life, so that it may be more evident that nothing can be concluded from either in favor of the opinion that makes our saint Berengar’s disciple in philosophy.

The love of truth now compels me to place before the reader one further point that in some way obstructs or at least does not support our opinion. Among the saint’s funeral titles, which number nearly 180, there is none that was composed for him by the church of Tours. From this it might appear that the alumnus of the Calabrian Charterhouse did not visit Tours. The Carthusian who circulated the encyclical letter concerning Saint Bruno’s death would seemingly have done this if the saint had studied philosophy at Tours, since it was customary in his age for such encyclical letters to be delivered especially to churches in which the deceased was known, or at least presumed to be known.

73. Thus may those who oppose our opinion that Bruno heard philosophy from Berengar at Tours argue. Yet it is quite probable that not all of the saint’s funeral titles were inscribed on the same roll which the Carthusian of Calabria circulated with the encyclical letter concerning the saint’s death, and which certainly contained several replies or funeral titles. Separate sheets on which some of these titles had probably been written could easily have perished through the passage of time.

What if this happened to the funeral title with which the church of Tours honored the saint? Moreover, the alumnus of the Calabrian Charterhouse who circulated the encyclical letter announcing Saint Bruno’s death may not have approached all the churches to which he was known during his lifetime, having departed from the usual custom for reasons unknown to us.

In any event, it does not follow from the fact that no funeral title bearing the name of the church of Tours is found among the saint’s titles that Bruno was not known at Tours or that he did not devote himself there to philosophy. For there is no possible doubt that the saint was extremely well known at Cologne, since he was born and largely raised in that city. Yet among his funeral titles there is none bearing the name of the church of Cologne, whether the cathedral church or the collegiate church of Saint Cunibert, in which the saint had nevertheless served as a canon.

Thus the difficulty just raised does not weaken the opinion that the saint learned philosophy at Tours under Berengar.

It further follows from this and from the other points stated above that, when the saint was already eighteen years old, he most probably had not yet studied at Paris. For when he was about fourteen, or even younger, he pursued at Rheims the humanities whose rudiments he had begun at Cologne; and after he had been instructed in them there, he began to hear philosophy at Tours, a course which he most probably completed in no fewer than two years. At what time, then, could he have studied at Paris before completing his eighteenth year?

Whether he later studied there or even taught there will be revealed by what follows.

§ IV. Where Saint Bruno went after leaving Berengar at Tours, what he first did there, when he began to teach at Rheims, and what sciences he taught and offices he discharged there

74. Saint Bruno’s departure from Tours after leaving Berengar occurred about the year 1048, or certainly no later than 1050. This is made exceedingly probable by the evidence presented in the preceding section. But where did the saint then go? To Paris or to Rheims? There is no ancient monument that enables me to assert either alternative with certainty.

Nevertheless, I would prefer to decide in favor of the city of Rheims, since it will be clear from what follows that the saint both studied and taught there for a long time.

Morkensius, in his manuscript *Chronological-Diplomatic Disquisition on Saint Bruno*, holds the opinion that, after Berengar’s heresy was discovered, the founder of his order returned to his homeland, Cologne. This certainly seems plausible, although it likewise cannot be proved by any sufficiently ancient monument.

But what should be said of Morkensius’s further assertion that our saint was then first made a canon of the church of Saint Cunibert? This also does not appear improbable, nor does the claim that Bruno at that time devoted himself there to Sacred Scripture and theological matters.

If matters in fact stood as they may have, Saint Bruno could also have been called by Manasses, archbishop of Rheims, a canon of Saint Cunibert in the sense explained in section 53, even though he had not served as a canon in the church of Saint Cunibert before leaving his homeland for Gaul for the first time in order to study letters.

Thus, even if it must be admitted that he had already been a canon of the church of Saint Cunibert for a long time before the year 1067, approximately when, as will be explained below, he resigned the direction of the schools at Rheims, it could not rightly be inferred from Manasses that he had certainly adopted this way of life at the time when he had not yet visited Gaul.

Add this to what was said in sections 52 and following and in section 65.

75. It would be far more probable that Saint Bruno returned to his homeland after studying philosophy at Tours, first began to serve there as a canon, and at the same time devoted himself to theological matters, if what the aforementioned Morkensius also reports could be established by sufficiently certain evidence: namely, that Bruno was recalled from Cologne to the city of Rheims by Gervasius, archbishop of Rheims, who had been promoted to that see in 1055, so that Bruno might teach there the sciences he knew.

In support of this, Morkensius cites an ancient manuscript mentioned in section 49, belonging to the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu in Picardy and praised by Surianus in his annotations to Surianus’s *Life of the Saint*, p. 79.

But since I have no independent knowledge of the manuscript’s antiquity or authority—Surianus, Morkensius, and Martini, who is likewise mentioned in section 49, are all silent about these matters—the manuscript, however ancient those writers may call it, cannot possibly suffice for me to regard it as certain that Saint Bruno was truly recalled by Gervasius from Cologne to Rheims in order to teach there.

I therefore leave this matter undecided, as I also leave undecided whether Bruno, when he left Tours after having studied philosophy there, returned to his homeland and for some time served as a canon there while devoting himself to Sacred Scripture and theological matters. I now proceed to discuss other matters concerning the saint that rest on more certain and more solid foundations.

76. It must be certain, above all, that Bruno served as master of the schools at Rheims, even though by that time he had probably already cultivated Sacred Scripture and theology diligently, whether in that city itself or elsewhere. This is established by the sole *Chronicle of the Four First Priors of the Charterhouse*, or rather by the brief eulogy of the saint that I transcribed from it above in section 7, since in that passage a contemporary author expressly calls him master of the schools of the church of Rheims.

This is also confirmed by Sigebert of Gembloux and Hugh, bishop of Die and papal legate in Gaul. The former, in his *Chronography* under the year 1084, and the latter, in a letter to Pope Gregory VII written in 1077 and preserved in Labbe, vol. X of the *Councils*, col. 365—a letter that will also be mentioned below—likewise call Bruno “master of the church of Rheims.”

Add to these Meinard, prior of Cormery in the territory of Tours. In a funeral title, among the 176 to be reprinted, with which he honored the saint, he says:

> “I, Meinard, who am prior of the monastery of Cormery in name rather than in deed of many monks, was born in the city of Rheims. For several years I heard the teaching of this lord Bruno, and by God’s will I made considerable progress.”

Thus he speaks. Although he does not explicitly say that he studied at Rheims under Bruno, the matter most probably stood that way, since he declares himself to have been born at Rheims and probably studied letters for some time in the place of his birth.

77. These considerations, in my judgment, prove more than sufficiently that Saint Bruno taught at Rheims or served there as master. What sciences he taught there, however, and approximately when he first undertook this work or office must now be investigated.

First, it appears that the saint taught poetry there. This may be concluded from his funeral title 126, in which the school of Saint Vedast at Noyon in Arras addresses him as follows:

> . . . . . . . . to you, Bruno, keen master.  
>
> The world was held in contempt here in its bloom and barren beauty;  
> The flower was in the hay. It flourished beneath a clear sun,  
> While your muse sang and devoted itself to study,  
> While now it nourished Rheims with milk, now fed it with bread.

The saint appears to have taught at Rheims not only poetry, one of the lower sciences or arts, but grammar itself as well. For in the school verses of the church of Saint Mary of Coutances, which constitute his funeral title 156 among those to be reprinted, he is declared to have been “the teacher of many grammarians.”

Although the verses do not say whether he trained grammarians at Rheims or elsewhere, it nevertheless appears probable that he did so at Rheims, because it cannot be demonstrated from any ancient monument capable of establishing unquestionable credibility that he ever taught anywhere other than Rheims.

No other evidence presents itself that could help establish that the saint taught the lower sciences or the humanities at Rheims.

78. But what should be said about the higher sciences, namely theology and philosophy? It seems that our saint also taught both of these at Reims. First, since various praises appropriate to Bruno—an almost exclusively public professor of philosophy and theology—are attributed to him in several funerary titles, especially titles 31, 32, 107, 124, 126, 131, 146, 166, 168, and 173, without any mention whatever of the place where he taught these sciences, it follows from the very argument just advanced, by which he appears to have taught grammar at Reims, that he also taught philosophy and theology there. I nevertheless wish to establish the matter in another way as well.

In the historical fragment extending from the time of Robert, king of the Franks, to the death of Philip I, which Marlot cites as no. 57, the anonymous author knew Bruno not so much from his homeland as from the studies to which he had devoted himself for a very long time at Reims, both as a student and as a teacher, and from the dignities he had obtained there. Accordingly, as I showed in no. 12, the author calls him “of Reims” (*Remensem*). Since, moreover, the author applies this designation to the saint in the very passage where he reports that Bruno flourished “in both divine and human philosophy”—that is, by teaching or publicly professing these two sciences—it is most likely that he did so chiefly because he knew the same man especially through human and divine philosophy, or through theology and philosophy, both of which sciences Bruno was then teaching at Reims.

79. Thus we now have it that Bruno taught both philosophy and theology at Reims. As for the latter science in particular, I demonstrate the point additionally as follows. We know that our saint held the office of schoolmaster or scholarch, a position that was entrusted only to the most learned and most eminent men. This is clear both from his funerary title 173, in which the regular canons of the church of Saint Vincent at Noyon assert that he had formerly been “the supreme teacher of the church of the see of Reims,” and from Guibert of Nogent, a contemporary writer, who writes of our saint in book I, chapter 11, of *On His Life*: “Not long before these days there was a certain Bruno in the city of Reims, a man instructed in the liberal arts and director of great studies.”

In former times, even in the age of Saint Bruno—that is, in the eleventh century—the principal responsibility of a schoolmaster or scholarch in the greater churches was to educate the clergy in the liberal arts and consequently, and apparently above all, in theological disciplines; to form them in good morals; to promote ecclesiastical discipline; and, whenever questioned, to answer on all matters pertaining to divine worship. These points, or at least matters not far removed from them, may properly be gathered from Thomassinus, *On the Old and New Discipline of the Church*, vol. I, book III, chapter 70, no. 8, and from Papirius Masson’s *Annals*, under Philip, even though in the meantime the office of scholarch or schoolmaster, since there are now others who teach the liberal arts elsewhere, has largely ceased to be an actual function in both the greater or cathedral churches and the others, and has remained almost exclusively as a dignity and title.

Now, since it has already been proved that the saint certainly discharged the office of schoolmaster or scholarch in the church of Reims, there can be no doubt that he taught theology to the clergy there.

80. I think it most probable that at that time he taught only these higher sciences, and among them theology. For the cathedral church of Angers, in its funerary title 166, which is to be reprinted and in which it celebrates the saint magnificently, sings of him as follows:

> He surpassed these teachers; he made  
> the highest teachers, not by instructing lesser men;  
> he was the teacher of teachers, not of little clerics.

By these three verses it is indicated that the saint taught not little clerics—that is, younger clerics suited only to learning the sciences of the lower order—but men of more advanced age. It is therefore implied that the lower sciences were not taught at Reims. This implication could not accord with the truth, since, according to what was said above, Bruno did teach poetry and grammar at Reims, unless the reference is to the saint after he had become scholarch of the church of Reims and director and prefect of the highest studies. For it does not seem probable that, before being appointed to this office, he taught the higher sciences, but that after his appointment he taught only the lower ones.

Bruno, therefore, after he had obtained the direction of the schools of Reims, taught only the higher sciences, especially theology; before he had been honored with this office, he taught the lower sciences as well. Let this suffice concerning the sciences that the saint taught at Reims. We must now inquire, in a general way, about the time when he undertook this work.

81. If Morkensius is correct in noting, at no. 75, that Saint Bruno was summoned from Cologne to teach letters at Reims by Gervasius, archbishop of Reims, Bruno certainly did not begin teaching letters at Reims before the year 1055, since Gervasius was first elevated to the see of Reims in that year. If, however, we should follow Marlot, who writes in volume II, page 115, of the *History of the Metropolitan Church of Reims* that Bruno was appointed by Gervasius in 1056 as head or director of the schools of Reims, then it appears that our saint began teaching in the schools of Reims before 1055, since he does not seem to have obtained the prefecture of the schools unless he had already been teaching for some time.

But since neither Marlot nor Morkensius inspires confidence here, as can readily be gathered from what was said above, we must turn elsewhere in order to determine, at least approximately, the time when the saint devoted himself to teaching among the people of Reims.

Baldric, abbot of Bourgueil, in his verses to Godefrid of Reims, who was substituted for Bruno in the direction of the schools of Reims by Manasses, bishop of Reims, around the year 1077, teaches in no. 62, transcribed below, that this Godefrid of his—whom he praises enthusiastically—studied at Reims with Herimann and Bruno, and then adds:

> You were young, and sharper than they;  
> therefore you came third, yet were already first.  
>   
> Your prince, Manasses, succeeded Gervasius,  
> and he advances you to the school.

These four verses clearly indicate—nothing else seems capable of being signified by them—that Godefrid reached the direction of the schools of Reims in third place, that is, after Herimann and Bruno, although he surpassed them in sharpness of intellect, Manasses promoting him to that office.

82. From this it follows, insofar as it concerns our present purpose, that Herimann had been prefect of the schools of Reims, and had held that position before Godefrid. Since he had likewise held that office before Bruno, to whom Godefrid was immediately appointed as successor, we shall learn approximately when Bruno began to discharge it by determining when Herimann laid it down.

Let us therefore investigate that point. Mabillon, in volume IV of the *Analecta*, prints a letter written by Gozechin, scholastic of Liège, from Mainz, to which he had withdrawn after abandoning the teaching office of the see of Liège. In this letter, lamenting the vices and evils of his age, which arose chiefly from the errors of Berengar, he says on page 385:

> All these things Herimann of Reims, Drogo of Paris, Huoremann of Speyer, Meinhard of Bamberg, and many other men, both distinguished and of the highest authority, wisely despised; having cut off their incomes—that is, as Mabillon interprets it in his preface to the sixth century of the Benedictine order, “having renounced their stipends and emoluments, and having laid aside their labors, they bade farewell to studies and, following a wise counsel, withdrew into the leisure of theology”—that is, as the authors of the *Literary History of France*, vol. IX, page 234, interpret it from what precedes and follows, into solitude, intending to devote themselves exclusively to meditation on divine matters and to true wisdom.

83. The Herimann mentioned here appears to be none other than the Herimann recently named as prefect or scholarch of the schools of Reims before Bruno. He had already withdrawn into solitude, abandoning his studies and consequently resigning the office of scholarch, when Gozechin wrote the letter in question.

Since he certainly did this before the year 1060, as can easily be understood from Mabillon’s discussion in the passage just cited, Herimann had already resigned the direction of the schools of Reims before that year. Now, since according to what has been said our saint immediately succeeded Herimann, it follows that he most probably received from Gervasius, archbishop of Reims, the direction of the schools of Reims before that same year 1060. Thus Marlot, who—as I have already twice noted—places the event in 1056, may perhaps not be far from the truth.

Therefore, since the saint appears to have taught letters, or at least the sciences of the lower order, at Reims for some time before he was made prefect of the schools of Reims, or “director of the great studies,” as Guibert of Nogent, cited above, calls him—or, as the regular canons of the church of Saint Vincent at Noyon likewise write in their funerary title of Saint Bruno, “supreme teacher”—it follows that he first began teaching at Reims between the years 1050 and 1060. In the meantime, he may either already have been living in the city of Reims and pursuing theological studies there, or he may then have been summoned by Gervasius, the archbishop, from Cologne, where Morkensius above says that he had cultivated these studies.

84. It certainly appears beyond doubt that he did not undertake this burden before 1050, since at that time, as is readily gathered from what was said above, he had emerged from the study of philosophy only one or two years earlier and, after completing it, had probably devoted at least some time to theological studies before beginning to teach.

We now therefore know not only approximately when the saint first acted as a teacher in the city of Reims, but also approximately when he was promoted to the prefecture of the schools of Reims, or the office of supreme teacher.

Furthermore, the saint not only held the prefecture of the schools at Reims, a matter already sufficiently discussed, but also served as canon and chancellor of the metropolitan church. The former is established both by the *Chronicle of the First Four Priors of the Carthusian House*, or by the eulogy of the saint extracted from it and transcribed above at no. 7, and by the *Chronicle of Sigebert of Gembloux*. In both of these genuinely ancient records, considering the time at which they were written after Bruno’s death, he is given the title “canon of the church of Reims.”

As for the office of chancellor, which he likewise held, this is clear from the charter alone to which Bruno, writing as chancellor, also subscribed. It was granted in 1076 by Archbishop Manasses in favor of the abbey of Saint Basolus. I therefore transcribe it here as it appears in the fourth book of the *Carthusian Annals*, not yet published.

85. It reads as follows:

> In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. I, Manasses, by the ineffable providence of God archbishop of Reims, mindful of past and future things, and recognizing how all things suffer irrecoverable loss through ruin and decline, because I know that the condition of my life will not last forever, have endeavored, by extending the hand of charity, to prepare a most tranquil harbor for my soul.  
>   
> Compelled, therefore, by this necessity and by concern for the churches entrusted to me, and at the request of Abbot Stephen, I have given and subjected to the monastery of Saint Basolus two altars, namely those of Alteia and Caprilla, so that the brothers may hold them perpetually without personal tenure, paying only the *summatici*, and may celebrate for me, for as long as I live, two Masses each week, one privately and the other publicly. Each year, moreover, on the day of my anniversary, the brothers of that church shall dine regularly in the refectory from the revenues of those altars. If anyone removes them from there, let him be accursed.  
>   
> Done at Reims in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1076, in the seventeenth year of the reign of King Philip, and in the seventh year of the archbishopric of our lord Manasses. In the fourteenth indiction.  
>   
> Sign of Guido, archdeacon. Sign of Guarinus, archdeacon. Sign of Manasses, provost. Sign of Leuvinus, dean. Sign of Odo, cantor. Sign of Henry, abbot. Sign of Jotzelinus, abbot. Sign of Gebuinus, abbot. Sign of Raimbaldus, abbot. Sign of Dudo, dean. Sign of Dominicus, dean. Sign of Lambert, dean. Sign of Bavo, dean. Sign of Wido, knight. Sign of Albert, knight. Sign of Rodulphus. Sign of Haymo. Sign of Lambert.  
>   
> Bruno, chancellor, wrote and subscribed this.

86. This charter also appears in Marlot, although he does not say where he obtained it, in volume II of the *History of the Metropolitan Church of Reims*, pages 170 and following. It is also found in the manuscript treatise on Saint Bruno mentioned at no. 28, which the Carthusians of this place shared with me. I therefore have three copies of the same document before me.

In all the details—the chronological notes by which they are dated as well as the wording in which they are composed—the three copies agree with one another almost exactly. They do not agree in the same way, however, in the witnesses subscribed to the instrument. For, apart from the fact that Marlot’s copy presents the names of some of these witnesses in a form different from that found in the other two copies, it adds to the abbots who subscribed the charter the names of the monasteries or abbeys over which each presided. This is not done in the other two copies, and I have not sufficiently established whether it is correct in Marlot’s copy.

Meanwhile, the anonymous Carthusian, author of the fourth book of the order’s *Annals*, adds the following note to the charter he has transcribed, thereby declaring that he took it from the original:

> It was extracted—that is, the instrument or charter just recited—from the original, sealed with the large seal of yellow wax, in whose matrix was impressed an image of the Blessed Virgin Mary holding the child Jesus in her right and left hands. This instrument was found in the aforesaid abbey of Saint Basolus at Reims by a certain venerable Benedictine monk of the reformed congregation, residing at Compiègne, in the year 1649, and lent to a Carthusian of the house of Mont-Dieu, from whose writings we extracted it.

87. Mabillon, however, who in book LXIV, no. 129, of the *Benedictine Annals* quotes part of the charter here transcribed in full, and who suggests that the original of this instrument, or at least an authentic copy of it, had been before him, observes there as follows:

> After the two archdeacons, the provost, the dean, and the cantor of the church of Reims, the signatures of Henry, abbot of Saint-Remi; Jotselinus, abbot of Hautvillers; Gibbuinus, abbot of Mouzon; Raimbaldus, abbot of Saint-Thierry; and others were appended. “Bruno, chancellor, wrote and subscribed”—the same man, apparently, who not long afterward withdrew from Manasses on account of his deeds and founded the Carthusian order. Attached to the authentic instrument is the seal of Archbishop Manasses, displaying the image of Blessed Mary bearing the child Christ on her left arm, with this inscription: “Manasses, archbishop of Reims.”

Mabillon adds to the abbots who subscribed the charter or instrument in question the names of the monasteries or abbeys over which they presided. I cannot say, however, whether he took these from the original itself—which he may perhaps have had at hand—or from Marlot, whom he cites in the margin. I therefore leave undecided whether these names are correctly attached to the abbots in Marlot, and now inquire into the time when the saint was first made chancellor of Reims.

88. Marlot, so often cited already, writes in volume II, page 134, of the *History of the Metropolitan Church of Reims*:

> A fragment of the *History of France*, which begins with Philip, speaks of Bruno as though he had been born at Reims. But a letter of Manasses, which will immediately be cited, removes the difficulty with these words: “This Bruno was neither born among us nor reborn among us.” He is therefore called a man of Reims, as I conjecture, because he is said to have taught letters with distinction at Reims and was granted the dignity of chancellor on account of his legal expertise, which he continued to exercise under Manasses, as is clear from various charters, especially from the instrument of the foundation of Saint Martin of the Twins in the diocese of Amiens. This instrument was publicly read before King Philip while Manasses was holding a synod at Reims, and Bruno subscribed it as chancellor in the year 1073.

From this passage of Marlot and from the charter just transcribed, dated 1076, the authors of volume IX, page 234, of the *Literary History of France* assert that Bruno served as chancellor of Reims from at least the year 1073 through the year 1076. This is certainly correct, provided that there is no error in the year Marlot gives for Bruno’s subscription to the charter or foundation instrument of Saint Martin of the Twins.

The manuscript treatise on Saint Bruno, which I have already cited several times and which the Carthusians of this place shared with me, gives me serious reason to doubt this point.

89. For at no. 12 it says:

> About the same time as this charter was issued—the charter just recited—Manasses confirmed the foundation of the abbey of Saint Martin of the Twins in the diocese of Amiens, which had been made three years earlier. Bruno added the following confirmatory words to the instrument: “In the seventh year of his episcopate, Archbishop Manasses confirmed it. Sign of Wido, archdeacon; and of Guarinus Waricus, archdeacon; and of Manasses, provost; and of Leuvinus, dean; of Odo, cantor. Bruno, chancellor, wrote.”

If these statements, whose source is not given, accord with the truth, then the charter of the foundation of Saint Martin of the Twins—or rather the instrument by which this foundation was confirmed—must have been issued in the seventh year of Manasses, who did not obtain the see of Reims until 1069. It was therefore not issued in 1073, as Marlot notes in the passage cited—since he seems to be speaking there of the same charter mentioned in the treatise—but in 1075 or 1076.

Perhaps Marlot mistakenly assigned to the year in which the confirmation occurred the year in which the foundation of the monastery of Saint Martin of the Twins took place, three years earlier, as the words of the treatise just cited and again quoted above indicate. Perhaps, too, he had at hand only faulty or untrustworthy documents from which he drew the information he reports concerning this matter.

90. I suspect the latter especially because Marlot writes that the instrument of the foundation—or, more accurately in view of what has been said, of the confirmation—of Saint Martin of the Twins was publicly read before Philip, king of the Franks, while Manasses was holding a synod at Reims. Yet there is no mention whatever, either among the collectors of councils and synods or even in the authors of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, who in volume IX list at least the principal acts of Manasses among the archbishops of Reims, of a synod held at Reims by Manasses in which Philip, king of the Franks, took part.

They do say there, in column 72, that a council was held by Manasses in the city of Reims in 1074 to ratify the unlawful marriage of King Philip and Bertrada. But they do not add that Philip was present. Nor would they assuredly have said that the council—or general synod of the archdiocese of Reims—which Manasses truly held in 1074 was convened to ratify Philip’s marriage to Bertrada if they had considered that this marriage was not contracted before the year 1092 at the earliest.

91. In any event, from all that has now been said it becomes doubtful whether the instrument discussed at length here was granted to the monastery of Saint Martin of the Twins as early as 1073, as Marlot notes, and consequently whether our saint, who subscribed it as chancellor, was already chancellor—as the authors of the *Literary History of France* judged, as noted above—as early as that same year 1073.

Nevertheless, even if this is so, some believe that the saint had held the office of chancellor of Reims before the year 1073 itself. Indeed, Bruno would have held it long before that year if Marlot writes correctly in volume II, page 115, of the *History of the Metropolitan Church of Reims*. There, concerning Gervasius, archbishop of Reims, who died in 1067, he records the following:

> In order to benefit the commonwealth in every way, and especially the commonwealth of letters, Gervasius resolved to make the schools of Reims, which had fallen into decay through age, more illustrious through the work of Saint Bruno of Cologne, who had been raised from childhood in the church of Reims. He appointed him head or director of the schools and added the office of chancellor, which Bruno discharged with distinction until Manasses I, when he himself, trampling underfoot the pomp of dignities, withdrew into the wilderness, as will be said below.

92. Thus far Marlot. He plainly teaches that our saint was made chancellor of the church of Reims by Gervasius, bishop of Reims, and consequently before the year 1068, by which time Gervasius had died—indeed, as early as the year 1056, to which he refers this appointment.

Later, however, Marlot himself brings forward evidence suggesting that Bruno was not appointed to this office so early. First, on page 139 and the two following pages, he transcribes a charter issued by Archbishop Gervasius in 1067, as is noted at the end, for the foundation of the famous monastery of Saint-Denis at Reims; it was written and subscribed by Odericus, the chancellor, who is also found under the variant names Odalricus or Oldaricus.

Then, on pages 166 and following, he cites another charter, granted by a nobleman named Walter in favor of Saint Peter of Rumi, and concluded as follows:

> Publicly enacted at Rumi in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1070, while Alexander was pope at Rome, Philip was reigning as king of the Franks, Manasses was archbishop at Reims, Odo was archdeacon, and Odalricus was chancellor.

Since, therefore, as is clear from these two public instruments produced by Marlot himself, Odalricus was still chancellor of the church of Reims in 1067 and in 1070, the saint certainly did not receive that dignity before 1070, much less before 1067.

93. Indeed, it may not have happened even before 1074. For in the same Marlot, same work and volume, pages 168 and following, there is a charter granted by Manasses, archbishop of Reims, confirming the foundation of the monastery of Morimont in the diocese of Châlons. It ends with these words:

> In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1074, indiction XII, on the Kalends of November, with the first epact, while the venerable King Philip was reigning, I, Odalricus, wrote and subscribed this charter, ratified and confirmed in the general synod of Reims.

Although at that time two men named Odalricus flourished at Reims—one chancellor of the church of Reims, the other provost of the same church and subsequently the first abbot of the monastery of Saint-Denis at Reims, as Marlot records in the same work and volume just cited, page 151—the subscription to the charter granted to the monastery of Morimont appears to belong to Odalricus the provost. For it lacks the title of chancellor, contrary to the custom normally observed in charters written by the chancellors of churches, in which the title is attached to the name of the chancellor.

Nevertheless, it is more probably to be attributed to Odalricus the chancellor, because it was the responsibility of chancellors to write public charters granted by the church whose chancellors they were, whether by its chapter or by its bishop, and to authenticate them by adding their names.
