It could easily have happened that here he neglected to add the title of chancellor to his name, since it was probably not required for the validity of a charter solemnly ratified and confirmed in a general synod of the diocese of Reims.

94. But, whatever may be the case with the charter mentioned here—whose epact, moreover, as given in the preceding paragraph, does not agree with the year according to the ancient computists—the subscription may be understood as follows. Bruno was certainly chancellor of the church of Reims in 1076; and in 1069 he had not yet obtained this dignity. He must therefore unquestionably have first received it either in the year immediately following 1069 or in one of the next six years, while the see of Reims was occupied not by Gervasius but by Manasses.

Although Bruno, for some time, as may readily be gathered from what has already been said, and his successor Godefrid discharged both the duties of scholarch and those of chancellor at Reims, the person who served as scholarch of the church of Reims was not always also its chancellor. For in 1192, when the chancellorship was vacant, Garnerius, as Marlot teaches in volume II, pages 427 and following, held the direction of the schools.

Thus the fact that, according to what was said above, the saint had served as prefect of the schools of Reims long before 1070 cannot be used to infer that he had likewise already been chancellor, contrary to the conclusion just reached. Mabillon seems to have thought otherwise, however. Agreeing with Marlot’s words, transcribed above at no. 91, although he does not cite them, he writes of Bruno in no. 85 of his *Preface to the Second Part of the Sixth Benedictine Century*:

> In that same church of Reims, while Gervasius was bishop, he was made canon, master of the schools, and chancellor.

These, then, are the points that arise concerning both the office of chancellor held by Bruno at Reims and the time when he was first appointed to it.

95. As for the time when he was first enrolled among the canons of the church of Reims, most recent writers believe that this occurred before he took charge of the schools of Reims and therefore long before he served as chancellor. Although this cannot be confirmed by any testimony of antiquity, it nevertheless appears sufficiently probable, if only because no more suitable time seems capable of being assigned for Bruno’s obtaining that honor.

There are also those who maintain that, while the saint was still living at Reims, he served as a preacher of the divine word. They rely, as I believe, partly on the following verse, which is included in the funerary title of the church of Angers, title 166 among those to be reprinted:

> He delivered many sermons throughout the regions.

But who could assert with certainty that this refers to Bruno while he was still living at Reims? Immediately after the verse just quoted, another is added there:

> He passed through the city of Rome and sought the Calabrians.

Surius, however, joins the two verses without punctuation, altering the first slightly, as follows:

> Passing through the regions while delivering many sermons,  
> he passed through the city of Rome and sought the Calabrians.

In any event, it is perhaps not far from the truth that Bruno also occasionally addressed the people at Reims, and likewise that he taught there more sciences than those listed above. Nor do I think there is any doubt that he also explained the sacred Scriptures to his students there. He knew these writings very well, as well as the Greek and Hebrew languages, which contribute greatly to their understanding, as will become clear from the matters to be discussed concerning his commentaries on the Psalms and the epistles of Saint Paul.

### § V. What kind of disciples the saint had, whom he formed no less in good morals than in learning, and what gifts and virtues of soul then shone forth in him

96. That there was a very large number of disciples whom our saint taught, and whom he instructed in letters with wholly desirable success—so that his diligence in imparting these studies shone forth magnificently—is indicated clearly enough by his funerary title 131 in the following verses, of which part reads:

> He was the splendor of speech and the light of religion.  
> His religion is known sufficiently everywhere.  
> Through his teaching so many wise men have been made,  
> whom my mind does not know and my pen is silent to name.

Saint Bruno’s disciples were not merely numerous; several of them also became distinguished by their virtue and moral integrity, as well as by the offices and dignities with which they were later honored. Since the probity and renown of disciples redound, in a certain way, to the glory of their teachers, I wish to list here some of the more illustrious among them as examples.

By far the foremost is Otto or Odo, born of noble stock in Gaul, formerly prior of Cluny, then bishop of Ostia, and finally supreme pontiff, elected in 1088 under the name Urban II. He became especially famous both for the excommunication of Philip, king of the Franks, and Bertrada, his concubine, and for promoting the holy war at the Council of Clermont. That Bruno was once his teacher is shown by the *Chronicle of the First Four Priors of the Carthusian House*, or by the eulogy of the saint transcribed from it at no. 7. The matter should therefore be beyond all controversy, as Ruinart rightly maintains in volume III of the *Posthumous Works*, in the life of this pontiff.

Robert of Burgundy must also be added. Born from the royal lineage of the dukes of Burgundy—specifically, the son of Henry of Burgundy, grandson of King Robert of France—he was promoted to the see of Langres around the year 1085, as the authors of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana* teach in their account of the bishops of Langres. In the funerary title 39, among those to be reprinted, which he dedicated to our saint, Robert himself professes that he had been Bruno’s disciple.

97. To these I add Lambert, abbot of the monastery of Pultaria on the Seine belonging to the Order of Saint Benedict; Peter, likewise abbot of the regular canons of Saint John in the Vines near Soissons; and Mainard, prior and subsequently abbot of the monastery of Cormery or Cormaric in the territory of Tours when the encyclical letter announcing the death of Saint Bruno was delivered to him. All three likewise profess in their funerary titles—numbers 45, 79, and 176, which they dedicated to the saint—that they had been his disciples.

I shall show below that these three abbots, as well as Robert, bishop of Langres, and Urban, supreme pontiff, had no teacher other than Bruno at Reims, when I inquire whether, after resigning the prefecture of the schools of Reims around 1076 or the following year, and before withdrawing into the desert of the Carthusian house, the saint taught letters at Paris.

For now I shall show only that they were all distinguished in virtue; this is evidence that they were formed by Bruno not only in letters but also in good morals. First, as regards Urban, that this is in accordance with the truth is demonstrated sufficiently and more than sufficiently by the life of this most celebrated pontiff, written by Ruinart and included in volume III of the posthumous works of that author and of Mabillon.

As for Robert, bishop of Langres, and the three abbots just mentioned—Lambert, Peter, and Mainard—Robert, after fulfilling all the duties of an excellent shepherd in governing his diocese, brought his approximately twenty-five-year administration to an end by a most devout death, as is clear from what the authors of the enlarged *Christian Gaul* report concerning this praiseworthy bishop in volume IV, column 566.

98. Although Lambert was abbot of his monastery at Pultaria, he nevertheless calls himself its servant and humble steward in the funerary title 45, which he composed in honor of our saint. From this, certainly, his great humility shines forth.

Peter, abbot of the regular canons of Saint John in the Vines near Soissons, uses the following words, among others, in the saint’s funerary title 79, addressed to the Carthusian hermits of Calabria:

> To the beloved brothers in Christ and worthy of God, the reverend hermits of Calabria, serving God in the monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin, Peter, humble abbot of the regular canons of Saint John of Soissons, and the entire community of brothers living and serving God there: may you have begun well, persevere better, and bring your work happily to completion.  
>   
> Having heard of the blessed death of your holy father and my teacher Bruno, from whose mouth I was often permitted to drink the streams of sound doctrine, although I did not complete the work in practice, we are deeply saddened by his absence. Yet we rejoice even more deeply that he has escaped bodily constraints, attained rest, and lives with God, insofar as we are able to form such a judgment from the purity and perfection of his life, which was sufficiently known to us.  
>   
> We therefore promise to commemorate him in this way: for thirty days we shall have Masses celebrated, both because he was our teacher and because we trust in his prayers and yours, which are all the more effective before God the holier they are, etc.

99. By this method of writing, this man—worthy of the highest praise—clearly displayed the utmost modesty and humility of spirit, as may rightly be inferred from the Calendar of Saint Gervasius, which records the following about him under 21 March in Claudius d’Ormay’s *History of Suession*, vol. II, book V, chapter 13:

> “Peter, abbot of Saint John, died: a man of complete integrity, in every respect praiseworthy before God and the world, and celebrated in memory.”

Mainardus, prior and later abbot of Cormery, speaks thus to the Calabrian Carthusians in the funeral title that he composed for the Saint:

> “I certainly rejoiced at the glorious death of so great a man—Bruno—but because I had an unremitting intention of going to him shortly, seeing and hearing him, pouring out all the emotions of my soul upon him, and, together with you under his leadership, obeying the Holy Trinity, I was so disturbed by his unexpected departure that I could not restrain the reins of my tears, which flowed forth of their own accord. I, Mainardus, then, was born in the city of Reims and was, in the monastery of Cormery, prior of many monks in title, though not in fact. For several years I listened to the teaching of this lord Bruno and, by God’s will, made very considerable progress,” and so forth.

100. These words plainly show the extremely strong inclination of mind that possessed him to visit Saint Bruno and follow in his footsteps, had Bruno remained alive longer. It also seems beyond doubt that a man who had so strongly directed his will toward the austere and holy way of life taught by Bruno, once his teacher, diligently cultivated his soul through the practice of virtue. Such were Saint Bruno’s disciples, whom he very probably instructed no less in virtue and moral integrity than in the perishable sciences of the world. The monks of Saint Dionysius at Reims may perhaps have alluded especially to this method by which the Saint taught when, in their funeral title—number 61 among those being reprinted—they sang of Bruno:

> Like four springs flowing from a single source,  
> which Paradise possesses and sends streaming through the realms of the world,  
> so he overflows upon the earth, adorning those whom he instructed;  
> he fills, forms, kindles, directs, arms,  
> forges, enlightens, and still governs, cultivates, and equips them.  
> He was like a star to all whom he himself taught.

101. The Saint did not make his disciples eagerly absorb both doctrine and virtue merely through words that breathed them forth; his outstanding moral integrity and the rare virtues that then shone in him contributed greatly to this as well. His moral integrity, by which Bruno at that time made himself conspicuous, is celebrated in funeral title 66, belonging to the cathedral church of Saint Mary of Laon in the archdiocese of Reims, in these words:

> Bruno, glory of the clergy and wisdom of the world,  
> while he lived on earth, flourished in keenness of mind;  
> while he was among us, he flourished also in instruction.  
> Integrity of character completed the accumulation of honors.

Funeral titles 29 and 31 likewise bear upon this. In the former, belonging to Holy Cross and Saint Faron of Meaux, the Saint is adorned with these verses:

> Bruno, the wise hermit, was well known for his learning  
> and for his blessed character and life;  
> he shone in the first principles and in the highest and lowest matters,  
> and afterward became a monk.

In the latter, written by the church of Saint Mary of Chartres, he is honored with these epithets:

> Just, sincere, severe in the gravity of his character.

102. As for the virtues that then distinguished him, an anonymous Carthusian, who wrote the fourth book of his Order’s *Annals*, hitherto unpublished and in my possession, sets before us these virtues, together with the remarkable qualities of mind by which the Saint then shone, drawing them from various funeral titles. He writes:

> “The qualities that shone forth in Bruno and may especially be noted are wisdom, eloquence, gravity free from pride, gentleness and integrity of character, irreproachable learning, and finally an exemplary life, after the pattern of which all good men would not hesitate to fashion themselves and order their conduct. I wish briefly to touch upon a summary of these virtues from his same funeral titles—not, indeed, the virtues that shone more abundantly and perfectly in him after his conversion, but only those virtues by which, while he still remained in the world, he illuminated it.”

Having prefaced his discussion thus, he immediately addresses the subject itself. I transcribe his words here, adding the numbers of the funeral titles he cites, by which each is distinguished in the edition. Thus they read:

> “His wisdom, learning, and exemplary life are commended by title 112 of Saint Peter of Neocastro in these brief but vigorous verses:”

> In whatever district he lived, while alive he remained an image  
> of true justice, learning, and philosophy.

103. And in title 31 of the church of Saint Mary of Chartres:

> Bruno was an unshaken wall of the Church,  
> for he was good and possessed a devout mind,  
> and he was a true teacher of wisdom, and so forth.

Later, in the school-verses of title 32, these qualities are not merely proclaimed; testimony is also given to the greatness of his spirit, when it says:

> He was the flower of the Fathers, the comfort and glory of the brethren,  
> a follower of truth, a lover of divine law,  
> the path of justice, the source and fountainhead of wisdom,  
> the light and mirror of the world, the sublime summit of things,  
> the staff of the fallen, the sweet relief of the wretched.  
> His mind was neither broken by misfortunes nor excessively elated by prosperity.

Title 150 of the church of Saint Mary of Bayeux likewise supports this:

> Comfort of the brethren, lover of holy virtue,  
> just reformer of morals, pious hope of the wretched,  
> ruler of justice, guardian everywhere of what is good;  
> adorned in character, a vessel full of devotion,  
> bravely armed with the shield of true integrity.

104. But no one commended his wisdom as highly as Lambert, abbot of Saint Nicholas of Angers, who speaks thus in his title 131:

> … Bruno’s wisdom shone forth with such brilliance  
> that among the stars of the Franks he alone  
> was the flower of all and the fountain of philosophers:  
> he was a beautiful flower and a deep fountain.  
> From him such wisdom flowed throughout the world  
> that those whom he instructed he made philosophers.

Although the sublimity of his intellect can become known from the books that he wrote before his conversion, the titles of various churches also testify to it. Among them, title 66 of Saint Mary of Laon contains the following:

> Bruno, glory of the clergy and wisdom of the world,  
> while he lived on earth, flourished in keenness of mind;  
> while he was among us, he flourished also in instruction.

105. In title 173 of the church of Blessed Vincent at Niort he is called an incomparable philosopher, and the following is added:

> “For who would not be astonished—or rather, who would not groan from the depths of his heart—on hearing that such a man, the light and foundation of all knowledge and almost all the clergy, had yielded to nature?””

Writing similar things, Nauclerus, in his *Chronographia* (vol. II, generation 37), called Blessed Bruno a most distinguished teacher of philosophy and Sacred Scripture, and the most eloquent teacher of the scholars at Paris—whether Bruno ever taught there I shall investigate below.

Lest anyone suppose that this holy teacher lacked an educated tongue with which he could sustain the weary by a word, let him consider title 64 of the holy martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris, where we read:

> Such was the power of this Teacher’s heart and mouth  
> that throughout the whole world he surpassed all other masters.  
> All wisdom gave itself to him and took its seat in him,  
> a rich guest in the hidden chambers of his inmost being.  
> What I say I know; France too knows it with me,  
> and the whole world knows it through its four regions.

106. He taught others not only by the word—which would have been a small thing—but also by example, as we learn from certain titles. Thus we read in title 120 of the church of Saint-Omer:

> You were accustomed to be an example for wretched mortals,  
> so that they might worship Christ, whom you, Bruno, always worshiped.

And in title 124 of Saint Mary of Arras:

> Bruno, guide and source of the right way,  
> taught people to live no differently from the way he himself strove to live.

Thus far the anonymous Carthusian whom I have cited. Although in all the funeral titles he praises there may not always be an allusion to the virtues and rare qualities of mind of which the Saint gave examples while he was still carrying out the office of teaching and had not yet renounced the world, there is no doubt that this is the case in most of them, as will be clear to anyone who considers the matter. In any event, it seems highly probable that while the Saint was still serving at Reims as head or director of the schools, he shone forth in various examples of virtue and thereby partly induced his disciples to embrace these virtues as well.

107. This is suggested both by the exceptional courage with which, as we shall see below, he opposed the wicked conduct of Archbishop Manasses, even disregarding the loss of rank and fortune, and by a letter written in 1067 or the following year to Gregory VII, the supreme pontiff, by Hugh, bishop of Die and legate of the Apostolic See. In that letter, which will be mentioned several times below, Hugh speaks as follows about another Manasses, provost of the church of Reims, and about our Saint, who at that time had not long since relinquished the direction of the schools of Reims and had not yet withdrawn into the desert:

> “We commend Manasses … our friend in Christ, who in the Council of Clermont resigned into our hands the provostship of the church of Reims, which he had acquired improperly, to the grace of Your Holiness as a sincere defender of the Catholic faith; and we commend Lord Bruno, master of the church of Reims in all uprightness. Both are worthy to be confirmed by you, with your authority, in the things that belong to God, since they have been deemed worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus. Therefore, employ them as advisers who will advance the cause of God and as fellow workers in the regions of France.”

The same anonymous Carthusian, whom I have just cited, indicates in section 104 that books were written by the Saint before his conversion—that is, before he abandoned all the perishable things of the world and withdrew into the desert. But since this is not sufficiently certain, I shall examine whether the matter is so or otherwise only when I discuss the life that the Saint led in the Calabrian desert and the two letters certainly written there by him. Thus, in one and the same place, I shall discuss all the works that either belong to the Saint or are attributed to him.

§ VI. He opposes the wicked designs of his archbishop, Manasses; on this occasion he suffers much and resolves to become a monk.

108. When Gervasius, archbishop of Reims—a man who had rendered great service to his church in many respects, and especially because he had made the schools of Reims, previously famous and illustrious, still more famous and illustrious through Bruno’s work—had been taken from this life in 1067, Manasses obtained, or rather invaded, the archiepiscopal see left vacant by his death through simony. He was distinguished by the nobility of his birth, not by the adornment of virtue. In an old manuscript codex from Reims he is found called Manasses of Gournay, as the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana* testify in volume IX, column 71.

Although he had not entered the sheepfold through the door, he nevertheless conducted himself at the beginning of his promotion and consecration, which took place in 1069, in such a way that, if not in every respect, at least in many, he fulfilled the office of a true shepherd. At that time he is known to have repeatedly defended the rights of the Church with great zeal and to have acted generously toward monasteries, as is reported both by Marlot, volume II of his *History of the Metropolitan Church of Reims*, pages 165 and following, and by the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana* in the place just cited. Nor did that simoniacal prelate at that time provoke the hatred of all good men against himself, although meanwhile he may have treated some of them unjustly. On the contrary, he seems to have taken care to earn the goodwill even of men distinguished by seriousness of character and virtue.

109. Our Saint is evidence of how true this is. As can easily be inferred from what has been said above, Manasses either himself advanced Bruno to the office of chancellor of the church of Reims, which had become vacant through Odalric’s death, or worked to have him advanced by the canons of his church. He may have done so because he had observed in the Saint the extensive learning and moral integrity especially required for the worthy exercise of that office; or because he desired above all to secure for himself the friendship of Bruno, a man of the highest renown and great authority in the city of Reims, lest he should someday find him opposed to the wicked plans that he may already have been turning over in his mind.

For his part, the Saint seems to have remained attached to Manasses, with a mind not wholly hostile, for as long as Manasses’ actions and conduct permitted this. It is also quite plausible that, through his counsel, Bruno meanwhile induced a man of ruined conscience to perform some good deeds and refrain from the evils he was contemplating. But as Manasses grew worse day by day, selling ecclesiastical benefices, plundering sacred furnishings, unjustly excommunicating many, and attempting either to seize or actually seizing the property of clerics, churches, and abbeys—in short, behaving as a wolf rather than a shepherd—our Saint openly made himself his opponent, perhaps especially because the simoniacal promotion of the man to the see of Reims, of which Bruno had previously been unaware, had at last become clear to him.

Since, however, if he had remained longer at Reims in opposition to Manasses, he would certainly have been exposed to considerable danger, it is highly probable that he left Reims, together with the dignity he held there and several of the more distinguished clerics of the church of Reims, both to withdraw from danger and to avoid being compelled to witness the impious deeds of a man whom he could not prevent.

110. Guibert of Nogent, in his *Life*, book I, chapter 11, either explicitly teaches nearly all this or at least allows it to be inferred. Hear how he argues there:

> “A certain Manasses,” he says, “after the death of Gervasius, the most renowned archbishop, intruded himself by simony into the government of that city—namely, Reims. He was indeed a noble man, but possessed none at all of that serenity which is the first adornment of nobility. For he had conceived such arrogance from this new position that he seemed to imitate the royal majesties—or rather the ferocity of the majesties—of foreign peoples.”

After inserting a few matters that do not concern us here, he continues:

> “This Manasses, then, being exceedingly fond of soldiers and neglectful of the clergy, is reported once to have said: ‘The archbishopric of Reims would be a good one if it were not necessary to have Masses sung there.’ Since every honorable person detested his thoroughly wicked character and utterly foolish behavior, Bruno, then highly renowned among the churches of Gaul, left the city with certain other noble clerics of Reims, out of hatred for that infamous man”—namely, the city of Reims.

So Guibert. At the very time when, as Guibert says, the Saint abandoned the city of Reims out of hatred—whether because he himself was driven not so much against his bishop as against the bishop’s utterly wicked conduct, or because the bishop himself regarded him as an enemy—he very probably, indeed almost certainly, renounced the direction of the great schools, or headship of the schools, and the office of chancellor. Or, if one prefers, he was stripped by Manasses of all his dignities and thereby lost them.

111. About what year did this departure of the Saint from the city of Reims take place, and which of the more distinguished clerics of the church of Reims accompanied him? Where did he first go? To answer each of these questions in order: Bruno certainly did not move away from Reims before 1076, nor after the year immediately following it; he therefore unquestionably did so either in 1076 or the following year.

That he did not leave Reims before 1076 is clear from a charter granted by Manasses at Reims in that very year in favor of the abbey of Saint-Basle and transcribed above, which ends as follows:

> “Bruno, chancellor, wrote and subscribed.”

That the departure did not occur after 1077 is evident from the fact that in that year, at the Council of Autun, and most probably also at Clermont, which preceded it, he accused Manasses, archbishop of Reims, of simony and other crimes, as we shall soon see. It is very probable that he did not do this before leaving the city of Reims in opposition to Manasses, as is suggested both by the grave danger to which he would otherwise have exposed himself before a prelate inflamed and uncontrolled by anger, and by the subsequent course of events. From that course it becomes highly probable, indeed certain, that after accusing Manasses at the Council of Autun, our Saint did not return to the city of Reims until Manasses had been deposed at the Council of Lyon in 1080, as anyone may easily infer from what will be said below.

112. Let us now turn to the more distinguished clerics who, opposing Manasses along with the Saint, departed from the city of Reims. It seems very likely that among them were Radulfus Viridis, to whom the Saint wrote a letter from the Calabrian desert that will be mentioned repeatedly below, and Fulcius Monoculus, who is mentioned in the same letter. This seems especially likely because of the conversation that, according to that letter, he held with them concerning the perishable pleasures of this world and the everlasting joys of heaven, on the occasion—as is acknowledged by almost everyone—of the great sufferings that the church of Reims was enduring at the hands of Archbishop Manasses.

It is certain that Manasses, then provost of the church of Reims, and a certain Pontius accompanied the Saint when he departed from the city of Reims, since both of them, together with Bruno, were accusers of the simoniacal prelate at the Council of Autun and elsewhere. This Bruno himself partly declares in his *Apology*, published by Mabillon in volume I, part II of the *Museum Italicum*, page 121, which I have already cited more than once above and shall cite several times below; the matter will also become clear from what follows.

As for the place to which the Saint withdrew when he left Reims, some infer that he went to Paris. Among these, Bulaeus is especially prominent. Inclining also toward the view that the Saint then devoted himself to teaching at Paris, he writes in volume I of his *History of Paris*, page 468:

> “From this passage of Guibert, already transcribed above, it is clear that Bruno, having left Reims, moved elsewhere with certain other noble clerics of the church of Reims. Although Guibert does not name these companions, we understand from Bruno’s own letter to Radulfus Viridis, provost of Reims, that these three friends departed together: Bruno, Radulfus, and Fulcius Monoculus.”

113. For he writes as follows:

> “Your affection remembers that, when I, you, and Fulcius Monoculus were together one day in a little garden adjoining the house of Adam, where I was then staying, we discussed false pleasures.”

> “Therefore Bruno was then staying with Adam, certainly not at Reims. For since he was a canon of the church of Reims and a teacher, it is not likely that he would have remained in someone else’s lodging. Hence I infer that Bruno came to Paris with these two friends, chose Adam’s house as his lodging, and then resumed the profession of teaching. Perhaps this was Adam the Parisian canon, who became cantor of the same church after Gualeramus around the year 1100 and held that office beyond 1123.”

So Bulaeus. Yet although, as I shall show below, it is highly probable that Bruno’s letter to Radulfus Viridis does not concern lodging in which he had been received by Adam at Reims, it by no means follows that, when he discussed false pleasures of the world with Radulfus Viridis and Fulcius Monoculus in the passage quoted by Bulaeus, the Saint was staying with Adam in Paris. Why could he not at that time have lodged somewhere outside the city of Reims just as well as in Paris? Nor does anything follow from what Bulaeus adds about Adam, a Parisian canon, since at that time other men—or even, if one wishes, several canons—could have flourished elsewhere who were likewise named Adam.

114. In order somehow to prove that the Saint went immediately to Paris when he left Reims, Bulaeus also adds to the words just quoted:

> “The Guibert cited above supports this, for when writing about his—that is, Saint Bruno’s—conversion, he says: ‘There was, not long before these days, a certain Bruno in the city of Reims, a man trained in the liberal arts and director of great studies, who is known to have found the beginnings of his conversion through the occasion described below.’”

> “By these words he seems to indicate that Bruno was director both of the Parisian and of the Reims schools, which Aimoinus, the monk of Fleury, in the *Life of Abbo*, calls the greater workshops of wisdom or learning.”

But why could the Saint not have been called by Guibert director of great studies because at Reims he presided over both philosophical studies and theological studies, which are the greater or higher sciences? Certainly that Guibert did not call him director of great studies in the sense suggested by Bulaeus is clear from the fact that, in the very words produced by Bulaeus, the same writer indicates that Bruno exercised that office not at Paris but at Reims, as will be evident to anyone who considers the passage.

Moreover, even if I granted that Guibert called the Saint director of great studies in the sense intended by Bulaeus, would it follow that, when the Saint left Reims, he immediately became director of great studies at Paris and therefore went there directly after departing from the city of Reims? No one, I think, would assert this.

115. Indeed, it is highly probable that when the Saint left Reims to avoid Manasses, he withdrew not to Paris but to Reciacum—also called Roceium, Rocus, Roscium, or even Rauciacum, for it is named differently by different writers—a fortified and famous castle of French Champagne on the Aisne, as may be seen in Marlot’s *History of the Metropolitan Church of Reims*, volume II, page 195, and in Valesius’s *Description of Gaul* under the entry “Rauciacum.”

This seems probable to me for two reasons. First, Manasses, provost of the church of Reims, and others who adhered to him—and therefore also our Saint—were in 1078 under the protection of Count Ebalus in the aforementioned castle, as can be inferred from a letter of Archbishop Manasses himself to Pope Gregory VII, written in 1078, which will be partly quoted below in section 123. I find no other count named Ebalus to whom this could apply.

Second, Ebalus, the lord or local ruler of that same castle, where he too apparently had established his residence, stood entirely on the side of the clerics of Reims and therefore of our Saint against Manasses, the simoniacal archbishop of Reims. For, as is likewise understood from the same letter, when Archbishop Manasses appealed to the supreme pontiff against the sentence pronounced against him in 1077 by Hugh, bishop of Die and legate of the Apostolic See, at the Council of Autun, and in fact went to Rome to defend his case there, Ebalus also went to Rome to protect Manasses the provost and the other clerics who had fled the city of Reims against the archbishop’s machinations.

Thus it has now been established, at least to some extent, both with whom and approximately in what year our Saint departed from the city of Reims, and also where he then withdrew. Let us now continue the sequence of events to be discussed.

116. Among the various councils held in the Saint’s time against the simoniacs and against investitures received from laymen, mention must here be made of the council that Hugh of Die, legate of the Apostolic See in Gaul, held at Clermont. There, as Hugh of Flavigny reports in the *Verdun Chronicle*, preserved by Labbeus in volume I of the *New Manuscript Library*, page 201, he pronounced a sentence of excommunication against Stephen, the invader of the church of Le Puy.

Gregory, who in 1073—the year during which the pontifical indiction XI ran from January to the end of December—had been raised to the supreme see of the Church, later confirmed this sentence in two different letters, one to the canons of Le Puy and the other to the bishops of Gaul, as may be seen in Labbeus, volume X of the *Councils*, column 164. Both letters were written on the same day, namely the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifteenth indiction.

Since this latter chronological indication, as is clear from what has already been said about the year in which Gregory obtained the pontificate, designates the year 1077, it follows that the aforementioned council held by Hugh of Die at Clermont was most probably celebrated either at the beginning of 1077 itself or toward the end of the immediately preceding year.

From the castle of Reciacum, where, according to what has already been said, he was then staying with Bruno and others, Manasses, provost of the church of Reims, presented himself at this council. There, before the hands of Hugh the legate, as the letter of Hugh that will be transcribed below makes clear, he resigned the principal dignity of the church of Reims, improperly acquired from the simoniacal archbishop Manasses around 1076.

117. It further appears probable that Bruno and the other clerics of the church of Reims who had moved with him to Reciacum also attended this council and presented to it the charges they held against Manasses, archbishop of Reims. It also seems likely that the council decreed that Manasses should be summoned to the next council in order to clear himself of the charges brought against him.

The opportunity for this soon arose. For Gregory, the supreme pontiff, in a letter dated the fourth day before the Ides of May, in the fifteenth indiction—which, as I have already said, designates the year 1077—instructed Hugh, his legate in Gaul, to assemble a synod of the bishops of France and carefully examine the case of Gerard, the elected bishop of Cambrai. After his legitimate election, Gerard had received investiture from King Henry, being unaware both that the latter was excommunicated and that the pontiff had forbidden anyone to receive investiture from lay princes.

The pope also instructed Hugh to settle the cases of certain other churches of Gaul and such affairs as seemed to him conducive to the benefit of those churches or of the universal Church, summoning Hugh, abbot of Cluny, to the synod on behalf of the church of Auvergne. Hugh obeyed the pontiff’s command, summoned the council at Autun, and celebrated it there in that same year, 1077, in which the pope had written the aforementioned letter to him.

118. This is expressly reported by Hugh of Flavigny, a contemporary author whose account cannot be convicted of error here. In the *Verdun Chronicle*, preserved by Labbeus in volume I of the *New Manuscript Library*, page 199, he writes:

> “In accordance, therefore, with these apostolic commands”—given by Pope Gregory to Hugh of Die in the letter just mentioned—“a synod of venerable Fathers was assembled at Autun under the guardianship and protection of Christ the Lord … in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1077, where many illustrious men from France and Burgundy gathered.”

Manasses, provost of the church of Reims, and our Saint, together with the other clerics of Reims who had withdrawn with them from Reims to Reciacum, attended this council and accused their archbishop Manasses of simony and other crimes. When he had been summoned to the council but neglected to appear, scorning the warnings and commands of the legate, a sentence of suspension was pronounced against him as a contumacious person.

Manasses soon appealed from this sentence to the pontiff, as it appears, and, meanwhile burning for revenge until he could reach Rome, laid many ambushes along the road for the canons of the church of Reims—his accusers—when they were returning from the council to Reciacum, as is evident from what has already been said above and will be said below. He broke open their houses at Reims, sold their prebends, and plundered their property.

Hear Hugh of Flavigny explain these events in his own words in the place just cited:

> “At the same council”—namely, the Council of Autun—“the simoniacal invader Manasses of the church of Reims was accused by the clerics of Reims and suspended from office, because, having been summoned to the council to clear himself, he did not come. When he had prepared many ambushes for the canons of the church of Reims, his accusers, as they were returning from the council, he eventually broke open their houses, sold their prebends, and plundered their property.”

119. So Hugh. That this is entirely consistent with the truth is also clear from a letter sent to Pope Gregory by Hugh the legate after the council had been held, when he had heard of the various injuries that Manasses had inflicted upon Bruno and the other canons of the church of Reims returning from it. In that letter he declares that our Saint and Manasses the provost “had been deemed worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus,” evidently, indeed unquestionably, alluding to the injuries that both had suffered, on the road and at Reims in their property, when returning from the Council of Autun to Reciacum.

Because that letter also proves conclusively what I asserted above concerning the attendance of Manasses, provost of the church of Reims, at the Council of Clermont or Auvergne, and contains other material concerning this matter—especially concerning Archbishop Manasses—I transcribe it here in the mutilated form in which it survives in Labbeus, volume X of the *Councils*, columns 365 and following. It reads:

> “To the most reverend Father and lord, Pope Gregory, Hugo, the most unworthy servant of His Holiness, humble priest of Die: greetings. Since we have learned that your R., the Parisian, has returned—he whom we had instructed to report faithfully to you, as your son, the proceedings of the Council of Autun, which he attended, but who neither returned through us nor wrote anything to us about your condition—we ask Your Paternity kindly to write us your judgment concerning the appointment of the churches of Reims, Bourges, and Chartres.”

120. “Let Your Paternity also know that the man called bishop of Noyon, whom we privately pressed under threat of a public examination, confessed his simony to us in the presence of the bishops of Laon and Langres and certain others. He also confirmed to us by oath upon the holy Gospels that, when he had seen your letters or your legation, he would properly relinquish the church that he had wrongfully occupied and would assist, to the best of his ability and understanding, in its being ordered according to God.

“The bishop of Senlis, after receiving investiture from the hand of the king, was ordained by that Reims heresiarch”—he means Manasses, the simoniacal bishop, or rather invader, of the church of Reims—“whom by your letters you forbade to receive men of this kind as bishops. The bishop of Auxerre, ordained before the proper years, did not receive investiture from the hand of the king, although he obtained the king’s favor through the king’s intimates.

“As for the archbishop of Sens, how great an insult and injury he inflicted upon Your Authority during my legation, you have, I hope, heard sufficiently from the aforementioned R. Nor, God is my witness, do I seek my own glory in saying this.

“The bishop of Bordeaux, too, because he was summoned in the preceding year to the Council of Auvergne but neither came nor offered a canonical excuse, was suspended from episcopal office at that same council. Disregarding this, he usurped the office from which he had been forbidden. Summoned again to the Council of Autun, because he sent us no explanation, we also suspended him from the priesthood.”

121. “Concerning all these matters, therefore, we ask Your Greatness to write to our lowliness what you have judged and what you wish us to do.

“Furthermore, we earnestly request that you send us the pallium through Bishop Valentine, in order to confirm the appointment of the most religious archbishop of the church of Lyon, against the barking heretics and those who, in their fleshly pride over the king’s indignation at God’s appointment, boast against it.

“For he himself would most devoutly present himself before Your Holiness, setting aside every inconvenience and danger of poverty and travel, if the church entrusted to him—so long sick and deprived of the comfort of its shepherd—could in any way endure his absence without great harm. Give instructions to Bishop Valentine and receive security from him in your hand, so that around the feast of Saint John the Baptist, as we have agreed with him, his church may receive him to celebrate the office, since he seems highly suitable for opposing the arrogance of the provincials.

“We commend Manasses, our friend in Christ, who in the Council of Clermont resigned into our hands the provostship of the church of Reims, improperly acquired, to the grace of Your Holiness as a sincere defender of the Catholic faith; and we commend Lord Bruno, master of the church of Reims in all uprightness. Both are worthy to be confirmed by you, with your authority, in the things that belong to God, since they have been deemed worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus. Therefore, employ them as advisers who will advance the cause of God and as fellow workers in the regions of France.”

### 122.

“The deposition of the heretic of Rheims, con… [Col. 0072D] revealed iniquity, the blood of heaven, and … cries out; strengthen [it] by a written declaration of your authority … these men, we ask, send to the Church of Rheims … his satisfaction, or command that he himself, if he is unwilling … or that it be received by us. Because … they made an episcopal election without consulting you, contrary to your excommunication. Your son Tiezo would already have returned to you, unless he were being detained to summon the council to be celebrated at Poitiers, God willing, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February. At that council we humbly entreat that the patronage of your merits be present for us. Pray for us, most holy Father.”

Such is the letter sent by Hugh of Die to the supreme pontiff after the Council of Autun, apparently in 1077 or, at the latest, at the beginning of the following year. From it, what I stated above both concerning the injuries inflicted on Saint Bruno by Manasses the archbishop and concerning the presence of this Manasses and of the provost at the Council of Clermont is most firmly confirmed.

Let us now pursue the sequence of events. Bruno and the Rheims clerics who were his companions, having avoided the ambushes which Manasses the archbishop had laid for them as they returned from the Council of Autun, withdrew once again to Count Ebalus’s castle at Reciacum, from which they had gone to that council, there to await the outcome of the very serious litigation pending between themselves and their archbishop.

### 123.

I infer this because Manasses the archbishop, in the letter cited above which he sent to Pope Gregory VII and which Labbe prints in volume X of the Councils, column 363, speaks as follows:

“Concerning Count Ebalus, who was attempting to accuse me in your presence and was commending himself and his loyalty to you with deceptive words, you have ample opportunity to recognize whose loyalty toward you appears the more sincere: whether mine, who am prepared to obey God and you in all things, or his, who, both through Manasses and his followers received in his castle, persecutes blessed Mary.

“For Manasses, of whom we have spoken, to whom, at your command, we granted pardon for what he had committed against us, provided that he returned to his mother Church, oppressed by the consciousness of his crime, neither wishes to return to you nor to be reconciled to the peace of the Church. Rather, with those followers of his, since he cannot do so by deeds, he does not cease to tear the Church and me apart by words and curses.

“Therefore, leaving aside this Ebalus, against whom, I believe, you are exercising a just and apostolic judgment, I earnestly beseech Your Holiness concerning Manasses: either command him to return to his own place and no longer attack the Church, or direct against him and his supporters and collaborators the punishment of apostolic severity. Deign also to write a suitable letter to those who receive them, so that they may either not retain them contrary to the rights of the Church or acknowledge that they have been punished by the same sentence.”

From these words it will be clear to anyone who considers them that Manasses the provost and those adhering to him, one of whom was our Saint, remained with Count Ebalus in the castle of Reciacum, or Rauciacum, certainly at the time when this letter was written by Manasses the archbishop—something which, as I shall show below, occurred in 1078. Since this is so, they had very probably withdrawn there in 1077, on returning from the Council of Autun, in order to evade the snares of Manasses the archbishop.

### 124.

From the words of Manasses’s letter just quoted we learn not only what I have now set out, but also that Count Ebalus, or Oebalus, who protected Saint Bruno and his companions against Manasses the archbishop in his castle, acted at Rome as their accuser before Pope Gregory. I shall explain how this happened.

Manasses the archbishop, who, as I showed above, had probably appealed to the supreme pontiff from the sentence passed against him at the Council of Autun, went to Rome in 1078, after letters had been delivered to him—as Hugh of Flavigny testifies in the passage cited immediately above—“to purge himself in a council” (that is, in another council to be held again in Gaul) “with six bishops.” Count Ebalus, having heard of the departure and purpose of the simoniacal prelate, likewise set out for Rome, so that there he might defend the cause of the Rheims clerics whom he had received into his castle and under his protection; several of them accompanied him.

That Pontius was among these is made certain by the frequently cited *Apology* of Manasses the archbishop, in Mabillon, volume I, part II of the *Museum Italicum*, page 121. It appears probable, however, that Fulcius Monoculus was also among them. First, that Fulcius mentioned by Saint Bruno went to Rome—as the very letter itself makes clear—immediately after the conversation held with Bruno and Radulphus Viridis concerning the false delights of the world and the true joys of heaven, in which they decided to assume the monastic habit. Second, this seems to have happened after the Council of Autun, in 1077 or the following year, and nowhere other than in the castle of Reciacum.

### 125.

To establish this, insofar as possible, I shall first transcribe here the words in which Saint Bruno recalls that conversation. They read:

“Your love remembers that one day, when you and I and Fulcius Monoculus were together in the little garden adjoining the house of Adam, where I was then staying as a guest, we discussed for some time, as I think, the false pleasures and perishable riches of this world, as well as the joys of everlasting glory. Inflamed by divine love, we therefore promised and vowed to the Holy Spirit that we would soon abandon the fleeting things of the world and pursue the eternal, and that we would also receive the monastic habit. This would in fact have been carried out shortly afterward, unless Fulcius had then gone to Rome; we postponed its fulfillment until his return. While he was delayed, and other causes intervened, divine love grew weak, the spirit cooled, and the fervor vanished.”

When Saint Bruno therefore held the conversation mentioned here, in which he vowed to become a monk, with Radulphus Viridis and Fulcius, he was staying not at home but in another person’s lodging. It follows from this that he certainly did not have this conversation at Rheims before he left that city, together with Manasses and other Rheims clerics, around 1076.

For it does not seem likely that Bruno was then living in another person’s house at Rheims, where he was not only a canon but also a teacher and chancellor, as Bulaeus correctly argues from the words quoted in section 113. Indeed, as the author of the *Treatise on Saint Bruno*, communicated to me by the Carthusians of this place, correctly observes in section 20 of his work, there can be no doubt that Saint Bruno then had a residence appropriate to his dignity as chancellor, canon, and teacher—indeed in the common cloister itself, which the canons of Rheims used both long before and long after Saint Bruno’s time. This may properly be gathered from Flodoard, *History of Rheims*, book II, chapter 11; the *Chronicle of Mouzon* in D’Achery, volume VII of the *Spicilegium*; and Letter 160 of Stephen of Tournai to Radulphus, dean of Rheims, distinct from Radulphus Viridis, written around 1176 or, as appears, not very long afterward.

### 126.

I transcribe here the relevant words of Stephen, from which it is chiefly understood that the canons of Rheims led a common life in the cloister in Bruno’s time, from the already frequently cited but hitherto unpublished fourth book of the *Annals of the Carthusians*. They read:

“A report has gone around among many that some of you are attempting to alter the ancient footsteps of the Fathers, practices established by holy councils and observed for a long time by the glorious Church of Rheims, and are striving by a certain singularity to erase, cast down, and trample upon the golden plate of religious custom which shines, fixed upon the forehead of the metropolitan Church, for all who are in the kingdom.

“By a singular privilege, the see of Rheims stood out among the other Churches of Gaul, persevering with the Apostles in the communion of bread and prayer, and, in social communion, preferring sacramental communion; it was a spectacle to the greater and an example to the lesser.

“From the remnants of the regular institutions they had retained two places for themselves: the dining hall and the sleeping quarters. In the one they followed disciplined abstinence; in the other they observed spotless continence … In these and other regular observances the Church of Rheims proceeded, terrible like an army arranged for battle, beloved by its own and admired by outsiders.

“If these things begin to be altered, what will its sister Germany say, equal to it in place and order? Among the other ecclesiastical institutions, Germany still observes the fraternal communion of eating and repose in such a way that it does not admit modern dissolution?”

### 127.

Since, then, as it is easy to infer from these words, the canons of Rheims in the age of our Saint led a common life in buildings that were separate, as was then customary, but enclosed within one and the same cloister, he certainly did not live in another person’s house while he was among them before his departure from the city of Rheims—that is, before approximately 1076. Consequently, he did not at that time hold the conversation with Radulphus Viridis and Fulcius Monoculus, since that conversation took place while Bruno was staying in another person’s house.

For the same reason, it appears rather unlikely that this conversation took place after Saint Bruno, once the simoniacal intruder Manasses had been removed and expelled, had been restored to nearly his former condition, or perhaps to an even better one—as we shall see below, with regard to how and when this occurred.

Moreover, from the fact that Saint Bruno was staying in another person’s lodging when he conversed with Radulphus Viridis about the false pleasures of the world, it further follows that this did not happen at Paris. Those who place the conversation at Paris assert that our Saint was then carrying out a teaching office there. But if Bruno had ever actually taught in that city, it does not seem that he would then have been using another person’s house as a guest.

Furthermore, there is absolutely nothing else from which it can in any way be shown that Saint Bruno’s conversation with Radulphus and Fulcius took place at Paris. Thus, just as it probably did not happen at Rheims, so it probably did not happen there either.

On the other hand, it appears most probable from the circumstances of Saint Bruno’s situation there that the conversation occurred at Reciacum, or Rauciacum, after the Council of Autun.

### 128.

For at that time both he and the other Rheims clerics, his companions in exile, were staying in other people’s houses. They had evidently been received as guests, with the permission of Count Ebalus, by various inhabitants of that castle—Valesius’s passage cited above leaves no doubt that it comprised several houses—whom Manasses the archbishop probably designated in section 123 as “the receivers of Manasses the provost and those adhering to him.”

In addition, during the period when Saint Bruno was staying at Reciacum with the other Rheims clerics and could already have held the conversation concerning the false pleasures of the world after the Council of Autun, Ebalus, the lord of that castle, set out for Rome, as I showed above. Several Rheims clerics accompanied him, as I likewise showed above. And, as the words quoted above from our Saint’s letter to Radulphus Viridis indicate, not long after the conversation which Bruno held with Radulphus and Fulcius, Fulcius departed for Rome.

It follows further from what has been said that Radulphus Viridis and Fulcius Monoculus were at Reciacum with our Saint before Count Ebalus left for Rome.

The writers of the *Literary History of France*, volume IX, page 235, list only three canons of the Church of Rheims—namely, Manasses the provost, Pontius, and Bruno—who accused Manasses the archbishop at the Council of Autun in 1077 and afterward withdrew to the castle of Reciacum. They assert that Bruno’s conversation with Radulphus and Fulcius concerning the vanity of the riches and pleasures of this world took place before this withdrawal.

But what of that?

### 129.

One need not accept the number of Rheims clerics who accused Manasses and withdrew to the castle of Reciacum assigned by those writers, with the consequence that Radulphus Viridis and Fulcius neither belonged to the household of Count Ebalus at the castle of Reciacum nor held there with Bruno the conversation in question.

For Manasses himself reveals in his *Apology*, preserved in Mabillon, *Museum Italicum*, volume I, part II, page 121, that there were more Rheims canons who accused Manasses the archbishop. He writes to Hugh of Die as follows:

“You said that we should come to the council to answer our accusers, namely Manasses and his companions. I say to you that Manasses and I made an agreement concerning all his companions, except two. One of them, namely Bruno, is neither our cleric nor our son, whether begotten or reborn, but is a canon of Saint Cunibert of Cologne, situated in the kingdom of the Teutons. We do not greatly desire his companionship, since we know nothing at all about his life or his liberty, and because, when he was among us, we were treated badly and wickedly despite the many benefices we had conferred upon him.

“The other, namely, Pontius, was found guilty of falsification in the Roman council in our presence. Therefore we neither wish nor ought to answer either one in an ecclesiastical judgment.”

Since, then, as is understood from these words, there were certainly more than three canons or clerics of the Church of Rheims who accused Manasses the archbishop, and who consequently withdrew to the castle of Reciacum after the Council of Autun, there is no reason to deny that Radulphus Viridis and Fulcius Monoculus were among them.

Since this is so, there is likewise no reason to suppose that our Saint did not hold with them in the same castle the conversation of which we are speaking—although concerning that castle one should consult the *Addenda and Corrigenda* to page 519, section 124.

### 130.

Indeed, both the considerations I have already brought forward and those I now add suggest that Bruno held it there.

That conversation, in which the vanity of the world, the eternity of heaven, and the assumption of the monastic habit were discussed, corresponds perfectly to the condition in which the Saint was at Reciacum after the Council of Autun. There he had been stripped of his goods by Manasses the archbishop and was suffering adversity—a condition that commonly leads mortals, when oppressed, to despise earthly things, esteem heavenly things, and turn themselves toward God.

Furthermore, the words of Saint Bruno himself transcribed above indicate that he and the others delayed for a long time fulfilling what they had vowed in that conversation. In fact, this occurred according to the view that the conversation in question was held at Reciacum after the Council of Autun.

For Saint Bruno, as I shall prove below, certainly did not withdraw into the wilderness and devote himself to the better life before 1081. Before he did so, the celebrated conversation discussed here took place with Fulcius at least three years earlier, as is easy to infer from what has already been said.

According to this account, Fulcius went to Rome with Count Ebalus in 1077—the year 1078 entered section 124 by mistake—and this journey was preceded by the conversation which he held with Bruno after the Council of Autun, likewise celebrated in 1077, concerning the false pleasures of the world. Thus the conversation occurred in that same year, 1077, and therefore at least three years before Saint Bruno withdrew into the wilderness.

Let us now settle the remaining matters relating to the litigation initiated by our Saint and the other clerics of the Church of Rheims against Manasses the archbishop.

## VII. Manasses defends his case at Rome in a council and obtains from the pontiff the rescission of the sentence of suspension passed against him at Autun; what else he subsequently did, and who was finally ordered to restore Bruno to his former honor

When Manasses, archbishop of the Church of Rheims, had already arrived at Rome to appear before the supreme pontiff, Gregory VII, to whom, as has been stated, he had appealed, he was received kindly by Gregory, who still hoped that the man would return to a better way of life. He attempted to defend his case in the council then held there—that is, in March 1078—in the presence also of Count Ebalus and the Rheims clerics who, as I have shown, had accompanied him and had come to speak on behalf of the Rheims clergy. See the words transcribed above from Manasses’s letter in section 123.

I have not found in the records what resources he used in conducting his defense. But he himself explains how successfully he proceeded in his *Apology*, preserved in Mabillon’s work cited above, page 119, writing there to Hugh, legate of the Apostolic See:

### 131.

“It is known throughout almost all Gaul, and also in Italy and Rome, how, nearly two years ago—that is, in 1077—in that same province, you and certain others acted violently and unjustly against us. Having suffered violence and prejudice, I proceeded to Rome and there appealed concerning this matter to the Roman and Apostolic judgment.

“But since you were absent, by command of the apostolic lord I remained in that region and awaited your arrival for nearly eleven weeks. When you did not come, at last, in the presence of the apostolic lord and in a general council, a dispute arose between us and those who were present in your place, as having been sent by you. From their accusation and our defense, it was judged and corrected that everything we had suffered had been done rashly and violently and ought not to stand.”

In this way Manasses—although he is excessively unfair toward Hugh, the legate of the Apostolic See, and although he sets out the matter with little sincerity, as is clear from what has already been said and from what will follow—correctly indicates that the sentence which Hugh had passed against him at the Council of Autun was corrected or rescinded.

### 132.

For Gregory, hoping that apostolic clemency would bring Manasses to a better way of life, absolved him from the sentence of suspension by which he had been condemned at Autun, and sent him back to Gaul restored to his former rank and office, though with certain conditions added which he does not mention here.

Gregory himself teaches this in Labbe, volume X of the Councils, in a letter written on the seventh day before the Ides of March, in the first indiction—which, according to what has been stated above, designates the year 1078. He writes:

“Because it is the custom of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authorization we serve, although unworthy, sometimes also to overlook certain matters, following the moderation of discretion rather than the rigor of the canons, we have investigated, not without serious labor, the cases of the bishops of France and Burgundy who had been suspended or condemned by our legate Hugh, bishop of Die.

“Finally, Manasses, archbishop of Rheims, who had been accused on many counts and had withdrawn from the synods to which Hugh, bishop of Die, had invited him, was restored to his former rank and office, because the sentence passed against him did not appear consistent with the gravity and customary gentleness of the Roman Church. This was done on the condition that he swear over the body of Saint Peter as follows:

“‘I, Manasses, archbishop of Rheims, did not refuse through pride to come to the Council of Autun, to which Hugh, bishop of Die, summoned me. If I am summoned by messenger or letter of the Apostolic See, I shall not withdraw by any evil device or fraud, but, coming, I shall faithfully obey the decision and judgment of this Church.

“‘If it pleases the lord Pope Gregory or his successor that I answer before his legate concerning the charges brought against me, I shall do so in every respect. I shall faithfully administer the treasures, ornaments, and estates of the Church of Rheims entrusted to me, for the honor of that Church, and I shall not alienate them in order to resist justice.’”

### 133.

This letter, or rescript, is subsequently followed by several other matters that do not concern our subject and therefore need not be transcribed here. It concludes as follows:

“Done at Rome on the seventh day before the Ides of March, in the first indiction.”

The later chronological note included in this clause designates the year of Christ 1078; see what was said in section 116. Therefore, the sentence of suspension passed against Manasses—who, as has been stated, had gone to Rome in 1077 after the Council of Autun, without waiting for the time appointed, although he had been summoned to the other council to be celebrated at Poitiers at the beginning of 1078, and who, after awaiting Hugh of Die’s arrival there for nearly eleven weeks, as his words transcribed in section 131 indicate—was rescinded by Gregory VII, the supreme pontiff, from March 1078 onward, subject to the condition contained in the words just transcribed.

Yet Gregory’s indulgence and kindness toward Manasses, the simoniacal prelate, most probably displeased Hugh of Die, bishop and legate of the Apostolic See in Gaul, considerably. This may properly be inferred from a letter written by Hugh to that supreme shepherd of the Church after the Council of Poitiers was held in 1078. Although it does not concern Manasses, Hugh says near its end, in Labbe, volume X of the Councils, column 367:

“Let Your Holiness therefore take care that it not continue to be shamefully reproached to us that simoniacs or any criminals suspended, deposed, or even condemned by us gladly run to Rome, and that, where they ought to experience a greater rigor of justice, they carry away from there what is, as it were, mercy according to their own desire. Those who previously did not dare to sin even in small matters afterward carry on a most suitable commerce with tyranny in the churches entrusted to them.”

### 134.

By these words he further teaches that simoniacs had then become worse and more insolent because of the indulgence they had experienced at Rome. How true this was, Manasses clearly demonstrated by his conduct.

Although he had solemnly promised in an oath given at Rome that he would answer the Apostolic legate concerning the crimes charged against him whenever the pontiff wished—see the words of Pope Gregory transcribed in section 132—he had scarcely returned to Gaul from the Roman council at which, as has been stated, he was heard and acquitted in 1078 when he sent a letter to the pontiff, to whom he had to write for other reasons.

In that letter, besides the complaints expressed in the words given in section 123 against Count Ebalus, Manasses the provost, and the other Rheims clerics who followed the latter, he argued from the privileges of his church that he ought to answer concerning the charges only to the pope himself or to the pope’s legates who were Italians or at least had been educated at Rome.

Thus Manasses attempted to evade the judgment of Hugh of Die—who had neither been born in Italy nor educated at Rome—and whom he feared above all lest he should again summon him to a council to purge himself of the charges. Hear what he brings forward on this subject in the said letter, in Labbe, volume X of the Councils, page 363.

### 135.

“I also beseech,” he says, “the benevolence of your dignity to deign to preserve for me the dignity which your predecessors preserved for my predecessors, the archbishops, and which they left recorded for the memory of posterity in privileges and other writings.

“May the privilege which you yourself granted me not be rendered void or broken—namely, that I should answer to you yourself, whether summoned or not, and to your Roman legates, not to those from beyond the Alps, who, joined to the Romans, seek what is theirs and not what is Jesus Christ’s, and who, under respectable names, serve their own greed rather than the Church of God.

“Therefore, because of the shameful reproaches and summonses of such men, I, who ought to summon all the bishops of Gaul, may rely upon you without a summons from the legates until I come to you at Easter, God willing.”

Thus Manasses sought to ensure that he would never be compelled to answer Hugh, the legate of the Apostolic See, concerning the crimes charged against him.

Gregory, however, did not listen to him in this matter. He refuted sharply whatever Manasses had written in the words quoted, whether concerning the legates of the Apostolic See or concerning the privilege of the Church of Rheims. Nevertheless, Gregory did take account of the complaints which Manasses had made against Count Ebalus, Manasses the provost, and the others. This is shown both by the letter in which he answered Manasses and by another which he sent at the same time to Hugh of Die, his legate in Gaul.

Both letters are recorded by Labbe, who prints them in volume X of the Councils, columns 196 and following, as “given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, in the first indiction.” This date designates the year 1078 according to what has been stated above.

It follows that the letter which Manasses the archbishop sent to Pope Gregory—the one just mentioned—was certainly written in 1078, since it preceded both of these letters but followed the Roman council held in that same year. I have thought it useful to establish this here in order to substantiate what was stated in section 123.

### 136.

I now transcribe the words in the two letters of Gregory just mentioned which bear, in whatever way, upon the present subject.

The first contains the following:

“Concerning Manasses, who does not cease to harass you and your church with curses because he cannot do so by evil deeds, and concerning all the other matters about which you may wish to bring a complaint, we have sent our letters to our aforementioned brothers, namely the bishop of Die and the abbot of Cluny, so that they may diligently investigate everything, carefully examine it, and judge what has been examined and investigated fully, justly, legally, and canonically.”

The second contains these words:

“Because we ought to watch attentively over the governance of the holy Church of God, over which by divine disposition we preside, we ask you through your constant prayers to obtain divine assistance for us. Therefore, we admonish and command you to apply the greatest diligence, so that you may investigate and, insofar as you can, endeavor to bring to a canonical conclusion the affairs about which our brother, the archbishop of Rheims, has complained to us in his letters.

“For he complains about our brother, Warmund, archbishop of Vienne, who deposed priests in his archbishopric and restored those same men … [lacuna]

“Concerning Manasses, about whom he likewise complains, who does not cease to burden him and the Church with the refuge and assistance of Ebalus and his followers, labor so that he may return to peace and cease disturbing the Church and persecuting the archbishop.

“If, however, he persists in his contumacy and refuses to obey, unless you find that he has a just excuse, do whatever seems most just to you.

“As for his other needs, assist the same archbishop, if he obeys you, as is fitting, and defend the Church entrusted to him by the authority of blessed Peter, as you ought also to do with the other churches.”

### 137.

It was therefore the pontiff’s wish—as appears chiefly from these words of the letter which he sent to Hugh of Die—that, if this could in any way be accomplished, Count Ebalus of Reciacum and Manasses, provost of the Church of Rheims, should be reconciled with Manasses the archbishop.

I therefore infer that Manasses the provost, having been informed of the pontiff’s wish either through Hugh, the legate of the Apostolic See, or through Manasses the archbishop himself, made peace with him. The simoniacal prelate himself records this in his frequently cited *Apology*, preserved in Mabillon, volume I of the *Museum Italicum*, part II, page 121, in these words:

“I say to you that Manasses and I made an agreement concerning all his companions, except two. One of them, namely Bruno, is neither our cleric nor our son, whether begotten or reborn, but is a canon of Saint Cunibert of Cologne, situated in the kingdom of the Teutons. We do not greatly desire his companionship, since we know nothing at all about his life or his liberty; and because, when he was among us, we were treated badly and wickedly despite the many benefices we had conferred upon him.

“The other, namely, Pontius, was falsified in the Roman council in our presence. Therefore we neither wish nor ought to answer either one in an ecclesiastical judgment.”

I am confirmed still more strongly in this conjecture by the fact that, when the pontiff later decreed that a council should be held at Lyons in 1080 to investigate and determine the case of Manasses the archbishop, this Manasses the provost, most attentive to the pontiff’s will, again presented himself there and even became one of the accusers of that simoniacal prelate with whom, as has been stated, he had previously made peace.

This seems to be gathered from a letter of Gregory VII to Manasses, archbishop of Rheims, preserved in Labbe, volume X of the Councils, column 241. It was written after he had been deposed at the Council of Lyons, in the third indiction—that is, according to what has been stated above, in 1080.

From the same letter it also appears that Manasses the provost, having most probably been restored to his goods after making peace with Manasses the archbishop, was again stripped of them by the latter because he had once more joined the archbishop’s accusers at the Council of Lyons.

### 138.

For the pontiff speaks as follows:

“We grant you permission to purge yourself, on this condition, namely that, after Manasses and Bruno, who appear to have spoken against you on behalf of justice, have been fully restored to their property, you leave the Church of Rheims entirely free from all occupation by the next Ascension of the Lord.”

Manasses the provost therefore not only made peace with Manasses, archbishop of Rheims, after the two letters mentioned in section 135—one of which Pope Gregory sent to Manasses the archbishop and the other to Hugh, his legate in Gaul, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, in the first indiction, or in 1078—but also went to Rheims to negotiate with him on behalf of the other Rheims clerics who, as has been stated, had left that city with him and Bruno in 1076 or the following year, and settled the matter.

I infer this from the frequently cited *Apology* of Manasses the archbishop. In it, first, he says in Mabillon, volume I of the *Museum Italicum*, part II, page 121:

“Manasses and I made an agreement concerning all his companions, except two,” and so forth.

Then, on page 122, he writes:

“Although we expect no accusation from the aforementioned Manasses and his companions, because they themselves—unless perhaps on the occasion of this council they return to their vomit—made an agreement of peace with us, except for the two I mentioned, Bruno and Pontius, to whom, for the reasons already given, I neither wish nor ought to answer.

“And if some of those whom we have said were reconciled through Manasses’s embassy have gone there after breaking the peace and wish to say anything against us, they must not be received.”

### 139.

This reconciliation between Manasses the provost and Manasses the archbishop, having taken place after the letter which Gregory sent to the bishop of Die on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September in 1078, most probably occurred either in that very year or at the beginning of the following one.

But I do not know whether at that time all the Rheims clerics, apart from Bruno and Pontius, returned to Rheims together with Manasses the provost, when he made peace with Manasses the archbishop on their behalf, as he himself had already done.

The letter praised immediately above, which Gregory sent to Manasses the archbishop after he had already been deposed at the Council of Lyons in 1080, gives me considerable reason to doubt this. In it Gregory orders Manasses the archbishop to permit the clerics—namely, the Rheims clerics whom Manasses had forced to leave Rheims by his wicked conduct—

“who have suffered exile for so long on behalf of justice, to serve God securely in the church.”

Whatever the truth may be, I infer from the peace mentioned above, which Manasses the provost and the other Rheims clerics had made with Manasses the archbishop, that Bruno and Pontius, because they did not wish to consent to it—as the words quoted in section 137 from Manasses’s *Apology* demonstrate—separated themselves from Manasses the provost and the other Rheims clerics who had consented to him, and went elsewhere.

This may especially have happened because Count Ebalus, under whose protection they were at Reciacum, had also made peace with Manasses at that time. I am led to suspect this by a letter written by Pope Gregory to Ebalus in 1080, preserved in Labbe, volume X of the Councils, column 265, in which Gregory orders him “from now on to withdraw from that man’s”—namely, Manasses’s, who had by then been deposed—“pernicious friendship.”

### 140

That Bruno indeed—there is no need here to say anything about Pontius—then returned from Reciacum to Cologne and was enrolled among the canons of the church of St. Cunibert seems to me exceedingly probable. For in the *Apology* so often cited above, which Archbishop Manasses wrote in 1080 or certainly toward the end of the preceding year, he is said to have been a Cunibertine canon in these words:

> “Bruno is neither our cleric, nor our son or one reborn among us, but he is a canon of St. Cunibert of Cologne, situated in the kingdom of the Teutons.” [Col. 0083C]

As I explained in § III, these words are more plausibly understood to mean that the saint was then—that is, in 1079 or at the beginning of the following year, when Manasses wrote this— a canon of the Cunibertine church.

Nevertheless, even if the matter stood thus, and the saint was therefore no longer in Gaul, he did not desist from the suit which he, together with the other clerics of Reims, had brought against Manasses, the simoniacal bishop. The facts will become clear from what follows.

As we have seen above, the pope had instructed Hugh of Die on 22 August 1078 to address the complaints brought before him by Manasses, Archbishop of Reims, and, if Manasses proved obedient, to assist him. [Col. 0083D]

### 141

To the letter in which he imposed this duty upon Hugh, the pope had added, as Hugh himself testifies immediately after the words transcribed above in no. 136, a copy of another letter written to Manasses. After several preliminary remarks, he addressed him as follows:
