> “Meanwhile, in the name of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, we admonish Your Fraternity that, just as we instructed you when you were in Rome, so before the bishop of Die and the abbot of Cluny, to whom we have entrusted our authority in this matter, you should be ready on every occasion, once all obstacles and excuses have been removed, to answer concerning all the charges brought against you, to make legal satisfaction, and to clear yourself canonically; lest, if anything else should be done by you—which God forbid!—it be attributed by many to evasion, flight, and consciousness of crimes, rather than to the enforcement of justice and equity.” [Col. 0084A]

From this letter to Manasses, which the pope communicated to Hugh of Die, and from the other letter mentioned immediately above, which the pope issued to Hugh himself, the historians of the *Literary History of France*, vol. VIII, p. 653, suspect that Hugh announced a council to be held at Troyes, a council mentioned by Manasses in his *Apology* published by Mabillon in the repeatedly cited volume of his works, p. 120. Indeed, the words already quoted from the first letter seem to provide reasonable grounds for such a suspicion. However the matter may stand, the council announced for Troyes did not take place—for whatever reason, I do not know.

### 142

When Pope Gregory learned this, he instructed his legate Hugh to hold a council elsewhere for deciding the case of Archbishop Manasses. The letter in which he did so is inserted in the *Chronicle of Verdun* in Labbe, vol. I of the *New Manuscript Library*, p. 205. It contains the following words, which are especially relevant to our present purpose:

> “Since you were unable to hold a council usefully in the previously designated region—namely, at Troyes—we judge it appropriate that your diligence should find a suitable place where, once a synod has been assembled, the case of the Archbishop of Reims may be examined. If suitable accusers and witnesses are found who canonically prove the charges brought against him, we wish you, without hesitation, to pronounce whatever sentence justice dictates. Otherwise, if the persons are such that they cannot reasonably be admitted, then, since an evil reputation concerning him has filled not only Gaul but nearly all Italy, let him, after taking to himself six bishops whose lives are not marked by infamy, if he can, clear himself before them; and, thus purged, let him remain in peace in his own church and dignity.” [Col. 0084B–C]

After receiving the letter in which the pope imposed these and other instructions upon him, Hugh the legate announced a council at Lyons, as the *Chronicle of Verdun*, or Hugh of Flavigny, its contemporary author, attests at the place cited. He summoned Manasses, Archbishop of Reims, to attend it.

### 143

But Manasses, who had already refused to appear at the councils held at Autun and Poitiers, was unwilling to come to the council soon to be held at Lyons either. Yet, as we have shown above, he had previously sworn before the pope at Rome that, whenever he was summoned by the apostolic legate to answer at a council concerning the crimes charged against him, he would obey him.

Accordingly, he sent the pope a letter, cleverly designed to excuse him in some fashion for refusing to go to the council announced by the legate at Lyons. In it he alleged that, because he feared the disorder of the kingdom, he could not go to the council at Lyons to which he had been summoned. He added that, when the roads were safe, he would again travel to Rome and hear the judgment pronounced by the supreme pontiff himself with filial submission.

All this is inferred from Gregory’s reply to Manasses, published by Labbe, vol. X of the *Councils*, col. 235 and following. The pope did not accept Manasses’ statements and sharply rebuked him in these words, which are particularly relevant here:

> “Mindful neither of your promise, by which at Rome you bound yourself before the body of blessed Peter, you put forward another excuse—namely, that because you fear the disorder of the kingdom you cannot come to the council at Lyons, to which you have been summoned. How unstable your excuse is in this matter can readily be assessed …” [Col. 0085A]

### 144

> “Although you could cross all the dangers of that road, if any exist, with the safest and most secure guides—namely, the Archbishop of Lyons and the Bishop of Langres, who would treat you with fraternal charity and lead you without any fear to the aforesaid place … If, however, you should not go to the aforesaid council, and should refuse to incline your ear to your mother, the Roman Church, which has long borne with you, then, if the Bishop of Die acts against you with the agreement of our religious brothers, we shall not only refuse to alter the sentence pronounced against you, but shall confirm it by apostolic authority.

> “If it should seem to Your Fraternity that the sentence pronounced against you can reasonably be challenged, we wish you rather to present your arguments before our vicar—the Bishop of Die—and before the other religious men in that region, where a greater number of accusers and defenders can be found, than to seek in vain, with the hope of a trial, to come to Rome through so many labors and difficulties, where neither is available.

> “Meanwhile, in the name of almighty God and by the authority of blessed Peter, we admonish Your Fraternity that, if you recognize yourself to be guilty in this matter, you should not suppose that you must excuse yourself by any worldly ingenuity; rather, strive to free your soul through worthy fruits of repentance.” [Col. 0085B–C]

### 145

This speech of the pope was certainly forceful and urgent. Manasses, however, was not moved by it at all. When the council had shortly afterward been held at Lyons, as we shall see, he did not appear before it; he contented himself with sending to Hugh of Die, its president, the *Apology* so often cited above, published by Mabillon in vol. I, part II, of the *Museum Italicum*, p. 119 and the following eight pages.

In that work, after briefly describing what had been done in his case both at Autun and at Rome, he brought forward—or rather pretended—various reasons why he could not come to the council at Lyons. These reasons appear outwardly just, and such that, if the character of Archbishop Manasses had been less notorious than it was, one might have believed that the sentence against him had been pronounced unjustly, precipitately, and out of envy, as the clerics of Noyon claimed in their letter to the clerics of Cambrai, published by Mabillon in vol. I, part II, of the *Museum Italicum*, pp. 128 and following.

Most of them, however, were not genuine. They had merely been devised or fabricated by Manasses so that, with his customary cunning and astuteness—by which, as Pope Gregory says in Labbe, vol. X of the *Councils*, col. 199, he “sought delays in order to evade”—he might either elude or avoid the ecclesiastical judgment which, according to the canons, had to be pronounced in his case.

How greatly he shrank from that judgment is also shown by the enormous gifts which, in order to make himself exempt from facing it, he offered to Hugh of Die when the time for the council at Lyons was already approaching. [Col. 0086A]

### 146

Hear Hugh of Flavigny in Labbe, vol. I of the *New Manuscript Library*, pp. 205 and following:

> “When, therefore,” he says, “the place of the council had been fixed at Lyons, and the Archbishop of Reims—namely, Manasses—was summoned to that same council, according to the tenor of the letters, in order to clear himself, Hugh was staying near Vienne for the treatment of his body. The messengers of the aforesaid archbishop came to him, wishing to incline him by many and very great entreaties and gifts. For this purpose they offered him immediately three hundred ounces of the purest gold, together with precious gifts for his household, and, in addition, wished to swear an oath of secrecy that they would reveal the matter to no mortal.

> “They asked him to allow Manasses to clear himself with six bishops whom he himself, the Archbishop of Reims, would choose from among his suffragans, without any investigation of the infamy alleged against him. They added—although they could scarcely hope for this, yet wished to leave nothing unattempted—that, if he alone were granted the opportunity to clear himself, they would swear to give him immeasurable treasures of gold, treasures that would even exceed all reckoning, and would in addition swear an oath not to reveal the matter to anyone. The source reads *ei solo [soli]*: “if he alone [or: if to him alone] were granted the opportunity to clear himself.” [Col. 0086B]

> “The manly spirit of that legate rejected all of this. And because Manasses saw that his resistance to money was unconquerable, fearing for himself, he refused to attend the council.”

From this alone, even if the matter were not otherwise established—as it plainly is—it becomes evident that our saint, and the other clerics of the church of Reims who had left Reims with him, had very justly accused Manasses of many crimes. For if he had not been guilty, if he could properly have dispelled the charges brought against him, why would he have striven with such effort, such gifts, and such frauds to avoid a judgment that was to be pronounced in a council by men of the utmost integrity and entirely free from suspicion?

But let us continue the sequence of events. [Col. 0086C]

### 147

When the time appointed for the council at Lyons arrived, Bruno and Pontius, as can be gathered from the words of Manasses quoted in no. 137, together with other clerics of the church of Reims—including, apparently, Manasses the provost—appeared before the council. They set forth the same principal charges against Archbishop Manasses as they had previously presented at the council of Autun.

After hearing these charges, and also reading, as seems probable, the *Apology* that Manasses had sent to them, the Fathers nevertheless rejected the excuses he had offered in it for not attending the council. They deposed the simoniacal bishop by synodal judgment, both because, as Hugh of Flavigny says at the place cited immediately above, “he refused to clear himself,” and because “he evaded the hearing of Autun, Poitiers, and Lyons itself.” They sent the sentence pronounced against him to the pope for approval and confirmation.

This occurred, and the date of the council can consequently be established, between 3 January and 17 April of the year 1080. The letter partly transcribed above, in which Pope Gregory most urgently urged Manasses to attend the council at Lyons, is dated “on the third day before the Nones of January, in the third indiction,” which, according to the foregoing, designates the year 1080. Another letter, in which Gregory likewise confirmed the sentence pronounced against Manasses at that council, is found in Labbe, vol. X of the *Councils*, col. 241. It too bears the third indiction, or the year 1080, and, as the chronological notes supplied at its end attest, was written on 17 April. [Col. 0087A]

### 148

I transcribe this letter in full from the place cited in Labbe, both because it sheds light upon and strengthens what has been said above, and because it provides eloquent testimony to the fairness of our saint in accusing Manasses, while ordering that the latter restore the saint’s possessions in full. It runs as follows:

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Manasses of Reims.
>
> “Let Your Fraternity know that we too, guided by justice, have confirmed by apostolic authority in the Roman synod the sentence of deposition pronounced by our legate, the Bishop of Die, with the counsel of religious men at the council of Lyons. Nevertheless, moved, if I may put it so, by an excessive mercy contrary to the custom of the Roman Church, we grant you permission to clear yourself until the feast of St. Michael, provided that you can obtain and assemble the Bishops of Soissons, Laon, Cambrai, and Châlons—or their equals—together with two others whose testimony we may equally trust, if you have confidence in your justice.

> “This permission is granted on the condition that, after restoring in full their possessions to Manasses, Bruno, and the others who appear to have spoken against you on behalf of justice, you completely relinquish your occupation of the church of Reims by the next feast of the Ascension of the Lord. You shall withdraw to Cluny or to the House of God, where you shall live religiously at your own expense with one cleric and two laymen.” [Col. 0087B–C]

### 149

> “If you wish to do this, take care to notify the aforesaid Bishop of Die, so that in his presence you may confirm by oath that meanwhile you will alienate nothing from the possessions of the aforesaid church except what is reasonably sufficient for you and the companions mentioned above.

> “Permit the clerics who have suffered exile for justice for so long a time to serve God securely in the church. And since it would be burdensome for you to come all the way to us, we grant you permission to clear yourself of the infamy before the Bishop of Die and the Abbot of Cluny—or, if the abbot should happen to be absent, before Amatus—in the manner stated above and with the witnesses mentioned above.

> “But if you disdain to obey this command of our dispensation, know that we can no longer bear your iniquity, and that the sentence of deposition will not only remain unaltered, but no hearing will be left to you thereafter.”

> “Given at Rome on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the third indiction.”

This letter makes clear that Gregory treated Manasses with the greatest kindness and indulgence. Manasses, however, with his mind hardened in his crimes, did not fulfill what the pope prescribed. In particular, he did not restore Bruno or the other clerics of the church of Reims—whom he had afflicted with the gravest losses, as see no. 118 and following—to their dignities and possessions, as the pope ordered in the letter just quoted. The next section will reveal what was later done regarding our saint. [Col. 0088A]

## § VIII. Who restored the Saint at Reims, and when, to his former or even better condition; and whether, after his departure from that city under Manasses, or at any other time, he taught at Paris

After Manasses, the deposed Archbishop of Reims, had failed to carry out anything of what Gregory had commanded him in the letter transcribed in the preceding section—and after he had descended to such madness that he attempted, even by force of arms, to retain the bishopric which he had acquired by simony and which he ought by then to have relinquished both by the pope’s command and by the sentence pronounced against him at the council of Lyons, or at least to claim its property for himself—the pope, judging that the man’s impiety had to be checked promptly, wrote four separate letters on the same day, 27 December, apparently not long after the council of Lyons at which Manasses had been deposed, and therefore in the year 1080.

One letter was addressed to the clergy and people of Reims; another to Hebolus—or, as he is also called elsewhere, Ebalus or even Oebalus—the Count of Reciacum; a third to the suffragan bishops of the archdiocese of Reims; and finally a fourth to Philip, king of the Franks. In these letters generally he earnestly commended to all and each of them that, no longer recognizing Manasses as bishop, they should provide him with a successor. More specifically, he seriously admonished the clergy and people, as well as Count Ebalus and the suffragans of the church of Reims, to resist Manasses, as an unjust usurper, with all their strength. To Philip, king of the Franks, he imposed by apostolic authority the command not to obstruct the election that the clergy and people of the church of Reims were to conduct.

All these letters are extant in Labbe, vol. X of the *Councils*, col. 264 and following. I transcribe here the words of the first that are especially relevant, since they show that, even after Manasses had been deposed at the council of Lyons and had received from the pope the letter transcribed in the preceding section, he still attempted to retain by force of arms the ill-gotten archbishopric of Reims and to plunder its treasures. [Col. 0088B–D]

### 151–152

Here it is:

> “After carefully examining that sentence—the sentence pronounced against Manasses at the council of Lyons—and approving it as most just in view of the enormity of his iniquities, we confirmed it in the Roman synod at the request of many brothers, granting him, during the interval allowed him, permission to come and clear himself of the charges brought against him and a free opportunity to speak on his own behalf. On the condition, however, that in the meantime he should relinquish the governance of that church and reside at Cluny or in some religious monastery, so that it might be proved how obedient and humble he was.

> “Nevertheless, as you yourselves know, he not only failed to obey this decision, but, in contempt of our prohibition, dared to invade your church and disgrace it by shameless devastation. He entered it not through the door, as a shepherd, but from elsewhere, as a thief and most savage robber, in order to slaughter and destroy the Lord’s flock, not to protect and defend it with a shepherd’s vigilance.

> “Indeed, the iniquity of his actions has grown so immeasurably that he deserves to be subjected most justly to condemnation and excommunication, so that he should never entertain any hope of restoration. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we admonish you to have no part in his perverse actions; rather, to ensure that he is removed from your midst and handed over to Satan for the destruction of his flesh, so that his spirit may be saved; and to resist him in every way.

> “Take care also that, by common counsel and with equal agreement, and with the assent of our aforesaid brother, the Bishop of Die, you choose for yourselves, according to the Lord, a father.” [Col. 0089A–B]

Nor was Gregory, who—as these words of his make clear—also wished Manasses expelled from Reims, disappointed in his desire. For not only the people and clergy of the church of Reims but also its leading men rose up against the simoniacal and already deposed bishop and drove him from the see he had usurped.

### 153

Guibert of Nogent, the contemporary author already cited many times, teaches this. Immediately after the words concerning Manasses transcribed above in no. 110, he adds:

> “Later, when he was repeatedly struck with anathema by Hugh—called Bishop of Die and later Archbishop of Lyons—the apostolic legate, a man most renowned for the abundance of his justice, and when he was attempting by military force to squander the treasures of the church, the nobles, clergy, and burghers drove Manasses from the see which he had wickedly occupied. Banished into perpetual exile, after he had gone to the excommunicated Emperor Henry, himself also excommunicated at that time, he wandered here and there and finally died without communion.”

Thus Guibert. Although, on the basis of the observations made by the historians of the *Literary History of France*, vol. VIII, pp. 655 and following, it may reasonably be questioned whether Manasses ended his life under the excommunication with which he had been struck chiefly because of his crimes and obstinacy, there can nevertheless be no doubt that what Guibert likewise reports is true: that this simoniacal bishop was expelled from the see of Reims by the clergy, people, and leading men. All the learned who have examined the matter affirm this unanimously, and, unlike the preceding case, no testimony of a contemporary or nearly contemporary writer can be produced that in any way contradicts it.

This expulsion of Manasses, being later—by an interval that can scarcely be doubted—than the letters sent by the pope on 27 December 1080 (see no. 151), did not occur earlier, in all probability, than 1081. That it did not occur later is clear from the fact that Rainaldus of Bellay, as the authors of the enlarged *Gallic Christian History*, vol. IX, col. 75, teach, was raised to the see of Reims in 1083, after Elinandus, Bishop of Laon, had held it for two years following the expulsion of Manasses. [Col. 0090A]

### 154

Let us now return to the subject of our saint. After the simoniacal bishop Manasses had been expelled, as just described, Bruno returned to Reims and was restored there to his former condition, or perhaps to an even better one. I establish the matter as follows.

An epitaph dedicated to him by the cathedral church of Reims itself—whose provost, the repeatedly mentioned Manasses, and whose canons certainly knew him very well—was composed and placed among the epitaphs to be reprinted, no. 52. It reads:

> Here this outstanding Father, founder of religion,  
> Presented himself as an example to his brothers,  
> Giving them a model for despising the world’s worthless things  
> While he pursued the rewards of the heavenly homeland.  
> For whose fault we do not believe one ought to mourn him,  
> Whom we believe already rejoicing in rest.  
> For if a good life earns rest for any saint,  
> Then for him also, according to his merits, the highest rest is granted.  
> When he flourished in many ways in our city,  
> Becoming comfort and honor to his own,  
> And when fortune favored him in everything, so that  
> We preferred him above all others—and rightly so;  
> For he was kind, skilled in every art,  
> Sufficiently eloquent, and powerful in wealth;  
> He set everything aside for Christ, and, following Christ naked,  
> This wilderness received him together with many others.  
> Therefore we believe that rest has been prepared for him.  
> Yet if any slight stain clung to him—  
> For it is clear that no one remains on earth without blemish—  
> May God wipe it away by granting him pardon.

### 155

Thus, as these verses most plainly reveal, at the very time when he possessed great influence in the city of Reims, with authority and wealth and with fortune smiling upon him especially, the saint withdrew into the wilderness after casting these things aside.

This cannot refer either to the period during which he lived at Reims before his departure from that city because of the abominable conduct of Archbishop Manasses, or to the period between that departure and Manasses’ expulsion from the see of Reims. For although, during the time when he had not yet left Reims while avoiding Manasses, the saint enjoyed good fortune there for a long time, it is nevertheless universally acknowledged that he did not then withdraw into the wilderness after abandoning his wealth.

As for the period between his departure from the city of Reims—which, according to what was said above, must be assigned to 1076 or the following year—and the expulsion of Manasses from the see of Reims, the saint was not then living at Reims, much less flourishing there in wealth. This is readily inferred partly from what has already been said, and partly from the letter of Pope Gregory VII transcribed above in no. 148 and following, written, according to the foregoing, in 1080. In it he commands Archbishop Manasses, already deposed at the council of Lyons, to restore the possessions of Manasses and Bruno in full and to permit the clerics “who have suffered exile for justice for so long a time”—one of whom was our saint—“to serve God securely in the church.” [Col. 0091A]

It remains, therefore, that Bruno’s enjoyment of a second period of prosperity at Reims, followed by his withdrawal from there into solitude, can correspond only to the period after Manasses’ expulsion from the see of Reims.

### 156

Accordingly, it is certain that the saint was then restored at Reims to his former condition, or perhaps to an even better one. But did this occur immediately after Manasses’ expulsion, which, according to what has been said, took place in 1081?

Some maintain that the matter must be postponed until the time when Rainaldus of Bellay, first raised to the see of Reims in 1083, had already occupied it. Their opinion, however, should probably not be accepted. For, after being restored to his former condition, the saint was probably also desired or sought as a candidate for the see of Reims—something that could not have occurred under Rainaldus, as will be shown—and this happened before he withdrew into the wilderness.

I now demonstrate this. Hugh of Die, legate of the Apostolic See, says near the end of his letter to the supreme pontiff, written after the council of Autun in 1077 or the following year and transcribed above in no. 119 and following, concerning Manasses the provost and Bruno:

> “We ask that you assign these men to the church of Reims.”

By these words he seems to have asked the pope to arrange for either Bruno or Manasses the provost to be appointed in place of Archbishop Manasses, whom he presumably thought ought to be deposed.

It therefore seems probable that the same legate, after Manasses had been expelled, acted with the greatest zeal among the clergy and people of Reims—whom the pope, in a letter sent toward the end of 1080 (see no. 151), had urged to substitute a new bishop for the deposed Manasses “by common counsel and equal agreement, with the assent” of Hugh of Die himself, the pope’s legate—to persuade them to choose either Bruno or Manasses the provost as their bishop. [Col. 0091B–C]

### 157

This leads me to adopt the opinion preferred by the author of the *Treatise on St. Bruno*, communicated to me by the Carthusians here, according to which it is probable that, when the saint withdrew into the wilderness, it had already been decided and firmly resolved among many of the people and clergy of Reims to elect him bishop.

This is indicated both by the following verses from the epitaph of the cathedral church of Reims, transcribed above:

> And when fortune favored him in everything, so that  
> We preferred him above all others—and rightly so;  
> He set everything aside for Christ, and, following Christ naked,  
> This wilderness received him together with many others;

and also by these other verses contained in another epitaph of the cathedral church of Reims, among those to be reprinted, no. 53:

> As Joseph scorned the love of his mistress  
> And fled her incestuous embraces with manly resolve,  
> So, Bruno, the glory of the world lies despised for you,  
> While she desired to embrace you and stretched out her arms toward you.  
> The world displayed many riches and many honors,  
> But you escaped, rejecting your splendid garment;  
> Embracing the wilderness, you are clothed in a blessed lot. [Col. 0092A]

### 158

The following epitaph, no. 146, also confirms me more and more in this opinion. In it the canons of the cathedral church of St. Mary of Rouen celebrate Bruno in these terms:

> Let the whole order of the holy Church mourn,  
> Weeping the irreparable loss of the human race.  
> Bruno, father and founder of holy religion,  
> Has departed from the world, a victor over worldly honor.  
> Such great holiness commends his pious life  
> That no one can equal him.  
> He himself was wise, a noble man, radiant in character,  
> Imbued at the fountain of all philosophy.  
> In him, while the living virtue of integrity shone forth,  
> By this virtue he was able to merit glorious offices.  
> He trampled wealth beneath his feet, despised every honor,  
> And crushed the world’s foolish ambition underfoot;  
> By his devotion he founded a holy religious life.  
> Turning away from the world, avoiding the world’s high things,  
> He chose instead to live a private life.

Although these verses perhaps allude to the bishopric of Reggio, which the saint refused because, as I shall explain below, he had been elected or sought for it, I nevertheless think that they more probably allude to a future election of the saint as Archbishop of Reims, an election which he deliberately avoided by withdrawing into the wilderness.

The reason is that in the verses quoted, contempt for honors and wealth—the contempt for which Bruno is praised there—is immediately followed by praise of his flight from the world. His flight from the world did not follow his election to the archbishopric of Reggio; it preceded it. [Col. 0092B–C]

### 159

It therefore seems sufficiently probable from everything brought forward that, when the saint withdrew into the wilderness—and consequently had already been restored at Reims to his former condition or perhaps to an even better one—he was desired by many both of the clergy and of the people of that city as their bishop and indeed would actually have been elected, had he not anticipated the event by departing.

Since this is so, and since Rainaldus, who had been raised to the see of Reims as early as 1083, did not die before 1096—by which time Bruno, according to what will be said below, had long since withdrawn into the wilderness (see the authors of the enlarged *Gallic Christian History*, vol. IX, col. 77)—it follows that, once Rainaldus was bishop, the saint could not have been desired or sought for the see of Reims. Consequently, both that event and his restoration to his former or perhaps better condition must have occurred earlier.

But by how much time did the saint’s restoration and his being sought for the see of Reims precede Rainaldus’ promotion to it? The authors of the enlarged *Gallic Christian History*, vol. IX, col. 75, write as follows:

> “After Manasses—the simoniacal bishop of Reims mentioned above—had been deposed, it is reported that Bruno, whom he had stripped of his benefices, was desired by many as bishop, since he had long distinguished himself in the church of Reims by the gravity of his learning and morals. But Elinandus, Bishop of Laon, held the archbishopric for about two years, having received it from the king—Philip of France—through gifts and the efforts of his friends, from 1081 to 1083. After spending a great deal of money, however, he was warned by the supreme pontiff to resign the other benefice, since a man who had a wife could not introduce another woman. He burned with such greed, says Marlotus, that he is reported to have declared that he would spare no effort if he could in any way attain the supreme pontificate.” [Col. 0093A]

### 160

If, therefore, the report praised here by the authors of the enlarged *Gallic Christian History* agrees with the truth, our saint was desired or sought for the see of Reims immediately after the expulsion of the simoniacal Manasses and his restoration to his former or even better condition.

Indeed, since Gregory, who then occupied the Roman see, had urged the people and clergy of Reims in a letter sent toward the end of 1080 (see no. 151) to substitute a new bishop for the expelled Manasses, it seems sufficiently probable that immediately after Manasses’ expulsion they considered and acted upon the choice of a new bishop, specifically the appointment of our saint—especially since, according to the public report recorded by the authors of the enlarged *Gallic Christian History* at the place cited immediately above, this is said to have happened at that time.

The matter, however, is not certain. Since Elinandus was extremely eager to obtain the archbishopric of Reims, it is possible that immediately after Manasses’ expulsion he secured from Philip, king of the Franks, with the assistance and money of his friends, the grant of that archbishopric, and that, supported by royal aid, he completely deprived the clergy and people of Reims of both the opportunity and the time to deliberate about the election of a new bishop. [Col. 0093B–C]

### 161

Hear what Guibert, a contemporary author, says concerning Elinandus or Helinandus—by whose account we also learn that he truly held the archbishopric of Reims for two years—in book III, chapter 2, of his *Life*:

> “Helinandus,” he says, “was a man born of a very poor and obscure family, with very little learning and a rather insignificant appearance. Through the acquaintance of Walter, the elder Count of Pontoise, from whose county he derived his origin, he gained access to the favor of Edward, king of the English. His wife had formed some sort of relationship with the aforesaid count—I do not know what kind.

> “He became Edward’s chaplain. And because he knew French refinement, that English king repeatedly sent him to Henry, king of the Franks. Since Henry was very greedy and accustomed to the sale of bishoprics, Helinandus dealt with him by means of very lavish gifts, so that, if any bishop of France should die, Helinandus himself might succeed to the episcopal insignia.

> “Placed in the service of the king and queen, and since England at that time flourished with immeasurable wealth, he had amassed many mountains of money. Therefore, because of the aforementioned reason—his lavish gifts—his voice was readily heard by King Henry.

> “And so it happened. Once installed at Laon, because he thought he could prevail neither through the distinction of his ancestors nor through literary knowledge, he turned to the abundant wealth at his disposal, which he had learned to administer with the greatest care, and in which he had placed his hope through generosity.

> “He therefore devoted himself to adorning and constructing churches. Although he appeared to do many things for God, he nevertheless gave the clearest indications that in his good works he sought only the favor of men and only the expansion of his reputation.

> “By these same arts he took possession of the archbishopric of Reims. After obtaining it for two years through the payment of great sums to King Philip, a man most venal in matters concerning God, he heard from the lord pope that a man who had a wife could not introduce another woman.

> “When a certain person consulted him as to why he was pursuing this course, he replied that, even if it were possible for him to become pope, he certainly would not conceal that ambition.” [Col. 0093D–0094B]

162. Since Elinandus, as can be understood from these words of Guibert, was a man of the greatest ambition—and since this made him entirely unafraid to purchase for himself, with money for which he had been exceptionally well provided, the highest ecclesiastical dignities and benefices—it appears by no means unlikely that, through his largesses, he immediately after Manasses’ expulsion secured from Philip, king of the Franks, that no discussion should be held by the clergy and people of Reims concerning the appointment of a successor to Manasses’ deposed position. This is especially likely since it is universally acknowledged among all who have written on the matter that, in reality, he prevented the election of a new archbishop of Reims for a full two years after Manasses’ expulsion. The author of the work on St Bruno communicated to me by the Carthusians of this region writes as follows in no. 20:

> “When the aforesaid Elinandus, bishop of Laon, yielded the right which he claimed to the archbishopric of Reims, peace was restored to that church; and when the canons expelled by Manasses had returned from exile toward the end of 1083 or at the beginning of the following year, the clergy and people began seriously to deliberate on the appointment of a shepherd. It is reasonable to believe that Bruno and Manasses the provost were proposed to the electors by the legate Hugh of the Apostolic See, since, as we saw above, the legate had already recommended both of them to the Supreme Pontiff for this very purpose: ‘We commend these men,’ he says, ‘to the church of Reims.’ We infer next from the eulogy composed by that same cathedral church of Reims—in which, when Bruno died, the aforesaid provost Manasses was presiding—that our patriarch, then restored to possession both of his property and of his dignities, was desired by many. The eulogy is found in these words, transcribed below from no. 154.”

163. Thus far his account. Although he seems to suggest that only in 1084—contrary to what the date of Rainald’s accession to the see of Reims appears to allow—the clergy and people of Reims may have discussed the appointment of a successor to Manasses, nevertheless it does not appear unlikely that, as he reports, St Bruno was first desired by many for the episcopate when Elinandus, in 1083, relinquished the right he had arrogated to himself over the archbishopric of Reims.

I hold this opinion because, when the Saint was sought or requested for the bishopric of Reims, he had already been living at Reims for some considerable time, having immediately been restored to his former, or perhaps even to a better, condition, as the verses transcribed above from the funeral eulogy of the cathedral church of Reims, no. 154, seem to indicate. This cannot readily be understood as consonant with the truth if he was requested or sought for that office immediately after Manasses had been expelled from the see of Reims.

Moreover, even if this perhaps first occurred in 1083, as has just been said, the Saint, having been restored to his former condition and fortune for some time previously, was already living at Reims. It may even be inferred from what has been said that he had been sought for the archbishopric of Reims as early as 1081; or, immediately after Manasses’ expulsion—that is, either from 1081 or not long afterward—having returned from exile to Reims, he probably recovered his former position of honor and resources. This is what had to be demonstrated here.

Nor should one object that, during the interval extending from Manasses’ expulsion to Rainald’s election, Elinandus, supported by the king’s assistance, held the cathedral see of Reims, and that it therefore seems unlikely that Bruno would have wished to return to Reims and remain there under such a bishop. For although Elinandus was not free from the stain of simony, he was nevertheless generous toward churches, and is not found to have been unjust toward the clergy.

164. Guibertus continues with these words concerning Elinandus, quoted above in no. 161:

> “Whatever sort of ambition or whatever other human quality may have existed within him, this honor must certainly be preserved for him: that he magnificently defended the liberty of the Church and advanced both that see itself—namely, the see of Laon—and its dependent churches by the most abundant generosity. It was fitting that external goods should be available to him, goods that could be expended on the adornment of the houses of the Lord.”

Since Elinandus was therefore such a man, I do not see why, while he held the see of Reims, Bruno should not be believed to have returned to Reims and lived there—especially since he may perhaps have been unaware of the man’s simoniacal stain. What if the Saint was even invited by Elinandus himself to return to Reims?

Certainly, since it had been Gregory VII, then Supreme Pontiff, who above all desired that Bruno should be restored to his possessions, one may reasonably and not rashly conjecture that Elinandus himself acted, by letter or by some other means, so that the clerics of the church of Reims who had been expelled by Manasses, and consequently also our Saint, might return to Reims and be restored to their property. He may have been driven to this lest, if he acted otherwise, he should lose by papal authority—as later happened—the archbishopric of Reims, which he had greatly desired and had obtained with insufficient propriety through royal favor.

165. There are, however, those who maintain that, before he was restored to his former condition, the Saint went to Paris from 1081, or even from about 1076, when he withdrew from Reims because of Manasses’ wicked conduct, and that he taught there until the year 1082, when the miracle occurred of the temporarily revived doctor who proclaimed from his bier that he had been condemned.

Bulaeus, in volume I of his *History of the University of Paris*, p. 468, indeed believes that the Saint—although, according to what has been said, he remained with Count Ebal from about 1076 until 1078 or even the beginning of the following year—then moved from Reims to Paris because of Manasses’ wicked conduct and resumed the teaching office there, although from what has been said it is extremely doubtful whether he had ever previously held that office there.

But the several conjectures and arguments by which he attempts in some measure to support this opinion prove absolutely nothing, as is clear from what was said above. We must now examine whether other arguments are of greater weight—arguments brought forward both by him and by others who wish the Saint to have taught at Paris, if not immediately from about 1076, when he withdrew from Reims, then at least from 1079 or one of the following two years.

They say that it is not plausible that Bruno, so great a man, spent three, four, or even more years immediately before his withdrawal into solitude in a completely idle life. That this is indeed implausible may be granted. But since, as I have shown above, the Saint was restored to his former condition at Reims in 1081, what if he also recovered the direction of the schools at that time and held it until his departure for the wilderness? In that case he would not have led an idle life from 1081 until that departure, even if it is maintained that he did not teach at Paris.

Nor should it be thought that he led an idle life in 1079 and the following year, when, according to what was said above, he was more probably living among the canons of the church of St Cunibert at Cologne. It may be that during that period he devoted himself diligently both to the Psalms and to the Epistles of St Paul the Apostle, the two parts of Sacred Scripture which, as I shall show below, he illuminated with highly learned published commentaries.

166. If this is displeasing, and if one wishes to maintain that the Saint did not remain at Cologne during those two years, even granting this, it does not follow that Bruno spent his life in idleness if he was not teaching at Paris. For what if it is asserted that he then withdrew to the monastery of St Mary at Dol and taught there?

It seems reasonable to say that the Saint either then or at another time exercised the office of teacher in that monastery, or at least that, when he carried on this work at Reims, he had there as pupils very many students from that monastery. For the religious inhabitants of that monastery, in the funeral eulogy numbered 169 among those to be published, which they composed for the Saint, seem to profess themselves his disciples in these words addressed to the Calabrian Carthusians:

> “As your holiness is worthy to request; and we, the brothers of the monastery of Dol, moved by compassion for the desolation of your brotherhood, immediately after we heard of the death of our blessed father and master Bruno, took care to offer to Almighty God the assistance of our most devout prayers.”

From the life, therefore, which the Saint would have led in idleness if one refuses to admit that he taught at Paris in 1079 and the following years, it cannot in any way be concluded that he taught there at that time.

Indeed, it appears most probable that the Saint not only did not teach at Paris then, but never taught there at all. For three contemporary or at least nearly contemporary writers—the author who composed the *Chronicle of the Four First Priors of the Grande Chartreuse*, Guibert of Nogent, and the author of the funeral eulogy numbered 173 among those to be reprinted, in which the canons of the church of St Vincent at Noyon lamented the Saint—either indicate or expressly distinguish him as master of the schools of the church of Reims. They would almost certainly have distinguished him by the title “master of the Parisian schools” as well, had he ever taught there as he taught at Reims.

Furthermore, absolutely nothing is found anywhere in any ancient writer of comparable authority and reliability from which it may in any way be inferred that the Saint ever taught at Paris.

[Col. 0097B] 167. But the anonymous author of the hitherto unpublished fourth book of the *Carthusian Annals*, having brought forward three different conjectures by which Egassius Bulaeus wrongly argues that Bruno taught at Paris—see what was said on this subject in no. 112 and following, and elsewhere—reasons as follows:

> “We may add a fourth conjecture, drawn from the funeral eulogies by which the memory of holy Bruno was piously honored by almost all the churches and monasteries of Gaul. How could a man who became so highly esteemed and renowned throughout the entire kingdom of France, and in the churches of that same kingdom—as Guibertus says—have become so famous, if this can scarcely be asserted of the school of Reims and must rather be understood of the Parisian school? For Paris was the seat of the kingdom, the center of France, its most celebrated marketplace, and the queen of academies; and it seemed more fitting that so many friends and disciples who celebrated his funeral should have gathered there.

> “There is no doubt that the students of the suffragan churches and monasteries of the province of Reims studied literature at Reims under Bruno. But when the churches most remote from it are read as having followed his death with lamentations and tears—such as the English, Breton, Norman, Poitevin, Touraine, Sequanian, and many others—we consider it absurd to say that the students of all these churches were educated at Reims. It seems much more consistent with Bulaeus’ view that they came to the Parisian academy, to which Bruno had at some point been transferred.”

[Col. 0097D] 168. He continues:

> “But what shall we say of the Parisian churches that mourned the death of St Bruno with celebrated eulogies, as of a man exceedingly well known to them—namely, the cathedral church of St Mary, the abbey of St Magloire, the abbey of St Germain-des-Prés, the abbey of St Denis, the abbey of St Maur-des-Fossés, and the abbey of St Peter at Lagny? Is it not incongruous that so many clergy and so many monks, established within the fountain of knowledge that is the Parisian academy, should have gone to a foreign diocese to acquire learning? And what we say of the Parisians we testify also concerning the religious of the other monasteries farther away: it was more fitting that they should be educated at Paris rather than at Reims.”

Thus far the anonymous author. He supposes, or even argues, that the Saint taught at Paris chiefly on the basis both of the remarkable fame which he enjoyed throughout the kingdom of France—though, if he had not taught at Paris, he would not have acquired it—and of the great number of churches and monasteries that honored him with the inscription of funeral eulogies and that, had he not taught at Paris, would not seem to have known him in any special way or possessed him as their teacher.

But I do not see why the Saint, even if he had never taught at Paris and had taught only at Reims, could not have acquired that remarkable fame which spread throughout the whole kingdom of France and even through several provinces outside it. Is he not called “of Reims” by the contemporary authors of the *Chronicle of Malleac* and of the historical fragment extending from the time of King Robert to the death of King Philip—see no. 41 and following—because, from the fame of his name, they knew him almost exclusively through what he had acquired at Reims by studying, teaching, and carrying out various duties?

169. Could he perhaps also have been known for a similar reason as “the Parisian”? If you affirm this, I ask you to name even one ancient writer of approved reliability who calls him “the Parisian.” If you cannot do so—as certainly you will not be able to—how will you prove that the fame by which the Saint became renowned had to be acquired by teaching at Paris rather than at Reims?

Moreover, according to the nearly unanimous agreement of all those who assert that he taught at Paris, Bruno did not begin that office there until about 1076, when, as has been said, he withdrew from the city of Reims because of Manasses’ wicked conduct. Yet Guibert of Nogent, a contemporary author, expressly states that he was already renowned before he withdrew from Reims, compelled by Manasses, and before he had therefore taught at Paris.

“Bruno,” he says in book I, chapter 11 of his *Life*, “then exceedingly renowned in the churches of Gaul—at the time when Manasses was miserably afflicting the city of Reims with his wicked conduct, before the Saint’s departure from it—departed from the city with certain other distinguished members of the Reims clergy, out of hatred for that infamous man,” namely Manasses, from the city of Reims.

Therefore even those who maintain that the Saint taught at Paris must in almost every case admit that, although he had never taught there, he could have acquired the immense fame that he did acquire.

It may also be added that those who maintain that the Saint taught at Paris before withdrawing from Reims under Manasses can be answered as follows: Bruno could have become widely renowned, by the time of his death, solely through his highly learned commentaries on the Psalms and the Epistles of St Paul, which he composed and which had perhaps already been widely circulated—even if, in the meantime, he had never taught either at Paris or even at Reims.

170. As for the great number of churches and monasteries that celebrated the Saint in the inscriptions of their funeral eulogies, it does not follow that he was known to all of them, or that he had been their teacher, in the special manner suggested by the Carthusian anonymous author.

For the inhabitants of the Calabrian charterhouse or hermitage did not announce his death and request prayers for his soul only to those churches and monasteries to which he would have been known in this way or of which he would have been the teacher. This is clear from the beginning of the encyclical letter by which they made the announcement. In the following words it indicates to whom it was addressed or to whom it was to be delivered:

> “In the first place, we, the humble hermits of the Calabrian monastery of St Mary, Mother of God, whose founder and superior Father Bruno was while he lived in the flesh, venerate and greet with due submission him whom we believe and confess to be the primate and head of the Church, the bishop of the Apostolic See, together with that entire principal court; and we announce the death of our holy Father on the day before the Nones of October, so that he may be assisted before God by their merits and prayers.
>
> “We also greet the whole holy Church in all its orders and professions: canons, monks, hermits, and holy virgins consecrated to God. Before them all we prostrate ourselves in spiritual presence, asking that they be willing to remember our deceased Father, so that, if any stain adhered to that beloved soul—for there is no just person who does not sin—it may be cleansed through the multiplied intercession and earnestness of prayers, and that he may pass into rest.”

The encyclical letter, announcing his death, was therefore sent to whatever monasteries and churches, whether they knew the Saint or not, as can be understood from this text. Consequently, the immense number of responses or funeral eulogies by which he was honored—since they proceeded from those same monasteries and churches—cannot be used to argue that he was known to all of them in some special way or had been their teacher.

Thus, even if I granted that our Saint, had he not taught at Paris, could not have been known in any special way to all those monasteries and churches, or have been their teacher, it would still not follow that he actually taught at Paris.

171. Nor does it matter that several Parisian churches mourned the death of St Bruno with celebrated eulogies as a man exceedingly well known to them. They may have done so because, although he was not known to them personally or in some other special way, as teachers usually are known to their disciples, he was nevertheless exceedingly well known by reputation, since, as has been said, he had become renowned through the greatest fame.

The same judgment should be made concerning certain other churches and monasteries that mourned the Saint’s death as that of a man exceedingly well known to them. Even if some of the funeral eulogies by which the Saint was honored were inscribed by persons to whom he was known personally or in some other special way, or whose teacher he had been, nothing nevertheless compels us to admit that these persons studied under him not at Reims but at Paris.

For why could the Saint not have had many foreign disciples at Reims as well? Certainly, in the eleventh century, during which Bruno flourished, the schools of different cities and churches were frequented to a greater or lesser degree by foreigners and outsiders according to the fame enjoyed by their teachers, as the authors of volume IX of the *Literary History of France*, p. 30 and following, show.

Therefore, since, while he was master of the schools of Reims, the Saint was, as is sufficiently clear from what was said above, celebrated for the fame of his learning not only throughout all Gaul but also in several distant regions, there can be no doubt that he attracted to Reims an immense multitude not only of natives but also of foreigners and outsiders, so that they might study literature under a teacher of such distinguished renown.

172. Among these, I believe, were Odo or Otto, later Supreme Pontiff under the name Urban II, Robert of Burgundy, bishop of Langres, and three other distinguished men listed in section V—both for the reasons already given and because absolutely nothing can be brought forward to make it likely that they studied anywhere other than at Reims.

Indeed, as regards Urban in particular, he should be said to have studied at Reims rather than elsewhere because it is known from other sources both that he spent some time at Reims and that he served there as a canon of the metropolitan church, as may be seen in Ruinart, volume III of this author’s works, and in Mabillon’s posthumous works.

I therefore hope that anyone who carefully considers everything brought forward thus far will judge it unnecessary to admit that the Saint ever taught at Paris, whether because of the fame of his name, by which he became renowned, or because of the multitude of his disciples or of those who knew him in a special way. The arguments I have brought forward above point in the opposite direction.

But, you may object, the Saint at least taught at Paris when he withdrew into solitude with several companions attached to him. For this is found to have been reported and believed by not a few writers.

That is certainly what they maintain. Yet they were by no means contemporaries of the Saint, and their opinion is not satisfactory: first, because from what has been said it appears that the Saint never taught at Paris at any time; and especially because, when Bruno withdrew into the wilderness, he had already been restored for some time—not at Paris but at Reims—to his former, and perhaps even better, condition, and was living amid the highest favors of worldly fortune, as the diligent reader will easily perceive from what I have chiefly brought forward in no. 154 and the two following numbers.

173. Consequently, even if that dreadful miracle in which the Parisian doctor proclaimed from his bier—first that he had been accused, second that he had been judged, and finally that he had been condemned—really occurred at Paris, as I shall examine below, and even if it was the true reason why Bruno withdrew into solitude, it still could not for that reason be admitted that he was teaching there when it occurred.

For since the Saint appears not to have left Reims, after Manasses’ expulsion from the archbishopric and his restoration to his former possessions or resources, in order to establish his residence elsewhere and cease living in that city before withdrawing into solitude, it follows that, if he taught at Paris at the time when the said miracle occurred—that is, about the year 1082—he had not yet been restored at Reims to his former possessions. Consequently, he must have been restored to them only after the aforesaid miracle, although, according to what has been said, this restoration occurred before he withdrew into solitude.

But, apart from the fact that, according to what has been said, the Saint had more probably already been restored at Reims to his former and perhaps even better condition before 1082, it also does not appear that the restoration occurred after that miracle. For, in the opinion of those who defend the miracle, Bruno decided most firmly on the basis of it to renounce the world, and, once his affairs had been arranged as best he could, he carried out his resolve. It therefore seems scarcely plausible that, after witnessing the miracle, he would have been willing—much less eager—or would even have gone to Reims, in order to recover the possessions and dignities that he had lost there under Manasses.

Accordingly, if the aforementioned miracle must be admitted as true—as I have said, I shall examine it below—it most probably occurred, for the reasons already given, while St Bruno was not teaching at Paris but was merely present there, either to visit friends or for some other reason.

174. Nor should this seem strange or newly invented to anyone. For from the *Chronicle of the Five First Priors of the Grande Chartreuse*, or rather from the eulogy of our Saint contained in it under the title of his *Life*—before whose author, it is thought, no one had committed to writing the miracle of the revived doctor that occurred at Paris—it seems that St Bruno was present at the miracle only because he happened to be staying at Paris.

Listen to the author’s words after he has narrated that miracle, in no. 5:

> “At that time,” he says, “there was there”—namely, at the place in Paris where the miracle occurred—“Master Bruno, a German by nationality, born in the city of Cologne to parents of no obscure standing, a canon of the church of Reims and master there of the schools in theology. Terrified and salutarily moved by the words written above”—namely, the doctor’s cries from the bier that he had been condemned—“he addressed certain companions who were present there,” and so forth.

Thus the older *Life* of the Saint, whose anonymous author would surely have called St Bruno master of the Parisian schools rather than, as he does in the quoted words, master of the schools of Reims, if he had believed that Bruno was teaching at Paris when the miracle he narrates occurred. He is speaking of an event that took place at Paris and that was witnessed there by the Saint while he was teaching.

The reason, I think, that not only Puteanus and the other biographers of St Bruno who flourished at the beginning of the sixteenth century, but also writers of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries whom I shall cite below, are found to report that our Saint taught there at the very time when the aforesaid miracle occurred at Paris—or at least to call him, in the place where they mention this, “master of the Parisian schools,” or to imply that he was so—is that they had either read somewhere that the miracle occurred at Paris or had received this through a tradition communicated to them. Finding that the Saint was present at the miracle and that he had been a master of the schools, they consequently judged that he had been teaching there at that time, even though they found no written testimony to this among writers who were either contemporaries of the Saint or at least nearly his contemporaries.

§ IX. Whether Guibert of Nogent assigns the true reason for St Bruno’s withdrawal into solitude, and whether, besides the vow he had made to assume the monastic habit, Bruno needed another and more serious reason for this withdrawal

Launoius, in a published dissertation on the true reason for St Bruno’s withdrawal into the wilderness, counts the miraculous resurrection of the Parisian doctor among fictions. He asserts that the true reason for St Bruno’s conversion or withdrawal into the wilderness is given by Guibert of Nogent, a contemporary author, in book I, chapter 11 of his *Life*.

I do not transcribe here the whole of Guibert’s text, which Launoius quotes for this purpose in chapter 1, section 4 of the dissertation mentioned above. I give only those words of his that can in some way serve the conclusion Launoius desires. They are as follows:

> “Not long before these days there was in the city of Reims a certain Bruno, a man instructed in the liberal arts and a master of great studies, who is recognized to have received the beginnings of his conversion from the circumstance that follows. After the death of the most famous archbishop Gervasius, a certain Manasses intruded himself by simony into the governance of the aforesaid city. He was indeed a nobleman, but possessed none of the serenity that befits nobility above all. For he had conceived such great arrogance from this novelty that he seemed to imitate the royal majesty—or rather the ferocity of the majesties—of foreign nations. … Since, therefore, he greatly favored soldiers and neglected the clergy, he is reported once to have said: ‘The archbishopric of Reims would be a good thing,’ he said, ‘if it were not necessary to have Masses sung there.’ When every honorable person abhorred his utterly wicked conduct and most foolish ways, Bruno—then exceedingly renowned in the churches of Gaul—with certain other distinguished members of the Reims clergy, out of hatred for that infamous man, withdrew from the city,” namely from Reims.

176. Thus far Guibertus. But does he in fact mention the true reason by which St Bruno was driven into the wilderness? The aforementioned Launoius emphatically asserts that he does, chiefly for two reasons: first, because in his view our Saint, when he left Reims because of Manasses’ wicked conduct, immediately withdrew into the wilderness; and second, because he thinks that the Saint’s departure from the city of Reims was preceded by the conversation mentioned above, which he held with Radulphus Viridis and Fulcius Monoculus concerning the false pleasures of the world.

But neither did the Saint, when he left Reims because of Manasses’ wicked conduct, immediately hide himself in solitude, nor was the conversation mentioned above held before his departure from the city of Reims. Both points are sufficiently clear from what has already been said.

First, since, as I proved clearly in no. 111, the Saint left Reims in 1076 or the following year in order to avoid Manasses, and since, as I shall show below, he did not go into the wilderness and renounce the world before 1081, it is perfectly clear that he did not do so immediately after his departure from the city of Reims because of Manasses’ wicked conduct.

Some, indeed, wish it to be indicated by Guibertus himself, in the place cited above, that the Saint did not withdraw into the wilderness until after Manasses, the archbishop, had been expelled from the see of Reims, that is, shortly after the year 1080, when this occurred. They hold this opinion because, after the words quoted above, Guibertus adds:

> “The nobles, clergy, and burghers afterward drove him”—the archbishop Manasses—“from the see which he had wickedly occupied, when he was repeatedly struck with anathema by Hugh”—called Hugh of Die, later created archbishop of Lyon—“the legate of the Apostolic See, a man most renowned for his zeal for justice, and when Manasses attempted by military force to squander the treasures of the Church.”

Then, after inserting several remarks which, although they concern Manasses, are less relevant here, he continues:

> “But Bruno, having abandoned the city”—namely, Reims—“also proposes to renounce the world; abhorring knowledge of his own people, he proceeded to the territory of Grenoble.”

But, as I shall show below, these writers should not be followed in this matter.

177. In the meantime, even if this is so, the further point made by Launoius in the cited passage does not work against us. He says that the Reims clerics who left the city of Reims with the Saint because of Manasses’ wicked conduct would, unless Bruno then withdrew into the wilderness, have had to follow him for a long time wherever he went, while they waited for God to intervene and convert them and drive them into the wilderness with the Saint.

For, as Guigo, the fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, testifies in our volume I for April, p. 40, no. XI, in the *Life of St Hugh, bishop of Grenoble*, the following persons withdrew into the wilderness with the Saint: Master Landuin, born at Lucca in Tuscany—see in Labbe, volume I of the *New Library of Manuscripts*, p. 639, the *Chronicle of the Four First Priors of the Grande Chartreuse*, of which I supplied the notice in no. 6—two Stephens, one of Bourg and one of Die, Hugh the chaplain, and two laymen or conversi, Andrew and Guarinus. Yet none of these is found to have been among those distinguished Reims clerics who left Reims with the Saint because of Manasses’ wicked conduct.

As for the conversation held by the Saint with Radulphus Viridis and Fulcius Monoculus, the material I brought forward in no. 125 and following proves more than sufficiently that it did not precede Bruno’s departure from Reims because of Manasses’ wicked conduct. Guibert of Nogent also supports this point in the passage cited immediately above, since, after his account of the Saint’s departure from the city of Reims because of Manasses’ wicked conduct and after inserting a few remarks that are irrelevant here, he adds:

> “But Bruno, having abandoned the city”—namely, Reims—“also proposes to renounce the world.”

178. Since, then, the Saint neither went into the wilderness immediately after his departure from the city of Reims because of Manasses’ wicked conduct, nor did that departure follow the conversation held with Radulphus and Fulcius, during which they and Bruno vowed to assume the monastic habit, who will accept Manasses’ wicked conduct as the true reason for which the Saint withdrew into the wilderness?

Certainly Guibertus does not support such a conclusion. Although in the words quoted above he asserts that Saint Bruno “received the beginnings of his conversion from the circumstance” of Manasses’ wicked conduct, he does not say that this conduct was the reason for which the Saint withdrew into the wilderness and completely converted himself.

Indeed, he suggests the opposite when he merely reports that Manasses’ wicked conduct provided the occasion for the beginnings of the Saint’s conversion, and these beginnings are distinct from conversion itself when perfected.

Guibertus should therefore be understood to have written in accordance with the truth in something like the following sense. Compelled to leave Reims because of Manasses’ wicked conduct, Bruno experienced a highly adverse fortune—the sort of pressure under which mortals most often begin to think about God and conceive a reform of life. This led him to hold with Radulphus and Fulcius Monoculus the celebrated conversation in which he vowed that he would shortly assume the monastic habit.

Since that vow may rightly be regarded as the beginning of the Saint’s completed conversion, and since Manasses’ wicked conduct provided the occasion for the conversation in which the vow was made, Guibertus can properly be understood to have written that our Saint received the beginnings of his conversion from the circumstance of Manasses’ wicked conduct—whether, in the meantime, it was from that vow or from the conversation in which it was made that the Saint eventually came to establish the new Carthusian religious order, or whether some new circumstance intervening impelled him to do so.

179. Launoius argues in chapter 1, section 3 of his dissertation on the true reason for St Bruno’s withdrawal into the wilderness that Bruno received from the aforesaid conversation the occasion for establishing his new religious order.

But the anonymous author of the hitherto unpublished fourth book of the *Carthusian Annals* thinks that this conversation contributed absolutely nothing to the establishment of the new Carthusian order. He responds to Launoius, who maintains the contrary, in no. 89 of his work as follows:

> “There …”—namely, in St Bruno’s letter to Radulphus Viridis, in the words transcribed above in no. 125—“Saint Bruno does not speak of a plan to found some new order, but only of a vow to receive the monastic habit. Some opponent may perhaps mock this distinction, which nevertheless will be observed more easily than the distinction noted by Launoius in Bruno’s words quoted immediately above concerning the occasion for establishing the Carthusian order, by anyone who considers the words of St Bruno attentively and without prejudice.
>
> “‘We promised,’ he says, ‘and vowed to the Holy Spirit that shortly we would leave behind the fleeting things of the world and pursue eternal things, and also receive the monastic habit.’ Who does not see that it is one thing to vow to assume the monastic habit and another to form a plan to establish a new religious order?
>
> “Since he immediately adds, ‘This vow would also have been carried out shortly, had Fulcius not then gone to Rome,’ these words sufficiently indicate that they were thinking only about putting on the monastic habit—not in a new order which they themselves would establish, but in a monastery belonging to some other order.”

[Col. 0105A] **180.** “For if they had discussed a new religious order in this conference, they could not have brought such a plan to completion so quickly—as in fact they did not—since they would first have had many things to arrange for carrying out so great an undertaking: the kind and manner of life, the habit, buildings however humble, above all a place suitable for the purpose, and many other matters of this sort, both temporal and spiritual, absolutely necessary for properly instituting a new religious order. Moreover, from the context of the words of the same letter it appears as clearly as daylight that this entire plan, undertaken at that conference, in the course of time came to nothing, as the blessed man himself candidly admits in these words: ‘It would have been carried out shortly afterward, had Fulcius not then gone to Rome; upon his return we postponed carrying it out. Since he delayed, and other causes intervened, divine love grew faint, the spirit cooled, and fervor vanished.’ What could have been said more plainly? For what does it mean to say that ‘divine love grew faint, the spirit cooled, and fervor vanished,’ except to say openly that they not only did not then renounce the world, but that Radulphus and Fulcius also abandoned their plan of renouncing it, while Saint Bruno deferred it to another time? This is signified even more clearly by the words ‘fervor vanished,’ and it becomes clearer still if we consider that Saint Bruno bade farewell to the world not with those with whom he had held the conference and made the vow, but with six others who had not attended the conference.”

[Col. 0105C] **181.** “Nor does it help to reply with Launoius that Saint Bruno was not speaking of his own delay, but of Radulphus’s procrastination.” For Bruno spoke in the plural: “upon his return we postponed carrying it out,” thereby indicating that not Radulphus alone, but he himself also, had delayed with him, and consequently that fervor too had then vanished for a time. For he adds: “Since he delayed, and other causes intervened, divine love grew faint,” and so forth.

“But so that the truth of this matter may become still more evident, account must be taken of the time that elapsed between the said conference and the year in which Saint Bruno withdrew into solitude. For it is certain—and especially so if this conference was held at Reims, as Launoius wishes to place beyond doubt—that between it and Saint Bruno’s withdrawal” (assuming, that is, as will be examined below, that he first devoted himself to the better life in 1084) “eight or ten years elapsed. For we saw above that Saint Bruno was expelled from Reims around the year 1076, and below we shall prove that he instituted his religious order” (that he withdrew into the hermitage of Chartreuse in 1084 will be proved below) “in the year 1084 or 1086, as Launoius himself wrote after Baronius.

“Therefore, whatever Launoius may protest against the distinguished Saussaius, Bruno, who was delaying and postponing the fulfillment of the vow he had made, needed a stronger incentive by which he might finally obey the divine call. That incentive was the horrifying spectacle of the condemned man, by which he was at last shaken to the depths; [Col. 0106A] summoned by God to higher things, he not only thought of taking the monastic habit, but conceived and successfully carried out the plan of embracing a new and most austere way of life.”

Thus far he argues, and rightly, that in the conference Saint Bruno held with Radulphus Viridis and Fulcius Monoculus concerning the false pleasures of the world and the eternal joys of heaven, there was no discussion of instituting a new order. Consequently, that conference was not the occasion—or at least not more than a very remote occasion—for instituting a new order. Indeed, the vow made at it could in no way have imposed upon the saint any obligation to embrace the new and more austere life that he led in the deserts of Chartreuse and afterward of Calabria.

[Col. 0106B] **182.** But I cannot at all accept what he says at the end: that “Bruno needed a stronger incentive by which he might finally obey the divine call” and fulfill what he had promised and vowed at that conference. For although the saint in fact delayed fulfilling what he had promised at the aforementioned conference—most probably held in 1077, according to what was said above—until at least 1081, as I shall prove below, and thus, if not for eight or ten years, at least for a long period of time, I nevertheless do not see why he should have needed to be driven to fulfill his vow by the arrival of some new and stronger incentive.

Since the vow he had made must undoubtedly have come to the saint’s mind from time to time, why could he not have been moved to fulfill it by the very arguments with which, in his letter to Radulphus, he urges Radulphus to satisfy the same vow? Those arguments were certainly most serious and perfectly suited both to reproving Radulphus’s hesitation and to stirring his spirit toward promptly fulfilling his vow. In particular, the saint impressed upon him the strict obligation of fulfilling the vow, and that Radulphus, by failing to satisfy it, would incur eternal punishments.

Hear Bruno speaking to Radulphus: “Although,” he says, “our bodies are separated from one another by a long stretch of land and an even longer passage of time, my affection has nevertheless been unable to be torn away from your friendship.” A little later he continues: “But in the regions of Calabria I dwell with religious brothers and several well-educated men in a hermitage sufficiently remote on every side from human habitation”; [Col. 0106D] and then, after a further interval, he says: “Would that you, dearest brother, might love contemplation alone, so that, warmed by its embrace, you might burn with divine love.”

**183.** A little later he writes: “Flee, therefore, my brother—flee all these troubles and miseries, and transfer yourself from the storm of this world to the safe and quiet anchorage of a harbor.” And again afterward: “Therefore it is worthwhile for you to weigh these matters with careful examination of your prudence. If the love of God does not invite you, if the advantage of such great rewards does not summon you, at least necessity and fear of punishments ought to compel you to do so. For you know by what pledge you are bound, and how almighty and terrible is the one to whom you have devoted yourself as an offering, a gift pleasing and wholly acceptable—one whom it is neither lawful nor expedient to deceive. For he does not tolerate being unjustly mocked.”

Then follow the words transcribed above in section 125, containing the conference discussed here and the vow made at it; immediately afterward, without any intervening material, these words are added:

“What, then, remains, dearest brother, except for you to free yourself more quickly from the bonds of so great a debt, lest, for so grave and so prolonged a crime of falsehood, you incur the wrath of the Almighty and on that account suffer immense torments? Who would leave unpunished the defrauding of a promised gift by anyone subject to him, especially if the gift were of great value and worth in his eyes? Therefore yield—not to me, but to the prophet, indeed to the Holy Spirit, who says: ‘Vow and pay to the Lord your God, all you who bring gifts around him, to the one who is terrible, and to him who takes away the breath of princes, terrible among the kings of the earth.’ Why does the Spirit of God impress all these things upon you, except to press you, having made a vow, to render what you vowed?”

**184.** Here he most earnestly warns Radulphus not to withdraw from “so exalted a pledge” or be recalled from divine charity on account of his riches, dignities, and especially the favor of the archbishop, which he enjoyed. A little later he adds:

“Would that you not despise a friend who admonishes you! Would that you not hear the words of the Spirit of God with deaf ears! Would that you satisfy my desire and my long expectation, beloved, lest my soul be tortured any longer on your account by cares, anxieties, and fear! For if”—which God forbid—“you should depart from this life before fulfilling the vow of your debt, you will leave me wasting away in continual sadness, without any consolation of hope.”

Finally, near the end of the letter, he adds: “I earnestly desire that your brotherhood may long remain safe and mindful of our plan, flourishing without forgetfulness of the vow.”

These are the incentives, these the goads, which Bruno diligently and skillfully employed to draw Radulphus toward fulfilling the vow he had made at the conference held with him. Who could say that our saint, who undoubtedly recalled that vow repeatedly, needed greater and sharper incentives in order to fulfill it? Bruno therefore had absolutely no need of an incentive stronger than that which the making of the vow and the obligation arising from it supplied, in order to put on the monastic habit and thereby fulfill the vow of assuming it. But [Col. 0107D] can the same be said of the new and more austere way of life that he maintained at Chartreuse and afterward in Calabria?

**185.** Since, as I shall show below, the saint probably lived for some time as a monk—or, if you prefer, as a hermit—in the desert of Sèche-Fontaine before withdrawing into the hermitage of Chartreuse, it is possible that, having gradually conceived a greater ardor of divine love there and consequently an increased desire to perform penance, he withdrew into the hermitage of Chartreuse in order to lead a more austere life with others in whom he had inspired the same desire.
