It is also possible that, after making the vow to assume the monastic habit, he went there for no other reason than that, because he had long delayed fulfilling his vow, he wished to satisfy the divine goodness—which he therefore considered offended—by adopting a stricter and more austere manner of life. Thus our saint seems not to have needed any new or stronger incentive than the obligation of the vow he had made in order to withdraw from the world into the hermitage of Chartreuse.

Yet even if this is so, it does not at all follow that, in reality, no stronger and more effective stimulus was added to the vow he had made to assume the monastic habit—a stimulus by which he was finally driven into the hermitage of Chartreuse. Some writers report that this occurred through the horrifying spectacle of the famous Parisian doctor who, restored to life for a time, proclaimed from his bier that he had been condemned by divine justice. Whether we should certainly agree with them must now be investigated.

In order to discuss this important matter suitably—for during the immediately preceding century it exercised the minds and pens of many scholars—I shall divide the whole treatment of it into various articles or sections, so that I may proceed more distinctly and orderly. I shall also frequently express what must be said in the very words of the anonymous Carthusian who composed the fourth book of the Annals of his order, hitherto unpublished: both to provide some specimens of this work, whose absence I understand many people regret, and lest anyone suppose that I have diminished the force of the arguments it contains—which I understand are held in high esteem—for proving the resurrection of the Parisian doctor. I begin with events relevant to this matter that occurred during the two immediately preceding centuries.

## § X. Whether the resurrection of the Parisian doctor, through which Bruno was converted, was removed from the Roman Breviary in the preceding century because it was regarded as false; who first began to attack it, either then or earlier; and who opposed them.

[Col. 0108C]

For a very long period it had already been believed that the most mournful and famous story of the Parisian doctor—who supposedly declared to those standing by that he had been condemned, speaking with his own mouth from his bier—had provided either the cause or the occasion for Saint Bruno’s withdrawal into the hermitage of Chartreuse. At length, during the two immediately preceding centuries, men were found who dared either to call the story into question or even to attack it with arguments gathered from every quarter.

“‘The first,’ as far as we know,”—these are the words supplied by the anonymous author of the fourth book of the Carthusian Annals—“who began to call it into question was Renatus Benedictus (or, more probably, as I shall show below, Papyrius Massonus, who should be named here only in second place), or someone else who published under his name, toward the end of the immediately preceding century—that is, since this was written in the preceding century, before the year 1600—a French version of the Legend of the Saints. In the Life of Saint Bruno, opposite the account in question, he wrote in the margin: ‘Guigo has nothing of this sort in the Life of Saint Hugh, bishop,’ and added: ‘The clerics of the church of Paris contradict this.’

“From this we infer that no one would ever have opposed this story if mention of the Parisian canonicate had not entered into the simple account of what happened; this alone and exclusively seems afterward to have been the seedbed of the entire dispute. Whether that man was a canon or a doctor, we shall say below. The second person to reinforce this doubt was Papyrius Massonus, who died in 1611, a man of more exacting learning.

**87.** “In Book III of the Annals of France, page 232, when discussing the time of the foundation of the Carthusian order, after reporting briefly on Saint Bruno and Landuinus, he adds these words: ‘Peter of Cluny, surnamed Mauriacenus, who lived under Crassus and Louis, names Bruno and Landuinus as the founders of this order. Although he describes the origin, institution, and customs of the Carthusians with the greatest precision, he makes no mention of the Parisian canon who is said to have spoken after his death during the solemn funeral rites.’”

That is what he says; his entire doubt seems to turn on Peter’s silence and on the condemned man’s canonicate. Yet the observations of Renatus Benedictus and Massonus were not weighty enough to prevent Pope Gregory XV from ordering that, after he had established throughout the Church the feast of Saint Bruno, to be celebrated each year by all clerics and religious, an Office for him should be composed, reviewed and approved by the Sacred Congregation of Rites, and inserted into the Roman Breviary—namely, in the year 1623. The three lessons of the second nocturn were taken from his Life; the second of them contains the whole story of this resurrection under the name of “a certain master,” without specifically mentioning either a doctorate or a canonicate.

**188.** “Urban VIII as well, Gregory’s successor, wished the Office of Saint Bruno, together with the account of this astonishing history, to be inserted anew into the Roman Breviary, as the distinguished Saussaius testifies in a didactic letter in these words:

“‘Meanwhile a Roman breviary was published, into which, by decree of Urban VIII, the Office of Saint Bruno had recently been inserted. In it that account was contained in a brief but clear narrative. At that time I, together with other delegates of the most illustrious lord archbishop and of the venerable chapter, was engaged in revising the Parisian breviary. On this occasion the Parisian Carthusians urged that the feast and Office of Saint Bruno be entered for the day of his birth, since it had hitherto had no place in our breviary. Their honorable request seemed deserving of approval. Saint Bruno was therefore entered in the Parisian calendar, but on the condition that the aforementioned account should in no way be mentioned in the lessons of his Office. Shortly afterward it could also be seen that this account had been suppressed in the Roman book of the divine Offices.’”

His words reveal the true cause of the entire dispute, which, as we said above, was nothing other than the mention of the canonicate in certain versions of the account of this history.

**189.** “After several years had passed, Joannes Launoius, properly seeking the highest doctoral distinction, publicly asserted in the theological schools, in a thesis published in print and prompted by Marsyas, a most learned man: ‘Whatever had been circulated concerning the three voices uttered from the bier by the deceased doctor was entirely fictitious and fabricated—in short, an old wives’ tale.’ The bystanders approved, for

> ‘This is not the time for such spectacles.’

“Nevertheless, to speak truthfully and sensibly, he did not receive the degree on that account, but deservedly received it for other specimens of his excellent and learned talent. Pleased with himself because of the approved thesis against the story of the revived man, he went to Rome to establish it with a stronger argument. There he employed every means and effort available to him so that this prodigy might be cut out of the lessons of the Roman Breviary, pretending especially that, because of what had been done when the feast of Saint Bruno was accepted at Paris, the clergy and the Parisian Carthusians themselves desired this.

“These are the methods he used to obtain his goal, as the author—Theophilus Raynaudus, namely—reproaches him on pages 114 and 115 of the *Hercules Commodianus*, in these words:

“‘And you were able to make that excision easier because you, who were present, pressed it by methods known to you: especially with a great uproar, you urged the infamy of the Parisian clergy and academy, and the petitions of the royal city, fabricated by you, so that the account might be passed over even if it were true. Your letters proved the latter. The former matters, which contain the genuine cause of the change’—that is, the change made in the Office of Saint Bruno—‘were clearly confirmed both to me and to others by the wisest theologian of the Congregation of Rites.’

“And a little later: ‘It must be said elsewhere who in Paris assisted you at Rome, causing it to be believed that the Carthusian fathers desired the removal of this account from the breviary,’ and so forth.”

**190.** “The religious men who presided over the Sacred Congregation of Rites, when, by order of Urban VIII”—who nevertheless had earlier, as we saw in section 188, ordered that the Office of Saint Bruno, containing the resurrection of the Parisian doctor, be inserted into the Roman Breviary—“were undertaking the revision of the entire breviary, were men of religious character and incorruptible integrity. They were not deceived by Launoius’s methods, but persuaded by wiser arguments. They arranged for removal from the same breviary not only the account of this history, but also that distinguished and most pious confession of faith uttered by Bruno himself when near death and inserted by order of Gregory XV as the third lesson of the second nocturn, along with many other passages from the lessons of other saints.

“Later, when Christopher Puteanus, prior of the Roman Charterhouse, submitted a petition on behalf of the Reverend Father Prior of the Grande Chartreuse and minister general of the entire order, they were asked about this removal and gave the following answer, as Theophilus Raynaudus testifies:

“‘It was never the intention of the Sacred Congregation to condemn or call into doubt the truth of this account. It seemed more prudent to remove it because the custom of the Church is that, in the sacred Offices of saints who founded religious families, their Lives should be recounted, not the causes that moved them to institute their order.’

“And a little later he adds that he had learned from a very wise man then residing in Rome:

“‘Since the lessons of the Office of Saint Bruno had to be shortened for other reasons, nothing occurred that could be removed with less inconvenience. In any event, the Sacred Congregation did not even consider attacking the truth of his account or depreciating it.’”

**191.** “Shortly before, Bartoldus Nihusius had given similar testimony in a letter to the distinguished Andreas Saussaius”—see the letter, printed at Cologne in 1645, whose title describes it as a didactic epistle—“in these words:

“‘Through Janus Nicius Erythraeus I inquired at Rome of the Sacred Congregation that oversees and presides over the direction of the Rites what its judgment was. And behold, the answer was that what we have mentioned had not been removed from the breviary because it was judged fabulous, but for another reason.’

“This reason is expressly and clearly revealed in a book preserved in the Vatican Library, concerning the changes made in the revision of the Roman Breviary. There, among the acts of the Congregation held on Thursday, 16 January 1631, the following decree is found:

“‘It was resolved that, from the lessons of Saint Bruno, that passage should be removed which is said to have been the cause of his conversion, for the sake of greater brevity and because it contributes nothing to the sanctity of Saint Bruno.’

“These words were taken from the cited book by the learned Emanuele Schelstratius, prefect of the same Vatican Library, at the request of the Very Reverend Father procurator general of our order, who recently sent them to us.

“Therefore this history was not removed from the Roman Breviary because it was considered fabulous, as those who pressed for the correction attempted to persuade people, but for the sake of greater brevity and because it contributed nothing to the sanctity of Saint Bruno. Nor was it the intention of the Sacred Congregation to prohibit those who wished to insert it into their own breviaries from doing so.”

**192.** “For this reason it was afterward restored—namely, in the breviaries printed at Paris in the years 1648 and 1652, ‘at the printing society for books of the ecclesiastical Office, printed by decree of the Council of Trent’—with no one objecting.

“We have necessarily placed this before the reader so that he might be warned that Doctor Launoius ought not to have asserted that the only thing deleted from the lessons of Saint Bruno was whatever concerned that prodigy, and that no more important reason for removing anything from the Breviary was prescribed by the ecclesiastical regulations than the discovery of falsity. For, as we have already seen, that famous profession concerning the body and blood of Christ in the Eucharist, made by Saint Bruno near death, was also removed by the very men who presided over the Sacred Congregation. No one will be so foolish as to think that it was deleted for the reason that it was false, as Joannes Columbi of the Society of Jesus wisely pointed out before us.”

He said this in his dissertation on the beginnings of the Carthusians, especially in section 8, where he also brings forward at numbers 94 and following several matters cited in the words already quoted from the anonymous author of the fourth book of the Carthusian Annals. He writes:

“Likewise, the censors of the Sacred Congregation of Rites in Rome removed from the Breviary that famous profession concerning the body and blood of Christ in the Eucharist, made by Bruno near death. No one will be so foolish as to think that they removed it because it was false. For those who had attended the dying man at Torre in Calabria wrote to their companions dwelling at Chartreuse, and to monks throughout the world, that the dying man had spoken these words:

> ‘I believe that the bread and wine consecrated upon the altar are, after the consecration, the true body of our Lord Jesus Christ and the true blood.’”

[Col. 0112B] **193.** This is what Columbi wrote, followed by the anonymous Carthusian just mentioned. From these statements, and from others brought forward above in this later work, it is clearly evident that the mournful history of the condemned doctor was not removed from the Roman Breviary in the preceding century because it was thought false.

Nevertheless, although this is so, everything else that the same anonymous Carthusian relates in the quoted words does not correspond so certainly to the truth. First, concerning the writers who first began to call into question the prodigy of the Parisian doctor temporarily returning to life, he most probably assigns the first place wrongly to Renatus Benedictus and grants only second place to Massonus.

For although Massonus did not exchange life for death until the year 1611, he had nevertheless published in 1578 his *Annals of France*, in which he expressed his doubts about the matter. Since Renatus Benedictus devoted little attention to critical scholarship, it appears more probable that the marginal note mentioned in section 186 was added not in the first editions of the legend—namely, the edition published in 1577 under Renatus’s own direction—but only in later editions, those of 1585 and, alone among them, the edition of 1593 that I possess, which others prepared.

Furthermore, since in 1631 “that passage from the lessons of Saint Bruno which is said to have been the cause of his conversion” was removed from the Roman Breviary, as is understood from the words cited in section 191, I do not sufficiently understand how Launoius’s journey to Rome, undertaken to arrange for its removal from the Breviary, could—as the words quoted in section 189 imply—have been postponed until a time when he had already presented publicly, in a thesis, the history of the condemned Parisian doctor as a fabricated and childish tale. This occurred around 1635, as he himself indicates in the preface that he placed before his dissertation *On the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Hermitage*, first printed in 1646.

Moreover, although Gregory XV, when the Sacred Congregation of Rites approved the Office of Saint Bruno in 1622, containing the resurrection of the Parisian doctor, granted and conceded by bull in the following year that it might be freely and lawfully recited as a semidouble Office by all the faithful everywhere, Urban VIII nevertheless seems to have been the first to order that this Office be inserted into the Roman Breviary, as I understand from a treatise communicated to me by the Carthusian Fathers of this place.

**194.** I omit other observations of lesser importance that could still be made concerning the words of the anonymous Carthusian quoted above, and now proceed to the principal writers who must be added to those already mentioned: both those who rejected the resurrection of the Parisian doctor, which supposedly drove our saint to Chartreuse, and those who attempted, against Launoius, to defend it as true.

First, since among these are some whose works, being hitherto unpublished, are not available to me, although they are mentioned by the anonymous author of the fourth book of the Carthusian Annals, I shall for that reason transcribe the words of this writer that concern the matter. They are as follows:

“Among those who attempted to prove that the story of the Parisian doctor, who proclaimed from his bier that he had been condemned, was not fabulous, Francis Ganneronius, the most learned monk of Mont-Dieu, would easily deserve first place if his work, hitherto unpublished, had not remained hidden within private walls. When he heard that Launoius had tried, in a publicly presented thesis, to prove that everything previously circulated about the condemned man was fictitious, he took up his pen and wrote a sufficiently extensive treatise. He sent it to the Charterhouse in 1640 under the title *Vindiciae geneseos Carthusiensium* [*Defenses of the Origin of the Carthusians*].

“Several years later Andreas Saussaius, first made famous by his published *Martyrology of the Gallican Church*, defended our cause and clearly refuted several objections of the adversaries in that most learned letter to Bertoldus Nihusius, which Nihusius himself printed at Cologne in 1645 under the title *Epistola Didascalica* [*Didactic Letter*].

“Feeling himself attacked in it, though his name was suppressed, Launoius published in 1646 a dissertation *On the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Hermitage*. Theophilus Raynaudus of the Society of Jesus immediately replied to Launoius in a book entitled *Hercules Commodianus*, published under the name Honoratus Leotardus. Not long afterward, Archangelus Monchozon, professed of the Charterhouse of Toulouse, composed a large volume dedicated to the Reverend Father Pegonius, prior of the Grande Chartreuse. He prefixed to it the title *Carthusianus Alitiphilus*—or *Alethophilus*—‘the Carthusian truth-lover, contending for the ancestral tradition concerning the institution of the Carthusian order.’”

**195.** “In this volume he collected not only the reasons and arguments of the authors mentioned above, but also their entire treatises, copied word for word, adding many refined arguments of his own invention. This work still lies hidden, known almost exclusively to us.

“Finally, Joannes Columbi of the Society of Jesus, the latest champion of them all, arose. In a recent dissertation, *On the Beginnings of the Carthusians*, published in 1668, he added new and powerful arguments and the most certain authorities to those of his predecessors.”

Thus writes the anonymous Carthusian. Although he rightly asserts that Columbi brought forward new and powerful arguments to establish the story of the revived doctor, these were nevertheless not such as to compel the assent of everyone.

In particular, Mabillonius, in more than one place in his works, treats that history—if not as an invention or fable—as at least a very uncertain and doubtful account. Nor are those who wrote after Mabillonius any more favorable to it: the authors of the *Literary History of France* and other learned men who, in works they published, expressed their opinion of that prodigious event, whether only in passing or in some degree deliberately.

Although Papebrochius wrote in Part I, page 32, number 17, of his *Chronological-Historical Attempt* that Columbi “has witnesses for the prodigious resurrection of the Parisian doctor from the years 1391, 1383, 1313, and even 1298 and 1150, so that the last is separated by only forty-nine years from the death of the holy founder, which occurred in 1101,” and although Janningus consequently spoke of Columbi, in his *Apology for the Acts of the Saints*, printed in 1685, as one who had no doubt whatever about the history, in number 24 of his friendly remonstrance, Papebrochius himself later wrote, in his replies to the presentation of errors, published in 1697, article 15, section 20, words that seem to indicate that he was not entirely free from scruple concerning the truth of that history, even though he confirmed what Janningus had said in the place just cited.

**196.** For there he writes, at number 291:

“‘If these two testimonies’”—one from the foundation charter of Chartreuse, signed in 1084, and the other from the Grandmont manuscript, written in 1115, cited by Polycarpus de la Riviere—“‘were sound, I do not see what more could be required for complete certainty. But Columbi’s silence—though he wrote thirty years after Launoyus and refuted him—and his failure to produce these two testimonies make Polycarpus’s reliability suspect to me, and, if Theophilus copied him, make Theophilus’s credulity suspect as well.

“‘Therefore, whether I wish it or not, I am compelled to examine Launoyus, and on page 135 I read that in the cited “charter” there is “not even a single letter concerning the doctor or the Parisian canon,” which “the prior general himself candidly admitted when questioned.”

“‘And on page 137: “In the Grandmont Chronicle, under the year 115, where the page was blank, the following was written in a different script and by a recent hand, in a place not belonging to it: ‘A horrifying spectacle occurred at Paris,’ and so forth, just as we ourselves saw it.”’

This explains why Columbi disregarded those testimonies, silently acknowledging Polycarpus’s bad faith, and why I, knowing nothing about him or about Theophilus, was content for the time being with the authorities used by Columbi—until circumstances require me to treat the argument expressly and examine Launoyus’s replies to the remaining testimonies.

“In the meantime, perhaps others, much more sincere than Polycarpus, will find many more and much older testimonies, closer to the event itself, than Columbi found, although he was assisted by the entire diligence of the order. Thus, as we desire, Launoyus’s contradiction may be completely dissolved and doubt concerning the truth of this history erased from everyone’s minds.”

**197.** Thus far Papebrochius. Since he writes that he was content for the time being with the authorities by which Columbi attempted to prove the history of the condemned doctor, until the matter should be examined expressly, and since he hopes that more and older testimonies than those found by Columbi may still be produced, by which Launoyus’s contradiction might be completely dissolved and doubt concerning the truth of the history erased from everyone’s minds, he seems sufficiently to indicate that he was not entirely free from scruple concerning it.

Nor do I know whether he would have advanced so readily as he nevertheless did into the opinion of those who count the horrifying spectacle of the revived doctor, proclaiming himself condemned, among true histories, if he had foreseen that the older testimonies which, when he wrote these words, he thought might perhaps be found to establish the story with complete certainty would not be discovered down to our own time. Conversely, he might have known that what has now occurred would be uncovered: namely, that the *Chronicle of the Five First Priors of Chartreuse*, or *Treatise on the Account of the Beginning and Advancement of the Carthusian Order*, which Columbi and, after him, Papebrochius thought had been written around 1150—or scarcely fifty years after the death of “Saint Bruno”—was certainly not written before the thirteenth century had already begun several years earlier, as the evidence I brought forward in section 12 and following sufficiently demonstrates.

Whatever judgment Papebrochius reached concerning the mournful account of the condemned doctor, it ought not to prevent us from freely investigating its truth. I therefore proceed from the writers who, during the two immediately preceding centuries, attempted either in some manner to reject that account or, on the contrary, to defend it, to the testimonies of earlier writers in its favor. I shall produce not only earlier testimonies, such as those cited by Columbi, but also others supplied by writers of the fourteenth century and later, which are less ancient. I do this partly because they will occasionally be useful below, but especially because I find that the anonymous author of the fourth book of the Carthusian Annals did the same. The reason given at the end of section 185 chiefly urges me not to depart from him here.

## § XI. Testimonies of Carthusian writers earlier than the sixteenth century concerning the resurrection of the Parisian doctor who publicly proclaimed his condemnation from his bier, and what should be judged concerning the circumstances afterward added to it.

[Col. 0115D]

Not all the Carthusian writers who committed to writing the dreadful spectacle of the Parisian doctor, who cried out from his bier that he had been condemned, presented it with the same accompanying circumstances; consequently, even among those who still believe the story today there is insufficient agreement about how it occurred. For some of them maintain that it happened publicly in a church, or at least before a vast multitude of people gathered around; others, on the contrary, hold that it occurred privately in the hall of the dead man’s house, with only his friends present, among whom were Bruno and several of his companions. Others again assert that the wails of the unfortunate doctor occurred three times on one and the same day, and at one and the same hour of the recitation of the Office; others, by contrast, assign a separate day to each cry.

Indeed, if the aforesaid spectacle took place not publicly before a vast crowd, but within the private walls of the dead man’s house, and if the voice of the unfortunate doctor returned not on three different days but on one and the same day, there would surely be no reason to wonder greatly at the constant silence of all contemporary writers concerning so memorable a story. Thus the gravest difficulty—on account of which this account appears so extraordinarily difficult to believe—would disappear. But since far more writers say that the dreadful spectacle of the condemned doctor occurred publicly in a church, or at least before a vast multitude of people, I shall first inquire what credibility they deserve in this matter, or whether their narrative can appear sufficiently credible and plausible; afterwards I shall examine the opinion of those who maintain that the event occurred within the private walls of the dead man’s house.

I begin by reviewing the testimonies of the older Carthusian writers who have handed down the memory that the dreadful event occurred before a vast multitude, preserving the chronological order in which they were written. Below I shall report those of other writers who did not belong to the Carthusian order.

### 199

Although the author of the *Chronicle*, or treatise *On the Narration of the History of the Beginning and Advancement of the Carthusian Order*, was not as ancient as Columbius believed him to be in his dissertation *On the Origins of the Carthusians* (see no. 12 and the following three sections), he is nevertheless, by common opinion, regarded as older than all the others who committed the story of the temporarily revived doctor to writing. This is so even though, on account of what was said in the passage cited immediately above and what will be said below concerning the Carthusian of Majoreven, the point cannot be regarded as entirely certain.

Before everything else, therefore, I transcribe here the complete testimony supplied by this author, since it ought occasionally to be kept before our eyes. I take it from the older *Life of the Saint*, which, as I have already noted, must be placed before two others that are less ancient, as an appendix to this Commentary. It runs as follows:

> “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1082, or approximately then, while the solemn university flourished at Paris, especially in philosophy, theology, and canon law, as was generally customary, a prodigy of this kind is said to have occurred there. For a certain eminent doctor, who in life—as it seemed—and in reputation, learning, and knowledge was excellently honored and wonderfully esteemed above all the doctors of Paris, having been overtaken by a serious and final illness, did not lie sick for long before he ended his last day.
>
> “Since, throughout the entire day on which he died, the divine Offices had been continuously sung in the hall, according to Parisian custom, while the corpse lay in its bier, on the following morning the whole University of Paris, both students and doctors, having gathered there to provide such an honorable man with a solemn and honorable funeral service and burial, wished to lift the reverend man’s bier, in which the corpse lay, in order to carry it to the church. Suddenly, to the astonishment of everyone, he who seemed and indeed was dead raised his head, sat up in the bier, and, with all hearing, cried out in a loud and terrible voice: ‘By the just judgment of God I have been accused.’ After saying this, he lowered his head and lay down dead, as before.”

### 200

> “At this cry everyone was stunned and terrified, and they decided that he should by no means be buried on that very day, but should be kept until the following day. Accordingly, on the next morning, when a very great multitude had assembled and they wished to carry the aforesaid corpse to the church as before, the dead man, as before, raising his head, thundered in a sorrowful and terrible voice: ‘By the just judgment of God I have been judged.’
>
> “The multitude present, clearly understanding and hearing this cry, was more astonished than before. Consulting with one another about what such extraordinary and unprecedented cries of the dead man might signify, they again decided that he should not be buried until another day had passed. On the third day, however, when, on account of these prodigies, almost the whole city had gathered, and when they wished to carry the corpse to the grave, everything having been prepared, the dead man, as before, resounded for the third time with the loudest and most mournful cry: ‘By the just judgment of God I have been condemned.’
>
> “When this dreadful sentence had been heard, almost everyone was struck with immense fear and trembling, having been informed of the condemnation of so great a man, who among others, and above others, appeared to shine forth in integrity of life, brilliance of reputation, excellence of dignity, and manifold knowledge and wisdom. At that time Master Bruno was there, a German by nationality, born in the city of Cologne of parents of no obscure standing, a canon of the church of Reims and there a master of theology in the schools. Terrified and salutarily moved by the voices written above, he addressed certain companions who were present there in the following or similar words: ‘Come, dearest friends, what shall we do? Let us all together—’ etc.”

The anonymous author of Book Four of the *Carthusian Annals* incorporated into his own work the same testimony transcribed here, as it appears in the Thuanean manuscript, which uses several words different from those expressed here but does not alter the substance of the account. Since he then observed that the anonymous author from whom he transcribed it had possessed great authority among all the later writers of the Carthusian order—as I also noted at the beginning of this Commentary—he lists several of those writers as well.

### 201

First of all, he grants the place of honor among them to Boso, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, in these words:

> “Among these”—namely, those who held the authority of the *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Grande Chartreuse*, or, if you prefer, of the anonymous Carthusian who composed it—“let Boso, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, a man of no ordinary holiness, which God also manifested through miracles, come first. As we have already said, in the treatise *On the Origin and Truth of Perfect Religion*, hitherto wrongly attributed to William of Hyporegia, as we shall prove in its proper place, he reported the entire *Chronicle* of our anonymous author, together with his account of the same prodigy—namely, the resurrection of the Parisian doctor—in the same words, with only a few omissions or alterations, none of them essential.
>
> “And to show how much confidence that author deserved to enjoy among everyone, he first urges his reader ‘not to neglect to write, read, or hear, for edification, the following treatise on the narration of the history of the beginning and advancement of the Carthusian Order.’”

Thus he attributes to Boso most explicitly the treatise *On the Origin and Truth of Perfect Religion*, which our Columbius, as he showed above, assigns to William of Elbura or Hyporegia. Since I hoped that something might perhaps be gathered from the arguments by which that treatise could be proved to belong to Boso, in order to determine more closely the period in which the *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Grande Chartreuse* was written, I inquired about this in a letter to the Parisian Carthusian mentioned above at no. 28. When he referred the matter by letter to the Grande Chartreuse, the reply was that those arguments were indeed unknown, but that this made no difference, since the said treatise, although attributed to William of Hyporegia, could also be ascribed to Boso, under whose auspices William had in some manner composed it.

### 202

The answer differs little from the treatise *On Saint Bruno*, communicated to me by the Carthusians of this place. Its author writes as follows in no. 22 of his work:

> “Nor would Boso have departed from the path of the Fathers”—who had not published what concerned their Carthusian order—“unless, in order to defend his Institute against the calumnies of certain religious of another order, he had been forced to violate the laws of that humble and holy silence, which had been observed for so long, by publishing a very extensive treatise, whether by his own initiative, as they themselves maintain, or by his command, using the pen of William of Hyporegia, an Italian Carthusian and learned man whom he had summoned to the Grande Chartreuse about three years before his death. He entitled this treatise *On the Origin and Truth of Perfect Religion, for the Defense of the Carthusian Order*.”

So far the author. But whoever may ultimately have been the author of that treatise, he certainly held the *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Grande Chartreuse* in high esteem and therefore approved, by his own judgment, the account of the Parisian doctor’s prodigy transcribed from it, since he also urged the reader to read or write it. I now turn to the others who did the same.

Columbius writes as follows in no. 56 of his dissertation *On the Origins of the Carthusians*:

> “The Carthusian of Majoreven wrote a very brief treatise with the title *How the Carthusian Order Began*. The following words are contained in it verbatim:
>
> “‘The matter had reached the point that the body of the dead man was to be placed in a tomb. Therefore, with the clergy standing around, the dead man cried out, saying: “By the just judgment of God I have been accused,” etc. On the following day, etc. Again the dead man cried out and said: “By the just judgment of God I have been judged,” etc. Again he cried out: “By the just judgment of God I have been condemned.” At that time there was a certain master of theology named Bruno, a man of great holiness, etc.’
>
> “The treatise itself is said by its author to have been written ‘in the year 1298.’”

### 203

Since, as I showed above, the length of time before the year 1313 in which the *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Grande Chartreuse* was composed cannot be determined with sufficient certainty, its author may perhaps not have begun writing before the Carthusian of Majoreven mentioned above—that is, before the year 1298, in which the latter himself declares that he wrote.

Whatever the case may be, I place this testimony after the two others that I have already cited from the *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Grande Chartreuse* and from Boso—or, if you prefer, from William of Hyporegia—for the following reason: according to common opinion it is more recent than the first of those two, and I find that the anonymous author of Book Four of the *Carthusian Annals* followed this order.

After briefly mentioning the testimony of the Carthusian of Majoreven from Columbius, he adds:

> “Another anonymous Carthusian, who lived under Elisarius, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, around the year 1360, and wrote a chronicle of that house—or rather continued and expanded the aforesaid treatise or chronicle *On the Beginning of the Carthusian Order* concerning the first five priors of the Grande Chartreuse—related the same history in the same words, though with some parentheses inserted and with the words *hall* and *church* altered. For where the older author has ‘in the hall,’ the more recent one put ‘in the church’; and where the earlier author mentions the church, the later one reads ‘tomb.’ From this it is clear that writers very often adapt the circumstances of histories to the use of the time in which they write.
>
> “That this author had seen the cited *Chronicle On the Beginning of the Carthusian Order* we infer from these words near the beginning of his preface: ‘Although the first five priors described below are found in several Chronicles, nevertheless their successors,’ etc. When he says ‘in several Chronicles,’ he seems also to imply that he possessed Boso’s treatise, into which the aforesaid *Chronicle* had been incorporated, as we have said.”

He does not seem to have been different from the chronicler of the priors of the Grande Chartreuse, whom, as Columbius teaches in no. 54 of his dissertation *On the Origins of the Carthusians*, wrote around the year 1390. Or, if the matter is otherwise, he should be regarded among the Christian writers who recorded the prodigy of the revived Parisian doctor, immediately alongside that chronicler.

### 204

I now continue the series of these writers from our anonymous Carthusian:

> “Henricus Kalkar, formerly a doctor of Paris, prior of the Carthusian houses of Cologne and Strasbourg, and for many years visitor and commissary of various provinces, after resigning all his offices and withdrawing into solitude, composed, among the many books he published, one entitled *On the Origin and Progress of the Carthusian Order*. Many copies of it are preserved in the libraries of the Carthusian houses of Cologne and Dijon, and of the city of Basel, as well as elsewhere.
>
> “In this treatise he included the wretched end of this condemned man in more concise words, as follows:
>
> “‘But behold, amid those dark upheavals of the Church, arising especially from faithlessness . . . by God’s mercy a new light through faith arose at Paris, where at that time students of every nation under the Most Christian king were gathered. It concerned that man dead for four days: after funeral rites had been performed for him on one day, when he was to be buried on the second, he cried out that he had been summoned before the just judgment of God; on the third, that he had been judged; and on the fourth, that he had been condemned, as this is commonly found written among the Carthusians.
>
> “‘This terrible and prodigious event taught those who then heard and saw it most faithfully that the resurrection of the dead and the future judgment are to be awaited; afterward their report of it went out into all the earth. By its horror it instilled fear and dread in every person, so that repentance should be undertaken and one’s condition and life amended.’
>
> “And shortly afterward:
>
> “‘For the venerable man Bruno, who was present at the time, observing that those Parisian cries had not been given for the salvation of the condemned man, but for himself and the others who heard them with him, as a summons to change their condition and life,’ etc.”

This is what Kalkar says. Since he died more than eighty years old, he had already learned this history—or could have learned it—before the year 1340. Nor does he present it as something recently invented by idle men, when he says that he related it “as this is commonly found written among the Carthusians,” that is, among the Carthusians or in the houses of the Carthusians throughout France, Germany, Spain, England, and other regions.

Nor was it found only among the Carthusians, but also among outsiders generally, since, as we shall show below, this history had already been written down by several English authors before the year 1370.

### 205

> “Hermannus Steenkenius, or a Petra, a native of Schüttorf, a contemporary of Henricus Kalkar, professed at the Carthusian house of Diest around the year 1390 and subsequently of the house at Trier, and, as those times required, served for many years as vicar of the Bruges nuns, among whom he died in 1428 with a reputation for holiness. In his treatise *On the Lord’s Prayer*, printed by the typographer John of Westphalia in 1484, he gives testimony concerning so great a spectacle in these words:
>
> “‘The same was true of that wretched master who taught theology at Paris, concerning whom one reads in the Chronicles of the Grande Chartreuse:
>
> “‘“Although he was regarded as a man of great learning and of a good and holy life, he died around the year 1082. At his funeral, when almost the whole body of masters and scholars had assembled and he was to be buried, he said in a loud voice, with everyone hearing: ‘By the just judgment of God I have been accused.’
>
> “‘“On the following day, when many more had gathered, he said: ‘By the just judgment of God I have been judged.’ Therefore, when he had been kept until another day and the whole city had assembled, he said before everyone: ‘By the just judgment of God I have been condemned.’
>
> “‘“Behold how he, falsely and only apparently shining, was expelled from his light into true darkness.”’”

The same treatise was published at Rouen in 1512 by Richard Goupil; but the author is wrongly called Arnold, since the chapter records of the order establish that he was called Hermann.

### 206

> “Aymarus Savelli, a professed monk of the Grande Chartreuse, whose procurator he served for more than twenty years—from the year 1438 until his death in 1459—wrote, or commissioned others to write, several books throughout this period, called *Recognitions*. Among them there is still one written in 1455, in which our history is expressed in exactly the same words in which it appears in our old anonymous author, with this title at the beginning:
>
> “‘How the Carthusian Order Had Its Origin.’
>
> “Immediately after the account of the history, the foundation letters of the Grande Chartreuse from the year 1084 follow. Hence we think that the error of D. Polycarp de la Rivière arose: when listing among the authors who mention this kind of prodigy, he also lists those same letters. For this reason Launoy seems to have attacked him somewhat too sharply, as though he were a man of bad faith in writing.”

### 207

> “Dionysius Richelius, commonly called the Ecstatic Doctor, who flourished among us from about the year 1423 until 1471, when he died, writes the following in the first article of his treatise *On the Proclamation, or Praise, of the Carthusian Order*, frequently printed among his minor works, in the section concerning the origin of our institution:
>
> “‘That miracle is clearly acknowledged and famous: the resurrection at Paris of a dead man, a master of theology, virtuous in outward appearance and externally adorned with great refinement of morals. On the second day after his death, at his first resurrection, he raised himself in the bier and, in a terrifying display, declared: “By the just judgment of God I have been accused.” On the following day he said more terribly: “By the just judgment of God I have been judged.” But on the third day, in the most terrifying voice, he uttered: “By the just judgment of God I have been eternally condemned.” On account of this prodigy the Carthusian Order began. For Master Bruno, a man of profound contemplation,’ etc.”

When Dionysius says “clearly acknowledged,” adding “and famous,” he indicates more brightly than the sun that in the period in which he lived—namely, around the year 1423—there was no doubt whatever about the aforesaid spectacle, but rather that it was regarded as absolutely certain and true, since it had been spread everywhere. The expressions “clearly acknowledged” and “famous” signify this.

This also agrees with what Henricus Kalkar, whom we said had already flourished by the year 1340, stated: namely, that the story was commonly found written among the Carthusians.

### 208

> “Bernard of Egra, a professed monk of the destroyed Carthusian house of Liegnitz in Silesia, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, as Trithemius says, composed in 1481 a dialogue *On the Praises and Miracles of the Blessed Virgin Mary*, printed at Leipzig in 1493 immediately after the author’s death. In it he narrates the origin of the Carthusian Order almost as it is read in the Chronicle of the Grande Chartreuse, which, as we have said, was written by another anonymous author during the flourishing of Elisarius.
>
> “Henricus Arnoldi of Alveldia, who, after serving for five years as a notary at the Council of Basel, entered the order at the Carthusian house of that city around the year 1436 and lived with universal praise until 1487, after having governed that house for more than thirty years to the greatest advantage of both estates, left, among the other monuments of his piety and learning mentioned by Petreius, a *Life of Saint Bruno*. We have not seen it ourselves, but the Reverend Father Mabillon testifies in his *German Journey* that it is preserved in the library of the city of Basel and that it mentions the condemned man. He writes as follows:”

### 209

> “In Lesser Basel, which is joined to Greater Basel by a bridge of piles over the Rhine, there stood before the Swiss disturbances a distinguished Carthusian house. Many manuscripts from it were transferred to that public library which we described above. Only two are worth noting: one contains Guigo’s statutes; the other contains the *Life of Saint Bruno*, beginning with these words: ‘What the wise man says for the sake of exhortation.’
>
> “At the end one reads:
>
> “‘Brother Ludwig Moser, a professed monk of this valley of Saint Margaret at Basel, of the Carthusian Order, transcribed this from the printed work of Father Henricus of Alveldia, formerly prior of the same house, in the year 1486, on 18 April, in the fiftieth year of the aforesaid Father Henricus’s membership in the Carthusian Order.’
>
> “I thought it worth recording this because that little book discusses the famous funeral of the Parisian doctor.”

This is what Mabillon says.

Peter Dorlandus, a contemporary of Henricus Arnoldi, a monk of unimpeachable life, professed and formerly vicar of the Carthusian house of Diest, where he also died most piously in 1507, wrote, among the many works of learning that he left to posterity, a *Carthusian Chronicle* divided into seven books. Our Petreius published it with notes in 1608.

In it he related the substance of this story, changing the style but adding no circumstance that differs from those found in the Chronicle of the anonymous writer who wrote around the year 1360, mentioned above. Nor does he mention the fourth reading of the Office of the Dead, as Launoy carelessly believed, or believed through a lapse of memory.

### 210

These, then, are the Carthusian writers earlier than the sixteenth century from whom I find the prodigious resurrection of the Parisian doctor recorded. Dorlandus is rightly counted among them as well, although he died after the sixteenth century had already begun, because he flourished chiefly in the preceding century and most probably committed to writing at that time what he says concerning Bruno.

There were also writers who enlarged the history of the prodigious resurrection of the Parisian doctor with circumstances not found among the older writers already reviewed. Two later writers of the sacred Carthusian order, namely Puteanus and Blömenvenna, who deliberately described the Life of their holy patriarch at the beginning of the sixteenth century, followed them.

Whether rightly will become clear from what follows. For the words of Blömenvenna, so that it may be evident, by comparison with what has already been given from the older anonymous author at no. 199 and following, what those additional circumstances were, I now transcribe them here. They run as follows:

> “It happened while the venerable Bruno was laboring in these excellent studies, in the time of Saint Gregory VII, Roman pontiff, and Henry IV, emperor, around the year 1082 of our salvation, when the solemn university flourished in the city of Paris, abounding equally in a multitude of students and a large company of distinguished doctors, that a spectacle so dreadful and memorable for all ages occurred there.
>
> “For a certain solemn doctor, foremost among the other doctors, excellently adorned with knowledge and morals and honored above the rest, having been overtaken by a certain serious illness, lay sick in bed and ended the last day of his life. When solemn funeral rites were being prepared for him according to custom, a large multitude of masters, students, and other citizens gathered to honor him. As they accompanied and followed the funeral procession, the body of the deceased was carried to the church in which it was to be buried.
>
> “When the customary Office for the Dead was being sung by the invited clergy who were present, and they had reached the reading that begins ‘Answer me,’ the man who was dead rose, raised his head slightly, and sat up in the bier. With everyone seeing and hearing, and with all astonished at the novelty of the event, he began to cry out in a loud and dreadful voice: ‘By the just judgment of God I have been accused.’”

### 211

> “After saying this, he lay down again. Those who had heard and seen these things, greatly and not without reason terrified, prudently and carefully decided to postpone his burial until the following day, awaiting the outcome of the event.
>
> “On the following day, therefore, when so great a spectacle had already become known throughout the entire city, a very great and almost innumerable multitude of both sexes gathered at the aforesaid church. When the funeral rites had been resumed and continued from that point, and they had reached the beginning of the aforesaid reading, the same dead man, raising his head as before, began to cry out and say: ‘By the just judgment of God I have been judged.’ After saying this, he withdrew again within the bier.
>
> “Yet the astonishment among those standing around increased greatly, as they marveled at an event more terrifying than can be believed. Since, however, they had not yet become certain from these words that he had been rejected—for the expressions ‘I have been accused’ and ‘I have been judged’ could also be understood in a favorable sense, as though he had first been unjustly accused before the tribunal of Christ by him who hastens to destroy all things, and had then been freed from his slanderous accusation by God’s just judgment—it pleased everyone to postpone his burial until the third day.
>
> “On the third day, therefore, there was an enormous gathering of men and women, so that almost the whole city streamed together to await so astonishing a judgment of God. And behold, while the funeral rites were being continued and performed in the former manner, the same dead man rose for the third time and said, with a great bellowing and a despairing voice, dreadful to all mortals: ‘By the just judgment of God I have been condemned.’
>
> “Having said this, he laid back his head, swallowed up in everlasting destruction. This voice, so astonishing and dreadful and unheard of since the beginning of the world, left almost all who were present lifeless with terror. Nevertheless, judging him to be rejected by the Lord and condemned by His just judgment, as he himself had testified, they declared him unworthy of every suffrage of the Church and of ecclesiastical burial, and had him buried in a dungheap.”

### 212

> “But since in Paris and in the other neighboring churches the fourth reading in the Office for the Dead begins in this way: ‘How many iniquities and sins I have!’ etc., some report that the preceding words, namely ‘Answer me,’ were thereafter removed from that reading in memory of the judgment, so that fear of it might remain perpetual and indelible.”

Puteanus also presents this account in no. 4 and the two following sections of his edition of the Saint’s Life, and indeed in exactly the same words. It is easy to understand why this is not surprising from what I discussed in § I concerning the Life of the Saint composed by Blömenvenna.

Now compare these words of Blömenvenna, and consequently also those of Puteanus, with the words transcribed here from the *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Grande Chartreuse* at no. 199 and following. You will see that in the latter the history of the Parisian doctor is not furnished with the same accompanying circumstances as in Puteanus and Blömenvenna.

In the first place, the author of the aforesaid Chronicle writes that the doctor’s three resurrections and cries occurred in the hall of the dead man; Puteanus and Blömenvenna, by contrast, write that they occurred in the church. But this divergence of these two writers from the Chronicle, since the same difference is also found among older writers—see the words of the anonymous Carthusian transcribed above at no. 203—and will be encountered again below, need not detain us here.

Turn your attention instead to the two other differences that follow. Puteanus and Blömenvenna report that the doctor, having revived momentarily, uttered his three cries from the bier when the recitation of the Office for the Dead had reached the reading whose beginning is “Answer me,” and that his body was also buried in a dungheap. The *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Grande Chartreuse*, however, makes absolutely no mention of these two circumstances accompanying the dreadful history of the Parisian doctor.

### 213

Since other ancient writers likewise do not mention them—whether the Carthusians already cited or others belonging to whatever institution, who will be mentioned below—I believe that these details ought to be removed from the history of the Parisian doctor, even if the history itself is admitted as true.

But from where, finally, did Blömenvenna—or rather Puteanus, from whom Blömenvenna took them—draw those two circumstances, which according to what has been said are found nowhere among the ancient writers?

The anonymous author of Book Four of the *Carthusian Annals*, not yet published, writes opportunely for the present purpose at no. 85 of his work:

> “Berthold Rembold committed to print at Paris in 1508 a *Life of Saint Bruno*, which he prefixed to his commentaries on the Epistles of Saint Paul. The anonymous author of this Life described the history of the condemned man at length. But he was the first of all to publish that the man had uttered the words of his condemnation at the words ‘Answer me.’
>
> “He does not, however, assert this outright, but adds it only tentatively, with the following parenthesis: ‘if any credence is to be given to the reports.’ Our Sutor, who lived at the same time and published his treatise *On Carthusian Life* shortly afterward, does mention the same words, but says: ‘as some writers have recorded, while the others remain silent.’
>
> “Certainly all the authors whom we listed above were silent about it. But he does not say who those writers were among whom Sutor had read mention of this circumstance. Nevertheless, we believe that the anonymous author of the aforesaid Life of Saint Bruno was among them.”

The first of the two circumstances mentioned above is therefore found in two writers of the sixteenth century. Since one of them speaks not assertively but only doubtfully, he sufficiently indicates that the authors from whom he had read this detail were neither of great antiquity nor of great authority. The other, since he does not name the authors in whom he found it, cannot make us believe that they were not much more recent than those reviewed above, who make no mention of the same detail.

### 214

Since this is so, it remains established that the aforesaid detail is not found among the older writers who were either the very first, or immediately followed the first, to commit the fatal spectacle of the Parisian doctor to writing.

Nor should you object here with Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Trond, who, as some report, mentions it in a book entitled *On the Sacred Calculation of Time* as follows:

> “Seven years ago, while Gregory VII occupied the first chair, when I was in Paris for the sake of study, I saw an astonishing event worthy of all remembrance, and I was not the only one to marvel and praise God. A cleric named Raymond Milleban died. On three alternate days, at the same hour of the Office at which the reading said to begin ‘Answer me’ was being recited, he rose from his bier and cried out in a dreadful voice: ‘By the just judgment of God I have been accused’; on the second day, ‘Judged’; on the third, ‘Condemned.’ After this, all the clergy ceased praying, and the corpse was immediately expelled from the church and given an ass’s burial.”

This testimony is so clear in support of the prodigious resurrection of the Parisian doctor that, if it really belonged to Theodoric, who—as the words just quoted suggest—was an eyewitness to the event, it would place the story beyond all controversy. Nevertheless, it is very probably—indeed, not to say undoubtedly—fictitious, as I shall show below.

As for the burial of the unfortunate doctor in a dungheap, which Puteanus and Blömenvenna assert, I do not doubt that they drew it from authors who preceded their own age. But there is no reason whatever to suppose that those authors were among the first, or even among the first immediately following them, to commend the spectacle of the revived Parisian doctor to writing.

Thus, from everything that has been said, it is clear that Launoy could not rightly reject the story as an invention or fable on account of the two details now mentioned concerning the prodigious resurrection. Even if these details are regarded as false, for any history to be pronounced true or false, account must be taken only of the circumstances with which it was clothed by the earliest and oldest writers, not of those with which later writers arbitrarily embellished it.

## § XII. The testimonies of writers earlier than the sixteenth century who did not belong to the Carthusian order are produced.

Among authors who were not members of the Carthusian order and who before the sixteenth century bore witness to the prodigy of the Parisian doctor’s return to life, the anonymous author of Book Four of the *Carthusian Annals* assigns first place to Caesarius of Heisterbach, who flourished toward the end of the twelfth century and the beginning of the next. But since I have resolved here to bring forward only those testimonies [Col. 0126B] that unquestionably support the prodigious resurrection of the Parisian doctor and the subsequent withdrawal of our saint into the wilderness—as the memory of his biographer and other earlier writers, either already cited above or soon to be cited below, attests—and since there are some who maintain that Caesarius was not speaking of the prodigy of the Parisian doctor’s return to life, I shall not list here this author’s testimony, although I shall discuss separately below what judgment should be formed concerning it. Nor shall I list the testimony mentioned above, which, although some attribute it to Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Trond, will nevertheless, as I have already indicated, be shown by what follows most probably to be spurious and fabricated.

I also pass over here [Col. 0126C] the testimony produced by the anonymous author of Book Four of the *Carthusian Annals* from the author of a work mentioned below, entitled *On the Four Rivers of Paradise*. For according to this account, the prodigious resurrection of the Parisian doctor did not occur in a church or publicly before an innumerable crowd, but privately in the dead man’s house, before only a few of his friends. The present undertaking requires that only those testimonies be reviewed which assert that this dreadful prodigy occurred publicly. Here, then, are the passages relevant to the matter, transcribed from Book Four of the *Carthusian Annals*, hitherto unpublished and very frequently cited, together with the observations that its anonymous author added to them.

[Col. 0126D] 216. “There still exists,” he says, “at Mont-Dieu a substantial volume, written on excellent parchment, containing the Lives of the Saints. Brother John, a monk of the Abbey of Saint-Arnulf of Metz, brought it with him to Mont-Dieu; he assumed the Carthusian habit around the year 1324. The codex bears this title: *The Golden Life concerning the Legends of Many Saints, with Certain Very Useful Additions.* At the end, in red letters, the following is written concerning the date when the codex was written:

“‘Brother John, monk of Saint-Arnulf of Metz, son of Bertrand called Trancon, surnamed of the Holy Cross, caused this book to be made and written, and it was completed in the year of the Lord 1322, on the vigil of Saint Vincent the Levite and Martyr. When the book is finished, praise and glory be to Christ. Amen.’

“In this [Col. 0127A] volume, then, the history of the man condemned is described under the following title: ‘Here begins how the Carthusian order was instituted.’

“‘As our fathers have related to us, there was a certain great cleric, actually teaching theology at Paris, a man of great name and of no ordinary reputation. He was brought at last to the end of his life. Because of the loss of such a man and such a master, all the other clerics who were present were greatly saddened and assembled for his funeral, as is customary at Paris. When everything pertaining to the funeral had been honorably and properly prepared, the time came for the dead man’s body to be placed in the tomb. As the clerics stood around, he who had died cried out, saying: “By the just judgment of God I have been accused.”’

[Col. 0127B] 217. “When the said masters and clerics heard this, and were not without reason astonished, they took counsel and carried the body back into the church, reserving it until the following day. On the next day, after the funeral rites had again been celebrated, when they wished to place the body in the tomb, the dead man cried out again and said: ‘By the just judgment of God I have been judged.’

“Then the said clerics were more and more astonished. As they consulted among themselves about what they ought to do, some said that ‘judgment’ could signify something favorable or unfavorable. Accordingly, it was commonly agreed that the dead man should be kept unburied until the following day also; and this was done.

“When the rumor of these events had spread, almost the entire city assembled on the following day. As they were placing the dead man in the prepared grave, he cried out again [Col. 0127C]: ‘By the just judgment of God I have been condemned.’

“The said masters, having heard these words and held careful deliberation, declared that he was damned. At that time there was a certain canon of Reims, a master of theology, named Bruno, a man of great holiness and profound understanding. After carefully considering what he had heard, he secretly called some of his students and said to them:

“‘Behold, you see . . . what we ought to do. If a man of such knowledge, such a life, and such reputation says that he has been accused, judged, and condemned, what ought we, miserable sinners, to hope for?’

“When they said to him, ‘Master, we are ready in all things to follow your counsel,’ he replied: ‘I advise that we flee the world and the things of the world and dwell in solitude, according to the saying: “Behold, I have fled far away and remained in solitude” (Psalm 54:8). And let us begin for ourselves an order of penitence and security.’”

218. “And he added:

“‘We have a holy bishop in the regions of Burgundy, in the city of Grenoble, in whose diocese there are deserted and almost inaccessible places. Let us go to him and do everything according to his counsel.’

“Thus seven men came, united and of one mind. When they entered the aforesaid city, it happened that the holy man, the bishop mentioned above, fell asleep in his chamber. In a dream he saw—and behold, seven stars were falling before his feet and afterward ascending over various mountains and through many deserts to a certain place [Col. 0128A] very terrible and remote from human beings; and there they stood.

“When the said bishop awoke and was reflecting on the vision of the seven stars, Master Bruno arrived with his companions. As the seven men fell before the holy man’s feet, he considered in his heart the seven stars, for they themselves were seven. He graciously raised them up to kiss them. After asking and carefully learning the reason for their coming, he said to them:

“‘I know the place prepared for you by God.’

“And with great labor he led them to the place where the seven stars had stood and said: ‘Behold your place.’

“There, with the holy man himself assisting them, they began to build the first house of the Carthusian order, which is now called the Charterhouse.”

[Col. 0128B] 219. “These are the passages found there. They do not differ from the others, but it should be noted that Saint Bruno is said to have addressed his companions privately. It is also probable that the author of this codex had seen the *Chronicle* published by our anonymous author”—see the words transcribed from it in nos. 199 and following, and in no. 12 and the two following sections—“around the year 1220.

“Fifty years ago, a manuscript codex of the church of Longpré in the diocese of Amiens was preserved in the Charterhouse of Montreuil. A certain monk of Mont-Dieu then read the aforesaid history in it. This codex also contained many French poems together with a letter or treatise *On the Solitary Life*, addressed to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu in the name of William. The codex was given to the Charterhouse of Montreuil around the year [Col. 0128C] 1330, as is recorded in it: ‘By Sir Robert Bataille, canon of Longpré in Santerre, to the Carthusians of Montreuil.’

“From these facts it is clear that this history was extremely well known at the beginning of the fourteenth century, and consequently that its origin was very ancient. For it is not likely that it was invented at the same time in so many places by unanimous agreement.”

After making these observations, the Carthusian anonymous author intersperses the testimonies already cited and those still to be cited below with ancient paintings and panels which depict the fatal spectacle of the doctor crying out that he was condemned and may therefore in some way serve as testimonies. I therefore add immediately the words with which he introduces them.

220. They read as follows:

“Pope Innocent VI of that name ordered the origin and progress of the Carthusian order to be painted in the refectory of the Charterhouse of Villeneuve, which he founded in 1356, beginning with the conversion of Saint Bruno and his companions. Among the other panels, one can still be seen there depicting the frightening spectacle of the condemned man.

“Although Launoius despised and ridiculed the paintings and colors in this history, we cannot fail to append to the aforesaid panels a prayer book used by John, Duke of Berry, son of King John of France, born in 1340 and deceased in 1416. We now have this book in our hands in the Charterhouse: it is written in polished and graceful letters, with gilded characters interspersed, and is ornamented here and there with many images painted with exquisite workmanship in oil. Among these are eight that depict the entire history of Saint Bruno’s conversion. Three of them most elegantly represent the condemned man’s threefold resurrection, with captions for the threefold utterance—namely, accusation, judgment, and condemnation.

“Someone who had not seen the book, wishing to make the testimony of its paintings appear older and more striking, wrote that the aforesaid duke was not the person who commissioned these images and therefore believed that they had been painted long before. But we frankly admit that they were not older than the lifetime of that prince, as appears from the first leaf of this book, where we read the following:

“‘Ces heures fit fair tres-excellent et puissant prince Jehan, fils de roy de France, duc de Berry et d’Auvergne, conte de Poitou, d’Estampes, de Bouloingne et d’Auvergne’—

“that is:

“‘These prayer hours were made by order of the most excellent and powerful prince John, son of the king of France, duke of Berry and Auvergne, and count of Poitou, Étampes, Boulogne, and Auvergne.’

“Then the name of the writer or painter is subscribed as follows: ‘Flamel.’ Everyone who sees his work admires it so greatly that it deserves a place among the outstanding painters of this period.”

221. The Carthusian anonymous author now returns to the testimonies of writers who were not members of his order and continues as follows:

“Ranulf Higden, a monk originating in the western part of England, who was living in 1363, published, among the many works he wrote, the *Polychronicon*, comprising seven books. In its seventh book, chapter 4, speaking of Saint Bruno and the reason for his conversion, he says:

“‘Bruno, born at Cologne, went to Paris, then most famous for its studies, for the sake of learning. There, after becoming a canon, he held a position among the professors. Moved by the voice of his teacher, for whom funeral rites were already being prepared and who, with his head protruding from the coffin, was complaining that he was condemned, he went out into a certain wilderness, accompanied by six others, and led a hard life. The place where they lived gave its name to the order of the Carthusians. After six years he was recalled by his disciple Urban, who was already presiding over the Roman Church, and for some time he rendered him assistance in the affairs of the Church. But weary of the labors of the sacred court, he returned to his former place, at the same time rejecting the archbishopric of Reggio—which he was being ordered to accept.’”

This author is mistaken when he says that Saint Bruno became a canon at Paris and, after rendering service to Pope Urban, returned to his former place, by which he appears to mean the Charterhouse. But such lapses are minor and cannot detract from his credibility concerning what he relates about the history of the condemned man. These details, moreover, agree sufficiently with the narrative of the Metz codex, in which—as will be mentioned repeatedly below—that unfortunate man is said to have been the master or teacher of the three men who had spent the night in prayer around his corpse.

Launoius did not criticize this author because he did not know him. We obtained these materials twenty years ago from the Charterhouse of Villeneuve in our province of Aquitaine. Whether they were excerpted from a manuscript codex or from a printed treatise by the author, we confess that we do not know.”

222. “At about this time—that is, in the fourteenth century—there lived John Iperius, a Benedictine of the Abbey of Saint-Bertin in the diocese of Saint-Omer. In the chronicle of that monastery, while discussing the foundation of the Carthusian order, he mentions our history. The exact words of this chronicle—which is now included in Martène, volume III of the *Anecdota*, but had not yet been printed when this was written—are given below, as they were courteously sent to us by the Reverend Father Mabillon:

“‘At the University of Paris a certain very distinguished doctor of theology died, and a multitude of masters and students assembled for his funeral. [Col. 0130B] When the dead man’s body was to be placed in the tomb, he cried out, saying: “By the just judgment of God I have been accused.” The masters, astonished, carried him back into the church.

“‘On the following day, after Mass and the funeral rites had again been celebrated, when he was to be buried, he cried out again: “By the just judgment of God I have been judged.”

“‘On the next day, after Mass and the funeral rites had been celebrated, as he was being placed in the tomb, he cried out again: “By the just judgment of God I have been condemned.”

“‘Believing that he was truly condemned, they departed. Among the others there was a certain distinguished doctor named Bruno, a canon of Reims. Terrified by this event, he said to some of his students: “What shall we do, when a man of such knowledge says that he has been accused, judged, and [Col. 0130C] condemned?” When they promised to follow his counsel, he said: “Fleeing the world, let us begin in solitude an order of penitence.”

“‘With this purpose, Master Bruno and six companions of one mind came to the city of Grenoble, among the mountains of Burgundy.’”

223. “On that day the holy man who was bishop of that city saw in a dream seven stars falling before his feet, then ascending [perhaps: to or through] the deserts as far as a certain terrible place, remote from human beings, and standing there. Immediately, that same morning, Master Bruno arrived with his companions, falling before the bishop’s feet. The bishop, considering in his heart the seven stars—for they themselves were seven—graciously raised them up to kiss them. After learning [Col. 0130D] the reason for which they had come, he led them to the place where the seven stars had stood, saying: ‘Behold the place prepared for you by God.’

“There, with the holy bishop’s assistance, they began to build the first house of the order, which is called the Charterhouse.”

This is his account, relating the vision of Saint Hugh somewhat differently from the way it is read in his Life, published by our Guigo. Launoius did not know this author either. Iperius died in 1383.

The authority of John Gerson, the most celebrated chancellor of the illustrious University of Paris, follows. Launoius thinks that he was the first to write about the doctor’s resurrection. But since it is clear from what has been said above that the story had been committed to writing more than two hundred years before Gerson’s death”—which occurred in 1429—“according to the view of the Carthusian anonymous author”—namely, by the anonymous author who wrote the *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Charterhouse* around the year 1220, though the writer of the present work is uncertain about that date—“Launoius’s arguments, by which he attempted to undermine the testimony of so great a man, collapse.”

224. “But more on this below. Saint Antoninus was almost Gerson’s contemporary, and he gives a lengthy account of this history. Launoius asserts that this saint greatly enlarged the account transmitted by Gerson with additions of his own invention. But the contrary is evident from the words of the Carthusian anonymous author, who wrote around the year 1220”—namely, the *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Charterhouse; see the relevant material cited in no. 12 and following—“quoted above. Antoninus appears to have taken his narrative from him, changing only the style and a few words, such as *ecclesia* for *aula*, ‘church’ for ‘hall,’ and *sepulcrum* for *ecclesia*, ‘tomb’ for ‘church,’ together with a few other similar changes.

“Another anonymous author had already done this before him, compiling the *Chronicle of the Charterhouse* around the year 1360, as we have noted in its proper place. Saint Antoninus added absolutely nothing except the asinine burial.

“The prayer of Saint Bruno to his companions, which Launoius attacks as though Saint Antoninus had invented it, is found in our Boson”—or at least, as you may see from what was said in no. 8, in the author of the treatise *On the Origin and Truth of Perfect Religion*—“who had borrowed it from the same anonymous author, as can also be proved from the Thuaneus codex, where it is written out in full just as it was read in the older codices.

“For this reason that old author should not be attacked along with Antoninus. Following the custom of many historians, he described Saint Bruno as addressing his companions and exhorting them to despise the world—not in the blessed man’s very words, but in similar ones, as he himself acknowledged, writing as follows:

“‘There was Master Bruno, who, salutarily terrified and moved to compunction by the words mentioned above, addressed certain of his companions who were present there in these or similar words,’ etc.”

225. “After Saint Antoninus’s testimony, Launoius adds that he deliberately passes over Dionysius the Carthusian, John Nauclerus, Hartmann Schedel, Polydore Vergil, Sixtus of Siena, Gabriel Prateolus, and other more recent writers, whom he asserts to have ‘changed almost nothing in Antoninus’s narrative, although they changed something in its wording.’

“That is true of Nauclerus, Schedel, and Prateolus, but not of the others. For our Dionysius mentions only the three days on which the condemned man uttered those terrifying words; he says nothing about the church, the asinine burial, or Saint Bruno’s prayer to his companions. The same is true of Polydore Vergil and Sixtus of Siena, who say in a few words that Saint Bruno, having heard a certain friend of his cry out after death, ‘By the just judgment of God I have been condemned,’ was thereby terrified and withdrew with some companions to a deserted place. In these words, certainly, the whole substance of the event is contained, and we assert that substance to be entirely true.”

The Carthusian anonymous author, so frequently cited, then adds the words transcribed above in no. 213, in which he makes certain observations concerning the anonymous author of the *Life of Saint Bruno* published in Paris by Berthold Rembold in 1508. He then discusses several matters relevant to his own position concerning the testimony of Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Trond, already cited above.
