He sufficiently indicates that he is uncertain whether this testimony is genuine or spurious—and with good reason, as will become clear from what I shall bring forward in the following section.

§ XIII. Whether Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Trond, may rightly be counted among the writers who testified in favor of the Parisian doctor’s resurrection and its accompanying circumstances

The anonymous Carthusian who composed Book Four of the *Annals of his Order*, hitherto unpublished, is about to bring forward the more ancient writers who, although not Carthusians, nevertheless bore witness to the resurrection of the Parisian doctor and to its principal accompanying circumstances. He introduces them in no. 73 of his work as follows:

“Having set forth above the testimonies drawn from authors belonging to the Carthusian profession, we now pass to the testimonies of external authors, that is, those who are not of the Carthusian order. Among them we could include Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Trond, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Liège, and begin this series with him, because he lived around the year 1100 and was a contemporary of Saint Bruno. Nevertheless, we omit him because we have not seen his works, although we know from trustworthy men that his words have been reported, in which he narrated this history” of the unfortunate Parisian doctor. “We shall nevertheless speak of him more fully below when the occasion arises.”

This is what he says. He fulfills in fact the promise made at the end of this passage after citing the testimonies of several external writers, writing in no. 86 of his work as follows:

“There is also another man who is said to be the first author and eyewitness of these words”—namely, of the fourth lesson, at the beginning of the recited Office for the Dead, to which the unfortunate doctor responded: first, that he had been accused; second, that he had been judged; and finally, that he had been condemned—“namely, Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Trond, who lived around the year 1100, or else, whoever he may be, the author of the book *On the Sacred Reckoning of Time*, in which they assert that the Parisian prodigy is described . . .”

The words of no. 214, already transcribed and therefore not to be transcribed again here, in which this event is said to occur in that work, are merely repeated by the anonymous Carthusian, who then continues:

“If the authority of this narrative could be established, nothing clearer or more certain could be produced to substantiate the truth of this history.”

227. “The first person to bring Theodoric forward as a witness was John Galaudus, a priest of Toulouse and doctor of theology, who, moved by a pious affection toward the Carthusian order, composed its *Chronicle* in 1615. Since he was prevented by death from publishing it, he left and donated it to the Charterhouse of Paris. In that work, where he discusses the doctor’s resurrection, he used the testimonies of two authors to prove it: namely, Caesarius of Heisterbach and Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Trond in the diocese of Liège. He himself reported their exact words as we transcribed them above, saying of Theodoric that he had these words ‘in his very elegant volume *On the Sacred Reckoning of Time*.’

“From this it is clear that the Carthusians did not ‘heap a new falsehood upon’ this history, as Launoius reproaches them in the conclusion of chapter five, when, in order to confirm it, they presented the authority of Theodoric to Bartholomew Nihusius in good faith on the basis of Galaudus, an honest and learned man.

“Nevertheless, we know that neither Trithemius nor Possevinus expressly lists among the books written by the said abbot a *Chronicle* or a book entitled *On the Sacred Reckoning of Time*, which Galaudus attributed to him—unless perhaps it is included under this general statement by Trithemius: ‘He wrote many other things that did not reach me.’

“However that may be, let trust remain with Galaudus, the first transcriber of this text, until something more certain is revealed.”

Thus far the frequently cited Carthusian anonymous author, who rightly judges that nothing more suitable or better adapted to establishing unquestionable faith in the prodigious resurrection of the Parisian doctor could be produced than the testimony of Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Trond, transcribed above in no. 214—provided only that its genuineness could be established.

228. But that testimony appears very probably to be spurious because it seems most probably to contain matters alien to the truth and consequently inconsistent with Theodoric, a contemporary author and eyewitness. The matter will become clear from what I am now about to say.

The fact that a lesson beginning with the words “Answer me,” and therefore taken from the Book of Job, was used in the Parisian Office for the Dead in the time of our saint is indeed indicated very plainly—see no. 214. But John, bishop of Avranches, in a book that he composed *On Ecclesiastical Offices* in the time of Saint Bruno, reports the following. Launoius bears witness to it in chapter 3 of his dissertation *On the True Reason for Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Wilderness*; on this point I find that no one disputes Launoius’s reliability:

“On the day after All Saints’ Day, let a solemn celebration of all the dead be held, in which neither hymn nor invitatory is to be said. Two clerics shall sing each responsory; two shall direct the choir; two, wearing copes, shall sing the Gradual; four shall sing the Tract at Matins; and the Hours of the day shall in no way be omitted, but the festive Office for the Dead shall follow these said in the ferial manner.

“After Prime has been said, let three psalms be sung in one tone: *Ad Dominum cum tribularer* [‘To the Lord when I was in distress’], *Levavi* [‘I lifted up’], and *Laetatus sum* [‘I rejoiced’]; and, after the verse has been said, let *Kyrie eleison* be sung. After the Lord’s Prayer has been completed, with only the first chapter, let the prayer *Requiem aeternam* follow. The same is to be done at the remaining Hours, except Matins.

“At Terce: *Ad te levavi* [‘To you I lifted’], *Nisi quia Dominus* [‘If the Lord had not been’], *Qui confidunt* [‘Those who trust’]. The versicle shall be *A porta inferi* [‘From the gate of hell’].

“At Sext: *In convertendo* [‘When the Lord restored’], *Nisi Dominus aedificaverit* [‘Unless the Lord builds’], *Beati omnes* [‘Blessed are all’]. The versicle: *Non intres in judicium* [‘Enter not into judgment’].

“At None: *Saepe expugnaverunt* [‘Often they have attacked me’], *De profundis* [‘Out of the depths’], *Domine non est* [‘Lord, it is not’]. The versicle: *In memoria aeterna* [‘In everlasting memory’].

“At Compline: *Deus misereatur* [‘May God have mercy’], *Deus in adjutorium* [‘O God, come to my aid’], *Domine exaudi orationem meam auribus* [‘Lord, hear my prayer; give ear’]. The versicle: *Requiem aeternam* [‘Eternal rest’].”

229. It should be carefully noted that in these words there is no mention whatsoever of the lessons that were then to be recited in the Office for the Dead.

Moreover, according to Launoius in the same passage cited immediately above, concerning the anniversary of King Dagobert, which Abbot Adam of Saint-Denis, successor of Suger, prescribed shortly after Bruno’s death, the following words are found at the end of the ancient Martyrology:

“‘We have appointed these same things”—those appointed at Vespers—“also for Matins. Let four singers, wearing copes, chant the Invitatory. After the lessons from the Gospel of the first and second Nocturns, let the final lessons follow, concerning his life and death.’”

The lessons recited in this Office for the Dead, therefore, were not taken from the Book of Job but from the Gospel. Since, moreover, there is no evidence from elsewhere by which it can be proved that lessons were recited in the Office for the Dead at Paris in the time of our saint, it appears more probable, on the basis of the words of John, bishop of Avranches, and of those found at the end of the ancient Martyrology cited by Launoius, either that this was not done then or that the lessons were taken from somewhere other than the Book of Job.

Since this is so, the testimony concerning the prodigious resurrection of the Parisian doctor transcribed above and circulated under the name of Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Trond, departs from the truth—or at least from what is more probable—when it indicates that, in the Parisian Office for the Dead in the time of our saint, there was a lesson beginning with the words “Answer me” and consequently taken from the Book of Job.

230. This, then, is the first point on which the testimony attributed to Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Trond, probably departs from the truth. I now present another point on which it probably suffers from the same defect.

It explicitly states that Theodoric was then in Paris for the sake of study, at the time when the fatal spectacle of the doctor’s return to life occurred there. But not only can it in no way be proved from any ancient and trustworthy document that Theodoric ever devoted himself to study at Paris; the contrary appears from the *Chronicle of Saint-Trond* written by Radulph, Theodoric’s immediate successor as abbot of Saint-Trond, which is preserved in Dacher, volume VII of the *Spicilegium*.

For, as this work teaches on page 396 and the two following pages, Theodoric—who had been educated from childhood in the Abbey of Saint-Trond and had afterward assumed the monastic habit there—was summoned to govern the Abbey of Saint-Trond from the monastery of Saint Peter at Ghent, to which he had withdrawn when that abbey was being disastrously disturbed by conflicts, by Olbert, bishop of Liège, and by the monks of Saint-Trond, his brothers, in the year 1099—or rather, according to the manuscript *Chronicle of Saint-Trond* in our possession, in the year 1098.

At the time this occurred he was a man thoroughly instructed in the liberal arts, second to none of his contemporaries in skill with either formal or informal style, and, as the same *Chronicle* says, already advanced to middle age. [Col. 0135A]

Since this is so, Theodoric must have been at least forty years old in 1098—or, if one prefers, in 1099, the year in which he assumed the government of the Abbey of Saint-Trond. Consequently, since he had most probably assumed the monastic habit in that same Abbey of Saint-Trond before he was twenty years old, where, as has been said, he had been educated from childhood, it follows that he most probably did so before the year 1082, in which, as the cited *Chronicle of Saint-Trond* preserved by Dacher on page 369 attests, Adelard II, abbot of Saint-Trond, died.

231. This conclusion becomes still more probable from the fact that, when Lanzon and Luipo were contending for control of the abbey after Adelard’s death—a contest that first began in 1085, as the *Chronicle of Saint-Trond* shows on page 370 and the following pages—Theodoric, already a monk of Saint-Trond, withdrew to the monastery of Saint Peter at Ghent, as the same *Chronicle* again teaches on page 396. It appears in no way probable that he first assumed the monastic habit under Lanzon, who, through the agency of Henry, bishop of Liège, and Herimann, bishop of Metz, had been appointed in place of Adelard II, against the unanimous wishes of the monks.

Since, then, it appears extremely probable from what has been said that Theodoric assumed the monastic habit at Saint-Trond under Adelard II, and since, while Adelard governed the Abbey of Saint-Trond, the study of letters flourished there to the greatest degree—as the writers of the *Histoire littéraire de la France* correctly teach from the cited *Chronicle of Saint-Trond*, volume VII, page 30—it appears altogether improbable that Theodoric, already a monk, should at that time have left the monastery of Saint-Trond, where he had been educated and had learned letters as a boy, to study at Paris, or that he should have been sent there by his abbot.

This is especially so because the aforesaid *Chronicle of Saint-Trond* makes no mention at all of any monk of Saint-Trond who, under Abbot Adelard, went to Paris for the purpose of learning letters. Nor was there any need for the pupils of the Abbey of Saint-Trond to go to Paris for that purpose, since they were abundantly provided at home with the necessities for learning letters.

Thus, from what has just been said, we have the conclusion that Theodoric most probably was not at Paris for the purpose of learning letters while Adelard II was abbot of the monastery of Saint-Trond, before the year 1082, in which Adelard ceased to live—see again the *Chronicle of Saint-Trond*, page 369.

But did he perhaps go there for the same reason after Adelard’s death, either in that same year, 1082, around which the prodigious resurrection of the Parisian doctor is said to have occurred, or in the following year?

232. There may perhaps be someone who suspects this on the basis of the frequently cited *Chronicle of Saint-Trond*. For, as it records in Books II and III, Herimann, bishop of Metz, and Henry, bishop of Liège, appointed Lanzon, abbot of Saint Vincent at Metz, to govern the Abbey of Saint-Trond after Adelard’s death, apparently in the year 1083, rejecting Gerard, whom the monks of the abbey had chosen as abbot from among themselves.

Consequently, almost all the monks of Saint-Trond, extremely angered and also realizing that they were about to be driven into exile, abandoned their monastery and fled, each going to a different place. From this one might suspect that Theodoric then went to Paris.

But to remove this suspicion, the *Chronicle of Saint-Trond* itself supplies the answer in the very passages where these events are narrated. To make the matter clear, I shall transcribe the actual words of the *Chronicle* that relate to it in the already cited Books II and III.

Book II contains the following:

“‘The bishops”—namely, Herimann of Metz and Henry of Liège—“neither agreeing to the just petition of our men nor understanding that God was persecuting them for their sins, both their own and ours, disregarding the worthy election of our men, which could not be rejected by any regular objection, just as they had long before decided . . . before the astonished eyes of the monks they introduced into our monastery a certain Lanzon, abbot from the monastery of Saint Vincent at Metz . . .

“‘On the day of the chapter, all our brothers assembled in the choir for Vespers, filling the choir with fine men of high rank, and men exceptionally learned in all the offices of ecclesiastical institutions.’

233. “‘The church would indeed have been blessed with so many, such great, and such excellent men, if it had not had God the Father angered against it, or if it had known how to bear his anger in humility of heart and contrition of flesh for its sins. But why do I delay?

“‘That same night, learning from friends that on the following day they would be violently and disgracefully thrust into exile if they remained united in the cloister, they were overcome by fear and, as is human nature—especially the fearful simplicity of monks—sought safety in flight.

“‘Only one of them, named Luipo, choosing exile rather than flight, was sent to Liège under Abbot Berengarius, at Saint Lawrence. Very few remained with Abbot Lanzon, namely Gerard the provost, the man whom our community had elected, and Blingerus; also the elder Herimann with another Herimann, his nephew. Hugo was sent shortly afterward into exile at Metz. Many of the others were dispersed throughout Flanders and England, Denmark and Saxony, [Col. 0136D] and throughout the kingdom of the Germans.

“‘A small number, retaining their habit, were given hospitality in various monasteries; the majority, retaining nothing of the monk in themselves, wandered about through various parishes in the manner of priests.

“‘But at Liège and Cologne, after God’s anger against our place had been appeased and his mercy toward our people had been restored, we saw some of them grow old among the clerics, in the order of canons: at Liège, in the monastery of the Holy Cross; and at Cologne, in the monastery of Saint George, at Saint John’s.’”

Book III contains the following:

“‘In the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1082, Abbot Adelard II died, on the eighth day before the Ides of December. On the third day before the Ides of August, a chapter was held concerning our brothers by the two bishops, namely Herimann of Metz and Henry of Liège. On that night all our brothers were dispersed, except for the few whom we named above.’”

234. Although, then, as is clear from these words, after the death of their abbot Adelard II almost all the monks of Saint-Trond fled from their monastery and withdrew elsewhere—and among them, in all likelihood, was Theodoric, since Radulph did not number him among the few who remained at Saint-Trond under Abbot Lanzon—it nevertheless appears from the same words already quoted that he did not go to Paris at that time. For among the various regions to which the monks of Saint-Trond then fled, they list not Gaul, where the city of Paris is situated, but only Flanders, England, Denmark, Saxony, and Alemannia. But someone may object: where, then, did Theodoric withdraw when, along with many others, he fled from his monastery at Saint-Trond after Lanzon had been imposed upon it? I think that he remained not far from Saint-Trond. For among those monks of Saint-Trond with whom Theodoric then departed, there were some who, not long afterward and with Lanzon’s consent, returned to their monastery. This is again gathered from the Chronicle of Saint-Trond, which, in D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, cited volume, p. 370, says the following about Luipo, a monk of Saint-Trond, who was still enduring the exile to which he had been driven after Lanzon had become abbot of Saint-Trond:

> “When he [Luipo], through all those whom he thought could be useful to him, and even through the emperor himself, had entreated Abbot Lanzon with all humility that he might be received back into the cloister in which he had been brought up and might enter it in the same order as the others, he was unable in any way to obtain this.”

These words, together with what follows, imply that at that time—or, as appears from the immediately preceding passage of the same Chronicle, in the year 1085, when Luipo tried to obtain permission to return to his monastery at Saint-Trond—some other monks of Saint-Trond who had left it, not indeed after being driven into exile but having fled, had already returned. Since these men returned not long afterward to the monastery they had abandoned, as also appears from the immediately cited passage of the Chronicle of Saint-Trond, they do not seem to have gone to distant regions when they withdrew from it in flight. Consequently neither did Theodoric, since he was evidently one of them, as is readily inferred from the fact that, when Lanzon and the aforementioned Luipo later contended for the abbacy of Saint-Trond, he withdrew from there to Ghent, to the monastery of Saint Peter, as the Chronicle of Saint-Trond again relates in D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, cited volume, pp. 369 and following.

235. I transcribe here the words in which it records this, together with several others added at the same place, since most of what has already been said about Theodoric for the present purpose was drawn from them. They read as follows:

> “Accordingly, when Olbert, bishop of Liège, had resolved to come to the aid of the monastery of Saint-Trond—which had been reduced almost to ruin by prolonged dissensions—the most diligent inquiry was made whether any son of our church still survived to whom the task of assisting his mother could suitably be entrusted. Our brothers, as well as the clerics and laymen who had known him, said that one of our brothers, named Theodoric, was staying at Ghent in the monastery of Saint Peter. He had withdrawn from our house during the dispute between the abbots Lanzon and Luipo. If he could be brought away from there, he seemed to them suitable to govern the abbey. For he was proficient in German and Walloon, excellently educated in the liberal arts, and in prose and verse would have been second to no one of his time. He was sonorous in voice, sweet and exceptionally deep; short in stature but handsome, and of middle age. He would also know better how to sympathize with the infirmities of his brothers, having been brought up with them from childhood, and having seen and heard the evils they had suffered in their tribulations.”

Thus the aforementioned Chronicle.

Now, since Theodoric, as is clear from everything already said, did not go to Paris when Adelard II, abbot of Saint-Trond, died in 1082, but, shortly after he had abandoned his monastery when Lanzon was imposed upon it in 1083, returned to Saint-Trond from the nearby place to which he had withdrawn, and since it appears that he remained there with Lanzon until 1085, when, after a dispute had arisen between Lanzon and Luipo, he withdrew to Ghent, to the monastery of Saint Peter, it follows that he probably did not study in Paris around the year 1082, since before that time he had not been there for study either, as I demonstrated above.

236. To make this clearer—and indeed to show that Theodoric never studied in Paris—I shall set out briefly and in order all that he did from early childhood until the time when, recalled from Ghent, he undertook the governance of the abbey of Saint-Trond.

While still a boy, he was educated in the monastery of Saint-Trond, according to the custom of those times, and was assigned to the study of letters. When he had grown older and had been enrolled among the monks by Abbot Adelard II, he continued cultivating his mind through learning until the year 1082, when Adelard died, in the school of his monastery, which at that time, according to what has been said, was flourishing greatly. After Adelard’s death in 1082, and after Lanzon had been placed in charge of the monastery against the wishes of the monks, Theodoric departed from Saint-Trond with many of them. He then returned to the monastery from the place not far away, apparently, to which he had withdrawn, with the consent of Abbot Lanzon. When a dispute arose between Lanzon and Luipo in 1085, he again left the monastery and went to Ghent, where he remained in the abbey of Saint Peter until the year 1099, or at least until 1098. In one of those two years, he was summoned from there by letters from Olbert, bishop of Liège, and accepted the governance of the monastery of Saint-Trond as its abbot.

Such were Theodoric’s activities up to the time when this occurred. They plainly do not allow us to believe that Theodoric ever studied in Paris, and specifically around the year 1082. Since this is so, the testimony transcribed above at no. 214 and attributed to Theodoric, by which that claim is asserted, is in all likelihood spurious and fabricated. The same appears also from other considerations, which I now add to what has already been said.

237. That testimony—and likewise the claim that the condemned doctor was called Raymund Malliban or Milleban, or, as others maintain, Raymund Diocres—seems to have remained unknown even to the Carthusians themselves before the beginning of the immediately preceding century, or before the year 1615, when the anonymous Carthusian says in the words transcribed above that it was cited by the priest Galaudus. This may be inferred from Petraeus alone, a member of the Cologne Charterhouse, who in his *Elucidations* on the first book of Dorlandus’s *Carthusian Chronicle*, printed in 1608, carefully investigates in a separate section “why the name of that condemned and thrice-unhappy doctor”—that is, the man who had proclaimed from his bier in Paris that he was damned—“had not been committed to the records of literature.”

Lest one suppose that Petraeus was mistaken, Peter Sutor, prior of the Paris Charterhouse, who died in 1537 and whose work *On Carthusian Life* first appeared in print at Cologne in 1609, writes as follows in the first book, treatise 1, chapter 3:

> “We frankly admit that we have cited no name for that doctor—the condemned Parisian—because no name of his has been revealed in any written record that we have seen. Therefore we wished not to invent a new one, but to remain silent about what was unknown.”

Nor should you object here to the manuscript *Life of Saint Bruno*, already cited by the anonymous Carthusian in the words of no. 209 and preserved in the Basel library, written in 1486 and therefore long before the sixteenth century. For although I find the following words written in the lower margin of p. 376 of volume II, part II, of Launoy’s *Works, with Their Authors and Illustrators*, printed at Geneva (Colonia Allobrogum) in 1731:

> “Around the year of the Lord 1082 a dreadful prodigy occurred in Paris involving a certain master, whose name, according to some, was Raymond,”

it does not follow that the unhappy Parisian doctor was called Raymond Diocres, or even Milleban, as the testimony attributed to Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Trond, reports. Consequently that testimony may rightly be regarded either as spurious or as highly suspect, unless perhaps the book from which it is said to have been taken by Galaudus is brought to light and accepted as a genuine work of Theodoric.

238. But where is this book located, and in what corner of which library is it kept? From where did Galaudus obtain it—or, if you prefer, the copy from which he excerpted the words quoted at no. 214? Does he anywhere in the *Chronicle of the Carthusians* that he composed identify the library, or the person by whom such a precious document was communicated to him? The anonymous author of the fourth book of the *Carthusian Annals*, which has not yet been published, the sole source from which it has been possible to learn nearly everything I have said about Galaudus, leaves all these matters obscure.

He does indicate that Galaudus was an honest and learned man. But who would therefore assert that he possessed such penetrating judgment that he could neither be deceived by an impostor nor accept as a genuine work of Theodoric a text falsely attributed to him? Meanwhile, it must be admitted that Berthold Nihusius—or, if you prefer, the Carthusians who supplied him with the testimony of Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Trond, which he praises in the letters prefixed to his *Didascalic Epistle* addressed to Andrew Saussaeius and printed in 1645—was wrongly accused of falsehood by Launoy in his dissertation *On the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Wilderness*, chapter 5, section 3, whether for citing or for presenting that testimony. Nihusius could have cited it in good faith, and the Carthusians could likewise have presented it to him as something received from Galaudus.

Let us now examine other matters relevant to this question, which the anonymous Carthusian did not include in the words quoted at no. 227. Among us there are several copies of the testimony attributed to Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Trond, transmitted from different places. One of them, however, bears at its head the following words:

> “Andreas Quercetanus (Du Chesne), in book IV of the *Fragments of History*, cites a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Theodoric near Reims, entitled *On the Reckoning of Times*, where the following is read:”

After these words, the testimony transcribed above at no. 214 is added, and at the end the phrase “Thus there” is appended as a conclusion.

239. When I first encountered this copy of the testimony attributed to Theodoric, excited by the words I saw prefixed to it, I eagerly seized the fourth book of the *History of France’s Writers* by Andreas Quercetanus, or Chesnius, and carefully examined the whole volume from beginning to end. But behold! On p. 162, the only page in that entire book, or volume, of Chesnius on which the manuscript of the monastery of Saint Theodoric near Reims, entitled *On the Reckoning of Times*, is cited, there is supplied a historical fragment in which, as will become clear to anyone who examines it, there is not even a syllable about the miraculous resurrection of the Parisian doctor or about Saint Bruno’s withdrawal from that event into the wilderness.

From this I understood that the copyist intended by the words I have just quoted to indicate that the testimony attributed to Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Trond, was written not in book IV of Chesnius, or in the volume he cites, but in the manuscript *On the Reckoning of Times*, from which Chesnius incorporated a historical fragment into that volume.

Yet I do not think even this accords with the truth. For if the matter were so, it would in all likelihood have been mentioned by several other writers; nevertheless, I have so far been unable to find it mentioned by any of them. On the other hand, according to the information available to me, there are some who affirm that in the library of the monastery of Saint-Trond in the diocese of Liège there is preserved a book attributed to Theodoric, who once governed that monastery as abbot, entitled *On the Sacred Reckoning of Times*, in which he supplies the testimony quoted at no. 214 concerning the miraculous resurrection of the Parisian doctor. They add that no one ought to be surprised by the silence concerning this book of Martène and Durand, writers of the Order of Saint Benedict, in their *Literary Journey*, where they discuss that abbey of their order and its library.

240. They make this assertion because those two writers did not possess a complete knowledge of all the manuscripts preserved in the library of the abbey of Saint-Trond, as they themselves declare. In the first volume of the cited work they write that the library of Saint-Trond was quite good and furnished with rather notable manuscripts; but in the second volume they report that, when they had again visited the abbey of Saint-Trond and wished to examine its manuscripts anew, they had been unable to obtain permission from the abbot.

Although I could scarcely bring myself to believe that the manuscript *On the Sacred Reckoning of Times* was hidden in the library of the monastery of Saint-Trond, I nevertheless thought that the matter required diligent investigation, lest I should seem to have neglected anything that might contribute to discovering the cause of Saint Bruno’s conversion. I was prepared to travel to the monastery of Saint-Trond if I could learn that permission would be granted to examine the manuscripts preserved in its library, and through friends I urgently requested that this be allowed me. But just as it had been denied to Martène and Durand, so it was denied to me.

Meanwhile, letters written from there indicate that the book in question is not found in the abbey of Saint-Trond—or at least that it does not contain the testimony quoted above concerning the miraculous resurrection of the Parisian doctor. Among these letters is one written by the abbot himself in 1745, in which he says:

> “I remember that a few years ago, at the request of the most reverend abbot of Saint-Laurent, I saw the same transcript—that is, the testimony attributed to Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Trond—and I then carefully investigated whether I could find it in the original. But I nowhere found it in the Chronicles of Abbot Theodoric, from which the transcript apparently could have been made.”

Since that book is also not found in the abbey of Saint-Victor near Paris, although I had found a note indicating that it was preserved there, as I learn from letters written to me after the matter had been most carefully investigated, the testimony of the abbot Theodoric, which some assert to be contained in it, must, in view of everything already said, be regarded as entirely fabricated.

## XIV. The testimony of Caesarius of Heisterbach is examined, and a judgment is formed concerning it.

241. The anonymous author of the fourth book of the *Carthusian Annals*, not yet published, about to introduce the testimony of Caesarius of Heisterbach concerning the miraculous resurrection of the Parisian doctor, begins as follows:

> “The first among outsiders in whose writings we read an account of this prodigy is Caesarius of Heisterbach, of the Cistercian Order. He was already flourishing in the year 1188, that is, approximately fifty years after the death of the first fathers of the Carthusian Order who had been instituted with Saint Bruno; or at least in the first century after Saint Bruno’s death, within which he lived for approximately twenty years.”

He then transcribes Caesarius’s words containing that testimony and argues at length against Launoy in order to prove that it supports the Parisian prodigy. To avoid appearing to have weakened the force of any of the arguments contained in them, I transcribe all his words here and shall add at the end several observations that I judge appropriate. They read as follows:

> “This Caesarius of Heisterbach, in his work arranged in twelve books in the form of a dialogue and entitled *On Illustrious Miracles and Memorable Histories That Occurred in Germany, Italy, and Gaul before or around His Own Time*, in book XI, entitled *On the Dying*, presents this spectacle in precisely these words:
>
> “There was in the kingdom of France a certain cleric, noble and rich—two qualities that often exalt men and subject them to evil vices. When he had died and had been placed in a bier, with a crowd of people sitting around, both clerics and laymen, he himself rose and, with everyone listening, burst into these words:
>
> “‘The Just Judge has judged, has condemned the one judged, and has handed the condemned man over into the hands of the impious.’
>
> “After saying these things, he reclined again but did not fall asleep; rather, he passed from rest to toil and from delights to misery.”

242. “In these very few words Caesarius perfectly represents the terrifying spectacle of the condemned man, conforming in every respect to the account that we earlier assembled both from the anonymous Carthusian and from the manuscript of Metz—which will be mentioned here more than once below—so that there is no difference between these authors concerning the substance of the event, nor even any contradiction in the circumstances themselves. We therefore think that no one will judge this to be a different account, however much Launoy may protest.

“This testimony, then, is of great weight, being given by a very ancient writer, a man of the highest authority, renowned for piety and learning. Archbishop Henry of Molenarck of Cologne, under whom Caesarius lived, chose him alone from among the most sensible men of Germany to adorn in noble style the life of his predecessor, Saint Engelbert, archbishop and martyr. Cardinal Bona commends the merits of Caesarius and his works in a few but weighty and concise words:

> “Caesarius of Heisterbach, of the Cistercian Order, pious, truthful, and simple in his memorable histories.”

“The Cistercians also write that he became illustrious through miracles after his death. In order to evade Caesarius’s very strong authority, Launoy tried to prove that the history he relates was different from the one narrated by Saint Antoninus. But he labored in vain by comparing Saint Antoninus’s account with Caesarius’s, as though Saint Antoninus had first made it public. For in fact what Caesarius records agrees with the ancient chronicles of the Order cited above, which were compiled almost 250 years before Antoninus and at the same time as Caesarius was living.

243. “But since Saint Antoninus differs little from the Chronicles, let us now see whether the mutual disagreement that Launoy claims to find between the accounts of Antoninus and Caesarius is so great that one may rightly be called different from the other and that the truth of the entire history must consequently collapse. Launoy attacks them as follows.

“‘First of all,’ he says, ‘Caesarius does not indicate the precise time when his prodigy occurred, whereas Antoninus specifies the very year in which his prodigy took place.’

“But what reader, however perceptive, will detect even the slightest disagreement between the two authors on this point? Certainly, if Caesarius specified a definite time different from and far removed from the time indicated by Antoninus, there would indeed be a conflict here. But since he says nothing about the time, he asserts nothing contrary to Antoninus, and therefore the substance of both accounts remains the same.

“We could satisfy this and Launoy’s following objections with a single answer if we said what is entirely true: Caesarius touched upon this history only in summary. It is therefore not surprising if he omitted many circumstances later related by Antoninus.

“‘Next,’ Launoy adds, ‘Caesarius does not define a specific place in the kingdom of France, whereas Antoninus defines a specific place in the kingdom of France, namely Paris.’

“This is an objection like the preceding one and deserves a similar answer: there is no contradiction between the two authors. There would be one if Caesarius had specified Spain, Italy, or some other region or kingdom. But he said that the prodigy occurred in the kingdom of France, while Antoninus said that it occurred in Paris, which is in the kingdom of France. Thus Blessed Antoninus supplied what Caesarius had omitted. Andrew Saussaeius’s excellent reasoning in support of the identity of the two accounts is comparable to this, however harshly Launoy may exclaim against it:

> “‘O miserable evasion!’

244. “Caesarius speaks of a certain noble and wealthy cleric, whereas Antoninus describes an outstanding doctor.”

“At first sight the words ‘cleric’ and ‘doctor’ seem to possess some distinction between them, but they can easily be reconciled. We are taught by various examples that men distinguished for learning and education were often called clerics. In Orderic Vitalis, book III, we read:

> “‘He was called a cleric because he was thoroughly instructed in letters and in other arts.’

“In the *History of the Bishops of Eichstätt*:

> “‘This Bishop John was a great cleric in canon law.’

“John Birellius, prior of the Charterhouse, was also called by Innocent VI, who had heard that he had died, ‘the cleric of the world,’ as we shall see under the year 1360, not only because he was a perfect monk—for monks too were sometimes called clerics—but especially because he had no superior in either divine or human knowledge.

“Thus Caesarius and Antoninus do not contradict one another when the former calls the unfortunate man a cleric and the latter an outstanding doctor.

“But Launoy persists:

> “‘Caesarius indicates that his cleric, exalted by nobility and wealth, became proud, whereas Antoninus signifies a doctor who flourished in a great reputation for knowledge and integrity.’

“This objection is no more weighty than the preceding ones. Nothing can be concluded from it, nor can it be used to demonstrate even the slightest difference between the two accounts. Caesarius does not explain what sort of cleric the man was, whether proud or subject to evil vices; he says only that he was ‘noble and rich, qualities that often exalt men and subject them to evil vices.’ These facts do not conflict with the common account, which describes the man as ‘powerful in eminent knowledge, integrity of life, and the greatest reputation,’ but only according to what appeared outwardly. For this reason the author of the Metz manuscript thinks that he was condemned because of the vice of vainglory.

245. “From this objection Launoy proceeds to the fifth, which he presents as follows:

> “‘Caesarius does not touch even in a word upon the University of Paris, whereas Antoninus praises it. And yet Caesarius mentions the University of Paris and events occurring in the University of Paris in many places.’

“Launoy then gathers numerous citations from Caesarius in which Caesarius mentioned the University of Paris. But what is the purpose of these citations? Just as we have shown that one cannot rightly conclude that Caesarius’s account is different from Antoninus’s because Caesarius did not specify the particular place in the kingdom of France that Antoninus specifies, so Caesarius’s silence about the University of Paris, which Antoninus praises, cannot imply any disagreement.

“But let us hasten to dispel Launoy’s other objections.

> “‘Caesarius plainly indicates that his cleric said, at one and the same time: “The Just Judge has judged, has condemned the one judged, and has handed the condemned man over into the hands of the impious.” Antoninus, however, expressly asserts that his doctor spoke on three distinct days.’

“We have already seen above that some of the cited authors of the Carthusian Order wrote that this threefold utterance was spoken by the condemned man on one and the same day, while others said that it was spoken on three distinct days. Thus Caesarius’s words agree with the former, and Antoninus’s with the latter. The two accounts should not for that reason be judged different, since they agree in the substance of the matter.

“Moreover, Caesarius does not indicate as plainly as Launoy claims that his cleric spoke at one and the same time. He does not expressly state that these words were uttered all together and once, or on three distinct occasions; he says only, in summary, that the man pronounced them. The words are therefore the same in sense as those that Antoninus testifies his doctor pronounced—not precisely the same words, nor spoken in the same manner, but others signifying the same thing. Thus there is no contradiction in the essence of the matter, nor any difference except that Caesarius, intent upon brevity, did not take care to express the matter as fully and extensively.

246. “It should also be noted that the author of the Metz manuscript mentioned above expressed that threefold cry of the condemned man in nearly the same words as Caesarius had used before him. Moreover, how many and how great are the similar differences found in Sacred Scripture, even among the holy Evangelists, who narrate the same event in different ways? It would be a crime not only to say but even to think that they were therefore opposed to one another.

“Caesarius does not write that his cleric uttered these cries while the Office appointed by the Church for the dead was being celebrated, whereas Antoninus explicitly writes this.”

Who would not be astonished that such a difference should be alleged by Launoy, a sensible and learned man? It is true, and we cannot deny it, that Caesarius did not explicitly mention the Office for the Dead. But who would deny that he implied it when he wrote that the deceased man “had been placed in a bier, with a crowd of people sitting around, both clerics and laymen”?

“Caesarius in no way indicates whether the cleric had been deprived of ecclesiastical burial or not, whereas Antoninus clearly indicates this.”

Nor did the cited Carthusian authors indicate it. Therefore they too would be opposed to Antoninus; therefore their account too would be different from Antoninus’s account. Who could think such a thing?

“Caesarius does not say that Bruno, the founder of the Carthusian Order, was present at the spectacle he relates, whereas Antoninus says that Bruno, the founder of the Carthusian Order, was present at the spectacle he describes.”

Caesarius was silent because perhaps he did not know that Saint Bruno had been present at the spectacle; for Bruno withdrew to the Charterhouse only two years after it occurred. Or, if Caesarius knew, he nevertheless did not wish to mention it because it was foreign to his purpose. His purpose was to present various examples concerning the dying, not to explain conversions or the foundation of religious orders.

247. “Moreover, Bruno’s conversion did not take place in public, just as it is not established whether the spectacle occurred in a church or in the deceased man’s hall—which is more probable—in the presence of many people or of only a few. Nor did Bruno’s conversion occur at the same moment as the spectacle, but within private walls and long after the spectacle had taken place, as is clear from the authors cited. Therefore it could not have been perceived by anyone who had been present at the spectacle. Antoninus said this because he read it in a written account and heard it reported.

“Caesarius does not say that Bruno took the occasion for founding his order from his spectacle, whereas Antoninus does say this.”

This objection of Launoy’s is no different from the preceding one. He has divided into two parts what could have been said together, attempting to overwhelm with many words what he could not establish by solid arguments. The objection has therefore already been sufficiently answered by the preceding response. For what is surprising if Caesarius, who made no mention of Bruno, also remained silent about the occasion for founding the Carthusian Order, for the same reasons that we touched upon above?

“Caesarius does not report that his prodigy occurred in Paris, whereas Antoninus does.”

This objection too is the same as the second. What Launoy says here he had already said above in second place, merely changing the terms and manner of expression. Indeed, both objections closely resemble the fifth. From this it is evident how excessively anxious Launoy was to exaggerate differences of this sort.

“Finally, Caesarius says nothing about the entire matter of the fourth reading of the Vigils for the Dead, which was treated after Antoninus’s time by the anonymous author of Bruno’s Life.”

But Antoninus too says nothing about the entire matter of the fourth reading. Therefore he does not differ from Caesarius. Nor do the ancient Carthusians, who likewise make no mention of this fourth reading or of the words “Answer me.” Therefore they too are not opposed to Caesarius.

248. “Furthermore, Launoy attempts to diminish Caesarius’s authority by invoking the authority of the most illustrious and reverend Nicholas Coeffeteus, a Parisian theologian, who in his *Response to the Mystery of Iniquity* says that Caesarius’s *Dialogues* are full of fables. But since Coeffeteus merely confirms the judgment of Conrad Gesner, a Zwinglian—as Launoy himself admits—we place greater trust in Cardinal Bona, a man equally pious and learned, who praises Caesarius as truthful in his memorable histories.

“And not without reason, since Caesarius himself most solemnly swears that he invented nothing, saying:

> “‘God is my witness that I invented not even a single chapter in this Dialogue.’

“Therefore we prefer to the authorities of Coeffeteus and Gesner the authorities of the most illustrious Saussaeius, of Jacob Breullius, distinguished for piety and learning, and of others who judged Caesarius more favorably. Above all, we prefer the authority of the outstanding doctor of sacred theology and canon of Saint Gereon at Cologne, Tilmann Bredembrach, a man distinguished by many titles of learning and virtue. Through his study and labor many records of ancient writers were brought to light. He also devoted much work to revising and purging the books of Caesarius’s *Dialogues*, intending to publish them; but when he had almost reached the end, he was summoned to heaven.

“Yet, lest the pious labors of so great a man should perish, among others Jacob Fischer, doctor of sacred theology, ensured their preservation. He completed what Bredembrach had begun and, in his preface, thoroughly refuted Gesner’s slander against Caesarius.

249. “Finally, in the conclusion of the third chapter of his dissertation, Launoy attacks Saussaeius—or rather the Carthusians through Saussaeius—because, in the account of Caesarius, he said that the substance of the event must be distinguished from its circumstances. Launoy then foolishly turns this distinction of Saussaeius, contrary to every rule of propriety, against Joan the Popess.

“But since we profess that we do not repel injury with injury, we leave it to the reader’s judgment whether this is the best method of disputing in order to assert the truth and reconcile authors who describe the same event in different ways.

“Yet Launoy misrepresents Saussaeius when he says that Saussaeius placed the substance of the event in the fact that Caesarius reports the prodigy as having occurred in the kingdom of France and not in his own time. For Saussaeius said nothing of the kind. After reporting Caesarius’s entire account, he adds:

> “‘This is Caesarius, who plainly comprehends the substance of the event under discussion in this description.’

“In saying this, Saussaeius does indeed indicate that the substance of the event is found in Caesarius’s description, but he does not explain what that substance consists in.

“Immediately afterward he speaks of the circumstances:

> “‘Although not all the circumstances are expressed with equal completeness in this description, since he does not record the year or the particular place in Gaul where the events he relates occurred.’

“These are the circumstances also noted by Launoy, which Saussaeius says are touched upon summarily in Caesarius’s description, when he adds shortly afterward:

> “‘Nevertheless, he says everything, since he asserts that the event took place in the kingdom of France and, by the word “was,” sufficiently clearly indicates that it occurred not in his own time but earlier.’

“Thus, by the words ‘he says everything,’ Saussaeius means those circumstances which he had just said were not ‘expressed with equal completeness’ by Caesarius, since Caesarius did not record the year or the particular place in Gaul, and so forth.

“This is the true and honest meaning of Saussaeius’s words. Launoy inverted their order in order to twist them more conveniently toward his own position and more easily persuade the reader that Saussaeius had placed the substance of the event in the fact ‘that Caesarius reports the prodigy as having occurred in the kingdom of France and not in his own time.’

250. “Toward the end of the conclusion of the third chapter, Launoy again attacks Caesarius, or rather the Carthusians through Caesarius, when he fully describes two examples drawn by him from the same treatise of Caesarius. From these examples he wishes to argue that idle men combined into one prodigy the elements that supposedly supplied the occasion for fabricating the beginning of the Carthusian Order as it now exists—or, more precisely, the beginning that he attempts to overthrow.

“One example concerns a certain Parisian canon who, after his death and honorable burial, appeared to a friend and announced that he was damned because true contrition had been lacking in him as he was dying. The other is that history which Launoy earlier tried to prove different from Antoninus’s account.

“Who would not be astonished at Launoy’s cunning? He joins together two examples that he claims possess great similarity, in order to dazzle the reader’s eyes and mind with greater subtlety. But we consistently deny that there is any similarity between those two examples beyond the common misfortune of condemnation suffered by both men; or that ‘idle men’ fabricated from these two prodigies—or even from only one of them—the cause of Saint Bruno’s withdrawal as time passed, as Launoy wishes.

“For we have already proved above that the anonymous Carthusian who first committed the matter to writing lived at the time of Caesarius. It was from that anonymous author, not from Caesarius, that the other Carthusians cited above borrowed their account of the same history.”

Thus far the cited author of the fourth book of the *Carthusian Annals*, against whom I shall now make several observations.

251. Therefore he rightly argues first of all against Launoius that, from the various circumstances attached to the account supplied by Antoninus—or rather by the anonymous author of the Chronicle of the First Five Carthusian Priors, from whom Antoninus drew it—concerning the deceased man who proclaimed from his coffin that he was damned, and absent from the account given by Caesarius concerning a deceased man who likewise shouted from his coffin that he was damned, one cannot reasonably infer either that Antoninus’s—or the anonymous author’s—account conflicts with the substance of Caesarius’s account, or that the prodigy which is the subject of the latter is certainly different from the prodigy presented in the former. For what is more commonplace than to find historical events reported by different writers and, although they are the same events, adorned by one with circumstances passed over in silence by another? Nor is there any reason for this to seem surprising, since it often happens that one writer gives a full account of a matter, omitting none, or at least very few, of its circumstances, while another reports it only in summary, stripped of nearly all its circumstances. Indeed, even from circumstances that conflict with one another and cannot by any means be reconciled, it cannot always be inferred that the accounts in which they occur concern different events.

Firmianus Lactantius, in Baluzius’s *Miscellanies*, book II, p. 37, records that the Emperor Constantine the Great was divinely warned in a dream to use in the army, when it was about to fight against Maxentius, a military sign formed in the shape of a cross. Eusebius does the same in book I, chapter 29, of his *Life of Constantine*. Yet the two writers do not at all agree about the time at which that vision was presented to Constantine. Lactantius connects it with the night immediately preceding the battle fought at the Tiber bridge on 27 October 312, in which Maxentius perished; Eusebius, however, by what he writes in the cited chapters 28, 29, and 37 of his book *On the Life of Constantine*, clearly indicates that it occurred while Constantine was still in Gaul, before he had crossed the Alps to take up arms against Maxentius, and therefore some considerable time before the night mentioned above. Thus Eusebius and Lactantius disagree about the circumstances, and yet it is not certain that the two accounts concern different visions presented to Constantine.

252. Various contemporary or nearly contemporary writers report the death of Julian the Apostate in battle; but with how many mutually conflicting circumstances do they embellish this event! To add an example from the very subject we are treating: the writers reviewed in § XI and following assert that the dreadful prodigy of the condemned scholar occurred publicly before a vast multitude of people; but the author of the Codex of Metz, to be cited below, states that it occurred privately within the walls of the deceased man’s house. Yet who would therefore say that the prodigy he relates is different from the prodigy reported by the others?

Although, then, the writers just mentioned also record that the three cries of the Parisian scholar—the first declaring himself accused, the second judged, and the third condemned—were uttered on three different days, while Caesarius appears, as Launoius understands him, to say that his cleric or scholar was judged, condemned, and “delivered into the hands of the wicked” all at once and therefore on one and the same day, it nevertheless does not follow with certainty that the prodigy he relates is different from the prodigy they report. Nor, however, is it certain that it is one and the same.

Columbius, in his *Dissertation on the Beginnings of the Carthusians*, no. 64, writes as follows:

> “Some make this prodigy—that is, the one reported by Caesarius—the same as the Parisian prodigy of which we are now speaking; others deny this. For my part, I do not now wish to assert either that it is the same as that one or that it is different from it. Certainly Caesarius does not add that it compelled Bruno and his companions to withdraw into the wilderness; but that is the one circumstance which led me to discuss the Parisian prodigy here. I would rather assert—and this is entirely appropriate to the present discussion—that the opponent, namely Launoius, ought not to have written the following words in his *Dissertation on the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Wilderness*, p. 145: ‘The Cistercian Caesarius relates two things which provided idle men with the occasion for fabricating the beginning of the Carthusian order in the form which we are now examining.’”

For since one of the two is precisely the event I have just related—the man in the kingdom of France who returned to life and cried out that he had been condemned by God—I do not see why idle men would have needed, in fabricating the Parisian story, to add the case of the Parisian canon who, a few days after his death, allowed himself to be seen without a body by a close friend.

253. “Certainly this canon had nothing in common either with the Parisian man who returned to life, of whom we are now speaking, or with the other man who, while his tomb was being prepared, was restored to life in the kingdom of France.” Thus he writes; and rightly indeed he argues that the prodigy related by Caesarius is not certainly one and the same as the Parisian prodigy recorded first by the author of the Chronicle of the First Five Carthusian Priors and subsequently by Antoninus.

But is he equally right to add, against Launoius, that this last prodigy was not assembled or fabricated by idle men from the prodigy reported by Caesarius and from the other prodigy of the Parisian canon who appeared to his friend after death and announced that he had been condemned? I say that it is so for this reason: if that story is perhaps in reality to be regarded as a fable or fabrication, the prodigy related by Caesarius alone could have sufficed for its invention; and no reason suggests that the other prodigy of the Parisian canon also contributed to it. Indeed, the greatest possible dissimilarity between that event and the Parisian prodigy by which Bruno was driven into the wilderness suggests the contrary. The difference between them is so great that the two prodigies have scarcely anything in common, as will be clear to anyone who considers the matter.

Moreover, although—as I have already said, and as Columbius also implies in the words just quoted—the Parisian prodigy by which the saint was driven into the wilderness is not certainly one and the same as the prodigy reported by Caesarius, it nevertheless appears probable that the one is not distinct from the other, because their substance is the same: namely, that a man who had died and had already been placed in a coffin returned to life for a time and announced his condemnation to those standing by. Nor does it stand in the way that the circumstances of the two prodigies differ from one another, since those circumstances must be distinguished from the substance which, according to what has just been said, is common to both prodigies. I shall demonstrate this below. Thus, at least in some measure, the other prodigy—that by which our saint withdrew into the wilderness—is confirmed by the prodigy related by Caesarius.

254. But Launoius does call Caesarius’s own account into question, and not without good reason. For whatever our anonymous Carthusian may bring forward against him in the words quoted above, and whatever commendation Caesarius may deserve for the sincerity with which he wrote, all more experienced modern critics nevertheless agree that he was excessively credulous. In his twelve *Dialogues* he did not distinguish true histories from false ones with sufficiently careful judgment, and at times inserted, without any discrimination whatsoever, trifles and fables gathered from every source.

Our Stiltingus, in volume I of September, in the *Life of Blessed Margaret of Leuven, Virgin and Martyr*, p. 590, no. 44, writes appropriately to the present purpose:

> “As regards the credibility to be accorded to these Acts—namely, those of Blessed Margaret, written by the contemporary Caesarius in book VI, chapter 34, of the *Dialogues*—the judgment of all may perhaps not be the same, unless a careful distinction is made among the various things narrated by the same author. For Caesarius was certainly a pious and learned man, but, for the time in which he lived, simple and credulous. Hence his *Dialogues* are not without certain little narratives which are nowadays read as fables. Yet we shall not judge rightly if we pass precisely the same judgment on all of them, because he related many things that are not contrary to probability and that he could have known accurately, since he was close to them in both place and time. Therefore, since suspicion of falsehood does not attach to Caesarius, a pious and sincere man, and since, in matters as close to him as those concerning Margaret, there is scarcely any danger of error, we cannot deny Caesarius credibility in these matters; and here his authority seems preferable to that of all who wrote later. For this reason I shall publish first the account of our blessed woman which he composed, as deserving preference over the later narratives.”

255. Caesarius, then, even according to Stiltingus—who nevertheless, as his very words sufficiently show, applies to this writer a criticism less severe, though certainly entirely fair—cannot secure indisputable credibility for the prodigy which he relates in the words transcribed above at no. 241. For, if it ever actually occurred, it must have taken place both long before Caesarius’s time and in Gaul, far from the monastery of Heisterbach; and this writer, as is clear from the words of Stiltingus just quoted, does not deserve unquestioned credibility in matters to which he was not close either in time or place.

Launoius is therefore right to call it into question because of the weakness of the authority on which it rests. Nevertheless, since, as I have already shown, it is probably one and the same as the Parisian prodigy by which Bruno was driven into the wilderness, and since this prodigy was committed to writing by the anonymous author of the Chronicle of the First Five Carthusian Priors, who flourished in the thirteenth century, it appears somewhat less open to suspicion of falsehood, being founded at least on two thirteenth-century writers—unless someone should wish to maintain either that the aforesaid author of the Chronicle of the Carthusian Priors, or the person from whom he drew his material, took from the prodigy reported by Caesarius a Parisian prodigy that never occurred, and enlarged it with circumstances invented at will. Mabillonius also seems to have been inclined to this view in assessing the matter.

256. For in the *Benedictine Annals*, book LXVI, no. 64, he writes:

> “Some authors, at least two hundred years later, brought forward another cause for that withdrawal—Saint Bruno’s withdrawal into the wilderness. They said that, while Bruno was teaching in the schools at Paris, he was terrified by the prodigy of a canon who returned to life and cried out that he had been condemned; that he then withdrew into the wilderness with the companions he gathered around him and founded the Carthusian order. This account, subsequently enlarged with various circumstances, was approved by Saint Antoninus and by Gerson himself, a man of sound learning and piety. It is therefore not surprising that it was accepted and asserted in good faith by members of the whole sacred order, to which Caesarius of Heisterbach seems to have provided the initial impulse.”

Whether Caesarius truly provided the initial impulse for the Parisian prodigy by which the saint was converted, or gave idle minds the occasion for fabricating it, I leave to be examined in what follows. Meanwhile, the suspicion that this account was drawn from Caesarius may be strengthened by the fact that this writer certainly flourished at the beginning of the thirteenth century, whereas the anonymous author of the Chronicle of the First Five Carthusian Priors probably did not compose his work, in which he reports the Parisian prodigy, before approximately 1250, as is sufficiently clear from what I discussed in § 1.

Moreover, if it were certain that the prodigy reported by Caesarius had occurred and that it was not different from the Parisian prodigy by which Bruno is said to have been driven into the wilderness, the opinion of the Carthusians, who on this basis trace the cause of the conversion of their holy patriarch, would indeed appear sufficiently probable, even though Caesarius does not state that Bruno was driven into the wilderness by the prodigy he relates.

Hence the principal question to be investigated is not whether it was the cause of the saint’s conversion, but whether the Parisian prodigy accords with the truth. I shall state my own opinion on this matter only after, in addition to the ancient writers already reviewed who support the prodigy with their testimony, I have also examined the ancient writers whose silence seems to count against it.

§ XV. Whether anything can be established against the *anastasis*, by which the scholar publicly proclaimed himself condemned, from the silence of Saint Bruno, Guigo, or Guibert of Nogent

257. All more experienced modern critics admit that, in historical matters, a negative argument often possesses considerable force. It will suffice to cite Muratorius as an example. In volume II, chapter 21, of his *Anecdotes*, he writes:

> “But I seem already to hear certain people replying that this method of argument is weakened and made worthless, since, as logicians call it, nothing can be proved by a negative argument. Let those reply in this way who have not even saluted ecclesiastical learning from the threshold and who have devoted their entire brains to scholastic subtleties. For how much force a negative argument possesses is shown by the clear treatise on this subject, and is daily experienced by the whole republic of learned men. How, I ask, could the inventions and fables that have crept into the histories of later times be exposed and hissed off the stage, unless the silence of earlier writers were valued more highly than the ignorant and audacious loquacity of later ones? The latter make assertions at will and dream up deeds remote from their own times; the former left not even a feather or footprint of those events—though they certainly would have left one had they known of them. Shall we allow ourselves to be guided by the incompetence of those who assert rather than by the learning of those who remain silent?”

This is what Muratorius says generally about the force of a negative argument. How great that force sometimes is, and also when and under what circumstances it may properly be applied, will readily be drawn from what I shall now say.

258. It is nearly universally acknowledged, and cannot reasonably be denied, that many events—some of them extremely worthy of notice—took place in past centuries without being committed to writing, and perhaps without ever having been recorded. It does not immediately follow, therefore, that events mentioned only by more recent writers are certainly false. They will nevertheless be certainly or merely probably false according as it is either established—which will indeed happen rarely—or merely probable or plausible that the ancient writers, or at least one or another of those whose silence suppresses them, were of such a kind that, had the events occurred, they would have known of them and would have mentioned them.

Our Papebrochius does not depart far from this position. In the *Propylaeum* for May he writes, most appropriately to the present purpose, as it seems to me:

> “Although in strict dialectical reasoning it does not follow: ‘It was not written or said; therefore it did not happen’—for Lazarus would have been raised by Christ even if John and the other three evangelists had remained silent, and even if the disciples of the apostles and all who were closest to them in age had also remained silent—it nevertheless rightly follows: ‘This or that lacks the testimony of suitable antiquity and authority; therefore it is not prudently credible that it happened.’ Thus the resurrection of Lazarus would not be credible amid the universal silence of all who had either themselves witnessed the event or had learned of it from eyewitnesses, and so forth. Moreover, the demonstration arising from a negative argument becomes more certain and evident in proportion as knowledge of the fact whose credibility is in dispute ought to have reached more people and been committed to writing by more people, on account of its exceptional notoriety.”

Papebrochius thus teaches that, although a negative argument does not irrefutably prove that the events against which it is directed are alien to the truth, it nevertheless possesses sufficient force to make those events approach more or less closely to the class of incredible things.

259. Let us now examine whether, and what, according to what has just been said, can be established from the silence of the ancient writers—or from negative arguments formed out of that silence—against the Parisian prodigy by which Bruno is said to have been driven into the wilderness: namely, the prodigy of a scholar who, having returned to life for a time, proclaimed himself condemned before an almost countless multitude of people.

In his *Dissertation on the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Wilderness*, Launoius brings forward twenty-nine ancient authors. Since they do not mention the Parisian prodigy, he argues that by their silence they testify that it was fictitious. Some of these writers were contemporaries or near-contemporaries of the saint; others flourished about one or two centuries after him; and the last of them, John of Saint Victor, completed his writing in 1322.

Yet there is nothing surprising about the silence of some of these writers concerning that prodigy, and consequently the negative argument formed from their silence has either no force or certainly very little. I therefore wish to examine specifically the silence of those authors—not all of them, but only the principal ones, especially those who would probably have mentioned the prodigy had it occurred, and whose failure to do so may therefore reasonably seem surprising—and to weigh the value of each of the negative arguments advanced by Launoius.

I begin with the silence of Saint Bruno himself. In this section I shall add two others who likewise remain silent about the prodigy: Guigo, the fifth prior of the Carthusians, and Guibert of Nogent.

In the letter already quoted several times above, and to be recited here in full below, which Saint Bruno wrote to Ralph the Green in order to encourage him to fulfill the vow he had made to assume the monastic habit, the saint makes no mention whatsoever of the horrifying spectacle of the condemned scholar. Yet, if Bruno had seen that spectacle and had thereby fulfilled his vow and withdrawn into the wilderness, mention of it would have been highly suitable for moving Ralph to fulfill his own vow.

260. Hence Launoius, in his once again cited *Dissertation on the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Wilderness*, chapter 1, argues as follows:

> “Ralph required sharper goads to spur him on to fulfill his own vow—the vow he had made with Bruno during the conference mentioned above concerning the assumption of the monastic habit. Hence Bruno proposes in this letter, just as glory for the one who fulfills his vow, so eternal punishment for Ralph if he does not fulfill it. Certainly this was the place for him to introduce that horrible spectacle, if what happened at Paris had earlier impelled Bruno to fulfill his vow. For what was more ready at hand for overcoming Ralph’s hesitation than to impress upon him, at every opportunity and out of season, that kind of spectacle by which Bruno’s own hesitation had been overcome, if we believe the *Didactic Epistle*—written by Saussay to Berthold Nihusius and, as I showed above, printed at Cologne in 1645? Nor does the didactic author, who foresaw that he would be attacked by this weapon, adequately ward it off; rather, he exposes his breast to be pierced when, comparing the obligation of the vow binding Bruno and Ralph with the horrible spectacle that he says drove Bruno into the wilderness, he regards that horrible spectacle as the stronger incentive. But if Bruno needed this stronger incentive, why, I ask, did Ralph not need it, since he postponed fulfilling his vow so long that, as far as I know, he never fulfilled it? Yet surely it would be cause for just astonishment in Bruno if, in a letter where he employs every device for moving Ralph, he passed over—or did not repeatedly emphasize—the punishment awaiting him, suggested by the spectacle that lay ready to hand, if indeed it had ever occurred. Since, then, among the arguments by which Bruno moves Ralph to fulfill his vow he omitted the horrible spectacle of which the didactic writer—namely Saussay, as he is called here after the *Didactic Epistle* mentioned shortly below—professes to have been instructed from childhood, he omitted what he could not say. And he could not say what had not happened to him and what some Carthusians introduced only long afterward as the origin of their order.”

261. Thus far Launoius. Now let us hear how the anonymous Carthusian, the author of the fourth book of the *Annals of his Order*, hitherto unpublished, answers this argument against the extraordinary resurrection of the Parisian scholar:

> “Why,” he says in no. 90 of his work, “mention this spectacle, which did not concern Ralph, since he had perhaps made his vow long before? And since the Chronicles of the Order—that is, the Carthusian Order—say that it occurred at Paris in 1082, when the Rheims clerics, expelled earlier by Manasses, had already returned to their church, it is possible either that Ralph did not know of it, if the event took place in a hall among friends, as may be gathered from the same Chronicles, or at least that he was not present. But even if we conceded that he was present at the time, it would not follow that Bruno ought to have refreshed his friend’s memory of the prodigy rather than of the vow he had made. For what was more ready at hand for overcoming Ralph’s hesitation than to impress upon him, at every opportunity and out of season, the vow by which he was bound, the fulfillment of which he was obligated to undertake under pain of mortal sin, and through failure to fulfill which he would incur eternal damnation—damnation he would not otherwise incur even if he neither heard nor obeyed the spectacle mentioned above? For this reason Saint Bruno introduces nothing more frequently in his letter than the obligation to fulfill the vow and the punishments with which God threatens those who do not fulfill what they have promised him.”

Thus he argues that Launoius’s proposed argument proves absolutely nothing against the history of the condemned scholar, principally because, in his letter, the saint ought to have mentioned the vow—or the obligation attached to it—rather than the gruesome history of the condemned man, since the latter was less suited than the former to compel Ralph to fulfill his vow.

262. Yet even if this is so, it is certainly true that mention of that sorrowful spectacle would have been highly suitable and especially effective for moving Ralph’s mind. Since it therefore appears sufficiently probable that Bruno, a prudent man, would have mentioned the same horrible spectacle in a letter in which he used every device to bend Ralph toward fulfillment of his vow, if the spectacle had occurred publicly—even in Ralph’s absence—and since Bruno nevertheless omits it throughout the whole of his lengthy letter to Ralph, the event, which is supported by no other testimony of either contemporary or near-contemporary writers, is thereby rendered in some measure suspicious of falsehood, or at least more difficult to believe, although it is not for that reason certainly false.

I now proceed to the second negative argument to be examined in this section, which Launoius derives in his *Dissertation*, and in the immediately cited chapter of it, from the silence of Guigo, the fifth prior of the Carthusians.

Launoius therefore transcribes the following words from the *Life of Saint Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble*, written by Guigo, the fifth prior of the Carthusians:

> “Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, was engaged in these matters, and behold: before three full years had yet passed in his episcopate after his return from the monastery, Master Bruno appeared, a man renowned for religion and learning, almost a living likeness of honesty, gravity, and every kind of maturity. He had as companions Master Landuin, who later became prior of the Carthusian house; two Stephens, one of Bourg and the other of Die; and these had been canons of Saint Rufus, but, with the abbot’s approval, had joined him out of a desire for the solitary life. They also had Hugh, whom they called the Chaplain because he alone among them performed the office of priest; and two laymen, whom we call conversi, Andrew and Guarinus.”

263. “They were seeking a place suitable for the eremitical life, but had not yet found one. Drawn, therefore, by this hope and by the sweet fragrance of his holy way of life, they came to the holy man, who received them not only gladly but reverently, treated them with honor, and enabled them to attain their vow. Under his counsel, assistance, and guidance, they entered the solitude of Chartreuse and built there their dwelling. At about that time he had seen in a dream God building in that same solitude a dwelling-place for the manifestation of his favor, and seven stars also leading him on his journey. These seven were in fact the seven men.”

Then, implying that these words of Guigo contain no mention whatsoever of the Parisian prodigy, Launoius concludes as follows:

> “This author—Guigo, that is—describes the beginnings of the Carthusian religion and pursues every detail with the greatest diligence, yet he does not even touch upon those two matters,”

namely, the Parisian prodigy in which the resurrected scholar cried out from his coffin that he had been condemned, and Saint Bruno’s withdrawal into the wilderness that followed from it.

Thus Launoius. Let us now see how the anonymous Carthusian, the author of the fourth book of the *Annals of his Order*, hitherto unpublished, answers him:

> “To this,” he says in no. 92 of his work, “we reply that Guigo’s sole purpose was to compose the life of Saint Hugh, not of Saint Bruno. Indeed, he did not undertake even that task until compelled by the Supreme Pontiff. For that reason he mentioned Saint Bruno only incidentally, insofar as Bruno concerned Saint Hugh; nor did he wish to relate more about the Carthusian Order, restrained by the consideration about which Peter of Cluny wrote as follows: ‘I have learned from many that many miracles occurred in that holy Order of the Carthusians, but they themselves, by the virtue of humility through which the servants of God always conceal their wondrous works with all the effort they can, have scarcely been willing to disclose any of them.’”

264. “But let us now see whether Guigo described the beginnings of the Carthusian religion and pursued every detail so diligently that his silence about the spectacle can serve as an argument for its falsehood.
