In a few words he does indeed relate that Bruno came with six companions, whose names he lists, drawn by the reputation of Hugh’s holiness, in order to obtain from him a place suitable for the eremitical life; and that, under Hugh’s counsel, assistance, and guidance, they entered and built in the solitude of Chartreuse. But he does not relate how these things came about.

Nor does he say where Saint Bruno came from—whether from Rheims, where he was a canon, or from Paris, where he had most recently taught, or at least conceived the plan of abandoning the world. He is silent about Bruno’s dignities in the church of Rheims and about the labors he had undertaken in various councils in defense of the liberty and rights of the Church, by which he had earned the glorious titles ‘Pillar of the entire metropolitan church’ and ‘Sincere defender of the Catholic faith.’

“He is silent about the conference between Saint Bruno, Ralph, and Fulk; about the vow to assume the monastic habit; and about the persecutions of Manasses, so that he says absolutely nothing about the cause or occasion of Bruno’s conversion, whatever it may have been. Finally, he is silent about everything Bruno did from his departure from the city of Rheims until his withdrawal to Chartreuse.

“All these matters, and many others of the same kind that need not detain us longer in enumeration, were genuine details—though great ones and plainly necessary for a proper description of the beginnings of the Order—which Guigo nevertheless omitted, just as he omitted the Parisian spectacle, because none of them contributed anything to the life of Saint Hugh, which alone he had undertaken to write. If, therefore, everything else that could be reported about Bruno’s history becomes uncertain because of Guigo’s silence, then we must hold only to what Guigo wrote. To say or even think that would be judged more than ridiculous.”

265. Thus far the anonymous Carthusian just cited, who rightly argues that nothing whatsoever can be concluded from Guigo’s silence against the resurrection of the Parisian scholar and Bruno’s consequent withdrawal into solitude. For, apart from the fact that he passed over many other matters concerning Saint Bruno and did not set out to write Bruno’s life, there is no reason to think that Guigo, even if he certainly knew that prodigy had occurred, would have committed it to writing in the cited *Life of Saint Hugh*, to which it was in no way relevant.

But what are we now to say about the silence of Guibert, abbot of Nogent in the district of Laon, which must still be examined in this section? Launoius writes as follows in his *Dissertation*, in the chapter cited above:

> “Guibert, abbot of Nogent, composed a treatise on his own life in which he explains the origin and institution of the Carthusians still more closely and closes every avenue to the fables of certain more recent writers.”

After transcribing a substantial portion of chapter 11 of book I of Guibert’s *Life of Himself*, he adds:

> “According to this author, Guibert, no room remains for the prodigious resurrection of the scholar which drove Bruno into the wilderness. For he assigns an entirely different cause for it in these words: ‘The occasion from which he is recognized to have obtained the beginnings of his conversion is the following: After the death of the famous Archbishop Gervasius, a certain Manasses intruded himself by simony into the administration of the aforesaid city, Rheims. He was indeed a nobleman, but possessed none of that serenity which is the first mark of noble character.’”

And later:

> “Since every honorable man detested this man’s utterly wicked conduct and his disgracefully stupid character, Bruno, then the most renowned man in the churches of Gaul, left the city, together with certain other noble clerics of Rheims, out of hatred for that infamous man.”

That was when he conceived the plan of leaving, after the conference with Ralph, which Bruno mentions in his letter to him.

266. “But I ask you: in this very lengthy account of Guibert, where is there even one word about Paris, which at that time possessed an academy flourishing in every branch of learning? About the resurrected scholar who, during solemn funeral rites, said three times that he had been condemned? Finally, about the solemn funeral rites which the entire ecclesiastical order honored?”

Thus Launoius.

But that Guibert does not assign the true cause of Saint Bruno’s withdrawal into the wilderness in the way this writer understands the words just quoted is demonstrated sufficiently and more than sufficiently, in my opinion, by what I brought forward in § 9.

As for Guibert’s silence concerning the resurrection of the scholar, Columbius responds to Launoius on this point in nos. 35 and following of his *Dissertation on the Beginnings of the Carthusians* in the following manner:

> “Guibert relates that Bruno obtained the beginnings of his conversion from the occasion just described,”

and Launoius himself points out that Guibert remained silent about the resurrected man who, at Paris, cried out from his coffin in a terrible voice that he had been condemned. Yet, as he meditated upon conversion after the occasion recounted above, conceived through pious conversations with Ralph the Green and Fulk the One-Eyed and confirmed by a vow, that event was a great incentive—more powerful than any speech—to undertake in Chartreuse a life far harsher than the one he had considered and already vowed to undertake.

“I am pleased to answer the exclamation with an exclamation. I ask you: in this very lengthy account of Guibert, where is there even one word about the little garden adjoining Adam’s house, about Bruno’s discussion with Ralph and Fulk, or about Fulk’s journey to Rome, which he undertook so that Bruno and Ralph did not immediately assume the monastic habit after making their vow?

267. “But why, then, do you not reject these matters as Guibert’s omissions, when you assert that those matters—namely, the resurrection of the scholar and Bruno’s consequent expulsion into the wilderness—are not true because Guibert remains silent about them? Yet, as I have shown, Guibert proposed to relate the occasion from which Bruno obtained the beginnings of his conversion, not the causes of his conversion. What therefore ought not to have been mentioned by him ought not to be demanded from his narrative by us.

“These causes were two: the discussion in the little garden adjoining Adam’s house, at an unknown place outside Rheims, concerning the false pleasures and perishable riches of this world, as well as the joys of eternal glory, held with Ralph and Fulk; and the horrible and fatal voices of the resurrected man at Paris, crying out from his coffin that he had been accused, judged, and condemned. The first caused Bruno to vow with Ralph and Fulk that they would undertake conversion and assume the monastic habit; the second, as he contemplated the conversion confirmed by his vow, compelled him, together with Landuin and five other companions, to enter Chartreuse, more powerfully than any speech or discussion. Just as Bruno therefore placed the first event, which concerned Ralph, in his letter to him without the second, which did not concern Ralph, so Guibert omitted both, because he had not proposed to speak of the causes of Bruno’s conversion, but of the occasion, to which neither of them pertained.”

Thus Columbius. Yet since Guibert does indeed recount Bruno’s resolve to renounce the world, as well as his withdrawal into the wilderness, or perfect conversion, and in that very place where he does so explains the occasion from which the saint obtained the beginnings of his conversion, it would most probably also have been appropriate for him to mention the cause of the conversion—or the resurrection of the scholar—which, if it had ever occurred, would have been much more noteworthy than this occasion and would likewise have been known to him.

268. Nor is it relevant that certain other matters concerning Bruno—namely, his conference with Radulph and Fulcius; his journey to Rome; and the subsequent relaxation, both of their resolve and of Bruno’s, to fulfill their vow to assume the monastic habit—were passed over in silence by Guibertus. For all these matters, as will be clear to anyone who considers them, are of such a kind that they could easily have been unknown to this writer. But as for the Parisian prodigy of the risen teacher, if it really occurred publicly before an almost innumerable multitude of people, as some of those whose account we are here examining have transmitted to memory, it appears in no way plausible that Guibertus, who was a contemporary of the event, could have been unaware of it. Moreover, as regards the occasion of the beginnings of Saint Bruno’s conversion—which Guibertus intended to mention exclusively, and not also the causes of his conversion—this cannot make it in any way plausible that Guibertus would have passed over that prodigy in silence, if it had occurred. For who would not be persuaded that this writer, when he recorded not only the beginnings of Saint Bruno’s conversion but also his complete conversion, or withdrawal into the wilderness, would have wished or intended to mention the occasion of those beginnings, namely Manasses’ wicked conduct, which was less worthy of remembrance, rather than the cause of his complete conversion—namely, the Parisian teacher’s resurrection, if it had ever taken place: an event, certainly, which, if it occurred, would have been far more worthy of the memory of all ages? The anonymous author of the fourth book of the Carthusian Annals, hitherto unpublished, in order to weaken the argument drawn by Launoius from Guibertus’ silence against the dreadful story of the condemned teacher, takes another path.

269. For he accuses Guibertus himself of ignorance concerning matters relating to Saint Bruno and the Carthusians. He also contends that chapter 11 of the first book of Guibertus’ Life, in which the story of the condemned teacher ought to have been recorded but is nevertheless passed over in silence, has been conspicuously interpolated, or even has an author other than Guibertus. The principal, or rather the stronger, arguments by which he either endeavors to prove this opinion of his, or actually presents it as proved, may be seen if I once again transcribe here the man’s own words. Thus, first, in no. 94 of his work, after prefacing certain matters that I pass over here, he writes:

> “He [Guibertus, that is, in the passage cited] describes the Great Chartreuse in the condition in which it was after the death of our Guigo, who died in 1136. ‘They have,’ he says, ‘a cloister sufficiently suitable for cenobitic observance, but not in the cloistered manner of the other inhabitants. For each of them has his own cell arranged around the cloister,’ etc.”

By these words he describes the new monastery of the Chartreuse, built after 1132, following the monks’ being overwhelmed by snow at the former site (see Labbe, *Bibliotheca nova manuscriptorum*, vol. I, p. 640). For at the time when Guibertus is believed to have written—namely, before or around 1124—the cells were not arranged around the cloister but were entirely separate from the cloister itself, as we shall prove in the Annals under the year 1134.

When he adds:

> “They have water both for drinking and for other use, from a conduit supplied by a spring which goes around all the cells and flows into each of the little buildings through specific openings,”

he indicates the time of Saint Antelmus, the seventh prior of the Chartreuse. For, as the author of his Life says:

> “Constructing an aqueduct through great but unremitting labor, he directed through long channels to the cells, the kitchen, and the other workshops such an abundance of water,” etc.

Guigo had indeed undertaken this work first, but death prevented him from carrying it through the cells.

270. “Guibertus [obviously in the passage cited above] writes that the Carthusians hardly speak anywhere; for if something must be requested, it is demanded by a sign.” But let us see from the customs of our Guigo whether Guibertus understood our practices correctly. Guigo speaks as follows:

> “We who live alone know either none, or only a few, of the signs used in monasteries, considering the tongue alone sufficient, and not wishing to involve the other limbs in the faults of speech as well; and therefore, when such necessity presses, we preferred that what the matter requires should be indicated in one or two words, or certainly in the very fewest words.”

We therefore demand what is necessary for us not by signs, as Guibertus maintains, but by speech.

“‘There are,’ says Guibertus, ‘below that mountain [the Chartreuse], dwellings containing laymen, more than twenty in number, and retaining men of the greatest fidelity.’” But Guigo established the following rule:

> “The number of laymen, whom we call lay brothers, is fixed at sixteen.”

Hence we suspect either that Guibertus did not die in 1124 but lived until the time of Basil, prior of the Chartreuse—that is, beyond 1150—or that this chapter—namely, chapter 11 of book I cited above—was inserted into Guibertus’ work by someone else. For around the time of Basil the number of lay brothers and hired workers began to increase, as is evident from the charters of the general chapters and is confirmed by Peter of Cluny. In chapter 28 of book II of his *Miracles*, which he published around 1150, as we shall say in its proper place, Peter writes that the number of lay brothers at that time was eighteen.

Guibertus asserts that the Carthusians

> “are borne along with such fervor of the contemplation they have begun that they do not desist from their institution through any length of time, nor grow lukewarm through any duration of that arduous way of life.”

From these words we certainly infer that a great “length of time,” or “duration of the way of life,” had elapsed from the foundation of the Order up to the time when this was written, so that the matter was worthy of admiration—which it surely would not have been if it did not extend beyond the lifetime of Guibertus, who was a contemporary of Saint Bruno. Nor, on that account, would the Carthusians have been so deserving of praise.

271. Guibertus continues to reveal his ignorance concerning Saint Bruno by saying:

> “From there also [from the Chartreuse], this remarkable Bruno, departing—I do not know on what occasion—after he had furnished, by repeated inculcation of what we have already mentioned, many rudiments of words and deeds, withdrew—I do not know whether to Apulia or to Calabria—and there established a somewhat similar manner of life.”

Saint Bruno left the Chartreuse unwillingly, at the command and compulsion of Urban II, the supreme pontiff, whom he assisted for several years with pious counsels, especially in the councils then being held. But Guibertus alone was ignorant of what was known to everyone: he admits that he does not know on what occasion Saint Bruno left the Chartreuse.

Next, he supposes that the holy patriarch traveled directly from Gaul to Apulia or Calabria, but he does not know to which of the two he actually withdrew. While Saint Bruno was at Urban’s court, the clergy of Reggio, with the pope’s approval, requested him as archbishop. He refused to consent to the election and, having received permission from Urban himself, withdrew into the solitude he had chosen in Calabria.

But Guibertus, ignorant of all these matters, writes that while Bruno was hiding in the wilderness, he was nevertheless exposed by the radiance of his virtues and, when sought out and detained by the supreme pontiff so that he might become a bishop, fled:

> “There,” says Guibertus—without knowing whether he means Apulia or Calabria—“he conducted himself with great humility and shone all around through the fullest display of pious examples. Sought out and detained by the Apostolic See for the dignity of a bishop, he fled.”

From this it is clear that Guibertus was entirely ignorant of whether Saint Bruno had ever attached himself to Pope Urban, although he ought to have known this especially well, since he had been Urban’s contemporary and had come, as it were, from the same region. Guibertus himself was originally from the city of Beauvais and later became abbot of Nogent in the diocese of Laon; both cities belonged to the metropolitan province of Reims. Urban, meanwhile, came from the territory and clergy of Reims, as Guibertus himself writes.

272. Immediately after the words copied by Launoius from Guibertus, as we reported them above, Guibertus adds in the same chapter:

> “These persons, I say, advanced the beginnings of conversions at that time. Crowds of men and women immediately joined them; every order soon hastened together.”

And later:

> “Likewise distinguished women, having abandoned the marriage-bond with famous husbands and abstained from children out of pious motives, contributed their resources there and committed themselves to ecclesiastical maintenance.”

What is the meaning of this? Guibertus died around 1124, and yet he speaks of Carthusian women, or nuns, who, as we shall prove in the Annals, were admitted into the Order only around 1145. Moreover, he speaks of women who, “having abandoned the marriage-bond of their husbands,” had embraced our institution, although it is certain that no women—whether widows or married women—were ever received into our communities of virgins. Only women, that is, virgins entirely untouched by marriage, were admitted, on account of the consecration that has always been practiced among our nuns and that is granted only to virgins.

Furthermore, during the entire first century of our Order, only one Carthusian community of women was founded. Guibertus continues in the same place:

> “What shall I say about their ages, when ten- and eleven-year-old children meditated on such things and performed many practices more austere than their tender age could bear?”

Who has ever heard or written such things about the Carthusian Order? No access was ever open to boys; indeed, they were always prohibited, in accordance with the statute of our reverend father Guigo, who writes concerning the age of those to be received:

> “We do not receive boys or adolescents, because we regret that many things have happened to monasteries through them . . . but men who, in accordance with the Lord’s command through Moses, may proceed to the sacred wars at not less than twenty years of age.”

273. “There are also many other things of this kind in the same chapter of Guibertus, so alien to the institutions of our Order that, when we read them, it occurred to us either that they are not Guibertus’ words or at least that they have no connection whatsoever with us,” although Dacherus, otherwise a most perceptive man, holds the opposite opinion. In marginal notes to the same words he writes, after the *Notes on Saint Bruno*:

> “Men and women adopt that manner of life. Even ten- and eleven-year-old children. He [namely Bruno, who built no other monastery besides the Great Chartreuse and the monastery in Calabria] established countless monasteries.”

And in his index to the same Guibertus:

> “The origin of the Carthusian Order, p. 465 or 467; description of the Chartreuse, 466 or 468. Men, women, and children adopt that manner of life. They establish countless monasteries, in the same place. They are richly endowed. 467,” etc.

Guibertus did indeed write in that same passage that, for the men—whether Carthusians or others—of whom he was speaking, “new monasteries had begun to be built everywhere, and great revenues of provisions were supplied from every direction by those who flocked together.” But to us, who investigate the more hidden facts of Carthusian history, the foundations of these countless monasteries have nowhere appeared. Indeed, it will be evident in our Annals that before 1124 scarcely five or six Chartreuses had then been founded, and those were exceedingly poor.

Thus far the anonymous Carthusian—quite rightly, and contrary to the opinion he had previously held, Dacherus believing that the matters reported by Guibertus in the cited book and chapter concerning the vast multitude of women and children devoting themselves to a religious or monastic life did not concern the Carthusians.

274. For the words that he immediately adds there to his statements about Saint Bruno—“These persons . . . advanced the beginnings of conversions at that time”—must be referred not solely to Saint Bruno but also to Saint Simon of Crépy, a count who became a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, whose life has already been published in our work under 30 September; to Ebrard, count of Breteuil; and to others who had converted to monastic life, or at least to a better life different from the Carthusian one. Guibertus had spoken of these immediately before discussing Saint Bruno.

Consequently, what he adds afterward—“Crowds of men and women immediately joined them; every order soon hastened together. What shall I say about their ages? When ten- and eleven-year-old children meditated on things appropriate to old age and performed practices far more austere than their tender age could bear. This occurred in those conversions, etc.”—must be understood to mean that at that time women and men, and even children, devoted themselves to a better and more disciplined life, but did not all embrace the Order founded by Bruno. Rather, each embraced this or another order according to what was appropriate to his or her sex or condition, and thus joined Bruno and the others whose conversions Guibertus had discussed by devoting themselves to one of the various forms of better life that those people had either instituted or followed.

Since this is so, there is no reason why the accounts given by Guibertus in the cited book and chapter concerning men, women, and children should be condemned as errors or falsehoods, and consequently rejected as though Guibertus could not have committed such matters to writing. Otherwise this would indeed have to be done, since certainly in the lifetime of Guibertus, who died in 1124—as Mabillon teaches in book LXXIV, no. 71, of the *Benedictine Annals*, followed by the authors of the *Literary History of France*, vol. X, p. 438—there were no nuns belonging to the Carthusian Order at all, nor had any women who had experienced widowhood or marriage ever been admitted into it.

275. But what should be said about the other matters likewise mentioned by Guibertus that, as our anonymous Carthusian believes, require a date later than 1124, and therefore could not have been committed to writing by Guibertus if he did not live beyond that year? Such matters include—see no. 269—the number of lay brothers or conversi, which suits only a later period; the construction of cells around the cloister; and finally the conduit carrying the spring water around all the cells and flowing into them.

Yet Guibertus could have made the number of lay brothers or conversi greater than it was on the basis of an erroneous account given to him. For the same reason he could also have been mistaken in assigning the location of the cells. As for the water conduit, since the work was begun by Guigo, who presided over the Chartreuse from 1110 until 1136, as our anonymous Carthusian himself teaches, what if Guibertus persuaded himself that the work which he understood Guigo to have begun with great diligence and labor had also been brought to completion? What if a superior conduit was later substituted by Antelmus for the spring conduit that, in Guibertus’ time, ran around all the cells of the Chartreuse and sprinkled them with water?

It is therefore unnecessary either to suppose that these matters were written by someone other than Guibertus or that Guibertus lived beyond 1124. The same may be said of the following words with which Guibertus praises the Carthusians in chapter 11 of book I of his cited Life:

> “They are borne along with such fervor of the contemplation they have begun that they do not desist from their institution through any length of time, nor grow lukewarm through any duration of that arduous way of life.”

For why could Guibertus, who died only in 1124, not have said this of Carthusians who had persevered steadfastly for thirty—or even only twenty—years in the discipline of the exceedingly austere life undertaken at the Chartreuse, a life whose institution Bruno had first begun in 1084?

276. Since all these matters stand as described, the arguments brought forward above by the anonymous Carthusian historian do not at all prove that chapter 11 of Guibertus’ Life did not have Guibertus himself as its author, or that it was inserted into this work by a later writer. Nevertheless, it must be admitted that these arguments plainly show Guibertus to have been insufficiently informed about everything concerning Saint Bruno and the Order founded by him.

In saying this, however, there is no reason to suppose immediately that Guibertus also departed from the truth in other matters he relates about Bruno, that he was unaware of the Parisian prodigy by which Bruno was driven into the wilderness, and that consequently no one should find his silence about it surprising. For the matters undertaken by our saint at the Chartreuse, where he was withdrawn from the sight of almost all people, and afterward in Calabria, far removed from Gaul and from the abbey of Nogent, must be distinguished from those he accomplished at Reims and in other places not far from Nogent.

Although Guibertus is sometimes found to have been mistaken concerning the former matters, he should not for that reason be considered to have been similarly mistaken concerning the latter, since he was near them not only in time but also in place, unless a solid argument proving this can be brought forward from elsewhere.

As specifically concerns the Parisian prodigy, since, according to the opinion we are examining, it occurred publicly before an almost innumerable multitude of people and not very far from the abbey of Nogent, it is in no way plausible that Guibertus was ignorant of it merely because he had not acquired sufficiently certain and precise knowledge of some events undertaken by the saint either at the Chartreuse or in Calabria, far from Nogent and indeed outside the sight of almost everyone.

277. Yet in the treatise on Saint Bruno communicated to me by the Carthusians of this place, the author writes additional remarks in no. 36 of his work by which he indicates that the work written by Guibertus about his own life and edited by Dacherus ought to be regarded as suspect and interpolated. Here are his words:

> “When Claudius Hemeraeus, a doctor of the Sorbonne, had dedicated a sufficiently substantial work in 1672 to Bruno d’Affringues, the superior general of our Order, and had arranged for it to be entitled *The Carthusian, or the Way to Wisdom*, and for an excerpt from Guibertus’ treatise containing praises of Saint Bruno and our institution to be appended at the end of that work, the same superior general wrote the following concerning the authenticity of this excerpt to John de Bacca, prior of the Carthusian house of Paular in Castile:
>
> “‘That gentleman Hemeraeus acted imprudently when he inserted into his *Carthusian* an excerpt concerning the origin of our Order which is false and fictitious, as the Parisian prior warned me when writing about the aforesaid Mr. Hemeraeus, the author of the book entitled *The Carthusian*.’
>
> “And indeed Lucas d’Achery, a Benedictine monk who deserved well of the Church through his published texts, admits that the copy of the entire treatise was written by a recent hand and is full of numerous errors: words have been transposed, and sentences have sometimes been altered or completely removed, so that, on closer examination, some passages were scarcely anything less than matters to be guessed by him. For this reason, when he wished to publish all of Guibertus’ works, he moved every stone in order to discover the autograph of the aforesaid treatise, which he had heard shortly before had fallen into the hands of a certain Parisian doctor; but in vain.”

278. Thus far the anonymous author. But although only a copy of the work Guibertus wrote about his own life had come before Dacherus, and although that most diligent editor of manuscripts hidden in libraries informs us in the preliminary Notice prefixed to the works of Guibertus that it was full of numerous errors and that he had been unable, despite the most diligent investigation, to find the autograph, that copy of the work does not appear to have been so corrupted that it contained entire chapters, or even fragments of chapters worthy of notice, inserted into it although they were not Guibertus’ work.

This may reasonably be inferred from Dacherus’ own words concerning the matter in the preliminary Notice just mentioned. I therefore transcribe them here. They read as follows:

> “It was permitted me to find only a copy of the books of our abbot [Guibertus] concerning his own life, written in a fine but recent hand, yet full of very many errors: words were transposed, and sentences were sometimes altered or completely removed—by the writing of one word or another, evidently either erroneous or difficult to read—so that, on closer examination, some passages were scarcely anything less than matters to be guessed by me. For the remaining words that had escaped me, I supplied dots in their place or wrote certain alternatives in the margin. I had indeed heard, and had learned through repeated reports, that the autograph was preserved into our own time among the ancient manuscripts of the church of Laon and had afterward been lent to an expert in antiquities, Mr. Dey, a Parisian doctor who has since died. I moved every stone to discover into whose hands it had later fallen, insofar as I could ascertain, but in vain.”

These are Dacherus’ words. But since he says only that the words and sentences were afflicted with errors in the manner I have described, who could conclude from this that entire chapters or notable fragments not belonging to Guibertus had been added to the work?

Since this is so, the passage cited more than once above, in which the occasion of the beginnings of Saint Bruno’s conversion is mentioned, cannot be regarded as an addition made to Guibertus. Consequently, the negative argument formed from Guibertus’ silence in that passage concerning the resurrection of the Parisian teacher retains all the force that I attributed to it above.

§ XVI. What should be thought of the silence of the Carthusian Order, as Launoius calls it, and of Peter the Venerable

279. The five eulogies of the first five priors of the Chartreuse preserved in Labbe, vol. I of the *New Library of Manuscript Books*, pp. 638 and following, possess the highest antiquity; and specifically, the first four were written before 1138. The evidence brought forward in § 1 proves this sufficiently and more than sufficiently. Hence Launoius, in chapter 1 of his *Dissertation on the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Wilderness*, rightly counts their authors—or rather, if only the first four are under discussion, their author—among the ancient writers who mention Saint Bruno.

But is he equally justified in arguing that the silence of the Carthusians concerning the miraculous resurrection of the teacher, preserved in those five eulogies found in an old manuscript codex of the Statutes and Customs of the Carthusian Order, bears witness against the Carthusian Order, as he calls it? Before stating my opinion on this matter, I shall transcribe here both Launoius’ words and the response made to them by our anonymous Carthusian in the fourth book of the Annals of his Order, hitherto unpublished.

After describing the eulogy of our saint from the manuscript codex just mentioned, Launoius argues as follows:

> “Here there is no mention of the dead Parisian teacher or canon, who during solemn funeral rites replied that he had been condemned, nor of this prodigy which drove blessed Bruno into the wilderness of the Chartreuse. Yet Raynaudus did not hesitate to write that these two matters were accepted by all the ancients.
>
> “Among ancient writers I cannot but count those who copied that codex of the Statutes at Paris, where it is now preserved among the Carthusians, or elsewhere, and who published the history of the first five priors of the Chartreuse in such a way that, if anything miraculous had been found in them, they would have observed it.”

280. “Therefore there is no reason at all for you to complain that these authors of whom we are speaking passed over in silence matters that would contribute to commending the conversion and flight from the world of those priors. Nor do I have any reason to suppose that the more ancient Carthusians omitted the principal memorial of their origin, which some of the more recent among them eagerly insert into their books and walls and call ‘a dreadful spectacle, worthy to be remembered throughout the ages.’ This memorial is certainly not of such a kind that it could have escaped all the ancient Carthusians and been known only to more recent writers, who, if they judged correctly in this matter, ought to draw their knowledge only from the accounts of their predecessors.

> “For, as Baronius says, ‘Whatever is reported concerning matters so ancient without the authority of some older source is disregarded.’”

So far Launoius. Now let us hear what the anonymous Carthusian cited above replies:

> “We call upon the kindly reader,” he says in no. 102 of the book of his Annals cited above, “to judge whether what the author of the codex—who, according to the preceding number, was available to Launoius—prefaced above about Bruno and his successors, namely his four immediate successors, in that meager Breviary of their lives, using so few words (see Labbe, the immediately cited passage of the *New Library*), carries such weight that Launoius could justly and reasonably draw from it the following conclusion:
>
> “‘Among ancient writers I cannot but count those who copied that codex of the Statutes at Paris, where it is now preserved among the Carthusians, or elsewhere, and who published the history of the first five priors of the Chartreuse in such a way that, if anything miraculous had been found in them, they would have observed it.’
>
> “See how many inflated phrases he throws out, in accordance with the poet’s saying, in order to magnify his authorities with swollen style. ‘I cannot but count those who copied that codex.’ Would he not have spoken better and more accurately if he had said ‘the person who copied that codex,’ since it contains scarcely thirty leaves—unless he wishes there to have been as many writers as there are leaves in the codex?”

281. But these are minor matters. Hear the more inflated claims:

> “Those who copied that codex published the history of the first five priors of the Chartreuse in such a way that, if anything miraculous had been found in them, they observed it.”

But, I ask, what are these miracles that those writers observed in so brief a narrative, contained on a single folio? Certainly none—at least none in the eulogies of the first four priors, which we reported above from the oldest of all codices of this kind (see the statement in no. 4). We now say nothing about Guigo, because, as we noted, his eulogy was added by a recent hand.

Does this mean that no miracle occurred among these first fathers or was performed by them? Let Peter of Cluny answer for us once again:

> “I have learned from many people that many miracles occurred in that holy Order”—that is, the Order of the Carthusians.

Are they therefore false because the writers of the codex were silent about them?

But let us return to Saint Bruno. The writers—or rather, to speak more accurately now, the writer—of this codex embraces his entire life, from infancy to his withdrawal to the Chartreuse, in these very few words:

> “Bruno the Teuton, born in the city of Cologne to parents of no mean standing, highly equipped in both secular and divine letters, a canon of the church of Reims and master of the schools, having abandoned the world, founded and governed the wilderness of the Chartreuse for six years.”

There you have Saint Bruno’s entire conversion contained in five words: “Having abandoned the world, he founded the wilderness of the Chartreuse”—words that could be said of the conversion of anyone who renounces the world.

Did that writer publish Bruno’s history in so few words “in such a way that, if anything miraculous had been found in it, he would have observed it,” as Launoius maintains? Just as he was silent about the vision of the seven stars shown to Saint Hugh; about Saint Bruno’s six companions; about the persecutions of Manasses; about Bruno’s vow; and about many other things he accomplished splendidly, so it is not surprising if he also omitted the spectacle.

282. Finally, it must be noted that the writer’s sole purpose seems to have been to compile a catalogue of the priors of the Chartreuse and specify the years of their governance. For he appears to describe nothing with greater precision than the fact that Bruno “governed the Chartreuse for six years and died in Calabria,” approximately eleven years after leaving the Chartreuse.

He carefully records the same information about the others, so that toward the end he repeats in summary the years that had elapsed from the foundation of the Chartreuse to the death of John the Tuscan:

> “Thus,” he says, “from the first year of Master Bruno to the last year of this man [John], twenty-five years are reckoned, completed around the birth of blessed John the Baptist—before his death, which occurred on the Nones of October. For it was at such a time that the aforesaid wilderness first began to be inhabited by Master Bruno.”

This was also observed by the person who inserted Guigo’s eulogy into the same codex.

Such is the response of the anonymous Carthusian to the negative argument drawn by Launoius from the silence of the codex praised in no. 279. Indeed, since the author of the codex—that is, the chronicle of the first four priors of the Chartreuse—did not undertake to describe the whole life and all the deeds of our saint, and says nothing about Bruno concerning many matters that he nevertheless knew especially well, particularly if, as appears, he was Guigo, the argument formed from his silence has here either no force at all or at least very little force. This is especially so since no reason can be given that would make it in any way plausible that this writer would not have passed over in silence the Parisian prodigy, which, if it occurred, he undoubtedly knew.

283. Let us now proceed to the second negative argument, which must also be examined in the present section and which is formed from the silence of Peter, surnamed the Venerable.

This man, born around 1093, after serving honorably for several years in military life, abandoned the world and joined the monks of Cluny. He was subsequently placed in charge of them as abbot in 1122 and held that office for more than thirty-four years. In 1156 he departed to the Lord, distinguished both by the holiness of his life and by the various works he left behind after composing them.

Among these works is one written about miracles and divided into two books. In the second of them Peter prefaces that he had resolved to write “miracles for the strengthening of faith and the formation of morals,” miracles “performed either in his own time or around his time, whose knowledge is certain.” Yet nowhere in the whole of this celebrated work does he mention the miracle or prodigy by which the Parisian teacher publicly declared before an immense multitude of assembled people that he had been condemned.

From this Launoius concludes, in chapter 3 of his *Dissertation on the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Wilderness*, that every account of this mournful story must be regarded as a fable. But did he rightly value Peter the Venerable’s silence on this matter so highly, surpassing Papirius Massonus?

Our anonymous Carthusian, who composed the fourth book of the Annals of his Order, hitherto unpublished, attempts to show that Peter ought not to have mentioned the Parisian prodigy in his entire work on miracles. He first brings forward certain matters concerning the purpose that this holy abbot of Cluny set for himself in composing the work, and at the same time examines what miracles, and of what kind, he reports in it. He then endeavors to refute with contrary arguments the reasons that led Launoius to suppose that Peter’s silence concerning the matter possessed great force against the resurrection of the condemned teacher.

Since the anonymous Carthusian believes that the entire argument he constructed for this purpose has considerable force in refuting Launoius, because of the reason given at the end of no. 185, I transcribe it here in full, however long it may be. I shall add at the end my own opinion on the matter.

284. Thus he prefaces his work in no. 105:

> “Launoius, following Papirius Massonus, places such weight on Peter the Venerable’s silence concerning our spectacle—that is, the spectacle of the risen and condemned teacher—that he boldly declares from this that the account must be regarded as a fable. But before refuting his arguments, it is useful to examine minutely the work of Peter the Venerable, entitled by its author *On Miracles*, which is in question, so that after a careful examination of it readers may cease to wonder that he was silent about so astonishing a prodigy.”

He then immediately takes up the matter itself and continues in this way:

> “This work is divided into two parts, or books. In the brief preface to the first book the holy abbot gives the following reason why he undertook to write on this subject—that is, on miracles:
>
> “‘Lest those miracles which occur in our own times, since there is no one who applies himself to writing them down, perish hidden beneath unfruitful silence, although their disclosure could benefit readers.’
>
> “This book comprises twenty-eight chapters. Twenty-one of them contain remarkable events that took place either in the abbey of Cluny itself or in other monasteries of the same Order. In five other chapters are reported stories that occurred in places not far from Cluny, except for one or two. For the abbot himself declares in chapters 9 and 23 that he will report what he had heard had happened in the monastery of Cluny or in its vicinity. Finally, two chapters mention a certain priest and a certain young man in the Teutonic regions who were abusing the divine mysteries and Holy Communion. [Col. 0169A]”

### 285

“Peter had received one account from the bishop of Clermont, who seems to have been Aymericus, formerly abbot of Casa Dei of the Cluniac order; another from the prior and brothers of a certain monastery situated in the same regions. But what he means here by ‘the German parts’ he seems to indicate later, when, speaking of the city of Mâcon, in whose diocese Cluny is situated, he writes as follows:

> ‘This same Mâcon lies on the borders of the kingdom of the Franks, which the river Saône, arising in Lorraine, and the Rhône, flowing into the Mediterranean Sea, divide from the empire of the Germans or Romans.’ [Col. 0169B]

From these words it may be conjectured that these two miracles also took place in a region not far from Cluny. Hence Peter’s purpose seems to have been merely to relate what had occurred within his own order, while nevertheless adding certain events that he had happened to hear had taken place around Cluny.

All these events contained in these twenty-eight chapters seem to have occurred while the abbot himself was already presiding—that is, after the year 1122—with the exception of certain matters concerning the Cluniac order that took place under Hugh, who had governed that same abbey for approximately sixty years and died in office in the year 1109. Moreover, it should be noted that everything Peter records in this book, except for two or three examples, had been reported to him by persons of the same order; among them must also be counted, as we have said, Aymericus, bishop of Clermont.

### 286

“In the prologue to the second book the venerable abbot writes as follows:

> ‘Since I have resolved to write down miracles performed in our time or around our time, whose occurrence is established beyond doubt, for the strengthening of faith and the formation of morals,’ etc.

These words concern not only the following book but also the first, in which, as we have pointed out, certain events had occurred around his own time—that is, in the time of Saint Hugh the abbot—and indeed only events relating to the Cluniac order. [Col. 0169C]

This second book contains thirty-two chapters on miracles. In the first, Peter relates, on the basis of common report, how a certain count of Mâcon was once visibly carried away by the devil. In the second he treats of a man “who, buried beneath the earth, was fed by an angel through the sacrifices and prayers of the Church”; he asserts that this occurred in the diocese of Grenoble, and perhaps had heard of it when he came to the Grande Chartreuse, to which, as we shall say in the appropriate places in the Annals, he ascended more than once.

From the third chapter through the twenty-third, inclusive, he writes out the life of Matthew, a Cluniac monk and bishop of Albano, who died most holy in the year 1139. In the twenty-fourth, twenty-fifth, twenty-sixth, twenty-seventh, thirty-first, and thirty-second chapters he records events that had occurred, while he was presiding, within his own order. [Col. 0170A] In the twenty-eighth chapter he treats “of the institutions of the Carthusian monks.” In the twenty-ninth, “of a certain Carthusian brother who, while awake, saw marvelous things.” In the thirtieth, “of the miracle of the Roman candles,” which, he asserts, takes place every year in the church of Saint Mary Major, “even to our own age,” he says, “and for as long thereafter as it may please God.”

Of these thirty-two chapters, twenty-seven concern the Cluniac order. The first two, together with the twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth, which concern the Carthusians, deal with events that occurred in regions not far from Cluny. Only the thirtieth chapter relates an event performed far from Cluny, namely at Rome, which Peter himself may perhaps have heard or witnessed when he had lived there some years earlier. [Col. 0170B]

### 287

“Thus the entire work, divided into two books, contains sixty chapters, of which forty-eight concern miracles perpetrated among the Cluniacs under Peter himself as abbot or under Saint Hugh, who had made him a monk. In ten others—for the moment we are not speaking of the two concerning the Carthusians—the subject is marvelous events which, as may be inferred from their narratives, occurred during Peter’s lifetime or even while he was presiding. With the exception of one portent concerning the count of Mâcon, these events were foreign to the Cluniac order, but they took place either around Cluny—as the abbot himself observed, with the Roman miracle alone almost entirely excepted—or were related to Peter by monks of that same order. Five or six, however, he learned from outsiders who were trustworthy and lived near Cluny. [Col. 0170C]

“All these matters, carefully and perhaps somewhat extensively examined, make it sufficiently clear that Peter of Cluny’s silence detracts nothing from the truth of our history. For what is surprising if, among five or six miracles unrelated to his order, he did not record our spectacle? These events, apart from one or two, seem to have occurred around Cluny during Peter’s lifetime and to have been reported to him by neighboring friends. The portent concerning the condemned man, however, occurred in Paris, quite far from Cluny, and perhaps within private walls—if indeed it happened before only a few people, no argument drawn from Peter’s silence has any force—and it took place nearly fifteen years before that same abbot was born.

“Nor should there be any doubt that many other portents occurred in Gaul, Spain, England, and Italy during Peter’s lifetime or around his time. Yet, apart from those relating to his own order, he mentions none of them, although he is reported to have traveled to these foreign regions not only to advance the affairs of monasteries belonging to his order but also the affairs of the whole Church. Why, then, would he have inserted our portent in his work rather than those other portents?

### 288

“But I hear someone answering on Launoius’s behalf: I. Peter had resolved to commit to writing miracles that had occurred everywhere in his time. II. He had included in two books every miracle that he had witnessed with his own eyes or received from trustworthy people. III. At the end of the second book he had described in fuller discourse the origin, statutes, and customs of the Carthusian order. IV. He had expressed the greatest sorrow that he could not relate more miracles concerning the Carthusian order, which he loved so dearly. V. Among the miracles that he records as having occurred throughout Gaul in his time, and among those about the origins and miracles of the first Carthusians that he discussed, the astonishing account of the dead man is missing. Finally, Peter himself had said that ‘the Carthusian order was instituted in his time.’

“These are the arguments that Launoius derived, both from the words and from the silence of Peter the Venerable, against the truth of the Parisian portent. To I we reply that Peter did indeed say that he intended ‘to transmit to the memory of posterity miracles performed everywhere in his time.’ But we have shown that he also said that his purpose was to relate events that had taken place around Cluny; and from an examination of the entire work we have learned that nearly all the miracles he recorded which do not concern his own order were performed in regions not far distant from Cluny. Those that occurred in foreign or more remote places either took place in monasteries of his order or were related to him by members of that order.

“To II we have given an adequate answer by showing that throughout his entire work he included only miracles relating to his own order, [Col. 0171C] apart from ten, of which he learned four or five from Cluniac monks and the rest from friends living near Cluny.

### 289

“To III. We admit that Peter described the statutes and customs of our order in a lengthy account, but he did not describe its beginnings as fully as Launoius claims. For he writes of them as follows:

> ‘In the regions of Burgundy, among all the professions of our European monastic order, there is preserved a certain profession more holy and more cautious than many others of the same monastic purpose. It was instituted in our time by certain great, learned, and holy Fathers: Master Bruno of Cologne, Master Landuin the Italian, and certain other truly great and, as I have said, God-fearing men. Having been forewarned by the lukewarmness, negligence, and sloth of certain ancient monks, they wished to renounce the world and to provide more cautiously for themselves and for those who follow them on the way of God,’ etc.

“He then adds much about clothing, revenues, customs, and statutes. This is his fuller—or rather, more barren—account of the origin of the order. For he says only that ‘a certain profession, holier than others, was instituted by Master Bruno of Cologne, Master Landuin the Italian, and certain other truly great Fathers.’ But afterward, as Launoius correctly observed, ‘he describes the statutes and customs of the order in fuller discourse.’

“This indeed was his purpose, as the learned Saussaeius wisely noted: ‘to treat of the institute, not of the institution of the Carthusian order.’ And in fact, if he had decided to describe the institution of the order, he would have related many other things that he could not have been ignorant of. Thus he says nothing about the reason for its institution—whether it arose from the conference held between Saint Bruno and the other clerics of Reims, or from the persecutions of Manasses, or from the terrifying cries of the condemned man. [Col. 0171D]

“He says nothing about the manner of Saint Bruno’s arrival at Grenoble with his six companions; nothing about their approach to Saint Hugh, the bishop; nothing about the vision of the seven stars granted to that same bishop—although he can hardly be thought to have been ignorant of these matters. Indeed, he does not utter a single word about Saint Hugh, whom he knew extremely well and under whose counsel, assistance, and companionship the first Fathers went to and built the solitude of Chartreuse. [Col. 0172A]

“So firmly does Peter adhere to his purpose—or rather, to the aim with which he had undertaken to speak only of the institutions of the Carthusians—that, what is even more noteworthy, he does not name either Chartreuse itself or the order of which he was speaking. One might therefore wonder what he was discussing, unless he had given his narrative the following title: ‘On the Institutions of the Carthusian Monks.’

“Launoius therefore ought not to ridicule Saussaeius for distinguishing the institution from the observances.”

### 290

“To IV. We do not know what Launoius means when he describes Peter of Cluny as ‘grieving that he could not relate more miracles concerning the Carthusian order, which he loved so dearly.’ If it is nevertheless permissible to guess, we believe that by these ingenious words he subtly intended to evade the objection that could be brought against him from the venerable abbot’s own words—an objection whose force he foresaw would completely overturn all the conclusions he draws from Peter’s silence.

“For by these words he indicates that other miracles had indeed been performed within the Carthusian order, but that the pious abbot was distressed because he could not relate them. The holy man immediately declares that this was the cause of his distress in the words quoted above, but necessarily repeated here:

> ‘I have received from many people that many miracles occurred in that holy order; but because they themselves, through the virtue of humility by which the servants of God always conceal their wondrous works with all the effort they can, scarcely wished to disclose any of them to anyone, few—indeed, exceedingly few—miracles to which complete faith could be given have reached me. Nevertheless, those which I have discovered beyond doubt to be certain, I neither wish nor intend to keep silent about.’ [Col. 0172B]

“He then relates two marvelous events concerning a certain lay brother, and nothing more about him or about others.

“Peter wrote this long after the year 1145, as we gather from chapter 25 of the second book, where he says:

> ‘At the beginning of the pontificate of Pope Eugene, I went to Rome to visit both him and our common mother, the Roman Church.’

“Eugene was elected in the year 1145. But Peter indicates that several years had already passed when he wrote this, since he says ‘at the beginning of the pontificate of Pope Eugene.’ Since he mentions our order only in chapters 28 and 29 of that same book, it is clear that what he reports about the ancient Fathers was written by him long after the year 1145. It is therefore not surprising if that spectacle was concealed from Peter by the Carthusians, who hid their works—an event that had occurred nearly seventy years earlier, or even more, and long before that abbot’s birth, as we shall soon prove. [Col. 0173A]

### 291

“To V. This argument has been sufficiently answered by the preceding replies, in which we proved that most of the miracles he records as having occurred throughout Gaul in his time concerned monasteries of the Cluniac order, while the very few that did not concern it were published as having occurred around Cluny. Even if we granted that they had likewise occurred throughout Gaul, Peter’s silence would still do us no harm, since, by describing so few events in his entire work, he either did not know or omitted many others.

“As for the final point, we concede that Peter wrote that the Carthusian religion had been instituted in his time. But it is clear from this very fact that his words must not be taken so strictly: he was born several years after the order had been founded. For since he is said to have been elected abbot in the year of Christ 1122, and to have been approximately twenty-eight years old at that time—unless one calculates otherwise, as in no. 283—he must have been born in or around the year 1095, that is, fourteen years after the cries of the condemned man had been uttered. Therefore the order was instituted not in Peter’s time but before it.

“Nor does it help to reply that he also related histories and miracles performed around his own time. This is indeed true of events concerning the Cluniacs, but not of portents unrelated to that order; as we have shown in the preceding examination, nearly all of these, with only one or two exceptions, occurred while Peter was alive or even while he was presiding.

“Finally, we infer from Peter’s preface to the second book on miracles that many miracles escaped him or remained unknown to him. There he complains that no one applies himself to writing down miracles:

> ‘The sloth of this unfruitful silence has now reached such a point of barrenness,’ he says, ‘that almost everything performed in the Church of God or in Christian kingdoms during approximately four or five hundred years is unknown to us and to everyone else.’ [Col. 0173B]

### 292

“For such a great distance appears between our times and those earlier periods that events performed five hundred or a thousand years ago are very well known to us, whereas those carried out from then until our own days are entirely unknown. Hence it is that we abound in ancient histories, ecclesiastical deeds, and numerous books of instruction containing the teachings and examples of the Fathers; but of what happened in times close to our own, I do not know whether we possess even one account.”

Thus he spoke, although earlier he had said that he “grieved and, beyond what many might believe, grew angry at the sluggishness of so many who, though rich in knowledge, learning, and eloquence, were reluctant through laziness to commit to writing, for the memory of posterity, the wondrous works of almighty God that frequently occur in different parts of the world for the instruction of the Church.”

For this reason, toward the end he professes that he would “according to the strength given by God, if he should be able to discover anything worthy or useful, make it known to his contemporaries or to posterity for the praise of God or the benefit of readers.” [Col. 0173D]

And yet, although he was possessed by so great a desire of this kind, he said nothing about the wonder-worker of his own time, Saint Bernard, who was his very dear and intimate friend. A broad field of miracles performed by Bernard with the greatest frequency lay open to him, from which he could at least have selected a few, and those the most remarkable, including the noteworthy conversion of William, duke of Aquitaine.

He said nothing about Saints Norbert and Robert of Arbrissel; nothing about so many other most holy men who lived at the same time as Peter; nothing about the monastic orders that then shone forth through many signs and virtues. In short, he wrote nothing about any of these matters. [Col. 0174B]

“And although he could have related more about the Carthusians—whom, in a letter that we shall present under the year 1156, he admits to have ‘shone throughout the world with innumerable miracles,’ which therefore could not have remained unknown to him—he nevertheless mentions only one lay brother. This was not merely because the first Fathers did not wish to advertise their works, but certainly also because of a defect in his memory, as seems evident from that miraculous story of Auduin, a monk of Chartreuse, who was found alive after twelve days amid the snow and ruins of the monastery. Peter omitted this story, although he knew it very well, since he wrote a consolatory letter to Guigo about that fall of snow and rocks. We shall present the letter in its proper place in the Annals.

### 293

“But what will surprise you even more is that Peter said nothing about Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, from whom he had received the monastic habit, except for a certain vision. Yet in the Life of Saint Hugh we read of many splendid and astonishing miracles performed both during his life and after his death.

“Launoius, together with Masson, therefore searched out a weak argument from the silence of Peter of Cluny and, on that sole basis, denounced this history as a fable and an old woman’s tale. If we were bound by his rules, we would count among fables everything that Peter left unsaid about other saints.”

These are all the words of our anonymous Carthusian. But do they remove all force from the negative argument formed from Peter of Cluny’s silence?

It is said that Peter the Venerable records only five or six miracles that do not concern the Cluniac order; consequently, it is not surprising that among so few he did not include the miraculous resurrection of the condemned doctor, especially since Peter also passed over in silence the vision of the seven stars shown to Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, when Saint Bruno approached him with his six companions, as well as several other matters concerning Saint Bruno.

This appears to be the principal reason why the argument drawn from Peter’s silence against the history of the condemned doctor is considered feeble and weak. Yet even if nearly all the miracles Peter committed to writing concern the Cluniac order, this writer nevertheless intended to transmit to posterity miracles that had occurred elsewhere as well, outside his own Cluniac order.

> “This,” he says in book II, chapter 28, “was my principal reason for writing throughout this entire work, as I have often already said: to transmit to the present or to the memory of posterity miracles performed everywhere and at every time.” [Col. 0174C]

“Listen also to what he had prefaced in the same second book, which is relevant here:

> ‘Since I have resolved to write down miracles performed in our time or around our time, whose occurrence is established beyond doubt, for the strengthening of faith and the formation of morals—these are Peter’s words—other matters no less useful, as I believe, to readers or hearers must be added to what has already been set forth.’ [Col. 0175A]

### 294

“Among these matters, as I have already said above, I observe no chronological order and avoid no kind of miracle; rather, just as I learned of them long ago or am able to learn of them daily from various trustworthy people, I entrust them to writing.”

Why, then, did Peter, who—as may be understood from these quoted words—had resolved to commit to writing miracles performed everywhere and of every kind, pass over in silence that dreadful portent, if it ever occurred: the event in which the Parisian doctor, briefly restored to life, proclaimed from his coffin before an almost innumerable crowd of people that he had been condemned by the just judgment of God?

You say that Peter likewise enveloped many other portents and miracles in silence. But the matters he does not mention are of such a kind that he could easily have been ignorant of them, or could have failed to retain them in memory when he was writing, or could finally have passed them over as less worthy of notice. [Col. 0175B]

The Parisian portent, however, since according to the opinion we are examining it occurred before an almost innumerable crowd and consequently would have been spread far and wide and transmitted to posterity, could hardly have remained unknown to Peter. And because it was at once especially worthy of notice and particularly suited to the end Peter intended—namely, “to strengthen faith,” as his words quoted immediately above say, and to inspire good morals—it would very probably have remained in his mind and been mentioned by him.

This is especially so because Peter also devoted effort and attention to gathering from every source miracles relating to the Carthusian order and committing what he discovered to written records, as he himself indicates in book II, chapter 29, in these words: [Col. 0175C]

> “I have received from many people that many miracles occurred in that holy order—the Carthusian order—but because they themselves, through the virtue of humility by which the servants of God always conceal their wondrous works with all the effort they can, scarcely wished to disclose any of them, few—indeed, exceedingly few—miracles to which complete faith could be given reached me. Nevertheless, those which I discovered beyond doubt to be certain, I neither wish nor intend to keep silent about.” [Col. 0175D]

### 295

“Peter writes as follows in book II, chapter 28:

> ‘In the regions of Burgundy, among all the professions of our European monastic order, there is preserved a certain profession more holy and more cautious than many others of the same monastic purpose, instituted in our time by certain great, learned, and holy Fathers: Master Bruno, Master Landuin the Italian, and certain others.’

“Since in these words he mentions at least a little about the institution of the Carthusian order, it appears probable that this writer, who is entirely occupied with recounting miracles and who had a suitable opportunity to explain the reason for the establishment of that holy order, would not have passed over in silence the mournful as well as miraculous history of the condemned doctor, if this event had ever taken place.

“Therefore, having duly weighed all the arguments contained in the words quoted above from the anonymous Carthusian, I would not dare to deny all force whatsoever to the negative argument formed from the silence of Peter the Venerable against the resurrection of the Parisian doctor. Nevertheless, I am very far from agreeing with Launoius, who in his Dissertation on the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Desert declares that, solely because of Peter the Venerable’s silence concerning the miraculous resurrection of the doctor, this history must be counted among fables and inventions. [Col. 0176A]

“Indeed, since Peter expressly affirms—as his words quoted in the preceding section show—that he had learned of rare, indeed exceedingly rare, miracles relating to the Carthusian order and deserving complete faith, and that he nevertheless committed to writing those which he discovered to be beyond doubt, it is possible that he did not consider the dreadful history of the condemned doctor, although it was not unknown to him, worthy of being mentioned. He may have learned of it not from any written records at all but solely through tradition or popular report, and therefore may not have regarded it as entirely certain and indisputable.” [Col. 0176B]

## XVII. What Should Be Concluded from the Silence of the Other Ancient Writers Whom Launoius Further Cites

### 296

“I have already indicated above that among the ancient writers who, according to Launoius, testified by their silence that the miraculous resurrection of the Parisian doctor was contrary to the truth, there are also some whose silence carries either no force or very little force against it.

“But, in addition to those whose silence I discussed in the two immediately preceding sections, I wish here to add several others cited by Launoius and brought forward by Bulaeus in volume I of the *History of the University of Paris*. I do so because the anonymous Carthusian, author of the fourth book of the Annals of his order, which has not yet been published, contends that the silence of all of them has absolutely no force against this writer, who attaches the greatest importance to it. I shall therefore bring forward all his arguments that in any way support the history of the condemned doctor.

“I begin with Sigebert of Gembloux. In his *Chronography*, under the year 1084, he writes the following about Saint Bruno:

> ‘Bruno, a German by nation, from the city of Cologne, highly learned in letters, canon and master of the schools of the church of Reims, abandoning the world, founded the desert of Chartreuse and established a sufficiently arduous program of monastic life. Hugh, of blessed memory, bishop of Grenoble, a fellow-worker and rival of this holy purpose, received the monastic habit from that same Bruno and provided an outstanding example to all who lived there.’ [Col. 0176D]

“Launoius, after quoting these words in his Dissertation on the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Desert, adds:

> ‘These words are found in Pistor’s edition but are absent from Miraeus’s edition. Miraeus nevertheless cites in his edition a certain manuscript of Sigebert from the library of Justus Lipsius, in which the following words about Bruno occur: “In the vast desert called Chartreuse, near Grenoble, he began to build a monastery and cells.”’ [Col. 0177A]

### 297

“‘I did not wish to conceal any of this from the reader, lest he complain that he was being misled by Sigebert. But whether we follow the Lipsius manuscript or Pistor’s edition, it will always be clear from them that among all the ancients the account concerning the doctor was not accepted as established.’

“So Launoius writes, correctly implying here that Pistor’s edition of Sigebert’s *Chronography* departs from Sigebert’s genuine text in the words recently quoted from it.

“Our anonymous Carthusian further explains this in no. 101 of his work as follows:

> ‘Sigebert is said to have died in the year 1113. If this is so, it must necessarily be conceded that these words, quoted above, were added to his *Chronography* by someone else. For, as we noted above, in the fifth testimony concerning Sigebert, the first part about Bruno appears in nearly the same words in the *Chronicle of the Four First Priors of Chartreuse*, which was evidently published only after Sigebert’s death.

> “‘Nor should the author of the chronicle be said to have borrowed them from Sigebert. For what follows in Sigebert makes it perfectly clear that these words were written after Saint Hugh had died, although Hugh survived Sigebert by approximately twenty years. “Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, of blessed memory,” says this interpolated Sigebert, “a fellow-worker and rival of this holy purpose, received the monastic habit from that same Bruno and provided an outstanding example to all who lived there.”

> “‘Who does not see that these words speak of Hugh as though he were dead and already numbered among the saints, since he is adorned with the title “of blessed memory” and is said in the past tense to have “provided an outstanding example”? Moreover, it is clear that a gross error has entered these same words, where the holy bishop is said to have received the monastic habit from Bruno; we shall prove in the Annals under the year 1087 that this is entirely false.’” [Col. 0177C]

### 298

“‘Sigebert, who lived at the same time as Saint Hugh frequented Chartreuse and died many years before him, would certainly not have fallen into these errors. But even if it were granted that these words had been written by Sigebert himself, they would do us no harm, since he should be called less a historian than a compiler, one who contains none of the matters arranged by other writers.’

“Certainly, our anonymous Carthusian, with Launoius also supporting him—as the latter’s words quoted just above sufficiently indicate—rightly insists here that the words transcribed above from the *Chronography* of Sigebert of Gembloux are not Sigebert’s, but belong to a later writer who inserted them into that work.

“He establishes this sufficiently—or, I should say, conclusively—even though he wrongly supposes, on the basis of the words he cites, that Hugh is being discussed as dead and already numbered among the saints solely because he is adorned in these passages with the title ‘of blessed memory.’ For, as Cangius teaches in his *Glossary* under the word ‘Memory,’ and as other authorities show, ancient writers sometimes applied this title even to people who were still living.

“But is the silence concerning the miraculous resurrection of the doctor, preserved in the quoted words of Sigebert’s *Chronography*, rightly considered worthless even if they are granted to be genuinely Sigebert’s? I absolutely think so, because there is no reason at all why it should appear even moderately likely that Sigebert would have mentioned that mournful history, however well known it might have been to him, in the very few matters he records for posterity about Bruno.

“Therefore the silence preserved in these same words appears entirely weightless, whoever the ancient writer may have been who, as has been said, inserted them into Sigebert’s *Chronography.” [Col. 0178B]

### 299

“Let us now examine whether a stronger argument against the Parisian portent can be drawn from the silence of Robert of Torigni, who continued Sigebert’s *Chronography*.

“‘He discusses many matters concerning the institutions, customs, and very origin of the Carthusians,’ Launoius says of this writer in chapter I of his Dissertation on the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Desert, ‘yet he offers no testimony whatsoever concerning the condemned doctor.’

“The anonymous Carthusian transcribes all the words that Launoius attributes to Robert and places before this objection against the Parisian portent, and he also responds to it. I transfer here his complete text, together with the words of Robert that it includes. It reads as follows:

> ‘Robert of Torigni mentions the Carthusian monks under the year 1131 in these words: “The Carthusian monks were gradually multiplying. More continent than others, they set limits to the plague of avarice, which we see afflicting many under the appearance of religion, by establishing a fixed number of men, animals, and possessions which they could in no way exceed. Each of them had his own separate cell, and they met only rarely, either for the worship of God or for mutual consolation in charity. They chose to die to the world more perfectly and to live for God more diligently than others, because they lived more secretly.”’

“These are Robert’s words in the edition used by Launoius. But in the edition that we presently have at hand, published in Paris in 1651 by Jean Billaine through the learning and labor of the most learned and devout Luc d’Achery, absolutely nothing appears under the aforementioned year 1131, nor anywhere in the entire appendix concerning the Carthusians. The same is true of the year 1132, under which Launoius read the following about Saint Hugh in his copy:

> ‘A holy man died, Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, whose exceedingly devout life Guigo, prior of Chartreuse, wrote down.’” [Col. 0178D]

### 300

“‘Dacherius considered the copy he possessed to be an autograph. From this it is clear that the material concerning Saints Bruno and Hugh found in other copies was added by someone more recent.

“‘Although this would be sufficient for us to reject the authority of the words reported by Launoius, nevertheless, even if they were genuine words of Robert, we reply to Launoius as follows:

> ‘I. In the entire appendix to Sigebert, according to our edition, Robert records nothing that occurred before the year 1101, when he began to continue Sigebert’s chronicle, except when he is dealing with the genealogy of princes or the succession of bishops; in such matters he occasionally, though rarely, goes further back.

> ‘II. The words reported by Launoius do not speak of the beginnings of the order but of its progress, as the very words themselves show: “The Carthusian monks were gradually multiplying.” Indeed, in the year 1131—that is, almost fifty years after the order had been founded—there were only five or six houses of the Carthusian institute in the whole Church. [Col. 0179A]

> ‘III. Robert’s principal purpose in this appendix was to describe the history of the Normans and the English, as he himself declares in the prologue in these words: “Since the aforesaid Sigebert begins his chronicles with the year 381 from the Lord’s Incarnation and carried them forward to the year 1100 of that same Incarnation, I shall thereafter undertake to collect, under the years of the Lord’s Incarnation, the events that occurred in various provinces, especially in Normandy and England, and that came to my knowledge, continuing them until the year 1182. I shall do this all the more willingly because I wish to record briefly, year by year, the deeds of Henry I, the most energetic king of the English and duke of the Normans, with whom I must begin.”’

### 301

“‘Robert kept his promise. For throughout his entire work he passes over no year without reporting many matters concerning the Normans and the English, while often writing nothing or very little about other provinces.

> ‘IV. In this appendix Robert wrote almost nothing about other orders or about their origins and institutions. It is therefore not surprising if he was silent about the Carthusians as well, or said so little about them, in accordance with the citation made by Launoius.

> ‘Finally, it should be noted that in his prologue this author does indeed imply that he will relate many portents, and he did so; but it is clear that he mentions only those that occurred from the year 1101 onward, as we noted above. Robert therefore should not be numbered among the authors who would not have omitted the famous resurrection of the condemned man if they had either read or heard that it had occurred.’ [Col. 0179C]

“Nor should the contrary be inferred from the words of that same Robert, who in his *Treatise on the Transformation of the Monastic Order*, chapter II, concerning the abbots and abbeys of Normandy, writes the following about the origin of the Carthusians:

> ‘At approximately the same time at which the Cistercian order arose in the parish of Chalon, the Carthusian order was also devised in the diocese of Grenoble. This kind of hermits acts under a prior, and their number does not exceed thirteen. Each person, separated from the others in his own cell on ordinary days, prays, sleeps, and eats; nevertheless, the cells are adjacent and joined in one place. On feast days they gather in the church and at table, and confer among themselves about spiritual matters. They perform the offices of the day and night according to the rule of Saint Benedict.’” [Col. 0180A]

302. “This is the author who gives no cause or occasion that impelled Saint Bruno into the wilderness, because he says absolutely nothing about Saint Bruno and does not even mention his name. He speaks only of certain Carthusian customs, which he seems to have drawn from the *Customs* of our Guigo. Thus, also with respect to the founders and patriarchs of other orders, he gives so summary an account that he reports scarcely anything memorable about them, content merely to assign the time of their conversion, together with the year or century in which they renounced the world or began their institution.”
