These statements most clearly establish that the silence preserved by Robert of Monte, whether it be considered very little or nothing at all, does not damage the mournful history of the condemned man. Nor did Launoius himself think that either this silence, or that of Sigebert of Gembloux—or of the ancient writer who inserted the words transcribed above into this *Chronography* at no. 296—contributed much toward demonstrating the falsity of the horrifying prodigy. From the quoted words of both writers, in which absolutely nothing is found concerning the resurrection of the unfortunate teacher, he inferred only against Raynaud that this account was not accepted as established among all ancient writers; but this conclusion does not require that the mournful event itself be false.

Let what has been said suffice concerning the silence of Sigebert and of Robert of Monte, who continued this *Chronography*. Among the ancient writers listed by Launoius, whose silence regarding the condemned teacher Bulaeus valued more highly, there is also Geoffrey, prior of Vigeois, who composed his *Chronicle*, published by Labbe in volume II of the *New Library of Manuscript Books*, toward the end of the twelfth century.

303. In chapter 21 of this work that writer says:

> “The most holy order of the Carthusians began at this time, namely in the year 1086 (or rather in 1084, as we shall prove below), through Bruno, a holy man, by nationality a German from Cologne Agrippina, a master in theology, together with six other venerable men in the diocese of Grenoble. This order, according to Blessed Bernard, holds primacy among all ecclesiastical orders, not by reason of its age but by the strength of its holiness; hence he calls it the most beautiful column of the Church. Pope Victor, while he was a monk of Monte Cassino, saw in a dream God, in His gracious condescension, constructing a dwelling in the Carthusian wilderness, and it is said that he possessed the gift of prophecy.”

But is Launoius, followed by Bulaeus, right to argue from the fact that Geoffrey does not mention the story of the condemned man that the story is therefore fictitious, or at least suspect as a fabrication? After the anonymous Carthusian had incorporated the words of Geoffrey just quoted into his work, he added:

> “This is Geoffrey, who reveals to us new and hitherto unheard-of matters, mentioned by no one, when he says that Pope Victor foresaw the foundation of the order through the prophetic spirit (what should be made of this will be examined below); we shall discuss his vision under the year 1086. To these words of Geoffrey [just quoted] Launoius adds: ‘Here was the broadest possible opportunity for speaking of the condemned teacher and canon; Geoffrey was silent because at that time idle men had not yet introduced the story.’”

304. “But the story had already been not introduced merely, but committed to writing by our anonymous Carthusian and by Caesarius of Heisterbach, Geoffrey’s contemporaries, as it had been reported to them by trustworthy persons. Nor is it surprising that Geoffrey omitted it, since he also omitted nearly everything else that might be said about Saint Bruno and the order. He could even have been unaware of a history that had taken place a hundred years or more earlier, and whose memory was then preserved almost exclusively among the Carthusians.”

But if that story had occurred publicly, before a vast crowd of people, it hardly seems credible that in Geoffrey’s time its memory should have survived among almost the Carthusians alone. Geoffrey flourished less than a hundred years—and perhaps not even sixty years—after Bruno’s death. Who, then, would believe that he was unaware of so dreadful a prodigy and therefore did not mention it?

Nevertheless, since this writer, as the anonymous Carthusian also correctly observes, omits nearly everything relating to Bruno, and since the Parisian prodigy, however well known and verified he may have considered it, does not appear to be something he would have mentioned among the few matters he reports about the saint, the argument supplied by his silence is plainly very weak.

I now present considerations that appear to possess somewhat greater force. The monk of Auxerre, who flourished toward the end of the twelfth century and the beginning of the next, or certainly during the pontificate of Innocent III, writes as follows in chapter 1 of Launoius’s *Dissertation on the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Wilderness*:

> “About that time Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, saw in a dream God, in His gracious condescension, constructing a dwelling in the wilderness of Chartreuse, and also seven stars offering themselves as guides for his journey. And behold, seven men, drawn to him by the fragrance of his holiness, came to him; all were inflamed by one desire and were seeking a place suited to the eremitical life, but had not yet found one. The first of them was Master Bruno, a man renowned for religion and learning; four others were educated men, and two were laymen. Saint Hugh gladly received them and granted them the fulfillment of their desire. With his help, counsel, and companionship they entered the wilderness of Chartreuse. Thus the Carthusian order began, distinguished among the other orders by purity of mind and devotion to contemplation.”

305. Launoius, who, as I have indicated, quotes these words in his aforementioned *Dissertation*, then adds:

> “No more with this monk”—namely, the monk of Auxerre—“than with the others” whom he had previously cited “is the account of the teacher, or the terrible event that drove Bruno into the wilderness, established. Indeed, that monk would certainly not have passed over the teacher’s dreadful resurrection, since he frequently records uncertain outcomes of events, the precarious fortunes of life in many people, apparitions, and prodigies of that kind.”

Now hear what our anonymous Carthusian replies. Thus, in book IV, no. 116 of his *Annals of the Order*, he writes:

> “This is what the anonymous author cited by Launoius says—the words of the monk of Auxerre having just been transcribed from Launoius. He appears to have copied all these things from the *Life of Saint Hugh* edited by Guigo, merely changing the order of the words. For that reason we oppose his testimony with the same arguments that we previously opposed to Guigo’s testimony (see nos. 263 and following). Moreover, let learned men judge what weight negative authority possesses. ‘The monk of Auxerre says nothing about the spectacle; therefore the spectacle is false.’ If one were permitted to reason in this way, even the truths of the Gospel would collapse, many of which rest upon tradition alone.

> “But suppose that, as Launoius asserts, that monk ‘frequently records uncertain outcomes of events, the precarious fortunes of life in many people, apparitions, and prodigies of that kind.’ Does he record them all, or record them in every person? To assert this would surely seem rash. He therefore omitted some, indeed very many, outcomes of events, and among them he could have omitted this prodigy, just as the three holy Evangelists omitted the exceedingly remarkable pool of Bethesda and the astonishing raising of Lazarus.”

306. “Finally, according to Launoius, that monk flourished under Innocent III, supreme pontiff; at that time our anonymous Carthusian (see his testimony at no. 199 and following, as well as what is said at no. 12 and following) was the first of all to begin committing this story to writing. Its memory was preserved almost exclusively among the Carthusians, whose numbers were still only gradually increasing. It is therefore not surprising if the monk of Auxerre, who perhaps had no association with the Carthusians, did not know the true origin of the order, and consequently supplied no reason for it, but merely copied the words that he had read in the *Life of Saint Hugh*. Finally, since we do not currently have the *Chronicle* of the aforementioned author at hand, we cannot extract more from it against Launoius.”

So he writes. Whether he is right in every respect must now be considered.

First, since there can be no doubt that the monk of Auxerre drew the words transcribed above from the *Life of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble*, written by Guigo, the fifth prior of Chartreuse, and since the silence preserved by Guigo in that work regarding the resurrection of the Parisian teacher has absolutely no force against the story (see no. 265), it follows that the silence preserved by the monk of Auxerre in the same passage is likewise of little weight.

As for the silence by which he passes over the horrifying prodigy in all the other parts of his *Chronicle*, it does not follow from this either that the story is false. Since, as the anonymous Carthusian rightly observes, he does not mention every outcome of events, the teacher’s horrible death may be among those he suppressed in silence. Nevertheless, since that monk, as Launoius suggests, is indeed very much occupied with recording prodigies, it seems less probable that, if it had occurred, he would have omitted to commit to writing the Parisian spectacle of the condemned man—a prodigy plainly far more worthy of remembrance than all the others he narrates.

307. It follows from this that the opinion of those who deny the mournful event receives at least some support from the silence of the aforementioned monk of Auxerre, who passes it over. Nor is it helpful to reply that the horrifying story was unknown to the monk of Auxerre because, according to the evidence cited, its true memory had survived almost exclusively among the Carthusians in the thirteenth century. How little credible this is has already been made clear.

Furthermore, almost the same and equal considerations as those by which, as I have just shown, the silence of the monk of Auxerre acquires force against the teacher’s prodigious resurrection also make the silence of the author of the Malleacensian *Chronicle* detrimental to the story. Its author flourished around the year 1140. Launoius speaks of this *Chronicle* in chapter 1 of his *Dissertation on the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Wilderness* as follows:

> “It is full of visions and memorable events, which the author recounts with the greatest eagerness; so that from this alone one may judge that he would nowhere have passed over such a spectacle, had it occurred in the manner in which it is said to have occurred, and in a manner that would have filled the books of all writers.”

That Launoius is to be followed in what he says here about the Malleacensian *Chronicle*, or rather about its author, the *Chronicle* itself will show when examined; it is now included by Labbe in volume II of the *New Library of Manuscript Books*.

Nor is the silence concerning the teacher’s resurrection preserved by Adam in the manuscript *Flowers of Histories*, by Vincent of Beauvais, and by the writer of the *Chronicle of Saint Martin of Tours* entirely without force. Although these three writers, as our anonymous Carthusian rightly observes, undoubtedly took their words, quoted by Launoius, either from Guigo, the fifth prior of Chartreuse, or from Geoffrey of Vigeois, or finally from others whose silence, for the reasons stated, does nothing or very little to weaken the prodigious resurrection, they nevertheless also employed a considerable number of other writers older than themselves, who flourished in the thirteenth century. If they found anything worthy of remembrance in those sources, they regularly incorporated it into their own works.

308. Since these writers nowhere mention the teacher who returned to life and publicly declared from his bier before those standing around him that he had been condemned by God’s just judgment, this indicates that Vincent and the other two writers did not find the fatal story in the writers they used—some of whom may now have perished through the ravages of time. Thus these three writers tell against the story to no small degree, since by their silence they somehow testify to and encompass the silence of all the others whom they employed. At least some of those other writers would probably have known of and mentioned such a mournful and supremely noteworthy event if it had ever taken place.

Moreover, to the ancient writers whose silence, since they would probably have mentioned the horrifying prodigy if it had occurred—whether because of the subjects they treated or for some other reason—works in some measure against it, one might add Hugh of Flavigny and many others not mentioned by Launoius, whom there is no need to enumerate here. Above all, one might add ascetic writers and preachers of the divine word. Since they delivered pious sermons, published sacred treatises, and composed religious meditations in order both to draw people away from vices and sins and to inflame them toward virtue, they would probably have mentioned that horrifying prodigy somewhere in those works, since scarcely anything more suitable or more useful to their intended purpose could have been devised or invented.

For this reason Launoius, in chapter 1 of the dissertation so often mentioned, also counts among the ancient writers whose silence works against the teacher’s prodigious resurrection Humbert of Burgundy, the fifth master general of the Preachers, and Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. He is right concerning the former, but not concerning the latter, even when the letter written to the brothers of Mount God is taken into account.

309. For this saint, in order to incite his readers and hearers to avoid vices and embrace virtue, was accustomed to employ almost exclusively the incentives supplied by Sacred Scripture in the pious sermons he delivered and the sacred treatises he published. The letter written to the brothers of Mount God, however, is the work not of Bernard but of William, abbot of Saint-Thierry’s monastery near Reims. Mabillon, in volume II of the works of Saint Bernard, p. 198, and after him the authors of the *Literary History of France*, volume XI, p. 654, clearly demonstrate this; and it is now generally acknowledged among learned men that the letter cannot be attributed to this holy abbot.

Nevertheless, one cannot infer from this that William, abbot of Saint-Thierry’s monastery near Reims, to whom the aforementioned letter actually belongs, should be counted among the ancient authors whose silence damages the mournful story of the condemned teacher. Although William is genuinely ancient, nothing appears that makes it at all probable that, had he known of the horrifying prodigy, he would have mentioned it in that letter.

As for the other writers whom Launoius still brings forward for his cause, I shall pass over the task of listing them individually here, as I said above that I would, since—unless perhaps John of Saint-Victor is excepted—they are not writers who, if they had read the famous account of the teacher’s resurrection anywhere or had heard that it occurred, would probably have mentioned it by name. I therefore proceed to examine the conclusions that Launoius draws, especially those relevant to our purpose, from the silence of the authors he cites.

## § XVIII. The principal conclusions that Launoius draws from the silence of the ancient writers whom he cites are examined

310. In order that it may become still clearer what force the silence of the ancient writers—or rather the negative arguments formed from it—has against the mournful history of the condemned teacher, and whether it has as much force as Launoius wishes, it will be useful, now that these matters have been discussed, to examine also the conclusions that Launoius claims follow from the same evidence.

I shall do this in such a way that I may not appear either to have attributed too much to this writer, whose *Dissertation on the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Wilderness* was newly entered by Roman censure in the Roman Catalogue of Forbidden Books, or to have weakened the arguments that the anonymous author of book IV of the *Carthusian Annals*, not yet published, brings against Launoius. I shall generally transcribe the words of both authors themselves, and only afterward add my own judgment concerning Launoius’s conclusions and the Carthusian’s replies to them.

Launoius therefore first concludes from the silence of all the authors whom he has cited:

> “That colored and embellished history”—especially in the Parisian Charterhouse—“which is said to have given Bruno the cause of withdrawing into the wilderness, is overwhelmed by the obstinate silence of all the authors who flourished from the year of Christ 1084 to the year 1322 and beyond. This is sufficient for sensible and learned men to refute the fable. To this is added, as a further confirmation, the authority of Bruno himself, the founder of the Carthusians, who writes that he received the cause of his departure into the wilderness not at Paris but at Reims; and, on the other side, the testimony of Guibert, abbot of Nogent, who specifically identifies the certain cause of his departure into the wilderness. Each of them cuts away the Parisian fable about the canon and the teacher who returned to life, and sets forth the simple truth.”

311. Now hear what our anonymous Carthusian replies to these words of Launoius:

> “This is what Launoius says, as though he were saying: ‘These writers kept silent about this story; therefore they denied that it was true.’ Let the reader judge the force of such an argument. But let us say what we have sufficiently demonstrated above: these authors kept silent about this prodigy just as they kept silent about Saint Bruno’s other splendid deeds.

> “None of all the writers cited by Launoius undertook to describe the *Life of Saint Bruno*. Whatever they wrote about him or about the Carthusian order, they all reported in very few words, in the manner of epitomators. Indeed, most of them mentioned Saint Bruno by name alone; others did not even express his name. For those who spoke at greater length about him, it was enough to say in four or five lines that he was the founder of the Carthusian order and that he founded it in such a year and under such a pontiff.

> “Some who were well disposed toward the Carthusians wrote more about their statutes, morals, and customs; but no one intended to treat individually of their foundation, the cause of their origin, or their other noble achievements, whether among them or among us. It is therefore not surprising that nothing concerning the spectacle of the man who returned to life appears in the authors cited.

> “But when the Carthusian order began to spread, our anonymous author—who was the first, around the year 1220 (or, more probably, as I have shown at no. 12 and following, not before the year 1250), deliberately to undertake committing its beginnings to writing, describing the acts of Saint Bruno more fully and at greater length—did not fail to explain that this resurrection had been the cause of his withdrawal into the wilderness.”

312. Afterward he transcribes the words of Launoius that I have already quoted:

> “To this is added, as a further confirmation,”

and continues:

> “We have already shown sufficiently above that Saint Bruno received the resolve to withdraw into the wilderness not at Reims but at Paris, as the learned Bulaeus also holds. Moreover, how uncertain the testimony of Guibert is appears from the many errors that we detected in the text of his narrative.”

I shall briefly state my own view of these matters. Launoius wrongly concludes from the silence concerning the fatal resurrection of the teacher maintained by all the authors whom he cites that the story must be regarded as a fable, or is certainly false, as I shall show below when I inquire what force the universal silence of all writers—both contemporaries and later authors—has against the mournful event.

Above, however, I have demonstrated that the silence of some of the writers cited by Launoius, and the negative arguments formed from it, are not wholly weak and feeble, but are not entirely without force. In particular, the argument drawn from the silence of Guibert, abbot of Nogent, possesses some strength. In my judgment, this is more than sufficiently established by what I brought forward at nos. 267 and following, although Guibert was not sufficiently well informed about matters concerning Saint Bruno and the order he founded, as I also acknowledged there.

Let us proceed to Launoius’s second conclusion.

313. “The second conclusion,” he says, “that follows from the silence of the authors cited is that the correctors of the Roman Breviary, in removing these matters from the Lessons of Saint Bruno, followed most exactly the canons of the Church, which decree that whatever contrary to truth has entered the books of the sacred offices must be removed.”

But what does our anonymous Carthusian reply?

> “Therefore,” he says, “if this reasoning of Launoius is sound, whatever the correctors of the Roman Breviary removed from the Lessons of Saint Bruno was contrary to truth. Therefore that celebrated profession of faith uttered by Saint Bruno when he lay dying, and removed from his Lessons, is also contrary to truth. Who would say or even imagine this? Certainly we do not believe that Launoius himself would say it, had he observed the matter more attentively.

> “The correctors themselves indicated the true reason that moved them—men most learned and wise—to remove both that spectacle and the profession of faith from the Breviary: namely, that those Lessons were too long.”

Certainly, the prodigious resurrection of the teacher was removed from the Lessons of Saint Bruno not because it was considered false. This is made certain by what was brought forward at no. 190 and the two following numbers.

There is no reason for anyone to reply on Launoius’s behalf that discovered falsity alone can be the reason why something is removed from the Breviary. Launoius himself plainly admits that this is contrary to fact in chapter 5 of his *Dissertation on the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Wilderness*, where he writes in his conclusion:

> “No other more compelling reason [for removing something from the Breviary] is prescribed by ecclesiastical regulations than discovered falsity.”

When he says that there is no more compelling reason than falsity for removing something from the Breviary, he clearly acknowledges that another reason may exist in addition.

[Col. 0187B] 314. But let us hear what Launoius goes on to conclude from the silence of the authors he has cited.

> “The third conclusion,” he says, “is that the claim that Bruno was a Parisian theologian and at some time directed the schools at Paris can still be removed, not only because none of the ancient authors made Bruno a Parisian master or said that he directed schools at Paris, as we have seen, but also because it could scarcely be proved that the study of theology had been established at Paris before Bruno’s time, or that a master’s degree in theology was customarily conferred there.”

The reply made to this by our anonymous Carthusian is of no force. For Bulaeus, contrary to what he says, does not in any way establish through the authorities and arguments he adduces that Bruno studied at Paris or directed its schools.

The matter is clear from what was said above, especially from the arguments by which we showed that Bruno most probably never taught at Paris and that it is also doubtful whether he ever studied there. I cannot therefore oppose Launoius when he argues that Saint Bruno was neither a theologian at Paris nor a teacher of its schools.

Nevertheless, this writer wrongly calls into doubt whether the study of theology had been established at Paris before the time of our saint. For although at that time a master’s degree in theology was not yet conferred there—indeed, the various degrees now customary in universities had not yet been devised—the liberal arts and every kind of learning were taught. The city of Paris already possessed a celebrated and flourishing academy, lacking almost nothing of the splendor of a university except the name, as the authors of the *Literary History of France*, volume VII, pp. 102 and following, demonstrate.

Let us now examine Launoius’s fourth conclusion.

315. “The fourth conclusion,” he says, “that follows from the silence of the ancient authors cited is that Theophilus Raynaudus wrongly asserted that the account of the teacher’s threefold resurrection, which drove Bruno into the wilderness, was accepted among all the ancients. It was likewise falsely added that ‘the silence of Peter of Cluny concerning the teacher’s prodigious resurrection and Bruno’s consequent impulse toward solitude is supplied by very ancient authors and by most writers of the period in which the event is said to have occurred.’

> “For we have made it clear that Peter of Cluny wrote under such circumstances of time and events that an argument equivalent to an affirmation may be drawn from his silence. We have further shown that there are no contemporary or near-contemporary writers of Bruno or Peter of Cluny who support this account of the teacher’s resurrection. Indeed, the sole Guibert, abbot of Nogent, who has been produced, both firmly confirms the argument drawn from Peter of Cluny’s silence and clearly explains the whole cause of the establishment of the Carthusian religion.”

Here also our anonymous Carthusian offers nothing that overturns this conclusion of Launoius. As for the first point contained in it, there is no reason to think it contrary to the truth. Since quite a considerable number of ancient writers whom Launoius cited for his purpose nowhere mention the Parisian prodigy, or the mournful story of the condemned teacher, by what appearance of truth can it be asserted that the story was accepted among all the ancients?

As for the silence of Peter of Cluny and Guibert, I have shown above that the negative arguments formed from it possess some force, though not the force claimed by Launoius. Launoius is nevertheless right to affirm that Peter of Cluny’s silence concerning the teacher’s prodigious resurrection is not supplied “by ancient authors and by most writers of the period in which the event is said to have occurred.” For the writers of this kind whom Raynaudus praised, he praised on the authority of Polycarp de la Rivière, whom Launoius contends acted in bad faith in imposing these materials, and whom Columbius and, after him, our Papebrochius tacitly acknowledge to have done so (see no. 196).

316. “The fifth conclusion,” Launoius continues, “is that the didactic writer did not weigh sufficiently carefully, or at least concealed, all the implications of the letter that Bruno sent from Apulia (or rather Calabria) to Ralph, provost of Reims . . . He also erred no less when he taught that Peter the Venerable did not recount the aforementioned spectacle because he had decided to recount only those miracles that had occurred in his own time—as though Peter himself did not expressly affirm that the Carthusian order had been founded in his time.”

Our anonymous Carthusian replies:

> “Certainly, what Launoius reproaches Saussay with here may be reproached to Launoius himself with even greater justice. For if he had carefully weighed the words in which Saint Bruno admits that after making his vow, ‘through intervening causes divine love grew weak, his spirit cooled, and his fervor vanished,’ and had examined them with a more even balance of judgment against Guibert of Nogent’s account, he would not have concluded that Saint Bruno made his vow at Reims and immediately after leaving the city of Reims went without delay to Chartreuse. It is established by the extensive proofs we gave above that Saint Bruno did not enter the wilderness until eight years after departing from Reims.

> “As for the age of Peter of Cluny, we also demonstrated clearly that the order was founded several years before he was born, and that he wrote nothing about miracles performed among the Carthusians except certain visions granted to a lay brother around the time when he composed his work on miracles—that is, approximately seventy years after the foundation of the order.

> “Let the reader judge, then, how carefully Launoius weighs Peter of Cluny’s words when he asserts that the order was founded in Peter’s time. But someone may reply on behalf of Launoius that Peter the Venerable expressly affirms this. For the aforesaid abbot speaks as follows: ‘In the regions of Burgundy there is preserved . . . a certain profession . . . established in our time.’”

317. “It is true that these words are Peter’s, but it is also true that he wrote them seventy years after the spectacle of the condemned man. That is not a short interval of time but a very long one. Together with the various affairs by which he was occupied because of his office, it was quite sufficient to remove every recollection of the said spectacle from his mind, just as it also removed his recollection of many miracles performed in his time by very holy men, both in his own order and in the other orders of the Church.”

Although the negative arguments drawn from Saint Bruno’s own letter written to Ralph the Green and from Peter the Venerable’s silence concerning the teacher’s prodigious resurrection do not possess anything like the force that Launoius attributes to them, both above and here in his conclusions, I have nevertheless shown above that they are not entirely weak or devoid of strength. Nor do the replies that our anonymous Carthusian makes here to Launoius establish the contrary.

Even if it be granted that Peter did not begin his work on miracles until seventy years after the Parisian prodigy, it nevertheless seems scarcely probable that he omitted the matter through ignorance or a lapse of memory, since, as has been said, he then diligently investigated miracles relating to the Carthusian order.

Nor does it matter that he also passed over in silence other miracles—indeed, miracles that had occurred in his own time and within his own order. For, as he himself indicates in the words transcribed at no. 293, he had resolved to recount those miracles that would serve “to strengthen faith and establish morals.” He could therefore have omitted certain miracles relating even to his own order, not because they were unknown to him or had previously been known but had slipped from his memory, but because they did not seem sufficiently suitable for the purpose just mentioned.

Since scarcely anything more useful to that purpose than the Parisian prodigy could be imagined, it seems to me for this reason alone less probable that Peter the Venerable would have failed to mention the mournful event, if it had occurred—an event that, as has already been said, he would in all likelihood have known.

318. In his sixth and seventh conclusions Launoius assigns almost exclusively what he considers to be the difference in reasoning between Raynaudus and Saussay; this need not detain us here.

In his eighth conclusion he asserts that the “common account of Saint Bruno’s conversion”—that is, the Parisian prodigy in which the teacher, having returned for a time to life, publicly declared from his bier before those standing around him that he had been condemned by God’s just judgment—“if traced back to its origins, is ultimately reduced to a public rumor without an author.”

Against this, the anonymous Carthusian argues that, if that cause of Saint Bruno’s conversion is traced back to its origins, it will be traced not to a public rumor without an author but to Saint Bruno himself and his companions. He also attempts to prove this:

> “For they knew well,” he says in book IV, no. 124 of his *Annals of the Order*, not yet published, “for what cause and in what manner they had renounced the world, and without doubt they handed this down to their followers. We do not think there is anyone who would stubbornly assert that Saint Bruno and his companions did not teach their followers how and for what reason they had embraced so arduous a way of life, or that the Carthusian order itself was unaware of the occasion and cause of its foundation.

> “Among these followers there was one who, approximately eighty years after their death”—here he is speaking of the anonymous author cited at no. 199 and following, concerning whose most probable period of activity I gave evidence at no. 12 and following—“committed this cause to writing. Perhaps someone had done so even before him, but his book may have perished through the passage of time.

> “As the number of houses of the order increased, so too did the number of copies of the book published by our anonymous author, until around the end of the thirteenth century and the beginning of the fourteenth it was found in all the provinces of the order. From there the fame of this story spread among the entire populace.”

Thus far he. Whether he is right or wrong, and whether there is a true and genuine tradition in the Carthusian order upon which the Parisian prodigy—or the common account of Saint Bruno’s conversion—is built, will be examined below. Let us proceed to the remaining conclusions of Launoius.

319. “Ninth,” says this writer, “hardly any fiction can be found in history that is refuted more forcefully and more frequently [than the Parisian prodigy, that is]. More forcefully, if one considers the array of so many writers marshaled against the account of the doctor’s horrifying spectacle and the Carthusian beginning inferred from it; more frequently, if one considers the several writers among them who separately overturn the same account and its appended episode.”

Thus Launoy argues that the celebrated [Col. 0190D] account of the spectacle of the condemned doctor is false: first, because all the writers he cited are entirely silent about that dreadful story; and second, because several of them, who—if the event had occurred—would have known of it and mentioned what they knew, by their particular silence demonstrate that it must be regarded as manifestly false.

Our anonymous Carthusian understood the words of Launoy just quoted somewhat differently, and perhaps not without reason, as is clear from his response, which runs as follows:

“Who would not be astonished at the empty hyperbole in these words, by which only simple people could be deceived? Not one of all the writers cited by Launoy refutes or denies the story; they merely do not relate it—indeed, they neither can nor ought to relate it according to their purpose. For they say little about Saint Bruno and nothing about his conversion, as can be seen above, if one excepts Guibert of Nogent. Nevertheless, Launoy dares to pronounce that hardly any fiction can be found which is more forcefully and more frequently refuted” [Col. 0191A]—although, on the contrary, nothing is weaker than the negative authority on which he relies, producing so many testimonies that say nothing against the truth of this story.

320. “As for what he adds—that it is refuted more frequently, if one considers among the writers whom he cited ‘several who separately overturn the same account and its appended episode’—this certainly does not appear true from the examination we made above of the authority of those writers. Not one of them, either separately or together, overturns the account in question or its appended episode; indeed, they do not even shake it in the least” [Col. 0191B].

Thus far the anonymous Carthusian. His purpose is evidently to show that the negative argument against Launoy—who attributes too much to it—has no force at all, and consequently that the ancient writers’ silence concerning the prodigious revival of the doctor does not merely fail to deny it, but does not shake it in any way, much less overthrow it.

I have already shown above, however, that the silence of some of the principal ancient writers praised by Launoy does possess a certain degree of force against this event. The following section will show how much weight the silence of absolutely all the writers who flourished during the passage of the entire first, and perhaps also the second, century after the event carries against it. It will also show whether Launoy, in the conclusion presently under discussion, rightly regards the celebrated account of the spectacle of the condemned doctor as false solely on the basis of the silence of the authors whom he cites, and whether he rightly dismisses it as an invention and a fable in his tenth and final conclusion. Since my purpose requires me to say a few things about that conclusion beforehand, I shall proceed to it now [Col. 0191C].

321. Finally, then, according to Launoy’s position, the unanimous silence of all the authors whom he has cited entails that “more than 240 years after the founding of the Carthusian Order, that account of the revival of the Parisian doctor or canon was fabricated—the account that drove Saint Bruno into the wilderness. Here,” he says, “is the terminal stake by which this narrative is held fast; this is the chronological boundary that leaves no room for evasions by the defenders of fables” [Col. 0191D].

Thus, if Launoy is to be followed here, the famous story of the doctor who supposedly cried out publicly from his bier that he had been condemned must have been fabricated by idle people only after the year 1324, since by that point exactly 240 years had elapsed from the founding of the Carthusian Order, or, according to what will be explained below, from the year 1084, the date assigned to its foundation, to the year 1324. But if that account was in fact fabricated—as whether this happened will be determined from what follows—it must have been fabricated long before the year just mentioned.

For several ancient writers reviewed in sections 11 and 12 committed it to writing before that year. In particular, leaving the others aside, there were the anonymous Carthusian author of the *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Grande Chartreuse* and the likewise anonymous Carthusian of Majoris [Col. 0192A]. The former (see numbers 12 and following) certainly began writing before the year 1313; the latter, in 1298, as he himself expressly states.

Our anonymous Carthusian, who compiled the fourth book of the annals of his Order, supplies somewhat more material relevant to this matter. I have not thought it necessary to transcribe his words here, since the few passages already cited sufficiently establish what had to be proved.

Those passages establish not only this point; they also show that, contrary to what Launoy further maintains in chapter 2 of his *Dissertation on the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Wilderness*, Gerson was not the first to commit to writing, around the year 1420, the grim story of the unfortunate Parisian doctor—or, as Launoy calls it, the fable—which had already been fabricated some time earlier [Col. 0192B].

Let us now proceed to the other matters that, as I said, are to be examined in the following section.

§ XIX. What the universal silence of all the writers who flourished during the passage of the entire first, and perhaps also the second, century after the event signifies against the prodigious revival in which the Parisian doctor publicly declared from his bier that he had been condemned; and whether, despite this silence, the ancient testimonies cited above can make that account certain or even probable.

322. In the four immediately preceding sections I showed, from the material brought forward by Launoy against the mournful story of the Parisian doctor, that there are several writers whose silence is somewhat adverse to that story. It must now be considered what weight the universal silence concerning that dreadful event carries—especially the silence of those writers who flourished during the passage of the entire first and perhaps also the second century after the event, when the matter had not yet been committed to writing [Col. 0192C].

In several passages of his frequently mentioned *Dissertation*, Launoy presents that astonishing and, if it occurred, most memorable prodigy as an undoubted falsehood, an old wives’ tale, and a foul invention, solely because it was not commended to writing by the ancient writers whom he cites. But is this correct? Certainly not, as is sufficiently clear from what I said in number 258, and will become even clearer from what I am now about to say.

Here is one example, among others, by which we learn that events reported as having occurred, yet not found recorded by contemporary writers, must not immediately be classified as fables and inventions. Pope Benedict XIV records the following near the end of *On the Beatification of the Servants of God and the Canonization of the Blessed*, book III, chapter 10, number 3:

“There was a report that Saints Faustinus and Jovita, patrons of the city of Brescia, had appeared in golden armor to protect it against Niccolò Piccinino, commander of the Milanese forces, who was besieging and attacking it with the greatest violence. But most people doubted this miracle of the remarkable apparition, since the Brescia historians contemporary with the event were silent about it, while Elias Capreolus—who died eighty full years after the siege had been lifted and inserted certain fabulous materials into his commentaries—did relate it. Then, through the work and diligence of Cardinal Angelo Maria Querini, two letters of Ludovico Foscarini to Saint Lawrence Justinian, then patriarch of Venice, were discovered, and these placed the whole matter in the open” [Col. 0192D–0193A].

323. “For fourteen years after Brescia had been freed from the siege, Foscarini assumed the administration of that city, entrusted to him by the Venetian Senate. Two days after taking up the province, a rumor spread that certain religious men had resolved to carry the bodies of Saints Faustinus and Jovita away to Venice; and that, unless he had opportunely rescued those religious, they would have perished by the fury and weapons of the people.

“In the letters mentioned above, Foscarini, explaining the cause of the pious rage that had inflamed the minds of the people of Brescia, writes as follows:

“‘They remember that, when they were surrounded and confined, suffering from hunger and undergoing the ultimate dangers, their most holy protectors were seen by the enemy defending Brescia in golden armor. Struck with astonishment by this miracle, Niccolò Piccinino, that most valiant commander, abandoned hope of capturing the city and restrained his eagerness both to seek punishment and to obtain gold. For these reasons they would the more reluctantly be deprived of those bodies’” [Col. 0193B].

Foscarini’s complete letters were included in the printed letter of the aforementioned cardinal, addressed to Father Cyprian Benaglia, abbot and general president of the Cassinese Congregation. After this, the learned cardinal adds the following relevant observation:

“It remains finally for you to acknowledge with me that the argument which the masters of critical method call negative—and which some of those very men not infrequently abuse in order to overthrow the authority of ecclesiastical monuments—can easily be found entirely deprived of authority. Certainly it seemed to triumph most powerfully in the matter appended to this letter, for the silence of the ancient writers could be directed against it all the more forcefully because several commentaries composed at the time of the Brescia siege concerning the events of that siege are still available” [Col. 0193C].

324. But the letters of Foscarini, which I discovered, showed how empty that triumph would have been. “From where, by the immortal God, does that tribe of critics confidently believe that it can know for certain that the ancient monuments against which they rashly declare war once lacked testimonies of this kind, when, over the passage of so many centuries, they may perhaps have entirely perished through adverse fortune, or may still lie hidden in darkness?” [Col. 0193D].

Here, surely, is an excellent example of an event which, although it truly occurred, is nevertheless not found recorded by contemporary authors, and which therefore would always have been considered false, or at least called into doubt, unless the letters of Foscarini—offering it the clearest testimony—had been discovered by the most eminent Cardinal Querini.

At the same time, however, Querini appears to diminish too greatly the force of the negative argument. Although that argument is not sufficient to pronounce anything against which it is directed false, it nevertheless often has an added force (see number 258) by which, according to the circumstances of events and times, it makes the fact against which it is directed more or less improbable [Col. 0194A].

For a negative argument to have a place, it is not necessary that it be certain, but only that it be probable that the matter was not recorded by ancient writers who have perished. This condition is met when it is certainly known that the matter is not found recorded by any ancient writers still extant, and when one or more of those writers are plausibly of such a kind that, if the event had occurred, they would have known of it and mentioned what they knew.

Consider now another example of an event that occurred but was not recorded by contemporary writers.

325. Saint Francis of Assisi is said to have asked Pope Honorius III for, and then obtained from him, the celebrated indulgence called the “Portiuncula.” No contemporary writers mention this at all—not even those who, with the greatest diligence and by deliberate design, described his entire life and deeds, namely Thomas of Celano and Saint Bonaventure [Col. 0194B].

For this reason, especially in the sixteenth century, there were some who either resolutely denied that Honorius had ever granted that indulgence to Saint Francis, or at least called it into doubt. They were further led to this position by the consideration that the grant of an indulgence as extensive as the Portiuncula indulgence was wholly inconsistent with the ecclesiastical discipline and practices prevailing in Saint Francis’s time.

But in the century just past, testimonies were finally brought to light from ancient manuscripts (see our work, volume II of October, pages 887 and following). They had been given approximately forty years after Saint Francis’s death—at a time when the indulgence had already been called into doubt or even denied by some because no papal documents concerning it survived—by Blessed Benedict of Arezzo, formerly admitted into the Order by Saint Francis himself, and by Raynerius of Mariano, Benedict’s companion [Col. 0194C].

These testimonies state that the indulgence in question had been both requested by Saint Francis and granted by Honorius III. Their account was based on a narrative given to them on this subject by Brother Masseo of Marignano, who had been present.

Most importantly, another testimony was added: Peter Zalfanus (see the same work, volume II of October, page 890) testified that he himself had been present in the church of Saint Mary of the Portiuncula when Saint Francis, in the presence of seven bishops, promulgated the indulgence he had received from Honorius [Col. 0194D].

These three testimonies no longer permit doubt that this notable indulgence was in fact requested by Saint Francis and granted to him by Honorius. Yet, as already stated, no contemporary writers whatsoever—and not even Francis’s biographers, although they carefully embraced in writing all his deeds—mention the event. This is certainly a very strong argument that it does not invariably follow that events not mentioned by contemporary writers are unquestionably false.

326. Since it is extremely easy for events which, although they occurred, are not mentioned by contemporary writers to be passed over in silence by writers of a later age as well, it certainly does not follow that what is omitted both by these and by others should be considered false or unhistorical. Consequently, Launoy wrongly dismisses the prodigious revival of the Parisian doctor as an empty invention and an old wives’ tale, wholly remote from the truth, simply because it is not found recorded either by contemporary writers or by others who flourished later [Col. 0195A].

Nor should you reply on Launoy’s behalf that ancient testimonies supporting the Portiuncula indulgence have already been brought forward, and that a legitimate reason can be given why contemporary writers did not mention it. For even though a reasonable explanation for the silence of contemporary writers and of Saint Francis’s own biographers concerning the Portiuncula indulgence can in fact be offered—as may again be seen in the same work, volume II of October, page 890—it nevertheless remains possible that the writers of both the eleventh century, in which the prodigious revival of the doctor is said to have occurred, and the following century failed, for a reason unknown to us, to mention it [Col. 0195B].

Or, if that explanation is unsatisfactory, they may have omitted all mention of that prodigy and mournful event not because some legitimate reason compelled them to do so, but because, in reporting events that occurred in their own time, they exercised almost no accuracy, or at most only moderate accuracy.

The Brescia historians contemporary with the event did not commit to writing the apparition by which Saints Faustinus and Jovita terrified Niccolò Piccinino, commander of the Milanese forces, and his soldiers while they were besieging the city of Brescia with the utmost force. Yet I find no sufficiently certain legitimate explanation offered for this silence. Their omission therefore appears attributable either to causes unknown to us or to the limited accuracy they employed in recording the events of their own time [Col. 0195C].

327. As for the testimonies praised above, which, despite the silence of contemporary authors, make the Portiuncula indulgence certain, they have no bearing on the present matter. It is clear from them that an event reported by later writers may have occurred in reality even though all contemporary writers passed over it in silence [Col. 0195D].

Since this is so, it is plainly wrong to pronounce the story of the doctor who publicly declared from his bier, in the presence of those standing around him, that he had been condemned, false solely because it was not commended to writing by contemporary authors.

Nor, as I have already said, does Launoy rightly assert that it is unquestionably false because it is also passed over in silence by other writers who flourished later.

But can that mournful event at least be regarded as highly doubtful, or even as probably or plausibly false, because it is passed over in silence by all writers, both contemporary and later, who flourished during the passage of the entire first and perhaps also the second century after the event? I think so entirely.

For although, among all the arguments from silence supplied by the silence of several of these writers—some of whom have also been cited above—there is scarcely any one that is very strong when taken separately, all of them taken together do make it quite probable that the event never occurred. This is much as several reasons contributing to the establishment of a proposition sometimes make it solidly probable when taken together, even though each of them, considered separately, is of little force [Col. 0196A].

Indeed, to whom would it not appear probable that a prodigy of this kind never occurred when it is passed over in silence by all the writers just mentioned, although, if it had happened, it would have circulated through everyone’s mouths and pens, since, according to the opinion under discussion—which asserts that it occurred publicly before an almost countless multitude of people—it would simultaneously have been an event most worthy of notice and universally known [Col. 0196B]?

328. Nor should you reply that the prodigious revival by which the doctor, temporarily returned to life, terrified a vast multitude of people by publicly announcing the dreadful judgment passed upon him was nevertheless mentioned by those who flourished not very long after the contemporary and near-contemporary writers, even though the latter suppressed it in silence.

The first person to commit this mournful story to writing was an anonymous Carthusian who compiled the *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Grande Chartreuse*, whose contents I described in section 1. But, as I also showed there, he most probably did not begin writing before the year 1250, and perhaps not even before approximately the year 1300. Consequently, he would not have done so until more than 150 years, and perhaps 200 years, had elapsed after the event—that is, after the horrifying occurrence [Col. 0196C].

You may say that this writer perhaps flourished from approximately the year 1220, or even somewhat earlier, and had before him an older writer from whom he drew what he reports about the miracle of the doctor restored to life and the consequent withdrawal of his holy Father into the wilderness.

But neither assertion appears in any way consistent with the truth. To answer first the second point, it seems clear from the very form of expression with which the author of the *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Grande Chartreuse* begins that no older writer from whom he drew his material stood before him. His words are as follows:

“About the year 1082 of the Lord’s Incarnation, or around that time, while solemn study was flourishing at Paris, it is said that such a prodigy occurred there. For a certain doctor,” and so forth [Col. 0196D].

By these words, that anonymous chronicler appears to indicate that he had not read the prodigy of the doctor restored to life, which he goes on to relate, in older writings or monuments, but had received it from others who recounted the matter orally.

329. Moreover, whenever this same chronicler inserted into the Life of our saint something received elsewhere from writers who preceded him, he informs the reader of the fact and even gives their names.

In number 10, when he is about to transcribe what is related about Saint Bruno and his six companions in the *Life of Saint Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble*, written by Guigo, the fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, he first says:

“To use precisely the words written in the aforementioned *Life of Saint Hugh, Bishop*” [Col. 0197A].

After quoting all that concerns Saint Bruno and his companions, he adds, in Guigo’s own words:

“All the foregoing are the words of Lord Guigo, written in the *Life of Saint Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble*.”

In number 24, the final number, after assigning the date on which the saint closed his final day after leaving the Grande Chartreuse from the *Chronicle of the Four First Priors of the Grande Chartreuse*, prefixed to Guigo’s ancient *Customs* (see number 6), he immediately adds:

“As is contained in the books of Lord Guigo’s *Customs*, which are in the house of the Grande Chartreuse” [Col. 0197B].

If, therefore, he had drawn the prodigious revival of the doctor which he relates from older writers, he would most probably have indicated this or named those writers—especially since, when about to relate that dreadful story, he begins: “It is said that such a prodigy occurred there.” It would have been easy and appropriate, in order to establish the credibility of so extraordinary an event, for him to add by whom it was said or reported.

Since these matters stand thus, it appears extremely probable, not to say certain, that the older writers by whom the Parisian prodigy had been handed down did not precede the anonymous chronicler of the first five priors of the Grande Chartreuse, or the older biographer of our saint. Consequently, on this ground he cannot lend any greater credibility to his account of the revival of the condemned doctor [Col. 0197C].

Furthermore, since the aforementioned chronicler or biographer, as has been said, would most probably have named any older writers whom he had used for the horrifying account of the doctor, and yet does not name Caesarius, it follows that he most probably either did not see the account given by that writer in number 241 or considered it different from his own.

330. As for the year 1220, around which time, or even somewhat earlier, the anonymous chronicler of the first five priors of the Grande Chartreuse, or the biographer of our saint, is supposed to have flourished, the matter is probably otherwise, as appears from what was said in numbers 12 and following [Col. 0197D].

Nor, even if the matter were as supposed, could anything be established from it that would make the mournful story of the Parisian doctor sufficiently certain or even probable.

Suppose, for the sake of argument, that the aforementioned chronicler, who first committed the story to writing, actually began writing around the year 1220. Even so, he would still have been approximately 140 years removed from the event, and therefore separated from it by too long an interval to make his account unquestionably credible.

Although it sometimes happens that an event, even if mentioned only by writers who flourished more than a full century after it occurred, must be regarded as probable, or even certain, this cannot apparently be the case when, as here, the event under dispute is of such a kind that, if it had ever occurred, it would probably have been mentioned even by contemporary and coeval writers.

But, you may object, the slaughter of Saint Maurice and his companions, the martyr-soldiers of the Theban Legion, is not found recorded by contemporary writers. It may be the sort of event that, if it had occurred, would probably have been mentioned by them; nevertheless, no one would rightly pronounce it false or insufficiently probable on that account [Col. 0198A].

I grant that this is so. But what follows? Reasons that are not ineffectual for explaining why contemporary writers passed over that slaughter in silence, despite its being extremely notable and famous, are given in our volume VI of September, where the saints are discussed from page 308 onward, in the preliminary Commentary on their Acts, section 7. Since such an explanation is possible—or rather, since it is in fact available—it is universally acknowledged that arguments from the silence of writers possess no force in this case.

331. Furthermore, the slaughter of those most celebrated martyrs is established—and thus whatever probability might otherwise arise against it from the silence of authors is removed—not only by the many testimonies brought forward in the Commentary just cited, but especially by Saint Eucherius, bishop of Lyon. He was the first to commit the event to writing, and although he flourished only in the fifth century, he drew his account from a genuine source of tradition, which he himself identifies [Col. 0198B].

But no sufficiently suitable explanation can be given for the universal silence by which writers who flourished during the passage of more than the entire first century after the event passed over the prodigious revival of the doctor. Nor is this horrifying story established by any monument, much less by the anonymous author of the *Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Grande Chartreuse*, who neither states from where he drew it nor is known to have obtained it elsewhere.

Indeed, since I have already shown that this author had no older writers before him from whom he could have drawn his material, from what source could he have derived his account—a source on which we could safely rely [Col. 0198C]?

Perhaps from public reputation or common rumor? But everyone knows how uncertain such an authority is.

Perhaps from the tradition of his Order? This is certainly what those who defend the story of the Parisian prodigy and of Saint Bruno’s consequent withdrawal into the wilderness believe; indeed, they must assert it in order to defend their position.

But whether that Carthusian tradition deserves the name of genuine tradition, and also how much weight it carries in establishing the truth of the Parisian prodigy, I shall examine below, after first investigating, as I have resolved to do in the present section, whether the remaining testimonies of ancient writers brought forward in sections 11 and 12 in favor of the revival of the Parisian doctor—who publicly declared that he had been condemned—can, despite the universal silence of writers just described, make the event certain or even probable [Col. 0198D].

332. Since all those writers received their account either from the already examined narrative of the chronicler of the first five priors of the Grande Chartreuse, with only certain arbitrary alterations made in it, or certainly from other writers whose own account likewise derived its origin from that narrative, they cannot give the prodigy greater credibility than the aforementioned chronicler deserves, who was the first to commit it to writing.

Nevertheless, as I have already shown above, their testimonies do establish that the prodigious revival of the Parisian doctor was unquestionably and for a very long time believed by many, and that it was committed to writing long before the time of John Gerson, contrary to Launoy’s position [Col. 0199A].

There is therefore no need to investigate at length what authority the individual writers listed in sections 11 and 12 possess in this matter.

Nevertheless, however the matter may stand, and although no sufficiently solid argument can establish the contrary, some people, as I learn from manuscript notes in my possession, insist that the testimony of John Iperius, transcribed in number 222, should be given great weight.

They argue this because, although Iperius did not flourish before the fourteenth century and therefore, considering the long interval separating him from the assigned date of the Parisian prodigy—that is, the year 1082—could not by his own authority make the event certain and unquestionable, he nevertheless had before him an older author contemporary with the event, from whom he drew what he reports about it [Col. 0199B].

The basis for this last judgment was supplied by Martene in his preliminary Admonition to Iperius’s, or Saint Bertin’s, *Chronicle*, included in volume III of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*. Near the end of that Admonition he writes:

“From this you will conclude that this Bertinian Chronicle deserves so much greater credit among the learned because it possesses more ancient authors who committed to writing the events of their own time, just as they had seen them or heard them from eyewitnesses. Nor should it seem surprising that later authors held it in such high esteem that they did not hesitate to receive from it what they had to say about Belgian affairs” [Col. 0199C].

333. Thus, as Martene teaches here, Iperius received the events related in his *Chronicle* from older writers who had either seen them themselves or heard them from eyewitnesses. According to Martene’s preliminary Admonition, there were three such writers: Folquinus, the Bertinian monk, who gathered the ancient documents of his monastery into a single volume in the tenth century; Simon, abbot of Sithiu or Saint Bertin, the forty-second abbot, who died in 1148 and wrote the chronicle of the Bertinian or Sithian church from the time of Roderic—that is, from the beginning of the eleventh century, when Roderic was abbot of the monastery of Sithiu—down to his own time; and finally an anonymous writer who was writing in 1229 and continued Simon’s work down to his own time [Col. 0199D].

Now, since only one of these three writers who preceded Iperius in composing the Bertinian Chronicle—namely Simon the abbot—was contemporary with the mournful story of the condemned doctor, as is clear from what has just been said, they concluded that Iperius had introduced the story into his Sithian Chronicle from Simon, and therefore from a contemporary author who had at least heard it from eyewitnesses; hence they concluded that it deserved the highest credibility.

Indeed, if Martene’s broad judgment of the Sithian Chronicle composed by Iperius is to be accepted, there would certainly be reason to suspect, not without justification, that Iperius really did draw the story of the condemned doctor from the work of Simon the abbot.

But Martene’s judgment of the aforementioned Chronicle is far from being accurate. To make this clear, and so that the attentive reader may understand that Iperius’s testimony concerning the mournful story of the doctor can add no weight—or at most very little weight—to it, I shall transcribe here the response supplied by our Stilting, volume II of September, page 555, number 25 onward, to Martene’s judgment of Iperius’s Chronicle [Col. 0200A].

334. He writes there as follows:

“I would have preferred the editor mentioned above”—that is, Martene—“to have supplied an accurate critical examination of this Chronicle rather than exaggerated praise. In that way the attentive reader would have understood more clearly what he could safely accept from it and what, on the contrary, he ought to avoid.

“Certainly the chronology is for the most part defective in the earlier centuries of this Chronicle, as will become clear in the course of the work. Indeed, I am often compelled to show that even the events related in this Chronicle are not so certain and so free from errors that they do not require fairly frequent correction.

“Martene attempts to establish the authority of the Chronicle because Iperius followed Folquinus the deacon, Simon the abbot, and their anonymous thirteenth-century continuator, whom he says wrote in 1229” [Col. 0200B].

“From these sources,” Martene says, “John Iperius appears to have composed his Chronicle in such a way that he may rightly be considered to have inserted their complete works into his own.”

He attempts to establish this by certain words he cites, which Iperius could not have spoken about himself and which therefore must be attributed to the older writers whose statements, without alteration to that point, Iperius inserted into his Chronicle.

But I strongly suspect that Martene never compared Iperius’s Chronicle with the three writers from whom he says Iperius borrowed so much. Certainly, if he had carefully compared Iperius’s words with those of the anonymous continuator, who is the compiler of the *Life of Saint Bertin* edited by Mabillon, he would have seen that Iperius completely altered the sense of the words in the event related in number 25 of the *Appendix of Miracles*, as I shall observe there [Col. 0200C].

355. “Moreover, if he had carefully compared and examined those three authors, he would have seen that very few events are reported by them as witnessed personally, while most are presented as having occurred long before. For this reason he would not have said: ‘This Bertinian Chronicle deserves so much greater credit among the learned because it possesses more ancient authors who committed to writing the events of their own time, just as they had seen them or heard them from eyewitnesses.’

“These statements were made inconsiderately and without sufficient examination. For Iperius drew little from writers who had themselves seen the events or had written down events occurring in their own time; at least in the earlier centuries of his Chronicle, he drew far more from writers who lived long after the events they reported.

“Moreover, Iperius possesses material from more writers than those three, of whom Martene makes him virtually a mere continuator.

“I have thought it necessary to make these observations about Iperius so that no one, deceived by Martene’s excessive praise, may immediately think me deserving of criticism when he sees that I do not submit to the authority of this writer.

“Nevertheless, I do not wish to deprive Iperius of the praise due to him. I judge his Chronicle useful and by no means contemptible, but it must not be followed blindly.

“He himself indicates in his second prologue where he drew his material and with what fidelity he wrote, in these words:

“‘We have gathered this present little work with grateful labor from many volumes and authentic writings, taking from each whatever seemed relevant to our purpose and inserting nothing that is not approved by authentic writings.’

“He then explains what he means by ‘authentic writings’: many Lives of the saints, quite a few Chronicles, antiquities, annals, histories, and archives both of the church of Sithiu and of other monasteries of Belgium and France; other historical books; and finally charters of privileges” [Col. 0200D–0201A].

336. “From all these monuments he claims to have composed his Chronicle: ‘By date and consulship, reconciling periods with periods, and events with events according to the causes contained in them’ [Col. 0201B]. I do not doubt that this pious and learned man carried this out diligently and in good faith; yet it is clearer than daylight that he did not do so without errors. Indeed, to compose such a work in the century in which Iperius lived, without various errors, was beyond human industry: first, because many of the monuments that had to be used were not entirely free from error; and second, because various matters had to be reconciled by conjecture. This reconciliation was all the more difficult because chronological and critical scholarship was then much less advanced toward its present perfection.”

Thus far our Stiltingus, who subsequently proves with great force and clarity, in more than one place in his Commentary prefixed to the Life of [Col. 0201C] Saint Bertin, what he here asserts concerning the Chronicle of Iperius, as will become evident to anyone who reads it through. Now, since Iperius—not to mention other matters—drew the events narrated in his Chronicle not only from the three writers mentioned by Martene, namely Folquinus, a monk of Sithiu, Simon the abbot, and the anonymous continuator, but also from many others whom Stiltingus will presently identify, there is no reason for us to suppose that the prodigious resurrection of the Parisian doctor which he relates was taken from the chronicles of Simon, abbot of Sithiu. Consequently, the fullest credence that would otherwise attach to the famous account of that event collapses. Indeed, since the matter stands thus, the Parisian miracle is not even rendered in any degree probable by the Chronicle of Iperius, as is readily inferred from what has already been said [Col. 0201D].

§ XX. Whether tradition, despite the universal silence of the foregoing writers, can also render certain, or at least probable, the miracle by which the doctor, proclaiming himself condemned, announced this publicly to those present

Innocentius le Masson, following the recension of Morotius, forty-ninth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, in the work he compiled under the title *Annals of the Carthusian Order*, published in 1687 by the Correrian press, discusses at length in Book I, chapter 1, the prodigious resurrection of the doctor through which Saint Bruno was driven into the wilderness; and he also adduces the tradition of that celebrated order in order to prove that this event truly occurred. So that no one may complain that I have passed over in silence anything that might in any way contribute to proving, or at least rendering credible, that horrible story [Col. 0202A], I transcribe here from that work—which is not commonly in everyone’s hands—the whole of Masson’s reasoning that bears on the matter, however lengthy and unpersuasive it may be. It is expressed in the following words, placed there as no. 8 and following:

“Those are mistaken who think that abstinence from meat, even in illnesses, together with other austerities, shortens the lives of Carthusians. For experience shows us that many among us live to extreme old age, reaching eighty years, and sometimes almost ninety. We therefore not infrequently see monks who have lived sixty years or more in the order, even in this century, when everyone admits that human life has been shortened if compared with earlier centuries. As an example of this more robust health, let us take the reverend Father Dom Joannes Pegon, of holy memory, our predecessor, who lived more than sixty-six years in the order, died at the age of eighty-five, and possessed such vigor of mind that on the day before his death he still used a pen to make arrangements for the order [Col. 0202B]. Let two nuns also serve as examples, who in our own days ended their lives: one of them had lived seventy years in the order, the other seventy-two. It would be easy here to cite many similar cases of those who died in our century.

338. “But if we go back to earlier centuries, we shall find persons who lived eighty years or more, indeed one who lived more than a hundred years in the order. The Reverend Father Jancelinus will come to mind, who governed the entire order for fifty-eight years [Col. 0202C]. Yet, after making the calculation and reducing the longer lifespan to only seventy years spent in the order—a span which it is certain many attained in each century, and even greatly exceeded—we shall find that the old man who in this century lived seventy years in the order could have seen and learned from another old man of the same age what that other had heard from yet another old man, and that the last old man had in turn learned and heard the story in question from someone else. Thus the tradition of those four old men extends over almost three hundred years. It is clear that they could easily have received it from one another, since three of them could have seen and conversed with one another without any violence being done to the ordinary course of nature. For nothing prevents the beginnings of the last from overlapping the end of the first, and a monk in his twentieth year from seeing and hearing a ninety-year-old [Col. 0202D]. We have at hand pictures affixed at the beginning of the ancient statutes, printed for a hundred and eighty years, in which that story is depicted, together with the account that we related above. If, therefore, we take as our starting point the time when those pictures were printed, and place the four old men earlier than that time, we shall find that they could have learned that story from those who immediately succeeded the first Fathers of the order. Indeed, peasants could then have been found in the village near the Chartreuse who had seen Saint Bruno and his companions. For peasants in these rocky regions, where the air is purer [Col. 0203A] and the manner of life very frugal, live a long time.

339. “I myself saw, and more than once questioned, an elderly household servant of the Chartreuse, named Nicolaus Planes, originally from the village of Corbel, who had seen the Reverend Father Dom Bernard Carrassus, who died around the year 1586. Nicolaus related many things that he had heard in his youth from others who, at that time, were already in extreme old age and had seen the Reverend Father Franciscus a Puteo, who died around the year 1521. This Nicolaus was about a hundred years old when he ended his life in 1677. To set out and explain the matter still more closely and distinctly, let us suppose that one of Saint Bruno’s companions lived only thirty years from the day when they came to the rocks of the Chartreuse, and that one of those whom the first Fathers received into their institution survived him by seventy years. There we already have almost a hundred years, and so we reach the year 1184. If we add to these the lifespan of the four old men, which reached 280 years, we arrive at the year 1464, and thus at the lifetime of the Reverend Father Franciscus a Puteo, a man highly versed in both branches of learning and an eminent scholar, who arranged for these ancient statutes to be printed. At their beginning was placed a picture representing that story, together with the account mentioned above. If he had suspected it to be a fable, a man of such intelligence would never have allowed it to be fabricated.

“Add to this that the house of the Chartreuse, although repeatedly consumed by fires, possessed ancient writings from which the truth of this story was plainly established. Many people read and saw them, just as we too learned it from elderly monks whom we saw in our youth [Col. 0203C], and who had heard it from eyewitnesses. Finally, this tradition has always and everywhere prevailed in the order, without anyone ever objecting. Who, then, would not acknowledge that such a tradition rests upon firm foundations?”

340. Thus far Masson, whose lengthy discourse serves only to show that, through a continuous tradition begun already in the time of Saint Bruno and his companions and transmitted by one Carthusian to another, it could have happened that the grim story of the condemned doctor reached the knowledge of Franciscus a Puteo, who prefixed it, cut in wood, to the statutes of his order published by him in 1510. But that this actually happened in this way he in no respect proves, as will be clear to anyone who considers the matter [Col. 0203D]. Yet this was entirely necessary if he was to establish anything in support of the miracle—or rather, in support of establishing a genuine tradition, begun from the very occurrence of the event, through which the story had come to Puteo’s knowledge. For it can easily happen that what, after more than three hundred years have elapsed since the event, is asserted to have been transmissible from its very beginning, as Masson claims, in reality began to be transmitted only long afterward, and thus derives its origin not from a true tradition but from an uncertain rumor.

Hence I do not sufficiently understand why our anonymous Carthusian, in no. 47 of his frequently cited work, writes as follows:

“As regards the tradition of the Fathers, the Reverend Father”—namely Innocentius le Masson [Col. 0204A]—“has established it sufficiently and more than sufficiently by solid reasoning in Book I, chapter 1, clearly and brilliantly demonstrating that all the Carthusians who ever were or are in the Christian world have never recognized any other cause or occasion for the institution of our religion than the tragic resurrection of this man. They assert that they received this account from their elders, who themselves learned it from their Fathers, to whom it had come from Saint Bruno and his companions, and from their disciples and followers, through a long tradition extending over many years.”

341. Yet although he speaks in this way here, he nevertheless tacitly acknowledges that the age of Puteo, to which Masson brings the Parisian miracle by tradition, is more remote from the event than to allow that tradition—being, as has been shown, of doubtful standing—to provide it with certain and unquestionable credibility in the manner assigned by Masson. For, in the words quoted immediately above, in order to shorten that long chain of tradition, he adds the following:

“Yet, lest so unusual and astonishing a matter, and one so difficult to believe, should appear wholly incredible on account of such a long chain of tradition—especially to the wicked men of this age, who believe almost nothing except what, as the common proverb says, leaps into the eyes of those who look—we shall shorten this argument, derived from tradition, by almost five centuries, if I may put it so.
