We shall extend this tradition only through a period of sixty years, or at most eighty, after the death of Saint Bruno’s companions, as follows.

“He who first committed this story to writing among the Carthusians lived around the year 1220, or even earlier, as we shall prove below—that is, eighty years after, and not much more than eighty years after, the death of Stephen of Die, one of Saint Bruno’s companions. In our Annals we shall see that Stephen was still alive around the year 1136. Nor is it impossible that some others among the seven first founders of the order lived longer. For who would deny that some of those who had not yet reached their twenty-fifth year when they withdrew into solitude could afterward have reached their seventieth or even eightieth year of life, and the year 1140 or later of the Christian era?

342. “This first writer of the story had certainly seen many monks who knew, or at least could have known, some of the disciples of the aforementioned seven leaders of the order. We know that some of these disciples lived beyond the year 1200 [Col. 0204D], such as Saint Artaldus, professed of the house of Portes, who was sent around the year 1132 to found the Chartreuse of Arvernia, later became its prior and bishop of Belley, and finally returned to Arvernia, where he died in 1206 at the age of 105; Garnerius, lord of Balmeto, co-founder of the house of Majorevia, established in 1116, who, after his wife’s death, became a lay brother there and lived to see the year 1214; and Brother Aynardus, a lay brother, professed of the Grande Chartreuse [Col. 0205A], who may have seen Saint Bruno, since the Life of Saint Hugh of Lincoln establishes that he died only in the 126th year of his age, which was the year 1204 of Christ, or somewhat later, as we learn from that same Life, written by a contemporary author, and shall relate more fully in its proper place.

“It must therefore be clear that the aforementioned writer received this story rather from monks who had lived with these and other disciples of Saint Bruno’s companions—among whom may also be counted the Reverend Father Jaucelinus, prior of the Chartreuse, who died in 1233 after governing it for almost sixty years, and whom our author himself had undoubtedly known—than ‘from the uncertain rumor of a credulous populace and the fables of certain recent writers,’ as Launoius charged us, as though we were idle men.

343. “‘From where, I ask, could that uncertain rumor at that time have been scattered through our cloisters? Should it not rather be said to have gradually spread far and wide from those same cloisters? Indeed, from the pupils of those very Fathers, men certainly most grave and holy. Guillielmus Durandus, an author of great reputation and learning, valued the credibility of these men and their successors so highly that in the *Speculum juris*, which he dedicated to Adrian V at the time when this story had already been made public by our men, he judged that ‘the legal rule which forbids anyone to give testimony in his own case does not apply to Carthusians and Cistercians, because of their holiness.’

“While Durandus was writing this, Boso, prior of the Chartreuse, and Guillelmus of Hyporegia, a monk of the same house, were flourishing in the order; both, or at least one of them, mentioned this story in their writings, as we shall say shortly. Durandus would certainly not have believed that men whom he regarded as so worthy of trust had originated the account of this resurrection—or fiction, as our adversaries maintain—in order to proclaim the cradle of their order to the people with puffed cheeks on the basis of so extraordinary a miracle. The vanity of such an idea is plainly frivolous and childish: it was surely born first in the mouths of our slanderers, not conceived in the hearts of our own people.

“Even if this were a fable, or had some connection with a fable, the Carthusian religion would nevertheless be no less held in the Church of God, since everyone knows that it shines with distinguished prerogatives from other sources.”

Thus far our anonymous Carthusian, whose principal purpose is to maintain that the anonymous writer who first committed to writing the prodigious resurrection of the Parisian doctor and his public proclamation that he had been condemned, and inserted it into the Chronicle of the first five priors of the Chartreuse that he composed, flourished only sixty, or at most eighty, years after the death of Saint Bruno’s companions—that is, already around the year 1220—and received the story from their own disciples, and consequently from a genuine tradition, “not from the uncertain rumor of a credulous populace.”

344. The reasoning just transcribed, by which our anonymous Carthusian attempts to prove this, is presented by the author of an anonymous treatise on Saint Bruno, communicated to me by Carthusians of this region, with several additions. In doing so, while proposing to prove something later, he says: “As we shall say in its proper place in the Annals”; elsewhere he also cites these matters as though he were going to publish them. On this account, I thought that the following observation was appropriate: it may reasonably be doubted whether the Masson mentioned above, when writing the *Annals of his Order*, did not compose that treatise from which our anonymous Carthusian afterward transferred certain passages into Book IV of the *Annals of the Carthusians*, hitherto unpublished.

Whatever the case may be, so that I may not seem to have omitted anything that could in any way support the genuineness of the tradition concerning the Parisian miracle, I transcribe the author’s words here. They are as follows:

“From the foundation of the order until the time of Boso, who governed the houses of Saint Hugh and the Grande Chartreuse together with the entire order from the year 1272 to 1313, when he died in extreme old age, the Carthusians maintained profound silence in their cloisters. They did not permit anything to be made public either concerning the origin of their order or concerning the wonders that frequently occurred among them. Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, gives testimony to this and complains of it amicably: ‘I have learned from many people that many miracles occurred in that holy order; but they themselves, through the virtue of humility by which the servants of God always conceal their wonderful works with all possible effort, scarcely wished to disclose anything of them.’

“Boso would not have departed from the path of the Fathers had he not been compelled to violate the laws of this humble and holy silence, maintained for so long, in order to defend his institution against the slanders of certain religious belonging to another order. He published a very extensive treatise, either on his own initiative, as some maintain, or at his command, employing the pen of Guillelmus of Hyporegia, an Italian Carthusian and learned man whom he had summoned to the Grande Chartreuse about three years before his death.

345. “He entitled this treatise *On the Origin and Truth of Perfect Religion*, for the defense of the Carthusian order. He said nothing in it about the tragic end of the condemned man—for this question had not yet been raised at that time—but he wished to have appended to its end a Chronicle concerning the beginning of the Carthusian order, recounting this story. It had formerly been written by an author of uncertain name, but professed in the same order; for that reason we shall henceforth designate him by the name ‘the Anonymous.’

“We possessed from the Chartreuse of Mont-Dieu one manuscript of the treatise of Boso or Guillelmus of Hyporegia, containing the Chronicle of the aforementioned Anonymous. It was written at the beginning of the fourteenth century, that is, around the end of Boso’s administration, as we infer from its script. A very learned man, highly experienced in such scripts, whom we consulted in Paris through the intervention of a friend, agreed with us in this judgment.

“Since Boso professed our institution in the middle of the thirteenth century, there is no doubt that the author of the Anonymous Chronicle was slightly older than he. This can also be proved from a manuscript in the Colbert Library, in which a copy of the same Chronicle is found, transcribed before the middle of the thirteenth century. Étienne Baluze, a man distinguished for his learning and most zealous in deserving well of everyone, informed us of this by letter in the following words:

“‘In manuscript 3806 there is a certain table containing fifty-one chapters on the perfection and privileges of the Carthusian order. It is incomplete and begins with chapter XVI. That manuscript is 460 years old’—that is, it dates from around the year 1240. ‘It contains a chronicle on the origin of the Carthusian order’—so it is also entitled in our manuscript—‘up to the year 1137, when Guigo died. Bernard’s work on contemplation follows. It begins: “One day, when …”’

“It is probable that this copy was transcribed from the actual ‘original, which has now been lost,’ and was ‘brought from the Grande Chartreuse to Paris by one of the first Carthusians of the Parisian house, and afterward entered first the library of Thou and finally that of Colbert’” [Col. 0207B].

346. “Since this Anonymous wrote his Chronicle around or before 1240, he could have become a monk at the beginning of that century and therefore could have received this story from the elder Fathers who were then still alive. Among them were some who are known to have been disciples of Saint Bruno’s companions and, with him, founders of our institution. Such were Blessed Artaldus, who, while Saint Anthelmus governed the order, became prior of the house of Arvernia, then bishop of Belley, and finally, after resigning his episcopal insignia, prolonged his life until 1206, when he died in his cell at more than a hundred years of age; and Aynardus the lay brother, professed of the Grande Chartreuse, concerning whom marvelous things are related in the Life of Saint Hugh of Lincoln. There it is also said that he died in sound mind in the 126th year of his age, approximately four years after Saint Hugh, namely around 1204. This could scarcely be believed unless someone who knew him had affirmed it in writing, as we shall say in its proper place in the Annals.

“Among these may rightly be numbered the truly venerable old men Bovo, successor of Saint Hugh of Lincoln in the priory of Witham, although Jancelinus was much older in years spent in the order; Jancelinus governed the mother house of the Chartreuse and the entire order for nearly sixty years, shortly after Basilius, the successor of Saint Anthelmus. There was also Guifridus, a lay brother of the Chartreuse, who, being sixty years old in the order in 1212, testified in a certain letter that he had seen Brother Olmarus, who had become a lay brother in the time of the Great Guigo, and who had undoubtedly known some of the seven founders of the order.

“From these and certain other monks of equal trustworthiness and authority, our Anonymous—or rather, those who related the story to him, to Boso, and to Boso’s contemporaries—received this account, not from the uncertain rumor of a credulous populace or from the fables of certain recent writers, as Launoius charged.

347. “For from where, I ask, could that uncertain rumor at that time have spread through our cloisters? Should it not rather be said to have gradually spread far and wide from those same cloisters, and indeed from the pupils of the first Fathers themselves, men certainly most grave and holy? Guillielmus Durandus valued the credibility of these men and their successors so highly—a renowned author—that in the *Speculum juris*, which he dedicated to Adrian V at the time when the first writers of this story were flourishing, he judged that the legal rule forbidding anyone to give testimony in his own case did not apply to Carthusians and Cistercians because of their holiness.

“These men, whom Durandus considered so worthy of trust, would certainly not have persuaded themselves to initiate the account of this resurrection, if it were a fiction, as our adversaries maintain, in order to disseminate the origins of their order among the people with puffed cheeks on the basis of so extraordinary a miracle. Whether true or false, it could bring their religion no glory or disgrace, no benefit or harm, since their religion already shone abundantly with the distinguished prerogatives of piety [Col. 0208B]. Nor would they have believed, as Launoius reproaches them, that the history of Bruno was not sufficiently illustrious unless it were enhanced by that event.

“For if both they and their successors loved, as someone—namely Columbius, in his *Dissertation on the Beginnings of the Carthusians*, no. 20—observed on our behalf, to seek out and say things about Bruno that were illustrious and suited to excite the people’s admiration, they would certainly have made his Life far more illustrious and much better suited to hold the common people in wonder if they had attributed to Bruno and his companions the things we read about Paul, Antony, and other earlier monks or anchorites. But as men who loved truth and hated every fiction, they honestly related about Bruno what they had heard from the Fathers, in accordance with the saying of Moses: ‘Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you’” [Col. 0208C].

348. “Therefore, since our Anonymous copied this story from the mouths of narrators who knew Bruno’s companions, or at least had professed our institution before the thirteenth century—that is, during the first century of our order—it follows that this tradition did not lack the authority of written testimony for more than sixty or seventy years after the death of some of the authors of our order. Something similar is scarcely found in many traditions of the holy Church.

“For how many and how great were the matters—not to draw any comparison—which the Church believed, honored, preserved, and observed for one, two, three, or even more centuries, resting solely on tradition and not yet established in writing [Col. 0208D]? Hence its enemies had nothing, and still have nothing today, more at heart than to attack tradition itself. Launoius also used these weapons against us above all, as we shall see later.”

Thus far the cited anonymous author. The principal purpose of his entire argument, transcribed above, is to persuade us that the anonymous author of the Chronicle of the first five priors of the Chartreuse—the first among them to commit to writing the miracle of the Parisian doctor who, for a time, returned to life and loudly proclaimed in public that he had been condemned—derived or learned it from the actual disciples of Saint Bruno’s first companions, or at least from monks of the same institution who had heard it from them. The latter is apparently the only point intended by the author of the similarly transcribed reasoning in Book IV of the *Annals of the Carthusians*, hitherto unpublished.

Both men are not without reason in laboring to establish one or the other of these claims. For if either the anonymous author of the Chronicle of the first five priors of the Chartreuse, or those who narrated it to him, heard the grim story from the disciples of Saint Bruno’s companions, who would readily dare to pronounce it false? But who proves that the anonymous author of the Chronicle of the first five priors of the Chartreuse drew his account from so trustworthy a source?

349. “Since, then,” says the author of the treatise on Saint Bruno communicated to me by the Carthusian Fathers of this region, “this Anonymous”—namely, the writer of the Chronicle of the first five priors of the Chartreuse—“wrote his Chronicle around or before 1240, he could have become a monk at the beginning of that century and therefore could have received this story from the elder Fathers who were still alive at that time, among whom, as is established, were some disciples of Saint Bruno’s companions and, with him, founders of our institution.”

So he speaks. The anonymous author of Book IV of the *Annals of the Carthusians*, hitherto unpublished, does not differ greatly from him:

“He who first committed this story to writing among the Carthusians,” he says, “lived around the year 1220”; and later, after inserting several intervening remarks: “This first writer of the story had undoubtedly seen many monks who knew, or at least could have known, some of the disciples of the aforementioned seven leaders of the order; and we know that these disciples prolonged their lives beyond the year 1200 … It must therefore be clear that the aforementioned writer received this story from monks who had lived with these and other disciples of Saint Bruno’s companions.”

They therefore maintain that the author of the Chronicle of the first five priors of the Chartreuse was already living, or even already professed as a Carthusian, at the very time when some of Saint Bruno’s companions and their disciples were still alive; and that from these men he, or at least those who narrated the story to him, derived the mournful account.

But is there any independent evidence that the Anonymous who first committed the Parisian miracle to writing was then already alive, or even that he was already a Carthusian [Col. 0209D]? I showed in no. 12 and following that this writer probably did not begin writing before the year 1250. I had decided not to debate further the length of his life or the time when he began to live or to act as a monk. But since the two writers discussed here, as has just been said, want the Anonymous who first committed the Parisian miracle to writing to have been alive from the beginning of the thirteenth century, and consequently insist above all that he learned it either from Saint Bruno and his companions’ disciples or at least from those who had once lived with them, I now wish to examine whether they are assigning the Anonymous an excessively early date, or whether they in any way prove that he lived from the beginning of the thirteenth century.

350. The anonymous author of Book IV of the *Annals of the Carthusians*, hitherto unpublished, entirely agrees with us—see no. 12—that the Anonymous did not write his Chronicle around the year 1151, although he mentions the Chartulary existing at the Chartreuse, “near” whose “beginning the papal letters of Urban II and the instrument of Siguinus” are found—the latter and the former being quoted below. Yet, in order to prove that he was already living around the year 1220, he argues as follows:

“We conjecture that this man”—namely, the author of the Chronicle of the first five priors of the Chartreuse—“lived before the time of the Reverend Father Boso, who entered our order around the year 1260 and assumed the government of the Chartreuse in 1277. We establish this conjecture from the Chartularies that we now possess at the Chartreuse [Col. 0210B].

“There are two of them. One was made under the administration of the Reverend Father Franciscus a Puteo and under his direction in 1507. It contains two volumes, in the first of which, toward the end rather than near the beginning, as the cited Chronicle says, are the aforementioned letters of Urban II. The instrument of Siguinus is described earlier, but well after the middle. Hence it is clear that the author of the treatise did not have this Chartulary in mind. Indeed, the Thuane manuscript, which everyone can consult, although more recent than our manuscript, was written long before this Chartulary.

“The other Chartulary of the Chartreuse consisted of three volumes, the first of which was lost in the most recent fire, as the officials of the Chartreuse affirm to us with grief. The other two are still preserved, unharmed and completely intact, written in different hands. The earlier of these two, which was the second volume, bears the following title at the head of the index of the charters contained in it: ‘This volume contains the charters and letters of the house of the Chartreuse pertaining to the county of Savoy.’

351. “Then, at the top of the first folio, which contains the first instrument, dated only in the year 1303, we read: ‘Here begins the new Chartulary of the county.’ From the words ‘new Chartulary’ we understand that another, older one had existed, which also later perished. The second instrument in this volume is dated 1306. Many others then follow, concerning events occurring at various times from 1207 to 1326, with one exception, dated 1331, which is recorded on a separate folio.

“Since the charter with which this volume begins is dated 1303, while its most recent charter is from 1336, we rightly infer that the volume was compiled under the administration and care of Aymo, prior of the Chartreuse, who presided from 1313 to 1330—and indeed after that deplorable fire which occurred in 1320. Since the older Chartulary may have been consumed by its flames, the Reverend Father Aymo arranged for a new one to be copied.

“The other volume, which was the third, was also written by several hands, none of which, however, appears later in character than the script of the preceding volume. Hence we infer that it was begun under the same Aymo and continued under his successors until 1346, when the latest instrument in this volume was dated [Col. 0211A]. We also infer this from the following words placed at the head of the index:

“‘Let this Chartulary be bound in its entirety, with its covers, when it appears sufficiently substantial and complete; afterward let another be begun.’

“There follow bulls of the supreme pontiffs from Alexander IV through John XXII, inclusive. After them, instruments are copied in another hand. The first of these is dated 1300 and has the following heading: ‘Here begins the new Chartulary of the Dauphiné.’

352. “Finally, as in the earlier volume, charters and letters from 1215 to 1346 are inserted without distinction. In certain transcribed copies there are also some earlier documents, such as the letters of Saint Hugh of Grenoble [Col. 0211B] and others. But neither of the two volumes contains the bulls of Urban II or the instrument of Abbot Siguinus.

“There is therefore no doubt that the first volume of this same Chartulary, which is now missing, was copied under the direction of the same Reverend Father Aymo. Had it still existed, it might perhaps contain the aforementioned bulls and the instrument of Siguinus, although this is not established. But even if we granted that point, it would not follow that it was the same volume of which our anonymous author speaks. Indeed, since we have seen that the two following volumes were called ‘new,’ it follows that this first volume too was recent at that time. Accordingly, it was different from the one which we believe was devoured by the fire of 1320.

“But all this doubt is removed by the treatise of the Reverend Father Boso, *On the Origin and Truth of Perfect Religion*, in which the entire Chronicle of our Anonymous concerning the beginning of the Carthusian order is inserted. Since Boso governed the houses of the Valley of Saint Hugh and the Grande Chartreuse from 1272 until 1313, when he died, it is clear that the Chartulary cited in the aforementioned Chronicle was written before Boso’s time. It therefore follows that the author himself was already flourishing before 1272. When we assign the time of his life to around 1220, we do not think that this exposes us to any reproach, since he may also have lived several years earlier and may even have seen that blessed old man Jancelinus, prior of the Chartreuse, as well as many other monks who were disciples of the disciples of Saint Bruno or even of his companions.”

Thus speaks our anonymous Carthusian annalist, also indicating in more than one place in his work that the anonymous chronicler whom he here places among the living from around 1220 or even earlier composed, in that same year or earlier, his work concerning the first five priors of the Chartreuse. But in the entire argument transcribed above there is absolutely nothing that proves that this anonymous chronicler, the author of the Chronicle of the first five priors of the Chartreuse, was already alive in that year, or that, if he was, he composed his Chronicle.

### 353

Suppose, then, that the Chartulary which he mentions as having at its head the letters of Pope Urban II and the instrument of Abbot Siguin was not the one that was written, under the direction of Aymo, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, after the year 1320, but another and older one, which V. G. had already composed from the year 1120—or, if you prefer, even earlier. Would it follow from this that the anonymous chronicler who cited it was already alive from that same year, or that he had composed his work then? Since the older Chartulary, which contained the letters of Urban II and the instrument of Abbot Siguin, may perhaps have been consumed by the flames only in the year 1320, when the fire occurred at the Chartreuse—or at any rate there is no certainty that it perished earlier—why could not the anonymous chronicler, even if he did not take up his pen until as late as 1290 or somewhat later, have cited it?

Nor does it advance the argument that our anonymous Carthusian—compare the words quoted immediately above—adds that Boso presided over the houses of the Valley of Saint Hugh and of the Grande Chartreuse from 1272 until 1313. For even if the Chartulary praised by the anonymous author in his Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Chartreuse was in fact written before Boso’s time, it still would not follow that this anonymous writer flourished before that time, or before 1272, and composed his work then. Why could he not, even if he wrote long after that year, have cited a Chartulary completed much earlier? Moreover, from the fact that Boso inserted into the treatise composed either by himself or at his command—the work entitled *On the Origin and Truth of Perfect Religion*—the entire Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Chartreuse, it by no means follows that its anonymous author wrote it before 1272.

### 354

For Boso, as the author of the treatise on Saint Bruno communicated to me by the Carthusians of this place teaches in the words just transcribed, either wrote the treatise mentioned above himself, or had it written, only three years before his death, which occurred in 1313. Nothing, however, prevents the Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Chartreuse from having been inserted into it even though its author had composed it only ten years, or fewer, earlier. Thus none of all the evidence brought forward in the immediately preceding words by the anonymous author of the fourth book of the Carthusian Annals proves at all that this work was composed about the year 1220, or even earlier. Indeed, it does not in any way follow from that evidence that the anonymous author of the same work had already begun to live among the living from that same year 1220, or earlier.

But the anonymous author of the treatise on Saint Bruno communicated to me by the Carthusians of this place takes another route in attempting to prove that the anonymous author of the Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Chartreuse had lived from about 1220, indeed that he had already professed as a Carthusian, and therefore that he could have understood—or actually did understand—from disciples of Saint Bruno’s companions, or at least from others who had heard the matter from them, what he records concerning the miraculous resurrection of the Parisian doctor. He therefore says that the Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Chartreuse was written not as early as 1220, but at least around 1240, and consequently that its author had not merely been alive from 1220 onward but had also professed as a Carthusian.

But does this establish the matter in any way? Stephen Baluze explained, in a letter addressed to the Carthusians, that the copy of that Chronicle preserved in the Colbert Library had been written four hundred and fifty years earlier; and since the letter was written in the previous century, when it was already nearing its end, this would place its composition around 1240. Such, in substance, is what the anonymous author of the treatise on Saint Bruno communicated to me by the Carthusians of this place, whom I have just cited, says.

### 355

But how did Baluze discover that the said copy of the Chronicle was of such great antiquity? The distinguished man ought surely to have added that, if he wished to make his testimony credible on this point. I suppose that he derived the great antiquity he asserts solely from the characters in which that copy of the Chronicle was written. Yet although the century in which ancient monuments were written can to some extent be determined from the characters used in them, who could thereby determine with sufficient certainty even the approximate year in which they were written?

Whatever, then, may have been the judgment of Stephen Baluze concerning the date at which the copy of the Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Chartreuse preserved in the Colbert Library was written, I remain as doubtful as before whether that Chronicle might not have been written thirty or even forty years later than he states. Nor does the doubt disappear because, as the Carthusian just cited teaches in number 24 of his work, the Chartulary of the Grande Chartreuse, which is cited in the Chronicle under discussion, was probably completed around 1240. Why could it not have been cited by the author of the Chronicle, writing only much later—or even thirty or forty years later?

Now, since all these things are so, and it is consequently doubtful whether the anonymous author of the Chronicle of the First Five Priors of the Chartreuse did not first begin to flourish only when one or two decades beyond the middle of the thirteenth century had already passed, it must likewise be doubtful whether he could have seen the disciples of Saint Bruno’s first companions, and others who immediately followed them in the Carthusian institution, and learned from them what, as is commonly believed, the first of all committed to writing concerning the miraculous resurrection of the Parisian doctor.

### 356

From this it further follows that it must be questioned whether the dreadful account of the condemned doctor was transmitted to posterity by a true tradition—whether from Saint Bruno himself and his first companions, contemporaries of the event, by word of mouth or in some other manner—and then passed from them to the Carthusians of a later age, and finally reached the anonymous writer who was the first of all to consign it to writing.

Since this is so, the Parisian prodigy must be regarded as insufficiently probable, especially because of the universal silence about it among all the ancient writers. Among these, as I have already shown above, there are probably some who, if it had happened, would have known of it and would have mentioned it as known to them.

This, then, is how the matter stands if it is held that the chronicler of the First Five Priors of the Chartreuse had not been alive from about 1220, still less that he had lived as a Carthusian. Nor would the matter stand otherwise even if we were for the moment to grant that he had already been alive then and had professed as a Carthusian. For although the two anonymous writers rightly teach in the words quoted immediately above that, if he had been a Carthusian from about 1220 onward, he could have learned the dreadful account of the condemned doctor from the disciples of Saint Bruno’s companions, or certainly from those to whom they had related it, they do not at all prove that this actually happened.

Their words rather indicate that the chronicler in question should be thought to have learned the matter from those persons rather than from the uncertain rumor of the credulous common people. But, apart from the fact that they do not establish even this by any argument, the contrary seems more likely: first, because he does not say from whom he derived his account, although, if he had drawn it from so trustworthy a source, he would probably have said so, as I showed in number 329; and secondly, because, when relating the Parisian prodigy, he says, “It is said that such a prodigy occurred there”—that is, at Paris—and thus speaks of the dreadful story in the manner of one who is uncertain rather than one who is affirming it. Yet if it had been reported to him either by the disciples of Saint Bruno’s companions or by those who had heard it from them, he would probably not have been doubtful about it.

### 357

Furthermore, even if the anonymous chronicler of the First Five Priors of the Chartreuse is held to have lived from about 1220 onward, he was still approximately one hundred and forty years removed from the Parisian prodigy. Now, although it sometimes happens that events reported by non-contemporary writers must be believed to have reached them through a true tradition, this can scarcely be the case when—as here—the events related are of such a kind that, had they occurred, they would probably have been mentioned even by contemporary writers, yet are found mentioned by none of them.

Nor does what the author of the treatise communicated to me by the Carthusians of this place adds about the traditions of the Church advance the argument. For when he says that what was received through such traditions had long been believed, honored, and observed in the Church, indeed for one, two, three, or even more centuries, he is plainly speaking of divine and apostolic traditions. “But just as nothing,” in the words of our Papebrochius in his *Responses to the Exhibition of Errors*, article 19, number XI, “is received as a divine and apostolic tradition if it is not proved from the holy Fathers to have been observed in the universal Church in their own age as something handed down from the beginning, so we do not prudently admit as human traditions those alleged to be such which either conflict with more certain authorities or could not have remained untouched by the ancients at some point if they were true.”

“But,” you will say, “if the Parisian prodigy was not received through a true tradition, how could the uncertain rumor, as Launoy wishes, have arisen in the Carthusian cloisters? Did they perhaps invent it?” This is nearly what the two anonymous Carthusians cited above also say.

Yet even if it is held that the anonymous chronicler of the First Five Priors of the Chartreuse did not learn the matter through a true tradition, it does not follow that he received it either from an uncertain rumor or from inventions of the ancient Carthusians. For what if the dreadful story of the condemned man occurred not publicly but within the private residence of the deceased, in the presence of only a few people, and was then corrupted over the passage of time in its details, without any invention intervening? That this could indeed have happened will become clear from what follows below, as will the manner in which it might have happened.

## XXI. Other considerations favorable to the prodigy in which the Parisian doctor publicly declared from his bier, before the assembled crowd, that he had been condemned; and an examination of whether the event can ultimately be rendered at all probable by these considerations

Since some of the funeral titles with which various churches and monasteries honored our Saint seem plainly to indicate that he withdrew into the desert from fear of divine judgments and of hell, the anonymous author of the treatise on Saint Bruno communicated to me by the Carthusians of this place conjectures that those titles allude to the mournful history of the condemned doctor. If, however, the stated titles really allude to that dreadful event, it follows that the event not only occurred but occurred publicly, since otherwise the churches and monasteries to which the titles belong would not have known of it.

Therefore, so as not to pass over unnoticed anything that may in any way seem favorable to the Parisian prodigy, I transcribe here the words of the anonymous author just mentioned, which contain the conjecture in question, together with the funeral titles on which he bases it; afterward I shall add my own opinion on the matter. They are as follows:

“The true cause of his—namely, Saint Bruno’s—withdrawal into the desert could not have been known so particularly by anyone as by the canons of the Church of Saint Mary of Reims, in which the Saint had once served as a canon. In their Title, which is number 54 among those to be published, they suggest it as follows:

> Fearing the judgment of the Judge who is to come,  
> Bruno despised worldly wealth and sought the desert;  
> There he brought forth sweet fruit of fragrance,  
> Calling back to Christ those whom vain glory had deceived.

### 359

“Radulphus Green, who enjoyed the dignity of provost in that church, perhaps alludes tacitly in these words to the invitation by which Bruno had shortly before been urged, in a letter, to assume the monastic habit as a fulfillment of his vow. He says:

> Calling back to Christ those whom vain glory had deceived.

“The particular church of Saint Bartholomew on Mont-Or, not far from the same city, supports the Church of Reims. Its eulogy, number 65 among the funeral Titles to be published, is entirely concerned with fear of death and hell, by which Bruno is said to have been terrified into entering the desert:

> The world, growing bitter, was weighed down and became lame beneath the burden of death,  
> And through the byways of human destiny it drags what is made visible.  
> Everything, wasting away, sinks into exile from its own nature;  
> Why, miserable man, do you swell with pride in this age that grows old?  
> You are plunged into the Charybdean spring toward the final limit;  
> And you will be dissolved as ashes into ashes, like the shadow of lamps.  
> His labor is love, and his error cannot be disentangled;  
> Through its failure, horror embraces the soul,  
> After it has been stripped from the prison of the flesh  
> Or surrounded here by the ranks led by Satan.  
> Fearing this, courageous Bruno, in this peril,  
> Entered the desert of combat in a single-minded service;  
> He abandoned wealth and the world’s splendor, lest glory  
> Become punishment unto destruction, and so forth.

### 360

“Something similar is sung by the canons of the principal Church of Paris, who honored their friend Bruno with a funeral Title—number 109 among those to be reprinted:

> O you worldly men, who rejoice in a vain thing,  
> Despise the cultivation of the flesh, which will suddenly perish.  
> For the vast body, fed on varied fatness,  
> The more it is filled, the more putrid it will become.  
> Why is the flesh fattened, when worms are fed by it?  
> Why do we desire so greatly goods that we cannot retain?  
> The world leads astray those whom it misguides,  
> And deceives the followers of the flesh through honors;  
> It offers flattering things while spreading nets for us.  
> In this world, too, worldly people are beset by anxiety,  
> And punishment earns punishment: the flesh is tortured twice.  
> Those who pursue profits are hurled down by sudden death,  
> And their flesh and souls enter the cavern of the abyss.  
> Bruno, having carefully pondered these things, suddenly—  
> He, the glory of teachers and the pattern of morals,  
> The chief helmsman of the Reims crowd in the great city—  
> Despised the world and turned his journey toward heavenly things;  
> Clothed in humble rags, he followed you, Christ.  
> Therefore may heaven be opened to him, and may he be joined  
> To the faithful people with whom Bruno rejoices forever.

### 361

“The monks of Saint-Germain in the same city—that is, Paris—also testify, in funeral Title number 26, that Bruno was terrified by the remembrance of the Last Judgment:

> The light in which the wicked will receive evil and the just good  
> Should always be held in our minds.

“Bruno, the true lover of wisdom, feared this.

“From these and certain other titles, which indicate similar things, we may not unreasonably conjecture that Bruno’s friends implicitly alluded in them to the spectacle of the man who returned to life, but did not clearly designate the story, lest they should seem to violate the reputation of him and of his relatives. We admit that the same things could be said of anyone else bidding farewell to the world whose reason for conversion was concealed; but since it was always accepted among all Carthusians that Bruno renounced the world after being shaken by the dreadful judgment of the condemned master, a weighty conjecture is thereby drawn that the same judgment is contained in the words of the titles mentioned above.

“For why did his dearest friends, who knew perfectly what the cause of his conversion had been, bring forward no reason other than fear of death, judgment, and hell? Why did they say nothing of Manasses’ accusations against the simoniac, or of his wicked character, if these were what drove Bruno into the desert, as Launoy necessarily wishes to infer from Guibert?”

Thus far the anonymous author. Since he admits that everything contained in the funeral Titles transcribed above and in others of the same kind is such that it could be said of anyone who bade farewell to the world, he plainly acknowledges that the conjecture he has formed from them possesses little force. In this matter we must indeed agree with him, as will be evident to anyone who considers it. Let us now proceed to other arguments that in some way appear to support the miraculous resurrection of the doctor.

### 362

In his didactic Letter, cited more than once above and published at Cologne in 1645, Saussaye also invokes, in support of the Parisian prodigy, images and the celebrated painting of the Paris Charterhouse, which represent the dreadful history of the condemned doctor.

First, concerning this argument, he writes on page 22:

“Figures and images were also present, by which that fatal spectacle was represented. They had been depicted in the little books of sacred prayers which they call the Hours, and even in certain Breviaries and Missals, not only of this diocese—that is, the Parisian diocese—but also of several others.”

Then, on the same page 22, he says:

“Moreover, we were shown that celebrated painting which can still be seen in the cloister of the monastery of the Carthusian Fathers of this city—that is, Paris—in the part nearer to the church. It portrays the sequence of the life of this wretched man, his fatal end, his dreadful condemnation publicly declared by him in the church after death, and the terrible catastrophe of his corpse being cast into an unconsecrated place.”

So much for Saussaye. Launoy responds to the latter point in his *Dissertation on the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Desert* as follows:

“This painting has no more authority than the books from which it derives its origin. It does not exceed in date the period represented by its subject, but follows it by a long interval. It was drawn, as it appeared recently to have been written above the gate leading from the smaller cloister to the larger, around the year 1582—recently, I say, when, as the previous year was passing, that celebrated painting had partly been destroyed and was partly hidden by new structures attached to the walls, arranged in arches, some of stone and some of wood.”

### 363

“The recent date of the image was also clearly established by the form of the cap with which Bruno was shown covered as he instructed his hearers here and there. For this head-covering, which in the old books of the university was both called and was a round *birretum*, began around 1520 to be fashioned differently and to end in a square, hornlike shape. Such was the cap, or *birretum*, the insignia of the master’s degree, with which, as we have said, Bruno’s head was covered.

“As for the man who painted the prodigy, and the brothers who had it painted, I think that they believed the event had happened as they depicted it; but they were deceived by those who supplied the subject of the false thing to be painted.”

To the earlier point he replies:

“We have also seen many books of this kind in which nothing of the sort appeared. Anyone who wishes may conjecture why these figures and images were painted in some books of Paris and other dioceses but not in others. We, however, believe the author—namely, Saussaye. But these figures and images are of no importance, since they are supported only by the authors whom we have rejected. We would embrace as witnesses of the truth those images that had been painted in Bruno’s time.”

Thus Launoy; and certainly with complete justification:

“For from paintings and images,” as he later states in the conclusion of chapter 3 of his *Dissertation*, “no sound argument can be drawn until the time when they were produced has been established with certainty. The reason is that, as he also adds in the same place, painters ordinarily form their images according to the model of things commonly believed or practiced in their own time. Thus, if we suppose an image to have been painted one or two hundred years ago, it will follow that the event represented in it was then commonly believed or was thought to have taken place in that manner.”

Accordingly, the images and paintings that represent the event cannot establish belief in the Parisian prodigy—whether the images and paintings of the fourteenth century mentioned here in number 220, or the panels prefixed to the statutes and customs of the Carthusian Order printed at Basel in 1510. These show only that the dreadful story was believed both in the fourteenth century and in 1510; it by no means follows that the event ever actually occurred. But enough has been said about the paintings and images representing the mournful event.

### 364

In the same Letter, page 22, Saussaye says, in proof of the horrible story, that it became more probable to him because, as he had learned, in the Parisian Office of the Dead the beginning of the fourth Lesson, “Answer me,” had at some time been deleted. He says that the miserable deceased man had answered the cleric who customarily pronounced these words in the Office for the Dead:

“By the just judgment of God I have been accused, then judged, and finally condemned.”

But I have already shown above that in the Parisian Office of the Dead in the time of our Saint there were probably either no Lessons recited at all, or that the Lessons which were recited—and from which, consequently, one of them might have begun with the words “Answer me”—were not taken from the Book of Job.

Since this is so, it is certainly very doubtful, to say nothing more, whether those who reported to Saussaye that the words “Answer me” had once been removed from the fourth Lesson of the Parisian Office of the Dead for the reason expressed in the words just quoted were telling the truth. See what Launoy supplies on this subject in his *Dissertation on the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Desert*, to which, on this point, I find no one has offered a contradiction.

Here is yet another argument brought forward in support of the Parisian prodigy. It is said that in the Parisian church dedicated to the Most Holy Mother of God there is a chapel called the Chapel of the Condemned Man, having supposedly acquired this name from the condemned man—whether canon or doctor—who, in that church, publicly proclaimed before an almost innumerable multitude of people that he had been accused, judged, and finally condemned by the just judgment of God.

But Robert of Torigni, in the Appendix to Sigebert under the year 1177, teaches that the Parisian church of Saint Mary that now exists had not yet been built in the time of Saint Bruno. He writes:

“Maurice, bishop of Paris, has for a long time been laboring and making progress in the construction of the aforesaid church of the city of Paris. Its main structure is already complete, except for the principal roofing. If this work is completed, there will be no work this side of the mountains that can plainly be compared with it.”

### 365

“But,” they say, “at the place where Bishop Maurice built the Parisian church of Saint Mary, another church had previously existed, containing the Chapel of the Condemned Man, and this chapel was retained and preserved in the new building.”

“Certainly,” Launoy says ironically in the passage just cited, “for the everlasting remembrance of so great an event, so that the name of the man who had been denied the honor of burial might be ennobled by such a basilica. Far from being consigned to perpetual obscurity, the man whom the Parisian clergy had ordered to depart for Morbonia (*Morboniam*) was thereby commemorated forever. Those who do not distinguish truth from falsehood are driven, whether they wish it or not, into these straits.”

So he speaks, again clearly suggesting that the mournful story of the condemned man must unquestionably be counted among fables.

And indeed, as I have already shown above, even if it is not certainly a fable or invention, the story appears quite improbable; nor can anything be added to its probability by the chapel called the Chapel of the Condemned Man.

For what if it was called this by the people, who mistakenly believed that the dreadful story, although it had never occurred, had nevertheless taken place in the church mentioned above? What if it acquired that name from an image or representation there of a condemned man—not of the man who had publicly declared his condemnation in that place, but of someone else? What if, from this as well, the passage of time gave rise among the people to the erroneous belief that a canon or doctor had publicly proclaimed in that same church that he had been condemned?

However the matter may stand, the chapel in the Parisian church could certainly have received its name for more than one reason. Consequently, no strong argument can be drawn from it in favor of the mournful history of the condemned doctor.

These, then, are the principal arguments favoring the Parisian prodigy that I have found in addition to those already mentioned. As is clear from what has been said, they contribute either nothing or at least very little toward establishing it. I omit other arguments of still lesser force, lest I make the discussion entirely useless and superfluous.

### 366

For this reason I had initially decided not to mention here, or above, the foundation-charters of the Chartreuse dated 1084, nor the Grandmont codex written in 1115. I had been persuaded by the words of our Papebrochius transcribed here in number 196 that Polycarp de la Rivière, a member of the Carthusian Order, had cited both the latter and the former in bad faith, or at least improperly, in support of the Parisian prodigy, just as he had cited certain other items that therefore need not be mentioned here.

But since I now understand that it is possible that the two monuments were cited by that Carthusian writer neither in bad faith nor improperly in his work entitled *Angelica*, published at Lyon in 1626, and since the arguments advanced by Theophilus Raynaud in the *Hercules Commodianus* seem to suggest this, I wish, before bringing the examination of the Parisian prodigy to an end, to place those arguments before the reader and examine their weight.

Raynaud, therefore, in the work cited, series 2, question 3, in order to show that Polycarp de la Rivière had not cited in bad faith the charter of the foundation of the Chartreuse in which the Parisian prodigy was mentioned, writes as follows:

“The most excellent and religious Father Justus Perrot of Paris, who shortly before had been promoted from being a scribe of the Chartreuse to become its General and had died with the greatest holiness, confirmed that he had seen that charter—the charter, namely, of the foundation of the Chartreuse—written not by a recent hand but by a very ancient one, and containing at the beginning of the book the prodigy of the condemned doctor.

“Nor am I the only one asserting this. I was honored by the conversation and kindness of that Nestor when he graciously summoned me to the Chartreuse. The same thing, received from his own mouth, has been attested to me not once but repeatedly by Dom Chrysanthus Paulinus, prior of the Valley of Benediction near Avignon, a man who by his merit and the prerogative of his antiquity must be counted among the principal fathers of the Carthusian Order. Many other survivors also testify to it, so that there can be no room for doubt except through sheer obstinacy.”

### 367

So much for Raynaud. From this evidence it appears to me sufficiently probable that Polycarp did not cite the charter of the foundation of the Chartreuse in bad faith in support of the Parisian prodigy.

But what if both this writer and Justus Perrot, whom Raynaud cites, mistakenly thought that the charter contained something that in fact it did not? The following words of our anonymous Carthusian, transcribed above in number 206, show us how—or rather, the way in which—this could have happened:

“Among the books written by Aymar Savelli, a professed member of the Grande Chartreuse, there is still one, written in 1455, in which our story—that of the condemned doctor—is expressed in precisely the same words in which it appears in our old anonymous author, with the following title at the beginning: ‘How the Carthusian Order Had Its Origin.’ Immediately after the story has been narrated, the letters of the foundation of the Chartreuse from the year 1084 follow.

“From this we think that the error of Dom Polycarp de la Rivière arose when, among the authors who mention this kind of prodigy, he listed those same letters. For this reason Launoy appears to have attacked him somewhat too sharply as a man of bad faith in writing.”

Whatever, therefore, the Carthusian General of the Order, Perrot, may have affirmed concerning the charter of the foundation of the Chartreuse in which he found a mention of the Parisian prodigy, he most probably made that assertion only because he had fallen into the error, in the manner explained here by this anonymous Carthusian author. Consequently, although Polycarp perhaps did not act in bad faith, he nevertheless cited that monument improperly or without justification as evidence for the mournful story, since it did not mention the story. Our anonymous Carthusian himself candidly acknowledges this here.

Nor should you reply here with Raynaud that the charter of the foundation of the Chartreuse was distinct from the charter of its donation, and that the prodigy was mentioned not in the latter charter, which still exists, but in the former, which perished in the burning of the Chartreuse. For that a charter of the foundation once existed that was distinct from the charter of the donation of the Chartreuse appears neither probable nor capable of proof by any argument.

### 368

As for the Grandmont codex, which Polycarp likewise cited in support of the doctor’s miraculous resurrection, Raynaud attempts to weaken the authority of Launoy, who asserted that what was written in that codex or Chronicle concerning the prodigy had been written by a later—or indeed very recent—hand.

But I think Launoy should be believed when he makes this assertion after inspecting the codex with his own eyes. I think so both because the evidence Raynaud adduces is not of great force and because Columbi, in his *Dissertation on the Beginnings of the Carthusians*, does not cite the Grandmont Chronicle in support of the doctor’s miraculous resurrection. If Launoy’s statements had not been true, Columbi would undoubtedly have cited it; by failing to do so, he tacitly acknowledges Polycarp’s bad faith in citing that monument, as our Papebrochius observed before me in the words transcribed here in number 196.

Moreover, Polycarp’s bad faith in citing several other monuments is established, so that for this reason too it becomes extremely likely that he acted in bad faith when citing the Grandmont Chronicle.

Now, since the matter stands as has been said with regard to this monument and the charter of the foundation of the Chartreuse, the Parisian prodigy cannot be made certain either from the one or from the other.

Nor, as a kind of conclusion that I wish still to note here, did the Carthusian author of the fourth book of his Order’s Annals, which has not yet been published, himself regard the dreadful story as altogether certain if it is held to have occurred publicly.

### 369

For in number 127 of his work he speaks as follows:

“Why, then, should faith be denied our anonymous author”—namely, the author of the Chronicle of the Priors of the Chartreuse, who writes that the mournful event occurred publicly—“does not seem clear.”

Then, without inserting any other words at all, he immediately adds in the following number:

“We say and request not divine faith but human faith, or rather the piety of faith. For we admit that the truth of this spectacle is not a matter of faith; therefore it makes no difference whether it is accepted or not. Nevertheless, we do not think that sensible readers can deny it a place among those truths which, without injury to the faith, may obtain some credibility among devout people.

“Of these truths John Gerson, a man equally pious and learned, speaks in his *Declaration of the Truths That Must Be Believed as Necessary for Salvation*:

‘Finally, in the sixth degree—which is the fourth in the arrangement just mentioned—are placed those truths which serve only to nourish or foster religious devotion. They are introduced more to inflame the affections than to instruct the intellect, where devout piety is regarded more than certain truth,’ and so forth.”

These words of Gerson neither undermine nor condemn as false, nor accuse of falsehood, our account of the condemned man. Indeed, who does not see that it can most appropriately be placed among “those truths which serve only to nourish or foster religious devotion”? And although in such truths “devout piety is regarded more than certain truth,” nevertheless the most pious doctor calls them “truths” and places them, in the sixth degree, among “truths to be believed.”

What could have been said more suitably to confirm and establish the truth of our account? We experience every day how greatly it “serves to nourish or foster religious devotion,” since many people “do not disdain to see in it both devout piety and truth.”

370. “Nevertheless, Gerson, no less prudent than religious, lest he should seem to neglect the truth under the guise of ‘devout piety,’ immediately added a qualification to the words cited above, saying: ‘In this one case it is disapproved, if there were rashness of assertion before the truth had been elucidated in another way by the Church or by certain reason’ [Col. 0222C]. That is, if something were rashly asserted about whose truth there was such doubt, and which was so doubtful that it deserved to be elucidated ‘by the Church or by certain reason.’ But in the truth asserted concerning the condemned man there is no ‘rashness of assertion’; nor did Gerson himself believe that there was any rashness in it, when later he proposed this ‘one famous example,’ as he himself puts it, ‘out of very many,’ in order to inspire ‘those who are exercised’ with fear of the Lord and ‘to nourish or foster religious devotion.’ Nor was it necessary that this be elucidated by ‘the Church or certain reason,’ since it was sufficiently clear; and for that reason Gerson called it ‘famous,’ as having been received and approved without contradiction from the institution of the Order—although, in view of what was said above, this is highly doubtful.

“So many authors asserted it; no one condemned it; and until now the whole Christian people has lent an ear to it. The entire Carthusian Order, although the matter bears only very remotely upon his praise, for six hundred years—again, in view of what was said above, this is very doubtful—has steadfastly, perseveringly, and unanimously believed and believes to this day that it is certain and true, with only Launoy opposing it. Finally, the supreme pontiffs approved it: both Gregory XV and Urban VIII openly approved its inclusion in the Office of Saint [Col. 0223A] Bruno, although afterward the Sacred Congregation of Rites judged that it should be removed from the Breviary lessons together with the profession of faith issued by Saint Bruno as he breathed forth his soul—not for any other reason than that the two pieces, once combined, had become excessively long, as the most learned censors later explained when those responsible for the removal raised the matter.”

371. “And indeed, if it had then been removed from the Breviary as something fabulous, why was it afterward restored to other Breviaries newly published in the years 1648 and 1652? Why do learned men daily confirm, in their own handwriting, the Legends of the saints, in which the Life of Saint Bruno is described together with the account of the same spectacle? They certainly act in this way, and the Sacred Congregation of Rites permits it, because nothing contrary to the faith is found in this account. In accordance with this, the same Master Gerson judged in the passage cited that the Lives of the Saints belong to the sixth degree of truths to be believed. ‘This degree,’ he says, ‘concerns the Legends and miracles of the Saints, the Lives of the Fathers, visions of devout persons, and the reports and opinions of sacred doctors. The Church accepts all these and permits them to be read—not because it determines that such things must be believed as necessary for salvation, but because they help to move the pious affections of the faithful and to edify them, provided that in such matters nothing is known with certainty to be false, even though it is not known with certainty to be true.’

“These are Gerson’s words. Having said above, in general, that ‘those truths which serve only to nourish and foster religious devotion’ are to be placed ‘in the sixth degree,’ he here declares specifically what those truths are: ‘Legends,’ namely, and so forth; the miracles of the Saints, the Lives of the Fathers, visions, and the like. All these are placed among truths, recognized as such, and judged as such by the Church, which permits them to be read, though it compels no one to believe them as it compels belief in the Bible. It permits them to be read by neither prohibiting them nor commanding that they be believed to be true. Indeed, it permits them to be read ‘because,’ as Gerson says, ‘they help to move the pious affections of the faithful and to edify them.’ And this is permitted with the condition ‘that in such matters nothing is known with certainty to be false, even though it is not known with certainty to be true’” [Col. 0223B–D].

372. “Therefore, in accordance with the statement of Master Gerson, the Church permits the Lives and miracles of the Saints, as well as visions and miracles of this kind, to be read and places them among truths—that is, it judges them to be true and not false—although ‘it does not determine that such things must be believed as necessary for salvation, provided that in such matters nothing is known with certainty to be false.’ Now this miracle, or remarkable event, concerning the condemned man belongs to the Legend of Saint Bruno, and in it ‘nothing is known with certainty to be false, even though it is not known with certainty to be true. Therefore, according to Master Gerson’s rule, received by the Church, it must be placed among truths.’”

Thus far our anonymous Carthusian, asking that scarcely anything more be attributed to the Parisian prodigy than we attribute to it. For he asks only that it be placed among those truths which are truths in name only, and which apply solely to things or assertions that are neither certainly true nor certainly false. In this respect, there is complete agreement between our Carthusian and ourselves: we likewise assert that the extraordinary story is neither certainly true nor, contrary to what Launoy infers from the foregoing, certainly false.

But there is also this difference between us and the same Carthusian: he must regard the mournful event as at least probable, since he affirms that it was judged true by the Church—although this is not in fact the case—and that for six hundred years [Col. 0224A] up to his own time it was steadfastly, perseveringly, and unanimously believed certain and true by the whole Carthusian Order. We, however, regard the same event as scarcely probable, or, to put it more strongly, as probably false, if indeed it occurred publicly before an almost innumerable multitude of people, as the opinion we have been examining maintains.

Moreover, it must be carefully noted against our anonymous Carthusian that the Church, by permitting the Lives, Miracles, and so forth of the Saints to be read, does not thereby judge them to be true. Let us now consider what should be thought of this mournful story according to the opinion of those who maintain that it occurred within the private walls of the dead man’s house, in the presence of only a few of his friends—including Saint Bruno and several of his companions—and not on three different days, but on one and the same day.

§ XXII. The opinion that the prodigy of the condemned man occurred within the dead man’s private house in the presence of a few persons is presented, and it is examined whether it should be rejected as foolish and recently invented.

Our anonymous Carthusian does not, on the basis of what has now been said, regard the condemned doctor’s prodigy as certainly consonant with truth if it is asserted to have occurred publicly. But if it is maintained that it happened not publicly but within the dead man’s private house and in the presence of only a few persons, he appears to regard it as undoubtedly consonant with truth. In this case, after omitting and cutting away the various circumstances found in other writers, which greatly impair its probability according to what has already been said, he proposes that the mournful story be conceived as follows [Col. 0224B–D]:

“In the year 1082, a certain man of distinguished learning and probity of life, as appeared from outward indications, died at Paris. While he lay at home awaiting transport to the church, and his friends were offering prayers for the repose of his soul, he raised his head from the bier and, in a terrible voice repeated three times, declared that he had been accused, judged, and finally condemned by the just judgment of God. On hearing this, Master Bruno, who was then present, was terrified and moved to compunction. Taking companions to himself, some of whom had witnessed the spectacle, he persuaded them by his pious exhortations to flee the world and withdrew to the wilderness of Chartreuse in the year 1084.”

He immediately adds:

“Once the matter is considered in this way, there is surely no reason to wonder at the silence of contemporary authors, who make no mention of this story [Col. 0225A]. Nor can we be reproached as though we were inventing a new account of this prodigy, since we put forward nothing that is not found written in older authors. For all agree that a learned man, although he had apparently lived and died piously, raised his head three times after being placed in the bier and, with three cries, announced to those present in amazement that he had been condemned.

374. “Some report that such a spectacle took place not in the church but in the hall of the dead man’s house. Some say that the threefold voice returned not on three days but on the same day, at the same time as the recitation of the Office. Others relate that friends, not a multitude of people, were present, among them Bruno and some of his companions, who afterward withdrew from the world with him” [Col. 0225B].

These are the words of our anonymous Carthusian. In this matter, however, he had already been preceded by the aforementioned Innocent Le Masson, who writes as follows in book I, chapter 1, section 3 and following of his *Annals of his Order*:

“Concerning that story of the doctor commonly called ‘the condemned,’ considerable difficulties have arisen among critics. Some assert that it is most true; others place it almost among old women’s tales; while others say that the story is true in substance but was enlarged by various circumstances not unlike fables. Among these circumstances, the one most commonly listed is that the deliberation concerning the condition of the dead man was deferred for three different days, so that it might be determined by the lifeless mouth of the corpse crying out, while meanwhile, at the appropriate hour, the funeral ceremonies and prayers for the dead instituted by the Church were repeated. As the rumor spread throughout the whole city, everyone could freely come to see the spectacle, as though, in accordance with an agreement, God were supposed to give, through the speaking mouth of the corpse, a sign by which those present could unanimously pronounce judgment concerning the dead man’s condemnation, with the same words—‘Answer me’—returning during each of the three distinct cries. To attempt this is to tempt God, and for that reason it would never have been permitted by the bishop, especially in that flourishing city, which abounded in so many learned and wise men” [Col. 0225C–D].

375. “Whatever may be said of this third opinion, which appears the more plausible—for if the circumstances of the story are set aside and the event is said to have taken place within the private walls of the dead man’s house, where Saint Bruno and his companions were performing the duty of charity toward the corpse of their beloved dead by reciting the Office of the Dead, during which the deceased, as though awakened from the sleep of death, cried out three times in a horrible voice that he had been accused, judged, and condemned—all the arguments drawn from the silence of contemporary authors collapse. These authors, when speaking of Saint Bruno’s departure into the hermitage of Chartreuse, are said to report absolutely nothing about that story.

“For although those authors were contemporaries of Saint Bruno, it was easy for them to have remained ignorant of the event, which for a long time and as far as possible was suppressed in silence and kept secret, both out of respect for the distinguished dead man and for his family [Col. 0226A]. Moreover, at that time there was no means of communicating promptly to distant regions what had happened in one place. The service of public couriers and runners, which was then very rare, was lacking. Whatever, I say, may be said of that opinion,” and so forth.

Certainly, if the prodigious story of the condemned man is held to have occurred in the manner in which some, according to Masson’s testimony here, and our own anonymous Carthusian in the words quoted immediately above, explain it, it will have far less to make it depart from probability. But two questions may now be raised. First, should an account in which the event is said to have taken place in this way be regarded as newly and foolishly invented—or rather, can it be confirmed by ancient testimony, and by what testimony? Second, what credence does it deserve? That is, did the prodigious resurrection of the condemned man really occur as the account relates, and did it impel our Saint into the wilderness? I wish to examine the first question in the present section and the second in the following one.

It often happens that historical events—even events that no one at all calls into doubt and that certainly did take place—are found, upon proper examination, to have been adorned with circumstances wholly alien to the truth and entirely fictitious.

376. Historians, both sacred and profane, committed to writing the holy contests of martyrs, the savage persecutions raised by tyrants against the faithful of Christ, the battles fought between hostile armies, the sieges laid against cities, and very many other events that occurred in ages long past. Yet how often did they—whether deceived by impostors or by the rumors of a credulous populace, carried away by misguided emotions, or finally led into error for some other reason—disfigure the events or deeds they recount with wholly false and fabulous circumstances [Col. 0226B–C]!

The discovery of the Holy Cross by Helena, the mother of Constantine the Great, belongs among historical events supported by certain evidence and was first commended in writing by Theodoret. Yet afterward it was polluted by very many fictions, as may be seen in our volume I for May, page 363. The glorious struggle of Saint Maurice and his companions, the Theban soldiers and martyrs, for the faith is altogether certain and beyond doubt. Yet the *Acts* of those holy martyrs as presented by Surius clothe it in not a few false circumstances, as is clearly shown by what we have said about them in our volume VI for September, pages 340 and following [Col. 0226D]. I shall add no more, since scarcely anything is more obvious than that true histories are found corrupted by false and fictitious circumstances.

Hence, in historical events, contrary to what Launoy wishes in his dissertation *On the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Wilderness*, the substance of what happened must be distinguished from its circumstances; and it does not immediately follow from the falsity of the latter that the former is likewise false. According to what has just been said, some of the circumstances with which Surius adorns the passion of the Theban martyrs are false; nevertheless, the event itself must be regarded as most certain.

377. The same applies to many other contests of other martyrs and to other historical events, much of whose history, both sacred and profane, would have to be erased if everything clothed in false and fictitious circumstances were to be counted as fiction and fable or held certainly false. These observations apply even more strongly to events known only through tradition, transmitted from the origin of the event through one, two, or even several centuries.

For although an event can easily be transmitted orally by those who witnessed it or heard it from eyewitnesses, and then passed on by them to others without any notable alteration, this can scarcely—or indeed scarcely at all—happen when events are transmitted for more than a century from one person to another through continuous tradition, without being secured by the support of writing [Col. 0227A–B].

Now, according to what was said above, if the prodigious resurrection of the Parisian doctor ever took place, it occurred more than a hundred years before it was committed to writing. It would therefore be remarkable if, by the time it reached the anonymous author of the *Chronicle of the First Five Carthusian Priors*, who first committed it to writing, it had not been greatly corrupted and altered in the circumstances accompanying it.

Hence it is highly doubtful whether that writer, even if the prodigy really occurred, did not clothe it in false circumstances that he had learned through a corrupted tradition. I shall explain how this could have happened. The substance of that horrifying event seems to consist solely in the fact that the dead man, who had apparently lived piously, declared to those present that he had been accused, judged, and condemned by the just judgment of God, uttering three cries from the bier in which he had already been placed. As a result, Saint Bruno, who was present, was moved to compunction by the terrible event and withdrew into the wilderness [Col. 0227C].

378. What if, then, as time passed, someone recounted what had happened and embellished this story, almost stripped of all its circumstances, by arbitrarily supplying circumstances—or circumstances that seemed more similar to the truth—and this embellished version subsequently reached the anonymous author just mentioned?

It certainly sometimes happens that writers arbitrarily adorn events they find stripped of circumstances with plausible details, or even replace the circumstances in which they find the events clothed with new ones that they judge more probable. Evidence of this may be found in the Carthusian chronicler mentioned at section 203, who flourished under Elizarius, prior of Chartreuse, in the fourteenth century.

For although he adopted in full the account of the condemned doctor that he had found in the anonymous author of the *Chronicle of the First Five Carthusian Priors*, he nevertheless writes that the horrifying event, which the anonymous author reports as having occurred in the hall of the dead man, took place in the church. He presumably made this change in the anonymous account because the latter relates that almost the entire city of Paris had gathered for the dreadful spectacle, whereas the chronicler did not consider it plausible that such a large multitude could have assembled in the dead man’s hall, which was incapable of holding it [Col. 0227D–0228A].

Perhaps for the same reason some people later recorded that the three cries of the condemned man returned not on three different days but on one and the same day. Sutor mentions some of these in book I, treatise II, chapter 2, of his *On Carthusian Life*.

379. Indeed, since the horrifying prodigy, if it ever occurred, probably reached the anonymous author of the *Chronicle of the First Five Carthusian Priors* through a tradition corrupted in its circumstances, as has been said, those who altered what seemed less plausible in those circumstances appear not unreasonably to have assigned only a single day to the unfortunate doctor’s cries, rather than three different days as he did.

This is especially so because the substance of the account remains intact and unharmed whether the three cries are held to have occurred on one day or on three different days, as will be clear to anyone who considers what was said in the preceding section.

Now, since this is so, and since it appears even more probable that the horrifying prodigy, if it occurred at all, took place not publicly before an innumerable multitude of people but within the private walls of the dead man’s house in the presence of a few persons, the writer who maintains that it happened in this latter way and on one and the same day does not seem to have acted foolishly, especially since the substance of the account assigned in the preceding section is not thereby damaged.

But did he not at least introduce something newly fabricated? This too, as appears, is no reason to reject his account. For there were also ancient writers who believed that the three cries of the condemned man occurred both on one and the same day and within the private walls of the dead man’s house.

This may properly be inferred from the author who composed in French the commentary entitled *The Four Rivers of Paradise for the Purification of the Soul’s City*. Launoy quotes this author’s account of the condemned doctor, translated by Launoy himself into Latin, in chapter 2 of his dissertation *On the True Cause of Saint Bruno’s Withdrawal into the Wilderness*. Our anonymous Carthusian afterward incorporated the same account into book IV of his *Annals of the Order*, not yet published at that time, both in the French in which it was originally written and in Latin.
