380. When doing so, and speaking of the author of the said Commentary—who differs from the anonymous author of the *Chronicle of the First Five Carthusian Priors* in the circumstances of the Parisian prodigy—he introduces him as follows [Col. 0228D–0229A]:

“This is the author of a manuscript codex on goatskin parchment, written in an obsolete character and style, found in the archive of the Castellione family and now kept in the library of the Jesuit college at Metz. It contains that story written in French. We count its author among the Carthusians because he professes that he received his entire account from an aged and highly respected monk of our Order. We have not seen the codex itself, but we here reproduce word for word the testimony of this story transcribed from it, just as it was sent in the year 1639 by the Reverend Father Claude Tifanius of the Society of Jesus, superior of the province of Champagne, while he was inspecting the college at Metz, to the Very Reverend Father Charles le Bret, prior of Mont-Dieu Charterhouse—without omitting or altering even a single letter—so that the reader may judge more soundly and surely concerning its antiquity and our notes upon it, without omitting or altering even a jot.”

He then transcribes the account of the condemned doctor, composed in French, together with a Latin translation appended at the end. For my present purpose, it will be sufficient to transfer only this account. It runs as follows:

“It is related that there was at Paris a certain master who surpassed all the other masters of his time in talent and learning. Externally, he appeared to lead an honorable life; no depraved conduct or disgraceful vice was detected in him, except perhaps vanity on account of his outstanding learning and exceptional judgment, with which the Lord had splendidly endowed him [Col. 0229B].

“It happened during his lifetime that three students of the highest nobility came to Paris for the sake of study. They immediately placed themselves under the discipline of the aforesaid master, since he was the most eminent of all the other masters.

381. “After they had devoted themselves to study under him for a long time, he died. The disciples were greatly saddened, for they had loved their master during his life. Continuing to honor him even after death, they decided, out of special devotion, to keep vigil that night beside the dead man’s body. After the Office of the Dead had been recited, they began the psalter.

“When they had completed the first Matins, or Nocturn, the body that lay dead there raised itself and, sitting up in the bier, spoke these words: ‘Just and fair is he who judged me’ [Col. 0229C].

“Then the three clerics and the companions who were present around the body, although exceedingly terrified, nevertheless did not desist from their pious work. They continued with the second Nocturn of the psalter. When it had been completed, the dead man’s body raised itself as before and said: ‘Just and fair is he who judged and condemned me.’

“The three clerics were then even more astonished than before. Making the sign of the cross over themselves, they began the third Nocturn with the greatest devotion. When it had been completed, the same body raised its head for the third time and said: ‘Just and fair is he who judged and condemned me, and consigned and delivered me over to terrors.’

“After these words, a sudden whirlwind came, seized the dead man’s body, and carried it away from the sight of everyone [Col. 0229D]. Thereafter it was impossible to discover what had happened to it.

“The three clerics, who had been his disciples, were struck with profound astonishment and bitter grief at the disastrous end of so unhappy a master. They then returned to their own homes and asked their acquaintances and relatives for what reason so great a man had been consigned to eternal punishments. After diligent inquiry, they could find nothing that, according to the outward indications, ought to be judged a mortal sin, except vainglory.

“Therefore, these three clerics, men distinguished by power and nobility of birth, seized with fear of the divine judgments, resolved by common agreement, in order to save their souls and escape the danger of eternal condemnation, to abandon worldly life and undertake and endure a harsh and severe way of life in solitude [Col. 0230A].

382. “Moved, therefore, by the divine Spirit, they went into Burgundy, to a deserted and uncultivated place surrounded by mountains. There, having built cells among the mountains, they lived a highly religious and austere life. Thus, through these three holy men, and through those who followed their example and adopted the same way of life, the Carthusian Order began, continues, and is observed to this day. I heard all these things from one of the senior and most ancient members of that same Order, who related them in the presence of the Lady Countess of Saint-Paul.”

This is the entire account of the unfortunate doctor given by the author of the book *The Four Rivers of Paradise*, as translated by our anonymous Carthusian [Col. 0230B]. To determine approximately the period in which the author of that book flourished, he adds the following:

“Launoy thinks that the author of this account lived around the time of Gerson or Antoninus, and he infers this from two things: from the French expression, which he wishes to assign to their period, and from the manner of speaking, which he likewise maintains implies knowledge of a matter not yet sufficiently established and accepted.

“But other learned men think otherwise. Claude Tifanius, mentioned above, judged from the style both of this account and of the entire codex that it belonged to the thirteenth century. This may also be supported by the following somewhat obscure words, which Raynaudus asserts occur in the same account—as indeed they do occur here as well. One is *Useille* [French: “Vigil” or “Vigil service”], the other *Graigneur* [French: “Great” or “Greater”]. The first means ‘Vigil,’ and the latter means ‘Great.’ This last word occurs in the same chapter of the cited codex, where the author translates these words of Ecclesiasticus, ‘The greater you are, humble yourself in all things,’ in that obsolete French idiom as follows: ‘De tant humilie toy plus, comme tu seras Graigneur’—‘The greater you are, the more humble yourself.’ And in the copy sent by the aforesaid Claude to Mont-Dieu, these additional ancient and obsolete words are read: ‘Que Dieu absoille,’ that is, ‘May God absolve’” [Col. 0230C].

383. “From all this it is sufficiently evident that the author of this account is older than Launoy supposed. It will be even more evident if we consider who this Countess of Saint-Paul was. There can be no doubt that she was the wife of a certain Count of Saint-Paul [Col. 0230D].

“We read the history of the family of the lords of Châtillon-sur-Marne, from whom the ancient Counts of Saint-Paul descended, edited by André Du Chesne. Among the wives of the Counts of Saint-Paul, we found none especially inclined toward our Order except Mary, daughter of John II, Duke of Brittany, and Beatrice of England; wife of Guy III, Count of Saint-Paul; mother of Mathilda, wife of the Count of Valois; and, with him, foundress of the Chartreuse of Notre-Dame de la Fontaine.

“Her husband Guy became Count of Saint-Paul after the death of Joan, his kinswoman, daughter and heiress of John, Count of Blois, Guy’s uncle. We first thought that this Joan, wife of Peter, Count of Alençon—who, after his death without children in 1283, remained a widow—was the Countess of Saint-Paul mentioned in the account, because she was a great benefactress of the Charterhouse of the Valley of Saint Peter and almost a second foundress of the Parisian Charterhouse, in which she built and endowed fourteen cells.

“Yet although she enjoyed the revenues of the County of Saint-Paul until the year 1291, when she died, we have nowhere found, either in the documents of the two Charterhouses or in Du Chesne’s cited History, that she bore the title of Countess of Saint-Paul; only the titles of Alençon and Blois are assigned to her. For this reason, we judged that the Countess in whose presence this account was given was more probably the aforementioned Mary, whose maternal relatives—the kings of England—were great supporters of our Order.

“She lived with her husband Guy from the year 1292 until 1337, when he died. She long survived him, remaining a widow until her death, which occurred in the year 1319” [Col. 0231A–B].

“Since, therefore, the writer of this codex was a contemporary of the aforesaid countess, and since, as he testifies in the same place, he received this story from a very ancient Carthusian monk, we infer that this monk was approximately contemporary with our anonymous author, who first committed the story to writing. He could already have been living in our Order before the year 1280. It is therefore clear that the event was already regarded as certain in the thirteenth century—that is, at most eighty years after the death of Saint Bruno’s companions—and at the time when the Carthusian Order began to spread more widely from its principal house.”

384. These are the words of our anonymous Carthusian, given in order to determine approximately the period in which the author of the account transcribed above flourished. Indeed, from what he brings forward concerning the Countess of Saint-Paul, it appears sufficiently probable that he flourished either toward the end of the thirteenth century or, rather, at that time and during some of the immediately following years.

The two conjectures of Launoy, one of which this writer repeats here, do not establish the contrary. Launoy derives the first from the French expression and the second from the manner of speaking, arguing that both this writer and that expression belong to the age of Gerson and Saint Antoninus.

The manner of speaking employed by the author may in fact imply, as Launoy wishes, knowledge of a matter not yet sufficiently established and accepted. It does not, however, follow from this that his account belongs to the age of Gerson and Saint Antoninus. Launoy thought so only because he wished Gerson—who speaks of the prodigy almost as one who doubts it—to have been the first to commit it to writing. But that this is contrary to the truth is sufficiently clear from what has already been said.

Moreover, since Launoy asserts that the mournful account of the condemned doctor was fabricated before Gerson committed it to writing, why could someone who wrote before Gerson’s time not have spoken of it as of a matter not yet sufficiently established and accepted?

As for the French expression used by the author of the book *The Four Rivers of Paradise*, whose period we are discussing, our anonymous Carthusian teaches in the words quoted immediately above that he received the mournful account of the condemned doctor that he supplies from an aged Carthusian in the presence of Mary, Countess of Saint-Paul, who lived until the year 1339. It is therefore possible that this occurred not long before that year. And since it is possible that he did not commit the matter to writing when he first heard it, he may perhaps have done so only around the year 1350.

I do not find it sufficiently probable that at that time the French language could have differed so greatly from the language used in Gerson’s age, that is, at the beginning of the fifteenth century, that Launoy could infer from the difference that the author who used it must have written only then. A period of merely fifty years, or somewhat more, does not ordinarily bring about so great a change in languages or idioms [Col. 0231C–D].

385. Hence I would not dare to adhere unreservedly to Tifanius, who judged, solely from the style used by the author, that the account in question, and the entire codex containing it, belonged to the thirteenth century. Nor do I see why the style could not still have been much the same around the year 1350 as it is thought to have been toward the end of the thirteenth century, or around the year 1292, before which the account was probably not committed to writing, as may readily be inferred from what our anonymous Carthusian teaches in the words quoted immediately above.

Be that as it may, it is also understood from the same words of our anonymous Carthusian that the same account was heard by the author who committed it to writing from a very aged Carthusian at the time when Mary, daughter of John II, Duke of Brittany, was Countess of Saint-Paul—that is, during the period extending from the year 1292 [Col. 0232A] to the year 1339. Thus we have a defined period in which the account probably became known to the author who committed it to writing. This is the principal point here and is almost sufficient for the present purpose.

In the meantime, however, it appears highly doubtful whether the very aged Carthusian from whom he learned the mournful story flourished no later than eighty years after the death of Saint Bruno’s companions. For I find that none of them lived beyond the year 1145. And, as may readily be inferred from what has already been said, it could easily have happened that the writer who committed the story to writing did not hear it from that aged Carthusian before the year 1330.

Now hear what judgment our anonymous Carthusian gives concerning the account in question:

“Such an account,” he says, “appears sufficiently frank and sincere, and expresses with complete candor the very marrow of the entire story on the basis of ancient testimonies. For in it you have the fact that the prodigy occurred at Paris, as well as the fact that the Carthusian institution had its origin on that account.”

### 386

“It is also reported that a triple cry was heard by the friends of the condemned master alone in his house. Nothing occurs that is inconsistent with the account of our earlier anonymous author, except for that threefold repetition of the voices, which he says took place three times on the same day, not on three days. As for the report that the corpse disappeared after being lifted from the sight of those standing by in a whirlwind, this involves no contradiction, since our anonymous author and the other authors cited have remained silent about what happened to it. For only the more recent writers remember that it was buried in a dung heap, inferring this suitably from the fact that his damnation was certain.”

So he writes. Yet there is rather more difference than he indicates between the account of the anonymous chronicler of the first five priors of Carthusian and the other account supplied by the author of *The Four Rivers of Paradise*. The former, unlike the latter, clearly indicates that an immense crowd of people had rushed to the deadly spectacle and had been present when the master proclaimed that he had been condemned by God’s just judgment. If this detail was absent from the account, that narration would consequently become less difficult to believe and less unlike the truth, as is sufficiently clear from what has already been said, and will become even clearer from what I am about to say, after I have transcribed what our anonymous Carthusian sets against Launoy, who rejects the aforesaid account as worthless.

Thus, after the words quoted immediately above, he continues:

“Launoy, who confuses the circumstances of ancient and modern writers and greatly exaggerates their disagreement, attacks this account as foolish and full of ignorance, chiefly on three grounds. First, because it attributes the beginning of the Carthusian order to adolescents, or to three clerics or scholars; second, because it reports that the foundations of that order were laid in the mountains of Burgundy; third, because what it says about the removal of the master’s corpse does not agree with the paintings and wall pictures of the Parisian monastery.”

### 387

“To the first objection we reply that this account was given by that monk only orally, word for word, and that therefore the writer of the manuscript, who perhaps wrote it down long afterward, could easily have been deceived by a failing memory. For we admit that only three clerics are expressly mentioned there, although in fact there were seven, including two laymen who laid the foundations of the order; yet it is not established that all of them were present at the spectacle. Let the discerning reader judge whether it follows from this that the whole history is false.

Indeed, what differs there from the accounts of other authors can readily be reconciled from the context of the same narration. Although the author mentions only three in the course of his account, he nevertheless implies that more established the order when, near the end of his speech, he adds:

‘And by these three holy men, and by those who followed their example and lived and conducted themselves likewise, the Order of Chartreuse was begun and is still maintained and observed’—

that is:

‘And thus, through these three holy men and those who followed their example and led the same kind of life, the Carthusian order began and still exists and is observed.’

And earlier:

‘Then these three clerics and their companions, who were around the body’—

that is:

‘Then these three clerics and their companions, who were around the body.’

Could not the four others who, together with these three clerics, gave the order its beginning have been included in that group? But even if we granted that no mention at all was made there except of three clerics, could it not have happened that, of that group of seven, only three were present at the funeral, while afterward they withdrew into solitude with the other four?”

### 388

“For in fact we infer that they wished to persuade several others to adopt the same way of life, from the case of Ralph and Fulcher, whom Saint Bruno had endeavored to win for God and with whom he had even made a vow to assume the monastic habit. Nevertheless, one may properly doubt whether they were present at the spectacle, since they could have made such a vow before it took place.

Moreover, of the seven first Fathers, only three seem properly to be called clerics, namely Saint Bruno, Landuinus, and Hugh. Of the other four, two were canons of Saint Rufus and two were laymen.

Finally, in that account the master is said to have died long after he had taught those three clerics. For it reads:

‘And when they had been there, their master died a long time afterward’—

that is:

‘When they had studied under him, their master died long afterward,’ or, as we rendered it above:

‘While they were devoted to study under him, after a long time that man died.’

Launoy, however, interprets these words as follows:

‘After he had taught them for some time, he departed this life.’

But in this interpretation, I must say unwillingly, he was not candid. For *aliquandiu* does not mean *long-temps*, or ‘for a long time,’ but ‘for some time.’ Since that man died long after he had taught those three clerics, they were not then adolescents in the strict sense, as Launoy seems to understand the term, so that the account might thereby appear more foolish. Nor were they scholars; two of them were already doctors and masters, as is clear in the case of Saint Bruno and Landuinus.

This does not prevent some of Saint Bruno’s other companions from perhaps having been scholars at that time, for the two Stephens were still quite young and had not yet been ordained priests.”

### 389

“Therefore nothing foolish will be found in this account by any reader who interprets its meaning with goodwill and without any preconceived bias. Whatever the adversaries may say in reply, the foundation, so to speak, of the history itself and its entire substance will nevertheless remain firm, nor will such slight discrepancies in circumstances be able to overturn it.

We cannot sufficiently marvel at the carelessness of Launoy, a most perceptive man, in this observation. Earlier, in chapter 1 of his *Dissertation*, while explaining the testimony of Peter of Cluny, he had read and written:

‘There is preserved within the borders,’ or ‘regions,’ ‘of Burgundy, as it is read elsewhere, a certain profession,’ namely the Carthusian profession, ‘more holy than many others devoted to the monastic way of life.’

And, in explaining the testimony of James of Vitry, he had written:

‘There is another congregation of saints, whom they call Carthusians, in the farthest regions of Burgundy.’

Yet here he accuses the manuscript’s author of foolishness and ignorance because he reported that the foundations of the order had been laid in the mountains of Burgundy.

Although the Grande Chartreuse is now considered to lie in Dauphiné, it was formerly reckoned as belonging to Burgundy, since both Savoy and Dauphiné were parts of ancient Burgundy. This also supports the antiquity of the Castiglionese manuscript: if its author had written after the year 1346, around which time Dauphiné began to be assigned to the kingdom of France, he would have spoken differently of Dauphiné.

As to the third objection, we believe that we have already given a sufficient answer when we said above that only later writers—including those to whom we attribute the paintings and wall pictures of the Parisian Charterhouse—devised this kind of burial in a dung heap, although it appears more like the truth than the story that the corpse was carried away by a whirlwind.”

These are the arguments that our anonymous Carthusian sets against Launoy, who rejects as foolish and ignorant the account supplied by the author of *The Four Rivers of Paradise*.

### 390

And indeed Launoy rejects it quite unjustly, whether because it reports that the foundations of the Carthusian order were laid in the mountains of Burgundy, or because it suggests that the corpse of the unfortunate master was seized and carried away by a demon, contrary to what is represented in the paintings of the Parisian Charterhouse.

For the mountains encompassing the Grande Chartreuse truly belonged, in the time of our saint, to ancient Burgundy, as is clear from what Valesius brings forward in the *Notitia Galliarum* under the heading “Burgundy.”

As for the claim that something happened to the condemned man’s corpse other than what is represented in the paintings of the Parisian Charterhouse, this is entirely irrelevant. Even if we grant that the Parisian prodigy occurred, the paintings of the Parisian Charterhouse do not possess such authority that whatever conflicts with them must be rejected.

Nor should the account under discussion be considered foolish because it attributes the beginning of the Carthusian order to three adolescents, whether clerics or scholars. It implies that, when they did this, they were no longer adolescents. Moreover, although it reports that only three were present at the horrible spectacle of the condemned man, the context of the speech indicates that more established the order; and none of the ancient writers who mention the spectacle asserts that all of them stood present at it.

Even if most of those writers expressly made such an assertion, the only conclusion would be that there is not exact agreement in the circumstances between them and the author of *The Four Rivers of Paradise*. But what of that? It proves only that this author did not draw from the same source from which they did; it does not prove that the account he supplies differs in substance from theirs, or that for this reason it is remote from the truth.

For, as is clear from what was said above, the substance of a narrative can agree most exactly with the truth even when it is clothed in circumstances that are either certainly false or only doubtfully true.

Indeed, I am persuaded that all the circumstances embellishing both the account supplied by the chronicler of the first five priors of Carthusian and the other account attributed to the author of *The Four Rivers of Paradise* are of this kind. They arose from tradition alone, which continued down to a time more than a hundred years removed from the origin of the event. When tradition lasts so long without the protection of written testimony, it commonly causes many circumstances—unknown at the beginning—to be added to the substance of the event.”

### 391

Accordingly, even if we grant that the mournful story of the condemned man occurred, I shall always doubt whether our saint ever studied in Paris, although this seems to follow from the account of *The Four Rivers of Paradise* transcribed above.

Even on that supposition, I shall likewise always doubt whether the man who made his condemnation known to those standing by from the bier was a cleric or a doctor. I have nevertheless generally called him a doctor above because the chronicler of the first five priors of Carthusian and others who follow him adorn him with that title.

Thus, even if the account we are discussing differs in its circumstances from the account supplied by the older biographer of our saint and by others who follow him, it does not follow that it must therefore be rejected.

Nor should you object that it is the only account which places the prodigy of the condemned doctor not in public but within the private house of the deceased, before only a few people. For even if that is so, the author of *The Four Rivers of Paradise*, who committed the account to writing, learned it from an aged Carthusian, as was said above.

Since he had undoubtedly heard this mournful story from the Carthusians with whom he lived, it ought to be regarded as equivalent to the testimony of many; and for this reason I have also spoken above of the story as one handed down by several people.

Moreover, the ancient testimonies cited above, which place the prodigy in public, were taken from the account of the anonymous chronicler of the first five priors of Carthusian. Consequently, all of them taken together constitute, in a certain sense, only one testimony.

Since this is so, and since nothing further militates against the account of *The Four Rivers of Paradise*, neither that account nor the opinion founded chiefly upon it—namely, that the Parisian prodigy occurred not publicly but only before a few people—should be rejected as foolish and recently invented.

## § XXIII. How much credibility should be granted to the opinion that the resurrection of the condemned doctor occurred in his private house before a few people, and what should finally be judged concerning this opinion so considered

[Col. 0236D]

It is not uncommon for historical events known only through tradition, however falsely clothed in circumstances, nevertheless to contain something true. This follows readily from what was said in the preceding section.

Nevertheless, in order that what must now be said about the mournful story of the condemned man may become clearer, I wish to bring forward certain observations supplied by our Papebrochius that are not wholly foreign to the present subject.

In his *Responses to the Exhibition of Errors*, article XIX, no. 10, he writes:

“It often happens that the substance of a tradition is such that, although it can only rashly be called into doubt, even when it lacks the testimony of contemporaries. For example, that a certain Saint Ursula, together with a very large company of companions, was killed by barbarians before the walls of the city of Cologne, which they had besieged; that Saint Dionysius, sent from Rome into Gaul, preached the faith at Paris and sealed it with his blood; and other similar matters.

I say, it often happens that those things subsequently added to the substance of the original tradition as though from tradition or revelation—for example, through the composition of legendary works, such as the Dionysian Legend in the ninth century and the Ursulan Legend in the eleventh—are rightly rejected as the dreams and inventions of later writers, unknown to all earlier antiquity. I mean ‘later’ not in relation to us, who live today, but in relation to the event itself, which preceded them by many centuries.”

Thus, as it seems to me, Papebrochius speaks most correctly. In the same article, no. 13, he supplies the following further observations relevant here:

“Popular traditions, sacred or profane, generally contain some truth as regards their substance, but much chaff is successively sprinkled over them, from which it is difficult to cleanse them so thoroughly that the understanding of a prudent person may safely rest upon them as upon things certain.”

And later, in no. 19, he adds:

“Rumor, arising usually from a very small beginning and often not from truth,

Gains strength through mobility and acquires power as it goes,

Small at first through fear, soon it raises itself into the air,

It enters from the ground and hides its head among the clouds.”

### 393

“Popular tradition is much the same. Its beginning is usually some memorable event, either something that really happened at some time but is clothed, as time passes, in such ornaments and additions that afterward it marvels at itself and scarcely recognizes itself; or something invented by an idle imagination investigating the origins of ancient events in order to promote its own reputation or that of its associates. The credulous common people eagerly adopt what they desire as true and honor it as such, often for many centuries.

Examples occur in both sacred and profane history.”

All this Papebrochius says about traditions, and indeed, as I have already said, most correctly.

Therefore, since according to these principles it often happens that traditions—or, if you prefer, narratives built solely upon traditions—are infected with many falsehoods while nevertheless being true in substance, or at least containing something true as regards their substance, it may easily be that the Carthusian tradition concerning the horrible Parisian prodigy by which Saint Bruno was driven into the desert—or, if you prefer, the account of that prodigy given by the anonymous chronicler of the first five priors of Carthusian and by the other writers praised above, an account originally derived from that tradition—is true in substance, or at least contains something true as regards its substance, even though many false circumstances were added to it over time in the manner explained above.

To speak more clearly: it may be that our saint was driven into the desert by a prodigy in which the deceased man, already placed in his bier, first declared to those present that he had been accused, then judged, and finally condemned; that Saint Bruno’s first companions or disciples related this to their followers; and that their successors, as the event was enlarged over time by false circumstances, then believed that the prodigy had occurred publicly before an almost countless crowd of people, and that the condemned man’s voice had returned on three different days—although in reality the mournful event had occurred within the private house of the deceased, before only a few people, one of whom was Saint Bruno, and the condemned man’s voice had been repeated not on three different days but on one and the same day.”

### 394

What if, then, the event happened in this latter way? Surely anyone who judged that it had truly happened in this manner would not be far from probability; indeed, the opinion could appear fairly plausible.

I think so because, as I have already indicated sufficiently above, it sometimes happens that historical events, even when suppressed in silence by all contemporary writers and transmitted only through tradition to those who eventually committed them to writing—tradition separated by more than a hundred years from the origin of the event—must be regarded as true.

Nor does the universal silence of all writers who flourished during the entire first century, and perhaps even the second century, after the event prevent the Parisian prodigy from being counted among such events, if it is held to have occurred not publicly but before only a few people within the private house of the deceased. For there is an adequate explanation for this silence, namely ignorance of the event.

Since the mournful event, if it did not occur publicly, could easily have escaped the notice of Guibert of Nogent and the other ancient writers reviewed above, there is no reason to be surprised by their silence concerning it or to argue from that silence that the event was false.

Furthermore, unless it is admitted that the Parisian prodigy by which Saint Bruno was driven into the desert took place, at least before a few people within the private house of the deceased, one must conclude either that the Carthusians themselves wholly invented the horrible story or that they adopted it after it had already been invented by others.

But who could easily bring himself to believe that religious men, most devoted to truth and haters of fables, did the former? Shall we then assert that they fell into the latter error?

### 395

“If it is a fable,” says the aforementioned Masson, speaking of the story of the condemned man in his work entitled *Annals of the Carthusian Order*, book I, chapter 1, no. 11, “by whom, I ask, was it composed? Certainly it cannot be said to have been devised by anyone other than secular people. But how could such a fable, fabricated by secular people, have been accepted as a most certain fact by the first Carthusians and their successors, and transmitted so firmly to their posterity without ever encountering any contradiction or protest? Everyone can see that this is morally impossible.”

Certainly, everyone will readily acknowledge that the mournful account of the condemned man, if it is a fable, was not adopted and transmitted to later generations by the first Carthusians—that is, by Saint Bruno’s companions or their disciples.

But someone may object: why could it not have happened that Carthusians of a later age—that is, those who flourished in the thirteenth century—accepted that story, however fictitious, as true after being deceived by an impostor?

Indeed, someone may perhaps bring forward Blomenvenna, who, in the life of Saint Bruno composed by him, relates three different prodigies. One of them is beyond all doubt an invention; the other two, to say nothing worse, are extremely suspect.

At first I had intended not to bring these three prodigies, or rather fables, forward here, lest I give anyone cause to suspect the ancient Carthusians unjustly. But since my duty requires me to present to the diligent reader both what may harm and what may support the Carthusian tradition concerning the prodigy by which Bruno was driven into the desert, and since the life of our saint composed by Blomenvenna is not in everyone’s hands, I transcribe here the writer’s own words containing the aforesaid miracles, or rather fables. At the end I shall add both what difficulty can be constructed from them against the Parisian prodigy and what answer ought to be given to that difficulty.

### 396

Thus the biographer of our saint writes:

“It must not be passed over in silence that, at the first entrance into the Charterhouse, before they had established a rule of life for themselves, a wondrous miracle is said to have occurred.

On one occasion, when blessed Hugh was about to visit his diocese according to custom—as he was accustomed to do during Advent and Lent—he took leave of the brothers and blessed them, meat having been provided for their meal.

On the very Sunday of Quinquagesima, after the divine office had been completed and at the hour of dinner, the tables having first been blessed, Saint Bruno, a man of profound heart, offered a most salutary admonition in place of the reading, saying among other things:

‘Let us beware, I beg you, dearest brothers, because the ancient enemy is deceiving us. For we have come into this desert to perform penance after the manner of the ancient Fathers—Paul the first hermit, Anthony, Arsenius, Hilarion, Macarius, and others. Did these men eat meat, as we have begun to do?’

Those who were sitting at the opposite table answered him:

‘Are we, venerable Father, greater and better than the apostles, to whom the Lord commanded: “Whatever house you enter,” and so forth, “eat and drink what they have”?’

Since Bruno and those who were sitting at his table held the contrary position, the dispute continued until evening. At last, wearied, they bent themselves down to the ground and fell asleep.

The bishop, having returned from his visitation, sent messengers to the holy brothers, informing them of his return and that, as usual, he wished to celebrate the new commandment with them on the following day, that is, on Holy Thursday.

The messenger, however, found them sleeping beside the tables. Seeing meat smoking upon the tables, he was greatly scandalized, returned, and reported to his lord what he had seen. But the bishop did not believe his words until, after sending a second and a third messenger, he received the same report.”

### 397

“The bishop was astonished but still did not believe it. Saying, ‘Unless I see it myself, I will not believe,’ he mounted his horse and came to the mountain.

When he found everything as the servants had reported, he turned away from them and, in indignation, was about to leave. But as soon as he placed his foot upon the threshold, Saint Bruno and his companions awoke, reverently greeted the bishop, and offered him devout thanks for all the benefits he had bestowed upon them. For the bishop himself was accustomed to distribute generously to them from his resources and to provide everything necessary.

The bishop then asked Bruno, ‘What day is it today?’

He replied, ‘The Sunday of Quinquagesima.’

The bishop said, ‘Why have you delayed so long before eating?’

When Bruno had related the sequence of what had happened and the dispute that had taken place among them, the bishop secretly summoned the steward of his household and asked whether this was the same meat that he had supplied on the Sunday of Quinquagesima. After carefully examining it, the steward reported that it was the same.

Then the astonished bishop turned to the brothers and said:

‘Know, my dearest brothers, that today is the Wednesday after Palm Sunday.’

When the servants, at the bishop’s command, wished to remove the meat, as soon as they touched it, it turned to dust, to the amazement and astonishment of all.

When the bishop saw this, he and his household knelt and humbly begged pardon from Saint Bruno and the brothers for the false judgment with which they had begun to judge them.

For the brothers this became an occasion to resolve that they would abstain from meat perpetually. Later, when other miracles followed, this resolution was confirmed with the greatest strictness, and they have observed it to this day.”

### 398

“For at another time a certain young man of noble birth and outstanding learning, having put on the monastic habit in the Charterhouse, lived honorably into old age. He advanced so far in the spiritual life that he was deemed worthy even to possess the spirit of prophecy.

At last, worn out by age and afflicted with a very serious illness, he earnestly requested that the prior, who was visiting him, provide him with meat. The prior, however, thinking that because of old age or illness he was not of sound mind, or at least that he was being deceived by the tricks of the ancient enemy, pretended not to hear him and departed.

Three days later, when the prior returned, the sick man, burning with desire for meat, said that by God’s grace he had not been mentally deranged when he had spoken thus. Rather, he knew for certain that he would die unless he were granted the use of meat. Saying this, he solemnly warned the prior that, unless he promptly satisfied his desire, he should know that he would have to give an account of the sick man’s death on the day of judgment.

When the prior heard this, knowing that the sick man was a holy man, he was greatly afraid, summoned the community, and explained the whole matter. They unanimously resolved that meat should be supplied to one placed in such extreme necessity.

The sick man was then asked what kind of meat he particularly desired. He answered, partridge.

Immediately the prior summoned a certain young noble monk, a novice from Grenoble, and ordered him to bring the sick man a partridge obtained from hunters. The novice set out without delay, both because of obedience to his superior and because of charity toward the sick man, whose disciple he had been. Without troubling to go by the bridge, which was the ordinary crossing, he crossed the river by walking upon the water and quickly brought back the partridge.”

### 399

“When the prior presented it to the sick man, perfectly cooked and in the presence of the community, the sick man looked up to heaven and said with tears:

‘Lord Jesus Christ, hear me, your sinful servant, who humbly begs your goodness: if this vehement appetite is pleasing to your will, may this food come to me for the health of body and soul. But if otherwise, most merciful Lord, who hold dominion over life and death, deign to restore life to this creature of yours, which was killed for my sake, so that, flying away on its own path, it may make us, your servants, understand that it is contrary to your will for me or for any monk of our order to eat meat on any occasion or because of any illness.’

When, at the conclusion of the prayer, all who were present had answered, ‘Amen,’ the bird immediately, having recovered life and being covered with feathers, disappeared in sudden flight before the eyes of all who were present, who were astonished and gave thanks to God, who performs great wonders in heaven and on earth.

At another time, certain bishops and other men came to the Charterhouse before Quinquagesima. When they saw some elderly men weakened by age, they attributed this to the lack of meat and earnestly begged the prior to give those weak men some refreshment from the meat that the whole world was using at that season. They added that many learned men had feared, and still feared, that the order was excessively severe in this matter.

But when the prior absolutely refused, they asked him at least to have meat purchased for themselves and their companions.

What more is there to say? Meat was bought and brought to the Charterhouse. When the bundles were opened, it was seen to have been changed into real and excellent fish, in color, smell, and taste.

When he saw this, the prior said:

‘It appears that it is not the Lord’s will for us to nourish flesh with flesh.’

The fish was then cooked and set before the community and the others; by tasting it, the sick and weak were healed and strengthened.

The bishops did not believe that the meat had been changed into fish until they sent to the butcher shops and made the most careful inquiries, from which they heard exceedingly astonishing and evident testimony concerning the matter.”

### 400

These are the three different prodigies reported by Blomenvenna. The first of them, as I have already said, is beyond all doubt fictitious.

Guigo, the fifth prior of Carthusian, does not mention it in the life of Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble. There can be no doubt that, if such a prodigy had ever occurred, that biographer would have known of it and would have mentioned it in his work, since it concerned both the Carthusian order and Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, who had played no small part in it. In that work he has most diligently included the whole life of Saint Hugh and even events far less memorable.

As for the other two prodigies likewise mentioned by Blomenvenna, they too, as I have already noted, are most probably fictitious. Although I do not possess a sufficiently strong argument to prove this conclusively, I nevertheless believe it for the following reason: both these prodigies and the first appear to have been invented to show, against detractors, that the Carthusians’ perpetual abstinence from meat—even when they were dangerously ill—was wholly approved by God. Once they had already been invented, Blomenvenna seems to have inserted them into the life of Saint Bruno that he composed for this sole purpose.

But someone may object: since, of the three prodigies reported by Blomenvenna, one is certainly and the other two probably fictitious, what if pious men were once found among the Carthusians, as among the monasteries of other orders, who were nevertheless so simple-minded that they thought it permissible to devise new prodigies at will—prodigies that might contribute either to the splendor and reputation of their order or to the glory of God and the saints—and who in fact invented some during the thirteenth century, when it is especially known that many people in monasteries devoted themselves to fabricating stories?

### 401

What if the prodigy of the doctor who returned briefly to life and proclaimed publicly from his bier that he had been condemned was one of those inventions, first committed to writing in the thirteenth century, as is clear from what was said above? What if it was then fabricated to provide a justification for the extremely austere life instituted by Saint Bruno, which some people formerly criticized?

The prodigies—or rather, fabrications—reported by Blomenvenna lead to this conclusion.

But whatever the case may be, they cannot make me regard the mournful story of the condemned man as an indubitable invention or fable, especially when the opinion in question, as it is presented here, holds that the event occurred not publicly before an almost countless crowd of people but within the private walls of the deceased man’s house, before only a few.

For not everything committed to writing by thirteenth-century writers is fictitious. Nor, even though Blomenvenna inserted the three aforementioned prodigies—or rather inventions—into the life of Saint Bruno, is it found that the entire Carthusian order either regards them or ever regarded them as true. It therefore appears that the order would not have regarded the Parisian prodigy as true and indubitable, as it has consistently done for several centuries, if it had been nothing more than an invention and a fable.

In any event, the opinion that the Parisian prodigy occurred within the private walls of the deceased man’s house is much less remote from probability than the opinion asserting that it occurred publicly before an almost countless crowd of people.

Whether, meanwhile, the mournful story truly took place—whether it is held to have occurred publicly or within the private walls of the deceased man’s house—and whether it drove our saint into the desert, I leave the diligent reader to judge from everything that has been discussed at length about it. The arguments advanced above do not seem sufficient to me to pronounce the story either certainly true or certainly false.

Let us now continue the sequence of events relating to our saint.

## § XXIV. Whether the saint withdrew into solitude from Reims or from Paris, when he did so, and whether he then went directly to the desert of Chartreuse

[Col. 0243A]

The anonymous chronologist of the first five priors of Carthusian, who composed the more extensive eulogy of our saint that, as I noted above, was to be published under the title *The Earlier Life*; Francis of Puteo, or Puteanus; Peter Blomenvenna; and his other more recent biographers, who committed to writing the Parisian prodigy in which the doctor publicly proclaimed from his bier that he had been condemned, record that after this had happened Bruno, having delivered a most forceful and effective sermon, persuaded certain men who themselves had been present at the horrible spectacle to renounce the world and its vanities and to withdraw with him into the desert.

The anonymous author, who does not write that the saint was teaching in Paris at that time, indicates that all these men were his companions or intimates. The more recent writers, however, who wish Bruno to have been acting as a master there at that time, also make some of them his disciples.

I transcribe here the relevant words both of the anonymous author and of the more recent writers—or rather of Blomenvenna, who will stand here for all the others, since the rest agree with him.

The anonymous author writes in section 5:

“At that time there was there a master, Bruno by name, a German by nationality, born in the city of Cologne of parents of no obscure standing, a canon of the Church of Reims and there a master of the schools in theology. He, salutarily frightened and moved to compunction by the aforesaid voices—that is, by the doctor’s proclamation that he had been condemned—addressed certain companions who were present there…”

After recounting the speech that the saint delivered to them, he adds in section 8:

“With these or similar words and sentiments, Saint Bruno addressing and exhorting himself and certain companions, he and six other good men resolved to renounce the world and its vanities with him, and to seek suitable deserted places for the practice of perpetual penance,” and so forth.

### 403

Here is what Blomenvenna relates:

> “Therefore, terrified and salutarily moved to compunction”—namely, Saint Bruno—“having summoned some of his companions and disciples who were more closely associated with him, among whom were Master Lauduinus, who afterward became the first prior of the Carthusian monastery; two Stephens, one [Col. 0243D] of Bourges and the other of Die, both canons of Saint-Rufus; also Hugo, whom they called ‘the chaplain,’ because he alone among them exercised the priestly office; and two laymen, namely Andreas and Guarinus, all of whom had been present at the aforesaid horrifying cries of the dead man, he addressed them tearfully in these or similar words, saying: ‘O friends and companions,’ etc.”

Thus he plainly teaches that some of those whom Saint Bruno addressed with the greatest earnestness after seeing and hearing the dreadful prodigy had been disciples of the saint. Yet even granting that the horrifying story of the condemned doctor really took place, this seems to me quite unlikely, because, as I showed in § VIII, it is most probable that the saint neither taught at Paris at the time when the mournful event supposedly occurred nor ever taught or acted as a master there [Col. 0244A] at any other time.

Moreover, in the anonymous chronographer of the first five priors of the Carthusian order, or rather in the older biographer of our saint—who certainly has greater authority than Blomenvenna and the other more recent writers—those to whom the saint is said to have delivered an address after the fatal event are described only as his companions, not also as his disciples.

Be that as it may, it certainly does not appear implausible on any ground that some of those whom the saint drew with him into the wilderness had previously been his disciples, and that on this occasion he inspired them with the resolve to withdraw with him into the wilderness. This is especially plausible since, while Bruno was teaching at Reims, an immense crowd from every direction—not only natives but also foreigners and outsiders—flocked there to study, as I explained above in no. 171.

### 404

But the question may now be raised whether the saint withdrew into solitude from Reims or from Paris, and likewise in what year he did so. Blomenvenna, Puteanus, and the other more recent writers who have deliberately composed a Life of Saint Bruno report that Bruno, while teaching at Paris, was driven into the wilderness by the horrifying prodigy of the revived man; they also plainly indicate that, once he had settled his affairs, he withdrew there from Paris. Our earlier biographer, or the chronographer of the first five Carthusian priors, does the same, although, as I have just shown, he does not record that the saint taught at Paris.

Yet when the saint withdrew into the wilderness, he was at Reims, having there been restored to his former position after the expulsion of Archbishop Manasses. This is taught by the verses concerning Bruno which those who composed the epitaph for the saint, as canons of the cathedral church of Reims, inserted in part among the epitaphs to be reprinted as no. 52. They were quoted above in no. 154:

> Although he shone in many ways in our city,  
> And became a solace and an ornament to his own,  
> And fortune favored him in everything, and we already  
> Preferred him to all, and rightly so;  
> For he was kind and skilled in every art,  
> Sufficiently eloquent and powerful in wealth,  
> He set everything aside for Christ, and, following  
> The naked Christ, the wilderness received him with many others.

Since this is so, it appears highly probable, indeed virtually certain, that Bruno—granted even that he had been present at Paris during the prodigy in which the doctor declared himself condemned—afterward, because of that prodigy, renounced the world, returned to Reims to settle his affairs, and withdrew into the wilderness not from Paris but from Reims.

### 405

This, then, is the first matter that had to be determined. The second concerns the time when the saint, having abandoned the world, sought the wilderness. For those who uphold the mournful story of the condemned doctor and maintain that Saint Bruno was driven by it into the wilderness, it necessarily follows that this did not happen before approximately the year 1082, since they unanimously write that the fatal spectacle occurred around that year, as will be clear to anyone who examines the three different Lives of our saint that are to be appended to this commentary from the evidence already given.

But since the fatal story is not certain on the basis of what has been said above, another method must necessarily be followed, by which either the date of Saint Bruno’s withdrawal into the wilderness, or at least the earliest time before which it cannot be placed, may be determined more safely and certainly.

As the statements made in § VIII demonstrate, our saint was not restored to his former position at Reims before the year 1081. Since, according to what has just been said, he did not withdraw into the wilderness until after that restoration had taken place, it follows altogether that he did not do so before that same year 1081. The writers of the *Literary History of France* therefore seem to depart from the truth when, in vol. IX of their work, p. 236, they assert that Bruno’s withdrawal into the wilderness occurred either in 1078 or at least at the time when Manasses, the deposed archbishop of Reims, was attempting by force of arms to reclaim the archbishopric that he had wrongly acquired—that is, in 1080.

Nor do these authors merely place our saint’s withdrawal into solitude too early in the passage cited; they also assert that the companions who accompanied him there belonged to the Reims clergy, although it is doubtful whether any of them did. I shall deal with this below; for now, we must first investigate the time when the saint’s withdrawal into solitude occurred.

The writers just mentioned, who, as stated, associate it with the year 1080 or even 1078, appear to do so because they place the conversation of the saint with Radulphus Viridis and Fulcius Monoculus—concerning the false delights of the world and the eternal joys of heaven, which endure forever and which have already been discussed at length above—around the year 1077. They therefore suppose that Bruno, who at that time had joined them in resolving to renounce the world and assume the monastic habit, did not long delay fulfilling his vow to God.

Yet the saint himself plainly indicates, in the letter praised above more than once, by which he urged Radulphus Viridis to fulfill that vow, that he did not carry it out immediately.

### 406

For in that letter to Radulphus he writes:

> “Your affection remembers that one day, when you, Fulcius Monoculus, and I were together in the little garden adjoining the house of Adam, where I was then staying, and when, as I think, we had for some time been discussing the false pleasures and perishable riches of this world, as well as the joys of eternal glory, we, inflamed by divine love, promised and vowed to the Holy Spirit that we would soon abandon the fleeting things of the world and seek the eternal, and would also receive the monastic habit. This would have been accomplished shortly afterward, had Fulcius not then gone to Rome; we postponed carrying it out until his return. Because he delayed, and because other causes intervened, divine love grew weak, the spirit cooled, and our fervor vanished.”

Thus our saint, by saying in the plural, “we postponed carrying it out,” unquestionably speaks not only of Radulphus, who delayed fulfilling the vow he had made, but also of himself, who likewise did so. Therefore the writers of the *History of France* ought not to have been led by any supposed promptness on Bruno’s part in fulfilling his obligation to place his departure into the wilderness in the year 1078, the year in which they believe the vow was made, or at least not to postpone it beyond 1080.

Nor is there any reason to think, on the authority of Guibert, abbot of Nogent, so frequently praised above, that our saint’s withdrawal into solitude took place before 1081. This writer indeed says in book I, chapter 11, of his *Life*:

> “Since every honorable man recoiled from the utterly wicked morals and disgracefully foolish conduct of this Manasses, archbishop of Reims and a simoniac, Bruno, then the most renowned man in the churches of Gaul, together with certain other nobles of the Reims clergy, out of hatred for that infamous man, departed from the city of Reims.”  
>   
> He adds shortly afterward: “But Bruno, having abandoned the city—that is, Reims—proposed also to renounce the world. Dreading recognition by his acquaintances, he proceeded to the territory of Grenoble. There, choosing to live on a lofty and exceedingly terrifying mountain, toward which a very difficult and highly unusual road leads, beneath which the chasm of a precipitous valley opens, he established this way of life; and his followers still live in this manner today.”

### 407

Yet although that writer, as is clear from the words just transcribed, joins our saint’s withdrawal from the city of Reims to his retreat into the wilderness of Chartreuse, he does not state that any interval of time—or only a very short interval—came between the two, nor does he say that Bruno went into the wilderness immediately after leaving the city of Reims because of Manasses’ wicked conduct. Nor could he have said this without compromising the truth, as is readily inferred from what was stated above both concerning the time when the saint left the city of Reims and concerning the events that he afterward carried out.

But, you will say, does Guibert supply nothing else by which the time of the saint’s withdrawal into the wilderness can in some measure be determined? Between the two passages just quoted he inserts the following words:

> “Later, when the nobles, clergy, and citizens, while Hugh—called of Die—archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, a man most renowned for his zeal for justice, repeatedly struck him with anathema, and when he attempted by military force to squander the treasures of the Church, they expelled him from the see which he had wrongly occupied. Condemned to perpetual exile, and having gone to the excommunicated Emperor Henry, himself also excommunicated at that time, he wandered here and there and finally died without communion.”

Since this writer immediately precedes these words—which he also places after the two passages transcribed above in the preceding section—with the expulsion of Manasses from the city and see of Reims, he thereby places our saint’s withdrawal into the wilderness afterward. It might therefore seem to some that Guibert intended to indicate that the expulsion preceded the withdrawal; and consequently, if this writer is to be followed, Saint Bruno did not go into the wilderness before 1081, since Manasses was not expelled from the city and see of Reims before that year.

Yet even though Guibert places Bruno’s retreat into the wilderness after Manasses’ expulsion, it does not consequently follow that he intended to signify that the expulsion preceded the retreat.

### 408

For, after recounting our saint’s departure from the city of Reims because of Manasses’ wicked conduct, he seems merely to have intended to inform the reader what afterward happened both to the one and to the other, without observing the order in which the events occurred.

This is entirely apparent. While actually narrating what happened both to Manasses and to Bruno, he places even the death of Manasses before the saint’s withdrawal into the wilderness, although there can be no doubt that the former occurred long afterward. Guibert himself seems to indicate, in the words quoted immediately above, that Manasses died only a long time after being expelled from the city of Reims, as will be clear to anyone who considers the passage. This is strongly confirmed by what the writers of the *Literary History of France*, vol. VIII, pp. 655 ff., record. From what will be said here, you will easily gather that the saint withdrew into solitude not very long after Manasses’ expulsion from the city of Reims.

Since matters stand thus, it by no means follows from Guibert’s placing our saint’s withdrawal into the wilderness after Manasses’ expulsion that he intended to indicate that the expulsion preceded the retreat, even though, in reality, as was stated in § VIII, the saint did not withdraw into the wilderness until after Manasses had been expelled from the city of Reims.

### 409

From this it further follows that Guibert did not intend to signify that our saint’s plan to renounce the world—although he too places it after Manasses’ expulsion in the words quoted above—was later than that expulsion.

I have thought it necessary to note this carefully because someone might argue from these passages that the vow of assuming the monastic habit, which the saint made in his conversation with Radulphus Viridis and Fulcius Monoculus, likewise occurred after Manasses’ expulsion from the city of Reims in 1081, contrary to what we established above.

Nevertheless, this matter would not be entirely certain even if Guibert expressly asserted that Manasses’ expulsion from Reims preceded the plan to renounce the world of which he speaks in the words quoted in no. 406 and elsewhere. For it is very doubtful whether, by those words, this writer is speaking of a vow made by the saint to withdraw into the wilderness and renounce the world, or of his actual withdrawal into the wilderness—which was certainly connected with his plan or intention to withdraw—especially since, as was shown above, Guibert was less well informed about events not publicly undertaken by Saint Bruno. He could easily have been unaware of the vow which our saint made with Radulphus Viridis and Fulcius Monoculus within the private walls of Adam’s house, where he was staying, apart from the company of other people.

This is why, in § VI, when establishing the opinion that the conversation held by Bruno with Radulphus Viridis and Fulcius Monoculus, together with the vow made there to renounce the world and seek the wilderness, occurred after Bruno’s departure from the city of Reims, I did not call upon the words of Guibert quoted above in support of that view, although I stated in no. 177 that those words might support it if Guibert intended by them to speak of the vow made by the saint.

Having now noted these points, let us continue our inquiry into the time when the saint withdrew into the wilderness—a withdrawal that, as has been established, did not occur before 1081.

### 410

Saint Bruno unquestionably first entered the wilderness of Chartreuse in the year 1084, as I shall show below. Therefore, if the wilderness which the saint first entered after renouncing the world was the Carthusian wilderness—that is, if he went directly to Chartreuse—there can be no doubt that he first bade farewell to the world and concealed himself in solitude in that same year, 1084.

This is precisely what the anonymous author of the hitherto unpublished fourth book of the Carthusian annals maintains. He places the prodigy of the doctor declaring himself condemned in the year 1082 and insists that the saint entered solitude only in 1084. He seems to do this in order to defend the reality of the prodigy, or rather to provide a suitable explanation for the silence with which Guibert, abbot of Nogent, passed it over.

Indeed, if the prodigy occurred in 1082 and the saint’s withdrawal into solitude only in 1084, it could easily have happened that Guibert did not know whether the former had caused the latter, and therefore passed over the mournful story in silence, although he knew it perfectly well, when he discussed the saint’s conversion and its beginnings in book I, chapter 11, of his *Life*.

Listen to how the Carthusian anonymous writer just mentioned speaks of this matter at the end of no. 99 in the fourth book of his order’s annals, still unpublished. I shall answer him shortly, so that the force previously assigned to Guibert’s silence—or to the negative argument formed from it against the prodigy—may remain intact:

> “Nor does it help to reply that Guibert kept silent about the spectacle. For he kept silent either because he did not know of it, if it took place only within private walls, or, if it was public and occurred before a great crowd, because he did not know whether it was the cause of Saint Bruno’s withdrawal, since he withdrew only about two years afterward, as is read in our anonymous writer and in the cited Chronicles published by Carthusian authors.”

### 411

> “Hence it is not surprising if this cause became known only to the Carthusians, especially since such plans are customarily kept secret and disclosed and communicated only to a few intimate persons. It is credible that Saint Bruno did this in accordance with that famous maxim commended by Peter of Cluny, as we have already said, by which the holy patriarch inspired his followers: ‘Conceal marvelous works with all the effort they can muster.’  
>   
> Nevertheless, this is to be understood only of present and personal works, not of the glorious deeds of the ancient Fathers, which God commands us to commend to posterity for its edification through Ecclesiasticus, who says: ‘Let us praise glorious men and our fathers in their generation.’”

Thus far the Carthusian writer. He tacitly acknowledges, meanwhile, that Guibert would have known that Saint Bruno had been driven into the wilderness by the Parisian prodigy if Bruno had withdrawn into it soon after the fatal story had publicly occurred.

And indeed, if the saint had gone into the wilderness immediately after the prodigy, or certainly not long afterward, accompanied by his six companions, it would surely have been widely known to Guibert and others that the horrifying event had driven him to do so—especially since the saint then stirred both those whom he drew with him into solitude and many others to undertake penance by means of that dreadful example of the condemned doctor, as all who defend the prodigy unanimously assert.

But our anonymous Carthusian says that the saint did not withdraw into the wilderness until nearly two years had elapsed since the doctor’s miraculous resurrection, and that Guibert therefore did not know that the saint had done so because he had been driven by the horrifying event.

But who, I ask, would find it probable that Bruno, who had long been bound by the obligation of a vow already made to assume the monastic habit, and who, by delaying longer to fulfill that obligation, would expose himself to the danger of a new and graver fault, did not withdraw into solitude until nearly two years had elapsed since the prodigy by which, as some put it, he had been shaken to the depths of his soul?

### 412

That certainly does not accord with the desire for eternal salvation and heavenly things which, after seeing the horrifying spectacle, he had conceived with such ardor.

Nor should you reply that the saint needed so long a period to settle his affairs and prepare what was necessary for undertaking a new kind of life. For although there can be no doubt that, after the prodigy—if it really ever occurred—he spent some period of time settling his affairs and preparing what was necessary for a new way of life, there is no reason whatsoever to think that this period was, or ought to have been, about two years. Why could he not, within merely two or three months, have renounced his possessions, taken leave of his friends, and prepared the few things that would be necessary for him, who was going to lead an extremely poor life?

“But,” says our anonymous Carthusian, “the chronographer of the first five Carthusian priors, or the older biographer of our saint, expressly states in no. 11 that the saint entered the wilderness of Chartreuse in 1084. The other Carthusians who flourished afterward, who have already been cited in § XI as witnesses in favor of the miraculous resurrection of the condemned doctor, agree with him.”

I admit that this is what he says. But what then? He nowhere asserts that, after the prodigy, the saint did not hide himself in a solitude different from the Carthusian wilderness before entering the latter. Nor, even if he did assert this, would it follow that, in view of what that writer records, our saint allowed approximately two years to elapse from the miraculous resurrection before withdrawing into solitude.

For although that anonymous chronographer, or our older biographer, connects Bruno’s withdrawal into the wilderness of Chartreuse with the definite year 1084, his manner of writing does not make it necessary to connect the Parisian prodigy with the year 1082. When reporting it, he says in no. 1:

> “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1082, or around that time, while the solemn schools were flourishing at Paris, especially in philosophy, theology, and canon law, as was generally customary, such a prodigy”—namely, that a Parisian doctor, revived for a short time, declared himself condemned to those standing around the bier—“is said to have occurred there.”

### 413

Therefore, in view of what our older biographer records, the miraculous resurrection of the condemned doctor occurred not in the definitively fixed year 1082, but either in that very year or in one of the years immediately preceding or following it. Nothing found elsewhere compels us, if the fatal story ever occurred, to assign it specifically to 1082.

What if, then, it is supposed that, if it occurred at all, it actually took place in the year 1083, when that year was nearly over—as, according to what has been said, it may indeed have done? In that case, the interval between it and the saint’s withdrawal into the wilderness of Chartreuse—which, according to what will be said, occurred in 1084 around the feast of Saint John the Baptist—would not have been approximately two years, but a much shorter period. The saint could have spent that time settling his affairs and preparing what he considered suitable for carrying out his plan.

If even that period appears too long to have been spent by the saint in settling his affairs and preparing what was necessary for embracing the eremitical life, it can be shortened further by postponing the Parisian prodigy even until the year 1084, since, according to what has already been said, it did not necessarily occur before that year.

However the matter may stand, it does not follow from what the anonymous chronographer of the first five Carthusian priors, or the older biographer of our saint, records that an interval of approximately two years intervened between the year in which the saint went into the wilderness of Chartreuse and the date of the Parisian prodigy.

For the present, and not without reason in view of what has already been said, we shall adopt the position of our Carthusian anonymous writer to this extent: when our saint left Reims in order to bid farewell to the world, he withdrew directly into the wilderness of Chartreuse—that is, he went to Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, by whom, as will be shown below, he was led into it.

### 414

Yet before doing this, the saint seems to have visited a solitude different from the wilderness of Chartreuse and to have remained there for some time.

Various funeral epitaphs of the saint provide grounds or a basis for this opinion, as does Mabillon in the *Annals* of his Benedictine order, book LXVI, no. 66. Speaking there of our saint, who, on approaching Chartreuse, is said—if Blomenvenna has correctly recorded the matter from Henry of Kalkar—to have consulted a hermit of great reputation on the way, Mabillon records the following:

> “No one has yet discovered, not even by conjecture, who that hermit of great reputation was whom Bruno consulted on his way to Chartreuse. I once conjectured that it was Stephen of Muret, who at that time was living the eremitical life with his companions at Muret among the Limousins, not without great renown. But certain documents lead me to believe that the famous hermit was none other than Robert, abbot of Molesme.  
>   
> “In the archive of his monastery there is a charter of Rainard of Bar-sur-Aube and John of Lantages, by which they grant to the church of Molesme ‘land at Sicca-Fontana, partly already leveled by human labor,’ with the approval of Count Valens of Brienne and Bar-sur-Aube, whose ‘holding’ it was.”

### 415

> “When the church of that place, which Peter and Lambert, disciples of Master Bruno, who were with him in that territory and lived as hermits, had built, was dedicated by Lord Robert, bishop of Langres, in honor of the blessed ever-virgin Mary, and its atrium was blessed, the aforesaid count, Rainard himself, and Acelenus were present with many others.”

From this it is understood that Bruno lived for some time as a hermit at Sicca-Fontana—a place in the diocese of Langres, in the archdeaconry of Bar-sur-Aube—with the aforesaid Peter and Lambert, his disciples, and that he could have consulted Robert, abbot of Molesme, who at that time was of great renown and was widely living the eremitical life.

No chronological note is attached to the aforesaid document; but the year 1081 has been written in a later hand in the margin, and that date may fit Bruno’s withdrawal extremely well. Nor is it an obstacle that Robert, bishop of Langres, himself a disciple of Bruno, who dedicated the church at Sicca-Fontana, did not occupy that see before 1085. For this dedication took place some time after Bruno’s departure.

Certainly, when Bruno was traveling from Reims to Grenoble, the monastery of Molesme—and therefore Robert, its abbot—lay in his path. No hermit or monk who was striving for perfection in those regions would have failed to wish to have Robert as a guide and leader.”

So far Mabillon. Among the funeral epitaphs, from which I infer that the saint did not withdraw directly to Chartreuse when he bade farewell to the world, the first is that of Saint Peter of Troyes. It is numbered 47 among those to be printed and reads as follows:

> As the epitaph says, the wise man Bruno conquered the world’s temptations,  
> Carrying out the commands of God.  
> He despised great riches, and had no resources of his own;  
> But whatever he could, he bestowed upon his brothers.  
> He fled this life, became a monk, and then a hermit.  
> Because he thus abstained, he merited the kingdoms of heaven, etc.

### 416

The second, which is the epitaph of the nuns of Saint John the Baptist and will be reprinted as no. 68, includes these two verses among several others:

> Bruno still lives; life is entrusted to him by the Father.  
> He was first a cleric, became a monk, and then a hermit.

The third, to be reprinted as no. 139, with which Albert, a canon of the Church of Beverley, honored the saint, consists only of a hexameter and a pentameter:

> May the piety of Christ grant you, Bruno, what you have deserved:  
> In this life you first became a monk, and then a hermit.

The fourth, numbered 143 among those to be reprinted, which the church of Saint Peter of Castres inscribed to the saint, is composed chiefly of these verses:

> Bruno was the glory of the righteous and the sole comfort of the guilty  
> While alive, and their equal grief in death.  
> The ornament of the entire clergy and also a model of truth,  
> Death, a grief, snatched him away when the Father died.  
> First made a monk and then a hermit,  
> May the highest grace of God be favorable to him.

Thus, as is apparent from these funeral epitaphs just quoted, the saint first assumed and practiced the life of a monk [Col. 0252B] before embracing the eremitical life. This is presumably how, as the writers of the *Literary History of France* observe in vol. IX, p. 237, the authors of those epitaphs intended to designate the period during which the saint inhabited a solitude before withdrawing into the wilderness of Chartreuse—or, what amounts to the same thing, to indicate that our saint inhabited a solitude different from the Carthusian wilderness and lived a monastic life there before hiding himself in the latter.

### 417

The writers just mentioned agree with them in substance, adding also the place where the saint spent some time before withdrawing into the wilderness of Chartreuse: they say that it was the solitude of Sicca-Fontana.

The evidence brought forward by Mabillon in the passage cited above makes it quite probable, not to say certain, that the saint lived there for some considerable time before going to Chartreuse, although Mabillon is also cited in the margin.

But if it is understood from that evidence that the saint lived there not a monastic but only an eremitical life, how can this agree with the various funeral epitaphs just quoted, by which we are taught that Bruno first became a monk and then a hermit? This certainly appears to be a difficult and very tangled knot.

But what if the saint is said in the aforesaid epitaphs to have first become a monk through the monastic habit which he put on as soon as he hid himself in the solitude of Sicca-Fontana, and afterward to have become a hermit through the manner of life which he subsequently embraced there?

What if he actually lived as a monk in the abbey of Molesme, near the solitude of Sicca-Fontana, having also assumed the monastic habit, and then devoted himself to the eremitical life both in the solitude of Sicca-Fontana and in the wildernesses of Chartreuse and Calabria?

The funeral epitaphs just mentioned and the vow to assume the monastic habit which, as has been shown, the saint had previously made, make me think that this last possibility is extremely probable. To establish either alternative, there also appears to be evidence in the funeral epitaph, numbered 40 among those to be reprinted, by which the monks of the Church—or abbey—of Molesme, or Molesmien, honored the saint.

For these monks state that Saint Bruno had been very closely associated with them:

> “By our verses, we who dwell at Molesme, adding you who are at the Tower, inform you that, for Lord Bruno, your patron and our very close associate, we celebrated the solemn Masses for thirty days; we also entered the anniversary of his death in the catalogue of our brothers.”

### 418
