But, you will say, although the chronographer of the first five Carthusian priors, or the older biographer of our saint, and the more recent writers do not prevent the Parisian prodigy—if it ever occurred—from being postponed beyond the year 1082, nevertheless, according to what they write, our saint seems to have withdrawn directly to Chartreuse when he bade farewell to the world, and not to have remained elsewhere for some time before going there.

For, to begin with our older biographer, immediately after recounting the address that the saint delivered upon seeing the horrifying spectacle, he continues:

> “Addressing and exhorting himself and certain others in these or similar words and sentiments, he himself and six other good men resolved to renounce the world and its pomp with him, to seek a suitable deserted wilderness in which to perform perpetual penance, and there, having abandoned all the riches, pleasures, and honors of this world, each to take up his cross and follow the naked Christ along the narrow way that leads to life, while abandoning the broad and spacious way that leads the lovers and followers of the world to the punishments of the damned.  
>   
> “And therefore, because they had heard of the holiness of Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, who is believed to have previously been for some time a fellow student of that same Master Bruno in the schools, they resolved, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, to approach the aforesaid holy bishop together and seek his help and advice, so that in his diocese—which they had heard abounded in many deserted mountains—they might merit to obtain a suitable place where they could put their holy and salutary purpose into effect.  
>   
> “Thus the seven holy men mentioned above, for the aforesaid reason and led by the Holy Spirit, came to the aforesaid holy bishop.”

Since, after the address delivered by Saint Bruno following the prodigy, he immediately adds the decision of Bruno and his companions to approach Hugh, and then their approach to that holy bishop, without mentioning any intervening event whatsoever, he plainly indicates that, after the Parisian prodigy, the saint went directly to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and did not remain elsewhere for any length of time beforehand. Anyone who considers the matter attentively will, I think, readily recognize this.

### 419

Blomenvenna indicates the same thing no less clearly in the *Life* of our saint which he composed.

After recounting the address with which Bruno, having seen the spectacle of the condemned doctor, first addressed certain of his disciples and close companions whom he had summoned to himself and exhorted to undertake penance, he introduces the two Stephens—one of Bourges and the other of Die, whom he includes among these men—as speaking in the following manner:

> “Not far from the city of Valence, to which our monastery of Saint-Rufus is attached near the banks of the Rhône, at the boundary of the diocese of Die, lies the city of Grenoble, and in it the blessed Hugh, bishop of that city. We have often seen him and know him to be a holy, just, upright, God-fearing man, trained and perfected in every virtue.  
>   
> “He has in his diocese very lofty mountains containing many deserted places, separated from all human passage and company and therefore exceedingly suitable for doing penance. Moreover, since by his example and admonitions he invites everyone to penance, he will rejoice at our arrival and fulfill your desire if we approach him. For he is extraordinarily devout, kind, and merciful.  
>   
> “Since we have often traveled the road by which one goes to him, we can lead you to him.”

He then explains how Bruno and his companions, after all had soon approved the advice contained in these words, went to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, once they had settled their affairs and had consulted on the way a hermit of great renown. He makes no mention whatsoever of their having stayed elsewhere before approaching Hugh.

Moreover, in the *Life* of the saint which he composed, Puteanus agrees almost exactly with Blomenvenna—apart from the fact that his failure here to mention the hermit whom they consulted on the way is irrelevant. Consequently, according to both of these biographers of our saint and according to the other writer mentioned in the preceding section—the chronographer of the first five Carthusian priors—when Bruno and his companions renounced the world and sought the wilderness, they went directly to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, by whom, as will be shown below, they were led not long afterward into the solitude of Chartreuse.

420. But since Puteanus and Blomenvenna composed their works on the saint only in the sixteenth century, and since the chronicler of the first five priors of the Carthusian order, who is older than they, flourished only after more than a hundred years had already elapsed since Bruno’s death, all are too recent and too remote from Bruno’s withdrawal into the Carthusian wilderness ever to be able to establish with certain and unquestionable credibility what they relate about him—much less when they conflict with an older monument of unimpaired authority [Col. 0254D]. The latter situation, however, obtains here. For the ancient charter of the monastery of Molesme, which Mabillon praises in the words quoted above, reports that, before concealing himself in the Carthusian wilderness, the saint had led the eremitical life for some time in the solitude of Séche-Fontaine; and this ancient monument, contemporary with our saint, does not appear spurious or forged on any ground. Furthermore, Guigo, the fifth prior of the Carthusian order, supports the view that, when the saint took leave of the world, he did not withdraw directly into the Carthusian wilderness, in the Life of St. Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, which he himself composed. For when he recounts Bruno’s approach, together with his companions, to Hugh—see the words transcribed from it below in no. 422—he writes of them as follows: [Col. 0255A] “They were seeking a place suitable for the eremitical life, but had not yet found one.” By these words he clearly indicates that Bruno and his companions, before they came to Hugh, had already undertaken to find a place suitable for the eremitical life. Hence, first, it seems contrary to fact that Bruno and his companions, when after the miracle they were on the point of bidding farewell to the world, should, as the biographers soon to be cited relate, have decided by common agreement to go to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, in order to obtain from him a place suitable for the eremitical life in the mountains of the diocese of Grenoble. Secondly, it becomes plausible from this very consideration that our saint, before approaching Hugh, had spent some time in the solitude of Séche-Fontaine, in order to investigate whether that place was suitable for the eremitical life [Col. 0255B]. Accordingly, whatever weight may be attached to the aforesaid charter of the monastery of Molesme, praised by Mabillon, is increased, since it reports that this is what occurred.

421. The funeral inscriptions praised above also support this conclusion. If our saint, when he took leave of the world, had withdrawn directly to the Carthusian monastery, where he led the eremitical life, they cannot be understood as corresponding sufficiently well to the truth. When everything has therefore been carefully weighed, it scarcely appears doubtful that, when the saint renounced the world, he did not go directly to the Carthusian monastery but first withdrew elsewhere. The place he then sought and inhabited for some time was indeed the solitude of Séche-Fontaine, as the monastery of Molesme’s charter, praised above by Mabillon [Col. 0255C], establishes. But for how long did Bruno remain there before going to the Carthusian wilderness or to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble? Nothing at all presents itself from which anything certain can be established on this point. Since the monks of the church or monastery of Molesme, adjacent to the solitude of Séche-Fontaine, call Bruno in the funeral inscription by which they commemorated him “their most familiar companion,” it seems quite plausible that he remained in that solitude—or even in the monastery of Molesme itself, where according to what has been said he served as a monk—for a sufficiently long period to become so well known to them. What if, then, he stayed there for about a year, or even longer, and only afterward, when he discovered that the place to which he had devoted himself was less suitable for the eremitical life, went to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, in order to obtain from him a more suitable one? This certainly seems to me far from implausible. Now, since these things are so, and since, as I established above, the saint certainly did not go into the wilderness after leaving the world before the year 1081, while, as will be shown below, he entered the Carthusian wilderness no later than around the feast of St. John the Baptist in 1084, it follows that either in 1081 or in one of the two following years he first withdrew, after abandoning the world, into the solitude which, according to what has been said, was undoubtedly Séche-Fontaine. I have been unable to discover anything else by which to determine more closely the time at which this occurred. Let us now proceed to examine the other events that followed.

§ XXV. The saint’s approach to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble; what sort of companions he had; and whether he had by then been ordained a priest

[Col. 0256A]

Since our saint and his six companions, whom he had apparently inspired with the desire for the eremitical life, had not yet found a place sufficiently suitable for this kind of life, despite having diligently searched for one, they finally came to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, in order to obtain from him some place suited to their purpose. They had heard of his outstanding virtues and the holiness of his life. It is permissible to gather this and several other facts from Guigo, the fifth prior of the Carthusian order, who, in the Life of that holy bishop published by us in the first volume of April, no. 11, writes as follows:

“While St. Hugh was occupied with these matters, behold, before three years had yet been completed in the episcopate after his return from the monastery, Master Bruno arrived—a man renowned for religion and learning, almost a living likeness of integrity, gravity, and every form of maturity. He had as companions Master Landuin, who afterward became prior of the Carthusian monastery; two Stephens, one of Burgundy and the other of Die (they had been canons of Saint Rufus, but, with the abbot’s approval, had joined him out of a desire for the solitary life); also Hugh, whom they called the Chaplain, because he alone among them performed the office of a priest; and two laymen, whom we call lay brothers, Andrew and Guarinus. They were seeking a place suitable for the eremitical life, but had not yet found one. Drawn both by this hope and by the sweet fragrance of his holy way of life, they came to the holy man. He received them, treated them, and enabled them to attain their desire, not only gladly but also reverently. With his counsel, help, and company, they entered the solitude of the Chartreuse and built there. At about that time he had seen in a dream, in that same solitude, God constructing a dwelling for His honor, and also seven stars guiding him on his journey. These seven men were the seven stars.”

423. An anonymous writer, who compiled from the chronicle of the first five priors of the Carthusian order, so often praised above, and from other sources, a brief history of the Carthusian order, inserted by Martène in volume VI of his *Amplissima Collectio*, col. 151 onward, also supplies a narrative in which, as Guigo does here, he relates both our saint’s approach to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and the vision divinely granted to Hugh. Yet he differs somewhat from the narrative of Guigo transcribed above, although he declares both that this account was drawn from Guigo by the chronicler of the first five priors of the Carthusian order and that this chronicler used Guigo’s very words. I wish to transcribe here the passages relevant to our subject, since they offer several matters worthy of annotation. I begin with the part in which he describes the saint’s approach to Hugh. He writes as follows:

“Master Bruno arrived, a religious man renowned for learning, almost a living likeness of integrity, gravity, and every form of maturity. He had as companions men sharing his purpose: Master Landuin, who afterward became prior of the Carthusian monastery [Col. 0257A], and two Stephens, one of Burgundy and the other of Die. Both had been canons of Saint Rufus; but, moved by the desire for the solitary life and with their abbot favoring them, they had joined him. Also Hugh, whom they called the Chaplain because he alone among them exercised the priesthood; and two laymen, whom they call lay brothers, namely Andrew and Guarinus. They were seeking a place suitable for the eremitical life and had not yet found one. While the aforementioned bishop was keeping vigil and reflecting on the vision of the seven stars—which had been granted to him shortly before—the aforesaid seven men appeared: Master Bruno with his six companions just named. As these seven fell at the feet of the holy man, the holy man himself reflected in his heart upon the seven stars he had seen in the vision. He kindly raised them and gave them the kiss of peace; and, after asking and carefully learning why they had come, he said to them: ‘I know the place prepared for you by God.’ He led them, not without great labor, to the place where the seven stars had stood, and said: ‘Behold your place.’”

424. Thus the anonymous author of the aforementioned *History of the Carthusian Order* differs somewhat from both Guigo and the anonymous writer who incorporated the words of Guigo just quoted into his little work, and also from the chronicler of the first five priors of the Carthusian order, or the earlier biographer of our saint, as will be clear to anyone who compares the words of the latter, likewise quoted immediately above, with Guigo’s words. Listen now to how he reports that the vision divinely granted to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, occurred when our saint approached this holy bishop. Guigo, and the aforementioned anonymous writer following him, mention the vision only briefly in these words:

“The aforementioned bishop (namely Hugh) had seen at about that same time—that is, when St. Bruno and his companions were approaching him—in a dream the Lord constructing in that same solitude of the Chartreuse a dwelling for His honor, and also seven stars offering him guidance on the journey.”

That writer, however, immediately before the words quoted above, gives a fuller account, adding several details absent from Guigo, in the following manner:

“Accordingly, the seven men described below—Bruno, namely, and his six companions—came for the aforesaid reason, namely to find a place suitable for the eremitical life, to the aforementioned holy bishop, Hugh of Grenoble, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. When they entered the aforesaid city, Grenoble, it happened that the aforementioned holy bishop fell asleep in his chamber. In his sleep he saw a holy vision: behold, seven stars fell before his feet, and afterward ascended through various mountains and many deserts to a certain very rugged and remote place, called the Chartreuse; and there they stood.”

Thus far the author of the praised *History of the Carthusian Order*. Since, moreover, when he was about to give the narrative transcribed in the preceding paragraph, he indicates that he would reproduce the very words of the chronicle of the first five priors of the Carthusian order, he seems to have had before him a copy of this little work [Col. 0258A] enlarged with additions which a later writer, who added them, considered plausible, but which, in my opinion, he did not find in the older author or monument.

425. I infer this concerning the latter point chiefly because he says that the vision was granted to St. Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, only when Bruno and his six companions were entering the city of Grenoble for the first time. This does not agree sufficiently with Guigo’s narrative. For this biographer of St. Hugh reports that the event occurred not when Bruno and his companions arrived in Grenoble, but “at about that same time,” so that, in view of Guigo’s authority, the vision granted to St. Hugh preceded the saint’s entry into the city of Grenoble by some interval.

The more recent biographers of our saint—namely Puteanus, Blomenvenna, and Surius—embellish the saint’s approach to St. Hugh of Grenoble and the vision granted to Hugh with various details not expressed either by Guigo or by our earlier biographer. On the time at which these events occurred, they speak more plausibly and more consistently with Guigo’s narrative. Puteanus reports that the vision was granted to Hugh during the night preceding Bruno’s and his companions’ arrival in the city of Grenoble; Blomenvenna, and Surius following him, say that it occurred when our saint and his six companions were traveling toward Grenoble. Because of what I said in no. 23, I transcribe here all Blomenvenna’s words concerning that vision and our saint’s approach to St. Hugh [Col. 0258C]. First, then, he relates that, as our saint was traveling toward Grenoble, he consulted on the way with a hermit of great renown and continued the journey; then he adds what concerns our present subject.

426. His words are as follows:

“At that same time, St. Hugh the bishop had seen in a dream God constructing in the solitude of the Chartreuse a dwelling for His honor. He had also seen seven golden stars arranged in the form of a crown, slightly raised above the earth, and differing from the other stars fixed in the firmament in position, motion, color, and brilliance, guiding him on his journey. While he was reflecting upon the vision, the aforementioned men—namely Bruno [Col. 0258D] and his companions—appeared before the doors of the episcopal palace. The venerable Guigo recalls this matter in the Life of the same St. Hugh in these words: ‘Master Bruno,’ he says, ‘a religious man renowned for learning, almost a living likeness of integrity, gravity, and every form of maturity, is here. He had the companions named above.’ They were seeking a place suitable for the eremitical life, but had not yet found one.

“When the bishop was informed that the aforementioned men, requesting an audience with him, were waiting before the doors, he immediately ordered them to be admitted. When they entered and humbly prostrated themselves at his feet, he bestowed on them the blessing they desired. After he had raised them and they had sat down together with him, he carefully asked the reason for their arrival. As Bruno recounted what had happened at Paris amid the outcries against the aforesaid teacher, and also their mutual agreement concerning the practice of the solitary life, asking in addition for assistance in finding a place suitable for penance, the bishop was first astonished at the novelty of the matter. Yet, turning his attention to their conversion, the steadfastness of their minds, the usefulness of their arduous purpose—which would benefit many—and its correspondence with the vision shown to him, he embraced the men with great joy and received them, not only gladly but also reverently, and treated them kindly. When the Spirit of the Lord had entered into him, he understood the vision, recounted to them in order everything he had seen, and declared that the place they were seeking had already been divinely revealed to him.”

427. “He did not hesitate to recognize in the number of seven stars the seven men who despised earthly things, sought the deserts, and shone like stars through their desire for eternal things.”

Thus far Blomenvenna, who, as I have already noted, preserves the tradition that the vision was granted to St. Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, not for the first time when Bruno and his companions were already entering the city of Grenoble, but somewhat earlier, when they were still traveling toward it. In fact, it is exceedingly plausible that the vision occurred either at that time or certainly, as Puteanus reports on the basis of what has been said, during the night immediately preceding the arrival of the saint and his companions in the aforementioned city, and not for the first time when they were already entering Grenoble. This is so both because, according to what has been said, that interpretation agrees better with Guigo’s narrative, and because the vision, having been granted to Hugh in a dream, most probably occurred at night, whereas the saint and his companions most probably entered Grenoble during the day, not at night.

Let us now examine the other details that Blomenvenna and others relate about the vision granted to Hugh. According to this writer, when Bruno and his companions had already arrived in Grenoble and were standing before the doors of the episcopal palace, Bishop Hugh reflected upon the vision divinely granted to him. The very brief *History of the Carthusian Order*, written by Martène in volume VI of his *Amplissima Collectio* and, as has been said, of uncertain provenance, likewise records this, as does Puteanus in no. 29 of his *Life of our Saint*. And indeed, whether the vision occurred for the first time when Bruno and his companions entered Grenoble, or during the night immediately preceding their entry [Col. 0259D], it certainly does not appear implausible that Hugh thought about it when they were already standing at the door and requesting an audience with him.

428. Although Guigo, in the words quoted above, merely implies that Bishop Hugh reflected upon the vision granted to him while Bruno and his six companions were already standing before him, nothing prevents Hugh from having thought about the same vision both then and a little earlier, before Bruno and his companions had yet been brought into the bishop’s presence. Nevertheless, since according to what has been said the vision was most probably not granted to Hugh for the first time when Bruno and his companions entered Grenoble, and since it is likewise uncertain whether it occurred during the night immediately preceding the saint’s entry into the city of Grenoble or somewhat earlier, and since, if the latter was the case, there is no reason to suggest that Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, meditated upon the vision while the saint was still waiting for an audience at the palace door, it cannot be asserted with certainty that the holy bishop actually did so at that time. Such a claim has no foundation in the authority either of Guigo or of any other ancient writer.

For the same reason, it appears to me highly doubtful that the seven stars which appeared to Hugh in the aforesaid vision were such as Blomenvenna reports them to have been in the words transcribed immediately above—Puteanus in no. 29 of his *Life of the Saint* agreeing with him on this point—or that they presented themselves to Hugh for viewing in the manner assigned to them either by these two biographers of St. Bruno or by the very brief *History of the Carthusian Order*, repeatedly mentioned above. It is likewise doubtful whether one of them, representing St. Bruno, was brighter than the others. I find this detail recorded not indeed by Blomenvenna or Puteanus, but by Zacharias Benedictus in his *Life of our Saint*, composed in an elaborate style at the beginning of the sixteenth century on the basis of what has been said, and by several other recent writers whom it is unnecessary to name here.

429. I wish to transcribe here all the verses in which that metrical biographer of the saint sings both of this matter and of the complete vision of the seven stars granted to Hugh, since I hope this will not be displeasing to the reader. They run as follows:

“Now Bruno was drawing near, accompanied by his company,

to Grenoble, once called Misora by the ancients.”

And after several intervening lines:

“Then, from the highest ether, the heavens sent down

seven stars; one of them moved more brightly than the others,

and from the rising of Phoebus seemed

to direct its steps toward the lofty dwelling

of Bishop Hugh, and to climb the rugged mountain

which was nearby and rested upon a lofty rock.

While he was lying in sweet sleep,

he beheld these things; and after awakening from sleep,

he turned the whole event over in his mind,

weighed it, and weighed it again.

‘Good God,’ he said, ‘what does this wondrous sign mean?

What, I ask, do these seven stars portend for the world?’

While he was thinking about these things more deeply,

the teacher, accompanied by his six companions,

approached the city and entered the bishop’s house.

He declared that he wished to see the bishop

in a private conversation. He was led inside

to the inner chambers of the hall,

and his companions likewise.

Bruno bent his knees and kissed

the consecrated hands, and thus began to speak, etc.”

430. Not only are the details just mentioned concerning the vision granted to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble—reported by Puteanus, Blomenvenna, Zacharias Benedictus, and other recent writers without an ancient guarantor—of highly uncertain and doubtful credibility [Col. 0261A], but so too is what Blomenvenna asserts (see his words transcribed immediately above) concerning the account given by Bruno to Bishop Hugh of the mournful story of the condemned Parisian teacher.

Apart from the fact that, as has already been shown above, it is not certain that this event ever occurred, I find no other writer at all who was capable of lending the matter any credibility recording in writing that our saint told Hugh about the fatal miracle. Whatever the truth may be, from the manner in which both Blomenvenna and the other writers already praised relate the aforesaid vision of the seven stars and its details, it is plainly entirely consistent with the truth—as I established in § 22—that in historical matters or events the substance of the event must be distinguished from its circumstances, and that it sometimes happens that later writers embellish with circumstances of their own choosing those events which they found in ancient writers either almost entirely stripped of circumstances or completely without them [Col. 0261B], adding details which they considered plausible.

In the Life of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, Guigo (see his words quoted in no. 422) reports only the vision in which Hugh saw in a dream God constructing in the solitude of the Chartreuse a dwelling for His honor or majesty, and in addition seven stars offering themselves to Hugh as guides on the journey leading to it. The writers cited immediately above added to the substance of this event the manner and time of the vision, as well as other details. Yet all these details, individually and collectively, are not plausible, contrary to what those writers seem to have thought, as is clear from what has already been said. I also find, however, a writer who says that this vision was granted to someone other than Hugh, bishop of Grenoble. That writer is Gaufred, prior of Vigeois.

431. This matter must now be examined, so that I may fulfill the promise made above. This writer, in his *Chronicle*, published by Labbe in volume II of the *Bibliotheca nova librorum manuscriptorum*, p. 289, records the following:

“The most holy order of the Carthusians began at this time, namely in the year 1086 (rather, according to what will be said below, in 1084), through Bruno, a holy man, a German by nation, from Cologne Agrippina, a master in theology, together with six other venerable men, in the diocese of Grenoble. This order, according to Blessed Bernard, holds primacy among all ecclesiastical orders, not by reason of its age but by the strength of its holiness; hence he calls it the most beautiful column of the Church. Pope Victor, while he was still a Cassinese monk, saw in a dream God constructing in the solitude of the Chartreuse a dwelling for His honor, and it is said that he possessed the gift of prophecy.”

Gaufred flourished in the twelfth century, and consequently fewer than a hundred years, or perhaps not even fifty, had elapsed since the death of St. Bruno. It might therefore appear that he had sufficiently well investigated what he committed to writing concerning Bruno and the order founded by him. But whatever may be thought of Gaufred’s age or authority, in this matter we must stand by Guigo, the fifth prior of the Carthusian order and biographer of St. Hugh.

Apart from the fact that he was a contemporary and intimate associate of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, whatever Guigo records in the Life of Hugh, composed by him at the command of the supreme pontiff, he either saw with his own eyes or learned from eyewitnesses or from St. Hugh himself. It is therefore exceedingly likely that he also heard from Hugh himself what he writes concerning the vision mentioned above.

“But,” you will say, “even if this is so, it still does not follow that Gaufred should attribute to Pope Victor III, formerly the Cassinese monk Desiderius, the vision in which he saw God constructing for Himself a dwelling in the solitude of the Chartreuse. For God could have revealed to both Victor and Hugh, in two different visions, what He intended to do in the solitude of the Chartreuse.”

432. I admit that this is how the matter stands. But that Gaufred is also speaking of the one and the same vision of which Guigo speaks is clear from the fact that the following words—“He saw God constructing in the Carthusian solitude a dwelling for His honor”—with which Gaufred describes it, occur almost verbatim in Guigo’s narrative given in no. 422. Indeed, it seems to follow from this that Gaufred borrowed those words from the Life of St. Hugh written by Guigo, or at least from another work into which they had been transferred from it, and that, through some unknown error, he wrongly attributed to Pope Victor the vision which those words ascribe to that holy bishop.

Moreover, as the anonymous Carthusian author of the fourth book of the *Annals of the Order*, not yet published, rightly observes in the words transcribed here in no. 303, Gaufred reveals something new and unheard of in doing this. For among the writers who mention Pope Victor there is not one who records that the vision under discussion was granted to him. Furthermore, why, I ask, would the Lord have granted such a vision to Victor while he was still a Cassinese monk, when God granted it to Hugh both to reveal to Hugh where a place for the eremitical life was to be assigned to Bruno and his companions, who were about to come to Grenoble, and to stir Hugh to give Bruno and his companions favor and assistance? This may properly be inferred from the words with which Guigo introduces and then follows the vision he narrates.

433. For immediately after the words transcribed in no. 422, in which he relates the vision divinely granted to Hugh, he adds:

“And these seven men were those seven. Therefore he gladly embraced the counsels not only of these men but also of those who succeeded them, and until his death he always supported the inhabitants of the Chartreuse with counsel and benefactions.”

By these words he clearly indicates that St. Bruno and his six companions were designated by the seven stars that had appeared to St. Hugh in the vision. Hence it came about that the holy bishop of Grenoble, who had been inwardly persuaded of this by God, remained beneficent throughout his life not only toward St. Bruno and his companions but also toward their successors.

Nor was it for any other reason that Hugh assigned the Chartreuse to Bruno and his companions as their dwelling, joined them as they traveled there, and provided help and assistance for the construction of the necessary buildings. Guigo likewise indicates this clearly enough, as will be evident to anyone who considers his words transcribed in no. 422.

Now, since this is so, divine goodness certainly had reason to offer Hugh the vision narrated by Guigo. But why, I ask again, would it have shown a similar favor to Pope Victor, who was still a Cassinese monk? This would plainly have been of no use whatever—for Victor, as I shall establish below, should not be thought to have confirmed the order founded by Bruno—and consequently it appears from this also that the event did not occur.

One could now discuss here St. Hugh’s benevolence toward St. Bruno and his companions, the fact that Hugh brought them into the Chartreuse, and several other matters related to this subject. But these will be treated more conveniently in the following section, when I have clarified here a few further points concerning the saint and his companions.

“Now he had as companions” (these are Guigo’s words concerning St. Bruno as he approached Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, already quoted in no. 422) “Master Landuin, who afterward became prior of the Chartreuse; two Stephens, one of Burgundy and the other of Die (they had been canons of Saint Rufus, but, with the abbot’s approval, had joined him out of a desire for the solitary life); also Hugh, whom they called the Chaplain, because he alone among them exercised the priestly office; and two laymen, whom we call lay brothers, Andrew and Guarinus.”

434. Thus, when the saint approached Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, he had six companions attached to him. Since all of them, together with the saint, sought a place suitable for the eremitical life—as Guigo establishes in the words quoted in no. 422—and since they had not yet found such a place when they came to Hugh, it seems that for some time all of them, together with our saint, had led the eremitical life in the solitude of Séche-Fontaine before going to Hugh in Grenoble.

Now, since in the charter of the monastery of Molesme, praised above from Mabillon and partly quoted, Peter and Lambert—whom Guigo does not count among the six companions who went with Bruno to Grenoble—are said to have been Bruno’s disciples in the solitude of Séche-Fontaine, it appears that, when he took leave of the world, the saint departed from Reims with more than six companions, or at least that, when he was already staying in the solitude of Séche-Fontaine, he probably had more companions attached to him: namely, the six listed above by Guigo, Peter and Lambert mentioned in the charter praised from Mabillon, and perhaps several others who remained in the solitude of Séche-Fontaine together with these two. Our saint later left that place with the companions enumerated by Guigo and went to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, in Grenoble, seeking a place more suitable for carrying out his purpose.

But did all these men belong to the clergy of Reims? The authors of the *Literary History of France*, volume IX, p. 236, plainly indicate that some of those who withdrew into the wilderness with the saint belonged to the clergy of Reims. Yet whether Peter and Lambert—who, according to what has been said, left Reims with the saint for the wilderness, or at least joined him when he was already staying in the solitude of Séche-Fontaine—truly belonged to that clergy, I do not know. As for the saint’s companions listed by Guigo, it is highly doubtful whether any of them belonged to the same clergy. This appears from the evidence I shall now present concerning each of them, in the order in which Guigo lists them above.

435. In Labbe, volume I of the *Bibliotheca nova librorum manuscriptorum*, p. 639, the oldest chronicle of the first four priors of the Carthusian order—of which a notice was given in no. 4 and following—contains a remarkable eulogy of Landuinus. It is composed in these words:

“Landuinus, a Tuscan by nation, from the city of Lucca, himself learned in both divine and human letters, presided over the Chartreuse for ten years. As he was traveling to Master Bruno, he fell into the hands of the schismatic Guitbert, which he greatly dreaded. Against his threats and promises, his deceits and violence, with divine grace assisting him, he remained steadfast and unbending in every way. When Guitbert died in his error, Landuinus mourned him with such tears that those standing around reproached him for grieving over one from whose perversity the goodness of Christ had liberated His Church. On the seventh day after Guitbert’s death, Landuinus himself also died and was buried in the monastery of Saint Andrew, at the foot of Mount Sirapto, near the castle where he had been captured and held in custody.”

Such is the eulogy of Landuinus in that very ancient and highly trustworthy monument. Yet it contains not even a word from which one might in any way infer that he belonged to the clergy of Reims [Col. 0264C]. On the contrary, since it says at the beginning of the eulogy transcribed above that he was a Tuscan by nation, he seems to have belonged to a clergy other than that of Reims.

Immediately after Landuinus, Guigo mentions the two Stephens, one from Burgundy and the other from Die. Since, according to the same Guigo, they were canons of Saint Rufus, they were regular canons and consequently certainly not clerics of the clergy of Reims. Meanwhile, listen to what the anonymous Carthusian writer so frequently praised above, author of the fourth book of the as-yet-unpublished *Annals of the Order*, says about these two canons, so that matters concerning them may be clarified further.

436. “Guigo,” he says, “simply calls them—the two Stephens—canons of Saint Rufus who, with their abbot’s approval, joined the holy Bruno out of a desire for the solitary life.”

But he does not say whether they came from Saint Rufus itself, the head of the entire order, or from one of the houses of that order. After the anonymous author of the *Life of St. Bruno* prefixed to his works—printed, as I established above, by Berthold Rembold—Surius writes that they were pupils of the monastery of Saint Rufus. This is not implausible, but he errs, together with his anonymous source, in saying that this monastery was then situated near Valence. For he introduces the aforesaid Stephens as speaking with St. Bruno in these words:

“Not far from Valence, where our monastery of Saint Rufus is situated, near the banks of the Rhône on the borders of the diocese of Die, from which one of us originated, lies the city of Grenoble,” and so forth.

It is certain, however, that the abbey of Saint Rufus, the head of the regular canons, was originally established outside the city of Avignon. Chopin, book II of *Monasticon*, title I, no. 1, says: “But, with the holy war against the Albigensians raging, the religious were forced to transfer their homes and hearths elsewhere, toward Valence in Dauphiné, where a larger monastery was erected under the name of Blessed Rufus.”

The Sammarthani and others state that this transfer took place only in 1210; others place it earlier. But this is irrelevant to us. Therefore, what is repeatedly read in Surius and others concerning the same monastery being situated near Valence must be corrected, since at the time when the Carthusian order was founded it still stood near Avignon.

In the place cited, the Sammarthani preserve a letter of Pope Urban II, dated 1096, in which the supreme pontiff confirms to the abbey of Saint Rufus outside the walls of Avignon the churches of Saint Mary within the city of Lyon and Saint Peter near Die.

437. “It could indeed be the case that both our Stephens were canons of the aforementioned church of Saint Peter of Die; but it is not established whether churches or priories of this kind, which they also called cells, admitted novices in those times for profession, or received already professed canons from the mother monastery at Avignon—as may be conjectured from the following example. Among the titles written before the year of Saint Bruno’s death, one reads: *Title of the brothers of Saint Rufus in the Costa of Saint Andrew, in the territory of the Allobroges* [Col. 0265C], near the metropolitan city of Vienne. In this title—which is among those to be reprinted, no. 14—the canons of that church speak as follows:

“‘We, brothers from the canons of Saint Rufus, residing in a certain cell of Saint Andrew, commonly called Costa, shall celebrate matins and Masses for seven consecutive days for the soul of the most devout Bruno. And, just as we shall give a prebend to one of our number for the consolation of his soul, so we shall have his name written in the catalogue of our brothers.’

“When they describe themselves as ‘brothers from the canons of Saint Rufus, residing in a certain cell of Saint Andrew,’ and so forth, they plainly indicate that they were dependants of the principal abbey of Saint Rufus. It is therefore more probable that our Stephens also came from it; and this seems rightly inferred from the words of our Guigo, in which he says that they ‘joined themselves to Saint Bruno with the abbot’s approval.’ The abbot can be no one other than the abbot of Saint Rufus at Avignon.

“Moreover, since the aforementioned canons, then inhabitants of the cell of Saint Andrew, conferred so great a benefit upon Saint Bruno and entered his name in the catalogue of their brothers, it is not an implausible conjecture that they granted this favor to the blessed man at the request of the two Stephens, once their fellow soldiers in the principal monastery of Saint Rufus, but then monks of the Carthusian order.”

Thus far our anonymous Carthusian annalist, who is chiefly striving here to establish two points: namely, that the principal monastery of the regular canons of Saint Rufus was situated near Avignon in Bruno’s time [Col. 0266A], and that two of its pupils were the two Stephens, the one of Bourges and the other of Die, companions of our Saint.

438. Against Surius, then, and against Puteanus and Blomenvenna, who preceded him and indicate, by a speech they attributed to one of the Stephens, that this monastery was then situated at Valence, he establishes the first point beyond doubt; as for the second, he at least renders it probable. Whatever monastery the two Stephens were pupils of, however, they were certainly regular canons and therefore—as is chiefly relevant here—plainly not from the clergy of Rheims, as I have already pointed out above.

It remains for us to provide some information, of whatever kind, about Hugh, who is named last among the companions who accompanied Saint Bruno to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble. Morotius places him sixth among the priors of the Grande Chartreuse in his *Chronological Theatre of the Sacred Carthusian Order*, and honors him with the following eulogy:

“‘Hugh, fourth of Bruno’s six fellow initiates when Bruno withdrew from the world, and distinguished from the others by the title of chaplain because, since they had not yet been ordained to the priesthood, he was responsible for sacred functions, governed the Chartreuse, begun at the beginning of his conversion, for two years, already weakened by old age. When that period had passed, he joyfully received the successor whom he had earnestly begged for, and lived on for seven years, during the whole of which time he prepared himself for eternity.’

“Guigo, the fifth prior of the Chartreuse, died in 1137. Therefore, if Morotius is reporting the truth here, Hugh prolonged his life until the year 1145, as will be clear to anyone considering the words of this writer just quoted. However the matter may stand [Col. 0266C], Morotius’s quoted words provide nothing from which one can in any way conclude that Hugh was from the clergy of Rheims. Since this cannot be proved from elsewhere either, the claim is highly doubtful, although at the same time there is nothing that would reasonably establish that Hugh belonged to another clergy rather than to that of Rheims.

“It is therefore very doubtful—as becomes clear from all the evidence just brought forward (for Andrew and Guarinus, being laymen, should not be mentioned here)—whether any of the companions whom the Saint took with him when he renounced the world and departed from Rheims belonged to the clergy of Rheims.”

439. The praised authors of the *Literary History of France* would not have asserted that several of these men were clerics of Rheims if they had considered that the Saint departed from the city of Rheims twice to migrate elsewhere: first, in order to avoid Archbishop Manasses, in the year 1076 or the following year, according to what has already been said; and second, in order to withdraw into the desert, after he had been restored at Rheims—Manasses having been expelled—to his former condition, or perhaps an even better one, in 1081 or the other year mentioned above.

Certainly, on the first occasion, but not likewise on the second, it is clear from the foregoing, and especially from the testimony of Guibert, abbot of Nogent, that the Saint had several clerics of Rheims as his companions. Moreover, Guigo’s words, transcribed above in no. 422, require still further discussion.

For since they say that Hugh, one of Saint Bruno’s companions [Col. 0267A], was called chaplain “because he alone among them performed the office of a priest,” one may now ask, first, whether the Saint and his other three clerical companions—namely, the two Stephens and Landuinus—were ever ordained to the priesthood; and second, whether the Saint, already at the time when he approached Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, had not yet been raised to that dignity.

As for Landuinus and the other of the two Stephens, namely Stephen of Bourges, although they may not yet have been priests when they came with Bruno to Grenoble, our anonymous Carthusian annalist seems to prove sufficiently well that they were later promoted to this dignity. I therefore transcribe here his words bearing on the matter:

[Col. 0267B]

440. “Later,” he says, “it must be entirely beyond doubt that Landuinus and Stephen of Bourges were raised to the dignity of the priesthood,” because, as he adds, “otherwise they could not have exercised the governance of souls within the order, as Landuinus did in the Grande Chartreuse, over which he presided after Saint Bruno, and Stephen of Bourges in the house of Majorevi, of which Guigo appointed him first prior.

“Nor can examples be brought forward of certain abbots who governed monasteries although they had never been priests. For at the time when the Carthusian order began, it had been decreed that no one should become an abbot unless he also became a priest, according to the decree issued at the Roman synod under Eugenius II, which expressly states that abbots must also have attained priestly honor [Col. 0267C]. This was renewed under Hugh and Robert, kings of the Franks, as may be seen among the canons of Abbo, abbot of Fleury, in chapter nineteen: ‘Let abbots who are not priests become priests or lose their prelacies,’ as the Council of Poitiers, held in 1078 by Hugh of Die, apostolic legate, had decreed; this was later inserted into the decretals.

“According to these decrees, Saint Bruno, instructing his followers, ordered that no one should be elected prior unless he could be promoted to the priesthood. Hence Guigo, describing the customs of the order as Saint Bruno had established them long before by word and example, declares that, after the prior’s death, the conventuals should ‘by the counsel of the greater and better among themselves elect one, either a priest or one who is to be promoted to the priesthood, who shall sing the principal Mass on the more solemn feasts and whenever a brother is to make his profession.’”

441. From these words it plainly appears that Landuinus and Stephen of Bourges were at some time ordained priests. As for Stephen of Die and Saint Bruno himself, whether that Stephen was ever a priest is highly doubtful, and nothing has appeared that could remove the doubt.

As for Bruno, however, even if he was not a priest when he approached Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, I am persuaded that he later became one by the baptism he conferred upon the son of Count Roger, observing all the Church’s ceremonies, as we shall see later [Col. 0268A]. Moreover, in his commentary on chapter 10 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, our Saint himself seems in some way to indicate that he had been a priest. For he writes there as follows:

“‘You must flee from the worship of idols, because the cup—that is, the blood of Christ—is a cup, I say, of blessing, through which we receive blessings of grace; for through the blood of Christ, if we receive it worthily, we are both freed from former sins and strengthened against those that are to come. We bless this cup, praising him because there has never been a cup of this kind which both freed from sins and strengthened us so that we would sin no more. Or, the cup of blessing means the cup which God himself blesses and consecrates; and we bless it through our ministry. For God accomplishes this through the priest, his minister.’”

Through these words Bruno speaks here in a manner in which he would not seem likely to have spoken had he not been a priest; and therefore he appears, in some fashion, to indicate that he was one.

442. But had he already been raised to that dignity when he approached Hugh, bishop of Grenoble? Guigo, in the passage cited above concerning Saint Bruno’s approach to Hugh at Grenoble, says:

“‘Master Bruno is present . . . . He had as companions Master Landuinus . . . . the two Stephens, of Bourges and of Die . . . . and also Hugh, whom they called Chaplain because he alone among them performed the office of a priest.’”

From these words, since in that very passage, where both Bruno and his companions are being discussed, Hugh alone is said to have performed the priestly office [Col. 0268C], it appears that we must conclude that our Saint had not yet been ordained when he approached Hugh.

Some, however, including our anonymous Carthusian annalist so frequently praised above, say that Guigo’s quoted words, in which Hugh alone is affirmed to have been a priest, seem to refer not to Saint Bruno himself but only to his companions. Since, they say, after listing the names of the clerical companions whom the Saint had with him, Guigo immediately adds of Hugh, “whom they called Chaplain because he alone among them performed the office of a priest,” the words “among them” seem to refer only to the clerical companions of the Saint and not also to Bruno.

That is their view. But I do not know whether this interpretation of Guigo’s words will appear sufficiently exact and suited to the author’s intention. Certainly the words “whom they called Chaplain” seem to be understood both of Saint Bruno, who called Hugh Chaplain, and of the Saint’s companions, Landuinus and the two Stephens. I therefore see no reason why the other two words, “among them,” should not likewise refer to Bruno as well as to his companions.

443. Furthermore, if Guigo’s complete wording is taken in the more obvious and natural sense, which this writer certainly followed, it seems to require us to understand him as speaking of a priesthood enjoyed at that time by Hugh alone, while the Saint and his other companions lacked it. Accordingly, if Guigo’s words are understood in the manner that appears more probable, our Saint seems not yet to have been ordained when he approached Hugh, bishop of Grenoble.

Unless, perhaps—and even this I scarcely dare assert—one wishes Guigo to have declared that Hugh alone performed the priestly office, not because he alone was a priest, but because he alone carried out the duties appropriate to a priest, while Bruno himself and his other companions abstained from them out of humility or for some other reason.

“But,” you will say, “in several funerary titles of the Church our Saint is called the wall of the Church, the light of the churches, and the pillar of the metropolitan church of Rheims, even before his withdrawal into the Carthusian desert; this is either expressly asserted or at least clearly suggested.”

I admit that this is so. But why could he not have been adorned with such titles because he was conspicuous both for his learning, by which he had instructed the pupils of the church of Rheims and of other churches, who flocked in great numbers to Rheims to hear him, and also for his virtue, by which he had long defended the church of Rheims against the impious efforts of Manasses, the simoniacal prelate?

Thus even from the honorary titles with which the Saint is adorned, whether in those funerary verses or elsewhere, no support can be added to the opinion that he had already been ordained when he approached Hugh, bishop of Grenoble. On the whole, therefore, it appears much more probable to me that he was not yet a priest at that time.

Let us now continue the sequence of events concerning the Saint.

## § XXVI. The Saint enters the desert of the Chartreuse: when this occurred

[Col. 0269C]

444. When Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, had informed Saint Bruno and the six companions named above that the desert or mountain of the Chartreuse was the place destined by God for them as a dwelling in which to lead the eremitical life and establish their home—having identified them with the seven stars divinely shown to him in a dream, and having related the vision in which he had seen God building himself a dwelling in that desert—and when he had also apparently urged them to choose that place as their habitation, they all showed themselves entirely ready both to obey the divine will and to withdraw into the dreadful solitude.

[Col. 0269D] They had spent little time recovering their bodies, exhausted by the journey, in the episcopal palace, where Hugh had most kindly arranged for their refreshment, when they set out toward the Chartreuse, taking Saint Hugh himself as their companion and guide. “For it was under the counsel, assistance, and companionship of that Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, that they entered the solitude of the Chartreuse and built there,” says Guigo concerning Saint Bruno and his companions in the passage cited above from the life of that holy bishop.

There seems no doubt that this most holy prelate arranged for the necessities both of that journey and of the construction and transport to the place of whatever houses or cells were required for himself, Bruno, and his companions in the desert of the Chartreuse. Zacharias Benedictus also plainly indicates that this was in fact done [Col. 0270A]. In his metrical *Life of our Saint*, after recounting events that, according to him, occurred between Saint Hugh and our Saint and his companions on the day before their withdrawal into the desert, he adds a description of the solitude of the Chartreuse. I transcribe here the verses in which he relates this:

445. When Jupiter brought the ether down upon the highest peaks,  
and the intervals of daylight returned with the new sun,  
the bishop orders horses and much food to be prepared,  
and various craftsmen to be summoned.  

Everything is ready; the craftsmen hurry through the buildings.  
Cement, bricks, and timber are carried as loads.  
The beasts send forth loud neighs beneath the heavy burden.  
Now all seek the mountains; the difficult track carries them  

toward the sunny summit. The hollow depths of the valley  
lie open; already from above they survey on their way  
the level land and the towers and towns all around.  
The procession of horses climbs over the hillocks,  

the grooms sweat and strive eagerly to proceed.  
At last they reach the highest summit.  
They see jagged rocks and cliffs terrifying on every side.  
There are no groves there, nor any trees bearing wood for construction.  

Hardly are there low green grasses and humble broom,  
with larches and firs, and pines stretching toward the stars.

Blomenvenna, although he makes no mention at all of the things Benedictus here says were prepared at the bishop’s command for the journey and for the dwelling to be established at the Chartreuse, nevertheless introduces the prelate Hugh explaining to Bruno and his companions what the solitude of the Chartreuse was like as they were about to enter it [Col. 0270C]:

“‘The place designated for you by God is a certain desert among very high mountains, and it is called the Chartreuse. It is spacious, indeed, but completely uninhabited [*non habitata*, “not inhabited”], accessible only to wild beasts and, because of the harshness of the place, almost unknown to human beings and to other domestic animals.

446. “‘It is surrounded on every side by high cliffs and crags, as though cut away, planted with barren trees, exceedingly cold, and covered with snow for most of the year. It is so precipitous, sterile, and unproductive that nothing there can be sown or harvested; the ascent to it is heavy and laborious, and the entrance difficult and dangerous, lying between two rocks of astonishing height which rise upward like straight lines and finally meet at the summit, so that to those entering they are a source of horror and terror.

“‘In its midst there is a small river called the Gnerus Mortuus, “the Dead Gnerus,” as though it were an image of death. Gathered from the mountains surrounding it on every side, it flows with great noise like a torrent or flood of waters. In short, the harshness of that place and its terror are so great that it might be called a prison or purgatory rather than a dwelling for human life.’”

Thus far Blomenvenna, borrowing nearly all of this, as he often does elsewhere, from Puteanus. And so, from Benedictus and Blomenvenna, and, if you wish, also from Puteanus, you now have, studious reader, a general account or description of the desert of the Chartreuse. A much more detailed account, extending to its principal features, is supplied by Innocent le Masson, mentioned several times above, in book I, chapter 2, of the work he entitled the *Annals of the Carthusian Order*, which he published in print at the Correrian press in 1687.

I wish to transcribe this account as well, since Masson had lived for several years in the Chartreuse itself and was therefore thoroughly familiar with the matters about which he writes, while his work is not generally in everyone’s hands. Thus each reader may have readily available a picture of what that famous desert is like—situated about ten miles, or three leagues, north of Grenoble, and first inhabited by our Saint. The description is given in these words:

[Col. 0271B]

447. “Our desert at that time, when the Saint withdrew into it, appeared much harsher than it does now; for it was entirely uncultivated and its approaches were extremely difficult.

“Forests occupied almost everything, but later they were cleared in many places and turned into sufficiently pleasant meadows. The form of this desert is like an elongated amphitheater, enclosed on every side by lofty cliffs. Its floor is much lower on the southern side and rises gradually in the form of hillocks overtopping one another, until at the place where the chapel of Saint Bruno stands it rises like a high mountain, immediately shut in by cliffs that are almost precipitous.

“On its slope the Carthusian house is now built, at a distance from that chapel requiring a walk of an hour and three quarters. In the lower and more depressed part of the floor of our naturally formed amphitheater, the part facing south, a torrent flows. It is first formed from springs bursting forth in various places throughout the desert and converging there; then, swollen by rainwater and melting snow descending from the highest cliffs, it commonly rivals moderate-sized rivers. When the rains are abundant, however, it equals great rivers.

“It also produces excellent fish, called rock trout. In the upper, northern part, it is enclosed by the cliff called *le Col*, on whose summit lies a broad and pleasant meadow, set upon that cliff like a diadem. On the right it has the cliff called Bovinant, and on the left another, at whose summit—for these cliffs rise one above another almost in steps—is the extremely high cliff called Alienard.

448. “On the eastern side rise extremely high cliffs, as though holding one another by the hand. Among them the first place belongs to the one called *le Grand-Son*, which in Latin means ‘the great summit,’ because it is considered the highest of all the cliffs. Thus, like walls, these cliffs extend until, at the place where the Carthusian bridge now stands, they fall away in a precipitous drop and open an entrance to the desert only thirty or forty feet wide.

[Col. 0272A] “For immediately another precipitous cliff rises on the other side of the torrent, so that the two cliffs appear to rise up and, becoming closer together higher above, almost rush into each other’s embrace. This is certainly a marvelous work of nature. A torrent flows between the two cliffs, and there stands the bridge by which access is given from the side of the city of Grenoble to the desert and the Carthusian house.

“In the same place the holy bishop Hugh also arranged for a small house to be built, so that a keeper might live there and grant or deny entrance to those wishing to enter. About halfway between that bridge and the Carthusian house stands the house of Correria, which in the customs of the Reverend Father Guigo is called the Lower House; there the procurator and lay brothers lived while attending to household affairs.

[Col. 0272B] “Between that bridge and the chapel of Saint Bruno, at the place where the Carthusian house was first built, there is a journey of one hour. From this one may infer the length of our amphitheater floor from south to north.

“Beyond the torrent lies a very pleasant meadow called Valombrey, enclosed by cliffs that gradually overtop one another and finally raise their heads toward the sky as though competing with one another. All of them are surpassed by the cliff called Charmanson, at whose summit a very broad meadow can be seen—one that those looking at the cliff from the Carthusian house could scarcely believe to exist, since its summit seems to terminate in the form of the teeth of some crag.

449. “But most of what lies beyond the torrent had not been granted to the first Fathers, and their boundaries were closed off by the torrent. That part was later given to the Carthusian house by devout laypeople, as will be explained more fully in its proper place in the second volume.

“Proceeding from the southern toward the western side, one immediately encounters very high cliffs separated from one another, between which a torrent flows toward the little town of Saint-Laurent-du-Pont. Along the bank of this torrent, a road has been opened with great labor, by removing or cutting through the rocks, or by blasting them with gunpowder, by which one reaches the Chartreuse from Saint-Laurent.

“From there the cliff comes into view on whose summit stands the grange called Chartrousette. We believe that the first Fathers kept agricultural operations and the raising of livestock there; for there are very extensive meadows and pastures, as well as certain fields that are plowed.

[Col. 0272D] “The cliffs continue in this way, like walls formed by rocks touching one another, until they reach the cliff above which we said the lofty Alienard rises, and they close the circle of our amphitheater.

“Running through it, as though cutting it in two, is a little stream that rises at the spring of Saint Bruno and also receives the waters of the neighboring cliffs. It carries them from north to south until it empties into the torrent.

“Moreover, in our amphitheater, naturally formed as we have said in an elongated shape, three distinct levels of elevation appear to those looking at it. On the lowest are green meadows; on the second are forests filled with ancient trees; these forests surround the place like an immense belt [Col. 0273A]. Finally, on the third level are cliffs which, with their uneven summits, resemble the jagged teeth of a saw, slightly separated from one another.”

This is the desert into which the Saint, while it was still entirely uncultivated, withdrew together with his six companions: Landuinus, the two Stephens—of Bourges and of Die—Hugh, Andrew, and Guarinus, with Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, accompanying them and providing, as it appears, the necessities both for their food and for the construction of dwellings in which they could live.

450. It plainly appears that, as soon as they had entered the desert, they set their hands to the work. I shall discuss this matter below; for now we must investigate only the time when the Saint and his companions approached Hugh, bishop of Grenoble; when, with this holy prelate accompanying them, they first entered the desert of the Chartreuse; and when they began to set their hands to building a monastery there.

Some place this event in the year 1084; others, on the contrary, contend for 1085 or even 1086. Baron, for his part, places the approach of our Saint and his companions to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and their entry into the Chartreuse, which followed not long afterward under Hugh’s leadership, in the year 1086 in his *Ecclesiastical Annals*, writing there for that year as follows:

“Since it was said above, from the acts of the life of Saint Hugh—that is, Hugh, bishop of Grenoble—that he was made bishop of Grenoble in the year 1080, but that two years later he went to the Cluniacs, where he remained for one year, and that he then returned to the episcopate and spent three years in it, you will find it clear that in the sixth year after his ordination, namely in the present year, he sought the Chartreuse with his companions.”

Thus the highly learned father of the ecclesiastical annals derived the date he assigns for the withdrawal of Saint Hugh and Saint Bruno with their companions into the desert from the acts of Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble—or rather from Guigo, the fifth prior of the Chartreuse, who was their author. Since this writer was contemporary with both Saint Hugh and Saint Bruno, and thoroughly familiar with matters concerning both of them, and since his reliability cannot reasonably be suspected or weakened on any ground, it will scarcely be possible not to agree with Baron, provided that he correctly interpreted Guigo. This must therefore now be examined.

451. Columbius, in his dissertation on the beginnings of the Carthusians, nos. 102 and following, first states that two different opinions are in circulation concerning the year in which Saint Bruno approached Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and withdrew into the desert of the Chartreuse: one belonging to the ancient Carthusians, and the other to Baron.

He asserts that the latter opinion, which derives from the acts of Saint Hugh, written by Guigo, and assigns the year 1086, is false, while the former, which maintains the year 1084, is true. He then adds:

“‘To make this clear, let us compare both opinions—namely, concerning the year of Saint Bruno’s withdrawal into the Chartreuse [Col. 0274A]—with Guigo’s words. Hugh speaks as follows: “Two years after his consecration”—which took place at Rome in 1080, as I shall show below—“having renounced everything, he became a monk of Casa-Dei of the Cluniac order. There he lived for one year as a novice. After this”—that is, after this year of novitiate, and therefore in the third year after his Roman consecration—“compelled by Gregory VII, he returned from the monastery into which he had entered fervently, more fervent still, keeping vigilant discernment in place of the cloister . . . justice in place of an abbot . . . and, in place of a congregation, either religious whom he never wished to lack, namely companions, or the universal Church . . . . He lived in this way,” that is, he seemed to himself to have a cloister, an abbot, and a congregation, “and behold, before three years had yet been completed in the episcopate after his return from the monastery, Master Bruno is present.”’

Thus far Guigo.

Baron interprets his words to mean that Hugh first spent two full years after his Roman consecration and the third in the monastery of Casa-Dei; then, after returning from Casa-Dei to Grenoble, he spent almost another three years in the episcopate before Bruno’s arrival. He therefore wishes Bruno to have come to him when he was not far from the end of the sixth year of his episcopate.

Nor does he think so without reason, and he interprets Guigo’s words accordingly. For if the ‘three years in the episcopate, which had not yet been completed,’ are considered to have elapsed after his return from the monastery of Casa-Dei, and if that return was preceded by the three years ‘after his consecration,’ as Guigo’s language seems at first sight to require, Hugh must be considered to have spent approximately six years, and no fewer, between his consecration and Bruno’s arrival.”

452. The author just cited affirms that Baron correctly interprets the words of Guigo, which Baron had quoted and which Columbius himself has now repeated, when they are considered according to the sense they offer at first sight, and that Saint Bruno’s withdrawal into the desert of the Chartreuse may reasonably be assigned to the year 1086.

Nevertheless, since he thinks that one ought to adhere to the opinion of the ancient Carthusians, who assigned this event to 1084, he contends that those words must be interpreted in another way than the one they appear at first sight to bear and than the one Baron actually gave them.

“‘But,’ he immediately adds after the words transcribed above, ‘nothing compels us to interpret Guigo as Baron did, namely to understand the expression “after his return from the monastery” as meaning “following his return from the monastery,” or “immediately, and not long after his return from the monastery,” with the phrase placed out of its proper position before the words “completed years.”

“‘The sentence will therefore be: “Behold, before three years in the episcopate had yet been completed, Master Bruno is present a short time after his return from the monastery.”

“‘But observe that the years said not yet to have been completed are years spent in the episcopate after his consecration and return from Rome, and devoted to episcopal care. For if you count the years from Hugh’s Roman consecration, three had already been completed and the fourth was running when Bruno came to him. This is what Guigo had said: “Two years after his consecration had been completed, Hugh was a novice for one year in the monastery of Casa-Dei.”’”

Such is the interpretation Columbius assigns to Guigo’s words as he quotes them. It is, however, altogether forced and strained.

453. Apart from the fact that Columbius must assert that Guigo—who should not nevertheless be rashly accused of disorder in writing—placed the words “after his return from the monastery” out of their proper position, his interpretation seems to have been sought with excessive zeal so that the words of Guigo’s text, as quoted above, might be understood as true even while maintaining the opinion that fixes Saint Bruno’s withdrawal into the Chartreuse in 1084. Moreover, leaving aside its other defects, it is wholly foreign to any customary method of calculating the years that bishops spend in their episcopate.

I demonstrate this as follows. Guigo, according to Columbius, states in the words quoted above that our Saint came to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, when Hugh had not yet completed three years in the episcopate. Columbius must interpret this in such a way that by those “three years in the episcopate” not yet completed are meant the years spent by that holy prelate in episcopal administration after he had been consecrated bishop at Rome at the beginning of the year 1080, from the same year 1080, already advanced beyond the month of June, until June of 1084, when Saint Bruno came to him, as will be explained below.

But since, between the earlier of these two chronological limits and the later, not merely three but four years had elapsed, it is necessary for Columbius to subtract from them the one year that Hugh spent meanwhile as a novice in the monastery of Casa-Dei, situated in Auvergne, without episcopal administration. Only in this way can he obtain the “three years in the episcopate,” or, as he explains them, “three years in episcopal administration not yet completed,” after which Bruno came to that holy prelate.

454. Yet although the years that bishops spend in their episcopate are sometimes counted not only from the time when they were elected or consecrated but also from the time when, already consecrated, they took possession of their bishoprics, I nowhere find this done in such a way that the years during which bishops, absent from their flock, did not exercise its care are subtracted from the years spent in the episcopate in order to arrive at a more exact total. Since this subtraction must be made according to the interpretation Columbius imposes upon Guigo’s words, that interpretation clearly does not appear suitable.

Nor, in my opinion, would Columbius himself have resorted to it in order to defend the opinion assigning our Saint’s withdrawal into the Chartreuse to 1084 if he had kept before his eyes all the individual words by which Guigo defines the time Saint Hugh spent after his episcopal ordination and before he sought the monastery of Casa-Dei, both in Surius and in our volume I for April, page 40.

For the biographer of Saint Hugh does not say there, “Hugh, after two years following his consecration had been completed, became a monk of Casa-Dei of the Cluniac order,” but rather, “Hugh, before two years following his consecration had been completed . . . became a monk of Casa-Dei of the Cluniac order.”

Thus either Columbius omitted the word “before” (*necdum*) through an error when transcribing Guigo’s text above, or he had before him a text from which that word had been erased by another person. This is what forced him to interpret Guigo’s words incorrectly in order to maintain that the Saint withdrew into the desert of the Chartreuse in 1084.

Otherwise, Guigo’s words can most appropriately be explained in a way that both allows Guigo to be understood as having written the truth and does not conflict at all with the opinion that assigns Saint Bruno’s withdrawal into the desert of the Chartreuse to 1084, as I shall show when I have briefly dealt with Pagi in his *Critica*.

### 455

This writer, who, in opposition to Baronius, likewise assigns Bruno’s withdrawal into the wilderness, or the foundation of the Carthusian Order, to the year 1084, writes as follows under the year 1086, no. 7 [Col. 0276B]:

> “Baronius therefore postponed the foundation of the most holy Order—namely, the Carthusian—to this year because Guigo, the author of the Acts of the Life of St. Hugh, to whom he was bound by the closest relationship, speaks as follows: ‘After two years had been completed after his consecration, Hugh, having despised all things, became a monk of the Cluniac Order at Casa-Dei. There he lived for a year as a novice. After this’—that is, after this year of novitiate, and therefore in the third year after his ordination—‘compelled by Gregory VII, he returned from the monastery which he had entered fervently, more fervent still … And behold, before three years had yet been completed in the episcopate after his return from the monastery, Master Bruno appeared.’”

Baronius interprets these words as meaning that Hugh first spent two full years after his consecration at Rome, where it had taken place, and a third at the monastery of Casa-Dei; then, after returning from Casa-Dei to Grenoble, he spent nearly another three years in the episcopate before Bruno’s arrival; and in the sixth year after his ordination—namely, the current year—he went to Chartreuse with his companions.

At first sight, that passage does indeed seem to require this interpretation. But the charter of the foundation of Chartreuse, which Baronius had not seen, contradicts it and demonstrates that the passage must be understood as follows: “Bruno, after his return from the monastery”—that is, immediately or shortly afterward—came to Hugh, who at that time had not yet completed three years in the episcopate.

Nor does it matter that Guigo says that Hugh became a monk “after two years had been completed after his consecration.” For, as I have shown in the *Hypatic Dissertation*, as well as repeatedly in this *Critique* by various testimonies, writers often understand expressions such as “three years having elapsed,” or “a three-year period having passed,” and similar phrases, to mean three incomplete years taken together, and they use “a two-year period” for a single year when the matter was begun at the end of one year and completed at the beginning of the next.”

### 456

Thus far Pagius. Although he borrowed most of his material from Columbi, as becomes evident to anyone who compares their words, he nevertheless decided to refrain from naming him. I do not know whether he did so in accordance with his usual practice—by which he generally names authors only when refuting them—or because he differs somewhat from Columbi as well.

In fact, however the matter may stand, he does differ somewhat from Columbi [Col. 0277A]. For although he introduces Guigo as defining the time when our saint approached St. Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and withdrew into Chartreuse in precisely the words used above by Columbi, he does not, in order to prove that this occurred no later than the fourth year after Hugh’s episcopal consecration, interpret with Columbi Guigo’s following words—“And behold, before three years had yet been completed in the episcopate after his return from the monastery, Master Bruno appeared”—as referring to three years not yet completed by Hugh in his episcopal administration when St. Bruno came to him.

Rather, he thinks that Guigo’s other words—“After two years had been completed after his consecration”—namely, his episcopal consecration, received at Rome in the year 1080—can be explained to mean that Hugh became a monk at the monastery of Casa-Dei after the portion of the year 1080 in which he had been consecrated as bishop, together with the portion of the following year that had elapsed after that consecration: that is, only one year after his consecration.

He holds this opinion because, as he says, it is not uncommon for writers, by “a completed two-year period,” or even by “two years having passed,” and similar expressions, to signify only one year whose beginning and end are connected with two different years of Christ.

### 457

But even if we concede this point to Pagius for the moment, it cannot have force when authors themselves indicate, by their manner of writing, whether they take the years and other periods or intervals of time about which they are speaking as complete or incomplete.

Now, in the text containing the words “after two years had been completed,” Guigo must be thought to have done precisely this, if Columbi and Pagius have reported him correctly; consequently, he should not be understood to have taken those words as referring to two incomplete calendar years of Christ, or to one complete year whose beginning and end are connected with two different years of Christ.

For in that same text, as preserved by Columbi and Pagius, when speaking of the three years which St. Hugh spent “in the episcopate after his return from the monastery” before our saint approached him, Guigo indicates by adding the word *necdum*—“not yet”—that those years were incomplete:
