> “Behold,” he says, “before three years had yet been completed in the episcopate after his return from the monastery, Master Bruno appeared.”

Therefore, if in the same text, by the words “after two years had been completed,” after which he writes that Hugh became a monk at Casa-Dei, he had wished to signify only incomplete years—one year, or a period of somewhat more than one year, whose beginning and end were connected with two different years of Christ—he would unquestionably have indicated this in the same way by adding *necdum* or a similar word.

Since he does not do so in that text as transmitted by Columbi and Pagius, Pagius wrongly interprets the two years in question as incomplete years, or as a single year whose beginning and end were connected with two different years of Christ, namely 1080 and the following year.

If, meanwhile, the matter were otherwise, and if—while accepting as genuine the text of Guigo as reported by Columbi and Pagius—it could therefore be admitted that Hugh went to the monastery of Casa-Dei in the year 1081, that text, even so understood, would fit perfectly with the opinion that assigns our saint’s withdrawal into the wilderness of Chartreuse to the year 1084.

What follows will make clear what must now be said about the genuine text in which Guigo explains when St. Bruno approached St. Hugh, bishop of Grenoble.

### 458

The text, as printed by us in volume I of the *Acta Sanctorum*, April, page 40, reads as follows:

> “Hugh … before two years had yet been completed after his consecration, having despised all things, became a monk of the Cluniac Order at Casa-Dei, where … he spent … a year as a novice … After this, compelled by … Gregory VII, he returned to the episcopate from the monastery which he had entered fervently, more fervent still … and behold, before three years had yet been completed in the episcopate after his return from the monastery, Master Bruno appeared.”

If both the two years which St. Hugh spent after receiving episcopal consecration and before putting on the monastic habit at Casa-Dei, and the three years which that holy bishop, after returning from Casa-Dei, spent in the episcopate before St. Bruno’s arrival, are understood as incomplete years—so that the former were not a full two-year period and the latter not a full three-year period—the whole text of Guigo can readily be reconciled with the opinion that assigns our saint’s approach to Hugh to the year 1084.

Indeed, it can be explained in such a way that St. Hugh, after returning from the monastery of Casa-Dei, had spent not yet three complete years in the episcopate—that is, somewhat more than two years—before St. Bruno came to him, while nevertheless Bruno’s arrival occurred in the year 1084.

To present the matter in an orderly and clear fashion, we must first determine when St. Hugh was consecrated bishop at Rome. Guigo writes as follows in his *Life of St. Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble*, printed by us in volume I of the *Acta Sanctorum*, April, page 37, no. 5:

> “After some interval of time had subsequently elapsed, the same legate held at Avignon, a distinguished city of Provence, a great council, at which he accomplished many things worthy of praise for the honor of God and the benefit of the Church.

### 459

> “To this council came the canons of Grenoble, lacking a bishop and seeking one. When they discovered that the aforesaid young man presided over the present assembly, they humbly requested, with the council’s support, from his venerable patron—whose service of grateful companionship he was rendering—that he give him to them as bishop without delay. The latter immediately and gladly consented: rejoicing both in the honors of his beloved count and favoring the advancement of the Church, whose sacred offices he did not doubt that the future bishop would suitably serve.”

Thus Guigo, after inserting some intervening matter, also teaches that, once the Council of Avignon had ended, St. Hugh, together with Hugh of Die, legate of the Apostolic See, went to Rome so that he might there be consecrated bishop by the supreme pontiff.

Hugh of Flavigny likewise records the matter in the *New Library of Manuscript Books* of Labbe, volume I, writing as follows concerning Hugh of Die, legate of the Apostolic See:

> “He also held the seventh council at Avignon, at which Achard, the usurper of the see of Arles, was deposed, and Gibelin was elected archbishop of Arles … Hugh [was elected] bishop of Grenoble … After the council had ended, he took them with him to Rome, and they were consecrated by the pope who had summoned the council at Rome.”

Hugh, therefore, was requested and appointed bishop of the church of Grenoble at the Council of Avignon; and afterward, when the council had ended, he went with Hugh, the legate of the Apostolic See, to Rome, so that there—as indeed happened—he might be ordained bishop by the supreme pontiff.

### 460

But when was that council held? Since the determination of the time when this occurred, and therefore of the time when Hugh was consecrated bishop at Rome, depends to some extent on the date of the council, and since some assign its celebration to the year 1078, while others—and more commonly—assign it to the year 1080, I wish on this occasion to investigate the matter somewhat more carefully, so that the year in which these events occurred may finally be known with certainty.

First, it is clear from a letter written on the Kalends of March in the year 1079 that the council was not held in 1078. In that letter Pope Gregory VII admonished the clergy and people of Arles (see Labbe, volume X of the *Councils*, column 213) to choose an archbishop for themselves—the man who was appointed at the Council of Avignon whose date we are investigating, as is understood from the recently quoted words of Hugh of Flavigny [Col. 0279C].

As for the year 1080, to which others assign that council, the author of the treatise on St. Bruno communicated to me by the Carthusians of this place writes as follows in no. 17 concerning that council and Hugh’s election there as bishop of Grenoble:

> “Baronius and others defer the aforesaid Council of Avignon and the election of Hugh to the year 1080; but it is easy to prove that they must be referred to the preceding year. For our Guigo—whose authority Baronius also used—writes, in the *Life of St. Hugh of Grenoble*, that St. Hugh died on 1 April in the year 1132 from the Incarnation of the Lord, at least in the eightieth year of his age, in the fourth month—that is, in his seventy-ninth year and four months.”

### 461

> “From this we rightly conclude that he was born around November of the year 1052, and consequently completed his twenty-seventh year only in that same month of the year 1079. Since the same author says that he was nearly twenty-seven years old when he was requested as pastor by the clergy of Grenoble at the Council of Avignon, it seems necessarily to follow that this council was convened in that year before November.

> “This may also be conjectured from Gregory VII’s letter issued from the Lateran on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in the second indiction. In it the supreme pontiff admonishes a certain Boson that, if he trusts that he has any claim of justice in the church in question, he must present himself before the legate, the bishop of Die, at the council which the latter was about to hold.

> “Gregory certainly is not speaking of the Council of Lyons, which, as he attests in another letter to Manasses, archbishop of Reims, was to be held only in January of the following year. Moreover, according to the same Guigo, Hugh afterward went to Rome with Hugh the legate, so that he might be consecrated by the supreme prelate of the Apostolic See. Hugh of Flavigny reports the same thing when speaking of that legate:

> “‘He also held the seventh council at Avignon, at which Achard, the usurper of the see of Arles, was deposed, and Gibelin was elected archbishop of Arles … Hugh [was elected] bishop of Grenoble … After the council had ended, he took them with him to Rome, and they were consecrated by the pope,’ who had summoned the council at Rome in the year 1080 during Lent, the first Sunday of which fell on the Kalends of March. From Gregory’s letters we learn that the legate Hugh, and consequently our Hugh as well, were present at that council.

### 462

> “From these facts it is again clear that Hugh’s election to the episcopate—which Baronius does not distinguish from his consecration—as well as the celebration of the Synod of Avignon, must be assigned to the aforesaid year 1079, while his consecration belongs to the following year. This must also be established decisively from Guigo’s additional words, according to which Hugh died ‘in at least the fifty-second year of his consecration.’ By a proper calculation, counting from the year 1080, we find that this fifty-second year had already been completed in March 1132, when, as we have said, he died on 1 April.”

Thus the author of that treatise, relying chiefly on the *Life of St. Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble*, written by Guigo, a contemporary author of the highest credibility, argues both that the Council of Avignon was held in 1079 and that St. Hugh, who at that council was requested and appointed bishop by the people of Grenoble, was consecrated at Rome in the year 1080.

And indeed, when the evidence by which he seeks to prove the matter is considered—namely, the words of the aforesaid *Life of St. Hugh*—it appears certain that the council was held in the year he assigns. For, as Guigo says, St. Hugh “died in the year … from the Incarnation of the Lord 1132, in the … eightieth year of his age, in the fourth month … on the Kalends of April.” This is equivalent to saying that Hugh died in 1132 either when he was already entering his eightieth year or when he was more than eighty years old.

But if he died when more than eighty years old, it follows that he was born before the year 1052; consequently, the Council of Avignon, which according to Guigo he attended at nearly twenty-seven years of age, would have been held before the year 1079. Since that cannot be admitted on the basis of what has been said, he must be understood to have died in the eightieth year of his age, in the fourth month. Consequently, the Council of Avignon, which according to the foregoing he attended at nearly twenty-seven years of age, was held in the year 1079.

### 463

But Hugh of Flavigny, likewise a contemporary author, appears to oppose this calculation through the words recently quoted [Col. 0281A], which are enclosed within the words of the author who composed the treatise on St. Bruno communicated to me by the Carthusians of this place.

For this writer, after listing six different councils held in Gaul by Hugh of Die, legate of the Apostolic See, immediately adds the Council of Avignon to the list and calls it the seventh. He thus seems to indicate that the Council of Avignon occurred after those six councils—although, according to the common opinion of all scholars, one of them, namely the Council of Lyons, was not held before the year 1080—and consequently that Avignon too was not held before that same year 1080.

This may therefore be brought forward against the calculation that places the Council of Avignon in 1079. But since Hugh of Flavigny (see the *Literary History of France*, volume X, page 79 and following) does not always observe, in recounting events both of the eleventh century in which he flourished and of earlier centuries, the chronological order in which each event occurred, it is possible that he did not observe it here either in listing the Council of Avignon and the six councils that preceded it.

Nor should one reply that this writer explicitly calls Avignon the seventh council after discussing the other six. He may have done so with reference not to the order in which that council and the six others were held, but solely to the order that he himself follows in mentioning them.

Moreover, Hugh of Flavigny (see again the recently cited volume of the *Literary History of France*) sometimes departs from true chronology and historical accuracy even when recounting events that occurred in his own time. Guigo, however, is not found to suffer from this defect. Therefore, even if Hugh were to assign the Council of Avignon explicitly to the year 1080, it would still be more reasonable to believe that it was held not then for the first time, but in the immediately preceding year, namely 1079, as is derived from the chronological indications supplied by Guigo and from the recently quoted words of the anonymous author of the treatise communicated to me by the Carthusians of this place.

### 464

Nor should you bring forward here, with Mabillon, in the preface to Part II of the *Benedictine Century VI*, no. 86, on behalf of Hugh of Flavigny—or rather concerning the time at which some infer from that author that the Council of Avignon was held—the letter written by Pope Gregory VII to the clergy and people of Arles. In that letter they were admonished to choose an archbishop; it was written on the Kalends of March in the year 1079 and inserted by Labbe in volume X of the *Councils*, column 213.

Although in this letter the supreme pontiff admonishes the clergy and people of Arles to choose an archbishop, and although this pontifical injunction was obeyed at the Council of Avignon, it by no means follows that the council was held no earlier than the year 1080. Why could it not have been held after the Kalends of March of that same year 1079, in which Gregory wrote the letter just mentioned?

Certainly, the interval from the Kalends of March of the year 1079 to the beginning of the following year was not too short for this to have occurred. Indeed, Mabillon himself, in the *Annals*, book 66, no. 34, indicates clearly enough that the year 1079 should be substituted for the year 1080 to which he had initially assigned that council in the passage cited above.

Furthermore, the letter cited by the author of the treatise on St. Bruno communicated to me by the Carthusians of this place also lends some support to the year 1079, to which he assigns the aforesaid Council of Avignon. This letter was written by the same supreme pontiff to a certain Boson on the fourth day before the Kalends of July in the year 1079.

In it the pontiff mentions a council soon to be held by Hugh of Die, his legate. It therefore appears to designate the Council of Avignon as one that was to be held in that very year 1079, because the two councils held immediately after the Kalends of July of the year 1079 were the Councils of Avignon and Lyons, and the latter certainly did not take place before the year 1080.

### 465

When all these considerations are taken together, it appears beyond doubt that the Council of Avignon, at which St. Hugh was requested and appointed bishop by the people of Grenoble, was held in the year 1079, and before the month of November of that year, as the author of the aforesaid treatise on St. Bruno, communicated to me by the Carthusians of this place, also teaches from Guigo.

The additional point that he makes there, however—concerning St. Hugh’s journey to Rome with Hugh, legate of the Apostolic See, after the Council of Avignon, and concerning both his episcopal ordination there and his presence at the council held in the year 1080 during Lent—does not confirm the date that he assigns to the Council of Avignon.

For Hugh the legate went to Rome not in the year 1079 but only in the following year, in order to be present at the council held there. This is clear from the Council of Lyons, which he held before doing so. After he had held that council in the year 1080—see what was said in no. 147—after the third day of January, he could have held another at Avignon before proceeding to Rome.

As for St. Hugh’s episcopal ordination and his presence at the council held at Rome, the author of the aforesaid treatise on St. Bruno, communicated to me by the Carthusians of this place, teaches—see no. 461—that this council was held during Lent, whose first Sunday fell on the Kalends of March, in the year 1080.

Thus, once the year 1080 had begun, Hugh the legate could have held the Council of Avignon, and after doing so could have reached Rome in time to attend the council held there during Lent. Consequently, although, according to what has been said, the Council of Avignon was held in the year 1079, the fact that St. Hugh, already elected bishop of Grenoble, was present at the Roman council cannot be used to prove that the Avignon council was held in 1080.

### 466

Nor can this be inferred from the episcopal ordination which St. Hugh received from the supreme pontiff at Rome in the year 1080. Nothing at all compels us to place it so early in that year that Hugh could have been at Rome to receive it only if he had already begun his journey from Avignon in the year 1079.

Indeed, it is certain that St. Hugh did not set out for Rome before the year 1080, because he undertook that journey with Hugh, the legate of the Apostolic See, and the latter did not undertake it before the year 1080—or rather, before the month of February of that year. I demonstrate this as follows.

Pope Gregory VII admonished Manasses, the simoniacal archbishop of Reims, in a letter dated “the third day before the Nones of January, in the second indiction”—that is, according to what was said in no. 147, in the year 1080; see Labbe, volume X of the *Councils*, column 223—that he should present himself at the council to be held at Lyons by Hugh, the legate of the Apostolic See.

There can be no doubt that enough time elapsed between the writing of this letter and the celebration of the Council of Lyons for the letter to be delivered to Manasses and for him, after receiving it, to reach Lyons for the council.

Now, since a period of no fewer than four or five weeks appears to have been necessary for this, it follows that the Council of Lyons was not held before February of the year 1080. Consequently, St. Hugh and Hugh the legate, who according to the foregoing did not depart for Rome until after the Council of Lyons had been held, did not undertake that journey before the same time.

### 467

Since this is so, St. Hugh certainly did not receive episcopal ordination at Rome so early in the year 1080 that he could have been there at that time only if he had already begun his journey from Avignon toward that city in the year 1079.

This is sufficient concerning the time when the Council of Avignon was held, and concerning the arguments by which its celebration in the year 1079 is either proved or disproved.

But when, after that council had been held, was St. Hugh ordained bishop at Rome? Since, according to what has been said, he did not go to Rome with Hugh the legate until after the Council of Lyons had been held, and since that council likewise was not held before February of the year 1080, he most probably did not reach Rome before March of the year 1080. Consequently, he was not consecrated bishop there by the supreme pontiff before that time.

But might the event not have occurred somewhat later still? Guigo testifies, in his *Life* as printed by us in volume I of the *Acta Sanctorum*, April, page 46, no. 33, that St. Hugh:

> “in the year … from the Incarnation of the Lord 1132 … in at least the fifty-second year of his consecration, on the Kalends of April … departed to the Lord.”

From the first day of March in the year 1080 to the first day of April in the year 1132, when St. Hugh died, fifty-two years had elapsed, together with only a few weeks. It therefore appears highly probable—or rather, one might say certain—that he was consecrated bishop by the supreme pontiff no later than March of the year 1080.

Since, according to what has been said, he did not receive episcopal consecration from the pontiff at Rome before March of that year, it follows that it most probably occurred in that very year and month.

### 468

We have now also established the time when St. Hugh was consecrated bishop at Rome. The next task is to demonstrate how the words quoted from Guigo in no. 458—words by which this writer of wholly tested credibility defines, or rather indicates, when St. Bruno approached St. Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and went to the wilderness of Chartreuse—can be understood as consistent with the truth, according to the opinion that assigns Bruno’s approach to St. Hugh and his withdrawal into the wilderness of Chartreuse to the year 1084, at a point already advanced into the month of June.

Since, according to what has been said, St. Hugh was consecrated bishop at Rome in March of the year 1080, what if he went to the monastery of Casa-Dei in May or June of the year 1081, when that year had already advanced, as could indeed have happened, and put on the monastic habit after renouncing all worldly things? What if, after spending approximately a year there as a novice—or nine or ten months, for Guigo does not seem here to indicate a full year—he returned from that monastery to the episcopate at approximately March of the year 1082, at the command of the supreme pontiff?

In that case, Guigo could certainly have said, without any loss of truth, that Hugh became a monk at Casa-Dei “before two years had yet been completed after his consecration,” lived there as a novice for about a year, and finally, at Grenoble, received St. Bruno in the year 1084, when Bruno came “before three years had yet been completed in the episcopate after the return from the monastery”—that is, after Hugh’s return from Casa-Dei.

Anyone who considers the matter carefully will, I think, readily perceive this. It must therefore be understood—or, if one prefers, it must be admitted—that the matter really occurred in the manner just assigned. Otherwise, since it is established from other evidence that St. Bruno’s approach to St. Hugh must be assigned to the year 1084, one would have to believe that Guigo wrote something contrary to the truth.

### 469

“But,” you will object, “on this account Hugh became a monk at the monastery of Casa-Dei only one year and approximately two months after his consecration, while after his return from that monastery he spent only two years and approximately two months in the episcopate before St. Bruno approached him. Yet Guigo’s words as quoted seem to indicate that ‘before two years had been completed’ signifies a period somewhat longer than one year and two months, while ‘before three years had been completed’ signifies a period longer than two years and two months.”

I admit that the matter does indeed appear so if the passage is taken in its most obvious sense. But if it is considered according to the strict meaning of the words, I do not see why Guigo could not have intended one year and two months by “two years not yet completed,” and two years and approximately two months by “three years not yet completed.”

For someone who has completed only one year and two months has not yet completed a full two-year period; likewise, someone who has completed only two years and the same number of months has not yet completed a full three-year period. Nor do I see that one would depart from the truth by designating one year and two months as “a two-year period not yet completed,” and likewise designating only two years and the same number of months as “a three-year period not yet completed.”

Whatever the case may be, the aforesaid words of Guigo seem to be understood in the manner just explained. This is necessary both to avoid being forced, with Columbi, to say that the following three words—“after the return from the monastery”—have been placed out of their proper position, which seems implausible and insufficiently supported, and to avoid having to assert that Guigo, a man upon whom suspicion of falsehood cannot fall, contradicts the opinion that assigns St. Bruno’s approach to St. Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and his withdrawal into the wilderness of Chartreuse to the year 1084.

Many considerations that I shall now bring forward strongly suggest that this opinion is entirely consistent with the truth. I begin with the charter of the donation of Chartreuse.

### 470

I shall publish the charter in full below, from the copy appended by Michael Morkensius to the end of his *Chronological-Diplomatic Dissertation* concerning St. Bruno. Near its conclusion it reads as follows:

> “The aforesaid land”—namely, Chartreuse—“enclosed within these boundaries”—that is, the boundaries specified above—“began to be inhabited and built by Master Bruno and by the brothers who were with him in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1084; in the fourth year of the episcopate of Lord Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, who praises and confirms this gift made by the persons written above and, together with the whole assembly of his clergy, grants in full whatever appears to belong to his jurisdiction.”

Thus it is established from the charter itself, by which Chartreuse was founded, that the saint entered the wilderness of Chartreuse in the year 1084.

I shall explain below how the fourth year of the episcopate of St. Hugh—which, according to what has been said, began when he was consecrated bishop in March of the year 1080—could still have been in progress when our saint first entered and began to inhabit the wilderness of Chartreuse in the year 1084, at a point already advanced into June, as will be demonstrated.

It remains to prove further here that St. Bruno’s approach to Hugh of Grenoble and his withdrawal into the wilderness of Chartreuse occurred in the year 1084.

As I shall show below, St. Bruno was summoned from Chartreuse to Rome by Pope Urban II, who had once been his disciple. When he was leaving, Landuin and the others with whom he had withdrawn into that sacred solitude also wished to leave the wilderness of Chartreuse; Bruno therefore resigned it to Siguin, abbot of Casa-Dei. Later, when Landuin and the other disciples of the saint returned to the place that Bruno had abandoned, Siguin restored it to them by a public charter. This charter is dated to the year 1090, which shows that in that year Landuin and the other disciples of our saint had already returned to Chartreuse, which they had abandoned when Bruno went to Rome.

### 471

Now, in the *Chronicle of the Four First Priors of Chartreuse*—a monument of very great antiquity and credibility, as I explained in § 1—our saint is said to have governed Chartreuse for six years before going to Rome in obedience to the pontiff’s will.

If those six years are to be understood as complete years, counting backward from the year 1090 to June, when, as will be demonstrated, he first withdrew into that wilderness, they lead to the year 1084. If they are to be understood as incomplete years, as in fact they were, then, counted backward from the same year 1090 to a point before June, or from the year 1089 after June had already advanced, they likewise lead to the year 1084.

It follows even from this that St. Bruno came to St. Hugh in that year and entered Chartreuse; the matter is entirely certain.

Moreover, in the same *Chronicle*, or rather in the eulogy of our saint contained in it, Bruno is said to have exchanged this mortal life for the immortal one “approximately eleven years after his departure from Chartreuse” (see no. 7).

Since, as has already been said, the saint governed Chartreuse for six years before departing from it when summoned by the supreme pontiff, it follows that the year 1101—in which, as everyone agrees, he died—was the seventeenth year after his entrance into Chartreuse. Consequently, he must first have entered it in the year 1084.

This is also established by the eulogy of Guigo, the fifth prior of Chartreuse, which is appended to the *Chronicle of the Four First Priors of Chartreuse* in Labbe, volume I of the *New Library of Manuscript Books*, pages 639 and following. The eulogy appears to have been composed by an author either contemporary with St. Bruno or only slightly later.

In it Guigo is said to have died “when the fifty-third year from the beginning of the wilderness of Chartreuse was in progress.” Since Guigo, as everyone agrees, died in the year 1137, and counting backward fifty-three years from that year leads to 1084, it follows that the wilderness of Chartreuse began in that year; or, what amounts to the same thing, that our saint first entered it then.

### 472

“Finally,” says Mabillon in the preface to Part II of the *Benedictine Century VI*, no. 86, that this occurred then is also “proved by St. Bruno’s epitaph, copied from an old manuscript in these words:

> “In the thousandth year—add the fourth and the eightieth too, if you reckon correctly—the Carthusians arose.  
> The exalted Master Bruno gave them their origin,”

and so forth.

Mabillon nowhere states how ancient the manuscript was from which he extracted these verses, nor have I been able to discover this elsewhere.

The testimony of Sigebert of Gembloux could also be brought forward in confirmation, together with a charter granted in July of the year 1084 by Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, in favor of the Carthusians, as Mabillon mentions in the passage just cited.

But since that charter is not at hand, and since the words attributed to Sigebert concerning St. Bruno in the Pistoia edition have, according to what was said in no. 298, been shown to be spurious, while the words found in Miraeus’s edition are not expressed with the same characteristics as those which certainly belong to Sigebert, I have decided not to do so.

Nor was this in any way necessary, since from the other evidence that I have already brought forward it appears altogether certain and beyond all controversy that our saint approached Hugh of Grenoble in the year 1084 and entered the wilderness of Chartreuse.

473. Since this is so, Guigo’s words, from which Baronius and others concluded that this happened in 1086, must beyond all doubt be understood in the manner explained above, especially since the Saint’s withdrawal to Chartreuse took place in June, as I now demonstrate. The chronologer of the first four priors of Chartreuse—how much credit he deserves I explained in § 1—records the following in Labbe, *Bibliotheca nova librorum manuscriptorum*, vol. I, p. 639, in the eulogy of John the Tuscan, the fourth prior of Chartreuse:

> “Thus twenty-five years are reckoned from the first year of Master Bruno up to the last year of this man [namely, John the Tuscan]. They are completed before his death, which occurred on the Nones of October, around the Nativity of blessed John the Baptist. For at that time the aforesaid wilderness began to be inhabited by Master Bruno.”

The Saint, then, as these words make clear, first withdrew into the wilderness of Chartreuse around the feast of Saint John the Baptist. Since the feast of the Lord’s holy Forerunner falls every year on 24 June, and since neither our Saint nor his companions, after arriving at Grenoble, appear to have remained long with the city’s holy bishop before going to Chartreuse, it seems beyond doubt that, in that same month of June into which the feast of the Lord’s Forerunner falls, they both approached Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and, with him accompanying them and supplying what was necessary for the purpose they intended, entered the wilderness of Chartreuse and laid the foundations there of the new order which, from that place where it began, is called Carthusian. And so, now that the year, month, and even almost the precise day on which this highly memorable event occurred have been determined, it remains for us to examine what Bruno and his companions did next, once they had found a place ideally suited to the eremitical life according to their wishes, and what way of life they adopted there.

§ XXVII. What the Saint and his companions first did after entering Chartreuse, and what manner of life they followed.

[Col. 0287D]

474. Concerning Saint Bruno and his six companions, who entered Chartreuse accompanied by Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, Blomenvenna writes in the *Life of that holy Patriarch of his Order*:

> “There, in the wilderness of Chartreuse, on the upper part of the mountain, at the place now called Sainte-Marie-des-Casals, they began to build a church, as well as small cells near a certain spring which to this day is called the Fountain of Saint Bruno. The cells stood not far from the church, distinct and somewhat separated from one another, so that no one might disturb another’s solitude. Living two by two in each cell, after the manner of the ancient Egyptian monks, they devoted themselves to silence, reading, prayer, purity of heart, and contemplation; thereafter they also applied themselves to manual labor, especially the copying of books.”

So writes the celebrated biographer of our Saint, from whom Puteanus, in the *Life of Saint Bruno* which he composed, differs little. That the matters Blomenvenna records in these words are entirely true may also be inferred from what Guibert of Nogent says in book I, chapter 11, of *On His Life*; from what Peter the Venerable says in book II, chapter 28, of *On Miracles*; and from what Guigo, the fifth prior of Chartreuse, says in no. 12 of the *Life of Saint Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble*, whether concerning Saint Bruno and his companions already living at Chartreuse or concerning the institutions of the Carthusians. I gladly transcribe the passages most relevant here. I shall begin with what Guigo provides.

475. In the place already cited, concerning Saint Hugh, who lived in the wilderness of Chartreuse with our Saint and his companions, Guigo writes:

> “Although even earlier [that is, before he had yet gone to Chartreuse with Bruno] he was wholly aflame with the fires of divine love, he nevertheless became fervent in the exercises of heavenly discipline through their example and companionship in the same way as if someone were to place several other burning torches around a flaming one. He was with them not as lord or bishop, but as the humblest companion and brother, ready, insofar as he could be, to serve everyone. Thus the venerable William, then prior of Saint Lawrence and later abbot of Saint Theofredus—himself also bound to Master Bruno by no slight religious devotion—complained rather bitterly to Master Bruno, as blessed Hugh’s companion [for at that time two lived in each cell], that Hugh took almost all the duties belonging to humility away from him within the cell, and that, although a bishop, he behaved toward him not at least as a companion but rather as a servant. Sadly, he declared that he was not permitted to perform any of the servile tasks which, according to custom, they ought to carry out by turns, because Hugh took them all away from him.”

From Guigo’s account it is established, first, that cells were built by Saint Bruno and his companions when they initially entered the wilderness of Chartreuse; second, that the monks did not at that time occupy one monk to each cell, as later became the case, which is made clear by what Guibert and Peter the Venerable report in the passages cited above concerning Carthusian institutions, but that two lived together in each cell, as Blomenvenna teaches in the words just quoted; and third, that each pair who shared a cell had to perform the domestic duties by turns. Now hear what Guibert says on this subject:

476. “The church,” he says in the passage cited, “there in the wilderness of Chartreuse, is not far from the foot of the mountain, whose slope bends slightly. In it there are thirteen monks. They have a sufficiently suitable cloister for a coenobitic community, but they do not live cloister-fashion like the other inhabitants. Each has his own cell around the cloister, where he works, sleeps, and eats.”

Thus writes Guibert, who, as I demonstrated in no. 170, died around 1124. Since he mentions the church which, in his own time, had been built at the foot of the mountain embraced by the wilderness of Chartreuse, it appears highly probable, indeed almost certain, that the church mentioned by Blomenvenna—very probably the same church—had already been built by our Saint and his companions when they first entered Chartreuse.

Indeed, the extraordinary love of God which they possessed leaves no room for doubt that, once they had entered Chartreuse, they would have considered nothing more urgent than to build a house or church—or at least a chapel—dedicated exclusively to his worship. I now turn to the words of Peter the Venerable that bear most directly on this point. In book II, chapter 28, of *On Miracles*, he supplies the following account of the Carthusians living in the wilderness of Chartreuse in his own time, that is, in the twelfth century, when, as that century had advanced to its twenty-second year, he began to serve as abbot among the Cluniacs:

> “After the ancient custom of the Egyptian monks, they continually inhabit separate cells [when Saint Bruno and his companions first entered Chartreuse, they lived two by two in each cell, as has already been said], where they devote themselves without interruption to silence, reading, and manual labor, especially the copying of books. In those same cells, summoned by the church’s signal, they render to God the appointed offices of the canonical hours, namely Prime, Terce, Sext, None, and Compline. At Vespers and Matins they all assemble in the church.”

477. Since, then, in Peter the Venerable’s time the inhabitants of the wilderness of Chartreuse regularly assembled at fixed times for Matins and Vespers, as we understand from Peter’s words, and since they certainly conformed their life to the pattern which Saint Bruno and his companions had expressed in their own practice, there can be no doubt that the Saint and his companions likewise wished to assemble for Matins and Vespers. Consequently, in order to have a place where they could do this, they most probably—indeed, I would say certainly—arranged for at least some sort of church or chapel to be built immediately after entering the wilderness of Chartreuse, with Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, most generously supplying the expense.

Moreover, Masson, whom I have already often cited, asks himself in book I, chapter 2, no. 10, of his work entitled *Annals of the Carthusian Order*, “how Saint Bruno and his companions began to establish a dwelling for themselves in that wilderness of Chartreuse, on the prominent site where the Chapel of Saint Bruno is now visited” (see no. 447). To confirm that the Saint and his companions, on first entering the wilderness of Chartreuse, set their hands to building a monastery or cells and a church or chapel, he answers in these words:

> “Tradition records that he [Saint Bruno] had a cell there, and even a nearby chapel in which he celebrated Mass; for it is believed that the altar of that chapel has remained unmoved to this day. Three or four large fragments of rock can also be seen there, once detached and cut away from the lofty cliffs and standing somewhat separated from one another. Many have conjectured that they built their huts at their foot; and it is indeed probable that this was done almost casually, as a temporary measure.”

478. “But it is to be believed that immediately afterward they discussed with Saint Hugh, and under his assistance, the construction there of a small monastery and the erection of the regular buildings. For the vision which the holy bishop had seen in his sleep—Christ building a house for himself in that wilderness—impelled him to this.”

Thus Masson writes. He further adds that, in order to prove that both a church and, specifically, a monastery had then immediately begun to be built by Bruno and his companions, many buildings were already standing in Guigo’s time, and that this would not have happened unless the Saint had set his hand to the work immediately after entering Chartreuse.

But since twenty-six years elapsed between the time when the Saint and his companions first withdrew into the wilderness of Chartreuse and the time when Guigo assumed its governance—as Masson himself admits in the passage cited—I do not see why the buildings encompassed by Chartreuse in Guigo’s time could not have been constructed even if Bruno and his companions had not begun building them immediately upon entering Chartreuse.

In any event, both what has already been said and the necessity under which Bruno and his companions were unquestionably placed of protecting themselves against the elements leave no doubt that immediately after entering Chartreuse they built whatever cells they could, all of them together presenting a kind of monastic appearance. Raynaudus does say in *The Mystical Stylite*, point 2, no. 3, that at that time they established their dwelling in cavities of the rocks; and others assert that they used huts hastily constructed. But even if this was perhaps their situation at the beginning, it did not last long. That cells and a church were meanwhile built by Bruno and his companions is demonstrated by the charter of the foundation of Chartreuse, which will be quoted below and in which we read, among other things:

> “The aforesaid land of Chartreuse, enclosed within these boundaries, began to be inhabited and built upon by Master Bruno and the brothers who were with him in the year 1084 from the Incarnation of the Lord.”

479. Blomenvenna affirms in the words quoted in no. 474 that the church and cells were then built by Saint Bruno and his companions beside the spring which even today is called the Fountain of Saint Bruno. This appears certain; nor can there be any doubt that those buildings, whatever their form, were erected “for the honor of God and of blessed Mary ever-Virgin and of blessed John the Baptist,” since Guigo, a witness beyond all exception, expressly asserts this in chapter 23 of his *Customs*.

There are, however, writers who say that this spring was miraculously brought forth. Some of these, whom Raynaudus mentions in *The Mystical Stylite*, point 2, no. 3, attribute it to the merits of Saint Bruno; others, including Dorlandus in book II, chapter 8, of the *Carthusian Chronicle*, attribute it to the prayers of Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble.

Zacharias Benedictus attributes the spring to the prayers of Saint Bruno and of all the others who were with him at Chartreuse, when, having first entered it and begun to construct the necessary buildings, they were suffering from a lack of water. In the metrical *Life of Our Saint* which he composed, he celebrates the event in the following manner:

> On the highest plain they build cells and shrines,  
> And a sacred altar is dedicated to the Mother who bore Christ.  
>   
> The place was deprived of flowing waters;  
> There was no cistern, no well, nowhere at all.  
> In a hollow, like rainwater,  
> Stagnant water lay, sometimes stinking with muddy odor.  
>   
> In sorrow they all endured such great hardship.  
> But what does steadfast faith not obtain and deserve?  
> That renowned company gave itself to tears and prayer  
> And obtained, suppliantly, what it sought from heaven.  
>   
> For immediately they began to dig into the hard rock;  
> Without delay fresh waters flowed forth,  
> And broad streams were driven out, like a river.  
> All rejoiced and resounded, giving praise,  
> And from the depths of their hearts they saluted heaven.  
>   
> Even now that spring, with winding course,  
> Washes the mountain’s summit  
> And flows in a glass-clear stream around the gardens of the cells.

480. Thus far Benedictus, whom I have praised. Although he does not state that the spring of which he speaks is still called the Fountain of Saint Bruno, he unquestionably celebrates the same spring which the authors cited above affirm is so called to this day, since both the spring he describes and the spring they describe are said to have arisen through a miracle.

But did that spring truly owe its origin to a miracle? I do not think so. When something is asserted by more recent writers to have happened miraculously, as here, without the support of any ancient witness whatsoever, it should not be believed to have happened miraculously unless an entirely solid and compelling reason dictates the contrary.

What reason, then, is there for supposing that the spring which still preserves Saint Bruno’s name at Chartreuse was once produced by a prodigy? Is it because it is still called “the Fountain of Saint Bruno”? But why could it not have acquired and preserved that name to the present day because it supplied the Saint and his companions with the water necessary for their daily needs? Why could it not also have been so called because Bruno had built near it the cell in which he lived?

In any event, although Puteanus, Blomenvenna, and Surius all mention a spring beside which Saint Bruno’s cell stood, they are completely silent about any miracle by which it was produced. Yet they had certainly examined, and especially Puteanus had before him, the metrical *Life of Saint Bruno* by Zacharias Benedictus, which its author himself inscribed and dedicated to him in 1510—that is, five years before Puteanus composed his work on this holy father—and in which the matter of the miraculous spring is recorded. Their silence therefore appears to indicate that they did not at all approve it.

But enough has been said about the spring which, according to the account, was brought forth by a miracle when the Saint and his companions entered Chartreuse. Whoever wishes to know more about it should consult Surius, in his *Observations on chapter 12 of Surius*, no. 12, and Raynaudus, in *The Mystical Stylite*, point 2, no. 3.

481. In the metrical *Life of Our Saint* which he composed, Zacharias Benedictus adds to the miracle of the divinely produced spring the consecration of the new church, which, together with the other buildings of whatever kind at Chartreuse, had begun to be built immediately after the Saint and his companions entered that wilderness and had by then been completed. The consecration, he says, was performed with great solemnity by Hugh, bishop of Grenoble.

To provide here something which I hope will not be unwelcome to the curious reader, I transcribe the principal verses in which that metrical biographer describes and celebrates the event. They read as follows:

> And now the solemn day had come when the rising structure  
> Could provide the monks with suitable lodging.  
> Hugh summons the clergy and invites the citizens from the town  
> To the mountain’s highest approaches and uncultivated thresholds,  
> To see the dedication of the festive church.  
>   
> The lofty bronze resounds and calls the crowds to the feast.  
> Then they prepare the shrines and adorn them with green leaves.  
> Ivy with hanging clusters is fitted to the wall;  
> They bind boxwood and the foliage sacred to Tritonia; from the lofty beams  
> The Peneian laurel puts forth leaves,  
> And bristling tamarisks join to form garlands.  
>   
> Flowers are scattered, and violets across the lofty roofs;  
> Lilies are not lacking, nor narcissus, acanthus, and Ajax,  
> Nor purple roses, which the attendants gathered  
> Throughout the neighboring towns; there are crocus and fragrant myrtle.  
> You might think that the gardens and fields of Paestum were here.  
>   
> Here hang tapestries; here painted carpets gleam.  
> The bishop sent varied cloths and gifts  
> For the new shrines, with which the walls and altars  
> Were to be covered.  
> The altars all around glitter with purple and lights.

482. After these verses Benedictus immediately adds several others in which he records—or rather, in the poetic manner, and with somewhat greater license than the subject warrants, imagines—that the heavenly beings themselves assembled for the solemnity. He then continues as follows:

> The bishop arrives, receives the sacred vestments in the customary order,  
> And places the dignity upon his head, the two-horned tiara.  
>   
> Fragrant smoke arising from Sabaean incense  
> Mounts higher and fills the vaults of the shrine.  
> One prepares a chair for the pontiff; another spreads the coverings.  
>   
> Now the priests, with voices evenly joined,  
> Begin the chants; the shepherd rises before the shining altars,  
> And, raising his palms toward heaven’s heights,  
> Offers the mystical holy things and presents the gifts to the powers above.  
>   
> The trumpets fill the air with their blast; the hollow pipe breathes  
> Sweetly sounds its ivory note; the organs give applause.  
> The trumpets alternate verses in divided song;  
> Lyres and plectra are present, and all the equipment of Phoebus.  
>   
> Meanwhile the priest dedicates the church and cloister  
> And decrees that the new house shall be called Chartreuse,  
> And that the houses yet to be founded shall bear its name.  
>   
> He donated estates and fertile acres to the house,  
> So that the monks might live without pursuing gain.

Thus writes the celebrated metrical biographer of our Saint. And indeed, I suppose that anyone will readily believe, even without an ancient witness, that the church of Chartreuse, once it had been completed, was consecrated by Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble. Yet the writer in question cannot persuade us that this was carried out with all the elaborate display he suggests, since, apart from having lived more than four centuries after the event, he speaks in the manner of poets, who generally enlarge the events they treat with various fictions serving, as it were, in place of ornament.

[Col. 0293B]

483. Yet I am far from being equally inclined to believe what the same Benedictus subsequently relates, likewise without any ancient witness, concerning the monastic habit which Saint Bruno and his companions supposedly received from Saint Hugh on the very day on which the aforesaid dedication of the Carthusian church took place.

Listen to how he sets out that event in verse immediately after recounting the solemn dedication of the Carthusian church. His account is composed in the following lines:

> Then Bruno enters the sanctuary, and the aged companions with him.  
> Each removes his precious and soft cloak;  
> They all immediately draw off their shoes from their legs,  
> And their hair is shorn from their noble heads.  
>   
> The noble, milk-white limbs of the young men appear;  
> They remain naked, bent at knees and body.  
> Their panting breasts sent forth sweet sighs,  
> Nor could their pious hearts restrain pious lamentation.  
>   
> O fervor of the young men, O divine love’s affection!  
> Soon the grieving shepherd covers the tender white backs  
> Of the teacher and his brothers with a cilicium,  
> And with a rough sackcloth; he places upon them a white garment  
> Of virgin wool, then girds them with white hemp,  
> And covers their shoulders with a white, closed hood,  
> A sign of everlasting enclosure and purity.  
>   
> Innumerable crowds stood by, and all groaned,  
> Moved by so great an example and such great sweetness.

484. The celebrated metrical biographer of our Saint further adds that the voices of angels applauding the events that took place that day at Chartreuse were heard. But anyone can readily understand from what has already been said what judgment should be formed about this matter.

As for the monastic habit which Bruno and his companions are said to have received at that time from Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, although it appears from Peter the Venerable, book II, chapter 28, of *On Miracles*, that they used clothing at Chartreuse which was poorer and rougher than before, I do not believe that the Saint was then first clothed in a monastic habit by Hugh.

For, apart from the fact that I have found no ancient writer who records this at all, what was already brought forward in § XXIV suggests that Bruno had been clothed in a monastic habit from the time when he was still living in the solitude of Sèche-Fontaine and therefore had not yet gone to Chartreuse, and that he was in fact already a monk.

Nor should you object that Guigo, in the *Life of Saint Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble*, calls the Saint “Master” at the point where he narrates that Bruno approached Hugh. Apart from the fact that the Saint could have been honored with the title “Master” by Landuin and the others who had come with him to Grenoble and placed themselves under his discipline, Guigo could also have called him “Master” even though he had already resigned the mastership or headship of the schools at Reims, because of the office he had formerly held.

I think Guigo uses the title in this latter sense because he also calls Landuin “Master” in the same place, and the title seems to have been attributed to him for no other reason than that he had once held the mastership of a school somewhere or had taught the higher branches of learning.

In any event, the fact that Guigo calls the Saint “Master” at the point where he relates that Bruno approached Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, with six companions cannot prove that Bruno was not then yet clothed in a monastic habit, much less that he was not a monk. For in the charter of the donation of Chartreuse, which will be transcribed below and which was issued in 1086, when he had already spent two years as a Carthusian, he is also called “Master.” He continued to be honored by that same title until his death, even after he had begun living in the Calabrian wilderness.

485. Let us now turn our discussion to the manner of life which the Saint and his companions followed at Chartreuse. It appears beyond doubt that the inhabitants of the Carthusian wilderness who flourished less than forty years after the Saint’s death, that is, in the time of Peter the Venerable, preserved the same manner of life—or at least one not greatly different from it—as that which Saint Bruno and his companions had followed at Chartreuse.

To give the reader some idea of the way of life they followed, I shall present from Peter the Venerable the principal features of the life they led. This writer, who is unquestionably most worthy of credence in this matter, records the following concerning the Carthusians of his own time in book II, chapter 28, of *On Miracles*:

> “To tame the beast of their body and, in the Apostle’s words, to subdue the law of their members, which resists the law of their mind, they continually roughen their flesh with harsh hairshirts. Through nearly uninterrupted severe fasts they afflict, weaken, and dry out their bodies. Hence they always use bran bread and wine diluted with so much water that it may rightly be called more a cheap drink [*vilum*] than wine. They perpetually abstain from all eating of meat, whether healthy or ill. They never buy fish, but sometimes accept it when given out of charity. Only on Sunday and Thursday do they permit themselves cheese or eggs. On Tuesday and Saturday they use either cooked legumes or vegetables. On every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday they are content with bread and water alone. They always eat once a day, except during the eight days of the Nativity of the Lord, the eight days of Easter, the eight days of Pentecost, Epiphany, the Presentation of the Lord—that is, the Purification of Saint Mary—the Annunciation of the Lord when it falls during the Easter season, the Ascension of the Lord, the Assumption and Nativity of the aforesaid holy Virgin, his Mother, and the feasts of the twelve Apostles, Saint John the Baptist, Saint Michael, Saint Martin, and the feast celebrated on the Kalends of November, All Saints.”

486. “In addition to all this, following the ancient custom of the Egyptian monks, they continually inhabit separate cells [in Saint Bruno’s time, according to what was said in no. 475, two lived in each cell], where they devote themselves without interruption to silence, reading, prayer, and manual labor, especially the copying of books. In those same cells, summoned by the church’s signal, they render to God the appointed canonical Hours, namely Prime, Terce, Sext, None, and Compline. At Vespers and Matins they all assemble in the church, and there, not perfunctorily like some, but with the utmost attentiveness, their eyes lowered to the ground and their hearts fixed upon heaven, they offer prayers and thanksgivings to God. By their habit, voice, and expression, with everything else despised, they show that their whole inner as well as outer person is intent—indeed fixed—upon realities surpassing the visible.

“They exempt from this custom those feast days written above, on which they eat twice and on which, in the manner of monks living together rather than separately in cells, they not only sing all the canonical Hours together in the church, but also eat communally in the refectory after Sext and after Vespers, with no person in health excepted. On these days alone, in imitation of the ancient hermits, so that they might not be hindered from other sacred works, though of lesser dignity, they offer the saving sacrifice to almighty God for their own salvation and that of the world. Because of its ancient usage, it is called Mass, from the word meaning that it is sent to God.

“On the sacred days which, by a special privilege from the Lord or from his Resurrection, are called Sundays, and on the often-mentioned solemnities of the Lord himself or of his Saints, they celebrate Masses. On the days when they are permitted to use legumes, they receive them by measure, prepare them, and cook them for themselves.”

487. “This is the practice when they do not eat together in the refectory, but when eremitical discipline requires them to eat alone in their cells. They take wine at no time, either before or after the meal. But if someone should then suffer thirst, he may drink water, not wine.”

Guibert of Nogent, whom I have so often cited above and who died in 1124, records much the same practices, or certainly practices not greatly different, as those observed by the Carthusians flourishing in his time, in book I, chapter 11, of *On His Life*. I therefore refer the curious reader to him, contenting myself with having brought forward the relevant words of Peter the Venerable, who in this matter is certainly a more credible and authoritative witness than Guibert.

I cannot, however, refrain from transcribing here the words in which this writer praises the Carthusians’ devotion to copying books, a devotion unquestionably transmitted to them by their father, Saint Bruno:

> “Although they reduce themselves to complete poverty,” he says in book I, chapter 11, of *On His Life*, “they nevertheless accumulate an exceedingly rich library. For the less they abound in the material supply of this bread, the more laboriously they toil after that food which does not perish but endures forever.”

He then confirms this by the example of the count of Nevers. When the count learned that the gifts of silver which he had sent to the Carthusians had been rejected, “he sent them many ox hides and parchments, which he recognized as almost unavoidably necessary for them” [namely, for writing and binding books].

Guigo tells us why they applied such extraordinary diligence and effort to copying books. In chapter 28 of the *Customs* he writes:

> “We wish books to be guarded with the greatest care and produced with the greatest diligence, as the everlasting food of our souls, so that, because we cannot preach with our mouths, we may preach the word of God with our hands. For however many books we write, we seem to make just as many preachers of the truth.”

It may also be added that they did this partly to provide for their poverty—for they were truly poor and called themselves either “the Poor” or “the Poor of Christ,” as may be seen under the word *pauper* in Du Cange—and partly so that they would not appear wholly useless to the Church, thereby giving malicious people an opportunity to slander their institution.

§ XXVIII. Whether the Saint wrote a new Rule, and whether he bound himself and his disciples to observe any previously written Rule, especially that of Benedict.

488. The extremely austere life which the Saint and his disciples led at Chartreuse is sufficiently demonstrated even by the few features of the rule according to which they ordered it, presented in the preceding section from Peter the Venerable. But the question may now be asked, first, whether Saint Bruno imposed on his disciples the observance of this or some other Rule; and second, whether he bound them, together with himself, to any previously written Rule, and specifically to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

In book I, chapter 3, no. 3, of his work entitled *Annals of the Carthusian Order*, Innocentius le Masson writes:

> “We believe that no rule of life was written by Saint Bruno. Rather, the teachings and examples of that holy man were for them like a living Rule, which they learned to fulfill and, through their own examples, to transmit also to their successors. Nevertheless, we do not doubt that it was the very same Rule which the Reverend Father Guigo later committed to writing. We do not believe that anything is found in his *Customs* which he did not learn, as it were from the mouth of Saint Bruno, through the disciples who had seen and heard him. For Saint Bruno had died scarcely five or six years before our Guigo entered the Order.

> “Therefore, in the *Customs* written by the Reverend Father Guigo, we must firmly believe that the mind, teachings, and manner of direction of Saint Bruno are depicted and contained as though they had been written by his own hand. Anyone will more easily convince himself of this when he becomes more certain that blessed Landuin, whom Saint Bruno had placed over his companions when they were returning to the wilderness of Chartreuse, undertook a very long journey to visit the founder of the Carthusian Institute, who was then living in the Calabrian wilderness, in order to discuss the observances of the Carthusians with him and hear from his own mouth what was to be observed by his followers, and how, in the Carthusian way of life and conduct.

> “The first constitutions of the Carthusians, therefore, were not unlike the law of grace. They were written rather on tablets of fleshly hearts, not with letter but with spirit, than in manuscript books.”

489. Thus Masson teaches that no Rule was written by Saint Bruno. On this point I cannot but agree with him, since I have found no writer, either recent or ancient, who records that the Saint did this.

But did he likewise bind himself and his disciples to none of the previously written Rules, and especially not to the Benedictine Rule? Mabillon writes in the Preface to the second part of the *Benedictine Sixth Century*, no. 87:

> “The occasion now requires us to discuss the first Rule of the Carthusians, which Saint Bruno prescribed for them before the first statutes of that Order were reduced to writing by Guigo. That this Rule was the Rule of Saint Benedict is established by many arguments.
>
> “First, Guigo himself issued his statutes according to the spirit of this Rule, as is shown by the inscription of those statutes in the Codex of Portes, where they are found under the title: ‘The Statutes of Guigo, Prior of Chartreuse, and of the Other Fathers, According to the Rule of Saint Benedict.’ Hence Guigo himself says in his preface that he delayed writing these statutes because he believed that almost everything which, as he says, ‘we customarily do here in a religious manner’ was contained either in the letters of blessed Jerome, or in the Rule of blessed Benedict, or in the other authoritative writings.
>
> “Certainly, in chapter 23 he proposes no other form of profession than the Benedictine one. Furthermore, in the privilege granted by Eugenius III to the Chartreuse of Mont-Dieu, he decreed ‘that the monastic order according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, together with the rule and institutions of the Carthusian brothers, be preserved there inviolably for all time.’
>
> “In addition, Paschal II granted Landuin, prior of Squillace after Saint Bruno, permission to establish a monastery in a certain church belonging to the wilderness, situated near Squillace, ‘so that the brothers who are unable to endure the austerity of the wilderness may there serve almighty God according to the Rule of blessed Benedict.’ He further says: ‘We decree that this habitation be governed and administered by a provost and a dean, yet in such a way that the provost of the wilderness always takes precedence and is regarded as superior; and in such a way that the same monastery remains subject to the administration of the wilderness, and that its provost and dean likewise be subject to the master of the wilderness.’ Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February.”

490. “From these things it is understood that there were there two kinds of Carthusians, anchorites and cenobites, as among the Camaldolese; and that the prior of the hermitage presided over both according to the rule of Saint Benedict, who instructed both kinds in his rule. This [Col. 0298A] document, however, concerns the monastery of Mentauri, which lay three miles from Squillace, as we shall relate more fully in our Annals, where we shall report the constitutions of both groups, namely the anchorites and the cenobites of Squillace. Finally, before the canonization of Saint Bruno, the Carthusians called Saint Benedict ‘their Father’ in their profession, and even now retain the arrangement of the divine office from the rule of Saint Benedict, whose feast they have always observed with solemn ritual according to their custom.”

Thus far Mabillon. He argues that Saint Bruno, who, according to what has been said, did not compose a new rule, nevertheless prescribed a particular rule for his followers, or bound himself and his disciples to a certain particular rule, and that this was the rule of Saint Benedict. But [Col. 0298B] do the arguments that he brings forward really establish the matter? I certainly do not think so. Indeed, from the following words supplied by Guigo in the preface placed before the Customs—or statutes—composed by him for the Charterhouse, and cited by Mabillon in support of his position, the opposite rather appears:

“We long delayed undertaking this task”—namely, writing down the Customs of the Charterhouse—“for what we believe to be reasonable causes: namely, because we believed that almost everything which we customarily practice here”—that is, in the Charterhouse—“religiously was contained either in the letters of blessed Jerome, or in the rule of blessed Benedict, or in the other authoritative writings.”

It therefore seems to follow that Saint Bruno did not bind himself and his followers to any particular rule at all.

[Col. 0298C] 491. Hear how Masson comments on these words in his work entitled *The Annals of the Carthusian Order*:

“From this”—that is, from Guigo’s words just quoted—“it is evident,” he says, “what freedom Saint Bruno and his successors wished to exercise in choosing and arranging their purpose and manner of life for themselves, according as the Spirit and prudence suggested, and in refusing to bind themselves to those specific rules or constitutions which had long before been composed in various monastic orders, both in the East and in the West. Saint Bruno chose nothing for his manner of life that had not been praised in the writings of Saint Jerome, Benedict, and others; but for that reason he did not subject himself to their rules, although, like a spiritual bee, he gathered from them what he might use to compose his own honey and wax. Therefore the professors of his institute cannot be reproached for not following this or that institution and practice of the saints—whether Antony, John Climacus, Benedict, Bernard, or the ancient Eastern Fathers—for these were not the rules of their own purpose, nor did they choose them for themselves to observe.”

Certainly, since Guigo’s quoted words teach that what had until the time of his writing been customarily practiced religiously in the Charterhouse was contained not only in the rule of Saint Benedict, but either in the letters of Saint Jerome, or in the rule of Saint Benedict, or finally in other writings, they sufficiently indicate that at that time the Carthusians were not bound to observe only the rule of Saint Benedict. Rather, they followed those excellent institutions of life which they judged more suitable to the kind of life they had embraced, whether found in Saint Jerome, Benedict, [Col. 0299A] or any other holy Fathers. Thus the anonymous author of the hitherto unpublished fourth book of the Carthusian annals rightly maintains:

“Saint Bruno and his disciples never bound themselves to any one determinate monastic rule, but, as arbiters, accepted from the writings and examples of the ancients whatever seemed suited to the perfection of the eremitical life.”

492. But in the words quoted immediately above Mabillon says that the statutes composed by Guigo bear the following title in the Codex of Portes:

“Statutes of Guigo, prior of the Charterhouse, and of the other Fathers, according to the rule of Saint Benedict.”

This is the first argument that the writer advances for his opinion. But although, as he says, Guigo’s statutes bear this title in that codex, it does not follow from this that Guigo brought them into conformity with the mind of the Benedictine rule. Since the title itself apparently does not name Guigo as its author, it is possible that it was added to the aforesaid codex by someone who had only an imperfect understanding of the manner in which Guigo had composed his statutes.

Whatever the case may be, Guigo himself indicates clearly enough in the preface that he prefixed to these statutes that he did not bring them into conformity with, or compose them according to, the mind of the Benedictine rule alone. For he says that he was committing to writing not new precepts or statutes, but the Customs—that is, those things then habitually practiced in the Charterhouse. Since these, as he himself indicates in the words [Col. 0299C] transcribed above, were contained not only in the rule of Saint Benedict, but either in that rule, or in the letters of blessed Jerome, or in other authoritative writings, it follows that Guigo did not frame his statutes according to the rule of Saint Benedict alone, and consequently that Saint Bruno and his disciples did not bind themselves and their followers to observe that rule exclusively.

Nor does the privilege granted by Eugene III to the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu, which Mabillon also cites, prove that the Saint and his disciples bound themselves to the sole rule of Saint Benedict.

493. In that document the pope decreed that the monastic order there should be preserved inviolably not only “according to the rule of blessed Benedict,” but also “according to the norm and institutions of the Carthusian brothers.” [Col. 0299D] Therefore, by virtue of that papal privilege, the monastery of Mont-Dieu was to observe neither the rule of Saint Benedict alone nor even the whole of it, but only those portions of it that agreed with the particular institutions of the Carthusians. From the fact that certain institutions of the Benedictine rule were adopted and observed by Saint Bruno, his disciples, or their followers, it does not follow that Saint Bruno and his disciples intended to bind themselves to observe that rule, one and entire.

Thus Mabillon could establish nothing in support of his opinion, even if we were for the moment to grant what he further adduces as an argument: that the Carthusians still retain the arrangement of the divine office from the rule of Saint Benedict. [Col. 0300A] But even this does not appear to accord exactly with the truth. For Masson, in his work entitled *The Annals of the Carthusian Order*, comments as follows on these words of Guigo’s statutes:

“In this”—that is, in the divine office—“they are found to agree much with the other monks, especially in the regular psalmody.”

Masson writes:

“He does not say ‘in everything,’ because in fact, in composing the Carthusian divine office, the monastic rite was adopted in the twelve psalms, three canticles, and twelve lessons, and in other similar matters; but quite a few elements were also added from the rites of both the Church of Lyon and the Church of Grenoble, in whose diocese the Charterhouse is situated. This can be proved from the ancient missals of the Church of Grenoble and from the manner of celebrating Mass then customary there, which are reproduced almost exactly in our own; likewise from the old antiphonaries and prayers which are known to have been transferred from the Church of Lyon for our use.”

494. A Carthusian anonymous author, the writer of the fourth book of the annals of his order, hitherto unpublished, supplies some further material relevant to this matter on page 56 of the fuller copy of his work, which is at the Charterhouse of Val-de-Dieu and is not in my possession. The Parisian Carthusian mentioned above, who, as he himself informed me, has that copy at hand, and who in every possible way wishes his name to remain undisclosed, has kindly transcribed the words in question and communicated them to me with his customary courtesy. They are as follows:

“From the very beginnings of our order we have venerated Saint Benedict, the restorer of the cenobitic life in the western regions, always celebrating his feast as especially solemn, as may be seen from Guigo’s Customs. Nor without reason, since from his rule they have drawn certain provisions suited to the cenobitic life, especially those concerning the divine office. Thus Robert of Mont, treating of the origin of the Carthusians in his work on abbots and abbeys, says: ‘They perform the offices of the night and of the day according to the rule of Saint Benedict.’ And our Guigo, in the prologue to his Customs, says ‘that in the divine office they are found to agree much with the other monks, especially in the regular psalmody.’

[Col. 0300D] “Nevertheless, we do not observe the rite of Saint Benedict so strictly that we do not differ from it in certain respects, especially regarding the ceremonies both of the Mass and of the divine office, the readings at Matins, the prayers of the Hours, chants, hymns, and other matters of this kind, some of which Cardinal Bona enumerates.”

Thus he also indicates why the Carthusians have always regarded the feast of Saint Benedict as solemn: namely, because they had assigned to the order’s statutes or Customs not the sole and entire rule of this holy Father of monks, but at least certain chapters from it. From this it may also have happened that, before the canonization of Saint Bruno, the Carthusians called Saint Benedict “their Father” in their profession. Consequently, Mabillon by no means proves from this that the rule of Saint Benedict was prescribed by Saint Bruno to the first Carthusians.

495. Nor does he prove it by the two other arguments that remain to be discussed. One is drawn from the privilege granted by Paschal II to Lanvin, prior of Squillace after Saint Bruno; the other from the formula of profession used among the Carthusians.

For who would reasonably conclude from the fact that this formula is the same as that of the Benedictines that the rule belonging to the Benedictines likewise belongs to the Carthusians? In substance, the formula of profession is nearly the same in most, not to say all, religious orders; yet it does not follow that the substantive rule of all these orders is likewise the same.

Nor does it matter that the profession formula of both Carthusians [Col. 0301B] and Benedictines is expressed in exactly the same words. Just as, from the fact that certain statutes of the Benedictine rule have been transferred word for word into the Carthusian rule, it does not follow—according to what has already been said—that Saint Bruno prescribed that entire rule, and that rule alone, for the first Carthusians to observe, so it cannot follow, as will be clear to anyone who considers the matter, from the fact that the Carthusians adopted for their own use the same words in which the profession formula is expressed among the Benedictines.

As for the privilege granted by Paschal II to Lanvin, it concerns exclusively the particular monastery of Mentauri, erected by the pope’s indulgence by Lanvin three miles from Squillace. Those who were not suited to the eremitical life maintained there a manner of living different from that of the other Carthusians. Therefore, even if we were for the moment to grant that the new inhabitants of that monastery had expressly been prescribed the sole and complete rule of Saint Benedict, it still would not follow that this rule had likewise been prescribed by Saint Bruno for the first Carthusians.

Thus, from none of the arguments by which Mabillon argues that the Carthusians were bound by Saint Bruno to the Benedictine rule is the matter in any way established. This is sufficiently clear from everything that has been said.

496. Indeed, to state my opinion openly on this matter, it is evident even from the fact that Saint Bruno did not bind either himself or his followers to observe the sole and entire rule of Saint Benedict that almost everything he imposed upon himself and his followers as something to be observed, and actually observed in practice, was set down by Guigo in writing in the Customs, while the Customs are very far from containing the sole and entire Benedictine rule.

Mabillon, in my view, eventually perceived this, and, turning somewhat from his earlier opinion, wrote in *Benedictine Annals*, book 66, no. 65, that Bruno proposed to himself and his followers only “the rule of Saint Benedict insofar as it expressed the institution of the anchorites.” But this too is not established by the arguments brought forward above from that author, whom Martène nevertheless follows here in *Veterum Scriptorum*, volume 6, Preface, no. 32, as is easy to infer from what has already been said and what will be said hereafter.

On the contrary, the anonymous Carthusian author of the hitherto unpublished fourth book of the Carthusian annals rightly maintains that Saint Bruno and his followers adopted a particular kind of life, or bound themselves to a certain special rule distinct both from the Benedictine rule and from all others previously composed. The Parisian Carthusian mentioned again in no. 494 also informed me of this. At the place cited there, the author writes:

“Haeften, in the first book of his *Monastic Investigations*, treatise 9, *On Rules Written in the Twelfth Century*, investigation 4, distinguishes our statutes—which he admits may truly be called a rule—from the rule of Saint Benedict. And in treatise 2 of the second book, investigation 5, where he discusses the Carthusians, he speaks of them as distinct from the Benedictine order:

“‘To omit those who serve God under the rule of Saint Benedict—who ought rather to be regarded as various congregations of one order than as distinct orders—the Carthusian order has borrowed many things from Saint Benedict,’ and so forth.”

By these words he plainly implies that the Carthusians, although they borrowed many things from Saint Benedict, nevertheless do not serve God under his rule. Indeed, in treatise 6 of the same book, investigation 4, when he lists the orders that profess the Benedictine rule, he makes no mention of the Carthusians.
