497. “Two hundred years earlier Saint Antoninus held the same opinion, writing as follows” —namely, in part 2 of his history, title 15, chapter 14—:

“After Benedict, all the monks of the West serve under the rule of blessed Benedict and have him as their father, except the Carthusians, who have their own particular constitutions.”

And in fact, when Guigo, our first legislator, says at the place cited:

“In the letters of blessed Jerome, or in the rule of blessed Benedict, or in the other authoritative writings, almost everything which we customarily practice religiously in the Charterhouse is contained,”

he sufficiently and plainly indicates in these words that the Carthusians had prescribed for themselves a special norm of life, different from the other rules.

For this reason Francis of Puteo, explaining a statute of our Raynaldus which forbids those professed in the Cistercian order and similar orders, when transferring to us, to hold any obedience, declares that by the word “SIMILAR” are meant all monks who serve under the rule of Saint Benedict. Who would not see that our Puteanus tacitly distinguishes the Carthusians from the other monks of Saint Benedict, as subject to another rule?

Our Boso, writing against those who say that the Carthusian order has no rule, indeed acknowledges that our statutes were composed from various writings of the holy Fathers:

“For it is clear,” he says, “from these same statutes that the things written there are either taken from the rule of blessed Benedict, or from the letters of blessed Jerome, or from the Conferences of the Fathers, or from the Lives of the Fathers, or even from the books of Cassian and of other holy doctors of the Church.”

He then lists many rules and adds:

“But the Carthusian order could not adopt any of the rules mentioned above, because all those rules either are or were institutions of the common and cenobitic life. For the eremitical life there is found a praiseworthy and devout rule, composed and arranged by Peter Damian in a most eloquent style; but the Carthusians could neither adopt nor wished to adopt that rule either, because the life of the Carthusians, as has been shown above, although it must be judged eremitical in its greater and more excellent part, is nevertheless composed of both the solitary and the common life.

498. “And therefore, since no such religious order previously existed, it was wholly necessary for them to make a special rule for themselves. For according to the rules mentioned above, of blessed Augustine, Benedict, and the other writers cited above, monks or canons must live together, eat together, sleep together, and so forth in each matter, as the cenobitic and common life requires. Therefore the Carthusians, who for the most part lead an anchoritic life and frequently eat alone and sleep alone, as has been shown above, could not adopt any of the aforesaid rules. Instead, inspired by the Holy Spirit, they issued for themselves a new, holy, and reasonable rule, which, through the operation of that same Spirit, the holy Roman Church, with certain knowledge, confirmed most perfectly, as we shall prove elsewhere.”

From these and the other things we have said above, it is clear that the Carthusians adopted a particular kind of monastic life and consequently established in the Church of God an order distinct from the other orders.”

Thus far the anonymous Carthusian author cited above. Drawing upon the arguments that he reports from Boso in these very words, as well as those that he derives from elsewhere, he maintains that the Carthusians—and consequently Saint Bruno, who had taught them this rule by his example and manner of life—established for themselves a rule distinct from all preceding rules and prescribed it for their observance.

Indeed, since, as Boso says, the manner of life of the Carthusians is partly eremitical and partly cenobitic, and since none of the rules written before the time of Saint Bruno was suited to such a form of life, they necessarily had to prescribe for themselves and their followers another rule possessing this distinctive quality, or shape it for them by their own example.

Our Saint and his first disciples must therefore be considered to have done precisely this, as the anonymous author of the Carthusian annals maintains in the words quoted above. Since this also appears sufficiently evident from the other matters mentioned earlier, I bring this discussion to an end.

§ XXIX. Whether Pope Victor III approved the Carthusian order, and whether the Saint had Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, reverent toward him and obtained the gift of the Charterhouse hermitage for himself

499. Zacharias Benedictus accepted as reliable the account of the vision divinely granted to Gaufred, prior of Vosi, who, as I explained above, reports that Pope Victor III saw the Lord constructing a dwelling for Himself in the hermitage of the Charterhouse. He incorporated this account into the metrical *Life of our Saint* which he composed.

He therefore judged that the vision had been shown by God—who does nothing without purpose—to Victor, undoubtedly not yet as a monk, as Gaufred says, but already as pope, so that Victor might understand from it that the foundation of the Charterhouse made by the Saint was God’s work and might consequently be moved to confirm it by apostolic authority. Zacharias consequently persuaded himself that Victor had in fact confirmed the foundation of the Charterhouse. The following verses, in which he sings of this event, are offered as evidence:

> When Gregory, seventh in lofty titles,  
> Sat upon the Latin throne and held the reins of the world,  
> And when he died, Victor took command of Peter’s see.  
> He then, as it happened, looked toward the heavenly axes,  
> And saw the blessed choirs flashing with radiant splendor,  
> From their holy seats joyfully joining the Thunderer.  
> As the Thunderer proceeded to visit the Carthusian hills,  
> they were building worthy dwellings for him in the rocks.  
> He marveled at those mountains and observed the region;  
> He sent a swift messenger and rapid letters there,  
> And wrote to Hugh of the miracles he had seen.  
> Hugh, astonished, wrote back everything that had happened at that time,  
> And with his swift pen recorded what the Almighty had done  
> In those regions: the Teacher and six companions  
> Turned away from the world’s whirlpool,  
> The lights of seven stars, and likewise  
> The course and strict rigor of the order they had begun.

500. The messenger departed and returned to the Latin city.

> When the greatest Shepherd received the new tidings, rejoicing,  
> He immediately summoned the Fathers, the holy senate,  
> Those whom Roman purple makes exalted, and disclosed  
> Everything that had occurred and had been divinely advanced.  
> With the unanimous wishes of the court he confirmed the work,  
> And, after completing the document, fortified it with divine gifts;  
> He enriched it with various endowments,  
> And the bronzes marked with double-faced signs are preserved.  
> This man had earlier been abbot, before attaining the highest summit,  
> Of the Mount of Olives, whose name came from the city of Cassino,  
> Once celebrated as a colony of the descendants of Aeneas.  
> Many other supreme Fathers did the same,  
> Those who encircle their lofty heads with the triple diadem.

Thus he records that the vision he describes was shown to Pope Victor—not, as I have already said, while he was still a Cassinese monk or, if one prefers, an abbot, but after he had been created supreme pontiff, contrary to Gaufred’s account—and that Victor, having learned from Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, that the foundation had been made by Saint Bruno, confirmed it by apostolic letters.

But neither Gaufred himself, who writes that the vision was shown to Pope Victor, nor any other writers whom I have so far seen mention such a confirmation, all of whom are earlier than Zacharias Benedictus. Therefore I strongly suspect—or rather, I regard it as virtually certain—that the metrical biographer of our Saint constructed this account solely from a conjecture formed on the basis of the vision that he believed had been shown to Victor.

But since, as was stated above, Gaufred departed from the truth when he committed to writing the vision in which Pope Victor III supposedly saw God constructing a dwelling for Himself in the solitude of the Charterhouse, there can be no doubt that the conjecture he formed from that vision likewise departs from the truth.

501. Furthermore, Victor was raised to the papal throne in 1086 and did not live beyond the following year, when Urban II succeeded him. That no papal letters mentioning the Carthusian order existed before the time when Urban II began to occupy the see of Saint Peter is shown with some clarity by the anonymous chronicler of the first five priors of the Charterhouse—or by the earlier biographer of our Saint—whose authority and reliability are certainly greater than those of the metrical biographer Zacharias Benedictus discussed here.

For after reporting, in no. 19, that letters had been written by Urban II—letters that I shall transcribe below—in which Siguin, abbot of Casa-Dei, was ordered to restore the Charterhouse to Landuin and his companions, who had abandoned it when Bruno departed for Rome, he immediately adds in the following number:

“These appear to be the first papal letters found to mention the Carthusian order.”

Now, since those letters, which according to the foregoing were written by Urban, are the first found to mention the Carthusian order, it must be regarded as certain—especially in view of the universal silence of all the ancient writers on the matter—that no letters were written by Victor III confirming or approving the foundation of the Charterhouse. Consequently, Zacharias Benedictus wrongly recorded that this had occurred.

Nor is this the only error for which this metrical biographer of the Saint must be censured. He also records that Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, received the Carthusian habit from Saint Bruno and was therefore enrolled among the Carthusians. Guigo, however, nowhere mentions this fact. He was the most exact and most trustworthy biographer of Hugh and, had the event occurred, would certainly have known of it and committed it to writing.

502. Yet this error, which first arose from the spurious Sigebert—see no. 297—seems in some way excusable. Although Hugh never put on the Carthusian habit, he could nevertheless in a certain sense have been regarded as a Carthusian, both because he is known to have burned with the desire to profess as a Carthusian after resigning his episcopate, and because of the exceptional affection he bore toward the Carthusians and his frequent stays with them in the Charterhouse.

That Saint Hugh had the greatest affection for Saint Bruno and the Carthusians is evident both from the words of Guigo transcribed above and from the fact that, as Guibert of Nogent teaches in book 1, chapter 11, of *On His Life*, that holy bishop did not shrink from exercising, after Bruno had departed from it, “the functions, in a certain sense, of abbot” and “administrator” of the Carthusian house.

The earlier biographer of our Saint further says in no. 14 that Hugh was so beneficent toward both the Carthusian order and house that he may be called, together with Saint Bruno, “the founder, and although not the first, nevertheless in a certain sense the principal institutor” of both.

As for Hugh’s residence in the Charterhouse, Guigo again teaches us that it was certainly very frequent and that during the same period Hugh conformed his life exactly to the model and standard of the Carthusians, so that he could in a certain sense have been regarded as a Carthusian. Guigo does this partly in the words of the holy bishop’s *Life* already transcribed above, and partly in the following passage:

“Saint Hugh, so devotedly and assiduously inhabited the hermitage”—that is, the Charterhouse with Saint Bruno and his companions—“that Master Bruno sometimes compelled him to leave, saying, ‘Go, go to your sheep and render to them what you owe.’ At that time, inflamed by a great ardor of poverty and humility, he wished to sell all his riding animals and, distributing the proceeds to the poor, to travel about on foot in preaching. But Master Bruno, a man of profound understanding, whose counsels he obeyed no otherwise than the commands of an abbot, did not consent. He feared that Hugh might perhaps become proud in his own eyes, or be judged by the other bishops to be seeking singularity; or”—and this was not doubtful—“that he might be unable to complete the undertaking because of the roughness and unevenness of the roads.”

503. These words of Guigo reveal not only what I have just stated, but also that Hugh possessed no less reverence for Saint Bruno than affection for him, and that this reverence was so great that he regarded Bruno in a certain sense as his abbot.

For this reason the earlier biographer of our Saint, after transcribing both these words and others of Guigo already given above, appropriately adds in no. 14:

“All the foregoing are the words of Lord Guigo, written in the *Life of Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble*. We have judged that they should be inserted here because they reveal the beginnings of the foundation of the Charterhouse, and make known the excellence of Master Bruno, especially in showing how such a venerable and holy bishop adhered to him with such reverence, fervor, and humility.”

One may also rightly conclude that our Saint and his companions were held by Saint Hugh in the greatest love and esteem from the charter which, if Mabillon is correct—and I do not know whether it exists anywhere—this holy bishop wrote to the priests and laymen of his diocese scarcely one full month after Saint Bruno’s arrival. In it he ordered:

“that women”—these are Mabillon’s words—“should not pass through the land of the brothers of the Charterhouse, who, desiring to please God, were fleeing the world and crowds; and that no one should exercise fishing or hunting within the boundaries of their property, or lead his animals there to graze.”

This may also be inferred from the fact that the Saint willingly ceded to him and his companions whatever right he possessed in the Charterhouse, and very probably also, as Blomenvenna, Puteus, and other biographers of the Saint agree in asserting, caused others who possessed any right in the same hermitage to renounce it in favor of Saint Bruno and his companions by issuing a public charter.

Since the place seems to require it, I now transcribe the charter in full from the copy inserted in the *Chronological-Diplomatic Disquisition* of Morkensius, cited so often above. It reads as follows:

“By the grace of the holy and undivided Trinity, mercifully reminded of our salvation, we have remembered the condition of human existence and the unavoidable falls of this fragile life, which we spend without end in sins. Therefore we have judged that we, servants of sin, should redeem ourselves from the hand of death, exchange temporal things for heavenly ones, and purchase an eternal inheritance at the price of a possession destined to perish, lest we be crushed by a twofold affliction and begin the miseries of the present life with labors and sorrows.

504. “Therefore, to Master Bruno and to the brothers who came with him, seeking a solitude in which they might devote themselves to God, and to them and their successors in perpetual possession, we have granted a spacious hermitage for habitation: I, Humbert of Miribel, together with my brother Odo and the others who held any right in the aforesaid place.

“These are: Hugh of Tolnone; Anselm Garcinus; then Lucia and her sons Rostan, Guigo, Anselm, Pontius, and Boso, at the prayers and intervention of their aforesaid mother; Bernard the Lombard with his sons; and likewise Lord Abbot Siguin of Casa-Dei with the assembly of his brothers. Whatever right they appeared to possess there, they have likewise granted to the aforesaid brothers.

“The hermitage itself, which we gave them, has these boundaries: within the place called Clusa; and the rock enclosing the valley and extending as far as the millstone that encloses and divides Combe-Calde, and reaching as far as the middle rock situated above Borghesos; then another boundary-marker, which descends as far as the rock at Bonviant. From there, another boundary-marker descends along the edge of the plane-tree grove from Bonviant as far as the rock above the oven of La Follia. Likewise, from that mountain which extends from the same rock as far as Mount Aillinart; and from Mount Aillinart, descending, it stretches beside Morta toward the west as far as the rock above Correria; and from that rock it extends as far as the rock of Pertuso. Finally, from there it stretches downward as far as the river called the Dead Guerus. From there it is enclosed by the same river as far as Clusa.

“But if any person, powerful or powerless, should violate this donation, let that person, as guilty of sacrilege, be separated from the grace of Almighty God and from the fellowship of the faithful, and be struck by the anathema *Maranatha* and consumed by the fire of eternal punishment, unless he makes worthy satisfaction; let him be burned with Dathan, Abiram, and the traitor Judas.”

505. “The aforesaid land, enclosed within these boundaries, began to be inhabited and constructed by Master Bruno and the brothers who were with him in the year 1084 from the Incarnation of the Lord. It was the fourth year of the episcopate of Lord Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, who praises and confirms this gift made by the persons written above, together with his entire assembly [Col. 0308A] of clergy, and, insofar as concerns himself, wholly grants whatever appears to be his right.

“The witnesses are Hugh the dean; John of Puy; Rostagnus; Guigo of Lanz; Walter Bueta; Peter and Gilbert; Agelbert and Aldelemus; Peter and Richard.

“This charter was read at Grenoble in the church of the blessed and glorious perpetual Virgin Mary, on the fourth day of the week”—Wednesday—“of the second week of the Lord’s Advent, in the presence of the aforesaid Lord Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and his canons, and many others, both priests and clerics of the other orders, who were celebrating a holy synod, on the fifth day before the Ides of December.”

Since this charter, as the chronological indications with which it is authenticated show, was read on the Wednesday of the second week of Advent—a day which falls on 9 December—and since Saint Bruno was still inhabiting the Charterhouse, it must undoubtedly have been issued during the period comprising the year 1084, the following five years, and part of the year 1090. Since, as will become clear to anyone who calculates the date, or even merely consults Labbe’s *Technical Chronology*, the Wednesday of the second week of Advent fell on the fifth day before the Ides, that is, on 9 December, only in the year 1086, it is perfectly clear that the charter transcribed above was read or issued in that very year.

506. And this is the first point that calls for notice concerning it. To prevent anyone from supposing that there is an error in the chronological notes, it must now be explained in what sense it can rightly be said that the desert of Chartreuse began to be inhabited by the Saint and his companions in June 1084 [Col. 0308C], as stated above, in the fourth year of the episcopate of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble. For Hugh, as I have shown above, had already been elected bishop of Grenoble in 1079 and consecrated at the beginning of the following year; consequently, when the Saint began to inhabit the desert of Chartreuse, Hugh had already entered upon the fifth year of his episcopate—if, that is, his episcopal years are to be reckoned either from his election or from his consecration. But is it necessary to reckon them in this way?

The author of an anonymous *Treatise on Saint Bruno*, communicated to me by the Carthusians of this place, having stated beforehand that the years of Hugh’s episcopate were customarily reckoned not from his election or consecration but from his taking possession of the episcopal see, and that Hugh did not take possession of the bishopric of Grenoble until the end of 1080 [Col. 0308D], immediately adds the following, by which both points are demonstrated:

> “There is preserved in the archive of the Grand Chartreuse a donation made by Count Guigo and his wife, Queen Mathilda, to the house of Cales, dated in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1110, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, in the thirtieth year of the pontificate of Lord Hugh, bishop of Grenoble. This thirtieth year of Hugh’s pontificate is not reckoned from his election or consecration; otherwise—for Hugh was elected in 1079 and consecrated bishop of Grenoble at the beginning of the following year, as I have again just noted—it would have had to be designated the thirty-first or thirty-second year. It must therefore be called the year of his possession of the see, which he had not yet obtained in October 1080 [Col. 0309A], as follows from the specified date, the eleventh day before the Kalends of November.”

507. “The same conclusion must necessarily be drawn from another instrument, published in *On the Use of the Fiefs of the Dauphiné*, whose beginning and end are as follows:

> ‘I, Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, at the request of the canons, granted to Boso, abbot of Sainte-Marie de Cruas, and to his successors, three churches . . . . This donation of the three aforesaid churches was made . . . . on the fourth day before the Nones of November, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1110, in the thirtieth year of the pontificate of Lord Hugh, bishop.’

Therefore Hugh had not yet entered upon the episcopate at the beginning of November in the aforementioned year 1080.”

To this I add, as the purpose of the present discussion requires, that since Hugh—having, as stated above, been elected bishop of Grenoble in 1079 and consecrated at the beginning of 1080—had, by the fourth day before the Nones of November, that is, by 2 November 1110, advanced into the year 1110, the year from his election and consecration would have been not the thirtieth but the thirty-first. Yet the instrument whose beginning and end the anonymous author of the *Treatise on Saint Bruno* exhibits is dated to the thirtieth year of Hugh’s episcopate. It follows that, both in this document and in the other by which Count Guigo and his wife Mathilda made a benefaction to the house of Cales, Hugh’s episcopal years were reckoned not from his election or consecration, but from his taking possession of that see after his consecration.

Since this is so, and since, as the Carthusian anonymous author cited above affirms, it appears consistent with the truth that Hugh’s episcopal years were customarily reckoned not from his election or consecration but from his first taking possession of the see, there is certainly no reason for regarding the charter of the donation of Chartreuse transcribed above as suspect on account of an error in its chronological notes, or for accusing it because it states that the desert of Chartreuse began to be inhabited by Saint Bruno and his companions in the fourth year of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble. According to what has been said above, this can be true only if the reckoning is begun from the time when Hugh took possession of the bishopric.

§ XXX. The Saint, summoned by the supreme pontiff, is compelled to leave Chartreuse, now duly organized and increased in population: when this occurred, and with what grief Bruno’s disciples received it.

[Col. 0309D]

508. It is not open to doubt that, after four or five years—or even somewhat fewer—from the Saint’s and his companions’ entry into Chartreuse, everything had already been properly organized in a manner most suited to the eremitical life, both as regards the dwellings of the religious inhabitants of the desert and as regards their rule of life. It is likewise clear that the Saint and his companions had become widely renowned for the austerity and holiness of the life they had undertaken.

I therefore think that this was the reason why some others came to the previously uncultivated and almost inaccessible desert and requested to be enrolled among the disciples of the celebrated man who governed it. First, Peter and Lambert—who, before the Saint had entered Chartreuse, had for some time led an eremitical life together with him in the solitude of Sicca-Fontana, as is attested more than once by the charter of the monastery of Molesme already cited from Mabillon—appear, according to the writers of the *Literary History of France*, vol. IX, p. 241, to have eventually embraced Bruno’s manner of life, either at Chartreuse or in Calabria.

There they make it fairly clear that Peter was distinct from Peter who, although born at Béthune, was surnamed “the Frenchman” because of his long residence in France, and who became the second prior of Chartreuse after Saint Bruno—see Labbe, vol. I of the *New Library of Manuscript Books*, p. 639. And, they indicate, Lambert was distinct from Lambert who, as prior or master of Calabrian Chartreuse, prescribed excellent laws for its religious inhabitants [Col. 0310B].

Indeed, since it could easily have happened that Peter and Lambert, who had earlier been unwilling to follow Bruno when he left the solitude of Sicca-Fontana for Grenoble, later changed their minds when they heard that the Saint had established a permanent residence at Chartreuse, and, with his approval, went to that rugged desert, it is by no means implausible that they actually did so. Nevertheless, I would not dare assert that Lambert, who had been with the Saint in the solitude of Sicca-Fontana, was the same person as Lambert, prior of Calabrian Chartreuse.

509. But whatever the facts may be, that the Saint had more disciples when he left the desert of Chartreuse than when he first entered that solitude is suggested to me by two charters [Col. 0310C], which I shall transcribe in full below. In one, Roger, count of Calabria and Sicily, gives the Calabrian desert to Saint Bruno and his companions; in the other, Roger, duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, whose uncle Roger the count was, confirms this donation.

In the first charter the count speaks as follows:

> “Roger, by the grace of God, to all his faithful throughout Calabria and Sicily and to the sons of the Church of God, present and future, greeting. We wish your brotherhood to know that, by the mercy of God, from the regions of Gaul there have come to this land of Calabria men of holy religion, namely Bruno and Lanvinus, with their companions, etc.”

In the second, Duke Roger speaks in this manner:

> “Roger, by the grace of God duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, to all faithful Christians, present and future, greeting in the Lord. We wish your brotherhood to know concerning two men, namely Bruno and Lanvinus, who, inflamed by zeal for holy religion, came with their companions from the regions of Gaul to the land of Calabria, God so disposing, etc.” [Col. 0310D]

Thus, when the Saint came to Count Roger in Calabria—which, as will be shown, occurred not long after his departure from Chartreuse—he had with him several companions who had come from Gaul and are mentioned in these charters. Since at least one of them, Lanvinus, was different from all six of the Saint’s companions who first entered the desert of Chartreuse with him, it follows that, when the Saint left the desert of Chartreuse to visit the pontiff, his disciples were more numerous than when he first entered that solitude.

I shall now show that Lanvinus, mentioned in the two cited charters, was different from all six of the Saint’s aforesaid companions—or rather, from Landuinus, a point which some might regard as especially doubtful. As will become clear from what follows, the Saint did not withdraw with Lanvinus to the Calabrian desert, nor obtain the donation and confirmation of that desert mentioned in the two charters, until after Landuinus had returned with the disciples—or Carthusians—whom Saint Bruno had placed under his direction, to the Grand Chartreuse, which they had left. It is therefore necessary that Landuinus be different from Lanvinus.

510. Moreover, Lanvinus, who withdrew with the Saint to the Calabrian desert, was born in Normandy, a province of France, whereas Landuinus, who returned to the Grand Chartreuse at Saint Bruno’s direction, was born in Tuscany [Col. 0311B].

Furthermore, Landuinus the Tuscan died in the year 1100, when he had come from the Grand Chartreuse, over which he presided as prior, to visit Bruno in Calabria—see Labbe, vol. I of the *New Library of Manuscript Books*, p. 639. Lanvinus, on the other hand, survived Saint Bruno, who, as will be shown, died in 1101, and was appointed to succeed him in the governance of Calabrian Chartreuse, as may be seen in Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, book LXX, no. 30.

It is therefore certain that Lanvinus, who lived with the Saint in the Calabrian desert, was distinct from Landuinus the Tuscan. This should be carefully noted, lest in what follows one be confused with the other [Col. 0311C].

Moreover, among the Saint’s companions mentioned in the two charters just cited, there were, in all probability, at least several others who were different from the six companions of the Saint who first entered the desert of Chartreuse with him. Thus, when the Saint departed from Chartreuse and set out for Calabria, the number of his companions had already increased.

Nor should one reply that the companions with whom the Saint is said in the two cited charters to have come to Calabria—and specifically Lanvinus, for whom see Zanotti’s *Life of Bruno*, chap. 17—did not join him until he was already in Italy, after leaving Chartreuse. For the claim that, during the brief period which, as will be shown, he spent with the pontiff before withdrawing to Calabria, the Saint immediately found at Rome men who had arrived from Gaul and placed themselves under his direction appears scarcely probable—yet such a circumstance would be needed to establish anything against our opinion [Col. 0311D].

511. Since this is so, there seems to be no reason to question whether the Saint saw the number of his disciples increased when he left Chartreuse; indeed, it is certain that he would have seen it increase still further if he had been able to remain longer at Chartreuse.

But after he had governed the desert of Chartreuse for six years as prior—or rather as “master,” for this is the title assigned to him and to his immediate successors by nearly all writers—a papal mandate was brought to him by which Pope Urban II, raised to the papal dignity in 1088, most strictly ordered him to proceed to the Roman Curia [Col. 0312A].

Urban had formerly been our Saint’s disciple at Reims, as I have already shown above. He therefore had a particularly clear knowledge of the man’s rare prudence and intellectual insight and wished to have him near him as a counselor during those extremely difficult times, when the affairs of the Church in Italy and Germany were being disastrously disturbed by the emperor Henry IV, who was opposed to the pope and frequently took up arms against the papal party in Italy.

As soon as that message reached Bruno’s disciples, an immense grief immediately entered the hearts of all. Hear what Blomenvenna records on this subject in the *Life of our Saint* which he composed:

> “And behold,” he says, “when scarcely six years had been spent in such a manner of life, he was again put to the test . . . . Pope Urban II—formerly named Otto, abbot of Cluny, who had once been a disciple of blessed Bruno—having attained the supreme pontificate and wishing to administer it worthily, mindful of the outstanding learning and probity of that same teacher of his, summoned him to the service of the holy Church, adding also a precept of obedience.”

512.

> “When this mandate had been read, a voice was heard in Rama: the howling and loud lamentation of the sons of Saint Bruno, who refused to be consoled and protested to their Father that, deprived of his comfort, they could in no way remain in that place of horror and vast solitude. If he remained, they would remain; if he departed, they too would depart [Col. 0312C].
>
> “The most devout Bruno, deeply disturbed and moved to compassion by their tears—for it was also exceedingly hard for him, after the rest of such a peaceful and tranquil solitude, to become entangled again in external cares and disturbances—nevertheless tried to calm and console their hearts.
>
> “He knew that it was written: ‘Whoever hears you hears me,’ and that what God speaks once, he does not repeat a second time. Therefore he accepted the Apostle’s command as a voice that had descended to him from a heavenly oracle.
>
> “Accordingly, addressing his followers, he said: ‘It is most pleasing to me, my dearest brothers, to remain with you; separation from you is most grievous. But it is necessary for me to obey the apostolic commands. For what good would it do to wear down my flesh here with fasts and abstinence together with you, if through disobedience I should incur the damnation of my soul, etc.’”

After inserting several further exchanges in which he represents the Saint and his disciples conversing with one another, he continues:

> “When blessed Bruno heard this and saw that they would accept no consolation and could not be persuaded to remain, he feared that, after his departure and theirs, the desert of Chartreuse—which was already a place consecrated to God—might again fall into lay and profane hands. He therefore considered returning there with his companions, and entrusted and gave it to the venerable lord Siguinus, abbot of the monastery of Casa-Dei, who had been one of the first donors mentioned above. A public instrument was drawn up concerning this.
>
> “And so blessed Bruno, having received the blessing of Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, set out for Rome, compelled by obedience” [Col. 0313A].

513. Thus far Blomenvenna, in close agreement with Puteanus, from whom he again borrowed nearly all his material, and not in conflict with the older biographer of our Saint, or with the chronicler of the first five priors of Chartreuse.

All three of these writers, as well as Surius, who drew his material from two of the more recent among them—Puteanus and Blomenvenna—appear to have correctly recorded that all the Saint’s disciples were overcome with the deepest grief when they learned that the pontiff had summoned him from Chartreuse, and that, upon the Saint’s departure, they resolved to leave Chartreuse.

Although I have found this reported by no contemporary or nearly contemporary author, it nevertheless appears consistent with the truth because of the charter for the restoration of Chartreuse, which I shall transcribe in full below. In that charter it is implied that the companions of Saint Bruno withdrew from the desert because of his absence [Col. 0313B].

The more recent biographers of our Saint cited above also indicate that, when Bruno gave Chartreuse to Siguinus and left it to proceed to the pontiff, he intended to return there afterward. This seems to me rather improbable, since the instrument by which the Saint, while on his way to the pontiff, donated Chartreuse to Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei, contains no mention whatsoever that it was to be returned to Bruno and his companions should they return.

Nor is it more plausible that the instrument by which the Saint transferred Chartreuse to Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei, was given to him while the Saint’s disciples had not yet dispersed from Chartreuse because of the departure of their beloved master, but when Bruno merely foresaw that they would disperse shortly afterward—a view nevertheless held by some.

514. For the charter of the restoration of Chartreuse states that Bruno gave and commended Chartreuse to Abbot Siguinus when he “saw the place deprived of its brothers because they had departed on account of his absence.” Therefore the instrument by which the Saint gave Chartreuse to Siguinus cannot have been transferred to him while the first inhabitants of the Grand Chartreuse, the Saint’s disciples, had not yet dispersed or left Chartreuse—especially since the departure of the Saint’s brothers or disciples from Chartreuse is expressly reported in the letter which I shall likewise transcribe in full below. In that letter Pope Urban II orders Abbot Siguinus to restore the desert of Chartreuse to the disciples of Saint Bruno when they return there [Col. 0313D].

But, you will say, if the Saint gave Chartreuse to Siguinus in the course of his disciples’ dispersal from Chartreuse, or at their departure from that desert, how are we to understand that they had dispersed from Chartreuse because of the Saint’s absence, or while he was already on the journey from Chartreuse toward the pontiff, as the repeatedly cited charter of the restoration of Chartreuse indicates?

Mabillon writes in the *Benedictine Annals*, book LXXVII, no. 92:

> “At the same time as Bernard was born, Bruno, the first founder of the Grand Chartreuse, was summoned to Rome by Urban II, who had been his disciple at Reims, so that he might use his counsel in the governance of the Church [Col. 0314A]. The young flock, deprived of the comfort of so great a shepherd, bore this departure with difficulty; and, in his absence, the habitation and austerity of life at Chartreuse seemed intolerable to all. But at length obedience had to be rendered to the authority of the supreme pontiff, who commended the place to Seguino, abbot of Casa-Dei.
>
> “Bruno therefore left Chartreuse after six years from the time he had begun to inhabit it. His departure disturbed the brothers, who, as is human temptation in difficult circumstances when a leader of great merit is lacking, abandoned the place. When Bruno learned of this, he transferred Chartreuse to him and to his monastery by a letter written to Seguino, abbot of Casa-Dei.”

515. Thus Mabillon indicates that Bruno drew up the instrument by which he transferred Chartreuse to Abbot Seguino only later, when he was on the Roman journey or even at Rome, and sent it to him by letter.

Indeed, once the matter is considered in this light, anyone can readily understand how, while the Saint was already absent—either on the journey toward the pontiff or at Rome—his disciples could have dispersed from Chartreuse, and how he, after or rather while they were dispersing, could have donated to Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei, the public instrument by which he transferred Chartreuse to him, without compromising the truth of any of the statements found in the charter of the restoration of Chartreuse.

Nevertheless, since the Saint appears to have transferred Chartreuse to Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei, before undertaking the Roman journey, at the very moment when his disciples were departing from Chartreuse, I would prefer to conceive the course of events as follows:

Saint Bruno, after he had already left Chartreuse, with Landuinus substituted in his place, went to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble—as Blomenvenna and others relate that he actually did—to bid him farewell. Meanwhile, the disciples whom he had left at Chartreuse, having heard of the Saint’s departure and being unable to endure their longing for him, likewise abandoned Chartreuse [Col. 0314C].

This makes it quite easy to understand how the Saint, as he was leaving Chartreuse, could soon have learned that his disciples were dispersing from it, and could have drawn up the instrument by which he commended Chartreuse to Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei—either delivering the completed document to him personally or arranging for it to be delivered by someone else.

516. Moreover, from the charter of the restoration of Chartreuse [Col. 0314D] one may also infer that the opinion of those who maintain that the Saint had all his disciples at Chartreuse accompany him on the journey he undertook toward the pontiff cannot in any way agree with the truth.

For in that charter, by which Siguinus restored Chartreuse to them, Bruno is said, at his departure, to have placed Landuinus over all his other disciples who remained at Chartreuse. But how could this have happened if both Landuinus and all his other disciples had undertaken the journey toward the pontiff with the Saint?

Yet did the Saint not have at least some of them as companions on his journey? There is certainly reason for someone to believe this, since, as I showed above, the charters of Count Roger and Duke Roger say that the Saint came to Calabria from the regions of Gaul with companions attached to him; and it does not seem possible to say this appropriately unless the Saint began the journey toward Calabria from Gaul itself together with the companions whom he had with him [Col. 0315A].

If this should nevertheless seem unsatisfactory, there can be no doubt that, once all his Carthusian disciples had followed him to Italy, the Saint retained some of them with him while sending the others back to Chartreuse. Otherwise, where would he have obtained companions from the regions of Gaul when he came to Count Roger in Calabria? See no. 509 and following.

But enough has been said about the disciples whom the Saint had under his direction when, by command of the supreme pontiff, he left Chartreuse and set out for the Roman Curia. Let us now investigate the time at which, after leaving Chartreuse, he proceeded to the Roman Curia [Col. 0315B].

517. Baronius places this event in the year 1092, because, as he understood it, the Saint was summoned to the Roman Curia in the sixth year of his residence at Chartreuse, and six years from 1086—the year in which, as we saw above, the Saint’s withdrawal to Chartreuse is recorded—lead to the stated year 1092.

But since, according to what has been said above, Bruno did not first establish his residence in the desert of Chartreuse in 1086, but already in 1084, and since, as the oldest and most trustworthy *Chronicle of the First Four Priors of Chartreuse* attests in the Saint’s eulogy, no. 7, transcribed above, he went to the Roman Curia after governing the desert of Chartreuse for six years, it follows that he certainly did so in 1090, after June—the month in which, according to what has been said, the Saint withdrew to Chartreuse—had already passed, provided that the six years during which the chronicler of the first four priors of Chartreuse says he remained at Chartreuse are understood as completed years [Col. 0315C].

Mabillon, in the *Benedictine Annals*, book LXVII, no. 92, assigns the Saint’s departure from Chartreuse to the year 1090. The writers of the *Literary History of France*, vol. IX, p. 239, agree with Mabillon, as does Pagius in his *Critica*, along with virtually all other learned authorities.

But in the *Life of Pope Urban II* included in volume III of the posthumous works of Mabillon and Ruinart, p. 69, the latter of these two writers, after recounting that Pope Urban II held a council or synod at Melfi in 1089, transferred the relics of Saint Nicholas to Bari, consecrated Bishop Elias, and finally traversed Calabria as far as Reggio, reports as follows:

> “On the same occasion it is more than probable that Bruno, the father of the Carthusians, traversed Calabria with Urban. For Bruno, summoned by the pontiff who had once been his disciple—as we have said, when the holy man was teaching letters at the school of the church of Reims—came to him in that year, namely 1089; and there is no doubt that he also followed him into Apulia and Calabria, since Urban had summoned Bruno with the intention of using his counsel in the most difficult affairs that were then frequently arising.
>
> “There is another indication of the same fact: Bruno’s holiness was, from that time, so well known among the Calabrians that shortly afterward he was given a place in that region to inhabit, which he actually occupied the following year with some of his companions. This is established by the charter of Count Roger, published by G. Surianus in his notes to the *Life of Saint Bruno*, and by Ughellus in volume IX, together with the confirmation of Theodore, bishop of Squillace” [Col. 0316A].

518. If Ruinart is correct in this statement, then our Saint came to Pope Urban II already in 1089, and indeed before that year had advanced beyond September. For, according to Ruinart, he accompanied Urban when the latter set out for Apulia in that year and was present with him at the council held there in September.

But is there nothing that prevents us from accepting Ruinart’s opinion, or that clearly proves it to be erroneous?

The older biographer of our Saint records the following concerning Bruno, no. 24:

> “He governed the desert of Chartreuse for six years and afterward, as was stated above, was summoned by the pope. Not long afterward he went to the desert of Calabria, called La Torre, and there, after a monastery had been built, became the ruler and minister of many servants of God who lived as anchorites. Having completed the course of his life there happily, he departed to the Lord in the eleventh year after leaving Chartreuse, neither more nor less, as is contained in the books of the Customs of lord Guigo, which are in the house of Chartreuse.”

So he writes. If this testimony is to be accepted, Ruinart unquestionably assigns the Saint’s departure from Chartreuse, or his arrival at Pope Urban II, incorrectly to 1089, before September had ended [Col. 0316C].

For since it is universally acknowledged, and will be demonstrated below, that the Saint died on 6 October 1101, his departure from Chartreuse must have occurred—not in 1089, as Ruinart maintains, before September had ended, but in 1090, after 6 October had already passed—if the eleventh year that elapsed after his departure from Chartreuse is to be reconciled correctly with the year of his death, 1101, as the quoted words of our older biographer require.

For from a date in 1089 before the end of September to 6 October 1101, more than twelve full years elapsed; whereas from a date in 1090 before 6 October to that same date, 6 October 1101, more than eleven full years elapsed. Thus, contrary to what our older biographer writes, the Saint would have died not in the eleventh year but either in the twelfth or even in the thirteenth year after his departure from Chartreuse.

But is the chronicler of the first five priors of Chartreuse—or the older biographer of our Saint—correctly reconciling the year 1101, the year of the Saint’s death, with the specified eleventh year after his departure from Chartreuse?

519. Certainly not. For it is entirely certain and indisputable from the charter which I shall transcribe below, by which Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei, restored Chartreuse to the Carthusians returning there—the Carthusians who, when Bruno departed for Urban, had left it—that the Saint went from Chartreuse to Pope Urban II before the year 1090 had advanced to October, indeed before 17 September. The charter is dated “in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1090, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October”; and more than eleven years elapsed from 17 September 1090 to 6 October 1101, the date of our Saint’s death.

It is therefore now clear that our Saint’s older biographer incorrectly assigns the year of Bruno’s death to the specified eleventh year after his departure from Chartreuse. Indeed, in doing so, while also stating in no. 23 that the Saint’s disciples withdrew from Chartreuse at the end of the sixth year from his entry there, when he had gone to Rome to Pope Urban II, he contradicts himself, as will be clear to anyone who considers the matter [Col. 0317B].

But does he perhaps also cite the books of the Customs of lord Guigo incorrectly? Or was the copy of those books that he had at hand corrupted in its chronological notes, which state the year in which the Saint died after his departure from Chartreuse?

It must certainly have been corrupted. For the books of the Customs which he cites are undoubtedly none other than Guigo’s *Statutes* or *Customs*—see what was said above in § 1, from no. 4 through no. 7—with the *Chronicle of the Four First Priors of Chartreuse*, or their four eulogies, prefixed to them. It is in those eulogies, not in the Customs themselves, that he found the chronological notes specifying the year in which the Saint died after his departure from Chartreuse.

But the oldest and genuine copy of the *Chronicle of the First Four Priors of Chartreuse*—see again § 1—records that our Saint died “after leaving Chartreuse, more or less in the eleventh year,” not, as the older biographer claims from Guigo’s books of Customs, “in the eleventh year, neither more nor less.”

520. Since this is so, it cannot be argued from the fact that our older biographer writes that Bruno “died in the eleventh year, neither more nor less, after his departure from Chartreuse” that Ruinart’s opinion departs from the truth—namely, the opinion that, according to what has been said, places the Saint’s departure from Chartreuse, or his arrival at Pope Urban II, in 1089, before September had ended.

But does the *Chronicle of the First Four Priors of Chartreuse* not oppose that same opinion, since it states that the Saint departed to the Lord “more or less in the eleventh year” after his departure from Chartreuse?

This expression appears to mean that the Saint died not in a precisely defined eleventh year after his departure from Chartreuse, but either in the eleventh year after that departure or somewhat before or after it. Thus, since it seems to designate a period neither much earlier nor much later than that year, I do not know whether, given the wording used by the chronicler of the first four priors of Chartreuse, the death of our Saint—who, as has already been shown, certainly did not die before the twelfth year after his departure from Chartreuse—can be placed so far beyond the eleventh year after that departure that, as Ruinart’s opinion requires, it could be postponed until the thirteenth year [Col. 0318A], when no other consideration provides support for doing so.

Ruinart does indeed say that Bruno was summoned by Urban with the intention that he should serve as a counselor in the most difficult matters that were then frequently arising, and therefore that this was done early enough for Bruno not to die until the thirteenth year afterward.

But I do not see why it could not have happened that Urban, even though he held Bruno, formerly his teacher, in the highest esteem and very much wished to use his counsel, nevertheless chose to refrain from summoning him to himself until the year 1090—that is, for approximately two years after he had already been made supreme pontiff [Col. 0318B].

521. Nor does the note concerning the Saint’s holiness among the Calabrians, which Ruinart also adduces as evidence, require that this occurred already in 1089. For, apart from the fact that Ruinart does not prove that Bruno had already become renowned among that people, the reputation for holiness which he had acquired through the exceptionally austere life he led in the solitude of Chartreuse, and through his contempt for wealth, honors, and the world—a reputation that had spread throughout much of Gaul—could already at that time have reached the Calabrians.

It follows that neither from the place which, as will be shown, the Saint obtained for habitation in Calabria from 1090 or certainly from the beginning of the following year, nor even from his election at that same time to the archbishopric of Reggio, can a sufficiently solid argument be drawn to establish Ruinart’s opinion [Col. 0318C].

Moreover, although the fact that he was elected archbishop by the people of Reggio in 1090 may lead someone to think that he was known to them in some special way, and therefore that he had already been present in the city of Reggio—which lies at the farthest corner of Calabria—from the year 1089, when Urban II visited it, it may nevertheless have happened that he was elected archbishop by the people of Reggio, although he was scarcely or entirely unknown to them, solely on the recommendation of the pope. For, as the chronicler of the first four priors of Chartreuse attests, this election occurred “with Pope Urban’s approval” [Col. 0318D].

But Morkensius, who likewise places the Saint’s departure from Chartreuse and arrival at Urban in 1089, says in his *Chronological-Diplomatic Dissertation on Saint Bruno* that between the Saint’s departure from Chartreuse and the eventual return there of his disciples—who, unable to endure the absence of their beloved Father, had likewise left Chartreuse for Italy as he departed—there must have intervened at least the space of one full year. The events that took place in the intervening period require this. Therefore, since, according to what has already been said and what will be said further, Saint Bruno’s disciples returned to Chartreuse before October 1090, it is necessary that Bruno left Chartreuse in 1089, before October had arrived.

Such, in substance, is his argument.

[Col. 0319A] **522.** Yet I do not see that, between the Saint’s departure from the Chartreuse and his disciples’ return to it, so many and such important events occurred that they could not have taken place in a period considerably shorter than one year. For what happened? Bruno, having left the Chartreuse and commended or donated it to Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei, went to Italy, to Pope Urban II, by whom he had been summoned. He received kindly the disciples who had followed him to Italy when he departed and likewise left the Chartreuse; he urged them to return to the Chartreuse, and actually secured for them letters from the Pope to Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei, by which Urban ordered him to restore the Chartreuse to Bruno’s disciples when they returned there. Thus they returned to their beloved hermitage, provided with papal letters as well as with others by which Bruno himself earnestly requested this of the abbot. [Col. 0319B] But why could all this not have been accomplished within only about six or seven months? Indeed, why could the Saint not also—as will truly be shown below—have returned to Calabria in that very year in which he left the Chartreuse and came to Pope Urban II, having obtained from him permission to resume the eremitical life?

Therefore neither what Morkensius adduces nor what was cited above from Ruinart obliges us to place the Saint’s departure from the Chartreuse, and his approach to Urban II, by whom he had been summoned, before the year 1090. Since this is so, and to state my own opinion openly at last, our Saint cannot, without solid reason, be held to have died after a period longer than is permitted by the expression by which, as already mentioned, the chronologist of the first four priors of the Chartreuse is said to have closed his life “about the eleventh year after his departure from the Chartreuse.” Since there is no proof whatever that the Saint left the Chartreuse for the Pope as early as 1089, before October had begun—a date from which his death at such a time would follow—I am persuaded that he did not do so before 1090, as Mabillon and others more commonly maintain. [Col. 0319C]

**523.** But approximately in what month of that year did this occur? Since, according to the chronologist of the first four priors of the Chartreuse, whose testimony must be followed here, Bruno died “about the eleventh year after his departure from the Chartreuse,” and since this event, which according to what will be said below occurred in 1101, appears to have taken place not long after the eleventh year from the Saint’s departure had elapsed, Bruno probably left the Chartreuse around March of that year and reached Pope Urban in the following month, April, or certainly at the beginning of May. Urban had by then returned to Rome from Apulia and Calabria, as Ruinart most clearly proves more than once in the Life of the Pope cited above.

I chiefly suppose that the matter happened in this way because, on this view, our Saint, having died in 1101, would have closed his life no later than after approximately five or six months had elapsed beyond the eleventh year from his departure from the Chartreuse. Nothing appears to prevent his death from being placed that long after the eleventh year, despite the expression by which the chronologist of the first four priors of the Chartreuse says that he died “about the eleventh year after his departure from the Chartreuse.” [Col. 0320A] I also suppose it because, on the same view, it is readily understandable that the events said to have occurred between the Saint’s departure from the Chartreuse and his disciples’ return there could actually have taken place, as will become clearer from what I shall provide in the following section.

Furthermore, since the Saint appears to have left the Chartreuse not long before his disciples followed him, this opinion is also supported, as will be evident to anyone who considers the matter, by our older biographer. In section 23 he writes that they withdrew from the Chartreuse “at the end of the sixth year” from their entrance into it, which, according to what was said above, took place in June 1084.

### § XXXI. The Saint comes to Rome to Pope Urban, urges his disciples to return to the Chartreuse, obtains from the Pope letters for them to Abbot Siguinus, refuses the archbishopric of Reggio, and obtains from Urban permission to withdraw again from the curia into the hermitage.

**524.** Blomenvenna records the following in the Life of our Saint that he composed:

> “Blessed Bruno, having received the blessing of Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, went to Rome, compelled by obedience. When the supreme pontiff heard of his arrival, he received him with the greatest kindness, being filled with indescribable joy—for he loved and venerated him most intimately—and always counted him among his foremost and principal personal familiars, counselors, and faithful friends, continually making use of his advice in the Church’s difficult affairs.”

So writes that biographer of our Saint, once again borrowing almost word for word from Puteanus. Puteanus, however, like Surius, states more explicitly than Blomenvenna that Bruno’s approach to Urban took place at Rome, or that Urban was then at Rome when Bruno came to him.

But was Urban really at Rome when our Saint came to him? Those who maintain that the Saint approached Urban as early as 1089, before September had ended, must suppose that Pope Urban was most probably not at Rome when this happened. The evidence cited by Ruinart in the Life of that pontiff proves that during the last four months of that year Urban was either in Apulia, where he celebrated the council of Melfi in September, or in Calabria. [Col. 0320D] But since, as the same Ruinart shows in his Life of Urban, p. 77, the Pope had already returned to Rome on 28 March 1090, the fifth day before the Kalends of April, and remained there until approximately midsummer, it certainly follows from the opinion adopted above—that the Saint did not come to Urban before April 1090—that this pontiff was at Rome when our Saint came to him.

**525.** As for the other matters contained in Blomenvenna’s words just quoted, it is plainly evident that they are entirely consistent with the truth, especially that the Saint was employed by Urban in giving counsel, since, according to the chronologist of the first four priors of the Chartreuse, he had been summoned for this very purpose.

Let us now turn to the other matters requiring discussion. It appears that our Saint had not been with the pontiff for very long when, according to the unanimous testimony of all his biographers, his disciples also came to their beloved Father, having left the Chartreuse. Blomenvenna adds to the words of his own text, recently transcribed here:

> “They all came to him, through the working of the Holy Spirit—those who had been with him in the Chartreuse—greatly grieving, though he himself grieved still more, that they had left the aforesaid place of the Chartreuse, which the Lord had chosen for him and in which he seemed to have built a dwelling for himself. They recalled in their minds not meats, cucumbers, or melons, as did those murmurers in the desert, but the devout meditations, prayers, readings, and spiritual consolations that they had previously enjoyed in the hermitage of the Chartreuse. Therefore, when they now saw themselves in the curia surrounded by the greatest tumult and noise after the deeply pleasing silence of their former repose, they could not restrain their tears.”

Thus far Blomenvenna; Puteanus, from whom he drew his material, agrees with him almost exactly, as does Surius. But two questions may now be asked. The first is whether the Saint’s disciples truly followed him to Italy and Rome. The second is whether, if that is so, they were divinely moved to do so in some extraordinary and miraculous manner, as Blomenvenna’s words just quoted seem to suggest. [Col. 0321C]

**526.** To begin with the first question, it appears that the Saint’s disciples went to him before he had yet left the papal curia and gone to his hermitage in Calabria. This may be concluded from the charter that will be transcribed in the present section, by which Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei, restored the Chartreuse to Landuinus and his companions when they returned there. For the charter suggests that Bruno, already having gone to Rome and being with the Pope, brought about their unanimous return to that famous hermitage which they had abandoned when their beloved Father departed for the Pope. It states:

> “At the request of our father Pope Urban, and through the prayers of the aforesaid brother Bruno, and with those same brothers—namely, his disciples—greatly encouraged by their prior Bruno to remain there, I relinquished to brother Landuinus, whom Master Bruno, when departing—namely, from the Chartreuse to the Pope—placed over the other brothers, and to him, the other brothers living under him, and their successors, the gift which the aforesaid Bruno had made to us when his disciples, as is stated at the beginning of this charter, withdrew from the Chartreuse, before the congregation entrusted to us … I, brother Siguinus, abbot of the aforesaid Casa-Dei …”

Since, according to the unanimous testimony, the Saint caused his disciples to return to the Chartreuse they had left, he could probably have accomplished this through letters only if he had them present with him; otherwise he could scarcely, or perhaps not at all, have done so. It therefore appears that they were actually with the Saint at that time and consequently followed him to Italy after his departure from the Chartreuse.

This is supported both by the Carthusian tradition and by our older biographer, who also appears to indicate in section 19 that all the Saint’s disciples came to him while he was at the papal curia. These considerations, and especially the public letters by which Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei, restored the Chartreuse to the Saint’s disciples when they returned there, make it to me highly probable, indeed almost certain, that this really happened.

**527.** As for the manner in which it happened that all his disciples, having left the Chartreuse, came to the Saint while he was at the papal curia, our older biographer appears likewise to place the matter among miracles. For he indicates that the Saint’s disciples did not immediately follow their beloved Father to Italy after his departure from the Chartreuse, but went away in different directions. Then, after recounting that the Saint obtained from Urban permission to withdraw again from the papal curia into the hermitage, he adds:

> “Before he withdrew from the curia, however, divine mercy, as is believed, through his merits and prayers, recalled all his companions and subjects, so that absolutely all agreed to return to the Chartreuse.”

By these words, with reference also to what he had previously implied—that the Saint’s disciples had dispersed in various directions after his departure from the Chartreuse—the biographer seems to assert a divinely wrought miracle by which they gathered to the Saint before he left the papal curia and agreed to return to the Chartreuse.

Yet although, as I have said, I regard it as almost certain that the Saint’s disciples came from the Chartreuse to Bruno while he was at the papal curia, I would not readily believe that any miracle intervened. For this miraculous occurrence, unlike the disciples’ journey to him in Italy, is not founded on the oft-cited charter of Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei; nor are our biographers, including the oldest of them, sufficiently ancient that what they alone report concerning the Saint and his disciples can be accepted as indisputable. Let us now examine what the Saint chiefly did when the disciples he had had at the Chartreuse came to him at Rome. [Col. 0322D]

**528.** There can be no doubt that he arranged with the Pope for them to be received in suitable lodgings where they could perform exercises appropriate to their state, although this cannot be confirmed by the testimony of any ancient writer. But since the Saint was deeply distressed that the hermitage of the Chartreuse, which he loved, had been deserted by its religious inhabitants, he repeatedly tried to persuade them to return there—and not in vain. Although they had probably been received, as stated, in lodgings suitable to their condition, they did not enjoy the customary quiet in which they had rejoiced at the Chartreuse. They therefore regretted the deserted hermitage of the Chartreuse and readily listened to Bruno when he urged them to return.

Provided with letters, both papal letters by which Pope Urban ordered Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei, to restore the Chartreuse to Saint Bruno’s disciples when they returned there, and other letters in which Bruno himself earnestly requested the same from the abbot, they finally set out on the journey back to the hermitage they had abandoned, as all our biographers unanimously report.

I transcribe here Urban’s letter, copied from the previously mentioned copy of Book Four of the *Annals of the Carthusians* of Vallis-Dei, not yet published, and communicated to me by the Parisian Carthusian, who, as has often been said, refuses by any means to have his name disclosed. It is composed in these words:

> “Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei, and to the whole congregation, greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “Those who are wearied by labors on account of obedience to the Roman Church ought also to be relieved through the assistance of the Roman Church. Since, therefore, we summoned Bruno, our dearest son, to the service of the apostolic see, and since he has come to us, we cannot—and ought not—to permit his cell to suffer any loss.
>
> “We therefore ask your affection, and in asking command you, to restore that cell to its former freedom. For love of us, also return the chirograph—the written deed—which our aforesaid son made to you concerning that cell when the brothers dispersed, so that it may remain in its former freedom. For now the brothers who had dispersed have returned, inspired by God, and will agree to remain in that place under no other condition.
>
> “When this letter has been delivered to you, do not delay, out of reverence for our command, returning the aforesaid chirograph within thirty days.” [Col. 0323C]

**529.** As soon as these letters and those of Saint Bruno had been presented to Siguinus, he obeyed the papal command, as all Bruno’s biographers again relate, and restored the Chartreuse to Landuinus and the other disciples of Saint Bruno who were returning there. I append the public charter by which he did this. It reads:

> “I, brother Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei, wish it to be known to those present and those to come that, when brother Bruno was summoned to Rome by the lord Pope Urban, he saw that the place had been deserted because the brothers had departed on account of his absence, and he gave the place of the Chartreuse to us and to the congregation entrusted to us.
>
> “Afterward, at the request of our father Pope Urban, and through the prayers of the aforesaid brother Bruno, and with those same brothers greatly encouraged by their prior Bruno to remain there, I, brother Siguinus, abbot of the aforesaid Casa-Dei, in the presence of the congregation entrusted to us and in our chapter, relinquished to brother Landuinus—whom Master Bruno, when departing, placed over the other brothers—and to him, the other brothers living under him, and their successors, the gift that the aforesaid Bruno had made to us.
>
> “With the consent of our brothers, I made the place of the aforesaid Chartreuse completely free for them and their successors according to their will, and I entirely transferred it to their right. But the charter that the aforesaid Bruno had made to us was not returned, because, having been sought by our brothers in chapter under penalty of interdict, it could not be found. If it is ever found, that charter itself shall belong to them.
>
> “This was done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1090, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October [17 September]. I, Siguinus, abbot, subscribed, and in the presence of Archbishop Hugh confirmed this charter in its entirety.” [Col. 0324A]

**530.** Morkensius, from whose copy I transcribed this charter—having incorporated it into the chronological-diplomatic *Dissertation on Saint Bruno* that he composed and, as he says, compared it with the original—rightly declares that the Hugh whom Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei, says was present when he confirmed the charter in its entirety was distinct from Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, since the latter was not an archbishop. Morkensius suggests that this was Hugh who, in 1080, was created archbishop of Lyons after having been bishop of Die and legate of the Apostolic See, the man so frequently mentioned above.

Columbius makes the same observation, and correctly, in section 108 of his *Dissertation on the Beginnings of the Carthusians*, where he likewise transcribes the charter given above. I know of no other Archbishop Hugh whom it would be plausible to suppose was present when Siguinus confirmed the charter.

There is no reason to find it strange that one Hugh is mentioned in the charter and another in the subscription to the charter. Nothing prevents us from believing that Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, was present when Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei, restored the Chartreuse to Landuinus and his companions, while Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, was present when he confirmed the charter by which he made that restoration.

If this interpretation is unsatisfactory, consider whether the following words of the charter may be read with the punctuation after *fecerat* omitted and placed after the name *Hugonis*:

> “The gift that the aforesaid Bruno had made to us before the congregation entrusted to us in our chapter, in the presence of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, I, brother Siguinus … relinquished …”

On that punctuation, the meaning would be that Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, was present when Bruno gave the Chartreuse to Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei, while Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, was present when Siguinus restored it to Landuinus and his companions.

Whichever way the matter stood, it plainly follows that this ancient monument should not be regarded as suspect merely because two different Hughs are mentioned, one in the charter itself and the other in its subscription. [Col. 0324D]

**531.** From this charter, in addition to several other matters discussed above, we learn that Landuinus and the other disciples of the Saint returned from Rome, where they had followed Bruno, to the Chartreuse on the seventeenth day of September 1090, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, on which date the document is recorded as having been issued.

It consequently follows that they remained with Bruno at the papal court not for more than a year, as some assert without the support of ancient authority, but only for a few months.

But did all those who had previously inhabited the Chartreuse return there with Landuinus? Almost all of them must have done so if Zanottius is to be believed. In the *Life* or *History of Bruno* that he composed, p. 89, Zanottius says that only two—namely Lanvinus and Lambertus—remained with the Saint.

Although I cannot determine the number of those who returned to the Chartreuse with Landuinus or of those who remained with Bruno, it is nevertheless clear that more than the two mentioned by Zanottius stayed with him. This is shown by the two diplomas cited above, one granted by Roger, duke of Apulia and Sicily, and the other by Roger, the uncle of that Roger and count of Calabria and Sicily, in favor of Saint Bruno and his companions who had withdrawn to Calabria after the Saint’s other disciples had already returned to the Chartreuse.

For in both documents (see section 509), Bruno and Lanvinus are said to have come from the regions of Gaul to Calabria with companions. Therefore, while Landuinus and several others returned to the Chartreuse, more remained with the Saint than Lanvinus and Lambertus. Otherwise—see section 510—how could Bruno and Lanvinus, if only Lambertus had been with them when they came to Calabria, be said in both diplomas to have had companions who joined them from the regions of Gaul?

It can scarcely be doubted, then, that the Saint retained with him at least two companions besides Lanvinus, while the others were sent back to the Chartreuse. [Col. 0325C]

**532.** Let us now examine what happened to these men and afterward to the Saint. The chronologist of the first four priors of the Chartreuse writes the following in his eulogy of our Saint (see section 7 of this Commentary) concerning Bruno, who was already staying with Pope Urban:

> “But since he could not endure the tumult and customs of the curia—that is, the papal curia—he left the curia and, having also rejected the archbishopric of the church of Reggio, to which he had been elected at the Pope’s own wish, withdrew into the hermitage of Calabria.”

Or, as it is better written elsewhere, he “seceded” into it.

The Saint, therefore, who, as we are taught here by a truly trustworthy writer, withdrew to Calabria after leaving the papal curia, had also been elected to the archbishopric of Reggio before withdrawing to that region. Since, as will be shown below, this withdrawal occurred during the same year 1090, he must have been nominated to that dignity no later than that year.

But did this not also occur earlier than 1090? There is no indication of that from any point of view. For, according to what has already been said, Bruno did not come to the Pope before the year 1090, and it is in no way probable that he was elected archbishop by the people of Reggio before he had come to Urban, his former disciple.

Moreover, Ughellus, in volume IX of *Italia sacra*, among the archbishops of Reggio, column 324, adorns our Saint with the following eulogy:

> “Arnulphus, archbishop of Reggio, died in the year … 1090. In his place, the senate of the clergy is said to have chosen Saint Bruno, patriarch of the Carthusians, as their archbishop. But they write that he refused that dignity and humbly rejected it out of love for solitude. Then Bruno, having shaken off the yoke of worldly glory, sought a hermitage near Squillace, in the territory of Calabria. There, after building a monastery dedicated to Saint Stephen, he led an angelic life under Duke Roger and, full of merits and renowned no less for holiness than for miracles and learning, fell asleep in the Lord in the year 1101. He was buried in the monastery mentioned above, where he is still honorably venerated.” [Col. 0326A]

**533.** Thus Ughellus affirms not only that our Saint was elected to the archiepiscopal see of the church of Reggio, as the chronologist of the first four priors of the Chartreuse, cited again shortly above, also states, but also that Arnulphus, archbishop of Reggio, after whose death this occurred, died in the year 1090.

Morkensius likewise reports that Severus of Naples, a member of the Carthusian Order, found the same fact recorded in an ancient manuscript catalogue of the archbishops of Reggio, as Morkensius explains in his chronological-diplomatic *Dissertation on Saint Bruno*. It therefore cannot be doubted that Arnulphus died in the said year 1090, especially since nothing appears that would in any way recommend assigning another date to this event.

Since this is so, and since Arnulphus, as the aforementioned Ughellus also shows, was made archbishop of Reggio while Gregory VII, who died in 1085, occupied the chair of Saint Peter—or, if it seems objectionable that Arnulphus’s predecessor appears to have been still alive in 1086, while Urban II had not yet been raised to the papal see—it follows that the see of Reggio did not become vacant before 1090 during Urban’s pontificate. Consequently, the election of our Saint to it, since it was made “at Pope Urban’s wish,” as the chronologist of the first four priors of the Chartreuse records in the words just quoted, did not occur before that year.

By a similar line of reasoning it can readily also be proved that the election did not occur later, if Rangerius was elected to the archbishopric of Reggio in 1090 itself, as is more probable. Since he held that see at least until 1106, it follows that our Saint’s election to it certainly did not occur after 1090, for after that year, while Urban was still alive and the see remained under his pontificate—as, according to what has been said, was the case—it was no longer vacant. [Col. 0326D]

**534.** For this reason Ruinart, in section 81 of his frequently cited *Life of Pope Urban II*, rightly writes:

> “We assign Bruno’s election to the archbishopric of Reggio to this year—namely 1090—although commonly published authors usually place it in 1095, because the see was vacant under Urban’s pontificate only in this year, namely through the death of Archbishop Arnulphus. When Bruno refused that dignity, Rangerius was substituted for him toward the end of the year.
>
> “This is confirmed by the previously mentioned privilege of Theodorus, bishop of Squillace—which we shall cite below—which was confirmed on 17 December 1090 by the elected archbishop of Reggio. He is subsequently recorded as subscribing various councils and public instruments through the year 1106 under the title of archbishop, as may be seen in Ughellus, volume IX of *Italia sacra*.” [Col. 0327A]

It therefore appears completely certain, and established beyond all dispute by the arguments just brought forward, that Saint Bruno was elected to the archbishopric of Reggio neither later nor earlier than 1090. Accordingly, our more recent biographers and the other writers who maintain that our Saint was first nominated archbishop by the people of Reggio at the time of the Council of Piacenza—or at the time of that council, which was not held before 1095—must not be followed.

But in approximately what month of 1090 did Saint Bruno’s election as archbishop of Reggio occur?
