Since, according to what has been said, the Saint did not arrive at Rome to see Pope Urban before April 1090, and since it likewise appears from what has been said that he was not elected or nominated to the see of Reggio before approaching him, it follows that this did not happen before April of that year. Whether it happened in that month itself or later, I cannot determine, since every argument that could in any way suffice for deciding the matter is lacking.

Nevertheless, let us examine whether anything can be inferred from what followed the return of Saint Bruno’s disciples to the Chartreuse that might define more precisely the time of the Saint’s election to the archbishopric of Reggio.

**535.** Ruinart writes the following concerning Pope Urban in section 82 of his Life:

> “Around the middle of this year—namely 1090—it seemed advisable, since he could scarcely breathe freely at Rome, to visit the provinces subject to Roger, duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, and to Boamund, the duke’s brother, so that he might there attend somewhat more freely to ecclesiastical affairs. Certainly it is known that he was in Campania around the middle of August of this year, from the privilege of Saint Basolus, issued at Sinuessa on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September of this year and addressed to Burchard, abbot of that place.”

The fact that Urban, as Ruinart says, could scarcely breathe freely at Rome must undoubtedly have resulted from the fact that, when the Emperor Henry had crossed the Alps and was advancing with a hostile army against the Pope and his supporters—as can be understood from the appendix to that year in the work of Berthold, priest of Constance, concerning Hermannus Contractus—the Roman supporters of the antipope Guibert, emboldened by this, could scarcely be kept in line and left Urban no secure way of remaining at Rome. [Col. 0327D]

But to return to the matter at hand: someone might perhaps suspect that our Saint was elected archbishop of Reggio while that pontiff was in Campania, having followed Urban there, because the Pope had then drawn nearer to the city of Reggio.

Indeed, if Urban had been at Reggio in 1090, as he had been in 1089, there would certainly be reason for such a suspicion. But since the pontiff appears to have remained in Campania for the rest of that year after leaving Rome, and since he could have arranged Saint Bruno’s election as archbishop of Reggio no less effectively while he was still at Rome than after he had reached Campania, it is entirely uncertain whether he did this while still at Rome or after he had already gone to Campania.

Consequently, it is also uncertain whether our Saint was elected archbishop of Reggio before or after the middle of the summer of 1090, when, as has been said, Urban departed from Rome for Campania. In any event, it is certain from what has been said above that this occurred in 1090, and at least after April of that year had begun. [Col. 0328A]

**536.** It is no less certain, being founded on the irrefragable testimony of the chronologist of the first four priors of the Chartreuse (see section 532), that Saint Bruno, after refusing the very exalted dignity offered to him, withdrew “into the hermitage in Calabria called Torre.”

But when did the Saint do this? Or, to begin with what must first be certain, when did he obtain permission to do so from Pope Urban?

Blomenvenna records the following in the Life of our Saint that he composed:

> “Blessed Bruno, after having remained with the supreme pontiff for a few years out of obedience and having greatly benefited the Church by his incomparable counsel, prudence, and wisdom—as may be inferred from the decrees and other acts of that same Pope Urban, in which Saint Bruno, without doubt, labored with tireless effort—nevertheless always desired to return to the embrace of his beloved Rachel, to the quiet of the hermitage and solitude. He always found the noise and tumult of the curia most burdensome. When he could no longer suppress the flame of so great a desire, before the aforesaid supreme pontiff passed from Piacenza into Gaul, he finally obtained, though only with great insistence, permission to leave the curia and return to the hermitage he had inhabited, or to choose another if he preferred.”

Thus far Blomenvenna, who borrowed at least the principal points he records here from the Life composed by Puteanus. Surius, who compiled his account of Saint Bruno from both these biographers, does not differ much from either of them.

But if they are correct in noting that the Saint did not obtain permission from the Pope to leave the papal curia and withdraw to a hermitage until Urban was about to depart for Gaul after celebrating the council at Piacenza, then, since this occurred in 1095, as everyone agrees, it follows that the Saint did not obtain permission to leave the curia and return to the hermitage before that year, or before approximately five years of residence with Urban had elapsed—for according to what has been said, he came to him in 1090. [Col. 0328D]

**537.** Yet just as the charters of Count Roger, the bishop of Squillace, Mesimerius, and others, which will be transcribed below, prove that the Saint was elected archbishop of Reggio before 1095, contrary to what those same biographers of Bruno write, so they also prove that he obtained from Urban, before that year, permission to return to the eremitical life. From these documents it is clear that the Saint was living in a Calabrian hermitage after leaving the papal curia before 1095, indeed as early as 1090 or certainly by 1091, as everyone will easily understand from what follows below.

Indeed, the biographers just mentioned—or rather those from whom their older source, Puteanus, derived his account—may perhaps have written that our Saint remained with Pope Urban for so long for no other reason than that, during the preceding five-year period in which he inhabited the Calabrian hermitage, he was summoned from time to time from his solitude by that pontiff, who wished to make use of his counsel in the difficult and complicated affairs that frequently arose during those most difficult times, as I shall show below.

In any event, it is clear that the Saint did not remain with Urban after his departure from the Chartreuse for five years, but only for that many months, or perhaps fewer. For, according to what has been said, he did not approach him before April or May of 1090, and during that same year, while it was still in progress, he was already in Calabria. There he obtained from Count Roger of Calabria and Sicily a public charter granting him the hermitage that he either began to inhabit in that same year 1090 or certainly not long afterward, as the matters to be discussed below will make clear.

Nor, apparently, did the older Carthusians believe that the Saint remained with Pope Urban any longer than I have just determined before obtaining permission to withdraw from the papal curia after his departure from the Chartreuse and to proceed to Calabria.

538. For the chronologer—or rather, the earliest biographer—of our saint, of the first five priors of Chartreuse, who, as stated above, flourished in the thirteenth century, records the following concerning Saint Bruno, first in no. 16 and following:

> “The venerable Father, coming to the Supreme Pontiff, attended upon him—not for a long but for a short time—and by salutary counsels and assistance bore many of his burdens, while by his prompt readiness he greatly relieved his solicitude in governing the holy Church of God. Yet he could not long patiently conceal the sadness and grief he had conceived over the dispersal of his sons, nor could he endure the din and tumult of the papal court, which impeded the sweetness and tranquility with which he had been accustomed to enjoy and nourish himself in the hermitage. Unable to bear this any longer, he laid his desolation before the Supreme Pontiff and with the greatest insistence implored and obtained permission to withdraw from the court, so that he might return to the hermitage and to the sweetness of the cell already tasted and the rest he desired.”

He then supplies the following in no. 24, which is also relevant here:

> “Bruno, therefore, a most holy man endowed with a twofold science, both divine and human, … ruled the hermitage of Chartreuse for six years; afterward, as has been said, he was summoned by the Pope, and not long afterward, going to the hermitage of Calabria called Torre, he became, after a holy monastery had been built there, rector and minister of many servants of God who were anchorites.”

Thus, in both passages, so far as appears, he indicates by the expressions he uses that Saint Bruno remained with Pope Urban not for five years, but for a much shorter period, before obtaining permission to leave the papal court and withdraw to Calabria. Therefore, since the earlier Carthusians who committed anything to writing about the holy founder of their Order drew nearly all their material from the aforesaid chronologer of the first five priors of Chartreuse—the words just quoted being his—it is most probable that, following his example, they assigned our saint a stay with Pope Urban lasting not five years but considerably less. Nor without good reason, since the saint did not come to him before April of the year 1090, and in that same year left the papal court, as is sufficiently clear from what has already been said and will become still clearer from what follows.

§ XXXII. Whether Saint Bruno was discovered by Roger, count of Calabria, while the latter was hunting, in the cave in Calabria where Bruno had withdrawn with his companions; where Bruno first went after leaving the papal court; and why he did not then return to Chartreuse.

[Col. 0330B]

539. All the principal biographers of Saint Bruno whom I have at hand and who are later than the fifteenth century—namely, Zacharias, Benedictus, Puteanus, Blomenvenna, and Surius—report that our saint, after leaving the papal court with the consent of Pope Urban, withdrew to the Calabrian hermitage called Torre and established his residence there in humble huts; that, while hunting, he was discovered in the caves where he was staying with his companions by Roger, count of Calabria and Sicily, who at that time did not yet know him; and that on this occasion he obtained that hermitage from the prince. Since Blomenvenna’s account agrees almost exactly with the others and can therefore stand for all of them, I transcribe the relevant words, omitting nearly everything else. He writes:

> “Thus, having been dismissed—with the consent and blessing of the Supreme Pontiff—Saint Bruno, together with several men of the same purpose whom by his most fervent exhortations he had led to contempt of the world, sought the deserts of Calabria. For he had heard that there were many deserted places there most suitable for practicing penance and pursuing a solitary life. He desired, as he had often resolved, to return to Chartreuse to his beloved brothers whom he had sent ahead; but because the Supreme Pontiff, with his court, was traveling into Gaul, within whose boundaries Chartreuse is situated, he feared that he would not be able there to avoid the court from which he was fleeing. Therefore he turned instead to the deserts of Calabria. …
>
> “The holy man came, therefore, to a certain hermitage in Calabria called Torre, in the diocese of Squillace. There they built—not costly cells, since they lacked the means for them—but humble huts of worthless material, though precious in Christ. …”

540.

> “When they had first begun to inhabit the said hermitage, it happened, through the working of the Lord, that one day Roger, count of Calabria, while engaged in hunting in the same hermitage of Torre with a considerable retinue and a great number of dogs, came to the place where the servants of God had begun to live. The dogs, following by scent the various tracks of wild animals, reached the caves or huts in which Saint Bruno and his companions lived. There they stopped, and by much barking indicated to their master that they had found great prey.
>
> “When the count saw this, he and his men came at a swift run and found the aforesaid Fathers in those same caves, kneeling, with their faces and hands raised toward heaven, praying together and praising God. At this sight the count was filled with great amazement. He leapt down from the horse he was riding, greeted them devoutly and humbly, and carefully asked about the reason for their arrival and their condition. When he had learned everything from them in due order, he rejoiced greatly, praising and glorifying God for judging him worthy of such prey.
>
> “For the religious count hoped that, through their merits and prayers, he and his land would be assisted by God and preserved in peace. Therefore, so that they might live there more peacefully and persevere longer, he gave them the church of the Blessed Mary and of Saint Stephen of Cremo. He frequently visited them and provided them with the necessities of life, while gladly listening to their teachings concerning salvation. He often summoned blessed Bruno, the shepherd and father of them all, to himself; he always held him in great reverence, and, treating him as the first person in his household, followed his counsels and continually commended himself to his prayers, in which he placed the greatest confidence.”

[Col. 0331C]

541. Thus far Blomenvenna—or rather, all the biographers of Saint Bruno mentioned above. We must now examine individually, or at least the principal ones, the claims established by the words quoted, and especially whether the saint, having obtained from the Pontiff permission to return to a hermitage, went directly to the Calabrian hermitage of Torre and was there discovered by Roger, count of Calabria and Sicily, while the latter was hunting and, as Blomenvenna’s quoted words indicate, still did not know him.

Roger, son of Robert Guiscard and brother of Count Roger, mentioned immediately below, was duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily. In a diploma, which will be transcribed below and by which in 1093 he confirmed the donation of the Calabrian hermitage made by his uncle, Count Roger, to Saint Bruno and his companions, he speaks as follows:

> “We wish it to be known to your fraternity that two men, namely Bruno and Lanvinus, inflamed by zeal for holy religion, came with their companions from the regions of Gaul into the land of Calabria by God’s ordering. Under my guidance they sought in the aforesaid land a place suitable for their purpose; since they found none suitable for them in my possession, they chose to remain between the place called Arena and the town called Stilo. That place Roger, count of Sicily, my uncle, … gave to them; for it belonged to his county through my grant.”

Since, then, our saint and his companions, as Roger the duke declares here, came into Calabria, part of which was subject to him and part to Count Roger, and since they first sought, under the guidance of Roger the duke, a place suitable for their purpose in lands subject to the duke but found none, and finally chose such a place within the county or territories subject to Count Roger, it follows that, after obtaining from the Pontiff permission to leave the court and seek a hermitage, they did not go directly—as Blomenvenna’s recently quoted words state—to the Calabrian hermitage of Torre, subject to Count Roger; rather, they went into lands subject to Duke Roger, intending to search there for a place suitable for the eremitical life.

542. Indeed, since, as I have just said, they found no place in those lands which they considered suitable for their purpose, but sought such a place in territories subject to Count Roger, as the recently quoted words of the diploma granted by Duke Roger attest, it is probable that before this the saint and his companions had been brought to Count Roger by Duke Roger, so that they might achieve their desire and obtain from that prince a place, if they should find one in his territories suitable for their purpose.

The diploma by which Count Roger granted the Calabrian hermitage to Saint Bruno and his companions also leads me to this conclusion. In it the count speaks in the following manner:

> “We wish it to be known to your fraternity that, by the mercy of God, men of holy religion, namely Bruno and Lanvinus with their companions, have come from the regions of Gaul to this region of Calabria. Having despised the vanity of worldly glory, they had chosen to serve God alone. Knowing their desire, therefore, and wishing to be assisted before God by their merits and prayers, I obtained from their charity, by many prayers, that they should choose for themselves in my land a suitable place in which they might prepare whatever dwellings they wished for the service of God.”

Since by these words the count indicates that he brought it about that Bruno and his companions should choose in his land—namely, in the Calabrian hermitage of Torre, as is understood from what follows—a place suitable for their purpose in which they could construct whatever dwellings they wished, it follows that before doing so they had dealt with Count Roger and had probably been brought to him by Duke Roger, who, according to what has already been said, had earlier assisted them under his guidance in searching his lands for a place.

From this it further follows that, once they had chosen their residence in the aforesaid hermitage and built dwellings of whatever kind, they were not discovered while hunting by Count Roger, who, as Blomenvenna and the other cited biographers indicate, was entirely unaware of the matter.

543. I therefore think that Count Roger offered Bruno and his companions the choice of a place within his dominions suitable for the eremitical life not on the occasion of a hunt during which he found them hidden in a cave and intent upon prayer, but through the intervention of Duke Roger. Having heard from the duke something about the extremely austere life and most holy conduct of Bruno and his companions, and hoping—as he himself indicates in the words of the diploma quoted above—that through their prayers and merits he would receive assistance from the Lord, he desired such men to establish their residence in his dominions. He therefore had them brought to him and asked them to choose for themselves whatever place they wished there.

Indeed, the account that Saint Bruno and his companions—whom Count Roger had never previously seen and knew nothing about—were discovered by him while hunting in a cave, intensely engaged in prayer to God, and were therefore enriched by him with numerous benefits, is reported by the cited biographers of our saint. Yet, as I have just shown at length, it does not agree very well with the two diplomas already cited. Before me, I find this same observation made by Caesar de Eugenio in his *Neapoli sacra*, in the annotations on Surianus’s rendering of our saint’s Life, p. 189.

Nor did Morkensius, a member of the Carthusian house of Cologne, in his chronological-diplomatic *Dissertation on Saint Bruno*, and Zanottius, in the Life or History of the same saint composed by himself and the Bolognese Carthusians in Italy, dare to declare the observation contrary to the truth. Nevertheless, they attempt to show that our saint and his companions really were found praying in a cave by Prince Roger while he was hunting, and that this was the reason why the prince bestowed numerous benefits upon them. They do so in two different ways.

544. The first asserts that the saint was found not by Count Roger in the Calabrian hermitage of Torre or Squillace, but by Duke Roger in a certain cave or grotto within his dominions, together with Lanvinus and the other companions whom he had associated with himself. Since Morkensius declared that he adhered to this opinion rather than to the other, which maintains that the saint was found by Roger the count, on account of the words of the diploma granted by Duke Roger quoted above, he also gives the reader the reason why he believes that Saint Bruno was in fact found by one or the other Roger while engaged in prayer in a cave. Concerning the history that reports the event, he writes as follows:

> “This is in accordance with the truth of the history, which I recognize as most true from the tradition of our ancestors, and which was also recognized by the compiler of the *Fasciculus temporum*, Henry of Kalkar in *On the Origin and Progress of the Carthusian Order*, Puteanus, the writer of the Life, and all the domestic writers.”

Lest anyone argue against that tradition, as he calls it, on the grounds that no mention occurs in the diplomas of either prince cited above of the saint’s being found in caves by Roger—whether duke or count—while the latter was hunting, he immediately adds the following after the words just transcribed:

> “Nor is there any reason why anyone should hesitate or doubt the truth of the matter because neither duke nor count—both named Roger—mentions it: the former in the aforesaid diploma, the latter in his charters, for he issued several in favor of Saint Bruno and his companions, more of which will be recited below than the one already mentioned more than once. Yet the latter, in another charter issued much later, does mention the Capuan treason revealed to him by Saint Bruno in a nocturnal vision. The condition of this matter and of that one is different. In the former he grants a place abandoned by human cultivation, and he could lawfully do so without giving any reason; in the latter he hands over to Saint Bruno, for perpetual servitude, men condemned to death as guilty of the Capuan treason, and according to the laws the cause of such an enslavement had to be formulated.”

545. Thus far he, arguing that there was no reason why the event should be mentioned in the aforesaid diplomas even if the saint really had been found by Roger—whether duke or count—while the latter was relaxing his mind through hunting, with his companions and praying to God in a cave, and therefore that the event could not be disproved from the silence of those documents.

So be it. Yet the claim that the saint was found by Duke Roger while hunting, which Morkensius considers more probable, cannot be confirmed by any testimony whatsoever of either a later or an earlier writer. It therefore appears to have been invented by Morkensius without foundation. Meanwhile, against this opinion of his—as also against the opinion of Blomenvenna and the other biographers, who state that the saint was found in the Calabrian hermitage of Torre by Count Roger, who was unaware that he was staying there—no positive argument at all can be constructed from the diplomas so often cited. Nor does anything else prevent our believing that our saint may have been found by Duke Roger in a cave within his dominions, since the words quoted above from the duke’s diploma attest that before entering Count Roger’s territories he had been in Duke Roger’s lands.

But Surianus, who supports the opinion that our saint was found in a deserted cave by Count Roger, to whom he was still entirely unknown—or rather, who transmits this opinion after Surius—invokes in his annotations on Surius, p. 192, against Caesar de Eugenio, who, as already stated, had observed in his *Neapoli sacra* that this story did not fit very well with the diplomas cited above, a diploma or privilege that will be recited below, which Bruno received from Mesimerius, bishop of Squillace.

546. He writes there as follows:

> “The aforesaid Caesar says that he applied painstaking diligence in investigating this truth—namely, that Bruno was found by Count Roger, to whom he was still entirely unknown, in the hiding places of the deserted or Calabrian hermitage. I do not deny it. Nevertheless, many things persuade me that he did not see, or at least lightly considered, the diploma of Mesimerius, bishop of Squillace. For if he had weighed that document, he would have agreed with what he says there: Saint Bruno had spent a sufficiently long time in the deserts of Calabria before transferring to the hermitage of Squillace, and therefore had lived not in fixed tents but in natural caves and such underground shelters.”

Thus far Surianus. Yet Mesimerius, the Greek bishop of Squillace, nowhere states in his diploma, written in Greek, that Saint Bruno had spent a sufficiently long time in the deserts of Calabria before transferring to the hermitage of Squillace, contrary to what Surianus’s words imply. In that document, the only words concerning Saint Bruno and his companions that might be thought to support this are quoted by Morkensius from his translation as follows:

> “These men, living in deserted places for a sufficiently long time, migrated there to the region of Stilo in my diocese.”

Or, if one prefers Ughellus’s translation in vol. IX of *Italia sacra*, col. 425:

> “After they had spent many years of their lives in solitary places, they migrated here to the region of Stilo in my diocese.”

But these words do not state whether, before withdrawing with his companions into the hermitage of Squillace, the saint had spent a sufficiently long time in the deserts of Calabria or in other places. What if Mesimerius is speaking only of the deserts of Chartreuse and of Sicca Fontana, where the saint had stayed for a sufficiently long time, or for many years, before going to Calabria? This certainly appears in no respect unlikely, much less incredible.

547. Furthermore, even if Mesimerius’s statement concerns deserts other than those of Chartreuse and Sicca Fontana, does it follow that our saint was found there by Count Roger, while hunting, when he was still entirely unknown to the count? Certainly not, as anyone, I think, will readily recognize.

“But,” you will say, “it could indeed easily have happened that our saint was found—not by Count Roger, but by his homonymous duke, whose uncle the count was—while hunting, in the cave into which he had withdrawn with his companions, when he was still entirely unknown to the duke.” I admit that this is possible, and the diplomas mentioned above do not contradict the possibility. Yet whether it actually happened remains doubtful to me, if only because the matter cannot be proved by any monument of established and certain credibility.

Let us now come to Zanottius. To defend the account transmitted by Surius and the other biographers of the saint—that he was found in a cave by Count Roger while the count was hunting—Zanottius maintains that this event occurred not before but after the saint had become known to Count Roger and had already received from him the Calabrian hermitage of Torre or Squillace for habitation. Since this does not even appear to conflict with the diplomas cited above, as anyone who considers the matter will see, and since those documents therefore cannot prevent us from believing that the event occurred then, Zanottius’s opinion appears no less credible than Morkensius’s.

Nevertheless, whether it actually agrees with the truth is wholly doubtful, since it is founded on no sufficiently reliable ancient author or monument. Nor can the biographers of our saint mentioned above make it certain, since, apart from clothing the event with circumstances different from those supplied by Zanottius, they are all too recent for their sole authority to establish as certain and indisputable the facts they relate about Saint Bruno.

548. Accordingly, after properly weighing everything, I consider it most probable that the saint’s withdrawal from the papal court to the Calabrian hermitage of Torre occurred approximately as follows.

According to what has already been said, Saint Bruno accompanied the Pontiff when he left Rome for Campania and the territories subject to Roger the duke and his brother Bohemond in the middle of the summer of 1090. There he earnestly requested permission from him to leave the court and return to a hermitage. Having finally obtained it, he soon went to Calabria, where he had heard that there were many deserted places, and sought Roger the duke, whom he may already have seen somewhere in Campania and to whom he had explained his desire to return to the solitary life.

When, with the duke’s consent and guidance, he had searched the part of Calabria subject to the duke for a place suitable for the eremitical life and had found none, he was brought by that same prince to Count Roger, who perhaps was hurrying there for other reasons. Having obtained from the count—who had been strongly commended to him by Duke Roger because of the remarkable holiness of his life—the right to choose for himself, in the part of Calabria under the count’s authority, whatever place he considered suitable for his purpose, he chose the hermitage of Torre and obtained from Count Roger the donation of it, as we shall soon see.

This arrangement and reconstruction of events contains nothing that conflicts either with the diplomas mentioned above or with probability of any kind. Since this is so, I consider it almost certain and indisputable that the saint withdrew to Calabria in the manner just described and obtained the donation of the hermitage of Torre.

If, meanwhile, anyone should argue with Zanottius that the saint, while intensely praying to God, was found in this hermitage after it had already been given to him by Count Roger, who was hunting; or if anyone should insist with Morkensius that this happened to him in Apulia at the hands of Duke Roger, I shall not strongly oppose him, since, although the latter opinion is less probable, it would not conflict with the diplomas cited above.

However all these matters may finally stand, our saint, when he left the papal court, withdrew to the Calabrian hermitage of Torre, as has already been said. Zanottius relates in chapter 18 of the Life of the saint composed by him that, while traveling toward it, he visited the church of Saint Nicholas at Bari and that of Saint Michael on Mount Gargano, that this archangel appeared to him twice, and several other things. Yet he himself supports none of these claims by any testimony of antiquity, nor do I find them supported elsewhere.

549. It remains to examine why the saint then preferred to withdraw to Calabria rather than return to Chartreuse, which he loved.

“[Bruno] desired to return to Chartreuse to his beloved brothers whom he had sent ahead; but because the Supreme Pontiff, Urban II, was traveling with his court into Gaul, within whose boundaries Chartreuse is situated, he feared that he might not be able there to avoid the court from which he was fleeing, and therefore withdrew instead to the deserts of Calabria.”

Thus writes Blomenvenna in the passage quoted above. But the reason he gives cannot explain why Bruno withdrew to Calabria rather than returning to Chartreuse. The chronology alone of Urban’s journey into Gaul and of the saint’s withdrawal to Calabria disproves it.

For Urban, as everyone agrees, did not enter Gaul before the year 1095, after celebrating a council at Piacenza in Italy and then proceeding to Clermont, where he was to celebrate another, much more famous council, at which the foundation was laid for the sacred expeditions against the infidels for the recovery of the Holy Land. Bruno, however, as is easy to infer from what has already been said and will further be said, withdrew from the papal court to Calabria in 1090.

I therefore think that the saint went to Calabria rather than returning to Chartreuse because the Pontiff, foreseeing that in the extremely difficult times in which he lived he would sometimes be compelled to leave Rome and withdraw into the lands subject to the two homonymous princes, Roger the duke and Roger the count, did not wish Bruno—whom he wanted occasionally to summon to himself and employ in his counsels—to depart for Gaul, or Chartreuse, situated far from the territories of both Rogers.

550. I am led to this opinion by the fact that, when the saint was already living in the hermitage of Torre, Urban summoned him from time to time, either to attend councils that had been announced or for some other reason. Mabillon supplies a fragment of evidence for this in book LXX of the *Benedictine Annals*, no. 30: a letter written by Pope Paschal II, the immediate successor of Urban, to Lanvinus, a disciple of our saint and his immediate successor in the priory of the Calabrian hermitage, on 26 November 1101.

The letter, which a Parisian Carthusian mentioned above more than once shared with me in full, copied from a manuscript of the fourth book of the *Carthusian Annals* of Val-de-Dieu, not yet published, reads as follows:

> “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Lanvinus, greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “What we greatly desired and awaited with intense longing has, by the Lord’s favor, been accomplished. For, when our brother R., bishop of Albano, returned, we learned that peace and concord had been restored to the hermitage and that you had succeeded the master Bruno of holy memory. Therefore may the spirit of that same man be in you; may there be the same rigor of eremitical discipline and the same steadfastness of conduct and gravity. For, with the Lord’s help, whatever authority and power the master’s sound wisdom and religious devotion merited personally from the Apostolic See, this we grant to you also, with that same spirit accompanying you.
>
> “We wish you to visit us in the coming Lent, so that we may speak more fully face to face about the secrets of the heart. Meanwhile, we admonish you to strive, together with our brothers and the religious men who are around you, to restore the peace of the land, which we have heard has been greatly disturbed, and to endeavor to admonish others to do the same.
>
> “Command in our name that the abbot of Saint Julian, whom we have heard to be blameworthy, present himself before us; and sharply rebuke him for disregarding the letters of our legate.
>
> “Given at Rome, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December.”

551. Since, then, as is clear from this letter of Pope Paschal, Lanvinus—the immediate successor of the saint in the priory of the hermitage of Torre—was summoned to Rome by Paschal, the immediate successor of Urban II in the chair of Saint Peter, it does not appear doubtful that Saint Bruno himself, whom Paschal here extols with the highest praises, had also been summoned by Urban II.

Since this is so, one may reasonably infer that the Supreme Pontiff, wishing to be able to summon Bruno to himself from time to time, did not want him to depart far from the regions in which he foresaw that he would often reside; and that this was why Bruno did not return to Chartreuse but withdrew to Calabria.

This conjecture is further confirmed, in some measure, both by the tradition of the Carthusian Order, as it is called, and by the fact that, according to the unimpeachable testimony of the chronologer of the first four priors of Chartreuse, in the eulogy of our saint transcribed here in no. 7, Bruno was summoned from Chartreuse by Pope Urban II to assist him with his counsels. It is therefore probable that, when Urban granted Bruno permission to leave his court, he still wished to make use of his counsels and, for this purpose, summoned him from time to time while Bruno remained not too far from Calabria.

Moreover, unless one maintains that the saint withdrew to Calabria because the Pontiff wished him, for this very purpose, to remain not far from the places where the Pontiff himself was staying, what reason can finally be given for his having done so after obtaining from the Pontiff permission to withdraw to a hermitage, rather than returning to Chartreuse?

§ XXXIII. Saint Bruno Is Given the Calabrian Hermitage of Torre by Count Roger; the Donation Is Subsequently Confirmed for Him by Mesimerius, Bishop of Squillace, and Later by Pope Urban II.

552. After the arrangement described in the preceding section—namely, that Count Roger of Sicily and Calabria granted him the right to choose in the prince’s territories a place he considered most suitable for conducting the eremitical life—Saint Bruno carefully explored Calabria. When he found the hermitage called Torre, situated between Stilo and Arena and enclosed within the boundaries of the diocese of Scyllacium, or, as others write, Squillace, he judged it very suitable for his purpose, since it was extremely mountainous and difficult and arduous of access. Count Roger most generously granted him this place by a public instrument or diploma, and the donation was subsequently confirmed by Mesimerius, bishop of Scyllace, and by Pope Urban II.

It will be useful to place before the reader’s eyes the charters or instruments by which they did this, since not all of them are readily available everywhere and since they shed light on much of what has already been said and will be said about the saint. At the end of each I shall add several observations, whether concerning the chronological notes with which the documents are furnished, the persons whose names are recorded, or anything else requiring clarification or commentary.

I begin by transcribing Count Roger’s diploma. In Morkensius’s recension it runs as follows:

> “Roger, by the grace of God count of Calabria and Sicily, to all his faithful subjects and to the sons of the Church of God, present and future, greeting in the Lord.
>
> “We wish it to be known to your fraternity that, by the mercy of God, men of holy religion, namely Bruno and Lanvinus with their companions, have come from the regions of Gaul to this region of Calabria. Having despised the vanity of worldly glory, they have chosen to serve God alone.

553. “Knowing their desire, therefore, and wishing to be assisted before God by their merits and prayers, I obtained from their charity by many prayers that they should choose for themselves in my land a suitable place in which they might prepare whatever dwellings they wished for the service of God.

> “They have indeed chosen in my land a certain solitary place situated between the place called Arena and the town called Stilo. I have given this place to them and to their successors who will serve God there, for the honor of almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and for the honor of the most blessed Mary, ever Virgin, Mother of Christ our God and Lord, and of all the saints, together with the entire forest, land, water, and mountain, for the space of one league [or: leuca] in every direction of the adjoining area. I grant and establish that they may possess this place freely and peacefully, together with its adjacent territory, forever, and that they shall render from it no forced labor or service to me or to any other person.
>
> “Moreover, on behalf of almighty God, holy Mary the perpetual Virgin, all the saints, and myself, I protest and forbid that any of my men or outsiders—whether a *stratygotus* [or: *strategus*], viscount, peasant, knight, slave, or free man—should cause the servants of God any trouble or injury in this place on account of pasture, agriculture, fishing, timber, or anything else. Rather, it shall be in their power to possess, dispose of, arrange, and distribute the aforesaid place, together with all its adjacent territory, according to their will.
>
> “If anyone hereafter should presume to act against the constitution of this document, let him first incur the wrath and curse of God unless he makes due satisfaction; and, his attempt having been brought to nothing, let him suffer in our court a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold for so great a presumption.

554.

> “Therefore, so that this constitution may remain inviolable and wholly firm, with the consent of my wife, Countess Adelaide, and of my son Goffredo, I made this donation in the presence of good men and ordered it sealed with my seal.
>
> “I, Goffredo, bishop of the Church of Malta, although unworthy, wrote this charter with my own hand at the request of Count Roger, approving and confirming this constitution, but condemning with anathema and excommunication anyone who should presume to violate it, unless, repenting, he makes satisfaction.
>
> “These things were done in the year 1090 from the Incarnation of the Lord. In addition, I gave Mule with his sons to guard the forest.
>
> “The witnesses present were these: Stephen the priest, Giraldus the priest, Peter of Moritono [or: Moritonio], Richard Maletus, Ragnulfus the almoner, Nicholas the notary, and many others.”

Morkensius, whose recension I have followed in presenting this charter, adds the following after the complete text:

> “Note: I received this charter of the donation of the Calabrian hermitage, etc., taken from the original in Italy. It is also found in the annotations—namely, pp. 199 and following—on the Life of Saint Bruno by our Surianus. From it it is manifest that our holy father Bruno, with Lanvinus and several companions, had already come from the regions of Gaul to Calabria in the year 1090, and had been asked by Count Roger to remain in that land of his and choose a hermitage suitable for his purpose.”

Thus far Morkensius, and rightly, so far as I can see. Yet there are some who contend that the charter of the donation made by Roger was not issued before the year 1091, because they want it to have been written in January or February. Since, according to the method of reckoning the years of the Lord followed by Count Roger—which reckoned them from the Incarnation rather than from the Nativity of the Lord and thus ran three months ahead of our computation—these two months ought to fall not in the year 1090, during whose January and February the saint was most probably, indeed almost certainly, still living at Chartreuse, but in the year 1091.

555. But the fact that Roger customarily reckoned the years of the Lord not from His Incarnation but from His Nativity is demonstrated by various charters of his preserved in Rocchus Pirrus, Ughelli, and others, as anyone who wishes to consult them will readily discover. Moreover, Mabillon, in Book LXVIII of the *Annals*, no. 32, confuses the charter of donation just quoted with the charter—also to be quoted below by us—by which Count Roger later marked out or assigned the boundaries of the Turritan hermitage, which he had already donated to Bruno and his companions; and, in addition, he wrongly attributes this charter to Duke Roger. I cannot but marvel at both errors, since this very charter, which he transcribes in part at that place, and which, as I have noted, he attributes to Duke Roger, bears at its head not the name of Duke Roger but that of Count Roger, and contains the following words in its text:

> “We have therefore donated this place, namely that situated between the place called Arena and the town called Stilo, that is, the Turritan hermitage and everything adjoining it on every side within the space of one league, to God and Blessed Mary, and to them and their successors in ownership, just as these lands were ours, with complete immunity and freedom . . . . Furthermore, we asked the venerable man Goffred, bishop of Melitine, to draw up a charter of confirmation of this donation of ours, which we also sealed . . . . This donation of ours, moreover, our lord the pope Urban, as well as Theodore, bishop of Squillace, in whose diocese the place itself is situated, praised, confirmed by privileges, and fortified with a terrible anathema.”

Since these words state that Pope Urban confirmed the donation of the Turritan hermitage of Calabria, made to Saint Bruno by Count Roger, and since the charter by which he did so was issued in 1092, as Mabillon himself admits in the cited passage, I do not see how this author could rightly have taken the charter that he partly transcribes, and presents as dated 1093, to be the charter by which Roger first donated that hermitage to Saint Bruno and his companions.

556. Nevertheless, since Mabillon appears not to have had at hand the charter by which Roger, count of Calabria and Sicily, truly donated the Turritan hermitage to our Saint, he may perhaps have fallen into this error for that reason. Yet nothing of this kind excuses the other error by which, as I have already noted, he attributes to Duke Roger the charter that he transcribes in part and that proceeded from Count Roger, whose nephew Duke Roger was. Anyone who has even glanced at a history of Sicily knows that the latter was different from the former; Mabillon himself was not unaware of this, so it would be superfluous to prove it here.

Nevertheless, so that everyone may distinguish between the two Rogers and judge fairly the genuineness of the charters to be transcribed here—charters granted both by Duke Roger and by Count Roger in favor of Saint Bruno and his companions—I wish to bring forward a few facts chiefly concerning those two princes, their Norman stock, and their descendants.

Tancred of Hauteville, as Geoffrey Malaterra, a contemporary author, reports in Book I of the Sicilian History that he composed, was born of noble family near Coutances in Normandy, a province of Gaul, and flourished in the eleventh century. By two different wives he fathered twelve sons. By the first, whose name has been lost, he had William, surnamed Iron Arm, Drogo, Humphrey, Geoffrey, and Serlo; by the second, who was called Fressenda, he had Robert, later called Guiscard, Malger, William, Alfred, Hubert, Tancred, and finally Roger. Except for two of them, who remained in their native land to secure a portion of their paternal inheritance, all went to Italy. There, distinguished by their military deeds especially in Apulia and Campania, they gradually subjected to themselves these regions and others nearby, after expelling the Greeks and Saracens, their rulers.

Among them, however, Robert, surnamed Guiscard, and Roger, the youngest of all, stood out particularly. They acquired a great name among even the latest posterity through their benefactions to Saint Bruno, and no less through their extraordinary generosity toward other persons and sacred places than through their arms.

557. Robert held the duchy of Apulia together with part of Calabria and several other neighboring territories, and in 1085 exchanged life for death. He left behind three or four sons, the second-born of whom, Roger, succeeded to the duchy of Apulia and the greater part of his paternal inheritance. He married Adela, daughter of Robert the Frisian, count of Flanders.

Roger, however, although he held only part of Calabria, was called count of Calabria no less than of Sicily, even though supreme lordship over the whole region appears to have belonged first to Guiscard and then to his son Roger. He had three different wives, if the first of these, whom Orderic Vitalis, in Book III of his *History of the Normans*, p. 484, calls Judith, but whom Geoffrey Malaterra, in Book II, chapter 29 of his *Sicilian History*, calls Delicia, may properly be regarded as his lawful wife.

The first bore him no children, as the aforementioned Orderic Vitalis states in the cited passage. The second, called Elemburga by Malaterra in Book IV, chapter 14, and Eremburgis by Cangius in the *Sicilian Genealogy* included among his notes on Anna Comnena, bore him a son, Geoffrey—or, as others write, Goffred—and several daughters. The third, named Adelaide, or, as others record it, Adelasia, was the daughter of Boniface, marquis of Montferrat. She was married to him in 1089, and by her he fathered two sons. One of them, named Simon, died in infancy; the other, called Roger like his father, later became king of Sicily.

I have prefaced these details, partly from Geoffrey Malaterra and partly from Orderic Vitalis, so that what must be noted concerning the various charters of Count Roger, and one charter of Duke Roger, granted in favor of Saint Bruno and his companions, may be understood.

From these facts it is already clear that nothing can be brought against the genuineness of the charter recently transcribed here, by which Count Roger granted Saint Bruno the Turritan or Squillacian hermitage of Calabria in 1090, on the ground that it is said to have been issued with the consent of Count Roger’s wife Adelaide and his son Goffred. Nor is there any reason to suspect the document because it was issued in Calabria and because Count Roger is not known to have been in Calabria at the end of 1090, when it was issued. For although Malaterra and others who committed his deeds to writing do not expressly state that the prince was there at that time, they likewise record nothing from which the contrary can be established with certainty.

558. I now come to the charter by which Theodore Mesimerius, bishop of Squillace, in whose diocese the Turritan hermitage was situated, as I have already noted, approved the donation made by Count Roger to Saint Bruno.

Morkensius states in his notes to this instrument that he had in his hands a copy taken from the Greek original and sent to him from Italy. Since it was in Calabria, where public instruments were customarily written in Greek even at the beginning of Norman rule, the instrument had originally been given in Greek to Mesimerius, a bishop of the Greek Church. Morkensius translated it into Latin and appended it to the end of the chronologico-diplomatic treatise that he composed concerning Saint Bruno.

I endeavored to obtain a copy of the Greek document itself for presentation here to the reader; but since my efforts were unsuccessful, and since I am forced to be content with another’s translation—whether that of Surianus in his notes, pp. 207 ff., to the Life of the Saint written by Surius, or that of Ughelli in volume IX of *Sacred Italy*, among the bishops of Squillace, or finally that of Morkensius—I transcribe the instrument here as this latter author translated it into Latin.

According to his recension, it reads as follows:

> “Theodore Mesimerius, by the mercy of God bishop of Castra, Squillace, Stilo, and Taberna, and protosyncellus, to the petition of the most illustrious count, our lord Roger, who deigned to ask me on behalf of the most honored monks and hermits, namely lords Bruno and Lanvin—not indeed dealing with me by supreme and tyrannical authority, but, as I have said, deigning to ask me on behalf of the aforesaid monks, who inhabit the place preserved by God called Turris, in the very venerable church of our most glorious Lady, the Mother of God, and of Saint John the Baptist, the Forerunner. These men, living in deserted places, migrated there after a sufficiently long time, to the territory of Stilo in my diocese.”

559. “And just as our lord the count has donated to you the mountain, fields, and mills around the church, extending for two miles, so may you, the monks mentioned above, and your companions and successors who will inhabit this place, possess them perpetually until the end of the ages, without anyone’s prohibition or disturbance. Let no one—neither I myself nor others who may be chosen as bishops after me—impose upon you or your other companions and successors any tribute, tithe, or harassment whatsoever.

“But if anyone should dare to despise this our seal—that is, charter—let him be accursed by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and by the 318 God-bearing Fathers of the Council of Nicaea. Let this seal remain firm and inviolable until the end of the ages. For I have made this present sealed charter on behalf of the aforesaid monks, and, having sealed it, I have marked it with my leaden seal: + on the seventh day of the month of December, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1090.

“I, Raingerius, by the mercy of God elected archbishop of the holy metropolitan Church of Reggio, have confirmed the present document exactly as it is written; and let it remain ratified and fixed with those servants of God mentioned above, Bruno, Lanvin, and their other companions, as well as with those who will succeed them, and let it retain its validity until the end of the ages.”

To the Greek charter of Mesimerius, here already given according to Morkensius’s recension, there is appended, as this author and Surianus, p. 209, testify, another Latin version—or rather, a somewhat freer interpretation of the Greek charter itself, apparently made by Mesimerius. So that the learned reader may form his own judgment concerning the donation approved by Mesimerius, which Count Roger made to Saint Bruno, I wish to transcribe that Latin charter as well.

560. It is worded as follows:

> “I, Theodore Mesimerius, by the grace of God bishop of Squillace, and of Stilo and Taberna, and protosyncellus, freely give, not under compulsion but consenting to the pleas of Count Roger and the advice of many of his nobles: the land of Turris, namely two miles around the church situated on the mountain, on every side, to Lord Bruno and Lanvin and their companions and successors who inhabit that mountain, in such a manner and under such terms that during their lifetime they may freely have and possess it; and after their death their successors may likewise freely possess the mountain and land, with the woods within the boundaries of the aforesaid two miles on every side around the church established on the said mountain.

“They shall pay no service to the bishop of Squillace, nor to the count, nor to any person whatsoever; and if they wish to make any ordination or consecration, let them do so as they please. Whoever wishes to contradict these provisions, let him perish with Judas the traitor, unless he comes to the brothers of the Church to make satisfaction and reparation. I, Raingerius, elected archbishop of Reggio, confirm and approve this charter.”

Here now is what Morkensius observes at the end of the instrument he transcribed, chiefly in addition to what I have already said:

> “Mesimerius, Πρωτοσυγκελλὸς—that is, in the interpretation made from the words of Mesimerius himself which is appended to this Greek charter—wrote in Latin *PROTOSYNQUILLOS*. I, imitating certain Latins, wrote *protosyncellus*. Another may perhaps translate it *first chaplain*, but that is irrelevant; let everyone read it as he wishes. The original has attached to it, by a white hemp cord, a small leaden seal. On one side is a certain saint, with arms and palms extended. I think it is Saint Agathius the martyr, patron of the people of Squillace; on the other side are very small Greek characters, scarcely legible.”

561. So much for him. He correctly renders the Greek word Πρωτοσυγκελλὸς into Latin as *protosyncellus*. But whether anyone has also correctly translated the same Greek word as “first chaplain” is another question. *Protosyncellus*, or Πρωτοσυγκελλὸς, means the same as “first of the syncelli”; but what meaning properly belongs to the word *syncellus*, I cannot state with certainty. Consult Cangius in his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin* under the entries *protosyncellus* and *syncellus*.

I now turn to the chronological features that the Greek charter of Mesimerius offers for observation and clarification. The year in which the instrument is recorded as having been issued does not agree with the indiction. What, then, shall we conclude about it? Shall we declare it spurious or forged for that reason?

Cangius, in his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin* under the entry *annus*, firmly demonstrates that charters should not readily be rejected because they contain chronological difficulties. It will be useful to transcribe here the whole passage, although it is somewhat lengthy, lest anyone too readily repudiate the charter of Mesimerius, or even merely regard it as suspect, especially if the chronological difficulty from which it suffers can in some way be removed.

It reads as follows:

> “Nevertheless, certain papal diplomas are found,” says the same author, Mabillon, in *De re diplomatica*, Book II, chapter 25, no. 9, “whose reckoning anticipates our more recent one. The learned Chifflet supplies us with two of this kind in his *History of Therench*. The first is: ‘Given at Alba by the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, indiction XIV, in the year 1122 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Callixtus [lacuna].’ The second has the same chronological indications.”

562. “Yet indiction XIV agrees not with the year 1122 according to our reckoning, but with the preceding year. Hence Chifflet, in the heading of the first privilege, notes that the privilege was issued in the year 1122 counted from 25 March, that is, insofar as the Incarnation precedes the Nativity by nine months; but according to the Dionysian year it was 1121, as indiction XIV shows.

“There appear to be other pontifical diplomas of this kind. Yet some are found whose reckoning precedes the Dionysian year by one entire year, not merely by the nine months that consequently cannot be adapted to the Pisan reckoning”—which begins from the Lord’s Incarnation and therefore, since the Incarnation preceded the Nativity by nine months, anticipates the common reckoning by the same number of months.

> “There is an unmistakable original of this kind in the Dionysian archive, dated: ‘On the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, indiction X, in the year 1103 of the Lord’s Incarnation, but in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.’ This indiction, just as the third year of Paschal’s pontificate, agrees with March of the year 1102 and cannot agree with the following year, even if the Pisan reckoning is admitted—unless this Dionysian diploma is said to have preceded it by an entire year.

> “Another, entirely similar, appears in Puricellus, p. 512, concerning the same Paschal: ‘Given at the Lateran by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, indiction X, in the year 1103 of the Lord’s Incarnation, but in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II.’

> “Here we have the same chancellor, the same chronological indications, which are offered for discussion to learned men, together with others of a similar kind that occur not rarely. These matters are taken almost word for word from Mabillon, though at greater length, and not without usefulness, to show that charters containing chronological difficulties should not readily be rejected, since such difficulties are also observed in diplomas that cannot in any way be called into question.”

563. Thus far Cangius, and rightly so, as I have already noted. But how shall we now remove the chronological difficulty that occurs in the charter of Mesimerius?

Shall we say that an error lies either in the year or in the indiction, arising from the carelessness of copyists who failed to observe accurately which year and which indiction were designated by the Greek letters written beneath Roger’s charter?

Yet the chronological characters with which not only the original of this instrument but also the copy that served as Morkensius’s model was furnished were not abbreviations expressed by letters standing for numbers. Rather, as this author himself reports in a marginal note, they were written out in full words in the following form:

> Μηνὶ Δεκεμβρίῳ εἶς τὰς ἔπτα, ἰνδικτιόνος δεκατὴς πεμπτὴς τοῦ ἐννεακοστοῦ χιλιοστοῦ ἔτους

That is:

> “On the seventh day of December, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1090,”

as Morkensius correctly translates it. Although the noun with which the feminine article τὰς agrees is not present, a plural accusative noun, ἡμέρας, “days,” is nevertheless understood, together with the participle προβεβηκότι, which refers to the noun μηνί, “month.” The sense is therefore:

> μηνὶ Δεκεμβρίῳ εἰς τὰς ἕπτα ἡμερὰς προβεβηκότι,

that is:

> “in the month of December, which had advanced to the seventh day.”

Thus, in the appendix to Bernard de Montfaucon’s *Palaeography*, p. 512, the following Greek inscription—or rather clause—from a manuscript of the *Octateuch* preserved in the University College at Oxford is rendered into Latin:

> Τέλος εἴληφεν ἡ Ὀκτάτευχος βίβλος Νοεμβρίῳ είς τὰς κʹ

That is:

> “The Octateuch received its completion on the twentieth of November.”

From the material supplied by Surianus in his notes to the Life of the Saint composed by Surius, it appears that the copy which served this author’s purpose read εἱς τῆς rather than εἰς τὰς ἕπτα. But this must be attributed either to an error of the copyist or to a dialect that Mesimerius may perhaps have followed.

Whatever the case, the error in the chronological characters marking Mesimerius’s charter—or rather, the copy of it transcribed here according to Morkensius’s recension—does not appear to have been committed by copyists. How, then, is the chronological difficulty presented by those characters finally to be removed?

564. At the end of his chronologico-diplomatic work, Morkensius proposes various explanations for reconciling the chronological characters attached to the several charters or public instruments that he has produced. Concerning Mesimerius he says that he “follows us Sicilians by one year, and therefore the date of his document must be extended to the following year according to our reckoning.”

If this is true, the charter of that bishop of Squillace, quoted above and marked as issued in 1090, was issued in the immediately following year. Thus the fifteenth indiction with which it is marked will agree perfectly with the year in which it was actually issued, and the entire chronological difficulty affecting the instrument will disappear.

But since this method of reckoning the years of Christ is not known to have been generally used among the Sicilians, it must be investigated whether it was certainly never employed by anyone.

Rocchus Pirrus, in the first part of his *Notice of the Church of Palermo*, under the year 1144, states that the year of Christ’s Nativity was commonly equated by the Greeks with the year 5508 from the creation of the world, and that this method of reckoning passed from them into Sicily. He writes as follows:

> “Fridericus Sylburgius presents the Sicilian *Fasti*, extracted from a chronicle that Jerome Zurita discovered in an ancient Sicilian library and that was subsequently brought into Italy by Antonio Agostini, and later transferred to Spain. In it, he reports that the year of Christ’s Nativity was placed under the consulship of Lentulus and Piso and in the year 5507 from the creation of the world.

> “Nor should this variation disturb the reader, if he observes that several writers anticipated the common Christian era by one year or another. I therefore think that in our Sicily the number of years from the creation of the world must be explained in documents according to this method of reckoning: namely, that one should subtract 5508, and the remainder will indicate the year of Christ in the common and ordinary era that we now use. For Sicily held that Christ was born after the year 5508 from the creation of the world, and that the first year of Christ fell in the year 5509.”

565. So much for him. What if, then, just as others mentioned here by Rocchus Pirrus anticipated the common Greek Christian era—namely, the year 5508 from the creation of the world—by one year or another, Mesimerius likewise followed it by one year, and considered Christ to have been born not in the year 5508 from the creation of the world but in 5509?

Since different people assign Christ’s birth to different years from the creation of the world, it certainly does not seem at all unlikely to me that Mesimerius, bishop of Squillace or Scyllace, held this opinion. According to it, the year 6599 from the creation of the world—which, as calculation shows, was in progress in the year 1091 of Christ according to the common Sicilian and Greek era just described—would have fallen in the year 1090 of Christ.

Consequently, this latter year of Christ, in which the charter granted by Mesimerius in favor of Saint Bruno and his companions is dated, ought properly to be regarded as the year 1091. To that year, already advanced to the seventh day of December, as the same charter states, the fifteenth indiction marked in the instrument agrees perfectly, as calculation will show.

For this reason I cannot dare to regard the document as spurious or suspect merely because, although it is marked as 1090, it was in fact issued in 1091. This is especially so since Ruinart, in the Life of Pope Urban II composed by him, p. 86, and other learned men praise it as genuine in various works that they have produced; and since not only Surianus, in his notes to the Life of Saint Bruno composed by Surius, but also Ughelli, in volume IX of *Sacred Italy*, have inserted it in full. Nor have I so far found any author who marks it with a less favorable judgment.

566. Nor is there any reason to regard as suspect the fact that it defines the size of the Squillacian or Turritan hermitage granted by Count Roger to Saint Bruno as two miles, whereas the charter of donation made by Count Roger and transcribed above assigns it the extent of one league.

Although a league was sometimes understood by the ancients as three thousand paces, this did not always hold among all of them. Nor, even if it did, would Mesimerius therefore be said to contradict Count Roger concerning the size he assigned to the hermitage given into Saint Bruno’s possession.

For in the charter of Roger just mentioned, the league is evidently understood as a measure of land. A league understood in this sense, among the Franks or in France—Normandy, the province from which Roger came—consisted of two thousand paces or miles, as Cangius teaches under the entry *leuca* in his *Glossary*.

But someone may object that in the charter granted by Mesimerius, Raingerius is called “archbishop-elect of Reggio,” so that he appears not yet to have been consecrated or ordained when it was issued. Yet from what was said above, he was elected to the see of Reggio in 1090. It therefore does not seem likely that on 7 December 1091, when the charter is dated, he was still not a consecrated or ordained bishop. It would consequently follow that the instrument was probably issued not in 1091, as we have determined, but in 1090, the year in which it is actually dated, and that it therefore bears an indiction inconsistent with the year of its date.

Those who wish to regard Mesimerius’s charter as spurious may argue in this way. Yet although it is more probable from what has been said that Raingerius was elected to the see of Reggio in the very year 1090 in which our Saint declined it, this is not altogether certain.

For why could it not have happened that, when Bruno refused promotion to that dignity, the people of Reggio—whether voluntarily or prevented by some outside circumstance from acting otherwise—delayed for some time the election of another to the same office?

567. Whatever the case may be, if it cannot be admitted that Raingerius had not yet been consecrated archbishop of Reggio in December 1091, while nevertheless having already been elected in 1090, then it must be concluded that he was promoted to this dignity not in 1090 but in 1091. This follows because the aforementioned charter, which he confirmed and approved as elected archbishop of Reggio, does not appear capable of having been issued before 1091.

I demonstrate this as follows. Bruno and his companions are said in that charter to have inhabited the church of our most glorious Lady, the Mother of God, and of Saint John the Baptist, situated in the Squillacian or Turritan hermitage. But, as I shall explain below, this church was first built when that hermitage had been donated by Count Roger to Saint Bruno.

Since, according to what has been said above, this donation did not take place before the year 1090 was already drawing to a close, it is not at all probable that from that same year there existed in the Turritan hermitage a church dedicated to the glorious Mother of God and Saint John the Baptist, which the Saint and his companions also inhabited during that very year. It is therefore necessary to conclude that the aforementioned charter of Mesimerius, which implies this, was issued not in 1090 but in 1091.

Thus the argument that could still be brought against the genuineness of the charter granted by Mesimerius also collapses, and it ought not to be considered spurious.

The next task is to carry out what I decided to do in the present section: I shall now also transcribe the Bull by which Pope Urban II confirmed the charters of Count Roger and Theodore, bishop of Squillace, quoted above, and bestowed a new favor upon Bruno and his companions.

It is worded as follows:

> “Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ Bruno and Lanvin, greeting and apostolic blessing. The affection of a pious will ought to be brought to completion by diligent pursuit. Since, therefore, it is our duty to provide, insofar as the Lord grants us power, for the peace of God’s servants, we mercifully assent to your petitions, most beloved and most reverend sons in Christ.

568. “By the page of this apostolic privilege, therefore, by apostolic authority we decree that the place which, by the Lord’s direction, you have chosen for your habitation shall remain entirely free from the yoke, power, injury, and disturbance of all men, together with its whole forest and mountain, land and water, extending for one league [elsewhere, *leucae*] on every adjoining side, under your unrestricted control and that of your successors, just as it was granted to you by our beloved son Roger, the count, and confirmed by our brother Theodore, bishop of Squillace.

“Let no one within the aforesaid space be permitted, on account of pasture, agriculture, fishing, the cutting of wood, or any other cause, to inflict injury or disturbance upon you or your successors. Rather, possess, dispose of, regulate, and distribute everything according to your will.

“Moreover, if you should require any episcopal service, we grant you free permission by this present decree to have recourse to whichever of the neighboring bishops you prefer. We also decree that the use of the tithes from your own labor or that of your boys (*pueri*) shall belong to you. If any offense should occur on the part of your boys, let all correction of them remain solely in your hands.

“Let no one, without your consent and under any pretext, interfere in matters pertaining to you, so that you may devote yourselves with free minds to the contemplation of almighty God and, by his favor, attain the sweetness of his countenance.

“Certainly, if in the future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or viscount, judge, or any powerful or powerless person, knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our privilege, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not make amends with suitable satisfaction, we decree that he shall be exposed to the danger of losing his rank and office, and by the authority of apostolic power we separate him from the body of Christ and of the Church.

“But peace from God and mercy shall be preserved for those who maintain this privilege, in the present and future ages. Amen. Amen. Amen.

“Given by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the day before the Ides of October, in the first indiction, in the year 1092 of the Lord’s Incarnation, but in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II.”

569. Morkensius, from whose *Chronologico-Diplomatic Treatise on Saint Bruno* these pontifical letters of Urban II have been taken, appends the following note:

> “This Bull of Pope Urban II,” he says, “as it is reported from Italy, has been lost. Nevertheless, a copy of it exists in a very ancient manuscript entitled *Brief of the Privileges of the Calabrian House*. It contains all the privileges written on parchment that were granted to this hermitage from the year 1090 to the year 1200.”

So much for him. But lest anyone think that the chronological indications with which the quoted letters of Urban are dated—namely, the year 1092 and the fifteenth indiction—do not agree with one another, Urban began counting the year from January but the indiction from the beginning of the preceding year, according either to the Greek practice beginning in September or, certainly, from 24 September, the eighth day before the Kalends of October, following the Constantinian or Caesarean indiction among the three commonly recognized systems.

This is clear from various Bulls issued by the pontiff, and especially, to omit the others, from another Bull granted in favor of Saint Bruno in 1098, which will be transcribed below and is dated “at Salerno, in the month of September, indiction 6,” and from another granted by him when he consecrated Elias archbishop at Bari, dated “at Bari, in the year 1089 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate, indiction XIII, on 7 October.”

Since this is so, and since the Constantinopolitan or Greek indiction began from the beginning of September while the Caesarean indiction began on 24 September, the first indiction began in the year 1092. Thus the year and indiction by which the letters transcribed here of Pope Urban II are dated—Urban being in Calabria in this year and month, as Ruinart demonstrates in his Life, no. 116 and following—agree perfectly with one another. The entire chronological difficulty on account of which someone might perhaps declare these letters spurious therefore disappears.

§ XXXIV. What Saint Bruno did after Count Roger’s donation of the Calabrian hermitage, and how Duke Roger later confirmed it and Count Roger defined its boundaries.

570. It appears that Count Roger gave Saint Bruno and his companions not only the Turritan hermitage but also the church dedicated to the Most Holy Mother of God Mary and Saint Stephen, immediately after he had found them dwelling in the cave, as Blomenvenna seems to indicate in the words transcribed above at no. 540. Puteanus and Surius do not disagree with him on this point.

Yet the statement appears contrary to the truth. For that hermitage was given to Saint Bruno and his companions not, as they maintain, in 1095, but in 1090; and at that time it does not yet seem to have contained a church dedicated either to the Most Holy Mother of God or to Saint Stephen.

I reach this conclusion because the church of that hermitage dedicated to Saint Stephen was built only much later, as will become clear from what follows. The church dedicated to the Most Holy Mother of God, likewise, was not consecrated before 1094, as will also become clear from what follows. It therefore appears highly probable, not to say certain, that it was founded under the direction of our Saint himself.

Just as Bruno, when he first entered Chartreuse, took care that a church should be built in honor of God, the Most Holy Mother of God, and Saint John the Baptist, according to what has been stated above, so too, after obtaining the Calabrian hermitage from Roger, he very probably took care that one should be built there.

I am especially confirmed in this opinion by the fact that Count Roger, in the charter transcribed above by which he gave the aforementioned Calabrian hermitage to Saint Bruno and his companions, makes no mention of a church dedicated there to the Most Holy Mother of God. Since the hermitage was almost uncultivated and deserted, and since such a church would have constituted its principal feature, he would very probably have mentioned it if it had already existed at that time.

571. Furthermore, in another charter, which will be transcribed below and which, as will emerge from what follows, was issued in 1099, I find an indication of something that seems to have happened when the Calabrian hermitage was first given to the Saint, and which should therefore be recorded here. In this charter Count Roger speaks of Saint Bruno as follows:

> “I also humbly asked him to deign, for the love of God, to accept in the land of Squillace the ample revenues which I was offering him. He refused to receive them, saying that for this reason he had left his father’s house and mine: so that, detached from worldly affairs, he might serve his God freely. He had been, in my entire household, as though first and foremost.”

From these words it appears that the Saint had spent some time in Count Roger’s household. I think that this occurred after the Turritan hermitage had been given to him, while buildings of whatever kind were being constructed there, especially those that were most necessary. Yet the anonymous author of Book IV of the *Annals of the Carthusians*, still unpublished at that time, although he indeed believes that the Saint spent some time at the court of Count Roger, nevertheless thinks that this happened before the Saint withdrew to the Charterhouse. Hear how he speaks in no. 13 of his work, still unpublished:

> “Those who know only superficially the deeds of Saint Bruno may perhaps think that we were seriously mistaken when we said that the holy Patriarch had once stayed with Roger, Count of Calabria, before his conversion, whereas he is said to have been seen only after he had planted the Major Charterhouse in Calabria. We admit that we are revealing something new, but we assert that it is entirely true on the basis of the letter which the same count gave to Saint Bruno—not merely after his conversion, but when he was already established as master, or prior, of the Calabrian Charterhouse. In it he says that Saint Bruno refused to accept the many gifts offered him by Roger himself, because ‘for this reason he had left his father’s house and mine’—these are Roger’s words in the diploma—‘so that, detached from worldly affairs, he might serve his God freely. He had been, in my entire household, as though first and foremost,’ and so forth. From these words we infer, if we judge correctly, that the blessed man remained at Roger’s court and in his retinue not after, but before his conversion; for the seriousness of the eremitical way of life prevents us from thinking that this could have happened afterward. Nevertheless, we allow the discerning reader to think otherwise.”

572. Thus he. But I do not at all approve the opinion he proposes in these words. Apart from the fact that, as he himself admits, it is wholly novel, it rests on absolutely no foundation. For what he says—that the Saint’s staying at Roger’s court would have been contrary to the seriousness of the eremitical way of life—proves nothing whatever. Why could the Saint not, after obtaining from Count Roger the Calabrian hermitage, have stayed with him for a while until the church and the other buildings most necessary had been constructed, and, when he was pressed to remain there longer, have courteously declined? It seems to me exceedingly likely that this is what happened, especially since I do not see how the words of the preceding charter transcribed above can otherwise be understood in a manner consistent with the truth; nor is the Saint read anywhere in Italy before his entry into the Charterhouse.

I now proceed to the charter by which Duke Roger confirmed the donation of the Calabrian hermitage made by Count Roger. It reads as follows:

> “Roger, by the grace of God duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, to all faithful Christians, present and future, greetings in the Lord.
