We wish your fraternity to know about two men, namely Bruno and Lanvinus, who, inflamed by zeal for holy religion, came with their companions from the regions of Gaul into the land of Calabria, God so disposing. Under my guidance they sought in the aforesaid land a place suited to their purpose. When they found no suitable place with me, they chose to remain between the place called Arena and the town called Stilo. That place Count Roger of Sicily, my uncle and faithful servant, desiring through their prayers to be helped by God, gave them with all his heart. For it belonged to his county by my grant, and he freed it forever from every obligation of servitude and from every forced service, so that none of his people or outsiders—whether strategus or viscount, peasant or soldier, slave or free—might at that place, on account of pasture, agriculture, fishing, hunting, timber, or any other cause, inflict trouble or injury upon the servants of God. Rather, the aforesaid place was to be entirely in their power, so that they might possess, arrange, and dispose of it as they wished.

573. “I, Roger the duke, approve and confirm this donation of that place and the grant of the aforesaid freedom. Since that land belongs to my duchy, I oppose in every way any attempt to subject it to harassment in perpetuity. If anyone should presume to act against the judgment that has been issued and violate our command, let him know with complete certainty that he will either be forever expelled from all our territories or struck down by my sword or that of my successors.

> “Therefore, so that everything granted above may remain firm and unimpaired, I, Roger the duke, and my wife Adela ordered this little charter to be written by one of our clerics, Rodolphus, and we marked it with our seal. In the year 1094 of the Lord’s Incarnation. Indiction I.”

After transcribing this charter in full at the end of his *Dissertation on Saint Bruno*, Morkensius adds that he found a copy of it among the published *Analecta* of the ancient hermits’ lives by Garnefeltius, an alumnus of the Cologne Charterhouse, and that it agreed with the original. Surianus, although he did not think it appropriate to include this document, together with the other public instruments relating to Saint Bruno and the Carthusian cause, in his annotations to the Life of the Saint written by Surius, nevertheless cites it on page 395 and says that it was issued in 1094.

Yet although the charter itself gives this year, it may appear to have been issued not then but in 1093, on the basis of the indiction I appended to it, which corresponds not to 1091 but to 1093. Nor, because the two chronological indications with which the charter or diploma is furnished do not agree with one another, should it be regarded as spurious. For, as was said above, public instruments should not readily be rejected as forged. It may be that an error entered these chronological signs through the fault of the copyists, or that the notary who drafted the instrument mentioned here at Duke Roger’s command reckoned the years of Christ not from the Nativity, as is customary, but according to the Pisan manner, from the Incarnation—since the Incarnation precedes the Nativity by nine months. By this method of reckoning, from 25 March 1093, that is, from the feast of the Annunciation of the Most Holy Mother of God, the year 1094 from the Lord’s Incarnation was already in progress, and it continued through the remainder of that same year 1093 and through the following feast of the Most Holy Mother of God.

574. It might indeed be objected that this method of reckoning the years of Christ was customary for Duke Roger, but that it cannot be proved by any diplomas issued in his name either in Sicily or in Calabria. Yet, apart from the fact that the contrary likewise cannot be proved by such diplomas, it may be that, although in Calabria and Sicily Duke Roger and most others began to reckon the years of Christ from his Nativity—or, if one prefers, from the Kalends of January—the notary who drafted the diploma or instrument in question followed a method of reckoning the years of Christ that was still less customary there.

Certainly, even if Sicily did not depart in its reckoning of the years of Christ from the common practice of others, contrary to what Zanottius claims in chapter 16 of his Life of Saint Bruno, nevertheless, as the distinguished Rocchus Pirrus teaches in *Notitia I of the Church of Palermo*, under the year 1144, a custom persisted in notarial instruments until his own time:

> “They themselves set the beginning of the year on 25 March, although the people, and even the magistrates, reckoned from the Kalends of January. Thus, where we say 18 February of the year 1630, they would say 18 February of the year 1629.”

Just as, therefore, the notaries mentioned by Rocchus reckoned the years of Christ not from the Nativity but, contrary to accepted custom, from the Incarnation while following the Nativity by a three-month interval, so the notary who wrote the charter of Duke Roger quoted above may have begun their reckoning from the Incarnation, or from 25 March, by anticipating the Nativity by nine months, as actually occurred, and by following the Pisan calculation. If he really reckoned the years of Christ in this way, then, according to the common calculation, this charter was granted in 1093 before September, as will be evident to anyone who considers the matter; and thus it would not bear an indiction at variance with the year in which it was actually issued.

Moreover, that charter exists in full in Book IV of the *Annals of the Carthusians*, which had not yet been published. There, as I learn from information sent to me by a Parisian Carthusian whom I have often cited, it is noted as having been issued in 1094, indiction II. But if the original charter was truly furnished with these chronological indications, it has no chronological difficulty whatsoever, since indiction II corresponds to the year 1094; and it follows that the copy lying before Morkensius contained an error.

575. Yet because this writer says that, according to letters received from Italy—or, as I believe, from the Calabrian Charterhouse—he learned that in the original itself indiction I was joined with the year 1094, it is more likely that the anonymous author of the *Annals of the Carthusians* had before him an erroneous copy.

In any event, whether one follows this writer or admits the Pisan method of reckoning the years of Christ in the diploma under discussion, the entire chronological difficulty that seems to trouble it disappears; it should not therefore be rejected on that account. For my part, I have decided to discuss this charter here because, as can readily be inferred from what has already been said, it was more probably issued in 1093, and may perhaps even have preceded another charter issued in that same year, by which Count Roger assigned the boundaries of the Calabrian hermitage previously donated by him to Saint Bruno and further strengthened and enlarged the donation.

I shall also transcribe that other charter in full, both for other reasons and especially so that, in the future, no one may confuse it, following Mabillon’s example, with the charter by which Count Roger first granted that hermitage to the Saint, and so that a precious monument of antiquity may not be withheld from the learned reader. It is composed in the following words:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Roger, by divine mercy count of Calabria and Sicily. Let it be known to all the faithful of Christ and of ourselves, future as well as present, that divine mercy sent to us men of holy religion, namely Bruno and Lanvinus with their companions, who were seeking a solitary place suited to their holy purpose. Rejoicing in their desire and trusting that through the merits and prayers of such men we would be helped by God, we earnestly urged them to choose in our land a suitable place for themselves, where they might prepare dwellings of whatever kind they wished for serving God.

576. “They therefore chose a certain solitary place situated between the place called Arena and the town called Stilo. We accordingly gave this place and everything adjoining it within the space of one league [or *leuca*, here and below] to God, to blessed Mary, and to them and their successors as their property, just as it had been ours, with complete immunity and freedom, together with everything situated within it—lands, forests, waters, pastures, and all other cultivated or uncultivated, movable or immovable things.

> “We further asked the venerable man Goffredus, bishop of Mileto [or Melito], to write a charter confirming this donation, which we also sealed. But afterward, when we had visited the brothers mentioned above in order to commend ourselves to their prayers and had received their fellowship—thanks be to God—we ourselves clearly marked out for them the extent of the aforesaid league by the following boundaries, and ordered the names of the boundaries to be written down for the memory of future generations:

> “On the eastern side, the castle, which is situated on the summit of Mount Stilo; from there it proceeds along the ridge of that same mountain to Malareposta, that is, to the upper hill of the mountain; from there, through the great ravine facing west, it descends as far as the foot of the mountain, where water flows; from there it crosses two streams and a valley in a straight line to the ridge of the mountain lying to the west, toward which the aforesaid ravine faces; from there it runs along the ridge of that same mountain to Brontismenon; from there it crosses the valley directly to the road that comes from Arena and goes to the place called Santa Croce; from there in a straight line [or *directe*, “directly”] to the summit of Mount Embacaht; from there it descends through the ravine, following the course of the water, through the spatula as far as the river Enchinar; from there it ascends that river as far as another river called Alba; from there it ascends that same [or “that”] river to the great ravine which the Greeks call Bachiriache; and it ascends through that ravine as far as the castle from which we began.”

577. “This donation of ours was approved, confirmed by privileges, and fortified with a terrible anathema both by the Apostolic Lord Urban and by Theodorus, bishop of Squillace, in whose diocese the place itself lies. Therefore, commanding we ask, and asking we command, in the name of almighty God, of blessed Mary, of those to whom we have granted this place, and in our own name, that no one ever, whatever his dignity or power, whether one of our people or an outsider, claim for himself anything, great or small, throughout the aforesaid space—not even we ourselves.

> “Let no one ever, for any occasion or reason, inflict injury or trouble upon the brothers who will serve God there, or cause them any disturbance; and let neither they nor their men be compelled to perform any forced service or labor. Let no one, not even we ourselves, be permitted there to cultivate anything, pasture any animal, cut timber, hunt, fish, or do anything whatsoever without the brothers’ permission. Rather, everything contained within the aforesaid space shall be in their power, for them to possess, dispose of, arrange, and distribute according to their will, as God’s possession and their own, immune and free.

> “If anyone should at any time presume to violate any part of this constitution of ours, let him make fitting satisfaction to the brothers living there. If he refuses, let him pay one hundred pounds of gold to the prince of the land, whoever he may be.

> “Therefore, so that this constitution may remain inviolable and entirely firm, with the consent of my wife Adela, the countess, and of our son Goffredus, we made this donation in the presence of good men and marked it with our own seal.

578. “Moreover, I gave Mule and his sons to guard the forest. Given in the meadows of Squillace, where at that time I was staying with an army assembled. In the year 1093 from the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction I, on the Nones of May [7 May].

> “+ Roger, count. + Adela, countess. + Goffredus, son of Count Roger. + William of Hauteville. + William Culchebret. + Gosbertus of Luciaco. + Roger, priest of Stilo. + Bastard.”

Morkensius, from whose frequently cited *Dissertation on Saint Bruno* I also obtained this instrument, adds the following note at its end:

> “I found this charter among the *Analecta* of our George Garnefeltius. But because it had been interpolated here and there, I feared that it might also have been corrupted; therefore I thought it best to compare it with the original”—that is, if I am not mistaken, with a copy of the original, for I do not think that Morkensius had the original itself in hand—“and I did so, marking these interpolations in the margin. From the original hangs, on a white silk cord, a leaden bulla bearing an image of Mary, the Mother of God, holding her Son on her left arm and a bird in her right.”

The interpolations mentioned here by Morkensius, which he says he marked in the margin, are for the most part merely variant readings; I have accordingly also entered them in the margin as such.

579. Furthermore, in his *Dissertation on Saint Bruno*, cited again shortly afterward, in the place where he sets out the chronology of events concerning the Saint, Morkensius writes the following under the year 1093 about Count Roger:

> “In 1093, while visiting the brothers in the hermitage—that is, Saint Bruno and his companions—he earnestly commends himself to their prayers and begs them to make him a participant in their merits. Having obtained his wish, he draws up a charter on 7 May, accurately and sufficiently broadly marking out and delimiting the boundaries of the hermitage; and he causes Roger, Duke of Apulia, his nephew through his brother, to confirm the donations by a diploma issued in the same year—and perhaps, as I have already suggested, even before the aforesaid 7 May.”

Thus he derives what he records here from the two charters just transcribed, one belonging to Duke Roger and the other to Count Roger. And, as will be clear to anyone who considers the matter, what he derives from the latter is entirely correct. For Count Roger himself teaches in the charter just quoted that in 1093 he visited Saint Bruno and his companions “in order to commend himself to their prayers,” and that he “received their fellowship”—for which he also gives thanks to God. From these words it seems rightly to be concluded that Count Roger begged the Saint and his companions to make him a participant in their merits, and that he obtained his desire.

Surianus, however, in his annotations to the Life of Saint Bruno composed by Surius, says on page 221, relying on the words of the same diplomas already quoted that were granted by Count Roger, that in 1093 this prince asked Bruno and his companions “to deign to receive him into their fellowship and to write his name among their names,” and that he actually obtained this. Yet this does not conflict at all with the interpretation Morkensius applies to the words of the diplomas granted by Roger. Although for the moment I find it permissible to call the matter into doubt, it very probably did take place, as seems inferable from the diploma for the foundation of the Latin episcopate in the city of Squillace, still to be cited below, preserved in Ughelli’s *Italia sacra*, vol. IX, col. 426, in which Count Roger calls Lanvinus “his brother.”

580. As for the diploma by which the donations previously made to Saint Bruno by Duke Roger were confirmed, with Count Roger acting as Morkensius says, it seems very doubtful to me whether Duke Roger granted that charter of his own accord or at the urging of his uncle Roger. For, as is sufficiently clear from what was said above, he was also very well disposed toward Saint Bruno and therefore needed no prompting to do him a kindness.

Moreover, lest anyone perhaps be troubled by a doubt concerning the charter of Count Roger transcribed immediately above because it is recorded as having been issued by the count while he was staying with an army in the meadows of Squillace, Bohemond, the brother of Duke Roger, was in Calabria in 1093. When he had falsely heard that Duke Roger had died, he occupied several castles belonging to him in Calabria. Enraged by this, Count Roger ordered his soldiers to attack Bohemond, and expelled him from all Calabria.

This is what the often-mentioned—and henceforth to be mentioned again—contemporary author Geoffrey Malaterra, a monk of the Benedictine order, says in Book IV, chapter 20 of his *Sicilian History*, which he composed at the command of Count Roger himself, as Muratori explains in his preface to the work, which he included in volume V of the *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*. Nothing therefore prevents us from believing that Count Roger, having assembled an army, stayed in 1093 in the meadows of Squillace, as is asserted in the charter under discussion.

Indeed, since it cannot be doubted that the prince really was there, and since Squillace is situated not far from the Turritan hermitage of Calabria, it could easily also have happened that Count Roger visited Saint Bruno and his companions, commended himself to their prayers, and granted them the charter in question—something which, according to what has been said, he himself further states that he did in the same charter.

Since this is so, and since the chronological indications attached to the charter—that is, the year and the indiction—agree with one another, while nothing else appears from any quarter that militates against the instrument’s authenticity, there is no reason to regard it as suspect, much less as spurious. I therefore turn to other matters concerning our Saint.

## § XXXV. The Saint arranges for the church constructed in the Calabrian hermitage to be consecrated with great ceremony, and increasingly finds Count Roger favorably disposed toward him.

581. When Bruno saw that the church which, as was said, he had caused to be built there as soon as he had obtained the Turritan hermitage of Calabria from Count Roger, in honor of God, the Most Holy Mother of God, and Saint John the Baptist, had been brought to completion, he very probably approached Count Roger to arrange for its solemn consecration.

Whatever the precise circumstances, that church was consecrated with the greatest ceremony by Aicherus, archbishop of Palermo, with five bishops assisting; and the distinguished Count Roger not only arranged for this to happen but also enriched the sacred building on that occasion with a considerable number of gifts bestowed upon Saint Bruno, as is clear from a charter granted by the same count at that time in favor of the church and Saint Bruno.

Ughelli, in volume IX of *Italia sacra*, col. 425, transcribes only part of this charter or diploma, and Rocchus Pirrus does the same in his *Notitia of the Church of Catania*. But so that I may not withhold from the eyes of the curious reader a venerable monument of antiquity which I have not yet had the opportunity to see printed and made publicly available in its entirety, I transcribe it here in full from Morkensius’s recension.

582. It reads as follows:

> “In the name of the eternal God and our Savior Jesus Christ. In the year 1094 from the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction II, when I, Roger, count of Calabria and Sicily, for the love of God and for the remedy of my soul, and for the salvation of the soul of my brother Robert Guiscard, most glorious duke of Apulia and Calabria, and for the remedy of the souls of my brothers and of all my relatives and wives, wished to have the church of the hermitage dedicated in honor of God, blessed Mary, and blessed John the Baptist—the church situated between Arena and the town called Stilo, in the territory of that town of Stilo—by the venerable and most holy Fathers, the archbishop of Palermo and the bishops of Melito [or Mileto], Tropea, Nicastro, Catania, and Squillace, with those same most holy Fathers approving, I gave to blessed Father Bruno, master of that hermitage, for himself and his successors, the monastery of Saint Mary of Arsasia with all its appurtenances, wherever they may be. From this day forward and forever I exempted that same church, or monastery, of Arsasia from every temporal service and from the tower-service to which it had been liable to my town of Stilo, so that the church of the hermitage and the brothers might possess it forever in peace, without any claim and without temporal service, with every *tremari* and *placario* removed, and with all harassment of these kinds removed.

583. “I gave these endowments to the aforesaid church of the Bosco and to the brothers serving God there as a dowry, with the advice and approval of my wife Adela and the consent of my son Goffredus and my son Malgerius.

> “The monastery of Arsasia was my chapel, exempt from episcopal jurisdiction by the Holy Roman Church. I caused this to be made known to the aforesaid archbishop and bishops, who are witnesses of this donation, as are Gosbertus of Luciaco, Paganus of Gorgis, Roger Bonellus [or Tonellus], and Fulco, my chaplain, who wrote this. I made these grants with the testimony of the witnesses written above. The following are the boundaries and limits of Saint Mary of Arsasia, namely, from the oak tree, and so forth.”

Here Morkensius says:

> “The description of the boundaries follows, which I omit because it contributes little or nothing to our subject, and I merely transcribe the places enclosed by this boundary.”

They include two enclosed hamlets, namely Saint Andrew and Roseto, free and exempt from every communal obligation owed by my hamlets of the town of Stilo; likewise the place called with the two hamlets Vingi and Buaungi, similarly free and exempt from every communal obligation owed by my hamlets of the aforesaid town of Stilo; likewise the church of Saint Fantinus, exempt from the jurisdiction of the bishop of Gerace [or Girace], which belongs to the same church of Arsasia and is situated in the territory of Agroteria, within the district of Gerace [or Girace], with all its rights and appurtenances; likewise the hamlet of Arunchi in the territory of the city of Squillace, with all its rights and appurtenances, just as that church of Arsasia has been accustomed to hold and possess them.

584. “I give and grant these places, noted above [or ‘previously noted’], as a dowry for the same church, to Father Bruno and his successors, with all their rights, watercourses, mills, groves and trees, cultivated and uncultivated lands, mines of copper and iron and of every metal, pastures, and all rights which I and my court have hitherto been accustomed to possess, so that no one may have anything there except the aforesaid church of the hermitage, just as from that time no one had any right there except me.

> “I also grant to the same church of the hermitage, throughout the remainder of my land, free use of the copper and iron mines and free pasture on that same land for the animals of the church, of its keepers, and also of those who live in the aforesaid hamlets. I further grant that the aforesaid church of the hermitage may have dependants in the aforesaid hamlets and places which I have given to the same church.

> “Let no one presume to pursue or possess any right in the aforesaid places, either in his own name or in mine or that of my heirs and successors—not even I myself. Rather, let everything be preserved solid and intact for the same church, since it is a small thing, for the love of God, to give his servants something, when he has bestowed many things upon me with a generous hand.

> “But if any person—my son, or any heir or successor—should annul this gift or privilege of mine, let him pay one hundred pounds of gold to me, to my descendants, or to the Roman Church, unless he makes fitting satisfaction, and let him be subject to the condemnation of the brothers serving God there and to perpetual damnation.”

585. “These things were enacted in the month of August, when I had returned from the expedition which I had undertaken against William and from the siege of Castrum-Villa. I ordered, commanded, and caused this privilege of mine to be secured with my hanging seal for perpetual validity.

> “+ Roger, count. + Adela, countess. + Goffredus, son of the lord count. + Malgerius, son of Count Roger. + Paganus of Gorgis. + Gosbertus of Luciaco. + Roger Bonellus [or Tonellus]. + I, Fulco, chaplain of the lord Count Roger, wrote this privilege at his command and subscribed my name.”

I also have the note which Morkensius appends to the charter he transcribed:

> “I found this constitution of the church of the hermitage, also interpolated, among the *Analecta* of our Garnefeltius. I transcribed it again after checking it against the original, and entered in the margin the interpolations marked by an asterisk. The seal is lead, as above, and hangs from a saffron-colored cord.”

The interpolations mentioned again by this writer are almost entirely somewhat variant readings; I have likewise added them here in the margin.

There are, however, other matters to be noted concerning this instrument. First, the chronological indications it bears at the beginning—that is, the year 1094 and indiction II—agree perfectly with one another. Nor is there any reason for anyone to be troubled by the statement at the end that it was issued after Count Roger had returned from the expedition undertaken against William and from the siege of Castrum-Villa.

586. For, according to Geoffrey Malaterra in Book IV, chapters 21 and following of his *Sicilian History*, William of Grantavul, or, as others write, of Grantemanil, who was married to Mabilia, the sister of Duke Roger, in 1093, like Bohemond mentioned above, falsely believing—after hearing the same unfounded report—that Duke Roger had died, occupied various castles and towns belonging to that prince, his wife Mabilia’s brother, including Castrum-Villa.

When, despite having learned that the report was false, he refused to return these places to their rightful lord, claiming a right to them through his wife Mabilia, Duke Roger made war upon him. Together with Count Roger, his uncle, who had joined him, he besieged and captured Castrum-Villa.

But another difficulty arises in that diploma of Count Roger, one that may perhaps make it seem suspect to some. For, as I have shown above, Count Roger had no children at all by his first wife Judith, also called Delicia, and by his second wife, named Elemburga or Eremburga—who had already died in 1089—he had produced only one son, besides several daughters. How, then, or who was this Malgerius, who is subscribed to the diploma quoted above as the son of Count Roger?

Roger certainly does not seem to have fathered him by any of his legitimate wives. What, then? Shall we call him illegitimate? Yet Geoffrey Malaterra stands in the way. In Book IV, chapter 18 of his *Sicilian History*, speaking of Jordan, who was an illegitimate son of Count Roger—as the same author teaches in Book III, chapter 36—he writes as follows:

> “Jordan . . . the count’s son, beloved by all on account of his valor, whom many suspected would become the count’s heir, since he had no other male child—for Goffredus was already afflicted by elephantiasis, which did not lessen the grief—was struck by a fever at Syracuse, a city under his own authority.”

587. Since, therefore, as is understood from these words of Geoffrey, when Jordan, his illegitimate or bastard son, lay ill with fever at Syracuse—a sickness which the distinguished Malaterra says in the immediately cited chapter of Book IV occurred in 1092—Count Roger had no other male offspring besides the aforesaid Jordan and Goffredus, it follows that Malgerius, who subscribes the charter just transcribed, issued by Count Roger in 1094, was neither an illegitimate nor a bastard son of that count.

It remains, therefore, either that Elemburga, Count Roger’s second wife, or Adelasia, his third, was a widow when she married him and had Malgerius from a previous marriage; or that this Malgerius, who signed his name as the count’s son, had been lifted by him from the sacred font or had even been adopted as a son; or finally that, besides the daughters attributed to Count Roger by the *Sicilian Genealogy*, inserted by Cangius in his annotations to Anna Comnena, and by Malaterra’s genealogical tree of the Norman princes prefixed to his *Sicilian History* in Muratori’s fifth volume of the *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, Count Roger had at least one further daughter, and that this Malgerius had married her.

In any event, since it could have happened on one of these grounds that this Malgerius was called the son of Count Roger, there is no reason to regard the charter of this prince transcribed here as spurious or suspect merely because the name “Malgerius, son of the count” is attached to it.

Something more may seem to count against it: the title “Blessed,” which it applies to the Saint (see no. 582). Nevertheless, even if that title were absent from the original charter and had perhaps been added imprudently by a more recent copyist to a copy out of veneration for the Saint, it is not wholly incredible that Count Roger himself, who regarded Bruno as a saint—as will become clearer from what follows—could have bestowed the title “Blessed” upon him while he was still alive.

I therefore would not on that account dare to reject as certainly spurious this instrument, which otherwise bears no signs of fabrication, especially since everything it relates about the consecration of the Turritan church and the time when that consecration took place agrees with the truth.

### 588

So that the learned reader may see that I am asserting nothing here contrary to the truth, I wish to transcribe from Morkensius’s recension the public instrument preserved by Rocchus Pirrus in *Sicilia sacra*, by Ughellus in volume IX of *Italia sacra*, column 425, and by other writers. For Alcherius himself, archbishop of Palermo, who celebrated that solemnity with great ceremony and pomp, testifies that this church was consecrated in the presence of five bishops—namely, those of Malta, Tropea, Nicastro, Catania, and Squillace—and the monument supports the charter of Count Roger that was cited above, in which the same thing is reported. It is worded as follows:

> “In the year of Our Lord Jesus Christ 1094, in the month of August, on the feast of the Assumption of Blessed Mary, I, Alcherius Hic . . ., archbishop of Palermo, consecrated this church in honor of God and of Blessed Mary the Virgin, and of Blessed John the Baptist, in the presence of the bishops of Malta, Tropea, Nicastro, and Squillace, together with Lord Roger, count of Calabria, Countess Adelaide, Master Bruno and Lanvinus, and the other Fathers assisting, and in the presence of good men.
>
> “I, Alcherius, archbishop of Palermo. I, Tristerius, bishop of Tropea, was present. I, Angerius, bishop of Catania. I, Theodore, bishop of Squillace. I, N., bishop of Nicastro, was present.”

Since the charter of Count Roger transcribed above, in which the consecration of the Turritan church is mentioned as something soon to occur, is dated in August (see no. 585), while the testimony of Alcherius, archbishop of Palermo, just cited assigns the fifteenth of August to this consecration, the chronological indications with which both instruments are dated agree perfectly.

### 589

Yet although the testimony of Alcherius transcribed here by Morkensius, like the cited charter of Count Roger, says that five bishops were present at the consecration—namely, those of Malta, Tropea, Nicastro, Catania, and Squillace—it nevertheless presents as subscribers not five but only four bishops who attended the solemnity: those of Tropea, Catania, Squillace, and Nicastro, with the bishop of Malta omitted. It follows that either a copy of that testimony, corrupted in the episcopal subscriptions, lay before Morkensius, or he himself made an error in transcribing it—especially since the testimony, both in Rocchus Pirrus’s *Notice of the Church of Catania* under the year 1094, no. 10, and in Ughellus, volume IX of *Italia sacra*, column 425, has not only the four bishops just mentioned but also the bishop of Malta subscribing, as follows:

> “+ I, Archerius Nic . . . ., archbishop of Palermo.  
> + I, Tristanus, bishop of Tropea, was present.  
> + I, An., bishop of Catania, was present.  
> + I, Theodore, bishop of Squillace, was present.  
> + I, Goffridus, bishop of Malta, was present.  
> + I, Henry, bishop of Nicastro, was present.”

Morotius, who reproduces the same monument in part VI of his *Chronological Theatre of the Sacred Order of Carthusians*, under the year 1090, likewise does not list the bishop of Malta among its subscribing bishops, contrary to Camillus Tutinus, who nevertheless says there that he took the monument from Morotius.

### 590

I therefore think that Morkensius derived the testimony of Alcherius transcribed here from Morotius; consequently, the omission just mentioned must be attributed to Morotius. I am especially confirmed in this opinion by the fact that the following words—

> “Who granted to all truly penitent and confessed persons . . . forty days of true indulgence . . . in the year . . . of his archbishopric,”

—which in the monument at the places cited immediately above in Ughellus and Rocchus Pirrus follow the words “in the presence of good men,” and which Morotius omitted, although they appear in Camillus Tutinus, are likewise omitted by Morkensius, who does not disclose from where he took the monument under discussion.

Moreover, in the various already mentioned copies of the testimony given by Alcherius, variant readings occur not only in the two matters just explained, in which Morotius and Morkensius differ from Rocchus, Ughellus, and Tutinus, but also in other matters, where Ughellus and Rocchus differ from Morotius, Tutinus, and Morkensius, and where those two themselves differ from each other both in the wording of the monument and in the names of the bishops who subscribed it.

To mention the principal variants and pass over the rest: where Morotius and Morkensius read in the body of the testimony “with Master Bruno and Lanvinus and the other Fathers assisting” (Tutinus has “Brothers”), Ughellus, omitting the conjunction *and* after the word *Bruno* and substituting a comma, reads:

> “with Master Bruno, Lanvinus B., and the other hermit brothers assisting”;

while Rocchus, also omitting the comma, has:

> “with Master Bruno Lanvinus and the other hermit brothers assisting.”

But this latter reading is plainly beyond all doubt erroneous.

### 591

This, above all, led Rocchus to make Bruno and Lanvinus incorrectly into one and the same person. At the place cited above, in the testimony of Alcherius that he himself transcribes, he observes as follows:

> “From these words, *e Magistro Brunone Lanvino*, you will easily understand that the diploma which we reported in the *Notice of Messina* under the year 1094, no. VIII, was sent by Pope Paschal II to this Bruno. For in it one reads: ‘Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Lanvinus, greeting and apostolic blessing, concerning the case of the bishop of Messina,’ etc.”

Of the bishops subscribing the testimony, the archbishop of Palermo who issued it is called Alcherius by Tutinus, Morotius, and Morkensius, but Archerius by Ughellus and Rocchus, with a change in one letter of the name. A further addition is made: after the word *Hic*, Morotius—and after him Morkensius—supply part of the name in the charter’s text, represented by “Nic . . .” in Ughellus and “Nico . . .” in Rocchus.

Since, however, Rocchus himself calls that archbishop Alcherius in the *Notice of the Church of Palermo*, under the year 1094, no. 6, in a diploma that Roger, count of Sicily and Calabria, gave to the church of Palermo in 1095, I think that his name should be given as Alcherius rather than Archerius, as it is by Tutinus and those who follow him, Morotius and Morkensius.

As for the fragment of the name, “Nic.” or “Nico.,” which is found only in the subscription of the charter in Rocchus and Ughellus, Tutinus may perhaps have thought it should be omitted because the complete word was not present. But to inform the reader of whose name it is probably a part, Rocchus, at the place cited immediately above—where he states that Alcherius occupied the archiepiscopal seat of the church of Palermo from 1083 until at least 1099—thinks it may be said that Alcherius was perhaps given the designation “Nicodemus,” either as a second name or as a surname; and the evidence he adduces there makes this sufficiently probable.

### 592

Among the bishops subscribing the testimony concerning the consecration of the Turritan church, immediately after Alcherius, archbishop of Palermo, appears the bishop of Tropea, or, as others write it, Tropeia, in Further Calabria. In the places cited above, Ughellus and Rocchus call him Tristanus; Morotius and Morkensius call him Tristerius, although Tutinus calls him Tristenus.

Ughellus, in volume X of *Italia sacra*, column 450, writes the following about this bishop:

> “Justegus or Justeyrus, and Tusteius, who is also Tristanus, was the first of the Latins to assume the episcopal office of the church of Tropea, around the year of Our Lord 1094.”

After some intervening material, he adds that a diploma granted in 1094 by Roger, duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, to the church of Tropea names Justegus as the man who was then its bishop.

The bishop who follows the bishop of Tropea among those subscribing the testimony is designated by Ughellus and Rocchus only by the first two letters of his name, as the bishop of Catania. Tutinus calls him Augerius, and Morotius, who follows him, does likewise; Morkensius calls him Angerius.

It is clear from what Rocchus Pirrus brings forward concerning him in the *Notice of the Church of Catania*, beginning in the year 1091, that this bishop’s proper name was Ansgerius and that he held the see from 1091 until the year 1124.

As for the bishops of Squillace and Malta, whose subscriptions immediately follow that of the bishop of Catania, the name of the former—who, as I shall show below against Ughellus, died in 1095 or the following year—is rendered everywhere in the same way. Nor does the latter, whose subscription is omitted by Morotius and Morkensius following him, undergo any variation in Rocchus, Ughellus, and Tutinus, by whom he is listed.

### 593

It should also be noted that this man was bishop not of the most famous island of Malta, but of Malta—or rather Militensis—a city of Further Calabria, as is clear from what Rocchus Pirrus records in the *Notice of the Church of Malta* immediately before the year 1089, and what Ughellus writes in volume I of *Italia sacra*, in the section on the bishops of Malta, column 942 and following.

I now come at last to the bishop of Nicastro, who was the last of all to subscribe Alcherius’s testimony concerning the consecration of the Turritan church. The evidence cited by Ughellus in volume IX of *Italia sacra*, column 402 and the two following columns, suggests that he held the see from 1094 until at least 1112. Rocchus and Ughellus call him Henry.

Although Tutinus, and after him Morotius and Morkensius, list him among the bishops subscribing the testimony soon to be mentioned again, he is not identified by either the name Henry or any other name, because Tutinus perhaps found no name in the copy of the testimony that lay before him. Thus Rocchus Pirrus and Ughellus differ considerably from Tutinus and those who follow him in their reading.

Nevertheless, although this is so, since all of them agree perfectly concerning both the year 1094 and the testimony that the consecration of the Turritan church was performed on the feast of the Most Holy Mother of God assumed into heaven, and since nothing else appears to make that monument, which according to what has been said is read in such varied forms by different writers, suspect or spurious, it should by no means be rejected on account of the variant readings in the various copies, which are for the most part merely errors of copyists or scribes.

From this, and partly also from the diploma of Count Roger just cited, it follows that there can be no doubt that the dedication of that church—which Tutinus incorrectly confuses with the church of Saint Mary of Arsafia on page 7 of his *Prospectus*, as is also clear from this document—took place both in the year 1094, as already stated, and on the feast itself of the Most Holy Mother of God assumed into heaven.

## § XXXVI. Whether the saint attended the Council of Piacenza, at which he composed the Preface concerning the Blessed Virgin, and why, if he did, he did not return after its celebration to the Grande Chartreuse

### 594

After the saint’s withdrawal from the papal court to the Turritan hermitage of Calabria, two councils are known from contemporary writers and monuments to have been celebrated by Pope Urban II not far from that region before the year 1095: one at Benevento in Campania, and another at Troia in Apulia.

At the first, which was celebrated in 1091 against the antipope Guibert and his followers, as Berthold, priest of Constance and a contemporary writer, testifies in his appendix to Hermann the Lame, so many bishops and abbots assembled—as it is read in an old Roman codex from which Labbe published its canons—“that their number could hardly be recorded.”

Nor was the number of fathers who assembled at the second council small, as is confirmed by the title of that council, brought by Labbe into volume X of the *Councils* from ancient manuscript codices. It reads:

> “In the year 1093 of the Incarnation of the Lord, on the fifth Ides of March, a council of nearly seventy-five bishops and twelve abbots assembled at Troia in Apulia.”

It seems probable for this reason alone that Urban summoned Bruno from his solitude to these two councils, celebrated not very far from Calabria and from the hermitage in which he was living: since Bruno was already residing in the Calabrian hermitage, that pontiff very likely summoned him from there from time to time, wishing to use so prudent a man in councils dealing with matters of greater importance, as I have already shown above.

### 595

But was the saint also summoned by Pope Urban to the celebrated and very large council held in 1095, as the priest Berthold, cited again shortly below, testifies, at Piacenza, somewhat farther from Calabria—and likewise to the gathering held shortly before it at Guastalla, or, as others write, Guardistalla or Ewardastalla, at the end of 1094, which seems to have been not so much a council as a preparation for the Council of Piacenza, since nothing is recorded as having been decreed there?

Blomenvenna and all the other biographers of the saint, who are later than the fifteenth century, unanimously affirm that Bruno attended the Council of Piacenza, at which the antipope Guibert and the emperor Henry were again deprived of ecclesiastical communion. They maintain that from the saint’s departure from the Carthusian house until the year 1095 he remained with Urban, and that only then, after refusing the archbishopric of Reggio to which he had been elected, did he leave the papal court and withdraw to the Turritan hermitage of Calabria.

Although I cannot support their assertion with any sufficiently ancient testimony, I do not think it at all improbable. It could easily have happened that the pontiff who, as has been shown, had probably wished the saint to attend the councils at Troia and Benevento summoned him from the Calabrian solitude also to Piacenza, where matters of the greatest importance were to be discussed.

Ruinartius says in no. 171 of his frequently cited *Life of Pope Urban II*:

> “Nearly all the commonly circulated authors relate that Saint Bruno, the father of the Carthusians, was present at that synod”—namely, the Council of Piacenza—“as counselor to the pontiff, and I have no intention of attacking this opinion. But I cannot agree with those who assert that at that time the pontiff offered this holy man the archbishopric of Reggio in Calabria.”

Thus he does not differ greatly, as it appears, from the opinion that the saint probably attended the Council of Piacenza, though I think that the archbishopric of Reggio was not offered to him there.

### 596

There are, however, also those who maintain that Bruno not only attended that council but also composed the tenth of the Prefaces customarily recited at Mass—the one concerning Blessed Mary—which was promulgated at that council.

Surianus is the first to hold this opinion, in his notes on the Life of Saint Bruno compiled by Surius, pages 192 and following, and then in his chronological arrangement of the same Life, page 396.

I transcribe here all his words, especially because in the first passage he chiefly attempts to prove that the saint attended the Council of Piacenza. In the earlier place he writes:

> “It is considered a difficulty of equal weight that he”—namely Saint Bruno—“is said to have attended the Council of Piacenza, which was celebrated in 1095, since the charters concerning the donation” of the Turritan hermitage by Count Roger, “made in 1090 and confirmed by Urban II two years later, contradict this. Yet this too is not without foundation, since Antonius Beuter, the Valencian chronicler and distinguished investigator of antiquity, asserts it not obscurely in his little book entitled *On the Ceremonies of the Mass*, when he says that the Preface, which is the tenth, concerning the Blessed Virgin Mary, was then composed by him. Therefore he could still have remained with the pontiff around the time of the Council of Piacenza and nevertheless have presided over his Turritan monastery. For that this was then customary and usual is proved by various records, especially those of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, in which it is read that he was absent from Clairvaux for six years and more, undertaking various labors and journeys on behalf of the Apostolic See; to say nothing of others who were summoned from the most remote parts of the world to extinguish the common fire of the schism.”

In the later passage he writes:

> “Antonius Beuter, the Valencian chronicler and remarkable observer of antiquity, reports in his book, which he published on the parts and ceremonies of the Mass, that the Preface concerning the Blessed Virgin Mary was composed by a Carthusian at this council, which Urban held at Piacenza. Who was that man, if not Saint Bruno, whose wisdom Pope Paschal praises in a certain diploma and says that he possessed great authority with the Apostolic See?”

### 597

Thus far Surianus, citing only Antonius Beuter in support of the opinion that the Preface concerning the Blessed Virgin Mary was composed by Saint Bruno at the time of the Council of Piacenza.

But since this writer, being separated by a very long interval of time from the age of our saint and of the Council of Piacenza, cannot by his authority alone establish the matter beyond doubt, we must chiefly examine where he obtained this information.

Because Beuter’s work would be necessary in order that I might do this more conveniently and certainly, and because it is not at hand, Morkensius opportunely comes to our aid in his manuscript *Chronological-Diplomatic Dissertation on Saint Bruno*, where he writes:

> “In the following year, 1094, while the followers of Guibert, as the same Berthold testifies, still held the Tower of Crescentius, and Urban was by no means safe from his enemies, he left the City for Lombardy. At Guastalla, on the River Po, having assembled a gathering of sacred prelates, he took counsel concerning the needs of the Church, and there published the Preface of the Blessed Virgin Mary. A manuscript catalogue of the Roman pontiffs in Papebrochius, under Urban; Sigonius and Leander Alberti in their description of Lombardy, under Guardistalla. Antonius Beuter found that Preface, which is the tenth, composed by a Carthusian, among ancient monuments in his book on the parts of the Mass; yet he wishes it to have been promulgated at the Council of Piacenza, perhaps because it was repeated at that later council, as the more celebrated one.”

Beuter therefore obtained from ancient monuments his assertion that the Preface concerning the Blessed Virgin was composed by a Carthusian. But since Morkensius does not say how ancient those monuments were—most probably because Beuter did not record it—I still consider it highly doubtful whether that Preface was truly composed by a Carthusian, as Beuter learned from those monuments, since the monuments that lay before Beuter may perhaps have been of very uncertain authority.

### 598

Furthermore, even if we were to grant for the moment that the ancient monuments from which Beuter learned this were altogether trustworthy and of proven authority, it still would not follow that the tenth Preface, which concerns the Blessed Virgin Mary, was composed by Saint Bruno.

For Beuter reports from the monuments he cites that it was composed not by Saint Bruno but by “a Carthusian,” without determining whether that man was the saint or someone else.

It may indeed be replied that no other Carthusian besides Bruno attended the Council of Piacenza. But if the saint really attended that council, as is probable from what has been said, it appears highly probable, indeed almost certain, that he had a companion with him. Given this, there is no reason to think that the work should be attributed to Bruno rather than to any other Carthusian who accompanied him to the Council of Piacenza, although Bruno, as a man of the highest learning, would have been most suitable for composing it.

Besides, the work would not have required such great learning; and the saint himself, as he teaches in his letter to Raoul le Verd, provost of the church of Reims, which I shall transcribe below, had several well-educated companions—or, if you prefer, disciples—with him in the Turritan hermitage of Calabria. Thus the Preface could have been composed by one of these whom the saint brought with him to the said council.

There are, however, those who maintain that the Preface was the work neither of Bruno nor of any other Carthusian, but of Pope Urban II himself. Among the first to hold this view are Cardinal Bona, book II of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 10, no. 3, and Ruinartius in his Life of that pontiff, no. 176.

I transcribe all the words of the latter, especially because they contain ancient sources—whether testimonies or monuments—from which he derived what he records here.

### 599

They read as follows:

> “A tradition has been received among the commonly circulated authors that Pope Urban added to the nine ancient Prefaces at this council”—namely, the Council of Piacenza—“the tenth, which concerns Blessed Mary. This is expressly stated in an old manuscript codex of the Remigian archmonastery at Reims, written about five hundred years ago. After a decree attributed under the name of Pope Pelagius concerning the nine Prefaces has been reported, the same hand adds these words: ‘The tenth was added at the Council of Piacenza celebrated under Pope Urban.’
>
> “They say that the matter occurred in this way. While the pontiff was celebrating the sacred rites at Saint Mary’s in Campania, a temple of very ancient piety, praying that God would bring the council’s undertaking to a good outcome, and while he was already offering the Preface, he suddenly burst forth, by divine inspiration, into these most sweet words, to the wonder of the people:
>
> “‘And to praise, bless, and proclaim you in veneration of Blessed Mary the Virgin, who conceived your Only-Begotten Son through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit and, with the glory of virginity remaining, poured forth into this world the eternal light, Jesus Christ our Lord, through whom,’ etc.
>
> “The universal Church afterward approved this Preface by adopting it, and retains it even now. Some wish it to have been issued by Blessed Bruno; but Pandulph expressly relates in his Life of Urban that it was composed by Urban himself—not at Piacenza, but at the synod of Ewardastalla, as we have already noted above, no. 168. Petrus Maria Campus has more about this Preface in book XII of his *History of Piacenza*, under the year 1095; since his accounts are not sufficiently consistent, I have not thought it appropriate to report them here.”

### 600

Thus far Ruinartius.

From these words it is understood that the Preface concerning the Blessed Virgin Mary was composed not certainly at the Council of Piacenza, but either at that council, if the Remigian codex he cites is to be trusted, or at Ewardastalla, that is, Guastalla, if Pandulph is to be believed.

Whether it was composed at the one or, as I consider more probable, at the other of these two councils, the opinion of those who make our saint its author may still be true, since absolutely nothing prevents us from believing that he attended both the council at Guastalla, which was celebrated at the end of 1094 as has been said, and the Council of Piacenza, which followed Guastalla not long afterward.

But since the words cited by Ruinartius from the Remigian codex offer nothing whatever to suggest that the Preface was composed by Urban himself, the main point now to be examined is first whether Pandulph, who asserts that it was made by Urban, deserves unquestioned credence; and second, whether his assertion is so clear and distinct that no doubt remains that he intended to signify that the Preface was composed by Urban himself.

That Pandulph is worthy of unquestioned belief does not seem doubtful. Although Muratorius, in volume III of the *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, page 274 verso, rightly teaches with Pagius that he was different from Pandulph Masca, whom Lucius III, elevated to the pontificate in 1181, enrolled in the senate of the cardinal Fathers, he was nevertheless contemporary with Pope Urban II or at least nearly so, as is clear from what Muratorius says about this same writer in the place cited. He writes as follows:

> “Since the very rich treasury of the Ambrosian Library contains Lives of certain supreme pontiffs written by Pandulph of Pisa, my palatine colleagues and I thought it most useful to include them also in the present collection.”

### 601

> “They begin with Gregory VII and end with Alexander III, and they proceed from a writer who was alive in those same times and committed those events to writing. We already knew, on the testimony of Felinus, Onuphrius Panvinius, Ludovicus a Sancto Carolo, and others, that Pandulph had composed such Lives; and the great illuminator of ecclesiastical history, Baronius, had also transferred much from them into his *Annals*. Indeed, in 1638 Constantine Caietanus printed and annotated at Rome the Life of Gelasius II, written by that same Pandulph, from which we learn that this writer, enrolled in the ecclesiastical service in 1118, lived in the Roman Curia.”

There therefore appears to be no reason to doubt that Pandulph deserves credence in what he reports concerning Pope Urban II.

Let us now examine whether he says so clearly and explicitly that the Preface concerning the Blessed Virgin Mary was composed by that pontiff that he implies Urban did it on his own initiative.

His words bearing on this matter, in Papebrochius’s *May Propylaeum*, in the *Chronological-Historical Attempt toward a Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs*, under Urban II, and in Muratorius, volume III of the *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, page 352, are these:

> “Pope Urban II celebrated six councils: one at Clermont; another at Guardestalla in Lombardy, where he composed the Preface concerning the feasts of the Blessed Virgin Mary; another at Melfi; another at Rome in the church of Saint Peter; another at Troia in Apulia; and another at Piacenza.”

Thus far Pandulph.

From these words Ruinartius appears to think that Pandulph expressly asserts that Pope Urban II composed the Preface under discussion on his own initiative. And it must indeed be said that Urban composed it on his own initiative if the matter occurred in the way in which it is said to have occurred—as reported in the words of Ruinartius cited above in no. 599.

### 602

But to answer first the point placed second: apart from the fact that those who narrate the matter in this way—especially Petrus Maria Campus, whom Ruinartius cites—are all later writers and therefore cannot establish it beyond doubt, they place the event at Piacenza (see again the words of Ruinartius in no. 599 and Petrus Maria Campus at the place cited), in such a way that it could not even have begun elsewhere. They therefore contradict Pandulph so strongly—for he says that the same thing occurred at Guastalla, or Guardestalla—that the two accounts cannot even be brought into agreement by the method proposed above by Morkensius.

As for the words just transcribed, in which Pandulph appeared to Ruinartius expressly to state that the Preface concerning the Blessed Virgin was composed by Urban himself: since kings, emperors, pontiffs, and other persons in positions of authority are often said to have done things that were not done on their own initiative but merely by their command, I do not know whether anyone will, on the basis of Pandulph’s words, unquestionably attribute that Preface to Pope Urban as something he composed personally.

As far as I am concerned, since the matter stands thus, and since nothing in what has been said prevents us from believing that our saint attended not only the Council of Piacenza but also the Council of Guastalla—at the time of which the Preface concerning the Blessed Virgin was composed, as the quoted authority of Pandulph makes at least highly probable, and which I judge preferable to the Remigian codex cited above by Ruinartius—I would not dare unhesitatingly to deny the work to Bruno, although I strongly doubt that it is truly his work, both because of what has already been said and because I consider the opinion that attributes it to Pope Urban as his own work much more probable. The quoted words of Pandulph support that opinion when they are taken in their more natural and obvious sense.

Moreover, that Preface may perhaps be older than both Urban and Bruno. See the *Writers of the Literary History of France*, volume VIII, pages 533 and 553.

But it is enough to have discussed these matters: the tenth of the Prefaces customarily recited at Mass, which some attribute to the saint, and his presence at the councils of Guastalla and Piacenza.

Let us now examine where Bruno went after the Council of Piacenza, which, according to what has been said, he perhaps attended; why he did not then return to the Grande Chartreuse; and what he did—or rather, is reported to have done—at that time.

### 603

All the writers who assert that the saint attended the Council of Piacenza unanimously affirm that he immediately returned from that council to the Turritan hermitage of Calabria.

Yet they are far from agreeing among themselves concerning the reason why the saint then went to Calabria and did not return to the Grande Chartreuse. Some of them, including Puteanus, Blomenvenna, and Surius, maintain that he did so because, since the pontiff was then traveling to Gaul, where the Grande Chartreuse is situated, he feared, “if he too went there”—these are Surius’s words—“that he might be unable to avoid the court, or might seem not to have left it but to be following it.” Others give different reasons, which there is no need to enumerate here.

Nevertheless, although this is so, and although—as I have already shown above—the reason alleged by our biographers did not cause the saint not to return to the Carthusian house in 1090, they should not therefore be said to contradict one another, since it could have happened that he did not wish to return to the Grande Chartreuse for different reasons.

For my part, whatever may ultimately be thought of the reasons advanced by others, Bruno seems chiefly not to have returned to the Grande Chartreuse but to have gone back to the Turritan hermitage of Calabria because he knew that the latter still greatly needed his care, and because Roger, count of Calabria and Sicily, who had already from the year 1090 urgently begged the holy man—then scarcely known to him—to choose for himself any place in his dominions, hoping that through the saint’s most holy prayers he and his territories would receive protection from the Lord, now that he knew him well and revered him as a saint, wished by every means for Bruno to return to Calabria.

Bruno could not fail to satisfy the desire of so pious and benevolent a prince, whom he had found, as we have already seen, exceedingly generous toward himself and his companions.

### 604

In any event, the saint returned to Calabria from the Council of Piacenza, if he indeed attended it, and it did not seem right to him to return to the Carthusian house, however greatly he may perhaps have desired to do so.

Zanottius reports in chapter 25 of his *History or Life of Saint Bruno* that, when the saint was returning from that council to Calabria, he turned aside to a place two miles from Siena, stayed there for some time, visited the neighboring people of Siena several times, and finally persuaded them by his exhortations to submit to Pope Urban II, who had placed their city under interdict because they adhered to the antipope Guibert.

For this account he also cites the manuscript Life of Saint Bruno, whose author was Fulgentius Ceccaronius. But since I find this event mentioned by no other writer at all, and since Fulgentius Ceccaronius cannot, considering the period in which he flourished after Saint Bruno, be regarded as an ancient writer, I cannot assert that Zanottius’s account is consistent with the truth. Leaving the matter therefore undecided, I turn to the events that befell the saint after his return to the Calabrian hermitage, and to what is reported to have been suffered by his disciples in the Carthusian house.

## § XXXVII. In the saint’s absence, the religious inhabitants of the Grande Chartreuse suffer a most serious temptation; the saint baptizes a son born to Count Roger and is affected by a new benefit from him
### 605

If our biographers’ account is true, Bruno’s failure to return from the celebrated Council of Piacenza—which, according to what has been said, he may have attended—to the Grande Chartreuse was exceedingly distressing to its religious inhabitants. For, if these writers are correct, they suffered a very grave temptation from the devil, during which the holy man, had he been present with his beloved disciples, could have offered them both consolation and assistance.

It is worthwhile to relate here, in Blomenvenna’s words, that temptation which, if it truly occurred, seems to have taken place not long afterward, as you will understand from what follows, after the Council of Piacenza and another council that immediately followed it, namely, that of Clermont. This biographer of the Saint, from whom Surius and Puteanus likewise borrowed what they provide concerning the same matter, writes as follows:

> “Nor was the ancient serpent absent from this spiritual paradise—that is, from the Carthusian monastery. For, foreseeing how great the losses he would suffer from that order, whose foundations were then already being laid, he disturbed them with the greatest faintheartedness and perplexity, chiefly through tongues—that is, through those who accused them of novelty and thereby exposed them to the danger of being killed. Thus they were utterly uncertain what they ought to do, both because of the rigor of the life they had undertaken and because of the dreadful wilderness in which, moved by the words of those men, they too feared that they were in danger. On the other hand, they feared that, if they departed, they would offend their guides, their stars, and God.”

### 606

Such was the temptation with which the inhabitants of the Grande Chartreuse were harassed by the evil spirit while Bruno was absent. The Saint would certainly have been especially well suited to dispel it; but what he could not accomplish because he was absent, divine clemency, if we are again to trust the writers just mentioned, graciously chose to accomplish.

Blomenvenna adds to the words quoted above:

> “And when they had been harassed for some time by these perplexities, behold, the most merciful Lord, who never abandons those who hope in him, sent to them, while they were discussing this matter—as it is written of the Spirit, ‘You do not know from where it comes or where it goes’—a venerable man with curly and gray hair, who said to them: ‘You are perplexed, brothers, whether you ought to remain in this place or withdraw; but I tell you on God’s behalf that the blessed Mother of God, Mary ever Virgin, will preserve you in this place, if you recite her Hours before the canonical Hours, but Compline after them.’ Having said this, the man disappeared. They, however, rejoiced with great joy and chose the blessed Virgin Mary as patroness of the order, and Saint John the Baptist as its patron. They inferred above all that this holy man had been the apostle Peter from the fact that his successor, Urban II, instituted in the Council of Clermont that the Hours of blessed Mary should be recited daily by clerics. By this vision they were so greatly strengthened in the Lord that neither death nor life could separate them from the charity of Christ.”

Thus far Blomenvenna. We must now make several observations concerning his words—or rather, concerning what he records and teaches in them.

### 607

First, as regards the apparition in which Saint Peter is said to have appeared to the first inhabitants of the Charterhouse, namely Landuin and his companions, assuming the appearance of an old man; to have trained them in the daily recitation of the little Office of the most blessed Virgin Mary; and thereby to have brought it about that they were freed from an extremely dangerous temptation and chose that same blessed Virgin Mary as patroness of their order and Saint John the Baptist as its patron: although this event is confirmed by the testimony or authority neither of a sufficiently ancient nor of a contemporary writer or monument, I would nevertheless not dare to deny it absolutely, since it is supported both by the established tradition—as it is called—of the entire order and by the continuous practice within it of reciting the little Office of the most blessed Virgin.

Yet is there nothing that might reasonably cause us to doubt whether that apparition, or the events said to have followed it, ever took place? The most blessed Virgin Mary as patroness, and Saint John the Baptist as patron, since Bruno, according to what has been said above, probably founded the Charterhouse in their honor, had most likely been chosen by the Saint and his disciples long before the apparition just mentioned. It is therefore doubtful whether that apparition existed as the cause of this choice, as Blomenvenna suggests in the words quoted. This is especially so since, according to his account—see the words of Blomenvenna just given—it was not Saint John the Baptist but the apostle Saint Peter who appeared to Landuin and his companions. Consequently, if the said apparition had caused the choice, they would seem to have chosen the latter of these two saints, not the former, as their patron.

Moreover, Ruinart, in the frequently cited *Life of Pope Urban II*, no. 226, writes as follows:

> “They also report that, on this very occasion of the sacred expedition, the canonical Hours of blessed Mary—which had previously been instituted by Peter Damian in his monasteries—began to be frequently recited, at Urban’s command, by clerics and even by laypeople, so that in this way those who were unfit to undertake the expedition might at least assist the soldiers by these prayers, earning for them the patronage of so great a Virgin.”

### 608

Since, then, according to Ruinart’s quoted words, Pope Urban is said to have instructed clerics to recite those Hours of the most blessed Virgin, commonly called her Office, and since, as appears, the instruction was in fact given at the Council of Clermont—see Labbe, volume X of the *Councils*, column 517—the Carthusians could have been moved to do the same by that recent command of Urban. Therefore, since they had no need of the apparition reported above in Blomenvenna’s words, it may seem doubtful whether they were truly impelled by it to undertake the recitation of those prayers.

Someone, however, may perhaps defend the claim that this was accomplished by the reported apparition by arguing that the apparition occurred before the celebration of the Council of Clermont. Petreius seems to have held this opinion. For in his *Elucidations of Dorland’s Chronicle*, book IV, chapter 4, he writes:

> “When the apostle Peter appeared to them—the Carthusians—he offered them salutary counsel, namely, that they should chant the canonical Hours daily in honor of the most sacred Virgin. The whole clergy afterward undertook to imitate this practice, as is clear from the decrees of the Council of Clermont.”

So he writes. Yet he proves what he asserts by no argument whatsoever, nor can his authority alone make us believe him. Dorland, whom Petreius intended to elucidate by that observation, introduces Saint Peter as speaking thus to the Carthusians to whom he appeared:

> “Know this: the most sacred Mother of God, Mary, will preserve you here from every trouble and will become the patroness of your Order, provided only that you chant her Hours, as has recently been instituted in the Roman Church.”

### 609

Dorland therefore believed that Saint Peter appeared to the Carthusians and admonished them to chant the Hours of the most blessed Virgin Mary at a time when the recitation of those Hours had recently been established in the Roman Church. Since no place other than the Council of Clermont is found where this had been established at approximately the time when the apparition occurred, he consequently held that the apparition was later than that council.

Blomenvenna held the same view, as is sufficiently clear from the following words, which he immediately adds after relating the apparition of the apostle Peter, and which were quoted above:

> “They inferred above all that the holy man had been the apostle Peter from the fact that his successor, Urban II, instituted at the Council of Clermont that the Hours of blessed Mary should be recited daily by clerics.”

Surius likewise agrees with Blomenvenna. Although neither he, nor Blomenvenna, nor Dorland adduces any testimony or ancient monument by which to strengthen their opinion, nevertheless, if the reported apparition of the apostle Saint Peter ever took place, I think that these three writers should be followed rather than Petreius alone. Petreius seems to place it before the Council of Clermont merely because of a preconceived opinion according to which he believes that the custom of reciting the Hours of the most holy Virgin Mary was first practiced by the Carthusians and then spread by them to others. But this is undoubtedly far removed from the truth.

### 610

For, according to Peter the Deacon, in chapter 64 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, the Hours of the most holy Virgin were already being added daily to the principal Office on Monte Cassino by order of Pope Gregory II, who began his pontificate in 715, and therefore long before the Carthusian order arose.

Furthermore, Peter Damian, who had already departed this life before the beginning of the Carthusian Order and before the Council of Clermont, teaches in letter 32 to the hermits of Gamugno that the recitation of these same Hours had been divinely confirmed in one of his monasteries, where they were accustomed to be frequently recited, against the monk Bozo, an opponent of this holy practice.

Since this is so, I consider it more probable, on the authority of Dorland, Blomenvenna, and Surius—which, for the reasons already given, ought here to outweigh the authority of Petreius alone—that the apparition in which Saint Peter appeared to the Carthusians and admonished them to discharge the daily burden of the Hours of the most holy Virgin occurred after the Council of Clermont.

Since the matter stands thus, it may, as I have already said, be doubted whether that apparition caused the custom among the Carthusians of reciting daily the little Office of the most holy Virgin Mary to become established. Moreover, since, for the reasons given above, it is also reasonably doubtful whether they were moved by that same apparition to choose the most holy Virgin Mary as patroness and Saint John the Baptist as patron, it likewise appears doubtful whether the apparition ever took place.

For the present, however, I have thought it appropriate to mention it here because, although, according to what has been said, it would have occurred after the Council of Clermont if it ever took place, it may nevertheless have happened in the very year 1095, in whose November that council was held. We are here dealing with events occurring at approximately this time and relating to the Saint.

Let us now continue the sequence of events that touch him somewhat more closely.

### 611

Bruno had not long returned from the Council of Piacenza—if it is indeed true that he attended it—when Count Roger demonstrated in another way how highly he valued and loved him, apart from the lavish donations he had previously made to the Calabrian wilderness of Turrita.

Camillus Tutinus, again cited above, records the following in his *Prospectus of the History of the Carthusian Order* under the year 1097:

> “A son is born to Count Roger by Adelaide; Bruno baptizes him in the church of Mileto, and Landuin lifts him from the font. He was Roger, the first king of Sicily. Maraldus, himself also a Carthusian, was present and composed a melic poem on this occasion.”

But did he correctly assign the birth of Roger, the first king of the island after the Saracens had been expelled from Sicily, to the year 1097?

Romuald of Salerno, a contemporary author, writes as follows about Roger, the son of Count Roger and the first king of Sicily, in his *Chronicle*, printed by Muratori in volume VII of the *Writers of Italian Affairs*, column 196:

> “The most glorious King Roger, after so many victories and triumphs, died at Palermo of a fever and was buried in the archiepiscopal church of that city in the fifty-eighth year of his life, two months and five days having passed, on the twenty-sixth day of February, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign; but in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1152, Indiction I.”

So Romuald writes. Since he could have known very well in what year of his life King Roger died, I am persuaded that he actually died, as the quoted words state, in the fifty-eighth year of his age.

Pagius, in his *Critica* under this year, proves with very clear arguments that Roger did not exchange life for death on 27 February of the year 1152, as Romuald—or rather, the words quoted and attributed to that writer—indicate, but in the year 1154. There is no doubt that other errors also lie hidden in the chronological details contained in the passage of Romuald copied above.

### 612

These details, however, are written only in abbreviated letters serving for numerals. Experience shows that errors very easily, and not rarely, creep into such forms through the carelessness of copyists. But in the quoted text of Romuald the year in which Roger closed his life is expressed not by abbreviated numerical letters but by complete words, into which, as all learned men know, an error enters with difficulty—or at least not so easily and not so frequently.

Moreover, nothing appears anywhere that could in any way suggest that Roger died in a different year of his life. Thus, if it is not certain, it is at least most probable that he died in the fifty-eighth year of his life specified in Romuald’s text, and indeed, as I shall show below, after two months and five days had already been completed—these details likewise being expressed in the same text by complete words.

Since this is so, and since subtracting fifty-eight years, two months, and five days from the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1154, advanced to 27 February—the date on which Pagius proves most clearly from the foregoing that King Roger died—brings us to the year 1095, which was already close to its end, it follows that King Roger, whose birth we are investigating here, was born in that later year, when December was already well advanced.

### 613

But, you will say, Geoffrey Malaterra, frequently praised above and apparently deserving greater confidence here than Romuald, writes in book IV, chapter 26 of his *History of Sicily*, concerning Capua, which had been besieged by Roger, duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, together with his uncle Roger, count of Calabria and Sicily:

> “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097, there—in the camp before besieged Capua—Countess Adelaide conceived by Count Roger.”

Since the subject here is Roger, later king, conceived by Adelaide or Adelasia from her husband Count Roger, and since, as will become clear from what follows concerning the time of the siege of Capua, Count Roger, the husband of Adelaide, could not have been in the camp before Capua before Pentecost—which fell on 24 May in the year 1097—even granting that the city had been besieged by Count Roger in that year, it follows from Malaterra’s quoted words that Roger, the first king of Sicily, was born not at the end of the year 1095 but only at the beginning of the year 1098.

I admit that this is what the passage says. Nevertheless, apart from the fact that it still cannot be proved that the birth occurred in the year 1097, to which Camillus Tutinus, according to what has been said, assigns it, it cannot be established that the words of Malaterra’s *History of Sicily* copied here concern Roger, the future king, whom Adelaide conceived in the camp before Capua by her husband, Count Roger.

Nor, even if the matter were otherwise, would anything follow from it in favor of assigning the king’s birth to the year 1097, since those words should not be attributed to Malaterra. Rather, they were written by an incompetent annotator in the margin of the page and later transferred from the margin into the text by an unskilled copyist. I shall show this below, when I discuss both the date of the siege of Capua and the diploma by which, after that siege, Count Roger bestowed many possessions upon Saint Bruno and the Calabrian wilderness.

### 614

After considering everything, I therefore remain of the opinion that Roger, the son of Count Roger and later king of Sicily, was born not in 1097, as Tutinus maintains, but toward the end of 1095.
