This seems still more probable, partly because of the words of Romuald concerning King Roger that I quoted above: “He died … in the fifty-eighth year of his life, two months and five days”; and partly because, although in his *Chronicle* Romuald generally does not take a year designated by an ordinal number appended to it as a completed year unless he adds an expression explicitly indicating this, here the fifty-eighth year must nevertheless be understood as having been completed by two months and five days, as is clear from the funerary inscription of King Roger.

This inscription appears in Rocchus Pirrus’s *Chronology of the Kings of Sicily*, prefixed to volume I of *Sacred Sicily*, page 8, and reads:

> “He lived 59 years; he reigned 34; he died in 1154.”

Since this is so, and since fifty-eight years, two months, and five days counted backward from 27 February 1154—the day on which, according to what has been said, that prince unquestionably died—bring us to the end of 1095, it follows that King Roger was born then, as has already been stated.

Since this is so, we have at the same time determined the date on which his baptism by Bruno took place. But what establishes that Count Roger conferred upon the Saint the honor of wishing him to baptize his son?

### 615

Among the inhabitants of the Calabrian wilderness who took part in the election of the new prior or master to govern the entire wilderness after Saint Bruno’s death, Maraldus is listed in the catalogue of those men transcribed below. The catalogue was found in an ancient document on which each of them had written his own name.

Rocchus Pirrus frequently mentions Maraldus, a Carthusian monk who compiled a certain chronicle, both in his *Chronology of the Kings of Sicily* and elsewhere. Morotius, in his *Chronological Theatre of the Carthusian Order*, affirms that Maraldus was rich in poetic talent and flourished around the year 1095.

From all this I am persuaded that Maraldus, a member of the Calabrian Charterhouse, truly attended the baptism of Roger, later king, as Tutinus says, and that Roger, the first king of Sicily after the expulsion of the Saracens, was truly baptized by our Saint, as Tutinus and others testify in the melic poem that Maraldus composed on the subject.

I think that it is worthwhile to transcribe the entire poem here from Tutinus, although in some places its verses have been so badly fashioned either by the author himself or corrupted by the errors of copyists that one can scarcely, or not at all, understand what they signify.

### 616

The following verses establish this:

> The whole world shines, the world  
> In a bright nativity.  
>   
> The niece of Boniface the Italian,  
> Marquis of Mileto,  
> Adelaide, his wife, adorns  
> Roger, Count of the Brutians and Sicilians,  
> And the noble, glorious woman  
> Endows the revered Norman with offspring.  
>   
> The count, present, perceived an ancestral inheritance [or perhaps an increase; *avitum* / *auctum* is uncertain],  
> And recognized himself in a son,  
> Who, after ten months,  
> Covered by the earthly burden,  
> Emerges.  
>   
> The ancient city of Mileto  
> Becomes filled with immense joys.  
> All things below stand bound  
> In rejoicing, and Trinacria likewise.  
>   
> A joyful and discerning chorus  
> Plays joyful songs.  
> For the holy sacred washing,  
> The cleansing waters.  
>   
> The count prays and prevails upon  
> Bruno the German,  
> For his devotion is held  
> As though bound to him.  
>   
> Summoned, not unwilling,  
> He comes rejoicing.  
> The boy is baptized and washed  
> In the sacred stream.  
>   
> Landuin is the godfather,  
> A noble Norman.  
> And then, after the sacred washing,  
> He is anointed with olive oil by Bruno.

### 617

> They suspend the war after the birth of the boy,  
> For Christ God most high.  
>   
> A happy omen: the boy  
> Is called Roger.  
> All sing; they remain sleepless,  
> Rejoicing in metrical songs.  
>   
> The hearth [or “fire”? E. P.] burns; the marriage-bed rejoices  
> With exceeding joy.  
>   
> For the church of Mileto,  
> Displayed in splendor, rejoiced,  
> Since it was seen adorned  
> With tapestry and fir branches.  
>   
> It is green with foliage; no one is silent;  
> All play in their rejoicing.  
>   
> Then Urban, yet humane,  
> Rejoices at the birth;  
> He, the second, whom the whole world  
> Immediately adores,  
>   
> From the seat of Christ,  
> With the reward of the most blessed kingdom.  
>   
> He prays, while the boy is lifted,  
> To the youthful Lord,  
> For a saving and equal life,  
> Christ’s celibate life.  
>   
> Therefore, once born and reborn,  
> May Christ grant the boy kingdoms,  
> Together with heaven’s gift of zeal  
> And of what is most just.  
>   
> To the highest God be forever  
> The praise of enduring fruit. Amen.

### 618

Whether Adelaide, the wife of Count Roger, had Boniface as her father, grandfather, or uncle cannot be determined from the third verse of this poem and the three following verses, since they are extremely obscure. Of the remaining verses—among which everyone will easily see, even without my saying so, which are especially defective through obscurity—the most important for our present purpose are those that show both that Count Roger asked the Saint to baptize his son and that the Saint performed this office. They are the following:

> For the holy sacred washing,  
> The cleansing waters.  
>   
> The count prays and prevails upon  
> Bruno the German,  
>   
> For his devotion is held  
> As though bound to him.  
>   
> Summoned, not unwilling,  
> He comes rejoicing.  
>   
> The boy is baptized and washed  
> In the sacred stream.  
>   
> Landuin is the godfather,  
> A noble Norman.  
>   
> And then, after the sacred washing,  
> He is anointed with olive oil by Bruno.

What these verses signify is sufficiently clear. Nevertheless, lest anyone perhaps doubt the meaning of the final verse—which is particularly relevant here—*Bruno* is a dative, derived from the noun *Brunus*, which the poet uses here for the name *Bruno*, as is evident from the two preceding verses, “The count prays and prevails upon Bruno the German.” It is employed, after the Greek manner, in place of an ablative with the preposition *a*. Thus the sense of the verse is: “He is anointed with olive oil by Bruno.” Together with several verses immediately preceding and following it, the line teaches that Roger, the son of Roger, count of Calabria and Sicily, was baptized by Saint Bruno at Mileto in Calabria with solemn rites, and that this occurred, as can readily be inferred from what has already been said, toward the end of 1095.

### 619

Not much time had elapsed after the baptism of Roger, later king of Sicily, when the Saint again experienced the benevolence of Roger, count of Calabria and Sicily, toward himself.

Surianus records this in his annotations to the *Life of Saint Bruno* written by Surius, page 397:

> “In the year 1096 Count Roger gave certain peasants to Saint Bruno, by a diploma in which he styled himself an assistant of Christians.”

The donation mentioned here by Surianus is undoubtedly the same one concerning which Camillus Tutinus speaks under the year 1096 in his *Prospectus of the History of the Carthusian Order*, using these words:

> “Another donation was added by the same count to Bruno and Landuin, and to their successors in the said monastery—that is, the Turritan monastery in Calabria—of fifty households of men bound to them by fealty and homage. The privilege was written in the Greek language.”

I have nowhere been able to find the privilege or diploma by which Camillus Tutinus and Surianus, in the words quoted, affirm that this donation was made to the Saint. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that it was available to one of these writers, namely Tutinus, who says that it was written in Greek.

I am therefore persuaded that this donation too was truly made to the Saint by Count Roger, although I would have wished to have that privilege or diploma here to show the reader, so that I could make the matter more certain for him.

### XXXVIII. After Theodore Mesimerius, the Greek bishop of Squillace, dies, the Saint advises that John of Nicephorus, a Latin, be appointed in his place; from the latter he then obtains an extensive privilege for the Turritan wilderness, where a new monastery of Saint Stephen has now been built, and arranges for it to be confirmed by the pope

### 620

As long as Calabria had been subject to the Greek emperors of the East, almost no bishops other than those belonging to the Greek Church had occupied the see of Squillace. But after that region had been subdued in the eleventh century by the Norman people and princes, who followed the rite of the Latin Church, and after Theodore Mesimerius, the Greek bishop of Squillace, had died in the year 1095 or at the beginning of the following year, Count Roger of Calabria and Sicily—whose dominion included Squillace, or, as others write, Squillacum or Squillacium—judged that no bishop other than one belonging to the Latin Church should be appointed to replace him.

At the urging of Saint Bruno and Landuin, together with several bishops of the Latin rite, Roger therefore appointed John of Nicephorus as the first bishop of that see belonging to the Latin rite.

All these facts are recorded in a surviving diploma preserved by Ughellus in volume IX of *Sacred Italy*, in the section on the bishops of Squillace, column 426. It is dated 1096, Indiction V. From this it is clear that Ughellus incorrectly placed Mesimerius’s death at the end of 1096 or the beginning of the following year. By that diploma Roger also bestowed many possessions upon the see of Squillace and in a certain sense refounded it.

The relevant words are as follows:

> “I, Roger, count of Sicily and Calabria, together with my wife, named Adelaide … with the counsel of Saxo, bishop of Cassano and vicar of the Lord Pope Urban, and of Lord Robert of Messina, Stephen … Angerius of Catania, Stephen of Mazara, Engerland of Agrigento, and Roger, bishop of Syracuse, with the consent of these bishops, and with the counsels of Lord Bruno and our brother Landuin, hermits and holy men, appointed Lord John of Nicephorus, who was a canon and dean of the venerable church of Saint Mileto, an honorable and prudent man, rich in every virtue, to that see as its master and bishop. I enriched his church with as many and as great benefits as pleased me, honored it with dignities, and, insofar as it depended upon me, assigned and described its parish,” and so forth.

### 621

Since Roger here honors Saint Bruno and Landuin with the title “holy men,” and since, as he himself acknowledges, he appointed John of Nicephorus to the see of Squillace and bestowed no small amount of property upon that see partly on their advice, this diploma is also clear evidence of the esteem in which that prince held Landuin and, specifically, Saint Bruno.

Not long after Mesimerius, the Greek-rite bishop of the Church of Squillace, had died, John of Nicephorus, who belonged to the Latin rite, had been appointed in his place by Count Roger at the urging of our Saint and Landuin. Bruno then began to establish a new church and monastery in the Calabrian wilderness of Turrita under the name of the most holy Virgin Mary and Saint Stephen the protomartyr.

Camillus Tutinus says in his *Prospectus of the History of the Carthusian Order*, under the year 1097, page 12:

> “The number of monks in the wilderness of Saint Mary had already increased, and since that place could not contain them, at the command of Count Roger a very spacious and magnificent monastery was built near the wilderness under the title of the same Virgin and of the protomartyr Stephen.”

If Tutinus is to be trusted here, then the Saint not only added a new monastery to the earlier one, which, according to what has been said, he had built immediately after entering the Calabrian Charterhouse in honor of the most holy Virgin Mary and Saint John the Baptist, but did so both because Count Roger wished it to be done and because the number of monks had grown so large that the monastery dedicated to Saint Mary and Saint John the Baptist could no longer contain them.

I think it probable that Bruno acted partly for this latter reason because in the year 1101, when, according to what follows, the Saint departed to the Lord—and therefore only five years after John of Nicephorus had been promoted to the see of Squillace—there were more than thirty monks in the wilderness of Turrita. This is demonstrated by the previously cited catalogue of the monks of that place who, after the death of their holy father, promised obedience to Landuin as master of the wilderness. The catalogue was excerpted from an ancient document on which each of them had written his own name and was incorporated into the fourth book of the *Annals of the Carthusian Order*, not yet published.

### 622

A Parisian Carthusian, frequently praised above, was kind enough to communicate this monument to me, copied from a manuscript of that book belonging to the monastery of Val-de-Dieu, together with many other materials. Since it has already been cited here and earlier and will still be cited below, I think it worthwhile to share it with the reader, who, I believe, will not find this unwelcome.

It reads as follows:

> “Brother Hugh promised obedience to Master Landuin. Likewise Brother Leo; likewise Brother Maraldus; likewise Brother Romanus; likewise Brother Stabilis; likewise Brother Ralph of the Crucifix; likewise Brother Ursus, subdeacon; likewise Brother Rainerius, subdeacon; likewise Brother Guildericus; likewise Brother Gerard; likewise Brother Tricus; likewise Brother Walter Morinus; likewise Brother Landulf; likewise Brother Herchen—the anonymous author of the fourth book of the *Annals of the Carthusian Order* notes that this name is incomplete because the parchment is damaged; likewise Brother Reginald the mason; likewise Brother Albert; likewise Brother Rembald and Brother Hugh; likewise Brother Odo; likewise Brother Longuisus; likewise Brother Odo; likewise Brother Anselm; likewise Brother Gumbert; likewise Brother Bernard; likewise Brother Durand; likewise Brother Loinus; likewise Brother Hato; likewise Brother Fulk, deacon; likewise Brother Heldicus; likewise Brother Guarinus, subdeacon; likewise Brother Lambert.”

Thus the cited catalogue includes more than thirty monks of the wilderness of Turrita who promised obedience to Landuin after the Saint’s death, as anyone who counts them will see. It therefore seems quite probable, as I have already said, that approximately five years earlier—when John of Nicephorus was first promoted to the see of Squillace—the number of monks had been much greater than at the beginning, and that this was partly the reason why the Saint built the new monastery of Saint Stephen.

### 623

The anonymous author of the fourth book of the *Annals of the Carthusian Order*, not yet published, assigns a very different reason for Bruno’s action. Here are his relevant words, copied from a manuscript of the said book belonging to Val-de-Dieu and sent to me by the Parisian Carthusian, already so frequently praised, who declines to reveal his name:

> “Moreover, he wished the Calabrian wilderness itself, which Saint Bruno had obtained from Roger, to be constructed in honor of Saint Mary and Saint John the Baptist, whom he had already chosen as special patrons in the Charterhouse, as we saw in the letters of Theodore, bishop of Squillace, quoted above, and he arranged that it should be dedicated under the same names in the year 1094 with great solemnity …  
>   
> “But what sort of wilderness this was, which the holy Patriarch inhabited, he himself described in his letter to Ralph, then provost of the church of Reims, saying: ‘In the regions of Calabria with religious brothers,’ and so forth, up to and including these words: ‘For if a bow is kept constantly stretched, it becomes slack and less fit for use.’  
>   
> “Thus Saint Bruno described his solitude, where he frequently stayed with those of his companions whom he had tested as called by God to lead the anchoritic life. But when he saw many people of different conditions and varying strength coming to him for the sake of conversion, he decided to retain with him in his wilderness those who were stronger and in whom he had discerned a divine vocation to this way of life. For the others, whom he judged less suited to the eremitical life, he built a monastery dedicated to Saint Stephen the protomartyr, situated about one mile from the wilderness, where they might live an eremitical life, indeed, but one somewhat more relaxed and less austere.”

624. Therefore, if we are to rely on the anonymous author of Book Four of the *Annals of the Carthusians*, hitherto unpublished, Bruno built the new monastery of Saint Stephen in order to provide assistance to those who were less suited to the eremitical life. This too may be true, since there is absolutely nothing to prevent us from believing that he did so partly for this reason and partly for the reason assigned above.

Whatever the facts may meanwhile be, it is beyond doubt that he added to the monastery consecrated to the most holy Mother of God and to John the Baptist—called the Monastery of Saint Mary of the Desert, or of the Tower—a second one, dedicated to the same most holy Mother of God and to Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. It is likewise certain that this second monastery was already inhabited on 2 August 1099. For Roger, count of Calabria and Sicily, in the charter transcribed below, which he granted in favor of Saint Bruno in that year and on that day, mentions the monastery of Saint Stephen, which then existed in the Turritan desert and was inhabited by brothers. He says:

“I wish it to be known to all faithful Christians what benefits God has granted to me, a sinner, through the prayers of the reverend man Father Bruno, most holy father of the brothers who dwell in the churches of Saint Mary of the Desert and Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, which are situated in my land between the town called Stilo and Arena.” [Col. 0383C–D]

From this it is now clear that Blomenvenna is entirely mistaken when, after transcribing part of the charter by which Count Roger granted many gifts to Saint Bruno, he immediately adds:

“By virtue of this donation, therefore, he first built there”—in the Turritan desert of Calabria—“a church in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary beside a certain underground cave or cavern in which he himself lived. He also built another church not far from it, in honor of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, together with a monastery adjoining it, in which the other brothers dwelt, serving Christ under the care and governance of so great a Father.”

[Col. 0384A] 625. Thus he reports that Saint Bruno did not first construct the church or monastery of Saint Stephen until after Count Roger had made him the donation expressed in the charter whose part he quotes. Since that very charter mentions the monastery as already existing or already built, he clearly falls into error. This error—into which two others, namely Puteanus before him and Surius after him, also fell—is all the more surprising because the very portion of the charter quoted by all three expressly mentions the monastery of Saint Stephen as already built.

Moreover, both Blomenvenna in the words just quoted and the two biographers of our Saint mentioned shortly afterward, Puteanus and Surius, report that Saint Bruno likewise did not first construct the church dedicated to the most holy Mother of God in the Calabrian desert until after Count Roger had granted him the donation expressed in the aforesaid charter. Their account is no less erroneous than their preceding account of the church of Saint Stephen, since it is clear from what has already been said that the church of the most holy Mother of God had already begun to be built in 1090 and was consecrated in 1094.

Nor do I see how what these three biographers say about the church of Saint Stephen—namely, that Saint Bruno first built it in the Calabrian desert after the charter just mentioned had been issued—can be reconciled with other statements of theirs, in which they had previously recorded that the churches of Saint Mary and Saint Stephen were given to Saint Bruno by Count Roger when, while hunting, he found Bruno in the Turritan desert, though he did not yet know him.

For if Saint Bruno was ever found by Count Roger while the latter was hunting and did not yet know him, this certainly occurred, as the biographers themselves must admit from what has already been said, no later than 1095 or the beginning of the following year. Since this is so, how can it be true that Count Roger then granted Bruno the church of Saint Stephen, while at the same time that church was not built until after the charter mentioned above, which was issued no earlier than 1099, as will be shown below?

626. Could there perhaps have been, during the lifetime of our Saint, four churches in the Calabrian desert: two of them—one dedicated to Saint Mary and the other to Saint Stephen—already existing before Bruno entered that solitude, and two others—again one dedicated to Saint Mary and the other to Saint Stephen—first built after the Saint entered the same solitude? But this neither appears probable nor is it recorded, so far as I can find, by any writer, whether more recent or more ancient.

Indeed, the anonymous author of Book Four of the *Annals of the Carthusians*, hitherto unpublished, mentions not four but only two churches or monasteries inhabited by Bruno and his disciples, which existed in the Turritan desert of Calabria during the lifetime of our Saint. Under the year 1114, as the Parisian Carthusian—whom I have cited so frequently that I do not wish to name him—has again taught me, he writes:

“In the years 1090 and 1097 we see that there were already two monasteries”—namely, in the Turritan desert of Calabria—“in the time of Saint Bruno: one dedicated to Blessed Mary (one may add, and to Saint John the Baptist), where he himself dwelt; the other not far distant from the first, built in honor of the same Blessed Mary and Saint Stephen, in which, together with all the lay brothers, certain monks also lived, whether less fervent or rather weakened, of whom Lanvinus himself was prior.

“But all had lived an eremitical life until the present year”—namely, 1114—“as though forming only one community, as seems evident from the encyclical letter sent to his friends after the death of Saint Bruno. In it they mention only one monastery, since they style themselves ‘the humble hermits of Calabria, of the monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God.’” [Col. 0385A–B]

627. “And in many letters sent by Pope Paschal II to Lanvinus, which we transcribed above in their proper places, the Pope himself calls Lanvinus ‘superior of the hermits and father and teacher of many anchorites.’ Nor does he speak of more than one monastery:

“‘We have learned,’ he says, ‘that the peace and harmony of the desert have been restored’”—see no. 550.

“And, writing to all of them: ‘Greetings to Lanvinus and the other brothers who inhabit the desert of the lord Bruno.’ And to the master of the desert himself: ‘We greet your brothers, the inhabitants of the desert.’

“Thus they were called and remained hermits until finally, in the present year”—namely, 1114—“a third monastery was erected for cenobites at Squillace, as is stated in the letters transcribed above.”

Thus far the anonymous author, listing, as I have said, only two monasteries inhabited by the Carthusians, which existed in the Calabrian desert not only during Saint Bruno’s lifetime but long afterward, up to the year 1114.

One of these, dedicated to the most holy Mother of God and to Saint John the Baptist, began to be founded in 1090 and was consecrated in 1094 with solemn rite and great ceremony, as I have already shown. The monastery of Saint Stephen, although it also had its own prior, was subject to the prior or master of this monastery.

The other, dedicated to the same most holy Mother of God and to Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, was afterward called the monastery of Saint Stephen of the Woods or of the Forest. On 2 August 1099, the day on which the charter mentioned above is recorded as having been issued, it was already built, as is clear from what I have discussed.

But how much earlier had its construction begun? Since, according to what has been said above, the monastery or church dedicated to the most holy Mother of God was not consecrated with solemn rite before 1094, and since the monastery of Saint Stephen does not appear to have been founded before that consecration, its construction most probably took place between 1094 and 1099, as anyone can easily infer from the foregoing. Accordingly, Camillus Tutinus may perhaps rightly have assigned its construction to 1097 in his *Prospectus of the History of the Carthusian Order*, as did the anonymous author of Book Four of the *Annals of the Carthusians*, hitherto unpublished. [Col. 0385C–D; 0386A]

628. Indeed, since in the charter which, as I have shown above, Count Roger granted to Saint Bruno in 1096 there is, so far as I believe, no mention whatsoever of the monastery of Saint Stephen as already existing, whereas it is mentioned in the other charter of 1099, which I have just discussed, I think it extremely probable that the monastery began to be founded under Saint Bruno’s care around 1097. It was evidently a large building, by common agreement, and at least two years seem to have been required for its construction; by 1099 it had already been brought to completion, as anyone will understand from what has been said.

Not long after this building had begun to be founded, John of Nicephorus revealed how favorably disposed he was toward our Saint, on whose advice, as has been stated, he had been raised to the see of Squillace and whose Turritan desert he had in mind.

For in the year 1098, perhaps before he had occupied the see for a full year, in the presence of Henry, bishop of Nicastro, and others, he confirmed all the donations and privileges granted to Saint Bruno and to his successors in the monastery of Saint Mary of the Tower. He also granted that monastery such extensive freedom that he deprived himself and his successors of episcopal jurisdiction over it, as the public instrument, or privilege, by which he did this makes clear.

The frequently mentioned Parisian Carthusian, with great kindness, deigned to share this instrument with me, copied from the Vallis-Dei manuscript of Book Four of the *Annals of the Carthusians*, hitherto unpublished. Since it is a precious monument of antiquity and, as I think, may not be unwelcome to the reader, I am pleased to share it here as well. [Col. 0386B–C]

629. It is composed in these words:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, John, by the will of God bishop of the see of Squillace, following in the footsteps of the holy Fathers who preceded me, wish to imitate their religious deeds and decrees and, to the best of my ability, preserve them inviolate.

“Therefore I praise, affirm, and confirm that the monastery called Saint Mary of the Tower, presided over by the venerable Father Bruno, is free, with the same liberty with which it was founded by Count Roger, granted by the blessed Pope Urban, and confirmed by my predecessor, Bishop Theodore, of good memory.

“Let all the faithful and lovers of truth therefore know that the aforesaid monastery, and likewise that place called Arsafia, with which the aforesaid monastery has been endowed, together with all its appurtenances and all the people—both clergy and laity—whom the said monastery presently has or will have in the future, and also all outsiders who live or will live under its authority, have been endowed with this liberty.

“Neither I nor any of my successors shall have any episcopal right there without the common and spontaneous consent of the brothers of the aforesaid monastery. Let them obtain consecrations, ordinations, chrism, and the other necessities of episcopal office from whichever bishop, near or far, they prefer, and let no one prevent them. Let their tithes belong to them. Let the punishment of offenses committed by their subjects and their correction be entrusted to them.

“These things that we have stated were confirmed by the authority and privilege of my predecessor Theodore, a Greek by nationality. These same things we too attest and confirm by the present privilege and by the authority which we have received from God; and let it never be lawful for me myself—God forbid that I should think otherwise—or for any of my successors to violate them.

“If anyone should obstinately attempt, by craft or power, to erase this judgment of ours, truthfully pronounced, written, and signed as a token of stability, let him himself be erased from the book of the living.

“But upon those who assent to and defend it, let peace and life rest, with Him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.” [Col. 0386D–0387A]

630. This charter or privilege bears no chronological notes attached to it, either at the beginning or at the end. Nevertheless, the anonymous Carthusian, from whose fourth book of the *Annals of the Carthusians*, hitherto unpublished, it was communicated to me, asserts that it was issued in 1098, in the sixth indiction, on the seventh day before the Ides of May, that is, on 9 May.

But he does not say whether he found those chronological notes in the original privilege itself, or in the copy that lay before him, or somewhere else. I was therefore initially uncertain whether the instrument had really been issued in 1098, until I discovered that Ughellus assigns it the same date in volume IX of *Italia sacra*, column 427.

Although Ughellus and the aforementioned anonymous Carthusian assign the same year, and likewise the same indiction, to this charter and the benefits granted through it to the Saint, they do not agree at all about the month in which it was issued. The latter, as I have shown, asserts that the privilege was issued on 9 May; Ughellus, on the contrary, says that it was issued on 9 March.

But should that difference make the ancient document suspect? Camillus Peregrinus observes the following in the annotations he added to Lupus Protospata’s chronicle under the year 1098:

“It is evident that March was often substituted for May elsewhere as well; this perhaps arose because, when proper names were abbreviated in the age of the Normans by being written only in capital letters, the month of March, written in that form, was very often taken by later scribes for May. This is like the ancient calendar of the Campanian Breviary, in which the feast of Saint Potentiana the virgin is incorrectly recorded on 19 March, although it is celebrated on 19 May.”

Perhaps, then, the month in which the privilege of John of Nicephorus, transcribed above, was granted to Saint Bruno was originally expressed only by the capital letter M. Hence some scribes or copyists recorded it as having been issued in May, while others, on the contrary, recorded it as having been issued in March. [Col. 0387B–D]

631. Since this is the situation, there is no reason to regard that ancient document as suspect merely because the anonymous Carthusian cited above records it as issued in May, whereas Ughellus records it as issued in March, even though this means that it cannot be determined in which of the two months it was actually issued.

This conclusion is also supported, in my judgment, both by the fact that nothing else appears anywhere that would in any way render that charter or privilege suspect, and by the fact that another charter confirms that the charter or privilege really was issued to Saint Bruno by John of Nicephorus, bishop of Squillace. In that other charter Pope Urban II confirmed what John had granted.

I am pleased to transfer here from Ughellus that document as well. It concerns our Saint no less than the preceding one and appears in volume IX of *Italia sacra*, column 427 and following. It reads:

“Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ Bruno and Lanvinus, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Since it is the responsibility of our office to provide, insofar as the Lord grants us power, for the peace and welfare of the servants of God, we mercifully assent to your petitions, most beloved and most reverend sons in Christ.

“By the text of this apostolic privilege, therefore, by apostolic authority we grant and confirm as firm, stable, and everlasting the donation of the lands given to you in the territory of Squillace, written down, delimited, and marked out by definite boundaries by our beloved son R., the count, with the consent of our brother John, bishop of Squillace, and confirmed.” [Col. 0388A–B]

632. “Therefore, by the aforesaid authority, we command and decree, and forbid under penalty, that from this day forward neither the count himself nor any of his heirs may violate or diminish your aforesaid donation or this confirmation of ours.

“Nor may anyone intrude upon any of the things that we confirm without your consent, so that you may devote yourselves with free minds to the contemplation of almighty God and, by his favor, attain the sweetness of his face.

“If any person or heir of the count violates it, unless he comes to an appropriate satisfaction, we decree that he shall be exposed to the danger of losing his honor or office, and, separated from Christ and from the body of the Church, shall be subjected without interruption or remedy to strict punishment at the eternal judgment.

“But may God and his mercy preserve in the present and future ages those who piously preserve these things.

“Amen.

“If, however, so lawful a count or his heir should wish to add anything to this donation, we decree that it shall stand valid under this confirmation of ours.

“Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church.

“I, Cardinal Rainerius, have subscribed.

“I, Cardinal John, have subscribed.

“I, Alphanus, archbishop of Salerno, have subscribed.

“I, Amatus, chaplain and priest, have subscribed.

“I, Dis, chaplain, have subscribed.

“I, Constantine, bishop of Catanzaro, have subscribed.

“Given at Salerno in the month of September, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1098 from the Incarnation of the Lord.” [Col. 0388C–D]

633. Ruinart, in his *Life of Pope Urban II*, after recounting the meeting of this pontiff with Roger, count of Calabria and Sicily, at Salerno following the capture of Capua by that prince in June 1098, as I shall prove below, records the following under the same year, 1098:

“Shortly afterward, namely on 20 July of the following year, the pontiff, at the request of another Roger—namely, the duke of Apulia—and of Archbishop Alphanus, granted an important privilege to the church of Salerno, conferring upon it primacy over the two metropolitan sees of Compsa and Acherontia, which had formerly been subject to it by metropolitan right.

“The bull is dated 20 July”—the manuscripts apparently read 13 Kalends of August—“in the year 1099, but the year must be reckoned from March of the preceding year, so that it may be assigned to the present year. The fourth indiction appended there, however, cannot be excused except by attributing it to the copyists’ error.

“This would be the place to discuss another rescript of Urban, by which the privileges of the monastery of Cava were revoked in favor of the same church, if it were not said to have been issued at Rome; and the seventh indiction which it bears could agree with this year. More on this below.

“Entirely authentic and beyond all doubt, however, is the document which Urban granted in September of this year”—namely, 1098—“to Saint Bruno, the father of the Carthusians, who was then living in the Squillace desert, in order to confirm and uphold all the possessions that had been granted to his monastery by Count Roger and John, bishop of Squillace.

“It was issued at Salerno in September of this year”—namely, 1098, as I have already noted—“in the sixth indiction. From this we infer that Urban remained in that city until the Council of Bari,” which was held in October of the said year, 1098. [Col. 0389A–C]

634. Thus far Ruinart concerning the charter granted by Pope Urban to Saint Bruno. From this we learn that in 1098 Urban was at Salerno, the place and year in which the charter is recorded as having been issued. Since that city is not very far from the Turritan desert, perhaps our Saint—at whose request, together with Lanvinus’s, the pontiff implies that he issued the privilege just quoted—went to Salerno with Lanvinus at that time and attended the Council of Bari, held not long after the privilege was issued.

As for the chronological notes by which the pontifical privilege is dated: since Pope Urban II used the Caesarean or Constantinopolitan indiction, as I showed in no. 569, and since the seventh indiction of this system ran from 24 September 1098 to 24 September of the following year, not the sixth, it follows that the pontifical privilege, being dated in 1098, in the sixth indiction, and in the month of September, must have been issued before that month had advanced to the twenty-fourth day. [Col. 0389D]

### § XXXIX. The Saint delivers Count Roger from the gravest danger by a vision in which he warns him during the siege of Capua, and on this occasion obtains a new charter by which Roger grants him very extensive possessions.

635. Among all the charters which the Saint obtained either from Count Roger or from anyone else in favor of the Turritan desert in Calabria, none is more illustrious or more celebrated by writers than the one he obtained from that prince on the occasion of the siege of Capua, in the year 1099, as I shall prove below.

It happened, says Geoffrey Malaterra in Book IV, chapter 26, of his *History of Sicily,*

“that Richard the Younger, son of Prince Jordan, himself prince of Aversa, left an orphan by his deceased father and surviving as a small child, had for a long time been unjustly deprived of the city of Capua through the treachery of the Lombards. When he had reached the age of understanding, seeing and lamenting the injury done to him and preparing to seek vengeance from its authors, he sent suppliantly to his kinsman the count”—namely, Roger, count of Calabria and Sicily—“prudent men, asking that he not delay in hastening with his forces to bring him aid.”

Moved by the embassy of his kinsman, the count assembled a considerable army. Having brought it into Campania to assist Richard and joined it with the forces of Roger, duke of Apulia, whose uncle he was, and of Richard, prince of Aversa, his kinsman, he besieged and captured Capua in 1098, as I shall show below.

During the siege, however, the count incurred great danger. Sergius the Greek, whom he had placed in command of two hundred Greek soldiers, had made an agreement with the Capuans for money: he promised to open an entrance for them so that, during the night, they could burst unexpectedly into Roger’s army, slaughter it, and kill the count himself.

The night had now arrived on which the treachery was to be carried out, and the forces of the Capuans stood ready, as they had agreed with Sergius. Then Saint Bruno—or rather, as will be explained below, an angel appeared to the count in his sleep under Bruno’s appearance and form, through the merits and prayers of Bruno—and warned him of the imminent danger.

Struck with fear, the count awoke, summoned the soldiers to arms, frustrated the ambush prepared for him, put the enemy to flight, captured most of those guilty of the treachery, and shortly afterward subdued Capua. [Col. 0390A–C]

636. After this expedition had been brought to a successful conclusion, the count first went to Salerno, where Pope Urban II met with him and where he remained for some time, and then proceeded to Squillace in Calabria.

While he was there suffering from ill health for fourteen days, Saint Bruno came to him, in order to console him in the difficulties of his illness, accompanied by four other religious inhabitants of the Calabrian desert. The count received the holy man with the greatest kindness, as was his custom, and gave him his warmest thanks because Bruno had cared for him even while absent during the siege of Capua, offering him many gifts as a token of gratitude.

Bruno, however, insisted that it was not he but the angel who stands beside princes in time of war who had appeared to the count during the siege of Capua, and therefore refused to accept the gifts.

Nevertheless, when the Saint afterward consented to accept at least something from the count, the latter issued a charter by which he greatly increased the possessions of the Turritan desert beyond what they had previously been. He also handed over to the desert in perpetual servitude the soldiers guilty of the Capuan treachery, whom he had brought with him to Squillace to be put to death but had spared at the intercession of our Saint.

All these facts are established partly by Geoffrey Malaterra, in the chapter cited immediately above and the following two chapters, and partly by the charter which Count Roger gave to our Saint after the military expedition just mentioned had ended.

Because of this, and also because Puteanus, Blomenvenna, Surius, Baronio in his *Ecclesiastical Annals*, Summontius in his *History of the Kingdom of Naples*, and nearly all the other writers who mention it reproduce only portions of the charter in their respective *Lives of Saint Bruno*, I shall place the complete document before the reader, taken from Morkensius’s recension of the present section, with additions at the end concerning matters that can conveniently be noted here.

The determination of the date both of its issuance and of the siege of Capua, and consequently of the time when Saint Bruno appeared to Count Roger in a dream and delivered him from the impending danger, I have decided to postpone to the following section, lest this one otherwise grow excessively long. [Col. 0390D–0391B]

637. The document reads as follows:

“In the name of the eternal God and of our Savior Jesus Christ.

“In the year 1098 from the Incarnation of the same Lord, in the sixth indiction, the glorious King David, inspired by the Spirit, said: ‘I will tell of all your wonders.’ Therefore I, Roger, by the mercy of God count of Calabria and Sicily, wish it to be known”—alternative reading: “known”—“to all faithful Christians what benefits God has granted to me, a sinner, through the prayers of the reverend man Father Bruno, most holy father of the brothers who dwell in the churches of Saint Mary of the Desert and Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, which are situated in my land between the town called Stilo and Arena.

“When I was at the siege of Capua on the Kalends of March, and had placed Sergius, a Greek by nationality, in command of more than two hundred soldiers of his own nation and as master of the army’s watch, he, having been anticipated by satanic persuasion, promised the prince of Capua, who had offered him a considerable quantity of gold, that he would provide an entrance at night for the purpose of attacking me and my army.

“The night of the treachery arrived, and the prince of Capua and his army stood ready for battle as promised. While I had given myself over to sleep, after some part of the night had passed, an old man of reverent appearance stood beside my bed. His garments were torn, and he could not restrain his tears.

“When in the vision I asked him the reason for his weeping and tears, he seemed to me to weep even more bitterly. When I asked him again who he was and why he wept, he said:

“‘I weep for the souls of Christians, and for you together with them. But rise as quickly as possible and take up your arms, if God permits you to free yourself and the souls of your fighting men.’

“Throughout the vision he appeared to me to be in every respect the venerable Father Bruno.” [Col. 0391B–D]

638. “I awoke in great terror, frightened by the vision. At once I took up my arms, shouting to the soldiers that they should arm themselves and mount their horses, striving to determine whether the vision was true.

“At the sound of the tumult and the trumpet blast, the impious Sergius and his followers fled, following the prince of Capua in the hope that they would find refuge in the city. The soldiers captured one hundred and sixty-two men, both wounded and unwounded, and from them we established that the vision had been true.

“By God’s will I returned to Squillace on 29 July, after the city of Capua had been taken. There I was ill for fifteen continuous days.

“The aforesaid venerable Father Bruno then came to me with four of his brothers, and they consoled me with holy and devout conversations. I recounted the vision to that reverend man and offered him humble thanks because, even while absent, he had cared for me in his prayers.

“He humbled himself and declared that it was not he”—alternative reading: “had not been he”—“whom I had believed it to be, but the angel of God who stands beside princes in time of war.

“I also humbly asked him, for the love of God, to accept in the land of Squillace the generous revenues which I was offering him. He refused to receive them, saying that for this reason he had left his father’s house and mine: to serve his God freely, as one detached from the affairs of the world.

“He had been, as it were, first and foremost in my entire household. At last, with difficulty, I was able to persuade him to agree freely to accept my small gift.” [Col. 0391D–0392B]

639. “I gave to the same Father Bruno and to his successors, to possess in perpetuity without temporal service, the monastery of Saint James of Nuntauro”—alternative reading: Mentauro—“together with the castle situated below the said monastery, built in ancient times, and the wooden castle situated on the summit of the mountain toward the sea. The mountain descends directly from the site of the built castle; the local inhabitants call this castle Belvider.

“I also gave the village of Saint Mary, situated on the bank of the said mountain between east and south; likewise my house called Buttarium, with the vats”—or troughs—“that are in that house, which belonged to my brother Robert Guiscard and were given to me by Roger, duke, my dearest nephew.

“I give the villages of Mentabri, Oliviani, and Gasparina, where formerly there had been a village, with all their appurtenances, as they are written here divided, namely, from the land of Coxanus”—and so forth.

Morkensius has omitted here the description of the boundaries of this land, since, as he says, it had nothing to do with his subject.

“Everything within”—alternative reading: below—“these boundaries, both the vassals who now dwell in the said villages and those who will dwell there in the future, I grant to be under your jurisdiction, Father Bruno, and that of your brothers who succeed you.

“I also grant that you and your successors may retain as dependents persons both from the county of Calabria and Sicily and from outside it, wherever they may be.

“You and your successors may exchange the dwellings of the villages whenever you wish. You may also do with the monastery of Saint James itself, which I have donated, and with everything in it and belonging to that land, whatever I could have done when it was permitted to me.” [Col. 0392B–D]

640. “No one within these boundaries may claim or possess anything as his own, since I have made a sufficiently satisfactory voluntary settlement and exchange with everyone who held possessions there: land for some, money for others, and perpetual freedom for certain people because they were villeins.

“There are many lands within”—alternative reading: below—“these boundaries that belong to you, Father Bruno, and to your successors, which I gave to you together with Arsafia at the time of the dedication of your principal church.

“Let no one within these boundaries dare to fowl, hunt, or fish in the sea without the consent of the aforesaid brothers. In all these matters the said brothers shall have your rights: to take pasture or acorns, cut wood, divert waters, possess forests, or possess meadows.

“Let no one whatsoever do anything contrary to this or infringe it in those lands on the pretext of any custom, under the pretext of being a nobleman or baron, or demand from their vassals, villeins, or dependents any temporal service—whether from those who now exist or those whom they will have in the future.

“Let no one compel those vassals or villeins to maintain communal obligations with the land of Squillace, Severetus, or their villages. Instead, they shall be preserved in complete freedom, for the use and dominion of the brothers, to possess perpetually.

“In the sea beside the boundaries that I have fixed, they shall have every right that I myself have had in times past.” [Col. 0392D–0393B]

641. “At the request of Brother Lanvinus I have ordered the boundaries of the village of Arunchum and its holding to be set down here; from ancient times it has belonged to Arsafia.

“I also gave to the same Father Bruno and to his successors the garden of Saint Nicholas, which I held as my own property.

“I also gave them the inheritance of my villein Calogericus, who had died without tongue and children, together with the vassals and villeins dwelling in that same village. In the same freedom and peaceful use as in the other places granted above and, by my will, freed from every servile yoke, both the said brothers and the vassals, dependents, and villeins shall enjoy every liberty in this place called Arunchum.

“They shall enjoy it also in all places that may be joined to these boundaries and that, God willing, they will possess, or [as to] villeins; I have provided that they themselves enjoy it both [as] lords and faithful Christians, as in the places written above [the syntax of the transmitted clause is corrupt].

“I also give to you, Father Bruno, and to your successors in perpetuity, my mill and fulling mill, which are below Squillace beside the spring called Alexius, with complete freedom and immunity, so that you shall owe no service for them to anyone—not to me nor to my successors.

“You may take all the water you require from my watercourse, and, if you wish, alter for the better the position of the water-channel serving the mill and fulling mill on that land of mine, without any person, or I myself, or my successors, offering any opposition.

“And with the waters that are on your land, you may make every use according to your own will.” [Col. 0393B–D]

642. “I also give you, Father Bruno, and your successors, one hundred and twelve lineages of slaves and serfs and their sons, as perpetual slaves and serfs forever, wherever they may be and dwell, with all their possessions. I reserved them for the service of you and your successors because they were found at the siege of Capua participating in the treachery of that pestilent Sergius. I had kept them liable to death, to be punished by various deaths, upon my return to Squillace; [Col. 0394A] but, freed at your petition, I bind their sons to you and your successors, and their sons’ sons forever as perpetual slaves and serfs, for the personal and perpetual servitude of blessed Mary and the protomartyr Stephen.

“Moreover, at your petition, Brother Lanvin, I grant that the animals of your vassals, commendati, and serfs may freely pasture throughout the holdings of the surrounding lands and places, and may gather acorns throughout all my woods. This privilege was written on the second day of August, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1099, indiction seven, by the hand of Fulco, my chaplain, at Squillace in the chapel of Saint Matthew, in the presence of and with the confirmation of the venerable and most holy Father John, [Col. 0394B] bishop of the see of Squillace, residing there beside the doors of the church; and with the consent of Adelaide, countess, my wife. Also residing with me and serving as witnesses to this donation were Rodulphus, count of Lorotello, my nephew; William of Hauteville; Odo Bonus, marquis; Josbert of Luciaco; Borello Malgerius, my son; Malduith Berengerius; Niellus of Ferlit; Richard of Treveris; Rodulphus Pain Evin; Hubert of Solma; Reynald of Chincham; Robert of Cuculo; Ermenfred, chaplain of Saint Matthew; Robert of Layna, stratigotus of the town; Blasilius, protospatharius; and Theodore Manchino.”

643. “Let no one presume to do or say anything whatsoever, whether small or great, against this voluntary and desired donation of mine. If he is a peasant or a townsman, let him understand that my court will take whatever he possesses in movable goods; nevertheless, he shall pay the brothers ten pounds of gold, and, if he is accused and convicted, the brothers’ losses, should they have suffered any, shall be made good from the property of those evildoers. If he is a knight or baron, he shall pay two hundred pounds of gold to the court of my successors or of myself. If he does not have that much, all his movable goods shall be mine, and, unless he makes due satisfaction to those same brothers, he shall pay them fifty pounds of gold.

“Neither I nor my successors may henceforth alter, do, or contradict anything, whether small or great, concerning all that I have freely granted. But if I—or, God forbid, my successors—should at any time act contrary to this, in anything small or great, may we incur the everlasting wrath of God, of blessed Mary, and of blessed Stephen the protomartyr, in all the matters stated above. And Father John, bishop, at my petition, pronounced the gravest anathema against such persons in his principal church, before all the people present and the witnesses named above; but may those who preserve the communion of the saints receive a good reward from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen, amen, amen.

“+ Roger, Count. + Adelaide, Countess. + William of Hauteville. [Col. 0395A] + Rodulphus, Count of Lorotello. + Odo Bonus, marquis. + Josbert of Luciaco. + Niellus of Ferlit. + Malgerius, son of Count Roger. + Rodulphus Pain Evin. + Richard of Treveris. + I, Fulco, chaplain of Lord Roger, by his command wrote and subscribed this privilege.”

644. Such, then, is that very extensive and celebrated privilege or charter which Count Roger granted to Saint Bruno, since he had no doubt that he had been delivered from the most immediate danger during the siege of Capua through the warning and merits of the person who appeared to him—so it seemed—to be Saint Bruno. Mörckensius notes at the end that a leaden bull was attached to its original.

Several matters must now be observed concerning it, and first of all concerning the vision in which Count Roger says that Saint Bruno—or at least an old man resembling that holy man in face and in the appearance of his entire body—appeared to him in sleep and was heard warning him. To deal with this matter in the appropriate way, it will almost suffice to quote here what the anonymous author of the fourth book of the Annals of the Carthusian Order, not yet published at that time, committed to writing and what the frequently mentioned Parisian Carthusian again communicated to me, copied from a copy of this work belonging to Vallis-Dei.

The Carthusian annalist writes as follows:

“From the apparition of Saint Bruno made to Count Roger, a question may arise: whether Saint Bruno truly appeared to Count Roger. For, when the count, after returning from the siege—see no. 638, the charter now transcribed—visited him while ill, Bruno expressly denied that he himself had been the one who appeared, but said that it was an angel of God who stands beside a prince in time of war, as is read in the earlier charter—that is, the one already quoted. Whether Saint Bruno said this out of humility or from the truth of the matter may be resolved from what Saint Augustine writes, in *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, chapter 10 and following, and in *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 29, and after him Durandus, in book 7, chapter 35 of *On the Duties of the Dead*: namely, that the living often appear in dreams to those who sleep, although they themselves do not know that they appear, and hear from those who have dreamed this that they saw them doing or saying something in a dream. It is therefore credible that these are the operations of angels, appearing in the form and appearance of those whose merits occasion the apparitions, through the dispensation of God’s providence, for some kind of consolation of the living. Thus it is probable that an angel of God appeared to Count Roger in the form and appearance of Saint Bruno, through whose grace and merits the apparition took place. Let the reader consult Thyraeus, in *On the Apparition of Spirits*, and Cardinal Bona, in *On the Discernment of Spirits*, who treat these matters excellently.”

645. Thus far the anonymous annalist, and correctly, so far as appears. Since, moreover, in the words quoted from these charters—“I wish the benefits to be known which God has granted me through the prayers of the reverend man, Brother Bruno, most pious father of the brothers who dwell in the churches of Saint Mary of the Desert and of Saint Stephen the protomartyr”—mention is made of the two churches, Saint Mary of the Desert and Saint Stephen the protomartyr, as though they were two distinct monasteries, and since it is also implied that Saint Bruno presided over both, he makes the following observation:

“Although Saint Bruno is called the father of the brothers of both churches, this must nevertheless be understood only of the supreme authority that he possessed in both, as their patriarch. For Lanvin is called prior of Saint Stephen in the other charter—that is, the one issued in 1101 and quoted below. ‘At the petition,’ it says, ‘of Brother Lanvin, prior of the church of Saint Stephen.’

“Nevertheless, the possessions granted by Roger were held in common by both. This is clear from the earlier charter—the one already given—in which Roger grants the conspirators ‘and their sons’ sons’—that is, the sons of those conspirators—‘as perpetual slaves and serfs forever, for the personal and perpetual servitude of blessed Mary and Saint Stephen the protomartyr.’

“Furthermore, since in the transcribed charter of the monastery of Saint James of Mentauro, which Roger bestowed upon Saint Bruno and his disciples, mention occurs of the prince of Capua to whom Sergius wished to betray Roger, the same author also supplies some information about both this prince and the monastery of Saint James of Mentauro. Concerning the prince he writes as follows:

“‘The name of the prince of Capua, to whom Sergius promised that he would provide a nocturnal opportunity to attack Roger, could not be found among writers,’ Michael the monk admits in the *Capuan Sanctuary*, published by him in 1630. ‘But in the revision of his work made in 1637, he gives the name of this hitherto unknown prince.’ He says to me: ‘The prince’s name, long unknown, has at last been learned. Don Camillo Tutini, a Neapolitan investigator of antiquities, preserves a manuscript chronicle in which it is read that Landon, count of Teano, of the race of the Lombard princes, was elected prince by the Capuans after the expulsion of the son of Richard.’

“But since the prince expelled by the Capuans was not the son of Richard but of Jordan, as Malaterra teaches in book 4, chapter 26, contrary to what is read in that manuscript chronicle preserved by Tutini, this appears suspicious to me. Consequently, it cannot make me regard it as certain that Landon was the prince of Capua to whom Sergius wished to hand Roger over.”

646. With regard to the monastery of Saint James of Mentauro, the aforementioned annalist of the Carthusian Order makes the following observation:

“The monastery of Saint James of Mentauro, granted by Roger to Saint Bruno, is, according to the notes of our Constantius, a grange now called Saint Anne, in which, at the beginning of the restoration of this Charterhouse, one lay brother continually lived. There, after Saint Bruno’s death, Lanvin established certain monks who were less suited to the eremitical life, with the permission of the pontiff, so that they might lead the cenobitic life, as we shall say in its proper place.”

The author of the *Annals of the Carthusian Order*, whom we have cited, subsequently fulfilled in fact what he promises to say here, under the year 1114, writing there as follows:

“As regards Carthusian affairs in Calabria, in this year—namely 1114—Lanvin, since, in accordance with the permission obtained the previous year from Paschal, the supreme pontiff, he had received into the eremitical life many persons not only from various nations but also from distant regions, as the papal bulls say, observing that some of them were less suited to it, decided to establish another monastery in which they might at least live as cenobites. He conceived this wisely. For, according to the Rule handed down by the holy Patriarch not in writing but by word of mouth, a novice was received among us only on this condition: ‘that if by chance he could not or would not endure our way of life, he should by no means return to the world, but should instead undertake some other form of religious life that he could bear.’ Thus provision was made for the honor and salvation of the novice who departed, since he could pass immediately from the desert to a monastery.

“The master of the desert held responsibility for both monasteries, and the man who presided over the cenobites under the title of provost, dean, or even prior obeyed that same master, as supreme prior, in accordance with the decree of the supreme pontiff Paschal, from whom Lanvin obtained the following letter for this purpose: ‘Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God,’ and so forth.”

647. These are the words of the anonymous annalist cited above. There are scarcely any other matters concerning the transcribed charter of Count Roger that need to be observed here. Something further could indeed be noted concerning the words by which the instrument implies that the Saint had spent some time in Count Roger’s household; but these matters have already been sufficiently treated in nos. 571 and following. The same is true of Malgerius, who is called “son of Count Roger” both in the text and in the subscriptions of the charters, although he was neither his legitimate nor his illegitimate son; see also nos. 586 and following.

As for the others who either subscribe the charter or are mentioned in its text as having been present as witnesses to the donation made through it, Rodulphus, count of Lorotello, whom Count Roger here calls “his nephew,” was very probably his paternal uncle, as can easily be understood from Cangius’s *Annotations on Anna Comnena*, pages 238 and following. Of the others, some of whom also subscribe other charters already issued by Count Roger, many are likewise found subscribed to certain public instruments preserved in Rocchus Pirrus’s *Sacred Sicily* and issued by Count Roger, as anyone who wishes to consult these documents will discover. It was useful at least to note this here, since I cannot provide detailed information about each individual.

Furthermore, so that the commentary, which by its bulk already nearly exceeds all reasonable bounds, may not grow still further without necessity, I do not explain here what the various barbarous terms occurring in the charter mean. I have therefore thought it appropriate to do the same both for this charter and for the other charters granted to our Saint, since the diligent reader can easily find the meaning of those terms both in our onomastic indexes and in Cangius’s *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*.

§ XL. The time at which Count Roger besieged Capua, and whether the charter which, after the subjugation of that city, this prince granted to Bruno was issued in the same year in which that event occurred.

648. Count Roger himself makes sufficiently clear in the charter recently transcribed here, which he granted to Saint Bruno, when it happened that he besieged Capua. At its beginning he speaks as follows:

“ In the name of the eternal God and our Savior Jesus Christ. In the year from his Incarnation 1098, indiction six, the glorious King David, preceded by the Holy Spirit, says: ‘I shall recount all your wonders.’ Therefore I, Roger, by the mercy of God count of Calabria and Sicily, wish all faithful Christians to know the benefits that God has granted to me, a sinner, through the prayers of the reverend man Brother Bruno, most pious father of the brothers who dwell in the churches of Saint Mary of the Desert and of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, which are situated in my land between the town called Stilo and Arena, when I was in the siege of Capua on the Kalends of March and had appointed Sergius, a Greek by nation, as prince over two hundred armed men of his nation and master of the army’s watch, etc.”

By these words he indicates that he was in the siege of Capua in the year 1098. For all the words inserted between the two expressions “indiction six” and “when I was in the siege of Capua” must be regarded merely as a prefatory clause enclosed in parentheses, so that the sense is: “In the year from the Incarnation of the same Jesus Christ 1098, indiction six … when I was in the siege of Capua on the Kalends of March.”

I hold this first because, in the other charter, which will be transcribed below and which is dated to 1101, Count Roger himself most clearly indicates that the Capuan siege occurred in 1098, in these words:

“These are the names of those … who were found in the siege of the city of Capua on the Kalends of March, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098, indiction six, whom I, Roger, etc.”

Moreover, the year in which the charter under investigation in this section was issued cannot be identified as 1098, since, as will be shown, Count Roger did not grant it to the Saint before the year immediately following the Capuan siege and the apparition of the Saint offered to the prince during that siege. It is otherwise established that this military expedition occurred in 1098, as I now proceed to prove.

649. Lupus Protospata, a contemporary author who, as must be carefully noted, begins the year according to the Greek practice in September, writes in Muratori, volume 5 of the *Writers of Italian Affairs*, page 47:

“In October of the year 1098 a comet-star appeared … and in this year Capua was captured by Count Roger in the month of March.”

But Michael the monk, having prefaced his discussion of the charter at issue here by saying that it had been given to him to read after being copied in full from the royal archives, writes as follows:

“Lupus Protospata, published by P. D. Antonio Caracciolo, writes that the year 1098 was the year of the siege of Capua. But one must not depart from the reckoning of Baronius, who, following Geoffrey’s account, assigns the year of the siege as 1097; the anonymous Cassinese, printed together with Protospata, agrees with him. Indeed, this privilege itself supports that view. Roger returned from the siege to Squillace on 29 July. On 2 August he granted this privilege to Saint Bruno. But because many days intervene between the granting of the privilege and Roger’s return, especially those fifteen days during which Roger—see no. 638—was ill, was visited by Saint Bruno, and discussed making the donation, the named months of July and August cannot belong to the same year. Rather, July, with its twenty-ninth day, belongs to 1097, and August, with its second day, to 1098.”

Thus far his words; and correctly indeed he asserts that the month of July, in which Count Roger returned to Squillace from the siege of Capua, and the month of August, in which the charter was dated, belong to two different years. For, as the count himself teaches in the charter—see again no. 638—he returned to Squillace on 29 July, whereas the charter is dated to 2 August. Thus, if the count’s return and the granting of the charter did not belong to different years, only three days would have intervened between them; but, as appears from the very text of the charter itself—see again the same no. 638—that is not plausible.

650. Nevertheless, although the author cited above correctly assigns to two different years the July in which Count Roger returned to Squillace from the siege of Capua and the August in which he granted the famous charter to the Saint, he wrongly places the siege of Capua in 1097 with Baronius, from whom he says that one must not depart, against the explicit testimony of Lupus Protospata, relying on the authority of Geoffrey Malaterra, an equally contemporary writer.

For although in the Sicilian author’s *History*, book 4, chapter 26, there occur words that seem to assign that siege to the year 1097, those words are not Malaterra’s. The date given by Lupus Protospata in the words just quoted must certainly be retained. Both assertions will become clear from what follows.

I begin with the posterior argument, that is, with the truth of the date which Lupus Protospata assigns to the Capuan siege by connecting it with the year 1098. Romuald of Salerno, a near-contemporary author, writes in his *Chronicle*, concerning the Christian crusaders waging war in the East against the unbelievers:

“They captured Antioch, a most famous city, in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1098, indiction six.”

Then, after inserting several matters irrelevant here, he adds:

“In that same year, in the same indiction, Duke Roger, together with Roger, count of Sicily, besieged the city of Capua and, on the fortieth day of its siege, captured it and restored it to Richard, the prince.”

It may indeed be objected that the chronological notes by which Romuald fixes the time of the events he narrates often contain errors. But even if that is so, as will become evident to anyone who examines Romuald’s work, it applies chiefly when he expresses chronological indicators in abbreviated form by numbers or letters standing for numbers. In the case of the year 1098, in which the Christians captured Antioch and in which he also records that Capua was besieged by Duke Roger and his uncle, Count Roger, he does not use an abbreviation by numbers or letters standing for numbers, but gives the date in full words. It is universally acknowledged that Antioch was truly captured by the Christians in the year 1098 as he states. Therefore, since he does not err in assigning that event to 1098, he should not be judged to err when, in the same place, he assigns the Capuan siege to that same year, 1098.

651. But even if the matter were otherwise and Romuald’s testimony concerning the correct assignment of the Capuan siege to 1098 were to be considered of little weight, Eadmer makes it certain that this writer and Lupus Protospata correctly assign the siege to that year. Eadmer not only flourished at the time of that siege but was also present during it.

He remained a constant companion of Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, throughout his life, including when Anselm departed from England for Rome in 1097 and then proceeded to Roger, duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, who was in the camp before besieged Capua. As may be seen in our April volume 2, page 865, Eadmer composed not only Anselm’s life, divided into two books, but also the six books of his *History of Recent Events in England*, printed first by Selden and later included in the aforementioned volume of our work. In the first four books he also recounts matters relating to that holy archbishop of Canterbury, particularly the journey to Rome just mentioned and his approach to Duke Roger before Capua.

At the end of book 2, chapter 2, number 19, of this history, after informing the reader that Anselm had finally obtained from the king permission to go to Rome, Eadmer adds:

“In the year from the Incarnation of the Son of God 1097 these things took place, on Thursday, which was the Ides of October.”

Then, after inserting several events that took place shortly after 15 October in the year thus assigned, he narrates the journey of that holy bishop toward Rome. It is therefore beyond doubt that Anselm undertook it in the same year, 1097.

On that journey, as can be understood partly from Eadmer’s *Life of Saint Anselm*, composed as described above and included in the aforementioned volume of our work, book 2, chapter 4, and partly from the *History of Recent Events in England*, also by Eadmer, book 2, chapter 2 and following, Anselm celebrated the feast of Christ’s Nativity with Abbot Hugh at Cluny. From there he proceeded to Lyons; continuing his journey, he passed through Susa unrecognized, celebrated the solemn rites of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection at Saint Michael of Clusa in Piedmont, and, successfully avoiding the ambushes of the Guibertines that had been prepared for him, finally reached Rome not long afterward.

652. After spending ten days in Rome, Anselm, invited by John—formerly his disciple at Bec and then abbot of Saint Savior near Telesia—turned aside to that city in the Land of Labor. When John had taken him to a village of his monastery called Sclavia, situated on a nearby mountain, and he had stayed there for some time, Anselm proceeded to Duke Roger, who at that time was in the camp before besieged Capua. Having learned of the man’s eminent holiness, Roger had invited him to come to him.

This is substantially what Eadmer relates, as I have noted, partly in the *Life of Saint Anselm* written by him and partly in the passages cited above from the *History of Recent Events in England*.

Now, since Anselm, according to Eadmer—who was a contemporary author and accompanied this holy bishop on that journey—set out from England toward Rome in October 1097, reached Rome not long afterward, after the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection that immediately followed October of the year 1097, and soon afterward approached Duke Roger, who at that time was besieging Capua together with his uncle, Count Roger, and his kinsman Richard, it necessarily follows from what Anselm’s unimpeachable testimony records that Capua was besieged in 1098 beyond all doubt.

This is the first point that had to be demonstrated. The second is now to be proved: that the words in Geoffrey Malaterra’s Sicilian history which indicate that the siege of Capua, during which Saint Bruno appeared to Count Roger and rescued him from imminent danger, occurred in 1097, do not belong to that author.

Those words are as follows:

“In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097, Countess Adelaide became pregnant there”—that is, in the camp before besieged Capua—with Count Roger.

As Peregrinus correctly observed before me in his annotations on the *Chronicle of Lupus Protospata*, these words are merely a marginal gloss written by an idle annotator in the margin of the page and subsequently transferred from the margin into the author’s text by an incompetent copyist.

653. I demonstrate this as follows. At the end of book 4, chapter 26, of his *History of Sicily*, Malaterra writes:

“The count himself”—that is, Roger—“rising every day before dawn, used to cross the bridge”—which, as the aforementioned Peregrinus notes in the cited passage, he had built over the Volturnus so that his own army and the joint army of Duke Roger and Prince Richard, who were besieging Capua across the river to the north, would have an open and convenient route—“and visit both armies to see whether they were attentive to the watches. The young men themselves, and especially those to whom the duty more particularly belonged, were flushed with shame because they were more sluggish than the count, a man of more advanced age and made more vigilant by the hardship of bodily wounds and labors. Indeed, his vigilance was a source of wonder to the entire army, and all became more watchful by his example.”

Thus far the text, which is unquestionably Malaterra’s. Immediately after it, however, there are appended the words quoted in the preceding number concerning Adelaide’s pregnancy before Capua, words that end book 4, chapter 26 and whose authorship we are investigating. Then chapter 27 follows, beginning as follows:

“While these things were taking place, Pope Urban, desiring a meeting with the duke and the count, set out from Rome and came to Capua, where they were maintaining the siege.”

Such is the beginning of book 4, chapter 27, in Malaterra’s *History of Sicily*. But who does not see that the words concerning Adelaide’s pregnancy in the camp before Capua, inserted between this passage and Malaterra’s genuine text—which I have just quoted and which is supplied by the preceding chapter—make the author’s narrative confused and divided?

Since this is so, and since such a defective manner of narrating events does not appear characteristic of Malaterra, those words must be attributed not to him but, as I have said, to an inept annotator. To make the matter more certain, it will be useful to strengthen it with another argument.

654. In the preface to book 2 of his work, the *History of Sicily* composed by him, Malaterra promises that he will preserve the chronological and annual order in his narrative. He makes the same promise again in book 4, chapter 18. After twice binding himself to this chronological order, he relates in chapter 25 of that same fourth book that Count Roger gave his daughter in marriage to the king of Hungary and arranged for her to be taken to Pannonia by sea under the care of Henry, bishop of Leocastrum, in May 1097.

Here are his exact words:

“Accordingly, in the year of the Incarnation 1097, after the necessary preparations had been made, in the month of May the count has Henry, bishop of Leocastrum, and certain of his faithful men escort his daughter with three hundred soldiers as far as Thermae; from there he sends them with the girl by sea to Pannonia. After preparing the ships and bringing the girl aboard with many bridal gifts, they give the sails to the wind and, with a favorable breeze blowing, are carried over the sea until they safely reach the port of Alba, which belongs to the kings of Hungary.”

These events, partly in May 1097 and partly somewhat later, are narrated by Malaterra in book 4, chapter 25. In the following chapter he explains that Count Roger was asked by his kinsmen Richard, prince of Aversa, and Duke Roger to bring them assistance against the Capuans, who were rebellious against Richard, and that the duke’s wife was also sent to him by Duke Roger. He then adds in the same chapter:

“But the count, moved and persuaded by affection for his kinsman the prince and by the many words of the duchess, who had been delegated by the duke to make the petition and who set it forth with entreaty and humility, assembled with strong authority an army such as he is known never to have had before, drawn from all Sicily and Calabria, and in the second week of April crossed the Strait in peace and hastened there”—that is, toward Capua, or toward Richard, prince of Aversa, and Duke Roger, whom he was going to assist.

655. This is what Malaterra says in the cited passage.
