He also relates there how Roger, after crossing the Strait in April, led his army through Calabria and Apulia; met Duke Roger on the way; celebrated Pentecost near the river called “Sabatus,” or, as he himself writes, “Sabbatum”; finally set up camp at Capua; and besieged that city together with Duke Roger and Richard, prince of Aversa.

Since, after narrating what had taken place in May 1097, this writer—who professes to preserve the chronological and annual order in his narrative—sets all these events down in writing, it follows from his own account that the April in which Count Roger crossed the Strait, the Pentecost that he celebrated near the river Sabatus, and thus also the time shortly afterward when he set up camp at Capua and besieged that city, belong not to 1097 but to the following year.

Indeed, unless this is so, Malaterra must be said to contradict himself. For, according to his account, Count Roger crossed the Strait in April, celebrated Pentecost near the river Sabatus, and then besieged Capua. If that April belonged to 1097, when Easter fell on 5 April and consequently Pentecost was celebrated on 24 May, it would follow that in May 1097 Count Roger was partly in Calabria or at least Apulia and partly in the camp before Capua.

But Malaterra makes this prince present in that same year and month neither in Calabria or Apulia nor in the camp before Capua, but in Sicily. In book 4, chapter 25, as I have already shown, he records that while Roger was then in Sicily—as is clear from the context of what he writes—his daughter was sent from that region to be married to the king of Hungary, by sea, under the guidance of Henry, bishop of Lecce, in that same year and month.

656. Since this is so, and since no one would say that Malaterra wrote mutually contradictory accounts, he cannot be accused of placing Count Roger, whom he makes present in Sicily throughout May 1097, in that same month in Apulia and in the camp before Capua, far removed from Sicily. It is therefore wholly necessary that the April in which, according to that writer, Count Roger crossed the Strait, the Pentecost which he celebrated near the river Sabatus, and the time shortly afterward when he besieged Capua, belong—even according to Malaterra himself—not to 1097 but to the following year.

It follows further that this writer assigns the Capuan siege to the same year as Lupus Protospata. Consequently, either the words concerning Adelaide’s pregnancy in 1097 in the camp before Capua, transcribed above, are not Malaterra’s, or, if they do belong to him rather than to an inept annotator, an error concerning the year 1097 to which they are attached must have entered through the fault or negligence of copyists, and 1098 must be substituted for that year.

Pagius, in his *Critica*, had thought that Malaterra assigned the Capuan siege to 1097 because of the aforementioned words concerning Adelaide’s pregnancy before Capua in that year. Seeking to reconcile him with Lupus Protospata, who connects the same siege with 1098, Pagius argued that the siege of Capua began in 1097 but was not completed until 1098, when the month of May had advanced.

But since, from what has already been said, Malaterra himself places the Capuan siege not in 1097—as some have persuaded themselves because of the words concerning Adelaide’s pregnancy before Capua in that year—but in 1098, that writer must be corrected.

### 657

For if one were obliged to stand by that account, it would follow that the siege of Capua lasted for several months. But this is clearly contrary to the truth, both from Malaterra, who teaches—partly in the cited chapter of Book IV and partly in chapter 27 and the two following chapters—that Count Roger celebrated Pentecost near the River Sabato in 1098, when that feast fell on 16 May, and only then moved his army toward the siege of Capua, accepting the city’s surrender not very long afterward [Col. 0404C]; and also from Romuald of Salerno and the anonymous Cassinese monk, first brought to public light by Antonio Caracciolo and then by Camillo Peregrini, and finally included by Muratori, together with the annotations of that later editor, in volume V of *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores* along with Lupus Protospata. Both expressly state in their chronicles that Capua surrendered on the fortieth day of the siege, or that it was subdued by Duke Roger and his uncle, Count Roger. The former does so in the words numbered 650 and transcribed above; the latter in these words:

> “Duke Roger, together with Count Roger, besieging Capua for forty days, captured it and restored it to Richard, son of Jordan.”

These words are indeed referred to the year 1097 in the Cassinese manuscript 47, from which the anonymous monk’s *Chronicle* was first edited by Caracciolo, and are printed as such by him and by Muratori; hence someone might perhaps argue that the siege of Capua must be assigned to that year. But Peregrini makes the following observation concerning this place in that manuscript:

> “As usual, Codex XLVII anticipates the year, and the edition made from it does the same. Not so Codex CXCIX, in which this passage occurs under the year 1098.”

So much for him. From what he observes in his preliminary notice to that *Chronicle*, however, you will readily see that the reference of the siege and surrender of Capua to the year 1097 in Cassinese manuscript 47 must be attributed not to the anonymous monk, who flourished at approximately the time when Capua was besieged, but to a more recent copyist, who arranged and divided by years, at his own discretion, what the monk had committed to writing. Since this is so, the anonymous monk provides nothing contrary to the opinion by which we assign the siege of Capua to 1098, and we must therefore remain with Lupus Protospata, who records that year for the military expedition of Duke and Count Roger.

### 658

Although this is indeed how the matter stands regarding the year in which this writer records Capua’s surrender, a different judgment must be made concerning the month to which he assigns it. For he notes that the city was “captured by Count Roger in the month of March.” Yet it is clear that this occurred later than March 1098, both from the *Life of Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury*, written by Eadmer, [Col. 0405B] and from Geoffrey Malaterra.

To demonstrate first that this is established by the said *Life of Anselm*: Eadmer, in the edition printed among our April volumes, volume II, pp. 886 and following, records that he celebrated the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection—which in 1098 fell on 28 March—together with Saint Anselm at the monastery of Saint Michael, situated in Piedmont; that he then came to Rome; that after spending ten days there he went to the monastery of Saint Saviour in the Terra di Lavoro, where he had been most cordially invited by its abbot, formerly his disciple; and that finally he went to Duke Roger, who was besieging Capua and had ordered that Saint Anselm be invited to come to him; he and Eadmer then went to him, remaining with him for a considerable period.

Now, since this was so, and since Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, who according to the foregoing took part in the siege of Capua for some time, could in no way have done so if Capua had surrendered as early as March 1098, as anyone can easily understand from all the passages just cited from the life of this holy bishop, it becomes completely clear from that life that Capua did not surrender to Count Roger in March 1098. The same is no less clearly established by Malaterra. For since, as has already been stated, this writer records that Count Roger did not bring his forces against Capua until after celebrating Pentecost near the River Sabato, on 16 May 1098, it is indisputable from Malaterra that the city had not already surrendered in March of that year [Col. 0405D].

### 659

“But,” you will say, “what month, then, should be substituted for March, which Lupus Protospata assigns to the surrender of Capua?” Pagius, in his *Critica* under the year 1098, Henschenius in his annotations on Book II, chapter 2, of Eadmer’s *History of England*, and other learned men pronounce in favor of May. Peregrini, however, hesitates over whether June may be substituted for March in the passage of Protospata concerning Capua’s surrender, transcribed above.

He writes there as follows:

> “Capua was therefore recovered, apparently no earlier than the end of May and the beginning of summer, if the forty days of the siege—assigned, as I have shown above, by Romuald and the anonymous Cassinese writer—are to be reckoned not from the arrival of the count, but from the day on which Prince Richard II, who held Aversa, the neighboring city, had himself surrounded Capua. Otherwise it must be said that it was recovered in June; and I should not object to this if June, rather than May, is to be restored in Lupus in place of March. For it is quite evident that the month of March was often substituted for May, perhaps because, in the Norman period, proper names were abbreviated by being written only in capital letters. Thus the month of March, written in this manner, was very often taken by later copyists for May. The same thing occurs in the calendar of the ancient Campanian Breviary, in which the feast of Saint Potentiana the virgin is incorrectly entered on 19 March, although it is celebrated on 19 May.”

### 660

So far Peregrini. As I have already noted, he hesitates somewhat over whether May should be restored in place of March, the month in which Lupus Protospata’s *Chronicle* states that Capua was captured; nevertheless, he leans more strongly toward the opinion that May must be substituted for March altogether. To defend this view, he asserts that Capua was surrounded by Prince Richard of Aversa, although Count Roger certainly did not bring his army against it before 16 May, as can easily be gathered from the foregoing; and he maintains that the forty days during which, according to the testimony of Romuald of Salerno and the anonymous Cassinese writer cited above, the siege lasted must be counted from the time when this surrounding was carried out, not from the time when Count Roger first arrived at the camp with his army [Col. 0406C].

But it appears from what Malaterra records in Book IV, chapter 26, and the two following chapters of his *History of Sicily*, that Capua was neither surrounded before Count Roger’s arrival nor subdued while May was still in progress, when that prince established his camp before it. For, as that writer relates in the same place, when Count Roger was leading his army from Calabria toward Apulia, he encountered Duke Roger near Liscum. After they had conferred with one another, the former moved his army toward Melfi and the latter toward Benevento. Consequently, while Count Roger was already hastening to besiege Capua, Duke Roger’s army had not yet encamped before that city, so that Prince Richard—who, as will be explained below, did not possess sufficient forces of his own—could not at that time have kept it surrounded [Col. 0406D].

Count Roger, after resting his army for some time near Benevento, moved on and encamped at the River Sabato. There he celebrated Pentecost, which in that year, 1098 after Christ’s birth, fell on 16 May. Not long afterward, as appears from the envoys whom he had sent to the Capuans, he learned that they would neither accept terms of peace nor wished to be reconciled with Prince Richard. He then finally entered Capuan territory with his army in order to besiege Capua.

### 661

Listen now to what else Malaterra supplies that bears on this matter in chapter 26. Speaking of Count Roger, he says:

> “But when he heard from the returning envoys that they were undertaking nothing, but were persisting arrogantly and utterly in their wickedness, he moved from there—from the River Sabato—and crossed into Capuan territory. At dawn he approached the city, preceding the army with a thousand armed men; he militarily overthrew and disastrously mocked many who had come out, and would have injured many more had not the dust, raised by the horses’ feet and driven together in the thickest clouds by the wind, intervened. Thus he returned to his camp. On the following day, moving closer to the city with his whole army, he surrounded it with a siege from the southern side, enclosing it from the eastern bank to the western.”

Since, as these words of Malaterra show, the Capuans sent an armed body against Count Roger, who approached their city accompanied by only a thousand soldiers before he had brought his army up to it, it is clear that Capua had not yet been surrounded. Moreover, since Malaterra states in the words just quoted that Count Roger, after bringing his army up to Capua, enclosed it on the eastern and western sides, and immediately adds:

> “But the duke and the prince, besieging the city with their army from the northern side, strive to weigh it down,”

he seems to indicate that Capua was first surrounded at that very time from the southern and western sides by Count Roger and from the northern side by Duke Roger and Prince Richard. It should therefore not be thought that the latter had surrounded it before Count Roger’s arrival [Col. 0407C].

### 662

Nor does Prince Richard appear to have had sufficient forces to do so at that time. Apart from the fact that he held under his authority only Aversa and a small tract of land adjoining that city, Malaterra adds the following immediately to the words just quoted:

> “Moreover, the count, on whose counsel everyone depended, because he was more anxious and more prudent in all undertakings, and watchful with vigilant care, constructed a bridge of wood and arranged it across the river—the Volturnus, namely—in such a way that, with free passage open, it served as a crossing for his own army and that of the duke. Thus the city was so hard pressed by both armies that no safe entrance or exit, by land or water, was open from any side.”

From these words, in which Malaterra mentions only two armies—one subject to Count Roger and the other to Duke Roger—it appears that only a small number of Prince Richard’s troops were incorporated into Duke Roger’s army. Nevertheless, Richard doubtless brought almost all the forces he possessed to that expedition, since the success of the undertaking was of the greatest concern to him. Malaterra therefore calls that army both Richard’s—because the prince had at least some troops in it—and Duke Roger’s, as is also shown by other words of Malaterra transcribed above [Col. 0408A].

Now, since Prince Richard appears, as has been said, to have been provided with very few troops, it seems scarcely credible that he could have surrounded Capua before Count Roger’s arrival, especially since, according to the foregoing, Duke Roger’s army was not yet with him at that time.

### 663

It follows from this that the siege of Capua probably began only when Count Roger brought his army up to the city. Consequently, since according to the foregoing it was not begun before 16 May, and since it lasted forty days, it cannot have ended in May.

But even if we grant for the moment that Prince Richard had surrounded Capua before Count Roger arrived there with his army, it will still appear probable that the city did not surrender during May. For since, as is clear from the foregoing, Count Roger halted with his army at the River Sabato, not far from Benevento, on 16 May—the day on which Pentecost fell in 1098—and celebrated that feast there, and since he does not appear to have moved from there immediately afterward, it is most probable that he did not establish his camp before Capua before 20 May. Consequently, if the city surrendered while May was still in progress, it would follow that Count Roger could have taken part in its siege for only about ten days.

But it is clearly apparent from what both Malaterra records in Book IV, chapter 26, and the two following chapters of his *History of Sicily*, and what Eadmer records in the *Life of Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury*, in our April volume II, p. 887, no. 45 and following, that the count was present at that military expedition for more than ten days. For the sake of brevity, I shall omit what Malaterra supplies in the cited passage concerning this matter, since it proves the point less clearly than Eadmer; I shall transcribe only the words of the latter writer, and only those most relevant here.

### 664

After briefly relating that Saint Anselm had been invited to go to Duke Roger of Apulia, who was occupied with the siege of Capua—an expedition to which, as he says, Count Roger of Sicily had brought many thousands of Saracens and in which he was therefore engaged—Eadmer continues:

> “We mounted, went, and spent several days in the siege, remaining apart in tents from the crowds and tumult of the resounding army. Where we were there was a certain little church, utterly deserted, and beside its entrance a cistern broken open above, displaying through its rupture a great and exceedingly deep opening. In that church, as though in a chamber, we lived as we pleased, devoting ourselves there to quiet and to our work, and having the duke himself and his men at hand with us every day, whenever we wished. One night, while we were sleeping there, it happened that Anselm, compelled by bodily necessity, rose silently and, so as not to disturb us, made his way slowly toward the entrance, according to his custom. When he had gone out and, forgetting the pit, turned aside in the darkness, he fell into the depths, crying out loudly as he fell: ‘Holy Mary!’ At the sound, we and our companions, who were resting in the tents, awoke and sprang from our beds. Running up, we saw the man in the depths, and were almost overcome by fear and anguish of heart. Perceiving this, he immediately raised his head and, with a cheerful expression, signaled to us by his look that he had suffered no injury. Some of our number then descended on the other side of the precipice, where there was a path down, and brought him out of the place completely safe and unharmed.”

### 665

> “After this, when Pope Urban, the pontiff of the Apostolic See, came there, Anselm and the leaders of the entire army went out to meet him. He was escorted with the great pomp of worldly glory and conducted to a tent that had been prepared for him near us, superior to the others. Thus, until the city surrendered, the siege had the lord pope and Anselm nearby, so that the households of both seemed to be one rather than two, and scarcely anyone would turn aside to the pope without also visiting Anselm. The pope was honored by all as their common father and shepherd; Anselm, however, was loved by everyone as a gentle and mild man, and one who, in their judgment, owed nothing to anyone.”

Since, as Eadmer teaches in the words just quoted, Saint Anselm—who, as Eadmer had stated shortly before, was then staying at the village of Sclavia, belonging to the monastery of Saint Saviour near Telese—was invited by Duke Roger to come to him at the camp before Capua, and since he remained for several days in that camp, where, as Eadmer again testifies shortly after the words already quoted, Count Roger was present; and since Pope Urban II afterward came to the same camp and remained there with Anselm until the siege ended with the city’s surrender, Eadmer, by stating that all these events occurred during the siege of Capua and while Count Roger was present, seems altogether to indicate that the siege lasted for more than ten days after the said count had joined it. This is especially so because in the words immediately following he adds details that clearly indicate that Anselm was frequently present in the camps of the duke and the count during the siege [Col. 0409D].

Since this is so, Count Roger very probably took part in the siege of Capua for more than ten days. Consequently, even if it had begun before his arrival, it remains highly probable—indeed, I might say certain from Eadmer’s account—that the Capuans did not surrender while May was still in progress.

Furthermore, Peter the Deacon teaches in Book IV, chapter 10, of the *Cassinese Chronicle* that Capua was subdued not in spring but in summer. Eadmer supports him by stating in no. 43 of his *Life* of this holy bishop that Saint Anselm was staying at the village of Sclavia, from which Duke Roger invited him to the camp before Capua, during the summer. Therefore, since May, strictly speaking, is not included within the summer season [Col. 0410A], Capua cannot have been subdued in that month, given what Peter the Deacon and Eadmer write.

### 666

I have wished to prove at greater length and with greater care that this city did not surrender while May was still in progress, both so that the time of the apparition in which the Saint—or rather, as stated above, the angel appearing in his form—delivered Count Roger from the most imminent danger may be determined as nearly as possible, and so that it may be evident that June, or even July, though I find the latter less satisfactory, must be substituted—not May—for March, to which Lupus Protospata assigns Capua’s surrender. In this way the month required by Count Roger’s diploma, transcribed above at the end, will not make that document suspect.

For Count Roger states in it that he was present at the siege of Capua “on the Kalends of March,” that is, on the first day of March. Yet it is certain from the foregoing that he did not bring his army against Capua before 16 May—or, what amounts to the same thing, that he was not present at the siege of that city before then. Therefore, in place of March, whose Kalends, or first day, he says he was present at the siege of Capua, June, or perhaps even July, must be substituted.

Lest anyone reject that instrument as spurious or forged because of this chronological error, I shall explain how the error could have arisen, and how it very probably did arise. Since, as Peregrini teaches above in his annotations on the *Chronicle of Lupus Protospata*, proper names in the Norman period were abbreviated by being written only in capital letters [Col. 0410C], it is possible that the month in which Count Roger affirms in the said diploma that he was present at the siege of Capua was expressed in this manner only. Then, when the capital letter by which that month had been represented had either been worn away by age in the original document or rubbed off by some accident, an inexperienced copyist, transcribing it, may have noticed that at that place there had been—or still remained—a letter that he could not read, either because it was almost erased or because of its unusual form. To complete the sense after the word “Kalends,” he may therefore have added “March,” supposing, on the authority and trustworthiness of Lupus Protospata—whose *Chronicle* he had perhaps read—that the city of Capua, at whose siege Count Roger is said in that passage to have been present, had surrendered in March.

### 667

“But,” you will say, “although the chronological error noted above could have entered the diploma of Count Roger just cited—or rather its copy or transcript—it cannot be proved with sufficient certainty by any argument or indication that this is really what happened.”

I admit that this is so. Nevertheless, if the error did not enter in the manner just explained, it must have entered the document in some other way of the kind by which errors are known to have slipped even into genuine documents, or rather into their transcripts. For the instrument has no other defect whatsoever on account of which it should be considered suspect, much less certainly spurious; it is praised by very many writers as genuine and authentic, and, so far as I know, rejected by absolutely none [Col. 0411A].

It remains for me to demonstrate that it was issued not in 1098, the year in which the siege of Capua occurred, but in 1099. The ancient monument—or rather, the copy of it from which I transcribed the document—preserved in Mörkens’s manuscript *Chronologico-Diplomatica de S. Brunone*, has the following at the end:

> “This privilege was written on the second day of August, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1099, indiction seven.”

The diploma under examination was therefore granted to Saint Bruno by Count Roger not in 1098, the year in which Capua was besieged, but in 1099, the year immediately following that siege.

I find, however, two well-learned writers who oppose us here: Michael the monk, praised above, and Camillo Peregrini in his annotations on Lupus Protospata. The former, although he wishes the diploma to have been issued in a different year from that in which Capua was besieged, nevertheless, since he simultaneously maintains that the city’s siege occurred in 1097, thinks that the diploma was issued in 1098. His opinion rests on the fact that, as he says, he read in a copy of the diploma preserved in the records of the royal chancery that it had been issued in 1098.

Let that be so. Since he nevertheless admits that the same document is dated to 2 August and to indiction seven, he must also admit that the copy preserved in the royal chancery contains an error either in the year or in the indiction [Col. 0411C].

### 668

For from 1 September 1097 to 1 September 1098, indiction six was in progress; and from 1 September of the latter year to 1 September 1099, indiction seven was in progress. The copy of the diploma in the royal chancery, therefore, which Michael the monk was allowed to read and which, as he says, was dated 2 August 1098, indiction seven, presents a year that does not agree with the indiction. Since it is thus clear that its chronological notices are corrupt, the year alone cannot establish for us, with certainty and without dispute, the year in which the diploma was actually issued.

Since this is so, and since it seems scarcely probable that Roger granted the diploma to Bruno on 2 August of the very year on whose 29 July—thus only three days earlier—he had arrived at Squillace from the siege of Capua, which, according to the foregoing, occurred in 1098, I think that we should stand by the chronological notices that indicate the time when the document was issued or written, as they appear in the copy transcribed above from Mörkens’s *Chronologico-Diplomatica de S. Brunone*. The document was therefore issued in 1099, as that copy records.

But now I come to Camillo Peregrini, who wishes Capua to have been besieged by Count Roger in 1098 and the diploma under discussion to have been granted by that prince to our Saint in the same year. In the annotations that he appended to Lupus Protospata’s *Chronicle* under the year 1098, he writes as follows concerning the date of the diploma that we are investigating:

> “But another error lies in this very diploma. In my opinion it should read that Roger, having returned to Squillace on 29 June”—not July—“unless you prefer 9 July—after Capua had been fully subdued, remained there continuously for a fortnight in ill health”; and that he issued the privilege “on 2 August, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1098, indiction six” (some editors incorrectly print indiction seven), “with John, bishop of the see of Squillace, residing beside the church doors, confirming it.”

### 669

> “Nor should one agree with the learned man who holds that the privilege was indeed issued in 1098, but that Capua was not besieged and recovered, as Lupus asserts, in that same year, but in the preceding year, as Geoffrey Malaterra states, who says that during the time of that siege Countess Adelasia became pregnant by Count Roger in 1097.”

No, I say: the year in which the diploma was issued does not seem to be distinguishable from the year of the siege of Capua and of Count Roger’s illness. Nor does it seem that the count postponed his voluntary donation until the following year after receiving the benefit, when no reason for such a delay is given—indeed, it is much more appropriate to say that Roger returned to Squillace before a full or anniversary year had elapsed, and that as soon as he arrived there from Capua and was sufficiently restored in health, he granted the aforesaid privilege.

Thus far Peregrini. He argues that the diploma or privilege was granted to Saint Bruno in the very year in which Capua was besieged and restored to Count Roger, apparently chiefly, if not solely, because he did not think it probable that the prince, who was most favorably disposed and benevolent toward Bruno, would have delayed for more than a full year after receiving the benefit a privilege generously granted to the Saint by Count Roger in gratitude for having escaped, through the Saint’s apparent warning and intervention, the gravest danger before Capua. He was led to this conclusion because he believed either that the count could have had no reason for postponing it until the following year or, at least, that he did not know what such a reason could have been.

Even if the count had been fully prepared to grant that extensive privilege to Saint Bruno in the very year in which he returned from the siege of Capua, and would undoubtedly have granted it in fact if he had been entirely free to do so, the diploma or privilege itself nevertheless supplies the reason why he did not do so at that time [Col. 0412D].

### 670

For in this document Count Roger speaks of himself, after returning to Squillace from the siege of Capua, as follows:

> “I also humbly asked him”—Saint Bruno, namely—“to accept, for the love of God, the generous revenues that I was giving in the territory of Squillace. But he, refusing to receive them, said that he had left his own house and mine for this purpose: to serve his God freely, as a stranger to the affairs of the world. He had been, as it were, first and great in my entire household. At last I could scarcely persuade him to consent freely to accept my small gift.”

The reason, therefore, why Count Roger did not grant Saint Bruno the extensive privilege under discussion in the very year 1098, in which Capua was besieged and subdued by him, was not the count but Saint Bruno himself. Bruno did not wish to accept the very large and generous gifts then offered to him by that prince. Finally, after more than a full year had elapsed from the time when Count Roger had offered him those gifts at Squillace, he reluctantly consented to have some part of them recorded in a public document.

If 29 July, the day on which Roger is said in the diploma to have returned to Squillace after the capture of Capua, could be replaced—as Peregrini prefers—by 29 June or even 9 July, the chronological dates contained in the document itself would certainly not prevent us from believing that it had been issued in 1098. But since we must not admit errors in ancient documents unless they are established with certainty, and since there is no evidence anywhere that 29 July was incorrectly recorded in this document, I cannot agree with Peregrini on this point. For the reasons already given, I consider that it was not issued before 1099, especially since that year is also recorded by Surianus, and since the original itself is likewise dated to that year, as the excerpts communicated to me by the frequently mentioned Carthusian of Paris from an as-yet unpublished copy of the fourth book of the Carthusian *Annals*, concerning the Charterhouse of Val-de-Dieu, show. Severus of Naples had discovered these excerpts.

Nor should you object that Count Roger was at Squillace in 1098 and that the diploma just discussed is also stated to have been issued at Squillace. Why could Roger not have been at Squillace in 1098 and again in 1099?

### § XLI. The Saint again experiences Duke Roger’s benevolence toward him; he is visited by Landuin, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, and through Landuin, whom he reluctantly lets depart, writes a letter to the brothers of the Charterhouse. These letters, together with the letter written to Ralph the Green, are presented here.

[Col. 0413D]

### 671

Not only after the siege of Capua, in which, according to the foregoing, Count Roger was delivered from the most imminent danger through the merits of our Saint, did the Saint again experience the benevolence of this prince; he also experienced that of Duke Roger of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, who was the count’s uncle.

“In 1099,” says Surianus in his annotations, p. 400, on the *Life of the Saint* written by Surius, “Roger, Duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, in the fourteenth year of his dukedom, gave to the church of Saint Mary, situated in the wilderness at a place called by the inhabitants Turris, the peasants whom he had at Squillace, for the love of God and out of reverence for Master Bruno, who presided over the monastery. The following subscribed the diploma: Roger, Archbishop of Reggio; after him Roger the duke; Fallow, Bishop of Castan; the pope’s vicar; Arnulf, Archbishop of Cosenza; Tustenus, bishop; and Guido, son of Duke Robert.”

Camillo Tutini also mentions this donation in his *Prospectus of Carthusian History*, p. 14. But since the diploma by which Surianus says it was made is not at hand, I do not think it appropriate to add more about it; I therefore proceed to other matters.

### 672

Surianus comments as follows in his annotations, p. 172, on these words of Surius concerning the Saint: “He frequently wrote to them”—that is, to the religious inhabitants of the Grande Chartreuse:

> “When his return”—that of Saint Bruno, namely—“was postponed from day to day, Landuin, the prior of the Charterhouse, was sent to him, so that he might, as it were, open negotiations with him and confer concerning the Order’s general institution. Having set out to him by long journeys, he conferred with him as far as circumstances and time permitted. When he began to return by the route on which he had come, he fell into the hands of the antipope. Since no prayers or threats could induce him to deny the legitimate pontiff, he was thrown into a most dreadful prison, where he died, bearing witness to his true fidelity to Christ’s vicar to his final breath.”

So much for him. First, the letters that are to be read in the present section, which the Saint sent through Landuin to his disciples staying at the Grande Chartreuse when Landuin was returning there, make it certain from their very beginning that Landuin came to Saint Bruno in Calabria. Therefore, the following words concerning this second prior of the Grande Chartreuse in the eulogy with which the chronicler of the first four priors of the Charterhouse—an authority, as has been shown in section 1, highly worthy of confidence—honors Landuin in Labbe’s volume I of the *Bibliotheca nova librorum manuscriptorum*, p. 639:

> “As he was journeying to Master Bruno, he fell into the hands of the schismatic Guibert,”

must be understood to include both Landuin’s arrival at Saint Bruno and his return from him—in other words, the entire journey that Landuin undertook in order to visit his holy father.

For since, as the same chronicler teaches, Landuin, after falling into the hands of the antipope Guibert, was thrown into the prison in which he died, it would follow that he never reached Bruno in the Calabrian hermitage at Turris if he encountered Guibert while traveling toward that place to visit his holy father, as the quoted words of the chronicler seem at first sight to indicate [Col. 0414D].

### 673

As for the reason why Landuin came to the Saint in Calabria by such a very long and perilous journey, it is most probable that he did so not only to confer with the holy Patriarch about the way of life they followed, but also, if this could in any way be accomplished, to bring the holy man back from Calabria to the Grande Chartreuse. I am persuaded of this both because Landuin and the others who lived under him in the Grande Chartreuse were possessed by an intense longing for their most holy Father—as is clear from what has been said [Col. 0415A] concerning their departure from the Charterhouse because of his absence—and because the Saint concludes the letter that he wrote to them and sent through Landuin, as I have already said and shall transcribe below in full, with these words:

> “Concerning me, brothers, know that, after God, I have one desire alone: to come to you and to see you. And whenever I can, I shall fulfill this in deed, with God’s help.”

From these words it is evident that the Saint had been asked by his Carthusian disciples—or, if you prefer, by Landuin on their behalf—to return to the Charterhouse.

Zanottius likewise supposes, in the Life of the holy Patriarch that he composed, chapter 29, that Landuin came to the Calabrian hermitage at La Torre in order to persuade St. Bruno to return to the Charterhouse; and he is right, as is apparent from what has already been said. But the additional claim he makes—that a lay brother had previously been sent to the Charterhouse from Calabria with a letter from Bruno, and that Landuin joined this brother on his return journey to the holy Father—is supported by no ancient monument of certain authority. Nor can I support it myself. He does indeed cite, as often elsewhere, in the lower margin of the page, the manuscript *Monumenta Calabriae*; but he nowhere states what these records are or what their character may be. Indeed, since he occasionally indicates that he doubts whether what they report is true, he himself does not appear to have regarded them as documents of certain and unquestionable authority.

### 674

Nevertheless, even if this is so, no one can reasonably doubt that Landuin, as he likewise relates there, was received by St. Bruno with the greatest affection, or that the Saint and Landuin discussed the institution of the Carthusian life [Col. 0415C]. The ancient writers are silent about these matters; but, apart from the fact that their testimony is not required for such things to be believed, the already twice-mentioned letter that the Saint sent through Landuin, when he was returning to the Charterhouse, to his disciples who were living there confirms that the Saint conversed with Landuin about the Carthusian institution and its followers in the Charterhouse. For in that letter he indicates that he had learned from Landuin certain things about their religious life, the rigor of their discipline, and their holy conduct, as will be evident to anyone who reads it.

The same letter no less clearly shows that Landuin was received by St. Bruno just as a most loving son is received by his father. Here are the words that make this plain:

> “I wished to keep Brother Landuin with us because of our grave and frequent illnesses; but because he considers that nothing is wholesome, nothing joyful, nothing life-giving or useful to him without you, he did not consent. He protested to me, with a fountain of tears flowing forth on your behalf and with many sighs, how highly you are esteemed by him and with what perfect charity he loves you. Therefore I wished to use no compulsion, lest I injure either him or you, whom, because of the merit of your virtues, I hold most dear.”

Thus the Saint spoke. Who, then, would not suppose that he received with supreme love and kindness the man whom he would so willingly have kept with him, although he was already afflicted by grave and almost constant illnesses, as the words quoted make clear? Yet Landuin, although received with such benevolence and affection by the holy Father, and although he wished to remain with him for a longer period in the hermitage at La Torre, preferred, despite the Saint’s most earnest appeals, to revisit the inhabitants of the Charterhouse whom he loved most dearly, lest his prolonged absence distress them. Nor did the Saint wish to deny him permission to return to them, although, by virtue of the obedience by which he could have held the man bound to him, he would have been able to do so.

### 675

Accordingly, with the same expression of love and benevolence with which he had received Landuin when he came to him in Calabria, he sent him away, placing in his hands the letter that he had written and that Landuin, once he had returned to the Charterhouse, was to deliver to its religious inhabitants.

But when Landuin was returning to the Charterhouse by the same road by which he had come to the Saint, he was captured by the followers of the antipope Guibert. Because he refused to acknowledge Guibert as the legitimate vicar of Christ on earth, they threw him into a foul prison, where he died, consumed by hunger.

I transcribe again here the principal words of the chronologer of the first four priors of the Charterhouse, already quoted above, because they make especially clear approximately when St. Bruno wrote the letter just mentioned, when Landuin visited him in the Calabrian hermitage, and, after being captured by Guibert’s followers, shut his eyes in prison, leaving a remarkably outstanding example of faithfulness to the Apostolic See. That writer speaks of Landuin in these terms:

> “He fell into the hands of the schismatic Guibert, which he greatly abhorred. Against his threats and promises, his deceits and violence, he persevered, with divine grace assisting him, steadfast in every way. When Guibert died in his error, he mourned him tearfully, so much so that those standing around reproved him for weeping for one whose perversity the goodness of Christ had liberated His Church from. On the seventh day after his death, he too died, and was placed in the monastery of St. Andrew at the foot of Mount Siraptis, near the fortress where he had been captured and held in custody.”

Thus, according to these words of that writer—whose reliability, as has been shown, is beyond doubt—Landuin migrated to the Lord on the seventh day after the death of the antipope Guibert, leaving the prison into which he had been cast because he refused to abandon the cause of the legitimate pope.

### 676

Therefore, since the antipope Guibert, as Pagius teaches under the year 1100 in his *Critica*, following Hugh of Flavigny, died in the year 1100 while the Council of Valence was being held—the council having begun in that same year on 30 September, that is, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, and having ended shortly afterward—it follows that Landuin, who survived Guibert by only seven days, exchanged this mortal life for immortal life during October of the year 1100.

Nevertheless, according to what I learn from Mörkens’s *Chronologico-Diplomatic Dissertation on St. Bruno*, Landuin is recorded in the Carthusian Menology as having died on 14 September. Yet since the text of Hugh of Flavigny, from which Pagius determines the time of Guibert’s death in the place cited, consists only of these words—“During the period in which the Council of Valence was celebrated, Wibertus died”—I do not know whether Hugh may not be understood to have meant merely that Wibertus, or Guibert the antipope, died at approximately the time when the Council of Valence was being held. If Hugh can be understood in that way, then it must be said that Guibert died on 7 September, by which date that writer can be reconciled with the Carthusian Menology.

In any event, it is certain from the text of Hugh of Flavigny that the antipope Guibert, and consequently, as has been shown, Landuin also, died in the year 1100, and that Landuin had reached at least the month of September when this occurred.

Now, since this is so, it follows that neither could Landuin have visited St. Bruno, who was living in the Calabrian hermitage at La Torre, later than the year 1100, nor could Bruno, through Landuin as he returned from Calabria to the Charterhouse, have sent the frequently mentioned letter to the religious members and beloved disciples of that house. But did these events perhaps occur even before the year 1100?

### 677

Mabillon writes as follows in the *Benedictine Annals* under the year 1099, no. 109:

> “In this year Landuin, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, went to Bruno, who was living in Calabria, both to visit him and to consult him about various doubts concerning his institute. His arrival was so welcome and pleasing to the venerable Father that he attempted to keep him with him. But Landuin could not bear to deprive his brothers whom he had left in the Grande Chartreuse, and whom he had informed of his return, of his presence and guidance. The holy Father, assenting to so just a purpose, allowed him to depart, giving him a letter for the brothers of the Grande Chartreuse, the first part of which I wish to reproduce here.”

Mabillon then transcribes the first part of the letter he has mentioned. Afterward, having also quoted the second part of the same letter, with some material inserted between them, he adds:

> “At the end”—that is, at the end of the letter, many of whose words he incorporated into his work—“the holy man declares that, after God, his sole desire is to revisit them, and that he will carry this out in deed at the earliest opportunity, if it can be done. But Bruno was not granted a return to Gaul, nor was Landuin himself, who on his return was seized by the antipope Guibert and, steadfast against his threats and promises, detained in prison until the schismatic remained alive—that is, until the following year.”

Mabillon therefore believed that in the year 1099 Landuin both came to St. Bruno in Calabria and, when returning from there to the Grande Chartreuse, was captured by Guibert, thrown into prison, and held there. Thus, in his view, the letter sent by the Saint through Landuin to the members of the Grande Chartreuse—the date of which is chiefly at issue here—was also written in the year 1099.

### 678

Yet since the aforementioned Mabillon offers no reason at all for this opinion, and since the eight months of the year 1100 preceding September—before which, as has been shown, Landuin certainly did not die—constitute a sufficiently long interval for Landuin to visit St. Bruno in the Calabrian hermitage, remain with him for some time, and afterward, on his return to the Charterhouse, be captured by Guibert, thrown into prison, and die there of starvation, I am very much in doubt whether Landuin visited Bruno in 1099 or at the beginning of the following year, and whether the latter then sent through Landuin, as he was leaving him, a letter to his first disciples in the Charterhouse.

Whatever the truth of the matter may be, it is sufficiently clear from what has already been said that these events took place either in 1099 or very soon afterward, and therefore not earlier than 1099. This is why, so as not to depart from the chronological order that I have decided to follow, insofar as conveniently possible, in presenting matters relating to the Saint, I have wished to discuss here both Landuin’s visit to our Saint in Calabria and the letter that the holy man gave Landuin as he was departing, to be delivered to the religious inhabitants of the Charterhouse.

Although Landuin was not granted the opportunity to return to Gaul, the letter nevertheless reached the hands of those to whom it was addressed, if the *Writers of the Literary History of France*, volume IX, page 249, report correctly. Indeed, it seems likely that they are correct, since that precious monument has been transmitted to posterity. The whole letter, of which Mabillon incorporated only two portions into the *Annals* that he composed concerning the Benedictines, is included in volume III of the Saint’s works, printed at Cologne in 1611 and again in 1640, as well as in Surianus’s annotations to the Life of Bruno composed by Surius. I wish to transfer it here from those sources.

### 679

It reads as follows:

> “To his brothers, uniquely beloved in Christ: Brother Bruno sends greetings in the Lord.
>
> “Having learned from the frequent and sweet report of our most blessed brother Landuin of the rational and truly praiseworthy discipline that you maintain with inflexible rigor, and having also heard of your holy love and unceasing devotion to those things that belong to integrity and uprightness, my spirit rejoices in the Lord. Indeed, I rejoice and am carried away into praise and thanksgiving to the Lord, and yet I sigh bitterly. I rejoice, as is just, over the increase of the fruits of your virtues; but I grieve and blush that I lie inert and sluggish in the filth of my sins.
>
> “Rejoice, therefore, my most beloved brothers, over the portion of your blessedness and over God’s generous hand of grace toward you. Rejoice, because you have escaped the manifold dangers and shipwrecks of the wavering world. Rejoice, because you have obtained a quiet and safe anchorage in a more secluded harbor, to which, although many desire to come and many also strive with no little effort, they nevertheless do not arrive. Many, indeed, after gaining possession of it, have been excluded, since it has been granted from above to none of them.”

### 680

> “Therefore, my brothers, let it be certain and established for you that whoever has enjoyed this desirable good, if he should lose it in any way, will grieve until the end, provided that he has any regard or concern for the salvation of his soul.
>
> “Concerning you, my most beloved lay brothers, I say: ‘My soul magnifies the Lord,’ because I behold upon you the greatness of His mercy, according to the report of your prior and most loving Father, who greatly boasts and rejoices on your behalf. We too rejoice, because although you are without knowledge of letters, almighty God writes upon your hearts with His finger not only love but also knowledge of His holy law. For by your deeds you show what you love and what you know.
>
> “When you observe true obedience with every care and zeal—obedience which is the execution of God’s commandments, the key and seal of all spiritual discipline, which is never without great humility and excellent patience, always accompanied by chaste love of the Lord and true charity—it is manifest that you wisely read the sweetest and most useful fruit of divine Scripture.
>
> “Therefore, my brothers, remain in the state to which you have attained, and avoid like a plague the diseased flock of certain utterly vain laymen who carry their little writings about, muttering things that they neither understand nor love, and contradicting them by their words and deeds. They are idle and wandering, and they slander all good and religious people, thinking themselves praiseworthy if they defame those who deserve praise; they hate obedience and every form of discipline.”

### 681

> “I wished to keep Brother Landuin with us because of our grave and frequent illnesses; but because he considers that nothing wholesome, nothing joyful, nothing life-giving or useful exists for him without you, he did not consent. He protested to me, with a fountain of tears flowing forth for you and with many sighs, how highly you are esteemed by him and with what perfect charity he loves you.
>
> “Therefore I wished to use no compulsion, lest I injure either him or you, whom, because of the merit of your virtues, I hold most dear. For this reason I earnestly admonish your fraternity, and humbly and uniquely beg you, to show by works toward him—your most beloved prior and Father—the charity that you carry in your hearts, kindly and prudently supplying what his varied state of health requires.
>
> “But if he should not consent to you in this act of kindness, preferring to endanger his health and life rather than omit anything of the rigor of bodily discipline—which is wholly to be condemned—perhaps he will be ashamed that, although he is first in religion, he should be found last in this respect, fearing that on his account any of you might become more lax or lukewarm. I do not think this is to be feared at all.
>
> “So that you may not be deprived of this grace, we yield our place in this matter to your charity alone, allowing you reverently to compel him to do what you judge beneficial to his health.”

### 682

> “Concerning me, brothers, know that, after God, I have one desire alone: to come to you and see you. And whenever I can, I shall fulfill this in deed, with God’s help. Farewell.”

After Surianus had quoted this letter in full, he immediately makes the following observation concerning it:

> “Of this exhortatory letter one may say what Peter, abbot of Celle, wrote in Letter 3 of Book III to the prior and brothers of the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu:
>
> “‘You have written from the fullness of a well-fed soul, from the abundance of God’s sweetness, and, as with the fat and richness of spiritual joy, you have filled my throat. For your speech is not such as, by superimposed counterfeit forms, presents an appearance of piety while denying its power. This belongs to those who speak with a double heart, or who soften their words more than oil, while they themselves are arrows. Your word, however, is not thus insipid; strengthened by the fullness of grace, it fills the innermost parts of the saints, and so forth.’”

These words of Peter the Venerable, which Surianus affirms may rightly be applied to the letter written by Bruno to the members of the Grande Chartreuse, may with no less justification be applied to the other letter, mentioned so often above, in which the holy man most earnestly exhorted Radulphus Viridis, provost of the church of Reims, to fulfill the vow that he had once made during a discussion with Bruno and Fulcius the One-Eyed concerning the false pleasures of the world.

That letter was written with such affection of soul toward his old friend, with such an outpouring of the heart, so to speak, and with such an anointing of the divine Spirit. At the beginning of this Commentary I could not present it in full, because no books in which it was inserted without mutilation, not even the works of St. Bruno printed at Cologne in 1611 and reprinted there in 1640, were at hand.

### 683

But when the Carthusians of this city at last graciously consented to lend me these books, I wish also to transfer here the precious monument copied from them, so that the reader may have readily available what is found in only a few books—and what, to my surprise, was not even included in the Saint’s works printed in Paris by Jodocus Badius in 1524, copies of which are in our possession—and so that I may discharge the promise I have made more than once above.

It reads as follows:

> “To his venerable lord Radulphus, provost of Reims, worthy of respect for his most sincere devotion to charity: Bruno sends greetings.
>
> “The faithfulness of an old and approved friendship appears in you all the more distinguished and worthy of greater praise because it is found so rarely among human beings. Although our bodies have been separated from one another by a long stretch of land and an even longer passage of time, my spirit could not be torn away from your benevolence as a friend. You have shown this sufficiently by your most delightful letters, in which you addressed me with friendly affection, and by your benefactions, generously bestowed not only upon me but also upon Brother Bernard on my account, as well as by several other indications.
>
> “Therefore we return thanks to your kindness—not equal to your merits, indeed, but nevertheless flowing from a pure source. Some time ago we sent you, with a letter, a certain stranger who was sufficiently trustworthy in other missions, but he has not appeared to this day. We judged it appropriate to send one of our own to your charity, who might explain at greater length by word of mouth everything concerning us, since we are not sufficiently equipped with pen and ink for these matters.”

### 684

> “We therefore inform your affection and your graciousness—for we think that this will not be unwelcome to you—that we are well in body (would that we were equally well in mind), and that in matters pertaining to our outward circumstances everything is sufficiently according to our desire.
>
> “But as for my inner state, I beseech the hand of divine mercy to heal all my inward infirmities and to satisfy my desire with good things.
>
> “In the borders of Calabria, with religious brothers and several well-educated men—who, remaining at their divine watch, await the return of their Lord so that, when He knocks, they may immediately open to Him—I inhabit a hermitage sufficiently remote on every side from human dwellings.
>
> “What worthy account could I give of its pleasantness, the temperate and healthy air, or the broad and agreeable plain extending lengthwise among the mountains, where there are green meadows and flowering pastures? Who could adequately describe the view of the hills gently rising on every side, the recesses of the shaded valleys, or the pleasing abundance of rivers, streams, and springs? Nor are irrigated gardens or the fertility of various trees lacking.
>
> “But why do I linger over these things any longer? There are other pleasures, more pleasing and far more useful to a prudent man, because they are divine. Nevertheless, when the weaker spirit, wearied by stricter discipline and spiritual studies, is frequently relieved and breathes again through such things, they are not without value. For a bow, if it is constantly kept taut, becomes weaker and less fit for its function.
>
> “What benefit and delight solitude and the silence of the hermitage bring to those who love them is known only to those who have experienced them. Here vigorous men may return into themselves as much as they wish, dwell with themselves, diligently cultivate the seeds of virtue, and happily enjoy the fruits of paradise. Here that eye is acquired whose serene gaze wounds the Bridegroom with love, by which God is seen in a pure and cleansed heart. Here leisure is celebrated as active business, and one rests in quiet action.”

### 685

> “Here God repays His athletes for the labor of combat with the desired reward, namely, the peace that the world does not know and joy in the Holy Spirit.
>
> “This is that beautiful Rachel, fair in appearance, more beloved by Jacob, though less fruitful in children than the more fertile but bleary-eyed Leah. For there are fewer children of contemplation than of action. Nevertheless, Joseph and Benjamin were loved by their father more than the other brothers.
>
> “This is that better part which Mary chose and which shall not be taken away. This is that most beautiful Shunammite, found alone throughout all the borders of Israel, who was to warm the aged David and give him heat. Would that you, dearest brother, might love her uniquely, so that, warmed in her embraces, you might grow hot with divine love!
>
> “If her charity once settles in your soul, that seductive and flattering deceiver, the glory of this world, would immediately become foul to you, and you would lightly cast away anxious riches, which are truly burdensome to the mind. You would also utterly despise pleasures, equally harmful to soul and body.
>
> “For your prudence knows who says: ‘He who loves the world and the things that are in the world’—the pleasures of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age—‘does not have the charity of the Father in him.’ And again: ‘He who is a friend of this world is made an enemy of God.’
>
> “What, then, is so unjust; what is so characteristic of an insane and headlong mind; what is so harmful or more wretched than to wish to wage enmity against Him whose power you cannot resist and whose just vengeance you cannot escape? Are we stronger than He? Because the patience of His mercy now calls us to repentance, will He not finally avenge the injuries inflicted by contempt?”

### 686

> “For what is more perverse, what attacks reason, justice, and nature itself more directly, than to love the creature more than the Creator?
>
> “What, then, do you think should be done, dearest? What else but yield to divine counsels, yield to the truth, which cannot deceive? For Wisdom counsels all alike, saying: ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.’
>
> “Is not the labor most evil and useless when one is stretched out by desire and continually afflicted by cares and anxieties, fear and sorrow, for things desired? What burden is heavier than that which casts the mind down from the lofty fortress of its dignity into lowliness, namely, every injustice?
>
> “Flee, therefore, my brother, flee all these troubles and miseries, and transfer yourself from the storm of this world to the safe and quiet anchorage of the harbor.
>
> “Your prudence also knows what Wisdom says to us: ‘Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple.’
>
> “Who does not see how beautiful, how useful, and how delightful it is to remain in her school under the discipline of the Holy Spirit and to attain divine philosophy, which alone grants true blessedness? Therefore it is worthwhile for you to weigh these matters by careful examination. If the love of God does not invite you, if the usefulness of such great rewards does not move you, at least necessity and fear of punishment ought to compel you to this.”

### 687

> “For you know by what promise you are bound, and how omnipotent and terrible is the One to whom you devoted yourself as a pleasing and wholly acceptable gift, and to whom it is neither permissible nor expedient to lie. For He does not permit Himself to be mocked with impunity.
>
> “Your affection remembers that one day, when you and I and Fulcius the One-Eyed were together in a little garden beside Adam’s house, where he was then lodging [or, better, ‘was lodging’], we discussed for some time, as I think, the false pleasures and perishable riches of this world, as well as the joys of everlasting glory. Inflamed by divine fervor, we promised and vowed to the Holy Spirit that we would soon abandon the fleeting things of the age, seek eternal things, and receive the monastic habit.
>
> “This would have been carried out shortly afterward, if Fulcius had not then gone to Rome; we postponed its accomplishment until his return. While he delayed, and while other causes intervened, divine love grew faint, the spirit cooled, and the fervor vanished.
>
> “What, then, remains, dearest, except for you to free yourself quickly from the bonds of so great a debt, lest you incur the wrath of the Most High, and terrible torments on account of so grave and prolonged a crime of falsehood?
>
> “Who would leave unpunished the defrauding of a promised gift by anyone subject to him, especially if the gift were of great value and price in his estimation?
>
> “Therefore believe not me but the prophet—or rather the Holy Spirit—who says: ‘Vow and pay to the Lord your God, all you who surround Him and bring gifts. He is terrible, and He takes away the spirit of princes; He is terrible to the kings of the earth.’
>
> “Why does the Spirit of God repeat all these things unless to urge you, who have made a vow, to pay what you have vowed?”

### 688

> “Why are you reluctant to repay what causes no loss or diminution of your possessions, and which increases profits for you rather than for the one to whom you repay it?
>
> “Therefore let not deceptive riches detain you, since they cannot drive away poverty; nor let the dignity of the provostship detain you, since it cannot be administered without great danger to the soul.
>
> “To convert into one’s own uses the possessions of others, whose steward and not owner you are—to speak with your permission—is as hateful as it is unjust. If, however, you desire splendor and glory and wish to retain a large household, then, when what you justly possess does not suffice, must you not somehow seize from some what you may give to others?
>
> “That is not beneficence or generosity. Nothing is generous that is not also just.
>
> “But I also wish to persuade your affection of this: do not, because of your connection with the lord archbishop, who greatly trusts and relies upon your counsels—not all of which can readily be called just or useful—withdraw from so sublime a promise. Let divine charity recall you, for the more just it is, the more useful it is.
>
> “What is so just and useful, or so implanted in and fitting for human nature, as to love the good? And what else is so good as God? Indeed, what else is good except God alone?
>
> “Hence the holy soul, perceiving in part the incomparable beauty, splendor, and loveliness of this Good, and inflamed by the flame of love, says: ‘My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?’”

### 689

> “Would that you did not scorn a friend giving counsel; would that you did not hear the words of God’s Spirit with deaf ears; would that you satisfied my desire and long expectation, dearest, lest my soul be tortured any longer on your account by cares, anxieties, and fear.
>
> “For if you should depart from this life before you have fulfilled your vowed obligation—which God forbid!—you will leave me wasting away in continual sadness, without any consolation of hope.
>
> “Therefore I ask and entreat you that, at least for the sake of prayer, you would deign to come to St. Nicholas and from there as far as us, so that you may see the man who loves you uniquely, and so that we may discuss face to face the state of our affairs, the order of our religious life, and whatever concerns the common good.
>
> “I trust in the Lord that you will not regret undertaking the labor of so great a journey.
>
> “I have exceeded the bounds of epistolary brevity, because, since I cannot possess you bodily, I shall at least remain with you longer by conversing with you. I earnestly desire that your fraternity may long remain safe, mindful of our counsel and not forgetful of your vow.
>
> “I beg you to send us the Life of St. Remigius, since it is found nowhere in our region. Farewell.”

The words of the letter itself, quoted in no. 684, make clear that the Saint wrote it while he was living in the Calabrian hermitage at La Torre. To understand why Bruno invites Radulphus to St. Nicholas near the end of the letter, one should know that the body of that holy bishop of Myra was transferred from Myra to Bari, a city of Apulia, in the year 1087, as Lupus Protospata and others report in their chronicles. Since it became renowned there through many miracles from that time onward, it was honored by very frequent pilgrimages undertaken to Bari even from the most distant regions.

### 690

Moreover, before the Saint wrote the letter just quoted to Radulphus Viridis, he had already been addressed by him in writing and had sent another letter to that old friend, although it is doubtful whether the latter letter was delivered. All these facts may be gathered from the Saint’s letter to Radulphus that I have already presented.

For at its beginning it reads:

> “Although our bodies have been separated from one another by a long stretch of land and a more extended period of time, my spirit nevertheless could not be torn away from your benevolence as a friend. You have shown this sufficiently by your most delightful letters, in which you addressed me with friendly affection, and by your benefactions, generously bestowed not only upon me but also upon Brother Bernard on my account, as well as by several other indications. Therefore we return thanks to your kindness—not equal to your merits, indeed, but nevertheless flowing from a pure source. Some time ago we sent you, with a letter, a certain stranger who was sufficiently trustworthy in other missions, but he has not appeared to this day. We judged it appropriate to send one of our own to your charity, who might explain at greater length by word of mouth everything concerning us, since we are not sufficiently equipped with pen and ink for these matters. We therefore inform your affection, and so forth.”

Such is the beginning of the letter written by the Saint to Radulphus Viridis. From the words just given, which establish that it was sent to this old friend of Bruno through one of the inhabitants of the hermitage at La Torre, it is clear that the Saint entrusted the letter to one of those members of his community.

But who this was, to whom the Saint assigned that duty, I cannot state with certainty. Nor can I determine who that Brother Bernard was whom Radulphus is remembered to have benefited on account of our Saint, according to the words of the letter to Radulphus just transferred here. The ancient *Catalogue of Monks*, which I have already cited above, listing those who after the Saint’s death promised obedience to Lanvinus as prior in the hermitage at La Torre, does mention a certain brother named Bernard.

### 691

Yet I would not dare to assert that this Bernard was the same as the Brother Bernard who was received with such affection by Radulphus on Bruno’s account. For if the matter were so, the Bernard mentioned in that catalogue would have had to be sent from the hermitage at La Torre by the Saint to Radulphus; and it appears that this did not happen. Had Bruno done so, he would most probably have sent a letter to Radulphus through him. Yet, before giving Radulphus the letter just transcribed, he appears, from the words of that letter, to have written to him only one other letter, which he sent through the stranger.

Furthermore, just as it is obscure who that Bernard was whom Radulphus received so kindly on Bruno’s account, so also the year in which the letter that the Saint sent to Radulphus through one of his own was written is completely unknown to me.

Nevertheless, although this is so, I have wished to mention the letter here because the letter that the Saint wrote to his first disciples in the Charterhouse was due to be examined, and the proper order seems to require that both letters be treated in one and the same place. For this reason also, in the very place above where it was appropriate to discuss the two letters already mentioned, I decided to treat in continuous sequence all the remaining writings that either truly belong to the Saint or are at least attributed to him. In fact, I shall do so in the two following sections.

## § XLII. The Saint truly composed the Commentaries on the Psalms and on the Epistles of St. Paul the Apostle that circulate under his name; when and by what method he composed them, and what other writings should certainly be attributed to him

[Col. 0425B]

692. Jodocus Ascensius published at Paris in 1524, through the printing press, two Commentaries—one on the Psalms, the other on all the Epistles of St Paul the Apostle—together with certain minor works or treatises and a fairly extensive collection of sermons, from a manuscript which he had received from Guillaume Bibaut, Prior of the Grande Chartreuse, under the name of St Bruno, founder of the Carthusian Order. These same Complete Works, with several other pieces added, were subsequently divided into three separate volumes—although they had been published by Ascensius in a single volume—the first containing the Commentary on the Psalms, the second the Commentary on St Paul’s Epistles, and the third the minor works and sermons. They were reprinted at Cologne in 1611 and again in 1640, likewise under the name of Bruno the Carthusian. Some of these works, however, certainly have our Saint as their author; concerning others it is disputed whether they are his. In the present section, then, I now undertake to discuss the former, since I have decided to inform the reader which works, besides the two Letters cited in the preceding section, should be attributed to the holy Father of the Carthusians; discussion of the latter is reserved for the following section. I begin with the Commentary on the Psalms.

693. The *Scriptores historiae litterariae Franciae*, vol. IX, p. 243, after stating that some people had deleted from the catalogue of works composed by St Bruno the Carthusian a certain Commentary on the Psalms for no other reason than that they had confused St Bruno of Segni with St Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, add approximately the following in substance:

“To clarify this difficulty more fully, it is useful to know that, within the space of scarcely a century—from the year 1040, that is, to the year 1123—there flourished three Brunos, all men of distinguished reputation, and all devoted to explaining or commenting on the Psalms: namely, St Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, who died in 1045; St Bruno, of whom we are here speaking; and St Bruno, bishop of Segni, who died in 1123.

“The work of the first on the Psalter, together with his other writings, had already been printed in 1494; it was then separated from them and printed at Würzburg in 1531, and again at Leipzig in 1533. This latter edition was prepared from the immediately preceding one, produced by Johann Cochlaeus. Finally, it was incorporated into the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, and appears in volume XVIII of the Lyon edition of that work. The Commentary of the bishop of Segni was brought to light by Marchesius and forms part of the first volume of his works, where it is placed between the Commentary on Deuteronomy and the Commentary on the Song of Songs.”

694. This is more or less what they say, as I have indicated, in substance; and thus they chiefly inform the reader which exposition of the Psalms should be assigned both to St Bruno of Würzburg and to St Bruno of Segni, who both commented on the Psalms. Before explaining, however, what should be attributed to St Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, whom they likewise acknowledge to have explained the Psalms, they first bring forward the arguments by which they endeavor to prove that our Saint really did comment on the Psalms. I would like to employ substantially the same arguments here in order to prove that point, since I have been unable to find others that are stronger.

Among the few verses with which the monks of the abbey of Micy, near Orléans, celebrate the Saint in title 107 of the funeral titles being reprinted, the following occupies the first place:

> “A learned psalmist, most renowned and a sophist.”

The canons of St Vincent at Noli, in the monastery of the Lower Poitou province, have the following in funeral title 173, by which they paid tribute to the Saint:

> “For Bruno possessed true knowledge and prudence in the liberal arts, as well as the other cardinal virtues, and he preserved them, bringing them to perfection in a good end. Formerly, indeed, he was the supreme teacher of the Church of Reims, being exceedingly learned in the Psalter and in the other sciences, and for a long time he stood as a pillar of the entire metropolitan church.”

Since, therefore, in the first of these two funeral titles the Saint’s learning in the Psalms is celebrated, and in the second, as appears, his distinction in explaining and commenting on them, there seems to be an allusion to an exposition or Commentary which he composed on them. From this, then, it appears that Bruno truly explained the Psalms in a Commentary, as may be concluded with the authors of the *Scriptores historiae litterariae Franciae* mentioned above.

695. Nevertheless, since someone might argue that these two funeral titles allude not to a Commentary on the Psalms which the Saint committed to writing, but to the explanation of the Psalms which he delivered orally when teaching the higher branches of learning at Reims or elsewhere, I am willing, with the aforementioned authors of the *Scriptores historiae litterariae Franciae*, to strengthen the case that Bruno really composed a Commentary on the Psalms by further arguments.

It was so firmly believed that, in the same century in which the Saint died, he had composed a Commentary on the Psalms that, if a copyist happened to come upon a similar manuscript which did not bear the author’s name, he would identify the copy taken from it both at the beginning and end of the dedicatory letter and in the title of the work itself by the name of St Bruno, founder of the Carthusians.

A copy of this kind was preserved in Mabillon’s time at the Cluniac monastery of Souvigny, situated two hours from Moulins in Burgundy. In it, as that writer himself—who found it there—testifies in the second volume of his *Posthumous Works*, p. 29, one read:

> “Here begins the Letter of Bruno, prior of the Carthusian house, to Hugh, bishop of Asti. To his lord Hugh, etc. … Here ends the Letter of Bruno, prior of the Carthusian house, etc. Here begins the exposition of the Psalter, taken by Bruno, prior of the Carthusian house, from the treatises of the holy Fathers.”

Mabillon, in no. 29 of book 70 of the *Benedictine Annals*, believed this copy to be an exemplar of the Commentary on the Psalms composed by St Bruno, bishop of Segni, although its beginning differed from the printed copies. The authors of the *Scriptores historiae litterariae Franciae*, however, say in the passage cited that it is an exemplar neither of the work composed by that bishop nor of the work composed by the holy founder of the Carthusian Order. The opening words of the work itself show that the Commentary was composed by Odo, a monk of Asti, and that Marchesius later published it at the end of the works of Bruno of Segni, to whom it is dedicated.

The copyist, therefore, of whom we have just spoken, erred not only in the name of the author to whom the writing should be attributed but also in the name of the patron to whom it was dedicated—unless perhaps, as is sometimes found to have happened elsewhere, it had been dedicated to two different persons: namely, to Hugh, bishop of Asti, as the manuscript copy reads, and to Bruno of Segni, as the printed copy states.

696. Such, in substance, is what the aforementioned authors of the *Scriptores historiae litterariae Franciae* say. Now, since ancient copyists, whenever they happened to find a Commentary on the Psalms lacking the author’s name, assigned to it the name of St Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, it cannot be doubted that they held the opinion that such a work had been composed by that Saint. This is therefore a very strong argument that it really was produced by the Saint.

To this must be added the fact that almost all writers who enumerate the more celebrated authors in literary matters and the books written by them mention a Commentary on the Psalms composed by St Bruno, founder of the Carthusian Order.

Someone may perhaps object that the Commentary on the Psalms which one of the several Brunos—someone other than St Bruno the Carthusian—had composed may, because of their shared name, have been mistakenly attributed to the latter by the copyists. I admit that this could entirely have happened; yet it seems to me scarcely probable that this is what actually happened.

For if the Commentary on the Psalms was attributed to our Saint merely because several Brunos shared the same name and one of them had composed such a work, why did the same not happen with the Commentaries which St Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, composed on all the Canticles of the Old and New Testaments, or with those which St Bruno of Segni composed on the books of Moses, Job, the Song of Songs, and the Apocalypse, so that these too were attributed to our Bruno?

Since no ancient or recent writer is found to have done this at all, whereas, as has already been said, nearly all of them attribute some Commentary on the Psalms to Bruno the Carthusian, this circumstance greatly confirms the opinion that a Commentary on the Psalms was truly prepared by him. That opinion, supported both by this consideration and by the other reasons already brought forward, is so highly probable—or even entirely certain—that it must be accepted.
