697. Since this is so, it likewise appears beyond doubt that the Commentary on the Psalms written by St Bruno the Carthusian is the very one that first appeared at Paris in 1524 from the press of Jodocus Ascensius, and thereafter in the Cologne editions of 1611 and again of 1640.

For this Commentary differs greatly from the Commentary attributed to Bruno, bishop of Würzburg. Nor is it, as some once mistakenly supposed—thereby improperly depriving our Saint of the honor of having composed a Commentary on the Psalms—the same as the Commentary bearing the name of Bruno, bishop of Segni. This too is an argument that the Commentary on the Psalms was composed by our Saint.

Thus all the evidence converges to attribute it to him, as the authors of the *Scriptores historiae litterariae Franciae*, whose observations have for the most part been cited above, rightly note in vol. IX, p. 245. There they go on to express their judgment of this work of St Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, approximately as follows:

“Anyone who reads it with even moderate attention will readily admit that it is exceedingly difficult to find a work of this kind which is at once more substantial and clear, more concise, and more free from obscurity. Had it been better known, it would also have been more commonly used, and would not have been neglected as it has been until now. It would rightly have been judged most suitable for imparting an understanding of the Psalms. It presents an author skilled in every science and filled with the Spirit of God, such as we have shown St Bruno to have been after those who knew him best.”

This is more or less what they say in substance. How consonant these general statements about the Saint’s work are with the truth is shown by the more particular observations which they subsequently add, after inserting some intervening material, concerning the method followed in it.

698. Their observations amount approximately to the following:

After the Saint has explained in a brief Preface what is meant by the Psalter and has distinguished in the Psalms their various senses—namely, the literal, moral, and mystical—he proceeds to expound the text. He follows this method in such a way that, whenever he assigns the literal sense, he always refers it to the spiritual or mystical sense, which the Holy Spirit chiefly intended in the Psalms.

Thus Bruno almost everywhere reveals Jesus Christ and his members—that is, Christ and his Church. Indeed, this is the only path that leads to a perfect understanding of the Psalms.

Our Saint had read the ancient Fathers who had explained them before him, and sometimes cites them, especially St Ambrose and St Augustine, though without transcribing their words. In this way he made what he received from them in some sense his own, so that the entire work seems to have been drawn from his own resources.

When he explains the titles of the individual Psalms—which he does while shedding much light on obscure matters—he reveals most clearly that he knew the Hebrew language. The same is evident from various passages occurring throughout the work, as well as from the fact that he has recourse to the original, or Hebrew, text in order to explain more fully what the Vulgate offers.

Throughout the Commentary he inspires admiration, especially when he explains the mysteries of Jesus Christ and expounds a passage from the Psalms by means of another text of Sacred Scripture.

His style is concise, simple, vigorous, clear, polished, and as thoroughly Latin as the style of any other writer who flourished in the same century as the Saint could have been.

We know of no other editions of this excellent Commentary besides those which bear its title at the beginning as a work printed under the name of St Bruno—at Paris in 1524, at Cologne in 1611, and again in 1640—as has already been stated. Meanwhile, it would be desirable for the work to be constantly in the hands of all the faithful, and especially of those devoted to the public ministry of divine prayer.

699. Such is the judgment which the authors of the *Scriptores historiae litterariae Franciae* deliver concerning this distinguished Commentary of our Saint on the Psalms. It seems entirely fair to me, except for what they imply by saying that the whole work was drawn from the Saint’s own resources while nevertheless acknowledging that part of it was received from the holy Fathers.

It remains now to determine when Bruno composed it. Since our Saint appears to have had leisure for the study of Sacred Scripture, especially while he was staying first at the Grande Chartreuse and later in the Calabrian wilderness of La Torre, it may seem probable that he composed the Commentary of which we are speaking during that period.

Nevertheless, nothing prevents him from having done so while he was still in Reims, directing the schools and teaching the higher branches of learning. Nor does anything occur in this work of our Saint which concerns more the instruction of the anchorites whom he governed in solitude than that of other faithful people. It therefore remains very doubtful and uncertain whether he prepared it after he had already renounced the world or before.

Nor can the time be determined more certainly when the other work—the Commentary on all the Epistles of St Paul the Apostle, which occupies no mean place among the works printed under the Saint’s name and fills the entire second volume of the Cologne edition—was composed, as will become clear from what I shall say when I have shown that this work truly belongs to Bruno the Carthusian.

700. The homonymy of the several Brunos, which, as has been explained above, once caused the Commentary on the Psalms—although he had indeed composed it—to be taken away from our Saint, can have no place here whatsoever.

For there is no writer or author bearing Bruno’s name who flourished in the same century as this Bruno, or at least in the same period, and who composed a Commentary on the Epistles of St Paul the Apostle.

Therefore, if it can be proved by sufficiently solid evidence obtained elsewhere that St Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, commented on these Epistles, then all the copies of the work which bear the Saint’s name support the opinion of those who attribute it to him.

In fact, a sufficiently strong argument that our Saint commented on the Epistles of St Paul is derived from his Commentary on the Psalms, since the latter has certainly been shown by the foregoing to be his work.

The same style and the same method which the Saint followed in commenting on the Psalms are also found in the Commentary in which he explained St Paul’s Epistles. The expressions *id est*—that is, expressions which he frequently uses when explaining the Psalms in order to make an earlier expression clearer or better explained by means of another expression or phrase—also recur frequently in the Commentary on the Epistles of St Paul the Apostle.

Moreover, what removes every ground for doubting that this latter work truly belongs to St Bruno is the closing formula found by Mabillon in an ancient copy of the Commentary, expressed in these words:

> “Here ends Bruno the hermit’s Glossary on the Epistles of the blessed Apostle Paul.”

701. We now have sufficient grounds for rightly attributing to the Saint the Commentary on all the Epistles of St Paul the Apostle which was published under his name. Let us now speak about the time at which Bruno composed it.

Some maintain that it is more probable that the Saint composed this work when he was already living in solitude, whether at the Grande Chartreuse or at La Torre. Certainly, since he could then have been free from every other concern and easily devoted himself to writing books, there seems to be good reason for judging that he did so at that time.

Nevertheless, since Bruno, while still at Reims and not yet having abandoned the world, continually cultivated his mind through study and could easily have composed the work in the meantime, there is likewise no reason why we should assume that he certainly did not write it then.

Accordingly, it seems exceedingly doubtful whether he produced it at that time or after he had already withdrawn into solitude. Since nothing appears—not in that work itself, nor anywhere else—that would put an end to the doubt, the time at which the Saint wrote the Commentary just mentioned appears no less uncertain than the time at which he composed the Commentary on the Psalms.

Leaving this matter unresolved, I shall now explain what must be said about the method which our Saint followed in composing that work.

First, he transcribes the entire text of each chapter and then explains each sentence clearly and concisely in order, devoting himself solely to making plain to the reader everything contained in them, whether in the sphere of ethics or of faith and doctrine.

Sometimes he explains the words of the sentences according to the rules of grammar; sometimes he explains what meaning is conveyed by the same words in Greek and Hebrew—evidence that he knew both languages.

This is approximately what the aforementioned authors of the *Scriptores historiae litterariae Franciae*, vol. IX, p. 247, also provide concerning the method which our Saint followed in his Commentary on St Paul’s Epistles. They add some observations concerning the Saint’s teaching about divine grace and human free will under grace.

702. But since these matters do not concern the method followed by the Saint in the work of which we are speaking, and since they would carry us farther than is appropriate from our purpose—which requires only that we examine which works are attributed to the Saint and at what time and in what manner those which truly belong to him were written—we shall pass them over.

Of the *Paraenetic Epigram* urging the pursuit of heavenly things, and of the distinguished confession of faith, which still remain to be mentioned among the writings certainly attributable to our Saint, I now wish to bring forward a few observations.

First, that the *Paraenetic Epigram*, or, as others call it, the *Elegy on Contempt for the World*, certainly belongs to Bruno is clear even from the fact that neither recent nor ancient writers attribute it to any other author. Its value I leave to each reader to judge both from an examination of the work itself, which I recited in full in no. 56, and from the inferences repeatedly drawn from it in various works. It would not be worthwhile to list all of them here.

As for the distinguished confession of faith, which likewise certainly belongs to the Saint, the holy man uttered it when he felt himself near death. He inserted in it, in particular, statements concerning the Most Holy Trinity and the Incarnation of the divine Word. At the end, most probably in order to show, in accordance with the custom then prevailing—see no. 69—how greatly he detested the heresy of Berengar, he added:

> “I also believe the Sacraments which the holy Church believes and venerates, and especially the bread and wine which are consecrated on the altar: that after consecration they are the true body of our Lord Jesus Christ, true flesh and true blood, which we too receive for the remission of our sins and in the hope of eternal salvation.”

His biographers had inserted only certain fragments of this writing into the Lives of the Saint which they composed. Surianus, however, published it in full in his Notes on the Life of the Saint composed by Surius, pp. 253 ff., and Mabillon subsequently did the same in the fourth volume of his *Analecta*, pp. 400 ff.

We too shall insert it in full into this Commentary when we discuss the time of the Saint’s death. We must now deal with the works attributed to the Saint which nevertheless are not certainly his.

§ XLIII. Whether the works published under the Saint’s name, besides those already mentioned, truly have him as their author.

703. The writings published under the Saint’s name, though it is disputed whether he truly authored them, are divided into individual minor works or treatises, and sermons or homilies.

So that what will be said in the course of the discussion may be presented more clearly to the scholarly reader, I shall first provide some sort of account of each of these writings before investigating whether our Saint truly authored them. For the moment I shall at least translate the titles attached to each work in volume III of the works published under Bruno’s name at Cologne in 1611 and again in 1640.

First, the titles by which the minor works and their chapters are designated are as follows:

> “Book on the Praises of the Church, containing eight chapters: I, On Paradise; II, On Noah’s Ark; III, On the Tabernacle of the Covenant; IV, On Solomon’s Temple; V, On the Woman by Whom the Church Is Signified; VI, On the Holy City Jerusalem; VII, On Basilicas Established by Bishops; VIII, On Gospel Readings.
>
> “Book on the Ornaments of the Church, containing twelve chapters: I, On Faith; II, On Hope; III, On Charity; IV, On the Four Cardinal Virtues; V, On Humility; VI, On Mercy; VII, On Peace; VIII, On Patience; IX, On Chastity; X, On Obedience; XI, On Abstinence; XII, In Which Virtues the Church Is Adorned.
>
> “Book on New Things, containing ten chapters: I, On the New World; II, On New Heavens; III, On New Clouds; IV, On New Mountains; V, On New Trees; VI, On New Animals; VII, On New Powers; VIII, On the New Sea and New Fishermen; IX, On New Birds; X, On New Rivers.”

704. These, then, are the titles of the minor works, to the first of which is also appended, as its final chapter, a sermon on the dedication of a church.

The sermons or homilies contained in the book entitled *On the Festivities of the Festivities* have the following titles:

> “Three sermons on the Most Holy Trinity.
>
> “One sermon on the Nativity of the Lord.
>
> “One sermon for the Octave of Epiphany.
>
> “Two sermons on Palm Sunday.
>
> “One sermon on the Lord’s Supper.
>
> “Two sermons on Good Friday.
>
> “One sermon on Holy Easter Day.
>
> “Two sermons on the Lord’s Ascension.
>
> “Two sermons on Holy Pentecost.
>
> “Five sermons on the Blessed Virgin: I, On the Praise of Blessed Mary, City of God; II, On Her Nativity; III, On the Purification; IV, On the Annunciation; V, On the Assumption.
>
> “Five sermons: I, On Martyrs; II, On Christ the Vine and His Vineyard; III, On Martyrs; IV, On Good and Evil Brothers Dwelling Together, or on Martyrs Slain Together; V, On Praising God with Musical Instruments, by Which the Torments of Martyrs and the Afflictions and Confessions of Confessors Are Signified.”

To these sermons or homilies, which are included among the works published under the Saint’s name that I have already mentioned, are added eleven sermons on holy confessors and three others.

Of the latter three, the first is entitled “On Virgins”; the second, “On St Michael the Archangel”; the third, “On Contempt for Wealth.”

Of the other eleven, which precede these, the first is:

> “On Salt and Light from the Words of the Lord, and on the City Set on a Mountain, concerning the Apostles and the Other Teachers and Confessors;
>
> “II, On the Lamp Placed on a Candlestick, Applied to Solomon, Christ, and Blessed Benedict, on Whose Feast It Was Delivered, and Applicable to Any Confessor;
>
> “III, On Various Eyes and on Bishops;
>
> “IV, On the Wells of Abraham, That Is, of Sacred Scripture, Which the Apostles and Catholic Teachers Open;
>
> “V, On the Girded Loins and Burning Lamps of Confessors;
>
> “VI, On the Talents Entrusted by the Lord to Each Person, but Especially to Bishops and Other Prelates, in Order to Gain Profit from Them;
>
> “VII, On Confessors Who Must Keep Vigil;
>
> “VIII, On Continence and Purity of Heart, and on the Office of Bishops Signified by the Breastplate;
>
> “IX, On Any Saint Who, Having Left Everything, Followed God, Including the Virgin;
>
> “X, On the Holy Apostles, Evangelists, and Teachers;
>
> “XI, On Holy Teachers and Preachers.”

705. These, then, are all the minor works or treatises, as well as the homilies or sermons, which make up the third volume of the works printed under the name of our Saint at Cologne in 1611 by the efforts of Theodor Petreius and again, after his death, in 1640.

The authors of the *Scriptores historiae litterariae Franciae*, vol. IX, p. 242, after generally listing all the minor works or treatises and the sermons attributed to Bruno the Carthusian both in this edition of his works and in the other edition mentioned above, which was prepared in 1524 by Jodocus Badius—also called Ascensius after his native place—add the following:

> “But from that great number of writings printed under the name of St Bruno in those two editions, all the minor works or individual treatises on the one hand, and all the sermons or homilies on the other, must be removed. Neither the former nor the latter belongs to him, although they have been adorned with his name; they came to be attributed to him solely through an error arising from that name itself. They are all likewise products of the pen of St Bruno, bishop of Segni, who died in 1123 and was therefore a contemporary of the founder of the Carthusians.
>
> “There can be no doubt about this, since we see them attributed to him by Peter the Deacon, librarian of Cassino, who wrote before the middle of that same twelfth century, in two of his works—namely, the minor work *On Illustrious Cassinese Men* and the *Chronicle of the Monastery of Monte Cassino*—where he enumerates them individually.
>
> “Mauro Marchesius, dean of Cassino, took care to assert that these works belonged to their true author and to restore them to him. He had them printed at Venice under his name, in two volumes which together make up only one volume of proper size. The edition is from the year 1641 and was prepared from several ancient manuscripts containing other works of that prelate, including some which had escaped Peter the Deacon’s diligence.”

706. Thus far they. But since among the works which Mauro Marchesius published at Venice in 1651 under the name of St Bruno of Segni, or the bishop of Segni, there are also—as they themselves admit—some pieces which do not appear in the catalogue supplied by Peter the Deacon of the works composed by this holy Benedictine prelate, why did they agree with Marchesius, as they do in the words quoted, when he asserted that these too belonged to St Bruno of Segni?

Was it because Marchesius had found them in ancient manuscripts containing other works which certainly belonged to the bishop of Segni? That they formed this opinion for that reason is clear from the final sentence of the passage translated above.

But since the common name Bruno, shared by the founder of the Carthusians and by St Bruno, bishop of Segni, could have caused—or indeed, as the cited authors of the *Scriptores historiae litterariae Franciae* maintain, actually did cause—works expressly attributed by Peter the Deacon to St Bruno of Segni to be assigned by copyists to St Bruno the Carthusian, why could not the same cause have led some minor works or writings not expressly mentioned in Peter the Deacon’s catalogue of the works composed by Bruno of Segni to be attributed in error by the copyists to that bishop, because they were found by Marchesius in ancient manuscripts, even though they belonged not to him but to St Bruno, founder of the Carthusians?

It is indeed said that, in these ancient manuscripts from which Marchesius recovered them, they had been attached to other works whose authorship by Bruno of Segni is entirely certain. But what of that?

The ancient manuscript from which Jodocus Ascensius published the works of St Bruno the Carthusian in 1524, and another manuscript which was then preserved at the Grande Chartreuse, contained, together with the Commentaries on the Psalms and on all the Epistles of St Paul the Apostle—which certainly belong to our Saint—other minor works as well, as the aforementioned Jodocus Ascensius attests in the dedicatory letter prefixed to them. He published those works here together with the Commentaries, although none of them belongs to St Bruno the Carthusian. I shall shortly demonstrate this, while partly agreeing with the authors just mentioned, who attribute none of these pieces to him.

707. For my part, I think that these writings were inserted into the aforementioned manuscript codices—or into one of them, from which the other was later copied—through the ignorance or hasty judgment of a copyist. Having undertaken to copy all the works of our Saint, he may have happened by chance upon minor works which bore simply the name Bruno, without any additional designation in the title, and may have judged them to be by our Bruno without any examination at all, or after only a very brief one. He consequently appended them to the genuine works of the Saint which he had already copied.

But, since this is so, why could it not likewise have happened that some minor works which are not by St Bruno, bishop of Segni, were inserted into the ancient manuscript codices used by Marchesius—or at least into one of them, from which the others were later copied?

Of the minor works and homilies which first appeared at Paris and later at Cologne under the name of our Saint, and which Marchesius and the authors of the *Scriptores historiae litterariae Franciae* who followed him nevertheless attribute to St Bruno, bishop of Segni, those seem truly attributable to the latter which, both because of the unusual or uncommon title they bear and because of the subject they treat, correspond to the works which Peter the Deacon explicitly testifies—in his minor work *On Illustrious Cassinese Men*, chapter 34, and elsewhere—to have been composed by Bruno, bishop of Segni.

I adopt this view because, although this writer is occasionally found to have departed from the truth, and although he cannot be compared in gravity and authority with Leo Marsicanus, who began the *Cassinese Chronicle* which Peter later continued, he should nevertheless not be thought to have attributed to Bruno of Segni works which did not belong to that holy prelate. Peter had served as librarian at the Cassinese monastery not long after Bruno’s departure to the Lord, as John Baptist Marus—the first person to publish his work *On Illustrious Men*—teaches in his preface to it, printed in Muratori’s *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VI, together with other bibliographers. It is therefore credible that he had at hand the works which, in the cited passage, he asserts had been written by that holy bishop, who himself had formerly been a monk and even abbot of the monastery of Cassino.

708. Accordingly, after Peter the Deacon has stated in the cited chapter that Bruno of Segni composed expositions of the Psalter, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, the Song of Songs, and Judges, he immediately adds:

> “He also composed these sermons: On the Praises of the Church at the Dedication of a Temple; On Paradise; On Noah’s Ark; On the Tabernacle of the Covenant; On Solomon’s Temple; and On the Woman by Whom the Church Is Signified; On the Holy City Jerusalem; On Basilicas Dedicated by Bishops; likewise, On the Gospels; On the Ornaments of the Church; On Faith; On Hope; On Charity; On the Four Virtues; On Humility; On Mercy; On Peace; On Patience; On Chastity; On Obedience; On Abstinence; On How the Church Is Adorned; On the New World; On New Heavens; On New Clouds; On New Mountains; On New Trees; On New Powers; On the New Sea and New Fishermen; On New Birds; On New Rivers; On New Animals.”

It appears highly probable from the unusualness or novelty of the titles—which express the subjects treated and also occur here in Peter the Deacon—that the three books or treatises listed in no. 703 and attributed to our Saint in the editions of his works mentioned above were in fact composed by St Bruno, bishop of Segni.

The first is divided into eight chapters and entitled *On the Praises of the Church*; the second contains twelve chapters and is entitled *On the Ornaments of the Church*; the third is divided into ten chapters and is entitled *On New Things*.

As for the book entitled *On the Festivities of the Festivities*, however, the situation is different. In the form in which it was published under either our Saint’s name or that of Bruno of Segni, it contains a considerable number of sermons whose authorship by that holy prelate is established neither by the distinctive or unusual title—which also occurs in Peter the Deacon in the passage cited immediately above—nor by any other evidence.

It is therefore doubtful whether these sermons should be attributed to Bruno of Segni or to our Saint. For, apart from the fact that there is no evidence, either from Peter the Deacon or elsewhere, that they belong to the former of these two Saints, it is possible that they were inserted into the manuscript codices in which Mauro Marchesius found them together with works certainly authored by Bruno of Segni, through the process explained above, even though they did not truly belong to that holy prelate.

709. “But,” you will say, “Peter, in the supplement to the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book IV, chapter 31, writes the following about Bruno of Segni: ‘This man should not be thought to have lived here idly, since he expounded for us such extensive and important books of Scripture—of those, namely, which have come into our hands, the sum of which we are taking care to set forth—on the Psalter, on Genesis, on Exodus, on Leviticus, on Numbers, on Deuteronomy, on Isaiah, on the Song of Songs, on Judges, and on the Apocalypse. Moreover, he composed sixty-nine sermons on all the festivals and Sundays of the year, and one hundred and fifty-five homilies.’ Since by these words Peter the Deacon attributes more sermons and homilies to Saint Bruno, bishop of Segni, than he lists in chapter 34, *On Illustrious Men*, and at the same time implies that he did not have at hand all the works composed by this saintly bishop, it may easily be the case that the sermons published under the name of this holy Patriarch in the editions of the works of Saint Bruno the Carthusian mentioned above—although they are not found in Peter the Deacon’s catalogue of the homilies and sermons of Bruno of Segni under the somewhat unusual or uncommon titles indicating their subjects—were nevertheless genuinely composed by him.

“I admit that this is so. Yet since it is not certain, as already stated, from Peter the Deacon that the said homilies and sermons had Bruno of Segni as their author, and since, according to what has already been said, they were found both in ancient manuscript codices containing works certainly belonging to Saint Bruno the Carthusian and in equally ancient manuscript codices containing the writings which no one denies to Bruno of Segni, it still remains doubtful whether they should be attributed to this saintly Benedictine prelate or rather to Saint Bruno, founder of the Carthusian order.”

710. Nor should you reply that it is at least established from Peter the Deacon that several sermons were composed by Bruno of Segni, and that therefore the sermons of which we are speaking should be assigned to him rather than to Bruno the Carthusian. For just as there can be no doubt that Bruno of Segni composed several, indeed very many, sermons, so it cannot be called into question that our Bruno did the same. I think this may be inferred both from the saint’s epitaph and from his funeral inscription, which are to be reprinted below at no. 166. In the former of these two ancient monuments, which was placed upon Bruno’s tomb, this saint, the founder of the Carthusians, is introduced speaking as follows:

> I was the first founder of Christ’s fold in this wilderness;  
> I earned the right to be covered by this stone.  
>   
> Bruno is my name; Germany was my mother, and kindly  
> Rest in the wilderness transferred me to the Calabrians.  
>   
> I was a teacher, a herald of Christ, etc.

In the latter inscription, with which the church of Saint Maurice at Angers honored our saint, the following verse is read, among many others, about Saint Bruno: “He preached many sermons throughout the regions.”

Since, then, it is clear from the testimonies just quoted, supplied by the two aforementioned ancient monuments, that our saint acted as a herald of Christ, there can be no doubt that he also composed the sermons he delivered to the people. This being so, there is no sufficient reason why, because of the multitude of sermons composed by Bruno, bishop of Segni, we should attribute to him rather than to our Bruno the sermons published under the latter’s name, which are not distinguished by unusual or uncommon titles expressing the subjects they treat.

711. It may indeed be objected that the sermons which the saint delivered to the people were certainly written not in Latin but in the vernacular, and that therefore the multitude of sermons he composed cannot be used to argue that the Latin sermons under discussion here should be attributed to him. Yet from the fact that Bruno prepared many sermons in the vernacular, it appears credible that he also composed many in Latin, which he delivered to his disciples—whether those at Reims who were devoted to the higher sciences, or the monks in the hermitages of La Torre and Calabria. Consequently, it is far from improbable that he was truly the author of at least some of those that appeared under his name and are not expressly attributed by Peter the Deacon to Bruno of Segni.

Nevertheless, I would not dare assert this concerning all of them, and especially not concerning the sermon that holds second place among the eleven attributed to him *On Confessors*. For, as Marchesius rightly observes in his historical dissertation on Saint Bruno of Segni and his works, prefixed to that work, its conclusion contains material that seems capable of being spoken only by a monk professing the Benedictine Rule.

The first Carthusians, certainly from the very time of Saint Bruno, called Saint Benedict their father and still celebrate his feast with solemn rites. Thus, even if the author of that sermon had honored Saint Benedict with the title “Father”—which he does not do—it would not yet follow that the sermon must certainly be denied to Bruno, the founder of the Carthusians. But at its conclusion it also speaks both of Saint Benedict and of Benedictine houses in terms which, I do not know, all who carefully read the sermon in question will readily admit as fitting a man who did not profess the Rule of Saint Benedict.

712. Be that as it may, I am led to believe, on the basis of what I have already brought forward, that some of the sermons attributed to our saint in the editions of his works praised above may in fact belong to him, although the manner of style in them does not appear to be precisely the same as in his other works. For what is surprising about one and the same author occasionally employing a somewhat different style in different kinds of writing?

But when did the saint compose these sermons? Since the exhortations they contain are for the most part suited to monks, they were probably composed by him when he was already living in either the Carthusian or the Turritan wilderness, and were delivered to those who had placed themselves under his discipline there.

Nor should you therefore think it improbable that our saint, while still at Reims, ever addressed words to the people, contrary to what we established in no. 95. Although at that time he most probably did not possess Latin sermons of the kind discussed here, he may have had others composed in the vernacular, which have either perished or were never committed to writing.

The same may be supposed concerning any sermons which the saint may have delivered to the people after he had withdrawn from the world into solitude. Indeed, it does not appear at all improbable that this actually happened. Why could it not have occurred that our saint, although he had embraced the manner of life of hermits, who ordinarily do not speak to the people, nevertheless sometimes preached to the people, either during the journeys he undertook, as has been stated, or in churches near the hermitage—whether the Turritan or the Carthusian one—in which he lived, having been summoned there by bishops who wished, through the pious and fervent admonitions of a man whose rare holiness of life they had recognized, to benefit the flock entrusted to them?

“He preached many sermons throughout the regions”—these are the words of the funeral inscription, mentioned immediately above, with which the saint was honored.

713. But enough has been said concerning the sermons which the saint composed and delivered to the people or to his disciples. There remain two other works attributed to our saint in addition to those already listed.

The first is the work mentioned by Possevinus in the *Sacred Apparatus*. After listing all the works which the saint either truly composed or which he knew some people believed to have been composed by him, Possevinus adds: “There is also a manuscript book *On the Praises of the Solitary Life*, written by the same Bruno, in the possession of Paul Roger, a Carthusian of the Venetian Charterhouse.”

For this reason Theodorus Petreius, when he was arranging for all the works of Saint Bruno to be reprinted at Cologne, wishing to have that book printed together with them, added the following in the *Carthusian Library* which he prepared, on page 33, after listing all the works he thought belonged to Bruno: “To these works”—namely, those composed by Bruno—“Possevinus adds a book *On the Praises of the Solitary Life*, which he says is preserved in manuscript at the Venetian Charterhouse by Paul Roger, a religious of our family. If only it were possible to obtain it, so that it might likewise be committed to the press together with the other works of Saint Bruno, which we are now about to revise and reprint with the permission of our superiors!”

Surianus also mentions, in his notes on the life of Saint Bruno composed by Surius, page 251, the book *On the Praises of the Solitary Life* preserved by Paul Roger, a member of the Venetian Charterhouse.

Yet since Petreius committed these matters to writing in the *Library of Carthusian Writers* compiled by him and printed in 1609, and since, so far as I know, the aforementioned book *On the Praises of the Solitary Life*, said to have been written by Bruno, has not until now been brought to light, I strongly suspect that Possevinus was mistaken in believing that this manuscript book existed in the possession of Paul Roger, a member of the Venetian Charterhouse.

714. What if a certain book did exist in Paul Roger’s possession, containing several short works attributed to Saint Bruno the Carthusian, and had been given the title *On the Praises of the Solitary Life* because it also contained a letter written by the saint to Ralph the Green, in which several matters in praise of the solitary life were mentioned?

This is what may be said about the first of the two works which are absent from the editions of the works attributed to the saint, although, as I have noted, some people assign them to him.

As for the second, it is a prayer addressed to Jesus crucified, beginning with the words, “Before your eyes, Lord, we bring our sins,” etc. Meleager Pentimalli prefixed this prayer to his short life of Saint Bruno, printed at Rome in 1622, and attributed it to this saint, founder of the Carthusians.

But, says Zannottius—often mentioned above—in his *History or Life of Saint Bruno*, Pentimallius is greatly mistaken here, at least in substance. For, as Antonius Maggius, an Augustinian of Bologna, demonstrated in a work he published in 1700, that prayer was composed by Saint Augustine for the city of Hippo, of which he was bishop and which was besieged on every side by the Vandals. He composed it both to encourage the flock entrusted to him to implore divine assistance and to enable him, kneeling before the Crucified One, to mourn his own sins bitterly.

I find nothing more to say about the works which either belong to the saint or are attributed to him. I therefore now hasten to other matters concerning him.

§ XLIV. The saint once again experiences the benevolence of Count Roger toward him, when Roger is already lying ill with a terminal illness; shortly afterward he follows him in death, after having first obtained from Pope Paschal confirmation of all the donations and privileges which he had received either from Count Roger or from others.

715. In 1099, according to what has already been stated, the saint had received in perpetual servitude all the soldiers who, during the siege of Capua, had wished to betray Count Roger, their lord, to the people of Capua, and who, after being captured, had been on the point of carrying out their treacherous plan. This was done by a charter, almost the whole of which I quoted in § XXXIX.

Since, however, that document did not specify the names of the individual soldiers or of their sons, whom the prince had likewise delivered at that time to the saint and to the Turritan wilderness in perpetual servitude, Lanvinus, prior of the monastery of Saint Stephen, requested from Count Roger, who was lying ill at Mileto with the illness from which he died, another charter for greater security of the donation, one in which these matters would be set out individually. The prince, evidently moved in no small degree by his exceptional love for Saint Bruno, granted Lanvinus’s request and supplied the charter he desired.

It survives, though, as I believe, mutilated at the beginning, in Surianus’s notes on the life of the saint composed by Surius, pages 234 and following.

716. It is drawn up in these words:

> “These are the names and lineages of the one hundred and twelve servants and villeins who were found with Sergius the traitor during the siege of the city of Capua on the Kalends of March, in the year 1098 of the Incarnation of the Lord, in the sixth indiction. I, Roger, by God’s will count of Calabria and Sicily, because of the miracle which God deigned visibly to show me, through the prayers of Blessed Bruno, for the salvation of the Christian faithful who were with me and for my own salvation, have given to Father Bruno and to his successors not only these men themselves but also their sons and their sons’ sons, forever, as perpetual servants and villeins, with all their movable and immovable possessions, present and future, wherever they may be, whatever their craft or business, or whether they are sailors.
>
> “I had condemned these traitors to death by various kinds of punishment according to the judgment rendered against them; but at the request of the said Father Bruno I spared them their destructive death. I bound them instead to perpetual servitude and villeinage for the churches of Blessed Mary of the Wilderness and of Blessed Stephen the Protomartyr. I therefore caused a written charter to be made at Squillace, together with the donation I made of the monastery of Saint James of Muntauro and its estate.
>
> “Their names and lineages, however, are not contained in that charter. At the request of Brother Lanvinus, prior of the church of Saint Stephen, I have ordered these names and lineages of the said servants and villeins to be entered in this privilege, for perpetual remembrance.”

717. Roger now lists the names of the families whom he gave in perpetual servitude to Saint Bruno and his successors. Anyone who wishes may find them in the cited place in Surianus. At the beginning of his transcription of some of these names, Surianus observes:

> “The names of these families still survive for the most part, and they live in the villages subject to the monastery—namely, the Turritan monastery in Calabria, or Saint Stephen of the Wilderness—in both jurisdictions. These villages are Serra, Spatul, Bivongi, Gasparina, and Montauro; and in Montepaone, subject only in temporal matters, as Oliviano or Arunchum is thought to have been; and in other surrounding villages and towns. Some have changed their vowels or a few syllables.”

He then gives the names of the remaining families whom Roger gave to the saint in servitude and appends the conclusion, or closing clause, of the charter or privilege whose beginning I have just quoted. It reads as follows:

> “These are the one hundred and twelve lineages of servants and villeins whom I have given to Father Bruno and his successors, with all their possessions, wherever they may be, in perpetuity, and wherever they may dwell. They were almost all from the estate of Squillace and of Suberato.
>
> “This privilege was written on the fourth day of June, in the chapel of Saint Martin, situated in the middle of the city of Mileto, while my lord the count was ill, by the hand of Fulco, chaplain of the said lord count. It was read aloud in the chamber where the same lord count lay ill, in the presence of my lady Adelaide, countess, and with the consent of Malgerius, son of the lord count, in the presence of Peter of Moritono, Robert of Layna, Toraldus Carbonellus, Raynaldus of Climpcam, and Hubert of Solona, in the year 1101 of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the ninth indiction. Amen.
>
> “+ Roger, count. Adelaide, countess.
>
> “Peter of Moritono. Malgerius, son of Count Roger. Robert of Layna. Thoraldus Carbonellus. Raynaldus of Climpcam. Hubert of Solona.
>
> “I, Fulco, chaplain of Lord Count Roger, wrote this privilege at his command and subscribed it.”

718. Morkensius, who incorporated part of this instrument into the manuscript *Chronological-Diplomatic Dissertation* which he compiled concerning Saint Bruno, observes that a lead seal was attached to the original by a cord. He says that he received this information from letters sent from Italy—that is, if I am not mistaken, from the Turritan Charterhouse—and he agrees almost exactly with Surianus both in the closing clause of the document, which he gives in full, and in the persons who subscribed it.

He also does not fail to observe that the names of those who subscribed the charters he presents are not written everywhere in the same way. Thus, for example, the man who is called Hubert of Solma in one charter is called Hubert of Solona or of Selona in another. He adds—and this too must be said here—that since he does not have the originals of those instruments at hand, he cannot determine whether those names should be written in one form or the other.

This is what Morkensius says about that instrument. Yet since it is possible that someone might hesitate over whether Roger, who delivered the men guilty of the Capuan treason to Bruno in servitude, and the saint, who allowed them to be subjected to him in this manner, had acted contrary to Christian gentleness, Surianus rightly shows in his notes on the life of the saint composed by Surius, pages 247 and following, that Bruno was entirely free from guilt according to the custom accepted in his age for just reasons.

Moreover, if this author is to be trusted, Count Roger granted not only the charter or privilege under discussion, in favor of Saint Bruno and the Turritan wilderness, in 1101, but also two others.

719. For after Surianus had recorded in the chronology which he appended to his notes on the life of Saint Bruno the grant of the charter in which Count Roger listed, with the names of each, those guilty of the Capuan treason whom he had delivered to Saint Bruno in servitude, he referred to that grant in the words quoted above under the year 1101. Immediately afterward, under the same year, he adds:

> “Likewise, under another charter, the aforesaid Count Roger gave to the church of Blessed Mary of the Wilderness and to Master Bruno the estate of Arunchum with all its appurtenances and all its villeins. Moreover, he granted to the same church of Blessed Mary and to the aforesaid brothers the mill below Squillace, situated at the spring of Alexius. The aforesaid count again confirmed this donation during his grave and terminal illness before Robert, elected bishop of Mileto, and John, bishop of Squillace.”

Camillus Tutinus, in his *Survey of the History of the Carthusian Order*, does not differ entirely from Surianus. Under the year 1102 he writes:

> “Count Roger gives to the monastery of Saint Mary of the Wilderness, and likewise to Bruno and Lanvinus, the monks, and their successors in perpetuity, the three fortresses of Aruncum, Monte Aureum, and Oliviano, together with their citizens, and in addition a mill in the city of Squillace.”

But apart from the fact that Tutinus unquestionably assigns these matters erroneously to the year 1102, by which time, as will be explained, Count Roger had already died, I do not understand how it can be true that either the three fortresses—Aruncum, Monte Aureum or Montauro, and Oliviano—together with the Squillace mill, as Tutinus writes, or even merely Aruncum and the aforementioned mill, as Surianus says, were first granted to our saint by Count Roger after 1099, as both writers maintain.

For the charter quoted at no. 637 and following makes clear that the mill and two of the three fortresses just mentioned—namely, Montauro and Olivano or Oliviano—had already been granted by this prince to Saint Bruno and the Turritan wilderness from the year 1099 onward; while the third, which some call Aruncum or Arunchum and others Aruncium, had likewise been granted from the year 1094 onward, as is clear from the charter transcribed here at no. 582 and the two following entries.

I therefore believe either that the two writers just mentioned mean only that the donations of those fortresses or—see no. 717—villages, previously made to our saint, were confirmed once and again after 1099 by new charters, or, as I consider more likely, that not only Tutinus—which everyone will readily admit was mistaken about the year, since he is certainly wrong about the very year in which the event occurred—but also Surianus was in error.

720. I am led to accept this rather readily concerning the latter writer as well, because in the portion of the charter mentioned shortly before and dated, according to what has been said, in 1099, which he himself transcribes in his work on pages 223 and following, the donation of both Aruncium and the Squillace mill is found as having been made by Count Roger to Saint Bruno.

Nor should you reply here on Surianus’s behalf that Count Roger mentions in the charter of 1101 only the persons guilty of the treason whom he delivered to the saint in servitude by the charter of 1099, and the monastery of Saint James of Montauro, which he likewise granted to Saint Bruno by a charter of 1099; and that therefore it is not Surianus, who writes that Arunchum and the mill below Squillace were given to Saint Bruno by Count Roger in 1101, who is mistaken, but rather that the charter of 1099, transcribed here at no. 637 and following, in which the count granted the saint these and many other possessions, some of which are mentioned in the words of Tutinus quoted immediately above, must be corrupt.

For the count did not first grant Arunchum or Aruncum to Saint Bruno by the charter of 1099. He had already granted it earlier, by the charter of 1094—see no. 583—and ordered that its boundaries or limits be marked; see no. 641. As for the mill below Squillace, Count Roger indeed first bestowed it upon the saint together with Oliviano or Olivano and several other possessions by the charter of 1099.

But apart from the fact that many of these possessions belonged to the monastery of Saint James of Montauro, so that when Roger mentions that monastery in the charter of 1101 he likewise mentions them, it is possible that in the aforesaid charter of 1101 the prince wished to recall not all the donations he had made to Saint Bruno in 1099, but only the principal ones. It therefore does not follow that those which he does not list in that charter were not made in 1099.

Since this is so, not only Tutinus but also Surianus, when he writes that Arunchum and the Squillace mill were given to our saint by Count Roger in 1101, was in error.

721. I suspect that this happened because, having read somewhere that Count Roger confirmed in 1101 the donations of Arunchum, the Squillace mill, and many other things which he had previously made to the saint, Surianus took this confirmation as the first donation, so far as Arunchum and the Squillace mill were concerned.

He was led into this erroneous opinion partly because he did not have at hand the charter given at no. 582 and the two following entries and did not pay attention to the charter of 1099 which he himself had transcribed, and partly because he had at hand only the portion of the charter by which Count Roger confirmed in 1101 all the donations previously made by him to Saint Bruno—the portion reproduced above, in which neither Arunchum nor the Squillace mill is mentioned.

Lest anyone think that what I transcribed above from Count Roger’s charter of 1101 is improperly regarded as only part of it, Morkensius writes the following under the year 1101 in his *Chronological-Diplomatic Dissertation* concerning Saint Bruno:

> “During his terminal illness, Roger, count of Calabria and Sicily, confirmed the donations, immunities, and privileges previously granted to Saint Bruno and the brothers of the Calabrian wilderness, by a charter issued at Mileto on 4 June, in which he also specified by name the persons guilty of the Capuan treason.”

This is what Morkensius says. He himself states that he had the entire charter of Count Roger, transcribed last, before him. Since, however, the charter he mentions by the quoted words was issued, as he says, on 4 June, he is plainly speaking of a charter other than the one in which, according to Surianus, Count Roger listed the names of the individuals he delivered to the saint in servitude.

Since this is so, it follows that Roger not only listed those names in that document but also confirmed all the donations previously made to Saint Bruno. Therefore, since the charter as it survives in Surianus does not contain that confirmation, it cannot be regarded as the complete document but only as a portion of it.

722. After Surianus has presented this matter, he inserts only a few details which need not be recalled here and then adds:

> “Moreover, in this very month”—that is, in the month in which the charter last mentioned is recorded as having been issued—“Count Roger died in June, on the twenty-first day, as is read in the death register of that Charterhouse, namely Saint Stephen’s in Calabria, or on the twenty-second, as in the Cassinese register, in the year 1101, according to the *Chronicle of Lupus Protospatharius*, who was living in Apulia at that time, although he incorrectly gives July instead of June, perhaps through the copyist’s error.
>
> “Fortunate, therefore, was this prince even in this respect: after this most generous donation, he immediately departed to God, as though he were about to receive his reward in another age, adorned with the fairest fruits of mercy. Saint Bruno followed him only three months later, being taken away in the same year as Roger from the storms of this world, joyful at his approaching death and confident of his imminent summons, after seeing that the man had gone before him whose salvation alone still compelled him to remain concerned.
>
> “He seemed to wish to follow him all the sooner and more hastily so that, if his soul were perhaps still held in places subject to purgation, he might more confidently intercede for its release before God, the supreme Judge, after first offering the sacrifices of the body and blood of Him who was once redeemed by His Mother for five shekels.”

Thus Surianus argues—and rightly, in my opinion—that Count Roger died in June, not July, as Lupus Protospatharius writes, relying on the necrology of Saint Stephen’s Charterhouse. Fazellus, however, book VII, decade 2, and after him Rocchus Pirrus, in his *Chronology of the Kings of Sicily*, assign his death to July.

Fazellus’s designation of July as Roger’s month of death appears to rest solely, unless I am mistaken, on the authority of Lupus Protospatharius. It often happens that in the chronicle of Lupus, in whose autograph the names of the months seem to have been written with only a single capital or initial letter, March is found substituted by copyists for May, or vice versa, and July for June, or vice versa.

Since the matter stands thus, Roger remained alive for only seventeen or eighteen days after the issuing of the charter by which he confirmed all the donations he had previously made to Saint Bruno.

723. Zanottius writes in chapter 30 of the life or history of the saint composed by him, as he calls it, that our saint, together with Lanvinus, hurried to Roger, who was suffering at Mileto in the final stages of his illness, and continually consoled him amid the severe trials of his terminal disease with pious exhortations and admonitions.

He also adds that when Bruno had returned from Mileto to the Turritan wilderness after Count Roger had died, he arranged for funeral rites to be celebrated for that prince, to whom he was certainly under the greatest obligation, and for a great number of Masses to be offered. He further ordered his monks to implore divine mercy for the soul of the prince, who had been so generous toward the Turritan wilderness, by multiplying their prayers, fasts, and other penitential works.

That is what he says in the cited passage. And indeed, so far as I believe, no one who considered that the saint was unquestionably very far removed from the vice of ingratitude would readily have called this last matter into doubt—something which Surianus also implies was done by the saint in the conclusion of the words quoted immediately above—even though no testimony of antiquity at all has been found to confirm it.

Nor does it seem doubtful that the saint either went in person to Count Roger, who was lying ill at Mileto with the grave illness that brought about his death, in order to comfort him in the trials of his sickness and prepare him through pious admonitions for the journey to eternity, or at least sent Lanvinus or another of his companions to perform this service.

For in 1098, as we saw above, he had visited the same Count Roger—who was then lying ill at Squillace with the illness he had contracted after returning from the siege of Capua—in order to console him in his sufferings, taking four companions with him. Moreover, Mileto is not much farther from the Turritan wilderness than Squillace is.

724. Nevertheless, since from the year 1100, or even from the year 1099—see no. 678—the saint had been afflicted almost continuously by serious illnesses, as the letter already given above, which he then sent through Landuinus to the brothers of the Great Charterhouse, itself confirms, and since not long afterward, as we shall see below, he passed from this mortal life to the immortal one, I have considerable doubt whether illness prevented him at that time from personally visiting the count, who was suffering at Mileto.

Nevertheless, as I have already said, I do not think it doubtful that either the saint himself did so or that he sent one of his companions in his place to Roger.

Whatever the precise circumstances, everyone can readily understand from what has been said that Saint Bruno was deeply concerned for the salvation of this most loving prince, from whom he had received so many benefits.

Nor does it appear improbable that by his prayers he obtained from God that Count Roger, whose life had been spent amid almost continual turmoil of war, should at last bring it to a happy conclusion and be transferred from this wretched valley of tears and troubles to the eternal joys of heaven.

As I have already noted, Saint Bruno himself departed this life not long after the death of Count Roger. Before that occurred, however, he obtained from Paschal II, supreme pontiff—who had succeeded Urban II in the chair of Saint Peter after Urban’s death in 1099—the confirmation of all the donations, immunities, and charters previously granted to the Turritan wilderness.

In the year 1101, when July was already advanced, Paschal had come to Mileto. On this occasion Bruno arranged to have the pope petitioned—or perhaps the saint himself personally made the request—that the pope should strengthen with a new bull whatever had been granted to the Turritan wilderness either by Count Roger or by anyone else. The pontiff most graciously granted the holy man’s request.

725. “Pope Paschal,” writes Surianus under the year 1101 in his *Chronology*, appended to his notes on the life of Saint Bruno composed by Surius, page 403,

> “while staying at Mileto on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, at the request of Saint Bruno and Lanvinus, again confirmed by his charter the donation of the place which the illustrious Count Roger had made for their dwelling—that is, for Bruno and his companions—and which Urban II had confirmed. He likewise confirmed the other donations and privileges granted to them.”

Tutinus writes in his *Survey of Carthusian History*, page 14, that the only donation confirmed by Paschal was the one by which Count Roger had granted Saint Bruno the three fortresses of Aruncum, Monte Aureum, and Olivanum, together with the Squillace mill.

Morkensius, however, persuades me to agree with Surianus. He states in his *Chronological-Diplomatic Dissertation* concerning Saint Bruno that the bull—or, if you prefer, the brief—which Paschal granted to Bruno is still preserved in its entirety in the Calabrian house or Charterhouse of Saint Stephen. He further writes as follows:

> “Pope Paschal II, while staying at Mileto on the sixth day before the Kalends of August in the year 1101 [printed: 1011], confirms by a bull all the donations, immunities, and other privileges granted by Roger, duke and count, approved by the bishops of Reggio and Squillace—see no. 558 and following—and confirmed by Urban II.”

This is what he says, and rightly so, in my opinion, although I would wish to have the papal bull itself at hand, so that I could pronounce with greater certainty concerning the matters he records here.

726. But when only a short time had elapsed after Paschal’s bull had been granted, the weakness or illnesses with which the saint had been struggling, as stated above, since the year 1100 or even somewhat earlier, gradually grew worse. He fell into a very serious illness and, at last, being brought to the point of death, passed from this mortal life to the immortal one, the Lord calling him to the heavenly marriage feast.

When the holy man perceived that death was approaching, he summoned his brothers or disciples to him and explained to them the entire course of his life from infancy, as well as other matters which the religious inhabitants of the Turritan wilderness recount in the encyclical letter they wrote concerning the death of their holy father and which I shall place in full before the funeral inscriptions.

“Knowing,” they say, “that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, he summoned his brothers and, beginning with his infancy, reviewed each stage of his life. He proclaimed the knowledge and judgment of his entire life worthy”—that is, as Mabillon interprets it in the *Annals*, book LXX, no. 29, “he declared it worthy of divine scrutiny.”

“Afterward he set forth his faith concerning the Trinity in an extended and profound discourse and concluded it in this way.”

They then append part of the profession of faith which the saint made at that time. But both to fulfill what I promised above and to prevent the learned reader from being left without this precious testimony to the saint’s venerable antiquity and pure, uncorrupted faith, I wish to transcribe it here in full from the fourth volume of Mabillon’s *Analecta*, where it is inserted on page 400.

### 727

Thus it reads:

> “I firmly believe in the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit: the Father unbegotten, the Son only-begotten, the Holy Spirit proceeding from both, and these three Persons one God. I believe that this same Son of God was conceived by the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary. I believe that the most chaste Virgin was a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and remained a virgin forever after childbirth. I believe that this same Son of God was conceived among human beings as true man, without sin. I believe that this same Son of God was seized enviously by the treacherous Jews, treated insultingly, bound unjustly, spat upon, scourged, dead, and buried. He descended into hell in order to free his captives from there; he descended for our redemption and rose again. He ascended into heaven, and from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. I believe the Sacraments that the Catholic Church believes and venerates; and, specifically, that what is consecrated on the altar is the true body, true flesh, and true blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom we also receive for the remission of our sins and in hope of eternal salvation. I believe in the resurrection of the flesh and eternal life. Amen.
>
> “I confess and believe in the holy and ineffable Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—one natural God, of one substance, one nature, one majesty, and one power. And we profess that the Father was neither begotten nor created, but unbegotten. The Father himself derives his origin from no one; from him the Son received birth and the Holy Spirit procession. He himself, therefore, is the fountain and origin of the whole divinity. This same Father, in an ineffable essence and by his substance, ineffably begot the Son, yet not anything other than what he himself is. God begot God, Light Light. From him, therefore, comes all fatherhood in heaven and on earth. Amen.”

### 728

In Mabillon, this monument bears the following title at its head—or, if one prefers, the note written by the Saint’s disciples:

> “We took care to preserve in writing the faith of our master Bruno, which he professed publicly to his brothers when he sensed that the hour was approaching for him to enter upon the way of all flesh, because he earnestly asked us to be witnesses before God of his faith.”

Surianus, who likewise quotes the entire monument in his annotations to Surius’s Life of Saint Bruno, pp. 253 and following—though it differs from Mabillon’s copy only in some readings of little importance—observes that it had been found in the house of Saint Stephen in 1514, when it happened to be restored to the Carthusian order, at the end of an old Menology. Consequently, the note preserved in Mabillon and transcribed above, in which the Saint’s disciples living in the Calabrian hermitage say that they took care to preserve it, should not be regarded as suspect.

Nor is there any reason for anyone to be troubled by the fact that the inhabitants of the Turritana hermitage, in the encyclical letter mentioned shortly before, say of the Saint:

> “He expounded his faith concerning the Trinity in an extended and profound discourse and concluded as follows: ‘I also believe the sacraments that the holy Church believes and venerates; specifically, that the bread and wine consecrated on the altar are, after consecration, the true body of our Lord Jesus Christ, true flesh and true blood, which we also receive for the remission of sins and in hope of eternal salvation.’”

Yet these words do not constitute the entire profession of faith that the Saint made when he was near death. For although, in the monument just quoted from Mabillon’s *Analecta*, several further statements concerning faith in the most holy Trinity follow these words about the hidden sacrament of the Eucharist, nevertheless, at the very beginning of that monument are placed the words in which the Saint expounded his faith concerning that same most holy Trinity. Only after the words in which the Saint professed what else he believed do the words transcribed above follow immediately—words by which he declared to the brothers standing around him his faith concerning the most holy and hidden sacrament of the Eucharist.

### 729

Since this is so, the inhabitants of the Turritana hermitage, or Saint Bruno’s disciples, were in any event justified in saying in the aforementioned encyclical letter that their holy Father concluded or ended the profession of faith which he made as he was dying with the things he believed concerning the Eucharist, even though several further statements concerning the most holy Trinity follow the words cited by the Saint’s disciples.

If this explanation is unsatisfactory, it seems preferable to say that the Saint’s disciples of the Turritana hermitage were less exact in their wording than to suppose that the ancient document which I have taken from Mabillon’s *Analecta* is corrupt, or that the order in which its contents are arranged, both in Mabillon and in Surianus, has been disturbed.

What this additionally offers for consideration with respect to doctrine—doctrine diametrically opposed, as regards the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist, to the Berengarian doctrine—anyone can easily perceive from what was said in no. 68 and following. I shall therefore be content to refer the reader there and now dispose of what remains to be said here concerning the time when the Saint passed to heaven.

The Saint’s disciples in the Turritana hermitage, in the encyclical letter written to various churches and monasteries, already often mentioned, by which they announced the death of their beloved Father and requested prayers for his soul, write near the end:

> “On the following Sunday that holy soul—namely, Bruno—was released from the flesh on the day before the Nones, that is, on the sixth day of October, in the year of our Lord 1101.”

Of the poems composing the epitaph placed on the Saint’s tomb, and to be transcribed below, the penultimate reads:

> “The sixth day of October released the bonds of the flesh.”

Therefore, since the encyclical letter was written immediately after the Saint’s death, and since the epitaph likewise appears to have been placed on his tomb not long afterward, there can be no doubt that Bruno passed to the Lord both in the year 1101 and on the sixth day of October. It is consequently astonishing that Tutinus, in his *Prospectus of Carthusian History*, p. 14, assigned Saint Bruno’s death to the year 1102.

### 730

It is no less astonishing that the authors of the *Literary History of France*, vol. IX, p. 239, lower margin, should have noted that it could not be understood how Ruinart, in the *Life of Pope Urban II*, no. 2, p. 8, assigned Saint Bruno’s death to the year 1099. For there Ruinart is speaking not of Bruno but of Pope Urban II, who died in that year; nor, so far as I know, does he assign the death of our Saint to any other year than the one we give elsewhere in the same *Life of Pope Urban*. Thus the authors mentioned above very probably misinterpreted him.

Moreover, the Saint’s older biographer records the following in his final chapter:

> “He passed to the Lord after the eleventh year from his departure from Chartreuse, neither more nor less, as is contained in the books of the Customs of Dom Guigo, which are in the house of Chartreuse.”

But it is clear from what I brought forward in § XXX, when discussing the time at which the Saint was summoned from Chartreuse to Rome by Pope Urban II, in nos. 518 and following, that there is an error in these words and that “in the eleventh year, neither more nor less” must be replaced by the following wording supplied by the chronologist of the first four priors of Chartreuse and already given here in no. 7 in the Saint’s eulogy: “in approximately the eleventh year.”

Let what has been said concerning the year and day on which Bruno passed from this mortal life to immortality suffice. Let us now proceed to what followed the Saint’s death.

## § XLV. In which church of the Turritana hermitage the Saint was buried, and what should be thought concerning the miracles following his burial, together with certain other matters in any way relating to him and preceding the time when he was entered in the catalogue of the saints—or rather, of the blessed

### 731

Since, as I have already shown above, two churches existed in the Turritana hermitage in the Saint’s time—one dedicated to the most holy Mother of God Mary and Saint John the Baptist, the other to the same Mother of God and Saint Stephen the Protomartyr—it may reasonably be doubted whether he was buried in one or the other. Some decide in favor of the former of these two churches, or at least in favor of the cemetery of that church, which was also simply called “the Church of Saint Mary of the Hermitage”; others, by contrast, decide in favor of the latter of the two churches. Nevertheless, it may perhaps be possible to reconcile all these views to some extent, as will readily be gathered from what follows.

Blömenvenna, and Surius following him in the Life of the Saint which he composed, explicitly affirm that Bruno was buried in the Church of Saint Stephen, which in the course of time was also called “the Church of Saint Stephen of the Grove” or “of the Wood.” These two biographers were subsequently joined by Mabillon in the Benedictine *Annals*, book 70, no. 29; the authors of the *Literary History of France*, vol. IX, p. 240; and several others.

Camillus Tutinus, however, states no less explicitly in his *Prospectus of the History of the Carthusian Order* that our Saint was buried in the Church of Saint Mary of the Hermitage. He writes on p. 15:

> “The body of Saint Bruno was handed over by the monks for burial in the Church of Saint Mary of the Hermitage, near its altar.”

In addition, Zanottius writes in the *Life or History of Saint Bruno*, chapter 31, citing the manuscript *Monuments of Calabria* in his support, that after the body of the Saint, who had died, had been exposed for public veneration in the Church of Saint Mary of the Hermitage for three days, it was then carried, as he himself had ordered, to the farthest part of the cemetery attached to that church and buried there in a marble sarcophagus.

Although he nowhere states what these *Monuments* were or how ancient they might be, it nevertheless seems that we should believe that the Saint was buried not in the Church of Saint Stephen but either in the Church of Saint Mary of the Hermitage, as Tutinus relates, or at least in the cemetery attached to it, as Zanottius records from those *Monuments*. For it seems likely that he wished to be buried in the church—or at least in the cemetery—of the monastery in which, according to what has been said, he had led an eremitical life for approximately ten years, rather than in the church of another monastery which he had never inhabited and which he had built for monks less suited to the eremitical life.

### 732

Morotius writes as follows in the *Chronological Theatre of the Carthusian Order*, p. 226:

> “After Saint Bruno had been entered in the catalogue of the saints, his body was transferred from the Church of Saint Mary of the Tower to another, Saint Stephen of the Wood.”

That is what he says. Since several other writers also agree with him, it appears certain that the body of Saint Bruno—already enrolled among the saints, or rather, for reasons to be explained, among the blessed—was transferred from the Church of Saint Mary to the Church of Saint Stephen, especially since no writer at all is found who records the contrary.

Since this is so, and since the Saint was probably transferred from the place where he had been buried to the Church of Saint Stephen, it seems likely that he had originally been buried in the Church of Saint Mary of the Hermitage.

But, someone may object, after the monastery of Saint Stephen defected from the Carthusian institute to the Cistercian in 1192, its abbots, fearing that the Carthusians might reclaim the sacred relics of their Founder, always guarded them with the greatest care, as Blömenvenna and, after him, Surius record in their works on Bruno, on the basis of a report made by the prior of the Neapolitan Carthusians (see no. 780). To guard them more securely, they placed the sacred relics now in one place and now in another, with only the abbot and another trustworthy man knowing where they were.

Therefore, from the fact that these relics were transferred from the Church of Saint Mary of the Hermitage to the Church of Saint Stephen of the Wood or Forest after Bruno happened to be entered in the catalogue of the saints or blessed in 1514, it by no means follows that he had been buried in that same Church of Saint Mary.

This may be argued against the opinion which holds that the Saint was buried not in the Church of Saint Stephen but in the Church of Saint Mary, or at least in its cemetery.

### 733

But what if what Blömenvenna and Surius report concerning Saint Bruno’s relics having been concealed by the Cistercians was conveyed to the aforementioned Carthusian prior only by a false rumor? There certainly seem to be grounds for thinking so.

For the Saint’s sacred body was found in the Church of Saint Mary in 1513, the year immediately preceding Saint’s canonization, as it is called, as Tutinus records in his *Prospectus of the History of the Carthusian Order* under the year 1513. Nor does it seem likely that this happened because the abbots of Saint Stephen had transferred the precious treasure from the monastery of Saint Stephen, their place of residence and the church in which it had originally been kept, to the Church of Saint Mary, separated or distant from that monastery, in order to conceal it.

Since this is so, all things considered, it appears more probable that Saint Bruno was buried in the Church of Saint Mary, or at least in the cemetery attached to it.

Nor should you object here that the bull of Pope Leo X, issued in 1513 and to be quoted below, contains the following words (see no. 755):

> “In whose church—that is, in the church of the monastery of Saint Stephen—the body of Saint Bruno, founder of that order, is said to be kept.”

For, apart from the fact that the pope speaks there on the report or opinion of others, who could easily have been mistaken, the cells built by Saint Bruno near the Church of Saint Mary of the Hermitage, and presenting together with it something like a monastery, appear to have ceased to be inhabited from the year—or even earlier—when the religious inhabitants of this place and of the monastery of Saint Stephen transferred themselves, as will be explained below, to the Cistercian order in 1192.

Meanwhile, the Church of Saint Mary remained under the care and dominion of the monastery of Saint Stephen, so that from that time the latter possessed two churches, one called Saint Mary and the other Saint Stephen; and it seems that under the name “the monastery of Saint Stephen of the Wood” not only that monastery but also the monastery of Saint Mary of the Hermitage was included.

I am entirely convinced of this because in all documents later than 1192 in which the religious houses of the Turritana hermitage are mentioned, only the monastery of Saint Stephen of the Wood is named.

### 734

Since this is so, even if Saint Bruno’s body had been kept in the Church of Saint Mary, Pope Leo could say without compromising the truth in the cited bull that it lay in the church of the monastery of Saint Stephen.

Nor is it apparent that Blömenvenna and the others who write that the Saint’s body was buried in the monastery of Saint Stephen, or in its church, could not have meant the Church of Saint Mary.

But whether the Saint finally received a tomb in this or that church of the Calabrian hermitage, the following epitaph was placed upon it, as Blömenvenna testifies when he begins his account of Bruno’s burial in the Life of the Saint which he composed:

> Christ’s first sheepfold is founded in this hermitage;  
> I earned the right to become one covered by this stone.  
> Bruno is my name; Germany was my mother, and grateful  
> The quiet of the hermitage transferred me to the Calabrians.  
> I was a teacher, a herald of Christ, a man known throughout the world;  
> From above came that grace—it was not merit.  
> The sixth day of October released the bonds of the flesh;  
> You who read this, pray for rest for the spirit.

Thus writes the biographer of our Saint. Puteanus also agrees with him in the Life of the Saint which he composed. In the later edition of that work, however, prepared by Jodocus Ascensius in Paris in 1524, a change was made in the poems comprising the epitaph just given.

In place of the first hexameter, most probably because in it the second syllable of *eremus* is contracted contrary to the rules of prosody, the following was substituted:

> “The first founder of Christ’s sheepfold in this hermitage.”

In the second pentameter, probably for the same reason, the following was substituted:

> “Grateful peace of the grove transferred me to the Calabrians.”

In addition, Surius gives the following in place of the final pentameter of the epitaph quoted above:

> “The bones remain in the tomb; the spirit seeks the stars.”

But since in the earlier edition of the Life composed by Puteanus, prepared at Basel not long after 1514, and in the ancient documents appended to the end of that edition, the three poems just mentioned are read in the same form as in Blömenvenna, it appears exceedingly probable—indeed, I would say certain—that they were originally written and placed on the Saint’s tomb in that same form.

### 735

Let us now examine what is reported to have occurred after the Saint’s burial.

Blömenvenna says in the Life of the Saint:

> “The man of God was buried in his monastery of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, behind the high altar. At his tomb a living spring flows, which by divine mercy and through his merits brings the faithful many desired remedies of health. There also, as is read elsewhere, one may see the blind given sight, the deaf restored to hearing, the maimed and mutilated healed, lepers cleansed, and those possessed by demons quickly purified.
>
> “Yet, if Saint Jerome is to be believed, there is something more astonishing than all these miracles: nearly all those in the aforementioned roll—containing the series of funeral titles to be published—show that they marvel at this, when they repeat so often and proclaim with one harmonious voice that he was able to trample glory and honor underfoot and happily complete the course of his life amid such austerity, truth, and perfection.”

Thus he writes. But lest anyone perhaps doubt the truth of the spring miraculously raised at the Saint’s tomb, as he seems to assert here, he immediately adds:

> “No one should be troubled if that spring is no longer seen at the tomb of the man of God. For springs produced miraculously are not always perpetual, just as the spring of oil which is said to have flowed at Rome at the time of Christ’s birth was not perpetual. I myself saw at Saint Mauricius, at the place of his beheading, a hole without oil, through which the inhabitants of that place asserted that oil had once flowed.
>
> “For miracles are performed by the Lord for the revelation and commendation of the holiness of his servants; and therefore, when their holiness has become perfectly known, miracles sometimes cease.
