It is read of Saint Nicholas that oil flowed from his sacred bones, but that, because of the people’s demerits, it ceased to flow when one of his successors had been unjustly expelled from his seat.”

### 736

> “The same should be thought concerning the spring of Saint Bruno: namely, that religion—which he himself had begun with the utmost holiness—had departed from his monastery. For when the holy man had fallen asleep in the Lord, that monastery remained committed to the eremitical life, or to the Carthusian order, which Saint Bruno had first instituted in the hermitage of Chartreuse and afterward in the Calabrian hermitage.
>
> “Five priors succeeded him in the government of that house, up to the time of the venerable Guigo, Prior General of Chartreuse. But while all the elders who had seen, heard, and known all the works of the Lord which he had deigned to perform through his servant Bruno were still alive, the monastery remained in its purpose. When others who did not know these things eventually succeeded them, and when the Carthusian order had begun to multiply in France, around Chartreuse and elsewhere, that Calabrian monastery alone remained, degenerating through lukewarmness from the holiness and fervor of so great a Father.
>
> “Since, however, it could not obtain visitors and reformers from the house of Chartreuse because of the great distance, it transferred itself to another purpose—namely, the Cistercian order, which, newly planted and watered by Saint Bernard through word and example, persevered in great fervor. This occurred after it had endured for sixty years in the purpose of the Carthusian order in which it had been founded.”

Thus far Blömenvenna. Surius agrees with him here in substance, as he often does, though not Puteanus, who writes only in general terms that the Lord deigned to perform many miracles through the Saint’s merits after his death.

But what should now be thought concerning the spring raised by a miracle at the Saint’s tomb; concerning the many miracles performed there through the Saint’s merits; concerning the time when it dried up or ceased to exist; and finally concerning the reason why this happened?

### 737

To begin with the spring miraculously raised at the tomb: since neither Puteanus, in the Life of Bruno which he composed, nor any writer, whether contemporary or nearly so, so far as I know, mentions it, there appears to be good reason why some people have called into question whether a spring truly burst forth by a miracle at the Saint’s tomb.

Indeed, since some have been found who, as we saw above, have asserted—or at least through error believed—that a spring was divinely raised at Chartreuse when the Saint and his companions first entered it, why could it not also have happened that, either through error or through the license of invention, it was written that a spring had bubbled forth miraculously at the tomb of our Saint, and that it was afterward believed more readily and confidently than was proper by lovers of marvels?

Nevertheless, since the following words are supplied by the chronologist of the first five priors of Chartreuse, or by the older biographer of our Saint, in his final chapter:

> “Immediately beside his tomb—namely, Saint Bruno’s—a living spring flows, which by divine mercy, through the merits of this holy man, brings the faithful the desired remedies for many illnesses,”

and since, as I have already shown above, he flourished in the thirteenth century, perhaps not yet two centuries after the Saint’s death, it does not appear unlikely that he drew this account of the spring miraculously raised at the Saint’s tomb either from an older document or at least from tradition.

I therefore cannot confidently assert that a miraculous spring did not burst from the earth at Bruno’s tomb—or, if one prefers, from the tomb itself—although I have serious doubts about the matter, since it is not supported by evidence of wholly certain and indisputable faith.

### 738

Nor can the doubts—already considerably increased by the fact that, as Blömenvenna himself admits in the words quoted above, the spring is no longer found at the Saint’s tomb—be removed by what this biographer chiefly states to have been the cause of the miraculous spring’s drying up or ceasing to exist.

For even if we grant that a spring was truly raised miraculously at the Saint’s tomb, it seems scarcely probable that it ceased because, as he appears to intend by the words quoted in no. 736, the inhabitants of the Turritana hermitage had embraced the Cistercian institute.

For they did this only so that, after religious discipline among them had collapsed, they might pass from the less austere way of life into which they had fallen after abandoning the original rigor of their institute to a stricter and holier rule of life, and thus serve God more perfectly. Blömenvenna himself seems to indicate this in the words quoted above, and the bull or brief of Pope Celestine, which will shortly be quoted, also confirms it.

Some maintain that they withdrew from the Carthusian institute for reasons which would have been less pleasing to God. Others, however, insist that this should not be accepted; and it does not greatly concern our present matter which side is right.

For even if we grant that there was no entirely just reason why the inhabitants of the Turritana hermitage should have departed from the Carthusian institute for the Cistercian, it still would not become probable that a spring miraculously raised at the tomb of Saint Bruno dried up because of their defection to the Cistercian institute.

Whatever the reason may have been, they transferred themselves to a way of life which was in no respect contemptible and was highly commendable in many respects; nor did they do so without the agreement and approval of Pope Celestine, as is clear from the bull by which he granted them permission to pass to the Cistercian order.

### 739

For this reason I wish to transfer here the bull from Surianus, who inserted it in his annotations—or rather, in the chronology—appended to his version of Surius’s Life of Saint Bruno, pp. 469 and following. It reads:

> “Celestine, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the brothers of the monastery of Saint Stephen of the Wood in Calabria: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “By the duty of our office we ought to devote especially diligent care to the propagation of the religious order and the extension of its branches, and to hold and foster it, as far as we can, while it grows through divine fervor.
>
> “Since, therefore, prompted by divine inspiration, you have wished to serve under the observance of the Cistercian order, and since your prior, coming to us, has earnestly requested apostolic confirmation and favor in this matter, after consultation with our brothers, since this change appears to be the work of the right hand of the Most High, we commend your purpose. We confirm by apostolic authority, saving the right of the Roman Church, that henceforth you must live under that same observance and under the correction of the abbot and brothers of Fossanova, and render to God a service pleasing to him.
>
> “Let no human being, therefore, be permitted in any way to violate this page of our constitution and confirmation, etc. Given at the Lateran, on the third Ides of December, in the second year of our pontificate.”

Since, therefore, as is understood from this papal bull or brief, the brothers of the monastery of Saint Stephen of the Wood in Calabria—that is, the religious inhabitants of the Turritana hermitage—passed to the Cistercian order not only without the pope’s opposition but with his approval and praise of their purpose, and since in doing so they undoubtedly did not sin against God, I do not know whether anyone will regard it as sufficiently probable that their transfer could have been the cause for which the spring of the Turritana hermitage, miraculously raised at the Saint’s tomb, ceased to exist—or, if one prefers, dried up.

Since the matter stands thus, it remains, on the basis of what has been said above, and especially because the spring raised by a miracle no longer exists, just as doubtful as before whether such a miracle ever took place there.

### 740

Nor does it greatly advance the case that miraculous springs are not always perpetual. Even if we grant that this is true, the only conclusion will be that, although a spring is no longer found at the Saint’s tomb, a miraculous spring could once have existed there. From this, however, no one will certainly regard it as an established fact that such a spring actually once existed there.

If, nevertheless, a miraculous spring ever existed at the tomb of our Saint and ceased only for the reason given by the writers mentioned above, it must have lasted longer than fifty or sixty years.

For Pope Celestine II died in 1144, at a time when it is admitted by all who accept this miracle that the monastery of Saint Stephen of the Wood had not yet been transferred to the Cistercian order and, consequently, that the spring miraculously raised at Saint Bruno’s tomb had not yet ceased to exist. Since the monastery did not pass to the Cistercian order later than the twelfth century, the Pope Celestine who granted the already quoted bull to the brothers of Saint Stephen of the Wood can be none other than Celestine III.

Since he was elevated to the supreme chair of the Church in 1191, after April had already begun, and since the bull is dated on the third Ides—that is, 11 December—in the second year of his pontificate, it follows that the brothers of the monastery of Saint Stephen of the Wood, or the religious inhabitants of the Turritana hermitage, passed to the Cistercian order only in 1192 or at the beginning of the following year.

Consequently, that monastery remained in the way of life followed there by Saint Bruno not merely for approximately sixty years, as Blömenvenna relates in the words transcribed above, but for nearly one hundred years or more; and it had more than five priors of the Carthusian institute before passing to the Cistercians.

### 741

Indeed, Camillus Tutinus, in the brief *Chronicle* of the Priors which he appended to his *Prospectus of the History of the Carthusian Order*, lists not merely five but thirteen priors who governed the Turritana house of Saint Stephen according to Saint Bruno’s rule, up to the year 1192, before it embraced the Cistercian institute, giving each of them his individual name. He notes that the prior who flourished after the fifth died in 1138.

It appears exceedingly probable that Tutinus correctly enumerates more than five priors who lived according to the rule established by our Saint in the Calabrian Turritana hermitage, both from what has already been said and from the relevant material which Columbius brings forward in his *Dissertation on the Beginnings of the Carthusians*, no. 20 and several following sections, as will become clear to anyone who consults him.

Since this is so, and since Blömenvenna and the others who share his opinion do not assert that the spring which arose miraculously at Saint Bruno’s tomb dried up, or ceased to exist, before the monastery of Saint Stephen passed to the Cistercian institute, it follows that the spring must have lasted not merely approximately fifty or sixty years but more than ninety years after our Saint’s death.

This is so even though, in the opinion of those writers—who place the Calabrian hermitage’s defection to the Cistercians as early as 1160 or even earlier—that conclusion is wholly contrary to the truth.

These, then, are the matters which arise for discussion both concerning that miraculous spring, said by the writers cited above to have arisen at the Saint’s tomb, and concerning the time when it ceased to exist and the reason why it did so. The next step is to discuss the miracles which, according to Blömenvenna’s words transcribed above and the testimony of others, were performed in great number through the Saint’s merits, especially for the benefit of those who drank from the miraculous spring mentioned.

### 742

Blömenvenna says of Saint Bruno:

> “Although he is said to have shone through many miracles, nevertheless—as I cannot recall without grief—miracles of this kind were not recorded with the diligence they deserved; or, if they were recorded, when monks of another religion—that is, the Cistercian—entered his monastery, they were first preserved with insufficient care and afterward lost.”

Thus he writes. Surius agrees with him exactly, and Puteanus likewise agrees as far as concerns the number of miracles generally performed through the Saint’s merits. Yet they do not recount a single particular miracle performed by the Saint.

I would like the assertion that many miracles were performed by the Saint to be confirmed by the testimony of at least one contemporary and trustworthy writer.

The older biographer of our Saint does indeed affirm, in the words given above, that many sick people who drank from the spring miraculously raised at the tomb were restored to their former health. Yet he is not sufficiently ancient for us to be able to trust him safely.

Nor does it help that, using verbs in the present tense, he writes as follows:

> “Immediately beside his tomb a living spring flows, which by divine mercy, through the merits of this holy man, brings the faithful the desired remedies for many illnesses.”

Thus he appears to speak of a miraculous spring which still existed in his own time and of miracles then performed by water drawn from it.

Even if we grant that this biographer is speaking of miracles performed in his own time, it will nevertheless be very difficult for him to secure among all readers a confidence that is altogether certain and indisputable in his account, since he wrote at the Great Chartreuse, situated at a considerable distance from the Turritana hermitage.

Furthermore, he may perhaps be speaking in the manner of historians, who quite often describe events that took place in past times by means of verbs in the present tense.

743. Blomenvenna and Surius, in that very passage where they acknowledge that the fountain miraculously raised at Bruno’s tomb no longer existed in their own time, speak of it as though it still existed, using the present tense. The former writes: “At his (namely, Saint Bruno’s) tomb a living fountain flows”; the latter: “At his tomb a living fountain bursts forth.” In the same place they likewise use only the present-tense verb when declaring that many people formerly recovered their health after drinking water drawn from that fountain. Consequently, from the fact that the earlier biographer of our Saint speaks in the present tense about miracles performed through Saint Bruno’s merits, it does not follow [Col. 0457D] that he intended to signify that these miracles had occurred in his own time.

Since this is so, it is exceedingly doubtful whether he is speaking only of events that had taken place long before his own age. Therefore what he records concerning the great number of miracles performed through the Saint’s merits cannot be made altogether certain and indisputable, although meanwhile it does not seem doubtful that the Saint, even before he had been enrolled among the blessed, performed at least some miracles, given the reputation for holiness by which he had been renowned among the Calabrians for more than four hundred years.

Indeed, Surius, in his annotations on the Life of Saint Bruno, after stating on page 314 that many miracles which God deigned to work at the invocation of Saint Bruno, His confessor, for the manifestation of his glory, had not come down to our knowledge because of the scarcity of written records and the ravages of time, brings forward a considerable number of miracles said to have occurred through Bruno’s intercession after his canonization, as it is called. He also places before these two miracles that occurred before Bruno was entered in the catalogue of the saints or blessed.

744. Since I am now treating events that occurred before ecclesiastical worship—the worship proper to the saints—was conferred upon the Saint by papal authority, I am pleased to insert here those two prodigies as well. I believe that the reader will not find it unwelcome to have them included in the small number of the many miracles performed through the Saint’s merits before his authorized ecclesiastical cult and that have come to our knowledge.

The first, although it is uncertain whether the Saint had any part in it, is as follows:

“In the year of the Lord 1131, when the illustrious Geoffrey of Lorotello, count of Catanzaro in Calabria, son of Count Rudolf of Lorotello, nephew of Count Roger, founder and benefactor of the hermitage of Saint Mary of Torre, had revoked certain donations of a church of All Saints, together with lands and vineyards in the territory of the town of Badolato, which had been made by himself and by his mother Berta, he was, with God as avenger, struck in the chest by a severe abscess. He thereby came to the point of death, and, after making his will, when he was near death, was admonished by Roger of Arenis to restore the things unjustly taken away. As soon as he restored what had been taken away, with blood flowing from his mouth and nostrils, he was restored to his former health. This will become clearer from his own words and from the instrument of restitution, where he says as follows:

“‘In the year 1131 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the eighth indiction, in the month of October, when I, Geoffrey of Lorotello, count of Catanzaro, was held by youthful desire—not to confirm, but rather to revoke, what my venerable lady mother Berta had given to the church of All Saints in the territory of Padulato, namely cultivated and uncultivated lands, domestic and also wild trees, peasants, and vineyards, which she had given to Blessed Mary of the hermitage and to the blessed Protomartyr—desiring temporal things more than eternal things, God permitting it, three years after my revocation I was so severely afflicted in the stomach by a horrible abscess that, my vital powers diminishing, I was despaired of by the physicians.’”

745. “But after the will had been drawn up, Lord Roger of Arenis, who was then present as a witness to the will at Castelnuovo, where I was ill at that time, said to me: ‘Confirm, with a sincere intention of restoring them, the things that you revoked from Blessed Protomartyr Stephen. For he has such merit with God that he will be able to free you from this abscess.’ When I heard these words, I ordered that they be confirmed by a new will, which I drew up again at once. In a wondrous manner I suddenly began to be freed as foul blood flowed from my mouth and nostrils.

“When he saw this miracle, I devotedly sent letters to the hermit brothers on the day when the Genoese ship, coming from Alexandria into the harbor of Castelnuovo, suffered shipwreck. Rudolf of the Crucifix, master of the hermits of Saint Mary and of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, came to me at my castle of Catanzaro, together with Brother Arnold, Odo, and Guido, monks. In their presence I ordered this present privilege to be written by the hand of the notary Robert, together with the things that my lady mother had given,’ and so forth.”

Such, according to Surius’s recension, is the first miracle that I thought should be mentioned here, one also confirmed by a public instrument. Since, however, it may seem—perhaps not without reason—that it is doubtful whether Saint Bruno had any part in this event, Surius immediately adds to the public instrument by which he confirms it:

“Nor is there anyone who doubts that this miracle”—namely, the one just related—“must also be attributed to Saint Bruno, because, now that he is in heaven, he cares for his household.”

Thus he indicates that he has no doubt that at least some part in the reported miracle should be attributed to Saint Bruno. But in the other miracle, which must also be given here, or rather in the apparition, it is entirely certain that the Saint had a part, as anyone will readily admit who merely reads the account.

746. These are the words in which the celebrated Surius relates it on page 317 and following:

“About the year 1510, at Valencia in Aragon, John Aloysius Bertran, a notary, who for a long time had been a benefactor and procurator of the Carthusian house of Porta Coeli, had, because of the great devotion he bore toward Saint Bruno, come from a prolonged illness to the threshold of death before the Wednesday of Holy Week. When the physicians had given up all hope of his recovery, he suddenly opened his eyes and asked for clothes to put on. To those who questioned him he replied that Saints Vincent Ferrer and Bruno had entered to see him and had told him that he would certainly not die on that occasion, but must go to church on that Wednesday to hear the divine offices. This he actually did.

“Afterward he loved Saint Bruno so greatly that, when Leo X later granted his feast to be celebrated solemnly in the churches of the Order in the year 1514, he himself, going to the same Carthusian house at his own expense, arranged that the feast should be celebrated both in the church and in the choir, and continued to do so until his death.”

John Aloysius Bertran, to whom the apparition related here occurred, later fathered Saint Louis Bertrand of the Order of Preachers by his second wife, whom he had married after the death of his first. Our account of that saint will be given on the ninth day of this month, on which he is celebrated. This is taught both by the very Life of this holy confessor, in which the same apparition is related—a Life written in Spanish by Vincent Justinian Antist, a Valencian and a member of the Order of Saint Dominic, and afterward translated into Italian by another religious of the same Order—and also by the celebrated Surius in his account of another apparition granted to the same Aloysius Bertran, which he places below, in the Appendix to the posthumous glory, immediately after the apparition already related.

Thus, through the apparition just mentioned, and through the merits of both Saint Bruno and Saint Vincent Ferrer, Aloysius Bertrand, who was lying dangerously ill, was suddenly and unexpectedly restored to his former health. We therefore now have a miracle that was performed at least partly through the intercession of our Saint and that preceded his canonization—or rather, the oral declaration by which, as will be explained, Pope Leo X permitted him to be honored in the Carthusian Order with the worship proper to the saints. Yet although I conducted the most diligent investigation, I was unable to discover other miracles performed at that time in which the Saint had any part.

747. Zanotti, moreover, who in chapter 34 of the Life of Saint Bruno composed by him also relates the apparition of Saint Bruno and Saint Vincent Ferrer granted to the father of Saint Louis Bertrand, reports in chapter 32, following several earlier writers, that a fountain burst forth from our Saint’s tomb. Drawing upon the Calabrian records contained in the manuscripts that he cites, he adds that the power of healing diseases, divinely imparted to the water of that fountain, passed to the waters of a small lake in which, while he was alive, the Saint used from time to time to immerse his body in order to discipline it, when the monastery of Saint Stephen at Torre first departed from the Carthusian institute and turned to the Cistercian one.

To prove this, the same author adds that even in our own time, and especially during Pentecost, when the Saint’s sacred body was transferred from the church of Saint Mary to the church of Saint Stephen, innumerable benefits are almost every year divinely bestowed during the three feast days through the power of those waters, and miracles are performed. As for the credibility owed to him both concerning these matters and concerning the transfer of the power from the waters of the prodigious fountain to the waters of the lake just mentioned, the judgment must remain with the reader.

To close this section with the miracle that is said to have begun immediately after the Saint’s death and to continue even today, Blomenvenna, later followed by Surius, writes near the end of the Life of the Saint that he composed:

“From that monastery”—namely, the Turritan monastery of Saint Stephen—“one proceeds by a level path along the bank of the torrent for 1,500 paces to a most devout cave. It is sufficiently enclosed by mountains and surrounded by woods, which close off the extremities of the valley; these are remote and solitary and offer no further access for human use. Above this cave a small chapel has been built, with an altar under the title of Saint Bruno, the Cologne master, the first founder of the Order of the Carthusians of Saint Mary of Torre; his image can be seen painted there.

“In this cave the same servant of God remained with incredible fervor from the time when he first came there until the day of his death. As a sign and testimony of his outstanding holiness, the place where, after the ecstatic transports of contemplation, he used to strike his relaxed naked limbs against the bare earth has, even to the present day, never produced grass over the area corresponding to the length of his sacred body, although grass can be seen growing all around it. All the inhabitants of that place most steadfastly affirm this evident miracle.”

748. Thus far his account. But whatever may be the truth concerning the miracle said to persist even today, which is mentioned in these words and which, I think, must be left undecided, I am entirely convinced and certain—if only by the diploma or privilege of Mesimerius, bishop of Squillace, numbered 558 and following—that, contrary to what Blomenvenna relates here, the Saint did not remain or live in the cave designated by these words from the day on which he first entered the hermitage of Saint Mary at Torre in Calabria until his death.

For in this document that prelate speaks as follows:

“Count Roger was pleased to ask me on behalf of the most honored monks and hermits, namely Lords Bruno and Lanvin, . . . who inhabit the place preserved by God called Torre, in the most venerable church of our most glorious Lady, the Mother of God, and of Saint John the Baptist, the Forerunner.”

By these words he clearly suggests that both Bruno and Lanvin lived in the most holy church of the Mother of God. How, then, can anyone prudently believe, without an ancient witness, the assertion of Blomenvenna and others that the Saint spent the entire period during which he was in the Calabrian hermitage in the cave mentioned above? Some more recent writers support Blomenvenna, but they too cite no authority or ancient monument in their favor.

Nor should anyone here adduce in their support the following words, which Zanotti, at the end of chapter 31 of the Life of the Saint, testifies were inscribed in the cave:

“This place, dearest brothers, must be held in the highest veneration and reverence, in which Bruno, the faithful servant of Christ and teacher of sacred Scripture, afflicted his body with many kinds of punishments; in which, after the course of this miserable life, he flew away to heaven.”

For who can assert with certainty that these words were placed in the cave either immediately after the Saint’s death or at least not long afterward? As for me, I think it must be very much doubted whether they are older than his canonization, as it is called.

I would therefore readily believe that Bruno occasionally withdrew to the cave mentioned by Blomenvenna, which was not far from the church or monastery of Saint Mary of the Hermitage where the Saint lived, so that he could devote himself more quietly to prayer and meditation on divine matters. But whether he actually lived there, I shall remain in doubt until stronger arguments are brought forward—arguments capable of removing all doubt about the matter from my mind.

§ XLVI. Pope Leo X orders the monastery of Saint Stephen at Torre in Calabria to be restored to the Carthusian Order and permits the Saint’s ecclesiastical cult.

[Col. 0461D]

749. In the numerous funeral inscriptions to be reprinted below, and likewise in the letters addressed to various churches and monasteries that are also to be reprinted below, by which the death of Saint Bruno had been announced to them by the Saint’s disciples from the hermitage of Torre, the Saint is praised in the replies not only for his outstanding teaching and virtue, but it is also declared that those who gave those replies needed his prayers more than he needed theirs. This clearly indicates that he was already generally recognized as a holy man.

Nevertheless, even if the matter stood thus, more than four hundred years had already passed since his death—a fact that may seem surprising—when, so far as appears, no one had yet attempted anything by which that most famous and holy man, who had founded a most illustrious Order and had greatly adorned first the Carthusian house and then Calabria through his wholly exceptional virtues, might be enrolled by the supreme pontiff among either the saints or the blessed.

750. Baillet adds in volume III of the Lives, column 91, that Saint Bruno’s memory had been so completely neglected among the people of Calabria throughout that entire span of four hundred years that no religious cult whatsoever had been offered to him by them. Yet it appears probable that this writer was mistaken in the matter, judging from what Blomenvenna committed to writing near the end of the Life of the Saint that he composed. For he writes there:

“Moreover, crowds of people come to these places”—namely, to the cave in which the Saint lived and to the church of Saint Mary of the Hermitage—“old and young, children and women, noble and common, princes and lords, out of veneration and devotion for the most holy Bruno and also to obtain his benefits. They attend him as though he were still living among human beings; they come eagerly and approach reverently, pray, and adore.

“Above all, the cave or grotto mentioned above, in which he served the Lord almost always alone, is visited with such reverence, affection, and unbelievable faith that several are sometimes seen approaching it from the aforesaid monastery”—namely, Saint Stephen’s—“only with bare feet. Others walk on their knees around the sacred cave, licking the earth and rocks out of devotion and going around them drenched in tears. Moreover, they take away a piece of the cave or rock itself, considering it a most precious relic, and thus return home rejoicing.

751. “No one could adequately express in words the devotion with which the bishops, abbots, prelates, religious, princes, counts, barons, and the entire populace of Calabria are attached to this most holy Father Bruno. In addition, not far from the aforesaid monastery, at a distance of 300 paces, there is a very extensive wood called Folo, set apart by the servant of God himself solely for the restoration of his monastery. If anyone attempts with rash audacity to act against the ordinance of the holy man—and this is a report confirmed by the long experience of all the peoples of Calabria—he does not escape divine vengeance.”

Thus far his account. Since he committed these things to writing when the Saint had not yet long been enrolled by Leo X among the saints—or rather, as will be explained, among the blessed—it appears probable that an outstanding and singular cult, such as he depicts in the words quoted, was already being offered to the Saint in Calabria, and not for the first time after this had been done by that pontiff.

I therefore do not dare to agree unreservedly with Baillet when he asserts that, when Bruno was enrolled among the blessed by Pope Leo, he had almost entirely been erased from the memory of everyone in Calabria and was honored there by no cult whatsoever. This is especially so since, from the veneration that the words of Blomenvenna just quoted indicate the Calabrian people bore toward the Saint even before he had been enrolled among the blessed, it appears probable that they had also offered him the worship proper to the saints.

752. But whatever the truth may be, it is permissible to conclude from the account already given of the apparition in which Bruno, together with Saint Vincent Ferrer, appeared to the sick Aloysius Bertran, that Bruno was regarded and honored as a saint even before he had obtained from the Carthusians a public bestowal of the honors of the blessed. In that account Aloysius is said to have been affected in a special manner toward Bruno as a saint.

The same may also be inferred from the fact that the Carthusians—who, as Baillet himself admits, honored Bruno privately, at least, with the honors of the saints in Carthusian houses outside Calabria—eventually began to consider procuring either his canonization or his beatification.

Camillus Tutinus, already very frequently cited, records the following in his Survey of the History of the Carthusian Order under the year 1504, although 1503 is incorrectly written there:

“In the general chapter celebrated that year, the Carthusian priors discussed procuring the canonization of Saint Bruno and recovering the Carthusian house of Saint Stephen in the Wood. It had been in the possession of the Cistercians for nearly three hundred years and afterward”—namely, at the beginning of the fifteenth century, or perhaps somewhat earlier, if the brief chronicle of the monastery of Saint Stephen in the Wood correctly records the matter on page 195 of Tutinus’s work—“had passed to commendatory abbots.

“For this reason James of Aragon, prior of the Carthusian house of Naples; Matthew, prior of Bologna; Louis, prior of the Carthusian house of Mantua; and Hugh, prior of the Roman Carthusian house, were appointed to pursue the litigation. At that time the commendatory abbot was Louis, Cardinal of Aragon, nephew of Ferdinand I, king of Naples. James, whom we mentioned above, being related to the cardinal, dealt with him in Rome, together with the other priors, concerning the restoration. After many articles had been discussed on both sides and conditions had been imposed, the cardinal allowed himself to be divested of the monastery.

“But since its revenues were held under emphyteutic right by Evangelista Tornafrancia of Catanzaro, who had also promised to relinquish his right, James, having completed the remaining matters, came to Naples. Evangelista, however, regretting the conditions that had been offered, fled. After being intercepted through royal measures and compelled to keep his promise.”

[Col. 0463D]

753. Thus he reports that the Carthusians had applied themselves not only to procuring the canonization of their holy Father but also to recovering the Calabrian monastery of Saint Stephen in the Wood, and that they had continued to work toward this end.

Nor was the effort of those religious men unsuccessful. First they obtained the restoration of the house or monastery of Saint Stephen to their Order, and afterward they obtained, if not the enrollment of their first founder among the saints, at least his enrollment among the blessed by papal authority. This will become clear from what must here be said, in accordance with the purpose of my work, concerning these two matters.

I begin with the recovery of the Calabrian monastery, since this preceded the Saint’s canonization, or rather beatification. First, however, whether the Carthusians had already begun considering the recovery of that monastery in the year 1504 is called into doubt by Camillus Tutinus himself, who says in the words just quoted that they had done so at that time.

For in the chronicle that he appended to the Survey of the Carthusian Order composed by him, he records as follows:

“In the year 1505 the Carthusian monks, in the general chapter, entrusted James of Aragon, prior of the Carthusian house of Naples; Matthew, prior of Bologna; Louis, prior of Mantua; and Hugh, prior of Rome, with arranging for the restoration of the monastery of Saint Stephen to the Order. After various negotiations with the aforementioned cardinal and Tornafrancia, prolonged for ten years, and after mutual petitions had been settled on both sides, they brought the dispute to the point that the cardinal resigned the monastery into the hands of the supreme pontiff Leo X. When this had been done, the pontiff once again granted and handed it over to the Carthusians with all its possessions, and suppressed the abbatial title by a bull issued at Rome in 1513.”

Since Tutinus here writes that the Carthusian priors named above were commissioned by the general chapter only in 1505 to attempt the recovery of the monastery of Saint Stephen, although in the words quoted above from his Survey he had taught that this had already been done in 1504, he himself makes it genuinely doubtful whether the Carthusians decided to attempt the recovery of Saint Stephen’s in the former year or the latter.

754. Nevertheless, since in the words quoted immediately above he also states that, after ten years had already elapsed from the beginning of the negotiations for its restoration to the Carthusians, the monastery was resigned into the hands of the pontiff, who afterward returned it to the Carthusians, it appears more probable that the Carthusians had in fact been negotiating the recovery of that monastery from as early as 1504. The bull by which Pope Leo X ordered it to be returned to them is dated 1513, as Tutinus himself admits in the words quoted, and it can readily be understood that ten years elapsed from 1504 to 1513, but not from 1505 to 1513.

I transcribe here the instrument that I had requested be given a place here and that also confirms several matters already stated. It is formulated in these words:

“Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, for perpetual remembrance of the matter. Because of the apostolic office entrusted to us, by which we preside over the governance of the universal Church, we are continually and carefully concerned to direct successfully and beneficially the condition of churches, monasteries, and all other regular places. Therefore, so that a more pleasing observance may flourish in some of these monasteries and places, divine worship may increase, and the devotion of the faithful may grow, we sometimes entrust them to be governed by new rulers, through whose diligent effort and prudent care those monasteries and places may also, in spiritual and temporal matters, advance through desired increases.

755. “Indeed, the monastery of Saint Stephen in the Wood, of the Cistercian Order and in the diocese of Squillace, which our beloved son Aloysius, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, had recently obtained in commendam by apostolic grant and dispensation—this commendam having ceased because the same Cardinal Aloysius today voluntarily and freely resigned it into our hands, and we decided to accept that resignation—remains vacant in the same manner in which it was vacant while it was commended to the same Cardinal Aloysius.

“Since we regard the latest manner in which the said monastery became vacant as expressly set forth here, even if from it there results any general reservation enclosed in the body of the law, we are devoting paternal and anxious attention to providing quickly and successfully for the government of that monastery, lest it be exposed to the disadvantages of a lengthy vacancy. After careful deliberation with our brothers, we have finally turned the eyes of our mind toward our beloved sons, the brothers of the Carthusian Order, in whom observance of regular discipline, holiness of life, and exemplary conduct are known to flourish daily like new branches in the Lord’s field.

“We hope that, if in the aforesaid monastery, in whose church the body of Saint Bruno, founder of the said Carthusian Order, is said to lie buried, the abbatial dignity and the Cistercian Order were perpetually suppressed and extinguished, and this Carthusian Order were instituted and planted; if thereafter the monastery itself were called a house under the same invocation of Saint Stephen; and if it were perpetually granted to the brothers of the said Carthusian Order to govern and administer it according to their rites, customs, and regular institutions, just as the other houses of that Carthusian Order are governed and administered, then through this act a good and blessed way of life would be introduced into the monastery, to God’s favor and acceptance; divine worship would be increased; and the condition of the monastery in spiritual and temporal matters would be happily provided for, together with the spiritual consolation of the faithful living nearby.

756. “Having weighed all these matters with due consideration, with the advice of the aforesaid brothers and by apostolic authority, through the tenor of these presents, we perpetually suppress and extinguish in the same monastery the abbatial dignity and the Cistercian Order, no matter in what manner or through whose person it may be vacant, even if provision for it on any account belongs specially or generally to the Apostolic See. We institute the said Carthusian Order there, so that henceforth it shall be and be called not a monastery but a house of the same Saint Stephen.

“We perpetually grant it, with all and singular its movable and immovable goods, rights, and appurtenances, to the aforesaid brothers, to be governed and administered by one prior and a suitable number of brothers according to their aforesaid rites, customs, and regular institutions, just as the other houses of the said Carthusian Order are governed and administered.

“Therefore let the beloved sons who are at present visitors of the said Carthusian Order in the province of Further Lombardy—within whose boundaries the said house of Saint Stephen is situated—be permitted, according to the custom of that Carthusian Order, in the name of the Carthusian Order and of its brothers, freely to take possession by their own authority, either personally or through another or others, of the house of Saint Stephen and of the aforesaid goods, rights, and appurtenances, and, as stated above, to retain it perpetually under their government and administration, converting its fruits, revenues, and income to the use and benefit of the brothers and their house, without requiring for this the permission of the diocesan of the place or of anyone else.

757. “We also grant, with similar advice and by the aforesaid authority, that the prior and brothers residing for the time being in the house of Saint Stephen may freely and lawfully use, possess, and enjoy all and singular the privileges, graces, immunities, indulgences, exemptions, prerogatives, favors, and spiritual and temporal concessions by which the other houses of the said Carthusian Order, or the priors and brothers residing in them for the time being, generally use, possess, and enjoy, or may in any way hereafter use, possess, and enjoy.

“This is notwithstanding apostolic constitutions and ordinances, as well as the statutes and customs of the said Orders, even those strengthened by oath, apostolic confirmation, or any other firmness, and all other contrary provisions whatsoever. For from this moment we decree null and void anything that anyone, with any authority, knowingly or unknowingly, may happen to attempt otherwise in these matters.

“Let no one at all be permitted to violate this document of our suppression, extinction, concession, and decree, or rashly to oppose it. Whoever should presume to attempt this shall know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

“Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1513, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the first year of our pontificate.”

Thus, as is evident from the bull transcribed here, Leo X restored to the Carthusians the Calabrian monastery of Saint Stephen in the Wood, which had been resigned to them by Louis, or Aloysius, of Aragon, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, mentioned by Oldoinus in volume III, column 187, of the Lives of the Pontiffs and Cardinals. The restoration took place on 16 December 1513, and they took possession of it soon afterward.

758. “James of Aragon,” Camillus Tutinus says in his Survey of the Carthusian Order under the year 1514, “the prior of Naples, together with the prior of Clermont and other Carthusian monks and lay brothers, took possession of the monastery of Saint Stephen in the Wood on 27 February.”

The Carthusians therefore took possession of the said monastery on 27 February 1514, and thus only three months had elapsed after it had been restored to them. Zanotti explains the event in his History of Saint Bruno, chapter 33, approximately as follows:

James of Aragon, prior of the Carthusian house of Naples and visitor of the province, and Peter Acerri, prior and co-visitor of the Carthusian house of Clermont in Basilicata, in the Kingdom of Naples, who had been appointed for this purpose, took with them the priors of Bologna, Mantua, and Rome. Armed with letters from the pontiff and the king, and aided by Adam Toraldus, baron of Badolato, they proceeded to the monastery of Saint Stephen.

When they arrived, the Cistercians, who had already been informed of the pontiff’s will through letters received from him, came out to meet them like suppliants amid the festive ringing of the bells. The Carthusians were then received and entered the church. After the papal and royal letters had been read aloud, they took possession of the monastery in the manner prescribed by law, giving solemn thanks to God after the transaction had been completed.

This is approximately what he relates in substance from the manuscript Calabrian records, which I think deserve credence here because they record events of relatively recent memory.

Leo, who had shown himself well disposed toward the Carthusians by restoring the aforesaid monastery, soon afterward favored them with an even greater favor. For in that same year, 1514, without judicially examining the miracles that were said to have been performed by Saint Bruno, he granted the Carthusians, by an oral declaration, permission to celebrate his annual feast with an ecclesiastical office and to commemorate him daily in the liturgical prayers.

This is made clear by the letter that Cardinal Anthony of Pavia, protector of the Carthusians, sent to them concerning the matter in that same year, 1514. Since the letter also contributes greatly to the glory of our Saint, I transcribe it here from Pope Benedict XIV’s work On the Canonization of the Blessed and the Beatification of the Servants of God, book I, chapter 41.

759. It is formulated in these words:

“Anthony, by divine mercy priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes of the holy Roman Church, Cardinal of Pavia, and protector of the entire Carthusian Order, sends eternal greetings in the Lord to all and each of those who shall see and read this present letter.

“Today, in accordance with the office of our protection and because of the goodwill and affection with which we are devoted to the entire aforesaid Carthusian Order, we presented before the feet of our most holy lord Leo X, pope by divine providence, the venerable religious men, Lords Matthew of Bologna, Louis of Mantua, James of Naples, and Hugh of Saint Cross in the City, priors of houses of the same Carthusian Order.

“Both we and the aforesaid religious men had reported and explained to His Holiness many things concerning the praises, honors, and holiness of life of Blessed Bruno, confessor, the first founder and institutor of the same Carthusian Order. This blessed man, as Christian warfare was declining and charity was growing exceedingly cold because of the abundance of iniquity, like a brave commander established and organized a new army in the Church to resist the enemies. And in the vineyard that the Lord had planted with His right hand, now overgrown with the brambles and thorns of vices, like a most diligent steward he brought in so many faithful laborers that day by day more abundant fruits might come forth from it for the holy Church, and that it might bring forth an odor of sweetness and holiness.”

### 760 [Cols. 0468B–0468C]

“For the manifold example of doctrine, most disciplined life, innocence, and purity furnished by that blessed confessor himself, generating very many sons of holy adoption, continues to generate and nourish them unceasingly day by day. By his merits the aforesaid Order is adorned, is confirmed by miracles, and continually rises, as it were, from virtue to virtue, watering the mountains from his heights, and the earth is satisfied with the fruit of his fragrances. Therefore, together with the aforesaid priors, we humbly petitioned that same Lord, our Lord, on behalf of the venerable men Francis of Puteo, the present minister general, and the other priors, and of all the monks, nuns, lay brothers, and persons of the said Order, that, for the glory of almighty God, who rejoices in the veneration of His Saints; for the honor of the aforesaid blessed confessor and of his most evident works of holiness and signs of virtue, by which he shone while in the flesh and, summoned to heaven, shines forever; and for the dignity of so distinguished an Order, he might deign, out of apostolic munificence and kindness, to grant permission that every year, on the sixth day of October—the day on which, having laid aside the burden of the flesh, that blessed confessor Bruno flew away to everlasting glory—the feast in his memory might be celebrated with fitting praises and honors in the Lord, together with a solemn Office, and that his commemoration might be made on the other days, although the same blessed confessor Bruno is not found to have been otherwise canonized by his predecessors, the Supreme Pontiffs, as is customary.”

### 761 [Cols. 0468D–0469A]

“That most holy Lord our Pope, asserting that he had long before learned many things concerning the praises and holiness of the same blessed confessor, judged it worthy and consonant with reason that he who had been distinguished by God in this world with such great gifts and graces, and who, having been taken up into heaven, ought to be venerated ever more greatly—he to whom the Almighty, while he was living, had given a heart obedient to the commandments and to the law of life and discipline—should now, while present before the throne of divine glory, receive on earth the service of due devotion. Accordingly, he willingly assenting to our petitions and those of the aforesaid priors, graciously and favorably granted and conceded to the said lord Francis, the present minister general, and to the other priors, monks, nuns, lay brothers, and persons of the said Order, permission, from that time forward and perpetually, with God’s blessing, solely in the houses of that Order and in their churches or chapels, to keep the aforesaid feast solemnly and celebrate it with due devotion; to honor and venerate the body and memory of the aforesaid Bruno with fitting praises in the Lord; to perform and chant a suitable Office in honor of that blessed confessor; and also to make his commemoration each day—without prejudice to the fact that the same blessed confessor Bruno is not found to have been otherwise canonized, as stated above. Present there also were the most reverend Father in Christ, Lord Lord Laurence Puccio, priest cardinal of the title of the Four Holy Crowned Ones of the Holy Roman Church, and the reverend Father Lord Francis Armellini, cleric of the Apostolic Chamber.”

### 762 [Cols. 0469B–0469D]

“Therefore, so that no doubt concerning this concession might arise in anyone, we ordered these present letters to be drawn up, subscribed by our own hand, and secured by the affixing of our customary seal; and we also caused them to be subscribed by our secretary, for the strengthening, confirmation, and testimony of the foregoing and of the truth. Given at Rome, in the Apostolic Palace, on 19 July 1514, in the second year of the pontificate of our Lord. Antonius, cardinal of Saint Praxedis, protector, by his own hand. Antonius Testa Verulanus.”

Such are the letters by which Antonius, priest cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedis of the Holy Roman Church, Cardinal of Pavia, and protector of the Carthusian Order, publicly testified that Leo X, the Supreme Pontiff, had granted by word-of-mouth authority to all persons belonging to this Order, both men and women, the power to render Saint Bruno the worship expressed in the same letters.

Zanotti, in the history or Life of Saint Bruno composed by him, chapter 33, writes substantially as follows:

“Pope Leo X, in the year 1514, on the nineteenth day of July, subscribed a Brief presented to him by Antonius, Cardinal of Pavia, protector of the Carthusian Order. By it he granted that monks, nuns, and all other persons professing the institute of Saint Bruno might celebrate every year, in their monasteries, the feast of Saint Bruno with solemn rite and a proper Office on the sixth day of October, and might make a commemoration of that same holy Father in the daily ecclesiastical Office. The autograph of this Brief is now preserved in the Major Carthusian House, and in it Cardinal Laurence Puccio and Francis Armellini, cleric of the reverend Apostolic Chamber, are said to have been witnesses of the pontifical approval.”

### 763 [Cols. 0469D–0470A]

This is substantially what Zanotti says, as I have already noted. But there can be no doubt that this writer mistakenly took the letters of Antonius, Cardinal of Pavia, which have been quoted, for the Brief granted by Pope Leo X. For he writes that this was issued in the same year and on the same day as those letters are dated, and he asserts that the same persons—although he writes their names somewhat differently—namely, Laurence Puccio, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, and Francis Armellini, cleric of the Apostolic Chamber, were present at the approval or subscription made by the pontiff, although in the very letters of Antonius, Cardinal of Pavia, they are recorded as having been present when the Pope granted the aforesaid faculty to the Carthusians by word-of-mouth authority.

Moreover, the letters quoted from Antonius, issued in that same year 1514 and on 19 July, demonstrate that Leo did not grant the Carthusians the ability to honor the holy founder of their Order by a Brief, but solely by word-of-mouth authority. This was precisely the year and day on which, according to Zanotti’s opinion, such a Brief would have been issued. Thus there can be no doubt that this writer was mistaken here.

Nor do those who contend that Saint Bruno was enrolled among the Saints by Leo X through canonization, at least equivalent canonization, appear to be free from error, as the following section will make clear.

## XLVII. Whether Pope Leo X also canonized Bruno, and what events contributing to the posthumous glory of the Saint immediately followed the faculty granted by that pontiff to render him worship

### 764 [Cols. 0470B–0470D]

Some believe that Pope Leo X not only granted that ecclesiastical worship should be rendered to Bruno, but also enrolled or canonized him among the Saints. Among these, the most learned father of the Ecclesiastical Annals, Baronius, appears especially to have held this view, since in his annotations on the Roman Martyrology he now observes concerning Bruno:

“He died in the year of the Lord 1101 and was enrolled among the Saints by Pope Leo X.”

Pope Benedict XIV, however, thought very differently. In his work *On the Beatification of the Servants of God and the Canonization of the Blessed*, book I, chapter 41, section III, he maintains that it cannot in any way be said that Saint Bruno was canonized by Leo X—and rightly so, as is proved both by what he himself adduces there and by what we are about to adduce here.

Since canonization, as I shall explain below, entails a precept of worship, it is plainly evident from the quoted letters of the Cardinal of Pavia that Bruno was not enrolled or canonized among the Saints by this pontiff through the word-of-mouth authority by which Pope Leo X merely granted permission in 1514 that ecclesiastical worship might be rendered to him. Therefore, if it is to be true that the holy founder of the Carthusians was canonized by Leo, the Pope must have done this on another occasion, either by a further declaration—likewise made by word-of-mouth authority—or by an express document. But no writer at all mentions a declaration made by word-of-mouth authority and distinct from the declaration recorded in the letters of the Cardinal of Pavia, by which Pope Leo enrolled Bruno among the Saints.

### 765 [Cols. 0471A–0471B]

As for a declaration expressed in a letter or bull by which he did this, Tutinus, in his *Outline of the History of the Carthusian Order*, page 135, after narrating that Leo X granted in 1514, by word-of-mouth authority, that public worship might be rendered to Saint Bruno, adds under the year 1515:

“Leo X sent a bull of the canonization of Saint Bruno to the minister general of the Carthusian Order, and in it imposed several obligations to be observed in the Order.”

Some others also agree with Tutinus in reporting here that Leo issued a bull by which the Saint was canonized. I do not know, however, whether Surius should be counted among them. For although, at the end of the Life of our Saint written by him, he describes his canonization in verse as follows:

> Pope Leo, venerable for his deeds and majesty,  
>   
> Surrounded by the cardinal fathers in solemn assembly,  
>   
> Was informed more certainly how holily  
>   
> Bruno once had lived, what service he rendered to the city while alive,  
>   
> And how through him the Church grew in divine worship.  
>   
> He had also heard of certain miracles of his.  
>   
> Therefore, with the Fathers’ votes in agreement, he  
>   
> Enrolled him among the Gods; he granted him a feast  
>   
> To be celebrated every year on the sixth light of October  
>   
> (That is, on the day when, dying, he ascended Olympus).  
>   
> He permitted statues to be erected to him and chapels to be built,  
>   
> And presented the documents drawn up concerning these matters.  
>   
> The Major Carthusian House, mother of our Order, preserves these  
>   
> Among the many instruments of the Roman senate;

nevertheless, he prefixes to this description the title: “The Canonization, as it is called, of Saint Bruno, written in verse.” From these words it might appear that he was uncertain whether Bruno had truly been canonized by Pope Leo.

Moreover, by the document he mentions here, he may perhaps understand, together with Zanotti (see no. 762), merely the Brief by which Leo permitted the Saint’s worship. Whatever the case may be, it must be regarded as certain that no bull by which Leo X canonized Saint Bruno was issued.

### 766 [Cols. 0471C–0472A]

I demonstrate this as follows. If such a bull had been issued by Leo in 1515—a bull which, despite the most diligent investigation both at Rome and elsewhere, could not be found—it would certainly have been known either to the general chapter of the reverend Carthusian Fathers held in the Major Carthusian House on 7 May and the following days of that year 1515, if it had preceded May, or, if it had been issued later in that month, at least to the general chapter of those same reverend Fathers held in the Major Carthusian House on 21 April and the following days of 1516. Yet that bull appears in no way to have been known to either of these general chapters.

For, in order that, as Leo the Pontiff had granted, the feast of Saint Bruno might be celebrated every year on 6 October with solemn rite, that a suitable Office might be said for him, and that a daily commemoration might be instituted in the ecclesiastical Office, the Fathers ordered this in the first of those two general chapters. They confirmed the order in the later chapter by a newly enacted ordinance, adding that Saint Bruno should also be invoked in the conventual Litanies and entered in the Martyrology. But they make no mention of a bull by which the pontiff had canonized Bruno and commanded that worship be rendered to him. Had they known of such a bull, they certainly would not have failed to mention it.

So that the diligent reader may see how true this is, and so that I may omit nothing pertaining to the Saint’s posthumous glory, I transcribe here both ordinances, obtained for me from the Major Carthusian House by the Carthusian from Paris whom I have already so frequently praised.

The first, namely, the one enacted in the general chapter of 1515, reads as follows:

“Since our most holy lord, Lord Leo, tenth Pope by divine providence and the present pontiff, has by his grace given and granted to us and to our Order the permission and authority that in each house of our said Order and in their churches or chapels we may solemnly honor the feast of blessed Bruno, our Father, and celebrate it with due devotion; that we may honor and venerate his body and memory with fitting praises in the Lord; that we may perform and chant a suitable Office in his honor; and also that we may make his commemoration each day and do other things, as is more fully contained in the letters drawn up concerning this matter above”—namely, the letters of the Cardinal of Pavia, which I gave in the preceding section.

### 767 [Cols. 0472B–0472D]

“Therefore, lest we appear to have neglected so great a grace, for the praise and honor of God and of that same Father of ours, for the increase of the Order, and for the salvation, consolation, and peace of ourselves and of all our members, following the meaning and tenor of the said letters, we will and ordain that from now on, in every future year perpetually, on the sixth day of October—the day on which that same Father of ours, released from the flesh, was clothed with blessed immortality—the aforesaid feast shall be solemnly celebrated with candles in all and each of the houses of our entire Order and in their churches or chapels, in honor and under the name and title of that same blessed Bruno the confessor. It shall be honored with due devotion by all and each of the priors, monks, lay brothers, and other persons of our said Order, and his body and memory shall be venerated with fitting praises in the Lord.

A solemn Office shall be performed and chanted for him on that sixth day of October, with twelve lessons, Chapter, refectory, and the other ceremonies customarily observed on solemn candle feasts, in the following manner.

At First Vespers: antiphon over the psalms, “Let your loins be girded.” Responsory, “Blessed is that servant.”

At Matins, the first eight lessons shall be a sermon of blessed Augustine, bishop, beginning, “Our Lord Jesus Christ,” as on the feast of Saint Martin. The final four shall be a homily of blessed Pope Gregory, beginning, “The Holy Gospel,” on the Gospel according to Luke, “Let your loins be girded,” as on the feast of Saint Benedict.

At Mass, the Gospel just mentioned, “Let your loins be girded.” Everything else, both at Mass, at both Vespers, at Matins, and at the other Hours, shall be done as for a single confessor who is not a bishop, except for the prayers, which shall be said as they are noted below at the end of this present ordinance.

We likewise will and ordain that on the vigil of the said feast there be abstinence, and that on the day itself a sermon be given in the Chapter of the monks and lay brothers to the praise of the same Saint and for the reform of the Order. All work shall cease on that day, so that we may be able to devote ourselves more readily and more devoutly to divine praises.”

### 768 [Cols. 0473A–0473C]

“We further ordain that the said feast be written in the Calendars of the Order under the sixth day of October, and that he be placed and written in the Litanies after Saint Benedict, and that from then on it be said: ‘Saint Bruno, pray for us.’

We likewise ordain that on each day when the customary suffrages are said at Matins and Vespers, immediately after the commemoration of Saint John, a commemoration of him be made in the following manner:

Antiphon: ‘I will compare.’

Verse: ‘He led the just man.’

Prayer: ‘Almighty and everlasting God, etc., that through his intercession and merits we may deserve to obtain divine grace in the present and eternal glory in the future.’

The prayers to be said at Mass follow. The first of them shall be said on the day at both Vespers, at Lauds, and at Terce, and every day at his commemoration in Matins and Vespers.

**Prayer.** ‘Almighty and everlasting God, who prepare mansions in heaven for those who renounce the world, we humbly implore your boundless mercy, so that, through the intercession of blessed Bruno your confessor, we may faithfully fulfill the vows that we made in our profession and may attain safely to those things that, for those who persevere in you, you have deigned to promise. Through.’

**Secret.** ‘We offer you, Lord, this sacred gift, humbly entreating your majesty that, through the intercession and merits of blessed Bruno your confessor, having been absolved from all sins and from the punishments of all sins, we may be able to offer you an acceptable sacrifice in memory of your Passion and our Redemption. You who live.’

**Post-Communion.** ‘Through these holy things which we have received, Lord God, kindle in us a devoted affection for holy Religion, so that, following the footsteps of him whom we honor as our father on earth, we may deserve, with you granting it, to fulfill what we have promised, with you working in us, and, when the end of life arrives, to come to you, who are the way, the truth, and the life. You who live,’ etc.”

### 769 [Cols. 0473C–0474A]

The later ordinance, namely the one prescribed in 1516, is formulated in these words:

“We confirm the ordinance made in the preceding chapter concerning the celebration of the feast of blessed Bruno, our Father, and we will and command that it be observed perpetually in our Order. We add that, just as he is to be placed and written in the private Litanies, so also he is to be placed and written in the conventual Litanies, and from then on it is to be said: ‘Saint Bruno, pray for us.’

And in the Martyrology, under the sixth day of October, these words are to be written:

‘In Calabria, the deposition of blessed Bruno the confessor, first founder of the Carthusian Order.’

Nevertheless, we ordain that a newly printed Life of him be read in the refectory every year, in each house of the Order, on the said feast.”

These two ordinances, which are noted as having been taken from the book of ordinances enacted by the general chapters, under the title prefixed to them at the beginning, are certified by the Most Reverend Francis Biclet, minister general of the Carthusian Order, who himself subscribed them, to agree with the original documents.

Now consider, diligent reader, these two documents just quoted, and I scarcely doubt that you will acknowledge that, at least in the latter of them, the Carthusians who were Fathers of the general chapter celebrated in 1516 would have mentioned the pontifical letters by which Saint Bruno had been canonized, had those letters come to their knowledge and had they therefore been sent, as Tutinus reports in the words quoted immediately above, to the minister general of the Carthusian Order.

For since, in the first general chapter of 1515, the Fathers did not fail to mention the faculty by which the pontiff had publicly granted them permission, solely by word-of-mouth authority, to honor the Saint, who would suppose that the Fathers of the chapter of 1516 would not have mentioned a pontifical bull permitting but also decreeing or commanding Bruno’s ecclesiastical worship, if they had known of such a bull? This is especially so in the latter of the documents, where they confirmed what they had previously established concerning the worship to be rendered to their holy Father, when that worship had been not commanded but merely permitted by the pontiff.

### 770 [Cols. 0474B–0474D]

Furthermore, in the latter of the two ordinances, enacted in 1516 as stated, the Fathers of the general chapter then celebrated not only fail to mention a pontifical bull sent by Pope Leo X to the minister general of the Carthusian Order by which this pontiff canonized Saint Bruno; they also provide grounds for inferring from this very ordinance that no such bull had been sent by Leo to the minister general of his Order.

For when they command that the founder of their Order be entered in the Martyrology, they do not direct that this be done under the title of Saint, but only under the title of Blessed. They would, in all likelihood, have acted otherwise if, by virtue of a pontifical bull, Bruno had been canonized by at least what is called equivalent canonization, and if they had understood that the title of Saint belonged to him.

Nor should you reply that Bruno is also honored with the title of Saint in the aforesaid ordinance, since it commands that he be invoked in the conventual Litanies with the words, “Saint Bruno, pray for us.” For among the heavenly beings invoked in such Litanies, which are not customarily recited publicly, the title of Saint is commonly applied both to those who have and to those who have not been enrolled in the catalogue of the Saints by formal or equivalent canonization.

But let us even grant that the arguments we have so far brought forward from the capitular ordinances of the Carthusians against the bull of Saint Bruno’s canonization asserted by Camillo Tutino—a bull which Pope Leo X supposedly sent to the minister general of the Carthusian Order in 1515—are entirely without force. It must nevertheless be regarded as certain that no such bull was ever issued by that pontiff, and consequently that none was sent to the minister general of the Carthusian Order. The reason is that Saint Bruno, the father and founder of the Carthusians, was enrolled by Leo X neither by formal nor by equivalent canonization among the number of the Saints, as the matters I shall now relate will plainly demonstrate.

### 771 [Cols. 0475A–0475B]

First of all, so that it may be more clearly understood whether he was truly canonized as a Saint by Leo, let us examine what canonization and beatification are, and thus what distinction exists between them.

Canonization, as Benedict XIV teaches in *On the Beatification of the Servants of God and the Canonization of the Blessed*, book I, chapter 41, no. 1, is of two kinds: one formal, the other equivalent.

Formal canonization is that which is performed by the Supreme Pontiff, with the judicial form observed, a sentence pronounced, and the customary ceremonies observed.

Equivalent canonization occurs when a servant of God, in possession of ancient worship and renowned for the reputation of his virtues and miracles, is ordered to be honored throughout the universal Church on a certain day through the recitation and celebration of an Office and Mass, without any sentence having been pronounced, without the judicial procedure having been observed, and with the customary ceremonies omitted, and with the rite—double or semidouble—by which this is to be done expressly and specifically determined or prescribed, unlike in the bulls of formal canonization (see the cited work of Benedict XIV, book I, chapter 38, no. 5 and following), as is understood from the various examples of equivalent canonization adduced by Benedict XIV in the work cited again, book I, chapter 41. Consequently, no further constitution is required for the Saint who has been canonized by equivalent canonization to be honored in this manner (see again the cited work of Benedict XIV, book I, chapter 38, no. 5 and following).

As for beatification, this too, like canonization, is divided into formal and equivalent beatification. Formal beatification occurs when, after a formal examination of the virtues and miracles, the pontiff grants that a servant of God may be honored as blessed in a particular place. Equivalent beatification occurs when the Supreme Pontiff, after a judicial proof of the reputation for virtues and miracles, approves a sentence delivered by an ordinary or delegated judge concerning a case exempt from the decrees of Urban VIII.

This is Benedict XIV’s teaching in substance in the cited work, book I, chapter 42, no. 8.

### 772 [Cols. 0475C–0476A]

Canonization, whether formal or equivalent, therefore differs chiefly from beatification, whether formal or equivalent, in this respect: beatification entails merely permission, whereas canonization entails a precept of worship. Likewise, in beatification worship is confined to a particular province, diocese, city, or religious family, while in canonization it is extended to the universal Church.

Since this is so, and especially since, in examining matters concerning the blessed person who is to be canonized, a judicial procedure or form is required for formal canonization, it is manifest that Bruno was not enrolled among the Saints by Leo in this manner. Nor does anyone contend that he was.

As for equivalent canonization, Leo did not enroll Bruno among the Saints by this either. For he never commanded that Bruno be honored throughout the universal Church through the celebration of the Office and Mass in the manner included in the definition of equivalent canonization given in the preceding number.

This is clear from the fact that, as I shall prove in the Appendix concerning the Saint’s posthumous glory, it was only in 1623 that Pope Gregory XV, at the supplication of the Carthusians, finally granted that “the feast of Saint Bruno . . . on the sixth day of October . . . might be placed in the Roman Missal and Breviary, and that an Office for him, semidouble”—these are the words of the bull issued by Gregory on this matter and to be quoted below—“might be recited freely and lawfully by all the faithful everywhere.” Hence it follows that Pope Leo X had not previously commanded that the Saint be honored throughout the universal Church through the celebration of the Office and Mass in the manner implied by the definition of equivalent canonization given in the preceding number.

From this, and also from what was said earlier, it further follows that Leo did not issue a bull canonizing Saint Bruno in 1515, much less send one to the minister general of the Carthusian Order, contrary to the account of Camillus Tutinus in the words quoted above and to the present opinion of several others who, as I believe, have been led into error by him.

### 773 [Cols. 0476B–0476D]

Since our Saint, who according to what has already been said was not canonized by Leo X, is found to have been enrolled by that pontiff among the Blessed only through the word-of-mouth authority by which the Carthusians were granted permission to render ecclesiastical worship to him, anyone, I think, will readily understand that this was not done by formal beatification, but only by equivalent beatification. This follows partly from the description or account of both formal and equivalent beatification of the servants of God already given, and partly from the manner in which Pope Leo is said to have proceeded in granting Saint Bruno the honors of the heavenly ones, both by Blomenvenna and by Surius, who followed him, in the Lives of the Saint composed by them, and by Antonius, Cardinal of Pavia of the Holy Roman Church, in the letters transcribed above.

For formal beatification (see no. 771) requires a formal examination, preceding or preliminary to it, of the virtues and miracles of the servant of God who is proposed for enrollment among the Blessed. But the manner in which Leo X proceeded in granting Saint Bruno the honors of the heavenly ones was as follows.

When the Carthusian priors appointed for this purpose, and Antonius, Cardinal of Pavia of the Holy Roman Church, acting in the name of the entire aforesaid Order, of which he was protector, petitioned that this pontiff might deign to grant the Carthusian Order permission to honor Saint Bruno with an annual feast and ecclesiastical Office and to make a daily commemoration of him in the canonical prayers, the Pope “had long since learned many things concerning the praises and holiness of that same blessed confessor. He judged it worthy and consonant with reason that he whom God had distinguished in this world with such great gifts and graces, and who had been taken up into heaven, should be honored ever more greatly; and that he to whom the Almighty, while he was living, had given a heart obedient to the commandments and to the law of life and discipline should now, while resting before the throne of divine glory, receive on earth the service of due devotion.” He most willingly consented to their petition.

### 774 [Cols. 0477A–0477B]

Thus read the letters of Antonius, Cardinal of Pavia, already given above in numbers 759 and following. In this matter Blomenvenna does not differ greatly from them; Surius agrees with him exactly in substance. Here are the words relevant to the matter. They read as follows:

“Our most holy lord”—namely, Pope Leo X—“having frequently heard from the reports of many about the outstanding holiness of blessed Bruno, considered it unworthy, after setting aside an investigation of miracles, that he whom God had adorned with such great gifts and graces in this world, now taken up into heaven, should not be extolled with the highest praises; and that he to whom the Almighty had given a heart obedient to the commandment and the law of life and discipline should not now, while resting before the throne of divine glory, receive on earth the service of due devotion.

Therefore, not only did he generously consent by apostolic authority, but he also willed that in every house of the entire Carthusian Order . . . the feast of the most holy Bruno the confessor, every year on the sixth day of October . . . should be solemnly honored and celebrated with fitting and due devotion.”

Since Pope Leo permitted ecclesiastical worship to be rendered to Saint Bruno, not after a formal examination of his virtues and miracles, but merely on the basis of the reputation of his holiness, as is understood from the words of the Cardinal’s letters and of Blomenvenna already given, it is entirely clear that he did not do this through formal beatification, for formal examination of virtues and miracles is required for that, according to what has been said. Consequently, it was not by formal beatification but only by equivalent beatification—such as was then in use—that our Saint was enrolled among the Blessed. The latter did not require pontifical approval of a sentence delivered by an ordinary or delegated judge concerning an exception from the decrees of Urban VIII, since those decrees did not yet exist.

### 775 [Cols. 0477C–0478A]

Whatever, then, may ultimately have been the manner in which Bruno, the most holy founder of the Carthusians, came to be enrolled among the Blessed by Leo X, it was certainly granted by that pontiff to the Carthusians that they might publicly render to him the honors of the heavenly ones. They did not long leave that faculty unused.
