For, so that in every house of their Order the worship permitted by the Supreme Pontiff might be rendered to their holy Father by absolutely all, whether clerics or lay brothers, they strictly decreed this in the general chapter celebrated in 1515, immediately after the granting of the said faculty, as the ordinance enacted there and transcribed above bears witness.

Already in the year 1514 itself, in which the pontiff had granted them that faculty, they had transferred the body of Saint Bruno from Saint Mary of the Tower to the church of Saint Stephen in the Wood, as Tutinus, in the work cited, page 136, and others relate, without anyone contradicting them in this matter.

Tutinus writes in the cited place that this took place only in the same year 1515 in which the ordinance mentioned above was enacted in the general chapter of the Carthusian Order. But just as this writer, who flourished no earlier than the immediately preceding century and was therefore long removed from the event, was mistaken, as has been said, in asserting that a bull was sent to the Carthusians by which Pope Leo X canonized Saint Bruno, so too he is beyond all doubt mistaken here in assigning the year in which the sacred relics of the Saint were transferred from the church of Saint Mary to the church of Saint Stephen in the Wood.

For Blomenvenna, who was alive at the very time when the aforesaid transfer of the Saint’s sacred relics took place and was prior of the Cologne Charterhouse (see Morotius in the chronological *Theatre of the Carthusian Order* and Petreius in the *Carthusian Library*), records in the Life of Saint Bruno composed by him, on the testimony of Matthew, prior of the Bologna Charterhouse, who had taken part in the event, that it had already taken place in the year 1514. All the other writers who have treated the matter, at least all whom I have seen, agree with him.

### 776 [Cols. 0478B–0478C]

The words by which Blomenvenna assigns the said transfer to the year 1514, on the testimony of the aforesaid prior of Bologna, who had been personally present at it, are these:

“In the year of the Lord . . . 1514, Lord Matthew, prior of the house of Bologna, who himself had also been appointed to press forward the undertaking mentioned above—the restoration of the monastery of Saint Stephen—personally took part in the transfer of the bones of Saint Bruno. He held the Saint’s sacred head in his hands so that it would not be placed upon the altar together with the bones.

But when crowds gathered and feared that they would be deprived of the sacred relics of their most beloved Patron, he satisfied them by saying that the sacred head, separated from the bones, was to be clothed in gold and silver and adorned with precious stones. Thus removing from them any suspicion of insufficient care, he, by special permission of the Supreme Pontiff, detached a portion of the head and distributed it to others.

In particular, he gave a small portion of that same head to the venerable Father Gregory, prior of the house of Freiburg, in the year of the Lord 1515, at the time of the general chapter. Gregory divided it into minute portions and distributed them among the houses of the Rhine province entrusted to him as principal visitor.

Because Saint Bruno was of Cologne by nationality, the aforesaid Lord Matthew had reserved a small portion of the same head for the prior of the house of Cologne. He gave it to him in the presence of the reverend prior of the Major Carthusian House, to the latter’s great joy and devotional reception, in the year 1516. Returning to Cologne that same year, the prior deposited this most precious and welcome gift in the church of his house on the feast of the Invention of Saint Stephen.

The powders that fell away during the division he distributed among the houses of the Teutonic province: Saint Saviour near Utrecht, Saint Mary at Monichusen, Saint Andrew near Amsterdam, and Saint Bartholomew near Delft.”

777. “The body of Saint Bruno was transferred in the year of the Lord 1514 by Lord John Rufi, abbot, and—as Lord Matthew, mentioned above, reported to me—it was placed upon the principal altar, constructed of white marble and surrounded by a wooden casing four fingers thick; an iron grating also encircled the altar on every side, whose mensa too is of white marble [Col. 0478D]. This altar is situated at the head of the church of Saint Stephen of Bosco.” Thus he plainly teaches that the sacred body of Saint Bruno was transferred in 1514.

From the words of Blomenvenna just cited we have not only this, but also that the translation was carried out by John Bufi, abbot—whom Surius and others perhaps more correctly call John, abbot of Saint Rufi—and that Matthew, prior of the Carthusian house at Bologna, was also present. Furthermore, Zanottius says in chapter 33 of the Life of the Saint that he himself composed that not only this prior but also the priors of the Neapolitan, Clermont—in Basilicata, in the province of the kingdom of Naples—Mantuan, and Roman Charterhouses were present at this solemn occasion. Although I nowhere find this confirmed by the testimony of a contemporary or near-contemporary writer [Col. 0479A], nevertheless, from the fact that these same priors had previously been appointed to see that the monastery of Saint Stephen at Turris was restored to their Order, I consider it most probable.

But it is enough to have said this about matters pertaining to the translation of the sacred treasure. Let us now say something about the treasure itself. Blomenvenna shows in the words quoted immediately above that, while this solemn ceremony was being performed, a portion of the head was removed by Matthew, prior of the Carthusian house at Bologna, in the manner he describes. He also shows that one portion of that part was given in 1515 to Gregory, prior of the Carthusian house at Freiburg, and another in 1516 to the prior of the Carthusian house at Cologne, by the aforementioned Matthew, prior of the Bolognese Carthusians.

778. The prior of Cologne, to whom this sacred gift was presented, was Blomenvenna himself—the very man who committed these matters to writing and who, because he was born at Leiden, or Lugdunum Batavorum, is also frequently called Leidensis, after his native city. This is clear both from the period during which Petreius and Morotius are said to have found him presiding over the Cologne Charterhouse and from Surius. The latter, recounting in the Life of our Saint that he composed the same things that Blomenvenna has just stated, records the following for posterity:

“Because Saint Bruno had Cologne Agrippina as his homeland, the same Lord Matthew gave a small portion of his head to Lord Peter of Leiden, prior of the Cologne Charterhouse. This gift was exceedingly welcome to him, and when he had returned home in the year 1516, he reverently placed the most precious gift in the church of the Cologne Charterhouse on 3 August.”

Thus Surius.

But how did it happen that Matthew, prior of the Bolognese Charterhouse, gave a portion of Saint Bruno’s head to Gregory, prior of the Freiburg Charterhouse and visitor of the Rhine province, in 1515—as Blomenvenna testifies in the words quoted—at the general chapter of the Carthusian Order, customarily celebrated at the Grande Chartreuse, yet did not at the same time place in the hands of Blomenvenna, who was also then visitor of the Rhine province, the portion of the head intended for the Cologne Charterhouse, which likewise lies in the Rhine province?

Since, as Innocentius le Masson teaches in book III, chapter 22 of the work entitled *Annals of the Carthusian Order* [Col. 0479D], only one of the two visitors of each pair of Carthusian provinces is required to attend each year the general chapter celebrated at the Grande Chartreuse, and since Gregory, prior of the Freiburg Charterhouse, attended the general chapter of 1515 as visitor of the said Rhine province, it is easily understood how it could have happened that Blomenvenna, although he too was visitor of the Rhine province, did not attend the general chapter in 1515. Consequently, Matthew, prior of the Bolognese Charterhouse, did not place in his hands before 1516 the small portion of Saint Bruno’s head that he had destined for the Cologne Charterhouse because the Saint had been born in that city; rather, he reserved it for delivery until the time when he knew that Blomenvenna would attend the general chapter.

[Col. 0480A] 779. On the occasion of the Saint’s translation, not only did the prior of the Freiburg Charterhouse receive one portion of his sacred relics and the prior of the Cologne Charterhouse another—those who, together with the other Charterhouses of the Rhine and Teutonia, or Belgium, provinces, shared the sacred gift, as Blomenvenna also teaches in the words transcribed above—but many others from the Carthusian Order likewise received portions, as there can be no reasonable doubt.

In particular, the alumni of the Paris Charterhouse obtained a bone of one of his fingers, which even today, as Baillet teaches in volume III of his *Lives*, column 91, can be seen at the foot of the statue representing Bruno. Zanottius, however, in the Life of the Saint that he composed, chapter XXXIII, supplies a further assertion relevant here, concerning whose conformity to the truth I remain uncertain [Col. 0480B]. He says that at the very time when the sacred body of our Saint was transferred, James of Aragon, prior of the Neapolitan Charterhouse, took from Saint Bruno’s body a portion of the lower jaw together with two teeth, having received permission from the Pope for this purpose, and sent these sacred relics as a gift to Francis of Puteo, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, who had contributed greatly to securing the solemn cult of the Saint.

Blomenvenna, however, who, as has already been said, was a contemporary of the event and who probably heard the account from Matthew, prior of the Bolognese Charterhouse, who was present at the Saint’s translation, records that this sacred gift was given to Francis of Puteo, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, earlier than the year 1514, and that it was not sent to him as a gift but was presented to him in person by James of Aragon, prior of the Neapolitan Charterhouse.

780. Here are Blomenvenna’s relevant words:

“When the matter of this restoration—that is, of the Calabrian monastery of Saint Stephen—was being pressed or discussed, at the time when the general chapter was being celebrated at the Grande Chartreuse, the prior of the Neapolitan house, to whom this matter had been entrusted, came and presented to the reverend father Lord Francis, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, a portion of the jaw together with two teeth of Saint Bruno. He also related to all who wished to hear that the abbots of the house of Saint Stephen, in which the sacred body of blessed Bruno rests, had guarded his sacred relics with such diligence, out of fear of the Carthusians lest they should steal it, that they had separated the bones and deposited them in various more secret places, frequently changing those places, so that no one could know where the sacred relics were except the abbot and another trustworthy man.” Thus far he.

In these words, as will be evident to anyone who considers them, he most plainly records that the jaw of the Saint together with two of his teeth was not sent as a gift by the prior of the Neapolitan Carthusians to Puteo, prior of the Grande Chartreuse. Rather, contrary to Zanottius’s account, the Neapolitan prior, being present with the latter at the time of the general chapter, offered that sacred gift to the said prior of the Grande Chartreuse.

As for the time when the event occurred, Blomenvenna writes that it took place while the Carthusians were insisting that the monastery of Saint Stephen be restored to their Order, and therefore before it had been restored to them. Now, since the business of this restoration was concluded in February 1514 through the execution of the papal decree issued in 1513, by which the restoration was ordered, and since the general chapter of the Carthusians for 1514—during which James, the Neapolitan prior, could have offered the aforementioned sacred gift to Francis of Puteo—had certainly not yet been celebrated (for the Carthusians never hold their general chapters before Easter), it follows plainly from what Blomenvenna records in the words quoted that, contrary to Zanottius’s account, the jaw of our Saint together with two of his teeth was offered to Francis of Puteo, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, by James, prior of the Neapolitan Charterhouse, before the year 1514 [Col. 0481B].

781. “But,” you will say, “since the Cistercians, while the monastery of Saint Stephen was in their possession, concealed Saint Bruno’s sacred bones with great care and cunning, as is clear from Blomenvenna’s own words quoted above, how did it happen that James, prior of the Neapolitan Charterhouse, obtained from them the jaw, which he gave as a gift to the prior of the Grande Chartreuse together with two of the Saint’s teeth, before that monastery had been restored to the Carthusians?”

I admit that there is indeed reason for this knot to appear difficult to untie. Nevertheless, since the place where Saint Bruno’s body—or, if you prefer, his sacred bones—was hidden had already been divinely revealed to Antonio Sabino, appointed by Cardinal of Aragon, the commendatory abbot of the monastery, as administrator or prefect of all the monastery’s possessions and revenues, either as early as 1513, if Tutinus is correct, or even as early as 1502, if Zanottius is to be trusted, it is possible that James, prior of the Neapolitan Charterhouse, received the jaw and two teeth before 1514 from the said cardinal, who was favorably disposed toward the Carthusians and related to James by kinship.

Since this was so, it appears to me more probable that Saint Bruno’s jaw together with two of his teeth was given to Francis of Puteo, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, before 1514, on the basis of what Blomenvenna, a contemporary author, records concerning the matter, than that the contrary account transmitted by Zanottius, a later author, is correct [Col. 0481D]. Nevertheless, Camillus Tutinus also supports Zanottius in this respect. In his *Survey of the History of the Carthusian Order*, he writes that in 1514 several relics collected from Bruno’s body were distributed among the Grande Chartreuse, the Cologne Charterhouse, and the Paris Charterhouse.

But since, as has already been shown above, this writer is certainly mistaken concerning the relics of the Saint that the Cologne Charterhouse obtained in 1514, he cannot add any weight to Zanottius’s written account of the time when the Saint’s jaw together with two of his teeth was handed over to Francis of Puteo, or to the Grande Chartreuse [Col. 0482A].

782. Although what Zanottius records in writing concerning the time and manner in which Francis of Puteo, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, obtained Saint Bruno’s jaw together with two teeth from James of Aragon, prior of the Neapolitan Charterhouse, cannot be regarded as certain and indisputable, as the foregoing arguments prove, nevertheless it appears that we may accept without hesitation his assertion, in the frequently praised chapter 33 of his work, that the remaining portion of Saint Bruno’s head is still honorably preserved in the Calabrian monastery of Saint Stephen, enclosed in a silver reliquary representing the Saint.

For, in addition to the fact that Matthew, prior of the Bolognese Charterhouse, declared during the Saint’s translation, in the presence of the assembled people, that the sacred head of the Saint, separated from the remaining bones, ought to be clothed in gold and silver and adorned with gems, as Blomenvenna teaches in the words quoted above, that writer could certainly have learned from the Calabrian records, which he so often cites, what he records concerning this matter [Col. 0482C]. For this reason alone there is no need to doubt that his account accords with the truth.

The same may be said of what he states in the cited passage concerning the rest of the Saint’s body, which is still preserved in the monastery of Saint Stephen beneath a magnificent altar in a marble chest—also, as I suppose, on the basis of Calabrian records. Nevertheless, although these records cannot establish indisputable certainty in matters more remote from our own age, and although I have therefore judged that quite a few things Zanottius derived from them, which it would not have been worthwhile to refute individually, should simply be passed over or disregarded in the course of this commentary, I have treated them just as I have certain other matters transmitted by more recent writers, which I judged to lack a sufficiently established basis of truth or even probability.

[Col. 0481]

## EARLIER LIFE

By an anonymous chronicler of the first five priors of the Grande Chartreuse,

drawn from the most ancient manuscript of the Cologne Carthusians [Note: Concerning this Life of the Saint, its author, and the period in which it appears to have been written, see the preceding Commentary, no. 8 and following, where I have brought forward whatever I judged necessary and appropriate. The same is true of the most ancient manuscript, from which this Life was extracted and communicated to us, a copy of the chronicle of the first five priors of the Grande Chartreuse.]

[Col. 0481D] CHAPTER ONE

The occasion of Saint Bruno’s conversion: he resolves to seek solitude, draws others to the same purpose, goes to Grenoble, withdraws into the wilderness of the Grande Chartreuse, is summoned from there to the Pope and obtains permission from him to return to solitude; he conceals himself in the Calabrian wilderness of Turris and dies there.

1. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1082, or thereabouts, while the renowned school flourished at Paris, especially in philosophy, theology, and canon law, a portent of the following kind is said to have occurred there, as was generally customary. A certain distinguished doctor, honored among all the Parisian doctors and remarkably esteemed for his life—as it appeared—his reputation, his teaching, and his learning, having been overtaken by a grave and final illness, did not lie sick for long before he died.

2. Throughout the entire day on which he died, the divine offices were continuously sung, according to Parisian custom, in the hall where the body lay in its coffin. On the following morning, when the university of Paris, both students and doctors, had assembled there [Note: It appears highly probable—indeed, almost certain—that this Life of the Saint was not composed before the thirteenth century, on the basis of the name “University,” by which the Parisian academy is here honored. See the preceding Commentary, nos. 12 and 15. To what was said there it may be added that the Roman pontiffs Innocent III, who died in 1216, as well as Honorius III, Innocent IV, and Alexander IV, all in the thirteenth century, granted privileges to the Parisian academy. Since the letters issued for this purpose began with the words “Let your university know,” or “The university of masters and scholars,” it happened—as nearly all learned men now agree—that the Parisian academy was first called a university.], in order to provide so honorable a man with a solemn and honorable burial service, the reverend man’s coffin, in which the body lay, was about to be lifted and carried to the church when suddenly, to the astonishment of everyone, the man who seemed and truly was dead raised his head, sat up in the coffin, and cried out in a loud and terrifying voice, with everyone listening: “By the just judgment of God I have been accused.” Having said this, he lowered his head and lay down dead, as before.

3. Terrified and stunned by this cry, everyone decided that he should by no means be buried that day, but should be kept until the following day. On the next morning, therefore, when a very great crowd had gathered and they again wished to carry the body to the church, the deceased, as before, raised his head and thundered in a sorrowful and terrifying voice: “By the just judgment of God I have been judged.”

[Col. 0483C] 4. The crowd present clearly understood and heard this cry and was even more astonished than before. Consulting with one another about what these extraordinary and unprecedented cries of the deceased might be intended to signify, they again decided that he should not be buried until another day had passed. On the third day, when the city had assembled because of these portents and, everything having been prepared, they wished to carry the body to the grave, the deceased, as before, cried out for the third time in a very loud and mournful voice: “By the just judgment of God I have been condemned” [Note: What should be thought about the Parisian deceased described here, who shouted from his coffin that he had been condemned—whether the dreadful spectacle is asserted to have occurred publicly before many people or with only a few present—and also whether Saint Bruno was driven into the wilderness by this grim story, I leave to the judgment of the diligent reader on the basis of what I discussed in sections 10 and following of the preceding Commentary.]

5. When this horrifying sentence was heard, almost everyone was struck with immense fear and trembling, having become certain of the condemnation of so great a man, who appeared to shine among and above the others in integrity of life, brilliance of reputation, excellence of rank, and manifold knowledge and wisdom.

At that time Master Bruno was there [Note: Even if the horrifying spectacle of the condemned man occurred at Paris and Saint Bruno was also present, it still does not follow that the Saint was then teaching there. See the preceding Commentary, no. 173 and following.], a Teuton by nationality, born in the city of Cologne of parents who were not obscure [Note: On Bruno’s noble lineage, see the second section of the preceding Commentary.], a canon of the church of Reims and a master of theology in its schools [Note: Bruno taught theology at Reims, as I have shown in the preceding Commentary, no. 78 and following.]. Salutarily terrified and moved by the words just mentioned, he addressed certain companions who were present in the following or similar terms:

6. “Come, dearest friends, what shall we do? We shall all perish together; no one will be saved except the one who flees. If such things happen in the green wood, what will happen in the dry? If a man of such rank and such learning, who appeared to lead so honorable a life and enjoyed such a celebrated reputation, has been unquestionably condemned, what shall we wretched little men do? If the mournful voice of one little man has struck and stunned us with such dreadful and astonishing fear and trembling, what shall we do when the roar of the lion, together with the trumpet of the final judgment, strikes our ears? When we all hear: ‘Rise, dead; come to judgment’? Where shall we flee then? How shall we be able to appear at so dreadful a judgment, where the pillars of heaven will tremble, and the angels will be terrified and, once terrified, will be purified [or: will be thrown into confusion]? Where shall we hide then?

7. “It will be impossible to hide and intolerable to appear. Let us therefore flee from the face of God’s sword; let us anticipate his face in confession. Come, let us adore and fall prostrate before God; let us weep before the Lord who made us. Since today we have heard his astonishing voice, let us not harden our hearts, but let us go out from the midst of Babylon; let us leave Pentapolis, already burning with fire and sulfur; and, following the example of blessed Paul the hermit, of the blessed Anthony, Arsenius, Evagrius, and the other saints, together with blessed John the Baptist, let us seek the caves of the desert. Let us save ourselves in the mountains, so that we may escape and reach the harbor and tranquility of eternal salvation from the wrath of the eternal Judge, the sentence of eternal condemnation, and the flood of sins [Latin: *diluvii*; perhaps *diluvium*]—in the ark of Noah and in Peter’s little boat, in which Christ caused the wind and storm to cease—that is, in the ship of repentance.”

8. Addressing and exhorting himself and certain companions in these or similar words and sentiments, Bruno and six other worthy men decided to renounce the world and its vanities, to seek suitable desert places in which to undertake perpetual penance, and there, having abandoned all the riches, pleasures, and honors of this world, to take up their individual crosses, follow naked the naked Christ along the narrow way that leads to life, and forsake the broad and spacious way that leads the lovers and followers of the world to the punishments of the damned.

9. Because they had heard of the holiness of Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, who was believed to have been for some time a fellow student of the same Master Bruno in the schools [Note: We treated Saint Hugh of Grenoble on 1 April, the day on which his name appears in the Roman Martyrology. According to Guigo, the fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, who was Hugh’s contemporary and was joined to him by holy friendship throughout his life, Hugh passed from this mortal life to immortality in 1132, as Guigo testifies in no. 33 of the Life he composed at the command of Pope Innocent II, at least in his eightieth year, in the fourth month. Since he does not appear to have been born before 1052, whereas Bruno had already been born around 1030, as I showed in section 2 of the preceding Commentary, and had begun teaching at Reims as early as 1060 or even earlier, according to what I stated there in section 4, their respective ages make it clear that Hugh was more likely at some time to have been Bruno’s pupil in the schools than his fellow student, contrary to what our biographer says here. Nevertheless, I would not venture to assert even this, since it cannot be confirmed by any testimony of antiquity.], they resolved, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, to approach the aforesaid holy bishop together and seek his help and counsel, so that in his diocese—which they had heard abounded in many deserted mountains—they might deserve to obtain a suitable place where they could put their holy and salutary purpose into effect.

Thus the seven holy men mentioned above came to the aforementioned holy bishop for this purpose, guided by the Holy Spirit [Note: The biographer says here that our Saint and his companions, after witnessing at Paris the grim spectacle of the condemned man, went straight to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble. But what I have brought forward in the preceding Commentary, nos. 414 and following, proves that this is not true.]

10. To use exactly the words written in the approved and confirmed legend of the Life of the aforesaid Saint Hugh, approved and confirmed by the Supreme Pontiff who canonized him [Note: Pope Innocent II instructed Guigo, the fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, to commit to writing all the deeds of this holy bishop after he had enrolled Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, among the saints at the Council of Pisa in 1134—see volume I of our work, April, page 36, no. 4—only two years after Hugh’s death. I do not find, however, that ancient writers record that the work in which Guigo obeyed the papal command was approved and confirmed by that pontiff, as this biographer relates, although the matter is by no means implausible.]:

“Master Bruno, a religious man renowned for his learning, is present—a kind of embodiment of honesty, gravity, and every form of maturity. He had as his companions Master Landuin, who later became prior of the Grande Chartreuse; two Stephens, the man of Bourges and the man of Die (they had been canons of Saint Rufi, but, out of desire for the solitary life, he had joined himself to them with the abbot’s support); also Hugh [Note: Concerning Landuin, the two Stephens—the Burgundian and the Diezian—the monastery of Saint Rufi from which they came, and Hugh the chaplain, who is said here to have accompanied the Saint to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, see section 25 of the preceding Commentary, from no. 434 through no. 441.], whom they called the Chaplain because he alone among them performed the office of a priest [Note: Whether it follows from Guigo’s words that the Saint had not yet been ordained a priest when he approached Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, is discussed in the preceding Commentary, nos. 442 and following.]; and two laymen, whom we call converts, Andrew and Guarinus. They were seeking a place suitable for the eremitical life, but had not yet found one [Note: See the preceding Commentary, no. 420, for what appears to follow from these words of Guigo.].

“Drawn by this hope and at the same time by the sweet fragrance of holy fellowship, they came. The bishop received them, treated them, and granted them the fulfillment of their desire not only gladly but also reverently.

11. “With his counsel, help, and companionship, they entered the wilderness of the Grande Chartreuse and built there in the year of the Lord 1084. The said holy Hugh’s episcopate was in its fourth year [Note: That the year of Christ given here is correct, and that the Saint and his companions entered the wilderness of the Grande Chartreuse, is demonstrated most clearly by what I brought forward in the preceding Commentary, no. 470 and the three following, especially against Baronius and others who contend that this occurred in 1086. It is also clear from what I discussed there in nos. 506 and following that this event is not wrongly placed in the fourth year of Hugh’s episcopate, even though he had been promoted to that office as early as 1079.

“In the meantime, all the words expressing the time of Saint Bruno and his companions’ entrance into the Grande Chartreuse, which are cited here as having been supplied by Guigo in the Life of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, are absent from that work both in our edition and in Surius. Thus either the copies from which the Life of Saint Hugh composed by Guigo was published both by us and by Surius had been corrupted through the omission of these words, or our biographer used a corrupt copy of that work, since in several other readings as well he differs from the Life of that holy bishop as it was published by us and by Surius. I consider the latter explanation more probable, partly because the copy of the eulogy given in no. 7 of the preceding Commentary, which he had before him and nevertheless regarded as uncorrupted, was also corrupt, as is clear from what was said in no. 519 of that Commentary.].

“The aforementioned holy bishop had seen in a dream, around the same time, the Lord building in that same wilderness a dwelling for his worship, with seven stars also showing him the way [Note: Concerning this vision offered to Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and its circumstances, see the preceding Commentary, no. 423 and several following numbers.]. There were seven of them. Therefore he gladly embraced not only the counsel of these men but also that of those who succeeded them, and until his death he always supported the inhabitants of the Grande Chartreuse with benefits and advice.

“Although he had previously burned wholly with the fires of divine love, through their example and companionship he nevertheless became inflamed with the exercises of heavenly discipline, just as someone might place several other burning torches around a blazing fire.

12. “He was with them not as a lord or bishop but as a companion, indeed as a most humble brother, prepared, insofar as it lay within him, to serve everyone. Thus the venerable man William, then prior of Saint Lawrence [Note: This is a cell or priory in the suburb of the city of Grenoble, dependent upon the monastery of Saint Theofridus mentioned immediately below, in the notes to letter d of page 41 in volume I of our work, April. The William mentioned here later became abbot of that cell’s monastery. Although he lived the eremitical or solitary life in the Grande Chartreuse with Hugh and Bruno, he was for that reason no more a Carthusian prior than either of these two Saints. See the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume II, column 766.], who later became abbot of Saint Theofridus and was himself bound to Master Bruno by considerable religious devotion, and who at that time was Saint Hugh’s companion—for two men lived in each cell—complained rather seriously to Master Bruno that the bishop was taking for himself within the cell almost all the duties pertaining to humility, and was not living with him merely as a companion but rather as a servant.

13. “He inhabited the wilderness with such devotion and diligence that Master Bruno sometimes compelled him to leave it, saying: ‘Go, go to your sheep and render to them what you owe.’ At that time the said bishop, inflamed with a great ardor for poverty and humility, wished to sell all his horses and distribute the proceeds to the poor, and to travel about on foot while preaching. But Master Bruno, a man of profound judgment, whose counsel the bishop obeyed no differently than commands, did not consent. He feared that the bishop might perhaps become proud of this in his own heart, or that the other bishops might judge him guilty of singularity, or—as was beyond doubt—that he might be unable to carry it through because of the harshness and unevenness of the roads.”

14. All the foregoing are the words of Lord Guigo, written in the Life of Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble. We judged it appropriate to insert them here because they reveal the beginnings of the foundation of the Grande Chartreuse, make known the excellence of Master Bruno, and show how so venerable and holy a bishop adhered to him with such reverence, fervor, and humility. Together with Hugh, Bruno may truly be called the patron and founder of the house and Order of the Carthusians; and although he was not the first founder, he was in a certain sense the principal institutor.

Thus the house and Order were happily founded and begun during the pontificate of Pope Gregory VII. He was succeeded in the papacy by Pope Victor, who lived for a very short time—only about one year and four months. After his death Urban II was elected. Master Bruno had previously been his teacher and instructor [Note: The first of these three pontiffs died in 1085. Since the man who succeeded him and assumed the name “Victor,” Desiderius, also died in 1087, Otto or Odo was eventually raised to the chair of Saint Peter and took the name Urban II. At one time he had studied under Saint Bruno at Reims, as I have shown in the preceding Commentary, no. 96.]

15. Soon after his election, Urban remembered the wisdom, holiness, and exceptional prudence of his teacher Bruno. He immediately considered obtaining him to direct and assist him in bearing the cares and burdens of the apostolate [Note: That the Saint was summoned from the Grande Chartreuse by Pope Urban II is beyond doubt from the chronicle of the first four priors of the Grande Chartreuse in Labbe, volume I of the *New Library of Manuscript Books*, page 638. It is likewise certain that before this occurred Bruno had governed the Grande Chartreuse for six years, as is stated below. Anyone can easily infer, however, that the latter period should not be regarded as six complete years but only as six incomplete years, from what I discussed in section 30 concerning the time when the Saint approached Pope Urban II.].

When the aforementioned Master Bruno had inhabited the wilderness of the Grande Chartreuse for six years and, summoned to the Roman court, was obliged to obey the Supreme Pontiff and, at least for a time, to leave the most beloved companionship of his sons, the inhabitants of the cells, his subjects were so shaken by grief and disturbed by such sorrow that they declared that they would not remain at the Grande Chartreuse at all if they were to be deprived of the presence and care of so gentle and beloved a Father.

16. Master Bruno, therefore, deeply distressed by the desolation of his sons, nevertheless neither wished nor was able lawfully to deny the Supreme Pontiff the debt of obedience. And lest the site of the Grande Chartreuse, abandoned by its inhabitants, should fall into profane and unworthy hands or secular uses, he left it, after making a donation and transfer, to the abbot of Casa-Dei, who had been one of its first founders, having drawn up a public instrument to this effect [Note: Concerning this instrument, granted by Saint Bruno to Seguin, abbot of the celebrated monastery of Casa-Dei in the diocese of Clermont in Auvergne—who is correctly said here to have been one of its first donors, as the letters of donation of the Grande Chartreuse cited in the preceding Commentary, no. 503 and the two following, make clear—see the preceding Commentary, no. 513 and the two following.].

Then the venerable Father came to the Supreme Pontiff and, attending him for a short rather than a long time, bore many of his burdens through salutary counsel and assistance, and greatly relieved his solicitude in governing the holy Church of God by his readiness to serve.

17. Nevertheless, he could not long patiently conceal the sadness and grief he had conceived over the dispersion of his sons. He also found the noise and tumult of the court burdensome, since they obstructed the sweetness and tranquility that he had been accustomed to enjoy and feed upon in the wilderness. Unable to endure this any longer, he laid his desolation before the Supreme Pontiff and with the greatest insistence implored and obtained permission to withdraw from the court and return to the wilderness and to the sweetness of the cell whose taste he had already experienced and whose rest he desired.

18. “And when the supreme pontiff wished to confirm him as archbishop of Reggio, to which church he had been elected with the pope’s approval [Note: [Col. 0489C] Our saint was elected or postulated to the archbishopric of Reggio in Calabria in the year 1090, as is proved by the evidence concerning this matter which I presented in the preliminary commentary, no. 532 and following], he in no way consented. Rather, spurning and despising that dignity, he bade farewell to the Apostolic See and, with God as his guide, reached a certain hermitage in Calabria called La Torre. There, after gathering many clerics and laymen, he established a monastery in which, until the end of his life, steadfast in the humility of the solitary life, ardent in charity, and fervent in devotion, he remained always attached to God; and there he happily completed the course of his earthly pilgrimage [Col. 0489B] [Note: [Col. 0489D] This was in the year 1101, as I demonstrated in the preliminary commentary, no. 729. By then he had gathered around himself approximately thirty disciples in the hermitage of La Torre, as may reasonably be inferred from the catalogue of the monks of La Torre who promised obedience to Landuin after the saint’s death, reproduced in the preliminary commentary, no. 622]. Divine mercy declared that this glorious Father had obtained the prize and crown of eternal happiness through several miraculous signs.

19. “Before he departed from the papal court, however, divine mercy, as is believed, through his merits and prayers, recalled all his companions and subjects, so that they all entirely agreed to return to Chartreuse [Note: [Col. 0489D] Our biographer seems here to suggest that all Bruno’s disciples came to Rome to join him by means of a miracle. I stated my opinion on this matter in the preliminary commentary, no. 527]. Therefore Master Bruno obtained from the supreme pontiff letters to the venerable man Siguin, abbot of the monastery of Casa-Dei, ordering him to return and restore the place of Chartreuse, abandoned by Master Bruno, to his companions and subjects, with all its former liberty, absolutely within thirty days of receiving the papal letters.

[Col. 0489C] 20. “These appear to be the first papal letters found to mention the Carthusian order [Note: [Col. 0489D] I gave those papal letters in full in the preliminary commentary, no. 528. In them, however, mention is made not of the Carthusian order, but only of the cell or monastery built by Bruno]. They were written near the beginning of the Chartreuse Cartulary. Abbot Siguin, having received the apostolic mandate, obeyed gladly and cheerfully, and freely returned the place of Chartreuse, as a free possession, to Master Landuin and his companions through a public instrument, which is transcribed near the beginning of the Chartreuse Cartulary [Note: [Col. 0489D] I inserted this instrument in the preliminary commentary, no. 529. For the conclusion to be drawn from the Carthusian cartulary, which he mentions here, concerning the period in which this biographer of our saint flourished, see what is explained in the preliminary commentary, no. 12 and following [Col. 0490C–D].]. Master Bruno had appointed the aforesaid Brother Landuin prior of Chartreuse before he crossed over to the regions of Calabria [Note: [Col. 0490D] Saint Bruno did not appoint Landuin prior only at that time, when he was already with the pontiff, as seems to be indicated here; rather, he appointed him when he departed from Chartreuse, as is clear from the letters cited in the preliminary commentary, no. 529, by which Siguin, abbot of Casa-Dei, restored Chartreuse to Landuin and the other disciples of the saint].”

21. “Since, therefore, the judgments of God are incomprehensible [Col. 0490A] and a great abyss, the place of Chartreuse should not be judged less worthy because, after having been dedicated to divine worship for six years, it was abandoned by the aforesaid holy men. Rather, for this reason it should be regarded as more remarkable and more worthy: it was so powerful even when abandoned that it deserved and prevailed upon its inhabitants to return, and could not remain without worshipers of God or without divine praises.

22. “Just as the Providence of divine dispensation permitted the apostles—already established by eternal predestination as the princes of heaven and earth—to fall during Christ’s Passion and to be separated from the truth of the Christian faith [Note: [Col. 0490D] Only heretics assert that all the apostles fell away from faith during Christ’s Passion; therefore the biographer is mistaken here], so also, when certain disciples had abandoned the sanctified city of Jerusalem and, scattered by the wind of unbelief among the outlying villages, were wavering amid the waves of despair, they themselves rose spiritually when Christ rose bodily, and afterward remained more constant and firmer in faith and in love of Christ. Since they had already withdrawn sixty stadia from Jerusalem, they returned that same day and were restored, together with the other disciples, by the vision of Christ. In the same way God first allowed the inhabitants of Chartreuse to depart, so that afterward, on returning, they might be more steadfast and stronger in holy perseverance.

23. “Those who had departed at the end of the sixth year returned in the seventh [Note: [Col. 0490D] It is clear from this that, even according to this biographer of ours, the six years during which Saint Bruno governed Chartreuse before Pope Urban II summoned him to Rome were incomplete]. This was intended to signify that, just as on the seventh day the Lord rested from his laborious works in the original creation, and after the Passion likewise rested in the tomb on that same day, and just as the seventh year under the law [another reading: ‘under natural law’] had been devoted to rest, and the seventh seven-year period is called the jubilee, so the inhabitants of Chartreuse, returning in the seventh year, ceased there from similar works of sin, were refreshed by the spiritual rest of contemplation, and rested hidden in Christ’s tomb—that is, in the cloister and cells. At last they themselves, then seven in number, might happily attain the seventh seven-year cycle of jubilee, which signifies the praise and eternal rest of everlasting glory.

24. “Bruno, therefore, a most holy man endowed with a twofold science, both divine and human, distinguished by Ciceronian eloquence, eminent in discernment, devotion, and the excellent integrity of his conduct, enriched and adorned with a plentiful treasury of heavenly virtues, beloved and pleasing to God and to men, governed the hermitage of Chartreuse for six years. Afterward, as has been said, he was summoned by the pope; and not long afterward [Note: [Col. 0491D] Bruno remained with Pope Urban only a few months before withdrawing to the Calabrian hermitage called La Torre, as is clear from what is stated in §31 of the preliminary commentary], he went to the hermitage in Calabria called La Torre. There, after building a holy monastery, he became the ruler and servant [another reading: ‘master’] of many servants of God and anchorites [Col. 0492A]. Having completed the course of his life happily, he departed to the Lord in the eleventh year after leaving Chartreuse—neither more nor less—as is contained in the books of the Customs of Dom Guigo, which are kept in the house of Chartreuse [Note: [Col. 0491D] There is unquestionably an error here in our biographer. See §30 of the preliminary commentary]. Immediately beside his tomb a living spring flows forth; by divine mercy, through the merits of this holy man, it grants the faithful who suffer many illnesses the desired remedies of healing [Note: [Col. 0491D] Concerning the miraculous spring mentioned here, and the miracles performed through the power of its waters, see the preliminary commentary, no. 735 and several following numbers].”

[Col. 0491]

# THE SECOND LIFE

By Francis of the Well, prior of the Greater Chartreuse,

from an edition prepared at Basel around the year 1315.

## PROLOGUE

The author explains why he undertakes to write the life of the saint.

[Col. 0491B]

1. We are commanded to praise not only the Lord in his saints but also the saints themselves in the Lord, as it is written: “Let us praise glorious men, and our fathers in their generation [Note: [Col. 0492D] Ecclesiasticus 44:1]. Men rich in virtue and devoted to the pursuit of beauty, making peace in their households. Their bodies have been buried in peace, and the Church proclaims their praise.” Let us praise, I say, and by word and imitation show to be worthy of praise men who are thus called from virtue—not travelers, since the Truth says, “Greet no one on the way [Note: [Col. 0492D] Approximately Luke 10:4]”—but glorious, that is, already received into glory and secure in their immortality; [Col. 0491C] and our spiritual fathers, whose faith and works we ought to imitate, and by whose teaching and examples we have been begotten for God, according to the Apostle’s statement: “Through the Gospel I begot you [Note: [Col. 0492D] First Corinthians 4:15].” “In their generation,” that is, according to what they did in their life.

2. “Men rich in virtue.” For true virtues are riches that cannot be violently taken away. “Devoted to the pursuit of beauty,” through true faith and the proper ordering of thoughts, affections, and works. “Making peace,” that is, possessing and making peace in their households. Their bodies have been buried in expectation of the perfect peace that will be given in the resurrection; and the Church proclaims their praise—that is, it proclaims their examples and glorious deeds, to the honor of God and the instruction of others [Col. 0491D]. This is the perpetual sacrifice that is offered without interruption in the Church of God [Col. 0492B]: an acceptable sacrifice, a rich burnt offering—not of goats or calves, but of praise—when God is praised in his saints by the human being whom he created, whom he redeemed, and to whom he promised the heavenly kingdom. This sacrifice is pleasing to God and useful and necessary for believers. It is necessary because the Lord says through the prophet, “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise [Note: [Col. 0492D] Psalm 49:14].” It is pleasing and acceptable to him because, he says, “the sacrifice of praise will honor me [Note: [Col. 0492D] Psalm 49:23].” It is useful to us because there, he says, I will show him the salvation of God—that is, Christ, who is the head of all the saints and their reward.

3. Let us therefore praise, dearest brothers, the Lord in his saints, and especially in this most blessed father of ours, Bruno, whose feast is celebrated today [Col. 0492C], who begot us in Christ, who prepared for us the way of life in the desert, and who showed us a rule of living by his example. Although we are not sufficient to praise him as he deserves, we must nevertheless not cease from praising him. Let us therefore exalt and praise him as much as we can, because he is greater than all praise. Let us recount his wonders, which he performed; let us proclaim his works among the nations, so that God may be glorified through them, and so that we may deserve to have in heaven as our companion and brother, through his merits and prayers assisting us, the one whom we were privileged to have as our father on earth.

# CHAPTER ONE

On the occasion of a deceased man who, during his solemn funeral rites, proclaimed from his bier that he had been condemned, Bruno decides to withdraw into solitude, draws others to the same purpose, and undertakes the journey with them to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble.

[Col. 0492D]

4. In the time of Gregory VII, Roman pontiff [Note: [Col. 0492D] This holy pontiff was raised to the chair of Saint Peter in the year 1073 and died in 1085, as we demonstrated in the preliminary commentary to his Life, under 25 May, the day on which he is commemorated and entered in the Roman calendar], and of Henry IV, emperor [Note: [Col. 0492D] He succeeded his father in 1056 and died in 1106, as Pagius and other writers show in their discussions of both years [Col. 0493C]], around the eighty-second year above the thousandth year of our salvation—that is, around 1082—when a distinguished school flourished in the city of Paris, crowded with a multitude of students and a very large company of eminent teachers in every branch of learning, a horrifying and memorable spectacle occurred there.

A certain distinguished master, foremost among the other teachers, outstandingly adorned with learning and character and honored above the rest, was overtaken by a serious illness. Lying in bed, he brought his life to its end. When solemn funeral rites were prepared for him according to custom, a large crowd of masters, students, and certain citizens gathered to honor him. With them accompanying and following the funeral procession, the body of the deceased was carried to the church in which it was to be buried [Col. 0493B]. As the customary Office for the dead was being sung by the invited clerics who were present, when they reached the lesson beginning, “Answer me,” the man who had died rose, lifted his head slightly, and sat up in the coffin. In the sight and hearing of everyone, who were stunned by the novelty of the event, he began to cry out in a loud, though dreadful, voice, saying:

“I HAVE BEEN ACCUSED BY THE JUST JUDGMENT OF GOD.”

5. After saying this, he lay down again. Those who had heard and seen these things, greatly and understandably terrified, prudently and carefully decided to postpone his burial until the following day, awaiting the outcome of the matter. On the next day, since so extraordinary a spectacle had already been spread throughout so large a city, a vast and almost innumerable crowd of both sexes gathered at the church. When the funeral rites had been begun again and continued from that point, as they reached the beginning of the same lesson, the deceased man, as on the previous day, sprang up from the coffin in which he lay dead and said:

“I HAVE BEEN JUDGED BY THE JUST JUDGMENT OF GOD.”

After saying this, he withdrew again into the coffin, and the astonishment among those standing by increased considerably. Yet they were not still certain from this that he had been rejected, since the words “I have been accused” and “I have been judged” could also be interpreted favorably—as though he had first been unjustly accused before Christ’s tribunal by the one who hastens to destroy all things, and then, by God’s just judgment, had been freed from that false accusation [Col. 0494A]. Everyone therefore agreed to postpone his burial until the third day.

6. On the third day an enormous crowd of men and women assembled, so that almost the entire city gathered to witness such a wondrous judgment of God. And behold, while the funeral rites were continued and performed in the former manner, the same deceased man rose for the third time and, in a powerful voice terrifying to all mortals, said:

“I HAVE BEEN CONDEMNED BY THE JUST JUDGMENT OF GOD.”

This voice, so astonishing and horrifying, and unheard of since the beginning of the world, left nearly all who were present half dead with terror. Nevertheless, judging him to have been rejected by the Lord and—according to his own testimony—condemned by God’s just judgment, they considered him unworthy of every suffrage of the Church and of ecclesiastical burial, and had him buried in a dung heap [Note: [Col. 0493D] What the learned reader should think about that entire sorrowful story of the condemned man may be gathered from the discussion of the matter at length in §10 and the thirteen following sections of the preliminary commentary. For the present, let him note especially that the account of the horrifying prodigy supplied here by Francis of the Well differs considerably in its details from the account contained in the Life composed by the earlier biographer of our saint. Besides the fact that the latter does not mention burial in a dung heap, he reports that the prodigy occurred not publicly in the church, as Francis of the Well says here, but within the private walls of the deceased man’s house, when his body was being taken to the church for burial. Nevertheless, like the account of Francis of the Well, he records that the event took place in the presence of a vast multitude of people].

Since, in the churches of Paris and the neighboring churches, the fourth lesson in the rites for the just dead begins, “Because of how many iniquities I have,” with the earlier words or phrases “Answer me” omitted, it is reported by some that those words were from then on deleted because of the perpetual and indelible memory of that terrible judgment [Note: [Col. 0493D] It is doubtful whether, in Saint Bruno’s time, any lessons were recited in the Parisian Office for the Dead, and likewise whether, if they truly were recited, one of them began with the words “Answer me” [Col. 0494C–D]. See the preliminary commentary, no. 228 and following].

7. Among the other teachers present at this horrifying spectacle was blessed Bruno, a Teuton by nationality, from the distinguished and royal city of Cologne, born of parents illustrious and noble not so much by lineage as by virtue [Note: [Col. 0494D] Everyone agrees that the saint was born of noble stock in Cologne]; a canon of the church of Reims, a doctor, and master of the Parisian scholars [Note: [Col. 0494C] It is explicitly stated in the account of his life given in the preliminary commentary, no. 7, that Bruno was master not of the Parisian scholars but of the schools—or, as it is written here, of the scholars—of Reims. Moreover, even if one grants that the saint witnessed the ominous prodigy of the condemned man at Paris, he never taught letters there, as is shown by the evidence relevant to this matter which I brought forward in §8 of the preliminary commentary]. A doctor especially learned in divine letters, as his writings testify [Note: [Col. 0494D] In particular, the two commentaries he composed, one on the Psalms and the other on all the Epistles of Saint Paul the Apostle. See §42 of the preliminary commentary], and honored above the rest.

Terrified and almost overwhelmed in a salutary way by these extraordinary, horrifying, and repeatedly uttered words, he summoned several companions and disciples who were especially close to him. Among them were Master Landuin, who afterward became the first prior of Chartreuse; two Stephens, one of Bourg and the other of Die, both canons of Saint-Ruf near Valence of the Allobroges; Hugh the chaplain; and two laymen, Andrew and Guarinus [Note: [Col. 0494D] Concerning Landuin and the others whom the saint is here said to have addressed, and likewise concerning the monastery of Saint-Ruf [Col. 0495D], see what is presented in the preliminary commentary, no. 433 and several following]. He said [Col. 0495A]:

“Many times, when we read the Apostle, we heard; but now, through experience, we have also learned, my dearest and most beloved brothers in Christ, how incomprehensible are the judgments of God and how unsearchable are his ways.

8. “While this deceased man was still alive, we both saw and knew him: a man learned in human wisdom, adorned with virtues—if indeed such things are true virtues—and with good conduct; according to outward wisdom, chaste, prudent, modest, well governing his household, honored by everyone and held in high esteem. But now we have heard from his own mouth that he has been condemned by the just judgment of God.

“Just, indeed, because the Lord is just and has loved justice; therefore his judgments can only be just, although they are often and for the most part hidden. ‘I have been condemned,’ he said, ‘by the just judgment of God.’

“This is certainly a terrifying and fearful voice. Would that it might sound continually in our ears and penetrate the depths of our hearts, so that we might fear the one whose judgment we cannot escape and, by fearing, flee from the coming wrath and seek the timely means of salvation while there is still time!

“Let us consider, I beg you, my brothers, what benefit the knowledge acquired with so much effort now gives this man in hell, since he suffers continual and perpetual blindness and ignorance. What do riches avail him, since he cannot have even a drop of water to cool his tongue [Note: [Col. 0495D] An allusion is made here to the rich man, Dives]? What do honors and pleasures avail him, when he must now undergo as many torments as he had enjoyments in the world?”

[Col. 0495C] 9. We have seen his body buried without honor in a dung heap. Let us consider that his soul is buried in hell, to be eternally tormented in everlasting fires with the impious—where their worm will not die and the fire will not be extinguished; where the burning is incomparable, the stench intolerable, and the pain without end. There people will seek death and will not find it. For then death will be immortal: it will consume them, not so that they may die, but so that they may be renewed for punishment.

“What, then, shall we do? To whose counsel shall we flee? For all of us have gone astray like sheep; each has turned to his own way. There is no one who does good, not even one. We have all sinned; we have acted unjustly; we have committed iniquity. We are all children of wrath [Col. 0495D], and therefore all worthy of the same punishment, unless the mercy of Christ rescues us from it.

“What shall we do? Shall we not all perish together? If he did not spare this man, nor the angels when they sinned, nor the natural branches, shall we suppose that he will not spare us either? Shall we suppose that his hand has been shortened, so that he can no longer show mercy? Or that he will restrain his mercies in his anger? God forbid.

10. “What, then, shall we do? O my brothers, in a matter so perplexing, so difficult, and so serious, let us seek counsel, lest we appear to have trusted in our own strength [Col. 0496A]. Not from the Jews, who believe that they are justified by the observance of the law alone. Not from the Greeks and their ancient philosophers, who trust in their own virtue. Not from the other seekers and wise men of this world, who are ignorant of the things of God. Rather, let us seek it from those who fear the Lord and walk in his ways.

“Let us first consult our advocate, whom we have with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who is the propitiation for our sins, and let us hear what he says. ‘The time is fulfilled,’ he says, ‘and the kingdom of God has drawn near; repent and believe in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0495D] Mark 1:15],’ for ‘unless you repent, you will all likewise perish [Note: [Col. 0495D] Approximately Luke 13:5].’

“Let us also hear John, the Lord’s forerunner, of whom it is written that among those born of women none has arisen greater than he [Note: [Col. 0495D] Matthew 11:11]. For, preaching in the desert of Judea a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, he says: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near [Note: [Col. 0496D] Matthew 3:2].’”

11. And again to the Pharisees and Sadducees: “‘Brood of vipers,’ he said, ‘who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Produce therefore fruits worthy of repentance [Note: [Col. 0496D] Approximately Luke 3:7–8].’”

Let us also hear the prince of the apostles, Peter, speaking to the Jewish people in the Acts of the Apostles: “Repent and turn back, so that your sins may be blotted out [Note: [Col. 0496D] Acts 3:19].” And again, when some of them, pierced in heart, said to Peter and the other apostles, “What shall we do, men and brothers?” [Col. 0496C] Peter replied on behalf of them all: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0496D] Acts 2:38].”

For this reason the prophet says: “If this nation repents of its evil, concerning which I have spoken against it, I too will repent concerning the evil that I had planned to do to it [Note: [Col. 0496D] Jeremiah 18:8].” And the Wise Man says: “If we do not repent, we shall fall into the hands of the Lord, and not into the hands of men [Note: [Col. 0496D] Ecclesiasticus 2:22].”

“This, then, my brothers, is sound and salutary counsel: if we wish to escape God’s just vengeance and his dreadful judgment, let us repent and cleanse our sins with tears. For this is the way that leads to life. This is the second plank after shipwreck, by which sinners are saved and by which God is inclined to mercy.

12. “Therefore, dearest brothers, casting away all uncleanness and abundance of wickedness, let us meekly receive the implanted word, which is able to save our souls. Let us turn to the Lord, and he will have mercy on us, for he is kind and ready to relent concerning evil; he does not desire the death of sinners [Col. 0497A], but rather that they should turn and live.

“Let us not delay turning until tomorrow, because he who promised forgiveness to the repentant did not promise tomorrow to sinners. Therefore those who lose the fitting time for repentance come in vain with prayers before the gate of the kingdom. To them the Lord says through Solomon:

“‘I called, and you refused; I stretched out my hand, and there was no one who looked. You despised all my counsel and neglected my reproaches. I too will laugh at your destruction and mock you when what you feared comes upon you. When sudden calamity and ruin descend like a storm, when tribulation and distress come upon you, then they will call upon me, and I will not answer; they will rise early, and they will not find me [Note: [Col. 0497D] Proverbs 1:24, 28].’”

[Col. 0497B] 13. Let us therefore be doers of this word and not hearers who deceive ourselves. Let us at least imitate those Ninevites who were converted by the preaching of Jonah, proclaimed a fast, wrapped themselves in sackcloth, and did penance. The Lord saw their works, that they had turned from their evil way, and he had mercy concerning the evil that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it.

“Let us do the same, because one greater than Jonah is here, who says: ‘Repent and believe in the Gospel.’ Let us open to the one who knocks; let us follow the one who calls—or rather, most certainly, who draws us and compels us to enter.

“For this voice that we have now heard was not made for the sake of the man who has died. Although there is repentance in hell, it is nevertheless too late and fruitless. It was made for us, so that this very voice might benefit us, whom divine patience still awaits with long-suffering [Col. 0497C]. Let us therefore no longer delay from day to day, because we do not know at what hour the Lord will come, and we cannot foresee the uncertain hour of death.”

14. After hearing these things, one of those standing by—Master Landuin, namely, a Tuscan by nationality, from the city of Lucca, a learned and God-fearing man—said:

“Good Master, now we know that you are truthful and teach the law of God in truth.” For your words are entirely true: we cannot escape God’s wrath and just indignation unless we cleanse our sins with tears.

“But since it is written that ‘everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life [Note: [Col. 0497D] First Epistle of John 2:16],’ who, I ask, can live safely and innocently among the wicked or produce fruits worthy of repentance where pride inflates, greed weakens, and lust defiles? Where there are lawsuits, quarrels, rivalries, slanders, and envies? Where robberies are committed, murders perpetrated, false testimonies uttered, adulteries, incest, fornications, sacrileges, sorceries, and similar crimes carried out? [Col. 0498A]

“Where simplicity has perished from human conduct, charity from fellowship, justice from action, truth from speech, and compassion from the needs of one’s neighbors? Where, finally, charity has grown cold and every iniquity has abounded, as the prophet testifies when he says: ‘There is no mercy, there is no truth, there is no knowledge of God in the land [Note: [Col. 0497D] Approximately Hosea 4:1].’

“I looked at it, and behold, it was empty; and at the heavens, and there was no light in them. I saw the mountains, and behold, they were trembling, and all the hills were shaken. I looked, and behold, there was no righteous person, and every bird of heaven had fled [Note: [Col. 0497D] Somewhat differently in Jeremiah 4:23–25].”

15. Therefore it seems difficult—indeed, almost impossible—for anyone who is pure and free from every sin to live in the world or produce fruits worthy of repentance in it. For, as Augustine says, “Repentance is vain when the sin that follows defiles it [Note: [Col. 0497D] This does not mean that the preceding sins were not truly forgiven for the penitent, but that the person who falls again loses the fruit gained from it].” Lamentations are of no benefit if sins are repeated. A wound that is reopened is healed more slowly.

And Gregory says: “Whoever mourns what he has done but does not abandon it subjects himself to a heavier punishment.” Therefore true repentance necessarily requires that the causes of sins be cut away completely [Note: [Col. 0497D] That is, repentance by which a person, having abandoned sin, strives toward perfection [Col. 0498D]].

“Therefore, if we wish to reach this degree of perfect repentance—for we cannot entirely abandon this visible world, which we see, as long as we live in the flesh—it is necessary at least that we completely leave behind everything that is in the world, since the Lord says:

“‘Everyone among you who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple [Note: [Col. 0498D] Luke 14:33].’

“And again, to the young man asking about eternal life: ‘If you wish to be perfect,’ he said, ‘go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me [Note: [Col. 0498D] Approximately Matthew 19:21].’”

16. When the young man heard these words and went away sorrowful, the Lord said to his disciples: “Amen, I say to you, a rich man will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty [Note: [Col. 0498D] Matthew 19:23].”

For this reason the Wise Man says: “He who trusts in riches will fall [Note: [Col. 0498D] Approximately Proverbs 11:28], and he who hastens to become rich will not remain innocent.” And again: “If you become rich, you will not be free from sin [Note: [Col. 0498D] Ecclesiasticus 11:10].” For “those who desire to become rich,” the Apostle says, “fall into the devil’s snare [Note: [Col. 0498D] First Epistle to Timothy 6:9].”

“Having therefore trampled upon, sold, and distributed to the poor all these things according to the Lord’s counsel, let us follow and imitate Christ, who, although he was rich, became poor so that we might be enriched by his poverty.”

“And because, most learned Master, under your instruction we have recognized the way of truth and the path of justice, and since it is dangerous to sleep beside a serpent and difficult to walk unharmed among flames, it remains for us to seek a place where, although in the world, we may live as though without the world, separated from the company of men, and may mourn our sins and produce fruits worthy of repentance [Col. 0499A]. Teach us, therefore, we beg you, and show us such a place; whatever you decide concerning it, we will do. For our salvation is in your hand.”

17. To this blessed Bruno replied:

“Brothers and fathers, listen—not to me, but let us listen together with me, I say, to that supreme knower of God’s secrets, the outstanding prophet David, to whom the Lord revealed the hidden and secret things of his wisdom. Let us first hear what he said; then let us hear what he did.

“He at that time, just as we are now, troubled in his exercise and disturbed by the voice of the enemy and by the tribulation of the sinner, said:

“‘My heart is troubled within me, and the fear of death has fallen upon me; fear and trembling have come upon me, and darkness has covered me.’

“And he said: [Col. 0499B] ‘Who will give me wings like a dove, and I shall fly away and rest?’

“Then he continued and said: ‘Behold, I have fled far away, and I remained in solitude [Note: [Col. 0499D] See Psalm 54:3, 8].’

“Behold, he says, I have withdrawn far from every occasion and circumstance of sin; fleeing this world in mind and body, I have remained steadfast—not in the city, but ‘in solitude.’

“For, as Gregory says, the one who flees withdraws far away when he raises himself from the crowd of earthly desires into the heights of contemplation of God; but he remains ‘in solitude’ when he perseveres in a remote concentration of mind.

“Therefore the same prophet, in order to deserve to see God’s power and God’s glory, testifies that he sought a place of solitude, saying:

“‘In a deserted, pathless, and waterless land, so I appeared before you in the sanctuary, to see your power and your glory [Note: [Col. 0499D] Psalm 62:3].’”

18. Solitude is the road that leads to life, where earthly things are exchanged for heavenly things, and transitory things for eternal ones. This is the place of repentance, the way of justice, the path of grace, and the ladder of glory.

“This is, I say, that ladder which Jacob saw standing on the earth in solitude and touching heaven; it carries human beings into heaven and receives angels for our assistance. It is the nurse of virtues, the guardian of patience, the teacher of pure simplicity, and ignorant of deceitful duplicity.

“It is the rest of those who labor, the consolation of those who mourn, and refreshment in the heat. In it stands the tower of David, built with battlements, from which a thousand shields hang, and in which there is every kind of armor for the strong [Col. 0499D].

“In it is the field of divine combat, the spectacle of angels, and the wrestling ground of athletes who fight courageously. In it Adam remained safe as long as he remained alone. But when a woman was given to him as a helper, he immediately fell.

“For this reason Enoch was snatched away into the solitude of paradise, lest wickedness change his heart. In it Abraham, while sitting alone beneath the oak of Mamre, saw three and worshiped one. In it Jacob, when he had sent everything ahead and remained alone, became blessed both by a blessing and by a change of name, gaining more in one moment alone [Col. 0500A] than throughout his entire life in company.

19. When Moses had driven the flock toward the inner parts of the desert, he was deemed worthy to see and hear the Lord in the burning bush saying to him: “Remove your sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground [Note: [Col. 0499D] Exodus 3:5].” The Lord never appeared to him except when he was alone. David, fleeing into the wilderness, escaped Saul’s snares. Jeremiah, asking that water be given to his head and a fountain of tears to his eyes, so that he might mourn the slain of his people, also asks for a place where he might more freely devote himself to such a holy work, saying: “Who will give me a lodging for travelers in the wilderness [Note: [Col. 0499D] Approximately Jeremiah 9:2],” as though he had no leisure to do this in the city; by this he indicated that [Col. 0500B] companions impeded the grace of tears. Moreover, when he had said: “It is good to await in silence the salvation of God,” and had added: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth,” he further added and said: “He will sit solitary and keep silent, because he will lift himself above himself [Note: [Col. 0500D] Lamentations 3:27–28].” Elijah, alone on the mountain at the entrance of the cave, recognized the Lord passing by. And Elisha received a double portion of his spirit when he was taken up. John the Baptist, filled with the Holy Spirit from the womb, secure neither in his wondrous birth nor in the holiness of his parents, fled the company of human beings as dangerous and sought the deserts of solitude. What virtue and merit he acquired there was shown by Christ’s baptism and by the death he accepted for righteousness. For in solitude he became such that he was worthy alone to baptize the One who washes [Col. 0500C] all things, and for the truth to shrink neither from prison nor from death.

20. What more need be said? Jesus Christ our Lord, whose power could neither be aided in secret nor impeded in public, was led into the desert—there is no doubt that this was by his own Spirit—in order to be tempted by the devil. The same Christ, leaving the crowds, went up the mountain alone to pray. Christ fed the crowds in the desert, suggesting to us by his example how greatly solitude benefits us. Consider for yourselves also how much the holy and venerable Fathers—Paul, Antony, Hilarion, the two Macarii, Eulalius, Arsenius, Evagrius, Basil, Benedict, and countless others—advanced in solitude. And you will find that the sweetness of psalmody, the study of reading, the fervor of prayer, the subtlety of meditation, the raptures of contemplation, and the baptisms of tears can be aided by nothing more than by solitude. Hence, concerning the sinful soul whom the Lord desires to call back to himself, the prophet says: “I will lead her into solitude, and there I will speak to her heart [Note: [Col. 0500D] Approximately Hosea 2:14].” But concerning the soul that, freed from the bonds of the flesh, has deserved to enter eternal joys, it is said in the Song of Songs: “Who is this that comes up from the desert, overflowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved? [Note: [Col. 0500D] Song of Songs 8:5].” [Col. 0501A] She is not found in the streets or squares of the city, but in solitude. Therefore, my brothers, let us pray to God that he may deign to show us such a place, where we may accomplish in deed what, with his inspiration, we have already conceived in our minds.

21. After the prayer had been offered, the two canons Stephen—one of Bourges and the other of Die—said: “Venerable fathers and teachers, not far from the city of Valence, to which our monastery of Saint-Ruf is adjacent [Note: [Col. 0501D] Concerning this monastery, see the preliminary commentary, no. 436], near the banks of the Rhône, on the borders of the diocese of Die, from which one of us derives his origin, there is another city, Grenoble. It is so called either because it was founded under the emperor Gratian, or from the etymology of its name, as though it meant gracious, noble, and populous. In it is blessed Hugh, bishop of that same city, who, before [Col. 0501B] his elevation to episcopal dignity, was a canon of the Church of Valence, born at Château-Neuf on the River Isère, only four miles distant from the city [Note: [Col. 0501D] Concerning this holy prelate, about whom we have already treated under 1 April, the day on which he is commemorated, see also the annotations appended to the preceding Life, under letter g]. We ourselves have both seen and known him, a man truly holy, just and upright, and fearing God.

22. “For if chastity is praised, who is purer than he? If truthfulness of speech, who is more cautious in speaking? If love of God, who is more fervent? If love of neighbor, who is kinder? If humility, who is more lowly? If almsgiving, who is more generous? If prayer, who is more devout? If rivers of tears, who pours himself out more abundantly in them? If contemplation, who is more exalted? If endurance, who is stronger in tribulation? If justice, who is stricter? If prudence, who is more watchful? If temperance, who is more moderate? [Col. 0501C] Apart from the good things that came through him to the clergy and the people, he possesses in his diocese very high mountains, and in them very many deserted places separated from all human passage and companionship, and therefore admirably suited for carrying out this strict penance. Since by his example and teaching he invites and draws people to penance, if we are willing to approach him, we shall easily be able to obtain from him the place we seek. For he is pious, kind, and merciful. He will rejoice at our arrival and will grant us our desire. We shall also guide you on the road, which we know and have often traveled.”

23. Then Hugh, whom they called the Chaplain, because alone among them, without a canonical or pastoral benefice, he performed the office of a chaplain-priest [Note: [Col. 0501D] Guigo, speaking in the Life he wrote of Saint Hugh about Bruno and his companions approaching Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, states that only Hugh among them, who was called the chaplain, exercised the priesthood. Puteanus, however, interprets him here in such a way as to suggest that the only meaning intended was that Hugh was then alone—not that he had been ordained to the priesthood, but that he alone had in addition been elevated by either canonical or pastoral dignity. Yet who would not see how little such an interpretation accords with Guigo’s words (see the preliminary commentary, no. 442)?], said: “I have certainly heard much about this man, whose reputation now spreads everywhere, because he is a man of God and holy, thirsting for the salvation of souls. Since the charity with which [Col. 0502A] he is filled never fails, he will, I hope, gladly receive us.
