And although I am already old and weak, and this road is narrow and difficult, yet because ‘the narrow way leads to life, while the broad way leads to destruction,’ and because no age is too late for penance, since the Lord says: ‘At whatever hour the sinner groans, I will no longer remember his iniquities [Note: [Col. 0502D] Ezekiel 18:21–22: ‘If the wicked man does penance … I will not remember any of all his iniquities …’],’ and since he also ordered a single denarius to be given to each of those laboring in his vineyard, to the last as to the first—if you decide to go there and undertake this road, I too shall follow; and wherever you go, I shall go. Whatever land receives you shall receive me also, and there I shall take my place of burial; only death shall separate us from one another.”

24. When the other two, namely Andrew and [Col. 0502B] Guarinus, heard this, they said together: “We have always heard, and from hearing have believed, that God is kind and merciful, surpassing malice in goodness, desiring that no one should perish but rather that all should be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. With him there is no partiality, but in every nation whoever does his will is acceptable to him. Although neither of us knows letters, we nevertheless know Christ, and him crucified, by faith; without him all knowledge is ignorance. Whatever the Church believes, we firmly believe and simply confess, hoping to be saved in this faith and to receive the remission of sins through his word. Yet we would like to be instructed, since the Lord, through his prophet and more than a prophet, admonishes us to produce fruits worthy of penance, what these [Col. 0502C] worthy fruits are.”

Blessed Bruno answered them: “Penance is a tree planted by the heavenly farmer in the midst of his Church. Its root is contrition of heart, its branches are good works, its leaves are full confession, and its fruit is the penalty of satisfaction.

25. “Thus, a person does penance but not worthy fruits who merely grieves over his offenses. Another performs penance and bears fruit, but not worthy fruit, who both grieves and makes partial satisfaction. But the person produces worthy fruits who, in sorrow of heart, is afflicted by punishment to the degree that he sinned by guilt, according to the saying in Revelation: ‘As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much torment and mourning give her [Note: [Col. 0502D] Revelation 18:7].’ And in Deuteronomy: ‘The measure of the punishment shall correspond to the measure of the sin [Note: [Col. 0502D] Deuteronomy 25:2].’ Hence he admonishes us to perform not merely [Col. 0502D] fruits of penance, but also worthy fruits of penance. For this, Gregory says, justice demands: if someone has fallen into guilt, he ought to cut away from himself lawful pleasures to the same extent that [Col. 0503A] he knows he has committed unlawful acts. Therefore, my most beloved brothers, let us no longer neglect the time of penance, nor delay from day to day. For we do not know at what hour the Lord will come, and none of us knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred. Already the axe has been placed at the root of the tree. Already this man, whom we knew while he was alive, has been condemned by God’s just judgment and consigned to eternal torments, as we have often heard from his own mouth.”

26. “What, then, shall we sinners and wretches do, who cannot be justified by the works we have done? Is God a respecter of persons? Far be it. For with God there is no change or shadow of alteration; rather, he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens. What else, I ask, shall we do [Col. 0503B] except flee from the coming wrath? For the Lord has given those who fear him a sign, that they should flee from the face of the bow. Hence the prophet also says: ‘Flee from the midst of Babylon, so that each may save his own soul [Note: [Col. 0503D] Approximately Jeremiah 51:6];’ and again: ‘Withdraw from the midst of Babylon, and go out from the land of the Chaldeans, and be like young goats before the flock [Note: [Col. 0503D] Jeremiah 50:8].’ And again: ‘Flee, save your souls, and you will be like tamarisk trees in the wilderness [Note: [Col. 0503D] Jeremiah 48:6].’ Another prophet likewise says: ‘Oh! oh! oh! Flee from the land of the north, for I have scattered you toward the four winds of heaven [Note: [Col. 0503D] Approximately Zechariah 2:6].’ And blessed Job says: ‘Flee from the face of the sword, for it is the sword of iniquities, and know that there is judgment [Note: [Col. 0503D] Approximately Job 19:29].’ And the bride says to the bridegroom in the Song of Songs: ‘Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle and a young stag upon the mountains of spices [Note: [Col. 0503D] Song of Songs 8:14].’ [Col. 0503C] What else, I ask, do all these exhortations urge us to do except flee by despising this world, which is rightly signified by Babylon and the north? For Babylon is interpreted as ‘confusion,’ while from the north every evil is spread abroad.”

27. “Let us flee, therefore, because we overcome it in no better way than by fleeing. Let us flee, I say, not like Jonah from the face of the Lord, but toward the Lord himself, who is present everywhere, humbly beseeching him to turn away from us by his mercy the indignation that we have justly deserved, lest we too perish together with this man and the other impious persons [Note: [Col. 0503D] The biographer requires a charitable interpretation here; for it should not be thought that Jonah perished or was damned, as he seems to intend].”

As he said this, both he himself and all the others who were present, unable any longer to restrain their tears, wept together. Prostrating themselves on the ground, they raised their voices and said:

“Lord [Col. 0503D] God almighty, whose mercy surpasses every judgment; who do not rejoice in the destruction of those who die, but rather grant them time and opportunity for repentance; who commanded your servant Abraham to leave his land, his kindred, and his father’s house; who led your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand [Col. 0504A]; who promised pardon to those who truly repent—extend your mercy over us, we beseech you, and deign to send your holy angel from heaven to teach us what we ought to do, to guide us in the way of justice and in the paths of your commandments, and to show us the place that you will choose, where we may be able to serve you worthily, escape the dangers of this world, and produce worthy fruits of penance.

28. “Defend us, Lord, from the snares of our enemies, who hasten to destroy all things, and do not enter into judgment with your servants. Rather, through the merit of the passion of Jesus Christ, your Son, our Lord, cleanse us from all sins and grant that, after our departure from this life, we may happily reach him who is the way, the truth, and the life, freed from every [Col. 0504B] punishment, to our Lord Jesus Christ, who with you, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God, forever and ever.”

When they had all answered, “Amen,” they rose from there and, with one mind and the same resolve, sold everything they possessed and gave it to the poor. Having taken leave of all their dear ones and acquaintances, they came, led by the Holy Spirit, though by a long and laborious road, with the angel of the Lord going before them, directing and protecting them, to the most blessed Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, already mentioned [Note: [Col. 0504D] See what has been noted in the preceding Life, annotation 8].

## CHAPTER II

Bruno, together with his companions, comes to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble; obtains from him the hermitage of Chartreuse; lives there in great austerity; and, after approximately six years, is summoned by the pope, but resolves to obey the summons.

[Col. 0504C]

29. As they were approaching the city, that same bishop saw in a dream God constructing for himself a worthy dwelling in the solitude of Chartreuse. He also saw seven golden stars, arranged in the form of a crown and raised slightly above the earth, differing from the other stars in the firmament in position, movement, color, and brightness; these seven stars provided guidance on the journey to seven men of the same number—for that is how many they were [Note: [Col. 0504D] Concerning what should be thought about the vision of the seven stars here mentioned, divinely granted to Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and about the circumstances reported here but not grounded in Guigo, the ancient biographer of this holy prelate, or in any other ancient authority, see the explanation in the preliminary commentary, §25].

When morning came, while he was troubled by such a vision, the seven men appeared, knocking at the doors of the episcopal palace—namely, blessed Bruno with his small but holy company. When this was reported to the bishop, he immediately ordered them to be admitted. They entered [Col. 0504D] and humbly prostrated themselves at his feet. Having requested and obtained his blessing, they explained the reasons for their coming to him and asked him to deign to show them some place in his diocese and, in his kindly clemency, to grant it to them as a pious gift: a place where, separated from the dangers of this world and from the company of other people [Col. 0505A], they might fulfill their desire, serve God alone worthily, and build a dwelling worthy of him.

30. When the most blessed bishop heard this, no longer troubled by the vision, which he now saw fulfilled, he received them with immense joy—not only gladly but also reverently—and treated them kindly. He recounted to them the vision he had seen in his sleep that night and said:

“My most beloved brothers and sons in Christ, I not only do not reject your purpose and desire, but strongly commend them. For this world is so full of snares, dangers, calamities, and miseries, so many and so great, that it often compels the elect to despise every prosperity and to seek God through adversity [Col. 0505B], since they cannot love God and the world at the same time. These two loves establish two cities that oppose one another: the city of God and that of the devil. God, however, is good—indeed, the highest good. But the whole world lies in the power of evil. Hence the apostle, beloved above all others, says: ‘If anyone loves the world, the charity of the Father is not in him [Note: [Col. 0505D] First Letter of John 2:15].’

“When God had determined to destroy the cities of the Sodomites, the angel said to blessed Lot, who belonged to the city of God: ‘Save your life, and do not look back, nor remain anywhere in the surrounding region, but save yourself on the mountain, lest you too perish in the same way [Note: [Col. 0505D] Approximately Genesis 19:17].’ For those saints of whom the world was not worthy, as the Apostle testifies, ‘in want, distressed, afflicted, wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, in deserts, mountains, caves, and caverns of the earth [Note: [Col. 0505D] Hebrews 11:37–38].’ [Col. 0505C]

31. “And so they were found approved by the testimony of faith. It is praiseworthy and beneficial to follow and imitate their footsteps, but it is especially difficult in these cold regions, which are not like Egypt, the Thebaid, Scythia [Note: [Col. 0505D] Our biographer is clearly speaking here not of Scythia, the northern region of Asia, whose climate is no less cold than that of the tract of land containing the hermitage of Chartreuse, but of the Egyptian desert of Schetes or Sciti, also called Schytia by some. As with the other deserts of Egypt and Palestine, it was once inhabited by a great [Col. 0506D] multitude of anchorites, as may be seen in Rosweyde’s Lives of the Fathers], or Palestine.

“For among these very high mountains that you see, amid the other solitudes, there is a certain wilderness called Chartreuse, about ten miles from the city. It is broad indeed, but completely uninhabited and accessible only to wild beasts. Because of the harshness of the place, it is almost unknown to human beings and other tame animals. It is enclosed on every side by high rocks and crags, as though cut away, planted with unfruitful trees, excessively cold, and covered with snow for most of the year. It is so precipitous, barren, and unproductive that nothing can be sown or harvested there. In its midst there is a small river called the Dead Gnerus, as though it were an image of death. Gathered from the mountains surrounding it on every side, it flows with great noise like torrents or floodwaters [Col. 0506A].

“The approach to this Chartreuse wilderness is difficult and laborious, while the entrance is hard and dangerous, being between two rocks of astonishing height that rise upward like straight lines and finally almost meet at the summit, so that they inspire horror and terror in those who enter.

32. “To put it briefly, the harshness of that place and its terror are so great that it could be called a prison or a place of purgatory rather than a dwelling-place for human life [Note: [Col. 0506D] To find a more detailed account of how dreadful the solitude of Chartreuse was before our saint entered it with his companions, see the preliminary commentary, §26]. Hence it will seem difficult, without a special gift from God, for human beings to live there or at least to persevere for long—for with God nothing is impossible. But you know, my brothers, how serious it is, after putting one’s hand to the plow, to look back [Col. 0506B]. Therefore, we must fear the example of Lot’s wife, who looked back; and where she looked, there she remained, and she was turned into salt, so that the prudent might be seasoned by her example [Note: [Col. 0506D] Everyone, I think, will readily conclude that this speech or exhortation, supposedly delivered by Saint Hugh to Bruno and his companions, was entirely fabricated by the biographer].”

When the most blessed bishop had finished these words, blessed Bruno replied:

“Most reverend Father, this place is certainly terrible, as we have heard and now partly see. But we are seeking just such a place in which to do penance. Although we are weak and fragile, we nevertheless trust in the mercy of God, who is powerful, and we hope that he who gave us the will to come here will also give us the power to persevere, since his hand has not been shortened so that he cannot show his mighty works to us now as he did formerly. For he inclined the crags of the torrents [Col. 0506C], so that the people might rest in Arnon and recline within the borders of the Moabites. He delivered Jonathan and his armor-bearer, crawling on their hands and feet over high rocks and crags, jagged like teeth, from the hands of their enemies, granting them victory over those enemies.

33. “He fed such a great multitude of the children of Israel, and an innumerable people in the desert, with manna sent from heaven. Will he now be unable to give bread or prepare a table for his people? He commanded the ravens to feed Elijah on Carmel, and they fed Paul in Egypt. He sent to Daniel in Chaldea the meal that Habakkuk had prepared for the harvesters in Judea. He multiplied the loaves in the desert, with which he satisfied so great a multitude of people. He gives [Col. 0506D] their food to the beasts and to the young ravens that call upon him. He feeds the birds of the air, which neither sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns. Are we not worth more to the Lord than they? Therefore, even if human comforts fail us, we shall not distrust God’s presence and providence, since he is powerful [Col. 0507A] enough to make bread from these stones that we have seen and to turn water into wine. When he wills, he is also able to give snow like wool and scatter mist like ashes.

“Trusting, therefore, in such power and goodness, we humbly beg again and again that you do not delay our desire any longer or put us to shame in this petition [Note: [Col. 0507D] It is evident that this response was likewise arbitrarily attributed to Bruno here, just as the words that follow are attributed to Hugh].”

Then blessed Hugh, considering their steadfastness and perseverance in the undertaking they had begun, lest he seem to resist their vocation and the divine will, said:

“My beloved, I too desire to fulfill your desire; I did not delay for the purpose of taking it away, but rather so that it might be increased by delay.

34. “Seeing that your will is rooted and founded in the charity of Christ, I now grant to you and to those whom the same charity may draw with you, both now and in the future, brothers, [Col. 0507B] the aforesaid place and whatever right or claim I possess in it, with complete freedom. I shall also arrange for the same to be done by all the others who hold any right in it, and throughout my life I shall gladly provide you and all your people with every human assistance possible for me.

“Moreover, for your peace and quiet, in order to remove whatever is contrary to your purpose, I wish a house to be built over the bridge situated between the two aforementioned rocks, at the entrance to the said solitude. By divine authority I shall prohibit women from passing through your boundaries in any way, as well as men bearing arms. Likewise, within those boundaries I shall prohibit fishing, hunting, and the capture of birds, [Col. 0507C] and the grazing and passage of sheep, goats, and all domestic animals. I shall pray to God that he multiply in his grace those who obey this gift and prohibition of ours and grant them a share in all the good works to be carried out there until the end of the world. Those who disobey I leave to divine judgment for punishment, and I shall also see that they are punished by secular authority [Note: [Col. 0507D] Mabillon mentions, in the preface to part II of the sixth century of the Benedictine Annals, no. 86, a charter given in the month of July 1084 to the priests and laypeople of the diocese of Grenoble, in which Chartreuse is situated. In it Bishop Hugh ordered that women should not cross the land of the brothers of Chartreuse, who, desiring to please God, were fleeing the world and crowds, and that no one should fish or hunt within their boundaries or lead his animals there to graze. Yet, despite the most diligent investigation, I have been unable to find that charter anywhere].”

35. After saying this, he rose, embraced them, and wept for joy over each one of them, praising and blessing God for their arrival. Then he blessed them, saying:

“Almighty and eternal God, whose mercies we can neither measure nor limit in time; who call those whom you will, and justify and magnify those [Col. 0508A] whom you call—look, we beseech you, with the eyes of your clemency upon these servants of yours, whom you have deigned to invite to the service of your worship, and grant the help of your grace, so that they may accomplish with all their strength whatever is pleasing to you. Fill them with your venerable virtues, so that, armed with them, they may overcome the snares of the flesh, the world, and the demons, and thereafter receive the unfading crown of victory. Cause them to increase a thousandfold, and deign to join them, as well as those who follow in their footsteps and persevere in true humility and charity in the said solitude until the end of their lives, free from every guilt and punishment, to the company of your saints. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.”

[Col. 0508B]

36. After this, because the aforementioned Bruno and all his companions were considerably, and not without reason, fatigued by the exertions of the journey, the same most blessed bishop kept them in his episcopal palace and, with his customary kindness, cared for and refreshed them for several days. When these days had passed, and everything necessary for the journey had been prepared and arranged, they climbed the mountain, entered the wilderness of Chartreuse, and began to inhabit it around the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, in the year of our salvation 1084 [Note: [Col. 0507D] That Puteanus correctly established this date for Bruno’s entry into Chartreuse is clear from what I brought forward in the preliminary commentary, nos. 470 and following], with the aforementioned blessed Bishop Hugh going before them, guiding them, helping them in all things and in every way, and providing what was necessary [Note: [Col. 0508D] That this is truly reported is clear from what was said in the preliminary commentary, no. 502 and following].

There, in the upper part of the mountain, which is now called [Col. 0508C] “To Blessed Mary of the Casales,” they began to build a church, as well as small cells not far from that church, near a certain spring that to the present day is called Bruno’s Spring. The cells were distinct and somewhat separated from one another, so that no one might impede another’s solitude [Note: [Col. 0508D] Concerning the spring, still distinguished by Saint Bruno’s name, and the other matters mentioned here, consult the preliminary commentary, §27]. In these cells they lived, one in each, after the manner of those ancient Egyptian monks [Note: [Col. 0508D] Puteanus, who agrees with Blomenvenna in most of what he writes about Saint Bruno and his companions when they first entered Chartreuse, wrongly disagrees with him here. Guigo records in the Life of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, as may be seen in the preliminary commentary, no. 475, that at that time they inhabited the cells not singly but two to a cell. This contemporary and highly trustworthy writer must be followed, even though shortly after the saint’s death the Carthusians occupied the cells singly rather than two by two]. There they continually devoted themselves to silence, reading, prayer, and manual labor, especially the copying of books [Note: [Col. 0508D] See the preliminary commentary, no. 487]. From then on they were called Carthusian brothers, taking their name from the name of the place; from them this Carthusian order likewise received both its origin and its name.

[Col. 0509A]

37. These seven men—for blessed Bruno directed the others, who had chosen him as their prior and shepherd of their souls and, with the approval of Bishop Hugh, had submitted themselves to his obedience [Note: [Col. 0509D] Since the Saint lived for some time as a hermit in the solitude of Sicca-Fontana before withdrawing to Chartreuse, as I have shown in the preliminary commentary, nos. 414 and following, it seems doubtful whether he was not elected prior by the companions who followed him to Chartreuse before he had yet come with them to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, contrary to what Puteanus seems to have thought on the basis of what is written here]—wishing to subject to themselves the world they had abandoned and everything in the world, namely the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, established a sufficiently arduous rule of life. They themselves observed it and commanded their successors to observe it.

For the defeat of pride, which is the beginning of every sin, and of its wicked offspring—namely envy, ambition, vainglory, and whatever else belongs to it—they made for themselves short and narrow garments of coarse, white, cheap, and rough cloth. These garments made them contemptible and degraded in the eyes of those who saw them [Col. 0509B], and caused them to inspire horror rather than honor. Although pride sometimes lies hidden beneath a filthy habit, they nevertheless did everything they could to drive it away.

Against greed, which is called the root of all evils, and avarice, which is called the service of idols, they established fixed boundaries, greater or smaller according to the fertility or sterility of their lands, so that outside those boundaries, even if the whole world were offered to them, they would not be permitted to possess even as much as a human foot could occupy.

38. They also imposed upon their animals and livestock a definite number that could in no way be exceeded. And so that they would never be compelled either to add more land to their possession [Col. 0509C] than had been specified or to increase the number of livestock, they decreed that twelve monks, together with a thirteenth prior, sixteen lay brothers, and a few hired workers—and no one added beyond this—should remain permanently in their houses.

To tame the lust of the flesh and the law of the members that struggles against the law of the mind, they always wore harsh hair shirts next to the flesh. On Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays they were content with bread, water, and salt, as they wished. On Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays they received vegetables or something of that kind and wine from the cook; on Thursday they also received cheese or something else. Yet both the healthy and the sick perpetually abstained from all eating of meat. They did not eat white bread, but only cakes [Note: [Col. 0509D] Guigo’s Customs, chapter 34, no. 3, reads: “Bread, although made of wheat, is a cake; for we do not make white bread.” Masson, however, in the work entitled Carthusian Annals, in his note on that chapter, interprets the cake as brownish bread]. They never drank pure wine, but wine well diluted, which they call “watered” (*limphatum*), and this only at lunch and dinner, and on those days when they were permitted to use it and to dine. They disciplined their flesh with almost continuous fasts and prolonged vigils. They never bought fish [Col. 0510A], but if fish happened to be given to them freely, they received it charitably and distributed it according to the donors’ wishes, though only on days when they were permitted to eat it.

39. They performed the divine office, both by day and by night, with the greatest devotion—not perfunctorily, as some do, but with intense attention, their eyes lowered to the ground while their hearts were fixed on heaven—both in the church, on the days and at the hours when they assembled there, and in their cells. They presented their entire human being, interior and exterior, directed—indeed, fixed—upon God, through things surpassing what is visible, in habit, voice, and countenance, with everything else despised.

On Sundays and on certain feasts of the saints alone, following the custom of the ancient hermits, they offered the sacrifice of the Mass, lest they be hindered from other sacred works, though lower in dignity; on these occasions they all assembled. On those same days they ate together in the refectory according to the rite of monks. On the other days, in their cells and under strict silence, they devoted themselves without interruption to prayer, meditation, contemplation, and the other pious and devout exercises. Thus, where previously there had been caves and lairs of wild beasts, one could then see choirs of soldiers, bands of prophets, assemblies of monks, and gatherings of angels [Note: [Col. 0510D] Concerning the rule of life observed by the Saint and his companions at Chartreuse, see the preliminary commentary, nos. 485 and following].

### 40

The holy bishop Hugh mentioned above frequently visited them and loved them most tenderly as sons. Until his death he always supported them—and not only them, but also those who subsequently succeeded them—with counsel and benefactions. Among them he was not as a lord or bishop, but as a most humble companion and brother, ready, insofar as lay within him, to serve them all.

He was so devoted to inhabiting the desert that Blessed Bruno sometimes had to compel him to leave it and return to his sheep. “Go,” he said, “go to your sheep and discharge what you owe them.”

[Note: The saint truly found Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, so obedient. See the preliminary commentary, no. 502.]

Moreover, at the urging and through the efforts of that most blessed bishop, all the people living nearby—ecclesiastics, nobles, and commoners alike—seeing the holy, honorable, and devout manner of life of Blessed Bruno and his companions, gave them whatever rights they held in those mountains and within the boundaries and limits of that solitude.

[Note: I have given the entire instrument by which they did this in the preliminary commentary, nos. 503 and following.]

These, then, O blessed Carthusian desert, were those first Fathers who first began to inhabit this vast solitude and first established in it this order, which received from you a name that has spread throughout the world like oil poured out everywhere. These are the seven pillars which Wisdom hewed out and upon which she built her house. These are the seven oxen ascending from the river, and the seven ears of grain on one stalk. They are also the seven trumpets whose use belonged to the Jubilee.

### 41

These are the seven lampstands, in the midst of which John, writing to the seven Churches that were in Asia, declares that he saw one like a son of man, clothed in a long robe (*poderes*), holding in his right hand seven stars, which are the angels of the seven Churches; and in the midst of the throne, a Lamb standing, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God sent into all the earth.

These are the seven baskets full of fragments, the seven seals of the closed book, and the seven men full of the Holy Spirit whom the apostles chose as deacons for service. They are also the seven steps which Ezekiel saw for ascending to the outer court.

This is the number seven, consecrated on account of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. This number seven is the first number made perfect in units when its parts are added together. For one and six, two and five, and three and four—its aliquot parts—make seven. Hence the seventh day, the seventh week, the seventh month, and the seventh year, as perfect things, were days of rest according to the Law.

### 42

The whole of time is also marked out and recurs in periods of seven days: “And on the seventh day God ceased from all his work.” On the seventh day Christ also rested in the tomb. In all these things the perfection of this consecrated number seven is signified, and in it the perfection of this holy religious institution, which was first established by these seven men of the same number.

This perfection is rightly represented by those seven stars which the Lord showed to blessed Hugh at the time of their blessed arrival, both because of the great mystery of this number seven and because of the sublimity, stability, brightness, purity, and number of the stars. These virtues not only befit all religious persons but are also necessary to them. They must be like stars in the heavens through contemplation, with their minds’ affections directed upward, not toward the earth.

“For the beauty of heaven is the glory of the stars,” says the Wise One.

[Note: Ecclesiasticus 43:10.]

Second, they must be firm and steadfast in the purpose of religious life they have undertaken. For this reason God placed the stars in the firmament, so that they might serve as signs for seasons, days, months, and years. Hence it is written that the stars, remaining in their course and order, fought against Sisera—that is, against the devil.

[Note: Judges 5:20.]

For *Sisera* is interpreted as “excluding the joyful.” Third, they must be patient in tribulation, so that they may be like the morning star in the midst of mist.

### 43

For God made the moon and the stars to precede the night. Fourth, just as, according to the philosopher, corruption, falling, and error do not befall the stars, so religious persons must preserve the integrity of the flesh without corruption, so that they may say the words of the Apocalypse:

“I am the offspring and root of David, the bright and morning star.”

[Note: Apocalypse 22:16.]

They must ensure that it is not said of them that “the stars are not pure in his sight.”

Fifth, just as each of the stars is larger than the whole earth, although it appears brief, almost point-like, and small in outward appearance, so religious persons must always increase through charity and decrease through humility. These two virtues—humility and charity—are the two extremities of religious life, its beginning and its end. Without them, all the things lying between are more deserving of punishment than of merit.

O blessed Carthusian desert, therefore, once again and again! For so long barren, but now fruitful! Blessed are the mountains that were deemed worthy to have such inhabitants and cultivators! Finally, blessed is this religious institution, divinely founded, which surpasses the other religious orders in antiquity after Augustine and Benedict, and surpasses them also in the austerity of its life!

Of its origin, then, let these few remarks suffice, so that we may return to the subject we began.

### 44

Blessed Bruno, of whom we are speaking, persevered in this austerity of life with his companions in that solitude for almost six years, devoting himself without interruption, day and night, to fasts, prayers, and other religious exercises.

[Note: Add what has been noted in the preceding Life, note 17.]

It happened that, after Gregory VII, Roman pontiff, had died, Victor III succeeded him in the papacy. When Victor likewise died after a few months, Urban II succeeded him. Formerly called Otho, he had been a monk and abbot of Cluny and, while still in the lesser orders, had been a disciple of that same Blessed Bruno.

[Note: See what I have brought together in the annotations to the preceding Life, note 16.]

Shortly after his elevation to the apostolic dignity, Urban, mindful of the teaching and probity of Blessed Bruno, his former teacher, and wishing to use his counsel in the administration entrusted to him by Christ, summoned him to the service of the holy Roman Church, adding a command of obedience.

When Blessed Bruno received this command, he was greatly troubled, since he had already tasted the sweetness of solitude. Mary held him back so that he might rest; Martha drew him onward so that he might labor; the brothers begged him not to abandon them; and the pope commanded him to obey. The court frightened him if he were to go there, while his anxious conscience did not know what to do in so perplexing a situation.

### 45

At last obedience prevailed. He knew that true obedience admits no delay and allows neither excuse nor postponement. Thus he said to his brothers and disciples:

“It is most pleasing to me, my dearest brothers, to remain with you; to be separated from you is most grievous; but to obey the apostolic commands is necessary for me. For those in higher positions have the authority to govern and command; those in lower positions have the obligation to obey. Therefore to resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse assent is like the crime of idolatry, because the Apostle says that ‘every soul must be subject to higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God; and those that exist have been ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance, and whoever resists acquires condemnation for himself.’”

[Note: Romans 13:1–2. There, however, instead of the words “and those that exist have been ordained,” the following words concerning authorities are read: “Those that exist have been ordained by God.”]

“What good would it do me, then, to wear down my flesh outwardly here with you through fasts and abstinence, while through disobedience acquiring the condemnation of my soul? Therefore, brothers, do not grieve over my departure, lest you add sorrow to sorrow. Rather, persevere in the vocation to which you have been called. And when I have fulfilled the obedience imposed upon me, I shall return to you, if the Lord permits.”

### 46

Then they all began to cry out with tears and great lamentation, saying:

“Why do you abandon us, Father, or to whom do you leave us in our desolation? For after God you are our entire hope and our whole refuge. In adversity you are our protection; in prosperity, our consolation; in temptation, our counsel; in weakness, our support. What, then, shall we do when you depart, or to whom shall we turn in your absence? Surely we shall be like wandering sheep without a shepherd.

“If obedience draws you to the Roman pontiff, then supreme charity, which is in Christ Jesus and which neither death nor life nor any creature can prevent us from hoping for, will draw us with you.”

When Blessed Bruno heard this, he feared that, because of his own departure and that of his companions, the place mentioned above—which had already been dedicated to God—might again fall into lay and profane hands. Since he did not wish to abandon it altogether, but intended to return to it with his companions after completing the penance imposed upon him, he entrusted and gave it to the venerable lord Siguinus, abbot of the monastery of Casa-Dei. Siguinus had been one of the first donors mentioned above and possessed a certain cell near his own, close to Grenoble, beneath the castle of Curnilhion.

[Note: The charter by which the saint did this was later not found. See the preliminary commentary, no. 529.]

## CHAPTER III

The saint travels from the Carthusian desert to Rome; his disciples follow him, and he persuades them to return to the Carthusian desert. Having obtained permission from the pontiff to withdraw, and having refused the archbishopric of Reggio, he hides himself in the deserts of Calabria, where he enjoys the goodwill of Count Roger, founds new churches, and lives and dies most holily.

### 47

Then, having received the blessing of Blessed Hugh the bishop, he went to Rome.

[Note: This was in the year 1090, when March was already well advanced, as I have shown in the preliminary commentary, no. 523.]

For the apostolic command pressed upon him. The pontiff, greatly rejoicing at the arrival of one whom he loved so intimately, received him kindly and counted him among his foremost and principal personal and intimate counselors and faithful friends. He used him and relied upon his counsel in the Church’s weightier causes and difficult affairs.

Meanwhile all the other brothers who had previously been with him in the Carthusian desert came to him, through the working of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: This did not happen through a miracle. See the preliminary commentary, no. 527.]

They were exceedingly sorrowful—and he even more so—that they had left the aforesaid place of the Carthusian desert, which the Lord had chosen for himself and in which he had built a worthy dwelling for him.

[Note: This refers to the vision divinely granted to Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, shortly before Saint Bruno and his companions came to him. See §25 of the preliminary commentary.]

Whenever they recalled—not like those murmurers in the desert, meat, cucumbers, or melons, but—the devout meditations, prayers, readings, and spiritual consolations that they had previously enjoyed in that solitude of the Carthusian desert, and whenever they saw the turmoil, noise, and dangers of the court, they could not restrain their tears.

### 48

At last, through the persuasion and urging of Blessed Bruno, since he himself was still unable to obtain from the pontiff permission or leave to return, as though he were necessary to the pontiff in the matters then occupying him, they all unanimously agreed to return to the Carthusian desert. First, however, they obtained from the same supreme pontiff letters to the aforesaid abbot Siguinus for the restoration of that place.

[Note: I have reproduced those letters in full in the preliminary commentary, no. 528.]

When Blessed Bruno departed from there, he had sent Siguinus back, as has already been said. Under the leadership of Master Landuin, whom Blessed Father Bruno had appointed prior in his place over the other brothers, they all returned to the Carthusian desert.

[Note: This was when he was summoned from the Carthusian desert by Pope Urban II and went to Rome. See the preliminary commentary, nos. 516 and 529.]

Siguinus the abbot, at the request of the supreme pontiff and of Blessed Bruno, with the consent of his convent and in the presence of the aforesaid Blessed Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and another Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, freely restored the aforesaid place of the Carthusian desert to them and granted it to them and their successors for perpetual possession.

[Note: On this restoration of the Carthusian desert by Siguinus, abbot of Casa-Dei, and on the circumstances mentioned here, see the preliminary commentary, no. 528 and the following two numbers.]

From that time onward, the aforesaid Landuin, as prior, the other brothers, and their successors down to the present day have held and possessed that desert of the Carthusian order, with its boundaries and rights. They have persevered there under the common obedience of the general chapter of the Carthusian order, which is held there every year, according to the rule of life first given to them by Blessed Bruno, then by the other priors of the Carthusian desert, and by the said general chapter.

[Note: It was under Saint Anthelm, seventh in Morotius’s reckoning among the priors of the Great Carthusian monastery, that the Carthusians first began to consider summoning an annual chapter of the entire order. It was finally put into practice under Basil, Anthelm’s immediate successor, as Colombius demonstrates in his dissertation on the origins of the Carthusians, nos. 57 and following. Since this is so, not everything that this biographer records here accords with exact historical truth.]

### 49

Blessed Bruno, beloved by that same pontiff Urban, served usefully and faithfully in the governance of the Church. At that time the Church was in the greatest turmoil because of the persecution by the aforementioned Emperor Henry IV, who had in fact intruded into the papacy a certain Gilbert, whom he called Clement.

[Note: This occurred in the year 1080, as Berthold, priest of Constance, shows in his Appendix to Hermann the Lame under that year. Other writers who treat of the calamities suffered by the Church under Henry IV—called Henry III by some—especially during the pontificates of Gregory VII and Urban II, agree with him.]

Both Henry and the antipope Clement persecuted the true pontiff Urban. Seeking to avoid their fury, and placing no confidence in the Romans—and rightly so—Urban held a council at Melfi, then went to Piacenza and celebrated another council there.

[Note: As Ruinart clearly demonstrates in his Life of Pope Urban, Urban II held the council of Melfi in 1089 and another at Piacenza in 1095. Therefore the pontiff did not go to Piacenza immediately after the council of Melfi, as one might suppose from the manner of writing used by this biographer, but only six years later. Nor did Urban then do this in order to avoid Henry’s fury, contrary to what Puteanus further teaches here. At that time the supporters of the pope were prevailing almost everywhere against the antipope Guibert and his followers, as the aforementioned Berthold the priest relates under the year 1095. Indeed, in the middle of Lombardy, in the city of Piacenza, a general synod was announced against the schismatics—that is, the Guibertines—and was actually celebrated there around the middle of Lent in that same year, 1095.]

At that council, according to Gratian, he courageously restrained the insolence of certain ecclesiastics. He also issued many decrees against them, especially against incontinent and simoniacal clerics, and against monks who possessed property and were unstable.

[Note: On the matters decreed by Pope Urban II at the council of Piacenza, one may also consult the contemporary writer Berthold, priest of Constance, under the year 1095, as well as Labbe, *Councils*, vol. X, col. 500 and the following five columns.]

Then, no longer safe there and again fleeing the fury of the same emperor, Urban left Italy and crossed into Gaul.

[Note: The Council of Clermont, which was convened chiefly to decide upon and prepare the expedition to the Holy Land, and which is more widely known than anything else connected with that matter, was held in December 1095, as everyone agrees. It is therefore clear, both from this and from what is said below in note 120, that Pope Urban did not at that time go into Gaul to avoid Henry’s fury when he summoned the council, contrary to what is related here.]

There, once again considering the welfare of the faith, he caused another council to be convened at Clermont, a city of the Auvergne. At that council, according to the same Gratian, he enacted several other constitutions which seemed directed toward restoring the fallen condition of the Church. Among other things, he decreed that the Hours of Blessed Mary should be recited daily by clerics and that her Office should be solemnly celebrated on Saturdays.

[Note: On this matter see Ruinart, *Life of Pope Urban*, no. 226, and also the preliminary commentary, no. 607 and following.]

### 50

I have read in a certain history called the *Fasciculus temporum* that this was revealed by the Blessed Virgin to the brothers in the Carthusian desert—without doubt to Blessed Bruno and his companions, when they alone were still called Carthusians.

[Note: The author of the work known by the title *Fasciculus temporum*, in which this is indeed read under the year 1094, was Werner Rolevinck, a member of the Carthusian order. But since he did not flourish before the fifteenth century, he is too late to establish certain and unquestionable credibility for this event.]

At the same council he accomplished something worthy of remembrance. For he so stirred up the princes of Gaul and the rest of the multitude gathered at the council to undertake an expedition against the Turks for the recovery of the Holy Land that three hundred thousand men enrolled their names in the army of Christ and received the sign of the cross.

Among them was Godfrey of Bouillon, duke of Lorraine. Under his leadership they moved through German territory and Pannonia, went to Byzantium, and then, after crossing the Hellespont, captured Nicaea first, then Antioch and several other cities of the Saracens, and finally Jerusalem, the holy city, together with the entire surrounding region.

[Note: What Puteanus asserts here is entirely consonant with the truth. The dates of the individual events may also be seen in the histories written about the expeditions to the Holy Land by William of Tyre and other ancient historians of those expeditions, published together at Hanau in 1611 by the Wechelian press under the title *Gesta Dei per Francos*.]

When the Christians were about to crown the aforesaid Godfrey as king, he refused, saying that he did not wish to wear a golden crown in the city where Christ had worn a crown of thorns.

[Note: So William of Tyre, book IX, chapter 9.]

The aforesaid Godfrey and seven other Christian kings after him held the worthy kingdom of Jerusalem for eighty-eight years, having defeated the Babylonians and Egyptians with great slaughter of the unbelievers and a great increase of the Christian name.

[Note: Jerusalem was conquered by the Christians in the year 1099 and taken from them by Saladin in 1187, as the unanimous testimony of all writers who treat of the matter confirms.]

The same pontiff Urban gave the cause of all these events at the aforesaid council of Clermont.

### 51

Since Blessed Bruno had therefore remained with that same pontiff for a number of years, although not many, on account of the merit of obedience, and had benefited the holy Church of God by his counsels, both in its reform and in the recovery of the Holy Land—as the decrees subsequently issued by that same Urban and his other deeds mentioned above testify—and since he could no longer endure such great disturbances and the turmoil and noise of the court, continually longing for the quiet of the solitude and cell that he had left, before that same pontiff went from Piacenza to Gaul he humbly and repeatedly asked him, and at last obtained, permission and leave to leave the court and return to the desert he had abandoned, or to seek another that the Lord might deem worthy to show him.

[Note: Bruno asked for and obtained permission to return to solitude earlier than this, namely before Pope Urban II, after celebrating the council at Piacenza, went to Gaul. See the preliminary commentary, no. 536 and the following two numbers.]

When the same pontiff wished to confirm him in the archbishopric of the Church of Reggio—the first metropolitan church of all Calabria—to which he had been elected with the pontiff’s approval, Bruno refused to consent to the election made on his behalf. From what he had read in Holy Scripture and from what he had both seen and heard at the court, he knew what and how great the dangers of prelacy were.

[Note: The saint was elected to the archbishopric of Reggio no later than the year 1090, contrary to the biographer’s supposition. He refused it. See the preliminary commentary, no. 532 and the following two numbers.]

He did not refuse obstinately, but solely from love and desire for quiet, while always maintaining—as was proper—obedience and humility toward his superior and charity toward his neighbors.

### 52

For, as Blessed Gregory used to say, true humility is preserved before God’s eyes when a person does not obstinately refuse what he is commanded to undertake usefully. Thus even a suitable person may laudably refuse the office of prelacy out of humility, since the same Gregory says that prelacy should be avoided for the sake of a better intention, especially when the will of heaven is recognized as directing this.

With the pontiff’s consent, permission, and blessing, Blessed Bruno therefore left the court and entered the deserts of Calabria—not alone, but accompanied by several other men of the same purpose, whom the good fragrance of his life had drawn to seek solitude.

[Note: One of these was Lanvinus the Northman, distinct from Landuinus the Tuscan. It appears, however, that the saint did not first attract him and the others with whom he left the papal court for the deserts of Calabria to the purpose of solitary life when he was staying at Rome, but had already had them as companions from the time when he was still living in the Carthusian desert, as can readily be inferred from what is said in the preliminary commentary, no. 510.]

For he had heard that there were many deserted and solitary places there, most suitable for performing penance. Although he intended and desired, as he had already decided many times, to return to the Carthusian desert that he had left and to follow there the brothers whom he had sent ahead, nevertheless, because—as has been said—the pontiff and his court were traveling to Gaul, within whose boundaries the Carthusian desert lay, he chose Calabria rather than the Carthusian desert, lest he appear to be following the court from which he was fleeing, but rather to remove himself from it.

[Note: When the saint withdrew to Calabria, Pope Urban II did not go to Gaul; consequently, the reason given here for his not then returning to the Carthusian desert does not stand. See the preliminary commentary, no. 549 and the following two numbers.]

He nevertheless always retained the intention and desire that, once matters had been settled, he would return to the Carthusian desert as soon as he conveniently could, as appears in certain letters that he wrote from Calabria to his brothers who were in the Carthusian desert. Their words are these:

“Know this of me, brothers: after God, my one desire is to come to you and see you; and whenever I am able, I shall fulfill this in deed, with God’s help.”

[Note: Since these words conclude the entire letter given in §41, which the saint sent to the brothers of the Carthusian desert through Landuin when Landuin was returning to them, this must undoubtedly be the very letter of which our biographer speaks here.]

### 53

He therefore came with the aforesaid companions to a certain desert place on the borders of Calabria called Torre, in the diocese of Squillace.

[Note: On this desert place see the preliminary commentary, no. 552 and following.]

There, because they lacked the resources to build cells, he constructed several caves or grottoes suitable for hermits. They were made of humble material, but precious in Christ. In these, he and the brothers who had gathered with him devoted themselves, during the night watches as well as by day, to divine praises and prayers, in the austerity of life that he had previously maintained in the Carthusian desert and had led his companions to maintain.

It happened, through the Lord’s providence, that one day the prince of Calabria, Roger, was hunting wild animals in that desert of Torre with a considerable retinue and a large number of dogs.

[Note: Who this prince—or rather count of Calabria and Sicily—was is explained in the preliminary commentary, no. 556 and following.]

The dogs, following by scent the various tracks of the beasts, came upon the caves where Blessed Bruno and the brothers who had come with him were living. There they stopped, indicating to their master with much barking that they had found some great prey. The prince and his men came swiftly to the spot and found the aforesaid Fathers in those caves, kneeling, with their faces and hands raised toward heaven, praying and praising God.

[Note: It appears to be clearly demonstrated by what I have brought forward in the preliminary commentary, no. 541 and the following two numbers, that our saint—still unknown to Count Roger of Calabria and Sicily—was not found by him in the caves while he was out hunting.]

### 54

When the prince saw this, he was filled with great astonishment. He leapt down from the horse on which he was riding and greeted them devoutly and humbly. He carefully questioned them about their arrival there and the condition of each one. Once he had learned these things, he rejoiced greatly, praising and glorifying God for deeming him worthy of such a splendid prey. He hoped that both he and his land would be helped by their merits and prayers and preserved in peace.

Therefore, so that they might live there more quietly and persevere longer, he gave them the churches of Saint Mary and Saint Stephen of the Desert.

[Note: It appears not to accord with the truth that these two churches were given to Saint Bruno and his companions by Count Roger immediately after he found them praying in the cave while hunting. See the preliminary commentary, no. 570.]

He frequently visited them there and provided what was necessary for their life, gladly listening to teachings concerning salvation from them. He also frequently summoned Blessed Bruno, the shepherd and Father of them all, whom he loved more intimately than the others. He always held Bruno in great reverence, treating him as though he were first in his household. He followed his counsels and continually commended himself to his prayers, in which he placed the greatest confidence.

[Note: What is recorded here about Count Roger’s supreme reverence and love for Saint Bruno is entirely consonant with the truth, as is amply proved by what I have discussed in many places in the preliminary commentary.]

### 55

Nor was his expectation disappointed. For God, through Bruno’s merits, delivered him from a treachery prepared against him during the siege of the city of Capua.

[Note: On the occasion of this siege and the danger to which Count Roger was exposed by the treachery prepared against him during it, see the preliminary commentary, nos. 635 and following.]

The prince himself testifies to this in his letters patent in the following words:

[Note: I have included these letters, or diploma, in the preliminary commentary, no. 637 and the following six numbers. The evidence set out in the same §40 shows that it was issued not in 1098, when the siege of Capua occurred, but in 1099.]

“I, Roger, by the mercy of God count of Calabria and Sicily, wish it to be known to all faithful Christians what benefits God granted to me, a sinner, through the prayers of my reverend brother Bruno, the most devout Father of the brothers who dwell in the churches of Saint Mary of the Desert and Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. These churches are situated in my land between the town called Stilo and Arena.

“When I was at the siege of Capua on the Kalends of March, I appointed Sergius, a Greek by nationality, prince over two hundred armed men of his nation and commander of the army’s watches. Having been anticipated by Satanic persuasion, after the prince of Capua had first promised him a considerable amount of gold, he promised that he would provide access for attacking me and my army by night.

[Note: Whether Sergius, the leader of the treachery, was among those captured or escaped by flight is not known to me. If he was truly among the captives, he must not have obtained Count Roger’s pardon but must have been put to death, since his name is not found among those captured as guilty of the Capuan treachery in the list given by Surianus, all of whom Roger gave into servitude to Saint Bruno and the desert of Torre.]

### 56

“On the night of the treachery, the prince of Capua and his army were ready for battle as promised. While I had given myself over to sleep, after some time had passed during the night, an old man of venerable appearance stood beside my bed, wearing torn clothing and unable to restrain his tears. When I said to him in the vision, ‘What is the reason for your weeping?’ he replied:

“‘I weep for the souls of the Christians, and for you together with them. Rise as quickly as possible, take up your arms, if God permits you to be delivered, and save the lives of your fighters.’

“This man appeared to me in every respect as though he were the venerable Father Bruno. I awoke in great terror, trembling at the warning. Immediately I took up my arms and shouted to the soldiers to mount their horses in armor, eager to discover whether the vision was true.

“At the sound of the commotion and shouting, the impious Sergius and his followers fled, following the prince of Capua in the hope of finding refuge in that city. Our soldiers captured one hundred and sixty-two men, both wounded and unwounded, thereby proving that the vision had been true.”

### 57

“By God’s will I returned to Squillace on the twenty-ninth of July, after first having secured the city of Capua, where I had been ill continuously for a fortnight. The aforementioned venerable Bruno came with four of his brothers, and they consoled me with their holy and devout conversations.

“I related the vision to that reverend man and humbly gave thanks to him, since, even while absent from me, he had cared for me in his prayers. He humbly declared that he himself was not the one whom I believed I had seen, but an angel of God who stands by princes in time of war.”

[Note: On the apparition related here by Count Roger, which was presented to him not by Saint Bruno but by an angel under Bruno’s appearance and clothing, see the preliminary commentary, no. 644.]

“I also humbly asked him to accept generous revenues from my estates in the land of Squillace, which I was giving him. But he refused, saying that he did not wish to receive them, because he had left his father’s house and mine for this very purpose: to serve our God entirely free from dependence on external possessions. He had been, as it were, first and great in my entire household.”

[Note: It does not follow from these words that the saint had spent any length of time at Count Roger’s court before withdrawing to the Carthusian desert. See the preliminary commentary, no. 571 and following.]

“At last I could scarcely persuade him to agree to accept my small gift without charge.”

58. For I gave to that Father Bruno and to his successors, to possess in perpetuity and without temporal service, the monastery of Saint James together with the castle, and numerous other properties and possessions, with very extensive liberties specifically declared in the said charter. [Col. 0520C] Accordingly, by virtue of the aforesaid donation, blessed Bruno first built there a church in honor of the blessed Virgin Mary, beside a certain cavern or underground grotto in which he alone lived. Finally, he likewise built another church, not far distant from the former, together with the monastery adjoining it, under the title of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr [Note: [Col. 0520D] As I have shown in § 38 of the Preliminary Commentary, the saint did indeed build, besides the church dedicated to the most holy Mother of God, which he had previously constructed in the Turritan hermitage, another church dedicated to Saint Stephen. But it is wholly contrary to the truth that either one or the other of these two churches, as this biographer indicates, was not begun until after Count Roger had made to Saint Bruno the donation expressed in the charter partly quoted above. Anyone who carefully considers what is said in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 624 and the two following numbers, will readily recognize this.], in which the other brothers lived and, under the care and governance of so great a Father, served Christ the Lord as soldiers [Col. 0521A] [Note: [Col. 0521C] It is thought that the saint placed in this monastery monks less suited to the eremitical life and appointed Lanvin as their prior, reserving the supreme prefecture to himself. See the Preliminary Commentary, nos. 623, 626, 645, and 716.]. With them he persevered until the day of his death in the observance which he had earlier begun and taught at Chartreuse, and he did not depart from it.

As he approached death, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, he summoned his brothers, reviewed one by one the several periods of his life from infancy, and, with the knowledge and judgment of his whole lifetime, declared what was worthy [Note: [Col. 0521D] For what this phrase most probably signifies, see the Preliminary Commentary, no. 726.], exhorting and admonishing them to charity, humility, and perseverance.

59. Afterwards he explained his faith concerning the Trinity in an extended and profound discourse and concluded as follows:

“I also believe the sacraments which the holy Church believes and venerates, and specifically that the bread and wine consecrated upon the altar, after consecration, [Col. 0521B] are the true body of our Lord Jesus Christ, true flesh and true blood, which we too receive for the remission of sins and in hope of eternal salvation” [Note: [Col. 0521D] I have included in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 727, the complete profession of faith uttered by Bruno when near death, although it did not end with these words.].

On the following Sunday, that holy soul was released from the flesh, on the day before the Nones of October, in the year of the Lord 1101. His brothers honorably buried his body there. At his tomb the following epitaph was placed:

> I deserved to become the first founder  
> Of Christ’s sheepfold in this wilderness, I who am covered by this tomb.  
> Bruno was my name; Germany, my motherland; and grateful  
> Rest in the wilderness transferred me to the Calabrians.  
> I was a teacher, a herald of Christ, a man known throughout the world;  
> That distinction came from above: grace, not merit.  
> The sixth day of October released the bonds of my flesh;  
> Reader of these words, seek rest for my spirit.

[Col. 0521C] [Note: [Col. 0521D] Here, as in several other places, the later Paris edition of 1524 differs somewhat from the Basel edition of this Life (see the Preliminary Commentary, no. 734). I have occasionally followed the former, though not here, when it offered better or more agreeable readings, since this work is not of such importance that its primitive text need everywhere be reproduced with scrupulous exactness.]

60. Many miracles followed this holy life and precious death of his, which the Lord deigned to perform through the intercessions and merits of his glorious confessor. Yet miracles do not make a saint, since the Apostle does not deny that mountains can be moved without charity. Therefore miracles of this kind, which may be shared even by the wicked, are not to be desired or sought. For the magicians of Pharaoh also performed many signs by their incantations. [Col. 0522A] Judas too, the son of perdition, performed miracles while he lived, and he received with the other apostles the power to cast out demons. Many others also performed signs, yet were not on that account holier; rather, they became worse and more deserving of condemnation.

When such persons say at the judgment, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?” the Lord will answer them: “Because I do not know you. Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0521D] The wording differs somewhat from Matthew 7:22 and following.].

This is why, when the disciples returned and said to the same Lord, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name,” he said to them: “Do not rejoice because the spirits are subject to you.” And as though they were asking, “In what, then, good Master, shall we rejoice?” he replied: “Rejoice in this, that your names are written in heaven” [Col. 0522B] [Note: [Col. 0521D] Luke 10:20.].

61. On the other hand, many are saints of whom no miracles, or only a few, are recorded, such as numerous martyrs whose holiness no one doubts. There are also many confessors who wrote much for the illumination of the faith and possess, in the eminence of their teaching, the proof of their holiness—Augustine, Gregory, and others like them.

Thus, when they were inquiring about miracles during the canonization of Saint Thomas Aquinas, the pope replied that there was no need to inquire into them. For he had performed as many miracles as he had settled questions [Note: [Col. 0521D] Pope John XXII enrolled Saint Thomas Aquinas among the saints in 1323, as may be seen in our treatment of that holy Doctor of the Church on 7 March. But he did not say that there was no need to inquire into the miracles performed by Saint Thomas; on the contrary, he ordered that they be investigated with the greatest care. This is clear both from the bull of the saint’s canonization, inserted by Laertius Cherubinus in volume I of the Bullarium, and from the investigative proceedings concerning the life, conduct, and miracles of the late Brother Thomas Aquinas, included under 7 March in the first volume for this month of our work, pp. 686 and following. Moreover, although, as Guilielmus de Thoco, a contemporary author, records in the Life of Saint Thomas Aquinas written by him and inserted in the same March volume, no. 81, Pope John, inspired by the divine Spirit, said to the Dominicans’ representatives who had come to request that he order an apostolic investigation of Saint Thomas’s miracles that he believed Saint Thomas’s teaching could not have existed without a miracle, and then made several other statements greatly commending it before the cardinals in consistory, I nowhere find that he asserted of Saint Thomas what Puteanus writes here. Nor do I consider it sufficiently probable that that pontiff said that this saint had performed as many miracles as he had settled questions.].

There were therefore many who lived in the wilderness, withdrawn from human society in an austere way of life, persevering in continual struggle against temptations [Col. 0522C] and vices, denying themselves, abandoning father, mother, and everything they had possessed, carrying their cross and following Christ, such as Paul the first hermit, in whose regard Antony said that he alone bore the name of monk. Likewise Arsenius, Hilarion, Macarius, Eulalius, and many others. Such also was this father of ours, blessed Bruno, who seems to have done no less than the others. For all of them the Lord’s word, spoken in the person of Wisdom, is sufficient as a testimony to holiness:

> “Those who make me shine forth will possess eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0523D] Ecclesiasticus 24:31.].

62. And again, speaking of the same Wisdom:

> “I loved her above health and beauty”;  
> “I resolved to have her for my light. I learned her without deceit, and I share her without envy, and I do not conceal her honor. For her treasure is infinite; those who have used it have become participants in the friendship of God, commended by the gifts of discipline” [Note: [Col. 0523D] Wisdom 7:10, 13–14.].

And in the Gospel, when Simon Peter had said to Christ, “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what, then, will there be for us?” he replied:

> “Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for the sake of my name will receive a hundredfold [Col. 0523B] and will possess eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0523D] Matthew 19:29.].

And again to his disciples:

> “Amen, I say to you, you who have followed me: in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0523D] Ibid., 27 and following.].

And to the young man who asked about eternal life he said:

> “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess and give it to the poor, and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0523D] Nearly the same wording occurs in the same chapter, verse 21.].

63. With these testimonies alone to the holiness of our father Bruno, our most holy pope, the lord Leo X, at this time Supreme Pontiff [Note: [Col. 0523D] Puteanus wrote this Life of our saint around 1515; Leo X occupied the chair of Saint Peter from 1513 until 1521.], content without any investigation of miracles, judged it worthy and consonant with reason [Col. 0523C] that he whom God had distinguished in this age by such great gifts and graces, now taken up into heaven, should be extolled with the highest praises, so that he, to whom the Almighty while he lived had given a heart for the commandment and law of life and discipline, might now, while resting before the throne of divine glory, be rendered on earth the tribute of due devotion.

For this reason that pontiff wished, and by apostolic authority granted to us and to our order, that in every house of our entire order and in their churches or chapels the feast of our same father Bruno the confessor should be solemnly observed each year on the sixth day of October and celebrated with fitting and due devotion. On that day his blessed soul, released from the bonds of the flesh, migrated to the heavenly realms [Note: [Col. 0523D] Since Pope Leo X enrolled our saint among the saints neither by formal nor by equivalent canonization—both of which impose an obligation of worship—but only, as I proved in the final section of the Preliminary Commentary, by equivalent beatification, granted through permission for worship alone, expressed in the letter of the Cardinal of Pavia given in § 46 of the Preliminary Commentary, our biographer does not write here with exact conformity to the truth if, by the past-tense verb, he means what the pontiff likewise imposed by a past-tense verb.]. He further granted that the saint’s body and memory be venerated with fitting praises in the Lord, that a suitable Office be performed and sung in his honor, and that we be able to commemorate him each day.

The same pontiff also restored to our order the aforesaid house of Saint Stephen—which, as has often already been said, our father blessed Bruno had founded in the regions of Calabria after first establishing the Charterhouse, and where his body is said to lie buried—after it had been occupied for many years by monks of another order [Note: [Col. 0524D] At present the sacred body of the saint is honorably preserved in the Turritan church of Saint Stephen; yet it was more probably buried in the church of Saint Mary. See the Preliminary Commentary, no. 731 and the two following numbers.]. He entrusted it to be governed and administered under the care of our order, according to its rule, customs, and regular institutions, as is contained in the apostolic letters drawn up concerning the matter [Note: [Col. 0524D] I have given in full, in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 754 and the three following numbers, the bull or apostolic letters by which that pontiff accomplished this.].

64. Let us all rejoice, then, my dearest brothers; let us all rejoice in the Lord as we celebrate the feast [Col. 0524B] in honor of our blessed Father Bruno, at whose solemnity the angels rejoice and praise the Son of God.

For this is the day which the Lord has made—the day, I say, which the angels continually celebrate in heaven, while we on earth commemorate it annually with devotion, to the praise of God and the memory of so great a Father. Let us therefore exult and rejoice in it, and humbly offer to almighty God such praises and thanks as we can, because in his mercy he went before the leader and prince of our warfare with such great and remarkable gifts and graces on the way, and afterward rewarded him with such endowments and such glory in his homeland. Let us proclaim the merits of this saint with worthy praises.

For we have a commandment concerning the honoring of parents—not only of those related to us by flesh, [Col. 0524C] but even more of those who begot us spiritually in Christ. Hence it is written that “the glory of a man comes from the honor of his father, and a father without honor is the disgrace of his son”; and that “he who honors his father will live a longer life, will rejoice in his children, and on the day of his prayer will be heard, and a blessing from God will come upon him, and his blessing remains at the last” [Note: [Col. 0524D] Ecclesiasticus 3:6, 7, 13, with somewhat different wording.].

65. Let us moreover offer praises and thanks to God, who, just as four hundred and thirty years after the promise made to Abraham he freed the children of Israel from the slavery of the Egyptians by the hand of Moses, so now, after the same number of years—namely, four hundred and thirty—has deigned to redeem this Father of ours, and the aforesaid house of Saint Stephen, founded through him, by the hands of the supreme lawgiver, the Roman pontiff, Christ’s vicar on earth, from the hands of strangers, and to restore it to the possession and obedience of our order. For four hundred and thirty years are reckoned from the beginning of that order, as if by a certain divine omen, until the year 1514 [Note: [Col. 0525B] Namely, the year 1084, when the saint and his companions first entered the hermitage of Chartreuse; the Carthusian order is considered to have begun at that time.], in which year the same pontiff freed this Father of ours and the aforesaid house, where, as has often been said, he lies buried, from the servitude mentioned above.

We worthily venerate and honor the Lord in his saints, and the saints in the Lord, when we imitate and follow the virtues and conduct of the saints—just as the one who perfectly loves God is the one who keeps his commandments.

66. Therefore, venerable fathers and brothers, dearly beloved in Christ, if we are true sons and not degenerate ones, let us follow and, insofar as we can with the Lord’s help, imitate the conduct and footsteps of this father of ours, blessed Bruno. For it is fitting that sons should resemble their father, since the Lord, speaking of himself, says that the Son can do nothing of his own accord except what he sees the Father doing, and that whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does [Note: [Col. 0525B] John 5:19.].

Therefore, just as he acted, so let us also act. For we are Carthusians, and, as we have already heard, we received our name from Chartreuse. According to the etymology of its name, Chartreuse is said by Jerome, in his interpretation of Hebrew names, to derive from *chartus*, which means “perfectly called” or “perfect calling,” and from *ia*, which means “lord” or “ruler,” as though it signified “a perfect calling from the Lord.” Hence a Carthusian is so called as one “perfectly called by the Lord,” or “called by the Lord to perfection” [Note: [Col. 0525B] Puteanus adds and publishes here a number of things under the name of the Life of Saint Bruno, just as he did those already given. Since, however, they contain nothing at all that was done by the saint, but together with what I have just given in the three final sections merely constitute an exhortation addressed to the Carthusians, I have rightly refrained from recounting them as part of the Life of our saint. Meanwhile, I wish to present here to the reader what Theophilus Raynaudus observes concerning the etymology of Chartreuse supplied here by our biographer, in *Stylita mystico*, point 4, no. 9. He writes there as follows:

“Whatever may be the case concerning the original derivation of the word—namely, Chartreuse—who could deny that the man who affirmed that the name Chartreuse seems to derive from *caro tusa et macerata*, ‘flesh beaten and emaciated,’ spoke in accordance with the truth? I would not dare assert that this was the original derivation of the word, since I know that the place already had that name before Saint Bruno and his companions arrived there, as is clear from chapters 9 and 10 of the *Acts of Saint Bruno* edited by Surius. Unless, after the saints’ habitation there and the bodily mortifications and bruisings they underwent there, the name then bestowed happened to be projected backward to the time before the saints inhabited it, whenever the earlier period was being discussed. For Scripture itself often derives the names of places from later events, as Saint Chrysostom explains at length. Although, therefore, the etymology of the name Chartreuse from ‘flesh beaten and emaciated’ may seem uncertain, the meaning underlying that etymology is plainly true. It fits much better than the other explanation, for which Peter Sutor argues—after Puteanus, that is—deriving the word Chartreuse from two Hebrew words, one of which, *CARTUS*, according to Saint Jerome, means ‘perfect calling,’ while the other, *IA*, designates God, so that the meaning is that Chartreuse is God’s perfect calling. Add this to what was said in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 28.”]

[Col. 0525]

# THIRD LIFE

Collected by Surius from the Lives written by Puteanus and Blomenvenna.

## CHAPTER ONE

The deceased publicly proclaims from his bier that he has been condemned; on the occasion of this spectacle the saint resolves to withdraw into solitude to do penance, and, with several others whom he moved to do the same, sets out to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and is kindly received by him.

[Col. 0525D]

1. Most blessed Bruno, the first author and architect of the sacred Carthusian institute, a German by nationality, had parents of distinguished lineage and virtue in the celebrated city of Cologne Agrippina [Note: [Col. 0525] Concerning the homeland, parents, and noble birth of Saint Bruno, see § 2 of the Preliminary Commentary, as well as the notes to the funeral title, no. 97.]. Yet he brought greater splendor to them, and indeed to his entire family, by the holiness of his life.

From his very cradle, with God’s grace directing him, he always strove to advance toward better things. Even while still a boy he displayed nothing childish, but surpassed his age in the gravity of his conduct and, as it were, presented a kind of preview of his future religious vocation. By divine preparation he was being fashioned into the father and founder of many monks.
