The Lord granted him, to use the words of Scripture, a good soul: an outstanding disposition, a distinguished intellect, a tenacious memory, and a will eagerly inclined to pursue every excellent thing.

2. Accordingly, he was sent to Paris so that there he might be educated in letters and the liberal disciplines. There he progressed so far beyond his contemporaries that he was counted among the leading philosophers [Note: [Col. 0527D] Saint Bruno completed at Reims the studies of refined literature that he had begun at Cologne Agrippina, and afterwards received the teachings of philosophy at Tours under Berengarius. It is not known that he pursued any other higher disciplines at Paris. See §§ 3 and 4 of the Preliminary Commentary.], and he became master of the schools [Note: [Col. 0527D] It is in fact highly probable that Bruno never taught at Paris, as is clear from what I discussed in § 8 of the Preliminary Commentary.].

He also devoted himself to the study of sacred theology and was regarded as highly learned and renowned among theologians. His surviving writings can offer particularly distinguished testimony to this [Note: [Col. 0527D] Among these, the chief place is occupied by two commentaries, one on the Psalms and the other on all the Epistles of Saint Paul the Apostle. I explained what should be thought of them in § 42 of the Preliminary Commentary.]. He was also a canon of the Church of Reims [Note: [Col. 0527D] What I cited in no. 84 of the Preliminary Commentary proves this to be extremely probable.].

While Bruno was engaged in these excellent studies, Gregory VII was the most holy Roman pontiff [Note: [Col. 0528D] See the remarks on note 35 of chapter 1 of the preceding Life.], and Henry III was emperor [Note: [Col. 0528D] The prince who is called Henry IV both in the preceding Life and in the other Life composed by Blomenvenna is here called Henry III by Surius merely on the basis of the example of several other writers. Surius did not consider Henry I, surnamed the Fowler, who ruled Germany from 919 to 936 but was never crowned emperor, to belong among the emperors.]. Around the year of salvation 1082, studies of letters were flourishing at Paris. There was both a large crowd of students and no small number of distinguished teachers.

A truly horrible spectacle occurred there, one destined to be remembered throughout the ages, and it provided the occasion for establishing the Carthusian way of life. Divine providence brought this about, desiring to provide for the salvation of many.

3. A certain highly celebrated doctor, endowed above all others with extensive learning and exceptional moral integrity—as far as people who look only at outward things can infer and judge, since they cannot see the secrets of the heart—who was honored above others on account of that very learning and probity, fell into a serious illness. Lying in bed as the illness worsened, he ended his final day, though first, in Christian fashion and as a Catholic man, fortified with the sacraments of the Church.

Since, according to the custom received among Christians, a solemn funeral was being prepared for him to honor his burial, a great multitude of masters, students, and citizens gathered. As they accompanied the funeral procession, the lifeless body of the deceased was carried into the church where it was to be buried.

When the clerics who had been invited for the purpose were performing the customary office and reciting the prayers called the vigil for the dead, they came to the lesson that begins, “Answer me.” At that moment the man who had died raised himself in the very bier. Lifting his head slightly, and with everyone seeing and hearing him, while all were understandably astonished at so unprecedented an event, he said in a loud and dreadful voice:

> “I have been accused by the just judgment of God.”

Having said this, he lowered his head again onto the bier.

[Col. 0527D]

4. Those who heard his words and saw his gestures [Col. 0528A], greatly terrified, prudently and deliberately decided to postpone his burial until the following day, so that they might await the outcome of such an extraordinary event.

At daybreak, when the report of what had happened had spread throughout the city and filled everyone’s ears, an almost countless crowd of people of both sexes flocked to the church. When the funeral rites were repeated and the beginning of the aforementioned lesson had been recited, the same deceased man again raised his head and cried out in a tremendous voice:

> “I have been judged by the just judgment of God.”

Then he immediately laid himself back in the bier.

All those present were seized by the greatest and most incredible astonishment, and the dreadful spectacle overwhelmed everyone with stupor. Yet because what he had said so far—that he had been accused and judged by the just judgment of God—did not yet clearly signify his condemnation, since it could also be understood in a favorable sense, everyone decided to postpone his burial until the third day.

For it was possible that he had first been unjustly accused before Christ’s tribunal by the one who hastens to destroy all things, who is rightly called the devil, that is, “the accuser,” because of his practice of slander; and that afterward he had been vindicated from the devil’s accusations by the sentence of the most just Judge.

5. When that day dawned, nearly the whole city hurried there, eager to learn the meaning of such an unprecedented and terrible judgment of God. The rites of the funeral were again performed in the same manner, and when they reached the lesson of which we have spoken,

> Then once more the lifeless man lifted his head from the bier,  
> And, contemplating his unhappy state, spoke,  
> Saying in immeasurable grief and with a mighty roar:  
>   
> “Spare the funeral rites; you can do nothing to help me.  
> Alas, why did my parents give birth to me?  
> Ah, wretched man! I go condemned to eternal fires.”  
>   
> Thereafter he fell silent forever and lay on his back [Note: [Col. 0528D] These verses are taken from the metrical Life of the saint written by Zacharias Benedictus, concerning which see the Preliminary Commentary, no. 19; only slight changes have been made in the third and fifth verses.].

At that voice, who could have a heart so hard as not to lose all composure? The Prophet rightly said: “The judgments of God are a great abyss.” That man was known to the entire people, and although no one suspected anything unfavorable about him, he declared himself condemned by the just judgment of God.

That dreadful voice—“I have been condemned by the just judgment of God”—seemed to penetrate to the very marrow of the bones, and all those present appeared almost lifeless [Col. 0528D].

6. They were not being shown an ordinary example, nor was the event a game or a matter of little importance. He declared himself condemned who had appeared to have lived among men in such a way that everyone considered him holy.

They said to one another: “If this has happened to so great and distinguished a man, what should we wretched people expect?”

At length, since he had openly confessed that he had been condemned and rejected by the just judgment of God, everyone agreed that he should be considered unworthy of the support of the whole Church and even of ecclesiastical burial, and that he should be buried in a profane place, in a dung heap. This was done [Note: [Col. 0529D] See what is said in the notes appended to chapter 1 of the preceding saint’s Life, note 37.].

There are some who affirm that, because of the perpetual remembrance of this terrifying judgment, the two words “Answer me” have since that time been omitted from the lesson so often mentioned [Col. 0529B] [Note: [Col. 0529D] See what is noted in note 38 to chapter 1 of the preceding saint’s Life.].

That unheard-of miracle certainly became for many an effective stimulus to correct their lives and minds.

7. The venerable Bruno himself was present and had absorbed everything said and done with his own eyes and ears. Overwhelmed with excessive fear and astonishment at the example, he dissolved entirely into tears and wept bitterly, considering within himself the severity of divine judgment, the uncertain outcome of this life, and how dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the living God.

Terrified and salutarily moved to compunction, he summoned to himself some of his closest companions and disciples: Master Landuin, who afterward became the first prefect, or prior, of Chartreuse; the two Stephens, the Burgundian and the Diensis, both canons of Saint Rufus; Hugh, whom they called the Chaplain, because he alone among them had been ordained a priest [Note: [Col. 0529D] Concerning Hugh the Chaplain, who alone among those whom the saint summoned to himself is here said to have been ordained a priest, and likewise concerning Landuin and the others listed here, see § 25 of the Preliminary Commentary, from no. 434 to the end.]; and two laymen, Andrew and Guarinus, who had also witnessed this spectacle.

Weeping, he said to them:

“Behold, my brothers and friends, uniquely dear to me in Christ, during these past days we have seen and heard things truly astonishing and terrifying. Yet they can bring us great benefit if, as is right, not the danger or uncertain fate, but the most certain condemnation, of this deceased man—utterly unhappy in every respect—makes us cautious and anxious to appease the Lord, whose hand no one can escape.”

[Col. 0529D]

8. And who, I ask, could have a heart so stony that such an example would not merely invite but compel him to do penance? Or who could be so weighed down by the deadly sleep of vices that he would not be roused and awakened by the ill-omened cries—even the thunderous cries—of this desperate man, to care for his salvation?

We knew that this man was endowed with great wisdom, adorned with good morals, chaste, modest, prudent, honored by everyone, and held in high esteem. Yet [Col. 0530A] from his own mouth we have now heard that he was condemned by the just judgment of God.

What could be said or imagined more terrible than that voice? Who would not tremble utterly upon hearing it? For what is it to be condemned except to have fallen into evils that no mind can grasp and no tongue explain?

If these evils ever came to an end, they might at least seem somehow tolerable. But since they are exceedingly bitter and never receive an end, even after countless myriads of years, those who fall into them cannot fail to be the most wretched and unhappy of all.

9. Let us now consider, my brothers, what his knowledge, acquired through so much labor, will profit him in hell, since there he suffers eternal blindness and ignorance [Col. 0530B]. What will wealth and abundance profit him, since not even a single drop of water is available to him with which he might cool his tongue, scorched by the fires of burning Gehenna? What will honors and pleasures profit him, since now he is compelled to endure throughout all eternity as many torments as he had pleasures in the world?

We saw his body buried with the greatest disgrace in a dung heap. Let us consider his soul, forever burning in sulfurous flames and buried in hell, where their worm will not die and the fire will not be extinguished; where intolerable fire rages, loathsome stench torments, and ineffable pain lays waste.

Let us consider these things, my brothers—not superficially but seriously—and, by embracing the remedy that brings salvation to our souls, let us take thought for ourselves, lest we also perish with him.

The one remedy that remains is true repentance, since the Savior himself says:

> “Unless you do penance, you will all likewise perish” [Note: [Col. 0530D] Nearly the wording of Luke 13:3.].

Scripture is full of exhortations to repentance. Let us therefore embrace it, dearest brothers, if we wish to escape the just judgment of God. Let our tears be our bread by day and by night, and with them let us wash away the filth of our sins.

10. Those voices that we heard were not uttered on his account, for he was already dead, but on ours, so that they might benefit us, whom divine patience still awaits with forbearance.

Let us not postpone the correction of our lives from day to day, since we do not know at what hour our Lord will come. For, as the most blessed pontiff Gregory says, the Lord promised forgiveness to the penitent, but he did not promise the sinner a tomorrow.

All those men were moved to compunction in their hearts by these words, and they ardently desired to give themselves to penance; but they did not yet see the manner or place.

Therefore, when Landuin, a learned and devout man, asked him about these matters, Saint Bruno replied:

“Let the spectacle we have seen—the spectacle that has afflicted us with salutary grief, troubled and terrified us, and brought us to repentance through fear of eternal punishment—produce this effect in us: that we despise this world with our whole heart and, insofar as possible, flee from it.

Let Saint David’s former words come to our aid—how, saddened in his exercise and troubled by the voice of the enemy and by the tribulation of the sinner, his heart was disturbed within him; how the fear of death fell upon him, and fear and trembling came upon him, and darkness covered him. All these things, as you know, we too have experienced,”

### 11.

“Who will give me wings like a dove,” he says, “and I shall fly away and rest? Behold, I have gone far off in flight and remained in solitude [Note: Psalm 54:5–8].” He admonishes us to flee the crowds of men and occasions of sin, and to dwell in solitude, which is a fitting place for carrying out penance, a teacher of virtues, and a revealer of glory. It is therefore right that we seek it with the greatest diligence, remain in it most carefully, and never set foot outside it until the final day of our life.

We have examples in the Savior himself, whom we know often to have sought deserted places, so that he might summon us to similar things. John the Baptist—than whom no one greater has arisen among those born of women—was in the deserts until the day of his manifestation. It would take too long to mention all the other holiest men who withdrew into the deepest solitudes, unwilling to have any dealings with this most deceptive world.

Meanwhile their spirits were inflamed, and they burned with desire for the solitary life. But since they were uncertain which place they should chiefly seek, Saint Bruno said that some good and faithful man ought to be sought who could point out a suitable place for them. Then the two Stephens, of Bourg and Die, said that not far from Valence, to which our monastery of Saint-Ruf is adjacent [Note: In assigning the location of this monastery, Surius is mistaken, together with Puteanus and Blomenvenna, whom he followed. See the Preliminary Commentary, no. 436], there was the city of Grenoble, and in it Blessed Hugh the bishop, whom they had often seen and knew well [Note: See what the annotations on this holy bishop of Grenoble provide in the note to the older Life of the saint, note 7].

### 12.

That man was most holy, just and upright, fearing God and thoroughly practiced in every kind of virtue. In his diocese were very high mountains, with many deserted places in them, separated from all human company and habitation and, for that reason, especially suitable for the practice of penance. Since the holy bishop invited everyone to penance by his words and example, when they came to him their arrival would be most welcome to him, and he would grant them the fulfillment of their desire. For he was exceedingly humane, kind, and merciful.

“You shall have us as guides for this journey,” they said, “for we have often traveled it.” Soon Hugh the priest also said:

“I too have heard much about this man, whose reputation is already spreading everywhere; and I have ascertained beyond doubt that he is a holy man, deeply devoted to the salvation of souls. There is no doubt that he will receive us most willingly and help us in every way. Although I am already advanced in age and in poor health, and this road is steep and difficult, nevertheless, since the way that leads to life is narrow and no age is too late for penance, if you decide to go there I shall offer myself as your companion. Nothing will separate us except death, for we shall be joined and united forever by the love of Christ.”

Andrew and Guarinus, laymen and uneducated, also displayed the same eagerness and readiness, and briefly asked to be taught how they might offer God fruits worthy of penance.

### 13.

When Blessed Bruno had done this, and had also recalled certain things about the frailty and instability of this life, the vanity and deceptiveness of the world, the uncertainty of our departure from this life, and the recent condemnation of their teacher, sweet streams of tears flowed from everyone’s eyes. Then all of them together entered into a new oath of allegiance to the service of Christ the eternal King. They begged almighty God to confirm them in their holy purpose and send them his good angel to be their guide on the journey and lead them to a place pleasing to his majesty.

Afterward, when they had made arrangements concerning their possessions and affairs and had properly settled everything, they said farewell to their friends and acquaintances. With the holy Spirit leading them, and with the angel of the Lord going before them, guiding and protecting them, they traveled by a long, tiresome, and arduous road to Blessed Hugh, bishop of Grenoble [Note: Whether the Saint, even after being driven into the wilderness by the portent of the dead man who cried out from his bier that he had been condemned, proceeded directly with his companions to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, as this biographer seems to indicate, is discussed in the Preliminary Commentary, beginning at no. 414].

On the journey itself they turned aside to visit a hermit of great holiness, so that from him, as one experienced in the matter, they might learn about the solitary life [Note: Concerning this hermit, whom the saint and his companions consulted on their journey, and whom Surius found mentioned by Blomenvenna from Henry Kalbar but not also by Puteanus, see the Preliminary Commentary, no. 414]. Made more eager by his words and pious exhortations, and inflamed with an even greater love for that life, they continued on to Grenoble.

### 14.

At about the same time, Saint Hugh the bishop saw in a dream God building for his majesty a house in the wilderness called Chartreuse, and also seven stars of gleaming color, arranged in a circle and raised slightly above the ground. They differed from the heavenly stars in position, motion, color, and brilliance, and provided him with guidance on his journey [Note: Concerning this vision granted to Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and the additions with which Surius and the two earlier biographers of our saint—Puteanus and Blomenvenna—embellish it, see the Preliminary Commentary, no. 423 and several following numbers].

While he was reflecting on this vision, seven men—Blessed Bruno with six companions—appeared at the doors of the palace. The venerable Guigo mentions this in the Life he wrote of the same blessed man:

“Master Bruno was present,” he says, “a man famous for religion and learning, a kind of embodiment of integrity, gravity, and complete maturity. He had with him the companions mentioned above. They were seeking a place suitable for the eremitical life, but had not yet found one.”

Thus Guigo [Note: Namely, chapter 11 of the Life of Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, cited by Surius immediately below and published by us in volume I of April, which he composed at the command of Pope Innocent II. See also what I noted in note 9 to the older Life of Saint Bruno].

When the bishop was informed that seven men were standing outside who wished to speak with him, he immediately ordered them to be brought in. After they had entered and humbly prostrated themselves at his feet, he bestowed upon them the blessing they desired. When they had been raised up by him and had sat down together, he carefully inquired the reason for their arrival. Saint Bruno explained what they had seen and heard at Paris and how they had holy agreement among themselves to embrace the solitary life; then he asked the bishop for a place suitable for penance.

### 15.

At first the bishop was astonished at the novelty of the matter. But when he carefully considered their conversion, their steadfastness of spirit, and the great usefulness of their arduous purpose—which would one day benefit many and corresponded to his vision—he embraced them with immense joy. He received them not merely willingly but reverently, and treated them with the greatest affection and kindness.

Instructed by the divine Spirit, he understood the vision at once and recounted it to them in full. He said that the place they sought had already been divinely shown to him. He had no doubt that the seven men who despised earthly things, sought deserted places, and, through their desire, zeal, and love for heavenly things, shone like stars, were signified by the stars he had seen [Note: Although most of the circumstances of Bruno’s and his companions’ meeting with Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, which Surius reports here from Blomenvenna and Puteanus, appear by no means unlike the truth, they cannot nevertheless be confirmed by any testimony of antiquity. This applies specifically to Bruno’s account of the condemnation of the teacher. See the Preliminary Commentary, no. 430].

Therefore, wishing to encourage them to perseverance—for perseverance alone obtains the fullest crowns of eternal salvation—he quoted the following passage from the Apostle Paul:

“Saints, of whom the world was not worthy, needy, distressed, afflicted, wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, in deserts, on mountains, in caves, and in the caverns of the earth [Note: Hebrews 11:38].”

“To follow their examples,” he said, “and to walk in their footsteps is praiseworthy and very salutary, but certainly difficult, especially in these cold regions, which are not like Egypt and Palestine [Note: In the deserts of Egypt and Palestine, lands enjoying a warmer climate than that around Grenoble, a great multitude of anchorites formerly lived, as may be seen in Rosweyde’s Lives of the Fathers].”

### 16.

“But to you a place has been assigned by God: a certain wilderness in the highest mountains, called Chartreuse. It is spacious, certainly, but completely uncultivated and inhabited by no one, accessible only to wild beasts, and, because of the harshness of the place, almost unknown and inaccessible to human beings and other domestic animals.

“It has high, almost sheer cliffs and crags on every side, as well as wild and fruitless trees. It is exceedingly cold and covered with snow for much of the year. It is also so precipitous, barren, and unproductive that nothing can be sown or harvested there. Access and approach to it are difficult and dangerous because of two lofty cliffs which rise directly upward and seem almost to join at the summit, so that they inspire both horror and terror in those entering.

“In its midst is a little stream which, gathered from those mountains, runs down with a great roar like torrents or overflowing waters.”

### 17.

“To sum up much in a few words, the harshness of that wilderness and its horror are so great that it deserves the name of a prison rather than of a human habitation. It hardly seems possible that anyone could live there, or at least endure there for long, without the singular favor of almighty God [Note: I presented the lengthy description of the wilderness of Chartreuse from Innocent Masson for the reader in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 447 and the following two numbers].

“You yourselves know, my brothers, how shameful and disgraceful it is, after putting one’s hand to the plow, to look back. You know that Lot’s wife, when she looked back, remained standing there and was changed into a pillar of salt, so that she might season the prudent by her example.”

When that most blessed bishop had said these and many other things, Saint Bruno replied:

“Indeed, most reverend father, this is a terrible place, and its wildness could frighten us away if we had come here with any other purpose than to receive such a place, being willing to endure everything for the love of Christ. Although we are fragile and truly weak, nevertheless, relying on divine mercy—which is our support, not our own strength—we are fully persuaded that the one who granted us the intention and ready will to come here will also give us the ability to persevere.”

### 18.

“For this reason we humbly and earnestly beg you not to postpone the fulfillment of our desire, nor allow us to suffer rejection in this request of ours.”

When the blessed bishop saw their steadfastness and their unshaken resolve to persevere, he said to them:

“Indeed, dearest ones, I both approve this holy desire of yours exceedingly and greatly long to fulfill it. Even now I shall lead you to the place you desire and which has been shown by God.”

He gave them the wilderness of Chartreuse and whatever rights and claims he possessed in it. He also promised that he would obtain the same from others who claimed any rights in it [Note: See the Preliminary Commentary, no. 503 and the following two numbers]. He further promised to build a house on the bridge between the two cliffs mentioned above, so that women and even men carrying weapons could be barred from entering. Finally, he promised to prohibit all hunting and fishing there [Note: See the annotations to note 94 on the second chapter of the preceding Life].

After this, he embraced them and wept over each of them for joy, praising and blessing God for their arrival. He kept them with him and, in accordance with his humanity, cared for them for several days so that they might recover from the fatigue of the journey.

## CHAPTER II

Saint Bruno enters the wilderness of Chartreuse, where he lives most holily; Pope Urban II summons him from it; he persuades his disciples, who have followed him to Rome, to return to Chartreuse; he refuses the archbishopric of Reggio and afterward obtains from the pope permission to return to solitude.

### 19.

When those days had passed, they ascended the mountain and began to inhabit the wilderness of Chartreuse around the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist in the year of our salvation 1084 [Note: I have demonstrated conclusively in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 470 and the following three numbers, that Saint Bruno entered the wilderness of Chartreuse in the year assigned here, in the month of June, whose twenty-fourth day is dedicated to Saint John the Baptist]. Blessed Hugh, the bishop, preceded, accompanied, guided, and assisted them in everything, also supplying them with the necessities of life.

They then built, in the higher part of the mountain—now called “at Blessed Mary de Casalibus” [‘of the cottages’]—a church, together with small dwellings or cells near a spring that is still called Saint Bruno’s Spring [Note: A chapel dedicated to Saint Bruno now stands there—see the Preliminary Commentary, nos. 447, 448, and 477. Since neither Surius nor Blomenvenna and Puteanus ever mention it in the Lives of the Saint that they wrote, I infer that it was built after the time of Surius, or at least after the time of Blomenvenna and Puteanus]. The cells stood not far from the church, but were separated from one another so that no one would disturb another’s quiet and solitude.

Two brothers lived in each cell [Note: Not long after Saint Bruno’s death, the Carthusians no longer inhabited their cells two by two but singly. See the Preliminary Commentary, nos. 475 and 486]. Like those ancient Egyptian monks, they devoted themselves to silence, prayer, reading, purity of heart, and contemplation of divine things. At set hours they also engaged in manual labor, especially copying books, both to provide for their poverty and to give no opportunity to those who seek an opportunity to slander their holy institution by claiming that they performed no service for the Church of God but attended only to their own affairs [Note: I explained the manner of life which the Saint and his companions maintained at Chartreuse in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 485 and the following two numbers].

### 20.

Uninstructed people often consider those idle and of little use to the holy Church who, separated from human beings, devote themselves solely to God and themselves. Ignorant and inexperienced in spiritual matters, they do not know how much the prayers of holy men can accomplish with God, even when those men dwell in the most hidden solitudes. Such men can more easily preserve the purity and innocence of their lives outside human society than those who mix with crowds of people—unless holy obedience compels them to do so. Even a certain pagan was able to say that he had never been among people without returning less than his former self.

Nevertheless, our most holy Fathers, who laid the first foundations of the Carthusian life, without attributing anything of this kind to themselves, also wished to devote themselves to writing books. They urged their successors to do the same, so that at least with their hands they might preach the word of God when they could not do so with their mouths. Thus speak the statutes of the ancient Fathers [Note: Namely, the Customs written by Guigo, chapter 28, as I explained in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 487].

### 21.

Thus, occupying themselves with these and other pious exercises, they cast all their care upon the Lord, as the Psalmist admonishes [Note: Psalm 54:23]. They were not anxious about the morrow or concerned in thought with matters belonging to the following day, casting every thought upon the Lord. They were not unaware of the prophetic saying:

“But I am needy and poor, and the Lord is mindful of me; the earth is his and all its fullness. He gives food to the animals and to the young ravens that call upon him [Note: Psalm 39:18].”

There was such charity among them that each tried to anticipate the others by mutual services, and such humility that each eagerly desired to transfer to others the praise and glory of whatever he had done well. Thus, while each wished to hide beneath another’s shadow, the reflected splendor of their virtues illuminated everyone more brilliantly.

In all of them gravity and maturity of conduct were conspicuous. Yet amid so many adornments of virtue there was also a horror and contempt for every kind of vanity, which, like a moth eating clothes, consumes all virtues and merits. In them one could admire an angelic life. They lived in great patience, in vigils, in fasts, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in gentleness, in the Holy Spirit, in sincere love, in the word of truth, and in the power of God.

### 22.

At first, when they had arrived in that solitude, they built for themselves huts rather than cells. The most holy Bruno lived among them and laid the foundations of the Carthusian order; by his words and example he trained them splendidly. As the sun among the stars, so he seemed to excel among the others in holiness of life.

In his breast Christ, the eternal wisdom of the eternal Father, dwelt as in a lofty ark, and the Holy Spirit had established in him a dwelling most pleasing to itself. The future architect of a sublime and arduous institution had to excel through the singular privilege of heavenly grace.

It is clear, moreover, that even before his residence at Chartreuse he had been a man of rare integrity, uprightness, and gravity [Note: How entirely this accords with the truth is especially clear from what is said in section 4 and the following four sections of the Preliminary Commentary]. This is partly attested by what has been said above and will also be confirmed by what we are about to say. From this it can easily be inferred what kind of man he proved to be when, having despised the whole world, he wished to lead an eremitical life—that is, a life dead to the things of this world and yearning only for heavenly things.

### 23.

For the man who, while living among people and prospering in the favorable circumstances of this world, had been devoted to virtue, conducted himself much more splendidly and sublimely in that harsh solitude, so that he could rightly be seen not merely as a lover of virtue but as adorned with the exceptional brilliance of every virtue.

There is no doubt that examples of virtue flowed from his outstanding holiness into all the monasteries of the Carthusian institution. As a result, the Carthusian order still appears today—though we wish to say this with the consent of all—to retain its ancient rigor more than the others. This is not because it has relaxed nothing of that rigor, but because it has not departed from it so far as to be judged to have suffered a major collapse.

Certain abstinences, tolerable only to a few, have been somewhat relaxed; nevertheless, the perpetual eating of fish remains, along with many fasts, prolonged vigils, lengthy prayers, and many other practices truly burdensome to the flesh.

Furthermore, although the most blessed Hugh the bishop—whose reputation for holiness had already spread throughout every region—treated all who lived with Saint Bruno in the wilderness of Chartreuse with great love and reverence, he held Bruno himself in such honor and respect, because he saw in him greater adornments of divine grace, that he obeyed his counsels no otherwise than he would the commands of an abbot.

### 24.

Although, as Guigo says in his Life, Hugh had previously burned wholly with the flames of divine love, through their example and companionship he nevertheless grew fervent in the practices of heavenly discipline, just as when someone places several other burning torches around a flaming one.

He lived among them not as lord or bishop but as the humblest companion and brother, ready, as far as he was able, to serve everyone. Thus the venerable William, then prior of Saint Lawrence [Note: See the annotations to note 15 in the older Life above], afterward abbot of Saint-Thierry, who himself was bound to Master Bruno with considerable religious devotion and was Hugh’s cellmate—for at that time two inhabited each cell—complained rather seriously to Master Bruno about Blessed Hugh.

He said that Hugh took away from him almost all the duties belonging to humility within the cell, and that the bishop did not behave toward him merely as a companion but rather as a servant. Sadly, he asserted that he was not permitted to perform any of the servile tasks which, according to custom, they ought to carry out in turn, since Hugh took them all from him.

Hugh lived in the wilderness with such devotion and diligence that Master Bruno sometimes compelled him to leave it, saying: “Go, go to your sheep, and render them what you owe.”

### 25.

At that time, inflamed by a great ardor for poverty and humility, Hugh also wished to sell all his horses and, distributing the price among the poor, travel about on foot preaching. But Master Bruno, a man of profound insight, did not agree. He feared that Hugh might perhaps become proud in his own eyes, or be judged by the other bishops to be seeking singularity, or—and this was beyond doubt—might be unable to complete the undertaking because of the harshness and unevenness of the roads.

Thus writes Guigo, whom we have mentioned, a particularly serious and most trustworthy authority, in the Life of Blessed Hugh, which the reader will find on the first day of April [Note: Also in our volume I of April, where the same Life of that holy bishop of Grenoble is included, page 40, no. 11 and following].

From this it can clearly be seen how great was the authority and esteem enjoyed by Blessed Bruno with so distinguished a bishop: Hugh obeyed him, as he would his own abbot, an uncommon and exceptional example of humility, undoubtedly because of Bruno’s outstanding holiness and wisdom.

Some writers claim that this same bishop received the monastic habit of the Carthusian institution from Blessed Bruno [Note: Those who write this are mistaken. See the Preliminary Commentary, no. 501 and following].

### 26.

At Hugh’s insistence and through his efforts, all the neighboring people—both ecclesiastics and nobles and commoners—willingly granted Blessed Bruno and his brothers whatever rights they possessed in the mountains of Chartreuse and within the boundaries of that wilderness, having observed their holy, honorable, and religious way of life [Note: I included the entire public charter by which they did this in 1086 in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 303 and the following two numbers].

Although Blessed Bruno, formerly celebrated in the world, now trampled underfoot all the glory of this world and strove with the utmost dedication to lie hidden in the wilderness, cling to God alone with ardent love and desire, taste how sweet the Lord is, and desire absolutely nothing apart from him, he could not wholly obtain what he wished.

For when he had spent not quite six years in that small but holy fellowship, Pope Urban II—who had once been the blessed man’s disciple—having been raised to that lofty summit of supreme honor and wishing to fulfill so great an office carefully, remembered the outstanding virtue and illustrious learning of his former teacher. He summoned Bruno by letter to perform services for the holy Church, gravely commanding him not to delay coming to Rome [Note: Concerning Saint Bruno’s summons from Chartreuse by Pope Urban II, who, as I showed in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 96, had once been his student at Rheims, see section 30 of the Preliminary Commentary. From what I discussed there, you will understand that our Saint, as Surius says here, had not lived at Chartreuse for a full six years but only five years and six or seven months when he was summoned from there by Urban, who had been raised to the supreme chair of the Church in 1088].

### 27.

When all his brothers and sons had read the pope’s command, immense grief seized them, and they would accept no consolation. They protested that there was no way they could remain in that vast solitude if they were deprived of the presence of so great a Father. They would stay if he stayed; if he left, they too would leave.

The most devout man was deeply distressed by their tears and moved by great compassion. Since it also seemed exceedingly bitter to him to be called back from the quiet of such a beloved solitude, from such tranquility of spirit and serenity of conscience, to the cares and tumult of this world, he tried to console them gently.

He knew that it was written: “Whoever listens to you listens to me [Note: Luke 10:16]”; and likewise: “Let every soul be subject to higher authorities [Note: Romans 13:1].” For this reason he received the pope’s command no otherwise than he would have received a voice conveyed to him by a heavenly oracle. He said to the brothers:

“To remain with you, dearest brothers in the Lord, is most pleasing to me; to be separated from you is most grievous. But to obey apostolic commands, as you yourselves know, is necessary.”

### 28.

“You know that a pontiff has succeeded to the place of the one to whom Christ said, ‘Feed my sheep [Note: John 21:17].’ Therefore no one can be counted among Christ’s sheep who refuses to obey the man to whom Christ entrusted the feeding of his sheep.

“What benefit could it bring me to afflict my body here with you by hunger and fasting and wear it down through the harsh labors and exercises of the discipline we have undertaken, if meanwhile I were to lose my soul through disobedience? Therefore, my brothers, do not distress my heart with these excessive tears and add your sorrows to my sorrows. Rather, remain in the vocation to which you have been called and persevere in this place.

“I trust in the Lord, who appeared to have built for himself through us, humble men, a dwelling in this wilderness for Blessed Hugh the bishop, that he will not allow the purpose of his grace to be frustrated by this separation of ours. Rather, in his kindness he will grant that, found obedient and faithful in this trial—which is truly very burdensome to me—I may return to you joyfully, strengthened by his blessing.

“You ought not to doubt that, even if I am separated from you bodily for a time, I shall always be with you in spirit.”

### 29.

As he said this, they all raised their voices with tears and said to him:

“You are, venerable Father, after God, our hope; you are our refuge, our consolation, and our counsel. When you depart, what shall we do? In your absence, to whom shall we turn? Surely we shall be like sheep without a shepherd.

“Therefore, if obedience draws you to the pontiff, let the surpassing charity that is in Christ Jesus draw us with you. Neither death nor life nor any creature will be able to separate or tear apart that charity.”

When Blessed Bruno heard this and saw that they would accept no consolation and that he could not persuade them to remain at Chartreuse—for he wisely feared that the place, once dedicated to God, might again fall into lay and profane hands—he commended it and entrusted it to the venerable man Siguin, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, who had been one of the first donors [Note: According to Mabillon in the Benedictine Annals, book 65, no. 35, this named abbot was appointed to govern that celebrated abbey in Auvergne in 1078; and, according to the same author in book 68, no. 103, he resigned the office in 1094. That he was among those who gave the wilderness of Chartreuse to the Saint is confirmed by the public charter, cited in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 503 and the following two numbers, by which it was granted to the Saint and his disciples in 1086].

He did this, however, while fully intending to return with his companions to Chartreuse [Note: This appears scarcely credible. See the Preliminary Commentary, no. 513]. After everything had been completed and he had received the blessing of the most blessed Bishop Hugh, he set out for Rome, compelled by the pope’s command.

### 30.

From this too it can clearly be perceived, though not obscurely, how exceptional was the virtue of the man on whom those religious brothers depended so completely that they considered life itself entirely joyless and burdensome if they were deprived of his presence.

When Blessed Bruno arrived at Rome, the pope was extraordinarily delighted by his arrival and received him with the greatest kindness, since he loved and revered him uniquely. He always kept Bruno among his first and most intimate counselors and faithful friends, continually using his advice in the Church’s difficult affairs.

All the brothers whom he had kept with him at Chartreuse came to him, moved by the Spirit of God [Note: See the Preliminary Commentary, no. 527]. They began to suffer great sorrow, while he himself was especially grieved that they had left the solitude of Chartreuse, which the Lord had chosen for him.

They remembered not meat, cucumbers, or melons, as did those murmuring Israelites in the desert, but the holy meditations, fervent prayers, diligent readings, and spiritual consolations which they had enjoyed in the Carthusian wilderness. They could not restrain the tears that burst forth when they saw that they had been thrown from such profound quiet and tranquil silence into the most troublesome noise and varied turmoil of worldly affairs.

### 31.

But since Blessed Bruno could not yet obtain permission from the pope to depart, he persuaded the brothers to return to Chartreuse. He obtained from the pope a letter to Abbot Siguin [Note: I presented this letter in full to the learned reader in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 528], so that he would restore the wilderness of Chartreuse to them.

He also appointed Landuin prior in his place, under whose leadership they all returned to Chartreuse [Note: Surius seems here to imply that Bruno appointed Landuin over the brothers of Chartreuse only when they had already come to Rome to join the Saint and had agreed to return to Chartreuse. But the public instrument by which Siguin restored the wilderness of Chartreuse to the Saint’s disciples, cited in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 529, confirms that this had already occurred when the Saint, obeying the pontifical command, left Chartreuse and set out for Rome].

From this the reader may also perceive what sort of man Blessed Bruno was and how highly he was esteemed by the supreme shepherd of the whole Church, who wished Bruno to hold such a place of familiarity and authority with him. We do not wish to elaborate on every detail, lest we become too lengthy.

After the brothers had come to Chartreuse with Landuin and had presented the pope’s letter to Abbot Siguin, the brothers of that monastery agreeing, and with Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, present, Siguin freely restored the Carthusian wilderness to them and then granted it perpetually to them and their successors for possession [Note: See what was brought forward concerning this restoration of Chartreuse in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 529 and following].

These were the first letters of a Roman pontiff concerning the Carthusian institution. They provide strong evidence that, from the very beginnings of the Carthusian order, it was approved by the Apostolic See [Note: The letters mentioned here certainly show that Urban II, the supreme pontiff, approved the manner of life which Saint Bruno and his companions maintained at Chartreuse. But in these letters—see the Preliminary Commentary, no. 528—mention is made only of the cells or monastery of Saint Bruno, not of the Carthusian institution].

### 32

From that day onward, the Carthusian wilderness always remained in the possession of the Carthusians, and the Carthusian religion has continued there down to the present. When Saint Bruno, residing at the papal court, learned that those brothers had returned safely to the Chartreuse, that they retained the place, and that they enjoyed tranquil peace and quiet, he frequently wrote to them, urging them to persevere steadfastly in the way of the Lord.

Yet that crooked serpent, the ancient serpent, was not absent from this spiritual paradise. For already foreseeing how great the losses and injuries that illustrious institution of sublime and angelic [Col. 0542A] life—whose foundations were then being laid—would inflict upon him, he brought excessive faintheartedness and perplexity upon those brothers. He employed for this purpose, as most suitable instruments, the deceitful and fallacious tongues of certain wicked men, who accused them of novelty and declared that they were throwing themselves into mortal danger.

And they succeeded in making the excellent fathers utterly uncertain what they ought to do, both because of the austerity of the life they had undertaken and because of the horror and desolation of that wilderness. Influenced by the speeches of those wicked men, they themselves now feared that they would come into danger of their lives. On the other hand, they were greatly afraid that, if they withdrew from there, they would offend God and the stars as guides, which Bishop Hugh had seen.

[Col. 0542B]

### 33

While they were for a considerable time being sorely harassed by these perplexities, behold, the most merciful God, who never abandons those who hope in him, sent to them, as they were discussing these matters among themselves, a venerable man with gray hair and curly locks. He said to them:

“You are perplexed, brothers, whether you ought to remain in this place or depart from it. But I tell you, in the words of almighty God, that the Mother of God, the ever-virgin, will preserve you in this wilderness if you are willing daily to recite her Hours.”

After saying this, he suddenly vanished from their sight. But they, filled with extraordinary joy, chose as patroness of the entire Carthusian institution that most holy Virgin, whom they knew to be one to whom her Son, the immortal King of all ages, could refuse nothing; and they chose the most blessed forerunner of the Lord, John, as their patron.

They inferred especially that the man who had appeared to them was the holy apostle Peter because his successor, Urban II, at the Council of Clermont, had established that the Hours of the most blessed Mother of God should be recited by the whole clergy. By this vision they were so strengthened in the Lord that neither death nor life could separate them from the love of Christ.

[Note: See what is said about this vision and the circumstances accompanying it in the Preliminary Commentary, nos. 605 and the following five numbers.]

[Col. 0542D]

### 34

When blessed Bruno had served the supreme pontiff energetically for a few years and had been of no little benefit to the Church of God through his counsel, prudence, and wisdom, he meanwhile suffered most painfully from the noise and tumult of the court. Setting these aside, he always longed to return to the tranquil harbor of solitary life. At last, unable any longer to endure the flame of so great a desire, and before the pontiff departed from Piacenza for Gaul, he finally obtained, with much persistence in prayer, permission and the opportunity to withdraw to his own hermitage—or, if that seemed preferable, to seek another.

At that time, with the same pontiff’s approval, a most holy man was elected archbishop of the Church of Reggio, which is the first metropolitan church of all Calabria. Pope Urban was very eager to confirm him in that dignity. But Bruno, knowing how many dangers, cares, and troubles accompany such ecclesiastical offices, did not wish to consent to the election.

[Note: The saint was not first elected to the archbishopric of Reggio during the period of the Council of Piacenza, held in 1095, nor did he obtain permission from the pontiff to return to his hermitage, contrary to what Surius says here. See the Preliminary Commentary, nos. 532, 533, 536 and the following numbers.]

Nor did he act stubbornly in this matter, but modestly and humbly, moved only by his love of quiet, while preserving obedience and submission toward the pontiff and charity toward his neighbors.

[Col. 0543A]

### 35

At last, leaving the court with the pontiff’s good will and blessing, he sought the deserted places of Calabria, accompanied by several men of the same purpose, whom the good odor of his life and his fervent exhortations had already led to contempt for the world.

[Note: Consult what I noted concerning the third chapter of the preceding Life, note 130.]

For he had learned that the region of Calabria contained many solitudes exceedingly suitable for doing penance and pursuing a solitary life. He would indeed have preferred what he had often resolved within himself: to return to the Chartreuse to his beloved brothers, whom he had sent there. But because the supreme pontiff, with his court, was departing for Gaul, within whose borders the Chartreuse was situated, Bruno feared that, if he too went there, he might either be unable to avoid the court or seem not to have left it but to be following it.

It therefore seemed preferable to seek Calabria, without in the meantime changing his resolve to visit his own brothers in the Chartreuse once matters had been arranged and settled.

[Note: Since the pontiff, after celebrating the Council of Piacenza in 1095, went to Gaul, while Bruno had already gone to Calabria from the year 1090 onward, it is clear that the reason stated here for his not returning to the Chartreuse when he withdrew to Calabria cannot stand.]

His letters, written from the solitude of Calabria to the brothers living in the Chartreuse, make this sufficiently clear. At their conclusion he writes:

“But concerning myself, brothers, know that, after God, I have one sole desire: to come to you and see you; and whenever I can, I shall fulfill this in deed, with God’s help.”

[Note: The complete letter ending with these words, which the saint sent to the brothers of the Chartreuse through Landuinus when Landuinus was returning there from Calabria, is given in the Preliminary Commentary, nos. 679 and following.]

### 36

In Calabria itself he came to a certain hermitage called Torre, in the diocese of Squillace.

[Note: See the Preliminary Commentary, no. 552.]

There, since they lacked sufficient funds for the expense, they built not costly cells but humble huts, made of base material yet precious in Christ. Who could express in words how great was the integrity and holiness of the life he led there with his companions, or what exercises of piety and religion occupied them?

Something of this can indeed be learned from a letter that the holy man wrote to Ralph, then provost of the Church of Reims and later its bishop. Among other things he says:

“In the borders of Calabria I inhabit a hermitage, together with religious brothers and several well-educated men who, remaining constantly vigilant in divine service, await the return of their Lord, so that when he knocks they may immediately open to him. It is situated far enough on every side from human habitation.

“Of its pleasantness, of the mildness and healthfulness of its air, or of the broad and agreeable plain stretching lengthwise among the mountains, where there are green meadows and flowering pastures—what worthy thing can I say? Or who could adequately describe the view of the hills gently rising on every side, the recesses of the shady valleys, and the delightful abundance of rivers, streams, and springs? Nor are irrigated gardens lacking, nor the fertility of various trees.”

### 37

But why do I linger over these matters any longer? The prudent man has other delights, far more pleasing and useful, because they are divine. Nevertheless, when the weaker spirit has been wearied by stricter discipline and spiritual pursuits, it is often refreshed and recovers its breath through these things. For a bow, if kept constantly taut, becomes slackened and less fit for its work.

What benefit and delight solitude and the silence of the hermitage bring to those who love them is known only by those who have experienced them. Here men of energy may return into themselves as much as they wish, dwell with themselves, diligently cultivate the seeds of virtue, and happily enjoy the fruits of paradise.

Here that eye is acquired whose serene gaze wounds the Bridegroom with love, by which God is seen in purity and cleanliness. Here leisure is celebrated as fruitful activity, and one rests in peaceful action. Here God repays his athletes for the labor of combat with the desired reward—namely, the peace unknown to the world and joy in the Holy Spirit.

This is that beautiful Rachel, fair in appearance, more loved by Jacob, less fruitful in children than the more fertile but bleary-eyed Leah. For there are fewer children of contemplation than of action. Nevertheless, Joseph and Benjamin were loved by their father more than their other brothers.

This is that better portion which Mary chose and which shall not be taken away. This is the most beautiful Shunammite, found alone throughout all the borders of Israel, who warmed and cared for the aged David.

This is what the holy man writes in that letter.

[Note: To see what the biographer is truly praising here, consult § 41 of the Preliminary Commentary, where I cited the entire letter and added the observations I judged appropriate.]

Much could be drawn from it in praise of him, but we shall pass on to other matters.

## CHAPTER III

Bruno is found by Count Roger in the hermitage of Torre; he rescues him from imminent danger; through Roger’s generosity he builds two monasteries there; in one of them he lives most holily until death; after his death he shines through miracles; and finally, with the pontiff’s permission, he is honored among the saints by the Carthusians.

[Col. 0544D]

### 38

After blessed Bruno had first begun to live in that hermitage of Torre with his companions, it happened, by God’s arrangement, that one day Count Roger of Calabria, while hunting in that same wilderness with a considerable troop of his men and a great number of dogs, came, entirely unaware of the matter, to the place that the servants of God had chosen for their habitation.

[Note: For information about this prince, see the Preliminary Commentary, no. 556 and the following number.]

When the dogs skillfully followed various tracks of wild animals, they ran toward the huts in which blessed Bruno was staying with his brothers. There they planted their feet and, with loud barking, announced to their master that they had found rich prey.

When the count saw this, he quickly rushed there with his men. He found the fathers in their caves, kneeling, with their faces and hands raised toward heaven, praying and praising God together.

[Note: Concerning this apparently fictitious discovery of the saint and his companions by Count Roger while he was hunting, see the Preliminary Commentary, no. 541 and the following two numbers.]

Then, filled with great amazement, he leapt down from the horse on which he was riding, greeted them piously and courteously, and carefully asked why they had come there and what their condition was. After learning everything from them, he rejoiced greatly, praising and glorifying God, who had judged him worthy of such splendid prey.

### 39

For he was convinced—and not without reason—that through their merits and prayers he and his land would be helped by God and preserved in peace. For this reason, so that they might live there more peacefully and remain longer, he gave them the church of Saint Mary and that of Saint Stephen of the Hermitage.

[Note: In the Preliminary Commentary, no. 570, I explained what should be thought concerning the two churches that Count Roger gave to Saint Bruno and his companions immediately after finding them praying in the cave.]

There he also frequently visited them, supplied them with the necessities of life, and willingly listened to what concerned the salvation of the soul. As for blessed Bruno himself, the pastor and father of the others, he not only embraced him more closely than the rest, but also often summoned him to himself. Showing him great reverence, he always gave him first place in his household, willingly obeyed his counsels, and continually commended himself to his prayers, in which he placed the greatest confidence.

[Note: See what I noted concerning this in chapter 3 of the preceding Life, note 137.]

Nor was his opinion mistaken. Through the merits of that blessed man, the Lord rescued him from the most imminent danger and from dangers laid against him. The count himself left this recorded in writing, for the glory of God and so that Saint Bruno’s holiness might be made known everywhere, in these words:

### 40

“I, Roger, by the mercy of God count of Calabria and Sicily, wish all faithful Christians to know the benefits that God, though I am a sinner, granted me through the prayers of my revered brother Bruno, the most devout father of the brothers who live in the churches of Saint Mary of the Hermitage and Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, situated in my land between the town called Stilo and Arena.

“When I was at the siege of Capua,

[Note: This siege, the occasion of which I explained in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 635, took place in 1098, as I showed in § 40 of the Preliminary Commentary.]

“on the Kalends of March, I had placed Sergius, a Greek by nationality, in command of two hundred armed men of his own nation and as master of the army’s watches. Having been forestalled by a satanic persuasion, he had promised the prince of Capua, who offered him a considerable quantity of gold, that he would provide access by night for an attack upon me and my army.

### 41

“The night of the treachery arrived. The prince of Capua and his army were ready for battle as promised. While I had surrendered myself to sleep, after some time had passed during the night, an old man of venerable appearance stood beside my bed, wearing torn garments and unable to restrain his tears.

“When in the vision I asked him what was the reason for his weeping and tears, he seemed to me to weep even more bitterly. When I asked again who he was that was weeping, he said:

“‘I weep for the souls of Christians—and for you together with them. Rise as quickly as possible and take up arms, if God permits you to rescue yourself and the souls of your fighting men.’

“This man appeared to me in every respect to be the venerable Father Bruno. I awoke in great terror, trembling because of the vision. Immediately I took up arms, calling to the soldiers that they should mount their horses while armed, and striving to test whether the vision was true.

### 42

“At that uproar and trumpet blast, the impious Sergius and his followers fled and followed the prince of Capua, hoping to find refuge in the said city. The soldiers captured one hundred and sixty-two men, both wounded and unwounded.

[Note: Whether Sergius was among them is uncertain. Consult what is noted concerning this in chapter 3 of the preceding Life, note 140.]

“From this we established that the vision was true. God willing, I returned to Squillace on the twenty-ninth of July, after having stayed in the city of Capua, where I had been ill for fifteen consecutive days.

“The venerable Bruno already mentioned came with four of his brothers, and they consoled me with their holy and devout conversations. I related the vision to that reverend man and offered humble thanks to him, since, even while absent, he had cared for me in his prayers.

### 43

“He humbly declared that he was not the one whom I had believed him to be, but an angel of God who stands beside a prince in time of war.

[Note: Concerning this vision offered to Count Roger in sleep, see the Preliminary Commentary, no. 644.]

“I also humbly asked him to consent on that account to receive abundant revenues from my possessions in the land of Squillace, which I was giving him. But he refused and said that he did not wish to accept them, because he had left his father’s house and my household for this purpose: to be entirely free from external possessions and serve his God. He had been, as it were, first and foremost in my entire household.

[Note: Do not infer from these words of Count Roger that Saint Bruno had spent some time at the prince’s court before his withdrawal to the Chartreuse. See the Preliminary Commentary, no. 571 and the following number.]

“At last, with difficulty, I obtained from him that he would graciously agree to accept my small gift. For I gave to that same Father Bruno and his successors, to possess perpetually without temporal service, the monastery of Saint James together with the castle, and many other estates and possessions, with the extensive liberties specifically set out in the said document.”

[Note: You will find these documents cited in full in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 637 and the following six numbers.]

Thus far the count.

### 44

Relying upon this generosity and donation of the count, blessed Bruno first built there a church in honor of the Mother of God, near a certain underground cave in which he lived. Then he also built another, not far from it, in honor of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr.

[Note: After withdrawing to the hermitage of Torre, the saint did not immediately live in a cave, as Surius seems to intend here; nor did he build the two churches mentioned here after the issuance of the charter, part of which is cited immediately above. See the Preliminary Commentary, no. 624 and the following two numbers, and also no. 748.]

He joined to the latter a monastery in which the other brothers lived, serving Christ under the care and governance of so great a Father.

[Note: The saint placed Landuinus in charge of this monastery as prior. Consult the Preliminary Commentary, nos. 626, 645, and 716.]

With them the holy man persevered until the final day of his life in the same manner of living and austerity of life that he had begun and taught earlier at the Chartreuse. Meanwhile he diligently cared for those who lived in the wilderness of the Chartreuse,

[Note: This appears entirely true from the letter cited in § 41 of the Preliminary Commentary, which the saint sent to the brothers of the Chartreuse through Landuinus when he was returning to them from Calabria.]

having appointed over them, as we said earlier, Master Landuinus.

### 45

That venerable man, so that he might not depart from the footsteps and institutions of so great a Father and teacher, nor instruct his own brothers in any way other than he had learned from Bruno together with his companions, undertook a very long journey to the hermitage of Calabria itself, intending to inquire carefully about every matter from Bruno.

But when he was returning from the most holy man, he fell into the hands of the schismatic Guibert. Since he could not be induced to abandon his position, he was detained in custody in defense of justice. Released shortly afterward, he returned his spirit undefiled to Christ not long thereafter.

[Note: Landuinus, who had gone from Calabria to see Bruno and was returning to the Chartreuse, fell into the hands of Guibert, the antipope, and was thrown into prison. It is permissible to conclude from what I discussed in § 41 of the Preliminary Commentary that he died there of starvation. Surius is therefore mistaken when he writes here that Landuinus died only after he had been released shortly afterward from the prison into which he had been thrown.]

### 46

Blessed Father Bruno also fell into a very grave illness. As the disease grew worse, his brothers and sons describe in a certain written account how he conducted himself:

“So that you may know with what confidence and certain hope of his liberation you should pour out your prayers, we make known his passing in a brief account, so that at the completion of the holy man you may gather the truth and perfection of the life he had lived.

“For, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, he summoned his brothers and, beginning from his infancy, reviewed the successive stages of his life. He declared the whole course of his time worthy of knowledge and reflection.”

[Note: For the meaning of this expression, see the Preliminary Commentary, no. 726.]

[Col. 0547D]

### 47

Afterward he explained his faith concerning the Trinity in an extended and profound discourse and concluded as follows:

[Note: I presented the saint’s complete profession of faith, uttered when he felt himself near death, for the attentive reader in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 727. The words that follow here do not conclude it there.]

“I also believe the sacraments that the holy Church believes and venerates, and specifically that the bread and wine consecrated upon the altar are, after consecration, the true body of our Lord Jesus Christ, true flesh and true blood, which we also receive for the remission of our sins and in hope of eternal salvation.”

On the following Sunday that holy soul was freed from the flesh, on the day before the Nones of October, in the year of Christ 1101, and his brothers honorably buried his body there.

[Col. 0548A]

### 48

The following epitaph was placed upon his tomb:

> First founder of Christ’s fold in this wilderness,  
> I deserved to become the one covered by this stone.  
> Bruno is my name; Germany was my motherland,  
> And grateful woodland rest brought me to the Calabrians.  
>   
> I was a teacher, a herald of Christ, a man known throughout the world;  
> The grace came from above—it was not my merit.  
> On the sixth day of October the bonds of the flesh were dissolved;  
> My bones remain in the tomb, while my spirit seeks the stars.

[Note: Several of these verses differ from the verses in which the saint’s epitaph was originally composed. Consult the Preliminary Commentary, no. 734.]

Many miracles followed his most holy life and precious death, which Christ performed on account of his excellent merits. After his death and burial, the brothers of his monastery sent letters, as is customary, to various provinces and even to Britain itself. In them they announced his departure from this life and asked that prayers be offered to the Lord for his holy soul.

[Note: Consult the Preliminary Commentary, no. 24 and the following number.]

### 49

For they knew that no one is just who does not sin. First his brothers and disciples, and afterward also others who had known him and to whom his outstanding learning and holiness of life were known, added testimonies concerning these matters to those letters, either in prose or in verse.

If we wished to recount all of them, we would be excessively lengthy; if we omitted all the testimonies of so many most distinguished men, we would not escape the charge of ingratitude and shamelessness—especially since from them the exceptional holiness of the blessed man can be perceived without difficulty. It is certainly useful that what we are about to record should not remain unknown, above all because certain foolish and senseless men have dared to persuade themselves and others that this blessed man was the teacher whom, at the beginning of this history, we said had been condemned.

That is an utterly groundless invention—I know not whose dreamer’s fabrication—for it is sufficiently clear that the condemned teacher gave the most blessed Bruno and his companions the occasion to think seriously about establishing a holier way of life and, abandoning all the possessions of this world, to move into the harsh wilderness.

[Note: So Surius writes here, and rightly, since he thereby refutes the impious slander against the saint. He immediately adds several funeral titles with which various churches had honored the saint. But since I shall give below not only these, but also all the others with which many churches and persons in Italy, Gaul, and England celebrated Bruno after his death, I refrain from transcribing here those listed by Surius.]

[Col. 0549A]

### 50

These splendid testimonies of so many eminent men and distinguished communities and persons are, if I am not mistaken, abundantly sufficient to demonstrate the excellent learning, moral integrity, and holiness of life of the most blessed Father Bruno, even if no miracles of his remained.

Yet it is also recorded that he became renowned for many miracles. These, however—a matter I cannot recall without sorrow—were not recorded with the diligence they deserved, or, if they were recorded, were first preserved carelessly and then lost by monks of another institution who took possession of his monastery.

[Note: These testimonies are expressed, of course, in the funeral titles cited from the note immediately preceding.]

The most distinguished man was buried in his monastery of Saint Stephen, behind the high altar.

[Note: Concerning the church of the hermitage of Torre in which Saint Bruno obtained burial, see the discussion in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 731 and the following two numbers.]

At his tomb a living spring bursts forth, which through the power of Christ and his merits brings many varied remedies of health to many people. The blind are given sight there, the deaf hear, the maimed and mutilated are restored, lepers are cleansed, and the possessed are quickly purified.

But more marvelous than all these miracles is that, as the testimonies already cited so often repeat, he was able to reject all glory and honor and persevere in such great austerity, integrity, and perfection of life.

### 51

No one should be troubled by the fact that the spring is no longer seen at the blessed man’s tomb. Springs that bubble up miraculously are not always perpetual, and sometimes such divine benefits are withdrawn because of human demerits.

Miracles are performed by God so that the merits of the saints may be commended and made known. Once these seem sufficiently known, miracles sometimes cease. Nor is it greatly surprising if that spring has disappeared, since the most holy manner of life that the most holy man had instituted there has gone into exile from his monastery.

[Note: Concerning the spring said here to have been miraculously raised at the saint’s tomb, and the reason given for its ceasing or drying up, consult what is said in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 735 and several following numbers.]

For after he had fallen asleep in the Lord, that monastery continued in the institution of Carthusian life under the five priors who succeeded him, down to the time of the venerable Guigo, prior of the Chartreuse. From that time, while the Carthusian order was flourishing in Gaul, that monastery of Calabria alone degenerated by growing lukewarm in the fervor and holiness of the blessed Father Bruno.

Its inhabitants did indeed ask the Chartreuse for visitors and reformers, but the great distance between the places made this difficult to obtain.

[Col. 0550A]

### 52

Accordingly, they transferred themselves to the Cistercian institution. At that time it was newly arisen and, through the remarkable holiness and great labor of the incomparable man, blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, wonderfully spreading and continuing in great fervor.

[Note: Concerning Saint Bernard, the first abbot of Clairvaux, the matter has already been treated among us in volume IV of August, on the twentieth day of that month, on which he is commemorated and is included in the Roman Martyrology. He gave his name to the Cistercian Order, which began in 1098 and was approved by Pope Paschal II in 1100; he entered it in 1113 and most happily ended a life lived with the utmost holiness in 1152, as is demonstrated by what is said about that holy abbot in the volume mentioned above.]

Until that time the monastery had remained for sixty years in the profession of the Carthusian religion.

[Note: The monastery of Saint Stephen at Torre remained attached to the Carthusian institution longer than is stated here. See the Preliminary Commentary, no. 740 and the following number.]

But when the Cistercian religion also gradually grew lukewarm there, the monastery of Saint Bruno eventually became commendatory.

[Note: For the time when this occurred, see the Preliminary Commentary, no. 752.]

It remained so until these times of the most holy pontiff Leo X. This pontiff, having repeatedly heard from many people about the outstanding holiness of blessed Bruno, judged it unworthy—without investigating the miracles—that he whom almighty God had so greatly enriched in this life with gifts and charisms, and whom he now blessed with heavenly happiness, should not be proclaimed on earth with exceptional praise and commendation, nor should the due offices of pious devotion be offered before the throne of divine glory to one who rests there and to whom the Lord had given a heart for the commandment and the law of life and discipline.

### 53

Therefore he not only graciously assented by apostolic authority, but also willed that in every monastery of the entire Carthusian order and in their churches or chapels the feast of the most holy Bruno, confessor, should every year on the sixth of October—the day on which he departed this life—be solemnly honored and celebrated with suitable and due devotion. He further decreed that Bruno’s body and memory should receive worthy praise and veneration in the Lord, that a fitting office should be performed and sung in his honor, and that he should also be commemorated daily in the divine office.

[Note: See what was noted in chapter 3 of the preceding Life, note 157.]

Moreover, in the year of salvation 1514, the same pontiff recalled from the Cistercians to the Carthusians the house of Saint Stephen that blessed Bruno had founded in Calabria and in which his sacred body rests.

[Note: The bull by which Pope Leo X restored the monastery of Saint Stephen at Torre to the Carthusians is recorded as having been issued in 1513; they took possession of it in 1514. See § 46 of the Preliminary Commentary, where I gave the complete bull.]

This was done so that from then onward life might be lived there according to the Carthusian manner and institution.

When this matter was being arranged, the prior of the Carthusian monastery of Naples, who had been entrusted with advancing and promoting it, presented to the reverend Father Lord Francis, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, part of Saint Bruno’s jawbone together with two teeth.

[Note: See the Preliminary Commentary, no. 779 and the following numbers, for the consequences of what Surius here reports after Blomevenna.]

He said that the abbots of Saint Stephen, where, as stated, the sacred body of blessed Bruno rests, had always guarded his sacred relics with such care, fearing that the Carthusians might reclaim them, that they had placed the bones in various hidden locations and frequently changed those locations. No one except the abbot and another trustworthy man had any knowledge of them.

[Note: It is not certain that Saint Bruno’s relics were concealed by the abbots of Saint Stephen in the manner stated here. Consult the Preliminary Commentary, no. 733.]

[Col. 0551D]

### 54

In the year of Christ 1514 those sacred bones were transferred, and Lord Matthew, prior of the Carthusian monastery of Bologna, was present at the transfer. He held the saint’s sacred head in his hands so that it would not be placed upon the altar together with the bones. To the crowds who feared that they would be deprived of the sacred relics of their beloved Patron, he gave this explanation:

“The sacred head,” he said, “must be separated from the bones and adorned with gold, silver, and precious stones.”

By these words he removed all suspicion from the common people. With the special permission of the supreme pontiff, he removed a portion from the head and distributed it to others, especially to the venerable Father Gregory, prior of Freiburg, who distributed fragments throughout the houses of the Rhenish province, of which he was visitor.

Since Saint Bruno’s homeland was Cologne Agrippina, Lord Matthew also gave a small portion of his head to Lord Peter of Leiden, prior of the Carthusian monastery of Cologne.

[Note: That is, in the year in which this prior himself attended the general chapter of the Carthusian order, 1516. See the Preliminary Commentary, no. 777 and the following number.]

This gift was exceedingly welcome to him. Returning home in 1516, he reverently deposited the most precious gift in the church of the Cologne Charterhouse on 3 August.

[Col. 0551C]

### 55

John, abbot of Saint Rufus, transferred the sacred body of blessed Bruno in the year mentioned, 1514, and placed it in the church of Saint Stephen upon the high altar, which was constructed of white marble.

A very sacred cave lies one thousand five hundred paces from this monastery. It is situated in a narrow place among the mountains, surrounded by woods that close off the far ends of the valley; it is entirely remote and inaccessible to human beings.

Above this cave a small chapel with an altar has been built. There an inscription bears the title:

> Saint Bruno of Cologne, master of the hermitage of Saint Mary of Torre,  
> first founder of the Carthusian Order.

His image is also painted there.

In this cave that man of God remained with incredible spiritual fervor from the time when he first came there until his death.
