[Note: Concerning the continuous residence of the saint in the cave asserted here, see what I stated in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 748.]

Furthermore, as evidence and commendation of his holiness, even to the present day that place where, after the excesses of contemplation had wearied his limbs, he would cast them upon the bare ground never produces grass to the measure of his body, although the surrounding area grows green. All the inhabitants of the place most firmly assert this illustrious miracle.

[Note: I left this miracle undecided in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 748.]

There is also, within a stone’s throw, a church of the most blessed Mary, built by Count Roger for the servant of God, Master Bruno, and for Master Landuinus the Norman, his companion.

[Note: As you will understand from the Preliminary Commentary, no. 733, the Carthusians who inhabit the monastery of Saint Stephen at Torre have charge of this church. This place, now called the “House of Saints Stephen and Bruno,” with Bruno’s name added to that of Stephen, is not the very one that Saint Bruno built, but another situated approximately a stone’s throw from the one that has now collapsed. I understand this from information copied from the as-yet-unpublished fourth book of the Annals of the Carthusians in the Vallis-Dei exemplar and communicated to me by a Parisian Carthusian, frequently praised in the Preliminary Commentary.]

[Col. 0552B] **56.** To these places crowds of people—old and young, men and women, nobles and commoners, princes and magnates—flock in eager rivalry out of veneration for the most holy Bruno, devotion of heart toward him, and also to obtain his benefits, contemplating him in their minds as though he were still living among men. They approach reverently, venerate him, and pray. They especially visit that cave in which he almost always served God alone with such reverence, faith, and affection that many are seen to go there from the monastery already mentioned only with bare feet. Others crawl on their knees, lick that sacred cave, its earth, and its rocks out of inward piety, and go around it in tears; they scrape off some small portion of the cave itself, intending to regard it as a great relic, and so depart joyfully to their homes. No one, indeed, could express in words with what devotion and zeal the bishops of Calabria, abbots, prelates, religious, princes, counts, barons, and the entire people honor the most holy man [Note: [Col. 0552D] That Saint Bruno is still held in the highest veneration among the Calabrians is shown by Zanottius in the Life of him that he composed, chapter 34.].

Finally, not far from the monastery mentioned above there is a very extensive woodland, which they call Folo, assigned by the man of God solely for the restoration of the monastery. If any rash person should dare to act against his will, then, as a firmly established tradition confirmed by long experience among all the Calabrians testifies, he does not escape divine vengeance. In this and in many other matters almighty God acts to declare the holiness of his most faithful Servant. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0553]

## ENCYClical LETTER [Note: [Col. 0553B]

This letter, sent in every direction according to the custom then prevailing (see the Preliminary Commentary, no. 24 and following) to announce Bruno’s death, and prefixed to the Funeral Titles or responses sent in reply to it, which are appended to the end of the Life of Saint Bruno written by Puteanus and printed at Basel about the year 1515, is preceded by seven verses. In that work they are put forward as another epitaph of the Saint; others, however, maintain that they are the funeral title with which the religious inhabitants of the Turritan hermitage mourned the Saint. Neither opinion pleases me. The first does not, because the verses do not seem to have the appearance of an epitaph; the second does not, because the verses were not sent as a response to the letter already given—although, according to what was stated in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 24, that would have been necessary for them to constitute a funeral title. Be that as it may, one might aptly call them an ethopoeia, by which Saint Bruno’s character is set before the reader’s eyes; nor does it seem entirely unlikely to me that they were attached to the encyclical letter already given by the Saint’s disciples, so that they might teach, to some extent, what kind of man he had been. The context therefore requires me to transcribe them here also, before proceeding to the funeral titles. They are as follows:

Bruno was praised in many things and in one.

He was a man of even life, a man distinguished in this respect.

His face was always cheerful, his speech restrained.

With the terror of a father he displayed his mother’s entrails.

[Col. 0554C] No one experienced him as a great man, but as gentle as a lamb.

He was wholly, in this life, a true Israelite.

Take him, God, from punishments, and bring him to pleasant heavenly dwellings.

Moreover, I stated in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 24, that I would explain certain matters occurring in the Funeral Titles of the Saint, which are about to be supplied here. To prevent anyone from thinking that these titles are spurious, I shall also indicate, whenever I can and judge it useful, the age of the sacred places whose names identify them; or at least, after each section by which I shall separate the titles, I shall note whether, and especially what, I have been able to discover concerning them. In the meantime, however, I have decided generally to pass over unnoticed the faults with which these pieces conflict with the laws of correct prosody and construction, since they are excessively frequent.]

The disciples of Saint Bruno in the Turritan hermitage announced his death in every direction and requested the customary suffrages for his soul.

[Col. 0553A] In the first place, we venerate and greet with due submission the bishop of the apostolic see—whom we believe and confess to be first and head in the Church—and that entire principal court, the humble hermits of the monastery of Calabria of Holy Mary, Mother of God, whose founder and superior Father Bruno was while he lived in the flesh. We announce the death of our holy Father on the day before the Nones of October, so that through their merits and prayers he may be helped before God.

We also greet the whole holy Church in its orders and professions: canons, monks, hermits, holy virgins consecrated to God. Before all these we prostrate ourselves in spiritual presence, asking that they may be willing to remember our deceased Father; that, if any stain adhered to that beloved soul—for there is no just person who does not sin—it may be cleansed by multiplied intercessors and the urgency of prayers, and that he may pass to rest.

We also ask that the communities or religious persons of whatever places commemorate him; let them not hesitate to subscribe their names individually on this sheet. If any wish separately to observe his written and annual commemoration, let them be enrolled, so that we may repay each one with a suitable return, insofar as our few numbers permit.

But so that you may know with what confidence and with what certain hope of his deliverance you should pour out prayers, we briefly make known his passing, for his benefit, so that in the completion of the holy man you may gather the truth and perfection of his life already lived. Knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, he summoned his brothers and, beginning from infancy, reviewed each of his ages; with the knowledge and judgment of his entire life he declared it worthy. Afterwards he explained and concluded his faith concerning the Trinity in an extended and profound discourse, thus:

“I also believe the sacraments that the holy Church believes and venerates, and specifically that the bread and wine consecrated on the altar, after consecration, are the true body of our Lord Jesus Christ, the true flesh and true blood, which we too receive for the remission of our sins and in hope of eternal salvation.”

On the following Sunday that holy soul was released from the flesh, on the day before the Nones of October, in the year of the Lord 1101. Pray for him and for us sinners. We commend to your charity our brother, the bearer of this letter, who is traveling as an act of obedience. Farewell.

[Col. 0555]

## FUNERAL TITLES

Or various responses to the preceding letter [Note: [Col. 0555A] On the manner and reason for which it seemed appropriate to publish here the Funeral Titles, or responses sent to the encyclical letter by which Saint Bruno’s disciples announced his death in every direction, see the Preliminary Commentary, no. 24 and following. There you will also find the basis for forming a general judgment about them.]

### SECTION I

[Col. 0555A]

#### Title of the Brothers of Monte Amiata [Note: [Col. 0555B] Lubinus, in his Brief Notice of the Abbeys of Italy, p. 226, lists an abbey of the Order of Saint Benedict bearing the title of the Holy Savior of Monte Amiata, situated in the territory and diocese of Clusium in ancient Etruria. Ughellus, in the Clusian Bishops in vol. III of Sacred Italy, followed by Mabillonius in vol. II of the Benedictine Annals, book XXII, no. 24, states that it was founded about the year 743 by Ratchis, king of the Lombards. It seems to me almost certain that the brothers from this abbey are those in whose name this Funeral Title is signed, although the monastery to which they belonged is called here Mons Amatus rather than Mons Amiatus, through the omission of a single letter.]

**1.** We make known to your holiness that we, the brothers of Vivo, humble inhabitants of Monte Amato, together with our lord Prior Jerome, have jointly decided, for the most reverend and most beloved Bruno, father of your Congregation, to celebrate Vigils [Note: [Col. 0555C] That is, the office customarily sung for the dead, as it is still called today.] and Masses for seven days after his venerable passing, to enter him in the register [Note: [Col. 0555C] Here this word means a catalogue in which monasteries or churches used to enter the deceased for whom they had decided to pray in a special way.], and to observe his anniversary. We pray and earnestly ask that you remember us in all your good works. Farewell.

#### Of the brothers of the monastery of Fiscicla [Note: [Col. 0555C] This is an abbey in the diocese of Lucca, or Lucensis, in Italy, famous under the title of the Holy Savior and founded in the tenth century. See Lubinus, Brief Notice of the Abbeys of Italy, p. 134; he nevertheless explains there that this abbey or monastery is called not Fisciclense but Fisceclense, Ficiscli, or even Ficoclense.]

**2.** We, the brothers of Fiscicla, will offer for the most reverend and most religious lord Bruno, that most eminent hermit, prayers of supplication with the greatest intensity and very willing spirit to God the Creator, together with the offering of the sacred sacrifice; we will enter his venerable name among the most beloved names of our brothers, and, as your charity requests, we will celebrate his anniversary with still greater devotion [Note: [Col. 0555C] In the encyclical letter announcing Saint Bruno’s death, placed above the Funeral Titles, his Calabrian disciples ask that those who, upon receiving it, are going to observe the anniversary of their deceased Father should enter their responses to that letter not on the roll containing the letter itself, but on a separate sheet. Thus it could easily have happened that, when the person carrying the encyclical letter announcing Saint Bruno’s death visited two monasteries—Fiscicla and Monte Amato, which were not very far from each other—one immediately after the other, and they promised to celebrate Bruno’s anniversary, these two monasteries entered their responses or Funeral Titles on the same separate sheet in the order in which they are placed here. I think the same applies to certain others inserted between the next title and Title Fifteen, which expressly promise the celebration of the Saint’s anniversary. For the person who carried the encyclical letter proceeded from Etruria—which included the two monasteries just mentioned, Fiscicla and Monte Amato—to Lyon. Since the sacred places to which these titles belong are not far from the road leading from Etruria to Lyon, he most probably visited them all in the order in which they are supplied here.]

#### Of Rangerius, Bruno’s disciple

**3.** I, Rangerius, formerly a disciple of the venerable Bruno [Note: [Col. 0556B] Some wish Rangerius, whose name identifies this Title, to be the same Rangerius who, after our Saint had declined the archbishopric of Reggio, to which he had been elected in 1090, was promoted to that see, as may be seen in Ughellus, vol. IX of Sacred Italy, among the archbishops of Reggio. But the anonymous author of a manuscript Treatise on Saint Bruno, which the Carthusians here shared with me, judges that Rangerius who wrote this Title and calls himself Saint Bruno’s disciple is rather the Rangerius who, according to Ughellus in vol. I of Sacred Italy, among the bishops of Lucca, occupied the see of Lucca in 1098 and died in 1112. Indeed, since Rangerius’s Title, in which the same thing was promised, is placed between two Titles entered on the same separate sheet—one from the monastery of Saint Fiscicla in the diocese of Lucca, the other from the monastery of Saint Frigidianus, situated in the city of Lucca itself, as will be explained below—it is very probable that this title too was written on the same separate sheet. If so, Rangerius, who wrote it, was probably in the city of Lucca or not far from it when he did so; and the opinion of the anonymous author praised above may therefore seem sufficiently probable, although it can in no way be held as certain, since neither from the Title itself nor from the inscription it bears is it established that Rangerius, whom it names as its author, was a bishop.]

I desire to offer prayers of supplication to almighty God, so that he who honored him with such great grace and adorned him with such great piety may, according to the merit of his faith, grant him also a crown. In particular, both as a special duty and as a privilege of love, I shall, as circumstances and time permit, perform his anniversary commemoration.

#### Church of Saint Frigidianus of Lucca

**4.** We, the humble brothers of the Church of Saint Frigidianus [Note: [Col. 0557B] Within the walls of the city of Lucca, as Lubinus explains in his Brief Notice of the Abbeys of Italy, p. 192, there is a monastery founded in the sixth century, called Saint Frigidianus or Frigianus. There seems to be no doubt that this present Funeral Title belongs to that very place.] of Lucca, willingly perform an office of commemoration for so great and glorious a man [Note: [Col. 0557C] I do not know whether those who wrote this Title promised by this formula of speech that they would observe the Saint’s anniversary. Be that as it may, it seems that this was indeed promised both here and in two other Funeral Titles that likewise do not express the matter explicitly, namely the sixth and the ninth, one belonging to the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre and the other to the Church of Segusium. Since all three are inserted among several Titles entered on a separate sheet (see what was said in note 258), it seems probable that they too were entered on the same separate sheet. By the very fact that they were entered on a separate sheet, those who wrote them apparently promised that they would celebrate the Saint’s anniversary, as appears from what was said in note 258.], believing that through his holy merits we are commended before God.

#### Church of Piacenza

**5.** We, the brothers of little merit of the mother church of Saint Mary and Saint Justina of Piacenza [Note: [Col. 0557C] That is, the cathedral church. See Du Cange, Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin, under the words *Ecclesia Matrix*.], willingly promise, with fervent hearts, to perform the due funeral rites for the most glorious soul of so venerable a man, and we shall lovingly insert his holy memory in our register [Note: [Col. 0557D] See note 256.].

#### Monastery of the Holy Sepulchre [Note: [Col. 0557D] Since this Title immediately follows the Title of the cathedral church of Piacenza, the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre whose name it bears is undoubtedly, as may easily be gathered from what was just said in notes 258 and 271, the Benedictine abbey of Piacenza called by that name, founded in 1056, as Lubinus explains in his Brief Notice of the Abbeys of Italy, p. 300.]

[Col. 0557B]

**6.** The community of the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre will willingly fulfill what you request [Note: [Col. 0557D] See note 261.]

#### Church of Saint Martin of Petra

**7.** We, the canons of the Church of Saint Martin, which is called Petra [Note: [Col. 0557D] I have nowhere been able to find information about this monastery. Nevertheless, from what I said above in note 258, I think it was situated between Piacenza and the Clusian monastery of the diocese of Turin, whose Title follows immediately here.], gratefully receive this sheet and, with humble mind, enter its commemoration in our register, observing the memory of this religious man, Bruno, on the day of his anniversary.

#### Monastery of Clusium [Note: [Col. 0557D] Lubinus, in his Brief Notice of the Abbeys of Italy, lists two Benedictine abbeys bearing the name of Clusa, one dedicated to Saint Victor and the other to Saint Michael, p. 104. There can be no doubt that the latter is the monastery of Clusium mentioned here, both because it alone is older than the Saint and because the Title that follows includes this verse:

“So that he may grant him everlasting rest, with Michael interceding.”]

**8.** The college of Clusium, sufficiently humble and small, will daily [Note: [Col. 0558C] That is, every day.] pray to the Lord for Bruno, a companion in religion and an outstanding teacher of eminent faith, who devoted himself in his lifetime to the prayers of our most holy Father Benedict. It mourns that it will be deprived of the consolation of so great a man. It will impose Masses upon the brothers and complete its Psalter, namely a thirty-day office [Note: [Col. 0558C] That is, an office of thirty Masses, to be completed over as many days for the dead. See Du Cange, Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin, under *Tricenarium*.]. It will also carefully enter him among the names of the brothers, celebrate his annual feast devoutly, and pray:

“So that he may grant him everlasting rest, with Michael interceding.”

We wish to be fortified by the shield of your prayers, through which we do not doubt that we and our dead may be admitted among the company of the saints.

#### Church of Segusium [Note: [Col. 0558C] Segusium, called Susa by its inhabitants, is an Italian city in Piedmont, at the foot of the Cottian Alps, through which there is passage into Savoy and Gaul. Since at the time when our Saint died, that is, at the beginning of the twelfth century, this city contained several churches besides the abbey church of Saint Justus, although none of them was a cathedral, I cannot determine whether one particular church is designated here, or whether perhaps all of them together are meant. Or perhaps the church of the abbey of Saint Justus is called the Church of Segusium by excellence because its abbot exercised considerable episcopal rights at Segusium, as Francis Augustine ab Ecclesia explains in chapter 22 of his Chronological History of the Cardinals, Archbishops, and Region of Piedmont?]

**9.** Divine authority has decreed, and the apostolic judgment likewise teaches, that brothers should bear one another’s burdens. Therefore, supported by the teaching of this authority, our humble and small Church of Segusium implores God’s mercy by pouring forth prayers, so that the soul of so great a religious man, namely the deceased Bruno, may obtain pardon for his sins through the perpetual grace of God [Note: [Col. 0558D] See again note 261.]

#### Provostship of Ulcium

**10.** We, the humble brothers of the Church of Saint Lawrence of Ulcium, which is otherwise called the Parish of the Martyrs [Note: [Col. 0558D] In the geographical map of the Dauphiné and neighboring regions prefixed to the historical monuments published at Paris in 1711, not far from Segusium in the direction of Lyon there appears the village of Ulcium. It occupies the same position in other geographical maps of the Dauphiné and is distinguished by the French name Oulx. Thus the brothers who administered that village’s church, dedicated to Saint Lawrence, or inhabited its provostship, most probably wrote this Title (see what was said in note 258).], for so great and religious a man, for whom the whole world ought also to pour forth prayers without ceasing, shall perform an office with a thirty-day observance [Note: [Col. 0558D] That is, if I am not mistaken, the office for the dead called Vigils, together with thirty Masses. See note 269.] and thereafter, with divine grace supplying the means, shall perform his anniversary.

#### Church of Grenoble

**11.** The Church of Grenoble, for which Lord Bruno, monk and hermit, first intended to make himself a hermitage and a dwelling [Note: [Col. 0559C] This means the hermitage of Chartreuse, which the Saint inhabited before he withdrew to Calabria and which is situated in the diocese of Grenoble.], rejoiced so greatly in his presence, thinking that it would have him permanently, and now grieves all the more, above others, at the absence of so great and incomparable a man. Therefore it willingly performs an unceasing office of his commemoration until the thirtieth day [Note: [Col. 0559C] That is, the thirtieth day. See Du Cange, Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin, under *Trigesimus*.]. It also distributed bread and wine, together with the other foods consumed meanwhile by the brothers of the same Congregation, to the poor for the soul of that same man. It has placed the day of his departure, on which he returned his soul, worthy of remembrance, to God, in the catalogue of the greatest and most illustrious men, and has continually promised to observe it as an anniversary and solemn day. Therefore we ask you with humble prayer to remember us, so that we may become participants in your prayers and supplications.

#### Hermitage of Chartreuse near Grenoble

**12.** We too, the brothers of Chartreuse, left more miserably than all others without the consolation of our most devout Father Bruno, a man of the highest renown, cannot decide what we should do for his beloved and holy soul. For the merits of his benefits toward us surpass whatever we can do or are able to do. Therefore, as for our only father and lord, we shall pray for him now and forever; and whatever custom of Masses and other spiritual exercises concerning the dead is maintained among us, we shall perform continually for his soul, as sons [Note: [Col. 0559C] The religious inhabitants of the hermitage of Chartreuse also promise quite clearly here that they will observe the anniversary of their holy Father.]

#### The Brothers of the House of God beneath Curnillion, near Grenoble

**13.** We, the brothers and servants of the servants of the House of God, living in the cell of Blessed Mary, which is otherwise called [Col. 0560A] Cornelio [Note: [Col. 0559D] This cell or priory, dependent upon the celebrated abbey of the Order and Rule of Benedict called the House of God in Auvergne, lies beside the part of Grenoble facing Lyon, on the right bank of the river Isère, as I learn from the geographical map of the Dauphiné cited above.], and which is near the hermitage of Chartreuse, shall, for the holiness of so great a man—through whose teaching and example so great a stock has borne fruit in Christ—celebrate the office and Masses for seven days. We shall give bread and wine, together with the other foods, to the poor as to one of our brothers, and we shall enter his anniversary commemoration in our catalogue.

#### The Brothers of Saint Ruffus at the Costa of Saint Andrew

**14.** We, the brothers from the canons of Saint Ruffus, living in a certain cell of Saint Andrew, commonly called Costa [Note: [Col. 0559D] On the same geographical map, between Grenoble and Lyon, there appears a place called Costa of Saint Andrew. It is therefore either the very cell or priory mentioned here, dependent upon the monastery of Saint Ruffus, now situated near Valence, or at least includes it, if it still exists.], shall celebrate Matins and Masses for seven consecutive days for the soul of the most devout Bruno [Note: [Col. 0559D] The office once called the Septenary, which was performed for the dead over seven consecutive days, is promised here. See Du Cange, Glossary, under *Septenarius*.]. We shall also give, for the consolation of his soul, a provision [Note: [Col. 0560C] If I am not mistaken, *praebenda* here means an alms consisting of a monastic portion, or a portion supplied by the monastery; thus the brothers whose Title this is seem to promise that for seven days they will give the poor as much food and drink as their community would have consumed during that time. See Title XI.] as to one of our own, and we shall keep his name written in the catalogue of our brothers.

#### Monastery of Athanacum at Lyon [Note: [Col. 0560D] This Benedictine monastery, formerly outside the walls of Lyon but now enclosed within them, was built at the confluence of the Saône and Rhône in the sixth century or earlier. Consult the enlarged Christian Gaul, vol. IV, col. 233.]

[Col. 0560B]

**15.** The community of Athanacum, forewarned by a divine oracle, has performed a general office [Note: [Col. 0560D] That is, an office for the dead celebrated with the most solemn rite possible. See Carpentier in the Supplement to Du Cange’s Glossary under *Officium generale*.] for the soul of the religious and God-beloved Bruno, together with prayers and supplications, and, having entered him with the brothers in writing, has rendered the services of commendation.

#### The Greater Church of Lyon

**16.**

Death spares the prudent no more than the foolish.

Bruno was prudent, yet swiftly fell beneath death.

Behold, Bruno lies pressed down in a single tomb,

Who, as far as he could, devoted himself to justice.

He flourished in life, having become a simple hermit.

If this man was guilty, spare him, O God,

[Col. 0560C] To whom beautiful songs are offered uselessly in place of psalms.

It would profit him more to say three times, “Have mercy on me.”

#### Saint Mary of Blois [Note: [Col. 0560D] In the city of Blois, as the writers of the enlarged Christian Gaul, vol. VIII, col. 1388, explain, there is an abbey of Canons Regular, served in the ninth century by secular canons, called Saint Mary of Blois or Middle Borough. This is undoubtedly what is designated here by Saint Mary of Blois.]

**17.**

There is no need to mourn or grieve at the father’s death.

Bruno has not died, for he fixed his portion in the one thing [Note: [Col. 0560D] There seems to be an allusion to Luke 10:42: “But one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better portion.”].

God received him; the devout multitude welcomed him as a companion.

#### Monastery of Saint Peter of Cluny [Note: [Col. 0561C] Since I find nowhere a monastery called Climiacum, I think an error has entered the name as written [Col. 0561D] and that *Climiacensis* should be read as *Cluniacensis*, so that the monastery founded in the year 910 is designated here.]

[Col. 0561A]

**18.**

By right, grief ought to be expressed for the death of a patron [Note: [Col. 0561D] That is, a teacher, lord, or even prior.].

Let the mother rejoice, and let the father himself rejoice.

We have performed the service that the little sheet ordered to be performed.

And may you do the same for us.

#### Saint Romanus, archdeacon of the Church of Lyon [Note: [Col. 0561D] I do not sufficiently understand what this inscription of the Title means.]

**19.**

Lord Bruno, who always under one ruler

Kept the sacred law and did not violate it,

The end of life is here; therefore the hermits grieve.

After death, the highest joys of life have been given to you.

Therefore let the hermits not utter laments for you.

While living in the world, you entered deserted places.

Now, having gained the heavens, you rejoice in Christ’s company.

#### Church of Saint Vincent of Chalon [Note: [Col. 0561D] The cathedral church of Chalon, or Cabillonum, received the name of Saint Vincent the Martyr as early as the year 541, replacing its former dedication to Saint Stephen; thus no other church than this is evidently designated in the inscription.]

**20.**

Since the written record testifies that his life was well spent,

And since the ability to die diminishes no one’s honor,

Tears ought to be laid aside for the death of the patron.

For God has granted him a dwelling in the heavenly abode.

Now, therefore, brothers, as we sing psalms and Masses,

Let us return praises and songs to our Christ,

So that it may benefit all that we have honored him.

#### Church of Saint Mary of Beauvais [Note: [Col. 0561D] In the city of Beauvais, or, as it is now more commonly written, Bellovacum, besides the cathedral church dedicated to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, there are six collegiate churches, one of which is dedicated to the most holy Mother of God, Mary. Unless *Belvensis* is written here incorrectly for *Belnensis*, and the church dedicated to the holy Mother of God in the city of Beaune—which is not very far from Chalon in Burgundy—is intended, the following Title most probably refers to this church.]

**21.**

Bruno, the simple hermit, has departed from this life;

He is lifted to the citadel of heaven, leaving the earth beneath the stars,

And so rests with Christ, freed from this world,

Praying for all who live and for those who have now died [Note: [Col. 0562D] This Title plainly indicates that Saint Bruno has been received into heaven and prays there for the living. Nearly the same is said in the four Titles immediately preceding and in many others below; this is certainly evidence that not a few regarded him as a Saint immediately after his death. See also the Preliminary Commentary, no. 749, and the Saint’s Life written by Surius, no. 45.]

#### Saint Anthony of Conty [Note: [Col. 0562D] Could this perhaps designate the church of Saint Anthony of Conty, or Contiacum, in Picardy, listed on p. 22 of the general catalogue of benefices of the diocese of Amiens, printed at Paris in 1648?]

**22.**

Whatever the world contains, whatever is called living,

If I have discerned rightly, remains subject to change.

Thus we are held beneath uncertain mutability.

Both unstable things and we ourselves, together with what is ours, seem so.

Fate turns, and the daily fates turn with it.

They themselves totter, as though they were being shaken in an urn.

The world’s sweetness is a fleeting and fearful thing,

And it must be avoided like a flame of fire placed beneath it.

All receive death through such sweetness.

Perish that sweetness which brings gall and vinegar.

It deceives all who are bound to it by a pleasing fetter;

At last it gives the deceived the same reward.

That reward is indeed given to all: the outcome is the same.

O miserable everyman, although you see that you are deceived,

[Col. 0562A] You nevertheless seem to care little about it,

And I judge that you possess a deceived light of the heart.

For it is darkened, so that you may not see your losses.

You neither hold fast what ought to be retained nor wish to move what ought to be removed.

Alas, miserable minds, fearing too little what ought to be feared,

Who care for what lasts briefly rather than for what lasts a long time,

Too intent upon things suddenly changed!

Death, a frightening name, offered a pitiable omen

To the race to come, first ill-known to its parent.

Death arrives, and the living die; no certain end is found

In this life: Bruno the hermit proves this.

Bruno has fallen, whose home was the forest and whose food was grass;

Because he was pure, he scorned to possess the world.

Holy Mother of Christ, who alone pleased God,

[Col. 0562B] Grant that a seat of rest may be given to him.

#### By the same

**23.**

Bruno, worshiper of God, noble avenger of vices,

May you possess rest before the face of God.

Reader, be confident, since he is now safe and about to enter [into rest; the reading is uncertain]; nevertheless, once his due offices have been completed, say for him: Amen.

#### Saint Peter of Chartres [Note: [Col. 0562D] Already before the tenth century, as may be seen in the enlarged Christian Gaul, vol. VIII, col. 1213, there existed at the foot of the hill on which the city of Chartres stands a Benedictine monastery called Saint Peter in the Valley. This is undoubtedly what is designated here by Saint Peter of Chartres.]

**24.**

The assembly of Silvester, sparing its flowing tears:

The shepherd’s life, redeemed by the practice of faith,

Gives us a reason to rejoice, not to shed tears.

If he dies to the world, he gains a seat in paradise.

He subdued the flesh; while he reaches toward the citadel of heaven,

He joins himself to Christ as he departs from this world.

Yet if any fault, however small, wounded the innermost parts of the Father’s flesh,

Let abundant mercy wipe it away—

[Col. 0562C] The mercy of him whom he hastened with his whole desire to behold.

O soldier of Christ, who departed victorious from the battle,

How well you fought, since by fighting you overcame!

Scorning earthly things, you receive pleasant wages;

You live and rejoice, and knock at the thresholds of the palace.

Christ, because this weary man seeks you, meet him face to face,

Giving him rest, giving him a day without end.

#### Saint Denis near Paris

**25.**

If prose or verse could bring salvation,

Neither prose nor verse, Bruno, will bring you salvation,

For prose or verse flies from the talkative mouth about you,

And benefits you in this way: if they could prevent you

[Col. 0563A] From being tormented and devoured by the threatening mouth of the serpent,

Then prose or verse could bring salvation.

Therefore, let the melody of the heart sound with the voice’s resonance,

So that we may meditate upon what prose or verse contains,

And pray from the heart to the Lord that what it sounds may come to pass.

Worthy Father Bruno, may you be saved from the fire

Which will belong not to the just but always to the rejected.

And if anything is lacking, which perfection does not provide,

May our devotion be able to have that granted and added

To your shortcomings, if God hears us.

But God will hear and will act, because we ask for what is just.

Therefore may God hear and grant what we ask justly,

So that unfailing heavenly light may be granted to you,

And to you together with us and all those named in this title.

#### Saint Germanus of Paris [Note: [Col. 0563C] There is no other church or monastery of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, at Paris than that called Saint Germanus of the Meadows. I therefore think that this institution, whose foundation dates back to the sixth century, is designated in the inscription of the Title below.]

[Col. 0563B]

**26.**

The light in which the wicked will undergo evils and the just [receive] good things

Ought always to be present in our minds.

Bruno feared it, a true lover of wisdom;

Here, in mortal flesh, he stripped off the old man.

Christ carried him from earth to the stars.

Servant of God Bruno, may your Creator receive you.

May you enjoy everlasting rest in paradise.

May all our people and all the faithful possess it.

#### Saint Magloire of Paris [Note: [Col. 0563C] This Parisian monastery, founded long before Saint Bruno’s time, has now been suppressed. See the enlarged Christian Gaul, col. 306 and the following three columns.]

**27.**

When the bodily diseases have been dissolved, why does the world grieve?

The punishment having ended, if they enjoy pleasant peace,

There is no need to weep, because they rejoice in perpetual light.

A man is worthy of praise; nevertheless, you must help him in this respect:

Spare him, Redeemer, who is made of earthly matter.

#### Saint Peter of Fosses [Note: [Col. 0563C] The Basel edition of these titles adds: “At which place Saint Maurus, disciple of blessed Benedict, rests bodily.” Thus the monastery designated by this inscription can be none other than Fosses of Saint Maurus, which was built in the ninth century, as the writers of the enlarged Christian Gaul, vol. VII, columns 282 and 284, explain, and has now been abolished.]

[Col. 0563C]

28. May his soul, in the name of Christ, rest in peace. Amen.

A thousand verses do no good for a soul;

Yet pray that it may rest in peace. Amen.

**[The title of] the monastery of the Holy Cross and Saint Faro of Meaux**  
[Note: The writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 1688 and the following two columns, provide extensive information about this monastery, which is much older than Saint Bruno.]

[Col. 0564A]

29. This man was well known for his learning and blessed

Conduct and life: Bruno, the wise hermit;

In first principles, highest things, and lowest, he shone.

After becoming a monk, he gained heavenly joys.

Behold, Bruno lies enclosed in a single tomb.

For thus the wise are taken away when they die,

Into the camp of the Lord, beneath the powerful stars.

Let no one wonder if Bruno is held to be holy:

By his life, this simple hermit deserved to be called so.

But if he sinned, and perhaps has not yet atoned for it,

May the Lord forgive him this and crown him in heaven.

**[The title of] the monastery of Saint Peter of Casiacum**  
[Note: This monastery, situated on the left bank of the Marne, two leagues below Château-Thierry in the diocese of Soissons, is believed to be older than the ninth, indeed than the eighth, century. See the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 427 and the following columns.]

30. May he who deigned to become

Man for the salvation of humanity

Deign to grant forgiveness to your patron.

## SECTION II

[Col. 0564B]

**The title of the church of Saint Mary of Chartres**  
[Note: The cathedral church of Chartres venerates as its patron the blessed Mary assumed into heaven, as the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 1091, informs me; hence I think that no other church than this is designated here. Moreover, since between the title of this Chartres church given below and the twenty-fourth title, which belongs to the monastery of Saint Peter situated in the city of Chartres, several other titles are inserted—namely, those of Saint Denis near Paris, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Saint Maglorius of Paris, Saint Peter of Fossat, Saint Faro of Meaux, and Saint Peter of Casiacum, situated in the diocese of Soissons—and since it in no way appears probable that the brother of the hermitage of Tournus, who carried about the encyclical letter announcing Saint Bruno’s death, would on his journey for this purpose have returned to Chartres after proceeding from that city to Paris, then to Meaux and Casiacum, a monastery of the diocese of Soissons, it is clear that all the funeral titles which were not written on the separate sheet mentioned in the notes attached to the preceding section, note 258, are not listed in the Basel edition, which I follow, in the precise order in which they were placed on the Roll. Those responsible for that edition, as appears, especially disrupted that order by inserting certain titles which had been written on separate sheets because an annual commemoration of the saints’ day had been promised to them. The matter will become clearer from the annotations made below in their proper places.]

31. Bruno was the church’s wall, not destined to fall,

For he was good, possessed of a devout mind and wisdom.

He was a true teacher: let the good people and clergy mourn him.

Just, sincere, severe in the gravity of his character,

Bruno died while fighting beneath one king.

He fought in such a way that he overcame the Duke’s enemies;

He was his soldier, and therefore let him seek a reward

From the Duke of the saints: the joyous kingdoms of heaven.

And let us pray in a thousand ways, with psalms and hymns,

That Christ may give him the light of supreme rest.

For if anyone deserved to have this reward,

Let no one suppose that Bruno is deprived of it.

**Scholars’ verses**  
[Note: In former times every cathedral church had its own school, where those who wished were instructed in refined letters and other sciences. The title following this inscription therefore belongs to those who attended the school of the cathedral church of Chartres.]

[Col. 0564C]

32. Whoever does not know who Bruno was, in a single moment,

Let him come here if he wishes to learn.

He was just, exceedingly wise, and gracious;

Yet it harmed no one to learn what he was able to teach.

[Col. 0565A] To him we offer devout prayers, and we ask our father

That, fleeing madness, he may possess rest.

If Bruno lived as he is thought to have lived,

May he live forever and enjoy the seat of paradise.

He was the flower of fathers, the comfort and glory of brothers,

A follower of truth, a lover of divine law,

The path of justice, a fountain and source of wisdom,

The world’s light and mirror, the lofty summit of all things,

A staff for the fallen, a sweet relief for the wretched;

His mind was neither broken by misfortunes nor excessively exalted by prosperity.

He did not live for himself, but for the world, which he governed well.

It is not he but life, bereft of him, that mourns this hermit.

He had no need of life, since he lived for the world and not for himself.

To tell briefly: who could tell it adequately?

[Col. 0565B] As Phoebus [is] to Phoebus, as the other stars [are] to the moon [the wording is corrupt],

So may the whole world attend you, Gallic Bruno.  
[Note: Do not infer from this that Saint Bruno was of Gallic nationality. See the preliminary Commentary, no. 42.]

**[The title of] the monastery of Saint Margaret**  
[Note: The Basel edition adds: “which is situated in the wilderness.” Yet I have found neither a monastery nor a church to which this inscription applies. Nor would I dare assert that this monastery was situated either in the diocese of Chartres or near it. Neither conclusion can be drawn from the fact that its title is placed here after the title of the cathedral church of Chartres, since the funeral titles not written on the separate sheet mentioned in the Notes attached to the preceding section, note 258, are not always listed in the same order in which they were placed on the funeral Roll containing the encyclical letter announcing Saint Bruno’s death, as I have already shown at note 253.]

33. To the Father, with the Son, be praise, and with the holy Spirit;

He sustains the world and governs heaven by his authority.

May the angels with the seraphim, and likewise the blessed cherubim,

Together with all the other saints, the just, and the blessed,

Meet him together, rejoicing and glad.

And yet, with those hosts standing all around,

With the thrones of virtues and the just powers,

May they truly bless the Lord and praise the King,

Ready to attend the soul of illustrious Bruno.

Soon may Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Job, and Elijah,

Isaiah, Daniel, David, and the most holy Joel,

Habakkuk, Obadiah, Zephaniah, and Jeremiah

[Col. 0565C] With the other prophets present him before the sight of Christ.

May they beseech him humbly and gladly to be enriched by this gift,

And may we, with them, offer devout songs of praise.

Although we are unworthy, may he deserve to be blessed with light;

Heaven rejoices, earth groans, and now echoes the rejoicing.

**[The title of] Saint Mary’s of the New Monastery**  
[Note: Unless the title given below refers to the abbey of Nogent in the diocese of Laon, dedicated to the most holy Mother of God and founded in 1076, as the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 603, report, I likewise cannot determine what monastery is designated here or approximately where this monastery of Saint Mary of the New Monastery was situated. The reason for this uncertainty is clear from what was said in the preceding note.]

34. We, the brothers of the New Monastery, as you requested,

Will earnestly implore the Lord’s mercy for your father,

The lord Bruno, a man worthy of holy remembrance.

**[The title of] Saint Benignus of Dijon**  
[Note: The monastery bearing the name of Saint Benignus, to which this inscription and the following title belong, is situated in the diocese of Langres. See the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 668, who state there that it was founded around the year 500.]

35. Since one must rise again, there is no need to grieve over death.

Death does not know how to spare; the just man rests well in death.

We offer mutual prayers and ask the same services for our own.

**[The title of] Saint Stephen of Dijon**  
[Note: The ancient secular church of Saint Stephen of Dijon, in the diocese of Langres, which adopted the Rule of Saint Augustine in 1113 and returned from the regular to the secular state in 1611, does not itself know its origins, as the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, who trace these only to the beginning of the ninth century, report in vol. IV, col. 752.]

36. May he who rules all that exists free him from every fault.

May he who rules all that exists join him to the just.

Pay to our own the same services that you request from us:

Offices, psalms, hymns, vows, and prayers.

May Bruno’s spirit be received in heaven,

[Col. 0566B] And may it be with Christ, whom he followed while he lived.

May he obtain for us that we may approach him—

Us whom this world desires to perish in the dregs of sin.

**[The title of] Saint Peter of Beza**  
[Note: This is a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, situated four leagues from Dijon in the diocese of Langres; it was built in the seventh century. See the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 703.]

37. Bruno, the supreme hermit, passes from this life,

And all the wise and learned mourn him.

He lived wisely and departed wisely to the heights.

May he now possess heaven, may he now diligently stand beside Christ,

Praying securely for the brothers devoted to him.

**[The title of] Saint Mary of Châtillon**  
[Note: In the suburb of the city of Châtillon there was a church adorned with the name of Saint Mary (see the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 770). Canons were first instituted there toward the end of the tenth century by Bruno, bishop of Langres—for the city lies in the diocese of Langres—and it subsequently became a parish and finally an abbey. This is undoubtedly what is designated here.]

38. This great and simple man, Bruno, was like a lamb;

Seeing the world becoming worthless, and scorning everything,

He changed his life and mortified his body with hunger.

After becoming a monk and entering the vast wilderness,

[Col. 0566C] Leaving this place, he ascended to the dwelling of heaven,

Where may the desired place of rest be granted him;

And if he injured anyone, or if any guilt clung to him,

May the great grace of God forgive him this.

**[The title of] the bishops of the church of Langres**  
[Note: On this bishop of Langres, whose title follows, see the preliminary Commentary, nos. 96 and following.]

39. Robert, servant of the church of Langres, asked the canons and priests of that same church, the monks, [Col. 0567A] and the hermits serving the Lord in the bishopric of Langres, to pray for the soul of their most beloved master Bruno and to distribute alms to the poor; and, insofar as he can, he will have the written commemoration of his death observed in the churches.

**[The title of] Saint Mary of Molesme**  
[Note: Beyond doubt the famous monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict is designated here, distinguished by the name Molesme or also Molernium. It was built in honor of the most holy Virgin Mary by Saint Robert, its first abbot, in the territory of Langres between Montbard and Mussy, at a time already well advanced in the eleventh century, as we explained under 29 April, when Saint Robert was commemorated among us.]

40. At the appointed time Bruno departs from the body;

While he lived, his life pleased God.

May those to whom authority has been entrusted come to his aid,

That rest and endless day may be his.

By our little verses, we who dwell at Molesme, we inform you who are at Tournus

That, for the lord Bruno, your patron and our closest friend,  
[Note: This confirms the opinion that Saint Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, before withdrawing into the wilderness of Chartreuse, spent some time in the solitude of Sèche-Fontaine. Consult the preliminary Commentary, no. 417.]

We celebrated solemn Masses for thirty days, and also entered the anniversary

[Col. 0567B] Of his death in the catalogue of our brothers.

**[The title of] the monastery of Saint Michael of Tonnerre**  
[Note: This monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, situated in the diocese of Langres on Mount Volutus, overlooking the city of Tonnerre, was restored in 980 by Milo, count of Tonnerre, with the assistance of Widricus, the diocesan bishop. See the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 712.]

41. The holy death of the just man enjoys the kingdom of heaven,

And by his death Bruno was joined to the sacred company.

May he live and enjoy the gifts of wisdom in rest;

May he, blessed, rejoice and also behold the face of the Father,

Which Christ will enable the blessed to see forever.

**[The title of] Saint Germanus of Auxerre**  
[Note: This most ancient monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict is situated in the city of Auxerre and was built a very long time before Saint Bruno’s age, as may be seen from the information supplied about it by the brothers of Sainte-Marthe in the old *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, p. 477.]

42. May Bruno’s dwelling be wholly everlasting in heaven,

And may life become his companion with God.

Take care always to pray that prayers may be granted to us

Through his merits in the heavenly abodes.

**[The title of] Saint Stephen of Auxerre**  
[Note: The cathedral, or church, of Auxerre is dedicated to Saint Stephen. I therefore think that the following title belongs to it; for I see no other church or monastery to which it could belong.]

[Col. 0567C]

43. Bruno was a devout shepherd, a lover of pure devotion;

Everywhere he overcame the fiery arrows of the devil.

He was exceedingly generous to his subjects and sparing toward himself;

By his deeds he fulfilled whatever he taught in words.

He did not desire to be called a prelate, but wished to be loved.

May he rejoice in heaven, for he lived faithful in heart.

**[The title of] the monastery of Saint Mary and Saint John of Réomé**  
[Note: There is no doubt that the monastery of Réomé, or Réome, in the diocese of Langres, is designated here. Since it was originally dedicated to the most holy Virgin Mary, it was later also named after Saint John, its first abbot, who founded it around the year 440. See again the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 658.]

[Col. 0568A]

44. Giving good things, Christ, grant Bruno, your servant, the kingdoms of heaven,

To him who exchanged the world’s flower and all its beauty

For the worthless wilderness, which was dearer to him than a kingdom

In this life. Now the many writings have ceased;

Let the vows owed to the teacher be rendered to Bruno,

And also to all his own and to our departed,

The true servants of Christ and righteous followers,

Who now inhabit the beloved stronghold of the wilderness, the Tower [the transmitted wording is corrupt];

May it lead you, like your own Master, to the stars.

Know, dearest ones, that we, your brothers of Réomé, observed the memory of your Patron in Masses and prayers for thirty days, and wrote his name, as was fitting, together with the names of our brother monks.

**[The title of] Lambert, abbot of Pultaria**  
[Note: On Lambert, the abbot to whom the following title belongs, and on the monastery of Pultaria, which he governed, see the preliminary Commentary, nos. 97 and following, as well as the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 724 and following.]

[Col. 0568B]

45. I, brother Lambert, by the necessity of apostolic obedience a servant and humble procurator of the monastery of Pultaria, a disciple from the beginning of my conversion from the world in the knowledge of literary learning and in the instruction of Catholic conduct and true religion under this outstanding master Bruno, will not grow weary of arranging and devoutly pursuing, with the sons and brothers entrusted to me, the memory of this most devout father and teacher through weekly and thirty-day offices and on the anniversary of his death, with spiritual songs and the annual refreshment of the poor; and we will rouse to pray for him as many as we can.  
[Note: Lambert, abbot of Pultaria, here shows himself exceptionally grateful toward Saint Bruno, once his teacher. To see what he promises by the weekly and thirty-day offices, consult notes 269 and 279.]

**[The title of] the monastery of Saint Peter of Aremar**  
[Note: This monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, situated four leagues from Troyes in the diocese of Troyes, was founded in 837, as may be seen in the brothers of Sainte-Marthe’s old *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, p. 78.]

[Col. 0568C]

46. Jesus, fountain and source of goodness, be merciful to Bruno;

Lest the lion touch the sheep, bring help, good Shepherd.

Let Bruno be your lamb, not the devil’s kid;

If he deserved punishment, spare the guilty man, O Goodness—

**[The title of] Saint Peter of Troyes**  
[Note: Since in Troyes there is no sacred place bearing the name of Saint Peter except the cathedral church, that church is undoubtedly designated here.]

47. As the title says, Bruno, a wise man who obeyed God’s commands,

Conquered the world’s trials.

He despised great wealth and possessed no resource of his own,

But whatever he could, he provided for his brother.

He fled this life, became a monk, and thereafter a hermit;

By such abstinence he earned the kingdom of heaven.

But since it is right that we should pray equally for a brother,

We ask that rest may be yours each day.

**[The title of] Saint Peter of the German Island**  
[Note: I have nowhere been able to find information about this place.]

48. Would that you, O death, had died or been shut in prison,

And had not stolen from the world so great a teacher!

For him we ask Christ, the source of goodness,

To grant Bruno the gift of his accustomed mercy.

Christ, Word of the Father, grant the heavenly kingdom

To Bruno, your servant, who in a pure heart

[Col. 0569B] Joined himself to you while living and scorned worldly joys.

Therefore, brothers who dwell in hermit cloisters,

Return now to our own what we do for yours:

May those taken away by death thereby attain paradise.

**[The title of] the church of Saint Stephen of Châlons**  
[Note: I think *Catalmiensis* is written here mistakenly for *Catalaunensis*, and that the cathedral church of the city of Châlons is therefore designated—the church which recognizes Saint Stephen the Protomartyr as its patron, as the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, cols. 858–859, report.]

49. The first-created man sinned; why should his later offspring,

Paying the penalty for the father’s deed, move toward destruction?

All perish, but not all are tormented.

Death comes to the unjust; life and salvation come to the good.

This Bruno, then, a man of holy religion,

Scorning the world, earned heavenly things.

Therefore we devoutly pray to the Lord

That he who was just may be justified still further.

**[The title of] the monastery of Saint Peter on the Mount**  
[Note: This monastery is situated in the diocese of Châlons and had already been built in the eleventh century. See the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 927.]

[Col. 0569C]

50. Dying, Christ bore us; rising from death,

God is hope in death, God alone is glory.

Grant Bruno everlasting rest, Christ,

And may joys with the saints be his according to his merits.

**[The title of] Saint Basolus**  
[Note: This monastery, situated in the diocese of Reims, was built after Saint Nivard, archbishop of Reims, had died around the year 673, as the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 196, report; this was shown under 1 September, when he was commemorated among us.]

51. May Bruno enter the heavens, which his strenuous life adorns,

And may the glory of his faith deservedly increase for him.

**[The title of] Saint Mary of Reims, the metropolitan church**

52. This outstanding father, founder of religion,

Presented himself as an example to his brothers,

Giving them a model for scorning the worthless things of the world,

While he pursued the rewards of the heavenly homeland.

[Col. 0569D] For whose fault we do not believe that we ought to grieve,

Whom we believe already rejoicing in rest.

[Col. 0570A] For if a good life earns rest for any saint,

The highest rest is likewise granted to him according to his merits.

Although he shone in many ways in our city,

And became a comfort and an ornament to his own people,

And although fortune favored him in everything, so that already

We preferred him to all others, and with good reason—

For he was kind, skilled in every art,

Very eloquent, and powerful through his wealth—

He set everything aside for Christ and, following Christ naked,

Was received into the wilderness with many others.  
[Note: From this you may infer that when Bruno withdrew into the wilderness, he had been living not in Paris but in Reims, amid the highest favors of prosperous fortune. See the preliminary Commentary, no. 154 and the following two numbers.]

Therefore we believe that rest has been prepared for him.

Yet if any slight stain clung to him

—for it is clear that no one remains on earth without blemish—

May God wipe it away by granting him forgiveness.

**Another of the same church**

[Col. 0570B]

53. As Joseph, scorning his mistress’s love,

Fled her incestuous embraces with manly resolve,

So, Bruno, the world’s glory lies scorned by you.

While it desired to embrace you, stretching out its arms toward you,

The world displayed much wealth and many attractions;

But you escaped, rejecting splendid clothing,

And, embracing the wilderness, clothed yourself in blessed fortune.

We believe that such a man, so great, is a companion of the heavenly beings.

The whole devotion of the brothers asks him

To deign to pour out prayers to the Lord on their behalf;

Yet if his inner self has drawn from the outer

Any stain, O God, wash it away with the dew of your mercy.

**Another of the same**

54. Fearing the examination of the coming Judge,

[Col. 0570C] Bruno scorned worldly wealth and sought the wilderness.  
[Note: The anonymous author of a *Treatise on Saint Bruno*, communicated to me by the Carthusians of this place, conjectures that this alludes to the Parisian portent concerning the dead man who himself proclaimed his damnation. Yet that writer himself admits that this conjecture has little force in establishing the gruesome story. Consult the preliminary Commentary, §21.]

There he put forth the sweet fruit of fragrance,

Calling back to Christ those whom vain glory had deceived.

Night and day he watched over God’s commandments,

An example to all whom the life of the wilderness adorns.

Oh, with what happy reward for their merits do they rejoice,

Those who become companions of the heavenly hosts,

And find places of light, ignorant of corruption,

Where eternal joys are celebrated at everlasting feasts—

Places for which he longed, desiring here to be dissolved,

So that in Christ he might reign together with the blessed!

Finally, when the struggle was ended and he was freed from the flesh,

Enjoying what he desired, he ascended freely to heaven.

But if anything belonging to earthly fortune [or: earthly stain] clung to him,

[Col. 0570D] So that nothing might be lacking from the tomb [or: sum] of his reward,

[Col. 0571A] Let us assail the Lord with prayers, whom all things revere,

That no torments of hell may hold power over him.

**Another again of the same**

55. This man was like Elijah and John the Baptist;

He was a cultivator of the wilderness and a lover of goodness.

Like Abraham, he was devout and faithful;

Like Peter, he followed the Lord’s commands,

Scorned everything, and clung to Christ in poverty.

He preferred to be poor with Christ rather than live rich in the world,

And thus he completely fulfilled God’s commandments.

But since death carries away with it everything that belongs to the world,

It took him from the world and joined him to the heavenly beings.

Let us, however, ask the Lord’s mercy,

[Col. 0571B] That if any worldly dust clung to so great a father,

God, the fountain of mercy, may wipe it away.

**Still another of the same**

56. Mother Reims, who taught Bruno as her tender pupil,  
[Note: From this we infer that Saint Bruno, while still very young, devoted himself to learning in the city of Reims. See the preliminary Commentary, no. 54.]

Rejoicing that he kept faith with his purpose,

Greets Bruno as he departs to the Lord with tears and prayers.

**[The title of] the monastery of the holy martyrs Sergius and Bacchus at Angers**  
[Note: The monastery named after these holy martyrs, situated in the suburb of the episcopal city of Angers, is said by its religious inhabitants to have been built in the eighth century. See the brothers of Sainte-Marthe in the old *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, p. 820.]

57. The just and the reprobate alike face the single fate of dying,

And the same passage brings all alike to the end;

But the Judge of deeds distinguishes their destinations:

The good man passes to rest, the sinner to fire.

**[The title of] the monastery of Saint Peter for women**  
[Note: Two monasteries of sacred virgins bearing the name of Saint Peter once existed in the city of Reims; one was called the Upper, the other the Lower. The latter of these (see the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 178) had most probably already been abolished in Saint Bruno’s time. I therefore conjecture that the former is designated here—the one built toward the end of the sixth century, as may be seen in the same writers, vol. IX, col. 270, and which still survives today. Yet perhaps, though I do not think so, this should instead be understood as a women’s monastery situated elsewhere.]

[Col. 0571C]

58. Bruno, father, model of a devout life and the whole treasury of wisdom,

If he has departed from this life,

It is clear that he was released from the flesh at the Lord’s command,

Who wished to grant the just man a crown according to his merits.

Although we trust that he is among the heavenly choirs,

The consolations of our service will nevertheless not be lacking.

**[The title of] Saint Symphorianus the Martyr in the city of Reims**  
[Note: This abbey of the Order of Saint Benedict was founded in the eleventh century. See the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 807.]

59. If it were useful and beneficial to grieve over death,

Then let us mourn and weep over this father as well;

But since neither mourning nor a cry raised to heaven

[Col. 0572A] Can restore anyone from death to life,

Let us pray to Christ, who was fastened to the cross for us,

That this hermit may enjoy heavenly life.

We write this to you and ask the same in return: grant us the same.

**[The title of] the church of the Holy Trinity**  
[Note: I cannot determine with certainty what sacred place is designated here.]

60. As you ask, brothers, so will we do for you;

But Bruno reigns with Christ, as we believe,

This hermit who followed him with the cross held before him,

Repelling the world’s allurements with steadfast mind.

**[The title of] Saint Denis of Reims**  
[Note: This monastery of Reims was founded long before Saint Bruno’s time, as is clear from what the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 288, record about it.]

61. For you, Christ the Father, for the gift of heaven,

Bruno abandoned all wealth and all the world’s honors;

Made poor, Bruno set out on the path of those whose teacher he had formerly been.  
[Note: You may reasonably infer from this funeral title that Bruno, by his example, led some whom he had previously taught sacred or secular sciences to withdraw into the wilderness in order to do penance.]

As four springs flowing from one source,

Which paradise possesses and sends through the realms of the world,

Flood the lands, so he adorns those whom he instructed,

Fills them, forms them, inflames them, guides them, arms them,

Fashions and enlightens them, and still rules, cultivates, and prepares them.

Like a star, he prays for all whom he himself used to teach.

May he rest among the citizens of heaven in Christ’s court.

**[The title of] Saint Remigius, apostle of the Franks**  
[Note: This distinguished monastery is situated in the city of Reims and preceded Saint Bruno’s time by no small number of years. See the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 219 and following.]

62. Do not grieve, sheep, weeping at the death of your Shepherd;

For he is not to be mourned for whom Christ was life

And death gain, since he overcame the devil’s deceit—

This outstanding father, whom we rightly venerate;

And not only we, but those whom the fiery sun burns.

Since God himself cherishes him, and paradise now holds him

In the rest of peace, why, I ask, do you grieve for such a man?

[Col. 0572C] For he has been snatched from the world and granted life in heaven,

And truly lives, because he strove to live justly.

Grant, we ask, that he may reign with you, O God,

Giving him everlasting rest, to remain forever with you.

**[The title of] Saint Nicasius, archbishop of Reims**  
[Note: This monastery too is situated in the city of Reims and is much older than Saint Bruno’s time. See again the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 204 and following.]

63. O God, light of faithful souls,

Release the soul of this Catholic man from every bond of sin.

**[The title of] the holy martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris**  
[Note: At Reims there is a collegiate church called Saint Timothy. Unless I am mistaken, it is designated here.]

64. Such was the strength of this Teacher’s heart and speech

That throughout the whole world he surpassed all teachers:

Thus he was good in meditation and eloquent in speech.

All wisdom gave itself to him and took its seat

As a rich guest in his secret chambers.

What I say, I know; France too knows it with me,

And the whole world knows it throughout its four regions.

This knowledge taught him to scorn the affairs of this world

And made him seek only the joys of heaven.

If any stain from the law of the flesh clung to him

—for we are all completely burdened by the law of the flesh—

May the Almighty remove it, he who loosens our sins,

And fulfill for him the desire that he has always cherished.

**[The title of] Saint Bartholomew the Apostle on Mount Or**  
[Note: Since the monastery of Saint Thierry, situated on a mountain called Or by the ancient Gauls, three miles from the city of Reims, and built around the year 500, was formerly also known by the name of Saint Bartholomew, as the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 181, report, there can be no doubt that it is designated here.]

65. The world, growing bitter, limps beneath the weight of death,

And, wasting away, drags each person toward the appearance of human destiny

Through the byways of exile.

Why do you swell with pride, wretched man, growing old in this age?

You will be submerged in the Charybdis-like fountain at the furthest end,

And, as ashes, dissolved into ashes like the shadow of lamps.

Its labor is love and an inextricable error,

Through whose failure horror embraces the soul,

After it has been stripped from the prison of the flesh

Or, alas, surrounded by hosts led by Satan.

Fearing this, Bruno, courageous in such danger,

Penetrates the wilderness of struggle in a single service;

He abandons wealth and the world’s splendor, lest glory

Become punishment leading to destruction, but, as a vein running with nectar,

May sweeten the soul’s currents and the course of the heart,

Constricting within himself the love of sins,

Through the various courses of good works performed virtuously,

Mortifying the head of death together with the law of evils.

Therefore he deserved the companionship of the citizens of heaven,

Freed from the enemy of the Styx and from the things of Tartarus,

And he is joined to him through whom the world will be restored,

As long as the goal is distant, so pure at last from sickness,

That he may rest, rising again from wretched death,

And that the serpent, swelling with foul irritation, may not harm him.

## SECTION III

**The title of Saint Mary of Laon**  
[Note: The cathedral church of Laon, or rather of Laon, is dedicated to the most holy Mother of God; hence it plainly appears that the following title belongs to it.]

66. Bruno, the glory of the clergy and the glory and wisdom of the world,

While he was on earth, flourished in keenness of mind;

While he was among us, he flourished also in instruction.  
[Note: Among the Gauls, that is; or, if you prefer, among the inhabitants of the archdiocese of Reims, of which the bishopric of Laon is a suffragan.]

Integrity of character completed the sum of his honors;

[Col. 0574A] But after he chose to withdraw from our life,

Your colleague and hermit in your territories,

He laid aside all concern for honor,

Embracing concern only for the love of Christ.

Therefore, brothers who cultivate the deserts of the wilderness,

Seeing that this excellent Father has now overcome the deceptive world,

Do not bear his death with sadness;

We believe that he has reached the divine kingdoms of heaven.

Since he is a citizen of heaven, what greater thing could he have?

While he was on earth, these were his desires.

**Another of the same**

67. Rejoice, Bruno: France received you as a teacher;

Now Calabria encloses you in its earth as a hermit;

All proclaim that rest may be yours.

**[The title of] the nuns of Saint John the Baptist**  
[Note: Within the boundaries of the city of Laon (see the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 587 and following), the virgin Saint Salaberga built in the seventh century a convent, later called for a very long period by the name of Saint John the Baptist. Sacred virgins remained there until the year 1128, when, in a synod of the province of Reims held at Arras, it was decreed that monks should replace the nuns. The following title therefore unquestionably belongs to this convent. It also supports the opinion—something worth noting here—that Saint Bruno, when he bade farewell to the world, did not withdraw directly to Chartreuse, since the verse it contains reads: “He himself was a cleric, he becomes a monk, then a hermit,” as I showed in the preliminary Commentary, no. 416.]

[Col. 0574B]

68. Bruno, you are praised; your worthy life is renewed

In verses and writings, though it cannot be remembered as greatly as it was.

He himself was devout, simple, full of love for God,

Diligent and pure, worthy of every honor.

Bruno still lives; life is handed down to him by the Father.

He himself was a cleric; he becomes a monk, then a hermit.

Now his lifeless body lies, yet it is venerated.

Bruno still lives, whose breath rejoices.

Though wearied by the passage of time and also by guilt,

May God now grant him to rest forever.

**[The title of] Saint Nicholas of the Vedocian Forest**  
[Note: This monastery, situated about three leagues from the city of Laon in the forest called Vedogia, or Voegia, and here distinguished by the name Vedocian Forest, appears to have been founded around the year 1080. See the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 610 and following.]

69. Let no one grieve that anyone succumbs to death,

Since he rather lives. Whoever destroys the body’s fever

[Col. 0574C] Here avoids the bitter right of death forever;

And may he grant you, Bruno, unending rest with the saints.

**[The title of] Blessed Mary of Noyon**  
[Note: I have nowhere found a sacred place that is or ever was called by this name.]

70. The outstanding Bruno is not to be praised in only one respect:

He taught the clergy, became the father of monks,

And, dear to God, shone through illustrious deeds.

He should always be remembered by all of us,

That God may grant him an unstained condition

And join him, through Masses and psalms, to the blessed citizens.

**Another of the same**

71. While Bruno lived, he warned us and acted according to his warning,

So that the world might become worthless to us and we might not perish.

The world possesses deceits and joins arts to these.

[Col. 0575A] Finally, with honeyed weapons it wounds the unwary,

And sweetens its tricks, so that it may wickedly destroy the incautious.

It could never dominate our Bruno;

So that it might not dominate him, he sought the wilderness stripped bare,

And remained in peace, so that a long peace might remain his.

**[The title of] the church of Soissons**

[The supplied source ends here.]

72. The mother church of Soissons [Note: [Col. 0575C] That is, the cathedral church. What meaning the word *Matricula*, occurring in this Title, has here, you will find explained in the Note appended to note 256 of the first section.] sends to the most beloved brothers, dear to God, dwelling in the wilderness called Turris, greetings and the wish always to have a heavenly way of life through Christ.

When we learned of the holy and glorious death of the most devout and God-beloved Father, the truly venerable Bruno, we were sweetly moved by the passing of such a great man. We performed the Office for his blessed soul according to the custom of the faithful, and, to commemorate annually the day on which he departed from the prison of the flesh, we entered in our register the day of his holy release, as we received it announced by you. [Col. 0575B] We pray and beseech that, through his most holy prayers and yours, we may be assisted, both the living and the dead. Amen.

### SS. Medard and Sebastian of Soissons

[Note: [Col. 0575D] There can be no doubt that the celebrated monastery of Saint Medard is designated here. It was founded in the city of Soissons in the seventh century. See the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume IX, column 405 and following.]

73. Pious people of Medard, the royal and renowned people of the Saint,

Give sweet consolations of salvation to those who weep and mourn.

You who grieve for the dead, lay aside your mourning for the departed;

It helps nothing to lament the extinguished or grieve for the buried.

Rather, let holy offerings benefit him through your vow.

Let these be offered for whoever fears and dreads the dangers of death;

Let him assist and help, through continual prayers, all who are perishing in the world.

While each person asks and entreats, each also labors for himself.

When Moses prays, the Israelite people prevail;

When he ceases his prayers, it immediately falls, and the enemy conquers.

Let us pray together, and let no spirit cease.

Vows help a person while he lives and departs at the appointed hour.

Wicked death, which destroys life, has carried off the hermit;

That which harms and injures the just has injured him with sufficient impiety.

This cruel, insatiable Charybdis slays those whom the all-begetting power devotes, sparing no one from every kind of pain.

May the One who endured death on the cross save a person from this,

And grant him a life that Proserpina cannot cut short.

### Saint Mary of Blois

[Note: [Col. 0575D] This same inscription is borne by the seventeenth Title. I therefore believe that this abbey of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine at Blois—see note 283—offered three distinct Titles to Saint Bruno: the aforementioned seventeenth and the two placed here. Those who arranged the Saint’s funeral Titles separated the latter two from the former and from the following one. Thus what I remarked above is true: these Titles were not arranged in the order in which they had been inscribed on the funeral roll containing the encyclical letter announcing Saint Bruno’s death.]

[Col. 0576A]

74. Bruno, a man of outstanding integrity, a gem of wisdom,

Whose honesty this present document bears witness to,

Has received the pledge of peace, translated to the dwelling of heaven.

Therefore let us praise, revere, and love the Lord,

Through whom the life of his servants is adorned.

Another by the same author.

75. You were accustomed to the wilderness; you abandoned earthly things, Bruno,

And death, by your death, did not wholly acknowledge your rights.

The body is dissolved into ashes; he becomes heir of heaven.

### Saint Krileff of Blois

[Note: [Col. 0575D] In the general catalogue of the benefices of the diocese of Chartres, printed at Paris in 1648, p. [Col. 0576C] 87, a distinguished priory near Blois is listed under the name of Saint Carilef or Krilef. The town of Blois lay in the diocese of Chartres before an episcopal see was granted to it in 1697. I infer that this is the place designated here.]

76. Every person incurs the dangers of the first fate,

And the defect of Eve harms all her descendants.

Therefore, while exercising its task, death’s impiety

Attacks and releases a man of such integrity.

### Saint Mary of Bernay

[Note: [Col. 0576D] The enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume XI, column 830, lists among the monasteries of the church of Lisieux one built in the eleventh century in honor of the most holy Mother of God. They call it Bernaicum; it is plainly the same place that is called Bernacum here, with only one letter changed.]

[Col. 0576B]

77. He was a teacher of teachers and a model of the good,

The outstanding Bruno of our times.

We believe that he has nothing of punishable guilt;

May he himself reconcile God to us by his merits.

### Holy Cross of Orléans

[Note: [Col. 0576D] The cathedral church of Orléans, as I understand from the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume VIII, column 1409, is dedicated to the Holy Cross. This, therefore, is undoubtedly what is designated here.]

78. Bruno, the highest honor and glory of this age,

You lie in the flesh, but you remain surviving in the better part,

And now receive the welcome rewards of righteous labor,

Rightly associated with illustrious teachers.

Living in Christ, holy man, remember us,

And your teaching, which shines throughout the whole world.

Pour forth prayers to Christ, that we may deserve to be your followers;

[Col. 0576C] And may we, who beseech God for you in brotherly fashion,

Always be helped by your prayers, Bruno, holy man.

You too, most holy brothers, who have sent so great and such a patron to heaven: having set aside all sorrow of human compassion, rejoice and exult in the Lord.
