Show by your conduct that you were worthy of so great a Father, so that, while he intercedes for us, the Lord may graciously provide you with a Father equal to him in knowledge, or, if not, at least similar in upright life. Farewell.

### The abbot of the monastery of Saint John of Soissons

[Note: [Col. 0576D] The monastery undoubtedly designated here is situated on the mountain or hill adjoining the city of Soissons. It is now called Saint John in the Vineyards and was founded in the eleventh century. See the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume IX, column 456. Concerning Peter, the abbot of that monastery, whose Title follows, see the preliminary Commentary, no. 97 and the two following numbers. It should also be noted, from the Notes appended to note 298 of the second section, that neither this Title, nor the two immediately preceding it, nor no. 73, was inscribed on the funeral roll in the order in which they are placed here.]

79. To the beloved brothers, worthy of God and beloved in Christ, the venerable hermits of Calabria, serving God in the monastery of Saint Mary, the ever-virgin Mother of God:

Peter, humble abbot of Saint John of Soissons, belonging to the Canons Regular, and the whole community of brothers living and serving God with him, wish you to have begun well, to persevere better, and to finish happily.

Having heard of the blessed end of your holy Father and my master Bruno, from whose mouth I often had the opportunity to drink the streams of sound doctrine, and, although I did not fulfill this in deed, we grieve deeply at his absence, we rejoice exceedingly that he has escaped the constraints of the flesh, obtained rest, and lives with God, insofar as we can judge from the purity and perfection of his life, which was well known to us.

We therefore promise that, both because he was our master and because we trust in his prayers and yours—prayers all the more effective with God the holier they are—we shall honor his memory in this way: for thirty days we shall celebrate Masses and Vigils for his relief and for that of your deceased brothers. In the book in which the names of the deceased brothers are written, we enter his name. With God’s will, we shall celebrate the anniversary of his burial with due reverence, and we desire him to share in all the benefits performed among us and in the places belonging to us; and we receive you as sharers in them.

### Saint Symphorian the Martyr of Beauvais

[Note: [Col. 0577D] This monastery was begun in the eleventh century on a hill overlooking the city of Beauvais, as the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume IX, column 807, records.]

80. The writings report that this man was a holy abbot,

And that he taught the flock entrusted to him the path of virtue.

Therefore, as this roll bears witness that he lived,

[Col. 0577C] we ask you, Christ, to grant him perpetual rest.

### Saint Quintin of Beauvais

[Note: [Col. 0577D] This monastery was built not far from the walls of Beauvais in 1067, in honor and memory of Saint Quintin the Martyr. So says the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume IX, column 818.]

81. The humble community of Saint Quintin of Beauvais, hoping to be assisted with God through the patronage of its venerable Father Bruno, obediently enters him in the thirtieth-day commemoration [Note: [Col. 0577D] I supplied the meaning of this word in the Notes appended to the first section, at note 269.] and will henceforth keep his memory, and that of all of you, together with his brothers.

The hermit, snatched from this life while thirsting for Christ,

Lest present evils alter his holy life,

Proved by dying whatever he had resolved while living.

It will benefit the Church to know the traces of his faith.

A certain brother of the aforesaid Church, named Gauherius, of holy memory, who loved the man greatly and proclaimed that he alone in our times had renounced the world, will perform the thirtieth-day commemoration and, as long as he lives, will carefully keep him in memory among his household.

### Saint Lucian, Apostle of Beauvais

[Note: [Col. 0577D] This monastery was built in the sixth century, three hundred paces from Beauvais. See again the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume IX, column 778.]

82. The leader of hermits, the light of churches, has fallen;

The wilderness mourns him, whom every faithful person honors.

For he is worthy, since he himself was kind.

He despised the world and abandoned all worldly things,

Practicing the life of one who made himself a hermit.

May he himself be a true hermit in the heavenly choirs,

Living with our brothers who are listed here. [Note: [Col. 0578C] I think it should be inferred from this that some deceased persons were entered under this Title, for whom the monks of Saint Lucian’s monastery requested the religious inhabitants of the wilderness of Turris to pray. [Col. 0578D]]

### Saint Fuscian of the Forest

[Note: [Col. 0578D] This undoubtedly designates the monastery in the diocese of Amiens called Saint Fuscian in the Forest by the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume X, column 1302. As is clear from what they record there, it was much older than Saint Bruno’s time.]

83. Bruno, an excellent and upright man, rejecting what is vicious,

You were a disciple of Christ, as your life bears witness.

Life, rest, day without night, wondrous restoration—

May these, given to you by Him, open the way to true joys.

### Saint Peter of Corbie

[Note: [Col. 0578D] This monastery was built in the seventh century four leagues from Amiens; its principal basilica was dedicated to Saints Peter and Paul. See again the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume X, column 1263.]

84. Bruno, you placed worldly riches second,

And by your example taught that they should be placed second,

And you cultivated the desert places for the King of heaven.

With sweet words you watered the hearts of many.

By such deeds you at once appear an imitator

Of the holy Fathers who flourished in teaching.

There you remained for many years, enduring

[Col. 0578C] the snares of the enemy, whose deceits you overcame.

Now, however, in Christ, with a blessed end,

You have completed the course of mortal life,

And, having died, possess the joys of everlasting life.

This is your reward.

### Saint Quintin of Vermandois

[Note: [Col. 0578D] This monastery, also called Saint Quintin of the Mountain, lies one mile from Péronne, in the region of Vermandois and the diocese of Noyon. It appears, from what the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume IX, column 1097 and the following five columns, relate, to have existed before the eleventh century.]

85. When Bruno dies, what he drew from the One dies;

His merit stands, because his spirit lives.

May the life of the blessed, the hope and crown of the devout,

Join him above the stars in the heavenly choirs.

### The church of Saint Peter of Lehun

[Note: [Col. 0579C] The writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume III, column 411, mention the cell of Lehun. From what they write there, it is credible that it already existed before Saint Bruno’s time.]

[Col. 0579A]

86. Though dead, he lives, because, having spurned everything, he went

With the cross after Christ, when he abandoned this world.

He harmed no one here, because he always clung to the Lord.

Therefore, avoiding punishments, he receives pleasant dwelling places,

To which the Most High, who grants pious rewards to the just,

May grant that we come to live.

### Saint Furseus of Péronne

[Note: [Col. 0579C] Erchinoald, mayor of the palace under Clovis II, built a monastery near his fortress at Péronne in the seventh century for Saint Furseus, a Scot by origin, and his monks. A college of canons, still surviving today, succeeded the monks there from the ninth century onward. I therefore think that this is the institution designated by the inscription. [Col. 0579D] See the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume IX, column 1035 and following.]

87. May this man of virtue, followed by virtues,

Receive unfading beauty through the flower of his merit.

May God himself, by whom all things are ruled and in whom all things stand,

Grant joys to your spirit, Bruno.

Although the lowly earth covers your fleshly limbs,

May your spirit pass into the heights of heaven.

May Bruno, the pious shepherd who led the life of a hermit,

By God’s gift, deserve the joys of life.

### The church of Saint Mary of Alren

[Note: [Col. 0579D] I have nowhere been able to find a sacred place bearing this name, and therefore think that it has been incorrectly written here.]

88. Holy Bruno, revered Father, revered offspring,

Keeping the commands of heaven, may you live as a heavenly image.

### The church of Saint Peter of Ducourt

[Note: [Col. 0579D] In the diocese of Cambrai, near the river Scheldt and not far from the town of Saint Quintin, stands a monastery which is mentioned in the division of the monasteries of the kingdom of Lothair, made in 870 between Louis and Charles, kings of the Franks. Some call it Hunnocourt, others by other names, though without much alteration of this name. I think no monastery other than this is designated in the inscription of the present Title.]

89. The wisdom of the world does not know how to decline toward death,

Nor does either sex decline the matter together with the word.

But I, unless I am mistaken, Bruno declines both.

Yet he falls in Libra, because his lot was just. [Note: [Col. 0579D] That is, the Saint migrated to the heavenly realms on the sixth day of October, or at the time when the sun by its own motion traverses the sign of the zodiac called Libra.]

His life was pure; this hermit was wise.

Placed upon the scales, may he know no danger of anger.

We therefore inform you, dearest brothers, as you requested, that we have devoutly entered in writing for this son of the Catholic Church the thirtieth-day observance, the anniversary day, and his inscription in the catalogue of our brothers.

### The monastery of the Savior of Aquicain

[Note: [Col. 0580C] It appears beyond doubt that the monastery to which the following Title belongs is the same one called by the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume III, column 408, the monastery of Saint Savior of Aquicain, Aquicinctum, or Aquicinum. It was built in the eleventh century and lies by the river Scarpe, two miles from Douai.]

90. I, Aimeric, abbot of this aforementioned monastery, although with inadequate prayers, implore from the eternal and merciful Savior eternal rest for the soul of the illustrious and famous master Bruno, and I have recorded Bruno’s day of death in the Calendar.

### The monastery of Marchiennes

[Note: [Col. 0580C] I think the Benedictine monastery called Marchianum by the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume III, column 393, is designated here. It was built in the seventh century. [Col. 0580D]]

91. At last he departed, his body long since dead,

While famous Bruno, surpassing himself in spirit and song,

Endured exile from the world while living in the body.

For this reason he withdrew himself; the good hermit concealed himself.

Yet he conceals himself well, while he shines with the light of his deeds.

There he delights in the hope of beholding the Godhead,

Which he now enjoys forever, having entered the heavens.

### The church of Saint Amand of Elnon

[Note: [Col. 0580D] This Benedictine monastery lies about three leagues from Tournai, on the river Elnon, and was built by Saint Amand himself in the seventh century. Consult the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume III, column 254.]

92. While he lived, he settled in the citadel of the mind;

Whatever is done by the devil’s art was displeasing to him also.

After the death of the flesh, he is buried in the heavenly city.

A dwelling worthy of his merits is granted to him,

A dwelling worthy of the wisdom which he pursued while living with unfeigned love of heart.

Therefore let the flock cease mourning the Father’s death,

Although it has been deprived of the honor of so great a light.

Rather let it rejoice deservedly, as the Father himself rejoices.

What we do for you, do the same for ours.

### The church of Saint Peter of Lille

[Note: [Col. 0580D] Since the city of Lille in Flanders is also called Isla and possesses a distinguished collegiate church dedicated to Saint Peter, it clearly appears that this is what is designated here.]

93. The true faith of Christ loosens the sins of the world;

His flesh, made an offering to the Father upon the wood of the cross.

Whoever imitates this in good-hearted faith and by vows

Deserves the joyful fellowship of his life.

That Father Bruno may become his fellow citizen,

Let worthy devotion be carried to the Judge’s throne.

May mutual prayer benefit our dead.

### The church of Saint Mary of Mecines

[Note: [Col. 0580D] This undoubtedly designates the abbey of noble Benedictine virgins, called by some Messines and by others Mesen, built in the eleventh century two leagues from Ypres. See the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume V, column 341.]

94. Father Bruno, worthy of remembrance, may the pious Mother of Christ

Deign to ask her Son, who suffered for us upon the cross,

And may the heavenly King grant you the rewards of his kingdom,

Where our brothers and sisters may be with you.

### The church of Saint Mary of Formeselles

[Note: [Col. 0581C] This monastery, situated not near Furnes, as the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume V, column 351, report, but near Ypres, was founded in 1068, as those same writers state there.]

[Col. 0581A]

95. We complain in vain if the just man is lulled to rest by death.

One common road, coming to all, has different outcomes:

It brings sadness to the mourners and full joys to the blessed.

Therefore blessed will be the one who has passed through well.

Happy is this Bruno, whose praise, uttered with one voice,

Is in harmony with the devout and adorned by so many studies.

We pray that the light of day may shine for him—

A light that does not fall with times or changes.

You too should pray for ours as you remember them.

Thus, thus I conclude briefly, most illustrious Bruno:

May you enjoy Christ without end, for whom you served.

### The church of Saint Donatian of Bruges

[Note: [Col. 0581C] This church, now a cathedral, was only collegiate in Saint Bruno’s time.]

96. This man, a worshiper of truth and, while living, the glory of the clergy,

Now released from the flesh, may safely possess joys.

Grant to ours what you ask for yours, brothers,

And you who are present as reader, say: “May he have rest.”

### The church of Saint Nicholas of Melte

[Note: [Col. 0581C] Since I can find neither a temple nor a monastery called Melte and dedicated to Saint Nicholas, I cannot determine which sacred place is designated here. [Col. 0581D]]

97. Death has a short name, but beneath that name a harsh

Lot lies hidden—a lot whose dominion is not brief.

It tramples wealth, shakes scepters, and overturns cathedrals;

No one knows where, when, or from where it comes.

Sense, honor, merit, appearance, strength, possessions, lineage, age—

All vanish at the moment of death.

Although all these things were yours, Bruno [Note: [Col. 0581D] Bruno is plainly said here to have excelled in rank, wealth, and lineage. Therefore, both from this passage and from what I brought forward in section 2 of the preliminary Commentary, it must be regarded as certain that he was born of noble stock.], nevertheless you yourself died on the day before the Nones of October.

Great Father, who can do all things, to whom alone it belongs

To see the inner depths of a man completely,

And to pardon sins and give healing after death,

Spare this great man, and be his remedy.

## SECTION IV

### Title of Saint Peter of Poitiers

[Note: [Col. 0581D] Since the cathedral church of Poitiers, which had Saint Hilary as its bishop in the fourth century, is dedicated to Saint Peter the Apostle, the following Title must undoubtedly be attributed to it.]

98. Death’s spectacles are the grim scenes of a harsh lot.

Death is free from no one and from no fortune;

It weighs the ruin of all on the same balance.

It spares the private person no more than the noble,

And empties narrow homes just as it does the dwellings of the great.

For, apart from divine things, youth, flowers, honor, beauty, possessions, and dignities

All lie beneath Libitina.

Therefore do not be surprised that this man has died.

But if some ignorant person asks what sort of man he was,

Let him unfold and read the document, and read it again. [Note: [Col. 0581D] That is, the funeral roll, which contains both the encyclical letter announcing Saint Bruno’s death and several funeral Titles, or responses sent to it, in which much is said about the Saint.]

### Saint Mary of Poitiers

[Note: [Col. 0581D] Several churches in the city of Poitiers bear the name of the most blessed Virgin Mary. One of them, a collegiate church that has existed since the tenth century, is called Saint Mary Major. I suppose that this is designated here by “Saint Mary,” standing alone and taken antonomastically. [Col. 0582C]]

99. You live and rejoice in heaven, faithful hermit;

Blessedness follows you, and every necessity flees.

O holy Father, for whom it is a crime to offer lamentation,

Whose joy no plague can abolish;

For whom God is life, light, and true salvation!

Well done: you enjoy the heavenly reward of God’s servant.

You receive the talent discovered with little toil,

Which wisely you repaid to the Lord at double interest.

For such great merits the words of the Thunderer cry out to you:

“Enjoy, good servant, the highest realm with me.”

### Saint Hilary of Poitiers

[Note: [Col. 0582C] Since there are two churches in Poitiers, older than Saint Bruno—see our treatment of Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, on 13 January—one called Saint Hilary of the Cell or Minor, the other Saint Hilary Major or Great, it may reasonably be doubted which one is designated by the following Title. Nevertheless, since “Saint Hilary,” placed alone and without an addition, appears by antonomasia to mean not the Minor but the Major church of Saint Hilary, I would decide in favor of the latter rather than the former. [Col. 0582D]]

100. Let hermits contemplate the course of Bruno’s life:

He saw the flourishing world deceiving worldly people,

But, while he observed it, he remained free from the world’s stain.

While it became worthless to him, while he knew not its foul pleasures,

He clung to Christ and departed from this age.

Bruno, the blessed hermit, was deprived of this life;

He found the Lord, since his deeds corresponded to his words.

Therefore we do not mourn him whom we see to have departed in this way.

Another by the same author.

101. While you lived in this world, Bruno, you followed Christ’s footsteps,

Stripped of many vices.

Therefore Christ granted you the kingdoms of heaven,

Where the most joyful throng of the blessed rejoices.

### Saint Radegund of Poitiers

[Note: [Col. 0582D] Saint Radegund, the queen treated by us on 13 August, withdrew to Poitiers after divorcing her husband, Clotaire, king of the Franks. In that city, as we explained there, she founded two churches, one for the sick and the other for holy virgins. The latter, together with its convent, is still honored under the name of the Holy Cross. The former, initially named Saint Mary, was later called the Basilica of Saint Regina or Saint Radegund, as I learn from volume II, column 1299, of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*. This collegiate church, therefore, is very probably—or rather certainly—the one designated here. [Col. 0583C]]

102. Immense King and God, who created all things by your word,

Who prepared heavenly kingdoms of rest for the saints,

And who lead your own people to the heavenly joys of light,

Make this man rejoice with the saints in the seat of heaven,

Where the assembly of the blessed rejoices truly and without end.

### Saint Mary and Saint Cyprian the Martyr

[Note: [Col. 0583D] It plainly appears that the ancient and noble abbey of Saint Cyprian is designated here. King Pippin of Aquitaine built it in the suburb of Poitiers in 828. See the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume II, column 1230. It has undergone various changes, including changes of name.]

103. Be every good thing to Bruno, merciful Christ;

He was a hermit, and for this reason he pleased you.

Having forgotten what lies behind and longing to see this shore,

He sees you not through an image but face to face.

### Saint John the Evangelist of Poitiers

[Note: [Col. 0583D] This Benedictine monastery was built in the city of Poitiers in the eleventh century under the title of Saint John the Evangelist. See again the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume II, column 1263 and following.]

104. Gaul, setting aside festive songs and odes,

Now receive mournful songs and sorrowful laments.

For your teacher, once a guide through heavenly things,

The pious Bruno, is dying; the flower of hay is buried beneath the earth.

This is why you grieve; but he lives—put away your complaints.

Truly, by his righteous merits, he is celebrated among the stars, [associated].

With whom may joys of light belong to us and to you.

### The monastery of Saint Peter of Virson

[Note: [Col. 0583D] This monastery is situated in the diocese of Bourges and was built long before Saint Bruno’s time, as is clear from what the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume II, column 133 and the following three columns, record about it.]

105. May there be peace for all the monks of Turris throughout the ages.

When Phoebus began to spread his golden rays across the world,

Your messenger came here, weeping over the death of the Father,

Whom hostile death had killed.

We celebrated the appointed prayers for his soul,

As is known to be the custom of the holy Church,

And entrusted his blessed soul to Christ.

For as long as he lived, he desired to serve the Lord,

Instructed in character and strengthened by divine light;

He remained beloved by the brothers and by God forever.

### Saint Martin of the Full Foot

[Note: [Col. 0583D] This abbey of the Order of Saint Augustine, situated in the diocese of Bourges two leagues from Avaricum, was founded around the year 1080. So says the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume II, column 186.]

[Col. 0583C] 106. Since no one can in any way escape the unavoidable shipwreck of this deadly life by the oar of his own virtues or prayers and obtain the heavenly unfading reward, you ask, brothers, for what befits the Catholic religion. Therefore, so that the rust of our sins may be most healthfully boiled away by his prayers and yours, we may be cleansed, we shall commemorate annually the day of your Father.

### The monastery of Saint Maximin of Miciacum

[Note: [Col. 0584C] This monastery of the diocese of Orléans, called partly from the district of Miciacum in which it was built and partly from Saint Maximin, its second abbot, whose feast is celebrated on 15 December and whom we included in our work, began at the beginning of the sixth century. See the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume VIII, column 1526 and following.]

107. A learned psalmist, most illustrious and a sophist—that is, a philosopher.

Gaul ought wondrously to have buried him,

But, as is said, Bruno is now buried in the Calabrian fields.

Having completed this life under established times,

May he pass to life established without times.

Another by the same author.

108. May Bruno rise to the King who cleanses sins,

To Christ of the saints, for whom he lived in this world.

The monk, the wise hermit, has departed from life.

Let the grieving clergy be admonished by these verses

To entreat the thundering Lord, who grants rewards,

That he grant Bruno rest; let the pious people say, “Amen.”

### Saint Mary of Paris

[Note: [Col. 0584D] The cathedral church of Paris is dedicated under the name of the most blessed Virgin Mary. I therefore judge it exceedingly probable that this is what is designated here; it originated as early as the first times of the kings of France.]

109. You worldly people who rejoice in an empty thing,

Despise the cultivation of flesh that will soon perish.

For the enormous body, nourished with varied fatness,

The more it is filled, the more putrid it becomes.

Why is flesh fattened when it feeds the worm?

Why do we desire so greatly goods that we cannot keep?

The world seduces people badly and leads them along crooked paths;

It deceives the followers of the flesh through honors,

And holds out flattering things while spreading nets for us.

There is also in this world worldly anxiety,

And punishment earns punishment; the flesh is tortured twice.

Those who pursue profits are hurled down by sudden death

And enter the pit—the abyss of flesh and souls.

Bruno, having carefully considered all this,

That ornament of teachers, instructor of morals,

The oar of the people of Rheims, the leading man in the city,

Despised the world and turned his path toward heavenly things,

Following you, Christ, dressed in humble garments.

Therefore may heaven be opened to him and to the faithful people,

With whom Bruno rejoices and is forever associated.

### Saint Peter of Resbac

[Note: [Col. 0584D] You will find information about this monastery, built in the seventh century by Saint Audoen, archbishop of Rouen, in the diocese of Meaux, in the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume VIII, column 1679 and following, and also in our volume IV for August, where Saint Audoen is treated, p. 812, under letter m in the Notes.]

110. In our times, while the end of the world draws near,

This man appeared in the world close to God.

For he had been rich and conducted his life wisely;

He despised everything and afterward became a poor hermit

For the Lord, who alone reigns on high.

He followed the way of the flesh; may he be blessed throughout the ages

By the piety of God, who redeemed the ages through death.

### Saint Peter of Lagny

[Note: [Col. 0584D] I think *Latunacensis* should be replaced here with *Latiniacensis*, designating the monastery of Lagny in the diocese of Paris, situated in the Brie region on the bank of the river Marne. Saint Furseus, a noble Irishman, built it in the seventh century, as we explained on 16 January, the day on which we treated him. After it had later been ruined by the Northmen, Count Herbert III, son of Herbert II, count of Vermandois, arranged for its restoration in the eleventh century. [Col. 0585D]]

111. Adam had tasted the fruit of a certain tree;

Afterward, from that tree, an equal fate hangs over all.

If he had not sinned, he would have restored the human race.

But because he sinned, he prepared every evil for death.

Therefore, O grief, mourning, pour forth waves of tears,

Because death bites in this way, rages, rushes upon everything, and swallows all.

Every human being falls through this because of the evil-tasted apple.

Here he flourishes and lives; soon he lays down his limbs in the earth.

Thus the flesh is a flower of hay and the glory of the world becomes hay,

While the flowers and beauties of youth wither.

The great passes away with the small; the wicked with the just.

Every person proves this, but what every person approves,

The father himself introduced; but what the father introduced,

God himself expelled; but what God expelled,

He made into a noble work; but the work that he made noble

Is felt by the succeeding origin; and what that origin feels,

Bruno also felt here. Since Bruno too feels this,

He lives eternally; therefore let us not mourn on his account.

Yet if he did anything that did not please the Lord,

Let mouth, mind, and tongue not refuse to ask God:

“O God, alpha of goodness, grant heavenly kingdoms to Bruno.”

### Saint Peter of Neufchâteau

[Note: [Col. 0585D] Since there are quite a few places distinguished by the name of Novum Castrum or Neocastrum, in French Neufchâtel, and I have been unable to find any whose church I know to be dedicated to Saint Peter, I cannot determine with certainty which sacred place is designated here.]

112. While this blessed hermit lived this life,

He was called the good Bruno, our patron in all things.

In the region where he lived, he remained a living image

Of true justice, teaching, and philosophy.

As an example to all who possess reason,

He built a structure which he knew would not collapse:

An airy dwelling that would endure throughout all ages,

In the highest heavens, where faithful Bruno rejoices.

As we marvel at his life and imitate his conduct,

Let us all pray with whatever prayer we are able,

That he, so worthy, so truthful, and so kind,

Pouring forth for us entreaties with his whole desire,

May make us rejoice with him and remain with him,

Supported by the heavenly summit where he rejoices happily.

### Holy Trinity of Falaise

[Note: [Col. 0585D] Falaise, called *Falesia* in Latin, is a city of Lower Normandy with an adjoining castle situated on a rock. It contains two parish churches, as Martinière states in his *Geographical Dictionary*: one of the Most Holy Trinity and the other of Saint Gervase. It therefore appears beyond doubt that the following Title concerns the former.]

113. We ought to have grieved at the death of so great a teacher,

And all good people ought to lament day and night,

If mourning could recall a buried man,

And if tears produced fruit, so that it were not foolish to lament.

But since the suffrages of Masses, together with tears,

And righteous prayers, carry a person above the heavens,

Let the faithful flock of Christ therefore ask for help with hymns,

Psalms, and prayers, abandoning all complaints,

That he may cause Bruno’s soul to dwell in the heavens,

And preserve the sheep, lest the predator’s mouth devour it.

### Saint Gervase of the same place

[Note: [Col. 0585D] The Basel edition adds “of the Castle”; therefore it is very probably the latter of the two churches mentioned in the preceding note, the one belonging to the castle of Falaise, that is designated here. [Col. 0586C]]

114. Gaul, mother and nurse of many men,

When will you have men equal to this one?

Once your teacher gave a stream of learning

To peoples and clergy. Alas, good reputation perishes!

You perceive that the literature of the Frankish nation contributes nothing;

With this man’s death, you now have proof of it.

A Calabrian tomb covers this man’s bones.

May the great grace of God grant him life.

S. Mary of Tournai [Note: [Col. 0586C] The cathedral church of Tournai is dedicated to the Most Holy Mother of God; therefore the heading placed here must be assigned to it.].

[Col. 0586B]

**115.** Cologne gave him birth, and France wishes that she had nurtured him—

Bruno, glory and father, shared by both peoples.

With easy ascent he is joined to the hosts of heaven,

whose citizen he was even while life remained.

Yet the fitting prayer is not offered here in vain.

May the Lord supply what was lacking in his merits.

S. Peter’s monastery of Blandinium [Note: [Col. 0586D] This most distinguished monastery of Ghent is today ordinarily known simply by the name of St Peter, under whose patronage, together with that of St Paul, it was built, although originally it was called Blandinium, after Blandinium Mount, near the city of Ghent, on which it was built by St Amandus in the seventh century. See our work, volume I for February, p. 822, and also the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume V, column 184.].

**116.** It is common to die; death spares no rank.

Death is life to the devout, but daily punishment to the wicked.

We shall go without delay, but we do not know at what hour,

for life is brief, fleeting, falling, and light.

Behold, we know well enough that we cannot escape it;

and what will the end be? Spring, and thereafter ashes.

While he lived, this Hermit’s life shone brightly enough;

[Col. 0586C] yet now dead, may he rest in peace: amen.

S. Leodegarius the Martyr [Note: [Col. 0586D] Since there are various sacred places distinguished by this Saint’s name, as we explained in the commentary preceding the Acts of St Leodegarius on 2 October, and since the funeral headings are not listed in the order in which they were written on the roll, I cannot determine which church or monastery is designated here.].

**117.** You ask for the help which Christ may grant forever;

we ask the Most High for Bruno, whose body is departing,

that he may grant him the longed-for gifts of the kingdom.

S. Bavo’s in Ghent [Note: [Col. 0586D] This distinguished monastery, later called by the name of St Bavo, was founded in the seventh century by St Amandus in the castle of Ghent, at the confluence of the Scheldt and the Lys. After various changes, it finally passed in the sixteenth century from the regular status—for it belonged to Benedictine monks—to that of secular canons. When it was then to be converted into a fortress, the canons moved to St John’s basilica, then a parish church and now the cathedral of St Bavo, which, with the name John removed, was called by Bavo’s name; thereafter they formed there the cathedral chapter of the recently established bishopric of Ghent. See our work, volume I for October, the posthumous glory of St Bavo, § 5, and also Sanderus, *Rerum Gandensium*, book IV, chapter 3, and the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume V, columns 171 and following.].

**118.** Although we possess great skill in words,

let us not wish to utter words merely according to our ability;

but, weeping, let us say briefly: “Most High Master,

grant that Bruno, dear to you, O King, and faithful in the flesh,

[Col. 0587A] he to whom the joys of heaven pleased above every good,

may possess that which never knows absence.”

S. Mary’s of Conatrensis in England [Note: [Col. 0587D] Since I find no sacred place bearing this name either in the *Monasticon Anglicanum* or elsewhere, I think that an error has entered its transcription, and that *Conventrensis* should be read instead of *Connatrensis*. Thus the cathedral church of this name in England is designated here; it is dedicated to the Most Holy Mother of God and is older than St Bruno’s time. See Mabillon, volume IV of the *Annales Benedictini*, book LVIII, no. 69, and the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, volume II, p. 428.].

**119.** May Christ the King, by his piety, place him in the citadel of heaven

and grant him to enjoy the rest of those who dwell there.

S. Audomarus, bishop [Note: [Col. 0588C] I think that the monastery of monks designated here is the one mentioned in the commentary preceding the Life of St Gerard, abbot of Brogne, in the preceding volume of our work, no. 245; there we also showed that it had already been converted into a house of secular canons in the ninth century.].

**120.** You used to be an example to suffering mortals,

so that they might worship Christ, whom you, Bruno, always worshiped;

for his sake you spurned the riches of the whole world,

so that the Author of the whole world might grant you eternity.

Therefore may the true faith, which you always cultivated,

draw you to Christ’s rest, which you, Bruno, sought.

S. Paul the Apostle of London [Note: [Col. 0588D] The cathedral church of London in England is dedicated to St Paul; therefore I think that the heading placed here refers to it.].

**121.** The fame of so great a man, spread beneath the world’s final heavens,

awakens minds burning with worthy prayers.

And although we wish, as far as we can, to fulfill what has been requested,

the vows promised everywhere by approved men

urge us, as we are able, to remember Bruno,

and to celebrate his departure each year with Masses.

The archdeacons Renger, Walter, Quintilian, Robert, and Durand the schoolmaster, Theobald, Arthur, and all the other canons of the church of St Paul of London greet and extend fraternal affection to the hermits of the church of Holy Mary, Mother of God, at the Tower of Calabria. We grant, as you requested, that an anniversary be observed each year on the day before the Nones of October for the reverend master Lord Bruno, servant of God, and for all the brothers of your monastery. We granted this by the public consent of our brethren, and entered his name among those of our brethren in remembrance of the aforesaid commemoration. [Col. 0587C]

The church of St Peter of Cassel [Note: [Col. 0588D] Cassel, a town in western Flanders, called *Cassel* in French and Flemish, could therefore have been called *Cassella* or *Cassellum* in Latin by those who wrote the heading placed here. It has two collegiate churches, one dedicated to St Peter and the other to St Mary; it is accordingly permissible to conjecture that the former is designated here.].

**122.** The worms feed upon Bruno’s defenseless flesh—

alas, upon the vessel of immeasurable understanding and goodness!

Yet that is not why I grieve; for I know

that he is a fellow citizen of the saints;

rather, because his own community mourns

its kindly Father, taken from it.

S. Mary’s of the see of Arras [Note: [Col. 0588D] The cathedral church of Arras, dedicated to the Most Holy Mother of God, is undoubtedly designated here.].

**123.** God is eternal light, apart from whom nothing can exist;

he who wished to be born for us from Jesse’s seed—

may he make you, Bruno, a participant in his goodness,

he who is the overflowing source of wondrous mercy.

Another by the same author.

**124.** Bruno, guide of the right path and fountain of philosophy,

he taught no differently from the way he strove to live.

By living well he did whatever a good man

would show by speaking; he shone forth from heaven.

Therefore may everlasting glory be granted him as his reward,

and enduring rest and day without night.

School of the monastery of St Vedastus at Nobiliacum [Note: [Col. 0588D] The monastery of St Vedastus at Arras, formerly called Nobiliacum, was built in the seventh century. There is therefore no doubt that the heading placed here proceeded from the school which that monastery, according to the custom prevailing at the beginning of the twelfth century, maintained.].

**125.** Let life weep over the brief sequence by which time passes;

for whatever is now seen to be present passes away.

Thus it must be, and nature requires it to be so.

The glory of things stands, but its end perishes in time.

[Col. 0588B] Nothing is eternal unless it is an imitation of the true.

Therefore whoever wishes to seem a prudent man

should love only those things which are gifts of salvation to him.

If his concerns stand well, loving the good things of the light to come,

let him not pursue those things which flee like air.

Whatever the world possesses is a kind of capture of the mind,

so that the ever-watchful art of the enemy may seduce it.

That roaring lion, the enemy, seeking whom he may devour,

never sleeps and grants no rest to his limbs.

All his care remains restless through the hours;

this fury has no setting, nor does his unholy will.

Therefore, I beg you, man, beware lest you be seized by him.

With mind attentive to heaven and with all your senses,

devote every effort to it, so that, having fulfilled the true honor,

you may always enjoy divine and pure love.

[Col. 0588C] Everything that exists perishes, wise man and fool alike;

poor, needy, and rich alike, whom the contemptible urn covers.

By the law of death, thus ordained, they become dust and bones.

The just man dies; he dies, wounded by some fault,

nor does anyone created under the common law lack a stain.

For he submits to the fate which father Adam

earned through the mother whom Scripture calls Eve.

While my mind laments these things, it wanders through many matters;

too vast a reasoning multiplies itself through the mind.

[Col. 0589A] Clear Father Bruno, I ask that everlasting life be yours;

let every faithful person who answers me say, “Amen.”

Another by the same author.

**126.** The light and ordered guide of the path leading to the heights of wisdom

has set, withdrawing from nature as Bruno departs.

Equal to a brute beast. For you, Bruno, keen master,

this world was worthless, with its blossom and sterile beauty.

It was a flower in hay, flourishing beneath a serene sun,

while your Muse sang, while she was free for study,

at one time nourishing Rheims with song, at another feeding it with bread [Note: [Col. 0589C] It appears that he taught poetry at Rheims; see the preceding commentary, no. 77.].

Yet thereafter, having cast aside wealth and rejected studies,

shut away in darkness, you enjoyed harsh seclusion,

following nothing varied, Bruno, founded upon the One alone;

thus, Father—O Bruno—captured by the One, you grasp the One [Note: [Col. 0589D] This also seems to allude to Luke 10:42: “But one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part.”].

## SECTION V

Heading of the church of S. Mary of Morlaix [Note: [Col. 0589D] Since I find no place called either *Morlivum* or *Morliva*, but in Lesser Brittany there is a city called *Morlaeum*—in French *Morlais* or *Morlaix*—which has a church dedicated to the Most Holy Mother of God, it appears probable that the heading placed here refers to that church, and that *Morlivensis* was written here incorrectly for *Morlaeensis*.].

[Col. 0589B]

**127.** In the world there flourished a prudent man of profound speech;

his lot and final norm are beneficial and fitting [the wording is corrupt or obscure].

For he truly knew that the world could not remain.

He trampled its flowers and despised its honors.

Now let there be rest for him, since Holy Scripture has said:

“The death of the just is not harmful, but precious.”

Bruno has ascended to spiritual Jerusalem.

The churches of St Peter and St Augustine, Apostle of the English [Note: [Col. 0589D] I think that the distinguished monastery at Canterbury is designated here. St Augustine, bishop of Canterbury in England and called the Apostle of the English—concerning whom we treated on 26 May—built it at Canterbury in the seventh century in honor of the Apostle St Peter. See volume I of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 23, and also volume VI of our work for May, p. 440.].

**128.** Bruno, hermit, may you live in heaven through a devout life.

We have rendered to yours what was due; may what is due be rendered to ours.

S. Edmund, king and martyr [Note: [Col. 0590C] See concerning this monastery the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, volume I, pp. 284 and following, where it is shown that it was built long before St Bruno’s time.].

**129.** Father and hermit Bruno passes from this life;

may his spirit pass into rest: Amen.

Another by the same author.

[Col. 0589C] **130.** May the true Lord grant Bruno joys,

and the hosts of the saints who contain the lofty ranks of the devout.

The church of S. Mary of Spalinga and S. Nicholas of Angers [Note: [Col. 0590D] The Angevin monastery of the Order of St Benedict, which received its name from St Nicholas, was founded in the eleventh century, as the Sammarthan brothers explain in volume IV, p. 688, of the old *Gallia Christiana*. I think that this is designated here by “the Angevin church of St Nicholas”; the name “S. Mary of Spalinga,” which precedes it, denotes one of the churches that the monastery possessed according to custom—for formerly the larger monasteries had several churches.].

**131.** In the world the sun’s ray gleams and, gleaming,

passes beyond the bright stars of the heavens;

so too Bruno’s great wisdom shone forth,

so that among the stars of the Franks he alone

was the flower and fountain of all philosophers.

He was a beautiful flower and a deep fountain.

From him such wisdom flowed throughout the world

that those whom he instructed he made philosophers.

He was the splendor of speech and the light of religion;

[Col. 0590A] his religion is known everywhere.

Through his teaching so many wise men were formed

that my mind does not know them and my pen is silent;

through his example there are many religious men

and followers and disciples of the cross.

He himself bore Christ’s cross and abandoned all that was his;

by denying himself he benefited himself.

Rich, famous, eloquent, and noble,

he shone in the world, but the world displeased him.

The world, its possessions, and worldly power

were not dear to him; he abstained from everything.

No love or honor harmed the man thirsting for God;

but in seeking God he [fled] into exile.

He was an exile from his homeland; he obtained

places and the protection of Mary, whose son he himself was.

[Col. 0590B] Happy was the exile whom the Virgin Mary received.

May she provide him refuge and help;

may she be the harbor for him whose immaculate origin

was the eternal Son; may certain salvation be yours.

To the religious brothers devoutly serving God in the place called the Tower, Lambert, abbot, and the entire community of St Nicholas send greetings and affection. Sharing from the depths of charity in your sorrow and desolation, rejoicing with the lord Bruno, who, as we believe, has passed from this world to the Father, and fulfilling the duty owed to a triumphant funeral, we satisfy your just petitions and desires by agreeing that his deposition be entered in the Martyrology among the names of our brothers and be commemorated in perpetual memory.

The church of S. Mary of Lincoln [Note: [Col. 0590D] The cathedral church of Lincoln in England is dedicated to the Most Holy Mother of God Mary, as may be seen in volume III of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, pp. 257 and 259; therefore there is no doubt that the heading placed here refers to it.].

[Col. 0590C]

**132.** You passed through the world securely, great Bruno,

and because you despised it, I think it harmed you not at all.

It wished to entangle you with deceitful things,

but, looking ahead, you did not fall into the snare.

Indeed, it offered what the foolish worship when they bow down:

riches and goods that perish.

And since no one can be made happy by their splendor—

for they are of no benefit, but greatly harmful—

after casting all these things aside, you gladly sought the wilderness,

desiring only to be able to please God.

Nor was the good man’s fame hidden, scattered as it was throughout the world;

it informed many peoples wherever it wandered.

It benefited many by giving an example of serving

him who is good, who is the Lord God.

What better thing could anyone meditate upon than this?

This salvation benefited many and benefited you.

Who ever knew anyone so happy and wise?

I know no such man, nor anyone like you.

In you true wisdom truly appeared;

the Lord’s piety nourished and taught you.

You chose him above all and loved him also;

whoever worships him need not be ashamed of having done so.

May light, homeland, rest, and glory be won for you—

for whom serving him was your sole glory.

S. Mary’s of York [Note: [Col. 0591D] This monastery, distinguished by the name of St Mary, had likewise been built long before St Bruno’s time. See the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, volume I, p. 384, and Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, book VII, no. 69.].

**133.** The son of the Church, released from mortal flesh,

Bruno, a wise man, as his deeds prove,

is not to be mourned, since he will never fall again;

he possesses what hope, love, and faith earned.

Another by the same author.

**134.** O, if the solemn pageant of this divine matter and its triumph

could be praised or fully made known by speech!

But since my voice would fail unless it restrained itself,

what I am granted to wish, I am denied the power to accomplish perfectly.

Nevertheless, without delay, let my prow rise upon the sea,

so that, if permission be granted, it may pray while praising Christ.

Praise to you, Most High Father, to whom dark hell is subject;

praise to you, praise, Christ, to whom this world is subordinate.

Grant Bruno, I beg, the rewards of heavenly gift,

so that he who lived and crucified himself to the world

may live forever and not be touched by death’s abyss.

What you ask for yourselves, grant in return to us.

The church of S. Peter of York, metropolis of England [Note: [Col. 0591D] There is no doubt that the cathedral church of York, dedicated to St Peter, is designated here.].

[Col. 0591C]

**135.** May he for whose sake Bruno rejected the harmful things of this brief life

repay him with the gifts of eternity.

Another by the same author.

**136.** Fame told us first, before your letter did,

not indeed of the man’s death, but of his goodness.

Bruno was a gem and pillar of the house of the Lord,

and a true cultivator of apostolic faith.

His true faith, built upon virtues,

built heavenly dwellings for him.

Glory, riches, personal distinction, and knowledge of things

were sufficiently brilliant in him, but he pressed them beneath his feet.

There are things which enable a man to live after death,

yet these cannot grant freedom from death.

Death weighs upon every head; and if it could spare anyone,

[Col. 0591D] it certainly ought to have spared Bruno.

Good death, happy death, if that may be called death

which is followed by rest and everlasting life.

[Col. 0592A] If earthly corruption has given him any stain—

for no one can live without sin—

may God, who lives Three and One, wash it away,

grant him rest, and let everyone say: Amen.

What you ask, we have already done and shall do;

and we ask that you do the same for ours.

The church of S. John, archbishop of Beverley [Note: [Col. 0591D] This church, which is collegiate and situated in the district of Beverley, existed long before St Bruno’s time, as may be seen both from what we explained concerning St John of Beverley, archbishop of York, on 7 May, when we treated of him, and from what has been recorded in volume III of the *Monasticon Anglicanum* among the collegiate churches of England, p. 1.].

**137.** Bruno left behind in death what he had despised while living,

for he fled the world and called worldly things worthless.

He served Christ; therefore he entered heaven.

But since brothers such as these sent a letter,

our lords wished, for so great a servant who had died,

to perform at the end a service pleasing to all servants.

Of Richard [Note: [Col. 0592D] This man, who, together with those who in the four headings immediately following explicitly lamented the Saint, was undoubtedly a canon of the collegiate church of Beverley. In the Basel edition, *Ad eumdem*—“to the same”—is added to each man’s name; what this probably signifies may be gathered from the notes to be appended to section VI at note 421.].

[Col. 0592B]

**138.** You who grieve at the chance of death, when the Father has been taken away,

set aside your sadness: the same end awaits everyone.

From this we must learn that the world’s glory is hay;

for a time it blooms, blooming it passes away and withers.

And because it blooms in this way, and blooming passes and withers,

let us turn away from it, seeking rather what is to come.

You have already gone before, Bruno; you were already the rule;

you have already brought to completion what you prudently proposed.

You flourished in the fragile world, but, in its fleeting flower,

you despised the fragile world and its fleeting blossom,

seeking to enter the contemplative life,

which may he grant you who reigns through all ages.

Of Albert.

**139.** May Christ’s piety grant you, Bruno, what you have deserved,

having first become a monk in this life and thereafter a hermit [Note: [Col. 0592D] This heading supports the opinion of those who hold that, when the Saint bade farewell to the world, he did not withdraw directly into the Carthusian order. See the preceding commentary, nos. 415 and following.].

Of Turstan.

[Col. 0592C]

**140.** May you have, Bruno, rest, light, and everlasting glory;

may God be your true salvation and true healing.

Of Richard.

**141.** He deprived us of an eternal dwelling and home,

having first himself become an exile from the eternal dwelling and home.

While Eve offered the taste of the forbidden tree,

she tasted, and by tasting added mortality to mortals,

and extended it to her husband, destined to fall by a similar mishap.

He was immortal, like the image of the Godhead;

he was immortal, the woman taken from his rib;

but immediately after the tasting they became mortal,

and by grievous expulsion they were cast out of paradise.

Savage death entered the world and subjected it

to its own laws: everyone who is born dies.

It knows not how to spare, nor did it spare you, Bruno.

It added you to the fathers; now may Christ be your life,

and may he restore you, snatched from the world, to paradise.

Of William.

[Col. 0593A]

**142.** If poems could do anything for so great a Patron,

my tuneful Muse would already have helped him.

She would have sung poems destined to enjoy an everlasting title;

in a thousand ways she would have sung for so great a man.

She would have sung for the man, magnifying him

with diligent mind and hand and tongue.

But since songs of praise benefit the dead nothing,

may the supreme power of God be merciful to him.

Phoebus had warmed Libra for twice six and eight days

when the hermit departed from this life [Note: [Col. 0593D] That is, in the year 1101, when St Bruno died. The Gregorian calendar reform had not yet been made, and the sun entered the sign of Libra on 17 September; from that day to 6 October, the day of the Saint’s death, twenty days elapsed, counting both endpoints.].

The church of S. Peter of Chester [Note: [Col. 0593D] Perhaps the English collegiate church of Chester, dedicated to St Peter, is designated here.].

**143.** Bruno, while living, was the glory of the just

and the sole consolation of the guilty;

the ornament of the entire clergy and likewise an example of truth,

[Col. 0593B] but death—grief!—snatched him away when the Father fell.

First made a monk, and thereafter a true hermit,

may the supreme grace of God be merciful to him.

To this end our prayers are directed, that complete propitiation

may be granted to fragile life, confined within its brief span.

The sixth day of October brought him to its end

with grievous reproaches; may he now have rest.

Another by the same author.

**144.** The title of the person named above,

the Virgin and Mother whom, after the Lord, he worships,

makes the whole world resound everywhere with diverse laments,

as it leads hosts along with itself to many deaths.

It prostrates all who have been washed in holy baptism,

as Bruno’s clear lamp demonstrates.

Although he is praised by the voices of many men

and is distinguished by the merits of outstanding conduct,

nevertheless the impious lot of death carried him to its gates.

We weep with you, but what use is there in all this except to ask Christ

that after his funeral he may have everlasting rest?

As we have fulfilled what was due for yours, so fulfill it for ours.

The church of S. Mary and S. Aldhelm of Malmesbury [Note: [Col. 0593D] The monastery of Malmesbury, discussed in volume I of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, pp. 49 and following, situated in Wiltshire, is probably designated here; accordingly *Malmesbenensis* is written incorrectly for *Malmesburiensis*.].

**145.** Here is the good athlete whose most celebrated life

is recounted here and proved worthy of praise.

For if he lived as this little document has said,

and if he was generous, devout, and chaste,

if sparing toward himself and generous to the needy,

if he trampled wealth and despised pleasures,

if he was refined in speech and well mannered,

what need is there of words? Why do I labor to say more?

[Col. 0593D] By the art of such great virtues he now possesses heaven,

for according to his merits the starry vault has been given back to him.

Now therefore Bruno rejoices and clings to the One;

Bruno has received the One, having abandoned many things.

Yet this One alone is superior to all.

If it is worthwhile to learn how great this gain is,

I shall say it briefly and explain it clearly in a few words.

He received Christ, the sweet consolation of labors.

What profit, then, is there in our composing verses for him?

Yet I think there is profit if I say: “God, have mercy.”

But since no one is without the blemish of sin,

if he has any wrongdoing, good God, wipe it away.

The church of S. Mary of Rouen [Note: [Col. 0593D] Since the cathedral church of Rouen is dedicated to the Most Holy Mother of God, it is certain that it is designated here.].

**146.** Let the entire order of the holy Church mourn,

weeping over the irreparable loss of the human race.

Bruno, Father and founder of holy Religion,

the victorious honor of the world, has departed from the world.

Such great goodness commends his holy life

that no one can equal him.

He himself was wise, noble, and radiant in character,

imbued with the fountain of all philosophy.

Since living virtue shone in him,

he earned glorious authority.

He trampled wealth, despised all honors,

crushed beneath his feet the world’s foolish ambition,

and by his devotion founded holy Religion.

Turning away from the world and avoiding the world’s high places,

he chose instead to live a private life.

Although a humble hermit, renowned for his merits,

no one can recount the sequence of his splendid piety

or the deeds of his holy goodness;

setting these matters aside, let us devote ourselves to prayer

and entreat the supreme Father with devout mind,

[Col. 0594C] that the excellent Father may enjoy the light of life,

and, just, may be joined to the ranks of the just.

We, the canons of the metropolitan church of Rouen, shall celebrate each year the anniversary of the venerable Bruno.

S. Trinity at Rouen [Note: [Col. 0594D] This monastery, situated on a hill near Rouen, was built in the eleventh century and continued under abbots until 1597, when its abbatial revenues were assigned to the Charterhouse of Gaillon, as the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume XI, columns 124 and following, explain.].

**147.** Although the human mind cannot discern what the end

of all things may be, the fountain and origin of good things

to whom what is hidden is open and who leaves nothing unpunished,

nevertheless, judging from the outward signs of his conduct,

the sweet and worthy completion of his holy life,

we believe that your Hero has passed to the heavenly beings.

What you celebrate in your prayers and vows,

we ask that you do the same for ours:

that those whom he released from this prison may live for Christ.

S. Leodegarius [Note: [Col. 0594D] The monastery of St Leodegarius at Pratellum, situated in the diocese of Lisieux and built in the eleventh century, as the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume XI, column 853, explain, is most probably designated here.].

[Col. 0594D]

**148.** Here the heading of the blessed Leodegarius is described.

No one can stand firm against the face of death,

[Col. 0595A] but a man’s barren life is like smoke.

Beautiful youth, once born, slips away like the wind.

The worst and the good alike are taken away.

All fall in death and seek the earth as corpses;

they come to nothing and flow away as food for worms.

Bodies decay—bodies that were once proudly alive—

and all flesh becomes hideous when dead.

As soon as a man dies, his grave is immediately prepared;

afterward no dear friend takes care to keep him.

The stinking body is already joined to the ashes of its companion.

O how vain is love, when all honor falls!

We have rendered to Bruno what due custom requires;

you too render the same for ours, those named in the heading [Note: [Col. 0595C] See note 352.].

S. Mary’s of Potilevium [Note: [Col. 0595C] This monastery, dedicated to the Most Holy Virgin Mary and also called Pontilevium, is situated in the diocese of Blois and was built in the eleventh century, as the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume VIII, column 1379, explain.].

**149.** A man, a despiser of the world, went out from the world to him

who made the world and whom he sees without end.

And although Bruno is called “dark” here, as though obscure [Note: [Col. 0595C] This alludes to the name Bruno, which may be derived from the Teutonic name *Braun*, the Flemish *Bruyn*, and the French *Brun*, all signifying in Latin “dark” or “somewhat black.”],

he is nevertheless radiant in fame and merits.

He enjoys God’s light because he rejected this light,

and in place of the wilderness he cultivates the heavenly kingdoms.

Therefore, brothers, do not grieve over one who is joyful;

he himself wishes you to be joyful as his companions.

If anything is lacking to him, may God complete it for him,

and join our prayers to yours on his behalf.

## SECTION VI

Heading of the church of S. Mary of Bayeux [Note: [Col. 0595D] The cathedral church of Bayeux is dedicated to the Most Holy Mother of God, as the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume XI, column 346, explain; therefore I think that the heading placed here must be referred to it.].

**150.** Energetic and strong protector of monks,

prudent concerning death and founder of monasteries,

first a kind imitator of the holy Fathers,

consolation of brothers and lover of holy virtue,

just corrector of morals, pious hope of the wretched,

guide of justice and guardian of the good everywhere,

adorned in conduct, a vessel full of piety,

bravely armed with the shield of true integrity,

Bruno submitted to the law of human condition,

to be joined to the ranks of the angelic host.

There dwell no robbers, nor any rebellious crowd;

[Col. 0596A] there are no wicked customs there, but everyone is faithful.

May the eternal King grant us access to that place,

and spiritual protection after death’s decease.

May this spirit of Bruno enjoy supreme peace

and, through God’s mercy, obtain the radiant light.

Scholastic verses of the same city [Note: [Col. 0595D] In the notes appended to section II I explained that formerly almost every cathedral had its own schools, in which those who wished were taught letters. But besides these schools, which were called episcopal, and the monastic schools established in monasteries, there were also in some cities schools founded outside the cathedrals and monasteries by teachers approved by the bishop. Since I do not know how matters stood in the city of Bayeux in St Bruno’s time, I cannot state with certainty whether the heading placed here refers to the episcopal school or to another Bayeux school. It may have proceeded from all the schools of the city of Bayeux together, if several happened to exist there.].

**151.** This grief, O Bruno, has proceeded from more than one source;

hence it grieves and laments, since your death troubles it utterly!

The common crowd of the schools does not shed its tears sparingly,

nor, deprived of such a Patron, does it kneel without grief;

in fitting measure it pours forth vows in prayer

and asks the King, who knows all hidden things,

to give you life, receiving you as a hermit.

S. George of the same city [Note: [Col. 0596C] In the general list of the benefices of the diocese of Bayeux, printed at Paris in 1648, p. 23, a church called St George is counted among the served churches of the city of Bayeux. Since I find no other sacred place, whether destroyed or still existing, which in the city of Bayeux either is or formerly was named for St George, I infer that this church is designated here.].

[Col. 0596B] **152.** Flower of hermits, wondrous and brilliant light,

star, Bruno, strength, order, and rule of the Fathers,

example of the heavenly way and fountain of wisdom,

you have reached the boundaries by which every age is enclosed.

We have enrolled you among the number of the brothers, best of Fathers,

pouring out diligent and devout prayers for you,

that through God’s piety a share of rest may be granted you.

S. Stephen [Note: [Col. 0596C] In the Basel edition there is *S. Stephani ad eumdem*, “S. Stephen, to the same,” that is, if I am not mistaken, to the same heading. Since the word “heading” was also sometimes used in St Bruno’s time to signify a circular letter announcing someone’s death, as is clear from the circular letter transcribed immediately before these funeral headings, announcing St Bruno’s death, this inscription is equivalent to the following: “The response of St Stephen to the same circular letter announcing the death of St Bruno.” Since the diocese of Bayeux contains in the city of Caen a monastery distinguished by the name of St Stephen and built in the eleventh century, it appears probable that this funeral heading—the response to the circular letter by which St Bruno’s death was announced everywhere—proceeded from that monastery.].

**153.** If this world could give life either through groaning or through tears,

the world would give both,

so that it might draw forth Bruno, once taken away, alive again—

Bruno, hope, honor, and help for the wretched—

who, pursuing the wilderness and bearing his own cross,

fulfilled in action what he taught with his lips,

and, holding the oar of faith, fixed hope among the stars,

and has now crossed the sea in a fortunate vessel.

And because no one can be blessed through his own power,

may the immeasurable grace of God justify this man.

The monastery of S. Vigor of Cerisy [Note: [Col. 0596D] This monastery of the diocese of Bayeux, also called Cerisy, had been destroyed by the Northmen while they were still pagans and ravaging Neustria; after they became Christians, it was restored by them in the eleventh century. See the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume XI, columns 408 and following.].

**154.** The humble flock of the monastery of blessed Vigor at Cerisy,

[Col. 0597A] instructed by a divine oracle, has performed the general office for the soul of the religious and God-beloved Bruno [Note: [Col. 0597C] See note 282.], praying that the supreme mercy of God may spare him.

The church of S. Mary of Coutances [Note: [Col. 0597C] The episcopal city of Coutances lies in Lower Normandy. Its cathedral church, as the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, volume XI, column 863, explain, is dedicated to the Most Holy Mother of God Mary; therefore I do not think that a sacred place distinct from that church is designated here.].

**155.** Christ, teacher of teachers, fountain and source of good things,

grant Bruno what the good have deserved.

That he is the true God entails that he is not severe;

therefore may God be gracious to him without end.

For this Father taught the human race,

worn down by vain guilt, as well as he could,

unfolding Christ’s commandment, which gives the beloved gift

of eternal life to the one who keeps it.

Nor does he teach only with words, like a harsh and bitter teacher;

he pursues the lesson with his own deeds.

[Col. 0597B] Why should this hermit lack perpetual life?

Because there is only one true God in the world.

What you ask for yours, may Christ also grant to ours,

so that together they may be companions of God forever.

Scholastic verses of the same city [Note: [Col. 0597D] The Basel edition adds “of the city.” See note 419.].

**156.** Bruno, teacher of many grammarians,

announces to all the bodily end.

Grammarian, rhetorician, dialectician, and astrologer,

Would escape death, if death were something to be fled.

But since no medicine can remove death,

Let each person always contemplate his own end.

### Saint Michael of Peril of the Sea

[Note: This monastery of the Abrincensis diocese, which is called by others Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea and which long preceded Saint Bruno’s lifetime, is discussed in volume VIII of our work, September, p. 80 and following pages, as well as in the writers of the expanded *Gallia Christiana*, volume XI, column 510 and the three following columns.]

157. The wondrous power of God brings wondrous deeds to completion.

[Col. 0597C] It justifies some and rescues others from death.

Whom He wills, He leaves unknown; whom He wills, He firmly establishes for Himself.

Among these Bruno, a man devoted to religion,

Is gathered, received, and happily numbered,

As the work of this roll testifies.

### Saint Peter Casalis

[Note: I nowhere find a sacred place distinguished by this name, nor one that could with any plausibility be the place designated here.]

[Col. 0598A]

158. If Bruno’s life, faith, and works were such as the inscription says,

He is not to be mourned, since he has been joined to the heavenly ones.

But while we endure the burdens of fragile flesh,

If no one appears who lives so free from sin

That he avoids offending either in deeds or in words,

For this reason we beseech Christ that, if this Father offended in anything, He may deign to forgive him.

### Monastery of Saint Mary of Louleium

[Note: This monastery, situated in the diocese of Le Mans and called Lonleyum, was built in the eleventh century. This is clear from the foundation charter supplied by the brothers Sammarthani in volume IV, p. 579 and following, since Sigefridus, bishop of Séez, subscribed it—not long after the eleventh century had begun, as the writers of the expanded *Gallia Christiana*, volume XI, column 680, show. Moreover, I think that this monastery, which, as the same Sammarthani brothers report in the same place, was founded in honor of the most holy Virgin Mary, is precisely the one distinguished in this inscription by the name “monastery of Louleium,” with the alteration of a single letter. In the meantime, it is strange that the title below explains not what this monastery, but what the mother church of Le Mans—that is, the cathedral church—did for Saint Bruno and was later to do. [Col. 0598C]]

159. When the death of the most blessed hermit Bruno was heard of, the mother church of Le Mans had a thirty-day office celebrated for him [Note: See note 269], intending to commemorate the anniversary of his burial.

### Saint Julian of Le Mans

[Note: Since the cathedral church of Le Mans is dedicated to Saint Julian, the first bishop of the people of Le Mans, and no other place distinct from it, bearing the name of Saint Julian, appears suitable to the title below—and since no sacred place in either the city or diocese of Le Mans seems to have existed in the twelfth century, in whose first year our Saint died—I think that the cathedral church itself is designated in this inscription. If this opinion of mine is correct, however, Claudius Robert and, after him, the brothers Sammarthani, who write in their compiled *Galliae Christianae* that the cathedral church of Le Mans, after having first been consecrated to Blessed Mary and then to Saint Gervasius, was finally dedicated to Saint Julian in the year 1201, when the saint’s sacred body was transferred into it, must necessarily have departed from the truth—unless, as I nevertheless do not think likely, this inscription of the title below originated solely with those who arranged for the Saint’s funeral titles to be published in the sixteenth century.]

[Col. 0598B] 160. We do not believe that your death, excellent Bruno, should be mourned,

You who, fleeing the empty honors of the perishing world,

Wisely imitated an angelic life on earth

And, while still living in the body, sought heavenly things in your mind.

Therefore, released by Christ’s mercy from the evils of the body,

You enjoy eternal peace in the ethereal dwelling places.

Would that I could follow your holy footsteps

And gladly endure the losses of this body for that purpose!

Another by the same author.

161. Bruno lived in the Church as its strongest column;

He has fallen, and therefore the Church’s glory trembles.

The earthly world mourns; the heavenly court rejoices.

The former has lost so great a man; the latter receives him.

He paid what nature owed, pursuing better things,

[Col. 0598C] For which eternal life will be his in place of brief death.

Another, likewise by the same author.

162. The worshiper and companion of the Most High withdrew to the heavenly ones,

Committing to the earth what belonged to it.

[Col. 0599A] He despises the light burdens and the world that acts like Proteus,

Having obtained, as a poor man, eternal riches.

Meanwhile, what has been entrusted to the ashes is mingled with them,

And in an equal lot it hopes for and awaits its rewards.

I suspect that the angelic hosts rejoice for him

And that the citizens of heaven applaud their new fellow citizen.

It was the sixth day of October when Bruno, having followed

Nature, went to the heavenly ones, freed from his burden.

Another, still by the same author.

163. This man, seeking heavenly things in sincere religion,

Reigns with the saints in the celestial realm.

He labored—blessed labor—from which there called him

The glory of the saints, the wondrous reward of labors:

Giving you, Bruno, to yourself, He gives you a kingdom under one King—

Under that King, I say, whose majesty

[Col. 0599B] Shines in Olympus and is light, glory, and everlasting life for the saints.

Therefore it is fitting for us to commend this man’s labor

And fitting also to praise the giver of the eternal gift.

May our devotion in praise obtain for us as well

That by the divine gift we may reign under that King.

### Saint Vincent of Le Mans

[Note: This abbey of the Order of Saint Benedict, situated in one of the suburbs of the city of Le Mans, was built in the sixth century by Saint Domnolus, bishop of Le Mans. Mabillon teaches this in the *Benedictine Annals*, book VI, no. 43.]

164. If life could be restored by tears and mourning,

With great lamentation, tears, and vehement grieving,

I would mourn sorrowfully, deprived of light, Bruno—

The flower of the whole world and the glory of the clergy.

### Blessed Julian of the Meadow

[Note: This monastery of Benedictine nuns is situated in the diocese of Le Mans and existed long before Saint Bruno’s time, as is clear from what Mabillon records about it in books I and II of the *Benedictine Annals*.]

165. May everlasting life be granted to this Bruno;

May his spirit, received into its heavenly dwelling,

Now and forever reign happily with the Lord.

[Col. 0599C] This illustrious man, blessed in life and as a teacher,

Shone happily among the clergy through his teachings to the world.

Therefore, with devout lamentation and abundant tears, let us too

Pray to Christ that He now grant him paradise.

### Saint Maurice of the See of Angers

[Note: The cathedral church of Angers is dedicated to Saint Maurice; there can therefore be no doubt that Saint Maurice of the see, or episcopal chair, of Angers is designated here.]

166. Gaul grieves; the Calabrian people weep.

This one mourns a good teacher, that one weeps for a patron.

The former praises him by the testimony of his present life;

The latter everywhere celebrates his outstanding wisdom.

Bruno’s tongue is praised more highly than Virgil’s,

[Col. 0600A] And Plato’s glory grows insignificant beside Bruno’s praise.

Here he surpassed teachers; here he produced

The greatest teachers, not by training lesser ones.

He was a teacher of teachers, not of little clerics.

For Bruno possessed neither the mere proprieties of words nor their mere solemnity,

But the qualities of a man of great reason.

The rule of the prudent surpassed the sharpness of the intellect,

So that he proved an excellent teacher of these doctrines.

He chose to place above them a more perfect school,

Announcing an excellent wisdom by teaching divine things.

He first demolished the former teachings and regarded them as frivolous;

Formerly a guide of error, he afterward showed the way of better doctrine [Note: Do not infer from this that Saint Bruno ever departed from the truth of orthodox faith. See the preliminary commentary, no. 69 and following],

Which grants joys without end.

But worldly wisdom gives nothing except empty things.

The one makes people arrogant through pomp; the other makes them blessed.

[Col. 0600B] By his deeds he completed in practice what he taught with his mouth.

He preached many sermons throughout the regions.

He passed through the city of Rome and visited the Calabrians.

At last he became an abbot and obtained heavenly things.

Hence that people grieves, because misfortune has taken away its father.

And although it mourns such a spiritual man,

Its sorrow is caused not by the shepherd’s death but by its loss.

### Monastery of Saint Florentius of Glamuensis

[Note: We have already dealt with Saint Florentius, priest and confessor, on 22 September, the day on which he is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology and other sacred calendars, and on which he exchanged life for death, probably at the beginning of the fifth century. There, in the commentary preceding his acts, it was explained how the monastery situated on Mount Glonna in the present duchy of Anjou—called by others Glomea or even Glomna—which bears its name from that Saint and is now called Old Saint Florentius to distinguish it from the new monastery of Saint Florentius, built later near Saumur, was restored in the tenth century after the double destruction it had suffered, first from the Bretons and then from the Northmen. This sacred monastery, also discussed by the brothers Sammarthani in the old *Gallia Christiana*, volume IV, p. 388, is beyond any doubt the one distinguished here by the name “monastery of Saint Florentius of Glamuensis,” with a change of one letter in the word, very probably through error. [Col. 0600C–D]]

167. The body is distinguished in various members,

Whose head is Christ, ruler of Catholics.

In it we monks, placed as modest members,

Believe that there are true and exalted hermits.

Among their number, great Bruno, we acknowledge you,

As the despising of worldly honor testifies to us,

[Col. 0600C] And as the good end of your holy life confirms.

Since we entirely approve the praises written for you

And think that we can be supported by your merits,

Yet, in order that we may comply with the prayers of our brethren who pray,

We make known that we have poured out prayers for you;

Therefore we have no doubt that you will repay us in turn.

### Saint Nicholas of the Same City

[Note: That is, if I am not mistaken, of Angers; so that here the monastery of Saint Nicholas of Angers is again designated—the one mentioned in the notes appended to the preceding section, where I already discussed it under note 402.]

168. Before your roll-bearer had yet reached our homes [Note: See the preliminary commentary, no. 24, for the meaning of this word], our abbot Lambert had already received him and had already written worthy verses about so great a Father. We willingly grant what he promised, and we now promise again to increase what was promised [Col. 0601A] [Note: It is clear from this that this title, and another given above in its proper order as no. 131, were written by Lambert, abbot of the monastery of Saint Nicholas of Angers. Observe also that, since the funeral titles of some other places intervene between this one and that one, the two were either written separately on two sheets of parchment (see note 290), or, if the matter was otherwise, were not published in the order in which they were written on the common funeral roll. [Col. 0601C]] for Bruno, whom we believe already to reign with God.

Bruno was a fountain of doctrine, a standard of true dogma,

Surpassing the depths of Aristotle and Socrates,

Outstripping Plato through the sacred gift of chrism.

He lived as a human being, pressed down by the weight of flesh,
