Yet while living he subdued the flesh, reaching toward heavenly things,

Despising the dying world for the sake of the heavenly kingdoms.

May Bruno live happily in heaven with the heavenly assemblies;

May he behold the King, whose law he preserved by his deeds.

And you, fathers and brothers, pray for the brothers.

### Monastery of Saint Mary of Dol

[Note: Since there is no monastery at Dol in Lesser Brittany, nor at Dol in the county of Burgundy, dedicated to the most holy Mother of God, it plainly appears that the monastery of Dol is designated here. It was built in Berry in honor of that same most holy Mother of God by Ebbo, lord of Dol, in the tenth century for Benedictine monks, who were finally replaced by secular canons in 1623, as the writers of the expanded *Gallia Christiana*, volume II, column 148, report.]

69. As your holiness deigns to request, we brothers of the monastery of Dol, moved by compassion for the desolation of your brotherhood, immediately upon hearing of the death of our blessed Father and master Bruno, took care to offer to almighty God the support of our most devout prayers for his soul. Besides the suffrages of thirty Masses [Note: That is, if I am not mistaken, Masses to be celebrated for thirty days, or perhaps for thirty years] and of alms, we devoted to him, with paternal affection, the benefit of an annual Mass, which is offered daily and, with the Lord’s consent, will continue to be offered. We also commend his memory in writing to our register [Note: I explained the meaning of this word in note 256], so that each year the affection of fraternal devotion may be stirred to commend him to almighty God when his name is read.

### Hermitage of Saint Michael

[Note: This very ancient monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, commonly now called Saint Michael in the Wilderness [Col. 0602C], is situated in the diocese of Luçon and was founded around the year 680 by Ansoaldus, bishop of Poitiers. See the expanded *Gallia Christiana*, volume II, column 1418.]

[Col. 0601C] 170. The cruel death of human beings, which Eve brought upon us,

Harms everyone, as this book teaches.

It crushes everyone and seeks a kingdom above all things.

Bruno was just, as this book has taught.

Bruno was just, simple, humble, and gracious;

Yet, when death willed it, he could not continue living.

[Col. 0602A] And since his limbs lie dead, let the groans for his funeral cease,

Because no one receives forgiveness on account of grieving.

Therefore let us persevere and repeatedly entreat the Lord God

That He grant him rest before His face.

### Saint Mary of Luçon

[Note: This formerly abbatial church, dedicated to the most holy Mother of God and raised by Pope John XXII to cathedral rank in 1317, is older than the eighth century, as is clear from what the writers of the expanded *Gallia Christiana*, volume II, column 1404 and following, record about it.]

171. Brothers who are in the valley called the Tower, let it be known to all of you that, for Lord Bruno, we are to perform charitably seven vigils [Note: See note 255 for the meaning of this word] and seven Masses, together with bread and wine, under the authority of Lord Reginald, abbot [Note: This abbot is listed first among the successors of Goffridus, abbot of Luçon, who died in 1091, in the *Chronicle of Maillezais*. See the writers of the expanded *Gallia Christiana* in the place cited immediately above.].

### Saint Peter the Apostle of Maillezais

[Note: The famous abbey of Maillezais, or Mallaisais, undoubtedly is designated here. It was built as early as the tenth century and dedicated to Saint Peter; it was formerly situated in the diocese of Poitiers and was later itself made an episcopal see by Pope John XXII. See again the expanded *Gallia Christiana*, volume II, column 1362 and the following two columns.]

172. May the Lord grant him a place of rest,

Whom he always worshiped while he was able to live.

### Monastery of Saint Vincent of Niort

[Note: This monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, formerly in the diocese of Maillezais and now in that of La Rochelle, is said in the manuscript *Chronicle of Maillezais*, as the writers of the expanded *Gallia Christiana*, volume II, column 1395, report, to have begun to be built in 1068, or alternatively 1069.]

[Col. 0602B] 173. While the community of Niort, attentive to chanting at the canonical hours in the church of blessed Vincent according to the regulations of the supreme Father Augustine, was gathered together, a letter was seen that revealed the death of Bruno, the incomparable philosopher. Such fear and horror seized them that they could scarcely complete the Office due at the time.

For who would not be astonished, indeed groan from the depths of the heart, on hearing that so great a man, the light and foundation of all knowledge and almost all clerics, had departed from nature? But since it is established that this cannot be avoided, and since we believe that our Savior also submitted for a time to the law of death, we transform into joy in Bruno the grief that we would have felt for others.

For Bruno possessed and preserved true knowledge and wisdom in the liberal arts, as well as the other cardinal virtues, and he brought them to perfection in a good end. For a long time he had been the supreme teacher of the church of the people of Reims, outstandingly learned in the Psalter and the other sciences [Note: This seems again to allude to the commentary composed by the Saint on all David’s Psalms. See the preliminary commentary, no. 694], and he long remained a pillar of the entire metropolitan church.

But because he understood that all this is truly transitory, after a stricter and highly unusual eremitical life he sought a wilderness in the regions beyond the sea [Col. 0603A] [Note: Those who wrote this title do not seem to have known well where the Turritan wilderness was situated, into which the Saint finally withdrew after leaving Gaul. For, contrary to their suggestion here, it was not situated beyond the sea in relation to Gaul. But perhaps, through an error originating with the scribes, *transmarinis* is written here for *transalpinis*—“beyond the Alps.” [Col. 0603D]]; and from there, when the Lord called him, he proceeded joyfully to the banquet of the supreme King.

There, although we believe that he chants the angelic Psalter with Christ, let us nevertheless continually ask the Fountain of all piety and mercy, by prayer and inward devotion, that if, while he lived, he neglected to remove any stain arising from his first parent or from his actual life, through forgetfulness or negligence, He may be willing to forgive him. To obtain this for him, we shall offer Christ for seven continuous days the Office owed to the dead.

### His School

[Note: That is, the monastery of Niort—or rather, as the writers of the expanded *Gallia Christiana* write in the place cited immediately above, the monastery of Niort. The two titles that follow here undoubtedly refer to the school that this monastery maintained according to the custom then prevailing.]

174. Bruno was the light of the French while he lived,

The light of the clergy; now he enjoys the light of the heavenly citizens.

[Col. 0603B] For he is worthy to receive such an honor,

Since in this life he lived a heavenly life.

He is plainly deranged and has a heart devoid of reason—

Whoever testifies otherwise or imagines something different,

As the man who brought us this document relates.

If any earthly impurity clung to him,

May He who cleanses the sins of the world wipe it away.

Another by the same author.

175. Bruno had been a light while he lived in this world,

But now he shines again, because he shines from heaven’s dwelling.

He knew the Psalter [Note: Here again there seems to be an allusion to the commentary composed by the Saint on all David’s Psalms, or at least to his truly outstanding understanding of them], but now he sings heavenly instruments above.

He taught many; now he sees the saints in heaven.

Now, alone among the heavenly citizens, he is teacher of teachers.

A teacher on earth, he now applauds Christ on high.

[Col. 0603C] Therefore pour out prayers for us, illustrious Bruno,

And we, in return, will strive to fulfill our vows.

For we desire to live above with you and with Christ,

And all of us ask to be placed in the tenth order.

### Saint Paul the Apostle of Cormery

[Note: This monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, situated in the diocese of Tours, was built in the eighth century in honor of Saint Paul the Apostle, as the brothers Sammarthani teach in the old *Gallia Christiana*, volume IV, p. 299.]

176. To my lords and brothers serving almighty God in the monastery of Saint Mary of the Wilderness, which is called the Tower: Mainardus, to make use of the world and enjoy God. In the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1102, on the Kalends of November [Col. 0604A], I received this roll [Note: The person who carried the encyclical letter announcing Saint Bruno’s death therefore did not visit the monastery of Cormery until some time after a year had elapsed since Saint Bruno’s death. I therefore think that he first visited the sacred places of England, whose funeral titles for Saint Bruno appear above, and only afterward crossed into Normandy, from which he then proceeded to the monastery of Cormery and other nearby sacred places.].

I read in it that the blessed soul of my most gentle master Bruno, by persevering in true charity, had breathed out the fleeting vapor of this age and, on the wings of the virtues, ascended to the heavenly kingdoms.

I rejoiced, certainly, at the glorious end of so great a man; but since I had an unflagging intention of going to him shortly, seeing and hearing him, pouring out all the passions of my soul into him, and obeying the most holy Trinity with you under his guidance, I was shaken beyond what I can express by his unexpected death and could not restrain the reins of my tears, which flowed freely.

I, Mainardus, then, in the monastery of Cormery, Prior [Note: See the preliminary commentary, nos. 97, 99 and following, concerning this most devoted disciple of Saint Bruno] in the name, though not in the work, of many monks, was born in the city of Reims. For several years I heard the teaching of this lord Bruno and, by God’s will, made considerable progress. Since I could not render thanks for my progress to Lord Bruno in this life, I have now resolved at least to offer them to his soul.

Accordingly, I shall keep him and all his beloved in Christ in my remembrance for as long as I am able to breathe. I shall summon, rouse, and encourage all my fellow-dwellers, spiritual sons and brothers, to the same work according to my ability. I shall offer to God and the Trinity prayers, offerings, and alms for him no differently and no less than for myself, for as long as there is breath in my nostrils.

### Saint Savior of the World and Saint Gildas the Confessor of Dol

[Note: This formerly Benedictine monastery, situated sixteen leagues from Avaricum of Berry, at the Indre River in the diocese of Bourges, was founded by Ebbo, lord of Dol and founder of the monastery of the same name mentioned under note 439, for the abbot and monks of the monastery of Saint Gildas of Rhuys, who had fled the fury of the Northmen, who were ravaging Armorica, where that monastery was situated, during the ninth century and the beginning of the tenth. The writers of the expanded *Gallia Christiana*, volume II, column 153 and the following two columns, explain how this was done, as well as how secular canons were finally substituted for the monks there in 1623.]

177. Since prayer must faithfully be poured out to the Lord for all human beings whom holy Mother Church, cleansing them from every error and from original sin through water and the Holy Spirit throughout all the regions of the world, regenerates day by day, especially for those whose help and benefit we believe can aid us, every Catholic ought to offer urgent prayers and perpetual remembrance.

Therefore, having heard that this most excellent man Bruno had been called by the Lord, we have determined to perform three fuller offices in the community. May his soul rest in peace.

### Church of Saint Mary of Tropea

[Note: Tropea, an episcopal city of Further Calabria, possesses a cathedral church dedicated to the most holy Mother of God, as Ughellus teaches in volume IX of *Sacred Italy*, column 449. I therefore think that this very church of Saint Mary of Tropea is designated by this inscription, especially since no other sacred place appears that could suit the title below. Nevertheless, the person who carried the encyclical letter announcing Saint Bruno’s death seems, from the different verses of which the title below is composed, to have visited this church only after the other places whose funeral titles precede it. It may therefore seem strange that he visited it so late, and only when he was already about to return home, since the church is not far from the Turritan wilderness. [Col. 0605D]]

[Col. 0605A]

178. Because Bruno was pleasing to God, he was therefore blessed.

If I were to praise him, I would not make him blessed by that praise.

I give thanks to God that he possessed as many virtues

As the tongue of a wise friend can express.

Therefore the skin of the neck is worn away beneath the weight of the roll,

And the neck of the roll-bearer can no longer lift the roll [Note: I supplied the meaning of *rolli* and *rolligeri* in the preliminary commentary, no. 24],

On which so many things of such great importance are written in the court of the Thunderer.

The sun with the moon, the course of the stars as well,

Light, heaven, air, earth, sea, Tartarus, sulfur, and smoke;

A livid, foul place, full of stench and corruption—

That realm of Pluto is far removed from Bruno’s lot.

[Col. 0606A] The parchment was large; now it seems small and confined,

On which the lot, the fate, and every created thing are written,

And the timeless time of the Creator’s honor.

Such was the life of this hermit in this life,

So devout and gentle, simple, and without any train of strife.

If I knew how to express it, there would be no place on which I could write it.

So it is being written on the inside and on the back of the skin.

What more shall I say? I no longer know how to say anything.

Yet, so that the blessing may increase, I say: may he rest.

I say that he has been given peace, since he has been placed above the stars.

Even if in the grave his flesh becomes dust and bones,

He has not died; he lives and has gone back seeking his homeland.

May we be able, in the One, to live the life that Bruno lives [Note: It is plainly evident that frivolous and empty things, as Cangius states under the word *Titulus* in the *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, were sometimes written in funeral titles with which the dead were formerly honored. This is clear from several passages occurring both in this and in several other funeral titles for Saint Bruno given above, although these titles almost always simultaneously include material useful for displaying Bruno’s reputation both for learning and for the holiness in which he became renowned immediately after his death. [Col. 0606D]].

## APPENDIX OR SUPPLEMENT TO THE POSTHUMOUS GLORY OF THE SAINT

### § I. The veneration shown in Calabria to the Saint, already enrolled among the Blessed and transferred to the church of Saint Stephen, and the numerous miracles performed at his invocation, several of them preceding the year 1600

[Col. 0605B]

1. After the sacred body of Bruno, enrolled among the Blessed by Pope Leo X in 1514, as I explained in the preliminary commentary, § 47, had been transferred in that same year 1514 from the Turritan church of the most holy Mother of God, where it lay buried, to the Turritan church of Saint Stephen, all the Carthusians everywhere, and especially those of Turris, increasingly manifested by more than one sign the singular veneration they bore for the holy founder of their Order.

First, the monastery of Saint Stephen of Turris, which at that time, after the original name of Saint Mary and Saint Stephen had been changed, was accustomed to be called solely Saint Stephen of the Wood or of the Forest—and under whose name, then as now, the Turritan church of Saint Mary and the entire complex of buildings belonging to the Turritan wilderness were included—was thereafter called by them not merely Saint Stephen, as Pope Leo X had decreed (see the preliminary commentary, no. 755 and following), but, with the name of Saint Bruno added to that of the holy martyr, the House of Saint Stephen and Saint Bruno, in honor of their holy Father. In the course of time, and for the same purpose, they also called the province of their Order that now includes the Charterhouse of Turris, and which had previously been distinguished by the name of the Province of Further Lombardy, the Province of Saint Bruno—a name it still bears today. I learn this partly from Morotius’s *Chronological Theater*, p. 226, and partly from Camillo Tutini’s *Survey of the Carthusian Order* under the year 1514. [Col. 0606B]

2. Yet the Carthusians who inhabited the Turritan wilderness, which had finally been restored to them from the Cistercians by order of Pope Leo X, did not stop at naming their monastery after Saint Bruno; such a name would plainly have been little enough. Their remarkable veneration for that holy Father went further.

For what Matthew, prior of the Charterhouse of Bologna, had said should be done with Bruno’s sacred head in the presence of the people standing by while his precious relics were being transferred (see the words quoted in the preliminary commentary, no. 776), they arranged to have carried out. They enclosed the Saint’s sacred head—or rather the portion of it that still remained in their possession—in a finely worked silver bust.

Nor were they content merely to ensure that this precious pledge should be guarded with suitable and proper reverence. Not long afterward, apparently, they instituted the practice that every year, so that the Saint’s cult might also increase among the people, his sacred head, already enclosed in the silver bust as I have said, should on the second day of Pentecost be carried in solemn procession from the church of Saint Stephen, where it is kept, to the church of Saint Mary, and on the following day be carried back from there to the church of Saint Stephen in the same manner.

This institution of the solemnity did indeed enjoy happy success. For not only did the Saint’s cult greatly increase through it; it also happened afterward that sick people who had come to the celebration, having implored Saint Bruno’s help, were restored to their former health. [Col. 0607A]

3. Various persons testify to this who committed to writing the miracles that the Lord then deigned to perform to manifest the glory of His servant. In this section I wish to recount, in the chronological order in which they occurred, some of these and several others that were performed at Saint Bruno’s invocation on other occasions before the year 1600.

To avoid disturbing that order, I begin with those that took place outside the time of the aforementioned solemnity. Surianus writes as follows in his notes on the Life of Saint Bruno written by Surius, p. 319:

“In the year 1523, on the first day of February, the Very Reverend Father James of Aragon, professed member of the Charterhouse of Naples and prior of the aforesaid Charterhouse of Saint Stephen, together with the other conventual monks, wrote the following miracles to the general chapter of the Carthusian Order. They had occurred shortly after the house” (namely, the Calabrian house of Saint Stephen) “had been recovered:

“In our own days, the noble Neapolitan Alphonsus Toraldus, the brother by both parents of the excellent Lord Adam Toraldus, baron of Badolato, who was deeply devoted to Saint Bruno, was staying at Tropea, a maritime city of Calabria [Col. 0607C]. While walking for recreation beside the sea on a steep cliff nearly one hundred cubits high, it happened that, his foot slipping, he slid headfirst into the abyss.

“As he fell, he tried to grasp a crumbling wall with his hands so that he would not fall to the bottom; but the wall itself collapsed upon him. Placed in such danger, he invoked Saint Bruno as his helper, and immediately saw a monk, handsome in appearance and dressed in white, holding his right hand and gently leading him down to the lower ground.”

4. “As a result, he suffered no injury from the fall, although his companions, who had run to the falling man, thought that he had either been killed or that his body had been shattered by the fall. He therefore returned home on foot, needing neither a vehicle nor anyone else’s assistance for the journey; and he gratefully attributed this great benefit to the merits of Saint Bruno. This happened around the year 1522.”

Camillo Tutini also records this miracle in the survey of the Carthusian Order that he composed. However, whereas Surianus here assigns it approximately to the year 1522, Tutini refers it to the year 1518.

Even if this is so, the two writers should not for that reason be considered to contradict one another. Surianus does not strictly attach the miracle to the year 1522, but merely writes that it occurred around 1522—a formula that allows an interval of three or four years.

In any event, that miracle seems to have preceded three others, which Surianus proceeds to relate from the account of James of Aragon and the other religious inhabitants of the Charterhouse of Saint Stephen in the notes mentioned above on the Life of Saint Bruno.

The first is as follows:

“Lady Laura Carafa, daughter of the Duke of Nevers and countess of Arenas, while pregnant, fell into a very serious illness. When she was at the point of death, her husband, Lord Francis, count of Arenas, who had always devoutly honored Saint Bruno, made a vow that he would offer a silver chalice at the Saint’s altar.

“Then, as the count and countess themselves testified, she was cured of that grave illness and, at the proper time, gave birth to a child, whom they named Bruno at baptism. And so that the mother might never be forgetful of the benefit she had received, she vowed to wear white clothing of the kind in which Saint Bruno himself, who had appeared to her in a dream, seemed to be clothed.”

### 5

The second is related in these words:

> “In the year 1522, a certain man from the town of Zimbario, in the diocese of Squillace, situated about four miles from the monastery” (namely, that of St Stephen), “named Garetus Scopa-Casa, brought his only daughter to the monastery gate with his wife Isabella. The girl was possessed by an unclean spirit. When relics of St Stephen and of other saints had been brought to her, so that the demon might be expelled—as had happened on other occasions—and when no hope of its departure appeared, the Very Reverend Father Vicar, Father de Corduba, advised the girl’s parents to take her to St Bruno’s grotto, which was a mile from the monastery.
>
> “When they had arrived there, they went around the chapel three times on their knees, praying devoutly. Then, after kissing the imprint of St Bruno’s feet on the image, the girl swallowed a little dust from the same grotto. Wonderful to relate: after she had taken the dust, the hostile spirit began to course through the girl’s bowels; then, migrating into her arm, it finally reached her hand. In order to leave a sign of its departure, it formed a swelling at the tip of one finger and, opening the pores more widely, made an exit for itself, not without blood, and completely departed. Freed from so evil a guest, the girl returned with her parents to the monastery, where she rendered immense thanks to God and to St Bruno, her liberator.”

Here is also the last of the three miracles mentioned above. It is set forth in the following words by Surianus, page 323:

> “About the same time” (namely, in the year 1523, shortly before the more certain general chapter of the Carthusian Order at which the account of the three said miracles was established), “in the town of Pizzone, in the diocese of Mileto, situated six miles from the monastery” (namely, the Turritan monastery of St Stephen), “a priest from the secular clergy named Sophranus Miriano, who had an abscess in his chest near his vital organs, made a vow to St Bruno. He was immediately restored to health and, as he himself testified in writing, sent a candle of virgin wax to the altar of the Holy Father Bruno, on which the account of his cure and recovery was inscribed.”

Surianus then adds other miracles performed through the merits of St Bruno. As he says, these “were copied from the manuscript papers of Don Nicola Ricci of Taverna, professed of the same house” (that of St Stephen), and were arranged more carefully, with several others added, by the Very Reverend Father Severus of Naples.

### 6

But since the first of these is said to have occurred only in 1524, and since the divinely granted apparition of St Bruno and St Vincent Ferrer to Aloysius Bertran, or Bertrand, father of St Louis Bertrand, perhaps occurred sooner than I promised in no. 746 of the preceding Commentary to relate it here, I wish to present that apparition first, before recounting any of the others, so as not to depart from chronological order.

Surianus therefore narrates it in the following manner on pages 318 and following:

> “On another occasion, after his first wife had died, he” (namely, the father of St Louis Bertrand) “was going to the same house” (the Carthusian house of Portaceli), “which is four leagues from Valencia” (that is, the city of Valencia in Tarraconian Spain, where he lived), “intending to request the religious habit. On the journey those same saints, Vincent and Bruno, appeared visibly to him, saying that it was not God’s will that he become a religious, but that he return to the secular world. From his second wife, Joanna Angela, whom he later married, he had Blessed Louis Bertrand in 1526, a member of the Order of Preachers, who, renowned for holiness and miracles, ascended to heaven in 1581.”

Thus Surianus relates the matter at the place cited. There he also adds that this account had been copied by Father John Madariaga, Part I of the Life of St Bruno, chapter 22, § 3, from the Life of St Louis Bertrand written by Brother Justinian Antist. Since the same account is found in that work, I think this is certainly consistent with the truth.

I now proceed to the miracles which Severus of Naples extracted from the manuscript papers of Nicola Ricci, arranged more carefully—as Surianus’s statements show—and supplemented with several others.

### 7

The first, according to Surianus’s recension, is as follows:

> “In the year of the Lord 1524, when the Very Reverend Father David de Charcascolis of Milan, professed of the Charterhouse of Pavia, was prior of this house” (St Stephen’s), “the distinguished lord John Baptist Carrafa of Naples, then count of Agrottaria and lord of Castelvetere and Rocella, fell ill unto death. When he was at the point of death, deprived of every medical aid, St Bruno appeared to him one night in a vision and said: ‘John Baptist, if you delay restoring the territory unjustly occupied by your people from my house of St Stephen of the Wood, you shall die and not live.’
>
> “He replied in a similar voice: ‘What territory, Father?’ He answered: ‘The territory which you call Ninfo, granted to me and to my successors by Count Roger the Norman.’ After saying this, he vanished.
>
> “The aforementioned count resolved privately to investigate the matter more carefully and to restore everything. Wonderful to relate: scarcely had he formed this resolution in his mind when he began to improve, and was entirely freed from his fever and every danger to his life. He then summoned a notary and witnesses, related the vision, and restored the territory, which had been occupied for many years. He also obtained many other benefits from the Holy Father Bruno, which are set forth more fully in the instrument of restitution.
>
> “This was executed at Naples on 18 November 1519” (there is an error here: the year in which that restitution was made, as will be found below in no. 13, must be substituted—namely, 1529), “by the notary Virgil de Bulvito of Naples, between the Very Reverend Don Octavian of Mantua, then prior of the house of St Stephen and visitor of the province, and the aforementioned count. As the instrument states, the count, recognizing and considering the good faith and the greatest devotion which he professed toward the monastery of St Stephen, and the reverence which he held for St Bruno, whose holy relics are honorably preserved in the aforesaid monastery, and through whose merit and intercessions he had continually been assisted, especially in obtaining offspring from the Lord, and being concerned for the salvation of his own soul and those of his predecessors—having first been informed and fully instructed concerning the monastery’s jurisdiction—freely and with a good, pure, and uncoerced will released the aforesaid territory of Ninfo and, by means of a staff, resigned it to the Very Reverend Father Prior, and so forth.
>
> “Physical possession of it was taken on 29 January 1530 by the aforementioned Octavian, the prior, in the presence of other monks and of Don Stephen of Surianus, professed of the same house.”

### 8

This is the first account which Surianus, in the place cited above, reports from the papers of Nicola Ricci of Taverna, arranged more carefully and supplemented from other sources by Severus of Naples. He immediately appends the following:

> “About the year 1540, when Blessed Catherine Thomas of Majorca, later a canoness of the Regular Order of St Augustine in the monastery of St Mary Magdalene in the city of Majorca, was about five years old and was traveling with her grandfather in a sloping place near the Charterhouse of Majorca, a certain monk appeared to her in a white habit, the distinctive dress of the Carthusians. He was believed to be St Bruno, and he foretold that she would become the bride of Christ and would not, as her grandfather wished, be joined in marriage.
>
> “On another similar occasion, before she had reached her tenth year, she had entered a certain cave and fallen into a pit from which she could not escape without human assistance. When that assistance failed, she appealed to God, and it came immediately. For a man of imposing appearance, in human form and dressed in white, stood beside her; in her judgment he appeared to be a Carthusian. But it must have been the Holy Father Bruno, who had appeared to her on the former occasion in the same guise. He consoled her, warned her not to be afraid, and told her to grasp and hold firmly the staff which he carried in his hand. When she had taken hold of it, she easily climbed out of the pit, and he immediately disappeared from her eyes.”

This prodigy of the two apparitions, however, may reasonably be doubted as having truly been attributable to Bruno. Severus of Naples seems to have drawn it not from Nicola Ricci’s papers but from another source. Surianus leads me to this opinion, since at the end of the account he notes that it was taken from the Life of Catherine Thomas, who is listed among those passed over by us on 5 April. The work was written in Spanish by the Very Reverend Father Bartholomew Valperga, a monk of the Charterhouse of Majorca, and printed at Majorca in 1617—

### 9

Here is now a miracle of another kind: not one by which the Saint conferred a benefit on anyone, but one by which a man who had injured him was divinely punished. Surianus immediately appends and relates it as follows:

> “In the year of the Lord 1544, on 5 October, the eve of the day sacred to the Holy Father Bruno, a certain man noble and illustrious by birth, but miserably led astray by the exceedingly cunning heretic Martin Bucer, was sitting in the Cologne Charterhouse at the time when the hourly evening prayers are celebrated, in the guesthouse where visitors are usually received. He was eating and drinking a little with the religious Father Peter Boechem, then procurator of that Charterhouse and later prior of Koblenz. When he heard from him that on the following day the solemn feast of St Bruno was to be celebrated, he replied angrily:
>
> “‘Do you suppose that he has been enrolled among the saints? Certainly, if he is a saint, may I never enjoy good health after drinking this cup.’
>
> “He spoke, drank, and soon, as though occupied with something else, began to sit pensively, as fanciful people do. Shortly afterward he mounted his horse and departed for his castle. Without delay he fell into bed and, a few days later, died of his illness just as he had called down upon himself—unwillingly approving the holiness of St Bruno.”

Erard Winheimius also relates this prodigy, or divine vengeance for the injury inflicted on God’s servant, in the *Agrippine Sacrarium*, page 214. Neither he nor Surianus, however, states the name of the nobleman who, because of the insulting words he had spoken against St Bruno, miserably perished. In all likelihood, both thought that they ought to spare the honor of the very noble and still highly distinguished family from which he came. Indeed, they acted according to an entirely commendable judgment; therefore I too, following their example, refrain here from disclosing the name of that nobleman, although I know it very well from an ancient and trustworthy document of the Charterhouse of Serra San Bruno.

### 10

Of the miracles preceding the year 1600 which Surianus reports from the papers of Nicola Ricci of Taverna, enlarged by Severus of Naples from other sources, and which must here be brought forward, let us now recount another:

> “When the monastery of St Stephen” (see Surianus in his annotations on Surius’s Life of St Bruno, page 331 and following) “was being enlarged in the year of the Lord 1553, under the prior Don Peter Paul Lumbulo of Gaeta, professed of the house of Naples, a man whose life was full of gentleness, piety, and religion, the upper part of the refectory, constructed with a vaulted roof—the kind which the Italian inhabitants call a *lamia*—was already very solid and carefully built at great expense. It appeared to have become sufficiently firm and stable that, once the moisture had dried, the wooden supports holding the stones bound with cement could be withdrawn and removed. The masons began demolishing the structure somewhat sooner than they should have done. Suddenly they heard a terrible crash from the collapsing vault.
>
> “It happened that a certain Bonellus, the master builder, together with others of the same trade assisting him, found themselves in such immediate danger and peril that they all began with one voice to cry: ‘St Bruno, help us!’ At these words they saw someone in the form of a monk, venerable in appearance, who grasped their hands and transferred them to another place outside the refectory. Immediately the collapsing vault fell.
>
> “Having thus escaped unharmed through the merits of Blessed Bruno, they rendered immense thanks to God and to the blessed Father.”

This last miracle clearly revealed how powerful St Bruno’s patronage is in heaven. So that no one might doubt its truth, Surianus immediately adds:

> “That this miracle occurred in the year 1553 is confirmed, besides John Madariaga, who asserts it on the basis of the sworn testimony of the Very Reverend Father Silvius, Book I, chapter 22, also by a painting in the same refectory. It indicates that the work” (namely, the work resumed after the earlier vault had collapsed in 1553) “was completed in 1554, and even now the memory of the event, received from our forebears, remains alive there.”

### 11

Another miracle, which I now add, proves no less how great St Bruno’s merit is before God. It is recorded by Surianus on pages 335 and following in these words:

> “At approximately the same time, namely before the year 1558, a certain Don Stephen Carozza of the town of Suriano, in the diocese of Mileto, about six miles from the monastery” (that of St Stephen), “one of the first professed members of this house in 1535, was expelled from the Order and declared alien to it as incorrigible, because of various crimes committed by him, ‘to the great scandal of the Order’ (these are the words of the charter of the general chapter of 1535 in the disposition concerning the province and this house), and because of his frequent apostasies.
>
> “He then lived for several years in the same town in the manner of secular clergy. At length he fell into severe pain in his sides and a fever. Thus brought to the point of death and entirely deprived of every aid, he began to cry out in a loud voice: ‘Holy Father Bruno, help me!’ He was seen rolling his eyes fiercely and moving about the bed with a sorrowful face. Nevertheless, he continually repeated in a loud voice, ‘Holy Father Bruno, help me,’ and, having no other words in his mouth, was tormented more and more.
>
> “When his brother James Carozza and the other members of the household observed this, they were moved by compassion and went to the prior of the monastery. Upon hearing what had happened, the prior immediately sent Father Francis Micelotto of Binungio, a professed member and procurator of this house, with full power and authority to reconcile him to the Order and clothe him in its habit.
>
> “He went there and, entering the house according to the customary rite, said: ‘Peace be to this house,’ and so forth. Immediately the sick man, who had been lying as though lifeless, cried out: ‘Clothe me, Father, for I cannot die unless I am first received back into favor and have recovered the habit which I abandoned. The most holy Father Bruno has obtained this gift for me from God.’
>
> “As soon as he had been clothed in the habit, he began to improve. He confessed his sins to the same father and humbly asked for and received the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist. Then, with great contrition of heart, he was anointed with holy oil. Thus fortified, he ended his life. His body was brought to the monastery and buried in the common cemetery.
>
> “This must have occurred around the year 1558, for in 1559 Brother Micelotto was appointed prior of the house of Trisulti by the chapter, and he died in 1560.”

### 12

Surianus, who received this miracle—or benefit—bestowed by St Bruno upon a priest who had once been a member of his Order from the papers of Nicola Ricci, enlarged by Severus of Naples, adds at the end that it was originally drawn from a charter of the chapter of the Carthusian Order, as is indicated at the beginning of the account already given.

After inserting several other matters, which I omit for the sake of brevity, he appends on page 354 the following account. It concerns Fabricius Carrafa, who, after his grandfather John Baptist Carrafa had restored the territory of Ninfo to the Charterhouse of St Stephen (see no. 7), occupied it again. The account had been entered in the same papers from the archives of the Turritan Charterhouse of St Stephen:

> “In the year 1586, in the month of October, Don Fabricius Carrafa, marquis of Castelvetere, grandson of Jerome F. and John Baptist Carrafa, continued the obstinacy of his ancestors by occupying and wrongfully retaining the aforesaid territory of Ninfo. When he was summoned to court by the prior of that time, the Very Reverend Father Peter Bono of Agrottaria, for its restitution, he treated the summons with contempt and fell into a most acute fever, so severe that the physicians gave up hope of his life. His family summoned his most religious mother, who was still living in a nearby town, to mourn the funeral of her unfortunate son.
>
> “But she, having learned from the misfortunes that had befallen her predecessors because of the usurpation of the aforesaid territory, replied to the messengers: ‘I shall come and cure him, God willing and St Bruno assisting.’
>
> “Immediately going to her son, who was already near death, she addressed him as follows: ‘You rightly suffer these things, because you unjustly occupy the territory of Ninfo belonging to St Bruno. Now heed my words: summon the prior of St Stephen and restore that place to him, and you will immediately be freed. You will know that the hand of the Lord is upon you, afflicting and rescuing you.’”

### 13

> “He immediately obeyed his mother’s admonition and, in the presence of many bystanders, declared that he would do so. But merciful God, who does not desire the death of a sinner but rather that he be converted and live, immediately commanded the fever, and it departed. Once restored to health, he fulfilled in action what he had promised by means of a public instrument executed on 18 October 1586, in the fifteenth indiction, by the hand of Consalvo Ermogida of the town of Spatula. In it he confessed that he had recovered his health miraculously, in these words:
>
> “‘Because of the supreme devotion owed to the aforesaid St Bruno, and because of the merits and benefits received and obtained in various ways, and which he hopes to receive from the aforesaid St Bruno and receives day by day, especially in his present grave illness,’ and so forth.
>
> “He also confirmed the cession made by his grandfather John Baptist on 18 November 1529, as stated above (see no. 7). On the same day he also wrote a letter to the community, commending himself to their prayers.”

I now come at last to the miracles drawn from the frequently mentioned papers and performed through invocation of the Saint during the annual solemnity in which, as has just been stated, the sacred head of Bruno is customarily carried from the Turritan church of St Stephen to the likewise Turritan church of St Mary.

Surianus writes as follows on page 356:

> “In the year 1589, when, according to custom, a great many priests and crowds of both sexes from the surrounding encampments and towns had gathered, during the solemn procession by which, on the Monday after Pentecost, the monks carry in procession from the monastery of St Stephen to the church of Blessed Mary—one mile distant from this place, near which there was formerly a hermitage constructed by St Bruno—a silver image, represented to the waist, in which the head of the Holy Father Bruno is preserved, and likewise an entire finger of St Stephen the Protomartyr, enclosed in a silver hand, which is said to have been donated to this house” (namely, the Calabrian house of St Stephen) “by Urban II at the insistence of Count Roger, many people were cured of various illnesses through the aid of the Mother of God and the merits of St Bruno. Many of our people saw them with their own eyes, for twenty-five monks and lay brothers were present there.”

### 14

> “There you might have seen some imploring the help of the Blessed Virgin and others calling upon the name of the Holy Father Bruno—and not in vain, for they were healed of whatever illness afflicted them.
>
> “Among them was a woman from the neighboring town called Pizzone who was mute and had not uttered a word for eighteen years. At once, in the church mentioned above, she began to cry out, ‘Mercy!’ and then recovered the free use of speech. In memory of the benefit she had received, she thereafter always wore the white habit in the manner of our nuns, and every year she came among the first to the annual feast of that church.
>
> “Another woman from the town of Suriano came to the church mentioned above. She had been ill for twelve years and had spent almost all her property on physicians, to no avail. Before everyone, she knelt in prayer and began to cry out:
>
> “‘Servant of God, St Bruno, I have now confessed; I have now received the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist. If it is beneficial for the salvation of my soul, obtain health for me; but if not, obtain a blessed death. For I shall gladly die if that should happen to me in this church.’
>
> “Wonderful to relate: she immediately died, and everyone saw her as though she were smiling. She was buried in the same church.”

These are the two miracles—or benefits—which still had to be recounted in the present section. Perhaps someone, however, will call into question whether the first of them was performed through St Bruno’s patronage, since the mute woman, for whose benefit it occurred, is not said to have invoked him.

Nevertheless, since she subsequently wore the white habit in the manner of Carthusian nuns in memory of the benefit received, she seems thereby to have attributed it to Bruno and to have confessed that she had invoked him. Since this is so, it appears that one must admit that the Saint had some part in that miracle or benefit—unless, as I do not think likely, the whole matter should rather be attributed to the most holy Mother of God.

Let us now proceed to the matters which I have decided to address in the following section.

## § II. Several miracles performed in the seventeenth century, but before its twenty-fourth year, are recounted; and it is explained how the cult of the Saint was eventually extended to the universal Church and how his feast was then celebrated at Cologne

### 15

Surianus, in his annotations on Surius’s Life of Bruno, having prefaced his account with a reference to the above-mentioned Nicola Ricci of Taverna, relates that many miracles were performed for the benefit of the sick and afflicted by means of dust scraped from the stone of the grotto or cave in which, as some maintain on the basis of statements in the preceding Commentary, § 45, St Bruno lived continuously after withdrawing to his Turritan hermitage, and in which he also appears in fact to have stayed at times (see the same preceding Commentary, no. 748).

He now presents, on page 361, the following miracle or benefit performed through the use of that dust, according to the account of Severus of Naples, who states beforehand that he heard it from Basil, a lay brother of the Turritan Charterhouse and an eyewitness of the event. He gives it in Severus’s own words:

> “Brother Blasius of Pace, a lay brother of the same Order, professed of that house, from the nearby town of Serra, one mile from the monastery” (St Stephen of the Wood), “was miserably tormented, by God’s permission, as one possessed by an evil spirit.
>
> “The aforesaid Reverend Prior” (namely, Louis Suespeckh), “moved by the great charity with which he was endowed and desiring to rescue his sheep from the attack of the infernal wolf, knowing also that a certain kind of demon is expelled only by prayer and fasting, lived for three days on bread and water alone. Suspending his other business, he remained devoted solely to prayer.
>
> “After the third day, having first made a more careful general confession of his sins, he celebrated Mass as devoutly as he could at the altar in the sacristy. In a finely made reliquary of ebony mixed with silver and variously embossed, the head of the Holy Father Bruno is preserved there in a silver image, together with other relics of the saints. Brother Blasius, the possessed man, and the aforementioned Brother Basil were present.”

### 16

> “After Mass, the exorcisms were begun. When the demon hesitated to depart, Father Prior remembered the stone of St Bruno’s cave and immediately ordered Brother Basil to mount a horse and bring him as quickly as possible some dust taken from the stone in the cave.
>
> “Having carried out the order, Basil took the dust and was returning home. In the middle of the journey he suddenly felt a powerful wind rushing violently against him. He was thrown forcibly from the horse and fell heavily to the ground. At that very moment the demon, bursting into laughter through the mouth of the possessed man, cried out in the Calabrian dialect:
>
> “‘At come buono conzato se ne terra!’
>
> “These words mean in Latin: ‘How well received he returns!’
>
> “Thus the same Brother Basil reported the matter to me precisely. The horse, now without its rider, returned straight to the monastery. Thinking that the fallen man was still unable to rise from the ground, people ran out to him and carried him back to the house.
>
> “The prior took the dust from him and applied it against the demon, forcing it to leave the man. He was immediately freed and remained unharmed until his death. He died afterward, on 1 August 1625.”

Since Louis Suespeckh, while he was prior of the Turritan Charterhouse of St Stephen and of St Bruno, expelled the demon from the possessed Brother Blasius by using dust from the stone of St Bruno’s cave, as related here, and since Severus of Naples states in the place cited by Surianus that Suespeckh was first appointed prior in 1608 and died in 1611, this prodigy must have occurred during the period between those two years. Since it may perhaps have occurred before 1609, I thought it best to place it before the other miracles still to be recounted, which occurred either in that same year or later.

### 17

Here is one that occurred in 1609. Although it was not performed through dust taken from the stone of Bruno’s cave, it was nevertheless accomplished through the Saint’s patronage. Surianus records it on pages 363 and following in these words:

> “Under the same Reverend Prior” (Louis Suespeckh of the monastery of St Stephen), “in the year 1609, when a large stone was being transported to the monastery, quarried from a nearby stonepit, square and measuring eight or more palms on every side, with a diameter of nearly one and a half palms, intended for the slab of the church’s high altar, it was so heavy that it could be hauled with difficulty by several pairs of oxen on a wooden machine. Many people came to see it.
>
> “A certain David Müller of Brandenburg, an excellent sculptor in stone and wood, who produced many admirable emblems in this monastery from multicolored pieces joined together, and who was the builder of the aforementioned machine and superintendent of the work, was attempting midway through the journey, with one knee bent, to adjust the cart. As he looked beneath it, one of the wheels pressed his leg so violently that it sank into the earth, the soil yielding completely under the weight. David himself cried out: ‘St Bruno, help me!’
>
> “When many people ran up out of compassion, thinking that his leg had been crushed, it was found to have suffered only a slight injury to the tendons, which was also completely healed shortly afterward.
>
> “At the same place the aforementioned sculptor arranged, at his own expense, for a small shrine or chapel on the hill to be erected in perpetual memory of the event. It still exists.”

To the two miracles already related and recorded by Surianus I now add another, not previously published in print, so far as I know. It was performed in 1610 before an image of St Bruno at Caballion—or, as others write, Cavallion—a city in the episcopal county of Venaissin in Provence belonging to the Apostolic See. It was communicated to our predecessors at the Grande Chartreuse in 1668, as the note assigned to it informs me.

### 18

It is described in the following words:

> “In the year of the Lord 1610, in the month of August, Alexander Maurissius, a citizen of Cavallion, saw in the choir of the Capuchin Fathers of Cavallion a small painting in which the image of St Louis, bishop of Toulouse and professed of that same Order” (namely, that of St Francis of Assisi; for Capuchins did not yet exist in the thirteenth century, when St Louis of Toulouse flourished), “had recently been portrayed by Father Bernardino. Delighted and exceedingly impressed by the elegance of the image, he approached Father Fabian de Sault, who was a friend of his, and urgently begged him—and obtained his agreement—to have the little image of St Bruno hanging there, which he had preserved out of his longstanding devotion to the Saint, transformed by Father Bernardino’s work, with superimposed colors, into a similar representation of St Louis.
>
> “Father Bernardino therefore laid the first stroke to the work on the twentieth of that month and began, as is customary, to coat the background of the image with indigo. But since the work displeased him because of its small size, he handed the brush to a painter who happened to arrive, named L’Empereur, and asked him to complete the work, already well begun, in the likeness of the image of St Louis.
>
> “The painter agreed and darkened the background of the image, the Savior himself hanging on the cross, and the skull beneath him with black soot mixed with oil. He changed St Bruno’s white habit to a grayish one, lengthened the cowl, shortened the sleeves, and sewed a piece of hempen cloth in place of the cowl. Finally, removing the pontifical insignia—the crozier and mitre—and St Bruno’s head, he transformed the entire image into another.
>
> “When the day was already far advanced toward evening, he left the panel in this condition with Father Bernardino and departed. The next day, at dawn, Bernardino, curious to inspect another man’s work, looked more closely at the image. He stood astonished and, struck by the unprecedented result, could scarcely believe his eyes. There was no brushstroke, no trace of color or indigo: everything was pure, as though wiped clean with a sponge. Only the sandarac remained, as if to provide a perpetual memorial of the event, while the original features were intact. Thus St Bruno appeared in the natural whiteness of his habit, having cast off the added form and colors.
>
> “Father Bernardino, uncertain whether to be overcome by fear or joy, hurried to Father Andrew d’Arles, Guardian of the convent, communicated the entire matter, explained it in detail, and displayed the image.”

### 19

> “All the Fathers of the house hastened to the spot when they heard of the extraordinary event. They questioned, listened, examined the image, and with one voice exclaimed that it was a great miracle.
>
> “Joseph L’Empereur, the painter, also arrived, mindful of his promise and intending to complete the task. But Father Bernardino informed him of the miracle that had occurred and forbade him to apply his hand any further to the work, since the undertaking had turned out so inauspiciously, or ever again to attempt to change an image of one saint into that of another.
>
> “After seeing and hearing all this, Don Maurissius, not without shame and fear, received the image returned to him with the greatest veneration. Eventually, after many people had seen and reverently inspected it, he presented it as a gift to Don Denis Sailly, prior of the Charterhouse of Bonpas.
>
> “An authentic instrument exists concerning the matter. It was signed by the Reverend Official and Vicar General of the Most Reverend Bishop of Cavallion, Alexander Maurissius, Joseph L’Empereur, and John Baptist Gemifrem, notary and secretary of the spiritual court of Cavallion, and was secured with the episcopal seal. Together with the aforementioned image, reproduced above, it was sent by the same Don Denis to the Charterhouse and is preserved there intact in the house archives.”

Our predecessors, as I already indicated above, noted in the margin that they had received from the Grande Chartreuse the account of the miracle performed in the image of St Bruno in these words. They also added a note stating that, when they were there in 1662, they had seen both that image of the Saint and the authentic instrument itself mentioned at the end of the account, in the chapel dedicated to St Bruno at the Grande Chartreuse.

It is evident from the words with which the account is formulated at its beginning and end that a copy of that image was sent to our predecessors together with the account of the miracle. I, however, was unable to find it among the collected notices concerning St Bruno, although otherwise I would here present it to the reader engraved on copper.

There is only one more miracle attributed by Surianus to the Saint and which preceded the year 1624. Before I turn to other matters relating to the posthumous glory of the Saint, I shall present it here for the benefit of the attentive reader.

### 20

It is related in these words:

> “In the year 1623, when Don John Manduci of the town of Seminara, in the diocese of Mileto, was prior, he had the chapels of St Stephen and St Bruno, situated in the transept of the church, ornamented with variegated marble brought from Rome at great expense. For the purpose of fitting the marble, a certain Gaspar, a marble worker, also came there from elsewhere.
>
> “One day, prompted by the enemy of the human race and goaded by the incentive of the flesh, he was speaking with another craftsman of the same trade, named Michael the Sicilian, inside the church of St Mary” (namely, St Mary of the Tower). They were alone near a small door on the right side of the church, exchanging words about a certain woman in order to solicit her to indecency.
>
> “Suddenly they heard four powerful blows striking the steps—at that time wooden, though later made of stone—by which one ascends from the exterior part of the church to the choir constructed above the church vestibule. Terrified by the noise, Gaspar went outside through the side door and clearly saw the back of a monk dressed in our habit, heading toward and entering a nearby grove.
>
> “He was struck by even greater fear at the sight, since he knew very well that none of our monks was there on that day or at that hour, nor did they ever customarily come there alone. He therefore reasonably supposed that it had been St Bruno, whose concern always was, and still is, the honesty and holiness appropriate to the house of God.
>
> “Then, pierced by fear, he disclosed the entire matter to Don Matthias Nucifero, a professed monk and at that time sacristan of the monastery. On his report, these events were entered in the records.
>
> “In the same year the woman was killed by her relatives. At night, during the time of Carnival, Gaspar, turning aside to a nearby village, was gravely wounded in the head, but soon recovered after commending himself to the Holy Father Bruno. He also entreated me, who am writing this, to offer a Mass at the Saint’s altar and in his honor. I willingly did so, unaware that the matter was secret.”

21. Since the date given in this account itself reveals that what Severus of Naples here relates at Surianus, p. 365 and the two following pages, occurred in the year 1623, and since the worship of our Saint also happened to be propagated in that same year, the chronological order which I have decided to follow requires that I deal with this matter here.

Public veneration of Saint Bruno, ever since the year 1514, when he had been enrolled among the blessed in the manner explained in the Preliminary Commentary, § 47, had existed almost exclusively among the Carthusians. At last, through their efforts, Pope Gregory XV granted that the feast of Saint Bruno should be entered in the Roman Missal and Breviary, and that an office for him, of the semidouble rite, on 6 October—the day on which he departed for heaven—could be freely and lawfully recited everywhere by all the faithful who are bound to the canonical Hours.

Pope Benedict XIV received the apostolic brief by which this was done from the Grande Chartreuse, as he himself states, and included it in the first book of his work on the beatification of the servants of God and the canonization of the blessed. There, in chapter 41, no. 7, it is worded as follows:

> “Gregory, Pope XV, for perpetual remembrance of the matter. We, although unworthy, exercise on earth the place of our Lord Jesus Christ, who grants his servants the reward of eternal glory in heaven. By the obligation attached to the pastoral office entrusted to us, we are bound to see to it that the fitting veneration of these servants of Christ is daily advanced, and that the Lord is praised in his saints. For this reason, we willingly accede to the petitions of all the faithful, but especially of those who serve the Most High under the gentle yoke of religion, whenever we perceive in the Lord that their requests, directed toward the particular worship and veneration of such saints, are beneficially expedient.”

22. 

> “Accordingly, moved by the petitions humbly presented to us by our beloved son, Don Bernardo Gazio, procurator general of the Carthusian Order, and acting on the advice of our venerable brothers, the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church assigned to sacred rites, we grant and concede by the authority of these presents that, for all future time, the feast of Saint Bruno, founder of that Order, on 6 October, the day on which he departed for heaven, may and shall be placed in the Roman Missal and Breviary, and that an office for him of the semidouble rite may be freely and lawfully recited everywhere by all the faithful.
>
> “Therefore we command and enjoin upon our venerable brothers, the patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches established throughout the whole world, that they cause these our present letters to be solemnly published in their respective churches, provinces, and dioceses, and to be observed without exception by all secular ecclesiastical persons and by the religious of every order, notwithstanding any apostolic constitutions and ordinances or anything else whatsoever to the contrary.
>
> “We further decree that transcripts of these presents, even printed ones, signed by the hand of any public notary and authenticated by the seal of any person established in ecclesiastical dignity, shall be given exactly the same credence as would be given to these presents themselves if they had been produced or displayed.
>
> “Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, under the Fisherman’s Ring, 17 February 1623, in the third year of our pontificate. S. Cardinal of Saint Susanna. Thus it is: Silvester Spada, notary of the most illustrious and most reverend lord Cardinal Vicar.”

Place of the seal.

23. This apostolic brief had already been preceded by an indult of the Sacred Congregation of Rites, by which the same thing that is granted here through the brief had already been granted in 1622. It likewise appears in Benedict XIV at the place cited immediately above, and reads as follows:

> “In response to the petition presented to the Sacred Congregation of Rites by Lord Bernardo Gazio, procurator general of the Carthusian Order, the same Congregation, moved by the common assent of the most illustrious reverend fathers, and having also obtained the confirmation of our Most Holy Lord, granted that the feast of Saint Bruno, founder of that Order, on 6 October, the day on which he departed for heaven, should be placed in the Roman Missal and Breviary, and that an office for him of the semidouble rite should be recited by all the faithful everywhere.
>
> “For those who founded sacred religious families and left to the Church militant the unfailing assistance of their prayers seem especially to demand the universal veneration of the Church among the saints.”
>
> Signed: Francis Maria, Cardinal del Monte. Place of the seal. Giovanni Battista Rinuccinus, secretary.

Ambrosius Crollet, the secretary who communicated this document to Benedict XIV by order of the reverend father general of the Carthusian Order, notes that it was dated 19 November 1622. It was granted to the Carthusians at their request by the Sacred Congregation of Rites, with the pope himself assenting, as the words quoted—which establish the matter—make clear, under Pope Gregory XV. Thus it appears that he had previously granted, by an oral declaration, precisely what he later granted to the Carthusians at their request in 1623 through the brief recited in no. 21 and the following section.

Nor did this pope grant only that Saint Bruno might be publicly venerated throughout the universal Church. He also very willingly granted that, so that Bruno might in fact be honored with suitable veneration even by those who are not bound to the canonical Hours, the sacred churches of the Carthusians should be visited and the customary prayers offered there in order to gain plenary indulgences. I am pleased to transcribe here the apostolic letters preserved in Surianus by which he did this.

24. In the following words, therefore, the commentator on the Life of Saint Bruno composed by Surius presents them:

> “Gregory, Pope XV, for perpetual remembrance of the matter. The splendor of the Father’s glory, who illuminates the world with his ineffable brightness, especially follows with benign favor the devout prayers of the faithful who hope in his most merciful majesty when their devout humility is assisted by the prayers and merits of the saints.
>
> “Therefore, wishing to illuminate all and each of the churches of the monasteries of Carthusian monks existing anywhere with some spiritual gift, trusting in the mercy of almighty God and in the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we mercifully grant in the Lord a plenary indulgence and remission of all their sins to all faithful Christians of either sex who are truly penitent and have confessed and received Holy Communion, provided that each year, on the feast of Saint Bruno, customarily celebrated on 6 October, they devoutly visit any one of the said churches from First Vespers until sunset on that feast-day, and there offer pious prayers to God for harmony among Christian princes, the extirpation of heresies, and the exaltation of Holy Mother Church.
>
> “These presents shall remain in force perpetually for all future time.
>
> “We further decree that transcripts of these presents, even printed ones, signed by the hand of any public notary and authenticated by the seal of any person established in ecclesiastical dignity, shall be given exactly the same credence as would be given to these presents themselves if they had been produced or displayed.
>
> “Given at Rome, at Saint Mary Major, under the Fisherman’s Ring, 3 July 1623, in the third year of our pontificate.”

25. After reciting this bull of Gregory XV, by which a plenary indulgence was granted to those who frequented any Carthusian church on 6 October, the day consecrated to Saint Bruno, Surianus adds on p. 266 and the following page:

> “At the sound of this bull, as though a trumpet had been blown, peoples of various regions were stirred up, and each in rivalry, according to his more religious devotion toward Saint Bruno, bestowed upon him exaggerated worship.”

He then relates with what solemnity and splendor the Saint’s feast was celebrated at Cologne, Liège, and Lier in Brabant. To be brief, I wish merely to inform the reader, through the commentator on the Saint’s Life written by Surius, what was done in the first of these three cities, where the Saint was born.

Before transcribing the words with which that writer explains the matter, however, something must be said about the year in which this solemnity occurred at Cologne, lest anyone perhaps suppose that, because it is placed by Surianus immediately after the apostolic letters just quoted, dated 1623, it also occurred in that year—whereas, as will be shown, the facts indicate otherwise.

The solemnity at which Saint Bruno’s feast was celebrated at Cologne, after the papal bull mentioned above had been issued, was preceded by an edict in which Ferdinand, prince-elector and archbishop of Cologne, strongly exhorted all the clergy of his archdiocese to celebrate the approaching feast of Saint Bruno with the appropriate and required devotion, and prescribed certain matters relating to it. I am pleased to transcribe in full that document, which I found among the notices concerning Saint Bruno preserved by our predecessors—not only so that I may omit nothing worthy of note that contributes to the Saint’s posthumous glory, but also because it shows that the solemnity under discussion was celebrated at Cologne not in 1623 but in 1624, as I shall demonstrate shortly after quoting it.

26. It is worded as follows:

> “Ferdinand, by the grace of God elected and confirmed Archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne, archchancellor of the Holy Roman Empire throughout Italy, and prince-elector; bishop of Paderborn, Liège, and Münster; administrator of Hildesheim, Corvey, and Berchtesgaden; prince of Stavelot; count palatine of the Rhine; duke of both Bavarias, Westphalia, Engaria, and Bouillon; margrave of Franchimont; count of Loss, Loon, and Horn; born legate of the Apostolic See, etc.
>
> “To the venerable clergy and to all and each of the Christian faithful of our city and archdiocese of Cologne: everlasting salvation in the Lord.
>
> “Since God Almighty, that Father of mercies, in accordance with his paternal providence and his infinite love for us, distributes his saints in various places and times, so that in this dark world, amid so many errors of doctrine and morals, they may carry a torch before us and, as it were, lead us by the hand along the way of eternal salvation; and since he has continually looked upon this our Church of Cologne with the eyes of his most gracious mercy and made it more distinguished than the other regions and provinces of the world, when in his clemency he willed and granted that it should be the parent, nourisher, dwelling-place, and guardian of many great saints;
>
> “through whose merits and intercessions, after it received the faith, it did not relapse but remained steadfast in the faith, is so still, and hears itself called the faithful daughter of the Roman Church, and receives the other benefits that flow and are derived from that source as from an everlasting fountain of all good;
>
> “among these saints Saint Bruno shines forth like the morning star: a great glory and ornament of the Church of God, a citizen of Cologne, born and educated at Cologne in the noble family of Hartenfaust, who died in the year 1101; enrolled among the saints by Leo X in 1514; and founder and patriarch of the most celebrated and holy Carthusian Order, ‘whose praise is in the Church.’
>
> “Moreover, letters of our Most Holy Lord Pope Gregory, of blessed memory, concerning the celebration of the aforesaid feast of Saint Bruno, have recently been presented and communicated to us, in the following tenor.”

27. The brief of Pope Gregory XV, who died on 8 July 1623, and therefore before this edict of the Archbishop of Cologne was issued, is then recited. It is the brief given in nos. 21 and 22. The document continues as follows:

> “We, therefore, both on account of the obedience which we owe to the Apostolic See and because of our religious affection and veneration toward the saints of God, especially those who are more closely connected with us and with our Church, hereby notify you, the persons mentioned above, of the apostolic letters, by the apostolic authority entrusted to us and also with the advice and consent of our venerable chapter.
>
> “For their execution, we earnestly request and admonish in the Lord both the secular and regular clergy to celebrate this day solemnly, with due and exemplary devotion, according to the tenor of the aforesaid apostolic brief, and to lead the other Christian faithful by their example.
>
> “We strictly and seriously command the rectors and pastors of churches and the preachers of the divine Word to publish this to the Christian people on the feast of Saint Michael, which falls on Sunday, the seventeenth after Trinity, 29 September, in a loud and intelligible voice, and, after explaining the Saint’s life, diligently exhort them to observe his feast piously and religiously.
>
> “They should entertain the firm hope that this Saint, our countryman by origin and education, will continue to protect and preserve us and the flock entrusted to us, through his prayers and intercessions before the divine majesty, in these most dangerous and deeply troubled places and times, with pious affection for his homeland. This is all the more necessary for us because more serious dangers surround us from heresy and war.
>
> “Moreover, so that the Christian faithful may be more readily encouraged to undertake the veneration and devotion owed to him, we further announce and attest that our Most Holy Lord Pope Gregory XV, by other special letters—which shall remain in force perpetually for all future time—has mercifully granted in the Lord a plenary indulgence and remission of all their sins to all faithful Christians of either sex who are truly penitent and have confessed and received Holy Communion, provided that each year, on the feast of Saint Bruno, customarily celebrated on 6 October, they devoutly visit a Carthusian church from First Vespers until sunset on that feast-day, and there offer pious prayers to God for harmony among Christian princes, the extirpation of heresies, and the exaltation of Holy Mother Church.”

28. 

> “This we declare in such a way that the faithful of the female sex—who are barred from access within the monastery enclosure and the church doors—may and can gain the same indulgences by praying outside, in front of the monastery or church itself.”

Since in the year in which Ferdinand, Archbishop of Cologne, issued this edict, the seventeenth Sunday after the feast of the Most Holy Trinity fell on 29 September, as the document itself makes clear, and since this occurred not in 1623 but, as calculation shows, in 1624—the year in which Easter fell on 7 April and therefore the feast of the Most Holy Trinity was celebrated on 2 June—it is necessary that the edict was issued in this latter year. It is also recorded at the end of the copy printed at Cologne by Peter Cholinus.

Now, since this edict preceded the Cologne solemnity under discussion, as already stated, it follows that the solemnity did not occur before 1624. Nor does it seem doubtful that it occurred in that very year, since it took place not long after the aforesaid edict, as may reasonably be inferred from the very words in which the document is composed.

Let us now transfer here the words in which Surianus describes it. They are as follows:

> “The feast—of Saint Bruno, that is—was celebrated and inaugurated with solemnity throughout the entire city of Cologne, in the manner of rejoicing people. The entire senate spent the joyful day at the Charterhouse, before the faces of the saints, both in the choir and in the outer choir. The whole clergy and all the religious of the other orders joined in the celebration.
>
> “And so that the female sex might not grieve or complain that it had been excluded, a platform and an altar of remarkable size were erected before the gate. In that place a very large crowd of women received Mass, Communion, and the sermon with eager minds.”

29. 

> “There was also no lack of most pleasing singing by the singers at both Vespers and at Mass. A procession was then made through the greater cloister with the gravity and splendor befitting the saints, followed by the senate of Cologne, both the patricians and the people.
>
> “On the actual radiant feast-day, the Mass was sung by a baron and canon of the metropolitan church; a count and canon served as deacon; and a priest-canon as subdeacon.
>
> “During the octave—for throughout the entire octave there was no lack of a gathering of the people—the vicar of the most serene prince also sang Mass, assisted by two canons, while the singers performed their office with truly outstanding skill both at Mass and at both Vespers.
>
> “To conclude in a word: since that Charterhouse was established, it had seen nothing comparable or equal to that solemnity. Finally, the most serene prince-elector and archbishop himself added the crown to the entire solemnity. After the octave, on the following Sunday, he visited the Charterhouse, received the Holy Eucharist, and spent that night as a guest in the priests’ residence.”

The Archbishop of Cologne, Ferdinand, mentioned here, was the son of William V, Duke of Bavaria, and Renata of Lorraine. Born in 1577, he was appointed coadjutor to his uncle Ernest, Archbishop of Cologne, in 1595, and succeeded him in the archbishopric of Cologne when Ernest died in 1612. He administered it most capably until the year of his death, 1650.

Surianus immediately adds to the words just quoted that at Liège and afterward at Lier, once Pope Gregory XV had granted in 1623 that Saint Bruno could be venerated throughout the universal Church with the semidouble rite on 6 October, his feast-day was likewise celebrated solemnly by men of the highest standing who were not members of the Carthusian Order. But since I have decided, in the interest of brevity, to refrain from reproducing the words in which that writer describes the solemnity then carried out in those two cities, as I have already stated, I now proceed to other matters that likewise concern the Saint’s posthumous glory.

§ III. Whether the Saint was canonized in 1623 by Gregory XV, or only later by Clement X, is examined; and other matters that contribute to his posthumous glory and appear especially worthy of notice are brought forward.

30. From the apostolic letters recited in the preceding section, by which Pope Gregory XV granted in 1623 that the feast of Saint Bruno on 6 October, the day on which he departed for heaven, should be entered in the Roman Missal and Breviary, and that an office for him of the semidouble rite could be freely and lawfully recited everywhere by all the faithful, Pope Benedict XIV concludes in his work on the beatification of the servants of God and the canonization of the blessed—a work cited more than once in the Preliminary Commentary—that Saint Bruno was not thereby canonized by equivalent canonization.

For in book I, chapter 41, no. 6, he writes:

> “It certainly seems impossible to say—see what was discussed on this matter in § 47 of the Preliminary Commentary—that Saint Bruno was canonized by Leo X. Rather, his equivalent canonization, based on the outstanding merits of so great a man, the foundation of so distinguished an Order, the continued fame of his remarkable miracles, and the concession of worship—first granted to the entire Carthusian Order by Leo X and afterward granted at will to the whole Church by Gregory XV—seems to be attributable to Pope Clement X, as may be gathered from the following decree:
>
> “‘In response to the earnest petitions presented to our Most Holy Lord Clement X by the Most Eminent Lord Cardinal Nithardus in the name of the Most Serene Queen of Spain, in which she begged His Holiness to grant that the office of Saint Bruno, confessor and founder of the Carthusian Order, which had hitherto been recited by the universal Church under the semidouble rite [supply: at will], should henceforth be recited under the double rite by all persons of either sex, both secular and regular, who are bound to the canonical Hours; and after the matter had been referred by His Holiness to the Sacred Congregation of Rites, that Congregation, upon the report of the Most Eminent Lord Cardinal Sforza, judged that the aforesaid favor could be granted if it pleased our Most Holy Lord, on 3 March 1674. After the aforesaid report had been made to His Holiness by me, the secretary, His Holiness graciously assented on 14 March of the same month and year, 1674.’”

31. Thus the cited Pope Benedict XIV teaches, not obscurely, that Saint Bruno was canonized by Clement X, and therefore not by the aforementioned apostolic letters of Gregory XV.
