He formed this opinion because, as the parenthesis inserted in the decree of the Sacred Congregation of Rites, which he quotes here, sufficiently indicates, those letters did not include a precept of worship.

Ambrosius Crollet, secretary to the most reverend father general and the chapter of the Carthusian Order, who communicated the same letters to Benedict XIV by order of that same most reverend Father, judged the matter in an entirely different way. For before the following words, which appear in the same Benedict XIV, book I, chapter 41, no. 7, he writes:

> “In the year 1623, the aforementioned Pope Gregory ordered that on 6 October all secular and regular persons throughout the world should recite, under the semidouble rite, the office of Saint Bruno, our confessor and founder, and also decreed that the feast of the same Saint Bruno should henceforth be described in Breviaries, Missals, and Calendars to be printed.”

From these words it is plainly evident that Ambrosius Crollet held the opinion that the apostolic letters of Pope Gregory XV quoted above included a precept of ecclesiastical worship.

But which of the two should be followed—the Carthusian member or Benedict XIV? Although Pope Gregory XV initially says in the aforementioned letters only that he was granting that Saint Bruno could lawfully be honored by all the faithful everywhere who are bound to the canonical Hours with an office of the semidouble rite on 6 October, he then adds words that sound like a command. He states that he commands and enjoins the patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches established throughout the world “to cause the aforesaid letters to be observed by all secular ecclesiastical persons and by the religious of every Order.”

This may perhaps have led Crollet to believe that Gregory intended to bind all the faithful who are obliged to the canonical Hours to recite the office of Saint Bruno, on 6 October, the day of his death, under the semidouble rite.

32. Perhaps, unless it is assumed that Gregory ordered them to do this, Crollet also did not sufficiently understand how it could have happened that Pope Urban VIII, Gregory XV’s immediate successor in the chair of Saint Peter, ordered Bruno’s office to be entered in the Roman Breviary without issuing a new decree by which he ordered Bruno to be venerated. See the Preliminary Commentary, nos. 188 and 193.

The matter certainly seems, as I now state my own opinion, extremely complicated. And indeed, since the decree of the Sacred Congregation of Rites included in the words of Pope Benedict XIV transcribed in no. 30—by which it granted, with the assent of Pope Clement X in 1674, that the office of Saint Bruno, which until then had merely been recited by the universal Church under the semidouble rite, should thereafter be recited under the double rite—contains no word that plainly expresses a precept of worship to be rendered to Saint Bruno, it seems not without reason that the question whether the worship of the Saint was prescribed by Clement X rather than by Gregory XV may be reopened.

Since this is so, and since a precept of worship is necessary for canonization, I do not dare assert with certainty that Saint Bruno was canonized—by what is called equivalent canonization—by Clement X rather than by Gregory XV.

Nor did Benedict XIV himself regard it as altogether certain that this had been done by Clement. For, as his words quoted in no. 30 show, he does not positively attribute Saint Bruno’s canonization to Clement X. Rather, using the mode of expression customary among those who are uncertain, he merely says that it seems that it should be attributed to that pontiff.

Nevertheless, even if the matter stands thus, and even if it may seem doubtful whether the Saint was canonized by Clement or by Gregory—or therefore whether he was ever truly canonized at all, since no pontiff after Clement is found to have prescribed the worship of Bruno—it is nevertheless certain that Clement X granted in 1674, as the decree of the Congregation of Rites cited above by Benedict XIV attests, at the petition of the Queen of Spain, that the office of Saint Bruno, which had previously been accustomed to be recited only under the semidouble rite, could thereafter be recited under the double rite by all who are bound to the canonical Hours.

I have thought it appropriate to mention here this matter concerning Clement’s concession and the decree of the Sacred Congregation of Rites by which it was declared, although three miracles preceded that papal indult and are to be related in the present section; they may perhaps have contributed in part to its being granted.

33. Since enough has now been said concerning the aforesaid papal concession, learned reader, I shall now also relate in continuous sequence the miracles that are found at Surianus, extracted from the documents already so often cited, on pp. 369 and following. They read as follows:

> “The Reverend Father Bernard Gort of Barcelona, professed religious of the Charterhouse of Scala Dei in Catalonia, formerly prior of Lisbon and afterward of Évora in Portugal, reports the following miracle.
>
> “The most illustrious and most reverend Don Theotonius of Braganza, Archbishop of Évora and munificent founder of the Charterhouse of Scala Dei—also called Scala Coeli—near Évora in Portugal, obtained from the reverend father prior general of the Carthusian Order a certain portion or relic of the head of our holy father Bruno. He enclosed it in a silver bust representing the same Saint down to the waist, which he donated, together with many compositions of emblems, hieroglyphics, and poems, to that Charterhouse of Évora, where it is still reverently preserved.
>
> “At the end of January 1628, after a great eclipse of the moon had occurred, Theodosius II, Duke of Braganza, fell into an extremely serious and dangerous illness. His household was so afraid for his health that they allowed only physicians to enter him.
>
> “Knowing this, the Reverend Father Antonio Coello, then prior of the Charterhouse of Évora, went with Don Álvaro de Fonseca, procurator of the same house, to the town of Vila Viçosa, where the sick duke lay. He took with him the aforesaid relic of Saint Bruno, intending to present it to the duke for veneration, and reminding him that the relic had once been sent by the father general to Lord Theotonius, his illustrious uncle.
>
> “The duke immediately composed himself with due decorum. The said prior showed him the sacred relic with the greatest reverence and, after reciting certain prayers with his companion, together with the prayer of the aforesaid Saint, offered it to the duke for veneration. Present were the Duke of Barcelos, his firstborn son, now Duke of Braganza, and two other sons, Don Edward and Alexander, kneeling and holding lighted candles.
>
> “When the duke had venerated the sacred relic, he said in the presence of his sons that he had great confidence in God that he would recover his health, since in his illness he had been deemed worthy to be visited by that Saint.”

34. 

> “The prior and his companion left the chamber, taking the sacred relic with them, for fear that the duke might wish to keep it with him, as they knew he desired to do.
>
> “Afterward the duke’s illness began to abate, and that same night he recovered so completely that the physician found him without fever; shortly thereafter he was entirely restored to his former health.
>
> “In the year 1631, a certain monk—whose name I deliberately omit because he is still alive—a professed member of one of the houses in the province of Saint Father Bruno, was staying at the house of Saint Stephen of the Wood. After suffering severe mental distress for a long time, he finally reached the point of openly discussing leaving the Order and arranging this through a suitable person in the Roman Curia.
>
> “When the procurator general of the Order was informed of the matter by the monk himself, he not only did not oppose it but even assented to his departure from the Order, in order to free himself from the man’s importunity.
>
> “Moreover, the monk had contracted an illness of the eyes, so that at night he could scarcely bear enough light to recite his sacred prayers. Finally, commending himself to Saint Father Bruno, he washed his eyes with water taken from Saint Bruno’s lake. This water is collected from a flowing stream near the grove of the church of Saint Mary, in a basin enclosed by a wall on the side of the road, oblong and circular in shape, in the middle of which a wooden cross has been placed; Saint Bruno is said to have been accustomed to drink and wash from it.
>
> “As soon as he washed his eyes with this water, he immediately felt himself illuminated both externally and internally. He abandoned his plan to leave the Order and confirmed himself in his holy purpose. He informed the Reverend Father Joseph Laudinus, prior of the Roman Charterhouse and procurator general of the Order in the Roman Curia, of this illumination in letters dated from that house in December 1631, which he also read to other acquaintances. He is still alive and in good health.
>
> “Many people drink from the water of this lake out of devotion and carry it to their homes. They also find it most effective in dispelling various illnesses when they take it with some feeling of piety.”

35. 

> “As the year 1633 was drawing to a close, the most illustrious Lord Henry Loffredus, Neapolitan, Marquis of Trivico and Count of Potenza in Lucania, was in danger of death from a very serious illness. Therefore, abandoning the aid and services of the physicians, he fled to the protection of the saints.
>
> “At the urging of Brother Angelo Massei of Naples, a lay brother professed at the Charterhouse of Saint Lawrence near Padula, who was then staying at a grange of that Charterhouse situated within the city of Potenza, he commended himself with devout affection of heart to Saint Father Bruno. He also took some powder from the cave of that same Saint, which the lay brother gave him as a medicine. By God’s favor, through the merits of Saint Bruno, he soon recovered, and likewise through the help of Blessed Giles the Minorite, whose body is preserved incorrupt at the town of Laurenzana, to whom he had been commended by his mother.
>
> “For this reason, in 1634, in order to repay the saints the thanks and service owed to them, he went to the aforesaid Charterhouse of Padula around the beginning of July to give thanks to Saint Father Bruno. This will be clearer from his letter addressed to the Reverend Father Giovanni Battista Manducius, prior and visitor of the province:

> “‘Most Reverend and most respected Father,
>
> “‘In recent months I fell into such danger of death from a very serious illness that, considering the physicians’ efforts already useless, I fled to almighty God and the holy citizens of heaven, but with particular devotion to Saint Bruno and Blessed Giles.
>
> “‘Now, so that I may in some measure satisfy the great debt I owe these saints, I have decided to go in person to venerate them: Father Saint Bruno there at Saint Lawrence of Padula, and Blessed Giles at Laurenzana.
>
> “‘Therefore I ask Your Reverence to grant me the favor and permission for Brother Angelo to come with me. For, since I know in part that I owe my recovery both to his prayers and to his urging me to commend myself to Saint Father Bruno, I desire this consolation from Your Reverence: that the aforesaid brother, just as he helped me obtain my recovery, may likewise help me give thanks.
>
> “‘Finally, offering myself always as ready to serve you and your religious community, I ask that you commend me in your prayers.
>
> “‘Potenza, 27 June 1634.’”

36. These, then, are the three miracles worked through the invocation of Saint Bruno which preceded the decree of the Sacred Congregation of Rites that elevated the Saint’s worship from the semidouble to the double rite with the assent of Clement X, and which I have judged should be related here.

Although the second of these miracles does not at all confirm Zanottius’s assertion in the Life of the Saint which he composed that the virtue of a miraculous spring’s waters had been transferred to the waters of the lake named after Saint Bruno (see the Preliminary Commentary, no. 747), it nevertheless provides some kind of evidence that a miraculous power truly resides in the waters of that lake through the merits of our Saint.

Several other miracles, which Zanottius himself relates in chapter 34 of his celebrated treatise on Saint Bruno, demonstrate this much more clearly. They were performed in the present age through the power of those waters and therefore after the decree issued by the Congregation of Rites in 1674.

I am pleased to present these here, translated from Italian into Latin, together with many others that remain both in Surianus and elsewhere. Since Zanottius, unlike his usual practice, cites no writer or document for them, I do so solely on the authority of this writer, although I nevertheless believe that he drew them from a reliable source.

Our Saint’s biographer relates them in the following words:

> “In the year 1715, Oliva Spani of Cantaci was possessed by an evil spirit in such a way that one day she was violently thrown by it upon a mass of burning coals, from which she contracted an incurable wound. Her husband, who was deeply distressed by this, invoked the holy Father—Bruno, that is—with great faith. When he had taken the woman to Saint Bruno’s lake and washed her there, he immediately saw that she had been freed from the infernal enemy and healed of her wound.
>
> “In the year 1719, on 28 May, Giovanni Bernardo of Saint Peter of Cosenza, who had been afflicted for seven years by an illness and had become contracted in many parts of his body, so that he was a pitiable sight to behold, was carried by his parents in their arms to Saint Bruno’s lake. By merely washing himself, he was restored to complete health.”

37. “In the same year Angela Rizzi of Cantaci, possessed by a demon for several months, felt herself freed from it as soon as she entered the said lake; and the same thing happened that very day to many other demoniacs. In the year 1721 Baron Leffelhol, captain of the imperial troops in Calabria and a Lutheran by sect, visited the small lake of Saint Bruno in order to satisfy his curiosity. When, in a single day, he saw twenty-four miracles obtained through the Saint’s intercession for various demoniacs, he was inwardly moved to embrace the Catholic faith. Accordingly, obeying the divine call, and abjuring Lutheranism on 24 June, he made his profession of the Catholic faith at Reggio in Calabria, in the Capuchin church, in the presence of Father Columbanus Theysen of Cologne, a Conventual Franciscan and chaplain to the imperial army, and Augustine Maria of Lucania, a Capuchin preacher. The two aforementioned fathers absolved him from the censures according to the customary form of the holy Church. The captain then wished an authentic instrument concerning the whole matter to be drawn up, to which the two religious men mentioned above and others besides would subscribe and swear that everything was true. In the following year, when he had come to give thanks to Saint Bruno by visiting his tomb, he himself deposited this authentic document in the Carthusian monastery of Saint Stephen.”

Since, on the two later of the three feasts of Pentecost—on one of which the sacred head of the Saint is annually transferred from the church of Saint Stephen to the church of Saint Mary at Turrita, and on the other brought back to it—there is, as Zanotti himself testifies in that very chapter of his *Lucubration* in which he reports the miracles already recounted, a huge gathering of people at the Turrita Charterhouse, and since the sick and demoniacs are then habitually brought there from every direction for healing, the twenty-four miracles by which, in the persons of as many demoniacs, the Saint’s intercession converted the captain of the imperial troops to the Catholic faith in a single day may perhaps have occurred on one or the other of those feasts of Pentecost. If the matter truly happened in this way, then it will be more credible than otherwise that the demon was expelled from twenty-four demoniacs on one and the same day.

38. Be that as it may, it appears credible that, when the waters of the lake called Saint Bruno’s were applied, no small number of miracles were performed—miracles which therefore, as I have already noted, display the extraordinary power of those waters more conspicuously than the single miracle reported in no. 34—and that they were performed chiefly upon demoniacs. Nor do the accounts which I have given above from Surianus and others allow us to doubt that further miracles were performed merely through invocation of the Saint, especially at the Turrita Charterhouse of Saint Stephen, which now also bears Saint Bruno’s name.

I now wish to add there, as a kind of conclusion, one further miracle—or benefit—performed elsewhere, in addition to those already performed and recounted there. Morkensius, in his manuscript *Chronological-Diplomatic Dissertation on Saint Bruno*, which I have very frequently cited in the preceding Commentary, writes at the end as follows:

> “To bring this inquiry finally to an end, I add here the remarkable event which, as I mentioned shortly beforehand, recently occurred on the occasion of this writing of mine, drawing it from a letter of the most distinguished man, Lord Judocus Hermannus Nunninghius, Doctor of Both Laws, apostolic protonotary, and highly distinguished scholasticus of the collegiate church of Vreden, etc. I had sent him this dissertation of mine on Our Holy Father Bruno so that he might read it and judge it, and, out of affection and friendship for me, write back what he thought of it. He satisfied my request completely; but before expressing his judgment he prefaced it as follows:
>
> “ ‘But before I address your writings, let me first relate an event which, to speak frankly, has seemed to me extraordinarily strange and full of marvels. Your manuscript dissertation on the life of Saint Bruno had already come into my hands when the residual heat in my veins from a fever unexpectedly provoked a nosebleed. Beginning in the evening, it continued through most of the night and presented a sufficiently alarming spectacle; surgeons summoned from the neighboring town promptly supplied appropriate assistance. My physician interpreted the hemorrhage, as a favorable omen, as a critical discharge beneficial to my health.
>
> “ ‘Meanwhile, while I was diligently occupied in examining your writings, within a week a second attack suddenly assailed me, far more dangerous than the first. It was about eight o’clock in the evening, and I was preparing to give my sick body some rest. I had scarcely laid back my head when, from the same little vein as before, a copious stream of blood burst forth, giving warning that I would soon be drained of life. Two streams ran continuously from my mouth and nostrils, with such force and such a loss of blood that they distressed those present and drove them to tears. I endured the misfortune with a calm spirit, as something sent from heaven.
>
> “ ‘Meanwhile the flow, no less violent, continued until the third hour of the night. The surgeons of Borcken were summoned again, but because of closed gates and other obstacles caused by the military garrison, as well as the darkness of night, they arrived more slowly. While they were delayed and the danger increased, deprived of human assistance I turned to heavenly aid. I made a vow to Saint Bruno, the patriarch, asking him to rescue me from the present danger of death, if heaven had decreed that I should continue the pious undertaking which, for your sake, I was then pursuing in some measure for his glory. I had scarcely finished my vows in words and in my heart when—despite the continuing flow of blood, my head thrown back upon the pillow, and sleep gently overcoming me—the deadly trickle came to an end. My brother and the others standing around were astonished at the extraordinary event. At last, about four in the morning, the surgeons arrived and learned by this miraculous example how greatly the assistance of the heavenly powers surpasses all human aid. Forgive the outpouring of my pen, which necessarily manifests the work of God.’ ”

40. Having appended a brief conclusion to Nunninghius’s account of this miracle—or rather, this benefit—conferred through invocation of Saint Bruno, Morkensius brings his treatise to an end.

Before I too conclude here my discussion of the matters that remained to be said concerning the Saint’s posthumous glory, one further striking proof must be recalled, thereby fulfilling the promise made at the beginning of the preceding Commentary: the wholly exceptional veneration shown to the Saint in his native land, indeed in the very house at Cologne that is believed to have been his birthplace.

Augustine Aldenbruck, a priest of our Society, in a letter which he sent to us on 27 July 1767 after inspecting that house called *At the Red Stess* (see the preceding Commentary, § 2), adds the following, among several other matters relating to Saint Bruno:

> “I also saw in the ancient house, called *At the Red Stess*, as it is still named, a room which the inhabitants said had been occupied by Saint Bruno while he was still living at Cologne. It has always been treated with such reverence that no one was permitted to spend the night there. In the same room they showed me the bedstead which he had used for rest. It was certainly extremely old and made of oak; yet, to my astonishment, it has to this day not been attacked by the bite of woodworms, much less damaged. Because it was repeatedly being diminished by excessive fragments torn from it by members of the household, servants, and others who were admitted to view it, the present owners and tenants of the house have recently enclosed it beneath a covering.”

Whether Saint Bruno truly used the room and bedstead mentioned here while he was still living at Cologne I do not investigate. But, whatever the truth of the matter, the exceptional care with which that bedstead—believed to have been used by the Saint for rest—is guarded, and the eagerness which seized certain people to acquire fragments of it for themselves, are unmistakable signs of the extraordinary veneration in which many people at Cologne are said to hold the Saint. For this reason it seemed fitting not to place an end to this Appendix on Saint Bruno’s posthumous glory until this matter too had been brought forward.

# The Works of Saint Bruno, Most Distinguished Patriarch of the Carthusians and Most Learned Theologian of Paris, newly revised through the diligence of Father Theodor Petraeus of Kampen, alumnus of the Cologne Charterhouse, and now divided into three volumes

*(Cologne, at the press of Bernard Gualtheri, in the year 1611.)*

[Col. 0633]

## To the Most Reverend Father in Christ and Lord, the Lord Bruno d’Affringues, Prior of the Grande Chartreuse and therefore most worthy General of the entire sacred family of the Carthusians, etc.

Ever since I began frequenting the solitudes of the Carthusian family in the provinces of both Germany, most Reverend Father in Christ, one thing above all has been a source of admiration to me: that everything there seemed modeled upon impregnable cities and fortresses. Before each sacred sanctuary stood triple guards, breastplates and helmets capable of withstanding iron and flame unharmed, and provisions sent down from heaven lest they be intercepted by land or sea. Their positions were made completely secure against the enemy’s open attack by the nature of the place; their battles were more ardent than any qualification can express. Just as they are not extinguished by the blood poured out, so they are perpetuated by weapons and spirits kindled with hatred and love.

But since Satan is tireless and immortal, against whom the communities of Carthusian brothers deployed throughout the whole world fight as so many bronze battle-lines beneath the standards of the Lord Bruno, it was neither fitting nor acceptable that I, a spectator, should stand by such a difficult contest without taking part. Father Theodorus Petraeus, a man distinguished by the outstanding characteristic of your congregation, would not allow this. As soon as he had rightly inferred my affection for the Carthusian family, he wished to summon me, alone among others, to share in his concern and labor, so that I might assist him in restoring the writings of the aforesaid Lord Bruno, the first and most sacred patriarch of the Carthusians. And indeed he will testify that he called upon a Theseus, for after he had deterred many people—some by the length of the books, others by the necessity of the labor and expense, while the printing presses of others had already seized books of this kind—I nevertheless hastened forward with the greatest eagerness, undertook the task immediately, and omitted nothing that belonged to their dignity and splendor.

I was moved to this especially by three reasons. First, so that this most powerful resource of these books, after they had been thoroughly cleansed of the rust of errors by the keen judgment of the aforementioned Father Petraeus and illuminated by learned distinctions, might not henceforth be lacking in your houses. Second, so that the image of the glorious patriarch depicted in those works, worn away by the hands and almost the eyes of readers, might live again in the colors of my types. Third, so that future generations of Carthusians might remember that the monuments of their most blessed leader were restored during the age and under the auspices of Your Most Reverend Paternity, who, strengthened in name and office by being the first Bruno, governs the Grande Chartreuse with steadfastness amid the common agitation of princes and peoples.

Therefore, Most Reverend Father in Christ, you recognize and approve, as I am led to hope, the intention of my will. If you peacefully accept the labor and diligence which I have contributed to these volumes for the public good—and especially to the first, which I offer and dedicate to you, the Father and primate of the entire family—press your thumb upon it and smooth your brow, so that I may be the more certain and joyful that I have answered the unspoken desires of your soul.

Farewell.

Cologne of the Ubii, in the year 1611, on Saint Bruno’s day.

The most devoted servant of Your Most Reverend Paternity,

**Bernardus Gualteri**, citizen and bookseller of Cologne.

[Col. 0635]

## Greeting to the Benevolent Reader

When several learned men of this age complained sorrowfully that it was impossible to find more copies of the works of Saint Bruno, since they had not been reprinted for a hundred years, and when the advice and wish of my superior were added—that I should devote some time and labor to preparing a new edition—I could not fail to satisfy the desire of both parties.

I was all the more inclined to undertake this burden because I had found a printer who promised not only clean paper but also exceptionally elegant and attractive type. It is clear that in this matter he has fulfilled his duty admirably.

Moreover, since the old typefaces abounded in abbreviations which the printers of today cannot readily accommodate, we took care that each word should be expressed throughout in completely expanded characters. We also made every effort to place the citations of Scripture, which occupy the margins here and there, in their proper locations together with their verse numbers, and to distinguish the words of sacred Scripture from the author’s context by a different kind of type.

It would be difficult to say how much time and labor this required of us amid all the daily exercises of our order. In any case, since the contents of the third volume are attributed by some people to Bruno, bishop of Segni, it is especially appropriate to know that several very ancient manuscript copies found in the mother Charterhouse everywhere bear the name of Blessed Bruno the Carthusian.

“But,” they say, “he calls him Father Benedict and repeatedly commends him.” He also calls Abraham “Father,” because he urges us to imitate him, and he willingly conforms himself to the footsteps of Saint Benedict, who first led an eremitical life and afterward a cenobitic one. “But he wrote on Exodus and the Apocalypse of John.” Nothing prevents our Blessed Father Bruno from having written commentaries on those books, which may perhaps have perished through the injury of time and the carelessness of men. If anyone thinks otherwise, each person may, by our permission, abound in his own judgment.

You yourself, most upright reader, will easily recognize the other things accomplished by us in this work. Meanwhile, farewell, and enjoy these books.

[Col. 0635]

## To Saint Bruno, Founder of the Carthusians, on behalf of Father Theodor Petraeus of Kampen, professed member of the same order among the Ubii

Until now, a match for a child and driven back  
by great fear of your divinity, divine Bruno,  
you who, seated among the stars with a blazing crown  
of rays, shine forth and renew the world with splendors,  
I rightly held back from the vast field of your praise,  
scarcely opening my unskilled mouth in mortal song.

But now, as your follower and rival, Petraeus,  
has renewed the love of my neglected Muses,  
the ready poem urged me on with ready mind,  
while he, still wholly filled with your spirit, said:

“Stop! In vain are you contemplating these honors for me,  
since I have now ceased openly to be my own master.  
If there is any devotion in my heart, or any desire,  
let it go to him to whom my transferred rights have passed.  
Whatever you prepare, let Bruno alone receive it—  
he who lives in my inmost heart and has bound me to himself  
as his own and other self.  
Either sing of him, or abandon the poem you have begun.”

He spoke, and I blushed. For what else could I do?  
An anxious mind cannot raise its senses  
so far above human things.

For as many creatures as the forest contains,  
as many fish as the vast sea,  
as many birds as the empty heavens contain stars:  
so many gifts of your mind, Bruno,  
are honored in heaven and honored on earth.

Yet see: when Petraeus revisits your writings  
and diligently examines the sacred volumes,  
devouring old age has corrupted much through decay,  
and much through the careless hand of scribes.  
What remains of your works, long denied to the press,  
is sought by many who desire it.

Nothing, therefore, is more worthy of you,  
nothing more sacred for the lecterns,  
than that, once more opened under your pure name,  
the streams of moral instruction and knowledge should burst forth.

This is what the leader and protector of your people desires and commands—  
he who, Bruno, is not unequal to you in name or office,  
your own Bruno, than whom no other is more illustrious,  
whom the Order regards with murmuring voice:  
if law and right delight him, sacred Astraea  
is believed to have fixed her seat in his breast.

Or rather, if the honor of piety and the gracious beauty of character delight,  
this very man is the summit of religion.  
Thus you gave to one man everything  
that ordinarily adorns others individually.

These things, having issued from vast depths,  
like a flame unable to be contained, or increased by winds,  
shine forth widely. And just as the Pole Star  
and Helice guide trembling sailors  
upon the storm-tossed sea,  
so he revives and leads the way  
whenever one of his clients gasps for breath  
or some weary traveler loses the path.

He commands. But what labor could compare with his?  
What sweat is harder than that owed to one alone?  
Therefore, like the eagle that bears Jupiter’s weapon,  
the prince of birds, who launches himself on swift wings  
toward the heights of the stars,  
he rises toward you and utters his lament,  
and Petraeus calls you to share in his wishes  
and in a portion of his labors.

O Father, O charioteer of our order,  
who, invoked, have never frustrated a prayer,  
great desire carries away his mind and spirit:  
watch over the undertaking, favor its beginnings,  
and mercifully bring them to completion.

With you may those things be born for me  
which, conceived under you as father,  
first came forth beneath the heavens in greatness.  
With you may the same pledges rise  
to towering increase. These and other matters  
he turns over in his inmost heart.

Since you, divine one, long ago wounded in your breast  
by devoted love and care, assent beyond the petitioner’s request,  
revealing by your embrace and expressive face  
the hope of his vow and the recesses of your mind,  
and displaying their signs upon your brow,

thereafter, just as a little flower, watered by warm rains  
during the night, raises itself more joyfully in the garden,  
so he upon whom your divine grace has poured its dew  
does not reject countless hours of labor,  
nor fear this as a foolish or sluggish undertaking.  
With you as ready helper and patron, he dares to begin it;  
with great skill he now weighs each part  
and with diligent effort polishes many pages.

Now, if any fortunate passages have slipped in,  
he separates them out.  
He distributes the harvests of your field  
according to a well-considered order.  
From your genial mouth the crop  
of your eloquence blooms again.

But just as things reborn with new life  
and greening everywhere upon the moist turf  
owe their existence to rains and the sun,  
and just as the gifts of clients  
are shared with their patrons,  
so he, sharing his palm of victory with you,  
dedicates to your altars whatever labor  
and whatever praise he has received.  
Whatever hope of greater increase future years may bring,  
he wishes it to be your gift,  
and he declares and consecrates it  
as a votive offering placed beneath shining vaults.

Therefore, divine one, joined to Theodor,  
whose body is made radiant throughout  
by distributing torches from his breast,  
if a true son honors his father,  
and a client rightly honors his patron,  
do not delay to love him.

If, like Phosphorus when it rises  
from the glassy waves, you shine forth again  
restored with greater light,  
continue to stand beside the undertaking.  
As a kindly genius, losing nothing yourself  
through your gift, make him your partner,  
so that his eloquent mind may produce  
sayings equal, or at least close, to yours,  
and may transmit devout thoughts into later ages—  
rich with you as father and powerful with you as protector.

[Col. 0637]

## Approval of the Censor

I judge these works of Saint Bruno, divided into three volumes and revised and reviewed with diligent care by Father Theodorus Petraeus, alumnus of the Cologne Charterhouse, entirely worthy of being reprinted and published. They breathe, in every respect, their former piety and learning.

In our Cologne convent, 10 August 1611.

**F. Gisbertus Spechtius**, prior of the Dominican convent and inquisitor of heretical depravity.

[Col. 0637]

## The Will of the Reverend Father General of the Carthusian Order concerning the Revision and Reprinting of the Works of Blessed Bruno

Your intelligent judgment will be worthily employed in undertaking the task of ensuring that the works of the Lord Bruno come forth into the light and fame of humanity more correctly and more elegantly. I think this will require only a few months’ labor, especially for you, who are already thoroughly worn by emending these old works. Therefore pursue eagerly this opportunity to deserve well of the public good.

For I cannot praise sufficiently this holy leisure of yours, occupied with much work and consecrated to the common benefit of the whole Church, with great praise for the order.

From a letter given at the mother Charterhouse, 10 June 1608.

**F. Bruno d’Affringues**, prior of the Charterhouse and minister general of the order.

[Col. 0637]

## The Life of Saint Bruno

*(It appears above among the Acts of Saint Bruno and is the Third Life.)*

[Col. 0637]

# Volume or Part I of the Works of the Most Holy and Most Learned Theologian Saint Bruno, First Founder of the Carthusians: Exposition of the Psalms

## 1. Prologue

[Col. 0637B]

The Psalter is a certain musical instrument that resounds from its upper cavity. Since the melody of the psalms was sung upon such an instrument, the entire work rightly received its name from the instrument. For just as the psalter resounds from above, so this whole work resounds concerning what is above—that is, concerning the praise of God.

The purpose of this work is shown to be manifold by the diversity of the individual titles. It intends to prophesy sometimes concerning the Incarnation, Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, and other acts of Christ, and sometimes concerning the salvation of the good and the condemnation of the wicked; in all these matters the praises of God are contemplated. In the Passion and in Christ’s other acts, and in the salvation of the righteous, the praises of his humility and mercy are discerned; in the condemnation of the wicked, the praises of his justice.

For this reason this book is rightly called among the Hebrews the *Book of Hymns*, that is, of the praises of God. Hymns properly mean praises of God composed in meter, whereas psalms were composed in lyric meter, as Arator says:

> “Lyric feet composed the Psalter.”

Three things are considered in divine books, just as in secular books. For just as secular works tend partly toward physics, partly toward ethics, and partly toward logic, so among divine works some tend toward physics, though in such a way that a figure is represented within that physics—as in Genesis, where the origin of the world is treated, and in Ecclesiastes, where many natures of things are treated mystically.

Others tend toward ethics in place of logic, such as the Book of Job, the psalm *Blessed are the undefiled*, and certain other psalms. Others, in place of logic and ethics, tend toward theory, that is, contemplation: namely, those which contain within themselves the sublime mysteries of God, remote from common knowledge, such as the *Song of Songs*. In it God is introduced, through a wonderful mystery, as speaking to the Church like a bridegroom to his bride.

This book too, although in some respects it tends toward ethics, appears principally to tend toward theory, since its chief concern is the mysteries of the Incarnation, Nativity, and the other acts of Christ.

It must be understood that there are very many kinds of prophecy. One kind is prophecy through deeds, such as the crossing of the children of Israel and their other actions, which “all happened to them in a figure,” as the Apostle says (1 Corinthians 10:11). Another is through words, as God is read to have spoken future things to Moses and many other prophets through angels.

Another is through revelation, as many things are said to have been revealed to Ezekiel and Daniel in portentous dreams. Yet another is through the hidden inspiration of the holy Spirit, as the mystical Passion of the Lord and his other acts were intimated to the prophet David—not through deeds, words, or any kind of revelation, but through the hidden inspiration of the holy Spirit.

It should be noted that, because of the extraordinary swiftness of the holy Spirit, the prophets speak of future things as though they were present and past. Everything future is present to the holy Spirit and known as though it were past.

It should also be noted that when Christ is sometimes introduced in the Psalms praying and acting humbly, he is to be understood according to his humanity; when he is introduced in a lofty manner, he is to be understood according to his divinity.

It should likewise be noted why the first psalm lacks a title, although the others appear to have titles: namely, because it is regarded as the title of all the other psalms. Since this psalm is concerned with the praise of Christ, it indicates that in all the others he will treat of Christ in various ways.

The purpose of this psalm is to remove from Christ the three deaths by which the first man came to death, and conversely to praise in him the threefold obedience of which the first man was deprived. It is the voice of the prophet considering the condemnation of the human race through Adam’s disobedience and foreseeing its future restoration through Christ. It is as though he were saying:

## Psalm I

### Blessed is the man, etc.

He says “man” not with respect to the distinction of sex, but with respect to maturity of understanding. The passage is expounded as follows:

Adam, dying through the pleasure, consent, act, and habit of sinning, dragged the entire human race down with himself, and thus was rightly unhappy. But there will be someone in the future who will be a man, one who will do everything not weakly as Adam did, but manfully and maturely. Because he will be a man, he will be blessed—that is, he will be so richly endowed by God with the blessedness of virtues and works, and afterward with immortality, that no one has the ability to reveal its extent.

He will be shown to be blessed because he will be such a person: one who “has not walked”—that is, will not walk—one who will not depart from the Lord in such a way as to be placed in the counsel of the wicked, that is, in the pleasure and consent of sinning, through which Adam and Eve came to death.

And he rightly says “counsel.” For before they committed the sin, they received the counsel to sin and took pleasure in that counsel. He calls them “wicked,” not according to the strict meaning of the word, as though they were ignorant of God, but because they became apostates while retaining knowledge of God. Properly speaking, the wicked are those who are ignorant of God.

“And he has not stood in the way of sinners”—that is, he will not stand in evil action, in which Adam and Eve stood. They were sinners, that is, evil-doers, when they ate the fruit contrary to God’s command.

“And he has not sat”—that is, will not sit, or remain—“in the seat of pestilence,” that is, in the habit of sinning. In that seat Adam and Eve sat when they excused themselves for the sin of eating the fruit, just as a teacher sits in a chair. By giving us instruction in sin, they brought us into pestilence, that is, into common death.

Pestilence is commonly understood to mean a death inflicted upon the people in common by some corruption of the air.

It should certainly be noted that he says one departs in pleasure, stands in action, and sits in habit. When someone is moving toward another place, he first departs from the place where he is in order to reach it; when he arrives there, he stands; afterward, wishing to remain, he sits down. Thus our first parents, moving toward evil action, first departed from God through the pleasure of evil action—that is, they withdrew from him—then finally stood in evil action, and at last, not rejecting the habit of sinning, sat in the seat of pestilence. That is, sitting there and remaining there fully, they brought others to death by sinning after their example.

They are rightly said, by analogy, to have sat in a chair, since teachers customarily sit in a chair. And action is rightly called a way: for it is exposed, like a well-trodden road, and is public, whereas pleasure lies hidden.

It should also be noted that it is not superfluous, after denying that he walked, to deny also that he stood and sat, even though the two latter denials necessarily follow from the first. Everyone who departs neither stands nor sits. This is done so that, by denying these things of Christ in this order, he may indicate that everything occurred in Adam in the same order.

After denying these three things, he indicates that three other things contrary to them, of which Adam was deprived, were present in Christ:

He will not walk, he will not stand, he will not sit. Rather, his will shall be in fulfilling the law of the Lord: that is, he will fulfill God’s law willingly, not unwillingly.

This indicates that he will take pleasure in its fulfillment, just as Adam took pleasure in transgression, and that he will fulfill God’s law by doing good, just as Adam transgressed by doing evil.

I say that he will fulfill God’s law according to God’s will, and that he will not do so for a brief hour; rather, he will meditate day and night on fulfilling his law—that is, at all times. He rightly says “he will meditate,” meaning that he will fulfill it not negligently but with meditation.

The word “meditate” also indicates that, just as Adam became accustomed to doing evil, Christ will become accustomed to doing good. And because he will not walk, stand, or sit, but will meditate on God’s law, he will be like a tree—indeed, truly a tree of life for others—which was prefigured in the tree of life that is read to have been in paradise (Genesis 2:9).

He shows by what means Christ will be a tree of life for others when he adds: “which is planted”—that is, conceived in the Virgin—“beside streams of waters,” that is, through the outpourings of the gifts of the holy Spirit, which refresh and cleanse like waters, so that Gabriel’s statement may be fulfilled: “The holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke 1:35), and so forth.

It is as though he were saying: He will truly be a tree of life, since he will be such a tree as is planted—that is, he will be conceived in the Virgin’s womb through the operation of the holy Spirit.

He will not be a tree of death, like Adam.

Or the passage may be understood in this way: He will be a tree of life, and although he will be destined to be a tree of life, he will nevertheless be such a tree as is planted—that is, he will be conceived beside streams of waters, meaning beside the streams of peoples. It is as though he were saying: Although he is a tree of life, he will be conceived in such a way as to possess a nature destined to flow toward death, like the peoples, who are called waters because they are unstable and flow downward toward death, just as waters flow downward.

By this he commends Christ’s obedience unto death and strengthens our faith, so that, because of the sublimity of his divinity, we may not fail to recognize the humility of his mortality.

And because he had called him a tree, lest anyone suppose that, as soon as he came into being, he would immediately give the fruit for which he was to come, he determines what the tree will give:

Not immediately upon his coming into being, but “in his time”—that is, in the time of his mortality—“his fruit,” namely, the restoration of the human race, which will be the fruit of his death.

And since he is a tree of life, “his leaf”—that is, his word—“will not fall,” meaning it will not be destroyed, as he himself testifies: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24:35).

Or the passage may be connected in accordance with another interpretation:

Although he himself is planted beside streams of waters—that is, beside peoples, and although he flows toward death like the peoples—nevertheless his leaf, that is, his word, will not fall.

The word is rightly called a leaf. For just as leaves adorn a tree and the fruit lies hidden among them, so the words themselves are an ornament of the Church, and in them there is fruit still hidden—namely, eternal life.

Or there may be a comparison here, as follows:

Because he will meditate on the law, he will be like a tree planted beside streams of waters, which will give its fruit in its time. Its leaf will not fall. That is, he will be comparable to a tree planted beside abundant waters, giving fruit in its time, whose leaf will not fall. For just as moisture is not lacking to that tree for producing fruit in its time, so neither will the vigor and teaching of the holy Spirit be lacking to him for making spiritual children fruitful for God in the time of fullness. And just as the leaves of that tree do not fall, so neither will his word fall.

And since his fruit will be so great and of such a kind, all the works and miracles that he performs will prosper for those who believe in him. That is, whatever he does in this world will contribute to the benefit and edification of his people.

The text continues:

### Not so the wicked, etc.

When he says, “Not so will the wicked be,” he makes Christ understood by aposiopesis, because the righteous will be as Christ is. The same point is expressed in the words: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 11:42; Matthew 5:48).

This does not mean that anyone will possess as much holiness as Christ possessed, but that each person retains something of God’s holiness—one person much, another less—and, as the Apostle says: “As was the earthly Adam, such also are the earthly” (1 Corinthians 15:48), namely, those conformed to him. “As is the spiritual one,” that is, Christ, “such also are the spiritual,” that is, those who obey him.

The verse is therefore connected and expounded in this way:

The blessed man will not walk, stand, or sit, but will meditate on the law of the Lord. Therefore he will be like a tree, and those who resemble him, namely the righteous, will likewise be so. But the wicked will not be so—not so.

This repetition is intended to strengthen the righteous and terrify the wicked. The repetition is not found among the Hebrews.

Rather, they will be like dust—that is, like dust, dry from lack of teaching, just as dust is dry from lack of moisture—which the wind casts away. The devil separates them from the face of the earth, that is, from the presence of Christ, upon whom the faithful lean, just as we lean upon this earth.

And therefore, because the wicked will be dust, they do not rise—that is, they will not rise—“in judgment,” meaning for the purpose of being judged. The Apostle bears witness to this: “Those who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law” (Romans 2:12).

It should be understood that on the day of judgment some will rise for judgment and others not for judgment, such as the Gentiles. Of those who rise for judgment, some rise in order to judge, such as the perfect, while others rise in order to be judged.

Of those who are judged, some will be saved, such as the good, while others will be condemned, such as false Christians, heretics, and Jews.

It is uncertain—and there is no authoritative testimony concerning the matter—whether the voice at the judgment will be a material one or not. If, however, according to some authorities, it is said that there will be no such voice, then “in judgment” will be expounded as follows: The wicked do not rise in judgment, that is, so that it may then at last become certain that they are to be condemned; for this is already certain.

But in the case of false believers, judgment—that is, certainty—will then at last be made. For it will then finally be evident to everyone that they are worthy of condemnation. If this were already certain, the diligence of the living would certainly not offer prayers and sacrifice to God on their behalf.

The perfect, however, when they judge—that is, when by comparison with their holiness they show themselves to be like those who are to be saved, and unlike those who are to be condemned—will do so.

Since he had said that the wicked would not rise in judgment, and had thereby greatly humbled them, lest false believers should think that they would rise in judgment and be saved by faith alone without works, he removes this possibility as follows:

“The wicked shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners”—that is, those who apostatize from God—“in the council of the righteous,” that is, so as to be in the congregation of the righteous, even though they rise in judgment. In the Hebrew, however, it reads “in the synagogue.” Therefore, “in the council” is more correctly found in the Latin. Nevertheless, it may be read “in the counsel.” For we call a *council* a gathering assembled for the establishment of something useful [Col. 0643A]. “Synagogue,” however, is interpreted as “congregation.”

Or this verse may be read in the following way: if “the wicked” above is taken generally, both for unbelievers and for sinful believers, the wicked will not be such. He shows in parts why this is so, saying:

This is because the wicked—that is, unbelievers—do not rise in this world from their unbelief in judgment, that is, through judgment, so as to judge, that is, condemn, their unbelief by confession. “For if they judged themselves,” as the Apostle says, “they would certainly not be judged by the Lord” (I Cor. II, 31). Nor do sinners—that is, false believers—rise so as to be in the council of the righteous, that is, so as, like the righteous, to subordinate their wills to the will of God.

Both statements may also be understood of unbelievers: the wicked are those who do not know God [Col. 0643B] and do not rise in judgment; while sinners are those who prefer their own wills to God’s will, and therefore are not in the council or counsel of the righteous.

It follows: “For the Lord knows,” and so forth. The passage continues in this sense:

The godly will be like a tree, that is, like Christ. This is because the Lord knows—that is, approves and loves—the way of the righteous, that is, the good life in this world, which is the way to eternal life. The wicked, however, will not be so; and this is because the Lord does not know their path, that is, their life. And although he ought to have said “does not know,” he expresses the equivalent result through its cause, namely, “will perish” instead of “will not know.”

“The way of the wicked will perish,” that is, their perverse life, which is their way to hell, will perish—more precisely, it will cause them to perish—because it is ignored by God, that is, not loved by him. The same is testified in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. XXV, 12), that is, “I do not love you.”

Or the passage may be connected differently, without changing the exposition: “Sinners will not rise in the council or counsel of the righteous, and the wicked in judgment.” This will happen because the Lord knows the way of the righteous, while “the way of the wicked will perish,” that is, he does not wish them to be with the righteous because the life of the righteous pleases him, whereas the life of the wicked displeases him.

## PSALM II

The psalm that follows this one is said by some to be one psalm with the preceding psalm, and by others to be a different one. For in the Acts of the Apostles this psalm is called the second psalm (Acts XIII, 33). That it is called the first is easily resolved: it is the first of the psalms that bear titles, since the first psalm lacks a title [Col. 0643D]. As regards the order of the psalms, however, it is the second; otherwise there would not be one hundred and fifty psalms.

Whether it is the second psalm, or is considered one with the first, it is always connected with the preceding psalm.

It should be understood that the titles of the psalms indicate their purposes either through the event itself, through the interpretation of the wording, or through both. They indicate it through the event when some event that pertains to the figure is identified, as when it says, “A psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom,” which was done as a figure of Christ.

They indicate it through the interpretation of the wording when the purpose of a psalm is designated solely by interpreting its words, without reference to an event, as in this second psalm, whose title is: “A psalm of David.” This is interpreted as follows:

“Psalm”—that is, this treatise—is to be attributed [Col. 0644A] to Christ, who is rightly called David. For David is interpreted as “desirable.” Christ, moreover, is desirable, according to Jacob’s saying: “He himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10).

David is also interpreted as “strong of hand.” Christ likewise is strong of hand, because he defeated the devil, according to the saying: “Now the prince of this world shall be cast out” (John XII, 31).

“Psalm” is sometimes used for the treatise itself, and sometimes for a good work. For a psalm is a symphony performed with a musical instrument together with the work of the hands; therefore it is sometimes used for a work.

This psalm is the voice of the Head, rebuking the Jews and the nations who afflict him because of his Passion. He does this in order to show in what follows that they gained no benefit from it, but on the contrary will receive condemnation in the future; while he has received the glory of the Resurrection and Ascension, and the rule of the whole world, insofar as he was man. For insofar as he is God, he existed before the ages with the Father as Lord of all.

And he says this as follows:

“Why did the nations rage”—that is, why will the nations rage—“that is, the Roman soldiers who will crucify me? Why”—that is, for what benefit will they rage?—“that is, act irrationally against me?” None. To rage is characteristic of lions, which are irrational. Therefore he says that the nations, that is, the Gentiles, raged against him in his crucifixion—that is, irrationally, without any opposition grounded in a cause, they crucified him.

The Jews, although they had no cause, nevertheless claimed that they had one, according to the saying: “This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath” (John IX, 16) [Col. 0644C]. And elsewhere: “According to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John XIX, 7).

Therefore he appropriately adds: “And the peoples”—that is, the Jews, who ought to be my people, as it is written: “I shall be your God, and you shall be my people” (Lev. XXVI, 12). “Why”—that is, in pursuit of what benefit—“did they meditate on vain things,” that is, will they meditate on holding me in death, so that the world may not follow after me, although this will be in vain?

By saying “meditate,” he indicates that they will labor greatly to find a justification for his death. And not only the lesser people labored, but also kings—not merely kings of his own people, but “the kings of the earth,” that is, earthly kings: both of them, namely, Herod—one at the Nativity, the other at the Passion—and Pilate.

“Why did they stand by”—that is, why will they stand by? The expression is used for “they pressed on,” since in the Hebrew it reads: “And the rulers of the priests”—that is, Caiaphas and Annas and the others—“assembled,” that is, will assemble together, acting maliciously against the Lord the Father and against me, Christ, that is, against his king, that is, the one appointed by him [Col. 0644D].

By saying not “the Father” but “the Lord,” he marks the offense as more serious, as though he were saying: Since they themselves were servants while he was Lord, it was disgraceful for them to oppose his decree when they rejected me, the king appointed by him, and wished to hold me in death.

When he says, “Let us break,” and so forth, he turns in an apostrophe to his own people, exhorting them not to be incorporated into those others through fear or flattery, lest they be condemned in the future along with them. They will rage and meditate, and will assemble against the Lord [Col. 0645A].

But I, and you who are my members, say: “Let us break”—that is, destroy—“their bonds,” namely, their flatteries, by which they wish to overcome you and make you imitate them. “And let us cast away from us”—that is, despise—“their yoke,” namely, the threat of the tribulations of death by which they wish to compel you, as though by a yoke.

It is as though he were saying: Do not be seduced by flatteries, and do not be terrified by fear.

When he says “Let us break” and “Let us cast away,” he does not say this because he himself has not already broken and cast them away. Rather, in order to urge them more strongly toward this, he uses this manner of speaking; or he implies that they cannot break and cast them away by themselves or without his help.

When he says, “He who dwells,” and so forth, he shows what they will obtain from that opposition, namely, condemnation. The passage therefore continues as follows:

I said: “Why did they rage,” and so forth. They will come to this outcome: he who dwells not among the wicked but in the heavens—that is, among the holy, who are exalted in virtues—will laugh at them as the heavens do. That is, in the future he will show that they were worthy of mockery, when he makes his own appear glorious and makes those others appear cast down, according to Solomon’s saying: “The righteous shall stand with great confidence against those who afflicted them” (Wis. V, 1).

He will not laugh at them in just any manner, but “the Lord”—that is, the one who is Lord over all things, powerful to condemn the wicked and save the righteous—“will mock them,” that is, will show them to be worthy of mockery, namely, of derision arising from indignation. For to mock is to contract the nostrils because of indignation.

And when he laughs at them, he will speak to them, namely, to the Jews, “in his anger,” that is, in the threat of death, which is usually the evil effect of anger, saying: “Depart from me” (Matt. XXV, 41), and so forth.

Afterward, “he will trouble them,” that is, condemn them, “in his fury,” that is, in death, which is called his fury—that is, his vengeance. For vengeance is usually the effect of anger.

Or, if it is said that the utterance there will not be *elementaris* [“elementary”; reading uncertain], there will be one exposition; another is as follows: “He will speak to them in his anger.” This will not be verbally, but he will trouble them in his fury, that is, in his vengeance—and not in an unjust fury, but in his own, that is, a just one. For he himself is the just judge. This means that the condemnation itself will be the speech of judgment to them.

It follows: “But I,” and so forth. The passage continues as follows:

Those who thought my death would benefit them will be troubled. But I, whom they thought they could annihilate, have been appointed, that is, will be appointed, king over Sion because of my obedience unto death—that is, over the Jews, namely, those who are Sion, that is, those who contemplate eternal things.

I say “Sion” as an existing mountain, that is, those who are a mountain by being Sion. He explains in what respect they are a mountain: not in wickedness, but in holiness; and this through him, not through themselves. This is what he means by “his holy mountain.” They will be a mountain through this: I will be to them one who proclaims his commandment.

And I will not be appointed only over Sion, but also over the nations. He shows this by authority as follows:

“For the Lord”—that is, the Father, who is Lord over all things and is powerful to subject everything to me—“said,” that is, established in his providence, “to me,” that is, something such as whatever pertains to me.

And he explains what he said:

“Ask of me”—that is, be obedient to me unto death. Through that obedience, as though by words, “ask of me the nations.” And I, who am powerful as Lord, “will give you the nations as your inheritance,” that is, so that they may be your inheritance, so that you may cultivate them as someone cultivates an inheritance.

And I will not give you a few nations, but “I will give you the ends of the earth as your possession.” By “the ends of the earth” he designates all nations—not because he would give all of them, but because he was going to give people from all of them, as the Apostle testifies: “At the name of Jesus every knee shall bow” (Phil. II, 10), that is, every kind of knee.

Or the qualification may be understood in this way: “I will give you the nations,” and not all of them, but “the ends of the earth,” that is, those who terminate in themselves earthly existence, that is, those who bring it to an end.

He appropriately first calls them his inheritance and afterward calls them his possession. At first he will cultivate them as an inheritance; afterward he will possess them, that is, rule them. “I will give you the nations, and Sion” [Col. 0646B]—and rightly so. “For you shall rule them with an iron rod,” that is, with inflexible government, so that neither by death nor by life will they be separated from charity (Rom. VIII, 38).

And so that they may be governed well, “you shall break them like a potter’s vessel,” that is, in the part in which they are fragile, like a potter’s vessel—namely, according to their vices.

And since someone could ask why, because of his obedience unto death, he would give the nations to him, when he did not give this to any of the prophets who died for him, he explains this by first stating:

“I will give you the nations alone, for you are my Son.” You were not begotten carnally or temporally, but “I have begotten you today,” that is, eternally.

He rightly says “today,” for in divinity there is no change or shadow of alteration (James I, 17). There “today” means an immutable present. He also rightly says “I have begotten,” which is a completed tense, lest, because he had said “today,” it should appear that his begetting was only now beginning. For he was perfectly begotten.

It is as though he were saying: You are my consubstantial Son.

Having shown by the authority of the Father that he is king, he turns in an apostrophe to those whose king he is, exhorting and instructing them as follows:

Since I am your king—and you were formerly servants of sin but have now become kings, for serving me is reigning—understand. And you who cannot understand—for understanding belongs to the perfect—be instructed by teachers.

He explains whom he calls kings as follows:

You are kings, I say, who judge—that is, condemn within yourselves by confession—the earth, that is, earthly-mindedness. I say: understand, be instructed, and thus serve the Lord, and do not do so negligently. For “cursed is he who performs the work of the Lord deceitfully” (Jer. XLVIII, 10), but serve him in fear, since “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. I, 7).

And do not serve in slavish fear, but “rejoice in him,” that is, serve him with rejoicing and fear. It is as though he were saying: Serve him with chaste fear, and thus rejoice, lest you become insolent; rather, always remain in trembling, so that “he who stands may see that he does not fall” (I Cor. X, 12).

And if, in serving the Lord, discipline should come upon you—that is, tribulation, which is his discipline, namely, correction—“take hold of that discipline,” that is, receive it willingly rather than unwillingly. To take hold means to accept willingly.

And you who understand, do this for a twofold reason, lest, if you do not serve and do not accept discipline, the Lord should at some time become angry. It is as though he were saying: Do not serve through fear of punishment, as servants serve their masters, but lest God be offended, just as a son serves his father not from fear of punishment but lest he displease him [Col. 0647A].

Therefore serve and accept discipline, lest you perish from the righteous way. This means: lest the righteousness that is the way by which one comes to life perish within you.

It is as though he were saying: Do not lose righteousness. And you who are not so perfect that you serve and accept discipline for these reasons—be instructed, and serve and accept discipline for this reason: for blessed will be those who, serving well, trust in him.

There is no confidence among those who do not serve, but presumption. And by saying, “Blessed are those who trust in him,” he makes it understood indirectly, through aposiopesis, that all who do not trust are wretched.

That blessedness and happiness will appear when his anger—that is, his vengeance—has burned forth. This will occur in a short time. He rightly says “has burned forth.” For now it burns according to the blinding of the soul; then it will burn outwardly, that is, it will burn more intensely, for the condemnation of both body and soul.

## PSALM III

The title of the third psalm is: “A psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom his son.”

This title of the third psalm expresses the psalm’s purpose both according to the indication of its historical event and according to the interpretation of its wording. For the statement that David was persecuted by his son signified that Christ would be persecuted by his disciple, who was his special son.

Absalom, the son of David, is interpreted as “the father’s peace.” This does not mean that he had peace toward his father, but that, while he was persecuting him, the father always maintained peace toward him.

So also Christ, when he was betrayed by Judas, his son, maintained peace toward him and did not even deny him a kiss. And just as Absalom perished by hanging because of his wickedness, so Judas perished because of the crime of his sale.

He appropriately placed this title before the title “Have mercy on me, O God” (Ps. L), which is: “A psalm of David, when he went in to Bathsheba.” For by this he indicates that this psalm is not to be understood according to the historical account. If it were to be understood historically, it would certainly have been placed after “Have mercy on me, O God,” according to the sequence of the history.

The title is therefore explained as follows:

“A psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom his son.” This means: “Psalm”—that is, this treatise—is to be attributed to David, that is, to Christ. It contains the event that happened to Christ himself when he fled, that is, withdrew, “from the face,” that is, from the presence, of Absalom, that is, of Judas, his son, that is, his disciple: “When the devil had put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon, to betray him” (John XIII, 2).

It is the voice of the Head, expressing amazement at the multiplication of those who persecute him without cause—not because he is amazed, since he knows that it will occur by God’s disposition, but because anyone could be amazed at it. He does this to show what he will obtain from that persecution, so that no amazement may remain for those who believe in him.

And he says this as follows:

“Lord, why have those who afflict me become so numerous?” This means: Since you, Father, are Lord of all, and nothing in your kingdom ought to be left to chance, why did you permit this to happen—that my enemies should multiply, afflicting me by their actions, counsels, and will? They will multiply to such an extent that my disciple will join them. As he says elsewhere: “Fat bulls have surrounded me” (Ps. XXI, 13).

It follows, concerning the very people who afflict me: “Many rise up,” that is, will rise up, against me with accusations, as it is read in the Gospel: “And they accused him of many things” (Mark XV, 3).

And many of those who afflict me also say—or will say—of my soul, insofar as they are harmful to it: “Come, let us kill him” (Wis. II, 10), “for there is no salvation for him in his God.”

This means: He makes the Creator his God and Father, but he himself has abandoned him, as it is said elsewhere: “He calls himself the Son of God. Come, let us oppress him, for there is no one to deliver him” (ibid., 3).

After presenting the amazement that someone might have, he proceeds to show the fruit of his Passion, saying:

They afflict me with death and with manifold anguish. But you, Lord, who are powerful to come to my aid, since you are Lord of all, are—that is, will be—my protector, that is, my physician and advocate: “you will raise me up.”

To protect is the work of physicians, so that they may heal the sick, and of advocates, so that they may defend the oppressed.

They say, “There is no salvation for him.” But you will be not only the salvation of the Resurrection, but also my glory, that is, the one who makes me glorious through the Ascension and through rule over the whole world.

They rise up, accusing, slandering, and humiliating me, calling me a deceiver. But you exalt my head, that is, my mind, through virtues and freedom from sin. The head is called the mind because it is the nobler part of a human being, just as the head is the nobler part of the body.

When he says, “With my voice,” and so forth, he turns in an apostrophe to his hearers, instructing them, when they are placed in tribulation, to cry out to the Lord after his example and to be heard. He says this as follows:

O hearers, so that he may receive me, be my glory, and exalt my head, “I cried out”—that is, I will act with an intense cry—“with my voice,” not with a vain voice, but with my voice, that is, one proceeding from my good intention; or “my” in the sense of “useful to me,” “to the Lord,” that is, to God, who is powerful to come to my aid. For he is Lord of all.

And I cried out for my good—that is, I will cry out. For “he heard me”—that is, he will hear me—so that I may obtain what I ask.

He heard me, I say, “from his holy mountain,” that is, from the eminence of his holy righteousness, which is called a mountain because it is high and lofty, as he says elsewhere: “Your righteousness is like the mountains” (Ps. XXXV, 7).

Or, “he will hear me from the mountain,” that is, on my behalf, because I am his holy mountain, that is, exalted in virtues.

Or, “he will hear me from the mountain,” that is, because I will become his holy mountain, as it is written: “The mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains” (Mic. IV, 1), that is, the protection of the whole Church, just as a mountain is a protection for those who flee to it, according to the prophetic saying: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” (Isa. II, 3).

And it is necessary that he hear me. For “I slept”—that is, I will sleep—“and I was overcome with sleep”—that is, I will be overcome with sleep—and afterward, so that I may be heard by him, “I rose up”—that is, I will rise up [Col. 0649A].

He rightly says not “I shall rise” but “I shall rise up,” that is, I shall rise beyond the resurrection of others. For I shall be more glorious than all the others who rise.

By saying “I shall sleep,” he indicates that this death will not be long, but will last only for a time, so that I may be quickly awakened from it, like someone awakened from sleep.

By saying “I shall be overcome with sleep,” he indicates that it will occur peacefully and with the security of rising again. A person who sleeps securely is said to be overcome with sleep.

Or, because he had said “I shall sleep,” that is, “I shall suffer a brief death,” lest we think that he would rise immediately, he adds: “I shall be overcome with sleep,” that is, “I shall sleep for a little while.”

Having shown the benefit that came to him from his death, he also shows the benefit that came to his members. Thus I say: The Lord will be my protector, that is, he will protect me, that is, he will raise me up.

“I shall not fear thousands of people surrounding me,” that is, surrounding my people. By saying “thousands of people surrounding,” he indicates that the crowd of persecutors will be great.

It is as though he were saying: Because I have conquered, and my people will conquer, I will not fear that my people will be conquered. As he says elsewhere: “Take courage, for I have overcome the world” (John XVI, 33).

I say: “I will not fear.” And so that they may conquer, you, God, who are powerful but appear powerless to those who persecute, “rise up,” that is, show yourself powerful. “And save me,” that is, my people, lest they yield to their enemies.

And this is fitting, for you are my God, that is, the God of my people, and there is no other.

I see this through an opposite statement, because you will save my people: you will destroy their adversaries. This is demonstration through the contrary. He says it as follows:

You will save my people. And I know this from the fact that you have struck—or will strike—that is, destroy—both in body and in soul, all who opposed me without cause in the Passion; or, “opposed me,” that is, my people.

And not only the lesser ones, but also “the teeth of sinners,” that is, those who are teeth among sinners, incorporating the lesser ones into evil, just as teeth grind food in order to incorporate it.

“You have crushed”—that is, you will crush—“them completely,” or “the teeth,” that is, those who gnaw at and slander me or my people.

And because he had prayed for his people, someone might say: Why do you pray for them? If they live well, they could be saved by themselves.

Therefore he adds: I necessarily pray to God that he rise up, for “salvation belongs to the Lord.” No one will be able to be saved from incorporation into his enemies except through him, who is Lord, powerful to save the righteous and condemn the wicked.

Now, in the excess of his affection, he turns an apostrophe to him as follows:

Through you there is salvation from enemies in this world, and not only this, but also blessing—that is, eternal reward—will come upon your people, that is, will come from above upon those who, formerly sons of perdition, will become your people.

It will be yours, that is, given through you, as it is written: “No one can come to me unless my Father draws him” (John VI, 44).

## PSALM IV

The title of the fourth psalm follows, and it is this: “To the end: a psalm of a song of David.”

It is explained as follows:

This psalm, this song—that is, this treatise—is called “a psalm of a song,” because it treats principally of the psalm, that is, of the good work, and secondarily of the song, that is, of the reward of the good work.

It is to be attributed to David, that is, to the perfected Church, which is strong of hand against the devil. David, I say, is “directed toward the end,” that is, toward Christ, the end of prophecy and of the law.

A psalm is that symphony which is made through the exercise of the hands on some musical instrument, commonly called a *luydas*. Because it is pleasing and is performed through the work of the hands, it is used for a good work, which, when accomplished through the exercise of the hands, pleases God.

A song is a symphony expressed with the living voice, through which the soul is delighted more than through a psalm. Therefore it is used for the future reward, which will be sweeter than the good work.

It is the voice of the perfected Church, first instructing the lesser members by her example not to cease praying in tribulation, as she herself does, and to be heard, as she herself is heard. Then she turns to the unbelievers, calling them back from unbelief to faith and to repentance, to the abandonment of evil and to good works, and thus by her example leads them to hope for reward.

And she says this as follows:

“When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me.”

This is explained as follows:

O lesser members, call upon God in your tribulation, and you will be heard. For “when I called, he heard me,” that is, he heard me so that I might obtain what I asked, the God who makes my righteousness, that is, who made me righteous, so that I might be worthy to be heard.

Now, in the excess of her affection, she turns an apostrophe to God, as though giving thanks and explaining in what way he heard her. I say: You heard me.

And this is true: when I was placed in tribulation, “you enlarged me,” that is, you gave me enlargement.
