It is as though she were saying: When those who afflicted me wished to make my righteousness narrow and small, you did the opposite and made it great and extensive.

And you who have already heard, hear my prayer again, that is, the prayer useful to me and proceeding from my upright intention. She explains what she means by “hear”:

I say, hear—that is, have mercy on me, lest I yield to those who afflict me; or have mercy on me, that is, on my people, lest they yield.

By praying repeatedly, she instructs the lesser members to pray without ceasing, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Pray without interruption” (I Thess. V, 7), and the Gospel’s: “Pray that you do not enter into temptation” (Luke XXII, 20).

Having instructed the lesser members in a few words, she turns to the unbelievers, instructing them at greater length, since they require more instruction than those who have been instructed to some degree. First she shows that the things they worship are vain, insofar as the Gentiles are concerned, and that the Jews offer a lying excuse. She says as follows:

“Children of men,” and so forth.

This is explained as follows:

I have already been heard, and if you cried out in the same way, you would likewise be heard.

And you, “children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” This is said generally to both Jews and Gentiles.

He rightly says “children of men,” as though saying: You who have not proceeded from irrational animals but from rational beings, namely, from human beings who worship not the creature but the Creator.

For no one—not even a Gentile—who belongs to those who have possessed knowledge of God is without descent, however long the succession of his bloodline may be, from people such as Abraham, from whom many descended, and Noah and the other faithful [Col. 0651A]. And all descend from Adam and Eve, who possessed knowledge of God.

He rightly says, “How long will you be heavy of heart?” as though saying: You who, until Christ’s coming, have had a heavy heart weighed down by earthly things, how long will you continue to have it so—that is, why do you not finally convert after his coming?

He explains in what respect they have a heavy heart when he adds:

You Gentiles, “why”—that is, for what benefit—“do you love vanity,” that is, worship idols, which are vain and empty of the divinity that you believe to be in them?

And you Jews, “why do you seek a lie,” that is, an excuse for your cruelty, saying that the Messiah has not come? This is a lie.

Know, O Gentiles, that those things are vanity, and know, O Jews, that your excuse is a lie.

And with this, know that the Lord—that is, the Father, who, since he is Lord, is powerful to make him wondrous—“has made wondrous,” that is, made miraculous, “his holy one,” that is, his Son, who by antonomasia is called his holy one.

This can be shown by the following result, which proves that he truly made him wondrous: the Lord the Father “will hear me when I cry out,” that is, when I pray to him with a righteous request, as it is written: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will grant you” (John XIV, 13).

Or I say that he “made him wondrous,” that is, made him Lord of all; and he himself, having become Lord insofar as he was man, “heard me,” and so forth.

After the prayer, she instructs them concerning conversion, repentance, cessation from evil, and good works. She says first: Know, and so forth.

And so “be angry with yourselves,” that is, repent of the crimes you have committed, and afterward “do not sin.”

Since she had said indefinitely, “Do not sin,” and this is impossible—for no one exists who does not sin at least in thought, as John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I, 8)—she specifies her meaning.

Thus I say: “Do not sin.” And because you cannot cease from the thought of sinning, at least “be pierced with remorse,” so that you do not proceed to consent to those unlawful things that you say—that is, think—in your hearts, namely, in those hearts that are then the lairs of beasts, that is, of demons. For lairs properly belong to beasts.

After this she instructs them concerning good works. Thus I say: “Be angry and do not sin,” and then “sacrifice the sacrifice,” for previously you could not do so. And not a sacrifice of bulls, but “a sacrifice of righteousness,” that is, such a sacrifice as makes you righteous—namely, good devotion and good action.

Therefore “hope in the Lord,” that is, place your hope of reward in the Lord.

And afterward, lest you lose hope, do not be like those many who say: “Who will show us good things?” This means: You Christians say that eternal good things exist, but who, possessing and visibly displaying those good things in himself, can show us by this that they truly exist?

No one can show this to them. After showing that certain unbelievers say that eternal good things do not exist, she says that she herself does not believe that they do not exist, in order to draw others to hope for them. Thus they speak: No one can show them these things.

But to us they have been shown by our reason. For, O Lord, “upon us,” that is, in the higher and more excellent part of us, namely, in the soul, “the light,” that is, the brightness, “of your countenance,” that is, of your Son, “has been marked,” that is, impressed.

It is as though she were saying: Because we are rational, made according to your image, that is, according to the likeness of your Son, who is your countenance and your image—that is, similar and equal in divinity, so that in no respect is he dissimilar—your light has been impressed upon us.

He rightly says “marked” by way of likeness. For just as a seal, being an image, when impressed upon wax places there a figure similar to itself, though in some respect different, so rationality is impressed upon our minds in likeness to the rationality of the Son of God, who is the countenance of the Father.

And because I am rational, you have given me joy—not in earthly things, but in things existing in my heart, that is, in the eternal good things that I hope for in my heart.

But those who say, “Who will show us good things?” rejoice in earthly things instead. For “they have multiplied,” that is, they have a manifold joy arising from the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil.

He rightly says “their,” for because they do not distribute these things for God, they retain everything for themselves.

By these three parts he gives us to understand all earthly things. And because he had said, “You have given joy in my heart,” he explains what this joy concerns as follows: They have multiplied from the fruit, and so forth.

But to me you have given joy from this: that in the future I shall sleep and rest from present tribulations, placed in peace—not in a changeable peace, but in peace tending into itself, that is, into eternity—as it is written:

“God shall wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, and there shall no longer be mourning, nor crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away” (Rev. XXI, 4) [Col. 0652C].

It follows: “For you, Lord,” and so forth.

The passage continues in this way: I say that I will rest, and this is because I hope for this alone. He expresses this equivalently as follows:

“For you, Lord”—that is, you who are powerful and Lord of all—“have established,” that is, made me firm, “in hope alone,” that is, in this singular hope, so that I hope for and desire nothing apart from you.

## PSALM V

The title of the fifth psalm follows, and it is this: “To the end, for her who receives the inheritance. A psalm of David.”

Here he directs us to the history of Abraham’s two wives. One of them was expelled from the inheritance, namely Hagar; the other received the inheritance, namely Sarah.

Through Hagar the handmaid, the Synagogue is represented, since it obeyed the law carnally through servile fear. Through Hagar’s son, false Christians and heretics are represented, who, like the Synagogue, have their minds set on the things of the flesh, although they were formerly God’s wife, being joined to him in knowledge.

These will be driven away from the inheritance of everlasting glory, as it is written: “Cast out the handmaid and her son” (Gen. XXI, 10; Gal. IV, 30).

Through Sarah and her son, however, the Church with her children is represented; she will inherit eternal glory in the future.

The title is explained as follows:

This psalm is to be attributed to David, that is, to the perfected Church, directed toward the end, that is, toward Christ, who is the end, or limit, of the righteous. No righteous person exists either on this side of him or beyond him, but in him, according to the Apostle: “We, though many, are one body in Christ” (I Cor. XII, 20).

David, I say, is praying for her who receives the inheritance of the eternal homeland—now in hope, and eventually in reality, that is, by possessing it in herself.

But by saying “for her who receives the inheritance,” which implies by contrast that there is another who will not receive it—namely, the Synagogue, false Christians, and heretics—he intends in this psalm that the Church should pray to God so that she may finally be able to attain that inheritance.

Afterward she declares that she will inherit it, while those others will be expelled. Therefore she prays in such a way that she may exercise herself toward God not only in action and thought but also in voice, and thereby possess greater affection toward him [Col. 0653B].

For this reason she announces that she will inherit, while those others will be disinherited, so that she may thereby draw them back from their injustice.

And she says this as follows.

My words—that is, words that are not empty and fanciful, but are such as I ought to utter, proceeding from right intention—perceive with your ears, that is, hear, O Lord. In saying “perceive with your ears,” he speaks according to human usage, as though he said: Hear me so that I may obtain what I ask. He rightly says “Lord,” when he could have said “Bridegroom,” so that he might be more humble, as though he said: You who are my Lord, whose will I place before my own will. And because I cannot always pray in words, if at some time I pray with good devotion, understand my cry—that is, regard favorably that devotion which prays to you like an intense [Col. 0653C] cry—and, so that my words may be increasingly worthy of being heard by you, attend—that is, grant intention, that is, perseverance—to the voice of my prayer, that is, to my voice as I pray, and rightly so. For you are my king—that is, you rule me—and I have myself not according to my own kingdom but according to yours, and you are my God. I am not one of those “whose god is their belly” (Phil. III, 19); I do not take away a place for your deity within me. As though he said: You ought to heed me, because I order myself according to your will, not according to mine.

After making his prayer, he declares that he will be heard, as follows: I say, “Perceive and understand,” and indeed, “In the morning you will hear my voice”—that is, on the day of judgment, which will be clear like morning, you will fulfill my petition, O God who are powerful, to whom I have made myself a servant [Col. 0653D]—because I pray and shall pray to you perseveringly in order to merit you, not for anything earthly. As though he said: I ask for what I ought to ask for, namely, you. When he says, “In the morning you will hear,” he indicates that you will fulfill his petition at the very beginning of the day of judgment. For morning is the beginning of the day. And he explains what he means by “you will hear,” as follows: I say, “You will hear,” and thus, “In the morning”—that is, on the day of judgment—“I shall stand,” that is, I shall be present before you with bodily presence, according to the words: “Where I am, there also my minister shall be” (John XII, 26), and: “Heirs indeed together with Christ” (Rom. VIII, 17). And I shall not merely stand, but shall see you face to face, according to the Apostle: “Now we see through a mirror, but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII, 12). From this I know that I shall stand, because although you are God and belong to your own nature, [Col. 0654A] namely, since iniquity is opposed to you, you do not will iniquity. For it would be unjust if you did not admit me when I seek only you, as I ought to seek you. And, conversely, I am again certain that I shall stand and see you: for neither shall the malicious one—that is, the Jewish people, which is malicious, being barren of good—dwell beside you, that is, it will not be an heir with you to the eternal inheritance, as you have testified: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXI, 43); nor shall the unjust—that is, false Christians who do not desist from their injustice—remain before your eyes, that is, before your presence. They will indeed come before you for judgment, but they will not remain—that is, they will not stay long—in your presence, as it is written: “Let the impious be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI, 10).

In truth, they will not remain, for you hate, and will always hate, all who practice iniquity—not those who have practiced it and ceased, but those who practice it perseveringly for as long as they live. And you will destroy, in body and soul, all who speak falsehood—that is, heresy—those for whom it is not enough merely to think unless they utter it with their mouths; not those who have spoken and rejected it, but those who speak perseveringly. And because he had spoken indeterminately of “falsehood,” since many falsehoods are venial, he specifies which liars he has in mind, turning to the hearers in order to deter them from that falsehood. Thus he says: He will destroy—and this is true—for the Lord, that is, the one who is Lord, powerful, and just, will abominate—that is, he will curse so vehemently [Col. 0654C] that he will not even regard him as a human being—the bloodthirsty man, that is, the liar who is a shedder of human blood, that is, a murderer of human beings. And he explains how he is a murderer when he adds: “And the deceitful man,” that is, the bloodthirsty man who kills his neighbors by the deceit of his words, namely, by his heresy.

He does not call him “bloodthirsty” because he sheds blood, but because he kills as one who sheds blood does. And he rightly says not merely “man” but “male,” since he strives with all his strength toward lying. He also rightly uses the singular “man” after having used the plural “all,” in order to show that, in being liars, they form one mass. When he says of these that you will destroy them and that he will abominate them, whereas he had said of the others that they would not dwell and would not remain, he indicates that these are to be punished more severely.

When he then adds, “But I shall enter,” and so forth, this means the same as what he said earlier in other words: “In the morning I shall stand and see.” But because he had said that he would stand and see on account of his merits, since he prayed both rightly and for what ought to be prayed, he repeats this in order to show that he will enter not merely because of his merits, but also through God’s mercy. He says this as follows: The Lord will abominate the deceitful man, but I shall enter your house—that is, the heavenly Jerusalem—trusting in the abundance of your mercy, that is, in your manifold mercy, and not, nevertheless, in my own merits. And, so that I may be able to enter, being first established here in fear—not servile fear, but your fear, that is, chaste fear— [Col. 0655A] which is yours, that is, very pleasing to you, I shall adore you, making you God and myself a creature. I shall come to your holy temple to receive it—that is, to receive your body, which is the holy temple of the Godhead—or in this way: I shall come to become your holy temple, according to the Apostle: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God?” (I Cor. VI, 19).

And so that here I may rightly adore and thus enter, O Lord, as I am established here, guide me in your justice—that is, lead me from virtue to virtue. And so that I may be able to be led, direct—that is, make straight before me, that is, in my understanding—your way, that is, your divine Scripture, which was given to us through you as the way of faith. As though he said: Do not permit me to stray in it, but grant me right understanding of it. And I ask this because of my enemies, [Col. 0655B] who lie in wait for me in order to make me stray. I ask because of my enemies for this reason: there is no truth in their mouths, that is, they speak falsely; and this is because their heart is empty, that is, full of vain thoughts. For out of arrogance, so that they may appear clever, they speak falsely about God. And since there is no truth in them, they not only destroy themselves, but their throat is an open tomb: that is, by the voice proceeding from their throat they may be compared to an open tomb. For just as a tomb is open so that it may receive a body and make it putrid and foul, so their evil doctrine is open so that it may receive the innocent as examples of itself and make them foul. And, in order that they might be an open tomb, they had first acted deceitfully with their tongues, that is, with their words, previously mixing truth with falsehood so that they might deceive more easily. And because they are such, O God, who are a just judge, judge them—that is, condemn them. This is not a curse, but a concession to divine justice, made in order to terrify them. And he explains in separate parts how he judges them: here, let them fall from evil into evil, according to what is said elsewhere: “Let the one who is filthy become filthy still” (Apoc. XXII, 11). This fall will not come from your harshness, but from their worst thoughts. And in the future expel them from your kingdom, which they arrogate to themselves through their presumption. Do this not according to your severity, but according to the multitude of their impieties—that is, because they have committed many impieties. And truly they have committed many, because they provoked you: although you were naturally sweet, they made you, God, bitter, even though you are Lord and they are servants.

Having made this concession, he prays as follows on behalf of his faithful, who are to inherit: Let those others be expelled, and, conversely, let all who hope—not in themselves but in you—rejoice in the future. Having prayed, he declares that what he prays for will come to pass, so that he may encourage his faithful to await it more eagerly and, by the prospect of this joy, draw unbelievers toward conversion. I say, “Let them rejoice”—and this will truly happen. They will truly exult, and not for a short time, but forever, and rightly so, because you will dwell in them, that is, you will pour out upon them the brightness of your Godhead, as it is said elsewhere: “When God will be all in all” (I Cor. XV, 28). And they will not exult merely a little, but will glory, that is, rejoice in the greatest glory. And this glory will be in you, not in themselves, since they will attribute it not to themselves but to you.

All who love your name—that is, who do not fear this fact, that you are Lord, on account of their evil conscience, but love your name, that is, the fact that you are Lord—will rightly glory, because you, who are just, powerful, and merciful, will bless the just, that is, will grant them eternal blessing. And he rightly says “the just,” not “the just ones,” in order to show that they will become one thing in themselves, as the Apostle says: “We shall meet in a perfect man” (Eph. IV, 13). I say that you will bless them, and, so that we may be worthy to receive blessing there: O powerful God, you have crowned us, that is, here you have surrounded us like a shield with the shield of your good will—that is, with your good will, namely, mercy—as with a shield, so that it may be our defense, just as a shield is a defense to one equipped with a shield. When he says, “You have crowned us,” he speaks by comparison with patrons who, in order to rescue one who has been oppressed, crown him—that is, surround him—with shield-bearing soldiers. So Christ, in order to rescue us from visible and invisible enemies, surrounds and protects us with the virtues of his mercy.

## ON PSALM VI

The title of the sixth Psalm follows, as follows: “For the end, in hymns, for the eighth; a Psalm of David.” This is explained as follows: This Psalm is to be attributed to David, that is, to the penitent, who, having first been overcome by the devil through sin, at last again became David, that is, “strong of hand,” intending once more to fight against the devil; and now made desirable to God through repentance. I say, David tending toward the end, that is, toward Christ, in hymns—that is, through praises—because by his repentance and good works he praises him, that is, shows him to be worthy of praise. I say, in hymns performed for the eighth, that is, with regard to the eternal rest that is to come on the eighth day, namely, on the day of judgment. And it appears that the same matter is treated in this Psalm as in the preceding one. For both Psalms treat of eternal rest. They differ, however, in this: in the preceding Psalm the faithful, already certain of that rest, pray for it; in this one the penitent, grieving over sins committed and sighing for that very rest, which he sees himself to have lost through evil merits, humbly prays for the remission of his offenses, as follows.

O Lord, to whom I make myself a servant through repentance, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger. As though he said: I do not indeed dread being rebuked and corrected here through tribulations, for according to Solomon: “The Lord corrects the one whom he loves” (Prov. III, 12). Indeed, “God scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII, 6); and elsewhere: “He who spares the rod hates his son” (Prov. XIII, 24). But I ask that you not rebuke me—that is, convict and show that I have done evil—through your fury inflicted upon me, that is, through eternal vengeance. And because many will be punished not in fury but in anger, that is, in prolonged purgatorial punishment lasting until the day of judgment, only then escaping it, he adds: Nor correct me in your anger, that is, in that prolonged punishment. Here “correct me” has the same meaning as “rebuke me.” But have mercy on me, O God: rebuke and correct me in this world with temporal scourges, with mercy.

And it is necessary that I ask this, because I am weak, that is, feeble and unable to heal myself by my own power; or “weak,” that is, sick with sins. And because my bones are troubled, that is, because I am so weak that even my bones—that is, the virtues that are the strength of the soul, just as bones are the strength of the body— [Col. 0657A] are troubled, that is, entirely lost and destroyed because of sins, heal me, O Lord, because you are a good and powerful physician. Or the passage may be connected in this way: I am weak, that is, unable by myself to be healed. Therefore heal me, O Lord, who are powerful; and it is necessary that I ask this, because my bones are troubled, that is, my virtues. You ought to have mercy on me because you are my Lord and I am weak. And therefore he continues:

Because my soul is greatly troubled, that is, pierced by compunction for its sins, and you, O Lord, to whom I have made myself a servant, how long will you delay comforting me by forgiving my sins? As though he said: Do not delay long, but turn by grace toward me, who have turned to you through repentance. And deliver my soul—that is, forcibly draw it out—from sins; then save me, restoring me to the justice in which I was before I sinned so grievously. Do this not because of my merits, but because of your mercy, since you are merciful by nature. And I am not yet in death: medicine can rightly be applied to me. That is, I am not in despair of your mercy. He proves this by an argument from the whole, as follows:

For one who remembers—that is, remembers you, namely, one who remembers your mercy—is not to be said to be in death, that is, in despair. And I do remember; therefore I am not in death. And he shows by an opposing statement that no one who remembers is in death, as follows: For who, being placed in hell—that is, in despair, by which one reaches hell—will confess to you, that is, praise you for your mercy? No one.

“ I have labored,” and so forth. This is connected as follows: I say that you ought to have mercy because my soul is troubled, that is, pierced by compunction. And I have not merely this, but, already established in mourning, I have labored in fasts, vigils, and other acts of satisfaction. In this he shows himself now more worthy of being heard; for having already labored is more than merely having mourned. And I shall wash—that is, cleanse—my bed, that is, my conscience, weeping, traversing every night, that is, all nights, not parts of nights. I shall remember each night, that is, each sin, which leads to night, namely, eternal death; and for each sin I shall weep and make satisfaction. Thus I shall cleanse my conscience, which until now has been foul. And afterward I shall water—that is, irrigate and make fertile with good thoughts pleasing to God—my couch, that is, my conscience, which until now has been dry and barren while I thought evil thoughts.

Here “couch” and “bed” mean the same thing. Conscience is called a couch and a bed by comparison. For just as a healthy person rests on a bed, while a sick person cannot rest at all, so conscience is rest for the good, but torment and anxiety for the wicked. And therefore I have labored, because my eye—that is, the consideration of my mind—has been troubled, that is, pierced by compunction. And he said this above in another way: “My soul is greatly troubled.” But he repeats it here in order to add why it is troubled. I say that it is troubled, and this disturbance proceeded from your fury, that is, from the thought of fury, namely, of perpetual vengeance, because I feared that fury. And this was because I grew old, that is, I fell from the newness of Christ in which I had previously been into the oldness of Adam, while existing among all my enemies—not among some, but among all, both visible and invisible: among the vices that made me sin, and among sinners who, by threats, flatteries, or their evil example, recalled me from the way of justice.

Having completed his satisfaction and being secure concerning forgiveness, out of excessive joy he turns to his visible enemies, telling them not to labor any longer to recall him, because they will not be able to do so. He says this as follows: I formerly grew old among you, and therefore, while making satisfaction, I prayed to God to heal me, and he healed me. Therefore, all you who practice iniquity—not those who practiced it and ceased, but those who still practice it and by your example wish to recall me—depart from me, that is, cease altogether from trying to recall me, because you will not be able to do so. For the Lord, to whom I have made myself a servant, has heard—that is, heard so that I might obtain what I asked for—the voice of my weeping, that is, the prayer I made with my weeping, which proceeded from my guilt.

The Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has received my prayer. He repeats this three times because, from excessive joy, it is not enough for him to say it once. Or these three statements may be distinct, as follows: The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping, granting remission of sins; the Lord has heard my supplication, so that I might not fall again; the Lord has received my prayer, restoring my justice to me, because he prayed for it and was heard.

He prays to God to make them convert, following his example, because they cannot convert by themselves. He says this as follows: Because you have heard me as I blushed and converted, so that you may likewise hear them, O God, let all my enemies blush—that is, truly be ashamed of their sin through you—and let them be greatly troubled, that is, pierced by compunction, and afterward let them turn to you through repentance and satisfaction. I say, let them blush, and I say this so that they may blush greatly, not slightly, and quickly, not slowly. For the one who promised indulgence to the penitent did not promise tomorrow to the one who delays (Gregory, Homily 12 on the Gospels). And it should be noted that he introduces the prophet here as a penitent praying in order to instruct us to repent and to pray for our sins so that we may obtain forgiveness.

## ON PSALM VII

The title of the seventh Psalm: “For the end, a Psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord concerning the words of Cush, son of Jemini.” Where we have “for the end,” the Hebrews have *for the victor*. The authors interpret this title in different ways. According to Augustine, the story of Cush is introduced figuratively: Cush once remained with Absalom during David’s persecution, while secretly reporting to David all the counsels of Absalom that would harm him. It is said that this same Cush destroyed the counsel of Ahithophel, which he had given to Absalom (II Kings XVII, 7), namely, that he should pursue his father through the wilderness. According to Augustine, Cush is interpreted as “silence.” But what follows, “son of Jemini,” does not seem to fit the story well. For blessed Jerome writes that this Cush was an Arachite, not the son of Jemini, and says that Augustine did not examine the historical matter carefully. Jerome also writes that in the name found in this title there is one letter among the Hebrews that is not written in the name of the man who appears in the historical account. Accordingly, “Cush” is interpreted as “Ethiopian,” and here *Cush* is a common noun, not a proper name.

Even if Cush is understood in this way in the historical account, perhaps no historical narrative is introduced, since no Cush son of Jemini is read of in the history—unless perhaps, through this common name, Cush is understood as Saul, who unjustly persecuted David. Saul truly was “Cush,” that is, an Ethiopian, black in sins, just as an Ethiopian is black in body. He is also read to have been a son of Jemini, that is, Benjamin, born from that tribe. Benjamin was first called “Benoni” (Gen. XXXV, 18), that is, “son of sorrow,” because his mother Rachel died from the pain of giving birth to him. But his father changed his name and called him Benjamin, because of the similarity of the sound, that is, “son of the right hand,” since he loved him more than the others and always made him sit at his right hand. It is also read in the historical account that the sons of Benjamin are sometimes called Jeminites and sometimes sons of Jemini. Through Saul, who wickedly persecuted David, the Jewish people are signified, since they unjustly persecuted Christ.

According to Jerome, the title is explained as follows: This Psalm—that is, the words understood in this exposition—is attributed to Christ, who is truly David, persevering toward the end, that is, toward victory, so that he may not yield to his persecutors through fear of death; for victory is the end of war. This Psalm—that is, the words of this Psalm—the Lord sang to the Father in his Passion, that is, he uttered them with the greatest joy, just as a singer utters his words with delight. I say that he sang it, and he did so concerning the words of Cush, that is, with regard to the words of Cush, son of Jemini—namely, concerning the Passion that came upon him through the words of the Jewish people, which is called Cush, that is, Ethiopian, black in sins. It is nevertheless called “son of Jemini,” that is, “of the right hand,” according to certain converts who are to be saved on the day of judgment and will be at his right hand.

The voice in this Psalm is that of the Lord’s humanity, praying for its members and for its persecutors—not by way of imprecation, but by way of concession. It is not that he is uncertain about himself or his members, but that he may instruct us to pray in tribulation. He says this as follows:

O Lord, the Word personally united to me, who, although you are God to others, are nevertheless my God—that is, more especially my God—in you, not in another, I have always hoped. This is a claim of merit. And because I have hoped in you, save me, restoring immortality and impassibility. I say, save me, rescuing me from all who persecute me. And first deliver me; this order is reversed so that he may add from what he is to be delivered. Deliver me thus: lest, like a lion—that is, lest the Jewish people, gnashing against me like a lion and seeking someone to devour (I Peter V, 8), at some time seize my soul from its good purpose and incorporate it into itself. For it wishes to compel me to deny that you are personally united to me, as in the Gospel: “According to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John XIX, 7).

I say, save and deliver me, and rightly so because of my merit: namely, because I have hoped in you, and because I still hope that there is no other who may redeem me, that is, deliver me, or who may save me. And I pray to you, O Lord my God, under this condition: If I have done this—that is, if I have caused this persecution. He had indeed done something of this kind, which was the cause of this persecution, although it was not a legitimate cause: he called himself the Son of God and drove the Jews from the temple, saying: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. XXI, 13), as it is said elsewhere: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. LXVIII, 10).

He adds: I say, if I have done this—that is, if there is iniquity in my hands, that is, in my works; for we perform actions with our hands. As though he said: If I have done any iniquity for which I deserve to be persecuted. And, in order also to remove that which appears more freely available among human beings, namely this: if I have repaid evil to those repaying me—that is, to the Jews, to whom I had done many good works, but who repaid me with evil—then let me be empty, that is, having empty hope, if this is due to my merit and not to your fault; let me fall from my enemies, that is, from the hope concerning my enemies. For I hope that after my death some Jews and Gentiles will be incorporated into me through the preaching of the apostles; let me fall from that hope. And not only let this evil befall me, but also let what is much worse happen: let the enemy—that is, the Jewish people—persecute my soul, and so seize it as to comprehend it, that is, incorporate it into itself, which until now it has not been able to do; and let it trample my life, that is, my soul, which is heaven by the dignity of virtue, and subject it to itself, making it inferior. Let it trample it after it has been brought down to earth, that is, to earthly things, so that it may savor and desire only earthly things, like their mind; and let it bring my glory—that is, the glory of my resurrection, which I await—down into the dust. That is, let it hold me, who expect to be glorious in the resurrection, in death, and thus cause me to return to dust. All of this is as though he said: You ought to deliver and save me because I have always hoped in you and not in another, and still hope in you, nor have I committed iniquity for which I would deserve persecution.

Nor have I repaid evil to those who repaid me with evil, and therefore I do not deserve that they should persecute me so as to seize and trample me and bring my glory down into the dust. I say, deliver and save me from those who persecute me. And because they persecute me, O God, who appear powerless to those Jews, arise—that is, show yourself powerful—in your anger, that is, in the vengeance you exercise against them, namely, in the blinding of their heart. And not only in your anger, but also exalt yourself, that is, show yourself powerful in removing the boundaries of my enemies’ homeland. This means: Blind them in mind and cause the boundaries of their homeland to be taken away, and thus show yourself powerful in vengeance. This is not a curse, but a concession to divine judgment, indicating to us that it is just.

After acknowledging divine justice against his enemies, he prays for his members as follows: Arise in anger against the enemies, and, conversely, arise in aid for the work of those who are not enemies but disciples, in obedience—that is, in obedience to the command—which you gave them through me: that they should love one another, take up their cross, and follow me (Matt. XVI, 24). As though he said: Help them by sending the Holy Spirit, so that they may be able to obey your command given through me: to love you and follow me, preach the words of life to others, and obey the other commands that I gave them.

And if you arise through their preaching, the Synagogue, that is, the congregation of peoples, will surround you, that is, will be in the fellowship of your faith. And he rightly says “of peoples,” even if this refers only to the Jews: for many peoples, that is, many Jewish crowds, were converted, as three thousand are read to have been converted on one day and five thousand on another (Acts II, 4). The text continues.

“And because of this, rise on high,” and so forth. The passage is connected as follows: I said that the Synagogue will surround you. And because of this Synagogue, not merely because of the disciples, return on high, O Word, that is, to the highest equality with the Father. It is not that you were not always there; rather, it is as though he said: You who existed and exist equal to the Father before the ages—because you permit me to suffer and therefore appear unequal—show them that you are equal by making me ascend into heaven, so that you may send the Paraclete to them, namely, to the Synagogue and the disciples. Thus, through my ascension, return on high to the height of your glory: you who were believed by the prophets and many other faithful to be equal, but now are not believed equal, show again that you are equal, and thus return on high in order to send them the Paraclete.

What follows, “The Lord judges the peoples,” is a turn toward the hearers, to show that he must be delivered and saved in every respect. The passage is connected as follows: I pray to be delivered and saved, and this will truly happen. For the Lord, the Word, judges all peoples as they ought to be judged, namely, in equity; and he will judge me in equity by delivering and saving me, according to what is said elsewhere: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22).

When he says, “Judge me,” and so forth, he turns to the Word personally united to him. Thus: Since you judge all peoples as they ought to be judged, judge me also, O Lord, according to what my innocence and my justice have merited—namely, by causing me to rise, ascend into heaven, and cause the world to follow after me. And this is how it stands in the book: “Judge me, O Lord, according to my justice and my innocence.” And he rightly says “my,” for it belonged especially to him, since no one was just and innocent before God. And although I call it “my justice” and “my innocence,” nevertheless they were above me, that is, they were given from above, from God’s disposition, according to the words: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James I, 17).

“Let the wickedness be brought to an end,” and so forth. This is connected as follows: Earlier I said, “Deliver and save me.” Afterward I inserted that I do not pray to be saved and delivered in such a way as to flee death, but so that wickedness may be brought to completion—that is, may be perfected—in me by giving me over to death. And thus you will direct the just one, namely me, that is, show me to be directed, by raising me gloriously and exalting me above the heavens, and by subjugating the world, which now calls me unjust and a perverter of the law.

And truly you will direct me, for you search hearts, that is, know thoughts, and kidneys, that is, works or pleasures. Since you know all thoughts and works or pleasures, you also know that mine are just; therefore you direct me. And truly you search hearts and kidneys, because you are God. He does not use “searching” because anything needs to be searched out—for he knows everything—but because it belongs to those who search to know, “searching” is used for “knowing.” He uses “kidneys” for works or pleasures because we perform generation through the kidneys and take pleasure there.

Because he had earlier said, “Judge me according to my justice,” lest it be thought to have been said arrogantly, he shows that his justice had rightly merited assistance. He says this: I rightly say, O hearers, “Judge me according to my justice,” for my help is just from the Lord, that is, it is just that he should help me, since the Lord saves those who are upright in heart. This is a proof from the lesser. As though he said: Since he saves all who are upright in heart, even those who are less worthy than I, it is much more just that he should help me by saving me.

The text continues: “God the judge,” and so forth. “And not converted,” and so forth. The second verse must be read first, and is connected as follows. Because he had said, “Let wickedness be brought to an end,” he turns to the sinners themselves, exhorting them to do penance for that wickedness, lest God brandish his sword against them. He makes this exhortation on behalf of certain people who are to be saved, and in order to teach us to pray for our enemies, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 44).

Thus he continues: I said, “Let wickedness be brought to an end,” and it will truly be brought to an end. And lest you perish because of that wickedness, be converted by doing penance. For unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword—that is, his vengeance—against you; he will prepare it against you, and rightly so. For that just judge cannot fail to repay you what will be deserved. And he is powerful enough to do this, as he says through Moses: “There is no one who can snatch anyone from my hand” (Deut. XXXII, 39).

And truly he is powerful and just, for he is God. And although he is just and powerful, he is nevertheless patient, that is, he patiently awaits you so that you may not perish, as he himself says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11). And truly he is patient. For does he become angry—that is, punish us—in anger, that is, in vengeance, every day, when we deserve this? As though he said: If he were not patient, he would be angry with us each day.

And so that you may not have any opportunity to escape the sword unless you are converted, here he stretched it—that is, he fitted his bow, namely, the Scripture of the New and Old Law, which threatened eternal death to the unrepentant, just as a drawn bow threatens death to those whom it pursues. He did not stretch it in secret, but prepared it, that is, placed it in the open, as it is said elsewhere: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. XVIII, 5). And he rightly says “he stretched,” by comparison. For just as the horns of a bow, previously distant from each other, appear to draw near when the string is tightened, so the two laws, which had seemed far apart, were made to draw near to one another and agree through Christ.

I say that he stretched and prepared the bow; and, so that that bow might be fully manifested, he prepared in it—that is, equipped and instructed—vessels of death, namely, those who are vessels of death, the preachers. For they are vessels of preaching, which is death to those who do not receive it, as the Apostle bears witness: “To some we are the aroma of life unto life, to others the aroma of death unto death” (II Cor. II, 19).

And he made the vessels themselves into arrows, that is, he made effective arrows. And not for evil, but his own arrows—that is, effective for his benefit—in those burning with faith and charity. This means: He will make them into shooters, that is, into those who strike for the good by their teaching, destined to burn with faith and charity.

Because he had earlier prayed that he might be delivered and saved, he asks from what he had prayed to be delivered, and explains this: I pray to be delivered, and behold, there is presently something from which I ought to be delivered. For the Jewish people is in labor with iniquity, that is, it strives to bring about my death—which is unjust—after the likeness of a woman in labor, that is, of one laboring to give birth. And it conceived this iniquity, not from any merit of mine or from another’s counsel, but by itself conceived in its heart—that is, it thought upon—pain, that is, my death, from which pain will come upon them. And because it has already conceived and is in labor, it has given birth—that is, it will give birth—to iniquity: it will unjustly accomplish my death.

And because it conceived, is in labor, and will give birth, it opened and dug out a pit—that is, by digging it out, it opened it; that is, it made it open and spacious—and it fell—that is, it will later fall—into the pit which it made, that is, which it prepared for me. This means: Because it wishes to hold me in death, it will be like someone digging out and opening a pit into which he intends to cast someone, yet he himself falls into that same pit. For the death which it prepares for me will be the cause of its ruin.

And he explains its fall through clearer comparisons, as follows: Truly, it will fall into the pit. For its pain—that is, the punishment of death which it prepares for me—will turn upon its own head, that is, upon its mind, which will therefore be blinded; and not only upon its head, that is, its mind, but its iniquity—that is, the punishment of its iniquity, namely, of my death—will descend upon its crown. And he rightly says “upon its crown”: for a yoke is customarily placed upon the crown of the head. And in place of their iniquity the Roman yoke will be imposed upon them. As if he said: It will not only be blinded for this reason, but will also be subjected to servitude.

Then follows: “I will confess,” and so forth. He addresses the hearers, instructing them to confess and sing psalms to the Lord, and thus connects the passage: I said, “Deliver,” “Save,” “Arise,” “Judge,” and “the pain will turn upon his head.” And so that all these things may happen, O hearers, I will confess to the Lord, the Word—that is, I will speak his praises—according to the justice given to me; that is, I will confess to him according to the measure of justice: just as he made me more just than all others, so I will offer him praise above all others.

And I will not only confess, but I will also sing psalms—that is, I will do good works—to the name of the Lord, that is, for the honor of the Lord’s name, presenting myself as his servant and acknowledging him as God, rightly for the honor of the name of the Most High. For he is the Most High, namely, the Lord of lords. Properly speaking, “to sing psalms” means to produce melody with the movement of the hands upon the psalter; therefore it is used here for “to work.”

## ON PSALM VIII

Next follows the title of the eighth psalm: “For the end, concerning the winepresses, a psalm of David.” This is explained as follows: This psalm is to be attributed to David, that is, to the prophet himself, directing himself toward the end, that is, toward Christ; or toward the end, that is, toward the perfection of good things. I say “David,” acting for the winepresses, that is, for the Church.

He says “winepresses” in the plural because of the two Churches, from the Jews and from the nations; or because of the many individual Churches, which are called winepresses by comparison. For just as wine and grapes are contained in the winepress, so good and evil are contained in the Church; and at length they will be separated on the day of judgment, as wine is separated from the grape, according to the Lord’s saying: “The angels will go out and separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous” (Matthew XXIII, 49).

In this psalm there is properly the voice of the future Church, in contemplation of the praise of God, so that it may instruct others to praise him, breaking forth in wonder.

“O Lord, our Lord”—that is, you whom we Jews alone acknowledge to be our Lord, for the nations do not yet know you—“how wondrous your name will be,” that is, with what wondrous glory your name will be. Namely, that you are Lord of all, throughout the whole earth, that is, among the nations of the whole earth. As if he said: You who are now known only in Judea will be acknowledged by nations of every kind, according to the saying: “All nations will run to you” (Isaiah IV, 5); and elsewhere: “All the nations which you have made will come and worship before you, O Lord” (Psalm LXXXV, 9).

And he explains how it will become wondrous, as follows: I say that it is wondrous, and this is because your magnificence—that is, your Son, who is emphatically called “magnificence,” making his own people magnificent—has been lifted up, that is, will be exalted above the material heavens; or above the heavens, that is, the divine Scriptures, which are lofty in comparison with secular things, just as the heavens are high. That is, he will be higher in holiness than the divine Scriptures have testified.

Or above the heavens, that is, above rational creatures: he will be more worthy than angels and human beings, who are more worthy than the other animals, just as the heavens are more worthy than the earth and are therefore called “heavens.”

And so that it may appear that your magnificence is to be exalted, you have perfected praise—that is, you will make praise perfect—from the mouth of infants, and not of the great, but, so that it may be wondrous, of sucklings, that is, of little ones, who did not have this from themselves but from the working of the Holy Spirit.

This means: To convict the Jews that Christ is your magnificence and is to be exalted above the heavens, the infancy of children, through the grace wrought by the Holy Spirit, will bear witness to you, saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matthew XXI, 15). And you will perfect this praise because of your enemies, the Jews, who will deny that you are the Son of God, so that by their children’s wondrous testimony you may destroy the enemy and avenger—or defender, that is, convict him—proving the Jewish people, which will be your enemy, to be a liar, since it will claim to be the avenger and defender of its law, according to the saying: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John IX, 16). And elsewhere it is said: “According to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.”

And therefore magnificence will be exalted, because through that magnificence I will see your heavens, that is, your preachers, who will be exalted in virtues. This means: Now I see in hope; one day I will see in reality—not by the sight of the body but by that of the soul—through your magnificence, exalted above your heavens, that is, your preachers.

I say “heavens,” which will be the work of your fingers, that is, will be established by your fingers, that is, by the gifts of the Holy Spirit. He is called a finger because through him the Father works, just as someone works through his fingers, according to what is said in the Gospel: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke XI, 20).

And through the heavens I will see the moon established, that is, the universal Church. It is called “moon” because, just as the moon sometimes appears to diminish during a time of persecution and sometimes to increase during a time of peace, so does the Church. And I will see the stars, that is, the particular Churches, which are small in comparison with the universal Church, just as stars are small in comparison with the moon.

You, O God, founded these—the moon and the stars—that is, you will found them. They cannot be established by those heavens themselves unless you lay the foundation, as the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ” (I Corinthians III, 11). And again: “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (ibid.).

But seeing that the heavens are to be established and God’s magnificence exalted, and that all this is to happen for the sake of humanity, which might seem vile and despised because of the weakness of the body, the prophet, in order to render humanity favorable toward God, breaks forth into his praise in this way: Since magnificence will be exalted and the heavens established, and all this will be for the sake of humanity:

“What is man?”—that is, how great a thing is man? And this can be seen from the fact that you remember him, that is, will remember him: him whom you seemed to have consigned to oblivion through Adam’s fault, you will remember through Christ’s obedience, making him immortal.

After praising humanity, he praises the Son of Man still more, in order to show that all things have been subjected to him, saying: I say, “What is man?” Or I can speak more worthily in this way: “What,” that is, how great a thing, “is the Son of Man,” that is, Christ? And that this is a great thing can be proved because you visit him, that is, will visit him, in that you diminished him, that is, made him lower, “a little lower than the angels.”

As if he said: Because you will make him lower than the angels for the sake of redeeming humanity—lower than the angels, that is, mortal and capable of suffering—you will visit him, bringing him out of that mortality and capacity for suffering.

And he explains how he will visit him as follows: Truly, you will visit him. For you crowned him—that is, will crown him—with the glory of the resurrection and with the honor of the ascension; or with glory, that is, with the illumination of the underworld, because he will descend to the dead with the glory of majesty; and with honor, that is, with victory over death.

And afterward you established him—that is, will establish him—over the works of your hands, that is, over rational creatures, which are said to have been made by God’s hand, that is, to be more worthy than the others, since they are said to have been made by God’s hand.

And you subjected—that is, will subject—not a few works, but all works, beneath his feet, that is, beneath his humanity. This means: You established him as Lord of all not only according to his divinity, but also according to his humanity. And humanity is rightly called a “foot,” since it is lower than divinity, just as the foot is lower than the other members.

And he proves this from the parts as follows: You will subject the sheep to him, that is, those who possess the highest simplicity and innocence, like sheep; and all the oxen, that is, the preachers, who are rightly called oxen because they cultivate the lesser and feed them with their teaching, just as oxen cultivate the fields and nourish their calves with milk.

Moreover, you will subject the beasts of the field to him, that is, those devoted to pleasure, who are so intent upon pleasure that they satisfy their desires, just as beasts linger in the pastures of the fields in order to serve their bellies. And pleasure is rightly compared to a field, since it is broad enough to satisfy the desires of the flesh, just as a field is broad.

And you will subject the birds of the heavens to him, that is, those who wander irrationally through vanities, like birds through the sky; and the fish of the sea, that is, the curious people of this world. This world is called “sea” because it is disturbed by frequent tribulations, like the sea.

The curious—that is, the avaricious people of this world—are called “fish” because, just as fish are submerged in the waves, so they are submerged in worldly anxieties. These fish traverse, that is, swim around, the paths, that is, the ways of the sea, that is, the affairs of this age, which are the ways by which one comes to worldly profit.

Or the fish are called the philosophers of this world because, just as fish are enclosed in the sea, so they are entangled in secular knowledge. And they are rightly said to traverse the paths of the sea, that is, the subtle judgments of that secular knowledge.

Having shown all the members of the Church who are to be subjected to Christ, just as he began with praise, so he intends to end with praise, drawing this conclusion: Therefore, because the sheep and the rest which I have mentioned will be subjected through you to the Lord’s human being: “O Lord, our Lord,” and so forth. And this is explained as above.

## ON PSALM IX

Next follows the title of the ninth psalm: “For the end, concerning the hidden things of the Son, a psalm of David.” This is explained as follows: This psalm is to be attributed to David, that is, to the perfect Church, directing itself toward the end, that is, toward Christ, so as to be conformed to him.

I say “David,” acting in praise for the hidden things of the Son, that is, for Christ’s judgments. He is called “the Son” antonomastically, as he himself testifies: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John VIII, 36). These judgments are hidden from many.

And he rightly says “hidden things.” For he does not speak of only one thing but of several: how God secretly judges some of the impious so that they may be converted, but others so that, becoming more blinded, they may be justly punished; and how he judges his own to be punished in this world and afterward to be blessed. Finally, he speaks of the future persecution in the time of Antichrist, which will occur through God’s hidden judgment.

In this psalm there is the voice of the perfect Church, instructing the lesser members to praise God and promising to praise God for his hidden judgments, by which many are scandalized, as follows:

“I will confess to you, O Lord.” As if he said: Many are scandalized by your hidden judgments, which seem unjust to them. But I will confess to you, that is, I will praise you, with my whole heart, that is, with the whole affection of my heart, with no illusory thought intervening.

For you are Lord and therefore worthy of praise. I will proclaim to others with my mouth all your wonders, that is, all your hidden judgments, which are worthy of wonder because of their dignity and justice. They are yours, that is, they are not rash or unjust, as some think, but such as befit you—namely, just. Or “yours,” that is, given to you by God the Father, according to the saying: “The Father has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22).

Then follows: “I will rejoice,” which is connected as follows: I say that I will confess, and this not unwillingly, but in this I will rejoice; and not moderately, but I will exult, that is, I will rejoice exceedingly. For one is said to exult when one has such great joy that it is also shown by bodily leaping.

I say, “I will rejoice and exult,” and this in you, not in earthly things. And I will not only confess with my intention and proclaim to others with my mouth, but I will sing psalms, that is, I will work well, to your name, that is, for the honor of your name, so that you may be praised through it, not so that I may become proud.

O Most High, it is fitting that I sing psalms to your name, since you are the Most High. Or “most high” is used adverbially, that is, with a most high and upright intention. This is as if he said: I will praise you with affection, mouth, and work, for your hidden judgments.

And he explains those judgments in this way: I will confess, I will proclaim, I will sing psalms.

“In the turning back of my enemy,” that is, in contemplating the conversion of my enemy: in this, namely, that I contemplate my enemy being turned back, that is, being overcome by my steadfastness, so that he will not be able to recall me from my good purpose.

And he says “turned back” by comparison. For it is characteristic of the conquered and fleeing to be turned backward. And he shows how they will be turned back: they will become weak, that is, they will be found weak and powerless to overcome me. And in the future they will perish from your face, that is, by withdrawing from your presence, as is read in the Gospel: “These will go into eternal punishment” (Matthew XXV, 26).

Or “they will become weak,” that is, those who appear strong and firm here will appear weak in the future, when it is said: “Depart from me,” and so forth (ibid.).

Or as follows: I will confess, I will proclaim, I will sing psalms, in the turning back of my enemy, that is, in contemplating that I will turn back my enemy through preaching and example. My enemy means certain people among my enemies; “back” means that I will cause them to turn from evil to good.

And he explains how: they will become weak, that is, those who are strong and firm in their unbelief will gradually become weak in it. And thus they will perish, that is, they will be utterly destroyed insofar as they are unbelievers. And this will happen from your face, that is, from your knowledge.

He says “enemy” in the singular and “they will perish” in the plural because they are both one mass and many individuals. He says “enemy” also of heretics and foreign enemies.

And therefore I will still confess, proclaim, and sing psalms, because you have made my judgment, that is, something useful to me, and my cause, that is, something useful to me.

Or as follows: “Because you have made my judgment and my cause,” that is, you have made or ordained the fact that I have been judged and brought to trial. It did not happen rashly, as some think. He calls it “judgment” because, through God’s hidden judgment, she has been afflicted with tribulations. He calls it “cause” because, when she disputed with heretics or unbelievers about God, she overcame them. All these things turned to her own advantage, as the Apostle says: “We know that for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans VIII, 28).

And you made this judgment and cause because you sat upon the throne, judging justice, that is, what is just. You do not merely begin to sit, but you have always sat and will sit, because you are the judge of all and not unjust, but judging justly.

And when he ought to have said that you are a judge, he gives a description in place of the thing described, namely, sitting upon the throne. For it is characteristic of judges to sit upon a throne. A throne is called a judicial seat.

Since he had earlier said, “I will confess in the turning back of my enemy,” someone might ask why he would confess for the conversion of his enemy. Therefore he adds the reason as follows:

I will rightly confess for the conversion of my enemies. For I cannot convert them by myself; but you rebuked them with an inward rebuke—that is, you will rebuke the nations through fear of judgment—namely, enemies living like the nations; and the impious man perished, that is, will perish, from his impiety, that is, he will cease to be impious.

And because he will perish, you erased—that is, will erase—their name, namely, their name “impious.” You will never again regard them as impious, nor punish them any further for it, as Scripture testifies: “If the impious man turns away from his impiety, I will remember none of his iniquities” (Ezekiel XVIII, 22).

I say that you will erase it, and this forever, that is, you will never, for as long as this age endures, regard them as impious. And not only forever, but unto the age of the age that follows it: in this age and in the future you will erase it.

He uses “forever” not for all time, as it is often used, but for the whole span of this age, as elsewhere: “The Lord will reign forever and beyond” (Exodus XV, 18).

I say that the impious man will perish, and thus the swords of the enemy failed—that is, will cease—utterly, to the end of cessation, as far as cessation can go: the tribulations and torments which they used to inflict upon me.

By “swords” the tribulations of martyrdom are signified, because many are afflicted by swords. And you destroyed—that is, will destroy—the cities, that is, their conspiracies, so that they will no longer conspire against me.

We customarily call a gathering of men a “city,” when they are joined together under one law in conspiracy. Therefore the multitudes of those conspiring together against the Church are called cities.

But when he says, “Their memory has perished,” and so forth, he turns to the hearers, because someone might ask whether the impious man would perish, as he had said. The passage is therefore connected as follows:

I said that you would rebuke the nations and the impious man would perish; and I speak truly. For truly the memory of those enemies has perished with sound, that is, the memory of their name will perish: they will never again be called impious.

And it will perish with sound, that is, with great rumor, because it will be widely proclaimed; it will not be hidden. And afterward the Lord remains forever, that is, always, in them, as he himself says: “We will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23).

And he himself, who will remain in them, will judge, that is, will reward in the future, with equity the world of the earth, that is, those who will be from the earth, who were formerly the earth of his world, that is, his crown surrounding him.

He uses “world” for “crown” because it is round. And he will judge the peoples, that is, he will reward the unbelievers in justice, that is, he will justly condemn them, even if this may seem unjust because they are impious.

I say that he will judge the world of the earth and the peoples, and rightly so. For he himself prepared his throne, that is, his judgment-seat, when he was established in the judgment of death for obedience to the Father—that is, by the judgment of death which he voluntarily endured—and thereby acquired for himself the judgment of the whole world, as the Apostle testifies: “Christ became obedient to the Father unto death; therefore God also exalted him” (Philippians II, 8).

He calls the wicked “peoples” because they will be many in comparison with the good, according to the saying: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew XX, 22).

I say that he will judge in the future. And meanwhile he has become—that is, will become—a refuge, that is, security, for the poor, that is, for one who will humble himself before him with such great submissiveness as a poor man shows toward a rich man in order to acquire something.

Or “for the poor,” that is, for one who in this world has chosen to be poor for his sake. And he is not only a refuge, making them steadfast and fearless—for many heretics are found to be fearlessly useless in tribulations—but also a helper in tribulation, acting through his hidden judgment so that the tribulation itself may aid them in increasing their merit, as it is written: “Let them become more radiant through the exercises of labors.”

I say “in tribulation,” ordained by God at suitable times, that is, according to what is suitable, so that they may be able to endure and not fail if it should exceed the proper measure, according to what is said elsewhere: “He will give us drink in tears by measure” (Psalm LXXIX, 6).

But when he says, “And let them hope,” and so forth, he turns to God, praying for the lesser members, as follows:

I say, O God, that you will judge the world and the peoples, and that you have become a refuge; and so that they may be judged in the future, let them hope for mercy in you, not in earthly things. And let all who know your name not fail, namely, those who know that you are Lord of all and powerful to save the just and destroy the impious.

Or “your name,” that is, that you are eternal, so that through you they may become eternal. And he repeats in other words the reason for which he prays that they should hope. Therefore let them hope, because you have not abandoned—and will not abandon—those who seek you, not worldly things, [text uncertain: “in adjutos Deus”].

As if he said: For you are Lord of all and can do nothing unjust. And this is the same thing which he said above: You have become a refuge for the poor, a helper in tribulation.

After the prayer, he turns to the lesser members, urging them to do what she herself does in praise. Since he will judge and is a refuge and helper, you lesser members, sing psalms to the Lord, that is, work well for his honor. And he indicates the benefit of this as follows:

“He who dwells in Zion,” which is as if he said: He who dwells in all who are Zion, and will dwell in you if you are Zion—that is, watchers of the heavenly homeland. And not only should you sing psalms, but also, while living and walking among the nations, proclaim to them his purposes, that is, the affections of his charity: with what great affection he redeemed us, and with what great affection he will reward the good in the future.

And he rightly says “purposes.” For he did not redeem us, nor will he reward us, rashly, but with great care and most powerful reasoning.

And you will sing psalms and proclaim for your own good, because he remembered—that is, will remember in the future in order to reward—the cry of the poor. And if he now seems to have forgotten it, he will remember the poor’s fervent prayer, made for his sake, which proceeds from right affection and action.

And because he had said “he remembered,” someone who does not pay careful attention might think that he had forgotten them. Therefore a correction follows:

I say “he remembered,” yet he was never forgetful of the cry of the poor. I said this only because it seems so to some. And that he will remember them by rewarding them he shows by contrast when he adds: “Seeking their blood,” that is, seeking their death from the hand of the impious in order to punish the impious, as it is said elsewhere: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 35).

This is as if he said: Since he will condemn the impious because of their persecution of the just, he will certainly reward the poor who suffer for his sake.

And he adds the cry of the poor itself, saying:

“Have mercy on me, O Lord,” that is, repay me mercifully, since you are Lord over all things and can do all things. And so that the cause for repayment may not be lacking: See, so that I may please you, my humility, that is, my abasement, inflicted by my enemies—namely, the tribulation which I suffer for you.

I say, “Have mercy,” you who so greatly exalt me in the dignity of life, me who have been brought out from the gates of death, that is, from vices, which are the gates through which one enters into death. And you exalt me for this purpose, so that I may proclaim to others all your praises, that is, your hidden judgments, on account of which you ought to be praised.

I say that I exist in the gates of the daughter of Zion. This is said intransitively: “of the daughter of Zion.”

This means: I exist in virtues, or in the sayings of the apostles, which are the gates through which the Church—which is the daughter of God and of the apostles—enters into life. And lest she be understood to be the daughter of Babylon, he specifies her by adding “Zion,” which means: she who contemplates the future.

And all this is as if he said: I know that you will have mercy on me, since you are already making me exalted. I say, “Have mercy on me,” and thus I will exult in your salvation, that is, in the salvation given to me by you, namely, in the fact that you restore me to immortality.

Having shown the cry of the poor, he returns to the subject with which he had begun, saying as follows:

“They are fixed in destruction,” and so forth. The passage is connected as follows: Earlier I said, O lesser members, “Sing psalms to the Lord who dwells in Zion,” because he has remembered and has not forgotten the cry of the poor. And do not sing psalms with this consideration alone, but also praise him with intention, words, and action, because the nations, that is, those living like the nations, are fixed in the destruction which they made.

That is, they are fixed inwardly in their soul; they are firmly situated in destruction, that is, in the blinding of the mind, which they made for themselves, not God. Their destruction came upon them because of their own evil merits, not through any fault of God.

As if he said: Praise him not only for the rewarding of the just, but also for the blinding of the wicked; and although this was done by a hidden judgment, it is nevertheless unquestionably just.

And he explains how they are fixed in destruction as follows: Rightly in destruction. For their foot has been caught in the snare which they hid, that is, which they secretly prepared for others.

When he says “their foot has been caught,” he speaks by comparison with a man who secretly places a snare in order to catch someone. He himself, however, is caught in it.

As if he said: They rightly perished, because they unjustly prepared the snare of deception for others, and this snare became the cause by which they reached destruction, that is, the blinding of the heart.

And they themselves do not now recognize that God judges them in this way; but at last, in the future, they will recognize it when he justly destroys them. “The Lord will be known as he executes judgments,” that is, it will be known that the Lord makes a hidden judgment upon the impious in this world.

And he explains that judgment as follows: In this, namely, he executes judgment: the sinner has been caught, that is, deceived and blinded, in the works of his hands, that is, through his wicked actions, because here he acts in every way to draw the just away from the way of God.

He calls actions “the works of the hands” because we work with our hands.

But what follows—“Let them be turned,” and so forth—is not an imprecation, but a concession of divine judgment concerning what the agility of the Spirit sees will happen, so that he recognizes it as just. The passage is therefore connected as follows:

I say that the nations are fixed here in destruction; but in the future sinners will be turned into hell, that is, from this judgment of blinding they will come into the judgment of condemnation in hell.

And since it will happen that sinners will be turned into hell, he explains whom he calls sinners: all the nations, namely, those who forget God—that is, those who, when they hear his preaching, consign it to oblivion and do not care to obey.

And he proves that they will be turned by contrast when he says: From this I know that they will be turned, because there will be no forgetfulness of the poor who strive toward the end, that is, toward perseverance in good works. The patience of the poor will not perish, that is, the reward of the patience of the poor who strive toward the end.

This means: From this I know that he will condemn sinners, because he will reward the poor, that is, the just.

Or as follows: There will be no forgetfulness of the poor at the end of the world, even if now their forgetfulness seems to exist. Or: If no poverty of forgetfulness is found from beginning to end, no forgetfulness of the poor will be found.

But when he says, “Arise, O Lord; let man not grow strong,” he foresees in prophetic spirit the tribulation that will occur in the time of Antichrist, a tribulation such as has never before existed, and he prays for those who will persevere in that tribulation, so that they may not fail. This is connected not with the preceding wording but with its meaning, as follows:

Earlier I said that the impious persecute the just here, both by the snares of flatteries and by the humiliation of tribulations. And this will not occur only in the present time; but someone will also arise in the last days—namely, Antichrist, who will make himself God, although he will simply be a human being filled with the devil, and who will inflict many tribulations upon your people.

And, O Lord, arise to help your people, so that that man may not grow strong against them. That is, so that Antichrist, who will simply be a man and not God, may not be found strong enough to overcome your people.

And although I say, “Let him not grow strong against your people,” I nevertheless concede that the nations, that is, those living like the nations, will be judged in your sight, that is, will be blinded by his deception. And although this does not appear to them, it will be certain in your sight.

Or “will be judged,” that is, will be blinded in your sight, that is, in the soul which you alone see. As if he said: Although I pray that he may not grow strong against the just, I nevertheless concede that those who are to be blinded by him will be blinded by your just judgment.

And he explains how he concedes that they will be judged: I concede that they will be judged; that is, establish, O Lord, who are powerful, a lawgiver over them. Because they did not wish to obey your law of truth, on account of their evil merits establish over them—or permit to rule over them—Antichrist, who will be for them the bearer of a law of falsehood and will blind them.

And finally, on the day of judgment, let the nations, that is, his obedient followers living like the nations, know that they are human beings: let them recognize, when they are justly condemned, that they are merely human beings, not deified by Antichrist, as they themselves believed.

But when he adds, “Why, O Lord,” and so forth, he raises a question which someone might ask and then resolves it himself. The passage is therefore connected as follows:

I prayed that he might not grow strong, even though I know that he will persecute them greatly. And when you permit him to persecute them, O Lord, why have you withdrawn? That is, why will you seem to withdraw far from your people?

And he explains how: Why will you despise them, that is, why will you seem to despise your people when they are unheard amid the tribulation inflicted by Antichrist? At the proper times—that is, in what tribulation will it be appropriate for you to help them?

After the question, the answer follows:

He will seem to despise them in order to permit Antichrist to grow proud against them. For while the impious man grows proud—that is, will grow proud, namely, Antichrist, the impious man antonomastically—the poor man is burned, that is, purified from the remaining filth by the fires of tribulations, just as gold is purified by burning. The poor man is one who is poor for God’s sake, that is, the faithful.

This means: You will permit him to grow proud so that your people may be tested through his tribulation. And there is another reason as well: while he grows proud, his accomplices, who grow proud with him, are caught—that is, will be caught, or deceived—as birds are caught in a snare, in the schemes by which they plan to catch your people.

As if he said: Not only will he be condemned, but also his supporters, because they will plot to kill others in soul and body; for such schemes they will be killed, that is, they will be more deeply blinded.
