And he adds the reason why he himself will grow proud, as follows: I say that the impious man will grow proud, and this because the sinner himself, antonomastically, is praised—that is, will be praised—by his accomplices when the desires of his soul are fulfilled. That is why he will grow proud: they will praise him for the fulfillment of his desires in the tribulation of the faithful, as it is said elsewhere: “The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins.”

And he will not only be praised, but he himself, the wicked man antonomastically, is blessed—that is, will be blessed, or worshiped, by them.

And because the sinner will act proudly (by antonomasia), the sinner has provoked—and will provoke—the Lord [Col. 0673C], that is, by calling himself God he will blaspheme God, and thus from what was sweet he will make something bitter for himself. Therefore the Lord will not seek him, that is, he will not cause him to be converted, according to the multitude of his anger, that is, of his vengeance. It is as though he said: Because he has deserved His great anger, God will not seek him. In saying “will seek,” he speaks by comparison with a shepherd who seeks a straying sheep until he brings it back to the fold. And he will still not seek him because God is not before his eyes, that is, in the consideration of his mind: he does not regard Him as merciful, so that he might repent. And again he will not seek him because his ways, that is, his deeds, are polluted unto death, that is, they will be defiled by vices; and this throughout the whole time of his life.

[Col. 0673D] And again, Lord, you will not seek him because your judgments are removed—and will be removed—from his face, that is, from his knowledge. His vanity will blind him so completely that he will not know that, in the future just judgment, you will reward the wicked. And because your judgments are removed from his face, and he will not think himself destined for condemnation, he will rule over all his enemies, that is, those who refused to obey him—not in their souls, but by tormenting their bodies. And truly he will rule. For he said in his heart, that is, he will think in his heart: “I must rule. For without evil, that is, without the tribulation of the righteous, I shall not be moved from this generation, which already worships me, to that generation which does not yet worship me.”

[Col. 0674A] This means: Unless I afflict those who resist me, my dominion will not extend from those who know me to those who do not know me. Or alternatively, he said in his heart: “I can rule securely. For I shall never be removed from my dominion, that is, I shall not be disturbed by anyone; rather, I shall be without evil, extending from this generation into the future generation, that is, forever.” This the one whose mouth is full—and will be full—of cursing will say in his heart: of bitterness, that is, of blasphemy against God, since he calls himself God alone; and of deceit toward the saints, that is, of flatteries by which he will desire to seduce them.

[Col. 0674B] And beneath his tongue, that is, in his heart, there is—and will be—labor and sorrow, that is, the thought of how he may make them labor and suffer. “Beneath the tongue” signifies the thought of the heart by comparison, just as the things that are in a chest are said to be beneath its key. For the tongue is the key of the heart’s secrets. The whole passage is as though he said: He will speak very presumptuously in his heart, “I shall not be moved,” although his mouth will be full of bitterness and deceit; and therefore he will be worthy of punishment.

I say that his mouth will be full of deceit, and this will not be merely momentary. Nor will he merely be full of deceit: he himself sits—and will sit—rather than stand, that is, he will remain for a long time in ambushes of flattery, with the rich in secret places, that is, with his supporters, who, like him, will be rich—abounding greatly in vices that are hidden from everyone. And he sits—and will sit—for this purpose: to kill the innocent.

Thus, certainly, his eyes look—and will look—upon the poor, that is, he will pretend to pity him, promising him many things in order to seduce him. In saying, “His eyes look upon the poor,” he speaks by comparison. [Col. 0674C] For the person whom someone pities he looks upon kindly with his eyes. I say that his eyes will look upon him. And so he lies in wait—and will lie in wait—in secret, that is, by concealing his treachery and pretending to be merciful.

Like a lion hidden in its den, he will lie in wait, I say, in order to seize the poor man and make him like himself. And because “to seize” is usually said only when something is taken by force or through ambush, he adds: “To seize the poor man,” I say, while he draws him by flatteries. This means: I rightly say “to seize,” since he directs his flatteries toward the same end toward which he would direct force: incorporating that holy man into himself.

And if he cannot draw him by flatteries, he will humble him, that is, cast him down and afflict him, in his snare, that is, in the tribulation which will be a snare to him—an entanglement of blindness. [Col. 0674D] For this reason he will be permitted to be blinded still more by the Lord. I say: “He will humble him.”

And when he has gained dominion by afflicting the poor man, he will bend him down, that is, cast him into eternal death. Since he had spoken obscurely in saying “He will bend,” he explains it in this way: “He will bend him down. And afterward, through this, he himself will fall into death.”

He then adds two reasons why he will rule in this way. Truly he will have gained dominion. For he said, that is, he will think in his heart: “I am able to rule securely. For God has forgotten them; He will never help them.” And again, because He has turned—and will turn—His face, that is, His thought, away, to the full extent of turning away, so that He may not see the persecution which I inflict upon them and avenge it. It is as though he said: “I can rule securely because God will not help them, and therefore He will not punish me.”

[Col. 0675A] But when he says, “Arise, Lord God,” and so forth, he assigns each statement to its corresponding statement, as follows. Antichrist will say, “God has forgotten and has turned away His face.” But you, Lord, who are powerful—and you, God, who are just—arise, that is, show yourself powerful, though you may seem powerless.

He explains for what purpose He should arise: namely, against what Antichrist will say, “He has turned away His face.” Arise, then, so that your hand may be exalted over him, that is, so that your vengeance, namely his condemnation, may appear great. In saying “may it be exalted,” he speaks by comparison with one who raises his hand in order to strike someone forcefully. It is as though he said: “Condemn him utterly.” This is not a curse, but a concession.

And against what he will say, “God has forgotten,” arise to help, so that you may not forget the poor, that is, your faithful. And if you may appear to have forgotten them while they are being tormented, nevertheless do not forget them forever. It is as though he said: “Rescue them at last.”

[Col. 0675B] When he says, “Why?” and so forth, he rebukes Antichrist, because he will claim that God will not reward him; yet God would be unjust if He did not reward him. He speaks as follows. He will say: “God has turned His face away,” that is, “He will not avenge.” “For what reason has the wicked man provoked—and will provoke—God?” By antonomasia, the wicked man will provoke Him by blaspheming, calling Him unjust and saying that He will not reward him.

And truly he will provoke Him. For he said, that is, he will say in his heart: “God will not require vengeance from me; I can rule securely.” This is as though he said: “For what reason will that wicked man provoke God by his blasphemies, saying in his heart, ‘He will not require it’?” He will have no reason at all.

[Col. 0675C] From this point he turns in an apostrophe to God, announcing the condemnation of Antichrist and his followers, so as to deter his hearers from resembling them. He speaks as follows: “O God, he himself and those who belong to him will say, ‘God will not require it’; but you already see, in your providence, that in the future you will deliver them into your hands, that is, into your vengeance—namely, into eternal death.”

And truly I know that you see, because you who behold all things consider the labor and sorrow which they will inflict upon your faithful. This means: Since you are a just judge, and see the labor and sorrow which they unjustly impose upon your own, you cannot fail to avenge them.

And he will say, “God has forgotten”; but, in opposition to this, you will be a helper, that is, a rewarder, of the orphan, that is, of the faithful one who continually suffers for you, whose father—the devil, so far as the faithful is concerned—will be dead, and whose mother will have been unbelief. And rightly will you be his helper. For the poor man has been—and will be—left to you, that is, entrusted to you by God the Father.

[Col. 0675D] Here “orphan” and “poor” are taken as referring to the same person. Or: the poor man has been left to you, that is, the poor man himself will leave himself to you, that is, entrust himself to your help, placing no confidence in himself.

What he says here—“Crush,” and so forth—is a concession made through prophetic foresight. I said that you see, so that in the future you may deliver them into your hands. And not only condemn them in the future: but here and now crush, that is, utterly destroy, the arm of the sinner and the wicked man, that is, his power, which extends itself and is strong like an arm.

I speak of his arm: he will be a sinner with respect to those whom he will mistreat wickedly; and he will be wicked, that is, barren, with respect to himself, since he will possess no virtue. [Col. 0676A] And it will be necessary for you to crush him quickly. For his sin will be sought by many and will not be found, that is, he will deceive very greatly because he will appear good. Many will seek to discover whether they might perhaps find sin in him; and when they cannot find it, they will yield to him. Therefore it is necessary that you crush him quickly, lest he deceive everyone.

But when he says, “The Lord will reign,” and so forth, this is an apostrophe to the faithful, so that they may not fear. For after the death of their bodies the Lord will reign in them forever. The passage is connected as follows: “I said, ‘Crush him,’ and truly he will be crushed. But the Lord will reign in you, O faithful,” that is, He will make you His kingdom. And although “forever” is usually used for the period extending to the end of the world, he determines it as follows:

[Col. 0676B] “I say, forever—and unto the age of the age,” the latter expression following the former, that is, always.

Afterward he turns in an apostrophe to the wicked, so that by frightening them he may draw them away from their wickedness. He speaks as follows: “The Lord will reign among the good; but you, nations,” that is, wicked men living in a pagan manner, “will perish from His land,” that is, you will be separated from fellowship with that land—namely, from fellowship with the saints, whom He Himself cultivates as someone cultivates his own land. In accordance with the Gospel: “He will separate the sheep from the goats” (Matthew 25:32).

I say that you nations will perish. And this is evident from the opposite. For the Lord has heard the desire of His poor, that is, He will hear it; He will show that He has heard it when He rewards them. He explains which desire this is, making an apostrophe out of great affection: “the preparation of their heart,” that is, the desire which they will not have from themselves, but which you will prepare in their hearts.

[Col. 0676C] “Your ear has heard”—that is, it will hear—where “ear” means the power of your mercy, which is rightly called an ear. For just as someone hears through the ear, so God hears through the power of His mercy. This is as though he said: “From this you can see that you nations will perish, because the righteous will be saved.”

Or the passage may be connected otherwise. He said that the Lord will reign in His own, and this is true because the Lord has heard—and will hear—the desire of the poor, who with great longing seek His kingdom. They will not have this desire from themselves, but He has heard—and will hear—the preparation of their heart, that is, your ear will hear the desire which you have prepared in them. In this he commends His mercy: He not only hears those who desire good things, but also causes them to desire good things.

He explains that desire as follows. I say that He will hear the desire of the poor—namely, the desire that He judge for the orphan and the humble. And he rightly says not “the orphan and the humble man,” but “for the orphan and the humble man,” that is, they desire you to make such a judgment as will benefit the orphan and the humble man, that is, the faithful one, who is an orphan because his father, the devil, is dead, and who is humble toward you.

[Col. 0676D] He explains the judgment they desire: namely, that the man of perdition, who will not be God—that is, Antichrist—may not continue to magnify himself by tormenting upon the earth of God, that is, upon the bodies of the saints, which are God’s earth. He rightly says “continue,” that is, that the one who here on earth—not over souls but over the bodies of the saints—has been magnificent in torments may not add another magnificence to this magnificence, so as to rule over them again.

[Col. 0677A]

## ON PSALM X

The title of the tenth psalm follows: “For the end. A psalm of David.” This title does not specifically indicate the intention of the psalm, for it can apply to all the psalms. It is explained as follows: This psalm is to be attributed to David, that is, to the perfect Church, tending toward the end, that is, toward perseverance in good works. Or, “toward the end,” that is, toward Christ.

It is the voice of the perfect Church speaking reproachfully to the heretics who wish to deceive it. It shows how, in order to deceive the good, they pervert Sacred Scripture, so that those who are less mature may learn to avoid them. It also shows, for the exhortation of the good, that they are not left without God’s help, while their plotters are blinded by God’s just and hidden judgment. It speaks as follows.

[Col. 0677B] “In the Lord I trust. How then do you say to my soul: ‘Migrate to the mountain like a sparrow’?”

This is explained as follows. You heretics, who wish to harm my soul, that is, my soul’s salvation, how—that is, for what reason—do you say to me: “Migrate,” that is, “Migrate from the humility of your own judgment to the mountain,” that is, to the lofty subtlety of our judgment?

You, I say, who are now like a sparrow, that is, unstable and trembling before our arguments, just as a sparrow trembles at a sound. Or: “like a sparrow,” that is, “Migrate so that you may be like a sparrow which dwells in high places.”

How, then, do you tell me to migrate to the mountain, when I trust in the Lord, who is a firm mountain and will not permit me to be deceived by you? This means: “You say this pointlessly and without reason.”

And because one might ask why he says this, he explains it as follows: “Behold, I shall explain why I said this.”

[Col. 0677C] Because sinners—by antonomasia, the heretics—have aimed, that is, have drawn tight and carefully, subtly expounded the bow, that is, Sacred Scripture. Not everywhere, but in some places: it is God’s bow, as was said in the seventh psalm.

And they have prepared their arrows, that is, perverse interpretations which kill like arrows, which are theirs, that is, invented by them and not given by the Holy Spirit—I say, they have prepared them in a quiver, that is, in their evil conception, which contains interpretations just as a quiver contains arrows.

It is as though he said: They have drawn the bow, that is, they have interpreted certain passages carefully, in order secretly to mingle their own interpretations with them.

[Col. 0677D] Or: “They have drawn the bow,” that is, according to their ability they have distorted and expounded it; and thus they have prepared, that is, brought forth, their arrows fitted in the quiver, that is, in their evil conception.

And they prepared them for this purpose: so that in secret, that is, with hidden cunning—pretending that the interpretations are good—they might shoot, that is, kill in faith, those who are upright in heart.

And the fact that, by drawing the bow, they prepare arrows is not the fault of the bow itself, but of those men. For “the things which you perfected,” namely, the divine Scriptures which you made perfect, they have destroyed with respect to themselves, not with respect to the Scriptures themselves; that is, by interpreting them wrongly they have perverted them.

But what did the Lord, who is just, do? That is, since it is just that He help His own, and since He Himself is just, what did He do for His own? Did He leave them without help? He raises this question benevolently, in order to answer it afterward.

[Col. 0678A] I ask what He did, and the answer is as follows. He was—and is—in His holy temple, that is, in the faithful who are His temple, as the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3).

And just as the Lord, that is, He is in them in such a way as to rule them and govern them lest they be deceived. I say: He is in the temple. And this is not temporary: His seat, that is, His enduring and eternal dwelling, is in heaven, that is, in those faithful themselves, who are called not only a temple but also heaven—namely, in those who are lofty in virtues and who, by their teaching, rain upon the less mature, just as heaven rains upon the earth.

[Col. 0678B] He says the same thing again in other words, inserting a reason. I say: He is in heaven, and His eyes, that is, His mercy through which He sees him, look upon the poor. This means: Because the poor man is heaven for His sake, and is disposed toward Him as a poor man is toward a rich man, He looks upon him with the eyes of mercy, that is, He mercifully helps him.

Since he had said above, “They have destroyed the things which you perfected,” one might ask why God wished the Scriptures to be so obscure that they could be perverted. He answers this objection as follows.

I say: “They have destroyed them,” and He therefore wished them to be obscure in such a way that they could be perverted, because His eyelids, that is, the Scriptures called “eyelids,” since they close and open in the manner of eyelids—at one time closing in order to blind the wicked, at another opening in order to enlighten the good—test, that is, prove, the sons of men.

He uses “to question” for “to prove” by a certain affinity, since a proof is accustomed to follow an inquiry.

[Col. 0678C] And because he had said, “They test the sons of men,” he sets this out in parts as follows: Truly, through the eyelids, the Lord tests the sons of men. For the Lord tests the just and the wicked through the eyelids, that is, He makes them manifest to others: He blinds the one in such a way that he wishes to draw others into error, and enlightens the other in such a way that he strives to enlighten others.

I say that He tests the just and the wicked. But the one who loves iniquity, that is, the wicked man, hates his own soul, that is, the salvation of his soul—namely, sound interpretations.

[Col. 0678D] Therefore, because he has hated his own soul, that is, sound interpretations, God rightly rains snares upon sinners—by antonomasia, upon the heretics. That is, He rightly gives them such rains, namely, Scriptures that are snares to them, deceiving and blinding them.

The Scriptures are called “rains” by comparison: just as rains, when they fall upon good soil, produce excellent fruit, but when they fall upon bad soil, produce thistles and thorns, so the Scriptures produce in the good the light of virtues, but in the wicked blindness.

And He will not merely rain snares, but “fire and brimstone and the spirit of storms are the portion of their cup,” that is, of their intoxication. He will intoxicate and fill them with fire, that is, with an excessive ardor for perverting the Scriptures; with brimstone, that is, with the stench of their corruption of the Scriptures; and with the spirit of storms, that is, with excessive talkativeness, which generates storms, that is, disturbances in the Church, just as a spirit, that is, wind, generates storms at sea.

[Col. 0679A] Or “fire” may signify the ardor of avarice; “brimstone” the stench of an evil action by which one’s neighbor is corrupted; and “the spirit of storms” that eternal damnation which will come through the administration of evil spirits, who are ministers of storms, that is, of tribulations.

It is as though he said: He not only rains snares upon them in accordance with their evil merits, but here also fills them with fire and brimstone; in the future He will intoxicate them with the spirit of storms.

[Col. 0679B] The passage continues: “For the Lord is just,” and so forth. It is connected as follows: I said that the Lord is in the temple and that His seat is in heaven, and that His eyes look upon the poor. And rightly so. For the Lord is just, and therefore He has loved righteousnesses, that is, since He is a just judge, He cannot fail to love righteousnesses, that is, the assistance He gives His own.

And he rightly says “He has loved.” For with the greatest love He has helped His own and will always help them.

Therefore, as I said, He rains snares upon sinners. And rightly so, because He is just. And therefore His face, that is, the appearance of His vengeance, has seen equity, that is, the equitable blinding of the wicked. It is as though he said: He cannot fail to rain snares; this is equitable, since He is just.

[Col. 0679C]

## ON PSALM XI

The title of the eleventh psalm: “For the end. For the eighth. A psalm of David.” This is explained as follows: This psalm is to be attributed to David, that is, to the assembly of the faithful which existed before Christ’s coming. David, I say, tending toward the end, that is, toward conformity with the End, namely Christ, who was the end of prophecy and of the law. Or, “toward the end,” that is, toward perseverance.

David is said to act “for the eighth,” that is, for the desire for eternal rest, which is to come on the eighth day.

Here the prophet introduces the assembly of the faithful who existed before Christ’s coming, praying God to send the one whom He is going to send, through whom the human race—having lost eternal rest through Adam’s sin and fall—will be saved.

He also prays that it may not conform itself to the example of the wicked, who pursue vanities. He further shows with what confidence he prays: namely, because God the Father has already promised them His Son through the Holy Spirit. The prophet introduces their words for this reason: to instruct us to have great love toward Him, since he presents to us their immense affection for Him. He speaks as follows.

[Col. 0679D] “Save me, Lord,” that is, Lord who are powerful, save me—not resisting your command like Adam, but obeying it. Save me, that is, by sending the one whom you are going to send; save me by restoring me to the eighth day which I lost.

And it is necessary that I pray for this because the holy one, that is, Adam, whom you made holy, in your image and likeness, fell from your command and therefore ruined both himself and all of us.

And again I pray so earnestly because truths have been diminished by the sons of men, that is, by the Jews, who were sons of the prophets and of other faithful men, who were “men,” that is, rational beings. They have been diminished in their desires for eternal goods, which are true and certain.

[Col. 0680A] This means: Those who, following the example of their fathers, ought to seek eternal goods desire them less and less from day to day, and by their example they wish to draw me back. Therefore it is necessary that I pray in this way.

“Truths have been diminished by the sons of men.” And it is not enough for them to diminish the truths within themselves and to be vain; they have also spoken vanity, each one to his neighbor, that is, they have spoken vain things to their neighbors in order to make them like themselves. Specifically, they have said that earthly things are the highest goods, although they are vain.

Since he had spoken generally by saying “each one,” he demonstrates this in parts as follows. I say that each one has spoken vanity, and this is true. For some, having deceitful lips, have spoken with a heart and a heart, that is, with a double heart.

[Col. 0680B] Not because they have two hearts, but because they have one thing in their heart while they truly understand that present things are not the highest goods, and another thing they falsely claim with their mouth to have in their heart—namely, that these are the highest goods. For this reason they are said to have a double heart and to be deceitful, since they think one thing and pretend another.

When he says “deceitful lips,” he speaks emphatically.

He hints at another group of those who cling to the vain goods of this world—those, namely, who prove by false arguments that these things are true goods, and who believe what they prove. He indicates this when he subsequently says: “Those who said, ‘We will magnify our tongue.’”

[Col. 0680C] But he first inserts the prayer in this way: I say that deceitful lips have spoken vanity. And so that they may not speak vanity any longer, may the Lord destroy all deceitful lips, and also the tongue that speaks great things.

It was not that He should destroy those who have deceitful lips and a tongue that speaks great things, but rather their deceitfulness and their grandiloquence, so that they might not harm themselves or others.

He explains whom he means by those who have a tongue that speaks great things as follows: “A tongue that speaks great things,” I say, belonging to those who said, that is, determined among themselves: “We will magnify,” that is, we will make our tongue great and glorious—our eloquence, that is.

And we can rightly do this. For “our lips are our own,” that is, our eloquence comes from our own side; it belongs to us as it does to them. It is not small or insignificant, but broad and distinguished. Therefore we can greatly magnify and exalt it.

[Col. 0680D] And since our lips are our own, “Who is our lord?” That is, who will rule over and prevail against our eloquence? No one.

He calls those men “grandiloquent” who, believing only in present things and not also in future things, strive by every means to appear blessed and eloquent here.

And because he had earlier prayed, “Save me,” one might ask with what confidence he prays for what he rightly lost through Adam. He answers as follows:

I prayed, “Save me,” and I said this with good confidence. For the Lord the Father said to me inwardly through the Holy Spirit: “Now,” that is, in the present, after a short time, “I shall arise to help.”

And I shall do this because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, that is, because of the misery of suffering and corruptibility into which my faithful have fallen through Adam.

[Col. 0681A] They are needy, that is, without help; they can be delivered by no one’s help except mine. And they are poor, that is, humble toward me, as a poor man is humble toward a rich man.

Therefore I shall arise, because they do not excuse themselves concerning their misery, as Adam did, but humbly groan because of it.

He explains how He will arise. I say: “I shall arise,” and I shall place that arising, that is, that help, in the Savior, that is, in Christ my Son, who will be the Savior, that is, the salvation of the poor, as Isaiah says: “He himself will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21).

I say: “I shall place it in the Savior.” And when I have placed it there, I shall act confidently in him, that is, through him I shall securely accomplish my will. For he will not fall as Adam fell.

[Col. 0681B] And not in him alone, but also in his preachers I shall act confidently. For the Lord’s utterances, that is, those preaching the utterances of my Son, whom I shall establish as Lord over created things, are pure utterances, that is, corrupted by no falsehood, by comparison with a virgin who is called pure because she has not yet been corrupted by a man’s stain.

And they are silver, that is, shining in their preaching as polished silver shines. Or “silver,” that is, sounding clearly in their teaching, just as silver rings more clearly than all other metals.

Silver, I say, tested by fire, that is, proved by the Holy Spirit, who is rightly called fire because, by inflaming the breasts of the faithful, He makes them ardent with faith and charity, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12:49).

[Col. 0681C] He explains from what it has been tested as follows: I say, “tested by fire,” namely, proved and purified from earth, that is, from every earthly impurity.

And he explains how it has been proved through fire: namely, purified sevenfold, that is, through the seven gifts of that fire. At this point is inserted what the Lord says especially to that assembly; then, in an excess of joy, it makes an apostrophe to Him as follows:

“Since you have promised this, I am truly secure, because you, Lord, will preserve us,” and so forth. This will be explained in what follows.

[Col. 0681D] Where it says, “The utterances of the Lord,” and so forth, these may be the words of the assembly of the faithful which spoke above. If so, the Lord says: “I shall place it in the Savior,” and so forth. And these utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, that is, corrupted by no falsehood.

And to commend them still further, he praises them by another comparison: “They are silver tried by fire,” and so forth, that is, like silver tested by fire, proved and purified from earth, that is, from every earthly impurity, in a furnace, sevenfold, that is, repeatedly.

This means: Just as such silver is bright and free from every impurity, so His utterances are bright and free from every stain of falsehood.

And because they are so bright and true, and because through them you promise us these things, you, Lord, who are true in all things, will preserve us, that is, save us in the future, restoring us to impassibility through the obedience of that Savior.

And so that we may be able to attain this salvation, in the meantime you will preserve us from this generation of deceitful and grandiloquent men, so that we may not be incorporated into them. I say: You will preserve us, leading us afterward into eternity.

I say that you will preserve us, so that we may not be deceitful, that is, promising blessedness in temporal things.

[Col. 0682A] But the wicked, that is, the deceitful and grandiloquent men about whom I spoke above, walk in a circle, that is, they resemble someone walking in a circle. For just as such a person will never reach the end, so they, while seeking blessedness in temporal things, will never reach the end.

He says this to show that, by God’s hidden judgment, they are made rich in this way so that they may justly perish in it. He adds as follows: I say, “They walk in a circle,” that is, in the pleasure of present goods, and thus they are blinded.

And this does not happen by an unjust judgment. Rather, you, God, according to your loftiness, that is, according to your lofty and inscrutable judgment, have multiplied earthly goods for the sons of men, that is, for the sons of the prophets and of other faithful people, who ought to have acted rationally and did act rationally.

[Col. 0682B]

## ON PSALM XII

The title of the twelfth psalm: “For the end. A psalm of David.” This is explained as follows: This psalm is to be attributed to David, that is, to the assembly of the faithful, tending toward the end, that is, toward Christ or toward perseverance.

The same assembly that spoke in the preceding psalm is introduced here, sighing from its immense desire for Christ’s coming and praying God to look upon the human race by sending Him quickly.

It does not pray in this way because it is uncertain that it will ever see Him, but because it has already conceived this through the Holy Spirit, since He will be sent, as was shown in the preceding psalm. Since the eager soul hastens greatly toward this, it prays that He may come at the appointed time, so that it may see Him with bodily eyes.

We likewise read that Moses prayed to God with excessive affection for what could not happen, when he said: “Show me your face, and that is enough for me” (Exodus 33:18).

[Col. 0682C] In this psalm the same assembly also prays that He free it from the death of serious sins, so that it may be able to rejoice at His coming. The Prophet introduces it here for this purpose as well: to instruct us, by its example, in love for Him. He speaks as follows.

“How long, Lord, to whom I have made myself a servant, will you forget me?” That is, how long will you appear to forget me by not restoring what I committed through Adam?

Afterward the same speaker answers herself, so that she may teach the less perfect how long this forgetfulness will last: “You will do this until the end,” that is, until Christ, who will come as the end of prophecy and of the law.

Or “until the end of the times of our misery,” that is, when the time of fulfillment will come.

[Col. 0682D] Or it may be read in this way, not as an answer but as a sigh: “Will you forget me to the end of forgetfulness,” that is, to the full extent that forgetfulness can exist, namely, for all time?

“How long will you turn your face away from me,” that is, away from my eyes, delaying to send the one whose coming will remove Him from my sight? This is not said as a question but as a lament.

The Son is called “the face,” because through His visibility the invisibility of the Father has been made known, just as the whole person is known through the face. As He Himself says in the Gospel: “Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9).

“How long shall I place counsels in my soul,” that is, how long, while I remain in this delay, shall I resemble a person placed in distress, who forms various plans in his soul concerning how he may escape?

[Col. 0683A] And how shall I place sorrow in my heart day by day, that is, daily, the sorrow which I have over this delay? By saying “I shall place it day by day,” he indicates that he did not place it only once, but daily, more and more.

“How long will my enemy,” that same devil, “be exalted over me,” that is, how long will he rejoice in what I lost through Adam, whom he deceived? Thus he will be exalted over me, that is, he will regard himself as the victor and me as having been overthrown through Adam.

Do not turn your face away for long, but look upon me through that very face of yours, sending it. And he rightly says, “Look upon me,” that is, “Visit me again”—you who looked upon us kindly in Adam when you made us impassible, but afterward seemed, because of his sin, to have forgotten us.

And when that face has been sent, hear me through it by restoring me to life, which I repeatedly ask you to give back.

Lord, who are powerful, my God, to whom I do not deny the place of divinity within me, but obey you as best I can.

[Col. 0683B] Seeing that she has prayed with excessive desire for what is impossible, she also prays for what can happen, as follows:

Since I am certain that you will not look upon me in such a way that I see your face with bodily eyes, at least enlighten my eyes with spiritual light, that is, the eyes of my heart, so that I may never fall asleep by sinning and thereby come into death, that is, into a serious sin through which one comes to death.

Then, on the day of judgment, my enemy the devil may not say: “I have prevailed against him,” that is, “I have conquered him.”

This does not mean that he will speak then, since he is incorporeal, but that, through the tribulation which he will inflict upon the wicked, he will show as though by words that he has conquered them.

[Col. 0683C] Therefore enlighten me still, so that the enemies, that is, the evil spirits, may not rejoice when I sin seriously, since it is not fitting that they rejoice over me, who am subject to you.

For those who trouble me by evil suggestion will rejoice if I am moved, departing from devotion to you and falling into sin.

“But I”—that is, “But I, so that I may remain immovable—have hoped, and hope, and shall hope in your mercy, not in myself.”

And because I have hoped, and hope, in your mercy, my heart, that is, my soul, will rejoice in your Savior, that is, in the coming of your Son the Savior, who will deliver me.

And so that I may then be able to rejoice, in the meantime I shall sing to the Lord, that is, praise Him with a good affection, which will be a song to Him, that is, a great delight.

The Lord has bestowed these good things upon me, so that I may hope in His mercy. And I shall not only sing, but also play the psalm, that is, act well.

And this will be not for my own pride, but also for the name of the Lord Most High, that is, for the honor of His name, so that He may be praised through it.

[Col. 0683D] And rightly so. For He is Most High, that is, Lord of lords; therefore He is worthy that I sing a psalm to His name.

## ON PSALM XIII

The title of the thirteenth psalm: “For the end. A psalm of David.” This is explained as follows: This psalm is to be attributed to David, that is, to Christ, who looks toward the end, that is, toward the salvation of the righteous and the destruction of the wicked, which will occur at the end of the world.

[Col. 0684A] Here the Head Himself is introduced reproaching the Jews, who, when they saw Him, did not receive Him as the God of glory, although the preceding psalm showed with what affection their holy fathers had desired to see Him.

It also shows that the greatest condemnation will come upon them for this, while everlasting salvation will come to His own, so that His people may be wholly deterred from their unbelief and strive more earnestly toward obedience to Him.

It speaks as follows.

The fool—that is, the Jewish people, by antonomasia—is the one who said this, being foolish because he does not believe what the prophets said about me: finding this in his heart, not possessing it from the Scriptures. “This man is not God.” In accordance with the Gospel saying: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John 9:16). And elsewhere: “Though you are a man, you make yourself God” (John 10:33). And therefore they said, “There is no God,” because they were corrupted in their mind, that is, blinded. And they were corrupted for this reason: because they had become abominable—that is, accursed—to God, persisting in their pursuits, that is, in the evil thoughts and deeds to which they devoted themselves intensely. It is as though he said: Because they devoted themselves to evil, God cursed them and thus blinded them.

But because they said, “There is no God,” they were deservedly blinded, so that there is no one who does good. He repeats this in order to reproach them more strongly: “There is no one who does good,” that is, who reaches even one, that is, reaches Christ, who is one—singular and incomparable. For there is no other God who is both God and man. And he rightly says, “There is no one who does good”; “there is no one who reaches even one,” as the same person testifies in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

They say, “There is no God,” although the Lord—that is, God united to me—looked down from heaven, that is, from the realm of the heaven of heavens, by antonomasia, upon the sons of men, that is, the Jews. And he rightly says, “He looked down upon them.” For someone who looks down upon another from an upper room through a window is above him: he neither entirely conceals himself nor entirely reveals himself. So too the mercy of the Godhead partly revealed itself to those below through the man who is the Lord, although it was wholly known to no one.

And he looked down for this purpose: to see—that is, to make his own see—whether there was among the Jewish people anyone understanding God through faith, or seeking him through good works. Or it may be understood in this way: “to see,” that is, he who previously saw by providence might see by the experience of the event itself, whether there was anyone understanding, and so forth. That is, he came so that they might be without excuse, as the same person says in the Gospel: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15:22).

I say that the Lord looked down; but they all turned away from the understanding of faith. Together with this—that is, at the same time as they turned away—they became useless, that is, fruitless and harmful to themselves and to others.

And truly they were useless to themselves. For there is no one who does good; there is no one who reaches even one, that is, Christ, namely me. And truly they were useless to others. For their throat—that is, the voice proceeding from their throat—is an open tomb, that is, comparable to an open tomb. Just as a tomb is open for the purpose of receiving and corrupting a body, so their voice is open for the purpose of incorporating the innocent and making them corrupt in thought and deed.

And they are not open merely to corrupt others; but first they deceitfully acted against me with their tongues, that is, with the lying and flattering tongues they deserved, saying: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful, and so forth” (Matthew 22:16).

And while they acted deceitfully, the venom of asps—that is, the incurable hatred they had for me—was under their lips, that is, in their hearts, as it is said through the prophet: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29:13; Mark 7:6). And he rightly calls their hatred the venom of asps: for just as one who drinks the venom of asps never escapes, so they too will not be emptied of the hatred with which they are filled until they die.

I say: they all turned away; and the mouth of all of them is full of cursing and bitterness, that is, of bitter cursing, as it is written: “You have a demon” (John 7 and 8).

Their feet—that is, their affections—are swift to shed my blood, as it is written: “And they were seeking how to kill him” (ibid.). Their affections are called feet because the mind advances by its affections just as the body advances by its feet. And they are rightly called swift, since they killed him unexpectedly, without even waiting for the feast day to pass completely.

The whole meaning is as though he said: It can be seen from this that they turned away, because their mouth is full of cursing and their feet are swift to shed my blood, as the Apostle says: “If they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

And because they turned away, and are such and such, destruction and misery—that is, miserable destruction—will be in their ways, that is, on account of their evil deeds and thoughts, which are ways for them to condemnation. Miserable destruction will come upon them, namely from the Romans, as the same Lord testifies in the Gospel: “They will surround you and hem you in on every side, and they will strike you down to the ground; and they will not leave in you one stone upon another” (Luke 19:44).

And although destruction will come upon them because of their turning away, yet, when at last they ought to have come to know, they did not know—that is, they will not know—the way of peace, that is, me, who am the way by which one comes to eternal peace, and who am also eternal peace, as the same person says in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). And the Apostle says: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14).

And therefore they will not know, because there is no fear of God before the eyes of their mind, that is, because they do not fear God. “For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclesiasticus 1:16).

After predicting their destruction, he also sets forth their condemnation with a rebuke, and the reward of his own, in this way. Since they are a tomb, deceitful, and swift to shed blood:

“Will they not know—all those who work iniquity,” that is, my death, which they unjustly inflict? And those who devour—that is, wish to devour by incorporating and killing—my people, that is, my faithful, like food? Like bread—that is, daily, just as bread is eaten daily.

And therefore they work iniquity, because they did not call upon the Lord. That is, God permitted them to fall into iniquity because they did not call upon him, that is, because they did not acknowledge him as Lord and themselves as servants.

And they still work iniquity because they trembled there with fear where there was no fear, that is, where there ought not to have been fear: namely, at the loss of the land, as it is read in the Gospel: “What are we to do? This man is performing many signs. If we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation” (John 11:48).

Will not all these people, who are such and such, know—although they now refuse to know—that the Lord is in this generation, that is, that his grace is always in this generation, in order eventually to reward them?

It is as though he said: They will truly know one day that the Lord is now among the righteous, in order eventually to reward those who now appear contemptible to them. Conversely, it is understood that they will know, when they are condemned, that the Lord was not in them.

Now he turns directly to them and rebukes them in this way:

Truly you wish to devour my people. For you have put to shame—that is, have judged shameful, and still judge shameful—the counsel of the poor, that is, the counsel of my people, who are poor, that is, needy on my account. This is their counsel: that the hope of the poor—that is, the one in whom he himself places his hope—is the Lord of all, that is, me, whom he believes to be Lord of all things.

And because it might be asked who this Lord is, he himself asks the question in order to answer it. I say: The Lord is his hope. Who? That is, who is this Lord?

He then describes him in this way: That Lord who was born from Zion, that is, from the Jewish people according to the flesh, will give salvation to Israel, that is, salvation to each person who sees God through faith and contemplation. That is, he will save Israel from original sin; and in the future, when the Lord turns away the captivity of his people, that is, the corruption and mortality of the body, Jacob, that is, the less perfect, will rejoice, and Israel, that is, the most perfect, will be glad.

And Jacob rightly signifies the less perfect, while Israel signifies the most perfect. For Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter,” whereas Israel is interpreted as “seeing God.” The less perfect are merely supplanters of vices; they do not yet see God in contemplation. The perfect both supplant vices and already see God in contemplation.

It is as though he said: I am that Lord who will save Israel here, and in the future, by turning away captivity, will make Jacob and Israel rejoice.

## ON PSALM XIV

The title of the fourteenth psalm: “A psalm of David,” that is, to be attributed to Christ. The man who is the Lord is introduced as speaking, because he had said: “He will give salvation to Israel, and Jacob will rejoice and Israel will be glad.” He does this so that no one who is called by the Christian name alone might presume that he will be saved and rejoice. He intends to show who the person is who will possess these things.

And since no one will rejoice in this way who has not first been here in the service of Christ, he asks, out of goodwill, who should be said to belong here to his service and to rejoice in eternal rest in the future, so that he may answer later. He uses “tabernacle” for military service, because soldiers customarily make tabernacles. And he says this:

“Lord, who will dwell,” that is, remain continually here, “in your tabernacle,” that is, in your service? Or I may ask in this way: Who will rest in the future on your mountain, that is, in sublime Jerusalem? I say “holy mountain,” that is, one in which no one will be except a holy person.

The answer follows in this way. He will dwell and rest who enters—that is, walks—in this life without blemish, that is, without mortal sin; that is, who is innocent; and who practices righteousness, that is, who is righteous in deed. For it is not enough to abstain from evil unless one does what is good.

And he shows what it means to be without blemish, that is, to be innocent, and what it means to practice righteousness, by setting out several aspects of innocence and righteousness together.

I say that he will dwell and rest who walks without blemish and practices righteousness. And understand that person to be without blemish, that is, innocent, and to practice righteousness, who speaks truth in his heart, that is, who has in the conscience of his heart an utterance of truth, namely, a thought of true faith.

For faith is the foundation of all virtues: that is, he does not err even in thought concerning the faith, but speaks the true faith in his heart, that is, thinks it. The speech of the heart is thought; and this pertains to righteousness, in accordance with the saying: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Romans 1:17).

And he is one who has not acted deceitfully with his tongue. “The deceitful and fraudulent,” as the Apostle says, “will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:9). This does not mean those who are deceitful in praising someone, but those who are deceitful in order to harm someone.

Not acting deceitfully pertains to innocence. Nor has he done evil to his neighbor by intention or in deed, which is innocence. Nor has he accepted reproach against his neighbors, that is, he has neither consented to nor taken pleasure in the reproach inflicted upon his neighbors. This too pertains to innocence.

And he has not merely refused to accept reproach; but the wicked person—that is, one acting wickedly against his neighbor—has been brought to nothing in his sight, that is, in the consideration of his mind. Not so that the person may become nothing, but he considers in his mind that one who, by acting wickedly, is separated from Christ, the true Being, is brought to nothing, that is, to not being with Christ.

In accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “If I do not have the love—that is, the affection—of God and neighbor, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:2). And this pertains to righteousness.

I say that he considers the wicked to be brought to nothing. But those who fear the Lord—that is, those who serve the Lord with chaste fear—he glorifies, that is, he regards as glorious. This indeed belongs to the righteous.

He who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive him. This is not to be understood as meaning that everyone ought to swear, since the Lord says in the Gospel: “You shall not swear by heaven, nor by the earth, nor by your head” (Matthew 5:36). Rather, it is the same as saying: He who is like one who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive him, that is, who is so truthful toward his neighbor as one who swears and does not lie. This too is righteousness.

He who does not lend his money at interest, which pertains to innocence. This is not to be understood only of earthly money, but also of one who freely expends upon his neighbors, for God’s sake, prayers and whatever other benefit there may be. In accordance with the Lord’s saying: “You received freely; give freely” (Matthew 10:8).

And he who does not accept gifts in order to prevail over the innocent, that is, in order to oppress him. This too belongs to innocence: that they do not accept such gifts.

Whoever does these things that I have set forth above, and things like them, will not be moved in this world from the tabernacle of God; in the future he will be led into it forever.

Alternatively, the four principal virtues may be understood through the foregoing. By the words “who walks without blemish,” “has not acted deceitfully with his tongue,” “has not done evil to his neighbor,” “has not accepted reproach against his neighbors,” “has not lent his money at interest,” and “has not accepted gifts against the innocent,” temperance is signified, since all these are its parts.

By the words “he practices righteousness,” righteousness is understood; its parts are intermingled when he adds: “But those who fear the Lord he glorifies,” and “he who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive him.”

By the words “who speaks truth in his heart,” prudence is understood. And by the statement that “the wicked person is brought to nothing in his sight,” fortitude is signified.

## ON PSALM XV

The title of the fifteenth psalm: “An inscription to David,” which is explained as follows. The inscription of the title, that is, the victory contained in this psalm, is to be attributed to David. And it does not mean David in the sense of the prophet, but David himself, that is, truly the one signified by David, namely Christ.

“ himself” is added for distinction, as in Ezekiel: “Behold, I myself will seek out my sheep” (Ezekiel 34:11).

And in this passage “title” is rightly used for “victory,” since at times victory is customarily signified by a title. Thus by this title Christ’s victory over the Jews was signified: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.” For when it says “King of the Jews,” it indicates that some of the Jews would be convicted by him and led from evil to good, and that he would become their king. This psalm concerns that victory.

Here the man who is the Lord prays to God the Father, or to the Trinity, to preserve him in his passion so that he does not yield, from which victory will follow. And for this reason he prays, so that in tribulation he may teach us to pray.

In what follows he also treats of the conversion of the Jews, who will become his inheritance, determining whom he calls his inheritance. He also promises that he will bless God for his passion and his inheritance, so that he may teach us to bless God both in prosperity and in adversity.

Furthermore, at the end he treats of the resurrection and ascension, so that by his example he may give those who hope in him hope of resurrection and immortality. And he says this:

“Preserve me in my passion, lest I yield, Lord, to whom I have made myself a servant.” And I am worthy of preservation because I have hoped in you, not in myself. And therefore, because I said to the Lord—that is, because I established in my heart, for the honor of you who are Lord—“You are my God; there is no other.”

It is as though he said: I am worthy to be preserved because I have always placed my hope in you and established you as my God. Yet I do not pray to be preserved because I would say that you lack those good things that must be provided to the human race through me—namely, the remission of sins, immortality, and freedom from suffering. For you do not need these goods of mine, as it is said elsewhere.

Therefore he is truly Lord who does not need the servant, while the servant needs him. [Col. 0689A] In this he provides us an example of humility, so that we may not in any way think that God needs our salvation or service, as the same person says in the Gospel: “When you have done all that was commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants’” (Luke 17:10), that is, bringing no benefit to God.

Or it may be understood in this way: Truly you are God; and this can be seen from the fact that you do not need my goods. And he expresses what those goods are, turning to his hearers in order to instruct them, as follows:

Truly he himself does not need my goods, O hearers—namely, those that I have made marvelous, that is, will make marvelous, that is, will make all my purposes appear marvelous to the saints who are in his land, that is, who are in hope in the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the land of the living, concerning which it is said elsewhere: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 114:9).

I say that my purposes are to be fulfilled in them: that is, I will not merely make my purposes appear marvelous to them, but I will also teach them to fulfill them.

And before I make my purposes marvelous to the saints who are in his land, their infirmities have been multiplied, that is, I will cause their infirmities to multiply, making them recognize and confess that their infirmities have been multiplied. He speaks of the infirmity in which the law was weak, as the Apostle says: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, in order to destroy sin through sin” (Romans 8:3); and elsewhere: “The law entered so that the offense might abound” (Romans 5:20).

It is as though he said: First I will give them compunction, so that they may recognize and confess that their infirmities are many, as James says: “Confess your sins to one another” (James 5:16).

And after they recognize that their infirmities have multiplied, they hastened—that is, they will hasten—to God through faith and works. And they will hasten in such a way that I will no longer gather—that is, cause to be gathered—their assemblies, that is, their congregations, from blood, that is, for the shedding of blood.

“From” has a causal force, meaning: They will hasten to the faith in such a way that I will no longer cause them to gather for the fulfillment of carnal observances.

And after they hasten, I will not remember their names, that is, I will not reproach them with the names they had on account of their crimes; I will not call them unbelievers, impious, or by their other names.

I say: Nor will I remember them with my lips, that is, when I seem to act with my lips, saying: “Depart from me” (Matthew 25:41), and so forth.

Or, if we say that he will not act with his lips, we shall explain it thus: Nor will I remember their names. And this is made clear by “my lips,” that is, by the prophets called my lips because they revealed my purposes, just as the lips of the heart reveal the will. That is, I have already made this known through my prophets, in accordance with the saying: “If the wicked person turns away from his wickedness, I will not remember any of his iniquities” (Ezekiel 18:22).

I say that afterward they will hasten. And they will hasten so greatly that the Lord will be the portion of my inheritance and my cup, that is, those saints of whom I said: “I have made marvelous those who are my inheritance,” whom I cultivate.

And my cup—that is, those who intoxicate me with their good life, filling me with joy—just as the finest cup of wine intoxicates the drinker and fills him with joy. They have chosen no portion except the Lord; that is, they do not wish to be on the devil’s side but on the Lord’s side, as it was said of Mary in the Gospel: “Mary chose the best portion, which will not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42).

When he adds, “You are,” and so forth, he turns directly to God out of great affection, as though giving thanks:

I say: The Lord is the portion of my inheritance, which I, insofar as I am human, will not obtain through myself; but “you are,” that is, you truly remain immutable, in accordance with the saying: “For God, being is true and proper.”

I say: You are the one who will restore my inheritance in blessedness, from which it fell through Adam. And this is “to me,” that is, for my honor.

Or it may be understood thus: You, who are powerful and Lord, are the one who will restore to me the inheritance that I possessed insofar as I am God and lost through Adam, as the same person says in the Gospel: “They were yours, and you gave them to me” (John 17:6).

And so that no one might presume that he will be in that inheritance merely on the basis of faith without works, he defines his inheritance. I say: You will restore my inheritance. And my inheritance will not consist of just anyone, but you will arrange cords, that is, choices.

“Lots have fallen,” that is, will fall, “for me,” that is, will fall to my lot, “in glorious places,” that is, I will choose only those who will be glorious in virtues.

He calls his arrangements “cords” by way of comparison, because just as fields are measured and selected with cords, so God by his arrangements selects those who are to be saved from those who are to be lost.

And he rightly says, “They have fallen”: for God’s arrangements are unknown, like things that happen by chance.

And because he had said “in glorious places,” while some may have been ragged, someone might say that they were not glorious. Therefore he adds:

I rightly said “glorious,” for my inheritance is glorious when I consider it not according to the outward person but according to the inward person.

And because he restored a glorious inheritance to me, I will bless the Lord, that is, magnify him, who gave me understanding, that is, the plan for redeeming that inheritance.

Moreover, I will bless him because my kidneys—that is, my Jewish relatives, from whose line my mother came—rebuked me, saying: “Ah! You who destroy the temple of God” (Matthew 26:61), and other blasphemies. In rebuking me they will pursue me until night, that is, leading me into the darkness of death.

I say that they rebuked me; but I continually looked upon the Lord as before me, that is, I will look upon him in the consideration of my mind. And I can rightly and securely look upon him, because here, for the present, in tribulation, he is at my right hand, that is, as my help, so that I may not be moved from my good purpose.

And he rightly says “at my right hand”: for by the right hand prosperity is signified, while by the left hand adversity is signified.

It is as though he said: Because he is at my right hand, that is, favorable to me, I can securely look forward to the fact that in the future he will raise me up. I say that he is at my right hand.

And for this reason my heart, that is, my soul, rejoiced. And my tongue exulted, that is, my tongue will utter words in exultation: “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46).

Moreover, my flesh will rest in the tomb in the hope of resurrection, that is, in such a way that the soul will hope that the flesh is to be raised.

Or “my flesh” means the Church, which is one body, whose head I am. It will rest in the hope of rising again, so that, just as I rose, it too may rise. And in this hope it will rest, that is, take great delight, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “If we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus” (1 Thessalonians 4:14).

And he rightly calls the Church his flesh, as the Apostle says: “The two will be one flesh. This mystery is great; but I am speaking of Christ and the Church” (1 Corinthians 6:16; Ephesians 5:32).

I say that my heart rejoiced and my tongue exulted.

And deservedly, because you will not abandon my soul in hell, so that it may be held there like the souls of sinners; but, after it has been stripped of its spoils, it will return with the procession of the saints. Nor will you give your Holy One—that is, the holy body of your Son—to see corruption, that is, you will not permit my most sacred body to decay.

And therefore you will not abandon my soul in hell, because you have made known to me the paths of life, that is, your commandments, which are paths to life for those who obey.

It is as though he said: Because I have striven to obey your commandments, which you made known to me, you will not abandon my soul in hell.

And you will not merely refrain from abandoning it; you will also fill me with joy in your presence, that is, with your presence. This means: When I enjoy your presence in heaven, I will rejoice greatly.

And afterward there will be delights for me at your right hand, that is, among your superior gifts. This means: I will take great delight in the faithful whom you will give me and establish at your right hand.

And my delights will not be small, but delights extending to the end, that is, to perfection—perfect and great delights.

## ON PSALM XVI

The title of the sixteenth psalm: “The prayer of David himself,” that is, of Christ—truly David.

And this psalm is given this title, although prayer is found in many other psalms as well, because it pertains principally and almost entirely to prayer. Here the head prays for the members, and first for himself, so that he may teach us to pray.

He also treats, by way of concession, of his enemies, setting forth their merits, because he and his own are worthy of reward, and because his enemies are also worthy of destruction. And he says this:

Hear, O Lord, my justice—that is, hear me according to what my justice deserves. And he shows from where he hears: “Give heed,” that is, make my prayer straight and earnest; that is, make me earnestly entreat you. And afterward, “with your ears perceive,” that is, hear. He speaks in human terms. Or by “ears” his power is signified, since ears possess the power of hearing. I call it “my prayer,” not one made with deceitful lips. We are said to pray with the lips when, while the lips are praying, the thought of the heart wanders.

Or “supplication” and “prayer” may be different. Supplication is on behalf of the members—that is, a prayer for the removal of vices, when he says, “Make your mercies wonderful,” and so forth; prayer, however, is on behalf of himself and the members, for perfection and perseverance. If we understand them as distinct in this way, then *intende* (“give heed”) will mean “understand.”

He says: “Perceive my prayer”—namely, this: “Let my judgment proceed from your countenance,” that is, the judgment by which I am now judged by the Jews, which seems to proceed solely from their counsels, but may appear to have proceeded from your will, as the same Pilate said: “You would have no power over me at all, unless it had been given you from above” (John XIX, 11). The will is called the “countenance” because a person’s will is often discerned in his face.

I say, “Let my judgment proceed from your countenance,” through this, namely, that “your eyes behold equity.” He speaks in human terms: that is, let your eyes behold equity—let them see to it that you fulfill what is just: by causing me to rise again, subjecting the world to me, saving and perfecting my people, and justly rewarding my enemies. Thus it may become evident that you willed the judgment of my death, so that such effects would follow.

The eyes may also be understood as signifying the power of Providence. And he sets forth his merit, as follows: “Truly you ought to perceive my prayer and behold equity, because you have tested my heart.” This does not mean that one from whom nothing is hidden needs testing. Rather, it is as though he said: “You have shown as approved the holy intention of my heart, which was almost unknown to everyone.”

And he explains how he tested it: “I say, You tested me; and you did so in this manner: You visited me by night” (42), that is, by a hidden temptation brought by the devil, as it is written in the Gospel: “And the tempter approached,” and so forth (Matthew IV, 3). He rightly says “you visited.” The temptation was a great visitation and exaltation, since he yielded to it in no way. “With fire you tested me,” that is, with the manifest and most grievous tribulation of the Passion; you showed me to have been examined and approved.

Thus “iniquity has not been found in me”: through this twofold temptation you make it evident that no iniquity could be found in me. The whole meaning is as though he said: “I am worthy that my prayer be heard, since there is no iniquity in me.” This became clear because, when tempted by the devil, I did not yield; and it will become even more evident that I shall not fail in the fire of tribulation.

And that there is no iniquity in me will be made manifest in this way: “so that my mouth may not speak”—that is, so that it will not be necessary for my mouth to say this. For it will be entirely obvious.

Indeed, iniquity has not been found in me, for “I have kept, and have not rejected, harsh ways,” that is, the works of human beings—those things, namely, that are commonly inflicted upon human beings, that is, upon those who do not do the things of God but the things of human beings. These are evil things: I shall willingly endure tribulations and the torments of the cross, which are customarily inflicted upon those who do evil. These are “your ways,” that is, given by you to lead me to glory.

He rightly says “I have kept,” using the likeness of travelers who, when they hold to the right road, keep to it faithfully even though it is very rough, lest they turn aside from it.

I have kept these ways “for the sake of fulfilling the words of your lips,” which foretold these things. The prophets are called “lips” because they disclosed God’s will, just as the lips of the heart open what is willed by the heart . . .

Or the passage may be punctuated in this way: “I say, There is no iniquity in me; and I say this so that my mouth may not speak the works of human beings,” that is, so that I may not speak of these things boastfully and arrogantly, since such utterances are works of human beings. The meaning is: “I speak of these things in such a way that I do not become proud because of them, as human beings commonly become proud of their merits.”

Or thus: “I say, There is no iniquity in me; and so utterly is there no iniquity in me that, what is greatest of all, my mouth does not speak the works of human beings,” that is, vanities. For vain speech is a work of human beings; thus I do not sin even with my tongue.

I say: “With fire you tested me.” But I, your innocent Son, have kept the harsh ways of tribulations for the sake of the words of your lips. And since I have kept the harsh ways so that through them my steps might be perfected, “perfect my steps,” that is, make my disciples perfect, through whom I shall come to the knowledge of human beings.

For this reason they are called “my steps” in your paths, which are paths to life. They are “steep,” that is, hard for the flesh and narrow, just as paths are narrow, in accordance with the saying: “Narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matthew VII, 14).

Perfect them in such a way that “my footsteps may not be moved” from them—that is, the examples of my good works impressed upon their hearts. Make them perfect and steadfast.

Up to this point he has prayed on behalf of the perfect. Afterward, on behalf of all unbelievers who are to be converted, he intends to pray as follows:

“I cried out to you,” saying, “Perfect,” and so forth. And I know that you have already heard me—not in deed, but because you have already fulfilled it in your purpose. And since you have heard me praying in this way, I pray again: “Incline your ear,” that is, make the power of your mercy condescend toward me—that is, toward those who will become mine, though they are still unbelievers—and hear the words I have poured out for them.

He rightly says “incline,” using the likeness of a physician bending over the sick, who because of their excessive illness are unable to rise up to him. In the same way the clemency of God bends down—that is, condescends—to those who are sick with sins and unable, through their own merits, to rise up to him.

I say, “Hear my words”—namely these: “Make your mercies wonderful,” that is, make those who will be saved through your wondrous virtues and works; “your mercies,” that is, those who, though unbelievers, will be saved by mercy alone and not by their own merits. They are emphatically called “mercies,” because your mercy toward them is exceedingly abundant.

I say, “Make them wonderful,” you “who save in soul from vices those who hope in you,” not those who hope in themselves—that is, my disciples. Of them it is written: “We were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke XXIV, 21).

And so that these may be made wonderful and placed over others, save them “from those who resist your right hand,” that is, from the Jews who, by persecuting me, will resist your Word personally united to me, the Word that made me king.

And what is your “right hand”? It is that through which, according to John, all things were made by you: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 2). It protects me, so that I do not yield.

“Keep me, O Lord, as the pupil of the eye,” that is, as one existing like the pupil of the eye. For just as the whole body is illuminated by the pupil, although it is the smallest part of the body, so the whole body of Christ—that is, the Church—is illuminated by Christ, who appeared small and insignificant. As he himself says: “I am the light of the world” (John VIII, 12).

I say, “Keep me”: protect me in such a way that I am not wounded in soul, even if I am wounded in body. I say, “placed under the shadow of your wings,” that is, under the protection and love of charity, using the likeness of a bird protecting its young beneath its wings so that they are not harmed by the heat.

I say, “Protect me from the face,” that is, from the assault of the impious Jews, who afflicted me—that is, will afflict me. He uses “face” for “assault,” because when enemies press upon someone, they show their face.

And he explains how they will afflict him, so that from their evil merits he may grant them future punishment—which will be just, since above he had said, “Let your eyes behold equity.”

Truly they will afflict me, because my enemies, the Jews, “have surrounded me”—that is, they will hem in my soul with their counsels, so as to hold me in death, saying: “Come, let us oppress the poor righteous man” (Wisdom II, 10).

And they will do this—that is, they will be so foolish—for “they have enclosed their fat,” that is, their fattened, carnal understanding; they have firmly retained it within themselves. They did not cast it away, as they ought to have done, thinking that I was merely human and not both human and God.

Therefore their mouth “has spoken”—that is, will speak—pride, namely, “Crucify him!” and “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX, 15).

And they will not merely speak pride against me; they themselves, casting me out of the city at the time now granted to them by God, as it is written in the Gospel, “This is your hour, and the power of darkness” (Luke XXII, 53), will at some point be expelled from that same city. They have surrounded me—that is, they will surround me fixed to the cross, spitting upon me and mocking me.

And they will do this because they have determined to turn aside—that is, have firmly turned aside—“their eyes,” that is, the considerations of their minds, “toward the earth,” that is, toward the desires of retaining their earthly possession. They will do this because they will think that by this means they can retain their place and nation, though by it they will rather bring destruction upon themselves.

Or the passage may be understood in this way: “I say, They have surrounded me. And for this reason they have determined to turn their eyes toward the earth.” Because of such great cruelty they will be like any cruel person who, having someone punished so that he need not see him, strives to turn his eyes toward the ground, lest, moved by the other’s misery, he should show mercy.

I say: “Casting me out, they have surrounded me and afflicted me in many ways.” Yet by their own power they could not do this; rather, they received me as one handed over by God the Father, as it is said elsewhere: “God did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans VIII, 32).

I say, “They received me,” being “like a lion ready for prey and like a lion’s cub.” By “lion” and “cub,” dwelling in hidden places, he means those who resemble a lion with regard to the elders and rulers, and a lion’s cub with regard to the common people, who had been generated by their elders in this wickedness, just as a cub is generated by a lion.

He rightly says “ready for prey” and “dwelling in hidden places.” Although they could do this whenever they wished, they were always ready for it, secretly planning it.

Having shown their evil merits, he speaks concessively of their punishment as follows:

Since they will do this and that, you, Lord, who appear powerless in my affliction, “arise,” that is, show yourself powerful. And he explains in what way: “Go before him and trip him up,” that is, conquer him. The one who goes before another conquers him, as does the one who trips him up. He uses these two likenesses to intensify the enormity of their crime.

Conquer him in this way: “Deliver my soul,” which is innocent, “from the wicked one,” that is, from the will of the wicked Jewish people, so that it may not be held in death.

He calls my soul “your sword,” because by its descent to the underworld you will defeat the devil. It is as though he said: “Deliver it, since it is your sword, from the enemies of your hand,” that is, from the Jews, who are enemies of your Word personally united to me.

This Word is your “hand,” through which you made all things, as the Psalmist says elsewhere: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Psalm XXXII, 6).

And do not merely deliver me from them; “divide them.” And lest this be understood of that division which will occur on the day of judgment, when the sheep will be separated from the goats (Matthew XXV, 32), he adds: “In their life,” that is, in this present life divide them throughout the world, separated from the few faithful of their lineage who are in Jerusalem. The Spirit told these faithful to move into the kingdom of Agrippa, so that they would not suffer the affliction of the siege of Jerusalem.

And rightly will you divide them, for “their belly,” that is, their carnal will, “has been filled”—their will has been satisfied—“with your hidden things,” that is, they will greatly rejoice in my tribulations and death, which proceed from your hidden judgments and not from their own power.

And they have not merely been filled; they have also been “sated with sons,” that is, for the evil example of their children, so that children who have not yet been born may be sated—that is, may delight—in their evil example.

Nor will the fathers alone be condemned; “they have divided their remnants,” that is, the punishment left to them by God for that satisfaction, “among their little ones,” saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew XXVII, 25).

Afterward, out of his great affection, he turns in apostrophe to God:

Thus they will be divided according to their merits. But I, who now appear contemptible in the sight of the Jews, shall appear glorious in your sight when I am present with you after ascending into heaven.
