And at the end of the age I shall be “satisfied,” that is, completely filled with joy, when your glory appears in those who are now contemptible—that is, when the eternal blessedness given by you appears in them—in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians III, 4).

## On Psalm XVII

**The sixteenth title:** “For the end: for David, the servant of the Lord, who spoke to the Lord the words of this song on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.”

Some say that this title directs us to that history in which David is said to have been delivered from the persecution of Saul and, after Saul’s death, from all his other enemies. This is certainly understood as having been done as a figure of the Lord.

For through Saul, whose name is said to be interpreted as “desired,” death is most fittingly signified. Just as Saul was desired by the Jews against the will of God, so death was desired by Adam and Eve through the transgression of God’s will. Even now it is desired daily by the wicked through evil works.

But just as David was delivered from Saul by Saul’s own death, so Christ was delivered from death in the resurrection, when death itself was destroyed.

Through David’s other enemies we understand the Jews and the Roman soldiers who persecuted Christ, from all of whom he was delivered in the resurrection.

The whole passage may also be referred to the Church: by David, the Church, which is strong of hand; by Saul, David’s persecutor, the devil, who is the head of all the Church’s persecutors; and by David’s other enemies, the visible persecutors of the Church, who are members of the devil. From all of these the Church has already been delivered according to the soul, so that it may not be incorporated into them; in the future it will also be delivered from their persecutions.

The title is explained as follows:

“The words of this song,” that is, of spiritual delight. The word “this” is not placed to designate present location but dignity, as was said above in another psalm: “A Psalm for David.” The meaning is: These words, spoken with spiritual delight, are to be attributed to David.

And he specifies which David: David the servant, that is, the servant of the Lord, “directed toward the end,” that is, toward perfection and completion. This means: he was perfectly obedient to the Lord, as no one else after him was.

These are the words that he spoke to the Lord, that is, for the Lord’s honor: partly addressing him as a second person, and partly instructing his members for his honor.

David is placed for judgment on the day—that is, in hope of the day—on which the Lord delivered him, that is, in hope of the day of the resurrection, on which the Lord will deliver both him and his members “from the hand,” that is, from the power, of all his enemies.

With regard to him, these are the Jews and the Roman soldiers; with regard to his members, all the persecutors of the Church.

And “from the hand of Saul,” that is, from death, with regard to him, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Christ, rising from the dead, will never die again” (Romans VI, 9).

With regard to the members, “from the hand of Saul” means from the hand of the devil, so that he may no longer have power to condemn them through original sin, in accordance with the Gospel’s saying: “The ruler of this world will be cast out” (John XII, 31).

This is first the voice of the Head giving thanks to God for his own deliverance; afterward, it refers to his being delivered by God, so that he may instill in his members, who are to be delivered through him, the hope of salvation.

He also sets forth, for the instruction of the members in faith and for the rendering of thanksgiving, what benefits ought to result from his death and deliverance. He says this as follows:

“I shall love you, Lord,” that is, while I am now before death I shall love you, and by loving you I shall obey you even unto death. After the resurrection, when no obedience will remain for me to perform, I shall at least love you.

In this he intimates that in the future, after immortality has been received, nothing will remain for the saints except love alone, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Whether prophecies will be abolished or tongues will cease, charity never fails” (1 Corinthians XIII, 8).

And he sets forth the reason for his love as follows: “I shall love you so greatly because you are my strength,” both in me and in my members—that is, through you I and mine are strong.

And he explains in what way he is his strength with regard to himself, turning in apostrophe to the members in order to add faith and hope of salvation to them:

“I speak the truth, hearers: he is my strength.” For he is my “firmament,” that is, my support, so that I do not fall away from holiness, using the likeness of a house supported by columns so that it does not collapse.

And he is “my refuge,” that is, my security, so that I do not fear the assault of enemies, using the likeness of a fortified tower to which the pursued flee in order to be safe.

And he is “my deliverer,” so that I may not be incorporated into my enemies.

And he himself, being God—that is, my Creator according to the flesh—is “my helper,” that is, the co-worker of what is good. The meaning is: Just as he was powerful to create, so also he is powerful to help.

And because he is my firmament, refuge, deliverer, and helper, “I shall hope in him for the resurrection,” passing over into him—that is, into his suffering and glory, insofar as I am human.

The meaning is: These things that I have foretold are for me like a pledge and guarantee of rising again and of passing over into him.

Or the passage may be understood thus: “I shall hope in him for the resurrection,” looking toward him, so that just as he is my firmament, refuge, deliverer, and helper, so also he may be my resurrection.

And because he had inserted “I shall hope in him,” he repeats, with an equivalent expression, what he had earlier said, “my helper,” adding:

“He is my protector,” so that enemies may not wound my soul by incorporating it into themselves, using the likeness of a defender who holds up a shield so that flying arrows do not inflict wounds.

And he is not merely my protector; he is also the author of my salvation, so that I may not be incorporated into them. “He is my horn,” that is, my power of attack, just as horns are the weapon of horned animals.

Through him I attack the treacherous judgments and objections of the Jews, as it is written in the Gospel: “All his adversaries were put to shame” (Luke XIII, 17). And elsewhere: “No one dared to question him any longer” (Matthew XII, 46).

And he will be “my receiver,” by raising me up, so that he may make me, who now exist as mortal, immortal. This uses the likeness of a good physician who receives a sick person in order to make him well.

He explains how he will attain this reception: He will be my receiver because I shall invoke the Lord as my helper, praising him with good affection and action. And thus I shall be safe, delivered from my enemies—that is, he will receive me.

Someone might ask: “Why do you say this? What do your enemies inflict upon you?”

He answers: “Through those enemies the pains of death have surrounded me”—that is, they will hem me in—pains leading me to death.

And these pains, being “torrents of iniquity,” that is, swift and excessive like torrents, proceeding from their iniquity and not from my merits, have troubled me—that is, they will trouble me according to the flesh—as in the Gospel: “He began to be sorrowful and troubled” (Mark XIV, 33).

He rightly says “torrents.” For those pains flowed upon him with the force of torrents, so that they might very quickly wrench away his life.

And because he had said “the pains of death,” lest they be thought to have occurred according to both natures, he repeats the phrase and specifies it by inserting the following:

“The pains of hell,” that is, pains occurring according to the lower nature, namely, according to the flesh, have surrounded me—that is, will surround me.

And for this reason: “The snares of death have anticipated me,” that is, mortality and passibility, which are snares—the causes by which I am drawn into death.

Or thus: “And so the snares of death have anticipated me,” that is, the Jews, who will be the cause of my death, will think that they have prevailed against me. I say this because the pains will surround me.

But “in my tribulation,” that is, in tribulation received not unwillingly but willingly, “I called upon the Lord” as helper—that is, I shall call upon him.

This is the same thing he said above: “I shall invoke the Lord, praising him.” But he repeats it in order to specify how he will invoke him and to add that he will be heard.

I say: “I shall invoke him,” and not with a deceitful invocation, but “I cried out to my God,” that is, I shall call upon him with an intense cry.

And I shall cry out for my good, for he heard—that is, he will hear—my voice.

And this will proceed from his holy temple—that is, from me, who am the temple of his divinity. “From” is used causally. The meaning is: “I, who am his holy temple, am the cause of my being heard.”

And because he had said above, “I cried out to my God,” so that each phrase may be matched with its counterpart, he adds: “And my cry, having been made in his sight,” that is, in his good pleasure, “entered into his ears,” that is, it will be heard by him.

This is spoken in human terms. Or “entered into his ears” means that it will be received by his ears, that is, by the power of his mercy.

Or the earlier phrase, “I cried out to my God,” may be explained in this way: “I shall cry out with the cry of the heart.” Then the meaning of “my cry, having been held in his sight” is “in the heart that he alone sees”; and it entered into his ears.

Having shown his tribulations and his escape from them, he also foretells the benefits that will follow from them:

Because the pains will surround me, and I shall invoke the Lord, and, having been heard, I shall be delivered, “the earth was moved”—that is, it will be moved—to faith: those who are now intent only upon earthly things.

And first it trembled—that is, it will tremble—because of the evil things it has done.

Not only the lowly earthly people, but also “the foundations of the mountains,” that is, the supports of lesser persons, namely, princes, dukes, and counts, were troubled with a good troubling because of their sins—that is, they will be troubled.

And thus they were moved—that is, they will be moved—to faith.

This will happen because he was angry with them—that is, they will recognize that the Lord will be angry with them in the future unless they repent.

And after they are moved, “smoke ascended in his anger.”

Or the passage may be connected in this way: “I say that the earth will tremble because smoke ascended”—that is, will ascend—in those earthly people: smoke, that is, a tearful supplication, which will provoke their eyes to weeping like smoke, and this “in his anger,” that is, in the recognition of his future anger.

He rightly says “ascended,” as though he were saying: “There will be smoke in them which will ascend to God,” that is, which will please him.

And after the smoke, “fire blazed forth,” that is, the ardor of divine love will greatly increase in them; and this will come “from his face,” that is, from the knowledge of him.

For as they ascend toward the Lord, their ignorance is illuminated and their weakness strengthened: understanding is given to them, by which they may see, and charity, by which they may burn.

And from that fire “coals were kindled,” that is, those who were first made alive in Adam and afterward extinguished through his sin. They are rightly called “coals,” that is, dead with respect to the love of God.

They were kindled—that is, they will be kindled and brought to life.

And because one might ask through which ministers these things will occur, he explains as follows:

I say that the earth will be moved, and also the foundations of the mountains; and this will happen through the heavens. For God bent down—that is, will bend down—the heavens, that is, the preachers, who are high in knowledge, just as the heavens are high in comparison with the earth. He will make them humble in preaching according to the capacity of those who receive them.

In accordance with Augustine’s saying: “Whether they are small or great, they have the means by which they may be nourished.”

And in the Apostle: “I became weak to the weak, so that I might gain the weak” (1 Corinthians IX, 22).

And in the Song of Songs: “Honey and milk are under his tongue” (Song of Songs IV, 2).

Through these bent-down heavens he descended into the knowledge of human beings—that is, the one who, because of his sublimity, could not be known descended, that is, adapted himself to their capacity.

And thus, through that descent, “darkness was under his feet,” that is, those who are not wholly ignorant but possess some degree of light were subjected to him, so that they might obey him, like those who, through humility, prostrate themselves beneath the feet of princes.

Of them it is said in the Gospel: “There is still a little light among you; walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John XII, 35).

And from among the darkened he will make some “cherubim,” that is, full of knowledge.

Afterward he ascended—that is, he will cause them to ascend to knowledge of him, once they have been made cherubim. Yet he remains above the cherubim and is not wholly knowable by them, as the Apostle John says: “No one has ever seen God” (John I, 18).

Thus he is incomprehensible, so that it is impossible at any time for him to be fully comprehended.

But he flew—that is, he will fly—“upon the wings of the winds,” that is, upon the swift intellects of spiritual men, who are called winds because of the speed of their understanding.

He rightly repeats “he flew,” as though he were saying: “When they begin to meditate upon him, he flies away from them.” And if they gradually draw nearer, he flies farther and farther away, as the bridegroom says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away” (Song of Songs VI, 4).

And this will not occur only through my tribulations—that darkness will be under his feet and that he will ascend above the cherubim. It will also occur because the pains of death have surrounded me.

God himself placed—that is, will place—“darkness as his hiding place.” Of this the evangelist John says: “The darkness did not comprehend it” (John I, 5).

The meaning is: He will make the impious, who will be darkened in their unbelief and entirely lacking the light of truth, into those in whom he may be hidden; that is, through their tribulations he will secretly work the salvation of the godly.

In accordance with the saying: “The wicked man lives for the godly.”

And the prophet says: “Assyria is the rod of my wrath” (Isaiah X, 5).

He himself did not know. I say that darkness will be his hiding place, that is, they will not know what God will accomplish through them.

But “his tabernacle will be around him,” that is, the faithful who will serve as his soldiers, like soldiers dwelling in tents, will be in his knowledge, after the likeness of those who recognize the one around whom they are stationed.

As the Apostle says: “But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed from glory to glory” (2 Corinthians III, 18).

The meaning is: Those who serve him openly will know what God is accomplishing in them. In this he greatly exalts them and humbles the impious, since he asserts that they do not know what is being accomplished through them.

But because he had said, “He bent down the heavens,” and that through them he descended and ascended, one might ask why he descended and ascended through these persons and not through the prophets. He therefore gives the individual reasons as follows:

He was going to descend through the apostles; through the prophets he did not descend, because there was “dark water,” that is, obscure doctrine, in the clouds of the air—that is, in the prophets, who, in their teaching, were clouds bringing rain upon others in the manner of clouds.

In another translation it reads: “in the clouds of the ether.” And the clouds of the ether are rightly so called, because they preceded the apostles in time, just as the clouds of the ether precede the lower clouds in place.

And therefore he will descend and ascend through the heavens, because they will be clouds bright with radiance—that is, exceedingly luminous clouds bringing rain—before him, that is, in his consideration. They will consider him openly and preach manifest doctrine, as the Apostle says: “Not as Moses placed a veil over his face, so that the children of Israel would not look intently at the face whose end was being brought to nothing,” and so forth (2 Corinthians III, 13).

But when he calls the prophets “dark,” this does not pertain to their disparagement; rather, having shown this, he intends in what follows to say that their obscurity will be made manifest through the luminous teaching of the heavens. And they, being clouds because of their brightness, will preach not to the Jews alone, but will pass over—that is, they will pass over to the Gentiles by preaching to them—as they will be commanded: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15). He says this in order to commend their teaching for the conversion of the Gentiles, when he proclaims that they will become their teachers.

I say that the clouds will pass over—clouds, I say, that are hail and coals of fire: that is, at first they will crush the vices of unbelievers and threaten the vengeance of the Day of Judgment, just as hail crushes the crops and, falling with a din, threatens injury. Afterwards, when those people have become believers, they are burning coals—that is, they kindle them in the ardor of faith and love, just as burning coals kindle what has been extinguished. Paul was hail when he said: “It is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:31). He was a burning coal when he said: “Brothers, I appeal to you by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice,” and so forth (Romans 12:1).

I say that the clouds are hail and coals; and they do not possess this from themselves. Rather, the Lord, existing in them as hail and coals of fire, thundered through them—that is, he will threaten in the manner of thunder—as Paul says: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me, namely Christ?” (2 Corinthians 13:3).

And afterwards the Most High himself, who is powerful, gave—that is, will give—through them his voice, that is, his teaching, just as the Lord says in the Gospel: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).

I say that the clouds will pass over, and they will not have this from themselves; rather, God himself sent—that is, will send—them as his arrows, that is, as smiters of unbelievers, just as arrows strike. And thus he scattered—that is, will scatter—them to whom they will be sent: that is, he will divide them, taking one part of them through their preaching and leaving another part. And for the building up of those who will be taken, he multiplied flashes of lightning—that is, he will perform many miracles through them. These are rightly called flashes of lightning because, like lightning, they render those who see them astonished. And through the flashes of lightning he troubled—that is, will trouble—them: that is, he will prick them to faith. And when they had been troubled, there appeared—that is, there will appear—springs of water, that is, vessels of pure preaching. It is as though he were saying: Those who had previously been judged by them to be deceivers will at last be judged by them to possess the purest teaching.

And through the springs the foundations of the world were revealed—that is, the obscure prophets will be revealed, who were the foundations of the Church. The Church is the world chosen from all lands, that is, the crown of God. He uses “world” for “crown,” since a crown is round.

I say that the springs will appear to them, and that this appearance will not proceed from the springs themselves, O Lord, but from your rebuke. For you will rebuke them secretly within, and he expresses the rebuke in this way: “And as a result”—that is, from the inspiration of the Spirit of your wrath, because you will inspire them through the Holy Spirit with your wrath that is to come upon unbelievers—as it is written: “If anyone is ignorant, let him be ignorant” (1 Corinthians 14:38). God sent—that is, will send—that Spirit, O hearers, from on high, that is, from the summit of his divinity. He says this for the instruction of our faith, just as it is also said through Joel: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh,” and so forth (Joel 2:28).

And through that Spirit he took—that is, will take—me, that is, my Church, and assumed—that is, will assume—me, that is, my Church, chosen from many waters, that is, from my many peoples. They are called waters because they flow from generation to generation, in the manner of flowing waters. As it is said in the Apocalypse: “Many waters: many peoples.”

Or it may be understood in this way: Since he had said, “The earth will be shaken and will be troubled,” one might ask through what means this would happen. He shows it as follows: I say that it will be shaken and troubled, and this through me; for God sent—that is, will send—his Word from on high, that is, from his equality with himself. And the Word itself took me—the Lord’s human being—that is, he joined him personally to himself; and through me he assumed me, that is, my Church, from many waters.

According to the first interpretation, “took” and “assumed” mean the same thing, but they are said by means of two different comparisons. “To take” derives from the likeness of fugitives who are captured; “to assume” derives from the likeness of those who, although weak, are taken up by someone so that they may be led to high places. God took us when we were departing from his law and faith; and, in order to make us high from the lowest places, he took us up.

And he rescued me—that is, he will rescue my Church—from my enemies, that is, from his strongest enemies, namely vices and evil spirits; and also from those who hate me, that is, from visible enemies who wish to incorporate me—that is, my people—into themselves. And it is necessary that you rescue me from those who hate me, because they have been strengthened—that is, they will become strong—against me, that is, against my people.

And he explains how: They went before me on the day of my affliction—that is, they will prevail over my people, like a runner who gets ahead of another, at the time when God permits me to be afflicted. And in that affliction the Lord became—that is, will become—my protector, that is, the protector of my people, so that they may not give way. He is not a protector in such a way that they will not be afflicted, but in such a way that he led—that is, will lead—me, that is, my people, out of the affliction itself into the breadth of faith and love, so that they may not become narrow in faith and love because of affliction, but may be made ever broader, according to the Apostle: “When I am weak, then I am strong and powerful” (2 Corinthians 12:10). He says this for the strengthening of the faithful who are to be afflicted.

Since above he had said, “He will take and assume me,” but had not explained it, he repeats the equivalent statement in order to define it, as follows: I said, “He will take and assume me,” and truly he saved me—that is, he will save my people—from unbelief and original sin. And this is not because of their merits, but because he desired me—that is, solely by his gracious will—as the Apostle says: “Not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Titus 3:5).

And because he will save freely, afterwards the Lord will repay me—that is, my people—according to my righteousness, that is, according to what my people will deserve in accordance with their works, so that “the one who is righteous may be righteous still.” This is an inference from the greater, as the Apostle says: “For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life” (Romans 5:10).

And he will also repay me according to the purity—that is, the innocence—of my hands, that is, of my affections. They are rightly called “hands,” because they are the causes of good works, just as hands are the causes of works. This means: He will repay my people according to what their innocence will deserve—namely, those who will be innocent, that is, who abstain from many vices, will become more innocent, that is, will abstain from still more vices. This again is an inference from the greater.

And he explains according to which righteousness and according to which innocence. According to righteousness, namely because I kept—that is, my people will keep—the ways of the Lord, that is, the commandments of the Lord, through which their fulfillers will come to life; and therefore they are called “ways,” since they will fulfill them with the utmost diligence and observance. And according to innocence he will repay, because I did not act impiously against my God—that is, my people will not act impiously against their God by departing from him.

For these reasons they will keep the ways of the Lord and will not act impiously: because all his judgments are before my eyes—that is, they see all his judgments. This means that they see that, by his hidden judgments, he permits the wicked to be exalted here and the good to be brought low, while in the future he will save the latter and condemn the former. And because this reason would not be sufficient, he adds: “And they will consider those things that are just.”

Although this lies outside the book, it is understood from the words that follow in the book. But since even this second reason is not sufficient, he adds a third: “And I did not cast away his righteous judgments”—that is, my people will not cast them away. This means that they will not displease them, by comparison with those who cast away from themselves whatever they hate.

I say that they will keep his ways and will not act impiously; and they will do this not temporarily, but with him—that is, while I work well with his help—I will persevere unstained; that is, my people will be unstained. And “I will observe myself from my iniquity”—that is, my people will restrain themselves from their iniquity, which has been allowed and forgiven them by God.

And because they will restrain themselves, the Lord will repay me—that is, in the future he will repay my people with blessedness—according to my righteousness, that is, according to the merit of my people’s righteousness, and according to the purity—that is, the innocence—of my hands, that is, of my affections, existing before his eyes, that is, in his good pleasure.

It is as though he were saying: According to the merit of my people’s innocence, which pleases him, as he himself testifies in the Gospel: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:13). And the Apostle says of himself: “From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will repay me” (2 Timothy 4:8). And in the Song of Songs the bridegroom says to the bride: “Come, you will be crowned from the head of Amana, from the summit of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards” (Song of Songs 4:8).

When he says “before his eyes,” he speaks by comparison: whatever pleases us, we often behold with the eyes of the body.

Since above, by twice saying “the Lord will repay me,” he had not explained those repayments, he intends to explain them, making an apostrophe to God with thanksgiving, as follows:

I said that the Lord will repay my Church here according to righteousness, and it is true. For you, God the Father, holy by antonomasia, will be cooperating with the Holy Spirit so that it may become holier. And I said that he will repay it here according to innocence, and it is true. For you, by antonomasia innocent, will be cooperating with an innocent man so that he may become more innocent, that is, abstaining from more vices.

It is as though he were saying: You will cooperate with his holiness and innocence, which merit this from him; and you will do something further: You, the chosen one whom my people will choose in order to obey you, will cooperate with the chosen one—that is, with the one called to salvation—so that he may become innocent. Yet he will not have this from free will alone, namely that he should become innocent after his calling; rather, you will cooperate in it, although his faith will merit it.

And that you will be holy with the holy, innocent with the innocent, and chosen with the chosen can be seen by contrast: for you will pervert yourself with the perverse, cooperating in his perversity. That is, you will be turned from assistance toward perversion together with the one who turns himself away from you. This means: If he had not been perverted from you, you would have assisted him; but because he has turned himself away from you and from the assistance you would have given him, you will be perverted—that is, you will be turned toward the purpose of perverting him by blinding him still further.

He also explains the future repayment as follows: I said that in the future the Lord will repay my people according to their righteousness and purity; and it is true, Lord. For in the future you, who are powerful, will save my humble people by bringing them back to eternity—that is, those who will be humble toward you—according to the saying: “The righteous will go into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46). This can also be seen by contrast: for you will humble—that is, annihilate—the eyes of the proud, that is, their pride, which is understood through the appearance of the eyes.

Having shown the benefits that would arise from his Passion—namely, the salvation of unbelievers—he prays for them, and thus instructs us also to pray for our enemies, as follows:

I said that he will send, take, and assume my people from many waters; and so may it happen, O my God, to whom I do not deny the place of divinity within me, as Adam did: enlighten my darkness with the light of faith—that is, those dark ones who are to become mine. And it is necessary that I pray for this, since they cannot be enlightened through anyone else, because you alone are the one who already enlightens by faith and love my lamp, that is, the apostles, who are my lamp, that is, the vessels of my light. According to the saying: “Let your light shine before men,” and so forth (Matthew 5:16). And it was said of John the Baptist: “He was a burning and shining lamp before the Lord” (John 5:35).

This is an illustration by comparison. I say, “Enlighten the darkness,” and it is beneficial for them that I pray for this, because in this way I shall be rescued from temptation in you—that is, my people, enlightened by trusting in you, will be rescued from temptation. This does not mean that they will not be tempted at all, but that in my God I will pass over the wall—that is, although they are tempted, they will not sin. Rather, through you, whom they will regard as their God, they will pass over the mass of sins, which is a wall set up between sinners and God. Concerning this wall it is said through the prophet: “You have set a cloud before you, so that prayer may not pass through” (Lamentations 3:44). Concerning the removal of the wall the Apostle says: “With the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

Afterwards he makes an apostrophe to his hearers, instructing them that they ought to have him as their God and showing how this may be recognized:

I say that in my God—that is, the God of my people—they will pass over; and rightly, O hearers, I place my hope in him. For he is my God—that is, my people ought to have him as their God—and they can see this from the fact that his way is undefiled, that is, clean innocence, through which one reaches him. They can also see it from the fact that the sayings—that is, the commandments—of that Lord have been tested, that is, approved and perfected by fire through the Holy Spirit. Therefore they ought still to make him their God, because, if they do this, you will protect them. For he is the protector of all who hope in him—not in earthly things. According to the saying: “The one who comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

And therefore they ought still to make him their God. For who is God besides God? Or I may put it this way: Who is God besides our God, who is my God and the God of my people? None, understood. It is as though he were saying: They ought to have him as their God because no other is to be called God.

And it can also be seen through the benefits conferred on me by him that he is God—namely, because that God is the one who girded me with strength so that I would not give way in the Passion. He fortified me by comparison with a soldier who is girded with a sword so that he may be protected by it. And he made my way blameless, that is, he gave me firm innocence—the clean way through which, insofar as I am human, I may reach his glory—as the Apostle says: “Holy, innocent, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 3:26).

And truly he is God, who perfected—that is, made perfect—my feet, that is, my affections, by which the soul walks just as the body walks by its feet, like the feet of deer—that is, in the manner of deer’s feet—so that, just as they are ready to leap over thickets, so my affections are ready to leap over every vice. And he is the one who establishes me in hope upon the heights, that is, in the heights, namely the heavenly places.

And truly he is God, who teaches my hands for battle, that is, makes my affections learned for fighting against the devil. He calls affections “hands” because through them we defeat the devil, just as someone defeats an enemy with his hands.

Afterwards he makes an apostrophe to God, giving thanks with great affection:

I say that you have taught my hands; and you have made my arms—that is, my strength—like a bronze bow, that is, an unyielding bow, as a bronze bow would be unyielding if one could find such a thing. This is a comparison with something that does not exist. He uses “arms” for strength because strength is accustomed to reside in the arms.

And through me you made it bronze; you gave me—that is, you will give my people—the protection of salvation, that is, your salvation. That is, you will protect them so that they do not give way; and that protection will be the cause of their salvation. And your right hand received me in the future—that is, by your grace placing them at your right hand, it will receive my people. According to the saying: “Come, blessed ones,” and so forth (Matthew 25:34).

And meanwhile your discipline—that is, temporal adversity permitted by you so that they may become more glorious—corrected me unto the end, that is, will correct my people completely. Concerning this it is said through Solomon: “My son, do not neglect the Lord’s discipline, nor grow weary when you are rebuked by him” (Proverbs 3:11; Hebrews 12:5).

And he explains in parts how he will correct them, as follows: “And that is”—namely, that same discipline of yours, of which I have spoken here—“will teach me,” that is, it will teach some of my people who need to be purified to some degree so that they may not fall again, according to the Apostle: “God scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:9, 6).

And through discipline you enlarged my steps, that is, you will make those who have been enlarged in your love perfect. They are called my “steps” because they carry me into the knowledge of others. “Beneath me”: by discipline you will bring them under me, that is, you will make them more humble toward me, as in the Acts of the Apostles: “They went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41). And the Apostle says: “We ourselves had within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we might not trust in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead” (2 Corinthians 1:9).

And when they are enlarged through discipline, my footsteps are not weakened—that is, the marks of my virtues impressed upon their hearts will not be weakened in them. For according to the Apostle: “Power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

And by my steps I will pursue my enemies—that is, the faithful who make themselves my enemies by their evil life. And I will overtake them; that is, I will rationally convict them of error, as is read concerning Stephen: “They could not resist the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke” (Acts 6:10).

And I will not turn back—that is, I will not cease pursuing and overtaking them until they fall away from unbelief. And they will fall away through this: that I will break them—that is, destroy their earthliness—as the Psalmist says elsewhere: “You will break them like a potter’s vessel” (Psalm 2:9).

And once broken, they will no longer be able to stand—that is, persevere—in their unbelief, but will fall beneath my feet—that is, they will be humbled beneath me, like those who humbly prostrate themselves at the feet of the wealthy.

And so that the steps may be effective for pursuing and overtaking them, you girded me—that is, you fortified my people with strength for battle, for defeating those enemies. And through those who were girded, you overthrew—that is, will defeat—those rising up against me, reducing them beneath me; that is, you will subject the Jews to me. Concerning them the Psalmist says elsewhere: “Unjust witnesses rose up against me” (Psalm 26:12).

And through them you gave me—that is, will give me—the backs of my enemies, that is, the Gentiles, as my followers and imitators, by comparison with those who go behind another’s back. Above he said this universally when he said, “They will fall beneath my feet”; here he shows it in parts.

And you destroyed—that is, will destroy—those who hate me, that is, those unwilling to convert, by removing their place and nation, so that afterwards they will not return to their homeland. But they cried out, and there was no one to save them—that is, they will cry out in the synagogues, praying that they may be brought back. Nor will there be anyone to save them by bringing them back from exile.

I say that they will cry out to the Lord, not to a foreign god. And he did not hear—that is, will not hear—them so as to bring them back.

And they will not merely become exiles; I will also crush them in their strength, so that they will be like dust before the face of the wind. Just as crushed dust, consolidated by no rain, is quickly carried away and scattered by the force of the wind, so they, crushed in their strength and unwilling to be consolidated by the rain of teaching, will quickly be carried away and destroyed by the evil spirit.

And not only this: I will also erase them from the glory in which they now are, making them like the mud of the streets—that is, vile and to be trampled by every passerby, just as mud is vile and trampled. And he rightly adds “of the streets,” for the mud of the streets is trampled more frequently. They will be erased in a way they least expect.

But me, whom they think they can overcome, you will rescue by making me rise again from the contradictions of the people who say: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John 9:16). That is, they will no longer be able to contradict me.

And when I have been rescued, you will establish me as head of the nations, that is, you will make me head of the nations, as the Psalmist says elsewhere: “I will give you the nations” (Psalm 2:8). And in Hosea: “I will say to the one who was not my people, ‘You are my people’” (Hosea 2:23).

And since one might ask whether he would possess the nations, he responds by making an apostrophe to his hearers, in order to make those nations subject to him by magnifying them:

Truly I will become head of the nations, for the people whom I did not know—that is, whom I appeared not to know, because I did not give them the Law or prophets—served—that is, will serve—me. And they will not be slow to do this, but at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me—that is, as soon as the bodily ear receives my preaching, they will immediately obey me.

And “ear” is rightly placed as a reproach to the Jews, because although they heard both with the ear and through the testimony of the Scriptures, they did not wish to believe with understanding. The Gentiles, however, lacking the Scriptures, assented through hearing alone.

I say that the Gentiles will obey; but my sons—that is, the Jews, who ought to be my sons, but who have become alienated from me through their own fault—according to the prophetic saying, “I nourished and exalted sons, but they despised me” (Isaiah 1:2)—lied, that is, they will lie. And this will happen to my honor, when those sons say: “The disciples stole him, and they told the people, ‘He has risen’” (from the conclusion of Matthew).

And this was to the Lord’s honor. For when they said that the disciples had stolen him while the guards were sleeping, it clearly became evident that this was a lie. For how could those who were sleeping at that time have known that the disciples were stealing Christ’s body?

And through the fact that the alienated sons will lie, they have grown old—that is, they will remain in the old age of Adam, unwilling to be renewed through Christ’s resurrection. And they, having grown old, will limp—that is, they will err by departing from their paths, that is, from the subtle meanings of their Scriptures.

A person is called lame when he walks correctly with one foot but unevenly with the other. So they too will limp: they will have one correct understanding in the Scriptures, namely the literal one, but the other will be crooked, namely the allegorical one.

And truly they will lie, for the Lord lives—that is, I, who have been established as Lord by the Father, live in reality, although they said that I would not rise, according to the saying: “He will rise on the third day” (Mark 8:31).

And because I live, blessed—that is, praised—be my God, both by me and by my people. And let God, the author of salvation—that is, of my resurrection—be exalted—that is, glorified through my resurrection: God, I say, who magnifies—that is, will magnify by his mighty works—the deliverances of his king, according to the Apostle: “Those whom he justified, these he also glorified” (Romans 8:30).

He will make great, I say, those who are to be saved by me, who am his king, according to the saying: “I have been established as king by him” (Psalm 2:6). He uses “salvations” emphatically. I say that he magnifies them, and this not because of their merits, but first by showing—that is, by showing in the future—mercy to Christ, that is, to his king David, namely to me, by raising me up; and afterwards to his seed, that is, to his spiritual sons, extending mercy to them from generation to generation into the age to come.

The words inserted here, “God, who gives,” and so forth, are an apostrophe to God with thanksgiving for what he showed above that the Father would give. He says it as follows:

I say, “Blessed be God,” and so may it be. Blessed are you, God, who give—that is, will give—me vengeance upon the Jews, as he showed above in this way: “You destroyed those who hate me,” and “I will crush them,” and “I will erase them.” And blessed are you who subject—that is, will subject—peoples beneath me, as I said above: “They will fall beneath my feet,” and “the people whom I did not know,” and so forth.

And therefore may you still be blessed, because you will be my deliverer, so that I do not yield to my enraged enemies, namely the Jews, who, solely because of anger, will strike me with scourges and kill me. One is called “enraged” who becomes angry easily and without reason.

And you will not only deliver me, but you will exalt me by making me not yield: me, I say, rescued from those rising up against me, that is, from their power. And before you exalt me, you will rescue me by resurrecting me from the unjust man, that is, from the power of the Jews. They are called “man” in the singular because they are one in iniquity.

And because you will exalt and rescue me, I will confess to you among the nations, Lord—that is, I will produce true confessors—and among the Gentiles, as the same is said in the Gospel: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice” (John 10:16).

And I will not confess with the mouth alone; rather, for your name—that is, for the honor of your name—I will sing a psalm, that is, I will cause those Gentiles to praise you by good works.

Through these acts of thanksgiving, he instructs us to render acts of thanksgiving to God.

## Psalm XVIII

The title of the eighteenth Psalm: “A Psalm, to be attributed to David the prophet; directed toward the end,” that is, looking toward Christ; or “toward the end of time,” that is, in the time of fullness, whence the Apostle says: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10:11).

The prophet, foreseeing that preachers would be sent by God for the instruction of the Church, and that through their marvelous office the Law would be presented through the Holy Spirit—an immaculate and holy Law—intends, for the instruction of their successors, to proclaim joyfully, as though it were present, what will come to pass through the activity of the Holy Spirit.

54. “The heavens declare the glory of God”—that is, the apostles, who on account of the sublimity of their virtues are rightly called “heavens.” They will proclaim openly the glorious essence of the Son of God, as the evangelist John says: “In the beginning was the Word,” and so forth (John 1:1). And, from another perspective, these same heavens—called the firmament—announce his works, that is, the holy works which proceeded from his hands, meaning from his affections: works which he performed while existing bodily as a human being, as the Apostle says: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2). And he rightly calls them the firmament here, for since they were firm in announcing this, they were the firmament of faith for the weaker.

Although, in proclaiming Christ as God and man—even though dead, afflicted, and surrounded by human necessities—they would be judged foolish by unbelievers for announcing him nevertheless as Lord of all, king, and consubstantial with the Father, yet in this they remained firm and immovable, never blushing with shame, as the Apostle says: “I am not ashamed of the Gospel, for it is the power of God” (Rom. 1:16); and elsewhere: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. 1:25).

Because he had said that they would announce the glory and the works, lest we think that they would indiscriminately announce everything to everyone, he foretells that they will do this with discernment, as follows: I say that they will announce both the glory and the works, and they will do so with discernment. “For day pours forth the word to day, and night declares knowledge to night”—that is, those who are called “day,” namely, those who are bright and radiant in teaching, pour forth the Word to those who are “day,” that is, splendid in understanding, as Paul did to Dionysius. The essence of the Word of God is brought forth to them from the profound and inward wisdom given to them by God, like something produced by one belching up what is within. Hence the Apostle says: “Comparing spiritual things with spiritual” (1 Cor. 2:13).

And those who themselves are “night,” that is, small and not very radiant in teaching in comparison with those who are “night” in understanding—namely, small and not radiant—declare knowledge to them: that is, they declare those things which their knowledge, meaning secular understanding, cannot grasp. Hence the Apostle says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. 3:2); and elsewhere: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal” (ibid.). And they do this wonderfully.

“For there are neither utterances nor speeches,” and so forth—that is, there are no languages so diverse, nor speeches so ornamented, whether in dialectic or rhetoric, in which their voices are not heard. He uses “of which” in place of the ablative, according to Greek usage: there is no language, nor any ornament of speech, which they do not know, and to which they cannot adapt their voices, as in the Acts of the Apostles: “The apostles were speaking in various languages” (Acts 2:4).

And they will not announce these things secretly or to a few, but broadly. “For their sound has gone forth”—that is, their fame will go forth—“into all the earth, and their words”—that is, their preaching—“to the ends of the inhabited world.” Hence the Prophet says: “Tell it in the islands that are far away: He who scattered Israel will gather him,” and so forth (Jer. 31:10).

I say that they announce these things, and that God the Father “placed his tabernacle in the sun”—that is, he placed the Lord, the human being in whom his Word waged war, amid the heat of tribulations, after the manner of cavalrymen who fight in military tents; and the one so placed endured this willingly. But he who had fought through the prophets himself exulted in his own person to run the course—that is, to complete quickly the Father’s obedience, which was his way to glory—from the time when he proceeded from the bridal chamber, that is, from the Virgin’s womb, his own—that is, appropriate to him. I say that he existed as a bridegroom, truly made in that moment the bridegroom of human flesh, which he then joined to himself.

According to his divinity, I say, he is the bridegroom of his flesh. Concerning this betrothal, the bride Church says to the Synagogue in the Song of Songs: “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon with the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal” (Song 3:11). He is also the bridegroom of the Church—not to the same degree as in the Song of Songs: “How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride” (Song 4:10)—but he is the bridegroom of the Church according only to the adoption of grace. He is the bridegroom of his flesh according to the union of person.

He calls the Virgin’s womb a bridal chamber because the Word of God was joined there to the flesh as a bridegroom is joined to his bride in a bridal chamber.

I say that he exulted to run the course, and in running it he was not weak, but was like a giant—that is, strong, comparable to a giant whom no one can hinder. I say that he proceeded, and although he proceeded from the Virgin’s bridal chamber, nevertheless his going forth—that is, his generation—was from the highest heaven, that is, from the Father, who is called “heaven” on account of the dignity and sublimity of divinity.

“Highest” is said not because the Father is greater than the Son, but because the Son was ineffably begotten from him, according to the saying: “Who will declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). And although, according to his going forth, he is another person, nevertheless his meeting extends to his own summit—that is, he meets at the summit of his divinity, namely, the Father’s. This means: although he is another in person, he is nevertheless equal in essence.

He rightly speaks of “course,” by comparison with those who meet one another so that they may come together into one mass. Thus the Son meets the Father at the summit: that is, he is united with him in divinity.

According to the Hebrew translation, in which we read, “He placed his tabernacle in the sun, in them,” it may be explained in this way: I said that the heavens declare the glory and the works, and that their sound has gone forth into all the earth and their words to the ends of the inhabited world—and this is true, because in them, that is, through them, God placed his tabernacle, namely, the humanity of his Son, in the sun, that is, in the open and manifest place, which the prophets had foretold obscurely. Through them also he placed in the sun the fact that he himself, proceeding like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber, exulted like a giant to run the course. The exposition does not change.

Behold the manifestation of the works and of knowledge. Thus above he said that the firmament announces the works of his hands, and that night declares knowledge; and through them he placed the Lord’s glory in the sun—namely, that his going forth was from the highest heaven and that his course reached to the summit of that heaven. The exposition of this also does not change.

He uses “sun,” because it is open to all, to signify what is open. And although he is so great that his going forth is from the highest heaven and his course reaches to the summit, there is no one among his hearers who can hide himself from his heat—that is, no one who can protect his unbelief by arguments from the assault of his Spirit, who speaks through his preachers.

He speaks of hiding by comparison with combatants, who conceal themselves by protecting themselves beneath shields. These unbelievers, seeking to hide themselves, protect themselves with human arguments and make themselves excusable; but they cannot, according to Solomon: “There is neither strength nor wisdom against God” (Prov. 21:30).

He calls the Holy Spirit “heat,” because just as heat dissolves water hardened into ice, so the Holy Spirit loosens those hardened in sins and unbelief, making them relaxed in faith and virtues. Concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel: “When he comes”—that is, when he is given to the apostles and speaks through them—“he will convict the world”—that is, he will render worldly people inexcusable—“concerning sin, indeed, because they did not believe in me.” This means that he will prove them inexcusable for not believing in him, that is, on account of their unbelief. This is properly called “sin” by antonomasia, since the virtue of faith is the foundation of all virtues.

“Concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer” (John 16:8–10). Previously they used to say that they could not be justified, since they had no just person at all in comparison with whom they might become just. But concerning the righteousness which they refuse to possess, they will no longer be excusable. For I am entirely just and without blemish, and after my example they can possess righteousness. By this the Holy Spirit will prove me to be entirely just and without blemish: “because I go to the Father,” and therefore you will no longer see me afflicted, distressed, and crucified bodily, as you saw me; from now on I shall be glorious and immortal. For unless I were entirely just and without blemish, I would not become immortal by ascending so gloriously to the Father.

“Concerning judgment, indeed, because the prince of this world has already been judged” (ibid.). It is as though he said: Previously, by judgment—that is, by the condemnation of original sin—they excused themselves concerning unbelief and righteousness, saying, “Why should we have faith and righteousness? We shall never be so faithful and just that we do not undergo judgment, that is, the condemnation of original sin.” But concerning this judgment—that is, by means of this judgment—they will no longer be able to excuse themselves, because the prince of this world, namely the devil, who until now possessed the world’s judgment, has already been judged by me. That is, the dominion of his power has been removed, so that he may no longer possess original right over the faithful and the just.

Having explained this digression, let us return to the psalm. I say that there is no one who can hide himself from his heat. Through this heat the law will be given. And the law of the Lord, namely of the Son, was given through his heat as immaculate; he explains this by saying that it converts souls from sins, not merely bodies, as the old law did, which withdraws the members from sins through fear of punishment, but not the wills. This is as if he said: It is immaculate—that is, it makes people immaculate—with assisting grace cooperating.

“And the testimony,” that is, the law of the Lord, “is faithful,” that is, it makes people faithful. The law is called a testimony because, just as a testimony left by a father to his son is a pledge and guarantee of inheritance, so the law left to us by God is an eternal pledge and earnest of our inheritance.

And this testimony “gives wisdom to the little ones,” that is, to the humble: spiritual understanding, according to the Gospel saying: “You have hidden these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to little ones” (Luke 10:21).

“And the judgments of the Lord are right,” that is, his precepts are rightly called right. This is proved by the fact that the very author of the precepts first fulfilled them, as in the Acts of the Apostles: “The things which Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1). And they are “making the hearts of the faithful glad,” not grieving them through fear of punishment as the old law did, according to the Lord in the Gospel: “My yoke is sweet, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30).

“And the commandment of the Lord is enlightening the eyes of the heart in understanding.” This is equivalent to what he said above, “giving wisdom to the little ones,” but he repeats it here in order to insert the reason why it enlightens the eyes: namely, because it is luminous, that is, manifest to understanding, and not obscure like the old law.

“And through that commandment the holy fear of the Lord is conceived,” that is, the fear which makes people holy, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “He who fears God will do good” (Ecclus. 15:1).

Since there are two fears—servile fear and chaste fear—and both are holy, for both cause people to cease from sins, he determines which one he intends here: “the fear,” he says, “which endures forever and ever,” that is, which, once possessed, will endure always—namely, chaste fear. Concerning this the Apostle says: “Charity never fails” (1 Cor. 13:8). Servile fear, however, is expelled when chaste fear arrives, as the Apostle John testifies: “Perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

He set forth these praises of God’s law in order to commend it to those who would receive it as successors. He repeats two of the praises mentioned above, adding another which he had not previously stated, so that from these he might add something further.

“And because the judgments of the Lord”—that is, the precepts judged worthy to be fulfilled in the Lord’s law—“are true,” this is what he said above, that the judgments are right; and because they are “justified,” that is, make people just, this is what he stated above by saying that the holy fear of the Lord makes people holy.

But the third point which follows had not been stated previously: namely, that they are “going forth in themselves,” that is, harmonious with one another, not discordant like secular judgments. They are “more desirable than gold and much precious stone,” that is, they ought to be desired above gold and many precious stones. By these highest riches he indicates that they are more desirable than all riches.

And they are “sweeter to the souls of the faithful than honey and the honeycomb.” This is an intransitive construction, meaning “than the honey of the honeycomb,” which is more pleasing than honey that has already been expressed. Alternatively, it may be read non-intransitively, since both kinds of honey are sufficiently pleasing. Through these two delights, which are exceedingly sweet, he indicates that they are sweeter than all delights, as elsewhere in the Psalms: “How sweet are your sayings to my throat” (Ps. 118:103).

He demonstrates this authoritatively as follows: Truly they are desirable and sweeter. “For your servant,” that is, one who does not make himself free of you but your servant, wholly obedient to you, “keeps them.” He keeps them in a manner he otherwise would not: not unwillingly, but diligently and with the greatest care he fulfills them, and he keeps them for his own good. “For in keeping them there is great reward.”

He rightly says “in keeping them,” for this reward is solely the reward which will be repaid in the future for those things kept. But this is also what they are allowed to be kept by God with the greatest reward.

I say that your servant keeps your judgments. But who understands sins as things to be kept? No one, certainly—not even the one who commits them. Therefore, Lord, cleanse me from my hidden sins, which arise from the hidden tinder of my sin. For this reason they are called hidden.

“And from the sins of others”—by taking me away from them—“spare your servant,” that is, spare me, so that I may not be defiled by those things which arise from the suggestions of others or from the prompting of the devil. For this reason they are called “others’,” concerning which the Wise Man says: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” (Prov. 1:10).

I say: cleanse me and spare me. And you will do this for my good. For if sins do not dominate me—that is, if they do not possess me in their dominion so that I serve them—“for everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34)—then I shall be immaculate, that is, innocent.

And then I shall be cleansed, that is, I shall be clean from the greatest sin, namely pride. Pride is rightly called the greatest sin because through it we first departed from God. For when we are disobedient, we are proud against God. And through that same pride many are finally conquered, when, after trampling down their vices, they glory in themselves because of their holiness. Hence Prosper says: “Only pride must be guarded against in upright deeds.”

Alternatively, it may be understood as follows: If my enemies—that is, the sins I mentioned—do not dominate me, and if they are not changed, then sins are said not to dominate when, although the tinder alone prompts, the act does not follow, nor does consent. Hence the Apostle says: “Therefore let sin not reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires” (Rom. 6:12). It is as though he said: Sin is in our mortal body, but let it not reign.

Once I have been cleansed, “the words of my mouth will be such as to please you,” that is, my praises, prophecies, and prayers will please you—things which otherwise would not please you. “For praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9).

And not only will my words please you, but also “the meditation of my heart,” that is, whatever I meditate upon will always be in your sight, that is, in your good pleasure; it will always please you, O Lord, my helper—that is, my co-worker, so that I may act well—and my redeemer from vices, so that I may not sin.

## IN PSALM XIX

Title of the nineteenth psalm: “A psalm of David the prophet. For the end,” that is, looking toward Christ. Or “for the end,” that is, toward the consummation of the ages, as in the preceding psalm.

The Prophet, foreseeing that Christ our king would fight on our behalf against the devil, and that he would also be our priest when he offered his body and soul to God on the cross, prays to God the Father on his behalf, asking that he hear him when he prays for himself in his Passion. He also asks that he not yield and that he rise again. And on behalf of the human race, he asks that God hear him praying for its salvation, fulfill his desires, and confirm his plans.

He does not pray for this because it is necessary to pray on Christ’s behalf, but in order to show that this will happen. He also indicates, by the example of his contemporaries, how great the desire for this event was. To us as well, in the time of fulfillment, he leaves an example of the good love which we ought to have toward Christ.

“May he hear you, O Christ”—that is, may the Lord, the Father or the Trinity, hear you praying for yourself and your members, so that you may obtain what you ask. “In the day of tribulation,” that is, in the time of the Passion, when you will pray in affection, words, and obedience, as will be explained below.

I say, may he hear you in this: May he protect you, who will fight on our behalf in the Passion, so that you do not yield. And “may the name of the God of Jacob” be the cause of this—that is, may this be the reason: that you seek to magnify the name of the Father, whom Jacob regards as God, that is, the God of strong wrestlers against vices.

Or, he is called the God of Jacob because he will be not only the God of the Jews but also of the Gentiles, who are “Jacob,” that is, those who supplant the blessing, and the younger ones, as Jacob was younger and also supplanted Esau (Gen. 27:36).

I say that the name of the God of Jacob is to be magnified, as in the Gospel: “I do not seek my own glory, but that of him who sent me” (John 7 and 8).

When he prays that Christ, fighting on our behalf, be protected, he presents him as king, for it belongs to kings to fight for the salvation of their kingdom. May he not only protect you, but also “send,” that is, give you assistance. This means: May he be your helper, so that you may conquer death and the devil.

“And may this come from the holy place,” that is, because of your holiness, which is so great that he may help you. “And may he guard you”—the same as he said above, “may he protect you”; he repeats it in order to add the reason.

From Zion, that is, may he guard you because of your “watchfulness,” since you contemplate eternal things and the future restoration of human beings. “From” is a causal particle. “And may he remember,” so that he may bring it to fulfillment, “all your sacrifice,” that is, each of the injuries and acts of obedience which you will suffer for human beings, and which will be sweet sacrifices to God.

“And your burnt offering”—that is, that supreme sacrifice in which you will offer yourself wholly to God for us on the cross—“may it be made fat,” that is, pleasing to God, by comparison with fat animals, which were pleasing for sacrifice.

He rightly says “burnt offering”: *holon* means “whole,” while *causis* signifies burning; he himself was a burnt offering, that is, wholly consumed, both in body and soul, by the fire of the Passion.

Here he presents Christ as a priest, for it belongs to priests to sacrifice for the people. When Christ thus sacrificed to God, he prayed to the Father through that very obedience for his resurrection and for the salvation of his members.

“May he grant you according to your heart,” that is, whatever your heart desires: namely, to rise again and save human beings. This has the same meaning as what he said above, “May he remember all your sacrifice.” But he states it in this way in order to show, through the excess of his affection, that Christ would pray not only by his obedience but also with the good affection of his heart on our behalf.

And since he would not merely possess some kind of affection of heart, but an affection ordered through the highest and ineffable plans, “may he confirm all your counsel,” that is, make all your plans firm and effective: namely, that blindness should come upon Israel, according to the Apostle, “until the fullness of the Gentiles enters” (Rom. 11:25), and that the old bond of Adam should be dissolved by your death, along with many other things which are ineffable.

When this happens, “we”—I and those like me—“shall rejoice in your salvation,” that is, in your saving work. And we shall not merely rejoice: we who do good works here “in your name,” that is, for the honor of your name and not for our own honor, “shall be magnified,” that is, through you we shall be great and glorious in participation in your immortality and blessing, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “The just will shine like the sun” (Matt. 13:43). And the Apostle says: “Those whom he called, he also magnified” [variant: “glorified”] (Rom. 8:30).

After inserting this, he returns to the prayer as follows: I say, may he remember. “And may he grant you according to your heart, and may the Lord fulfill all your petitions,” namely: “Father, glorify your Son” (John 17:1); and elsewhere: “Father, I will that where I am, my minister also may be there” (John 12:26).

This could be understood above, where he said, “May he grant you,” and so forth. But he states it here in order to indicate that Christ would pray not only through desire but also in words.

And lest anyone think that he prays out of uncertainty, but rather that he knows with complete certainty that what he prays for will happen, he confirms it as follows: Although I pray in this way—“May he grant you,” and so forth—“now I know,” that is, I am already certain. I shall not know only when it happens that the Lord has saved—that is, will save—his Christ, namely Jesus; that is, that he will raise him from the dead. And he will hear him praying for his members.

And this will be from his holy heaven, that is, because Christ is his holy heaven in the sublimity of virtues; here “from” is causal. Or, he will hear this, namely that those who are saved—those who are emphatically called “salvation” because they have been saved through him—“will be powerful in his powers,” that is, in the powers of his right hand. They will be powerful in virtues, which are called God’s “right hand” because they are more excellent than present goods, just as the right hand is more excellent than the left.

Present goods are called the “left,” because they are less worthy, as the bride says of the bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song 2:6).

I say that the saved will be powerful in the right hand. But these others, who are not saved, will be powerful in chariots, and others in horses. This means: They will be powerful in secular pomp, some more, others less. Greater pomp is signified by chariots; lesser pomp by horses. For the triumph celebrated in chariots was greater than that celebrated on horses.

I say that they will be powerful in chariots and horses. But we, doing good works in the name of the Lord our God and despising such things, will call upon him—that is, we shall pray to him with our voice, our deeds, and our good affection.

I said that they will be powerful in chariots and horses. Through this they think themselves happy, standing firmly and ready to do everything. But by this very means they have been bound, that is, hindered from working out their salvation. And those who think that they stand well have fallen into the death of vices.

But we, whom they consider oppressed, have risen through good works from sins; and not through ourselves, but we have been raised upright by you.

I said that we shall rejoice in Christ’s salvation and shall be magnified. In order that this may happen, Lord Father, save your kingly Son by raising him from the dead. And you, O king, having been heard, hear us: lead us out from the condemnation of original sin—that is, me and those conformed to me—on the day when we call upon you, that is, as soon as we pray to you. That is, we shall call upon you as soon as we pray to you: those who are alive in works and devotion, but those who are dead in spiritual affection.

## IN PSALM XX

Title of the twentieth psalm: “For the end, a psalm of David.” Here too it is explained as in the preceding psalm.

The Prophet intends to announce, for the sake of our faith and that of his contemporaries, what he prayed for in the preceding psalm: namely, that Christ would act courageously, save the world, and justly condemn his enemies, both in this age and in the future. He says this as follows:

“Lord Father, the king”—that is, Jesus, your Son—“will rejoice in your strength,” that is, you will give him the strength of steadfastness in the Passion; and he will act so courageously in it that by rising again he will attain the joy of victory.

And he will not rejoice only because of your strength, but will “exult greatly over your salvation,” that is, over those whom you will save through him. Or, he will exult greatly while looking toward your salvation, that is, while considering those whom you will save through him.

And truly he will rejoice and exult. For “you have granted”—that is, you will grant—“him the desire of his heart,” namely, to rise again and save the world. “And you have not defrauded him”—that is, you will not diminish—“the desire of his lips,” namely, the good will with which he will pray through his lips that he may rise again and save the world.

This is the same thing he said earlier: “You have granted him the desire of his heart.” But he repeats it here in order to show that he would not only desire this, but would also pray for it.

Alternatively, “you have not defrauded him” may mean that you have not denied him the desire of his lips. And behold the reason why you will grant it and will not defraud him: “For you have gone before him”—that is, you will cause him to go before all others—“with blessings of sweetness,” that is, with the exaltations of the sweetness of virtues. You will exalt him above all the saints in the sweetness of virtues, to such a degree that there will be no sin in him, something which will happen to no one else, according to the saying: “No one is clean from uncleanness, not even an infant whose life is one day upon the earth” (Job 14:4).

Or, “you have gone before him” means that at the beginning of his incarnation you will place him in blessings of sweetness, that is, in freedom from sin, and in virtues, whereas others ordinarily are first placed under the curses of original sin, which is erased in baptism. Through this he will be worthy not to be defrauded.

He explains that desire as follows: because he will become so worthy that you will thus go before him, “you have placed”—that is, you will give—“upon his head,” that is, at the beginning of his preaching, “a crown,” namely, a gathering of the faithful, by which he will be surrounded and adorned, just as a head is adorned by a crown.

A crown, I say, “of precious stone,” that is, of precious stones—namely, of the apostles, who are radiant in virtues and dear to God, just as a precious stone is radiant and dear to all.

And afterward “he asked for life”—that is, he will ask life of you both in affection and in good works. “And you granted”—that is, you will grant—“him,” after the completion of his obedience, “length of days,” that is, a very long life, lasting through this present age and through the succeeding age of this age, forever, as the Apostle Paul says: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more,” and so forth (Rom. 6:9).

And he will desire to possess great glory in the resurrection. “And great will be his glory in your salvation,” that is, in your saving work, when you raise him from the dead.

And he will desire to possess glorious and beautiful members. And you will place—that is, establish—upon him, so that he may be their foundation and head, “glory,” that is, glorious members, and “great beauty,” that is, magnificently beautiful members in virtue and holiness. Hence the Apostle says: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets,” and so forth (Eph. 2:20). And it will be fitting that these things be placed upon him.

“For you will give him in the blessings of his members,” that is, in their exaltations, so that he may exalt his own in virtues from generation to generation, forever and ever.

After inserting the reason, he returns to the good things which the Father will give him, which he began to enumerate: I said that he will desire, and you will place great beauty upon him. And he will also desire to rejoice in the joy of the blessedness of his own in the future.

“And you will make him glad with the joy of his own,” which they will possess “with your face,” that is, when they are in your presence in heaven. Hence the Apostle says: “We shall be caught up to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:17).

And rightly will he have all these things through you: “For the king himself hopes”—that is, he will place his hope—in you, Lord, not in earthly things, and therefore he will not be moved from his good purpose, trusting in the mercy of his Most High, as in the Gospel: “Not my will, but yours be done” (Luke 22:42).

He turns in address to the king himself, concerned with those who are to be saved and announcing what will happen to those who are to be condemned:

I said that you will be glorious in this way, as will be shown by what happens. And when you are thus glorious, “may your hand”—that is, the power of your virtue—“be found by all your enemies,” both Jews and Gentiles, that is, may they recognize you as powerful and turn to you.

He uses “hand” for “power,” because we work with our hands and possess strength through them. And if they cannot find you by themselves, since they are weak, may “your right hand”—that is, the power of your mercy—find all who hate you, both Jews and Gentiles unwilling to believe in you and obey you.

He does not say “all” because all will in fact be found, but because, out of his great affection, he prays for all. I pray that you may find all who hate you.

And truly you will find many, even if not all. But those whom you do not find, “you will place like a furnace of fire,” that is, like a burning furnace. For just as a furnace burns inwardly, so they will burn inwardly with an evil conscience, “at the time of your face,” that is, of your anger—namely, on the day of judgment. Hence Paul says: “Their conscience bearing witness, and their thoughts accusing one another” (Rom. 2:15).

Because anger usually appears in the face, he uses “face” for “anger,” as the Psalmist says elsewhere: “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Ps. 33:16).

And they will not merely be placed like a furnace; the Lord will also trouble them with sadness and fear, “in his anger,” that is, when he will appear angry to them, saying: “Depart from me, accursed ones,” and so forth (Matt. 25:41). And once troubled, he will devour them, that is, the eternal fire will engulf them, as in the Gospel: “These will go into eternal punishment” (Matt. 25:46).

And you will not merely trouble them, but you will also destroy “their fruit,” that is, their children, namely their imitators, by erasing them from the land of the living, as the Psalmist says elsewhere: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous” (Ps. 69:29).

And not only from the land of the living: here also you will destroy “their seed,” that is, those same children of theirs, by separating them here from the children of human beings—that is, from the faithful of the Church, who are imitators of the prophets and apostles, who were “human beings,” that is, rational.
