I said that you will place and trouble them, and rightly so. “For they turned evil things against you,” which they feared would come upon them if they made you their king—namely, the loss of their place and nation. For they wanted you to suffer the evil of the Passion so that they would not lose their place and nation.

Hence Caiaphas said: “It is expedient that one man should die, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John 11:50).

And they devised plans which they could not establish, that is, they could not keep me in death, as they themselves said to Pilate: “Order the tomb to be guarded” (Matt. 27:64), and so forth. And from this blindness will come upon them, so that they devise these plans.

“For you will place them as a back,” that is, rejected by you, like something cast behind one’s back; he emphatically calls them “back.” And lest we think that he would afterward show mercy to no one, he determines this by adding:

I say that you will place them as a back, but not all of them. For you will still “prepare”—that is, restore—“their face,” that is, the sight of their mind, which has been extinguished by unbelief. And this not in all, but “in the remnants,” that is, in those whom you will leave to be saved, as the Apostle says: “The remnants will be saved” (Rom. 9:27).

Or, “you will prepare their face in your remnants,” that is, through Elijah and Enoch, whom you have left alive for this work.

And in order that all these things may happen, O Lord, “be exalted,” that is, appear powerful, “in your virtue,” that is, by exercising the power I have mentioned: by rising again, glorifying your own, and destroying your enemies.

But we shall sing and praise your virtues, that is, celebrate these virtues of yours with the song of good affection and with a psalm, that is, through good works. This means: To the honor of your virtues we shall think and act well.

## IN PSALM XXI

Title of the twenty-first psalm: “For the end, for the taking up at dawn, a psalm of David.”

This is explained as follows: This psalm is to be attributed to David, that is, to Christ, who is striving toward the end—that is, toward the victory which is the end of the course of his obedience.

Where we have here “for the end,” the Hebrews have “for the victor.” Or “for the end,” that is, toward perseverance. David, I say, is acting “for the taking up at dawn,” that is, for the resurrection which occurred in the morning, in which God took him up from humility to glory and from mortality to immortality.

In the Hebrew translation, however, it reads “for the morning hind,” which has the same meaning in substance. It is as though he said: Acting for the morning hind—that is, for the joy of the hind, namely of his humanity, which would rejoice at dawn. This means: for the joy of the resurrection.

The hind signifies Christ’s humanity by comparison. For it belongs to hinds, and also to stags, to rejoice greatly at dawn, at the coming of day; so Christ’s humanity rejoiced at its morning resurrection at the coming of eternity.

He rightly uses the feminine “hind,” since the humanity of the incarnate Word is called his bride.

And here the voice is that of the Head, proposing something which might cause doubt, so that he may explain afterward why God, although Christ was so just, appeared to abandon him in the Passion, since he permitted him to be afflicted in this way.

He also prays concerning steadfastness in the Passion and concerning the resurrection, especially in order to instruct our faith. He also indicates the manner of his Passion and what fruit will result from it. He says this as follows:

God, who are God of all in common, and my God in particular, that is, personally united to me; or, my God, whom I specially obey above all others: look upon me, helping me lest I fall, and so that I may rise again—me whom the Jews, judging me vile, disdain to regard with pity. What he briefly says here, “look upon me,” he explains at length in what follows. I say, “My God”; and since you are specially my God, it seems necessary to ask: Why have you forsaken me? That is, why have you appeared to have forsaken me? The explanation follows.

[Col. 0719A] The words of my sins—namely, of my future members—are the petitions that my future members make for the cleansing of their sins: they ask that you be far from my bodily salvation, that is, that you not save me from bodily death. He does not say “words” because they act through words, but because, just as someone makes a petition with words, so they cried out to him through the miseries of their sins, as the Lord said to Cain concerning the blood of Abel: “Behold, the voice of your brother Abel’s blood cries to me from the earth” (Gen. IV, 10). It is as though he were saying: “The petitions of my members for the cleansing of their sins are the reason why I am thus forsaken by you.” Or the phrase may be understood as a removal expressed through a question, as follows: “I say, Why have you forsaken me? Do the words of my sins,” that is, the petitions of the sins I have committed, bring this about, that you are far from my bodily salvation?” Which is to say: “Do my sins demand that you not save me?” Certainly not.

[Col. 0719B] He explains in what respect he appears to have been forsaken, as follows: “I say, You have forsaken me.” And truly you have appeared to have forsaken me, O my God, in a special sense. For I will cry out, that is, I will appear to the Jews to cry out with the feeling of my heart throughout the day of my passion, so that I may escape. And you will not hear me, that is, you will appear not to hear me; or I will truly cry out both with voice and with feeling to be delivered, though I do not wish to be heard. Yet, for the strengthening of my weak members, who will be destined to fear amid torments lest afterward they despair of their reward, I will cry out, and you will not hear me so as to deliver me, as in the Gospel: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will” (Matt. XXVI, 39).

[Col. 0719C] And in the night, that is, at the dawn of the resurrection, while the darkness of night still remains, I will cry out to you—not with words, but through the very obedience of death. That cry will not bring me into folly, that is, on account of it I will not be judged by you foolish and unworthy to obtain my request; rather, then you will hear me by raising me from the dead. Another translation has: “And you will not be silent,” that is, you will answer my petition, not by speaking but by raising me. Or it may be understood thus: “There will be no silence from you for me, but an answer.” The meaning here is the same: “I say, You appeared to have forsaken me and to be far from my salvation; and you will not hear me.”

[Col. 0719D] But you—that is, you—although this is so, dwell, that is, remain continually, even though you appear to have withdrawn, in me, in the Holy of Holies, by antonomasia. Or, because he had said that he was forsaken in death on account of the words—that is, the petitions—of the sins of his members, so that they might be fulfilled, lest it be thought that they would be heard in every respect, the whole passage may be understood as a removal in this way: “I say that the words of those sins ask that you be far from my salvation; and in this they are heard, yet let them not think that they will be heard in every respect, O my God. For I will cry out”—that is, my members will cry out to you—“during the day,” that is, in prosperity, so that it may not fail, “and you will not hear me. And in the night,” that is, in adversity, so that it may fail, “and you will not hear me.” Their not being heard will not be to my folly, but for my benefit and instruction. For, according to the Apostle: “Power is perfected in weakness” (II Cor. XII, 9). And elsewhere the Psalmist says: “Your discipline corrected me,” and so forth (Ps. XXVII, 37). I say that you will not hear me, and therefore you will appear to have withdrawn. Yet you dwell, that is, although you do not hear me, in the holy place, that is, in the holy gathering of my members. Hence the prophet says: “I will dwell in them, and I will be their God” (II Cor. VI, 16; Lev. XXVI, 12).

Having shown one reason why he appears to have been forsaken, he adds another, more forceful, as follows. I say: “You have forsaken me.” And truly you appear to have forsaken me, O you who are the praise of Israel, whom the ancient fathers of the race of Israel praised with good devotion and action. Or, you who will be, through me, the praise of my future Israelites, that is, of those who will see you in contemplation.

[Col. 0720A] For our fathers hoped in you, though they were less worthy than I. I say, “They hoped”; and therefore you delivered them from tribulations. And they not only hoped, but cried out to you from their mouths and were saved. This is the same thing he said above, “You delivered them,” but he repeats it for another reason, namely, because he had said, “They cried out to you.” And they were not only saved, but hoped in you and were not confounded, that is, defeated by their enemies; rather, they were victorious, like the children of Israel under Moses. Here less is said according to the letter, and more is understood. For when he says, “They were not confounded,” it is understood that they were victorious.

[Col. 0720B] I say that they were saved. But I, though so righteous, am a worm and not a man, that is, I appear so vile that they kill me as a worm, which is destroyed without any consideration of the loss. And I am not even reckoned by them to be a man, that is, they kill me as though I were not a human being. Or it may be understood thus: I am a worm, that is, like a worm. For just as a worm is born from a nut or some other fruit without seed, so I was born from a Virgin without seed; and I am not simply a man, but also God. Yet although I am so worthy that I am a worm and not a man, I am nevertheless the reproach of men, that is, I appear so vile to them that I seem to be a reproach to all men, whose nature I share.

[Col. 0720C] And, to speak more forcefully, I am the rejection of the people, that is, the refuse of the whole people when I am killed, just as filth purifies houses when it is cast out of them. And because I am a reproach and a rejection, all who see me—that is, who regard me as such, as reproach and rejection, and not as God and man—mocked me by spitting upon me and striking me. And they did not mock me only in this way, but also spoke with their lips, not merely in their hearts; and by speaking they shook their heads derisively.

[Col. 0720D] I say, “They spoke,” saying: “He hoped in the Lord,” that is, “He says that he hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him from our power. Let him save him from death, for he wants him,” that is, he loves him, as he himself asserts. Thus it is said in the Gospel: “He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he wants him,” and so forth (Matt. XXIX, 43, as printed). All this is as though he were saying: “This is the reason why I appear to have been forsaken. You delivered our fathers, who were less worthy than I, when they were heard and freed from tribulations. But me, who am so worthy that I am consubstantial with you, you permitted to become so vile as a worm, a reproach, a rejection, and an object of mockery.”

Having resolved what he had proposed and explained the intervening causes, he prays that God not leave him entirely without help, first presenting the merit by which he is worthy to be heard. He says this as follows: “They all mocked me in this way, thinking that I had been forsaken by you. But you, do not depart from me, lest I fall, and so that I may rise again. And I truly know that you will not depart, because you are the one who drew me from the womb,” that is, you alone were the cause of my being born. In the case of others, their fathers who beget them are in a certain sense the cause why they themselves are drawn from the womb and born. And you are my hope from my mother’s breasts, that is, I have always hoped in you from the time I began to suck my mother’s breasts.

[Col. 0721A] And from the womb I was cast upon you, that is, so that I might be personally united to you, whereas all others at their first birth are cast upon Adam, so that they may be conformed to him in original sin. I said that you are my hope from the breasts; and, to say it more explicitly: “You are my God from my mother’s womb,” that is, I have had you as God from the time I was in the womb. Therefore do not depart from me, that is, do not leave me without help. And it is necessary that I pray for this.

[Col. 0721B] For tribulation is near, that is, in my flesh, not in my members and not in the loss of possessions. And there is no one to help except you. He explains the tribulation as follows: Many calves surrounded me in order to seize me, that is, many people from the common crowd, wanton like calves, seized me for no reason but their own wantonness. And after seizing me they besieged me, that is, they surrounded me with their accusations so that I could not escape.

[Col. 0721C] Fat bulls, that is, the stiff-necked and proud leaders of the Jews, like fat bulls—not because of any evil merits of mine, but solely because of their fatness, that is, their pride. And they, both the calves and the bulls, opened their mouths against me, standing over me—that is, judging themselves superior to me—and saying: “Crucify him” (Luke XXIII, 21). They were like a lion, that is, cruel as a lion, insofar as the calves seized me; they seized me irrationally. And they roared, that is, raged irrationally against me, in the manner of a lion. This applies to all of them, both calves and bulls.

[Col. 0721D] And they did not do only this, but I was also poured out, that is, my soul was poured out from my body. I say, “I was poured out,” existing as water, that is, resembling water, which, when poured out, customarily causes a ruin; so I too, when poured out, would bring ruin upon my enemies, that is, destruction. Hence the Gospel says: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel” (Luke II, 34).

Or it may be understood thus: I was poured out into death like water, that is, with as much contempt as water is poured out. Therefore all my bones were scattered in flight, that is, the people who are stronger in the Church, just as bones are the stronger parts of the body. Hence it is written: “Then all the disciples, leaving him, fled” (Matt. XXVI, 56). And the prophet says: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zech. XIII, 7).

[Col. 0722A] And they were not merely scattered; my heart also, that is, the teaching that had proceeded from my heart and that I had taught them—namely, that I would rise again—became like melting wax in the midst, that is, in the commonality of my belly, meaning the apostles. They had previously been bones, that is, strong in faith, but became weak like the belly. Which is to say: Just as wax melts at the sight of fire, so the teaching of faith in them failed at the sight of my passion—not in a few of them, but in all alike.

And therefore my heart became like melting wax because my power withered in them, though it had previously flourished in miracles; that is, my power appeared to have failed and was judged by them as fragile, like a potsherd, which can quickly be broken. Hence they themselves said: “We had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke XXIV, 21). And my power withered in them because my tongue clung to my jaws so that it did not speak, that is, because they saw me silent as though I were guilty.

[Col. 0722B] And this was still so because you led me into the dust of death, that is, because they thought you had permitted me to be led into death in such a way that I would become dust like other dead men. And therefore I appeared to have been led into the dust of death, because I was condemned to the most shameful death. He explains what kind of death this was.

For many dogs surrounded me in order to seize me, that is, many ministers, irrationally barking against me—though I had come for their salvation, just as dogs often bark at those who are helping them. And after seizing me, the assembly of the wicked, that is, the leaders acting wickedly against me, besieged me, that is, surrounded me with accusations so that I could not escape.

[Col. 0722C] And afterward: They pierced my hands and my feet on the cross. And they stretched them out so far that they could count all my bones, that is, they were able to count them. After committing this crime, they did not grieve; rather, they themselves whom I had come to save, for whom I had performed miracles, looked upon me and gazed upon me with delight as I hung upon the cross.

And afterward they divided my garments among themselves, and over my garment, which was seamless, they cast lots to determine to whom it would belong, “not wishing to tear it” (John XXIX, 24, as printed), because it was valuable. In the division of the garments he displays their avarice, also prophetically foretelling this for the instruction of the faith of those who would follow.

[Col. 0722D] This may also signify an allegorical meaning. The garments that were torn signify the Scriptures, which are garments—that is, the defenses—of the Church, which is the body of God. Heretics tear these garments by interpreting them wrongly, as the Psalmist says elsewhere: “What you accomplished, they destroyed” (Ps. X, 3). But the garment that was not divided and was given by lot signifies the incorrupt faith. This garment belongs to the faithful and cannot be torn by heretics; it is also given by lot, that is, by God’s election, to future believers, not on account of their merits.

Or the passage may be read in this way from the place where he said, “I was poured out like water,” and so forth. I say that they opened their mouths against me. And I was also poured out by them into death like water, existing as something comparable to water. For just as water washes bodies, so I washed souls from original defilement by my death. I say that I was poured out so that I might be water, that is, purification.

[Col. 0723A] And thus I was purification: all my bones were scattered, namely, my disciples, throughout the whole world after my death, to preach, according to the Gospel: “But they went forth and preached everywhere,” and so forth (Mark XVI, 20). Through those bones—that is, through my disciples—my heart, namely, the teaching of my prophets that had proceeded from my heart, that is, from my will, which heart had previously been hard to understand, became like melting wax, that is, soft and intelligible, just as wax, previously hard, becomes liquid when fire is applied.

I say that my heart existed in the midst, that is, in the commonality of my belly, meaning that it existed commonly in the disciples. They are called my belly because they retain my memory, just as memory is in a person’s belly, while the heart is in the belly.

[Col. 0723B] Through those bones my power, which appeared impotent and fragile in death, withered like a potsherd, that is, was shown to be powerful and strong, in the manner of a potsherd: although it is soft at first, it is fragile; but the more it dries, the stronger it becomes.

Through this my power was proved, because my tongue, that is, the preaching of my disciples, clung to my jaws, that is, to the commandments that proceeded from my jaws. Which is to say: They preached not according to their own inventions, but according to what I taught them. Through those bones you led me—that is, the knowledge of me—into the dust of death, that is, into unbelievers who, although dead in sins, were dust: dry in doctrine and easily moved by the devil’s impulse, just as dry dust is easily moved by the wind.

[Col. 0723C] After showing in what manner he was water, he wishes to show how he was poured out into death, saying as follows: “I said that I was poured out.” And this happened in the following manner: “For many dogs surrounded me,” and so forth, up to “But you, Lord, do not change.” Everything that he says in the past tense through the agility of prophecy is to be understood as future.

Having displayed his passion, he returns to his prayer, because he had prayed briefly in order to pray at greater length, to instruct us to pray, and afterward to show the fruit of his passion and resurrection. He says this as follows: “They will surround me and pierce me in this way and will think me forsaken; but you, Lord, do not distance your help from me,” that is, do not prolong the help of my resurrection until the general resurrection, but raise me after three days. And first look upon me for my defense, lest I fall in the passion.

[Col. 0723D] He explains these two petitions individually, matching each to the other. I said, “Do not distance your help from me,” that is: “Deliver my soul from the sword, O God, so that it may not be held in death.” He says the same thing in other words, out of his great feeling, adding the reason as follows: “And from the hand of the dog,” that is, from the power of the Jewish people, irrationally barking, so that they may not be able to hold me in death as they desire; “deliver my only one,” that is, my soul, because it is unique, distinguished above all others in goodness.

And I said, for my defense, “Look upon me,” that is, save me from the mouth of the lion, that is, from the Jewish people, which desires to devour my holiness, as a lion does, so that I may not yield to them. He repeats the same thing in other words, out of great feeling, adding the reason as follows: “And save my humility,” that is, save me because I am humble, “from the horns of unicorns,” that is, from the proud persuasions of the Jews, so that I may not consent to them. They are called unicorns, that is, possessing a single and preeminent pride above all others, just as a unicorn has a single horn. And rightly their proud persuasions are called horns, by which they intended to overcome him, just as horned animals fight with their horns.

[Col. 0724A] After making his prayer, he shows the fruit of his resurrection as follows: “I prayed that you would deliver and save me. If you do this, I will proclaim your name to my brothers,” as in the Gospel: “Father, I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me” (John XVII, 6). That is, I will make your name known to the apostles, teaching them that you are God and Lord. They are my brothers, that is, co-heirs of eternal blessing with me. Hence the Apostle says: “Heirs indeed of God, but co-heirs of Christ” (Rom. VIII, 17).

[Col. 0724B] And through those brothers, in the midst of the Church that will believe through them, I will praise you, that is, I will cause you to be praised both in action and in devotion by those who will believe through them. Hence the same Lord says in the Gospel: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 10).

He then turns by apostrophe to those who will believe, exhorting them to praise him both in action and in feeling, as follows: “Since I will be surrounded and pierced for you, through this I will bring forth true praisers of you: you who fear the Lord,” that is, you who will come to fear God, “praise him in words and deeds.”

[Col. 0724C] He says this also in parts, as follows: “I say, let all who fear him”—namely, the whole seed of Jacob—“glorify him,” that is, all of you who will believe from the seed of Jacob, that is, from the Jewish people, who will wrestle against vices, just as he himself wrestled (Gen. XXXII, 24). Show him to be glorious through good works, feelings, and words.

And let the whole seed of Israel fear him with chaste fear, that is, let those who, being from the seed of Jacob, will see God in contemplation and therefore be called Israel, fear him. They will praise and fear him for their own good, just as I praised and feared him for my own good.

[Col. 0724D] And truly for my own good. For this reason he did not despise or scorn the prayer of a poor man made poor for your sake, as the Apostle says: “Though he was rich, he became poor for us, so that we might become rich in him” (II Cor. III, 9). Which is to say: Because he did not despise me praying in the passion, he will not despise you who have become my imitators.

By saying “despised” and “scorned,” he expresses great feeling, saying the same thing twice in equivalent terms. Nor did he turn his face away from me, that is, he was not angry with me, after the likeness of angry persons who turn their faces away from those whom they hate. It is as though he were saying: “He loved me.”

[Col. 0725A] And therefore, when I cried out to him in action, words, and devotion, he heard me so that I might obtain my request, making me steadfast and raising me. Since he had shown above that he would suffer, lest he be thought for that reason altogether inferior to the Father, he shows himself to be equal in this way. I said that I would praise you, that is, cause you to be praised in the Church. And not only will you be praised personally, but my praise will be great with you in the Church: by praising you, the Church will praise me also. “For I and you, Father, are one” (John X, 30). And elsewhere in the Gospel: “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John III, 23).

And thus it will arrive at my praise, because I will therefore repay my vows. Which is to say: I, who from the beginning vowed to give them my body and my blood for their salvation, will repay my vows here also in the sight of those who fear him. That is, those who fear the Father, O hearers, will see those vows with pure faith, believing that the sacraments have truly been changed into my body and blood—not merely imaginatively, as certain heretics falsely assert when they perversely interpret the Gospel: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke XXII, 19).

[Col. 0725B] For they understand that in those sacraments there is only a remembrance of the Lord’s body and blood, without reality, although the Lord cries out to them: “This is my body, which will be delivered for you” (ibid.). And shortly afterward: “This is my blood, which will be poured out for you” (ibid.). He therefore did not assert that these were merely a remembrance or sign of his body and blood. Rather, he expressly testified: “This is my body,” and “This is my blood.”

As for the statement that follows, “Do this in remembrance of me,” no doubt remains if the Apostle’s statement is considered in a Catholic manner. For he says: “Whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you will proclaim the death of the Lord” (I Cor. X, 26).

[Col. 0725C] This, then, is the sacrament of the Lord’s passion, not a remembrance of himself. For nothing can be a remembrance of itself. Bread and wine, however, are called Christ’s body and blood by Christian truth, not with respect to their nature, but with respect to their appearance and odor. For the one who was able to assume flesh in the Virgin’s womb and unite it personally and ineffably to his Word, and who will also, by the power of his command, make our mortal bodies immortal, is able to transfer the substance of bread and wine into the substance of his body and blood.

These sacraments are also rightly called signs and mysteries—not signs of themselves, but of us. For great signs and mysteries are contained in them. The material—namely, the bread from which the Lord’s body is fashioned through spiritual blessing—is joined together from many grains crushed by the mill and mixed with water. The wine, which is transferred into blood, is likewise made from many grapes by the pressure of a winepress or some other weight.

[Col. 0725D] The grains and grapes are produced with the labor of cultivators; so we too, renewed in faith through the cultivation of preachers, are afterward crushed by fasts and vigils and made into one body, namely, Christ’s body, with the mixing of baptism cooperating. Hence the Apostle says: “So we, though many, are one body in Christ” (Rom. XII, 5).

These sacraments are also signs for us and a pledge of eternal blessedness, which we are to attain through them if we receive them worthily; hence they are also called viaticum. Water is joined to the wine in the making of this sacrament as a figure of us. For just as we flow downward toward death like water, so through the mystery of the Lord’s passion we are joined to Christ by the grace of adoption.

[Col. 0726A] When this body is received by the faithful, it is a sign that our mortal bodies are to be restored through Christ’s passion. Through the reception of the blood, we understand the restoration of souls. For the soul dwells especially around the blood. Although this sacrament is divided into parts, it nevertheless remains wholly and entirely present everywhere, as the Apostle Andrew testifies: “Although his flesh is eaten by the people and his blood is drunk, the lamb that was sacrificed nevertheless remains whole and lives.”

The text continues:

“They will eat, the poor,” and so forth. This is connected as follows: “I say that I will repay my vows in the sight of those who fear him.” Those who fear him, having seen him, will eat this, having become poor in spirit, that is, humbling themselves in soul and not becoming proud. Of them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. III, 3).

[Col. 0726B] And because eating is not enough, he adds: “And they will be filled,” that is, they will be filled with the reality signified by the sacraments, namely, the unity of faith, hope, and love, which are designated through the sacraments, since each sacrament is made one thing from many grains and grapes, as we have said.

And thus, by eating and being filled, those who seek him will praise the Lord with such praise, not with earthly praise. Which is to say: That eating and fullness will be the praise of God. I say that they seek him, and they do so for their own good. For their hearts, that is, their souls, will live forever and ever, that is, eternally, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever eats me will live because of me” (John VI, 57).

[Col. 0726C] This does not mean that bodies will not also live eternally in the future; rather, he designates the whole through a part. Since the soul rules more particularly in the heart, he uses “hearts” for “souls.”

Having shown the conversion of the Jews when he said, “Let the whole seed of Israel fear him,” he also shows the conversion of the Gentiles as follows: Not only will the seed of Israel and Jacob fear him, but all the ends of the earth—that is, many nations from all the ends of the earth—will remember the Lord, whom they knew in Adam but afterward consigned to oblivion through original guilt and unbelief. And thus they will be converted to the Lord through faith and repentance.

[Col. 0726D] And afterward all the families of the Gentiles, that is, many people from all the families of the Gentiles, noble and ignoble alike, will adore the Lord, that is, will venerate him in praise and action, acknowledging themselves to be creatures and him to be the Creator.

I say that they will adore him by existing in his sight, that is, always keeping him in view and never putting him second. Or they will adore him in his sight, that is, in the soul, which he alone sees, even if they cannot always adore him in their works.

[Col. 0727A] And rightly they will adore him, because the kingdom belongs to the Lord—namely, the kingdom that previously belonged to the devil. And afterward that same Lord will rule the Gentiles, not the devil, who previously ruled them.

I say that they will be converted and will adore him. And thus they ate, that is, they will eat, my vows; and afterward they adored, that is, they will adore.

This is the same as what he said above, “They will be filled.” Which is to say: They will adore, that is, venerate him, filled with the reality of the sacrament, namely, the unity of faith, hope, and love, which, as we have said, is designated through the sacrament.

[Col. 0727B] I say that all the rich of the earth will eat and adore, that is, all kinds of people rich in earthly possessions, not only the poor. For if only the poor were to adore and be saved, the Apostle Paul would certainly not admonish his disciple to instruct them as follows: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded” (I Tim. VI, 17).

And he rightly said, “the rich of the earth,” not those rich in spirit. Rich and wealthy in spirit are those who become proud because of earthly possessions and place their hope in them as in the true good. The poor in spirit, however, even if they abound in earthly things, do not become proud because of them and do not place their hope in them; rather, they distribute them generously to those in need.

[Col. 0727C] I say that the rich will adore. But all who descend into the earth, that is, into merely earthly desires, will fall into death. And this is constant in his sight, for whoever is not steadfast. I say that they will fall; but my soul, that is, the soul of my members, by adhering to him, will live.

Because he had shown the conversion of Jews and Gentiles, lest we think that they would remain in this state only once, he shows that this conversion will continue through many generations, from generation to generation, until the end of the world.

I say that the soul of my members will live in him. And through the preaching of those members, my seed will serve him, that is, their children, imitators of their goodness, will serve him through their preaching, so that they may live.

[Col. 0727D] And again, through that seed, the coming generation will be proclaimed to the Lord. This concise statement may be unfolded as follows: Through the proclamation of the preaching of that seed, another generation, coming after that seed, will be converted to the Lord. And some of that generation, having become heavens, that is, rain-bringers and preachers of others, will proclaim his righteousness, that is, his just commandments, to the people who will be born after them, whom the Lord made, that is, whom he has already ordained to be saved.

## ON PSALM XXII

### Title of the Twenty-Second Psalm

“A Psalm of David,” that is, of the faithful, concerning whom it was announced in the preceding psalm that they would believe and adore. For the instruction of those who would come after, he shows the benefits bestowed upon him by God, so that they too may strive to attain these benefits by living well. Afterward they turn by apostrophe to God, giving thanks for the benefits bestowed; hence they say:

[Col. 0727D] “The Lord governs me in a place of pasture,” that is, he himself is my ruler, so that I may not wander in the divine Scriptures, which are the place where the souls of the faithful feed upon the sweetness of doctrine.

And because I have such a ruler, “nothing will be lacking for me in the place of pasture,” that is, no understanding that ought to instruct me will be lacking in those Scriptures. And truly nothing will be lacking for me in the place of pasture. For there he has placed me, that is, he has caused me frequently to study.

[Col. 0728A] And he bestowed on me not only this benefit, but also, having first established me over the water of refreshment, that is, over the water of baptism, he brought me up, that is, nourished me with the milk of doctrine, and first converted my soul from unbelief to faith.

The water of baptism is rightly called the water of refreshment, because through it our righteousness and innocence, which failed in Adam, are restored. Baptism is also the foundation and beginning of all other goods.

And he not only placed me, raised me, and converted me, but also led me from virtue to virtue, from good action to good action. Or he led me lest I fail, having been set upon the path of righteousness, that is, upon the virtues and good works that are the narrow way to life.

[Col. 0728B] He rightly says “upon.” For when these things were exceedingly difficult at first, they could be said to be beneath them, that is, they afflicted and depressed the body through their practice. But once they have become habitual and are no longer so difficult, the faithful are said to be above them, that is, to have them ready at their command, though grace continues to cooperate as an aid.

I say that he led me. And he did this not on account of my merits, but to magnify his name. And he not only led me, but still leads me.

This is the reason: I will not fear evils, that is, the examples and persuasions of enemies, or the tribulations inflicted by them. And if I walk through the way of this life, that is, although I conduct myself in the midst of the shadow of death, among the wicked who are the shadow of death—cold because they lack the warmth of the Holy Spirit and dark in understanding, just as a shadow is cold and dark—and who lead others to eternal death through their examples and persuasions, just as a shadow kills the plants that remain beneath it for a long time, I will not therefore fear being bent by their evils.

[Col. 0728C] For you, who are omnipotent, are with me to strengthen me. It is as though he were saying: “This security does not come from me, but from you.”

Someone might say: “Why do you say that you do not fear evils? At least you fear tribulations, which are evils.” He answers: “No.”

For your rod, that is, lesser tribulation, which is your discipline, through which you correct and teach; and your staff, that is, greater tribulation, through which you chastise me again by scourging me—these very things that seemed likely to disturb me have instead consoled me, since through them I understand that I am cleansed from my sins, that my crown and virtues are magnified, and that I am guarded against pride, according to the Apostle: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me” (II Cor. XII, 7).

[Col. 0728D] And they consoled me because you prepared, that is, appointed, for me against those who afflict me, lest I fail through tribulations, a table, that is, the refreshment of your body and blood, which is received at the altar’s table.

I say that the table was set in my sight, and I see it as a sign of your death, so that I too may not fear suffering and dying for you. And because sight alone would not suffice, you anointed my head with oil, that is, made my mind gentle, not rebellious in the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is called oil because it makes the mind gentle in suffering, just as oil softens the head that it anoints.

[Col. 0729A] And therefore my cup, that is, that oil which intoxicates me so that I do not feel tribulations too severely, is exceedingly splendid; that is, it appears to me very splendid. Grace is called oil and a cup because, as has been said, it intoxicates the faithful, after the likeness of a cup of wine, which intoxicates those who drink it.

And once I have been anointed, your mercy, that is, your grace, will follow me, that is, accompany me, all the days of my life, so that I may advance from good to better. And it will follow me so fully that through it I will dwell in the future in the house of the Lord, namely, in paradise, going into the length of days, that is, into eternity.

## ON PSALM XXIII

### Title of the Twenty-Third Psalm

“A Psalm of David,” that is, of the Prophet, “on the first day after the Sabbath,” that is, concerning the one acting in contemplation of Christ’s victory, which occurred on the first day after the Sabbath, namely, on the Lord’s Day, which is called the first day after the Sabbath.

The Jews counted the days in this way: first day after the Sabbath, second day after the Sabbath, and so forth. They call the seventh day the Sabbath.

Here the Prophet exhorts the faithful who exist after Christ’s coming to prepare themselves well to receive Christ, their king, with triumph, increasing more and more in virtues and good works and removing vices, after the likeness of those who prepare themselves to receive their king with triumph when he returns victorious from somewhere.

They raise and enlarge the gates of the city so that the spoils and the chorus of the triumphant may enter easily. For Christ, returning victorious from the underworld, obtained the kingdom that the devil had usurped, namely, the Church.

The Prophet also shows which are the members of the Church, lest anyone unworthy claim this for himself. He says this as follows:

The earth is the Lord Christ’s—that is, the Church, over which the devil formerly ruled. It is called “earth” because it is stable, fruitful in good works, and cultivated by preachers, just as earth is a stable element and fertile, and is cultivated by farmers. And that earth is not small, but full. And the fullness of that earth belongs to the Lord—not because it did not belong to him before, but because it is now called his in such a way that it obeys his will, which previously it did not do.

And the inhabited world—that is, the Church chosen from all lands—belongs to the Lord. This is the same as what he said above, “The earth is the Lord’s”; but out of excessive joy he repeats it, to show that it is perfect and not defiled by vices, by comparison with a round object, which is also called a sphere. A sphere is more perfect than a square or triangular object, having no beginning or end, but always turning back upon itself. Nor can stains easily adhere to it.

And all who dwell in it—that is, in that sphere, meaning in the unity of its faith and love—belong to the Lord. This is the same as what he said here, “The inhabited world is the Lord’s.” But he repeats the point in other words so that, since he had said “the inhabited world” indefinitely, he may now speak universally. I say that the inhabited world is the Lord’s. This can be seen from the fact that he himself founded it upon the seas—that is, he made it so firm that it did not fear but despised the seas, namely, the bitter peoples who oppose it in tribulations, just as the seas are bitter. He also established it upon the rivers—that is, he set it firm and lofty in virtues above princes, so that it might despise their tribulations. Princes are called “rivers” because their care flows down upon the subjected people, just as rivers run down into the sea.

Since he had said, “All who dwell in it,” lest anyone false suppose that he dwells there, he asks who should be called a dweller, so that, by answering afterward, he may exhort us to strive to become dwellers. He says:

I say that those who dwell in it belong to the Lord.

And who will ascend the mountain of the Lord—that is, the Church, which has been made lofty in virtues by the Lord? Or rather, who, after ascending, will stand—that is, will dwell—in his holy place, namely, in the Church, which is the holy place in which God himself dwells? For there are many who ascend but afterward, by failing, do not remain inhabitants.

The answer is: The one innocent in hands will dwell—that is, innocent in works with respect to his neighbor. And because this would not be sufficient, he adds: And existing with a pure heart—that is, having no impure thought against his neighbor.

And the one who has not received his soul in vain, with respect to himself—that is, who has not held his soul acceptable in vanity. This means: If his soul, through the weakness of the flesh or through suggestion, has been driven to think something vain, it was not acceptable to him in such a way that he consented to it, but he utterly rejected it.

And he was not only innocent in hands and pure in heart with respect to his neighbor; he also did not swear deceitfully to his neighbor—that is, he did not make a firm promise in such a way as to deceive him. By this kind of expression, namely, deceitful speech, he removes every kind of evil speech directed against one’s neighbor.

And lest we think that this person stood in the Lord’s holy place by his own power, he adds: The one who is such will receive this blessing from the Lord—that is, this exaltation, so that he may stand in his holy place. And he will receive this not solely on account of his merits, but will receive this mercy from God his Savior—that is, from his saving God.

And rightly will he receive this mercy from God. For this is the generation of those who seek the Lord, specifically those who seek the face—that is, knowledge—of the God of Jacob, namely, of the strong wrestlers. It is as though he said: They are not innocent and such as I have described in order to acquire something else, but only your glorious knowledge in the future, which they cannot fully possess here. Hence the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

And he rightly says “generation,” lest we think there is only one person, since he had used the singular expression, “innocent in hands.”

Having explained this for our instruction, he returns to what he had begun, as follows: I said, “The earth and the inhabited world belong to the Lord.” Therefore, O princes—that is, you faithful, formerly servants of sin but now made princes and free through the Lord—lift up, that is, raise, your gates.

And afterward—that is, you who are emphatically called gates—eternal gates, namely, possessing within yourselves the virtues that are gates leading to eternal things, be lifted up from good to better.

Or in this way: Lift up—that is, remove—your gates, not God’s gates, namely, the vices that are closed gates and do not admit God’s entrance. Hence the Wise Man says: “Wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul” (Wisdom 1:4).

And once those gates have been removed, be lifted up—that is, grow—in the faithful, eternal gates, namely, virtues. Then the King, the giver of glory—that is, Christ—will enter, as he likewise says in the Gospel: “We will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

Or alternatively, you princes of darkness—that is, demons—lift up, and so forth. The rest is unchanged. Since he had said “King of glory,” lest he be thought to mean some ordinary king, he intends to magnify him in this way: I say, “King of glory.”

And who—that is, how great—is this King of glory? He is truly great. For he is the Lord in all things, strong in raising his flesh, who appeared weak in his Passion, and powerful although he appeared powerless. And truly the Lord is powerful, and this in battle—that is, on account of the battle he obediently waged against the devil and in which he prevailed over him. God the Father caused him to appear powerful in his ascension. Hence the Apostle says: “Therefore God also exalted him,” and so forth (Philippians 2:9).

Therefore, because he is strong and powerful, lift up the gates, and so forth. This is expressed as above. And who is this King of glory? The phrase is joined and explained in the same way as above.

But here he adds something else in order to magnify him more forcefully: The Lord of the heavenly powers—that is, of the celestial spirits, not merely of human beings—is himself, namely the one whom I have understood here and no other: Christ, the King of glory.

And truly he is the Lord of the heavenly powers. Hence the Apostle says: “At the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (ibid.).

That he says twice, “Lift up,” and, “Who is this King of glory?” contributes both to our exhortation and to Christ’s magnification; or he says this twice because of the Church’s two walls, namely, Jews and Gentiles.

## ON PSALM XXIV

**Title of the twenty-fourth Psalm.** A Psalm of David—that is, of less-perfect faithful people praying after abandoning their sins, so that God may make them persevere, lest they yield and thus be put to shame. It also presents the merit by which he ought to be heard. He likewise prays that God not withdraw his grace from them on account of their offenses and ignorances. Moreover, for our instruction, he shows that God, although sweet in showing mercy, is also righteous in justly punishing the wicked. Finally, he prays both for enemies and for the good. Thus he says:

To you, Lord, to embrace you, I have lifted up my soul, freed from earthly desires. I have also lifted it by doing good, O my God, my Creator, to whom I do not deny the place of divinity within me. In you I trust, not in myself, because I will continue to lift myself more and more.

And because I have lifted myself and trust, I will not be put to shame—that is, I will not fail—and thus I will not be put to shame. For I would be put to shame if I failed. I pray that I may not be put to shame. Nor may my enemies, both visible and invisible, mock me when I fail—that is, may they not rejoice at my failure, for they would rejoice if they saw me failing. I ask that I neither be put to shame nor be mocked.

And I pray this with good confidence. For all who await you—that is, who patiently await you as their helper and rewarder—or, those who await you, meaning those who patiently endure your commands by fulfilling them—will not be confounded, that is, they will not be put to shame.

And therefore, because I await you, I will not be confounded. But those who act wickedly in vain—that is, without benefit—who think they possess some benefit in the wicked things they do, will be confounded because they do not await you.

And because I see that this will happen, I grant it, not by cursing: Let all who act wickedly in vain be confounded—that is, be put to shame—in their conscience, both in this world and in the future, because no one is so wicked that he does not feel shame in his conscience over his wickedness. He makes this concession in order to deter the wicked from their wickedness.

Afterward he returns to prayer as follows: I say that I will not be put to shame. And in order that this may happen: Show me your ways—that is, those commands of yours that are common paths for all who are to be saved unto life, without whose fulfillment no one will be saved.

He does not say “show me” because he is ignorant, since he had said above, “I have lifted my soul to you,” and so forth. Rather, “show me” means, make me keep them in memory, so that I may fulfill them.

And teach me your paths, likewise so that I may fulfill them. He calls those commands “paths” that are greater and fulfilled by few, just as fewer people walk by a path than by a road—namely, selling everything and giving to the poor, and other similar things that belong only to the most perfect.

And by those roads and paths direct me, by doing good. And do this in your truth—that is, placed in conformity with Christ, who is the truth proceeding from you, as he likewise says in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Christ is called “truth” emphatically, since all truth proceeds from him. And in order that he may direct me along the roads and paths, teach me—that is, instruct my understanding in them—so that I may not go astray in them.

And you are powerful enough to do this, because you are God—that is, my Creator—and Savior—that is, my Restorer.

And it is fitting that you do this. For I have awaited you—that is, I have patiently waited; or, I have patiently fulfilled your commands—all day, that is, throughout the whole time since I began. By “day” he designates the whole period by a part.

I pray: direct me. And in order that you may direct me, you who appeared to have forgotten me when, by not knowing you, I sinned before baptism, remember your compassions, Lord, and your mercies, which are in you from eternity—that is, from everlasting.

This means: Remember how many compassions you have bestowed upon human beings from the beginning of the world, and how merciful you are by nature; and therefore have mercy on me as you have had mercy on others.

“Mercy” is what exists naturally in God. “Compassions,” however, are the benefits bestowed through mercy. Although he uses “mercies” in the plural, in God mercy is nevertheless to be understood as simple; but because of its many effects he uses “mercies” in the plural.

I say: Remember your compassions and mercies. And lest I be deprived of mercy, Lord, do not remember the offenses of my youth in order to punish them—that is, the venial sins I committed after, by stripping off the old man in baptism, I became young in faith.

And my ignorances—that is, the sins I committed unknowingly before baptism.

Or in this way: The offenses of my youth—that is, of my rashness. For young people sin more rashly than the old, and therefore he uses “youth” for “rashness.” It is as though he said: Do not remember the great offenses that I commit rashly, not necessarily.

And my ignorances—that is, the venial sins I commit unknowingly.

And by not remembering the offenses, remember me in order to have mercy on me—you who appeared to have forgotten me while I was an unbeliever—you, O Lord, who alone can have mercy in this way.

And do this because of your goodness—that is, because of the mercy you naturally possess—not solely because of my merits. And do not have a little mercy, but according to your mercy—that is, in proportion to your mercy: just as you are greatly merciful, so may you have great mercy.

Since he had mentioned God’s goodness, lest anyone, trusting too much in that goodness, persist in sins, he also says that God is righteous in avenging the sins of those who persist, as follows:

I say this because of your goodness. And truly the Lord is sweet—that is, good—and yet righteous, that is, just, in taking vengeance. This can be seen from the fact that he is both sweet and righteous.

For this reason he will give a law—that is, instruction—to those who sin while placed in the way of moral conduct, that is, to those who sin venially. For those who sin criminally are outside the way of moral conduct.

This means: He will give them instruction so that they may not perish by sinning criminally; and in this he is shown to be both sweet and righteous. For if he were only sweet, he would give the law uselessly, since he would forgive everything to all sinners. But if he were only just, he would never give a law of mercy, but would condemn everyone justly.

Or he calls “law” the discipline of tribulations, which he brings upon his own people in order to correct and teach them. Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “Your discipline corrected me” (Psalm 17:37), that is, it will teach me.

And in judgment—that is, in that law by which they will know how to judge what must be held to and what must be avoided, and which is therefore called “judgment”—he will direct the meek from good to better, not the rebellious.

And so that they may be directed well, he will teach especially the gentle his ways, by which they will reach him. And since one might ask what those ways are, he explains: All the ways of the Lord are these: mercy and truth.

Mercy, namely, so that each person may have compassion on himself, lest he sin and perish by sinning, and so that he may repay good for evil.

Truth—that is, justice—namely, so that he may love God above all things as is just, and repay good for good.

I say that mercy and truth are found by those who seek his covenant and his testimonies. This means: If someone searches carefully by seeking the new law and the old, he will find no more ways than these.

And he rightly calls the old law “testimonies” in the plural, since it was delivered by many witnesses, namely, by the prophets who served it. But the new law is called “covenant” in the singular, because it was given by one witness of eternal life, namely, Christ. The Apostles and the other teachers were not givers of the law, but interpreters.

Having shown, for our instruction, that the Lord is sweet and righteous, since he had prayed above, he announces with good confidence that he will obtain what he asks, so that he may also urge others to ask in order to obtain, as follows:

I prayed: “According to your mercy, remember me.” And you will truly do this. Truly you will pardon my sin, for the sake of increasing your name.

And it is fitting that you pardon. For it is great—that is, I regard it as very great. This means: I do not excuse myself by treating it as insignificant, but rather accuse myself by regarding it as very serious; therefore I deserve pardon.

And because he had said that his sin was great, so that he might also teach us to regard sin as serious and thus merit pardon, he adds: I said, “It is great”; and it is good that it is great. For the one to whom it is great fears God.

And who is the human being—that is, how great and how blessed is the human being—who fears the Lord? This becomes evident from the following. For he establishes a law for the one who fears him—that is, firmness—so that he may not fail on the way of good conduct that he has chosen.

He uses “law” for “firmness,” because a command that is firm and stable is customarily called a law. And through that law, when his soul departs from the body, it will dwell—that is, inhabit—the heavenly goods.

And in the future his offspring will inherit the earth—that is, the good works sown here will be the cause why, in the future, body and soul together will inherit the land of the living. Works are called “seeds” because they are the causes of rewards, just as seeds are the causes of harvests.

Since he had said, “He establishes a law,” he explains that law as follows: I say, the Lord establishes a law—that is, the Lord is the firmament of those who fear him, so that they may not yield.

And once they have been made firm, his covenant—that is, his promise—is made known to them in the future, as he likewise says in the Gospel: “I will manifest myself” (John 14:21). For in the present time God is not manifested to anyone in the way he will be manifested in the future.

He uses “covenant” for “promise,” because a covenant promises an inheritance.

And because the Lord is a firmament for those who fear him, my eyes—that is, my affections by which I look upon him in the manner of eyes—are always toward the Lord.

This means: In order that he may be my firmament, I never turn my eyes away from him, after the likeness of a good servant whose eyes are always toward his master, so that he may immediately obey him at his nod. Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “As the eyes of servants are toward the hands of their masters” (Psalm 122:2).

And rightly are my eyes toward the Lord, because he will one day draw my feet from the snare—that is, he will rescue me from the snare of mortality and susceptibility to suffering, by which I am now greatly hindered.

When he says “my feet,” he speaks by comparison with those who are caught by their feet in a snare.

And because my eyes are always toward you, look upon me—that is, be favorably disposed toward me. This is said by comparison with a master who often looks upon the servant whom he loves.

And he rightly says “upon me.” It is as though he said: Do not look upon me merely for an hour, but look upon me by fixing your gaze upon me and not quickly withdrawing it; and while looking upon me, have mercy on me by granting pardon.

And it is fitting, because I who ask this am solitary and poor. The order is inverted. This means: Because I am poor in spirit, not proud—that is, because I humble myself toward you in all things.

What it means to be poor in spirit was explained in Psalm XXI.

And I am so poor that I am also solitary—that is, among the number of the children of the Church, which is your one Church, and which is as dear to you as an only son is most dear to his father. Hence in the Song of Songs the bridegroom Christ says to the Church, his bride: “My only one, my dove” (Song of Songs 6:8).

He explains his poverty in parts.

He also explains in parts the matters for which he asks God to have mercy on him: Truly I am poor, namely in this respect: The tribulations of my heart have multiplied—that is, I have many tribulations and sorrows in my heart because of sins.

And therefore rescue me from my necessities—that is, from venial sins, which necessarily occur because of the weakness of the flesh: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (Psalm 50:19).

And do not rescue me only from my necessities, but also see—that is, look upon mercifully—my humility, that is, the extent to which I humble myself toward you; and my labor, which I undergo by fasting and afflicting myself in every way for my offenses.

And for these reasons forgive all my offenses—not only venial but also criminal offenses.

But after you have forgiven my sins, lest I fall again, look upon my enemies who want to overthrow me, so that you may render them ineffective.

And it is necessary for me that you look upon them, because they have multiplied—that is, they are many—and therefore I am insufficient to resist without you.

Nor do they have a just reason for being hostile to me, but they hate me with unjust hatred, not with good hatred—that is, they hate the goodness in me, and that hatred is unjust. They do not hate evil, which would be righteous hatred. Hence Augustine says: “Rightly, in the wicked we hate wickedness.”

I say: Look upon my enemies, because they have multiplied, and thus I will not be put to shame.

Nor is it unjust, because I have hoped in you, not in myself—that is, I have hoped, and I still hope, to be rescued and guarded through you. For I would be put to shame if you did not rescue and guard me.

And although he had said this very thing above, namely, “I will not be put to shame,” it is nevertheless not judged superfluous. For it is not enough for one who greatly desires something to pray only once; or, since he says “look upon them,” this may be a prayer for his enemies.

For we are commanded by the Lord to pray for our enemies in this way: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Luke 6:28).

And he continues in this way: I prayed, “Rescue me; forgive me.” And I pray not only for myself, but also for my enemies: Look mercifully upon my enemies, so that you may convert them.

And it is fitting that I pray for this, because they have multiplied and have hated me with unjust hatred—that is, because they are many, and it would be a great loss if so great a mass should perish. And they are greatly destructive to themselves when they hate me with unjust hatred.

Thus I have prayed for my enemies. And whatever may happen concerning them, at least guard my soul, and so forth. These words remain unchanged.

I said, “I will not be put to shame,” because I have hoped in you. And therefore, because many have attached themselves to me, having been made through me innocent and upright—that is, just in their works—because I awaited you—that is, hoped in you—so that they too might hope through my example, I will not be put to shame.

This means: Because I have encouraged many to await you by my example, without failing, I will not be put to shame, lest they too, perhaps, failing through my bad example, be put to shame.

He also prays for those innocent and upright people as follows: I say that the innocent and upright have attached themselves to me—that is, through my example. Therefore, O God, free those who have now become Israel from all their tribulations, lest they yield.

## ON PSALM XXV

**Title of the twenty-fifth Psalm.** A Psalm of David—that is, of the assembly of the completely perfect faithful, who, secure in their innocence and justice, grant that God judge them in the future according to what their innocence and justice deserve.

They also display in parts their innocence and justice, and promise that they will devote themselves increasingly to these things, so that by their example they may strongly invite the less perfect to pursue them.

Or this may be a prayer that God judge them—that is, distinguish them in the future from the mass of the lost, lest they be mixed with them, as they are in this world.

The rest concerning the intention remains unchanged. This, however, begins as follows:

**75** Judge me, Lord, in the future according to what is just. For I, who grant this, have entered in my innocence—that is, I have walked in the way of your commandments. This means: For I have persevered in my innocence.

Or in this way, so that it may be a prayer: Judge me, Lord, by your just judgment; distinguish me in the future from the lost, with whom I associate here.

What follows, however, as Augustine says, is not the arrogance of an exalted person, but the confession of one who is not ungrateful.

I say: Judge me. And rightly, because I, praying in this way, have entered in my innocence—that is, I have persevered—and I will continue to do so; I will not grow weak in perseverance, hoping in the Lord and not possessing hope of perseverance through myself alone.

I pray: Judge me. And so that I may await this judgment with good hope, first test me here. The order is inverted.

Test me—that is, show me, having been tested through tribulations and ineffective suggestions, to myself and to others who will adhere to me.

And afterward prove me—that is, show me proved, with no tribulation or any criminal suggestion having accomplished anything in me.

I say: Test me, as follows: Burn—that is, consume completely with spiritual fire—my kidneys and my heart.

He explains in what sense he uses “kidneys” here: namely, for the illicit movements of my heart, which are called “kidneys” because we take delight in them as in the illicit exercise of the kidneys.

Since no one will be saved by innocence alone—for “in your sight no living person will be justified” (Psalm 142:2)—he also prays to be saved through mercy.

I said, “Judge me, because I have entered in my innocence.” And I do not pray to be saved by innocence alone, but also because your mercy is before my eyes—that is, before the reflections of my heart.

It is as though he said: Because I trust in your mercy, and therefore also because, so far as I am able, I have been well-pleasing in conformity with your truth, namely your Son, both in works and in virtues.

He explains his innocence in parts as follows: Truly I have entered in innocence, because I have not sat with the council of vanity—that is, although I associate with them bodily, I have not sat among them in my soul; I have not lingered with them by consenting to them.

They are the council of vanity, that is, those who agree together in the desire for earthly things, which are vain.

I say, “I have not sat,” and I also promise: I will not enter by consent with those who act wickedly, namely, false Christians. And he rightly says “I will not enter,” for “to enter” means to enter into something hidden. Anyone who acts wickedly enters—that is, enters into something to be concealed, namely, into sins—as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3:20).

And not only have I not sat with them; I have also hated the assembly of the wicked—that is, I have hated their evil works, not the creature.

And not only will I not enter with those who act wickedly, namely, false Christians; I will not sit—that is, I will not linger in consent—with the impious, namely, heretics and idolaters.

This means: I will not consent to their unbelief and opinions.

But standing among the innocent, I will wash my hands—that is, I will cleanse what must be cleansed in my affections. They are called “hands” because by them we grasp opinions, just as with bodily hands we handle bodily things.

Having displayed his innocence in parts, and seeing that this was not sufficient, he also promises to do good works, as follows:

I say, “I will wash my hands,” and with washed hands I will surround—that is, adorn with good works and virtues—your altar, Lord, namely, the faith upon which all virtues are founded and good works are sacrificed to God. It is therefore called an altar, since sacrifice is customarily offered upon an altar.

Hence the Apostle says: “Without faith no one will please God” (Hebrews 11:6).

“Surround” is used for “adorn,” by comparison with an altar, which, when adorned with cloths, gold, or silver, is often surrounded.

I say, “I will surround it,” and I will do this in order to hear the voice of your praise—that is, to understand by what voice you wish to be praised, namely, by the voice of the righteous: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Sirach 15:9).

He rightly uses “hear” for “understand.” For the hearing of the soul is understanding.

And also in order to declare to others your wonders—that is, your commands and works, which are wondrous because of their exceeding excellence. Otherwise I would not be fit to declare them. Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my statutes?” (Psalm 49:16), and so forth.

I say, “I will surround it,” and indeed I will do this, O Lord. For I have loved the beauty of your house—that is, I have loved making your house beautiful with virtues—and I have loved the place where your glory dwells—that is, I have desired, by doing good, to make myself such a place that, by graciously dwelling in me through my good works, you may be glorified by others, according to the Gospel saying: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father” (Matthew 5:16).

Because I have loved this, I will surround it, I will wash my hands, I will not sit, and I will not enter.

Do not destroy my soul with the impious in the future—that is, with heretics and idolaters, O God—and do not destroy my life with men who shed blood, namely, false Christians. Do not destroy my life—that is, my soul, which is called “life” because through it we live.

Men of blood are those who kill souls by evil example and persuasion, just as those who completely pour out the blood of bodies cause the bodies of those whose blood they shed to perish.

These men of blood and the impious will rightly be destroyed. Here are the reasons:

In whose hands are iniquities—that is, in whose affections they are. This means: Even if they are not always able to act wickedly, they always desire to act wickedly.

And if at some time they do good, they do not act with good intention, but because their right hand—that is, their good work—is filled with gifts.

It is customary to signify good things by the right hand and evil things by the left.

This means: They do good works so that they may be filled with the favor of the people and with earthly advantages. Concerning such people the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:16).

The men of blood and the impious are such; therefore they will rightly be destroyed.

But I, acting here in my innocence, have entered. This is repeated out of an excess of affection, as explained above.

Therefore, because I have entered, redeem me from sins, namely, through the death you suffered for me; and, having redeemed me, have mercy on me by making me blessed in eternal glory.

And do not redeem and have mercy on me because of innocence alone, but also because my foot—that is, my affection—stood, that is, persevered, on the straight path, that is, in good action, which is straight and not crooked.

Affections are called “feet” because through them the mind walks by thinking, just as the body walks by moving its feet.

I say that my foot stood on the straight path. And also, O Lord, I will bless—that is, glorify and magnify—you—by doing good—in the churches, that is, in the presence of assemblies of the faithful, so that they too may glorify and magnify you by doing good.

## ON PSALM XXVI

**Title of the twenty-sixth Psalm.** A Psalm of David before he was anointed.

Here we are referred to the history of David, who was anointed king three times.

First, in Bethlehem, in his father’s house; this signified that he had been chosen by God to be king.

Second, after Saul’s death, in Hebron, so that he might reign over the tribe of Judah.

Third, so that he might reign over all Israel.

All these events preceded as figures of the Church. For the children of the Church are anointed in baptism with sacred oil, to signify by this that they have been chosen by the Lord, so that those who had been servants of the devil might, by spiritual grace, become kings of themselves.

Second, in confirmation they are anointed by bishops, so that, by receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit more abundantly, they may become increasingly kings of themselves—those who have already become Judah, that is, confessors of God.

Third, in the future they will be anointed by God with eternal blessedness, so that those who will then be Israel may, with God’s help, become so completely kings of themselves that neither visible nor invisible enemies will in any way rule over them.

It appears that here the assembly of the faithful is speaking. In the preceding psalm it spoke of the benefits already given to it by God, before it has reached eternal anointing; and it does so for the instruction of others, **77** so that those who possess the same goods may know that they have them from God, while those who do not yet possess them may hasten by every means to obtain them.

It also shows that it awaits that anointing in every way, and prays to attain it, so that it may instruct us both to await it and to pray for it.

This is briefly indicated in the title as follows: This psalm is to be attributed to David—that is, to the Church acting most perfectly concerning the benefits received from God—before he was anointed, that is, before he was anointed by God as king with that most perfect anointing.

Eternal blessedness is rightly called “anointing,” because through it one will be healed of all corruption, just as the sick are accustomed to be healed by anointing.

This psalm begins as follows:

The Lord is my illumination—this is said emphatically. This means: The Lord illuminated me by faith in baptism.

And my salvation—and this too is emphatic: he himself saved me from sins.

And since he has already bestowed these things, what invisible enemy shall I fear so that he may overcome me? None, of course.

And the Lord is the protector of my life. This means: To me, who was dead in Adam originally in my soul, he restored life, and he himself is the protector of that life, so that I may not lose it by sinning criminally.

Therefore, from what visible enemy shall I tremble when those who, by their will, wish to harm me, although they cannot do so in action, being above me—that is, superior and more distinguished than I with respect to the body—draw near, that is, prepare themselves, to devour—that is, consume through tribulations—my flesh?

I shall tremble before none, this being understood.

Or “to devour my flesh” may be explained in this way: They draw near, I say, for this purpose, although they did not intend it, and will come to devour my flesh by inflicting tribulations upon me—that is, to consume and reduce to nothing my carnal desires, so that, when I have been afflicted, they may be unable to accomplish whatever they wish in me.

Hence in the preceding psalm he also prayed: “Burn my kidneys” (Psalm 25:2).

And rightly I will not tremble when I consider this concerning the enemies who afflict me. They who by this appear powerful and lofty to others, and firm in dominion, have rather been weakened by it—that is, they have already appeared to me weak and wretched.

And, to say more, they have already fallen as far as I am concerned—that is, I have already foreseen their future fall.

He explains how they draw near. I say, I will not tremble when they draw near. And this is true. For if they encamp against me—that is, if multitudes of enemies appear in order to fight against me with tribulations—my heart will not fear in such a way that I yield through fear.

This is said by comparison with enemies who, when they wish to engage someone in battle, first enter his territory and pitch their camps there.

I say: I will not fear camps standing against me.

And, to say more: If a battle of tribulations rises against me, I will not only say, “I will not fear,” but also, in this very matter, I, who may appear to fear the enemies, will hope—that is, through this battle in which I will act courageously, I will hope to obtain one thing that I await from the Lord.

And truly I await one thing, because I have asked one thing from the Lord, both in deed, voice, and affection, namely, eternal blessedness. And I will seek this as the reward of my life.

He expresses that blessedness in parts. I will seek this: to dwell in the house of the Lord—that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem—and not merely for an hour, but all the days of my life, that is, in the eternity through which my life endures, namely Christ.

Hence the Apostle says: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:4).

And I will seek this also: once established in the house of the Lord, to see perfectly the will of the Lord, which here I cannot see perfectly. Hence the Apostle says: “Now I know in part, but then I shall know just as I am known” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

And by seeing his will, I will visit—that is, see—his temple, namely, the body of the Lord’s humanity, which was the temple of divinity. Hence he likewise says in the Gospel: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

I say that I will seek these things. And this is the confidence arising from such benefits, which he has already bestowed upon me:

For he hid me in his tabernacle—that is, he has already placed me in the hidden place of his tabernacle, namely, in faith and hope of the blessedness that I shall possess through Christ, who was God’s tabernacle. This blessedness is now hidden from us, though one day it will appear. Hence the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1). And elsewhere he says of blessedness: “Your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3).

And he not only hid me, but also, when I had been placed in the hidden place of his tabernacle, protected me in the day of evils—that is, in this time in which all evils abound; by his grace he defended me so that I would not yield. Hence the Apostle says: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. 5:16).

And he not only hid and protected me, but also, when I had been placed upon the rock—that is, in Christ, who is firm like a rock—or, upon the rock, that is, in steadfastness and strength, he exalted me in virtues. And he indicates when I was exalted. I say, he exalted me. And now, namely, in the time of persecution, when I seem entirely depressed, he exalted my head—that is, my mind—above my enemies, even though he permitted my body to be depressed. This is to say: I have been more exalted in virtues against them than they have been exalted in their tribulations against me.

Having shown the benefits granted to him by God’s grace, through which he has confidence that he will attain blessedness, he also shows the merits of free will, as follows: I do not hope to possess the blessedness that I shall seek only because he hid, protected, and exalted me, but also because I went around—that is, so that I would not be rash or negligent, I diligently investigated—how I ought to sacrifice to him.

And, having been placed in his tabernacle—that is, in faith in Christ and in his tabernacle—I sacrificed to him a sacrifice of shouting, namely, virtues and good works, which are sacrifices that cry out greatly to the Lord, in accordance with Prosper’s words:

> No sweeter fragrance arises by Christ’s example
