> Than when a man offers the libations of chaste conduct  
> And makes sacred offering from the gift of virtues.

When he says “a sacrifice of shouting,” it is as though he said: “A sacrifice greatly worthy of obtaining what is sought,” by comparison with those who, when they cry out greatly, usually obtain their request more quickly than those who act negligently. He says “I went around” by comparison with those who, when they investigate something diligently, usually go around a great deal.

But I not only went around and sacrificed; I shall also sing to the Lord—that is, I shall think well of him, which will be sweet to him like a song. And I shall not only sing, but shall also now say a psalm—that is, I shall place my good work in public, so that I may draw others by my example. He rightly says “I shall say it”: spoken words are in public, whereas thoughts are hidden.

Having shown the benefits and merits by which he trusts that he will attain blessedness, he prays that he may obtain it, as follows: I said, “I asked for one thing, and I shall seek it”; and you, Lord, hear my voice with which I cried out—that is, with which I acted toward you by an earnest cry, not negligently, in order to win your favor. And hear me not solely on account of my merits, but have mercy on me and hear me—that is, hear me mercifully.

I say, “I cried out.” And truly my voice was a cry. For while I was speaking with my voice, I had nothing else in my heart; rather, my heart said to you the very same thing as my mouth. Otherwise my voice would not have been a cry but something negligent. Or it may be understood thus: I say, “I cried out,” and it was not my mouth but my heart that said this to you.

And he states what it said: “O Lord, my face has sought you.” This is to say: I have diligently sought, both in work and in affection, to see face to face the one whom I now see in an enigma. And still, Lord, I shall seek your face, by thinking and acting well.

Therefore, do not turn your face away from me in the future, even if now you turn it away. What he adds, “Do not decline,” means the same as “Do not turn your face away.” But he repeats it in order to add this qualification: Do not decline your face, namely, in anger—that is, because of the anger that you may have toward me on account of my sins—for you will decline from no one except the one to whom you appear angry. Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “Then he will speak to them in his anger” (Ps. 2:5).

I say, “Do not decline from me,” namely, from your servant, as though he were saying: It is not fitting that you should decline, since I am your servant, obedient to you in all things as far as I can be. I pray that you do not decline; rather, be my helper for acting well. And, as my helper, do not abandon me to free will alone, because I would be insufficient by myself—even if you have sometimes abandoned me, so that, when I fall, I may not doubt that I am insufficient, just as you abandoned Peter when he denied you, so that afterward he would not trust in himself.

For he had said, trusting in himself: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. 26:35). At least, do not despise me—that is, do not abandon me in such a way that afterward you do not help me—as you despised Judas. And you ought not despise me, because you are God, that is, my Creator, and my savior, that is, my Redeemer.

It is as though he were saying: Since you alone are my God and Creator, it is necessary that you neither abandon nor despise me, because my father and my mother—namely, Adam and Eve—abandoned me, that is, cast me down into death.

He speaks by comparison with a father and mother who, when they abandon and expose a small infant, kill it, insofar as that depends on them. For it would perish from hunger unless someone else came to its aid. Thus Adam and Eve, who by their good example ought to have instructed us to obey God and thereby drawn us with them to life, abandoned us by failing and by their example instructed us otherwise, and thus dragged us into death.

I say that they abandoned me; but the Lord took me up, so that, being weak, he might sanctify me—that is, restore me to immortality. And he makes this apostrophe to his hearers, so that those who have been taken up may attribute this not to themselves but to the Lord, following his example, while those who have not been taken up may endure every hardship so that they may be taken up.

After the apostrophe he returns to the prayer as follows: I say, Lord, that you have taken me up; and so that I, having been taken up, may not again become weak, Lord, set for me, placed upon your way—that is, upon the way of your commandments, namely, in their fulfillment, which is the way to life—a rule for walking, that is, guidance, so that I may turn neither backward nor to the right nor to the left.

He is said to go backward who fails completely. He is said to go to the right who, while striving too greatly for holiness and exceeding the proper measure, cannot attain what he has resolved upon, as did the little hermit John, who failed while attempting to live angelically. And rightly this is called going to the right. For good things are usually signified by the right hand, and virtues are good things. That movement appears to approach virtue. No slothful person, however, strives beyond measure in any virtue.

He is said to go to the left who, although he does not fail completely, nevertheless relaxes too much in virtue. For vices are signified by the left hand, and vices are evil; evil things are often denoted by the left. To relax too much in virtue is characteristic of the vicious. For no holy person relaxes in virtue. Thus, to relax excessively is rightly called going to the left.

To go forward on God’s way is said of one who is deflected neither by relaxing too much nor by exceeding the proper measure, but walks along God’s way with due balance. The way of God means the common commandments, without which no one will be saved, as we explained in Psalm 21.

I say, “Place a law in my way,” and not only this, but also “direct me”—that is, make me straight—in the straight path. The straight path means the particular commandments, which apply to few, as was said in that same psalm.

And I make this request—“Place a law and direct me”—because of my enemies, who want to make me turn aside. Rescue me from them, so that they may not prevail against me. And thus, by rescuing me, do not hand me over to the souls—that is, to the wills—of those who afflict me.

This is to say: Even if you permit me to be afflicted by them, do not allow them to accomplish fully in me what they want, namely, to make me turn aside. I pray, “Do not hand me over.” And this is what I ought to pray, because unjust witnesses have risen up against me, afflicting me and making suggestions—namely, those who give unjust testimony, both in deed and in word, asserting that attachment to worldly things is the highest good.

And iniquity—that is, those very persons, emphatically called “iniquity”—has lied in order to make me turn aside, affirming that things which are evil, namely vices, are good, and that things which are good, namely virtues, are evil.

I say, “It has lied,” and this not to my disadvantage but to its own—that is, to its own condemnation. “For the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11).

Having made his prayer, lest he seem to have prayed out of distrust, he declares that he firmly believes he will attain what he has prayed for, as follows: I prayed, O hearers, that God would not turn his face away, and I did not pray this out of distrust. For I believe that I see—that is, shall see—the good things of the Lord, namely, his face and his will, which are truly good. And I shall see them not in the present life but in the land of the living—that is, in paradise, where no one will dwell except one who lives forever.

Therefore, hearer, following my example, await the Lord, believing that he will give you these same good things. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not abandon your confidence, which has a great reward” (Heb. 10:35).

I say, “Await”; and while awaiting, do not be negligent in works, but act manfully—by working, praying, and thinking well. And when you have acted manfully, do not cease through weariness, but let your heart be strengthened in this. “For whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22). And if the Lord delays, endure—that is, await the Lord patiently—so that you do not murmur.

## ON PSALM 27

### The Title of the Twenty-Seventh Psalm

A psalm to be attributed to David, that is, to Christ. And rightly it says “to David himself.” It is as though it were saying: Not to David speaking through his members, but to David himself—that is, to David acting in his own person. Here he pleads by presenting his merit, that is, his good intention, so that God may hear him as he prays concerning the resurrection. He also speaks concessively concerning the retribution of his enemies, announces the salvation of his own people, and at the end prays for them.

To you, Lord, the Trinity, I have cried out and shall cry out in order to obtain you—that is, I shall act with a good intention, which is an intense cry directed to you. He does not say “to obtain you” because God would not always exist fully in him; rather, it is the same as if he said: I shall cry out for this purpose, so that although according to mortality I am not conformed to you, I may be conformed to your immortality and impassibility—that is, that I may possess immortality and impassibility insofar as I am human.

Or: I shall cry out while looking toward you in your mercy, as though he were saying: Trusting in your mercy. Therefore, my God, do not be silent, having withdrawn from me. This is to say: Answer my petition. God’s answering is the fulfillment of the petition.

In another translation we find: “Do not become deaf to me,” that is, “Do not become deaf for me.” This means the same as “Do not be silent toward me.” And because he had said “Do not be silent,” lest we think that he wanted his petition fulfilled immediately, he qualifies it: I say, “Do not be silent toward me, having withdrawn,” when—that is, at some time.

This is to say: Even if you are now silent, not fulfilling it, do not remain silent when silence will no longer be appropriate. It is as though he were saying: At some time fulfill in me what must be fulfilled, so that you may make me immortal and impassible.

“Do not be silent” and “Do not be silent toward me” are repeated as a qualification. Or it may be understood thus: Do not be silent at any time or in any way about making me and my people immortal.

I pray, “Do not be silent.” For if you are silent, I shall not only fail to be immortal, but shall also become like those who descend into the pit—that is, into the depth of death—and who will not rise until the general resurrection. We call a pit a very deep hollow, and therefore it is used here for “depth.”

In another translation we find: “Lest, while you are silent, I become like those who descend into the pit.”

I said, “I shall cry out,” namely, with intention. And I shall also cry out with the voice of supplication—that is, with an articulate voice proceeding from my supplication, namely, from the intention of my heart, which earnestly supplicates you. And you, hear the voice of my supplication—that is, hear it so that I may obtain what I seek—the voice proceeding from my good intention with which I supplicate you.

And it is fitting that you hear me, since what I ask is directed toward obtaining you, not something earthly, and since this is what I do: I do not lower but raise my hands—that is, intensify my affections—in order to establish your holy temple.

This is to say: My affections are directed toward establishing the Church, which will be your holy temple, in which you will dwell. Hence the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Cor. 3:17).

Or it may be understood thus: While I raise—that is, lift—my hands upon the cross in order to establish your holy temple. The rest remains unchanged.

Since he had said “Hear,” he shows from what he should be heard, as follows: Hear this, namely, this request. Do not hand me over to death together with sinners, by antonomasia, as though he were saying: I do not ask that you not hand me over to death at all; rather, I ask that you not hand me over together with sinners—that is, by consenting to the desire of the sinners who want to keep me in death so that I may not rise again.

And because he had spoken obscurely, he explains: I say, “Do not hand me over together with sinners,” which is as if I were saying: And, that is, namely, do not destroy me—that is, do not destroy me completely—so that I may not rise again.

Do not hand me over with those who work iniquity—that is, by consenting to the Jews who work my death, which is emphatically called “iniquity” with respect to them. These workers of iniquity speak peace—that is, peaceful words—with me, their neighbor, born according to the flesh from their race, saying: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful,” and so forth (Matt. 22:16).

I say that they speak peace. But evil things—that is, evil thoughts concerning me—are in their hearts. He says this to heighten their guilt, so that afterward he may speak concessively of their condemnation, as follows: I say, “They speak peace,” and evil things are in their hearts.

Therefore, give them according to their works—that is, repay them with the condemnation that their works deserve—the death of me, namely, which they bring about not in deed but in counsel and word.

And lest their works be thought just or rash, he qualifies it thus: And, that is, namely, give them according to the wickedness of their inventions—that is, according to what they have deserved for the wicked counsels they devised concerning my death.

And not only give them according to works not performed by their hands, but repay them according to the works of their hands—that is, according to what they carried out with their hands, scourging me and treating me as though I were a thief.

And because he had said “give” and “repay,” he explains what he asks to be given, as follows: I say, “Give and repay”: namely, return to them their retribution—that is, the reward of their retribution, to them themselves. For they repaid me evil for good.

The verse that precedes, namely, “For they did not understand,” is read in reverse order as follows: I say, “Return their retribution”—which you will indeed do: you will destroy them, both here from their land and in the future from the land of the living, which they presume to possess. And afterward you will not build them up, either in this life or in that one.

And this is because they did not understand the works of the Lord—that is, they did not wish to understand through his works that he is Lord in the world, namely, through the glorious miracles that he performed before them. For no one else illuminated a man born blind or raised one who had been dead four days.

And they did not understand him through the work of his hands—that is, through his most excellent works, that he is Lord: namely, through the fact that he restored the innocence taken away through Adam, destroyed original sin, restored immortality to the world, and performed the other things wondrously. These are called the works of his hands because they are especially outstanding. For works performed by hand are more excellent than those carried out by other instruments.

Since he had said, “Hear the voice of my prayer,” and so forth, lest he be thought to have prayed out of distrust, implying that he would be heard, he praises God as though he had already been heard, as follows: I pray, “Hear”; and already I seem to myself to have been heard. And blessed—that is, exalted—be the Lord, both by me and by my members.

For he has heard—that is, because of the excessive certainty I possess, he already seems to have heard—the voice of my supplication, that is, the voice proceeding from my good intention.

And he shows from what he has heard me: he has heard me in this respect, namely, because the Lord will be my helper so that he may raise me up, and my protector, so that I may not yield in tribulations. And deservedly so. For my heart has hoped in him, not in another; and therefore I was helped by him.

And rightly he says, “My heart has hoped.” We are said to hope with the heart and mind when we hope rationally and for things pertaining to salvation. But we hope with the senses when we hope only for things that are pleasant and useful to the body.

Since he had said, “I was helped,” he explains in what he was helped, as follows: I say, “I was helped”; and because he helped me, my flesh has blossomed again—that is, my flesh will blossom again—with the glory of the resurrection, which was the flowering glory of the Nativity, when she was born from the Virgin without concupiscence.

Hence Isaiah says: “A shoot will come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root” (Isa. 11:1). And in the Song of Songs the same bridegroom says to his bride, the Church: “I am a flower of the field” (Song 2:1).

And because the flesh that appears to have withered in the Passion will blossom again, I shall confess to him—that is, I shall praise him—in my future members. “According to my will,” that is, according to the will of my members. Namely, I shall bring forth confessors for him who will praise him not through slavish fear, as the Jews did, but voluntarily, with good affection and action.

I say that I shall confess to him in my members. But the Lord will be the strength of his people—that is, the Lord will make those confessors whom I shall bring forth for him, and who will be his people, strong in virtues. And he will be the protector of the salvations of his Christ—that is, of those who are to be saved by me, his Christ; they are emphatically called “salvations.”

Having announced the salvation of his people, he prays for them as follows: I say that you will be their strength and protector; and so may it be. Save, Lord, your future people from vices. And bless your inheritance—that is, exalt in virtues the people whom you will cultivate through preachers, as someone cultivates an inheritance; therefore they will be called your inheritance.

And guide them so that they do not fail. And exalt them—that is, raise them from good to better—unto eternity, that is, to lead them into eternity.

## ON PSALM 28

### The Title of the Twenty-Eighth Psalm

A psalm of David, that is, of the prophet acting at the completion of the tabernacle—that is, in contemplation of the completion of the tabernacle, namely, the Church. It is called a tabernacle because the faithful who exist in it serve God by fighting against vices, after the manner of soldiers serving in tabernacles.

This title appears to have been placed according to the likeness of the historical account. For it is read that when David had completed the tabernacle of the Lord, the people of Israel offered many sacrifices there.

That tabernacle prefigured the Church, which was to be completed in virtues and good works by Christ, the true David, from both peoples. Foreseeing this completion, the prophet exhorts those who will be in the tabernacle, namely, in the Church, that when it has been completed by Christ they should bring themselves to sacrifice, following the example of the apostles.

The apostles are called rams because they are the leaders of all the faithful, just as rams are leaders of sheep; or because they have two strong horns, namely, the two Testaments, with whose aid they repel the errors of all people, just as rams drive away obstacles with their two horns. He also shows how this tabernacle is to be completed.

Bring to the Lord, O future adopted sons of God; bring yourselves to sacrifice, sons of rams—that is, imitators of the apostles. This is to say: Offer yourselves to the Lord, as the apostles did.

The faithful are truly called sons of God, that is, specially regenerated by him. Hence John the Evangelist says: “He gave them the power to become sons of God” (John 1:12). They are also called sons of the apostles because they are regenerated to God through their teaching and, insofar as they can, become their imitators. Hence the Apostle says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor” (Gal. 4:19), and so forth.

Because he says “bring” twice, he speaks as follows: I say, “Bring yourselves as sons of rams”; and in this, namely, be sons of rams. Bring to the Lord, as they themselves did, glory, so that you may think well about the glorious essence of the deity.

And bring honor. In another translation we find “authority,” which is to say: Understand that, according to his humanity, he is to be honored by all and has power and authority over all things. Hence he says in the Gospel: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18). And the Apostle says: “He gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. 2:9).

I say, “Bring glory and honor to the Lord”; and do this, insofar as you can, by thinking well about him, and also with respect to others: bring glory to the Lord’s name—that is, make him glorious among others by magnifying his name—and adore the Lord, that is, venerate him through good works, in his holy court—that is, once you have been made his holy court: not narrow in charity, but expanded, just as a court is spacious.

In another translation we find “in his holy hall.” This is the same in meaning, namely, that you should be his dwelling in the greatest possible charity, after the manner of a hall, which is a very spacious dwelling.

I say, “Bring yourselves, sons of rams”; and you must be brought, for the tabernacle has now been completed, and therefore sacrifice must be offered in it.

And he shows how it has been completed, and what that tabernacle is, announcing with complete certainty what is future in the past tense, as follows: Truly, they must be brought. For the voice of the Lord—that is, his preaching—thundered through preachers over the waters—that is, in the manner of thunder, which sounds openly to everyone and threatens them. It sounded openly to the nations and threatened condemnation to those who did not repent.

And rightly he says “over.” For that voice proceeded from the Father’s higher disposition. The nations are called waters because, like flowing waters, they flow into unlawful things.

And because he had said “the voice of the Lord,” lest the Lord appear to be just anyone, he commends him as follows: And this Lord, being God of majesty—that is, of omnipotence—thundered over many waters. And he repeats “over the waters” in order that, since he had stated it without qualification, he might add “many.”

I say, “The voice of the Lord working in strength,” that is, in the steadfastness he gave to the preachers, so that neither death nor life would separate them from the charity of Christ (Rom. 8:35). And I say, “The voice of the Lord working in the magnificence of the preachers’ miracles.” Hence the Gospel says: “The Lord worked with them and confirmed the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16:20).

And he explains what he worked in strength and magnificence as follows: The voice of the Lord, I say, breaks cedars—that is, those who are lofty in pride—turning them from evil to good, after the manner of a cedar, which is a lofty tree.

When he says “cedars,” he means in general all those who are proud against God through disobedience. And the Lord will not only break small cedars, but will also break the cedars of Lebanon—that is, those who are proud because of the splendor of nobility and riches. They are therefore called cedars of Lebanon, for Lebanon is interpreted as “splendor.”

I say that he will break the cedars, and he will still do something else that is more wondrous: he will break the cedars and, once broken, crush them—that is, he will humble them greatly in tribulations. I say that he will crush them as a calf of Lebanon—that is, making them acceptable to God through those very tribulations, just as the calf of Lebanon is acceptable for sacrifice, since it is exceedingly fat because of the good pastures of Lebanon where it was fed. For fat calves were suitable for sacrifice.

I say that he will crush them. And lest their being crushed seem disgraceful to them, the Beloved—that is, Christ, by antonomasia, of whom the Father’s voice says, “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3:17)—will be crushed, that is, humbled in tribulations.

And lest it be thought that he is crushed according to his divine nature, he qualifies it as follows: “As the son of unicorns”—that is, in the manner in which he is the son of the Jews, who are called unicorns because of the one and singular pride they possessed above all other peoples. Or because of the one Law: no other nations then possessed the Law.

Because he calls him the son of the Jews, that is, born from their blood, he says this to commend his humility: he did not disdain to be born even from the blood of those whom he knew would crucify him.

And lest it be thought that he breaks and crushes only those cedars which, although they belong to Lebanon, are not hostile to the Church, he also shows that he divides those who oppose the faithful, as follows: And the voice of the Lord, I say, cuts apart—that is, divides—the flame of fire, that is, the persecutors, taking some and leaving others.

They are rightly called a flame, because they devour the faithful through tribulations, as a flame devours wood. And rightly he adds “of fire” after “flame.” For just as a flame proceeds from fire, so their persecution proceeds from the excessive heat of anger and hatred.

After showing that the voice of the Lord thundered over the nations, which are called waters, and did so in strength and magnificence, breaking the cedars of Lebanon and crushing them like a calf, and cutting apart the flame of fire, he declares that by the same voice the desert of Kadesh is to be shaken and moved, through which the Jews are signified.

According to Augustine, Kadesh is interpreted as “holy of the Law.” But they themselves are a desert with respect to the holiness of the Law—that is, lacking the holiness of the Law and retaining only carnal commandments. Or they are the desert of the holiness of the Law, that is, abandoning the holiness of the Law that the Lord set before them. The meaning is the same, differently explained.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “You have made void the commandment of God because of your tradition” (Matt. 15:6). And the Apostle says: “Seeking to establish their own will, they have not been subject to the law of God” (Rom. 10:3).

According to Jerome, Kadesh is also called “the moth’s devouring.” But the Jews, being a desert, endeavored, after the manner of a moth, to eat the innocent through false apostles—that is, to consume them by confirming them in their own error.

And concerning their movement toward faith he says as follows: I said that the voice of the Lord thundered over the waters. The voice of the Lord, I say, shakes the desert through repentance, and he specifies which desert: and, that is, namely, the Lord will move the desert of Kadesh through repentance, that is, the Jews.

This is by comparison with a cultivator who shakes and moves the earth with ploughs so that it may become fertile.

And the voice of the Lord prepares the stags from that desert—that is, makes some stags, namely, those who devour the poison of serpents. And he will prepare stags because he will reveal to them the thickets—that is, the obscurities—of the prophetic Scriptures.

I said that the voice of the Lord thundered over the waters, and will break and crush the cedars; and it will move the desert of Kadesh. And all these—that is, the waters, cedars, and desert—existing in his temple, namely, the members of the Church, which is his temple, will give glory to him—that is, glorify him through good affections, words, and works.

And they will give glory for this reason: the Lord makes them inhabit the flood—that is, establishes them immovably in the hope of blessedness, which is given by God to the faithful through baptism. It is called a flood because all sins are washed away in it, just as all flesh was destroyed in the Flood.

And through the flood the Lord the King will sit—that is, dwell—in them, so that he may rule them from good to better, forever—that is, in this life and in the future. And he explains how he will rule: Here, the Lord will give strength to his people—that is, steadfastness, so that they do not fail—and in the future he will bless his people, that is, exalt them, establishing them in peace so that they may no longer be troubled by anything.

## ON PSALM 29

### The Title of the Twenty-Ninth Psalm

A psalm of a song at the dedication of the house of David. This title was placed according to the likeness of the historical account. For the prophet, foreseeing that his son Solomon would build a house for God and later dedicate it, and that at that dedication the dedication of Christ’s body and of the Church would be prefigured—both of which are God’s house, that is, his dwelling—introduces Christ promising that he will act well, so that he may be dedicated by God in the resurrection, that is, destined for immortality, glory, and the praise of God, just as Solomon’s house was dedicated, that is, destined for God to be praised in it.

He also announces the dedication itself of his resurrection, exhorting his members to act well and praise God, so that they may themselves be dedicated in the future, that is, freed from mortality and destined for immortality, joy, and the praise of God. He also shows his steadfastness in praying for that dedication, so that he may make us steadfast in prayer.

Because the title says “a psalm of a song,” some say that this is one part, while others say that it is two. When it is one part, the title is explained thus: This work, called “a psalm of a song,” contains within itself a psalm—that is, good action—and a song—that is, the reward for good action. It was made in contemplation of the dedication of the house of David—that is, of Christ’s body or of the Church. Both are the house of David, that is, of Christ, the true David.

But if “a psalm of a song” consists of two parts, although the meaning is the same, it is explained differently as follows: This psalm—that is, the good action contained in this work—is the cause of the song, that is, of joy. The song is for the future dedication of the house of David in that house.

Or it may be understood so that there is a difference in meaning: This psalm—that is, this work—is a psalm, that is, a work, of a song concerning the future dedication of the house of David.

I will exalt you, Lord—that is, I will regard you as high and great, by thinking well about you for your honor and by acting well. And deservedly so, because for the sake of exaltation you have taken me up—that is, you will take me up—making me immortal from mortal, by comparison with a physician who takes up a sick person in order to heal him.

And you will not permit my enemies, the Jews who exalt themselves over me, to rejoice over me. For they would rejoice if I were held in death.

I say, “You will take me up.” But so that I may be taken up, Lord of all, my God in a special way, I looked toward you in your mercy and cried out—that is, I prayed with an intense voice—and therefore you healed me, that is, you will heal me. “You healed” means the same as “you took me up.”

And he explains how he will heal: You will heal in this way, namely: Lord, you brought my soul out of hell—that is, you will bring it out of the local hell—returning it to the body on the third day; and you saved me from every sin, so that I might be worthy to lead others out of hell.

I say that I am separated from those who descend into the pit—that is, from the company of those who descend into the depth of vices.

Having shown his healing, he exhorts his members to sing psalms and confess to the Lord, so that, having been healed, they too may rejoice: I say that he has healed me. Therefore, so that you may be healed, O my saints, who are his children, sing psalms to the Lord—that is, act well for the Lord’s honor.

And confess to the memory of his holiness—that is, praise him with voice and affection for the memory of his holiness. This is to say: Praise him for the fact that he will remember his promise, namely, to sanctify you through me, you who became sinners through Adam.

I say, “Confess,” and do so for two reasons. Because his anger—that is, the vengeance he inflicted upon human beings because of Adam—will be in indignation, that is, in brief wrath. In another translation we find: “His anger is for a moment,” which is the same in meaning. For indignation is momentary wrath.

And life will be in his will. This is to say: You ought to confess to God himself because, although he could justly condemn you, he inflicted upon you a brief vengeance, namely mortality and suffering, which will not last long. And because life will be given in the future by his will—that is, through his gracious will—therefore continue to confess.

For in the evening—that is, for those who look toward Adam in order to be conformed to him—there will remain weeping, that is, eternal weeping in the future. And in the morning—that is, for those who look toward me, Christ—there will remain the joy of blessedness.

This is to say: Confess. For those who do not confess, but look toward Adam and are conformed to him, will weep. But those who, by looking toward me, Christ, sing psalms and are conformed to me, will rejoice.

Adam is rightly called “evening,” for he became dark through sinning, and from him our death followed, just as night follows evening, which is darker than morning. But Christ is “morning,” because in him the light of our faith had its beginning, and he was bright in holiness like the morning, which is bright, in which the light of day begins.

I said: Because for those who look toward evening, weeping will remain.

But I did not look toward evening; rather, in my abundance—that is, established in the fullness of my holiness—I said, that is, resolved within myself: “I shall not be moved from this abundance forever.” He says this in order to instruct us by his example, so that we may not be moved from holiness.

I said, “I shall not be moved”; yet this was not through myself, but you, Lord, supplied strength—that is, steadfastness—to my beauty, that is, to the abundance of my holiness, in your will, that is, by your grace. He shows what strength this was: namely, that even in tribulation I should not cease to cry out to you, although you allow me to suffer tribulation.

I say that you supplied strength, and to such an extent that you turned your face from me—that is, you will seem to turn the sight of your mercy away from me in the Passion, permitting me to be afflicted—and I became troubled, that is, I shall be spontaneously troubled in soul by fear of the Passion, and yet I shall not grow lax.

But looking toward you, Lord of mercy, I shall cry out—that is, I shall act with a clamorous affection—and looking toward you, God, that is, my Creator, I shall entreat you, saying:

“What benefit will there be in the shedding of my blood, while I descend—that is, if this is what it means for me to descend into corruption, that is, into putrefaction?”

This means: “Do not permit me to descend into corruption.” For since great benefit will in the future arise from my death if I rise again, if this means that, without rising, I shall descend into corruption, what benefit will there be in the shedding of my blood? None, certainly.

And he explains that benefit as follows: “Truly, then there will be no benefit in my blood. For will dust—that is, will dust produce true confessors for you? Or will that dust proclaim your truth—namely, that you are truthful, since you promised through the prophets that you would raise me?”

This means: “If, without rising again, I become dust, I shall neither produce confessors for you nor proclaim in my members that you are truthful, because by raising me you have fulfilled your promise.” He says this in the form of a question because of his exceeding affection, so that he may move him all the more strongly to complete what he can.

After making this prayer, lest he seem to have prayed out of uncertainty, he says—because of the certainty by which he already knows that he has been heard—even though this has not yet occurred in reality. He says it in this way:

“What benefit, and so forth.”

And although I say these things, I do not doubt that what I pray for will occur. For I am certain that the Lord has heard me—that is, will hear me. He shows that he heard him both because of mercy and because of his merits, as follows:

“I say, he has heard me. And this is because he has also had mercy on me and because he has become my helper.”

This means: “He will therefore hear me because he will have mercy on me and because, through my merits, I have made him my helper.”

[Col. 0751C]

He shows in what respect he will be a helper, turning in gratitude toward him and addressing him as follows:

“Truly, you will become my helper. For you have turned”—that is, you will turn—“my mourning,” that is, the sorrow of my Passion, “into joy,” that is, the joy of the Resurrection.

This means: “You will destroy my mourning by giving me joy.” And you have torn my sackcloth—that is, you will utterly destroy my mortality—and you have surrounded me—that is, you will enrich me completely with the joy of immortality.

Mortality is appropriately called Christ’s sackcloth. For since he had no sin, his mortality was the punishment for our sin, just as the sackcloth in which penitents are clothed is the punishment for their sins.

I say that you will surround me with joy; and this is so that my glory may sing to you—that is, so that my glorious Resurrection may offer you praise, not in words but by the very evidence of itself.

[Col. 0751D]

And I said that you have torn my sackcloth; therefore I shall not be pierced any longer by fear of death. Hence the Apostle says: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more” (Rom. VI, 9).

And because I shall not be pierced, Lord my God, I shall confess you forever—that is, I shall praise you in my members with every kind of praise.

Or it may be understood this way: I say that you have torn my sackcloth, and this is so that my glory may sing to you—that is, so that my wholly glorious members may praise you, and in such a way that they are not pierced—that is, that they do not regret having sung to you, whether through fear or through favor toward some ruler.

But, O Lord my God, forever, going from generation to generation, I shall confess you—that is, they shall praise you.

## INTO PSALM XXX

[Col. 0752A]

### The Title of the Thirtieth Psalm

“Unto the end. A Psalm of David.” Augustine alone, however, has: “Unto the end. A Psalm of David for ecstasy.”

This is explained as follows: This psalm is to be attributed to David, Christ, striving toward the end—that is, toward perseverance and victory. I say that the psalm was composed for ecstasy, that is, for his subtle contemplation.

“Ecstasy” (*exstasis*) is understood in two ways. We call ecstasy an excessive stupor of the mind caused by fear or wonder. Thus it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “They were filled with wonder and ecstasy at what had happened to him” (Acts III, 10). Such an ecstasy must never be said to have existed in Christ.

We also call ecstasy the mind’s secret elevation whenever the contemplation of the perfected lingers in the investigation of God’s hidden counsels, having entirely set aside worldly thoughts.

This psalm concerns such an ecstasy. For the Lordly man, considering that by the immeasurable and most excellent arrangement of divinity he was to be handed over to death, and that from that death the salvation of the human race would follow, prays, putting forward his merits, that God may make him steadfast in the Passion, so that he may not yield, and that he may be resurrected.

He also foretells his future Passion, speaking of it in the past tense. He further shows the salvation of his own people and prays for them. He exhorts them also to act manfully in God’s commandments. He likewise speaks, by way of concession, of the condemnation and shame of his enemies. And he begins as follows:

“In you, Lord, established and firm, I have hoped,” that is, I have placed the hope of my steadfastness and Resurrection.

[Col. 0752C]

Behold the claim of merit. Therefore, because I have hoped in you, I shall not be confounded forever—that is, I shall never be put to shame.

Or in this way: Even if I seem for a time to be put to shame in the Passion, this will not nevertheless be forever.

Because he had said generally, “I shall not be confounded,” he shows specifically the circumstance by which he would be confounded, as follows: I would be confounded if I were not freed from death, or if I yielded in the Passion.

And therefore free me from death, and do this in your justice. This means: “Because you are just, and because by hoping in you I have merited this.”

And in order that I may be freed, incline your ear toward me. Above he showed his merit by saying, “In you I have hoped,” and, “In your justice, free me.” Here, however, he prays to be freed through mercy, when he says:

“Incline your ear toward me, a mortal,” that is, make your kindness condescend to the lowliness of my mortality.

He speaks by comparison with a physician who, out of kindness, inclines his ear toward a sick person when the latter cannot speak because of his illness, so that, having recognized his illness, he may cure him.

The ear is rightly called God’s kindness, through which he receives the prayers of our lowliness.

I pray that you free me, and do not delay until the general Resurrection; rather, hasten to rescue me—that is, rescue me quickly—after three days, namely.

I pray not only to be freed from death, but I also pray this: “Be for me a protecting God.” This means: “I regard you as God, and, as God, may you become my protector, so that I may not fail.”

And be a house of refuge—that is, security, just as a fortified house is a cause of security for those who flee to it. Many are protected who are not secure; therefore he rightly adds, “And a house of refuge.”

I say, be my protector and house of refuge, so that you may save me from death in this way. Otherwise I would not be saved.

Truly, you ought to be protector and refuge, for you are my strength and my refuge—that is, because I regard you as my strength, that is, my protector, and as my refuge, that is, my security.

And in this temptation of death you ought to be protector and refuge, since in the other temptations of visible enemies and in the temptation of the devil you are always my strength and refuge.

And therefore you will lead me from good to good, causing me to persevere, and through this leading you will nourish me—that is, strengthen me, making me immortal—by comparison with a nurse who feeds a small child so that it may become strong from weakness.

He explains how he will nourish him, as follows:

“Namely, you will nourish me. You will bring me out of this snare that they have hidden for me,” that is, from the present death that they think they have secretly prepared for me, by comparison with one who secretly sets a snare in order to deceive an unsuspecting bird or beast.

And rightly you will bring me out. For into your hands—that is, into your power—I shall commend my spirit, that is, I shall commit my soul, so that through you, who are powerful, I may receive it again, in such a way that my enemies will no longer have the power to take it from the body, as they now do.

He speaks by comparison with one who entrusts something so that he may receive it again whenever he wishes. And I shall entrust it with good confidence, because you are—that is, you will be—my protector in the Passion, so that I may not fail.

He shows what benefit will follow from this, as follows:

[Col. 0753C]

“I say that you will bring me out, and by bringing me out you have redeemed me”—that is, you will redeem my people from death—“O Lord, being the God of truth,” that is, the giver of truth, making them seek true goods.

Or: “God of truth,” that is, the true God, who promised this and cannot fail to fulfill it. For my people would not be redeemed by my death unless I were brought out of this snare.

I said that you will redeem my people, for whom you will be the giver of truth.

“But you have hated those who observe vanity”—that is, those who embrace worldly goods, which are vain, with the greatest diligence—and who do this pointlessly, that is, without any benefit. Therefore you will not redeem those whom you will hate.

But I shall not be hateful to you; that is, my people will not be hateful to you. For I shall hope in the Lord; that is, my people will place their hope in you, Lord, and not in vanities.

And therefore I shall exult and rejoice—that is, they will exult in the future in the blessedness of the body. For exultation properly belongs to the body, since the word is derived from *saltare*, “to leap.”

And they will rejoice in the blessedness of the soul, and this in your mercy, not in their merits alone.

And truly they will exult in the body, because you have regarded my lowliness—that is, you will consider it mercifully, so that from it you may rescue them through the abasement of my body.

For they are subject to every kind of distress. He says “you have regarded” by comparison with those who kindly look upon someone oppressed, so that they may have compassion on him.

And truly they will rejoice in the soul. For you have saved—that is, you will save—the soul of my people from necessities, that is, from the weaknesses that occur through the necessity resulting from original sin.

It is fragile because, when filled with that knowledge of God which it would have possessed had Adam not sinned, it is deprived of it. It is also fragile when it fears and grieves and suffers everything of this kind.

And they will have not only this, that they may exult and rejoice in the future; even in this life you have not shut me up in the hands of the enemy—that is, you will not permit my people to be enclosed in the devil’s power, so that he may ensnare them through the suggestions of the wicked and lead them into conformity with himself.

He speaks by comparison with a captive who is first seized and afterward confined in prison.

Truly, you will not permit them to be confined. Rather, you have set my feet in a spacious place—that is, you will set the affections of my people in the spaciousness of faith and love—by comparison with one who, led out of a narrow prison, is placed in a spacious place.

[Col. 0754B]

Having declared the salvation of his people, he turns in prayer to God, asking him to complete in them what he had declared, and says:

“I have declared that my people will exult and rejoice. And in order that this may happen, have mercy on me”—that is, on my people—“Lord.”

And they need this, because I am troubled—that is, my people are troubled.

He explains this tribulation through the fathers. Truly they are troubled, for “my eye, my soul, and my belly have been troubled in anger,” that is, they have been weakened by the vengeance you took for Adam’s sin, as perceived by the reason of my people.

“Troubled” is used by comparison with an eye disturbed by darkness or some disease and therefore weakened for seeing.

And the soul of my people has been troubled—that is, the vitality and sensibility of my people have been weakened—and the belly has been weakened, that is, their body.

He designates the whole body by its softer part, so as to indicate that it is an extremely weak thing.

He explains how the soul is troubled, as follows:

Truly the soul—that is, vitality—has been weakened, because my life—that is, the vitality of my people—has failed in sorrow, that is, has become subject to failure through sorrow. This would not have happened unless Adam had sinned.

This means: “It has become a nature of such a kind that it can fail through some sorrow.”

And my years are subject to failure amid groanings. Here “years” and “life” mean the same thing.

It is as though he said: “It must not only be called subject to failure because it can quickly be ended by sorrow, but also because, while it endures amid the repeated groanings of adversity, it falls away from the blessedness of joy which it would have possessed continually if Adam’s obedience had persevered.”

By showing the failure of vitality, he also intimates that the body has failed, since it is enlivened by vitality. He also intimates that sensibility has failed. Indeed, it has failed, for we see and feel less even physically.

It should be understood that soul, sensibility, and vitality are the same thing, but they are called by different names according to their different functions.

“Soul” is its principal designation. It is called “sensibility” because it exercises various senses through bodily instruments, seeing through the eyes and hearing through the ears. It is called “vitality” because, by nourishing the body, it makes it live.

When vitality and soul are said to fail, although the soul appears to be everlasting, this means that it fails in the exercise of its function, not in its essence. For if its essence were entirely destroyed, it would certainly not be everlasting.

He also explains how the eye is troubled, as follows:

Truly the eye has been troubled; the eye is also called the virtue of my people because of its dignity. For my virtue—that is, the reason of my people—has been weakened in poverty, that is, it labors like the sick because of the lack of full knowledge of God.

And because the virtue has been weakened, my bones have been troubled—that is, the virtues of my people have been weakened. They are called “bones” because of the strength they possess, by comparison with bones, which are stronger than flesh.

Having shown one reason why he should have mercy—namely, because of their tribulation—he adds another, namely his own Passion and the injury he was to suffer for them, which he also sets forth.

He says this as follows:

I say, “Have mercy on my people,” because they are troubled. And therefore still more, because, in order that you may have mercy on them, I have become a reproach above all my enemies—that is, I shall become a reproach and object of derision to my enemies, more than they themselves will become a reproach and object of derision to the nations when they are led away captive and scattered by them.

Another translation has: “Among all my enemies,” that is, “I shall become a reproach to all my enemies.”

And also to my neighbors—that is, to those who have come somewhat near in order to know me, though they did not yet know me fully, as many of the Jews did—I have become a reproach. That is, they will be ashamed that they were my neighbors.

And I shall become fear—that is, a cause of fear—to my acquaintances, that is, to the apostles, so that they will not dare to confess me through fear of death.

Hence it is written: “My acquaintances have withdrawn from me like strangers” (Job X, 13).

I said that I would become a reproach to my neighbors. Therefore those neighbors who saw me outwardly—that is, who saw me according to my external nature, namely according to the humanity in which I would suffer—and who now, considering me according to my divinity, have fled—that is, will withdraw entirely from me, that is, from the hope they had in me.

Or in this way: Those who saw me—that is, who will know me to some degree—will flee from me, going outside, that is, yielding to those who are outside the knowledge of me, namely the Jews.

And they will not flee in such a way that they later return. Rather, I have been—that is, I shall be—given over to oblivion, as though dead in heart, that is, according to the soul in sin, just as they will see me dead in the body.

This means: “They will think me dead in soul through sins, and therefore they will think that I will not rise again.”

And I have become—that is, I shall become—to them like a discarded vessel.

[Col. 0755D]

This means: “Having previously placed their hope of salvation in me, they will regard me as useless for saving them, like a discarded—that is, broken—vessel, which is useless for holding anything in itself, since whatever is placed in it immediately leaks away.”

And therefore they will regard me as a discarded vessel, because I have heard—that is, I shall patiently hear, without answering—the reproach of many dwelling around me.

They do not dwell around me in love and knowledge of me, but at a distance, like a circle that is far from the point at its center.

Or “dwelling around me” means dwelling in the desire for earthly things. These are rightly called “circles,” because they are never stable but move in a circle—that is, they are always turning, sometimes toward prosperity and sometimes toward adversity.

This means: “Therefore they will regard me as a discarded vessel: because, when I am reproached, they will see me remain silent as though I were guilty.”

And therefore I have still become like a discarded vessel, because, while the Jews were in the circle I have described, when they gathered—that is, when they will gather—physically against me in order to slander me, they, remaining together—that is, agreeing in the same intention of my death—took counsel—that is, will take counsel—to seize my soul, that is, to take my life.

He speaks by comparison with one who is seized by enemies in order to be destroyed.

This is as though he said: “Because they will see them plotting my death and carrying it into effect while I do not resist, they will regard me as a discarded vessel.”

I said that they will take counsel to seize my soul. But I have hoped in you—that is, I shall place my hope in you—Lord.

And I said—that is, I shall say—in words, in deed, and in affection: “O Lord, rescue me from the hand,” that is, from the power, “of my enemies, the Jews, so that I may not be conformed to them.”

And rescue me from the Jews who persecute me.

This means: “Rescue me from the power of the Jews, so that they may not prevail over me, for they are my enemies and persecutors.”

For many are enemies who are not persecutors. Therefore he rightly adds: “From those who persecute me.”

He first sets forth the reasons from which he should be rescued, as follows:

I say, “Rescue me,” and this is fitting. For you are my God; I regard you as my Creator.

And because my lots are in your hands—that is, my choices are in your wills.

This means: “Because I choose only your wills.” He uses “lots” for choices because choices are customarily made by lots. But because actions proceed from wills, hands are mentioned; for works are carried out with the hands.

I pray: “Rescue me.” And not only this, but also enlighten your face—that is, make your kindness bright and manifest—by looking upon me, your servant, that is, one wholly obedient to you.

He uses “face” for kindness because kindness is often signified in the face.

He also rightly says, “upon your servant,” as though he were saying: “Since you are higher than I, your human servant, condescend to me”; and by this show your kindness to be bright.

I pray, “Enlighten me,” in this way, namely: “Save me from death.”

And do this in your mercy, Lord, so that I may not be confounded—which would happen if I were not saved—nor is this fitting, since I have invoked you, that is, prayed to you.

Or in this way: “Since I have invoked you,” that is, called you to dwell in me with good affection, in words, and in action.

I say, “Let me not be confounded.” But let the wicked—that is, my enemies, the Jews—be ashamed at my Resurrection, and afterward let them be led into hell, namely, the local hell.

I say, “Let them be ashamed,” and also, “Let their deceitful lips become mute.”

He does not say “mute” in the sense that they should say absolutely nothing, but “mute” in the sense that they will say nothing evil about me that appears to be true.

They are said to have deceitful lips who think one thing and say another; the Jews possessed such lips. For although, compelled by their reason and by Christ’s miracles, they truly recognized him to be God, they denied it only with their mouths.

This may also be understood as a prayer, if it is explained as follows:

I pray, “Save me.” And once I have been saved, let the wicked Jews be ashamed because of my death—let them be ashamed for the sake of good. And so that they may be ashamed more intensely, let them be led by their own thoughts into hell, into the depth of their sins.

This means: “Let them consider the depth of their sins, and thus let their deceitful lips become mute in their reviling of me.”

He shows in what respect they are deceitful when he adds:

“Those lips that speak against me, the just one,” that is, slandering me, the just one—and they do this in pride and abuse, that is, proudly and abusively.

They spoke proudly when they said: “Hail, King of the Jews” (Matt. XXVII, 29; Mark XV, 18; John X, 3).

They spoke abusively when, to his detriment, they misused false names, calling him, although he was just and innocent, a sinner and a deceiver (Matt. XXVII, 63).

Or in this way: They speak abusively, that is, they abuse their free will by speaking against me.

For free will was given to them for this purpose: that by abstaining from evil and doing or speaking what is good, they might become better than if they merely possessed the power to act well. They abuse this free will by speaking evil of me.

He shows what fruit follows from his salvation, as follows:

I pray, “Save me.” And through my salvation it will be revealed how great—that is, exceedingly great—the multitude of your sweetness, that is, your mercy, is, which you have hidden from those who are perishing, and this for those who fear you, that is, for the benefit of those who fear you.

This means: “You have hidden it from those who do not fear you, so that they may not know it; but you have revealed it to those who fear you,” in accordance with the Gospel saying: “You have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to infants” (Luke X, 21).

And you have not revealed it in such a way that they will not possess it; rather, you have perfected—that is, you will perfect—that multitude for those of mine who fear you, who hope in you in the sight of the children of men—that is, who confess that they hope in you in the sight of the imitators of evil, not denying you through fear of death.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also shall confess him before my Father” (Luke XII, 8).

Here he calls people “evil” because they are merely human—that is, because they consider merely human things and not spiritual things.

He shows in detail what the multitude of sweetness mentioned above is:

I said that you will perfect in them the multitude of sweetness, namely this:

“You will hide them, separated from the disturbance of men,” that is, of the wicked.

And you will do this in the hidden place of your face—that is, you will hide them from the wicked, so that they may not see their glory and disturb them as they do now.

And you will establish them in your presence, which will be hidden from the wicked.

Hence it is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI, 10).

I say that in the future you will hide them; and here you will protect them, as they dwell in your tabernacle—that is, in your army—from the contradiction of tongues, that is, from the contradicting tongues of heretics and of others who suggest vain things, so that they may not prevail over them.

Here, however, he makes this apostrophe to the members:

“Blessed be the Lord,” because he sees that what he foretold will come to pass for my people.

I said that God will hide and protect you, those who hope; and so it will be.

Therefore blessed—that is, praised—be the Lord, both by me and by you.

He repeats the reason why he should be praised in other words, as follows:

“For he has made his mercy toward me wondrous,” that is, God will make his wondrous mercy toward my people—that is, toward you.

And he will do this in a fortified city, that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem, which is called a fortified city because no assault of enemies can be made against it.

Hence it is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (Isa. LXIV, 4; I Cor. II, 9).

He turns to God, repeating the reason for the salvation of his people, so that he may make them more indebted to him:

I said that my people will be protected and hidden. But, so that they may be protected, I have been cast away—that is, I shall be cast away—from the sight of your eyes, that is, from the presence of your mercy.

This means: “I shall seem in the Passion to have been cast away from your mercy.” And I said—that is, I, who am to be cast away, understood—that this casting away occurs by how profound and reasonable an arrangement.

I say, I said this in ecstasy, that is, in the sublime subtlety of my mind. It is rightly called “ecstasy,” because it surpasses all the subtilities of all human beings and angels.

By saying that he understood this, he intimates that he will endure it willingly and that he is not ignorant of it.

I say that I shall be cast away. And therefore you have heard the voice of my prayer while I cried out to you—that is, you will hear it in such a way that I may obtain my prayer, which I shall utter aloud while I cry out to you on behalf of my people.

He turns in address to his people and exhorts them to love God and to act manfully, so that his prayer and his being cast away may benefit them, since otherwise they would not benefit them.

I say that I shall be cast away for you and that I shall be heard while I cry out.

Therefore, all his holy sons who are to come through me, love the Lord. For the Lord will require this truth—that is, this justice, namely love—from you, through the benefits that he will give you through me and that he has already given.

For it is equitable and just that creatures should love their Creator, and that those who have been restored should love the one who restored them to life.

Hence it is written: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart” (Deut. VI, 5; Matt. XXII, 37; Mark XII, 31; Luke X, 41).

And therefore still: “Love,” because he will repay abundantly—that is, he will give a great and exceedingly abundant recompense—to those who act proudly against him.

This means: “Those who make themselves proud against him by scorning his love.”

It is as though he said: “Therefore love. For if, by not loving, you have been proud, when he repays all the proud, he will repay you as well.”

I say, “Love.” And because love is nothing without good works, act manfully in good works.

Hence blessed Gregory says: “The proof of love is the manifestation of the work” (Homily 30, on the Gospels).

And the Apostle says: “No one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (I Tim. II, 5).

And by acting manfully, do not fail; rather, let your heart be strengthened in this—that is, persevere in it—you who hope for salvation in the Lord.

Otherwise it would be not hope but presumption.

## INTO PSALM XXXI

[Col. 0759A]

### The Thirty-First Psalm

### The Title

“Understanding for David.”

This is explained as follows: “For this David”—that is, for this faithful person who acts in this psalm—“there is understanding.”

This means: “This faithful person who speaks here is truly wise and discerning.”

When “understanding” is given without qualification, it suggests that he is more intelligent than if the term were determined by a specific qualification. We customarily call those who are most wise “wise” without qualification. Thus Solomon is called “wise” without qualification.

In this psalm, every faithful person acts who previously thought that he could be made blessed through free will without the remission of sins. But now, having set aside such an error, he shows for the instruction of others that no one can be made blessed except through the remission of sins, putting himself forward as an example.

For while he held this error, he was altogether weakened in the virtues. At last, therefore, having recognized his error, making confession on that account and seeking pardon, he obtained it. Thus he attained the blessedness of righteousness, and in the future he is made still more blessed.

He also exhorts others not to reject from themselves the understanding of remission, lest they be deceived by this error. And because they are insufficient for this by themselves, he afterward prays for them.

This psalm rightly follows the preceding one. For in the preceding psalm the subject was remission and the blessedness of the faithful. In this one, instruction is given concerning how blessedness is attained, so that no one may presume to reach it through free will.

“Blessed are those,” and so forth. This verse is read in reversed order, as though he said:

“Many strive to attain blessedness by free will alone, but only those are blessed whose sins are covered,” that is, hidden in such a way—whether by baptism alone or also by confession—that the Lord does not see them in order to avenge them.

“And whose iniquities are remitted,” that is, after their sins have been covered. Thus their evil desires—that is, their thoughts—are remitted, that is, rendered ineffective, so that they do not prevail over them, by comparison with a relaxed bow, which is powerless to shoot.

But lest anyone, after the covering of sins, think that iniquities are remitted in such a way that no sin is ever committed, or that, if sin is committed, he can no longer attain blessedness, he adds:

“And blessed is that man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin.”

It is as though he said: “I grant that no one can exist immune from sin after his sins have been covered; but only that man is blessed”—that is, just—or will be blessed in the future, to whom the Lord will not impute his sin for eternal punishment.

This is the man who will not sin criminally or excessively habitually—that is, in the ordinary course of life—in such a way that he does not afterward make satisfaction to God by confessing, mortifying the body, and giving alms.

For sin will be imputed for punishment to the one who, after the covering of sins, sins criminally or excessively habitually, so that he does not afterward make satisfaction to God.

Hence the prophet says: “If the just man turns away from his righteousness, will he live?” (Ezek. XVIII, 27).

Nor is there deceit in the spirit of that blessed man, that is, in his soul.

This means: The blessed man is also the one who does not fail but perseveres in his good purpose, because the one who has a deceitful spirit is said to be the person who, after promising faith to God, refuses to persevere in fulfilling obedience by his works.

From this it is understood that the one who, although his sins are covered and his iniquities remitted, is nevertheless deceitful in spirit, is not blessed.

Hence it is written: “It is better not to make a vow than not to fulfill one’s vows” (Eccl. V, 5).

It follows:

“Because I was silent,” and so forth.

This is explained as follows:

“Now I understand that those are blessed whose iniquities are remitted,” and so forth, but others are not blessed at all.

I was silent about this—that is, I did not understand it—when I thought that I could be made blessed through free will.

“Silence” is rightly used for not understanding. For just as we say that the mind speaks when it understands, so we also say that it is silent when it does not understand.

I say that what I now declare I previously kept silent about. And because I was silent, my bones grew old—that is, my reason, my free will, and my virtues were weakened. They are called “bones” because of their likeness to bones.

He says “grew old” by comparison with clothing, which becomes weaker the older it grows.

It is as though he said: “Because I presumed that I was sufficient by myself, my bones, in which I trusted, were weakened.”

I say that I was silent, even though I cried out all day, that is, continually.

The latter expresses the same thing as what I was silent about.

This means: While my very misery, as if by a cry, demonstrated what I was silent about in my understanding—namely, that only those whose iniquities are remitted are blessed, and so forth.

He explains how he cried out, as follows:

Truly I cried out, because your hand—that is, your vengeance, O God, which you took against me because I was silent in this way—was heavy upon me day and night, that is, continually.

It became heavy and burdensome upon me.

It is as though he said: “The very misery that your vengeance inflicted upon me with the greatest weight cried out what I had kept silent about, namely, the weakening of my bones.”

I say that your hand was heavy. And when it became heavy, at last I turned to you, understanding what I had previously kept silent about.

And this occurred in my affliction, that is, in my consideration of my affliction.

It is as though he said: “By considering my affliction, I was admonished by it to turn to you, and thus I turned.”

I say, in the affliction that truly was affliction, when the thorn was fixed—that is, when sin was fixed—in me.

Sin is called a thorn because it pricks the conscience like a thorn that pierces the body.

By saying “was fixed,” he indicates that many sins were fastened in him simultaneously.

Another translation has: “When my harvest was scorched.”

This means: “When my virtues were destroyed.” They are called “harvest” because the soul is sustained by them, lest it perish, just as the body is sustained by harvest when it is eaten.

I say that I turned. And having turned, I made my offence known to you.

This passage, as it has been explained here, can also be explained and punctuated in another way, namely as follows:

I said that I turned. And thus the thorn in me—that is, pride—was broken.

“Thorn” is the name given to that collection of bones which extends from the neck to the loins and makes the body stand upright. If it is broken, the body is immediately bent and humbled. Therefore it is used for pride.

For pride raises the human heart against God. But if the heart is broken, it is immediately humbled before God.

I say that the thorn in me—that is, pride—was broken. And when it was broken, that is, when the thorn in me was broken, I made known—that is, I revealed—to you my offence.

Not that you previously did not know it, but because, by excusing myself, I had previously hidden it, as far as depended on me, not as far as depended on you.

By confessing and accusing myself, I understood that I had made that offence manifest to you. And I did not hide my injustice, as before, but by confessing I revealed it, just as I did the offence.

An offence (*delictum*) is so called when we abandon what ought to be done, such as doing good, worshiping God, and other things of this kind. Injustice, however, occurs when we do what ought not to be done, such as killing a person, seizing another’s property, and other things of this kind.

I say that I made it known.

And he explains how, as follows: “And this I previously said,” that is, I resolved in my mind, saying: “I will confess my injustice to the Lord,” and I will do this by acting against myself, that is, I will accuse myself of my iniquity by confessing it to the Lord. Previously I was arrogantly excusing myself; this is what I meant when I said: “And I did not hide it.” Therefore you, in your mercy, forgave the impiety of my sin—not merely the sin, but also the impiety of that sin, that is, the pride of an unconfessed sin.

Having shown that confession leads to forgiveness, lest it be thought that only he, who had previously been a sinner, needed forgiveness, while the saints did not, he adds: “I say that you forgave.” This is a forgiveness for which not I alone, but every saint will pray to you, in order to obtain it at the appropriate time, that is, in this age, which is suited to repentance. The future age is unsuitable for this. Hence the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time” (II Cor. VI, 2).

I say that he will pray. And this prayer will not be fruitless. Nevertheless, although he is to be in a flood of many waters—that is, on the day of judgment, which will contain many sudden tribulations—those waters, that is, those tribulations, will not approach him. The day of judgment is called a flood because it will come unexpectedly, just as a flood arrives unexpectedly. Hence the Gospel says: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief” (I Thess. V, 2). This is as though he were saying: He will pray for his own good; therefore, on the day of judgment he will be touched by no tribulations.

He now turns in prayer to God, asking that the one who rescued him from the earlier tribulation—from impiety—also rescue him from the tribulation of external enemies, who seek to bring him down in many ways. He says this as follows: “I say that you forgave impiety. Therefore you too, who are my refuge,” that is, the one to whom I fled from the innermost tribulation that surrounded me, that is, that occupied me completely—namely, from the impiety of sin—and who are also my rejoicing, that is, the cause of my rejoicing, rescuing me from it: “rescue me also from the tribulations and suggestions that surround me,” that is, that persecute me intensely, [Col. 0762A] lest I yield to them.

This is as though he were saying: Make me persevere, so that I do not fail. And you ought to do this, for you promised me this inwardly, saying: “I will give you understanding, and I will instruct you in this way in which you will walk.” This should be read in reversed order: “I will instruct you,” that is, “I will teach you, in this way in which you will walk”; that is, “I will teach you how you ought to proceed along the way of my commandments.” And afterward: “I will not abandon you, but I will establish over you,” that is, “I will place firmly over you, so that you do not fail, my eyes,” that is, my loving-kindness. This is as though he were saying: “I will make you persevere.” And thus I will give you understanding, so that you may understand my hidden counsels; otherwise you would not have understanding.

Having prayed for himself, he exhorts his hearers not to reject from themselves the understanding of forgiveness, as follows: “I say that God forgave me my impiety. And so that he may likewise forgive you, do not become like a horse and a mule, which have no understanding,” that is, which are irrational. This is as though he were saying: Do not make yourselves comparable to a horse and a mule, becoming dull and sluggish with regard to this understanding of forgiveness, like the mule, which is a dull and sluggish animal. And do not be proud, thinking that you can be blessed by free choice, like the horse, which is a proud animal.

He also prays for them, because he sees that they are incapable of avoiding this by themselves, as follows: “I say, let them not become like a horse and a mule; but since they cannot avoid this by themselves, O God, constrain their jaws with bit and bridle.” They do not approach—that is, they are incapable by themselves of approaching you, that is, of attaining obedience to and knowledge of you. When he says, “Constrain their jaws,” this is the same as saying, “Constrain them.” Since he had mentioned a horse and a mule, which are restrained by their jaws, they are likewise named here on account of their likeness to them. By the bit we understand the heavier means of guidance, and by the bridle the lighter. For the bit—which in common usage is called a *canifrenum*, not a halter, as many claim—restrains a horse more heavily than a bridle does.

So too the most merciful guide constrains more severely those who need heavier guidance, bringing tribulations upon them so that, once chastened, they may not perish. Those who need lighter guidance are constrained more lightly. Hence Prosper says: “He mercifully applies temporal severity, lest he justly inflict eternal condemnation.” And Solomon says: “God chastises every son whom he receives” (Prov. III, 12; Hebr. XII, 6).

I say: Do not become like a horse and a mule. If you do become such, it will happen to your harm. For in the future there will be many scourges for the sinner, namely, for the one who refused to obtain forgiveness here. But the one who here hopes in the Lord will be surrounded by mercy, that is, will be entirely embraced by it in the future, both in soul and in body. Through this he strongly invites those who do not hope to hope in the Lord, since they will thus be surrounded by mercy.

He also turns to those who hope, exhorting them to rejoice in their good hope not in themselves but in the Lord, saying: “Therefore, since mercy will surround the one who hopes in the Lord, rejoice because of your hope in the Lord,” that is, in the praise of the Lord, “O righteous,” and not in yourselves, by attributing this hope to yourselves. And do not rejoice only a little, but exult, that is, rejoice greatly; let this joy be shown even by bodily dancing. And also glory in the Lord, that is, attribute your glory to the Lord, not to your own merits, all you who are upright of heart, that is, righteous, having a heart that is upright in thinking good things and not distorted by thinking perverse things. As the Apostle says: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31).

## ON PSALM XXXII

**The title of the thirty-second Psalm:** “A Psalm of David,” that is, of the faithful, to whom it was said in the preceding psalm: “Rejoice in the Lord; exult, you righteous”—of those exhorting one another to exult in the praise of the Lord, namely, to praise him both on the *cithara* and on the *psalterium*. And let them also sing to him a new song with a loud cry. He sets forth, however, the most honorable reasons why this should be done. He also shows at the end that no one is saved unless the grace of God assists him. He therefore says:

“Exult, you righteous, in the Lord,” that is, in the praise of the Lord. This is as though he were saying: Exulting, praise the Lord. And you ought to exult in this, for praise of the Lord befits you who are upright of heart, that is, the righteous. “For praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner” (Eccl. XV, 9), namely, of one who does not wish to repent and become upright.

He explains in parts how they should praise him, as follows: “I say, exult in this: Confess to the Lord on the *cithara*,” that is, praise the Lord through the praise of the mortification of your flesh. This is as though he were saying: “Put to death your members,” and so forth.

This mortification is rightly called a *cithara*. For from the lower part, that is, from sensuality once mortified, it resounds to God, that is, praises him—not by the voice, but by the evidence of what it is, like a cithara, which resounds from its lower hollow. Sensuality is mortified through the mortification of the flesh, so that it may no longer, as before, be intent upon vanity.
