“And on the ten-stringed *psalterium*”—that is, on the psalterium having ten strings—“play for him.” This is as though he were saying: Praise him through the enlivening of your mind, which is enlivened through the ten strings it possesses, that is, through the fulfillment of the ten commandments of the Law. They are called strings because they render a sweet song to God, not in voice or sound, but in the evidence of the deed itself, corresponding to strings that produce a sweet song by resounding.

The praise of an enlivened mind is rightly called a psalterium, because it resounds from the higher, that is, the more excellent, part of us—from the mind—like a psalterium that resounds from its upper hollow.

“And sing to him a new song,” that is, praise him with a new song, namely, through the fulfillment of the commandments established by the new Adam, in which God delights as in a song. Hence the Apostle says: “Strip off the old man with his deeds, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God” (Eph. IV, 24), namely: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Luke VI, 27). And: “Sell all that you have, give to the poor, and follow me, says the Lord” (Matt. V, 44; Luke IX, 12). Fulfill also commandments of this kind, which have been newly given by Christ and were not contained in the old Law, which said: “You shall love your friend, and you shall hate your enemy.”

I say: Sing to him a new song, and not carelessly. But play well for him with a loud cry, that is, praise him with great intensity of mind. It is called a loud cry because, like an elementary shout, it seeks an answer with excessive force. Hence it is written: “Cursed is the one who does the work of God negligently” (Jer. XLIII, 10), that is, without attention.

He then adds the reasons why one should confess and play. Thus I say: Confess and play. And this should be done because the word of the Lord is upright. This is as though he were saying: This word, that is, this commandment to sing, belongs to the Lord, and is therefore upright. For it is right that the Lord should command the servant, and the Creator the creature.

Therefore sing and confess to him, as we say, by acting: for all the works that he himself has commanded them to perform are upright for those established in faith, although they may appear unjust to unbelievers. Hence it is written: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VII, 9).

Therefore continue to sing and confess, because he naturally loves mercy and judgment. It is as though he were saying: Since he is naturally merciful, he will have mercy on you if you sing to him, in accordance with Joel: “He is merciful and gracious concerning evil” (Joel II, 13). And since he is naturally just and loves just judgment, he will condemn you by a just judgment unless you sing to him and confess. Hence it is written: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Deut. XXXII, 35; Rom. XII, 19).

I say that he loves mercy. This can be seen from the fact that “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord,” that is, the Church, which is God’s earth and which he cultivates through preachers.

He explains how it is full of mercy, as follows: Truly it is full of mercy, namely, through this: “By the word of the Lord”—that is, through the Son of the Lord—“the heavens,” that is, the preachers, have been established in faith and holiness. And afterward all their virtue, which they possess in innocence and holiness, “was confirmed by the spirit of his mouth,” that is, by the Holy Spirit, who proceeds not only from the Father but also from the Son. This Son is called the mouth of God because through him the secrets of God have been revealed to us, just as the secrets of the heart are revealed through the mouth.

For although they had first been strengthened in the virtue of faith and holiness through Christ’s teaching, afterward they were wholly confirmed in the same virtue through the Holy Spirit. Through Isaiah he is called “the spirit of counsel and fortitude” (Isa. XI, 2), because he makes people strong and steadfast.

I say that their virtue was confirmed by the Spirit of his mouth. It was confirmed for this purpose: to be “gathering,” that is, joining together, “the waters of the sea,” that is, the unrighteous, who flow through unlawful things as waters flow. They are bitter to God like the sea. They are gathered together “as waters in a wineskin.”

This is as though he were saying: Their virtue joins and constrains, through the law imposed upon them, in unity of faith, love, and action, those who previously flowed into every unlawful thing according to their own desires, just as waters that previously flowed away are joined together in a wineskin and restrained from flowing away.

[Col. 0765A] Or it may be understood as follows: “Gathering as into a wineskin,” that is, as though into a wineskin. This is as though he were saying: Joining them in the unity of the Church, which is rightly called a wineskin, since it is constituted solely from them. They have been mortified in the flesh, just as a wineskin is made from the skins of dead animals, in accordance with the Apostle: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh” (Gal. V, 24).

I say, “gathering the waters,” and not only the perverse waters, but also—and this is more wonderful—“placing the abysses,” that is, those who are deepest in sins, just as an abyss is deepest among treasures. This is as though he were saying: From those who are abysses, you make treasures out of abysses, that is, you fill them so abundantly with doctrine and holiness that they enrich others from it, like a treasure that enriches worldly people with worldly riches. Hence the Apostle says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Cor. IV, 7).

Having established these reasons, he returns to exhortation, as follows: Therefore, because the word of the Lord is upright, and his works are in faith, and he loves mercy and judgment, “let all the earth fear him” with chaste fear, that is, the Church: “For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX, 10). And the Apostle says: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. II, 12).

He also prays for them, as follows: I say, “Let them fear.” But since they are incapable by themselves, let all who inhabit and do not abandon “the world,” that is, the Church, be moved by him—that is, by his grace—to fear. The Church is God’s world, as we said in the exposition of Psalm XXIII.

He joins together other reasons why he should be feared, as follows: I say, “Let them fear,” and he must be feared because he, being so powerful, “spoke”—not verbally, but established by his own disposition—“and they were made,” that is, all things were formed, as is read historically in Genesis. “He commanded,” that is, he ordained by his disposition, “and they were created,” in a crude and formless creation.

This is as though he were saying: Their material, from which they were afterward formed—that is, the formless elements, namely heaven, air, and earth—was created, as is read in Genesis: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I, 1). “But the earth was empty and void,” and so forth.

I say that “they were made”; he commanded, and they were created. And by this—or rather, because everything that he says and commands will likewise come to be—the things that foolish and useless nations devise against God and the Church by counsels of words, and the things they also conceive in thought, will not come to pass.

For “the Lord frustrates,” that is, destroys, “the counsels of the nations.” But he rejects “the thoughts of the peoples,” that is, of the nations, who uselessly think that they can devour the Church through threats, tribulations, or suggestions. And he not only rejects the counsels of the common people, but also rejects the counsels of rulers, that is, by rejecting them he reduces them to nothing, so that they do not prevail over his own.

Hence Solomon says: “There is no wisdom, no counsel, and no strength against the Lord” (Prov. XXI, 30).

It should be noted, however, that he does not destroy all their thoughts or counsels. For he permits some things to occur for the benefit of the Church or for the just condemnation of the impious: namely, that his own should be persecuted, afflicted, and killed, and that the wicked should flourish in earthly matters. But whatever would be fulfilled to the detriment of his own, he entirely rejects and destroys—namely, lest they yield to their example or suggestion—and likewise anything else beyond these things whose completion would harm his own.

I say that the thoughts and counsels of peoples and rulers are rejected and destroyed. But “the counsel of the Lord,” that is, the counsel which the faithful verbally establish for the benefit of the Church, with the grace of the Lord cooperating, “remains forever.” That is, it is not destroyed.

And not only the counsel, but also “the thoughts of his heart,” that is, those things which they conceive for their own benefit and for the benefit of the hearts of his faithful, remain through “this generation and the generation to come,” that is, they remain forever.

All this is as though he were saying: Truly God must be feared by you, because he is powerful enough to destroy the counsels that are against you. He is also powerful enough to establish forever what is done and conceived by you through his counsel. The nations, however, should not be feared, since their counsels are quickly destroyed.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather, fear him who has power to cast both body and soul into the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. X, 28).

I said that the Lord is so powerful that he spoke and they were made, and that he destroys the counsels of the nations while his counsel remains forever. Therefore, because he is so great, “blessed is the nation whose Lord is its God,” that is, the nation that regards God as its Lord, so that it obeys him in all things and does not serve the belly or vices.

And this—that they regard God as Lord—they do not possess from themselves. Rather, “blessed is the people whom the Lord chose,” that is, separated from the mass of the lost, “as an inheritance for himself,” that is, so that they might be his inheritance.

It is as though he were saying: The Lord chose them for this purpose: that, being his possession, they might worship him as Lord, and thus be blessed. Hence the Apostle says: “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (I Cor. XII, 3).

He explains how he chose them, as follows: This is how he chose them: “The Lord looked down from heaven,” that is, although he was supreme and invisible, he visited the human race through Christ’s human nature. Hence the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman,” and so forth (Gal. IV, 4).

I say that he looked down from the heaven of heavens upon Christ, and through that heaven he saw—in order to have mercy—every kind of human being: Jews and Gentiles, poor and rich, slaves and free.

This is as though he were saying: He had mercy on every kind of human being. Where we have here “sons of men,” the Hebrews have “sons of Adam.” But “sons of men” is rightly used, namely, of the first human beings, Adam and Eve. They are not only sons by nature, but also sons in crime.

I say that he looked down from heaven. And not only from heaven, but also “looked upon all,” that is, every kind of person who inhabits the earth, that is, who remains in this earth, “from his prepared dwelling,” that is, through the teaching of the apostles, who are his prepared dwelling, chosen by him through gracious will. [Col. 0767A] Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV, 16).

Or it may be understood as follows: He looked upon them because he was above all who inhabit his earth, that is, those who possess and rule his earth, that is, the flesh.

I say that he himself looked upon them—he who afterward “formed their hearts individually.” This is as though he were saying: Since it would not have been enough for him merely to look upon them by forgiving their sins and then abandon them, he established for them individual hearts, that is, various good wills, in accordance with the Apostle, who says: “Each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (I Cor. VII, 7).

He rightly says “formed,” that is, easily fashioned. For we say that something is formed when it is easily fashioned from wax or clay or some other soft material.

But since even the forming of hearts would still not be enough, he adds: “He who understands all their works.” This is expressed concisely. This is as though he were saying: He makes them perform works pertaining to understanding. It is as though he were saying: Not vain and irrational works, but works corresponding to what they themselves understand.

This kind of grammatical construction is found in the Apostle when he says: “The Spirit intercedes for us,” that is, makes us intercede, “with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. VIII, 26).

I say that he looked upon them, formed them, and understands them. And thus every faithful person is saved, being called a king because he rules himself by restraining himself from evil, and a giant because he is strong in doing good.

But that king is not saved by great virtue—his own virtue, that is. Even though he himself is a giant, he will not be saved by the multitude of his virtue, [Col. 0767C] that is, by the multitude of the virtue attributed to him as his own.

This is as though he were saying: I grant that he will be saved through the great virtue given by the grace of God, but only in such a way that he does not regard it as his own. For if he regarded it as his own, that is, as originating from himself, he would not be saved.

I say that the one who is a king and a giant is not saved by a great virtue regarded as his own. But if someone who is not a king or a giant mounts a horse, that is, adopts a proud thought, thinking that he can attain salvation by himself, that thought is rightly represented by a horse, which is an exceedingly proud animal. The horse—that is, that deceptive thought—is false with regard to attaining salvation.

This is as though he were saying: His thought will deceive him. He will not attain salvation as he thinks. Hence it is written: “If anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself” (Gal. VI, 3).

And not only will the horse of the one who is not a king and a giant in virtue be deceptive; even if someone who was previously a king and a giant, abounding in virtue, mounts a horse in the abundance of his virtue—that is, relies even on the virtue in which he previously abounded—he will not be saved. For it is reduced to nothing, in accordance with Ezekiel: “His righteous deeds that he had done will not be remembered” (Ezek. XVIII, 22).

When he says, “The king is not saved, nor the deceptive horse,” and so forth, he says this so that no one may presume to be saved by himself, but may attribute his salvation to the grace of God.

Someone might say: If he is not saved by himself, how then is he saved? The answer is given: Behold, I clearly set forth through what he will be saved.

“The eyes of the Lord,” that is, his loving-kindness, “are upon those who fear him,” looking upon them so that they may persevere in good; and they are upon those who hope in his mercy.

I say that the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, namely, those who hope in his mercy. This is as though he were saying: They do not fear him out of fear of punishment, but out of hope of mercy. Hence it is said through Solomon: “Whoever fears God will do good” (Eccl. XV, 1).

I say that the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, in order that in the future he may rescue their souls from death, that is, from condemnation, and meanwhile nourish them here, that is, strengthen them with the bread of life, namely, good action and good understanding. I mean those placed in hunger for righteousness, that is, in an intense desire for it. If they did not hunger for righteousness, he would not nourish them in this way. Of such people the Gospel says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. V, 6).

Therefore, because the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, in order to rescue and nourish them, “our soul waits,” that is, patiently awaits, “the Lord.” And this with good confidence, since it already possesses from him a pledge, namely, that he is our helper for doing good and our protector, lest we fall in tribulations.

I say that it waits for the Lord, and this for its own good. For eventually “our heart,” that is, our soul, “will rejoice in him,” that is, in attaining him. And so that we may then be able to rejoice, “we have hoped,” that is, we have possessed hope of rejoicing—and we still possess it—“while dwelling in his holy name,” that is, in the magnification of his holy name.

This is as though he were saying: We aim at magnifying his holy name.

This, then, is the explanation of how our soul waits for the Lord, which I mentioned above: it waits for him by hoping in his name.

Or it may be understood as follows: “We have hoped in his holy name,” that is, in what his holy name signifies for us—namely, that he is merciful—which is attributed to him by antonomasia. This is as though he were saying: We have hoped in his mercy.

Therefore, because we have hoped and continue to hope in your name, we pray: “Lord, let your mercy be upon us in the future,” that is, may the blessedness of your mercy descend upon us, weak and infirm, “just as we have hoped,” that is, placed our hope, “in you.”

This is as though he were saying: Let it not be upon us sparingly, but as abundantly as we have abundantly hoped in you.

## ON PSALM XXXIII

[Col. 0768D] **The title of the thirty-third Psalm:** “A Psalm of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, who dismissed him, and he departed.”

The history suggested to us by this title is as follows. David, expelled from the kingdom of the Jews because of Saul’s envy—for the song was sung of him: “Saul struck down his thousand, and David his ten thousands” (I Sam. XVIII, 7; XXI, 11)—fled for refuge to Achish, king of the Philistines, and hid there for some time.

Achish was also called Abimelech by the common title of the rulers of the Philistines. All the kings of the Philistines, whatever names they had previously borne, were commonly called Abimelech, just as the kings of Egypt were called Pharaohs.

But because David, while previously living in Judea, had killed Goliath, who had been a Philistine, and had also killed many Philistines—hence, as we said above, the song was sung of him: “David struck down his ten thousands”—the Philistines were stirred up against him, partly by hatred and envy and partly by fear.

For they feared that, since he was brave in war, he would occupy their kingdom. By frequently accusing him before Achish, they managed to have David brought to him for execution. When he was being sought in order to kill him, he was beating a drum while remaining at the city gate.

But when, through a revelation by the indication of the Holy Spirit, he learned that he could in no way escape by force, he pretended to be insane in the manner of epileptics. He let spittle fall into his beard, carried himself about with his hands, completely altered his expression, and began rolling about face down.

Nevertheless, his pursuers, who had been sent by Achish, although they believed him to be insane, seized him and brought him to the king. When Achish saw him and judged him to be insane, he said: “Why have you brought this madman to me?” (I Sam. XXI, 11). David was immediately dismissed, departed, and escaped.

In this history, carefully examined, there is contained, according to Augustine, the following figure of Christ. Through David hiding with Abimelech, the humanity of Christ is understood. It endured violent persecution from the members of the devil, who is represented by Saul, and humbly remained for some time among the Jews, who are signified by Abimelech.

Saul, whose name is interpreted as “desired,” rightly expresses the devil, whom the evil activity and devotion of the wicked frequently desire. Abimelech, whose name is interpreted as “the kingdom of the father,” appropriately signifies the Jews. Through their fathers, namely, the contemporaries of King David, they possessed the kingdom of that same King David. He is called Christ’s father according to the flesh, since Christ was born from his seed. Hence in the Gospel we read that the blind man said: “Son of David, have mercy on me” (Mark X, 47).

When this David—that is, Christ—was being accused before Abimelech, that is, before the Jews, by the Pharisees, chief priests, and scribes, and was being sought for destruction, he beat a drum while remaining at the city gate. That is, with the apostles already established in the faith, which is the entrance into Jerusalem, the eternal city, he brought forth a sweet sound from the drum: the teaching of mortifying the flesh, which would then bring forth a sweet song to the Lord and is represented by the drum, made from the skins of dead animals and producing a sweet sound.

This Christ also let spittle fall into his beard, carried himself about with his hands, changed his expression, appeared insane before Abimelech, and departed after being dismissed by Abimelech.

He let spittle fall into his beard when he commanded the apostles to eat his flesh and drink his blood. This commandment is called spittle because, to many who did not understand it, it appeared to have been spoken foolishly and childishly, like spittle flowing from the mouths of children. Hence some of the disciples are also said to have asked: “How will this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John VI, 52).

That spittle fell into the beard, that is, upon the apostles, who, being his manly soldiers, did not reject it but received it by understanding it carefully. Hence Peter is reported to have said: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John VI, 68). The beard, which is a sign of manliness, signifies the manly.

He carried himself about with his hands in a wondrous manner when, carrying his body and blood in his hands, he handed them to his disciples at the supper, saying: “Take this; this is my body” (Matt. XXVI, 26). Shortly afterward he said: “Drink from this, all of you; for this is my blood” (ibid.).

He changed his countenance—that is, his will to sacrifice—before Abimelech, that is, before the Jews, when he himself, who had previously desired the legal sacrifices figuratively, showed, as John records, that the sacrifice of his body and blood was to be offered to the five thousand Jews whom he had fed with five loaves and two fish.

Why did he also appear insane to them, since they did not understand? For this reason he was dismissed by those same people called Abimelech. Thus, departing from them, he transferred himself to the Gentiles, of whom he had earlier said: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice” (John X, 16).

“Countenance” is used for “will,” because the will is very often signified by the countenance.

The figure and sequence of the history have been treated as far as possible. Let us now proceed to explain the words of the title.

This Psalm, that is, this treatise, is “of David,” that is, of Christ; it is to be understood by the faithful or fulfilled by the faithful, after David himself—that is, after Christ himself—“changed his countenance,” that is, his will to sacrifice, “before Abimelech,” that is, before the Jews; and after Abimelech dismissed him, that is, Christ, and Christ himself departed to the Gentiles and withdrew from those Jews.

Before he changed his countenance, this psalm was neither understood nor fulfilled by many. And it is the voice of the first believers, namely, the apostles and the other disciples, promising that, once David had changed his countenance—that is, his will regarding sacrifice—they would bless him, that is, praise him by living well and by giving others an example of good living, according to what his sacrifice demands, and also with their mouths.

He also exhorts others to magnify God, showing by his own example what benefit follows from this. He teaches them also to taste the Lord’s body and blood not rashly but with fear, explaining as well what the fear of the Lord is. At the end, he discusses the salvation of those who taste with the fear of the Lord, so that they may be drawn to taste, and the condemnation of the wicked who do not taste rightly, so that he may restrain them by terrifying them and draw them toward tasting rightly. He therefore says:

“I will bless,” that is, since David has changed his countenance, “I will praise him who exists as Lord,” by doing good according to what the countenance—that is, the will regarding sacrifice—which he changed demands. And this “at all times,” that is, in prosperity and adversity.

And I will not bless him only by my works, but “his praise will always be in my mouth,” that is, I will always praise him both with the mouth of my body and with the mouth of my heart. And thus I will bless and praise him, so that “my soul,” that is, my good life, “which is placed in the Lord,” that is, in his praise and obedience, “will be praised by others” for the sake of its good example. This is because David changed his countenance, and therefore I will bless the Lord.

Let the ears of the heart of the meek hear this, that is, let the faithful who are not obstinate hear it, unlike those who said: “How will he give us his flesh to eat?” (John VI, 52). And hearing, let them rejoice, and not be saddened as those others were saddened.

The assembly of the faithful, which speaks in this psalm, turns to the meek in an apostrophe, exhorting them to magnify the Lord, as follows: Therefore, since I promise that I will bless him and fulfill this promise in action, you who are meek, magnify the Lord with me, and so forth.

This may also be connected in another way: I said, “I will bless and praise.” And so that others may do the same thing by my example, let the ears of their hearts hear the exhortation that I will give them. Let the meek hear it—that is, those who assent and are not rebellious—and let them rejoice in it rather than be saddened.

The exhortation is as follows: “Magnify the Lord with me,” that is, praise him as I do, both by deed and by word. And let us not do this merely at intervals, but let us “exalt his name,” that is, magnify him who is called Lord, with an exaltation directed toward the same end, namely, perseverance. This is as though he were saying: Let us exalt him perseveringly.

And do not magnify him in order to seek something besides him through it. Rather, following my example, seek the Lord by magnifying him, and he will hear you.

For “I sought the Lord,” that is, I sought the Lord beyond all else by magnifying him; “and he heard me,” that is, he heard me so as to grant my request. And thus he rescued me from all my tribulations, so that I would not yield to them—not so that I would not suffer them; or “he rescued me,” that is, he will rescue me in the future.

I say: Magnify him. And so that you may be able to magnify him well, approach him with the steps of faith, and as you approach, be enlightened with spiritual understanding. For when one approaches the Lord, ignorance is enlightened.

And after you have been enlightened, “your faces will not be confounded,” that is, the thoughts you will have about God, through understanding rightly, will not be disturbed, as were the faces of those who, when they heard the Lord say: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI, 60), went away from him.

“Face” is used for “knowledge,” because we know through the eyes, which are in the face, or because anyone is recognized more quickly by the face.

I say: Because I sought the Lord, and he heard me—and I did not do this alone. But so that you may do this more willingly, know that “this poor man,” whom above I called the Lord when I said, “I will bless the Lord,” and so forth, that is, Christ, “cried out,” that is, sought the Lord with intense cries of deed and word. And the Lord heard him, and so forth.

This is explained as above: For although Christ was Lord of all, he became poor, that is, obeyed the Father in all things, just as a poor man obeys a rich man.

Or this may be a repetition, because he had inserted “approach,” and so forth, in order to add: The assembly of the faithful, which acts in this psalm, speaks about itself in the third person, as follows: I said that I sought him, and it is true; for “this poor man who speaks,” that is, I, “cried out,” that is, sought the Lord with an intense cry, and so forth.

The following words of this verse do not change. And because he is poor, he heard the one crying out and saved him.

The angel of the Lord will send forth [his angels] around those who fear him—that is, Christ, who is the angel, meaning the messenger, of the Lord the Father; he is called the angel of the great [102] counsel. He will send good angels around those who fear him. This means that he will fortify them on every side with his angels. Thus he will rescue them from tribulations, lest they fail—or he will rescue them in the future. Hence the same is said in the Gospel: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matthew 18:10).

I said, “Draw near and be enlightened”; and thus “taste” the body and blood of the Lord. For the Lord says: “Whoever eats me lives because of me” (John 6:57). And by tasting, “see”—that is, come to know by the experience of the thing itself [Col. 0772B] in the future, when you will be made blessed—that the Lord whom you will taste is a sweet food, that is, a pleasing one, giving life to the faithful. Hence in the Song the bride says of the bridegroom: “His fruit”—that is, his body and blood—“is sweet to my throat” (Song of Songs 2:3). I say “see” in the future; meanwhile hope here, because you will see. For blessed will be the man who hopes in him.

I said, “Magnify, draw near, and taste”; and thus fear—that is, with fear, venerate—the Lord, all his saints. And you will fear for your own good, because there is no lack of the true good for those who fear him. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Those who fear God lack nothing” (Ecclesiasticus 1:28). I said that those who fear him suffer no lack; but “the rich have become needy and hungry.” The order has been reversed. This means: The rich in spirit—that is, the proud—have hungered, and will always hunger [Col. 0772C], that is, they will desire that good. For no one is so impious as not to desire the highest good, although he does not rightly strive toward it. And they have been needy of that good, and will always be needy of it, that is, they will lack it. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:24)—rich, that is, in spirit.

But because he had said, “There is no lack for those who fear him,” he explains what “there is no lack” means, as follows. I say that “the rich have become needy and hungry”; but those who seek the Lord—that is, the poor and those who fear him, who seek the Lord most earnestly—“shall not be diminished in any good,” that is, they will never have less, since they seek the Lord, who is every good; that is, since he is the highest good, every good comes from him.

But because he had said, “Fear,” [Col. 0772D] and was afterward going to teach them the fear of the Lord, he exhorts them to listen in this way: I said, “Fear.” And so that you may know how to fear, O you “sons,” not according to the flesh but according to teaching, come with the steps of affection and listen to me with the hearing of the heart; and thus I shall teach you the fear of the Lord.

But in order to urge them more strongly toward what he is about to say, he exhorts them almost by way of a question: I say that I shall teach you. And lest I teach in vain, who is the man who desires life? He explains what life he means when he adds: Who is the man who loves to see, by the experience of the thing itself, “good days”—that is, the days of eternal life, in which there will be no tribulation, and which are therefore called good? These present days, however, are called evil, not because they are evil in their essence, [Col. 0773A] but because evils of various tribulations threaten within them.

This is as if he were to say: You, man, who desire life, listen, whatever others may do; and thus I shall teach you the fear of the Lord: restrain your tongue from evil—that is, from bitter words. And because some who are not bitter in their words speak deceitfully, and thus are not among those who fear him, he adds: “Let your lips not speak deceit”—that is, deceitful words. Also, turn away from evil action; and because that would not suffice, do good. And do this not for human approval, but through these things seek eternal peace; and do not seek it lukewarmly, but pursue it, that is, seek it perseveringly.

This means: When you turn away from evil and do good, do so with a view to eternal peace—that is, Christ, who is true peace. In accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14). [Col. 0773B] I say, “Turn away from evil,” and so forth. And toward this God will help you.

For the eyes of the Lord are upon the just, looking upon them—that is, his grace looks upon them to strengthen them, so that they do not fall away from his likeness, just as one who loves someone looks upon him. And his ears—that is, grace itself—are toward their prayers, that is, near their prayers, so that he may hear them and be their co-worker for good. Grace is rightly called both an ear and an eye, because through it we are both heard and seen by the Lord.

Or what he says, “Restrain your tongue from evil,” may be read more specifically in this way: I said, “Taste and fear,” that is, taste with fear. And so that you may taste with fear, you who love life, restrain your tongue [103] from evil—that is, from blasphemy against the sacrament. Also, let your lips not speak deceit [Col. 0773C]—that is, deceitful words about the sacrament itself, so that you speak well of it while understanding it wrongly. The rest is unchanged.

What he says here, “Restrain your tongue,” and so forth, is not the fear of the Lord but the effect of fear. Through the effect he indicates the cause.

It follows: “But the face,” and so forth. Because he had said that the eyes of the Lord are upon the just, he intends, by contrast, to show what will happen to the wicked, so that they do not think themselves unpunished, as follows: I say that the eyes of the Lord are upon the just. By contrast, the face—that is, the facial expression—of the Lord is upon those who do evil, that is, his anger is upon them, so that he may destroy even their memory from the land of the living, so that no mention of them and no prayer for them may be made there. He uses “face” for anger because anger usually appears in the face. The anger of God, however, is nothing other [Col. 0773D] than vengeance.

I said that the ears of the Lord are toward their prayers. This can be seen by analogy. For “the just cried out”—that is, the just in the Old Law, Abraham, Isaac, and others of this kind, acted with an intense cry. And the Lord heard them, and thus delivered them from all their tribulations. Therefore, through their example it can be demonstrated that the Lord is near—that is, close—to those who are troubled in heart: he hears those who tear their hearts by mourning over their sins, and not their garments. And he will save those just who are humble in spirit, not the proud.

The insertion gives the reason. This means: He will save them because they are humble in spirit. And it is necessary that he save them. For the tribulations of the just are many, both those that arise of themselves, such as fever and other things of this kind, [Col. 0774A] and those inflicted by others, such as being scourged and killed. And from all these the Lord will deliver them. This is an exposition of what he said above: “He will save the humble in spirit.”

I say that he will save them in the future. Meanwhile, the Lord guards all their bones—that is, all their virtues—in such a way that not one of them will be broken, that is, destroyed.

I said that he will save the just after they die, namely, the bodily death that will be a gate of life for them. But the death of sinners will not be a gate of life; rather, it will be very evil—that is, the gate of perpetual death.

And I said that the Lord guards the bones of the just so that they do not sin. By contrast, those who hate the just—that is, sinners—will offend, going from evil to worse.

But he explains how he will deliver the just and how he guards the just here, as follows: I say that he will deliver [Col. 0774B] the just—namely, he will redeem them, that is, the Lord will rescue the souls of his servants from these very tribulations by the price of his death. And I say that he guards their bones; and thus all who hope in him will not sin criminally—that is, no one who places his hope in him will sin.

## ON PSALM 34

### Title of the Thirty-Fourth Psalm

“A Psalm for David,” that is, to be attributed to David as signified—namely, to Christ. Wherever “for David” is placed in the Psalms, Christ, the true David, is understood.

Here the head—that is, Christ—is introduced as acting concessively concerning the judgment of the Jews [Col. 0774C], so that, blinded on account of their evil merits, they may hand him over to death. He also prays for the defeat of his enemies and for steadfastness, so that he may not yield in the Passion, and for the Resurrection. Afterward he prays for the salvation of certain enemies. He also acts concessively concerning the destruction of certain others. He shows the cause of their condemnation, namely, the death and insults that they freely inflicted upon him; afterward he explains these at sufficient length, also showing how great were the humility and goodwill he had toward them.

He seems to do this with the intention both of terrifying his enemies away from their impiety and of making those whose salvation he seeks more indebted to him.

“Judge, Lord, those who harm me.” It is as if he were to say: I know that, because their evil merits demand it, the Jews are to be judged by you—that is, blinded—so that they may harm me in intention, not in action, namely, by desiring to keep me in death. And because I know this, I consent. “Judge, Lord, [Col. 0774D] them,” blinding them so that they may be those who harm me, not in action but in mind.

And also “fight against”—that is, cause them to be overcome by their first desire, so that those who resist somewhat in their love for me, but who, compelled by their reason, yield to their perverse desire concerning my death, may, overcome by that desire so that they yield to it, be assailants of me according to the flesh in order to kill me.

After granting this, he prays for the defeat of his enemies and for steadfastness, as follows: I granted concerning them that you judge them; but so that you may help me, I pray: “Take hold of arms and shield,” that is, make me take hold of arms—namely, firm arguments, miracles, and other works by which I may openly convict them, as with weapons. And make me take hold of a shield—that is, the hope of your protection, which may protect me, in the likeness [Col. 0775A] of a shield, so that I may not be convicted.

Or it may be read by analogy alone: “Take hold of arms and shield,” that is, be like one who takes up arms, in that you make me overcome as one who takes up arms in order to help a friend overcome. And be like one who takes up a shield, protecting me so that I may not be convicted, as one who takes up a shield and holds it against the darts of enemies, protecting a friend so that he may not be overcome.

And thus, by taking up arms and shield, “rise to my help,” so that I may convict and not be defeated.

I say, “Judge and fight against.” And after my death, “draw out the sword”—that is, multiply your vengeance upon them. And “make a conclusion,” that is, bring a conclusion against them, namely, a conclusion directed against them by which they may be convicted as unable to resist.

[Col. 0775B] This means: Openly convict them by the arguments and miracles of the disciples, and by my Resurrection and Ascension, those who persecute me, as one is convicted by a conclusion.

The sword is used for vengeance because vengeance is usually carried out by a sword.

I say, “Make a conclusion,” in this way: “Say to my soul: I am your salvation.” This means: Make a conclusion by saying to my soul—not in words but by the experience of the thing itself, namely, by resurrecting me—that I am its salvation.

Or it may be read in this way: “Rise to my help, and afterward draw out”—that is, make known to the nations—“your sword,” namely, me, who am your sword, through whom you will convict the devil. And by my outpouring [Col. 0775C] make a conclusion against those who persecute me—that is, make a conclusion against them.

This means: They appear to speak of me with excessive arrogance, as though wandering about; but you make a conclusion against them that is very much opposed to them—that is, confine them through my exaltation and proclamation, so that they cannot wander in words against me in the same way as one confined in prison, who has no freedom to wander.

I say, “Draw out,” and draw out in this way: “Say to my soul,” by resurrecting me, “I am its salvation.” This means: Resurrect me, and thus make known that I am known by only a few.

Then follows the prayer for the salvation of the enemies, as follows: I said, “Pour me out, and thus confine them”; and when they have been confined through my outpouring, let some of them who are to be saved [Col. 0775D] be “put to shame”—that is, blush—and, having been put to shame, let them revere—that is, fear—the punishment, because they sought to take my life; and, by revering, let them turn away from their impiety, “backward,” that is, proceeding behind me.

This means: Those who now place their own desires before my desires, and thus go before me, should instead place their own desires after mine, and thus go behind me—that is, become my followers. And after they turn backward by following me, let them be put to shame—that is, let them blush more and more continually over the fact that they had been thinking evil against me, that is, against me.

It is as if he were to say: Let them not be put to shame only before they turn away, but, after their turning, let them persevere more and more in shame, so that they may thereby deserve pardon all the more.

After the prayer for those to be saved, [Col. 0776A] there follows a concession concerning those to be destroyed, so that they may become “like dust before the face”—that is, the presence—“of the wind.”

This means: At the beginning of their blindness let them become comparable to dust, which, being dry and not bound together by any moisture of the earth, is easily driven here and there by the face of the wind. So they too, adhering to the Church—which is firm earth—with no moisture of virtues, may be driven most easily by their evil desire toward unlawful things. That desire is therefore called wind because it drives one to do evil, like wind driving dust.

I say: “Let them become like dust before the face of the wind”; and, so that things may be still worse for them, let the angel of the Lord—that is, the evil angel, who is the Lord’s avenger against the wicked—be one who confines them by suggestions toward unlawful things.

And it should be noted that before anyone is confined by an evil angel [Col. 0776B], he is driven by an evil will arising from himself. But after they become like dust and are confined by the angel, “let darkness”—that is, ignorance—“and slipperiness”—that is, sliding from vice to vice, from an evil work to something worse—be the way by which they will come to death.

This means: After they have been driven by the wind of desire and confined by the angel, let them fall into the darkness of ignorance, so that they may never come to their senses; and thus let them slide from evil to worse, and let this be their way to death. And so that they may go on slipping even more, let the angel of the Lord, namely the evil one, pursue them, so that he may lead them through every unlawful thing.

He rightly places “darkness” and “slipperiness” by way of analogy, as if he were to say: Let things happen to them as badly as they do to one who, while his enemy pursues him, proceeds along a dark and slippery [Col. 0776C] road; for such a person falls very easily.

But he assumes the reason why this should happen to them, as follows: I grant that they become like dust, and so forth. And deservedly, because “without cause”—that is, without reason—they had secretly hidden for me the destruction of a snare. That is, they secretly thought to prepare destruction for me that would be the cause of a snare, namely, the reason why I would be ensnared and held so that I would not rise again, in the likeness of one who, being held by a snare, has no freedom to go wherever he wishes.

The snare, I say, was destined for them themselves—that is, through it they would themselves be ensnared unto death. And they reproached my soul, that is, they brought reproaches against my soul, calling it deceitful and sinful. Hence they are recorded as having said in the Gospel: “We know that this man is a sinner” [Col. 0776D] (John 9:24); and elsewhere: “He deceives the crowds” (John 7:12). And this was “needlessly”—that is, falsely, entirely empty of any rational cause. Therefore “needlessly” is rightly used, as though to say “very emptily.”

I say that they secretly hid destruction for me by means of a snare; therefore “let the snare come upon him unexpectedly”—that is, death at the hands of Titus and Vespasian. He does not know it now; hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “But now they are hidden from your eyes” (Luke 19:42). Or, “he does not know” means that he will not know that it is happening to him on account of his merits. For he will be so hardened that, even when placed under the vengeance for his sin, he will not recognize that vengeance.

And let the capture come upon him which he secretly hid—that is, which he thought to prepare for me in secret.

This means: Let the capture by which he seized me be the reason why capture also comes upon him.

I said, “Let the snare come upon him” [Col. 0777A]; and thus let him fall into the snare, namely, into the very snare that he wanted to prepare for me, so that he may be held in death, just as he wanted to hold me.

What he says, “let him fall into the snare,” is the same as what he said above, “let the snare come upon him”; but he repeats it in order to define it by adding “into it itself.”

It should be noted, however, that “capture” and “snare” are used with reference to different people. Some of them were captured; others were ensnared by death. I say that the snare and capture will come upon him, and so it will be.

But my soul, by contrast, which will be thought to have been ensnared, will rejoice in the Lord at my Resurrection. And it will also delight in its salvation—that is, in its own salvation, which will come to the human race through me.

And all my bones—that is, the disciples, who are stronger members of me—will say, both in words and in thought: “O Lord, who is like you in power?” No one. You, I say, Lord, are the one who rescues your needy people from the hand of those stronger than them [Col. 0777B] [106]—that is, from the power of evil spirits, who until now had been stronger, leading them into the darkness of death through Adam’s sin.

In saying “those stronger than them,” he follows Greek usage: the Greeks use the genitive for the ablative, which they lack.

And you are also the one who rescues your needy and poor people from those who plunder them, so that they may no longer plunder them—that is, from the evil spirits, who previously plundered their virtues for themselves.

A needy person (*inops*) is one who is without another’s help; a poor person (*pauper*) is one who is without his own help; and a destitute person (*egenus*)—which is the same as a beggar—is one who lacks both kinds of help. He is called a beggar because, lacking both kinds of help, he seeks it with lamentation and shame.

All of this occurred in the human [Col. 0777C] race. For it was never able to be freed either by its own help or by the help of the Law; therefore, in its misery, it begged to be freed.

But because he had said “the one who rescues,” and so forth, and someone might ask how he is the rescuer, he intends to explain this as follows: The bones themselves will say that I am the rescuer, and so it is. I am the rescuer in that I patiently endured all the things I shall mention.

It should be noted that the things here announced in the past tense with complete certainty are to be understood as future, namely: “Rising up against me, unjust witnesses, they questioned me about things I did not know,” not with respect to wisdom but by the experience of the thing itself—that is, they imposed things upon me, in the likeness of those who question someone about something he does not know. They are recorded in the Gospel as having said: “Are we not right [Col. 0777D] in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (John 8:48).

And “they repaid me evil for good,” which I had done for them by preaching, raising the dead, performing other miracles, and so forth. He explains in what follows what evils they repaid.

And they also repaid, in accordance with their impiety, the barrenness of my soul, so that, while through preaching I wished them to give birth with respect to grace and goodwill, they made it barren with respect to themselves, in accordance with what is read in the Gospel: “How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Luke 13:34).

I said that they made my soul barren. But when they were troublesome to me because of that barrenness, I put on sackcloth for them in the future—not in reality, but in hope.

This means: I was already planning [Col. 0778A] to clothe them—that is, to join them to myself, in the likeness of a garment which, when put on, is joined to the body. And he rightly says that they would become sackcloth—that is, penitents—for penitents are clothed in sackcloth.

And while I was planning that I would clothe them, I humbled my soul in fasting.

This means: Although I could freely exalt my vengeance over them, because they made me fast from their incorporation into myself, I humbly endured that fasting in the secret of my soul. And this because my prayer will be turned into my bosom.

This is said emphatically: those for whom I pray will be turned toward my protection, from which they had departed by living wickedly. He refers us here to the analogy of the story of Moses, whom the Lord commanded [Col. 0778B] to put his hand into his bosom and draw it out again (Exodus 4). When it had been drawn out and appeared leprous, it was put back in again at the Lord’s command and was healed. This was done as a figure of the Jews.

While subject to the Lord’s protection, they existed healthy in virtues; but once removed from it through their own evil merits, they were corrupted by various stains of sin, like leprosy. When, however, part of them returned to that protection through the preaching of the apostles, it was healed again.

And this is what he says here: “My prayer will be turned into my bosom.”

I say that I humbled my soul in fasting. And I also pleased myself in this, admonishing them—that is, I took delight in it as though in admonishing my neighbor. He explains which neighbor when he adds: as though in [Col. 0778C] admonishing our brother. By saying “our,” he hints at the Trinity of persons.

This is as if he were to say: I took such delight in admonishing them as anyone does in admonishing his brother. And thus I was humbled—that is, afflicted with grief—by the hardening of my own people, like a father or friend mourning and grieving over the death of a son or friend.

There follows an explanation [107] of the evils about which he earlier said: “They repaid evil.” I say that I was humbled on their account, and they, by contrast, rejoiced and assembled.

The order has been reversed. They assembled in order to seize me, and rejoiced at my capture; and “scourges were gathered against me,” that is, against me in order to crush me. And I did not know the reason for which I was scourged—not with respect to wisdom but with respect to the experience of the thing itself.

This means: I was not guilty.

By [Col. 0778D] saying “scourges were gathered,” he indicates the diversity and multiplicity of the scourges. For he was scourged in many ways, as is read in the Gospel (Matthew 27:26).

And because they did these things, they were scattered—that is, destroyed—in their virtues, and afterward they were not moved to repentance; they were scattered by God.

Or it may be read in this way: While they were gathering scourges against me, they were scattered—that is, separated from certain people of the same people who grieved over my death and are also said to have wept. To them he said: “Do not weep over me” (Luke 23:28). Yet they were not moved toward me by compassion, following their example.

By this he indicates their excessive hardness.

Or it may be read in this way: Because they rejoiced and assembled, they were scattered—that is, they will be scattered throughout the whole world. Nor will they then be moved [Col. 0779A] to repentance, when they ought to have been moved. Thus too he indicates their hardness.

I said that they assembled, and so forth. They also tested me, saying: “Prophesy: who is the one who struck you?” (Luke 22:64). And they mocked me—that is, ridiculed me—with mockery, that is, with excessive derision: “Ha! You who destroy,” and so forth (Mark 15:29).

To mock is to wrinkle the nose in excessive derision; therefore it is used here for excessive mockery. What he adds, “with mockery,” intensifies the expression, meaning with extreme mockery.

And they also gnashed their teeth against me while standing over me—that is, prepared to crush me, in the likeness of one who stands over someone in order to crush him.

When he says “they gnashed their teeth,” it is as if he were to say: They burned with such anger against me that they could not even [Col. 0779B] speak, but gnashed their teeth.

The future Passion is shown by the past tense.

Then follows the prayer concerning the Resurrection, as follows: I said that they did to me as I have recounted; and while I suffered humbly, I seemed to have been handed over to oblivion. And you, Lord, when will you look upon me, you who seem to have forgotten me? Do not hand me over to oblivion any longer, but restore my soul to my body, wrested away by their malice—that is, which those wicked men will take away from my body.

And he adds the reason why it should be restored, as follows: “And restore my only one, torn away from lions.”

This means: Restore it for this reason, because it is unique—that is, singular in holiness—and they are lions, that is, cruel, taking it away in their cruelty and not according to merit.

If you restore it, I will confess to you in the great Church—that is, [Col. 0779C] I will praise you through the great assembly of my members, which will not be small, as the Synagogue was. And that Church will not be unstable, easily bending toward vices like the Synagogue; rather, I will praise you in a weighty people.

This means: My weighty people—that is, weighty in virtues and not quickly moved—will praise you with every kind of praise.

I said that I should restore the soul because it is unique and because I will confess. And therefore, further, let those who oppose me—that is, those who are unjustly opposed to me, not opposed on account of merit—not rejoice over me.

This means: Let them not rejoice in keeping me in death, as though they were then over me—that is, superior to me and convicting me.

But because he had said indefinitely “those who oppose me,” lest some appear to be speaking peacefully [Col. 0779D] and thus not opposing him, making them inexcusable, he adds: Although all oppose me, some “nod with their eyes”—that is, they show favor to me.

This means: They favor me before my eyes—that is, in my presence—but when they are not before me, they oppose me greatly. Or they “nod with their eyes,” that is, according to the gesture of their eyes, not according to the assent of the flesh, like those who said: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful,” and so forth (Mark 12:14).

He explains by the past tense how they nod, as follows: It is true that I say they nod to me, because they spoke peacefully to me, while in their speech they were devising plots against me in order to destroy me, and this in anger over the loss of their land.

For they feared losing the land because of me.

Or it may be read in this way: not in good anger, but in “anger over the land”—that is, anger concerning earthly things, not spiritual things [Col. 0780A]. Anger over good things consists in being angry against vices. Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “Be angry and do not sin” (Psalm 4:5).

I say that they spoke peacefully, and not only this, but, standing over me—that is, superior to me in their own estimation—they “opened their mouths,” that is, spoke broadly and arrogantly, saying: “Crucify him” (Mark 15:13). And rejoicing, they said: “Good, good!”—that is, things are going well for us. For our eyes have seen what we desired, namely, him dying shamefully.

I say that they opened their mouths and did the other things that have been described; and I endured everything humbly. And you, Lord, saw both my humiliation and my justice, and their iniquity and arrogance.

Therefore, do not be silent concerning them—that is, do not refrain from rebuking them through vengeance—even if now you seem [Col. 0780B] to be silent.

This means: Prove by the vengeance you will inflict that they acted wickedly and justly, as though you were showing it by words.

And, looking upon my humility, do not depart from me, even if you seem to have departed. It is as if he were to say: Do not withdraw your help from me.

But “rise, Lord”—that is, show yourself powerful by helping me, though you seem powerless to them. And “attend to my judgment”—that is, consider it intently and carefully, not according to your act of considering, since you always see everything, but according to recompense.

My judgment is unjust, since they judged me worthy of death, and I humbly endured this out of obedience to you.

This means: Reward me because I was unjustly judged for you, you who are my God—that is, my creator—and my Lord, whom I serve in all [Col. 0780C] things. Attend to my cause, for which I suffered, and see how honorable it is. Therefore reward me. For I did not suffer on account of anyone’s wrongdoing, but on account of the salvation of human beings.

And also “judge me,” not only according to the judgment and cause mentioned above, but according to your justice—that is, resurrect me and glorify me—because I was judged for you and on account of this cause, and because you are just. And it is just that you do this, since I have deserved it.

And therefore, further, judge me according to the judgment by which I am to be judged, so that they may not rejoice over me. This is explained above: the expression is repeated out of excessive affection. For one prayer is not sufficient for what he greatly desires.

He shows what they should not rejoice over when he adds: Let them not say in their hearts [Col. 0780D], “Good, good for our soul.”

This means: Those who, as I showed above, said with their words, “Good, good,” should not say this in their hearts—that is, they should not understand that things are truly as they say aloud. Rather, when I rise again, let them appear to themselves as liars in their conscience, even if they deny it in words.

He shows why they should not say “good” when he adds: Let them not say in their hearts, “We have devoured him”—that is, we have utterly destroyed him so that he will not rise again, in the manner of food that is devoured. For if they could truly say, “We will devour him,” they would certainly say “Good,” and thus rejoice over me exceedingly.

I say, let them not rejoice exceedingly, but let them be put to shame for good and revere—that is, fear—their condemnation for what they did wickedly against me: those who rejoice only in my evils, together with those who both rejoice and act.

For many [Col. 0781A] were those who rejoiced but did nothing.

This means: Let both those who acted and those who merely rejoiced be put to shame.

It should be noted, however, that he does not pray for everyone, but for those who are to be saved; otherwise he would pray fruitlessly.

Above he prayed for this same thing, but it has been repeated out of excessive affection. I say: Let them be put to shame and revere, and not merely a little, but let them be clothed with shame—that is, let them be surrounded by blushing and reverence as a body is surrounded by clothing—and let them be so surrounded in soul and body.

Those who speak maliciously against me—that is, about me—should thus repent.

And, by contrast, let those who desire my justice—that is, the Resurrection which justly comes to me—rejoice and be glad, namely, the disciples.

What he says, “Let them rejoice and be glad,” has its order reversed [109]. It is as if he were to say: [Col. 0781B] Let them be glad, and not merely a little, but let them rejoice exceedingly—that is, be very glad.

Or “those who desire my justice” may mean those who desire to imitate it insofar as they are able.

And let those who desire the peace of his servant—that is, who desire to attain eternal peace, which I already possess, since I am his servant, namely, the servant of the Lord the Father according to the flesh, that is, obedient to him in all things—say, in mouth, affection, and action: “May the Lord be magnified forever,” that is, praised from generation to generation, in the conversion of the faithful and in their good works.

And when they thus rejoice, my tongue—that is, the tongue of my people—will meditate—that is, proclaim and preach diligently—to others your justice, namely, how just you were in this: that you resurrected me, who had merited it well. And all day—that is, continually—it will meditate on your praise, that is, it will diligently preach to others, both by mouth and by example, so that they may praise you in every way.

What he says, “it will meditate,” is the same as saying “it will announce diligently,” in the likeness of those who meditate well and say nothing rashly.

It is not said “it will meditate” as though the disciples ought to deliberate about what to say; for it is written concerning them: “Do not consider what you shall speak,” and so forth (Matthew 10:19). Or, if it refers to other faithful people, “it will meditate” may be understood as “it will speak thoughtfully,” not rashly.

## ON PSALM 35

### Title of the Thirty-Fifth Psalm

“To the end. A Psalm of David, servant of the Lord.” This is explained as follows: This Psalm is to be attributed to the servant of the Lord—that is, to any faithful person who, insofar as he can, has made himself the Lord’s servant; a servant, I say, who is David “to the end”—that is, strong-handed [Col. 0781D] in perseverance, acting manfully against the devil and vices.

Here every such faithful person intends to convict the unjust who excuse themselves for their sins and attribute their guilt to the necessity of divine providence—not by setting out the unjust persons’ own words, but by arguing against them. He shows that every sin proceeds not from God but from an abuse of free choice.

He also commends God’s mercy, without which no one can be made perfect, and which here saves both the good and the wicked in bodily health. He also treats of the blessedness of the good, for the attainment of which he prays.

“The unjust man said that he would sin within himself.” It is as if he were to say: Some people, excusing themselves, say that they sin by necessity, but no one can reasonably excuse himself [Col. 0782A] in this way.

For “the wicked man said that he would sin”—that is, he first determined in his heart that he would sin—not from the necessity of divine providence, nor from the necessity of his nature, but “within himself,” that is, it is under his own control: by free choice he can either do this or leave it undone.

Therefore no one is to be blamed for it except himself.

Someone might ask: Why, then, does he sin? The answer is: Because there is no fear of God in him—namely, in its effect. I say “fear” that is set before his eyes, that is, before the eyes of his heart. And it is evident that the fear of God is not in him in such a way as to make him cease, because he acted deceitfully, and this in his own sight. This means: he sees what, although it is hidden from human beings, he nevertheless acted deceitfully in such a way that his iniquity is found—that is, understood by him himself—to be hateful in the sight of God. This is as though he said: Truly, the fear of God is not in him. For he acted so deceitfully that he understood his iniquity to be hateful to God.

He explains his iniquity part by part in this way. Someone might say: What do you mean by “iniquity”? The answer is: “The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit.” This is said intransitively, and means: The deceitful words of his mouth are iniquity. And this is iniquity, because he did not wish to understand so as to do good; that is, he did not wish to direct the understanding he possessed toward doing good. No one is so brutish and stupid that he does not understand that good ought to be done.

“And he meditated iniquity in his bedchamber,” that is, in his heart, which is called a bedchamber because the devil lies there. And this is iniquity: “He stood by every way that is not good,” that is, he willingly persisted in carrying out every perverse action, which is a way that is not good but evil, leading to death. Or, “he stood by” means that he stood there perseveringly. Indeed, by a likeness, working is properly called standing. For just as anyone who is walking, after arriving where he was heading, stands there, so someone who first advances through an evil thought, after reaching the act, remains fixed there.

I said that his iniquity is found—that is, understood—to be hateful. “But he did not hate malice”; that is, he did not hate malice itself, namely iniquity.

After showing that the unjust person sins not from necessity but by himself, he shows that the fact that the faithful are heaven is from God’s mercy. Just as I said that when the unjust person sins, he sins “in himself,” O Lord, so “in heaven is your mercy, and your truth,” that is, your justice. This means: The fact that someone sins is from himself; but the fact that someone is heaven is accomplished by your mercy and justice. As though he said: This is not from him.

I say that mercy and truth are powerful “unto the establishment of the clouds,” that is, they can make heaven into clouds—preachers who rain upon others, after the manner of clouds raining upon the earth. And your justice, that is, your just ones, are through this same mercy and truth “like the mountains of God,” that is, established by you, God. This means: They are firm in virtues and stable after the manner of immovable mountains. Or they are a refuge for the lesser, because of their holiness, just as mountains are a refuge for those who fear, because they are fortified places.

[Col. 0783A] Someone might ask: Since God makes the just into mountains, why does he not justify the unjust, so that he might also make them mountains? The answer is: O God, “your judgments,” by which you judge the unjust to be rejected, “are a great abyss,” that is, exceedingly deep. This means: They are inscrutable, like an exceedingly deep abyss whose limit cannot be reached.

I said that your mercy is in heaven, and that you will also save “human beings and beasts,” that is, both those who conduct themselves rationally like human beings—namely, the just—and those who conduct themselves irrationally like beasts—namely, the unjust. You will save them, Lord, mercifully with bodily salvation, giving them the necessities of this age.

Therefore, O God, “how have you multiplied your mercy?” This means: From this it is evident how manifold your mercy is. He says this admiringly, in praise of God’s mercy.

I said that you will save human beings and beasts with such a salvation, and that the beasts seek no other salvation. But “the sons of human beings,” that is, those who are rational like human beings—namely, the just—will hope for another salvation, the future one, “placed under the shelter of your wings,” that is, under the protection of the two laws. These protect them through the consolation of their judgments, so that they do not fail in prosperity or adversity, after the manner of the wings of a bird, which protect its young from heat and rain.

Or it may be understood as follows: Lord, your mercy will be in heaven; that is, heaven itself will be constituted from human beings and beasts—from the wise and from those who are rightly rational, who are therefore called “human beings” here, and from beasts, namely the uneducated and simple, who are not very rational and are therefore called “beasts.”

“Therefore, how have you multiplied,” and so forth. These words are not changed. And they will have not only this, that they are heaven. “But the sons of human beings,” that is, those very sons of human beings who already exist as heaven—namely, the rational—will hope for another salvation, placed under the shelter of your wings. These words also remain unchanged.

I say that they will hope for another salvation: They will hope “to be made drunk from the abundance of your house.” And indeed they will be made drunk, that is, they will be filled abundantly by the abundance, namely by the plenty, of your house—the blessedness possessed by those who are already in your house, the heavenly Jerusalem.

He properly says “they will be made drunk” by way of comparison: They will be filled in such a way that every earthly sensuality will be driven out from them, after the manner of drunkards, who are free from all cares.

[Col. 0783D] He explains this abundance in the following way: I say that they will be made drunk, and this through you. For you will give them drink, that is, satisfy them, “from the torrent of your delight,” that is, from your delightful glory. It is properly called a torrent: it is abundant like a torrent, or it drives away all adversities from the faithful, after the manner of a torrent which, flowing with force, drives away everything that obstructs it.

And truly you can give them drink from it, because “with you is the fountain of life,” Christ, from whom that torrent proceeds. Hence John says: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1).

When he says “with you,” he indicates a distinction of persons. And because the fountain of life is with you, it is “in your light,” that is, in your Son, who is your light, as John testifies: “He was the true light,” and so forth (John 1:9).

[Col. 0784A] “We shall see you, the true light,” through spiritual contemplation. Hence the same person says in the Gospel: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9).

He prays for this very inebriation. Thus he says: “The sons of human beings will be made drunk”; and, in order that they may be made drunk, “extend, Lord, your mercy over those who know you.” That is: By your mercy, make innocent those who already have faith in you but are not yet innocent. And “over those who are upright of heart,” already innocent, extend your justice; that is, before that inebriation, give them your justice so that they may reach it—namely, justify them.

This is as though he said: Make those among us who are not innocent innocent, so that afterward they may be justified and thus saved. Justify the innocent also, and thus they will be saved.

After we have become upright of heart, “let not the foot come upon me, nor upon them,” that is, let not the inclination to pride come upon us, lest by boasting in our uprightness we fall. “Foot” is used for inclination, because the soul walks by means of its inclinations.

“And let not the hand of the sinner”—that is, the impulse of the suggestion of the sinner, namely the devil, by antonomasia, or any sinner—“move me or them” from a good purpose. For we push with our hands, and therefore “hand” is used for impulse.

There, that is, in pride, “they fell into condemnation, who work iniquity,” continually—that is, the devils. For this reason they were expelled from heaven and afterward could not stand in heaven.

Or it may be understood as follows: There fell those who work iniquity—Adam and Eve and those conformed to them, who still work iniquity in their descendants. For this reason they were expelled from innocence and life and afterward could not stand in it by themselves, unless God’s grace came to their aid.

[Col. 0784C]

# IN PSALM XXXVI

**Title of the Thirty-Sixth Psalm.** A psalm to be attributed to David, that is, to Christ. Or, if we say with certain commentators that it is simply “a psalm of David,” it will be the voice of the perfect Church.

Here Christ, or the Church, exhorts its simpler members not to become angry when they see the wicked flourishing in this world and the good being oppressed, imagining either that God is unjust or that he does not care about worldly affairs. Nor should they wish to imitate the wicked because they prosper. Rather, they should patiently endure these hidden judgments of God.

He also shows what the prosperity of the wicked and the adversity that will come upon the good are leading toward. He admonishes them to hope and rejoice not in themselves but in the Lord; and, if they sin, humbly to confess to him, thereby obtaining forgiveness and attaining justice.

“Do not be jealous,” that is, do not become angry “at those who do evil,” namely, in considering the prosperity of those who do evil, saying that God grants this to them unjustly. “Nor be zealous,” that is, do not love them so as to imitate those who commit iniquity.

He will make this clearer in what follows. I say: “Do not be jealous,” because “they will quickly wither from the flower of their prosperity when they die,” existing like grass, which quickly withers after the flower of its greenness, and they will quickly fall from that prosperity, existing like “the vegetables of herbs,” that is, green vegetables, which quickly wilt when cut.

It should be noted that the poorer are signified by grass, and the richer by vegetables. Vegetables are more valuable than grass while both remain green.

I say: Do not be jealous, but “hope in the Lord,” that is, hope for the eternal goods that are in the Lord. For hope without works is presumption. “Do good,” that is, good works, “and inhabit your land,” that is, possess and govern it, and cultivate well the sensuality of your earthly flesh, cutting away vices and evil works, after the manner of a good inhabitant who cultivates his land well, cutting away thorns and other useless growth.

And if you inhabit it, “you will be fed,” that is, refreshed in soul, “by the riches of that land,” namely, by the good works that will proceed from the cultivation of that land. “You will be fed” is properly said: Just as the body is nourished by bodily food, so the soul is fattened by good works.

And while doing good and inhabiting the land, do not delight in yourself by attributing this to yourself. Rather, “delight in the Lord” because of this: take joy and delight in this in the Lord, attributing it to him. And if you do this, he will at some time give you “the requests of your heart,” that is, what your heart, hoping with a good intention, asks—namely, eternal goods.

And if you sin, which is human, “reveal your way to the Lord” with humble confession. He already knows it through his provident consideration: that is, reveal the sin which would be your way to death if, by excusing yourself, you concealed it as Adam did.

And by revealing it, hope for forgiveness in him. He himself will act—that is, fulfill what you hope for—and, after he has forgiven you, he will justify you.

This is outside the book, but it is suggested by what follows when he says: “And he will bring forth…”

[Col. 0785C] That is, he will make your justice known to others as something existing like light; he will make it as open as light in darkness, so that others also may practice justice by your example, in accordance with Isaiah: “Your light shall rise in the darkness” (Isaiah 58:10).

“And your judgment”—by which you judge yourself to be a servant of God and the Lord, obedient in all things—“he will bring forth like midday,” that is, he will make it open to others after the manner of midday, so that others also may have that same judgment by your example.

And when he brings it forth in this way, do not become proud because of it. Rather, be increasingly subject to the Lord, and pray to him that you may not fail but may be increasingly justified.

He repeats what he placed at the beginning in order to state it more clearly as follows: Since he will bring forth justice like light, if you are subject to him, “do not be jealous,” that is, do not become angry in considering “the one who prospers in his way”—namely, do not become angry with the person who commits injustices, or with the prosperity of the person who commits injustices, since that prosperity will be his way to death.

Rather, “cease from anger,” the lesser anger, “and abandon wrath,” the greater anger. This means: Have neither a small nor a great anger because of it.

He also repeats the other part that he placed in the preceding verse, saying, “nor be zealous,” and so forth, in order to add the reasons.

I said: Do not be jealous, that is, do not become angry with the person who commits injustices. And also do not be jealous, that is, do not imitate that person, so as to do evil after his example and prosper similarly. For if you do evil, you will do so to your own harm.

“For those who do evil will be exterminated,” that is, they will be expelled beyond the boundaries of the heavenly homeland. This means: They will be disinherited from the land of the living, which they presumptuously suppose, in vain, that they will possess.

But “those who wait for the Lord,” in contrast—that is, those who patiently endure the judgments of the Lord without murmuring, although he judges the wicked to flourish here and the good to be oppressed—those who now appear vile and rejected will inherit the land of the living.

Since he had said that those who wait for the Lord will inherit the land, lest waiting seem tedious to anyone, he says that there will be little waiting.
