Thus I said: Those who wait will inherit. “And they will wait a little longer”; and after this little while, “the sinner will no longer be” in the condition in which he is now—flourishing and oppressing the just as he does now.

And you will seek his place by your reasoning and knowledge, and you will not find it. This means: If you seek by reason and meditation whether he will have a place there for becoming proud and oppressing the good, you will not find his place—that is, his opportunity. For once gold has been properly tested, it is no longer fitting for a fire to burn in the furnace.

Or you will seek his place, that is, whether he will remain there with the just, and you will not find it. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “The angels will go out and separate the wicked from the midst of the just” (Matthew 13:49).

I say that the sinner will have no place. “But the meek will inherit the land of the living,” in accordance with the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matthew 5:5).

He had already placed this above when he said, “Those who wait will inherit the land,” but he repeats it in order to add that when they inherit, they will not inherit in anxiety. Rather, “they will delight in the abundance of peace” in that land, that is, in great peace. This means: They will inherit that land with delight and peace.

He does not speak of an abundance of peace because there will be many peaces there, but because one eternal peace will come from many tribulations—or rather, from all tribulations—and through this he will come to that peace.

For here “the sinner will watch the just,” that is, lie in wait for the just in order to deceive him. “And he will gnash his teeth against him,” existing in an immoderate and irrational anger in order to oppress him, after the manner of irrational animals which gnash their teeth when angry.

“And afterward they unsheathed the sword,” and so forth, “to deceive the poor,” and so forth. The whole sense is as though he said: They will reach that peace because here sinners will lie in wait for them and gnash their teeth; they will unsheathe the sword and slaughter them; they will bend the bow in order to deceive them, but they will not be able to do so.

I say that the sinner will watch and gnash his teeth; but “the Lord will laugh at him” when he does this, that is, in his providence he will judge him worthy of ridicule, because he foresees that “his day” will come, the day of judgment, which will be the day of his retribution.

It follows: “They unsheathed the sword,” and so forth. This should be read in reverse order. They will not merely gnash their teeth against him; rather, “sinners have bent their bow,” that is, they will make the deception of their suggestions intense, “to deceive the poor and needy” by flatteries—that is, the just, whom they will believe to be poor, meaning unable to free himself by his own aid—and needy, meaning lacking another’s aid for deliverance.

When they are unable to deceive him with the bow, “they unsheathed the sword,” that is, they will bring forth open persecution through torments and death, “to slaughter,” that is, to kill bodily “the upright of heart,” namely the just.

The bow, because through it one is struck secretly and unknowingly, is used for deception. For many of the wicked attempt to make God’s servants conform to themselves by flatteries.

But because one is struck openly by the sword, it is used for the open persecution of the faithful. When the wicked cannot draw the just to themselves by flatteries, they at least attempt to turn them back by open persecution through threats and tribulations.

Therefore, because they will unsheathe the sword, I grant that “their sword will enter their own hearts,” that is, let death in their souls befall them in place of that sword, after the likeness of the person whose sword is turned back into his own heart when he intends to wound another with it.

“And let their bow”—that is, the deception of their flatteries—“be broken,” that is, utterly destroyed, so that it may not prevail against the just.

It should certainly be noted that he does not pray for the sword to be broken. For it contributes to the increase of the crown of the faithful who willingly suffer, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake,” and so forth (Matthew 5:10). But because the bow is useless against the just, he prays for it to be broken.

I said that the meek will inherit the land and that the sword of sinners will enter their own hearts. Therefore “it is better for the just to have little,” that is, to be poor and needy, than to have the many riches of sinners—that is, than for him himself to have many riches and be a sinner.

He adds the reason as follows. It is better for the just because “the arms of sinners will be broken,” that is, their riches and power, which are called arms because they trust in them, just as anyone trusts in the strength of his arms, will be utterly destroyed.

But the Lord strengthens the just through these very tribulations, so that they may become more radiant and stronger in virtues.

It is therefore still better for the just to have little because “the Lord knows”—that is, he has already foreseen in his providence—“the days of the blameless,” namely the days that he will give to the blameless, that is, to the just.

He explains what those days will be like when he adds: “And their inheritance will endure forever,” namely those days of blessedness that God will give to the blameless.

It is therefore still better for the just to have little because “they will not be confounded,” that is, they will not be disturbed by fear of punishment “in an evil time,” namely on the day of judgment.

And they will not merely avoid confusion; they will also “be filled with eternal glory in the days of famine,” that is, in the days of the future life, in which the wicked will hunger because they lack the true good.

He uses “days” in the plural because that day, although it will be single and eternal, will surpass the multitude of these days in duration.

Someone might ask why that time is called an evil time and those days evil days. He answers by giving the reason in this way: Because sinners will perish then—and not only then will they perish, but “the enemies of the Lord,” that is, those very sinners who are enemies of the Lord through their evil life.

Suppose that they were immediately honored, from infancy onward, with honor, and exalted in power so as to be kings or princes of some other kind. Nevertheless, inwardly they will fail. “Failing like smoke in riches,” that is, after the manner of smoke, which, the higher it rises, the more quickly it disappears.

I say that sinners will perish, and deservedly, because “the sinner borrows from the Lord”—namely, understanding, riches, health, and the other benefits—and does not repay God with interest.

He properly says not merely “borrows,” but “will borrow,” that is, he will persist in borrowing. For God gives one person understanding so that, by preaching well, he may repay God the interest—that is, the gain of children who are to be converted. He gives another health and riches so that he may return to God the interest of good works.

But when that person receives these benefits from God as a loan, he pays nothing.

The just person, in contrast, has mercy on himself by living well. Hence it is written: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclesiasticus 30:24). But the person who lives badly is cruel to himself, dragging himself toward condemnation.

He will also give others an example of living well, and thus have mercy on others. And because this would not be sufficient, he will give them what they need: instruction to those who need instruction, and worldly benefits to those who need worldly benefits.

It should nevertheless be noted that good will alone is sufficient for no one who is unable to bring his will into action.

The whole point is as though he said: Not all sinners will perish, but those who borrow and do not repay—and they perish because they do not repay.

But the just person will inherit forever because he has mercy and gives.

He will not do this for the sake of human favor, but with this aim: “Those who bless God,” that is, those who praise him by their good life, “will inherit the land of the living.” But “those who curse him,” that is, those who reproach God by their evil life, “will perish utterly,” that is, perish completely, both in soul and in body.

This means: He has mercy and gives, and thus blesses God, so that he may inherit the land and not perish by ceasing from God’s blessing and thereby reproaching him.

For he is certain that all who bless will inherit, and those who curse will perish.

It should be known that just as anyone blesses God by living well—that is, praises him—so by living badly he curses him—that is, reproaches him—as the Apostle testifies: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Romans 2:24).

In this way, the just person will not have from himself the fact that, by having mercy, he will repay and thereby inherit; rather, it will be “with the Lord,” that is, in God’s disposition.

“The steps of a man,” that is, the good inclinations and actions of the just person who conducts himself rationally, after the manner of a human being, by which he walks toward life, “will be directed” perseveringly from good to better.

Another translation has “by the Lord.” Nevertheless, “with the Lord” is properly placed by way of comparison. For just as, with some prince—that is, in his secret disposition—the arrangements of his entire kingdom are worked out, so in the divine disposition whatever is done by the good is ordered.

And because God will direct the steps of a man, that man himself will increasingly desire “his way,” God’s way—namely, his commandments, by which he will come to life.

Or it may be understood as follows: He will not only direct his steps after he has become just, but he will also desire “his way,” that is, his good life, which will be his way to life, and God himself will wish to have him—that is, by his gracious will he will give him this.

He explains how he will direct him: He will direct him in such a way that, when he gives him external tribulations, he will not be struck in soul so as to fail. He will not be struck because “the Lord places his hand beneath him,” that is, sustains him, after the likeness of someone who places his hand beneath a person who is wavering so that he does not fall.

Or it may be understood as follows. Lest anyone suppose that he would be directed in such a way that he would never fall at all, he adds: His steps will be directed so that, when he falls into a small sin, he will not be struck—that is, he will not be grievously harmed by descending into mortal sins. Or, when he falls into suggestions, he will not be struck by sinning mortally.

The verses that follow do not change.

[Col. 0789B] Someone might ask: How do you know that the just person will not be struck? The answer follows, to be stated if Christ is acting in this psalm:

“I was young among my members,” that is, in the time of the first just people. This means: I had younger members.

Or, if the Church is acting, it may be understood as follows: “I was young among my first just people,” that is, in the time of Abel and the others who came first. They are called younger either because they were first, or because they were not as mature in virtues as those who existed after Christ’s coming.

And in that youth “I did not see the just man forsaken,” that is, not aided by God.

Someone might say: What if you did not see this in youth? Perhaps afterward it happened that the just man was forsaken.

To this he replies by inserting: It did not happen. “For afterward I grew old,” that is, I had faithful elders—namely, apostles, martyrs, and confessors—who are called elders either because they came later in time or because they were more mature in virtues.

“And in old age I did not see the seed of the just man, who had been young, seeking bread,” that is, lacking the bread of life and understanding, after the manner of those who, having no bread, seek it by begging but do not find it.

The Gospel speaks figuratively of the five foolish virgins in this way (Matthew 25:5): Because they had no oil, they begged but did not find any.

The bread of life and understanding is called the teaching of God, by which the souls of the faithful are nourished and strengthened and led to eternal life.

The bread of life and understanding is also called that blessedness in which, after death, the souls of the faithful live forever, rejoice, and understand God more deeply.

The apostles and the other faithful of the New Testament are rightly called the seed of the first just people—namely, the patriarchs and prophets—because, with God’s grace cooperating, they were generated in faith through their teaching.

Hence the Lord said to the apostles: “Others have labored” (John 4:38), namely the patriarchs and prophets, “and you have entered into their labors” (ibid.).

Or it may be understood as follows: “I was young among the first faithful.”

Someone might ask why you say “I was” and not “I am.” He answers: For “I grew old” in the apostles and their successors, and I did not see, either in youth or in old age, the just man forsaken by God—that is, not aided in tribulations.

Nor did I see “his seed,” that is, good works, which are the cause of eternal life, just as seeds are the cause of harvests, “seeking bread,” that is, unrewarded through lacking the bread of life and understanding, by the same comparison used in the preceding statement.

From this it is evident that he is not forsaken by God. For “all day long,” that is, continually, he has mercy on himself and on others, and he lends others good preaching and the other benefits.

He properly says “lends,” that is, gives as a loan, so that they too may give to others in need and thus God’s gifts may be multiplied.

He had already stated this above, but because he had said it indefinitely, he repeats it by adding “all day long.”

And because he has mercy and lends, “his seed,” that is, his good work, “will be in blessing,” that is, it will be for him the cause of blessing—namely, exaltation in the future.

Therefore, because sinners will perish, you who wish to be saved must “turn away from evil” universally.

And because those who bless the Lord by their good life will inherit the land, “do good,” and not merely for an hour. Rather, “inhabit that good forever and ever,” that is, persevere in that good always.

And here are the reasons why one must turn away from evil and do good: Because “the Lord loves judgment,” namely, that we should judge and fulfill this together with him.

And therefore also because he will not leave his holy ones, who judge this together with him, without aid; rather, they will be preserved by God forever.

And therefore one must also turn away from evil because the unjust will be punished in the future.

Lest anyone suppose that they will be saved because of certain good works that they perform for the sake of favor, he adds: “And the seed of the impious will perish,” that is, the good work performed with an eye to favor will not be rewarded. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:5).

But the just, in contrast, “will inherit the land of the living, and will inhabit it forever and ever,” that is, they will remain over it forever, resting upon it and founded upon it, so that they may no longer be moved away from it.

He repeats this because it is the cause of the statement, “Turn away from evil,” and so forth. As though he said: Turn away and do good for this reason, so that, together with the other just, you may inherit the land—that is, Christ, who is the firm land upon which the faithful rest.

Someone might ask: Who are those just people who will inherit? He determines this so that no one may rashly declare himself to be such a just person.

“The mouth of the just man who is going to inherit will meditate wisdom,” that is, he will meditate on living wisely with regard to himself.

“And his tongue will speak to others,” that is, he will preach this judgment, which he judges that he himself must fulfill, so that they too may fulfill it. He will speak wisdom to them.

He will not meditate and speak in this way so as afterward to fail. Rather, “his law is always in his heart,” that is, in his will: he always loves it and wishes to fulfill it.

Thus it is in his heart, so that “his steps will not be overthrown” by that law—that is, his inclinations will not be displaced from it.

Someone might ask whether there is anyone who wishes to overthrow him. The answer is yes: The sinner sees the just person persevering in that law, and seeks to kill him—that is, to draw him away from the same law—by flatteries or tribulations, and thus, by making him act badly, to lead him to the death of the soul.

But the Lord will not leave him without aid, lest he yield. With him “placed in the sinner’s hands,” that is, he will make him steadfast while he is in the sinner’s power, not according to his soul but according to his body.

Nor will the Lord condemn him when he is judged—that is, when it happens that the just man is condemned by the sinner through bodily torments. And this will be “for him,” that is, for his own benefit.

As though he said: That judgment will not be for his condemnation but for his benefit.

Or it may be understood as follows: “Nor will the sinner condemn him,” as he supposes, when he is judged by him—that is, when it happens that the judgment which the sinner inflicts upon the just man by afflicting him instead becomes the condemnation of that sinner.

I said: Turn away from evil and do good. And if you do not immediately receive a reward for this, do not murmur as the children of Israel did, who, when they could not quickly reach the promised land from Egypt, wished to return to the pots of meat (Numbers 14:4).

Rather, await the Lord, who will reward you shortly, without murmuring.

And by waiting, “keep his way,” that is, his law, so that you do not turn away from it, since it will be your way to life. Otherwise your waiting would be vain.

Therefore keep it, so that you may inherit the land of the living, that is, so that it may be your inheritance.

You will see this land when sinners have perished in the future.

Or it may be understood as follows: When you begin to inherit the land, you will see when sinners have perished; that is, you will see the destruction of sinners.

By this he intends to recall the person from sin, lest he perish with sinners.

Someone might ask: How do you know that the sinner will perish? He confirms this by his own authority as follows: Truly, I know that they will perish. For “I saw,” that is, I considered in my mind, “the impious exalted over the pious in this world,” and raised up in riches “like the cedars of Lebanon,” which are taller than other trees.

Then, by consideration, I passed on to his end. And behold, “he was not,” that is, in the presence of my consideration, it became clear that he was not to remain so exalted.

This means: I considered that he would lose such exaltation.

And I sought him, that is, I investigated his place by careful reasoning—whether in the future he would have a place for becoming proud and oppressing the good—and “his place was not found” by me as I considered.

It should be known that he had placed this statement above in the second person in the following way: “You will seek his place and will not find it.” Here, however, he confirms it by his own authority, and therefore the wording is different.

Therefore, because if you wait, he will exalt you, and because, as I have shown, he will no longer exist in that way, “keep innocence” with regard to that impious person. Do not wish to harm him by words or deeds merely because he afflicts you.

And “see equity,” that is, recognize that it is equitable for you to remain innocent toward him.

And you will keep it for your own good, because “for the peaceful man,” that is, for the innocent, “there are remnants,” namely eternal goods that he has left for himself after despising worldly goods.

But the unjust “will perish utterly,” that is, they will perish completely, both in soul and in body.

Together with them, “the remnants of the impious,” that is, the worldly goods they have left for themselves after despising eternal goods, will perish, in accordance with: “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Luke 21:33).

Or it may be understood as follows: “The remnants of the impious,” that is, the eternal goods which they presumptuously leave for themselves after death, will perish with regard to them—that is, they will not be present for them.

Or as follows: The good works performed for the sake of favor, which they leave behind after death, will perish, that is, be annihilated.

He had already stated these reasons above, but here he repeats them for another purpose. He still insists upon them in order to draw the good toward what is better and terrify the impious.

Lest the just should in any way glory in themselves concerning their salvation, he says that all their salvation comes from the Lord in this way:

I said that the just will inherit the land, that when the just man falls he will not be struck, and that the Lord will not abandon him into the hands of the sinner. But this salvation does not come from the just themselves. “The salvation of the just is from the Lord.”

He explains salvation part by part as follows: “He is their protector in the time of tribulation,” lest they yield. He will help them to act well, free them from sins, and rescue them from sinners—that is, from the power of sinners, so that although their bodies are killed, the sinners may have no power over their souls.

Afterward he will save them from mortality and suffering, restoring them to eternal blessedness.

And this is because they hoped in him, not in themselves.

# IN PSALM XXXVII
## Psalm Thirty-Seven

### Title

“Psalm of David, for the remembrance of the Sabbath.” This is explained as follows: This psalm is attributed to David, that is, to Christ acting in remembrance of the Sabbath of eternal rest. For by “Sabbath,” which is interpreted as “rest,” eternal repose is signified.

In this psalm there is the voice of the Head, praying for the members who are to come, so that they may not be condemned in the future. These members, through Adam, had consigned eternal rest to oblivion; but at last, through Christ, they were to remember that rest and were to do penance for their sins both before baptism and after baptism. To show the excessive affection he has for them, he prays for them as though for himself, so that he may obtain his request more easily by showing the reasons why one ought to pray for them. He also adds several reasons why he ought to be heard on their behalf: namely, because they will repent and grieve over their sins, and will desire God alone; and because he is to suffer and rise again for them. He also reveals part of that Passion. Further, the members themselves will be ready to undergo scourging for Christ, just as he himself was scourged for them; and they will confess their sins and consider how to make satisfaction for them.

### “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger,” and so forth

It is as though he said: Lord, do not rebuke my members—that is, do not convict my members of having acted wickedly—by rebuking them in the anger of your judgment, when you will say to those who are to be condemned: “Depart from me, you accursed,” and so forth (Matt. 25:41). Nor, in your wrath—that is, in your eternal vengeance—correct me, that is, punish my members, in the likeness of one who, when corrected, is punished. This is as though he said: I certainly wish them to be rebuked and corrected here by passing scourges, but not in the future, when the reproof will take place in anger.

Someone might ask: Is it necessary for them that one pray on their behalf? The answer is yes: Your arrows—that is, mortality and liability to suffering, which you threatened to Adam before he sinned, saying, “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death” (Gen. 2:17)—have been fixed in me, that is, in my members. And I will say more: You have strengthened your hand over me, that is, you have made your vengeance very firm and heavy over my members.[^c0075-118] He rightly says “over,” after the likeness of one who, when striking someone harshly, presses his hand heavily and firmly upon him. Explaining in what way he strengthened his hand, he adds: In this, namely, you have strengthened your hand over my members: there is no health in my flesh, that is, in the flesh of my members.

This means: The flesh of my members, which had been healthy in relation to the tinder of sin, has become weak, always having within itself evil desire, which is called the tinder of sin because evil pleasure and occupation arise from it. Hence the Apostle says: “There is sin in your body, but let it not reign” (Rom. 6:12). And the fact that it is not healthy occurs from the face of your anger—that is, from the presence of your vengeance, which you exercise against it on account of Adam’s sin. Since the flesh is not healthy, there is no peace in my bones—that is, in the reason and virtues of my members. For they are always harassed; and this occurs from the face, that is, from the urgency, of my sins.

This means: There is no peace for them because sins—that is, evil desires, which are also called the tinder of sin—are pressing upon them and striving to overthrow reason itself and the virtues, according to the Apostle’s saying: “The flesh desires against the spirit” (Gal. 5:17).

Or the statement “Your arrows are fixed,” and so forth, may be understood in this way, so that “arrows” means more than in the preceding interpretation. Above, only mortality and liability to suffering were understood by “arrow.” They are rightly called arrows because God threatened Adam with them from afar before he sinned, just as arrows shot from afar threaten someone; or because through them the human race is afflicted, after the manner of one who is tormented by the wounds of arrows.

But “arrows” may also be taken more broadly, as follows: Your arrows have been fixed in my members—that is, mortality, liability to suffering, and the tinder of sin. And not merely for an hour, but you have strengthened—that is, made firm and enduring—your hand over my members, that is, your vengeance, namely the arrows mentioned above. He explains how he strengthened it: You strengthened and fixed it in such a way that there is no health in the flesh of my members because of the face of your anger—that is, on account of the presence of your vengeance. It is weak, mortal, liable to suffering, and subject to the tinder of sin.

This does not mean that the flesh itself suffers or desires, but that through its weakness liability to suffering and desire arise in the soul; this desire is the tinder of sin. Since the flesh is not healthy, there is no peace in my bones. This occurs from the face—that is, from the urgency—of the sins of my members, namely their evil desires.

And therefore it is still necessary to pray that they not be rebuked in anger and corrected in wrath, because my iniquities—that is, the evil desires of my members—have passed over my head, that is, have prevailed over the mind of my members, leading it into the pleasures of sin. They have also become heavy over me, like a heavy burden; that is, they have become burdensome to my members and oppress them, after the manner of a very heavy load. For just as a heavy burden does not permit the person whom it weighs down to rise, so desires burden their mind and do not allow it to strive upward to contemplate heavenly things.

All this is an argument from the lesser, as though he said: Since, on account of Adam’s sin, you punished them in the way I have shown—fixing your arrows in them and strengthening your hand—it is much more to be feared that, on account of the iniquities by which they are burdened, they will be punished more severely in the future.

I said that iniquities have passed over my head and have become heavy like a heavy burden. This is to be understood as occurring before baptism. And when they are freed from these iniquities in baptism, they again became putrid—that is, they will become putrid—and my scars were corrupted—that is, they will be corrupted—after baptism. The order of the words has been reversed in this way.

“My scarred members,” that is, those healed from the sins they committed before baptism, are named after scarred flesh that has been healed from a wound. They will be corrupted after baptism by evil desires, being led into consent and pleasure, after the likeness of scarred flesh that is corrupted if a sword is thrust into it. And the people, by acting wickedly, becoming accustomed to wickedness, and giving others a bad example, will become putrid after the likeness of a corpse.

This becoming putrid and being corrupted will occur from the face of my folly—that is, from the urgency of the tinder of sin belonging to my members. It is called folly because it is the cause of folly. Or it may be understood as follows: “From the face,” that is, from the presence, of my folly—that is, the folly of my members. It is as though he said: [^c0075-119] Nothing else will be blameworthy in this matter except their folly.

And because they will become corrupted and putrid, I have been made wretched—that is, they will become wretched, although previously they had been made happy by purification in baptism. And I have been bent down—that is, they will be weighed down by their sins—to the end of their bending, that is, as far as they can be bent, so that they cannot raise the eyes of their mind to eternal goods and act well by contemplating them, after the likeness of one who is bent over and cannot look upward.

Alternatively, everything he says—“the iniquities have passed over,” and so forth—may be understood as occurring after baptism, as follows: It is truly necessary to pray for them, so that they may not be rebuked and corrected in this way.

“For my iniquities have passed over,” that is, will pass over, “my head” after baptism; and “like a heavy burden they have become heavy,” that is, they will become heavy. Someone might ask: Will they not be rescued from these things in baptism? The answer is: They will be rescued, but afterward my scarred members will become corrupted and putrid from the face of their folly. Thus they will become wretched and will be bent down to the end. The explanation of all these statements does not change.

Having shown the reasons why one ought to pray for them, he adds other reasons why they ought not to be rebuked and corrected, as follows: I pray that you neither rebuke nor correct them, even if they ought to be corrected or rebuked.

“For throughout the whole day,” that is, continually, “I went about sorrowful,” that is, my members, being saddened by their sins, will enter from great grief into still greater grief; that is, they will continually become more and more sorrowful over their sins. Therefore they ought not to be rebuked and corrected in the future on account of them.

Or it may be understood as follows: “Throughout the whole day,” that is, continually, “they will enter,” that is, they will walk along the way of this life, saddened by their sins.

And they will not merely be saddened; I have also been afflicted and humbled exceedingly—that is, they will afflict themselves greatly in the body by fasts and other hardships, and will humble themselves in soul by placing their own wills after your wills, although previously they had been proud in their disobedience.

And, to speak more forcefully, I roared—that is, they will roar; they will grieve intensely, like a lion which, when saddened, is accustomed to emit a very loud roar. Or “they will roar,” that is, they will be very angry with themselves on account of their sins, also after the likeness of a lion, which roars when it is angry.

They will not roar with an outward voice, but that roar will proceed from the groaning of my heart, that is, the heart of my members. It is as though he said: First they will groan in their heart, and afterward their groans will grow into a roar. This means that they will roar in their heart, in such a way that they first groan.

They will be saddened, afflicted, humbled, and roar for this reason: My loins—that is, the hearts of my members, which are called “loins” because evil thought proceeds from them, just as lust proceeds from the loins—have been filled with illusions, that is, with evil pleasures, which are the illusions of evil spirits.

They are full for this reason: There is no health in my flesh, as was shown above. This means: It occurs because of the weakness of the flesh of my members, which is weak. This has partly been stated earlier in other words, when he said, “Like a heavy burden,” and so forth. But he repeats it here for another purpose.

All this is as though he said: You ought to pity them and neither rebuke nor correct them because they will repent of their sins in every way.

And you ought still to pity them because all my desire—that is, the desire of my members—is that they may at some time be before you, that is, in your presence, blessed with the glory they lost through Adam. This means: They desire nothing apart from you, and in desiring you they groan and sigh for this.

The groaning of my members is not hidden from you; rather, it is known and pleasing to you. Therefore it is most unfitting that it should go without reward.

Or it may be understood as follows: The groaning of my members, which they utter over their sins while sighing for blessedness, is not hidden from you, but is known and pleasing to you.

Someone might ask: Will they groan? The answer is: Truly, my heart—that is, the heart of my members—has been troubled by groaning. And this is because my strength—that is, all the strength of my members—has abandoned me through Adam: humility, chastity, and the other virtues.

This does not mean that all the virtues abandoned them completely, but that some abandoned them entirely, while those that remained were greatly diminished. Or “my strength” means free will, so that they cannot use it for salvation.

Their heart has therefore been troubled because [^c0075-120] the light of my eyes—that is, the understanding of the hearts of my members—or the light, namely Christ, the Sun of Justice, who will illuminate the eyes of their hearts, is not with me to illuminate my members. And I say that he is the light without which I am to be considered nothing.

He adds another reason: namely, his Passion, on account of which he ought to pity them, as follows: You ought to pity them because I suffered for them, since my friends, and so forth.

The preceding verse may also be read with reference to the Passion in this way: I say, “Do not rebuke or correct them.” For, so that you may pity them, my heart—that is, my soul—will be troubled voluntarily in the Passion. Hence it is written: “He began to be afraid and sorrowful” (Mark 14:33). And my strength has abandoned me—that is, to some it will appear that my power has abandoned me. Hence it is said elsewhere: “My strength dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21:16).

And the light of my eyes—and I say that this light is one without which I would be nothing—is not with me; that is, to some it will appear not to be with me. The divinity, namely, which illuminates the eyes of my heart, will appear not to be with me. Hence someone is recorded as having said: “God has abandoned me” (Isa. 49:14). Through this, my strength and my light will appear not to be with me.

“For my disguised friends and my neighbors,” that is, my relatives, “have drawn near,” that is, will draw near, “against me,” in order to seize me. “And they stood,” that is, they will stand steadfastly in accusing me, saying: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19:12).

And because they were near me—that is, they were in familiarity with me—the disciples stood at a distance; that is, they will stand at a distance, abandoning me out of fear of the Jews.

And those who sought—that is, who will seek by every means—to take away my life, namely the Jews, used force; that is, they will inflict violence upon me by scourging and crucifying me (John 19).

And those who sought—that is, who will seek—evil against me in their counsels, namely how they might kill me and hold me by force, spoke—that is, they will speak—vanities, saying: “This man said: ‘I can destroy,’” and so forth (Matt. 26:61).

They will not speak these vanities immediately; rather, to heap up the measure of their wickedness, throughout the whole day they meditated deceit—that is, they will continually meditate vain and deceitful words against me.

But I will not answer them in return. I will not hear, like a deaf man—that is, I will remain silent, as though I did not hear, like a deaf man—and like one who is mute, not opening his mouth.

This means: I will give no sign of indignation by groaning or weeping, like a mute person, who is not only unable to speak but cannot even open his mouth to emit any sound. For many mute people at least cry out and groan.

He repeats what he said, “I was like a deaf man; I did not hear,” in order to add this: I became—that is, I will become—like a man who does not hear and who has no reproofs in his mouth.

This means: I will appear to be silent like a deaf man because I have no means by which to rebuke them, although I could rebuke them in many matters.

All this is as though he said: You ought to pity them because I will suffer such things for them.

Since death without resurrection would not be a sufficient reason, he adds:

And therefore you ought to pity them, so that through my resurrection you may pity them. I have hoped in you, Lord—that is, I have placed my hope of resurrection in you. And you will hear me praying, Lord my God, so that you may raise me up.

And you will hear me not only because I have hoped, but also because I have said—that is, because I will pray in words, saying: O Lord, raise me up, so that my enemies may never—that is, at any time—rejoice excessively over me.

This means: May those who rejoice excessively in my death not rejoice excessively in any circumstance in which such rejoicing is unfitting.

He explains in what circumstance they are not to rejoice excessively when he adds: And when my feet are moved—that is, if my affections were moved from their purpose, namely if I yielded to them—they would rejoice excessively.

I know this because those standing over me in the Passion spoke great things—that is, proud things—saying: “He said, ‘I am the Son of God’” (Matt. 26:64).

Or it may be understood as follows: May they not rejoice excessively over me when rejoicing is unfitting, namely in my being retained in death. And I know that they would rejoice excessively because they spoke great things—that is, proud things—against me; that is, they will speak them when my feet are moved, that is, when my disciples are moved away from me by abandoning me in the Passion.[^c0075-121]

They are called “feet” because they will carry my name among the nations.

Or it may be understood as follows: May they not rejoice excessively over me when rejoicing is unfitting, that is, in my being retained in death. And when my feet are moved, they spoke great things against me—that is, may they not speak proud things against me while standing over me, saying that they have overcome me, when the fact is that my feet, that is, my affections, are moved from their purpose, namely when I yield to them.

This is as though he said: Do not permit my feet to be moved, lest those standing over me speak great things. For they would speak very proudly if they prevailed over me in this way.

The Hebrew translation directs us to this third interpretation, for it reads: “Lest, when my feet have wavered, they magnify themselves over me,” that is, lest they become great in pride.

And therefore you ought still to pity them.

“For I am ready for scourges to be received by me,” that is, my members will be ready to suffer scourges for me, just as I will suffer for them; otherwise my Passion would profit them nothing.

And therefore still pity them, because the pain of my members will be before my eyes—that is, my members will always have pain over their sins before their consideration.

And therefore still pity them, because I will announce my iniquity—that is, my members will humbly announce their iniquity to others through confession, according to the Apostle James: “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. 5:16).

And because this would not be sufficient, I will think on behalf of my sin—that is, they will think about making satisfaction to God for each of their sins by fasting and afflicting the body with other hardships.

I said that they will think of mortifying the flesh on account of their sin. But my enemies—that is, the enemies of my members, namely the wicked who will persecute them in many ways—live; that is, they will live prosperously in this world, flourishing in riches.

And they have been strengthened—that is, they will be strengthened in perseverance against me, that is, they will exalt themselves over my members. And they have multiplied—that is, there will be many who hate me, that is, who will hate my members, and this unjustly.

He explains how they will do so unjustly: namely, they will repay—that is, they will repay my members—evil for good, which is characteristic of the unjust.

He also explains this in part when he adds: They were slandering me—that is, they will slander my members—because I was following goodness, that is, because they will persevere in goodness.

This means: Because my members will give them a good example, they will unjustly slander them.

Therefore, because enemies will multiply against my members, do not abandon me, Lord my God—that is, do not leave my members without help in their tribulations, but make them steadfast, so that they do not yield.

And if you appear to abandon them by permitting them to be afflicted and sometimes to fall into sins, so that afterward they may be more humble, do not depart from me—that is, do not withdraw from them completely, so as not to help them afterward—but rather attend to my help, that is, to the help of my members, Lord my God.

This means: Him whom my members will regard as their Lord and their God.

## Psalm Thirty-Eight

### Title

“Toward the end, for Jeduthun. A song of David.” Jeduthun is interpreted as “leaping across.”

The title is explained as follows: This song—that is, this treatise, in which a song is contained, namely future joy, that is, eternal blessedness—or joy, that is, the immense happiness arising from hope of eternal blessedness—is David’s, that is, it is made by the perfected Church. This song, that is, this treatise, is “for Jeduthun toward the end,” that is, for the purpose that this David himself may leap across all the way to the end: leaping from vices to virtues and from earthly goods to eternal goods, which are the end of the expectation of the righteous.

Or it may be understood as follows: This song—that is, future joy—or joy, that is, the happiness of future joy, belongs to David, that is, to the perfected Church. I say that the song is to be possessed if it concerns future joy, or possessed already if it concerns the joy of future happiness, through this fact: David, who speaks here, is Jeduthun, that is, one leaping across all the way to the end.

In this psalm the perfected Church, rejoicing, shows that it has leapt from vices to virtues, so that it does not intend to sin even with its tongue, which is a great thing. It also says that it prayed when it was insufficient by itself, so that God might make known to it the end—that is, the proper measure of silence and the proper measure of speech—and might make known to it the vision of eternal goods, so that, despising worldly things, it might leap by hope toward [^c0075-122] those goods.

It also shows that it obtained its request and that it awaits those goods alone. It says this not out of arrogance, but for the instruction of others, so that they may strive toward the same thing by its example.

It also rebukes those who devote themselves to vanity, so that it may make them leap from vanity toward the goods that are true. It also prays to provide others with an example of prayer, so that God may rescue it from all iniquities and thus enable it to reach that for which it sighs. Otherwise it would not attain it.

It further prays that God may lighten its tribulations, lest it fail under too great a burden and thus lose what it awaits. It also says that it ought now to be spared, since it has been purified through enduring for a very long time.

### “I said: I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue”

It is as though he said: I have already guarded my affections and actions well, so that I would not sin in them; they will be my ways to life. But I could lose the benefit of these ways unless I ceased to sin with my tongue. Hence the Apostle James says: “If anyone thinks he is religious, not bridling his tongue but deceiving his heart, his religion is vain” (Jas. 1:26).

When a sinner stood against me, not prepared to offer a rational rebuttal but always to resist the truth shamelessly and wickedly, I might fall into quarrelling and chatter, and thus perhaps into blasphemy, as I had often done before.

I said—that is, I determined in my heart: I will guard my ways perfectly, so that I may not sin with my tongue against the sinner by doing anything improper, namely by giving what is holy to dogs and casting pearls before swine (Matt. 7:6).

For I would not guard my ways profitably if I sinned with my tongue by acting talkatively. Hence Solomon says: “In much speaking sin will not be absent” (Prov. 10:19).

And I did not merely say this; I also completed it in action: I placed a guard over my mouth, that is, I guarded my mouth so that I would not sin by speaking; I became silent.

And I did not do this out of indignation, but I was humbled in this matter, that is, I did it out of humility.

Or: “I was humbled,” that is, when I became silent, I was regarded by them as humble and defeated, unable to resist.

By this he implies that we ought to become silent before the sinner not out of indignation but out of humility. Even if we appear defeated and contemptible in this, it is not to be regarded as a concern, but is to be endured with joy.

And I became so silent that I also kept silent from good things.

This means: I kept silent not only from bitter words, but also from good words, fearing that by speaking well and resisting him improperly I might again fall into quarrelling.

Or: I did not merely become silent before the sinner, but I also kept silent from good things—that is, from instructing the good—so that the sinner, remaining bodily present with them, might not resist by hearing and render my words fruitless.

And because I saw that it was evil to be silent from good things, my pain was renewed.

This means: I had previously grieved over excessive talkativeness, but I grieved again over excessive silence. The renewal of my pain occurred because my heart grew hot—that is, it burned with love toward those before whom I was silent.

That heat was hidden within me, since I did not dare to reveal it in words. Then I began to consider what I should do, namely whether I should speak or remain silent. And during that meditation a fire will burn within me; that is, the love I had will begin to grow more and more, after the likeness of a fire that is blazing up.

Since I was insufficient to decide for myself what I ought to do, I spoke by praying to God. “With my tongue,” that is, with such a tongue as I usually use when praying—namely, a rational tongue, praying suitably; with the tongue of the heart, or with the bodily tongue.

I spoke as follows: Make known to me, Lord, by divinely inspiring me, my end—that is, the measure I ought to have in keeping silent and in speaking.

And after you have made that known, also make known to me the number of my days—that is, the multitude of my eternal days, which I shall have in the future. Here “number” means multiplicity.[^c0075-123] For we are accustomed to call multiple things “numerous.”

This does not mean that there will be many days there, but that that single, unique, and eternal day will surpass the multiplicity of our days.

I say “number” which truly exists and will never fail.

Or: Make known to me the number which truly exists. I say “number,” the author of my future days, namely Christ, through whom I shall have eternal days.

He is rightly called “number,” because, since he is the wisdom of the Father, all countable things subsist through him. He is also called “truth,” because all truth comes from him; or because he is unchangeable, after the manner of number, which, although it is considered in mutable things, is itself unchangeable. Thus three and seven, added together, unchangeably make ten.

This is as though he said: Give me a subtle understanding of that number, so that I may consider how great it is, even if not perfectly. By considering this, let me know—that is, understand—what, that is, how great a thing, is lacking to me, since I lack such a great good. Thus, increasingly despising worldly things, let me direct myself toward and sigh for that number.

After making his prayer, and certain that it had been granted, he declares that he has already obtained it, so that if we pray according to his example, he may give us hope of obtaining our request.

I spoke in this way while praying. And behold—that is, in the presence of my mind—you have made my days measurable; that is, by divinely inspiring me, you have made me understand that the days I have here are not eternal but measurable and passing.

By this he also implies that he showed him that future days are eternal and immeasurable. For how would he see that these days are measurable except by comparison with those that are immeasurable?

And you have also placed this in my consideration: that my substance, that is, my essence, which I now possess, is like nothing when compared with you—that is, in relation to that substance which will be future before you, when I shall be in your presence in the future.

Or: It is like nothing when compared with you—that is, in relation to your likeness, which I sigh to attain.

Or: It is like nothing before you—that is, it is considered as such in my mind, which is before you and which you alone see.

He rightly says not “nothing” but “like nothing.” For nothing does not exist; but “like nothing” means defective, to such a degree that it seems almost to be reduced to nothing by dying, so that it may be evident that it was made by God from nothing. For God made all things from nothing.

I say that our days are measurable and that our substance is like nothing. Nevertheless, although this is so, every living human being who is not God—that is, who by living badly conforms himself to the human being Adam, who behaved humanly and weakly, rather than sighing and striving to be conformed to God by behaving well—is universal vanity, that is, subject to every vanity.

His saying “universal vanity” is intended, by emphasis, as a very strong rebuke of them. Nevertheless, although he is vanity, he is without excuse. For he has passed into vanity from the certainty of the true good to which he ought to cling.

I say that he dwells in the image of God, that is, since he was made according to the image of God—rational, namely, so that he might know what ought to be sought and what ought not to be sought. Hence it is read in Genesis: “God made man according to his image” (Gen. 1:26).

Or it may be understood as follows: Nevertheless, although he is subject to vanity—that is, to the desire for earthly things, which are vain—he passes from life to death in an image, or he has passed into vanity while dwelling in an image, that is, in the likeness of the image of someone’s face, which, when seen in a mirror, quickly passes away, according to the blessed Apostle James: “He looked at himself and went away, and immediately forgot what he had been like” (Jas. 1:24).

By this he strongly calls them back from vanity, as though he said: He ought not to cling so closely to worldly things, which are vain, since he is passing away like an image.

I say that he is vanity, that is, subject to vanity; and he is not troubled in vain only for himself, but is also troubled—that is, he is anxiously occupied in desiring vanities—for others.

He explains how, when he adds: For he stores up treasure, and although he thinks he is storing treasure for a son or [^c0075-124] a friend, he does not know for whom—that is, for whose use he will gather it.

It may happen that an enemy or a servant, whom he does not expect, will become his heir.

And now—that is, since man has passed away in an image, and my days are measurable, and my substance is like nothing—what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord?

It should be noted that “now” is not a sign of time here but of cause. It is as though he said: I said that man has passed away in an image, that my days are measurable, and that my substance is like nothing. And now, that is, therefore, the Lord alone is my expectation; setting aside worldly things, I await him alone.

It should also be noted that, out of excessive joy and also for our exhortation, he states this in the form of a question.

And because I await you, my substance—which, in relation to this present state, is regarded as like nothing—has already been considered by me as being with you, that is, in conformity with you; it already seems to me to possess true being.

This means: When I consider that it will exist truly in the future, when it is with you—that is, in your presence and conformity—I already see by hope that it possesses that true being.

And so that my substance may possess true being with you, rescue me from all venial iniquities by forgiving me.

It is as though he said: I have guarded my ways from criminal sins well, as I showed at the beginning of the psalm, but you forgive venial sins. Thus I will be freed from all iniquities. Otherwise I would not attain that being, since nothing defiled will be in your kingdom (Rev. 21:27).

And you ought to rescue me, for you have made me a reproach to the foolish.

This means: Since, having despised worldly things, I look toward you alone, or, to express it more clearly, I am a mockery and reproach to the foolish people—and this on your account.

Hence Prosper says: “Those who wish to live piously must necessarily suffer reproaches from the wicked and those unlike them.”

And although I was a reproach to them, I gave no bitter reply but became silent. Thus I did not open my mouth in any way to show, by groaning or by any other means, a sign of sorrow or indignation.

He also prays that God may lighten his scourges, lest, if they should be excessively heavy, he fail under their weight and thus not attain what he awaits.

He says this as follows: I pray not only that you rescue me from iniquities, but I also pray: Remove your scourges from me. Do not remove them entirely, but partly. This means: Lighten the tribulations which you have inflicted upon me to purify me.

And you ought to remove them because you have already made me perfect and purified through those scourges.

He explains this when he adds: Truly, you have made me. For I have already wasted away from my impurities through rebukes—that is, through the tribulations with which you rebuked and corrected me.

I say “rebukes” inflicted by the strength of your hand. This is an intransitive expression, meaning: inflicted by your strong hand, that is, by your strong power or vengeance.

And these rebukes were not unjust, for on account of the iniquity committed you corrected this man, namely me, who had lived as a human being rather than as God.

Since he had said, “I have wasted away,” he explains in what respect he wasted away, as follows: I say that you corrected me, and by correcting me caused my soul to waste away—that is, to fail—from the impurities of its pleasures, through those very rebukes, like a spider; that is, after the manner of a spider, which gradually wastes away through its own work.

Nevertheless, although I am so perfect, and although others could waste away after my example and thus become perfect, every human being—that is, every person still living as a human being—is troubled in vain, that is, anxiously occupied in desiring earthly things, which are vain.

Having shown his wasting away, he returns to prayer as follows:

Therefore, because you have made me waste away in this way, hear, Lord, my prayer uttered aloud, and my supplication, proceeding from the intensity of my heart; receive my tears with the ears of your mercy.

Or: Do not be silent—that is, bring to completion what I request—because I, already existing by hope with you, that is, in your presence and conformity, am a sojourner and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were, namely my predecessors, whose son in holiness [^c0075-125] I am.

It is as though he said: I am not a son of this world, but I belong to another region, toward which I am tending, namely the eternal Jerusalem.

“Pilgrim” and “sojourner” mean the same thing, but the words are repeated out of great affection.

He says that the Fathers were sojourners and pilgrims in order that, at least by their authority, he might draw us away from this kind of pilgrimage.

I pray: Hear me, and hear me in this respect: Forgive me my sins before I depart from this life, so that, once they have been forgiven, I may be refreshed in the future, that is, may be in the refreshment of rest, although here I am continually afflicted by tribulations for your sake.

And if you do not forgive me before I depart, I will no longer be in the true being that I await.

## Psalm Thirty-Nine
## Title of the Thirty-Ninth Psalm

A psalm to be attributed to David, “for the end”—that is, to Christ existing as David, namely, as strong of hand, acting manfully against the devil and conquering him unto the end, that is, unto perfection, and fully accomplishing the obedience imposed upon him by the Father.

In this psalm he intends to show the Head, for the instruction and conformity of the members, with what constancy he awaited God and how intensely he would receive what he had awaited, so that his members too, following his example, might await it—not demanding their denarius before evening, but receiving intensely at the end what they will rightly await. He also shows that he not only waited but prayed for this, and that he was heard in this, adding the reason by which he was worthy to be heard. He further demonstrates that he would have many imitators in waiting, thereby also indicating to us that, if we wait, we shall have many imitators in this. Moreover, he indicates in what order others will become his imitators: namely, through his death and the preaching of his own. Afterwards he prays concerning the resurrection, showing why his resurrection is necessary. He also prays for his enemies and for his members.

“I waited expectantly for the Lord.” By saying “waiting,” he indicates perseverance in waiting, as though he were saying: “I did not grow weary or murmur, but awaited the reward.” “Waiting,” that is, not failing but persevering in expectation. And because I waited, and will still wait, “he inclined toward me,” that is, he will give me intensely what I awaited, by resurrecting and glorifying me. Since this was to occur with the utmost certainty, he expressed it as though it had already happened.

Yet I not only waited; I also prayed for what I awaited. Although this occurs outside the book, it is understood from what follows. And because I prayed, he heard my prayers. This too must be understood as future, as though he were saying: “I shall pray, and he will hear me.” And so that I might be worthy of being heard, he first brought me out of the pit of misery—that is, from the depth of vices into which other miserable people descend. He did not say that he brought me out because there had been iniquities in him, but because, with regard to the weakness of humanity, it could have happened unless the grace of divinity had prevented it. It is as though he were saying: “He made me free from sin.”

The depth of sins is rightly called a “pit,” because it makes people unstable, shifting, and insubstantial, just as a pit is unstable, fluid, and without firmness. “And he brought me out of the mud of filth.” This is the same as “out of the pit of filth,” but it signifies something else as well: the excessive foulness and stench of a bad example, just as mud from dregs is dirtier and more putrid than other mud. For those who are in the pit of misery are not only exceedingly foul themselves but also corrupt others through the stench of their bad example.

And he not only brought me out but also “set”—that is, established—my feet, that is, my affections, upon the rock, that is, upon the firmness of the virtues. “And he directed my steps,” that is, those same affections, perseveringly from one good work to another. “And he put into my mouth”—the mouth of the heart, namely—“a new song,” that is, a hymn or praise suitable to our God. In Hebrew it has *hymn*.

He calls it a “new song” because it means preferring God’s will to one’s own will—something from which the old Adam and his members were deprived, since they preferred to obey their own wills. But the new man, Christ, and those conformed to him possessed this.

It should be noted that the prophets and other faithful people who preceded Christ’s coming were members of Christ already in faith and hope, although he had not yet been born of the Virgin. This was prefigured by someone in the Old Testament whose hand preceded his head at birth.

I say: “I waited, and he inclined toward me. I prayed, and he heard me.” “And many will see these things,” that is, understand them, as it should be understood. And by seeing, following my example, they will fear the Lord with chaste fear—that is, they will love him and, in fear, hope in the Lord for their reward.

And because they will fear and hope, “the man will be blessed” in the future. The name of this man is “the Lord is his hope,” that is, he places the hope of salvation in the name of the Lord, which he loves and magnifies. He uses “man” in the singular, although he had used “they will fear” and “they will hope” in the plural, in order to show that they are one in hope and fear.

## [Col. 0804A]

But because this would not be sufficient, he adds: “And that blessed man did not look”—that is, he will not look back—“toward vanities and false insanities,” turning aside.

“For no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62).

By “vanities” he means earthly desires, which are vain. By “false insanities” he means the very goods that make people insane, since they turn them away from the law of God. They are called false because they deceive those who desire them by promising blessedness, or “false insanities” may mean the worship of idols. For what is more deceptive than to call a creature the Creator, or what greater insanity is there than to offer to a creature the worship owed to God?

Alternatively, “false insanities” means vices, because, by drawing people away from God, they make them insane; and although they appear desirable, they deceive. I say that he will not look toward vanities, that is, toward earthly things. And although I have called them vain, I do not mean vain in their nature, but with regard to human opinion, since people say that they are the highest goods when they are not.

Nevertheless, lest I seem to disparage those things themselves, I say that you, Lord my God, “have done many wondrous things”—namely, those earthly things, which exist as wondrous things—and I say that they are yours. This means: They are your creatures, not the Creator.

Or it may be understood thus: He will not look toward “insanities,” that is, toward idolatry. Nor should one look there, but toward you, Lord, so that you may be worshiped. For you, Lord, have done many wondrous things that are yours. This means: You have made many wondrous creatures, through which you, although invisible, are recognized as Lord and Creator. Therefore one should look toward your worship.

Hence the Apostle says: “His invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly perceived and understood through the things that have been made” (Romans 1:20).

And you have done these wondrous things according to your “thoughts,” that is, according to your dispositions, not those of another. Hence the same Apostle says: “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Romans 11:34). No one, certainly. Therefore, because you have done many wondrous things according to your own thoughts, it is evident that no one is in every respect like you—namely, in being the Creator of things—and therefore that you alone should be worshiped in this way.

Someone might ask: “You say that many will see these things, and so forth. Through what, then, will they see?” He shows this when he adds: “Through this they will see: because I announced and spoke, they were multiplied beyond number.” This means: My people will announce and speak to them, and through this they will be multiplied beyond a definite number, that is, they will be more numerous than can be counted.

“Announcing” and “speaking” are different. They will announce through the testimony of the prophets, who spoke of future things. For announcing properly concerns future things, while they will speak by their own authority and reasoning. Speaking, however, concerns past and present things.

He explains what they will announce and speak when he adds that they will announce this: that you did not desire a legal sacrifice or a legal offering. For many things were offered under the Law that were not called sacrifices, such as loaves and other things of this kind.

And I say that you did not desire “sacrifice and offering,” but “you perfected ears for me,” that is, you gave me perfect understanding. This means: They will announce that you gave me perfect understanding. Ears are used for understanding because by hearing with the ears we understand.

And this also: You did not request “burnt offering for sin,” which was considered a great offering. When he says “you did not request,” it must be understood by *litotes* as “you rejected.” For *litotes* occurs when less is said but more is understood.

*Holo* means “whole,” while *causis* signifies “burning.” Hence a sacrifice was called a “burnt offering” because, when it was made for some sin, the whole of it was burned. In other sacrifices, not everything but only a part was burned.

I say that they will announce this because you perfected ears for me, and also that which I then said—not with my voice but with my heart. This means: “Since you perfected them, I established this with myself: ‘Behold, I come,’” that is, I approach ready with the steps of my will, “to do your will, O God”—that particular will which, by antonomasia, is called your will—and also “to do your law,” that is, to fulfill the law given by you, which is still imperfect, as he himself testifies in the Gospel: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17).

This clause—“to do your will and your law”—is supplied from outside the book so that the continuity may proceed more clearly.

It is fitting that I do your will and your law. For it is written—that is, it has long been established and confirmed, in the manner of Scripture—“that I should do your will and your law,” which exists “in the midst of my heart.” This means: I do not have it merely around my heart, as though I cared little about it; rather, I hold it memorably in the middle of my heart.

I say that it is written, and he shows where it is written: namely, at the beginning of Book I of the Psalter, where it says: “His will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night” (Psalm 1:2).

Or, “in the beginning of the book,” in the disposition of the Word personally united to me—the Word being my head according to my humanity; I am the book.

Hence Paul says: “The head of a woman is man, the head of man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3).

Christ is called a book because, for the correction of our conduct, we ought to study his example of life, just as anyone studies a book for the sake of instruction. Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “In your book all shall be written” (Psalm 138:16).

But since he had said, “It is written in the beginning of the book,” lest he seem to fulfill it from necessity rather than from will, he inserts: “My God, this I desired”—I desired to do it; I am not compelled by necessity. Otherwise my merit would not be great.

## [Col. 0806A]

But I shall not merely announce that you did not desire sacrifice, and so forth. I have also announced—that is, I shall announce through my members in the great Church, established from both peoples, not a small church as the Synagogue was signified to be—that all justice is yours, that is, from you and not from the works of the Law, as some wrongly assert.

Or “your justice” means the justice to be given by you to the faithful, which they lost through Adam.

I say: “They will announce.” This is present to me, as a result of my excessive certainty: “I shall not restrain my lips,” that is, my members will not restrain their lips from announcing out of fear of punishment.

And they will not restrain them because you knew—that is, you willed—this. This means: They will know that you will this. Hence in the Gospel: “When you hear of wars and seditions, do not be terrified” (Luke 21:9).

And I did not hide your justice in my heart, that is, the justice to be given by you to the faithful. My members will not hide it; they will not carelessly conceal it in their hearts, unwilling to disclose it to others.

But I said—that is, they will say to others—“your truth and your salvation.” They will preach me, your Son, who am called Truth because all truth proceeds from me, and who am your Savior, through whom you will save the world.

It should be noted that, when he had said “I announced,” he did not add needlessly, “I shall not restrain my lips” and “I did not hide mercy,” although the meaning is the same. When he says “I shall not restrain,” he indicates that they will not be silent through fear of death. When he says “they will not hide it in their heart,” he indicates that they will not cease through negligence.

They would be held accountable if they ceased through negligence, in accordance with the prophet’s words: “If you do not announce his wickedness to the wicked man, I shall require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 3:18).

And “I did not hide”—that is, my members will not hide—“your mercy and your truth,” that is, your Son, emphatically called “mercy,” because through me God will show mercy to the human race, and “truth,” because all truth proceeds from me.

It should also be noted that this repetition is not superfluous. It is repeated in order to add: “They will not hide it,” I do not mean from a few, but not even from a large assembly. Hence the earlier psalm says: “I shall not fear the thousands of the people surrounding me” (Psalm 3:7)—that is, surrounding my members.

This may also be understood differently, as follows: I said that my members will not hide your truth and your salvation, namely, me. And they will not hide your mercy from the large assembly, that is, the remission of sins which, in your mercy, you will bestow upon people through me. Nor will they hide your truth, that is, your justice, by which you will reward the just in the future.

When he says “they will not hide it from the assembly,” it must be understood by *litotes*: they will proclaim your mercy and truth to a large assembly.

The overall meaning of this passage, beginning where it says “I announced and spoke” and continuing up to “But you, Lord,” is this:

Through this many will see, fear, and hope in the Lord: my members will announce and speak to them that the sacrifices and legal offerings which preceded as shadows of the New Testament have been abolished through my death, and that the New Testament itself has been completed through that same death, to which one must now cling.

They will also announce me as your Truth and Salvation. They will likewise announce your mercy, bestowed upon people through me, and your truth, by which you will reward the just in the future.

This means: Through this preaching of my members, which I have described, they will see, fear, and hope.

## [Col. 0807A]

“But you, Lord”: so that my members may announce and they may see, do not take your mercies far from me—that is, the benefits of your mercy. For if you took them far away, my members would not announce, nor would many see, fear, and hope.

This means: Do not take away from me the benefits that you mercifully granted me—namely, that you made me free from sin and girded me—by rendering them void, that is, by not resurrecting me. Do not permit such great benefits to be useless. For if I were held in death, they would be useless.

It is as though he were saying: “Resurrect me, so that afterward my members may announce to many what I have shown above, and so that those to whom they announce may see, fear, and hope.”

Someone might ask: “Has he made mercies with you?” He responds as follows: “For your mercy and your truth have always received me,” that is, guarded me. This means: “You have always been my receiver,” that is, my patron and defender, so that I might not fail in anything and might abound in every good.

You did this on account of mercy, so that through me you might mercifully save the world; and on account of truth, so that you might be true to what you had promised.

Or “on account of truth” means “on account of justice.” For it was just that you should always receive me as a just man.

He says “receive” by comparison with a patron who receives someone in order to act as his patron.

He then adds reasons so that he may more easily obtain his request, explaining why he should not take the mercies far away:

I say, “Do not take them far away,” and it is necessary that you not do so, because evils of various tribulations have surrounded me—that is, surrounded my members—on account of Adam’s sin. Their number is undefined, that is, they cannot be counted.

They would never be freed from these evils if you took your mercies far away. Therefore, do not take them far away even now, because “my iniquities have overtaken me,” that is, their iniquities have prevailed over my members, conquered them, and subjected them as captives.

This is by comparison with someone who pursues another so persistently that he both conquers and overtakes him. Hence the Apostle says: “I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin which is in my members” (Romans 7:23).

They overtook my members to such an extent that I could not see—that is, they were unable to see well, to recognize by inward vision what ought and ought not to be done. These iniquities are not few; rather, they have been multiplied beyond the hairs of my head—that is, the hairs of my members. This means: By their multitude they exceeded the number of my hairs.

But because he had said that their iniquities had overtaken his members, lest anyone, wishing to excuse them, should say that they had been created so weak by God, he adds:

## [Col. 0808A]

And this—that their iniquities overtook them—happens because “my heart has abandoned me,” that is, the reason of the heart of my members, which was created perfect by God, has for the most part abandoned my members; that is, it has become imperfect.

It should be noted that just as reason was created perfect in Adam and was weakened through his sin, so too a perfectly rational soul is created in each person, but is afterward weakened through the oppression of the corrupt flesh to which it is joined.

I said that evils surrounded my members and that iniquities overtook them. Now, so that they may be rescued both from the evils and from the iniquities:

“May it please you, Lord, to rescue me,” by resurrecting me from death. Otherwise they would not be rescued. And so that I may be worthy to be rescued:

“Look mercifully upon me to help me,” so that I may do good works and not fail.

He says “look” by comparison with someone who frequently looks upon the person whom he wishes to help. This means: “Help me to do good.”

When he says “may it please,” he signifies the Trinity. When he says “you,” he signifies the unity of essence.

And after you have rescued me, “let those who seek my soul be put to shame with a good shame and be afraid”—those who seek it in order to take it away, not in order to imitate it.

And not only those who seek it, but also, together with those who seek it, those who wish me evil: “Let them be turned back from their wickedness, walking behind me,” that is, let them become my followers, “and let them be afraid,” that is, fear.

Or it may be understood thus: Together with the joy they had from my death, let them be put to shame at the resurrection, and thus let them be turned back. Here “turned back” is placed in an inverted order.

Many indeed were evil in intention who did not seek me. Those also who falsely said to me, “Good, good,” pretending to be my friends, should immediately—that is, without delay after my resurrection—“bear their shame,” that is, believe it for their own advantage.

He rightly says “bear,” by comparison with someone who carries a heavy burden and is greatly weighed down by it. This means: “Let them be oppressed by their shame, and thus let them be turned back.”

It is as though he were saying: “I pray not only for those who wish and seek evil, who are not my false friends, but also for the false friends, for whom it would seem less likely that I should pray.”

It should be noted that he does not pray for everyone, but only for those who are to be saved. For he would pray uselessly for those who are to be lost.

I say that the enemies should be put to shame and be afraid. Conversely, “let all who seek you rejoice and be glad” through their good life, namely, my disciples.

This is an inversion: Let them be glad, and not merely glad, but let them rejoice, that is, be exceedingly glad, founded upon you so that they may not be moved.

And let those who seek you, who love your salvation—that is, who love me, through whom you will save the world, and who do not hate me like the wicked Jews—say, inwardly or outwardly: “Let the Lord always be magnified,” that is, let him be glorified more and more in the conversion of the wicked, since he has already been glorified in the resurrection.

I say that I am salvation. “But I”—that is, I am also a beggar and poor, O hearers, according to my humanity. This means: “I am not only Savior, but, in order to save you in this way, I am also poor,” that is, insufficient in myself to be saved; and “a beggar,” that is, seeking the help of another—namely, the Father.
