Otherwise you would not be saved.

And because I humbly consider myself a beggar and poor, “the Lord is concerned for me,” that is, he has provided for me in order to reward me. This is by comparison with a patron who is concerned for the person whom he intends to reward.

When he calls himself, although he is omnipotent, a beggar and poor, he instructs us by the example of his humility not to trust in ourselves, but to regard ourselves as beggars and poor, and thus finally to be rewarded, just as he himself was rewarded.

He also prays concerning the reward of resurrection, so that he may instruct us to pray likewise:

“O my God, since you are concerned for me, you who are my helper”—that is, my co-worker, so that I may rise again—“and my protector,” so that I may not fail in tribulations, “do not delay my resurrection until the general resurrection, but resurrect me after three days.”

By saying “helper,” he indicates that he works for resurrection through his merits, showing that divine grace will also cooperate in it, so that we too may be instructed to work for our salvation by doing good.

## IN PSALM XL

### Title of the Fortieth Psalm

A psalm of David, that is, of Christ “looking toward the end,” that is, toward future blessedness, which will be the end of the expectation of the just; or toward himself as the end of prophecy and the Law, who is also the end of all holiness.

It is likewise the end toward which all good people strive to attain.

But because he had called himself a beggar and poor, lest he be understood simply as a beggar and poor man according to his humanity alone, he instructs his members to understand something else in him above the beggar and poor man—namely, God—which those who handed him over to death did not understand.

He also shows that they will gain a twofold benefit from this: one here and one in the future. He likewise prays for them, saying that through his passion he merits these things, and he partly reveals that passion. Moreover, he prays concerning the resurrection, so that he may repay his enemies what they deserve and thereby deter his own from conformity with them. And he says that he is to be heard because he is innocent, thereby indicating that we too will be heard if we remain innocent.

“Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor.” It is as though he were saying: “In the preceding psalm I called myself a beggar and poor.” There are some, however, who, considering me simply as a man, understand me only as a beggar and poor man—namely, the Jews. But blessed will be the one who understands something else in me, something above the needy and poor man: namely, divinity, which rules over the humanity that is beggarly and poor.

He shows part of this blessedness when he adds: “On the evil day the Lord will deliver him,” that is, from everlasting death on the day of judgment. That day is called evil because condemnation will be assigned to the wicked on it. Hence it is written: “That day is a day of wrath, of calamity and misery” (Zephaniah 1:15).

He also shows another part of blessedness as follows: In the future he will deliver him; here he will preserve and vivify him, and will make him blessed upon the earth; and he will not hand him over to “his soul,” that is, into the hands of his enemies. This is outside the book but is perceived from the prayer that follows.

I say: “He will deliver and preserve,” and so let it be: “May the Lord preserve him and vivify him.” This is an inverted order.

May the Lord vivify him inwardly in his soul, restoring the virtues that he lost through Adam. “And may he make him blessed upon the earth.” This means: May he cause him to rule over and cultivate the earth well—namely, his sensuality—so that, properly cultivated, it may produce good fruit, that is, good works, rather than thistles and thorns, that is, sins, as before.

This was prefigured through Adam, to whom the Lord said: “Your land shall produce thistles and thorns for you” (Genesis 3:13).

And after the earth has been properly cultivated, may he make him blessed even in this world: “upon the earth,” that is, in the good fruits of his earth.

And afterward may he preserve him perseveringly in the vivification of his soul and in the blessedness of his earth. And in this way, namely, may he preserve him.

“May he not hand him over to his soul,” that is, to the will of his enemies. This means: Even if he hands him over into their hands so that they may afflict him, may he not hand him over into their desire, so that they may somehow draw him away from the vivification of his soul and the blessedness of his earth.

It is as though he were saying: “May he preserve him in such a way that his enemies cannot turn him back.” And may the Lord also help him in the future, freeing him from mortality and vulnerability.

I speak of the one who exists “upon his bed of pain,” that is, who rules his body, which is the bed of the soul and the bed of pain, in which such pains reign.

The “bed of pain” is rightly used by comparison. Just as a bed of pain is one on which a sick person lies and in which he cannot rest, so the body in which the soul has become sick is one in which the soul remains but cannot rest, being tormented in many ways. It is therefore called its bed of pain.

He explains how the body became a bed of pain.

Someone might say: “How did the body become a bed of pain?” He replies:

“O Lord, you have transformed his entire bed,” that is, you have altered his whole bed, changing that bed in all its parts and making it a bed of pain, although it had been a bed of rest in which the soul would rest, if Adam had not sinned.

This is by comparison with a bed which, when properly arranged so that someone can rest well upon it, is overturned and becomes disordered, so that rest can no longer be found upon it.

I speak of a bed “placed in his infirmity.” This means: You did not overturn it unjustly, but because of his evil merit, since he first placed himself in infirmity by transgressing your commandment in Adam.

He makes this apostrophe out of excessive affection, as though saying: “You, Lord, who justly overturned the bed and are powerful enough to restore it, mercifully restore it, making a bed of rest out of the bed of pain.”

I prayed: “May the Lord preserve him,” and so it will be, for my prayer merited this.

For I, who was suitable for this and had come in order to pray for them, said, inwardly or outwardly: “Lord, have mercy on me,” that is, on my members. Have mercy in this way: “Heal my soul,” that is, the soul of my members. It must be healed because it has sinned—or has sinned—against you, that is, it must be healed by you alone through remission. I say: Heal it, which you ought to do.

## [Col. 0811A]

For in order that you may heal, I shall endure all this. My enemies said—that is, will say—evil things to me, namely: “When will he die?” and the rest that follows up to “But you, Lord.”

This may also be continued as follows: I say that the one who understands above the needy and poor will be blessed, and rightly so, because he will not refuse to understand, although many do not understand, whose bad example could turn him back.

For my enemies, the Jews, said—that is, will say—evil things to me, that is, my misfortune, not according to the truth of the matter but according to their estimation. They said this evil thing:

“When will this man die, and when will the name of him perish?”—that is, the reputation of his name, which is so great.

It is as though he were saying: “Let us kill him, and by keeping him in death let us destroy the fame of his name.”

Nor will they say only these evil things. Even if—that is, although—one of them entered, that is, should enter, into my intimacy, presence, and dwelling, he will not enter with a good intention, but only in order to see—that is, in order to observe.

“Even if” may also be understood as two clauses, as follows: They will say these evil things to me: “And if one of those who speak them entered”—that is, should enter—into my intimacy and dwelling, he will enter for this purpose: to see, that is, to investigate whether there is anything in me worthy of blame.

And when he sees nothing, nevertheless he spoke—that is, will speak—vain things, that is, falsehoods, about me, as some are recorded to have said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons” (Luke 11:15).

And not only will he speak vain things, but “his heart gathered iniquity,” that is, he will gather wicked thoughts about me, and this for himself, that is, to his own condemnation.

And afterward he went out—that is, will go out—from my intimacy and dwelling, and he spoke—that is, will speak—evil things about me, with speech tending toward the same thing, that is, persevering in it.

This means: He will speak evil things about me perseveringly.

Or: He will speak about me, tending toward the same vanity, meaning that he will speak while he is with me. This means: Whether he remains with me or departs from me, he will not cease speaking vain things.

And not only will this man speak vain things about me, but all my enemies, the Jews who oppose me, “whispered”—that is, will speak evil about me in whispers—in accordance with the saying: “The Pharisees murmured,” and so forth (Luke 15:2); and elsewhere: “There was much murmuring about him among the people” (John 7:12).

And they not only whispered but also thought—that is, will think—evil things against me. And this “for me,” that is, for my exaltation, in accordance with the saying: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and rise again, and thus enter into his glory” (Luke 24:7).

And they will not only think, but “they established an iniquitous word,” that is, will establish one against me, saying: “He is guilty of death” (Matthew 26:66).

I say that they will think and speak in this way. And when they have done this, will one who sleeps—that is, sleeps in death—not add to this, so that he may rise again?

He puts this interrogatively as a rebuke to them, as though saying: “Do they think that I shall not rise again?” But the one who has the will to sleep—namely, I—will also add to that will the will to rise again.

Hence he says in the Gospel: “I lay down my life, and I take it up again” (John 10:17).

I said that my enemies will think and speak against me in this way, and this is quite believable because something greater and more wondrous will happen to me.

For “the man of my peace”—that is, Judas, a man simply and not specially so called, “one who shares my peace,” that is, one toward whom I have peace by bearing with him patiently, although he is exceedingly hostile to me—or “the pretender to my peace,” that is, one who will pretend to have peace with me in order to betray me with a kiss—

He “who ate my bread,” that is, who is my companion, or who ate my special bread, namely, the teaching by which the souls of the faithful are nourished, and the sacrament of my body and blood, being “above me,” that is, superior in his own estimation, “magnified his treachery against me,” that is, will prepare a great deception for me, namely, to betray me with a kiss.

Yet this is not deception with regard to me, but with regard to his own estimation.

He does not say this to excuse his enemies. Rather, it is as though he were saying: “For this reason the one who understands should be blessed: because the evil example of the one who betrays me will not remove them from their good understanding.”

I say that my enemies will think and speak against me in this way, and that the man of my peace will magnify his treachery against me.

“But you, Lord, have mercy on me.” And have mercy in this way: Resurrect me, and, once resurrected, I shall repay them what they have deserved—namely, a double condemnation in body and soul.

I prayed: “Have mercy,” and you will truly do so. And in this, because you desired—that is, loved—me by making me free from sin, I have known that my enemy, the Jewish people, will not rejoice over me, that is, over me not being resurrected.

This means: Your love toward me is from this a pledge and guarantee: the enemy will not rejoice.

“But you received me because of my innocence,” that is, you will receive me because I am innocent, as a physician brings someone from mortality to immortality.

And afterward, you established me—or will establish me—while I exist in your sight, that is, in your good pleasure. Or “in your sight” is said by comparison with a faithful servant who, always standing in the sight of his lord, is ready to obey him even at a nod. This means: You will establish me, always ready to obey you, forever—that is, in eternal glory—so that I may no longer die, in accordance with the saying: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more” (Romans 6:9), and so forth.

He then makes an apostrophe to the hearers, exhorting them to bless God on this account, as follows:

Therefore, because he will receive me and you will be confirmed, “Blessed”—that is, praised—“be the Lord God of Israel,” that is, by those who see God, “from age to age,” beginning in this age and proceeding into the age to come.

“Let it be, let it be.” He repeats this either because of the intensity of the exhortation or because of the Church’s twofold wall, as though saying: “Let this happen in the Church from the Jews, and let it happen in the Church from the Gentiles.”

## IN PSALM XLI

### Title of Psalm XLI

“For the end; an understanding for the sons of Korah.” Here “Korah” is not included as part of the historical figure but solely for the interpretation of the name.

For *Korah* is interpreted as “Calvary.” Since our Lord suffered at the place of Calvary, “Korah” is placed here on account of his passion.

It should be noted that he more suitably used *Korah*—which means “Calvary”—because of the similarity, than if he had used *Golgotha*, which is also the proper name of the place where Christ suffered. For just as Korah, a contemporary of David, had physical sons, so Christ, whose passion is understood through the name Korah, has spiritual sons, who, insofar as they are able, are imitators of his passion and goodness.

The title placed above is therefore explained as follows:

“For the sons of Korah,” that is, for the imitators of Christ’s passion, “who press toward the end,” that is, toward the highest good.

Because they are called “sons of Korah,” understanding must be attributed to them; that is, they must be said to understand well, since through imitation of Christ’s passion they understand that they will reach the end toward which they strive.

In this psalm the voice of the Church of the martyrs is introduced, oppressed by tribulations and understanding that, through those tribulations, it will reach the end. In this psalm it greatly sighs for that end, and, in view of that end, it also consoles itself amid its tribulations. Hence it also says that it will pray.

As the stag longs to reach the springs of water after consuming the serpent, so my soul longs to reach you, O God, after I have already consumed and destroyed the vices within me. Behold, here she sighs while striving toward the highest good. He rightly says not simply “waters,” but “springs of water,” which is to say: [Col. 0813C] unfailing waters, which always flow and are never dried up. For when the stag has devoured the serpent, it hastens, burning with intense heat, to a living spring whose water never fails; by its cooling and drinking it becomes young again. So too every believer, after absorbing within himself the poison of vices, strives toward Christ, the unfailing fountain of life, by the course of good works and continual endurance of tribulations. When he reaches him, having laid aside the old age of the flesh, he will be renewed with ineffable youth through the cooling and inebriation of that very fountain. Hence in the Apocalypse: “Behold, I make all things new” (Apoc. XXI, 5).

He shows why he desires to reach God by addressing his hearers, so that he may instruct them to desire the same, when he adds: [Col. 0813D] “I say, O hearers, that my soul desires—and not with a small desire—but my soul thirsted, and still thirsts,” that is, it desired with as great a longing as one who is thirsty, “to reach the strong God [fountain],” that is, the impassible one, whom no enemy can overcome, “the living” one unfailingly, according to the saying: “I live forever” (Isa. XLIX, 18). It is as though she said: “I thirsted for this purpose: that through him, the living and strong one, I might become living and strong.”

“And I, who thirsted and still thirst in this way, when shall I come”—having laid down the burden of the flesh—“before the face,” that is, the presence, “of God,” while, as long as I am in this pilgrimage, I seem to be far away? And after I have come, I shall appear to my enemies alive and strong, although here, while existing in the flesh, I am weak and continually subject to the danger of death, and do not even seem to be anything at all [Col. 0814A]. This he expresses interrogatively, out of his excessive desire.

Someone might ask: “Why do you sigh so intensely to come?” He therefore answers as follows: “For this reason I sigh, saying, ‘When shall I come and appear?’—because I am placed in tribulations from which I would wish to be delivered. For my tears,” that is, my miseries, which are the causes of tears, “were and are my bread,” that is, they were continual, like bread, which is a constant and daily food.”

He explains in what sense he uses “bread,” when he adds, “by day and by night,” that is, they were continual: while, that is, when the enemies say to me every day, that is, continually, both in words and through the very tribulations they inflict: “Where is your God, who does not deliver you from our hands? Nowhere.” Or in this sense: “Where is your God, whom you cannot point out with your finger, as we point out the sun and moon and the other gods whom we worship? Nowhere.”

“I say that my tears were my bread. And because they say, ‘Where is your God?’ I nevertheless remembered these things,” that is, I often considered them—“these tears, and this statement, ‘Where is your God?’ And therefore I poured out my soul”—not outside myself, but within myself I diffused it, that is, I expanded my soul in joy. Hence Augustine: “Joy is the expansion of the soul; sorrow, the contraction of the soul; desire, the advance of the soul; fear, the flight of the soul.”

“And therefore I poured out my soul, because through these things which I patiently endure I shall pass from this valley of tears to the house of God,” namely, the heavenly Jerusalem, which is not transitory like a tabernacle, but permanent in the manner of a house. Concerning it the apostle Paul says to the Corinthians [Col. 0814C]: “We have a building from God, a house of God, not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (II Cor. V, 1).

“I say that I shall pass to the house of God. I say this as one who has passed into the place,” that is, into the opportunity, “of the admirable tabernacle,” namely, the Church, which is God’s admirable tabernacle, in which the faithful serve as soldiers for God. This is to say: “I passed from idolatry and the desire for worldly things so that I might become a son of the Church, through which I shall arrive at the house of God.”

He rightly says “into the place of the tabernacle,” that is, “into the opportunity.” This is to say: into the opportune tabernacle. For the tabernacle is opportune in that through it one reaches the house. When, however, he calls the transitory tabernacle admirable, on account of the excellence of the faithful who serve as soldiers in it [Col. 0814D], he indicates that the house, which will be eternal, will be much more admirable.

“I say that I shall pass to the house of God, existing then in a voice,” that is, in the manifestation, “of exultation and confession,” that is, praise. He uses “voice” for manifestation because thoughts are made manifest through it. This is to say: “When I pass over, I shall openly exult in him and confess to him,” that is, praise him. “For now we see as through a mirror, but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII, 12).

He then adds the cause of the voice of exultation and confession, as follows: “I say, in the voice of exultation and confession. And this sound,” that is, this voice, “is the sound,” that is, the manifestation, “of my exultation and confession as one feasting.” This is to say: “I shall openly exult and confess for this reason: because I shall feast, not on earthly banquets, but on eternal blessedness, which will be my banquet.” Hence elsewhere the Psalmist: “Let the righteous feast in gladness” (Psal. LXXVI, 4). “Sound” also, because, like a voice, it is a manifest thing, is likewise used for manifestation. Or in this sense: “My tears were continual.”

And he explains: “I say, when I shall come before the face of God. And I am certain that I shall come. For my tears were my bread by day and by night,” that is, continually. This is to say: “I continually endured miseries for this reason: while it was said to me every day, ‘Where is your God?’” “My tears,” I say, “were the bread of my soul.” As though she said: “By them the soul is refreshed and strengthened, since through them it is cleansed from its defilements, even though the flesh is tormented by them.”

“And although my tears were my bread by day and by night, nevertheless I remembered these things which I shall say”—I who had at some time forgotten them because of tribulations—namely, that through tears I shall pass to the house of God, existing in the voice of exultation, which voice will be the sound of me as one feasting. I say this as one who has already passed into the place of the admirable tabernacle.

“And because I shall pass to the house, and have already passed into the place of the tabernacle, I poured out my soul within myself. Therefore, because I shall pass through tribulations, why are you sorrowful, O my soul, in tribulations? And why do you trouble me,” that is, make me troubled because of your sorrow?

He puts this interrogatively out of excessive affection. It is as though he said: “Cease to be sorrowful and to trouble me. And hope,” that is, place your hope, “in God, because there is still to come the time when I shall confess to him,” that is, praise him with perfect praise, “established in blessedness.”

Or in this sense: “Because, hoping until the end of life, I shall confess to him.” As though he said: “If I hope perseveringly, I shall praise him perfectly; otherwise I would not confess him.”

“And hope in him, because he is the salvation,” that is, the Savior, “of my countenance,” existing, that is, as my likeness, namely, a human being like me. Therefore he will have mercy on me, since I am of the same nature. “And he is my God,” that is, my Creator.

“Countenance” is used for likeness because human likeness is especially accustomed to be indicated in the face.

“I say, O hearers, why is the soul sorrowful?” And because it is sorrowful, “my soul was troubled by indignation against me,” that is, my soul was indignant against itself, because it became sorrowful over what it ought not to have mourned—namely, over tribulations [Col. 0815D]. In this he implies that we likewise ought to be indignant against ourselves if at some time sorrow over tribulation should occur, and thus depart from sorrow.

“I said that I shall pass to the house of God. And therefore, because I am certain of this, I shall remember you, always striving toward you, not henceforth consigning you to oblivion. This remembrance will come from the land of Jordan,” that is, from me, because you have made me the land of Jordan, namely, irrigated and fertile land through Jordan, that is, through baptism. Previously I was barren land, sterile in good works through the aridity of sins. Jordan is used for baptism because the Lord was baptized in it.

“And that remembrance will proceed from Hermoniim,” that is, from me, because through confession you have made me Hermon, that is, one who anathematizes my sins. “And it will proceed from the little mountain,” that is, from me, because you have made me a mountain, that is, exalted in virtues, after the manner of a mountain—and yet little, that is, humble, not proud on account of my virtues. Here *de* and *a* are used causatively.

This is as though she said: “For this reason I shall remember you: because you have made me the land of Jordan, Hermoniim, and a little mountain.”

“And I shall still remember you because of the abyss,” that is, my depth, namely, because of the multitude of my tribulations. This is supplied from outside the text.

Someone might say: “Why will you remember him because of the abyss?” He answers: “For this abyss,” that is, the depth of tribulations, “calls upon” or summons in my mind, through consideration, “the abyss,” that is, the depth of future condemnation, which will be eternal.

This is to say: “When I see that here I am permitted by you to be afflicted with tribulations because I consigned you to oblivion through sins, I consider that in the future I shall be condemned more grievously if I persistently consign you to oblivion; and thus through those very tribulations I shall remember you.”

He says “calls upon” by comparison with someone who calls a person separated from another, so that through his calling he may make him present. “Calls upon,” that is, calls into the mind. And it calls upon “in the voice of your cataracts,” that is, in the open testimony of your prophets, who testified to that future abyss. As though she said: “It calls upon through this, because it sees that the prophets testified to these things.”

“Voice,” as above, is used for manifestation. The prophets are called “cataracts,” because through them the water of teaching descends upon the human race, just as waters of rain flow down through cataracts onto the earth [Col. 0816C]. For cataracts are properly called the channels through which rainwater descends upon the earth. Hence it is read in Genesis: “The cataracts of heaven were opened” (Gen. VII, 11).

Someone might ask: “Is there an abyss within you?” The Fathers answer: “Yes.” For “all your heights,” that is, great tribulations, “and your waves,” that is, lesser tribulations, sent forth by your ordering, “passed over me,” that is, came upon me as though they were passing over me, so that they might oppress me.

When he says “passed over,” he implies that they came in such a way that they would pass over, to teach that they are not to be feared, since they are transitory. Tribulations are called “waves” because they oppress the flesh, just as waves oppress a ship.

“Your heights and your waves”—which the Lord, through the writings of teachers, commanded us, when established in the day, that is, in prosperity, to recognize as his mercy, that is, to understand that they are inflicted upon us through God’s mercy, so that, purified by them, we may not be condemned in the future. This accords with Augustine: “He mercifully applies temporal severity, lest he justly inflict eternal punishment.”

He rightly says “in the day,” that is, in prosperity, he commanded this, because believers are able to devote themselves to the study of Scripture when they are at rest from tribulations.

“And through those same Scriptures he commanded that in the night,” that is, in adversity, “his song,” that is, joy in him, should be present, according to the saying of the Gospel: “Rejoice and exult when people hate you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil on account of the Son of Man; for your reward is great in heaven” (Luc. VI, 22).

He uses “day” for prosperity because the day is bright; he uses “night” for adversity because it is obscure.

Since, then, he commanded that tribulations are mercy, and that in the night a song should be present, “with me,” that is, in my heart there will be prayer made to God, the author of my life. That is, I shall pray inwardly to God, the author of my life; inwardly I shall say to God: “O God, you are my protector,” that is, my physician and patron.

“Why, then, have you forgotten me?”—that is, why do you appear to have forgotten me? He explains in what respect he appears to have forgotten me, as follows: “Why do I walk sorrowful,” that is, why do you permit me to walk sorrowfully along the way of this life, “while”—that is, because—“the enemy afflicts me by tribulating me?”

“And while my bones are broken,” that is, the strengths of my patience are weakened, because I bear tribulations with difficulty, although they ought not to cause sorrow. He uses “bones” in the plural with reference to the many faithful of the Church.

“And why do I walk sorrowful while my enemies”—those who tribulate me—“have reproached me,” that is, inflicted reproaches upon me, saying that I am foolish and insane because I relinquish present goods and promise myself invisible and future things?

“And while they say to me every day: ‘Where is your God, who does not deliver you, and whom you cannot point out?’” He presents this prayer interrogatively, out of immense desire. The whole passage is as though he had said:

“Do not be so forgetful of me that I become sorrowful over the afflictions which I endure for you, that my bones are broken, and that I am sad because of the reproaches brought against me by my enemies for your sake” [Col. 0817C].

He then addresses himself, consoling his soul concerning its sorrow, as follows: “I say that God is my protector. Therefore, why are you sorrowful, O my soul, and why do you trouble me? Do not be sorrowful and trouble me. But hope in God, because I shall still confess to him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.”

This is explained here as above.

It should be noted that although this has been stated above, it is not superfluous to place it here also, since it is introduced for another purpose. He repeats it in this way out of excessive affection. For what one desires greatly is not sufficiently expressed by saying it only once.

## ON PSALM XLII

The title of the forty-second Psalm is: “A Psalm of David,” that is, of the Church of the martyrs.

Above, the Church of the martyrs appeared to have been speaking, sighing amid tribulations inflicted by enemies who are outside the Church; they also said twice: “Where is your God?” (Psal. XLI, 11.)

Here, however, the Church of the martyrs speaks while placed amid tribulations caused by false believers, praying that by God’s judgment her cause may be distinguished from theirs—that is, that it may then be revealed which is the better, something which is now unknown to many.

She also prays to be rescued from their fellowship after the dissolution of the body. At present she suffers much because of the wickedness and deceitfulness of those same unbelievers, whose bodily presence is now joined to hers. She also consoles herself concerning her tribulations, showing that no sorrow should be entertained on account of them.

[Col. 0818A] “Judge me, O God,” as though she said: “I do not shrink from your judgment, as the wicked do; rather, I pray: judge me as you ought to judge.”

“And judge in this manner”: namely, distinguish in the future “my cause,” that is, my case, “from an unholy nation,” that is, from the case of false Christians who pretend to be holy but are not. Thus, although it is now uncertain to many who will have the better case and merit in the future, it may be revealed through the judgment of you, the just Judge, when we shall be saved because of our merit, while they will be condemned because of theirs.

“Before reaching that judgment, rescue me through the dissolution of the body from an unjust man,” that is, from the fellowship of unjust men—namely, false Christians who openly persecute me in words or deeds, such as Arius and the other false believers and heretics who persecuted the true believers in every way [Col. 0818B].

“And rescue me from a deceitful man,” that is, from the fellowship of deceitful men—namely, false Christians and heretics, who inflict upon me a deceitful and hidden persecution.

He says “man” in the singular because they are one thing in wickedness.

It is fitting that you judge and rescue me, because “you are my strength,” that is, through you I am strong, so that I do not fail amid tribulations, even if, because I am sorrowful over them, I may seem less than perfect. This is an assertion of merit.

“Why, then, when you have already made me strong in this way, have you rejected me,” that is, appeared to reject me from grace? Namely, “Why do I walk sorrowful,” that is, why do I remain for so long, walking from sorrow to sorrow, “while”—that is, because—“the enemy afflicts me with every kind of affliction?”

This is to say: “Since, through the strength which I have received from you, I have deserved not to be rejected, do not reject me in such a way as to leave me walking sorrowfully because of the tribulations which I suffer from enemies for your sake.”

“I say: judge me. And also, by judging, send into me,” that is, send manifestly into me, so that I may know more fully, “your light,” that is, your wisdom. It is called your light because it illuminates the human nature personally united to it, and afterward all its members, according to the saying: “This was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (Joan. I, 9).

“And send your truth,” that is, manifestly send your truth into me—namely, the human nature—so that I may become conformed to it in impassibility and immortality. Human nature is called “truth” because, being impassible and immortal, it is wholly unchangeable. Hence it is written: “With whom there is no change or shadow of alteration” (Jac. I, 17).

He rightly says “send,” as though he were saying: “You have already sent your light into me,” that is, the knowledge and perceptiveness of your light; but it is obscure and as though seen through a mirror. “And you have sent your truth into me,” so that I may be somewhat conformed to it in virtues [Col. 0818D].

“But in the future send”—that is, send from yourself into me—“so that what is hidden in you may be fully realized in me, insofar as possible: so that I may know that light fully, insofar as it is possible for me to know, since now I know only in part.”

“And although I am not fully conformed to your truth, may I fully possess within myself, insofar as possible, conformity to the truth, so that, existing impassible and immortal, I may be wholly unchangeable.”

And it is fitting that you send the light and truth in the future. For the light and truth themselves have led me and brought me forward. The order is reversed: “They themselves brought me forward,” that is, Christ, who is light according to his divinity and truth according to his humanity, brought me from the valley of error to your holy mountain.

He explains which mountain when he adds, “and into your tabernacles”: “I mean that mountain on which those who serve you perfectly are situated,” namely, the height of the virtues by which they fight against vices.

“And after the light and truth have brought me forward, they have also led me onward from good to better and caused me to persevere on that very mountain” [Col. 0819B].

What he prayed for—“send,” and so forth—he promises, from the certainty he possesses, that he will attain it, so that by his example he may also invite us to pray, in order that we may likewise obtain it.

“I say that they have brought me forward and led me onward. And because I have already been brought forward, I shall enter in the future,” that is, I shall be admitted, “to the altar of God,” that is, to the vision and conformity of the Lord’s human being. It is called the altar of God because upon it, that is, in faith in him, all sacrifices are offered to God by the faithful. Otherwise they would be useless.

“And through that altar,” that is, through conformity to and vision of him, “I shall enter to God,” that is, to the knowledge and subtle contemplation of divinity. I mean God, “who will make my youth rejoice,” that is, who will then make me young and new after I have laid aside the sordid old age of the flesh [Col. 0819C], “or who already makes my youth rejoice in hope,” that is, makes me joyful in hope of becoming young in the future.

When he says “I shall enter,” he implies that the matter is secret and still unknown to us; for we are said to enter into secret things.

“I say that I shall then enter. And in order that I may deserve to enter, meanwhile here, O God”—who are commonly the God and Creator of all, and my God above unbelievers, whom I obey—“I shall confess to you,” that is, praise you, “with the harp,” that is, through the mortification of the flesh, when it is mortified because of the tribulations inflicted for your sake.

“But you, O my soul, since I shall enter through tribulations, why are you sorrowful in tribulations? And why do you trouble me through sorrow? Do not be sorrowful and trouble me, but hope in God, because I shall still confess to him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.”

This is explained as in the preceding Psalm.

## ON PSALM XLIII

The title of this forty-third Psalm is the same as that of the forty-first Psalm: “For the end, understanding, for the sons of Chore.” It will be explained there.

For it is chiefly the voice of the Church of the martyrs, imitating Christ’s passion, which is signified by Chore, and praying to be delivered through Christ from enemies, especially on the day of judgment. Hence they say:

“O God, we have heard with our ears.” He rightly says “with our ears.” As though he said: “We did not hear through dreams or through thoughts, but with our ears,” that is, we heard with complete certainty.

“And we did not hear from just any narrators. Rather, our fathers, men distinguished by authority [Col. 0820A], related it to us through their writings.”

“And they did not relate some matter of which they were ignorant, but the work which you performed in their days,” which they themselves saw with their eyes.

Lest anyone think that you performed that work in the days of people other than the ancient fathers, he adds: “And”—that is, namely—“in ancient days you performed this work.”

He rightly adds “work,” to indicate that what God did with them was something great. For what is great we customarily call a work and an undertaking.

He explains what work this was when he adds: “This, namely, that your hand,” that is, your power, “destroyed the nations”—namely, the Jebusites, Amorites, and Perizzites [138], and the other nations of the promised land. “And when those nations had been destroyed, you planted them,” that is, the fathers, “in their place.”

When he says “you planted,” he implies that you placed them there so that they might multiply and grow, not so that they would immediately depart from the place—by comparison with an herb or tree which is planted somewhere so that it may grow there.

Since he had said “destroyed,” lest anyone think that the nations were dispersed through sloth, fear, or negligence, he says that they were driven out through affliction, thereby increasing the manifestation of God’s power and making the matter more remarkable.

“I say: your hand destroyed the nations”—in this way: “You afflicted the peoples with wars and many other calamities, and thus expelled them from the promised land.”

“Nation” and “people” have the same meaning here. This is to say: “You expelled those peoples through manifold affliction.”

Someone might say: “Why do you say that God’s hand destroyed and afflicted the nations? Did not the fathers themselves afflict them in wars [Col. 0820C] and thus acquire the land for themselves?”

The answer follows by removing this objection: “Truly, your hand destroyed them. For the fathers did not possess the promised land by their own sword,” that is, through their sword, “and their own arm,” that is, their own strength, “did not save them from the wars and ambushes of those nations. Rather, your right hand,” that is, the prosperity of victory granted by you; “and your arm,” that is, your strength; “and the illumination of your countenance,” that is, the clear counsel of your wisdom or your grace, saved them.

Here “countenance” is used for grace, because a person’s favor can often be indicated in the face. Alternatively, God’s wisdom, that is, the Son of God, is called the illumination of God’s countenance because through his visible humanity the invisible divinity of the Father became known to the world, just as the secrets of the heart are often discerned in the face.

“And you did not save them on account of their merits, but because you were pleased with them,” that is, it pleased you to save them. This is to say: “You saved them solely by the good pleasure of mercy.”

Or in this sense: “Truly, your right hand, arm, and illumination worked for their salvation. And they did so with such manifest effect that through this you pleased the other nations by saving them,” that is, by saving their fathers.

This is to say: “When the other nations saw you working their salvation, it pleased them to recognize that you were the true God,” as certain people are said to have declared: “There is no other God besides the Lord God of Israel” (Dan. III, 17).

“I said that you saved the fathers in this way. You are the one who saved them, my king and my God,” that is, I regard you as my king and my God, and no other.

“You not only commanded salvation for the fathers through the prophets, but also command salvation through the Scriptures for Jacob,” that is, for us, who are wrestlers and overthrowers of vices.

You command this salvation: “In you,” that is, through you, “we shall winnow,” that is, separate from ourselves, “our enemies,” namely, unbelievers, when we sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matth. XIX, 28).

Or “we shall winnow,” that is, we shall be the cause, through our merits, of their being winnowed, that is, separated from us—by comparison with chaff, which is separated from grain by the horns of a winnowing fork and scattered, that is, carried away by the wind. Thus, in the future, unbelievers, separated from us, will be carried away by the force of evil spirits.

“And you command this: that, not trusting in your name,” that is, in the honor of the name which we glorify—or, according to another reading, trusting in your name, namely, in the name which means “merciful”—“we shall despise those who rise up against us,” that is, the devils who rise against us, fearing them in no way.

“And not externally, but within us,” that is, in our interior—namely, by suggesting evil thoughts in the soul.

Another translation has: “those who rise up against us.” According to this reading, they may be understood either as external or as internal enemies.

Someone might say: “You say that through God you will winnow and despise your enemies. Will you not be able to despise them through yourselves, trusting in your own strength?”

He removes this objection as follows: “Truly, through him we shall despise them. For I shall not trust in my bow, and my sword will not save me.”

This is to say: “We shall not suppose that we can be saved through our bow and sword.”

The bow signifies hidden defense, which is carried out through counsel and cunning, after the manner of a bow, which, by striking the enemy secretly, protects the one who shoots from the enemy.

The sword, however, with which one fights at close quarters and openly, signifies open defense.

Or by “bow” are understood lesser virtues, which are hidden; by “sword,” greater virtues, which cannot be concealed because of their magnitude. Through these virtues the faithful fight against both external and internal enemies.

This is to say: “I shall never suppose that I can be delivered either by my bow or by my sword, unless your mercy cooperates.”

“And rightly I shall not trust in bow and sword, but in you. For you saved”—that is, you will save—“us, as you command, from those who afflict us,” both externally and internally.

“And you confounded”—that is, you will confound—“those who hate us,” destroying the external enemies and rendering the internal ones unable to win.

“And you command this: that all day long,” that is, continually, “we shall be praised by those same external enemies,” existing “in God,” that is, in participation in God’s blessedness.

Those enemies will also say: “We considered their life madness, and their end without honor. Behold how they are counted among the sons of God!” (Sap. III, 4.)

“And you command this: that we shall confess to you forever,” that is, praise you eternally.

He presents these salvations as having been commanded by God as though they ought to be fulfilled in the present age. They will not be fulfilled then, so that he may attract them more strongly; but he does not specify when they will be fulfilled, so that he may urge them more strongly to investigate this.

“I said that you planted and saved our fathers, afflicted and expelled their enemies, and commanded these salvations for us. But now,” that is, in the time of fulfillment, “you have rejected and confounded us, and to such an extent that you do not go forth, O God, with our armies,” that is, in our forces.

This is to say: “You have so confounded and rejected us that we can no longer assemble armies against our enemies in which you might go forth to our aid through the ministry of angels, as happened in the days of the ancient fathers.”

For it is often read that when they were preparing to fight with enemies, angels came forth with them to battle as helpers. In this way God was said to go forth with their armies to their aid through his ministers.

Armies are rightly called “forces,” because the strength of commanders to fight is established in them.

He explains this in parts, first how God rejected them: “I say that you rejected us in this way: you rejected us. You turned us backward,” that is, you permitted certain people to be turned away from our holiness by the force of tribulations and to go backward, namely, behind our enemies, so that, yielding through fear of punishment, we might follow the example of our enemies and become conformed to them.

Lest anyone think that all had been turned backward, he specifies this when he adds: “And thus, I say, you turned us away, so that those who hate us,” namely, our enemies, “seized some of us for themselves,” that is, conformed certain of us to themselves.

As though he said: “They did not turn all of us away, but only a part,” by comparison with someone who, unable to take an entire object, tears away a portion of it for himself.

“I say that you permitted us to be turned away,” insofar as we were the deficient part.

But insofar as we were the part that did not fail, rather persevering in goodness, “you gave us into the power of our enemies as sheep for food,” that is, so that they might kill us without any regard for mercy, just as sheep, which are born for the purpose of becoming food, are killed without regard for mercy.

“And among the nations,” that is, among the nations, “you dispersed us,” that is, you permitted us to be dispersed and become exiles.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matth. XX, 23).

“I said that you gave us as sheep for food, so that we might be killed without any regard for pity. Yet no fruit of the Church resulted from this,” so that others might be converted by the example of our steadfastness [Col. 0822D].

“But you sold your people,” namely, us, “without a price,” that is, you permitted us to be killed in such a way that you resembled one who sells something without receiving a price for it.

This is to say: “For this reason God appears to permit his people to be killed: so that through their steadfastness he may produce sons for the Church, and this may be the price of their death. But when no conversion of unbelievers follows the killing of some, you appear to have sold them and received no price.”

“And if there was some conversion of unbelievers through the death of certain people, nevertheless there was no great exchange in their place,” that is, you did not exchange them in such a way as to raise up many sons because of their death.

It should be noted, however, that some were given over to death without any price; some for a small price; and some for a great price. But he does not discuss those who were given for a great price, since nothing concerning them requires investigation.

“And you made us a reproach to our neighbors,” so that, when you permitted us to be afflicted or killed, we would become a reproach to those who were already our neighbors and wished to be converted by our example, causing them to be ashamed that they had ever wished to become our imitators.

“And to those who are not in our neighborhood, but in our circuit,” that is, at a distance from us. Or “in our circuit,” that is, those who surrounded us and hemmed us in with threats and tribulations, by comparison with people who surround someone so that he cannot escape.

“You made us a taunt and a derision,” that is, a cause of taunting and derision. We call something a taunt when someone, out of excessive indignation, wrinkles his nose. Therefore “taunt” is used for indignation.

This is to say: “You made us such that they would be indignant against us and deride us.”

“And you made us a likeness,” that is, a parable, “among the nations,” so that, when they saw someone guilty, they would say: “You deserve a death such as that by which this or that person perished.”

“And you made us among the peoples a shaking of the head,” that is, a cause for shaking the head.

This is to say: “You permitted us to be afflicted to such an extent that the unbelieving peoples moved their heads in derision, asserting that we were foolish and insane.”

After explaining how God rejected them, he explains how he permitted them to be confounded, as follows:

“Since you made us a reproach, a taunt and a derision, a likeness, and a shaking of the head, all day long,” that is, continually, “my shame is before me,” that is, before me, in my sight, “never departing from me.”

And this is not a small matter. “But the confusion of my face,” that is, shame—not existing inwardly because of consciousness of crime, but appearing externally in the face because of the weakness of the flesh—“covered me,” that is, it was so great that it occupied me excessively outwardly, by comparison with a broad garment which covers the entire body.

Confusion, I say, which arose from the voice of one reproaching me—that is, the enemy, inflicting many kinds of insults upon me—and of one speaking against me, that is, speaking against me and attempting, by human arguments, to disprove the truth uttered by me; and from the face, that is, from the pressure, of the enemy; and also of one persecuting me with tribulations. Not merely the one reproaching and speaking against me: all these things we have mentioned came upon us, that is, for our oppression. Yet we have not forgotten you.

[Source-column anchors: 0823D, “attempting … to disprove the truth”; 0824A, “our heart … has not withdrawn”; 0824B, “in the future … no place of affliction”; 0824C, “a foreign god”; 0824D, “sheep for slaughter”; 0825A, “our poor ones”; 0825B, “our weakest part”; 0825C, *In Psalmum XLIV*; 0825D, “from mortality to immortality”; 0826A, “for their honor”; 0826B, “the essence of the Father”; 0826C, “Before Lucifer”; 0826D, “perfect eternity”; 0827A, “the Father’s generation”; 0827B, “tongue … for the Word”; 0827C, “the sword of preaching”; 0827D, “prepare yourself to preach”; 0828A, “God … in eternity”; 0828B, “the perfection of good works”; 0828C, “truth, gentleness, and justice”; 0828D, “insofar as they are evil”; 0829A, “the peoples … your dwelling”; 0829B, “the rod of correction”; 0829C, “anointed … with the oil of gladness”; 0829D, “the garment of divinity”; 0830A, “polishing ivory”; 0830B, “daughters of kings”; 0830C, “it may be read in this way”; 0830D, “these meanings do not change”; 0831A, “weak and fragile”; 0831B, “the primitive Church”; 0831C, “variety of virtues”; 0831D, “understand what you hear”; 0832A, “the house of your father”; 0832B, “the daughters of Tyre”; 0832C, “all the rich of the people”; 0832D, “all the glory … inward”; 0833A, “surrounded with varieties”; 0833B, “near to her in conformity”; 0833C, “mean the same thing”; 0833D, “bishops and the other pastors”; 0834A, “every generation”; 0834B, “not exhortatively or imperatively.”]

And in this way we have not forgotten you: namely, we have not acted wickedly in your covenant, which was left to us; that is, we have not acted wrongly by withdrawing from your covenant, meaning the promise that we made to you in baptism, in the presence of our sponsors—namely, that we would obey you alone, having rejected the pomp of the devil. And in this way also we have not forgotten you: namely, our heart, that is, the will of our heart, has not withdrawn from you by turning back, that is, by inclining toward unbelief. This is to say: We have not only acted without wickedness, but we have not even wished to withdraw from you, which is the lesser matter. And we have had this not through ourselves but through you.

For you have not turned aside—that is, you have not permitted our paths, namely, our works, which are paths for us to life, to be turned aside—from your way, that is, from the way of your commandments. This is to say: You did not permit us to do much of anything that would be foreign to your commandments. Therefore it is all the more astonishing that, although you made us persevere so greatly in what is good, you nevertheless rejected and confounded us as though we had deserved this by living wickedly.

Someone might ask: Why do you say that you did not forget, when there had been no cause for you to forget? The answer is: There truly was such a cause for us, because you humbled us—that is, you afflicted us with tribulations, or permitted us to be afflicted—in a place of affliction, namely, in this world, in which there is a place of affliction. In the future, however, there will be no place of affliction.

And you humbled us so greatly that the shadow, existing as a cause of death, covered us; that is, those who are emphatically called “shadow”—namely, shadowy and obscure in error, and who are a cause of death to others by incorporating them into themselves through evil example, suggestions, threats, and tribulations—completely overwhelmed us with tribulations.

Someone might say: Why did you claim that you had not forgotten, when you had forgotten? The answer is: We truly did not forget. For if we have forgotten the name of our God, by not acknowledging him as God and Lord, and ourselves as servants and creatures; and if, by forgetting the name of our God, we have spread out our bodily hands toward a foreign god, worshiping him; or if we have spread out our hands—that is, directed our affections—toward a foreign god, so that we might even wish to entreat him, will God not investigate these things in the future, so as to avenge them?

He certainly will investigate them. It is as though he said: We speak the truth when we affirm that we have not forgotten. For if we had forgotten, why would we lie about this, when we know that God will investigate it in the future? It is as though they said: We would not say this unless it were true.

Someone might say: He will not investigate it, because he does not know it. To this he replies: He does not fail to know it. For he himself universally knows the hidden things of the heart.

Then follows a prayer for those placed in affliction, as follows: I have said that you humbled us, and yet we have not forgotten you. Therefore, because for your sake we are put to death in the flesh all day long, that is, continually; and while we are being put to death, we have been regarded by our persecutors as sheep for slaughter, that is, we have been considered fit to be killed without any regard for mercy, like sheep that are born for the purpose of being killed and eaten—arise, Lord, that is, show yourself powerful, although you appear powerless.

Why do you sleep concerning us, that is, neglect us? For God’s sleeping means that he neglects someone. It is as though he said: Do not sleep concerning us, but arise. And arise in this manner: do not reject us from your help unto the end of rejection, that is, forever. Even if you now seem to reject us, do not reject us completely.

It has also been said concerning those who are sorrowful, as follows: And why do you turn your face away, that is, the kindness of your grace? You turn it away in this manner: you forget our poverty, that is, our poor ones; and our tribulation, that is, you seem to forget certain ones among us who are poor, namely, sorrowful in their tribulation, since you permit them to be sorrowful precisely where they ought to rejoice.

Those believers who are sorrowful in their tribulation are called poor, as though they doubted that they could be delivered by God’s help. For those who are without anyone’s help are called poor. Those who, although afflicted, nevertheless possess an abundant hope of being delivered are called rich. It is as though he said: Do not turn your face away, and do not forget the poor.

He also prays for those who are failing, as follows: I do not pray only for the poor; but because our soul—that is, the soul of certain ones among us—has been humbled, that is, cast down and inclined to turn away from its holiness; and this in the dust, that is, in the tribulation of its dust, namely, its flesh, which is nothing other than dust and earth; and because our belly, that is, our weakest part, has been glued to the earth, that is, joined to earthly things and made like them in its desire.

This is to say: Since some among us are altogether failing, so that they are not glued to the earth, while others are such that they are glued to it, arise, Lord, that is, show yourself powerful. And arise in this manner: help us in accordance with those who are poor but not yet failing, so that, with you assisting us, we may not fail; and redeem us from failure, in accordance with the portion of those who are failing.

This is to say: Let your death be the price by which we are rescued from the failure through which we would perish completely. I pray: help and redeem. And do this not because of our merits, but for the magnification of your name—both by us, if we do not fail, and by others, who will be moved to this by our example.

## IN PSALM XLIV

[Col. 0825C]

### Title of the Forty-Fourth Psalm

“For the end, for those who will be changed, for the sons of Korah, for understanding; a song for the Beloved.”

By “sons of Korah” he means here not only imitators of Christ’s passion, but also all those who are adoptive sons of the Church through the passion. The title is therefore explained as follows: The song—that is, this treatise, which contains joyful praise—is proposed to the sons of Korah for understanding, that is, so that they may diligently examine this song, which is exceedingly profound, and thus attain understanding.

I say “song” because it was formed and composed by the prophet for those who will be changed at the end, that is, in complete consummation—namely, from mortality to immortality and from passibility to impassibility—that is, for those who are to be saved. “For we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. XV, 15).

It was composed “for the Beloved,” namely, antonomastically for Christ, who is beloved by God the Father and by the Church. Concerning him the Father’s voice is reported to have thundered in the Gospel: “This is my beloved Son,” etc. (Matt. III, 17). And in the Song of Songs the bride, the Church, testifies concerning him: “My beloved is white,” etc. (Song V, 10).

He rightly says “for those who will be changed” and “for the Beloved,” for “for” is used causatively. It is as though he were giving the reason for those who will be changed and for the Beloved—that is, this song is made for their honor—so that, when their praise is contained in this treatise, it may invite others to praise and honor him.

For God the Father is introduced as praising him and instructing our faith concerning the ineffable and eternal generation of his Son. He also praises him according to his humanity, for his innocence and justice, and exhorts him to preach. He likewise praises those who will be changed at the end, that is, the primitive Church, which is God’s bride, for the perfection of her virtues; and he exhorts that primitive Church to hear and see, so that, having thus been made beautiful, she may be loved. He says that, following her example and preaching, the Church from the Gentiles will succeed her, and that this Church too will be changed at the end.

### “My heart has uttered a good word”

“Heart” is used here for the paternal essence, because that essence is secret and unknown, like the heart, which is hidden and unknown except to God alone and to the one whose heart it is.

“Word,” however, means the Son of God, that is, the Wisdom of God. He is called “Word” by analogy, because through him, once incarnate, the divine will was made known to us, just as the secrets of the heart are revealed through words.

He is also called “Word” because through him God the Father arranged all things and brought them into being. Thus, just as a prince arranges by his word what he intends to accomplish, and by the command of that same word compels his subjects to complete what has been arranged, so God the Father acts through the Word.

When he says, “has uttered,” he indicates that he brought him forth and begot him from his secret essence, ineffably, before the beginning of the world. The expression is drawn from the likeness of belching, which is brought forth from the body’s inner and hidden parts. Hence elsewhere: “Before Lucifer I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 9).

How the Father begets, how the Son is begotten, and how the Holy Spirit proceeds is beyond our investigation and unknown to us; nevertheless, it must be believed with the firmest faith. Hence we read: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. LIII, 8.) No one.

“Good,” however, is not used here adjectivally but substantively. The words above—“My heart has uttered,” and so forth—are therefore explained as follows: My heart, that is, my secret essence, has uttered, that is, brought forth and begotten, the Word. And not just any word, but a Word that is the consummate and supreme Good, from which all good things are good.

But because he had previously said “has uttered,” that is, “has begotten,” lest it appear that he is not now also begetting, and thus that mutability exists in the divine essence, rather than perfect eternity—for nothing is eternal that has been made changeable—he adds: I have not uttered in such a way that I do not utter now also. But even now I, who am one in essence with him, say, “My works to the king.” That is, I say—not with words, but by an ineffable saying—that I arrange and conceive my works through the Word, who is king of all, since he is one in essence with me and I am king.

Hence we read:

> The Word, begotten from the Father’s heart, creates and governs all things.

This does not mean that the Father and the Spirit do not create and govern, since they are one, but that through the Word they ineffably arrange, create, and govern all things. According to Augustine, “to say that the works are governed by the Father” is equivalent to saying that the Father begets the Son. For “generation” belongs to the Son as a paternal act, while “disposition” and “conception” are through him.

Nor do I merely say—that is, arrange—my works through him; but my tongue, that is, my Word, is my pen, the pen of a swiftly writing scribe, through that same tongue. This is to say: Through him I quickly compose all things.

This is said by analogy. For just as a scribe gives form to figures through a pen, so the Father impressed forms upon things through the Son. He rightly says “swiftly,” since, by the command of his will and without delay, he creates whatever pleases him. In accordance with this: “He has done whatever he willed” (Ps. CXIII). And elsewhere: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. CXLVIII).

“Tongue” is rightly used for “Word,” since the word is formed with the aid of the tongue.

Having shown the ineffable generation of his Word, he treats of him according to his humanity, praising him and exhorting him to preach, as follows: “Beautiful in form,” and so forth.

The verse that follows this one—namely, “Gird yourself,” etc.—is read beforehand in this manner: I say, “I have uttered the Word”; and you, most powerful one—that is, you, the Word, possessing with me equal power of divinity—“gird yourself with your sword upon your thigh.”

According to his humanity, let him be like an excellent commander preparing himself for war, who girds himself with his sword upon his thigh in order to destroy the enemy. Thus he should prepare himself to preach, by which preaching he will destroy the vices of others, in the manner of a sword by which the body is destroyed. Hence Paul says: “The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI, 17).

Or it may be read in this way: “Gird yourself with your sword,” namely, with the word of preaching; that is, prepare your sword, in imitation of one who prepares a sword for battle by girding himself with it. The sword, I say, is placed upon the thigh, that is, upon humanity.

This is to say: Humanity will not have this sword from itself, but it will be given to it from above, that is, from divinity. In accordance with the words of the apostle James: “Every perfect gift is from above” (James I, 17).

“Thigh” is used for humanity because human generation proceeds from the thighs. Hence we read that Abraham made his servant place his right hand under his thigh and made him swear by the God of heaven that he would not bring a wife of foreign blood to his son (Gen. XXIV, 2). This prefigured that someone would be born from his thigh who would exist perfectly as both man and the God of heaven.

I say, “Gird yourself,” that is, prepare yourself to preach; and you are fit for this.

For you are beautiful in form, that is, in interior beauty—namely, innocence—before the sons of men, that is, before the faithful who conduct themselves rationally as human beings.

This is to say: Since you are perfectly innocent above all the innocent, you are fit to preach, because nothing reprehensible is found in you.

And it is necessary for you to gird yourself, because upon your lips—that is, through the preaching that will proceed from your lips—grace has been poured out; that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, namely the remission of sins, will be poured out upon the human race.

And therefore, because you are beautiful and grace will be poured out upon your lips, God has blessed you, that is, magnified you forever, making you immortal and impassible from being mortal and passible.

In this he indicates that whoever, insofar as possible, will likewise be beautiful will also be blessed in the future.

Or it may be read in this way: It is fitting that you gird yourself. For this reason, in order that you might gird yourself, God has blessed you, that is, magnified you in innocence, making you free from sin. I, that is, God, am your God according to your humanity; and this blessing will be eternal.

But since you are beautiful, attend to your beauty, that is, make yourself intent upon your beauty, namely, your innocence—not by increasing it, but by persevering in it. In the Lord’s humanity, innocence was always perfect from the beginning.

And make yourself intent upon your beauty, that is, persevere in the perfection of virtues and proceed in the perfection of good works, going from one good work to another. For he did not perform all his good works at once.

And by making yourself intent, proceed prosperously to wage war against vices through your preaching, and to wage war against the devil. And proceed prosperously in this way: reign among the faithful. Having conquered vices and the devil, I say, reign.

And do this for the sake of truth, that is, for the sake of the preaching that you will give them; and for the sake of meekness, that is, because you will be meek rather than rebellious in your passion. In accordance with Isaiah: “Do not fear, daughter of Zion; behold, your king comes to you, meek” (Isa. LXII, 11). And do it for the sake of your justice, which you possess, in whose likeness they too will be made just; or for the sake of the justice that you will give them.

This is to say: Your truth, meekness, and justice will be the reason why you will reign in them.

I have said, “Reign for the sake of truth,” and your right hand, that is, your power, will lead you into that kingdom, that is, will enlarge you. And this will happen wonderfully, that is, through the wonders you will perform.

This is to say: Through the miracles that your power will perform, you will be led into the kingdom.

Your arrows too will lead you, that is, the pronouncements of your preaching, which are called arrows because through them you will strike hearts in the manner of arrows. For your arrows are sharp, that is, penetrating to the heart and effective.

And through these arrows the unbelieving peoples, struck by them, will fall among the enemies of the king, that is, according to that disposition of heart by which they will be your enemies. This is to say: Insofar as they are evil, they will be destroyed.

I say “peoples who are to be brought under you,” that is, who will be subjected to your authority. It is as though he were saying: Through the pronouncements of your preaching, which will be effective, the peoples will be subjected to you, and thus your kingdom will be enlarged.

He had already expressed this equivalently above when he said, “Reign for the sake of truth.” “Truth” and “arrows” mean the same thing. But because he had not stated that this truth of preaching would become effective, he repeats the thought equivalently when he says: “Your arrows will lead you into the kingdom,” adding that they are sharp.

This is to say: They will not be blunted, but effective.

I say that the peoples will fall beneath you. And afterward those peoples will be your throne, O God.

This is to say: O Son, who are not simply man but also God, those peoples will be your dwelling. And not only in this age, but also in the age of this world that follows, age upon age. In accordance with the saying: “The soul of the righteous is the throne of God.”

And after you sit among them, if they should at some time proceed crookedly, withdrawing from your subjection by acting and thinking wickedly, you will rule them with a rod, that is, with the correction of tribulations. The image is taken from a horse that, when it goes crookedly, is struck with a rod and brought back onto the road.

This is supplied from outside the book, but it is understood from what follows, when he adds: “And the rod of your kingdom,” that is, the correction by which you will rule your faithful, namely, those who will be subjected to your rule, “will be a rod of direction,” that is, a rod directing them and bringing them back onto the road. Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 33), etc.

He explains how it will direct them, as follows: I say that the rod of your kingdom will be the rod by which you will direct them. And you have loved righteousness and hated iniquity, that is, through that rod you will make them love righteousness and hate iniquity.

Or it may be read in this way: I have said that the peoples will be your throne, and that you will direct them, and that you are fit for this. For you have loved righteousness.

This is to say: You are just, and therefore you will be powerful enough to direct them. This is clear from the opposite: you have loved righteousness, for you have hated iniquity.

I have said that your right hand will lead you, that the peoples will fall beneath you, that they will be your throne, and that you will direct them with a rod; and this is because you have loved righteousness and hated iniquity.

And so that all these things may happen, O God—you, the Son, who are not only man but also God—I, your God, have anointed you with the oil of gladness, that is, I have filled you with special grace and freedom from sin, by which I would make you glad above your companions, that is, above the other faithful who are your companions, namely, co-heirs and participants in your holiness.

In accordance with the Apostle: “If children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ” (Rom. VIII, 17).

He says that he was anointed with oil by analogy with one who is anointed with consecrated oil in order to become king. So Christ was anointed by the Father with the oil of special grace and freedom from sin, so that he might be king.

From this it can be understood that he was anointed with the oil of gladness, because myrrh—that is, incorruptibility after the passion—cassia—that is, the exaltation of the ascension into heaven—and myrrh-like drop, that is, humility in the passion—will give forth fragrance from your garments.

He uses the plural for the singular, “garments” for “garment.” This is to say: From your humanity, which is called the garment of divinity because divinity lies hidden in it and is joined to it, as the body lies hidden within a garment and is joined to it, your faithful will smell incorruptibility and exaltation after the passion, and humility to be practiced in the passion.

And, following your example, myrrh, the drop, and cassia will give forth fragrance from ivory houses, that is, they will smell sweetly to you in your faithful, who are called your houses because you dwell in them.

They are ivory houses because they shine with the perfection of virtues and are white. This came about through many anxieties and labors: they become bright in the perfection of virtues like ivory, which, although previously lacking luster, becomes white and shining through continual work with files.

It should be noted, however, that myrrh, that is, incorruptibility, and cassia, that is, exaltation in God’s presence, will give forth fragrance from the ivory houses in the future. In this life, the drop, that is, humility, will give forth fragrance.

If the passage is referred solely to the soul, then even in this life the incorruptibility of faith and the exaltation of virtues will also give forth fragrance.

From these things—namely, from myrrh, the drop, and cassia, as they give forth their fragrance—“in your honor,” that is, for the purpose of honoring you through them, not so that they may become proud by attributing them to themselves—“the daughters of kings,” that is, the faithful who above were called ivory houses, have delighted you, that is, will delight you.

This is to say: You will be greatly delighted by these things.

Or it may be read in this way: From these things, as they give forth their fragrance, the faithful will delight you; they will be, according to the teaching, daughters of kings, that is, of the apostles, who will be kings of the Church. Hence the Apostle says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor” (Gal. III, 19); and in the Psalm: “Now therefore, O kings, understand” (Ps. II, 10).

I say “daughters of kings,” and this is “in your honor,” that is, they are daughters of kings in such a way that you are honored by these daughters, because they are daughters through your grace.

It should be understood that myrrh is used for incorruptibility because bodies, when anointed with it, become incorruptible. The drop, however, is a medicinal substance suited to dispelling swelling; therefore it is used for humility, which is powerful for suppressing the swelling of pride.

Cassia, because, according to Jerome, it is a tree that grows upward to a great height, is used here for exaltation.

Or this verse may be read in another way. Since he had said, “God your God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions,” they seem to be less fully anointed than he. Otherwise, “above your companions” would have been badly placed.

Someone might therefore ask: Are his companions anointed to some extent with the oil of gladness, that is, with special grace?

He answers as follows: They truly are anointed with oil; and this is apparent from the fact that from your garments—that is, from your companions, who are called garments because they surround you in faith as garments surround the body—myrrh, that is, virginity; the drop, that is, humility or chastity; and cassia, that is, faith, give forth fragrance.

I say that these things give forth fragrance from the garments, namely from the ivory houses, that is, from the companions who are called both garments and ivory houses, by the analogy already mentioned.

From these things, that is, from myrrh, the drop, and cassia, the daughters of kings will delight you in your honor. This meaning remains unchanged.

Myrrh, because it makes the flesh anointed with it incorruptible, is used for virginity, through which the flesh remains incorrupt from lust.

By the drop, through which all poisons are suppressed, charity is understood, through which all the poisons of vices are extinguished.

By cassia, which grows in watery places, baptism is signified. Through baptism, however, faith is signified, since faith is what brings one to baptism; therefore cassia is used for faith.

It should also be noted that he calls the faithful not sons but daughters, in order to humble them, so that they may not trust in themselves, since they are weak and fragile and easily fall, after the manner of the female sex, which is weaker than the male.

Alternatively, he does this to show that they greatly require the cultivation of preaching, after the manner of daughters, who require more care than sons. Through this he makes them very subject to the preachers who labor greatly in their cultivation.

In accordance with the Apostle: “Obey your leaders and be subject to them. For they keep watch over your souls as those who will have to give an account, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning” (Heb. XIII, 17).

The admonition and praise of the Bridegroom having been completed, he turns to praising and admonishing the bride, so that he may make her more attentive to obeying the Bridegroom. He does this as follows: “The queen stood,” etc.

He connects the passage in this way: I say, Son, that you will be exceedingly beautiful in form. The queen—that is, the primitive Church, betrothed to you, joined to you in the marriage of conformity and faith—which you will make a queen from a servant, and free from a slave through your death—stood, that is, will stand, before you, ready to obey.

She is like a good servant who always stands before his lord, ready to obey even at a sign. And the very fact that she will stand will proceed from your right hand, that is, from your propitiation, not from her merits.

He uses “right hand” for “propitiation,” because those who are to be saved in the future by divine propitiation are said to sit at God’s right hand.

I say that she will stand, and this in a garment, not a disgraceful one but a gilded one, that is, in the perfection of virtues with which she will be adorned, as a body is adorned with a precious garment.
