By gold, which is a precious and solid metal, the perfection of virtues is understood. And not in a simple garment, that is, in one virtue alone, but surrounded, that is, adorned, with a variety of virtues, after the manner of a bride adorned with various jewels.

It should be noted that he praises her by analogy with visible ornaments in order to draw her more effectively toward the perfection of virtues. Visible examples ordinarily provoke people more strongly than invisible ones.

Praise is followed by exhortation when he says: “Hear, daughter,” etc. He calls her “daughter” out of immense affection, because he will regenerate her through faith. He rightly uses the feminine form “daughter,” because he had begun to speak of her as a queen and as a bride.

He continues in this way: I say that the queen will stand in a gilded garment. But lest you lose this garment, O daughter, bride of my Son, hear the voice of the Bridegroom—not merely with outward hearing, but also see, that is, understand what you will hear, so that you may fulfill it.

Or it may be read in this way: Hear, see, and thus understand. For unless you believed, you would not understand.

And behold the voice of the Bridegroom that you will hear: Forget your people, that is, the carnal observances of your Jewish people, which were shadows of the New Testament. And also forget the house of your father, that is, the conduct of the devil, who until now has been your father. In accordance with the Gospel: “You are from your father the devil” (John VIII, 44).

He uses “house” for “conduct,” because human conduct takes place in a house.

Or it may be read in this way: Hear, daughter, what the prophets prophesied concerning your Bridegroom. And by hearing, see, that is, understand. And by understanding, forget your people, that is, the vices existing in you, which are called “people” because they are many, after the analogy of a people.

And forget the house of your father, the devil, so that you may no longer wish to be his house and dwelling.

He says this by analogy with a bride who, being closely joined to the bridegroom whom she loves, forgets her own people and her father’s house because of her love for him.

He shows what benefit will come to her if she forgets, so as to draw her more strongly toward this, as follows: And if you hear and see, and forget, the king—that is, your Bridegroom, my Son, who will rule you—will desire your beauty; that is, he will love you because of the beauty of your virtues, after the analogy of a bride who is loved by her bridegroom for her beauty.

And truly you ought to hear him and, for his sake, forget your people and your father’s house, because he is the Lord your God. For it is fitting that a servant should obey her lord, and a creature should obey her God.

[Col. 0832B]

He also announces the conversion of the Gentiles when he says: “And the daughters of Tyre will worship him,” etc.

The passage continues in this way: I have said that the queen, that is, the primitive Church, will stand before my Son. And not only will she stand before him, but the daughters of Tyre will also worship him, that is, the souls of the Gentiles, made daughters through faith.

By Tyre, because it is a place of the Gentiles, the Gentiles are understood. In the Hebrew translation it reads: “The strongest of Tyre will worship him,” that is, the martyrs from the Gentiles will venerate him, those who will be exceedingly strong amid the pressures of tribulations.

For Tyre is interpreted as “narrowness.” And they will not worship empty-handed, without gifts, but “with gifts,” that is, by offering themselves as gifts. In accordance with this: Whoever considers what he should vow to the Lord should prepare himself and make the vow. This is what is required; this is what is owed.

Nor will only the poor of Tyre worship you; but all the rich of the people—that is, people rich in plebeian, earthly things—will entreat your face, O queen. That is, they will entreat God to give them a face like yours, namely, the beauty of virtues, so that they too may be able to worship.

Because beauty ordinarily appears especially in the face, “face” is used for “beauty.” Or by “face” he means the inner sight, that is, understanding, by which one understands how God is to be worshiped. “Face” is rightly used for “sight,” since bodily sight is in the face.

But because he had praised the queen for her golden garment, lest it be thought that the glory of her beauty was outwardly located in the body, he determines the matter as follows: I have said that the queen will stand in a gilded garment. Yet this glorious garment is not to be understood as existing outwardly in the body; rather, all the glory of the king’s daughter—that is, the daughter of my Son, whom above I called the queen—will be inward, that is, from the soul, shining in golden borders, that is, in the perfection of charity, which appears through good works.

Perfection is signified by “borders,” because they are placed at the edge of garments. Charity is signified by gold, because it is more precious than every other virtue, just as gold is more precious than the other metals.

And she will not have glory only in golden borders; she will also be surrounded, that is, adorned, with varieties of virtues. This was also stated above when he said “surrounded with variety.” But because, in order to make the distinction, he had said “all her glory,” lest she be thought glorious only in the borders, he repeats the point.

Or the meaning may be different, as follows: I have said that the glory of the king’s daughter will be inward, and the daughter herself will also be surrounded, that is, encircled, with varieties, that is, with various nations, which will believe through her example and adorn her after the manner of garments, which adorn the body by surrounding it.

Someone might ask: How will she be surrounded with varieties of nations? He answers as follows: She will be surrounded in this manner: Other virgins from the Gentiles—that is, faithful souls who will be incorrupt in faith, after the manner of virgins who are incorrupt in body—will be brought through the teaching of the Fathers, that is, the apostles, to the king, that is, to Christ my Son, after her, the queen.

These virgins will not be alien from conformity, even though they are alien in origin. Rather, being near to her in conformity, they will be brought to you, that is, for the service of honoring you, O Son, through the teaching of the Fathers.

He rightly says “they will be brought,” in order to make them humble, indicating that they cannot approach by themselves, since they are weak in understanding; but they will be brought through the teaching of the Fathers, like a sick person who is carried by another because he cannot walk by himself.

These virgins will not be brought to you unwillingly; they will be brought in joy—and not in a small joy, but also, that is, specifically, in exultation, namely, in the greatest joy.

It should be noted that they will be brought in this manner in the present life. In the future, however, they will be brought by you into the temple of your king, namely, into the heavenly Jerusalem, which is your temple and dwelling.

It should also be noted that “surrounded with varieties” and “virgins will be brought to the king after her” mean the same thing. He repeats the statement, however, so that, by drawing them more strongly toward this, he may show that for this reason they will eventually be brought into the temple of the king.

Someone might say: You say that virgins will be brought to the king through the teaching of the Fathers. I confess that this is true; but after the Fathers have died—for they will truly die, since they are human—will no virgins be brought? For there will be no one to bring them.

He answers as follows: They will certainly be brought through their sons, that is, through bishops and priests and the other pastors of the Church, the successors of the apostles.

For the Fathers—that is, in the place of the Fathers, namely the apostles—sons have been born, that is, will be born in faith and in the office of preaching: sons, namely, bishops and the other pastors. And this is for you, that is, for your work.

And you will establish these sons as princes over the whole earth, that is, over the whole Church, which is stable and solid like earth, and which will generate fruits for you, namely good works, after the manner of earth, which produces the fruits of the harvest.

You will establish them as princes in such a way that whatever they bind or loose on earth will be bound or loosed also in heaven (Matt. XVI, 19).

Once established as princes, they will not be idle. Rather, I will remember your name, that is, I will make them mindful of your name, so that they may preach it in every generation of the Jews and in every generation of the Gentiles, through the succession of generations.

For until the end of the world there will be no generation, whether Jewish or Gentile, in which the name of God is not preached.

Because the sons will remember by preaching, the peoples of the Jews and of the Gentiles will confess you, that is, praise you by believing, forever—that is, for as long as this present world endures, until the age of the age that follows this one.

This Psalm may also be read as spoken in the person of the Prophet, making the reading clearer, if only the exposition of the first two verses is changed.

If it is understood as spoken in the person of the Prophet, it does not concern the ineffable generation of the Word, as it does when spoken in the person of the Father. Rather, in the first two verses he makes a kind of prologue, so as to make the hearers more attentive, setting forth what he will discuss in this work: namely, the king, that is, Christ, antonomastically the King.

To him he later says, not exhortatively or imperatively, but concessively and prayerfully, that he should gird himself with the sword of preaching. For a creature ought not to exhort the Creator, the ignorant one the one who knows, nor should a servant command the Lord.

He praises, after the king himself, the Bridegroom of the Church, for our instruction and conformity, so that he may also invite us to praise him and show him to be worthy of praise. He likewise praises his bride, the primitive Church, transformed from a handmaid into a queen, so that by his praise he may move her to obey the Bridegroom, through whom the bride is beautiful. He also exhorts her to hear the Bridegroom’s voice and obey him, calling her “daughter” out of excessive affection—either the daughter of his Prophet according to teaching, or of Christ himself according to regeneration. He also prophetically announces the bringing of the nations to faith through the preaching of the apostles and their sons.

[Col. 0834C] “My heart has poured forth a good word”—which is to say: My heart has arranged to bring forth a good word in speaking. By calling it “good,” he invites us to attend carefully to that word, because it is good. He shows how it is good when he adds: “Truly it will be good.” For “my works,” namely, my word, “I dedicate,” that is, I devote and consecrate, “to the king,” that is, to Christ, antonomastically the King. It is as though he said: Here I shall speak about the King, to whom I dedicate this work of mine. And *dico* is declined not as *dico, dicis*, but as *dico, dicas*, meaning “I devote and consecrate.”

But this word that I shall pour forth will not come from me; rather, “my tongue will be the pen of a swiftly writing scribe,” that is, of the Holy Spirit writing swiftly through that pen. He says this by way of comparison. For just as a pen does not form letters by itself, but does so when the scribe moves it, so my tongue will form words not by itself, but when moved by the Holy Spirit. And he rightly says “of one writing swiftly.” For the Holy Spirit speaks through him swiftly, without prior deliberation, so that it may be shown that the words themselves come not from the Prophet, but from the Holy Spirit. And behold the word that my heart resolved to pour forth:

“O most powerful King, Christ, gird yourself with your sword upon your thigh. For you will be beautiful in form beyond the sons of men,” and so forth. These words are not now changed, but are read here just as above.

# ON PSALM XLV

[Col. 0835A]

## Title of the Forty-Fifth Psalm

“To the end; for the sons of Korah; concerning hidden things; a psalm of David.”

This psalm is David’s, that is, of the primitive Church, which is strong-handed and acts manfully in tribulations. It is proposed for the sons of Korah, that is, for the sons of the Crucified, in faith and conformity. I say “for sons tending toward the end,” that is, toward the consummation of the true and highest good.

This psalm is understood as concerning hidden things, that is, in contemplation of and on account of hidden matters—namely, the secret counsels of God: specifically, that “blindness has happened in part to Israel, so that the fullness of the nations might enter” (Rom. XI, 25); that in the future the remnant of Israel will be saved; and that he permitted his own people to be afflicted by the Jews in the primitive Church. Those who afterward were converted became preachers to the nations, where they too were severely worn down by tribulations. All these matters are hidden, and few or none know why they have been so ordered by God.

It should also be noted that the primitive faithful are introduced here not as speaking of the past, saying that they were steadfast, but as promising that they will remain steadfast in the tribulations that will be inflicted by Jews and by the nations during the apostles’ preaching; and this is for the instruction of the other sons of Korah. They are more appropriately introduced as speaking of the future than of the past, so that, by showing through the prophetic Spirit that they already know beforehand that they will be steadfast and fearless, they may invite the succeeding sons of Korah to steadfastness by their example. They also show that preachers will be made joyful, strengthened, and assisted by the Lord amid tribulations, so that they may indicate to the sons of Korah, for whom they speak, that the same will happen to them [Col. 0835C] if they do not fail.

They also say that it is not surprising if the earth is shaken against the preachers during their preaching, since it was shaken even against the Lord’s voice. They likewise explain the voice and the benefit that came through that voice, for the instruction and exhortation of those same sons of Korah.

“Our God is refuge and strength.” This is to say: We have no refuge in anything earthly, but our God—that is, the one whom we acknowledge as God—is our refuge in every necessity. And he is not merely any refuge, but “strength,” that is, firm and unconquerable. “Strength” is used emphatically. He is not only refuge, so that we may not yield, but also “helper” in tribulations, that is, a fellow-worker, so that we may conquer our enemies by incorporating them into ourselves.

“I say, in tribulations that found us.” It is as though he said: We did not seek them, nor did we encounter them because of evil merits of our own; rather, they themselves, while troubling the Church and wishing to destroy it entirely, found us. And they found us “exceedingly”—not only by stripping us of our possessions, but also by afflicting our flesh severely and even to the shedding of blood.

And because our God is our refuge, strength, and helper, “we will not fear when the earth is troubled against the preachers.” “Earth” means Judaea, which was formerly God’s earth, cultivated by him through the teaching of the prophets; or it means the earthly, clinging to earthly things rather than spiritual ones. This is to say: We will not be fearful, but steadfast in the tribulations that the troubled earth will inflict.

“And while this occurs, the mountains”—that is, the apostles, exalted by the height of holiness and innocence—“will be transferred into the heart of the sea,” that is, into the depth of the nations, which flowed diffusely into every vice like the sea and made God bitter by serving idols. “Heart” is used for “depth,” because it is in the interior. It is as though he said: They will not be transferred merely into some small part, but into the fullness of the nations.

Or in this sense: “The mountains will be transferred,” that is, the teachings of the mountains will be transferred “into the heart of the sea,” that is, of the nations, so that they may receive them not only with the ear of the body, but also with the heart.

Lest it be thought that the mountains would be transferred among the nations in order to hide timidly there rather than preach to them, he adds: “I say that they will be transferred into the heart of the sea, and there they will not hide, but will sound forth,” that is, they will preach openly to them, in the manner of a sound, which is an open and manifest thing. “And by their sound,” that is, by their preaching, “they have been troubled,” that is, they will be troubled, “against the mountains—their waters,” that is, the peoples of that sea.

He uses “their” in the plural because *sea* is a collective noun and signifies many things. Why peoples are called waters was explained in the first psalm. Or “they will be troubled” means that their waters, that is, their doctrines concerning the superstitious worship of idols, will show themselves to be turbid and muddy. They are called waters because from them they give drink to fools who comply with them.

This is to say: Their waters, that is, their doctrines, which seemed good, clear, and useful, like clear water useful for drinking, will be shown by their sound to be turbid, useless, and foul, resembling muddy water, which is turbid, foul, and useless.

“And the mountains,” that is, the preachers themselves, “have been troubled,” that is, they will be troubled by carnal fear. For they are human beings amid the strength of that sea, that is, amid the powerful boiling of the sea’s tribulations. Nevertheless, they will not fail in their disturbance. For “the force of the river,” that is, the abundance of the Holy Spirit, “makes glad,” that is, will make glad inwardly, “the city of God”—namely, the mountains, which are a city well fortified by virtues.

The river is called the Holy Spirit because he waters and gives drink to his own with wisdom and counsel, like a river that waters abundantly. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, as the prophet says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” He said this about the Spirit (John VII, 38).

And by making them joyful in the very tribulations, “the Most High and Powerful One has sanctified,” that is, will confirm in steadfastness, “his tabernacle,” that is, the city of preachers who serve in his army [Col. 0836D].

He says this as an exhortation to the succeeding sons of Korah, for whom they speak, so that they may not fail if they fear in tribulations because of the weakness of the flesh, but may trust that they likewise will be made joyful and strengthened.

“I say that the Most High has sanctified.” The Most High is God, who always exists in the midst of that city—that is, he adheres to its reason not locally but in a special way—so that it may be steadfast. This reason is called “the midst” by comparison: just as, by the measure of the point that is the center, the whole circle is made equal, and could scarcely or never proceed rightly in another way, so by the measure of reason the whole human being is directed; otherwise he would be distorted.

Since God is in its midst, it will not be moved in tribulations from its purpose of steadfastness. And he will not only sanctify it so that it does not yield, but God will also help it conquer its enemies: “in the morning,” that is, at dawn—namely, through the illumination of his counsel and wisdom.

Here “morning” means the same as “dawn,” namely illumination. But lest it seem to have been placed merely to designate the morning time, which it signifies elsewhere as well, he adds “dawn” to specify this meaning. For the word *dawn* is related by composition to the word *light*.

With the Lord helping, “the nations have been troubled,” that is, they will be troubled with a good disturbance toward faith. And not just a few nations: “kingdoms have been inclined,” that is, many nations will humble themselves by approaching the faith, setting aside the pride of their unbelief. He rightly uses “kingdoms” for “multitude,” since when many nations are contained within one kingdom, many more are contained within many kingdoms.

Or in this sense: “Kingdoms have been inclined,” that is, they have been humbled for the purpose of becoming kingdoms of God, though previously they served the devil.

Above he had said that the earth would be troubled against the preachers. Lest this seem surprising, and lest it be wondered why God would permit it, he says that the earth was also moved against God’s own preaching; therefore it is not worthy of wonder if it is moved against his disciples. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John XV, 20).

He speaks of how the earth was moved against God as follows: “The earth will be troubled against the mountains,” and this is not surprising. For “the Lord of the heavenly powers”—that is, the one who is Lord of angels, not merely of human beings—“gave his voice,” that is, his preaching; and against him the earth was moved, namely Judaea, with an evil disturbance, calling him a deceiver and a sinner.

Where we have *Dominus virtutum* (“Lord of hosts”), the Hebrews have *Adonai Sabaoth*, meaning “Lord of armies,” namely of the heavenly armies. He explains how he gave his voice: “I say that the Lord of hosts gave his voice with us,” existing with us—that is, in our humanity. This is to say: He did not give his voice according to divinity, but according to human nature. In Hebrew it is *Emmanuel*, that is, “God with us.”

[Col. 0837D]

Someone might say: The earth should not be greatly blamed for being moved against him, since he existed with us, that is, was human just as we are. To this he adds: It truly should be blamed. For, existing with us, “he is our protector,” that is, our physician and patron.

This is to say: He became human so that by his death he might be our physician and patron. And it should still be blamed for another reason: he is not a newly made god, but the God of Jacob—that is, the God whom Jacob worshiped, the eternal God. What greater madness, then, than to rise up against one’s God, physician, and patron?

Someone might say: What is surprising if the earth was moved against his voice? Was that voice useful for anything? In response, to show what benefit came through that voice, he exhorts us by explaining its usefulness:

“I said that the Lord gave his voice, and it was nevertheless exceedingly useful. If you ask what it was useful for, come by faith and see with understanding the works of the Lord, who through that voice placed wonders,” that is, marvels, “upon the earth,” that is, upon the Church, which is his earth.

He rightly says “upon the earth.” For, after the likeness of the heavenly citizens, he placed those works on earth. He explains the works as follows: “He is removing wars,” that is, the enmities that they had toward God and neighbor through evil living. And he is not removing wars in only a few nations, but “to the end of the earth,” that is, throughout the whole world.

Or in this sense: He is not removing wars only in part, but “to the end of the earth,” that is, to such an extent that all earthliness in them is brought to an end.

This is as though he said: He gave peace to his earth, both toward God and toward neighbor—the peace possessed by the heavenly citizens. Hence the angels are read to have sung at his birth: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men,” and so forth (Luke II, 14). And he himself says in the Gospel: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV, 27).

But so that wars may be removed entirely, “he will crush,” that is, destroy in his earth, “the bow, and he will break the weapons and shields,” that is, destroy them completely. He explains how he will destroy them: He will burn all these things with fire, that is, consume them by the Holy Spirit.

The bow signifies deceit, both against God and against neighbor. The weapons signify open assault—against God by reviling him, and against one’s neighbor by treating him badly. The shield signifies the defense of error by false arguments. God destroys all these things in his own people, since otherwise complete peace would not be present among them.

Having shown the usefulness of the voice, he joins the voice itself to the instruction of those for whom he speaks, so that they may believe his word:

“I said that the Lord gave this voice: You who are destined to be my members, be free from concern for earthly things and from the worship of idols, and thus see with understanding; for otherwise you would not understand that I, who am speaking to you as a human being, am your God,” according to what he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII, 25).

“And I, who am God, will be exalted among the nations for the present.” Hence the Apostle says: “Blindness has happened in part to Israel, so that the fullness of the nations might enter” (Rom. XI, 25) [Col. 0838D].

“And I will be exalted in the earth at the end of the world,” that is, in Judaea. Hence the prophet says: “The remnant will be saved” (Isa. X, 21; Rom. IX, 27). And in Psalm XX: “In your remnants you will prepare their face.”

This is as though he said: My worship will presently be exalted throughout the nations; in the future, however, it will be exalted among the Jews.

He repeats what he said above: “The Lord of hosts,” and so forth, impressing it upon them so that he may commend the word placed here, as follows: “You ought rightly to believe this voice that I have given: ‘Be free,’ and so forth. For it is not the voice of just anyone, but he uttered it who is the Lord of hosts, our protector, and the God of Jacob.” This is explained here as above.

# ON PSALM XLVI

[Col. 0839A]

## Title of the Forty-Sixth Psalm

“To the end; for the sons of Korah; a psalm.”

This is explained as follows: This psalm was composed for the sons of Korah, that is, for the benefit of the sons of the Crucified, who tend toward the end, that is, toward the consummation of the true good. The apostles are introduced here exhorting all the sons of Korah to praise God by deed and affection, and also with a voice of exultation.

They add several reasons why they ought to praise him: because he is exalted and fearful, because he ascended into heaven, and because he subjected the whole world to himself. At the end they show how he subjected it.

“All nations, clap your hands.” It is as though he said: Not only the Jews, as under the old law, but all of you nations—Jews and Gentiles—clap your hands to God Christ, that is, rejoice in God’s praise through good works, after the likeness of those who clap their hands because of excessive joy. Since we work with our hands, “hands” is used for “works.”

And do not clap only with your hands, but also “shout in jubilation to God,” that is, praise God with jubilation, meaning inward joy that cannot be expressed either by letters or by syllables. And shout in jubilation so that you persevere “in the voice of exultation,” that is, in the voice of exulting while praising and preaching him.

For he says the same in the Gospel: “Whoever acknowledges me before men, I too will acknowledge him before my Father” (Luke XII, 8).

And behold the reasons why you ought to clap your hands to him, shout in jubilation, and exult: because Christ himself, who in his passion appeared lowly, almost like a servant, “is the exalted Lord of all” [Col. 0839C]. As the Psalmist says elsewhere: “Your magnificence has been exalted above the heavens” (Ps. VIII, 2).

And he who appeared terrified will be fearful to the unjust in the future. Hence blessed Gregory says: “He will appear gentle to the just and fearful to the unjust.” And the Apostle says: “It is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. X, 31).

And he who appeared powerless is a great king. And truly he is great, for he is king over the whole earth. Hence elsewhere: “I have been established as king by him” (Ps. II, 6).

And it becomes evident that he is a great king and God because he also subjected to us, his servants, the peoples of the Jews—namely, he placed the faithful and the nations under our feet, that is, subjected them greatly to us, after the likeness of one who is subjected beneath another’s feet.

This is to say: He subjected those who would believe from the Jews and the nations to our governance; and by this it is evident that they themselves are subjected all the more.

But that he subjected the nations to us did not occur through their merits. Rather, “he chose our inheritance,” that is, by the election of his mercy he subjected to us the nations, which are his inheritance and which he cultivates through us.

Since not all are his inheritance, he explains which inheritance he chose: “He chose the beauty of Jacob,” that is, the beauty of the nations prefigured by Jacob. For through Jacob, who stole the blessing from his elder brother, the nations were prefigured; they were destined to succeed the Jews.

The Lord loved Jacob while neglecting Esau, of whom it is written: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I, 3; Rom. IX, 13).

Or otherwise: “He chose the beauty of Jacob,” that is, beautiful Jacob—namely, those among the nations who are beautiful to the lesser ones, wrestlers and supplanters of vices. “Whom Jacob loved,” that is, whom he loved as beautiful before the foundation of the world, in his providence.

And therefore continue to clap your hands, shout in jubilation, and exult, because “God himself has ascended into the heavens,” although he seemed to be merely a simple human being. And this occurred amid “the jubilation of the apostles,” that is, while we apostles rejoiced with inward joy, which is called jubilation.

And the Lord himself, existing as Lord of all, ascended “with the sound of the trumpet,” that is, with the testimony of angels made in an elemental voice, which was manifest like the sound of a trumpet. Therefore it is called the voice of a trumpet, because the angels are read to have said: “Men of Galilee,” and so forth (Acts I, 11).

Therefore, because he ascended in this manner, and because he is exalted, fearful, and a great king, “sing praise to our God,” that is, work well to his praise, because he is our God.

I say, sing praise. “And sing praise to our king,” that is, sing praise to him because he is our king. He repeats “sing praise” so often in order to exhort them more strongly.

And not only because he is our king—that is, the king of us apostles—but because “God is king of the whole earth,” that is, of every kind of earth, sing praise to him. And do this wisely, that is, as praise ought to be sung, not with arrogance or negligence.

Someone might say: Why do you say that he is king of the whole earth, since God belongs only to the Jews? To this he adds: I rightly said “of the whole earth.” For God will reign not only over the Jews, but also over the nations.

He explains over which nations as follows: He will not reign in such a way that he does not reign now, but “even now he sits forever, destined to sit upon his holy throne,” that is, he sits upon those from the nations who are his holy throne, so that he may direct them from good to better. Hence the Prophet says: “His kingdom will have no end” (Mic. IV, 7; Luke I, 33).

Someone might ask: How did he prepare a kingdom for himself among the nations? He answers that “the princes of the peoples,” that is, kings, leaders, and others, “have gathered together for faith”—not with a newly made god, but with the God of Abraham, that is, with the eternal God whom Abraham worshiped by living well, not by disagreeing with him and living perversely.

By “princes,” their inferiors are signified as having gathered together.

It might also be asked: Did they gather by free choice? The answer is: By no means. Rather, they gathered through us, who are “the gods of the earth,” that is, the Church, which is God’s earth; or “gods of the earth,” that is, deified from earthly beings, which we formerly were.

For we, the gods of the earth, strong in the steadfastness of preaching, were greatly exalted in the power of miracles, “the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark XVI, 20). Through the preaching and miracles of those gods, the princes of the peoples were gathered.

The apostles are rightly called gods because they are spiritual sons of God; insofar as possible, they were conformed to Christ, who is God, in holiness of life; and in heaven, after the release of the flesh, they share in his glory. Hence the Psalmist says: “I said: You are gods” (Ps. LXXXI, 6).

# ON PSALM XLVII

[Col. 0841A]

## Title of the Forty-Seventh Psalm

“A psalm of a song, of the sons of Korah, for the second day of the Sabbath.”

This is explained as follows: This tract, that is, this psalm, is “a psalm of a song,” that is, a tract of joy, containing the foundation of the Church. Therefore joy ought to be held by all the faithful.

Or it is a psalm of joy, that is, one showing how great was the joy of the Church at its foundation.

In this psalm the sons of Korah are introduced—namely, the apostles—speaking about what was signified by what occurred on the second day of the Sabbath, that is, about the reality prefigured by the firmament created by God on the second day of the Sabbath. The Latins call this day Monday; the Hebrews, counting the days from the Sabbath, call it the second day of the Sabbath.

For the firmament made by God on the second day of the Sabbath, after the creation of light, prefigured the foundation of the Church. This foundation occurred after the radiant resurrection of Christ, which resurrection is the illumination of our understanding.

Hence Augustine also calls the whole period from Christ’s resurrection to the end of the world “the second day of the Sabbath,” because throughout that entire period the Church is founded by God from generation to generation, just as we understand the establishment of the firmament to have occurred on the second day of the Sabbath.

This firmament is rightly called the firmament of the Church, because it is made firm in the perfection of virtues. Concerning it, the Lord is read to have said to Peter in the Gospel: “Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI, 18).

In this psalm the apostles speak about this foundation of the Church, saying with what exultation of all the nations it was made from Jews and Gentiles, and how steadfast it is, so that it may not fail in any way through fear of earthly rulers, but may draw them to conformity with itself by the example of its steadfastness and by the admiration inspired by its glorious foundation.

And because the Church was founded in this way, he shows that the Lord Christ appears great and praiseworthy in it, so as to attract his hearers to his praise.

He commands the citizens who are in it, from Jews and Gentiles, to rejoice in its foundation; and he urges the nations, who are less perfect, to imitate the more perfect faithful from among the Jews; and, so that they may imitate only the good, he warns them to beware of false preachers.

He speaks of this glorious foundation of the Church in order to invite those who are not yet its citizens to approach it; and, once they have become citizens, to admonish them to persevere in it:

“Great is the Lord Jesus.” I do not mean in bodily size, but in the sublimity of power. “And praiseworthy,” that is, worthy of praise. And this “exceedingly,” that is, beyond human capacity, “in the city of our God”—namely, of Christ—“on his holy mountain.”

This is to say: The Lord Jesus, who appears great and praiseworthy in the foundation of his city, that is, of the Church, which is his holy mountain, made exalted in virtues after the manner of a mountain—this same Jesus will not only be seen to be Lord, but will also be recognized as God “in the houses of his city,” that is, in the contemplation of the faithful who are the houses of his city, whom he inhabits and confirms in every virtue.

This is to say: He will appear to be a great and praiseworthy Lord not only through the glorious foundation of his city; through the admirable firmness of the houses of that same city it will also be established that he is Lord.

Or in this sense: Though he is not recognized as God by everyone, in the houses of his city—that is, among the faithful—he will be recognized as God. And he will be recognized when he receives that city in order to preserve it in tribulations, so that it does not fail, after the likeness of a patron who receives one oppressed by another in order to protect him.

Since he had said that the Lord was great and praiseworthy in the city, someone might ask: Why is he praiseworthy in the city? To this he responds by inserting the reason why he ought to be seen as great and praiseworthy in the city:

“Truly he is great and praiseworthy in the city.” For that city of the great King, namely of the Lord Jesus, “is founded by the King himself,” that is, it is firmly established by him; and this occurs “with the exultation of the whole earth,” that is, it is founded in such a way that all peoples, both Gentiles and Jews, exult in its foundation.

And since they might be understood to exult as though they were not in that city, he shows that it is constituted from both peoples when he adds: “And the city itself is Mount Zion, and the sides of the north”—that is, it is constituted from Mount Zion and from the sides of the north, namely from Jews and Gentiles.

“Mount Zion” is called the people of the Jews, not because it was exalted in virtues, but in relation to the worship of God which it practiced; by practicing that worship it contemplated God, whereas the unbelief of the nations lacked it.

The “sides of the north” are called the nation of the devil, because, being his satellites, they always had him as their leader. This is after the likeness of clients who, by enclosing their lord’s side as they follow him, are called his sides—that is, those who press closely around his sides.

The north is called the devil because, being cold in relation to the warmth of divine charity, he makes others who consent to him cold in the same way, and thus sterile in good works. This is like the north wind, which, being a cold wind, makes the earth cold and constricts it, preventing the generation of flowers.

Hence the bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind,” and so forth (Song IV, 16).

Since he had said that the Lord would receive the city in tribulations in order to preserve it, someone might ask: Why, then, is it necessary for him to receive the city? To this question he responds:

It is necessary for him to receive it because, behold, “the earthly kings have gathered together,” that is, will gather together. He explains how they will gather when he adds: “They came together,” that is, they will come together with one purpose of malice, in order to persecute that city.

And when they who come together for this purpose see that it is founded in this way—namely, from Mount Zion and the sides of the north, and with the exultation of the whole earth—and that its Lord is great and praiseworthy, “they have admired,” that is, will admire, its firmness and steadfastness.

And while admiring, “they have been troubled,” that is, will be troubled, with a good disturbance, grieving that they had persecuted it; and, being troubled, “they have been moved,” that is, will be moved, from unbelief to faith and from wickedness to justice.

And they will not be troubled only a little, but to such an extent that “trembling seized,” that is, will seize, them—such fear, namely, that it will also be shown by trembling of the body.

He rightly says “seized.” They will strive, under the devil’s prompting, to escape death, but in vain; for it will pursue them so severely that it will also seize them, after the likeness of one who is caught while striving to escape.

He shows for what purpose they will be moved through this disturbance:

“I said that trembling would seize them; and there, in that trembling, the pains were not fruitless, but were like those of a woman in labor,” that is, similar to the pains of a woman in labor, who suffers pain for the purpose of giving birth afterward.

This is to say: From the pains of this trembling there will follow the birth of holiness and good works [Col. 0843B].

Lest they be thought to be troubled and moved through free choice, he adds: “And this disturbance will not be from them; but you, God Christ, in a vehement Spirit”—that is, a strong and effective Spirit—“will crush,” that is, destroy completely in them, “the ships of Tarshish,” that is, the wanderings and anxious pursuits of investigation—namely, of worldly joy.

This is to say: You will destroy in them the anxiety that makes them wander and toil in seeking how they may rejoice in worldly things. This is equivalent to saying: You will destroy in them concern for earthly matters, so that they will not seek joy in them, and thus you will make them conform to your own people.

Anxieties are called ships because by thinking we wander through them, just as one wanders by ship across the sea. *Tarshish* is interpreted as “exploration of joy.” According to Remigius, however, among the Hebrews it is interpreted as “sea,” and according to this it is explained as follows:

“You will crush the ships of Tarshish,” namely, you will destroy in evil what you will build in good: the kings themselves, who are called ships of the sea—that is, of this world—because, like ships that carry people across the sea, they too carry their subjects by the governance of their rule.

The world is called the sea because, like the sea, it is greatly disturbed by the storm of tribulations.

When he says, “As we have heard,” and so forth, he shows that the testimony of the prophets concerning the foundation of the Church was true, since in it the things they foretold are seen to have been completely fulfilled. By this he indicates that the foundation of the Church is by no means some worthless and despicable thing, since it was confirmed by the ancient authority of such great men.

The passage is connected as follows: Therefore, because the Church was founded from both peoples, as we said above, and is so steadfast that it not only does not yield but even conquers, just as had been foretold by the prophets, we can truly affirm that, “as we heard” with the hearing of understanding in the books of the prophets, so we have seen it fulfilled “in the city of the Lord of hosts,” that is, of the heavenly armies, “in the city of our God,” that is, of Christ—not in the city of another Lord of hosts, since there is no other Lord in the Church.

He explains what was fulfilled in it:

This is what we saw fulfilled in the city of the Lord of hosts: “God founded it,” establishing it with a foundation that will endure forever.

Someone might ask: Through which ministers? The answer is: Through us. He founded it in this way:

“Because at the beginning we received your mercy, O God Christ,” that is, the Paraclete Spirit, through whose gift you had mercy on humanity, and for this reason he is called “mercy”; and we received this “in the midst of your temple,” that is, in the manifestation of your temple.

Since the things placed in the middle are manifest, “middle” is used for “manifestation.”

This is to say: We received the Holy Spirit to such a degree that, through his grace cooperating in miracles through us, it might be manifested that we are your temple.

And once they had been made righteous through us, O God Christ, “according to your name,” that is, according to the measure of your name, “so also”—that is, likewise—“your praise is great,” namely, it has been spread “to the ends of the earth” [Col. 0844B].

This is to say: We have spread your praise so widely that it is proclaimed throughout the whole world, just as the name “God,” or another name equivalent to it, is proclaimed in every place on earth.

Among the Hebrews, this name is *El*; among the Greeks, Θεὸς (*Theos*); and among the other nations, other names of this kind.

Since God’s praise could be proclaimed in every region, but only among a few in each one, lest they seem to be few he adds:

“And your right hand is full of justice,” that is, your power or your mercy is full of just people.

This is as though he said: The just whom your mercy and power have acquired through us are not few, but many. You are entirely full of them and surrounded by them, after the likeness of a hand which, when it holds many things, is full and packed with them.

The right hand is used for power because greater strength and power are in the right hand than in the left. It is also used for mercy because by it he helps the one who is slipping, just as anyone’s right hand often extends assistance to one who is falling.

When he says that God’s praise has been spread through him, he does not say this out of a swelling of pride, but out of thanksgiving.

He exhorts the citizens of this city to rejoice in God’s judgments, recognizing that they are just and not murmuring against them, as follows:

Therefore, because the city of God has been firmly founded by God and subjected to such a king, you, its citizens, rejoice to his praise. “Let Mount Zion rejoice,” that is, the gathering of the faithful from the Jews; “and let the daughters of Judah exult,” that is, the faithful from the nations whom Judah gave birth to in faith—namely, the confession of the preachers of the primitive Church from among the Jews.

This is to say: They acquired them for God through the confession of their preaching, and for this reason they are called their daughters. They are rightly called daughters, not sons, because they are most beautiful in virtues; for greater beauty is usually found in daughters than in sons.

Or “your daughters” means the primitive Church, which was from the tribe of Judah.

I say, let them rejoice and exult, and let this be “because of your judgments, Lord,” because you judged that the Church should be constituted from Jews and Gentiles.

He also exhorts the daughters of Judah to strive in every way to imitate the perfect faithful from among the Jews—that is, the preachers, who are more perfect because they have possessed knowledge of the one God for a longer time.

[Col. 0845A] I said to you, O daughters of Judah, “Rejoice”; this also I admonish you: “Surround Zion,” that is, imitate the perfected ones from the Jews, investigating their holiness—after the likeness of someone who surrounds another and moves about him in order to observe his actions. And so that you may imitate perfectly, “embrace” her, that is, love her. Since embracing belongs to those who love, he uses “embrace” for “love.”

He explains in detail how they are to imitate her when he adds: I say, “Surround Zion,” that is, imitate her, in this manner: “Tell it to others in her towers,” that is, in conformity with her preachers of the primitive Church. They are called towers because they are impregnable to vices and fortify the Church of holiness by their strength, after the manner of towers.

And do not imitate her only in proclamation; in order that you may imitate Zion [Col. 0845B] in virtue also, “set your hearts,” that is, the consideration of your hearts, “upon her virtue”: consider how great her virtue is, so that you too may conform yourselves to her in virtue. By “virtue” he means either the force of her steadfastness or the charity that she has toward God and neighbor. This is called “virtue” by antonomasia because it is more excellent than the other virtues.

I said, “Tell it in conformity with the towers.” But lest you be led astray by false apostles, “who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matt. VII, 13), “separate,” that is, set apart, “her houses,” Zion’s towers, from those pseudo-apostles. This is to say: exercise discernment between the pseudo-apostles and the towers, so that you may proclaim in conformity with the towers “in the generation that will follow,” [Col. 0845C] not only in the present one.

Or in this way: proclaim not only in your own persons, but also “in,” that is, through, the generation that will follow. It is as though he were saying: If you conformed yourselves to the pseudo-apostles, your proclamations would not be authoritative, nor would they be recited from generation to generation. But conform yourselves to the towers, and what you proclaim will be authoritative. Another generation that follows will also proclaim it to others; and proclaim it through another generation, that is, let the generation that follows proclaim what has been proclaimed by you.

“For God is here,” that is, in the Church; and he is not another, but “our God, Christ,” “for ever,” that is, for as long as this world shall endure, “and unto the age of the age” that follows, never abandoning her. And he is not in her in such a way that he does nothing [Col. 0845D] there; rather, this same God of ours will rule us, lest we be turned aside from his way, “unto everlasting ages.” He says this in order to invite still more those who are unfaithful to become sons of the Church.

## ON PSALM XLVIII

### The Title of the Forty-Eighth Psalm

“Unto the end, for the sons of Korah. A Psalm of David.” This is explained as follows: This psalm belongs to David the prophet or to the apostles. David, I say, speaks to the sons of Korah so that they may strive to remain sons “unto the end of sonship,” that is, insofar as they are able to be sons. This means that they should be sons in perseverance and perfection.

In this psalm the apostles or prophets intend to recall all the sons of Korah—among both Jews and Gentiles, both the perfect and the imperfect, both the rich and the poor—from iniquity: specifically, from trusting in their own virtue and boasting in the multitude of their riches. They show that iniquity alone is the reason why they will fear and be condemned in the future, without ever being redeemed; and, in order to turn them back from iniquity more effectively, they affirm that the righteous will not be redeemed.

But in order to make those to whom they speak attentive to this instruction, they exhort them to listen, so that they may understand. They promise that they will speak wisdom, and not without forethought; yet they will not possess it from themselves, but from the teacher Truth, who presides within them.

“Listen with the ears of your heart to these things that I am about to tell you, O all nations,” that is, all the faithful from the nations; “and you faithful from the Jews who inhabit the world,” that is, you who are not mobile and temporary in the world, that is, in the perfection of virtues, [Col. 0846B] but who dwell there and remain steadfast: perceive these things with your ears, that is, hear them outwardly in such a way that you also perceive them with your heart.

He uses “world”—which means the same as “roundness”—for perfection. For just as dirt cannot cling to round bodies, so vices cannot cling to those who are perfect in virtue.

He does not say that the Jews alone inhabit the world, that is, perfection, because many from the nations did not inhabit it and still do not; rather, because certain Jews in the primitive Church were more perfect than others, he speaks universally: “Listen, all nations, and all you who inhabit the world.”

He explains this in detail, as follows: listen to these things, not only you who are perfect, but also “all you earth-born,” [Col. 0846C] and “all you sons of men,” that is, all you who still cling to earthly things and are imperfect; and “sons of men,” that is, those who use reason as human beings, who are perfect. And let not only the rich or the poor hear this, but “let the rich hear this, and let the poor hear this,” proceeding together into concord—that is, not with one listening carelessly and the other attentively, but with both listening attentively.

Let the rich hear in order to learn not to boast in riches, once I have shown that they produce condemnation rather than salvation. Let the poor hear in order that, by attending to these same things, they may be comforted concerning poverty and despise riches.

He then makes them attentive to listening in this way: I said, “Listen,” and I am to be heard. For I shall not speak empty and useless things, but “my mouth shall speak wisdom,” that is, something pertaining to a wise life. And I shall not speak without forethought, but “the meditation of my heart shall bring forth prudence,” that is, wisdom.

He rightly says, humbling himself, not “I shall speak,” but “my mouth shall speak.” For if he had said, “I shall speak,” it might appear that he possessed this from himself. But by saying, “my mouth shall speak,” he indicates that it will not be from himself, and that his mouth alone will be the instrument of this discourse. He clearly shows this in what follows, namely, that it will not be from himself:

I say that “my mouth shall speak wisdom,” but you should know that it is not from me, so that you may regard it as more authoritative. Rather, it is from the teacher Truth, who presides within me, and from the Holy Spirit. “I shall incline my ear to a parable,” after the likeness of a good servant who inclines his ear in order to hear his lord’s words attentively. I shall incline, that is, I shall direct the ear of my heart toward a parable, that is, inwardly toward hearing the work of the parable, from that teacher Truth. And after learning with my ear inclined, “I shall open,” that is, I shall manifestly display, my proposition, that is, the parable, not only with my mouth but “on the psaltery,” that is, through good works.

This means: I shall display it not only by my voice but also by good works; and this display through works is much more effective than through the voice alone.

Since a psaltery is a kind of musical instrument through which a song is expressed by the action of the hands, “psaltery” is used for good works. By “parable” he means the instruction that he is about to give, because it is not expressed in plain words but as if through certain likenesses: for example, when he uses “heel” for “condition,” and when he says, “He was compared to beasts” (Ps. XLVIII, 13), and similar expressions.

This is also called a “proposition,” because it is proposed for the correction of others. And since questions commonly arise from such expressions, because they are obscure, after making his exhortation he begins what he promised, as follows:

I said, “Listen”—namely, to this: “Why shall I fear on the evil day?” This is as though he were saying: Blessed is the one who will not fear on the evil day, that is, on the day of judgment. It will be an evil day with respect to the wicked, a day of calamity and misery.

For if I shall be on the evil day in such a way that I fear condemnation, why shall I fear? That is, what will be the cause of this fear?

He does not raise this question concerning himself because he doubts whether he fears, since he lacks the cause of this fear. Rather, by transforming himself into another person, he raises the question in order to resolve it for the benefit of his hearers and to teach them to avoid iniquity, as follows:

I said, “Why shall I fear?” I answer it in this way: I shall fear on the evil day if I fear that “iniquity will surround me,” that is, will occupy me greatly. This means: I shall be conscious, if I fear, that much iniquity is present in me.

I speak of “the iniquity of my heel,” that is, iniquity proceeding from my affection, which I have harbored in my affection. He calls affection “heel,” because through affection the mind advances by thinking, just as the body walks by the heel.

Or in this way: I speak of iniquity as “the overthrower of my heel,” that is, the destroyer of the condition of my holiness. It will never surround me then in any other way unless it has first overwhelmed the condition of my holiness here. Since one stands by the heel, he uses “heel” for “condition.” The condition of holiness appears to be nothing other than perseverance in holiness.

Or in this way: I speak of “the iniquity of my heel,” that is, of my perseverance. It is as though he were saying: Iniquity will not surround me unless it is the iniquity of the heel, that is, an iniquity in which I persevere unto the end. Since the heel is the final part of a person, it is used for perseverance, which continues to the end.

Through this he teaches that perseverance in iniquity must be avoided with the greatest care.

He explains who those are who possess iniquity, in order subsequently to show that they will be condemned for this reason and thus to terrify his hearers completely away from it:

I said that iniquity will surround me if I fear, yet I am free from it. But those possess it who trust in their own inward virtue, that is, those who believe that their holiness—indeed, holiness that ought not even to be called holiness—suffices for their salvation without God’s grace. Concerning such people the Psalmist says elsewhere: “The giant shall not be saved by the multitude of his strength” (Ps. XXXII, 16).

They also possess iniquity who glory not in God but in the multitude of their riches, placing their hope in them as though they were true and supreme goods.

The brother does not redeem those who trust and glory in this manner, that is, Christ, who is the brother of all the good because they will share in his blessedness. Hence, after the resurrection, he said concerning the apostles: “Go, tell my brothers, etc.” (Matt. XXVIII, 10); and elsewhere: “Whoever does the will of my Father, he is my brother,” etc. (Matt. XII, 50).

This means: Although the brother suffered for all, so that he might redeem all by his passion, as regards his own mercy, nevertheless he does not redeem those whom I mentioned above, as regards their iniquity, because by refusing to conform themselves to him they repel redemption from themselves.

And if they are not redeemed by the brother, will a man redeem them—that is, old Adam, the old man to whom they are conformed? By no means.

Or in this way: The brother, a man, does not redeem them here, that is, Christ, who is our brother according to his humanity, does not here redeem them from their injustice by his death. Will he therefore redeem them in the future? Certainly not. This is what he says: Truly he will not redeem them, for that brother will not give God his propitiation, that is, will not offer propitiation for them in the future.

This means: He will not make a prayer for them to God the Father by which he appeases his wrath against them. And here he will not give them “the price of the redemption of his soul,” that is, of their souls. This means: His death, which is the price of the redemption of the souls of the righteous, will not be the price of the redemption of the souls of the unrighteous, because they trust and glory as we have said above.

And because the one who trusts and glories will not be redeemed by the brother, that wretched man will labor, to be tormented eternally in the future.

And even here beforehand—that is, for a little while, not for long—he will live prosperously, life leading him to the end, that is, to that eternal life. In accordance with Solomon’s saying: “The prosperity of fools is their destruction” (Prov. I, 32).

I said that in the future he will labor. And although he lives prosperously here, he will not see, by inward reflection, his own destruction, by which he will labor in the future. For he will be blinded, so that he cannot see it, when he sees the wise living justly here and dying.

This means: When he does not see the wise becoming eternal on account of their justice here, but sees them dying a bodily death just as the unjust do, he will not think that he will be condemned in the future on account of his iniquity. For just as, when the righteous are brought to life, he considers God powerless or neglectful, so also, in his own condemnation, he regards God as impotent or unconcerned with vengeance.

And although he does not see the destruction, nevertheless in the future “the fool and the senseless shall perish together,” that is, they will perish in everlasting destruction.

A fool is one who does not fail to know something, yet through negligence pretends not to know it. Thus he may be called “not seeing,” specifically, not seeing for his own benefit. A senseless person, however, is one who is entirely ignorant, whose condemnation is just insofar as, through laziness, he has ceased to labor so that he might not remain ignorant. Hence the Apostle says: “The one who is ignorant will be ignored” (I Cor. XIV, 38).

Or in this way: I say that he will labor; and when this happens to him, he will not see in the future the destruction of the wise, although here he has seen the wise dying a bodily death. I say that he will see the wise dying; and not only will they themselves die, but together with those wise men “the senseless and the fool will perish” by the death of the flesh.

It is as though he were saying: If they could escape the death of the wise, then at least in some way their condition would be bearable. But since they cannot even escape this, it is utterly certain that the greatest accumulation of miseries threatens them.

It should indeed be noted that the impunity of the righteous here, and likewise the condemnation of the wicked for this reason, are discussed so that the wicked may be drawn toward conformity with the righteous by the example of the righteous’ impunity, and so that the wicked themselves may be terrified away from persevering in their iniquity by the threat of future destruction.

It should also be noted that he speaks of the wicked both individually and collectively for this reason: although there is a multiplicity of persons among them, there is also a unity of iniquity in those same persons.

The text continues: “And they shall leave,” etc. The connection is as follows: I said that they will perish, and, in perishing, they will not carry their riches with them for their consolation, although they will have devoted themselves so diligently to accumulating them. Rather, “they shall leave their riches to strangers.” For even if they leave them to their sons, those sons themselves will nevertheless be strangers to the aid of their fathers. They will not be able to help them by any benefit, since, according to the demands of their merits, they will have been condemned eternally.

And although they themselves built many spacious houses here, after death none of those houses will remain for them. Rather, “their tombs will be their houses for ever,” that is, for as long as this world shall endure.

In their spacious houses they will have no benefit except empty fame. For “their tabernacles,” that is, their houses—which should not even be called houses but tabernacles, since they are transitory in the manner of tabernacles—“they called their names in their lands,” that is, they were the reason why their names alone would be called; and not in distant lands, but only in their own lands.

For it will be said: “This was Octavian’s house; this was Pompey’s,” and similarly of the others. This will occur “in the present generation and in the generation to come,” that is, through many generations.

What follows—“and man,” etc.—gives the reason why the wicked man will labor, as follows: I said that the wicked man will labor, and deservedly so, because he himself, “man,” that is, one who possessed human nature and ought to conduct himself as a human being, rationally rather than irrationally like an animal, “when he was placed in honor,” that is, made rational in the likeness of God—which is exceedingly honorable—“did not understand,” that is, did not care to understand.

Although by reason he could understand his own destruction and escape it by living well, “he was compared to beasts,” that is, he was made comparable to beasts through senselessness, so as to behave irrationally.

And lest it be thought that he was compared to them falsely, he adds: “And being compared in this way,” that is, having been made like them “in senselessness”—I said that the senseless are like beasts—“this is their way,” that is, this senselessness by which they proceed, increasing it day by day. Therefore it is called a way, and “it will be a stumbling-block to them,” that is, a cause of stumbling, namely, eternal death.

Or in this way: I said, “They were placed in honor,” that is, in rationality. And this rationality, which would be their way to life unless they turned aside from it, will be a stumbling-block to them—that is, a cause of stumbling—because they set it aside.

I said that the wicked are compared to beasts in senselessness. But it will not be enough for them to have become senseless; after they have become senseless, they will also “please other senseless people,” who have made themselves so, “with their mouth,” that is, through the prompting of their speech.

This means: By their mouths they will prompt others—not only by their example—to trust in virtue and glory in riches, which is the height of senselessness. And those to whom this prompting is made will be pleased by it and will conform themselves to them.

Therefore, since they have become senseless like beasts and will please others by their speech, “they have been placed”—that is, they will be placed—in hell, “like sheep,” that is, they will be devoured by everlasting death, after the likeness of sheep, which are born for the purpose of being devoured.

But lest it be thought that they are devoured in such a way that they perish completely like sheep and afterward no longer feel the torments of death, he adds: “Death shall feed upon them,” that is, it will consume them in such a way that they nevertheless remain alive in torments, after the manner of grass which, when grazed upon, still remains. He says this to intensify their calamity. For it would be better to die altogether than to be grazed upon.

I say that they will be grazed upon by death. And in order that they may suffer more, “the righteous,” whom they rule here and afflict, “shall rule over them,” that is, shall judge them, “in the morning,” that is, at the morning resurrection. In accordance with the saying: “The saints shall judge nations and rule over peoples” (Wis. III, 8).

And “their help” in hell, where the wicked have been placed, “shall grow old,” that is, shall fail, after the likeness of an old garment that wears out. This means: There they will not obtain the help of their friends. The fact that their help will grow old will proceed from their glory, that is, the glory of their pride, which they possess here, will be the cause of it there.

Or otherwise: The help that they now expect from their glory will fail them when they have been placed in hell.

I say that death will thus feed upon them, and they will not be redeemed by the brother. Nevertheless, although I may appear to perish in the same way and not to be redeemed, since here I am subject to every misery, “God will redeem my soul from the hand,” that is, from the power, of the underworld.

This means: Although I undergo the death of the flesh, the Lord’s death will nevertheless be my redemption, so that I may not enter hell, since it was for this purpose that he assumed me, that is, my humanity, in order to redeem me. Through this he indicates that he will likewise redeem others conformed to him.

And therefore, since the wicked will be grazed upon and my soul and the souls of those conformed to me will be redeemed, let every righteous person not fear one who is simply a man and not even deified—namely, the wicked man—when that man has become rich [Col. 0851A] and powerful enough to afflict you. And when his glory, that is, the magnificence of his house, has increased here, remember that these things will not last for ever.

But when a man has died the death of the body, “he shall take nothing,” that is, he will possess no riches by which he may later exalt himself against you. Nor will “the glory of his house,” in which he glories and takes pride, descend with him into hell.

And truly he will take nothing, nor will the glory of his house be exalted, because “his soul,” that is, his sensuality, “shall be blessed,” that is, exalted, only in his lifetime.

This means: Truly it will not be exalted in the future, because only in this life will his sensuality be exalted in every kind of desire. This is an exposition by way of repetition.

His soul, I say, of one who says to himself: “Do good to your soul according to every desire.” For when you have done good to it, it will thank you, that is, someone will praise you by calling you good and generous.

The text continues: “He shall enter,” etc. The connection is as follows: Thus the wicked man will speak with himself—he will give thanks, and so forth—and will do good to his soul. And yet, although here he does good to himself, “he shall enter unto the generation of his fathers,” that is, into hell, where the generation of other wicked men entered, whose son he is in wickedness.

Or in this way: He shall enter into hell, where their fathers, the devils, entered through their pride; they are called “generation,” that is, those who beget him as a wicked man in unbelief.

And after he has entered, “unto eternity he shall not see light,” that is, the knowledge of God. And therefore he shall enter and shall not see, because “man, when he was placed in honor,” etc. This is explained above: he repeats it in order to draw him away from the likeness of beasts.

## ON PSALM XLIX

### The Title of the Forty-Ninth Psalm

“A Psalm of Asaph.” Asaph, Heman, Ethan, and Jeduthun were four musicians who presided over the other musicians who rendered David’s psalms.

Here, however, the name Asaph does not seem to have been attached to some particular historical figure, but because of its interpretation. For Asaph has the same meaning as Synagogue, namely, “assembly.” Therefore this psalm, that is, this treatise, is said to be of Asaph, that is, of the congregation of the faithful before Christ’s coming.

It must be understood that this assembly before Christ’s coming was not called “Synagogue,” that is, “assembly,” because it belonged to irrational and compelled persons; for many of them, being exceedingly perfect, were called “Church,” that is, “convocation,” which belongs to rational persons and not to those who are compelled, who approach only by convocation.

Rather, it was called this according to the greater part, because they did not serve the Law with their reason leading them to do so, but through fear of punishment, in the manner of irrational animals, which are gathered together not by reason leading them but by force.

In this psalm the faithful who existed before Christ’s coming are introduced as saying that God, who had previously spoken through the prophets, would speak to the world through his incarnate Son. And, once the legal sacrifices—which had existed only as signs of the new law—had been emptied of their force, he would establish a sacrifice of praise.

He shows that this sacrifice is absent from sinners, so that they may thereby be drawn away from sin, if not by love, at least by fear. The Prophet introduces these men for the purpose of making what is prophesied here more firmly confirmed by the testimony of such great persons.

“God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and called the earth.” It is as though he were saying: He who is Lord over created things, and who, being Lord, possesses the power to change and order what belongs to him according to his own will; and who is God, that is, creator of all things, and therefore to be believed in all things—not such a god as has been deified by another, as many perfected faithful have been—but “God of gods,” that is, of heavenly spirits and of the most perfect human beings, who are called gods because they share in his divinity: this God has spoken, that is, at the fullness of time he will speak to his people through the Son, having already often spoken beforehand through the oracles of the prophets.

Hence the Apostle says: “In many ways and by many means God formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in his Son” (Hebr. I, 1).

And after he has spoken through the Son, “he called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting,” that is, he will call to faith through preachers from among all the inhabitants of the earth, from the rising of the sun to its setting.

Although he ought next to have stated what he would say, he inserts that he will be born from the Jews, or that he will begin his calling from the Jews, in order that the unbelieving Jews, who were going to deny that he was God, might be compelled by his authority and invited to hear what he would say and to obey him.

He also inserts that “fire shall burn before him” and that “a storm shall be around him,” and that he will separate heaven, that is, the apostles, and earth, that is, the middling faithful, from those destined for destruction.

These apostles will also announce to others, who will be earth, the righteousness of that God. By prophesying this so long beforehand, he stirs unbelieving Jews to hear and obey Christ and his disciples.

He also exhorts the heavens themselves to gather together by their preaching those who will become God’s faithful, so that he may indicate how great his concern for this matter already is, existing as he does so long beforehand, and may teach others to have the same concern.

With this noted, let us return to the words of the book.

The text continues: “From Zion the beauty,” etc. The connection is as follows: I say that he will speak through the incarnate Son. “And the beauty of his splendor shall proceed from Zion,” that is, he himself, beautiful in innocence and splendid in every virtue, will be born from the Jewish people, which is signified by Zion, a tower in Judea.

Or in this way: I say that he will call the whole earth; and the beauty of the splendor of that God, that is, his preachers, beautiful in innocence and splendid in virtues, will proceed from the Jewish people.

Or in this way: He will call the earth. And the beauty of the earth’s splendor will begin from Zion, that is, the first beautiful and splendid people of the earth whom he will call will be from Zion—namely, the Church of the primitive believers.

By this he makes the Jews well disposed to hear him, since he will deign to be born from them and to begin his calling from them.

I said that God will speak through the Son, and that the Son himself exists as God with the Father. Accordingly, he will come invisibly, not locally, but he will come manifestly into human knowledge, that is, manifest and visible according to his humanity.

I say that he is God, and not a recent god, but our God, whom we and our fathers have worshiped. And this God himself will not conceal that he is God. This means: By word and deed he will show himself to be God, according to what is read in the Gospel: “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 10).

I said that he will come, and after he has come, “fire shall burn before him,” that is, the fervor of love will increase, after the manner of a blazing fire, in those who behold him with a special gaze, namely, in the faithful.

And “a mighty storm,” that is, an exceedingly great blindness—which is called a storm because it will cast them down in the manner of a storm [Col. 0853B] and carry them away into unlawful things—will be around him, that is, among the unbelievers who have neglected to draw near to him. They will be around him, that is, in separation from him.

Or in this way: a mighty storm, that is, blindness, will be among those who behold him—not in his divinity, but “around him,” that is, only in his humanity.

This means: There will be a storm among those who think that he is merely a man. His humanity is called “around” by analogy. This does not mean that it locally contains divinity within itself, but that divinity itself dwells in it secretly and spiritually. For when we dwell inside something, we are surrounded by that same thing.

Since he had said that he would call the earth but had not explained it, he now makes it clear so that this should not remain unknown. I say that he will call the earth, and in this manner: first he will call, that is, call to faith, “heaven,” that is, the apostles, who are called heaven because of the sublimity of their virtues.

And lest it be thought that he loses his divinity because of the humanity he assumed, he adds: “Existing from above,” that is, in the sublime equality of divinity with the Father. It is as though he were saying: Although he is manifest and visible as a man, calling and speaking with a human voice, he will nevertheless be from above.

Through this he refutes the unbelief of the Jews, who falsely claim that he is simply a man. Hence he himself testifies: “You are from below; I am from above” (John VIII, 23).

I said that he will first call heaven. And through heaven he will call earth, that is, the other faithful who will be his earth, watered by the teaching of the apostles, just as the earth is watered by the rain of heaven so that it may thereby become fertile.

He wishes through that heaven to distinguish “his people,” that is, his earth, from the mass of the lost. This means: Through the heaven already called, he will also call the earth to faith, in order to separate it from the lost—if not from association with the lost in the present, at least from conformity with them, and in the future from their presence as well.

The exhortation to heaven itself follows, and it is as follows: I say that through you, O heaven, he will call the earth; and since such an office will be entrusted to you, apply diligent effort to this office.

Specifically, by your preaching “gather into the unity of faith,” and do this “for his honor,” not for your own exaltation, “his saints,” that is, those whom, as they approach him in faith, he will sanctify.

He determines who these are as follows: I call those saints who “order,” that is, who will place, “his testament,” that is, his new law, “above the sacrifices” of the old law.

This means: they will regard the sacrifices as inferior, that is, less worthy, and the testament as superior, that is, more worthy, after the likeness of someone who places one stone above another, and similar examples.

After inserting this exhortation, he returns to what he had begun, as follows: I say that he called heaven, and through heaven the earth; and these heavens will announce to those whom they call “his righteousness,” namely, that he is just.

And since he who is God is also Judge—this means that, in order to terrify them away from sins, they will announce that he is a just Judge who will avenge sins in the future.
