Or the whole passage from “God will come manifestly” up to “Hear, O my people” may be understood of the second coming. He inserts it for this reason: having shown that the very Son whom he wishes to introduce as speaking will come as a terrible Judge at the second coming, he may at least by fear urge unbelievers to hear him and obey him.

“God manifestly,” etc. The connection is as follows: I said that God will speak through the Son and call the earth, and that the beauty of his splendor will be from Zion. And the same Son, who, while humble, will not appear to unbelievers to be God, will come manifestly to judgment in the future, that is, with power and majesty.

And thus he will appear to be God, according to what is read in the Gospel: “Then they will see the Son of man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty” (Luke XXI, 27).

I say that God the Son will come; he is not a recent god, but our God, whom we worship. And when he comes, he will not be silent concerning vengeance, as in his first coming.

This means: appearing in majesty, he will take vengeance upon those who neglected him when he first came in humility.

The manner in which he will take vengeance is explained as follows: Truly he will not be silent, for “elemental fire shall burn before him,” that is, in his presence.

It must be noted, however, that this fire will not be that eternal fire in which the wicked will afterward be tortured without end. Rather, as blessed Peter affirms, at the resurrection of the dead this fire will reach as high into the air as the floodwaters rose (II Pet. III, 10–12). By this fire all the impurity of the air will be cleansed. Through this fire the bodies and souls of the faithful, joined together as they now are, will meet the Lord in the air for judgment with the utmost speed and without any injury.

Hence Paul says (I Thess. IV, 17): “We shall be caught up to meet the Lord in the air.” But the wicked, weighed down by the burden of their sins and bearing great injury within themselves, will pass to judgment, immediately to be sent into the torment of eternal fire.

The text continues: Since fire will be there and “around him,” that is, locally surrounding him, or “around him,” that is, among those separated from him—namely, among the wicked—there will be “a mighty storm,” an exceedingly violent wind, namely, a multitude of evil angels. They are called a storm by analogy, because just as a storm, that is, wind, when it encounters grains and chaff mixed together, does not move the grains but carries off the chaff, so they, leaving the faithful untouched but carrying off the unbelievers, will thrust them into everlasting fire.

### He will summon

He will summon. This is connected as follows: I say that God will come manifestly. Coming from above in a localized manner—that is, from his lofty seat, which is at the right hand of the Father—he will summon heaven, that is, the most perfect, and earth, that is, the less perfect, wishing through the judgment of heaven to distinguish his people—that is, the less perfect—from those to be condemned. In accordance with this, he says in the Gospel: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28; Luke 22:30).

When he says, “Gather,” and so forth, he exhorts the good angels, out of their great affection, to gather the good, as follows: Since the tempest will carry away the impious, you good angels, through whose ministry the saints will be led to glory, gather for him—that is, for the honor of that Son—his saints, that is, heaven and earth. He determines who those saints are when he adds: those who in this world set his covenant in order—that is, regard in the right order his covenant, namely, eternal blessedness, which he himself promises in the New Testament to be above sacrifices—that is, to surpass in dignity the good works and virtues which they offer to God as sacrifices. This means: those who consider eternal glory more valuable than their merits, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18).

I said, “Gather the saints into glory,” and they—that is, the gathered saints, heaven—will announce his righteousness, namely, God’s. He explains what righteousness this is when he adds: they will announce, namely, that God is judge. This means: not with their voice, but by the blessedness of their glory they will show the unbelievers—as though they were announcing it—that God is a just judge who will reward them worthily.

After a useful digression, he begins to recount God’s speech, which he promised above, as follows: I said that the God of gods would speak through the Son. This speech is: “Hear, my people Israel.” This is as though he said: You assembly of the Jews, who are my special people, to whom I have bestowed so many benefits, who ought to be Israel—that is, one who contemplates heavenly things, not one whose heart is weighed down by earthly things—hear with inner hearing what I shall say. And I, who, being human, speak in human fashion, will testify to you—that is, through the testimony of your Scriptures and of my good works I will prove to you—that I am God, and not a stranger, but your God. It is as though he said: You ought to hear me and, by hearing, obey me, because I am your God; this is proved by the testimony of the Scriptures and of my works.

I say, “Hear”; and hear this in particular: Do not continue to offer me the legal sacrifices which until now were signs, but which now, after the thing signified by them has arrived, are no longer signs and are therefore useless.

“For I will not henceforth reproach you concerning your legal sacrifices,” which have not been offered. It is as though he said: If, while they were signs of the new law, which did not yet exist, you had failed to offer them, I would certainly have reproached you through the prophets and the Scriptures and through temporal tribulations. But now, because they are no longer signs of the new law, which already exists, I will not reproach you if you do not offer them, because henceforth I do not care about them.

“Your holocausts, however, which are signified rather than signifying, are always before me,” that is, within my good pleasure. This means: I am pleased not with holocausts made from oxen and other animals, but with your holocausts—that is, those made from you. I am pleased if you burn away your vices completely within yourselves by the fire of the Holy Spirit, and if you offer yourself wholly to me. This was signified by the holocaust made for sin, which was entirely burned; that is what will please me.

Because he had spoken indefinitely, saying, “I will not reproach you concerning sacrifices,” he removes this point by parts, as follows: Truly, I will not reproach you concerning sacrifices; for I will no longer accept calves—that is, sacrifices of calves—from your house, that is, from your household. Nor will I accept he-goats—that is, the sacrifice of he-goats—taken from your flocks. Through these two parts he also makes the others understood. This means: None of your sacrifices will be acceptable to me.

Someone might say: Even if they are not signs, since we wish to give these things to you, accept them. Against this he adds: Since they were not useful to you, as they formerly were while they were signs, it is not fitting that I should accept them. For I have no need of them, since all the wild beasts of the forests are mine, over which you have no authority. Mine also are the beasts that graze upon the mountains, and the oxen—that is, not only domestic animals are mine, but also the wild creatures, namely the wild beasts, oxen, and beasts grazing on the mountains, over which you cannot rule.

It is as though he said: While it benefited you for me to accept them, I accepted them—that is, when they were signs. Yet it is clear that they benefited me nowhere and will benefit me nowhere. But since henceforth they would not benefit you, because what they signified has now arrived, why should I accept them, as though I needed them? I do not need them, certainly, since all four-footed animals, both domestic and wild, are mine.

Nor are only the four-footed animals mine; I also know all the birds of heaven—that is, since I am their Creator, I know the nature of them all. Nor are birds alone mine: the beauty of the field is also with me—that is, the beautiful crops and fruits of the fields are in my ordering. For I am their Creator.

It is as though he said: I have no need for you to offer me birds and crops in a sacrifice that is useless to you. All these things are mine. When he says, “I know the birds,” he indicates that they are his creatures. But since the four-footed animals and the birds are mine, as is the beauty of the fields, if this were what I hungered for—which nevertheless will never happen—I would not tell you to offer these things to me.

He repeats the reason why he does not tell them to offer them, in order to confirm it, as follows: Truly, I will not tell you, nor is it necessary. For the world is mine—that is, the whole earth—and its fullness, that is, everything that is in it.

It is as though he said: Since these things are no longer signs, you appear to offer them for the purpose of satisfying my hunger. For this reason it is not necessary. If I were hungry, I would not seek these things from you; I could take them myself, since the whole earth and everything in it are mine.

Because he had said, “If I were hungry,” someone might suppose that he could in some way become hungry. He removes this supposition as follows: Although I said, “If I were hungry,” would I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of he-goats? Certainly not. This means: It is not necessary for me to urge you to offer these things to me. For I do not eat the flesh of bulls, nor do I drink the blood of he-goats.

After showing that he does not want these sacrifices, he invites them to the sacrifice that pleases him when he says, “Sacrifice to God,” and so forth. This is connected as follows: I said that I do not care for sacrifices of calves and he-goats, so that you should sacrifice them; rather, sacrifice to me, God, a sacrifice of praise—that is, this sacrifice: praise me both in affection and in good works, and also with your voice.

And with regard to the fact that you will praise me, do not suppose that you possess this from yourself; but also “render your vows to me, the Most High,” that is, sacrifices of praise. This means: Regard it as something that I give you, so that if you sacrifice to me and render these vows to me as a debt, you should not think that you are giving them as a gift. Such sacrifices are called vows because they are vowed to God by the faithful in baptism.

And if you sacrifice a sacrifice of praise, call upon me as Deliverer in the day of tribulation—that is, on the final day of your death, when evil spirits will confront you, wishing to lead you into tribulations—and I will rescue you from every tribulation. Once rescued, you will honor me—that is, you will praise me forever, established in perpetual glory. You will honor me, that is, not with your voice, but with your affection.

But because he had said that a sacrifice of praise must be offered to God, lest people suppose that sinners could offer this sacrifice—since they seem to praise him with their outward voice, though this should not be called praise when their affection and conduct disagree—the faithful Asaph shows, on the basis of divine authority itself, that a sinner announces the praise of God with his voice alone to no advantage, as follows:

I said that God commanded a sacrifice of praise to be offered in voice, work, and affection. The just man offers this sacrifice to his greatest advantage. But to the unrepentant sinner God said through the Scriptures, and also says through his Son: “Why do you recount my righteousnesses?” That is, for what advantage do you recount to others my commandments, which are just? And for what advantage to yourself do you take up my covenant—that is, my law—speaking it with your mouth and praising me with your voice alone? You do this to no advantage of your own.

This means: The just man praises God with his voice to his greatest advantage when his life does not contradict his praise. But the sinner, as he is convicted by the authority of the Lord himself, praises God with his voice to no advantage of his own, whether he announces God’s praise to himself or to others.

He shows, in the person of God himself, why such praise is useless, as follows: I say that you recount my righteousnesses to others with your voice and take them upon your mouth—righteousnesses which the just recount through their conduct and patiently, by bearing my discipline, and which are therefore useful to them. But you, while recounting and taking them up, hated—and still hate—discipline.

This means: If at some time, out of fatherly compassion and in order to correct your sins, I afflict you with the discipline of tribulations, you do not bear it patiently and lovingly. Rather, because you hate it, you endure it uselessly, with weariness and murmuring.

And you have not only hated discipline; you have also cast my words behind you—that is, you have neglected my commandments by living wickedly.

He shows by particular examples how you have cast them behind you, as follows: Truly, you have cast my words behind you. For I commanded that you should not steal, and when you saw a thief, you ran with him—that is, you quickly consented to him either in deed or in assent. And I said that adultery must not be committed, yet when you saw people practicing adultery, you placed your portion—that is, your participation—with the adulterers.

This means: You became a participant in adultery with them, either in deed or by consent. I also commanded that there should be no blasphemy, yet your mouth abounded in the wickedness of blasphemies against your neighbor. I likewise established that your neighbor should not be deceived by fraud, yet your tongue contrived deceits—that is, by joining and mixing truth together so as to deceive more effectively, it uttered deceits against your neighbor.

I say that your mouth abounded in the wickedness of blasphemies against your neighbor, and this not merely once, but while sitting—that is, remaining fixed and persevering—you spoke wicked blasphemies against your brother.

And because “brother” can be understood equivocally—either a brother only according to human kinship, or also according to faith, or even according to impiety—he specifies which brother he means when he adds: I say that, sitting, you spoke against your brother, and that is, namely, against the son of your mother, the Church, you placed a stumbling block.

This means: If you had sinned against the brother who is your brother only by human descent, or against the one who is your brother in impiety, although that would be evil, it would nevertheless not be so intolerable. But what is much more serious is that through the wickedness of your blasphemies you scandalized him who was your brother according to the unity of the Church.

Therefore, because you have cast my words behind you in this and in many other ways, you praise me—by recounting those just words—to no advantage of your own.

I say that when you saw a thief, you ran with him, and that you did other similar things; and it is true: you really did all these things. Yet I kept silence—that is, I did not rebuke you by immediately condemning you for what you had done. And because I kept silence, O wicked one, you supposed that I would be like you, consenting to your wickedness by not punishing you.

Alternatively, “wickedly” may be read adverbially, as follows: Because I kept silence, you supposed that I would be like you by not avenging your wickedness; and you supposed this wickedly—that is, your supposition was not true. For in the future I will rebuke you by your condemnation, and I will rebuke you in such a way that I will set you before your own face.

This is said metaphorically, as though he were placing you so manifestly before yourself that, whether you wished it or not, he would make you recognize your wickedness, which now you neglect to recognize—like someone who, if another person were set before his face, would recognize him.

It should be noted that he inserts this concerning the sinner in order to draw him away from sin by frightening him and to lead him to repentance.

After frightening the sinners, he invites them to understand what sacrifice they should offer, so that he may instruct them at the end, as follows: I said that the sinner does not honor me with his voice alone to any advantage. Therefore you sinners, who now forget God—that is, me—by not obeying my commandments, understand—that is, carefully grasp—the things I have said, so that you may not merely recount my righteousnesses with your voice, nor cast my words behind you.

Otherwise, if you do not understand, when—that is, at some time—God seizes you for vengeance, namely I, there will then be no one to rescue you from condemnation.

It is as though he were saying: When the devil at some time intends to seize you for evil, I rescue you; but if I seize you, no one will be able to rescue you.

But because he had frightened them away from their sins, they might ask: Since you do not approve of our recounting your righteousnesses in such a way that we cast your words behind us, instruct us what we should do. He responds to this request as follows: I said what it is not right to do—to recount my righteousnesses in this way, since this is not to my honor. But a sacrifice of praise will honor me—that is, it will be to my honor when someone praises me with voice, work, and affection.

And “there”—that is, in that sacrifice—“there will be a way,” along which I will show to the one who has done this the salvation of God—that is, the salvation which God will give to his own in the future.

It is as though he said: Each person ought to apply himself to the sacrifice of praise. This will be the way—that is, the path by which the one who applies himself to it will see the salvation which God, namely I, will give to his own in the future.

Alternatively, this verse may be connected without altering the exposition, as follows: Therefore you who uselessly recount my righteousnesses with your voice alone, understand these things that I shall say to you: “A sacrifice of praise will honor me,” and so forth.

## ON PSALM L

The title of the fiftieth psalm is: “For the end; a psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, when he went in to Bathsheba.” This is explained as follows.

This psalm is to be attributed to the prophet David, who looks toward the end—that is, toward Christ, the end of prophecy and of the law. Through faith in his mercy and passion, David considers himself destined to be saved from the homicide and adultery that he committed. This psalm was composed when Nathan the prophet came to him. “When” is used causally here, as though he said: The reason why he then composed the psalm was that Nathan the prophet came to him.

But because Nathan had come to him many times, lest it be unknown during which coming he was the cause of this psalm, he specifies this when he adds: “when he went in to Bathsheba.” “When” here is causal, as though he were saying: When Nathan the prophet came to him to correct him at the Lord’s command—since David had gone in to Bathsheba and committed adultery.

When he says “he went in to Bathsheba,” he indicates the shameful matter covertly. It was not necessary for it to be expressed more openly, since the story is well known. Nevertheless, the story should be touched upon briefly because of its allegorical meaning.

It is indeed read that David, from his rooftop, saw Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, coming out from bathing, and desired her beauty (2 Sam. 11). After knowing her in adultery, because he could not retain her in marriage, with her husband still alive, on account of the disgrace, he deceitfully caused her husband Uriah to be killed and thus joined her to himself in marriage.

Moreover, because he felt secure concerning so great a sin and neglected to satisfy God through repentance and affliction, he was rebuked at the Lord’s command through the prophet Nathan. Repenting of his sin, he composed this psalm. In it he prays to God with intense affection for the remission of his sin and, in the end, seeks to obtain God’s goodwill. He also prays for the remission of all his iniquities.

He further promises himself, through confidence in divine mercy and power, that he will be cleansed through faith in the Lord’s passion and in the future baptism, asking that, once cleansed, God not permit him to return to sins.

He also shows, in order to move God’s mercy more strongly toward forgiveness, that if God forgives him, many sinners will be converted to him in repentance by David’s example. He excuses himself for not offering legal sacrifices because he knows that God does not forgive sins through them.

Furthermore, he shows that sins are forgiven through the sacrifice of a contrite spirit, which is most pleasing to God. Because he foresees that this sacrifice will exist in the Church, he prays with intense affection for it, asking God to establish it graciously; once established, it will sacrifice itself to God upon the altar of faith.

It should be noted that, for our benefit, David’s offense, repentance, and remission of sin are set before us. When we see so great a man, so advanced in holiness, fall so grievously, we—who are utterly weak and have no confidence in ourselves—should always fear falling and take every possible precaution.

But if we should fall in the manner he did, or even more grievously, we should be brought back to repentance by his example. We should weep for our sin, strive in every way to satisfy God, and pray for forgiveness with excessive affection; thus we shall obtain pardon.

This history contains an allegorical meaning. Although that meaning does not seem to pertain to the intention of the psalm, it must not for that reason be said to lack usefulness for its hearers. The allegory is said to be as follows.

Through David, whose name is interpreted as “strong of hand” and “desired,” the Lord Jesus is understood. He showed himself strong of hand by acting manfully against the devil, and before the time of the fullness he was desired by the true faithful.

From his throne—that is, from the loftiness of his mercy—he looked upon the beauty of the Church as she emerged from the washing of baptism, in the beauty of holiness and innocence, and desired her. This Church was prefigured by Bathsheba, whose name is interpreted as “well of satiety.”

For the Church is a well filled with the teaching of the Lord’s doctrine, in accordance with what is read in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38).

Thus, in order that Christ might join the Church to himself as his bride, he destroyed by his death the devil, whose bride she had been while placed in unbelief—not according to essence, but according to power—so that, because of Adam’s sin, he might no longer exercise any authority over her.

That sin was destroyed through Christ’s obedience. The devil was prefigured by Uriah, Bathsheba’s husband, who was killed by David. Uriah is interpreted as “my light is God.” The devil is rightly called “my light is God.”

For, taking pride in the exceedingly bright appearance of his nature, he did not conduct himself humbly toward God as his creature. Rather, not with his voice but in the awareness of his arrogance, he said within himself: “My light is the light of God.”

This means: Since I exist from God as a being of exceedingly bright nature, I will regard myself not as a creature but as God. My great light proves that I am God. For the devil is said to have declared—not with his voice but with his affection—“I will set my throne toward the north” (Isa. 14:14), that is, in the coldness of love for the Most High, and thus, “I will be like the Most High” (ibid.).

It is as though he said: If, burning with the fire of his love, I submit myself to him as a creature, then, although I exist as a being of the brightest light, I will be unlike him, since he will be considered God and I his creature. But I will sit in the north—that is, I will remain in the coldness of his love—and I will not be subject to him. I will be like him: since I possess such great light, I will be considered God just as he is.

It should certainly be noted that it is not disgraceful if, through Bathsheba the adulteress, the Church, who is Christ’s virgin and chaste bride, is represented; through David the sinner, Christ, who is free from sin; and through Uriah, innocent and unjustly killed, the devil, who is guilty and justly slain by God’s death.

For this is no more disgraceful than the fact that the name of the devil is often written in letters of gold, while the name of God is written in ink, that is, in black coloring. The lowliness of ink contributes no dishonor to God, nor does the preciousness of gold confer any honor upon the devil.

“Have mercy on me, God, according to your great mercy.”

This means: Since you are God, and mercy belongs to you, have mercy on me. And have mercy not a little, but according to the measure of your great mercy. Since your mercy is great and my sin is great, have mercy on me according to the greatness of your mercy, whose sin is great.

“And according to the multitude of your mercies, have mercy on me,” that is, according to the benefits of your mercy, which are many; these benefits are called “mercies.”

This means: I ask not only according to the measure of the greatness of your mercy, that you may have mercy on the greatness of my sin, but according to the measure of the multitude of your mercies. Since your mercies are many, have mercy on me through them, who have committed many offenses through Bathsheba.

For I sinned in adultery; I sinned in homicide; I sinned also in neglecting you; and I sinned in making Bathsheba guilty. By saying that God’s mercy is great and that his mercies are many, while indicating that his own sin is great and manifold, he seeks to gain God’s goodwill by accusing himself and magnifying God.

He shows in what respect God should have mercy on him when he adds, as follows: Have mercy: “Blot out my iniquity,” that is, blot my iniquity from your memory, so that you do not punish it. Or alternatively: blot the stain of my iniquity from my soul.

And blot it out in this way: “Wash me more” from my iniquity than you have washed me from other iniquities. It is as though he said: You have already washed me from other iniquities, which were not so great; but since this one is greater than they were, I need a greater washing. Therefore wash me more.

Or alternatively: wash me more than I know how to ask you to wash me. For I neither know how nor am able to ask you as much as I ought. And wash me not a little, but cleanse me completely through your great mercy.

“From my sin.” Sin here is the same as iniquity. Or “sin” may be understood as evil desire, while “iniquity” is the act itself. For iniquity appears to signify something graver than sin.

Because he had prayed to be cleansed, he adds the reason why he ought to be cleansed, as follows: I pray, cleanse me, and you ought to cleanse me, because I, who ask you and who have sinned, know my iniquity—that is, my iniquity is not hidden from me.

And I do not know it only for a moment; rather, “my sin”—that is, my iniquity—is always against me—that is, before my inner sight.

This means: I always behold my sin with my inner eyes, so that I may groan over it, by analogy with something placed before someone’s gaze, which he continually sees.

It is as though he were saying: You ought to cleanse me through mercy. For, since I know that all criminal sins must be punished either by God or by the one who commits them, I do not disdain to acknowledge my iniquity. Rather, by continually beholding it within myself, I punish it with groaning and tears, with constant repentance and prayer.

All this is as though he briefly said: You ought to cleanse me and no longer punish me, since you are just. For I already frequently punish my iniquity within myself.

Having shown that God ought to have mercy on him because of his great mercy, and because of justice, since he already punishes his own iniquity within himself, he adds that God ought to cleanse him by his power, since only one who is free from sin and just can forgive sins.

I pray, have mercy, so that you may blot out my iniquity; and I pray with this confidence because I have sinned against you alone. This means: Since I have sinned against you, you are such that you can forgive, for you alone—that is, as one of singular power—can pardon sins.

For no one is clean from defilement except you. Therefore you alone have power to forgive. For this reason also I pray: have mercy, because I have done evil before you—that is, in such a way that it is not hidden from you, but is before you, in your sight, so that you see it.

It is as though he said: If I knew that my iniquity were hidden from you, I would certainly excuse myself; I would not pray that you have mercy. But because I know that, since you see everything, my sin is not hidden from you, I do not wish to excuse myself uselessly. Rather, humbly, I pray: have mercy.

In saying that God is of singular power and sees everything, he makes him greatly disposed toward mercy.

But because he had said, “Against you alone I have sinned,” lest by the inappropriate use of “alone” we understand him to mean that he had sinned only against God and not against Uriah, whom he had unjustly killed, and thus make him appear to be lying, he specifies how “alone” is to be understood.

I said, “Against you alone,” and I say “alone” because you are alone “so that you may be justified in your words,” that is, so that you may be found truthful in everything you have spoken through the prophets and will also speak through the Son. Hence the Apostle says: “God is truthful, and every human being a liar” (Rom. 3:4).

And likewise you are alone “so that you may prevail when you are judged,” that is, so that your goodness may conquer and surpass the goodness of all others whenever judgment is made by the consideration of the just between your goodness and that of other good people.

This means: Whenever your faithful compare your goodness with that of other good people, yours always surpasses theirs. Hence in the Gospel: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:18).

He shows from what it may be seen that God prevails when he adds: “For behold, in iniquities,” and so forth. This is connected as follows: I say that you prevail when you are judged by the faithful, and it is true.

For behold, there is presently a reason by which it may be perceived that you prevail over both me and the entire human race. Since you are free from sins, I was conceived in original iniquities.

This means: I, who already existed in original iniquities, was conceived by my mother. It is as though he said: Before I was conceived by my mother, while I was still in my father’s loins, I was already in original iniquities.

Hence the Apostle says: “Death passed to all” (Rom. 5:12)—that is, original sin, through which one comes to death unless it is cleansed by baptism.

I was not only in original iniquities before conception; my mother also conceived me in sins—that is, in original iniquities. That is, even in the very act of conception I was in those original iniquities.

All this is as though he had briefly said: In this you prevail over me and over all human beings, because you are always free from sin, whereas I and all human beings are burdened by original iniquities both before conception and in conception itself.

He rightly uses “iniquities” in the plural. For Adam sinned in multiple ways: through pleasure, through the act, and by leaving others an example of sinning.

And truly you prevail over all by your goodness. Behold, there is presently a reason by which it can be seen that you prevail over both me and all human beings by your goodness.

For you loved truth—that is, my true repentance and my acknowledgment concerning sin.

This means: While I, conducting myself negligently, hated repentance for my sin, you, most merciful, loved truth—that is, you loved my practicing true repentance—and you moved me to it through the prophet Nathan.

By this it is apparent that you prevail over me in goodness. For while I was impious toward myself, persisting in my iniquity, you were merciful in admonishing me to repent.

It is also proved by this that you prevail in goodness: You revealed to me, who had not deserved it and was about to fall so grievously, through the prophetic spirit, the uncertain and hidden mysteries of your wisdom—that is, of your Son.

This means: You revealed to me through the Holy Spirit the mysteries of the incarnation and passion of your Son, and that he would restore the world through his death. These things are uncertain to many who, although they have heard them from the prophets, do not possess full faith in them through the Spirit; and they are hidden from many who have heard nothing at all about them.

It is as though he said: So that I might be saved from original sin through faith in these mysteries, you revealed them to me out of gratuitous mercy.

Hence it is clear that you prevail, since you revealed these things to me for my salvation without any merit on my part.

And it is still further evident that you prevail in goodness because you will sprinkle me with hyssop—that is, you will make me like one who is sprinkled with hyssop—and thus you will make me such that I shall be cleansed.

This means: You will cleanse me through the sprinkling of Christ’s blood, which will be scattered with hyssop—that is, in humility. This was prefigured in the old law. For when the leper was sprinkled with the blood of the sacrifice by a bundle of hyssop, he was cleansed from leprosy (Lev. 14:6).

By hyssop, a lowly herb which grows in rocky places and is effective in reducing swellings of the lungs, the humility of Christ was prefigured. Christ is the firm rock; through the outpouring of his sacred blood he reduced the swelling of the devil’s power and destroyed the leprosy of the human race’s sins.

Through faith in this humility, David promises that he will be cleansed from his sin when he says: “You will sprinkle me with hyssop”—that is, you will make me like the leper who is sprinkled with blood by means of hyssop.

He explains how he will make him like that leper when he adds: “and,” that is, namely, “I shall be cleansed.” That is, you will make me like him in this respect: Just as that leper is cleansed in his body, so I, through faith in the sprinkling of Christ’s blood in humility, shall be cleansed in my soul from my sin.

And I shall not be cleansed only through faith in Christ’s passion; “you will also wash me,” that is, you will cleanse me from the sin itself, so that I may be dedicated to Christ in the faith of baptism.

And once washed in the faith of baptism, “I shall be made whiter than snow” in my soul.

This means: I shall possess in my soul a greater brightness of virtues than is, in its own way, the brightness of snow. Because he could find no greater brightness in bodies, he made the comparison with the brightness of snow.

It is also evident from this that you prevail in goodness, because you will give joy to my inner hearing—that is, to my understanding—concerning the remission of my sin.

This means: Now I am sorrowful because of the oppression of my sin, but there will be a time when I understand that, through your mercy, it has been blotted out—that is, through the repentance I am undertaking—and thus you will give me joy concerning the remission of that same sin.

Or you will give joy to my inner hearing because, once remission has been received—that is, fully received—I, who now cannot comprehend your hidden mysteries because of my sins, will at some time comprehend them.

And in the future you will give me the joy of reward, when, justified by grace, you grant me the recompense of eternal life.

And by this also you prevail in goodness: “My humbled bones will rejoice”—that is, you will make me rejoice in my bones, namely, in reason, free will, and virtues. Although these are now humbled through sin, at some time they will again be exalted through the remission of sin and the restoration of my righteousness.

Having sought God’s goodwill by commending his goodness, he appropriately returns to his prayer, as follows:

I have shown in many ways that you prevail in goodness. Since, therefore, you are so good, “turn your face”—that is, your consideration—“away from my sins,” which I committed through Bathsheba.

I do not say “turn away” so that you may not see them, which is impossible; rather, turn away so that you do not punish them. To turn the face away from sins is to see them in such a way that they are not punished; to turn the face toward sins is to consider them in such a way that they are punished.

Because sight is in the face, “face” is used for consideration.

I pray that you turn your face away not only from the sins I committed through Bathsheba, but also that you blot out all my iniquities, whatever I have committed, so that you do not punish them.

Once these have been blotted out, “create a clean heart in me, God”—that is, a heart so clean from every error that I may be able to contemplate your mysteries within myself.

And “renew a right spirit”—that is, your Son, through whom everything that is right is brought about—“within me”; that is, make him newly dwell in my inward parts.

This means: Your wisdom—that is, your Son—dwelt previously in my soul through the operation of grace, before I sinned so grievously. By sinning I drove him away from me. I pray that you make him dwell in me again.

He indicates why he prays that the spirit should be renewed—that is, that the Spirit, namely the Son, should be restored to him—when he inserts the word “right.” It is as though he said: I pray for this in particular, so that, since the spirit himself is right, he may also make me right in my conduct, although by sinning I have turned myself away from righteousness.

He says “renew,” not with respect to the renewal of the spirit’s essence, since it is immutable, but with respect to the restoration of good works, which had failed in him.

It is as though he said: Restore to me the right spirit, through whose indwelling grace the good affections that had failed may be renewed in my soul, so that I may practice good works.

He uses “inward parts” for the soul because the soul reigns especially in the inward parts.

And after you have restored the right spirit to me, do not cast me away from your presence [Col. 0865C]—that is, do not permit me, through sin, to cast myself away again from the righteousness of your presence, that is, of the Son, who is called the Father’s face because, through his obedience, the Father’s mercy looked upon us so that we might be saved, just as someone looks through the sight that is in the face. And do not take from me—that is, do not permit it to be taken from me any longer through sin—your Holy Spirit, that is, the indwelling grace of your Spirit, and specifically of that person who is commonly called the Spirit, who also proceeds from the Father and the Son. This is as if he were saying: Make the grace of the Paraclete Spirit dwell steadfastly in me.

And thus: Restore to me the joy of your salvation, that is, of your Son, who will be the Savior of the world; as if he were saying: Because of the gravity of my sin, I have lost the joy of the salvation of your Son. For I know that I shall gain no benefit from his coming unless here I obtain forgiveness of sins through repentance. Therefore, I beg you, forgive me, and thus restore to me the joy of the Savior who is to come. And strengthen me in that joy—that is, make me persevere, so that by sinning criminally I may not again be deprived of it.

I say: Strengthen me in it, and do so by your principal Spirit, that is, through you, the Father, dwelling specially within me. The Father, however, is called the principal Spirit—not because he rules over the Son and the Holy Spirit or is greater than they, but because the Son is ineffably begotten from him and the Spirit proceeds from him.

He properly treats first of the Son when he says, “Renew the right spirit,” and so forth. Afterwards he treats of the Holy Spirit when he says, “Your Holy Spirit,” and so forth. Finally he treats of the Father when he adds, “By the principal Spirit,” and so forth. For if he had spoken of the Father first, someone perhaps in error might have believed that the Father excelled the Son and the Spirit in dignity, since the Father is called principal. But now, because he treats of the same person only at the end, and it is clear that he is not inferior, there can be no doubt that equality is affirmed. It should also be noted that it is not inappropriate for the Father and the Son to be called Spirit. Every incorporeal substance is rightly called spirit; and the Father and the Son are incorporeal substances.

After he has shown that, through God’s mercy, power, and goodness, his sins ought to be forgiven so that he may obtain pardon more quickly, he shows what benefit will follow from his forgiveness, as follows:

I prayed, “Have mercy and blot out my iniquities; create a clean heart in me,” and I prayed for many other things as well. If you accomplish these things in me, by my example I shall teach the wicked—that is, other people who sin criminally—your ways, that is, the mercy by which you will forgive my sins, and the justice by which, after justifying me, you will justify me still more. These mercy and justice are called your ways because through them one comes to you.

This is as if he were saying: If through your mercy you forgive me and justify me, and after justifying me advance me through your justice to greater righteousness, I shall show to others who sin in the same way that you are merciful and just, by the example of my innocence and justice given by you. And the impious—that is, those who sin as I have—will be converted to you through repentance, led by my example.

But so that this may happen, so that the impious may be converted to you by my example, O God—that is, my Creator and the God of my salvation, the Creator of the salvation that will restore to me the salvation I lost through sin—deliver me from bloodguilt, that is, from my sins, namely the adultery and homicide committed through Bathsheba. They are called “bloods” because they proceeded from an excess of blood, or “bloods” may mean the many deaths I caused.

For I killed the innocent Uriah bodily. I also killed myself spiritually by committing adultery. I likewise killed Bathsheba by driving her to consent to adultery. Deliver me from all these deaths by mercifully forgiving me, lest through them I be dragged to eternal death and tormented forever. Blood is used for death because blood is often shed in killing. Hence the prophet says: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I shall require his blood,” that is, his death, “at your hand” (Ezek. III, 15).

And if you deliver me from bloodguilt, I shall not only teach the wicked by my example, but my tongue also shall exult in your justice—that is, it shall joyfully proclaim that you are just, since you will have justified me. Or it may be understood thus: It shall proclaim to other wicked people the justice you will have given me, so that they too, converted to you, may be justified.

He promises that he will obtain what he has prayed for out of confidence in divine mercy, and by this too he merits pardon: he does not distrust God’s clemency, but attributes hope to his confidence. I said that, if you deliver me, my tongue shall proclaim your justice; and just as I trust that, through your mercy, you will deliver me, so, Lord, by my deliverance you will open my lips [Col. 0867A], that is, make them fit to praise your justice.

This is as if he were saying: As long as I remain unpurified from sins, I shall in no way be fit to praise you, and so I shall rightly have closed lips. “Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. XV, 9). But when you have cleansed me from sins, you will immediately make me fit to praise you, and thus you will open my lips, granting me the right to praise you. And after you have opened my lips, my mouth shall proclaim your praise, that is, it shall praise your mercy and justice.

Because he had groaned so deeply over his sin and prayed for it, someone might say: Why do you groan so much? Do not groan, but offer legal sacrifices to God for your sins, and thus you will be delivered. To exclude this objection he adds:

It is necessary that I groan and pray; nor is it useful for me to offer legal sacrifices, which I shall not offer. For if you had desired sacrifice—if I had understood that you wanted me to offer a legal sacrifice—I would certainly have given it already; but you will not delight in burnt offerings, that is, in legal sacrifices.

It should be noted, however, that in the Old Testament God was in a certain sense pleased by burnt offerings. Otherwise he would have commanded through Moses that they be offered in vain. He was pleased by burnt offerings so that they might be signs of the sacrifices that would take place under the new law, and so that what the limited understanding of those who understood spiritual realities weakly could not grasp might nevertheless be represented to some extent through the image of legal sacrifices, lest they be entirely alienated from faith in the grace that was to come.

He was not pleased by burnt offerings as though through them he forgave sins when faith in what those sacrifices signified was absent. Therefore he says, “You will not delight in burnt offerings,” namely, in such a way that through them you forgive sins.

It should also be noted that, although David lived under the old law, in which burnt offerings were commanded, he did not offer them—not through negligence, but because he left them aside as instruction for the faithful who would live under the grace of the New Testament. Thus, as a man already belonging by faith to the New Testament, he indicated to the faithful who would live in the time of the New Testament that such sacrifices were in no way to be offered by them; with the arrival of the realities signified by those sacrifices, they were to be entirely abolished.

After this he intends to show what sacrifice is suitable for the remission of sins. I said, O God, that you will not delight in burnt offerings, but a sacrifice acceptable to you for sins is a troubled spirit—that is, a soul afflicted with grief and groaning, and greatly troubled, O God. But you will not despise—that is, you will regard as acceptable—a broken and humbled heart, that is, a soul thoroughly broken and completely afflicted in every form of satisfaction.

The Prophet, foreseeing that such a sacrifice would wholly come to exist in the primitive Church and in the Church that was to be established from Jews and Gentiles, prays for both. Thus:

I said that an acceptable sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit. I know that this sacrifice will exist both in Zion, that is, in the primitive Church, which, neglecting earthly things, will contemplate heavenly things, and in Jerusalem, that is, in the Church to be established from both peoples.

It will be Jerusalem—that is, one who sees eternal peace by hope, or one who sees peace within herself, not being hostile to God by evil conduct but having peace with him by good living. Therefore, Lord, because this sacrifice will exist in Zion and in Jerusalem, deal kindly with Zion, that is, bestow abundant benefits upon her, exalting her in innocence and holiness—not on account of her merits, which are nonexistent, but in your good will, that is, through your freely given will, which proceeds from the goodness of your mercy.

Then let the walls of Jerusalem be built by that will of yours—walls that were destroyed in Adam, namely the virtues and innocence by which Jerusalem will be fortified after the manner of walls. He calls them the walls of Jerusalem by way of comparison, as if he were saying: Jerusalem, which was constituted from angels and human beings, and which was afterwards destroyed in Adam with respect to human beings, while remaining inviolate with respect to the angels, will be restored when its human beings are restored as citizens. He speaks by comparison with a city whose walls, partly destroyed, are rebuilt.

Then—that is, after you have built Zion and Jerusalem—you will accept, that is, regard as acceptable, the sacrifice of justice, specifically the thing signified and not the sign, which will be offered to you by Zion and Jerusalem. I mean a sacrifice that truly exists, not symbolically: not offerings and burnt offerings, that is, the sacrifice signified by the legal offerings and burnt offerings. It should truly be called an offering and a burnt offering.

The legal offerings and burnt offerings were so called because they were signs of the true future offerings and burnt offerings. He explains that sacrifice of justice as follows:

I say that you will accept the sacrifice of justice that will be offered to you by Zion and Jerusalem. And truly they will offer you a sacrifice of justice, that is, a sacrifice that is just to offer for the forgiveness of sins. For then they will place—that is, offer—themselves as calves, that is, as new sacrifices through baptism, just as calves are young and new. And they will do this upon your altar, that is, upon the faith on which they are founded. Faith is called an altar because upon it all sacrifices acceptable to God are offered.

## On Psalm LI

The title of the fifty-first Psalm: “For the end; understanding of David, when Doeg the Edomite came and announced to Saul and said to him: ‘David has come into the house of Abimelech.’” [Col. 0868D]

In this title a historical account is introduced to indicate its figurative meaning. The account is as follows: One day, while fleeing Saul’s persecution, David came to the house of Abimelech the priest, and there ate the bread of the Presence (1 Kings XXI). A certain Doeg the Edomite, who was keeper of Saul’s mules, saw this and reported it to Saul, saying: “David has come into the house of Abimelech.” Saul, angered against Abimelech because he had received David into his house, killed him together with his entire family.

The figure of this history is as follows: Through Doeg the Edomite, whose name is interpreted as “earthly agitation” or “agitation of blood,” the Antichrist is signified. He is properly called, with emphasis, “earthly” or “bloody agitation,” because through tribulation and the shedding of the blood of those unwilling to believe in him he will intend to move the whole earth from the worship of God to his own worship.

Through Abimelech, whose name means “the kingdom of my father,” is signified the assembly of the faithful who will exist in the time of the Antichrist. They will receive David—that is, Christ—into their house, that is, into themselves, who will be his house, and they will not deny him through fear of punishment. [Col. 0869A]

When the Antichrist sees that they have received David and are unwilling to abandon him, he tells Saul to kill them—that is, he commands it, not by voice but by his disposition and intention. He commands him to kill Abimelech, that is, that assembly of the faithful which has received David. This means: He will kill all those who will be Abimelech, that is, the kingdom of David’s own Father, namely those in whom God the Father of Christ will reign.

Through Saul, whose name is interpreted as “desire,” death is appropriately signified, since it is frequently desired by unbelievers through evil works.

Since in this Psalm the Prophet will not deal with the history but with what the history signifies, the title is nevertheless set down according to the likeness of the history, not as concerning the future but as though concerning the past, although it is to be understood of the future. It is explained as follows:

The understanding of this Psalm—that is, the understanding conceived in this treatise—is attributed to the prophet David, who looks toward the end of the world. This understanding was acquired when Doeg the Edomite came, that is, when he considered that the Antichrist would come, meaning that he would reign, and announced to Saul and said to him: “David has come into the house of Abimelech.”

He does not say that Doeg announced and spoke to some being who would have a conversation with death, since death is either an incorporeal reality or rather nothing at all. He speaks according to the likeness of the history: the Antichrist will in this way stir up death against the faithful because they will receive David—that is, Christ—into themselves, becoming his house, just as Doeg the Edomite stirred Saul against Abimelech so that he might kill him.

Saul came to him, Doeg announced and said to him that David had come into the house of Abimelech and had been received by him. I say that Doeg announced to Saul and said to him—that is, in his own thought he will announce to death and say that it should kill the faithful because David—that is, Christ—will come into the house of Abimelech, that is, he will be received by Abimelech, who will be his house, namely by the assembly of the faithful.

Or it may be understood thus: Doeg the Edomite, that is, the Antichrist, will come—that is, he will reign—and will announce to Saul, that is, to his ministers who are executioners. He will say to them: “David has come into the house of Abimelech,” that is, Christ has been received by his faithful, who have become his house. Therefore kill those faithful.

His ministers are properly called Saul, either according to the likeness of the story or according to the meaning of the word itself. According to the likeness of the story, because just as Saul killed the innocent Abimelech because he had rightly received David, the Lord’s Christ, so at the end of the world those ministers will kill innocent faithful people because they will rightly receive Jesus, the Christ of God the Father, in faith.

According to the meaning of the word, because Saul means “desire,” while those ministers will be desired in every way by the Antichrist for the destruction of the faithful.

In this Psalm there is the voice of the Prophet, who understands that the Antichrist will exist at the end of the world and persecute the faithful. He rebukes him for his wickedness, showing that it will itself be the cause of his complete destruction. Thus he strengthens the faithful who will exist in his time, whom the Antichrist will persecute, in steadfastness and draws them away from conformity to him.

For their consolation he also foretells that those faithful will fear God and praise him, foreseeing the death of the Antichrist, lest, if they abandon the fear and praise of God, they too perish like the Antichrist. On the day of judgment he promises those faithful, for their consolation, that they will laugh at the Antichrist.

Why do you glory in wickedness—that is, for what benefit do you rejoice in the wickedness of words, thoughts, and actions against the faithful, O Antichrist, who are powerful in iniquity, that is, to whom God permits the power to exercise iniquity against the faithful, for no benefit whatsoever?

It is as if he were saying: You glory in wickedness as though it were an honorable thing or as though some benefit would follow from it. But wickedness is neither honorable nor will any benefit come from it; rather, condemnation will follow.

He explains this wickedness in its several parts, so that it may be seen to be a dishonorable thing. I said: Why do you glory in wickedness? And truly you glory in it. For all day—that is, continually—your inner tongue, that is, the meditation of your heart, has thought about injustice, that is, unjust thoughts concerning how you might turn the faithful away from God’s law.

Since “speaking with the heart” means nothing other than meditating, meditation is called a tongue. And not only have you thought, but you have also practiced deceit, that is, deceitful words, saying that you are God while understanding that you are merely human.

You are like a sharp razor—that is, comparable to a sharp razor—in this respect: you are as ready to carry out wickedness as a sharp razor is to perform its function.

Or it may be understood thus: You are comparable to a razor so that, under the appearance of righteousness, you may secretly corrupt and injure some in the faith, just as a razor, although it ought to shave hairs, sometimes wounds the skin.

Or thus: You are like a razor because, just as a razor cleanses the skin and makes it brighter by removing excess hairs, so you, although you do not intend this, will cleanse the faithful through your persecutions from the excess filth of sins and make them bright in holiness. This means: You will be the cause of their becoming clean and radiant.

I say that you have practiced and conceived deceit, and you did so not unwillingly, which would have been more tolerable, but you loved wickedness—evil and harsh thoughts—rather than goodness and good thoughts. This is as if he were saying: If your reason ever urged you to think well—for no one is so wicked that his reason never at some time exhorts him to think well—then, scorning the good thought, you thought wickedness.

In this he shows him to be exceedingly worthy of condemnation, since he knowingly prefers evil to good. You loved iniquity, that is, speaking iniquitous and blasphemous and harsh words against the faithful in order to make them conform to you, more than speaking righteousness, that is, just and good words.

This means: You loved to speak harsh and iniquitous words, but not just ones. When he says “more than righteousness,” he indicates that at times, admonished by reason to speak well, he rejected speaking well and spoke evil.

Nor did you merely love iniquitous and harsh words; you also loved words of precipitation, that is, every word by which you could hurl the faithful into the error of your worship—both threatening words and flattering ones.

You, I say, are a deceitful tongue. This is said emphatically, meaning: You are deceitful in speech, saying that you are God while understanding that you are human.

All this, although it is placed in the past tense in prophetic fashion, is to be understood of the future. I said that you loved wickedness, and so forth.

Therefore God will destroy you with utter destruction, that is, completely. Or he will destroy you after you have been advanced to the end, that is, to the perfection, of wickedness. This means: After you come to the end, that is, to the accumulation of wickedness, you will be destroyed by God.

And he will do this in the following manner: God will tear you away from your tabernacle, that is, from this life and from your power, which will be temporary like a tabernacle and in which you will serve the devil; and he will make you migrate from this tabernacle into something worse.

He shows by removing you from where he will make you migrate when he adds: I say, he will tear you from your tabernacle, and he will tear out your root from the land of the living, that is, because of the empty pride of your power he will tear you from the land of the living.

This is as if he were saying: By the power through which you make yourself God, you think that you will take root in the land of the living; but because of your pride God will tear you from it. Or he says that he will tear out your root merely by comparison, meaning that he will destroy you completely, by comparison with a tree or plant that is uprooted.

By saying that he will tear him from his tabernacle, that is, from this world, and from the land of the living, he indicates that he will make him migrate into hell, since no other state remains after these two from which he will be torn.

But the righteous whom you persecute will see—that is, foresee—that God will destroy you. They will take warning from your example for themselves, lest, if they conform to you, they perish with you, and therefore they will be on their guard.

And on the day of his destruction, that is, on the day of judgment, they who in this world are oppressed by you through tribulations, being set above you, will laugh at you—that is, they will judge you worthy of ridicule—and will say:

“Now it is evident that he is merely human, not God, as he used to say.”

He did not set God as his helper, that is, because he did not regard himself as a creature but as God, he did not wish to pray to God for help. But he hoped—that is, he had confidence that he would accomplish whatever he wished—in the abundance of his riches, that is, through his many inner and outer riches.

By inner riches he means worldly eloquence and wisdom, which he will possess. By outer riches he means gold and other earthly things. And in his vanity, that is, in his empty pride, he prevailed, that is, he was stronger than all others, so that he might have greater power than everyone.

Or it may be understood thus: Placed in the vanity of his power, he prevailed over us—not in the injury of souls, but in the injury of bodies.

Or thus: Placed in the vanity of his hope, he prevailed, that is, he thought that he prevailed over us, so that we might conform to him.

I say that he hoped in many riches. But I hoped in the mercy of God forever—that is, for as long as this transitory age lasted, and onward into the eternal age that follows the former age.

I say that I then existed in the house of God, that is, in the Church, not barren of good works, but like a fruitful olive tree, bearing the fruit of good works after the manner of a fruitful olive tree, and ever green in faith, both in prosperity and adversity, after the likeness of the olive tree, which lacks its greenness neither in summer nor in winter.

Or it may be understood thus: Existing like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, that is, insofar as I was the house of God. This is as if he were saying: I was not fruitful through myself, but through God, whose house I was.

I say that I then hoped in mercy, while he hoped in riches. I say thus, speaking with myself: O God, I will confess to you forever. This is as if he were saying: I will not deny you through fear of the Antichrist, but I will confess—that is, praise—you, looking toward the eternal age in which you will return the reward of my hope.

And I will confess because you have made me a fruitful olive tree, and I will not make myself God in this age. But I will await—that is, patiently await—your name, which you will give me in the future, namely the name “God,” which you will give me in the future when you make me a participant in your divinity.

And rightly I will await that name, because it is good, already existing in the presence—that is, in the inward contemplation—of your holy ones. This means: They already contemplate that name in hope.

Or it may be understood thus: I will await—that is, carefully consider—your name, which is “God.” I will not attribute to myself or to the Antichrist this name, which is “God,” but I will consider it to be your name, because this name signifies the highest good, namely you and nothing else. And this is constant in the inward presence of your holy ones, although it is not constant for everyone.

Or again: I will await—that is, carefully consider—your name, that is, the magnification of the honor of your name. I will consider that your name is greatly to be honored, not the name of the Antichrist, because your name is good, that is, the honor of your name is good in the presence of your holy ones.

This means: I will consider it for this reason, because I see that your holy ones regard it as good to consider this.

## On Psalm LII

The title of the fifty-second Psalm: “For the end; on account of Amalek; understanding of David.” [Col. 0872D]

Since the history introduced in this title as a figure is very well known, he indicates it briefly when he says “on account of Amalek.” The history is as follows:

The Amalekites seized by force the small city of Ziklag, in which David’s sons and his wife lived, and carried away those sons and his wife as captives. When David heard this, he gathered a very large force, pursued them, defeated them, and rescued his wife and sons (1 Kings XXX).

The figure of this history is as follows: David signifies Christ; Amalek, whose name is interpreted as “grieving” or “in labor,” signifies the unbelievers from both peoples, who persecute the faithful in this world and lead them captive by exercising power over their bodies.

Those unbelievers are aptly called “in labor” and “grieving,” because here they are always bringing forth evil works for eternal punishments, over which they will grieve without end in the future.

By David’s wife and sons rescued from Amalek is signified the primitive Church, Christ’s special bride, and the other faithful who were made Christ’s sons through the preaching and example of that Church. In the future they will be completely rescued from the power of unbelievers when they are enriched with eternal glory. The unbelievers themselves, however, will be condemned forever.

The words of the title are explained as follows: The understanding of David, who looks toward the end, was acquired on account of Amalek. This means: The understanding David had when composing this Psalm was acquired on account of Amalek, that is, because of Amalek.

David, I say, looked toward the end, that is, toward Christ. This is as if he were saying: Amalek, defeated by David, signifying the assembly of unbelievers from whom God will rescue his own in the future, was the reason David acquired an understanding of the end, that is, of Christ, by looking toward that end, namely Christ. Because of this understanding he composed this Psalm in honor of the end, considering that the end would rescue his own and condemn the unbelievers.

In this Psalm the Prophet introduces Christ himself, the head, speaking about the unbelieving and foolish people who persecute his own. In persecuting the faithful they do not regard God as their avenger. He says that they are corrupt in their morals and abominable to God because of their iniquities. He also shows them to be without excuse, since they despise the salvation offered to them by God: namely, Christ, sent by the Father for the redemption of the world, from whom they turn away completely.

He also demonstrates the condemnation of those unbelievers, both here and in the future, and the salvation of the faithful, both here and in the future.

It should be noted that, although this Psalm was placed earlier in the thirteenth position, it was not repeated here in almost the same words without reason. Since in the earlier location the title introducing the history of Amalek does not precede it, but only “A Psalm of David” is given, we are shown that the victory over the Amalekites had not yet occurred when the Prophet composed the Psalm. For if it had occurred, the title would have been placed there.

Afterwards, when Amalek had been defeated and David’s wife and sons had been rescued, the Prophet himself saw that this event of victory figured what he had foretold in the Psalm concerning Christ. He therefore repeated the same Psalm on account of this history, to indicate that the rescue of the sons and wife had been a figure of the future rescue of Christ’s sons.

Just as this rescue indicates that the event foreshadowed some matter belonging to the new law, so it also indicates that all the deeds of the old law preceded as signs of the matters belonging to the new law, as the Apostle Paul testifies: “All these things happened to them in figure” (1 Cor. X, 11).

Some maintain that the three verses read above in this Psalm were not placed there by the Prophet, since in the repetition neither they nor any words equivalent to them are found. But because Paul placed these three verses in his Epistle to the Romans, with one brief verse of this Psalm added to them, they are said to have been received into this Psalm on account of the Apostle’s authority.

For the Apostle writes: “As it is written: There is none righteous, there is none who understands, there is none who seeks God; all have turned aside” (Rom. III, 10–12), and so forth.

Those three verses are these: “Their throat is an open tomb,” and so forth; “whose mouth,” and so forth; “destruction,” and so forth.

Since this Psalm was explained earlier at length and as carefully as we were able, and since here the text and meaning are almost the same, we judge it unnecessary to treat the same subject again at length. We think it sufficient to touch on it briefly, so that, if there is anything unknown that we had not yet understood and therefore did not include in the earlier exposition, we may supply it here at least.

Or if some portion is set down here with a different wording, we shall likewise endeavor to explain it as best we can.

First, however, it must be said that although we stated earlier that the head in this Psalm reproaches the Jews, it should be understood that the Psalm may concern not only the Jews but generally all the persecutors of Christ and of his members.

The foolish Jewish and Gentile people, persecutors of me and of my members, said in their heart: “This Christ is not God, so that he could avenge himself and his own.”

Truly both peoples are foolish, since they do not recognize me as God, even though my works and miracles and those of my members at least show this.

Since they said, “There is no God,” they were corrupted—that is, they will be corrupted more and more inwardly through blindness—and, being corrupted, they became abominable, that is, they will become accursed to God by persevering in their iniquities.

This is as if he were saying: They will not merely be corrupted and abominable to God because they said, “There is no God”; they will also become so because of their wicked works, and they will be corrupted to such a degree that there is not—that is, there will not be—anyone among them who does good.

This verse may also be read in the past tense, as follows: The fact that they said, “There is no God,” happened because they were corrupted, that is, blinded and so corrupted that they became abominable to God. And it is evident that they are corrupted and abominable in this respect: there is none of them who does good.

“Good” is understood in many ways. We call God good, true, and supreme. Virtues and the works performed through them are also called good. All creatures are likewise called good insofar as they were created by God; hence it is written: “Whatever was created by the good Creator is good.” We also call benefits good, regardless of who bestows them, even if they are not performed through the exercise of some virtue.

Although the foolish are corrupted and abominable and say, “There is no God,” they are nevertheless without excuse for this foolishness. For the triune God mercifully looked down from heaven—that is, from me in my human nature—upon the sons of men universally, that is, upon all human beings, to see, that is, to make evident, whether there was anyone understanding or seeking God.

This means: He did so in order to make plain who are understanding and seeking, and who are not.

But all those foolish people turned aside from that regard, that is, they did not care about the regard of mercy, and together with their turning aside they became useless both to themselves and to others.

He shows how they became useless to themselves: There is none who does good; there is none who reaches faith even to the one, that is, to me, who am the one and supreme good, according to the saying: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30).

Or the verse may be read, “God from heaven,” and so forth, in this way: Lest all human beings be thought to be corrupted, he says as follows:

I said that the foolish were corrupted. But the sons of men are not corrupted. For God looked down from heaven, that is, through the teaching of the apostles, upon the sons of men, that is, upon the faithful who conduct themselves rationally, to see whether there was anyone understanding or seeking God—that is, to make evident which of them rightly understands or seeks God and could instruct others in this.

For there are many faithful people who are not sufficiently understanding to be instructors of others. I said that he looked upon the sons of men so that through them others might understand. But the foolish, unwilling to understand through them, all turned aside from understanding, and so forth.

I said that they say that I am not God. But will they not recognize in the future all who work iniquity, that is, perform wicked works, who devour my people through tribulations as though they were bread—that is, continually—that I am the God whom they now deny?

He puts this as a question in order to rebuke them and draw them away from such an error.

And therefore they have been so blinded that they work iniquity, because they did not invoke me, God, as their helper, and because there they trembled with fear where there was no fear to be had. The Jews feared abandoning carnal observances; the Gentiles feared not worshiping their idols. Neither of these things should have been feared.

Although he says “they trembled,” he does not add “with fear” unnecessarily. Many tremble not because of fear but because of a fever or some similar condition.

They were blinded in this way because they did not invoke God, since the triune God scattered the bones of those who please human beings. This means: God weakened, after the manner of something scattered and thereby made weak, their free will and reason, so that they would not wish to invoke him.

He did not scatter them unjustly, but because they pleased human beings in persecuting the faithful—that is, because they persecuted them in order to please one another, being merely human and not also belonging to God in their persecution. This means: They did so in order to glory in one another.

And those who have already been scattered were confounded—that is, they will be utterly confounded—here, so that they may become more blinded in the future and perish without end. They will therefore be confounded because God rejected them on account of their evil merits.

He raises a question and then answers it himself, as follows: I say that God rejected them. Which God? The answer follows: The one who, being born from Zion, will give salvation to Israel in this world—that is, he will give salvation to the faithful, so that they may not be blinded, contrary to the fact that he scattered the bones of the foolish here and contrary to the fact that in the future he will confound them.

In the future Jacob will exult and Israel will rejoice, that is, the faithful, both great and small, will rejoice when the triune God turns away the captivity of his people, Jacob and Israel—that is, their mortality and their liability to suffering.

## On Psalm LIII
### Title of the Fifty-Third Psalm

“Unto the end, in songs of understanding, of David, when the Ziphites had come and said to Saul, ‘Is not David hidden among us?’”

This title also appears to have been placed according to the historical account, which is as follows. When David was fleeing from Saul, he took refuge at a village called Ziph, where his fellow-tribesmen lived, and hid there. But the Ziphites, who were his kinsmen and ought therefore to have concealed him, went to Saul and said to him: “Why do you not kill David, since you now have the power to put him to death? For is he not hidden among us, where you can find him?” Having said this, they betrayed him to Saul (1 Kings 23).

The figurative meaning of this history is as follows. Through the Ziphites who betrayed David to Saul—“Ziphites” being interpreted as “those who flourish”—the Jews were signified. Although they flourished in earthly things, moved by the arrogance of their prosperity, they betrayed Christ, who is truly David, to Saul—that is, to death—fearing that they would lose their place and nation. Christ, according to his divinity, was hidden among them; that is, he was hidden in the flesh which he had taken from their blood in the Virgin. Why Saul signifies death has often already been explained.

The words of the title, however, should be explained as follows. “The understanding of David” means the understanding which the Prophet David possessed when composing this psalm. “Of David,” I say, “who looks toward the end,” that is, toward Christ; “in songs,” that is, in praises. In other words, he looked toward the end in such a way as to praise him by composing songs—namely, this psalm—to his honor. The Prophet received this understanding when the Ziphites had come and said to Saul: “Is not David hidden among us, where you can kill him?” And afterward they betrayed him to Saul. That is to say, the Prophet observed that the Ziphites, his fellow-tribesmen, who ought to have concealed him, had come to Saul and said to him, “Is not David hidden among us?” and afterward had betrayed him to Saul. Understanding through the Holy Spirit that this event, fulfilled in him, prefigured the betrayal of Christ by the Jews unto death, and looking toward Christ himself, he composed this psalm in his praise.

In it he introduces Christ, according to his humanity, praying to the divine Trinity that it make him steadfast in his Passion, so that he would not yield through fear when the Ziphites betrayed him to Saul. He also prays concerning the resurrection and on behalf of his enemies; he displays his Passion, for which it was necessary that he pray; and he promises that he will willingly offer himself upon the cross, with the resurrection in view. This sacrifice is the reason why God ought to hear him when he prays.

The words placed in the title, “Is not David,” do not seem to contribute anything figuratively to the force of the psalm, but rather to serve the historical exposition.

“God the Father, save me, so that I may not yield.” By “me” I mean: preserve me steadfast in the honor of your name, according to the saying: “I do not seek my own glory, but that of the Father who sent me” (John 8:50). “And judge me as I ought to be judged,” namely, by causing me to rise through your power—that is, through your might. In other words: You are powerful enough to raise me.

He shows himself worthy to be heard when he prays not only with words but also with inward feeling, adding: “I pray, save me and judge me.” He makes this prayer both with affection and with words. Therefore, O God, hear my prayer, which is made with inward feeling, and perceive it with your ears—that is, hear the words of my mouth, the prayer which I express in words. “Perceive with your ears” is said according to human usage.

It is necessary that I pray to you to save me, so that I may not yield, because strangers—that is, the Jews, who ought to be friends since they are my fellow-tribesmen, but who have become strangers to me through their pride and envy—have risen against me, seizing me, beating me, and blaspheming.
