Desiring to be strong themselves so that they might hold me in death, they sought my soul—that is, they will seek to take my life.

Although they ought to have recognized that I am God, and therefore ought not to persecute me, they did not set before themselves—that is, they will not set before their inward sight—God the Word, personally united to me, as my helper. In other words: They will not consider that I am both man and God.

Someone might say: “Do you have God personally united to you as your helper?” He replies: “Yes. They truly ought to set God before themselves.” For behold, in the present God is helping me, making me steadfast; and therefore, in view of my steadfastness, they ought to set him before themselves. And the Lord, personally united to me, is the protector of my soul—that is, he will receive my soul in order to restore it to my body after three days.

Then follows a prayer for his enemies:

“Although they rise against me and seek my soul, I pray only this, Lord: Turn away from me the evils which my enemies deserve. And destroy them according to what they are, in your truth”—that is, bring them into conformity with me, who am your truth, according to the saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Or this may be understood as a concession to divine justice, as follows: “I say that the strong will seek to hold my soul in death, and therefore I concede: Turn these evils away from me, so that I may not be held and yield; and give these evils to my enemies, namely, that they be defeated by the Roman enemies and condemned eternally.”

He explains part of these evils when he adds: “In your truth”—that is, in your true and just judgment—“destroy them”: destroy them through Titus and Vespasian, or destroy them with the destruction of eternal death.

He then adds the reason why God ought to hear him:

“I have prayed to you, God, that you save me and judge me, and this is just. For willingly—that is, gladly and not unwillingly—I shall sacrifice myself to you upon the cross. And afterward I shall confess”—that is, I shall bring forth true confessors—“to your name,” that is, to the honor of your name, Lord. For it is good to confess; that is, it is good that I should bring forth confessors.

“And therefore I shall sacrifice, because I am certain that you have delivered me”—that is, will deliver me—“from every tribulation,” making me immortal. “And my eye”—that is, my contemplation—“has looked down upon my enemies,” who now consider themselves inferior.

In other words: “I shall look down upon them”—that is, I shall cause my enemies to be seen below me, appearing above them: I shall subjugate some of them to myself by saving them, and scatter others throughout the world.

It is as though he were saying: “You ought to hear me when I pray, so that you may deliver me from tribulation. For I shall sacrifice to you because I have confidence that you will deliver me from every tribulation; and afterward I shall look down upon my enemies who now, while I am placed in humiliation, look down upon me—that is, consider themselves inferior to me.”

### On Psalm Fifty-Four

The title of the Fifty-Fourth Psalm is: “Unto the end, in songs, an understanding for David himself.” It is explained as follows.

The understanding of this psalm is to be attributed to David himself—that is, to Christ persevering “in songs,” meaning in praises, so that he may praise God in intention, voice, and deed, not ceasing even in the Passion itself, where God is especially to be praised.

By “in songs,” I mean persevering unto the end, namely, unto the end of his life, until his life was brought to an end through the death of the cross; or else persevering in songs unto the end—that is, unto the consummation of eternity.

In other words, he persevered in songs, that is, in the praises of God, both in prosperity and in adversity, until God restored him to complete and perfected immortality.

When the phrase “in songs” is used, the psalm often concerns the Passion. We are thereby reminded that, just as Christ persevered in the praise of God during his Passion, so we too ought not to cease praising God in our tribulations.

In this psalm the Head is introduced praying that he may not yield in the Passion and that he may rise again, while displaying his Passion, for which it is necessary that he pray. It also concerns the rejection of the Jews and the conversion of the nations. Concerning the condemnation of those Jews, it speaks concessively both with respect to body and with respect to soul. It also foretells that he will remain steadfast, rise again, and ascend to heaven. He presents all this for the instruction of those who are to be converted, so that they may love God because of their salvation and guard themselves against the destruction of unbelievers, lest, if they depart from God, they too should be condemned in the same way. Thus he says:

“Hear, God, my prayer, so that you may raise me again, make me immortal, and exalt me; and do not despise my supplication, by which I ask you not to allow me to fail in the Passion.”

We properly say that we “pray” when we ask in order to obtain something; we “supplicate” when we ask that some disadvantage be driven away from us by our prayer.

“Attend to me”—that is, grant me the intention of perseverance in virtue and in my good purpose, namely, that I may praise you continually. “And in this way, I say, hear me,” by granting me this intention.

He adds this out of great affection, or because the labor in the Passion is exceedingly great—or else “exercise” is used for “Passion” in any kind of trial. I say, then: “Hear me.” And this is just. For if I have been troubled in my exercise—that is, in my Passion—I have been troubled, or will be troubled, on account of the Jews because they refuse to submit to my teaching.

It is as though he were saying: “For this reason I am worthy to be heard: because I shall undergo the exercise of the Passion for you, and before long I shall be so troubled by the obstinate unbelief of my enemies that I shall grieve.”

The Passion is called an exercise by analogy: just as through the exercise of secular arts one arrives at knowledge of the divine Scriptures, so through the Passion Christ arrived at the sublimity of immortality.

Or it may be understood in this way: “In the exercise of my teaching”—that is, in perseverance in my teaching—“I have been troubled by the obstinacy of the Jews.”

Having shown the merit by which he ought to be heard, he sets forth the necessity as follows:

“I pray: hear me, and this is necessary. For I have been disturbed by the voice of the enemy”—that is, of the Jewish people—“and by the tribulation of the sinner,” namely, of that same people, called “the sinner” by antonomasia.

In other words: “I shall be troubled by voluntary fear according to the flesh.” This fear will arise from the voice of the threatening Jewish people—that is, because they will threaten me with death, saying, “Crucify him”—and from the tribulation of the sinner, because he will inflict tribulation upon me, seizing me, leading me away as a robber, spitting upon me, and afflicting me with blows.

He explains why he will be troubled by their voice:

“I shall therefore be troubled by their voice because they have turned aside their iniquities”—that is, they will turn their iniquities away from themselves onto me—“so that they may kill me, pretending that I am a seducer and blasphemer, although they themselves are seducers and blasphemers.”

Accordingly it is written: “If this man were not a malefactor, we would not have handed him over to you” (John 18; Mark 2). And elsewhere: “This man blasphemes” (Matthew 26; John 10).

“And I shall fear the tribulation,” because they were troublesome to me—that is, I foresee that they will inflict troublesome tribulation upon me. This is not because of my merits, but “in wrath,” that is, because of the impiety of their irrational anger.

Because he had said that he would be troubled, lest he be thought to be troubled involuntarily rather than willingly, he repeats that he will be troubled in order to define the matter as follows:

“I said: I shall be troubled by the voice and by the tribulation, and this is how it will be: my heart has been troubled”—that is, my soul will be troubled by fear of the voice and of the tribulation. And this disturbance will be “in me”—that is, within my own authority.

In other words: “I have the power to be troubled or not to be troubled.” It is as though he were saying: “I shall be troubled willingly.”

Nor will I fear only because of the voice and the tribulation: “The dread of death has fallen upon me”—that is, it will happen to me.

When he says, “It will fall upon me,” he indicates that the dread will be exceedingly great, so that it will oppress him violently. The expression is drawn from the likeness of a heavy object which, if it falls upon someone, crushes him excessively.

He displays this dread in its parts as follows:

“Truly dread will fall upon me; and it will not be a simple dread, but there will come upon me”—that is, they will come upon me for my oppression—“fear in my soul and trembling in my body. Nor will this fear be empty, for darkness has covered me”—that is, death will wholly occupy my body.

He uses “cover” by analogy with something which, when covered, is entirely occupied by that with which it is covered. Death is called “darkness” because it makes the bodily eyes dark.

“I say that they will turn their iniquities upon me and will trouble me in their wrath; and they will grieve me because they refuse to submit to my teaching.”

Then I said—that is, I shall say both with voice and with inward feeling:

“Who will give me wings like a dove’s, that I may fly away and rest?”

This is placed in the form of a question, but it is a prayer. He expresses it interrogatively because of his excessive affection. Such questions usually bear the greater weight of feeling.

It is as though he were saying: “O God, grant me, who am like a dove”—that is, truly a dove—simple as a dove is, without the gall of anger and hatred, and full of the love of charity, like doves which, out of affection, offer kisses to one another—“wings,” that is, the agility of rising again, so that my resurrection may not be delayed until the general resurrection. Make me rise quickly, namely, after three days.

He uses “wings” for agility because winged birds are agile.

“And after you have given me wings, I shall fly”—that is, I shall go most swiftly to the nations through my preachers, not locally but by faith, because they will believe in me—“and I shall rest in them,” that is, I shall delight in their faith.

Since the Jews reject me, I say: “Give me wings.” For while I exist like a dove—that is, while I lack the gall of bitterness, after the manner of a dove—who else will give me wings, so that I may fly and rest? No one except you.

Because he had said, “Who will give me wings?” lest he seem to have said this out of uncertainty, he turns in apostrophe to his hearers and shows himself certain of it, foretelling that he will fly as follows:

“I said: Who will give me wings, and so forth.” Yet I am by no means uncertain of this. For I know that—behold, in the present—I have withdrawn, or will withdraw, fleeing from the Jews, compelled by them because they reject me. This is taken from the likeness of someone fleeing who is compelled to leave a certain place.

“And afterward I remained in the wilderness”—that is, I shall remain forever among the nations, which were called a wilderness because they were deserted, lacking every good work and virtue and deprived of the dew of teaching. The expression is drawn from the likeness of a wilderness, that is, of a deserted land lacking the fertility of every good thing.

Or it may be understood as follows: “Who will give me wings”—that is, agility for rising again—“and I shall fly,” that is, I shall hasten most swiftly toward immortality and impassibility; “and I shall rest,” that is, I shall delight, I who am afflicted here by many anxieties.

It is as though he were saying: “Give me wings, and I shall fly and rest. For who else will give them, except you? No one, certainly.”

He also shows himself certain of this, just as in the preceding statement:

“Although I said, ‘Who will give me wings, and I shall fly,’ I am nevertheless not uncertain of this. For I am secure, because behold, in the present I shall withdraw, fleeing from death”—that is, swiftly, after the manner of one fleeing—“and I shall remain forever in the wilderness,” that is, in solitary blessedness.

And truly his blessedness is a wilderness, since no one besides him alone has attained, or will attain, to such great blessedness, although all the faithful will attain to it.

Since he had said, “Who will give me wings?” lest he seem not to know who the giver was, he adds:

“I said, ‘Who will give me wings,’ O hearers, and yet I do not fail to recognize the giver of the wings. Rather, I awaited him”—that is, I, who know him well, await him, and will await him patiently, without complaint or weariness—“who saved me,” or “will save me,” “from faintness of spirit,” so that I may not have a fainthearted spirit and fail in the Passion.

Those are said to have a fainthearted spirit who yield through fear. And he will save me from the storm—that is, from disturbance of mind—so that I may not be stirred in the Passion by anger and hatred against the Jews.

Such disturbance is rightly called a storm, because it troubles the mind and destroys the virtues, by analogy with the air that is commonly called a storm, by which the air is disturbed and the crops are destroyed.

He speaks concessively concerning his enemies:

“Enemies will turn their iniquities upon me and will trouble me, and for this reason I shall fly from them to the nations. These enemies, as I foresee, will afterward be cast down from the honor in which they now take pride.”

And so I concede: “Cast them down, God, from their honor.” But because they could be cast down from their honor while remaining in their homeland, he adds:

“And by casting them down, divide their tongues”—that is, make them divided and diverse.

It is as though he were saying: “While they remain in their homeland, they need only one language. But scatter them throughout the entire world, and then they will necessarily have different languages.”

And when I say “cast them down,” I do not say it out of malevolence, but because of their evil merits:

“For I saw in the city”—that is, in their assembly—“iniquity,” that is, wicked thoughts and wicked deeds, “and contradiction.”

In other words: “I saw that they were wicked in their thoughts and deeds and contradicted the truth.” Therefore I concede: “Cast them down.”

“City” is used by metonymy for “assembly,” because a city contains an assembly of human beings.

This iniquity will never afterward cease; rather, day and night—that is, continually—or “day and night,” meaning both in prosperity and in adversity, iniquity will surround it, that is, occupy it completely. The expression is drawn from the likeness of a city surrounded by enemies.

He shows in its parts how iniquity surrounds the city—that is, occupies it entirely—as follows:

“I say that iniquity will surround it. Iniquity, I say, exists upon its walls”—that is, it subjects the rulers of that city to itself, namely, the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees. They are called walls because, like walls, they ought to fortify the lesser people by their teaching, since they are elevated in knowledge.

“And in its midst”—that is, among the common people—“there is labor and injustice,” namely, laboring to obtain injustice.

In other words: “They labor altogether for this purpose, that they may be unjust.” The middle is called the common people because they ought to be protected by their superiors, just as the middle of a city is protected by its walls.

Or it may be understood in this way:

“Day and night iniquity will surround it, existing upon its walls,” that is, prevailing over the guardianship of its walls so that the walls cannot protect it—namely, the angels who had been given to them by God for their protection, whose guardianship they repel from themselves through iniquity.

In other words: “Its iniquity is so great that the walls cannot guard it.”

And therefore, in the midst of that city—that is, in the fullness of that city—there is labor and injustice, namely, laboring toward injustice.

In other words: “It is not merely a few who labor toward injustice, but the whole fullness of that city.”

When he says that there is injustice in its midst, this is said by analogy with enemies who, after occupying the middle of a city, are able to dominate it on every side.

It is as though he were saying: “Injustice has occupied that entire city.”

Or it may be read literally:

“Day and night iniquity will surround it, existing upon its stone walls,” that is, rising above the height of its walls.

In other words: “Although its walls are sufficiently high in their own measure, their iniquity is still higher in its own measure.”

And therefore “in its midst,” that is, in the open, there is labor and injustice. In other words: “They labor openly and shamelessly toward injustice.” Since what is in the middle is open, “middle” is used for “open.”

He explains the injustice in its parts as follows:

“And from its streets”—that is, from the public place—“usury and deceit have not ceased,” literally.

It is as though he were saying: “In the streets also they openly practice usury and deceit.”

Or it may be understood as follows:

“From its streets”—that is, from its rulers—“usury has not ceased,” namely, excessive punishment, “nor deceit.”

In other words: “If anyone sins against them, they demand a greater punishment than the offense warrants,” by analogy with a usurer who demands more money from a debtor than he lent.

But if at times they cannot exact usury from those who sin against them—that is, manifest punishment—they act deceitfully against them.

The rulers are rightly called “streets,” because through their governance and teaching the lesser people ought to walk, just as one travels through streets.

Since he had spoken about them concessively, someone might say: “Why do you rather concede that these people should be cast down, when there are also many Gentiles who do not obey you, concerning whom you do not say that they should be cast down?”

He answers by showing why these people are less tolerable than the Gentiles, even if the Gentiles had cursed him and spoken great things against him. In answering, he turns to them in an apostrophe of rebuke; although they are many persons, he addresses them in the singular as “man,” because they are one in wickedness.

“I said concessively, ‘Cast them down,’ and I conceded this justly. For it is unworthy that I should tolerate you”—that is, patiently postpone your punishment entirely until the future.

“For if my enemy”—the Gentile people, who never falsely claimed to be my friend, as you, the Jewish people, falsely claim, saying, ‘Teacher, we know that you are truthful,’ and so forth (Matthew 12:14)—“if that Gentile people, which openly acts as my enemy and does not have faith in me, had cursed me”—not with its voice but in deed, that is, had brought me low in tribulation, as you will curse me, that is, bring me low—“I would certainly have tolerated it,” that is, I would have patiently postponed its punishment entirely until the future. I would not have conceded that it be cast down here, as I concede concerning you.

“And if the one who hated me”—openly living wickedly and not pretending to be my friend, as you pretend—“had exalted himself over me through arrogance, after your manner, and had spoken great things with his mouth”—that is, proud things, as you do when you say, “Everyone who makes himself a king contradicts Caesar” (John 19:12), and other such things—“perhaps,” that is, truly, “I would have hidden myself from him,” that is, I would have hidden my power from him, postponing punishment until the future. I would not cast him down here, as I shall cast you down.

What he has placed in the past tense should be read as follows: “If my enemy had cursed me, as you will curse me, I would certainly have tolerated it. And if the one who hates me had spoken great things against me, I would truly have hidden my power from him.”

“But you, the Jewish people, being a man”—that is, animal and not spiritual—“united in mind”—that is, most friendly to me in pretense, but not in reality, and not according to everyone, but according to certain persons who deceitfully seek intimacy with me so that they may rebuke me—“my leader,” according to those whom I appointed as leaders of the people, although they do not lead them well, namely, the chief priests and the other rulers, who possess the keys of knowledge but neither enter themselves nor permit others to enter (Matthew 23:13).

They are called leaders although they do not lead, because they have the office of leading.

“And my acquaintance”—that is, my kinsman, according to some, because they belong to the same tribe—or “acquaintance,” according to others, because, although I was nourished bodily, I was brought up and lived among them from childhood—

“you who together with me took sweet foods,” that is, the sweet precepts of the Law, which are food for the soul, “and took them together,” that is, in the same place: in the synagogues and in the Temple.

In other words: “We all took them together, in the same place, and in the house of God”—that is, in the Temple—“we walked together,” that is, in harmony, so that we might jointly complete the sacrifices and other legal observances there.

“You, I say, Jewish people, who are such and such as I have said—are you to be tolerated by me?” By no means.

It is as though he were saying: “Truly I must concede that you be cast down, and I ought not to tolerate you by postponing your punishment until the future, because you are my fellow-minded man, my leader, and my acquaintance; you took sweet foods together with me, and with you I walked in the house of God in harmony.”

“And although all these things are so, you will nevertheless grieve and disturb me and reject me, when you ought not to reject me, but ought to submit to me as your king and Savior, whom you were able to recognize through the testimony of the prophets, and thus make me rejoice. Therefore you are altogether worthy to be cast down.”

“I say that I shall not tolerate you, although you are all these things, and yet you will both grieve and disturb me.”

I would tolerate the Gentile enemy who openly hates me if he cursed me, and I would hide my power from him if he spoke great things against me, since he is neither my acquaintance, nor united with me in friendship, nor my leader.

For the Gentile people are not as deserving of condemnation as you are. They could never have known me through the Law, which they lacked, as you could know me through the testimony of the Law. Nor did they ever deceitfully make themselves united with me in friendship. I did not appoint them as my leaders, as I appointed you; nor were they ever my kinsmen.

When he says, “But you, man,” this seems to have an effect not upon the sense but upon the order of the wording.

When he says “had cursed,” “to curse” is used for “to bring low,” just as “to bless” is often used for “to exalt.”

### The Condemnation of the Jews

Having conceded that the Jews would suffer condemnation in this world, and having shown the reasons why they ought to undergo that condemnation, he next discusses the condemnation that will occur on the day of judgment:

“I said, ‘Cast them down and divide them.’ And not only will they be cast down and divided, but at some point everlasting death will also come upon them—those who do not know that I am God, namely, the uneducated common people, who sin against me at the urging of their rulers—and they will descend alive into hell.”

By “those who are alive” he means those who knowingly and prudently kill themselves by sinning against me, although they do not fail to know that I am God.

He alludes here to the historical account of Dathan, Abiram, and their accomplices (Numbers 16). Dathan and Abiram, while contradicting the priesthood of Aaron and not being unaware that they were acting against God, the author of that sacrifice, had many accomplices who nevertheless did not know that they themselves were acting against God. They were swallowed alive by the earth and descended into hell. The others, who ignorantly consented to them, were consumed by fire.

Through Dathan and Abiram, who perished while alive, that portion of the Jews was signified which, although it knew that Christ was God, was nevertheless going to contradict him and, while living prudently in the knowledge of Christ himself, was going to descend into the condemnation of hell.

Through their accomplices, who were consumed by fire, that portion of the Jews was represented which, although ignorant that Christ was God, was going to contradict him and, when the infernal fire came upon them and overwhelmed them, was going to perish—not because they were alive and prudent, but because they acted perversely through the negligence of ignorance.

He alludes to the likeness of this history when he says:

“Let death come upon those who, while ignorant that I am God, contradict me,” just as fire came upon the accomplices of Dathan and Abiram and consumed them.

It is well said that death will come “upon” them, by analogy, as though he were saying: “May everlasting death so oppress them that they cannot rise from it and escape,” after the manner of those who are so crushed by some weight falling upon them that they are not permitted to rise.

“And let those who are alive”—that is, those who do not sin through ignorance—“descend into hell,” that is, let them come into the deepest destruction, which is indicated by the word “descend.” For we say that those come to the depths who descend.

“I say, let them descend into hell, and let death come upon them, because wickedness”—that is, wicked deeds—“is in their dwellings,” that is, in their bodies, which are the dwellings of souls.

“And wickedness”—that is, wicked thoughts—“is in their midst,” that is, in the heart, which is called the middle because it is situated in the middle of the body.

Or “middle” is used by analogy, because bodily actions are performed according to its measure, just as a circle is constructed according to the measure of a point, which is the center.

When he adds, “But I,” and so forth, he announces his salvation, lest he seem to have prayed out of uncertainty. The continuation is as follows:

“I said that they would be destroyed in this world and in the future. But I cried to the Lord with devoted intention, and the Lord will save me.”

He will save me by making me steadfast “in the evening,” that is, in the Passion, which occurred toward evening—at about the ninth hour, specifically—which was prefigured by the lamb that was sacrificed in the old Law toward evening.

“And he will save me in the morning,” that is, in the resurrection, which will occur in the morning, making me immortal and impassible.

“And he will save me at midday,” that is, in the ascension, which will occur around midday, exalting me above the heavens and subjecting the whole world to me.

“And I shall recount through my preachers to the whole world these salvations after they have occurred. And while they are still future, I shall announce them to my disciples, so that they may recount them to everyone after they have taken place.”

“Recount” properly refers to the past; “announce” to the future.

Or it may be understood as follows:

“The Lord will save me in the evening, in the morning, and at midday,” that is, both in prosperity and in adversity, so that prosperity may not lift me up, nor adversity depress me.

Prosperity is signified by evening and morning because at those times the air lacks heat; the heat of tribulations does not prevail in them. Adversity is understood through midday, which burns with the heat of the sun, because in adversity everyone is oppressed by the heat of tribulations.

And because he will save me through his preachers, “I shall recount” the benefits which he has given me, and “I shall announce” the benefits which will be repaid to my faithful in the future.

Or it may be understood as follows: “Through my preachers I shall recount the lesser benefits already given to me by him,” namely, freedom from sin, the power of miracles, and the practice of good works; “and I shall announce the greater benefits which he will give,” namely, immortality, impassibility, and the subjugation of the whole world.

“I said that I cried out inwardly with affection, and not only this, but I shall also pray with my voice.” This is not explicitly found in the book, but it is understood from what he adds: “And he will hear my voice.”

He will hear me in this way: “He will redeem”—that is, rescue—“my soul, to establish it in perpetual peace.” This was stated obscurely above when he said, “He will save me in the evening.” Therefore he repeats it equivalently when he says “he will redeem,” so that he may explain more clearly afterward from whom he will redeem me, when he adds:

“He will redeem me from those who draw near to me.”

And because “to draw near” can refer both to good and to evil, he defines it as follows:

“I say that he will redeem me from the Jews who draw near to me. And it is necessary that he redeem me from them, because they were with me”—that is, they are in my intimacy—“among many,” existing in the number of the unbelievers, who are many, not in the number of the faithful, who are few.

In other words: “They draw near to me in such a way that, without abandoning their unbelief, they lie in wait for me, so that they may accuse me and find an occasion for my death.”

Having announced his salvation, he also announces the twofold condemnation of his enemies, which he had discussed above concessively when he said: “Cast them down,” and, “Let death come,” and so forth.

In order, therefore, to announce this condemnation, he repeats what he had stated above, in order to confirm it as follows:

“He will hear me,” I say, “God the Word, so that he may redeem me. And, by contrast, God the Word, personally united to me, who existed before the ages”—that is, from eternity—“will humble my enemies from worldly honor and cast them down from their land.”

They say that he is not united to me. In other words: “I, who am God and man, eternal according to my divinity and born in time according to my humanity, will humble them, because they consider me only as man and deny that I exist from eternity.”

Someone might say: “Has mercy perished to such an extent that, although they might perhaps someday be converted from their impiety, God does not have mercy on them, so that they may not be humbled?”

He answers this by saying that they will never be converted:

“I say that God the Word will humble them, and justly. For there is no conversion for them”—that is, they do not ever wish to be converted from their wickedness so as to become good.

It is as though he were saying: “If they were converted, they would not be humbled. But because they do not wish to be converted, God will humble them.”

And therefore there is no conversion for them, because they did not fear God the Word; that is, they did not set before their consideration the need to fear God the Word. Certainly, if they feared him, they would also desire conversion.

He now discusses the condemnation that will occur on the day of judgment, as follows: I said that God will humble them, and he will not merely exact this vengeance from them; he will further stretch out his hand, that is, he will further enlarge his vengeance by repaying them with a greater condemnation in proportion to their evil merits. This is drawn from the likeness of someone striking who, when he wishes to strike someone heavily, stretches out his hand very far. The hand is appropriately used for vengeance, since by striking with our hands we often [188] avenge ourselves upon enemies. And he will rightly stretch out his hand, because they have defiled his testament, that is, they have corrupted his law by explaining it wrongly. Accordingly, we read in the tenth psalm: “What you have accomplished, they destroyed” (Ps. X, 3). They did indeed defile the law—not with regard to the law itself, which is holy and pure, but with regard to their left-handed interpretation of it. This is to say: They gave a corrupted exposition of the law. [Col. 0886C]

Having stated the reason why he will stretch out his vengeance, he explains the vengeance itself as follows: I say that he will stretch out his hand in this way, namely, because they have been divided from the anger of his countenance, that is, on the day of judgment they will be separated from the kingdom of God, in which they rashly presume to dwell. This separation will occur because of God’s anger, that is, because he will be angry with them. When he says “the anger of his countenance,” he speaks in human fashion, since anger is ordinarily made known in the face. “The anger of his countenance” means no more than anger simply, or than my anger, when on the day of judgment I shall appear in majesty, angered, to those by whom I was neglected—though I came in humility and peace—who am called the countenance and face of God, because through me God mercifully looks upon the human race, just as anyone looks upon another with his face. Or it may be read in this way: He stretches out his hand in repaying.

I say that they have no change from evil to good, and this because they did not fear God so as to obey his commandments. And although they did not fear him, nevertheless he stretches out his hand, that is, he makes his mercy abundantly generous in repaying good for evil: although they were wicked and disobedient to the precepts of the law, he would send them mercy, namely his Son, that is, me, who would lead them back to the way of life.

And they did not recognize God’s mercy, but defiled his testament by explaining it wrongly and twisting to another meaning whatever is written there about me; therefore, in the future they will be separated from the anger of his countenance. [Col. 0886D] When he says that he stretches out his hand, he uses a comparison, since when we wish to bestow benefits upon someone, we ordinarily stretch out our hand toward that person.

I say that they will be separated from the kingdom of God, whereas, by contrast, “that one’s heart of God has drawn near” (Matt. XXV, 34), that is, it will draw near to the kingdom of God in order to possess it. Hence we read: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom that has been prepared for you from the origin of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34). The good are called the heart of God because they know his secrets; or they are called the heart of God in the ordinary usage of the expression. We are accustomed to call our dearest friends “our heart.” And rightly will his heart draw near, because he has not defiled the Testament; rather, his words have been softened for him beyond oil—that is, his commandments, which seemed severe to others, have become for him soft to understand and easy to bear, in their own way softer and lighter than oil is in its own way. [Col. 0887A]

Since he had said “softened,” and since “soft” can sometimes be used to mean fragile and weak, lest it appear that it is being used here in the same sense for fragile and weak, he adds: “And those words are arrows to the heart itself.” This is to say: Although I said that the words are soft in one respect, they must nevertheless be called arrows in another respect, because with them the faithful strike back at the adversaries of the catholic faith, just as enemies are struck with arrows.

Since, then, he had said that the words are arrows, it is understood that the faithful sometimes suffer tribulations and quarrels from unbelievers. He exhorts them not to fear if they should at some time suffer persecution, but to cast the whole burden of their cares upon God, and he will deal with them effectively. [Col. 0887B]

I said that the words of God are arrows of the heart of God, that is, arrows for the faithful against unbelievers. If those unbelievers stir up tribulations and quarrels against you, O heart, do not fear, do not be anxious, but cast your care upon the Lord, that is, place upon him the entire burden of your anxiety, after the likeness of a weight placed upon someone. This is to say: Do not be anxious about how you may escape, but be secure, assign the whole care of your salvation to the Lord, and the Lord himself will [189] nourish you with his words, that is, he will feed and strengthen you so that you may be strong and wise enough to strike back at such enemies with these arrows.

And if no bodily tribulation has been inflicted upon you by your enemies, God will not give you, as a just person, fluctuation—that is, he will not permit you to fluctuate, or to labor—since this is what it means for you to be just. This is to say: Because of your righteousness he will make you so steadfast that you will in no way fluctuate. [Col. 0887C]

He turns in apostrophe to God, speaking of the impious’ perpetual death as follows: I said that the heart will not fluctuate.

But those who persecute your heart, you, God the Word, who are powerful, will lead away—that is, you will permit them to be led away by evil spirits—into the pit of destruction, that is, into the deepest destruction. From it they will not be able to emerge, after the likeness of a very deep pit. If someone falls into such a pit, he cannot rise from it. Of this pit of destruction it is written: “His mouth shall be closed; his worm shall not die, nor shall the fire be extinguished” (Isa. LXVI, 24). [Col. 0888A]

And this is as though he were saying: They will not only be separated from the anger of his countenance, which is exceedingly wretched, but after their separation they will also be led into the pit of destruction. And rightly so: for, being men of blood and deceitful, they will not halve their days. The order is reversed: when these deceitful men try by flatteries to make the good conform to themselves, and afterward, when they do not prevail by flatteries, being men who shed blood—that is, openly and through the shedding of blood wishing to draw them back from holiness—they will not halve the days of their life. That is, they will not make a distinction by assigning the past portion, which they have spent in wicked works and thoughts, to wickedness, and the future to good action and thought. This is to say: They will never lead even some portion of their life in holiness and innocence, but will live wickedly throughout all their days. [Col. 0888B]

Therefore they will justly be led into the pit of destruction. Or it may be read in this way: Someone might say, “You say where they will be led; does it not benefit them not to be led there, since they sometimes act well for a time and afterward fall away?” Against this comes the following denial: They truly will be led there, even if they act well for a time and afterward fall away.

For men of blood and deceit will not halve their days. This is to say: They are not permitted to divide their days, so as to serve God partly and the devil partly in alternation, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matt. VI, 34).

Or it may be read as referring to what was stated above, where it says: “God will humble them from the kingdom.” I say that God will humble them, and this humiliation will not be long delayed. For men of blood and deceit will not halve their days in their own land. [Col. 0888C] It is as though he were saying: They think that they will remain there from generation to generation, throughout all the days for which this world will endure; yet they will not be there even for half of those days that they assign to themselves and to their children, since in the forty-second year they will be expelled from there.

I said that they will be led into the pit of destruction, but I shall hope in you, Lord. This is to say: My people will not hope in earthly things, as unbelievers do, but will hope in you, that is, they will place their hope of salvation in you. Therefore they will not be led into the pit of destruction.

## ON PSALM LV

[Col. 0888D] The title of the fifty-fifth psalm: “For the end; for the people who have been far removed from the holy ones; for David; in the inscription of the title, when the Allophyli seized him in Geth.”

In this title, although certain words appear to have been placed according to the historical account—namely, “when the Allophyli seized him in Geth”—there are nevertheless some additions that clearly recall us from an historical understanding, where it says, “for the end; for the people who have been far removed from the holy ones.” These words are nowhere found in the historical account. Therefore the words mentioned above—namely, “when the Allophyli seized him in Gath”—must be understood solely according to their interpretation.

By the term *Allophyli*, which is interpreted as “foreigners,” the Jews are understood: they were formerly sons, but now have become foreigners, that is, alienated, according to what is read in the seventeenth psalm: “The sons of foreigners have lied to me” (Ps. XVII, 48). By *Geth*, which is interpreted as “winepress,” the pressure of the Passion is signified, since it is characteristic of a winepress to press. With this noted, let us proceed to explain the words of the title. [Col. 0889A]

This psalm speaks on behalf of the Jewish people, who are to be changed through faith, “for the end,” that is, for conformity and subjection to Christ, who is the end of prophecy and of the law. It speaks, I say, on behalf of the people “who have been far removed from the holy ones,” that is, who have become very unlike the apostles and the other faithful of the ancient law who believed Christ to be the King of the Jews, such as Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, and Gamaliel and many others, both their contemporaries and those who existed before their time. [190]

I say that the people have been far removed from the holy ones in this respect: in the inscription of the title made for David, that is, for Christ, by Pilate. This inscription is: “Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews” (John XIX, 19). I say that the inscription of the title was changed by that same people, when they, being Allophyli—that is, foreigners—formerly sons, seized him in Gath, that is, thought that they had seized him in the pressure of death so that he would not rise again. [Col. 0889B]

For this people changed the title, as far as their belief was concerned, saying to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but that he said, ‘I am King of the Jews’” (ibid., 21). And the whole matter is as though it said: This psalm speaks for the benefit of the Jewish people, who formerly became far removed from the holy ones by changing the inscription of the title both in word and in affection, since, being alienated, they wished to keep Christ in death, refusing, that is, to have Christ as their king. This people is to be changed from its unbelief and hardness into faith in Christ.

And rightly is this psalm said to speak for the benefit of the people who are to be changed. For in the preceding psalm, when the Passion and the portion of the people that is to be condemned were being discussed, Christ was introduced. In this psalm he is introduced praying before the Passion that he may not yield and that he may rise again. It displays his Passion and the change of the people who are to be saved. It says that this is for their benefit, so that, by predicting their change, it may incite them to that very change. [Col. 0889C]

Have mercy on me, God, so that you may make me steadfast and raise me up. It is necessary that I pray for this, and it is also worthy that you have mercy, because man has trampled upon me, God and Creator—that is, the Jewish people, who are man, that is, a creature, will trample upon me. It is unworthy that the creature should trample upon the Creator.

When he says “he has trampled,” he alludes to the comparison with a winepress, because he had placed *Gath* in the title, which is interpreted as “winepress.” For it belongs to a winepress to trample grapes.

Or it may be read in this way: Man will trample upon me, that is, the Jewish people, who simply are man, that is, an animal, certainly not spiritual. He explains how they will trample upon him when he adds: I say that he will trample upon me; thus he afflicted me, that is, he will crucify me with tribulations throughout the entire day of my Passion, attacking me with words by saying: “This man says: I can destroy the temple of God” (Matt. XXVI, 61), and so forth. [Col. 0890A]

He rightly says “throughout the entire day.” For on that day they never ceased from afflicting and attacking him. Or it may be read: He afflicted me on the day of the Passion, attacking me before the Passion with abusive words throughout the day, that is, continually, saying: “You have a demon” (John X, 20), and other such things.

It should be noted that Christ is introduced here speaking before the time of his Passion. But since he had foretold that he would be trampled, lest he appear to be trampled on account of his merits, he repeats the statement while adding the cause of the trampling, as follows: I say that man will trample upon me, and not because of anything I have deserved before God; rather, my enemies trampled upon me throughout the day, that is, they will trample upon me throughout the day of the Passion, for this reason alone: because they are my enemies. This is to say: Enmity alone will be the cause, not any merit of mine. [Col. 0890B]

But lest it appear that he would have fear during that trampling, he removes this under the form of a question: I said that they will trample upon me, and since many who will fight against me with words and tribulations will be hostile to me, men who will be powerful, that is, proud in the dominion that will be permitted them over me, shall I fear [191] the height of the day, that is, shall I fear because of the pride of their temporal and brief domination?

This is to say: Shall I fear that their height—that is, their domination leading me to death—will be the reason why I remain detained in death? By no means. When he says “of the day,” he indicates that this domination will last for a short time, since one day is a brief period. It is as though he were saying: Fear will not arise in me that I shall not rise again because of the height that will last only for a day. [Col. 0890C]

But I shall hope in you. It is as though he were saying: I shall not fear; rather, I, who am innocent, just, and obedient to you, shall hope for the resurrection in you, that is, in consideration of your power and mercy.

It should be noted that before the Passion, when he was close to the Passion, Christ is said to have feared voluntarily for the instruction of his followers. But when he had already been placed in the Passion, he is not read to have feared. Since hoping without a good life must be called not hope but presumption, he adds: I say that I shall hope, and this hope will not be presumptuous, for before the Passion, while existing in God—that is, in the work and praise of God—I shall praise the words, that is, I shall show my proclamations to be praiseworthy by my good life. [Col. 0890D]

This is to say: By living well I shall show my preaching to be praiseworthy. Hence it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I, 1). For if he had not fulfilled in action what he preached, his preaching would certainly not have been praiseworthy.

Since he had said, “I shall hope in you”—namely, in the Passion—lest it appear to be implied that he did not hope before the Passion, he adds that he will not only hope in the Passion, but that he has always hoped in God; therefore he will not fear what flesh may do to him.

This is to say: I shall fear neither their height, by which they might detain me in death, nor the tribulations, blasphemies, and ambushes that those who are merely carnal, and not spiritual, will inflict upon me. He explains what they will do in detail, as follows: Flesh will do this to me throughout the day, that is, continually they will judge my words execrable, saying: “Abraham is dead, and the prophets, and you say: If anyone keeps my word, he shall never taste death” (John VIII, 52), and other things of the same kind. [Col. 0891A]

And they will revile my words because all their thoughts will be against me. Since many people think against someone not in order to harm him, but to destroy him according to the perversity that is in him, he adds: Their thoughts will be for evil, not for good. This is to say: From the evil thoughts that they will think against me will proceed the reviling of my words. Hence it is read in the Gospel: “From the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Luke VI, 45).

And while reviling, they will inhabit my familiarity and conceal the reason for their inhabiting it—not with regard to me, who see everything, but with regard to their own opinion. This is to say: Although they will inhabit it with evil intention, they will pretend to inhabit it with good intention. [Col. 0891B]

He shows why they will inhabit it by adding: I say that they will inhabit it, and while inhabiting it they will watch my heel, that is, they will await my end, so that, since at the beginning they find nothing in me to criticize, they may at least find something at the end that they can censure.

The heel is rightly used for the end, because it is the final part of the body. Or it may be read: They will watch, that is, they will await my heel’s slipping. This is to say: They will wait to see whether perhaps they may observe me falling into some crime. Since a person slips by the heel, the heel is used for a fall.

The same meaning is understood in these words as in the preceding ones: I said that they will watch my heel. As they have held my soul, that is, as those who will hold my life, that is, those to whom my life will be a burden and a weariness, like someone holding up some heavy weight to whom that weight is exceedingly burdensome. This is to say: The fact that my life will be wearisome to them will be the reason why they will watch me. [Col. 0891C]

He now speaks of the change and salvation of the enemies as follows. [192]

I said that they will trample upon me, revile me, and watch my heel. And although they will do all these things perversely, nevertheless you will save them for nothing, that is, without any merit of theirs—from original sin and from actual sins. [Col. 0891D]

Or it may be read in this way: I say that they will watch my heel, and nevertheless you will save them for nothing, just as, for nothing—that is, without cause—they will hold my soul. The meaning is almost the same as above, but the division is changed. In the preceding reading, *sicut* is understood as “inasmuch as”; here it is taken comparatively.

And before you save them, you will break peoples, that is, the multitudes of enemies according to their wickedness, in anger, that is, in the knowledge of your future anger. This is to say: Through the knowledge of your anger, which you will give them, their impiety will be broken.

When he uses the plural “peoples,” he indicates that they will not be few but many, just as on one day three thousand, and on another five thousand, are read to have been converted (Acts II, 41; IV, 4). [Col. 0892A]

And before they are broken, O God, I proclaimed my life to you, that is, those who will be mine will proclaim to you, by confession, the foulness of their life. The whole passage is as though it said: My people will proclaim their sins by confession; you will break them according to their condition as sinners; and thus you will save them here. By saving them here, you have placed—or will place—in your sight, that is, in your presence and favor, my tears, that is, those very people for whom I often poured out tearful prayers.

Or “my tears” may be understood emphatically, that is, those for whose death I wept at the death of Lazarus (John XI, 35). It should indeed be noted that he did not then weep for Lazarus, who was about to be immediately raised, but for those whose death was represented in the death of Lazarus: they were so dead in sins that by their evil example they already stank to others, like Lazarus after four days (ibid., 39). [Col. 0892B]

I say that you will save them and place them in your sight; and likewise—that is, also—in your promise this is constant: you promised it through the prophets, whose promise the Gospel itself confirms. There, when the angel announced to Joseph, the husband of Mary, that a Savior was to be born, he said: “He will save his people from their sins” (Matt. I, 21). And the whole matter is as though he were saying: I announce this, and you promised this.

I said that they will proclaim and that you will break them, and then my enemies will turn back toward me, walking behind me, that is, becoming my followers, after the likeness of someone who follows another. This is to say: They will live well according to my conformity, becoming my followers insofar as they are able. [Col. 0892C]

I say that they will turn, and you will receive them not only in their first age or in their second, but on whatever day I call upon you, that is, at whatever time of life they call upon you with true contrition, so that afterward they do not return. According to that prophetic saying: “At whatever hour the sinner shall groan, as he ought to groan, he shall be saved” (Isa. XXX, 15, according to the Septuagint).

Since he had said that my people will proclaim their life, and since proclamation cannot exist unless the knowledge of God is possessed first, he adds: I say that they will proclaim, and first—behold, in the present—I knew that you are my God, that is, my people will know by faith that you are their God.

And because faith without works is dead, while existing in the Lord—that is, in the Lord’s work—they will praise the word, that is, they will show their word to be praiseworthy by their good life. “In God” and “in the Lord” have the same meaning here. [Col. 0892D]

But *verbum* and *sermo* differ. Properly and ordinarily, we call something *sermo* when someone speaks to one or more persons not in a composed written text or in a composed and ornate form of speech, but in ordinary language. We call it *verbum* when someone addresses anyone through the composition of Latin or ordinary speech.

And the whole matter is as though he were saying: After they have known God by faith, they will act well, and thus they will show both their *sermo* and their *verbum* to be praiseworthy. For if they lived badly, they would make them contemptible. In accordance with that saying of blessed Gregory: “When someone’s life is despised, it remains that his preaching also is despised” (*Homily 21 on the Gospels*).

Or it may be read as indicating the whole Trinity. I said that they will proclaim; and so that they may be able to proclaim, behold, in the present I [193] knew—that is, they will know—that he is my God, that is, God the Father is the God of my people. [Col. 0893A]

This is to say: They will know God the Father, and in God the Father, that is, in the equality of God the Father, I shall praise—that is, they will praise—the Word, namely the Son. And in the Lord I shall praise the *sermo*, that is, in the equality of the Lord, the Spirit, they will praise me, the Son, who am the Father’s *sermo*, through whom he spoke—that is, ordained—and all things were made (1 John I, 3).

And the whole matter is as though he were saying: They will know that the Father is God, and they will know me, whom they formerly denied and despised as equal to the Father, as God equal to the Father and the Spirit. Thus they will praise me by faith, by works, and by devotion.

And by knowing and praising the triune God, they will hope in that God, that is, they will have hope of eternal salvation; therefore they will not fear what man may do to me—that is, to themselves—man being the persecutor who is merely man, that is, an animal and not spiritual. [Col. 0893B]

This is to say: They will not fear the tribulations, death, and loss of earthly wealth that persecutors will inflict upon them. Someone might say: “The persecutor truly must be feared, because he will take away earthly goods, and afterward they will not have the means by which to fulfill their legal vows.” Against this he adds: I say that they will not fear what man may do to them, nor is there anything to fear. For although he may take away earthly things, he cannot take away their ability to sacrifice to you. In me—that is, in my people—are your vows, that is, your sacrifices, which I shall repay—that is, they shall repay—to you, namely praises.

This is to say: They possess within themselves what they will sacrifice to you, namely the means of praising you by voice, by works, and by devotion—something no persecutor can take away from them—and it will be worthy that they repay it. [Col. 0893C]

For you have rescued my soul from death, that is, you will rescue the soul of my people from the multitude of sins by which they would come to death unless you forgave them. And after rescuing them from death through the forgiveness of sins, you will rescue my feet, that is, the affections of my people, from falling, so that they may not fall away from holiness through some evil desire, in order that I may please—that is, they may please—God in the light of the living, that is, placed in conformity with me, who am the light of all living persons in the perfection of virtues, not in the mass of dead sinners.

This is to say: You will rescue them so that, having been made conformable to me, they may please you; I am the illuminator of all who live well. I say that they may please while existing before God, that is, in the manifest knowledge of God, so that they may see him specially with unveiled face, after the likeness of one who openly sees the person before whom he stands. [Col. 0893D]

## ON PSALM LVI

The title of the fifty-sixth psalm: “For the end; do not destroy [do not disperse]; for David; in the inscription of the title, when he fled from the face of Saul into a cave.”

In this title, as in the preceding one, certain words appear to have been added according to the historical account, namely, “when he fled from the face of Saul.” But what is added is not *into the cave* but *in the cave*, which does not work if it is referred to the historical account. For the text there has *into the cave*, whereas the expositors have *in the cave*. Indeed, David is read to have fled into a cave while Saul was pursuing him (2 Sam. XXII). [Col. 0894A]

The other expression added in the title—namely, “in the inscription of the title”—also appears in no way to pertain to the historical account, since nowhere is an inscription of a title recorded as having been made for the prophet David. It therefore seems appropriate to accept this title not according to the historical account, but according to the interpretation of the words. It is explained as follows.

This psalm looks toward the end, that is, toward Christ, and exhorts you, whoever you are who reads, not to corrupt David, that is, Christ, insofar as this depends upon you. It shows in what respect you should not corrupt him, adding: Do not corrupt him, I say, in the inscription of the title made for David, that is, for Christ, by Pilate, which we have displayed in the preceding psalm.

This is to say: Do not corrupt the inscription of the title, that is, what is signified in the inscription of the title, namely, that Christ is king. You would corrupt it, insofar as this depended upon you—not insofar as it depended upon him—if you denied him to be king either in affection, in speech, or through neglect of his commandments, as the Jews wished to corrupt it when they changed it. [Col. 0894B]

I say: Do not corrupt David in the inscription of the title, changed and made for David, when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave. [194]

This is to say: Do not corrupt him, since he himself, while lying hidden in the cave—that is, in his humanity—fled according to his divinity, that is, departed completely after the manner of one fleeing, from the face of Saul, that is, from the presence of the Jewish people’s knowledge.

It is as though he were saying: The Jewish people therefore corrupted the inscription of the title by changing it, because Christ, hidden in his humanity, departed from their knowledge; that is, they did not recognize him to be God. [Col. 0894C]

But you, reader, do not corrupt it on that account: while hidden in the cave, that is, in his humanity, he fled from the face of Saul, that is, from the presence of the knowledge of the Jewish people. The people are appropriately called Saul, that is, “desiring death” through their evil works. Or Saul is so called because he persecuted Christ, just as Saul persecuted David.

The cave is rightly called humanity, because it was humble, and the divinity lay hidden within it, just as a cave is a humble thing and someone may lie hidden in it.

It should be noted that although we say that this psalm exhorts the reader not to corrupt him, it nevertheless does not openly give this admonition. But if its words are carefully considered, it implies that he must not be corrupted.

For in this psalm the Lord’s man is introduced praying before the Passion that God may make him steadfast in the Passion and raise him again, and it displays his Passion. [Col. 0894D] It then discusses his resurrection and exaltation and the subjection of the whole world. From this it is understood that he is Lord and King, since he will rise again and be exalted, and thus the whole world will be subjected to him for governance. By this it implies to the reader that the inscription must not be changed or corrupted, since Christ is king of all.

Have mercy on me, God the Father, so that you may make me steadfast. Have mercy on me so that you may raise me and exalt me. Or it may be read: Have mercy on me so that you may make me steadfast, raise me, and exalt me. And have mercy on me—that is, on my people—so that they may be saved by my death.

And it is worthy that you do this, because my soul trusts in you, that is, in your mercy, power, and justice. I say that my soul trusts in you, and still I shall hope in the shadow of your wings, that is, in the refreshment of your protection, until iniquity passes away, that is, until the death which the Jews will wickedly inflict upon me is completed. [Col. 0895A]

This is to say: I shall hope continually in your protection until I am freed from death. This protection is refreshment for me amid the heat of tribulation, just as shade is refreshment for those overcome by the sun’s heat. He uses “wings” for protection because a bird protects its young with its wings from rain and heat and from the attack of predatory birds.

It should certainly be noted that trusting is more certain than hoping. Nevertheless, here they are taken in the same sense, except that one is present—“trusts”—while the other is future—“I shall hope.” [Col. 0895B]

I said that I shall hope, and not only this, but I shall also cry out, with devotion, voice, and works, to God Most High. It is as though he were saying: Since he is Most High, and since the height of his dignity demands that I cry out intensely, I shall cry out intensely to God, I say, who has done good to me.

“Has done good” is to be understood both in the past and in the future, as though he were saying: I shall cry out because he has already bestowed benefits upon me and will still bestow others.

He explains what benefit he has bestowed when he adds: “He sent from heaven.” It is as though he were saying: He bestowed this benefit upon my human nature, that he sent from heaven the Word, so that the Word might be personally united to me and make me free from sin.

It should be noted that the Word was not sent from heaven locally. Far be it from us to confess that God is local! [Col. 0895C] Rather, when it is said that God the Father sent the Word from heaven, this is explained as follows: The Word, of whom the heavenly citizens alone had knowledge, he sent from heaven—that is, from the knowledge of the heavenly citizens—specifically into the knowledge of human beings, when he caused the Word to be personally united to human nature.

This is to say: He extended to human beings through the human nature to which the Word was united the knowledge of the Word that the heavenly citizens possessed.

He also explains the benefits that he will confer upon human nature when he adds: I say that he sent the Word from heaven, but also through that Word he delivered—that is, he will deliver—me, innocent and holy human [195] nature, from the power of the Jews; and he gave—that is, he will give—them, who trample upon me, over to disgrace, scattering them everywhere: the Jews who afflict me with death and treat me with contempt, after the likeness of something utterly worthless that is trampled underfoot. [Col. 0895D]

Because he had said, “He sent from heaven,” but had not explained what he sent, and had also said, “He will deliver me,” but had not shown from whom he would deliver me, he explains both with a repetition, as follows:

“He sent,” I say, “his mercy and his truth, so that the same Word might be united to me; and through that Word he rescued”—that is, “he will rescue”—“my soul from the midst of lion cubs,” that is, from the common desire of the Jewish people, who desired to keep me in death. This people is figuratively called “lion cubs,” that is, the offspring of savage rulers like lions, because the people itself is generated in wickedness by its rulers, just as cubs are generated by lions. [Col. 0896A]

He shows how he will deliver me from the midst of the cubs, as follows:

“I say that he will deliver me from the midst of the cubs, and this will necessarily happen. For I, troubled by spontaneous fear, slept”—that is, “I will sleep in death through those cubs.” When he says “I will sleep,” he indicates that the death will be brief, like sleep.

The Word is called “mercy and truth” emphatically, because through it God has shown mercy to the human race, and because in it everything that God had promised through the prophets has been fulfilled.

He explains who those cubs are who will make him sleep in death, and with what weapons they will kill him, so that no one might wish to excuse them on the grounds that they did not kill him with arrows and a sword. He says this as follows: “The sons of men,” and so forth, up to “Arise.” These words should not be read in the sequence in which they are set out, but should be construed as follows. [Col. 0896B]

“I said that I would sleep while troubled, and this is true. For the sons of men”—that is, the Jews, who ought to conduct themselves rationally as human beings because they are sons of men, that is, of the prophets, who conducted themselves rationally as human beings—“prepared a snare for my feet,” that is, they will prepare death for my affections, by which they will restrain those affections from their intended effect. This is by comparison with a bird that, when its feet have been caught in a snare and it cannot escape, is held fast. Thus, although I have the affection—the desire—to rise again, to be exalted, and to subject the world to myself, they will restrain those very affections from their effect and render them futile.

“I say that they will prepare a snare,” that is, death, “and in that death they bent down,” that is, they will think that they will humble my soul in such a way that it will not rise again.

He repeats by another comparison what he had said, “They will prepare a snare,” that is, death, to indicate that this death is not being prepared for him without his knowledge, but with his knowledge. Through this it is understood that he is God, since he foresees future events.

“I said that they will prepare a snare, and this not without my knowledge, but they dug a pit before my face.” This means: “They will prepare for me the deepest death, from which I will not escape,” by comparison with one who digs a pit—that is, makes a very deep pit—in order to thrust someone into it who cannot get out. “They will dig that pit before my face,” that is, just as I will know and foresee it, like one who sees what is before his face.

All this is as though he said: “They will not prepare this death for me in such a way that I do not know it, but it will be as though it were before my face,” that is, before my knowledge.

“And they fell into it,” that is, they will fall into that pit. This means: When they prepare eternal death for me, after I have been delivered from it, they themselves will fall into it, so that they will never emerge from it—by comparison with one who, after digging a pit in order to cast someone into it, falls into it himself and afterward does not rise.

He shows how they will prepare that death for him when he inserts, “Their teeth,” and so forth, up to “Be exalted.” The passage is to be continued as follows.

Someone might say: “Why do you say that the sons of men will prepare death for you, when they will take up against you neither arrows nor a sword nor anything by which they might kill you?”

He answers as follows:

“Truly they will prepare a snare,” that is, death, “for me. For their teeth”—that is, their anger and hatred, which are called “teeth” because they are frequently displayed with the gnashing of teeth—“will be weapons,” that is, instruments of my death.

He shows what weapons they will be when he adds: “And,” that is, “namely, arrows.” This means: “Their hatred and anger will be the distant preparations for my death, just as arrows are distant weapons,” that is, weapons threatening death from afar. “And their tongue will be a sharp sword,” that is, their voice will be the public cause of my death, when they say, “Crucify him” (Luke 23:21), and, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19:12), by comparison with a sword by which anyone is openly killed.

All this is as though he were saying: “They are not excusable even if they do not kill me with weapons and a sword. For because of hatred and anger, not because I have deserved it, they will deceitfully prepare death for me, and afterward openly demand it with their voice.” [Col. 0897B]

The phrase that follows, “Be exalted,” and so forth, is a prayer arising from excessive affection, inserted before he had finished what he had begun. It is to be continued as follows.

“I said that the sons of men would prepare a snare for me, but you, God the Father, be exalted above the heavens by exalting me.”

This means: “Exalt me, insofar as I am human, above the heavens,” that is, above the rational heavenly creatures, namely, above the angels, “so that I, who now appear lowly and rejected, may appear great and exalted in power above them when I ascend gloriously into heaven.”

“And when I have been exalted above them, you too, that is, appear great and lofty in power above those angels, when you appear powerful by exalting me; and let your glory be extended over all the earth.”

This is as though he said: “May you be exalted not only among a few through my exaltation, but may your glory be extended over all the earth,” that is, “may you everywhere throughout the world be glorified because of my exaltation.” [Col. 0897C]

When he says, “My heart is prepared,” and so forth, he shows that he will suffer willingly, so that he may make us more indebted to him, for whose sake he suffered willingly. The passage is to be continued as follows:

“They will dig a pit for me, and my heart is prepared, O God the Father, to enter it. ‘My heart is prepared,’ that is, the will of my heart is prepared.”

This means: “I already have the will to enter it.” He repeats, “My heart is prepared,” to show how great is his affection for dying for the salvation of the human race.

“And because my heart is prepared, I will sing,” that is, I will preach the doctrine of life, which will be a song and a delight both to me and to God. “And I will also sing a psalm,” that is, I will place my good works in public view, by comparison with a spoken word, which is a public matter.

A psalm is used for a good work because it is performed through the exercise of the hands. All this is as though he said: “Since I am prepared to undergo death, and since I am certain that the song”—that is, my preaching—“and the psalm”—that is, my good works—“will be the causes for which they will kill me, nevertheless I will not cease from the song; I will not cease from the psalm.”

When he says, “Arise,” and so forth, rejoicing in his resurrection, he exhorts his body to rise. The passage is to be continued as follows:

“I say that I am prepared to undergo death. You, of whom the psaltery and the lyre are said to arise, arise; arise, that is, let my humanity rise from that death.” [Col. 0898A]

Christ’s humanity is called the psaltery because it sounded from above, that is, from the divinity, in the manner of a psaltery, which sounds from above.

This means: “From the divinity itself the report of miracles proceeded through the operation of the humanity.” For the humanity worked miracles by going to raise the dead, laying hands upon the sick, speaking, and in many other ways.

The same humanity is called the lyre because, in the manner of a lyre, it sounded from below, that is, it brought forth from below a sweet sound to God—a sweet praise of obedience—when it offered its body, which was lower than the divinity, to God on the altar of the cross; and also because, while placed in obedience, it hungered and thirsted.

“I say, arise from death, O humanity that is both psaltery and lyre. You are,” I say, “my future glory”—an emphatic expression. [Col. 0898B]

This means: “You are the humanity that will be immortal and impassible, in which I will glory and be glorious.”

“I say, arise, and so it will be: I will rise at dawn,” that is, in the morning resurrection.

He shows what benefit will follow from his resurrection, as follows:

“I say that I will rise, and when I have risen I will confess to you among the peoples,” that is, I will acquire true confessors among the Jewish people.

This means: “I will make many among the Jews your praisers. And I will sing a psalm to you among the nations,” that is, I will bring forth for you among the nations many who will sing a psalm to you, that is, who will place their good works in public view for your honor.

This means: “Through my glorious resurrection I will make many from among the nations do good works for your honor.”

He shows how he will establish both confessors and those who sing the psalm, as follows:

“I said that I would bring forth for you confessors among the peoples and those who sing the psalm among the nations, and I will do this through the heavens and through the clouds,” that is, through the preaching of the apostles. They are called “heavens” because of the sublimity of their holiness, and “clouds” because they rain doctrine upon others, like clouds raining upon the earth. [Col. 0898C]

“For your mercy has been magnified as far as the heavens are to be established,” that is, “I, your Son, and your mercy will be magnified to such an extent”—that is, “I will be so powerful”—“that I will make my disciples heavens. And your truth will be magnified as far as the clouds are to be established,” that is, “I, who am your truth, will be so great and powerful that I will make those heavens clouds.”

It should be noted that he is not said to be magnified as far as the heavens and clouds because he was not already great and powerful enough to accomplish this, but because that greatness and power had not yet appeared.

It is as though he said: “Although I now appear lowly and powerless, I will appear great as far as the heavens and as far as the clouds.”

“And so that I may confess to you among the peoples and sing a psalm to you among the nations, be exalted above the heavens, God the Father, by exalting me.”

This, as explained above, is repeated because of his excessive desire. “And through my exaltation above the whole earth, let your glory be extended,” that is, “let your glory, coming from above to human beings, be extended everywhere throughout the earth.”

Alternatively, when he says, “Be exalted, God,” this may be an exhortation addressed to the Word personally united to him: “Be exalted, God, Word,” that is, “let your height appear through the exaltation of my human nature; your height, which is not now apparent.” [Col. 0899A]

“And your glory above the whole earth”—this is not changed.

## ON PSALM LVII

The title of the fifty-sixth psalm: “For the end: Do not destroy; for David, in the inscription of the title.”

This is explained as follows:

This psalm, looking toward the end—that is, toward Christ—warns you, whoever you may be, not to destroy David, that is, not to destroy the kingdom of Christ, the true David, by denying that he is king, while the inscription of the title made for David, that is, for Christ, remains unchanged.

The Prophet speaks in this psalm, exhorting the Jews to read him in the Old Law concerning Christ and to understand him correctly: they should judge rightly about him, attributing to him what the books of the prophets say about him, namely, that he is king.

Accordingly, Micah testifies:

> “A ruler will go forth who will govern my people Israel” (Micah 5:2).

And another prophet says:

> “Your king comes to you, gentle” (Zechariah 9:9; Isaiah 52:11).

It should be noted that, although in the preceding psalm an exhortation not to corrupt may also be indicated, it occurs there in a different manner. There, when he was speaking about his resurrection and exaltation and about the subjection of the whole world, he indicated that the inscription of the title should not be corrupted. Here, however, the Prophet plainly exhorts them: since they say in the prophetic books that Christ is a just king, they should not corrupt the title by denying his kingdom. [Col. 0899B]

He also shows the condemnation of certain people who corrupt the title by acting wickedly in their hearts, so that they may be without excuse and so that all may be recalled from such conduct by fear of their condemnation.

“If you truly speak justice in the books of the prophets”—that is, Christ, who is antonomastically called “justice,” from whom all justice comes, and who has been set before us by the Father as redemption and justice, as the Apostle says (1 Corinthians 1:30)—“which indeed you do,” that is, “you speak of justice, O sons of men,” that is, “you Jews, sons of the prophets, who ought by their example to be human beings and not irrational creatures: judge rightly concerning justice itself,” that is, concerning Christ, “attributing the kingdom to him.”

For you will judge unjustly if, while you say in the prophets that Jesus, whom it is evident from the works and signs of the prophets to be the Messiah, is king, you deny that he is the Messiah and king and assert that another will come who will be the Messiah and king.
