It should be noted that, in prophetic fashion, the Prophet speaks of future events as though they were present. Later, at times, he speaks of them as past, when he says, “They are alienated,” and at other times as future, when he says, “God will crush,” and so forth. Nevertheless, they must always be understood as future. For what follows says, and so forth.

The passage is continued as follows. Since he had exhorted them to judge rightly, someone might say: “Why do you exhort us in this way? Do we not judge rightly?”

He answers as follows:

“My exhortation is necessary for you, since you judge unjustly. For you work iniquities in your heart,” that is, “you plot in your heart to commit iniquities,” namely, to seize Christ, kill him, and take the kingdom away from him—an act that will be reckoned to you as though it had already been performed. For when, by thinking, you already take the kingdom away from him, it is the same as if you had already taken it away.

“I say that you work iniquities in your heart. For in the earth”—that is, in consideration of Christ’s earthly flesh, because you consider him only an earthly human being and not also God; or “in the earth,” that is, in fear of losing the earth, because you fear that you will lose the land if you accept him as king; or “in the earth,” that is, in Christ’s earthly flesh, you plot to work iniquities, namely, to scourge him, spit upon him, and kill him; or you plot to work iniquities in the earth, that is, in your earthly and impious affection.

This means: “The iniquities that you plot against Christ, you do not plot out of a good zeal, as though you thought you were acting against him as a destroyer of the Law; rather, you do this from an earthly affection, that is, from anger and hatred, although through the works and signs of the prophets foretold concerning him you could recognize him as God and king.” [Col. 0900B]

“Not only do you work iniquities in your heart by thinking, but your hands also compose injustices,” that is, your actions jointly carry out injustices insofar as they are able; that is, they bring your unjust thoughts into action.

This means: “You agree in unjust deeds and unjust thoughts, so that your works are unjust just as your thoughts are unjust.” This is by comparison with singers who sing in harmony: just as they are harmonious in song, so your thoughts and works are harmonious in injustice.

He shows the cause for which they work iniquity, making an apostrophe to his hearers in order to instruct them not to act unjustly for the same reason.

“I say that they work iniquities, and they do these things for this reason: they, who are antonomastically sinners, when they ought to be generated through faith so that they might be sons of the Church, have been alienated through unbelief from the womb,” that is, from the Church’s spiritual birth.

“Womb” is used figuratively for birth because generation takes place in the womb.

He explains their alienation in parts when he adds: “Certainly they went astray in thought from the womb,” that is, removed from the Church’s spiritual conception.

This means: “They did not wish to become her spiritual children.” The womb, because conception takes place in it, is used for conception. Here “womb” and “vulva” seem to be the same thing. But to go astray and to be alienated are not wholly the same, because going astray is one part of alienation.

Another part of alienation follows when he adds: “They spoke falsehoods.”

This means: “It is not enough for them to go astray in thought; they will also speak falsely about Christ, saying: ‘This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath’ (John 9:16). And elsewhere: ‘He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee even to this place’ (Luke 23:5). And again: ‘We found this man perverting our nation’ (Luke 23:2). And once more: ‘We have no king but Caesar’ (John 19:15).”

Alternatively, the verse should be read in such a way that its continuity is not altered:

“The sinners,” antonomastically—that is, those who ought to be Christ’s children—“have been alienated from his sonship; and this alienation occurred from the womb,” that is, from Christ’s carnal conception.

He explains this alienation in parts when he adds: “Certainly they went astray in faith.” This error occurred from the womb, that is, from Christ’s conception. “And therefore they spoke falsehoods,” denying that he is God and king.

This means: “They were alienated from him, went astray, and spoke falsehoods because they saw him conceived in the womb and uterus of the Virgin according to the flesh”—something that is by no means disgraceful.

Alternatively, this verse may not be read generally of the Jews, but specifically of those who are to be destroyed, as follows:

“I say that they work iniquities in their heart; and some of those who work them have been alienated,” that is, rejected by God, “from the womb,” that is, from the time of their conception; “and they went astray,” that is, they were foreseen by divine providence as people who would err; “from the uterus,” that is, from their conception; “and they spoke falsehoods,” that is, they were foreseen as people who would speak falsehoods.

This means: “God therefore alienated them from the womb,” that is, rejected them, “because he foresaw that they would go astray in faith and speak falsehoods.”

Although they have been alienated, gone astray, and spoken falsehoods, “their fury,” that is, their madness, is “according to the likeness of a serpent,” that is, according to the fact that they are like a serpent. He shows which serpent when he adds: “Like that of an asp,” that is, “like an asp.”

It should be noted that he does not say that they have fury by comparison with an asp, since an asp does not have fury but cunning. When it does not hear the voice of the enchanters who would kill it if it heard them, he does not say that they have fury for that reason, but says that they have fury according to the fact that they are like an asp.

He shows in what respect they are like an asp when he adds: “Deaf.” This means: “They are like it in this respect, that they become deaf like an asp.” But lest anyone think that an asp is naturally deaf, so that they too might naturally be deaf by comparison with it and therefore excusable, he adds: “and stopping its ears.”

This means: “It is deaf of its own will, stopping its ears—one by applying it firmly to the earth, the other by stopping it with its tail.”

He demonstrates why it stops its ears by adding: “which, after it has stopped its ears, will not hear the voice of enchanters.” He shows for what kind of enchanter it stops its ears when he adds: “and,” that is, “namely, it will not hear the voice of the sorcerer who enchants wisely.”

It is as though he said: “It does not stop its ears because of the voice of a foolish enchanter, which would harm it in no way, but so that it will not hear the voice of the sorcerer who enchants wisely, who would make it fall asleep and kill it, and would draw out its venom.”

All this is as though he said:

“They are so mad that they willingly stop the ears of reason, partly with their tail,” that is, with the habit of past evils, which are signified by the tail because it is the posterior part of the body and those evils have already passed and lie behind; “and partly they stop the ears of reason by applying themselves to the earth,” that is, by attaching themselves to earthly and impious affections, like the asp, which stops one ear by applying it to the earth and the other with its tail.

“And they stop them for this reason: so that they will not hear the voice,” that is, the preaching, “of the enchanters—not of foolish enchanters, but of sorcerers who enchant wisely,” namely, the apostles and other preachers. They are called “enchanters” and “sorcerers” because through their preaching they make these sinners fall asleep in their sins, that is, cease from them, and thus kill them insofar as they are evil and remove the venom of depraved desire. This is like sorcerers who, by their voice, make an asp fall asleep and kill it and draw out its venom. [Col. 0902A]

This is equivalent to saying: Although they have been alienated, they have such great fury that through their past and present evil affections they stop the ears of reason, so that they do not hear the voice of the preachers and, ceasing from sins, are deprived of the venom of evil desire and thus become good.

He shows the destruction of certain of these alienated people who are to be saved—that is, their destruction in evil so that they may become good—as follows:

“I said that the sinners have been alienated. And since they are such, and since they could not otherwise be saved, God will crush through the opposition of his preachers their teeth,” that is, their minor gnawings and slanders—namely, those of certain people who are to be saved. “And the Lord will break through those same preachers the molars of lions,” that is, their greatest gnawings. These are “lions,” that is, those who devour the saints by their words and tribulations, like lions devouring prey. This will occur “in their mouth,” that is, in the response of their mouth.

This means: “He will make his saints so eloquent that by their eloquence they will destroy whatever the impious say wickedly about God and about them, and this also through the testimony of their mouth,” that is, they will dispute with them so rationally that by that very voice, leading them through contradictions, they will destroy both their lesser and their greater blasphemies.

He uses “teeth” for the gnawings of words, namely the lesser ones, and “molars” for the greater ones, because it belongs to teeth to gnaw and because molar teeth are larger than teeth that are not molars, namely, the front teeth.

Alternatively, “their teeth,” which are “in their mouth,” may mean those gnawings that are already public, namely, their evil words, while “molars” may mean hidden gnawings, namely, the thoughts by which they inwardly devour God and the saints. These are hidden like molars.

“The Lord will crush” them, that is, he will destroy them completely through the preaching of the faithful, so that they may no longer gnaw at them either by thinking or by speaking.

After their teeth and molars have been crushed, “they will come to nothing in their malice like water,” that is, like flowing water.

This means: Just as water gathered by rain rises and quickly runs away and is reduced to nothing, that is, quickly flows away from the place through which it runs, so they will quickly be annihilated in their malice and through this will come to nothing.

“For God will bend his bow,” that is, he will make the threatening of his Scripture intense through the preachers, “until they become weak in their malice,” that is, until their malice fails.

Having shown that God will crush the teeth and molars of certain people and that they will thus be annihilated in their malice, so that they may not perish, he shows the condemnation of the others as follows:

“I said that God will crush the teeth and molars of certain alienated people and that they will thus be annihilated so that they may not perish. But the others, who are to be condemned, will be taken away from the earth like wax that melts,” that is, in the manner of wax that melts before the face of fire. [Col. 0903A]

This means: “Just as wax is unstable before the presence of fire, so they will be unstable and weak before the attack of their enemies,” namely, the Romans. “For they will be conquered by them and led away captive.”

It should be noted that those Jews who had been converted were not taken away and led into captivity. Before Jerusalem was besieged, they had been warned by the Holy Spirit to transfer themselves to the kingdom of Agrippa, where they would be at peace (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 5).

Alternatively, “they will be taken away” in the future “from the face of the judging God,” flowing into hell like wax that melts from the presence of fire.

Meanwhile, here in this world, “fire has fallen upon them,” that is, fire will fall upon them: the heat of evil desires. When he says “upon,” he indicates that the fire of desires will be so great that it will completely weigh them down, like a burden falling from above.

This is as though he said: Since they are blind through their evil desires, he will multiply in them the heat of evil desires, so that they may become even more blind.

This will happen because they did not see through faith the sun of justice, Christ, who illuminates the whole world by faith and virtues, like the sun illuminating the world with its brightness.

“And this fire will consume them as living beings,” that is, it will devour them by blinding their reason. They are not truly living, but only like living beings: they live in the body according to sensuality, but in the soul they are dead through sin.

“I say that it will consume them, and this as in anger,” that is, not in the anger of God—which is truly to be called anger, namely, “in everlasting anger”—but “as in anger,” that is, in such anger as will be like anger, a shadow of everlasting anger. [Col. 0903C]

This means: The punishment by which God permits them to be consumed here by the fire of desires will not be the everlasting anger by which they are to be condemned, but a shadow of that anger.

He says this lest anyone think that they would have no other anger or punishment awaiting their condemnation besides this temporary blinding.

He makes an apostrophe to the impious themselves, indicating that eternal condemnation will come upon them, so that, even if they are not terrified, at least others may be frightened away from impiety. He speaks as follows:

“I say that the fire will consume you, and this consuming occurred before your thorns understood the bramble,” that is, before your sins—which they will one day understand through the experience of the matter itself—understood “the bramble,” that is, eternal condemnation.

He does not say that sins understand because they can understand anything, but by metonymy, as though he said: Before you, on account of your thorns—that is, on account of your sins—understand in the future, by suffering it, eternal condemnation, which here you neglect to understand so that you may avoid it.

The bramble is a shrub that, while young, has no thorns and is not rough. But after it grows and hardens, it becomes surrounded by many thorns and extremely rough. It is therefore used for perpetual condemnation, not by the comparison according to which, while tender, it is smooth and not rough to the touch, but rather by the comparison according to which, after it has hardened, it bristles with thorns and is extremely rough. For eternal condemnation will be harsher than all else.

All this is as though he said: “Here, before you come to eternal condemnation, you will be consumed by the fire of blindness; but in the future you will be consumed by perpetual condemnation.” [Col. 0904A]

It should be noted that, according to the explanation we have given, from the passage “God will crush” up to “he will rejoice”—there being four verses—two are explained concerning the crushing of the alienated who are to be saved in goodness: namely, “God will crush” and “they will come to nothing.” The other two concern the condemnation of those who are to perish, both here and in the future: namely, “like wax” and “before.”

All four, however, can be read as referring to those who are to perish, so that there is diversity in one part of the meaning but identity in another, if they are connected with the interpretation according to which the three verses—“They are alienated,” “their fury is like that,” and “which will not hear”—are explained specifically of those who are to perish.

The passage is then continued as follows:

“I said that they were alienated from the womb,” that is, from their conception; “that is, they were rejected. And this because they were foreseen by God as people who would go astray and speak falsehoods; and that their fury was like that of a deaf asp. Since they are such, they will be condemned both here and in the future.”

Here God will crush through the eloquence of the preachers their teeth, that is, the lesser gnawings and blasphemies that they direct against God and the saints; and the Lord will break their molars, that is, their greater blasphemies. This will occur “in their mouth,” that is, in their own voice, because they will be overcome by the saints through their own response—not so that they may blush and repent, as occurred earlier in the other interpretation, which concerned those who are to be saved, but only so that they may blush, having nothing to say, and appear liars to others. [Col. 0904C]

Alternatively, “their teeth,” that is, their open blasphemies, and “their molars,” that is, their hidden ones, the Lord will break “in their mouth,” that is, in their own voice.

Accordingly, it is written concerning blessed Stephen:

> “They were unable to withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke” (Acts 6:10).

Nor will this alone happen—that, after their teeth and molars have been crushed, they will appear to be liars. Rather, from the power and prosperity that they possess, they will come to nothing like flowing water when they are besieged by the Romans.

This means: Their prosperity will be transitory, like a torrent flowing away with the greatest speed, and truly they will come to nothing.

For God will bend his bow, that is, he will make his opposition against them intense, “until they become completely weak.” [Col. 0904D]

It is indeed read in Josephus that, while they were being attacked externally by their enemies, they themselves, blinded by the exercise of anger and hatred, fought one another to such an extent that they frequently battled among themselves within the city, until they were utterly weakened and failed both against themselves and against their enemies (Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book V, chapter 20).

He uses “bow” for attack because we attack an enemy with a bow.

“And when they have been weakened, they will be taken away from their land and led into captivity like wax that melts.” Alternatively, “they will be taken away in the future from the face of the judging God, like wax that melts.”

But what follows, “Fire has fallen upon them,” and so forth, up to “he will rejoice,” is in no way changed. [Col. 0905A]

I say that the impious will be condemned in this way.

But every just person will rejoice when he sees the punishment of the impious here. He will not rejoice in the punishment of the impious as such, but in his own innocence, since he himself does not suffer that punishment—so that the fire of blindness and the other condemnations that will occur among the impious may not fall upon him.

“And he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner,” that is, he will cleanse his affections in consideration of the blood, that is, the death, of sinners.

This means: When he has considered the death of the sinner, both here according to blindness and in the future according to condemnation, so that he himself may not die in the same way, he will cleanse his affections so that he may commit no criminal sin.

“And a man will say within himself, ‘If there is fruit,’” that is, benefit, “for the just person from his justice,” so that he may be justified more fully by God—“and indeed there is.” God is truly the one judging, that is, condemning, the impious by blinding them in this present earth.

He might say: “I must beware of wickedness, lest I be blinded, for I would truly be blinded by God.”

This may be understood by comparison. For just as the just person, because of his justice, is justified more fully by God, so the impious person, because of his impiety, is blinded, so that in the future he may be condemned without end.

He says this for our instruction: when we know that the just person is justified because of his justice, while the impious person is blinded because of his impiety, we should flee impiety and cling to justice.

Alternatively, he says this to remove the opinion held by certain people who assert that no one in this world suffers any loss by the judgment and disposition of God, but that everything happens by chance.

## ON PSALM LVIII

[Col. 0905C]

The title of the fifty-eighth psalm: “For the end: Do not corrupt; for David, in the inscription of the title, when Saul sent to guard his house in order to kill him.”

This is explained as follows:

This psalm looks toward the end, that is, toward Christ, and by its evident meaning exhorts you, whoever you may be, not to corrupt David, that is, Christ, by taking away his kingdom, so far as you are concerned, in the inscription of the title made for David and altered.

This means: “Do not corrupt him by altering the inscription of the title, which affirms that he is king,” which is true.

“I say, do not corrupt him by altering his inscription, when Saul sent,” that is, “since the Jewish people sent guards,” namely, soldiers, “to guard his house,” that is, the tomb, “in order to kill him,” according to the fame and honor that it had already killed according to the flesh—yet it was unable to kill him in this way.

The fact that it was unable to kill him is not contained in the title, but it is understood from the psalm, where it says at the end of the psalm, “You have become my protector,” that is, “my resurrector.” Therefore, to strengthen the argument, this is supplied outside the book. It is equivalent to saying:

“You ought not to corrupt him by denying that he is king, since it is evident that he is king of all.”

The matter is this: The Jewish people, wishing to kill him—that is, to extinguish the fame and honor of his name—sent soldiers to guard the tomb, saying that, unless it were guarded, the disciples would steal his body and tell the people that he had risen, and thus make them believe in him. Yet it could not kill him, that is, extinguish the fame of his name.

For he was not stolen by the disciples; rather, on the third day he openly rose again while the guards were terrified, and, having become known to every nation through the glorification of his resurrection, he subjected the whole world to his rule. [Col. 0906A]

The many guards stationed at the tomb greatly served as a testimony to his resurrection, although, corrupted by money, they falsely claimed that he had been stolen by the disciples while they themselves were sleeping.

Indeed, through the deceit of those same guards, the falsehood of the Jews became manifest: namely, that Christ had not remained held in death, as they falsely claimed, but had certainly risen.

For since the guards were present and had been appointed for the purpose of guarding him, they certainly would not have allowed his body to be removed secretly while they were watching. If the disciples had approached to steal it while the guards were asleep, the stone placed above it could not have been removed by the disciples without a disturbance; therefore, awakened by the disturbance, the guards would certainly have noticed it. [Col. 0906B]

Let it nevertheless be granted—even though it is entirely false—that the disciples could have rolled away the stone without causing a disturbance; the falsehood of the guards would still be no less apparent. For how do they know that his body had been removed by theft, when they claim that at that time they were weighed down by sleep?

Thus, from their very false statement it can be detected that he rose from the tomb.

The tomb is called his house—not because his body remained in it for a long time, but because his body rested there in peace for a short interval. [Col. 0906C]

It should be noted that he wished this to be understood by the prophet as referring to the future, although, in prophetic fashion, he placed the title in the past tense. For us, however, it is already past.

It may also be noted that in three titles he wrote, “Do not destroy,” or “Do not corrupt,” in the inscription of the title, because he placed this expression on account of the three kinds of language in which the title was written. For it is read that it was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin (John 19:20).

Therefore, when he says three times, “Do not corrupt,” he indicates that the title is to be corrupted in none of these three languages.

It should also be noted that this psalm does not exhort the reader in explicit words not to corrupt, but does so by its very clarity and devotion. For when this Lordly man speaks here about the conversion of the nations and the dispersion of the Jews, [Col. 0906D] and at the end about salvation...

Source column anchors retained for this supplied commentary: [Col. 0896A], [Col. 0896B], [Col. 0896C], [Col. 0896D], [Col. 0897A], [Col. 0897B], [Col. 0897C], [Col. 0897D], [Col. 0898A], [Col. 0898B], [Col. 0898C], [Col. 0898D], [Col. 0899A], [Col. 0899B], [Col. 0899C], [Col. 0899D], [Col. 0900A], [Col. 0900B], [Col. 0900C], [Col. 0900D], [Col. 0901A], [Col. 0901B], [Col. 0901C], [Col. 0901D], [Col. 0902A], [Col. 0902B], [Col. 0902C], [Col. 0902D], [Col. 0903A], [Col. 0903B], [Col. 0903C], [Col. 0903D], [Col. 0904A], [Col. 0904B], [Col. 0904C], [Col. 0904D], [Col. 0905A], [Col. 0905B], [Col. 0905C], [Col. 0905D], [Col. 0906A], [Col. 0906B].

Grant, however, even though it is altogether false, that the disciples could have rolled away the stone without causing a disturbance; nevertheless, the guards’ falsehood will appear no less clearly. For how do they know that his body was stolen, when they claim that at that time they were weighed down by sleep? Thus, by their very false statement, it can be detected that he rose from the tomb. That tomb is called his house—not because his body remained there for a long time, but because it rested in peace there for a short while [Col. 0906C].

It should be noted that he wished this to be understood of the future prophet, although, following prophetic custom, he placed the title in the past tense. For us, however, it is already past. It may also be noted that he placed three times in the title the words “Do not destroy” or “Do not corrupt,” because of the three kinds of language in which the title was written. For it is read that it was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin (John 19:20). Since, therefore, he says three times “Do not corrupt,” he indicates that the title is to be corrupted in none of these three languages.

It should also be noted that this psalm does not exhort the reader in explicit words not to corrupt it, but by its own evidence and devotion. Since this Dominical man speaks here about the conversion of the nations and the dispersion of the Jews, and finally about the salvation of the remnant of Israel, as well as about his resurrection through which all these things would occur, it is certainly understood that he is the King and Savior of Jews and nations. And when he is understood to be a king, it will most certainly be proved that the inscription of the title—which asserts that he is king—is not to be corrupted.

At the beginning of the psalm he prays concerning the resurrection, that he not be held in death according to the will of the Jews, whom he later says would kill him and think that they had kept him in death. He also prays for the salvation of the nations that are to be converted, and, by concession, speaks about the dispersion of the Jews; and at the end he prays for the salvation of the remnant that is to be converted at the end of the world.

“Deliver me from my enemies, my God.” This means: Although you are God of all, you are specially mine—either because you are personally united to me, or because I obey you above all others. Therefore, deliver me from the desire of my enemies, the Jews, who are hostile to me through envy and anger, lest they hold me in death, extinguish the glory of my name, and thus take my kingdom from me.

“And from those rising up against me, free me”—that is, from the Jews, lest they hold me in death. Deliver me by causing me to rise again. “From those who work iniquity”—that is, from the Jews working my death, which, with respect to them, is iniquity in the fullest sense. “And from men of blood”—that is, save me, by resurrecting me, after I have been removed from the power of the Jews, who are men of blood.

It should be understood that “deliver,” “free,” and “save” mean the same thing, and that “my enemies,” “those rising up against me,” “those who work iniquity,” and “men of blood” are the same people. But he repeats these terms so often in order to show that, step by step, they would first become enemies by thinking evil of him in their hearts; afterward they would rise up against him through blasphemies, accusations, and beatings; then they would work iniquity by killing him; and finally they would become men of blood—that is, men who kill both themselves and their children through their sin and evil example, as they themselves admitted: “His blood, that is, the sin of his death, be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25).

Alternatively, “men of blood” were those who shed blood, since they killed not only Christ but also many of the saints, such as Stephen and James; and although they did not kill many others, they afflicted them even to the shedding of blood.

It is necessary that I pray, “Deliver me,” because behold, at the present time they have seized my soul—that is, they will think that they have seized my soul, meaning that they have held me in death so that I cannot rise again. This is by comparison with a captive who, shut up in prison, cannot leave it. “And first they rushed upon me”—that is, they will rush upon me—“strong,” that is, effective in accomplishing their desire, so that they may hand me over to death, or because they desire this. The order is reversed, as though he said: “They will kill me; and, once killed and placed in the tomb, they will think that I will not rise again.”

It should be noted that he calls them enemies and gives the other designations that follow in order to show their impiety and to prove that their desire—that they should be able to hold him in death—is not to be fulfilled. He also shows himself innocent, so that he may more easily obtain what he prays for: “I pray, deliver me, as you ought to do; for there is no iniquity of mine, nor any sin of mine, Lord.” Iniquity is in thought; sin is in action. Or, iniquity concerns one’s neighbor, while sin is properly said with respect to oneself. This means: “I am neither harmful in thought nor in deed.” Or thus: “There is no sinner in me, nor am I a sinner against my neighbor.”

Moreover, not only was he not unjust, but, being without iniquity—that is, being not unjust—he ran, that is, swiftly completed good works; and not only this, but he also directed others who were walking crookedly toward the way of doing good, namely, his disciples. Therefore, because there is neither iniquity nor sin in me, and because I ran and directed others, “Rise up”—that is, show yourself powerful—“to meet me,” going toward me by resurrecting and exalting me [Col. 0907D–0908A].

This means: When I meet you—not locally, but by doing good and suffering for you—then you also meet me by rewarding me, namely, by resurrecting and exalting me. This is like a patron who goes out to meet someone fleeing to him in order to lead him into safety. “And see”—that is, make your meeting visible throughout the whole world: make manifest everywhere among the nations, through my preachers, my resurrection and exaltation. It should be noted that “Rise up to meet me” means the same as “deliver,” “free,” and “save,” which he said above.

But he repeated it in order to add, “and see.” I say, “Rise up and see.” And thus you, God, who are powerful—you, I say, God of the heavenly powers and God of Israel, that is, of the Jews [Col. 0908B]. This means: You whom the heavenly spirits and the Israelite people have already recognized as God.

“Pay attention”—that is, make yourself attentive—“to visit all the nations,” that is, nations of every kind. This means: You who have already revealed knowledge of yourself to the heavenly spirits, and to Israel, that is, to the Jewish people, reveal yourself also to the nations, and visit them so that you may bring them to faith and thus save them—intensely, that is, here from original sin and in the future through eternal salvation.

He calls all the heavenly spirits “powers,” using a part for the whole, since one part of them is called “powers.” And “powers” is appropriate, since they possess the greatest power of divine contemplation. I say: “Visit the nations.” And, in contrast, I concede what is just: namely, that you should not have mercy by visiting all who work iniquity—that is, those who work my death—so that they do not repent.

Having prayed for the conversion of the nations, he indicates their conversion as follows: “I said, Pay attention to visiting all the nations, and so it will be: they will truly be visited.” For they will be converted from error to faith, and this “at evening,” that is, in the sixth age, as though he had said: Those who, from the beginning of the world, had been idle with respect to the good life will at last be converted, now at the end of the ages, in the sixth age. This age is called “evening” because it is at the end of the world, just as evening is the final part of the day. The age extending from the time of Christ to the end of the world is called evening. In the Gospel it is also called, by comparison, the eleventh hour (Matthew 20:6).

And they will not only be converted, but some of them, existing as dogs—that is, preachers faithfully guarding the Church and barking at its enemies, namely, heretics, through their judgments so that they do not attack the Church, like dogs faithfully guarding their master’s house and barking at enemies and thieves—will suffer hunger, that is, the desire to incorporate others into themselves through preaching.

And those who will be like dogs will go around the city—that is, they will thoroughly fortify and guard the Church, which is the city of God, against visible enemies, namely heretics, and invisible enemies, namely evil spirits, through their preaching, example of good living, and prayer, so that those enemies do not prevail in the Church. This is like good guardians who carefully guard the city entrusted to them by going around it, lest enemies attack and thieves secretly enter [Col. 0908D–0909A].

They will not only suffer hunger; but behold—that is, openly—they will speak, not in their hearts or in writing, but with their mouths they will speak the word of preaching. “And a sword will be in their lips,” as though he said: Their preaching will not be ineffective, but in their lips there will be a sword—that is, preaching comparable to a sword, killing vices in the soul and evil works in the body, after the manner of a sword that kills. It should be noted that he uses “behold” in place of “openly” because it is customary to say “behold” of something that is present and visible.

Someone might say: You claim that they will speak openly, as though this were something wondrous and great. Do not other people speak openly? To this he adds: “Truly it is wondrous, for who has heard the things that they will speak?” No one—as though he said: They will speak things unknown and unheard: that a man born of a Virgin died, rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven; and, more wondrous still, that he is both God and man.

He also speaks prophetically about the condemnation of the enemies, as follows: “I said that you should not have mercy on all who work iniquity.” And you will not only fail to have mercy, but you, God, who are powerful and just, will also mock them—that is, you will show them worthy of mockery—when you cast them down from their honor and position. And I said that the nations would be converted, and that you would reduce all the converted nations to nothing with respect to their impiety and wickedness.

But since he had said of the enemies, “Do not have mercy on them” and “You will mock them,” someone might say: Since, O Christ, those who work iniquity will not obtain mercy, why do you not destroy them completely here and now? He answers this as follows: Although I concede that they will not obtain mercy, I will nevertheless not destroy them here completely in body and soul; rather, I will preserve my strength—that is, I will reserve my power until the future—so that I do not condemn them entirely, looking toward you, Father, that is, toward your disposition by which you have ordained that I should preserve it [Col. 0909C].

He then turns to his hearers, showing why he will preserve his strength: “I said that I would preserve my strength; and I will do this because God the Father, my protector”—so that my God, the Creator, may resurrect me—“and his mercy will come before me,” that is, will come upon me before others. This means: It will be greater in me than in others, so that he may exalt me and subject the whole world to me.

God, I say, showed this to me in my inward understanding—to me, I say, as I considered my enemies and rationally examined what ought to be done concerning them. He showed me this so that I would not destroy them, but would pray to the Father himself for them in this way:

“O God the Father, do not kill them for the present or ever afterward, in body or in soul, lest at some time the Christian people forget me”—that is, forget the benefit I bestowed on them, namely, that I died for them so that they might be saved—or lest my Christian people forget the prophets who foretold me.

This is as though he said: Since God the Father is my protector and creator, and since his mercy will come before me, I ought to obey him. He showed me in my reason that I should pray for them, so that they might not be killed by bodily slaughter, but might be witnesses to my death; that they might preserve the books of the prophets as testimony to me, who was foretold in them, and for the instruction of my people’s faith [Col. 0909D–0910A]. For if they were destroyed, my people would not possess the books of the prophets in which testimony to my resurrection and death is contained, and eventually those books would be forgotten. But when they see the Jews dispersed everywhere because of my death, they will retain the memory of that death without end.

I say: “Do not kill them, but scatter them everywhere throughout the lands in your strength,” that is, in your power, since you are powerful enough to scatter them. But since they could be scattered in such a way that they retained honor somewhere, he adds: “And you, Lord, who are my protector, do not yield”—that is, put them down from all honor [Col. 0910B].

He prays for the salvation of those who are to be converted at the end of the world as follows: “I say, Do not kill them here in body, but, in those who are to be saved, kill the sin of their mouth”—that is, destroy the sin they will possess because they will blaspheme me with their mouths, following the example of their ancestors. And after you have killed the sin, kill also the blasphemous speech of their lips—that is, do not let them speak blasphemy against me any longer. Thus, “let them be caught by their own reason in their pride”: let their reason grasp that they have gone astray when they spoke proudly in blasphemy against me and denied me worship.

Having shown one reason why he preserves his strength—namely, for the future, because God showed him that he should pray for them—he adds another, as follows: “And therefore I will still preserve my strength, because they will be announced”—that is, through the proclamation of preachers they will be converted from the curse and falsehood in which they formerly existed into consummation, that is, into the perfection of virtues.

This means: From what they formerly were, following the example of their ancestors—cursing me and lying by saying that I am neither God nor King—they will become perfect in virtues through the preaching of preachers, namely Elijah, Enoch, and the others. I say that they will be converted, and this “in the anger of consummation,” that is, in consideration of the future anger, which will be consummate, that is, perfect—not a passing anger, but an eternal one.

This means: Because they will consider the everlasting anger that is to come upon them, they will be converted through fear of that anger, and afterward they will no longer be impious as they were before. And those who previously did not acknowledge that I ruled over Jews and nations will know—that is, they will recognize—that God will rule Jacob and the ends of the earth. This means: They will recognize that I, who am not merely man but also God, will rule both Jacob—that is, the Jewish people—and all the nations to the ends of the earth. He uses “the ends of the earth” by metonymy for the nations themselves.

He also shows at what time this will occur: “I say that they will be converted through proclamation,” that is, through the teaching of preachers; “and this conversion will not be for the present, but they will be converted at evening,” that is, at the end of the sixth age, at the end of the world. And, existing as certain dogs, they will suffer hunger—the desire to incorporate others into themselves—and they will go around the city, that is, they will carefully guard the Church [Col. 0910D–0911A].

This verse is explained here as above, except that above he took “evening” to mean the beginning of the sixth age, which as a whole is called evening; here, however, he calls evening the end of the sixth age, and this properly, because we take evening to be the final part of the day. They will not only suffer hunger, but they will also be scattered through many places in order to eat—that is, to incorporate unbelieving Jews into themselves, after the manner of food, which is incorporated into the body when it is eaten.

But if they are not satisfied by incorporating others—that is, if they cannot incorporate many into themselves—they will not only grieve in their hearts, but will also murmur with their mouths, that is, they will complain to God in prayer that they may be satisfied. In this he indicates that they will be very perfect, since they will even pray for the conversion of others.

Having shown the conversion of Jews and nations, he also gives thanks to God for his strength and mercy, promising that he will praise God and act well in contemplation of his strength and mercy [Col. 0911B].

I said that nations and Jews would be converted through my death and resurrection. But, so that all these things may occur, I will sing with my mouth and devotion of the strength that is to be given to me, and I will rejoice—that is, I will praise with joy—your mercy that will come to me in the morning.

This means: I will praise you with my mouth and affection, both for the steadfastness of the strength you will give me in my Passion and for the morning mercy of the resurrection. He explains what he said in this verse when he adds: “I said that I would praise you for the morning mercy”; namely, I will praise you because you have become—or will become—my protector, that is, my physician, by resurrecting me and leading me to immortality [Col. 0911C]. And I said that I would praise you for your strength, namely, because you will become my refuge, that is, my security, so that I do not yield on the day of tribulation, that is, of my Passion.

I said that I would sing to you both of strength and of mercy. But I will not only sing with my mouth and devotion; I will also sing psalms to you—that is, I will work well for your honor—because you will be my helper, so that I do not yield; because you, God the Father, will be my protector, so that you may resurrect me; because you are my God, that is, my creator insofar as I am man; and because you are my mercy—an emphatic expression.

This means: You are merciful toward me, not only in resurrecting me, but also because you made me free from sin and will bestow many other benefits.

## ON PSALM LIX

[Col. 0911D] The title of the fifty-ninth psalm: “For the end, for those who will be changed, to David himself, in the inscription of the title. For instruction, when he set fire to Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Zobah, and turned Joab and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand.”

Although history appears to be indicated in this title, the psalm nevertheless does not seem to have been composed according to the analogy of the historical account. For although the history records that David conquered and killed his enemies, this passage is not about victory but about repulsion and destruction. Therefore, this title appropriately seems not to be understood according to the analogy of the history, but according to the interpretation of the words.

By David, therefore, Christ is understood. By Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Zobah, the Church from the Jews is understood, which was set on fire by Christ, the true David, with the fire of the Holy Spirit. Mesopotamia is interpreted as “elevated calling”; Syria as “sublimity.” The Church from the Jews is appropriately called elevated, called, and sublime. For it was to be set on fire by the Spirit’s fire through Christ’s death, called to faith through the apostles, raised above vices through repentance, and thus made sublime in virtues.

By the Syria mentioned again—which, as we have said, is interpreted as “sublimity”—and by Zobah, which signifies “vain antiquity,” the sublimity, that is, the pride, of the old law is designated. That law was vain, not because it was not good, but because it was insufficient for the salvation of the world, as many supposed. David—that is, Christ, or the Church from the Jews—set that pride on fire with the fire of the Holy Spirit, that is, utterly destroyed it [Col. 0912A–B].

By Joab, who is interpreted as “enemy,” and Edom, which means “earthly” or “bloody,” the people of the nations converted to faith are understood. They were converted from the enmity they had wickedly maintained against God through evil living to peace through good living. Although they were earthly, that is, intent on earthly things, and bloody, that is, persecutors who shed the blood of the faithful, or bloody, that is, shedder of the blood of sacrifices that they offered to idols, they were struck by Christ through preachers who threatened eternal death to those who would not be converted and promised eternal life to those who would be converted.

This means: Their earthliness, persecution of the faithful, and worship of idols were destroyed. By the valley, which is a low-lying place, humility is understood. By the salt-pits, through metonymy from what is adjacent, salt is understood, since salt is prepared in salt-pits [Col. 0912C].

By salt, which seasons all foods and gives them flavor, the flavor of humility is understood. Humility seasons the other virtues and makes them acceptable to God, since without it the other virtues, even when possessed, would be useless and unacceptable to God; indeed, they would not be called virtues in you, but imitations of virtues. Hence humility is also called the queen of virtues, just as pride is the queen of vices.

In this humility he placed Mesopotamia of Syria set on fire, and Joab and Edom converted and struck—that is, the Jewish and gentile peoples—so that by persevering in it they might attain exaltation.

By “twelve thousand” the same thing is understood as by Mesopotamia of Syria and by Joab and Edom—namely, the Jewish and gentile peoples—but something else is also signified. Earlier, the Jewish people were understood indefinitely through Mesopotamia of Syria, and the gentile people through Joab and Edom. Similarly, through the number one thousand, which is so perfect that no numerical variety proceeds beyond it, the perfect fullness of both peoples is understood: converted to faith, and still to be converted throughout the entire sixth age, even to the end of the world. This is the subject of the preceding psalm, and this fullness is greater than it had ever been before the sixth age.

But because, if he had placed only the number one thousand, the greatest fullness might have been understood, though not necessarily from all parts of the world, he added twelve. Through the number twelve, which is multiplied from three and four, the whole people of the world, converted in the sixth age from all four parts of the world to faith in the Trinity, is understood: three times four, or four times three, makes twelve [Col. 0912D–0913A]. Through the three and four, which are parts of seven, by which the twelve is multiplied, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are understood, by which the people converted to faith are filled most abundantly.

Having indicated the interpretation of the individual words, we must proceed to adapt them to the words of the title. This psalm is concerned with those who will be changed “for the end,” that is, for the perfection of blessedness: in the future, from mortality to immortality, from passibility to impassibility, and from imperfect knowledge to perfect knowledge of God.

I say that they will be changed, and this “in the inscription of the title,” made for David himself—that is, for Christ, whom they have received [Col. 0913B]. This means: They will be perfectly changed in the future because they have received Christ Jesus as king, which is designated in the inscription of the title.

But because it would not be enough to recognize and receive him as king unless one also obeyed his commands—as he himself testifies in the Gospel: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 7:21)—the words “for instruction” are added.

It is as though he said: I say that they will be changed, and this because they have received the inscription of the title; nevertheless, this is “for instruction,” that is, because they attend to his teaching in order to obey him, doing good works and abstaining from vices as he commanded [Col. 0913C].

Lest anyone suppose that those who will be changed received the inscription of the title and attended to the fulfillment of his teaching by free choice, without the help of God’s grace, he shows that they attained this through the grace of the Holy Spirit when he adds, “when he set fire to,” and so forth.

This is adapted as follows: I say that the psalm concerns those who will be changed through receiving the inscription and fulfilling the teaching, and that they did not suffice by free choice for receiving the title and fulfilling obedience. Rather, they received the title and obeyed the teaching when David himself—that is, Christ—set fire to Mesopotamia of Syria.

That is, he kindled with the fervor of spiritual grace the Jewish people, which had become Mesopotamia of Syria: called to faith, raised above vices, and made sublime in virtues. And in that Mesopotamia he set fire—that is, destroyed—Syria of Zobah, meaning the sublimity of vain antiquity, namely the pride of the old law, so that it would no longer grow proud by trusting in it [Col. 0913D].

And this also occurred when David himself converted Joab—that is, the gentile people, the enemy—from error to faith; and struck Edom—that is, through the preaching of the faithful he struck that same Joab insofar as it was Edom, earthly or bloody, so as to destroy its earthliness and make it spiritual; and so that he might consume in it what was bloody, namely its persecution and idolatry, and make it peaceful, gentle, and a worshiper of God.

I say that he set fire to Mesopotamia and converted Joab, and he did all this in the Valley of Salt, that is, in flavorful humility, so that he might make the proud humble [Col. 0914A]. And he did not set fire to only a small part of Mesopotamia or convert only a few of Joab, but he set fire to and struck twelve thousand—that is, the greatest fullness gathered from the Jews and nations from all parts of the world.

When he says “when he set fire to,” the word “when” is causal. The whole statement is as though he said: In this psalm the faithful from Jews and nations act, praying for those who will be changed at the end—that is, praying for themselves, so that God may change them into perfect blessedness. He has already changed them through his death from original sin to innocence of life; and therefore may he change them because they have received the inscription of the title and obey his teaching.

This occurred because Christ set fire, by spiritual grace, to Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Zobah—that is, he destroyed among the Jews the pride of the vain old law. Through this he made them elevated above vices and sublime in virtues, calling them to faith through the teaching of the apostles. Christ himself converted Joab from error to faith and struck it insofar as it was Edom. He did all this in flavorful humility, and he did not set fire to, convert, and strike only a few from Mesopotamia and Joab, but twelve thousand.

At the beginning of this psalm the faithful who act here show into what misery they came through Adam: from part of which they have already been rescued, while from part they must still be rescued. They show this so that, by lamenting it, they may deserve to be completely rescued. Afterwards they pray that they may be wholly rescued, since they are suffering harsh things for God and have already come to faith. They say that they must be completely rescued in the future, since God promised this through his Son, whom they introduce as speaking from the earth. They also promise that they will trust in no one except God himself.

“God, you have repelled us”—through Adam—from the manifest knowledge of you that we would have had if Adam had not sinned. And you have destroyed us with respect to the blessedness that we would have possessed, subjecting us to every misery: cold and heat, illnesses, sorrows, and other sufferings of this kind. You did not do this unjustly, but you were angry with us—that is, you did this because of your anger, meaning because of the just vengeance that you exercised against the human race on account of Adam’s fault. The anger of God is nothing other than his vengeance. Afterwards you had mercy on us through your death, so that you might redeem us from original sin.

He explains how God had mercy when he adds: “You shook the earth and troubled it.” The order is reversed. I say that you had mercy, and thus you troubled the earth—that is, us, who were earthly—with a beneficial disturbance, threatening through preachers that “whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16). Thus you moved it toward faith, rescuing it from the ignorance in which it was previously held because of its original and actual sins.

And you, who have already healed it in part in order to rescue it from ignorance and redeem its sins through baptism, heal its breaches—that is, heal it in the future from its breaches, so that although here it is crushed by all pains and sufferings, which are the punishment of original sin, once restored to impassibility it may no longer be crushed [Col. 0914D–0915A].

This means: You who have already healed it from sin, heal it also in the future from the punishment of sin. And you ought to heal its breaches in the future because it has already been moved from error to faith, so that it may receive you as God, Creator, and King, whom it previously refused to worship.

He also shows another reason why he ought to heal the earth, as follows: “I said that you should heal the earth because it has been shaken, and also because you showed your people hard things.” This means: You showed us, who are your people and your earth, an example of enduring hard tribulations, since you suffered hard and harsh things for us. Having shown this, you gave us wine of compunction—that is, you filled us with compunction through wine, meaning the cup of tribulations—so that through them we might be changed at the end, although before our conversion we had been drunk with sweet wine, that is, the cup of pleasure.

The whole statement is as though he said: You ought to heal us because for your sake we are drinking the draught of tribulations. Through the death of the Dominical man you gave us an example. Wine that causes compunction is called tribulation because it is bitter and harsh to the body, like wine that causes a stinging sensation and is bitter and harsh. Pleasure is also called sweet wine because it is sweet and makes people foolish, drawing them away from God like wine that makes foolish those whom it intoxicates.

Tribulations are also called draughts by comparison, because just as illness is driven away and health restored by the bitter potions of physicians, so the foulness of vices is cleansed by the bitterness of tribulations and everlasting life is restored. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” (Matthew 20:22) [Col. 0915B–C].

He shows the benefit for which he displayed to his people that hard things must be endured, as follows: “I say that you showed your people that hard things must be endured, and through those hard things you gave those who fear you a sign.” That is, you gave them hard things so that they might be a sign to them—a sign of the future judgment—so that, when they saw God exacting vengeance here upon the sins of the faithful through tribulations, they might judge from this that he would exact vengeance all the more upon the sins of those who do not confess them. As the Apostle says: “Which you endure as an example of the just judgment of God” (2 Thessalonians 1:4) [Col. 0915C–D].

I said that through hard things you gave the faithful who fear you a sign, namely so that, contemplating these signs of tribulation, they might flee through correction of their life “from the face of the bow”—that is, from the presence of his threat, meaning from everlasting condemnation, which worldly tribulation threatens, since it is its sign.

Temporal tribulation is rightly called a bow, because just as a bow threatens from a distance, so worldly tribulation threatens eternal death to those who are not converted; of that death it is a sign.

“Face” is also rightly used for “presence,” since we say that those placed before someone’s face are present. Therefore, those who fear you should flee here from the face of the bow through correction of their life, so that your beloved—that is, those who fear you—may be freed from the face of the bow, that is, from everlasting condemnation in the future [Col. 0915D–0916A].

And so may God act so that we may be freed: “Save me,” namely with eternal salvation, “your people,” by placing me at your right hand—that is, in the favor of your grace—and not placing me on the left with those who are to be destroyed. And concerning this for which I pray, “Save me,” hear me—that is, hear me in such a way that I may obtain what I ask.

They show that they will attain salvation and, at the end of the world, be separated from evils through God’s own promise. They introduce God as speaking here, and through the Dominical man he will separate the good from those to be destroyed and receive them. They introduce him as speaking in order that what they say he promises may possess greater authority.

I said that God would save me, his people, and truly he will do so: “God has spoken in his holy one,” that is, in the Dominical man, who is called “holy” by antonomasia [Col. 0916A–B].

“I will rejoice and divide Shechem,” that is, I will joyfully divide from those who are to be destroyed those broad-shouldered ones—that is, those who patiently bear my yoke upon their shoulders, carrying in the shoulders of their heart my law, which is a most gentle yoke, and carrying it in memory, like those who bear a yoke upon their shoulders. Shechem is interpreted as “shoulder,” and is said to be a place in Judea. Therefore, through Shechem the faithful from the Jews are understood.

But because he had placed Shechem without qualification, it is not clearly understood which “broad-shouldered ones” he will divide, since there are also some who bear the devil’s yoke, and some who, although they seem to bear the Lord’s yoke, do not endure it in humility but bear it unwillingly. Therefore, he determines which broad-shouldered ones he will divide, as follows [Col. 0916B–C]:

“I say that I will divide Shechem and”—that is, “namely”—“measure the valley of the tabernacles,” that is, those dwelling in tabernacles in the valley, namely those serving God in the humility of patience.

This means: I will gather them away from the assembly of the wicked, like a reaper who gathers ears of grain from the stalks. Hence it is written: “He will separate the nations from one another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats” (Matthew 25:32). The valley is appropriately used for humility because it is lowly. A tabernacle is used for military service because dwelling in tabernacles is characteristic of soldiers.

And I will not measure those soldiers in the valley who fall away from the service through fear of tribulation and martyrdom. “But Gilead is mine”—that is, those who are mine for measuring are those who are Gilead: martyrs serving as soldiers, perseveringly refusing to deny the name of God even in tribulation, where there would seem to be a place for fear and denial [Col. 0916C–D].

For Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony.” Hence martyrs are appropriately understood through Gilead, since they do not fear being witnesses to the Dominical faith even in tribulations. This is also understood through the word “martyr.” For *martyr* is Greek and means “witness” in Latin. Someone is not rightly called a witness if, through fear of death, he withdraws from bearing witness to the truth.

Martyrs are called a heap because they are many. For we call a collection of many things a heap. A single person can also be called a heap by another comparison, because through tribulations he grows upward into the height of perfection, like a heap that rises upward.

[Col. 0917A] Since, however, there were some who remained witnesses of the Lord’s faith even unto death—not moved by charity, but stirred up by human approval—the Apostle says: “If I deliver up my body so that I may be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3). He therefore determines whom he calls his Gilead when he adds: “And,” that is, namely, “Manasseh is mine,” that is, “forgetfulness.” This means: Those martyrs are mine who are Manasseh, that is, who forget every earthly approval and fight in tribulation for charity alone.

Manasseh is interpreted as “forgetfulness.” This Gilead, which is Manasseh, while also being Ephraim—that is, producing fruit in others through faith by his preaching and steadfastness—is “the strength of my head,” that is, he considers himself strong in steadfastness amid tribulations through me, who am his head, that is, his governor. Ephraim is interpreted as “fruitfulness.” The whole statement is as though he said: “I shall divide those shoulders away from the wicked; I shall measure out for myself those who will be my witnesses, even amid tribulations, forgetting every human approval, producing fruit in others as they are able, and attributing all the strength of their steadfastness not to themselves but to me, their head.”

Gilead is a region in Judea. Ephraim and Manasseh, moreover, were Jewish men. Hence, through these names, martyrs from the Jews are understood. But lest Jewish confessors seem not to belong to him, he also adds them, saying: “And Judah is my king,” that is, “My confessors from the Jews are those who rule themselves so that they do not slip into unlawful things.” For confessing God with the voice benefits someone little or nothing unless he also abstains from unlawful things by governing himself well and strives to do good. Hence Prosper says: “To speak well and live badly is nothing other than condemning oneself by one’s own speech.” The apostle John likewise says: “If anyone says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments, he is a liar” (1 John 2:4).

Judah is indeed interpreted as “confession.” Accordingly, Judah—a Jewish man, namely Jacob’s son—appropriately signifies confessors from the Jews.

After showing that the martyrs and confessors from the Jews are his and will be divided out in the future, lest the faithful from the nations think themselves excluded—since many of them became martyrs and many others confessors—he likewise adds them universally, saying: “And Moab is the pot of my hope,” [Col. 0917D] that is, the refreshment of my hope. This means: “The gentile people converted to the faith are mine, for whom I hope to be refreshed with joy when I divide them away from the wicked in the future.”

Moab was the son of Lot, whom Lot begot from his daughter; from his blood the greatest generation of gentiles proceeded, who were also called Moabites (Gen. 19:7). Moab is therefore interpreted as “outside the law,” because he was begotten contrary to the law from a daughter. Through Moab, therefore, the gentile people are understood, who were always outside the law and contrary to the law, since they denied God the worship owed to him.

“Refreshment” is not inappropriately understood through the pot, since the body is refreshed by food cooked in a pot. Or the passage may be read in another way, with both the meaning and the punctuation changed: “Moab is the pot of my hope,” that is, “That gentile people which has been boiled free of all earthliness by the fire of tribulation, like a pot that is boiled by fire so that it may be stronger, belongs to my hope,” that is, “I hope to divide it away from the wicked in the future.”

Or thus: “Moab is the pot belonging to my hope,” that is, “The gentile people that was the pot of my faithful,” meaning that it boiled them through the fires of tribulation free of every stain, like a pot in which food is boiled free of harmful moisture.

And since someone might ask, “How will you acquire Moab, that is, the gentile people?” he now shows how he will acquire it, saying: “I say that Moab belongs to my hope, and I shall acquire Moab for myself in this way: namely, I shall extend my sandal over Idumaea,” that is, “I shall extend preachers over the gentile people, and through their teaching they will acquire it for me.”

[Col. 0918B] Idumaea is called “earthly”; hence Idumaea signifies the people of the gentiles, who before their conversion devoted themselves solely to earthly things. “Sandal,” appropriately, signifies preachers, because by their preaching, example, and prayer they fortify the Church, just as the foot is protected by a sandal.

Or through “sandal,” by association, feet may be understood, since sandals are worn on feet; and through “feet,” preachers, because just as feet carry the body, so preachers carried the Lord’s name among the nations.

Or thus: “I shall acquire the gentile people for myself because I shall extend my sandal over Idumaea,” that is, “I shall extend knowledge of my sandal over Idumaea”—namely, over the gentile people—“so that, recognizing me, who was God, as having become man for the salvation of the whole world, it may submit itself to me willingly.”

A sandal is made from the skins of dead animals; therefore it stands for Christ’s humanity, which through many tribulations was mortified in the final suffering of the cross. Hence John the Baptist says: “After me there comes a man, namely Christ, who was made before me” (John 1:27)—according to his humanity, not temporally but in dignity. This means: “He who, according to his humanity, is later in time was made more dignified than I.”

“I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (ibid.), that is, “I am not worthy to explain the smallest part of the mysteries of his humanity.” This means: “I am neither worthy nor capable of explaining even the smallest secret of his humanity, much less am I sufficient to disclose the ineffable mysteries of his divinity.” Since the strap is the smallest part of the sandal, it rightly stands for the smallest part of the mysteries of Christ’s humanity.

Or thus: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal,” that is, “the question of his humanity”—namely, the question posed by some of how the one who was God became man. The question is appropriately called a strap, because just as a strap fastens a sandal, so a question binds the matter about which it is made.

I said that I would extend my sandal over Idumaea; thus the foreigners are subjected to me, that is, the Idumaeans will be subjected to me. Until now they were foreigners—that is, of another generation, generated by the devil and alienated from knowledge of me.

[Col. 0919A] It should be noted that although the things said here are not found in the Gospel as having been said by the Lord, the Gospel does record that God spoke things equivalent to them; these will readily appear to anyone who investigates.

After introducing the words concerning the Lord’s Passion, the gathered faithful, rejoicing over this promise, as though in the form of a question, pray to be led into a fortified city—that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem, where the enemy will make no assault. They say and pray as follows, so that this city may be enlarged more and more from day to day:

“O God, you promised that you would divide Shechem and Moab, the pot, away from those destined for destruction”—that is, the Church from the Jews and the nations. “May it therefore come to pass that you divide me and lead me, once divided, into the fortified city. For who will lead me into the fortified city?”

And because you promised that you would extend your sandal over Idumaea, “enlarge me here as far as Idumaea”—that is, as far as those who are still earthly—“so that they too may be joined to me. For who will lead,” that is, enlarge, “me as far as Idumaea,” that is, to the point that the Idumaeans may be joined to me?

“Is it not you, God, who have repelled us,” that is, who appear here to repel us while we are placed in tribulations, “and who will not go forth here with our forces,” that is, with our armies, “so as to make us gather armies against our enemies and go out with those armies to battle against our adversaries, just as you went out with the armies of our fathers through the ministry of angels?”

The whole statement is as though he said: “Since you have promised that in the future you will divide us away from the wicked and lead us into the fortified city, and that here you will extend your sandal over Idumaea, even though I appear to have been repelled by you, nevertheless lead me in the future into the fortified city; and here enlarge me as far as Idumaea. For who can do this except you? No one.” He expresses this from an immense desire in the form of a question.

I said that you had repelled us, that is, that you appear here to repel us who are placed in tribulation. Therefore, because here you permit us to be in tribulation, give us help from tribulation—that is, through this tribulation that we suffer. This means: “Make this tribulation a help to us,” that is, a cause of salvation, “while through it we are boiled free of our stains.” For this reason we ask to be helped through tribulations, because human salvation is vain.

It is as though he said: “We ask to be helped through tribulation, not through human aid, because human salvation is vain,” that is, human assistance is vain in bringing salvation.

I said, O hearers, that God will not go forth with our forces. We shall not now gather forces; rather, we shall make our strength in God, that is, we shall have God as our strength and trust in him more than in any force, so that he himself may make us overcome our enemies. And he himself will reduce those who afflict us to nothing, that is, through our preaching he will make them good instead of wicked.

Or he will reduce those who afflict us to nothing in the future, that is, he will destroy the power of those who afflict us, so that in the future they may not prevail over us as they now prevail in the body.

He addresses this apostrophe to the hearers in order to instruct them by his example to trust in God alone, not in earthly strength.

## Psalm 60

### The title of Psalm 60

“Unto the end, in hymns. A psalm of David.” This is explained as follows: “A psalm of David,” that is, of the Church of the perfect, persevering in hymns until the end of life—that is, persevering in the praises of God in deed, voice, and devotion. Or, “reaching toward the end,” that is, toward perfect blessedness, by persevering in hymns, that is, in the praises of God.

The assembly of the perfect prays that God may hear its prayer, which it makes in order that in this age it may dwell in God’s tabernacle and in the future possess an eternal inheritance. It also prays that he may hear the supplication it makes, asking God to protect it from vices by removing them from it and to protect it from everlasting punishment.

Here it should be noted that “prayer” refers to what is made for the acquisition of any thing, whereas “supplication” refers to the removal of something. The speaker shows that she will obtain both what she prays for and what she supplicates, both through the confidence of her merit and through the example of the benefits she has already obtained; and with this confidence she promises that she will recite the psalm because she will obtain them.

“Hear, O God, my supplication, so that you may protect me from vices and everlasting punishment by removing them from me. Attend to my prayer,” that is, hear my prayer carefully. Or, “attend,” that is, “make yourself attentive to my prayer”: namely, “As intensely as I pray, so intensely grant what I ask—that I, who have already begun to dwell in your tabernacle,” that is, in your warfare, “may dwell in it here more and more, and in the future may possess my inheritance.”

It is right for you to hear me, for I have cried out to you with mouth, deed, and mind in order to win your favor, not for anything earthly. This cry proceeded “from the ends of the earth,” that is, of earthliness. This means: “I arrived at this cry because I brought all earthliness to an end in myself, so that I might yearn not for earthly but for spiritual things, in anticipation of the reward.”

He shows the benefits already obtained, by whose example he believes that he will obtain what he prays for. I say: “Hear what I pray for and what I supplicate,” and you ought to hear me because you have already bestowed these benefits, namely, because you “exalted me upon a rock,” that is, in conformity with Christ, who is the firm rock, though I had previously been cast down in vices.

This means: “You exalted me in virtues so that I might be conformed to Christ.” Christ is called a rock because, in the likeness of a rock, he is the firm foundation of all the faithful, so that those founded upon him may not be moved in any way. Hence the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4); and the prophet says: “He will be a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal to the two houses of Israel” (Isa. 8:14).

He also shows from what condition he exalted her, adding: “I say: You exalted me when”—that is, while—“my heart was anxious from the consciousness of crimes,” that is, while my heart was mine and not yours. The heart is said to belong to the sinner when it thinks evil; but it belongs to God when it thinks well. Hence Prosper says: “When we think rightly, it is not the work of ourselves.”

The whole statement is as though he said: “You exalted me after freeing me from the anxiety of crimes.”

Or thus: “You exalted me, and it was necessary for this to happen while my heart was anxious; for previously it was sorrowful, because by myself I could not be exalted.” It is as though he said: “It was necessary for you to exalt me, since by myself I was insufficient to exalt myself, and therefore I was extremely anxious.” For a person is greatly anxious when he cannot reach what he strives for intensely.

And once exalted, you led me onward, that is, you made me persevere in that exaltation so that I would not fall. Or, you led me from great things to greater things, so that, once exalted, you might exalt me more from day to day.

He promises himself, from the certainty of the hope he possesses, that he will obtain what he prays for, when he adds: “Because you have become my hope, a tower of strength in the face of the enemy.”

“I shall dwell in your tabernacle forever; I shall be protected beneath the shelter of your wings.” The passage is connected and construed so that each clause receives its corresponding meaning.

I said: “Hear my supplication, so that you may protect me from vices and everlasting punishment; and attend to my prayer, so that you may make me dwell more and more in your tabernacle.” I am certain of obtaining what I supplicate and pray for, because you have become my hope—that is, because, by exalting and leading me onward, you have become one in whom my hope rests. I am certain, therefore, that I shall dwell in your tabernacle, that is, in your warfare, advancing more and more “forever”—that is, for as long as the earthly ages endure. I shall persevere in your warfare, into which I have begun to be led.

The words “You have become my hope” are expressed emphatically. And because you have become “a tower of strength in the face of the enemy,” that is, because you have become for me a strong defense against the attack of the visible and invisible enemy that seizes me, I am certain that, existing beneath the shelter of your wings—that is, in your protection—I shall be protected, here continually from vices and in the future from punishment.

The phrase “beneath the shelter of wings” does not mean that God has wings. It is drawn from the likeness of a bird, which protects its young with the shelter of its wings from heat, rain, and the attack of predatory birds. The meaning is equivalent to: “You will protect me in your defense.”

Or the wings may signify the two laws, the Old and the New, or also the twofold love of God and neighbor. Through the practice of these, the faithful of the Church are continually refreshed and protected: here, so that they are not overcome by tribulations; and in the future, so that they are not punished by everlasting punishment, just as the young of a bird are protected by its wings from every injury.

I do not hope merely that I shall dwell in your tabernacle because you have become my hope; I hope it also because you, God, who are powerful to complete what I pray for, have heard my prayer—that is, you have determined to complete my prayer, namely, that I should dwell in your tabernacle forever.

And you will not merely grant that I dwell here in the tabernacle; in the future you have given—that is, you will give—an inheritance of eternal blessedness to those who fear your name, namely, to those who approach this name of yours, “Lord,” with chaste fear, not grieving over and blaspheming the fact that you are Lord.

He calls eternal blessedness an “inheritance” by comparison, because the faithful, made adoptive sons through the death of Christ the Son, will possess it forever, just as sons possess their father’s inheritance after the father’s death for as long as they live.
