He explains this inheritance when he adds: “I say that you will give an inheritance: namely, you will add the days of the king to the days of the king.” This means: “While here we have days conformed to the days of Christ, who is pre-eminently called the king, so that here we may fight for you according to our ability, just as he fought for you, God, in this life, you will add to us after the death of the flesh other days conformed to other days of Christ the king. These will be days superior to our present days.”

They will be eternal days, that is, perpetual life, which will be conformed to the life of Christ that he attained after the death of the flesh, as he himself testifies: “I live, and you will live” (John 14:19).

Since he had said “days,” lest they seem to be something insignificant, he calls them by a more dignified name when he adds: “Namely, you will add the years of the king to his years,” that is, to the king’s years. Here “years” and “days” have the same meaning.

It should not be understood that perpetual life is called “days” or “years” in the plural because there will be a multiplicity of days in it. Rather, that one day will surpass the multiplicity of these days. I say that you will add days upon the days of the king; and you will do this in different righteous people, “unto the day of generation and generation,” that is, you will give those days according to the soul to different righteous people at different times: today to one who departs from this life, tomorrow to another, and the day after tomorrow to another, and so continually by succession until the day of judgment.

That day will be “the day of generation and generation,” that is, of a twofold generation, on which the faithful will be generated twice into eternity, according to both body and soul. Those who are generated according to the soul are generated immediately after the death of the flesh. The Lord calls this day “the day of regeneration” when he says: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits…” (Matt. 19:28), and so forth.

Or it is called “the day of generation and generation” because all who have been spiritually generated in faith will be generated together into eternal blessedness. This generation and generation remains forever in the sight of God: that is, those who have been generated spiritually, or according to body and soul, will remain forever in the presence and good pleasure of God, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “So we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:16).

Someone might say: “You say that they will remain in the sight of God, as though that were something great.” To this he adds: “Truly, that remaining is great. For who afterward will seek mercy,” that is, the remission of sins and deliverance from tribulations, “and truth,” that is, eternal, true, and unchanging existence? No one.

It is as though he said: “Blessed will be those who remain, for once they have entirely obtained mercy and truth, they will no longer need to pray to God for mercy and truth.”

Therefore, “so that I may remain in your sight, O God, I shall sing a psalm to your name,” that is, I shall set my good works openly before you for the honor of your name, not for human approval. I shall not do this by the hour or unwillingly; rather, from day to day I shall perform my works, which are called vows because they are done by the vow and desire of the heart, not unwillingly. And I shall do this “unto the age,” namely, the age that follows this one. This means: for as long as this world lasts.

## Psalm 61

### Title of Psalm 61

“Unto the end, for Idithun. A psalm of David.” This is explained as follows: This psalm is David’s, that is, of the Church of the perfect, composed through Idithun “unto the end,” that is, with regard to the meaning of the name Idithun; “unto the end,” that is, on the occasion that the Church herself is “leaping over” those against whom she argues here; and “tending toward the end,” that is, toward conformity with Christ, the end of prophecy and of the law.

In this psalm the Church of the perfect argues against heretics, gentiles, and Jews who wish to draw her away from God’s law and from submission to him, showing that they will in no way draw her away. She also shows several reasons why they will not be able to do so.

She reproaches their impiety in order thereby either to recall them or to turn away from conformity with them others who are still innocent—namely, the good. She also exhorts her own soul not to depart from submission to God after their example. She admonishes the good to hope in God, not in acts of robbery and riches, saying at the end of the psalm that God will repay each person according to his works: saving those who hope in him and justly condemning those who hope in riches.

“Will not my soul be subject to God?” It is as though he said: “You adversaries of the Catholic faith wish to remove it from submission to God. If you can accomplish this, you wish it not to be subject. By no means: it will truly be subject and will not be able to be moved by you.”

And rightly will it be subject: “For from him is my salvation,” that is, my salvation comes from him. This means: “He himself will save me.”

Someone might say: “Is he powerful enough to save you?” To this he responds: “Yes, truly my salvation can come from him. For he himself is also my God,” that is, my restorer through his death—since I had perished in Adam—and “my receiver” in the future, that is, my physician, who will make me, mortal and subject to suffering, immortal and free from suffering.

Or the passage may be connected without changing the meaning: “My soul will therefore be subject to him because my salvation comes from him; and for this reason also—for he himself is my God, my savior, and my receiver.”

It is as though he said: “He is not only my savior, but also my God, my savior, and my receiver.” Since there are such great reasons for being subject to him, “I shall not be moved any further from his submission.”

When he says “any further,” this does not necessarily imply that she had ever been moved; it is equivalent to saying: “I shall never be moved.”

Or thus: “I shall not be moved any further,” after I began to be subject to you; before I was subjected, I had been removed from you through unbelief.

After dealing with all his adversaries, he now proceeds especially against those who openly attack her through tribulations—namely, the Jews and gentiles. He shows that they desire in vain to draw her away and that by doing so they instead kill themselves in soul, so that in this way he may call them back. Or, if they refuse to be drawn away, they may be made without excuse.

He says this as follows: “I say: I shall not be moved.” And since I am immovable, “how long,” that is, until what time, “will you rush upon me through tribulations, a man”—that is, upon me, who am still a man, mortal and subject to suffering, in whom you have the power to attack?

This is expressed as a rebuke and is equivalent to saying: “Since I am immovable, cease attacking me for the purpose of recalling me. For by rushing upon me you all kill yourselves.”

This means: “The fact that you rush upon me is the reason that you are killed in soul.” I speak to you who exist “like a leaning wall,” that is, who are comparable to a wall already leaning and ready to fall.

It is as though he said: “When God made you rational and endowed with free will, and thus made you suitable to be a wall of the Church, by living wickedly you inclined yourselves,” that is, you made yourselves ready to fall into death, just as a leaning wall is ready to fall.

[Col. 0924B] He further demonstrates that they are weaker when he adds: “And to you I speak as to a pushed fence,” that is, as to people comparable not to an upright wall but to a fence that has already been pushed and is inclined to fall.

A fence, properly speaking, is a heap of stones placed in alternating courses without cement or any binding; it can quickly be destroyed. A wall, however, is a heap of stones placed in alternating courses and bound with cement or some other joining material; it is not as easy to make fall as a fence.

Accordingly, those who exist without the bond of faith and concord and who, driven by vices, are easily brought down into death are appropriately compared to a fence.

The whole statement is as though he said: “Since, because of your evil life, you are already about to fall like a pushed fence, you ought certainly to be bound by the cement of faith and submission to God, so that you would not fall.”

He makes an apostrophe to the hearers, showing the adversaries’ desire to draw the Church away from submission to God and thus also to take from her the God for whom she yearns.

He also deals with the heretics, who try to attract her outwardly by speaking well with their mouths, mixing false things with true statements in order to deceive her and thereby make her conform to themselves. He also shows his own perseverance in goodness, so that by saying this about himself he may instruct the hearers to avoid these same adversaries and persevere in goodness.

He says: “I said that I shall not be moved, O hearers, for the reasons stated above. I also said that my adversaries kill themselves while they rush upon me.”

Nevertheless, although for these two reasons they ought to desist, “they have thought to drive away my price from me,” that is, they have considered how to repel me from submission to God and thus take away from me the price of my labor—namely, God, for whom I yearn completely and toward whom I strive with every labor of good works.

Not only those who rush upon me through tribulations—the Jews and gentiles—have thought to repel me, but also the heretics. For when I ran along the way of good works, and did so “in thirst,” that is, in the desire to incorporate them into myself through the example of those same good works, they blessed with their mouths, that is, they pretended to utter certain good words. Yet “with their hearts they cursed,” that is, the same words that appeared good when pronounced by their mouths they considered evil and deceptive in the conception of their hearts.

This means: “They uttered certain deceptive words that appeared good, so that by secretly mixing falsehoods into them they might deceive me and thus, having removed me from submission to God, take away from me the price of my labor.”

He now exhorts his own soul when he adds: “Nevertheless, be subject to God, my soul.” This means: “Although they strive in every way to remove you from submission and thus drive your price away from you, do not yield to their evil example or exhortation; rather, be more and more subject to God, my soul.”

Someone might say: “If, while remaining subject, you refuse to yield to their exhortation, you will suffer many tribulations.” To this he adds: “I shall not depart from his submission because of fear of tribulations; rather, I shall patiently bear tribulations for his sake, because my patience comes from him,” that is, the example of my patience. For he gave me an example of suffering when he suffered for me.

Or, “my patience comes from him,” that is, he gave me patience so that I would not fear suffering for his sake. And for this reason also I shall not depart, because he to whom I am subject is “my God,” that is, my Creator and Savior, forgiving sins, and my helper, enabling me to do good.

It should be noted that the reasons he gives here, saying “because he is my God,” and so forth, are not repeated superfluously, although he had stated the same reasons above. Above, he stated them while acting against the adversaries; here, however, he turns to another purpose, namely, exhortation.

He intimates that his salvation came from God alone, not from any preceding merit of his own, lest anyone think that free will or any merit of his had cooperated in his salvation—as free will cooperates in a good action.

He says: “I said that God is my savior and my salvation,” that is, salvation itself was given to me in God alone, by the grace of God alone. “My glory,” that is, the fact that he made me glorious and my life praiseworthy through my salvation, “is in God alone,” not in any merit or in my free will.

But lest good action appear to proceed entirely from free will and not also from God, he adds: “And God is the maker of my help.” This means: “Although he saved me and made me glorious by a free gift of his will, he is also my helper in doing good, while my free will cooperates.”

Therefore, because he saved me freely, made me glorious, and is also my helper in doing good, “my hope is in God.” That is: Since he has already bestowed so many benefits on me, I hope to obtain those things that are in God—namely, immortality and freedom from suffering.

He exhorts the good to work in God by his own example, adding as follows: “I say that my hope is in God. Therefore, after my example, hope in him, every assembly of the people”—that is, you who have not been separated from Christ by your evil life and heresies, but all of you who are gathered in faith and conformity with Christ within the worldly people and are one in this, as the Apostle says: “We, though many, are one body in Christ” (Rom. 12:5).

And so that your hope may be upright and firm, “pour out your hearts,” that is, empty your hearts insofar as they are yours and not God’s.

This means: “Empty your hearts of evil thoughts, which come from your side and not from God, so that by pouring out your hearts you may be before God,” that is, in God’s good pleasure. For unless you pour them out, you will not be before God.

You ought to pour them out, “for then God will be our helper,” that is, he will help both me and you to do good, leading us into eternity through the help of his grace.

He reproaches the adversaries’ hardness for the benefit of the faithful whom he has just exhorted not to conform themselves to them. He adds:

“I said, O assembly of the people, that you should hope in God and pour out your hearts, and thus be before him, with him as your helper. Nevertheless, although the hearts of those who hope are before God and have him as their helper, the sons of men, conformed to the ancient ones”—that is, my adversaries, the gentiles conformed to the oldness of Adam and Eve—“are vain.” That is, they do not wish to hope in God, although that hope would be most certain; rather, they are vain, clinging to vain things, namely, earthly things.

Where we have here “sons of men,” the Hebrew translation has “sons of Adam.”

“And the sons of men”—the Jews and heretics—“are liars in the balances,” that is, in the divine Scriptures, which they interpret perversely.

[Col. 0926C] It was said by comparison with merchants who, when they ought to weigh equally on a balance, falsify the weighing by weighing unequally. The divine Scriptures are called “balances” because they are the test of all justice, just as balances are the test of just weight. This is what it means: Although the Scriptures have been set before both the Jews and the heretics as a test of uprightness, they do not, moved by those Scriptures, pour out their hearts; rather, they falsify them by perversely interpreting the Scriptures themselves, in order to deceive the good—those who seem good to some—going from vanity to the same thing, that is, into vanity. In other words, they deceive the faithful by proceeding from vain and false speech to speech still more vain and false.

After reproaching the enemies, he returns to exhorting the good, as follows: I say, hope in God; do not hope in iniquity in general—that is, do not hope to obtain some advantage from any iniquity—or alternatively, do not hope in iniquity, that is, in riches, which are called “iniquity” because it is unjust to gather them and not distribute them to the poor. [Col. 0926D] Hence the Lord says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke 16:9). This means: Do not suppose that retaining riches is profitable. And you who lack riches, do not covet acts of robbery—that is, riches which are called “robbery,” either because they are seized from someone by force or fraud, or because they are given to no one—according to Prosper’s saying: “What he gives to no one, he has robbed from the poor.” And if riches abound—that is, if they are plentiful for you—do not set your heart upon them, that is, do not attach your heart’s desire to them, lest, loving them excessively, you forget God. Hence the Apostle says: “The covetous person, which is idolatry, has no share in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Ephesians 5:5).

[Col. 0927A] Or, “do not set heart upon heart,” that is, do not add pride to the pride of your heart: when riches flow to you more and more, do not therefore become more and more proud. Hence Paul says to Timothy: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches” (1 Timothy 6:17).

Because he had said that one must hope in God and not in riches, in order to draw his hearers toward this he says that God is powerful for punishing those who hope in riches and merciful for rewarding those who hope in him. I said, O congregation of the people: Hope in God and not in riches, and do not set your heart upon them; and you ought obediently to fulfill this. For God has spoken, both through the Scriptures and through human nature, and he has spoken this once—that is, unchangeably.

[Col. 0927B] This means that he has spoken something that will be unchangeable and must be fulfilled. We rightly call that “one” which possesses no diversity of mutability; thus, although God is three in persons, he is called one because in his decree he is unchangeable and undivided. Hence “once” is used here for “unchangeably.”

I say that God has spoken, and among the things I perceived in his speech I heard two reasons why one must hope in him and not in riches, and why hearts must be poured out. These two are: that power belongs to God—that is, to you, O God, because you, God, are powerful—and that mercy belongs to you, Lord—that is, you, Lord, are merciful. He briefly explains these by adding: I say that power and mercy belong to you, which is as though I were saying that you will repay each person according to his works in the future.

[Col. 0927C] All this amounts to the brief statement: Hearts must be poured out, and one must hope in God and not in riches, because you, God, speaking to us in a most truthful and unchangeable utterance, have shown these things. Since you are powerful to condemn those who neglect you, you will in the future repay each person according to his works: punishment to those who neglect you, but everlasting salvation to those who hope in you and pour out their hearts.

Or alternatively: “God spoke once,” that is, he eternally and unchangeably ordained all things, and he still ordains them. This means that he unchangeably and eternally begot the Son, and still begets him in an incomprehensible manner. For the Son’s being begotten by the Father is nothing other than his ordering all things through him. We call God’s ordering an ineffable utterance; [Col. 0927D] and in that utterance I heard these two things with my inner hearing, and so forth. These things do not change.

## 220. ON PSALM 62

The title of the sixty-second Psalm: “A Psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Idumea.” This is explained as follows: This psalm is attributed to David, that is, to Christ. This psalm was composed by David himself when David was—that is, when he was bodily dwelling—in the wilderness of Idumea, that is, among the Jewish people, who were a wilderness because of Idumea, that is, because of their earthliness.

[Col. 0928A] This means: Because they were intent upon earthly things and had made God’s law void through their traditions, they were deserted by God’s grace and barren of good works, like deserted land, which is barren. In this psalm, however, the Lord’s human nature shows its desire, before the Passion, to reach God. Accordingly, he declares that he keeps watch in good works so that he may reach him; he promises that he will persevere in praising God both with his voice and by his good life; and he prays to be filled perseveringly with spiritual grace, so that he may not cease from praise.

He does this for the instruction of his own people, so that they too may keep watch by his example, desire to reach God, praise him in every way, and, filled with spiritual grace, pray that they may persevere in his praise; otherwise they could not do so. At the end of the psalm he speaks of the fact that his enemies will seek in vain to hold him in death. He also speaks of the enemies’ manifold condemnation, of the joy of the resurrection, and of the future praise of his own people.

[Col. 0928B] O God, who are commonly the God of all but specially my God, whom I obey above all, who have made me completely free from sin: I keep watch, by living well, in order to attain you.

This means: I do not conduct myself negligently in your will, but I keep watch—that is, I strive attentively and diligently to attain you—in order to obtain conformity with you insofar as I am human, namely, so that I may become immortal and impassible like you. This is by comparison with the good servant who, while awaiting his master, does not sleep but keeps watch; of him it is written in the Gospel: “Blessed is that servant whom, when his Lord comes, he finds watching” (Luke 12:37).

I say, “I keep watch,” and this watchfulness arises from the light of your virtues and knowledge, with which I am inwardly filled. [Col. 0928C] This means: The greatest light of the virtues and of your knowledge, poured into me, is the reason why I persevere in watchfulness.

Or, my watchfulness arises from light—that is, from your wisdom personally united to me—which continually illumines my soul; and from this too my good watchfulness arises. For my soul thirsted for you: my soul ardently desired, and still desires, what is in you, namely, impassibility.

This means: It has as great a desire to be conformed to you—that is, to impassibility—as a person who is very thirsty desires to drink. And my flesh thirsted to cleave to you in many ways! This means: In my flesh there are far more causes than in my soul for which I thirst to be conformed to you. In the soul there is only one reason why it thirsts for you: it is passible. In the flesh there are also the facts that it is much more passible than the soul and that it is mortal, which the soul is not.

[Col. 0928D] I say that soul and flesh thirsted for you; and I say that soul and flesh were placed in a deserted land, and so forth. Or the passage may be connected in this way, without changing the exposition: I say that I keep watch toward you—I, who am placed in a deserted, pathless, and waterless land. It is as though he were saying: Although I dwell among the Jews, who are land—that is, entirely earthly—and pathless—that is, without a way, since they refuse to receive me, who am the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6)—and because they are earthly and pathless they are also without water, that is, not watered by spiritual grace, but barren of every good and dry, nevertheless I am not turned away from my watchfulness by them, even if there could be a reason for ceasing.

When he says “in a deserted land,” he uses such words in accordance with the title, in which it was said: “A Psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Idumea.”

[Col. 0929A] Because he had said, “I keep watch,” lest he seem to have said this boastfully and not truthfully, he confirms that he keeps watch by the authority of the Father when he adds: I said that I keep watch and thirst, and I appeared to you in the holy place, that is, I am known to you in this holy watchfulness and thirst.

This means: My saying that I keep watch and thirst is not empty, for in this holiness I appeared to you—that is, I am known to you—in such a way that I might see your virtue. That is, you know me as persevering in this holy watchfulness and thirst, so that I may see the virtue and glory of revelation, that is, may regard it as yours and not mine. Through this he instructs us to attribute whatever good we have to God, not to ourselves.

[Col. 0929B] I said that I keep watch, and this is because your mercy—that is, living watchfully, which arises from your mercy—is better than lives, that is, better than all the lives of worldly men, however prosperous they may be. Or it is far better than lives, that is, more useful and more excellent than all the rules of life devised by philosophers.

This means: I resolved to keep watch because this life is far better than all lives.

When he says “better than lives,” although one ought to understand “better than all lives,” he repeats the expression for emphasis, as though he were saying: It is much better than all lives.

He promises that from now on he will praise, when he adds: I say, I keep watch by praising you with voice and life. And not in such a way that I might sometimes cease from your praise while drowsing, but my external lips will praise you without ceasing. Thus, because I shall also bless you, I will exalt you in my good life—that is, by living well—and in your name—that is, by doing good works in honor of your name—I will lift up my hands, that is, I will raise up my works.

[Col. 0929C] This means: I will work well in honor of your name, and thus my works will be exalted and worthy. But if I were to work in my own name, I would rather depress than exalt my works.

He prays to be filled continually with inner wisdom and the strength of spiritual grace, lest he fail at all in praise, when he adds: I said that I would praise you with my lips and bless you with my life, and this shall be so: Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness—that is, with inner wisdom, which is like fat, that is, comparable to fat, lying hidden within the soul just as fat lies hidden in the inner parts—and with the strength of spiritual grace, which is like richness, that is, comparable to richness, appearing outwardly through works just as richness appears outwardly through the limbs.

[Col. 0929D] “Fat” properly means what covers the vital organs, lying hidden within; “richness” means what appears outwardly, strengthening the limbs. He does not say “let it be filled” because his soul is not always filled with inner wisdom and with the strength of spiritual grace appearing outwardly through works; rather, it is as though he were saying: May my soul, which is already filled, not fail in any way, but persevere in fullness like fat and richness.

And may the lips of exultation—that is, my exultant lips—also be filled like fat and richness, that is, with words proceeding from inner wisdom and spiritual grace; and in this way my mouth will praise you.

Or it may be understood so that the wording is also different: I say, let my soul be filled, and thus my mouth will praise you with lips of exultation, that is, with exultant lips.

[Col. 0930A] He confirms by the example of remembrance that he will henceforth praise God, when he adds: I say that I will praise you with exultant lips, which I shall truly do if—that is, because—I have remembered you continually upon my bed, that is, while being on my bed.

This means: It can be proved that I will praise you without ceasing because up to now I have always remembered you—that is, your praise—on my bed, that is, in the purity of my conscience. This is called a bed because in it I rest and delight wholly in holy things, just as someone rests and delights in an excellent bed.

When he says “upon my bed,” it means the same as “in my bed.” But because someone lies upon a bed, “upon” is used here by comparison.

[Col. 0930B] But I will not praise you only with lips of exultation. Looking toward you—that is, with the gaze directed toward attaining the immortality and impassibility that are in you—I will meditate in the morning.

Or alternatively: I will meditate upon you as my helper, in the mornings—that is, in the completion of good works. Through your help I will be attentive so that, in completing good works, I may praise you. They are called “mornings” because they are bright and clear like morning.

From this it can also be proved that I will meditate continually upon good works, because you have been my helper in doing good up to now. This means: Just as you have helped me until now, so you will help me hereafter.

I said, let my soul be filled like fat and richness, so that through this I may praise you both with my mouth and in the mornings. And while praising you in this way, I will not fear that I might fail in tribulations, as though there were reason to fear and fail; [Col. 0930C] rather, I will exult, placed under the shelter of your wings—that is, I will work well exultantly, remaining in the refreshment of your protection.

This means: The protection of your mercy will be refreshment for me in tribulations, so that I may not desist from good work. “The shelter of wings” is used for the refreshment of protection by comparison, because a bird cools its young by the shelter of its wings and protects them from heat and harm.

And therefore I will exult because my soul has cleaved to you with the bond of love, following after you—that is, preferring you to itself and loving you above itself.

This means: I shall therefore exult in your protection because my soul is joined to you by an immense love. From this I am also certain that I shall exult, because your right hand has received me, [Col. 0930D] that is, the favor of your grace has always defended me, so that it would not permit me to offend in any crime. “Right hand” is used for favor because we are accustomed to place at our right those whom we favor.

I said that I would meditate in the mornings and exult under the shelter of the wings. But they—the Jews, whom I came to teach and save, and from whose blood I was born—sought, or will seek, what was least fitting: to hold my soul in death, lest they lose their place and nation.

And they will do this in vain, that is, their hope will be vain. For, expelled from their homeland, they will enter the lower parts of the earth. That is, when they have been expelled from their own land, which is fertile, they will enter the worse and lower regions of the earth. [Col. 0931A] For scarcely is there any part of the lands so barren that some portion of them cannot be found there. Or alternatively, they will seek my soul to their own harm, for this is why they will enter the lower parts of the earth—that is, hell, which is in the lower regions of the earth. Hence hell is also called *infernus*, as it were, “the lowest.” And some will be delivered into the hands—that is, into the power—of the sword, to be killed; and after they have been killed, they will become portions of foxes and other wild beasts, so that their unburied bodies may be eaten by them.

He says this to heap up the misery of their calamity. For if, expelled from their homeland, they were dispersed into some fertile region, it would seem less grievous than the fact that most of them were scattered through the harshest regions of the world.

[Col. 0931B] Or alternatively, according to the interpretation in which we said that they would enter the lower parts of the earth, that is, hell: they will not only enter hell and be delivered into the hands of the sword, but some of them will also become portions of foxes, that is, they will be divided up and led captive by foxes—namely, by rulers who are called foxes because they were cunning in conquering them, just as the fox is an extremely cunning animal.

In this he greatly magnifies their wickedness, showing that they will be dispersed among foreigners.

I say that they will enter the lower parts of the earth, be delivered into the hands of the sword, and become portions of foxes.

But the king will rejoice in God—that is, I, the king in the eminent sense, will rejoice in God’s mercy when he raises me from the dead and glorifies me. And not only will the king rejoice, but [Col. 0931C] all who swear by him—that is, all who in baptism firmly promise to persevere in him, that is, in his will—will be praised. In the future they will appear praiseworthy even to their enemies when they are enriched with eternal glory, although here they seem detestable while being worn down by continual tribulation. Of them it is also written that they will say: “We foolish people considered their life madness; behold, how they are counted among the sons of God” (Wisdom 5:4–5).

I say that the king will rejoice, and rightly, because the mouths of those speaking iniquity have been—or will be—stopped: namely, the mouths of the Jews, who deny that I am God and instead assert that I am a seducer and blasphemer.

This means: Through the testimony of my resurrection and exaltation they will be so confounded that, whether they wish it or not, they will be silent, having nothing that they can say about me, although [Col. 0931D] now they rise up against me with many abusive words.

## ON PSALM 63

The title of the sixty-third Psalm: “To the end. A Psalm of David.” This is explained as follows: A Psalm of David—that is, of Christ—looking toward the end, that is, toward the complete consummation of himself after the future death; or toward the end, that is, toward the perfect consummation of his own people, which will occur on the day of judgment, “when God will be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28).

In this psalm the Lord’s human nature prays concerning the resurrection and asks that God deliver him from the fear of the enemy. It also speaks of the enemies’ hidden and manifest persecution, of the exaltation of the resurrection, of the enemies’ ineffectuality, and afterward of the proclamation of God’s works that will take place through preachers, and of the future joy and praise of the righteous, when they will be enriched by eternal recompense.

[Col. 0932A] Hear, O God, my prayer, so that you may raise me up, and deliver my soul from the fear of the enemy, the Jewish people, so that when I entreat you I may not fall into conformity with them.

This means: Deliver me when I continually entreat you, just as I continually make this request. He declares that what he prayed for will happen in the future when he adds: I say, deliver me, and so you will act.

You have protected me—that is, you will protect me—from the assembly of the wicked, the Jews, so that I may not yield to them through fear when they rise up against me with wicked words. And you will not only protect me from their fear when they rise up against me with wicked words, accusing and slandering me; you will also protect me from the multitude of those who work iniquity, that is, [Col. 0932B] you will make me steadfast so that through fear I may not yield to the multitude, that is, to the assembly of the Jews, who are working my death—in the eminent sense, iniquity.

This means: Neither when they are acting wickedly will I fear them, nor when they are working iniquity.

But lest they excuse themselves from the working of iniquity on the grounds that they killed him neither with their hands nor with weapons, he adds: Truly they will work my death, even if not with weapons or hands, because they have sharpened—or will sharpen—their tongues and the sword.

This means: They will adapt the words of their tongues so that they may be effective in drawing me to death, saying: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19:12), and other such things by which they will compel Pilate, who would wish to release me, to crucify me. [Col. 0932C] This is by comparison with a sword, which is sharpened so that it may be more effective for killing.

And before they sharpen their tongue, they stretched the bow—that is, they made their deception ready, so that by speaking flatteringly they might catch me in speech, unsuspecting and unwary, and thus hand me over to Caesar’s ministers for condemnation, or accuse me of violating the law.

For they will question me as a teacher: “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matthew 22:17), so that if I say it ought not to be paid, they may hand me over to the Roman officials as a prohibitionist of Caesar’s tribute; but if I assert that it ought to be paid, they may charge me with violating the law, calling me an unjust judge because I judged those subject to the worship of God to be servants of the Roman king.

This is what he obscurely expresses by equivalence: “They stretched the bow,” namely, they prepared a bitter thing, [Col. 0932D] even if it appeared sweet. That is, they will prepare deceptive words which, although they seem sweet, will nevertheless be extremely bitter, so that they may shoot the innocent—that is, harm me, who am innocent, just as one who is shot is harmed.

And let them do this in secret, that is, let them shoot in such a way that it is hidden from me, so that I cannot take precautions.

It should be noted that he does not call the sword—that is, their open persecution—a bitter thing, because this is obvious. But he calls the bow, which seems to be a sweet thing, bitter. After they have stretched the bow, they will suddenly shoot the innocent, as far as their opinion is concerned: they will be certain that they really will shoot me, and this suddenly—that is, unexpectedly—so that I will not know how to take precautions.

[Col. 0933A] And they will not fear shooting me, although they ought to fear it greatly because of my holy teaching, which they will hear, and because of my miracles and good works, which they will frequently observe.

And when they cannot shoot me, they have strengthened—that is, they will firmly and steadfastly utter—a wicked word, saying: “Crucify him!” (Luke 23:21). And this will be for themselves, that is, to their own harm and destruction, because they will be destroyed on account of this deed.

Or alternatively: After they have sharpened their tongues, they will firmly and steadfastly utter a wicked word to their own harm, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25).

I say that they will stretch the bow in order to shoot, and they will think that they have shot me; and after their shooting has proved ineffectual, they related, and so forth.

[Col. 0933B] Or the passage may be connected in this way, without changing the exposition: I say that they will strengthen for themselves a wicked word, namely, “His blood,” and so forth. But before they strengthen it, they have related—or will relate—in their plan, in order to conceal snares: that is, in order to prepare a hidden death for me by which they may hold me back so that the world may not be subjected to me, and so that I may not escape, by comparison with a bird which is held by snares so that it cannot get away.

And they said—or will say—to themselves while thinking: Who will see them—that is, the snares? In other words, who will know that we have brought about his death? No one. It is as though he were saying: In their thoughts they will arrange to prepare my death secretly, handing me over through a disciple and killing me through Roman soldiers. They will think that no one will judge them guilty of this deed, since they will do nothing with their own hands.

Hence they are reported to have said: “Let us do everything in such a way that we seem to have done nothing” (Augustine, *On this Psalm*).

[Col. 0933C] And they investigated these iniquities—that is, they investigated how to conceal the snares: namely, how to hand me over through my disciple and kill me through the Roman soldiers. They investigated them—that is, they will investigate how they might accomplish this—and in vain. For while investigating these things with investigation—that is, with the most thorough and careful scrutiny—they failed: they will not be able to accomplish this without appearing responsible for the deed.

I say that they will arrange to prepare snares for me, that is, a hidden death, as though they knew in advance that I would want to escape it. But they would not need to labor for this. For the man will approach death voluntarily—that is, I, whom they suppose to be merely a simple man, will voluntarily approach death insofar as I am human—and this approach will be made by a profound heart, that is, by the deep and unfathomable disposition of my wisdom.

[Col. 0933D] For this is the highest mystery: why he preferred to redeem human beings by his own death, when he could have saved them by the command of his power. Indeed, it was fitting that, when he had thus been made mortal and was unjustly attacked by the devil, who instigated his death, the devil should justly be deprived of the power over the human race that he held by right.

I say that the man will approach death, and thus God will be exalted—that is, I will be exalted by rising again and ascending into heaven. Then I will also appear to be God, although I do not appear to be merely human. For “it was necessary for Christ to suffer and thus to enter into his glory” (Luke 24:26).

And he will truly be exalted by rising again, for their wounds—the wounds by which they will lead me to death—have become arrows of little children, that is, they will become comparable to arrows of little children. [Col. 0934A] Just as such arrows, being fragile and made of wood or some other fragile material, do little harm, and whatever harm they cause is healed very quickly, so their wounds, though causing harm for a short time, will be healed in a brief time: for I will rise again after three days (Matthew 27:63).

And after I have been exalted, their tongues have been weakened. This will be against them. It means: The words by which they will lie about me, pretending that I did not rise but that my body was stolen by my disciples, will appear weak and false; and they will also be against them, that is, suitable for proving them to be liars.

For if, as they claim, the guards fell asleep when the body was stolen, how did they know that it had been stolen?

I say that their tongues will be weakened, and all who saw—or will see—them weakened, not only with outward but also with inward vision, were—or will be—[Col. 0934B] troubled in their understanding. They will be troubled with a good kind of disturbance, fearing punishment, because they consented to his death.

And after the disturbance—that is, after servile fear—every human being feared him. That is, all those who are human, possessing reason, will fear him with chaste fear, once they have been troubled. For many, being irrational, will neither be troubled nor fear.

And having become fearful, they proclaimed God’s works and understood his deeds. This should be read in reversed order: After they have become fearful—that is, loving—they will understand God’s deeds: they will understand that my death, resurrection, ascension, and other works were accomplished by God’s merciful plan, not by chance. And by understanding them, they will proclaim those works of God.

[Col. 0934C] I say that they will be troubled; but every righteous person will rejoice in the Lord—that is, my disciples, who are righteous, will rejoice in the exaltation of my Lord—and will hope in him, that is, will place firm hope in him who will be powerful enough to bless them in the future and who will be powerful enough to raise himself after the third day.

At first, however, some of those righteous disciples will doubt whether he is indeed able to raise himself, and therefore they will not dare to hope firmly in the Lord himself, that is, in me. Hence they are reported to have said while doubting: “We thought that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21).

I say that they will rightly rejoice in the exaltation of my Lord, and in the future all the upright in heart will be praised: the righteous, upright in heart, will appear praiseworthy when they are made glorious and impassible.

[Col. 0934D] These three verses may also be understood of the apostles, with the passage connected as follows: I said that they would conceal snares and stretch the bow to shoot me; and all my disciples, using reason as human beings, will fear the punishment of those Jews whose blindness prevents them from knowing how to fear it. In their fear they will proclaim God’s works to them, so that they may be converted. That is, they will proclaim that the works of my death, resurrection, and miracles were accomplished by God’s plan.

And they understood his deeds—that is, they will make some of those Jews understand that they are to be saved, although now they neglect to understand.

But the righteous person will rejoice in the Lord and hope in him. This should be read and explained in the plural, as in the interpretation given above, and the passage continues as follows: I say that the righteous who see them blinded—that is, my disciples—will [Col. 0935A] be troubled, that is, saddened by their blindness. Yet those righteous will rejoice in the Lord, that is, in the exaltation of my Lord, and they will hope in him, that is, they will have firm hope in me, because I will be able to reward them in the future, since I am powerful enough to raise myself.

Hence they doubted at first, as we have already said. And in the future all the upright in heart will be praised. This does not change.

## ON PSALM 64

The title of the sixty-fourth Psalm: “To the end. A Psalm of David, a song of Jeremiah and Haggai, concerning the word of the pilgrimage, when they began to set out.”

[Col. 0935B] In this title the psalm seems to be indicated as having been composed, by analogy with the historical account, concerning the return of the Jews from their Babylonian pilgrimage. Jeremiah and Haggai foretold this pilgrimage by prophetic inspiration, as well as the return from that pilgrimage; Haggai was also present during the pilgrimage itself and its return.

Nevertheless, it is uncertain whether the Psalmist composed this psalm with consideration of that history. For it is clear that this history occurred long after his time. Yet it was possible that one who had foreseen many things through the Holy Spirit might also have foreseen this return from pilgrimage, through which the return of the whole human race to the heavenly Jerusalem was prefigured, and that he might have dealt in this psalm with that return of the whole human race on the basis of such a consideration.

[Col. 0935C] Ezra the scribe, who is said to have adapted the titles to the Psalms and who lived after the return from the Babylonian pilgrimage, seeing through the Holy Spirit that the likeness of this history could pertain to the subject of the present psalm, adapted the title in accordance with the history.

It is explained as follows: This psalm belongs to David the prophet, looking toward the end of the world, when the return of all the faithful to the heavenly homeland will take place; or looking toward the end, that is, toward the perfect and consummated blessedness in which the faithful, returned from this valley of misery to the heavenly homeland, will be restored; or toward the end, that is, toward the end of the ages, specifically the sixth age, which the Apostle calls “the end of the ages” (1 Corinthians 10:11), in which the fullness of the Gentiles will return from their unbelief to the knowledge and worship of God; or toward the end, that is, toward Christ, through whom the possibility of returning to the homeland is granted to us.

[Col. 0935D] And the psalm itself is a song of Jeremiah and Haggai, that is, the greatest delight and joy of all the faithful who, by living well, await the return to eternal life, which they foresee will come and which they will eventually attain.

These faithful are appropriately understood through Jeremiah and Haggai. For Jeremiah is interpreted as “exalted of the Lord,” while Haggai means “festive” or “solemn.” The faithful, already exalted in contemplation of the Lord—of whom the Apostle says, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20)—are rightly called “exalted of the Lord,” having already been raised up by the Lord in the perfection of the virtues.

[Col. 0936A] They are also rightly called solemn and festive, since, setting aside all concern for temporal goods, they dwell solely upon solemn and festive heavenly joys in contemplation of them.

I say that this psalm is a song of Jeremiah and Haggai, dealing with the word of pilgrimage: namely, with the word—that is, the thought—of Adam and Eve, who, thinking in their hearts, said: “We shall be like gods” (Genesis 3:5) if we eat the fruit forbidden by God.

This word was the cause of the pilgrimage of the whole human race, and indeed of a twofold pilgrimage. We were pilgrims away from the Lord because of this word, while, before Christ’s death by which we were redeemed, we were alienated from his faith, contemplation, and perfection of virtues.

[Col. 0936B] We also continue to be pilgrims after the redemption, while, because of that word, we remain mortal and passible and are separated from the divine presence and the company of the angels.

This word is treated briefly in the psalm, where it says: “The words of the iniquitous prevailed against us.” The psalm also deals with the time “when they began to set out,” that is, when and through whom they will begin to return from pilgrimage and set out for the homeland, when it says: “Blessed is the one whom you have chosen,” and so forth, to the end of the psalm.

This means that it speaks of the twofold return from this twofold pilgrimage, and of when and through whom each return will begin.

It should be known that both returns take place through Christ. One, which will last until the end of the world, begins in time, when the human race—previously burdened by the immense weight of its original and actual sins—began, [Col. 0936C] having received forgiveness for those sins through Christ’s death, to return to the faith of God, to contemplation, and to the perfection of virtues that it had lost through the word mentioned above. From generation to generation it will continue returning until the end of the world.

The second will begin and be completed on the day of judgment through the redemption of that same death of Christ. Then, when every punishment for sin—that is, mortality, passibility, and every imperfection—has been removed from us, we will become immortal and impassible, possessing the perfect nature of God, and will return to the eternal homeland, where we will dwell happily without end.

[Col. 0936D] The Prophet, who speaks in this psalm, deals with the first return from the place where it says “Blessed is the one whom you have chosen” up to the place where it says “You will bless,” and he shows through whom, by what ministers, and in what manner it will occur.

He deals with the second return where he says “You will bless,” and so forth to the end of the psalm.

He also prays that the Church may be constituted from every people, and that it may return in this way. He prays for the return itself, that it may happen, when he says: “Hear us, O God.” He also joins himself to the faithful of the Church when he says “Hear us,” although they are still future; and rightly so, since, although he already existed temporally, he was nevertheless a member of the Church by faith.

[Col. 0937A] He undertakes this exposition for the benefit both of those already converted and of those who are still to be converted: to urge those already converted, who have attained the first return, more and more toward the second return; and to draw those who are to be converted toward both returns. And when he prays concerning this return, he gives us an example of prayer.

You are owed a hymn, O God, in Zion—that is, in the Church which will be the earthly watchtower Zion. There will be a hymn, that is, such praise as becomes you, O God the Word—that is, as will become you. This means: the Church, which is to be established by you, will praise you with fitting praise, namely, by faith, voice, deed, and devotion. The Synagogue does not do this, since it lingers and places excessive confidence in carnal observances. And in the heavenly Jerusalem a vow will be rendered to you—that is, perfect praise will be paid to you with every vow and every desire by that same Zion, when, having returned to the Jerusalem from which it fell through Adam, it will be blessed forever.

“Rendering a vow” is used by comparison. Just as rendering a vow is a more perfect good than making a vow, although both are good, so that praise which will be paid by the faithful in the heavenly Jerusalem will be more perfect than the praise offered in the present age by faith, voice, deed, and devotion. Although this praise is holy and pleasing to God—for here too, even if the faithful praise him in this way, they nevertheless offend him in some respect whenever they commit at least some venial sin—in the future he will be praised with devotion so perfectly intense that he will in no way be offended. For then there will be no inclination to sin.

And since Zion will praise you fittingly, hear, O God the Word, my prayer made on its behalf, that you may establish it as Zion. Since he had mentioned Zion, and this word often serves to designate the Jewish people, lest it be thought that the Church was to be established solely from the Jews, he adds: I say that a hymn in Zion becomes you, and this Zion will not be constituted from Jews alone; rather, every flesh will come to you through faith—that is, all kinds of people: Jews and gentiles, poor and rich—who are now flesh, that is, carnal, wholly obedient to the flesh. From them you will establish Zion.

But since, by saying “Every flesh will come to you,” it was implied that flesh had departed from God, he shows how it departed from God by adding: Truly it will come to you, from whom it departed through the words of the wicked, namely Adam and Eve. For the words—that is, the perverse thoughts that were the words of the hearts of the wicked, apostatizing from God when they thought, “We shall be like gods” (Gen. III, 5)—prevailed over us, that is, prevailed against us. This means: They were so effective that they thrust not only Adam and Eve, but also all of us, Jews and gentiles alike, into death. For we all became participants in their wickedness, which they committed by eating the fruit. Hence the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death, and so it passed into all” (Rom. III, 12).

But lest it be thought that flesh could reach God by its own power, it is added: I say that the words prevailed over us, and you, God the Word, will be propitious toward our wickedness—that is, not on the basis of our merits, but through your propitiation you will erase our wickedness, both actual and venial, and thus we shall come to you, who are true life (John XIV, 6).

When he says, “The words of the wicked prevailed over us,” this is equivalent to saying: They prevailed in order to be over us—that is, to oppress us—by comparison with something that is violently oppressed beneath a heavy weight falling upon it.

He then shows through whom propitiation will be made, as follows: And you will do this through someone altogether blessed, namely the Lord Jesus, who will be free from sin, whom you will choose [Col. 0938A] from among all human beings as especially worthy and distinguished above the other faithful. Accordingly, the bride, the Church, says of him in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from thousands” (Song V, 10).

And you will take him up—that is, unite him personally to yourself—as Athanasius also testifies: “God and man are one Christ” (Athanasius, in the Creed). And that blessed one will dwell in your courts—that is, in the breadth of your love [Col. 0938B] and of good works. This means: He will be most perfect in every form of charity and good work.

A court is an exceedingly spacious hall within the houses of nobles; therefore it is used for spaciousness. Or: He will dwell after his resurrection in your heavenly courts—that is, in the heavens to which he will ascend, so that he may draw us to himself. As he himself declares in the Gospel: “If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John XII, 32); and again: “Where I am, there also my servant will be” (ibid., 26). This is adapted from outside the book, but it is indicated by what follows, when it is added: Truly, through the blessed one you will be propitious.

For the one whom you chose—that is, whom you will choose—and took up—that is, whom you will take up—will indeed be blessed, [Col. 0938C] and he himself will dwell in your courts. After you have become propitious toward our wickedness by erasing it, we shall be filled with the goods of your house by existing in those goods themselves, both in body and in soul. We shall be filled with the goods of the Lord’s man, who will be your house in which you will dwell. And through that blessed one we shall be filled with those goods.

When he says, “We shall be filled with goods,” he shows emphatically that we shall be filled with those goods to a very great degree, by comparison with someone who, being in water or some similar substance, is filled inwardly with that water. This means: Through the blessed one we shall be filled to overflowing with those goods, outwardly in the body and inwardly in the soul.

He explains part of those goods as follows: Truly, your house will possess goods, for your temple is holy—that is, it will be holy. The blessed one, who will be your house and temple, will be full of every holiness; and it will not merely be holy, but will be wondrous in the equity of its holiness. That is, the Lord’s man will be so equitable and holy that he will be wondrous to all. Through that holiness and equity we shall be filled by him, so that we become holy both in thought and in action, though not to the same degree as he.

He prays to God the Word himself to be propitious toward his own wickedness—he who exists so long beforehand through faith in the Lord Jesus, a faith that he already possesses—and to be propitious toward the wickedness of those who will be faithful at the time of fulfillment; to sanctify them; to increase him, though exempt from actual sins, in deed and devotion; and, at the time of fulfillment, though he will already be dead in the body, to lead him, cleansed, back to the eternal homeland [Col. 0939A]. As for those who are faithful, or who will become faithful at the time of fulfillment, may he cleanse them from both actual and original sin, sanctify them in deed and devotion, and lead them back to the eternal homeland. He says this as follows:

I say that you will be propitious toward us and will fill us with goods through that blessed one; and in order that this may happen, hear us, O God the Word, our savior—that is, our future savior through that man, myself in particular. Hear me now as I pray for propitiation and fulfillment, and hear the faithful who will one day pray to you for this same thing.

You, I say, who will be the hope of salvation for all the ends of the earth—that is, for all kinds of people, Jews and gentiles, dwelling throughout every region of the earth—and, to say more, you will be the hope of all those who are far away on the sea, that is, on the islands situated far out in the sea. This means: You will be the hope of salvation for all who dwell both on land and on the sea.

Hence we read: “Coming, he preached peace to those who were far away and to those who were near” (Eph. II, 17).

Or it may be understood in this way: You will be the hope of salvation for all the ends of the earth—that is, for all the faithful who are already bringing their earthly nature to an end, namely those from the Jews who have already acquired knowledge and faith in him before his coming. And in the future you will be the hope of those far away on the sea—that is, of unbelievers who are still far away, that is, very deeply immersed in the bitterness of their unbelief, and who will be converted to you at the time of the Lord’s man.

The sea is appropriately used for bitterness because it is a very bitter thing. He shows the conversion and salvation of those situated in the sea through the apostles, whom God will prepare, making them mountains—that is, exalted in life—and he says this as follows:

I say that you will be the hope of all the ends of the earth and of those far away on the sea; and you will be the one preparing the mountains—that is, the apostles—in your strength, that is, in the steadfastness of their preaching and in all the virtues that you will give them. And you will be girded with power—that is, with the powerful apostles in miracles, who will emphatically be your power—surrounded by them, by comparison with a vigorous commander who is girded, that is, surrounded, by his soldiers in order to conquer his enemies through them.

This means: You will prepare them so that they may be in your favor and obedience. You disturb the depths of the sea—that is, you will disturb through their preaching, and through their salutary disturbance those who are deep in the sea, that is, in the bitterness of unbelief, namely the gentiles. And after you have disturbed them insofar as they are a sea, you will also disturb the sound of the waves of that sea—that is, the contradiction and persecution of those who, because of the bitterness of their unbelief, will be waves, surging against your people in tribulations like waves that overflow.

This means: After you have destroyed their unbelief, you will also destroy their resistance, so that they will no longer contradict your people or persecute them. Their contradictions are rightly called a sound, because they were made with great noise.

He repeats what he had said, “You disturb the depths of the sea,” in order to add: The nations, I say, who are the depths of the sea, will be disturbed, so that they may fear on account of their sins with servile fear; [Col. 0940A] and afterward they will fear you with chaste fear—that is, they will love you. And this disturbance will result from your signs, that is, from the miracles of the preachers.

After they have been disturbed and have feared, you will make the morning’s departures and the evening’s departures delightful—that is, you will make departures from prosperity into adversity and departures from adversity into prosperity delightful. This means: You will make them pass from adversity into prosperity and from prosperity into adversity in such a way that they are neither broken by adversity nor lifted up by prosperity; and you will take delight in such passages.

Morning is used for prosperity because it is brighter than evening; evening, because it is darker than morning, is used for adversity. By this he shows that they will become most perfect, since such passages belong only to the most perfect. Thus you will take delight among the nations in the departures of morning and evening.

For you visited the whole earth—that is, you will visit both gentiles and Jews, who are earthly—and you did so by intoxicating it—that is, you will fill it with the Holy Spirit, who will not allow it afterward to experience either prosperity, so that it may be lifted up, or adversity, so that it may be broken. This is compared to wine, which largely takes away the senses of the one whom it intoxicates.

This means: You will visit the earth in such a way as to fill it with spiritual grace—not with simple grace, but you multiplied—that is, you will multiply—the enrichment of the earth; that is, you will enrich it in many ways with various gifts of the Holy Spirit. In accordance with the prophet Joel: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel II, 28).

Someone might ask: Are the enrichments of spiritual grace manifold? The answer follows: Truly, you will be able to enrich it in many ways with the grace of the Holy Spirit, for the river of God is filled with waters—that is, the Holy Spirit, who is called a river because he refreshes and satisfies the faithful like a river, is filled with waters, that is, with many different gifts by which the faithful drink as from water—and from that river you prepared food for them, that is, you will prepare it, by which they will be satisfied in soul.

This means: You will make the river itself their food, and that food is the bread of life and understanding, since its preparation is thus—that is, it is prepared in this way by you. This means: It is necessary for you to prepare food for them, since otherwise it could not be prepared.

He prays that what he has announced may indeed come to pass. When he adds, “I said that you will intoxicate the earth, and so let it be, O God: intoxicate its streams,” that is, the streams of the earth. In another translation we read, “its furrows,” and so forth. It is fitting that this translation has “streams” in place of “furrows,” since the furrows of streams bear a likeness to them, appearing to have banks like streams.

I say: Intoxicate the streams of the earth—that is, fill the hearts of that earth with spiritual grace, hearts split and furrowed by the plowshare of preaching, that is, opened to receive preaching, whereas they had previously been closed by unbelief, like earth that is split, furrowed, and opened by a plowshare so that it may receive seed. And by intoxicating its furrows, multiply its offspring—that is, give it many offspring: many successors, namely spiritual children, springing from its teaching and faith.

If you do this, each one who germinates will rejoice in the drops of its river as they are received—that is, they will joyfully receive the offspring of that earth, the drops of its river, namely the teachings that will drip from it.

Alternatively, these three verses could be read as follows: “You will make the departures of morning and evening delightful among the nations; and for this reason you will take delight, because you visited the earth”—that is, the nations alone—and you visited it in such a way that you intoxicated it and multiplied its enrichment. These changes are made in this interpretation.

He then shows the order in which he will visit the earth, as follows:

I say that you will visit the earth, and you will do this through the river—that is, through the primitive Church consisting of Jews—which is called a river because preachers will proceed from it, just as streams proceed from a river. For that river of God is filled—that is, will be filled—with waters, that is, it will have many preachers, who are called waters because through their teaching they will water others like waters.

And you, O God, prepared their food—that is, you will prepare food for that river. You will give it the Holy Spirit, who will be its food, that is, the bread of life and understanding. “Their” is not inappropriately referred to the river, for although it is singular in grammatical form, it is plural in meaning.

I say that you will prepare their food, since its preparation is such—that is, will be such—that it could not be prepared otherwise.

He prays for those preachers themselves when he adds:

I say that the river of God will be filled with waters—that is, with preachers—and you, O God, intoxicate its streams with spiritual grace, namely the preachers who proceed from the river like streams. And through the streams that have been intoxicated, multiply the offspring of that river—that is, make many children germinate from the streams of that river.

This means: Make many of the unbelievers in Judea germinate in faith from generation to generation through the preaching of the streams. And if you intoxicate the streams, the one who germinates will rejoice in the drops of that river—that is, in the teachings that will drip from the streams of the river. The one who germinates is the gentile people germinating in faith.

This means: They will cause not only the Jewish people but also the gentiles to germinate. The whole passage is as though he had said briefly: In this order you will visit the earth, namely the gentiles: first you will establish the primitive Church from the Jews, and it will have many preachers through whom the earth—that is, the gentile people—will germinate in faith and be intoxicated.

Having shown the first return from pilgrimage, he intends to show the second, as follows:

I said that you will visit and intoxicate the earth through the streams of the river, and you will do this in this world, namely in the sixth age. But in the future you will bless the crown of the year of your kindness—that is, you will exalt in heavenly glory your universal Church, consisting of Jews and gentiles. It will be the crown of the year of your kindness, that is, the redeemed multitude in the year of kindness, namely in the time of your Passion, in which you will act kindly toward the human race.

We customarily call a multitude of people standing around someone a crown. It is therefore fittingly used for the multitude of the faithful who will stand around the presence of the Lord Jesus in eternal glory. Or “crown” refers to victors, since victors are often honored with crowns. Thus it may be explained: You will bless the crown of the year of your kindness—that is, you will exalt in glory the victors who are to be saved in the year of your kindness, namely all the faithful who will conquer this world by living well. When he says, “You will bless the crown,” he is speaking of the whole Church.

[231] This is also explained in parts, as follows:

I say that you will bless the crown in such a way that your fields, which will be part of that crown—namely the faithful Jews, who are called fields because, already possessing knowledge of God, they were more suitable than the gentiles for receiving the seed of teaching, just as fields are more suitable than mountainous land for receiving seed—will in the future be filled, both in soul and body, with the abundance of eternal blessedness.

And the beautiful places of the desert, which are another part of the crown—that is, the gentiles, who, because they were previously a desert, lacking the law and knowledge of God, have become beautiful in faith and in the perfection of every virtue and good work—will grow fat, that is, they will be filled with and rejoice in the same abundance as the fields. “Grow fat” is said by comparison with a wealthy person who, filled with every kind of wealth, grows fat and rejoices in it.

Both the beautiful places of the desert and the fields also have their own parts: namely, prelates, who are called hills because they preside over others as hills over valleys; and those subject to them, called valleys because they are subject to the prelates as valleys are subject to hills; and, moreover, greater and higher prelates, who are leaders of all the hills and valleys, just as rams are leaders of sheep and lambs.

He shows by their parts what abundance both the fields and the beautiful places of the desert will have, when he adds:

I say that the fields will be filled with abundance and the beautiful places of the desert will grow rich; and so it will be. For the hills—that is, the lesser prelates of both the fields and the desert—will gird themselves, that is, will be filled and surrounded, both in body and in soul, with the exultation of eternal blessedness. This is compared with someone who is girded by some object, that is, completely surrounded by it.

And the rams, that is, the greater prelates, the leaders of the sheep—that is, of the lesser prelates—are clothed, that is, will be clothed, with the same exultation as the hills; that is, they will be filled with it both in soul and in body. This is said emphatically, by comparison with a body covered and surrounded by the garments with which it is clothed.

And the valleys, that is, those subject both to the hills and to the rams, will abound in grain—that is, in the blessedness of Christ’s presence, by which they will be spiritually nourished both in soul and in body—like grain, which is more excellent than other crops for nourishment.

The Lord Jesus is also called grain, since he satisfies us with the bread of his teaching. Of him it is written: “Unless a grain of wheat” (John XII, 24), and so forth.

And the valleys themselves, which will abound in grain, will cry out. He shows this by reference to the act of crying out: Truly they will cry out, for they will sing a hymn to God—that is, praise not with the mouth, but with the intensity of inward devotion.

## IN PSALM LXV

### Title of Psalm Sixty-Five

“Toward the end: a song of the psalm of resurrection.” This is explained as follows:

In this treatise there is contained a song—that is, a joyful reward—of the psalm, that is, of good work. This song belongs to the resurrection, which tends toward the end—that is, toward perfect and unchangeable completion.

This means: Here the joyful reward is discussed, the reward that will be given to the faithful for good devotion and good work in that perfect and completed resurrection which will take place on the day of judgment. He speaks briefly of this reward where he says, “You led us into refreshment,” and so forth up to “Come and I will tell.” According to one interpretation, he also discusses it where he says, “They will pass through the river,” and so forth up to “who rules.”

The apostles are introduced in this psalm inviting all the nations that have already been converted to praise God in view of the eternal reward. In order that they may praise God in humility, they urge them to consider his terrifying works: that he rejects the elect, namely the Jews, and chooses the rejected, namely the gentiles. In both works he is perceived to be terrifying.

For when he rejects the elect, it must be feared that, if the gentiles become proud, he may also cast them away. But when he has chosen those same gentiles by grace alone, they must greatly fear offending him, lest, once offended, he condemn more severely those whom he mercifully spared.

The rejection of the Jews is treated briefly where it says, “Your enemies will lie to you”; the election of the gentiles where it says, “He who turns,” and so forth up to “Bless”; and on their behalf his own people pray where it says, “All the earth,” and so forth up to “Come.”

They also exhort them to bless God with heart, deed, and voice, and not to fear blessing him before unbelievers through fear of punishments. [Col. 0943C] They also set before them their own steadfastness, which they possess amid manifold tribulations, so that those nations may become steadfast in tribulation by their example.

This occurs in the passage beginning with “Bless” and continuing to the passage where it says, “We passed through.” There he begins to discuss the reward that they will receive in the future for their steadfastness, so that by hope of that same reward they may invite the nations to steadfastness.

Where it says, “Come and I will tell,” and so forth to the end of the psalm, they display the benefits already bestowed on them by God on account of their good life, so that they may also indicate to the nations to whom they speak that these same benefits will be given to them if they persevere in living well, and thus invite them to a good life.

### “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth”

This means: All you converted nations, who are still earth and ashes—that is, mortal and earthly, not yet made spiritual and immortal—even while you are still earth, praise God with the inward joy of the mind, which cannot be fully expressed either by voice or in writing. Praise him, that is, with intense devotion.

But since it is not enough to praise him with inward joy alone, sing a psalm to his name—that is, openly perform a good work. Persist in this not for human approval but for the praise of his name: “So that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16).

And by saying, “Sing a psalm to his name,” give glory to his praise—that is, make the praise that you will offer him in deed glorious. This means: Sing a psalm to his name for this reason, so that the praise which you will render to God through the psalm may be glorious and pleasing to God. For if you sang the psalm for human approval, your praise would certainly not be glorious.

Hence the Apostle says: “It is better for me to die than that anyone should empty my glory; for if I preach the Gospel, it is no glory for me” (1 Cor. IX, 15–16).

Or it may be understood in this way: I say, shout joyfully and sing a psalm, and thus give glory to his praise—that is, make his praise glorious. This means: The praise of God will then be glorious if you praise him both with inward joy and with the psalm.

To shout joyfully alone, or to sing a psalm alone, would not suffice. And in order that you may shout joyfully and sing the psalm in humility, say to God with inward speech—that is, do not become proud because of your inward joy and your psalm, but consider this within yourselves for the honor of God:

O God, how terrifying are your works! That is, how greatly we can be frightened by the contemplation of your works!

He explains one part of those works as follows:

I say that your works are terrifying. And behold, this work that you ordain is terrifying to you: in the multitude of your power your enemies will lie to you.

This means: You permit the Jews, who were formerly friends but have now become enemies through their wicked life, to be so blinded and hardened that they have lied, are lying, and will continue to lie.

They do this while contemplating the multitude of your power—that is, while considering in many ways your power in your resurrection, in the subjugation of the whole world, and in the miracles that you performed and still perform through your own people. In view of these things they ought to praise you and confess that you are God. Instead they lie by denying that you have risen and that you are God, and they will continue to lie.

If they were to cease from their falsehood, it would be bearable. But he rightly says not “they lie,” but “they will lie,” in order to show their perseverance in falsehood.

I say that they will lie, and this will happen to your honor. For because of their great blindness it will happen that all the earth—that is, every kind of gentile people—will adore you, though it is still earth, that is, devoted to earthly things.

This means: Once those people have been cast out, the gentile people will venerate you in faith and devotion, recognizing you as Creator and regarding themselves as creatures.

Thus, O God, let all the earth adore you. And whoever would not be sufficient for this, let him sing a psalm to you. He explains this by adding: Let him sing a psalm to your name—that is, let him openly persist in good work, for the honor of your name and not for self-exaltation.

He exhorts them to contemplate not only that terrifying work by which he rejects the Jews, but also other terrifying works—namely, that he acquires those same gentiles for himself through gratuitous mercy—so that they may fear him all the more. He says this as follows:

We have shown one terrifying work of God, namely that the enemies will lie. There are still other terrifying works.
