In contemplation of these works, so that you may fear God, come, you nations, with devotion and faith—that is, prepare yourselves—and thus see with the inward sight of reason the works of the Lord, who is terrifying in the plans made concerning the children of men—that is, in the plans that he carries out among the nations, who are called children of Adam and Eve, the first human beings, according to their conformity to an evil life.

This means: That he is exceedingly terrifying appears in his plans concerning human beings, that is, plans by which he rules human beings and fulfills in them whatever pleases him. This is indicated when he says “over.”

He then displays the terrifying works themselves, adding:

I say, see the works of the Lord. The Lord turns the sea into dry land—that is, he turns the gentiles, who were bitter and flowing into vices, as the sea is bitter and flowing, into dry land, so that they may be his earth, which he cultivates with the plowshare of preaching. He makes them dry—that is, thirsty for the teaching that they previously neglected—like dry land that thirsts for water.

Nor will he bestow only this benefit, namely that he turns the gentiles into dry land; he will also do this: Those who are in the river will pass through it on foot—that is, through the humility in which they will persevere.

This means: He will make them cross the river in which they are on foot, that is, by the merit of their humility; or on foot, that is, securely; or on foot, that is, swiftly.

This mortal age is called a river because it flows quickly, like a river. He will make them cross it by leading them back to immortality, and this on account of their humility, swiftly after a short time, and securely, so that at their departure from this life they will not fear punishments arising from the awareness of sins, since they will have been cleansed beforehand.

“Foot” is used for humility because it is the lower part of the body. It is also used for swiftness because a person’s speed is based in the feet. It is likewise used for security because we rely securely upon our feet.

Or: They will pass through the river—that is, they will despise the abundance of worldly goods, which is called a river because it flows quickly. They will do this on foot—that is, swiftly and in humility, so that they may not become proud on that account.

And there we shall rejoice—that is, in that passage, both we apostles and the nations passing through it shall rejoice in God and shall not grieve over the loss of temporal things.

Or, according to the earlier interpretation: We shall rejoice in him—that is, in attaining him when we pass from this world.

In him, I say, who rules forever in his own strength—that is, in the power proper to him, not in another’s power—or in his own strength, that is, in the power of the resurrection.

This means: Through this the Lord became ruler, because he suffered and rose again. In accordance with the Apostle: “He gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. II, 10).

This means: It is not without reason that one should rejoice in him, since he rules forever in his own strength.

But because he had said, “He turned the sea into dry land,” lest the gentiles think that they were saved by their own merits, he adds:

I say that he turned the sea—that is, the gentiles—into dry land, and this not through the merit of the gentiles, but because his eyes of mercy look upon them—that is, he looks mercifully upon the gentiles in order to save them. This is compared with a compassionate patron who, from the lofty throne of his authority, looks with merciful eyes upon someone who is oppressed, in order to save him.

They then turn to the converts from the Jews, who asserted that no one except Jews should be admitted to the faith, saying that the Lord Jesus had come for the salvation of Jews alone. They exhort them not to insult the gentiles, since the eyes of the Lord look upon the gentiles.

Thus it is said: Since the eyes of the Lord look upon the gentiles, and not only upon the Jews, do not exalt yourselves—that is, do not continue to be proud in yourselves, in your lineage and in your knowledge. They are the people who, in their own estimation, provoke God’s mercy—not God himself, who in his nature is always gentle.

This means: They make that mercy harsh insofar as they judge that it ought to show mercy only to the Jews and not also to the gentiles.

He then exhorts the gentiles to bless God as follows:

Therefore, because his eyes look upon you, bless, you nations, our God—that is, praise him with every kind of praise in devotion and deed. His eyes look upon you; he is God, and he is ours—that is, he exists as a human being of our nature.

And do not praise him only in deed and devotion; make the sound of his praise heard—that is, praise him openly, so that others may hear and, following your example, praise him.

The text continues:

### “He has appointed my soul for life”

This is as though he were saying: If persecutions assail you while you are praising him, do not cease from praise through fear, but endure patiently, so that through this you may reach life, just as we also endure patiently in order to reach life.

God has appointed my soul, says the Church of the apostles, that is, he has humbled my sensuality in tribulations—that is, he has permitted it to be afflicted—and he did this in order that we might attain life, that is, eternal life, through this.

We properly use “appoint” when something is taken from a higher place and sent downward. It is therefore appropriately understood here as “humble.”

And although he appointed me, he did not allow my feet to be shaken—that is, he did not allow my affections to be shaken, so that through fear of punishments they would be moved away from a good purpose.

Someone might object: Was there anything by which you could be shaken? The answer is added by turning in thanksgiving to God concerning their steadfastness:

Truly, there was something by which we could be shaken, because you, O God, tested us.

He explains how he tested them when he adds: You examined us in the fire of tribulations, and not to our detriment, so that we might be entirely consumed by the fire of tribulations; rather, you examined us as silver is examined.

This means: Just as silver placed in fire is tested—that is, cleansed from every impurity—so you cleansed us in the fire of tribulations.

It should be noted that he does not say “you tested us” because God previously did not know their steadfastness. Rather, it is equivalent to saying: You showed us to be tested, although previously we did not appear steadfast.

He then describes the tribulations themselves in parts:

I say that you tested us with fire, and behold, you brought us into a snare—that is, you permitted us to be brought into various captivities, prisons, stocks, fetters, chains, bonds, and other things of this kind.

You placed—that is, you permitted—tribulations upon our backs, so that we might be afflicted by various beatings.

You placed men upon our heads—that is, you permitted wicked men to be placed upon our heads. They are rightly called “men” because they are not spiritual. You granted them power to rule over our heads, so that they could kill us; or you placed them upon our heads—that is, you subjected us to their power.

And why should I go through each detail for you?

We passed through fire and water, that is, through prosperity and adversity, in such a way that we were neither broken by hardship nor lifted up by prosperity. Adversity is rightly called fire, because it torments and afflicts and, in its own way, burns like fire. Prosperity, on the other hand, is called water, because in its own way it refreshes like water. Or alternatively: We passed through fire and water, that is, through every kind of torment that takes place in fire and water; and by these two he makes the other torments understood. And because we passed through all these things without failing, you brought us out—that is, you will bring us out—from them all, leading us into the refreshment of eternal rest.

He explains into what refreshment he will lead us, adding as follows: Truly, you will lead me into refreshment. For I shall enter your house, namely, the heavenly Jerusalem. I say, existing in holocausts, that is, in consummated and perfect burning: so that in me everything that is earthly, mortal, and subject to suffering may first be consummated, and I may become perfectly spiritual and immortal, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “This corruptible thing must put on incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:53). A holocaust was the name given to that sacrifice which was burned completely. Therefore the term is used for perfect burning. And after I have entered the house, [Col. 0947C] I shall repay my vows to you, that is, I shall render you my praises eternally, from every vow and desire. These vows my inner lips—that is, the lips of my heart, namely, my thoughts—distinguished, that is, understood as distinct, separate, and excellent above every praise that is offered in this world. For in this world God is praised imperfectly and sometimes with weariness; in the future he will be praised both perfectly and without weariness. “I shall repay my vows”: he says this by the same comparison with which it was said in another nearby psalm, “To you the vow shall be repaid in Jerusalem” (Ps. 64:2). And that these vows are to be repaid, my mouth also spoke, even in my tribulation. This means: Even in tribulation I did not remain silent about the fact that these vows were to be repaid, although it might have seemed an occasion for silence.

I say, I shall enter the house; and, so that I may eventually enter it, meanwhile I shall offer you marrow-filled holocausts, that is, sacrifices with marrow, namely with inner love, which is called marrow because it is inward in the soul, as marrow is inward in the body. He explains these holocausts when he adds, namely: I shall offer you burning oxen, that is, the burning of oxen, together with the burning of rams, that is, also the burning of rams, and with goats, that is, also the burning of goats. This means: I shall burn up in myself the ox, that is, every act of kicking against the goad, so that I may not kick against the yoke of your commandments and your chastisements through tribulations, just as an ox often kicks against the yoke and the goad; rather, I shall patiently bear the yoke and the blows. And I shall burn up in myself the ram, that is, rebellion and pride, so that I may not be rebellious or proud toward you, just as a ram is a rebellious and proud animal. And I shall burn up the goat, that is, lust, which stinks to you like a goat, an animal that has an offensive odor. These burnings will be most sweet holocausts to you, prefigured by the holocausts which, in the old law, were commanded to be offered from oxen, goats, and rams.

They exhort people to behold the benefits already conferred upon them by God, so that they too may strive toward this by living well, as follows: I said, “Come and see the works and terrible deeds of God,” and I recounted them to you, so that, by contemplating them, you might praise God with fear.

But so that you may strive more and more toward this praise, come—that is, prepare yourselves to hear, with the ear of the heart, like those who hurry in order to hear something. And hear, and I shall recount to you, all you who fear God with chaste fear, how many benefits he has bestowed upon my soul—benefits he will bestow upon you if you conform yourselves well to us. For it would be fruitless to recount these benefits to those who do not fear. And behold these benefits: he brought about in me the fact that I cried out, that is, that I acted with an intense cry: “With my mouth”—and not with an empty mouth, but with my own, that is, with the kind of mouth with which I am accustomed to cry out, namely, a devoted and attentive one. And again he brought about in me the fact that I exulted under my tongue, that is, in my heart, over the purity of my innocence. This means: He gave me innocence, from which I might exult exceedingly.

The two verses that follow are read in inverted order, as follows: I say, “I exulted under my tongue over my innocence, which I love.” And because I love innocence and exult in it, he heard—that is, he will hear—me praying to God for perfection [Col. 0948C] in the virtues. And he attended to the voice of my supplication, that is, he will diligently and attentively hear me when I pray for the removal of vices. He proves this from the opposite when he places the words first as follows: Truly he will hear me because of the innocence that I loved and in which I exulted. For if I regarded iniquity in my heart, that is, if I loved iniquity and exulted in it in my heart, the Lord would not hear me. “To regard” is used for “to love” and “to exult,” because we look more frequently upon a thing that we love and in which we exult.

He also brought about in me the fact that he did not remove—that is, did not allow my prayer to be removed—from me: he frequently caused me to pray to him, which is the highest benefit. And he did not remove his mercy from me, but multiplied it, that is, he did not remove from me the abundant benefit given through mercy, but increased all things. Therefore let the Lord be blessed—that is, praised with every kind of praise—who did not remove my prayer and his mercy from me. In this an example is given to those who hear, that they should bless God for the benefits conferred, so that they may be increased.

## ON PSALM 66

**Title of the sixty-sixth psalm.** “For the end, a psalm of David.” Some commentators, however, are said to have the reading: “For the end, in hymns, a psalm of a song of David.” Jerome, the most diligent investigator of the Hebrew truth, has: “For the end, a psalm of David.” This means that this psalm belongs to David, that is, to the apostles who look toward the end, that is, toward the perfect consummation [Col. 0949A] that God will grant to the converted nations: in this age according to faith and all the virtues, and in the future according to eternal blessedness, which will be far more perfect than the present consummation. Or, “for the end,” that is, for Christ, whom they pray for on behalf of themselves and the nations, since this perfection comes through him. In this they give those nations, which are less perfect, an example of praying, since they themselves, being far more perfect, pray for themselves, although prayer might not seem equally necessary to them.

“May God the Father have mercy on us,” so that he may restrain our carnal impulses, lest they prevail over spiritual impulses; “and may he bless us,” that is, exalt our spiritual impulses, so that they may prevail over carnal impulses. “May he illuminate his face upon us,” that is, may he grant the illumination of his Son within our soul, which exists above us with respect to the body—that is, which is the higher and more excellent part of us, ruling and dominating the body. In other words, may he grant us a clear and manifest knowledge of his Son, so that through this we may attain to knowledge of the Father himself, who is one in essence with the Son. The Son is appropriately called the face, because through him the Father’s invisibility is known, just as the whole person is known through the face.

But to indicate that carnal impulses will never be entirely restrained in this age, and that therefore we must frequently pray for their restraint even after blessing and illumination, lest they prevail, they repeat the prayer as follows: “And after he has blessed and illuminated, may he have mercy on us,” always restraining carnal impulses within us.

And in the intense desire to obtain this, they address God by apostrophe as follows: We have said, “May you have mercy, bless, and illuminate,” so that here and now we may know your way on earth. Otherwise we would in no way know it. This means: May we see the knowledge of your Son to be within us and among the nations, who are still earth, that is, possessing an animal body and not a spiritual one, in accordance with what is prayed in the Lord’s Prayer: “May your will be done, as in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 6:10). This means: Just as you wish the knowledge of your Son to exist among the heavenly spirits, namely the angels, so may you also will it to exist among human beings. The Son is called the way because through him one comes to knowledge of the Father, in accordance with his own testimony: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

And may we know your way not among a few, but among all; that is, among every kind of nation may we know your salvation—that is, may we see the knowledge of your Son, who is your salvation, through whom you save the world. Concerning him it was foretold through the prophet: “He will send them a savior and defender who will deliver them” (Ps. 29:20). It should be noted that the apostles pray for this knowledge on their own behalf, not because they lack it, but so that it may be increased in them, thereby giving others, as we said above, an example of praying.

After you have had mercy, blessed, and illuminated the nations: “Let the peoples praise you, O God,” that is, let the nations praise you with every kind of praise. And not merely a few peoples, but let all peoples praise you, that is, every kind of people, who previously would not have rendered you fitting praise. “For praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Sir. 15:9).

The verse that follows is read in inverted order, assigning each phrase to its corresponding phrase, as follows: We said, “May you have mercy, bless, and illuminate,” and thus “may they praise you”; and, while you do this, “May the nations rejoice, because you direct them from good to better.” Or, you direct those nations from evil to good, in this earth, that is, in this age. “And may they exult,” that is, may they have such great joy that it is also displayed by the leaping of the body, because you judge—that is, will judge in the future—the peoples with equity, rendering to each according to his works, saving the just and condemning the unjust. But if you do not have mercy on them, and so forth, they would not have reason to rejoice in your just judgment, by which they would justly be condemned on account of their injustice.

Or these two verses may be fitted together so that the first has a different meaning and the second the same meaning: We said, “May God have mercy both on us and on the nations.” And because the peoples—that is, the nations—could not attain this by themselves: “Let the peoples praise you, O God,” confessing their sins by repenting of them. And not merely a few peoples, but let all peoples praise you. Thus may the nations rejoice and exult because you judge in the future the peoples with equity, while you direct the nations on earth, which otherwise would not rejoice and exult but would instead be saddened.

He repeats what he said, “Let them praise,” in order to add the reason why praise is required, as follows: “Let the peoples,” I say, “praise you, O God; let all peoples praise you.” And from now on they must praise because the earth has given its fruit, that is, because God the Word became earth and man for us. He gave part of its fruit, namely innocence through the remission of sins, perfection in the virtues, and knowledge of God; and he promised that he would give a share of the fruit in the future, through the cooperation of the grace of the whole Trinity, namely eternal blessing.

And because he promised that he would give it: “May God the Father bless us in the future; may our God bless us,” that is, the Son, who shares in our human nature; “may God the Holy Spirit bless us.” And because otherwise they could not attain that blessing, meanwhile “let all the ends of the earth fear him” with chaste fear: all the righteous who bring earthly nature to an end in themselves, or all the ends of the earth, that is, every kind of nation dwelling in all the boundaries [Col. 0950D] of the earth.

## ON PSALM 67

**Title of the sixty-seventh psalm.** “For the end, a psalm of David, a song.” This is explained as follows: This psalm belongs to the prophet David, who looks toward the end, that is, toward the future consummation of the Church through Christ—in this age according to the perfection of the virtues, and in the future according to perfect blessedness. Or, he looks toward the end of the ages, that is, toward the sixth age, in which God was to build the Church, and toward the end of the world, when he will reward it with eternal blessedness. “A psalm of David,” I say, existing as a psalm of a song, that is, of great joy. For in this psalm the prophet rejoices as he speaks of Christ’s glorious future resurrection, which he desires; and of the blessedness, both here and in the future, of the earliest righteous, whom he exhorts to sing to God, to play psalms, and to preach to others. He also speaks of the universal establishment of the Church: how it will come about and through whom, and of Christ’s ascension. He further says that many who will appear to be Christ are by no means Christ. He speaks also of the Church’s future reward, and in this age of the heretics’ defeat by the Church and their rebuke. In all these future things that he foresees with joy, he gives us an example of rejoicing in the praise of God through these same things. One part has already been completed; concerning the other part, which is still to be completed, we are confident. He also speaks, not by wishing but by conceding, of the condemnation of enemies, both here and in the future, so that by terrifying us he may withdraw us from conformity with them, and indicate how great Christ’s power is.

“Let God Christ arise,” as if he were saying: I foresee that Christ, insofar as he will be man, will die and rise again, and that through this he will appear to be God. And because I foresee this as destined to happen, I grant and desire that he arise, being destined through this to appear as God. I foresee also that his enemies, the Jews who will rise against him with blasphemies and tribulations, will be scattered—therefore, throughout the whole earth—and will flee from his face in this age; and in the future they will fail like smoke and perish from the face of God.

And I grant that his enemies be scattered here throughout the whole earth, and that those who hate him flee from his face, that is, voluntarily withdraw from knowledge of him in the manner of one who flees, so that, blinded, they may refuse to know him. And let this happen because they hate him, that is, because they pursue him with hatred, not because of any merit on his part. And in the future may they fail from every rest and from every advantage that they suppose they will possess, being exalted by the flame of their hatred and wicked desire, just as smoke exalted by a flame fails, that is, vanishes.

Or, “may they fail” means in punishments: may they be consumed and tormented, not in such a way that they are utterly destroyed, just as exalted smoke fails not by becoming nothing but by being scattered so that it is no longer seen. In accordance with what is said elsewhere: “Death will feed upon them” (Ps. 48:15). And, so that they may be even more miserable, just as wax flows from the face of fire—that is, just as wax is unstable in the presence of fire—so may sinners perish, antonomastically meaning the Jews, from the face of God, that is, removed from God’s presence and contemplation, in accordance with what is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:10). For they would have some refreshment if, while established in punishments, they could enjoy the contemplation of God; but this will not be possible.

He then treats of the twofold blessedness of the righteous, when he says:

“And let the righteous feast,” as if he were saying: Just as I foresee that the enemies will be condemned both here and in the future, so, by contrast, I foresee that the righteous will be exalted and exult in this age, and in the future will delight; and thus I grant and desire this. Let the righteous feast and exult in the sight of God, that is, let them be refreshed by the various gifts of the Holy Spirit, after the manner of one who feasts and is refreshed by varied dishes. And while feasting, let them exult in the sight of God, that is, in the soul, which God alone sees. Or, “in the sight of God” means in the fact that they will have hope of seeing God in the future. And in the future let them delight in the joy of eternal blessedness, where there will be no weariness but eternal delight. For in this age God is sometimes served with weariness.

This was said concerning the righteous of the first age. He then addresses the righteous themselves by apostrophe, exhorting them to sing and play psalms to God so that they may deserve to attain that joy, as follows: I say, O righteous, that you will delight in joy. And so that this may happen: “Sing to God,” that is, praise God in contemplation, devoting yourselves to the theoretical life; “and sing a psalm to his name,” in the practical life, that is, act well for the honor of his name.

This is said with respect to different people: the less perfect should praise God through the practical life, and the more perfect through the theoretical life. The practical life, which is called active, consists in acting well, clothing the naked, and other similar works, but in such a way that one does not become wholly absorbed in earthly concerns. The theoretical life, which is called contemplative, consists in setting aside all earthly things and devoting oneself solely to prayers and the contemplation of God’s secrets.

And not only should you sing and sing psalms, but “make a way for him who ascends above the setting,” that is, above death. This is said with respect to preachers. It means: Through your preaching, make a way to knowledge of him in the hearts of unbelievers, which are closed through unbelief. And you ought to make a way for him, since he will be so powerful that he will ascend above the setting, that is, he will crush death, both in himself and in his own, like one who crushes something by treading upon it and ascending over it. Death is rightly called “the setting,” because it brings the body to decline.

Nevertheless, there is another reason why you ought to make a way for him: namely, because “the Lord is his name.” He says this more emphatically than if he had simply written, “He is Lord.” By this he indicates that this name properly and above all others belongs to him. And while making a way for him, “exult in his sight,” as if he were saying: If persecution arises while you are making the way, do not fail, but exult in his sight, that is, in hope of seeing him; or “in his sight” means in the soul, which he alone sees. Even if you appear outwardly sad in the flesh, you should exult, since through your preaching you will overcome them. For while you preach, the unbelievers will be disturbed with a good disturbance, and this will happen “from his face,” that is, from knowledge of God, whom they now do not know.

He is the one who exists as “the father of orphans” in this age and will be “the judge of widows” after this age. This means: He is now your Father, that is, he mercifully protects you in the manner of a most merciful father, so that you may not fail in tribulations, since you are orphans after your father the devil has died. Properly speaking, an orphan is one whose father has died. And in the future he will be your judge, so that he may justly reward you according to your merits. You are called widows by analogy, because you have been deprived of the consolation of earthly things, which have died within you, and you cling only to God, just as a widow is deprived of the consolation of her husband, who has now died. Through this he will draw them to obey him in making a way, since he is their Father here and will be their judge in the future.

They will not merely be disturbed; after their disturbance, God appearing in his place makes—or will make—them who are of one manner dwell in a house. This means: Since God himself is powerful, he is able to make them dwell in a house, that is, to make them persevere in the Church, which is his house, once they have been made of one manner, that is, of the same custom, the same will, and the same concord. It is as if he were saying: After they have been disturbed, he will cause them to have the same manner of believing and acting well, and thus he will make them persevere in the Church, never wandering away from participation in it.

The words “God in his holy place” have been inserted to show in what respect he can be proved to be God. I say: God Christ will make them dwell in the house. God, I say, in his holy place, appearing as God, that is, shown to be God through his faithful ones, who will be his place in which he will dwell. He will make them so glorious in miracles and so perfect in virtues and good works that, unless he were God, he could certainly not make them such.

And because one might ask how he will make them dwell there, he shows this by adding as follows: He will bring out those bound by sins, setting them in strength, that is, he will make those whom he frees from the weakness of sins strong and steadfast. It should be noted that he speaks of those bound who, although heavily burdened by sins, have not yet descended into the depths of sins.

Similarly, just as he brings out the bound, he will also bring out those who provoke God, that is, those who make God harsh, although by nature he is sweet and gentle, because they never wish to repent. He identifies who they are when he adds: Namely, he will bring out those who already dwell in tombs, that is, in the death of blindness, who already despair of salvation because of the depth of their sins.

This means: He will bring out from sins both those who are merely bound and not yet dead, and those who, through despair, are already dead; and he will make them dwell in the house. Tombs are used here for death, because the bodies of the dead are placed in tombs.

And before you bring them out, O God, “the earth being moved”—that is, earthly people, both among the Jews and among the nations, will be moved from unbelief to faith. This will happen when you go out—that is, when you will go out—appearing in the sight of your people, the Jewish people, which has already attained some degree of knowledge of you. This means: You who are now obscure and largely unknown to it will appear clearly in its sight, that is, in the consideration of its faith. And then the earth will be moved to faith when you pass through the desert, that is, when you pass from the Jews into the knowledge of the nations, which are now a desert, being without teaching, law, and the fruit of good works like a desert.

He shows through which ministers they will be moved to faith by adding as follows: Truly the earth will be moved.

“For the heavens,” that is, the preachers, “distilled voluntary rain,” that is, they will distill doctrine in different ways, freely and without payment; or “voluntary,” that is, given by God’s gratuitous will, [Col. 0954A] without any merit on the part of that earth. Truly they will distill doctrine in different ways, speaking great things to those who are more capable and small things to those who are less capable.

“I say, rain proceeding from the face of God,” that is, from the knowledge, illumination, and presence of God—and not of a recent god, but of the God of Sinai, that is, of the God who gave the old law, and of the God of Israel, that is, of Jacob. It is as if he were saying: He was also God before the law was given on Sinai; or “the God of Israel” means the God of the new people who see God in contemplation. This means: He is the God both of the old law and of the new.

“Sinai” is interpreted as “temptation.” Therefore it is appropriately used for the old law, which, through its transgression, was the cause of sinning, just as temptation causes one to sin. For it prohibited sins, but did not assist people in ceasing from them. Hence the Apostle says: “Sin, taking occasion through the commandment, deceived me” (Rom. 7:11). Or, because the law was given on Sinai, Sinai is used for the law.

In this he condemns the error of the wicked Jews, who deny that he is God, since he says that he is not a recent god but the God of Sinai and the God of Israel.

I say that the heavens will distill rain, and you, O God, will set it apart from those who are to perish, for your inheritance, that is, for the work of the faithful, who will share in your inheritance, namely, eternal blessedness; or, those who will be your inheritance, whom you will cultivate through the preachers. And in this he makes them very attentive and submissive, when he tells them that a thing so holy and precious is to be given only to them.

“And it was weakened,” that is, the earth will be weakened in its wickedness, because of the voluntary rain. But you, who are powerful for this purpose, perfected it, that is, you will make it perfect in every good thing after it has been weakened.

Or alternatively: I say that you will give the rain separately to your inheritance, and the inheritance was weakened—that is, will be weakened—in the tribulation of the flesh because of its reception. This means: The one who receives the doctrine and strives to obey it will be weakened by many tribulations inflicted by the wicked. But you, who are powerful, perfected it, that is: Because it will be weakened for your sake, you will make it perfect in the future and wholly blessed. It is as if he were saying: There is no need to be concerned if it is weakened because of the rain; that weakening will be the cause of your perfecting it in the future.

Everything from the point where it says “God in his place” is equivalent to arranging the order as follows: Through this the nations will be disturbed, because the heavens will distill rain, through which the earth will be moved, that is, disturbed with a good disturbance, when you go out in the sight of your people and pass through the desert. Then you will bring out the bound and those who dwell in tombs, and thus you will make them dwell in the house; afterward you will allow them to be weakened by tribulations, and in the future you will perfect them.

It should be noted that, since “they will be disturbed” and “the earth was moved” have the same meaning, the expression is repeated in order to show when the earth will be moved and through whom. But because he had said, “You will set it apart for your inheritance,” he indicated that there are some who are not in the inheritance. Therefore he determines who are to be said to be in the inheritance, so that it may become clear who are not in it and may thus strive to be in it. He says this as follows: I say that you will set the rain apart for your inheritance.

In that inheritance there will dwell—that is, they will remain there perseveringly—“animals,” that is, those who are gentle and simple, like those commonly called animals, namely oxen. And not animals of every kind, but yours, that is, those who have faith in and love for you, and who are subjected to the yoke of your subjection, just as animals are suited to being subjected to a yoke. For many people, although they appear gentle, are nevertheless not subjected to God’s yoke. Through this it is implied that those who are not God’s animals are not in his inheritance.

He also shows that God’s doctrine is not harsh toward the good, so that he may draw those who are unwilling to receive it, as follows: I say that you will set the rain apart for your inheritance. It will not be harsh to it, but you, O God, prepared—that is, will prepare—that rain for the poor, that is, for the work of the poor inheritance, namely, the inheritance that will be poor in spirit. And “in sweetness you will prepare it,” that is, in such a way that it will be sweet to it. “In your sweetness,” I say, that is, given by you. It is as if he were saying: They will not possess that sweetness from themselves, but from you. Through this he humbles them, lest anyone think that anything good comes from himself.

He also shows that the preachers do not receive doctrine through free will from the face of God, but have it as a gift from God, in order to humble them. He adds as follows: I said that the heavens will distill rain from the face of God; yet they will not have it from themselves, but the Lord will give the word of preaching—which above I called rain—to those evangelizing, that is, to the preachers whom I called heavens. And he will give that word with great power, that is, with manifold power of miracles, so that they may be powerful not only in preaching but also in miracles. Through this he also explains what he called rain and whom he called heavens.

The Lord, I say, existing as “the king of the powers of the beloved, of the beloved,” that is, the ruler of those evangelizers, who by emphasis will be called the powers of Christ, beloved by God the Father according to his divinity, since he is consubstantial with him, and beloved as man, since he will be free from all sins. They will be called powers because they will be full of every virtue. It is as if he were saying: He will give the evangelizers the power both to preach and to perform miracles, as well as the fullness of virtues, because these three things will be useful for the instruction of the Church. Their preaching would not be believed if they did not perform miracles. But if they preached well and performed miracles while lacking virtues and living badly, they would appear to be magicians, and thus would scarcely be believed.

Therefore he will give them the ability to preach, to perform miracles, and to live well. And he will not merely give the word to those evangelizing, nor merely be king of the powers so that they may not fail; he will also give them the ability “to divide the spoils,” that is, he will give them power to distribute the other faithful who will be spoils taken from the devil through those evangelizers, so that they may make some rulers in different ways within the Church and others subject.

I say that he will give them the ability to divide the spoils, and this division will be for the beauty of the house, that is, for the work of the beauty of the Church, so that the Church, which is God’s house, may be more beautiful because of the diversity of its children. In accordance with what the Apostle says: “God placed some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then powers” (1 Cor. 12:28).

He then addresses the spoils themselves by apostrophe, exhorting them to sleep among the intermediate lots and showing what benefit they will derive from this, as follows: I said that he would give them the ability to divide the spoils. And, O you spoils, so that you may be the beauty of the house of God, the Church, “sleep among the intermediate lots,” that is, rest in the manner of one sleeping among lots which have a middle. This means: Remain so at rest that you may be in the midst of two lots. For we call those things “intermediate” which have a middle.

“Clerus” is interpreted as “election.” Therefore a lot (clerus) is used both for the multitude of the sons of this world, who choose earthly things rather than heavenly things, and for the multitude of the citizens above, who have been chosen by God. Or a lot is used for temporal goods, which are chosen by earthly people, and for heavenly goods, which are chosen by holy men.

The faithful are said to sleep among the intermediate lots, that is, to rest in the midst of these two elections: temporal goods and heavenly goods, or in the midst of worldly men and heavenly citizens. They have already left behind the election of earthly goods and have already rejected conformity with worldly men, since by living well they strive toward heavenly goods and toward fellowship with the citizens above. Yet they do not hasten by murmuring about the delay of the election for which they wait, nor do they return to the worldly election that they have already left and rejected. Rather, they sleep in the midst of these two, that is, they rest by living well, so that they do not return to what they rejected and do not impatiently hasten toward what they await.

They would hasten prematurely if, before the time arranged by God, they grieved that they could not attain it. Or the wording may be adapted so that the meaning remains the same:

“Sleep,” that is, remain at rest, not existing in premature haste, among the intermediate lots, that is, among the gatherings of the faithful, which are lots, that is, chosen by God. They are intermediate lots, resting between the earthly lot and the heavenly lot, having already abandoned the earthly and not yet having reached the heavenly. This whole statement is as if he were saying: Sleep, existing among the gatherings of the righteous, who are intermediate lots, between the two lots, earthly and heavenly.

For if you sleep among the intermediate lots, that is, if you remain not murmuring and not hastening prematurely, but sleeping—that is, resting in patient expectation—in the midst of the two elections, the temporal and the heavenly, you will be “silvered wings of a dove.” That is, you will raise up the Church through good life, prayer, and also your preaching, in the likeness of wings that raise a bird aloft as they carry it through the air.

The dove is called the Church because it is simple and without the gall of blasphemy against God and neighbor, in the likeness of a dove, which is a simple bird without gall. Accordingly the Bridegroom testifies concerning it in the Song of Songs: “One is my dove” (Song 6:8), and so forth.

And such wings will be silvered, that is, made of silver. You will be perfect in steadfastness, so that you will not fail under the blows of tribulations, just as pure silver does not crack under the blows of a hammer.

And you will be not only wings, but also “its hind parts, the backs of it,” namely of the Church. This is said intransitively, as if he were saying: You will be such posterior members in the Church that you will be its back, that is, worthy to bear the burden of governing the Church, like the posterior parts of the body that we call the back and that are suited to carrying a burden. It is as if he were saying: You will be the back of the Church, that is, worthy of ecclesiastical authority—worthy to be bishops or presbyters and the other rulers in the Church—who carry the members subject to the Church through your preaching, example of good life, and prayer.

I speak of you as abounding in the pallor of gold, that is, in pale gold, namely in the perfection of virtues, which is signified by pale gold, which is more perfect than gold that is excessively white or red like copper. This means: You will rightly be rulers of the Church, because you will be perfect in every virtue.

Or this verse is explained as follows: “O spoils, sleep among the midst of the clans,” that is, remain diligently among the clans until the sleep of death, that is, among the many books of the Old and New Law. Not among all the books, since many of them are apocryphal, but among the “midst,” that is, among those books that are common to Catholic men and authoritative, which Pope Gelasius carefully enumerates. He uses “midst” for “common,” because a thing placed in the middle of those surrounding it is usually shared by them all. Properly speaking, we ordinarily call a multitude of clerics the *clerus*. Therefore, here he uses *cleros* for the multitude of the books of both Laws. He is not here indicating the interpretation of this word, *clerus* [Col. 0957C]. And he rightly says “among,” as though he were saying: Study the authoritative books until the sleep of death, so that you may be among them, that is, in their midst, confirming one through another: the new through the old, and the old through the new.

I say, “sleep”; for if you sleep among the midst of the clans, that is, if you study among the authoritative books until the sleep of death, you will be the wings of the dove, that is, those who exalt the Church. This is unchanged. And you will be such wings as are “silvered,” that is, possessing silver—namely, the literal understanding, which is bright like silver. And you will be not only silvered wings but also “the hinder parts of its back,” namely, of the Church: you will be worthy to bear the burden of governing the Church. This too is unchanged [Col. 0957D].

I say, “abounding in the pallor of gold,” that is, in pale gold—namely, in the mystical understanding, which the Greeks call *anagōgē* (ἀναγωγή), represented by pale gold, which is more perfect than all other gold because it is far more perfect than the understanding that is literal. It is as though he were saying: You will be worthy to be the wings and the back of the Church when you abound both in the literal and in the mystical understanding.

Some interpreters, however, read “in the greenness of gold.” According to them, the passage is explained as follows: If you sleep among the midst of the clans, that is, in the midst of the authoritative books, you will be the wings of the dove, that is, those who exalt the Church. This is unchanged. And the wings are “silvered”: in this interpretation *silvered* is used in its proper sense. For something is called silvered when, although it has silver on the outside, it contains something else within.

[Col. 0958A] Thus it is explained: Externally, in your mouth, you will possess clear and resonant eloquence, represented by silver, which is clear and bright and resounds better than every other metal. And you will not only be wings, but also “the hinder parts of its back,” that is, bearers of its governance, of the Church. This too is unchanged.

I say, “abounding in the greenness of gold,” that is, in the greenness proceeding from gold—namely, in charity, which is always green in each believer and never withers, and which proceeds from the inner wisdom that is perfect and precious like gold. Many indeed say that the finest gold sometimes has a color close to green.

Or again: You will be “silvered wings,” that is, bright exaltors, perfect in every virtue and work like silver, and this in the present life. In the future [Col. 0958B] you will be “the hinder parts of its back,” that is, bearers of the Church, in “the pallor of gold,” that is, in pale gold—namely, in perfect blessedness, which is understood through pale gold because it is perfect. That is, you will be such sons of the Church as will bear within yourselves in the future the great and weighty burden of eternal blessedness, like a back that bears a burden. This is as though he were saying: Here you will exalt the Church through the radiance of virtues, works, and preaching; and in the future you will bear the reward of eternal blessedness.

It should be noted that, in all the foregoing interpretations, after calling them wings he did not call them the back without purpose. For many are wings—that is, people who exalt the Church by their good life—who are not the back, that is, prelates. In this final interpretation, however, it is quite evident that the wings and the back are different, since one is understood in the present, namely the wings, while the other is understood in the future, namely the back.

The verse that follows, beginning “when he distinguishes,” is connected in two ways, although the interpretation does not thereby change. For if we take *cleros* to mean two elections, namely the earthly and the heavenly, the connection is as follows: I said, “Sleep among the midst of the clans,” that is, remain at rest in the midst of the two elections; and if you sleep, I have shown what you will attain from this.

One must not sleep for only an hour, but for as long as—that is, while—the heavenly King, namely God the Father, distinguishes kings over that dove, that is, appoints many prelates over the Church so that they may rule it by governing it well [Col. 0958C]. This is as though he were saying: One must sleep for as long as this present life lasts, during which God distinguishes kings over it. By this he commends these prelates to their subjects, since he says that they are appointed over their subjects by God.

It should be noted that no one will sleep among the clans throughout this entire life, since no one will live forever in this world; rather, this is said concerning all of them. Together they will complete this sleep—not each one the whole of it, but each one a part, according to his station. One will sleep for twenty years, another for thirty; one longer, another less; and so they will succeed one another from generation to generation. Each one, sleeping according to his station throughout this life, will sleep among the midst of the clans.

But if we take *cleros* [Col. 0959A] to mean the multitude of the books of the Old and New Law, the connection is as follows: I say that you will be wings, and this for as long as the heavenly King distinguishes kings over that dove, that is, throughout this entire life. Each one will be wings in his own station, from generation to generation.

These kings will be “whitened with snow,” that is, with the purity and brightness of faith, which is well signified by snow because it is exceedingly white; “in Selmon,” that is, through Christ, who is suitably understood by Selmon. For Selmon is interpreted as “shadow.” By shadow, refreshment is understood, since shade usually cools those laboring in the heat. Thus Christ is signified by Selmon, because he is the shadow of perfect refreshment.

Here he humbles the prelates, showing that they are not worthy in themselves to be distinguished as kings over the Church, but through Christ, by whom they are first whitened with the brightness of faith.

Someone might ask: Will Christ be able to whiten them? To this he adds: Indeed he will. For Christ will be “the mountain of God the Father,” that is, exalted by God the Father in every power, according to what is said in the Gospel: “The Father has given all things into his hand” (John III, 35). And such a mountain will be “a fat mountain,” that is, overflowing with rich and perfect wisdom, by which he will nourish and strengthen his own, like a fertile mountain that fattens and strengthens the animals dwelling upon it with its rich pastures.

And although, with respect to the perfect, he is fat in wisdom and teaching, with respect to the less perfect he will be “a coagulated mountain,” that is, a milky mountain, nourishing them with simpler teaching, like a child who is nourished with milk. Properly speaking, coagulum is a property of milk. Therefore “coagulated” is suitably understood as “milky.”

And although, with respect to the perfect, he is a fat mountain, and with respect to the imperfect, a coagulated mountain, he will also be a fat mountain in himself, that is, abounding in every perfection of wisdom and virtue.

And since this one alone will be a fat mountain, why do you, Jews, suspect—or will suspect—that “coagulated mountains” are this fat mountain? You will suspect this unjustly. He says this by way of correction, as though he were saying: Many saints will exist who, because of their excessive holiness, will be thought to be that fat mountain, Christ—John, Jeremiah, and others like them. Nevertheless, they will be coagulated mountains, not fat mountains, in comparison with him [Col. 0959D]; that is, they will be milky, small in teaching and wisdom in comparison with him. Therefore, although they are coagulated, do not suspect them to be that fat mountain.

I say that Selmon will be a fat mountain, and so fat that it will be a mountain in which God is well pleased, that is, in which he will be entirely pleased, so that nothing in it will displease him. It is as though he were saying: Although God is pleased with other mountains, nevertheless, in their holiness there will be something that displeases him. For no one is free from uncleanness, not even an infant whose life upon earth is only one day old. But since this fat mountain will be free from sin, in it God the Father will be well pleased in every respect.

Accordingly, the same one testifies in the Gospel: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew III, 17). This is as though he were saying: God will be well pleased in the perfection of this mountain, and God the Father will also be well pleased to dwell in that fat mountain. Indeed, he will be pleased to dwell in it—namely, in the Lordly man. For he will dwell in it “unto the end of dwelling,” that is, in perfect dwelling, namely, so that he may be personally united to it and thus dwell in it forever. What he says, “for he will dwell unto the end,” determines the manner in which he will dwell.

After exhorting them concerning the spoils and praising the fat mountain, he returns to what he had begun to discuss concerning the preachers and the constitution of the Church. First he commends the apostles, so that he may make those subject to them more submissive and obedient. He says this as follows:

I said that the Lord will give the word to those evangelizing. Having received the word with great power, they will be the chariots of God, bearing God into the knowledge of human beings through the harmony of their preaching, just as a chariot drawn concordantly by horses carries someone. For although one preacher may seem to differ from another in the wording, in their meaning there is harmony of understanding.

I say “chariot” existing as “many thousands of tens,” that is, the company of preachers will have many preachers—ten thousand, namely, such as are rightly signified by this number, ten thousand: they will be perfect in holiness and firm in faith, in the likeness of this number, ten thousand, which mathematicians call perfect and solid, because it seems to grow into a solid body—into a body in quantity, not a body in substance. This body, as is said, is composed of surfaces, and surfaces in turn are constituted from lines.

Let the number one hundred be set down as a line, and let one hundred be multiplied by the number ten, so that one says: ten times one hundred makes one thousand. This is called by mathematicians a surface, as though composed of ten lines—namely, of ten times one hundred. Let this surface, which is one thousand, likewise be multiplied by the number ten and by the number one hundred, and let one say “one hundred ten times ten times.” This is to say: ten times one thousand makes ten thousand. This is a solid body, composed of ten surfaces, namely, of ten thousand.

This number is perfect because no higher number is found beyond the number one thousand. Since, then, this number is perfect and solid, preachers are most rightly understood by the ten thousand: they will be solid in virtue, work, and faith [Col. 0960D].

And those thousands will be “rejoicing,” that is, those many preachers, perfect and solid, will rejoice in tribulations, not failing through fear of those tribulations. Therefore those thousands will be rejoicing because the Lord will be spiritually in them on Sinai, that is, in the temptation of tribulations, so that they do not fail. For Sinai is called “temptation.”

He will be in them “in the holy place,” that is, in holiness, so that he may make them holy and steadfast in that temptation, according to what he likewise testifies in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew VIII, 20).

He shows how they will become chariots by turning in thanksgiving to God, as follows [Col. 0961A]:

I said that they will become chariots, and by this they will become chariots: “You will dwell in them on Sinai, in the holy place; you ascended on high,” that is, ascending into heaven according to your humanity. For according to your divinity you are not local. And through your ascension, by sending the Holy Spirit into them, they will become your chariots. “For unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John XVI, 7).

And as you ascend, you took captivity, that is, you will take with you and lead the holy patriarchs and prophets who, dying before your coming, will be held captive in hell. By rising, you will lead them out from there, and by ascending you will lead them with you. By this he attracts the living to obey him, so that they too may be led away.

Nor will you take only captivity, but also “among human beings,” that is, among those who will still be human beings living in the flesh, you received—that is, you will receive—gifts. This is to say: From among human beings, through the teaching of your chariot, you will receive certain persons who will be your gifts, to be given to you by your Father.

He demonstrates this by a part, adding: Indeed, you will receive certain persons from among human beings who will be your gifts.

For you will receive, O Lordly man, those who do not believe that the Lord God dwells in you—namely, certain Jews who will not believe that the Lord God dwells in you. They will say this: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John IX, 16). By this example concerning the Jews he intimates that he will also receive some from the Gentiles.

He then turns to the hearers, declaring that salvation will come through the Lord. I said that the Lord Jesus ascended on high and will receive gifts among human beings. And that blessed Lord, that is, the exalted Lord, existing in the day—that is, through the illumination of his glory, which is understood by “day” because it illuminates the faithful, like the day illuminating the world—will “daily,” that is, continually from day to day, make our path prosperous toward our salvations, that is, toward our salvation.

This is to say: His illumination will be our way to salvation, that is, to the remission of sins and to obtaining eternal life. The illumination of his glory will save us from sins and lead us back to life.

When he says “for us,” he joins himself to the faithful of the New Law, showing that he is already a member of the Church by faith, as though he were saying: He will save both me, who existed before the time of fullness and possessed its faith, and those whom he will gather in the time of fullness, from sins, illuminating us with his spiritual grace and leading us back to the life that we lost. For no one was so holy that, before the time of fullness, he was saved from original sins.

And he rightly says that he will make the path prosperous daily. For every day the faithful come through God’s grace to salvation, each one according to his station.

I say, the Lord exists as “our God,” to whom we make a place of divinity in ourselves by obeying and subjecting ourselves to him, and he exists as powerful to save us, that is, he will be powerful for our salvation.

This is the same thing he stated above, “he will make our path prosperous toward our salvations.” But it is repeated in order to magnify God’s praise. And although he will be powerful to make his own people safe, nevertheless, “the exits of that Lord,” truly and antonomastically existing as Lord, will be “the exits of death.” This is to say: He will go forth through death to the glory of resurrection and immortality.

According to this: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise, and thus to enter into his glory” (Luke XXIV, 28). It is as though he were saying: Do not think him powerless because he will die; for through death he will go forth to glory. By this he intimates that the faithful too will likewise go forth through death to glory. In this he indicates that they should not grieve because they are going to die.

When he says “the Lord Lord” twice, he does so for his praise, as though he were saying: He is speaking of that Lord who is Lord *par excellence*, to whom every creature is subject.

But because he had said that he would die, lest he seem in any way to have diminished him, he commends him as follows: I say that the exit of the Lord will be an exit of death. Nevertheless, being God, he—the one who is believed to be Lord absolutely—will break the heads of his enemies, that is, he will break the power of the evil spirits, who are the heads of the unbelievers, who are enemies of God.

They are rightly called the heads of the unbelievers, because they dominate them, just as the head dominates all the limbs. This is to say: He will take power away from the evil spirits, so that they cannot dominate those who now make themselves his enemies by living wickedly.

And he will “break the crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins,” that is, the pride of the frivolous people who walk in their sins, persevering as they go from sin to sin. This is to say: In them he will break the heads—that is, the power—of the heads, because he will break in them the pride that proceeds from their vanity, through which the heads dominate them.

The crown is rightly understood to signify pride because it is the high part of a human being and exalts the mind beyond measure. Hair, because it is a very light thing and yields most easily to every wind, is suitably understood as vanity.

He shows this by authority, as follows: Truly, the Lord will break his enemies by turning them to himself.

For the Lord said this to me inwardly, through spiritual revelation: “From Bashan,” that is, from confusion, “I will convert some,” that is, I will convert some of my enemies to myself because of Bashan—that is, because of the confusion they will have within themselves, blushing and groaning over their sins. For Bashan is called “confusion.”

When he says “from Bashan,” the word “from” is used causatively. He shows in particular whom he will convert, adding: I will convert those who are in the depth of the sea, that is, those who are deep in the bitterness of vices. By this example he intimates that he will convert even more readily some who are not yet in the depth of the sea.

He then turns to God in thanksgiving, as follows:

I said, O God, that you will convert and break your enemies, and you will break them so completely that your foot will be dipped in blood, that is, the foot made from your enemies—your travelers, who, running throughout the world, will confess you—will be dipped in the blood of martyrdom.

He explains what they will be made into a foot when he adds: The foot, I say, made from enemies, will be the tongue of your dogs.

This is said intransitively, as though he were saying: Those who will become travelers from among your enemies will become your “tongued dogs.” And this will be from you yourself, not from their own free will.

This is to say: You will make them like tongued dogs, loyal animals to their masters and barking at their enemies, so that they too, being faithful to you, may bark at heretics and all unbelievers, running everywhere among the nations and scattering the seeds of teaching. For this they will not hesitate to be dipped in the blood of martyrdom.

Since one runs with the foot, the foot is not inappropriately taken for the travelers. By this they will be dipped in blood because they have seen your entrances, that is, they will see your footsteps, O God—namely, that you will walk through death. And therefore, following your example, they too will be dipped in blood.

Another translation has: “They saw your paths.” From this we conclude that *entrances* has been used in place of *footsteps*.

And lest it seem incongruous that he is God and walks through death, he confirms this for the instruction of his hearers by turning to them, as follows:

I say that they will see your footsteps. And truly, O hearers, such will be the footsteps of my God, my King, who is—that is, who will dwell—in the holy Lordly man. It is as though he were saying: The Word of God, existing as my God—though he may not seem God and my King to everyone—insofar as he will be in the holy man, will walk through death; that is, that holy man, personally united to him, will die.

This is as though he were saying: God the Word will give them an example of dying by walking through death. And therefore they will still be dipped in blood, because the princes—the apostles, who will be princes of the Church—went before them and will precede them in being dipped in blood. This is to say: God will give them not only an example of being dipped in blood, but also the apostles, who will be dipped first.

But because he had called them princes, lest they seem to become proud of their principate, he adds: Princes, I say, “joined to those who sing psalms,” that is, they will be joined to the lesser faithful who do good works, so that together with them they may be one body of the Church.

This is to say: They will not disdain to be joined to their subjects, so that they may be one with them; rather, they will be one company with them.

He expresses with which psalm-singing people they will be joined when he adds: They will be “in the midst of young women who beat tambourines,” that is, they will exist among those faithful so that they may be one company with them. These faithful will be called young women because they will be young in faith, that is, newly approaching the faith.

They are called “those who beat tambourines” because they will praise God with the tambourine, that is, through the mortification of the flesh, which is understood as the tambourine: this is a musical instrument covered with the skins of dead animals.

In this they give an example of humility, so that no prelate in the Church may exalt himself against his subjects. He calls the faithful subjects “those who beat tambourines” in the feminine gender because they are less perfect than the apostles in holiness, just as the feminine sex is less perfect and weaker than the masculine [Col. 0964A].

Then, turning to those whom above he called the feet of God and his tongued dogs, he exhorts them to bless God by dwelling within the common fellowship of the Church, not proudly separating themselves from it—a thing that would be displeasing to God, since the princes will be joined to the young women.

O you who are destined to be converted from Bashan and to become the feet of God, do not become proud because you will be feet. Rather, existing in the churches—that is, in the common fellowship of the churches among the Jews, whom I called young women—bless the Lord God, that is, praise that Lord who is God and powerful to reward your praise. Praise him with your voice, with your life, and by dying for him.

I say, bless God, and let this blessing proceed “from the fountains of Israel,” that is, after the example of fountains, namely, of the Church. Praise him by remaining in the common fellowship of the Church among the Jews, like the apostles, who are called the fountains of the Church because they give it drink through their teaching.

For it would profit nothing to do good if, through pride, you departed from the assembly of the Church. According to what the Apostle testifies: “If I deliver my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians XIII, 3).

You would then depart from the Church if, judging yourselves alone to be holy, you judged those within the Church to be merely sinners and unworthy of your companionship, and thus had no charity toward them.

Someone might ask: Who will those fountains be? To this he responds as follows: There, that is, among those fountains, will be “Benjamin, the young man,” that is, Paul, who will be from the tribe of Benjamin, as he himself testifies in the Letter to the Philippians: “Circumcised on the eighth day, of the race of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin” (Philippians III, 5), and so forth.

Paul is called a young man because he was the last of the apostles to come to the faith—not because he was less perfect in faith and holiness. For this reason he calls himself one “untimely born,” saying: “Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me” (1 Corinthians XV, 8).

I say that Benjamin, that is, Paul, will be among the apostles, and this “in an ecstasy of mind,” that is, through an elevation of the mind—namely, the ecstasy of mind in which he will be while going to Damascus, when a light from heaven will shine around him, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts IX, 3).

Or again: Benjamin will be there, existing in an ecstasy of mind, that is, in contemplation of heavenly secrets, when he will be caught up to the third heaven and hear secret words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak (2 Corinthians XII, 4).

Or again: Benjamin will be there, and this in “the ecstasies of the minds of human beings,” that is, in amazement. For many will be amazed when they hear of his conversion, since previously he will have been a persecutor of the Church.

And there also—that is, in the assembly of the fountains of Israel—will be the princes of Judah, the princes of Zebulun, and the princes of Naphtali, that is, the other apostles. Some of them will be from the tribe of Judah, some from Zebulun, and others from Naphtali.

Some interpreters have wished the apostles to have come from these tribes, even if this is perhaps not found written anywhere. The Prophet indicates this here for the clarification of his prophecy.

Or, by Judah, which is interpreted as “confession,” faith is understood, from which confession of God is generated. By Zebulun, which signifies “strength,” hope is understood, which makes the faithful strong in suffering. By Naphtali, which is called “enlargement,” charity is signified, which is enlarged even to the love of an enemy.

The apostles were the princes of the Church’s faith, hope, and charity when they preached that these three things must be possessed.

Princes, I say, who will be the leaders of those—namely, of Israel, that is, of the whole Church. Although *illorum* is a plural case, it is suitably referred to *Israel*, which is singular in case. It is plural in meaning but singular in grammatical form.

After declaring [248] the constitution of the Church, he prays God the Father that what he prophesied may be fulfilled through the office of the Son, as follows [Col. 0965B]:

I said that the nations will be disturbed, the earth will be shaken, God will break the heads of his enemies, and he will convert them from Bashan; and the other things that I foretold will likewise come to pass.

And in order that all these things may be fulfilled: “Command this, God the Father, to your Power,” that is, impose this office upon your Son, who by emphasis will be your Power, through whom you will wondrously conquer the devil.

And after you have fulfilled these things through the Son, “confirm what you have worked,” that is, what you have worked in us. This is to say: Constitute the Church from both peoples, perfect it in every holiness, and afterward strengthen it so that it does not fail.

When he says “in us,” he joins himself to the future Church, because he was already a member of the Church by faith.

I say, command—that is, impose the task of constituting the Church upon your Son—“beginning from your holy temple,” which is in Jerusalem. That is, begin to constitute the Church by converting those who, existing in Jerusalem—that is, among the Jewish people—will be your holy temple, in whom you will dwell spiritually once they have become faithful.

This is to say: Let the beginning of the Church be from the Jews. Jerusalem, because it is a city in Judaea, is suitably taken for the Jewish people.

And if you command this to the Son, “kings will offer you gifts,” that is, many from the Gentiles and the Jews, having become kings of themselves, will offer themselves to you as gifts, setting aside their own wills, submitting themselves to you, and obeying you alone.

But because the Prophet foresaw that many disturbances by heretics would arise in the Church, he prays God to restrain them, as follows:

I ask not only that you command this task to your Power, but, since I see that many heretics will arise in the Church—who will rightly be called beasts because they will be fierce and irrational, and will devour the faithful like beasts—I ask you to rebuke, that is, to convict through the rebuke of your preachers, “the beasts that devour the reed,” that is, divine Scripture, which they corrupt by interpreting it perversely.

Scripture is rightly understood by the reed because the ancients used a reed for writing.

Rebuke some of them so that they may be converted; others, who are not to be converted, rebuke so that they may be exposed and no longer deceive.

Or, “the beasts that devour the reed” means those faithful who will be light and unstable like a reed and will be carried about by every wind of doctrine.

It will indeed be necessary for you to rebuke them. For the assembly of bulls—that is, of heretics, who will be called bulls because they will be proud like bulls, which are stiff-necked—will be among the cows of the peoples, that is, among the faithful already mentioned, who will be weak like cows, which are weaker than bulls. This means: There will be many heretics who will make many simple people conform to themselves.

But lest God seem to permit them to dominate without any benefit to his own people—something that would be considered incongruous—he adds: “To this end,” namely, among the cows of the peoples, “exclude from the mass of the simple those who have been tested in silver,” that is, those who are perfect in Scripture, which is bright like silver; or “in silver,” that is, in eloquence that sounds beautifully, after the manner of silver. This means: So that, through their separation from the wise faithful, those faithful who have been tested in knowledge of the Scriptures and in eloquence may appear and be revealed. Otherwise they would not become manifest, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Cor. 11:19).

He uses “exclude” in the sense of “make manifest,” by comparison with someone who, while enclosed somewhere, is not visible, but who, once excluded, immediately appears and becomes manifest.

It should indeed be noted that he calls the greater heretics “wild beasts,” namely, those who are teachers of errors, because they are savage like wild beasts. But I ask not only that the wild beasts be rebuked; I also ask: “Scatter the peoples who desire wars,” that is, convict the lesser heretics, the disciples of the greater ones. I call them “peoples” because they will be numerous. I say “scatter,” that is, divide them, so that you may convict some in such a way that they are converted, while others, who must be destroyed, may merely be exposed. And rightly will you scatter them, because they do not desire peace but seditions and wars in the Church.

And so it will be. Truly, you will rebuke the wild beasts and scatter the peoples, O preachers who will be your legates. For legates will come from Egypt, that is, from the mass of sinners who are darkened by sins, who are suitably signified by Egypt; for Egypt is said to mean “darkness.” This means: Many sinners, made your legates, will come for the purpose of preaching.

And before Egypt has legates, Ethiopia—that is, Egypt—will anticipate it; that is, it will hasten beforehand to give its hands to God, namely, its hands, so that the mass of the darkened, destined to be saved, will hasten to subject itself to God through faith. This is by comparison with someone who, when he becomes subject to another, gives him his hands.

Ethiopia here signifies the same thing as Egypt—not because its interpretation is the same, but because the inhabitants of Ethiopia are extremely black. He then exhorts all the faithful to sing psalms and songs to God in view of all the matters mentioned above, as follows:

“Therefore, kingdoms of the earth”—that is, all of you who are to become kingdoms of God—“sing to God,” namely, to Christ, that is, praise God with a song, in the joy of the contemplative life. “And you who cannot sing psalms, sing psalms to the Lord,” that is, praise the Lord with a psalm, namely, through the good work of the active life.

This was said earlier in this same psalm, where he said: “Sing to God; sing a psalm to his name.” But earlier it was said to the first converts; here it is said to all the faithful.

Sing psalms, I say, to God who ascends above the heaven of heaven, that is, to God who, according to his humanity, will ascend above heaven—namely, above the firmament of the aerial heaven, which encompasses the whole air, the earth, the sea, and everything in them.

He also identifies the place from which he will ascend, for the confirmation of our faith, as follows: “I say that he will ascend into heaven, and this toward the east,” namely, from the Mount of Olives, which lies opposite Jerusalem on its eastern side.

Or “he will ascend” means that he will be exalted by his dignity “as far as the east,” that is, he will become worthy to be personally united to the Word of God, who eternally and ineffably rises—that is, is begotten—from the Father.

I say that he will ascend, himself existing exalted above the higher heaven, which encompasses the lower heaven; that is, he will be more worthy than the higher citizens of heaven, who, within the power of their principality, encompass lesser spirits.

I say: sing psalms and sing, and by doing this give glory to God, that is, give God glorious praise. Do not consider that you possess from yourselves the ability to praise him, but recognize that you have it from that same God. Otherwise the praise would not be glorious.

And it is fitting that you do all this. For behold, in the present age he will not delay long—namely, after the present age, which is exceedingly brief in comparison with God. He will give his voice the character of a voice of power; that is, he will make his voice powerful and mighty when he says: “Depart from me, you accursed” (Matt. 25:41), and so forth. In the Passion he will have a humble voice, saying: “My soul is sorrowful” (Matt. 26:38), and other things of this kind.

It is as though he said: Praise him who will appear powerful in judgment to those who were unwilling to hear him when he addressed them in humble instruction, lest he then justly condemn you if you have neglected to praise him.

And therefore continue to give glory, because then his majesty will be over Israel, that is, by his higher disposition he will glorify in glory the elect from the Israelite people. And his power will be in the clouds, that is, the blessedness and power to judge the world will be given by him to the apostles, who are clouds—that is, they will be the rain-bringers of the Church in this life. In accordance with what he says: “You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

Nor will God appear wondrous only in the clouds and in Israel by glorifying them; God will appear wondrous in all his saints, glorifying them from whatever people they may come.

“I say, God of Israel,” that is, the God of the patriarch Jacob, not a recently existing god. Or “God of Israel” means the God of the whole Church, which will then be seeing God.
