He explains in what respect he will be wondrous in his saints when he adds: I say “wondrous,” and in this respect: He himself will give power to his people, that is, immortality and impassibility, whereas here his people are weak because they are subject to suffering and mortal; and he will give strength to his people, so that they can no longer be deceived or sin.

I say, he is the blessed God who exists as the exalted God. It is as though he said: Since he himself has been exalted, in the sublimity of his divinity he can certainly exalt his people in the future by giving them strength and power. [Col. 0968A]

## On Psalm 68

### The title of Psalm 68

“On the end: a psalm for those who will be changed, of David.”

This is explained as follows: This psalm concerns those who will be changed, that is, for their benefit—those who will be changed by David, Christ; that is, having been changed from the oldness of Adam, they will be conformed to the newness of Christ.

I say “they will be changed,” and this “unto the end,” that is, unto perfect transformation. Here they will be changed and conformed to him according to holiness and innocence, insofar as this will be possible for them; but in the future they will be conformed to him according to immortality and impassibility.

And the psalm is rightly entitled as concerning the benefit of those who will be changed, since Christ’s resurrection will be the cause of this transformation, and since Christ is introduced here praying concerning perseverance and resurrection. There is also no doubt that he prays for the benefit of those who are to be transformed.

In this psalm he also reveals his Passion, so that, by the same Passion, he may make those redeemed by it subject to him and give them an example of suffering for his sake. Moreover, he treats in many ways of the condemnation of his enemies, in order to draw his own people away from conformity with them. At the end of the psalm he exhorts his own people to praise God, briefly treating their salvation.

“Save me, God the Father,” by making me steadfast and by raising me from the dead.

And it is necessary that I pray for this, because “the waters”—that is, the Jews—“have entered,” that is, will enter, “even unto my soul,” in order to take it away.

This means: Those who for a long time desired to bring about my death, but could not do so because the time of my Passion had not yet been arranged by God, will finally proceed to carry out my Passion, to such an extent that they will even take away my soul, having received this permission from God’s disposition. This is by comparison with someone who has long desired to enter a place but has been unable to do so, and who is finally permitted to enter.

“The waters have entered” is said by comparison: just as waters entering a ship sink the ship, so my enemies, having entered into the carrying out of my Passion, plunged me into death. They are therefore called “waters” because they plunged him into death; for it belongs to waters to submerge.

Or they are called waters because they are unstable and move themselves toward every evil, after the manner of water, which is a mobile and fluid thing.

They will have the power to enter even unto my soul because I am “fixed in the mire of the deep.” That is, I, your Word, Father, existing immutably and firmly united to human nature, am fixed in it. Human nature is called mire because it is earthly and, according to mortality, fragile; and it is called “deep mire,” that is, lowest, because it is a nature inferior to divinity. For something deep is sometimes understood as something low. Therefore “deep” is taken to mean “lowest.”

When he says “fixed,” it is understood that he is immutably and firmly united to human nature. For what is immovable and firm is customarily called fixed.

It is rightly that he says not “fixed” but “in-fixed,” as though he were saying “fixed inwardly,” so that he may indicate both that he is firmly united and that human nature lies hidden and does not appear visibly. In this he also instructs our faith, when he asserts that he is God and man.

And because I am fixed in the mire of the deep, “there is no substance”—that is, I will have no subsistence. This means: I will not subsist, that is, I will not live, but will die, since this has been arranged by my Father.

In another translation it reads: “I cannot stand.”

Or it may be understood in this way: Save me, therefore, because I am fixed in the mire of the deep. This is expressed only by comparison, as though he said: It is necessary that you save me because I will be like someone fixed in the mire of the deep, who, unable to escape, is submerged. I too, being fixed in tribulations, will not escape; and because I will be like one who is fixed, “there will be no substance.” This is not changed.

Or in this way: The waters will enter even unto my soul because I am fixed in the mire of the deep; that is, because I, living among the Jews, who are the deepest mire, am fixed—inwardly firm and steadfast in soul—so that I do not conform to them out of fear, even though outwardly I may appear weak in the flesh.

They are rightly called mire because they are filthy in their iniquities and muddy, after the manner of mud, which is a muddy and dirty substance. They are also rightly called “mire of the deep” because they are deepest in their filth.

But since he had said that they were mire, someone might think that God had naturally made them mire, and thus that all blame would be transferred to him, while they themselves would be excusable. He intends to remove this implication by adding:

“And this fact—that they are mire—is not substance,” that is, it is not some nature created in them by God.

This means: God did not create them muddy and filthy; rather, through their iniquities they themselves became muddy and filthy.

I said that the waters will enter even unto my soul, and this unjustly, without any evil deserving it on my part.

“For I have come into the height of the sea,” that is, by a gracious will I approached the Jews, who are high and deep in the bitterness of their sins. And when I came, I labored to instruct them, crying out to them through preaching and through works.

This means: By gratuitous clemency I came to them, and I labored with the insistent cry of preaching and works in order to lead them back to the way of salvation.

“And the storm submerged me,” that is, they themselves became stormy. Namely, amid the tribulations and blasphemies rising against me, like a storm they will submerge me—that is, they will plunge me from life into death.

He sends us here to the historical figure of Jonah, who, having been submerged by the storm of the sea and swallowed by the whale, escaped after three days, when the whale vomited him out upon the shore (Jon. 2:11). So too the Lord Jesus, existing for three days in the power of the Jews, by whom he was plunged into death, rose after three days.

I say that I labored, crying out. And while I cried out, “my throat became hoarse”; that is, my throat will be comparable to a hoarse throat. Just as someone whose throat is hoarse is not heard, so my preaching was not heard by them.

All this is as though he said: I am worthy to be saved, for they will unjustly kill me, although I came to instruct them for their salvation and they neglected to hear me.

By depressing the portion of his enemies, he seems all the more to exalt his own. In order to increase the merit of his salvation, he shows that the storm destined to submerge him will be exceedingly great, when he adds:

I say that the storm will submerge me; because of this storm “my eyes failed,” that is, the apostles will fail. They are called eyes because they illuminate my whole body, namely, the Church, through preaching and life. They will fail in this way: they will leave me alone and flee.

Yet this remains what I hope in my God. It is as though he said: Although they will fail me, they will not have the example of my failing. For I will not fail, but in my God, whom I obey above all, having hope of being raised, I will remain immovable.

And therefore it is necessary that you save me, because the Jews who hate me without cause—that is, the Jews who persecute me out of gratuitous hatred—“have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.” That is, they will be more numerous than the hairs of my head, namely, more numerous than my disciples, who are mine and adorn me by their good life, just as hairs adorn the head.

And they will not merely be numerous, but “they have grown strong,” that is, my enemies, the Jews who persecute me while I am innocent, will be strong and effective by divine permission.

What he says here, “they have grown strong,” seems to say the same thing as what was said above, where it says, “the waters have entered,” but here it is expressed more clearly. Therefore it is repeated.

And then, when they persecute me, “I will repay what I did not seize,” that is, I will pay the penalty for the thefts of Adam and Eve, which I did not seize, that is, which I did not commit.

A person is said to seize when he presumes to take for himself what is not his. Adam and Eve therefore committed theft when, by eating the fruit, they thought to make themselves divine.

I say that I will pay the penalties for another’s thefts. And this will seem the greatest folly to unbelievers: that, although I am God and innocent, I should wish to die for the sins of others.

But you, Father, who see all things, know my folly, that is, you ordain this which appears to be folly, although it is rather the highest wisdom. Hence the Apostle says: “What is foolish in God is wiser than human beings” (1 Cor. 1:25).

I say that I did not seize anything. But the Jews think that I am committing theft and am a sinner because I call myself the Son of God and King of Israel.

“And my offenses are not hidden from you,” that is, these things which they themselves consider to be my offenses. Rather, they are the highest justice and truth, and they are not hidden from you, that is, they please you.

What he says, “they are not hidden from you,” is stated by comparison. We do not wish those things that please us to be hidden from us; rather, we often look upon them.

And therefore continue to save me, so that those who place their hope of salvation in me may not be put to shame because I have not been raised—those who await you, Lord, to raise me. “Lord,” I say, not only of earthly beings but also of the heavenly powers.

This means: Raise me not only on account of my merits, but since you, being Lord of the powers, are able to raise me, raise me, so that the apostles, who place the hope of their salvation in me and await my resurrection, may not be put to shame. For they would be ashamed to have hoped in me if I remained in death.

But let them not only not be put to shame; let them also not be confounded because of me—that is, let my apostles, who seek you through their good life, not be confounded because I was not raised.

“God of Israel,” that is, God who make all who seek you into Israel. It is as though he said: My apostles, who seek you by living well so that you may make them Israel—that is, spiritually seeing you—would be confounded by the Jews if I did not rise. That is, they would be beaten, called deceivers and liars, and even killed.

And therefore, because through me they seek you, save me so that they may not be confounded.

And therefore continue to save me, because “for your sake I have endured reproach,” that is, in order to complete the obedience imposed upon me by you—the obedience of suffering. I will endure, that is, I will patiently bear, the reproach inflicted by the Jews when they call me a liar and a deceiver.

“And shame covered my face.” That is, shame will visibly occupy my face entirely.

This means: I will suffer what usually causes the faces of many to be covered with shame—spitting, blasphemies, and blows.

And I will endure reproach to such an extent that “I have become a stranger”—that is, I will become a stranger—to my brothers, the apostles, who are the adoptive sons of my Father. They will abandon and deny me as a stranger, like Peter, who will say: “Woman, I do not know him” (Luke 22:37).

And to the sons of my mother—that is, to all the Jews, the sons of the Jewish stock from which I was born—I will become a foreigner, so that they will show me no consideration of mercy, as though I were a stranger, that is, an alien.

Or “to the sons of my mother,” that is, to the members of my own family, my fellow tribesmen, I will become a foreigner, so that they will never assist me or take my side, as though I were an alien.

And therefore continue to save me, because “zeal”—that is, indignation—“for your house,” that is, for your temple, which has been treated wickedly, “has consumed me”; that is, it will be the cause of my being consumed, namely, the reason why they will devour me in death, after the manner of food that is eaten.

It is as though he were saying: The action by which I am justly indignant at your temple, which they make a den of thieves by buying and selling in it, and from which I will drive them out (Matt. 21:12–13), will be the reason why they will unjustly kill me. Therefore I am worthy of salvation.

And therefore continue to save me, because “the reproaches of those reproaching you have fallen upon me,” that is, will fall upon me; namely, they will be turned back upon me to oppress me, like a weight that, falling upon someone, crushes him.

It is as though he said: The Jews reproach you when, abandoning your commandments, they strive to observe their own traditions. They reproach you when, setting aside your commandments, they indicate that their traditions are to prevail.

But when I rebuke them for these reproaches, they will inflict the punishment of the cross upon me, by which I will fall into death. I am therefore worthy of salvation.

And therefore continue to save me, because, while I exist in the fast of their incorporation, I have covered my soul; that is, I will conceal from them that my soul is powerful enough to condemn them, since by its mere will it could kill them.

And this concealment will become—or will be made—my reproach. It is as though he said: When I wish to be filled by their incorporation, they will make me fast by refusing to be converted. And although I could immediately condemn them by the mere will of my soul, I will patiently endure in order to leave them an example of suffering. Thus I will conceal that my soul has the power to condemn.

For this they will reproach me, asserting that I am a liar because I have claimed to be Lord and king. And because I will be so patient in fasting, I am worthy of salvation.

“Cover” is rightly used in the sense of “conceal,” because we sometimes cover a thing that we wish to hide.

And therefore continue to save me, because I have put on sackcloth; that is, I have been so grieved over their destruction as someone who, at the death of a friend, puts on his sackcloth garment—that is, uses the garment called sackcloth. In ancient times people used sackcloth as a sign of mourning at the death of friends.

And therefore continue to save me, because I have become a parable to them; that is, I have spoken to them about myself in parables in order to incorporate them into myself.

For example, I spoke of the householder who sent his son to the vineyard, whom the tenants killed (Matt. 28; Mark 12), and in many other places I spoke about myself in parables in order to attract them to myself. Parabolic words usually attract the minds of hearers more readily than they would if direct speech were made to them.

And this is as though he said: I am worthy of salvation, since I am so compassionate that I grieve over the destruction of my enemies and deal with myself in parables before them in order to attract them.

But while I am concerned for their salvation, those who sat—and still sit—at the gate of knowledge, not entering and not permitting others to enter through their bad example (Luke 2:52), namely, the scribes and Pharisees, spoke against me; that is, they will speak against me by arranging for my death.

And those who drank wine, namely, the common people, who are filled and intoxicated with bodily pleasure, which recalls them from the true will and understanding like intoxicating wine, “sang a psalm against me” by their actions; that is, it will be an exceedingly sweet psalm to them to speak against me and arrange for my death.

It is as though he said: The rulers, who lead a somewhat austere life so that they may be regarded as learned, are nevertheless at the gate of knowledge, not in knowledge itself; that is, they appear wise but are foolish. And the insolent common people, intoxicated with every kind of pleasure, take great delight in speaking against me.

Or it may be understood in this way: Those who sit at the gate of the city to administer judgments—for it was the custom of judges to sit at the gate, prepared to judge those entering and leaving—and those who drink wine at banquets “sing a psalm against me” by their actions.

It is as though he said: Wherever they gather to exercise justice, and wherever they gather to satisfy their pleasure, they always act against me, and this is their sweetest psalm.

But although they speak against me in this way, I will direct to you, God the Father, my pure and holy prayer, proceeding from right devotion, on behalf of the portion of them that is to be saved.

Therefore I am worthy to be saved, since I am going to pray mercifully for my enemies.

My prayer is as follows:

“O God the Father, it is the time of your good pleasure,” that is, the time for exercising your grace, which is pleasing to you, with “the abundance of your mercy”—that is, the mercy to be exercised upon the human race through me, who am your abundant mercy, through whom you will bestow many benefits of mercy upon the human race.

It is as though he said: Have mercy on my enemies who are to be saved; for now is the time of grace, the time of fullness, in which you ought, through me, who am your abundant mercy, to forgive the sins of both Jews and Gentiles who are to be converted.

And because the time of fullness has arrived, so that through me you may have mercy on the human race, first hear me praying “in truth,” that is, in consideration of the truth of your salvation. I pray in this way because I consider you truthful in what you promised: that you would save me.

Or I pray “in the truth of your salvation,” that is, in asking for the true and eternal salvation that you are to give.

It is as though he said: You truly ought to hear me, since I consider you truthful in what you promised: that I would be saved by you. And since I do not seek the salvation of human beings, which is vain, but the salvation of eternal immortality and impassibility, to be given by you alone, hear me in this respect.

“Deliver me from the mud,” that is, from the corruption of the flesh. For what can putrefying flesh, composed of mixed moisture, more properly be called than mud?

And do not deliver me from the mud in such a way that I first enter the mud, but so that I am not fixed in the mud; that is, deliver me in such a way that I never come into corruption, just as it is said elsewhere: “Nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10).

And in this also hear me: deliver me from those who hate me, that is, from the Jews, who will persecute me with unjust hatred.

He explains how he asks to be delivered from them by adding:

“And”—that is, namely—“deliver me from the depths of the waters,” so that the storm of the water may not submerge me. That is, let the Jewish people, which exists as stormy water and wishes to drag me into conformity with itself, like stormy water that submerges whatever exists within it, not have the power to submerge me through fear of death into conformity with itself.

“Nor let the depth of hell swallow me up.” We say that someone is swallowed when he is received unwillingly by water or by a very deep abyss.

It is as though he said: I indeed wish to go into hell in order to strip it, but not in such a way that I am unwillingly swallowed by it on account of any actual or original stain, as all others are swallowed.

“Nor let the pit”—that is, the depth of hell—“close its mouth over me once I have been swallowed,” that is, constrain or shut me in.

This means: Let it neither swallow me nor, after swallowing me, close its mouth over me, lest I be unable to depart, by comparison with a pit: if someone entered it and the mouth of the pit were closed, the one who had entered would have no power to get out, but would perish, held within.

And this is as though he said: Let hell neither swallow me nor have the ability to retain me.

And so that none of these things may occur, “hear me, O God.” He repeats this because of his intense desire to obtain what he asks.

And therefore hear me, because your mercy is kind, that is, abundant; because you are naturally abundantly merciful, hear me mercifully.

“And look upon me mercifully,” that is, have mercy so as to raise me, by comparison with someone who kindly looks upon one to whom he wishes to show mercy.

I say: Look upon me. And do this “according to the abundance of your mercies,” that is, according to your many mercies, namely, according to the many benefits of your mercy.

It is as though he said: Since you mercifully bestow many benefits upon all your creatures, it is much more fitting that you bestow upon me, who obey you above all, the benefits I request.

I ask: Look upon me. And I also ask: Do not turn away “your face”—that is, your grace—from “your servant,” that is, from me, your servant, insofar as I am human.

Grace is signified by the face because a sign of grace commonly appears in the face. “Servant” is customarily used to mean “slave.”

This means: Since your grace toward me is great, do not permit me to fall in anything, so that you might thereby turn your grace away from me.

It should be noted that he does not pray because he fears falling in anything, but so that he may leave us an example of praying that we may not fall.

And because I am afflicted—that is, I am to be afflicted in your obedience—hear me so that you may raise me, and do this quickly, namely, after three days.

He repeated “hear me” in order to add “quickly.”

“And attend to my soul,” that is, give the intention of fame to my life, so that it may be publicly known among all peoples that I have risen.

And in order to give this intention to it, first deliver it from death. This is the same in meaning as “hear me quickly”; but he repeats it because he specifies how he is to be delivered when he adds: “Deliver me,” that is, free me manifestly, not secretly.

And I ask this on account of my enemies who will guard me, who will guard me so that I do not flee, in order that they may withdraw in confusion; or on account of my enemies, both Jews and Gentiles, who make themselves my enemies by living badly, so that, once my glorious resurrection has been revealed, they may be converted through it.

“Deliver me” is stated by comparison. Someone who is rescued is delivered not secretly but openly.

It is as though he said: Deliver me openly, whether they wish it or not, and in this way let my enemies be converted.

And you ought to deliver me, for you who know all things know that my reproach, which is to be inflicted by the Jews, is false—namely, their claim, in reproaching me, that I am a deceiver, the son of a craftsman, and other such things.

And you know that the shame they will impose upon me is false—namely, that they will unjustly reckon me to be inwardly ashamed because of the consciousness of sins, although I committed no sin and no deceit was found in my mouth (1 Pet. 2:22).

And you know that the false shame they will make my own is false—namely, that they will say I feel shame, that is, embarrassment, because of the accusation of false crimes, when they lie that I am a sinner because I assert that I am God and king. Therefore I will feel no shame. For it belongs to the imperfect to blush at the imposition of false crimes.

And in your sight, since you are the judge of all, are all those who afflict—that is, will afflict—me, though I am innocent.

This means: Since you know that my reproach is false, you also, who leave nothing deserving punishment unpunished, consider how unjustly they will afflict me.

I will not endure this reproach and affliction unwillingly. For “my heart”—that is, my soul—“has waited,” that is, has long desired to suffer this reproach and this misery of afflictions, which they consider misery, although it is not misery but the highest blessedness.

And when I have reached this misery, “I looked for one who would grieve together with me, but there was none,” that is, I will patiently consider whether there is anyone who will grieve with me over his own destruction, but there will be no one who grieves.

“And I looked for one who would console me, but I found none,” that is, I will endure to see whether there is anyone who will console my sadness through his conversion, but I will find none.

For then my sadness would be consoled to some degree if each person were converted from his ignorance.

And since they neglect to grieve with me and to console my sadness, “they gave”—that is, will give—“gall for my food,” that is, bitterness.

This means: When I wish them to be sweet, that is, obedient, so that they may be my food, namely, so that by conforming them to myself I may incorporate them into myself, they will make themselves bitter to me, that is, disobedient, unwilling to become my food, which is sweet.

This means: They will give bitterness for my food; that is, they will make themselves bitter, though I wished them to be my sweet food.

And when I thirst—that is, when I will greatly desire them as a sweet wine to drink, in order to draw them into conformity with me—“they gave me vinegar,” that is, they will give me old and sour wine, “in my thirst,” that is, in my desire to incorporate them.

It is as though he said: When I thirst for them as a sweet and refreshing drink, a new drink—that is, one conformed to me, the new man—they will make themselves vinegar, namely, sour and old wine; that is, they will conform themselves to the bitterness of the old man.

And with that vinegar they will satisfy my thirst, that is, they will fill me with bitter tribulations, after the manner of the old man, while I thirst for their salvation.

It should be noted that “They gave me gall for food” and “They gave me vinegar to drink in my thirst” are almost the same, except that here he expresses the same thing by another comparison, to heap up the wickedness of their impiety; yet vinegar also signifies their oldness, which gall does not signify. For by vinegar we mean old and sour wine.

Since, then, “They will give me gall for food, and in my thirst they will give me vinegar,” I understand the following: “Let their table become before them a snare,” and so forth. Because I foresee this, I grant: “Let their table”—that is, divine Scripture, by which they are accustomed to refresh themselves spiritually, just as anyone is bodily refreshed at a table—“become for them a snare,” that is, a deception. That is to say, when badly expounded, it causes them to be ensnared, that is, deceived, after the likeness of a bird which is caught by a hidden snare.

But lest Scripture itself seem so difficult that they could in no way understand it, and thus be without excuse, he adds: “Let their table, I say, be before them” [Col. 0976A], that is, present in their sight, insofar as the clarity of Scripture itself is concerned, not insofar as their obstinate blindness is concerned. This is to say: Let Scripture—which, insofar as it is clear in itself, would be manifest to them if they believed—become obscure, deceptive, and blinding to them while they persist in unbelief; “and let it become for them a retribution.” He explains what kind of retribution by adding: “And,” that is, namely, “as a stumbling-block,” that is, a fall from vice into vice. This is to say: Let Scripture itself, causing them to fall from vice into vice, thus be a retribution for their unbelief.

He expresses this by assigning each thing its corresponding effect, showing how Scripture becomes for them both a snare and a stumbling-block, as follows: “I say, let their table become a snare”—in this way, namely: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see” [Col. 0976B], that is, let the eyes of their reason be blinded, so that they may not see rightly, that is, rightly understand Scripture. “And make their back always crooked.” This is an exposition of what he said, “Let their table become a stumbling-block”; it is spoken by comparison, as if he were saying: Permit them to fall so deeply into sins that they are weighed down by the excessive mass of their sins and cannot rise from them, after the likeness of one whose back is bent beneath a very heavy burden and who is unable to straighten himself.

Nor should you pour out upon them only wrath—that is, your vengeance—by pouring it inwardly into their souls, so that you permit them to be blinded and to fall from sin into sin; rather, “pour out your wrath upon them,” that is, pour your wrath outwardly into their bodies, so that it may overwhelm them in this world. “And in the future let the pursuing fury of your wrath seize them” [Col. 0976C], that is, condemn them in such a way that they can in no manner escape.

“Fury” means that eternal vengeance by which God will punish them in the future. In comparison with the present vengeance, it will be as great as fury is in comparison with wrath. When he says “let it seize them,” he speaks by comparison, as if he were saying: In this world they will not be seized completely. Although they are punished on account of their evil merits, they will nevertheless conceal, by false explanations, that they are being punished for this reason. But in the future they will be punished more grievously, so that the cause of their punishment will be apparent to everyone, including themselves, after the likeness of one who, having fled for a long time, is finally captured and can no longer escape.

He explains how wrath is poured out upon them by adding: “I say, pour out wrath.” Pour it out in this way, namely: “Let their habitation” [Col. 0976D]—that is, the land in which they dwell—“become desolate.” And lest anyone think that he is thereby granting that it should be abandoned in such a way that no human being dwells there, he adds, to specify the meaning: “And let their tents,” that is, their houses, which are rightly called tents because they will soon change them, after the likeness of tents, “be without an inhabitant,” that is, without one who rules them as at present.

It is as if he were saying: I do indeed grant that foreign nations may dwell there, but not they. And he rightly says not “let them remain,” but “let them dwell.” For many of them remained there as slaves, but no one thereafter dwelt there, that is, ruled there. “To dwell” is commonly used to mean “to rule.” Thus we call one who governs himself well by living rightly an inhabitant of himself. This, therefore, will justly befall them.

“For the one whom you, who are powerful, struck with mortality and passibility, they persecuted”—that is, they will persecute me. It is as if he were saying: By sinning, Adam struck himself and the whole human race; that is, he made them mortal and passible. But I, free from sin, did not strike myself; rather, your dispensation struck me, making me mortal and passible, so that the world might be saved through me. They, however, will persecute me, though innocent and struck by you, and therefore it is just that they be driven from their homeland.

And therefore, because they have added to the pain of my wounds—that is, they will add guards to the tomb in order to hold me within death forever—what is fitting is this: “Add the iniquity of the children to the iniquity of their fathers,” so that the heap of their misery may be greater; that is, since they themselves are wicked and obstinate, let them have wicked and obstinate children until the end of the world, when the remnant will be saved. And although both are wicked, “let them not enter,” that is, let them not enter the way of life, “through your justice,” that is, by remaining in justification. This is to say: Let them not be justified by you through the remission of sins.

He explains what he had earlier granted—namely, “Let the fury of your wrath seize them”—as follows [Col. 0977C]: I said that all this would happen in this world, so that their habitation would become desolate, and so forth. “And in the future let them be blotted out,” that is, let them clearly know themselves to have been blotted out of the book of the living, namely, from your disposition in which all those who are to live eternally have been appointed, just as the names of many people are written in a book; hence it is called a book.

They are not to be blotted out in such a way that they had been written, or were to be written, in that book. For no one written in it will be erased from it. Rather, he says “let them be blotted out” because they consider themselves to have been written there. It is as if he were saying: Those who now appear to themselves to be written in it shall in the future appear to themselves to have been blotted out. And in order that this erasure may befall them in the future, “let them not be written here meanwhile,” that is, let them not be appointed by God’s disposition to be among the just; that is, let God not dispose them to be here in the company of the just, that is, of those who act well. For they will not be erased in the future, and it is just that they be erased.

[Col. 0977D] For through them I am—that is, I will be—“poor and sorrowful”: they will make me sorrowful, that is, cause me to suffer grief, and they will kill me in a poor life, that is, deprived of life. But for that very reason I rejoice rather than grieve. For “your Father,” God the Father, received—that is, will receive—me; that is, for these reasons, because I will be sorrowful and poor, you, the Savior, will receive me, that is, you will protect me like a loving patron by raising me again.

And because you will receive me, “I will praise,” O hearers—that is, I will cause my members to praise—“the name of God with a song,” namely, with their voice and joyful affection, “and I will magnify him in praise,” that is, my members will offer him magnificent praise by their good works. This is to say: I will cause them to praise him with voice, affection, and works. And this praise will please God, founded [Col. 0978A] “upon a young bull,” that is, upon faith in me, the young bull—namely, the one who will be offered as a sacrifice for the salvation of the world.

This was prefigured by the bull which, as we read in the Gospel, the father of the household offered for the return of his son from his wandering, the son who had been lost and was found, who had been dead and came to life again (Luke 15:32). He calls himself a bull because he was prefigured by this bull of which we have spoken, and because he was to be sacrificed for the salvation of the world, after the manner of the bull sacrificed under the old law.

He calls himself “young” because, being the new man who was created according to God in the righteousness and holiness of truth (Eph. 4:24), he had come to draw us out of the oldness of our first father and to restore us to conformity with himself.

“I say, a bull producing hoofs and horns,” that is, having extended horns and extended hoofs—namely, great power to drive away the enemy Jews, who is considered powerless, and great discernment, though he appears foolish and senseless. By extended horns, great power of expulsion is rightly signified, because an ox with extended horns is more powerful for driving away an enemy than one with short horns. By extended hoofs, great discernment is understood, because hoofs are split and distinct.

And this is as if he were saying: That praise will please God which is founded on faith in me, who am a young bull with extended horns and extended hoofs. He says this in order, insofar as possible, to draw us toward conformity with himself, so that we may strive in every way to drive away all visible and invisible enemies and to possess discernment in all things.

Alternatively, extended horns signify the greatest power to defend one’s own, even though he did not wish to defend himself in his Passion. For horned animals defend themselves with their horns.

He then exhorts his own to see, rejoice, and seek the Lord, as follows: I said that I am poor and sorrowful, that I am to be saved, and that I am a young bull; let “the poor in spirit”—namely, my faithful, who are humble in spirit and not proud—“see” all this, that is, understand it. “And let them rejoice in my salvation,” through which they will be saved.

And because this would not be sufficient, O you poor, “seek the Lord” by doing good, and through this your soul will live in eternal glory. By the life of the soul he also gives us to understand the life of the body, which will be granted in the future. And in seeking the Lord, pray to him to give you life, for “the Lord has heard”—that is, will hear—the poor who pray; that is, he will heed the prayers of the poor, “and he has not despised”—that is, will not despise—his bound ones.

Here the lesser is said by litotes, while the greater is understood. It is as if he were saying: He will not despise those bound by the bonds of mortality and passibility, who belong to him, that is, who are subject to him; rather, he will exalt those whom he seems here to despise. Or “his bound ones” may mean those united and joined by the bond of love and subjection.

He shows whom he calls poor by adding: “Let the heavens and the earth praise him.” This one word, “let them praise,” contains as much as the other three—“let them see,” “let them rejoice,” and “let them seek the Lord.” For the one who rightly understands God praises him, rejoices, and seeks him.

I say, let the poor see, and so forth; that is, let them praise him by seeing, rejoicing, and seeking him: “the heavens,” that is, the apostles; “the earth,” that is, the Church from the Jews; and “the sea,” that is, the Church from the Gentiles. Earth is rightly understood as the Jews and sea as the Gentiles. For just as the earth is surrounded on every side by the sea, so the land of Judah, which is a small part of the earth, is enclosed on every side by the Gentiles.

But lest the heavens, the earth, and the sea seem to have come of themselves to become the Church, he humbles them by adding: “And let the creeping things in them praise him,” that is, those who are in them—namely, those who formerly existed as creeping things. This is an intransitive construction. It is as if he were saying: I speak of the heavens, the earth, and the sea, which formerly were creeping things, that is, clung to earthly things and did not look toward heavenly things, after the manner of creeping things which crawl upon the earth.

It is as if he were saying: They ought to praise him because he has made them, from creeping things, people who strive toward heavenly things.

I say, let them praise him, and for this reason: “God will save Sion,” that is, he will save his own in the future with perfect salvation, restoring them to immortality and impassibility. I mean those of his own who have been made Sion, that is, who see God not through a mirror but face to face, manifestly.

Or it may be understood in this way: “He will save Sion,” that is, he will restore it to the heavenly Sion, which will be his city, composed of angels and human beings. As regards human beings, it was destroyed through Adam; as regards the angels, it was not. Meanwhile, “the cities of Judah” will be built here in virtues, that is, the churches of the faithful who confess God with pure faith. For Judah is interpreted as “confession.” Thus by the cities of Judah the churches of the faithful are signified, who are confessors of God and are strongly fortified in virtues, after the likeness of cities. He rightly uses “cities” in the plural.

For although all the faithful, according to the faith, are one catholic Church, there are nevertheless many churches according to the diversity of places.

I say that the cities of Judah will be built here. But in the future “they will dwell there,” that is, in Sion, in that blessed vision of God and in the city of God. They will not have this by themselves, but they will acquire Sion by inheritance, that is, because they are God’s inheritance; through my death they will be made my co-heirs.

Or it may be understood thus: They will acquire it by their good life and works, “by inheritance,” that is, for an inheritance, so that it may be an eternal inheritance for them.

“And the seed of his servants will possess it in the future,” that is, the seed proceeding from his servants will be the reason that those servants possess it—namely, the good works that they sow here in tears, so that in the future they may reap eternal blessedness with joy (Ps. 125:6).

But since doing good is nothing without charity, he specifies as follows: I say that the faithful will dwell in Sion through their good works, and, that is, those will dwell in it “who love his name,” namely, the name of God which is “Lord”; that is, they love with chaste love the one who is Lord. Hence the Apostle says: “If I distribute all my goods as food for the poor, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3).

[Col. 0980A] Through this he invites us to good works and to the love of God, by which one comes to dwell in the heavenly homeland.

Alternatively, these three verses may be read as follows: I exhort the heavens, the earth, and the sea to praise God. I exhort the heavens and the earth—that is, the apostles and the primitive Church—to praise God because I foresee that God will save Sion, that is, through my death he will save it by remitting sins and justifying the primitive Church from the Jews. He will make it Sion, that is, exalted in the contemplation of heavenly mysteries.

And I invite the sea—that is, the Church from the Gentiles—to praise God because I foresee that through my death the cities of Judah will be built by God the Father in virtues, that is, the churches of the Gentiles confessing God, which were destroyed through Adam. Those cities, once built, will dwell there in Sion, that is, they will continually dwell in conformity with that Sion, the primitive Church, which will be far more perfect. They will dwell there in such a way that they will acquire it by inheritance.

“To acquire” and “to dwell” mean the same thing, but he repeats himself in order to specify the manner, adding “by inheritance.” This is to say: They will acquire by faith and good works conformity with that Sion by inheritance, that is, by hereditary right, so that by right they are one inheritance of God with that Sion. For although the promise of the inheritance was made to the sons of Abraham, they will nevertheless be sons of Abraham not according to the flesh. Since they will become my spiritual sons, and I am the son of Abraham according to the flesh, through me they will become true sons of Abraham and by right will be God’s inheritance together with the Jews.

This has been said concerning the primitive churches of the Gentiles. He speaks of the churches that will succeed them when he adds: “And the seed of his servants will possess it.” It is as if he were saying: Not only will the primitive cities of Judah dwell in it, but the seed of his servants will possess it; that is, those who will be the seed, or spiritual children, of his servants—namely, of God’s apostles and of those primitive cities—will possess that Sion according to conformity, just as the cities of Judah will.

He specifies whom he calls the seed of the servants by adding: “And those who love his name will dwell in it.” This is to say: By “seed” I mean those who will dwell in it, namely, those who love his name, which is “Lord”; they do not fear him, but are pleased and delighted that he is Lord, and love him with pure love.

# ON PSALM LXIX

The title of the sixty-ninth Psalm: “To the end. A Psalm of David, for remembrance, because the Lord saved him.”

This is expounded as follows: This Psalm belongs to David, that is, these words are Christ’s; it is “for remembrance,” that is, for frequent recollection, “because the Lord saved him,” that is, will save him, with a salvation directed toward the end, that is, toward the perfection and completion of himself and his own: of himself, namely, according to immortality, impassibility, and ineffable glorification; and of his own, according to the remission of sins and justification in the present, and according to the perfect blessedness of body and soul in the future.

It is as if he were saying: Before his Passion, Christ, foreseeing the salvation of himself and of his own, frequently uttered this prayer, in which he prays for the resurrection, for steadfastness in the Passion, for the conversion of enemies who are to be saved, and for the joy and exultation of his own. He invites them to magnify God and humble themselves, and by his example exhorts them to prayer.

“God the Father, attend to my help,” that is, make yourself attentive to my help, so that, just as I merit an intense salvation, you may also grant it intensely, by raising me and making me immortal and impassible. And do not defer this help until the general resurrection; hasten to help me, so that by raising me after three days you may restore me to perfect blessedness.

And through the fact that you will help me, let those who seek to take away my soul—namely, the Jews—not be put to shame with a good shame, but be reverent, that is, fear on account of their sins. And not only those who seek my soul, but also those who merely wish me evil, let them be turned backward and put to shame.

“Let them be put to shame”: this is an inversion of the order, meaning, let them be ashamed of their wickedness and thus turn backward from it, following after me, that is, becoming my followers. For many wish me evil who do not seek my soul.

I say, let them be turned away, and let this turning not be deferred until the future age. Rather, let those who wish evil, saying to me, “Good, good,” be ashamed immediately—that is, shortly after my resurrection—and turn away from their wickedness: “Teacher, we know that you are true” (Matt. 22:16) [Col. 0981C], and so forth.

This is to say: Let those who strive to deceive me by their flattering words turn away. Let those who seek my soul be put to shame.

But let those who now seek you by doing good after my example—namely, my disciples—exult in the future in you, that is, in attaining the blessedness which is in you; and meanwhile let them rejoice in the hope of attaining it. Let those same people who love your salvation—that is, the salvation which you will give them in the future, through which they will be saved both here and in the future—say in their good desire after my resurrection: “Let God Christ be magnified.”

And let this be always, so that he who has already been magnified through the resurrection and glorification of himself may be magnified here continually by remitting the sins of his own and justifying them from generation to generation until the end of the world, and in the future may be magnified through the perfect glorification of his own.

I say, let them say of me, God: “Let God be magnified.” But let them say of themselves: “O God, help me” by cooperating with me and rescuing me from sins. For “I am needy,” that is, capable of being saved by the help of no one else except you, “and poor,” that is, incapable of saving myself by my own power.

I say, “Help me,” and you, Lord, “do not delay,” that is, do not be slow to provide my help and deliverance. For you alone are my helper in doing good and my deliverer from vices. This is to say: You alone can help me and deliver me.

# ON PSALM LXX

The title of the seventieth Psalm: “A Psalm of David, of the sons of Jonadab and of the former captives.”

Here a historical figure is indicated concerning Jonadab, who was a most holy priest of God under the old law and commanded his sons neither to drink wine nor to dwell in houses, but to live in tents (Jer. 35:6–7); and the obedience of his sons did not fail to observe his commands.

Jonadab, whose name is interpreted as “spontaneous for the Lord,” fittingly signifies Christ, who is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. Serving the Lord God the Father not out of servile fear but out of spontaneous and chaste love, he completed the course of his obedience.

Christ commanded his sons—namely, his spiritual faithful—not to drink wine, that is, not to love carnal pleasure, which, by drawing people subject to it away from God, makes them senseless, after the manner of wine that intoxicates. Accordingly, he says the same in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross daily and follow me” (Luke 9:23).

He also commanded them not to dwell in houses but in tents, that is, although they dwell among earthly things, not to dwell in them as in houses, but as if in tents: they should not suppose that these things remain, after the likeness of a house, but that they pass away, after the likeness of tents. In accordance with this the Apostle says: “As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (2 Cor. 6:10). And elsewhere: “Here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one to come” (Heb. 13:14).

The wording of the title is adapted as follows: This Psalm belongs to David, that is, to Christ praying for himself, that he might be raised again and made steadfast in the Passion. It is the Psalm “of the sons of Jonadab,” that is, of Christ; and he specifies which sons when he says, “and of the former captives.”

This is to say: They were formerly captives and exiles from their homeland through Adam, but afterward were led back to their homeland through Christ. This is said to distinguish them from the heavenly spirits, who, although they are adopted sons created by the Word of God, had never previously been captives.

And he rightly says that this is the Psalm of the sons of Jonadab. In this Psalm Christ speaks of the salvation, praise, and steadfastness in preaching of his sons. He also speaks, by way of concession, of the confusion and shame of his enemies.

“In you, Lord, I have hoped.” This asserts merit. It is as if he were saying: Lord Father, I have hoped for the things that are in you—immortality and impassibility. Therefore, “let me not be put to shame forever,” even if for a time I seem to be put to shame before the Jews. I would then be put to shame if I did not obtain what I have hoped for.

I say: Do not permit me to be put to shame, but “deliver me in your justice,” that is, according to what your justice requires. For it is just that you deliver one who hopes in you. And do not deliver me secretly, but rescue me, that is, deliver me openly, rescuing me by your power. And although you are exalted, incline your ear to me, who am weak and humble according to my humanity; that is, incline the power of your mercy, by which you hear those who cry to you—hence it is called an ear.

This is to say: Make your exalted power condescend to the prayers of me, who am weak and humble, and thus save me—both by delivering me, as I said above, and by making me glorious, immortal, and impassible, though here I am weak according to mortality and passibility.

This is spoken by comparison with a physician who kindly bends his ear toward a sick person unable to rise up to him and heals him.

I say, save me; and in order that you may afterward save me, first be for me “a protecting God,” that is, since you are my God and creator, proceed from being God for me to being my protecting God, who protects me in the Passion so that I do not fail through fear of punishment.

And “be for me a fortified place,” that is, a place of security, so that I may not even be afraid, just as a fortified place is security for those who flee to it. Many are protected who are not secure; hence the words “a fortified place” are not added superfluously.

From now on, therefore, you must be both my protector and my fortified place, because until now you have been “my strength,” that is, my strong protector, and “my refuge,” that is, my security [Col. 0983B].

It is as if he were saying: Since until now you have been my strength and refuge, and I have failed in nothing, from now on you must be my refuge and strength, so that I may not fail in the future.

Or it may be understood thus: I pray that you save me because you alone are my strength and my refuge, that is, because you alone can protect me and make me secure.

He explains what he earlier said, “rescue me,” and from whose hand he asks to be rescued, as follows:

And you also, my God, through a certain special obedience of mine, rescue me by raising me from the hand, that is, from the power, of the sinner, so that he may no longer have permission to afflict me.

He explains in detail from the hand of which sinner he asks to be rescued, saying: “Rescue me from the hand of the one acting against the law,” namely, the Jewish people, in that they neglect to obey me, although they have been commanded to do so by the law. Moses says accordingly: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him, and everyone who does not listen to that prophet shall be exterminated from my people” (Deut. 18:13; Acts 3:22–23).

“And rescue me from the hand of the unjust,” namely, the Gentile people, who will crucify me and guard me in the tomb. Although they do not act against a law which they do not possess, they are nevertheless unjust, that is, unbelieving and evil-doing.

He repeats what he prayed for—“Be for me a God,” and so forth—when he says, “Do not cast me away,” up to “because they said,” in order to place beforehand the reasons he did not previously state. These reasons are contained from the verse [Col. 0983D] “For you are my patience,” and so forth, up to “Do not cast me away.”

These words are read and construed as follows: I prayed that you rescue me from the hand of the sinner. I also pray that you do not cast me away, that is, do not despise me, so that you protect me when I am placed in the time of old age—that is, before the resurrection, for as long as I am temporal. For after the resurrection I will be eternal and without time.

I speak of the time of old age, that is, of oldness, in which I retain the oldness of Adam—not according to sin, but according to the punishment of sin; that is, in which I exist as mortal and passible, which is the punishment of Adam’s ancient sin. Therefore, do not cast me away.

For you, Lord, are “my patience,” that is, you are the cause of my patience; in order to obtain conformity with you, I will patiently endure tribulations. Therefore, do not cast me away further, because you, Lord, are my hope: in you I have hope of reward. This hope proceeds from my youth, that is, from my prudent counsel and vigor.

This is to say: I hope in you because I am prudent in counsel and vigorous in the activity of your obedience. Otherwise my hope would be in vain. He uses “youth” for prudent counsel and vigor because it belongs to the young to use prudent counsel and to be vigorous in action.

Therefore, do not cast me away further, because I have been confirmed in you, that is, made firm, “from the womb,” that is, from the time of my conception. I was not weakened in Adam through original sin, as other human beings are, who, when conceived according to the law of concupiscence—which is the punishment of original sin—become themselves guilty of original sin.

This is to say: From the time of my conception, you confirmed me, conceived without the law of concupiscence, in conformity with you, so that I might be free from sin, as you are.

Or it may be understood thus: “In you,” that is, in conformity with you, “I have been confirmed from the womb,” that is, according to the humanity which I received in the womb. According to my divinity, in which I exist as your equal, I did not need confirmation.

Therefore, do not cast me away further because you are my protector, so that I might not fall in any way: “from my mother’s womb,” that is, you have always protected me from the time when I came forth from my mother’s womb.

Or it may be understood thus: You are my protector according to that nature in which I came forth from the womb, namely, according to my humanity. It is as if he were saying: Because until now you have been my protector, I ask you henceforth not to cast me away.

And therefore, do not cast me away further, because in you my song is always founded, that is, my joyful praise, because I always praise you joyfully both in affection and in action.

Or “my song is in you,” that is, all my delight is in you. Because, having neglected all earthly things, I strive only in your praise and delight in you, I have become “like a portent to many,” that is, to the wicked, who are many in comparison with the good, whose number is small. I have become like a monster, so that they reject and abhor me entirely, as though I were a monster.

Therefore, do not cast me away further, because you are a strong helper in doing good.

Or it may be understood thus: I say that I have become a portent to many, and yet you are a strong helper, so that I may not yield to those many.

He prays that God make him persevere in his praise, as follows: Because you are my hope, and through you I have been confirmed, “let my mouth be filled with praise.” That is, since I have already praised you for the benefits you have bestowed, make my mouth entirely filled with praise; make me persevere in your praise, so that I may continually sing your glory—“all day,” that is, constantly—and your greatness.

That is to say: Make me attribute to you my glory and my greatness joyfully, considering that I am glorious and great through you.

Or it may be understood thus: Make me sing your glory and your greatness, that is, make me joyfully attribute to you the benefits mentioned above. These will be your glory and magnificence, that is, they will be the reason why you appear glorious and magnificent to human beings, namely, powerful [Col. 0985A].

All this is as if he were saying: Make me persevere in your praise in this way, so that I attribute all these benefits mentioned above to you, not to myself.

Having shown several reasons, with a prayer inserted incidentally, he finally states the purpose for which he supplied those reasons, as follows: Because you have bestowed upon me so many and such great benefits—namely, that you might be my patience, hope, confirmation, and song—do not cast me away in the time of old age.

He repeats the same thing in equivalent words, adding another reason when he says: “Do not abandon me, I say,” that is, do not cast me away in the time of old age, “when my strength will have failed.”

“Will have failed” is in the past tense, as if he were saying: You ought not to abandon me because all the strength that is in me has failed, so that it is not attributed to me; that is, I do not consider that I possess the strength I have from myself, but from you.

Or it may be a specification, as follows: “Do not abandon me, I say, when my strength fails,” that is, when my power is considered to have failed, namely, in death.

This sentence may also be read with “will have failed” if it is not understood as a past tense.

He repeats what he said above—“rescue me from the hand of the sinner”—in equivalent words when he says, “God, do not be far from me,” placing beforehand other reasons that he had not stated. These are contained from the place where it says “because they said,” up to “God, do not be far away.”

This is read as follows: I pray not only that you do not cast me away in the Passion; I also pray, O God, that you do not be far from me by delaying my resurrection until the future. But you, who are my God and whom I obey in a special way, “look to my help,” namely, so that you raise me after three days.

And I pray this because my enemies, the Jews, said—that is, will say—to one another, and said it to my disadvantage. He specifies whom he calls enemies when he adds: And those enemies, I say, who watched over my soul, that is, who will lie in wait for my soul, in case they should see anything in it worthy of reproach, “made”—that is, will make—“a conspiracy,” joining together in wickedness.

By saying “they made a conspiracy,” he notes something especially grave. For it is worse to deliberate about evil by counsel than to act rashly.

I say that they made a conspiracy, saying to one another: “Pursue him with tribulations; for God, whose Son he claims to be, has abandoned him,” that is, has despised him. And not only, “Pursue him,” but also “seize him,” so that he may not escape; that is, kill him, because there is no one to rescue him.

It is as if he were saying: He says that God will rescue him from death after three days, but he will not rescue him. Therefore seize him by death.

He speaks, by way of concession, of the confusion of the enemies, as follows:

I said that you should look upon my aid, and that, by contrast, they should be confounded in evil—that is, should be ashamed and deprived of every worldly prosperity—those who disparage the virtues of my soul; namely, the Jews who take away my virtues, as far as their own opinion is concerned, by saying that I am a deceiver and a destroyer of the Law. And let them not merely be confounded and deprived of prosperity, but let them be covered with confusion and shame—that is, let them be surrounded by blushing and bodily destruction. This is said by comparison with a body that is covered with garments on every side [Col. 0986A]. This means: Let those who seek evil against me—namely, in order to kill me and keep me in death—have complete confusion and shame. As if he said: Let them have not only confusion and blushing because they disparage me, but also because they seek evil against me.

Above, he used “confusion” for blushing and “deprivation” for destruction, where he said, “Let them be confounded and deprived.” Here, however, he uses “confusion” for destruction and “shame” for blushing.

He speaks as follows about the hope of his people and the praise they will offer to God: I say that the enemies will be confounded. But I will always hope—that is, my people will always hope in you for perfect salvation in the future, after the example of my salvation—and I will add to all your praise; that is, they will add praise belonging to you beyond all the praise given by the former people [Col. 0986B]. This means: They will praise you with every kind of praise, which will be more perfect than the praise of the former people, since they too will be more perfect in the future.

It should be noted that he does not say that the praise of the apostles and of the others who exist under the New Law is more perfect than the praise of certain people who, although they lived under the Old Law, were nevertheless men of the New Testament through faith, such as Elijah and the other most perfect men who utterly despised the world. Rather, he says that the praise of the new people is more perfect than the praise of those old people who were not so perfect, of whom there was a great number.

Or, “They will add praise beyond all your praise”—the praise bestowed on you for the creation of all things—so that, just as you are praised for the creation of the world, they will praise you much more for the restoration of the human race.

I say that they will add praise—that is, they will praise you through their innocence and justice, which they will not regard as their own:

“But my mouth”—that is, the mouth of my people—“will announce your justice”; that is, it will announce that all their justice comes from you. And “all day”—that is, continually—it will announce your salvation; that is, it will announce that future salvation will come from you, not from their merits.

Or it may be understood thus: I say that my people will always hope in you, and I say this generally. But “my mouth”—that is, the preachers, who are to be called “mouth” in my body, the Church—will announce that all your justice belongs to you, that is, comes from you, and will announce your salvation all day. These statements are not changed. Therefore my people will announce that all justice comes from you.

“For I have not known the letter to be justifying” [Col. 0986D]; that is, my people will know that the letter of the Old Law cannot justify anyone. “For the letter kills” (II Cor. III, 6). This means: They will know to be false what the Jews asserted—namely, that someone could be justified through the Law. For the Law merely indicates sin; it does not also help one to abstain from it.

And by recognizing through the letter that they cannot be justified, “I will enter”—that is, my people will enter—“into the powers of the Lord.” This means: Those who previously considered themselves capable of doing good through free will and through the Law, once they recognize their insufficiency for doing good, will enter into the powers of the Lord; that is, inspired by divine grace, they will enter upon this course so that they may regard their power to do good and abstain from vices as coming not from the Law but from the Lord [Col. 0987A]. Hence it is read in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5).

They will not merely announce that their justice is yours—that is, comes from you—but, O God, “I will remember your justice alone”; that is, my people will remember your justice, which alone exists, that is, which is unique, incomparable, and most perfect. Hence it is read: “No living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm CXLII, 2).

This means: They will say that you alone possess unique and most perfect justice, and they will say this with remembrance, not carelessly. Yet the fact that they will announce that their justice is yours, and will proclaim your justice alone and most perfectly with remembrance, will not come from them alone, but with your cooperation.

“For you, God, have taught me”—that is, you will teach my people by your spiritual wisdom, which you will inwardly impart to them—and therefore “I will proclaim your wonders”; that is, my people will proclaim your wonders to others: namely, the justice that you will restore through me to the human race, and your salvation, which you will give in the future.

This has already been said above, where he said, “My mouth,” and so forth. But he repeats it in order to show the perseverance of their proclamation, as follows: I say that my people will announce your wonders, and this from my youth—that is, from the time of the martyrs, who will be young, meaning ardent in faith and vigorous in action, like young people who are fervent in age and vigorous in action—and now, that is, during that very youth, they will continue to proclaim; that is, they will proclaim continually and steadfastly, not failing through fear of death. And my people will proclaim these things into old age—that is, until the time of the confessors, who will be old, meaning somewhat colder than the martyrs [Col. 0987C], since they will not undergo bodily death for God, just as old age is a colder period than youth.

And they will proclaim into extreme old age—that is, until the time of Antichrist, in which many will grow cold from the fervor of faith. For this reason it is called “extreme old age,” since extreme old age is the coldest and most failing period of life. At that time the Lord says in the Gospel: “Because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matthew XXIV, 12).

This means: My people will praise you steadfastly—both those who will be in youth, those who will be in old age, and those who will be in extreme old age.

Or he calls the time of the martyrs “youth,” the time of the confessors “old age,” and the time of Antichrist “extreme old age,” because the martyrs came first, the confessors followed them in time, and finally the time of Antichrist will come. Therefore my people will proclaim in youth, old age, and extreme old age.

“Do not abandon me”—that is, my people—“without help until they announce to every generation”—that is, until they announce to every kind of generation that will come until the end of the world—“your arm, your power, and your justice”: namely, me, who am your arm, through whom you will vigorously defeat the devil, just as someone overcomes a weak enemy through the strength of his arm; and who am your power, through whom you will make the faithful powerful in resisting vices; and who am your justice, through whom you will justify the faithful.

I say that I am your power and justice reaching to the highest places—that is, I am not powerful only among human beings, but also among the highest heavenly spirits [Col. 0988A].

Or this may be read differently, without changing “arm”: I say, until they announce your arm, your power, and your justice, going from the lowest rational creatures to the highest—that is, to the super-heavenly rational creatures.

This means: Until they announce that all power and justice come from you, beginning with the power and justice of human beings, who are lowly in comparison with the angels, and proceeding to the power of the angels themselves. As if he said: They will regard as coming from you the fact that the righteous will then be powerful in good works, as well as the fact that the angels are righteous in the affection of their love for God and powerful—that is, exalted—in blessedness.

He commends those angels to the praise of God, speaking of them with admiration, as follows: I say, “to the highest places,” and those great works of yours—that is, your highest works—which are called great because they are great in the excellence of their dignity; which is to say, how great are the things you have made, how worthy they are. And therefore, who is like you in the sublimity of power? No one.

As if he said: From this it can be proved that no one is like you. And because no one is like you, since you are so powerful, Adam and Eve wanted to make themselves like you by eating the apple, saying: “We shall be like gods” (Genesis III, 5). How many—that is, how great—tribulations you have shown me—that is, to my people—so that they would no longer grow proud! And how many and how evil—that is, how harmful—they were: death, namely, and every kind of suffering, which are most harsh and harmful to soul and body [Col. 0988C].

And you, turning away from anger—that is, from the vengeance you exercise upon them through tribulations—“gave me life”; that is, through my death you will give life to my people, making them innocent and just through inward vivification. And in the future you “brought me back”—that is, you will bring my people back—to the homeland from which they were expelled through Adam.

I say that my people will again be brought out of the depths of the earth—that is, from the lowest condition of earthly existence. Earlier you brought them out in Adam from the lowliness and utility of earthly existence, so that from the clay of the earth you might make them living and not subject to death. Through Adam’s sin they were cast back into the same condition, so that by dying they might become ash and dust; from this condition you will rescue them in the future.

We call an abyss an excessive depth, and therefore “abyss” is used for baseness [or: “lowly condition”; the manuscript reading is uncertain].

I say that you will bring them back from the depths of the earth. Then you multiplied your magnificence, O God—that is, you will make your magnificent glory manifold in them, making them immortal and incapable of suffering, and happy with every blessedness.

Earlier, having turned toward me, you consoled me—that is, you will give life to my people—and by this you will console them, as I said above where I wrote, “You will give me life.” He repeats this in order to show through the effects how he will take them up from the depths. Through these effects it will be proved that you have given them life.

“For I too will confess,” and so forth. “For” marks a connection, and it is rightly placed with respect to the order. As if he said: You will give life, and my people will confess to you—that is, to your honor—your truth: namely, that you are truthful in your promise concerning the restoration of the world, which has been completed through me, and concerning the future salvation that is to be completed [Col. 0989A].

I say that my people will confess to you. I say that some of my people exist in the “vessels of the psalm,” that is, in the psalterium, which is called the vessel of the psalm because the psalm is made in it—namely, in contemplation of heavenly goods, through which they will resound in God’s praise in the manner of a psalterium, which resonates from above. He uses “vessels” in the plural with reference to the many faithful.

And “I will sing to you”—that is, some of my people will praise you by good works—“existing in the lyre,” that is, in the active life. This is appropriately signified by the lyre, which resonates from below, since the active life is lower than contemplation.

I say that they will sing and confess to you. I say this to you who are “the Holy One of Israel”—that is, so holy that you are able to sanctify all the faithful whom you make Israel. It is from desire for this that they sing and confess to you.

This is as if he said: It will be possible to see in this that you have given them life, because they will sing and confess to you; otherwise this would not happen.

And when I sing to you—that is, when my people praise you—“my lips will rejoice”; that is, the lips of my people will rejoice in that very praise. And lest we understand external lips, he adds: “And in this way, namely, my soul”—that is, the souls of my people—“which you have redeemed”—that is, my people will rejoice in praising you through the affections of their souls—because you will redeem it through me.

The affections are called “lips” because through them the soul speaks inwardly to itself. And not only will the soul of my people rejoice in your praise, but “my tongue”—that is, the tongue of my people—“will meditate upon your justice”; that is, in praising you, they will announce with meditation, not rashly, that all justice is yours [Col. 0989C], that is, comes from you.

This was stated above, where he wrote, “My mouth,” and so forth. He repeats it here in order to add: They will announce it with this consideration. This will occur when those who seek evil against me—namely, the Jews—have been confounded in evil and have trembled; that is, when they are ashamed because of my resurrection and are afraid during the persecution of Vespasian and Titus.

This means: When they see that by your just judgment they have been made ashamed and fearful, they will announce this justice of yours to others, so that those others may withdraw from imitating them.

Or it may be understood thus: The tongue of my people will utter your justice meditatively; that is, it will say that you are a just judge, when those who seek evil against me have been confounded and have trembled—that is, when they have foreseen that they will fear and be confounded in every way in the future [Col. 0989D].

Those who seek evil against my people, who here do not appear fearful but secure, nor confounded but blessed. This means: They will announce that you are a just judge because they will foresee that their enemies will be confounded and fearful by your just judgment.

## ON PSALM LXXI

The title of the seventy-first Psalm: “A Psalm of David concerning Solomon.” It is explained as follows: This psalm belongs to the prophet David, who looks toward Solomon—that is, toward the true Christ, Solomon, meaning the true peaceful one, who made both one and who is our peace (Ephesians II, 14).

Although this psalm seems to contain certain things that happened to Solomon, the son of David—namely, when it says, “O God, give your judgment to the king and your justice to the king’s son,” and, “He will judge the poor of the people,” along with other such statements—nevertheless, since it also contains certain things that in no way happened to that Solomon, where it says, “He will remain with the sun and before the moon,” and, “All kings will adore him,” and similar statements, the whole psalm must appropriately be referred to Christ, the true and signified Solomon.

For Ezra, who imposed the titles of the Psalter and lived long after Solomon, king of Israel, recognizing that Christ had been signified by that Solomon both according to the interpretation of the name and according to the events themselves, gave this psalm—which is to be read as concerning Christ—the title “of Solomon.”

In Solomon’s time there was very great justice and peace in Israel. Hence he too is called “the peaceful one.” His kingdom was also greatly extended, and he himself was exceedingly wise, so much so that the queen of the South is said to have come from the ends of the earth to hear his wisdom (III Kings X, 1).

So too Christ, who was the true peaceful one, justified the world and reconciled it to God. Being most wise, he called to himself the queen from the ends of the earth—namely, the Church, whom he made a queen and his bride from a captive—and through preachers summoned her to himself; and he caused her to hear the wisdom of his commandments.

The Prophet speaks at considerable length in his praise about the extension of Christ’s kingdom, the justice and peace that will exist in his time, his eternity, how he will acquire his kingdom, who will belong to it, and the blessing and salvation of his kingdom.

At the beginning of the psalm he therefore prays that God the Father may grant him judgment, here and in the future, for the benefit of his people. He also prays that the mountains and hills may receive peace from God and communicate the peace they have received to the people. At the end of the psalm, by blessing the same king, he gives us an example of blessing him.

“O God, give your judgment to the king”: that is, give Christ the king the judgment that you exercise with the Holy Spirit over the world and will exercise in the future, according to his humanity, while according to his divinity he already possesses it.

He shows what judgment he means, and to which king, when he adds: “And your justice to the king’s son.” Here, through hendiadys, “justice” means the same as “judgment.” As if he said: Give your just judgment to the Son of your king, Christ.

And he rightly says “your,” since this judgment belongs to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Although some support this statement: “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22), this presents no obstacle, since it must be understood thus: “The Father judges no one” visibly, because he is invisible; “but has given all judgment to the Son,” according to the Son’s humanity, while according to his divinity he is equal to the Father and receives nothing from him.
