Thus he gave all judgment to the Son so that, appearing visibly, the Son might judge everything in the future, while the power of the whole Trinity cooperates invisibly.

He explains this judgment part by part, as follows: I say, give to Christ, the Son of your king, your just judgment; namely, grant him to judge your people in justice and your poor in judgment. “Justice” and “judgment” mean the same thing.

He calls the lesser faithful “the people,” but the holier faithful “the poor”—those who, utterly despising the world, follow Christ naked and destitute [Col. 0991A].

It is as if he said: Grant him the power in the future to judge your people—that is, the lesser faithful, who are called “the people” because their number will be very great in comparison with the wicked.

Or the two verses may be read as follows: O God, give your judgment to the king, both here and in the future; and, so that this judgment may benefit the people who are to be saved, give your justice—that is, the justice that comes from you—to the son of that king, namely, the Christian people, who will be the spiritual son of that king.

This means: Justify that son of the king, both through the remission of sins and through the perfection of virtues and good works. For if he were left unjust, he would be condemned by the king’s just judgment.

He explains the judgment part by part as follows: I say, give judgment—namely, grant him to judge here the people you have called the king’s son—in justice; that is, according to the justice that this people will deserve through what you have given them, so that, although this people is just in this world, it may be justified still more by that same king [Col. 0991B].

And grant that king to judge in the future, in just judgment, your poor—namely, the faithful who are not poor apart from their will, but are your poor, that is, poor for your sake.

By speaking of the greater faithful as “the poor,” he also indicates the lesser faithful, who, although they do not entirely abandon the world, will nevertheless be saved in the future.

But so that this judgment may take place both here and in the future, “let the mountains receive peace to be presented to the people”; that is, let the apostles, who are high like mountains in comparison with the hills, receive peace from that king: namely, the love of God and neighbor, through which peace is possessed toward God and toward one’s neighbor.

Therefore peace is rightly called what they are to announce to the people, that is, to the lesser faithful. And because the mountains would not suffice, let the hills—that is, the lesser preachers, who are called hills because they will be lower in holiness than the mountains, just as hills are lower than mountains—receive from the mountains justice to be announced to the people.

“Justice” means the same as “peace.” And the love of God and neighbor is rightly called justice, since everyone who possesses it perfectly is perfectly justified.

He now declares what he expressed through prayer and desire, where he wrote, “To judge the people,” and so forth: I say, let the mountains receive peace and the hills justice, to be presented to the people.

And after the mountains and hills have received peace for the people, that king will judge in the future the poor of the people; namely, he will reward by his just judgment those whom I called mountains and hills, who will be poor here among his people because they abandon the world.

And he will save the sons of the poor with eternal salvation—namely, their subjects, who will be the spiritual sons of the apostles and preachers—and he will humble the calumniator, namely the devil. He will cast him down so that he may no longer have an opportunity to tempt or accuse his own.

As long as this world lasts, he is a calumniator—that is, an accuser—not by voice but by his evil intention. He is also a calumniator in that he is, as far as he can be, a disturber of every good. For we ordinarily call someone a calumniator when he intends to disturb what is good.

Or “he will humble the calumniator” may mean: He will humble any impious person who here brings calumnies—that is, scandals—against his own people, so that he may no longer have an opportunity to slander them [Col. 0992A].

Or it may be read according to the interpretation we gave to the first two verses, without changing the connection:

After the mountains, hills, and people have received peace, he will judge here—that is, reward here—the poor of the people, namely the greater faithful, so that, since they are just, he may make them more just.

By this part he indicates that he will also reward the lesser faithful, although they are not equally perfect, in accordance with what their justice demands. And he will save in the future with eternal salvation the sons of the poor—that is, the lesser faithful.

By this it is understood that he will save much more the poor themselves, whose sons they will be. And he will humble the calumniator in the future. This statement is not changed.

He praises him for his eternity as follows: I say that he will humble the calumniator, and that same king who will humble him will remain in the future “with the sun”—that is, with the majesty of the Father, consubstantial with him according to his divinity.

The Father is rightly called “the sun,” whose nature is so radiant that no one can contemplate it perfectly, just as the brightness of the sun cannot be fully seen by human sight. And he will remain “before the moon”—that is, in the presence of the moon according to his humanity.

According to his divinity he is not local; that is, according to his humanity he will be present in the presence of his Church, so that he may continually be seen by that Church for the increase of its blessedness.

He shows what he calls “the moon” when he adds: “In generation and generation he will be,” that is, in the presence of every generation of the righteous. Since he repeats “generation,” he indicates all the generations of the righteous.

“Generation and generation” means the same as “the moon.” He calls the Church “the moon” because, during persecution, it diminishes through the imperfection of its children, like the moon, and during peace it increases through the growth of its children’s regeneration.

Or it may be understood thus: “He will remain with the sun,” that is, for as long as the sun endures. He explains this when he adds below: namely, until the generation of this generation that follows, and the final generation. By repeating “generation,” he indicates all generations.

As if he said: He will remain for as long as all the generations of the world are destined to last. And lest anyone think that he will not remain after the sun and the generations, he adds [Col. 0992D]: “And he himself is before the moon”—that is, he will be more excellent and more enduring than the moon, namely, than every changeable thing, which is signified by the moon because the moon often changes.

Or, lest he appear not to have existed before the world, he adds: “And he remained before the moon,” according to his divinity. For by the moon, which is a part of all creation, he wishes to signify every creature.

Since he had called him king and said that he would judge the poor and the sons of the poor, one might ask how he will acquire them for his kingdom. He shows this as follows:

I said that he will be king and will judge the poor and the sons of the poor. He will acquire these poor and sons of the poor for himself in his kingdom in this way: First he will descend—that is, he will come from his lofty invisibility into the knowledge of the primitive Church formed from the Jews—just as rain descends upon a fleece while the threshing floor remains dry in the time of Gideon [Col. 0993A].

And afterward he will descend into the knowledge of the Gentiles, like dripping drops of rain; that is, just as drops of rain descend upon the earth—that is, upon the threshing floor—while the fleece remains dry.

He appropriately says “dripping,” so that the comparison may be effective. For just as a drop of rain drips—that is, flows little by little—so his knowledge gradually flowed through preachers into the minds of human beings.

He refers us to the historical figure of Gideon. When the Lord had said that Gideon would liberate Israel from the nations that had oppressed it, Gideon asked the Lord for a sign of this salvation. The Lord granted it to him: he was to find a fleece placed on the threshing floor wet while the threshing floor was dry, and on the following day the threshing floor wet while the fleece was dry (Judges VI, 37–40).

By the fleece, therefore, first soaked by the rain, the Jewish people was prefigured. It had separated itself from God without causing God any loss, just as a fleece can be torn from a sheep without harm to the sheep. Yet this people was to be partially infused with the rain of spiritual grace while the Gentiles remained dry.

By the threshing floor, however, which was afterward wet while the fleece was dry, the people of the Gentiles was prefigured. It was afterward to be filled with that grace, while the Jews, for the most part, remained dry with respect to that grace, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “A blindness in part has happened in Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter” (Romans XI, 25).

And the Gentile people was appropriately signified by the threshing floor. For just as the threshing floor surrounded the fleece on every side, so the countless people of the Gentiles surrounded the Jews, whose number was not so great, on every side geographically [Col. 0993C].

They were also appropriately called a threshing floor because they were earthly in their affections and had no understanding of the things that belong to God. For a threshing floor is nothing other than earth.

Or this verse may be read as follows: I say that he will judge the poor and the sons of the poor, and first he will descend into the Virgin’s womb—not locally, but spiritually—as rain descends upon a fleece.

This means: Just as rain descended upon that fleece without corrupting the fleece, and was then wrung out without injuring the same fleece, so the Word of God will descend into the Virgin—that is, will become incarnate in the Virgin—and will be born without corrupting the Virgin. Afterward he will descend into the knowledge of human beings, so that, imbued with spiritual grace, he may cause them to bear good works for God, just as dripping drops of rain soak the earth and make it germinate [Col. 0993D].

He praises him for his justice as follows: I say that he will descend, and “in his days”—that is, in the time of his reign—“justice will arise”; that is, the human race, which fell through Adam into injustice, will be justified through him, something it could not attain through the Law and free will.

And not a small measure of justice, but “an abundance of peace”—that is, the most abundant peace, namely, the love of God and neighbor, which is called both justice and peace, as was shown above.

This abundance of peace will endure until “the moon is taken away”—that is, until the Church passes from its present condition into a perfect condition.

Or the moon that is in the heavens will be taken from its present condition into a perfect condition. For the moon, the sun, and the other elements will be changed.

In accordance with what is read: “Behold, I make all things new” (Apocalypse XII, 5). This means: His peace will last as long as this world passes away—not that it will not last forever afterward, but we often have expressions of this kind, as when we say, “Wait for me until I come,” without intending that he should depart afterward.

He also praises him for the greatness of his kingdom, as follows: I say that in his days justice will arise, and he will rule from the eastern sea to the western sea, and from the southern sea to the northern sea.

This means: His dominion will last from east to west and from south to north, and he will begin to rule from the river—that is, from the Jordan, which is called “the river” by antonomasia because it is the most distinguished river in Judea.

By the Jordan he signifies baptism, because the Lord was baptized in the Jordan. As if he said: His dominion will begin to appear from the time of baptism, through his preaching.

Before his baptism he did not preach—not because he was ignorant, for from the time of his birth, according to his humanity, he knew everything. For, as Augustine asserts, ignorance could not have had a place where the eternal wisdom of the Father was personally and unceasingly present. Rather, he chose to postpone preaching until after his thirtieth year and after baptism, in order to give the example that no one should preach before baptism and before the age of thirty.

Because he had said “from sea to sea,” and since there are many seas, one might understand the Mediterranean Sea or some nearby sea, and thus the whole world would not be understood as subject to his dominion. Therefore it is added: “From the river”—that is, from baptism—“to the ends of the earth he will rule” [the supplied text reads *damnabitur*, apparently an OCR error for *dominabitur*], that is, everywhere on earth.

Or “from the river he will begin to rule” may mean from the Jewish people, from which he will establish the primitive Church. This people is understood metaphorically through the Jordan, which is called “the river” by antonomasia because it is in Judea, extending to the ends of the earth—that is, to all nations [Col. 0994C].

And lest only those who would not be very sinful be understood as belonging to his kingdom, he shows that even those who are most foul in sins will be in his kingdom, thereby commending his justice still more, as follows:

I say that he will rule, and behold those over whom he will rule: “The Ethiopians”—that is, those who are blackest in character, as an Ethiopian is black in body—“will fall”; that is, they will humble themselves from their pride, and they will fall “before him,” that is, into his good pleasure.

Or “they will fall before him” means that they will adore him. For it is characteristic of those who adore someone to fall before the one whom they adore.

And his enemies, who will not wish to fall before him, “will lick the earth”; that is, they will cling to earthly things with excessive desire. This is by comparison with someone for whom the food he has eaten is not enough, so that he also licks the vessel in which it was placed; or by comparison with certain animals whose nature it is to lick the earth.

As if he said: Acting irrationally, they will embrace earthly things with excessive desire, and these things will be the cause of their destruction. He says this to heighten the misery of their condition.

He shows, moreover, for the praise of God, that these Ethiopians will possess various virtues, adding as follows: I say that the Ethiopians will fall, and they will become “kings of Tarshish”—that is, kings of themselves—and this in such a way that they will be kings of contemplation, contemplating heavenly things rather than earthly things. For *Tharsis* is interpreted as “contemplation.”

They will offer gifts to that king—namely, their contemplation and their other virtues. They will not attribute these to themselves, but will testify that they are gifts of that king; and thus they will offer those gifts to him.

And the Ethiopians, having also become “islands”—that is, innocent and casting far from themselves every surrounding sin, like islands that repel the force of the sea surrounding them and remain dry—will offer gifts to that king: namely, their innocence and their other virtues, which they will attribute not to themselves but to the king.

And those Ethiopians, having become “kings of the Arabs”—that is, humble and fruitful in producing others—and having become “kings of Sheba”—that is, kindled by the fire of charity and converted to the faith—will bring gifts to the king; that is, through their preaching they will bring others to God, whom they will cause to offer themselves as gifts to God through submission.

The Arabs are appropriately understood as the humble and fruitful. For Arabia is called “humble” or “level.” By “level” people, those who bear fruit are understood, since level fields are suited to producing fruit.

Sheba, however, is interpreted as “kindled” or “converted,” and therefore rightly signifies those who are kindled by the fire of charity and converted to the faith.

It should be noted that not all these virtues belong to everyone: namely, that all should be contemplative, innocent, humble, fruitful, converted, and kindled with charity. Rather, all of them belong to certain perfect people, while some belong to some, and others to others.

Or this may be understood literally: the kings of Tarshish, of that region, and the inhabitants of the maritime islands will offer themselves as gifts to that king through conversion; and the kings of the Arabs, those peoples, and the kings of Sheba, that land, will bring themselves as gifts to God through faith.

But lest, if it were understood literally, only those Ethiopians, the kings of Tarshish, the inhabitants of the islands, the kings of the Arabs, and the kings of Sheba be understood as adoring him, he adds:

“And all kings will adore him”—that is, they will venerate him through faith and good works—all kings, meaning rulers of every kind. By “kings” he signifies all rulers of the earth.

“All nations”—that is, nations of every kind—“will serve him with chaste love.” And rightly so, because by his death he will free the poor world, which cannot free itself by its own power, from the powerful devil, who exercises power over it through Adam’s sin. “For the ruler of this world will be cast out” (John XII, 31).

And he will free the poor one, I say, who had no helper; that is, the one who could not be freed either by himself or by any helper.

But since he had said “poor,” meaning insufficient in himself, it might appear that the poor one could be freed by someone else unless he added, “who had no helper.”

And he will not merely free him from the powerful one [Col. 0995D], but here he will spare the poor and needy—the world, namely, which is poor with respect to its own aid and needy with respect to the aid of another. He will spare it; that is, he will forgive its sins.

For he could free it from the powerful one without remitting its sins, and in that case the world would nevertheless be condemned.

I say that here he will spare it, and in the future he will save the souls of the poor with eternal salvation—namely, his faithful, who are poor, that is, humble in spirit.

When he says that the souls are to be saved, the salvation of the bodies is also understood. He explains this verse by assigning each phrase its proper meaning when he adds: “From usuries,” and so forth.

This is read in the following inverted order. I say: Here he will spare the poor and needy—that is, by his death he will redeem the souls of his own from iniquity; in other words, by the price of his death he will rescue them from every crime. And I say that in the future he will save the souls of the poor—that is, he will redeem them by the redemption of his death—from usuries, that is, from eternal punishments. These are called “usuries” because they will be greater and more enduring than the sins committed here, just as usury is greater than the principal.

And the name of those who exist before him—that is, in his good pleasure—will be honorable. This means that, because they will be in his good pleasure, he will give them an honorable name: those who were formerly called servants of sin, guilty and unjust, and who bore other such names, will be called sons, kings of themselves, just, and will be designated by other names of this kind.

Or it may be understood in this way: Their name will be honorable, and this will be before him, that is, in his sight. This means that he himself will regard the name as honorable, even if no one else does, and he will live in them. It is as though he said: Their name will therefore be honorable because he himself will live in them, that is, he will be with them forever. In accordance with this he likewise says: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew XXVIII, [Col. 0996C] 20).

Or it may be read thus: “And he will live.” Since, by saying above that he would redeem their souls, it was understood that he would redeem them by his death, he adds: I said that he would redeem them by dying, and yet afterward he will live forever by rising again; he will not be held by death, as the Jews’ wretchedness will falsely claim. In accordance with this it is written: “Death no longer ruled over him” (Romans VI, 9).

But because, while discussing the conversion of the Ethiopians, kings, and nations, he had said nothing about the conversion of the wise, he also treats of this, as follows: I said that all kings and nations will adore him; and gold from Arabia will also be given to him by God the Father, that is, certain of the wisest philosophers of this age. They are signified by the gold of Arabia, which is more precious than all other gold, because wisdom is most precious, in the manner of Arabian gold.

And those who will be the gold will always pray to him, that is, continually; receiving from him himself the means of doing this, namely, from his teaching, so that they may pray. This means: He himself will give the commands for prayer, just as the Gospel records that he gave them to his disciples, as follows: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matthew VIII, 9), and so forth.

Or “they will pray,” receiving this from him and not from themselves. It is as though he said: Even their ability to pray to him will come from him, not from their own strength.

Or it may be understood thus: They will adore him, that is, they will venerate him in faith and devotion, receiving this from him and not being sufficient for it by themselves; and they will bless him, that is, praise him, throughout the day—that is, because of the whole of his illumination, which will be as great as day. They will not ascribe to themselves the fact that they have been illuminated by faith and wisdom, but to him; therefore they will praise [Col. 0997A] him.

Or “throughout the day” means continually: they will bless him, that is, praise him in word and deed, for the benefits bestowed upon them by him.

And rightly will they bless him, for he will be the support on the summits of the mountains existing in this present earth. This means: He will make the greatest philosophers firm in every perfection of virtue. Because of their exceedingly great knowledge, they are to be called the highest mountains of the mountains, that is, among the other mountains, namely, the other philosophers.

Or the phrase “on the summits of the mountains” is used intransitively, meaning “on the highest mountains.” I say that he will make them firm, and in this present earth, where there is a place of falling away. Or he will make firm those who exist on the earth, that is, in their earthliness, namely, in the flesh. [272] This means: While they remain in this earthly flesh, he will strengthen them [Col. 0997B] so that they do not fall away—not only in the future, where they will be strengthened much more.

And because he will be their support, his fruit will be raised high above Lebanon. That is, those mountains whom he will strengthen, whom he will make fruitful in faith, will be raised above Lebanon; they will be exalted in the dignity of my shining ones—that is, of those who prosper in earthly things—who are signified by Lebanon because “Lebanon” is interpreted as “whiteness,” and whiteness very often signifies prosperity.

This means: They will be more dignified amid flourishing earthly things.

And those who are from the city—that is, from Lebanon, namely, from Babylon, which shines with earthly things and is the city of the devil—will flourish in present goods like the grass of the earth, that is, like earthly grass, “which today is, and tomorrow is cast into the oven” (Matthew VI, 30). [Col. 0997C] This means: The flower of the prosperity of those who are citizens of Babylon, that is, of the city of the wicked, which is the city of confusion, is transitory like the flower of grass.

Hence Isaiah says: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isaiah XL, 7).

Or it may be understood thus: I say that his fruit will be raised high above Lebanon, and those who are the fruit of this present city—that is, of the Church, which is the most strongly fortified city of God—who are going to another city, namely, the heavenly Jerusalem, will flourish in good works in order to produce a harvest, that is, the eternal blessedness to be received in the future, just as the grass of the earth flowers so that seed may be produced from its flower.

He says “grass of the earth” to distinguish it from the grass of roofs, whose flower is useless for the production of seed; that grass “withers before it is plucked up” (Psalm CXXVIII, 6).

And he rightly says “from the city.” It is as though he said: From this city, that is, from the Church, which is God’s city, the flowers of the righteous—that is, good works—will proceed, and in the future the harvests of good works will be gathered, namely, the reward of eternal blessedness. For the mountains will be strengthened, raised high above others, and will flourish.

“May his name as king be blessed,” that is, exalted throughout the ages to come. He ordinarily uses “name” to mean glory. For we customarily say that someone who is glorious is a person of great name.

I say that his name should be blessed by the mountains. Yet his name remains before the sun, that is, his glory remains. By “the sun” he understands the creation of the world, because the sun was created at that time.

And it is as though he said: I do not exhort you to exalt his glory except for your own benefit. For your exaltation will confer nothing upon him whose glory existed before the foundation of the world.

But because he had said, “He will be a support on the summits of the mountains,” lest it be thought that he would strengthen only the greater and not the lesser, he adds: I say that he will be a support on the highest mountains, and not only this; but in him—that is, in faith in him—all the tribes of the earth will be blessed, that is, all kinds of earthly tribes, both of Jews and of nations.

In accordance with the promise made to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations will be blessed” (Genesis XXVI, 4).

And because, by blessing him, all nations will magnify him—“nations” and “tribes” being the same—this means: All nations will exalt him in praise, saying: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel.” That is, may he be exalted because he is Lord in all things and God of the faithful, whom he makes Israel, that is, those who see their God in contemplation; or, “to whom God appears as Israel,” that is, as the faithful, even if God does not appear to everyone.

“Who does [Col. 0998B]”—and so forth. It is as though he said: Let him therefore be blessed because he has done wonders—not just any wonders, but great ones—and not with the help of another, but alone.

For it is a wonder that he was born of a virgin and redeemed the world by his death, brought the desperate back to life, and accomplished many other innumerable things.

And let him not be blessed for an hour only; rather, may the name of his majesty be blessed forever, that is, may the glory of his greatness be exalted, may his great glory be raised high.

I say that all the tribes of the earth will be blessed in him. And this will happen in such a way that the whole earth will be filled with his majesty, that is, all kinds of earthly people will be filled with the greatness of his spirit.

In accordance with what was spoken through Joel: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh” (Joel II, 20).

And this filling is to take place in the Church: let it take place among the Jews in the Church, and let it take place among the nations in the Church.

## IN PSALM LXXII

**Title of the seventy-second Psalm:** “The praises of David, son of Jesse, have ceased; a psalm of Asaph.”

According to Augustine, this is interpreted as follows: This psalm belongs to Asaph, that is, to the faithful synagogue, and is understood in relation to the statement “The praises of David, son of Jesse, have ceased.” This means that the praises of the Jewish people have ceased—the people that used to praise God with regard to temporal goods, not with regard to eternal goods.

For when Christ came, praises of this sort ceased, since Christ gave the command that one should be concerned not with temporal but with spiritual goods. As he himself declares in the Gospel: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat, or what shall we drink, or with what shall we be clothed?’ For your Father knows that you need all these things” (Matthew VI, 31–32). And he adds: “Seek therefore first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (ibid., 33).

The addition “son of Jesse” is appropriate, to distinguish the Church and Christ, who are customarily understood by the name David, so that, literally, David the king of Israel, who was the son of Jesse, may be understood.

By “David, son of Jesse,” Israel is clearly understood metonymically as a people, because that same David was its king.

And it is also fitting that this psalm is said to have been composed on the occasion that the praises of the Israelite people had ceased. For the Church, which is also called the faithful synagogue, had previously praised God with regard to earthly things. But after Christ’s coming, seeing the good afflicted and the wicked prospering, it became indignant and nearly fell away. It almost entirely conformed itself to the party of the wicked so that it too might prosper.

But eventually, with the help of God’s grace, it was freed from this error and came to understand that the prosperity of the wicked leads to their destruction, while the adversity of the good leads to their salvation. Thus adversity no longer displeases it; rather, it pleases it.

Therefore, in order to withdraw the good from error and indignation and to show that God should be praised not for earthly but for eternal goods, it burst forth in praise of God, showing that he is good even in the affliction of the good.

By rebuking itself, it also showed that it had erred, and it explained the reason for its error: it had considered the impiety and wickedness of the wicked, which they display in many ways. It also treats of their future consolation.

Moreover, it discusses, for the example of others, the change from its own error and its submission to God, saying that from now on it clings to God and places its hope in him.

The title is treated according to Augustine as follows. But if we turn to Jerome’s opinion, the title of this psalm appears to be simply “A psalm of Asaph.” Thus the phrase placed before it—“The praises of David, son of Jesse, have ceased”—the blessed Jerome affirms not to be part of this title among the Hebrews, but rather a statement appropriately added by Ezra that refers to the preceding psalm.

For Ezra, the composer of the titles, considering that the preceding psalm contained the subject of Christ’s coming and reign—in whose time the praises of the Jewish people would cease, praises that they offered with regard to earthly things—added this statement for the instruction of those who would live in the time of Christ. He presents it as though the king had already come, and it is related to the psalm in the following way:

When that king of whom the preceding psalm spoke comes—the king who is such and such, as he was shown to be in that psalm—the praises of David, son of Jesse, will cease, namely, the praises offered to God by the people of Israel with regard to temporal things.

This means: That king will instruct his people that God is not to be praised for temporal but for eternal things.

The psalm of Asaph that follows intimates that these praises have ceased; its purpose has already been shown in the exposition of the preceding title.

“How good is the God of Israel to those who are right in heart.”

In the Hebrew translation it reads: “Yet how good is the God of Israel,” and so forth.

It is as though he said: Although God permits his own to be afflicted and the wicked to prosper, some who do not consider the matter rightly judge him not to be good in this respect.

Yet he himself, who appears as God to all who are Israel, even to those to whom it does not appear how good he is—that is, exceedingly and ineffably good—appears as such to those who are right in heart: namely, to those who rightly consider what the exaltation of the wicked and the future affliction of the good will lead to.

“But my feet were almost moved.”

This is connected with what precedes as follows: God appears as good to those who are right in heart; but my feet were almost moved away from him. That is, my reason, by which the mind walks just as the body walks by its feet, was almost separated from him; in other words, I almost distorted the gaze of my reason away from him.

“And my steps were almost poured out,” that is, my good works, by which I walk toward God, were almost poured out like certain steps—that is, they were emptied and brought to nothing—after the likeness of a liquid which, when poured from a vessel, is wasted.

For if my reason had been moved away from him, all my good works would have appeared to be reduced to nothing. In accordance with this Ezekiel says: “If the righteous turns away from his righteousness, I will remember none of his righteousnesses” (Ezekiel III, 18).

He then adds the reason why his feet and steps were almost moved, as follows: His feet were almost moved because he was jealous, that is, indignant, when by the consideration of reason he looked upon the wicked.

And he explains why he was jealous of the wicked, adding: “I was jealous when I saw the peace of sinners.” That is, I was indignant because, when I considered the wicked themselves, I saw that they had a peaceful and undisturbed life, although they were sinners and deserving of disturbance.

He says “over the wicked” by comparison with someone standing in a high place and looking down upon those below.

He then proceeds to explain why peace has been given to sinners, as follows: I say that I was jealous when I saw the peace of sinners. I say that peace was given to them by God for this reason: “There is no regard for God toward their death.” That is, God allows them peace which will be greatly harmful to them in the future because he does not look toward the death that will come to them on account of this peace, so as mercifully to rescue them from it.

For if he wished to rescue them from it, he would certainly grant them not peace but adversity.

“And there is no strengthening of God in their wound,” that is, in those wounded by the wound of sins. This means: He grants them peace because he does not care to strengthen in health those who are wounded. For if he chastised them through adversity, he would by this very means strengthen the wounded in health.

[Col. 1000D] And rightly is there no strengthening in their wound. For they are not in the labor of human beings, that is, they do not share in the labor of human beings—namely, the faithful who conduct themselves rationally, in the manner of human beings.

This means: They neglect to labor for the attainment of eternal goods, for which the faithful labor.

And therefore they will not be scourged with human beings, that is, they will not be chastised with the faithful by the scourges of tribulations.

Or these verses may be read in another and better way, so that he continues to add the reasons why he was jealous, as follows: I was jealous because there is no regard for God toward their death, that is, toward their sins, which are called death because they are the cause of death.

This means: I was jealous because God does not look upon their sins in order to punish them in the present.

And because there is no strengthening in their wound—that is, if a wound, namely adversity, ever comes upon them, there is no strengthening in that wound. God does not strengthen the wound so that it may last a long time, as their evil merits seem to demand; rather, it quickly passes away.

And therefore I was still jealous because they are not in the labor of human beings, namely, of the faithful. That is, they do not share in the labor of the faithful, so as to labor in adversities in the same way as the faithful.

And he explains this when he adds: They will not be scourged in this world, nor are they scourged with the scourges of tribulations by God together with human beings, that is, together with the faithful.

This means: I am indignant because I see the faithful laboring and being scourged by God, while the wicked are not at all. For if at least the good neither labored nor were scourged, I would not be so indignant.

Or it may be read in the manner explained above. I say that God does not regard their death, that is, their sins; yet they are not in the labor of human beings, that is, of the faithful, so as to labor for eternal things as the faithful do. Although they thus seem deserving of scourging, they are not scourged by God together with human beings.

It is as though he said: I am all the more indignant when I see the good laboring for eternal things and being scourged, while those who neglect to labor for eternal things are not scourged at all.

And therefore, because they are not and will not be scourged, pride has seized them, that is, it has held and bound them, never to release them; and they become increasingly proud.

And therefore they are still covered, that is, surrounded, by iniquity—by iniquitous thought with respect to their neighbor—and by their impiety with respect to God, that is, by an impiety proceeding from them and not from the merits of God and their neighbors.

He says “covered” emphatically, by comparison with a body that is covered on every side with garments.

It is as though he said: They are completely filled with their own iniquity and impiety, which they possess willingly, with no one giving them the occasion for it.

And their iniquity, that is, their iniquitous thought, came forth as though from fat, that is, from earthly prosperity. Prosperity is said to be like fat because, just as the fat of fleshy animals is the reason why those animals become proud, so their earthly prosperity is the reason why they become proud.

And from iniquity, that is, from iniquitous thought, they passed into the desire of the heart, that is, into the excessive longing of the heart.

This means: They not only thought wickedly, but went so far as to harbor in their hearts the desire to complete the perversity of their will.

Or it may be read as “in the desire of the heart.” I say that their iniquitous thought came forth from fat, and this iniquitous thought was not small. Rather, they surpassed the other wicked, who do not prosper as they do, in the depraved desire of the heart.

This means: They surpassed all other evil people in the wicked desire of their hearts, so that they desire worse things than the others.

He repeats this when he says “they thought,” adding the following: It was not enough for them to surpass others in depraved desire and depraved thought; they also thought of iniquity.

And afterward they spoke iniquity—not in secret, which would certainly be more tolerable—but they spoke iniquity openly, that is, publicly, so as to draw others toward it, by comparison with someone who climbs to a high place so that his voice may be clear to all who are around.

And they did not speak just any iniquity, but “they set their mouth in heaven,” that is, they made their mouth steadfast in blasphemy against the God of heaven; or, “they set it against heaven,” namely, so that they might blaspheme the God of heaven.

Yet their tongue first passed through the earth, that is, through the things that are on earth. This means: First they blasphemed human beings and the things that are on earth, and from blaspheming them they passed over to blaspheming the heavenly God, so that afterward they might blaspheme him.

Or it may be understood thus: I said that pride seized them, and it seized them so completely that they set their mouth in heaven, that is, in conformity with the heavenly God, so that, just as he arranges affairs and brings them to completion by his ordering, they too might arrange future events according to their own will by commanding their subjects and strive to bring them to fulfillment by the command of their word.

And the tongue of those who exist on earth passed beyond earthly thoughts: although they were earthly, they did not think as earthly beings but as gods, considering themselves exceedingly exalted, as though they were gods.

It is as though he said: Although they are earthly and speak lofty things with impunity, they are the reason why I was jealous.

But because he had said that he was jealous and had shown the reasons for his jealousy, someone might ask him: Why do you say this?

He responds as follows: I say this because my people, that is, the people of the faithful who resemble me, will turn away from this very error here, that is, through consideration of these words.

It is as though he said: I have shown that I was jealous for such reasons, but that I eventually recovered from this state, because, on account of these words, a people of the faithful resembling me will turn away from this same indignation if they have fallen into it.

And thus, in those faithful people, full days will be found, that is, days of fullness.

This means: They will have the kind of life that belongs to those who are in the days of fullness. They will live in such a way that they praise God in adversities with regard to heavenly things, as those who exist in the days of fullness—that is, in the time of grace.

Or it may be understood thus: Because they will turn away from jealousy, in the future days of fullness will be found in them, that is, eternal and unending days.

This means: Their conversion will be the cause of their eventually attaining eternal life.

But to withdraw them more and more, he shows from what they will turn, as follows: I say that the people of the faithful will turn. And those faithful will say, both in voice and in thought: “How does God know?” That is, by what reasoning can it be proved that God knows all things? And if there is knowledge in the Most High—that is, if, although he is exalted, he knows all things—then he is unjust.

This is implied through aposiopesis; but because it would be disgraceful to state it, he did not state it openly.

He also shows the reason why they fell into this error, as follows: We say that God does not seem to know all things; or, if he does know them, he seems to be unjust. And here is why either of these alternatives seems possible: those very people, being sinners and abounding in the world—that is, in worldly goods—obtained riches, that is, possessed them for a long time. Both circumstances appear most unjust.

It is as though he said: If he knew all things, he certainly would not permit those who are sinners to abound in worldly goods. For if he permitted them to abound, he would at least not allow them to retain those goods, but would quickly deprive them of them.

If, however, he knows all things, then he appears unjust when he allows those who are sinners to abound in riches. And what seems much worse is that he allows them to possess riches, although they would rather deserve every kind of affliction.

I say that the faithful said what I have set out above, and I said this same thing to myself, together with what follows:

“Therefore, if the Lord does not know, or if he knows and is unjust, in vain”—that is, without benefit—“I justified my heart,” by thinking rightly, “and without benefit I washed my hands,” that is, I made my works clean, while existing among the guilty, whose example might have led me astray, but did not.

This means: I thought rightly and performed good and clean works in vain, if God does not know all things, or if, knowing them, he is unjust.

And it is evident that I did so without benefit because I was also scourged by God all day long, that is, continually, by tribulations.

“And my chastisement came in the mornings,” that is, with speed.

This means: If I commit anything, I immediately chastise myself for it.

And yet he himself scourged me. Thus I appear to have thought and cleansed my works uselessly, since he said that this would make me free from scourges.

He uses “in the mornings” to mean “with speed,” by comparison with those who rise early and quickly proceed to complete their tasks.

Having shown his error, he also shows how he turned away from it, as follows: I said the things I have set out above, and I spoke against them.

“If I recount it in this way,” that is, if I affirm either that God is ignorant or that he is unjust—behold, in the present this is the unacceptable consequence: “I rejected,” that is, showed as rejected, not with respect to the truth of the matter but with respect to my own judgment, “the generation of your sons,” that is, the multitude of the faithful who are your spiritual sons.

This means: As far as I was concerned, I showed that you rejected the whole multitude of the faithful, whom you would not reward if you were ignorant or unjust. But it is unacceptable and incredible that they should not be rewarded.

Or it may be read thus: If I recount this, namely, that God is ignorant and unjust and will not reward his sons, behold, in the present this is the unacceptable consequence: I rejected, that is, despised, the generation of your sons, that is, the authority of the multitude of the faithful, who affirm that God knows all things, is just, and will at some point reward the faithful.

And because this unacceptable consequence confronted me, “I supposed that I might understand.” The expression “I supposed” does not seem to have been used very precisely here; but since the Hebrew translation has “I thought,” it appears that “I supposed” has been used for “I thought.”

It is as though he said: I thought that I might understand why, although God knows all things and is just, he allows the good to be brought low and the wicked to be exalted in the present.

“And this labor is before me,” that is, beyond me, greater than I am, so that I cannot bring it to faith:

“Until I enter the sanctuary of God,” that is, until by divine grace I am admitted to see the disposition of God, which is called a sanctuary because it contains the holy mysteries of God.

This means: The labor of understanding this is so great that I will never bring it to completion until, by the granting of divine grace, I am admitted so that God’s just and hidden disposition may be revealed to me to some extent, through which these things are ordained.

He says “I enter” by comparison with someone who, after long desiring to enter a house, is finally admitted and enters.

And this labor is beyond me until, placed in the consideration of their final destiny, I understand—that is, possess a right understanding of—why God permits the wicked to prosper here.

It is as though he said: I will never understand why they are permitted to prosper unless I look toward their final torments, which will come upon them in place of their prosperity.

Or the passage may be read in this way: I say that this labor is before me because I thought that I might understand; and understanding this is a labor before me, that is, it is difficult to understand when considering the things that are before me—namely, their present prosperity and the afflictions of the good that are in my sight.

This means: If I look upon their prosperity and the adversities of the good that are before me, that is, in my presence, it is difficult to understand why these things happen.

“Until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their final destiny.”

The exposition of this verse does not change.

This means: I will not understand it until I refer myself to God’s disposition and to their final destiny.

Nevertheless, it may be possible to see through their very prosperity why these things happen to them, although I said that it is difficult to understand this except by considering their final destiny. For “you placed prosperities for them because of treacheries,” that is, according to treacheries, namely, in the likeness of treacheries.

This means: You gave them prosperity in such a way that it appears to be a deception, although in fact it happens justly.

He explains how it resembles deception as follows: Truly, you placed prosperity according to treacheries. For while they were being lifted up by those very prosperities, you cast them down inwardly, that is, you destroyed their reason so that they would become more blind.

This means: When you gave them prosperity for their pleasure, you appeared to have acted deceitfully, although it is just, by comparison with those who put forward deceptive goods in order by this means to deceive someone.

He then shows their final destiny: I say that I will understand in their final destiny—and in that final destiny, how they have been made desolation, that is, how great a desolation they will become, losing the temporal goods in which they now seem to have consolation, and from that desolation they will not be able to protect themselves.

For “suddenly they failed,” that is, they will fail suddenly and without warning, and they will be made desolate of temporal goods, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians V, 2).

And they will not only fail with respect to temporal things, which would at least be tolerable; they also “perished,” that is, they will perish without end on account of their iniquity, which they possess here, in accordance with what the same Apostle says: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ sudden destruction will come upon them” (ibid., 3).

He shows by a comparison how they will fail, as follows.

[Col. 1005A] I say that they will fail, “like the dream of those who awake.” That is, just as riches, when they are dreamed of by people, appear to be nothing to them when they awaken from sleep, so their prosperity, which is vain, will fail when they awaken in the future.

And not only will they then appear to be nothing; here also you will reduce their image to nothing in your city, namely, in the Church. That is, you will reduce their imaginary goods—namely, their earthly goods, which they regard as true goods although they are nothing but an image and, as it were, a shadow of goods—to nothing.

This means: In your Church in particular you will reveal that these imaginary goods, which the wicked regard as great, are nothing in comparison with eternal goods.

Someone might ask: How do you know that the wicked are destined for desolation, and that these goods are considered nothing in the Church?

He answers as follows: This is known to me from the fact that my heart has been inflamed, that is, illuminated and kindled by the flame of spiritual wisdom; and my reins have been changed, that is, my pleasures have been changed. The reins signify pleasures because carnal pleasure is located in the reins. They have been changed so that, whereas I previously delighted in worldly things, now I delight in spiritual things.

He then shows from what he was changed, adding: “And before I was changed, I was reduced to nothing,” that is, to nothingness with respect to my virtues and reason, so that I was entirely without them; or, “to nothing,” that is, to the desire for temporal things, which are nothing.

And I was reduced to nothing to such an extent that I did not know what should be done and what should be left undone.

And afterward my reins were so changed and my heart so inflamed that I, who had previously been rebellious and untamed while existing in your presence—that is, in your familiarity and good pleasure—became like a beast of burden, that is, a domesticated animal prepared to carry the burden of your commandments, in the manner of a beast of burden, which is a gentle animal and suited to carrying loads.

And I shall always be with you, no longer abandoning you.

He shows how he became a beast of burden through God, as follows: Truly, I became a beast of burden not through myself but through you. For you held—that is, made me persevere—my right hand, that is, my good work, which is signified by the right hand. Through the right hand prosperity is often understood, because good work leads to prosperity.

And you led me according to your will, that is, you caused me to advance from good to better in your commandments, so that I might fulfill them more and more and thus become a beast of burden.

And in the future you received me—that is, you will receive me—making me immortal and impassible from one who is mortal and passible, and doing this with glory, that is, making me glorious in both soul and body.

He discusses that glory admiringly in order to show that it is great, as follows:

Truly, you look upon me with glory.

For what is there for me in heaven—that is, how great a thing indeed has been prepared for me in heaven—namely, eternal glory; and although what is in heaven is great, and I ought always to have desired it, what a worthless thing I, wretched man, wanted to have given me by you upon earth—that is, how vile a thing I asked to have given me by you in this world—when I saw the peace of sinners and was jealous of it: I wanted earthly goods, which are utterly worthless, to be given me. [Col. 1006A] For this reason he reproves himself in such a way as to turn others away from desire for earthly things.

Someone might say: “How do you know that you are to be received with glory, since you previously desired earthly things?” To this he adds: I am confident that I shall be received with glory because my flesh has already failed—that is, insofar as it was mine—and my heart, insofar as it was mine. This is to say: Carnal desire and earthly thought have failed within me, and because God spiritually inhabits my heart, so that I think of him alone, he is my portion, so that from among all things I choose and desire him alone as my portion. And this forever, both here and in the future. This is to say: Therefore he will receive me with glory, since, having set everything else aside, I think of and desire him alone. [Col. 1006B]

He then supplies the reasons why he thinks of and desires God, assigning each cause its proper explanation, as follows: I say that God is the possessor of my heart, and here in the present there is the reason, O God, why I wish you to be the possessor of my heart: because those who distance themselves from you in thought will perish without end. And lest I perish, I do not wish to distance myself from you. And I choose and desire you as my portion. For you have destroyed—that is, you will destroy—everyone who commits fornication by departing from you and following the devil, who is an adulterous husband. This is by comparison with a fornicating woman who, having left her husband, joins herself to an adulterer. And lest you destroy me, I do not wish to commit fornication by departing from you, like one who commits fornication by departing from you—that is, by not obeying you with chaste love but through fear; this is by comparison with an adulterous woman who obeys her husband more through fear than love, and who, if she dared, would commit fornication. [Col. 1006C]

I say that you will destroy the one who distances himself from you and who commits fornication. But for me it is good—that is, useful—to cling to you, God, in thought, and to place in you, Lord of all and God—that is, Creator—my hope, that is, my desire. This is to say: But you will not destroy me. For I consider it useful to think of you alone and to desire you alone. And it is good—that is, useful—for me to announce to others all your proclamations, that is, all your commandments, which you order to be proclaimed.

I speak while existing in the gates of the daughter of Zion—that is, in the virtues which are the gates through which the Church will enter into Zion, that is, into fellowship with the angels. Zion is called her daughter because she stands innocent and pure in likeness to Zion’s purity and innocence; [Col. 1006D] or he speaks intransitively of the daughter of Zion, as follows: I speak while existing in the judgments of the prophets, who through their teaching are gates through which Zion, their daughter—that is, their imitator—may enter into life. It is as though he said: I shall preach to them in such a way that I persevere in the virtues: “Lest, having preached to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. 9:27). Or as follows: I shall preach in such a way that I do not dissent from the prophets. And because I consider it good to preach in this way, God will not destroy me with those who commit fornication against him. By saying this, he gives others an example of clinging to God, placing their hope in him, and preaching in the gates of the daughter of Zion.

## ON PSALM 73

### Title of Psalm 73

“An understanding of Asaph,” that is, of the faithful Synagogue, whether existing before the time of Christ or during the time of the persecution of the martyrs. [Col. 1007A] This is to say: This psalm, in which an understanding concealed beneath the text is contained, belongs to the faithful Synagogue, which here laments the rejection and persecution of the Jews carried out by the Romans. It prays for the salvation and conversion of those Romans, since they did not carry out that persecution with the intention of vindicating God, although that persecution served as God’s vengeance, but rather with the intention of destroying God’s name and winning a triumph for themselves.

It also deals with the persecution of the faithful, for whom it likewise prays, and it does so with the intention of generating in us an understanding of God’s just judgment. It adds the reason why unbelievers suffer persecution toward condemnation, and why the faithful suffer it toward salvation—both of which were obscure. [Col. 1007B] And since it prays both for the persecutors and for the persecuted, it gives us an example of how to pray.

It should be noted that whenever “understanding” is placed in the title, something obscure in understanding is contained in the psalm. For example, in this psalm, through its exposition one understands why God allows the good to be afflicted just as the wicked are, something that may perhaps seem unjust and that is obscure to understand.

It should also be noted that if faithful Asaph, existing before Christ’s time and foreseeing by the Holy Spirit the condemnation of his descendants, is introduced as speaking, then what he places in the past tense in prophetic fashion is to be understood as future. But if that faithful Synagogue of the Jews which existed during and after the time of the persecution is introduced as speaking, then what is placed in the past tense [Col. 1007C] is also to be read as past.

It should further be noted that, while it laments and has compassion for their condemnation, it also includes itself among them out of excessive compassion. Thus it gives us an example that we too ought to have compassion even for enemies and for those who are to be condemned. [Col. 1007D]

Why, O God, have you rejected with final rejection—that is, with complete rejection—both in body and in soul? He determines whom he calls rejected when he adds: And why is the fury of your anger against the sheep of your pasture—that is, so that it may oppress the Jews, who were the sheep of your pasture, that is, those whom you fed in the pastures of the Law, like a shepherd who feeds sheep in excellent pastures. [Col. 1008A]

“Anger” and “fury” sometimes mean the same thing. Sometimes “fury” is used for excessive anger. When he says here, “The fury of your anger is against,” he indicates the intensity of the fury. “Why, O God, have you rejected,” and “the fury of your anger is against,” have the same meaning in substance; but he repeats the statement, saying “the fury of your anger is against,” in order to add the specification, namely, “against the sheep of your pasture.” It is as though he said: Since you once loved the Jews so greatly, it seems remarkable to many—what is the reason that you rejected them in this way and that your fury thus burned against them? [Col. 1008B]

Later he shows the reason for their rejection, anticipating the persecution itself. Or this half-verse may be read in another way: “Why, O God, have you rejected the Jewish people with final rejection?” This part of the verse remains unchanged. And: “The fury of your anger is against the sheep of your pasture,” namely, against us, whom you feed like simple sheep of the pasture of your teaching. It is as though he said: Since you also allow us to be afflicted like unbelievers, you do this because you are angry with us. He raises this question so that he may resolve it later. [Col. 1008C]

But he prays for himself as follows: I say that you reject the Jewish people, whatever may be said about those who have earned eternal condemnation. At least remember your congregation, namely us who are your congregation, lest you reject us forever and remain angry with us. You possessed this congregation through our ancestors, namely the patriarchs and prophets, from the beginning of our nation. It is as though he said: Since you, God, are our possessor from the time of our ancestors, whose faith we imitate, and since you have already bestowed many benefits upon them and remembered them, I also ask you to remember us, lest we be rejected from your grace.

For we do not wish to be subjected to any possessor other than you, God. Therefore remember this benefit that you have already conferred upon us: you redeemed, by the price of your death, the rod—that is, the kingdom—of your inheritance, that is, us, who are your hereditary kingdom, a natural kingdom not previously subjected to any other god. This is by comparison with hereditary property, which someone possesses not by seizing it from another lord, but because it comes to him by hereditary right from his ancestors. [Col. 1008D]

It is as though he said: Since you redeemed us as your hereditary kingdom, I also ask you to remember us, lest that redemption be rendered void. By the rod, a scepter is meant; by the scepter, a kingdom is understood, since the scepter is the sign of a kingdom.

That rod—that is, the hereditary kingdom—is Mount Zion, exalted in the virtues, like a mountain, and contemplating eternal things. On this mountain you, who can do all things, dwelt—not locally, but according to operative grace. It is as though he said: Mount Zion is not a mountain in itself, but becomes so because you dwell in it according to operative grace, so that you advance it toward good work. And since you made that mountain itself, Mount Zion, the place of your dwelling, I also ask you to remember it. [Col. 1009A]

I say that you dwelt in it, namely in that which is both mountain and Zion—that is, in the understanding that they are exalted in holiness and contemplate eternal things. Or the wording may be adapted as follows, while the meaning remains the same: That rod is Mount Zion, in which—that is, in consideration of the fact that it is Mount Zion—you dwelt in that mountain according to operative grace. For unless you dwelt there, it could in no way be a mountain. And from the fact that it is a mountain, it can be understood that you dwell in it.

He also prays for the persecutors of the Jewish people, namely the Romans, who persecuted the people not for the sake of God’s vengeance but for the sake of disgrace, as follows: I said that you rejected the Jewish people from the land through the Romans; and you, God, lift up—that is, exalt—your hands, that is, your power, in order finally to bring down their pride, through whom you permitted the Jewish people to be rejected. [Col. 1009B]

It is as though he said: I ask not only that you remember us, but also that you display your exalted power by bringing down their pride and making them humble and subject to you. Or as follows: Lift up your hands, that is, your power, in order to bring down their pride. This is “to the end,” that is, for completion. This is to say: Exalt your power over them so greatly that you completely consume their pride.

He shows the components of their pride when he adds: Truly, they displayed pride. For the enemy Roman people, hostile to you through their evil life, how much wickedness did they commit in the holy place of holy places, that is, how great were the evils they practiced in your holy temple?

The Holy of Holies was called the inner part of the temple, which only the high priest entered once a year with sacrifices. The whole temple may also be called holy because it had been consecrated, although it was frequented by unworthy worshipers. [Col. 1009C]

Nor did they merely act wickedly; those who hated you also gloried in their wickedness. The Romans, by denying you the worship owed to you and desiring to destroy your name, did so in the midst of your Paschal solemnity, that is, during all the days of the Paschal festival, which they thought they were celebrating, although unworthily, in your honor. For this reason it is called yours. This is to say: The Romans gloried in their siege and persecution, and they did so with the intention of expressing hatred and disgrace toward you.

It is indeed read that because the Jews crucified the Lord Jesus at Passover, in the forty-second year after the Lord’s Passion they were besieged by the Romans at Passover (Josephus, *The Jewish War*). And just as the Jews rejoiced at the Lord’s death during that festival, so the Romans rejoiced at their siege and persecution during the same festival. This was exceedingly proud. [Col. 1009D] For it is worse and more arrogant to rejoice in the completion of an evil than to commit the evil itself.

And not only did they glory in it, but—something especially proud—they set their signs above the summit, that is, above some elevated place: signs, namely such signs as they themselves did not regard as signs of God, but as their own signs, that is, signs of their victory. And they placed them as signs are customarily placed at an exit, that is, on a triumphal arch beneath which people enter and leave. Hence it is called an “exit.” Or they placed them at a gate through which people enter and leave.

He refers here to the custom of the ancients. When they had captured and conquered a city, they placed a statue or some sign upon a triumphal arch or over a gate, in memory of their victory. But because the Romans, after Jerusalem had been utterly destroyed, had no gate on which to place the signs of their victory, they placed them upon some elevated site. [Col. 1010A] They did not regard them as signs of divine vengeance, as they ought to have done, but as signs of their own victory, which was utterly arrogant.

Or “as at an exit” may be read to mean: They placed them as conquerors place signs at an exit, namely when they leave a conquered city, and they did not recognize that this victory had come not from their own merit but from divine providence.

Or, if the reading is “upon the summit,” as in Augustine, and “they did not understand,” it may be read as follows: They did not understand how this victory came forth at the exit, upon the summit—that is, from the supreme disposition of God. This is to say: They did not understand how this victory proceeded from the disposition of the supreme King. If they had known this, they would never have been proud of it.

He shows by particulars how they acted wickedly in the holy place when he adds: Truly, they acted wickedly in the holy place, for, directing their wickedness toward the very same thing—that is, agreeing in the same evil thought— [Col. 1010B]

they cut down its doors with axes, as is done in a forest of timber. A forest of timber is properly one designated for the cutting down of its trees, not one preserved for the grazing of wild animals. Trees that have been cut are called timber.

This is to say: Without any reverence they cut down its doors, just as a forest of timber is felled without reverence. By the cutting down of the doors, which were the more ornamented parts of the temple, he also indicates the destruction of the other parts. For the ancients devoted greater care to building gates.

And they did not merely cut them down; they also threw them down, that is, knocked those doors flat, with axe and hatchet—that is, by blows of axe and hatchet. Through these two instruments he designates every kind of iron tool. When he mentions the hatchet, he indicates how great was their desire to destroy the temple. Whatever work of the builder they could not destroy with large tools, they destroyed with a hatchet and other small instruments. [Col. 1010C]

And they did not merely throw down the doors; they also burned your sanctuary with fire, laid upon the ground—that is, the temple which is called a sanctuary because holy things were contained in it, namely the ark, the lampstands, and other such objects. When he says that it was subjected to fire, he does not say this because it could have been burned only by fire, but to display the violence of the burning. And he rightly says “laid upon the ground,” as though he said: What was laid upon the ground could be burned; but in the heavenly temple, which this signified, they had no power. By this he exhorts us to strive toward that temple in which we shall suffer no assault from enemies.

Before they burned it, however, they polluted the tabernacle of your name—that is, of your glory—the temple, namely, which had been made for the glory of your name, with murder, sacrilege, and other perverse acts. It is called a tabernacle in relation to the heavenly temple, because that one is eternal whereas this one is transitory. [Col. 1010D]

And this happened—that they burned and polluted it—because they said in their heart. Nor did only a few of them say this; their whole kindred together, that is, their entire assembly, unanimously said in their heart: Let us cause all the festive days of the God of the Jews to cease from this land, namely from Judea.

It was as though they said: Rejecting our own gods, they worship some unknown God to whom they hold festivals. But let us destroy the temple, and thus we shall ensure that those festive days are no longer celebrated in this land. And because they said this in their heart, they also brought it to completion in action.

Having therefore described the persecution of the Jews and the wickedness and pride of the Romans, faithful Asaph adds the cause of that persecution: namely, that they did not recognize the time of their visitation. [Col. 1011A] He includes himself among their assembly when speaking about them, as though Asaph himself had been like them in ignorance of the time of the visitation (Luke 19:44). Yet he was not actually like them; rather, he acts in this way because, being of the same origin and having excessive compassion for them, he regards their error as his own—not according to the condition of the same error, but according to compassion.

I said: Why have you rejected? And I showed how they were rejected. This happened deservedly, for did we not see our signs? Indeed, we saw them. It is as though he said: It happened justly because, insofar as our side was concerned, we did not recognize the time of the visitation—many among us did not wish to recognize it—even though we saw the signs foretold by holy men. [Col. 1011B]

Or it may be read without interrogation: It happened justly, for we did not see—that is, some among us did not recognize—our signs, foretold by the prophets. If they had wished to see them, they would have recognized the time of the visitation and would not have deserved to be rejected.

And here is one of the signs: There is now no prophet for us who prophesies about the Messiah, which had been foretold by the prophets. They had been destined to cease after his coming, although they had always continued until his coming. Hence it is read: “When the Holy of Holies comes, your anointing will cease” (Dan. 9:24). Prophecy was no longer necessary where the experience of the reality itself had occurred.

And since there is now no prophet for us, it is apparent that the Messiah will no longer recognize us—that is, certain ones among us who say that he will come. He will not visit them in such a way as to come bodily to them and release them from their captivity. And the fact that he will not come again is a sign that the time of fulfillment has already arrived. [Col. 1011C]

The cause of the Jews’ rejection having been shown, a question and astonishment might arise as to why at least the faithful suffer persecution. He treats their persecution with wonder and raises the question so that he may resolve it later, as follows:

I have shown that the Jews were rejected because, although they saw the signs, they did not wish to recognize the time of the visitation. But persecution exists not only among the chaff—that is, among unbelievers who deserved it—but persecution also exists among the grain, that is, among the faithful who have deserved nothing. It exists both in words and in deeds.

And since the faithful are persecuted, how long will the enemy—that is, the unbelieving people—reproach your own through words? This “how long” does not indicate a period of time but a measure. [Col. 1011D]

It is as though he said: The place of persecution seemed to exist only among the chaff; but since it does not cease when it reaches the grain, how long—that is, to what extent—will you permit the enemy to inflict reproaches through words upon your faithful? This is to say: It was thought that reproach would cease when it reached the grain. But since it now has a place even among the grain, it is unknown what measure and what end it will have.

And to what extent will the adversary, the unbelieving people, provoke your name to the end of provocation? “Provokes” is stated here in abbreviated form. It is as though he had said: How long will the adversary, by provoking you to the end—that is, completely—through the persecution of the faithful, blaspheme your name, not by voice but by the very persecution of the faithful? For the persecution of the faithful is a blasphemy against God’s name.

It is as though he said: From this point it is unknown what end and what measure the provocation through the persecution of the faithful will have, since it does not cease among the grain.

After his astonishment he also raises a question, as follows: I say, how long will he reproach and provoke? And whatever you may do with the unbelievers, who are justly rejected, why at least do you turn away your hand to the end—that is, for what reason do you seem to turn it away completely from the midst of your bosom, that is, from your complete protection? And, namely, your right hand. [Col. 1012A]

This is to say: Why, by permitting your right hand to be afflicted—that is, the faithful through whom you conquer the devil—do you seem to turn them away altogether from your complete protection? And he rightly says not simply “from the bosom” but “from the midst of the bosom.” It is as though he said: I do not mean that you fail to protect them in any way, since you make them steadfast; but you do not protect them completely, because you permit them to be afflicted. What, then, is the reason that you turn them away?

The statement that the hand is turned away from the bosom is presented by comparison with the story of Moses, whose hand, when drawn from his bosom, appeared leprous (Exod. 4:6). It is as though he said: By rejecting them bodily from your protection, which was signified by Moses’ bosom, you make them appear worthless, just as the afflicted leprous hand appeared worthless; through that hand they were signified as destined to appear worthless in suffering. [Col. 1012B]

Having raised the question, he proceeds to the solution, as follows:

I said, O listeners, while raising the question: Why do you turn away, and so forth? And what I asked—namely, why God permits his own to be afflicted—may perhaps seem to happen unjustly and without any benefit. But God, that is, our God who is King before the ages, through this turning away of the faithful has worked salvation, and not the salvation of a few, but in the midst of the earth—that is, among the whole earthly community. [Col. 1012C]

This is to say: Their turning away should not appear accidental or unjust. For through it the one who is God—that is, our Creator and King, who existed before the ages and ruled us eternally before the ages by his providential ordering, but now rules by the experience of the reality itself—has worked salvation for the whole earthly community.

Or as follows: God worked the salvation of human beings through their turning away. God, I say, is our King existing in the midst of the earth—that is, dwelling bodily in Judea, which is situated in the midst of the lands. And although he dwelt in the midst of the lands according to his humanity, he existed before the ages according to his divinity.

It is as though he said: The Lord Jesus, our King, through their suffering worked the salvation of the world. He was indeed able to do this; for although he appeared on earth as a man, he nevertheless existed as God before the ages.

Or “existing in the midst of the earth” means in the midst of the Jews, who are simple earth, not spiritual. He then shows that salvation itself as follows: [Col. 1012D]

Truly you have worked salvation, O God. For you, who seemed powerless for this purpose, by the power given to the faithful—that is, through the steadfastness which you gave them in persecution—confirmed the sea, namely those who had been fluid through errors, like the sea, and whom you made steadfast in faith. The steadfastness of the martyrs accomplished very much for the faith of unbelievers. If their steadfastness had failed, so great a multitude of unbelievers would certainly not have believed through their example. 284

And you not only confirmed the sea by the power of your own, but, with that same power cooperating through their example, you also shattered—that is, destroyed in the waters of baptism—the heads of dragons, that is, principal vices. They are called heads because they are principal among the other vices, just as the head is the principal part of the body. [Col. 1013A]

I say “heads” brought in by the dragons through suggestion, that is, by evil spirits, who are called dragons because they are cunning and harmful like dragons.

This is to say: You not only confirmed in faith those who were the sea, but through baptism you also destroyed in them the principal vices brought in by evil spirits. You did this through the example of the steadfastness of your own. And not only this, but through the steadfastness of your own you also broke—that is, completely destroyed—in those whom you had confirmed the heads of the dragon, that is, the principality of the devil, the prince of all demons. [Col. 1013B]
