This is to say: Through the steadfastness of your own you annihilated in them the powers which the principal devil possessed in them through the sin of the first man. When those people were called to faith through the martyrdom of your own, those powers were destroyed. They were called heads because they ruled over them, just as the head rules over the other members.

And you not only broke the heads of the dragon; you also gave that dragon as food—that is, as something to be consumed—to the peoples of Ethiopia, that is, to peoples confirmed in faith, whom I previously called the sea, who had formerly been Ethiopians, that is, black through sins. [Col. 1013C]

This is to say: You not only took away his original power, but you also gave this power to your faithful, confirmed through the steadfastness of the martyrs, so that they might consume him—that is, consume his snares both in themselves and in others—and drive him away from bodies he had possessed, devouring him as food is consumed.

Or as follows: You gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia, that is, as incorporation, so that they might incorporate him into themselves in faith—not according to him, but according to his members. This is to say: You gave them the power to incorporate certain of his members into themselves.

But you did not do all these things only through the steadfastness of your own; you also did them by breaking open the springs—that is, causing the martyrs themselves to overflow with wisdom, like a closed spring whose enclosure is broken by the excessive overflowing of the spring itself. [Col. 1013D]

This is to say: You caused immense wisdom to flow from them, and you made those springs into torrents, that is, flowing with force like a torrent, and driving back all the objections of their adversaries, so that no one could resist the wisdom and the Spirit who spoke (Acts 6:10).

And through those torrents you dried up—that is, annihilated, like water dried up—the rivers of Ethan, that is, the various and false teachings of the pagan people, with which they instructed others like rivers. They had certain superstitious teachings which they called theological, that is, discourses about the origin of the gods. These were emptied out through the teachings of the preachers. For it would greatly hinder the instruction of faith if such deception survived.

For Ethan means “strong.” Hence by Ethan the pagan people are understood, since they were strong in their obstinacy in error.

And through those springs you made day and night—that is, some who were very bright in faith and understanding, in the likeness of day, and some who were simple and obscure in understanding, in the likeness of night. And that day is yours—that is, the ministry of the preachers was made by you—and the night is yours. [Col. 1014A]

He says this so that the conversion of unbelievers should not be thought to have occurred through the preachers alone. And you will fashion through the springs—that is, you made—the dawn and the sun: those less inflamed with love, signified by the dawn, when it reddens and the nocturnal cold begins to be driven away, although not completely, and the air begins to grow somewhat warm; and those more inflamed with the fervor of charity, who are rightly understood through the sun, by whose heat the nocturnal cold is driven away more thoroughly and the air becomes warm.

You also made through those springs the boundaries of the earth—that is, all those who bring earthly-mindedness to an end and terminate it in themselves. And you also made summer and spring, that is, labor here and reward in the future. 285 Through spring the labor of good works is understood, because in spring crops are sown and flowers are produced. Through summer eternal reward is understood, because in summer crops and fruits are gathered. Both of these became known to human beings through the preachers.

But by setting this forth in parts, saying, “Yours is the day,” and so forth, he confirms it universally, as follows: [Col. 1014B]

Truly, day and night, dawn and sun are yours, for you fashioned them—that is, you created them to be such. They were not created by the springs. And because you fashioned them as such, remember this creation, so that you may make it endure and prevent it from failing in them. It is necessary that I pray for this, for the enemy, the unbelieving people, has reproached—that is, will reproach—you, Lord of all; and what is more wicked, in order to turn them away from you, he will blaspheme you with words. [Col. 1014C]

And lest they be turned away by those reproaches, remember, so that you may make them persevere. And he will not only reproach you with words; the foolish people, namely the unbelieving people, have incited—that is, will incite—your name by persecuting your own.

“Will incite” is stated here in abbreviated form. It is as though he said: By inciting you, that is, exasperating you, he will blaspheme your name, that is, he will persecute your own; and that persecution will be a blasphemy of your name, and through it he will incite you to vengeance.

But lest your own fail in that incitement through fear, remember, so that you may make them persevere. Since the foolish people will reproach you and incite your name in order thereby to make your own like themselves, I ask, Lord, not that you hand over their bodies to affliction, which is very useful for them, but that you not hand over the souls of those who confess you. [Col. 1014D]

I mean the souls of your faithful, who praise you with every kind of praise, to beasts—that is, to unbelievers living bestially, irrationally, in the manner of beasts. This is to say: Even if you permit their bodies to be afflicted, at least do not permit their souls to be made like beasts, since they continually praise you.

And do not forget to the end of forgetfulness—that is, altogether. Even if you seem in the persecutions to forget the souls of your poor, by handing them over to beasts, you would then utterly forget them if you allowed them to be made like beasts.

“Do not forget to the end” has the same meaning as “do not hand them over to beasts,” but he inserts the reason when he says “of your poor,” as though he said: You ought not to forget them, since they are poor in spirit, having abandoned all worldly things for your sake. [Col. 1015A]

I say, do not forget, but rather look upon your covenant—that is, your firm promise—lest it be rendered void. For you promised: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). A covenant is a written document confirmed under the authority of witnesses. Therefore it is used for a firm promise, as though he said: Do not forget them, but help them as you firmly promised.

He shows why the adversaries are rightly called beasts, as follows: Truly they are beasts, because they are filled with iniquities—those who have been darkened, that is, blinded in understanding, in the houses of the earth, that is, by dwelling in earthly houses. [Col. 1015B]

This is to say: They are concerned only with bodies, which are earthly houses, conducting themselves voluptuously in the manner of beasts; therefore they are completely darkened and filled with iniquities.

Or “by dwelling in earthly houses” means being like those who are already dead in earthly houses, that is, in tombs. This is to say: Already completely dead in vices, they are filled with iniquities.

I pray, look [upon your covenant], and thereby let it come about that the humble people are not turned away from you, namely the poor who are humbly subject to you. This is the same as he stated above: “Do not forget the souls of your poor.” But he repeats it in order to show what would follow if they were turned away. [Col. 1015C]

I say, “lest the humble be turned away.” I call him humble, though he would be made confounded if he were turned away. This is to say: If he were turned away, he would be confounded with complete confusion. Therefore I ask that he not be turned away.

For if the humble people are not turned away from you, this will happen because the poor and needy will praise your name—that is, each of the faithful from your humble people, who regard themselves as poor, that is, insufficient to be freed by themselves, and needy, that is, insufficient to be helped by anyone other than you.

They will praise your name—that is, by praising you they will magnify your name with voice, heart, and deed. Therefore arise, O God—that is, show yourself powerful by helping them. And arise in this way: Judge your cause in your own people—that is, defend your cause in them by the just judgment of your ordering. [Col. 1015D]

It is as though he said: They have undertaken your cause in order to defend it against the adversaries of the catholic faith; but because they are insufficient by themselves, defend your cause in them by your just judgment.

And not only this, but remember the reproaches of your faithful, namely the reproaches which the foolish unbelieving people have continually—that is, all day long—inflicted upon them. This is to say: Do not forget, when you reward them in the future, that for your sake they endure reproaches from the ungodly, even if here you seem to forget them.

And do not forget the voices of your enemies, that is, the reproaches which they inflict upon your own through words, so that you may reward them in the future, even if here you seem to forget them. And it is right that you not forget. For the pride of those who hate you, by persecuting your own, always rises, that is, grows and is exalted.

## ON PSALM 74

[Col. 1016A]

## Title of Psalm 74

**For the end: “Do not destroy.” A psalm, a song of Asaph.**

Asaph, which is interpreted as “Synagogue,” is here understood as the unbelieving Synagogue, which intends to conform Christ’s members to itself. Against this Synagogue Christ acts in this psalm, strengthening his own in the praise of God and in the narration of his wondrous deeds. He shows that they will never fail through Asaph’s admonition, since he will reward them on the day of judgment: he will justly exalt those who are humbled here, and humble their adversaries, who are exalted here. He also exhorts the unbelievers to cease from acting and speaking wickedly, lest they be justly condemned by the powerful Judge.

He demonstrates the perseverance of his own in praising God and recounting his wonders, as well as the reward of his own and of the unbelievers, so that by drawing the perverse Asaph away from persecuting the faithful, he may invite her, through the example of his own people, to praise God.

The title is adapted as follows: This is a psalm of a song—that is, this is a discourse containing a psalm, namely a good work, and a song, namely the joyful reward of a good work. Therefore it is called “a psalm of a song.” It is set before you, O unbelieving Asaph, exhorting you by its clarity not to corrupt the discourse, looking toward the end—that is, toward Christ—to whom you should ascribe it, since he appears to act here. For if you attributed it to someone else, you would certainly corrupt it. No one but Christ can properly say: “I have established its pillars, and I will break all the horns of sinners,” and the other things he says here. Since it contains things that belong to Christ alone, its very clarity admonishes you, unbelieving Asaph, who interpret the Scriptures perversely, not to corrupt it but to attribute it to Christ.

“We will give thanks to you, O God, Trinity.” Out of his great love, and because spiritually he is one with them, he joins himself to his members when he says “we will give thanks,” as if he were saying: The unbelieving Asaph intends to draw my people away from your praise, but this is futile. For following my example, my people will give thanks—that is, they will praise you by their works.

He repeats the statement in order to add this: “We will give thanks,” I say, by our works, “and we will also call upon your name”—that is, inwardly, in the soul, we will call upon your name with good devotion. Your name is “Lord.” This means: My people have judged you to be God, and by calling upon your name in their interior selves they will venerate you.

Or it may be understood in this way: “We will call upon your name with our mouth.” That is: By calling upon your name, which is “Lord,” my people will pray to you according to my example. And not only this, but “we will recount your wonders to others.” This means: Through my people I will recount to others your wonders, namely my incarnation and birth, my redemption of the world, and the other wonders that you accomplish through me. When they hear these wonders, they will turn to you, and my people will give thanks, call upon you, and recount your wonders for their own good.

Therefore, when I have received from the Father’s disposition the time for judging, I—who was unjustly judged here by the Jews—will judge with justice, that is, with just judgments, rewarding my own as justice requires.

I say that my people will recount your wonders to others so that they may turn to you, and this is necessary. For the earth, which was made for the purpose of being solid and firm in virtues, has melted—that is, it has become unstable and fluid—in its vices and unbelief, like a liquid thing that flows away.

But lest we understand this as referring to the earth that we ordinarily call “earth,” which certainly has not melted, he specifies the matter when he adds: “And all who dwell in that earth.” This means: I say that all human beings have melted—those who dwell in that earth, both Gentiles and Jews. But I, who appear powerless and humble, “have established its pillars”—that is, by sending the Paraclete Spirit in faith and virtue, and preachers in doctrine. They will be the pillars of that earth, namely the Church, established from earthly people; through the ministry of their preaching, their example, and their doctrine, they will be its supports, just as the pillars of houses are their supports.

Through these established pillars I said to the wicked—that is, I will say to the unbelievers: “Do not act wickedly,” that is, cease from evil action. And to transgressors, that is, those who act perversely, I will say: “Do not exalt your horn,” that is, do not raise up your pride by boasting about your evil action.

For although acting perversely is evil, it is worse to exalt one’s horn—that is, by boasting about an evil action, to increase and raise one’s pride. Pride is signified by the horn, which reaches upward and is rigid, because pride itself makes the heart in which it resides excessively elevated and rigid. Hence pride is called the queen of vices.

“And do not raise your horn”—that is, do not lift your pride upward in exaltation, against God Most High. He explains how they should not raise their horn against God when he adds: “Do not speak wickedness against God,” by blaspheming him in any way. For the person who blasphemes against God raises his heart excessively high.

Or it may be understood thus: “Do not raise up against the Most High”—that is, against God—“your heart,” namely your pride, by thinking evil of him. “And do not speak wickedness with your mouth against God,” that is, blasphemy. This last statement remains unchanged.

I say: “Do not act wickedly, and do not speak against God.” You must observe this because the Judge is coming, namely Christ, who will judge those who act wickedly with severity.

I say that the Judge comes neither from the east nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains—that is, neither from the south, where the mountains of the desert are hot because of the excessive heat of the torrid zone, nor from the north, where the mountains of the desert are cold—so that he may say: That Judge is to be feared, whose presence no one will be able to escape.

He will not come as a localized being from the east, west, south, or north; rather, he is everywhere, and truly he will not come as a localized being from any region of the world. For that Judge is God. It is therefore clear that, according to his divine nature, he is not localized, although according to his human nature he is localized.

From this also it will be clear that he is the Judge, since he is God, and that he has the power to humble “this one”—that is, to humble by perpetual condemnation the people who act wickedly and are exalted here through pride—and to exalt “that one,” namely the other people, the faithful, who give thanks to God here. He will exalt them with eternal blessedness, though they are humbled here through tribulations.

Truly he will humble some and exalt others, because in the hand—that is, in the power—of the Lord Jesus who is to come there will be a cup full of unmixed wine, that is, a mixture of pure wine. This means: Judgment will be in the Lord’s power, overflowing with unmixed wine—that is, containing a mixture of an equitable reward. It is called wine because one part of it will be sweet with respect to the good, while the other will be bitter with respect to the wicked. Yet both parts will be pure, that is, just and free from every injustice.

The cup is called judgment because it contains both rewards mixed together, just as a drink is contained in a cup. This is as though he were saying: He will truly be powerful for humbling and exalting, for he will have in his power a judgment in which a twofold reward will be contained together.

“He inclined this cup”—that is, he will extend it—“from one drinker to another.” This is an image drawn from a cupbearer who, after one person has drunk, inclines the cup toward another. “From this to that” is used neutrally, as though he were saying: Once this one has drunk, he will incline the cup—that is, he will make his judgment ready—for another to drink. This means: After rewarding his own by saving them, he will intend to reward the wicked justly by condemning them.

Because he had called both rewards “pure wine,” lest the whole of it be understood as pure in such a way that no part of it appeared bitter, he shows that, with respect to those who will be condemned, it is harsh and severe:

“I speak of pure wine. Yet although the retribution is pure, the dregs of its cup have not been emptied.” That is: Although the retribution is pure, it nevertheless has dregs insofar as it is harsh and turbid toward the wicked, after the manner of dregs. Such dregs will never be emptied—that is, they will never be drained away, but will be eternal.

“All the sinners of the earth will drink from those dregs.” These are those who are earth, that is, those who desire only earthly things. For if he had simply said “all sinners,” he would have asserted that all good people must drink the dregs, since no one is so just that he does not sin at least venially.

Alternatively, “all the sinners of the earth” means those who are found throughout the earth, both Gentiles and Jews, specifically those who sin mortally. He says all this in order to frighten the wicked away from their sins.

After introducing his own people as speakers, from the place where it says “I said to the wicked” up to “I am,” he himself, speaking in his own person, shows in other words the perseverance of his own in goodness and their future reward, as well as the reward of the wicked. Just as he had shown both rewards in the person of his own people, he does this so that, by displaying both rewards, he may recall the perverse Asaph, against whom he acts here, more and more from wickedness. He says this:

“I say that sinners will drink from the dregs. But I will announce forever”—that is, my people, who will not drink the dregs, will announce, that is, recount your wonders to others, from generation to generation, into the future age. “And I will sing to the God of Jacob”—that is, with delight they will praise the God of those who struggle, so that he may enable them to struggle manfully against their vices.

“And I will break the horns of sinners in the future”—that is, I will utterly destroy sinners because of their horns, namely because of the elevations of their pride. “And the horns of the just will be exalted”—that is, the just will be exalted because of the elevations of their virtues and good works, which reach upward like horns.

Or, following Augustine, these two verses—“he humbles this one,” and “he inclined this cup”—are interpreted differently if the statement “I said to the wicked,” together with “do not act wickedly” and “do not speak wickedness against God,” is understood to refer only to the Jews, who are wicked by antonomasia.

The meaning is as follows: Through my people I said to the wicked Jews: “Do not act wickedly, and do not exalt your horn,” and so forth. This is because God is the Judge, who will not come from the east, and so forth, and who will judge you severely according to your works.

It is evident that he will judge severely in the future because already here, by his judgment, he humbles this one and exalts that one. He humbles the Jewish people, who were exalted in their knowledge of the law in comparison with the Gentiles, who were wholly ignorant of the law, by blinding them. And he exalts the Gentile people, who were humble and rejected, by enlightening them with a spiritual understanding of the law.

He explains how he humbles one and exalts the other when he adds: “Truly he humbles this one and exalts that one, because in the hand”—that is, in the power—“of the Lord is the cup,” namely the old law. It is called a cup because it contains understanding, as a drink is contained in a cup.

The cup, I say, is full of pure wine and full of a mixture—that is, overflowing with pure and spiritual understanding. This is called pure wine because it is pure, exceedingly sweet, and gladdens the hearts of the faithful after the manner of pure wine. It also overflows with mixed wine, that is, turbid and harsh wine, which is also called dregs—namely, the carnal understanding according to the letter. It is rightly called mixed wine and dregs because it is turbid and harsh, like mixed wine that is called dregs.

“He inclined this cup from one to another”—that is, after the Jewish people had drunk from it, he transferred it to the Gentile people, whom he caused to drink from it.

Yet although he inclines the cup by giving it to both peoples, he does not give both to drink in the same way. “The dregs of the cup have not been emptied”—that is, the carnal understanding of that law will not be emptied from the Jews, but will remain among them. This means: Behold, he will make the Jews drink from it continually.

By this he intimates that he will give the Gentile people to drink of pure wine. Although the Jews here drink the dregs while the Gentiles drink pure wine, in the future all will drink pure wine—that is, sinners of every kind on earth, not only Gentiles but also Jews.

This means: In the future he will give a spiritual understanding to the remnant of the Jews who will be saved, and thus sinners of every kind will drink pure wine.

I say that the Jews alone will drink pure wine at the end of the world. “But I”—that is, my people—“already having drunk from it, will announce forever,” and the rest of the psalm up to its end remains unchanged.

## On Psalm 75

### Title of Psalm 75

**For the end, in praises. A psalm. Asaph’s song for the Assyrians.**

This is interpreted as follows. This psalm belongs to Asaph—that is, to the faithful Synagogue directing itself toward the end, namely toward Christ—and not in reproach but in praises. For it praises him when it says, “You are terrible,” and so forth. This psalm is a song, that is, it is uttered with the greatest delight and joy, for the conviction and conversion of the Assyrians.

By “Assyrians” are meant the Jews, who are truly Assyrians because of the similarity of the wicked action they retained to that of the Assyrians. For just as the Assyrians, alienated from the law of Moses, persecuted the Jews, so the perverse part of the Jews persecuted everywhere the true Jews who had been converted to the faith of Christ.

According to the interpretation of this word, “Assyrian,” the Jews are falsely called Assyrians. “Assyrian” means “one who directs” or “one who guides.” The Jews are therefore called Assyrians not because they direct themselves according to divine commandments, but because they falsely claim that they alone direct themselves.

Accordingly, it is read in the Gospel: “We are disciples of Moses” (John 9:28). Elsewhere it is said of them: “This people honors me with its lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29:13; Mark 7:6).

This psalm is rightly said to act against the Jews. Since the perverse part of the Jews gloried in the names it unjustly claimed for itself—saying, namely, that it was called “Jews,” “Jerusalem,” “Israel,” and “Zion”—the faithful Asaph intends to humble them, proving that they do not rightly use these names. He also shows who are rightly called Jews, Jerusalem, and Zion. In addition, he demonstrates the blinding of the false Jews in this age and their great trembling in the future. He then adds the salvation of the true Jews because of their good thoughts and good works. By the example of these people, he admonishes the perverse Jews against whom he acts to vow good works through thought and to fulfill them through action, adding the reason why this must be done.

“God is known in Judea.” This is as though he were saying: Do not boast, unbelieving Jews, about the name “Judea,” which you unjustly claim for yourselves. For God is known in Judea—that is, among those who truly are Judea, namely those who confess God purely and possess knowledge of God’s Christ. Since you lack this knowledge, you are certainly not Judea.

“And great is his name in Israel.” This is as though he were saying: Do not boast about the name “Israel” either. For in Israel his name is great—that is, glorious. Those who truly are Israel glorify and magnify the name of Christ. Since among you it is not great but utterly despised, you are certainly not Israel, that is, those who see God.

“And his place has been made in peace.” Another translation has “in Salem.” But since Salem is interpreted as “peace,” he substitutes “peace” for Salem. It is as though he were saying: Cease boasting about the name “Salem” as well.

For Christ’s place has been made in Salem—that is, among those who truly are inhabitants of Salem, namely those who have peace with God and with their neighbor. God dwells there not locally but spiritually, just as someone dwells in a particular place.

Accordingly, the evangelist John testifies: “Whoever remains in charity”—which truly and rightly is called peace—“remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:16).

Since you refuse to be God’s place, you are not rightly called Salem either. “And his dwelling is in Zion.” This is as though he were saying: Do not arrogantly attribute the name Zion to yourselves either.

For Christ’s dwelling is in those who truly are Zion, namely watchers of eternal things. According to inactive grace, Christ dwells in them. But since this is far from you, you are certainly not Zion.

It is clear that he dwells in Zion because there—that is, in Zion and Israel—he “broke,” that is, utterly destroyed, “the powers of the bows.” By the powers of the bows are meant those instruments by which bows can inflict harm, namely arrows.

Arrows approach as if stealthily and unexpectedly and cause injury; they therefore signify deceptions that secretly do harm. “And he broke the shield.” By the shield, which protects a person, is understood the obstinacy of a sinner defending his guilt. He destroyed every such obstinacy in them, so that they would no longer excuse themselves for their sins but rather accuse themselves in humble confession.

“And the sword”—that is, open persecution, which is appropriately signified by the sword. Through the sword persecution is made manifest; he broke this in them, so that they would no longer presume to persecute the faithful openly.

And why enumerate each item? “He broke all war there,” so that they might be rebellious toward neither God nor their neighbor. Since these things have not yet been broken in you, O unbelieving Jews, it is certainly clear that you are neither Zion nor Israel.

He shows through what means he breaks such things in them when, with thanksgiving, he turns directly to God and says: “And through this you break in them what you are”—namely, enlightening them, O God, with faith and knowledge of you. You do this wondrously, through evident miracles worked by your people. This enlightenment proceeded through miracles from the mountains—not from evil mountains, but from eternal mountains, namely the apostles, who are mountains in virtues and eternal because they lead others toward eternity by their preaching.

He inserts, in a connected manner, a discussion of the blinding of the perverse Jews, in an attempt to draw them away from unbelief by rebuking them.

I say that you are enlightening Zion, Salem, Israel, and Judea—namely the Gentile people. At this enlightenment all the foolish in heart, that is, the perverse Jews, were disturbed by envy. They are foolish not only in their actions but also in the thoughts of their hearts, since they have been blinded because of their evil merits.

There are many who, although they act foolishly, are nevertheless not ignorant that they are acting badly. Such people are not foolish in heart. Hence it is read in the Acts of the Apostles that, when the Jews heard that Samaria had received the word of the Lord, “they were filled with jealousy” (Acts 8:14).

“And being disturbed, they slept their sleep”—that is, a sleep harmful to themselves. They will complete their unbelief so that they never cease from it, until the time of the remnant, at the end of the world, after the likeness of a sleeping person who is not awakened until he has completed his sleep.

Unbelief is called sleep because it weighs down souls just as sleep weighs down bodies. Hence the Apostle says: “Those who sleep, sleep at night” (1 Thessalonians 5:7). And elsewhere: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Romans 13:11).

Because they will sleep, “the men of riches” will, according to their reputation but not according to the truth of the matter, find nothing in their hands. This means: Those who suppose that they alone will be rich in eternal glory will find no blessedness present to them on the day of judgment, like a sleeping person who dreams that he is holding riches in his hands but, upon waking, finds nothing there.

He shows how and for what reason this sleepiness came about, lest it appear to have been permitted unjustly by God:

“They slept,” I say—that is, they will sleep. This will happen because of your rebuke—that is, because of your hardening—O God of Jacob, the God of the faithful who struggle manfully.

“Slept” means the same as “slept their sleep”; both are placed in the future tense. Their hardening is rightly called a “rebuke,” because it is a sign that they have acted wickedly against God and therefore ought to be punished. Rebuking words are likewise signs both of past evil action and of future vengeance.

It is as though he were saying: They will sleep because, by blinding them, you hardened them.

He adds the cause of their sleepiness: “All who mounted there, and who continually mount horses, will sleep.” By horses are signified prides, because horses are proud animals. This means: You hardened them because they raised themselves excessively in pride and continue to raise themselves, by neglecting Christ, like those who make themselves exalted by mounting horses.

### “You are terrible”

The statement continues in this way: I say that you are almighty, enlightening Zion. You, I say, are terrible—that is, you will be terrible when you come to judgment—as Gregory also testifies: You will appear gracious to the just and terrible to the unjust.

“And who will resist you then?” No one. This is as though he were saying: Even now they resist you in some way, saying that you are merely human and powerless, but then they will be unable to resist you at all.

“For from that time onward”—that is, from that time through eternity—“your wrath,” namely your vengeance, “will be manifest,” whereas now it is hidden. Accordingly, the Psalmist says elsewhere: “When his wrath is kindled in a little while” (Psalm 2:12).

Then, coming from heaven and localized according to what you are as a human being, you will make judgment—judgment that is not hidden but heard, that is, audible and manifest to all. As it is written: “All the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them,” and so forth (Matthew 25:32).

I say that he will make the judgment audible to those who hear it. “The earth trembled and was still”—that is, earthly sinners, those who here are intent only on earthly things, will fear greatly and will be still, whether they wish it or not. They will cease from their ungodliness, though not for their own advantage, because here they neglect to cease from it.

They will tremble and be still when God rises for judgment—that is, when Christ God, who appears powerless here, rises for judgment and appears powerful by coming to judgment—“to save,” that is, to make eternally safe, “all the meek of the earth.”

By the meek of the earth are meant the faithful, who, from being earthly—that is, what they formerly were—have been made meek by God: gentle, and in no way resisting God.

Alternatively, “all the meek of the earth” means all who are in this earth, both Jews and Gentiles.

He turns directly to his hearers in order that they may be drawn away from wickedness by fear of punishment and impelled toward good works by love of reward.

And rightly will you save the meek, O God, because “the thought of man will give thanks to you.” That is, each meek person who behaves rationally, as a human being, will praise you through the good thought of his mind.

“And the remnant of thought”—that is, the good works that remain after thought, or that remain to be completed—“will keep a feast for you,” that is, they will lead, for your honor, a festive and holy life in which they cease from evil actions, just as one ceases from servile work on a feast day.

Therefore, by analogy, it is called a feast day. This is as though he were saying: The good works they perform will be the reason why they lead a festive life in your praise.

He turns directly to the unbelieving Jews, against whom he acts in this psalm, in order to invite them to praise God in thought and deed—or, if they neglect to do this, at least to leave them without excuse. He says:

“Vow to the Lord your God”—that is, promise Christ good works by thinking rightly—because he is both Lord over all things and God, your Creator, whether you wish it or not.

After you have vowed through thought, fulfill the vow through action. “For it is better not to vow than, after vowing, not to fulfill” (Ecclesiastes 5:4). You ought both to vow and to fulfill.

For all who are “around him,” that is, in his good pleasure, will bring gifts to God consisting of good thoughts and works. This is as though he were saying: You ought to vow and fulfill because no one will be around him except the one who brings him here the gifts of good thoughts and works.

I speak of the Lord God, who will be terrible, as I have shown. This is as though he were saying: You must vow and fulfill to the one who is terrible. I speak of the Lord who “takes away the spirit of princes,” that is, who has the power to take away the souls of princes, namely to kill them.

And he is not only terrible in the future, but also terrible among the kings of the earth—that is, he is already feared by many kings of the earth, not only by princes.

Alternatively, “he takes away the spirit of princes” means that he is so merciful that he takes away the proud spirit of certain people whom he makes princes of themselves. This means: He removes pride from their spirit and gives them humility.

“And he is terrible among the kings of the earth” may also mean among the faithful who rule their earth well, namely their earthly flesh, lest it drift into unlawful things.

Or “he takes away the spirit of princes” means that, because of certain evil merits, he takes away the upright spirit from certain princes—that is, from certain faithful people who had previously been princes of themselves. It is read that he took it away from Solomon because he inclined his head toward idols, and from Judas because he betrayed him, although Judas had previously been said to perform miracles, and from many others.

Because he takes away the upright spirit from princes, while existing as one to be feared, he is feared here by the kings of the earth, who fear that if they fall, he may likewise take away their upright spirit.

The more terrible he shows him to be, the more he invites his hearers to obey him.

## On Psalm 76

### Title of Psalm 76

**For the end, for Jeduthun. A psalm of Asaph.**

This psalm belongs to Asaph—that is, to the faithful disposition of the Synagogue—and is given “for Jeduthun,” that is, for the reason that Asaph herself is Jeduthun. Jeduthun means “one who leaps over” those about whom he speaks in what follows, where he says “like sheep,” namely the unbelieving Jews. She leaps over them, proceeding all the way to the end—that is, toward Christ—showing that by faith, good works, investigation, and knowledge she leaps beyond them to the end.

For this reason, since she leaps beyond unbelief and all earthly things, and since she is directed toward the true end, Christ, she invites the unbelieving Asaph, by her example, to leap toward the end.

She shows how she makes these leaps: after having already reached him through faith, she later advanced partially toward his knowledge and love through investigation and consideration of God’s works, while in the future she will reach this more perfectly.

She also shows, in order to urge the unbelieving Asaph—that is, the Jews—to leap toward the end, that many Gentiles have leapt to Christ through faith and knowledge, by means of the teaching and miracles of the preachers. At the same time, she condemns the unbelief of those same Jews, since they do not wish to leap in knowledge toward the one who led them by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

“With my voice I cried to the Lord.” This is as though he were saying: You, unbelieving Asaph, cry out to the Lord, so that he may cause you to leap toward the end, following my example, and he himself will hear you.

For I, acting with my voice—that is, not with an empty and useless voice, but with a firm, attentive, and useful voice—cried out. By an inward cry of intense devotion I acted toward the Lord the Father. “With my voice,” I say, I acted toward God the Father.

When he says “with my voice” twice, the meaning is the same. But when he says “to God” and “to the Lord,” he indicates different reasons, as though he were saying: I truly ought to cry out, since he is Lord—that is, governor—and God—that is, Creator.

And because I cried out, “he attended to me”—that is, he gave me greater intention for crying out; or he made himself attentive to me, so that he might give me intensely what I prayed for by crying out intensely.

This means: He heard me concerning what I prayed for with intense crying.

He explains what he prayed for in his cry and how he was heard:

The Lord heard me crying out because, “in the day of tribulation,” when the place for failing seemed to have come, I sought the Lord with affection and voice.

Or “in the day of tribulation” means throughout the whole time of my life, in which there are nothing but days of tribulation. “The life of man upon earth is a warfare” (Job 7:1).

I say that I sought God, and I did so as I ought. For I sought him with my hands extended against him—that is, with my works raised before him through their multiplication—after the likeness of those who pray with extended hands.

I speak of hands, that is, of works raised up and enlarged for the honor of God. And I did this also at night—that is, in adversity, where many cease from good works. It is rightly called night because those who walk in it encounter many obstacles, just as people walking at night stumble.

Or “with my hands extended at night” means throughout my whole life, which is rightly called night in comparison with the future life because it is dark like night. The future life, by contrast, is like the brightest day.

This means: He heard me because throughout my whole life, in prosperity and adversity, with mouth, devotion, and action, I sought him—that is, I sought him beyond all other things, seeking him alone while despising everything else.

What I sought he has already granted in part, and in the future he will grant it more perfectly. In seeking him I was not deceived by any hidden suggestion or by any prosperity offered by the devil or by any member of the devil, which might have drawn me back from seeking God.

This means: Neither any suggestion nor any prosperity brought by the devil or one of his members could deceive me and recall me from seeking God.

He explains how he was not deceived: “My soul refused to be comforted” by anything except God alone. This means: I despised every consolation of earthly goods and remembered God alone. I always held him in memory through faith and exercised myself in his knowledge.

This is as though he were saying: Once I had leapt toward him through faith, I labored to attain knowledge of his mysteries, and in this exercise my spirit—that is, my soul—failed, because it was insufficient to attain perfect knowledge of his mysteries.

He explains how he exercised himself by adding:

I say that I exercised myself in investigating the knowledge of God, and not just a little. For my inner eyes anticipated the vigils of the other faithful. This means: My reason, which is the eye of the soul, anticipated—that is, surpassed—the other faithful who were watchful and diligent in exercising themselves in the knowledge of God’s mysteries. Though they were very diligent in this, I was more diligent than they.

Yet although I anticipated their vigils, I still failed. I was troubled in soul by grief because I was failing.

Although I grieved over my failure, I did not speak blasphemy against God, as many blaspheme what they cannot understand. It is as though he were saying: Although I grieved that I was failing, I was not indignant on that account, nor did I say anything blasphemous against God.

In this he gives us an example: We should not become indignant but patiently endure it if someone cannot quickly attain knowledge of a particular mystery.

That patience came to me because I did not speak out: I considered the ancient days, in which Adam and Eve, after becoming disobedient, passed from the perfect knowledge of God—which they would have possessed if they had persevered—into a state of deficiency. They drew all of us into the same deficiency.

I also kept in mind the eternal years that we lost through Adam—that is, eternal life. If we had possessed them, we would certainly not be failing.

This means: I endured this deficiency patiently and did not murmur because I considered that it had rightly come upon us through the guilt of our first parents, through which we also lost eternal life. Until we recover it, we should continually keep it in mind.

While thinking about this, I also meditated at night—that is, throughout my whole life—or at night, that is, even in adversity, in which many cease from such meditation. I meditated on whether we might ever escape this deficiency.

I acted with my heart as though with another person, proposing and resolving many matters within my heart. In this meditation I exercised myself, that is, I was frequent and diligent.

And I did not exercise myself only a little. Rather, I “scobebam”—elsewhere read *scopebam*—my spirit, that is, I dug into my soul and made it very deep by investigating, after the likeness of a pit that becomes deep through digging.

This means: I led my soul into profound questions.

Or, if *scobere* is taken to mean “to cleanse,” as many report, the passage is read in this way: So that no earthly thought might harm my exercise, I “scobebam” my spirit—that is, I cleansed my soul of every worldly concern.

He shows in what he exercised himself through meditation when he adds:

I say that I meditated with my heart, acting in this way: “Will God cast us away forever from the perfection of his knowledge, from which we were cast here because of Adam’s sin?”

This means: Will we always know God imperfectly, as we do now?

“And will God not add” that he should still be more pleasing to us—that is, more pleasing and more beloved?

This means: He who has already placed in us, in part, the capacity to love him and to find him pleasing—will he not add in the future so that he may be more pleasing, that is, more perfectly loved, when we have been perfectly enlightened with the knowledge of him?

Since, therefore, he had asked indeterminately, “Will he cast away?” and “Will he not add?”—and since it is established that many, namely all who will die in unbelief, are to be cast away forever, and that God will never again be more pleasing to them—he asks determinately concerning the regenerated, answering each point with its corresponding point, as follows:

“I spoke indeterminately. Will God cast us away forever from the perfection of his knowledge? Or may I ask in this determinate way: Will God cut off to the end of cutting off,” that is, forever, “his mercy,” namely the perfection of his knowledge, which is the highest mercy and blessedness, “from the first generation,” which is according to Adam’s old condition, “as far as the second generation,” which comes about according to the Spirit?

That is to say: Just as he will cut off from the unbelieving, who are generated only by the first generation, which comes through the desire of the flesh, the perfection of his knowledge, which is great mercy, “to the end,” that is, forever, will he also cut off that same knowledge “to the end”—both here and in the future—from the faithful, who are generated through the second generation by baptism?

“Or will God forget to show mercy?” This pertains to what he stated above: “And will he not add,” and so forth. It is read as follows: “I spoke indeterminately: Will he not add further, so that he may be more pleasing? Or may I say this determinately: Will God forget to show mercy?” That is, once God has begun to show mercy to the faithful by giving them love of himself, will he partly forget this mercy by failing to perfect it in them? This would be utterly incongruous—namely, that God should forget anything.

Having answered each point with its corresponding point, he gives a statement applying to both of the foregoing when he adds: “Or may I say this: Will he restrain his mercies in anger,” namely, the perfection of knowledge and love of himself? This is to say: Although by nature he is ready to show mercy to the faithful in the future through the illumination of perfect love and knowledge of himself, will he restrain these mercies from the faithful, refusing to confer them because of the anger he has against the human race on account of original sin? This too seems incongruous.

Having posed these questions, he proceeds to resolve them in this way: “I say that I meditated with my heart,” raising the objection as follows: “Will God cast us away forever?” Against this objection I stated the following solution: “Now I have begun.”

This is to say: Truly, he will not cast us away forever, and he will yet be more pleasing. I know this because now I have begun to know him—as though he were saying: A portion of his knowledge and love, given to me by him at the beginning as a pledge and guarantee, is a sign that I shall know and love him more perfectly.

I know this also because I shall know and love him more perfectly, since “this is the change of the right hand of the Most High”—that is, our being changed from ignorance of God to knowledge of him, and from hatred to love, occurs through the right hand of the Most High, namely through the Son of the Most High and Almighty Father, who is rightly called his right hand. For through him he defeated the devil.

This is to say: Since Christ, the Son of the Most High Father, who is so great and so powerful, has begun this change in us, there can be no doubt that he will perfect it in the future, so that we may love and know him perfectly.

He therefore shows from what it can be proved that he is the Most High Father, adding: “I said, ‘the right hand of the Most High.’” And in order to prove that he is Most High and Almighty, he says that he remembered the works of the Lord the Father—that is, he frequently called to mind how gloriously and wonderfully he had acted from the beginning of the world—and through this it became evident to him that he is Most High.

Therefore I will not cease from this remembrance, but will continually remember your wondrous works performed from the beginning of the world. From this, two benefits will come to me: I will meditate on all your works, so as to fulfill them, and I will exercise myself by acting according to your inventions—that is, according to your commandments, which you devised.

This is to say: From considering your wonders I shall gain these two advantages: I shall meditate on how to complete your commandments in action, and, insofar as I am able, I shall act accordingly.

Having inserted this passage to show by what means he proved God to be Most High, he repeats, in an equivalent expression, what he had stated above—“This is the change of the right hand of the Most High”—so that, on that occasion, he may burst forth into God’s praise as follows:

“I said that I have now begun, O God, to come to the love and knowledge of you. And your way, O God, by which we come more perfectly to the knowledge and love of you, has been set before us in the holy of holies, Christ—that is, in conformity to him.” This is to say: Through conformity to him we come to you.

Therefore, because you set your way before us in him, “what god is great like you, our God,” though you are not regarded as God by anyone? That is: What god is regarded by the nations as great in the way that you are, whom we regard as God? None.

For you are the God who works wonders, and no one else works wonders. And here are the wonders: “You made your power known among the peoples.” This is to say: It was a wonder that, through preachers, you made your Son known among the peoples, both Gentiles and Jews. He is called your power because through him you act wonderfully and powerfully.

And here is another wonder: “In your arm,” that is, in your Son, who is called your arm because through him you overcome the devil, “you redeemed your people,” made your own through faith, “a people,” I say, “made into sons”—that is, those who became your sons through regeneration. “Sons,” I say, “of Jacob and Joseph,” that is, the Jewish people and the Gentile people.

Jacob appropriately signifies the Jewish people, and Joseph the Gentile people. For Jacob wrestled with the angel, was struck by him, became lame in one foot, and received a blessing (Gen. XXXII, 24–25, 29). In the same way, the Jewish people, wrestling with the Lord, while they rendered his commandments ineffective, were struck by the Lord with blindness and became lame in one foot—namely, in their understanding of carnal observances, by which they understood only the letter and not the spirit—while in another understanding they remained upright, namely in their understanding of moral commandments, in which alone they ought to have adhered to the letter. Among those to be saved, they also received the blessing of adoptive sonship.

Joseph, however, is interpreted as “increase.” Hence the Gentile people are understood through Joseph, since they were added to the increase of the primitive Church from the Jews.

And here is another wonder: “Through knowledge of the Son, the waters”—namely the Gentiles, who previously were ignorant, unstable and fluid like water—“saw you by faith, O God the Father.” In order to expand upon this, he repeats as follows:

“The waters saw you,” I say, “and were afraid; and the abysses were troubled.” This is an inversion of the order. It is as though he said: Those very waters which had previously been in unbelief, deep like abysses, were troubled with a good disturbance and became afraid because of their evil deeds.

It was not a small number of waters, but “the multitude of the sound of the waters”—that is, many waters making a sound, rebelling against God’s commandments with an excessive clamor of words.

I say that you made your power known, and the waters saw you. This happened because “the clouds”—that is, the many preachers of the Church—“gave forth a voice of preaching,” through which the waters were converted to faith in and knowledge of God.

Someone might ask why the waters were troubled because of the preachers’ voice, since the preachers themselves were only from the Jews. To this he responds as follows:

Truly, the waters are troubled because of the preachers’ voice. “For your arrows pass over”—that is, those same preachers, called your arrows because through their preaching you wound the hearts of unbelievers, pass over from the Jews, who reject the kingdom of God, to the Gentiles.

He shows how far they pass when he adds: “The voice of your thunder passes in the wheel,” that is, throughout the whole world. Since the world is round like a wheel, it is signified by the wheel.

This is to say: The voice of the preachers, who are called thunder because, by preaching openly, they threaten those who will not believe with eternal death, passes in such a way that it is manifest “in the wheel,” that is, throughout the whole world: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. XVIII, 5).

The waters, however, were not troubled and afraid solely because of the preachers’ voice. The earth also—that is, the earthly people to be saved from Jews and Gentiles—trembled because of their sins and was moved to faith when “your flashes illuminated the world,” that is, when the flashing wonders of the preachers became manifest to the whole world, like flashes in the air that shine at the time of thunder.

This is to say: Through the preachers’ miracles, earthly people were moved.

And thus, after the disturbance in the sea—that is, among the Gentile people, who previously lacked all knowledge of God—“your way was in the sea,” that is, the knowledge of your Son, who is the way by which one comes to you, as he himself testifies: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV, 6).

“And your paths are in many waters,” that is, your commandments are among the many nations. They are called paths because, like paths, they are very narrow for the flesh.

He does not say that God’s way and paths are in the nations in order to suggest that they are not also found among those to be saved from the Jews. Rather, he treats the Gentiles specifically in order, on that occasion, to condemn the unbelief of the Jews as follows:

I say that your way and your paths are among the Gentiles, who had heard nothing more about you through the prophets and to whom you had not granted as many benefits as you had granted to the Jews.

“But your footsteps”—that is, your commandments and the preachers’ miracles, which are called footsteps because through them one reaches you—“will not be known by your people,” namely by the unbelieving part of the Jews, who ought to have been your people.

Yet you led this people of yours like sheep—that is, you led them from Egypt into the promised land—in the hand, that is, under the leadership of Moses and Aaron, as your sheep, since you fed and guarded them so diligently, just as a shepherd carefully feeds and guards his sheep.

It is as though he said: The Gentiles, whom you appeared until then to have neglected, obey your commandments. But the unbelieving Jews, whom you led like sheep in the hand of Moses and Aaron, and to whom you granted so many other benefits, will despise the footsteps of your commandments, miracles, and preachers. Certainly, they ought not to do this.

He condemns the unbelief of the Jews so that, by this means, the part of those to be saved may be kept from imitating them.

## On Psalm LXXVII

### The title of the seventy-seventh

“A psalm of understanding, of Asaph.” This is explained as follows.

This is a psalm of understanding—that is, of intelligence, in which mystical understanding is contained—of Asaph, that is, of the perfectly faithful Synagogue. It addresses the less-perfect faithful Asaph and recounts the former benefits bestowed by God on their ancestors in ancient times.

At the beginning of this psalm, it exhorts that same less-perfect Asaph to listen attentively and diligently to what it will say to her in parables and propositions—that is, to understand those benefits mystically and not merely according to the letter, as their unbelieving ancestors did. Those ancestors perished because they neglected the benefits, understanding them only according to the letter.

He recounts those benefits in order to instruct them, so that what occurred historically in the former people may also be understood as occurring figuratively in the Church.

It should be known that, although this psalm, read continuously according to the historical sense, contains an allegory within itself, it is nevertheless difficult, or scarcely possible, to read it continuously according to the allegorical sense everywhere.

It should certainly be noted that this psalm, like the others, properly pertains to prophecy, even if it is read historically. This is so first because the faithful Asaph, who did not yet exist at that time, is introduced as speaking through the Prophet; and also because, in the benefits that the Prophet presented here as having occurred historically, he mystically designated other benefits that would occur in the Church.

### “Attend, my people, to my law”

He uses “attend” in the plural because “people” is a collective noun. It is as though he said:

You, faithful but less-perfect Asaph, who are my people—that is, of my kind, since we belong both to the same nation and to the same faith—attend, that is, consider the old law carefully, not negligently as your ancient fathers did.

I call the law “now made mine” through understanding—that is, I may now rightly call it mine because I understand it. Otherwise it will not be yours unless you have understood it.

Since he had spoken of “the law” without qualification, lest we think he was sending us to understand the whole law while saying nothing further about it, he adds:

“And in order that you may diligently consider the whole old law through the example of my words, incline your ear, proceeding toward an understanding of the words of my mouth.”

This derives from the likeness of a diligent student who inclines his ear in order to grasp well the words of a good teacher.

It is as though he said: Listen carefully to the words I speak, so that, by understanding them mystically, you may likewise understand mystically the other things read historically in the law, using these words as an example.

It is necessary that you attend and incline your ear, “for I will open my mouth in parables,” that is, I will speak parabolically through likenesses. You must therefore attend carefully, so that what is said parabolically may be understood mystically.

I will not speak only in parables; I will also speak “propositions,” that is, obscure likenesses, beginning from the beginning of the old law. For this reason, it must be considered with even greater attention.

In Hebrew, the expression is *aenigmata antiqua*, “ancient riddles.” Hence we understand “propositions” to mean those likenesses that are more obscure to the understanding, while “parables” are those that are clearer. They are called propositions because they are proposed as questions.

Since parables are clearer to the understanding than propositions, he indicates this when he says: “I will open my mouth in parables,” as though he were saying: I will speak openly in parables.

To make them more attentive, he says that he did not invent what he will say, but heard and learned it from the fathers, who were men of great authority.

I say that I will speak of things I have not invented:

“How many things we have heard and known, and our fathers have recounted to us.”

This is to say: The things we shall speak of, whose magnitude—that is, whose great importance—our fathers, authoritative men, recounted to us, we heard carefully and learned mystically. Therefore we ought to be believed.

“These things were not hidden from the children of those fathers,” namely from us, “in another generation,” that is, from a generation different from us.

This is to say: We did not conceal them out of envy, but made them known to the generation of the Gentiles, which is another generation, different from us in origin.

He makes them very attentive in this respect also: even the Gentiles, to whom these benefits had not been granted, heard them attentively.

After this interruption within the verse, he returns to what he had begun, as follows:

I say that the fathers recounted great things to us. The fathers who recounted them were recounting “the praises of the Lord,” that is, the commandments through whose observance God is praised, and his powers, that is, those benefits in which he appeared to have acted with a kind of violent force—namely, the dividing of the sea, the drowning of Pharaoh, and the defeat of the enemies.

They also recounted his wonders, which he performed—that is, those benefits he worked wonderfully, not as though by violence, but by power alone, such as the manna he rained down, the water he gave from the rock, and other things of this kind.

He shows where they recounted these things as follows:

Truly they recounted God’s praises, powers, and wonders. For God “raised up testimony in Jacob,” that is, among the Jewish people, testimony consisting of written accounts of his powers and wonders. These are called testimony because they testify that he is powerful.

“And he set a law in Israel,” that is, among the Jewish people, through those same fathers: written commandments of his, which are his praises.

He appropriately says “raised up,” after the likeness of something dead being raised. It is as though he said: Since his miracles, powers, and commandments would otherwise have died, he caused the fathers to compose writings in which his wonders, powers, and praises might be raised up.

He says this briefly: “He raised up testimony in Jacob”—that is, in order to raise up his wonders and powers, he placed writings through the fathers among the Jewish people.

Alternatively, “he raised up testimony in Jacob” means that he placed writings of carnal observances among the Jewish people. These were called testimony because, through their manifest character, they testified to other mystical realities that would come about in the Church.

“He raised up testimony in Jacob,” that is, he placed it among the Jewish people in order to raise up his commandments, which had died through Adam’s transgression. “And he set a law of moral commandments in Israel.” He uses “Israel” and “Jacob” for the same people.

In that testimony and in that law, he commanded our fathers to make known through their writings how many wonders, powers, and praises he had performed for them, so that they might be made known to their children—that is, to us.

It is as though he said: Truly they recounted God’s praises, powers, and wonders. For God commanded them to leave writings for us, in which he ordered them to make known to us, their children, his great benefits—namely, his praises, powers, and wonders—so that through us “another generation,” namely the Gentile generation, might know them, that is, understand them mystically.

It should be noted that he had said nearly the same thing above, where he said “how many things we have heard,” up to the words “the fathers recounting.”

There is nevertheless this difference: here he says that they recounted these things by the Lord’s command, which he had not said above.

Nor will another generation alone know them. The children who will be born from us will also know them, and they will rise up—that is, they will be attentive to this knowledge, understanding it mystically. They will not lie down—that is, they will not take these things according to the letter alone—but will recount them to their children.

By this he makes those to whom he is speaking here very attentive, since he foretells that those who are yet to be born will not be ignorant of these things. For this reason they will recount them to their children.

“So that they may place their hope in God”—that is, after hearing of these benefits freely granted by God to the fathers, they should expect nothing from themselves but place all hope for benefits in God.

“And may not forget the works of God, as their fathers forgot them”—that is, may they not forget the benefits that God will work in them, which were signified through the benefits worked in the ancient fathers, who themselves forgot them.

“And so that they may seek his commandments,” that is, attentively know and love them, which their fathers neglected.

For this reason also they will recount them: so that their children may not become like their ancient fathers—namely, so that they may not become a morally perverse generation, provoking God by evil deeds as their fathers did.

He shows in what respect that generation was perverse when he says: It was a generation “that did not direct its heart,” so as to think rightly about God; “and its spirit,” that is, its reason, “was not believed with God”—that is, it was not believed capable of thinking rightly with God’s help, but only by itself.

This is to say: They believed themselves sufficient to think rightly without God’s help, and in this they were perverse.

Or it may be read this way: It was a generation that did not direct its heart toward thinking rightly; this part remains unchanged. And if at some time it thought rightly according to human custom, its spirit, existing with God, was not believed—that is, they did not trust their own reason, which, by thinking rightly, was with God, thinking what was pleasing to God, so that they might complete in action what they thought rationally.

Or it may be read concerning the fathers who lived in the time of Christ:

I say that our children, who will be born, will recount these things to their children who are to be saved, so that they may not become like their unbelieving fathers who lived in the time of Christ. Let them not become a morally perverse generation, provoking God by their perverse deeds, about whom the Lord testifies in the Gospel: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign,” and so forth (Matt. XII, 33).

It was a generation that did not direct its heart toward thinking rightly about God, and “its spirit was not believed with God the Son.” This is to say: It did not believe in the Son and the Holy Spirit. Here he implies that it did not believe in the Father either. For the Father is not known without the Son and the Holy Spirit, since they are one.

Nevertheless, the subsequent words seem to agree better with the earlier interpretation concerning the ancient fathers who lived in the time of Moses.

I say that the fathers were a generation that did not direct its heart. And not only those who were inferior among the fathers, but also those who ought to have been “the sons of Ephraim”—that is, imitators of Ephraim, the son of Joseph whom Jacob blessed—namely, the priests and Levites.

Although they were preeminent among the people, and ought by their good life to have sought this, so that they might receive from God, after the manner of Ephraim, a blessing (Gen. XLVIII, 8), “they bent the bow and shot arrows, but turned back on the day of battle.”

He presents this by way of a likeness. That is, they became like cowards who, before battle, engage in preliminary display, bend the bow, and shoot arrows, threatening that they will fight well; but on the day of battle, once the matter comes to action, they turn and flee.

They bent the bow and shot arrows when they promised that they would obey God well, saying: “Whatever the Lord and Moses his servant commands, we will hear and do” (Exod. XIX, 8; XX, 19). But as soon as they came to observing the commandments and fighting against vices, they immediately turned back to their crimes.

Through Ephraim, whose name means “fruitfulness,” the priests and Levites are signified. They ought to have produced the fruit of good works among the people, so as thereby to be sons—that is, imitators—of Ephraim, but they were sterile.

This also happens in the Church. For many prelates in the Church, who promise that they will act courageously through preaching and through the example of their good life among the people, turn back once they come to action. They ought to be sons of Ephraim, that is, producers of good works.

He shows how they turned back on the day of battle when he adds: “They did not keep God’s covenant,” that is, they did not fulfill God’s law. And if a few of them kept it in some respects, “they did not wish to walk in his law,” that is, they did not proceed willingly in fulfilling the law.

This is to say: Whatever they fulfilled, they fulfilled not willingly but unwillingly, out of fear.

Although they ought at least, out of consideration for his benefits, to have loved God’s covenant, they forgot his benefits, which he performed as though by violence—namely, the drowning of Pharaoh and other things of this kind.

They also forgot his wonders, which he showed them—that is, which he performed openly before them.

He calls those benefits wonders that he worked wonderfully, not as though by violence but by power, such as the manna and other things of this kind.

I say that they forgot the wonders he showed them—namely, the wonders and benefits he performed in Egypt.

He explains in which part of Egypt when he adds: “In the field of Taphnes” (alternative reading: “Taneos”). There he performed benefits and wonders for them.

Taphnis is a city in Egypt, where God worked many wonders and benefits for them. These wonders performed in Egypt he carried out before the fathers—namely, Moses and Aaron and the other leaders of Israel. They were called fathers not according to generation, but according to the paternal affection they had toward their subjects.

It is as though he said: Although the people did not understand those wonders, he nevertheless performed them in such a way that they were before the fathers—that is, so that their significance was manifest to them.

He then enumerates the things he did in Egypt, first recounting the things he did after the departure from Egypt, as follows:

I say that they forgot the wonders he showed them. And here are the wonders: When Pharaoh was pursuing them, he divided the sea for them and led them through the divided sea.

And so that the waters might not harm them in any way, he caused the waters of the sea to stand—that is, he made them stand so that they would not flow—just as water stands confined in a wineskin, unable to flow.

Thus, all the remaining benefits are read according to the letter up to the end of the psalm, and all of them are explained according to the literal sense in their proper place, continuously.

But since an allegory seems to be contained in each individual passage, the mystical meanings appear to require separate explanation, because it is difficult, or impossible, to read the psalm continuously according to the allegorical sense.

Therefore let us proceed to the allegory of what we have already read according to the letter. Beginning at the place where it says “the sons of Ephraim,” we shall first explain this verse differently from the historical explanation given above, and afterward we shall turn to the allegory.

Since, therefore, he had earlier promised, “I will open my mouth in parables,” and had inserted the preceding passage in order to make those to whom he was speaking attentive to his words, he now proceeds to speak parables and propositions as follows:

I said that I would open my mouth in parables. And now I set forth parables, from the place where I say “the sons of Ephraim” to the end of the psalm.

The first is this:

“The sons of Ephraim”—that is, the imitators and followers of Jeroboam, who was from the tribe of Ephraim. He is therefore called Ephraim here not with regard to the interpretation of the name—“bending the bow,” that is, making their deceitfulness intense, “and shooting arrows from the bow,” that is, sending from their deception deceitful injuries against their neighbors—“turned away from Jerusalem and from the tribe of Judah, going to Samaria after Jeroboam.”

They preferred to be “on the day of battle” rather than in concord—that is, in the fervor of rebellion against the tribe of Judah, the tribe of Benjamin, and the few from the tribe of Levi who remained in Jerusalem with Rehoboam, the king and son of Solomon, from the tribe of Judah.

And by bending the bow and shooting arrows, “they did not keep God’s covenant,” and so forth, up to “before the fathers,” which, as has already been explained above, is explained here as well.

Here the history is touched upon, and it is as follows (III Kings XIV):

In the time of Rehoboam, son of Solomon and king of Israel, another man arose from the tribe of Ephraim, the son of Joseph, named Jeroboam. He departed and established a kingdom for himself in Samaria. Ten tribes followed him. Only the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, together with certain sons of Levi, remained in Jerusalem with King Rehoboam.

Those who departed with Jeroboam, acting deceitfully against their neighbors, forgot the benefits and wonders that God had performed in their own time and in the time of their fathers. In consideration of these benefits, they ought to have been recalled from their deceitfulness and to have dwelt in Jerusalem with the tribe of Judah.

Through Rehoboam, who reigned in Jerusalem and was from the tribe of Judah, Christ is appropriately understood: Christ, the king from the tribe of Judah, of the eternal Jerusalem and of the earthly Church, which already sees eternal peace in contemplation.

Through the tribe of Judah and the others who remained in Jerusalem with Rehoboam, the faithful—who are members of Christ—were prefigured. They prefer to be subject to him and to remain in the Church.

Through Jeroboam, who, after abandoning Jerusalem, established a kingdom for himself in a foreign region, the devil is appropriately figured. After abandoning through pride the fellowship of the heavenly Jerusalem, he established for himself, through unbelief, a kingdom among those who are completely alienated from that Jerusalem by their unbelief.

Through the ten tribes, which abandoned Jerusalem and their king Rehoboam and adhered to the wicked king Jeroboam, heretics were signified. They despise Christ, the true and holy King, and the fellowship of the Church, and subject themselves to the devil.

Another parable follows when he says:

“He performed wonders before their fathers in the land of Egypt, in the field of Taneos.”

According to the literal sense, we have explained this above. In the same way, God performs wonders in the Church when he leads unbelievers back to the way of faith and performs countless other works.

Although these wonders are unknown to the uneducated, they are nevertheless before the fathers—that is, they are manifest to the faithful prelates in the Church, who preside over the people with paternal affection.

He performs these wonders in the present land, which is a land of affliction. For Egypt is interpreted as “affliction.”

And he performs them “in the field of Taneos,” that is, in the plain of the humble commandment. He performs these miracles—calling unbelievers to the faith—through the plain and intelligible teaching of the preachers, given in humility. This teaching is not burdensome and obscure like the old law.

Thus “the field of Taneos” is appropriately understood. For a field is level ground. Taphnis (or Thanis) is interpreted as “the humble commandment.”

Another parable follows. After they had gone out of Egypt, God divided the sea for them and led them through dry land; and, lest the waters harm them, he set the waters as though in a wineskin, so that they would not flow away. All this pertains to the historical sense, according to what is written: “The children of Israel went through the midst of the dry sea, while the waters were for them as a wall on their right and on their left” (Exod. 14:22).

This also takes place allegorically in the Church. For God divides the sea—that is, he divides the Gentile people through the teaching of preachers—so that he may take one part for salvation and reject the other as destined for condemnation. Through faith and good works he leads those who are to be saved to the promised land, namely, the heavenly homeland. And lest the waters—that is, unbelievers, who are unstable 301 like water—be able to disturb the good, he establishes them, that is, he restrains them as waters are confined in a wineskin, so that they cannot flow except at the cupbearer’s pleasure.

He does not, indeed, restrain the wicked in such a way that they have no power to rage against the good; rather, God permits them to flow in their raging only to a measured extent, so that, although at times they afflict the good with bodily torments, they can in no way make them like themselves. Or God divides the Red Sea—that is, God divides baptism—so that for some, namely the just, it is unto salvation, while for others, who are not just, it is unto condemnation. “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16). Baptism is signified by the sea because it is made from water, and because sins are wiped away in it, just as the enemies of the children of Israel were destroyed in the sea. It is called Red because it was consecrated through the shedding of Christ’s blood; and through the washing and faith of baptism it leads his own to the land of the living.

But lest his own, after the grace of baptism, be submerged by the waters—that is, lest they be led by the waves of evil desires to the death of wicked action—he sets the waters as though in a wineskin, that is, he restrains the waves of desire through the mortification of the flesh, lest they prevail. This mortification is fittingly figured by the wineskin, because a wineskin is made from the skins of dead animals. This is to say: He makes his own mortify their flesh through fasts and other afflictions; and through this he restrains their desires, lest they be able to prevail over them.

It follows: “And he led them in a cloud by day.” That is, after the children of Israel had crossed the sea, he led them, once they had emerged from the sea, through the desert in a cloud by day—that is, beneath a cloud that would be a cooling shade for them from the heat of the day (Exod. 13:21). And throughout the whole night he led them by the illumination of fire; namely, lest they suffer obstacles in the darkness of night, he gave them illumination from the fiery pillar that went before them.
