In the same way God cools his own as they proceed through this life—which, in comparison with eternal life, is called a desert—by day with a cloud, that is, by the protection of his humanity. For the sake of our salvation, his humanity cools us from the heat of vices and from the fiery exaltation of prosperity. The humanity of Christ continually intercedes for the faithful before the Father, lest they become overheated by any harmful heat. In accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “Christ Jesus, who also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:34). Christ’s humanity is fittingly called a cloud, because it cools his own from the heat of vices, just as the brightness of day is shaded by a cloud.

“And throughout the whole night he led them by the illumination of fire”—that is, throughout this whole life, which is obscure like night and lacks perfect knowledge of God, he leads them from good to better by the illumination of the grace of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is called fire because he kindles the good with the fire of charity.

It follows: “He divided.” This is joined literally as follows. He not only led the children of Israel in a cloud by day and throughout the night by the illumination of fire, but he also divided the rock for them in the desert through Moses, so that he might draw water from it. Hence it is written: “He struck the rock twice with the rod, and waters flowed out in great abundance” (Num. 20:11). And after he had divided the rock, he fully watered the children of Israel, as one could be fully watered in a great abyss, that is, in extremely deep water.

But because he had said that they were watered and had not yet stated that the waters had flowed from the rock, he adds: I say that he divided the rock and drew water from the rock. And lest we suppose that he drew from it water that would remain in one place alone, he adds: “And he brought forth waters from the very rock, flowing like rivers”; and these waters followed them as they moved their camps through the desert, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “The rock followed them” (1 Cor. 10:4). This is to say: Water proceeding from the rock followed them.

By the rock divided through the double striking of the rod, from which abundant water flowed through the desert, accompanying them and continually satisfying them, Christ was signified—Christ who is a firm and solid rock. Concerning him the Apostle cries: “But the rock was Christ” (ibid.). Through the double striking of the rod, the two timbers of the cross were prefigured: one set lengthwise, the other across it. 302 On that cross the Lord’s body, which we have said is a firm rock, was pierced by nails, and his side was divided by the blow of a lance. From that division there flowed forth for us the grace of remission. As we proceed through the entire desert of this life, that grace continually accompanies us, spiritually satisfies us, and does so without ceasing until the end of the world. Therefore this grace was fittingly prefigured by the water that proceeded from the divided rock and, following the children of Israel through the desert, physically and continually satisfied them.

It follows: “And they added.” This is joined literally as follows. I say that God divided the rock for them and conferred the other benefits. And the children of Israel, although they had sinned before these benefits and ought, in view of the benefits, to have ceased from sin, added still to sin against him. They sinned to such a degree that they stirred him to anger—that is, to vengeance—in the waterless place, that is, in the desert.

He shows how they sinned when he adds: “Truly they stirred the Lord to anger, because they also tempted God in their hearts,” that is, they hesitated in their thoughts concerning the omnipotence of the Lord, so that by tempting him they asked for foods necessary for their souls, that is, for their life. And they spoke evil of God. For they said: “Can God prepare a table,” that is, complete nourishment, for us in this desert, in which there is no human cultivation? Surely he cannot.

This is to say: They stirred God to anger because they thought him powerless, and they spoke evil of him with their mouths, saying hesitantly: Can he give us food here, since we are in a desert place? Surely he cannot.

And if their reason sometimes told them the opposite—“Surely God can give a table, since he struck the rock and waters flowed”—they, on the contrary, said: Since he struck the rock and waters flowed, and not merely a little water, but torrents also flooded forth from it, will he not also—that is, even—be able to give bread to his people, namely, to us? Or, if he gives a little bread, will he be able to prepare a table for us, his people? Certainly not.

This is to say: Although by striking the rock he caused waters to flow from it, he will not therefore be able to give us bread in full measure. And because, by saying these things, they did not believe in God as one able to give them bread, they did not hope in his salvation—that is, they had no hope of food in consideration of his salvation, namely, they did not hope that, just as he had saved them from Egypt, so also he could give them food.

God heard—that is, he took notice of their unbelief—and delayed vengeance, since he did not punish them immediately. And the more he delayed, the more fire was kindled in Jacob, that is, vengeance was increased against the children of Israel, more than if he had immediately punished them while they were sinning. And his anger was not kindled only a little, but it rose—that is, the anger, namely the vengeance, grew greatly—in Israel, that is, in the Jewish people.

This is to say: Because they were so unbelieving, God took notice of their unbelief; and by delaying the punishment, he increased his vengeance all the more.

And although they had tempted him and spoken evil of him, nevertheless, to show his omnipotence, he commanded the clouds above—that is, the clouds of heaven—to rain manna upon them. And he opened the gates of heaven, that is, he made waxen cataracts through which the manna might descend. And he rained manna upon them for food, and gave them the bread of heaven—that is, food created without human labor in heaven, namely in the air: manna.

“And man ate the bread of angels”: that is, the Jewish people, man in the merely human and non-spiritual sense, ate that manna which signified the bread of angels, namely Christ, by whom the angels are spiritually refreshed. I say that he gave them the bread of heaven, and not sparingly, but sent them provisions in abundance, namely, the bread of heaven that would be their food.

Another translation has “the bread of the strong.” Angels are appropriately called strong in comparison with us, who are weak. They are strongly refreshed by Christ, the true bread, in that nature in which he is the Word of God. But because our weakness could not feed upon such bread in the divine nature, which is invisible to us, “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), and through the eating of his flesh “dwelt among us” (ibid.). Having therefore applied these verses to the literal sense, let us approach the allegory.

I said that God the Father divided through the Passion the rock in the desert, namely Christ in this life, who is a solid rock and from whose division the grace of remission proceeded. Yet many heretics, having received this grace through baptism, add sins to those committed before baptism, continuing to sin against God after baptism. They sin to such a degree that they stir him to anger—that is, to vengeance—against themselves. And this occurs in the waterless place, that is, in the dryness of the heart, because they do not wish to be watered by that grace; thus they make God angry with them.

In this way they add to their sins after baptism. For they also tempt God in their hearts, that is, they doubt God’s omnipotence: whether he can give his body under the appearance of bread to be eaten. And they tempt him in such a way that they nevertheless ask for foods useful to their souls. They ask daily for the Lord’s body and blood with the voice alone and not with the heart, when they say: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke 11:3), that is, your body and blood.

This body and blood are one indivisible and incorruptible food, although they appear to be broken under the appearance of bread and crushed by the teeth of the faithful. This mystery is indeed insoluble: why it appears to be broken and crushed while remaining indivisible. Nevertheless, it must be believed with firm faith. He calls it “foods” in the plural, although it is one, according to the participation of many.

I say that they tempt him by thinking. And they tempt him, and speak evil of God with their mouths. For they say: “Can God in the desert”—that is, in this life, which he physically abandoned when he ascended into heaven—“prepare a table,” that is, make the creature of bread into a table, namely, into the nourishment of his body? Certainly not.

This is to say: Since he has abandoned this earth and is bodily and locally in heaven, how can he still prepare the creature of bread that now exists, so that it may become his flesh, which existed a thousand years ago? In no way.

But when Catholics object to them, “Surely God can do this, since he has done something even more wondrous—namely, he allowed himself to be struck as a rock, from which the water of spiritual grace flowed,” they, in their most wicked mouths, respond: Since he struck—that is, allowed himself to be struck—the rock in the Passion, namely himself, and from it waters of spiritual grace flowed, and not little waters, but torrents, that is, abundant waters, flooded forth, will it therefore also follow that God can give bread which is his body to his people, that is, to the people of the faithful?

Or we may put it more plainly: Will he therefore be able to prepare a table of bread—that is, make the nourishment of his body—for the people of the faithful? Certainly not.

As though he were saying: Even if through his Passion he bestowed the grace of remission, it does not therefore follow that he can make his body from bread, by which he might satisfy the faithful people.

And therefore those who still did not believe in God the Father by what they said, nor hoped in his salvation—that is, in Christ the Savior sent by God the Father—because they did not believe that, through the cooperation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, Christ’s bread could be made his body, the Lord heard this—that is, he took notice of their unbelief—and nevertheless delayed their bodily punishment until the future.

And fire was kindled in their soul, that is, the fervor of his vengeance, in Jacob—that is, in those very heretics who ought to have been Jacob, namely, vigorous wrestlers—and they failed. His vengeance was not kindled only a little, but anger—that is, vengeance—rose in the soul, that is, grew greatly, in Israel, that is, in the heretics who ought to be Israel: those who see God, yet have been made blind through pride.

This is to say: Because they did not wish to believe, although God had not yet punished them in the body, he nevertheless condemned them in soul by blinding them. And because they do not wish to believe, they are without excuse.

For God also commanded the clouds existing above—that is, the apostles, who are more exalted than the other faithful, to whom the heretics ought to have believed—he commanded them, that is, instructed them, to preach the mystery of the bread that becomes his body. And through the clouds he opened the gates of heaven, that is, he made open the Scriptures that had previously been hidden. These are the gates of heaven, that is, the entrance to God’s hidden mysteries, which are called heaven because they are high like heaven and are concealed from many.

This is to say: Through the preachers he made the Scriptures open, in which the mystery of this sacrament and the other mysteries are contained. Nor did he merely command the clouds to rain these things—that is, to proclaim them throughout the Church—but through the clouds he rained manna upon them, that is, his body for eating. Through the preachers he gave those heretics the teaching of eating his body.

“Manna” is derived from the Hebrew word *manhu*. For when the Jews rose in the morning on which it first fell and saw it falling, they marveled and said: “Manhu?” (Exod. 16:15), which means: “What is this?” Hence Christ’s body is appropriately called manna. For after he had first said to the disciples, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54), certain people who were hesitating said: “What is this? How can he give us his flesh to eat?” (ibid. 6:53).

He not only rained the teaching of eating that bread, but also gave them the bread of heaven to eat, namely himself, who is the true bread by which the heavenly spirits are continually refreshed. As he himself testifies in the Gospel: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (ibid. 6:41). And this bread of angels—that is, the bread by which angels are satisfied—is eaten by every kind of human being, both faithful and unbelieving.

I say that he gave the bread of heaven, and not sparingly, but sends them the provisions of his body and blood in abundance, abundantly for as long as the world lasts. Another translation has: “He sent them a grain harvest.” The Lord’s body is appropriately called grain, because it is more precious than every kind of food, just as grain is more precious than every harvest. If the passage is read literally, manna is rightly called grain because it was sweet and flavorful in the manner of grain.

It follows: “He transferred.” This is joined literally as follows. He did not give manna only to the children of Israel; but when they murmured because they had no meat and wished to return to the meat-pots of Egypt—although the manna had the taste of meat and of all the foods they desired—he transferred the south wind from heaven. That is, he removed that south wind from the higher air in which it was blowing, which is called heaven, and brought the African wind—that is, the south wind, which is called African because it comes from Africa—into the air nearer the earth.

This is to say: While it was blowing high above, it was not suitable for carrying quails, which remain on the ground and fly in the air close to the ground. He caused the African wind, removed from the higher air, to blow near the earth, so that by its force it would bring quails from the land in which they were abundant.

Or, if we say that the south wind and the African wind are two winds, the passage may be read as follows: He transferred the south wind from heaven, that is, he entirely removed the south wind from the air, since it was useless for this task; and he brought in the African wind, which was suitable for it. And he did this by his power, that is, by his authority. For he is omnipotent.

He says this as a reproach to those who do not judge him to be omnipotent. Another translation has: “He transferred the east wind from heaven.” It was unsuitable for this task; the rest of the verse remains unchanged. And through the operation of the African wind “he rained flesh upon them as abundantly as dust,” that is, he caused flesh to fall upon them plentifully, in the likeness of rain, like dust.

He explains what flesh he means when he adds: “and winged birds”—namely quails—“like the sand of the sea.” He does not say “winged” as though there were some flying creature without wings; rather, by this he commends God’s power, since he caused winged birds to fall as though they lacked wings. And, to make God’s benefit still greater, it was not necessary to seek those falling birds far from the camps. For they fell in the midst of their camps and around their tents—that is, around their camps: they fell both in the middle and outside beside the camps.

Having applied these three verses to the literal sense, let us approach the allegory.

I said that God rained through the preachers the teaching of eating his body. And in order that he might also rain other commandments upon them through those same preachers, he transferred the south wind from heaven. That is, he removed from the mystery of sublime contemplation the preachers who are fervent with the fire of charity and faith, in the likeness of the south wind, which is a hot wind coming from a hot region. And he brought the African wind into the earth—that is, he brought those same preachers down to earthly matters, so that they might preach to the people. The south wind and the African wind signify the same persons, since both come from a hot region.

Or, if we say, “He transferred the east wind from heaven,” it will be as though he were saying: He removed the preachers who are radiant in the sublime knowledge of God—who are signified by the east wind because it comes from the world’s luminous region, namely from the east—from the pursuit of contemplation, so that they might devote themselves to preaching. And, while they were African—that is, fervent in charity—he assigned them to the care of preaching.

And he did this by his power, that is, by his might. After he had assigned them to the care of preaching, through those preachers he rained flesh upon them—that is, upon the heretics and also the faithful. He uses the plural for the singular: *carnes* (“meats”) for *caro* (“flesh”). When he says “upon them,” he indicates that this teaching came from above, as though he were saying: He rained flesh upon them, that is, the teaching of the incarnation of the Word of God.

I say that this flesh was “like dust,” that is, light in every virtue and good work and free from every moisture of sin, just as dust is light and without moisture. And he did not rain flesh alone, but also winged birds, that is, all salutary commandments that raise the faithful toward heavenly things, like wings raise flying creatures.

And those commandments fell—that is, came down from above—in the midst of their camps, that is, openly, in the middle of their cities, which are called camps because, like camps, they are temporary. At times they fell around their tents, that is, around the houses in which they dwell briefly and temporarily, as in tents.

This is to say: At times they preached salutary commandments privately in houses, so as to attract their hearers; at other times, when it was suitable, they preached openly in the midst of the cities.

It follows: I say that God rained manna and birds upon the children of Israel, and they ate them, not merely to moderation, but were exceedingly filled, that is, they ate to gluttony. And although they ate to gluttony, their desire was granted them, and not merely in part, but to such a degree that they were not defrauded—that is, diminished—of their desire.

This is to say: He granted them whatever they desired. And because they had asked God for food while tempting him and ate it with gluttony, while the food was still in their mouths—that is, while they were still eating the manna and the birds—the anger of God came upon them, that is, God’s vengeance descended without delay, so that he might justly crush them.

He explains how this happened when he adds: “And that anger slew their fat ones,” that is, the proud, who through the fatness of prosperity had become arrogant. And he hindered the chosen ones of Israel—namely Moses and the other rulers and saints—from being able to proceed, since they were disturbed by their burial.

Or he hindered the prayer of the chosen, that is, he made it ineffective, as something obstructed, so that when they prayed for them they did not obtain what they asked.

And when the others who survived ought to have been chastised so that they would not sin, in view of the miracles mentioned above and this vengeance, nevertheless, even after considering all these things—that is, while considering all this—they sinned still, and did not believe that God would become their avenger in his miracles, that is, in consideration of his miracles.

This is to say: Although, in view of the miracles mentioned above, they ought to have believed that God would be their avenger, they nevertheless refused to believe, so as to cease from sinning. And therefore their days failed in the unity of those who existed.

This is to say: Their way failed, so that they died, because they were vain. Or it may be understood this way: They failed after the manner of those born in vanity.

This is to say: They died in such a way that they seemed to have been born in vain and without any usefulness. And they did not fail slowly, but their years failed with haste—that is, without delay. Here “days” and “years” mean the same thing.

But when God slew them, those who survived, compelled by fear, sought him in prayers, returned to him in repentance for their sins, and came to him with a promise of obedience. They did this at dawn, that is, earnestly, after the manner of clients who rise early and diligently attend to their lord’s business.

Then they remembered what they had forgotten in prosperity: namely, that God is their helper against imminent dangers, and that God Most High is their omnipotent redeemer, who had redeemed them from the hand of Pharaoh and from the Red Sea.

Then they loved him with their mouths, that is, in the manner of a pretender. This is to say: They uttered deceptive words that appeared to belong to love. And by loving with their mouths, they lied to him with their tongues, that is, by making the deceptive promise that they loved him.

He explains how they lied when he adds: I say that they loved him with their mouths, but “their heart was not right,” namely, it was not in harmony with that God, so as to will what God willed. It would have been right if it had been with him.

Nor were they regarded as faithful through good works in his covenant, that is, in the promise they had made to him. This is to say: They did not act well, so as to be faithful to their promise.

But although God could justly have taken vengeance on them, he is merciful by his nature. And he will be propitious toward their sins with regard to their remnant at the end of the world: namely, at the end of the world he will be propitious toward the sins of those who are still to be born. And he will not destroy them, that is, he will not destroy their descendants as he destroyed their unbelieving fathers.

Here, by *litotes*, it is understood that he will save them; for if he had killed all the fathers, no sons would have been born toward whom he could show mercy.

His mercy was so abundant that he turned away his anger—that is, his vengeance—from the fathers. Yet he did not turn it away in such a way that he killed no one; rather, he did so in such a way that he did not kindle all his anger so as to destroy them all.

As though he were saying: He killed some, but left others to beget sons toward whom he would show mercy in the future. And, so that mercy might abound, he remembered that they are flesh, that is, made of carnal and fragile matter and inclined to sin. They are fragile because their spirit—that is, their reason—is “going,” that is, departing from God through sin, and does not return by itself.

This is to say: He remembered that their reason can depart from God by itself, but cannot return by itself unless God’s grace brings it back. He does not say “remembered” because God had ever forgotten, but because, by killing some of them, he appeared to have forgotten them.

Having treated the literal sense of these twelve verses, let us approach the allegory.

I say that every human being, both faithful and unbelieving, eats the bread of angels. I mean that the faithful and the unbelieving eat it, but the faithful are satisfied by it, whereas the unbelieving are not. They are filled by that bread of angels with the reality of the sacrament, namely, with union with the Church and perfection of virtues.

And because here they are satisfied with the reality of the sacrament, it will grant them their desire, namely eternal life in the future, which they desire to attain through the sacrament. It will not grant their desire sparingly, but so fully that they will not be defrauded—that is, diminished—of their desire; rather, they will obtain more fully than they desire.

I say that for those who eat and are satisfied, it will grant their desire. But here it punishes without delay those who do not wish to be satisfied. For while the food is still in their mouths, the anger of God rises against them.

This is to say: In the very act of eating, God’s anger is multiplied in their oppression, blinding them inwardly because they eat irreverently and unworthily. Nor does God’s anger merely rise against them by punishing them inwardly; bodily also he slays their fat ones, namely the proud, who approach the eating of this sacrament arrogantly and without reverence.

Hence the Apostle says: “Therefore many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep” (1 Cor. 11:30)—sleeping the sleep of death. And because of their slaying he hinders the chosen of Israel, namely the rulers of the Church; he makes them hindered 307 by compassion for those whom he slays, since they cannot assist them by their prayers.

Or it may be understood this way: He not only punishes subjects if they become fat, but also hinders the chosen of the Church if they grow fat, either by bodily death or by diminution of virtues, when he disciplines them for this reason. He sets this down for the correction both of subjects and of rulers.

But when those who are not slain ought to have been chastised by considering the vengeance inflicted on such evils and by reflecting upon the miracles that God performed among them, as we have shown above, nevertheless they still sin after considering all these things—that is, although they consider all this—and do not believe that God will be their future avenger in view of his miracles. That is, although they know that he performed such miracles, as we have shown, they nevertheless do not seem firmly to believe that he is powerful enough to take vengeance.

And therefore, just as the days of the others of whom we have just spoken failed, so the days of these survivors who exist in vanity also fail, that is, they die, because they are vain.

Or it may be understood this way: Their days fail so that they appear to have been born in vanity and without usefulness, since they die in this manner; and their life did not fail late, but their years—that is, their life—failed with haste, that is, they die quickly.

And when God slays them, those who survive seek him in prayer, asking him to spare them, and return to him, promising obedience if he spares them. And at dawn—that is, earnestly—they come to him through repentance.

And what they had forgotten through pride they remember: namely, they remember that God is their helper in cooperating toward good, and that God Most High is their Redeemer through the death of the cross.

Then they love him with their mouths, that is, with lying mouths. They say that they love God, and with their tongues they lie to him—that is, they lie to him with a deceitful tongue, which belongs to them and not to God.

But their heart is not right, that is, it is wicked; it is not a participant with that God in a good will. Nor are they regarded as faithful—that is, truthful—in his covenant. They do not act well so as to be faithful to the promise they made to him in baptism, under the testimony of their sponsors.

I say that they are unbelieving. But although God could justly destroy them all because of their falsehood, he is merciful by nature, so that he does not become angry. And he will be propitious toward their sins, forgiving them in the future, and will not destroy them in the future, as they deserve; rather, in his clemency he will save them.

And lest he destroy them with eternal death in the future, his mercy abounds here, so that here he may turn away his anger—that is, his vengeance—and not kill them bodily, but, sparing them, grant them a place for repentance.

But lest he seem to turn away his anger in such a way that he would not afflict them even with transitory scourges, he specifies this when he adds: “And thus I say that he will turn away his anger, so that he does not kindle all his anger,” that is, so that he does not display all the vengeance that he could rightly display.

As though he were saying: In part he takes vengeance on them by chastising them with transitory scourges in paternal kindness; in part he spares them, so as not to kill them. And so that mercy may abound toward them, he remembers that they are flesh, that is, carnal and fragile, and that their spirit—that is, their reason—is going by itself, that is, departing from God through sin, and does not return by itself through repentance unless God’s grace grants precisely this, that they may repent.

And because he considers them to be fragile in this way, he turns his anger away from them and mercifully spares them. He does not say “remembers” because God ever forgets, but because, when he kills some by taking vengeance, he appears to forget; when he spares others, he appears to remember.

By saying that the Lord turns away his anger and remembers human frailty, he commends God’s mercy and humbles his hearers, showing them to be so exceedingly fragile.

It follows: “How often,” and so forth, up to “And they tempted and provoked God Most High.” This is applied to the literal sense as follows.

I said that they sinned by tempting God in their hearts, the children of Israel, in order to ask for food for their souls; and God granted them their desire, and afterward took vengeance on them. And they, turned by fear, sinned again, while he again showed them mercy. Yet they did not correct themselves so as to cease afterward.

But as often as they provoked him by sinning in the desert—that is, in the desert after the Red Sea, by sinning many times—they made God, who is sweet by nature, bitter to themselves. And they did not provoke him only a little, but to such a degree that they stirred him to anger—that is, to vengeance—and, as though by a certain force, compelled him to act against them in the waterless place while they were sinning there.

This was a place of great fear, since he fed them there with manna and gave them drink from water drawn from the rock by the force of his power. In this way they stirred him to anger, because they turned away from God to sin and tempted God, that is, they distrusted his power, hesitating whether he could free them from the hand of their imminent enemies, the Midianites and others.

And they provoked the Holy God of Israel—that is, of the Jewish people—by evil deeds: by making a molten calf, bowing their heads to it, and committing other evil acts. It was wholly unfitting that they should provoke by evil works one who is holy and able to sanctify those who obey him.

Yet they ought not to have tempted God by hesitating concerning his power, remembering how he had redeemed them from the hand of Pharaoh, who afflicted them, and what plagues he had inflicted in Egypt on their behalf.

They did not remember his hands—that is, his power and assistance—hands, I say, displayed on the day when he redeemed them from the hand of the one afflicting them, that is, from the power of Pharaoh, who oppressed them with various tribulations. Nor did they remember the signs that he performed in Egypt, just as he performed his signs in Egypt. It is as though he were saying: They certainly knew that God had performed those signs, but they did not remember them in the manner in which he gloriously performed them; that is, they did not remember them in such a way that, by contemplating them, they would thereafter no longer distrust his power.

I say that he performed his signs in Egypt—and not small signs, but prodigies, that is, his great marvels, appropriate to him, since he himself was great and powerful—in the plain of Tanis [Taphneos] in Egypt. Here he designates the whole by a part. Moreover, Taphnis or Taphnae, as we have already said, is a city where he performed many prodigies for them (Ezek. 30:18). And behold, the prodigies: he changed their—namely, the Egyptians’—flowing rivers and their rains, that is, the water from cisterns which they had collected from rainfall for drinking because of the scarcity of springs, into blood; that is, he made them bloody, so that they would not drink them for refreshment. Where we have *rains*, blessed Ambrose has *rainwaters*. After this prodigy, he sent against them the *coenomyia*, that is, he sent against them, to afflict them, a very great multitude of flies, and it devoured them, that is, it repeatedly bit them. In Hebrew it says “every kind of fly”; but when he writes *coenomyia*, he signifies the whole by a part. After this plague he sent upon them—namely, upon the Egyptians—frogs, that is, an abundance of frogs, and destroyed them, that is, made them dispersed. They could not live together because of the excessive flood of frogs, which soiled them.

After this he gave their produce to rust for consumption. Blessed Jerome wishes *rust* to be a certain kind of worm which, creeping secretly through the tree, entirely consumes the fruit together with the leaves—the creatures commonly called *canillae*. Augustine, however, says that *rust* is a harmful mist which destroys the fruit. Some maintain that *rust* means the caterpillar. After this he gave their labors to the locusts, namely, the crops which they had prepared by their labor; he gave them to the multitude of locusts for devouring. He killed their vines with hail, that is, he destroyed the fruit of the vines by the blow of hail, and their mulberry trees with frost. By *mulberry trees* he signifies all other trees. This means: He destroyed the fruit of the mulberry trees and of the other trees by excessive rain. And afterward he delivered their cattle to the hail for striking, and their possessions—that is, their houses and their other property—to fire for burning. [Col. 1046B]

Moses did not include this plague of fire in Exodus together with the other plagues. But since it is evident that he omitted many other things, it is believed that he omitted this one as well; the prophet, being no less authoritative than Moses, added it under the revelation of the Holy Spirit.

And to speak universally: He sent upon them wrath, that is, the greatest vengeance of his indignation, namely, the sequel to his lesser vengeance. Lest this seem to have been stated intransitively—that is, as though *wrath* and *indignation* were the same thing—he explains it when he adds that he sent indignation upon them, that is, a lesser vengeance, by destroying their lesser possessions; afterward wrath, that is, a greater vengeance, by destroying their more precious possessions; and afterward tribulation, that is, a much greater vengeance, by killing a portion of them. He carried out this entire infliction—of indignation, wrath, and tribulation—through evil angels, that is, through the agency of demons.

He introduces these matters concerning evil angels in order to increase the misery of the Egyptians, since he says that they were afflicted by the very beings whose servants they were; and by this he also recalls his hearers from subjection to demons. He likewise shows the order of his vengeance in this way: I say that he carried out this infliction through evil angels, through whose agency, namely, he made a road—that is, the breadth—of his wrath from the path that had previously existed. It is as though he were saying: When his vengeance had previously been narrow, like a path, he made it broad, like a road. By this he shows that his wrath was at first small but afterward great, and thereby instructs us not to neglect his small vengeance, lest perhaps we incur a greater one.

He therefore shows the greater vengeance in parts, when he says: Namely, he did not spare them from the death of their souls, taking them away. This means: He killed them inwardly in their souls, blinding and hardening them so that they would not wish to release the children of Israel. Hence it is written: “The heart of Pharaoh was hardened; he does not wish to release the people of the Lord” (Exod. 7:9). And because, having been killed in their souls, they did not wish to release the people, he enclosed their cattle in death, that is, he brought them to death by the blows of hail.

Although this was also stated above, where he said, “He delivered their cattle to the hail,” here he says something else; nevertheless, it could not clearly be understood above that he had killed the cattle, whereas here he states this plainly. He shows the greater vengeance in parts when he adds: “And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt,” namely, on that night when he led the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt; he killed all the firstborn, both human and animal. And first he struck in the tents of Ham, that is, in Egypt, where the sons of Ham dwelt in tents, the firstfruits of all their labor, that is, all the earliest and choicest crops which they had prepared with labor; or the firstfruits of labor, that is, the crops that were most ready to ripen, and therefore afflicted them more than if inferior or later crops had been struck.

I say that he afflicted the Egyptians in so many and such various ways, and that he took his people, namely the children of Israel, away from the power of the Egyptians like sheep—that is, as his sheep, for whom he cared as a shepherd cares for sheep. And he led those children of Israel who were in the desert—that is, the desert between the Red Sea and Egypt—through that desert as his flock, that is, as his own flock. He repeats what he said, “he led them through,” in order to add: “And he guided them,” I say, through the desert; and this in the hope of escape, so that they did not fear their enemies. He covered their enemies, the Egyptians, with the sea and killed them. He brought the children of Israel, rescued from the sea, into the mountain of his sanctification, that is, into Jerusalem, which is situated on a mountain and which he himself sanctified. The mountain, I say, which his right hand acquired—that is, his power—for the work of the children of Israel.

Since they could not otherwise dwell freely on that mountain, he drove out from their face, that is, from their presence, and at their insistence expelled the nations that dwelt on that mountain, namely the Jebusites and the others. After the nations had been expelled, he divided among the children of Israel the promised land by lot, among the tribes, and by a measuring cord of distribution, among the families. I say that he expelled the nations and made the twelve tribes of Israel dwell—that is, remain for a long time—in their tents, that is, in the houses of those nations. [Col. 1047C]

With the literal exposition of these seventeen verses thus completed, let the allegory be shown. I say that God turns his wrath away from unbelievers and heretics, remembering that they are flesh, and a spirit that goes away and does not return. Yet, although they ought to cease in view of God’s mercy, as often as they provoke him in the desert—that is, in the barrenness of the heart, because after the manner of a desert they make themselves barren of goodness and dry of spiritual grace—they provoke him. They do not provoke him a little, but so greatly that they stir him to wrath, that is, force him to vengeance against themselves in the waterless place, that is, in the barrenness of the heart. Desert and waterless place mean the same thing. Indeed, they truly stir him to wrath by their barrenness.

For they have turned from good to evil and have tempted him—that is, they tempt God through various heresies, doubting concerning him—and they provoke the Holy One of Israel by evil deeds, namely God, who is the Holy of holies and who sanctifies all who do not neglect to be Israel. Although they ought to remember the assistance he bestowed upon them in baptism, and thereby cease from evil, they do not remember his hands—that is, his assistance—so as to cease from evil. His hands, I say, are his assistance on the day when he redeemed them in baptism from the hand of the one afflicting them, that is, from the power of the devil, who afflicted them by leading them into unlawful acts.

Nor do they remember that he performed signs in Egypt, just as he performed his signs—that is, wonders—in the human race, which was Egypt, afflicted by original sin. It is as though he were saying: I do not deny that they remember them in some way; but they do not remember them fully and gloriously. I say that he performed his signs—not small signs, but prodigies, that is, exceedingly great and wondrous signs. He performed these signs in the plain of Tanis, that is, through the plain and humble teaching of the apostles. For it was a great and prodigious thing that through the teaching of the apostles he chose certain people from the mass of the lost and performed many other prodigies.

If they would recall this properly, they would not provoke the God who mercifully chose them. And so that they might fear returning to Egypt through sinning, they do not remember what vengeance God takes upon those who remain in Egypt. Namely, they do not remember how he changed the rivers of some of them—that is, the writings of the philosophers, which are called rivers because they flow toward posterity like rivers—into blood, that is, into death; and the rains, that is, those words which are called rains because they quickly pass away like rain, which, when it falls, is quickly absorbed and vanishes, into blood, that is, into death, so that they might not drink those rivers and rains—that is, so that they might not be refreshed by them for their benefit, as anyone is refreshed beneficially by drinking.

Blood signifies death, because blood is more often shed in death. It is as though he were saying: The philosophers, while still existing in Egypt, produce from their various errors writings and words which they believe to be for their own refreshment unto salvation, and through which they kill others. But God changes those writings and words for them into death, so that they do not drink them. I do not say that they do not drink them unto death; rather, they do not drink them in the sense that they are not for them the salutary refreshment they suppose them to be, just as drink is salutary refreshment for the one who drinks.

And upon some who are in Egypt God sends the *coenomyia*, and it devours them. That is, by withdrawing the assistance of his grace, he permits every kind of earthly desire to dominate them; these desires bite them inwardly with many anxieties, just as the *coenomyia* bites outwardly. Since they bite, they are appropriately signified by the *coenomyia*.

And upon some—namely, poets and sophists—he permits a frog to come, which destroys them, namely, useless chatter. This is rightly signified by the frog, which is talkative. That chatter destroys them, that is, makes them dispersed and divided: poets in their fictions, and sophists in their arguments, become greatly opposed to one another.

And if some fruits of good works exist in certain people who remain in Egypt—for without good works the life even of the worst person is found only with great difficulty—God gives those fruits to rust, that is, permits them to be consumed and brought to destruction by rust. Since rust dominates them, every good work in them is annihilated.

If, following Jerome, we understand *rust* as *canillae*, then by rust, which secretly creeps along and gradually consumes the fruit by eating it, lust is understood. Lust enters as though furtively, gradually taking possession of the wretched body; if any good work is in it, lust completely destroys it. For without chastity no one will please God. Or if we call rust caterpillars, we shall understand lust in the same way, since the caterpillar consumes fruit. But if, according to Augustine, rust is called a harmful and hidden mist which attacks and consumes fruit, then by rust is understood proud self-glory in the mind concerning one’s goodness, which chokes virtues and every good work.

And he gave their labors to the locusts, that is, the good works of certain people existing in the Egypt of unbelief. He permits what they labored over to be reduced to nothing through the rashness dominating them, which is understood by the locusts, since they move rashly, having no leader like a swarm of bees.

“And he struck their vines with hail” is stated intransitively. It is as though he were saying: He permits certain people remaining in Egypt—people who ought to be vines, fruitful in good works like vines—to be struck in their grapes by hail, and their fruits to be destroyed by despair of eternal goods, which is appropriately signified by hail. Hail, of course, is water frozen in the clouds of heaven. Hence despair is rightly called hail. For despair is nothing other than the freezing of hope in heavenly goods. Whoever despairs performs whatever good he does uselessly.

And he permits their mulberry trees to be struck by frost—that is, he permits certain people who ought to be fruitful in good works, like fruit-bearing mulberry trees, to be scorched and their good works consumed, if they have any, by hatred against their neighbor. Hatred removes the warmth of charity, just as frost in the morning—which we commonly call *frima*—removes the sun’s heat. Therefore hatred is rightly called frost. Hence John says: “He who hates his brother is a murderer. And we know that every murderer does not have life abiding in him” (1 John 3:15). [Col. 1049C]

“And he delivered their cattle to the hail,” that is, to destruction, which is signified by hail, since hail destroys crops and fruits by battering them. This too is stated intransitively, as though he were saying: He completely destroys some of those who are in Egypt, namely those who behave irrationally and excessively in accordance with pleasure, like cattle.

And he delivers the possessions of some of them—namely, their good works, which they possess—to fire for destruction; that is, he permits them to be annihilated by the excessive heat of anger, which continually dominates them. I say that he takes this vengeance upon some by permitting anger to dominate them, and that he sends rust upon others, while he punishes the rest in other ways, as we have shown.

And to speak universally: God sends wrath upon all who refuse to leave Egypt, that is, the great vengeance of his indignation, the sequel to his lesser vengeance. Lest this seem to have been said intransitively, he explains it when he adds that he sends indignation upon them, that is, a lesser vengeance, and wrath, that is, a greater one, and tribulation, that is, a much greater one. He carries out this infliction of vengeance through evil angels, that is, through the agency of demons.

He explains the order of vengeance by a comparison when he adds: Through the agency of those angels he makes a road—that is, a breadth—for the path of his wrath, that is, for the smallness of his vengeance. This means: When vengeance was previously small and narrow, like a path, he himself, through the agency of evil angels, makes it great and broad.

He shows how it was previously a path when he adds: Truly, it was previously a path; for previously he did not spare them from the death of their souls by delivering them. Here, by *litotes*, it is understood that he first kills them inwardly in their souls by blinding them. He also shows how he makes the vengeance broad, like a road, when he adds: After they have been killed in their souls, he encloses their cattle in death, that is, ends them in bodily death—the Egyptians themselves, existing irrationally like cattle.

Or it may be understood this way: I say that he made a road for the path of his wrath, and in this way he makes the wrath broad like a road, although previously it was narrow like a path. For he does not spare them in order to deliver them from the death of their souls; rather, he kills them in soul by blinding them, and he brings to an end in death—that is, kills—their cattle, namely their gentleness and the other virtues, if any are in them, through the excess of their vices. Those virtues are signified by cattle because cattle are gentle animals and provide human beings with support, as beasts of burden do.

And he does not kill only the ignoble; he also strikes with death every firstborn in the land of Egypt, that is, all those who are more worthy and distinguished in the earthly Egypt. He uses *firstborn* for “more worthy,” since firstborn things are ordinarily more worthy.

Before he strikes the more worthy with bodily death, so that nothing good may remain in them which could become a cause of salvation, he destroys the firstfruits of all their labor, that is, permits all their distinguished and good works in which they labored to be annihilated through the excess of evils, in the tents of Ham. These are the firstborn in the land of Egypt, who are the tents of Ham, that is, the dwellings of the crafty enemy, the devil, who is emphatically called Ham, that is, “craftiness.”

From all these vengeances God takes away his people who have left Egypt, like his sheep, that is, like those for whom he cares as a shepherd cares for sheep. And some of his people, although they have gone out from the Egypt of unbelief, have not yet reached the Red Sea, that is, the grace of baptism, but are still in the desert between Egypt and the Red Sea. That is, although they possess only the knowledge of faith, like catechumens, they are still in the barrenness of good works, none of which anyone can attain fully except after baptism. He leads them through the desert to the Red Sea, so that they may not return to Egypt, as his flock, that is, as those who already exist as his flock through faith. He brings them from the desert of barrenness to baptism, placing them in the hope of salvation.

Afterward they no longer fear Pharaoh, that is, the devil, and the sea covers their enemies, that is, original sin and the actual sins they have committed, and destroys them through baptism. After baptism he brings them into the mountain of his sanctification, that is, into the Church, so that they may be his children. By sanctifying it, he made it lofty in virtues, like a mountain. The mountain, I say, which his right hand, that is, his Son, acquired by his death. Through this he makes us indebted to God, since he acquired us by his death. Or, he acquired it by his right hand, that is, by the power of his right hand.

And so that they may dwell securely and without disturbance on the mountain, he drives out from their face the nations, that is, he drives vices away from their presence, so that they cannot dominate them. They are called nations because their multitude is very great; for we call a great multitude of human beings a nation.

And he divides among them the promised land, namely the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and this by lot, that is, freely. *Lot* is used for “freely,” because what is given by lot is given freely. The gifts of the Holy Spirit are signified by the promised land because they are freely bestowed by God, just as the promised land was freely given to the children of Israel.

I say that he freely divides among them the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and does so unequally, but by a cord—that is, according to a measure of distribution—so that he distributes more to one and less to another, as he wills. Hence the Apostle says: “To each of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. 4:7). *Cord* is used for “measure,” because land is customarily measured by a cord.

After expelling the vices, he makes the tribes of Israel dwell—that is, have dominion—in their tents, that is, in the dwellings of those vices. The tribes of Israel are the congregation of the faithful who see God in contemplation. This means: He makes those who have become Israel into inhabitants, that is, rulers and governors, of themselves, although previously they were dwellings of vices, under the yoke of vices. [Col. 1051C]

Next: “And they tempted,” and so forth, through the end of the psalm. The literal sense is joined together as follows: I have shown that God led the children of Israel through the desert and brought them into the mountain of sanctification, and bestowed many other benefits upon them. Yet they still tempted him, doubting whether he could deliver them from the enemies surrounding them on every side, and they provoked the Most High God against themselves.

They provoked him in this way: They did not keep his testimonies, that is, his commandments, which he had given them under the testimony of Moses. By despising his commandments, they turned away from God. They did not keep the covenant which they had made with him when they promised that they would obey him at all times if he expelled the nations from before them.

And just as their fathers turned aside into a crooked bow—that is, they turned aside in the likeness of their unbelieving fathers, who continually offended God after he had bestowed many benefits upon them—they turned into the likeness of a crooked, that is, ineffective, bow. For just as a crooked bow, when first bent, shoots a little, but afterward, gradually relaxing, fails altogether, so they, initially stretched by their promises concerning God’s commandments and carrying them out to some extent, gradually relaxed and completely failed.

When it says, “They did not keep his testimonies,” and “They turned away,” these mean the same thing; but the statement is repeated to heap up the account of their misery. When it says, “They did not keep the covenant,” it shows that they had promised this, and in this it censures them more gravely than if they had not promised. When it says that they turned into a crooked bow, it implies, by comparison with their fathers, that they began like them and failed like them. This is more serious than not beginning at all.

And they stirred him to wrath, that is, forced him to vengeance, by sacrificing on the hills according to the rite of the nations. The hills, I say, were their own, that is, invented by them, not commanded by God. For the Law commanded that no one should sacrifice to God on the hills, because of the uncleanness of those places, but only in the temple, in the tabernacle, or in some place consecrated for this work.

They, however, sacrificed on the hills according to the rite of the nations; and what was worse, they sacrificed not to God but to their graven images, that is, to idols made by themselves. And in their graven images, that is, in the sacrifices to their idols, they provoked him—that is, forced him by violence—to jealousy, that is, to extreme wrath.

For God heard—that is, God took notice—that they had sacrificed to graven images, something they did not think he perceived. Therefore he rejected them and reduced Israel very greatly to nothing, that is, he permitted the children of Israel to be reduced to utter destruction through the assault of the Philistines and the other enemies surrounding them.

He permitted them to be reduced to nothing in this way because he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, that is, he despised his tabernacle, which was in the city of Shiloh. In that tabernacle was the ark, and there sacrifices were offered to him by the people. I say “his tabernacle,” that is, consecrated to him and not to idols, where he dwelt.

Lest it seem that he dwelt locally in the tabernacle, he qualifies this when he adds: “Among human beings.” He dwelt in the tabernacle among the Jews who sacrificed there, not locally but according to the indwelling grace; he dwelt there as long as they were human beings, behaving rationally as human beings. It is as though he were saying: Because they behaved dishonorably, he despised both them and their sacrifices, as well as the tabernacle in which they sacrificed, although it had been dedicated to him. By saying that he despised the tabernacle on their account, he indicates that they had become extremely hateful.

After despising them, he delivered their strength into captivity, that is, he permitted the ark, which was in the tabernacle and by whose protection they were strong in wars, and which was therefore called their strength, to be captured by the Allophyli in the great city of Shiloh where it was located (1 Kings 4:11). He did this so that afterward the ark would not be a cause of strength for the Jews.

“And he delivered their beauty into the hand of the enemy,” namely, the Philistines. He calls the ark their beauty, just as he called it their strength; but he signifies something else: namely, that it had been the cause of their becoming so inwardly beautiful in virtues when they rendered worship to it in honor. Therefore, so that they might no longer become beautiful because of it, he took it away from them through the assault of the Philistines.

After the ark had been taken away, he enclosed the formerly Jewish people in the sword, that is, permitted them to be brought to an end by death through the blows of the Philistines’ sword (1 Kings 4:10). I say “the people,” and, to speak more forcefully, “his inheritance,” that is, he despised and permitted to be killed those whom he had previously cultivated as his inheritance. In this he censures them more severely, since he first says that they had been most beloved, but afterward, because of their evil merit, had become most vile.

He shows in parts how he permitted the people to be killed when he adds: Truly, he despised them. For the young men of the children of Israel, who were stronger in battle, the fire—that is, the heat of God’s wrath—devoured; that is, he permitted them to be devoured. This means: Because he was exceedingly angry with them, he permitted their young men to be killed by their enemies.

And their virgins, some killed and others subjected to violation, were not mourned by anyone. It is as though he were saying: The persecution was so great that there was no leisure to mourn the death and abduction of the virgins.

Their priests fell, that is, died, by the sword, that is, in the persecution of the sword, and were not mourned—namely, Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli the priest (1 Kings 4:11)—because they had greedily stolen the better portions of the sacrifices. And their widows, some killed and others subjected to incest, were not mourned.

After such a great persecution, the Lord was at last aroused, that is, appeared aroused by showing mercy to them, although previously he had existed as though sleeping, that is, like one asleep, while he permitted them to be afflicted. He was not like one gently sleeping, but like a powerful man drunk with wine, that is, like any powerful person who, drunk with wine and overcome by excessive sleep, does not protect his household even when a tumultuous assault of enemies occurs within it.

When aroused, he struck his enemies, the Philistines, who had persecuted the children of Israel not to carry out his vengeance but rather to insult them, in their hindquarters; that is, he struck them on their buttocks with a very severe disease, so that he made them putrefy. Through this blow he gave them everlasting disgrace. For the Jews frequently reproached them with this blow as the greatest disgrace.

After they had obtained mercy, the children of Israel asked God to give them a king from one of the twelve tribes. The Lord rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, that is, he despised the great multitude of the tribe of Joseph, which seemed more eminent, so that he would not choose a king from it. He uses *tabernacle* for “multitude,” because an army’s multitude commonly dwells there.

He therefore shows by the more eminent part that God despised the tribe of Joseph. Truly, he rejected the tribe of Joseph so that he would not choose a king from it. For he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim, the son of Joseph, either, although it was the more distinguished part of the tribe of Joseph, to receive a king from it; rather, he chose the tribe of Judah to receive a king from it.

Nor did he choose a place in which to dwell from any of the other tribes, so that that place might be the head of the kingdom. Instead, he chose Mount Zion, which he loved: namely, he chose Jerusalem to be the head of the kingdom, signified by a part, namely by the mountain on which the tower of Zion stood.

Afterward he built—that is, caused to be built—his sanctuary, that is, the holy tabernacle which was made before the Temple by King David, in the land which he founded, that is, made firm and stable, forever, that is, eternally, namely in Jerusalem. This cannot be said of Jerusalem as signified, as though it were founded forever, since afterward it was destroyed; but it is said of the Church signified by Jerusalem, even though the other words appear to have been set down according to the historical sense. When he includes something which cannot be read according to history, he indicates that this psalm is not to be read simply as history.

I say that he built the sanctuary. I say “sanctuary” like a unicorn, that is, as a unicorn. This means: Such a sanctuary in which unicorns sacrificed to him—namely, faithful Jews, who were called unicorns because they had one horn, that is, a firm faith in the one God, rising upward like a horn, since a horn is a firm thing that grows upward.

I say that he chose the tribe of Judah in order to receive a king from it; and from that tribe he chose David, his servant, that is, David who was obedient to him in all things like a servant. And he took him—that is, exalted him—after receiving him from the flocks of sheep.

Lest it seem that *from* had been used causally, as it often is, he specifies the matter by adding: Namely, he took him from what he was doing after the nursing ewes—that is, while he was tending the sheep of his father Jesse (1 Kings 10:19)—to pasture, that is, to pasture Jacob his servant.

This means: He chose him from being a shepherd for this purpose, so that, once made king, he might pasture Jacob his servant, that is, rightly govern the Jewish people, the Lord’s servant, according to the law of a shepherd.

And because he had called him a servant, lest he seem to have lowered him, he adds: “And Israel,” I say, that is, the Jewish people existing as his inheritance, that is, the people whom the Lord cares for as his own inheritance.

I say that the Lord chose him to pasture them, and he pastured them well in innocence, that is, by the example of the innocence of his heart, giving them in himself an example of innocence. And he led them from good to better, in the understanding of his hands, that is, in the rational principles of his works. This means: He gave them an example of acting well through his works, which he did not perform rashly but according to rational understanding.

With the exposition of the literal sense of these fourteen verses completed, let us now approach their allegory. I said that God removes his faithful, who are his people, from the condemnations suffered by those who remain in Egypt; and that he brings them into the mountain of sanctification and bestows many other benefits upon them.

Yet they, although in view of such a great benefit they ought thereafter to cease from tempting and provoking God, according to some still tempt him through various heresies and provoke God by their works. They provoke him in this way because they do not keep his testimonies, that is, his firm commandments given through the testimony of the apostles; they do not keep them so as to cease from evil works at their command. By neglecting his commandments, they turn away from him and go after the devil.

Although in baptism they promised that they would never abandon God, by turning away they do not keep the covenant which they made with him: that they would always obey him if he forgave them their original and actual sins. Instead, like their fathers, they turn into a crooked bow, that is, into the likeness of their unbelieving predecessors, whose children they are—not by generation, but by imitating their error. They turn into the likeness of a crooked, that is, ineffective, bow, which, when first bent, shoots a little and gradually comes to failure. So they, initially laboring only a little around baptism, afterward fail altogether.

Having explained how they provoke him, he also explains how they tempt him when he adds: I say that they tempt him. They tempt him in this way: Some stir him to wrath by sacrificing on their hills, that is, in their heresies, which proceed from lofty pride as they seek to appear novel and subtle. Therefore they are signified by hills, which are lofty. And some provoke him to jealousy, that is, to extreme wrath, through their graven images, that is, through the sacrifice offered to their graven images.

This means: They truly tempt God. For after baptism some entangle themselves in heresies, while others again sacrifice to idols, and they regard God as powerless to avenge himself. Yet God hears these things, that is, takes notice of them, and despises them—those whom he had previously held dear—and he despises them to such an extent that he greatly reduces, that is, permits to be reduced, those who had previously been Israel to the nothingness of the sanctity they formerly possessed. Or “to nothing” means to the mass of sins, through which they come to the nothingness of sanctity.

He explains how he despises them as follows: I say that he permits them to be reduced to nothing because of their evil merits. He permits them to be reduced to nothing by rejecting from his grace the tabernacle of Shiloh, that is, of rupture. For *Shiloh* is interpreted as “rupture.” He rejects from his grace those who had previously been the tabernacle in which he dwelt spiritually; they are rejected from his grace because they tear themselves away from him through heresy, idolatry, and evil action.

Because he had said “the tabernacle” without adding “his,” he repeats it in order to add: “His tabernacle,” I say, where he dwelt according to his inworking grace, namely among human beings. He dwelt in them—that is, they were his tabernacle—as long as they were human beings, that is, as long as they behaved rationally.

After he rejects them, he delivers—that is, permits to be delivered—their strength into captivity, namely their free will, which had previously been firm and, so to speak, virtuous. He permits it to be taken captive, that is, to become weak and powerless for acting well, like a captive who cannot use his own strength.

And he permits the inner beauty of their innocence and of their other virtues to be placed in the hand of the enemy, that is, in the power of the devil. This is to say: Because of their evil merits, God permits the beauty of innocence and the virtue of free will to be annihilated in them through the devil’s assault, so that they are unable to use it as before.

He repeats in equivalent expressions what he said—“He rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh”—in order to expound it in parts, as follows: I say that he delivers their virtue into captivity, and in this way he “shut up his people in the sword,” that is, he confines in his vengeance those who previously were his people. This is to say: He seized them in his vengeance, after the likeness of one who is shut up in prison. Vengeance is carried out by the sword; “sword” is used for “vengeance.”

I say “the people,” and, to say something greater, he despises his inheritance, that is, he despises those who previously were his inheritance, by shutting them up in the sword. The more he shows that they had been dear to him, the more he implies that, now that they have been despised, they are wretched.

He therefore shows in parts the vengeance that he takes upon them, as follows: Truly he confines them in vengeance. For “their young men fire consumed,” that is, he permits those who previously were strong after the manner of young men—namely, in virtues—to be consumed, and their virtue to be annihilated by the fire of desire that dominates them.

“And their virgins,” that is, those who previously were incorrupt in faith and innocence after the manner of virgins, when they are consumed by vices, “were not lamented” by the prelates of the Church. This is to say: They are brought so completely into a reprobate mind and into the depths of vices that the shepherds of the Church have no care for them, nor do they lament their destruction, which they see occurring by divine judgment.

“And their priests,” who ought to have been eminent and to have led others to life by their example, fall—because their evil works demand it—from the holiness they previously possessed, “by the sword,” that is, into the vengeance of God’s blinding.

“And their widows were not mourned”: namely, many among them who had previously been like widows, the world to which they had clung having died within them as a woman clings to her husband, became apostates. Because of their evil merits they fall from that holiness and perfection, and come to such a condition of vices that the faithful do not mourn their damnation.

It should be noted that the damnation of the perfect is discussed for this reason: that by means of it he may terrify those who are less perfect away from sins. For those who are so perfect that they are called priests, or young men, or virgins, are nevertheless so blinded by their evil merits.

Having therefore shown the just damnation of certain people who return to vices after baptism, lest it seem that no one who falls back into sins after baptism can be saved, and thus that the place of repentance might be removed, he shows the salvation of certain of those who fall back, when he adds the following: I say that God rejects and confines in the sword his people who tempt and provoke him after baptism. Nevertheless, for the sake of some of them who are to be saved, the Lord is roused, bringing them back to himself. I say that the Lord exists as one sleeping, that is, like a sleeper, in accordance with the greater part of those whom he confines in the sword, as I showed above.

And he is not like one sleeping lightly, but exists as one powerful, that is, like some prince made drunk with wine, that is, extremely drunk, who, sleeping heavily, gives no care to his household. I say that he is roused, and this happens in this way: in certain people he is roused. He strikes them, as they are his enemies by living badly, with the goads of repentance.

I say that he strikes them, and with a blow extending “into future ages,” that is, with such a blow as afterward endures throughout all their lifetime. And because he had said this obscurely, he explains it when he adds: I say that he strikes them “into future ages”; this is to say: He gives them everlasting disgrace, so that as long as they live they may have disgrace because of their sins and may repent.

Since, therefore, he had spoken of the damnation of certain people who tempt and provoke God, and of the salvation of certain others, but had not determined which would perish and which would be saved, he determines this when he adds: I say that he strikes certain people with the goads of repentance. And likewise he rejects from his grace the tabernacle of Joseph, that is, those who, although they had previously been his tabernacle in whom he dwelt, become Joseph—that is, become like Joseph. Just as Joseph was sold into Egypt, so they sell themselves into Egypt through the price of carnal pleasures, which they embrace—that is, into the affliction of eternal perdition.

This is to say: He rejects from himself those who persistently submit to pleasures, in accordance with what is written: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15:50).

And because there are many who, although they are not occupied with pleasures, are nevertheless justly rejected by God because of their other evil merits, he adds: “And he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim for salvation,” that is, universally, all the ungodly who are like the tribe of Ephraim—namely, those who abandon the Church and persist in subjection to the devil, just as the tribe of Ephraim is said to have abandoned Jerusalem and to have persisted in the kingdom of Jeroboam against God’s will.

“And likewise he chose the tribe of Judah,” that is, the multitude of those who confess—that is, who continually praise God—in deed, word, and heart. For Judah is interpreted as “confession.”

I say that the tribe of Judah was made by God’s grace “a mountain,” that is, lofty in virtues, and “Zion,” that is, contemplating eternal things. He loved this mountain because it is a mountain and Zion.

And from this tribe he built his sanctuary, that is, his holy temple in which he might dwell; namely, he constituted the Church from them. I say that the sanctuary was “founded upon the earth,” that is, made in the likeness of the earth, which he founded firm and immovable, destined to endure throughout all ages. Namely, he makes it firm and immovable, in the likeness of the earth, which is a firm element—that is, immovable and long-lasting.

I say that he builds his sanctuary by founding it in the Church, “as,” that is, as a sanctuary “of unicorns”: that is, a sanctuary made up of unicorns and of holy men. They are called unicorns because they possess one firm concord of good will and charity, directed toward heavenly things, after the likeness of a horn, which is a firm object directed upward.

And because no prophet or other faithful person was suitable for building this sanctuary, he chose for this work, from the mass of the faithful, David his servant—namely, Christ, truly strong-handed, his servant according to his humanity, that is, faithfully obedient to him and resisting him in nothing.

And he “took him up,” that is, exalted him, “from the sheepfolds of sheep,” that is, from the multitude of certain faithful Jews—namely, the apostles and others—who had only a knowledge of him.

This is to say: From the knowledge possessed by a few faithful Jews he exalted him, bringing him into the knowledge of the nations.

But because he had said “he took him up,” and this expression signifies a taking away, lest it seem that he had taken him away from the knowledge of the apostles when he brought him to the nations, he adds, in order to clarify: I say that he took him from the sheepfolds of sheep; namely, he took him from what he was “after the ewes that give birth,” that is, governing the apostles by his teaching, after the likeness of a shepherd who governs sheep while walking behind them.

The apostles are appropriately called “those after the ewes that give birth,” because they produce offspring for God, giving birth through teaching to faithful children for God.

This is to say: When he himself was known by a few faithful people, he took him from there, that is, he extended him into the knowledge and dominion of the nations. When he calls those whom he previously governed “those after the ewes that give birth,” he indicates that he did not abandon them. For it would be unjust for him to abandon them when they were those after the ewes that give birth.

I say that David chose to feed—namely, to feed by teaching and example—Jacob his servant, that is, the gentile people, strong as a wrestler against vices and obedient to him in all things. By Jacob are signified those who are still in the active life, wrestling manfully.

And he chose to feed “Israel, his inheritance,” that is, completely: the perfect, who devote themselves to contemplation, because they are already the Lord’s hereditary possession. I say that he chose him to feed Jacob and Israel.

And he fed them in innocence, that is, in the example of the innocence of his heart, and led them from good to better “in the understandings of his hands,” that is, in the example of his works, which he did not perform rashly but with rational understandings.

This is to say: He made them conformed to himself in innocence and in rational understandings, from which good works proceeded—works signified by the hands because we work with our hands.

# ON PSALM LXXVIII

## The heading of the seventy-eighth Psalm

“A Psalm of Asaph.” This is explained as follows: This Psalm belongs to Asaph, that is, to the faithful congregation of martyrs, who see the Church’s great persecution and grieve compassionately: certain weak members of the Church are incorporated into the impious through fear of tribulations; others, exceedingly strong because they refuse to yield to unbelievers, are killed, their blood being shamefully poured out like water, and their corpses being handed over inhumanely to beasts and birds.

Thus the faithful are a reproach to their neighbors and a mockery to their enemies. The congregation of the faithful also prays that God not permit them to fail in tribulations because of their sins, thereby giving others an example of praying that they may not fail in tribulation.

It also speaks concessively about the damnation of certain of their adversaries who are destined to perish, and prays for the salvation of certain others who are to be saved.

It presents the Church’s tribulation for this useful purpose: to instruct those who come after, if tribulations are inflicted upon them for Christ’s sake, that they ought not to bear them grievously, since they hear that the earliest faithful endured the same things.

“God, the nations have come”—that is, those living in a pagan manner, whether Jews or Gentiles; namely, impious and most savage peoples have come with barbarian assault “into your inheritance,” that is, into the Church.

And because he had not determined why they had come into the Church, lest it be thought that they had come into it for good, he shows what they accomplished when they came into it, adding: I say that they came, and when they came they polluted it by conforming certain people to themselves, people who had previously been your holy temple.

And by killing the stronger ones, they “set Jerusalem,” that is, the Church, “in custody,” that is, in the likeness of a fruit-watchman’s hut: namely, like any most worthless shelter situated in orchards, where watchmen who guard the fruit customarily stay before it is gathered. Once the fruit has been gathered, that shelter is abandoned.

So also the Church, after many of the faithful have been gathered through death, becomes abandoned and worthless.

But they did not merely make Jerusalem abandoned through the death of the strongest faithful; they also did something exceedingly inhuman: they made “the corpses,” that is, the dead bodies of your servants whom they cruelly killed, “food for the birds of the air,” and “the flesh of your saints,” who were killed for your sake, “food for the beasts of the earth.”

This is to say: They not only killed them cruelly, but, what is more cruel, after killing them in the body they gave them over to birds and beasts to eat.

He does not say “to the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth” merely to distinguish them. Rather, when he adds “of the air” and “of the earth,” he indicates their exceedingly savage intention: namely, that they exposed the corpses to them not merely so that they might be fed from them, but so that they might scatter them piecemeal through earth and air, lest Christians gather them.
