And they did not regard any consideration of loss or mercy in their death; rather, they “poured out their blood manfully,” and without regard for any loss, “like water,” in whose pouring out no one is moved by mercy and no loss is reckoned.

And they did not pour out their blood in one place alone, but also “around Jerusalem,” that is, around the whole world, wherever Jerusalem—that is, the Church—is found.

This is to say: They poured it out everywhere on earth, because the Church has spread everywhere on earth.

And they did not kill only a few, but so many that no surviving congregation of the faithful remained to bury them; that is, not enough of the faithful remained to suffice for burying the bodies of those who had been killed.

And so, in such a worthless manner and without manifest vengeance, you permit your own people to be killed. We, the remainder and survivors, “have become a reproach,” that is, a cause of reproach, “to our neighbors,” that is, to those who had just begun to approach the faith through our example. It is a reproach to them that they ever wished to be conformed to us.

And to those “who are around us,” that is, who are far away—unbelievers entirely unwilling to approach the faith—we have become “a mockery by the gesture of the nose,” so that they wrinkle their nostrils in derision of us, and “a laughingstock by words,” so that they spew insulting words against us.

This is to say: They deride us both by gesture and by words. To mock is to wrinkle one’s nose out of contempt for someone.

But in order to provide the later answer, he asks the question out of excessive compassion, as follows: I say that you permit us to be afflicted so shamefully, and in this you appear angry. “How long, O Lord, will you be angry?” That is, to what extent will this anger of yours against us continue?

This is to say: What will this anger against us come to? “Will you be angry forever,” that is, completely, so that you utterly destroy us?

The answer follows: Truly you will not be angry forever, but “your jealousy”—that is, this persecution, which is not jealousy but appears to be jealousy, although in fact it is the greatest mercy—“will be kindled in us like fire,” that is, after the likeness of fire.

Just as fire applied to gold purifies whatever impurities are in it and supplies it with brightness, so the fire of tribulations kindled against us, not for our harm, will wipe away the filth of sins and grant us the outstanding brightness of glory.

He speaks concessively about the damnation of certain unbelievers when he adds: I say that they exposed the corpses of your servants to beasts and birds, and poured out their blood like water. And because they did these things, “pour out your wrath upon the nations that did not know you.”

As if he were saying: You have already poured your vengeance inwardly upon them, blinding them in soul. I also grant that you may pour it out—that is, pour it outwardly—upon their bodies in the future, sending body and soul into the fire of Gehenna.

And therefore pour it out, because they did not know you; that is, they neglected to come to knowledge of you through our preaching.

And “pour out your wrath upon the kingdoms of the nations that did not invoke your name.” Here “kingdoms” and “nations” refer to the same people, but he adds another reason why wrath should be poured out upon them: namely, because they did not invoke—that is, neglected to invoke—the name of God, which is “Lord.”

And therefore pour it out still further, because “they devoured Jacob,” that is, they devoured the faithful who were your wrestlers: polluting some, as we said, by conforming them to themselves, and killing the rest.

And by devouring Jacob they “laid waste his place,” that is, they laid waste those who wished to succeed to his place in the faith, by terrifying them through Jacob’s death.

Or, “they laid waste his place,” namely, the Church, in which they remained harmoniously according to the unity of faith and charity; they made it desolate by his death.

On their own behalf they pray as follows: We grant, concerning the nations, that your wrath may be poured out upon them. But for ourselves we ask that you not permit us to fail because of our ancient iniquities.

“Do not remember our ancient iniquities,” because they were forgiven in baptism—namely, since afterward we partly fell back into them. Do not exact them from us to the last quarter-penny (Matt. 5:26), nor permit us to fail because of them.

Or “ancient iniquities” means those that our fathers committed, which nevertheless are ours when we become participants in them. Otherwise there would be no reason to fear them unless we were conscious that we participate in the same things. For a son will not bear his father’s iniquity if he has not consented to that same iniquity.

Or “ancient iniquities” means those long past, yet committed after baptism.

I say, do not remember the iniquities; but “let your mercies quickly anticipate us,” that is, your acts of compassion, namely, the benefits of your mercy.

This is to say: Before we come to failure through weakness, may the aids of your mercy come to our assistance most swiftly.

And it is necessary that they anticipate us, because through Adam’s sin we have become exceedingly poor. Although previously we were poor—that is, insufficient in ourselves—we have become exceedingly poor, that is, exceedingly insufficient and weak.

Therefore, because we are exceedingly poor, O God our Savior—that is, our Savior through the death of the cross—help us to conquer and incorporate our enemies, and deliver us, lest we be conquered.

And do this not because of our merits, but for the glory of your name, so that your name may thereby be glorified.

And lest we be hindered by present sins, be merciful toward our sins by forgiving them, for your name’s sake, so that your name may be magnified on this account.

And therefore deliver us, lest we yield, lest perhaps they say among the nations—that is, lest the nations say something foolish and absurd: “Where is their God?” As if they were saying: These Christians boasted that they had a God who would make them firm and steadfast, so that they would not yield. And where is he now? Either he is nowhere, or, if he exists anywhere, he is powerless.

He also prays on behalf of the portion that is to be saved, as follows: We pray that you deliver us.

And this also we pray: that the vengeance for the blood of your servants, which has been poured out, may be made known. I say, vengeance that is to be carried out by you upon the nations of the Gentiles may become known—that is, may become manifest before our eyes. Exercise upon them a manifest retribution that we may see with our eyes.

And in order that this retribution may become known before our eyes, “let the groaning of the prisoners enter into your presence,” so that it may be in your sight—that is, in your good pleasure. These are the prayers that we, your prisoners, pour out with groans for this retribution: prisoners bound by the fetter of your commandments, or bound for your sake by the fetter of tribulations.

He explains the retribution itself when he adds: I say, let the retribution become known; and what retribution is this? Possess those very nations as the spiritual children of the slain. As if he were saying: Make them become our children, acquired through our preaching—we who are put to death in the flesh for your sake through continual tribulation.

And possess them after this, that is, subject them to yourself and govern them.

And do this according to the greatness of your arm, that is, according to the greatness of your great strength—namely, because you are strong and powerful enough to accomplish this.

He calls God’s possessing them “retribution,” although it is useful to them and retribution is ordinarily understood only in an evil sense; but it is called retribution by way of comparison.

For just as a victor often exacts this retribution from an enemy whom he has conquered: he leads him behind himself at will and binds him with chains, so God makes those who previously resisted him by living badly into his followers, having conquered them through preachers, and binds them with the bond of his commandments.

I say, possess them. And because they reproach you by bringing reproaches upon us, make them, by approaching the faith, our neighbors. “Repay into their bosom,” that is, into their hearts, “sevenfold the reproach with which they reproached you,” by bringing reproach upon us.

This is to say: Because, by reproaching us, they also reproached you, make them our neighbors through faith; and for the reproach they inflicted upon us and upon you, repay them here with a reward—namely, a reproach seven times greater in their hearts than the reproach they inflicted upon us.

And this is as if he were saying: Make them reproach themselves seven times as much as they reproached us, because of what they reproached us for, while groaning in their hearts.

Through the number seven he shows the multiplicity of the reproach that they ought to make against themselves. Or “sevenfold” signifies the sevenfold grace with which they, having been imbued, will reproach themselves in many ways for what they did badly.

The heart is called a bosom because it is secret and hidden after the manner of a bosom.

I say, repay them their reproach. But we, if you do this, being your people and, to say something greater, being the sheep of your pasture—which you feed with teaching and inner wisdom—will confess you forever, that is, we will praise you with mouth, heart, and deed as long as this age shall last.

And we will also announce your praise in the generation of this world, and, proceeding into the future generation, when our bodies will be regenerated.

This is to say: Here we will praise you, and in the future we will announce your praise—that is, we will announce to the unbelievers who here neglect you that you are worthy of praise, through the greatness of our glorification.

# ON PSALM LXXIX

## The heading of the seventy-ninth Psalm

“To the end, for those who are changed: a testimony of Asaph. A Psalm for the Assyrians.”

This is explained as follows: This Psalm speaks for those who are changed “to the end,” that is, for the benefit of both Jews and Gentiles, who will be changed from oldness into newness.

And this is “to the end,” that is, toward perfection. Here they will be changed in part, according to the uprightness of virtues; and in the future, according to the perfect accumulation of glory.

Or “to the end,” that is, into Christ: they will be changed by being brought into conformity with him, who is the end of prophecy and of the Law.

This Psalm also speaks for the Assyrians, that is, for the benefit of the Assyrians—namely, Jews who say that they are Assyrians although they are not. They say that they are directed rightly in the Law, whereas they are rather distorting it.

This Psalm is a testimony of Asaph, both faithful and unfaithful. The faithful Asaph is a testimony of his belief, because he rightly believes that salvation comes through Christ, when he says: “Show your face, and we shall be saved.”

The unfaithful Asaph is a testimony in this way: it exposes him as erring because he denies that Christ is the Savior, while he openly shows the destruction of the Jewish people contemporary with Christ, which befell them because they denied that Christ himself was the Savior.

He therefore shows this destruction where he says: “You have destroyed its hedge,” and so forth.

It is rightly said to speak for those who will be changed and for the Assyrians. For the congregation of the faithful existing long before Christ—or that existing around his time, which was worthy to see him, such as the just Simeon, Nathanael, and many others—is introduced in this Psalm, sighing out of an excess of longing for Christ’s coming, which was greatly delayed for them, and praying that God the Father, sending the one whom he is about to send, might through his coming convert and save all who are to be saved in the time of grace, both Gentiles and Jews.

It also prays for the portion of the Jews who are to be saved at the end, and shows the destruction of Jerusalem because it did not recognize the time of its visitation.

It does this for the following reason: by showing how great was the desire for Christ’s coming, and also by showing the perdition of those who neglected to venerate him, it may make us more ready to venerate him.

“You who rule Israel, give heed.” This is to say: O God the Father, who rule Israel—that is, leading the faithful from among the Jews from virtue to virtue—we pray that you give heed, that is, make yourself attentive to the governance of this Israel.

And you who lead Joseph—that is, will lead the Gentile people who are to be converted from good to better, who will be Joseph, that is, “increased”—give heed, that is, make yourself attentive to leading Joseph.

As if he were saying: Since we know you to be powerful enough to rule Israel and increase Joseph, and foresee prophetically that you will do both, we pray that you hasten to rule and lead them attentively.

I say that you will lead Joseph. I say that Joseph is like a sheep, that is, as one whom you make gentle from a dog like a sheep. I say, give heed.

And do this in the following way: You who sit above the cherubim—that is, you who dwell continually and exercise dominion among the heavenly spirits, who are cherubim, that is, full of knowledge of your cognition—manifest yourself, that is, make yourself manifest through faith, before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh.

These are the faithful of both peoples, who, although they are now adopted children of perdition and wrath, will be made by you Benjamin, that is, “sons of the right hand”—adopted sons through faith who will be placed at the right hand of your majesty in the future.

Although they are barren in good works, you will make them Ephraim, that is, fruitful in goodness. And although they take pleasure in earthly things, you will make them Manasseh, that is, forgetful of earthly things.

For Benjamin is interpreted as “sons of the right hand.” Ephraim means “fruitfulness.” Manasseh means “forgetfulness.” Cherubim is called “fullness of knowledge.”

And this is as if he were saying: You who are already known among the angels, among whom you dwell without ceasing, manifest yourself also in the knowledge of the faithful of both peoples.

By the cherubim, who are one part of the heavenly spirits, the entire multitude of angels is understood.

I say, give heed in this way, so that you may be manifested before the faithful; and in this way also give heed.

“Rouse your power,” that is, the benefits signified long ago by the miracles of your power. As if he were saying: Rouse those miracles that you powerfully performed among the earlier people—rescuing them from Egypt, dividing the sea and the rock, and doing other such things—which, because they are past, appear to be dead. Rouse them, that is, bring them back to remembrance by working in the Church benefits worked for them by you.

Or “rouse your power” means the benefits signifying the power you exercised long ago.

And rouse it in this way: “Come according to your help to us.”

He explains how he is to come, lest we understand “coming” locally, as follows: I say, come—namely, come in such a way that you may save us; here from sins, and in the future with perfect salvation, just as you came to the earlier people according to the help of grace in order to save them from the slavery of the Egyptians.

I say, save us—and save us who existed before the time of Christ and will not see him, by rescuing us from the darkness in which we will be detained after death because of original sin; and save those conformed to us who will exist in his time, by rescuing them from sins.

But save both us—that is, both them and us—with perfect salvation in the future.

Since he had said “save us” without qualification, he explains that salvation as follows: I say, save us. And do so in this way: O God, “show your face,” that is, the Son, who is appropriately called your face because you are known through him, just as a whole human being is known through the face.

As if he were saying: Make your Son, who according to his divinity is invisible, incarnate; and thus show him as a visible human being.

And through the face that has been shown, convert us—namely, us who will then already be dead, converting us through him from darkness to light. And convert those who will be conformed to us and will be alive, from vices to virtues and from ignorance to perfect knowledge of you.

And in this way we shall all be saved in the future with perfect salvation.

The congregation of the faithful that speaks here sighs over the delay of its expectation, speaking as follows: I say, show your face. And while you delay showing that face, O Lord God—that is, creator of the heavenly powers—“how long will you be angry?” That is, for how long will you appear to be angry with us, not looking down from the height of your disposition upon the prayer of your servant?

That is, not fulfilling what we pray: that you show your face. We are a people serving you in all things as we are able.

As if he were saying: Because you delay so long, you appear to us to be angry. And although you are powerful enough to accomplish this—for you are Lord and God of the heavenly powers—you appear angry to us insofar as you delay it. We pray that you show your face.

Nevertheless, we are certain that you will not provide us through him with an abundance of earthly pleasures. Rather, after he has come, you will feed us who live and cling to him with the bread of tears.

This is to say: For his sake we will suffer many tears, with which you will feed us—that is, strengthen us as with bread—so that we may become more steadfast, just as one who is fed with bread is strengthened.

As it is written elsewhere: “Bread strengthens the human heart” (Ps. 103:14).

And you will give us drink, that is, joy in tears: namely, so that tears may be a cause of joy for us, because through them we will be certain of our reward, just as wine is a cause of joy to the one who drinks it.

As it is written elsewhere: “Wine gladdens the human heart” (ibid., 15).

I say that you will give us joy in tears. I say, tears that are given in measure: you will not give them beyond measure, but with restraint, so that once given to drink we may not fail, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able” (1 Cor. 10:13).

Because he had mentioned tears, he implies that they will suffer tribulations, and shows part of them by adding the following: I say that you will feed us with the bread of tears, and truly we shall weep. For you have set us—or will set us—“for contradiction to our neighbors,” that is, to our fellow tribesmen.

Namely, you will permit the Jews, who are our neighbors because they are of the same people, to contradict us, who will then remain as those who cling to him. And these same neighbors, having become our enemies, mocked us for this reason.

And although we know that we will suffer all these things for his sake, nevertheless, on the condition that he himself come, we do not fear suffering them. Rather, we pray: O God of powers, convert us; show your face, and we shall be saved.

By saying that they do not fear suffering for his sake, they instruct us not to flee from suffering for his sake.

Having made this prayer and shown their exceedingly great longing for Christ’s coming, he proceeds to show what loss the unbelieving Jews suffered, since they neglected his coming.

And in order to show that their perdition is deserved, he first mentions the benefits bestowed upon them by God, because of which they ought not to have neglected the coming of the Son of God.

Or he mentions these benefits beforehand for this reason: afterward, by lamenting the Jews’ perdition, he may say that it seems astonishing that God should afterward have permitted those whom he had previously cultivated so diligently, as his vineyard, to be afflicted so severely. By this means he deters his hearers from offending God, showing that the Jews, whom he previously loved so greatly, were punished so severely because they offended him.

He speaks as follows: We pray and desire that you show your face, and that through it conversion may take place. In order that it may be shown and conversion may take place through it, one must pray with great urgency.

For the Jews, who previously existed as your vineyard, O God, fruitful in good works but afterward became barren by living badly, will be severely punished because they neglected to have that face shown to them through faith and to be converted through it.

And yet you “brought that vineyard out of Egypt,” by the help of your grace, into the promised land. And so that it might remain there securely, you drove out the nations from that land, as was said in Psalm LXXVII, and planted it in the place of the nations that had been driven out. That is, you established it firmly, so that it could not be moved by the assault of neighboring nations.

The Jewish people were previously called God’s vineyard because they were fruitful in goodness after the manner of a fertile vineyard, and because God cultivated them through the teaching of the prophets.

I say that you brought the vineyard out of Egypt, and in that very journey you were its guide—and this not secretly, but in its sight.

This is to say: You led it with so open a guidance that it saw this with its own eyes, when a cloud appeared to them by day and a pillar by night (Exod. 13:21).

He repeats what he said—“you planted it”—in order to add: I say that you were its guide in its sight, and “you planted its roots,” that is, you planted it firmly in the promised land, after the likeness of a tree whose planting is more secure when it is planted with its roots than when it is planted without them.

And once planted, it “filled,” that is, completely occupied, the promised land.

Or by “roots” he means rulers, because through their care they support the people as a root supports a tree. They are planted firmly in it so that the rulers of neighboring nations could not prevail over them and drive them out; and the people, supported by their governance, filled the land.

Or he calls the ancient fathers “roots,” from whose seed the sons proceeded and filled the land, just as branches sprout from a root.

And it filled the land so completely that its shadow also covered the mountains—that is, its abundance occupied not only the level country but also the mountainous regions of Judea, which were steep and uncultivated—like a very dense vine growing so high that its shadow covered even the mountains. And its branches covered—that is, occupied—the cedars of God through the care of its governance. This means that the lowly members of that vine were supported by its shoots, namely by kings, judges, and prophets, who were the cedars of God: they had become as lofty as cedars in holiness, wisdom, and virtue. The comparison is drawn from vines, which are also called vine-plants (*arbusta*) and which, in order to be more fruitful, are supported by lofty trees that they cover. For, because of their weakness, they could not grow upward and support themselves.

He also shows the extent of the vine’s expansion when he adds: “And the vine itself, supported by the cedars, extended its branches”—that is, the generations of its sons, which are called branches because they came forth from the Jewish people, just as vine-shoots come forth from the branches of a vine—“to the western sea; and it extended its offshoots to the Euphrates River.” He uses “offshoots” and “branches” with the same meaning. Accordingly, we read: “From the great river, the Euphrates, to the western sea shall be your boundaries” (Deut. XI, 24).

Since, then, you planted this vine with such care, enlarged it so greatly, and dealt with it so mercifully, why did you destroy its hedge—that is, why will you destroy it? You removed your protection from it, by which it was defended, just as a vine is protected by a hedge placed around it. It is as though he said: Since you loved it so greatly in the time of the fathers whom you planted, it seems astonishing and grievous, and something that will not occur without a very serious cause, that you should despise it so far as to withdraw your protection from it completely.

And because you will destroy its hedge, those who pass along the way will gather it—that is, they will consume it—not only the worshipers of Christ, but also, what is more grievous for it, all who pass along the way, namely the unbelieving Gentiles who pass by Christ, unwilling to approach him through the teaching of the preachers, although Christ is the way to life.

He shows which part of the harvesters he means when he adds: “I say that those passing along the way will gather it; and they will truly gather it, for the boar coming out of the forest will destroy it”—namely Vespasian, who will be savage and unclean with the filth of vices, just as the boar is a savage and filthy animal. Vespasian, that is, coming from Rome, which is rightly called a forest because it was uncultivated with respect to teaching and full of bestial savagery, like a forest whose trees are uncultivated and which is the habitation of wild beasts. “And the solitary wild beast has devoured it”: Titus, namely, who is called “solitary” by the same comparison by which his father Vespasian is so called, will devour—that is, consume—it, like grass that is consumed by being grazed upon.

Vespasian indeed devastated all Judea, killed many Jews, and led still more into captivity. Titus, after besieging Jerusalem, captured and destroyed it; he killed a very great multitude of Jews and scattered the survivors in captivity.

Alternatively, this verse may be read as follows: Not only will the Gentiles who pass along the way consume it, but the boar will also destroy it—that is, he will destroy it in its virtues—the savage and filthy boar coming out of the forest, namely the devil coming from the Gentiles who will come to the faith. Those Gentiles, now occupied by him, are uncultivated like a forest. And in the future the solitary wild beast, the devil, will devour it—that is, he will consume it by eternal death—not so that it will be utterly destroyed and cease to exist, but so that, always being consumed in torments, it will remain. The comparison is with grass that is grazed upon and nevertheless remains forever.

At the end he prays for a portion of this vine that will be converted at the end of the world, as follows: We complain that you permit the vine transferred from Egypt to be so gathered and destroyed; and although you permit it, because of its evil merits, to be partly consumed in this way, we nevertheless pray, O God of the heavenly powers, who can accomplish what we ask, that you turn from anger to mercy. Turn it in this manner: Look down from the heaven of heavens upon Christ; and look upon him in this way, namely, see—that is, cause him to be seen through faith—and visit—that is, heal from sins—this vine according to the portion determined by faith and by the merit of the Lord’s Passion. The comparison is with the most compassionate physician who visits and heals the sick.

Alternatively, “look down from heaven” means “from the height of your providential ordering.” And after you have visited it, perfect it—that is, make this vine perfect in virtues—in the portion that your right hand planted, as was said, namely by your merciful power in the promised land. Perfect it in this way: by founding it upon the Son, that is, upon faith in and the protection of Christ your Son, whom you confirmed—that is, whom you will make firm in innocence—for yourself, that is, for your honor. “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ” (I Cor. III, 11); whoever is founded upon him is firm.

I say, “Perfect it”; and you will indeed perfect it, for at the rebuke of your face—that is, through the hidden and inward rebuke of your Son, who is your face, as has already been sufficiently explained—“those consumed by fire and those dug under will perish.” That is, when the Son rebukes them inwardly, by their hearing the teaching of the preachers, whatever things in them are “consumed by fire,” namely corrupted by the fire of desires, and whatever things are “dug under,” namely secretly committed through fear, will perish. In them will perish everything that they have committed through the burning of evil desire and through the hiding-place of fear.

Sin is committed in these two ways: either by the will or by fear. Sins committed through fear are appropriately signified by “things dug under,” because they are committed secretly. A thing dug under is hidden.

With this verse inserted, he returns to the prayer announcing the salvation of the remnants of that vine, as follows: I say that the things consumed by fire and dug under will perish through the rebuke of the Son; and, so that this may happen, O God the Father, let your hand—that is, your power—come upon the man of your right hand, namely upon Christ, who will be the man of your right hand, that is, of your compassion, through whose obedience you will be reconciled to the world.

This means: From your heavenly providence, grant him the power to conquer the devil. Since “the right hand” often signifies prosperity, God’s compassion is appropriately designated by the right hand. For what prosperity is greater than the manifestation of divine compassion?

He explains who this man of the right hand is when he adds: “And let your hand”—that is, let it be—“upon the son of man,” namely Christ, whom you confirmed for yourself, as has already been said. By saying “not of men, but of man,” that is, of the Virgin, he humbles the party of the Jews who asserted that he was merely a man, begotten from a human being.

And if you confirm him, we will not depart from you: those conformed to him, that is, those who will exist in that time, will cling firmly to you through his faith and will not afterward depart from you, whether through fear or through any circumstance. They will not have this firmness from free choice, but because we will invoke—that is, inwardly, in their conscience, they will call upon—your name, which is “Lord.” You will confer this firmness upon them because they will call you Lord not only with their mouth but also through the faith of their heart.

And because they will invoke you, you will give us life—that is, you will give life to our counterparts in their souls. Or, in the future, you will give us life both in body and in soul, with eternal life.

And so that this may happen: “Lord God of the heavenly powers, turn us; show your face, and we shall be saved.” This verse is explained as above. It is placed three times in order to signify the persons of the Trinity. It is as though he said: You, God the Father, show your face; and you, God the Word, show your face, namely the Lord’s humanity; and you, God the Spirit, show your face. Since he says “God of the heavenly powers,” the expression has force, as though he said: Since you are the God of the heavenly powers, who would not desire to see your face?

## ON PSALM LXXX

### The title of Psalm Eighty

“To the end, for the winepresses, on the fifth day of the Sabbath, a psalm of Asaph.”

He uses “winepresses” in the plural for the two Churches, namely that of the Jews and that of the Gentiles. In this psalm he addresses them, urging them to rejoice in the giving of life to the spirit and in the putting to death of the flesh, and openly admonishing them to preach both things to others.

He designates the Church from the Jews where he says, “the commandment is in Israel”; but he designates the Church from the Gentiles where he says, “a testimony in Joseph.” Both Churches are therefore called a winepress by this comparison: just as a winepress contains both wine and grapes, so both good and evil are contained in each Church. The good belong to the Church both through participation in the sacraments and through virtues and good works. The evil belong only through participation in the sacraments, since they are baptized and communicate in the Lord’s Body.

Thus, at the beginning of this psalm, faithful Asaph, after Christ’s advent, urges the good of both Churches to rejoice with psalm, lyre, and trumpet, speaking to them in his own person. Afterwards, however, so that the admonition might be more terrifying and carry greater authority, he introduces God speaking to the evil, urging those evil persons themselves to obey him and setting before them the benefits he has already bestowed upon them, on account of which they ought to obey him. He also shows what will happen to those who do not obey him and what, on the contrary, will happen to those who do obey.

Thus the title appropriately says “for the winepresses,” that is, for the benefit of the Churches whom he addresses here. The words of the title are adapted as follows: This psalm is Asaph’s—that is, it is the psalm of the faithful Synagogue acting for the winepresses. I say “for the winepresses,” signified by the event that occurred on the fifth day of the Sabbath. On the fifth day God created the flying creatures from the water (Gen. I, 20), as a figure of the Church. In the same way he recreates the children of the Church from the water of baptism, making them all lofty in innocence at baptism like flying creatures, although afterward they may debase themselves through vices.

For this reason he adds “on the fifth day of the Sabbath,” to specify which winepresses he means here: those designated by the event that occurred on the fifth day of the Sabbath, namely both Churches. I say that this psalm is Asaph’s. I mean Asaph exhorting those winepresses “to the end,” that is, toward the perfection of goodness—partly exhorting them in his own person and partly in the person of God—or exhorting them “to the end,” that is, toward conformity to Christ, the end of prophecy and of the law, so that after his example they may rejoice with psalm, lyre, and trumpet.

### “Rejoice in God our helper”

It is as though he said: You good children of both Churches, do not rejoice in earthly things; rather, rejoice to the honor of God, namely in those things that pertain to God. And do not fear, although of yourselves you are insufficient for rejoicing, for he himself is our helper, and he will help you to rejoice.

Do not rejoice only a little; but “shout for joy,” that is, rejoice with the inward intensity of gladness that cannot be expressed in words. Shout for joy to the God of Jacob—to the God to whom one must shout for joy, who is not the God of the sluggish but of Jacob, that is, of those who wrestle manfully. He is the God whom Jacob regards as God, whoever may deny it, and he will be your God if you are Jacob.

And behold in what things I urge you to rejoice: joyfully receive a psalm from God, which you cannot possess by yourselves, namely the vivification of the spirit in innocence and virtues, which are given by God’s higher clemency and are therefore received through the psalm. A psalm is a melody made on the psaltery, sounding from above.

And in order that you may deserve to receive the psalm, give God a tambourine, that is, mortification of the flesh. Mortification is appropriately signified by the tambourine, which is covered with the skin of a dead animal. This means: To the honor of God, mortify the flesh with fasts and vigils.

For the psaltery—that is, the spirit made alive—is pleasing to God, that is, very delightful, together with the lyre, namely with mortification of the flesh, which is understood through the lyre because it sounds from below. It is as though he said: It is pleasing to God that, by mortifying the flesh, your spirit should be made alive. Therefore it is fitting for you to rejoice in this.

“Sound forth also joyfully with the trumpet,” that is, resound through open preaching, which is signified by the trumpet because the sound of the trumpet is manifest.

I say that you are in the new moon, that is, in the renewal of the moon, namely in the renewal of your humanity through baptism. Humanity is rightly called “moon,” because it often declines through many anxieties, after the manner of the moon.

This means: Since your humanity has now been renewed through baptism—having fallen into old age through Adam—preach this renewal openly, so that others may approach it. This was prefigured by the earlier people, who were commanded to sound the trumpet at the renewal of the moon in the seventh month. For *neomenia*, “new moon,” is interpreted as “the renewal of the moon.”

I say that you are already in the new moon, namely in the notable day, that is, in the most noble brightness of your solemnity, or of your festival rest. This means: Your new moon is nothing other than the most noble and pre-eminent brightness of faith and understanding, through which you rest from every evil work. This was prefigured by the Jews, who on the notable and solemn day of the new moon rested from every servile work.

I say: Rejoice by receiving the psalm, giving the tambourine, and sounding the trumpet.

And you ought to fulfill this because “the commandment is in Israel,” that is, in the Church from the Jews, which is rightly called Israel because it is loftier in the contemplation of God than the Church from the Gentiles. This commandment is “judgment,” that is, just. For *judgment* (*judicium*) is so called as if from *justly spoken* (*jure dictum*). Therefore, whenever “judgment” is placed somewhere without “false” or anything similar being added, it is the same as if “just” had been written.

This just commandment must be ascribed to the God of Jacob, that is, of those who wrestle vigorously. It is as though he said: If the commandment came from the apostles or from other prelates, it would certainly have to be carried out. How much more, then, when it is commanded by the God of Jacob?

But it is not only a commandment in Israel; God also placed “that testimony”—that is, that commandment which bears witness to salvation for those who obey and to death for those who do not obey—in Joseph. He firmly established it in the Church of the Gentile people, who are called Joseph because they have been added for increase. For *Joseph* is interpreted as “increase.”

And when he came out of the land of Egypt through faith and the washing of baptism—that is, out of the earthliness of affliction and the darkness of ignorance—he heard from the wisdom inspiring him inwardly “a language that he did not know,” namely this commandment that he had not previously heard. Since the commandment is given through the tongue, “tongue” is used for “commandment.”

It is as though he said: While he was in Egypt, in affliction and ignorance, he was never commanded to rejoice with psalm, tambourine, and trumpet; but after he came out of Egypt, he received this commandment from the Lord.

This was prefigured through the Jewish people. While they were in Egypt, they never received the law from the Lord. But when, leaving Egypt, they crossed the Red Sea, the law was given to them by the Lord. Egypt is indeed called “affliction” or “darkness.”

Through this we are instructed that this commandment must not be preached to anyone until, by leaving Egypt, he has been reborn through the water of baptism.

I say that he was coming out of the land of Egypt; and it was necessary that he be made to come out from there, for through this departure he turned his back—that is, his conscience—away from the burdens of sins. While he was in Egypt, in unbelief, his conscience was weighed down by the burdens of sins, like a back burdened by an excessive weight. But, leaving Egypt, he was freed from those burdens through the regeneration of baptism.

This was prefigured by the people of Israel, who, leaving Egypt and crossing the Red Sea, were freed from the weight of Egyptian slavery.

It was necessary that his back turn away from the burdens, for while the Gentile people were in Egypt, their hands—that is, their works—served the devil in the basket, that is, in filling the basket. They filled themselves, who were the devil’s basket, with straw and mud, that is, with evil works. These are rightly called straw and mud because they are filthy like mud and fit to be burned in eternal fire like straw. From this straw and mud they built themselves into the devil’s city.

This occurred figuratively in the Israelite people, who, while remaining in Egypt, served Pharaoh in the basket, filling baskets with straw and mud and carrying them on their backs, so that from materials made from these they might build a city there for Pharaoh.

After making this exhortation to the evil, he introduces God exhorting the evil as follows: I say that God placed that testimony in Joseph. I mean that God exhorted you in this way, O perverse children of both Churches.

“Hear, O my people”—that is, you gathering of the perverse, who ought to be my people, since in baptism you promised me obedience. Hear what I command, hearing in such a way that you assent.

You ought to hear me in this way, since I have bestowed these benefits upon you: You called upon me—that is, you prayed to me, already converted to the faith, “in the day,” that is, at the time of tribulation before baptism, when you already possessed knowledge of the faith but nevertheless inwardly suffered great tribulation because of the consciousness of your sins, so that I might free you from this tribulation; and I freed you from it.

Afterward I heard you praying “in the secret place of the tempest,” that is, at the time of hidden tribulation. When, after baptism, a hidden suggestion arising from the evil habit of past vices disturbed you inwardly and invisibly like a most savage storm and tried to turn you back toward those same vices, you prayed that it might not prevail over you, so that I might rescue you from it; and you were heard by me.

But because he had not specified how he had freed him from the earlier tribulation, namely from the consciousness of sins, he specifies this when he adds: Before I freed you from the hidden place of the tempest, I tested you at the water of Contradiction. That is, I made you upright and clean from sins in the water of Contradiction, namely in the water of baptism, which you contradict by living badly, failing to do what you promised me in it, and by sinning again making void the grace of remission that you received there.

Therefore, because I have bestowed these benefits upon you, hear me with assent, you who ought to be my people; and I will testify to you—that is, I will make you certain through the testimony of my help—O Israel, you people who ought to be Israel.

Or, “I will testify to you” means “I will prove to you by the testimony of the Scriptures that, if you hear me in such a way that you assent, there will not be in you a new god, nor will you worship—that is, venerate—an alien god.” You will not have within you any vice that, by worshiping it—that is, by obeying it and satisfying it—you make into a god for yourself, although it is something new and alien to your reason.

This is as though he said: If you give me your assent, I will help you so that no vice will dominate you, causing you to worship and cultivate it as a god. And it is truly alien that you should cultivate and worship anyone other than me.

For I alone, who speak to you, am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, namely from the earthliness of affliction and darkness into which you had descended through Adam.

Therefore, because I have bestowed so great a benefit upon you, open your mouth—that is, enlarge your heart by desiring good things—and I will fill it with virtues, like a hungry young bird that opens its mouth so that its parent may fill it with food. The food of the soul is virtues.

It is as though he said: Do not merely flee vices, but desire virtues exceedingly, so that I may fill you with them.

After making this exhortation to the evil, because he sees that they will not accept it, he turns in apostrophe to the hearers. He shows what will happen to the evil because they are disobedient, and also what they would have attained if they had been obedient. He does this so that, by showing the condemnation of the disobedient, he may withdraw the hearers from disobedience, and, by recounting the benefit they would have had if they had been obedient, draw them toward obedience.

I said, O hearers, that if my people heard me, there would be no new god in them. But my people did not hear my voice with assent—the voice that I made for them, not in words but through hidden inspiration, giving them reason by which they might not worship the vices removed from them. Yet they do worship and adore what is alien.

And I said that they should enlarge the mouth of their heart by desiring good things, so that I might fill it with virtues. But Israel did not attend—that is, did not direct its attention to me—to enlarge its mouth attentively, as I commanded. Therefore I abandoned those who ought to be Israel, and they wished to go according to the desires of their hearts.

It is as though he said: At first I restrained them with loving blows, lest they should dissipate themselves through perverse desires. But because I saw that this correction was fruitless, I let them go according to what their evil heart desired.

And because I let them go, no longer restraining them, they will go from evil to worse, persisting in their own inventions, that is, in the evil works they themselves invented and did not receive from God.

But if the one who ought to be my people had heard me with assent, so that he would not worship an alien god—that is, so that he would serve no vice—and if the one who ought to be Israel had walked in my ways, that is, in my commandments, not by bodily movement but by the desire of his soul, namely by enlarging the mouth of his heart and desiring that I give him virtues, I would have humbled their inner enemies for nothing—that is, without difficulty. “For nothing” means lightly and without labor; to me it would indeed be nothing.

I would have depressed and emptied the power of the vices dominating them, so that they would not insult them. I say, “I would have humbled them”; and perhaps I would have done so—not “perhaps” with respect to me, who am omnipotent, but with respect to their doubt. For they doubt whether I can do this.

And I would have placed my hand—that is, the power of my repression—upon those who afflict them, namely upon the vices.

“To humble their enemies” and “to place my hand upon those who afflict them” mean the same thing. But by saying “those who afflict,” he notes another reason for detesting vices: they are not merely enemies but also afflictors. Therefore they must be avoided.

It should be noted that when he introduces Christ speaking to the evil, whom he nevertheless knows will not accept his correction, and showing compassion toward them, he teaches that we ought to have compassion for the evil. Although they despise the exhortation, we must nevertheless admonish them, so that we may save our own souls, since the Lord testifies through the prophet: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. III, 18).

After faithful Asaph had introduced God speaking to the evil, and, turning in apostrophe to the hearers, had sought to withdraw them from conformity with the evil, he shows that the evil are justly condemned because they are liars in their promise.

I showed, O hearers, that the Lord exhorted the evil, saying, “Hear, O people,” and so forth. But the enemies of the Lord, who ought to have been his people, lied in opposition, failing to fulfill what they had promised in baptism: namely, that after casting away vices they would obey God.

I say that they lied, and they lied to him in such a way that he did not fail to know their lie; it was open before him. Therefore the time of their punishment will be for eternal ages, which will come after this age. Or “time” means their wasting away in torments, and it will last through eternal ages. “Time” is used for “wasting away” because time is defective and quickly passes away.

And rightly will they fail throughout the ages, for they refuse to obey him although he bestowed these benefits upon them: he fed them with the fat of wheat, that is, with wheat that fattens souls, namely with the sacrament of his Body, which fattens souls as wheat fattens bodies; and he filled them with honey flowing from the rock, namely with the sweetness of wisdom proceeding from Christ, who is the firmest rock.

## ON PSALM LXXXI

### The title of Psalm Eighty-One

“A psalm of Asaph.”

This does not mean that Asaph himself speaks here, but that the prophet, speaking in rebuke to unbelieving Asaph—that is, to the assembly that did not recognize the time of its visitation, Christ—confirms that Christ, whom it falsely claimed to be a mere man, is God.

He also urges the leaders to judge rightly concerning him, and the lesser people to rescue him. Through this he teaches us to correct even those who will not be saved, out of a concern for compassion: when he foresees that they will not be recalled from sin, he nevertheless tries, through affection beyond measure, to draw them away from sin by chastising them.

He also treats of the just destruction of unbelieving Asaph and of the conversion of the Gentiles to the faith.

### “God stood in the assembly of gods”

It is as though he said: You unbelieving Jews will say that Christ is a mere man, but he himself will stand as God in the assembly of gods—that is, it will be established to the assembly of the faithful, whom he will make gods by grace, that he is God and not merely man.

He will not be God by grace like the other faithful human beings, although he is man. But “in the midst”—that is, he himself, standing in the midst, openly, existing as a visible man—“he judges the gods”: he will distinguish the faithful deified through him according to the various gifts of the Spirit that he will distribute among them, and according to their differing functions, making some evangelists and others prelates of another kind.

Through this he implies that he will be God by nature. For he could not distinguish gods unless he existed as God in nature.

Therefore, because he will be God, and so powerful that he will judge gods, O leaders of the Jews, “how long will you judge injustice?” It is as though he said: You have judged injustice in the killing of the prophets; and how long—that is, to what extent—will you judge injustice? You will judge injustice so far as to judge worthy of death the one who is the God of the faithful?

And you lesser people, “how long will you accept the faces of sinners,” that is, how long will you take on the conformity of the leaders, who are called “sinners” by antonomasia? It is as though he said: You have become like the leaders by consenting to their judgment concerning the death of the prophets; will you also become like them by consenting to their judgment concerning Christ’s death?

You leaders, do not judge injustice; rather, “judge the needy and the orphan,” that is, render a just judgment to the honor of Christ, who for your sake will be needy, although he is the exalted God, and an orphan, that is, humble and without assistance like an orphan.

He explains how they should judge him when he adds: I say, judge him, and judge him in this way: “justify the humble and the poor,” that is, do not regard him as a sinner; rather, regard as just the one who for your sake will not refuse to be poor and humble.

“Humble” here means the same as “orphan,” and “poor” the same as “needy.”

For if the leaders, unwilling to justify him, should prefer to condemn him to death, then you, the people, at least rescue him by force—the one who for your sake is poor. And if you do not do this by force, free the needy one by a ransom or by some other means from the hand of the sinner, namely from the power of the assembly of the leaders, who are sinners by antonomasia, so that they may not have the power to hand him over to death.

For the correction of the hearers, he shows the obstinacy of their unbelief as follows: I say that he himself, God, will stand and judge gods. But the lesser people did not know this—they will not know it, blinded by their unbelief—nor did the leaders understand it. They ought to have possessed understanding of this matter through investigation and the testimony of the Scriptures.

Therefore they walk in darkness: God will permit them to persist in the darkness of their ignorance, so that they may go from evil to worse.

In their place all the foundations of the earth will be moved toward the faith: every kind of earthly leader who sustains them by his care, and who is therefore called a foundation. Or all kinds of foundations of the earth will be moved toward the faith, namely those who establish their hope and desire upon earthly things.

He returns to his exhortation when he adds: I say, justify the humble and the poor; and it is indeed useful to do this. But they will not know or understand. Nevertheless I, who am the prophet and must be believed, have said, and I say to them: “You are gods,” that is, you lesser people will be gods, made divine so that you may be immortal and impassible if you do this.

But you lesser people who neglect to do it will die the death of the soul here and the death of the body in the future, deceived by the leaders to whom you will ignorantly consent. The first human beings died in the same way, deceived by the devil—namely Adam and Eve—who refused to be made divine through obedience, although they will afterward be freed from that death after a long time through Christ, because they repented.

And you leaders, because you will judge injustice, will fall into condemnation, not deceived but sinning knowingly, just as the devil, who had previously been one of the chief heavenly spirits, fell into condemnation, not deceived but sinning knowingly.

And so that this may happen—that these may die, those may fall, and the foundations of the earth may be moved toward the faith—“Arise, O God,” Christ, from the dead, since you will rise according to your humanity, and “judge”—that is, justly condemn—the earth, namely earthly people, that is, the Jews who will hand you over to death for fear of losing the earth.

And therefore arise, because after you have risen, you will inherit among all the nations: all kinds of Gentiles converted to the faith will be your inheritance, while the Jews are rejected. Hence the Apostle testifies: “A partial blindness has happened in Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter” (Rom. II, 25).

This entire psalm, expounded as spoken in the person of the prophet, may also be read in this way: in the first and last verses the prophet nevertheless speaks in his own person, while in the other six middle verses he introduces Christ rebuking the Jews, so that the meaning does not greatly change.

It is expressed as follows: I say that God, Christ, will stand in the assembly of gods, and, standing in the midst, will judge the gods, saying—Christ himself—“How long will you, leaders, judge injustice? Will you judge it so far as to call me worthy of death? And you lesser people, how long will you accept the faces—that is, the conformities—of the sinful leaders? Will you accept them to such an extent that you will consent to their judgment concerning my death, just as you have already consented to their judgment concerning the death of the prophets?”

You leaders, do not judge injustice; rather, judge what would be an honor to you in respect of me, the needy and the orphan for your sake: namely, justify me; regard me, the humble and poor, as just.

But if the leaders refuse to do this, you lesser people, rescue me, the poor, by force; and if not by force, free me, the needy one, by a ransom or by any other means from the hand of the sinful people’s leaders.

He turns in apostrophe to the hearers in order to show the hardness of both their leaders and their lesser people, as follows: I said to the lesser people, “How long will you accept the faces?” and “Rescue me from the hand of the sinner.” But they did not know what I said to them, and they acted badly.

And I said to the leaders, “How long will you judge injustice?” Nor did they understand that they were judging injustice, although they ought to have understood this through investigation of the Scriptures.

Therefore they walk—that is, persist—in the darkness of ignorance, so that they may become more and more blind; and in their place all the foundations of the earth will be moved toward the faith.

This is explained in two ways, as above. And because the foundations will be moved toward the faith, I, who am God and omnipotent, whose willing is doing, said—that is, I determined with the Father—“You foundations,” because you will be moved toward the faith, “are gods,” that is, you will be immortal and impassible like gods, and “you will all be adoptive sons of the Most High,” that is, of the omnipotent Father.

But you lesser people of the Jews, because you are ignorant, will die eternally, existing like human beings, namely like Adam and Eve, deceived by the leaders just as Adam and Eve were deceived by the devil.

And you leaders, deceived by no one, will fall from the prosperity in which you flourish because through pride you refused to understand. Just as the devil, previously one of the chief heavenly spirits, not deceived by anyone, fell with his angels from the height of heavenly glory through the arrogance of his pride.

After introducing Christ as speaking, the prophet speaks in his own person, turning in apostrophe to him, as follows: You say that the foundations moved toward the end will be gods and sons of the Most High, and that the unbelieving Jews will die and fall. And so that this may happen, arise, O God Christ, from the dead, since they will hand you over to death according to your humanity; and, having risen, judge the earth, that is, justly condemn the earthly Jews.

Someone might object: If he condemns the Jews, who have knowledge of him, among whom he will afterward reign, how will this be?

He responds to the objection as follows: Do not therefore refrain from judging them, thinking that you will lack those who might be your hereditary kingdom. For after these have been judged, you, whose inheritance is in the Jews, will inherit among all—that is, among every kind of Gentiles converted to the faith.

He foretells this for the instruction of the faith of the Gentiles, not in order to instruct Christ concerning among whom he will inherit after the Jews have been cast down.

## ON PSALM LXXXII
## Title of Psalm Eighty-Two: A Song of the Psalm of Asaph

This is explained as follows: This song of the psalm—that is, this treatise called a “song of the psalm”—belongs to Asaph, that is, to the congregation of the faithful that existed before Christ’s coming. Foreseeing through the Holy Spirit the tribulations that would arise in the Church and be inflicted by false Christians, heretics, and unbelievers, it foretells them for the benefit of the faithful who will suffer them, and shows by whom they will be inflicted. For darts that are foreseen wound less than those that strike suddenly. Therefore, so that they may remain more steadfast amid those tribulations, it foretells them.

It also prays concerning the recompense of those who will endure them [Col. 1076D], and, by way of concession, it likewise treats of the adversaries’ overthrow both in the present and in the future. It also prays for some among those very adversaries who are to be saved, and thereby teaches us to pray for our enemies, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Luke 6:28).

This psalm is called a song of the psalm because, although briefly, it treats here of the song of the psalm—that is, of the joyful recompense of the faithful’s good work—for which faithful Asaph prays when he says: “Do not be silent, O God, concerning their recompense in the future.” It does not, then, speak so explicitly about good work, except that where it says “against your holy ones,” it indicates that they will work well. For they would not rightly be called holy unless they worked well [Col. 1077A]. Nevertheless, their tribulations, which he recounts, may properly be called good works. For who should more rightly be said to work well than one who does not flee from suffering for Christ?

“God, who will be like you?” No one. Through this question he indicates the sorrow he feels concerning certain people who will set themselves above Christ by afflicting his servants. He immediately treats, by way of concession, of their destruction, as though he were saying: There are many who will set themselves above you by tormenting your people and will make themselves equal to you, judging that they do not depend upon you, just as you do not depend upon them; nevertheless, none of them will be like you.

Or he puts the question almost as an expression of wonder, to indicate the greatness of his power. As though he were saying: God, Christ, whom your adversaries will regard as powerless because you do not immediately reward your people or punish your adversaries—who, nevertheless, will be like you, that is, so omnipotent as you? No one. Therefore, since you are so powerful that no one can be made like you, you who now remain silent concerning the recompense of your people—that is, do not reward them in the present as they deserve—do not remain silent in the future, but reward them.

Nor, O God, should you be restrained in the future from avenging your adversaries, by whom you are restrained here only through mercy. Someone might ask why he says this, since no one has yet arisen who opposes him. To this he responds as follows: I say, “Do not be restrained,” because, behold, what your enemies have sounded forth in the present will not last long—or rather, they will sound forth: those who will become your enemies will sound forth in the persecution of your people [Col. 1077B]. That is, they will rage irrationally against your people by contradicting them, like inanimate objects whose collision produces a noise.

And they will not merely sound forth by contradicting; those who hate you—that is, the enemies who will hate you—have lifted up their head, that is, they will raise their minds against you. He explains how they will lift it up: they will lift up their head in this way, namely because they have devised, or will devise, a wicked plan against your people—that is, they have entered, or will enter, a wicked conspiracy in words in order to oppress your people. And not just any people: they have considered, or will consider, something against your holy ones, that is, they will think up something of such a kind as to harm your servants bodily.

For they have said, or will say—that is, they will arrange this among themselves, one saying to another:

“Come, and let us destroy them from the nation.” As though he were saying: These faithful are nations, that is, a very great multitude; but let us advance against them and destroy them by removing them from the nation—that is, let us diminish them so that they are no longer nations, or a multitude—and let us destroy them to such an extent that the name of Israel will no longer be remembered [Col. 1077D]. That is, let us destroy them so completely that no further mention will even be made of the name of those who call themselves Israel.

Someone might say: From where will they derive such confidence that they can extinguish the name of Israel? He replies: Their confidence in extinguishing the name of Israel comes from this: they have considered it unanimously—that is, they will consider it with one evil will. And they will not merely consider it, but together, existing with one mind against you—that is, acting in opposition to you—they have arranged, or will arrange, this covenant among themselves [Col. 1078A], namely this most firm pact, in order to destroy your people.

The tents of the Edomites—that is, the transient multitudes of the Idumeans, prone to fall; these are the earthly and bloodthirsty multitudes, namely false Christians, who, although they have been initiated into the Church’s sacraments, are nevertheless earthly, that is, yearning in every way for earthly things, and cruel toward the good, just as one who sheds his neighbor’s blood is cruel.

And the Ishmaelites will arrange themselves against you—that is, those same Christians who, although they have promised obedience to God, are nevertheless Ishmaelites, that is, obedient to themselves in all their shameful desires. The Idumeans are interpreted as “bloodthirsty” or “earthly,” while the Ishmaelites are interpreted as “obedient to themselves”; although Ishmael himself is said to mean “obedient to God.” The Ishmaelites, I say, will be Moab—that is, not merely obedient to themselves, but also a lawless people, without the law of God’s commandments; or begotten from the father the devil through unbelief; or separated from God the Father, namely, having withdrawn from him through unbelief, because they refused to be his sons through faith. For Moab is interpreted as “lawless” or “from the Father.”

And the Hagarenes will arrange themselves against you: namely, the heretics, who, although regenerated through baptism, nevertheless make themselves alien to the faith through their heresies. The Hagarenes are interpreted as “proselytes,” and proselytes means the same as “aliens.”

And Gebal will arrange itself against you: namely, the people of hypocrites, “who come in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matthew 7:15). Gebal is called a “vain valley.” Therefore hypocrites are signified by Gebal: although they are vain and proud, they make themselves valleys—that is, humble [Col. 1078C].

And Ammon will arrange itself against you—that is, the turbulent people, namely the leaders of the heretics, who are turbulent and who pour out turbulent and obscene teaching.

And Amalek will arrange itself—that is, the “licking people,” namely the Simonians, who are lickers: by money and ambition they embrace ecclesiastical doctrines as though with greedy appetite. Amalek is indeed interpreted as “licking” or “one who licks.”

And the foreigners will arrange themselves: the Philistines, indeed; because they have always been adversaries of the Jews, they have almost taken as their proper name this appellation, “foreigners.” Thus, when he says “foreigners,” it is the same as if he had said “Philistines.” Through the Philistines, who are interpreted as “those falling through drink” [Col. 1078D], are understood those false Christians who are adversaries of the good. Excessively steeped in the obscene drink of lust, they fall away from fellowship with the good and oppose them in every way.

I say that all these—although initiated into the Church’s sacraments, namely false Christians, hypocrites, and heretics—will arrange a covenant against you. They will be in agreement in this with those inhabiting Tyre, that is, with those living in “Tyre,” meaning “distress”: with unbelievers who persist in oppressing the good in every way. Tyre is also called by another name, Sor; for Sor means “distress.” Therefore, when he says “Tyre,” it is the same as if he had said “Sor.”

I say that unbelievers, false Christians, hypocrites, and heretics will arrange a covenant against you [Col. 1079A]. And truly they will arrange one.

For Assyria, that is, the devil, has come, or will come, with all of them through evil suggestions, in order to make them arrange this. The devil is rightly called Assyria, that is, “directing,” “depressing,” or “exalted.” For those whom he deceives he directs toward death—that is, he leads them by a straight path through sins; he depresses the good through the persistence of evil deeds; and he continually exalts himself arrogantly against God.

This devil was prefigured by Nebuchadnezzar, who, in the historical account, led a multitude of nations to oppress Jerusalem. Nebuchadnezzar is also said to have been of Assyrian origin.

And all of them have been made, or will be made, an aid to the sons of Lot, that is, to the sons of “declination”; for Lot means “declination.” Thus, by the sons of Lot are understood the evil spirits, who, although they had at first been special sons, withdrew from God through arrogance. Since they cannot persecute the good by themselves, they enlist all the wicked as their aid, and through their service afflict the good in many ways.

By way of concession he treats of the destruction of those adversaries who will have been initiated into the Church’s sacraments, as follows: Since Moab and the others will arrange themselves against you, deal with them as with Midian—that is, with those who are Midian, meaning “declining from judgment,” namely false Christians and heretics, who, in their own estimation, decline from the future judgment, since they do not fear that you will condemn them by a just judgment in the future—and as with Sisera, that is, with those who are Sisera, meaning “vision of a horse” or “exclusion from joy.”

They are those who, in their understanding, continually see a horse—that is, lust or the battle of contradiction against the good. Both are signified by the horse, which is an animal of lust and suited to war. By living badly they exclude eternal joy from themselves.

And deal with them as with Jabin—that is, condemn them—as those who are Jabin, meaning “understanding” or “wise”: those who consider themselves subtly intelligent, although they are erroneous and wise only in carnal matters. This indeed applies to heretics.

As Midian, Sisera, and Jabin, I say, who exist in the torrent of Kishon—that is, in an excessive abundance of hardness; Kishon means “hardness.” They are abundantly hardened in unbelief. The word “torrent” is used for abundance because it overflows excessively with waters.

I say that, concerning those initiated into the sacraments, I concede that you should do what is to be done regarding their condemnation. Their condemnation is not entirely certain, because they appear to be faithful. But concerning the condemnation of unbelievers I need not speak by way of concession, since it is already manifest.

For they, existing in Endor, have perished—that is, existing only in the fountain of generation and refusing to be in the fountain of regeneration. They will perish while remaining in their carnality, in which they were generated. It is therefore called a fountain, that is, the origin of generation. They refuse to reach baptism, which is the fountain of saving regeneration, and so they will perish—that is, they will perish utterly.

And although they perish completely, they should not nevertheless be thought to have been born uselessly. For they have been made like dung upon the earth, that is, comparable to dung, specifically manure scattered over the ground. Although it is foul in itself [Col. 1080A], it nevertheless enriches the soil and makes it fertile. So also unbelievers, foul and filthy in themselves, nevertheless make the good whom they afflict fertile in good works through tribulations and enrich them with divine grace.

Having inserted this distinction concerning condemnation and salvation, he returns to conceding the condemnation of those initiated into the Christian sacraments, as follows: I say, deal with false Christians as with Midian and Sisera.

But place their princes like Oreb, Zeb, Zebah, and Zalmunna—that is, those who stir them up to error and to the oppression of the good. Place them for condemnation like Oreb, that is, as those who are Oreb, meaning “dryness,” “like a raven,” or “a hole.” They are dry, namely, of the dew of spiritual grace; they strive to dry up the goods of others; they are black in sins like a raven; and they are a hole [Col. 1080B], that is, a serpent’s cave, in which the devil dwells, who by antonomasia is called the venomous serpent.

Through them he also hisses and pierces, when through the service of their tongues he infuses the poison of unbelief and error into others, after the likeness of the serpent, which lives in holes and caves, hisses from there, pierces those who approach it, and injects poison into them. This applies to heretics.

And as Zeb—that is, as those who are Zeb, meaning “wolf”—devouring others by afflicting them in the manner of a wolf. This applies to unbelievers.

And those who are Zebah, meaning “sacrifice of a wolf,” namely those who sacrifice to the devil through evil works and desire others to sacrifice as well. The wolf is called a ravenous animal by antonomasia. This applies to false Christians.

And those who are Zalmunna, meaning “shadow of disturbance” or “consummated”: those who are easily moved to every evil, like a shadow that moves according to the sun; those who are a shadow, that is, overshadowed by blindness; and consummated in wickedness, that is, perfected in it.

He also adds the reason why he treats their overthrow by way of concession in this manner. I say, place the princes in condemnation—all their princes, I mean—who have said, or will say, some with their voice, some with evil affection, and some by the persecution itself:

“Let us possess as an inheritance, in our dominion, the sanctuary of God,” that is, the holy people of God. Let us possess and cultivate God’s people according to our own pleasure, just as anyone possesses and cultivates his inheritance according to his pleasure. As though he were saying: Place them there for this reason, because they will say, “Let us possess God’s sanctuary as an inheritance.”

He shows how he concedes that they should be placed there when he adds: I say, place the princes—place them in this manner, O my God. Place them here like a wheel, that is, make them like a wheel, so that they are raised at the rear, namely in earthly things, which are always left behind when people pass on, and cast down at the front, namely in heavenly goods, so that they may not attain what they presume to attain—things that are in front, that is, still to come—in the likeness of a wheel, which is raised at the rear and cast down at the front.

That is to say: Permit them to prosper in secular matters so that they may be cast down in heavenly matters. And place them like straw before the face—that is, before the force—of the wind [Col. 1081A], so that they may be unstable and inconstant in resisting the devil’s suggestions, just as uprooted straw is unstable before the force of the wind.

And in the future you will pursue them in your storm, that is, in your judgment, which is called a storm because it will separate the good from the evil, just as a storm separates grain from chaff, carrying away the chaff and leaving the grain. Or it is called a storm because a multitude of angels will accompany it, and it will separate the good from the evil, according to what is read elsewhere: “Around him is a mighty storm” (Psalm 49:2).

And after the storm, in anger—that is, in your vengeance—you will trouble them when they are cast into the Gehenna of eternal fire.

I say, you will pursue them in this way, just as fire pursues a forest and consumes it; and not just any forest, but as a flame—that is, a fiery flame—consuming the mountains, meaning the forests of the mountains, pursues those mountain forests. That is to say: Just as fire in the forests of the mountains, where it is more violent because of the excessive force of the winds, pursues the forests so completely that it utterly destroys them, so you, O God, in the future, by your just judgment, will pursue them so as to destroy them completely.

But he prays for the salvation of some princes who are to be saved: I say, place the princes like a wheel—that is, those who are to be condemned—but fill the faces of some of them who are to be saved, that is, their consciences, here with disgrace, meaning shame, so that they may recognize themselves as disgraceful because they have sinned, and thus be ashamed.

And through this, O Lord, they will seek your name by living well, that is, the honor of your name. The conscience is called the face for this reason: just as a blush appears on the face as a sign of shame, so shame itself remains in the conscience.

He returns, however, to conceding the condemnation of those who are to be damned, as follows: I say that the faces of those who are to be saved should be filled with disgrace; but let those who are to be condemned in the future be put to shame to their harm, since here they refuse to be ashamed to their advantage. Let them be troubled forever and ever, that is, let them grieve eternally.

He repeats this in order to add: “And let them be confounded,” I mean, let them be troubled and perish by eternal death. Then let them know what they refused to know here: namely, that your name is God, that is, that you alone are rightly called God, meaning Creator, and that there is no other besides you; and that you alone are the Most High, that is, the Omnipotent One ruling over the whole earth [Col. 1081D].

As though he were saying: While they pursue their own desires here and despise yours, they will make themselves equal to you and will not think that you alone are the Most High. At last they will recognize this in the future, when they justly perish.

## On Psalm Eighty-Three

The title of Psalm Eighty-Three: “For the end, for the winepresses; a psalm of the sons of Korah.”

This is explained as follows: This psalm is to be attributed to the adopted sons of Korah, that is, to the perfect imitators of Christ’s Passion, who act concerning the winepresses that are effective unto the end—that is, who act concerning the pressures of tribulations, which are effective in leading those who endure them unto the end, namely to the perfection of eternal blessedness.

Or it may mean the sons of Korah looking toward the end, that is, toward Christ, through whom they trust that they will come to blessedness, and acting concerning the winepresses, that is, for the praise of the winepresses, which seem useless to some.

Winepresses are called the pressures of tribulations because, just as winepresses squeeze grapes, separate the must from the grapes, and make the must flow into the Lord’s storerooms while the grape-skins remain, so the pressures of tribulations depress the good and separate them bodily from the evil, when their souls, separated from their bodies, ascend into heaven. But the wicked, weakened by tribulations, cannot reach there.

The sons of Korah are introduced here praising these very tribulations, through which one comes from this valley of tears to the courts of heavenly life [Col. 1082B]. They do this in order to urge their hearers to endure these tribulations, which will be useful to them, so that through them they may reach blessedness.

Yet, so that no one may presume that he can reach this goal solely through the merit of enduring tribulations, they show that no one will reach it unless he grounds his works in hope, faith, and love, and unless God also assists him through his grace in ascending to blessedness.
