Therefore they pray that God may assist them in this through the merit of Christ’s goodness, saying that it is better to be the least citizen in eternal Jerusalem than to be here, in the city of sinful Babylon, the greatest and most distinguished.

“How beloved are your tabernacles,” that is, your warfare through tribulations, which are transient in the manner of tabernacles, “O Lord God of the heavenly powers!” As though he were saying: Since secular men regard it as beloved and dear to serve secular lords under the great burden of tribulations, how beloved are your tabernacles to us—that is, how greatly beloved are your armies—under the heaviest burden of tribulations, since you are so powerful that you rule even over the heavenly powers?

And through these tabernacles my soul longs to come into the Lord’s homeland, that is, into the expanse of heavenly Jerusalem, which is the Lord’s city. And it not only longs, but also faints through tribulations from this life, namely when it is separated from the body by torments, in order to reach the Lord’s courts themselves, after the likeness of a grape that faints in the winepress so that the expressed must may flow into the Lord’s storerooms [Col. 1082D].

Since he had said that the soul longs, and it is established that there are two powers of the soul—namely sensuality, which he here calls “flesh” because it gives life to the flesh and savors the things of the flesh, and spirituality, which is also called rationality, which he here calls “heart” because it rules and arranges sensuality and the body itself—he shows here that both powers desire with exultation to reach eternal blessedness, namely to attain conformity with the living God.

Nevertheless, unless sensuality is subdued by many fasts and other afflictions, it often resists spirituality, according to the Apostle’s saying: “The flesh,” that is, sensuality, “desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17).

When, therefore, he says that the flesh, that is, sensuality, exults amid tribulations so that through this it may reach the living God, he indicates that, subdued through many afflictions, it consents to spirituality. He also instructs us similarly to tame our own carnality, so that it does not resist the spirit.

He says this as follows: I say that my soul longs, through pressures, to reach the courts of the Lord; and it does not long for this according to only one power. Rather, my heart, that is, spirituality, and my flesh, that is, sensuality, have exulted—that is, they have desired with exultation—to reach the living God through the winepresses of tribulations, namely to attain conformity with the living God insofar as I can be conformed to him, so that I may live forever.

He does not add “living” superfluously. As though he were saying: Since he himself is living and immortal, who would not long to reach him in order to live? He then shows with what confidence he thinks he will attain this, when he adds: I say that my soul longs to reach the courts of the Lord, and I trust that I will reach them.

“For the sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest, where it may place and warm its young.” “House” and “nest” should be understood as referring to both birds; but for the sake of brevity he has joined “house” to the sparrow and “nest” to the turtledove.

The sparrow is rightly called spirituality because it always tends toward high places, and, like the sparrow, never builds its nest except in elevated places.

The turtledove, however, is called sensuality because it groans under many tribulations and, by being subdued through tribulations, becomes chaste, so that it neither indulges in lust nor resists the spirit, like the turtledove, which continually groans and is chaste.

He calls the young good works because they proceed from the faithful and are continually increased by them, just as young birds proceed from birds and are nourished and warmed by those same birds.

He calls love a house because it is not quickly transient, just as a house is not; but hope and faith he calls a nest because they will exist for a time in the likeness of a nest, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Love never fails” (1 Corinthians 13:8), and again: “But the greatest of these is love” (ibid. 13).

Through this he indicates that faith and hope will fail in the future. In this house and in this nest, therefore, the young are placed and warmed—that is, good works are founded and increased. Otherwise they would perish, like young birds placed in a nest and warmed so that they do not perish.

The words of this verse are adapted as follows: Truly I trust that I will reach the living God. For the sparrow—that is, spirituality—has found for itself, that is, for its own benefit, a house, that is, love, and a nest, that is, hope and faith. And the turtledove, that is, sensuality, has found a house and a nest where both may place their young, that is, where they may establish and increase their good works. For both birds work well in this way; therefore both are appropriately said to place works in the house and nest.

I say that the sparrow has found a house and the turtledove a nest; and these house and nest are your altars. They are truly altars, because just as sacrifices are offered upon an altar, so all good works ought to be offered to God upon hope, faith, and love.

He shows why he longs to come into the Lord’s courts: And this is why, O Lord, God of the heavenly powers, my king and my God, the blessed dwell in your house, heavenly Jerusalem.

As though he were saying: Who would not long to come into your courts, since you are God, that is, Creator and Lord of the powers, and king, and since all who dwell in your house are blessed? Here he takes “courts” and “house” in the same sense.

When he says “blessed,” he indicates that they possess as much blessedness as can be understood; and it is clear that they are blessed because they will praise you out of the love of devotion forever and ever, that is, eternally. For they would not praise you eternally unless they were eternally blessed.

No one, however, can reach this blessedness by himself, even if he possesses hope, faith, and love. Rather, blessed is that man—that is, only that man reaches this blessedness—whose help comes from you for the ascents of blessedness that he has arranged in his heart.

That is to say: Only that person should be called one who will reach blessedness who, while arranging in his heart to ascend to this blessedness, receives help from your grace through many ascents of virtues and good works. For no one can ascend by himself, as the Lord himself attests: “No one has ascended into heaven,” by himself, that is, “except the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

I say that he arranged ascents while existing in the valley of tears, that is, in this life, which is lowly and full of the tears of tribulations in comparison with the other life, which, compared with this one, must be called a mountain and is full of joy.

As though he were saying: It is fitting that he arrange ascents. For who, unless insane, would not wish to ascend from the valley of tears to the mountain of joy?

And so that no one might seem to be in the valley of tears without deserving to be there, he adds: in the valley of tears, I say, in the place that man himself made for himself by sinning. As though he were saying: It is not a place that every human being possesses through the fault of the Creator, but through his own fault.

Or it may be understood in this way: So that no one might bear impatiently being in this valley of tears, he adds: in the place that God assigned to the human race, that is, in which he established that we should be afflicted because of the crime of our first parent.

Since he had said, “Blessed is the man whose help is from you,” someone might ask: Does God help him to this end? He answers as follows: Truly, the blessed receive help from God. For the lawgiver, namely Christ, who gave us the law, gives and will give blessings perseveringly—that is, manifold gifts of grace—through which he will bless his people, that is, exalt them to blessedness [Col. 1085A].

And through these blessings they will go from virtue to virtue, ascending. And in the future, in heavenly Zion, Christ, the God of gods, will be seen—he who, although he is God, will also deify his own.

Or, while they exist in Zion, the God of gods will be seen spiritually, namely the triune God. That is to say: “By reason they will see in themselves the God whom here they cannot see; for God will be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28).

Or it may be understood thus: They will ascend to such a degree that in this life the God of gods will be seen—not bodily, but in Zion, that is, in the watchtower of contemplation. As though he were saying: He will bless his people and make them ascend from virtue to virtue to such a degree that he will also make them contemplate him.

He prays for this vision of God and for blessedness as follows: I say that the God of gods will be seen. And so that I may see you and become blessed, O Lord, who are powerful because you are the God of the heavenly powers, hear my prayer, because I pray that I may see you.

“Receive with your ears”—that is, receive in the power of your mercy, through which you graciously hear—the prayer itself, O God of Jacob. As though he were saying: I pray that, since you are my God as Jacob, you may also be my God as Israel, so that you who already make me struggle vigorously may also make me contemplate you.

Hear the prayer, receive it with your ears, and look upon us, O God. The same request is repeated so many times out of an excess of affection. And you, O God our protector, so that I may not fail amid the tribulations of this life, look upon us with the gaze of mercy—that is, mercifully grant us to be your contemplators—you who grant us this, that you may be our protector amid tribulations.

And because our merits do not demand that you look upon us, look upon the face, that is, upon the beauty of the virtues and good works of Christ your Son, our head. Consider that the beauty of your Son Christ demands that you have mercy on us through him.

He uses “face” for “beauty” because human beauty is usually observed in the face. Therefore I ask so earnestly to see you and to reach the blessedness of eternal life: because one day, and that day without end, which is in your courts, that is, in heavenly Jerusalem, is infinitely better than thousands of days of this life.

That is to say: I desire to reach you and attain eternal life because that one day of eternal life, which does not end, is more worthy and more excellent than the infinite thousands of days of this life, which will end. By commending eternal life in this way, he urges his hearers to seek it.

And because that day is such a day, I chose to be lowly—that is, the least citizen—in the house of God, heavenly Jerusalem, rather than to dwell, that is, to remain for a long time, distinguished and honored in the tents of sinners, that is, in the transient way of life of secular sinners.

He uses “lowly” for “least,” not because anyone there will be lowly, but because we customarily call the least “lowly.” Some there will indeed be least, while others will be greatest, according to the Apostle’s saying: “As star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:41).

I say that I chose to be lowly in the house of God. I do not believe that I will reach that house through my merits, O hearers, but through the mercy and truth of God, because God loves mercy and truth—that is, because God is merciful and true, and has promised that he will lead us to that house.

And because he is merciful and true, the Lord will give grace and glory, that is, freely given glory in the future, namely eternal life.

He explains to whom he will give it [Col. 1086A], and shows that he will give it forever: after he has given the goods of that glory, he will not deprive those who live in innocence and walk—that is, advance—from one good work to another.

That is to say: To the innocent, who will work well, he will give these goods; and after he has given them, he will not deprive them of them. No one will possess these goods if he has despaired of them.

But, O Lord of the heavenly powers, blessed will be that man—that is, that man will be blessed with these goods—who hopes in you for the things that are in you, namely these goods.

As though he were saying: Since you are the God of the heavenly powers, who is more blessed than one who hopes in you? Or, he will be blessed here who hopes in you and not in himself, namely one who does not trust that he can reach this goal through his own merits, but through you. Whoever trusts in himself alone will never reach it.

## 339. On Psalm Eighty-Four

[Col. 1086B]

The title of Psalm Eighty-Four: “For the end, a psalm of the sons of Korah.”

This is explained as follows: This psalm looks toward the end, that is, toward Christ, whose benefits to the human race it recounts. It is for the sons of Korah, that is, for the benefit of those who are to become sons of Korah, namely imitators of the crucified Christ.

By this psalm’s narrative he does not say “for the sons of Korah” because the sons of Korah speak here, or because the psalm is addressed to them. Rather, the Prophet, showing the benefits given to the human race through Christ, urges his hearers through this very narrative to become imitators of him, from whom so many benefits have been bestowed upon them. For this is exceedingly useful to them.

These benefits, although still future in their proper time, he announces in the past tense, as though they had already happened, following the usage of the past tense, and he prays for them.

“You have blessed”—that is, you will bless—O Father, your future land through blessing, which was previously cursed through Adam. As though he were saying: The human race, which must be called “land” according to sensuality, since it is intent upon earthly things, was cursed through Adam, that is, humbled toward vices and evil works.

This was prefigured when the Lord said to Adam: “Cursed is the earth in your work; it will bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Genesis 3:17).

But you, O Father, will bless that human race, that is, exalt it in virtues and works; and through this you will make it your land, so that it may produce for you the fruit of good works.

And before you bless it, you have turned away—that is, you will turn away—the captivity from Jacob, namely from the greater part of the human race, which you will make Jacob, that is, one who struggles manfully against the devil. You will turn away the vices so that they may not be in captivity, that is, so that they may not be held captive in subjection to the devil.

And after you turn away the captivity, you have forgiven—that is, you will forgive—the iniquity of your people, that is, you will forgive in your people their iniquity. You will restrain in them the tinder of sin, namely evil desire, so that it may not prevail over them or drag them into evil action.

And before you forgive iniquity, you have covered—that is, you will cover—their sins, namely you will bury and erase them in baptism, both original and actual sins.

This was prefigured in the sons of Israel when they crossed the Red Sea long ago: their enemies, following behind them, were covered in the sea, drowned, and killed.

[Col. 1087A] It should be noted that he does not recount these benefits in their proper order. First, one was turned away from captivity through faith; afterward sins were covered; then iniquity was remitted; and finally one was blessed with good works and virtues. Lest it seem that he would bestow no other benefit, he indicates that he will give something far more perfect in the future when he adds, “You have mitigated.” The passage may be connected as follows: I say that you will bless, turn away captivity, remit iniquity, and cover sins; and in this way you have mitigated—that is, you will mitigate—all your anger, that is, your vengeance of every kind. It is as though he said: You exercise your vengeance in many ways upon the human race because of Adam’s sin, permitting it to be subjected to the devil through evil works, to be taken captive, to have its iniquity increased, and to be mortal and subject to suffering. Yet you will not remove this vengeance here [Col. 1087B] entirely; rather, you will somewhat mitigate here your vengeance of every kind when you bless and turn away captivity.

In the future, however, “you have turned away”—that is, you will turn yourself away—from the anger of your indignation. “Indignation” is sometimes used for a lesser anger; but another translation has, “from the anger of your fury.” From this we infer that here “indignation” is used for excessive anger. It has been added as a qualifier so that the expression is intransitive, thus: In the future you will turn yourself away from the anger of your indignation, that is, from the anger that ought to be called indignation because it is great; in other words, you will turn yourself away from your great vengeance. It is as though he had said: Here you will remit to them the lesser vengeance that you exercise upon them because of Adam’s sin—namely, the increase of iniquity and other things of this kind, which are called lesser because they do not seem to burden the wicked so heavily, since they actually take pleasure in them. In the future, however, you will turn away from them the greater vengeance, which, because of its excessive magnitude, is called fury—namely, mortality and liability to suffering. These burden even the wicked very greatly; therefore they are called the greater vengeance and fury.

He prays that what he has declared may come to pass, as follows: I say that you will bless and turn away captivity, and so forth. Thus may it happen, O saving God, that is, our Savior: convert us from the curse to blessing, from captivity to freedom, from the increase of iniquity to remission, and from the persistence of sins to their covering and immersion.

And I have said that in the future you will turn away the anger of indignation; so may it be: In the future turn away from us entirely your anger, that is, your great vengeance. I pray for this because surely we must not believe what certain people falsely assert—namely, that you will be angry with us forever, failing to raise us up and restore us to immortality. You would indeed be angry with us forever if we were not raised up and restored to immortality. Or, if you raise us up and make us immortal, will you extend your anger—that is, your vengeance—from this earthly generation to the future generation, when we shall be raised? In other words, when you exercise this vengeance upon us here so that we are subject to suffering, will you extend this same vengeance into the future generation, so that we shall then also be subject to suffering, as certain people suppose?

Those people seem to have held this opinion who, as we read in the Gospel, asked the Lord whose wife the woman who had married seven brothers would be in the future resurrection. The Lord answered them: “In the regeneration they neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Luke 20:33, 35). He resolves this question point by point when he adds: Truly, you will not be angry forever; but you, God, turning in the future from anger to mercy, will give us life by raising us up and making us immortal. You will not extend your anger from generation to generation, because your people—that is, we and those conformed to us—will rejoice in you, that is, in participation in your freedom from suffering. It is as though he said: We shall be anxious under no fear of suffering, but shall rejoice in participation in your glorious freedom from suffering.

He also prays that this may come to pass, as follows: I say that in the future you will give us life, and we shall rejoice in you; and so, Lord, [Col. 1088B] show us in the future this mercy of yours—namely, the life and joy that are mercifully to be given. Do not show it in such a way that you do not give it—as when, to increase their misery, those destined for destruction will see the glory of the blessed, which they will not possess—but show us and give us your salvation, that is, that salvation consisting in life and joy. He uses “mercy” and “salvation” with the same meaning.

Alternatively, this may be a prayer concerning the coming of the Son, through whom these benefits were to be conferred, as follows: I say that we shall be given life and shall rejoice; and since these things cannot occur unless your Son becomes incarnate and appears visibly, show us, Lord Father, your mercy—that is, make your incarnate Son visibly appear to our children who will exist at that time. Through his obedience you will have mercy upon the world; for this reason he is called your mercy. And since he will not be visibly shown to all who are to be saved, at least give him, your Salvation—that is, your Savior—to all of us who are to be saved, both present and future. Give him so that he may be the Savior of all believers, both of those who see him and of those who do not.

Since the Prophet had announced these benefits, so that his words might be established as authoritative, he shows that he received this not from himself but from the Holy Spirit, as follows: I say that God will give us life and that we shall rejoice in him.

I do not say this from myself, but I frequently hear the Lord God, the Spirit, speaking these and similar things within me—not in words but through hidden inspiration. [Col. 1088D] And I not only hear this, but I shall continually hear what the Lord God speaks within me, that is, in my interior being. It is as though he said: No concern for earthly things will be able to recall me from this hearing. And it is fitting that I should always hear this, because what he speaks will not be trivial: he will speak of the peace that is to come to his people, namely the Jewish people—a peace that will be eternal, when we shall be disturbed by no suffering but shall continually rejoice in God.

By saying that he will frequently hear this, he instructs his hearers [341] that they ought always to be intent upon this peace. He properly calls the Jewish people his own by antonomasia, since it has always possessed knowledge of him. Lest it be thought that the promise concerned the entire Jewish people, he specifies those to whom it will come when he adds: I say that peace will come to his people; that is, it will come especially upon his holy ones—upon the holy ones who will be in the Jewish people—and this peace will be given according to God’s higher disposition.

Peace will come not only upon the holy ones from the Jews, but also upon those from the nations who are converted—that is, who will be converted from the error of irrational unbelief to the heart, that is, to the reason of the heart, so that they may know and worship their Creator. He properly says that the nations are to be converted to the heart. They were outside the heart when they offered to creatures the worship owed to God, worshiping idols, that is.

I say that there will be peace among the holy ones; nevertheless, his salvation will be near those who fear him—not near those holy ones who, becoming proud because of their holiness, will fall away. It is as though he said: Although I have spoken indefinitely of “holy ones,” there will nevertheless be many holy ones who will fall away from holiness, and from them the salvation of eternal peace will be distant. But salvation will be near those who fear him, that is, near those who always fear him here, so that they do not become proud. That salvation through Christ will be near them while they remain in this world.

I say that here salvation will be near the holy ones, and finally near those who fear him, so that at last, in the future, the glory of salvation may dwell—that is, remain forever—in our land, that is, in our earthly flesh, so that we may be glorious not only in our souls but also in our bodies, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “This corruptible body must put on incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:53).

Alternatively, the passage may be read as specifying among whom he will dwell, for the instruction of our faith; and this may be intended either to make the Jews, among whom he says that he will dwell, more obligated to him, or also to serve the faith of the nations. For he will not glorify only those among whom he will dwell, but all who will worship and believe in him. I say that his peace will come both upon the holy ones from the Jews and upon those who will be converted to the heart.

Nevertheless, although he will give peace both to the holy Jews and to the nations converted to the heart, Salvation—that is, his Son the Savior, through whom he will save the world—will dwell by bodily presence not among the nations but near them, that is, among those who fear him, namely, among the Jews who have possessed knowledge and fear of him from the time of Abraham. Yet this will occur in such a way that he will not make glorious only those among whom he dwells; rather, through his grace, the glory of immortality and freedom from suffering will dwell in the future not only in our soul but also in our land, that is, in our flesh, which is now earthly.

The preceding passage may also be joined to the words, “He will speak of the peace that is to come to his people,” because the two intervening verses were inserted. I say that there will be peace in his people, and not peace alone: peace will be in us, who are his people, in such a way that glory will dwell together with peace in our land. The exposition does not change.

We shall attain this peace not through our merits but through God’s mercy and truth, because he is truthful; and when he has promised this, he cannot fail to fulfill it. He is also merciful by nature. Truly, we shall attain this through God’s mercy and truth. For this reason mercy and truth [Col. 1090A] have met one another—that is, these two will agree among themselves to bring about our possession of peace and glory—after the likeness of people who meet one another in order to accomplish something harmoniously. It is as though he said: Now God’s mercy and truth will cooperate harmoniously so that we may obtain peace and glory.

Through this also we shall attain these things, because, through God’s mercy, righteousness—that is, remission of sins—and peace—that is, love of God and neighbor—have kissed one another, that is, will be brought into complete agreement, after the likeness of those who agree and kiss one another. This means that human beings will attain eternal peace and glory because God’s mercy and truth, and the righteousness and peace given to human beings through God’s mercy, will cooperate to this end. [Col. 1090B] Someone might ask: How will righteousness, that is, remission of sins, be given to them?

He demonstrates this as follows: Truly, there will be righteousness among human beings; for from the earth—that is, from human beings themselves, who are now earthly and not spiritual—truth will arise, that is, a true confession of sins. Through this true confession righteousness, that is, remission of sins, given from the heaven of heavens, will look upon them—that is, will come to them—after the likeness of someone who, looking compassionately upon a person gravely oppressed, comes to assist him.

Human beings do not possess this confession from themselves. For the Lord will give kindness, that is, the gracious inner illumination of his grace, from which that true confession will proceed. Through confessing and attaining the righteousness of remission, not only will the soul give the fruit of good thoughts, but our land also—that is, our earthly sensuality, belonging to those conformed to us who will exist at that time—will give God fruit, namely the fruit of good works. By saying “our,” he conforms himself to the future faithful of the Church, since according to faith he was already a member of the Church.

I say that righteousness and peace will be among human beings through truth. After they have been made righteous, righteousness will walk—that is, they themselves will advance from good to better—and it will walk not for human approval but before him, the Lord, that is, in order to please him. He uses a quality-word for the persons possessing that quality, using “righteousness” for “the righteous.”

And it will walk before him because righteousness will set its steps—that is, its works by which it will proceed toward life—upon the way, that is, upon Christ, who is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), since they will be conformed to Christ in their works; for by themselves they would not suffice to walk from good to better.

Alternatively: I say that it will walk, and not by itself; rather, the Lord will set his steps—that is, the steps of assisting grace—upon the way, that is, in the righteous themselves, who will be called God’s way because he will walk spiritually in them according to non-operative grace, not according to local movement, in accordance with what he says through the Prophet: “I will walk in them, and I will be their God” (Leviticus 6:12). Or they are called “ways” because they will be directed by the Lord toward life in the manner of a road.

## ON PSALM 85

[Col. 1091A]

The title of Psalm 85: “A prayer to be ascribed to David,” that is, to Christ. Although certain things are stated in this psalm as declarations, it is called a prayer because it principally concerns prayer. The Lord Jesus is introduced in this psalm as praying around the time of his Passion—for steadfastness, so that he might not yield; for the resurrection; and for the salvation of the nations and of the Jews who were to be converted—in order to give us an example of prayer both for ourselves and for our enemies.

His saying that he is poor according to his human nature, although according to another nature he was God and omnipotent, is intended for our instruction, so that we, who are simply human beings, sinners, and exceedingly frail, may consider ourselves utterly poor and needy and pray to be mercifully assisted by divine grace. [Col. 1091B]

“Bend your ear, Lord Father”: this is said after the likeness of a physician bending his ear toward a sick person who, because of excessive illness, cannot speak, so that by bending his ear he may perceive the extent of the person’s illness and have compassion on him. The ear signifies the power of divine mercy, because just as we perceive what is heard through the ear, so he perceives what we pray for and fulfills it through the power of his mercy.

It is as though he said: Bend your ear, that is, make the power of your mercy condescend to me, who am weak according to my humanity. This means: You who always regard me as weak, I ask you also to consider attentively the weakness of my humanity and hear me.

It is necessary that you hear me by condescending to me, because I, who am God and omnipotent according to my divinity, am needy according to my humanity—that is, unable to be delivered by the help of anyone except you—and poor, that is, unable to be assisted by my own power. And hear me in this respect: preserve my soul, so that it does not fall away from holiness through fear of death, since I am truly holy both in thought and in deed; and by raising me up, save me from this weakness of my humanity, your servant, my God.

I call myself your servant in a special sense, through a singular obedience, trusting in you and not in any other helper. It is as though he said: Since I am your servant, resisting you in nothing and obeying you in all things; since I hope in you alone and not in anyone else; and since you are God, whom I obey especially above all others, it is fitting that you preserve my soul and save me. [Col. 1091D]

Therefore continue to have mercy on me, by raising me up and preserving me, because all day long—that is, throughout my entire life, which was bright and radiant in goodness like the day—I cried out, that is, I devoted myself to attaining you with an intense cry of devotion.

And I also ask you to gladden my soul in the resurrection, since it is now sorrowful in the Passion. “Gladden my soul” is almost equivalent in meaning to “save your servant,” except that, when he says “gladden,” he makes clear, in order to manifest his frailty, that he had been sorrowful. I ask you: gladden me.

And this is fitting, because I have not depressed my soul by devoting myself to vices and evil works; rather, I have raised it up—that is, exalted it—in virtues and good works in order to win your favor.

And these reasons alone are not sufficient to make you hear me. Rather, hear me because you, Lord, are gracious—that is, an agreeable and pleasant food to holy people, who nevertheless are sinners to some extent and far beneath me; and because you are gentle toward sinners who have not yet repented, whom you do not immediately condemn justly but patiently await; and because you are of great—that is, infinite—mercy, forgiving sins to all who call upon you, that is, who affectionately pray for forgiveness.

Hear my prayer with your ears, that is, through the power of your mercy; and by hearing it, attend to the voice of my supplication, that is, make yourself attentive to my voice as it supplicates you. This means: Since you grant these benefits to those who are simple human beings and offend you in some respect—being gracious and gentle and of great mercy toward them—grant me, who am God and human and free from sin, with special intensity what I ask.

Hear me, therefore, because I cried out—that is, I devoted myself with an intense cry to winning your favor—in the day of my tribulation, that is, throughout the whole period of my life, which is nothing other than tribulation. This is almost the same as what he said above, “I cried out to you all day,” except that the word “tribulation” adds another implication. It is as though he had said: Although I have continually been in tribulation, I have never ceased crying out; therefore I am worthy to be heard.

He shows what benefit will follow from being heard, as follows: I say, “Hear my prayer”; and so you will do. Because you have heard me—that is, because you will hear me—by preserving and raising up all the nations you have made, nations of every kind, through my resurrection they will come to you by faith, although they are far away through unbelief. [Col. 1092C]

It is not without significance that he says, “you have made.” It is as though he said: It is fitting that they should come to you, since you created them. What could be more fitting than that the creature should be subject to the Creator? And after they have come, existing before you—that is, in your good pleasure—they will worship you, that is, venerate you with devotion and humble prayer. They will also glorify your name among others, that is, proclaim to their successors that your name is glorious.

The verse preceding this one, namely, “There is none like you among the gods,” and so forth, has been inserted parenthetically and should be read after this verse, “All the nations,” and so forth. I say that all the nations will come to you, abandoning their idols. And rightly so: no one among their gods—that is, among their idols, which will falsely be called gods—is like you in nature; and no one acts according to your works, that is, no one works wondrously after the manner of your wondrous works.

He assigns each statement to its proper counterpart when he adds: Truly, no one among the gods works according to your works, because you alone are great, that is, powerful and doing wondrous works. They, however, are neither great nor workers of wonders; and no one is like you in nature, because you alone are God, and none of them is God.

He prays either for the nations who are to be converted, as follows: I say that the nations will come to you; and on their behalf, Lord Father, lead me from virtue to virtue—that is, lead those nations who are to become mine, placed upon your way, that is, in faith and knowledge of you, through which they will come to you.

And I shall enter—that is, they shall enter—those of mine who are placed in life, into your truth, that is, into your true commandments; or, “they shall enter” means, they shall advance in your true commandments. In this leading and entering, let my heart—that is, the heart of those who are mine—rejoice. Let them not be saddened by fulfilling your commandments, but rejoice; yet not in such a way that they become proud because of this, but in such a way that they fear—that is, that those who are mine fear—your name, which is “Lord.” They shall fear what is signified in you by the name “Lord,” namely, that you are omnipotent and avenging, and that you will punish them if they become proud.

Thus the Lord says through the Prophet: “If I am your Father, where is my love? If I am God, where is my honor? If I am Lord, where is my fear?” (Malachi 1:6.)

He declares that what he prayed for will happen when he adds: [Col. 1093B] I pray that those who are mine will be led and will fear you, and so it will be: I will confess to you, Lord my God—that is, since you are the Lord and God of those who are mine, those who are mine will praise you with all my heart, that is, with the whole affection of their heart. They will not devote part of themselves to you and part to worldly things; rather, they will praise you with their entire affection. And I will glorify—that is, they will proclaim your name glorious to others—and this forever.

He repeats this in order to add: They will rightly glorify your name and confess to you with their whole heart, because your mercy is great toward me—that is, toward those who are mine—since through your mercy you will confer great benefits upon them, enlightening them with virtues and good works.

And earlier you rescued my soul from the lower underworld—that is, you will rescue the souls of those who are mine from the corruption of blindness. This blindness is properly called the lower underworld, that is, the lower degradation, in relation to the corruption of the body, namely, its liability to suffering and mortality. Since the corruption of the body, which is the baser part of the human being, may rightly be called “underworld,” that is, degradation and abasement, the corruption of the soul through blindness is appropriately called the lower underworld, that is, the lower degradation. For the more worthy and exalted a thing is, the lower and more grievous is its degradation.

Thus, here God frees his faithful from the lower underworld, that is, he illuminates by spiritual grace their soul, previously corrupted by blindness. In the future, however, he will rescue them from the underworld of the body when he makes them immortal and free from suffering.

Alternatively, this verse may more appropriately be read as referring to Christ: I say that they will confess to you and glorify your name. This will happen because your mercy toward me is great—that is, it will be great—so that you may give me steadfastness in the Passion, subject the whole world to my authority, and grant me the name that is above every name. And you have rescued—that is, you will rescue—my soul from the lower underworld, to which it will descend, so that from there it may draw out the faithful who are in darkness.

The lower underworld is appropriately called that local underworld in comparison with this world, which is higher and yet is called an underworld—that is, low and degraded—in comparison with the heavenly homeland, which ought to be called the mountain of joy.

After praying concerning the nations, he intends also to pray concerning the Jews who rise up against him. But in order to show that they need his prayer, he first demonstrates that they are guilty, as follows: I prayed to you, Lord Father, for the nations who are to be saved; I also wish to pray to you for the wicked Jews.

It is indeed useful for them that I pray for them, O God. For the wicked—that is, the lesser members of the Jewish people—rose up against me not because of any merit of mine but because of their own iniquity, crying out, “Crucify him!” (John 19:6), and other things of this kind. And the assembly of the powerful—that is, the congregation of the chief priests and the other rulers—sought to take my life away. They did not set before their minds that you would be the future avenger; that is, they did not consider within their minds that you ought to avenge in this way the fact that they had risen against me in iniquity, though they certainly ought to have considered it.

Yet you, Lord, should not justly punish them for this, but so that a portion of them may be saved. You, Lord God, are merciful by nature; compassionate in the manifestation of mercy; patient, awaiting sinners and not immediately punishing them; of great mercy, forgiving the sins of those who are converted; and truthful, fulfilling everything you promise.

Since you are truthful and have promised that I will be saved and glorified, look upon me, who am obedient to you even unto death; and in this way give me dominion over the whole world, me, your child—that is, your servant—who resist you in nothing. And before you give me dominion, after three days save from death the son of your handmaid Mary.

It is as though he said: My obedience is not the only thing that merits your saving me; the obedience of my mother also merits it. When, through Gabriel, you commanded her to conceive me, she did not become unbelieving or rebellious but obedient and faithful: “Behold,” she said, “I am ready, for I am the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1:38), and so forth.

Do not save me from death in such a way that this remains hidden, for my resurrection would then be useless to the world. But because you are merciful and compassionate and patient and of great mercy, perform with me a sign of resurrection for the good.

He properly says “with me,” thereby indicating that he is God. It is as though he said: I, insofar as I am God, will perform the sign of resurrection—that is, a wondrous and manifest resurrection. “Sign” is very often used for “miracle.”

I say that I will perform the sign of resurrection, and this sign will be “for good,” that is, for the benefit of the Jews and of the nations who are to be converted.

Or: “I will perform” means, I will fulfill the sign of Jonah—namely, just as Jonah came forth on the third day from the belly of the whale, so I will cause my flesh, raised up on the third day, to come forth from the tomb (Matthew 12:40). “For I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18).

I say that I will perform the sign for good; and you, Father, perform it with me—that is, cooperate with the Holy Spirit in this sign for good—so that the Jews who hate me may see by faith, insofar as they belong to those who are to be saved, that you, Lord, have helped me. You have helped me in this way: you have comforted me in the resurrection, although I am now voluntarily sorrowful in the Passion. By seeing this, may those who hate me be confounded with a good confusion and thus be converted.

## ON PSALM 86

The title of Psalm 86: “For the sons of Korah. A psalm of a song.” This is explained as follows: This psalm of a song—that is, of joy—is not so called because the Prophet treats in it of the joy of eternal reward, but because here the Prophet greatly rejoices while praising Zion, that is, the primitive Church composed of Jews. It is proposed to the sons of Korah, that is, to the adopted sons of the Crucified, for whose benefit the Prophet is concerned in this psalm.

In this psalm the Prophet praises the primitive Church concerning the foundation and glory of its gates. And, so that his praise might have greater authority, he introduces the Holy Spirit praising it. To this primitive Church, as an addition to its glory, he says that the Church from the nations will be joined, and that Christ, God and human, and Lord of that Church—which is the city of God—will be born within it.

He offers this praise for the benefit of the sons of Korah, so that those who, already made sons of Korah through baptism, are citizens of that city may, stimulated by this praise, never withdraw from participation in it; and so that those who are not yet its citizens may be drawn to it by such praise.

Christ is properly called Korah, that is, “bald,” because he was mocked by the Jews, who were foolish like children, after the likeness of criminals who, because of their crimes, are mocked when they have been made bald—that is, shorn of their hair. This was prefigured in Elisha the bald man. When, departing from Jericho, he ascended toward Bethel, children saw him ascending and mocked him, saying: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” (2 Kings 2:23). Immediately afterward, by divine vengeance, they were devoured by two bears coming out of the forest (ibid., 24).

So also the Jews, because they mocked Christ as he was preparing to ascend from Jericho—that is, from this life—and from Bethel—that is, heaven—through the departure of death, while he was ascending the cross, saying, “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matthew 27:40), were destroyed forty-two years later by two emperors, Titus and Vespasian, coming out from Rome.

This world’s life is properly called Jericho because, like the moon, it sometimes seems to increase through prosperity and sometimes to wane through adversity. Indeed, Jericho is interpreted as “moon.” Heaven is also suitably signified by Mount Bethel, because it is a lofty house, namely, its highest dwelling—not a local dwelling but a spiritual one. Bethel, in fact, is interpreted as “house of God.”

[Col. 1095D] “Its foundations are in the holy mountains.”

Although he appears to be praising the primitive Church, which is the city of God, as though he had already said something about it—he places at the beginning the relative word “its”—he indicates to us that he had already considered it much and frequently in his mind. By this he greatly commends it, since he, a man of very great authority, indicates that he had frequently thought about that Church.

It is as though he said: Zion, that is, the primitive Church, which will contemplate eternal things by paying no attention to present things, will be very worthy of praise. For its foundations will be in the holy mountains, namely, the apostles and prophets, who are to be called mountains because of their perfection in the virtues and works of the Most High.

This means that Zion will be founded upon the teaching of the prophets and apostles, so that, made firm, it will not collapse under the assault of visible or invisible enemies. These prophets and apostles are called exalted mountains to distinguish them from heretics and false preachers. Although the latter may be mountains—that is, advanced in worldly wisdom—they are not holy but dark. Hence Scripture instructs us through the Lord to beware of stumbling on dark mountains.

The prophets and apostles are called the foundations of the Church because through their teachings it has been founded in faith upon the one and immovable foundation, which is Christ, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:20).

“But the Lord loves…” This may be connected as follows: I say that Zion is worthy of praise because it is founded upon the holy mountains. It is also worthy of praise for the beauty and perfection of its gates, namely, the apostles, who are called not only its foundations but also the gates of the Church, because through their teachings unbelievers enter into fellowship with that same Church.

It is thereby shown that its gates are beautiful in virtues and works, because the Lord, who would not love them unless they were beautiful, loves the gates of Zion—that is, he will love them above all the tents of Jacob. He will love the apostles who serve him more than all those in the former Jewish people, who were descended from Jacob.

They are called tents because they served God in tents, that is, in the service of carnal observances, which were transitory like tents after the things they signified had come. It is as though he said: The Lord will love the apostles more for this reason: they served him in moral commandments. The faithful in the former people served God in carnal observances, which are shadows of the moral commandments.

A few who were already members of the Church by faith, although they served God in moral commandments, did not do so perfectly like the apostles; therefore they were deservedly loved less.

Alternatively, if we wish to understand this praise as concerning the whole Church, one part of which already rejoices in heaven with the angels while another part, living in this life, still serves God under the burden of troubles, we may understand the gates of Zion as the virtues that are its gates, through which one enters into life. The Lord loves these more than the tents of Jacob, that is, the transitory service of the carnal observances of the former people.

The text continues:

[Col. 1096D] “Glorious…”

This may be connected as follows: I praise you, Zion, for your foundations and gates; and I do not invent this from myself. Rather, these glorious things—namely, that you will be such in your foundations and gates—have been spoken to me concerning you by the Holy Spirit, O city of God, fortified in virtues and good works.

Thus he introduces the words of the Holy Spirit speaking inwardly to him when he adds, “I will remember,” and so forth. This may be adapted as follows: I say that these glorious things have been spoken to me concerning you by the Spirit, who continues to foretell such things to me for your praise.

I, who seemed to have forgotten Rahab and Babylon by not enlightening them with faith, will remember that Rahab and Babylon, so that I may bring them to the faith; and I will do this through those who know me, that is, through the preachers of the primitive Church who know me—that is, who know me by faith.

[Col. 1097A] Rahab and Babylon here appear to signify the same thing, namely, the multitude of the nations. For Rahab is interpreted as “pride” or “breadth,” while Babylon is interpreted as “confusion.” Thus the people of the nations are properly called Rahab and Babylon, because they have advanced broadly through pleasure and vices and, by denying God the worship owed to him, have become proud against him. For this reason they have made themselves worthy of confusion.

The same people are also called Rahab through a historical figure. For just as Rahab the prostitute in Jericho is said once to have received the scouts of the children of Israel and, by this merit, to have saved the members of her household from destruction when Jericho was destroyed, under the sign of the red cord (Joshua 2), so also that portion of the nations which received the apostles and believed them—for they were God’s scouts among the nations—will be saved, through the sign of the purple of Christ’s Passion, on the day of judgment together with all their imitators, when Jericho—that is, the declining city of the wicked—will be destroyed.

Jericho is so called because here it grows through prosperity, whereas in the future it will suffer decline in torments, after the likeness of the waxing and waning moon.

“Behold the foreigners,” and so it is adapted: I say that I shall remember Rahab and Babylon, and so it will be. For behold, it is already certain—as though it were present—that the foreigners, that is, the nations alien to the faith and of a different descent from the Jews, namely those foreigners whom I call both Tyre and the Ethiopian people, are there. Part of them is Tyre, that is, distress, which afflicts my faithful in many ways; and part is the Ethiopian people. Even if they are not Tyre—that is, black in sins after the manner of the Ethiopian people, which is black in body—all these, namely Tyre and the Ethiopian people who are part of the foreigners, were there, that is, will be joined to the fellowship of that primitive Zion through those who know me.

[Col. 1097C]

“If indeed, ‘Will he say?’” and so on. This is joined together and read in reversed order. I say, O hearers, that the Holy Spirit says this to me: “I shall remember, and behold, the foreigners.” And, to increase her praise, he testifies this about her to me: namely, that “someone was born,” that is, will be born in her—“a man,” that is, according to the human nature—and that he himself, who will be born in her, founded her, that is, will create her; and the Most High will establish her in faith and virtues, that is, according to the nature by which he will be almighty as God. This means: Christ will be born according to his humanity among the Jewish people, although according to his divinity he created that people and, according to his human part, will establish it in faith.

And this obscure statement that I make about you, O Zion: “Will a man say?” That is, will anyone who is simply a man—animal and not spiritual—be able to explain it? Truly he will not say it, that is, he will not be able to explain how this will happen: that a man will be born in you and that he himself will establish you. “For the natural man does not perceive the things that are of God” (1 Cor. 2:14). By this he intimates that this happened through an ineffable and most sacred mystery, which he says is insoluble to man.

Or it may be understood in this way: “I say that a man will be born in you, and he himself will establish you. And this, O Zion, will a man say?” That is, will anyone who is merely a man—animal and not also spiritual—dare to say it? Certainly not. For the weak did not dare to confess that Christ was God and man. Hence the Manichaeans falsely claimed that he was not truly human, but had assumed a phantom body. “For it was a stumbling-block to the Jews, but foolishness to the Gentiles” (1 Cor. 1:23), that anyone should be called both God and man.

He foretells this, moreover, to the praise of the preachers: namely, he indicates that they will steadfastly preach what the weak will not dare to confess.

“If the Lord will narrate it.” This is joined as follows. Because he had said, “Will a man say?”—so that no one might understand this to be so difficult that no one at all could or would say it—he adds: Although man will not say this, it will nevertheless not be entirely left unspoken. For the Lord God has narrated this, that is, will narrate it, in the Scriptures of the peoples, that is, in the Scriptures set before Christian peoples for understanding. It is as though he said: Those Scriptures will not be unintelligible and excessively obscure, like the writings of the philosophers, which are extremely obscure and understood by few, while they scarcely say anything true. Rather, since they proclaim what is true and manifest, they will be understood by many peoples. In this he greatly commends those Scriptures.

He also displays their authors, to heighten their praise, when he adds: “I say that he will narrate it in the Scriptures of the peoples,” that is, in the Scriptures of the rulers of those peoples who were, that is, who will be, in that Zion. This means: He will not narrate it in just any Scriptures of the peoples, but in the Scriptures of the apostles, who will be leaders in the teaching of those peoples who will be in that Zion.

It follows: “As of those who rejoice.” This continues as follows. Out of excessive joy he turns in address to her, thus: I say, O Zion, that the Holy Spirit says this to me about you: a man will be born in you, and he himself will establish you. Moreover, he says this about you: the dwelling-place of all who dwell in you will be like the dwelling-place of those who rejoice. This means: All who dwell in you by faith will be like those who rejoice in the purity of their conscience. In accordance with this the Apostle says: “For our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12).

He rightly says not “of those who rejoice,” but “like that of those who rejoice,” because although the faithful here truly rejoice greatly and abundantly in the purity of their conscience, yet, by comparison with the eternal joy to come, this present joy is not called joy, but likeness to joy—that is, a shadow of the future joy. By this he draws those who are outside the Church into fellowship with the Church, when he says that its inhabitants are rejoicing.

## ON PSALM 87

**The title of the eighty-seventh Psalm:** “A song of the psalm, for the sons of Korah, toward the end, for Melech [al., Maeleth], to respond; an understanding of Heman the Israelite [al., Ezrahite].”

It does not say “a song” because this concerns the joy of eternal reward, but because here Christ, speaking about his passion and praying that God make him steadfast and raise him up, instructs all who are his adoptive sons that, just as he himself willingly and joyfully endured the cross for us—although according to the weakness of the flesh he appeared sorrowful—so also his sons, if necessary, ought joyfully to endure adversities for him and to pray amid those adversities.

This is also suggested in the title when it says: “A song of the psalm, for the sons of Korah, toward the end, for Melech, to respond.” It is adapted as follows. The song of this psalm—that is, the joyful undertaking of this discourse, namely the undertaking of Christ’s passion, in which he suffered for the world’s salvation and sang beforehand—is therefore called a song. What is contained in this psalm is proposed to the sons of Korah, that is, to the sons of Christ, who were made his adoptive sons through his passion. It is proposed to them “to respond,” that is, so that they may answer him not with words but with deeds: just as he sang beforehand for them by suffering, so they too, if it should be necessary, may sing after him and respond by not fleeing death for his sake.

They are not to respond unwillingly or as though compelled, but “for Melech,” that is, according to the harmony of charity and love: just as he endured with charitable love, so they too should endure with charity and agree with him in this. For “if they hand over their body to be burned but do not have charity, it profits them nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3). And they must not make this response for a time only, but until the end of life. “For whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

*Melech* is interpreted as “choir.” Since harmony of singing normally exists in a choir, *Melech* is suitably understood as harmony.

And this is “the understanding of Heman the Israelite”: that is, Christ understood that it should be sung—that it should be joyful in the soul amid tribulation, even though there is outward sorrow according to the flesh. For *Heman* is interpreted as “brother,” while *Israelite* is interpreted as “seeing God.” Hence Christ is appropriately called Heman the Israelite: he is our brother both according to the humanity that he shared with us and according to his divinity, participation in which he granted us. Thus he himself says: “Whoever does the will of my Father is my brother” (Mark 3:5). And elsewhere: “Go, tell my brothers” (Matt. 28:10).

He is rightly called an Israelite. For who can be compared with him in the vision of God, whose humanity was joined to the Word of God in the ineffable union of the same person? Through this, then, he strongly draws the sons of Korah to sing amid tribulation, since he declares that Christ understood this. For he would not have understood it if he had not willingly hastened to obedience in his passion.

“Lord, Father, God, author of my salvation, by day”—that is, in prosperity—“and by night”—that is, in adversity—“I cried out,” that is, with an intense cry I performed the work of good devotion. “And this is before you,” that is, you see this, whoever else may be ignorant of it. Therefore, let my prayer, made in your sight—that is, made concerning something that is in your sight, namely, concerning the perfection of steadfastness and the resurrection, which are pleasing to you and for which I pray—enter, that is, be admitted so that it may be fulfilled, after the likeness of honorable ambassadors who are permitted to enter the Lord’s chamber.

When he says, “By day I cried out, and by night before you,” this is parenthetical, and it is as though he said: Since you are Lord of all and God, and since it is thereby evident that you are almighty; since you have already become the author of my salvation, and since I pray for such things as are before your sight, I ask that my prayer enter, that is, be admitted.

Because he had said “salvation,” he discloses that salvation itself when he inserts: You were the author of this salvation, namely, you made me so perfect that I was not negligent. Rather, “I cried out,” that is, with an intense cry of devotion I performed this work, both by day and by night—not becoming proud by day, nor being broken by fear at night. It is equally the highest salvation that no one desist from such a cry either by day or by night.

I say, “Let my prayer enter”; and, so that it may not be shut out, “incline your ear,” that is, make the power of your mercy stoop toward my humble prayer. This is said after the likeness of a physician who inclines his ear toward a sick person; or, as has already often been shown, it may be understood otherwise.

It is necessary that you incline your ear toward my prayer because “my soul is filled with evils,” that is, will be filled with tribulations. *Evils* are very often used for tribulations; for example, in Job: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not also receive evils?” (Job 2:10).

And my soul will be filled with evils to such an extent that “my life”—that is, the soul itself, which is the cause of my life—“has drawn near,” that is, will draw near, “to hell,” namely, it will be separated from the body and descend into hell under the excessive weight of tribulations, and will bring out from there a portion of the saved.

I say that my soul will be filled with tribulations. And, to increase my persecutions, “I have been reckoned,” that is, will be reckoned by my persecutors, the Jews, “with those who descend into the pit,” that is, with robbers descending into the depth of vices; I have been judged worthy to be shamefully handed over to death. Hence the prophet testifies: “He was reckoned among the wicked” (Isa. 53:12; Luke 22:37).

And I have become, that is, will become, in their estimation, vile and despised, “like a man without help”; they will think that I cannot be helped in any way. Yet I shall be free from the jurisdiction of death, while existing among the dead. That is, although I shall be dead in the body and numbered among the dead, I shall not be under death’s power, so that it can retain me; rather, I shall be free, so that whenever I wish I shall have the ability to rise again.

By calling himself free, because he will suffer willingly, he indicates the disposition with which he instructs us to suffer.

And I shall still be considered by the same persecutors to be a sinner, like many who were first wounded by an evil suggestion through consent and now sleep in tombs—that is, are stupefied and dead in their bodies through the operation of excessive pleasure.

That is, they will regard me as like sinners who, first wounded by their suggestion through consent, have now come to the habitual practice of pleasure, to such an extent that their souls are sleeping in tombs—that is, stupefied and dead amid the pleasures of their bodies, which are rightly called tombs by analogy. For just as bodies lying in tombs decay and stink, so souls that linger in vices by consenting to bodily pleasures emit outwardly the stench of an evil reputation.

“You no longer remember those who sleep,” that is, those who sleep so deeply that you no longer remember them, so as to raise them up.

I say that they will consider me like those who sleep; yet they themselves “have been rejected from your hand,” that is, from your protection, because of their evil merits, so that you do not remember them. It is as though he said: If those who regard me as such were just, this would not seem so remarkable. But since they are such sinners that, by the demands of their evil merits, they have already been rejected from your hand, it seems astonishing and utterly unworthy that they should regard me, who am just, as such.

Through this he instructs the sons of Korah to endure willingly the insults of sinners, even though they are just, since he himself, uniquely just and free from sins, endured so many insults.

“And they placed me,” that is, in their estimation they will place me, “in the lower pit,” that is, in the depth of sins. They reckoned that I had already reached the lowest depth of sins.

And “in their estimation they placed me among the dark,” that is, among the number of the dark. They reckoned that I was in the darkness of ignorance of God—not in just any ignorance, but in “the shadow of the cause of death,” that is, in that darkness of ignorance which is the cause of eternal death. Of this it is written: “The one who is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Cor. 14:38), namely, the one who is entirely without knowledge of God’s commandments.

There are, however, certain forms of ignorance that do not lead to death, such as when we are ignorant of the relation between the divine Trinity and unity, and of other such ineffable mysteries of God.

They will also reckon that “your anger has been made firm over me,” that is, that your excessive anger—your firm and immovable wrath—has come upon me, that is, has occurred in me in order to oppress me, after the manner of heavy things falling from above. This means: They will reckon that you are very angry and hostile toward me here, and that in the future, according to their estimation, “you have brought upon me,” that is, will bring upon me for my oppression and destruction, “all your waves,” that is, all your punishments through torments. These are suitably called waves. For just as waves rushing upon a shipwrecked person submerge him so that he cannot rise again, so God’s punishments will plunge the condemned into torments, so that they will no longer be able to escape.

Nor will this alone happen to me—that I should be regarded as such by my persecutors. To increase my miseries, “you have put far from me,” that is, will permit my acquaintances to be far from me. My persecution will be so great that my disciples, who are my acquaintances, will flee and become distant from me.

And not only will they become distant, but “they have made me an abomination,” that is, a cause of abomination to themselves. For some of them, despairing of my resurrection, will regard it as disgraceful that they had clung to me.

“And I have been handed over,” that is, will be handed over to the Jews by one of my disciples, Judas Iscariot. And when I am handed over, “I will not go out,” that is, will not go out from the obscurity of power, after the likeness of one who, existing in the darkness of some place, does not wish to leave lest he be seen.

It is as though he said: I could indeed exercise the vengeance of my power upon them when I have been handed over, but I will not reveal to them the greatness of my power, which is obscure and unknown to them. Rather, I shall patiently endure everything, so as to give my own an example of suffering patiently and without rebellion, even where they will have occasion to take vengeance.

And because I will not go out, “my eyes have languished,” that is, the apostles will languish, failing in hope of my resurrection through lack of inward light: because they will not yet be fully enlightened inwardly by faith, they will fail in hope of the resurrection. Hence certain of them are said to have spoken in despair: “We had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21).

In the Church the apostles are appropriately called “eyes,” because they look ahead for the lesser members with pastoral care, after the likeness of eyes that look ahead for the whole body.

I say that my soul will be filled with evils, that I shall be reckoned with those who descend into the pit, that I shall be handed over, and that my eyes will languish. Yet I was not thereby negligent. Rather, “I cried out to you, Lord Father”—that is, with an intense cry of devotion I acted toward you—so that you might make me steadfast and raise me up. And “all day,” that is, continually, “I spread out my hands,” that is, I opened wide the hands of my heart, namely, good affections, toward you, in order to win your favor; that is, so that I might deserve your grace and thereby become steadfast and rise again.

I say that I cried out, saying: O Lord, do not let me remain in the tomb. I do not say this in such a way that I should not be placed in it, but so that I may not remain in perdition, that is, so that I may not decay.

“Will you indeed work wonders for the dead?”—dead in soul, namely, will you work these wonders among people who are dead through original sin, so that you may bring them back to life through faith, as you promised, while I remain in the tomb and in perdition? Certainly not.

Or will the apostles, who will be your physicians, dispensing the medicine of teaching to those who are sick and dead in soul, raise those dead—the whole human race—to the life of faith through their teaching? And once raised, will they confess you—that is, praise you with mouth, heart, and deed—while I remain in the tomb?

“Will anyone also narrate your mercy,” that is, the restoration of the human race accomplished through your mercy, “in the tomb,” that is, in consideration of my tomb, if he considers me to remain in the tomb and not rise again?

“And will anyone narrate your truth,” that is, that you are truthful in fulfilling my resurrection, which you promised through the prophets, “in perdition,” that is, in consideration of my perdition, if you permit me to reach perdition so that I do not rise again?

“And will your wonders be known in darkness,” that is, among the dark—namely, will the nations who are in the darkness of ignorance learn through the apostles’ proclamation of your wonders, which you will accomplish through me, such as the defeat of the devil, the salvation of the world, and the other many wonders, while I remain in the tomb and in perdition?

“And will your righteousness be known in the land of oblivion,” that is, among the nations who are cursed earth through Adam and whom you appear to have handed over to oblivion? Will those nations recognize that all righteousness comes from you and not from themselves, if I remain in the tomb and in perdition? Certainly not.

This statement, however, which he presents in the form of questions, is a prayer made with greater force of feeling than it would have had if expressed without questions. It is as though he said: Raise me up. For if I remain in the tomb and in perdition, these incongruities will follow: you will not work wonders among the dead; nor will the physicians raise those dead through their preaching; nor will the dead, once raised, confess you; nor will any of the preachers narrate your mercy and truth; nor will the nations who are in darkness, the land of oblivion, recognize your wonders and that all righteousness comes from you.

By showing these incongruities, therefore, he more strongly urges God’s mercy to grant what he asks.

He repeats what he said, “I cried out,” in order to add: I say that these incongruities will occur unless I am raised. Therefore, in order to deserve resurrection, “I cried out to you, Lord Father,” I who am worthy to be heard.

And I shall not cease from crying out. Rather, my prayer, made with a cry, “in the morning”—not in darkness, but in the brightness of my good conscience and devotion—“will precede you,” that is, will precede your reward; namely, it will merit the reward, after the likeness of a vigorous soldier who precedes his gratuity by his service, so that afterward he may worthily receive the gratuity itself.

This means: In order to be worthy of resurrection, I shall first merit it through unremitting prayer and crying out. For one must labor first in the vineyard, and afterward receive the denarius.

He raises a question, which he then proceeds to resolve: namely, why God did not wish to hear him when he prayed to be able to avoid the tribulation of his passion. He adds: “Why?” and so on.

This is joined as follows: I say that I cried out in prayer concerning the resurrection. I also prayed that, if it were possible, the cup of the passion might pass from me. “And why, Lord, do you reject this prayer of mine,” permitting me to suffer, “and in this way turn away,” that is, appear to turn away, “your face from me,” that is, your goodwill—after the likeness of angry people who turn their face away from those with whom they are angry?

He uses “face” for goodwill, because goodwill is usually signified by serenity of face.

Although you reject my prayer, I, who am permitted to be afflicted, am nevertheless “poor,” that is, humble toward you, as a poor man is humble toward a rich man, and I am engaged in the labors of preaching “from my youth,” that is, from the beginning of my youth—namely, from the thirtieth year of my age, from which time it is lawful to undertake preaching.

And I am “exalted,” that is, greatly advanced in humility and in the labor of preaching; this too is a great exaltation. “I have been humbled,” that is, cast down in tribulations, and “I have been troubled” by fear of those tribulations.

It is as though he said: If I were proud and idle, it would not be surprising that my prayer were rejected. But since I am humble like a poor man, laboring in obedience to preaching, and greatly exalted in these things, it is astonishing why you permit me to be humbled and troubled so severely in tribulations.

The question has been posed, and he approaches its solution when he says: “Your wrath has passed over me,” and so on.

This continues as follows: I say that one might ask why you reject my prayer and why you permit me to be humbled and troubled. Behold why this happens: I am humbled because your “wraths”—that is, your punishments, which you exercise upon the human race because of Adam’s sin—have been cast upon me and “passed over,” that is, will pass over, from the human race.

This means: The sufferings cast upon me will be the cause by which mortality, vulnerability, and the other punishments that you, God, exercise upon the human race will be destroyed. Therefore “your terrors”—that is, the dreadful sufferings appointed by you—“have troubled me,” that is, will trouble me according to the weakness of the flesh.

Or the terrors of the many sufferings that I know I shall endure by your appointment will trouble me—not through compulsion, but with voluntary disturbance. Hence it is written: “Jesus began to be sorrowful and troubled” (Mark 14:33).

And truly the terrors will trouble me. For “they surrounded me like water,” that is, my sufferings will surround me all day long, “like water,” that is, after the manner of water, so as to oppress me—after the likeness of water that surrounds someone in order to submerge and overwhelm him.

“They surrounded me,” I say, “and this all at once,” that is, in such a way that none was excepted. It is as though he said: They will not surround me partly at one time and partly at another, but all of them will surround me simultaneously, to intensify my calamities. Therefore I shall be surrounded.

Moreover, to increase my hardships, “you have put far from me friend and neighbor.” The disturbance of my sufferings will be so great that you will cause my friends, namely the apostles who are my friends—that is, very familiar with me—to flee and become distant from me. “For you will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Mark 14:27).

And my neighbors, that is, my fellow tribesmen, will be put far from me; and my acquaintances, that is, my more hidden disciples, such as Nicodemus, Gamaliel, and the others, you will permit to become distant from me. Their departure will result from my misery: when they consider my manifold misery, they will leave me and flee.

By saying that friends, neighbors, and acquaintances would be put far from him, he indicates that his misery is manifold; and through this he instructs us all the more to suffer for him.

## ON PSALM 88

[Cols. 1099–1099D]

**The title of the eighty-eighth Psalm:** “An understanding of Ethan the Israelite.”

This is explained as follows: Here there is “the understanding of Ethan the Israelite,” not in the sense that Ethan the Israelite possesses this understanding, but because the Prophet, treating this subject in the psalm, has this figurative understanding concerning Ethan the Israelite—that is, concerning Christ, who is Ethan, meaning “strong,” because he conquers the strong, armed devil; and he is an Israelite, as was shown in the preceding psalm.

Since in the preceding psalm the Prophet had introduced Christ humbly treating of his passion, in this psalm he intends to show him great, powerful, and incomparable, by recounting the benefits of God’s mercy that will be conferred through him upon the human race. He also confirms this by the authority of the Father, whom he introduces as speaking and promising the benefits that he will effect in Christ and through Christ in the Church.

Here too the Prophet shows that the sufferings which will exist in Christ and in the Church are not to be understood as destined for destruction, but for the purification of those same faithful. He also prays both for the head himself and for the members, in order to show his good affection toward him and, by his example, produce good affection in us.

“I shall sing the mercies of the Lord,” that is, the benefits of the mercy of the Lord Father, which he will confer upon the human race and which will last forever; “I shall sing,” that is, I shall treat them with joy.

Because it could be understood that he sang only in his mind, he specifies this by addressing him directly when he adds: I shall proclaim in writing, and “in this present generation and unto the final generation,” that is, always, as long as the world shall endure, “your truth,” that is, the benefits of mercy that you will fulfill so that you may appear true in your promise.

I call this truth “prepared in my mouth,” that is, something that I do not merely consider in my mind or announce in writing, but bring forth from an excess of affection with my mouth. By thus indicating his affection, the Prophet makes his hearers attentive.

Or it may be understood thus: “I shall proclaim in my mouth,” that is, in the office of my mouth, “your truth, which will endure from generation to generation,” that is, forever. He uses “mercies” and “truth” for the same thing.

Someone might ask: Where are the mercies that you will proclaim? They appear nowhere. He answers this by confirming it on the authority of the Father himself, as follows.
