I say that I shall sing the mercies, which I do not have from myself but from you, Lord Father, because you said to me by your inward inspiration that “mercy,” that is, the benefit of mercy that will last forever, “will be built in the heavens,” that is, will be brought about in the apostles, whom you will enlighten in faith and knowledge of you, elevate in virtues and good works, and finally bless.

And in those heavens—that is, through them—your truth will be prepared in others, and thus the benefit of mercy, which your truth will fulfill.

He introduces the Father’s words as follows: I say that you spoke, and behold, your words are ordered from eternity: “My testament,” that is, the firmest new law that I shall give to my elect, namely to my faithful who will exist in the fullness of time, whom I shall choose from the mass of the lost; “and I swore,” that is, I firmly promised, as though with an oath, “to David my servant,” that is, to Christ signified by David, who will be my servant according to his humanity and obedient in all things.

This is what I promised you, O David: “I shall prepare your seed through the preachers in faith,” that is, your adoptive sons, who will be your followers as far as they are able. I say that I shall prepare the seed—a seed, I say, that will remain forever. “Whoever believes in you will not die forever” (John 11:26).

“And I shall build your seat in virtue and good works from generation to generation,” that is, one that will remain forever. These same people—the faithful whom I said were your seed—I shall build so that they may be worthy for you to sit among them and always rule them. For the soul of the just is the seat of God.

After briefly introducing the Father’s words, the Prophet, speaking in his own person, addresses the Son out of an excess of affection:

O Lord Son, since through you mercy will be built in the heavens, “the heavens will confess your wonders,” that is, they will proclaim with praise your wondrous benefits bestowed upon the human race. And he explains this in part: Truly they will confess. For “in the Church of the saints,” that is, in the congregation of the faithful, “they will confess your truth,” that is, the benefits that your truth will fulfill.

Or it may be understood thus: They will confess your truth as something to be fulfilled in the Church of the saints. And rightly they will confess, since it is more worthy and exalted than they are.

“For who among the clouds”—that is, among those very heavens, which will be called clouds because they rain doctrine upon others—“will be equal to the Lord Christ?” No one.

“And who among the sons of God”—that is, who among those very clouds, which will be sons of God—“will be like the Lord Son in sonship?” No one. For he is Son by nature, while they are sons through the grace of adoption.

This means: They ought truly to confess him, since they are unlike and unequal to him in dignity. Inequality is spoken of with respect to something that one person has less of and another more of, as when someone is taller than another tall person. Unlikeness, however, concerns something that one person has and another lacks, as when one person is white and another is not.

He shows them to be unlike when he says: Truly no one is like him. For “he will be God,” and such a God as is glorified in the council of the saints—that is, will be glorified—whereas they will not be such gods as are glorified in the council of the saints.

He rightly says not simply “among the saints,” but “in the council of the saints,” as though he said: The saints will glorify him in devotion, deed, and speech, and this not without deliberation but with reasonable counsel; this is certainly more worthy than if it were done without counsel.

He also shows them to be unequal when he adds: Truly no one will be equal to the Lord Son. For he will be great in the power of miracles and terrible in punishment, above all the preachers who are—that is, who will be—“around him,” that is, in his service. This is said after the likeness of servants who surround their lord in order to serve him.

It is as though he said: Although they are great in the power of miracles and terrible in the power of punishing the wicked, through the merits of their prayers, he is greater and more terrible than they.

He addresses him again with repetition in order to add: I say, O God the Son, who among the clouds will be like the Lord? No one. And rightly I say this: For, O Lord God of hosts, who among those clouds will be like you? No one.

Since you are Lord of the heavenly powers and God—that is, their creator—while they are not, they are unlike you. They are also unlike you in this: you are powerful, that is, you will possess a kind of power that they entirely lack. They are likewise unlike you because your truth will be around you, whereas it will not be around them. That is, they who will be called “your truth” by emphasis, because they will be made holy through truth, will be in your service.

But because he had said, “You are powerful, O God,” he displays this power by adding the following.

I say that you will be powerful—and here is the power: you rule, that is, you will rule, over the power of the sea, whereas they do not. That is, you will have under your dominion the power of those unbelievers who embitter you by their evil life: the very power they will have for persecuting your people will be under your dominion, so that they will not be permitted to rage and persecute except insofar as you allow them. And you will not merely have that power under your dominion so that you can restrain it: “You still the movement of its waves”—that is, you will still the movement of its waves, whereas they do not. That is, at some time you will cause the movement of the waves of that sea to cease: the anger of unbelievers, which will stir up waves against the saints, namely persecutions that overwhelm them like waves.

This is to say: You will calm the anger of certain unbelievers, so that, once converted, they will cease persecuting your faithful. It should be noted that the repeated use of “you” is meant to mark the distinction, as though he were saying: “You will do this, but they will not”; and by this they are shown to be unlike you.

I say that you rule over the power of the sea, and so forth, and you are also so powerful that you humbled—that is, you will humble—the proud one, antonomastically, “as one already wounded”; that is, you will first wound him by your death, taking away the right he has over the human race, and afterward completely humble him by depriving him of his kingdom, when through preachers you take the nations away from him. This is compared to an enemy who is first wounded and afterward cast down; or “wounded” is aptly used as meaning “like one wounded.” For it was not truly and properly a wounding, but something like a wounding.

And you scattered—that is, you will scatter—your enemies, the Jews, throughout the whole world, by the arm of your power, that is, by your powerful arm, so to speak: by the strong force of your power. Or “you will scatter” means “you will separate all your enemies,” namely all those in the human race who make themselves your enemies by their evil life, so that you take some to life and leave others to death. And you will do this by your arm, that is, by the power of your strength. He uses “arm” for “power,” because the arm is the more powerful member of the body in respect of strength.

And you are so powerful that the heavens are yours and the earth is yours, whereas they are not; and in this they are unlike you—namely, the preachers who are the heavens, because they pour down doctrine. They will be yours, that is, through you they will be heavens; and the earth is yours, that is, the Church watered by preachers. Though previously a sea, it will become fruitful earth in good works, and by your grace it will have what makes it earth.

He explains how he says that the earth is his when he adds: Truly the earth will be yours, for you founded—that is, you will firmly establish—the circle of that earth, namely its perfection in virtues and good works. And you founded—that is, in the first creation you created—the fullness of that earth: you will cause many nations to arise, from which you will constitute the Church.

He appropriately uses “circle” for “perfection,” because in circles—which we call orbs—there is a more perfect equality than in other figures. All the parts of a circle are equally distant from the point at its center, something that cannot at all be found in other figures. By analogy with this, philosophers are said to have defined virtue in this way: “Virtue is the equality of a life everywhere conformed to reason” (*Virtus est aequalitas vitae, rationi undique convenientis*). Reason should be like a center, in accordance with whose arrangement all the parts of life are led equally and proportionately, just as all the parts of a circle are directed equally according to the measure of its central point.

Or it may be understood this way: “And this truth of yours”—namely, that you are powerful—is in your circuit, that is, in those who are in your service. This is to say: Your obedient servants know truthfully that you are powerful, whoever may remain ignorant of it.

Nor did you merely found the circle of the earth and its fullness; you also created the north and the sea. That is, you created the devil, who makes unbelievers cold, away from the warmth of charity, like the north wind, the coldest of winds. And you created the sea, that is, the unbelievers themselves who embitter you.

This is to say: You created not only the good but also the wicked, and the devil, their head—not insofar as they are wicked, but because, when you created them good in Adam, they became wicked through Adam’s sin; and when you created the devil good and luminous, he made himself wicked through pride.

Or it may be understood this way: “You created”—that is, you will create—the north and the sea: you will dispose and order the devil and his members. In accordance with the saying of Isaiah, “forming peace and creating evil” (*Formans pacem et creans malum*, Isaiah 45:7). This does not mean that he himself is the author of wickedness—for it is impious to say that anything evil proceeds from him—but that he creates evil, that is, orders it, so that, although the wickedness itself proceeds from the devil and the impious, he orders it in such a way that it contributes to some benefit of his own people.

Since he had said, “The heavens will confess your wonders,” he wishes to explain which heavens they are when he adds: I say that the heavens will be yours, and that those who are Thabor and Hermon will be yours; that is, those who are enlightened and anathematize the devil. They will exult—that is, they will proclaim exultantly—in your name, that is, for the honor of your name, your arm, that is, your strength, with power, that is, with efficacy. They will proclaim that you are powerful and effective in overcoming the devil.

Thabor and Hermon are two places in Judaea. Thabor is interpreted as “coming light,” while Hermon means “anathema.” Accordingly, Thabor and Hermon aptly signify preachers from the Jews, to whom Christ, coming as the true light, gave the power to anathematize the devil and their sins. By this he made them proclaimers of his strength and power.

In this too they are shown to be unlike him, since he was not a proclaimer of their power and strength.

He also prays for them in this way: I say that they will proclaim your arm with power exultantly; and, so that they may not fail in this, let your hand be established in them—that is, work firmly and continually in them what you are going to work, namely the whole perfection of the virtues. And let your right hand be exalted in them—that is, let the grace of your kindness grow and multiply in them, so that the power of your grace, which will work the perfection of the virtues in them, may be greater.

By “right hand,” since prosperity is usually signified, God’s kindness is appropriately understood here. For what prosperity is greater than to obtain the favor of divine kindness? In this, moreover, by suggesting in prayer that they need God’s kindness and action, he shows them to be unlike him, since he himself does not need their kindness or action.

So that what he prays for may be fulfilled, he shows what benefit will result if God establishes his hand in them and exalts his right hand. I say: Let your hand be established in them, and let your right hand be exalted. If this happens, “justice and judgment of Thabor and Hermon will be the preparation of your seat.” This is to say: Through your establishing your hand in them and exalting your right hand, judgment will be in them—that is, they will judge themselves to be creatures and you to be the Creator, and they will judge themselves to possess from you whatever good they possess. Through this judgment there will be justice in them, that is, the justification of good works.

This judgment and justice will be the reason why they are considered worthy to prepare a seat for you in others; that is, by their preaching, example, and conduct they will win for you people in whom you may sit and reign. Otherwise they would not be worthy to prepare a seat for you. Here too he shows them to be unlike him, because they will prepare a seat for him as servants, whereas he will not prepare one for them.

He therefore shows how they will prepare a seat for him when he adds: I say that judgment and justice in Thabor and Hermon will be the reason why a seat is prepared for you. That seat will be prepared in this way: mercy and truth will go before your face, that is, before the knowledge of you.

This is to say: Before you are known by those who will be made your seat—Thabor and Hermon, who are called “your mercy and truth” by emphasis, because through your mercy and truth they will be made heavens—they will precede the knowledge of you by their preaching. Thus they will first proclaim you to them and, by leading them to knowledge of you, make them your seat. This is compared to energetic servants who go before the face of their arriving lord in order to prepare lodging for him.

In this also they will be unlike him, since he will not precede their face.

The Lord’s mercy is said to be in the preachers insofar as he forgives them their sins and restores innocence in them; truth is in them when he justifies those who are already just still more, as he promised.

Or it may be understood this way: Justice and judgment will be the preparation of your seat in those heavens. Through justice and judgment they will prepare themselves as a seat for you; and those same heavens, being mercy and truth by emphasis, will precede your face among others, so that they may make those others your seat.

I say that in all these ways the heavens will be unlike you, O Christ. That is, blessed will be the people who know the jubilation of this unlikeness—who know how to rejoice and will rejoice with inward jubilation because you will be so great that no one will be able to be compared with you.

This properly belongs to the principal intention, namely the praise of God. For in this he greatly commends him: he declares blessed the people who rejoice over his incomparable sublimity.

Or it may be adapted in this way: “Blessed is the people,” and so forth. I say that justice and judgment will be the preparation of your seat, and that people, having been made your seat through them, will know jubilation, that is, will know how to rejoice in God. If they rejoice with the intention of pure devotion, they will be blessed both here and in the future.

And here is the blessedness they will have here: Those who belong to that people, being in the light of your face—that is, in the illumination of the knowledge of you, which inwardly enlightens them—will walk, that is, will advance more and more in that light, so that those already enlightened may be enlightened still further. They will exult over their innocence all day long, and this in your name, that is, for your honor, so that they may ascribe to you, not to themselves, the fact that they are innocent. And they will be exalted in your justice, that is, in the justice given by you; they will grow in righteous works through you.

This is to say: They will have a threefold blessedness: those who are enlightened will be enlightened still further, they will rejoice over their innocence, and they will advance in good works.

I say “in your justice,” and rightly say “your,” by referring back to you whatever virtue will be in them, because you are the glory of their virtue, whereas they are not. In this they are unlike you: you will be the one in whom they ought to glory for every virtue they possess—for their illumination, innocence, and justice. Therefore I rightly say “your.”

He then shows why he himself will be the glory of their virtue by joining himself to their number, since he is already, by faith, a man of the New Testament.

I say that you will be the glory of their virtue, and this because our horn—that is, our virtue, which is called a horn because it is firm and grows upward like a horn—will be exalted not in our free will but in your good pleasure, that is, through the good pleasure of your grace. It will be raised up and increased by you.

Having shown the blessing that the rejoicing people will have in the present, he also shows the blessing of the future in this way. I say that the people who know jubilation will be blessed in the future. And truly we too will be blessed—we who exist so long beforehand, yet are already conformed by faith to that people and will be the same people in the future—because “our assumption is the Lord’s,” that is, will be the Lord’s.

This is to say: The Lord will take us from mortality and suffering into salvation. And “the Holy One of Israel our King”—that is, our assumption will belong to that Lord who will be holy, antonomastically holy among those who will be Israel, and who will sanctify those who will be Israel; and he will be our king. As if he were saying: He will be powerful enough to take us up, because he will be the Holy One of Israel and our king.

[Col. 1110D]

After the Prophet, acting under the inward influence of the paternal authority, had briefly indicated the benefits to be conferred upon the human race through Christ, and had used that occasion to treat those same benefits at greater length by acting in his own person, lest it be judged fictitious that he had testified that the Father spoke these things inwardly to him, he corroborates this by the authority of others. He says that the Father had said to other saints in a vision the very thing he had said to him, and also said it in his own time, so as to give it greater authority, lest the other prophets who came after him should seem to have received it from him rather than from the Father. For several prophets are read to have lived in David’s time, such as Nathan, Samuel, and the others.

He also introduces the Father himself speaking to those saints and more fully expressing to them the same benefits that he had declared to him. This is adapted in the following way. I say, O God the Father, that you said inwardly to me that mercy will be built up in the heavens, and so forth. And when you said this to me, you also spoke to your holy prophets, namely to my contemporaries, in an inward vision, that is, in a certain knowledge produced by your inspiration. By saying “in their vision” he lowers the status of those who falsely claim that prophets are ignorant of what they speak through the Spirit, like demoniacs, who do not know what they say.

I say that you spoke to your saints, and this is what you said: “I have placed help in one who is powerful.” As if he were saying: I will help the human race, which is insufficient of itself to free itself from condemnation, by freeing it; and I have placed this help—that is, I will place it—in my Son, who is antonomastically powerful. Through the obedience of his passion I will help it. And so that he may be powerful enough to accomplish this help, I exalted—that is, I will exalt—in the perfection of every virtue that chosen one from my people, namely the one whom I will choose for this purpose from the entire multitude of my saints. For no one else will be found worthy to carry this out. “He is beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (*Speciosus enim forma prae filiis hominum*, Psalm 44:3). Hence, in the Song of Songs, the bride says of him: “My beloved is white and red, chosen out of thousands” (*Dilectus meus candidus et rubicundus, ex millibus electus*, Song of Songs 5:10).

He then adds the reasons why he will exalt him, as follows: I say that I will exalt the chosen one, namely Christ, the true David. And I will exalt him for this reason: I found—that is, I will find through the experience of the matter itself—that David is my servant, that is, I will discover him to be my servant, obedient in everything and resisting in nothing. And because I will find him to be my servant, I anointed—that is, I will anoint—him as king and priest with my holy oil, that is, with freedom from sin. This is to say: I will give him freedom from sin, so that through this he may be worthy to become king and high priest, after the likeness of one who is anointed with oil for the purpose of becoming priest or king.

He shows through what he will be powerful, as follows: I say, “I will place help in David, the powerful one,” and truly he will be powerful. For my hand—that is, my Word, personally united to him insofar as he is human—will assist him in conquering his enemies, and my arm—that is, the same Word—will strengthen him, that is, will make him steadfast, so that he does not yield to his enemies. The Word of God is appropriately called hand and arm, because through it God the Father arranges and accomplishes all things, just as we act with our hand and arm. Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (*Verbo Domini coeli firmati sunt*, Psalm 32:6).

He therefore explains how he will strengthen him, as follows: I say that he will strengthen him, and he will strengthen him in this way: the ancient enemy, the devil, will accomplish nothing in him through his suggestions, whether criminally or venially; and the Jewish people, being a son of iniquity—that is, a son of the devil through obedience—the one who is called “iniquity” antonomastically because he is the origin of all iniquity, will not add to harming him. As if he were saying: The Jewish people will indeed have the will to harm him by conforming themselves to him, but it will not add actual harm to its will.

He also explains how he will assist him when he adds: I say that my hand will assist him, and I will assist him by my hand in this way: I will cut down—that is, I will destroy for the good—his enemies, the Jews. I will destroy a part of his persecutors from wickedness and cause them to be converted to him. This cutting down of the enemies will occur “from his face,” that is, from his knowledge, namely through knowledge of him: they will be destroyed from their wickedness and built up in goodness.

And I will not cut down only his persecutors, but also those who hate him, that is, a part of those who will not persecute him in fact but will merely hate him. I will turn them into flight from hatred, namely I will make them flee from hatred and approach his love.

And after he has conquered his enemies, I will not abandon him, but my truth and my mercy will be with him. This is to say: I will always be with him in assistance and strengthening, both because of my mercy and because of my truth, since I promised this and cannot fail to fulfill it, because I am true by nature. And because I will be with him, his horn will be exalted, that is, the power of his virtue will be raised up, so that the whole world will be subjected to him. This exaltation will be in my name, that is, in my honor, so that I may thereby be glorified by human beings. “Horn” is used for “power” because it is strong and in it resides the power of fighting.

Or it may be understood this way: I say that I will cut down his enemies, and I will cut them down by this means: my truth and my mercy will be with him, that is, I will be with him because of my mercy and truth. And because I will be with him, his horn will be exalted, that is, his sublimity will be exalted in my name, that is, in the magnification of my name. This is to say: Although he will be destined to be exalted in justice and innocence, he will be exalted more and more because he will strive to exalt my name.

Nor will I cut down only his enemies, the Jews, and turn the Jews who hate him into flight; I will also place his hand, that is, his activity, in the sea, that is, among the people of the Gentiles who embitter him. This is to say: I will cause him to convert a part of the Gentiles to the faith through the activity of the preaching of his disciples.

Nor will I place his hand only among the poor and subject people of the sea; I will also place it in the rivers, that is, among rulers, whose care flows down to the subject populace like rivers flowing down into the sea. I will place his right hand, that is, his activity; namely, I will cause him to convert some rulers through the activity of preachers. This is appropriately understood by “right hand,” because it is with the right hand that we act.

And I will do this for him deservedly. For he himself invoked—that is, he will pray to me—that I should make him firstborn and exalted, and that I should preserve my mercy for him, saying: “You are God,” that is, my creator, insofar as I am human, and “my Father,” insofar as I am God, and “my protector,” that is, my physician and patron, insofar as I am human; the one who works my salvation, that is, my steadfastness and resurrection. Or “my protector of salvation,” that is, the defender and preserver of my salvation, so that it does not fail.

It should be noted that when he sets down these pleasing words that Christ is read to have used in his prayers—namely “Father,” “God,” and “protector”—he does not state what he will pray for; this is understood from what follows, when he sets down what he will give by promise, adding:

I say that he will invoke me, and I, the one whom he will invoke and who am powerful enough to grant what he will pray for, will make him “firstborn of the dead,” that is, I will make him the first to be generated into immortality and incorruptibility, and through him all the dead who are to be saved will be generated in the future. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “Firstborn of the dead” (*Primogenitus mortuorum*, Revelation 1:5); and the Apostle says: “Firstborn among many brothers” (*Primogenitus inter multos fratres*, Romans 8:29).

And I will not merely make him firstborn, but also exalted in glorification above the kings of the earth, that is, above all the faithful who rule their earthly nature well within themselves, namely their sensuality, so that it does not resist spirituality excessively. This is to say: Although future believers will be exalted and glorified, he will nevertheless be exalted above all of them.

Or, literally: I will make him exalted above the kings of the earth, namely so that many kings of the earth will subject themselves to him and acknowledge that he is exalted. And I will preserve my mercy for him forever, both for his sake and for the sake of his members. This is to say: I will have mercy forever upon him and upon his members, so that I may always make them steadfast.

[Col. 1113C]

And thus my covenant—that is, my pact made with him—will be faithful, that is, true. This is to say: Because I will preserve mercy for him, the pact that I made—that is, that I will make by promising that I will preserve mercy for him if he is obedient to me—will be true. And I will establish his seed forever and ever, that is, I will establish his followers forever; namely, I will cause them to live forever. And I will establish his throne, that is, his followers, who will be his seat; I will make them glorious in the perfection of the inward nation. “As the days of heaven”: their glory will be splendid, as the glory of the heavenly spirits is splendid.

But since he had made so great a promise concerning his members, saying, “I will establish his seed forever and ever,” and so forth, lest those followers seem never afterward to sin, or, if they sinned, never to recover, he indicates that they will sin, that they will need correction, and that they will not lose God’s mercy, as follows:

I say that I will establish his seed forever and ever, and so forth. But if—that is, if his sons, his followers, namely the prelates—abandon my law, that is, the discipline prescribed in my law; namely, if they do not correct their subjects according to the discipline established in my law, but either correct them too harshly according to their own desire, exceeding the proper measure through anger, or too leniently, doing little because of someone’s favor; and if his sons, the prelates, do not walk in my judgments, that is, do not persevere in the judgments established by me; namely, if they do not maintain right judgments toward their subjects because they judge falsely out of love or hatred for someone; and if his sons, the subjects, profane my just decrees, that is, regard my just commandments as profane and unjust—as do many priests who consider it unjust and detestable that what has been established in the canons should prohibit priests from having wives, buying ecclesiastical offices, and doing other such things; and, to speak universally, if his sons, both prelates and subjects, do not keep my commandments (although it is more tolerable merely not to keep them than, by not keeping them, to profane them)—then I will visit their iniquities with a rod, that is, I will correct with a lesser blow the lesser offenses of those who do not keep my commandments. This is by analogy with children who commit lesser offenses and are corrected by a blow of the rod.

And I will visit—that is, I will correct—with blows, that is, with great and harsh corrections, the sins, that is, the greater faults, of those who have profaned my just decrees. This is by analogy with young men who offend more seriously and are chastised with blows from staffs. As if he were saying: If his sons offend, I will chastise them through illnesses and through other anxieties that I will bring upon them; all of these will be for them a most bitter and salutary visitation.

It should be noted that he makes this promise of correction and mercy only concerning those sons who are to be saved. He uses “law,” that is, “discipline,” because those institutions in which the punishment of offenders is treated are more forcefully called laws than those in which the rule of life is established.

I say that I will visit them with a rod and with blows. But I will not scatter my mercy from him, that is, I will not entirely remove the benefits of my mercy from his sons who are to be saved, whom I will visit. Namely, I will not take away from them faith and knowledge of me, nor the other benefits that I will confer upon them through my mercy. Nor will I harm them in the future by condemning them.

And this is certain and firm in my truth. As if he were saying: Since I am true and cannot deceive, my very truth requires that I fulfill what I promised—namely, that I will not scatter my mercy and will not harm them. Nor will I profane my covenant, that is, I will not make my pact with David my son profane, namely a lying pact, which I will establish by promising that I will not harm his sons. Nor will I make void—that is, empty and without any useful effect—the things that proceed from my lips, that is, those benefits that my prophets, called “my lips” because through them I speak beforehand of future things, proclaim concerning his sons.

As if he were saying: If I were to scatter my mercy from them, my pact with David would be a lie—a pact that I will make by speaking inwardly to him—which would indeed be profane, and it would be impossible for me to lie, since I am God; and the things that the prophets announce concerning the eternal salvation of his sons would be void and spoken without benefit. To prevent either of these things from occurring, I will not scatter my mercy, nor will I harm them.

And truly I will not scatter it, for I swore once—that is, I immutably and firmly decreed it—after the likeness of those who establish something firmly and with an oath. I swore once, that is, so inviolably that there is no need to repeat the oath.

[Col. 1115A]

I say that I swore once, and this in my holiness, that is, in my holy decree. As if he were saying: Since my decree is holy, it is impossible for what I decree not to occur. I say “I swore,” and this is what I swore: His seed will remain forever, that is, his followers will be eternal. And if I, David, lie—namely, if I fail to fulfill what I covenant with my son—then I am not God, or David is not a prophet to whom I foretold this.

And not only will his seed be eternal, but also his throne, that is, the seed itself, which will be his seat—not a local but a spiritual one—existing in the future in my presence, that is, in the open contemplation of me. Those who here see me through a mirror will then be luminous in soul like the sun, that is, after the manner of the sun. In accordance with the saying of Jesus: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father” (*Justi fulgebunt sicut sol in regno Patris mei*, Matthew 13:43). And the same throne will be splendid in body forever, as the full moon is splendid.

It should be noted that they will be brighter in their souls than in their bodies, since the soul is more excellent than the body. It should also be noted that, although all God’s followers may be called his throne, those who are more worthy and holier by a certain pre-eminence are called his throne, just as a certain order of spirits is called “thrones” because of its excellence.

And Jesus, their head, will be a witness in heaven to this promise concerning the sons. Having been taken up into the heavens, he will be splendid; he will be both witness and pledge that the members will be splendid. And he will be such a witness as will be faithful, that is, such that faith should be placed in him, since he is both God and man; or “faithful” means one who will provide assurance.

After setting down the promise of the Father’s authority, the Prophet, acting in his own person, raises an objection that many might raise, in order to resolve it: namely, why, if God the Father promised such great benefits to Christ and his members, he permits them to be afflicted by so many anxieties.

He states it as follows: O God the Father, you promised Christ that you would preserve mercy for him forever, and that his throne would be like the sun, and other such things. Yet you have deliberately rejected—that is, you will seem to reject—from all glory your Christ, whom you will permit to be treated shamefully; and you have despised—that is, you will seem to despise—him, namely, because he will be so afflicted, although you foretold through the prophets that he would be glorious in the future. He will seem not yet to have come, but still to be delayed. Hence the unbelieving Jews suppose that the Messiah is still to come.

And you will seem not only to reject and despise the head itself, but also to overthrow—that is, you will seem to destroy—the covenant of your servant, that is, the pact that you will make with Christ your servant by promising that his throne will be like the sun, and so forth. You will seem to overthrow it because you profaned—that is, you will permit persecutors to profane—the sanctuary of him which is on earth. Namely, you will permit those persecutors to drive away and persecute as profane those who are his martyrs, although they are your sanctuary, that is, your holy temple remaining on earth.

He says “on earth” to distinguish them from the citizens above, who, although they are God’s sanctuary, cannot be profaned by the impious.

Or it may be understood this way: You will permit your sanctuary to be profaned on earth, that is, you will permit the impious to persecute the faithful in the manner of profane people, as long as they are on earth, although they are your sanctuary, that is, his holy temple. After they depart this life, the persecutors will have no power to persecute them.

And you will permit the sanctuary to be profaned in this way: You destroyed all the hedges of that sanctuary, that is, you will permit the prelates of the Church, who protect the Church by their doctrine and example, to be destroyed through bodily death, after the manner of hedges enclosing and protecting a vineyard. And by permitting them to be destroyed, you placed—that is, you will place—the sanctuary’s support in fear, that is, causes of fear. Namely, by destroying the hedges you will cause those hedges, which during life will be a support and protection for them, once bodily destroyed, to become for them a reason to fear that they too will be destroyed.

And they ravaged David in his members, that is, they will tear apart the greater part of his members by killing them; or they will seize certain weak members of his and incorporate them into themselves. These are all those who abandon the way of right living, both Gentiles, Jews, and heretics, or those who pass by the way, that is, neglect Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life. This is to say: Because of fear arising from the destruction of the prelates, some weak persons among the subjects will conform themselves to the unbelievers.

And because they will have ravaged him, David himself—that is, those members who remain—has become, and will become, a reproach to his neighbors. This is to say: Those who are not ravaged will be a reproach to their neighbors, that is, they will be a cause of reproach to those who will already be neighbors, wishing to be converted to the faith of the Church by their example. Namely, those neighbors will be ashamed that they ever wished to believe them.

Having shown the abasement of the faithful, he shows the exaltation of those who abase them, as follows: I say that you will permit the members of David to be so abased that the hedges are destroyed and some of them are ravaged. And, by contrast, you have exalted the right hand of those who abase him, David in his members; that is, you will permit the strength of the persecutors who labor to abase his members to be exalted and increased.

This is to say: You will give them extensive power to abase the faithful. And by this you have gladdened—that is, you will permit to rejoice—all his enemies, David’s abusers, namely those who abase his members. As if he were saying: You will permit their strength to be exalted to such an extent that they will be greatly delighted by it. Hence certain persecutors are said to have ordered banquets to be prepared and games to be held at the place where martyrs were killed.

I say that you will exalt the persecutors. And, conversely, you have turned away—that is, you will turn away—the help of the sword of his reason, David’s, that is, of certain of his members. Namely, when they have a rational defense with which to defend themselves after the manner of a sword, showing that they believe rightly and are not worthy of persecution, you will turn away from them the aid of reason, which will be their sword. That is, you will make their reason unable to defend them from persecution and death, after the likeness of a soldier who cannot defend himself from an enemy with the aid of his sword.

And that sword was not a help to him, that is, that sword of reason will not help certain of his members in the battle they will wage against unbelievers. This is to say: When certain people fight against the impious with rational arguments, they will not be able to convert them, after the likeness of a soldier whose sword is ineffective at overcoming the enemy.

And you destroyed him, that is, you will permit certain of his members to be destroyed by death. Their destruction will result from the cleansing of those members: they will be destroyed because they will be pure and holy in faith and works, and the impious will be unable to endure their purity. This will indeed be more extraordinary than if they were destroyed because of impurity.

Or their destruction will result from cleansing, that is, on account of cleansing. This is to say: They will be destroyed by the impious because they will be regarded as profane, and through their destruction the cities from which they are removed will seem to be cleansed by their death.

[Col. 1117A]

Lest they therefore be thought to be destroyed both in body and in soul, he determines the matter as follows:

[Inherited source boundary: the supplied text ends here, incomplete.]

[Col. 1117B] I say that you will permit its members to be destroyed; and this destruction will not be both in body and in soul, but upon the earth, that is, in the body, which is earthly. You have dashed him, that is, you will permit his seat to be dashed down—David, that is, his members in which he will sit. This means: You will permit them to be destroyed in body, not in soul. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28).

And you have shortened, that is, you will shorten, the days of his time, that is, of certain of his members—David, namely, when he will have certain members, whether prelates or those newly approaching the faith. While others will desire that they live long, you will shorten the days of their time, that is, you will permit them to live less long than they wish.

And him, that is, many of his members existing in confusion, that is, amid many anxieties that will be causes of confusion, you have drenched, that is, you will permit them to be drenched and surrounded by that very confusion, namely, by anxieties that will be causes of confusion. This is said emphatically, by comparison with those who, being in water, are surrounded by it.

And when you will thus permit David and his members to be persecuted, how long—that is, to what extent—O Lord Father, will you turn away, that is, will you appear to turn away, your mercy from that David and his members? Will you turn it away to the end, that is, completely? Or to the end, that is, to destruction, so that you destroy them entirely? By no means. Rather, your anger, that is, your vengeance, will blaze, that is, will be inflamed, in them like fire, that is, by comparison with fire. For just as fire, when vehemently kindled, purifies gold but consumes and reduces wood to ash, so the persecution of Christ and his members will be expiation for those members, but destruction for the unbelievers persecuting them.

When, therefore, he says, “Your anger will blaze like fire,” he briefly resolves everything that he had proposed concerning the persecutions and overthrowings of Christ and his members, from the place where he had said, “But you…” When, however, he says, “Remember…,” he prays for the salvation of the members, namely, that God the Father, by remembering how great the future dignity of Christ’s merit will be, may have mercy on those members through him.

The passage is adapted as follows: I say that your anger will not blaze to the end, but like fire. And so that it may not blaze to the end: Remember, God the Father, what—that is, how worthy—my substance will be, namely, the human nature that your Word will assume from my seed, so that through the merit of that dignity you may have mercy on human beings.

And it is necessary that you remember. For did you establish, that is, create, all the children of human beings—that is, all human beings—in vain, that is, without benefit? Far from it. It is as though he said: Remember Christ’s dignity so that through it you may have mercy on human beings, because if you did not remember it and did not have mercy on human beings, you would appear to have created them without benefit, although they seem to have been created for this purpose: that the tenth order, which perished, should be filled up from them.

And I rightly say, “Remember what my substance is.” For who is the human being—that is, how great and how glorious will that man be who is to be born from my seed? And truly, he will be great. For he will be such that he will live, and thus will not see death.

[Col. 1118A] But lest he be thought never to die, this is specified as follows. And afterward—that is, he will not see death after he rescues his soul from the hand, that is, from the power, of the underworld. “For Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more” (Rom. 6:9).

And truly that man will be great. Where are, that is, in what will consist, O Lord Father, your ancient mercies, that is, the benefits of your mercy ordained from of old, that is, from eternity? This means: Through whose obedience the benefits of your mercy, ordained from eternity, will be conferred upon the human race, just as you swore to David, that is, just as you will firmly promise inwardly to that man who will truly be David. And this is in your truth, that is, in your most truthful promise.

I say, “Remember what my substance is.” I also pray: Remember the reproach of your servants, the members of that David, so that you may grant them recompense for it. I mean the reproach of many nations, that is, the reproach that will be inflicted by many nations; and therefore it will be heavier than if it were inflicted by a few.

I have not loathed that reproach, nor have I rejected it, but I have contained it, that is, I have embraced it lovingly in my bosom, that is, in my inner conscience, which is fittingly signified by the bosom, since the bosom is a hidden and secret place. By saying that he loves that reproach, which will be the occasion of salvation for those who endure it, he strengthens those sufferers to endure it.

What they reproached—that is, the reproach that, by reproaching, your enemies, the unbelievers, will inflict upon your servants, O Lord Father. He repeats this in order to show what the reproach itself will be. What they reproached, I say, that is, what they will say by way of reproach: They will reproach them with the transformation of your Son Christ, that is, with the fact that Christ will be changed from life to death, saying that those who believe in a dead man are insane.

And yet, although Christ will thus be changed, through this change the blessed Lord of all will appear, that is, he will be exalted forever in everlasting glory. Hence the Apostle says: “Therefore God also exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name” (Phil. 2:9). And in the Gospel: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise, and thus to enter into his glory” (Luke 24:46).

I say that the Lord will be blessed, and let this happen so that he may be blessed in the Church from the Jews, and let him be blessed in the Church from the Gentiles. By desiring his blessing in this way, he invites us to bless him.

## IN PSALM LXXXIX

**Title of the eighty-ninth:** “A prayer of Moses, the man of God.” This is expounded as follows.

In this psalm he introduces Moses praying to God the Son, who is to become man, that he may not turn man away from his mercy—man who, through Adam, has been cast down into humility—and he also shows and announces that, once freed from that fall, we shall finally rejoice.

And it is not just any Moses who is introduced here as praying, but Moses, the man of God. He more appropriately says “man of God” than if he had said “servant of God,” in order to show that Moses obeyed God freely and with chaste love, like a free man who serves his lord, not so much from fear as from love. A servant, however, serves more from fear. Concerning this Moses, the same Lord testifies: “Moses my servant is most faithful in all my house” (Num. 12:7; Heb. 3:2).

For this reason Moses, the minister of the old law, is introduced by the Prophet as praying to Christ: among the Jews he is regarded as more authoritative than all the prophets. Thus, by the authority of Moses praying to Christ and showing him to be both God from eternity and destined to become man in time, as well as the restorer of the world, the unbelieving Jews are convicted—those who deny that Christ is God and the restorer of the world. Concerning this same Moses he said to the most unbelieving Jews: “If you believed Moses, you would certainly believe me” (John 5:46). “For he wrote about me” [perhaps].

The Prophet composed this psalm in Moses’ person either because he saw in Moses’ writings something similar to the words of this psalm, or because, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, he learned that Moses had acted in this way. Ezra also, the giver of the titles, recognizing through the revelation of the same Spirit that the prophet David had wished this psalm to be understood in Moses’ person, inscribed it with that title.

**Lord, you have been our refuge:** You exist as the word of salvation for the human race in the generation of the old covenant and in the generation of the new. Or: You began to be a refuge from the generation of the old covenant and continued into the new generation. Or thus: Beginning from the old generation and proceeding to the new generation, you have become—that is, you who are the refuge will become—a creature, namely, you will personally assume human nature; and this for us, that is, for our benefit, so that you may restore the world.

Hence the Apostle says: “God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. 4:4).

But because he had said “become,” lest Christ appear in every respect to have had a beginning and to be merely a man, he adds: Although I call you “become,” nevertheless, before the mountains were made—that is, before the heavenly spirits were created, who are called mountains because they are exalted in the dignity of their nature—or before the earth was formed from the four elements, that is, before the earthly man was formed, who is lower than the angels; and, to speak universally, before the world was formed, namely, the whole world and everything in it; and, to say something even greater, from the age, that is, from eternity, and unto the age, that is, unto eternity—without beginning and without end—you are.

[Col. 1119D] And truly you are eternal, for you are God. When he says “you are,” and not “you were” or “you will be,” he indicates eternity. “Age” is sometimes used for eternity; at other times “eternity” is used for an age.

And he rightly says “mountains,” that is, angels, as not formed but made, and says that the earth was formed. For that is called “formed” which is made from some unformed matter. The earth—that is, man—was formed from the four elements, whereas the heavenly spirits were created from nothing.

And because you are powerful, as God, and for the salvation of human beings you will become a creature, do not turn away from your mercy the man cast down into humility, that is, human beings who through Adam have fallen into the greatest decline. This means: Restore the human race, for whose restoration you will become a creature.

And I pray this with such confidence because you have said inwardly to your faithful, speaking without the noise of words: “O children of human beings,” namely, of Adam and Eve, who were simply human beings and not spiritual beings. I say “children” not only according to origin, but also according to imitation in sin: Turn from being children of human beings to being my children through obedience, and I will turn toward you according to fatherhood. It is as though he said: I would not admonish them about returning unless I had foreseen that they were to be restored. With this confidence, therefore, I pray for their restoration.

Thus he shows into what humility man has been cast down when he adds: I say, “Do not turn away the man cast down into humility.” And truly he has been cast down into humility, since, although he had originally been created incapable of dying, he has now become so fragile that, even if he lived a thousand years—which nevertheless has never happened in any human being—those thousand years would be like yesterday, that is, comparable to yesterday.

He shows in what respect they are comparable when he adds: That yesterday has already passed and now does not remain. It is as though he said: Although they may seem to last for a little while, they are no more to be valued than yesterday, which has already passed. They too will pass in the same way, and in this respect they are rightly compared with yesterday.

Or the passage may be read thus: A thousand years are like yesterday, of little value before your eyes, that is, in comparison with the eternal life that is before your eyes, that is, which you contemplate.

And, to say less, a thousand years are to be considered a small thing, like a watch in the night that has already passed, that is, like a single watch, which was shorter because it lasted only three hours. And, to speak more accurately, their thousand years will be counted—that is, rightly reckoned—among those things that are regarded as nothing, that is, things so worthless that they are considered to be nothing.

Having shown the excessive fall of human beings, because he had said, “Do not turn away man,” lest he seem to wish man never to remain in this fallen condition and thus to oppose the divine ordering, he concedes man’s fall when he adds: I pray that you do not turn away the man cast down into humility, but restore him.

Nevertheless, I concede that man himself, existing like grass in the morning—that is, flowering and conspicuous like grass, which is more beautiful in the morning than at any other part of the day—passes from that beauty into death.

He determines how he passes when he adds: Namely, let him first flower in the morning, that is, let him be conspicuous like flowering grass in youth. Youth is signified by morning because it is the beginning of life and is vigorous, like morning, which is bright and the beginning of the day. From the flower of youth let him pass into evening, that is, into old age, which is called evening because in old age a person comes to decline just as the day tends toward sunset in the evening. And in the evening of old age let him fall into death, and let him become stiff, so as to become a rigid, hard, and inflexible corpse; then let him wither and become dry dust.

[Col. 1121B] When he makes this concession, he teaches us patiently to endure our fall. He also gives the reason why we have reached this humility, lest we seem to have been cast down without cause, when he adds: I say, “Do not turn away the man cast down into humility.”

And truly all of us human beings have come into great degradation, and rightly so, because we have failed, that is, become subject to decay, although before Adam sinned we had been created incapable of failing. And we reached this condition in your anger, that is, in your just vengeance.

He will repeat and explain this in what follows. And not only have we failed, but in your fury, that is, in your excessive vengeance, we have been troubled, that is, made subject to disturbance: we have become such that we can be disturbed by death and by all anxieties. This is indeed more serious than merely being subject to decay, and therefore it is rightly placed under “fury.” For fury appears to be greater than anger.

And truly through anger we failed, and through your fury we were troubled. For you did not overlook our iniquities, but you placed our iniquities committed through Adam before your sight, that is, you regard them in order to punish original sin, of which we are participants.

And you placed our age in the illumination of your face, that is, in the brightness of your knowledge: it cannot deceive you, but you see it openly. In another translation we find: “Our negligences in the light of your face.” Hence we appropriately understand “age” to have been used for negligences. For it is customary for us to say of someone living badly: “This man is leading a bad life.”

It is as though he said: The original sins committed through Adam, in which we have become participants, are not merely iniquities but also such iniquities as are negligences, that is, committed negligently by Adam, without any compulsion. Therefore they are more deserving of punishment. You did not put them aside but placed them before your sight so that you might avenge them.

He repeats what he stated above—“we have failed”—in order later to explain it. I said that man had been cast down into humility. And truly we have been cast down, because all our days have failed, that is, become subject to decay, although before Adam sinned perpetual life had been given to us in Adam.

He rightly says “all our days,” indicating that both the eternal days have failed and the days we possess are subject to decay, as the following verse explains.

And we have failed in anger, that is, in your vengeance; we have become subject to decay, occupied in works that are themselves subject to decay. And truly we are subject to decay, that is, occupied in perishable works, because our years will meditate like a spider, that is, throughout all our years we will meditate and act like a spider: we will act with deliberation in such things as are quickly transitory and very easily dissolved, like the work of a spider, which is extremely fragile.

When he says “we will meditate,” by using the future tense he indicates perseverance, and he denotes something more serious than if he had simply said “we will act.” For it is worse to act badly with deliberation than rashly.

He also explains how the days have failed when he adds: Truly our days have become subject to decay. For the days of our years are enclosed within seventy years, that is, within those seventy. By saying “those,” he indicates that our life ends within this number. It is as though he said: The days of our life have become so subject to decay that we live only seventy years.

If, however, some of us live in “potencies,” that is, in potent and fully endowed conditions of health, eighty years constitute our life. This means: If some of us—and only a few—lead a thoroughly healthy life, the span of their life is eighty years; and beyond their eighty years there is labor and sorrow.

When he says “of them,” following Greek usage, he uses the genitive in place of the ablative, since Greek lacks an ablative. It is as though he said: If some live beyond these years, namely, beyond eighty, that life will be labor and sorrow, that is, spent in labor and sorrow. It should not even be called life, but by emphasis it is to be called “labor and sorrow.”

The seventy years also signify the present life, because the number seventy is multiplied by seven and the present life revolves through seven days. By eighty years, however, the future day of judgment, the eighth day, is understood, because the number eighty is multiplied by eight.

According to this interpretation, the passage is adapted as follows: I say that in all our years we will meditate upon works that are dissoluble and fragile, like a spider. He explains how when he adds: Truly throughout our whole life we will perform such works through deliberate thought as the spider performs. For the days of our years will be meditating within those seventy years, that is, throughout all the days of our years we will meditate on what will be necessary for those seventy years in which we now exist, namely, on what pertains to the present life in which we are still detained.

I say that throughout all our days we will meditate on what pertains to seventy years. But if—that is, rather if—there are among us a few in potencies, that is, in virtues and good works, which are called potencies because they can lead us to life, the eighty years will be desired through those potencies, that is, the rest of the eighth day.

This means: Some of us who exist in potencies will not work like a spider. They will not perform works pertaining to the present life, but works pertaining to the future life.

And beyond their eighty years, to desire is labor and sorrow, that is, causes of labor and sorrow.

Because he had said “in potencies,” one might ask where certain people obtain this, so that they are in potencies. He responds as follows: We few have this because gentleness has come upon us, that is, the Son of God will come to us from the Father’s exalted seat. Through faith in him we shall already be coming into potencies.

He is emphatically called the Father’s gentleness because through him God’s anger has been softened toward us. But lest it be understood that our gentleness would be such that, once it had come, we would never afterward be chastised, he adds: Yet we shall be chastised, that is, corrected by mortality and susceptibility to suffering, after gentleness has come upon us.

If this interpretation is followed, the words at the beginning of the psalm, “Lord, Word existing as refuge, you have become,” that is, “You will become a creature from the Father,” are expounded as follows: Lord Father, you have become our refuge, that is, our security for escaping the fall into which we came through Adam. The rest need not be changed.

According to the earlier interpretation, in which we explained “the days of our years” literally as the seventy years, the verse that follows—“because gentleness has come upon us”—is expounded thus: I say that we have become subject to decay, so much so that we do not live beyond eighty years except in labor and sorrow.

And this is because, lest we become too fierce and unbridled against God, gentleness has come upon us, that is, from God’s higher disposition there has come upon us a taming that makes us gentle and humble toward God, namely, mortality and susceptibility to suffering. Through that taming of gentleness we shall be chastised as long as we remain in this life, lest we grow too insolent against God. This is by comparison with an unbridled horse, which is chastised with whips so that it may become gentle.

I say that gentleness has come upon us through which we are chastised, and we shall be chastised. And although you frequently chastise us, nevertheless, who among human beings knows the power of your anger, that is, the powerful efficacy of your vengeance, which you exercise against us? And who knows how to count your anger, that is, the multiplicity of your vengeance, in proportion to, that is, for the sake of, your fear—so that they may fear you in view of the power and multiplicity of that vengeance?

Few do. It is as though he said: Although we are continually punished by your powerful and manifold vengeance, nevertheless few among us, considering the power and multiplicity of your vengeance, fear you on its account, although they ought to do so. He says this, therefore, for the correction of those who do not fear, so that they may learn to fear.

He also prays for those who fear, as follows: I say that we are few who fear. Therefore, in accordance with the merit of the fear that we possess, make your right hand known to us in the future through experience of the reality, that is, the mercy of your salvation.

This means: Because we fear you here, grant us salvation in the future through your mercy. And because we could not otherwise attain this mercy, meanwhile make us instructed in heart, that is, in the understanding of the heart; grant us the ability to understand rightly.

And because it is not enough to understand rightly without good action, also make us instructed in wisdom, that is, in virtues and good works, which are called wisdom because they proceed from wisdom. This means: Give us knowledge of how to act well and embrace virtues.

Or this may be read with wonder, as follows: I say that we shall be chastised, and we are chastised, through your vengeance. And who is—that is, how great and how blessed is—the one who knows the power of your anger and knows how to count your anger in proportion to your fear, that is, so as to fear you? The explanation remains unchanged.

He also prays in this way: I say, “Who knows?” And only a few know this. Since it belongs to few to know, and those who know are blessed, I pray: Lord, make your right hand known to us in the future, that is, your mercy, so that first we may know the power of your anger and count your anger in proportion to your fear. For unless we first feared here, your mercy would certainly not be made known to us in the future.

And so that we may know how to count anger in proportion to fear, make us instructed in heart, that is, in understanding. And because understanding well would not suffice, make us instructed in wisdom, that is, in virtues and good works.

I say, “Make the right hand known,” and so that it may become known: Turn, Lord, from anger toward mercy, as far as—that is, to the extent that—it pleases you.

He explains this “as far as” when he adds: And, that is, be implorable, that is, be willing to be entreated, concerning your servants, that is, among your servants.

This means: Even if you do not wish to turn toward mercy with regard to those destined for destruction, nevertheless turn toward those who serve you, so that you may have mercy on them because they serve you.

When he says “concerning your servants,” it is the same as saying that this should occur through the Father’s higher disposition, so that he may have mercy on his servants. One is properly called implorable when he grants what is requested from him in prayer.

He therefore announces the future mercy for which he prayed, for the consolation of the faithful, as follows: I prayed that you would make your right hand known, that is, your mercy. And truly it will be made known to us through experience of the reality. For we have been filled, that is, we shall be filled, with your mercy, which will occur in the morning in you, Christ, that is, through the benefit of the resurrection, which you will give us through your mercy. This will first occur in you on the morning of the third day.

This means: You will mercifully make us rise on the eighth day, just as you, the first, will rise in the morning on the third day after the Passion.

And once filled, we rejoiced, that is, we shall rejoice, in the splendor of the body; and we were delighted, that is, we shall be delighted, in the blessing of the soul. And not for a time, but throughout all our eternal days, which are called many because of their duration, although they are one and continuous. And they are rightly called “ours,” that is, useful and necessary for us.

He repeats in an equivalent expression what he said—“we shall rejoice and be delighted”—in order to add the following: We rejoiced, I say, that is, we shall rejoice in soul and body, and this in place of the days, that is, in the place of the present days in which you did not humble us, that is, promised that we would be humbled, amid the anxieties of numerous sufferings.

But because he had said “days,” lest he seem to have said too little, he adds: For years, namely, we shall rejoice in those years in which we experience evils, [Col. 1125A] that is, fitting tribulations.

This means: Because here we suffer persecution for God, in the future we shall rejoice. In accordance with that saying of the Lord: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6:21).

What he prayed briefly above, when he said “instructed in heart in wisdom,” he repeats here in prayer so as to say more fully, as follows: I say that in the future we shall rejoice. And so that we may be able to reach this joy: Look with the regard of mercy upon your servants, that is, upon those who serve you, incorporating others into themselves; and look upon your works, namely, upon those who are good because they are so through the working of your mercy.

When he says “servants,” he indicates their merit; when he says “works of God,” he indicates mercy. It is as though he said: Look upon them for this reason, because they serve you by instructing others. And for this further reason: Whatever they are, they are so through your working.

And also direct their children, that is, their followers, toward good action.

He therefore explains how he asks God to look upon them. I say, “Look,” and look in this way: Let the splendor of the virtues and innocence of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon us, that is, in the higher and more excellent part of us, namely, in the soul.

This means: Let our soul participate in his splendor insofar as this is possible. And direct upon us, that is, toward eternal life, which is above us, the works of our hands, that is, the good works that arise from our good affections, which are called hands because through them the mind acts by thinking.

This means: Make us perform good works with regard to heavenly goods, not with regard to human favor. And direct into perseverance—that is, make us persevere—the work of our hands, that is, the good works of our affections. They are singularly called “the work” because, being performed with charity, they are not discordant but one unified whole.

## IN PSALM XC

**Title of the ninetieth:** “A praise-song of David.” This is expounded as follows.

This psalm is praise, that is, composed for the praise of God; and it is the praise of a song, that is, the praise of joy, or joyful praise. And this praise belongs to David, that is, to every faithful person, who is introduced by the Prophet in this psalm.

For in the first verse of the psalm, speaking in his own person, the Prophet intends to show who should be called one who dwells in the protection of the Most High and in the shelter of the God of heaven. He introduces this dweller throughout the remaining verses of the psalm as acting and attributing to the Lord, not to himself, the benefits that God will grant; he also recounts those benefits for his own exhortation. Through this he teaches others that whatever good they have must be referred back to the Lord, so that they too may obtain the same benefits.

**He who dwells in the help of the Most High:** That is, the one who is not a temporary visitor but a dweller, perfectly remaining in the help of God. It is good to remain in his help, since he is the Most High, that is, the Almighty. And he who will remain—that is, dwell perseveringly—in the protection of the God of heaven, that is, of the God of the heavenly spirits, will remain safely in his protection, since he is so powerful that he is the God of the citizens above.

He will say to the Lord, both in words and in thoughts, “My protector,” and so forth. This means: God continually helps no one else toward good action, nor does he protect anyone else in virtue so that he may not fail, except the one who attributes all the good he has not to himself but to the Lord and says to the Lord with thanksgiving: O Lord, you are my protector, that is, my patron, who guard me so that I may not fail; and you are such a protector that you are my refuge, that is, my security, so that, trusting in your patronage, I may fear nothing; and you are my God, that is, my renewer, who creates me in good action, namely, who helps me to act well.

And because it is not enough to say this to the Lord unless he also takes care to instruct his neighbor, he will say to his neighbors as well, for their instruction: I will hope in him, that is, I have no hope in myself, O hearers, but I hope and shall hope in the Lord, that is, I shall place my hope in him; or, I shall hope, abandoning myself and moving toward him so as to place my hope in him. The meaning is the same when we say “in him” and “into him.”

I say that I will hope in him, and this is what I will hope: He who is powerful enough to deliver me will deliver me from the snare of hunters, so that I may not be caught in it.

By comparison, he calls evil spirits hunters, because just as hunters set snares for unwary wild animals by which they deceive them, so evil spirits prepare snares for the faithful by which they may entangle them. Their snare, therefore, is gold and silver and other such things, which can become material for sin, as well as vices.

And he will deliver me from a harsh word, so that it does not prevail against me, that is, from a hidden suggestion, which is called a harsh word because it disturbs the mind, by comparison with a harsh word; or from the harsh word of heretics and unbelievers, so that, because of their harshest insults, I may not fall away from the right purpose of my faith.

I say that he will say to the Lord, “My protector,” and so forth; and he will say to his neighbors, “I will hope in him,” and so forth. He will also say what follows to himself, for exaltation and for giving thanks to God.

O my soul, place firm hope in the Lord. For he will overshadow you, who have already been carried to the folds of faith, upon his shoulders, that is, through the teaching of preachers. They are called the shoulders of God because through their teaching God brings back lost sheep, namely, human beings, to the path of faith and to the sheepfold of paradise, to which they cannot return by themselves—just as a shepherd, when he has found a sheep he had lost, carries it tenderly on his shoulders to the folds of the sheepfold because it cannot walk owing to its weakness (Luke 15:5).

He will overshadow you, that is, he will give you the cooling shade of his protection. This means: He will cool you by his protection from the incitements of vices, so that you do not fail under their excessive heat. This was prefigured by the children of Israel, who, as they proceeded through the desert, were overshadowed by a cloud so that they would not be harmed by excessive heat. It is also said by comparison with a vigorous commander who provides shade for his soldiers while they are fighting, so that they do not fail because of the heat.

I say that he will give you shade, and you, placed under his wings, that is, under the cooling shelter of his protection, will hope. “Wings” are used by comparison for protection, because a bird protects its young with its wings from predatory birds and cools them from the heat.

I say that you will hope, and behold what you will hope: You will hope that his truth, that is, his true faith, will surround you with a shield, that is, fortify you on every side.

It is as though he said: When heretics strive to bend you toward their error through their false arguments, the truth of his faith, remaining immovable within you, will fortify you on every side—that is, will fortify you against all heresies—with a shield, that is, with invincible protection, which will be for you like a shield, rejecting from you every missile of depraved thoughts sent by the devil.

And because his truth will surround you, you will not fear, that is, you will not need to have the fear that comes from nocturnal terror, that is, from the fraud of heretics. It is called “fear” emphatically because it inspires fear, and “nocturnal” because it is obscure, by comparison with night: hidden and deceptive, since heretics mix certain truths with their false arguments so that they may deceive more quickly.

This means: You will not need to fear being deceived by the hidden fraud of heretics.

And you will not fear the arrow flying by day, that is, the same fraud of heretics. It is rightly called an arrow because it wounds secretly like an arrow; and it flies by day, that is, it is elevated through human wisdom, which appears to be day, namely, clear and splendid, like the day.

And because he had said that it flies by day, since “day” is usually understood in a good sense, he adds: And you will not fear the business walking in darkness, that is, the same fraud of heretics, which is rightly called “business.” For “business” signifies an activity completed with the greatest zeal and labor; hence the word *negotium* is understood as if from *negans otium*, “denying leisure.”

The fraudulent opinion of heretics is therefore called “business” because they devote great zeal and labor to it. Although this business may seem to be in the day, it nevertheless exists in the darkness of folly: “The wisdom of this world is folly with God” (1 Cor. 3:19). And it will walk into those very darknesses, that is, it will advance entirely, so as to sink more and more deeply into folly.

And you will not fear the assault of those heretics, that is, the excessive force of their eloquence, by which they attack the faithful. Hence the bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “My locks are full of drops of the nights” (Song 5:2).

And you will not fear the noonday demon, that is, the gathering of heretics who appear to be in the noonday, that is, fervent like midday in good action, since they perform certain simulated good works; and they appear bright and splendid in their human and subtle, though utterly false, opinions. Nevertheless, they are a demon, that is, the shadow of a demon.

Hence the Apostle says: “Satan disguises himself as an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11:14).

It should be noted that although the same matter—namely, the fraudulent opinion of the heretics—is understood through nocturnal fear, the arrow flying by day, the business, and the assault, nevertheless these expressions denote different things concerning the same matter, as has been shown, and must accordingly be expounded in different ways.

You will not merely hope that his truth will surround you with a shield; you will also hope that a thousand will fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand. Since he says “at your right hand,” by which prosperity is usually signified, it is implied that we should supply “at your left side.” For the left frequently signifies adversity.

It should be noted, however, that he says ten thousand temptations will come from the right, that is, from prosperity. This number is greater than a thousand simply because a more abundant supply of temptations arises in prosperity than in adversity.

The wording is adapted as follows: You will also hope, O soul, through the security of divine protection, that a thousand inward enemies, arising at your left side—that is, a thousand hidden temptations proceeding from your adversity—will fall, that is, will be overcome by your prayer. And because many enemies will afterward fall, having previously prevailed to some extent, he adds: I say that they will fall, and they will not fall just anyhow; rather, they will fall in such a way that none of those thousand thoughts will approach you, that is, approach you in consent, so as to prevail over you in any manner.

Nevertheless, although none will approach you, you will consider them with your inward eyes—that is, with the eyes of reason, which considers subtle matters. It is as though he said: One does not usually know so well what something is when one does not experience it in oneself as when one is actually subject to it. Nevertheless, although the sins of temptation are not in you in action or consent, you will still know, through the consideration of reason, how foul and worthless they are. With the gaze of reason you will also see the retribution for sins—that is, for evil actions and unlawful consents—to be rendered by God in the future.
