This seems to belong sufficiently to the purpose of praising God: he illuminates his own people to such an extent that they consider the worthlessness and foulness of sins, as well as the retribution to be rendered for them in the future, and thereby abhor sinning. I say that a thousand will fall; and this will not come about through my own strength.

But because you, O Lord, are my hope—that is, you will cause them to fall because you are my hope, because I place all my hope in you—and because you have established, that is, will establish, my refuge in the highest place, that is, an unconquerable refuge, like a tower situated in a very high place, which is strongly fortified and impregnable. This means: You will make yourself my refuge, that is, my most strongly fortified protection.

He repeats the thought equivalently, adding this: Since I have said, “They will fall at my side,” and so forth, I say, O soul, that the Lord is my hope and my refuge. Therefore evil—that is, a hidden temptation—will not approach you through consent; and in the future the scourge—that is, vengeance for this evil—will not approach your tabernacle, that is, you who are here serving God. This means: Neither here will you be overcome by hidden temptation, nor in the future will you be punished on account of it.

I possess security concerning this because, since God is my hope and my refuge, he has commanded his good angels concerning you—not by words, but through the hidden inspiration of his power—to guard you, lest you fail in all your ways, that is, in the virtues and good works that are ways for you to life. For we read that good angels were given by God to holy men for their guardianship and protection, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1:14).

I say that he will command the angels concerning you. Those angels will carry you in their hands, that is, they will cause you to advance through the support of their assistance. “Hands” signifies assistance, because by raising our hands we help those who are falling. They will carry you, therefore, lest perhaps—that is, lest in any way—you strike your foot, that is, your affection, against the stone of stumbling, Christ.

Christ is appropriately called a stone because, like a stone, he is the firmest foundation of our faith. Whoever thinks perversely about him in his mind strikes the foot of his heart against that stone. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense; and whoever falls upon that stone will be shattered, while upon whomever it falls, it will crush him” (Isaiah 8:14; Matthew 21; Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 8).

Affection is called the foot of the mind because through it the mind advances by thought. And carried by the assistance of those angels, you will walk upon the asp and the basilisk—that is, you will trample upon and overcome the asp, meaning the devil, who secretly bites through unlawful suggestions, like an asp, a serpent that bites covertly. You will trample beneath your affections the basilisk, meaning the gathering of those who act wickedly. Through the foul example of their evil action, they draw others to act wickedly unto death, like the basilisk serpent, which kills human beings with the stench of its breath.

You will trample, as though you did not yield, the lion, that is, persecutors who openly harass you, like a lion openly attacking; and you will trample upon the dragon, that is, heretics, who first bind the unwary with their false arguments and draw them to themselves, and afterward, by making them firm in allegiance to themselves, devour them, like a dragon that first binds an animal with its tail and then devours the animal it has bound.

He also introduces the Lord himself speaking, and does so to produce a fuller thanksgiving and to exhort the hearers more strongly, as follows: I say that the Lord commanded the angels, saying to those angels: Guard him carefully, because he has hoped in me, that is, he has placed all the hope of his salvation in me. Therefore I will free him from every assault of inward and outward enemies, so that they do not prevail over him; I will protect him in his virtues and good works, so that he does not fail.

And this is because he has known—in the true sense of knowing—the name “Lord.” This means: He has known me to be the Lord and himself to be a servant, so that he would not neglect to obey my commands. He cried out to me with intensity of voice and devotion, and I will hear him. I will do this by being with him in tribulation, and I will be with him according to my assisting grace. This means: I will guard him in tribulation, so that he does not fail.

At last, in the death of the flesh, I will rescue him from tribulation; and in the future I will glorify him with the glory of eternal blessing. In place of this transitory life, which he despised, I will fill him with length of days, that is, with eternal life. “I will fill him” is said emphatically. And because here he did not care for the salvation of the flesh, then I will show him my salvation, that is, a salvation conformed to my salvation, so that, just as I rose and became immortal and incapable of suffering, so they too may rise and exist immortal and incapable of suffering.

It should be noted that “I will show him my salvation” means the same as what he stated above, “I will glorify him,” except that here the statement is specified.

According to Augustine, two verses of this psalm—namely, “He will surround you with a shield,” and so forth, and “from the arrow,” and so forth—are read differently from the way we have expounded them above, so that three kinds of temptation may be indicated as follows:

I say that you will hope under his wings, and specifically you will hope that his truth, that is, his true promise, will surround you—that is, fortify you on every side—with a shield, that is, with protection. Thus you will not fear nocturnal fear, that is, an obscure and hidden, slight temptation. It is called “fear” because it is not so severe as a great temptation, just as fear is less than danger, from which fear arises. This means: He will make you so secure that you will not fear a slight, obscure temptation that sometimes draws an unwary person into consent.

You will also not fear the arrow, that is, a slight and manifest temptation. It is called an arrow because it wounds less severely than a great temptation, like an arrow, which wounds less severely than a lance. I say, an arrow flying toward you by day, that is, assailing you in the clarity of knowledge. This means: You will not fear yielding to a slight and manifest temptation.

You will not fear the business, that is, the greatest and most serious temptation, which is called “business” on account of the magnitude of its severity. For business cannot be spoken of in relation to a small matter. I say, business walking in darkness, that is, moving and advancing in obscurity. This means: You will not fear yielding to a great and serious obscure temptation.

You will not fear the assault and the noonday demon, that is, the demon coming upon you at noon. This means: You will not fear yielding to a serious temptation brought upon you openly by a demon. It is called an “assault” because it is serious and very great; and it is called “noonday” because it is open and manifest like midday. There is no need to alter the rest of the psalm.

## Psalm XCI

### The title of the ninety-first psalm

“A psalm of a song, for the Sabbath day.” This is expounded as follows:

This treatise contains a psalm, that is, a good work. That psalm is the occasion of a song, that is, of a joyful reward to be given by God on the Sabbath day, that is, in the brightness of eternal rest. “Sabbath” is interpreted as “rest.” This means: It is the reward that God will give his faithful on the eighth day, which is called “the day” by an antonomasia on account of its surpassing brightness, and “the Sabbath day,” that is, the day of eternal rest.

Or it may be understood in this way: This psalm of a song, that is, this treatise of joy in which the faithful who work here greatly rejoice, belongs to those who have already been placed in the Sabbath day, that is, in the brightness of rest. They have such a clear conscience that it is like day, and they keep holiday from every evil thought; for this reason it is rightly called Sabbath, that is, rest.

In this psalm there is the voice of every perfect person, acting for the instruction of the lesser, concerning good work, because good work is performed with a song and on the lyre, and concerning the destruction of those unwilling to do good and the future retribution for good work.

It is good to confess to the Lord, that is, it is useful to praise you, Lord, in the purity of devotion, since you are Lord of all. It is also good to sing to your name, O Most High, that is, it is useful to act well, not for human favor but for the honor of your name, since you are Most High, that is, almighty, and therefore sufficient to reward those who confess and sing to you.

I say that it is good to confess and to sing, going from confession and psalmody to proclaiming in the morning, that is, in prosperity, your mercy to others. This means: After someone has confessed and sung within himself, it is good for him to proclaim to others who are still ignorant, and who think that prosperity has been given to them by God on account of their merits, that they are prosperous through God’s mercy.

He should also go to proclaim your truth through the night, that is, that your judgment is true and just in adversity. This means: The one who confesses and sings should also proclaim to the ignorant, who think that they suffer adversity unjustly, that the just judgment of God accompanies them throughout all their adversity, namely, that all their adversity occurs by the just judgment of God.

It should be noted that, by first saying that it is good to confess and sing, and afterward to proclaim, he implies that it is fitting first for each person to confess and sing to God within himself, and afterward to proclaim this same thing to others both by example and by words.

He shows in what manner one should sing to God and to others when he adds: I say that it is good to sing on a ten-stringed psaltery, that is, in a soul adorned with the ten commandments of the law, after the likeness of a ten-stringed psaltery adorned with ten strings on which it resounds.

This means: It is good to act well with the affection of a soul resounding with the adornment of the ten commandments, and not unwillingly but with a song, that is, with the greatest joy, and while existing on the lyre, that is, in the mortification of the flesh. For it is fitting to mortify the flesh, lest it be able to resist the law of the mind. “Those who belong to Christ,” as the Apostle says, “crucify their flesh” (Galatians 5:24).

He shows, as an example of humility, through what means it is good for him to confess and sing to God, when he adds: I say that it is good to confess and sing to God; and this very thing that is good for me does not come from me but from you, O Lord. For you have delighted me, that is, you have caused me to delight, O Lord, in your work, that is, in the confession and psalmody that you have caused to exist in me. I will not cease from this delight but will persevere in rejoicing in the works of your hands, that is, in the consideration of confession and psalmody, which are the works of your hands, that is, of your grace.

Grace is appropriately called a hand because you work through it, and therefore I shall rightly rejoice in these works. For how greatly—indeed, very greatly—your works have been magnified in me, O Lord.

Since someone might ask why, if you act well and sing by God’s grace, every wicked person is not also assisted by the same grace to do this, he shows that this is inscrutable when he adds:

I say that it is good for me to confess and sing, and that these works have been magnified in me; but your thoughts are exceedingly profound, that is, your dispositions are most profound and unsearchable: that you assist me to confess and sing, while you reject others.

Since he had implied that he did not know by what disposition he was assisted by God while many were rejected, lest he be thought likewise ignorant of what end the prosperity of the wicked would come to, he shows their destruction, which he says they themselves do not know. He does this for the instruction of his hearers, so that they may beware lest, through ignorance, they come to the same destruction.

The passage is therefore adapted by supplying something from outside the book:

I say that these thoughts of yours are exceedingly profound, and therefore they are unknown to me. But this I do not fail to know: the senseless and the fool will perish forever and ever, that is, eternally, although here they flourish briefly and transitorily, like grass, whose flower quickly falls.

Moreover, the senseless man, that is, the unbeliever who does not know God, and the fool, that is, the false Christian who, although he possesses knowledge of God and could understand that the wicked will perish by God’s just judgment, nevertheless, blinded by the obstinacy of his wickedness, will not understand this with a true and effective understanding, so that all who persist in committing iniquity will perish forever and ever, that is, will be destined to die eternally.

This is so although here they have sprung up like grass, that is, although here they have grown in earthly prosperity, in the likeness of grass, which grows quickly and quickly withers; and although here they have appeared to others in the flower of their prosperity, famous and glorious.

I say that they will perish. But you, O Lord, Son, who have appeared almighty, will appear Most High, that is, almighty, in the salvation of your own and in the just destruction of the wicked.

Since he had said that they would perish, someone might ask, “Why do you say that they will perish?” He answers as follows: I rightly say that they will perish, because behold, it is already certain to me as though present that your enemies, the unbelievers, will perish in the future, and all who practice iniquity, namely, the false Christians, will be scattered, that is, separated from the company of those who are to be saved.

His repetition, “Behold, your enemies,” serves to terrify the enemies more greatly. I say that they will perish and be scattered; but, in opposition to this, my horn, that is, the exaltation of my virtues, or my hope, which is strong and grows upward like a horn, will be exalted, that is, will advance higher and higher, like a unicorn—that is, my horn, since I am a unicorn, possessing one hope, faith, and charity, and not entangled in various heresies.

In the future my old age, that is, the life to be given me by God after death, which is called old age because it will be the last stage, after the likeness of old age, which is the final part of human life, will be in abundant mercy, that is, in copious mercy. This means: Having obtained God’s mercy here through the remission of sins, in the future I shall obtain abundant mercy in my old age, when I become immortal and incapable of suffering.

Or it may be understood as follows: My old age, that is, the gravity of my conduct, which is understood by “old age” because gravity of conduct exists in the old, will be in abundant mercy, that is, will be abundantly rewarded.

With this in view, my inward eye, namely, my reason, looked down—and will look down—upon my inward and outward enemies. When the wicked rise up against me, that is, when persecutors acting wickedly rise against me with persecutions, my inward ear, namely, the ear of reason, will hear, for my encouragement not to fail, the Spirit speaking inwardly to me.

And behold, this is what it will say to me: Do not fail through fear of those who rise up to turn you away from justice. For every just person will flourish like a palm tree, that is, after the likeness of a palm tree. Just as the palm tree is rough and full of knobs in its lower part, near the ground, but beautiful and flourishing in its upper part, so the just person in this lowly life is rough and full of tribulations, but in the higher life, eternal life, will be flourishing and conspicuous in blessedness.

He will be multiplied in blessedness like the cedar of Lebanon, that is, after the likeness of the cedar of Lebanon, which is taller than other cedars. This means: He will be exalted in manifold blessedness like the cedar of Lebanon.

Or it may be understood as follows: He will be multiplied like the cedar of Lebanon, that is, of whiteness, as one exalted in the whitening, that is, the purification, of virtues. For “Lebanon” is interpreted as “whiteness” or “purification.”

Having introduced these words of the Holy Spirit for his greater exhortation, he expounds them as actions performed in the Spirit’s own person, as follows:

The Holy Spirit says: O hearers, the just will flourish; and behold, I tell you how they will flourish. Planted here, namely through virtues and good works, in the house of God, that is, in the Church, they will flourish in the future, existing in eternal glory—not in the house of God, that is, in equality with the angels, who are the heavenly house of God, but in the courts of that house of our God, that is, in affinity with and subordination to the angels, which is signified by the court. Although a court is near the house, it is nevertheless less worthy than the house and less glorious.

This means: They will flourish in such a way that they will be to some extent akin to the heavenly spirits, though not altogether similar or equal to them. Hence the Lord testifies concerning John: “The one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he” (Luke 7:28). Blessed Jerome affirms that this was spoken of the least of the angels.

Since he had said that the just would have flowers and would be multiplied, he specifies when this will happen, lest it appear that it would happen in the present:

I say that they will flourish and be multiplied. This, however, will not happen immediately; it will happen after a long time. Then they will be multiplied and flourish, existing in abundant old age, that is, in the final life, namely, eternal life, which will be abundant in every blessedness.

Or it may be understood as follows: They will be multiplied in the future, existing here in abundant old age, that is, because here they remain in abundant gravity of conduct.

They would not otherwise be multiplied; therefore, in the meantime, they will exist here without murmuring in adversity but enduring well, that is, bearing it with charity and patience. They will endure so well that by other words and by their example they will proclaim that the Lord Jesus Christ, our God, is just—the one who ordains that his own suffer here so that through this they may be blessed with eternal glory.

He is not merely just in the way human beings are just, who are just in part and unjust in part; rather, he is perfectly just, so that there is no iniquity in him. In accordance with what Moses says concerning him: “The faithful God, without any iniquity, just and upright” (Deuteronomy 32:4).

## Psalm XCII

### The title of the ninety-second psalm

“A song of praise of David, on the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was founded.” This is expounded as follows:

This psalm is a praise of David, that is, made by the prophet for the praise of Christ, the true David. It is a praise of a song, that is, of exceedingly great joy, possessed on the day before the Sabbath, that is, in contemplation of the sixth day, which is before the Sabbath—namely, in contemplation of the sixth age, which was signified by the day before the Sabbath, in which God created humanity.

For the six ages of the world are read as corresponding to the six days of the week apart from the Sabbath. The first age, therefore, is from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to Moses; the fourth from Moses to David; the fifth from David to John the Baptist; and the sixth from John to the end of the world.

This sixth age is before the Sabbath, that is, near to the Sabbath, namely, eternal life, which truly is the Sabbath, that is, rest. It was the time when the earth was founded, that is, the time in which, during the sixth age, God founded through faith and virtues the immovable earth, namely, the Church.

Thus in this psalm there is the voice of the prophet showing, for the praise of God, the preparation of the Church through the teaching of the apostles, the persecutions inflicted upon the apostles by the rulers of the earth, and finally those persecutions calmed by the power of God.

The Lord has reigned, that is, the Lord Jesus, who will be handed over by the Jews to death, will finally reign, claiming for himself the kingdom of the whole world after trampling upon death. He will reign throughout the whole world because he has put on beauty, that is, he will put on and unite to himself through faith the apostles, beautiful in every perfection, and he will be adorned by them as a body is adorned by garments.

He has put on strength, that is, he will put on and unite to himself those same apostles, strong in steadfastness, after the likeness of a good king who has beautiful and courageous soldiers. With these strong and beautiful men he has girded himself, that is, he will gird himself, adorning himself on every side in order to subdue the nations and subject them to himself, after the likeness of a king who girds himself with a sword to conquer an enemy.

This means: Those beautiful and strong men whom he will put on will be his weapons, by which he will subject the enemy to himself.

He therefore shows for what purpose he will gird himself with them when he adds: Truly he will put on the beautiful and strong, and with them he will gird himself. For through their preaching he established, that is, will establish, the inhabited world, that is, the perfection of the Church, making the Church firm in every perfection through their teaching.

The inhabited world will be so firm that it will not be shaken, either in prosperity or in adversity. From that time onward—that is, from the time when the earth has been founded—your throne, O God, will be prepared in that earth; from that time your throne will be established there, although long before it had been the throne of the devil.

But lest he appear not to have existed before the preparation of his throne, he adds: Although your throne will be prepared from that time, you nevertheless exist from eternity, that is, from everlasting, without beginning.

Your throne will therefore be prepared through this, and the inhabited world will be made firm, because the rivers, that is, the apostles, who will water hearts toward God with teaching, have raised, O Lord, their voice, that is, they will raise the voice of their preaching, which had been suppressed by fear during your Passion.

I say, the rivers will raise their voice. He repeats this for confirmation. Against the voice of these rivers there are other rivers, namely, the earthly rulers, who are called rivers because their care flows over the people subject to them, after the likeness of rivers flowing into the sea.

They have raised their waves, that is, they will raise their persecutions, by which they will plunge the apostles into death, after the manner of waves. This will happen because of the voices of many waters, that is, on account of the voices of many nations, which will be unstable like water.

This means: The rulers will persecute them because very many nations will judge them to be profane and sacrilegious.

Or it may be understood as follows: This will happen because of the voices of many waters, that is, on account of the voices of many preachers. They will persecute them because, through the apostles, they will grieve to see many others become waters, that is, because they will observe many others, following the apostles’ example, becoming people who water human beings through teaching.

I say that they will raise their waves, and these raised persecutions of rulers who embitter God will be marvelous because of their excessive magnitude and harshness. But the Lord will be even more marvelous in calming these great and deep swellings.

This means: The Lord will be more marvelous because, whenever he wishes, he will calm these swellings. And you will calm them, O Lord, through this: Your testimonies, that is, your commandments, preached by the apostles, which testify to life for those who fulfill them, have become—or will become—exceedingly credible to the sea, however detestable they may initially appear to it.

Through this same sea, once transformed, your house, in which you dwell spiritually, is adorned by your holiness, that is, by the holiness to be given by you. This means: Through the fact that they believe your testimonies, they will become your house and will be adorned with fitting holiness.

I say, your house will proceed through holiness into length of days, that is, into eternal life, which is emphatically called “length of days” because it will never end.

Or it may be understood as follows: It will come into being through that very holiness in the length of days. The meaning is the same.

## Psalm XCIII

### The title of the ninety-third psalm

“A song of praise of David, for the fourth day of the Sabbath.” This is expounded as follows:

This psalm is a song of praise, that is, a praise of joy. This means: In this treatise there is contained praise performed with exceedingly great joy. It is the praise of David, designated by the fourth day of the Sabbath, namely, the praise of the faithful who are perfect in knowledge.

They were prefigured by the work that occurred on the fourth day of the Sabbath. On the fourth day God made the luminaries that illuminate the earth; they are firm and immovable from the purpose of their appointed function. Through them the perfect were prefigured, for they will illuminate the Church, which is God’s earth, firmly through their teaching and by their example.

Concerning them the Lord himself says: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

Or, according to Blessed Jerome, it may be understood as follows: David is designated by the fourth day of the Sabbath, that is, through the fourth day of the week, which among the Latins is called Wednesday.

The more perfect faithful in knowledge are appropriately understood through the fourth day. Just as the fourth day, situated in the middle of the week, has three days preceding it and three following it, so the perfect men of the New Testament exist in the middle of the two Testaments, namely, the preceding Old Testament and the subsequent New Testament, while striving to be the completion of both.

The two Testaments are suitably understood through the number three because, if both Testaments are carefully examined, the instruction concerning faith in the Holy Trinity is found in each. In the Old Testament the faith of the Trinity is indicated where it is read concerning Abraham: “He saw three and worshiped one” (Genesis 18:3).

Since this same faith is also signified in the New Testament, it can be made manifest by many examples.

This psalm is rightly called the joyful praise of the faithful. In this psalm the faithful who are perfect in knowledge, acting against false Christians who promise themselves impunity for their crimes, praise God while asserting that he will judge with just vengeance those whom he presently tolerates with mild patience.

They also speak concessively concerning the retribution of their condemnation. And lest they seem to be cursing them, they complain about their iniquity, which they also display in its several parts.

They further exhort the wicked themselves to live rightly and to understand rightly concerning God, showing by certain arguments that he both understands and sees their impieties and will punish them in the future. They show also that the tribulations of the good do not lead to their rejection but to blessedness.

They admonish these good people to resist the wicked, yet in such a way that they place their confidence not in themselves but in the Lord, so as not to fail.

All this is done for the instruction of the ignorant, who, when they see the prosperity of the wicked and the adversity of the good, become indignant because they do not know for what purpose these things are permitted by God.

God of vengeance, the Lord who works vengeance, is indeed God. I say, God who will work vengeance acted freely, that is, he will exercise the freedom of his power against the wicked. He appears powerless to them because he deals mercifully with them, waiting for them and enduring them.

It is as though he said: You promise yourselves impunity for your crimes, O false Christians; but in the future God will act freely against you by taking vengeance on you, since he is able to do so because he is God and since it belongs to him to do so because he is Lord.

They speak concessively of his vengeance against them, as follows: I say, O God, that you will act freely; and I concede that this should happen, O Christ: exalt yourself, that is, appear powerful. Although you may seem powerless or negligent concerning earthly affairs, you nevertheless judge this present earth according to your disposition, so that nothing occurs in it without your command or permission.

Exalt yourself in this manner: in the future, render the retribution of just condemnation to the proud, that is, to false Christians who do not repent but persist proudly in neglecting repentance.

Lest they seem to have uttered a curse, they piously complain about the wickedness of those same people, as follows:

Although, concessively, we say, “Render retribution to the proud,” nevertheless, O Lord, how long will sinners—by antonomasia, the false Christians—how long, that is, to what extent or for how long, will sinners glory in their iniquity?

By placing this in the form of a question, they indicate that they feel great sorrow for them. It is as though he said: Although we concede that retribution should be rendered to them, nevertheless we complain that they will live long and glory in their iniquity. For the greater and longer-lasting their glorying, the harsher their future retribution will be.

We would therefore prefer that their life and glorying should end quickly, so that their retribution might be milder.

They do not merely glory in their iniquity; they also utter this iniquity, that is, speak it outwardly—speak it publicly—and talk about it privately among themselves.

How long, that is, to what extent or for how long, will all who persistently practice injustice, living wickedly, publicly utter and privately speak iniquity, that is, speak iniquitous words?

It is as though he said: We would prefer their life to end, so that they could no longer speak and utter iniquity or practice injustice, and so that they might consequently be punished more mildly for it.

He therefore explains that injustice itself in its several parts, as follows:

Truly they practice and have practiced injustice. For they have humbled your people, O Lord, namely, those who serve you, with insults and verbal reproaches; and they have harassed that same people, who are your inheritance, whom you cultivate through the teaching of preachers as one cultivates an inheritance, with excessive tribulations.

And not only this: they have also slain the widow and the sojourner, and they have killed the orphans.

This means: They have killed bodily many of your faithful, who were comparable to widows, sojourners, and orphans.

They were comparable to widows because they had been deprived of the consolation of temporal goods, which they had already rejected, just as widows are deprived of the help of husbands who have died.

They were comparable to sojourners because they did not make themselves citizens of this earthly homeland but sought the future one, just as sojourners intend to return to the homeland from which they are absent.

They were comparable to orphans because they were without the devil, who had previously been their father, and without unbelief, which had been their mother, just as orphans are without a father and mother who have died.

Or this may appropriately be understood literally. Widows, sojourners, and orphans, existing without anyone’s assistance, are defended by the help of God alone; therefore they are called his people. Hence he is also called “the father of orphans and judge of widows” (Psalm 67:6).

I say that they have humbled your people, harassed your inheritance, slain the widow and the sojourner, and killed the orphans.

And in doing these things, as an addition to the sum of their misery, they said: “We may safely humble, afflict, and [Col. 1138A] kill them. For the Lord will neither see nor understand this, nor will the God of Jacob, so as to punish it.” It was exceedingly inappropriate, however, that they should say that he did not see this who is the omnipotent Lord, and that they should say that he did not understand it who is the God of Jacob—that is, of those same faithful people who struggle valiantly, whom they humbled, afflicted, and killed.

He therefore turns in direct address to these same wicked men, exhorting them to understand and see rightly concerning God, as follows: I say that you claim, O false Christians, that God neither understands nor sees what you wickedly do against his servants. Yet you, who exist among God’s people not by your conduct but by participation in the sacraments, and who are foolish—that is, capable of readily understanding rightly concerning God, since you have already advanced somewhat in knowledge of him, yet neglect to pay attention—understand, that is, take note, that the Lord sees and understands what you wickedly do against his servants. And you, fools among God’s people, who are unlearned and dull, and slow to acquire this understanding, finally become wise concerning what you have hitherto been unable to understand: namely, that God hears—that is, understands—and sees what you do wickedly, and that in the future he will rebuke these things.

And behold, this is how it can be proved that he both hears and sees all your evil deeds, and that these evils will be rebuked by him in the future. For “he who planted the ear, does he not hear?” Indeed, he will hear. And “he who formed the eye, does he not observe what you do?” Certainly, he observes it. And he who rebukes the nations here through the Scriptures, lest they sin—will he not rebuke in the future, through condemnation, those who here neglect his correction? Indeed, he will rebuke them. For he would rebuke them here to no purpose if he were not going to rebuke them in the future.

And he who teaches human beings knowledge—that is, he who through his teaching makes that human being knowledgeable, that is, rationally ordered—does he not know? Certainly, the Lord knows not only their deeds but also, what is more, he knows the thoughts of human beings, because they are vain. That is, he knows that your thoughts, since you are merely human beings and not spiritual, are vain and worthy of punishment.

The whole passage is as though he had put it this way: It is proved that he hears them because it would be inappropriate for him not to hear, since he planted the ears of all human beings—that is, formed them from the clay of the earth. And it is proved that he sees because it would be inappropriate for him not to see, since he formed every eye. And it is proved that he will rebuke in the future because otherwise he would rebuke here in vain. And it is thereby established that he knows, because it would be inappropriate for him not to know, since he teaches every human being whatever that person knows.

Having offered this exhortation to the false Christians, he intends to show that the tribulations of the good contribute to their blessedness, as follows: Therefore, because you see, know, and hear everything, it is thereby proved that every person whom you, knowing and seeing all things, instruct through tribulations will be blessed. That is, you will bring that person out of ignorance, instructing him through many anxieties that present things are not the highest goods and are not to be desired, and that there are other goods—namely, spiritual ones—which are to be desired.

God instructs his own through anxieties because, while he permits them here to be afflicted and deprived of present goods, he indicates that these goods are not the highest goods, since they are lost in this way; nor is this life happy, in which they are afflicted in this way. Rather, there are other highest goods and another eternal and blessed life, which are to be sought.

What he says, “Blessed is the person whom you will instruct,” is equivalent to saying: Instruction through tribulations will be the cause of blessedness. And lest the person who is to become blessed in the future fail here amid the instruction of tribulations, “you will teach him from your law”—that is, you will teach him through the instruction of your law that this instruction is to be endured patiently. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke 9:23).

He then inserts the reason why he will teach him, adding: For this reason, that is, you will teach him through your law, “so that you may give relief to him who is embittered by evil days.” That is, so that you may grant the relief of patience to the one who is embittered by days of tribulation, which are called evil because the evils of many tribulations press upon them. This is equivalent to saying: You will teach him for this reason, so that he may not fail under the burden of tribulations by which he is embittered.

I say, “by evil days” that will not last forever, but only until “the pit of the sinner is dug”—that is, until the future condemnation of the sinner who persecutes the faithful is completed. This was said by comparison with one whose pit is dug so that he may afterward be thrown into it. It should be noted that he says this for the consolation of the good and the terror of the wicked.

Having inserted the reason why he will teach, he shows what he will teach, as follows: The Lord will teach this through the instruction of his law: that the Lord himself will not reject his people, even though he permits them to be afflicted. That is, he will teach that he does not permit his people to be afflicted for the purpose of rejecting or neglecting them. He will also teach that, although he permits this same people of his, who are his inheritance, to suffer tribulation, he will nevertheless not abandon his inheritance.

When he says “he will not abandon,” it is understood through litotes that he will assist his inheritance through tribulations, so that the tribulations themselves may be the cause of salvation for them. I say that he will not abandon his inheritance, but will assist it, and will assist it until justice—that is, Christ, who is called “justice” emphatically because all justice proceeds from him—“is turned into judgment.”

This is equivalent to saying: He will not reject them but will assist them through tribulations until Christ comes to judge the wicked, whom he patiently awaits here. He does not determine this in such a way as to imply that afterward he will reject his own; rather, because it is certain that afterward he will not reject his own, he does not exclude what follows. What is said here, that he will not reject them, had to be stated because here they appear, through tribulations, to be rejected and abandoned.

And who will be “according to that justice”—that is, who here will be conformed in virtues to that justice, and in the future will reign with it at the Father’s right hand? The answer is: All who are upright of heart will be according to it—not those who appear righteous merely in outward appearance through hypocrisy. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Tear your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2:13).

That he says that those who are upright of heart will be beside Christ is stated by comparison with a king who makes his dearer and more capable leaders sit beside him in his palace. What he puts interrogatively is equivalent to saying: Justice will be turned into judgment, and beside it will be all who are upright of heart, not merely in appearance.

Therefore, since all who are upright of heart will be beside it, who, wishing to be upright of heart, will rise from a bodily bed, joined to me through conformity, against those who act wickedly—that is, contradicting the adversaries of the Church, namely heretics and false Christians? Or who will stand—that is, who will persevere in fighting with me through contradiction against those who practice iniquity? [Col. 1140B] For it is not enough to rise unless one also stands.

Those who act wickedly and those who practice iniquity are the same. This was said by comparison with citizens who, when attacked at night by enemies, rise from the beds in which they were sleeping, climb onto the city wall, and stand there to defend it against the assault of the enemy. The fact that he puts this interrogatively serves to intensify the exhortation. It is as though he were saying: Therefore, since only the upright of heart will stand beside that justice, all of you who wish to be upright of heart—and by this to be beside it—rise against those who act wickedly, and stand with me against those who practice iniquity.

Although I thus exhort people to rise and stand, I am nevertheless unable by myself to rise and stand. For unless it were that the Lord remained because he assisted me through his assisting grace, my soul would have dwelt—that is, would have persevered—in hell, that is, in the consent of the wicked, which is rightly called hell because through it one comes to hell; and my soul was only very nearly, that is, by very little, removed from dwelling there.

He said this as an example of humility, so that the unlearned might not trust that they could stand by themselves. If the reading is “has dwelt,” it should be understood as follows: Unless it were that, because the Lord assisted me, my soul had dwelt in hell, it was only very nearly—that is, it almost dwelt there. The meaning is the same.

And truly you assisted me, Lord. For when in humble confession I said, “Assist me, Lord, because my foot has been moved”—that is, my affection—your mercy, Lord, assisted me, so that I would not fail completely. This is equivalent to saying: When my affection was moved and troubled by some unlawful suggestion, and I humbly confessed this to you and prayed for your help so that I would not fail, you assisted me through your mercy.

And because I did not merely say this to you but also grieved in many ways over the movement of my foot, repenting and praying that this unlawful disturbance might be forgiven me, the consolations of forgiveness—which I understood spiritually to have been given to me by you through repentance—made my soul rejoice.

I say that the consolations were given in many ways, according to the multitude—that is, in accordance with the multiplicity—of my griefs, which truly existed in my heart and did not merely appear outwardly through hypocrisy. This is equivalent to saying: Because I grieved in many ways over my disturbances, you granted me manifold forgiveness and thus consoled my soul.

Through this he therefore instructs his hearers to grieve deeply over their sins, so that they may obtain pardon. I say that the griefs were in my heart, and rightly I grieved in my heart. For if I had not grieved, I would have been a seat of iniquity, and thus I would not have clung to you, neither here through conformity nor in the future through participation in blessedness.

For does a seat of iniquity—that is, one in whom iniquity sits—cling to you, when you impose labor in the commandment, that is, when you devise grief or labor in the commandment? Certainly, such a person does not cling to you. It is as though he were saying: No one who is a seat of iniquity clings or will cling to you, since you give the command that no one should be a seat of iniquity, and in that command you devise—that is, appoint—labor; namely, you ordain that this commandment be fulfilled not negligently but with the greatest labor and care.

Or, if we read “grief,” it should be understood as follows: You give the command that no one should be a seat of iniquity, and you devise grief in the commandment—that is, in completing this commandment you ordain the grief of tribulations. This is equivalent to saying: Since those who fulfill this commandment must undergo manifold griefs of tribulation, you devise—that is, ordain—the grief itself, distributing it to each person according to what he is able to endure. In accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

I say that you devise grief, and this grief is of such a kind: the wicked, proceeding according to their evil desire, go against the soul of the righteous and seek to capture that soul; indeed, they will still frequently seek to capture it through their deceptions and make it conform to themselves. And because they will not be able to capture it, they will condemn innocent blood—that is, the blood of the righteous—through its shedding and death.

According to the reading “you devise labor,” the following verse is connected in the manner already explained, without any change in the interpretation: I say that a seat of iniquity does not cling to you, and rightly so. For those who are seats of iniquity will seek to capture the soul, and so forth.

I say that the wicked will condemn innocent blood. But lest we fear and fail because of their condemnation, the one who is Lord—that is, who has become powerful for me and for those conformed to me—has become a refuge for us, that is, a source of security. And that same Lord, who is my God—that is, the Creator—has become a help for me and for those conformed to me, so that we may not fail.

I say that he exists as the cause of my hope, for these things are my pledge and guarantee that I will have hope of being gladdened in the future. I say that the Lord is a refuge and help for me and for those conformed to me. Or: My God has become my hope—that is, the thing hoped for by me. This is equivalent to saying: Through tribulations he assists me, so that at last I may reach the thing hoped for, namely, eternal blessedness.

And in the future he will repay those who seek to capture our souls and condemn our blood with their iniquity—that is, with the recompense for their iniquity—and, namely, in their wickedness, because of the merit of their wickedness, he will utterly destroy them. He will destroy them, I say, the one who is our Lord. Therefore he ought to concern himself with our vengeance; and because he is our God, he is able to destroy them.

He says this to deter the wicked from their wickedness, lest they promise themselves impunity on the grounds that the tribulations inflicted by them become salvation for the righteous. For God does not consider what they do to the righteous through their tribulations, but rather what they intend wickedly.

381. ON PSALM 94

The title of the ninety-fourth psalm is: “Praise of a song of David.” It is explained as follows: This psalm is the praise of a song—that is, the praise of joy and gladness—and it belongs not to David but to Christ.

In this psalm the Prophet, praising the Christ who was to come out of an excess of joy, exhorts the unbelieving Jews who would exist in the fullness of time to come to him by faith at last in the sixth age, and to rejoice, exult, and give thanks to him. He also exhorts them not to harden their hearts at the voice of Christ, and thereby to lose eternal rest, just as their fathers provoked God in the desert and therefore, having been struck down, did not reach the rest of the promised land.

It should be noted, however, that in this psalm the Prophet places certain words in the person of the Lord himself, namely when he says, “where they tempted me,” and so forth, through the end. He does not do this contrary to custom, since in histories and prophecies we frequently find angels and prophets saying many things in the person of the Lord.

Come, by faith in the time of the fullness, O Jews, who for a long time have been separated from God through unbelief; and by coming, let us exult in the Lord Christ. It is as though he were saying: Just as I, existing so long beforehand, rejoice with good affection over his coming, so you, who will exist at that time, should rejoice over his coming.

And we ought to rejoice in him because the Lord is omnipotent. Let us not rejoice in him only a little, but let us shout for joy to him, our saving God. This is equivalent to saying: Just as I already shout for joy to him—that is, rejoice with an exceeding and intense inward joy—so you too should shout for joy to him, because he is God, that is, the Creator, and saving, that is, the Savior.

Let us not merely rejoice in our hearts, but also, persevering in confession—that is, in praise by the mouth—let us go before his face. Let us be like servants who go before the face of their lord in order to make him attentive to them before he is occupied with other business.

This is equivalent to saying: Let us be diligent and persevering in confessing his praise, after the manner of servants who, as I have said, go before the face of their lord.

Or it may be understood this way: Let us diligently go before his face in confession of our sins—that is, let us anticipate his coming. This is equivalent to saying: Let us confess our sins in this life, lest at the second coming we be condemned with those who do not confess. “For now is the acceptable time; now is the day of salvation” (1 Corinthians 6:2).

The second coming is rightly called the face, because then Christ will be manifested to all, just as the whole person is known through the face.

I have said that we should shout for joy to God. And because this is not sufficient unless we also act well, let us shout for joy to him inwardly in psalms—that is, in good works—persevering outwardly.

It is fitting that we exult in him, shout for joy to him, and confess him, because he is God and exists as Lord over all things. And he is not just any kind of lord, but great in power and a great king in governance, existing above all gods—that is, more worthy and excellent than all the prelates of the Church, who will have been made divine in holiness.

In accordance with this, the Lord said concerning Moses: “I have appointed you god of Pharaoh” (Exodus 7:1). These same prelates are also the Lord’s, since they possess lordship and authority over their subjects. They are also their kings, since they rule them by their teaching and example.

He therefore assigns each quality to its proper subject, adding: Truly he is a great king, because in his hand—that is, in the governance of his operative grace—are the ends of the earth, that is, those who bring earthly-mindedness to an end in themselves.

This is equivalent to saying: The fact that the faithful bring earthly-mindedness to an end in themselves is due to his governance. And it is evident from this that he is a great king; indeed, the Lord is truly great, because the heights of the mountains—that is, the lofty mountains, namely the perfect—are his possession.

This is equivalent to saying: The fact that the perfect are lofty in virtues and holiness results from his dwelling in them, possessing them, and ruling them. And this shows that he is a great Lord, since it belongs to a great lord to have a great possession.

It is also clear from this that he is a great Lord, because the sea is his possession—that is, he possesses those unbelievers who embitter God, so that they are not permitted to rage against the saints except insofar as he himself permits.

382. And it is proved that God is great because he who is the possessor of that sea also made it—that is, he created the embittered people, not insofar as they are sea, but insofar as they are creatures.

It is also established by this that God is great: his hands formed the dry land—that is, the works of his grace made the Church, previously disfigured in Adam, beautiful in virtues and good works. It is “dry” because it thirsts for the teaching of God’s word, just as dry land thirsts to be filled with water.

Having interposed this praise of him, he repeats the preceding exhortation on the occasion of this praise, adding: I have said that Christ will be God, king, and great Lord. Therefore, because he will be such, O Jews who will exist at his coming, come to him by faith; and by coming, let us adore him—that is, just as I adore him, venerating him through intense and particular prayer, so you too should adore him.

And let us fall prostrate—that is, let us humble ourselves in soul, which is signified by falling bodily to the ground—and let us weep over our sins, not before the gaze of human praise but before the Lord, that is, before the gaze of the Lord who made, or created, us. Therefore we ought to adore him.

And because he who appears to have been born in time is nevertheless our God, he is not a newly made god but the eternal God whom we prophets worship and adore.

I say that he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture—that is, the people whom he fed with manna in the desert through our fathers, and whom he also feeds with the law. We are the sheep of his hand—that is, of his work—for he worked by grace in the desert so that we might be like sheep, neither plowing nor sowing, yet possessing everything necessary, just as sheep are provided with everything necessary by their shepherd without any labor on their part.

Having made this exhortation in his own person, he adds the warning of the Holy Spirit in order to attract them more effectively. The Spirit exhorts them not to harden their hearts at the voice of the Lord Christ, as follows:

I have exhorted you, O Jews, to exult in the Lord Christ, to shout for joy, and to adore him, since he is our Lord and we are the sheep of his pasture. The Holy Spirit also exhorts you to obey him, saying: If you hear the voice of his preaching—as indeed you will hear it “today,” that is, in the sixth age, which will be your “today,” namely the present time, just as the present day is called “today”—do not harden your hearts; that is, do not harden your hearts against this voice by neglecting it.

Do not be like your fathers, whose hearts were hardened in provocation—that is, at the time when God was provoked. The sixth age is also called “today” because it is bright through the teaching of Christ and radiant, after the manner of day.

Since he had said “as in provocation,” although their provocations against God had been many, he indicates which provocation he means by adding: I say, do not harden your hearts as in the provocation—namely, do not harden them according to the day of testing, that is, after the likeness of the day of testing that occurred in the desert, where, or in which desert, your fathers tested me, doubting whether I could give them drink and food.

You are their children not only according to generation but also according to conformity in unbelief. They tested me, I say—that is, they tempted me—and they saw with the eyes of the body the wonderful works that I performed among them for forty years in the desert.

The whole passage is as though it were briefly put this way: You unbelieving Jews, who are going to hear Christ’s voice, do not harden your hearts after the manner of your fathers, who tempted him in the desert and saw his works for forty years, yet nevertheless hardened their hearts.

I say that they tempted me, and therefore, being offended—that is, angered—I was against that most wicked generation. “Offended” is used for “angered,” because those who are offended customarily become angry.

I say that I was offended, and yet, for their correction, I always—that is, frequently—said through Moses and their other teachers: “They wander in their heart” through unbelief.

And although I had said this for their correction, they nevertheless did not understand in such a way as to complete my ways—that is, my commandments. For to those who complete them, they are ways to life; but to those who do not complete them, they are ways to death.

And because they did not understand, I swore that they would never enter my eternal rest—or, in my anger, that is, in my just vengeance, I firmly decreed that they would not enter. If this is not so, then I am not a true and just judge.

If this is set down with deliberate restraint for the sake of the hearers’ correction, lest they likewise harden their hearts and lose rest, it should be understood as follows: Because they did not understand my ways, they will not enter my rest. For I swore this in my anger.

Or, according to another translation: I swore to them in my anger that they would not enter my rest—that is, the promised land, where there will be rest, which I will give to their children. And since I swore that they would not enter, if they do enter that rest of mine, then I am a liar.

IN PSALM 95

The title of the ninety-fifth psalm is: “When the house was being built after the captivity, a song of David.” It is explained as follows:

This song—that is, this psalm called a song because it exhorts people to sing a new song, or because it was composed amid great joy and gladness—belongs to the prophet David. It was composed by the Prophet when the house was being built, in the Prophet’s contemplation, after the captivity.

This is equivalent to saying: He composed this song at the time when, through the spirit of prophecy, he already contemplated that the human race, which had been destroyed through Adam and led into captivity, would at last, after the period of captivity, be built up in virtues through Christ, so that it might be the house of God, in which he would dwell spiritually.

He rightly says “was being built.” For in the Prophet’s contemplation the house was already being built, although it was to be built in reality only after a long period. As the Prophet contemplated the future building of this house, he exhorted all who would be in that house to sing a new song to God.

In order that this song might be sung, he admonishes the prelates, the preachers of this house, to announce God’s wonders to the nations, and the nations to obey them. He affirms that all who are built into that house will exult when God judges the world justly.

He does this with the intention of drawing everyone to participation in the house that is to be built and to the singing of a new song.

Sing to the Lord Christ a new song. Sing, I say, not only you Jews, but every land—that is, all kinds of earthly people, both Jews and nations.

He calls those commandments “a new song” which were not given in the Old Testament but only in the New, and in whose fulfillment God delights as though in a song: such commandments as loving enemies, despising earthly things, dying for one’s neighbor, and other things of this kind.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 13:34). And elsewhere: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:20).

What he says, “Sing to the Lord a new song,” is equivalent to saying: Act with delight for the honor of the Lord in the new song; that is, fulfill the commandments that he will give in the New Testament. Do not do so unwillingly or for human approval, but sing—that is, fulfill with a song—with gladness, and do this for the Lord, that is, for the Lord’s honor.

Since he says “sing” three times, this serves for insistence, so that he may exhort more strongly; or he repeats it three times to manifest the Trinity. It is as though he were saying: Sing to the Lord the Father, sing to the Lord the Son, sing to the Lord the Spirit. And by singing, bless his name—that is, exalt and glorify this name of his, “Lord,” by living well and performing every good work.

This is equivalent to saying: Devote yourselves to good works, which are the reason that God’s name is blessed by those who see them. For just as through those who act badly “the name of God is blasphemed among the nations” (Romans 2:24), so through those who act well it is exalted.

He then turns in direct address to the prelates, as follows: I exhort all who will be in the house of God, both Jews and gentiles, to sing a new song to the Lord and to bless his name.

But because the gentiles would not otherwise sing this song, nor would the Lord’s name be blessed, you preachers announce his salvation—that is, the salvation of the Lord Christ—namely, how he will save the world through his death.

I say, announce it by going from day to day—that is, from the brightness of the New Testament into the brightness of the Old, and from the brightness of the Old into the brightness of the New. Announce it in such a way that you confirm your preaching by the authority of both Testaments, bringing forth “new and old things from the treasure of your heart” (Matthew 13:52).

Or, “going from day to day” means going from one bright virtue and work to another, brighter virtue and work, lest, while you preach to others, you yourselves become reprobate.

Or, “going from day to day” means going from the brightness of the Father into the brightness of the Son, and from the brightness of the Son into the brightness of the Father, so that through one you may show the other.

Or, literally, “going from day to day”: announce his salvation frequently, on each successive day.

Announce also among the nations—that is, in the fullness of the nations—his glory, namely the glory of the Lord Christ. Announce that he is glorious; announce that he is Lord, God, and omnipotent, and announce whatever else pertains to his glory. And among all peoples—that is, in the fullness of all peoples—announce his wonders, which he will perform in the human race.

He explains how they are to announce his glory, as follows: I say, announce his glory. Announce that he who will appear small and almost servant-like among the Jews is Lord; and not merely any lord, but a great one, to whom all things will be subjected.

And he who will appear contemptible is worthy of praise—that is, worthy of praise—and not merely a little, but exceedingly, beyond what every creature could praise.

And he who will appear to fear in the Passion will be terrible—that is, to be feared by his enemies—and not merely a little, but terrible above all gods, that is, more than all the perfect whom he will make divine. For although they will be powerful in punishing enemies through the merit of their prayers, and therefore terrible, he will be much more terrible, since he is more powerful in punishing.

But lest he appear to be speaking of the gods of the nations—which would certainly not be an extraordinary praise—he makes a distinction as follows: I say that he is terrible above all gods, but I do not say this of the gods of the nations, for all the gods of the nations are demons; therefore such a comparison would be unworthy.

For demons, entering the idols of the nations, gave responses, and for this reason were worshiped by the nations as gods.

He adds, to heap up praise: “But the Lord made the heavens.” Here “but” is used in place of “rather,” and it heightens the statement. The sense is as follows: He is not only more terrible than the gods, but, existing as Lord of all, he himself made those gods heavens—that is, they are what they are, exalted in holiness, because he made them so through grace.

He also explains how he exhorts the prelates to announce his wonders among the peoples, as follows: I say that you should announce his wonders among the peoples. And behold the wonders: in his presence—that is, in knowledge of him—there are confession, beauty, and magnificence; that is, those who confess are made beautiful in innocence and holy in every virtue, and will be magnificent in the future.

This is equivalent to saying: Announce this: those who behold him through faith will confess their sins. And although by this they appear ugly, through it they will become beautiful in innocence, holy in every virtue, and finally magnificent in eternal blessedness.

And this magnificence and holiness will be in his sanctification—that is, the fact that they are holy here and magnificent in the future will result from his making them magnificent, not from their own merits.

Having exhorted the prelates, he exhorts the nations to whom they will preach to obey, as follows: I have exhorted the prelates to announce to you, O nations, the glory and wonders of Christ.

I also exhort you, O lands of the nations—that is, the many and diverse kingdoms of the nations—to bring to the Lord Christ, through the preaching of the prelates, the glory of faith; namely, glorify him through faith. And bring to the Lord the honor of confession by the mouth; that is, confess praise of him with your mouths.

“For with the heart,” as the Apostle asserts, “one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

And bring glory to his name by living well. And if it should be necessary for you to die for him, take up—that is, offer yourselves as sacrifices to God, dying for him just as he died for you. In accordance with what he says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross and follow me” (Matthew 16:24).

I say, take up sacrifices, and thus enter his courts. Enter, namely, into conformity with his courts—that is, into conformity with the apostles, whose teaching leads one to God, just as one enters a house through its courts; for this reason they are called courts.

This is equivalent to saying: You truly ought to offer yourselves as sacrifices, if necessary, for in this way you will be conformed to the apostles; otherwise, not at all.

But because many hypocrites and heretics appear, through pretense, to conform to the courts while completely departing from union with the Church, he adds: And when entering the courts, adore—that is, rightly venerate the Lord Jesus Christ—by remaining in his holy court, that is, in the vigor of the charity of the Church, which is his holy court.

“For if,” as the Apostle testifies, “I deliver my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3).

The present Church is rightly called a court because through it one enters the heavenly Zion, just as through a court one enters a house.

I say that the lands of the nations should bring glory and honor to God. And not merely a few lands, but, to speak universally, let all the earth—that is, all earthly people—be moved from error to faith.

Or this may be read optatively: I have said that the lands of the nations should bring to God the glory of faith, and so may it be: let the whole earth be moved, and let this movement occur from the face—that is, from the knowledge—of the Lord Christ.

And after you, O nations, have been moved, so that later nations too may be moved, say among the nations—that is, announce in the fullness of those nations—that the Lord Christ has reigned, having acquired the kingdom of the whole world after trampling down death.

Or “say among the nations” means “say among the unbelievers.” I say that you ought to say this because the Lord has reigned, and from this it is proved that he has acquired the kingdom for himself.

Indeed, he set right the world, that is, the perfection of the earth: namely, those whom he made from the earth into a world, that is, into perfect people. When they had previously been distorted by vices, he set them right, [Col. 1148B] that is, made them upright in virtues. This world will not be shaken at all from its perfection, even if it is shaken in respect of certain weak members.

But do not say only that he has reigned; also, so that the unbelievers may be shaken more greatly, say that he will judge the peoples: the faithful in faith, and the unfaithful in equity, saving the good but justly condemning the wicked. And because he will be judge, let the heavens rejoice—that is, the prelates who rain upon others as the heavens do upon the earth, and who will be rewarded in that just judgment—and let the earth also rejoice, since it too will then be rewarded. Let those, namely, rejoice who have been rained upon and are bearing fruit, after the likeness of the earth which, when drenched, bears fruit.

But so that the sea—that is, the bitter and unbelieving people—may not be condemned in that just judgment because of unbelief, let the sea be shaken from the bitterness of unbelief toward the sweetness of faith; and not merely some small portion of that sea, but its fullness, that is, a very great multitude of that sea. With this security, all the heavens and the earth rejoice here, because in the future the fields and everything that is in them will rejoice: that is, the perfected among the Jews will rejoice because here they will be fields, cultivated in faith after the manner of fields; and everything that is in them will rejoice, that is, all the virtues that will be in them here will be causes of their rejoicing in the future.

But not only will the faithful from among the Jews rejoice, who are rightly called fields; at the time when the fields rejoice, everything also will rejoice, that is, every kind of tree [Col. 1148D] of the forests: namely, the Gentiles, who, previously uncultivated and wild like trees of the forests, will here be made cultivable through faith and will bring forth the sweet fruit of good works.

And this exultation will come from the presence—that is, from the knowledge—of the Lord. They will rejoice for this reason: because here they will know God through faith and good works. They will also exult because he has come—that is, will come. He will come, I say, to judge the earth, that is, all earthly people, both faithful and unfaithful.

He explains this in parts, as follows: I say that he will come to judge the earth. For he will judge the world, that is, those who will be made perfect from the earth, in equity, that is, by justly repaying them with eternal blessedness; and he will judge the unfaithful peoples in truth, that is, in true judgment, condemning them deservedly because of their iniquity [Col. 1149A]. He says this so that by means of it he may promote those who are already good toward what is better, while by frightening the wicked he may draw them toward faith and toward singing a new song.

Alternatively, “from the presence” may mean from the presence of the Lord whom they will see, because he has come—that is, will come—manifestly, and they will rejoice at his coming. Hence it is written: “Then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty” (Luke 21:27). And although they could greatly rejoice simply at his coming, they will rejoice much more because he has come to judge, that is, because he will come for this purpose: to judge all human beings.

## ON PSALM XCVI

**The title of the ninety-sixth:** “A psalm of David, when his land was restored.”

This is explained as follows. This psalm is of David, that is, of Christ, and was completed when his land was restored: namely, the prophecy of this psalm was fulfilled in Christ, the true David, when his land was restored. This means that the human race, which had previously been his land—that is, his kingdom and possession—was taken away from his rule through Adam’s transgression, but was restored to him so that it might again come under his rule through faith. This indeed took place through the obedience of his death.

This restoration of Christ’s kingdom was prefigured in the prophet David, to whom God restored the kingdom taken away by his enemies after all his enemies had been defeated. This psalm is said to be Christ’s, not because Christ speaks here, but because the Prophet, treating of Christ in this psalm, shows how [Col. 1149C] he acquired a kingdom for himself among the Gentiles through miracles and the teaching of the apostles. He does this with the intention that, by taking occasion from his kindness, which he displays, he may exhort them to hate evil and love good, since they are his kingdom. It should be noted that, in prophetic fashion, he declares what is still future as though it were past, because of his great certainty.

The Lord Christ has reigned, that is, he will acquire the kingdom of the whole world for himself, having trampled down death; therefore let the earth rejoice, that is, let human beings rejoice, having already become his fruitful earth. Since he had spoken indefinitely of “the earth,” he defines it when he adds: “Let the many islands rejoice.” By “many” he indicates that he wishes to speak of the many churches of the Gentiles [Col. 1149D], which are many with respect to the diversity of languages but one with respect to faith. They are also appropriately called islands, because they cannot be submerged by the tribulations rising against them within and without, after the likeness of islands, which are not overwhelmed by the waves pressing upon them from every side.

I say that he will acquire the kingdom for himself, and this through clouds and darkness. The clouds and darkness are “around him,” that is, in his service, so that they might prepare this kingdom for him. The apostles are called clouds because they rained upon others; and “darkness” by emphasis, that is, “full of darkness,” because they were filled with the most obscure mysteries of God, which, in relation to others, they did not see. Hence the Apostle says: “I heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak” (2 Cor. 12:4).

The fact that they were filled with such darkness contributed greatly to the establishment of the kingdom. For if they were entirely lacking inwardly in the mysteries of wisdom, they would not know how to distinguish what should be preached from what should not.

And those clouds are “justice and judgment,” that is, just in life and judges of that kingdom, possessing the office of instructing their subjects; and “the correction of his throne,” that is, by their correction they make those who were distorted through unbelief into his throne, that is, into people in whom the Lord spiritually dwells. Alternatively, “correction” means “correctors,” namely, if in some respect those subjects who are already the Lord’s thrones are distorted.

When he calls them clouds and judgment, he shows that they possess the office of preaching; but when he calls them darkness and justice, he proves that they are suited to this office. Moreover, when he asserts that they are the correction of this undertaking, he shows that activity is present in them.

That they will prepare his throne by their correction will not come from the clouds themselves. Rather, this will happen because fire—that is, the fervor and illumination of the Holy Spirit—precedes, that is, will precede, among the Gentiles before him, before the sitting of the Lord Christ. This means that they will be made his throne because the grace of the Holy Spirit will first come upon them; and that fire will inflame his enemies, that is, inwardly kindle with the flame of faith the very Gentiles who are enemies through unbelief, so that it may make them friends through faith.

Fire will come upon them because his lightning flashes have shone upon the world, that is, his miracles, which he will perform through the apostles, will shine upon all the nations inhabiting the world. They are called lightning flashes because, after the likeness of lightning touching human eyes with its brilliance, they make those who see them astonished and stupefied.

And the earth saw those lightning flashes and was shaken: that is, earthly people will see those miracles, and when the fire of a special grace comes upon them, they will be moved from earthliness toward what is special.

Alternatively, it may be understood as follows: I say that the clouds will be the correction of the Lord’s throne, but before the Lord himself—that is, before his sitting, beforehand, before he sits upon the thrones made in them—fire will precede: that is, the fervor of wrath will come upon the very Gentiles and will inflame them, inwardly kindling his Gentile enemies. For they will be indignant at their correction.

This fire will not be in only a few enemies, but “around him,” that is, in all those dwelling around him, everywhere throughout the earth. It should be understood that “around him” is read in the preceding sentence just as it is here.

I say that the fire will inflame the enemies, but this is not a matter for concern. For his lightning flashes will shine upon all the enemies existing in the world; and the earth—that is, the people of the enemies—will see these miracles and will be shaken.

The meaning of this final verse will not be changed. But not only will the people be shaken: “the mountains also melted,” that is, the rich, exalted in possessions, will melt away from their hardness and will become soft, that is, capable of doing good.

This will happen from the presence of the Lord, that is, from knowledge of the Lord; and not of just any lord, but from the presence of the Lord of the whole earth. Since they will know through faith the Lord of the whole earth, they will melt away from their hardness [Col. 1151A] like wax—that is, by comparison with wax melting at the sight of fire.

Therefore, so that the mountains may melt at the sight of the Lord, the heavens—that is, the preachers—announced, that is, will announce, his justice. They will announce this: that all justice, that is, all remission and justification of sins, will come from the Lord. And while they are announcing it, all peoples—that is, peoples of every kind—saw, that is, will see by faith, his glory: they will believe that he is glorious, namely, that he is God, and king, and almighty, and all the other things belonging to his glory.

And because peoples of every kind will see by faith, I wish and exhort that all who worship graven images—that is, who venerate them as gods—be put to shame with a good shame, by the example of believing peoples; and not only those who worship them, but also those who glory in their images, that is, in images made by themselves and then worshiped.

It is as though he were saying: If human beings worshiped all living creatures, it would be less pitiable. How much more pitiable, then, is it to worship an image of a human being, especially to worship the one who constructed that image?

He then turns in apostrophe to the angels, granting that they should worship God—not because the angels need his exhortation, but so that he may display his good desire and, by the authoritative example of the angels, draw unbelievers toward worshiping God—as follows:
