I say that some will be worshiping graven images while neglecting to worship God. But although these miserable little humans neglect this, at least you, all his angels, who are highly rational [Col. 1151C], worship—that is, venerate with supreme and special worship—the Lord Christ.

I say that the peoples will see his glory; this, however, “Sion heard,” that is, will hear, and “rejoiced,” that is, will rejoice. But because “Sion” is used both for the faithful Jews and for the unfaithful, he determines which Sion he means, as follows:

I say that Sion will rejoice, and, that is, specifically, “the daughters of Judah rejoiced,” that is, will rejoice, at the faith of the peoples: the daughters of confession, namely, the early faithful from among the Jews, confessors of God’s name openly and not failing in tribulations. They are appropriately called female daughters because they are most beautiful in the cultivation of virtues. For the cultivation of daughters is more beautiful than that of sons.

They are also called daughters because they are capable of generating others in faith, just as daughters are capable of giving birth to sons.

They will rejoice, I say, and this because of your judgments, O Lord: namely, because you will judge not only the Jews but also the Gentiles worthy of salvation. “For there is no partiality with God” (Rom. 2:11).

And rightly they will rejoice at your judgments, because you, who will appear almost as a servant, are the Most High, that is, the Almighty ruling over the whole earth, over both Jews and Gentiles, and you have been greatly exalted, that is, you will be greatly exalted by every nation above all their gods. This means: While the unbelievers still greatly exalt their gods, much more, after they come to the faith, will they exalt you in heart, voice, and deed.

Alternatively, the passage may be understood as follows: “Because of your judgments the daughters of Judah will rejoice”; and here are the judgments: “For you are the Most High Lord over all the earth,” that is, you will judge that every people of the earth, both Gentile and Jewish, should regard you as the Most High Lord and exalt you above all gods.

When he says that the faithful Jews rejoice at the salvation of the Gentiles, he indicates that, on the authority of the Jews, there should be no doubt about the salvation of the Gentiles. This was a major question in the early Church; and by this he makes the Gentiles themselves more obligated to God, since he assures them of their salvation.

At last the Prophet comes to the point toward which he was aiming, making an apostrophe to the Gentiles, of whom he is speaking in this psalm, as follows:

I say that the Lord Jesus will prepare his kingdom for himself in this way and that, through the clouds, and because he is the Most High. Therefore, O Gentiles who will become his kingdom, who will love—that is, who will come to love—the Lord Christ by coming to the faith, hate every evil and vices [Col. 1152B], that is, evil works. “For no one can serve two masters” (Luke 16:13).

And if, in hating evil, tribulations come upon you, stand firm. For the Lord Christ guards—that is, will guard—the souls of his servants, namely, your souls, so that you may not conform yourselves to evils through fear. And he has not only liberated their souls, but also “from the hand of the pursuing sinner he delivered those servants,” that is, he will at some time liberate their bodies, even if at first he permits them to suffer somewhat.

And if persecutors take away the present life, this is not a matter for concern. For in place of the loss of this life, the light of eternal life has arisen—that is, will arise—for each just person: in eternal life he will be given the immense light of divine contemplation. And in place of the sadness they will suffer here, the joy of eternal blessedness will arise for them in the future [Col. 1152C]. In accordance with the Lord’s saying: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh” (Matt. 5:5).

Therefore, because light and joy will arise for the just, do not yield or become sad in tribulations; rather, rejoice, you just, in the Lord: not in evils, but in the things that belong to the Lord, namely, in virtues and good works.

And confess the praise of the memory of his holiness, that is, praise him in heart, voice, and deed, because he will remember to sanctify you, although for a long time he seemed to have forgotten you, who were placed in unbelief and original sin.

## ON PSALM XCVII

**The title of the ninety-seventh:** “A psalm of David, of the Prophet, exhorting all the faithful who will exist in the time of fulfillment [Col. 1152D] to sing a new song to the Lord the Father, in view of the wonderful benefits accomplished through the Son in the human race”; benefits which he also narrates, so that he may draw his hearers more strongly toward the praise of God. Here too, although the events are future, he declares them as though they were past, in prophetic fashion.

Sing, that is, present to the Lord the Father with love, O all you faithful, a new song, that is, the completion of the new commandments, in which he delights as in a song.

Alternatively, sing to him a new song, that is, praise the Lord with joy in a new praise: namely, for the death of his Son and the restoration of the whole world, which is indeed new.

And therefore sing a new song, because he has done wonders in the human race. Here is one wonder that he did: his right hand and his holy arm saved the human race associated with him through adoption [Col. 1153A].

The Son is called the right hand because through him God the Father does all things. He is called the arm because he is the Father’s strength. For through him the Father acts powerfully and not weakly. The arm is indeed the strongest member of the body.

This is as though he were saying: The Lord Father did this wonder: through the death of the Son he saved the human race from original sin and joined it to himself through adoption.

It should be noted that, when he says that the works of the Son are the Father’s, he shows the identity of nature.

And here is another wonder, so that the human race might be saved: “The Lord made his salvation known,” that is, his Savior, Christ. This means: He made Christ, whom the prophets had prophesied obscurely, known to the part of the Jews destined to be saved, both through faith and through the evident reality itself.

He repeats what he said, “he made known,” in an equivalent expression, in order to add the following: “He revealed,” I say, that is, he made him known to the Jews by also placing the same Savior before the faith of the Gentiles. This means: He revealed him to the Jews in such a way that he also caused the Gentiles to behold the same one through faith.

I say that he revealed the Savior both to Jews and to Gentiles, and thus he remembered his mercy with respect to the Gentiles, and his truth—that is, his true promise made to the house of Israel, that is, to the family of Israel, namely, the Jews.

This means: He made the Savior known so that through him he might show mercy to the Gentiles, whom he seemed for a long time to have abandoned to forgetfulness, and so that he might fulfill the true promise made to the Jews. For through Moses he had promised as follows: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers” (Deut. 18:15), and so forth.

Since he had said indefinitely that he revealed him “in the sight of the Gentiles,” he states this universally as follows: I said that he revealed him to the Gentiles, and not merely to a few; rather, all the ends of the earth—that is, all kinds of Gentiles inhabiting the ends of the earth—saw the salvation, that is, the Savior, of our Lord God.

He rightly adds “our,” for the sake of authority. It is as though he were saying: He is not a recent deity, but is the Son of our God, that is, of the God whom we prophets worship.

Alternatively, this may be read allegorically. I say that he revealed him to Jews and Gentiles; and in reality he was not revealed to everyone, but “all the ends of the earth,” that is, all those—both Jews and Gentiles—who in themselves bring earthly existence to an end, saw by the true vision of faith the salvation of our God.

Nevertheless, the following seems to accord better with the preceding interpretation taken literally [Col. 1153D]. I say that Christ, the right hand of God, saved the human race and was revealed to Jews and Gentiles. On this account, let every earth—that is, all inhabitants of the earth—shout to the Lord Christ with intense affection of love and devotion; let them sing, that is, think well about him, which will be a song for him; rejoice inwardly by thinking well about him; and sing praise.

He explains how he commands them to sing praise when he adds: Sing praise, I say, to the Lord Christ, that is, sing; and do so “on the lyre”—on the lyre, that is, in the good activity of your members, which are mortal and of a lower nature than the soul. For this reason they are represented by the lyre, which produces sound from what is lower and is covered with the skin of dead animals [Col. 1154A].

He repeats “on the lyre” in order to impress the exhortation: to sing praise to God through the service of the members means extending the hand to almsgiving, moving the foot toward some good work, and other such things. And sing praise to him with the voice of a psalm, that is, of good action—namely, with an outward voice corresponding to good action.

This means: By acting well, exhort others to act well with the voice of your mouth.

And sing praise on stretched trumpets, that is, in the office of stretched trumpets, so that you may be trumpets openly proclaiming, after the manner of a trumpet sounding openly. Do not be just any kind of trumpets, but stretched trumpets: not contracted by the blows of tribulations, but increasingly extended into the breadth of love, after the manner of a stretched trumpet, which, being made from gold or silver, is extended by hammering [Col. 1154B].

The Apostle appeared to be a stretched trumpet when he said: “When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful” (2 Cor. 12:10).

And sing praise with the voice of a horn trumpet: with the voice of preaching proceeding from you in such a way that you are a trumpet, that is, openly proclaiming, and a horn, that is, remaining in the flesh but not waging war according to the flesh, so that you may not fight for earthly advantage. Rather, surpass carnal things, look toward heavenly things, and be firm in constancy, after the likeness of a horn, which, while remaining in the flesh, rises above that same flesh and, being rigid, reaches upward.

This was prefigured in the earlier people, the Jews, who on feast days sounded stretched trumpets and horn trumpets.

Shout, I say, with a shout of devotion [Col. 1154C], and do so in the presence of the Lord the King: that is, because you have deserved to be in the presence of his faith, who is King and Lord, whose presence should be greeted with great rejoicing.

But since someone might object that they truly will not rejoice because they will be unable to do so on account of the sea’s being shaken, he adds: I say, rejoice; and if the sea is shaken against you, what concern is that? Let the sea be shaken sufficiently through tribulations—the sea, that is, the bitter people. And not merely a small part of the sea, but its fullness, that is, the multitude of that sea.

But so that we might not understand “sea” literally, he adds a specification: let the world be shaken. And so that we might not take the world itself as immovable, he further specifies: namely, let those unbelievers who inhabit that world be shaken.

This is neither a wish nor a concession, but sarcasm, that is, hostile mockery. I say, “Let them be shaken,” which indeed is not a matter for concern.

For although they may be shaken, the rivers—that is, the faithful who proceed from Christ the fountain and do not fail like rivers, which flow without ceasing from whatever source they arise—will clap their hands, that is, will join their good works here with joy, and will do so together, that is, in harmony.

This means: They will act well harmoniously and joyfully. By this he indicates that, because of the shaking, they will not cease inwardly from rejoicing, nor will they be prevented outwardly from action.

To clap is indeed to join the hands vigorously out of joy.

I say that the rivers will clap, and that these same rivers, existing as mountains—that is, exalted in virtues—will rejoice in the future. This rejoicing will come from the presence of the Lord, that is, from the vision of the present Christ [Col. 1155A].

And truly they will behold him bodily, because he has come—that is, will come bodily—to judge the earth, that is, all human beings.

And then he will judge the world, that is, the perfected, in justice, rewarding them; and the peoples, that is, the unfaithful, in equity, justly condemning them.

## ON PSALM XCVIII

**The title of the ninety-eighth psalm:** “A psalm of David the prophet, acting against the unbelieving Jews who were angry at Christ’s kingdom, showing their anger to be useless and unjust.”

It is useless because their anger will harm his kingdom in no way, since he sits above the cherubim and already reigns in Sion and among the peoples of the Gentiles. It is unjust because they are moved against one whom Moses, Aaron [Col. 1155B], Samuel, and all those regarded as authoritative among the Jews worshiped; he is not a recent God.

He does this with the intention of recalling them from this anger, both because it is unjust and because it is useless, and thus of inviting them to confess God Christ. In prophetic fashion, however, he treats of what is future by means of the past tense.

The Lord Christ has reigned, that is, has obtained the kingdom for himself, having trampled down death. Therefore let the unbelieving peoples of the Jews be angry as much as they wish. He does not say this as a wish, but as mockery of them.

It is as though he were saying: The peoples are indeed angry about his kingdom, but what concern is that? Let them be angry as much as they wish; nevertheless, he reigns and will reign without end.

The Lord, I say, who sits above the cherubim, that is, who rules over the sublime spirits, the cherubim, while remaining in them according to the subtlety of divine contemplation.

Therefore let the earth be shaken, that is, let those earthly Jewish peoples be disturbed in their earthliness against him. Nevertheless, their opposition will not be able to abolish his kingdom, since he is so powerful that he sits above the cherubim.

He therefore shows where he reigns, as follows: I say, let the earth be shaken. Yet the Lord Christ himself is regarded as great in Sion, that is, the faithful from among the Jews, who are already Sion, recognize him as the great king; and he is exalted, that is, almighty, above all peoples, namely, the faithful from among the Gentiles, who recognize him as almighty and reigning over them.

Since he had said, “Let them be angry,” so that he would not seem to have spoken this as a wish, he adds: Although I said, “Let the peoples be angry,” nevertheless I rather wish, O Lord, that they confess your great name, which is “Lord”: namely, that they cease from this anger and, having faith, honor you with praise because you are called their Lord.

This is necessary because this name is “terrible,” that is, feared by the wicked, and “holy,” that is, beloved and delightful to the good. For when the wicked hear that he is Lord of all, they fear condemnation because of their wickedness; but the righteous expect reward because of their righteousness. “Holy” is used for “beloved,” because everything that is holy is worthy of love.

I say, let them confess—that is, let them praise and honor your name. And because the honor of you, the king, loves—that is, requires—judgment, let them confess their sins, namely, let them judge themselves to be sinners and repent of their sins. Otherwise they would not rightly honor God.

In this judgment they themselves are inexcusable. For unless they resist through the hardness of unbelief, you have prepared—that is, will prepare—through grace, paths of uprightness: you will make upright those who are distorted through unbelief.

He therefore explains what paths of uprightness he will prepare in them when he adds: Namely, you have done—that is, will do—in them, the deeds of Jacob, that is, of wrestlers, through grace that is active, judgment, so that they may judge themselves guilty in conscience, and afterward justice, so that they may be justified in virtues and works.

Alternatively, the explanation may proceed by analogy as follows: I say that the honor of the king loves judgment, and unless they resist, you will prepare that judgment in them through grace. This is proved by the fact that you have already prepared paths of uprightness in many others, the deeds of Sion, when they were distorted [Col. 1156B]. Namely, you did in them judgment and justice.

Having made his wish concerning the same people for whom he wished, he makes an apostrophe of exhortation as follows:

I wish, O unbelieving Jews, that you exalt God with a good confession, and see to it that you do so. Exalt the Lord Christ in faith, devotion, and deed—not as a recent God, but as the God who is ours, whom we prophets worship.

But because he had said “God,” so that he would not seem to wish only his divinity to be exalted, he adds: And worship—that is, venerate with supreme worship—the footstool of his feet, that is, his body, because it is holy in every perfection.

The seat of divinity is said to be the soul; the footstool of the feet, however, is his body, because although the deity dwells spiritually in both, the soul is nevertheless higher in dignity, while the body is lower. It is like the seat of someone being higher and his footstool lower, although the one seated dwells in both.

He rightly calls it the footstool of the feet, to indicate that the habitation of divinity is there, after the likeness of someone sitting above the footstool on which he places his feet.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not swear by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet” (Matt. 5:35).

What, then, is more appropriately understood by “heaven” than the soul of the Lord Jesus, surpassing every heavenly creature in dignity? And by “earth,” his earthly flesh is rightly signified. Therefore, when we pray, we also kiss the earth as a sign of Christ’s flesh, which was created from the earth.

But since he had asserted that the Lord Christ is God [Col. 1156D], he confirms this by the authority of Moses and the others, as follows:

I exhort you to exalt God, which certainly ought to be done. For he is worthy of exaltation, since he is not a recent God. Moses and Aaron, whom you regard as authoritative, were among the priests, that is, among the number of his priests. When he says “among the priests,” he indicates that he had many priests.

It should be noted that Moses was not a priest; he is placed among the number of priests, however, because he is read to have offered sacrifices and prayed for the people, which indeed belonged to priests.

And Samuel, my contemporary prophet, a man of no small authority among you, is among them, that is, among the number of those who invoke his name, which is “Lord”: that is, those who call him Lord in purity of faith [Col. 1157A].

But so that it might not be objected, “What concern is it if they invoked him? Perhaps they were deceived,” he adds: They invoked Christ, I say, as Lord; and he himself, who appears to you to be a simple and powerless human being, heard Moses and Aaron, so that they might obtain what they asked, and he spoke to them in the pillar of cloud, that is, in the office of the pillar of cloud, or existing in the pillar of cloud, although he was everywhere, not locally.

For it is written that the Lord spoke to them at the entrance of the tabernacle from the pillar of cloud (Exod. 33:9), which cooled them from the heat of the day. Whether he spoke to them through angels or in some other way is not known with certainty.

Through the pillar of cloud, Christ’s humanity was appropriately prefigured, for it brought us refreshment from the incentives of vices. Through it, the divinity is believed to have spoken to us, as the Apostle says: “In many ways and by many means God formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in the Son” (Heb. 1:1).

Humanity is also appropriately called a pillar because, like a pillar, it is the firmest support of our faith.

I say that he spoke to them. They, however, kept his testimonies by believing: that is, his firm promises concerning things that would take place after a long time, which he testified to them with an oath. They also kept every command of his by fulfilling the testimony that he mentioned above.

I say that God heard them, and you are also my witness that I speak the truth. For you, Lord Christ our God, heard them, though you are not a recent deity; and you were merciful to them by forgiving their sins [Col. 1157C].

But so that it might not be objected, “He was merciful because he was unable to take vengeance,” he adds: Although you were merciful in forgiving all their sins, nevertheless you took vengeance upon all their inventions, that is, all their sins, which they did not receive from you but devised themselves. You took vengeance by not permitting them to enter the promised land.

By this he indicates that all sins are to be punished either here or in the future: here through contrition and manifold affliction of the flesh; in the future through eternal condemnation. By this he frightens the unbelievers.

After adding the authority of Moses and the others, he repeats his exhortation as follows:

O unbelieving Jews, I said that Moses and Aaron worshiped the Lord Christ [Col. 1157D]. Therefore, convicted by their authority, exalt the Lord Christ your God in faith, mouth, and deed—not as a recent deity.

But so that he would not seem to remove his humanity, he adds: And worship—that is, venerate him with supreme worship—on his holy mountain, that is, in the worship of his humanity, which is a holy mountain in every goodness.

This means: By venerating the humanity, venerate the divinity. Otherwise the matter would not proceed.

It is necessary, however, for you to worship his mountain, because that holy mountain is the Lord our God. This means: His humanity must be worshiped because the divinity and humanity are one and the same person.

## ON PSALM XCIX

**The title of the ninety-ninth psalm:** “A psalm of David, in confession.”

This is explained as follows. This psalm is by the prophet David and was made “in confession,” that is, in an exhortation to the confession of divine praise. It is rightly called a psalm “in confession.” For in this psalm the Prophet invites all human beings to confess the praise of the Lord, since, as was shown in the preceding psalm, he has already obtained the kingdom for himself.

“Shout to the Lord, all the earth.” It is as though he were saying: Since the Lord Christ has reigned, all you peoples of the earth, both Jews and Gentiles, shout to that Lord with the inward shout of intense devotion.

And because shouting alone is not sufficient, serve the same Lord by fulfilling what he commands. Do this not unwillingly, as the earlier Jewish people did, and not with sadness, as worldly masters are still served, but with joy. For to serve him is to reign.

But I do not say, “Serve in joy” [Col. 1158B], so that joy may be simulated outwardly while sadness is held inwardly. Rather, being in exultation—that is, in joy—enter the secret place of your conscience.

This means: Have that joy inwardly. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “When you pray, enter your inner room” (Matt. 6:6), namely, your conscience.

I say, have exultation in his presence, that is, in what pleases him. This means: Let that inward joy be pleasing to God; otherwise it would not please him.

And while serving in joy, know that the Lord Jesus himself is God, although he appeared to unbelievers simply as a human being. He will be proved to be God by this: he made—that is, created—us, and thus we did not create ourselves.

He adds “not we ourselves” in order to define the first creation, in which we contribute nothing [Col. 1158C]. In the second creation, however, when we are created in holiness by God’s grace, we create ourselves in that same holiness through free will.

And know also that we are his people and the sheep of his pasture. This means: The fact that we are a people—that is, rational—we are so through him. For we call a collection of rational beings a people, not a collection of irrational animals. And the fact that we are sheep—that is, simple and free from evil, like sheep—is also through him; and we are the sheep of his pasture, whom he feeds with both earthly and spiritual food.

And therefore, all you who are human, existing in the confession of his praise, enter his gates, that is, the conformity of the apostles and prophets, who are gates through their teaching, by which we enter to him [Col. 1158D]. This means: Praise him with mouth, faith, and works, in conformity with the prophets and apostles. And enter his courts, that is, the breadth of charity, which is signified by courts because they are spacious. And after you have entered the courts, do not fail, but confess to him in hymns, that is, praise him in acts of thanksgiving, attributing nothing to yourselves, but assigning to him whatever good there is in you.

Or in this way: Existing in the confession of sins, enter his gates, that is, the beginnings of approach to him. This means: Approach him through confession of sins, after the likeness of one approaching a house who first enters through its gates. “For the beginning of wisdom is fear of the Lord (Ps. 110:10).” Through fear one comes to confession [Col. 1159A]. And after you have entered the gates, having become his courts, in which he may dwell spiritually—that is, being enlarged in charity and every virtue, after the likeness of courts—confess to him in hymns, that is, praise him in acts of thanksgiving.

And praise his name, which is “Lord.” This means: Let it not be hateful to you, but praiseworthy, that he is called Lord, for although he is Lord and has the power to oppress, nevertheless he is gracious. And in this respect he is gracious: his mercy, which he displays toward the human race by forgiving, will endure forever; and his truth—that is, the true promise of his justice, by which he promised that the one who is just would still be justified here and rewarded in the future—will endure to the last generation of this life [Col. 1159B], until which he will always justify the just more fully, and “to generation,” that is, to the generation that will exist on the day of judgment, in which he will duly reward those same just people.

## ON PSALM C

The title of the hundredth Psalm: “A Psalm of the prophet David, showing how innocently and justly he conducted himself in his office of leadership.” He does not say this with a purpose of boasting, but for the instruction of leaders, so that, following his example, they too may conduct themselves innocently and live justly in their office of leadership.

Attributing mercy and judgment to you, I shall sing, that is, I shall announce this to others with joy, Lord Jesus Christ. It is as though he said: Many leaders, considering you only merciful and not a just judge who punishes sins, by failing to punish their subjects consent to the sins that they themselves now commit. But I, regarding you as merciful in such a way that I also recognize you as a chaste judge, shall sing this to others for their instruction, that is, I shall announce it to others in song. And I shall not sing only this, but I shall also sing psalms, that is, I shall act well.

And, existing in an undefiled way, that is, in innocence, which will be the way to life, I shall understand this when you come to me in the future through reward. It is as though he said: I shall not expect to be rewarded here, but in the future on account of good action. In accordance with this: “And we shall come to him, and we shall make our dwelling with him (John 14:23)” [Col. 1159D].

Or in this way: I shall sing psalms, that is, I shall act well; and, existing in an undefiled way, that is, in innocence, I shall understand—that is, I shall possess rational understanding—what must be done and what must be avoided. And this will be when you come to me, not locally, but through grace that operates within. This means: I shall sing psalms and understand through the fact that you will come into me.

He then shows that he previously possessed innocence in this way: I said, “I shall sing of mercy and judgment”; and when I resolved to sing these things, I was already walking in the innocence of my heart, that is, in the innocence of good thought—not merely in the innocence of good action—and I was advancing greatly in that innocence. I speak of an innocence proposed for instruction, in the midst of my house, that is, openly before my household. This means: I made that innocence manifest in order to give my household an example of innocence [Col. 1160A].

Having shown the extent of his own innocence, he also shows that he did not consent to another’s injustice, as follows: I not only walk in innocence, but I also did not set an unjust matter before my inner eyes, that is, another’s unjust action. This means: I did not approve of another’s unjust action; indeed, I hated the one who committed transgressions, that is, unjust actions. For an unjust action is a transgression of God’s command, and therefore it ought to be hated.

Nor did I merely fail to consent to another’s wicked action; what is more, a wicked heart did not cling to me through consent, that is, another’s wicked will. This means: If I discovered someone’s wicked will, it did not cling to me so that I would consent to him.

And this was not so only with outsiders. If someone familiar to me turned away from my good will through an evil will, I not only held him in hatred, but did not know him, that is, I acted toward him harshly in rebuke, as though I did not know him.

Nor did I merely hate those who committed great transgressions; what may seem small, although it is great, was also hateful to me: one who slandered his neighbor—not publicly, but secretly, which might seem less serious. I not only hated him, but, what is more, pursued him, sometimes by punishing him, sometimes by rebuking him.

I also hated one who was proud in his eyes—not merely proud in action, but one who, even if he did not act proudly, was nevertheless marked as proud in the way he looked [Col. 1160C]. For pride is sometimes recognized in the eyes.

I also hated one who existed with an insatiable heart, that is, the greedy person who is never satisfied by the abundance of wealth, or the envious person who is never satisfied by another’s misfortunes. And I not only hated him, but also did not eat bodily with him. By this he indicates that he had no fellowship with him. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever loves his father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matt. 10:37).”

I say that I did not eat with one proud in his eyes and insatiable in heart. But since it is not enough to hate the wicked unless the good are also loved, my inner eyes, that is, the regard of my good pleasure, are toward the faithful of the earth, that is, of my kingdom [Col. 1160D]. This means: The faithful and good of my kingdom please me, so that I do not deprive them of the honor of leadership, but so that they may sit, that is, remain with me in the kingdom. This means: Faithful leaders please me, so that, in no way deprived of their honor, they may reign with me.

I say that my eyes are toward the faithful of the earth; and for a long time now, while walking—that is, persevering—in an undefiled way, that is, in innocence, he served me here in the administration of the commonwealth. Specifically, I appointed the innocent man as my minister, so that, existing under me, he might faithfully preside over his inferiors.

I say that I hated one who was proud in his eyes, and I shall still hate him. For the one who ever commits pride, that is, a proud action, will not dwell in the midst of my house, that is, he will not rule the household, after the likeness of leaders who exist in the midst of a house [Col. 1161A].

Or, “he will not dwell in the midst of my house” means that he will not be made manifest in the community of my household. This means: No proud person will ever be intimate with me.

And the one who speaks iniquity, that is, flattery, never made himself upright, that is, by flattering, he never made himself pleasing in the sight of my inner eyes. This means: No one ever pleased my rational judgment through his flatteries, as flatterers customarily please worldly lords. For the tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins.

I said that I pursued the slanderer, the one proud in his eyes, and the one insatiable in heart; and, to speak universally, existing in the morning, that is, in the brightness of innocence and complete perfection [Col. 1161B], I was killing—that is, desired to kill—all the sinners of the earth, that is, of my kingdom, insofar as they were sinners.

And this was so that I might destroy from the city, that is, from the people of the Lord over whom I presided, all who work iniquity. This means: I desired to kill them in such a way that none of them, remaining in the people of the Lord, would practice iniquity, but that all iniquity would be destroyed in them and goodness built up.

It should rightly be noted that when he says, “I pursued the slanderer,” and, “With him I did not eat,” and, “I was killing sinners,” he more appropriately uses the imperfect tense than the past tense. By this he indicates that he began long ago, had not yet finished, and still persevered in the same conduct.

## ON PSALM CI

[Col. 1161C]

The title of the hundred-first Psalm: “The prayer of the poor man when he is anxious and pours out his prayer before the Lord.” It is explained as follows: This Psalm is the prayer of the poor man, that is, in this Psalm Christ prays, having become poor for our sake, although he was rich, so that through his poverty we might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9).

He shows his poverty in the Psalm where he says: “My days are like a shadow,” and so forth. I say that this prayer is the prayer of Christ the poor man, made when he was anxious, that is, concerned about the destruction of the human race, and when he had poured out—that is, knew that he would pour out—this prayer of his before the Lord Father, that is, in the good pleasure of the Lord Father.

This means: He made this prayer because he was concerned about the ruin and destruction of the human race, and because he knew that it pleased the Lord Father for him to pour out this prayer for the salvation of human beings.

It should be noted that he indicates there that he is anxious about the salvation of human beings, since he prays for them as though for himself. He indicates there that this prayer pleases the Lord where, in what follows, he declares that the restoration of human beings will take place—the restoration for which he prays at the beginning of the Psalm.

He prays for them and declares the benefit of their restoration with this purpose: to make devoted and well-disposed those who have been restored through him, so that through that devotion they may attain eternal salvation.

Lord Father, hear my prayer, so that I may obtain what I ask. This prayer is not slack, but is an intense cry made with upright and intense devotion. And may this cry of mine come to you, that is, may it not suffer rejection, but be brought to fulfillment, admitted by you, after the likeness of ambassadors who are admitted into the Lord’s chamber.

He therefore explains what he is asking when he adds: “Do not turn away,” and so forth. This is explained as follows. I say: Hear the cry of my prayer, and this prayer is of such a kind: I ask that in the future you not turn your face, that is, the presence of your knowledge, away from me, that is, from those who are mine. Permit them in the future to attain the blessedness of knowing you.

And so that your face may not be turned away from them in the future, in whatever day I am troubled incline your ear to me, that is, at whatever time those who are mine are inwardly troubled by their sins, incline your ear to them. Cause your mercy to bend down toward them, so that you may rescue them from this tribulation, after the likeness of a physician bending his ear toward a sick person [Col. 1162B].

And he appropriately says “in whatever day,” on account of the diversity of time, as though he said: Since they will be troubled at different times, whenever they are troubled, bend your ear mercifully toward them.

I say, “Incline your ear to those who are mine.” For those who are mine will call upon you in their tribulations, that is, they will pray both with voice and devotion. And in whatever day I call upon you, that is, at whatever time of tribulation those who are mine pray to you, hear me, that is, hear those who are mine, so that they may obtain what they ask; and hear them quickly, that is, without delay, in this life, where the time of being heard exists. For in the future no one will be heard.

In meaning this is the same as “incline your ear,” except that it adds “quickly” and “in whatever day I call upon you” [Col. 1162C]. It is repeated out of excessive affection. I ask that in the future you not turn your face away from them, and that you incline your ear to them so that they may be rescued from tribulation.

But I ask not only this; I also ask that they be restored to immortality, because my days have failed like smoke, that is, the days of life belonging to those who are mine have been made quickly perishable through Adam, after the manner of smoke, which quickly dissipates.

And I also ask that the bones of those who are mine be strengthened. For my bones, that is, the intellectual faculty and free will—which are called bones, that is, the stronger parts of the soul—of those who are mine have dried up like fuel, that is, they have lost their strength through original sin, after the likeness of fuel placed in a frying pan and, as it burns, losing the power of its fatness.

They truly have perishable days and dry bones. For I have been struck like grass, that is, those who are mine, struck and punished by you, have been made perishable through the punishment of sin like grass, which quickly loses its greenness; and my heart has dried up, that is, the bones of the heart of those who are mine have dried up.

This means: Their life has thereby become perishable, and their inward bones have been weakened, because you struck them with mortality and blindness.

And they were not struck without reason, but for this reason: I forgot to eat my bread, that is, those who are mine forgot to eat their bread. Specifically, in Adam they forgot to be refreshed by their bread, that is, by obedience to the divine command, which would have been saving bread for them.

This means: On account of their disobedience they were rightly struck by you. And that forgetfulness of eating bread occurred because of the voice of my groaning, that is, of those who are mine. For the deceptive devil said: “If you eat, you will be like gods (Gen. 3:5).”

This means: They forgot to eat bread because the devil’s deceptive voice deceived them, through which they came to the condition from which they very often groan.

It should be noted that, when he says that they were struck deservedly because of their negligence, he makes them still more obligated to him, since he prays so earnestly for those who were struck because of their disobedience. But when he shows that they sinned through the voice of diabolical suggestion, he makes room for forgiveness for them. For if they had sinned without any suggestion, they would have been wholly unworthy of forgiveness, just as the devil lost all possibility of forgiveness because he sinned from pride alone.

I say that their forgetfulness occurred through the voice of the devil; and because those who are mine obeyed that voice, my mouth, that is, the rational faculty of those who are mine, which is the mouth of the soul [Col. 1163B], clung through consent to my flesh, that is, to the carnality of those who are mine.

This means: That voice caused the intellectual faculty of those who are mine to be overcome by sensuality. This is the same thing he had said above, “My heart dried up,” but it is repeated because of the excessive anxiety he has for those who are his, so that he may obtain the salvation of this matter more quickly.

Having shown the striking of those who are his, and the reason for their striking, so that he might obtain forgiveness for them more quickly, he declares how much he will suffer for their restoration, and how he will rise again and ascend into heaven, as follows:

I ask that you hear the prayer made for the misery of those who are mine, which must indeed be heard so that they may be restored. For in order that they may be restored, I have become like the pelican of the wilderness, that is, like a pelican dwelling in the wilderness.

For just as the pelican is a solitary bird, so I exist in solitude, while I alone persist in freedom from sin. Or I am solitary because I was born alone, uniquely, from a Virgin. No one else has been born from a virgin.

Or also solitary, that is, I alone will rise again through myself. For no one else has risen or will rise by himself. Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “Free among the dead (Ps. 87:6).”

I will also become like a pelican in the shedding of blood and in the giving of life to children. For physiologists say that the pelican kills its young because they strike it in the face. Then, distressed at their death, it makes them live again by pouring out the blood of its side over them.

So too Christ condemned his children, that is, the entire human race, to mortality, because they struck him in the face, that is, because through Adam’s disobedience they offended him greatly, after the manner of those who strike someone in the face. Afterwards, having compassion on their death, he gave them life again through the shedding of his blood [Col. 1163D].

But I shall not resemble the pelican only in the shedding of blood; I shall also be like the night-raven, that is, I shall resemble the night-raven in death. For just as the bird called in common speech the “raven of the night” flies at night, so I shall remain in death.

And this resemblance to the night-raven will occur in a dwelling, and through the dwelling, namely through the pride of the Jews, which is appropriately understood by “dwelling” because of its loftiness. For a dwelling is properly called the roof of a house, which is above in the house; and it is called *domicilium*, as if from *domus supercilium*, “the brow of the house.”

[Col. 1164A]

It should be noted that, when he indicates that he will be killed through the pride of the Jews, he makes them still more obligated to him, since he shows that a portion of them will later be saved through him, although they unjustly handed him over to death.

Or I shall be like the night-raven dwelling in a habitation. For just as the nocturnal bird called the night-raven dwells in a habitation, so I shall remain for the three days of my Passion in a dwelling, that is, in the proud power of the Jews, which is understood through “dwelling” because of the loftiness of their arrogance, since a dwelling is the upper part of a house.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “As Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster for three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights (Matt. 12:40),” namely, in the power of the will of the earthly Jews.

In another translation it reads “in the ruined walls” [Col. 1164B]. By *parietina* we mean the walls of buildings that are half-ruined and destroyed. Hence the Jews who killed Christ are also understood by *parietina*, since, although they ought to have been God’s building, through their pride and other sins they destroyed themselves.

I said that for the restoration of those who are mine I would become like the pelican; and for this same reason I kept watch, that is, I shall awaken from death on the third day. And afterwards I became—that is, I shall become—like a solitary sparrow nesting on a roof. Specifically, I shall resemble a solitary sparrow nesting on a roof.

For just as the sparrow, abandoning the company of other birds, lives alone on a roof, so I, having bodily abandoned the company of the apostles and ascending with the Father into heaven, shall possess a solitary kingdom.

Nor did I merely prepare, for the restoration of those who are mine, to make myself like the pelican, the night-raven, and the sparrow; but because I prepared myself for this, I was already suffering for their restoration. For my enemies, the Jews, reproached me all day, that is, continually.

And I also suffered this: those among the enemies who praised me, pretending to say, “Teacher, we know that you are truthful (Matt. 22:16),” and so forth, swore against me, that is, they formed a conspiracy against me concerning how they might deceive me by their praise.

He therefore explains why they reproached him when he adds: They reproached me for the very thing for which I ought to have been praised, namely, because I ate—that is, incorporated into myself through teaching—ashes, that is, repentant sinners, as bread, that is, like my disciples.

Or in this way: Because they had already become bread for me, that is, a pleasant refreshment. This means: They regarded me as deserving reproach because I drew repentant sinners to myself just as I did the righteous. They are understood by “ashes” because repentant people customarily placed ashes on their heads, which was a sign of sorrow.

And I mixed my drink in my intimacy, that is, the righteous, who were my pleasant cup, with weeping, that is, with repentant sinners who wept. This means: I joined both the righteous and sinners to my intimacy without distinction.

This is also what is meant by “I ate ashes as bread,” expressed through another comparison for emphasis.

One might ask: From where did they receive such great blindness that they reproached you in this way? He answers as follows: This occurred because of the presence of wrath, that is, of the small punishment of sin, and of indignation, that is, of the great punishment given to me by you [Col. 1165A]. “Wrath” and “indignation” are used for punishment because they are ordinarily the causes of punishments.

This means: Because they saw me bearing in my body both the greater and the lesser punishment of Adam’s sin, and thought me merely human, they did not hesitate to reproach me. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8).”

And truly both wrath and indignation are yours against me. For although you were raising me up, that is, exalting me in innocence, nevertheless you struck me down, that is, injured me.

This is how you struck me down: My days declined like a shadow, that is, the days of my life became perishable after the manner of a shadow that quickly passes, so that I might quickly pass from one age to another [Col. 1165B]. This punishment, however, is less than the suffering of anguish.

And you struck me down in this way as well: I dried up like grass. That is, not only did my limbs dry up, but I myself, in my own person, became subject to drying up after the likeness of hay. For just as hay quickly dries through separation from its greenness, so I, according to my humanity, became subject through continual sufferings to drying up from the greenness of impassibility, which human beings lost through Adam.

By the decline of the days he indicates mortality; by the dryness, however, he indicates passibility.

Or this passage may be read as follows: “Because of the presence of wrath,” and so forth. I said that my enemies reproached me because I ate ashes as bread, and this impiety came upon them because of the presence of wrath, that is, because of the presence of your wrath, which had blinded them. And it was not a small wrath, but indignation, that is, excessive wrath. In Hebrew it reads “fury.” And therefore they still reproach me, because they saw that you, while raising me up, struck me down. These and the other words remain unchanged.

Having made his prayer concerning the restoration of those who are his, he declares that their restoration will come through him in such a way as to make them still more obligated to him:

Those who are mine have become perishable like smoke, and their bones have dried up; and for their restoration I have declining days and dry up like grass. But you, Lord Father, remain forever, that is, you are both Lord and almighty and eternal. Therefore you can restore immortality and impassibility to me and to those who are mine.

For if you were not Lord and eternal, you would by no means possess the power for this matter [Col. 1165D]. It should indeed be noted that, when he calls him Lord and eternal, he indicates that he is powerful enough to give immortality and impassibility, and through this he merits immortality and impassibility for himself and his own.

I say that you are Lord and eternal, and therefore able to grant us eternity. But you not only possess the possibility of this, for your memorial—that is, your mercy, which is called a memorial because it is worthy of human remembrance, or through which you will remember the salvation of human beings—will be in this generation and to the last generation, that is, among all human generations.

This means: In all the generations of this world your mercy will be shown to human beings, or “in generation and generation,” that is, forever. Since he had spoken obscurely by saying “memorial,” he explains it by adding:

Truly your memorial will be in all generations.

For you, who for a long time seemed to lie inactive and to neglect the salvation of human beings, rising for salvation, will have mercy on Zion, that is, on the portion of the Jews destined to be saved, forgiving its sins through repentance and faith, because the time for having mercy on it has now come—that is, the time of fulfillment, which you ordained from eternity, so that at that time you might have mercy on your Zion.

Because the time for having mercy has come, he repeats this out of his excessive affection for the salvation of those who are his.

And you will have mercy in this way: because the stones of your Zion have pleased your servants, my disciples, that is, the Scriptures of the prophets, who were stones—that is, through their teaching they were stones of the foundation upon whose teaching the primitive Church would be founded.

And your servants, the apostles, imbued with the teaching of the stones of Zion, will have mercy on the earth of that Zion, that is, on those who are still earth in the Jewish people, that is, earthly; or “earth,” that is, cultivable, because, like earth receiving the seed of teaching in the heart, they will have mercy on it.

Specifically, they will have mercy on its earth by opening up the exceedingly obscure teaching of the prophets and thereby bringing it to faith and to the grace of baptism.

The whole verse is as though he said: Through the apostles you will have mercy on the Jewish people—through the apostles, I say, who will call it to faith by the testimony of the prophets.

But he will not have mercy only on the Jews by calling them to faith; the Gentiles also, called to faith through their teaching of mercy, will fear your name with chaste fear, Lord. That is, they will venerate you in faith and works and with their mouths, calling you Lord.

And not only the people, but all—that is, kings of every kind on earth—will fear your glory with chaste fear, that is, they will fear what is glorious in you.

And this will happen because, through the preaching of the apostles, the testimonies of the prophets, and the sacrament of baptism, the Lord, who alone gives the increase (1 Cor. 3:7), built—that is, will build; the past is used for the future because of the certainty of prophecy—Zion from living stones, that is, the Church.

This Zion had its beginning through Christ’s preaching, the working of miracles, and the sending of the Holy Spirit. And the Lord himself, who by his nature is invisible, will be seen visibly in his glory, that is, in the Son, who is the wisdom and glory of the Father, as it is written: “A wise son is the glory of his father (Prov. 10:1).”

He will be seen, I say, in the Son who said: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also (John 14:9),” namely, “when he comes in his majesty and that of the Father and of the holy angels (Matt. 25:31).” “Then, I say, every eye will see him, even those who pierced him (Rev. 1:7).”

The Lord himself therefore built the Church and delivered his Son visibly in the flesh.

For he looked not upon the arrogance of the proud Jews, who gloried in the Law, believing that they were justified through it, but upon the prayer of the humble patriarchs [Col. 1167A], namely, the prophets and other faithful people, who, filled with the Holy Spirit, believed, hoped for, and desired his coming in the flesh, and humbly sought it in their prayers: that he might come into the world to restore human nature, break the bonds of death, and open the entrance to life that the guilt of the first parent had closed.

They said:

“Would that you would rend the heavens and come down (Isa. 64:1).”

“Send the Lamb, Lord, the ruler of the earth (Isa. 16:1).”

“Send, Lord, the one whom you are going to send (Exod. 4:13).”

“Lord, incline your heavens and come down (2 Sam. 22:10).”

“Come, come, and do not delay (Hab. 2:3).”

“Show us your mercy, and grant us your salvation (Ps. 84:8),”

and similar words.

He therefore looked upon the prayer of these people and did not despise their petition, because he sent the one in whom they believed, whom they hoped for, and whom they sought with such great desire in their prayers; and he granted the request of those who implored him.

And because these things that have been mentioned—namely, that God looked upon the prayer of the humble through Christ’s incarnation, that he built the Church through Christ’s preaching and Passion, and that Christ will be seen in glory after the future resurrection—are great and worthy of remembrance, lest they be consigned to oblivion through ingratitude, let them be written for perpetual remembrance in another generation, that is, for the benefit of the generation that was to succeed the perverse generation of the Jews.

To that generation the Lord says: “Unbelieving generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you? (Mark 9:19).”

For the benefit, that is, of the Christian generation, concerning which it follows: “And the gentile people,” formerly dead through sins, “which will be created” through the bath of regeneration, so that it may be a new creation, “will praise the Lord” with a new song, on account of the new man who was given to the world, believing him in the heart, praising him with the mouth, and confessing him in works.

This generation, I say, will praise the Lord because the Lord, who “knows the lofty from afar (Ps. 138:6),” looked upon not only the Jews, who seemed to be near, but also the Gentiles; that is, he saw them from afar—from his holy height—when, through his incarnation, “the Dawn from on high visited us.”

He explains this more clearly when he adds: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the earth,” when he came from royal seats into the Virgin’s womb [Col. 1167D] (Wis. 18:15).

For this is the incorrupt earth that the Lord blessed, and which was therefore free from every contagion of sin. Through it we recognized the way of life and received the promised truth. Because this earth was worthy, the Lord looked from heaven upon the earth.

But for what purpose? “To hear,” I say, “the groaning of the fettered,” that is, the mournful prayers of those who, fettered in hell because of the sin of the first parent, were held in the bonds of darkness. Christ descended to the lower regions during the three days and, having broken the bonds of death, freed them.

Or he heard the groaning of the fettered, that is, of those who were held captive by the devil through the habit of sinning. For Christ came into the world especially for this purpose: to free the dead from the underworld [Col. 1168A] and to release the living from sins.

Hence it follows: “And to release the sons of the slain,” that is, of the first parents, who were both slayers and slain. They were slayers because they transmitted to their children the cause of their slaying, that is, original sin, and slain because of that same sin.

As the Apostle says: “Through one man,” that is, through Adam and Eve, who are two in one flesh (Gen. 2:24), “death entered into the world (Rom. 5:12).”

And therefore the Lord looked from heaven upon the earth, so that he might free from their ancestral errors the imitators of those who were slain through the devil’s deceit.

He did this so that they might announce in Zion, that is, in the Church militant, the name of the Lord, which is admirable above every name (Phil. 2:9), and there is no other name under heaven by which we ought to be saved (Acts 4:12).

And so that they might announce his praise—I mean the Lord’s—in Jerusalem, that is, in the Church triumphant.

He says that his name is to be announced in Zion and his praise in Jerusalem because “Zion” is interpreted as “watchtower,” while “Jerusalem” is interpreted as “vision of peace.”

In the present Church we see God through a mirror and in an enigma; in the heavenly Church we shall see him as he is. Now we know in part; then we shall know even as we have been known (1 Cor. 13:9, 12). In the present we understand by contemplating the power of the divine name; in the future, seeing peace, we shall raise the proclamations of his praise.

But he did not do only the things mentioned so that the Lord’s name might be announced in Zion and his praise in Jerusalem. He also did them in order to gather the peoples—the Jewish people and the Gentiles—into one worship and one faith, so that there might be “one sheepfold and one shepherd (John 10:16),” just as there is “one God, one faith, one baptism (Eph. 4:5).”

And he did so also to gather the kings of the earth, not only those who rule over peoples, but also those who rule themselves and their affections and movements of mind well, so that they may serve the Lord, that is, the one of whom it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve (Deut. 6:13),” for to serve him is to reign; and the one who has written on his garment and on his thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev. 19:16).”

Moved by these benefits and kindled with love for eternity, the Church responded—not so much with voice as with heart, not so much with word as with desire, not so much with tongue as with life—to that Lord, rejoicing and obeying his commandments in the way of his virtue, that is, in those who have already undertaken the way of his virtue and perfection.

With immense desire she asked and implored, burning with longing, that he might tell her whether, after a few days, she would reach the homeland of heavenly blessedness. She said: “Make known to me the small number of my days,” that is, show me whether I must remain only a few days in this exile of pilgrimage.

“For I desire to depart and be with Christ (Phil. 1:23),” and I long to reach the heavenly kingdom, praying continually that your kingdom may come (Matt. 6:10).

But lest anyone should think that, because of the small number of days she desires, the Church would come to an end before the end of the world, she added and said: “Do not recall me in the midst of my days,” that is, before the end of the world [Col. 1169A]. This is the appointed period of the Church’s duration, since Christ promised his faithful that he would be with them all days, until the consummation of the age (Matt. 28:20).

The middle period is that which lies between two extremes: namely, between the end of the present age and the beginning of the future one.

Therefore I do not desire a small number of days so that I may cease to exist before the end of the world, but so that the end of the world may draw near. And so that I may be with you throughout the years of eternity, because your years extend from generation to generation and never fail, since they have neither beginning nor end; there nothing is changeable, nothing past, nothing future, and there the saints will rejoice with the Lord in everlasting gladness.

These, I say, are the things to which the Christian people in the Church Militant will respond to you; and this will not come from themselves but from you. For you founded the earth in the beginning—that is, you will found the lesser members of that people who will respond, your earth—and you will make them firm in constancy through the Beginning, that is, through me, who am the beginning and the end of all things. And the heavens—that is, the higher and more distinguished members of that people—will be the work of your hands; that is, the fact that they will be heavens will come from the operations of your grace. And those heavens must respond to you. For those heavens will perish through bodily death, whether they respond or not—as if he were saying: Since they must necessarily perish, they would be insane if they hesitated to lose this perishable life for your sake.

I say that they will perish, but you—that is, yet you—remain in eternity. Therefore you can give eternity to them. In calling him eternal, he intends to attract them more strongly to respond. I say that they will perish, and not merely a few, but all of them will grow old like a garment; that is, they will gradually fail by growing old, like a garment that becomes worn out and reaches the point of deterioration. Therefore they must still respond to you, because if they do so, you will change them—though they are themselves subject to aging and decay, like some covering—from perishability into eternity in the future; and thus, that is, through you, they will be changed. Otherwise they would not be changed. “They will be changed” means the same as “you will change them”; but it is repeated for this reason, to indicate that they cannot change themselves.

I say that they will be changed; but you—that is, yet you—are the very same, that is, you are immutable. Therefore you can make them immutable. Nor are you immutable only for a time; rather, your years will not fail, that is, they are eternal. He said this above, where he said, “You remain,” but he repeats it here in order to add the following.

I say that your years will not fail. Your years will be inhabited—that is, possessed—by the sons, that is, by the good works which your servants will produce of themselves in the manner of sons. This means that good works will be the reason why your servants will possess your years. And in order that they may dwell there through good works, their seed will be directed—that is, the works they sow here will always be directed from good to better, until they reach the age to come.

This statement—that the sons of the servants will dwell there—was prefigured by the Jews who went out from Egypt, whose sons inhabited the Promised Land, which they would never have inhabited had they not been directed by Moses and the other leaders.

## ON PSALM 102

The title of the hundred and second Psalm: “A Psalm belonging to David,” that is, to Christ—not because Christ himself is speaking here, but because each faithful person who is introduced as speaking here exhorts his soul to bless God with good devotion, in consideration of the benefits that God gives the faithful here and will give them in the future, benefits that he also displays. He does this with the intention of urging others, by his example, to bless God. And it is rightly joined to the preceding psalm, so that he exhorts himself to bless Christ because in the preceding psalm he heard Christ concerned with the salvation of his own.

“Bless the Lord, my soul”—that is, Christ. It is as though he were saying: Since, as was shown in the preceding psalm, he prayed for you, became mortal, and blessed you by restoring you through his death, O my soul, bless him—that is, magnify him with inward devotion. He does not speak of the soul in such a way as to exclude the body from blessing through the praise of the outward voice; rather, when the soul truly blesses God, there is no doubt that the body too should bless him, whenever that is appropriate.

And let my soul bless him not in such a way that any of its powers resists, but let everything that is within me—that is, both my sensory faculty and my intellectual faculty, my free will, and all the powers that are in my soul—bless his holy name, which is “Lord.” It is as though he were saying: Exalt him by obeying him in all things, and do this in consideration of his holy name, because he is called Lord and Almighty. That name is holy, that is, worthy of love.

He repeats the exhortation in order to add the following: “Bless, I say, my soul, the Lord Christ; and, so that you may always have a reason to bless him, do not forget all his recompenses”—that is, commit to memory the benefits that he has already repaid to you and will repay in the future, although you have gravely offended him and, for those offenses, he could justly repay you with eternal damnation.

He explains these recompenses as follows: “His recompenses”—I mean, of the one who is merciful toward all your iniquities, both original and actual, by forgiving them; and, once the iniquities have been forgiven, he also heals your infirmities—that is, the weaknesses you have for doing good, arising from your evil habits of sinning. For after someone ceases from sin, those very habits of sin leave him weak and sluggish for doing good, like a sick person who, after recovering from a prolonged illness, remains weak for a long time and unable to work. God gradually heals these weaknesses when he makes people capable of acquiring the habit of good works.

And the Lord also redeems—that is, will redeem—your life from destruction by the price of his death, so that it may not be subject to the eternal destruction of the condemned. It should be understood that he redeemed everyone once, when he was placed upon the cross; but when it is said that he now redeems or will redeem, this means the same as saying that, by the price of redemption which he has already paid, he rescues and will rescue those who are to be saved from eternal destruction: in the present state, when they die, and others in the future, when they die, so that they may not live in eternal death and torment with the condemned.

And he is the one who crowns—that is, will crown—you with the crown of eternal blessedness. He will do this “in mercy,” that is, through his natural mercy, and “in mercies,” that is, through the mercies of this age. He will crown you on account of the good works you perform, which are his mercies—that is, benefits proceeding from his mercy. For his merciful benefits include the fact that anyone performs good works here.

And the Lord is the one who fills—that is, will fill—your desire with the eternal good things that you desire. This phrase is a qualification indicating the extent to which he will crown you. It is as though he were saying: He will crown you with eternal goods because you greatly desire them, and he himself will greatly fill your desire with those goods, so that you can say, “It is enough.”

And thus he will crown you, so that your youth—which you possess here in baptism through the forgiveness of sins—will be renewed, that is, made new again in the future through glory and impassibility, as the youth of the eagle is renewed. This means the following: When an eagle passes from youth into old age, it becomes extremely weak because the upper part of its beak grows excessively and prevents it from eating. Later, however, when it breaks off the excess of that same beak by striking it against a stone, it regains its former ability to eat and thus becomes young again—not in the smallness of its years, but in the former strength of its body.

So too you, O soul, who through Adam passed from the youth of eternal blessedness into the old age of sinning and suffering, have also become young in part through baptism, namely through the forgiveness of sins and the restoration of virtues. Much more will you become young in the future, when, by joining yourself to Christ, who is the firm stone, you lay aside the excess of the old suffering and ignorance that you have from Adam. Then at last you will be refreshed by the saving bread of divine contemplation, by which at present you are not fully refreshed because of the old age mentioned above. Therefore you continue to grow old and become weak. Hence it is written: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21:5).

Since he had said that his soul would be filled with eternal goods, which are not yet visible, and someone might doubt whether he would grant them, he intends to prove that he will truly grant them by means of the evident benefits that he has already bestowed, as follows:

I said that he would fill me and the other righteous with good things—namely, immortality, impassibility, and freedom from sin—and this is true. For if he did not fill us with those goods, he would truly be angry with us forever. But he will not be angry forever; that is, he will not always exercise anger against us, meaning the vengeance of original sin—mortality and suffering. Rather, at some time he will make us immortal and impassible. Nor will he threaten us forever through the Scriptures, so that we cease from sins, as he now threatens us when we sin. Instead, he will restore us to such perfection that we will sin no more and he will no longer need to threaten us.

[Col. 1172A] This is further demonstrated by the fact that he will not be angry forever, because here the Lord shows mercy to his own—that is, he bestows the benefits of his mercy upon the righteous, namely the forgiveness of sins and the justification of virtues and good works. He would do this in vain if he were going to remain angry forever.

It is further demonstrated by the fact that he imposes this judgment upon all his own who suffer injury in this life for his sake: he judges that they should suffer injury. This would certainly be most wretched if he were going to remain angry with them forever. Hence the Apostle says: “If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are more miserable than all men” (1 Cor. 15:19).

This is demonstrated not only by what I have just mentioned, namely, what the Lord himself accomplishes in the new people, but also by what he accomplished for the earlier people: namely, by the fact that he formerly made his ways known to Moses the lawgiver—that is, his commandments—and through Moses made his will known to the children of Israel, that is, his commandments. He would have done this uselessly if he were going to remain angry forever.

He repeats what he said in equivalent language. When he says, “showing mercy,” he says “merciful,” in order to add the following: He is merciful, I say—that is, he shows mercy—and the Lord is merciful by nature. He is also long-suffering, that is, patient with sinners in the breadth of his forbearance. I say that he is merciful, and not merely so, but greatly merciful. Hence it is clear that he will not be angry forever. For what purpose would his mercy and long-suffering serve if his anger were to last forever?

This too is demonstrated by the fact that he has not dealt with us according to our sins with the recompense of just condemnation; nor has he repaid us according to our actual iniquities with condemnation. Rather, he has forgiven all iniquities and sins. This would certainly be fruitless if his anger were going to last forever.

It is also demonstrated by the fact that, according to the height of heaven above the earth, he has strengthened—that is, made firm—his mercy, meaning the benefit of his mercy, over those who fear him chastely. Just as heaven is lofty and exalted in comparison with earth, so mercy has made us, who were previously unworthy and cast down, worthy and exalted in innocence. This too he would have done uselessly if he were not going to withdraw his anger.

It is further demonstrated by the fact that he has put our iniquities far from us—that is, he has removed the inward blindness that was the cause of our iniquities and has inwardly enlightened us through special grace.

And he has put the blindness of our iniquities far from us who have been enlightened, as far as the rising of the sun is from the west—that is, from the setting of the sun. Light is understood through the rising of the sun, because light follows its rising; darkness, however, is understood through its setting, because darkness follows it. It is as though he were saying: As far as light is from darkness—not locally, but by nature—so far has he made us, who were previously blind of ourselves, different from what we now are after being enlightened.

This would certainly be rendered void if he were going to remain angry forever. It is demonstrated further by the fact that, just as a father has mercy on his children when he sees them going astray and, in order to recall them to the way of righteousness, chastises them with paternal affection by scourging them, so the Lord has had mercy on us who fear him, chastising us piously through the scourges of tribulations. This too would be entirely pointless unless his anger were someday to end.

And he has had mercy because he himself, although he appears severe in scourging, nevertheless, by having mercy, recognized our formation—that is, he recognized that we are earthly and fragile, like a potter’s work. He explains how we are such a formation when he adds that he who seemed to have forgotten us for a long time remembered that we are dust—that is, earthly and readily inclined to sin—and, with respect to ourselves, barren of good, like dust, which is earth, easily moved and barren of fruit.

And he remembered how every human being is quickly passing away and perishable like grass, “which today is, and tomorrow is cast into the oven” (Matt. 6:30). Thus he is like grass, whose days—that is, whose life—will quickly flower, or rather wither away; that is, it will quickly pass from blossoming to decay, like the flower of the field, which quickly withers. It is fitting that he adds “of the field,” for the flower of the field withers more quickly when it is cut and uprooted as the field is plowed than does a flower of a garden or meadow when it is plucked.

He also remembered that the spirit—that is, the inclination of their heart within the person—will quickly pass away, insofar as that person is fragile, from good to evil. And it will pass away in such a way that it does not remain—that is, it does not stop. It will not cease passing away after it has once passed away, but will continually pass from evil to worse. And after it has passed away, it will not know its place by itself; that is, it will not know the state of innocence from which it passed away, so as to be able to return to it by its own power.

I say that, with respect to its fragility, it will pass away and will not know; but with respect to the mercy of the Lord, who mercifully assists it, it will know and will return to the state of innocence. This is what he says in equivalent words: “But the mercy of the Lord,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: Insofar as he depends upon himself, no one who has passed away will return; but the mercy of the Lord is over us who fear him chastely. It is in our higher part, namely in our rationality, so that after we have passed away, it may cause us to return through repentance and satisfaction.

I say that this mercy works in human beings from eternity and unto eternity—that is, from the first righteous person to the last righteous person. In accordance with this, he himself promises his own in the Gospel, saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

Nor is his mercy only over those who fear him; his justice also—that is, “so that the one who is righteous may be justified still further” (Rev. 22:11)—will be bestowed upon those who keep his covenant, that is, his law given to us. This means: His mercy will work not only in those who fear him, but also his justice, so that those who have been justified may be justified still further.

His justice, I say, will not only work in the righteous who are present, but will reach to the latest sons of sons—that is, to the final generation of the righteous.

He explains how they keep his covenant as follows: I say that they keep his covenant, and they keep it in this way: They remember his commandments, not carelessly consigning them to oblivion, but also advancing themselves toward carrying them out. For it would not be enough to remember them unless they also fulfilled them. And they do not have from themselves the fact that they remember and fulfill them, but from God.

For the Lord the Father prepared his seat—that is, his dwelling—in them, and he did this in heaven, that is, through heaven, namely through Christ. From him they have the fact that they remember and fulfill, because through Christ they have been made the seat of God. Or it may be understood in this way: They remember because the Lord Christ, in heaven—that is, in those who have been made heaven through the sublimity and dignity of their life—prepared his seat. This means that he first made them heaven, and thus made them his seat.

And he does not sit only in some of them; rather, his kingdom will rule over all. That is, he who is king will rule over all those who are in heaven, and he will always rule them well.

After displaying the benefits in consideration of which he exhorted his soul to bless God, he returns to the exhortation as follows:

I said that my soul should bless the Lord in consideration of his recompenses, which I have displayed. But these benefits should not be the only reason for me to bless the Lord. You also, all his angels, bless the Lord in me—that is, all of you apostles who are his angels, his messengers, bless the Lord. Be a reason for me to bless the Lord; that is, in consideration of your dignity, let me magnify the Lord who has made you so worthy and exalted.

He specifies which angels he means when he adds: “His angels,” I say, who are mighty in strength—that is, in miracles—who do his word, who fulfill his commandments, and who also advance yourselves toward hearing the voice of his words; that is, toward making others hear the voice of your preaching, which represents the words of the Lord.

And you also, all his supercelestial powers, bless the Lord in me; be, for me as I contemplate the nature of your dignity, a reason to bless the Lord. In Hebrew it reads: “all his armies.”
