You powers, I say, who are his ministers and do his will, which has been entrusted to you. Hence the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits?” (Heb. 1:14), and so forth.

But not only angels and powers should be a reason for me to bless the Lord. To speak universally, you, all his works, bless the Lord; that is, be a reason for me to bless the Lord.

And not only should you, O soul, bless the Lord in consideration of the good things that he himself performs; also bless the Lord, O my soul, in every place of his dominion—that is, by considering every place of his dominion, namely every state of his rule, both among good and among evil. This means: Consider how he rules not only over the good, so that they may turn out for good, but also over the evil, so that they may come to serve any advantage of his own people. And with this consideration bless the Lord, who possesses this wondrous power.

## ON PSALM 103

[Col. 1175A]

The title of the hundred and third Psalm: “A Psalm belonging to David,” that is, to Christ. It is not that Christ himself speaks here, but that the Prophet, speaking in this psalm for the purpose of instructing others to bless the Lord, exhorts his soul to bless the Lord Christ in consideration of the things that he will magnificently accomplish both through himself and through his own people. He explains these things at length, and in consideration of his wondrous power, which he demonstrates in what follows.

“Bless the Lord, my soul”—that is, Christ: magnify and exalt him with intense devotion and affection. Out of excessive affection he addresses him directly as follows:

Truly it is fitting that my soul should bless you. For, O Lord my God—that is, you, Christ, whom I, the Prophet, regard as my Lord and my God, although unbelieving Jews will say that you are only a man—you have been greatly magnified; that is, you will be exceedingly magnified in the wonders that you will accomplish in your own people.

And behold, you will be magnified in these wonders: in this, namely, that you have put on confession and beauty—that is, you will put on those who confess the ugliness of their sins and who, through this, will become beautiful in innocence and virtues. This means: You will join the apostles to yourself, making them inwardly beautiful because they will humbly confess the ugliness of their sins; you will be adorned by them as a body is adorned by clothing.

Hence it is said through the Prophet: “The Lord lives, for you will be clothed with all these” (Isa. 49:18).

And you will be clothed with light as with a garment; that is, you will be surrounded and adorned by those same apostles, who will be a light to their subjects through their teaching, just as a body is surrounded and adorned by the precious garment with which it is clothed. They are also called light by emphasis, because they will have been greatly illuminated inwardly by heavenly grace.

They will be inwardly illuminated because you will stretch out the heaven like a skin for them—that is, the teaching of the prophets, which is called heaven both on account of its dignity and because, just as the heavens conceal their secrets, you will stretch those teachings out for them in the manner of a folded skin that is extended. This means: You will illuminate them inwardly by opening prophetic writings to them, writings that lie hidden and are as though folded up.

The comparison is to a folded skin that, although it contains certain hidden things within itself, is revealed in every respect when it is stretched out.

I say that you will be magnified—you who cover, that is, will cover, the upper parts of heaven with waters, namely with the manifold grace of the Holy Spirit, by which the faithful are refreshed as by water. The upper parts of that heaven are charity toward God and toward one’s neighbor, which are the higher and more excellent commandments in that heaven, namely in that teaching of the prophets. It is as though he were saying: In order to make those same apostles, who will confess their ugliness, beautiful, you will protect and strengthen them through special grace, so that they may not fail in anything.

Or it may be understood in another way. “Stretching out the heaven like a skin” remains unchanged; and truly you will be magnified, you who cover—that is, obscure—the upper parts of heaven, meaning the surface of the written text of the prophecies, with waters, that is, with spiritual meanings by which the faithful are refreshed in soul.

It is as though he were saying: Although the surface of the written text of those prophecies is covered with waters—that is, filled with and obscured by spiritual meanings—you will nevertheless stretch out and open those prophecies to the apostles.

The upper parts are rightly called the surface of the written text because they are seen more quickly than the meanings contained within them, just as the upper parts of any object are seen more quickly than those that lie within. The prophecies are called both the sequence of the written text and the words collected in the writing, as well as the meanings.

And truly you will be magnified, you who place the cloud—that is, will place those same preachers, who will drench others in the manner of clouds—those whom I said above would be confessing and beautiful. “Your ascent” does not mean the means by which you ascend, but the means by whose teaching others ascend to you.

This means: You will make those apostles so worthy and exalted that, by their example and teaching, others will ascend to the knowledge of you.

And although ascent to you will take place through them, you will nevertheless be magnified, you who walk—that is, will walk—not locally but spiritually, upon the wings of the winds, that is, upon the agile and subtle contemplations of spiritual men. They are called winds because they are spiritual, just as wind, although bodily, is called incorporeal because it is invisible.

Their subtle contemplations are called wings because through them they fly toward contemplating the nature of God, just as a bird flies upward on wings.

This is as though he were saying: Although they will think subtly about you, and others will assent through them, you will nevertheless surpass their sublimities by the sublimity of your ineffable nature.

Hence John says: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18).

Or you will surpass the agility of their love by the sublimity of your love. I speak of the exceedingly excellent sublimity of your love. For although they will love you greatly, you will nevertheless love them much more. Hence the same Lord says in the Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16).

And truly you will be magnified, you who make your angels spirits—that is, you will make your apostles your messengers, who will announce your name throughout all nations, spiritual in understanding. It is as though he were saying: Although you surpass their subtle contemplations, they will nevertheless be spiritual in understanding.

Hence it is said through the prophet Joel: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:28). For “angels” means “messengers.”

And you will make those same angels, who are your ministers in administering your commandments to others, a burning fire—that is, comparable to fire in the nature by which fire burns. For just as fire, by burning, purifies and consumes the impurities of gold or silver, so they, by burning sinners through the chastisement of their teaching, will destroy the filth of their sins.

And truly you will be magnified, you who founded the earth—that is, by faith you will found your cultivated earth, the Church, upon its own stability—that is, upon its stable foundation, namely upon yourself.

Hence the Apostle says: “No one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Christ” (1 Cor. 3:11). And elsewhere: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone” (Eph. 2:20).

And because it will be founded in this way, it will not be shaken—that is, it will not be cast down—nor will it be moved from its stability by any attack of tribulations throughout the age of this world that is to follow, that is, throughout eternity. For it will be founded upon the firm rock.

It should be noted that, even if some of its weaker members are occasionally shaken, this does not obstruct the point. For it is said of the whole Church that it will not be shaken. Since he had said that it would not be shaken, someone might ask whether there would be any place for shaking. To this he adds the following:

It could truly be shaken. For the abyss—that is, the deep multitude of persecutors, deep in sins after the manner of an abyss—will be the covering of its earth; that is, it will be an enveloping of that Church like a garment. This means: Just as a garment surrounds and envelops the body, so the multitude of persecutors will envelop the Church on every side with tribulations.

And not only will the multitude of persecutors envelop the lesser members, but waters—that is, persecutors—will stand above the mountains, meaning the leaders of the Church, in order to plunge them into death as waters do. But so that the Church may not be shaken by the waters, those waters will flee at your inward rebuke; that is, the persecution will cease. This means: So that the Church may not be shaken by persecution that lasts too long, you will rebuke them inwardly, either through miracles or in some other way, although they themselves may not perceive it. And although they will not be converted, they will nevertheless at some time cease from persecution.

Nor will they merely cease from persecution; they will also fear—that is, they will feel fear concerning the fact that they have persecuted. This fear will arise from the voice of the thunder, that is, from the voice of the preachers. It is called the voice of thunder both because it is manifest and because it threatens death to those unwilling to obey, after the likeness of thunder, which is manifest and threatens death.

And after the waters have ceased through fear, the mountains ascend—that is, they will appear ascending—the mountains being the leaders; and the plains descend—that is, the subjects will appear descending and subordinate, like plains, which are low and subject to the mountains.

Both mountains and plains will come into the place—that is, into the state—which you founded for them. That is, you will establish this state, assigning each of them their position, so that the leaders hold the higher place and the subjects the lower.

It is as though he were saying: While persecution exists in the Church, the leaders will not be able to exercise their leadership; therefore it will not be possible to see who are leaders and who are subjects. But when persecution ceases and the leaders exercise their leadership, then at last the ascent of the mountains—that is, the sublimity of the leaders—and the descent of the plains—that is, the subjection of the subjects—will appear.

And all this will be for the magnification of the Lord, who will thus establish distinctions in the Church. Therefore he must be blessed. This was prefigured in the time of the Flood: while the surface of the earth was covered, there was no distinction between mountains and plains; but when the Flood receded, the ascent of the mountains and the descent of the plains appeared.

I say that waters will stand above the mountains, and in that very state of persecution you set—that is, will set—a boundary for the waters, which they will not transgress; that is, they will not cross it. This means: So that they may not completely overwhelm the Church, you will establish a limit for their persecution which they will not be permitted to exceed.

And I said that they would flee from persecution and fear at the voice of your thunder. Nor, after they have ceased in fear, will they turn back from that cessation to cover the earth; that is, they will not return to persecution in order to attempt once again to overwhelm the Church.

These two verses may also be read in another way, so that by “mountains” we understand not the leaders of the Church but the persecutors who wish to submerge the faithful, just as mountains of waves submerge ships at sea. The statement “the mountains ascend” means the same as the earlier statement, “The waters will stand above the mountains”; but it is repeated in order to add the following.

According to this interpretation, the text is arranged in this way: I say that waters will stand above the mountains. The mountains ascend, I say—that is, the persecutors will be raised above the faithful. This means: The waters will stand, and afterward those same mountains will descend—that is, they will descend from the height of persecution. They will become plains, that is, humble and fruitful in good, after the likeness of plains, which are low and fertile.

I say that the plains will come into the place that you founded for them; that is, they will come from a state of pride and persecution into a state of subjection, a state that you will found for them—that is, establish. It is as though he were saying: Their arrival at this state will not be their own doing; it will happen through your foundation.

And truly they will descend from their state of persecution. For in the ascent of their persecution you set—that is, will set—a boundary for them which they will not further transgress by ascending. But after they reach it, they will immediately descend, and after they have descended they will not turn back to cover the earth—that is, they will not return in order to fill the Church with persecution.

Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “You rule the power of the sea” (Ps. 88:10), and so forth.

He further shows how the Lord will be magnified:

Truly you will be magnified, you who send forth—that is, send out into the open—fountains, meaning the abundance of preaching by which the faithful may be refreshed and the incentives to vices extinguished, just as people are refreshed by fountains and fires are extinguished by them.

I speak of fountains that exist in the valleys, that is, in preachers who are humble like valleys. It is as though he were saying: The fact that the persecutors descend will occur through preaching, which God will cause to flow publicly from the preachers. Those waters of preaching will pass through—that is, they will pass through all peoples—and they will not be discordant, but will exist among the mountains, that is, in the midst of the mountains, namely in the harmony of the leaders.

For although there will be many of them, they will nevertheless agree in the power of faith. This was said by comparison with fountains flowing among the mountains.

I say that the waters will pass through; all will drink those waters, that is, beasts of every kind of the field—namely, Jews of every kind, both noble and ignoble, who have already been somewhat tamed by the old law, although for the most part they are still beastlike.

Therefore they are represented by “beasts of the field,” which are tamed, such as oxen, asses, and other animals of this kind. But not only will the beasts of the field drink them; the wild asses also—that is, the untamed Gentiles, represented by wild asses, which are not domesticated—will await them; that is, while placed in thirst, they will ardently desire to drink those waters, in a burning desire to drink them. Their thirst, I say, will be for what is most useful to them. And all this pertains to the magnificence of God.

I say that the waters will pass through the midst of the mountains, and above them—that is, above those mountains—birds of heaven will likewise dwell. These signify spiritual men of every kind, called “birds of heaven” because they rejoice in the purity of their minds, just as birds dwelling in the heaven—that is, in the air—rejoice in the purity of that heaven.

It is as though he were saying: Not only will the beastlike be refreshed by their teaching, but spiritual men also, founded upon their teaching, will rely upon their authority.

And while dwelling above them, they will utter voices of disputation concerning ecclesiastical matters. Voices, I say, that do not disagree with the preachers, but proceed from the midst of the rocks—that is, from the agreement of the preachers, who will be the rocks upon which those spiritual men will be founded.

Or this verse may be read as follows: I said that the beasts of the field will drink, and that the wild asses will await; and above them—that is, besides them—the birds of heaven also, namely those among the beasts and wild asses who will be flighty with regard to every unlawful thing and unstable like the birds of heaven, which are more wandering than terrestrial birds, will dwell—that is, will become fit for habitation, namely stable and constant in goodness—through the teaching of the mountains. And not only this, but, having been instructed, they will give to other uninstructed people voices of preaching, not discordant with their preachers, but proceeding from the midst of the rocks, that is, from the agreement of their preachers.

I said: “You send forth springs in the valleys,” that is, in preachers; “you,” I say, watering the mountains from their heights, that is, watering those preachers with the teaching of the higher apostles. I said that the beasts and wild asses will drink the waters of teaching, and through this the earth of God will be made cultivable, although it previously existed as a sea. And that earth will be satisfied—that is, it will be filled sufficiently and abundantly—with the fruit of your works, that is, of good works. This means: It will produce good works abundantly. When he says “your,” it is the same as though he had said “good.” For every good work is from God.

I say that the earth will be satisfied—the earth, I say, producing grass for cattle, that is, bringing forth bodily sustenance for preachers, who are called cattle because they help and sustain their subjects, after the manner of cattle. This means: The subject people will provide the preachers with the expenses of food, in accordance with what the Lord says: “The laborer is worthy of his wage” (Luke 10:7), and in the Law of Moses: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is threshing” (Deut. 25:4; 1 Cor. 9:9), and the Apostle says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. 9:11).

And that earth, established in subjection, will produce grass for the service of human beings, that is, for the work of human servitude—namely, for servants of human beings, that is, for the work of preachers. This is the same as “producing grass for cattle”; but he indicates something different by “servitude” than by “cattle”: namely, that they are servants of their subjects in the administration of teaching. For “cattle” could be understood as hearers, so that they would not be understood to be servants. But he speaks of “servitude” emphatically, so as to humble them and prevent them from becoming proud of their preeminence. Hence the Apostle says: “We are your servants through Jesus” (2 Cor. 4:5).

Grass and herb are called carnal because, like grass and herb, they are transitory. I say that the earth will produce grass; and for this purpose the earth mentioned above [410] will produce grass for the preachers, so that it may bring forth—that is, draw forth—the bread of teaching from that aforementioned earth. The prelates are truly called earth, because they feed their subjects with the fruit of their teaching, just as the earth feeds human beings with its crops. It is as though he said: For this reason the carnal subjects will provide food, so that they may receive from them the bread of teaching. For unless they provided it, being hindered by concern for these matters, they would be less able to preach. Their teaching is appropriately called bread, because it is more precious and more strengthening than earthly food, just as bread is more worthy than every other food.

And therefore the subject earth will still produce grass, so that the wine received by the prelate earth may gladden the heart of human beings—that is, the heart of the subject earth behaving rationally, after the likeness of a human being. This means: For this reason they will supply the prelates with carnal things, so that through faith in their teaching they may be able to receive heavenly grace, by which their heart will be inwardly gladdened. This grace is figuratively called wine because, just as wine, while it intoxicates the human heart, alienates it from knowledge, so heavenly grace alienates the heart of the person whom it imbues from secular knowledge. “For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3:19).

It is as though he said: And therefore the subject earth still produces grass, so that the prelate earth may gladden the inner face of the subject earth—namely, the reasoning faculty of the soul—in oil, that is, in the mercy of the remission of sins. This is called oil because it makes the soul bright and joyful, just as oil, when someone is anointed with it, makes the outer face bright. This is as though he said: For this reason the subject people supply them with carnal things, so that the prelates may mercifully absolve them from their sins after they have performed penance. “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 18:18).

It must nevertheless be noted that they ought to loose them not with the intention of carnal people, but solely out of mercy. Otherwise the absolution would not be valid. Alternatively, by wine is signified the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, without which no one is saved—for example, the spirit of counsel and of fortitude, and the other spiritual gifts. By oil, however, which makes the outer face bright, are understood other charisms of that same heavenly grace, which shine outwardly and without which salvation can nevertheless take place—for example, the grace of healings and miracles, the spirit of prophecy, and other things of this kind.

And not only does the prelate earth gladden the face of the subject earth with oil, but the living bread that came down from heaven (John 6:38)—namely, the sacrament of the Lord’s body, given by the prelate earth—also strengthens the heart, that is, the soul, of every person who worthily receives it, in complete perfection. Hence that same Lord says: “Whoever eats this bread”—namely, worthily—“will live forever in the soul” (ibid., 58).

I say that the subjects will produce grass for the prelates, so that they may be satisfied by them with bread, wine, and oil. And thus it will be:

They will indeed be satisfied with these riches through the prelates—not only the Jews, but also the trees of the field, that is, the faithful from the gentiles, who previously were not trees of the garden, which produce sweet fruits, but trees of the field, that is, producing the bitter fruits of evil works, like uncultivated trees of the field that produce bitter fruit. But not only will the lowly among the gentiles be satisfied; so too will the cedars of Lebanon, that is, cedars of whiteness—namely, exalted princes in the brightness of secular prosperity, after the manner of cedars, which are lofty trees. And not just any cedars of Lebanon, but those cedars whom he planted—that is, whom God will plant in faith and in those riches, and whom he will plant for the benefit of his own people.

There, that is, in those cedars, sparrows will build nests—that is, faithful monks and clerics will have consolation and support—because they will be separated from the company of worldly people, after the manner of sparrows, which are separated from the other birds. For the poor of Christ are sustained by the support of the resources of faithful princes. And he appropriately says “they will build nests”: just as a bird inhabits a nest temporarily, so they too will seek the earthly assistance of those princes for a time, but will not place their hope in it forever. “For cursed is the man who trusts in man, makes flesh his arm, and turns his heart away from the Lord” (Jer. 17:5).

It follows: “The houses of the heron are his leader” [411], that is, they will be their leader. The heron is a bird so strong that it can even overcome and kill an eagle; this bird lives in cavities of rocks. Therefore, as has often already been indicated, Christ is suitably understood by the rock. By the heron, however, are understood spiritual men, whom above he called sparrows. Although here they overcome the devil to a great extent when they resist his suggestions, in the future they will kill him completely by their merits, so that he will have no freedom of suggestion in them. That devil is understood by the eagle, which is a predatory bird, because he intends to snatch the faithful for himself.

Therefore Christ, the firmest rock of these faithful, is their house of refuge, leading them from the pilgrimage of this life to the heavenly homeland through the completion of his commandments.

The same faithful are also called stags, whom we have already called sparrows and herons. For just as stags consume the poisons of serpents, and when pursued by dogs leap over thorny thickets with the utmost agility and without impediment, and flee to lofty mountains, so these faithful men consume the poisons of vices in themselves and in others. When the thorny thickets of diabolical suggestions confront them, they leap over them unharmed through the agility of their holiness and flee to the heights of Christ and to the arduous commandments that must be fulfilled. These are compared to mountains because of their excellence, since they are exceedingly lofty [the reading “al a” is evidently corrupt] and are fulfilled only by the perfect—for example, virginity, contempt for the world, and other things of this kind.

The text is adapted as follows: I say that the sparrows will build nests in the cedars—namely, they will have earthly support for a time in the resources of faithful princes. While they are in this nest, however, they will sigh with every desire for the superheavenly house. Since they could not come to it by themselves, Christ, being the house of the heron—that is, being their house of refuge in this life—will be their leader. They are the heron: he will lead them from this nest, in which they will dwell for a time in this world, to their homeland.

He explains by what means he will lead them, as follows: “He will be their leader,” because the lofty mountains—that is, the arduous commandments—will be a refuge for the stags, that is, for those same faithful. This means: Through the completion of arduous commandments he will lead them to their homeland; here those commandments will be their refuge from the pressing suggestions of temptation.

Since, then, he had said that he would be the leader and refuge of the stags, lest anyone doubt that he would be a refuge for those who could be called neither stags nor sparrows, because they remain engaged in worldly concerns and are entangled in frequent sins, after the likeness of hedgehogs surrounded by many spines, he adds: Not only will the stags have a refuge, but the rock—that is, Christ—will also be a refuge for hedgehogs, that is, for worldly people comparable to hedgehogs.

He will indeed be their refuge through the completion of lesser commandments, even if they cannot attain the sublime commandments of God, which are not called commandments because God orders that they be fulfilled of necessity. Hence the Apostle says: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give advice” (1 Cor. 7:25).

I say that the stags and hedgehogs have a refuge; all of them are children of the Church. And it will indeed be necessary for the whole Church to have a refuge. For God made the moon to run through appointed times—that is, he will make his Church comparable to the moon—and this not forever, but enduring in the likeness of the moon for as long as these worldly times endure. This means: He will make it of such a nature that it can grow in virtues and decline after the manner of the waxing and waning moon.

It must nevertheless be noted that the faithful do not have from God the fact that they decline; rather, he made them only such that they could grow and decline. He explains when they will decline as follows: I say that the Church will be liable to decline like the moon, and then it will decline when Christ, the sun of righteousness, sets for them, withdrawing from them the radiance of his grace. And that sun will not set without reason; rather, he knew—that is, he will know—his setting, namely, he will know the reason why he must set in them. For he will set in them because of their evil merits.

He then makes an apostrophe to God out of great affection, as follows: I say, O sun of righteousness, Christ, that you will set in certain children of the Church, and by setting you have placed—that is, you will place—in them the darkness of sins. This means: By withdrawing from them the light of your grace, you will permit the darkness of sins to occur in them; thus night has come to be—that is, will come to be—in them, namely blindness, so that, remaining in sins, they may become still more defiled (Rev. 22:11). He says this in praise of God’s grace, so that we may desire it all the more, since without it we can do nothing good.

I say that the night of blindness will come upon them, and in that night—that is, for as long as the night of blindness remains in them—all the beasts of the forest will pass among them, going from temptation to temptation. These are wicked spirits, cruel and irrational after the manner of beasts, which customarily dwell in a forest—that is, among the gentiles, who are uncultivated like a forest.

Not only will the greater beasts—that is, the prelates among the wicked spirits—pass among them, but also the cubs of lions, that is, the lesser and subordinate ones, called cubs because they are subject to their superiors. Just as cubs are subject to lions, so they will pass among them through temptations, roaring—that is, fierce like cubs, whose fierceness is shown by their roaring. They will pass among them for the purpose of carrying them off through consent; and since they will not be able to carry them off unless the Lord permits it, they will pass among them so that, before carrying them off, they may ask God—not with their voice but by their desire—to make them their food. That is, they will ask God for permission to devour them, as food is devoured. Their only food is to devour the faithful through consent and evil works. Hence it is written concerning Job: “Satan asked to tempt him, and power was given to him by the Lord over his possessions and his flesh” (Job 2:5–6).

After showing how the Church declines when the sun of righteousness itself sets, he shows how it increases when that same sun rises for it, as follows: I say that the sun, Christ, will set for certain children of the Church, and thus there will be night in them, and all the beasts of the forest will pass among them. Afterwards the sun rose—that is, the sun of righteousness, Christ, will rise for them, restoring to them the light of grace. When the sun rises, they were gathered—that is, they will be gathered: the cubs, namely, will release them and will be placed in their dens. That is, they will not only release them, but will also cease from temptation.

This means: When the light of spiritual grace arrives, the wicked spirits will release them, and thereafter will cease from tempting them. This is said by comparison with wolves and lions, which emerge from the forests at night and scatter themselves for plunder; but when the sun rises, fearing the presence of human beings, they gather in the forests, are placed in their dens, and cease from plundering throughout the day.

I say that when the sun rises, the demons will release them and will cease thereafter from tempting them. Then each person who has been released will go forth to his work, that is, out of the good will he will possess inwardly. Each faithful person, having become human—that is, rational—who previously, when the sun had set for him, was bestial, will go forth—that is, will advance outwardly—to a good work that will be his, not the devil’s. And he will not go forth once only to his work; rather, he will go forth to his activity, that is, he will advance toward frequent good work. For a frequent work we call an activity. I say that he will go forth to activity—activity, I say, lasting until the end of life, which is understood by evening because it is the end of the day.

These verses can also be explained as follows. I say that the mountains will be a refuge for the stags, and the rock for the hedgehogs, and it is necessary for both of them to have a refuge. For God made the moon—that is, he will make his Church liable to decline and waxing like the moon, as was explained in the preceding sentence. He made the moon, I say, to run through appointed times—that is, one that will endure for as long as these times endure.

And through these things the Church will be established, because Christ, the sun of righteousness, knew his setting—that is, he will know death, namely, he will die—and through his death the moon, that is, the Church, will be established.

He explains by what means the sun will come to its setting, making an apostrophe to the sun itself with appropriate reasoning, as follows: I say, O sun of righteousness, that you will come to your setting; and behold how you will come to your setting. For you have placed darkness—I supply, in the Jews—that is, by withdrawing your grace from them, you will permit the darkness of blindness to exist in them because of their evil merits; and thus night has come to be—that is, that death will come to be. This means: They will be blinded through the withdrawal of grace, and thus they will hand you over to death.

And in that night—that is, at the time of that death—all the beasts of the forest will pass among the apostles through various temptations. These are wicked spirits wishing to recall them from hope in your resurrection, O Christ, and to extinguish the memory of your name. For at the time of the Passion the demons especially attempted to mislead the apostles, taking advantage of Christ’s death, when they caused Peter to deny him, and afterward caused Thomas to doubt his resurrection, as well as certain others who said: “We had thought that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21).

Hence the Lord is said to have told Peter around the time of the Passion: “Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, and when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:31–32).

And not only will the greater beasts of the forest pass among the apostles, but also the cubs of lions, that is, the lesser ones, roaring—that is, fierce—will pass among them in order to carry them off through consent, yet in such a way that they first ask God to make them their food. I have explained this in this interpretation as in the preceding one.

I say that the sun will know its setting, and at its death all the beasts of the forest will pass among them. Afterwards the sun rose—that is, it will rise—the same sun of righteousness, by rising again. Then the wicked spirits were gathered—that is, they will be gathered: they will release the apostles, and not in such a way that they afterward pass among them; rather, they will also be placed in their dens, that is, they will cease thereafter from temptation. This is said by the same comparison that was explained above in the other interpretation.

Then each of the apostles, who previously had been bestial through despair concerning the resurrection of the sun, having become a rational human being through belief in the resurrection, will go forth to his work and to his activity, which will last until evening. In this interpretation the verse is explained as it was explained in the preceding one.

The following four and a half of these five verses are explained in yet another way. I say that you will permit the darkness of blindness to be placed in the Jews, and through this night will come to be—that is, they will become obscure and blind, so that they will entirely lack reason. It is as though he said: They will not be blinded in any other way than by your blinding them, because of their evil merits, through the withdrawal of grace, so that they hand you over to death.

But not only will the Jews themselves be blinded; in that night as well—that is, while they remain in such blindness—all the beasts of the forest, that is, all the gentiles, fierce and untamed like the beasts of the forest, will pass among the primitive Church, going from persecution to persecution. It is as though he said: Since the preachers of Christ will announce his death and resurrection to the gentiles, the gentiles, blinded and unwilling to assent, will be stirred up against them in very many persecutions.

Not only will the greater and superior ones pass among them, but also the cubs of lions, that is, the lesser and subordinate ones, roaring—that is, fiercely—will pass among them through tribulations, in order to carry them off, that is, incorporate them. And since this cannot be accomplished unless the Lord permits it, they will pass among them so that they may ask God to make them their food—not with their voice, but by the very desire to incorporate them. They will ask God to have them as food, that is, so that they may incorporate them after the likeness of food that is incorporated. For they will demand from God the merit of their evil will, so that he may permit them to become the incorporators of those people; and by incorporating them they will become still more sinful.

Afterward, at last, the sun rose—that is, the sun of righteousness will rise in them according to the illumination of grace. They were gathered—that is, they will be gathered—into the unity of faith, having previously existed divided through the diversity of errors. Thus they will be placed in their inner dens: whereas previously they had been senseless and outside their rational faculties, at last, gathered in faith, they will move within their rational faculties, which are the dens of their souls, in which they dwell.

After they have been placed in their dens, each preacher, being a rational human being, will go forth to his work and to his activity. Whereas previously the preachers did not dare to perform the work of preaching openly, they will go forth to their work—that is, they will openly perform the good work—not once only, but to their activity, which will last until evening, that is, until the end of the world. At that time there will again be such great persecution of the faithful by the Antichrist and his ministers that scarcely anyone will dare to perform good works openly.

Having displayed the manifold magnificence of God’s works, he bursts forth in his praise at the sight of these works, as follows: Therefore, since you will wondrously perform all that I have shown above, how magnificent are—that is, will be—your works, O Lord! And truly they will be magnificent. For you made all your works in wisdom, that is, you will perform everything wisely.

And behold what you will wondrously perform: The earth—that is, the Jewish people, the earth of God already cultivated by the preachers—has been filled, that is, will be filled, with your possession at the end of the world, when the remnant of Israel will be saved (Rom. 9:27). This means: You will fully join the Jewish people to your possession through voluntary subjection.

And you will possess not only the Jewish people, but also this sea, which is present all around the earth—the sea, I say, great, that is, deep in its bitterness, and spacious, that is, broad and wide, spread throughout the whole earth. Spacious, I say, in its hands, that is, in the works of preaching, in which, since it is sufficiently spacious, the preachers will have room to labor. It will be filled with your possession.

This means: Not only will the Jewish people be God’s possession near the end of the world, but earlier, at the time of the fullness of the gentiles, the people spoken of here—so called because it is so great that it can be seen throughout the whole earth, and called a sea because it is unstable and bitter like the sea—will become fully and voluntarily God’s possession.

I say that the sea is spacious in the hands of the preachers, which are to be exercised there. And it will indeed be necessary for their hands to be exercised there. For in that sea, that is, among the gentile people, are reptiles without number. These are many wicked spirits, called reptiles because they creep secretly into the hearts of that gentile people, after the likeness of reptiles creeping stealthily.

He explains these reptiles in parts as follows: I say that there are reptiles there; namely, there are small animals there together with great ones, that is, wicked spirits both great and small, namely, superior and subordinate. When he says “animals,” it is the same as though he had written “beasts,” as above. For we commonly call animals “beasts.”

Jerome and Augustine say that they call the demons of night and the angels of light “animals.” They also say that angels have ethereal bodies, while demons have aerial bodies. Whether they possess these bodies by nature or assume bodies temporarily remains undetermined.

I say that in the sea there are small and great animals; and although this is so, ships will nevertheless pass through it. Namely, preachers will pass through that sea, not impeded by these animals. This means: These animals will not be able to impede or hold back the preachers in that sea, preventing them from crossing and overcoming it completely, carrying many whom they will capture there to the harbor of eternal life, after the likeness of ships which, in the middle of the sea, are not submerged by the waves but carry their sailors unharmed to the shore.

These two and a half verses can also be explained in another way. I say that your works will be exceedingly magnificent, which you will perform in wisdom. And behold what you will perform in wisdom: The earth—that is, the Church, the cultivable earth of God—will be filled with your possession, that is, with innocence and the other virtues, which will be your possession, namely, which you will rule and cultivate in them through grace, as someone cultivates a possession.

I say that the Church, your earth, will be filled with your possession. But this sea, which is present everywhere, great—that is, deep in bitterness—and spacious, broad and wide, has been filled with hands, that is, with infernal spirits, who are called Manes, because we commonly call infernal spirits *Manes*. This means: The people of unbelievers, called a great sea because of the excess of their bitterness, is full of wicked spirits whom it obeys.

And there too are reptiles without number, that is, in that people there are innumerable hidden temptations, which are called reptiles because, like reptiles, they creep secretly into human hearts. And there too are small and great brute animals, namely, there are bestial, crude, and foolish human beings—small and great, that is, noble and ignoble in every respect. The Manes, reptiles, and animals will strive, like waves, to plunge the faithful crossing the sea toward the harbor of life into persecutions and to hold them in the sea. Nevertheless, the ships will pass through there—that is, the faithful and saints will cross that sea to the harbor of life, called ships because they are not overcome by the assault of tribulations, just as ships crossing the sea are not submerged by the storms of the waves.

And in this sea too is that dragon of whom everyone knows, namely, the prince of the devil, who is called “that one” because he is known to everyone by report. O God, you formed the dragon in the sea to be mocked by the faithful—that is, you arranged him beautifully and splendidly, so that in that sea there would be a dragon who would strive to deceive the saints and would be mocked by them, when his temptation could find no place in them. This is like a wolf which, often thinking that it will soon be able to seize a lamb, is mocked by it when the lamb escapes its bite unharmed.

And he rightly says “you formed” him. For it is beautiful and very splendid, and pertains to God’s magnificence, that the dragon is mocked by the faithful.

I say that the earth of God, namely the Church, is filled with your possession, O God; and that in the sea there are animals and reptiles and a dragon; and all these await from you that you give them food, that is, refreshment. For the good, this consists of virtues and good works by which they may be refreshed; for the evil, it consists of permission to persecute and incorporate the good, and this at a time appointed by you.

It is as though he said: Neither will your earth, the Church, be able to have the food of virtues and good works, nor will the reptiles and animals be able to have refreshment for incorporating and persecuting the good, except at that time in which you determine to give food to all, to each according to its measure.

I say that all await food from you; but when you give them food, the reptiles and the other animals will gather the faithful. This means: After you give them permission to devour the good by persecuting and incorporating them, they will gather them—killing some through persecutions, but incorporating others. And when you open the hand of your generosity, so as to give the food of virtues to your earth, the Church, all the members of that earth will be filled with goodness, namely, with innocence and the other virtues.

All this pertains to the magnificence of divine power. I say that when you open your hand, all will be filled with goodness.

Afterward, when you turn your face away from certain faithful members of the Church, their inward face—that is, your grace—will be troubled by unlawful suggestions and by vices prevailing over them. It must be noted, however, that whenever God permits his own people to be troubled in this way, he either abandons them because of certain evil merits of theirs, so that they may perish, or permits them to be troubled for their own benefit for a time, so that, repenting again, they may become more humble and learn to spare others who sin.

For this reason he permitted Peter to deny him, namely, so that he would not become insolent because of the exaltedness of his preeminence and would learn to act more gently toward all those subject to him who sinned.

I say that you will turn your face away from them, and they will be troubled. Then you will remove, through the infusion of your grace, their spirit—namely, the spirit of pride, which will not be yours but theirs—and they will fail completely in that spirit. And so that they may fail completely in pride, they will return to their dust, that is, you will make them return to consideration of their dust. Namely, they will consider that at the end they will return to dust by decaying; and through this consideration they will be humbled, in accordance with Solomon’s words: “Remember your end, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. 7:40). And the Lord said to Adam: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19).

I say that you will remove their spirit and send forth—that is, from the unity of your ineffable nature you will send into them, not locally but spiritually—your Holy Spirit. Through that Spirit they will be created, that is, renewed in virtues; and through that renewal you will renew in innocence the inner face of your earth, the Church, which previously was growing old through consent to sin.

This means: Through the restoration of innocence you will renew the reasoning faculty of their souls, which is called the face because the soul is perceived through reason.

He then offers an exhortation to those who will be renewed, urging them to glorify God for their renewal by attributing to him all the good things that he works in them.

For then God will rejoice. I say that God will send his Spirit into you, O faithful, and will create and renew you; and therefore let the glory of the Lord, exhibited by you through good living and by attributing to him all the good things that will be in you, endure forever. This means: Glorify him by your good life, attributing to him all the good things that are in you, and let this continue forever, from generation to generation, through succession.

For the Lord will rejoice in his good works, that is, in works attributed to him. This means: The Lord will rejoice if you glorify him in this way, attributing to him, not to yourselves, the good works that he performs in you.

He explains these works when he adds: “The Lord, I say, who regards the earth,” and so forth; this will be explained in what follows.

It can also be read differently from the passage where he says, “when you open,” and so forth. I say that when you give food to those animals and reptiles, they will gather the faithful; and when you open the hand of your generosity near the end of the world, all—that is, all who will be on the earth, namely, in the Jewish people—will be filled with the goodness of faith and of all the virtues, when Elijah and Enoch preach to them.

But when afterward you turn your face away—that is, your grace, not in reality but according to human judgment—they will be troubled by the persecutions of the Antichrist. This means: After all have come to the faith, you will seem to turn your grace away from them when you permit the Antichrist to dominate their flesh. Thus they will be troubled in body, not in soul.

And then you will remove their spirit, that is, you will permit their souls to be removed through tribulations. I say that the spirit will be removed in such a way that they will depart from this life by bodily death. They will not merely die, but will also return to dust by decaying—their own dust, namely, that from which they were made by God in Adam. For it is written that the human being was created from the clay of the earth (Gen. 2:7).

After they have departed from this life and returned to dust, at last, on the day of judgment, you will send forth your Holy Spirit; and through its cooperation, with the Father and you cooperating as one, they will be created—that is, recreated by rising again—and you will renew the face, that is, the form, of the earth literally.

And he rightly says that the face of the earth must be renewed. For the earth, the air, and the elements, which are mutable for our uses, will become immutable, beautiful, and new. Hence it is written: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21:5).

This renewal of the face of the earth pertains to the magnificence of God. And because the face of the earth will be renewed and the faithful recreated, the glory of the Lord will endure forever—that is, unto eternity. I grant indeed that the glory of the Lord will endure forever, namely, that the Lord will be glorified through the glorification of his own people eternally.

In this he gives us an example of how to glorify God.

And then, when the faithful have been glorified and recreated, [Col. 1189B] the Lord Christ will rejoice in his works, that is, in the magnification of the good things that he works here in his own people, which will then bring about their glorification. This is to say: Then it will become manifest, through the reward of their glorification, that the Lord rejoices in the good works that he himself works in them. He briefly repeats part of those works, in order to commend his magnificence, as follows:

The Lord, I say, will rejoice—that is, he will be revealed through the effect of the reward—because the Lord rejoices in the good works of his own. I mean the Lord who here looks upon the earth, that is, who inwardly enlightens earthly people through faith. And he makes it tremble by causing repentance for sins. And not only does he look upon those subject to him; he also inwardly touches the mountains through reproof, [Col. 1189C] that is, the rulers, and they smoke, that is, they emit smoke—namely, tearful compunction, which compels the outer eyes to weep, like smoke. For this reason it is called smoke.

Or it may be understood in this way: When the faithful are recreated, the Lord will rejoice in his works, namely, it will please him that he will find nothing in them except his own works, that is, good works. For he will not find evil works in them, on account of which he might say: “It repents me that I made them” (Gen. VI, 7). The Lord, I say, who here looks upon the earth, and so forth. This remains unchanged and pertains to the magnificence of God.

Having displayed God’s magnificent works—so that by his example he might invite us to sing—he promises that he will sing to the Lord, as follows:

I have displayed the magnificent works of God: that here he makes the earth tremble and the mountains smoke, and that in the future he will recreate his own, [Col. 1189D] and renew the face of the earth. And because he is so magnificent that in the future I may deserve to be glorified by him, I will sing to the Lord, that is, I will perform good works to the Lord’s honor, and this will be a song for him. I will sing, I say, and I will do so in this present life of mine; and not merely for a time, but I will sing psalms to my God as long as I am—that is, I will perform good works to the honor of my God for as long as I live here. For “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22).

I say that I will sing psalms, and through this my speech will be pleasing to him, that is, the praise spoken by my mouth will be pleasing to him, which otherwise it would not be. “For praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Eccli. XV, 9). And I indeed pray that my speech may be pleasing to him.

But I will take delight in the Lord, as though he said: [Col. 1190A] Sinners take delight in their own works. But I, who am a prophet, whose authority and example ought to be followed, will take delight in praise and in good works that pertain to the Lord; I will take delight, I say. It is as though he said: I will perform good works with delight. Through this he instructs us to perform good works with delight.

He then prays for those who take delight in the Lord, as follows:

I say that I will take delight in the Lord; and so that sinners may be able to take delight in the Lord, let sinners, with regard to themselves—namely, those who work evil within themselves—fail from the earth, that is, from the delight of earthly things; and let those who are wicked with regard to others, namely, those who act wickedly toward their neighbors, fail, so that they may no longer be wicked.

But you, my soul, bless the Lord, with a good disposition and by contemplating his magnificent works, [Col. 1190B] which were mentioned above.

## ON PSALM 104

**Title of the hundred and fourth:** “Alleluia.” This is to say: “Praise the Lord.” For *alleluia* is interpreted as “praise,” and it is a certain name of God among the Hebrews. Thus to say *alleluia* is to say: “Praise God.”

This psalm is appropriately entitled “Praise God.” For the prophet, extending his consideration toward the time of fulfillment, exhorts the faithful who will believe from among the Jews to praise God by confessing their sins, by thinking and acting well, and by proclaiming his wonders to the nations. He does this also with regard to the fact that what he promised Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—namely, that he would give their offspring the land of Canaan—he fulfilled both literally and symbolically, and will still fulfill it completely. He also declares the benefits that he bestowed upon the patriarchs, and how he gave them the land of Canaan, so that by contemplating those benefits he might more greatly incite the faithful Jews, concerning whom he is speaking here, to praise God.

“Confess to the Lord and call upon him,” and so forth. The construction in fact begins with the sixth verse, which is as follows: “Seed of Abraham,” and so forth. It is adapted in this way:

You, the seed of Abraham according to the flesh—that is, you Jews. I am not speaking to all who are the seed of Abraham, but to his servants, namely, to those who do not refuse to be servants of the Lord Jesus. And because certain Gentiles descended from Ishmael, Abraham’s son, who have now come to the faith and become servants of Christ, he adds:

I mean you who are sons of the patriarch Jacob according to the flesh. I am not speaking of the unbelieving sons of Jacob, but of you who are his chosen ones—namely, those whom he chose by calling them to the faith.

Confess your sins to the Lord Christ; this confession will belong to the Lord. And by confessing, call upon his name, that is, call upon him with consideration of his name, which is “Lord.” This is to say: Consider that he is Lord of all, and with this consideration call upon him inwardly, praying with good devotion that he may dwell within you, according to his operative grace.

And so proclaim among the nations—that is, in the fullness of the Gentiles—the works performed by the Lord, both among the former people and among the new people.

But because it would not be sufficient for them to proclaim the Lord’s works immediately after confession and invocation, he adds: Before you proclaim his works, sing to the Lord, by thinking well of him, and sing psalms to him, by acting well. Then, having in this order been made fit to recount the Lord’s wonders, recount all his wonders performed among both the old and the new people—namely, that he was born of the Virgin, redeemed the world through his death, and performed his other wonders.

Or it may be understood thus: Recount all the wonders that are in you, declaring them to be his and not your own. That is, whatever makes you wondrous in confessing, singing, and singing psalms, ascribe not to yourselves but to him.

And when you have sung and sung psalms, do not do this with the sole intention of being praised for it, but “boast in his holy name,” praising him in such a way that his holy name may also be praised by others in consideration of your holiness. Hence the Lord says: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16).

And do not sing psalms unwillingly and out of sadness, as many did among the former people; rather, let your heart rejoice while you sing psalms—your heart, I mean, of those who seek the Lord, that is, who desire to have not human favor but the Lord as their rewarder in the future.

Seek to have the Lord as your rewarder in the future through affection, prayer, and action. Do not seek him only for a time; rather, be strengthened in seeking him—that is, be constant and steadfast. In this seeking, I say, seek to have the Lord as your rewarder in the future.

And here also, by considering your reason, continually seek his face, that is, knowledge of him, so that you may possess knowledge of his divine sublimity and thereby burn more intensely with charity toward him.

And you ordinary people, whose reason is not sufficient to seek his face, at least, so that you may have material for praising him, remember his wonders that he performed—namely, his birth from the Virgin, his resurrection from death, and the other things that he worked among the new and the old people.

I say, remember his wonders—that is, remember his prodigies—as though he said: Remember those wonders, I say, which are not ordinary things but prodigies, that is, things exceedingly wondrous. And remember the judgments of his mouth, that is, his commandments, which he himself judges ought to be carried out, so that you may fulfill them.

He adds the reasons why they ought to do these things, as follows:

I say: Confess to the Lord, sing to him, sing psalms to him, and remember his wonders and his judgments. And you ought to do all these things because he is the Lord our God.

I mean the one who previously spoke through the prophets and, coming in his own person, remembered his covenant, that is, his promise, in order to fulfill it forever—that is, to fulfill it continually for as long as this age lasts. This is to say: He who seemed for a long time to have forgotten his promise finally remembered it, so that he might fulfill it not only literally but also symbolically.

For he promised that he would give the sons of Abraham the land of Canaan, which he formerly gave literally in the time of Joshua. He also gives it to the spiritual sons of Abraham, namely, to the faithful who are saved each day as they depart from this life, and continually, until the end of the world, at different times he will give them eternal life, which was fittingly prefigured by the land of Canaan. For Canaan is interpreted as “humble promise.” Hence eternal life, promised to the faithful, is understood through Canaan; it will be attained through humility.

I say that he remembered the covenant, that is, the promised eternal life, which he will continually give to the faithful who die, until the future age.

He also remembered the word, that is, the new law, which was given through his word. Namely, he gave the new law that he had promised; it is called the “abbreviated word,” because all the moral commandments of the old law are briefly contained in it. Hence the prophet says: “The Lord, completing and abbreviating in righteousness, makes a word upon the earth” (Isa. X, 22; Rom. IX, 22).

He remembered, I say, the word that he commanded to be fulfilled through a thousand generations, that is, in all generations until the end of the world. By “a thousand,” which is a perfect number, all generations are suitably understood.

The statement inserted here, “his judgments throughout the whole earth,” is placed as proof that he is the Lord God. It is adapted in this way:

I say that he is the Lord God, and this is demonstrated by the fact that his judgments, that is, his commandments, have been fulfilled throughout the whole earth, among Jews as well as Gentiles. This would not be so unless he were God and Lord.

I say that he remembered the covenant, namely, the covenant that he established with Abraham—that is, promised to Abraham. Therefore he could not fail to fulfill it.

And he remembered his oath made to Isaac, that is, the firm promise made to Isaac, which he made with an oath by himself. For he fulfilled that oath both literally and symbolically.

And he established that covenant, that is, that promise, with Jacob the patriarch, leading us into his commandment, that is, into the fulfillment of his commandment. This is to say: The mystical promise of eternal life made to Jacob is the reason why we fulfill the Lord’s commandment, so that through this we may reach that promise.

He also established that covenant literally with Israel, that is, with Jacob, leading us through that covenant, already fulfilled literally, into the eternal covenant, [Col. 1192D] that is, into the understanding and hope of the eternal promise, eternal life, which is continually given to the faithful as they depart from this life.

This is to say: Through the promise fulfilled literally, we mystically understand the eternal promise, which is fulfilled daily in the faithful.

He therefore explains the promise itself literally, and how it was fulfilled literally, throughout the entire psalm until its end.

I say that he established it with Jacob and Abraham, saying through the ministry of angels:

“To you, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, I will give the land of Canaan; I will give it literally to your offspring.”

The prophet indicates the eternal promise prefigured through the land of Canaan when he adds on his own part:

I call the land of Canaan one signifying the portion of your eternal inheritance, to be given by the Lord—that is, signifying the measure of your inheritance.

This is to say: O faithful Jews, the land of Canaan given to your fathers with a measuring cord signifies the eternal blessedness promised to you. It will be given to you according to measure, so that although all of you will possess the same blessedness, one will nevertheless be more blessed and more glorious than another, according as he is holier, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “As star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV, 41). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John XIV, 2).

I say that he promised the sons of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob the land of Canaan. And so that their descendants might possess it, he did not leave—that is, he did not allow—anyone to harm them, namely, Abraham and Isaac, in such a way that they would be killed. He also rebuked kings on their behalf, so that they would not harm them, just as the king of Egypt and the king of Gerar are said to have been divinely rebuked lest they harm Abraham (Gen. XII, 17; XX, 3).

I say that he rebuked kings, saying in a mysterious utterance:

“Do not harm my anointed ones,” that is, those anointed by me with the oil of spiritual grace; “and do not act wickedly against my prophets.” They were indeed prophets, even though they did not publish books of prophecy.

I say that he then rebuked kings on their behalf, when they were few in number—or, to put it more precisely, when they were very few, and were sojourners, that is, resident aliens and inhabitants of that land.

And when Abraham and his household passed from nation to nation—and because they could pass from nation to nation, he specifies one kingdom as follows:

I say that they passed from nation to nation in such a way that they passed from the kingdom of the Chaldeans, where Abraham was born, to another people, namely, the people of the Canaanites.

For it is written that the Lord said to Abraham: “Go out from your land and from your possession, and come into the land that I will show you, and I will make you grow into a great nation” (Gen. XII, 1).

For unless Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had been preserved in order to beget children, their children—since they would have been no one at all—could never have possessed the land of Canaan.

And after he had preserved them as they passed from nation to nation, so that Jacob and his sons might go into Egypt and afterward return from there to the land of Canaan, he called—not with a voice, but by the command of his power—famine upon the land. That is, he commanded famine to rule over the land of Canaan, after the likeness of one who calls a servant in order to give him an order.

And so that famine might rule over the land severely, he crushed—that is, allowed to be crushed—every support of bread, namely, he allowed all bread to be destroyed, by which human sensuality is sustained.

But so that Jacob and his sons, who were to travel into Egypt during the time of famine, might have a protector and not perish from hunger, he sent Joseph ahead of them, a man who conducted himself manfully by refusing shamefully to consent to the wife of Potiphar, the eunuch of Pharaoh.

He sent him in this way: He was sold by his brothers to the Egyptians, passing from a free man into a slave. This was all the more wondrous because afterward he was made lord of Egypt, although he had been a slave.

The Egyptians to whom he was sold humbled his feet in fetters. For Potiphar’s wife, to whom he refused to consent, said that he had wished to do violence to her (Gen. XXXIX, 14). For this reason he was seized by Pharaoh’s servants, imprisoned, and bound in fetters (ibid., 20).

And there iron—that is, the harshness of tribulations—passed through his soul, that is, it caused anxiety in his vitality, after the manner of iron passing through a body.

I call the iron of tribulations something that lasted until his word came, that is, until the word of interpretation of Pharaoh’s vision came. Then the Lord’s utterance, namely, the word of interpretation given to him by the Lord, inflamed Joseph—that is, proved him to be holy, although previously he had been called an adulterer—after the likeness of pure gold, which is inflamed, that is, proved pure through fire.

Then King Pharaoh sent to the prison and released him from his fetters. And the prince of the Egyptian peoples—that is, King Pharaoh—sent for him, and not only released him but also dismissed him, that is, freed him from prison.

After he had seen that he was a wise man, he appointed him lord of his house and ruler over all his possessions, so that he might govern his household in the time of famine. He also appointed him to instruct Pharaoh’s princes in such a way as Pharaoh himself wished to be instructed—not only the young princes, who were not so wise, but also his old men, who were wise, so that he might teach them greater prudence.

This was indeed wondrous: that old men should be taught by a young man. And on account of Joseph, who ruled in Egypt, Jacob entered Egypt with his sons so that he might not perish from famine.

But lest it be believed that Jacob had been lord of Egypt, and that therefore his sons ought not to have departed from there, he adds:

And Israel, that is, Jacob, was a sojourner, that is, a resident alien in the land of Ham, namely, in Egypt, where Ham dwelt.

There the Lord greatly increased his people, that is, multiplied the sons of Israel. And he made them a strong people, that is, made them powerful in possession and wealth over—that is, more than—all their Egyptian enemies, who were hostile to them out of envy.

But so that the people of Israel might return to the land of Canaan through the occasion of the Egyptians’ persecution, he turned the hearts of the Egyptians away from friendship, so that they hated his people. Thus they acted deceitfully toward his servants, killing their children, the sons of Israel, and oppressing the Israelites themselves with slavery.

And so that his people might be rescued from slavery, he sent Moses his servant to deliver them, and Aaron, whom he chose as priest—Aaron, I say, who was very dear and familiar to him.

And in them, that is, in Moses and Aaron, he placed his words, that is, his commandments—words effective for producing his signs, and not merely ordinary signs, but prodigies performed in the land of Ham. For because they spoke the Lord’s words faithfully and fearlessly to Pharaoh, they performed many prodigies.

Moreover, because Pharaoh refused to release his people on account of the Lord’s words, he sent darkness into Egypt, [Col. 1195A] so great that it darkened the Egyptians, so that no one could see another (Exod. X, 23).

For it is written that the air was so dense that it could be touched (ibid., 21). In this way the Lord did not make his words harsh—that is, he did not allow his words to become a source of bitterness. For unless he had performed such miracles, the words that Moses and Aaron spoke to Pharaoh would have been bitter for them; indeed, they would have been the reason why they were harshly punished.

But when the darkness had ceased, the Egyptians still refused to release the people. Therefore he turned their waters into blood, so that they could not drink, and thus he killed their fish.

Nor did he punish them only in this way. The earth also brought forth frogs for them, not only in the fields but, to make the persecution more severe, in their inner chambers—that is, in the private bedchambers of their kings, [Col. 1195B] who are usually able to drive away other hindrances in some fashion but could not drive away the frogs.

And because they still detained the people, he spoke—not with a voice but by the command of his power—and there came upon Egypt a swarm of flies and gnats throughout all their borders, not merely in one part.

He also made their rains hail, so that the trees might be battered. And he placed the fire of lightning in their land, burning it—that is, so that it might burn the crops, the livestock, and the other things that were there.

I say that he made their rains hail; and with that hail he struck their vines and their fig trees. And to speak universally, with that hail I crushed every tree within their borders.

And because they still persisted in hardness, he spoke by the command of his power, and there came upon Egypt locusts without number, [Col. 1195C] and caterpillars whose number could not be counted.

The locust ate all the grass in their land, and the caterpillar ate all the fruit of their land. Afterward the Lord struck, through the striking angel, every firstborn in their land, both of human beings and of cattle, and the firstfruits of all their labor, that is, their finest crops.

Or “firstborn” refers only to human beings, while “firstfruits of labor” refers to cattle, which are raised with labor.

And after he had struck every firstborn, he led them out of Egypt with much silver and gold belonging to the Egyptians. For the Lord commanded them to borrow from their neighbors whatever gold and silver they could and secretly carry it away with them (Exod. II, 2).

And when he led them out, there was no one weak among their tribes. Then Egypt, which had been saddened at their departure because its gold and silver had been taken away, rejoiced when it heard that Pharaoh and his entire army had been drowned. It rejoiced at the departure of the sons of Israel—that is, it rejoiced because they would not return to occupy the land. And it rejoiced because fear of the sons of Israel had fallen upon the Egyptians.

I say that God led them out. And when they traveled through the desert, he spread a cloud over them for their protection, that is, to protect them from the heat, and a fire in the form of a column, so that it might shine for them by night and they might not stumble anywhere.

Then they asked for food (Exod. XVI, 3), and quail beyond number came spontaneously, without the labor of searching, falling in the midst of the camp (ibid., 13). And he satisfied them with the bread of heaven, that is, with manna falling from heaven (Exod. XVII, 6; Num. XX, 11).

And when they were thirsty, he split the rock through Moses, and waters flowed from it—not small streams, but rivers went forth from there behind the sons of Israel, and this in a dry place. This was exceedingly wondrous: it occurred in the desert, where there was no place for rivers.

And he did all these things because he remembered the word of his holiness, that is, his holy covenant, which he had made with Abraham his servant—that is, his slave—namely, that he would give his sons the land of Canaan, which they would otherwise not have possessed unless these benefits had preceded.

At last he led his people out of the desert with rejoicing. He did not lead out all the people whom he had brought out of Egypt, since many thousands of them had died in the desert, but he led out his chosen ones, namely, their sons, who had been brought out of Egypt and whom he had chosen to be brought out.

And after leading them out, he gave them the regions of the Canaanite nations—that is, after those nations had died and been expelled. He did not give them those regions empty; rather, so that the benefit might be greater, they possessed the labors of the Canaanite peoples, namely, the crops and other things that those peoples had prepared with labor.

And he bestowed all these benefits upon them so that they might observe his ordinances by fulfilling them, that is, his commandments by which they were justified. And they were not to observe them unwillingly; rather, they were to seek his law, that is, his commandments, with love, so that they might fulfill them.

Through this he instructs the faithful Jews concerning whom he is speaking here: in view of the mystical benefits that God works in them daily, they ought to observe his ordinances and seek his law.

## ON PSALM 105

[Col. 1196C] **Title of the hundred and fifth:** “Alleluia.” This is explained in the same way as in the preceding psalm, but this psalm has a different purpose from the preceding one.

For whereas in the preceding psalm he dealt with the faithful Jews, in this one he addresses the unbelieving, exhorting them to praise God by confessing the sins that they committed in imitation of their sinful forefathers. He also exhorts them to enumerate those sins and, by confessing them, to cease from similar sins; to pray as well that God may visit them through the Son; and to proclaim the Lord’s powers and offer his praises, because through this they will attain blessedness.

After they have confessed their own sins and those of their fathers, he admonishes them to pray for others. He gives this exhortation with the intention of recalling them from all sins and, after they have been brought to the faith, instructing them to pray for themselves and for others.

“Confess your sins to the Lord the Father,” you unbelieving Jews. And if you confess with a pure heart, you may be secure concerning forgiveness, because he is good in his nature—that is, easy to persuade to pardon. I urge you to confess to him, for he is not good only for a time; he is merciful. Confess, therefore, because his mercy, which he possesses by nature, endures into the future age, that is, forever.

This is to say: He is merciful forever. I say: Confess, and after confessing your sins, who will speak of the Lord’s powers and make his praises heard?

The order is inverted. First one must offer his praises, and afterward speak of his powers. And this statement, placed in the form of a question for greater exhortation, is equivalent to saying:

After confessing your sins, offer his praises, that is, perform good works in which he may be praised. And because someone might say, “We do not know those praises,” he adds “that have been heard,” as though he said: Those praises that you have already heard sufficiently through the Scriptures.

And after you have produced his praises in yourselves, speak to others by proclaiming the Lord’s powers. Proclaim, for the correction of others, that he is powerful to forgive sins, powerful to reward the good, and powerful also to punish the wicked.

For no one ought to preach to others before first fulfilling good works in himself. Hence the Apostle says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become rejected” (I Cor. IX, 27). [Col. 1197B] It is also written concerning Jesus: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I, 1).

I said: Confess your sins—and this is indeed necessary for you. For blessed, both here and much more so in the future, will be those who preserve within themselves—that is, embrace and do not neglect—the judgment of sins, that is, confession. I mean those who preserve confession in such a way that they confess frequently and, after confession, do not return to their vomit.

I said: Who will offer his praises, that is, good works? And you must indeed do so, because blessed will be those who practice justice, that is, just works, not merely for a time but at all times.

I say: Confess while praying in this way:

“Remember us, O Lord,” by forgiving our sins. You seemed to have forgotten us for a long time, while we remain under the condition of original sin.

I say: Remember us—not according to our merits, but according to the good pleasure of your people, that is, according to the good pleasure of your mercy, in accordance with the way you customarily show mercy to your people.
