And in this way, remember us: visit us in your salvation, that is, visit us, who are sick with sins and subject to death, through Christ your Savior, so that through the price of his death we may be restored to life.

I say: Visit us in obedience to your Savior, leading us through knowledge of that Savior to see you by inward contemplation. Lead us who are placed in the goodness of your chosen ones.

This is to say: Visit us in such a way that, by visiting us through forgiveness, you lead us to contemplate knowledge of you; lead us, I say, who are placed in goodness, that is, in the good works possessed by your chosen ones.

It is as though he said: Having visited us, make us perform good works in conformity with your faithful, who were chosen for life, so that by the merit of good works we may deserve to contemplate you.

I say: Visit us, leading us to see you while we are placed in goodness; and lead us also to rejoice in the goodness of works, in the joy of your nation, that is, in conformity with the joy of the just, who are your people.

This is to say: Make us perform good works in such a way that we do not undertake this good activity with sadness but joyfully, in conformity with the joy of the just. “For God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX, 7).

Lead us, I say, to the joy of good action, so that, while we joyfully perform good works through you, you may be praised by others together with your inheritance, namely, together with us.

This is to say: On the occasion of our good works, may we praise you, and may you be praised through us.

Having shown how they should pray, he explains at length, almost to the end of the psalm, how they ought to confess that they sinned in conformity with their fathers.

I say: Confess in this way: “O Lord, we have sinned with our fathers,” that is, we have sinned in conformity with our fathers, who existed long before us and gravely offended you.

He demonstrates this by parts, as follows:

Truly we have sinned like our fathers. For we have acted unjustly with regard to our neighbor, just as they did, and we have committed iniquity with regard to ourselves, just as they did.

Someone might ask: “Did your fathers sin?”

The answer is as follows: “They certainly did sin. For our fathers in Egypt, where you, O God, performed many wonders for them, did not understand—that is, did not take notice of—the wonders that you performed for them, so that by contemplating those wonders they might believe in and obey you.”

I say: They did not understand. And even if they understood for a time, they did not long remember the abundance of your mercy, that is, the many wondrous benefits that you bestowed upon them solely through mercy.

We say, O hearers, that they were forgetful of the Lord’s manifold mercy. And while forgetful, they provoked him to anger when they went up, that is, when they departed from Egypt.

He rightly says “went up.” For since Egypt is lower in situation than all the lands around it, no one can leave it in any direction except by ascending.

They went up, I say, and provoked him, and this in the sea, namely, in the Red Sea, where they ought not to have provoked him because of the enormity of the danger. For when they saw their enemies pursuing them and the Red Sea before them, they doubted whether God could deliver them, and thus they provoked him.

Or it may be understood thus: They provoked him when they went up from Egypt into the sea—the sea, I say, the Red Sea. For the Red Sea is higher than Egypt, just as is the land in which it lies.

Or thus: They provoked him when they went up in the sea, namely, in fear of the Red Sea.

“Red Sea” specifies how they provoked him and, although they had provoked him, he nevertheless saved them—not on account of their merits, but for the glorification of his name, so that through this he might make his power known to their descendants, that is, that he was powerful. In this way his name would be glorified by them.

I say that he saved them, and he saved them in this manner: By the silent command of his power he rebuked the Red Sea, so that it would not hinder them. Through this it was dried up in the middle, with the waters heaped up and standing on either side like a wall.

And he led them through the abysses, that is, he led them through the place where abysses, or great depths, usually existed, in such a way that it was dry, as through a desert—almost as through a desert where there had never been any water.

Then the water of the sea covered those who were troubling them, namely, the Egyptians who had rashly entered it, so that not one of them remained to pursue them afterward.

Then they believed God in the fulfillment of his words, that is, by contemplating the fulfilled words—namely, by considering that he had fulfilled the words that he had commanded them through Moses concerning their deliverance.

They believed that he was omnipotent, and then they praised him with the affection of their hearts, expressing his praise with their mouths.

This is to say: They praised him both with mouth and heart. But they did this believing and praising only briefly—that is, for a time—and not for long. Immediately afterward they forgot his works, by the continual contemplation of which they ought to have believed and praised him.

And when he himself had ordained by a hidden plan that they should not enter the land of Canaan immediately, they did not endure it—that is, they did not patiently await his plan—but murmured and distrusted the promise of the land of Canaan. Later, while they were in the wilderness, where there was no food, they desired a desire, [Col. 1199B] that is, the manna, which is called “desire” because it was sought as the object of gluttonous craving; or “a desire,” that is, the pots of meat which they had possessed in Egypt. By desiring, they tested God, distrusting his power and doubting whether he could give them food—and this in a waterless place, that is, in the wilderness, where at least through fear they ought to have ceased from testing him. Although they had tested him, he nevertheless granted them their request; and he granted it in this way: by sending manna, he sent fullness into their souls, that is, he filled their vitality. Although he bestowed these benefits upon them, they nevertheless provoked Moses, and this in the camp, where there was reason for fear; and they provoked Aaron, the holy priest of the Lord.

For we read that when Moses, at the Lord’s command, had appointed his brother Aaron priest, they murmured about this and did not acquiesce, saying that he had done it because he wished to exalt his own tribe (Num. XVI, 11). And because they provoked Moses and Aaron (ibid., 18), the earth opened and swallowed Dathan. It is to be understood that it also swallowed Abiron and covered him—that is, the earth closed over the congregation of Abiron’s family after it had been swallowed. It should also be noted that it swallowed Dathan’s congregation as well, but this is expressed in this way for the sake of brevity. Dathan and Abiron were in fact the authors of this murmuring, and therefore they were swallowed alive with their entire family.

Nor did the earth swallow only them and their family (ibid., 32); fire also broke out in the Synagogue, that is, in their congregation. It broke out in such a way that the flame consumed sinners from other families who had consented to them—namely, Korah and the other two hundred and fifty who had gathered with Dathan and Abiron and had been chosen to offer sacrifices against Aaron and his tribe (ibid., 35).

Nor did they sin only in this way: they also made a molten calf (Exod. XXXII, 4), and this at Horeb, in that place, namely, where obedience was owed to God, at least because of fear of the surrounding nations. After they had made the calf, they worshiped that carved image, namely, the calf; and thus they changed their glory, namely, the Lord, who ought to have been their glory, in whom alone they ought to have gloried by worshiping him. They did not change it into a true calf—which would itself have been sufficiently wretched—but, what is worse, into the likeness of a calf that eats grass. This is to say: they regarded the molten calf, which was the likeness of a real calf, as God. The added phrase “that eats grass” is not included to distinguish it from something else, but to their disgrace, since they said that likeness was God, although it is so weak and worthless a creature that it feeds on grass.

I say that they worshiped the carved image, and thus forgot God, whom they ought by no means to have forgotten: he who saved them from Pharaoh and from the Red Sea; who performed great deeds for them in Egypt—not merely ordinary deeds, but wonders in the land of Ham; and who also performed terrifying deeds for them in the Red Sea, that is, works of such a kind that he ought to be feared, since he drowned Pharaoh with his entire army. And because they forgot God, God said—that is, determined—that he would destroy them, if Moses, his chosen one, that is, his friend, for whom he was bound to do much, had not stood before him on their behalf in the breach, that is, in the greatest anxiety of concern, praying to God for them that he might spare them.

I say: if he had not stood in the breach, and this in his sight, that is, inwardly in the soul which he alone sees. This is to say: he would truly have destroyed them, unless his servant Moses, taking pity on them, had prayed for them with heartfelt devotion. For God had said to him: “Leave me, so that my wrath may burn against them” (Exod. XXXII, 10). He stood in the breach for this purpose, namely, by praying for them to turn his anger—that is, his vengeance—away from them, lest he destroy them.

I say that they forgot the Lord, and also regarded the desirable land, that is, the land of Canaan, which ought to have been greatly desired (Num. XIV, 7), as nothing. They distrusted its promise so completely that they considered it as though it were nothing and were unwilling to labor to obtain it. Although the Lord most certainly promised it to them (ibid., 30), they did not believe his words received through Moses. Instead, they murmured more and more while remaining in their tents, where there ought to have been fear and an end to murmuring, since they did not yet possess a secure dwelling-place. Even when the Lord chastised them through Moses so that they would cease murmuring, they did not heed the voice of the Lord delivered through Moses.

Although on this account they deserved condemnation, he lifted up—that is, separated and removed from them—his hand, that is, his vengeance. I call it a hand because it was impending over them on account of their evil merits: it was poised to strike them down worthily, that is, to kill them in the wilderness; and it was also poised to cast down their seed among the nations, that is, to permit their captive children to be scattered among the nations, and to destroy them, that is, to ruin them in various ways in the lands of the nations where they had been scattered.

This is as though he said: Since, on account of their distrust, the anger of God was impending over them in order to scatter some of them in the wilderness, to disperse others in the lands of the nations, and to scatter their children among the nations, he first postponed this vengeance lest they perish, like someone who lifts a burden so that it may not crush anyone.

Although he lifted his hand, they nevertheless initiated themselves into Behel-Phegor, that is, were consecrated to the idol Behel in the region of Phegor. It is as though he said: Although he mercifully spared them, they nevertheless offended him still more by consecrating and submitting themselves to Behel, and there, in Phegor, they ate the sacrifices of dead men whom the nations falsely claimed to be gods—such as Jupiter and others—who had been human beings, whose abominable sacrifices had been forbidden to be eaten.

I say that they ate unlawful sacrifices, and they also provoked God by their inventions, that is, by inventing the practice of fornication with the women of Midian, which had been forbidden by God. And because they provoked him, destruction multiplied among them, that is, many were killed by God.

When that destruction was taking place, Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, the brother of Moses, stood firm. He did not fall, but remained steadfast in the Lord’s command not to fornicate with the Midianites. Standing firm, he appeased God by piercing with a spear, in vengeance on God’s behalf, a Hebrew man and a certain Midianite woman whom he found joined illicitly (Num. XXV, 8). Thus the plague ceased, so that afterward God spared them. And because he had thus appeased God, this was reckoned to him as righteousness: that is, for this reason he was called righteous. In that present generation, in the generation that followed, and even forever, he will be reckoned righteous on this account.

I say that they provoked God by their inventions, and not only in this way: they also provoked him at the waters of contradiction, namely, before the rock, where by their reproach they contradicted Moses and Aaron, saying that they could not bring water out of the rock (Num. XX, 10). There Moses was troubled, that is, distressed, because of them, that is, because of their contradiction. He was truly troubled, because by contradicting they embittered his spirit, that is, made his soul bitter and angry. He was so embittered and thrown outside himself that he made a distinction with his lips, that is, introduced a distinction and variation into the words of his lips: although previously he had said nothing doubtfully concerning what had been commanded him by the Lord, he now spoke doubtfully. Thus these words were distinct and different from the words he had earlier spoken with certainty. For we read that he said: “Can we bring water out of this rock for you?” (ibid.).

Nor did they offend God only in these ways; [Col. 1201D] they also offended him in this way: after they had come into the promised land, and after the Lord had commanded them to kill all the nations of that land, they did not destroy all the nations which the Lord had told them to kill. They not only spared them, but also became joined to them through marriage with women among the Amalekites, whom they had spared against God’s command. Thus they learned their practices, namely, unlawful sacrificial rites; and by sacrificing they served carved idols (Num. XXV, 2–3). This became a scandal to them, that is, it became the reason why God permitted them to suffer many scandalous tribulations at the hands of those same nations.

I say that they served carved images, and by serving them they sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons, namely, to idols in which demons gave responses. He explains how they sacrificed them. I say that they sacrificed them, that is, by killing them in this way; and they poured out innocent blood, which is much worse than if it had been the blood of the guilty—the blood of their sons and daughters whom they sacrificed to the carved idols of Canaan. This was all the more cruel because they were their sons and daughters. They did not kill only a few; rather, the land was killed by them, that is, the greater part of the children of those dwelling in that land.

“In bloods,” that is, in the shedding of blood: the land was killed for the purpose that its blood might be poured out to idols. The slaughter was so great that the land where the sacrifice took place was polluted by their works, namely, by the works of the sacrifices in which blood was poured out. Thus they fornicated through the inventions of the nations, by making the nations’ invented sacrifices their own: in performing them, they fornicated by abandoning God and adhering to idols, after the likeness of a woman who fornicates when, having left her husband, she fornicates with an adulterer.

And because they fornicated, the Lord was angry with fury, that is, with excessive anger against his people; and he abominated his inheritance, that is, regarded his people as abominable and accursed, the people whom he had cultivated through Moses and the other teachers, as someone cultivates an inheritance. He delivered them into the hands, that is, into the power, of the surrounding nations. He delivered them in such a way that the Gentiles who hated them ruled over them, leading them into captivity and demanding tribute from them. Their Gentile enemies also afflicted them with countless tribulations, and they were utterly humbled under their hands, that is, under their power, so that at times they became their servants. From this humiliation the Lord often delivered them in many ways, as the history relates.

Although for this reason they ought never to have embittered him, they embittered him by their unlawful counsel, that is, by accepting the evil counsel of sinning. Again they were humbled by God under the power of their enemies in their iniquities, that is, because of their iniquities. Then, when they were afflicted, he mercifully looked upon them and heard their prayer, as they prayed to be delivered.

He heard them because he remembered his covenant made with Abraham, according to which Christ was to be born from his seed; and he would not be born unless they were spared. Because he remembered, he repented, that is, he delivered them as though he repented of their tribulation. In God there is never repentance, but it sometimes appears to exist when he changes some deed. He repented, I say, according to the abundance of his mercy, not according to their merits.

From anger he gave them over to mercies, that is, to benefits of mercy. Although he had first been angry with them, he bestowed upon them manifold benefits of mercy, and did so in the sight of all the enemies who had previously taken them into slavery. This is to say: after delivering them, he bestowed benefits upon them in such a way that all their enemies became aware of it. When he says “to mercies,” he speaks emphatically. It is as though he said: He surrounded them with many benefits of mercy.

After the Prophet had instructed them concerning how they ought to confess their own sins and those of their fathers, he also instructs them to pray in this way: I say that you should confess in this manner, saying, “We have sinned with our fathers,” and so also say: Since you heard the fathers when they prayed, delivering them from their tribulations, save us also when we pray, delivering us from the tribulations of our sins.

The Prophet also instructs them, after they have prayed for themselves, to pray for others in this way: After you have prayed for your own salvation, pray also for the salvation of the nations, saying: “We say, save us”; and we also pray, “Gather us into the unity of faith from the various nations of the Gentiles,” that is, gather those who will be conformed to us, namely, those from the Gentiles who will believe. As we say, “Save us,” so that, having been saved, we may confess praise to your holy name, by mouth, deed, and heart—that is, to the name which is the Lord—and may glory in that praise of yours, offering it not unwillingly.

Let us confess, I say, saying this: “Blessed,” that is, exalted, “be the Lord God of Israel”; let him be magnified who is our ruler and creator, we who are Israel. And let this be not for a time only, but from the present age and unto the age, that is, forever. This is what we shall say: “Blessed,” and so forth. And following our example, all people—that is, people of every kind, both Jews and Gentiles who are to be converted to the faith—shall say, “Let it be, let it be.” He places “let it be” twice either for emphasis or because of the two walls of the Church.

## ON PSALM CVI

[Col. 1203C] Title of the hundred and sixth. Alleluia, alleluia.

That “alleluia” is placed twice here, blessed Augustine affirms to have been done on account of the two walls of the Church: one “alleluia” for the Church from the Jews, to exhort it to praise God; the other with reference to the Church from the Gentiles.

Nevertheless, Saint Jerome, the diligent investigator of Hebrew truth, writes that in whatever psalms “alleluia” occurs twice, the first belongs to the preceding psalm, while the second is the title of the following one, as appears in the preceding psalms. For after the preceding psalm, where he dealt with the unbelieving Jews, had displayed the sins of their former fathers and how God, after afflicting them for their sins, delivered them from those afflictions when they prayed and repented of their sins, “alleluia” is fittingly added. It is as though he had said: Since, as I have shown, God bestowed such benefits upon your fathers that he may bestow the same benefits upon you, praise God in faith, voice, and deed.

The following “alleluia,” however, is appropriately the title of the following psalm. For the Prophet, who dealt with the Jews in the two preceding psalms, now deals with the faithful from the Gentiles, exhorting them to praise God, and to do so because he works manifold benefits in the Church. Since he rejected the Jews and admitted the Gentiles to the faith, he also declares these benefits in order to stimulate them all the more to praise God.

He explains how he delivers his own from four dangers. These deliverances do not apply equally to everyone. Not everyone falls into all these dangers, but there is no one in the Church for whom at least one, or indeed all, of these deliverances is not necessary.

The first danger is unbelief, from which everyone must necessarily be delivered through faith. The second is the habit of sinning, which remains after the reception of faith and, although it may rule over many, leads them back to their former vices. Yet there are few whom it cannot oppress. From this habit of sinning God delivers the faithful who entreat him, leading them through grace into the habit of good works.

The third is acedia, that is, slothfulness. It assails spiritual men alone: after they have attained the habit of good works, they acquire a certain torpor through the delay of their heavenly homeland and take the spiritual food of the soul—namely, reading and prayer—with less eagerness than usual and with weariness. From this danger God delivers those who cry out to him, when he arouses in them the fervor of charity.

The fourth danger is the danger that threatens pastors of the Church alone: an immoderate storm of tribulations. This occurs either when they are persecuted by external enemies who strive to devour the Lord’s flock, or when they suffer inward tribulation from subjects who behave immoderately and without correction, while the pastors deeply pity those whom they cannot restore to the way of righteousness. Divine clemency, entreated by those prelates, certainly calms this storm, either when it spiritually corrects the subject people or when, by the power of its command, it wondrously restrains in some way the assault of their external enemies.

Some also assert that the fact that “alleluia” is placed twice before this psalm was done for the sake of repetition and to give greater force to the exhortation. Since there are several opinions concerning this matter, Jerome, as one skilled in the Hebrew language, especially appears to deserve to be followed.

“Confess to the Lord,” and so forth, as though he said: You Gentiles, who are to be redeemed by Christ through his death, praise the Lord with mouth, deed, and devotion. Confess this with regard to the fact that he is good by nature, ineffably so.

But you simple people, who cannot suffice to confess him with regard to his goodness, at least confess with regard to this: that his mercy is forever—that is, because you perceive that the benefits of his mercy will endure in the human race unto the age, that is, forever.

Confess, I say. And the redeemed—that is, the Gentiles who are to be redeemed by the Lord Christ—should also exhort one another by saying what I command: “Confess to the Lord.”

He therefore explains from what they are to be redeemed when he adds: “Whom he redeemed,” I say, or “will redeem,” by his death from the hand of the enemy, that is, from the power of the devil, who opposes them out of envy. And he gathered, or will gather, those who are to be redeemed—not into one place, but into the unity of faith—from all regions.

By saying “from all regions,” he indicates that they are many and shows that the benefit is all the greater. He sets out those regions in parts when he adds: he will gather them from the rising of the sun, that is, from the east, and from the setting, that is, from the west, and from the north, that is, from the northern region, and from the southern sea.

This is as though he said: He will gather them from every part of the world. As for the phrase “from the sea,” blessed Jerome does not wish it to be understood as referring to the southern region, because Jerusalem has no sea on its southern side; but it may be referred to all the parts. It is as though he said: I say that he will gather some from the east, some from the west, and some also from the north. And all these you will gather, delivered from the sea, that is, from the bitterness of unbelief.

He intends to show the first danger when he adds, “They wandered.” This is adapted to the statement “I say that he will gather them.” Behold from where he will gather them: from error, namely, from unbelief.

For they wandered, or will wander, placed in a wilderness, namely, the wilderness of unbelief, solitary and not joined to the Jewish people, which possessed at least some knowledge of God. They were, or will be, placed in a waterless region, that is, in the dryness of the heart, lacking the water of doctrine and understanding.

Some of them, namely the philosophers, were hungry and thirsty, that is, they greatly desired, like hungry and thirsty people, to discover by reason the way by which they might reach the heavenly city. Yet they did not find the way of the city of habitation, in which there is no pilgrimage but perpetual dwelling. By this he implies that simple people who did not seek the way found it even less.

For we read that Plato disputed about the Trinity but had no knowledge of the incarnation of the Word. Hence, in the Song of Songs: “In my bed I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but I did not find him” (Song III, 1). In the same way, other philosophers disputed about God, the highest good, but lacked faith in that same incarnation. Therefore they wandered.

They wandered, I say, and their soul, trusting in those things, failed—or will fail—in understanding and every virtue. This is to say: because they will think that they possess virtues and understanding by themselves, they will fail in all these things. For virtues and right understanding are not properly to be called such when they are possessed without faith and charity.

Wandering and failing, they cried out—or will cry out—to God, not with voice or affection, but when they were, or will be, troubled, that is, when they were, or will be, afflicted by the anxiety of ignorance. “When” is causal, as though he said: The misery of their tribulation itself will cry out to the Lord, when they become less anxious because they are unable to attain the way of the highest good.

And the Lord delivered—or will deliver—them from their necessities, that is, from their poverty: from the fact that they were, or will be, lacking in faith, virtues, and understanding. It was therefore greatly necessary that they be delivered.

He will deliver them in this way: having delivered them from error, he led—or will lead—them into the right way of faith and understanding, so that by this way they might go, or may go, into the city of habitation rather than pilgrimage, namely, the heavenly Jerusalem.

Since he will bestow these benefits upon them, I exhort them to confess the praise of the Lord’s mercy: let these benefits of his mercy—that he will deliver them and lead them—be the reason why they praise the Lord with heart, mouth, and deed.

And the benefits will not be ordinary, but wonders to be displayed to the children of the first human beings, namely Adam and Eve, who will be their children not only according to origin but also according to participation in death. For it will be a wonder that he will raise the dead through faith.

He repeats these benefits, which are very numerous in relation to the many persons involved, in order to stimulate them all the more to praise God, as follows: Truly they ought to confess with regard to these mercies, because he satisfied—or will satisfy—meaning that he filled, or will fill, their previously empty soul fully and abundantly. Their soul was empty and hungry for good things, that is, it greatly desired them; he satisfied it, or will satisfy it.

He will fill it abundantly with those good things, namely, faith, virtues, and understanding. He repeats “the soul” in order to add “hungry,” as though he said: He will therefore fill their soul because it will hunger.

It is also understood that they will lead many simple people into the right way of faith, people who previously did not know how to seek it.

After displaying the deliverance from the first danger, he intends to display the deliverance from the second in this way: He will not only satisfy the hungry, but after this deliverance he will also free many of those who have been delivered, while they are sitting—that is, lingering—in the darkness of sins, and in that darkness which will be the shadow of death, that is, darkness leading to eternal death. He will free them from those darknesses, namely, from mortal sins.

Here “darkness” and “shadow” signify the same thing. Sitting in darkness, I say, and bound in that darkness by an evil habit, so that they cannot escape by their own efforts. By their liberation a greater benefit is signified.

Bound, I say, by persisting in beggary and iron, that is, in iron beggary—namely, in the unbreakable poverty of weakness. They will be so weakened by evil habit that they will be unable to resist sins, like a weak person who cannot escape the iron chains by which he is bound.

I say that they are bound in iron beggary, and that they will consequently be bound inseparably, because they embittered the Lord’s words: that is, they regarded the Lord’s commands as bitter and burdensome. If those commands appeared pleasant and lovable to them, they would certainly not be bound in this way.

They will embitter, I say, the Lord’s commands and counsel—that is, by embittering the commands given by the wise counsel of the Most High, they will provoke him to anger. This will indeed be extremely rash, since he is the Most High and powerful to avenge.

Since he had called them bound, he shows that they are bound in such a way that they cannot free themselves by any effort, so that the benefit of their liberation may appear greater. I say that they will be bound, and bound in such a way that, although they strive with all the effort of reason to free themselves, nevertheless, while persisting in their efforts to free themselves, their heart, that is, their soul, was—or will be—humbled beneath sins and overcome by them.

Thus they were—or will be—weakened, that is, weakened to such an extent that they fall into the habit of sinning. There was—or will be—no one to help them, that is, no one besides God who could help them by delivering them from this weakness.

Therefore they cried out—or will cry out—to the Lord when they were—or will be—troubled, namely, because they were—or will be—insufficient by themselves. They will cry out to the Lord with voice and affection when inwardly troubled by vices. And he delivered—or will deliver—them from their necessities, that is, from this poverty and beggary.

He will deliver them in this way: he led—or will lead—them out of darkness by grace, that is, out of those things which are the shadow of death, the shadow leading to death. He broke—or will break—their bonds, that is, the bonds of evil habit and weakness, breaking them within them and destroying them so that they will no longer be hindered by these things.

Since he will bestow these benefits of mercy upon them, let them confess to the Lord these mercies of his and his wonders to be displayed to the children of human beings. This is explained as above.

He repeats these mercies in order to commend them, as follows: Let them confess, I say, also for this reason: because he shattered—or will shatter—the bronze doors and broke—or will break—the iron bars. That is, he will utterly crush, break, and destroy in them the evil habit and weakness which are called bronze doors and iron bars, because they will hold them captive, after the likeness of bronze doors and iron bars that keep someone shut in prison so that he cannot leave.

Nor will he merely crush these things in them; he also received—or will receive—them as examples from their way of iniquity, that is, he will receive them after freeing them from evil habit, which is the way toward committing iniquity. He will receive them in such a way that afterward he will protect them, lest they be bound again by this chain.

He will receive them, I say, because they were—or will be—humbled on account of their injustices: that is, he will receive them because they will humble themselves before God with every devotion, in view of their iniquities, so that they may be forgiven. God indeed permits many people to fall so that through this they may be humbled.

The Prophet now begins to show the third danger and its deliverance, as follows: I say that God will receive them after delivering them, so that he may guard them from vices.

Afterward, however, the soul of some of them abominated—or will abominate—all spiritual food, namely, reading and prayer, by which the soul is refreshed. Although it had already been accustomed to enjoy that food, because of the delay of the heavenly homeland it will conceive weariness of it and will therefore approach—or will have approached—the gates of death, that is, sins, which are the gates through which entry is made into death. In other words, they will come to the point of almost committing mortal sins.

Considering themselves placed in such danger, they cried out—or will cry out—to the Lord with voice and heart when they were—or will be—troubled, that is, when they are troubled by inward weariness of spiritual food. And he delivered—or will deliver—them from their necessities, namely, from the poverty of fervent charity.

He will deliver them in this way: he sent—or will send—his word to their aid, not locally but spiritually, that is, the command of his power; and thus he healed—or will heal—them. This is to say: by the command of his power he will establish that they be healed, and immediately they will be healed of the languor of this weariness.

Through this healing he delivered—or will deliver—them from their destructions, that is, from the destruction of sins and from eternal destruction into which they would fall if they remained in this weariness.

Therefore let them confess to the Lord these mercies of his and his wonders to be displayed to the children of human beings, also in the manner explained above.

And when they confess to him with heart, mouth, and deed, let them sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to him. Let them dedicate to him not cattle or any such sacrifices, but praise, which will be a pleasing sacrifice to him.

They sacrifice a sacrifice of praise in this way: let them attribute to God in their minds the fact that they are not weary but fervent in charity, and let them also proclaim, for God’s praise and with rejoicing, to others the works of God existing in themselves. That is, let them proclaim that they are such through the work of God.

He also intends to show the fourth danger, which threatens prelates alone, and the deliverance from that danger, when he says: “Those who go down,” and so forth.

This is adapted as follows: Not only will those whom I discussed above consider and experience in themselves the works of divine mercy, but also the prelates, who descend from the sublimity of contemplation by descending into the sea, that is, into the subject people, just as the sea is disturbed by the most frequent storms of temptations.

They do not descend in such a way that they are submerged in the sea, but by existing in ships, that is, in governances, so that through their governance they may protect the subject people from the storm of tribulations, like ships that protect those who rely upon them from a storm at sea.

Through their governance they perform works in many waters, that is, among many peoples: they labor greatly through the governance of their preaching among the people subject to them, causing them to conduct themselves rightly and ecclesiastically.

They saw—or will see—the works of the Lord’s mercy. He rightly says “they,” to indicate that while the others discussed above will see the works of the Lord, those who descend into the sea will see his works of mercy more fully through the experience of the reality itself.

And these will not be ordinary works, but wondrous works of his mercy to be performed in the deep, that is, among those subjects who are deep in vices.

All this is as though he said: The prelates who descend from contemplation into the active life in order to govern their subjects will themselves experience God’s wondrous benefits toward subjects deeply immersed in sins. He will show these benefits in what follows.

He calls peoples “waters” because, like waters, they flow from generation to generation.

Since he had said that the prelates would see the Lord’s benefits, in order to display these benefits in sequence he first shows the danger in this way: They will see, I say, the works of the Lord’s mercy; and in order that they may see these things, he said, the spirit of the one who works the storm stood in the sea subject to them.

God permits the spirit of the storm to stand in the subject people, which we earlier called the sea. The spirit of the storm—that is, the evil spirit who produces the storm of sedition and discord—will remain in that sea. Thus the waves were exalted, or will be exalted and increased: the waves of the persecution of that sea will rise, so that the subject people may sometimes rise against their prelates through external persecutions and completely cast off from themselves the yoke of doctrine and ecclesiastical discipline.

Or, if the waves of external tribulations do not rise, the waves of inward tribulations will rise, pressing them excessively in their souls because of their compassionate concern, when the subjects refuse to amend their evil deeds in response to holy correction.

Then, when the waves of tribulation rise, the prelates ascend to the heavens and descend to the abysses. That is, they ascend in their contemplation to the heavens, as far as considering the life of heavenly people, which is sublime and holy and beloved by God; and they descend to the abysses, as far as considering the wretched—and therefore hateful—life of sinners, who will be deep in sins like the abysses.

Through this, the souls of the prelates were—or will be—wasted away and fail through excessive sorrowful anxiety amid evils, that is, in contemplating the evils of their subjects, who will be deep like the abysses.

For they will weigh against each other the sublimity of the heavenly people and the abasement of their own subjects, whose care has been entrusted to them.

It may also be read by mere analogy as follows: “Its waves will be raised up,” I say; and then the prelates will ascend to the heavens and descend to the abysses—that is, they will resemble men in peril during a storm at sea, who sometimes, when the waves lift them up, seem to ascend to the heavens, and sometimes, when the waves cast them down, seem to descend to the abysses. They will be placed in as great a danger in their prelatehood as those who, as has been shown, are endangered at sea. Therefore their soul will waste away, placed amid these evils of anxiety; and then “the prelates were troubled,” that is, their reason will be troubled. And lest they be understood to have been so troubled that they had never possessed sound reason, he adds: “And they were moved,” that is, they will be moved away from the soundness of their reason, as though he were saying: Although previously they had possessed a sound and undisturbed reason for governing their subjects, they will be moved from that soundness into disturbance because of the subjects’ excessive dissension—or they will be moved by indignation against their subjects. By this he therefore shows their excessive disturbance.

“They will be troubled,” I say, “from their reason as a drunken man,” that is, in the manner of a drunkard, who is alienated from the soundness of his reason. And they will be so troubled that “all their wisdom has been devoured,” that is, will be devoured and utterly destroyed: although before the disturbance they knew how to govern wisely, once placed in such great disturbance they will lose all the wisdom of governance. This is by analogy with sailors who, seized by an excessive storm, cannot make use of their skill in navigation.

“They will be troubled,” I say, and therefore, seeing that they cannot suffice, “they cried out,” that is, they will cry out to the Lord with heart, mouth, and deed, “when they were afflicted,” that is, when they are afflicted in so great a danger; “and he brought them out of their necessities,” that is, he will bring them out of the inadequacy and poverty of their governance. And behold how he will bring them out: “And he established them,” that is, he will establish them.

[Col. 1210A] This means: “He will change its stormy sea,” that is, the lesser tribulations, both external and internal, “into a breeze,” that is, into serenity and quiet; “and its waves were silent,” that is, will be silent and the greater storms of persecution by that subject people, whether external or internal, will cease altogether. This means that he will calm the dissension of the subject people by making them conduct themselves well, holily, and according to rule, so that the prelates will not need to sympathize with them and be anxious on their behalf. This is by analogy with the sea, which after a storm is sometimes so calmed that it is disturbed neither by squalls nor by waves, but only a light and serene wind, called a breeze, is present upon it.

We call lesser disturbances of the sea “squalls,” but greater ones “waves.” We also call a serene and gentle wind a “breeze.” Hence, by squalls lesser tribulations are understood, by waves greater ones, and by the breeze the serenity of concord is appropriately understood. Or, just as by the “spirit of the storm” we denoted an evil spirit, so by the breeze, which is serene and gentle, the Holy Spirit is understood, the author of all serenity and concord. Thus the text is adapted: “God will establish,” that is, he will change “the storm of diabolical dissension into a breeze,” that is, into the spirit of serenity, so that, every storm having been driven away, the serenity of spiritual concord may be present there. Thus “its waves will be silent,” that is, will cease—“the waves of its sea,” that is, the tribulations of the subject people—so that thereafter they will bring tribulation to the prelates neither inwardly nor outwardly.

And because “the waves were silent,” that is, will be silent, “they rejoiced,” that is, the prelates who had previously been saddened by the storm will rejoice. They will also rejoice because God led them into the harbor of their desire, that is, he will lead them into the tranquility and rest that they desire. He could indeed lead them to tranquility, but not to as much as they might wish; therefore, so that the benefit might appear greater, he adds: “into the harbor of their desire.” This is by analogy with sailors who, having escaped a storm, are tranquil and at rest after reaching harbor.

Therefore, since he will show these mercies to the prelates, “let these mercies of his confess to the Lord, and his wonders to the children of men,” that is, to the subjects, the sons of Adam and Eve. For the prelates, although placed in a storm, are not to be called “sons of men,” sons of Adam and Eve, according to death.

He explains how he speaks, so that these mercies may be the occasion for confessing praise to him, when he adds: “Let them confess,” I say—that is, let them be the occasion of confession—namely, “let those who see him exalt him with every kind of praise in the Church,” that is, in their consideration of the Church, the subject people, seeing what an excellent and orderly congregation of subjects there is; “and let them praise him in the chair of the elders,” that is, in their consideration of the governance of the prelates, who rule their subjects reasonably and peacefully. “Chair” is used for governance because governors customarily sit in chairs.

Having shown four deliverances, in order to incite the peoples more fully to praise God, and although he previously dealt with their salvation, he nevertheless treats the same matter in what follows, also treating the rejection of the Jews, so that the benefit of the salvation of the nations may appear greater by comparison with the rejection of the Jews.

“I say, let those who see the Lord in the chair of the elders praise him,” and let them also praise him for this: “He made rivers in the desert,” that is, preachers, who are called rivers because, like rivers, they refresh their subjects with their teaching. By sending them into the desert, God will place them there, that is, he will make them persevere for a long time; in this desert, that is, among the gentile people, so that he may refresh them with his teaching. That people is called a desert because, before the preachers’ teaching, they were barren in good works, like deserted land.

God will not only place lesser preachers in the desert, but will also place “in the thirsty land the outlets of waters,” that is, the apostles, among the gentile people, so that through their teaching they may be led to the faith. The apostles are called “outlets of waters,” that is, fountains, because the teaching of all preachers will flow forth from their teaching, just as streams flow out from fountains. The gentile people is emphatically called “thirst,” because it was exceedingly dry and parched with respect to the teaching of faith. I say that he will place rivers in the desert.

But “the fruitful land,” that is, the Jewish people, which previously possessed its own land fruitful in good works, he will permit to be made “salt-land,” that is, barren; barrenness is understood through salt-land because salty soil is sterile. Its becoming barren of good works will result from the wickedness of its inhabitants, that is, of those who rule it—namely, through the wickedness of the Pharisees and the other prelates, who by living wickedly and being barren will corrupt it by their example.

Conversely, he placed—that is, will place—“the desert,” that is, the gentile people, through the help of grace, “in pools of water,” that is, among preachers, namely certain people from the nations, whom he will cause to overflow with the water of teaching to such an extent that they may refresh others, just as pools overflow with water. He appropriately says “pools,” so that those prelates may be understood who remain in one place, not traveling through the various regions of the world to teach, as many bishops and the other ranks of prelates of individual churches do. This is by analogy with pools, which do not flow.

He will not only place the desert in pools of water, but also “the land without water,” that is, the gentile people lacking the water of teaching, in “outlets of waters.” Namely, he will make some of those nations apostles, so that, in the place of the apostles, they may traverse and teach many provinces, while other lesser preachers may proceed from the fountain of their teaching. Thus Dionysius the Areopagite did so in Gaul, and many others, sent by the apostles and their successors, did so throughout the various regions of the world.

And there, that is, upon the foundation of the faith and teaching of those pools and outlets of waters, he “placed,” that is, will establish, many others who are hungry, that is, ardently desiring to be refreshed by their teaching. Thus many are said to have been established in the teaching of the blessed and most glorious Martin.

And those pools and outlets “established a city of habitation,” that is, by their preaching and example they will establish those hungry people in such a condition that they may eventually become the heavenly Jerusalem, which, as was said above, will be the city of habitation. Or they will make the hungry whom they establish among them into preachers, who by preaching will make others into a city of habitation.

They will establish the city in this way: they “sowed,” that is, will sow, certain people who have been made cultivable fields of God, through faith, with the seed of teaching; and from those fields they “planted,” that is, will plant, vineyards. Namely, from believers who are to be generated for God through faith, they will firmly establish congregations of clerics and monks, which will be God’s fruitful vineyards. They will not be fruitful in evil, but they “made,” that is, will make, “the fruit of birth,” that is, natural fruit—the fruit, namely, of good works, for producing which they were born and created by God. For the fruit of evil works is contrary to nature. Sin is not nature but a defect of nature, as Prosper asserts.

And “he blessed” those vineyards and fields, that is, the Lord will bless them, namely, he will exalt them in virtues. “And they were multiplied,” that is, they will be multiplied with respect to the number of persons, “and exceedingly,” that is, beyond measure. This will be “exceedingly” because he did not diminish their beasts.

Here it is understood that he will permit their beasts to multiply, that is, those among them who will be simple and uncultivated, like beasts—namely, the unlearned. They are therefore said to have multiplied exceedingly because many of them, as will be shown below, were incorporated by heretics. For when heretics cannot devour the wise, they attack the unlearned. Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “The congregation of bulls among the cows of the peoples” (Ps. 67:31).

“I say, the fields will be multiplied.” And afterward “they became few,” that is, they will become few when the perfect are separated from the greater number of beasts who will be incorporated by heretics. “And the perfect were afflicted,” that is, will be afflicted, by the tribulation of the wicked, that is, of the heretics. For heretics are recorded as having inflicted bodily persecution upon holy men, such as Arius and many others. The perfect will also be afflicted inwardly by the grief of compassion, namely, by sympathizing with their error and destruction.

By becoming few and being afflicted, they will show that “contempt was poured out upon the princes of the heretics,” that is, upon their higher part, in the soul—namely, the disdain of God’s anger was and will be poured out upon them, blinding them inwardly. Or contempt will be poured out upon the princes, who are to be crushed by God’s just judgment, so that they may contend with one another through manifold schism and thus become still more blind.

“And he made them blind,” that is, he will permit them to err, “placed in a trackless region,” that is, in the deviating paths of various heresies, so that they are in no way on the way of faith. There are indeed many who, although they err through ignorance in certain minor matters, nevertheless remain on the way; concerning such the Apostle says: “And if you think differently in anything, God will reveal this also to you” (Phil. 3:15).

Since it might be asked how this matter concerning the heretics pertains to God’s praise, he shows what benefit will result from it for the perfect, thereby indicating that it pertains to God’s praise, as follows: I say that the heretics will err, and by their poverty—that is, by the fact that they will be poor in faith—“he takes away the poor man,” that is, the Lord will help the people of the perfect, who are poor in spirit and not proud.

Or by “poverty” he means their small number: that is, the fact that the perfect will be few will help them, since they will be few and surrounded by many heretics. And lest their households be led astray by the heretics, he “established,” that is, will establish and firmly ground, those households in the faith, “like sheep,” that is, resembling sheep, which listen only to the voice of their shepherd and do not follow a strange shepherd.

He explains how he will help his own through poverty as follows: Truly, he will help his own through the poverty of the heretics. For “the upright will see” through them—that is, having been harassed by their questions—and will see many things concerning the faith that previously had not been understood by them; and by seeing them they will rejoice.

And because they will be those who see, “all iniquity of the heretics will close its mouth,” that is, all the heretics will shut their mouths, not daring to attack them.

Therefore, since God will exercise so many mercies upon the human race, “who is wise and will keep these things, and will understand the mercies of the Lord?” He puts this interrogatively in order to increase the force of the exhortation. It is as though he were saying: Since God will bestow so many mercies upon his own, if anyone is wise, he will preserve these benefits after they have been given to him so abundantly, lest he lose them through his own fault; and he will understand that these mercies belong to the Lord alone.

## ON PSALM 107

[Col. 1213C]

### Title of the One Hundred and Seventh Psalm

“A song of the psalm, to David,” to be attributed to Christ. This treatise is called “a song of the psalm” because it deals principally with the song, that is, with joyful reward, and secondarily with the psalm, that is, with good works. In this psalm the Lord’s man acts, showing that he is prepared for obedience to suffering and for good works; and he also treats of the reward of that obedience, namely, the glorification of his resurrection and ascension, and the fact that through his death he will take up those among the Jews and the nations who are to be saved.

He does this with the intention of giving his own hope of glorification, if they should prove obedient to the divine commandments. It should certainly be noted that this psalm was not joined by the Prophet without reason from the ends of two psalms: namely, from the end of Psalm 56 and from the end of Psalm 59. This is indicated to have been done so that it might be removed as an interpretation that those two psalms should be understood only as histories, even though they are titled from the resemblance of histories.

For if the Prophet had composed them solely as histories, since the histories are entirely different, he would not have placed the portions of the psalms made from them into the composition of a single psalm; nor would Ezra have given this psalm any title other than one taken from those two histories. Ezra is believed to have supplied the titles through the same spirit of prophecy through which David composed the psalms. Otherwise they would not have been received by the Church as authoritative. This also indicates that the other psalms titled according to history are not to be understood as referring only to history.

“My heart is prepared, O God,” as though he were saying: Although, because of the weakness of the flesh, I may be seen to be saddened on account of the passion, nevertheless my heart is prepared. “My heart is prepared,” I say: that is, the will of my soul is prepared to suffer. He states this twice for emphasis, and by this he instructs his hearers even more strongly that they should likewise be prepared for his sake.

And I, thus prepared, will sing to you with inward devotion and will sing psalms to you through outward good works, and this “in my glory,” that is, in contemplation of my glory. For I consider that I am to be glorified for this reason, when I become immortal and incapable of suffering.

He exhorts his humanity to sing and to play the psalm, so that through this it may come to the resurrection. He does not state that it itself will sing and play the psalm, but equivalently says that it will “arise,” which is the effect of those acts; and through this their causes, namely singing and playing the psalm, are understood.

I say that my heart is prepared to suffer, and because I will sing and play the psalm, let it be so, O my humanity: “arise,” that is, merit to arise through obedience unto death and through song and psalm—you, my humanity, I say, who are “the psaltery and the harp.”

You are the psaltery according to what is above, that is, according to virtues and good works by which you praise God, like a psaltery that sounds from above; and you are the harp according to what is below, namely, according to mortality and passibility, which also praise God by suffering and dying in obedience to him, by analogy with a harp that sounds from below.

Or thus: I say that I will play the psalm in contemplation of my glory; and, so that you may be glorified, O flesh, “arise, psaltery and harp”—you who now exist as a harp according to the lower nature of mortality and passibility, arise from death so that you may be a psaltery by attaining the higher nature of immortality and impassibility.

I say, “arise,” and so it will be: “I will truly arise,” and this “at dawn,” that is, on the morning of the third day. By assigning the time of the resurrection, he contributes to the certainty of our faith and to a greater exhortation of his humanity.

“I will arise,” I say, and thereby “I will confess to you among the peoples,” that is, I will bring forth for you true confessors among the Jewish peoples; “and I will sing psalms to you among the nations,” that is, I will bring forth through faith among the gentile nations people of such a kind that they will sing psalms to you.

And I will confess and sing psalms not only because I will arise, but also because “your mercy is great”—I myself, emphatically, am your great mercy, since through the obedience of my passion you will bestow great benefits of mercy upon the human race. “I will be exalted above the material heavens,” ascending them bodily, “and I will send the Holy Spirit,” by whose kindling confessors and those who sing psalms will be formed.

Or, “I will be exalted above the heavens,” that is, above the angels, made immortal and incapable of suffering. For according to mortality and passibility I am now made a little lower than they; and thus I will establish confessors and those who sing psalms.

And “your truth,” that is, I myself, emphatically, your truth, through whom your promise will be fulfilled, “will be exalted as far as the clouds to be established,” that is, to such an extent that I will also establish preachers. I will bring forth confessors and those who sing psalms through my resurrection and exaltation; and, so that they may be brought forth, exalt me above the material heavens—or above the angels, O God the Word, personally united to me.

He does not say this concerning the Word as though the Word were not timelessly coequal with the Father and the Spirit. Rather, because of the indissoluble personal union of the human nature—which suffered and was exalted—the Word is sometimes read of as having suffered and as having been exalted above the heavens.

“Be exalted,” I say, “above the heavens, O God the Word,” that is, cause me, the human nature, to be exalted, and thus let your glory be exalted above the whole earth, both above the Jews and above the nations, so that through this exaltation every kind of people, coming to the knowledge of you, may recognize and glorify you as God above all.

Or thus: “Be exalted, God the Father, with me exalted above the material heavens or above the angels.” Namely, exalt me above the heavens, and through this you will be exalted among human beings; and, with me exalted above the whole earth, subjecting it to me through faith, let your glory be exalted above the whole earth, so that by knowing you in their knowledge of me they may glorify you in heart, mouth, and deed. “For no one will come to you, the Father, except through me, the Son” (John 14:6).

Make me arise, I say, and exalt me above the heavens, so that through this your beloved who are to come may be freed from the power of the devil. But in order that I may attain this exaltation, first save me from death by raising me up through your right hand, that is, through your power; and, so that I may be saved, hear me praying for this salvation.

Since he had said, “I will arise and confess,” and “your mercy will be exalted above the heavens, and your truth as far as the clouds,” and lest anyone doubt that this would be true because he had humbly prayed for it by the authority of the Word speaking inwardly to him, he confirms it as follows: “I said, I will arise, O hearers,” and so forth. And lest you doubt that this is true, know that God the Word, personally existing in me, his holy one, spoke these things to me.

And then, when I arise, I will rejoice, knowing that “death will no longer rule over me” (Rom. 6:9). And so that my own may rejoice with me in the future resurrection on the last day, I will divide from the mass of the lost “Shechem,” that is, my faithful who bear burdens upon their shoulders—namely, those who here carry confidently upon the shoulders of their heart the yoke of my commandments. And I will measure out, that is, gather from among those condemned, “the valley of the tabernacles,” that is, of those dwelling in tabernacles. Namely, I will gather those burden-bearers so that they may rejoice with me, who, although they are in the tabernacle, that is, in the service of my commandments, are a valley, that is, humble. For without humility, serving in God’s army is fruitless.

Therefore I will divide the burden-bearers from the lost because “Gilead is mine,” that is, the heap of testimony is devoted to me—namely, the congregation of the martyrs, who are Shechem. “Manasseh is mine,” that is, those burden-bearers are mine who, even if they are not Gilead, are at least Manasseh: those who forget earthly things and stretch themselves toward eternal things.

And those burden-bearers who are Ephraim, bearing fruit both in themselves and in others through their preaching of good works, are “my reception,” that is, they receive me here through obedience and conformity to me, their head—me, I say, whom they ought to receive since I am their spiritual head.

And so that I may encompass all of Shechem universally:

“Judah is my king,” that is, those burden-bearers of mine are those who, while they are confessors of their sins, are also rulers of themselves by good works. This is to be understood of the faithful from the Jews, because Shechem is a place in Judea and Gilead is a mountain. Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah were Jewish men.

He adds concerning the faithful from the nations as follows: “Not only are Gilead and Manasseh and Ephraim mine, but Moab also,” that is, the gentile people, which until now was lawless and without God as Father. “It is the cauldron of my hope,” that is, the refreshment of my hope, since I am refreshed by joy over its future separation from the lost, just as someone has hope of refreshment from a cauldron full of some kind of meat.

Or thus: “Moab, the cauldron,” that is, the gentile people that will become a cauldron—one that boils away all excess within itself and softens its heart through faith, which previously was hard through unbelief, just as hard foods are softened in a cauldron and their excessive moisture is boiled away—“will belong to my hope,” that is, it will pertain to my hope, since I hope to be refreshed by joy over its salvation. “Moab,” I say, “will be the cauldron of my hope.”

By this I will join the people of Moab, the gentiles, to myself: “I will extend my sandal into Idumea,” that is, I will extend my preachers into that gentile people. Or “my sandal,” that is, the knowledge of my humanity. Through this, “the foreigners,” that is, the gentiles who are foreigners—alienated from me by making themselves my enemies through unbelief—“have become friends,” that is, will become friends to me through faith.

Moab, Idumea, and the foreigners are the same. Why preachers and Christ’s humanity are called a sandal, and why the gentile people is called Idumea in Psalm 59, has been shown there.

Since, before I reach Idumea, I must first be led into a fortified city, who will lead me into a fortified city—that is, who will lead my soul bodily into hell, so that I may draw my faithful out from there and conquer the prince of darkness? And afterward who will lead me—that is, the knowledge of me—as far as Idumea, that is, as far as the gentile people?

Will you not, O God, lead me, you who rejected us—that is, you who seemed to have rejected mine from your grace by making them mortal and capable of suffering? This is asked interrogatively out of excessive affection. It is equivalent to saying: In order that I may join the Idumeans to myself, you, O God, who rejected mine through Adam, lead me first into hell to strip him and conquer the devil, and afterward lead me into Idumea.

Hell is called a fortified city because it is difficult for all who are inside it to get out, just as a well-closed and fortified city is difficult for captured enemies to escape. When he says “you rejected us,” he joins his members to himself out of excessive love, because Christ the members and the head are one.

And since you rejected mine by making them mortal and capable of suffering, and weakened their inward virtues, “will you not, O God, go forth in our virtues,” that is, will you not come by grace to the aid of my virtues? Indeed, you will go forth to aid my virtues, lest they be overcome by the devil, by analogy with a brave helper who goes out to assist those who are going to battle against enemies.

You will go forth, I say, but in such a way that mine must suffer many tribulations, which will be of assistance to them in attaining the crown. And so I grant that they should endure manifold tribulation; and from that tribulation “give us,” that is, mine, assistance—namely, make that very tribulation serve them as help in attaining the crown.

I grant that they should suffer for this reason: continuous bodily prosperity is vain, that is, it is fruitless and rather harmful for someone to enjoy earthly health continuously. “For God chastises every son whom he accepts” (Heb. 12:6).

He then turns to the hearers for their instruction, as follows: “God will go forth,” I say, “in the virtues of mine, O hearers,” and, firmly founded and supported upon God through this, “we will perform an act of strength,” that is, mine will do whatever pertains to virtue, namely good works. Or “they will perform an act of strength,” that is, they will achieve a strong and, so to speak, virtuous victory over all visible and invisible enemies.

And that same God who rejected mine in Adam “will reduce our enemies to nothing,” that is, he will reduce the enemies of mine—both visible and invisible—to such a condition through the help of his power that their attacks will have no place among them.

## ON PSALM 108

[Col. 1217C]

### Title of the One Hundred and Eighth Psalm

“To the end. A psalm of David.” This is interpreted as follows. This psalm is to be ascribed to David, Christ, who presses on toward the end, that is, toward the perfect completion of immortality and impassibility.

In this psalm Christ prays to God the Father to show him, whom his enemies strive to crush, as worthy of praise by raising him from the dead, making him immortal and incapable of suffering, and subjecting the world to him. He also treats of the craftiness, hatred, and attack of those same enemies. He further treats, concessively, of their manifold condemnation.

Moreover, he treats of the confession and praise of his own. He does this with the intention that, by praying, he may show himself to be truly human; but by showing their manifold condemnation and the confession and praise of his own, he may demonstrate himself to be God and omnipotent. He also treats of the condemnation of his enemies with the intention of frightening others away from conformity with them.

“God the Father, do not keep silent about my praise,” namely, do not permit my praise to be kept silent. This means: Make manifest through my resurrection and the subjection of the whole world that I am altogether worthy of praise.

I pray this on the occasion that “the mouth of the sinner,” antonomastically, and “the mouth of the deceitful man,” antonomastically—namely, Judas—has been opened against me, that is, will be opened so as to crush me. Judas is called “the sinner” by antonomasia because he betrayed his Lord and master. He is also called “the deceitful man” because he betrayed him with a kiss of peace. He opened his mouth for his oppression when he said: “What do you wish to give me, and I will hand him over to you?” (Matt. 26:15).

“The mouth of the deceitful man,” I say, “will be opened against me.” And not only this, but also the Jews, to whom he will hand me over, “spoke,” that is, will speak before I am handed over to them, “with a deceitful tongue,” saying: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful” (Mark 12:14), and so forth. They will speak “against me,” that is, they will speak deceitfully for the purpose of harming me by their deception.

And they will not only speak deceitfully against me, but “they surrounded me with words of hatred,” that is, will surround me, pouring out through so many bitter words, signifying hatred, that I may seem, emphatically, to be completely surrounded and enclosed by them. For the words of the deceitful do not signify hatred but pretend love.

Nor will they do only these things; they also “fought against me,” that is, will fight against me, with blasphemies and many tribulations, so that they may attack me in such a way as to make me deny what is true—namely, that I am the Son of God. They will fight against me, I say, “without cause,” that is, without occasion or advantage; and this is indeed more serious than if they did not do it without cause.

But they will not merely speak deceitfully and hatefully against me: “they were slandering me,” that is, will slander me secretly, although they ought to say something of such a kind as to love me, that is, so that by that saying they might show that they loved me. This means: Although they ought to utter words pertaining to love, they will utter words pertaining to slander.

But I, whom they will slander, “was praying,” that is, will pray for their salvation. In this they are all the more guilty, since they are slanderers of one who prays for them. I say that they will speak about me deceitfully, bitterly, and slanderously, and will fight against me.

“And they placed all these evils against me,” that is, they will place them against me for my harm, and this “in return for the many good things” that I did for them. This means: Although I did many good things for them, they, in return, will repay me with evils, and will therefore be all the more culpable.

“And they placed hatred in return for my love toward them”: although I love them, they will hate me. This is an illustration from the side of good and from the side of evil.

Having shown the deceitfulness and attack of the enemies, he treats, concessively, of their condemnation, first of the condemnation of Judas, since he is preeminent among them. He says as follows:

I say that “the mouth of the deceitful man will be opened against me.” Therefore, O Lord Father, “set a sinner over him,” antonomastically—that is, permit a sinner to rule over him completely. He explains which sinner he means when he adds: “And let the devil, antonomastically, stand at his right hand,” that is, let him be regarded by him as standing at his right hand; namely, let him regard serving the devil as good and useful.

He considered it good and useful to serve the devil when he wickedly conceived the betrayal of his master. By the right hand we customarily and consistently denote good and useful things.

Or thus: “Let the devil stand,” that is, persevere, “at his right hand,” that is, make use of his right hand; namely, let him persist in the vicinity of his good works, so that through evil works outweighing them he may render those good works entirely null.

“And when he is judged,” that is, since by God’s just judgment he has already been judged for his crime—that is, condemned—let him not escape that judgment salutarily by repenting in this life, but “let him go out from this life condemned,” that is, let him die in that condemnation.

“And let his prayer,” that is, his repentance, which is understood through prayer because penitents pray, “become directed toward sin,” namely, let his repentance serve to make him hang himself, which will be the gravest sin.

For Saint Jerome writes that Judas offended God’s clemency more by hanging himself than by betraying Christ.

Or “his prayer,” that is, his wish, which he will express with prayer, “let it become directed toward sin”: let him wish for nothing except what pertains to sin. “And let his days be few,” that is, let him live for only a few days.

And lest the rank of his apostleship appear to have been so dishonored because of his guilt that no one ought to be substituted in his place, he adds: “And let another receive his bishopric,” that is, the exalted rank of his apostleship—namely, Matthias (Acts 1:26). By this he indicates that in the rank from which unworthy prelates are expelled, others who are worthy ought to be substituted.

He also treats, concessively, of the condemnation of the enemies, the Jews, whom he calls Judas’s sons and wife by analogy. He calls them sons because they were then begotten by him in sin, when he provided them with the opportunity to kill the Lord. He calls them wife because they were joined to him in conformity for the production of evil works, just as a wife is joined to a husband for the procreation of children.

Previously they had been sons of God, destined to obtain an eternal inheritance unless they sinned, and God’s wife, joined to him through knowledge of him for the production of good works.

He says this as follows: I have treated, concessively, of Judas’s condemnation; concessively, I also treat of the condemnation of his sons. “Let his sons,” that is, the Jews, “become orphans,” without God the Father, whose sons they had been, because they will be the sons of Judas; “and let his wife,” that is, the Jewish people, “become a widow,” without the true God as husband, whose wife she had been, because she will become Judas’s wife.

Let them not only become orphans, but “let his sons also be transferred from their land,” and let them not have, as afterward, any fixed place, but remain always wavering, that is, firmly attached to no place; “and let them beg,” that is, always stand in need of another’s help.

Since they could be transferred either by deceit or in some other [Col. 1219D] way, he adds: “And thus I say, let them be transferred,” namely, so that they are forcibly expelled by the Romans from their dwellings. “And in the future let the creditor search out,” that is, demand, “all his substance,” that is, his sins—not because sins are substance, but this is said by comparison, 440 because just as some creditor lends his substance at interest, so the devil, since he has no other substance, inflicts sins so that in the future he may exact punishment from them. This is called “interest” because the interest itself exceeds the principal of the sin, since the sin is temporal whereas the interest is eternal.

God too is called a creditor, because he lends his substance at interest: namely, he gives understanding and the five bodily senses so that, through their service, he may collect the interest of good works. God certainly demands this interest, examining with punishments those who here neglect to multiply the principal entrusted to them.

According to both these interpretations, the passage is explained as follows. “Let Christ or the devil, the creditor, search out from Judas all his substance,” that is, let him demand punishment from him for all the substance entrusted to him. Christ demands punishment because Judas neglected to multiply the substance of understanding and the five senses which Christ had lent him. The devil, however, does so because Judas strove to multiply the substance of sins which he had lent to the devil. “And not only this, but if he has labored at any good works, let evil spirits, having become wholly alienated from him, seize those labors,” that is, let them snatch from him the accumulation of evil fruits—that is, the labor of those [Col. 1220B] good works.

“Let the creditor,” I say, “search out all his substance,” and then let there be no saintly helper for him who might intercede on his behalf; nor let there be any saint who, by his prayers, might have mercy on his orphans—that is, on the Jews, who, by being his sons, will become orphans from God the Father. “And let his descendants, the Jews themselves, become born,” that is, his sons, “for destruction”: through their sonship to him, let them be driven into eternal destruction. “Let the name of Judas be erased,” that is, destroyed, so that it is no longer in the book of the living. It had been written there insofar as it concerned God’s mercy, but he himself will erase it through his wickedness.

“Let his name,” I say, “be erased, and this in one generation,” that is, in the generation of the day of judgment, which is called “one” because then, among all the righteous, there will be “one heart and one soul” (Acts IV, 32). For God will be all in all.

But so that Judas himself may be punished in many ways, let the iniquity of his carnal fathers, who were exceedingly wicked, return to remembrance, although now it appears to have been consigned to oblivion. Let it return in such a way that it is before the Lord’s sight—that is, let the Lord behold it, so that he may punish it in Judas, because he surpassed those fathers in iniquity.

And let the sin of his carnal mother, who was exceedingly sinful, not be erased from the Lord’s memory, but be punished in him. It is certain that God punishes the sins of fathers in those sons who conform to their fathers in iniquity, according to the saying: “Visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation” (Exod. XX, 5). It is equally certain that God does not punish the sins of fathers in those sons who devote themselves to good works and refuse to conform to their fathers in iniquity. Hence the prophet says: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. XVIII, 20).
