“Let the sin,” I say, “of the mother not be erased”; rather, let the iniquity of the fathers and the sin of the mother always be against the Lord—that is, before the Lord—so that he does not forget them, by comparison with something placed before the eyes, which is not easily forgotten. “And let the memory of those sons of Judas perish from the land of the living,” which they rashly claim for themselves, so that there is not even any remembrance of them there.

And this I concede concerning Judas and his sons because Judas did not remember—that is, he will not remember—nor will he or his sons remember to show mercy toward me, the Lord and God, who bestowed so many benefits upon them. “And he pursued,” that is, Judas will pursue, “the killing of a poor and needy man,” namely, he will pursue me in order to kill me in that nature by which I am man: poor, that is, unable by myself to be delivered; and needy, that is, requiring the aid of another.

This means: He will pursue me in order to kill me as a mortal and passible man, and also as one pierced in heart by compassion for his condemnation. In this he will be more guilty, since he will have persecuted one who was pierced for his own sake.

“And he loved the curse,” that is, Judas will love the evil cause of the curse, namely, the evil deed; and therefore the eternal curse will come upon him. “And he did not desire the blessing,” that is, he will not desire the cause of eternal blessing, namely, the good deed, and the blessing itself will be removed far from him.

“And he put on the curse” [Col. 1221B] as a garment: that is, he will attach to himself the wicked intention of betraying me, which will be the cause of the curse, just as a garment is attached to the body. He rightly says that it is “put on” like a garment. For just as a garment is attached to the body even though it is not natural to it, so an evil will is attached to the soul through consent, although it is outside its nature.

“And it entered,” that is, it will enter, “into his inner parts,” as water enters even into the inner parts of flesh. An evil will is said to enter the inner parts of the soul when the soul not only consents but also strives with all its strength to accomplish the wicked will. This is by comparison with an enemy who is more greatly feared when he has already entered a city than when he is still very near outside it.

And, to put it more fully, it will enter so far that it is already “in all his bones,” that is, after the soul’s powers—reason and free choice—have been overcome, just as oil penetrates not only flesh but also bones. An evil will is then said to penetrate and break the bones of the soul when weakness reaches the point of action through reason and free choice. This is by comparison with an enemy who is more dangerous when he has already seized the city’s defenses than when he has merely entered the city.

Since, therefore, he has inwardly put on the cause of the curse, “let it be for him like a garment with which a man is clothed outwardly,” so that just as that garment appears outwardly, so the evil will may become manifest through his hanging himself. “And let it be for him like a belt with which he is always girded”: just as the belt with which he is girded makes him readier and more unencumbered for action, so that evil will may make him readier and more unencumbered to hang himself and be eternally killed.

God would not permit him to reach such a blindness that he killed himself unless the evil will of betraying the Lord had preceded as the cause of this killing.

I speak of Judas: he will pursue me, poor and needy; he will love the curse and put it on like a garment. And not only is it Judas’s work to pursue me, love the curse, and put it on, but the same will be the work of those who slander me—that is, the Jews will do the same, pursuing me and putting on and loving the curse.

They slander me while I exist “with the Lord,” that is, in equality of essence with the Lord God the Father. They slander me in this respect: they deny that I am the Son of God, although I am “with the Lord,” according to John’s saying: “The Word was with God” (John I, 1). By saying that he is with the Lord, he indicates that whoever slanders the Son also slanders the Lord Father, according to the saying: “He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father” (John V, 23).

Or it may be understood as follows. Because he had spoken of the curse of Judas and the Jews, lest he appear to have spoken thus imprecatively and out of ill will, he shows that he says this concessively, because of their evil merits, as follows: “I said, ‘Let his days, Judas’s, be few; let his sons be orphans; let there be no helper for him; let his descendants be brought to destruction,’” and other such things. “I do not say these things imprecatively, but concessively.”

For this evil work of those who slander me, who exist with the Lord—that is, the evil work of Judas and his sons—deserves this many-sided curse. And not only the evil work of those who slander me, but also of those “who speak evil against my soul,” namely, those who discuss among themselves how they may take away my life.

Therefore you, O Lord, Lord, who are powerful, since you are Lord of all, “act with me for resurrection and glorification.” It is as though he said: “By the merit of my obedience I accomplish my resurrection and glorification, and you accomplish these things with me by the aid of your power—and this for the glorification of your name. For when I am glorified, you too will be glorified, just as, when I am blasphemed, you too are blasphemed. For we are one.”

And therefore you ought to act with me, because your mercy is sweet to me, that is, delightful. It is delightful, not harsh, to me that you have mercifully determined to restore the human race through my death.

Since he had said, “Act with me,” without specifying what he should do, he clarifies this by adding: “Act with me,” I say, “and do this:

“Deliver me from mortality and passibility by raising me from the dead.” I must pray for this because I, who according to my other nature am God, immortal, impassible, and omnipotent, am according to my human nature needy, that is, unable to be delivered except by another’s aid, and poor, that is, insufficient to save myself by my own power.

This is as though he said: “I am mortal and passible, and not so powerful in suffering that I suffer nothing; rather, my heart has been troubled”—that is, my soul will be troubled by fear of death. Yet this disturbance is within me, that is, it is under my control; it does not occur against my will and determination, since I am God and omnipotent. He adds this so that it would not appear that he had prayed because he was compelled to suffer.

And not only will I be troubled, but I have also been “taken away, becoming like a shadow at evening, when it declines from the mountains,” that is, I will be taken away from my disciples when I am seized—not spiritually, but locally. I will be taken away, I say, like a shadow declining from the mountains, that is, descending. For just as toward evening a descending shadow gradually grows as it approaches night, so I, taken away from my own, gradually approach death through suffering.

And when I am taken away, with the Jews capturing me, “I have been shaken like a locust,” that is, my disciples will be shaken away from me and will flee, unstable like locusts, according to the prophetic saying: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zech. XIII, 7; Matt. XXVI, 31).

Nor will they merely be shaken away from me locally; “my knees also have been weakened,” that is, the apostles, who are called my knees because through them I am carried into the knowledge of human beings, just as the body is carried by the knees. They will be weakened in faith, so that they will even doubt my resurrection. Those were indeed weakened who said hesitantly: “We thought that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke XXIV, 21).

They will be weakened, I say, and this will happen because of fasting from that bread which descended from heaven (John VI, 41)—namely, from me. This is as though he said: “This weakness will happen to them because, in my absence, they will fast from my teaching.”

I said that I would be taken away from my own, becoming like a declining shadow. “And thus my flesh has been changed,” that is, it will be changed, so that from living it becomes lifeless. This will happen for the sake of the oil to be given to the human race, so that the grace of remission may be granted to all. It is called “oil” because it heals sins and illumines the soul, by comparison with oil, which heals wounds and clarifies the bodily eyes.

And after my flesh has been changed, “I became a reproach to them,” that is, I, who, suffering reproach for the salvation of human beings, ought by no means to have been a reproach, will become a reproach to those Jews. They will regard it as a great disgrace that I was born from their race.

Or: “I will become a reproach to them,” that is, the cause of reproach. For because of my crucifixion they will remain an eternal reproach among human beings. And not only will they crucify me, but “they saw”—that is, they will look upon me dead with delight, making me a spectacle—and “they moved,” that is, they will move, their heads in mockery, saying: “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matt. XXVII, 40).

And because my flesh will be changed and I will become a reproach, help me, Lord my God. Help me in this way: “Save me,” by raising me and making me immortal and impassible; and do this according to your mercy, so that just as your mercy is abundant, so my salvation may be abundant.

And once I have been saved, let the Jews know through the experience of the event itself that “this hand,” which they neglect, is yours—that is, that I am your hand, your Son according to divinity, which they deny. Although this hand is consubstantial with you according to divinity, nevertheless you, Lord, “made” it—that is, created it—according to humanity.

The Son is called the Father’s hand because through him the Father works all things. When he shows himself to be true God and true man, he destroys both the heresy of those who asserted that he was man alone and that of those who asserted that he was God only.

Or it may be understood as follows: “Through my salvation let them know that this hand,” that is, this deed of my death, “is yours,” not something accomplished by their power. It is yours in this way: you, Lord, “made” it, that is, you ordained it.

He states that what he prayed for will be future, lest he appear to have prayed out of disbelief, as follows: “I said, ‘Help me, Lord,’ and you will do this. They will curse me,” that is, the Jews will bring me down into death; “but you will bless me,” that is, you will exalt me by raising me.

And because they will curse me, “let them be confounded”—that is, let the Jews who rise up, or will rise up, against me in words and tribulations be put to shame, not for their benefit. But, in contrast, “your servant will rejoice”: I will rejoice in the perpetual glory obtained, because I am your servant and in no respect resist you.

“Let them be confounded,” I say, and not slightly, but “let them be clothed,” that is, let those who slander me be surrounded with shame, by emphasis, like a body that is surrounded by what clothes it. This means: Let them have complete confusion, not ordinary confusion; let them be covered, that is, openly surrounded by their shame—the shame they deserve through their evil deeds—like a *diploid*, that is, in the manner of a double garment.

Saint Jerome writes that a *diploid* is a double cloak, one part of which is inner and the other outer. Accordingly, the Jews are fittingly said to have been covered with double shame, like a *diploid*: one shame inwardly in the soul, whether or not toward repentance, at Christ’s resurrection and ascension; the other outwardly in their capture and dispersion.

I say this so that they may be confounded, but I will confess to the Lord with my mouth, O hearers. That is, my people will confess praise to the Lord not only in their hearts but also with their mouths, without keeping silent through fear of unbelievers; and they will do this exceedingly, that is, greatly. “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X, 10).

And my people will not praise the Lord before a few unbelievers only, but “in the midst of many I will praise him”: openly, before many unbelievers, they will praise him with their mouths, not fearing their threats. This praise will result from the fact that the Lord himself “stood,” that is, will stand, at the right hand of me, the poor one. He will protect me according to that nature in which I am poor, by comparison with a patron who stands at the right hand of a poor person whom he protects.

A patron is not said to be at the left but at the right, since prosperity is understood by the right hand and adversity by the left. He will stand, I say, at the right hand for this purpose: to “save,” that is, to save, my soul from the Jews who persecute me, by raising me from the dead so that I am not held in death.

## ON PSALM CIX

### Title of the One Hundred Ninth Psalm

“A Psalm of David,” either because David the prophet speaks here, or because the prophet speaks of David, Christ. This entire psalm concerns his praise. For because in the preceding psalm the Prophet had introduced Christ himself praying that his praise should not be silenced, he now shows him worthy of praise through the testimony of the Father’s authority.

For he introduces the Father himself speaking to the Lord Jesus and declaring that he is to reign with him, [Col. 1225A] showing that he is consubstantial and coeternal with him, and swearing that he will be a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. He also proves him worthy of praise because, in the future, seated at the Father’s right hand, he will crush here the kings who rebel against him; by judging among the nations he will exalt the humble, abase the powerful and proud, and receive this great power because he will drink from the torrent of suffering.

“The Lord said to my Lord.” This means: The Lord Father will say—not with words, but by an ineffable inward saying—to my Lord Christ; and he will say this continually, from the time when Divinity is united to humanity. And this is what he will say: “Sit at my right hand,” that is, reign with me, by comparison with a king who makes his son, whom he has appointed to reign with him, sit at his right hand on his royal throne.

When the Prophet calls the Lord Christ “his Lord,” he suppresses by his authority the position of the unbelieving Jews, who denied that he was God and Lord. In this psalm he appears to be acting against the unbelieving Jews, and it is equivalent to saying openly to them: “You will deny, O unbelieving Jews, that Christ is God and Lord, yet I understand him to be the one who will be Lord and reign with the Father.”

Or: “Sit at my right hand,” namely, after the suffering of death, rest from all labor through the merit of your obedience, by comparison with one who sits and rests. “Sit,” I say, “at my right hand,” that is, rest by existing in my superior qualities, namely, immortality and impassibility.

“Sit,” I say, “at my right hand, until I place your enemies”—Gentiles and Jews—“as the footstool of your feet.” This means: “Reign with me until I make all those who are hostile to you, unwilling to submit to you, a footstool,” that is, subject to you as a footstool is subject to the feet.

“A footstool of your feet,” that is, of your steadfastness, which is understood through the feet because one stands by the feet. That is: until I subject them to you in such a way that you stand over them, that is, reign over them steadfastly.

He does not say, “until I make your enemies subject to you,” because they are not also subject now—for otherwise God would not be God—but because, although they are subject to him in the truth of the matter, they are not subject with respect to their knowledge of it. Those who come to faith in this life will recognize that they are subject to him willingly; the rest, who here neglect to recognize their subjection to him, will finally recognize in the future, willingly or unwillingly, that they are eternally subject to him, through the infliction of torments.

Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “You have subjected all things under his feet” (Ps. III, 7). This is equivalent to saying: “Sit at my right hand, reigning with me, until I make all your enemies, both Gentiles and Jews, recognize that they truly are the footstool of your feet,” that is, always subject to you. Some will recognize this by coming to the faith; others will ultimately be led into just condemnation in the future.

It should be noted that he does not say that he sits at the right hand only until he makes his enemies a footstool, as though he would not sit forever afterward. Rather, because it would then be manifest that he sits, it was unnecessary to state that he would then sit. Now, however, he confirms for the instruction of our faith that he sits, since his sitting is not yet known to his enemies.

After he had added the Father’s words in praise of the Son’s authority, the Prophet, speaking in his own person for the Son’s commendation, proceeds as follows: “I said, O Lord Christ, that the Father will say this to you: ‘Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies in the future as the footstool of your feet.’”

Meanwhile, before all the enemies are made a footstool, the Lord Father will “send forth from Zion the scepter of your power,” that is, he will extend from Zion, from the Jewish people, the scepter of your power—that is, the kingdom of your power—which you will govern with the strength of righteousness.

By “scepter” we understand a staff, and by “staff,” which is the sign of a kingdom, we understand a kingdom. This is equivalent to saying: “In the primitive Church of the Jews the Lord Father will prepare a kingdom for you, and from the Jews he will send forth,” that is, extend, your kingdom among the Gentiles, so that many among the Gentiles may willingly submit to you through obedience.

Thus in this life you will rule “in the midst,” that is, commonly among your enemies, both Jews and Gentiles: you will rule commonly over the faithful from Jews and Gentiles, who exist as your enemies through unbelief. And I concede that it should be so: “Rule in the midst,” that is, commonly among, “your enemies, Jews and Gentiles”—that is, let your enemies commonly recognize you as Lord; and rule them by directing them from good to better.

Or: “Rule in the midst of your enemies,” that is, among the righteous who are called the midst of the enemies, namely, the unbelievers, because they are surrounded on every side by unbelievers who persecute them, just as what is in the middle is surrounded by those who are all around it.

The Prophet also adds, for the Son’s commendation, the Father’s words when he says: “With you is the beginning,” and so forth. This is adapted as follows. Someone might ask why God the Father would say to Christ, “Sit at my right hand,” since he has said this to no one else. The answer is added in this way:

“I said, ‘Sit at my right hand,’ and it is fitting for you to sit at my right hand because I begot you by an ineffable begetting, ‘from the womb,’ that is, from my hidden essence, which is understood by the womb because the womb is a hidden part of the body; and this was before Lucifer.”

By saying that he was begotten before Lucifer, who was the most worthy among the angels and therefore fell when he became proud, he indicates that he begot him before every creature. He also indicates by this that he was not begotten in such a way as to be a creature. According to the manner in which he was begotten by the Father, he shows this.

This is as though he said: “It is fitting for you to sit at my right hand because you are consubstantial with me as my Son.” But lest he be understood to have been begotten in time, “the beginning” is placed before “with you.” This means: “I begot you—I, who exist as the beginning with you of all things. I begot you in such a way that we are nevertheless the beginning of all things, that is, so that you are coeternal with me, and so that all things were made through you just as through me.”

He rightly says not “the beginning with me” but “the beginning with you.” For if he said, “You are the beginning with me,” those who understood it wrongly could err and say by this that the Father was greater than the Son. But when he says, “I am the beginning with you,” since no one doubts that the Father is not less than the Son, he plainly indicates by this that he is coeternal and coequal with that same Son.

He also shows in which nature he begot him, and in which he is coeternal and coequal with him, when he adds: “In the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones.” This is adapted as follows:

“I begot you, I say, and I am the beginning with you, and this in the day of your power and in the splendors of the holy ones.” That is, I begot you in the nature in which you are day: namely, I begot you according to divinity, and with you I am the beginning, which is day—that is, brighter than day. Hence Christ says of himself: “I am the light of the world” (John VIII, 12).

“In the day,” I say, “of your power,” that is, of your might, namely, because your divinity is your strength and power; and “in the splendors of the holy ones” I begot you, and with you I am the beginning—that is, in the same divinity through which you make the holy ones splendid. Hence he is called “the splendor” (Hebr. I, 3).

He rightly says “splendors” in the plural, because he makes many holy ones splendid in their conduct.

Or it may be understood as follows: “I am the beginning with you,” that is, coeternal and coequal, “in the day of your power,” that is, in divinity, and “in the splendors of the holy ones,” that is, in the equality of the splendors of the holy ones—namely, in the equality of the Holy Spirit, through whom all the holy ones are made splendid. They are called “splendors” in the plural because of his sevenfold grace.

This is as though he said: “I and you are the beginning,” that is, coeternal and coequal.

Or it may be read, much better, as follows: “I begot you,” I say, “while existing as the beginning with you. It will be evident that I begot you and that I am the beginning with you in the day of your power,” that is, on the day of judgment, when your power, which now does not appear to everyone, will be manifest. And it will be manifest “in the splendors of the holy ones,” that is, on that day of your power in which you will make your holy ones eternally splendid.

This means: Through your holy ones, whom you will make splendid on the day of your power, it will be evident that you are coeternal, coequal, and consubstantial with me.

After he had proved, on the authority of the Father himself, that Christ reigns with the Father and is consubstantial, coeternal, and coequal with him, he proves from that same authority of the Father that Christ was made a priest and that the Levitical priesthood would be changed forever into the priesthood of Melchizedek, as follows:

“I said, O unbelieving Jews, that the Lord Father said”—that is, will say—“to the Lord Son: ‘Sit at my right hand,’” and so forth. “And not only this, but the Lord Father also swore,” that is, will swear. He will firmly speak and promise, by an inward oath, to the Lord Son, and he will do so in such a way that he will not repent of it, that is, will not alter his promise, by comparison with one who repents.

He will swear, I say, and this is what he will swear to you, O Christ: “You are a priest,” established according to your humanity, “according to the order of Melchizedek,” that is, according to the many-sided dignity considered in an ordered way in Melchizedek.

Melchizedek is interpreted as “king of righteousness.” He was king of Salem, that is, “king of peace,” “without father, without mother, without beginning of days or end of life” (Hebr. VII, 3). Yet this was not so in reality. Rather, he is said to be without father, without mother, and to have had neither beginning nor end of days because in the historical account nothing is read about his father, mother, or the beginning or end of his days.

This Melchizedek is also read to have been priest of the Most High and to have offered a sacrifice of bread and wine. All these things, therefore, could be considered in Christ. He is truly king of righteousness and of all peace; according to his humanity he exists without a father and without a mother, and according to his divinity without beginning or end of days. He is also priest of the Most High Father and offered on the altar of the cross the sacrifice of true bread and wine, namely, his body and blood.

“You are,” I say, “a priest according to the order of Melchizedek,” and this “forever”: that is, your priesthood has been admitted in place of the now abolished Levitical priesthood, enduring forever in you and in your people.

In his own person he is called a priest forever—not because he offers the sacrifice of his body and blood forever, which he offered only once, but because he prays forever to the Father for his sons. For it is not only the priest’s task to offer sacrifice, but also to pray for the people.

In his people, however, he is a priest forever, both according to the offering which they offer continually forever—that is, until the end of the world—and according to prayer. Every day his priests offer the offering of the Lord’s body and blood and pour out prayer for the people.

It is entirely fitting that he is said, with the Father’s oath, to have been established forever as a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, so that he might indicate that the Levitical priesthood was wholly, firmly, and irrevocably changed into the priesthood of Melchizedek.

After treating of his priesthood on the authority of the Father, he now treats of his vengeance and future judgment as follows:

“You, O Lord Father, said to my Lord, Christ your Son, ‘Sit at my right hand,’” and so forth. “And the Lord himself, sitting at your right hand, broke”—that is, will break with the breaking of eternal condemnation—not only the lesser ones but also the kings who oppose him here, “on the day of his wrath,” that is, of his vengeance, namely, on the day of judgment, when his vengeance will be manifest.

“And then he will judge among the nations,” that is, he will render an equitable judgment among all classes of faithful and unbelieving people. “And through that judgment he will fill the ruins,” that is, he will fill with exultation those of his own who here cast themselves down and humble themselves rather than exalt themselves.

This means: He will exalt his humble ones, “and he will crush the heads of many upon the earth,” that is, he will crush the pride of many, which they possess in earthly prosperity. These are signified by “heads” because this part of the body is higher. Hence the prophet says: “Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low” (Isa. XL, 4; Luke III, 4).

Or: “He will fill,” that is, in the future he will make complete, “the ruins of the unbelievers.” Although here they cast themselves down through sins, he will cast them down completely when he condemns them eternally. “And he will crush the heads of many upon the earth”: this is not changed.

And from this such power will be given him by God the Father that, while placed on the road of this life—that is, in this life through which return is made to the heavenly homeland—he “drank from the torrent,” that is, he will drink from the cup of suffering. It is called a “torrent” because it was temporary and bitter, like a torrent that quickly swells from the rains and quickly subsides; and because, being turbid, it is bitter to drink.

And therefore, because he will not refuse to drink, God the Father will exalt his head, that is, he will exalt his majesty, so that, although he is already exalted in innocence, he may exalt him much more by giving him “the name that is above every name” (Phil. II, 9). By “head,” because it is high, exaltation is understood.

## ON PSALM CX

### Title of the One Hundred Tenth Psalm

“Alleluia.” This is as though he said: In its evident meaning, this entire psalm says “Alleluia” to all the faithful—that is, “Praise God in integrity of love and good works.”

For in this psalm the Prophet says that he will confess to the Lord in complete love and good works, showing that good works are great and come from the Lord. He explains what those good works of the Lord are. Therefore he says that he will confess praise to the Lord, in order to instruct all the faithful to confess. He also shows that they are without excuse regarding confession: first, because they are not ignorant, since the Lord has already given them the food of teaching through preachers; second, because they are not incapable of this, since the Lord works in them through grace, judgment, and truth; and third, because it is useful to confess, since the Lord’s commandments are faithful.

And because he has already sent the Redeemer, through whom he entrusted his testament, and because he wishes to exhort them more strongly to confess to the Lord, he affirms that the Lord is holy to those who confess him and terrible to those who refuse to confess.

I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart—that is, I will praise you continually with the whole affection of my heart, in complete love—and this in the council and assembly of the righteous; that is, I will make this confession in imitation of the righteous, who do not act rashly in this matter but with deliberation, and who are not few but, so that their authority may be greater, constitute an assembly—that is, they are many. By saying that he will praise the Lord with complete love, he indicates that he will also praise him by good works, since complete love cannot be idle, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words” (John 14:23). I will confess, then, to the Lord inwardly with complete love and outwardly through good works. And these works, which are confessed inwardly and outwardly, are great—that is, honorable—and they are not from me, but are also the Lord’s; that is, the Lord works them in me. They are also choice—that is, exceedingly excellent. He uses “choice” for “excellent,” because what is excellent is ordinarily sought out carefully.

Or it may be understood thus: These works of the Lord are great and choice—that is, if their nature is carefully investigated, they will appear great. But since he had said only, “I will confess,” and afterward had spoken in the plural of “great works,” someone might not understand from the words “I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart” that several good works are indicated, although this is in fact true. Therefore one might ask: Which works do you say are the Lord’s great works? To this he adds: I say that the Lord’s great works are to go in all his wills—that is, to carry out all his wills in action. And since one might again ask what the execution of his wills consists in, he proceeds to show this:

Behold, I speak of the execution of his wills. The confession of sins is the work of his will; that is, he himself wills each person to act in such a way as humbly to confess his sins. And after confession, magnificence is his work; that is, after confession he wills us, aided by his grace through free choice, to work within ourselves by refraining from sins. “Magnificence” means innocence, which is so called because it makes the soul great—that is, honorable before God. And afterward justice is also the work of his will; that is, the justice of virtues and good works. This is to say: He wills us to cleave to the virtues, that is, to strive earnestly to devote ourselves to righteous works. And this justice, being his work, remains in his faithful ones until the future age that follows this present age; and by this it appears to be something great.

Or it may be understood thus: I said that confessing to the Lord with complete love and confessing through perfect action are the Lord’s great works. This is proved from the lesser, since the confession of sins and magnificence—that is, innocence, which is much less than complete love—are his work. And justice—that is, the virtues—and that good action which is not worthy of God in the same way as complete love and perfect action, are nevertheless his work; and that justice remains in many of the faithful until the age of ages—that is, as long as this present age lasts—even if it is not wholly perfect. From the fact that it remains, it is evident that it is something great.

After promising to confess to the Lord, and after commending this confession sufficiently in order to draw the faithful of the New Law to confessing to the Lord, he shows that they have no excuse on the ground of ignorance, since the Lord will give them the food of instruction, as follows:

I said, “I will confess”—that is, I will praise the Lord with complete love and perfect action—and you also, faithful of the New Testament, should likewise confess, since you have no excuse based on ignorance. For the Lord, merciful by nature and compassionate in the bestowal of benefits, has made—or will make—a remembrance of his ancient wonders; that is, he will bring back to remembrance, in the time of fulfillment, the wonders he worked in the time of our fathers, which have already almost been consigned to oblivion through the passage of time, by granting the benefits prefigured through those mystical wonders.

He explains in part how he will make a remembrance of his wonders:

He will, I say, make a remembrance of his wonders, and he will do so by giving—or will give—the food of the instruction of the New Testament, that is, of the New Law, to those who fear him with chaste fear, namely, to the apostles. Through them, those who fear him will be nourished by such food. He will remember his covenant—that is, the New Law—forever in the future age; namely, that New Law promised through the prophets, which he seemed for so long to have consigned to oblivion. He will remember it by giving it frequently through the apostles and the other preachers, for as long as this world endures.

Thus he will remember not only to give preachers and apostles an understanding of the significance of his works, which he performed in the Old Testament as figures of the benefits of the New Testament, but also, through preachers who fear him, to announce to his Jewish people the power of the significance of the works he performed in the Old Testament. This is to say: He will make the faithful from among the Jews understand, through the instruction of preachers who fear him, what his ancient works signified, so that on this account they may confess inwardly.

He will, I say, announce through those who fear him the significance of his works to his Jewish people in such a way that he will give to those who fear him—namely, the apostles—and to his people, namely, converts from the Jews, the inheritance of the nations; that is, he will give converts from the nations to them as an inheritance, so that they may cultivate them through their teaching, just as someone cultivates his own inheritance. He will, I say, give the nations to them as an inheritance, and among those nations will be the works of his hands—that is, his excellent works—which are called “works of the hands” because the hands are more excellent than the other members for performing work.

His excellent works, I say, will be found among those nations. These works are truth and judgment: first judgment upon sins through humble confession, and afterward truth—that is, virtues and good works. They are called “truth” because they lead to true being.

[449] It is as if he said: So that the faithful from the nations may confess to him with complete love, he will work judgment and truth in them through the preaching of the apostles.

He adds another reason why they ought to confess, as follows:

I said, “I will confess with complete love and, by good action, fulfill his commandments,” and you also, faithful, should confess to him with complete love and the fulfillment of his commandments. For his commandments are faithful—that is, they are not useless but certain, and rewards have been promised for their fulfillment. Someone is called “faithful” when he fulfills what he has promised. His commandments, I say, are faithful provided that they are not completed merely for a time, but are confirmed—that is, completed with the steadfastness of perseverance—until the age of ages that follows this present age; and this is so if they are performed in truth—that is, on the foundation of true faith—and in equity—that is, with an equitable intention, so that they are not fulfilled with a view to temporal goods but to heavenly goods. Otherwise they would have no value.

Therefore continue to confess to the Lord with complete love and in the fulfillment of his commandments, because the Lord the Father has sent—or will send—to his people, namely, to you faithful ones from Jews and nations, redemption; that is, Christ, who will be redemption. Through that redemption he has commanded—or will command—you his new covenant, leading those who fulfill it to eternity. Therefore you ought to confess to the Lord in the fulfillment of the commandments of this New Testament.

And therefore continue to confess to the Lord because his name, which is “Lord,” is holy and terrible. Through the name “Lord,” the one who is holy—that is, pleasing and sweet to those who confess him, since he will save them—and terrible to those unwilling to confess, since he will justly condemn them—is signified.

Lest it seem useless that he is terrible, he shows what benefit follows from this:

He is, I say, terrible, and this is not without great usefulness. For the fear of the Lord—namely, servile fear—is the beginning of wisdom; that is, of the good life which is lived with wisdom. There are few who begin to live well without servile fear, yet through it one often reaches chaste fear.

I said that the works of the Lord are great, that he will make a remembrance of his wonders, that his commandments are faithful, that he will send redemption to his people, that his name is holy and terrible, and that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. The faithful of the New Testament ought to understand all these things, and this understanding is good—that is, useful—to all who put it into practice; that is, to those who strive to fulfill, as far as they can, what they understand. Understanding is useless to those who understand but do not act. And the praise of this good understanding—that is, its completion through action, which is called “praise” because whoever voluntarily completes something praises what he completes—remains perseveringly until the age of ages that follows this present age.

It is as if he said: This understanding is good when it is praised through completion, and not merely for a time, but when that praise remains perseveringly until the end of this life. “For whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

## ON PSALM CXI

Title of the hundred and eleventh: “Alleluia, of the return of Haggai and Zechariah.” This is explained as follows: Praise God, all of you who, in regard to what is accomplished here through virtues and good works—namely, the return of Haggai and Zechariah to Jerusalem—praise him. That is, praise God by a good life, through which you return from the exile of this life to the heavenly Jerusalem, in imitation of Haggai and Zechariah, that is, of the perfected ones who return by living well to the homeland of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Haggai, whose name is interpreted as “solemn” or “festive,” and Zechariah, whose name is interpreted as “one who is zealous,” were two prophets who, during the Babylonian captivity, foresaw the return of the children of Israel to Jerusalem and the restoration of the temple, and who were also present at the return to Jerusalem and the restoration of the temple. Hence by these two are understood all the perfected ones who, being zealous—that is, loving the Lord Jesus and imitating him as far as possible—are solemn and festive, while, placed in contemplation, they attend to the solemn festivals of the angels. Already, with certain hope, they foresee the perfect restoration in the future of the heavenly Jerusalem, which was partly destroyed through Adam—not with respect to the angels, but with respect to human beings. To this heavenly Jerusalem these same perfected ones are already returning from the exile of this life through virtues and good works.

The Prophet demonstrates the blessed return of these people in this psalm through fear, the will expressed in the Lord’s commandments, innocence, wisdom, justice, faith, firm and immovable hope, and the distribution of money—that is, of their words. His purpose is thereby to exhort all hearers who have not returned—both those who have not yet acquired knowledge of the faith and those who already possess an idle faith—to such a return, which is the highest praise of God.

Blessed is the man who fears the Lord, even with servile fear. Such a man is blessed here, while he returns to the homeland by living well, and he will be blessed in the future after he has returned. And that blessed man, persisting in the commandments of the Lord, will desire them exceedingly; that is, he will have an exceedingly great desire of love for those commandments. His offspring—that is, his teaching—will not be useless but will be powerful, that is, effective among his subjects, who will be capable of receiving that teaching, just as well-cultivated land is capable of receiving seed.

His seed of teaching, I say, will be powerful, and in this way: through that seed of teaching, the generation of the upright—that is, of faithful subjects—will be blessed; that is, it will either be exalted in virtues and good works or multiplied, so that many who were not upright may be added to their number through that seed.

Or it may be understood thus: Blessed is the man, I say, who will desire the commandments of the Lord, and his offspring—that is, that good will which is the seed of works—will be powerful in the earth; that is, it will bring forth good works in his earthiness, namely, in his sensuality. This is to say: That will does not submit to sensuality, but compels sensuality itself to act well. Through the example of that seed as it bears fruit, the generation of the upright will be blessed, either through multiplication or through the exaltation of virtues and good works.

And in his inner house—that is, in his heart, in which he dwells by thinking as though in a house—there is glory, that is, innocence. Hence he himself glories, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). And the riches of inner wisdom and the justice of the works of this blessed man remain until the age of ages.

This is to say: He acts well without ceasing, and, being innocent, wise, and just, he is thereby powerful in his teaching, so that through it the generation of the upright may be blessed.

But the fact that his seed is powerful and that glory and riches are in his house does not come from him himself but from the true light. For light has arisen, according to faith, in the darkness—that is, in the hearts of the blessed, who previously were darkness both because of sins and because of ignorance. Light has arisen, I say, in the darkness, and it has arisen for the upright—that is, for the work of the upright. It has arisen in order to make upright those who were previously darkness. This light that has arisen for them is Christ, merciful by nature, compassionate in the bestowal of benefits, and just.

By saying that he makes those who are already just more just, he implies that this same light will also rise for unbelievers if they approach it; and through this he renders them inexcusable.

And because God himself is merciful and compassionate, every person who shows mercy by forgiving those who sin against him is pleasing—that is, acceptable—to God, just as God pardoned that person when he sinned. And he not only shows mercy but also lends what is his own to those suffering need, just as God confers many benefits upon him. Thus, if he does not have money to lend, at least he arranges—that is, distributes—his words by preaching to others or exhorting them in some way to live well, and he does so with the judgment of discernment: judging how one ought to speak with the experienced and how with the inexperienced, how with the noble and how with the ignoble.

When he says “he lends,” he indicates that what the faithful give for Christ they give in such a way that they will receive it back. For what is lent is afterward received.

Or it may be understood thus: The man who shows mercy and lends what is his own to the needy is pleasing; and in showing mercy and lending, he will arrange his words for the judgment—that is, he arranges what he will answer on the day of judgment, when it will be necessary to render an account to everyone. This is by comparison with someone who, when he is about to enter into a dispute with another, first considers with himself how he will speak there.

The man is pleasing, I say. And he will be shown to be pleasing in this respect: he will not be shaken forever from his purpose of holiness. He would in fact quickly be shaken unless he were pleasing to God. He will not be shaken because, being just, he will be in eternal remembrance before the Lord; that is, he will always be aided by the Lord’s grace so that he does not fail. And because he will be in eternal remembrance, he will not fear an evil report—that is, the threatening report of persecutors. He will not fear when persecutors threaten him with death.

He will not fear, I say, for his heart is prepared—that is, it is always ready to hope in the Lord—and his heart is strengthened by that hope. Therefore, as I said, he will not be shaken from his good purpose, persevering until, when he departs this life, he sees his enemies proved despicable and defeated.

Or these two verses may be read as follows: I said that he lends; he will not be shaken forever. The pleasing man will not be shaken from his good purpose, and therefore, being just, he will be in eternal remembrance before the Lord; that is, the Lord will remember to repay him with eternal blessedness. And, possessing a good conscience, he will not fear in the future an evil report—that is, the harsh proclamation made to those who are to be condemned: “Depart from me, you cursed,” and so forth (Matt. 25:41). Nor will he need to fear it, for his heart is prepared in every virtue to hope in the Lord; that is, it is prepared in such a way that he can hope in the Lord for recompense. His heart is so prepared that it is strengthened in this readiness, lest he ever be heedless; and it is so strengthened that he will not be shaken, persevering in his purpose until he despises his despised and powerless persecuting enemies, who here have power over his flesh for a time.

Or it may be understood thus: It is evident that he arranges his words well here because he will not be shaken forever; that is, he will not be disturbed forever by any anxiety, but the just man will be in eternal remembrance before the Lord, so that the Lord may grant him eternal blessedness. And he will not merely remain unshaken; he will also not fear an evil report, which is a lesser matter, when it is said: “Depart,” and so forth.

Since he had said “he lends,” he determines to whom one ought to lend, as follows:

I said that his heart is prepared to hope in the Lord; yet he does not hope rashly for a good reward from the Lord. For he has scattered what was his own, and not among mimes or other worthless rogues, but he gave it to the poor. Therefore the justice of his virtues, preserved by God, remains until the age of ages—that is, for as long as this world lasts. And in the future his horn—that is, the exaltation of his justice—will be raised in the glory of eternal blessedness.

This is to say: He will be exalted in glory because of his horn.

Every sinner will see this exaltation and will be angry because he did not do such a thing, through which he too might be exalted in the same way. He will not be merely somewhat angry, but will gnash with his teeth—that is, he will be exceedingly angry, like someone who gnashes his teeth in violent anger. He will gnash, I say, and waste away—that is, he will wholly fail because of excessive anger.

Or it may be understood thus: He will not merely have this evil, that he is angry; he will also waste away—that is, he will perish in torments. He will be angry, I say, because then the desire of sinners will perish, namely, the riches they greatly desired here.

Or thus: He will be angry, desiring that he had done such a thing, through which he might be exalted; but that desire of sinners will perish—that is, it will be useless.

## ON PSALM CXII

[Col. 1235C] Title of the hundred and twelfth: “Alleluia.” In this psalm the Prophet invites all nations to the praise of God, considering that here he raises those nations from their earthiness and in the future will raise them from corruption; and that he makes the Church, long barren, fruitful, and in the future will make her dwell in his house.

Praise the Lord, you children. This is to say: Praise the Lord, O Gentiles, in such a way that you are children—that is, his servants; or be children in innocence, in accordance with the saying: “Do not become children in your thinking, but be infants in wickedness” (1 Cor. 14:20). This is the same as if he said: Praise the Lord with the praise of your innocence and obedience.

And praise the name of the Lord; that is, praise God in consideration of his great name—namely, because he is called “Lord.” And do this not with delay or merely for a time, but let the name of the Lord be blessed by you; that is, exalt the Lord with the highest praise in consideration of his name, from this time onward—that is, beginning in the present time and persevering—unto the eternal age.

And I do not say this only to a few nations, but let the name of the Lord be praised—that is, let the Lord be praised in consideration of his name—by all nations existing from the rising of the sun to its setting. Through these two regions he makes the other regions of the world understood.

Praise, I say; for he is worthy of praise. For the Lord is exalted—that is, omnipotent—ruling over all nations. And not only over the nations, but, what is greater, his glory—that is, his glorious power—is exalted above the heavens, that is, above all supercelestial rational creatures. He is exalted, I say.

For who is a Lord and God as exalted as the Lord our God, who dwells on high and regards the lowly in heaven and on earth; who raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dungheap, to set him with princes, with the princes of his people? He makes—or will make—the barren woman dwell in a house, a joyful mother of children.

No one, therefore, is exalted in comparison with him. This whole passage is placed under the form of a question for greater force; it proves that he is exalted above all, and is equivalent to saying: I say that our Lord is exalted, and truly he is exalted in power. Although many earthly lords appear powerful, what powerful lord is like our Lord? None. And what powerful god is like our God? None.

[Col. 1236B] It is thereby proved that he is exalted, since he is so great that he dwells not locally but by power in the heights—that is, in the heavenly spirits and in holy men who are lofty in holiness.

Lest they seem to be lofty through pride, he adds: Although I call them lofty, the Lord nevertheless regards the lowly in heaven and on earth; that is, in accordance with his mercy he works humility in heaven—that is, among the lofty heavenly spirits, namely, the angels—and on earth—that is, among the holy men who, while still remaining on earth, are his fruitful earth.

This is to say: He dwells in those who are lofty, yet they are made humble through the regard of his grace.

He is also proved to be exalted by the fact that in this life he raises the needy from the earth; that is, he raises each faithful person who is needy—that is, humble, like a needy person—through the aid of his mercy. He raises him from the earth; that is, he exalts him after removing him from earthiness, into which he came through Adam, making him spiritual instead of earthly through the forgiveness of sins.

[453] And in the future resurrection he will lift up the poor; that is, he will exalt each faithful person through immortality, taking him from the dungheap—that is, from the corruption of the flesh, which is rightly called dung because of its foulness. He will lift him from the dungheap in such a way that he will set him in eternal blessedness with princes, with the princes of his people—that is, with the heavenly citizens who here rule their people by guiding them from good to better, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “They will be like the angels in heaven” (Matt. 22:30). Whether they will be equal or unequal to them in glory has not yet been determined for us.

He will also be proved exalted by the fact that he is the one who makes—or will make—the barren Church dwell in the house; that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem, which is his eternal house. He will make dwell there not only the Church from the Jews but also the Church from the nations, previously barren of spiritual children but now made a mother by grace—not merely the mother of one child, but a spiritual mother of many spiritual children.

He will, I say, make her dwell in the house, and not in just any manner, but rejoicing with eternal joy, in accordance with the prophetic saying: “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1; Gal. 4:27).

This is as if he said: He will establish his house not only from the Church of the Jews but also from the Church of the nations, which for a long time was barren, bearing no spiritual child for God.

The Church of the nations is rightly called a mother: namely, the whole gathering of the faithful from the nations, because by drawing others to the faith through her authority she gives birth to them for God and nourishes them through her teaching. Her children are each of the faithful belonging to that same gathering, because, persisting in the harmonious unity of that gathering according to faith and love, they grow daily in virtues, just as children grow through their mother’s daily nourishment.

## ON PSALM CXIII

Title of the hundred and thirteenth: “Alleluia.” At the beginning of this psalm the Prophet, speaking in order to invite all people, both Jews and nations, to the praise of God, displays many of God’s benefits: namely, how, causing his own people to depart from the Egypt of unbelief and from the barbarous people of vices and evil spirits, he sanctified them and made them powerful; and how, through their example, he caused the unbelieving people and false Christians, who were failing through fear of persecutors, to be converted to the likeness of perfected Christians.

He also displays the exultation of rulers and subjects over the conversion of the unbelieving people, whom he calls “the sea” because of the bitterness of their unbelief, and over the conversion of false Christians, whom he calls “the Jordan,” since Jordan is interpreted as “descent,” because, by falling away from the height of communion with the Church, they descend through fear of tribulations into conformity with unbelievers.

Afterward, in order by the example of the rulers to draw everyone, Jews and nations alike, to the praise of God and to remove them from idolatry, he introduces those rulers speaking, displaying God’s benefits, dwelling both upon the overthrow of idols and upon the praise of God.

When Israel went out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people, Judah became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion.

In these two verses, each phrase is matched with one corresponding phrase, as follows: “When Israel went out from Egypt, Judah became his sanctuary.” This is to say: As Israel went out by faith from Egypt—that is, as the people of the faithful went out, although, being now Israel, they were not previously Israel—from the darkness of ignorance signified by Egypt, since Egypt is interpreted as “darkness,” Judah came to be in that people of the faithful; that is, confession of faith.

For it is not enough to believe in the heart unless confession is also made with the mouth. Hence the Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). Confession, I say, being the sanctification of that people of the faithful—that is, being the reason why it is sanctified by God through the forgiveness of sins.

And when the house of Jacob went out from the barbarous people, that house became Israel, and through this it became his dominion; that is, it became powerful over itself.

This is to say: After the departure from the Egypt of ignorance, when the house of Jacob—that is, the people of the faithful, who are now the house of Jacob, the household of God struggling against vices and supplanting them—went out from the barbarous people, that is, from the ravaging multitude of vices or evil spirits, that house became Israel.

That people is called “barbarous” because it devastates the mind of virtues, by comparison with a barbarous people devastating some homeland. The house of Jacob became Israel; that is, it became one who sees God in contemplation.

It is as if he said: After the people of the faithful had gone out from Egypt, the barbarous people resisted—that is, the multitude of vices and evil spirits made an exceedingly violent assault, through an evil habit, upon that people of the faithful, and thereby held it back greatly from contemplation of the divine height. But after that people had manfully wrestled against the barbarous people, defeated it, and escaped its excessive assaults through the help of heavenly grace, then at last it became Israel, which previously it had not been; that is, by the gaze of contemplation it saw God.

And being made Israel, it also became his dominion—that is, powerful over itself, ruling itself well in virtues and good works through the help of divine grace, whereas previously it had been under the power of the barbarous people.

Or it may be understood thus: The people of the faithful became Israel, and through this it became his dominion—that is, by becoming Israel it became the cause of its own power. Namely, the fact that it became Israel was the cause of its becoming powerful in miracles.

But when the people of the faithful became Israel and powerful, although previously it had been ignorant and powerless, the sea saw this—that is, the bitter people of unbelievers saw it—and, in order likewise to become Israel and powerful, fled from the bitterness of unbelief by approaching the sweetness of faith.

And the Jordan also saw this: namely, that the people of the perfected had become Israel and powerful. The Jordan is the people of failing false believers, who, through fear of tribulations, had descended from the height of faith into the sea—that is, into conformity with the unbelieving people. In order that the Jordan might become Israel and powerful and rise from the unbelief into which it had descended, it turned back, toward the height of the confession of faith.

This was once prefigured in the river Jordan. When the ark of the Lord passed through it, the river was divided so that it might provide free passage for the Levites carrying the ark. Its upper part stood still like a wall, while the lower part flowed down into the sea (Josh. 3:16). Whether the part that flowed down afterward turned back is not stated in the historical account.

I say that the sea fled and the Jordan turned back. Therefore the mountains—that is, the rulers—exulted like rams, that is, as rams, the leaders of the whole people of the faithful, just as rams are the leaders of the whole flock. And they rightly exulted, because this came about through their ministry of preaching.

And over this same flight and turning back the hills—that is, the subjects—exulted like lambs of sheep; that is, as young and innocent through faith, just as lambs are young animals and innocent animals. They are lambs of sheep because the fact that they are lambs came about through the sheep—that is, through the rulers, who are called sheep because by their teaching they nourish their subjects, after the likeness of sheep nourishing lambs with milk.

By saying that rulers and subjects exult over the salvation of unbelievers, he shows their exceedingly great charity directed toward the praise of God.

Alternatively, we may understand the mountains as the greater rulers and the hills as the lesser ones.

The Prophet poses a question about the flight of the sea, the turning back of the Jordan, and the exultation of the mountains and hills—not because he doubts these things, but in order to rouse the minds of his hearers to attend carefully to them. Through this kind of question he indicates that such events could not have occurred without God’s great purpose. He says this as follows:

The sea, I say, fled, and the Jordan was turned back, and the mountains and hills exulted. Therefore, what is the matter with you—that is, what occasion was there for you, O sea, because of which you fled? And you, Jordan, what happened to you, because you were turned back? And you, mountains, on what account did you exult like—that is, as—rams, and you, hills, like—that is, as—lambs of sheep? Truly, this did not happen without some great cause.

Having posed the question to the minds of his hearers [Col. 1239B], he introduces the very prelates whom he had testified to have exulted as answering, and makes them speak through to the end of the psalm, so that greater credence may be given to the authority of those through whose sound preaching this flight and turning occurred. He introduces them answering in this manner. Since the Prophet had said, “What is the matter with you, O sea,” and so forth, the prelates’ answer follows thus:

“Truly, it is not without some very great cause that we mountains exulted. For we exulted because the earth was moved from the face of the Lord—that is, the people of earthly things were moved from unbelief toward the end—and this happened from the face, that is, from the knowledge, of the Lord; and not of a recent Lord, but from the face of the God of Jacob, that is, from knowledge of that God whom the patriarch Jacob worshiped.

“He explains how they came to the knowledge of the God of Jacob, as follows [Col. 1239C]: ‘From the face, I say, of the God of Jacob.’ This God, by the illumination of grace, changed the rock into pools of water: namely, us prelates, who had been hard like rock in unbelief, he changed from the barrenness of ignorance so that we might become like pools full of water—that is, full of the waters of spiritual knowledge, just as pools are full of water. And he not only made us full of knowledge, but us who had previously been a crag—that is, hard and dry like a crag—he changed into springs of water; that is, he brought us to become like springs of water, supplying continual instruction to unbelievers, in the manner of springs continually flowing with water. Thus, through us, the earthly unbelievers came to the knowledge of the Lord.”

They then turn in address to God, praying that he may move the earth more and more toward faith, and this for the honor of his name. “We say that the earth has been moved, in large part; and, O Lord, move it more and more by the illumination of the knowledge of you. And give glory not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name”—that is, glorify your name through this more and more, since it has already been greatly glorified. This means: “We do not desire the conversion of unbelievers for our exaltation, but for the greater glorification of your name.”

Because he says “not to us” twice, he does so to emphasize the removal of self-glory. They repeat this emphasis for the instruction of their successors, so that no one may seek glory for himself in this world, but for God. “Give,” I say, “glory to your name,” and let this occur [Col. 1240A] “according to your mercy and your truth”—that is, from your mercy and your truth. Give glory to your name by calling the nations to faith through your mercy, and the Jews on account of the truth of your promise being fulfilled; for you promised that you would save the Jews.

Alternatively, “mercy” and “truth” may be understood with reference to both groups: for he saved Jews and nations through mercy, and had promised to save both. And so glorify your name among nations and Jews, lest the nations ever say, “Where is their God?” That is, let your power at some time become so evident through miracles that the nations will not say what they now say, namely, as a reproach to your faithful: “Where is their God?”—that is, the God of the Christians. “We are nowhere able to display our gods—Jupiter, Mercury, and the others—but their God nowhere appears; he is nowhere.”

After showing the reproach of the nations, they themselves praise God and scorn the idols in this way [Col. 1240B]: “The nations, intending to prove that our God does not exist, say, ‘Where is their God?’ But our God is in heaven.” This means: “Because he is invisible, the nations say that he exists nowhere; but our God is in heaven”—that is, in angels and heavenly men, not locally, but according to the grace that dwells within them.

Or it may be understood thus: “Our God, Christ, God and man, is locally in heaven according to his body. Although he is not seen by you, he is nevertheless so powerful that he has done whatever he wished.”

But the gods of the nations, who ought not even to be called gods but merely images, are utterly powerless [Col. 1240C]. To say nothing of images made of stone, wood, and iron, even the images of the nations that are made of silver and gold—and the fact that they are images—they do not possess from themselves, but are works of human hands. They have mouths, but they will not speak; and not real mouths, but imaginary ones. They have imaginary eyes, but they will not see. They have imaginary ears, but they will not hear. They have imaginary nostrils, but they will not smell. They have imaginary feet, but they will not walk. And although they have an imaginary throat, I do not say merely that they will not speak as human beings do; what is less, they will not even cry out through their throat—that is, there is no cry of beasts or birds in their throat.

From this, therefore, it is apparent that, being such, they are entirely devoid of power. Yet since they are such and are nevertheless worshiped by the most foolish nations, all who make them become inwardly like them; just as they worship them, so they become like them. Thus, just as the images are outwardly deaf and unable to see, so those who make and worship them lack inwardly, in their spiritual soul, the faculties of spiritual sight and hearing.

And not only those who make and worship them become like them, but also those who, even if they do not make them, at least place their trust in them, supposing them to be gods. This is not said as an imprecation, but concessively, in order to turn the nations back from the worship of images. “I say that the nations trust in images, and therefore become like them.”

But let the house of Israel not be like the images. For the house of Israel—that is, the family of faithful subjects who see God in contemplation—has hoped not in idols but in the Lord. Therefore, the Lord is their helper in good works and their protector, so that they may not be overcome by vices. And the house of Aaron—that is, the family of faithful prelates—has hoped in the Lord, and he himself is their helper and protector.

This is to be understood of the prelates and subjects of the Church who are from the Jews. By the house of Aaron, the assembly of prelates is understood, and by the house of Israel, the assembly of subjects, because under the Old Testament the tribe of Aaron ruled over all the tribes of Israel. This also corresponds well according to the interpretation of the name: for Aaron is interpreted as “mountain-dweller.” Prelates are appropriately called mountain-dwellers on account of the height of their pre-eminence; for we call those people mountain-dwellers who live on the summits of mountains.

But not only prelates and subjects from the Jews [Col. 1241B] hoped in the Lord; all among the nations who fear the Lord, both prelates and subjects, whether with chaste fear or servile fear, have hoped in the Lord. Therefore, he is their helper and their protector.

That both Jews and Gentiles hoped in the Lord did not come from ourselves, but from this: the Lord, who had long consigned us to forgetfulness while we were placed in unbelief, remembered us in order to bring us to faith and make us hope in him. Through this he blessed us—that is, exalted us—both according to the number of our multiplication and according to the increase of virtues and good works.

He explains in detail whom he blessed, as follows: “He blessed us,” I say. That is, “He blessed the house of Israel,” the family of faithful subjects from the Jews; “and he blessed the house of Aaron,” the family of prelates from Jews and Gentiles; “he blessed all who fear the Lord,” whether with chaste fear or servile fear, “the small with the great”—that is, subjects and prelates.

They pray for the addition of subjects and prelates in this way: “We have said that the Lord has blessed you, O prelates and subjects. May the Lord add to you others who are already joined to him through faith”—that is, after you who have already been joined to him through the adoption of grace, may he add others who are still unbelieving, and after you—that is, after you who are to be added—may he add others who will be sons, that is, your imitators. And after those sons of yours may he add still others, and so may he continue through all generations until the end of the world. May all of you, both those already added and those still to be added [Col. 1241D], be blessed—that is, multiplied and exalted in virtues—for the Lord, that is, for the honor of the Lord.

This means: “Let the fact that you will be blessed be ascribed not to you but to the Lord”—to the Lord, I say, “who made heaven and earth.” This means: “He is worthy of honor, since he himself made heaven,” that is, prelates, “and earth,” that is, subjects. And he not only made lesser prelates, but also made “the heaven of heaven,” that is, greater prelates who are the heaven of heaven—that is, prelates over lesser prelates. He himself made them what they are, and he made this for himself, that is, for the honor of the Lord.

Or it may be understood thus: “He did not merely make prelates and subjects what they are, but also the heaven of heaven,” that is, the Lordly man, who is heaven above all heavens. And he made this heaven of heaven for the Lord—that is, he made the Lordly man so that he might be personally united to the Lord the Word.

Or “the heaven of heaven” means the Lordly man whom he made for the Lord, that is, to be subject to the Lord according to his humanity. Hence the Apostle says: “The head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3). When he says “the heaven of heaven,” the addition of “of heaven” indicates that the prelates who are heavens with respect to their subjects are also subjects of the Lordly man, who is heaven with respect to them. Hence the Apostle says: “The head of the man is Christ” (ibid.).

According to Ambrose, the Father is also said to be the head of the Word—not because he is prior to or greater than the Word, but because the Word ineffably proceeds from the Father.

Since he had said that the Lord made heaven and earth [Col. 1242B], that is, prelates and subjects, lest it appear to subjects that they owed subjection to God alone and not to prelates, it is added as follows: “The Lord, I say, made heaven and earth; but he gave the earth,” that is, the subjects, “to be cultivated and governed by the sons of men,” that is, by prelates, who conduct themselves reasonably as human beings.

But although, O Lord, you have made heaven and earth, and these benefits that I have shown above, in view of the things mentioned earlier, the dead in unbelief will not praise you, nor all false Christians who descend into hell—that is, into the depths of vices. “Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner” (Sir. 15:9). The dead, I say, will not praise you; but we who live in faith and good works bless the Lord with mouth, heart, and deed, beginning from this moment—that is, from the present time—and persevering into the future age.

They say this in order to call the dead back from the death of unbelief, and those descending into the hell of vices back from that hell; and to invite those living in faith and good works to persevere.

Alternatively, they say this because they had prayed, saying, “May he add,” and so forth. In order to obtain more quickly what they had prayed for, they show that unbelievers will not praise him in any other way unless, by adding them to the faithful, he first rescues them from the death of unbelief.

It should be known that, although above we said that the prelates’ response begins where it says, “From the face of the Lord,” and so forth, the same passage may also be understood as the common response of the sea, the Jordan, the mountains, and the hills, continuing up to that apostrophe in the third verse where it says, “Not to us,” and so forth, which seems to apply only to the prelates. Nevertheless, the meaning is the same whether it is the response of all or only the response of the prelates.

If, therefore, it is the common response of all, it is adapted in this way: “You ask, O Prophet, why I, the sea, flee, why I, the Jordan, am turned back, and why we, the mountains and hills, have exulted. All these things happened because the earth was moved from the face of the Lord,” and so forth.

The Prophet introduces them answering in this manner so that no one might suppose that these things occurred through the power of the prelates, or through the free will of the sea and the Jordan. By removing this supposition, he implies that all these things are to be ascribed to God, for the magnification of his praise.

The apostrophe that follows, when he says, “Not to us,” which indeed concerns only the prelates [Col. 1243A], is adapted in the same manner as above.

## ON PSALM 114

**Title of the One Hundred Fourteenth:** Alleluia.

In this psalm there is the voice of the assembly of the faithful, displaying the complete love that they have for God in view of the benefits that he has already bestowed and those that he is still going to bestow. They display these things also for the instruction of their hearers, so that the hearers too, in view of these same benefits, may love God completely and thus praise him with complete love.

“I have loved”—the Lord, with complete love. When he says that he has loved the Lord, he also implies that he has fulfilled all the precepts of the law. For “the whole law and the prophets depend upon love” (Matt. 22:40).

He then adds the reason why he loved, as follows: “For this reason I loved the Lord completely, because I am certain that the Lord will hear, according to the effect that will occur in the future, what he already hears here according to his disposition—the voice of my prayer.” That is, the external petitioning voice proceeding from my inward prayer, that is, from a good affection.

This means: “For this reason I loved and love him completely, because I know that in the future he will accomplish what I have prayed and am praying for in affection and voice.”

When he says “I have loved,” he indicates that he has already persevered in love and is continually increasing in it; through this he more strongly invites his hearers to love. “I have loved,” I say, “because he will hear”; and not only because he will hear in the future, but also because here he has already inclined his ear to me in my weakness [Col. 1243C]. That is, he made the ear of his mercy incline toward me in my weakness, after the likeness of a physician who bends down his ear to a sick person who can scarcely speak.

This means: “He will not merely hear in the future what I pray, so that he may finally bring it to completion; but when I was weak, and prayed to him because of my weakness, although I had no merits to help me, he heard me through grace alone, so that he might complete what I was praying for.”

When he says that God inclined his ear to him, he implies that he prayed. In order to provide his hearers with an example of continual prayer—so that whoever stands may beware lest he fall (1 Cor. 10:12)—he affirms that he will pray as long as he remains in this life, as follows:

“He inclined his ear to me,” I say, “to me, a weak man praying. And so that he may continually incline his ear to me, I will call upon him”—that is, I will pray to him in inward affection—“in my days,” existing in them; that is, I will call upon him for as long as I remain in these transient days, which are mine because I made them mine when, by sinning in Adam, I acquired them for myself.

He explains from what source the Lord will hear him in the future, as follows: “I say that the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer.” And it is indeed necessary that he hear, because “the pains that cause death have surrounded me”—bodily pains, that is. I endure so many pains of mortality and passibility, through which one reaches bodily death, that I seem, by emphasis, to be wholly surrounded by them. In the future he must rescue me, once heard, from these pains, even if he does not rescue me from them now.

He also explains from what source the Lord inclined his ear to him, as follows: “He inclined his ear to me,” I say, which was certainly necessary for me. For not only have the pains of death surrounded me [Col. 1244A], but the dangers of hell have found me—that is, vices, which are dangers through which one comes to hell, pursued me for so long that they found me according to my consent and evil action. Thus they humbled me with such severe weakness that I could never rise by my own power.

Since, therefore, I was thus surrounded by pains and found by dangers, because otherwise I would not escape, I discovered, by attentive reflection, the tribulation of those dangers and the manifold pain of mortality and passibility by which I was surrounded.

This means: “I perceived what I had not previously perceived, namely, how great my tribulation and pain were; and so I called upon the name of the Lord”—that is, I prayed to the Lord by considering his name, which is “Lord.”
