It is as though he said: “Considering him to be omnipotent, on account of the greatness of his name, which is ‘Lord,’ I called upon him”—that is, I prayed to him inwardly in affection—saying:

“O Lord, deliver my soul, here from dangers and in the future from pains.”

The word “O” is not used vocatively here, but optatively. In Hebrew the expression is *anna Adonai*. *Anna* is a sign of wishing or supplication. Since we Latins do not have a word equivalent to this word *anna*, “O” has been placed here, because it is a sign of wishing. Hence in some translators one finds, “I beseech you, Lord.”

“I say that I called upon the Lord, saying: ‘O Lord, deliver my soul’—in the future from the pains of passibility, and here from the dangers of hell.”

Thus, in calling upon the Lord, I was humbled in inward affection; that is, I called upon him with humility of affection and devotion, considering myself insufficient to be delivered by my own power. And because I was humbled, the Lord has already delivered me from the tribulation of the dangers of hell, that is, from vices, so that they do not prevail over me to the same extent as before.

The Lord, I say, is merciful by nature, and just, and our God. It is as though he said: “He delivered me who ought to deliver me, since he is merciful and just, and who was able to deliver me, since he is our omnipotent God.”

He explains how he is proved merciful and just, adding a separate point to each, as follows: “He is merciful,” and he is proved merciful by nature because he shows mercy by bestowing many benefits of mercy. “And he is proved to be just because he guards the little ones”—that is, he guards his faithful who make themselves little, that is, humble—so that they may not fall away from his holiness. This is indeed just: namely, that the little ones should be guarded by him.

He then turns exhortingly to his soul, as follows: “I said that the Lord has already delivered me from dangers, and in the future will hear the voice of my prayer. Therefore, O my soul, turn away from regard for worldly things toward your rest”—that is, toward consideration and hope of your future rest.

This means: “Putting aside every concern for worldly things, direct yourself in action and affection toward the rest of eternal blessedness.”

And you must indeed do this because the Lord has done good—or will do good—to you in that rest. He will do good to me in this manner because “he has delivered,” or “will deliver,” my soul from eternal death [Col. 1245A].

Alternatively, “he will deliver my soul from death,” that is, my life from mortality and passibility; and “he will deliver my eyes from tears,” so that I will no longer need to weep, as is fitting here on account of the remembrance of sins and the postponement of the eternal homeland.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6:21). Of the future state it is written: “God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints” (Rev. 21:4).

“And he will deliver my inward feet,” that is, my affections, “from falling,” so that afterward I may not fall even in affection, although here I often fall into vice not only in affection but also in action.

Then I will please the Lord in all things, offending him in absolutely nothing, whereas here I displease him in many ways. “I will please,” I say, “existing in the land of the living”—that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem, in which no one will dwell except one who lives forever.

## ON PSALM 115

**Title of the One Hundred Fifteenth:** Alleluia.

The voice of the Church of martyrs, displaying the steadfastness of its faith and its suffering for the faith, and the offering of itself through martyrdom, in order to invite its hearers, by its example of faith and confession and martyrdom, to praise God.

“I believed; therefore I spoke.”

Among the Hebrews this psalm is regarded as virtually one with the preceding psalm, because it can be connected with it as follows: “I said that the Lord would deliver my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling, and that I would please the Lord; and I believed all this. Therefore I spoke openly of my belief.”

Or it may be understood as referring to faith in general, with the psalm standing on its own: “O believers, do not, through fear of the humiliation of tribulations, desist from openly confessing the faith; and take me as an example for yourselves. For I believed”—that is, I held the right faith in my heart—“therefore I spoke”—that is, I openly confessed that faith with my mouth.

And therefore, although I had believed rightly and spoken rightly, I ought not to have been humbled; yet I was humbled “in tribulations exceedingly”—that is, greatly. Or, “I was humbled in tribulations exceedingly”—that is, beyond the measure of my weakness, beyond what my frailty could bear.

Hence the Apostle says: “We were burdened beyond measure, so that we despaired even of life” (2 Cor. 1:8). Therefore, you too, believers, speak by my example, not fearing to be humbled.

But because he had said that he was humbled, someone might suppose that he would not have spoken if he had known that he would thereby be humbled. To remove this supposition, he shows that before he spoke he had foreseen that he would offer himself to God through martyrdom.

He says this as follows: “I spoke,” I say, “and for this reason I was humbled in tribulations; but this humiliation did not occur contrary to my will and disposition. For I, who believed rightly, said in my inward ecstasy”—that is, I thought and resolved in the secret of my reason, which surpasses all human reasoning in subtlety—“Truly, every man is a liar.”

That is, everyone who is simply a human being, earthly and not spiritual, preferring this life to the eternal life, is a liar if he hesitates to give up this life for the sake of the eternal one; even if he says nothing with his mouth, he is a liar when he supposes that this life ought to be preferred to the life to come.

And because I too would be a liar and guilty if I were simply a human being, what shall I render to the Lord for all the good things that he has rendered to me? Since, for my sins, he has mercifully rendered me the remission of those sins, justification, and other benefits, what worthy and precious thing shall I render to him for all these good things that he has given me?

Behold, I know what I shall render, since I can do nothing greater for him: “I will take the cup of salvation,” that is, of Christ the Savior—namely, the death that he willingly endured for me.

And lest I fail through fear of this cup, “I will call upon the name of the Lord”—that is, I will call upon God as my helper, considering the greatness of his name, which is “Lord.”

Death is called a cup by a double comparison. Either because it is bitter to the flesh, like certain cups of medicinal potions which, although most health-giving, are nevertheless exceedingly bitter; or because, just as a cup of the finest wine changes the person whom it intoxicates from the state in which he is into another state, so death changes the person whom it overtakes from the state of this life into another state.

The verse that says, “I said,” can also be constructed differently, with the intervening phrase “every man is a liar” understood as inserted. It may then be adapted as follows:

“I say that I was humbled, and this did not happen contrary to my will. For I said in my inward ecstasy”—that is, I resolved and judged in the excess of my reason—“What shall I render to the Lord for all the benefits that he has rendered to me? Certainly I will render this: I will take the cup of salvation; and, lest I fail in taking it, I will call upon the name of the Lord.”

And therefore I said this in my inward ecstasy, because every man who is simply human, not spiritual and not obedient to God unto death, is a liar in his promise. For in baptism he promised God obedience to all his commandments, but he is a liar in that promise when he fears to die for him, just as Christ himself died for all.

“I say that I vowed in my inward ecstasy that I would take the cup of salvation for the Lord. And I will not pay these vows of mine—that is, this promise of mine to carry myself to death—in secret [Col. 1246D], but I will pay them openly before all his people: openly, when I confess, and before the whole assembly of the faithful I will die—that is, I will die in order to give everyone an example of dying for the Lord.”

Lest anyone think it a small thing to die for the Lord, and so that he may more strongly incite his hearers to such a death, he shows that this is precious to God, as follows:

“I say that I will take the cup of salvation. This must indeed be done by me, for ‘in the sight’—that is, in the judgment—‘of the Lord, precious,’ that is, very dear, ‘is the death of his saints.”

This means: “However worthless it may seem to anyone, the Lord nevertheless regards the death of his saints as precious.”

Or it may be understood thus: “For this reason I will take the cup of salvation,” that is, death, “because the death of his saints, existing in the sight of the Lord”—that is, in the Lord’s good pleasure—is precious, that is, bought at a great price: namely, at the price of his death.

This means: “It is fitting for me to die for him because, by dying for me, he purchased this very thing: that I too might die for him.”

He then turns to God out of his great affection, as follows: “I say, O Lord, that the death of your saints is precious in your sight. Therefore, O Lord, I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise”—that is, I will sacrifice myself to you as a victim by dying in confession of you, a victim that you will praise.

And because, O hearers, I could not complete this sacrifice except with God’s help, “I will call upon the name of the Lord”—that is, I will call upon the Lord as my helper, considering the greatness of his name, which is “Lord.”

I will sacrifice myself to you as a victim not only for this reason, because the death of the saints is precious in your sight, but also because I am your servant.

“Your servant”—that is, I am wholly subject to you, as a creature is subject to the Creator; therefore I must obey you in all things.

But because he had simply said that he was a servant, and some servants are wicked, such as evil spirits, who, although unwillingly, nevertheless obey God’s disposition, while others are spontaneous servants, who serve willingly, such as holy men, he shows that he is a willing servant, in order to instruct his hearers to serve God willingly, as follows:

“I am your servant,” I say, “and such a servant that I am the son of your handmaid”—that is, an imitator of the heavenly Jerusalem, which is a handmaid, that is, subject to you, the gathering of angels and spiritual men.

Thus, just as they obey you not unwillingly but willingly, so I too will obey you by a free will. And in order that I might serve you freely, “you have broken my bonds”—that is, you have destroyed the bonds of my sins by forgiving them, bonds that held me captive and hindered me from obeying you.

It should be noted that the statement, “I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise, and I will call upon the name of the Lord,” is equivalent to what was said above, “I will take the cup,” and so forth. But it is repeated out of affection and in order to invite the hearers more strongly to martyrdom. For the same reason he says twice, “I am your servant,” and repeats what he had said above: “I will pay my vows in the sight of all his people.”

This is adapted as follows: “I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to the Lord, and I will pay these vows of mine”—namely, this sacrifice that I vowed to render to the Lord—“in the sight of all his people,” that is, I will render it openly, so that the whole faithful people may receive an example from it.

“I will pay my vows,” I say, “I”—already existing in hope in the courts, that is, in the spaciousness of the house of the Lord, namely, the heavenly Jerusalem. This means: “I will pay my vows in hope of attaining the spacious house of God, not for human approval.”

“I say that I exist in hope in the spaciousness of the house of God, the heavenly Jerusalem. And I do not exist in hope in a lesser rank of that Jerusalem; rather, I exist in hope in your midst, O heavenly Jerusalem”—that is, in your more distinguished rank—after the likeness of those soldiers who, being dearer to their lord, sit not in a corner of the house but in the middle, in a more honorable place.

Martyrs are said to obtain a higher rank than confessors. By saying that they are in the middle, they invite their hearers more strongly to martyrdom, so that they too may deserve to be in the middle.

## ON PSALM 116

**Title of the One Hundred Sixteenth:** Alleluia.

In this psalm the Prophet exhorts all Jews and Gentiles to praise God: the Jews in view of his true promise fulfilled in them, and the Gentiles in view of the mercy bestowed upon them.

“Praise the Lord with every kind of praise, all nations; praise him also, all believing peoples of the Jews.”

He appropriately uses “peoples” in the plural, to show that many were converted from all twelve tribes.

He therefore assigns separate reasons to the respective groups, as follows: “You nations, praise him for this reason: because his mercy”—that is, your salvation through the remission of sins and justification, which occurred solely through his free mercy—“has been confirmed over us,” that is, it has been made firm, immovable, and enduring in you, given by God’s superior disposition.

According to the saying: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James 1:17).

It is as though he said: “For this reason, O nations, praise him, because the salvation of his mercy, given over you—that is, bestowed upon you from the heavenly disposition—has been so confirmed in you that you will never be deprived of it.”

Hence the Apostle says: “The Gentiles are to glorify God for his mercy,” and so forth (Rom. 15:9).

Because the Prophet says “over us,” joining himself to the faithful from the Gentiles although he himself is a Jew, he does so in order to show that he and all the faithful, both from the Gentiles and from the Jews, are one mass in Christ.

“But you, Jews, praise the Lord for this reason: because the truth of the Lord remains in you forever”—that is, the fulfillment of his true promise, namely, your salvation, which he truly promised and fulfilled in you, will endure forever.

## ON PSALM 117

**Title of the One Hundred Seventeenth:** Alleluia.

In this psalm the assembly of the first martyrs is introduced speaking, exhorting Jews and Gentiles to praise God on account of his goodness and mercy. It also displays the benefits of that mercy in itself in many ways, recounting how far he rescued it from the tribulation of vices [Col. 1248D].

And because he is a helper in the external tribulation caused by enemies, making the person strong and steadfast in that tribulation so that he does not fail, and also enabling him to overcome his enemies, the psalm shows that this tribulation will give way to prosperity and correction, not to eternal death.

It also promises that it will always confess the Lord, because he has become its salvation through Christ, the rejected stone who was made by the Lord the cornerstone. It also prays for its salvation and exhorts its hearers to establish a solemn day.

Through its example, it instructs its hearers not to fear tribulations inflicted by enemies for the Lord’s sake, since such tribulations will likewise give way to their prosperity; it also instructs them to pray.

[Col. 1249A] “Confess to the Lord”—that is, praise him in every way—you faithful from Jews and Gentiles, with this consideration: that he is good by nature.

And if you are not sufficient to consider this, at least confess him with this thought: that “his mercy”—that is, the benefits of his mercy which he bestows upon his faithful—“endures into the future age,” that is, forever.

I do not merely exhort the faithful of both peoples to confess the Lord among themselves; let the house of Israel also—that is, the family of faithful subjects among the Jewish people—say now, without delay, exhorting others:

“Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.”

Or let them say this to one another, exhorting one another. And let the house of Aaron—that is, the family of faithful prelates among the Jewish people—say now, either to others or to one another:

“Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.”

And let those among the Gentiles who fear the Lord, whether prelates or subjects, say now, either to others or to one another:

“Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.”

It should be noted that the first verse of this psalm is to be repeated in full in each of the three following verses, although, for the sake of brevity, only its latter part appears to be repeated.

He explains the benefits of the Lord’s mercy in himself as follows: “The mercy of the Lord,” I say, “will endure forever.” And behold, the benefits of his mercy are apparent in me. For I, constricted by the inner tribulation of vices, called upon the Lord because of that tribulation—that is, I prayed to the Lord in order to escape it—and the Lord heard me when I called, rescuing me from that tribulation: I mean, placing me in the breadth of love and good works. As though he were saying: “He rescued me from tribulation by grace and placed me in the spaciousness of virtues and good works.”

Since, therefore, the Lord has been my helper in inner tribulation, I am certain that he will also be my helper in tribulation inflicted upon me by any persecutor, so that I do not fail. Therefore I shall not fear whatever a wicked person may do to me through persecution—that is, I shall not fear whatever kind of persecution wicked people may inflict upon me. The Lord, I say, will be my helper in outward tribulations. [Col. 1249D] Therefore I shall not fear human enemies; rather, although I endure much persecution from them, I shall despise my enemies, wicked human beings—that is, I shall despise their persecutions and regard them as nothing—which is indeed more than not fearing them. Or I shall despise my enemies, wicked spirits—that is, I shall despise their suggestions by refusing to consent to them.

Since, therefore, O hearers, the Lord is such a helper that he causes his own people not to fear and to despise their enemies, it is good to trust in the Lord while suffering for him, rather than to trust in a human persecutor in order to obtain earthly safety through him: “Vain indeed is the salvation of man” (Ps. 59:13). The comparative word “rather” is not used here as though he were saying: “It is useful to trust in the Lord while enduring tribulation for him, and it is not useful to trust in a human persecutor while seeking bodily safety from him.” I remove this confidence not only from any ordinary human being, but, to say what is better, it is more useful to hope for salvation from the Lord through the harshness of tribulations than from princes, even secular ones, through earthly prosperity. This is as though he were saying: “It is good to hope for salvation in the Lord, and not in secular princes.” Hence it is written: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man” (Jer. 17:5), and so forth.

This passage may also be read comparatively if we understand “princes” as heavenly spirits and spiritual men who are regarded as princes among God’s people. According to this interpretation it will be said: “It is good to trust in the Lord rather than in any human being, and it is good to hope in the Lord rather than in princes,” that is, in angels and holy men. As though he were saying: “Although it is sometimes useful to trust in a human being and to hope in the prayers and patronage of holy princes, it is much more useful to trust and hope in the Lord. For God can help without them, whereas they can do nothing without God.”

He then shows the tribulations inflicted by the enemies as follows: “I say that the Lord will be my helper against enemies, who have already been my helper against enemies. For all the nations”—that is, all those living in a pagan and irrational manner, both Jews and Gentiles—“surrounded me with tribulations,” that is, they inflicted so many tribulations upon me that I seemed to be entirely surrounded by them. And when they attempted to overwhelm me completely, “in the name of the Lord it happened that I avenged myself upon them by going against them,” that is, because I strove in the name of the Lord—in the Lord’s honor, not my own; namely, because I labored to honor God, not myself—it happened that I avenged myself upon them by going against them through preaching, in order to incorporate them into myself.

This means: “Because I devoted myself to God’s honor, the Lord granted me this vengeance against them: just as they sought to incorporate me into themselves through tribulation, so I might incorporate them into myself through preaching.” Or it may be understood in this way: “I avenged myself by taking vengeance upon them,” that is, against them—namely, against certain of them. This means: “I took such vengeance upon some of them that this vengeance was exceedingly harmful to them, since some of my persecutors are said to have been condemned by the Lord even in this life to a just bodily death.” Or it may be understood thus: “I have avenged myself”—that is, I shall avenge myself—“by taking vengeance upon them,” that is, against them, namely through the vengeance of eternal death, which will greatly harm them. He says this for the correction of the persecutors.

Having shown the multiplicity of the enemies, he also shows the persistence of their tribulations as follows: “All the nations,” I say, “surrounded me with tribulations,” and this was not merely for an hour; rather, “while surrounding me, they surrounded me,” that is, they were always present and persevering in that surrounding. It should be noted that when a present participle joined to a conjugated verb is placed in this way, it denotes persistence, as in *videns vidi*, “seeing, I saw,” *exspectans exspectavi*, “waiting, I waited,” and other such expressions.

“I say that, while surrounding me, they surrounded me, and yet in the name of the Lord it happened that I avenged myself upon them.” This is explained as above: “They surrounded me,” I say, “and this as bees”—that is, resembling bees in extreme ferocity and sharpness, which, when angered together, press on with great violence. Or: “as bees,” that is, resembling bees. For just as bees produce sweet honey, so they, through the force of their tribulations, produced a greater sweetness of charity toward God. “The weaker I am, the stronger and more powerful I am” (1 Cor. 12:10), and they blazed against me with tribulations as fire usually blazes among thorns. For just as fire kindled in a thorn thicket burns the thorns but leaves the trunk unharmed, so their tribulations consumed the thorns of sins in me. [Col. 1251B] They left me unharmed, and this happened in the name of the Lord, because I avenged myself upon them.

This too is explained as above: “They surrounded me,” I say, “and I was driven by their tribulations”—that is, struck—“so that I might fall,” that is, so that I might fail in my purpose. This means: “They drove me with tribulations intending to bring me to the collapse of failure.” I was not only driven, however, but, with respect to certain weak members of mine, I was also overthrown, “so that I might fall.” That is, through fear of tribulations some of my weak members wavered—not in such a way that they fell completely, but as though they were already falling, that is, as though they were at the beginning of their fall and already prepared to fail.

And lest I fall completely in that part in which I had been overthrown, the Lord received me [Col. 1251C] through the assistance of his protecting grace. This means: “He helped my already-overthrown weak members so that they would not fall completely,” after the likeness of someone who catches another person leaning forward to fall, whose foot has already turned aside, supporting him with his right hand so that he does not fall.

In that part of my strong members, however, in which I was merely driven and not overthrown, the Lord was “my strength,” that is, the cause of my strength. This means: “The Lord gave constancy of strength to my strong powers, which, when driven toward tribulation, did not waver, so that they might persevere in his good purpose.” Through this he became “my praise,” or “my act of praise,” that is, he became for me the cause of praise or of praising him. Namely, through strength he granted me this: that I might be regarded as worthy of praise in the Church. Or he became “my praise,” or “my act of praise,” in the sense that he brought this about in me: I praised him because of the strength he had given me, and through those very tribulations, reception, and strength he became for me one who leads toward eternal salvation.

This means: “Through this he has worked, and continues continually to work, my eternal salvation.” “For no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5).

I say that he is my strength with respect to my robust members. And he is so greatly the cause of strength in those robust members that “in the tents of the righteous”—that is, among the righteous who dwell in tents, namely, in my robust members, who are righteous and persevere in the tents of God’s warfare—there is not a voice of mourning but a voice of exultation, [Col. 1252A] signifying joy and eternal salvation. This means: “He makes them so strong in tribulation that even in tribulation they do not utter a voice of sadness, but one signifying eternal exultation and salvation.” Accordingly, it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “They went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41).

The Lord was not only my strength, with respect to my robust members, so that he might make me strong and steadfast against persecutions; “the right hand of the Lord also made virtue in me,” that is, the Son of God gave me victory. Namely, he caused certain members of mine, already made robust, to conquer all persecutors, so that they would not yield even in bodily death. Through this “the right hand of the Lord exalted me,” that is, [Col. 1252B] elevated and glorified those members of mine that had already conquered, so that they might be regarded as praiseworthy among the faithful.

“The right hand,” I say, “of the Lord made virtue.” He repeats this in order on this occasion to add a refutation. The persecutors might object: “You say that the Lord caused you to conquer, which certainly seems strange, since you appear rather to have endured in certain members things that pertain to death—namely, tribulations even to the shedding of blood, which the defeated are accustomed to suffer.” To this the refutation follows:

“I rightly say that the right hand of the Lord caused me to conquer through the suffering of those very tribulations. For I shall not die because of those tribulations, as you persecutors think; rather, through them I shall live eternally.” He appropriately says “I shall die,” although he could have said “he made,” which is in the past tense. As though he were saying: “I rightly say that I have already conquered with respect to certain members, which have already endured tribulations and steadfastly escaped them. Those members of mine did not die through the tribulations; rather, through this they began to live perpetually.”

Likewise, through the force of the tribulations I shall not die with respect to those members that are still to suffer; rather, through those very tribulations I shall live. That is, the tribulations will be the cause that my members, which are still to suffer, will live without end. This means: “The tribulations were not the cause of death for my members that have already suffered, nor will they be the cause of death for those that are still to suffer.” The bodily death that occurs through tribulations should not be called death, but the beginning of life. For after this death the saints begin to live happily. Hence the day of the martyrs’ death is also called their birthday. For then they are born into eternal life.

By this he draws his hearers toward martyrdom, saying that this temporal death is not death but the beginning of life. “I say that I shall live,” and this can be demonstrated by the fact that after the separation of body and soul I shall proclaim the works of the Lord—not with my own voice, certainly, but I shall be the cause that the works of the Lord are proclaimed and praised by others who survive. This would not be so unless I lived. For “the dead will not praise the Lord” (Ps. 113:17). This means: “My own steadfastness, firm unto the end, will itself be the cause that others, by proclaiming them, praise the works of the Lord”—namely, the steadfastness and victory, and the other benefits that he works in me.

[Col. 1253A] I say that I shall not die, and truly such a separation of soul and body should not be called death but chastisement. For through such death and tribulation the Lord has chastised me with respect to certain members of mine that have already suffered, and he is also chastising me with respect to those members that are now suffering and dying.

“Chastise” is not understood here in its customary sense, but is used for “purify.” Through the death of martyrdom and through tribulation, the Lord purifies both the sins that are in the martyrs and increases their crowns. “He chastised me,” I say, and, having chastised me in this way, he did not hand me over to eternal death. This means: “Through such chastisement he freed my members that had already suffered from eternal death.”

Since, therefore, tribulation—and this separation of body and soul—is for me chastisement and an occasion of life, I concede, O persecutors, and do not shrink back: “Open for me the gates of righteousness,” that is, prepare for me the tribulations and death that will be gates for me through which I shall enter into righteousness, that is, into the just recompense of eternal life, after the likeness of those who open the doors to someone wishing to enter a house.

He does not say this imperatively but concessively, since it is wrong to persuade anyone to do evil. He makes this concession in order to invite his hearers more strongly to endure tribulations and death willingly, by showing that these are the gates of righteousness.

“Open,” I say, “the gates,” and when I have entered into them—the tribulations that are the gates—I shall not be saddened but shall confess to the Lord, that is, praise the Lord with my voice, heart, and endurance. Indeed, I do not shrink from entering these gates because this same gate of tribulation belonged to the Lord Christ: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and thus to enter into his glory” (Luke 24:26).

And because it belonged to the Lord, all the righteous who enter it must do so either through the actual experience of suffering or at least through the wish to suffer if necessary. For no one who does not enter in some manner will be saved. Thus it is read concerning the blessed Martin: although the sword of the persecutor did not take him, he nevertheless did not lose the palm of martyrdom. For by his willingness he became a martyr.

Out of excessive affection he then makes an apostrophe to God, as follows: “I shall confess,” I say, “to the Lord, and rightly shall I confess to you, O Lord, because you heard me, so that you might free me from the inner tribulation of vices, and you became for me salvation”—that is, the cause of salvation—“both here,” namely, through the remission and justification of sins, [Col. 1253D] “and in the future,” when you will give eternal blessedness.

And through this you became for me the cause of salvation: “The stone, Christ, which the builders rejected, has become the cornerstone.” This means: “Through the rejection of Christ, the most firm stone, you saved me. Without him as foundation no one can build himself as a temple of God through virtues and good works.” “For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ” (1 Cor. 3:11).

This stone, without which no one can build himself as a temple of God, “the builders rejected,” that is, the Jews despised him while building themselves as a temple of God through their traditions. I say “builders” with respect to their own estimation, not with respect to the truth of the matter. For no one can become a temple of God unless founded upon faith in Christ, whom the Jews rejected, denying that he was the king of Israel and the Son of God, in accordance with the statement: “Do not write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but that he himself said, ‘I am the King of the Jews’” (John 19:21). And again: “According to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (ibid., 19:7).

Because this stone was rejected by the Jews and handed over to death, it became “the cornerstone.” Previously it had not been the cornerstone, that is, it became the head of the Church’s two walls: the wall of the faithful from the Jews and the wall of the faithful from the Gentiles—properly called a “corner.” For just as two different walls meet at a corner, and each embraces the other by means of a corner-stone placed above them and serving as their head, so those two walls—the Church from the Jews and the Church from the Gentiles—which had previously been wholly separate from one another, came together in the unity of faith, subject to Christ the cornerstone. He is the head of both and embraces both under his rule, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14), and so forth.

The story that the Jews tell concerning the cornerstone—namely, that during the construction of Solomon’s Temple one stone was rejected by the builders and finally placed in the corner—seems entirely to approach falsehood, since it is not found in the historical account.

It should be noted that the Prophet composed this verse with a particular kind of expression. Having written, “The stone which the builders rejected,” he ought, according to the order he had begun, to have added, “they made into the cornerstone.” Abandoning this order, he brought the verse to an end by another form of expression, adding: “It has become the cornerstone.”

In this he removes a notion that someone might wrongly entertain: namely, that the Jews rejected this stone with the intention that it should become the cornerstone. If they had done this with that intention and plan, the Prophet would plainly have written: “The stone which the builders rejected, they made into the cornerstone.” But by abandoning this order and speaking otherwise—namely, “it has become the cornerstone”—he clearly teaches that it became the cornerstone not by their plan but by another’s.

He shows by whom it became the cornerstone and by whose arrangement it was rejected—for its rejection did not occur without a great plan—by adding the following: “I say that they rejected the stone, and it has become the cornerstone. Both the fact that it was rejected and the fact that it became the cornerstone were done by the Lord,” that is, they occurred through the hidden disposition of God. Although among us it is ineffable and unknowable by what reasoning this happened, it is nevertheless wondrous in my inward eyes—that is, in the eyes of the mind.

This means: “We marvel exceedingly at why the Lord arranged that the people of the Jews, previously so dear to him, should be so blinded that they rejected and handed over to death Christ, the true stone about whom they had heard so much from the prophets, and that he should thus become the cornerstone.”

I say that they rejected him by handing him over to death. The day on which he was rejected and handed over to death is truly “the day which the Lord has made”—not because he did not make all other days as well, but because, on account of the dignity of that day on which we were redeemed, it is said by antonomasia that he made this day.

And because this day is so worthy, “let us exult in body and rejoice in soul” on that day—that is, in imitation of that day. Let us imitate, both in the soul’s desire and by suffering joyfully for Christ, if necessary, in the body, the passion that he endured for us on that day, insofar as this is possible for us.

Or the passage may be read concerning the day of the Resurrection: “I say that he became the cornerstone, and this occurred through the glory of the Resurrection. This day, on which, rising again, he became the cornerstone, is the day which the Lord has made.”

In this interpretation, as was already understood above, “this” is taken by antonomasia. Therefore, because this day is so glorious, “let us exult in body,” by doing good, “and rejoice in soul,” through a good disposition, “on that day,” that is, in contemplation of that day.

This means: “Whether that day is present or not, nevertheless, because such a great benefit happened to us on it, let us rejoice in soul through a good disposition in contemplation of it, and let us exult in body through good action.”

“Let us rejoice,” I say, “and exult,” each one saying: “O Lord, save me”—here by forgiving sins, and in the future by granting eternal blessedness. And: “O Lord, make prosperous,” that is, cause everything that happens to us here, whether prosperous or adverse, to work toward good prosperity for us in the future. In accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “We know that for those who love God all things work together for good” (Rom. 8:28).

I say, “Let us exult and rejoice on that day,” which indeed we ought to do. For on that day Christ was blessed—that is, exalted through the glory of the Resurrection—“he who is to come in the name of the Lord,” that is, in honor of the Lord the Father, in accordance with the statement: “I do not seek my own glory, but that of the Father who sent me” (John 8:50). And elsewhere: “I have come in the name of my Father,” and so forth (John 5:43).

Other translators have: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” From this it is gathered that if one says, “Blessed is he who is to come,” this is spoken with respect to the prophet, who lived before Christ’s coming, not with respect to the martyrs, who are introduced here as speaking and who lived after Christ’s coming.

The passage may also be read concerning Christ’s second coming: “He is blessed in the name of the Lord,” that is, he is exalted. He who is to come in the future to judge the world, namely Christ, was zealous for the honor of the Lord the Father.

Having recounted the benefits of the Lord’s mercy, the martyrs who speak here make an apostrophe to their hearers, in order to commend what they have said and draw them to imitate them in the praise of God. This apostrophe refers to everything said above and is read as follows:

“We said, ‘Let us exult,’” and so forth. “And, O hearers, we have blessed you,” that is, we have spoken well to you by announcing the benefits of the Lord’s mercy that appear in us martyrs. “We have blessed you,” I say, “as those who belong to the house of the Lord,” that is, to the household of the Lord; therefore we are worthy of your obedience.

And we did not possess from ourselves what enabled us to bless you, but from God the Lord. For God, who is also Lord of all, not only disclosed these things to us but also “shone upon us,” that is, shone in our minds through the illumination of knowledge of himself. By shining upon us, he made known to us the things with which we have blessed you; therefore we ought all the more to agree with us.

“We have blessed you,” I say. Therefore, O hearers, stirred by our admonition, “establish a solemn day,” that is, firmly establish your life as resembling a solemn day. Just as on a solemn day you cease from every servile work, so throughout your entire life cease from every servitude to sins.

“Establish,” I say, “persisting in the honor of God amid dense foliage,” that is, amid manifold sacrifices of virtues and good works. And establish a solemn day amid dense foliage until you reach “the horn of the altar,” that is, until you attain contemplation of Christ’s divinity, which is understood through the horn because of its sublimity, since the horn grows upward.

As though he were saying: “Persist amid dense foliage until in the future you may deserve to attain the perfect contemplation of the sublimity of Christ’s divinity, which is our altar, upon which we offer to God sacrifices of conduct and good works.”

Or “to the horn of the altar” means “to the sublimity of the mind,” that is, to the contemplation of divinity, which is the horn of the mind: it surpasses our mind in its sublimity, after the likeness of a horn, which, in horned animals, surpasses the whole body by extending upward.

The mind is also called an altar because in the mind we frequently offer to God sacrifices of virtues and good conduct, as upon an altar. Divinity is likewise called a horn, that is, a firm defense founded upon merits against the devil and vices, just as the horn is the defense of a horned animal.

After making this exhortation to the hearers, so that the hearers themselves might be more strongly moved to confess God, the assembly of the martyrs speaking here promises that it will confess God and exalt him, as follows:

“I said to the hearers, ‘Establish,’” and so forth. “Whatever they themselves may do, you are my God,” that is, my creator; therefore I shall confess your praise with my mouth. “You are my God,” I say, and therefore I shall exalt you through my action and devotion.

This means: “I shall confess you and exalt you; therefore, because you are my God, I shall confess you.” I say, “For you heard me and became my salvation,” as explained above, repeated here in order to provide an example of confession.

“I shall confess,” I say; therefore, following my example, O hearers, “confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.” This is repeated as explained above, so that just as the psalm began with praise, it might also end with praise.

## Psalm 118

Psalm One Hundred Eighteen. Although, according to blessed Ambrose, it is entitled “Alleluia,” among the Hebrews it nevertheless has no title. It was not necessary to place a title before it, since its purpose and subject are evident to those who consider carefully its beginnings and the number of its verses.

For among the Hebrews this entire psalm is arranged in sections of eight verses. At the beginning of the verses of each section, the individual verses are written according to the order of the Hebrew alphabet, so that all eight verses of the first section begin with the letter Aleph, the eight of the second with Beth, the eight of the third with Gimel, and so on in the remaining sections, with all eight verses of each section beginning in order with the individual letters of the Hebrew alphabet.

Since, however, the Latin language does not permit the eight verses of each section to begin according to the order of the letters of the Latin alphabet—for the eight verses of the first section cannot all begin with *a*, nor the eight verses of the second with *b*, and likewise for the rest, because Latin does not possess suitable words for this according to the interpretation of the Hebrew words placed at the beginnings of the verses of this psalm—among the Latins the names of the letters of the Hebrew alphabet are written in order before each section.

Thus before the first section is written *Aleph*, the name of the Hebrews’ first letter; before the second, *Beth*, the name of the second letter; and so the names of the remaining Hebrew letters are written in order before the remaining sections.

This is not done because these words are the titles of the sections, but so that they may serve as a sign to us that among the Hebrews the eight verses of each section begin with the letters mentioned above. In the number eight of the verses and in the inscription of the entire Hebrew alphabet, the purpose and subject of the whole psalm are indicated.

In this psalm the perfect faithful, whose voice this is, intend to instruct the lesser, teaching them how they may attain true blessedness. This is understood through the number eight because on the eighth day—namely, the day of judgment, which follows the seven days of this life—the saved will receive it.

Through the number eight, eight kinds of blessedness are also understood, which God gives to the faithful. The instruction concerning their attainment is contained in this psalm. Although there are eight of them, as the Lord shows in the Gospel when he says, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3), and so forth, they all nevertheless concern the same thing. All these are one blessedness.

Thus, to indicate that they all concern the same thing, each set of eight verses in the individual sections appears to have its beginning from the same letter. Since the purpose of this psalm is to instruct the lesser in attaining blessedness, the whole psalm is directed chiefly toward instructing them to obtain it through moral teaching. Moral teaching is the beginning and, as it were, the foundation of the good life. For moral conduct must come first; without it no one is saved.

From moral conduct one proceeds through the physical to the mystical understanding, so that one may understand the nature of each creature, what each signifies, and also in what manner and through what mystery the sacrifices of the old law and its bodily observances were established by the Lord.

From this kind of understanding the faithful ascend to the theoretical life, that is, to the contemplative life, so that, having set aside every concern for secular goods, they may contemplate only heavenly goods, desire to possess only these, and long for them with their whole affection. Finally, from the theoretical life they attain the possession of perfect blessedness after the dissolution of the flesh.

Although many simple people are saved through moral conduct alone, without physical and mystical understanding and without the theoretical life, no one is found to be wholly perfect without these two latter things. The principal purpose of this psalm, then, is that the perfect, whose voice this is, instruct the lesser through moral teaching to ascend to true blessedness.

And since the primary purpose of the whole psalm first concerns instruction in moral conduct and then blessedness, the arrangement of the Hebrew alphabet through the individual sections signifies this, and not inappropriately. For just as knowledge of the alphabet is the rudiment for children and the beginning of all literary learning, so moral instruction is, for the simple, a kind of foundation and beginning for reaching blessedness.

Its subject, moreover, is this: they treat in various ways of the matters pertaining to moral conduct and blessedness, as will become clear in the psalm itself. To discuss these matters is one thing; to intend, through that discussion, to instruct the hearers is another. For although some passages of this psalm may appear to pertain to the physical understanding and others to the theoretical understanding, its entire principal purpose and subject, as we have already said, concern ethics.

Since this common purpose is maintained throughout the psalm, each section also has in some way its own particular purpose. Alternatively, its subject may be discerned through the interpretations of the individual Hebrew letters that are written above it; this will be explained in order in each section.

First, then, we must discuss the first section, which has *Aleph* written at its beginning; *Aleph* is interpreted as “teaching.” Since this entire psalm concerns the teaching of conduct and blessedness, as was shown above, one may ask why this first section is rather inscribed with *Aleph*, which is interpreted as “teaching.”

The answer is as follows: This letter is inscribed on the section in order to indicate that this first section is a kind of *schema*, that is, a brief account, in which is briefly contained the summary of what he will address in all the following sections. For in this section he briefly indicates that throughout the psalm he will treat of the teaching of conduct and blessedness—teaching which is called “teaching” by antonomasia—when he explains as follows:

“Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.” As though he were saying: “O faithful, many who are wise according to earthly standards offer false teachings for attaining blessedness. But whatever they may say, let this be clear and established for you: truly, those who are undefiled while in the way will be blessed. Those will attain true blessedness who, existing through faith in the way—that is, in Christ, who is the way to blessedness—are undefiled, that is, innocent and not stained by any blemish of grave sin.”

Since it is not enough to abstain from evil unless one also does what is right, he adds: “Undefiled,” I say, “who walk in the law of the Lord,” namely, those who, placed with their whole will in the law of the Lord’s commandments, walk in this law—that is, advance in this law with perseverance unto the end—after the likeness of one who walks in order to arrive somewhere and rest there.

It should be noted that, when he says “undefiled,” he does not add “in the way” as a distinction, but in order to teach that no one can truly be undefiled unless he is placed in the way.

Behold, in this verse he has dealt with moral instruction, through which one reaches blessedness. But because no one can attain perfect blessedness through moral conduct alone, he instructs them to examine the divine testimonies and to contemplate, when he adds:

“Blessed will be those who, existing undefiled in the way and walking in the law of the Lord, are not idle in seeking his testimonies, but scrutinize his testimonies,” that is, diligently inquire into them in order to understand mystically his commandments, which are obscure and given through parables and riddles. They are called “testimonies” because they testify justly to life for those who fulfill them, but to death for those who do not.

To scrutinize the testimonies pertains to the mystical and physical understanding. “Blessed,” I say, “are those who scrutinize his testimonies and ascend from scrutinizing the testimonies to seeking him by devoting themselves to contemplation,” and this “with the whole heart,” that is, with the whole affection of the heart. Namely, having set aside every concern for secular goods, they long for God alone through contemplation; they seek and desire him alone with the whole affection of their heart.

Or: “They seek him,” that is, his most secret mysteries, “with the whole heart,” namely, they seek the hidden secrets of his divinity with the whole affection of the heart.

Alternatively, this verse may be read so that the qualification indicates how one can come to be undefiled:

“Blessed,” I say, “are the undefiled. But in order that you may be undefiled, O hearers, scrutinize his testimonies, and only then seek him with the whole heart.”

For those will be blessed who, in order to be undefiled, scrutinize his testimonies—that is, diligently consider in their reason his witnesses, namely, the angels whom God has appointed to guard the faithful. On the day of judgment they will also be witnesses of all their deeds, both good and evil, except those that will be remitted through repentance.

This means: “Those will be blessed who, while being pressed by illicit suggestions, do not doubt that heavenly spirits will be witnesses of their deeds; for this reason they desist from evil works and strive to be undefiled.”

And here they seek him with the whole heart; this is explained as above in the first interpretation.

Because he had said that those who walk in the law of the Lord are blessed, someone who misunderstands might infer: “Therefore, if everyone who walks in the law of the Lord’s commandments is blessed, then even those who commit iniquity, if they walk for an hour in the Lord’s precepts, are blessed.” He removes this misunderstanding as follows: “Blessed,” I say, “are those who walk in the law of the Lord; but those who commit iniquity will not be blessed.” For those who commit criminal iniquity have not walked in his ways, that is, they have not been moved by his commandments, which are ways leading to blessedness. He does not say “those who have committed iniquity and repented,” but “those who persist in committing it to the end of their lives.” Quite appropriately, therefore, he says that those who commit iniquity have not walked in the ways of the Lord. For although they have acted well for a time, they have nevertheless not walked in his ways. They are said to walk in his ways only if they act well with perseverance to the end. Since he excludes from them walking in the ways of the Lord—which is the cause of blessedness—it follows that he also excludes blessedness from them.

He shows, moreover, that they have not walked in the law of the Lord when he adds: “Truly, those who commit iniquity have not walked in your ways, Lord, because they have not kept your commandments exceedingly,” and no one walks in your ways except one who keeps your commandments exceedingly. For you, whom one must obey, who command nothing except what is just, and who can justly condemn those who do not obey you, commanded that your commandments—which are ways leading to blessedness—be kept exceedingly, that is, greatly, namely with diligence and perseverance, not with negligence. “For cursed is the one who does the work of the Lord negligently” (Jer. 48:10).

Since the assembly of the faithful that speaks here recognizes that, for human frailty, it is difficult to keep the Lord’s commandments exceedingly, it prays and desires that the Lord direct its ways toward keeping them. Through this it also teaches its hearers to pray and desire the same, since this too will be difficult for them. Thus it says:

“You, I say, commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly.” 471 “And because, Lord, although this is difficult, my frailty cannot suffice for it by itself, I desire and pray, Lord:

‘Would that my ways’—that is, my dispositions, through which the mind proceeds as though along ways when it thinks—‘which are not straight ways, but are inclined and twisted toward worldly things, might be directed by you,’ that is, might be made straight and turned toward the contemplation of heavenly things. Or, ‘might be directed’ means ‘might be advanced from good to better,’ and this for the keeping of your justifications; that is, may they be directed for this purpose, so that I may keep, that is, complete with perseverance, your commandments, which are called justifications because they are the causes for which those who complete them are justified.”

The following verse indicates that this is to be understood as referring to the keeping of all the commandments. “May my ways,” I say, “be directed toward keeping all your justifications.” If this happens, then I shall not be put to shame, that is, I shall not be embarrassed but shall rejoice, when I perceive that I am in all your commandments—that is, in the completion of all your commandments. No shame or confusion will then remain in me when, by the insight of my reason, I perceive that I am in all your commandments.

For if I were in some but not in all, those in which I was not would be the reason for my shame. This is said by comparison with a man who examines himself in a mirror: if he sees that all his limbs are beautiful, he rejoices; but if some are deformed, he is ashamed and confused.

When I perceive that I am in all your commandments, I shall in no way attribute this to myself. Rather, by attributing it to you, I shall confess to you, that is, praise you entirely, in the direction of my heart—that is, in consideration of the directions of my heart—namely, on the ground that you make the dispositions of my heart straight. I shall also confess to you in that contemplation because, through the illumination of your grace, I have learned the judgments of your justice, that is, I shall diligently complete your commandments.

Let this alone be what I desire and pray for, Lord: that you do not abandon me utterly—that is, with complete abandonment. I mean: may your grace not abandon me entirely, so that I arrogantly attribute to myself the fact that I have been directed and do not attribute it to you. For the one who attributes his goodness to himself and glories in himself rather than in the Lord has been utterly abandoned by divine grace.

It should be noted that, when he says this, he teaches his hearers that no one will truly keep the Lord’s justifications unless he confesses them to him, attributing to him whatever good there is in himself. For if he glories in himself, he will be utterly abandoned by the Lord, and thus he will not keep his justifications. Through this he urges his hearers to confess God.

## BETH

“Beth” is interpreted as “confusion.” Through Beth, therefore, which is the beginning of the verses of the second section, the particular intention of this section is signified: namely, that the assembly of the faithful here intends to instruct those who, because of their wicked life, are subject to eternal confusion and thus are alienated from the path of true blessedness, so that they may correct their morals, avoid confusion through this correction, and approach blessedness.

It also instructs these same people by offering itself as an example, so that after they have attained moral correction, they may pray to God. For here it prays while presenting its merits, as appears in the section itself. At the beginning, however, it engages in deliberation, thereby teaching that correcting one’s morals is a great undertaking, and that it must not be done without the greatest deliberation.

“In what does a younger man correct his way?” etc. It is as though he were saying:

“Above I said that those who are blameless in the way and walk in the law of the Lord will be blessed. No one will attain that blessedness if, by living wickedly, he is subject to eternal confusion, unless he diligently strives to correct his morals. In what way, then, does a younger man correct his way”—that is, his disposition and activity by which he proceeds as though along a way—in order to attain blessedness and escape confusion?

It is as though he were saying:

“Whoever up to this point has been a younger man by living wickedly”—that is, with the most foolish and depraved morals, like young people who, because of the foolish character of their age, are foolish and rash—“if he wishes to attain moral correction and seeks instruction from me about what he should correct in the way of his morals, I shall tell him: ‘O Lord, he corrects the way of his morals by keeping your words,’ that is, by diligently completing your commandments. He then corrects the way of his morals well if, just as he devoted himself to evil deeds, so also he strives to cling to your commandments.”

Or, “younger man” means one who is still young in age. “In what does he correct his way?” “In keeping your words.” Nothing is changed here except “younger man.” The reason he invites a younger person to moral correction is that the one who begins correcting his way from youth is more perfect than one who begins in old age. Hence the Prophet says: “Blessed is the man who has borne the yoke of the Lord from his youth” (Lam. 3:27).

Or it may be read in this way: “The younger man” is one who until now has been old, that is, conformed to the old man Adam in the oldness of life, but who wishes to be a younger man, that is, conformed to the new man Christ in the newness of life. In what does he correct his way? “In keeping your words,” as explained above.

Because he had said that moral correction consists in keeping the Lord’s words, in order to draw his hearers more strongly by his example toward keeping those words, he shows that he himself has kept the Lord’s words. For this reason he prays not to be driven away from God’s commandments, as follows:

“I say that, O Lord, the younger man corrects his way by keeping your words, and I have already practiced this correction in myself. For, O Lord, with my whole heart”—that is, with the entire disposition of my heart—“I have sought you through the keeping of your commandments,” that is, I have sought to attain you alone, out of all other things.

When he says that he has sought God with his whole heart, he indicates that he has kept God’s commandments, because the completion of God’s commandments is the cause of seeking him. Since, therefore, I have sought you with my whole heart, I pray, Lord, that you not drive me away from your commandments, that is, by withdrawing the help of your grace.

I also pray that, through the illumination of your grace, you teach me and do not allow me to be driven away from keeping your commandments. This is to say:

“Because, insofar as I was able, I sought you by keeping your commandments, I pray that you make me keep your commandments more and more through the help of your grace.”

I also pray that, through the illumination of your grace, you teach me your justifications, that is, teach me your commandments more and more, which I already know in part. It is fitting that you should reveal your commandments to me more and more. For I have not foolishly scattered what you have already revealed to me among the unworthy, casting pearls before swine or giving what is holy to dogs (Matt. 7:6). Rather, I have hidden them—that is, carefully guarded them—and I have hidden from the unworthy your utterances, that is, your commandments existing in my heart, not foolishly proclaiming them with my mouth.

I hid them, I say, so that I would not sin against you by proclaiming those utterances to the unworthy on account of any flattery or greed, or through boasting or carelessness. For one sins against the unworthy in all these ways when proclaiming the Lord’s utterances.

I hid your utterances so that I would not sin against you. Yet I do not attribute to myself the fact that I was able to hide them; I attribute it to you. Therefore you are blessed, Lord, that is, exalted and glorified.

Since it is not enough to hide the Lord’s utterances from the unworthy unless those same utterances are also proclaimed to those who are fit to hear them—for it is a sin for the Lord’s servants to deny people the food owed to them—he shows that he was ready to proclaim the Lord’s commandments to those fit to receive them. Through his example he thus instructs his hearers to do the same. He says:

“I have not only hidden your utterances from the unworthy, Lord, but I have also proclaimed what is just to those who are fit to hear it: the judgments of your mouth, which are ready on my lips.” That is, I have proclaimed to the capable your commandments, which you judge ought to be completed and which are always ready on my lips, so that whenever it is appropriate for them to be proclaimed, they may be proclaimed.

He rightly says “the judgments of God’s mouth,” to show that he is ready to proclaim those judgments which God revealed by his mouth: either by his own mouth, while he lived on earth, or by the mouths of the prophets, the apostles, or any teachers whatsoever. This is called the mouth of God because the Holy Spirit spoke through it.

There are certain hidden and secret judgments of God which God has revealed to none of the faithful; therefore they themselves cannot proclaim them to others.

“I have proclaimed your commandments,” I say—and not unwillingly. Rather, in the way of your commandments, which are to be proclaimed to those who are fit, I have delighted, as a worldly man would delight in all worldly riches.

This is to say: Just as someone delights in possessing all worldly riches, so I have delighted in announcing to others your testimonies, that is, your commandments, which are the way to blessedness.

Or this verse may be joined to the preceding ones without changing the meaning. I said: “With my heart I have sought you by completing your commandments.” I completed them not unwillingly, but delighted in the way of your testimonies when they were completed, just as any worldly man would delight in acquiring all worldly riches.

“I have delighted,” I say, “in the practice of your commandments.” Therefore I shall not grow faint; rather, I shall continue to exercise myself in completing your commandments. And, in order to exercise myself fully, I shall consider your ways through the insight of my reason—that is, I shall take as my example the holy Fathers whom you have set before us as ways, that is, as models for carrying out your commandments.

“I shall exercise myself,” I say, “in your commandments, and not rashly or without forethought. Rather, I shall meditate on your justifications,” that is, on the practice of your justifications. I shall exercise myself in the Lord’s commandments with the greatest meditation and reason.

Otherwise the practice would be fruitless. Thus I shall meditate so that I do not forget your words—that is, your commandments—at any time in my life, but keep them in eternal memory. “For the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

## GHIMEL

“Ghimel” is interpreted as “retribution.” Through Ghimel, therefore, which is inscribed on the verses of the third section, it is indicated that the assembly of the faithful here prays concerning retribution while presenting its merits. It does this in order to instruct its hearers that, once they have attained moral correction, they should pray concerning this same retribution.

If certain things stated above are repeated here, this causes no difficulty, since they are said with another intention, namely the intention of retribution. The retribution for which he prays becomes clear in the section itself, when he says:

“Repay your servant,” etc. When he says “servant,” there is both merit and a display of humility, as though he were saying:

“Since, Lord, I have now corrected my morals, and, as was said in the preceding section, I have sought you with my whole heart, hidden and proclaimed your utterances, and delighted in the way of your testimonies, repay your servant for these things—that is, grant me a just recompense, to whom you ought to repay, since I am your servant, resisting you in nothing and humbly obeying you in all things.”

He specifies the retribution for which he prays when he adds: “Give me life,” namely, “make this my recompense: that you give me life.”

He does not pray to be given life because he is dead, but, since he has already been given life, he desires to be given life more intensely. He indicates by the effect what kind of vivification he seeks when he continues:

“And in this way give me life: so that, having been given life, I may keep your words.” Give me life inwardly, in virtues, more intensely, so that through this I may keep your commandments more diligently.

I pray not only that you give life to my soul so that I may keep your commandments; I also pray that you reveal my inner eyes, that is, the eyes of reason. It is as though he were saying:

“Since you have already opened and revealed the eyes of my reason by removing from them the dark veil of ignorance, I ask you to reveal these eyes of mine more and more through the illumination of grace, cutting away whatever ignorance remains.”

This is said by comparison with eyes that were previously covered and obscured by a veil of darkness but are revealed by a physician through the removal of that darkness and are made clear-sighted.

“Reveal my eyes,” I say, “and with my eyes revealed I shall contemplate wondrous things from your law,” both new and old—namely, the mystical and secret things contained in both your laws. Because of their obscurity, these things are wondrous to those who do not understand them. I shall contemplate them, that is, I shall understand and perceive them diligently. I could not do this unless I had revealed eyes.

I say, “Reveal,” and this is fitting, for I do not present myself as a citizen of this world. Rather, I am an inhabitant in this land: while living in this land, I consider myself an inhabitant and pilgrim, directing all my affection toward the heavenly Jerusalem, whose citizen I am.

Hence the Apostle says: “We do not have here a lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come” (Heb. 13:14).

And because I am an inhabitant, do not hide your commandments from me—that is, from my understanding—the secret and mystical ones; instead, make them manifest to me.

He had already stated this equivalently above when he said, “Reveal my eyes.” But he repeats it here because he had added a merit for obtaining what he asks, namely, “I am an inhabitant in the land.” He adds another merit for which he may obtain from the Lord the gift of vivification, as follows:

“Give me life, I pray, so that I may keep your words.” And this is indeed fitting, “because my soul has desired to desire your justifications,” that is, I have wished to complete your commandments with desire—and not merely for a time, but throughout the whole time of my life.

“Desire” is greater than “long for.” For properly speaking, we call desire an excessive will.

He also sets forth the necessity arising from danger, showing why it is necessary for him to pray for vivification:

“I pray that you give me life, and it is necessary for me to pray for this, lest, if I am not given life and do not keep your words, I be condemned, like the proud first parents and the others who now depart from your commandments and will justly be cursed by you.”

“For long ago you rebuked the proud,” namely, the first parents, Adam and Eve, because in their pride they acted against you and did not keep your words. You rebuked them through a just condemnation when you expelled them from paradise and made them mortal and subject to suffering.

But you did not rebuke only those proud ones. Those who persistently depart from your commandments are also cursed by you here through a just execration, and in the future they will be cursed through eternal condemnation. These are those who, withdrawing from the loftiness of your commandments, turn toward evil deeds, which are low.

Therefore, lest I be rebuked and cursed along with them, remove from me, through the sending of grace, reproach and contempt—that is, both the greater disgrace and the lesser. This means:

“Do not allow me to commit something so grave that I become so base and infamous that I am a reproach to other believers because of it. Nor, even if this is lesser, allow me to do something for which I would be despised: even if I were not a reproach, I would nevertheless be held in contempt. For it is greater to be a reproach than to be despised.”

And therefore remove from me reproach and contempt, because I have sought your testimonies, that is, from all other things I have chosen only your commandments and sought them with the whole affection of my heart.

He adds another danger explaining why it is necessary to pray to be given life in order to keep the Lord’s words:

“It is indeed necessary, Lord, for me to pray that I may be given life and thus keep your words, lest I fail in them. For wicked earthly princes sat and spoke against me, and they still speak”—that is, by sitting they spoke against me: they spoke with deliberation and determination in such a way as to oppose me, namely, so that through their threats and flatteries they might call me away from keeping your commandments. These princes are terrifying because they possess the power to compel.”

When he says “they sat,” he indicates that they persisted in turning the saints away.

“Princes,” I say, “sat and spoke against me; but I, your servant, did not fail on their account. Rather, I exercised myself in completing your justifications.”

When he says that he exercised himself in God’s commandments, he presents his merit. When he says in the third person, “Your servant was exercising himself,” he displays humility; he would not do this if he said, “I was exercising myself.”

He also presents a merit for which he should be given life so as to keep the Lord’s words when he adds:

“Therefore give me life so that I may keep your words. For my meditation is your testimonies,” that is, I meditate on completing your commandments. “And my counsel is your justifications,” that is, I have a plan for how I may fulfill those commandments.

This is to say: I strive through both meditation and counsel to complete your commandments. Therefore I am worthy of vivification. To deliberate is indeed greater than simply meditating.

Or by “princes” he means the chief heretics who strive in every way to call the faithful away from their resolve of holiness.

These two final verses may also be joined to what precedes without changing the meaning, as follows:

“I say, ‘Remove from me reproach and contempt.’ And I pray for this because I fear incurring reproach and contempt by sinning. And behold why they are to be feared: for earthly princes—or heretics—not only begin to sit, but have already sat for a long time,” etc. “Therefore it is fitting that you remove from me reproach and contempt, for your testimonies also,” etc.

## DALETH

“Daleth” is interpreted as “fear.” Hence through Daleth, which is placed at the beginning of the verses of this section, it is understood that in this section the assembly of the faithful prays to be given life, as in the preceding section, but for another reason: namely, in view of the fear of a danger already escaped.

For it fears being put to death in soul, as it was already put to death when its soul clung to the pavement and when it dozed. It adds the reasons why it should obtain what it asks. Through this it also instructs by its example those who are in such danger and those who have already escaped it to pray.

It indicates the danger whose fear prompts this prayer at the beginning of the section, when it says:

“My soul clung to the pavement,” etc. It is as though he were saying:

“Above, Lord, I prayed that you would give me life as a retribution. I also pray for this same thing on another occasion, namely, ‘Give me life.’”

He explains what kind of vivification he seeks by adding:

“Give me life,” I say, “with a vivification according to your word.” This means: “Give me inward life in my soul, so that I may live according to what you command, namely, holily and justly.”

I await this vivification in view of the fear that I might again fall into the dangers from which I have already escaped, namely, lest my soul cling to the pavement, or lest it doze from weariness—which is the lesser danger.

“For my soul clung to the pavement,” that is, to the flesh, by consenting to its desires; or to earthly things, by embracing them in its affections.

The flesh is called the pavement of the soul by comparison. For just as the pavement is the lowest part and is made so that passage may be made across it, not so that one may cling to it, so the flesh is joined to the soul, although it is of a lower nature, so that the soul may pass from this pilgrimage to its heavenly homeland by doing good through the service of the flesh.

The soul clings to the flesh when it consents to it in any pleasure or vanity.

Or “pavement” means present goods, because they were created by God for the support of the body, not for excessive pleasure. Since they are lower than heavenly goods, they are to be trampled underfoot for God, like a pavement that lies below in a house and is trampled by passersby. It is made so that those who pass over it may be supported by it.

Because he had said that his soul had clung to the pavement, lest this attachment make him appear unworthy of vivification, he shows himself worthy of it when he adds:

“Give me life,” I say, “and it is truly fitting, although my soul has clung to the pavement by acting wickedly. For I, repenting of this attachment, declared my ways to you”—that is, my evil deeds, which had been my ways, not yours, along which I had proceeded—“confessing them and humbly praying that you would forgive them; and you heard me by forgiving them.”

Since, therefore, I declared my ways to you, and you conferred on me this benefit, namely, that you heard me, teach me your justifications more and more, that is, your commandments, through the completion of which I may be justified, and which you have already taught me in part.

I pray not only that you teach me your justifications, but also that you instruct me in the way of your justifications, that is, in the order of your commandments, namely, in what order I ought to act well—how I should ascend from virtue to virtue, lest I be zealous at the beginning but lax at the end.

Order is called a way by comparison, because one who proceeds in order goes rightly, just as one who walks along a way goes rightly. But if he abandons order, he is led astray, like a traveler who leaves the straight road.

“I say, ‘Instruct me in the way,’ and once instructed I shall exercise myself in your wonders,” that is, I shall exercise myself in your commandments through knowledge and action. They are called wonders because they make those who complete them wondrous in holiness.

Through this he merits obtaining what he asks, because he promises to exercise himself in God’s commandments. Through this he also instructs his hearers toward the same exercise.

“Lord, I prayed to be given life because I feared the attachment from which I have already escaped. I also pray: ‘Strengthen me in your words,’ and strengthen me more and more in your commandments, so that I may complete them.”

This is the same as he said above: “Give me life,” but it is repeated here because it has been added for another reason.

“Strengthen me,” I say, “and I pray for this because I fear dozing, as my soul has already dozed from weariness,” that is, because it became somewhat lukewarm and less fervent toward good work, since fasting, keeping vigil, and doing other good things were wearisome to it.

Dozing is less serious than clinging.

“I prayed that you would strengthen me. I also pray that by your grace you remove from me not only iniquity but also the way of iniquity,” that is, the habit of that iniquity, which remains after the iniquity itself, just as a well-worn path remains for a long time after the repeated passage of travelers.

“And by removing the way of iniquity, have mercy on me according to your law,” that is, according to your law and institution. Since you possess the law of healing, heal me mercifully as may be appropriate, by inflicting just tribulations and illnesses, after the manner of a physician who heals a sick person by cutting, burning, and imposing other discomforts.

“I pray: Remove from me the way of iniquity. I also pray: Do not put me to shame,” that is, by withdrawing your grace, do not allow me to be confounded by failing in the way of truth.

Nor would this be fitting, because I have chosen the way of truth, that is, from all other things I have chosen the completion of your commandments, which is the way to truth, that is, to true blessedness.
