I have chosen the way of your commandments in such a manner that I have not at any time forgotten your judgments, that is, your commandments, which you judge ought to be completed by the faithful.

Or it may be understood in this way: In order that I might choose the way of truth more and more, I have not forgotten your judgments. This means:

“I kept in mind how, in the future just judgment, you will bless those who choose this way, while you will condemn by a just judgment those who do not choose it.”

I chose not only the way of your commandments, which is the way of truth, in intention; I also clung to your testimonies, Lord, that is, in action I clung to your commandments.

I did not act only for a time; rather, I ran in the way of your commandments, that is, I carried out your commandments—which are the way to true blessedness—with spontaneous intention and perseverance.

This is signified by running. Yet I did not have from myself the fact that I ran; I had it from you. For I ran when this was the case: you enlarged my heart, that is, you enlarged my heart in charity, and this was the reason why I ran.

Hence Prosper says: “Narrow is the way that leads to life, and yet one does not run along it unless the heart has been enlarged.”

“‘When’” signifies either cause or time. Through this he gives his hearers an example of humility, so that they attribute nothing to themselves but everything to the Lord.

## HE

“He” is interpreted as “I live” or “he is.” Since, therefore, He is inscribed on the verses of the fifth section, it is shown that the intention here concerns the one who truly is and lives, namely Christ, who testifies of himself: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14). And elsewhere: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). The Apostle likewise says: “Death no longer rules over him. But the life that he lives, he lives to God” (Rom. 6:9–10).

Here the assembly of the faithful prays that the Lord the Father place before it the Lord Jesus Christ, who truly lives and is, as the law and governance of the way it has begun. That is, it asks him to grant it the ability to follow the Lord Jesus, who will be its guide and helper, through whom it may attain true being.

So that it may be able to walk this way perseveringly under his guidance and assistance, it also prays that understanding be granted to it for examining the old law, without keeping which it is impossible to attain true blessedness.

It further prays to be led in the path of the commandments of the new law, for its heart to be inclined toward his testimonies, for its eyes to be turned away from vanity, for the Lord’s word to be established in it, and for its reproach to be removed. It adds the reasons why it should obtain these things.

It does this in order to instruct its hearers, by its example, to strive toward this same true being, to seek Christ as guide and helper in attaining it, and to pray for the same things that it prays for.

“Establish a law for me, Lord,” etc. It is as though he were saying:

“I said that I chose the way of truth and ran along it. But in order that I may run this way without ceasing, O Lord Father, establish for me the way of your justifications, the law for traveling: namely, the Lord Christ, who is the way of your justifications, that is, the way by which one comes to your justifications, through whom the faithful come to the remission of sins.

“Establish for me, I say, the law for traveling; give him to me as governor, so that under him as guide, helper, and governor I may strive toward true being,” by comparison with a traveler who, trusting in a good guide, reaches the goal of the journey he has begun.

He uses “law” for governance because the law was given for the governance of the subject people.

“I pray: Establish the way as a law for me. I also desire and pray that I may always seek it,” that is, that from all other things I may always seek chiefly to imitate it with complete affection.

This means: “Give me the disposition always to seek it.”

But in order that I may always seek that law, namely Christ, give me understanding, that is, the power and capacity to understand. Then I shall examine your old law, namely what its mystical commandments signify, not rejecting it like the Manichaeans. “For the Lord Jesus did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17).

Examining it diligently, I shall keep it—not outwardly through carnal observances, but inwardly, mystically and morally, with my whole heart, that is, with the entire affection of my heart.

I pray not only that you give me understanding for examining your law; I also pray that, by your grace, you lead me—that is, direct me and make me persevere—in the path of your commandments.

These are the commandments of the new law, which are called “commandments” by antonomasia because of their dignity, and which are called a “path” because of their difficulty, since they are common to few, like a path along which few walk.

This means: “Make me directed and persevering in the difficult commandments of the new law.” These include loving one’s enemy, postponing everything for God, and other things of this kind.

It is fitting that you lead me into the path of your commandments because I have desired it; and whoever rightly desires something good is worthy of obtaining it.

“Lead me,” I say, “into the path.”

But when I have been led in this way, do not allow me to become proud because of it. Rather, “incline”—that is, humble before you—my heart, so that it may in no way grow arrogant.

I speak of my heart as intent upon your testimonies, that is, your promises, and not upon greed. Make my heart humble and persevering in your commandments, not with greed in view, so that I might intend to gain something earthly from them, as certain hypocrites do, but for the sake of obtaining your testimonies—that is, your promises—both in this life and in the future, which you testify in the Gospel, saying: “We shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

Behold the promise concerning the present. Concerning the promise of the future he says: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22; 24:13).

“I pray: Incline [my heart]. I also pray: Turn away my inner eyes so that they do not see vanity,” that is, turn away the dispositions of my heart so that they do not think vanity, namely, so that I do not act well for the sake of empty glory and human favor.

He uses “to see” for “to think,” because the heart sees in no other way than by thinking.

“I also pray: Give me life in your way,” that is, make me understand that it is a great vivification for someone to be in the way of your commandments.

This means: “In order that I may persist more firmly in your way, make me always see with the eyes of my mind that the one who persists in this way already possesses the face of vivification.”

I pray not only to be led into the path of your commandments; I also pray: “Establish your word in your servant,” that is, in me, because I am your servant. Make your commandment established and firm in me, so that it may never fall from my memory and so that I may never cease completing it.

“Establish your word,” I say, “in me, your servant,” and do this by grounding me in your pure fear.

This means: “Make me grounded in pure fear, and thus your word will be stable and firm in me.” For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10).

But in order that your word may be established in me through fear, remove from me through pardon my reproach, that is, take away from me every sin, which is the cause of reproach.

I say “reproach” because I suspected that it was in me. It is as though he were saying:

“I am not certain whether reproach is in me, but because I suspected that it was in me, I pray: Remove it.”

Through this he strongly urges those who are conscious of sin to pray, since he himself, although not conscious of sin, nevertheless prays in this way. Hence the Apostle says: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4:4).

“I say, ‘Remove it,’” etc. I pray for these things, although I am not conscious of sin, because I know that your judgments are gracious, that is, sweet and delightful. For you judge that those who confess should be pardoned; your judgments are not harsh like the judgments of human beings, who decree that punishment should be inflicted on those who confess their guilt.

I prayed that you would remove reproach. I also pray: “Give me life,” that is, make me alive in soul through the completion of the commandments. Do this according to your equity, that is, as your equity requires.

For behold, I have desired greatly to complete your commandments, and this is present and manifest to you. Therefore, because I have desired them, your equity requires that you give me life on this account, since you are an equitable judge.

## VAU

“Vau” is interpreted as “either he” or “he is.” Accordingly, Vau appropriately begins the verses of the sixth section, so that it may become clear that here the faithful assembly is praying for the coming of him who truly is the mercy of the Father and the Son, and the salvation of the faithful—namely, the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit is called the mercy of the Father and the Son because, through his illumination, the Father and the Son mercifully accomplish the salvation of the faithful.

Here the assembly of the faithful prays concerning this Holy Spirit that he may come especially into its mind and grant it eloquence of knowledge and speech, so that it may answer rationally those unbelievers who reproach it. It also prays that it may never fall away from the speech of God or from keeping the law. In addition, it sets forth the reasons why it ought to obtain what it asks. Through this, it teaches its hearers to pray for these same things.

That this is a prayer concerning the person of the Holy Spirit is indicated by the force of the interpretation of this letter. For since above he prayed to the Father concerning the Son, that the Son might be his law, and since Vau is written here—interpreted as “he”—the meaning is the same as if it were plainly said: “I prayed, Lord Father, that you might appoint for me as law the Son, who is the way of righteousness. I pray that the third in person, that glorious and magnificent one—namely, the Holy Spirit—may be sent especially to me.” For often, when “he” is placed in this absolute way, something great and notable is signified.

But if we examine another interpretation of this word, we shall understand the intention of this section. For since, as has been said, Vau is interpreted as “he is,” it wishes to indicate that he truly exists and is already approaching true being—the one into whom the Holy Spirit, concerning whose special coming the prayer is made here, comes. Hence it is plainly evident that he prays here for his coming with the intention of instructing his hearers to pray for his coming, so that they may be able to exist. The meaning is equivalent to saying plainly: “Since he truly is, in whom the Holy Spirit is, it is most useful for you to pray for his coming.”

### “And let your mercy come upon me,” etc.

The conjunction “and” refers to the other things that are placed in what follows, where it says, “and I shall answer,” etc.; “and do not take away,” etc.; “and I shall keep,” etc. The meaning is as follows: “I prayed, Lord Father, that you might appoint as law for me Christ, who is the way of righteousness, and give me understanding,” etc. “I also said that I desired your commandments, and this is evident to you. I pray also, Lord, since I desire your commandments, that your mercy may come upon me”—that is, the Holy Spirit—“upon me,” that is, into my higher part, namely, into my soul; “and let your salvation come upon me,” that is, let the Holy Spirit, who is the salvation of the faithful, come upon me. This is as if he said: “Let your salvation, namely the Holy Spirit, come upon me, and let this come from your mercy and your salvation.”

He specifies how he prays that the Spirit may come into him when he adds, “according to your word.” This is as if he said: “I pray that your salvation may come into me, and that it may come according to your word”—that is, according to this I pray that it may come into me, so that it may give me your speech, namely, the knowledge and eloquence that come from you. The meaning is equivalent to saying: “Give me the Holy Spirit, who may enlighten me with knowledge and eloquence.”

“And if your salvation comes into me and makes me eloquent, I shall answer a word”—that is, a rational speech—to the unbelievers and heretics who reproach me, namely, those who heap reproaches and insults upon me on account of the integrity of my faith and life. He appropriately calls it a “word,” that is, a rational speech. For the speech of heretics or of other unbelievers, since it is nothing but empty, windy chatter, ought not to be called words but empty wind.

He shows why he prays so earnestly that God’s eloquence be given to him when he adds: “For this reason I ask so earnestly, Lord, that your salvation may come into me and give me eloquence, because I have hoped in your words”—that is, because I have had, and still have, great hope and confidence in your words. If they are given to me, I shall be able to answer rationally those who reproach me.

Or it may be understood this way: “I shall answer,” I say, “a word to the heretics and unbelievers who reproach me.” I call them “those who reproach” because I have hoped in your words—that is, because I have certain hope in your promises, awaiting the eternal goods that you have promised. I pray that eloquence may be given to me through the coming of the Holy Spirit, so that I may answer those who reproach me with a word. And after I have this word with which to answer, I pray that you do not take away—that is, do not permit to be taken away from my mouth—the word of truth, that is, the true Word of confession of you.

### “[Col. 1272A] Do not take it away,” I say, “entirely”

That is, in no way: neither through any distress of tribulations nor through any deception of words. The meaning is: “I pray not only to have in my heart the word of confession of you, but I also pray that no cause may enable the wicked to take it from my mouth, so that I may always confess you,” that is, proclaim you.

For it is not enough to have this word in the heart unless it is also in the mouth. For the Lord says: “Whoever is ashamed of me before human beings, I also shall be ashamed of him before my Father” (Luke 9:26). And the Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

Someone might say: Why do you pray that the word not be taken from your mouth, since, unless it is taken away, you will suffer tribulations because of this word? To this he responds as follows: “For this reason I ask that the word not be taken away because, in your judgments, I have hoped beyond hope for remission”—that is, because of the tribulations that are called your judgments, since you judge that they must be endured for your sake, I have hoped for recompense.

He rightly says “beyond hope,” as if he were saying: “Since, from proclaiming your word, I have hoped for recompense on account of enduring those tribulations, I have hoped for a greater recompense, because I would not have suffered for it if I had simply proclaimed the word.” Or it may be understood this way: “Because in your judgments”—that is, in enduring tribulations—“I have hoped beyond hope,” that is, I have hoped for a greater recompense than the distress of the tribulations themselves. Therefore I pray that you do not take away the word.

Hence the Apostle says: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

He also prays that, in tribulations, he may not hate any enemy because of the tribulations, but may retain fully, amid those very tribulations, love of God and neighbor. He calls this love, by antonomasia, “the law,” because the whole law and the prophets depend upon it. For if he lacked this law, he would endure tribulations uselessly, according to the Apostle’s saying: “If I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3).

He says this as follows: “I pray that you do not take the true word from my mouth, and I also pray that in tribulations I may not fail in love, but may always keep your law inviolate.” He specifies which law when he adds: “The law,” I say, “that will endure for this age and for the age of ages”—that is, for the future age—namely, love, which never fails (1 Corinthians 13:8), neither in this age nor in the future.

### “And I walked,” etc.

After completing the prayer, he adds the reasons by which it is fitting that he should attain what he asks, when he says, “And I walked,” etc. This also refers to the preceding and following matters, as if he were saying: “I pray that in tribulations I may keep your law,” that is, love. “And it is fitting that I should have this from you. For when previously I was in tribulations and prayed to you to keep this law, I was already keeping, as far as I could, the law of love itself. I was walking in spaciousness”—that is, I was advancing and persevering in the breadth of love toward God and neighbor.

Therefore, because I kept it as far as I could, I deserved that you should make me keep it more fully. He further increases his merit when he adds: “And from this it happened that I walked in spaciousness, because I sought your commandments”—that is, I chose them above all other things.

Having stated the reason why the keeping of the law ought to be given to him by the Lord, he states the reason why he ought to be granted that the word of God not be taken entirely from his mouth: namely, because up to that time he had spoken this word without shame in the presence of kings.

He says this as follows: “I pray that you do not take the word from my mouth, and it is fitting that it not be taken away. For I was not only walking in spaciousness while placed in tribulations, but I was also speaking while dwelling in your testimonies.” This means: “By speaking about you, I bore witness that you are the true God.” Or, “I was speaking”—that is, I was proclaiming your testimonies, that is, your commandments—“while living well in those same testimonies, so that I might provide my hearers with an example of remaining in those testimonies, lest, while preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Corinthians 9:27).

“I was speaking,” I say, “not in secret, but in the presence of earthly, unbelieving kings who threatened me with death. And although I was clothed in rags and despicable, I was not ashamed”—that is, I did not blush to speak, even though there might have been cause for shame there.

Therefore you ought still not to take the true word from my mouth and should make me keep your law. But this is also because I not only sought your commandments by choice, and not only spoke in the presence of kings, but also meditated on fulfilling your commandments, since I loved them.

This means: “I meditated on how I might fulfill your commandments, and I did so not unwillingly but out of love, because I loved them greatly. And I not only meditated, but I also lifted up my hands”—that is, I advanced and directed my affections—“toward fulfilling your commandments in action, since I loved them.” The phrase “since I loved them” indicates that this was said not unwillingly but out of love, by comparison with someone who raises his hands in order to carry out some task.

Thus I lifted my hands to fulfill your commandments in action, and I was exercised in your righteousnesses”—that is, in your commandments, which I was fulfilling. This means: “With great exertion in action I was fulfilling your commandments in deed; therefore I have greater merit.”

## ZAIN

“Zain” is interpreted as “lead yourself” or “here.” The intention with which the assembly of the faithful prays in this seventh section is therefore indicated by the interpretation of this word.

For when it prays concerning the promise of blessedness, putting forward its merits, it does so with the intention of inviting its hearers to sigh and strive for that blessedness with every intention and good work. It is as if it said: “Whoever you are who acts well, direct yourself here, toward that to which I direct myself—namely, eternal blessedness. Whatever good you do, do it with the intention of attaining this blessedness, not for human approval.”

But if we observe the interpretation “lead yourself,” the meaning is equivalent to saying: “You, whoever you are, faithful person who acts well, direct yourself by your intention toward that to which I direct myself by praying and acting well—namely, toward eternal blessedness.”

### “Remember your word,” etc.

It is as if he were saying: “I said, Lord, that I was walking in spaciousness and speaking in your testimonies, that I was meditating on your commandments, and that I lifted my hands toward your commandments and was exercised in them.”

Therefore I pray, Lord: “Remember your word”—that is, your promise—“made to your servant, whoever he may be,” that is, the promise of eternal blessedness that you promised to give to every servant of yours. I pray that you fulfill it in me, since I am your servant.

He rightly says “remember,” not because God has forgotten, but because, since he does not presently reward his own, he appears to unbelievers to consign them to oblivion.

He shows why he prays so earnestly for the fulfillment of the word when he adds: “Remember,” I say, “your word, so that you may fulfill it in me,” in which you gave me hope—namely, through which you made me have certain hope of the promised blessedness. This hope, conceived from that word, has consoled me, cast down in humility—that is, it has given me the greatest consolation of salvation while I am in this humility, in this abasement of mortality and suffering that is mine, since I myself prepared it for myself by sinning in Adam.

Therefore I still pray: “Remember your word,” because your speech—that is, your promise—not only consoled me, but, to say something greater, it gave me life. Since I am already certain of the promise, I seem to myself already to be alive on account of the promise alone. What, then, will happen when I finally attain the promise? Therefore I pray: “Remember,” so that you may fulfill the word of promise.

And here are my merits, on account of which it is fitting that you should remember. The proud”—by antonomasia, the impious, who through pride cast off your yoke—“acted wickedly to the utmost,” that is, in every way: both against themselves and against their neighbor, by withdrawing from your law and striving in many ways to turn me and the other faithful away from that same law.

“But I nevertheless did not turn away from your law because of their exhortations and example.” This means: “Although the proud acted wickedly, desiring to turn me away, I nevertheless did not obey them by turning aside.”

Therefore still remember to fulfill your word, because I did not consign your just judgments to oblivion; rather, I remembered your judgments, Lord, from of old”—that is, judgments completed from the beginning of the age.

This means: “I kept in perpetual memory how, from the beginning of the age, you rewarded your saints even in this life according to your just judgments”—Noah and Abraham, and others of this kind. Therefore I was consoled, trusting that you will someday reward me by a just judgment. And therefore it is still fitting that you remember your word toward me.

For, in what is most perfect, I love my enemies—so much so that exhaustion has seized me on account of those enemies, who are sinners. This means: “Excessive grief has overwhelmed me on account of my sinful enemies; it is so great that I waste away and faint entirely in soul.” Hence it is called “exhaustion.”

### “On account of sinners,” I say, “who abandon your law”

This means: “I suffer exhaustion on their account because they abandon your law, not because they persecute me.”

Therefore still remember your word, because not only, when the proud acted wickedly, did I not turn away from your law, but your righteousnesses were also songs to me”—that is, your commandments were delightful to me, like something sung out of delight.

This means: “Your commandments, which are just, were delightful to me.” They were songs to me, I say, “in the place of my pilgrimage”—that is, in this life, in which I am a pilgrim far from my homeland, a pilgrimage that I myself prepared for myself by sinning in Adam.

Through this he increases the merit, as if he said: “Adam, when he was not in pilgrimage, did not have your commandments as pleasant and delightful; but for me, placed in pilgrimage, they are delightful.”

Therefore also remember your word, because I remembered your name by night, Lord”—that is, during the nighttime, which is a time of rest and in which illicit suggestions especially tend to arise. I remembered your name so that I might escape illicit suggestions, remembering that you are Lord and Creator and the avenger of the disobedient.

Or “by night” may mean during adversity, in which there can be exhaustion: I remembered your name, Lord. And by this I did not fail, but kept your law”—that is, your commandments—“so that I might not transgress them.

He shows, for the weight of his merit and as an example of humility, that he did not have this remembrance from himself when he says: “I remembered,” I say. “This remembrance did not come from me, but was made possible for me by you.” It was made possible because I sought your righteousnesses”—that is, I sought, or chose, your justifying commandments above all other things.

It should be noted that Zain, which is seventh in the order of the alphabet, is not inappropriately inscribed upon the section just explained, so that the number seven may indicate that in this section prayer is made for rest in eternal blessedness. For he says, “Remember,” which is understood through the number seven, since God is read to have rested on the seventh day, and in the old law rest was commanded to be observed on the seventh day, by which eternal rest was prefigured.

## HETH

“Heth” is interpreted as “fear.” It is therefore not inappropriate that it is inscribed upon the eighth section, whose verses are arranged in eights. In this section the assembly of the faithful prays that God may teach it his righteousnesses, putting forward several reasons by which it may attain this.

That this prayer is indicated by Heth, which is interpreted as “fear,” is because, although it has already risen to such dignity, as was shown in the preceding sections, it fears that it may somehow fall from this height. On account of this fear it prays so earnestly. “Blessed is the person who is always fearful” (Proverbs 28:14).

### “My portion, Lord,” etc.

Almost everything contained in this section consists of reasons set forth beforehand for the prayer placed at the end of the psalm, where it says: “Teach me your righteousnesses.” This can be adapted as follows:

“I prayed, Lord, ‘Remember the word of your promise,’ so that you may grant me the eternal blessedness you promised. In order that I may attain that promise, I pray, Lord, that you teach me more and more your righteousnesses”—that is, your commandments—in knowledge and in practice, which you have already taught me.

“And therefore teach me according to your commandments, because you, Lord, are my portion.” I chose you alone as my portion, rejecting all other things, and I fear losing such a great chosen possession through some occasion of sin.

“Therefore still teach me, because I not only chose you as my portion, but, in order to attain you whom I had chosen, I said in my heart”—that is, I resolved—“to keep your law,” that is, to fulfill your commandments.

“And not only this, but I also entreated with my whole heart”—that is, with the whole affection of my heart—“to attain your face in the future,” that is, your presence and the full knowledge of you, which is supreme blessedness.

Or it may be understood this way: “I entreated to attain your face, and I did so with my whole heart”—that is, so that in the future I may know you with my whole heart and see you with my whole heart directed toward you, not partly toward worldly things as now.

“I entreated,” I say, “saying: ‘O Lord, have mercy on me’”—that is, from your mercy give me your face—“according to your word,” that is, according to what you promised through the prophet, saying: “All shall know me, from the least to the greatest” (Jeremiah 31:34).

“Therefore still teach me, because I not only resolved to keep your law, but also considered my ways”—that is, I investigated with the utmost meditation what my ways were, namely, the ways useful to me by which I might reach you.

“And so, despising all worldly things, I finally turned my feet toward your testimonies”—that is, I turned my affections toward your commandments, which are ways for me to reach you. This is by comparison with someone who turns his feet from a crooked road onto a straight road.

By the fact that I considered my ways, I am prepared to resist courageously both interior and exterior enemies, and consequently I am not at all disturbed by those enemies. I am so prepared that I may keep your commandments by fulfilling them in action.

Someone might say: “You say that you are not disturbed. Was there any occasion for disturbance?” To this he responds:

“There certainly was. For the cords of sinners surrounded me”—that is, strong snares, which usually draw people into sins, enclosed me so as to drag me into sins. “Yet I did not forget your law, so that I might be dragged into sins.”

He uses “cords” for strong snares because strong snares are made from cords for trapping wild animals. He calls the things by which people are usually drawn into sins “the cords of sinners”: gold and silver, for example, draw one toward avarice, while a beautiful woman draws one toward lust.

### “Truly I did not forget your law”

“But in the middle of the night”—that is, in the middle of the nighttime, in which there is a place of rest and in which illicit suggestions commonly arise in great measure—“I rose to confess you,” that is, to praise you, “established upon the judgments of your righteousness,” namely, upon your commandments of righteousness, through which you justify those who obey you.

This means: “So that illicit suggestions might not draw me away from your commandments, I rose in the middle of the night to praise you, and I persisted in your commandments.”

Around midnight, because of rest and the flesh becoming insolent through the richness of the previous evening’s meal, suggestions commonly arise and destroy chastity and the other chief virtues. This was prefigured in Egypt under Moses, when at midnight the firstborn of the Egyptians were destroyed by the striking angel (Exodus 12:4–5).

But just as Moses at that time did not snore or act sluggishly, but delivered the people of Israel from the striking angel through the shedding of the lamb’s blood (Exodus 12:23–24), so, when suggestions assail at midnight, one must not grow numb but must keep watch and act courageously, and must fortify body and spirit through faith in the passion of Christ, who is the true Lamb.

Or it may be understood this way: “At midnight”—that is, in manifest adversity, in which I appeared to be oppressed—“I rose to confess you,” that is, I strove to praise you, “looking toward the judgment of your righteousness,” that is, considering those retributions to be your judgments, by enduring which you judge that your faithful are to be justified.

Therefore still teach me, because, although I am as I have said, I do not on that account place myself above your lesser members or arrogantly set myself outside their fellowship. Rather, I consider that I am a participant”—that is, a companion—“of all who fear you and keep your commandments.”

This means: “I judge myself to be a companion of the greater and lesser faithful.” He calls the lesser faithful “those who fear,” because, being at the beginning of faith, they still possess servile fear. “For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110:10).

He calls the greater faithful “those who keep the commandments.” Or “I am a participant of those who fear and keep,” that is, I share in their joy and sorrow, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15).

With this perspective I also pray, Lord, that you teach me your righteousnesses, because “the earth is full of your mercy.” This is said emphatically. The meaning is: “The benefits of your mercy are fully present in all earthly creatures, both living and inanimate. Therefore I pray that you mercifully teach me your righteousnesses.”

For it is by the mercy of the Lord that stones exist, trees and grasses put forth leaves and bloom, while animals live and feel.

## TETH

“Teth” is interpreted as “exclusion” or “good.” If we carefully attend to the interpretation “exclusion,” it seems to suggest that here the mass of the faithful, which seeks to be taught goodness, discipline, and knowledge by the Lord, has already excluded from itself every fear of suffering and is prepared to undergo the discipline of tribulations for the Lord. Concerning this discipline it prays by showing what benefit results from it.

But if we consider the interpretation “good,” it is indicated that here the assembly of the faithful seeks to be taught goodness, discipline, and knowledge by the Lord, with the consideration that the Lord is good by nature. And because he has already acted with it in goodness, it is also suggested that this same assembly of the faithful is here showing discipline to be good, since through it the law of the Lord’s mouth appears to be good.

The assembly of the faithful also sets forth merits by which it may obtain what it prays for. It does all this with the intention of inviting its hearers to goodness, discipline, and knowledge.

### “You have dealt well,” etc.

In the first verse there is a presentation of a benefit already bestowed, from confidence in which he prays in the second verse. The second verse should first be explained as follows:

“I prayed, Lord, ‘Teach me your righteousnesses,’ that is, your commandments, on the ground that you are my portion. And because I rose at midnight to confess you, and because of the other reasons set forth above, I also pray, Lord, that, according to this experience, you teach me goodness”—that is, the sweetness of living according to your word—“according to your word,” that is, your commandment.

“Grant that it may be sweet for me to abstain from evil and to act well, and teach me to undergo discipline”—that is, to suffer tribulations for you. These are called discipline because you permit them to be inflicted upon your faithful for this purpose: that, having been chastened, they may learn fully how they ought to obey you. This is like a disciple who is beaten so that he may learn completely.

For “discipline” is derived from *disco, discis*—“I learn, you learn”—and so forth, and means learning fully. The adversity of tribulations is discipline for the faithful when, as they endure them willingly, it serves as correction. But if they suffer unwillingly, it is neither discipline nor correction for them.

“And teach me, by its manifestation, the knowledge of your hidden things”—that is, give me knowledge so that I may know what must be done and what must not be done, and what is to be understood concerning you and what is not.

It is one thing to abstain from evil and act well, and another to know that one must abstain from evil and act well. Through these three words, the four principal virtues of the soul may be signified, concerning the attainment of which prayer is made here.

By “goodness,” temperance and justice are understood, since they concern good action. One scarcely abstains from evil without applying oneself to good action, which is the effect of justice. By “discipline,” fortitude is understood, because in the discipline of tribulations one must possess strength of perseverance. By “knowledge,” prudence is plainly signified.

“I say: Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge.” I pray for this with this consideration and confidence: “because you have already acted with your servant”—that is, you have acted with me because I am your servant—“in goodness of living according to your word.”

This means: “I am certain that you will give me what I ask because you have already bestowed this benefit upon me: you have made it sweet for me to live according to your commandment, abstaining from evil and acting well.”

Therefore I pray: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, because I believed your commandments”—that is, I believed that the eternal recompense and the other things promised on account of fulfilling your commandments are true.

It is as if he said: “It is fitting that you teach me these things because I did not regard as false what is promised to the faithful for fulfilling your commandments, but considered it true and certain.”

Or, “I believed your commandments”—that is, I devoted, entrusted, and subjected myself to your precepts, so that I might conduct myself according to their instruction, like a faithful servant who wholly entrusts and submits himself to his master’s laws, preferring all his master’s wishes to his own.

### The presentation of merit

Since he had prayed for discipline, someone might say: “It is useful to pray for the attainment of goodness and knowledge, but it seems strange that you pray for the discipline of tribulations, since it appears useless and exceedingly harsh.”

To this he responds by showing what benefit has resulted from this discipline:

“I prayed, Lord, that you give me discipline. Concerning this, it is still necessary to pray that it be given, since a benefit has already come to me from having received it. For before I was humbled”—that is, afflicted by this kind of discipline—“I went astray. And because I was humbled, I was corrected from that very offense, and I kept your word”—that is, your commandment.

This means: “The benefit that came to me from it was that, although I had previously gone astray by not keeping your word, afterward, corrected through this humiliation of tribulations, I kept your commandment by fulfilling it.”

Here he prays for what he prayed for above, but on another occasion, as follows:

“I prayed, Lord, ‘Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge,’ because you dealt in goodness with me, your servant, and because I believed your commandments. I still pray for this same thing on another ground: O Lord, teach me, according to the experience of the matter, your righteousnesses”—that is, goodness, discipline, and knowledge—which are called your righteousnesses because through them you justify your faithful.

“Teach me,” I say, and, leaving my merits aside, I pray for this because you are good by nature, and, in consideration of your goodness, teach me your righteousnesses.

He also adds merits when he says: “Teach me,” I say, “and here is why it is fitting that you teach me: the iniquity of the proud”—that is, of the impious who, through disobedience, act proudly against you—“has been multiplied against me in order to oppress me.”

This means: “It is not enough for them to act wickedly in themselves; they multiply their iniquity to such an extent that, by oppressing me with tribulations, they strive to make me turn away from the state of my holiness.”

“But although their iniquity was multiplied in this way, I did not cease from your commandments. Rather, with my whole heart”—that is, with the whole affection of my heart—“I shall search out your commandments.”

It is as if he said: “I am worthy that you teach me because, although the iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me, I have nevertheless not ceased searching out your commandments.”

Their iniquity was not multiplied merely for an hour, but with perseverance.

### “For their heart has coagulated like milk”

That is, it has been hardened in this iniquity, like milk—that is, in the manner of milk. Just as milk first becomes sour and then coagulates and hardens, so they, having first become sour toward me in iniquity, became, by persevering in that same iniquity, as though hard and immovable.

“Their heart has coagulated,” I say. But when they were thus coagulated against me, so that they might draw me away from meditation on your law, I nevertheless meditated continually on your law”—that is, your commandments.

Since he had spoken about the persecution of the wicked, which is the Lord’s discipline, lest he seem to have spoken of it as though complaining, he shows that this humiliation of persecution is good for him when he adds:

“I said, Lord, that the iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me and that their heart has coagulated like milk. I do not complain about this persecution of iniquity, because it is good”—that is, useful—“for me that you humbled me.” I consider it most useful that you willed me to be humbled and afflicted by the wicked persecution of the proud.

He explains the purpose for which this is useful when he adds: “You humbled me,” I say, “for this purpose: so that through this humiliation I might learn your commandments more and more,” like a disciple who is beaten so that, once chastised, he may learn better.

Therefore I also consider this humiliation good, because through it the law of your mouth”—that is, the law of your Son, namely the new law that your Son gave—“became good for me,” that is, it became dear and pleasant to me. Your Son is called your mouth because through him, incarnate, you revealed your will to the human race.

This means: “This humiliation accomplished in me that your new law, which seems unpleasant to some, should appear dear and pleasant to me, and this more than thousands of gold and silver”—that is, more than the abundant multitude of all worldly riches, which are signified by these two most precious things, gold and silver.

When he places silver after gold, he does not do so because silver is more precious than gold, but because the two together are more precious than either one alone.

## JOD

“Jod” is interpreted as “beginning.” From this it is gathered that here the assembly of the faithful prayed that what God created in it at the beginning, and what was destroyed in Adam, might be restored in it.

For since humanity was made rational in soul at the beginning, according to the image of God, and innocent and just according to the likeness of God, and since this was weakened in humanity through Adam, it prays to God with regard to that benefit which he created in it at the beginning, asking that he recreate the same thing in it—namely, that he give it rational understanding, which was weakened in it through Adam.

It also shows that those who fear him will rejoice because of this, so that by this means it may more readily obtain what it asks. It adds its merits as well, and prays for its enemies, so that it may obtain its request more fully.

It also prays concerning the glory of immortality and freedom from suffering, which it lost in Adam. It does this with the intention of drawing its hearers to pray for the same things.

It should be noted that although above it prayed for the attainment of knowledge, and here it prays for understanding—things that appear to be the same—nothing prevents this, since here it prays for another reason, namely, on account of that benefit which he bestowed upon it at the beginning of creation.

He demonstrates this at the beginning of the psalm when he says:

My hands made me and fashioned me. Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments.

As though he were saying: [Col. 1280D] Earlier, Lord, I prayed that you would teach me knowledge, considering that you had dealt kindly with me, your servant; that I had believed your commandments; and that you are good by nature. Now also, for another reason, I seek that same thing—namely, give me, in accordance with advancement, rational understanding, which was weakened through Adam, so that, possessing this understanding, I may learn your commandments more and more.

I pray for this because in the beginning, in Adam, your hands made me with regard to my soul, which you created perfectly capable of reason, and fashioned me from the clay of the earth with regard to my body, which would have been immortal and incapable of suffering had Adam not sinned. Something is said to be fashioned when it is formed from some shapeless material, as Adam’s body was formed from the clay of the earth. Whether, however, the soul or the angels were formed from some material, blessed Augustine asserts that this is uncertain.

When he says, “Your hands fashioned me,” this does not provide the occasion for the prayer that immediately follows, when he says, “Give me understanding,” but for what is set down later, where he says, “Let your mercies come to me.” But when he says, “Your hands made me,” with regard to the soul, this does provide the occasion for the present prayer.

When he says that he was made in his soul by the Lord’s hands, he does not say this because the Lord made anything with hands in the creation of the world. For he created all things solely by the command of his will. Rather, the expression is based on a likeness. Since among human beings works that are great and worthy are customarily done with both hands, and not with only one hand, a human being is said, by analogy with this, to have been made by God’s hands, so that it may be shown that he was a great and worthy work.

When he says that he was made by God’s hands, he does not say this boastfully, but to praise the Creator himself, who was able to make so great a work. The sense is as though he were saying: For this reason, Lord, I pray that understanding may be recreated in me: because I consider that in the beginning, in Adam, you created my soul so worthy that it was capable of rational understanding. Nor is it unjust for me to seek to have recreated in me what your mercy created in me at the beginning. I am not asking for something alien to my nature, but rather for that which I was created naturally fit to possess.

To make what he has prayed for more likely to be granted, he shows what effect will follow if he receives it, as follows: “Give me,” I say, “understanding.” If this happens, those who already fear you—that is, those who already possess fear of you through faith—will see, by the inward vision of my reason, that I have hoped exceedingly in your words, that is, in your commandments, and in those commandments have hoped for a reward in their pre-eminence, beyond what can be said or understood. On this account they will rejoice by doing good.

When he says “they will rejoice,” it has the same force as if he had said “they will do good,” since rejoicing is the effect of doing good. The sense is as though he were saying: Give me understanding to fulfill your commandments, because, if I possess understanding in fulfilling your commandments, your faithful ones who already fear you, when they consider through the insight of reason that I am intent upon your commandments, will, on account of this consideration, themselves possess understanding in your commandments and, following my example, will do good. That is: the vision of my understanding will work in them, so that they too, possessing understanding, may do good.

Nor is it surprising that the vision of understanding and the good work of the saints should produce understanding and good works in those who see them, since, as blessed Jerome affirms, there is an animal whose sight cures those who see it of jaundice.

He prays to obtain, through mercy, the same thing that he prayed for earlier on account of the beginning. He does this by humbly confessing that, through Adam and by God’s just judgment, he lost the sublimity of understanding, when he says:

“I have known, Lord,” and so forth.

The verse that follows this one is read in an inverted order, as follows: I prayed, Lord, that you would give me understanding, with this in view—namely, that your mercy might become effective for me, so that it might console me. The sense is: Console me through your mercy by giving me the sublimity of understanding that I lost through Adam; once it has been restored, it will be a great consolation to me.

“Let your mercy console me,” I say. I do not ask this on the basis of my merits, but “let it console me according to your word,” that is, according to your promise made to your servant Christ, who was obedient to you in all things (Phil. II, 8). The sense is: Mercifully console me, as you promised Christ, your Son, that through his obedience unto death you would bring consolation to your faithful.

[Col. 1282B] I pray for consolation from your mercy and from your promise because I have known, Lord, that your judgments by which you blinded Adam are justice emphatically—that is, they are exceedingly just. I have also known that, in your truth, that is, in your true and just judgment, you humbled me, that is, cast me down from the sublimity of understanding.

The sense is: I desire to obtain consolation of understanding from your mercy and promise because I have recognized that Adam and I lost it through your just judgment, and that I cannot recover it by my merits.

After praying for the acquisition of understanding, he also prays for the future glory of the body, when he says:

“Let your mercies come to me, and I shall live.”

This is joined to what he said earlier, “Your hands fashioned me,” as follows: I prayed, Lord, that, considering that your hands made me intellectual with regard to my soul, you would recreate understanding in me. I also pray—since at the beginning you bestowed this benefit upon me, and since your hands, with regard to my body, fashioned me so worthy that I would have been immortal and incapable of suffering had Adam not sinned—that your mercies may come to me in the future, that is, the benefits of your mercy which I lost through Adam: that I may be immortal and incapable of suffering, visible in the flesh, and may obtain the many other unspeakable benefits that those who are to be saved will possess with regard to the body.

“Let your mercies come to me,” I say, “and so I shall live,” never to die, though now I am mortal in the body.

To obtain these mercies, he puts forward his merit when he adds:

“For your law is my meditation.”

That is: because I meditate on fulfilling your law.

Having prayed for himself, he also prays for his enemies, that they may be put to shame and converted, and thereby he merits more fully what he prayed for earlier concerning himself. Hence it is written: “He who prays for others labors for himself.”

He therefore makes this prayer as follows: [488] I prayed, Lord, for myself, saying, “Let your mercies come to me.” I also pray for the proud who persecute me, namely, that your mercies may come to them as well. “Let the proud be put to shame”—that is, let them be ashamed of their iniquity—because they committed iniquity against me, striving through tribulations to cast me down from the state of my holiness, and did so unjustly, that is, without cause.

The sense is: Let those who persecuted me, not on account of any fault of mine but solely out of pride, in order to make me like themselves, be ashamed of having persecuted me in this way.

It should be noted that he says, “They committed iniquity unjustly.” This seems to suggest that some iniquity is committed justly. If, however, we consider the New Law, which commands us to love our enemies (Matt. V, 44), every iniquity—that is, every persecution—is committed unjustly. But if we turn to the Old Law, it permits “an eye for an eye” to be given justly (Exod. XXI, 24). If we turn to secular laws, in which it has been established that vengeance should be taken against enemies, that iniquity—that is, that persecution—which is undertaken for some reason is committed justly; what is done without cause is truly committed unjustly.

It is of this unjust iniquity that he says: “They unjustly committed iniquity against me,” and this is far worse than if it were done justly.

“They unjustly committed iniquity against me,” I say. “But I did not turn aside because of their unjust persecution; rather, I exercised myself more and more in your commandments, both in knowledge and in action.”

“Let the proud be put to shame,” I say, “and, having been put to shame, let them be converted from their iniquity of making me like themselves and of becoming fearful of you, though now they do not fear you. And let those who already know your testimonies,” that is, your commandments—namely, those who are already faithful, though not yet as perfect as I am—“be strengthened in me,” so that they may become perfect by exercising themselves more and more in the Lord’s commandments.

To be worthy of imitation by those who know your testimonies, I pray not only that I may not sin in deed or in speech, but I also pray for what is most perfect: let my heart become undefiled, so that it may not be stained by any thought of criminal wrongdoing. Let this take place “in your justifications,” that is, through your justifications, since by itself it cannot become undefiled; let it become undefiled through your justifying it.

He uses “justifications” in the plural with regard to the many cleansings of many illicit thoughts.

“Let my heart become undefiled,” I say, “so that I may not be put to shame,” that is, so that I may not blush in my conscience. For I would blush in my conscience if my heart were stained.

## CAPH

*Caph* is interpreted as “they have been bent down.” This eleventh section is appropriately inscribed with eight-verse stanzas so that it may be evident from this that the faithful, bent down and distressed under the excessive weight of tribulations, sighing for eternal life, already desire to be released and to be with Christ (Phil. I, 23). At the beginning of the psalm they put forward the reason why they ought already to attain eternal life.

Nevertheless, since they must still endure many tribulations for Christ before they are released from the flesh, they at least pray that he may help them amid the anxieties of those tribulations, lest they fail. They do this in order to instruct other faithful people who are placed in tribulation and sigh for eternal life: since they cannot so quickly be released and be with Christ, they should nevertheless not fail through weariness of tribulations, but await from God the help of perseverance.

[Col. 1284A] “My soul has failed, longing for your salvation,” and so forth.

In the first three verses of this section he puts forward his merits, by which he shows himself worthy to join the body of the faithful in eternal life. For this life he sighs in the fourth verse, when he says:

“How many are the days of your servant?”

This verse should be read first and then joined to what precedes, as follows:

I said, Lord, that the proud unjustly committed the iniquity of persecution against me. For them I prayed that they might be put to shame and converted. Yet, refusing to be converted, they continually bend and afflict me under the weight of tribulations.

Therefore, Lord, how many are the days of my affliction, while I am your servant? That is, for how many days will you permit me, your servant, to be afflicted so severely? When will you execute judgment upon my persecutors, namely, when will you reward me justly with eternal life after releasing me from the flesh, in return for their unjust persecutions?

What he sets down almost as a question, out of the excessive ardor of his desire, is equivalent to stating the prayer as follows: Since my persecutors do not wish to be put to shame and converted, but persecute me severely and continually, I pray that you shorten the days of my affliction and justly reward me with eternal life.

It is fitting that you do this for me. For my soul has failed with respect to every desire for temporal things, stretching with all its affection toward your salvation, that is, toward obtaining your Savior, the Lord Jesus.

The sense is: Having set aside every love and desire for worldly things, I desire only to obtain the Lord Jesus; I burn to enjoy his presence in heaven after the dissolution of the flesh. Therefore it is fitting that you shorten the days of your servant.

“My soul has failed,” I say, “stretching toward your salvation.” By stretching toward the Word, that is, toward your salvation, toward your Son, the Lord Christ, I have hoped exceedingly in him; I have hoped to obtain blessedness in him beyond what can be said or understood. Therefore it is fitting that you shorten my days and reward me.

Or: “In your word I have hoped exceedingly,” that is, I have hoped more and more for a reward: when I hoped the day before yesterday, I hoped more yesterday, and today I hope still more.

Nor has my soul alone failed with respect to the desire for temporal things by stretching toward your salvation; my inner eyes as well—namely, the eyes of reason—have failed with respect to every other form of understanding, looking only toward your word, that is, toward your Son, who is called your Word because through him you have spoken all your secrets.

The sense is: I have restrained my reason from every worldly understanding and turned all the vision of my reason toward understanding you. Therefore it is fitting that you shorten my days and reward me.

It should be noted that what he said earlier, that the soul had failed with respect to desire, is very different from what he says here, that the eyes of reason had failed with respect to understanding. Desire is one thing, and understanding another.

“My eyes have failed,” I say, “saying”—that is, compelling me to say, since they rationally force me for this purpose—so that, out of excessive longing, I say to you: O God, when will you console me by dissolving my flesh, thus freeing me from tribulations and rewarding me with eternal life?

What he sets down with suspended syntax, out of the ardor of his desire, has the same force as if he were praying as follows: Because I understand in part how great Christ is, and sighing to reach him in some measure, I pray, Lord, quickly to console me, desolate in tribulations, by releasing me from the flesh and drawing me into his presence.

For this reason also, Lord, shorten my days and execute judgment upon my persecutors, because I have become like a wineskin placed in frost—not like a wineskin placed in heat, which splits apart through excessive dryness and is consequently useless for holding wine, but like a wineskin placed in frost, that is, in cold water, where it is cooled so that it does not dry out and split from the heat. Since it is moistened by the frost itself, it is suitable for receiving wine or any other liquid.

The sense is: Just as a wineskin placed in frost, removed from the heat and cooled, is useful for receiving new wine within itself, so I, cooled by fasts, vigils, and prayers and thus protected from the heat of vices lest I be corrupted by it, am fit to receive and observe the commandment of the New Law.

By “frost” we do not mean that water which, hardened by excessive cold, has become ice, but an extremely cold dew in spring or autumn which has frozen slightly. [490] Therefore you ought still to execute judgment upon my persecutors, because I have not forgotten your justifications.

The sense is as though he were saying: I have kept your just commandments in mind so that I may fulfill them in deed.

The whole of this has the same force as if he were saying: I am not merely fit to receive your commandments; insofar as I can, I also fulfill them in deed.

By saying that he has been cooled from the heat of vices like a wineskin, he indicates that he possesses temperance. By saying that he has not forgotten the Lord’s justifications, he shows that he possesses diligence in doing good.

Having displayed his merits, he shows the necessity of prayer when he adds:

Therefore, Lord, sighing for eternal life, I say, “How many are the days,” and so forth, because it is useful for me to pray that these days be shortened, since I am placed in great danger.

For the wicked, in order to draw me away from your law, told me tales, that is, empty and useless words about the pursuit of worldly happiness. Since these things are false and fruitless, they should be called nothing other than tales.

“They told me,” I say, “fabulous words,” namely, so that I would believe them to be true and sacred. But I did not regard those tales as being what your law is, that is, as being like your commandments. For all your commandments are truth emphatically—that is, they are exceedingly true.

The sense is: I did not regard their tales as I regarded your commandments. I regarded your commandments as supremely true, but their tales as supremely false.

Since, therefore, by their tales they could not make me part of themselves, those wicked men persecuted me with bodily tribulations, so that at least by force they might compel me to fail.

Therefore I pray and entreat you, Lord, that, since for the present it cannot be the case that I am released and be with Christ, for which I sigh greatly, you may at least help me with the aid of perseverance, so that I may not fail amid persecutions.

It is necessary and fitting that I should pray to be helped, and that you should help me, because “they have almost finished me,” and so forth—that is, they have nearly completed in me what they began by casting me down from the sublimity of my holiness onto the earth, that is, into earthly things, namely, into vices.

The sense is: It is necessary for me to pray for your help because such persecution is inflicted upon me by the wicked that they have nearly accomplished in me what they intended: to make me like themselves in vices.

But because he had said “they have nearly finished me,” lest he appear to have consented to them in any respect, he removes this implication as follows:

“They persecuted me,” I say, “and thus nearly finished what they began. But I did not abandon your commandments by consenting to them in any way. Therefore I am worthy of help.”

When he says, “They have nearly finished me,” he shows the necessity of prayer. When he says, “But I,” and so forth, he puts forward his merit for obtaining what he requests.

Since, therefore, the persecution is so great and I have not abandoned your commandments, “give me life” more and more in the virtues. Do this according to your mercy, that is, according to the regard of your mercy; and once given life, I will steadfastly keep the testimonies of your mouth, that is, the commandments which your mouth—namely, Christ your Son—ordained to be kept.

## LAMECH

*Lamech* is interpreted as “heart” or “servant.” This section is inscribed with that name so that it may be clear from it that the faithful who live here below are most faithful servants of God for the instruction of the less advanced, and truly possess a rational heart, since they affirm that they will never forget God’s justifications. They give several reasons why they will not forget them, and pray to be saved by the Lord [Col. 1286C] so that they may not fail with respect to these justifications.

It is fittingly said that the faithful are servants of the Lord and possess a heart when they promise that they will persevere so firmly and truly in the Lord’s commandments. Those who despise God’s commandments are neither servants of the Lord nor thought to possess a heart; rather, they may be called senseless and insane.

[491] “Lord, your word remains forever in heaven.”

In the first four verses of this section he sets out the reasons for what he promises in the fifth verse. That verse should be read first and joined to what precedes as follows:

Earlier I said, Lord, that I had not abandoned your commandments. For the future I also promise that forever—that is, at no time—I will forget your justifications, that is, your commandments. Or: I will not forget your justifications, stretching through them toward eternity, that is, toward everlasting life.

I will not forget them because, Lord, your word, that is, your commandment, remains in heaven forever—that is, it always remains without end among the rational heavenly creatures.

The sense is: When I consider that the heavenly spirits observe your commandment without end, this gives me occasion also never to forget your commandments but always to observe them.

I will not forget them also because I consider that your truth, that is, your supremely true commandment, which is called “truth” emphatically, has remained among the generation of the faithful of the Old Testament, from righteous Abel until the time of Christ. [Col. 1287A] And this same truth of yours remains among the generation of the faithful of the New Testament, from the time of Christ until the end of the world.

One might ask: Since the author of falsehood, the devil, was cast down from heaven and descended upon them, raging with all his strength to make them liars, and since at first they were extremely unstable, how did they come to be so firm that divine truth remains in them?

To show this, he answers as follows: Your truth remains “from generation to generation” because you founded—that is, made firm—generation after generation, which was your earth.

The sense is: When they were previously unstable like the sea and easily yielded to every impulse of suggestion, you made them founded, firm, and immovable like the earth, which, on account of its heaviness, is an immovable element.

Or: You founded it so that it would be your fruitful earth.

Or again: You founded generation after generation, which was previously earth—that is, when it was still earthly, desiring earthly goods; you founded it in the virtues and thus made it spiritual, desiring spiritual gifts.

“You founded the earth,” I say, and, because you founded it, your truth remains in them. Therefore, because I consider that generation after generation does not forget your supremely true commandment, I too will not forget it.

“You founded the earth,” I say. This earth, because you founded it, became day, bright in virtues and understanding like the day. This day perseveres in its brightness so that it never falls away from it, and this happens by your ordinance, that is, through the ordering of your disposition.

Therefore, so that I too may be day and persevere in brightness, I will not forget your just and supremely true commandments.

I say, Lord, that your commandment is in heaven and from generation to generation. Since your word, that is, your commandment, possesses eternal remembrance in all these, all these serve you by fulfilling your commandment. And because all these serve you, I too will not forget your just commandments forever, so that I may serve you; rather, I will always fulfill them.

Or this may be understood as an argument from the whole: It is not surprising that the day perseveres by your ordinance, since you are so powerful that all things—that is, all creatures—serve you by fulfilling your commandments.

[Col. 1287D] I will also not forget your justifications, that is, your commandments, because, if it were not for the fact that your law is my meditation—that is, if it were not for the fact that I have meditated upon your commandments, which I still meditate upon—then, when the wicked persecuted me, as was shown in the preceding section, perhaps through my folly and lack of foresight I would have perished in the death of the soul, in my humiliation, that is, in the downfall caused by my persecution.

The sense is: I will not forget your justifications lest I perish in persecution by failing, just as I would already have perished if I had not kept them in continual meditation.

And therefore I will not forget your justifications forever, but will fulfill them insofar as I can, because you have already given me life while I exist in them—that is, because the fact that I persevere in them is already a great justification for me.

Since by himself he cannot be sufficient to persevere in these justifications, he prays God to preserve him, so that he may not fail with respect to them, as follows:

“I will not forget your justifications,” I say. So that I may not abandon these justifications because of some persecution and thereby perish, I pray, Lord, save me by giving me perseverance. And this is fitting. For I who seek this am yours and subject only to you, not to vices. I cannot serve two masters.

It is evident that I am yours because I have sought your justifications alone—that is, from among all other things I have sought, chosen, and investigated your just commandments.

It is necessary for me to pray that you save me, lest I perish by failing. For sinners have waited for me—that is, the wicked have long lain in ambush for me—“sinners” by antonomasia, so that they might destroy me in soul by making me fail with respect to your justifications through continual persecutions.

“Save me,” I say, so that I may persevere in your commandments. I ask this because I have understood your testimonies, that is, your commandments.

The sense is: I pray so earnestly to obtain this salvation, so that I may persevere in your commandments, because I have understood how worthy they are by their nature.

I also pray that you save me, making me persevere in your commandments, because I have seen the end of all perfection. That is, by my reason I have seen what end the person who has been perfected in all your commandments will reach.

The sense is: I desire to be perfected in your commandments with respect to perseverance because I have understood that the one who has been perfected in all your commandments will thereby reach the end—that is, eternal blessedness, which is called “the end” because the faithful will desire nothing beyond it, just as a traveler does not continue farther after reaching the destination that is the goal of his journey.

Therefore I also pray to be saved by persevering in your commandments, because “your every commandment is exceedingly broad.” It does not seem narrow, arduous, and difficult to carry out, like a narrow road that is more difficult to travel; rather, it seems broad, pleasant, delightful, and easy to carry out, like a broad and level road that is easier to travel.

Hence Prosper:

> Yet these paths, which the world’s vanities dread,  
> Are plains of a kind to noble souls.

[Col. 1288D]

## MEM

*Mem* is interpreted as “the inward parts,” or “from them.” Accordingly, through *Mem*, with which this entire section is inscribed, the law of God is signified: the faithful who live here below love the law of God from their inmost parts, with the inward affection signified by “the inward parts,” since these are interior and love is held in them.

Hence also we speak of “the bowels of mercy” (Luke I, 78), and we are commanded to love God with all our inward parts.

Here the faithful show that they love the Old Law exceedingly and meditate upon it all day. They also show that, through the illumination of the New Testament, they possess a sublime understanding of that Old Law above all Jews. Through this they instruct their hearers that the Old Law should not be rejected, as the Manichaeans wish, nor the New Law despised, as the Jews assert.

“How I have loved your law,” and so forth.

As though he were saying: Earlier I said, Lord, that your commandment—the commandment, namely, of the New Law—is exceedingly broad, pleasant, and delightful, and that I have loved it with certainty.

But I have not loved only the New Law, which is called “the commandment” by antonomasia. I have also loved, Lord, your Old Law—how greatly, that is, to what extent, I have loved it.

This is said with very great emphasis and admiration, and has the same force as if he were saying: I have loved your Old Law, Lord, exceedingly, beyond what I could say; I have not rejected it like the Manichaeans.

Or it may be read with aposiopesis, something being left understood: I have loved not only your New Commandment but also your Old Law. And how I have loved your law, Lord, you yourself are my witness, since you know all things. It is evident that I have loved and do love it because it is my meditation all day—that is, continually—as I seek to understand and fulfill that law.

Or again: I have loved it so greatly that my meditation upon this law is not in darkness, as is the meditation of the Jews, but “in the whole day,” that is, in complete and clear knowledge.

Since, therefore, I have loved the Old Law and it is my meditation all day, you have made me prudent in understanding that law, and this above my enemies, the Jews who are hostile to me because I understand the law spiritually.

The sense is: You have made me more prudent in that law than my Jewish enemies, and you have done this through your commandment of the New Law.

That is: Through the illumination of the New Law you have made me understand prudently the Old Law, which is the shadow of the New Law.

You have therefore made me prudent in the law because this law is my guidance forever, that is, toward the promise of eternity.

The sense is: I do not understand superficially that temporal things are promised to me through the fulfillment of this law, as the Jews do, who understand it only according to the letter. Rather, by understanding it spiritually, I understand that heavenly goods are mystically promised to me through it.

Because he had said without qualification, “You have made me prudent above my enemies,” he specifies which enemies he means when he adds:

“Above my enemies,” I say, “you have made me prudent.” I do not mean above the Gentiles, but “above all those who teach me I have understood,” that is, I have had greater understanding in this law than all the Jews. They are called those who teach me because, with a certain presumption, they claim to teach me, thinking that they understand me better.

Or they are called those who teach me because they teach me that law according to the letter, just as Jerome, the distinguished interpreter of the Hebrew law, was taught that law according to the letter by the Jews [Note: [Col. 1289D] This is established by Letter 4 to Rusticus, chapter 6.].

“I have understood above all those who teach me,” I say. This happened because “my meditation is” that this law contains “your testimonies”—that is, because I have meditated upon the fact that your testimonies are contained in this law: the testimony of the birth of your Son, of his passion and resurrection, of the salvation of the human race, and of your other deeds, which the Jews did not wish to contemplate and therefore did not understand as I did.

I say that I have understood above all those who teach me, and not only above all younger teachers, who are less experienced in the law, but, to state something greater, I have understood above the elders. That is, I have understood the law better than the Jewish elders, who are more learned and have grown old in the study of the law.

This happened because I have sought your commandments—the commandments, namely, of the New Law—both in understanding and in practice. For the Old Law could not be fully understood unless the New Law had first been understood.

Or: I have sought your commandments of the New Law, understood mystically in the Old Law.

It should be noted that, although he had said earlier, “You have made me prudent by your commandment,” he had not yet said that he had sought God’s commandments. Therefore it was not superfluous to add, “because I have sought your commandments.”

He shows through its effect how he loved the law, as follows:

“I have loved your law,” I say, and I loved it in such a way that, as it is established in that law, I restrained my feet from every evil way—that is, from every path of criminal iniquity by which one comes to death. By “my feet” he means my affections. When, through the weakness of the flesh, my affections were inclined toward sin, I restrained them from sins by the force of reason.

But since it is not sufficient to abstain from evil unless one does what is good, I have also loved and do love your law in such a way that I keep your words—that is, that I fulfill in deed the words of your Old Law, which command good works.

I have also kept the words, that is, the commandments, of the Old Law in such a way that I have not in any respect turned aside from your judgments—that is, from the commandments of the Old Law, which you judge ought to be fulfilled—by transgressing them through negligence.

But I had this observance of them not from my own powers, but from your grace. For you, who are almighty, established—that is, made firm and fixed for me—this Old Law of yours, so that I would not criminally transgress it in any respect.

“I have not turned aside,” I say, “from your judgments,” that is, from your commandments.

For “your words,” that is, your commandments, are “how sweet”—that is, exceedingly sweet and delightful—to my inward throats. The soul is said by analogy to have throats, since by the powers of reason it tastes God’s commandments and takes great delight in them.

Or: How sweet they are to my external throats, that is, to the throats of the body. It is sweet and pleasant for me to announce them to others by speaking with bodily lips.

“How sweet,” I say, “are your words to my external or inward throats—and this more than honey,” which is sweet to my external mouth.

The sense is: They are sweeter to my throats than honey is to my mouth. The sweetness of honey quickly passes away, whereas theirs endures.

Since, therefore, I have not turned aside from your commandments, and since they are so sweet to my throats, it follows that I have understood more and more—that is, that I have possessed increasingly advanced understanding—in those commandments.

And because they are sweet to me, and because through them I have come to understand more deeply, I have hated every way of iniquity—that is, every criminal iniquity, which is a way leading to death.

The sense is: Because your commandments were sweet to me, and through them understanding is given, I judged sins, from which ignorance is produced, to be hateful in contrast.

## NUN

*Nun* is interpreted as “the only one” or “their pasture.” It is appropriately placed at the beginning of the verses of this section because the body of the faithful, which earlier showed that it loved and observed the Old Law and sought the commandments of the New Law, does not attribute this to itself. Rather, it shows that it possessed these things through the Word of the Lord, namely, through Christ, the only natural Son of God, who is the spiritual pasture of those faithful people.

Here that same body of the faithful prays to him to give it life more and more, so that it may not fail under the humiliation of persecution. It also prays that he may make the voluntary good pleasure of its mouth effective, and it puts forward reasons why it may obtain what it requests.
