This is done in order to instruct its hearers that whatever good things they possess must be attributed not to themselves but to the Lord. They should also pray to him to give them life, so that they may not fail amid persecutions.

## “A lamp to my feet,” etc.

This is joined to what precedes as follows: “I said, Lord, that I loved your law, that I sought your commandments, that I restrained my feet from every evil way, and that I did not turn aside from your judgments. But I received all these things from you, not from myself. For your word [Col. 1291C] was a lamp to my inner feet,” that is, your Son was illumination for my affections. The Lord Jesus was my illumination: he illuminated my first affections.

This is to say: Those first affections of my free will, by which I desired to love and observe your law, were illuminated by your only Son through the help of your grace, so that they would not fail but grow from day to day. He also gave those affections to me. For by myself I would have been insufficient to possess them. And that same Word of yours, the Lord Jesus, was a light to my paths, that is, an illumination for my movements, which are understood through “paths,” since movement takes place along paths.

This is to say: He not only illuminated my first affections [Col. 1291D] through the help of his grace, but also gave illumination to what I pursued after beginning to love and observe the law.

Here, “lamp” is not understood as a vessel for light, as it usually is, but as a small light. This is clear from the Hebrew translation, where it has “candle” for my feet. The Lord Jesus is called a lamp, not because by his nature he is ever a great light, but because, in relation to those who are first approaching the faith and whom he illuminates less, he is called a lamp, whereas, insofar as he illuminates more those who have already advanced, he is called a great light, according to John’s statement: “He was the true light (John 1:9),” etc.; and elsewhere: “I am the light of the world (John 8:12).”

When it says “a lamp to my feet,” this is said by comparison with a person who is in darkness, for whom someone holds a light before his feet so that he may see where he ought to place them, lest he fall or stumble by walking badly. Since, therefore, the Word was a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths, “I swore and resolved”—that is, I resolved under oath; I firmly and immutably determined within myself—to keep the judgments of your justice, that is, your just judgments, namely, your commandments, which you judge ought to be fulfilled and which are just.

I could not have firmly made this determination unless your Word had illuminated me. The phrase “I swore and resolved” is taken from the likeness of someone who firmly determines something by establishing it under oath.

When I had sworn and resolved this, I did not thereby become proud in any way, but was humbled utterly—that is, I remained completely humble—neither attributing to myself the fact that I had sworn and resolved, nor despising anyone inferior to me in holiness on that account, nor regarding this as my merit.

As for the statement “I was humbled,” it adds: “Give me life according to your word,” that is, give me inward life with the vivification that takes place according to your word, namely, through your Son, the Lord Jesus. Give me life in the virtues, so that I may persevere in what I have sworn.

Or it may be understood thus: Because I swore and resolved to keep your just judgments, and kept them as I had sworn, “I was humbled utterly,” that is, I was afflicted in body by the torments inflicted by the wicked, who strive to withdraw me from keeping your commandments. And because I was humbled for your sake, I ask that in the future you give me life according to your word, that is, according to the vivification of your Word, after the likeness of the vivification of your Son.

This is to say: Just as you gave the Lord Jesus [Col. 1292C] your Son eternal life according to the flesh because he humbled himself to you, becoming obedient unto death (Phil. 2:8), so also give me life because I have been humbled for your sake.

And I ask not only to be given life, but further: “Make the voluntary offerings of my mouth pleasing to you, Lord,” that is, make the preaching about you that I voluntarily deliver with my mouth to others pleasing to you. More precisely, by your grace make me deliver it with discernment, so that it may please you; otherwise it would not please you.

And so that the voluntary offerings of my mouth may be pleasing to you, “teach me your judgments,” that is, by the illumination of your grace make me know how you judge that one ought to preach to the noble and how to the lowly, how to the foolish and how to the wise.

Or it may be understood thus: “Make the voluntary offering of my mouth pleasing.” And if persecutions come upon me because of these preachings, “teach me that they are your judgments,” that is, teach me that these persecutions are your judgments, since they occur by your judgment, so that through them I may be justified more fully.

It is fitting that you give me life, make the voluntary offerings of my mouth pleasing to you, and teach me your judgments, because “my soul is always in my hands,” that is, in my defenses, which are signified by hands, since defense against an enemy is made with the hands.

This is to say: I did not allow my soul to be overcome by my enemies through being incorporated into them; rather, by resisting them courageously through the virtues, I defended it, after the likeness of a vigorous soldier who does not surrender to his enemies the weapons he holds in his hands but defends those weapons from them. [Col. 1293A] In this way my soul is in my hands, because I have not forgotten your law.

This is to say: I observed your law and thus defended myself from them.

Someone might say: Were there any who tried to compel you to forget the law? He answers as follows: Certainly. “Sinners”—that is, heretics, unbelievers, and false Christians—“set a snare for me,” that is, deception through threats, flatteries, and false arguments, in order to draw me away from your commandments. Yet I did not err by withdrawing from your commandments.

What he says, “I did not err from your commandments,” seems to be the same as what he said above: “I have not forgotten your law.” But it is repeated because he had said: “Sinners set a snare for me.” Or, so that it may not be repetition, “commandments” refers to the new law, [Col. 1293B] and “law” to the old law, as in the preceding section; the faithful observe both, and sinners attempt to draw them away from both.

“I did not err,” I say, “from your commandments, but acquired your testimonies by inheritance,” that is, I acquired your commandments by hereditary right. This is to say: Through the help of your grace, by diligently investigating your commandments, I acquired them so firmly that I hold them as though by hereditary right, so that no one could easily take them from me, just as an inheritance cannot easily be taken away by law.

The reason I did not err from your commandments and acquired them as an inheritance is that, emphatically speaking, they are “the exultation of my heart.” This is to say: My heart greatly rejoices in your commandments, which I have acquired and kept. [Col. 1293C]

Although I did not err and acquired your commandments, I did not thereby become proud, but “inclined,” that is, humbled, my heart “to perform”—that is, to regard as yours—these acts of justification. This is to say: I humbled myself so that I might make what I have been justified in by persevering in your commandments your work and regard it as coming from you, not from the strength of my own powers.

Or it may be understood thus: “I inclined,” that is, humbled, my heart “to perform your acts of justification,” that is, to fulfill your commandments more and more. This is to say: I humbled myself so that by this merit you might assist me more powerfully in fulfilling your commands. For you do not assist the proud but the humble.

And I also inclined my heart “because of the reward that endures forever,” that is, in order to obtain the reward of eternal life.

Or it may be read: “I inclined my heart to perform them forever,” that is, always, “your acts of justification,” and this in order to obtain the eternal reward. The sense does not change.

## SAMECH

“Samech” is interpreted as “hear,” or “firmament.” It is certainly fitting that this word be inscribed at the beginning of every verse of the fifteenth section, so that it may serve as an exhortation to the reader: the things contained in this section, which on the surface appear contrary to the new law, are not to be heard superficially and in passing, but with attentive hearing of the mind and with the firmness of reason.

It is as though he were saying plainly: Whoever you are who read what I say—“I hated the wicked, and I loved your law,” etc.—hear attentively and with the greatest diligence these things that I set down here, which appear contrary to the new law unless they are properly understood; and in investigating them, maintain the firmament of reason. If they are heard attentively and examined diligently with sound reasoning, they will in no way be contrary to the new law.

In this section the faithful show that they hate the wicked, love God’s law, and have God as their helper and protector in this. It should be noted that they hate the wicked insofar as they are evil, not insofar as they are God’s creatures. They also exhort the wicked to cease trying to draw them away from God’s law, which is a cause of condemnation for the wicked themselves.

They pray that they may be received and helped by the Lord, and that their flesh may be pierced with the fear of God, adding reasons why one ought to pray. They say all this in order to instruct their hearers in all these same things. [Col. 1294B]

### “I hated the wicked,” etc.

This is joined to what precedes as follows: “I said that sinners set a snare of deception.” Therefore I hated the wicked—that is, those same sinners—not insofar as they are creatures, but insofar as they are evil. And I said that I did not err from your commandments. This was because I loved your law with every affection of my mind.

Or it may be understood thus: “I hated the wicked,” I say, and yet in hating them I loved your new law. It is as though he were saying: Although your new law commands that enemies be loved, I did not violate it by hating the wicked. I loved them according to their creation, but hated them according to their wickedness. Hence Prosper says: “Rightly, in the wicked we hate wickedness and love the creature.”

But to hate the wicked and love your law, you are my helper and protector. The order is inverted. It is as though he were saying: You are my protector, that is, my physician and healer. Formerly, when I was weak, I did not hate the wicked in this way and did not love your law, since I remained somewhat conformed to them. But you, who can do all things, became my protector by healing me of this weakness, so that I would not love them insofar as they are evil and would not neglect your law. You are also my helper in doing good and in keeping that law.

And because you are my helper and protector, as I advance toward your word—that is, toward fulfilling your commandment—through the completion of that word, I “hoped beyond hope” for a future reward, beyond what can be said or understood.

Or “I hoped beyond hope,” that is, I hoped more and more: yesterday I hoped greatly, and today I hope more.

Or it may be understood thus: Extending myself through the consideration of my mind toward your word, that is, toward your promise, I hoped beyond hope in that promise for a reward. This is to say: I expect to be rewarded according to what you have promised. “I hoped beyond hope” is explained here in the same way as in the preceding sense.

He then addresses the wicked themselves in an apostrophe: Since I hated you, O wicked, and still hate you, and loved God’s law and still love it, and since the Lord is my protector and helper, “depart from me, evildoers”—that is, you wicked people who act wickedly, both by sinning against yourselves and by attempting to draw me away. Withdraw from me, so that you may no longer attempt to draw me away; your effort is certainly futile and is an occasion of just condemnation for you.

You, I say, depart from your evil purpose, and I, without abandoning my own good purpose, will perseveringly investigate with action the commandments of my God—namely, the commandments of the one who is my God and my Creator, whose commandments ought to be investigated, not neglected. [Col. 1295A]

He also addresses God in prayer: So that I may be able to investigate your commandments intensely, “receive me, Lord,” that is, be my protector, physician, and healer, so that you may heal me of every weakness of mind by giving me the ability to act rightly.

“Receive me,” I say, and do this “according to your word,” that is, according to your promise—namely, as you promised that you would always protect your faithful, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age (Matthew 28:20).” And elsewhere: “I will not leave you orphans (John 14:18).”

“Receive me,” I say, and if I am received here, I shall live according to your word, and in the future I shall have eternal life. Thus, “do not put me to shame,” that is, do not allow me to be put to shame by being separated from my expectation, namely, from the eternal life that I await. For it would be the greatest shame for me if I ultimately failed to attain what I await with such great desire.

Or it may be understood thus: “Receive me, Lord,” that is, protect me by instructing me “according to your word,” that is, according to your commandment. This is to say: Protect me in such a way that you make me observe your commandment; and, with you receiving me, I shall live in that word, that is, I shall fulfill that word, and it will be life for me.

For I would not live unless you received me; and so, with you receiving me and with me living, “do not put me to shame,” that is, do not allow me to be put to shame by being separated from my expectation. For I expect to be received by you and thus to live through advancement and perseverance; and if I failed to obtain this and were put to shame, I would be ashamed of it inwardly and grieve.

Because by saying “receive me” he had indicated God’s grace alone, he also indicates free will when he adds: “I said: Help me.” I do not pray to be received in such a way that I become lazy and do nothing myself. Rather, “help me, Lord”: while I strive by myself through free will, help that free will by grace—that is, cooperate with me. With you helping me, I shall be saved [Col. 1295D] by persevering in your commandment; or I shall be saved in the future with eternal salvation.

And if you help what will be justified in me as I persist in your commandments, I shall not attribute it to myself: “I shall always meditate on these acts of your justification,” that is, I shall always meditate on this, so that I do not attribute these acts of justification to myself but regard them as yours.

I ask so earnestly to be received and helped by you in persevering in your righteousness because “you have rejected”—that is, will reject—those who depart from your righteousness, that is, from your just commandments.

This is to say: I ask to persevere in your just commandments so that you will not reject me, as you reject those who depart from your just commandments—rejecting them here by blinding them and in the future by justly punishing them.

And rightly you will reject them, because their thought is unjust. Some think that God does not care for human affairs; others think that God’s mercy forgives everything to everyone, even if they do not repent; still others think that it is good to depart from God’s commandments.

Therefore, lest anyone suppose that only those who are Jews, gentiles, or heretics are deserters from the Lord’s righteousness, while false Christians who sin criminally are not deserters, he shows that all who sin criminally are transgressors, as follows: “You will reject all who depart from your righteousness.”

And lest any Christian who sins criminally flatter himself into thinking that he should not regard himself as a transgressor, let it be certain to everyone that I have regarded—and regard—all the sinners of the earth as transgressors, that is, all who sin criminally. Since they are lowly in their vices and filthy, they are called “earth,” not “heaven.” I have regarded, and regard, them as transgressing your just commandments, that is, as violating them.

To depart from God’s commandments and to transgress them are the same thing. Therefore, because you reject all who depart from your righteousness, and so that I too may not be rejected, I did not depart from your righteousness but loved your testimonies, that is, your commandments, without rejecting them.

And so that I may love them more intensely, “pierce my flesh with your chaste fear,” that is, place your chaste fear in my flesh, by which you may pierce it—that is, join and subject it so closely to you that it cannot be torn away from you by any suggestions—after the likeness of someone fastened to a wall or to some piece of wood, who cannot move himself.

He does not say “pierce my flesh with your fear” because flesh can fear, since all fear is in the soul. Rather, it is as though he were saying: Since my soul has been fastened to you according to the power of reason, let it not dissent from you according to carnal sensuality. “Pierce my flesh with your fear,” that is, my carnal sensualities.

This is to say: Pierce my soul with your fear according to my carnal sensualities; that is, join and subject my soul to you in such a way that it does not oppose you according to any carnal sensuality—so that it does not offend you criminally through sight, hearing, or any other bodily sense.

I ask that my carnal sensualities be pierced by your fear because “I feared falling away from your judgments,” that is, because I feared, and still fear, that through my carnal sensualities I might fall away from your commandments, that is, from keeping your commandments.

## AIN

“Ain” is interpreted as “eye.” Through this inscription it is implied that the faithful, while acting here, possess the eye of right reason, as is clear at the beginning of the section, where the faithful say that they have carried out judgment and justice.

Later in this same section they pray that God preserve this eye for them by receiving them into goodness, lest, conformed to the Jews who bring accusations against them, they be blinded. They also add many reasons by which they may obtain what they pray for.

They say all this in order to invite their hearers to pray for possessing this same eye and, once they possess it, not to lose it.

### “I have carried out judgment and justice,” etc.

This is adapted to what precedes as follows: “I said, Lord, that I loved your testimonies”; and when I loved them, I carried out within myself the judgment of those testimonies, that is, I examined them with the eye of my reason and discerned how your commandments ought to be understood and observed.

After making this judgment, I carried out the justice of those same testimonies, that is, I rightly understood your commandments and fulfilled them in action. “Judgment” refers to the first deliberation itself concerning understanding and acting well; “justice” refers to the execution itself.

Because of this merit, therefore—because I have carried out judgment and justice—I pray, Lord: “Do not hand me over,” that is, do not allow me to be handed over in conformity with those who accuse me, namely, the Jews who oppose me unjustly and irrationally.

This is to say: The Jews accuse me by turning good into evil—specifically, by accusing me because I understand the old law spiritually and do not doubt that the Lord Jesus is true God. Therefore I pray, Lord, that because of this accusation I not be handed over to conformity with them, so that I lose the eye of my reason.

An accusation is properly an unjust opposition.

And so that I may not be handed over in conformity with those who accuse me, “receive your servant,” that is, protect me by the help of your mercy, since I am your servant. “Receive me,” I say, directing me toward goodness in advancement and perseverance, that is, from good work to better work.

I also pray for the proud Jews, who do not wish to submit humbly to you. In their pride they accuse me. May the proud no longer accuse me; for this accusation is an occasion of death.

This is to say: May they cease from this deadly accusation and join themselves to me.

Since he had prayed to be received into goodness, he presents the merit by which he may obtain what he asks and then repeats the same prayer in other words when he says: “Deal with your servant,” etc.

This is adapted as follows: “I have carried out judgment and justice.” I did these things so intensely that my inner eyes, that is, my intentions, “failed” from all worldly concerns, stretching toward your salvation, that is, toward your law, which is saving for those who fulfill it, and toward the word of your justice, that is, toward your just law.

“Salvation” and “the word of justice” designate the same thing, namely, the law; but through these expressions different qualities are indicated in that same law: that it is saving, and that it is just and therefore all the more worthy of being embraced.

It is as though he were saying: I have failed from every worldly business, and I have directed all my affections toward your saving and just law.

Since, therefore, my eyes have failed toward your salvation, I pray, Lord: “Deal with me, your servant, according to your mercy.”

When he says “deal with your servant,” he indicates free will. It is as though he were saying: Insofar as I am able, I act well in your law through free will. But because by myself I am insufficient, deal with me according to mercy—that is, according to the help of mercy—cooperating with me, your servant.

This is to say: Just as your mercy is abundant, so also cooperate abundantly with me.

And when you have dealt with me, “teach me that these acts of justification are yours.” This is to say: When, by cooperating with me in your law, you have justified me, [Col. 1298A] make me not attribute this to myself, but teach me through inward illumination that these acts of justification are yours and do not come from me.

I ask not only that you deal with your servant according to cooperation, but also that I may be more suitable as one with whom you cooperate: “Give me understanding more intensely, so that I may know”—that is, understand—“your testimonies,” that is, your commandments. Let me know how your commandments are to be understood and carried out.

It is fitting that you give me understanding because I am your servant, not the servant of any vice, obeying you in all things.

You should also give me understanding because, Lord, it is now an opportune time to do this, namely, to give me understanding. For the Jews who accuse me have “destroyed,” that is, demolished, insofar as they are concerned, your old spiritual law by rejecting its spiritual understanding and failing to observe it morally; and they wish to drag me into their error.

It is therefore necessary that I possess understanding so that I may escape their error.

You should also give me understanding because, in order to deserve understanding of your commandments, I loved your commandments [Col. 1298B] more than gold and topaz, that is, more than all worldly riches, which are signified by these two precious things: by gold, which is more costly than every other metal, and by topaz, which is an extremely precious stone. For the rarer topaz is, the more precious it is.

You should therefore give me understanding also because, in order to deserve understanding, I was directed long ago—that is, I was advanced—toward fulfilling all your commandments.

And in order that I might be able to obtain this understanding, I hated every way of iniquity, that is, every criminal action, which is a way to death. “For wisdom,” as Solomon asserts, “will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subjected to sins (Wisdom 1:4).”

## PHE

“Phe” is interpreted as “he erred.” It is therefore fittingly inscribed at the beginning of every verse of this section because the gathering of the faithful speaking here—by showing that God’s testimonies, namely, the testimonies of the old law, are wonderful; by showing that their soul has investigated them through the new law, which is the explanation of that old law; by praying that God give them understanding and performance of those testimonies; and by praying that God redeem them from the accusations of the Jews, lest they yield to them, for whose error they also say that they have wept greatly because they did not keep the law of the Lord—says all this in order to imply that the Jewish people have long been in error and still err.

Although these testimonies are obscure and wonderful, the Jewish people do not investigate them through receiving the new law. Rather, by understanding them only according to the letter, they accuse, insofar as they can, those who investigate them.

They say this also in order to draw their hearers away from that error and invite them to investigate these testimonies through the new law.

### “Wonderful are your testimonies,” etc.

This is joined to what precedes as follows: “I prayed, Lord, that I might be given understanding, so that I might know how to understand your testimonies,” namely, those of the old law.

I pray to obtain this understanding because, Lord, “your testimonies are wonderful,” that is, the institutions of the old law, considered according to the letter, appear astonishing. For it is indeed astonishing, if we look only at the letter, why you commanded certain sacrifices to be burned outside the camp, why you instituted circumcision for all the Jews, and why you prescribed many other things in the old law.

Therefore it is necessary that I pray to obtain understanding, so that I may understand these testimonies in this way.

And lest he appear sluggish in investigating these testimonies and thereby fail to deserve the acquisition of understanding, he adds: “Because your testimonies are wonderful, my soul has investigated them,” that is, my reason has diligently examined these testimonies.

I investigated these testimonies through the new law that I received, through faith and understanding [Col. 1299B]—the new law “which is the explanation of your words,” that is, which explains and discloses the obscure words of the old law.

“For the explanation of your words gives light and grants understanding to the simple.” This is to say: I investigated these testimonies through the new law so that through it I might be illuminated concerning them. For, existing as the explanation of your words, it illuminates those who are simple in spirit, that is, humble and not proud like the Jews.

It illuminates them in this way: It gives these simple people spiritual understanding, according to the Lord’s saying: “You have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to the simple (Luke 10:21).”

Since the old law is explained through the new law, this is gathered from the prophet’s words: “The Lord,” he says, “will accomplish and abbreviate the word in equity upon the earth (Isaiah 10:22; Romans 9:28).”

And so that I might investigate these testimonies more diligently through the new law, “I opened my mouth,” that is, I expanded the mouth of my heart through faith and did not constrict it through unbelief; and with my mouth open, I “drew in the spirit,” that is, drew the Holy Spirit to myself. I embraced the Holy Spirit, whom no one can obtain if he closes the mouth of his heart, as the Jews do.

He rightly says “I drew in.” The Holy Spirit, insofar as concerns his mercy, is ready to illuminate everyone. Whoever proceeds through faith, intimate love, and the other virtues, and does not close the entrance of his soul to him through vices, draws him to himself.

Since he says “I drew in the spirit,” this is spoken by comparison with someone overheated: if he comes into gentler and cooler air, he opens his mouth and draws that air toward himself in order to be refreshed by it. So every faithful person, if he is overheated by the fervor of unlawful suggestions, ought to draw the Holy Spirit toward himself by opening the mouth of his soul, as has been said.

When he says that he opened the mouth of his soul, this means nothing more than that he prepared his soul to receive the Holy Spirit; but it is said by comparison with someone overheated who, as has already been said, opens his mouth to draw in air.

I deserved to draw the Holy Spirit toward myself because I did not reject your commandments, that is, the commandments of the new law, which I desired to fulfill, as unbelieving Jews do. No one can draw the Holy Spirit toward himself unless he desires and embraces the commandments [Col. 1300A] of the new law.

“I opened my mouth,” I say, saying: “Look upon me,” that is, upon my inner part, namely, upon my soul, with the gaze of illumination, after the likeness of the sun, which illuminates whomever it looks upon.

And “have mercy on me,” that is, I say this so that you may look upon me in order to have mercy on me; look upon me out of mercy, because my merits are not sufficient to obtain this.

This is to say: Since you are the Sun of justice, illuminating all whom you wish with understanding, I ask that through the gaze of mercy you look mercifully upon me also, so that you may illuminate me with understanding.

“Look upon me,” I say, and do this “according to the judgment of those who love your name.” This is to say: Look upon me in the manner in which you judge that those who love your name ought to be looked upon.

It is as though he were saying: Since you judge and determine that those who love your name ought to be looked upon, I also ask you to look upon me, for I do not reject your name—which is “Lord”—as the stiff-necked and disobedient Jews do, but love it and embrace it with every affection and obedience.

I ask not only that you look upon me with respect to the illumination of understanding, but also: “Lord, direct my inner steps,” that is, my affections, “according to your word,” that is, make them direct toward right action, according to your commandment.

This is to say: I ask not only that I understand your testimonies, but also that I be directed to fulfill in action what I have understood.

And thus “let no iniquity rule over me,” that is, no iniquity considered in all its parts. This is to say: Let me be directed by you in such a way that no part of iniquity remains in me as my ruler.

There is one kind of iniquity: to fulfill none of God’s commandments in action. Another kind occurs when part of them is fulfilled and part is negligently omitted.

So that my steps may be directed and no iniquity may rule over me, “redeem me,” that is, free me by the price of the Lord Jesus’ death from the accusations of men, namely, of the Jews, who are simply “men,” earthly rather than spiritual.

This is to say: The Jews, who are earthly and unbelieving men, accuse me—that is, oppose me—by turning my good understanding and work into evil. Free me from their accusations, lest I fail because of them.

Once redeemed, I shall keep your commandments by fulfilling them in action, which I would not otherwise fulfill.

He then specifies how he prays to be looked upon, having said above: “Look upon me.” “I prayed: Look upon me,” and look upon me in this way: “Make your face shine upon your servant,” that is, place the illumination of your face upon the upper part of your servant—namely, upon me—which is the soul.

This is to say: Give me the illumination of your Son, so that he may illuminate me in my soul with understanding. He is called your face because through him, made visible, you are known by all, although you are invisible, just as the whole person is recognized through the face.

And “through the illumination of your face, teach me your acts of justification,” that is, teach me your just commandments, both in knowledge and in performance.

Or: “Teach me that the acts of justification are yours,” that is, teach me that the fact that someone is justified in your commandments comes from you, not from himself.

Or the verse may be joined as follows without changing the sense: “So that I may be redeemed from the accusations of men, make your face shine,” etc.

Or it may be joined thus: “I prayed: Look upon me; I also pray: Make your face shine,” etc.

And lest he seem to have said the preceding things out of contempt and disparagement of the Jews and out of exaltation of himself, he shows that he greatly grieved over their error, as follows:

What I said, Lord—that my soul investigated your testimonies and that I opened my mouth, which the Jews did not do, and that I prayed to be redeemed from the accusations of the Jews—I did not say in order to disparage them or exalt myself. I have so deeply sympathized with their error that my outer eyes “sent forth,” that is, released outward, “streams of water,” that is, a great abundance of tears.

This is to say: I wept greatly for them because they did not keep your law, refusing to understand it spiritually.

“Streams of water” is used for an abundance of tears because we customarily speak of streams of water when waters flow out abundantly from springs.

## SADE

“Sade” is interpreted as “justice” or “consolation.” It is therefore suitably the beginning of the verses of this section, in which the faithful show God to be just, since he has given them his justice, namely, the testimonies of the old law, which are the cause of their justification. They prayed to obtain this in the preceding section.

They also show that the new law has been given to them, which they observe exceedingly, to such an extent that they even love their enemies, for whose error they waste away in grief.

They further say that although they have been despised by their enemies and have suffered tribulations and distress, they have not for that reason forgotten either the new or the old law, because these laws are justice, truth, and equity, leading those who fulfill them to eternity.

When they judge that both laws have been given to them in understanding and in action, they show that they have obtained the greatest consolation in this. For someone conscious of good understanding and good action is greatly consoled in conscience.

They relate all this in order, by their example, to invite their hearers to seek this same consolation through the understanding and performance of both laws.

**You are just, O Lord, etc.** The second verse of this section is first read in this way and joined to the preceding verses: I prayed, “O Lord, look upon me, direct my steps, redeem me from the calumnies of men, and let your face shine upon your servant”; and behold, I obtained what I prayed for. For you commanded justice, your testimonies—that is, by the sole command of your will you gave me justice, namely your testimonies. That is, by your willing alone you gave me the precepts of your old law, both in understanding and in practice. These are emphatically called “justice,” because they are exceedingly just and justify human beings.

When he says “you commanded,” he indicates the greatness of God’s power: by the sole command of his will he gives understanding and practice of his precepts. “You commanded,” I say, your ancient testimonies. And you also commanded me your truth exceedingly—that is, your exceedingly great truth, namely the new law. It is emphatically called “exceeding truth” because it is very true, that is, just, commanding nothing except what is true and just. [Col. 1302A] Or it is called so because it is true in its promise of eternal blessedness. Or the passage may be read thus: You commanded me exceedingly—that is, by the sole command of your will you gave me greatly, both in understanding and in practice, your truth, that is, the new law. This means: You made me understand and fulfill your most truthful new law exceedingly well.

By the fact that you commanded me justice and truth, it is apparent that you are just, O Lord, by nature; and not only are you just by nature, but your judgment is also right—that is, whatever you judge and determine to give is right. “You commanded,” I say, your true law to me, to be understood and fulfilled in practice.

From this it can be demonstrated that I greatly fulfill the new law, because, since it commands the love of enemies, I love them so greatly that my zeal—that is, the excessive love I have for them—has made me waste away, that is, fail in my soul through great anguish on their behalf, because my enemies, the Jews, have forgotten your words. He does not say that they “forgot” because they once knew them; rather, it is as though he said that they neglected your words, namely the precepts of both laws, after the likeness of one who consigns to oblivion what he neglects.

I say that my zeal made me waste away because my enemies have forgotten your words. And indeed one ought to waste away on their behalf, because they do not keep your precepts: for your utterance is exceedingly fiery—that is, your fiery command greatly consumes the filth of sins in the faithful, illuminates the understanding, and makes them burn inwardly with charity, after the manner of fire, which consumes, illuminates, and burns. Since your utterance is so useful, it is exceedingly harmful to them to lose so useful a thing through negligence.

“Fiery,” I say, is your utterance, which is neglected by my enemies; and since it is fiery, your servant loved it—I, namely, who am obedient to you in every way and resist you in nothing. By loving it I became a young man, that is, exceedingly young, namely conformed through virtues to the new man, Christ, whereas previously I was conformed through vices to the old man.

I am a young man, I say; and although I am a young man, nevertheless—something that seems least likely to be said—I am despised by my enemies, the Jews, because I understand the old law spiritually and receive the new law. Although I am despised for this reason, I have not therefore forgotten your justifications, that is, the just precepts of both laws. For this reason I have not forgotten the old law: your justice—that is, the old law, which is most just and was given by you—is justice forever, leading those who understand and fulfill it spiritually into eternity. And for this reason I have not forgotten the new law, because your new law is truth, as was said in the second verse of this section. Hence John the Baptist says: “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).

Nor have I merely been despised by my enemies; tribulation in the body, from persecutions, and anguish in the soul, inflicted by those same enemies so that I might forget your precepts, have also found me. They afflicted me exceedingly, and yet my meditation is your precepts, [Col. 1303A] that is, I meditate on them constantly so that I may understand and fulfill the precepts of both laws. Not forgetting, however, is one thing, and meditating is another, although one may be understood from the other.

When he says “they found me,” he indicates that he was steadfast and capable, one who would endure tribulations and anguish manfully. For one who fails through fear and flees from suffering them is not “found” by tribulations, after the likeness of an ineffective soldier who, when he ought to begin battle, flees, and thus is not found by the enemies.

I meditate continually on the precepts of both laws because your testimonies of both laws, which lead those who fulfill them into eternity, are equity—emphatically, they are supremely equitable, commanding nothing except what is equitable. What he here calls “the equity of your testimonies” is the same as what he earlier called “your justice,” “justice forever,” and “your law truth”; but here it is applied to something else, namely to what he said: “My meditation is your precepts.”

“Equity,” I say, are your testimonies. Therefore I ask, O Lord, that you give me ever greater spiritual understanding of these things, and thus I shall live in their fulfillment—that is, I shall fulfill them, and this will be life for me.

**504. COPH** is interpreted as “conclusion” or “look.” Accordingly, Coph is suitably inscribed upon this entire section, in which the body of the faithful, suffering persecution from its enemies—persecution so great that it appears completely enclosed by them, after the likeness of one who, shut in and surrounded by enemies, cannot escape—shows that it has cried out to the Lord, asking him to hear it and make it seek his justifications and keep his precepts. It adds the merits and necessity explaining why it would obtain what it prayed for.

He relates this with the intention of instructing his hearers, so that if they should ever suffer a similar confinement, they may likewise cry out to the Lord and not be separated from him. This is clearly suggested by the force of the interpretation “look,” as though he plainly said: “When I report that, enclosed by enemies, I cried out to the Lord, I do this for your instruction, hearer, whoever you are, who are to be enclosed by enemies. Therefore, when you are so enclosed that you cannot escape by your own power, look to God’s mercy and cry out, and so you will escape”—after the likeness of a captive who, shut in by enemies, looks toward his fellow citizens or his lord and cries out to them to rescue him.

[Col. 1303D] **I cried with my whole heart, etc.** This is connected with the preceding passage in the following way. Earlier I said that, although I had been despised by my enemies, I had not forgotten your justifications; and although tribulation and anguish had found me, your testimonies were my meditation. This happened because I did not forget them and meditated upon them: when I was enclosed and surrounded by my enemies, I cried out—that is, I acted with an intense cry and did not conduct myself languidly.

I do not mean that I cried out externally, which would not be a great thing; rather, I cried with my whole heart—that is, I cried inwardly with the whole affection of my heart—saying: “Hear me, O Lord, so that I may seek your justifications,” that is, frequently seek, according to the desire of a good will and understanding, your justifications, namely the just precepts of both laws.

[Col. 1304A] He repeats what he said, “I cried,” in order to add this: “I cried,” I say, looking toward you, who can and will hear all who cry worthily to you. It is as though he said: “When I looked upon you as powerful and willing to do this, I cried out to you with good confidence, saying: Save me, O Lord, from my enemies, lest I become conformed to them; and save me in such a way that I may keep your precepts, new and old.”

It is as though he said: “My enemies intend to draw me away from keeping your precepts, but make me keep them—that is, fulfill them in practice—and this keeping will be salvation for me.” It is just that you save and hear me because of these merits of mine, since, while I was still placed in immaturity—that is, in immature age, namely youth, which is an immature age, hot and more inclined to every vice than old age—I anticipated others in good works, that is, I went before the other faithful who only began to act well later, in old age, which is a mature age.

It is as though he said: “It is worthy that you hear and save me for this reason: I began to act well from youth and acted more than those who began in old age.” Old age is called a mature age because, by nature, people have more mature character in old age. Youth, on the other hand, is called an immature age because, by nature, people’s character is more immature in youth.

“I anticipated,” I say, “others in good works while placed in immaturity”; and then, in that very immaturity, I cried out with intense devotion, at a time when few usually cry out. This “I cried” must be understood as having occurred at a different time from the other “I cried” placed at the beginning of the psalm. This one is to be understood as having occurred in youth; the other, after he had become more perfect in holiness.

“I anticipated,” I say, “others by acting well and going toward your words,” that is, toward your precepts. By acting well I hoped beyond hope—that is, from day to day I hoped more and more for the reward, adding hope to hope.

Nor did I merely anticipate others by acting well in immaturity; my inward eyes also—that is, my affections looking and directed toward you—anticipated others at dawn, that is, in the early morning, to meditate on your utterances, namely your precepts. This means: I anticipated others in meditating upon your precepts, beginning at the earliest morning hour, when the others ordinarily sleep and rest.

Or it may be read thus: My eyes—that is, my affections—being at dawn, namely in the excessive brightness of virtues, anticipated others, directed toward you, in order to meditate on your utterances. This means: Placed in the dawn of virtues, I was more intense than others in meditating on your utterances.

Therefore, since I anticipated and cried out, hear my voice according to your mercy, O Lord—that is, hear me so that you may give what I ask, namely that you may give me life in your precepts. Do this according to the regard of your mercy, and not according to mercy alone; but also give me life in these same precepts so that I may keep them continually, and do this according to your just judgment—that is, according to what your justice requires, so that you may justify me according to my merits.

It is necessary that you hear my voice and give me life, because those who persecute me have drawn ever nearer to iniquity: although they had previously been sufficiently wicked, by sinning they came closer to iniquity—that is, they became more wicked—trying to make me conform to them, after the likeness of one who, withdrawing from the light, proceeds into a dark crypt; the nearer he comes to the darkness, the more he is obscured.

“They have drawn near,” I say, “to iniquity, but they have become far from your law.” This means: The nearer they have come to iniquity, the farther they have become from the law of your commandments through their increasing iniquity. Therefore, lest they also make me draw near to iniquity and become distant from your law, it is necessary that you hear my voice and give me life in virtues and in keeping your commandments.

I ask with this confidence that you give me life because you are near, O Lord—that is, you are ready to aid all who cry out to you—and also because all your ways, that is, all your judgments by which you proceed, are truth, that is, true and just.

This is as though he said: “Since I see that, through your natural mercy, you are ready to help all who cry out to you, and since I know that you judge nothing except what is just, I trust that by your just judgment you will help me, who cry out to you and by my good life merit your aid.”

It should be noted that here he says that all the ways of the Lord are truth, whereas elsewhere he says: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10). These statements are not opposed, since everything he does through mercy is also truth, that is, justice. For it is just that, since he is merciful by nature, he should exercise his mercy by showing compassion.

Or the verse may be read thus: “I say that those who persecute me have drawn near to iniquity.” Yet they are inexcusable, while you, God, are beyond accusation, because you are near, O Lord—that is, you are ready, through your natural mercy, to give them life in virtues if they should wish to turn to you. Since you are near to them, while they do not wish to draw near to you through repentance, all your ways—that is, all your judgments which you exercise upon them—are truth, that is, justice. For it is just that they should be blinded here and punished without end in the future.

For this reason also I ask you to give me life in virtues and in your commandments, because from the beginning—that is, at the beginning—I understood from your testimonies, namely your precepts, that you founded them, that is, firmly established them, among your faithful forever, that is, so that they might lead them into eternity.

This means: “When I consider the beginning, namely Adam, to whom you gave your precepts, but in whom they were not founded so that he might persevere in them, and therefore he lost eternity, I understood conversely from consideration of this beginning that all in whom you have founded your precepts so that they may persevere in them will, through their observance, be led into eternity. Therefore I ask you to give me life by founding them in me, so that I may be led into eternity.”

**506. RES** is interpreted as “head” or “primacy.” By “head” or “primacy,” however, humility is signified. It is called the head or primacy of the other virtues because it is the beginning and first of all the virtues, and because, when possessed by the faithful, it guards all the virtues. Without it, all the virtues are weak and useless, just as all the other members of the body are governed by the head, which is its principal part. When the head is removed, the whole body is useless, like a lifeless trunk.

Hence humility is also called the queen of the virtues, just as pride is the queen of vices. Nothing prevents this from coexisting with blessed Gregory’s assertion that charity is the root of all the virtues. Humility is called the head and primacy of the virtues because, once acquired first, it guards the other virtues. Charity is called the root because all the virtues are situated in it, and when it is possessed, none is lacking.

[Col. 1306B] It is less hateful to God to possess humility alone than to possess all the virtues together with pride. Hence Augustine says: “In righteous deeds, pride alone must be avoided.” The Lord instructs us in the observance of this humility in the Gospel when he says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11:29). And elsewhere: “Be prudent as serpents” (Matthew 10:16). It is as though he plainly said: “Just as the serpent, which is a cunning animal, always protects its head so that it may not be struck there and perish, so you too, whoever you are who desire to escape eternal death, preserve your humility, because it is the head and guardian of the other virtues.”

This kind of head, namely humility, is treated in this section. For since the assembly of the faithful had earlier put forward its merits, saying, “I cried with my whole heart,” and “I anticipated in immaturity,” and so forth, lest it seem to have said these things out of boasting, it demonstrates in this section that it possesses humility. On account of this humility it asks God to rescue it from its enemies, lest it become conformed to them.

Moreover, lest it seem to be asking to be rescued from them merely so that they would not persecute it, it grants that these persecutions themselves should befall it. On their account it asks to be redeemed from torments in the future and to be given life. It also demonstrates the just condemnation of sinners, because they did not seek God’s justifications, and the many mercies of the Lord, by which it asks to be given life, adding also the merits by which it ought to attain this.

It does all this with the intention of inviting its hearers to observe humility, so that on account of it they may ask God to rescue them from their enemies and give them life, while nevertheless expecting to obtain this through God’s mercy and devoting themselves to attaining it through the merits of virtues and good works.

**Look upon my humility, etc.** This is connected in the following way: Earlier I said, “Hear my voice, so that you may rescue me from my enemies and give me life.” In order that I may obtain what I have asked, I beseech you, O Lord: look upon my humility—that is, see how humble I am and how devoted to you in all things.

I do not say “look” because you do not see this—you see all things—but look in such a way that through it you may grant me what I have asked. “Look,” I say, and on account of it rescue me from my enemies, lest they prevail over me in my soul.

He demonstrates his humility when he adds: “I said: Look upon my humility,” namely this humility, that I have not forgotten your law—that is, the institution of humility. This is my law and measure of life, which you gave me when you said: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Sirach 3:20). And elsewhere: “He who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11; 18:14). You also bestowed it upon me by your example when, though Lord and Master, you washed the feet of your disciples and, for my salvation, endured scourges, spittle, insults, the cross, and finally death.

Since he had said “rescue me” without qualification, lest he seem to be praying for rescue in such a way that he would suffer no tribulation from his enemies—and thus already depart from humility—he adds: “Judge,” etc. This is joined as follows: Although I prayed, “Rescue me,” I do not ask to be rescued in such a way that I suffer no bodily tribulation; rather, I ask and grant: “Judge my judgment”—that is, judge that I should suffer tribulations [Col. 1307B] here—which judgment is mine, that is, useful and salutary for me. Through this judgment of temporal tribulations, redeem me in the future from the punishment of fire, by which those who are to be saved after death will be purified if they have not been purified here through temporal tribulations.

Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3:15). And the prophet says: “A fiery sword has been placed at the entrance of paradise” (Isaiah 66:15). In Genesis also it is read that, after Adam’s expulsion from paradise, the Lord placed cherubim and a flaming, turning sword to guard the entrance to paradise (Genesis 3:24).

Appropriately, that purgatorial fire through which those who are to be saved will pass is called a sword and “turning.” It is called a sword because, in purifying them, it will cut away all the filth of sins, after the likeness of a sword that cuts. It is called “turning” because the perfected faithful will pass through it swiftly, so that they will not be harmed by it, after the likeness of a turning sword: if someone comes against such a sword and its edge is turned away from him, he is not injured.

It is also called “turning” with respect to those who will be purified there. Although those to be purified suffer there, they will not suffer eternally but will soon escape, after the likeness of a turning sword: if someone encounters such a sword and is wounded somewhat, he is nevertheless injured less if it turns than if it does not turn.

“Redeem me,” I say—and not only this, but also give me life, with eternal life—and do this on account of your utterance, that is, on account of your commandment kept by me, or on account of your utterance, that is, on account of your promise. For you promised, saying: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:10).

I say, “Give me life,” and you will truly do so. This salvation of life, however, will be far from sinners who sin mortally, and rightly so, because here they did not seek your justifications—that is, they did not seek with inward affection to suffer temporal tribulations, which are the justifications by which you purify and justify your faithful here.

This means: “They will not be saved in the future because here they refused to be justified through tribulations.” He says this in order to recall sinners from their sins and invite them to humility.

Lest God seem unmerciful on account of their just condemnation, he removes this impression as follows: Although salvation is far from sinners, your mercies, O Lord, are many—that is, the benefits of your mercy are many, and you work them in diverse ways in all your creatures. More is understood when he says without qualification, “Your mercies are many,” than if he specified God’s mercy in separate parts. It has the same meaning as if he said: “You, O Lord, are greatly and ineffably merciful.”

“Salvation,” I say, “will be far from sinners; but let salvation not be far from me. Give me life with eternal life according to your judgment,” that is, according to what your just judgment demands. This means: “Since you are a just judge, give me life, since it is just that I should be given life.”

And behold why it is just that you give me life. Many are those who persecute me, driving me from city to city for your sake, and afflicting me with bodily tribulations in order to force me to depart from your commandments; yet I have not departed—that is, I have not withdrawn—from your testimonies, namely from your commandments.

For this reason also you ought to give me life, because I am so perfect that I saw transgressors, that is, those who negligently passed over your commandments, and wasted away in my soul with excessive grief on their behalf because they did not keep your utterances, namely your commandments.

This means: “You ought to give me life because I waste away over the error of my enemies, who transgress your commandments.” They, I say, did not keep your commandments; but I both kept and loved them.

And look upon this, O Lord—that is, be my witness—because I loved your commandments. “Look,” I say, not because you do not see this, but look so that on account of it you may give me life. I ask you to give me life not only on account of these merits of mine, but also give me life in your mercy, that is, in consideration of your mercy.

“I loved,” I say, “your commandments.” And I loved them because truth—that is, justice and honesty—is the beginning of your words, that is, the principal cause of your commandments.

This means: “I loved them because I see that the principal reason why you gave these commandments to the faithful is that they are honorable and just, and it was honorable and just for you to impose them upon your faithful.” It is as though he said: “There are many reasons for which you imposed them; the fact that they are honorable and just in themselves, and worthy of execution, is one reason.”

For what is more honorable and just than to love God with one’s whole heart, to be chaste, humble, and moderate, and to possess every virtue? Another reason for which you gave them is that eternal blessedness might be prepared through their observance.

The fact that they are honorable and just in themselves is called their principal cause because one first considers whether what God has commanded is just and honorable in itself. Once it is clear that it is just and honorable, one then investigates what benefit will follow from it.

This principal cause of them—namely, their truth, that is, their honor and justice—made me love your commandments. And for this reason I still loved your commandments, because the judgments of your justice—that is, your just commandments, which you judge ought to be fulfilled—lead those who fulfill them into eternity. Therefore, so that they too might lead me into eternity, I loved them in such a way that I fulfilled them.

**SEN** is interpreted as “upon a wound.” Whatever is placed upon a wound to heal it is either some salve, a plaster, or any other medicine. Therefore, by “Sen,” interpreted as “upon a wound,” which is inscribed upon this section, it is indicated that the faithful who live here show that the persecutions they suffer for God are “upon a wound,” that is, are medicine by which the wounds of sins are healed. These wounds have already been healed in them to such an extent that they hate and abominate iniquity, rejoice over the Lord’s utterances and love his law, praise him seven times a day, and await his salvation.

They say this with the intention of inviting their hearers to endure persecutions.

**Princes persecuted me, etc.** This is joined to the preceding passage as follows. Earlier I said that many are those who persecute me; and so it is: earthly princes persecuted me without cause, namely without my deserving it and without any fault of mine requiring that persecution—kings, dukes, and other rulers—wishing by fear of punishments to force me into defection.

So that I might not fear their persecutions and thus fall away, my heart feared eternal punishments; and this fear arose from your words. For you said that those who fall away are to be condemned forever, in accordance with the Gospel passage: “He who loves his life will lose it” (John 12:21).

This fear of perpetual condemnation therefore drove out fear of temporal persecution. Through the persecutions I endured from the rulers, I became so perfect that under the pressure of these things I will no longer be saddened. Rather, I myself, while suffering, shall rejoice, established and founded upon your utterances—that is, upon your promises—as one who has found many spoils.

This means: Just as one who finds many precious spoils rejoices over those spoils, so I, founded upon the promises of eternal blessedness, shall rejoice in the hope of that blessedness. Your promises are the foundation of my joy.

Or it may be read thus: The persecutions will bring this about: I, founded here upon your utterances—that is, upon your precepts, which I constantly keep—shall rejoice in the future over the eternal blessedness that will finally be found, just as one rejoices who has found many spoils.

It is indeed appropriate that eternal blessedness be compared with spoils. Spoils properly refers to garments or possessions taken by force. Eternal blessedness is likewise acquired as though by a kind of force: by fasting, keeping vigil, and suffering many adversities. Hence the Gospel says: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11:12).

The persecutions also brought this about: I hated iniquity, and hated it so greatly that I abominated it, that is, cursed it; while I loved your law—that is, the persecutions themselves brought it about that I loved the law of your precepts.

They also brought this about: placed in the day of virtues, that is, in the brightness of virtues, I gave you praise, both with mouth and heart and by my works, seven times—that is, throughout my entire life, which is understood through the number seven because it unfolds through seven days.

Or “I gave you praise seven times” means: in the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit which you gave me. From this statement, “Seven times a day I have given you praise,” the practice arose in the Church that praise should be offered to God seven times a day: at Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline.

If Matins is said at night, this presents no difficulty, because among arithmeticians day and night are sometimes called together as one whole day.

“I gave you praise,” I say, “considering the judgments of your justice,” that is, considering your just judgments, namely the persecutions which you judge your faithful ought to suffer so that they may be justified through them. This means: “I praised you for my persecutions, considering that they are the cause of my justification.”

Or it may be read thus: I gave you praise with mouth and heart, founded upon the judgments of your justice—that is, upon your just precepts, which you judge ought to be fulfilled and which I have also fulfilled.

Since he had said, “I loved your law,” one might ask what benefit there will be for those who love your law. He answers as follows: “There will be great inward peace for those who love your law.” It is as though he said: “Although outwardly they endure the anxiety of adversities, inwardly they have great peace from vices, so that they are not excessively pressed by unlawful suggestions.”

Concerning this peace the Lord says in the Gospel: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27). And lest he seem to have been speaking of worldly peace, he added: “Not as the world gives do I give to you” (ibid.).

“Peace,” I say, “belongs to those who love your law.” And if they are in some degree tempted by certain vices, nevertheless there is no scandal for them, that is, no disturbance.

This means: Such temptations cannot perturb them so that they are drawn away from God’s law. Or there is no scandal for them in faith; or there is no scandal for them in the prosperity of the wicked and the adversity of the good.

This also resulted from the fact that princes persecuted me: through the merit of enduring those persecutions I had long awaited your salvation, that is, your salvation in the future. And in order to attain what I awaited, I loved your new commandments.

This seems to be the same as what he said earlier, “I loved your law,” but it is repeated here with a different application. Nor did I merely love your new commandments; my soul also kept your ancient testimonies with inward love.

This means: “I loved your new and old precepts.” And my soul did not love them in just any way, but loved them exceedingly, that is, greatly. Nor did I merely love them; I also kept them—that is, I fulfilled in practice your new commandments and your ancient testimonies.

That I loved and kept them, however, I did not have from myself, but from this: all my ways—that is, all my thoughts and actions by which I proceed—are in your sight, that is, in the sight of your mercy.

[Col. 1311A] This means: “By consideration of your mercy you have ordered all my ways.”

Or it may be read thus: “I say that I loved and kept them, and I do not lie about this, since I am certain that all my ways—that is, my thoughts and actions—are in your sight.” It is as though he said: “Since I know that you behold all my ways, it would be utterly foolish for me to say falsely that I loved and observed all your precepts.”

Or it may be read thus: “I loved and kept your commandments and testimonies; and this is proved by the fact that all my ways—that is, my thoughts and actions—are in your sight,” that is, in your good pleasure.

This means: “Since I neither do nor think anything except what pleases you, it is beyond doubt that I have loved and observed your commandments and testimonies, and that I still love and observe them.”

[Col. 1311B] **TAU** is interpreted as “he went astray” or “he completed.” Accordingly, Tau is suitably inscribed upon the eight-verse section at whose end the body of the faithful shows that, through Adam, it went astray from its homeland. Because of this error it prays that, through its merits and prayers, it may draw near and enter the homeland from which it wandered through Adam.

In order that it may draw near and enter, it asks to be given understanding in the Lord’s justifications, so that its lips may pour forth a hymn; and it asks to be rescued from this life.

Lest it seem still to be in the error of original sin, it shows that God has already completed it in holiness to such an extent that it has chosen God’s commandments, desired his salvation, and meditated upon his law.

Although it has therefore already been completed in holiness and still remains in that holiness, there remains in it not the error but the punishment of error—namely mortality, susceptibility to suffering, and exile from its homeland. It prays that the Lord’s mercy may lead it by his hand to salvation: that is, that, restored to its homeland, it may live forever, a life which it confidently promises itself.

It says all this with the intention of inviting by its example those who are still in the punishment of this error to sigh for the eternal homeland and pray for their return to it.

## “May my supplication draw near…”

“My supplication may draw near,” etc. This is joined to the preceding clause as follows. I said, Lord, that I have kept your commandments and your testimonies; on account of these merits I pray that my supplication may draw near in your sight—that is, that my supplication, being received in your sight, or in your good pleasure, may make me draw near to the heavenly homeland in this life through contemplation and good works. For by these means one draws near to it in this life.

May my supplication, I say, make me draw near, saying this supplication: “O Lord, give me understanding that accords with your word,” that is, with your commandment. This means: “Give me understanding of your commandments, so that I may thereby draw near to the homeland.” But let my supplication not merely make me draw near here; beyond this, let my petition enter into your sight. This means: “Let my petition, received in your sight,” that is, in your good pleasure, “enter”—that is, make me enter in the future—the heavenly homeland itself. To enter is more than to draw near. Here one draws near through good thoughts and good works; in the future one enters through the actual experience of the reality.

Let my petition, I say, enter, and it is this: “Deliver me, Lord, from the misery of this life through the dissolution of the flesh,” and do this according to your word, that is, according to your promise. For through the prophet you promised, saying: “For I shall take you from the nations, and gather you from the lands, and bring you into your own land” (Ezekiel 36:24).

I said: “Give me understanding of your commandments,” so that you may teach them to me. And when you have taught me your justifications—that is, your righteous commandments—my outward lips will pour forth a hymn; that is, from the inmost affection of my heart they will offer you praise, after the likeness of one who, from excessive fullness, belches outwardly. This means: “Such will be my inward affection that my lips will be unable to refrain from the hymn outwardly.” And I shall not merely praise you by speaking about you with myself; my tongue will also declare your word to others, that is, your commandment. It is honorable to declare it, for all your commandments are equity—by emphasis, they are supremely equitable. And who would not wish to declare equity?

But since in this proclamation I shall suffer many adversities from unbelievers, lest I then fail, let your hand—that is, your angelic army, appointed to help the faithful—be my help, so that it may save me; that is, may be the cause of my salvation in the future, for if it failed me, I would not be saved. Indeed, angels are read to have come to the aid of many martyrs when they were placed in the contest of suffering.

Or it may be understood in this way: Let your hand—that is, the power of your mercy—be my help here, so that I may not fail, and in the future may save me with eternal salvation. And it is worthy that this should happen, because I have chosen to proclaim your commandments to others; and also because I have desired your salvation, Lord—that is, I have greatly desired your future salvation. And in order that I may attain your salvation in the future, here your law is my meditation; that is, here I meditate upon the law of your commandments.

I have desired, I say, your salvation—that is, eternal life—and I know that I shall finally attain it. My soul, namely, will live with eternal life, and by living will praise you without end, with intense love. And to this end—that I may live—your just judgments will help me: judgments by which you have never judged anything except what is just, and by which you will not judge me unjustly when I have deserved well; rather, by a just judgment you will give me life.

When he says, “My soul will live,” he plainly indicates that the whole person will live, both in soul and in body. Since he had said, “Let your hand be such that it may save me, and my soul will live,” one might ask: “Why is it necessary for you to be saved and to attain life?” He therefore answers as follows:

“I prayed so earnestly that you might save me by bringing me back to the homeland of life because I have strayed from that homeland”—that is, through Adam’s error I have gone far away from it—and by straying I have perished, having become mortal and subject to suffering, and having fallen among enemies, namely, demons and vices, which strive to put me to death.

“I strayed,” I say, “and perished like some sheep that wandered from the fold and, falling among wolves, perished. Therefore, since I have strayed, so that I may be brought back, seek me, your servant, Lord, bringing me back to the homeland after death.” You have already sought me by bringing me from unbelief to faith. This is said after the likeness of the good shepherd who seeks the lost sheep and brings it back to the fold.

It is fitting, however, that you should seek me, because although at first I strayed from you through Adam, nevertheless, after you had imposed your commandments upon me when I was called to the faith, I did not forget your commandments as Adam did; rather, insofar as I was able, I loved them and fulfilled them in action.

## ON PSALM 119

### The title of Psalm 119

“A Song of Ascents.” This is explained as follows. This psalm is called a song of ascents—that is, a joyful discourse of ascents—because it contains within itself one of the steps by which every faithful person ought to ascend to the song, that is, to the most joyful heavenly reward. One ought not to ascend through sadness, but with a song, that is, with joyful gladness.

This psalm is called a song of ascents, as are the fourteen that follow, because in them fifteen steps are shown, by which all the faithful ought to ascend with the joy of hope, faith, and the other virtues to the Holy of Holies of the heavenly Jerusalem, since they are already placed here in the Church through faith. This was plainly prefigured in Solomon’s temple, in which there were fifteen steps, by which once a year the high priest alone ascended from the outer temple into the Holy of Holies.

It is also called a song of ascents because these steps concern not only the song of the future reward but also the present reward. For here too God rewards those who ascend them, when he hears their prayers and increases them in virtues and good works. He appropriately uses the plural “ascents,” to indicate that there are many steps.

The word *gradus*, “step,” signifies both the steps by which ascent is made and those by which descent is made, although here no steps are to be understood except those by which ascent to the heavenly Jerusalem is made.

For “ascents” we have *gradus*, whereas the Greeks have *anabathmos*; this word signifies only ascending steps. These steps are fittingly enclosed within the number fifteen. Since this number consists of seven and eight, the fifteen corresponding to these steps indicates that throughout this entire life—which revolves continually through seven days—we must strive by these steps toward the joyful reward of the eighth day.

Alternatively, by the number seven the whole Old Testament is understood, so that it may be designated in its entirety, because the Old Testament concerns the observance of the seventh day. Or the Old Testament is understood by seven because that Testament was fulfilled by the former people not for the sake of heavenly things but for the sake of attaining worldly prosperity. This worldly prosperity is signified by seven, because this worldly life revolves through seven days.

By eight, however, the New Testament is expressed, because that Testament was established through the Lord’s resurrection, which took place on the eighth day. The Lord is said to have risen on the eighth day because, although he had previously been in this life, which revolves through seven days, he did not rise again in order to possess this same life, but rose to eternal life, which will be given to the faithful on the eighth day of judgment. Or the New Testament is designated by eight because the faithful observe it not with regard to temporal things but with regard to the reward of the eighth day.

Since, therefore, these steps shown in these psalms are ascended through the fulfillment of the two Testaments, they are appropriately enclosed within the number fifteen. For without the fulfillment of both Testaments it is impossible to ascend by these steps to the heavenly Holy of Holies.

It should be understood that in all fifteen of these psalms of ascents the perfected faithful are represented as speaking. Since they have already ascended these steps, they speak about those same steps, so that the faithful who have not yet ascended them may thereby be invited to ascend.

The first of these steps, which is treated in the present psalm, is as follows. The assembly of the perfected shows that it cried out to the Lord when it was troubled by heretics and blasphemers, and prayed that arrows might be given to it for convicting them, and desolating coals for avoiding their assault. But because it says that its cry was heard, this does not belong to this first step but to the second. It hastens to assert that it was heard for this reason: so that by this it might kindle its hearers more strongly to cry out to the Lord, in order that they too, crying out, might likewise deserve to be heard.

### “To the Lord, when I was troubled…”

This is as though he were saying: “All you faithful, when you are troubled by the lying lips of blasphemers and by the deceitful tongue of heretics who attempt to make you like themselves, cry out to the Lord after my example, so that he may deliver you from them. For when I was troubled, I cried out to the Lord, and he heard me when I cried.”

He shows for what tribulation he cried out when he adds: “I cried out, I say, saying this: ‘Lord, deliver my soul,’” etc. This is as though he were saying: “Since you are powerful to deliver—for you are Lord—I ask not that the body be delivered from the sufferings of tribulation, but that you deliver my soul from the lying lips of blasphemers and from the deceitful tongue of heretics, lest it be turned by them toward evil.”

He also shows how he had deliberated about his deliverance, to indicate that the danger of the tribulation was great, and thereby to instruct more fully those placed in such danger to pray. For deliberation ordinarily occurs in great danger, not in a small one.

He therefore says this: “I say that I cried out, saying: ‘Lord, deliver me,’” etc. But before I cried out, I deliberated with myself, speaking to myself as though to another person:

“What weapons may be given to you for conquering the deceitful tongue of heretics? Or, if no weapons are given for defeating them, at least what defense may be placed—that is, joined—to you by God against the deceitful tongue, so that it may not be able to defeat you?”

This is said after the likeness of a shield or breastplate that a soldier places upon himself in order by these means to be protected from the arrows of his enemies.

It is as though the following were being said: “What weapons could be given me by the Lord for conquering the deceitful tongue? Or, if I lack weapons, what defenses could be given me so that I may not be conformed to the deceitful tongue?”
