It should be noted that, since he deliberates about the deceitful tongue but makes no mention of deceitful lips, it is indicated that it is more dangerous to contend against the deceitfulness of heretics, who appear to possess an argument, than against the wicked words of those who openly blaspheme God, who possess not even the shadow of an argument.

He shows what can be given or placed upon him as follows: “I say what may be given or what may be placed upon me. These things, namely, will be given: the arrows of the Mighty One”—by *antonomasia*, Christ—“sharp,” that is, the sayings of the words of the Lord Jesus, more penetrating than any sharpness. They are effective for convicting heretics, just as sharp arrows, when shot from the hand of a mighty man—that is, a strong man—are powerful for killing an enemy.

The arrows, I say, of the mighty Lord will be given, and this together with desolating coals being placed upon me. This means: “The arrows will be given in such a way that desolating coals will also be placed upon me, by which I may be defended against the deceitful tongue.”

He calls the prophets and apostles “desolating coals,” because all heresies were laid waste by them in their own times, just as fire-coals lay waste whatever buildings they have been kindled in; for this reason they are called desolating. The faithful who are not sufficiently learned to contend against heretics by arguments are therefore defended against them by the authority of these prophets and apostles.

He also shows the excessive anxiety of his tribulation as follows: “I say that I cried out to the Lord when I was troubled, and it was indeed necessary to cry out. For alas for me”—that is, woe to me—“there was excessive misery for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged,” that is, my pilgrimage has become excessively long: the pilgrimage, namely, of this life, in which, while I remain, I am an exile from the heavenly homeland.

It should be noted that he does not inquire about the prolongation of his sojourn because he now wishes to be dissolved from the body, since he has not yet reached perfection, but because he is distressed by dwelling together with the wicked. This is made clear in what follows:

“And therefore I say, ‘Alas for me!’ at the prolongation of my sojourn, because in this sojourn I dwelt bodily with those who dwell in Kedar,” that is, in darkness—namely, with blasphemers and heretics who remain in the darkness of ignorance.

He determines that his complaint concerns not the sojourn of the body but that of the soul when he adds: “And by dwelling bodily with those who dwell in Kedar.” Before I cried out to the Lord, my soul was a sojourner—that is, a stranger—and this for a long time, that is, it was very far from contemplating the heavenly homeland, since it was often troubled by those who dwelt in Kedar.

And not only were those with whom I dwelt inhabitants of Kedar, but I was also dwelling with those who hated the peace of the Church’s faith and sought to disturb it with many heresies. I was dwelling with those who hated peace—that is, with heretics—and therefore it was alas for me.

“I say that I was dwelling with those who hated peace, while I was myself peaceful”—that is, peaceable—“loving their salvation and desiring that they be brought back to the peace of the Church.”

By this he instructs his hearers that they ought to be peaceable with the enemies of peace. Hence Prosper says: “It belongs to Christian perfection to be peaceable even with the enemies of peace, in the hope of correction, not in agreement with wickedness.”

“I say that I was peaceful, and when I spoke peaceably to them, they attacked”—that is, assailed—“me with abusive words, and this gratuitously,” that is, without cause and without reason; or “gratuitously,” that is, in vain, since they were unable to defeat me.

## ON PSALM 120

### The title of Psalm 120

“A Song of Ascents,” as explained above.

After the first step has been shown—namely, that he cried out to the Lord in tribulation, praying that arrows and desolating coals be given him—he shows in the following psalm the second step: that he obtained what he prayed for, namely, knowledge of the Scriptures and the authority of the apostles and prophets. Hence he says that help will come to him from the Lord.

By this he invites his hearers to cry out, so that they too, crying out, may deserve to obtain what they ask. He also prays thereafter to be guarded so that he may not be shaken any further or sleep in the faith, and for the certainty of his hearers he declares that what he prays for is already present.

### “I lifted up my eyes…”

This is as though he were saying: “Earlier, when I was troubled, I cried out to the Lord, praying that arrows and coals be given me. When these had been granted to me through the illumination of divine grace, whereas previously I had kept the eyes of my reason lowered by ignorance, I lifted those inner eyes of mine to the mountains”—that is, I raised them by paying attention to the writings of the prophets and apostles, who are called mountains on account of the eminence of their dignity.

“From there my help will come to me.” This is as though he were saying: “Truly, the eyes must be lifted to the Scriptures. From there help will come to me, so that by their arguments I may convict my adversaries in the faith and remain fortified against them.”

Lest this help appear to come from the mountains alone, he removes that implication as follows: “Yet my help, which will come from the mountains, is from the Lord.” That is, I shall receive help from the mountains in such a way that this help comes principally from the Lord.

From the Lord, I say, who is powerful to help, who made heaven and earth—that is, who made the mountains themselves, which were heavens, that is, those who pour upon their subjects; and who made the earth, that is, those subjects upon whom they pour.

What follows—“May he not permit,” etc.—may either be a prayer concerning himself, addressed in the second person, that he not be shaken; or it may be understood concerning each hearer as follows:

“I say that I have now lifted my eyes to the mountains. And so that you may not thereafter stray from those mountains and may lift your eyes to them more and more, may he not permit your inner foot to be shaken,” that is, may he not permit the faith—which is the foot by which the mind strives toward higher things—to be shaken from the stability of the Scriptures and fall into error.

Nor, which is less, may he permit it to sleep—that is, may he not permit you to sleep, namely, to waver in the faith and in some way to doubt—he who guards you, God through the grace dwelling within you. This is said after the likeness of one who is drowsing, who is neither wholly asleep nor wholly awake.

The following can likewise be read as concerning himself, as though addressed in the third person. It is adapted to each individual hearer without changing the meaning:

“I said, O hearer, that I lifted my eyes to the mountains. So that you too may lift yours in the same way, may he not permit your foot to be shaken, nor let him who guards you sleep.” This is to be understood as explained in another interpretation.

Lest he appear to have prayed out of distrust, he declares what he prayed for as follows: “I pray that he may not permit your foot to be shaken,” etc. And behold, what I pray for will be present: “He will neither grow drowsy nor sleep”—that is, he will not permit you to grow drowsy in the faith, that is, to waver, nor to sleep, that is, to be wholly shaken in faith—he who, through the help of grace, guards each one who is Israel, namely God.

To sleep is certainly more than to grow drowsy. “I say that he will neither grow drowsy nor sleep,” but, being the Lord himself and therefore powerful to guard, he guards you with perseverance. The Lord, I say, who is your protection, who protects you by the help of grace so that you do not yield to the assault of your enemies.

The Lord, I say, existing through the reign of his grace, is “over the hand of your right hand,” that is, over the power which will be the cause of your right hand: over the power of faith, namely, which will be the cause by which you will be placed at God’s right hand. It is called yours because you desire it to be given to you and will be placed at it.

This means: “He himself exists over your powerful faith,” that is, he rules your faith, guiding it well and increasing it. Through him it is powerful and strong, and through it you will be placed at the right hand of God the Father. “For without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11:6).

Or he exists “over the hand,” and not over the left hand, but over your right hand—that is, over good action, which is understood by the right hand, since good things are often signified by the right. This means: “The Lord is not only your protection, so that you do not yield to the assault of enemies; he also rules and guides your good action well, so that he may increase it from day to day.”

The Lord, I say, guards you; therefore the Sun of righteousness, Christ, will not burn you by day. That is, he will not obscure the bright keenness of your reason by day, by the excessive brightness of his divinity, which is rightly called day in relation to his humanity, which is also called night because it is far less bright in comparison with his divinity.

Nor will the moon—that is, Christ—burn you; that is, he will not permit you to be burned. He will not permit the keenness of your reason to be obscured in blindness by night, that is, by his humanity.

This means: “The Lord both guards you and will guard you, so that he does not permit your reason to be obscured by any error in contemplating his divinity, so that you say that he is another God than the Father and lesser than he, as the Arians wished; nor, with respect to his humanity, so that you say that he was not a true human being but assumed a phantom body, as the Manichaeans asserted.”

The statement that he will not burn you “by day and night” is said after the likeness of those who, traveling either by day, are darkened by the sun, or by night, by the moon, and so lose the brightness of their skin; for this reason they are said to be burned. It belongs to those who are burned to be darkened. Although the moon does not heat like the sun, it is nevertheless of such a nature that it burns—that is, it darkens the skin and causes it to become black.

Christ is called both sun and moon: sun with respect to his divinity’s brightness; moon with respect to the flesh, which could decrease like the moon through adversity and death and increase through the prosperity of restored health.

But the Lord not only guards you so that you are not burned by day and night; the Lord also, to speak universally, guards you from every evil of heresies, so that you do not err concerning the resurrection of the dead, the baptism of infants, and the other heresies.

Since he had said without qualification that he guards him from every evil, lest this be understood as guarding him from every bodily evil, he makes clear what evil he means when he adds an optative expression:

“I say that he guards you from every evil, and may the Lord continually do this: may he guard not the body from tribulation, but your soul from every error.”

And may the Lord guard it in this way: through the illumination of grace, may he guard your entrance—that is, your faith, into which you have already entered, or which is your entrance into every good. For it is the beginning of all virtues. And may he guard your exit—that is, your end—so that when you depart from this life you may not in any way dissent from the faith. For at the time of departure many hidden suggestions and unlawful things are brought forward by the devil.

May he guard your entrance—that is, your faith—from this time onward, beginning in the present age and persevering into the age to come.

## ON PSALM 121

### The title of Psalm 121

“A Song of Ascents,” also as explained above.

After the assembly of the perfected has been confirmed in faith through the mountains to which it lifted its eyes, that assembly—which represents the second step—shows in the following psalm that it has ascended the third step, namely hope, through which it already lives in heavenly things. It asserts that it has had joy because of this hope, so that it may invite its hearers more strongly to the same hope.

It also shows, through the certainty of its hope, that many people of its confession have already ascended to the same heavenly peace toward which they strive in hope. It asks them to pray for that peace, so that it may be given to the faithful who still dwell on earth.

### “I rejoiced…”

This is as though he were saying: “By lifting my eyes to the mountains, I have now reached the point that I rejoiced in these things”—that is, in consideration of what has been said to me by the writings of the prophets and apostles—“namely, that we faithful will go after the death of the flesh into the house of the Lord,” that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem.

“I rejoiced,” I say, “because we shall go there.” But I do not merely now have hope that we shall go there. From the time when I rejoiced in this, our feet were also standing—that is, the affections of our hope were already dwelling firmly—in your courts, O Jerusalem, that is, in your spaciousness.

This means: “From the time when we rejoiced, we already dwelt in you through hope; because of your spaciousness you are said to have courts.”

When he says in the singular, “I rejoiced,” he shows that the assembly is one. When he says, “Our feet,” he shows that the persons speaking are many.

He determines which Jerusalem he means when he adds: “I mean the Jerusalem that is built daily from the faithful who depart from this world.” It is not truly a city but is called a city by likeness, because it is made from living stones, just as a city is made from lifeless stones.

Lest this be understood of some city that is now being built and called Jerusalem, he adds by way of distinction: “I mean that Jerusalem whose participation is in the One”—that is, whose tendency is toward him, toward immutability—“which participates in that good which is immutable and eternal.”

By this the heavenly Jerusalem is understood, whose citizens share in immutable blessedness.

The perfected who act in this psalm show that all their faithful predecessors have already gone into the house of the Lord; hence they are certain that they too will go there:

“We shall go,” I say, “into the house of the Lord, and from this we are certain. For tribes have already ascended there according to the soul, not according to the body.”

When he says “tribes,” he indicates human beings, since we speak of tribes of human beings, not of angels. It is as though he were saying: “We are certain that we shall ascend there because generations of human beings have already ascended there.”

He determines which tribes when he adds: “Tribes, I say, of the Lord”—that is, those people will ascend who have been regenerated in the Lord from the water of baptism and the Holy Spirit, according to the saying: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16:16).

“Tribes of the Lord have ascended.” And this, he asserts, is “as a testimony of Israel,” that is, as Jacob the patriarch testified in his vision, when he saw the ladder and angels ascending and descending upon it (Genesis 28:12).

This was a sign both of a past reality and of a future reality. For by those descending, wicked angels were signified, who descended through pride; by those ascending, the saints who were to become spiritual like angels and who would ascend there to restore the fall of those who descended—and some have already ascended.

Or it may be understood in this way: “There the tribes of the Lord have ascended as a testimony of Israel,” that is, testifying by their ascent to the same thing that Israel testified in the vision. This means: “By their ascent they testified that what Israel testified in the vision was true.”

The tribes have ascended, I say, “to confess praise to the name of the Lord,” that is, to praise the Lord in consideration of his great name, which is “Lord.” This means: “They ascended in order to praise God with everlasting praise of love.”

From this also we are certain that we shall go into the house of the Lord, because “thrones” have already sat there—that is, in that house judges have long since rested, and they are understood by “thrones,” either because it belongs to judges to have a seat, or because they are the seats of God.

He determines when they will be judges when he adds: “Thrones in judgment”—that is, those thrones which, although they are not yet thrones, will become thrones in the future judgment.

This means: “The apostles have already ascended there and have long since rested there; they are to be judges on the day of judgment over the house of David,” that is, over the Church, which is the spiritual house of Christ, the true David.

According to the Lord’s saying: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28).

The house of David—that is, of Christ—is said to include both good and evil believers, because all have been initiated into the same spiritual sacraments.

Since it had been said that tribes and thrones had ascended into the house of the Lord, he asks those who have already ascended to pray for those who are still to ascend:

“I say that thrones and tribes have ascended. And you who have already ascended, ask for us the things that belong to attaining the peace of the heavenly Jerusalem. Ask God to give us, who are still to ascend, those things by which we may come to the eternal peace of the heavenly Jerusalem.”

After inviting those who have already ascended to pray for that peace, the assembly of the perfected itself also prays for that peace, so that it may instruct its hearers to pray:

“We say: ‘Ask for the things that belong to peace,’ and we ourselves also pray that in the future there may finally be abundance for those who love you, O heavenly Jerusalem”—that is, that all those still dwelling here who desire to attain the abundance that is in you, being lovers of you, may obtain that abundance.

He explains what abundance he is praying for when he adds: “I say, ‘Let there be abundance for those who love you’”—namely, “Let them have peace in your power,” that is, through your power. Let eternal peace be given them through Christ, who is your power, making you strong and unconquerable, so that no assault of enemies can be made against you.

Or it may be understood in this way: “Let them have peace by existing in your power.” That is, let the peace that is in you be given to them in such a way that they also persevere in divine love, which is called, by *antonomasia*, your power because it is more worthy and more enduring than every virtue. For although all virtues are possessed here, in the future only charity will be possessed. Hence it is written: “But greater is charity” (1 Corinthians 13:13).

And let not a small peace be given them, but let an abundance of peace be given them—an abundance that is already in your towers. Such abundance may be given them in the future as is already in the apostles, who are called your towers either because of the eminence of their merits or because they are the protection of the faithful through their teaching and the patronage of their prayers.

After showing his joy and hope and his prayer for peace, he discloses the purpose for which he did these things as follows:

“I said: ‘Our feet were standing in your courts, O Jerusalem,’ and I prayed concerning your peace, saying: ‘Let there be peace,’” etc.

And when speaking about you, O Jerusalem, I spoke of peace—that is, I proclaimed your peace. Whenever I spoke about you, I proclaimed to others how great your peace is.

“I spoke,” I say, “of peace,” and this was for the sake of my brothers and my neighbors—that is, for the benefit of my brothers and neighbors, so that they might strive toward this peace.

He calls all the faithful “brothers,” because all are adopted sons of God. He calls the perfected “neighbors,” because they are near to them in conformity. This is gathered from another translation, in which “my friends” is found.

Since there can also be neighbors in evil, he determines which neighbors he means here by adding: “I spoke of peace for the sake of the house of the Lord our God being built.” That is, he did this so that, following the example of my speech, the faithful might strive more and more toward that peace of the heavenly Jerusalem, and so that it might itself be built more and more, since it is the house of God.

And thus: “O house of God, Jerusalem, I sought good things for you”—that is, I acquired good citizens for you, from whom, being built, you might become more glorious and more honored.

## ON PSALM 122

### The title of Psalm 122

“A Song of Ascents.”

After treating the third step—namely, after showing for the instruction of his hearers the certainty of his hope—he shows, for the instruction of those same hearers, that he has ascended the fourth step. This is so that he may now lift the eyes of his reason to attend to the Lord’s will, in order to fulfill it, and continue doing so until he has mercy on him by restoring him to immortality and freedom from suffering. He also prays for this mercy, saying as follows:

### “To you I lifted up my eyes…”

This is as though he were saying: “O hearers, after you have rejoiced that we shall go into the house of the Lord, lift the inner eyes of your reason to him who dwells in the heavens. Do this after my example. For after I rejoiced, I lifted my inner eyes—namely, the eyes of reason—to you who dwell in the heavens,” that is, who rule over the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem.

This means: “I lifted the eyes of my reason by attending to your wills, so that I might fulfill them. They had been lowered while I attended to fulfilling my own wills. And it was fitting that I should lift my eyes to you, since you are the one who rules over the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem; I would not come into their fellowship unless I lifted my eyes to you.”

He shows that he lifted his eyes attentively to God by a twofold comparison, so that he might draw his hearers more strongly toward the same thing:

“I lifted my eyes to you. And behold, O hearers, how attentively I lifted my eyes to God, and still lift them: just as the eyes of servants are fixed upon the hands of their masters, attending to those hands so that whenever the master gives them a sign they may immediately obey—and, to say something even greater, just as the eyes of a maidservant, who is more subject and ready to obey, are fixed upon the hands of her mistress, attending so that obedience follows her mere sign—so our inner eyes are attentive to the Lord our God, so that we may obey him in all his wills.”

We shall remain in this servitude until he has mercy on us, restoring us in the future to immortality and freedom from suffering and rescuing us from this servitude.

He prays for this mercy as follows: “I say, until he has mercy on us; and because I trust that you will have mercy, I pray: Have mercy on us,” finally rescuing us from this servitude in the future and restoring us to the perfect state.

He says “Have mercy on us” twice because of his excessive desire.

“I say, ‘Have mercy on us,’ and it is necessary to pray this because here we have been filled with contempt”—by emphasis, we are so contemptible that we appear to be filled with every contempt.

And it is necessary to pray this not only because we are despised in body, but also, and more importantly, because “our soul has been greatly filled with contempt,” being regarded as a reproach—that is, judged worthy of reproach—by those who abound in earthly riches, that is, by the rich of this age, and being regarded as contempt by the proud—that is, by those same wealthy people who are proud of their riches.

This means: “Our soul is despised and judged worthy of reproach by the proud rich of this age, since it is called foolish and senseless because it scorns worldly things.”

## ON PSALM 123

### The title of Psalm 123

“A Song of Ascents.”

After the fourth step has been shown—namely, attention to God’s will—the perfected treat the fifth step: when, because of their attention, they are tempted to be recalled from that attention, either by detractors or by flattering deceivers, and are unable to be recalled, they should ascribe this constancy not to themselves but to the Lord. They instruct all who desire to be Israel to do the same.

Unless the Lord had been among us, let Israel now say, etc.; as though he were saying: When I had kept my eyes attentively fixed upon God, and detractors and flattering deceivers wished to draw me away from that attention but could not, I said that the fact that I was so attentive came not from myself but from the Lord. Therefore, by my example, whoever is now lifting his eyes to God is Israel, and whoever has been tempted unsuccessfully to turn back should not attribute such steadfastness to himself, but let Israel now—that is, immediately—say both with his mouth and in the reflection of his mind: If he had not remained, because the Lord was among us according to his assisting grace; unless the Lord had been among us, I say, when men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive. It should be noted that his repetition of “unless the Lord had been among us” twice is either the result of excessive rejoicing and affection, or is made so that each phrase may correspond to another, as follows: Unless the Lord had been among us when wicked men rose up against us with flattering and deceptive words, attempting to turn us away from our attention, they would have swallowed us—that is, incorporated us into themselves—alive, that is, knowingly and deliberately in sinning. [Col. 1322D] And they might have done this—that is, suddenly and unexpectedly—519 so that we would have had no power to escape. Although we might have been swallowed knowingly; or perhaps—that is, as though we had been made without reason. And unless the Lord had been among us when their fury grew angry against us—that is, when detractors and slanderers, raging, became angry against us, and through their detractions and slanderous words—water would have absorbed us, that is, they themselves, becoming like water by flowing here and there through unlawful things; or, in their attempt to submerge me as water, they would have absorbed us, that is, incorporated us into themselves; and this, perhaps. This “perhaps” is of the same kind as the “perhaps” above. They would have absorbed us, I say, unless the Lord had been among us.

But because he was among us, our soul passed through—that is, escaped—the torrent, that is, their bitter and defamatory words, flowing with the violence of a torrent, so that they could not turn us back. I say “passed through,” and I say this perhaps—that is, timidly, because of the magnitude of the danger in which I was, and doubting whether I had offended in any respect. By this he teaches his hearers always to fear falling, so that “let him who stands take heed lest he fall (1 Cor. 10:12).” “For blessed is the man who is always fearful (Prov. 28:14).”

Our soul passed through the torrent, I say; and would that our soul had passed through it in such a way that it had offended in no respect—an intolerable water, so far as our frailty is concerned, though not so far as the help of divine grace is concerned. He treats “water” and “torrent” as equivalent. The soul passed through, I say; therefore let the Lord be blessed—that is, magnified and praised—who did not give us into their teeth, that is, into the grasp of the corrosions of their detractions and slanders; that is, he did not permit them to incorporate us into themselves through their detractions and slanders. We were not merely delivered from their teeth; our soul, moreover, being cautious like a sparrow, which is cautious in avoiding snares, was rescued from the snare of the hunters, that is, from the deceptive flatteries of worldly people, by which they attempted to capture me for themselves and make me conform to them, just as hunters deceive wild animals or birds with a snare.

The soul was not rescued in such a way that it had ever been caught in that snare, but in such a way that the snare itself was broken—that is, rendered ineffective for capturing and ensnaring us—like a broken snare, which is powerless to ensnare. And because it was broken, we were freed from it, so that it could not deceive us. This did not come from us; rather, our help came in the name of the Lord, that is, through the Lord’s honor—namely, through the Lord’s mercy. For he himself is honored by the faithful in view of his mercy; therefore it is called his honor. The name is frequently used in place of honor. This means: Because we were delivered, it happened through the help of the Lord’s mercy; or thus: Our help came in the name of the Lord, that is, on the occasion of the Lord’s honor—namely, we were helped because we earnestly endeavored to honor the Lord in every way. The Lord, I say, who made heaven and earth, that is, prelates and subjects. And since he is so powerful that he made heaven and earth, he is proved to be powerful enough to help us.

## ON PSALM 124

The title of the hundred twenty-fourth psalm: “A Song of Ascents.” After the fifth degree has been treated—namely, that they should attribute all their steadfastness not to themselves but to the Lord—the sixth is discussed: after one has reached such steadfastness that one cannot be drawn back from one’s attention, one must also ascend to the point of trusting in the Lord alone, setting aside every worldly confidence. The perfect, who are treated here, invite their hearers to this confidence by showing what benefit comes from it.

“Those who trust in the Lord,” etc.; as though he were saying: I not only lifted my eyes to God, and not only said, “Unless the Lord had been among us,” but I also ascended higher, so that I might trust in the Lord alone, despising every worldly confidence. Therefore, all of you who are Israel and have already ascended these five degrees, ascend higher still, so that you may trust in the Lord alone; and you will do this for your own good.

For the people who trust in the Lord, 520 and not in worldly things, will not be shaken forever from their good purpose, neither by prosperity nor by the adversity of tribulations, just as Mount Zion—that is, Christ—could not in any way be shaken from his stability. All who exist are founded upon and lean upon this Mount Zion. This means: Such a person will be steadfast and immovable, just as Christ was immovable—not that he will possess as much steadfastness as Christ possessed, [Col. 1324B] but, insofar as possible, he will be conformed to him in steadfastness.

He specifies who the people are who trust in the Lord, lest anyone rashly judge himself to possess this confidence when he lacks it, as follows: The people, I say, who trust will not be shaken; and I affirm that the one who has this confidence is the person who already dwells in the heavenly Jerusalem through hope and a manner of life. Hence the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in heaven (Phil. 3:20).” The trusting people will therefore not be shaken because mountains surround them—that is, the apostles and the other saints who have already departed from this life. They are called mountains because of the sublimity of their holiness. They surround them—that is, they are their fortification—protecting them by their merits and prayers from the injuries of visible and invisible enemies, like soldiers providing protection who, standing around someone, defend him from attacking enemies.

The Lord also surrounds his people, protecting them by the help of his grace, beginning now and continuing forever. Truly, they will not be shaken; for even if the Lord permits sinners for a time to rule over the just and scourge them, nevertheless the Lord will not long leave the rod—that is, the scourging or domination of sinners—upon the lot, that is, upon the election of the just, namely, upon the just elected for salvation. He does this so that the just themselves may not stretch out their hands—that is, may not extend their desires—toward iniquity. It is as though he were saying: If God permitted sinners to rule over the just and afflict them with tribulations beyond the measure of their endurance, they would indeed be shaken and would be moved toward iniquity.

Therefore, so that they may not only refrain from evil works but also not extend their desires toward iniquity, God adjusts their tribulations to the measure of their endurance, so that he does not permit those sinners to rule over them beyond measure or afflict them with tribulations. Hence the Apostle says: “He will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear (1 Cor. 10:13).”

He prays concerning what he has declared as follows: I said, O Lord, that you would not leave the rod of sinners upon the elect just; and so let it be, O Lord: “Do good to the good and upright in heart,” removing from them the rod of sinners. He calls those “good” who work well; but “upright in heart” are those who, although they cannot perform good works, at least possess the will to do good. He uses “lot” for “election,” because an election may take place; and “rod” for “scourging,” because one is scourged with it. Alternatively, by “rod” we understand a scepter; by “scepter,” a kingdom, since it is a sign of kingship. This is gathered from the Hebrew translation, where “scepter” is found.

He also shows the condemnation of those who will be shaken from their good purpose, in order by this means to deter his hearers from such a thing, as follows: I say that the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners long upon the elect just; rather, he will quickly remove that rod from them. But those who turn aside—that is, who deflect themselves from their justice—he will lead into bonds, that is, into iniquity, which is a bond and chain leading them to death; in the future, by his just judgment, the Lord will lead them into condemnation, [Col. 1325B] together with those who work iniquity—that is, together with those who make them turn aside. Therefore, by antonomasia, they are called “those who work iniquity.” This means: They will be led into the same condemnation as the wicked, to whom they have conformed themselves. Hence the prophet says: “If the just man turns away from his justice, will he live? (Ezek. 18:24).”

The Lord, I say, will lead those who turn aside into condemnation. The Lord, I say, who will be Israel’s eternal peace—a peace existing over Israel itself, to which Israel will be subjected by gratuitous love and will confess without end.

## ON PSALM 125

The title of the hundred twenty-fifth psalm: “A Song of Ascents.” Having shown confidence, which is the sixth degree, the perfect also discuss the seventh degree, [Col. 1325C] namely, that they have now reached the point of being turned from captivity into freedom, by which they have been comforted, filled with joy, and magnified. They also pray that they may attain this freedom more and more, since they can always increase in it. By this example they encourage their hearers to strive more and more toward this freedom.

We call it “captivity” when the faithful serve God through fear of punishment and by the authority of the commanding Lord. They would not serve if they were not certain that punishment would be removed from those who sin, and if the authority of the one commanding were absent; this is like servants and captives, who serve more through fear and the authority of their commanding master than through love. This kind of captivity is converted into freedom through delay, when the faithful are so inflamed with love toward God that they serve no longer from fear but from love alone and without any difficulty. They would nevertheless serve even if they knew that no punishment threatened them for their sins, like free persons, who serve willingly and are not compelled by necessity.

“When the Lord turned,” etc. This verse begins in a certain order but ends by omitting that order and adopting another. For although it begins in this way: “When the Lord turned the captivity of Zion,” it ought afterward to add “he became magnified,” or “he became glorious,” or something of that kind corresponding to the initial construction. But, abandoning that order of construction, it gives another which does not seem to cohere with the first; for it says, “we became as those who are comforted.” It seems to do this in order to suggest that what it had begun and then left unfinished is evident and manifest from what follows. It also omits the first construction because it does not pertain to the purpose of its intention.

The construction of this verse is therefore equally meaningful as if it were expressed in this way: O you who have now ascended to the degree of confidence, strive by our example to reach the point that your captivity may be converted into freedom, and that you may thus become comforted and joyful as we are. For when the Lord converted our captivity—that is, when the Lord mercifully converted our captivity into freedom—through that freedom we became as those who are comforted.

He calls the removal of the sadness by which they were desolated “consolation”; for when they served through fear of punishment, they were often pressed by sadness because of the burden of their service. Therefore he says not “comforted” but “as those who are comforted,” because this consolation must be called “as consolation,” that is, a shadow of consolation, in comparison with the future consolation, which will be more worthy. When he says “when turning,” he seems to indicate that consolation occurred not long after the conversion but immediately in the conversion itself.

Then, in this conversion, our mouth was filled with joy within—that is, our mind, with which we speak to God mouth to mouth. And not only within, but also our outward tongue was, by emphasis, filled with rejoicing—that is, with exultant words, by which we continually praise God for our conversion.

When our captivity had been converted, and we had become comforted and filled with joy and rejoicing, then they would say among the nations—that is, this would happen because certain people among the nations, namely, some unbelievers living in a pagan manner, observing our magnification, would say to one another: “Truly the Lord magnified his work with them.” That is, when he had first worked obedience in them—namely, that obedience which is “his work,” that is, his deed—and when he worked it with them, meaning that they themselves worked it through free will while God worked with them through assisting grace, he magnified it—that is, made it magnificent and wondrous. Thus, although they had previously obeyed out of fear, they now serve and obey out of love alone.

This “then,” placed at the beginning of the verse, is causal and has the same force as if it had been written “therefore.” After presenting the words of the nations concerning their magnification, he grants their words to the praise of God because of their excessive joy, as follows: Some, I say, among the nations will say: “The Lord magnified his work with them”; and they will speak truly. For the Lord magnified his work with us, and therefore we became joyful, both outwardly in the tongue and inwardly in the mouth.

But in order that we may rejoice more and more, we pray: Convert, O Lord, our captivity into freedom, according to our intention—that is, since it has already been converted, convert it further so that we may now obey through love of freedom; or, “convert” according to perseverance.

[Col. 1327A] Convert, I say, captivity into freedom, which may be like a torrent in the south, that is, in the time of the south wind. For just as, when the south wind stands, melting snow and ice, any torrent grows through the melting of the snow and ice and, thus flowing violently, drives away every obstacle in its path, so our free obedience, growing through the Holy Spirit—which dissolves all the ice of vices and kindles in us the fervor of charity—presses toward the heavenly Jerusalem with the force of good works and drives away all impediments of worldly pleasures. The Holy Spirit may appropriately be called the south wind, because it often kindles hearts hardened by the ice of vices with the heat of charity. Hence, in the Song of Songs: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind (Song 4:16),” etc.

Because he had prayed for the conversion of captivity into freedom according to his intention, someone might say: Why do you desire such freedom, which cannot even be called freedom, since those placed in this freedom of obedience must endure so many tribulations? To this he adds as follows: I desire this rightly. For if tribulations arise because of such obedience, one must not cease from obedience; rather, the works of good obedience must be sown all the more amid those tribulations.

Those who sow good works here in tears—that is, in tribulations, which are called “tears” because they are caused by tribulations—will reap in the future the reward of eternal blessedness, and this with rejoicing, like country-dwellers who sow with labor what they reap with joy. Good works must therefore also be sown in tribulations so that they may be reaped with joy in the future.

For the holy Fathers, our predecessors, went here toward death and wept—that is, they went toward death with weeping, namely, with the suffering of tribulations, which is understood through weeping because such suffering causes weeping. They went, I say, with weeping, yet they carried their seeds—that is, their good works. But when they come to the heavenly homeland, both in body and in soul at the resurrection, those who were in the sorrow of tribulations will come with perpetual rejoicing, carrying sheaves—that is, possessing a very great weight of eternal glory, which is implied by the words “carrying.” For when speaking of something great, we customarily say that someone “carries” it. This is said by comparison with a cultivator who, at harvest time, carries the sheaves of his seeds with the greatest rejoicing. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5:10).”

## ON PSALM 126

The title of the hundred twenty-sixth psalm: “A Song of Ascents of Solomon.” This means: This psalm is a song of ascents, as explained above. I say it is a song of admonition by Solomon—that is, one directing us to Solomon, the son of David and king of Israel. By its evident meaning it exhorts us, after we have ascended to freedom, not then to trust that we can no longer fall, and thereby fall through becoming insolent. We should always keep before the eyes of our mind the fact that if Solomon, who was so great a man, so wise, and also a prophet, fell into idolatry, it is much more possible for us, who are far lesser, to fall. Thus we should always be anxious about falling and persist in humility, holding as certain that we are always inclined toward falling; but when we stand, we stand because the Lord guards us.

This anxiety about falling is the eighth degree in humility. In this psalm there is the voice of those same perfect persons who are treated in the preceding degrees, showing, in order to generate anxiety in us, that just as no one can become God’s house unless God builds it, and unless God guards it, so, after it has been built, it cannot stand.

“Unless the Lord guards,” etc. This first verse is placed beforehand as proof of what follows. Hence it is clear that the following verse must be explained first in this way: The perfect who are treated here say to their hearers: O you faithful, whose captivity has now been converted into freedom, always be anxious about falling, reckoning that through your own guardianship you are powerless to stand. For unless the Lord guards the city by his grace—that is, each perfect believer, who is called God’s city because he abounds in a manifold abundance of virtues, just as a city abounds in a multitude of citizens—the one who guards it watches in vain, that is, uselessly strives with vigilant reason to guard it from falling. This may be either some prelate, whose duty it is to be watchful in guarding his subjects, or the city itself.

It is certain from this that the city cannot be guarded unless the Lord guards it, because, first of all, unless the Lord builds the house—that is, unless the Lord builds each believer into a house through faith, the remission of sins, and virtues, a house in which he might dwell spiritually—the preachers who continually build it, now largely built, have labored in vain by preaching. The very people who are the house have also sometimes labored in vain by devoting themselves to good works, since they continually build themselves into a house for God through free will and good works. This means: The house could not be built unless the Lord were building it.

Since, therefore, O hearers, although you are a city, you are nevertheless so weak that you cannot stand unless the Lord guards you—for here you are always inclined toward falling—it is vain for you to rise before dawn, that is, before the other life, which is called “light” by antonomasia because in it illumination will be perfect, into confidence that you will not fall. Here you must always be humbled by anxiety about falling; but after you have sat down—that is, after your sitting, which is your humiliation, has ended in this life—for here you have been humbled by mortality and susceptibility to suffering, which are still punishments for sin—after the end, I say, of your sitting, after you come to the exaltation of immortality and impassibility, then at last rise from anxiety into confidence. For then, by the gift of divine grace, you will be so confirmed that you can no longer fall.

“Sitting” is used for “humiliation,” because those who sit are low and humble in body, so far as the body’s posture is concerned. You, I say, after you have sat down, rise—you who here eat the bread of sorrow, that is, you who here are continually refreshed by sorrow as by bread, namely, for whom it is a pleasant refreshment to grieve continually here over sins, just as bread is a pleasant and constant refreshment. Hence the Lord says: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh (Luke 6:21).”

He specifies when they will rise, as follows: Rise, I say, after you have sat down. That will be the time when you rise, when the Lord gives sleep to all his beloved—that is, eternal rest, which is understood by “sleep” because people rest during sleep. But lest that rest seem to be postponed too long, he adds, for the consolation of those who await it: He will give his beloved sleep, that is, rest. This rest will not be delayed long; rather, behold, after a short time the Lord’s inheritance will be given: immediately the Lord will give those who persevere that rest to possess by hereditary right. Hence in the Apocalypse: “Wait yet a little while, until the number of your fellow servants and brothers [conservants] is complete (Rev. 6:11).” That is rightly judged short and little which will eventually be brought to an end.

He specifies which Lord he means as follows: Behold, I say, the Lord’s inheritance—namely, behold the Son’s reward, by antonomasia; that is, behold the inheritance which will be the reward that the Lord the Son will lawfully give to those who strive, or the inheritance which is the Son’s reward, namely, which the Son himself already possesses by hereditary right.

He also specifies which son he means: The sons, I say, are the fruit of the virginal womb—that is, the son proceeding from the most blessed Virgin’s virginal womb became the fruit, or benefit, of that Virgin and of the whole human race. 524 This the woman recognized when, raising her voice from the crowd, she said: “Blessed is the womb that bore you (Luke 11:27).” For we customarily call that which is useful a “fruit.”

But because he had humbled the faithful who had already been converted into freedom by saying, “Unless the Lord guards,” and “It is vain for you,” etc., lest they consequently appear worthless, he intends also to commend them as follows: Although I said that it is vain for the faithful, whose captivity has been converted into freedom, to rise before the light, nevertheless they should not for that reason be judged worthless.

For just as arrows in the hand of a mighty man—that is, in the hand of a strong archer—are effective for killing, so the sons of those who have been shaken off—that is, these faithful, who are the sons of the apostles—are powerful for destroying the wicked through their preaching, insofar as the wicked are wicked. The apostles are appropriately called “those who shake off,” because through their preaching they shook the faithful from the mouth of the most ravenous wolf, the devil, and from the mass of the lost. This is like vigorous soldiers who, by force, shake booty away from enemies, and like harvesters who are commonly called “those who shake off,” because they shake the grains from the chaff by blows.

Nor are the faithful, now made free, proved powerful only because they are the sons of those who have been shaken off; this is also shown by the fact that, since they are the sons of those who have been shaken off, that blessed man—blessed both here and in the future—will fulfill through them the desire he has received through example and teaching, namely, the desire to do good. Since it is clear that this man is made blessed through them, there is no doubt that they themselves are especially shown to be blessed.

That blessed man will be evident in this respect: He will not be put to shame—that is, he will not blush at being defeated—when he speaks in debate with his enemies, unbelievers and heretics, at the gate, that is, openly. This is understood through the expression “at the gate,” because citizens customarily conduct public judgments at the gates of cities. Or it may be understood in this way: When he speaks in debate with his enemies at the gate, that is, not as though they were enemies outside the gate, but as though they were at the gate—that is, in the faith, which is the gate and entrance to the other virtues.

## ON PSALM 127

The title of the hundred twenty-seventh psalm: “A Song of Ascents.” Having shown that, unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain—and that from this the anxiety of falling should arise, which is the eighth degree—the perfect discuss the ninth degree in the following psalm. It is this: to fear the Lord with chaste fear, that is, to love him in such a way that one walks in his ways through fear. This fear must be held in view of the consideration that no one can stand unless the Lord guards him. The perfect treated in this psalm invite their hearers to this degree of fear, showing that those who fear the Lord are blessed both here and in the future.

It should be noted that although chaste fear could have been understood in some of the preceding higher degrees, it differs here in this respect: here that fear is understood which is held in view of the consideration that no one can stand unless the Lord guards him.

“Blessed are all”—both here and in the future—“who fear the Lord”; as though he were saying: Since, as was said in the preceding psalm, no one can stand unless the Lord guards him, you who have now ascended to the point of recognizing that no one can stand otherwise, fear the Lord with chaste fear in view of this consideration—that is, love him.

For blessed are all, both here and in the future, who fear the Lord; and those, I say, who fear him in such a way that, existing in his ways—that is, in his commandments, which are the ways to life—they walk, that is, advance in those ways by fulfilling them perseveringly. He makes an apostrophe to each of his hearers in order to incite him more strongly to this fear, showing what benefit will arise from this fear both here and in the future.

I say that blessed are all who fear the Lord. And behold what blessedness you, whoever you are, will have both here and in the future if you fear him. Truly you are already blessed here in hope, and in the future it will be well with you—that is, you will be blessed through the experience of the reality itself. You are blessed, I say, here already in hope, and it will be well with you 525 in the future, because you will eat the labors of your hands—that is, you will be spiritually refreshed by the labors of your hands, namely, by the eternal blessedness which you will acquire through the labors of your good works—like a diligent laborer who, working with his hands in summer, acquires what will feed him in winter.

You are also blessed in the present, because your wife—that is, your sensuality, which will be subject to reason as a wife is subject to her husband, and is therefore called a wife—will be abundant in good works, like a vine abundant in clusters. Your wife, I say, will be abundant, and this in the sides of your house—that is, in the office of the sides of your house, namely, in the activity of the limbs, which are called the sides of the body. The body is the house of the soul, because the limbs are the outer parts of the body and surround the body itself, just as the sides of a house are its exterior parts and surround the house itself. Through the activity of the limbs, sensuality indeed produces good works, like a vine which, situated in the sunlit sides of a house, is more fruitful.

It should be noted that when sensuality is subjected to rationality, both are at rest; but when sensuality prevails, both are driven from their rest. This was foreshadowed in Adam and Eve, his wife. While Adam prevailed over Eve, both remained in paradise; afterward, when Eve prevailed over Adam, both were expelled from paradise.

Your wife, I say, will be abundant in sons—that is, in good works—and your sons who will be born from that wife, namely good works, will be like young olive plants, that is, resembling young olive trees. For just as a young olive tree, which is small, gradually grows into a mature olive, so good works, performed in the peace of ecclesiastical concord, will gradually grow through this peace until they bring the faithful to that perfect peace of the eternal homeland. Peace is appropriately understood through the olive, because the olive is a sign of peace.

Your sons, I say, will be like young olive plants, existing around your table—that is, around Christ, who is your table, namely, your spiritual refreshment. This means: I say that those sons of yours are comparable to young olive plants who are around Christ—that is, directing themselves toward Christ and begotten for his honor. This is said by comparison with children sitting around their father’s table so that they may be nourished from it.

I said that the one who fears the Lord will eat the labors of his hands in the future, and that here his wife will be abundant like a vine, and his sons like young olive plants. Behold, therefore, in this way, as has been shown concerning the present, the man who fears the Lord with chaste fear will be blessed—that is, made blessed.

Why then, O hearer, whoever you are, fear the Lord. If you do this, may the Lord bless you—that is, exalt you with blessedness. And may this happen from Zion—that is, from the fact that you will be Zion, contemplating future things and not attending to present things. May he bless you in this way: here may you see throughout all the days of your life the good of the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, goods resembling the goods of Jerusalem—so that you may rest from vices and burn with love of God, like the citizens of Jerusalem, although not with equal perfection. Hence Prosper says: “In this life rest has been granted to many saints.”

See here, I say, the good of Jerusalem. And in the future, through the experience of the reality itself, may you see [Col. 1332A] the sons of your sons—that is, sons to be begotten by your sons, namely, the reward of eternal goods, which are called “sons of sons,” that is, of good works, because they will proceed from them as sons proceed from fathers.

He explains what he means by “sons of sons” as follows: You will see, I say, the sons of sons, namely, eternal peace to be granted over Israel—that is, granted by the higher disposition of God—to those who here are Israel. I call it “sons” in the plural although it is one thing, because many will share in it.

## ON PSALM 128

The title of the hundred twenty-eighth psalm: “A Song of Ascents.” After the perfect had invited their hearers to fear, which is the ninth degree, because this fear cannot be idle but is accompanied by good action—which is indeed the blessed reward of this fear, and which, as was shown in the preceding psalm, is multiplied by the Lord for those who fear him—and because, on account of this good action and fear, bodily tribulations often arise from unbelievers or false believers, the perfect, treating of this psalm, exhort their hearers to unconquerable steadfastness, so that they may not fail amid these tribulations. This steadfastness is indeed the tenth degree; but they should be so steadfast in chaste fear and good work that, following the example of those perfect persons, they may truly say:

“Saepe expugnaverunt me, etc.”, as though they were saying: We have exhorted all the faithful to fear and to walk by doing good in the ways of the Lord. But since, on this account, assaults of tribulations will arise from sinners, we also exhort each faithful person who, after ascending to this fear and good works, becomes Israel, not to fail in these assaults, but to be so steadfast that now—that is, immediately and without delay—he may truly say to the praise of God and in thanksgiving, once he cannot be overcome:

“They have often assailed me,” that is, “they have attacked me.” He does not specify who the attackers are; for it is clear that the good are attacked not by the good but only by the wicked. “They have attacked me,” I say. “And this occurred from my youth,” that is, they attacked me because I had put off the old man with his deeds and, putting on the new man, who was created according to God, together with his deeds, had become young through the fear and good works of that new man.

Or, “from my youth,” that is, from the time of youth, namely, from the time when I acquired strength through fear and the other preceding stages; this strength is signified by youth because outstanding strength is found in the young. In an excess of rejoicing, he makes an apostrophe and adds: “Often, I say, they have assailed me from my youth.” And therefore they have done so often, because they were never able at the outset to prevail against me. The whole sense is as though he were saying: “Often they have attacked me from my youth, and in no way were they able to prevail against me.”

He then explains who attacked him, how they attacked him, and what they accomplished by their attack, as follows: “They attacked me,” I say, and indeed in this manner: “Sinners have worked upon my back,” by antonomasia. By “back” it is understood that they also worked upon the other members. When he says that they worked upon his back, he indicates the violence of the scourging: they devoted themselves to scourging him continually and violently, just as craftsmen vigorously and incessantly strike the anvil with hammers while working. By “back,” which is a part of the body, he also indicates that they attacked only that part of him; and because they accomplished something in the attack itself, he uses the likeness of craftsmen, who produce something by their work.

He therefore shows what they accomplished by their attack, adding: “They worked upon my back,” I say, “and by working they prolonged their iniquity.” When their iniquity was already great, while they had possessed only the will to attack, once they had worked upon my back by scourging it, they prolonged their iniquity, that is, they made it greater. For doing evil is worse than merely wishing to do evil. The expression is drawn from the likeness of iron, or some other metal, which is lengthened and extended by being worked.

When he says that the iniquity of the persecutors was prolonged, he teaches by contrast that the justice of the one who endured patiently was prolonged through the same working. Since, then, they worked and prolonged their iniquity, the Lord, who is both almighty and just and therefore must enact justice, will in the future cut down the necks of sinners—that is, he will cut down and destroy the sinners themselves forever because of their “necks,” that is, because of their stubbornness, namely, their prides, which are understood by “necks,” since they are signified by the raising of the neck.

But lest sinners be cut down, let them be confounded with a good shame at their proud conduct, and thus let them turn backward after us, so that all those sinners who hate Zion—that is, who persecuted us not because of merit but out of hatred while we were Zion—may become our imitators. For if they refuse to be converted, I grant concerning them what is just: namely, that by the just judgment of God they become dry of every virtue before they are taken from this life. And not in just any manner, but “like the grass of the roofs,” which, before it is torn up by anyone, has completely dried up of itself, since it has no foundation in the earth. So may they also, lacking Christ as their foundation, wither inwardly even while they live. By this he deters them from their iniquity.

When he says “before it is plucked up,” he intimates that sinners do not wish to depart from this life, as the just do, but must be plucked up—that is, drawn out by a certain force and against their will.

“Let them become,” I say, “like the grass of the roofs.” Since that grass is useless, the one who mows it will not fill his hand with it: the reaper, gathering the ears of grain and other useful grasses, will not gather any of this grass so as to fill his hand with it. Nor will the one who gathers sheaves of other useful grass or of grain fill his lap with it; that is, he will not gather much of it so that he can fill his lap with it, as he sometimes gathers enough good grass or grain to fill his hand, and sometimes enough to fill his lap.

This is to say: The grass of the roofs is so useless that no one will take the trouble to gather a little of it to fill his hand, or much of it to fill his lap. The same will happen to sinners. For when the angels appointed to reap the faithful gather some people from this life in such a way as to collect a small amount—namely, the less perfect, after the likeness of one mowing a little grass or grain in order to fill his hand—and gather others in such a way as to collect a great amount, namely, the perfect, after the likeness of one mowing much grass or grain in order to fill his lap, they will gather sinners neither as a small amount nor as a great amount.

And therefore they will not be gathered, because those who were passing beyond this life—namely, the preachers who were passing through and despising this life, “shearing toward the homeland” and not clinging to its pleasures—did not say to those sinners: “The blessing of the Lord be upon you.”

It should be noted that both by voice and by affection they said this concerning all, the good as well as the impious, so that God’s blessing might be upon everyone. Otherwise they would not be perfect, since the Lord says: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. III, 44).

Moreover, when he says, “They did not say: The blessing of the Lord be upon you,” this is a concise expression, as though he were saying: “They did not say”—that is, by the word of their preaching they did not bring it about that they could truly say, “The blessing of the Lord, produced through faith and virtues, has come upon you, O sinners.” This is to say: By the words of their preaching they were unable to lead them to such goodness that they would be worthy of divine blessing.

He explains how they did not bless them as follows: “I say: They did not say: The blessing of the Lord be upon you,” namely, “They did not say: We have blessed you who are placed in the name of the Lord.” That is, by the word of their preaching they did not bring this about in those who were hardened: that they could truly say, “We have blessed you”—that is, “we have exalted you,” namely, “we were the cause of your being exalted”—by placing you through our preaching “in the name of the Lord,” that is, in the Lord’s honor, producing this in you by preaching, so that you might devote yourselves to the Lord’s honor.

This is to say: By their preaching the preachers could not lead them to honor God by living well, and thus to be blessed by him.

## IN PSALM CXXIX

**Title of the hundred and twenty-ninth. A Song of Ascents.**

Having shown the tenth stage, namely, the steadfastness that must be maintained in tribulation, in the following psalm the perfect speak of the eleventh: the intense cry that must be addressed to God by those who are in the depths of tribulations, lest the Lord allow them to fail by observing their iniquities. They would indeed fail if God wished to observe their iniquities in order to exact punishment. For no one is so holy that no iniquity can be found in him.

Therefore, in this psalm, the perfect speak so as to provide an example to those who, through fear and obedience to the Lord, have been placed in tribulation. They show that they cried out to the Lord in this way, considering that, if the Lord wished to observe iniquities, no one could remain steadfast. They also show that they hoped in the Lord, not because of their merits but because he himself is propitious, so that they may instruct others by their example to place all their hope not in their own merits but in the Lord’s mercy.

“Out of the depths, etc.”, as though he were saying: Those who have now reached steadfastness amid tribulations, lest they fail in their steadfastness because of those very tribulations, should cry out to the Lord from the depth of their tribulations, and should do so following my example. For I, placed in the depths of tribulations, cried out after the likeness of one placed in the depths of the waves who cries out to those on the shore above, asking them to come to his aid.

From those depths of tribulations I cried out—that is, I uttered an intense cry—saying also with my mouth: “O Lord, hear my voice.” “Hear,” I say, and not faintly; but just as I prayed with an intense cry, so also let your ears become attentive—that is, let the power of your mercy, through which you mercifully hear those who pray to you, become attentive to the voice of my supplication. That is, let it hear intensely my voice by which I beseech you; let it be attentive in such a way that you intensely fulfill what I intensely request, namely, that you preserve me unharmed in the depths of tribulations.

Or, “to the voice of my supplication,” that is, to the voice proceeding from the supplication of my intense inward cry.

It should be noted that when he says apostrophically to God, “Out of the depths I cried to you, O Lord,” he does so in thanksgiving, because God made him cry out. By this he instructs his hearers that, when they become criers, they should give thanks to God for the very fact that they are crying out.

“Let your ears,” I say, “become attentive.” But lest they fail to be attentive, “do not observe my iniquities,” that is, do not keep them in your memory as though you were planning to punish them and thus permit me to fail in my steadfastness.

For if you observe both my iniquities and those of others in order to avenge them, O Lord, “who will endure you, O Lord?” That is, who, while enduring tribulations for your sake, will await you as rewarder? No one. It is as though he were saying: Do not observe my iniquities, so that you may permit me to fail because of them. For if you observe mine, it is clear, by analogy, that you will also observe those of others; and thus no one will henceforth endure for you without failing and, as a result, await you as rewarder.

Although I say, “Who will endure?”, nevertheless I have endured you, O Lord—that is, by enduring tribulations for your sake I have awaited you as rewarder. And I have done so not because of my merits, but because “with you there is propitiation,” that is, in your nature: it belongs to you by nature to be propitious toward us. I have also awaited you as rewarder because of your law—that is, because of your conditional ordinance, which I have fulfilled.

For you established: “Forgive your debtors, and it will be forgiven you” (Matt. VI, 12), and this I have fulfilled as far as I was able. Or, universally, “because of your law,” that is, because of all the precepts of your law, insofar as I have fulfilled them.

But in order to instruct his hearers to endure the Lord, he makes an apostrophe to them, saying that he endured the Lord, as follows: “I said, O hearers, that I have endured the Lord, and I speak truly. For my soul has endured him in his word”—that is, in consideration of his word. Because he promised that he would reward those who endure for him, my soul, by enduring tribulations for his sake, awaited him as rewarder.

And my soul did not hope in him as rewarder only in consideration of his promise; my soul also “hoped in the Lord”—that is, in consideration of the Lord—because I considered him to be Lord of all and therefore hoped that he could reward me.

“My soul,” I say, “hoped in the Lord, beginning to hope from the morning watch,” that is, from the time when, coming toward morning—that is, toward the brightness of faith—I began to guard myself from vices. And I shall hope in the Lord perseveringly “until night,” that is, until the end of this life.

And because I have hoped and shall always hope, let everyone who is Israel hope in the Lord after my example. Let him hope not because of his merits but because of the Lord’s gratuitous mercy. For “with the Lord there is mercy,” that is, in the Lord’s nature: it is natural to him to have mercy on those who hope in him.

Let him hope for this reason also: “With him there is plentiful redemption,” that is, because by his death he will redeem all who hope in him, both Gentiles and Jews. Or, “plentiful redemption” with respect to vices. For he redeemed us not only from original sins but also from actual sins.

And therefore hope still, because “he himself will redeem Israel”—that is, at the end of life he will save each person who is Israel—“from all his iniquities,” namely, although after the remission of sins in baptism each person who is Israel commits many iniquities. “For in many things,” as the Apostle James testifies, “we all offend” (James III, 2). By the redemption of his death he will save the penitent Israelite from those iniquities at the departure from this life, so that he may not perish because of them.

## IN PSALM CXXX

[Col. 1336D]

**Title of the hundred and thirtieth. A Song of Ascents.**

After treating the eleventh stage, namely, the cry amid bodily tribulation lest there be failure there, in the following psalm the perfect show, for the instruction of their hearers, the twelfth stage, acting apostrophically toward God in thanksgiving. They show that they always persevere in humility, which is the twelfth stage, so that they may ascribe the wonders of the higher stages to which they have already ascended not to themselves but to the Lord.

“Lord, my heart is not exalted,” etc., as though he were saying: When anyone has ascended to these higher stages, he must not become proud because of them; rather, he must then possess humility concerning them, judging that they come not from himself but from the Lord. This indeed is to ascend the twelfth stage.

Let them have this humility after my example. For although I have already ascended these higher stages, O Lord, “my heart has not been exalted” from them into pride, nor have my outward eyes been lifted up proudly; that is, no pride has appeared as a result in the elevation of my eyes. Sometimes pride lies hidden in the heart so that it does not appear outwardly; sometimes it is marked by the elevation of the eyes.

Because he had stated indefinitely, “My heart has not been exalted,” he determines the point in which it was not exalted as follows: “My heart has not been exalted,” I say, and I do not merely deny that it was exalted in small matters; “nor have I walked in great things, nor in wondrous things above me,” namely, I, placed in the great and wondrous higher stages, which are not from me but above me—that is, from the gift of God, who is above me—I have not walked, that is, I have not advanced myself proudly in those great and wondrous things, imagining that they came from me.

This is to say: I have not become proud at the sight of those great and wondrous things. Nor have I merely refrained from walking in great and wondrous things; I have also humbly judged them to come from you.

But if I did not judge humbly and, on the contrary, exalted my soul—that is, became proud in my soul—regarding these things as coming from me, then, just as a child who is still lying against its mother and being nursed by her dies if it is weaned—that is, separated from the milk—for it cannot yet live by itself, so may the fitting recompense of perishing come upon my soul; that is, may my soul perish.

He devotes himself to destruction under this condition in order to withdraw his hearers from pride, teaching that they will perish in themselves unless they judge humbly.

I have said that my heart was not exalted at the sight of the higher and greater things, but that I judged humbly. Therefore, after my example, let everyone who is Israel not trust proudly in himself, but let everyone who is Israel hope humbly that all great things are “in the Lord,” that is, in the Lord’s gift, not in his own merits.

“Let him hope,” I say, “beginning from this time,” that is, from the present moment, and persevering in hope until the future age.

Or it may be read in this way: “My heart has not been exalted,” I say, or “I have not walked”—that is, I have not advanced myself proudly—“in great things, nor in wondrous things,” that is, in considering great and wondrous things, stretching myself above myself so as to make myself greater than I was.

Hence the Lord says: “When you have done all that has been commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants” (Luke XVII, 10).

Therefore, whoever is Israel, following my example, should not be proud but should judge humbly; and thus let Israel hope for a reward “in the Lord,” that is, in consideration of the Lord: namely, by considering him to be Lord and powerful enough to reward. Otherwise no reward would be hoped for.

“Let Israel hope,” I say, “in the Lord, beginning from this time and persevering until the future age.” This is explained as above.

## IN PSALM CXXXI

[Col. 1338A]

**Title of the hundred and thirty-first. A Song of Ascents.**

After treating of the humility that must be maintained in great and wondrous things, which is the twelfth stage, the perfect also treat in the following psalm of the thirteenth stage. This stage is nothing other than the fact that they have now ascended to such dignity that they are already resolved to live in conformity with the apostles, dwelling together as one and possessing everything in common.

And because they cannot attain this by their own merits, they pray that they may attain it through the merits of Christ, their head, who was meek and, in all things, obedient to the Father, as he firmly promised.

They say that they pray with this confidence because the Lord the Father swore to David, Christ, that he would place upon his throne one from the fruit of his womb, and because the Lord chose Zion, saying: “This is my rest,” etc.

Here I call the whole of this a stage: both their resolve to live in conformity with the apostles and their prayer to attain this through the merit of David, Christ, in his meekness. They treat of this resolve and prayer with the intention of inviting their hearers, by their example, to ascend to this stage of resolve and prayer.

“Remember, O Lord, David,” etc., as though he were saying: O hearers, after you have ascended the higher stages, strive to ascend to this one also, so that you may resolve to live in conformity with the apostles and pray to attain this through the merit of Christ, the true David, in his meekness.

Take me as an example in this matter. For after I resolved to live in conformity with the apostles, I prayed to the Lord the Father concerning the attainment of this in the following way: Grant me what I have resolved upon, since my merits are not sufficient to attain it:

“Remember, O Lord the Father, David, Christ, my head, strong of hand, who acted manfully in his obedience; so that you may reward in me the merit of his manliness and strength, granting me through him what I have resolved upon and for which I pray.

And remember all his meekness,” namely, that in all things he was meek and patient, returning evil to no one for evil and never rejecting the yoke of the Lord’s commandments. Reward in me the merit of his meekness, granting what I have resolved upon and for which I pray.

Or this verse may be read without taking “David” according to the interpretation of the name, as follows: “Remember, O Lord, David, Christ, so that for love of him, whose member I am, I may attain what I have resolved upon. And remember all his meekness,” that is, keep in mind all his obedience, completed with meekness, so that through the merit of his meekness you may permit me to attain what I have resolved upon and for which I pray.

Isaiah speaks of this meekness: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 7).

“Remember,” I say, “his meekness,” that is, his meek obedience, completed “as he swore to the Lord the Father, as he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob,” that is, to the Lord the Father, who is the God of Jacob, that is, of manly wrestlers, whom it was fitting for him to obey, since he himself was Jacob above all others.

He does not say “he swore and vowed a vow” to indicate that he himself made an oath and vow, but by these two expressions he intimates that he firmly resolved within himself that this meek obedience should be fulfilled. By these two means—namely, by a vow or an oath—future things are customarily established firmly.

When he calls the Lord the Father the God of Jacob, he thereby invites his hearers to strive to become Jacob.

“He swore,” I say, “and he vowed a vow,” that is, he firmly resolved within himself, saying:

“If I enter the tabernacle,” that is, the dwelling of my house, “and if, having entered the tabernacle, I ascend upon the bed of my couch,” that is, upon a bed spread with cushions or other coverings. We call the bed itself the “bedstead”; the “couch” refers to the coverings and cushions placed upon it.
