“And after I have ascended upon the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes, and even what is less than this, if I give slumber to my eyelids”—that is, the briefest sleep, allowing my eyelids for a little while to close in sleep—and “if, even less than this, I give rest to my temples,” for the temples are weighed down by sleep before the eyelids close in slumber;

“If I admit these earlier gifts of repose, until I complete what has been enjoined upon me”—namely, until through my death and my preachers I find a place for the Lord the Father, that is, until I find people who are a place, or spiritual dwelling, for the Lord the Father, whom he may inhabit through assisting grace, and until I find such a place as is a tabernacle for the God of Jacob, that is, a good life serving the Lord the Father, whom one must serve since he is the God of Jacob, that is, of strong wrestlers—then I am unworthy of reward.

All these things are said only by way of likeness. The equivalent concise expression would be this:

Just as a good soldier, until he has completed the purpose of his military service, does not enter the tabernacle of his house in order to ascend his bed and satisfy himself by resting for a long time in sleep, or at least to rest a little by slumbering, or to give his temples a brief period of repose, so neither will I rest much or little—that is, cease—until I have completed the purpose of my enjoined obedience: namely, until through my death and through the teaching of my preachers I have acquired for the Lord people from both Jews and Gentiles whom he may inhabit spiritually and who may serve him through their good life.

With these words of Christ inserted to give authority and weight, the perfect, again speaking in their own person, confirm that he has already fulfilled what he resolved upon, as follows:

I say that he swore and vowed a vow to the Lord, saying that he would find a place, that is, a seat, for the Lord—namely, the Church. And behold, it is evident that he has already acquired a seat for the Lord. For we have heard that this seat, that is, the Church, is already in Ephrata, that is, in the Jewish people, which is suitably signified by Ephrata.

Ephrata is indeed a place in Judea, which is also called Bethlehem. Ephrata is also interpreted as “mirror.” The Jewish people, therefore, are suitably signified by Ephrata, because they were a people that looked into a mirror, doing all carnal things “through a mirror and in an enigma,” since they did everything with an obscure signification.

When he says, “We have heard that it is in Ephrata,” the pronoun “it” refers to the “place” mentioned above, where he had said, “a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.” This is certainly not inappropriate, even though “place” is masculine and “it” feminine. The relative pronoun is not determined according to grammatical gender but according to the meaning of the word itself. For when he says “place,” it is the same as if he had said “seat”; according to this equivalence, the relative word “it” refers to “place.”

I say that we have heard that it is in Ephrata. And not only have we heard that it is in Ephrata, but we have also found that it—the Lord’s seat, the Church—is “in the fields of the forest,” that is, in fields made from a forest, namely, in the peoples of the Gentiles. Although previously uncultivated like a forest, they have been made cultivated from their uncultivated state, in the manner of fields.

The whole meaning is as though it had been expressed in this way: We have now heard that the Church exists both among the Gentiles and among the Jews.

Since above he had prayed, saying, “Remember, O Lord, David,” without showing the resolve for which he prayed, he now shows it when he adds: “We will enter,” etc. The passage is adapted as follows:

I say: “Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness,” so that through the merit of his meekness you may grant us to attain what we have resolved upon. For we have resolved upon this: “We will enter,” through obedience, “into his tabernacle,” that is, into David’s service.

They explain how they will enter as follows: In this manner we will enter—that is, we will honor him with heart, mouth, and deed—remaining in that place, that is, in that state of life in which his feet stood, that is, in which they perseveringly lived. His “feet” are the apostles and his other disciples, who are called his feet because they carried him into the knowledge of human beings.

This is to say: Just as his feet served him by striving toward unity of faith and concord, dwelling together and possessing everything in common, since “they had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV, 32), so we have resolved to serve him, dwelling together as one and possessing everything in common.

But so that we may enter his tabernacle and adore in the place where his feet stood, “arise, O Lord the Father”—that is, appear exalted and powerful—“and go to your rest.” By this he asks that you manifest your power, so that you may come not locally but according to your operative grace to us, whom by your coming you will make your rest: you will make us so holy that you may rest in us, that is, take delight in us, as someone takes delight in repose.

“Arise,” I say, and through your rising “let the ark of your sanctification also rise,” that is, let your ark be exalted. This is the ark that you sanctified through your death and resurrection and through the remission of sins. Let us also be exalted, for we are called your Church and your ark, since the Church was prefigured by the Lord’s ark.

For just as manna was contained figuratively in the ark, and manna was spiritual food, so in the Church there is the spiritual food of the Lord’s body, which was prefigured by manna; and there is also the bread of understanding, signified by that same manna.

The law was also contained there, and here likewise both laws are found, namely, the new and the old. Aaron’s rod was there as well; here too there is the kingdom of Christ, that is, the kingdom given by Christ to the faithful, so that each person may be ruler of himself.

For by the rod, through contiguity, we understand the scepter, and by the scepter the kingdom, since it is a sign of kingship.

“Let it rise,” I say—that is, let the Church, the ark of sanctification, be exalted, namely, let us be exalted. And let your priests, namely, us, “put on justice.” For we sacrifice ourselves to you by living well, and therefore we are called your priests. Let us put on justice emphatically—that is, let us be greatly filled with and adorned by the justice of virtues and good works—after the likeness of a body that is surrounded and adorned by clothing.

This putting on of justice was prefigured in the Levitical priests, who at the time of sacrifice were clothed in a linen ephod, a long tunic, and other insignia. For just as they were adorned by those insignia visible outwardly, so we, the priests of the New Testament, will be adorned when justice appears outwardly through good works.

But not only should your priests, namely, us, put on justice; those same priests, being your holy ones—that is, sanctified by you through death and the forgiveness of sins—should also “exult in the gift of innocence.” Give them innocence, so that they may exult in it.

We do not pray to be clothed with justice and to exult in innocence because of confidence in our merits, but because of “David your servant,” that is, because of the merits of Christ, the true David, who according to his humanity was your servant, devoted and obedient to you in all things, whose members we are through faith.

We pray that you give us justice and innocence, and thus we will be conformed to Christ “in face,” that is, in the beauty of virtues, which is understood through the face because outward beauty is signified in the outward face.

But after we have attained Christ’s face, do not turn away—that is, do not permit that face, that beauty of your Christ, to be turned away from us through sins.

He makes an apostrophe to his hearers in order to show that he prays not from distrust and thereby urge them to pray for the same thing:

We pray, O hearers, that we may put on justice and innocence, and that Christ’s face may not be turned away from us. We pray for this confidently. For the Lord the Father swore to the Lord David, Christ his Son, “the truth”—that is, he swore by himself, who is truth. He swore, that is, he promised most firmly, in the manner of one swearing, that he would not frustrate him, that is, would not deceive him by failing to fulfill what he had sworn.

I say that he swore, saying: “From the fruit of your womb I will place upon your throne,” that is, I will cause some of your spiritual sons to reign with you in eternal blessedness in the future, after the likeness of a king who places upon his royal throne the son whom he wishes to reign with him.

He calls spiritual sons “the fruit of the womb,” not because they were generated from his womb, but after the likeness of sons, who are the fruit of the womb.

When he says “from the fruit,” rather than “the fruit,” he intimates that not all, but only a part, will be placed upon the throne. For “not everyone who says, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII, 24). All who come to faith are indeed sons, but not all will be saved.

Or: “From the fruit of your womb I will place some upon your throne here,” that is, I will cause them to reign with you, so that by living well they may rule themselves in conformity with you, who while living here ruled yourself well.

“Some,” I say, “from the fruit of your womb,” that is, from your sons, “I will place upon your throne.”

Yet I promise this under the following condition: if your sons and the sons of your sons—that is, their imitators—have kept by fulfilling my testament, that is, my promise, which they promised me under the testimony of their sponsors; and if, that is, they have kept my testimonies, that is, my commandments. I do not mean the commandments of the Old Testament, but these commandments that I will teach them through David, my Son, namely, the testimonies of the New Law.

“They will sit upon your throne,” that is, they will reign with you here by living well and ruling themselves in conformity with you “until the future age,” that is, until the end of this life.

Or, “they will sit upon your throne” in the future, that is, they will reign with you in blessedness, “until the age,” that is, forever.

Here “testament” and “testimonies” mean the same thing. But when he says “testament,” he intimates that the Lord’s commandments must be fulfilled because they have promised to fulfill them; when he says “these testimonies that I will teach them,” he intimates that they must be fulfilled because he himself teaches them.

With the words of the Father’s promise inserted to show its certainty, the perfected, speaking in their own person, demonstrate that the fact that the sons of David will sit upon David’s throne does not result from their merits but from God’s gratuitous election. Thus he says:

The Lord the Father says that David’s sons will sit upon his throne, and this will not happen because of their merits but by the gratuitous election of the Lord the Father. For the Lord the Father chose Zion—that is, the whole Church, which he made to be Zion—and chose it for himself as a dwelling, that is, so that he might dwell in it, according to his unworking grace. Hence we read: “Those whom he chose (Rom. 8:29), these he also called [predestined].” He chose Zion for himself, saying: “This, namely Zion, is my rest,” that is, my delight, “unto the age of the age,” that is, unto the age to come.

“Here I shall dwell,” that is, in this Zion I shall dwell according to unworking grace. And this is not because of Zion’s merits, but solely because I freely chose it for salvation. Since I have chosen Zion, I shall bless her widow—that is, those from that Zion who are called widows because they have been desolated of earthly things, to which they have now renounced their claim, just as a widow is desolated by a husband who has died. I shall bless them, that is, I shall exalt them here, and I shall do so blessing them, that is, remaining in that blessing. And her poor—that is, those same people whom I called widows, who are also poor in spirit, that is, humble, and therefore worthy of blessing and satiety—I shall satisfy in soul with loaves, that is, with manifold gifts of spiritual understanding. These will be loaves for them, that is, exceedingly sweet refreshments, just as loaves are exceedingly sweet refreshments.

He explains how he will bless them as follows. In this way indeed I shall bless them: I shall exalt those from Zion who are widows, namely, those same people who are her priests, when by living well they offer themselves as a sacrifice of praise. I shall clothe them with salvation, that is, I shall surround them and adorn them with conformity to Christ the Savior, so that they may be conformed to him in the exaltation of righteousness, insofar as this is possible. And they, being his holy priests—that is, sanctified through Christ’s death and the forgiveness of sins—shall exult with exultation, that is, with innocence. This is called “exultation” because it is the cause of exultation. Or perhaps he adds “with exultation” for emphasis, as though he were saying: “They shall exult exceedingly.”

These priests of his, I say, I shall clothe with salvation. In the future, however, I shall bring forth there the horn of David, that is, I shall extend to those same people the exalted glory that is already in David, my Son, so that they may possess the same exaltation, although to a lesser degree. Meanwhile, here, through the illumination of grace, I have prepared for them a lamp, that is, a vessel of light—a lamp, I say, for my Christ—in which he himself might shine upon the world through his teaching.

He properly says not “light” but “lamp,” since they themselves are not light but vessels of that light and its ministers. For we call a vessel a lamp. Hence it is written of John the Baptist: “He was not that light, but in order to bear witness concerning the light (John 1:7).”

In them, I say, I shall bring forth the horn of David. But his enemies—namely, the persecutors of the widow—I shall clothe, by emphasis, with shame; that is, I shall surround them both in body and in soul with the shame of eternal perdition. But my sanctification—that is, my widow sanctified by me, founded upon that David, Christ, in faith and conformity, and relying upon him—shall blossom. That is, from the flower of good works it shall pass into the fruits of eternal reward, by analogy with a flower that passes into fruit.

Or it may be understood as follows: I shall not only bring forth there the horn of David, but also his enemies—that is, the persecutors of his widow. In part, indeed, I shall clothe them, that is, I shall fill them here with shame, namely, with the shame of sins, and thus they shall be converted. But my sanctification—that is, my sanctified widow, founded upon that David in faith and conformity—shall blossom, that is, shall flower completely and perseveringly in good works, and through this shall reach the horn of David in the future.

## On Psalm 132

The title of the one hundred and thirty-second psalm: “A Song of Ascents.”

In the preceding psalm the thirteenth degree was shown, namely, that which they arranged in conformity with the apostles: dwelling together in unity in order to serve God. They prayed to attain this. In the following psalm the perfected speak of the fourteenth degree, which is nothing other than what they prayed for above, namely, that the brothers dwell together in unity. They declare this to be good and pleasant, so that they may draw their hearers toward ascending to this degree.

[Col. 1344A] “Behold, how good,” and so forth, as though they were saying:

You who have already ascended the preceding degrees, ascend also to this one, so that you too may dwell together as brothers and thus serve God. From us, indeed, take an example. For behold, it is already evident that we dwell together, having everything in common; and we dwell together in such a way that we are brothers—not wicked brothers, but spiritual brothers, tending together toward faith and concord. Otherwise dwelling together would not be beneficial.

And since we already dwell together, behold, it is present and evident among us how good—that is, more than exceedingly useful—and how pleasant—that is, more than exceedingly delightful—it is for us brothers to dwell together, tending toward unity of faith and concord. If this dwelling together were simply good, it ought to be desired. How much more, then, when it is both good and pleasant!

They show from what this dwelling together can be proved to be good and pleasant, as follows:

It is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together in unity, like ointment—that is, like a spiritual gift. It is proved to be good and pleasant because it is a spiritual gift. It is called ointment because through it we are spiritually anointed while dwelling together, so that we may be our own kings and priests, sacrificing ourselves to God by a good life, after the likeness of kings and priests, who are anointed at the time of their ordination.

“Like ointment,” I say, “existing upon the head,” that is, in the power of Christ the Head. This ointment is possessed only as a gift from the Head. That ointment descends from the gift of the Head upon the beard—that is, upon all who are good, strong against vices, and manly in conduct. They are fittingly signified by the beard, since a man becomes strong and reaches manhood when he becomes bearded.

He explains the beard itself in its several parts as follows. It descends, I say, upon the beard, namely, upon Aaron’s beard—that is, upon Christ’s manly and strong ones, namely, the apostles and disciples, the other early followers of Christ. They are called Christ’s beard by antonomasia, although all good people can also be called his beard, because those early followers were more manly and stronger. After the Lord’s ascension they are said to have dwelt together in Jerusalem for many days and to have had one heart and one soul.

Aaron was the high priest and the chief of all the priests in the Old Testament. His name is interpreted as “mountainous.” Therefore Christ is rightly understood through Aaron: Christ, being the chief and highest of all priests, was also mountainous, that is, exalted upon the lofty mountain of virtues.

Or “mountainous” may refer to one who came from the mountain, that is, from the heights into the world, sent by God the Father for the salvation of human beings. Hence he himself says: “You are from below; I am from above (John 8:23).”

And the ointment does not descend only upon Aaron’s beard; it also descends from Aaron’s beard to the hem of his garment, that is, upon the martyrs. Since they were pre-eminent after the apostles, they should be called the hem in God’s garment, that is, those who are higher in the Church, just as the hem is the upper part of a garment. The Church is called God’s garment because its adornment is like the garment of the body.

It should be noted that Aaron’s beard and the hem of the garment are parts of the beard that he had mentioned universally when he said that the ointment descended upon the beard.

They also show that this dwelling together, which he had demonstrated to be a spiritual gift, is gratuitous, as follows:

We said that this proves dwelling together to be good and pleasant, because it is like ointment. It is also so because it is like dew, that is, like a gratuitous gift, which is understood through dew because dew comes freely, without human labor, price, or effort.

“Like the dew of Hermon,” that is, of exalted light—namely, like a gift freely given by Christ, who is called Hermon, that is, exalted light. Although all the faithful may be called light because they illuminate others by teaching and example, he is the light exalted and elevated above all those lights.

Hence John says: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being, and so forth (John 1:9).”

I say, like the dew of Hermon, which dew descends from Aaron’s beard and from the hem of the garment upon Mount Zion—that is, upon all those who in Zion, namely in the Church, can be called mountains because of the exaltation of their life, such as confessors and any others who are perfect in the Church. This degree of dwelling together does not belong to all the children of the Church. It is appropriate, however, to those living under a rule, to canons, and to cenobites.

Hermon is interpreted not only as “exalted light” but also as “anathema.” According to this interpretation, the passage is read as follows.

I say that the dew is gratuitous, that is, a gift: dew, I say, given to Hermon—that is, to the primitive Church from the Jewish people. That people is properly called anathema by emphasis, either because it anathematized Christ, calling him a deceiver and one filled with a demon, or because it anathematized him, that is, separated him from God by its evil deeds. “Anathema” is indeed said to mean “separated.”

By the fact, therefore, that this gift was given to Hermon, it is proved to have been gratuitous. And the dew descends from Hermon upon Mount Zion, that is, upon those from the Gentiles who are mountains in Zion, namely, those exalted in holiness within the Church.

They further prove that dwelling together in unity is good and pleasant as follows:

Truly, dwelling together in unity is good and pleasant, because there, that is, in that dwelling, the Lord commanded blessing for brothers who persevere in that dwelling. In that dwelling the Lord bestowed a legacy, namely, he gave them exaltation on account of this cohabitation: exaltation in virtues and good works. And he commanded—that is, he will bequeath to them in the future—a life lasting unto the age, that is, everlasting life.

## 536 On Psalm 133

The title of the one hundred and thirty-third psalm: “A Song of Ascents.”

After the perfected had spoken, for the instruction of their hearers, about the fourteenth degree, they speak of the last, namely the fifteenth. This is nothing other than, after they have ascended these degrees, ascribing all of them not to themselves but to the Lord, performing all good works with regard to the heavenly homeland, and thus blessing God. Here, while speaking of this degree, the perfected invite their hearers to ascend to it as follows:

[Col. 1346A] “Behold, now,” and so forth, as though they were saying:

All you servants of the Lord who already declare that dwelling together in unity is good and pleasant: behold, now—that is, at the present time—bless the Lord. In the present time, without delay, exalt the Lord by your good life, persevering in the degrees described above, ascribing to him the higher degrees which you have already ascended, and performing all your good works with regard to the heavenly homeland.

It should be noted that when he says “behold, now,” the “behold” is placed to define “now,” because “now” is not only a sign of the present time but also of the immediately preceding and immediately following times. Hence we commonly say, “He has come now” and “I shall come now.”

Since he had said, “All servants of the Lord, bless the Lord,” and since some servants are wicked, he specifies which servants he means by adding:

You, I say, servants who stand in the house of the Lord—that is, who remain in the Church through faith—yet stand in the courts of the house of our God, that is, in the breadth of love which the perfected of the house of God, namely the Church, have toward God and neighbor, and in the breadth of the other virtues, which are signified by the courts because they are spacious.

Bless the Lord, I say, all servants of the Lord; and you who exist in the nights—that is, in these transitory days, which in comparison with the life to come are called nights because of the frequency of persecutions—lift up your hands toward the holy things, the heavenly things. Do not lower your works by performing them with regard to temporal things; instead, lift them up, that is, raise them, directing them through these works toward the holy things. That is, perform them with regard to the holy heavenly goods, so that you may attain them.

And bless—that is, exalt—the Lord by ascribing to him the very fact that you lift your hands toward the holy things, or that you persevere in the higher goods.

Since, however, whoever you are among the hearers cannot bless and lift up your hands by yourself unless the Lord blesses you: may the Lord Christ, proceeding from Zion—that is, from the Jewish people, insofar as he is human—bless you, that is, exalt you in virtues. He, insofar as he is God, made heaven and earth, that is, greater and lesser things; therefore he can rightly bless, since he is both God and human.

Or: May the Lord bless you, that is, exalt you more and more in virtues; and may this happen from Zion, that is, from the fact that you are already Zion, contemplating the future and not attending to the present.

The Songs of Ascents end here.

## On Psalm 134

The title of the one hundred and thirty-fourth psalm: “Alleluia.”

This is the voice of the Prophet exhorting all the faithful among the human race to praise the Lord: because he is good, because he chose Jacob and Israel, and because he has done everything that he wished. He demonstrates these things in many ways, so as to draw his hearers more strongly toward praising the Lord.

“Praise the name of the Lord,” that is, praise the Lord Christ with voice and affection, with regard to his name, which is “Lord.” Praise, I say, the Lord, you servants. As though he were saying:

You ought to praise him, since you are his servants, that is, subject to his power, and he is Lord of all. You, I say, praise him, who, remaining in the faith, stand in the house of the Lord and in the courts of the house of our God. This verse is explained as in the preceding psalm.

Praise, I say, the Lord with voice and affection, because he is good in nature; and sing psalms to his name, that is, perform good works in his honor, with regard to his name, which is “Lord,” because his name is sweet, that is, it signifies something sweet and gentle. It does not signify something harsh and hateful, as the names of secular lords do.

Praise, I say, the Lord and sing psalms to his name, and do this also with regard to the fact that, by gratuitous mercy, the Lord chose Jacob for himself as his possession—that is, those who, still living in the active life, are manfully struggling against vices. And he chose Israel—that is, those who have already been placed in the contemplative life and see God—as his possession, so that he might possess them through indwelling grace, directing them from good to better.

I say: praise and sing psalms. This is why I exhort you in this way: because I, who am a prophet, whose authority ought to be believed, have learned from Truth, my teacher, presiding inwardly within me, that the Lord is great in power. He is so great that he is our God, existing from so long ago and not a newly arisen god. He is great above all gods, that is, above all the saints deified by him, who nevertheless are very great, such as Moses, Abraham, and the others who were made gods by grace.

He himself is God by nature and therefore greater. When he says “our God,” he says this to overcome the unbelieving Jews, who denied that he was God.

He is shown to be great because the Lord did everything that he wished—that is, he made everything by his will alone—and everything that he wished, without exception. For his will is his act of making.

He made, I say, everything that he wished: in heaven and on earth, that is, in the greater and lesser faithful. He himself made in them what caused the former to be his heaven and the latter his earth. He did everything that he wished in the sea, that is, in lesser ungodly people who embitter him; and in all the abysses, that is, in all the greater people who embitter him, who are abysses, that is, deep in wickedness.

He effected this in them: that their persecution would turn to the benefit of his own people, whom they persecute for his sake. For the ungodly person lives for the benefit of the godly.

He explains what the things are that he did in heaven and on earth when he says, “bringing forth,” and so forth, up to “O Lord, your name.”

I say that the Lord did everything that he wished. The Lord, I say, brings forth clouds from the ends of the earth—that is, from those who were the ends of the earth, namely, the lowly among earthly people and those at the extremity in wealth, understanding, and lineage, such as Peter and Andrew, exceedingly poor fishermen, and the other disciples, who were of humble birth.

He made them clouds, that is, he made them exalted in holiness after the manner of clouds, and gave them the office of watering others with their teaching, after the likeness of clouds watering the earth.

He rightly says “bringing forth”: since they had previously been at the extremity, he brought them out from that extremity when he exalted them so greatly in holiness that they are regarded as pre-eminent among human beings.

In those clouds he made lightning, that is, the illumination of his knowledge. This is signified by lightning because it is brilliant. He uses the plural “lightning” on account of the many persons who were illuminated.

Lightning, I say, tending toward the rain of teaching—that is, he made this in them so that through those illuminations they might water others with their teaching. They could scarcely do this unless they had first been illuminated.

I say that the Lord did everything that he wished, bringing clouds forth from the ends of the earth. The same Lord brings forth from his treasuries—that is, from the hidden secrets of his disposition, which are called treasuries because they are concealed like treasures—the winds, that is, those spiritual men whom he previously called clouds. They are called winds because they are agile, after the manner of winds, in contemplating God.

This means that the fact that they become winds results from God’s hidden disposition; and the more incomprehensible he is, the more praiseworthy he is.

Or it may be understood otherwise: He brings forth from his treasuries—that is, from the heavenly seats—the winds, that is, the angels, so that through their service the clouds brought forth from the ends of the earth may be advanced toward preaching and performing other good works, after the likeness of winds advancing clouds by their blowing.

The winds are called angels both because they are invisible, like winds, and because they are agile in carrying out the office entrusted to them and in contemplating God.

The Lord also struck—that is, by his death he destroyed—the firstborn of Egypt in baptism, that is, the original sins of the human race. They are called “firstborn” because from the beginning of birth they ruled over the human race, as though by inheritance. The human race is called Egypt because it was held in affliction and in the darkness of ignorance. Egypt is indeed interpreted as “darkness” or “affliction.”

He struck, I say, the firstborn of Egypt, beginning with the human being and extending to the cattle, that is, he struck those firstborn both in human beings and in cattle: in the wise, who were rational in the manner of human beings, and in the ignorant, who were brutish like cattle.

This was foreshadowed in the striking of Egypt’s firstborn under Moses.

The Lord not only struck the firstborn but also sent forth—that is, sent outward and made manifest—signs. He sent not just any signs but prodigies, that is, very great signs, in your midst, Egypt, that is, in the common body of the human race.

He explains what those signs were by adding:

He sent forth signs in the destruction of Pharaoh and all his servants. These were the signs: in baptism he destroyed Pharaoh and all his servants. That is, he destroyed the devil and all evil spirits, not essentially but potentially.

This was prefigured in Pharaoh, who was submerged with his army in the Red Sea.

God destroyed the devil potentially, together with all his ministers, when, in baptism, he not only forgave original sins but also actual sins, reducing to nothing the power which they possessed over human beings through those sins.

The devil is rightly called Pharaoh, since he harshly oppressed the human race subjected to him, just as Pharaoh violently oppressed the children of Israel before they were liberated by the Lord.

Since “Pharaoh” is also interpreted as “destruction,” the devil is suitably called Pharaoh by emphasis: insofar as he can, he is the destroyer of all virtues and of all good things.

He also rightly says “he sent forth signs,” that is, he made the signs manifest, “in your midst, Egypt,” because the signs that Pharaoh and his servants were destroyed were openly manifested outwardly through the good works of the faithful. These works would indeed be nothing if Pharaoh had not been destroyed.

The Lord sent forth signs, I say, by destroying Pharaoh in baptism. After baptism, he also struck many nations in his own people, that is, he destroyed many sins, which are called “many nations” because of their great number. We call multitudes of human beings “nations.”

And he killed—that is, destroyed—in his own people strong kings, that is, the very sins which he previously called many nations. They are also called kings because before Christ’s coming they ruled over human beings in the manner of kings. They are called strong kings because by themselves human beings could not escape from their dominion.

The Lord certainly destroyed these sins in his own people after baptism. In some, he destroyed them in such a way that they could never prevail over them again after baptism; in others, he destroyed them in such a way that, after they had prevailed over them, they were again erased through grace by repentance.

The Lord wished this destruction of sins to be prefigured when, as the children of Israel entered the promised land, he destroyed before them many nations and strong kings who possessed that land, and, after taking the land away from them, gave it to the children of Israel as an inheritance.

He explains which sins those were that he destroyed and which he previously called strong kings, as follows:

He struck strong kings, namely, Sihon, king of the Amorites. “Sihon” is interpreted as “burning temptation” or “temptation of the eyes.” Through Sihon, therefore, a vehement temptation is understood. It is called burning because it burns intensely when it incites the faithful excessively to consent, assailing them repeatedly.

It is also called the temptation of the eyes, so that the whole may be designated from its principal part. Thus, through the eyes, since this sense is the chief among the bodily senses, the temptation of all the bodily senses may be understood.

This temptation is the king of the Amorites, that is, it is the prince of those who embitter; it rules those whom it draws to consent, making them Amorites, that is, people who embitter God. “Amorites” is indeed interpreted as “those who embitter.”

The Lord destroyed this kind of temptation in his own people—not so that it would not assail them, but so that it would not prevail over his people through consent, become their king, and make them Amorites.

In some, although it prevailed over them after baptism, he nevertheless destroyed it through repentance in such a way that it would no longer have the opportunity to prevail over them.

He struck not only Sihon but also Og, king of Bashan. “Og” is interpreted as “conclusion,” while “Bashan” is interpreted as “confusion.”

Through Og, therefore, evil action is signified. It is called “conclusion” because it so encloses and binds the person who acts wickedly that he can scarcely be released from it, after the likeness of those confined in prison, who cannot easily leave by their own power.

This action is the king of Bashan, that is, it is powerful in leading those who act wickedly to Bashan, namely, to the confusion of eternal perdition; or to that confusion in which, through the evil merit of that very confusion, they rush from bad to worse.

God destroys this evil action in his own people, either so that it may in no way prevail over them, or, if they have fallen into it in some way, so that he may empty it of its power through repentance.

And he struck all the kingdoms of Canaan, that is, all the kings of Canaan. Through Canaan, which is interpreted as “commotion” or “prepared for humiliation,” evil habit is expressed. By ruling those over whom it is king, it moves them, that is, separates them from God; and by separating them from God, it prepares them for humiliation, that is, for the eternal downfall of perdition.

God strikes this habit in some of his own people by removing it through repentance after it has taken hold of them; in others he strikes it in such a way that it never rules in them at all.

The wording is adapted as follows:

He struck not only Sihon and Og but also all the kingdoms of Canaan, that is, all those kings who are Canaan, namely, those who move human beings away from God and prepare them for the humiliation of eternal downfall. That is, he struck the evil habits so that they would not be kings of his faithful.

He struck Sihon, I say, and Og and the kings of Canaan. After striking them, he gave the land that had previously been their inheritance—that is, the earthly sensuality of the faithful, which had previously been the inheritance of these kings, namely, which these kings possessed as someone possesses an inheritance—as an inheritance to Israel, his people.

That is, he caused his people of the faithful, now Israel, after those kings had been expelled, to possess and cultivate their own sensuality as an inheritance, and, governing it well through reason, to make it God’s fruitful land in good works.

The verse “He sent forth signs” can also be read in another way, without changing the sense of what follows, as follows:

He struck the firstborn of Egypt, and he struck them for this reason: because he sent forth signs in your midst, Egypt—that is, he sent signs openly among you, O human race. And they were not just any signs but prodigies, namely, the miracles of the apostles, which were prodigious and great.

These signs were directed against Pharaoh and all his servants, that is, toward the destruction of the devil’s power and of all the evil spirits who are his ministers.

As though he were saying:

He sent forth the signs for this purpose: so that through them the human race might be called to faith, and through faith and baptism original sin might be erased in them; and thus, on the occasion of these signs, the power that the devil and his servants possessed over the human race might be taken away.

On the occasion of these same signs, he also struck through faith in baptism many nations and killed strong kings, namely, Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan. After striking these, he gave the land that had been their inheritance as an inheritance to Israel, his people.

These three verses are explained here as they were explained above. Through “many nations” and “kings,” actual sins are understood, struck down in baptism, namely, consent, action, and habit.

Therefore, because you struck the nations and kings and did everything described above, O Lord, your name will endure forever. That is, with regard to these things mentioned above, you will be glorified by human beings, and that glory of yours will endure forever.

And from this will come what will be forever: because, O Lord, your memorial endured in this present generation and unto the final generation. That is, the striking of nations and kings by you will take place in all the generations of this life, in the various faithful who are already born and who are still to be born, and therefore you will always be glorified by those faithful.

The striking of sins is called God’s memorial because, since it is performed by God and signifies the slaying of the king and the nations which occurred historically when the children of Israel entered the promised land, it repeatedly brings that history to remembrance.

Nor, O hearers, will the Lord’s glory be eternal only because of the benefits mentioned above. It will also be eternal because the Lord will judge, that is, by his just judgment he will exalt his people, the people of the faithful, in dignity and glory after they have departed from this life. Thus he will be glorified by those who live in this life.

He will exalt the people of his servants by such a just judgment that in those servants of his he will intercede, that is, he will be worthy of being entreated by those who ask, on account of the merits of his servants, so that through their interceding merits he may grant them what they request.

Hence the living faithful have the custom of asking the Lord to pray for them through the saints who have already departed from this life.

Having completed his exhortation to praise the Lord, and wishing to draw his hearers more strongly toward the praise of God by thoroughly turning them away from idolatry, he lingers over the humiliation of idols as follows:

I have said, O hearers, that the Lord is so powerful that he did everything he wished, as has also been shown point by point. But the gods of the nations, who ought not even to be called gods but images, neither wish nor can do anything.

They are proved to be powerless because the images of the nations are silver and gold according to their material, and the work of human hands according to their form. They have an imagined mouth, but they will not speak. They have imagined eyes, but they will not see. They have imagined ears, but they will not hear.

And I rightly say that they will not speak, for there is no spirit in their mouth, that is, no breath, without which speech cannot be formed.

Since, therefore, the images are so powerless and are nevertheless worshiped as gods by foolish Gentiles, may those who make them become inwardly like them, just as they worship them; and may all who, although they do not make them, nevertheless trust in them, unless they eventually recover their senses, become inwardly deaf and blind in reason, just as those images are outwardly.

He says this not by cursing but by granting the possibility, so that he may thereby deter his hearers from the worship of idols.

May those who make them, and those who trust in them, become like them.

But you, house of Israel—that is, the household of the faithful subject to God within the Jewish people—bless, that is, exalt, the Lord Christ in work and heart. And you, house of Aaron—that is, the household of the greater prelates among the faithful from the Jews—bless the Lord.

And you among the nations who fear the Lord with chaste fear, both prelates and subjects, bless the Lord, saying also outwardly with your mouth:

“Blessed,” that is, may the Lord Christ be exalted forever, who is from Zion, that is, born from the Jews insofar as he is human, and who, insofar as he is God, dwells in Jerusalem, that is, rules over the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem.

This means: He is to be blessed because he is God and human.

By Aaron the greater prelates are understood, and by Levi the lesser ones, although Aaron belonged to the tribe of Levi. But since the more distinguished part of the tribe of Levi was the tribe of Aaron, the greater prelates are appropriately understood through the tribe of Aaron. Therefore the word “Levi” is restricted to signify the lesser prelates.

## On Psalm 135

The title of the one hundred and thirty-fifth psalm: “Alleluia.”

This is the voice of the Prophet exhorting everyone to confess the Lord, both because he is good in nature and because his mercy is everlasting, and also because he is God of gods and Lord of lords, and because he performs great wonders, which he displays throughout almost the whole psalm to his praise.

541. Give thanks to the Lord the Father, or to the Lord the Son, with praise in heart, voice, and deed, all you faithful; and do so because he is good in nature. But if you are not sufficient to contemplate him as good in nature, give thanks to him because his mercy endures forever—that is, the benefit of his mercy, which he continually bestows upon the human race—or thus: because his mercy leads us into eternity, that is, into eternal life, through the forgiveness of sins and the increase of virtues.

Give thanks, I say, to him who is God of gods, that is, of the saints whom he has made divine—as though he were saying: We must give thanks to him, since he is himself the God who makes all the saints divine. Give thanks to the Lord of all lords—as though he were saying: We must give thanks to him, since he is the Lord of all lords. Give thanks to him to whom thanks are due, for he has performed great wonders, being alone God by nature and Lord by omnipotence.

He adds “alone” to exclude the implication arising from his having mentioned gods and lords, in order to show that he alone is God in nature and Lord in omnipotence. It should be noted that at the end of each verse of this psalm one must repeat, “for his mercy endures forever,” which the Prophet places there in praise of God; and this must be expounded in each verse as it was expounded in the first.

Alternatively, “mercy” need not be understood in every verse as broadly as it is understood in the first, but more narrowly, so that in each verse only that mercy is understood which is indicated in that verse. For example: Give thanks, I say, to him who, alone existing as Lord and God, performed great wonders, “for this mercy”—that is, the benefit of his mercy, namely, his performing great wonders—will endure forever, or leads us into eternity.

He explains what wonders he performed as follows. He performed wonders, namely, he who made the heavens, that is, exalted prelates in holiness after the manner of the heavens; and he made these heavens in his understanding, that is, in his wisdom. If we speak of the Lord the Father, we shall say that he made the heavens in wisdom, that is, in the Son. Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. XXXVI, 6).

But if we speak of the Lord the Son, we shall say that he made the heavens in himself, that is, through himself, who is the Father’s wisdom—not through alien powers—and that he established the earth in faith, that is, his subjects, who are a fruitful earth. I say “earth” founded upon the waters of baptism, which are the foundation and beginning of virtues. “For unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” [Col. 1353B] (John III, 5).

Or he established the earth in constancy of virtues, so that it would not be submerged by the waters—that is, by persecutors striving on every side, after the manner of waters, to engulf it through incorporation—but would stand above the waters, that is, be superior to the waters and unconquerable by them, so that it yield to them in no respect. This is said by comparison with that immovable earth which is asserted to have been founded upon the waters and which cannot be submerged by the marine waters pressing upon it from every side.

Give thanks, I say, to the Lord who made those whom I previously called the heavens and the earth—that is, prelates and subjects—into great lights by his grace: that is, into great beings in the illumination of his knowledge, so that they might also be lights to others by illuminating them with the same knowledge through teaching. This was prefigured in the lights that God placed in heaven so that they might illuminate the earth (Gen. I, 14).

He made great lights, I say; and behold what lights: he made the sun, namely, those who are to be called “sun.” He explains why he made the sun when he adds: He made the sun, I say, subject to the power of day, that is, to the power of the clearest knowledge, which is called “day” because of the excellence of its dignity. It is as though he were saying: He made some to be lights in such a way that, because of the greatness of their illumination—which is called “day”—they themselves are called “sun.”

That is to say: He made some more illuminated than others by knowledge. He also made the moon and the stars subject to the power of night, that is, he illuminated some with a moderate power of knowledge, so that they could be called “moon” in comparison with those who are more illuminated and are called “sun”; and he illuminated others with a lesser power of knowledge, so that they could be called “stars” in comparison with those moderately illuminated, who are called “moon.”

The sun is far brighter than the moon, and the moon than the stars. Therefore, those more greatly illuminated are appropriately understood by the sun, those moderately illuminated by the moon, and those less illuminated by the stars. The illumination of those who are called moon and stars may indeed be called “day” in itself; yet in comparison with the illumination of those who are the sun—which is, by antonomasia, “day”—it is called “night.” Accordingly, the Psalmist testifies elsewhere: “Day pours forth the word to day, and night declares knowledge to night” (Ps. XVIII, 2).

These lights, although, when compared with one another, some are greater, some moderate, and some lesser, are nevertheless all great and glorious in themselves. Therefore it is not without reason that it is said, “who made great lights.”

He explains by what means he made the heavens, the earth, and the lights when he adds: “Who struck Egypt,” and so forth. This is adapted as follows: Give thanks, I say, to the Lord who by this made the heaven, the earth, and the lights: by striking Egypt with their firstborn—that is, by destroying the Egyptians and their firstborn, namely, human beings who were Egyptians, that is, darkened by ignorance and afflicted under the burden of actual sins.

By faith he destroyed them insofar as they were Egyptians, and, once destroyed, he illuminated them in this way and freed them from the affliction of sins; and he destroyed their firstborn, that is, original sins.

But lest he seem to have destroyed all the Egyptians, he adds: Give thanks, I say, to him who brought Israel out from their midst, that is, from the common body of the Egyptians. It is as though he were saying: I say that he struck Egypt in such a way that repentance struck some of the Egyptians; through this he made them Israel, and thus brought them out from association with the other Egyptians who remained in Egypt.

He did this with a powerful hand, that is, through the powerful operation of his grace, and with an exalted arm, that is, with exalted strength—namely, the strength of that powerful operation of his grace, which is exalted, that is, lofty and glorious above all other strengths. This is signified by the arm, because strength resides in the arm. Here “arm” and “hand” signify the same thing, but “hand” indicates operation, whereas “arm” indicates strength.

He shows by what means he brought Israel out of Egypt—namely, through baptism—when he adds: Give thanks to the Lord who, in order to bring Israel out of Egypt, divided into divisions, that is, divided into diverse parts, the Red Sea, that is, baptism prefigured by the Red Sea, so that for some it would be ruin and for others salvation, as has been expounded in the commentary on Psalm 77, at the passage that reads: “He broke through the sea,” and so forth.

It should be noted that when he says “he divided,” the addition “into divisions” is not superfluous, but indicates the multiplicity of distinctions within baptism itself. For although baptism is one, many good people are saved through it in various ways, while many evil people are condemned through it in various ways.

He divided, I say, the Red Sea, and through the midst of that sea he led Israel—that is, the people of those who were to be saved—out of Egypt, that is, out of unbelief. When he says “through its midst,” we understand nothing more than if he had said “through that Red Sea”; but he uses these words in accordance with the historical resemblance. For the children of Israel are read to have been delivered from the Egyptians through the midst of the divided Red Sea.

He led Israel out through baptism, and he shook off Pharaoh—that is, the devil—and his power, that is, the army of evil spirits that previously ruled Israel while it was in Egypt. He shook it off from Israel, that is, he removed the yoke of its power from the neck of the faithful, drowning it in the Red Sea—that is, in baptism—and destroying Pharaoh himself together with his entire army.

After he had led his people through the Red Sea and drowned Pharaoh there, he led that same people across—and still leads it—to the heavenly homeland through the desert of this life, by virtues and good works. This was demonstrated beforehand in the children of Israel, who were led through the desert into the promised land.

And because he did not want his people to be hindered in this passage by the great and powerful kings who confronted them, he “struck great kings”: he struck great criminal sins, so that they would not be kings over his people. Nor did he strike them in such a way that they merely ceased to rule; he also killed them, that is, destroyed those great and powerful kings, who had previously existed in strength, so completely that they could in no way extricate themselves from it.

He killed, I say, great and mighty kings, namely Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan. After killing them, he gave their land, which had previously been their inheritance, as an inheritance to Israel—that is, to the people of the faithful servant, who obeys him in all things.

These seven verses are expounded in this psalm in the same way as they were expounded in the preceding psalm. I say that the Lord struck great and powerful kings, led us out of Egypt, and bestowed the other benefits; but he did this not because of our merits, but solely because of his mercy.

For although he seemed for a long time to have forgotten us, he remembered us in our humiliation, that is, in consideration of our lowliness, looking mercifully upon the degradation of our mortality and passibility into which we had fallen through Adam. Remembering us, he redeemed us by his death from our enemies, namely, from vices and evil spirits.

It should be noted that although he said above that he rescued us from our enemies, here he indicates the price of his death, to magnify the benefit itself and make us more ready to praise God, when he says, “he redeemed.”

I say that he redeemed us, and that even after the redemption he continually gives spiritual food of his body to every flesh, that is, to every kind of human being, Jew and Gentile alike, noble and ignoble alike; from this the soul is continually refreshed. “For there is no partiality with God” (Rom. II, 11). When he says “to every flesh,” it is the same as if he had said “to every human being,” designating the whole by a part.

Give thanks, I say, to the God of heaven—as though he were saying: Since he has performed so many wonders for the human race, give thanks to him. And since he is God not only of human beings but also of heaven, that is, of the heavenly spirits, give thanks to him for this reason as well.

Give thanks also to the Lord of lords—that is, give thanks also because he is the Lord of all lords—and therefore because his mercy endures forever. He repeats this so that, just as he began in praise, he may also end in praise.

## ON PSALM 136

**Title of Psalm 136.** “A Psalm of David because of Jeremiah.” This is explained as follows: This psalm is David’s—that is, it was composed by the faithful who act here—and it was composed because of Jeremiah, that is, in accordance with the prophet Jeremiah. It does not conflict with Jeremiah’s prophecy, but contains within itself, mystically, though briefly, what Jeremiah prophetically announced at length in the historical sense.

Jeremiah, however, at the end of his book mystically prophesied what he had foretold historically concerning the captivity of Jerusalem in Babylon, brought about by Nebuchadnezzar. That captivity was a sign of the captivity of the faithful, the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, who are truly to be called captives while they are exiles from the heavenly Jerusalem, dwelling bodily among the citizens of Babylon—that is, among the impious sons of this world.

This world is rightly called Babylon, that is, “confusion,” because it will hurl those who love themselves into eternal confusion. In accordance with the Lord’s saying: “But the sons of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness” (Matt. VIII, 12).

Concerning this captivity from the heavenly Jerusalem, the perfect faithful, placed within it, speak when they say that they sat beside the rivers of Babylon, and there wept in remembrance of Zion, and hung their instruments from the willows, and did not sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land.

They also promise that they will continually remember the heavenly Jerusalem, and pray that the Lord will remember the tribulations inflicted upon them by the sons of Edom, so that at some time he may requite them; and they also grieve over the misery of the daughter of Babylon. They say all this in this psalm in order to instruct the other faithful who are placed in the same captivity, so that they too may conduct themselves similarly in that captivity. The words of this psalm, however, are set down according to the historical sense.

544. Being beside the rivers of Babylon—not submerged by those rivers, but existing above the deceitful affairs of this world, not subject to those affairs but standing above them and despising them—or being above the rivers of Babylon, that is, above worldly things, which we despise and to which we refuse to be subjected. These worldly things and affairs submerge those who love them and drag them to condemnation, after the manner of rivers, which submerge those who fall into them and carry them into the sea.

There we sat, that is, while dwelling bodily there, beside those rivers of Babylon. Although we were not submerged by them, we nevertheless sat there—that is, we were cast down and distressed. We regarded it as a great misfortune to dwell bodily beside those rivers, and many anxieties consequently befell us. Sitting there, we wept, that is, we could not refrain from bodily tears.

But since they might have wept fruitlessly, like those who weep over the loss of possessions or for some similar reason, they specify the cause of their tears by adding: We wept, I say, while we remembered you, O heavenly Zion. We wept in remembrance of the heavenly Jerusalem, whose citizens we are, from which we are exiles while placed here in Babylon.

Or we wept in compassion, because we saw many citizens of this Babylon being submerged by those rivers. We wept, I say, because we were always remembering you, O heavenly Zion; and by remembering you we could not be submerged. It is as though they were saying: Although we ourselves were not submerged, we wept solely out of compassion for the submersion of others.

Or we wept over the submersion of others while remembering you, Zion—that is, while thinking continually of you, to whom we feared that those who had been submerged would never attain.

We sat, I say, and wept; and while dwelling bodily among the willows—that is, among the impious, who are barren of good works, and are therefore called willows, since willows are barren trees—we hung our instruments from those willows.

I mean, in the midst of that Babylon, which already existed in the depths of Babylon and therefore could in no way be rescued, we hung our instruments from those willows—that is, we removed and separated our preaching from those sterile impious people.

These preachings are called “instruments” in relation to the faithful hearers, whom they delight after the manner of musical instruments. It is as though they were saying: We therefore removed our preaching from them because we recognized them to be sterile and obstinate in evil.

Hence the Lord says: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine” (Matt. VII, 6). And the Apostle says to Titus: “Avoid a heretical person after the second and third admonition” (Tit. III, 10), and so forth.

Someone might object: Why do you say that you hung up your instruments of preaching? Was there anyone who desired your preaching? To this anticipated objection the following answer is given: We were right to hang up our instruments because those who led us captive—that is, the evil spirits who, through Adam, brought us into this captivity of mortality and passibility—were there, seated over those willows, and speaking through those willows, asking us for words of songs, that is, words of preaching, which are delightful to the faithful like songs.

They asked for them not so that they might obey them, but so that they might despise and trample them underfoot.

He specifies what words of songs they asked for when he adds: I say that those who led us captive asked us—and those same evil spirits who, through Adam’s disobedience, led us away from eternal blessedness into this captivity asked us through those willows, saying: “Sing us one of the hymns of Zion,” that is, joyfully proclaim to us one delightful sermon from those delightful preachings that pertain to the heavenly Zion.

They asked us, I say, for words of songs. But we, hanging our instruments away from them, said: How shall we sing the Lord’s song to you in a foreign land, that is, in consideration of a foreign land?

It is as though they were saying: Since we consider you to be a barren land, alien to God and unsuitable for the seed of the Lord’s teaching, we shall not sing the Lord’s song to you.

Or thus: While dwelling bodily in a foreign land, that is, among you earthly beings who are wholly alien to God, how shall we sing the Lord’s song to you?

Or thus: How shall we sing the Lord’s song to you who exist in a foreign land, that is, in your earthliness, which is alien to God and unsuitable for the seed of teaching? It would indeed be useless to sing the Lord’s teaching to you; therefore we shall not sing it.

Since they had said that they would not sing the song of the heavenly Jerusalem to unbelievers, lest they seem to have forgotten Jerusalem, they remove this implication as follows: Although we shall not sing the Lord’s song to unbelievers, I shall nevertheless never forget Jerusalem—that is, I shall not fail to direct all my devotion toward you, nor fail to sing of you among the faithful who are suited to this song.

If I forget you, O Jerusalem, if all my devotion does not attend to you, if I do not sing of you to those who will be fit for this, may my right hand—that is, my good work—be given over to oblivion, so that it may never be rewarded.

Or “my right hand,” that is, my placement at the right hand of God the Father, which I await, may be given over to oblivion, so that I may never attain it.

Or “my right hand,” that is, my good work, may be given over to oblivion, meaning that I may forget to act well. And not only may this misfortune befall me, but may my tongue also cling to my palate, that is, may I become mute with respect to good speech, by comparison with someone whose tongue clings to his palate and who therefore cannot speak.

May my tongue cling to my palate, I say, if I do not remember you. “If I forget you” and “if I do not remember you” mean the same thing, but the repetition is for variation.

Nor shall I merely remember you in some ordinary way; rather, O Jerusalem, I shall set you first—that is, place you at the beginning, or at the summit, of my joy. If it happens that I rejoice in many other things, you nevertheless, for whose attainment I already have hope, will be the beginning—that is, the chief cause—of my joy.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Seek first the kingdom of God” (Matt. VI, 33). He does not say “first” with respect to order; rather, it is as though he said: Seek above all, with mouth, heart, and deed, the kingdom of God, namely, the heavenly Jerusalem.

For if I do not place you, Jerusalem, at the beginning of my joy, let my right hand be given over to oblivion and let my tongue cling to my palate. This is supplied through aposiopesis.

They impose these conditions in order to show their good desire for Jerusalem and to indicate the greatest loss that will befall those who do not possess a good desire for Jerusalem.

They also pray for the requital of the tribulations they suffer for God, as follows: I say that I shall not forget Jerusalem and that I shall place Jerusalem at the beginning of my joy. For this reason many tribulations are inflicted upon us by the sons of Edom, that is, by earthly and blood-descended sons—namely, by the sons of Babylon, that is, by impious people.

They were prefigured by the sons of Esau, who is also called Edom, who, when the children of Israel returned from the Babylonian captivity to Jerusalem, hindered them as much as they could from rebuilding the city and the temple.

In the same way, the sons of this world strive through tribulations to prevent the faithful from building themselves into a temple for God by living well. “Edom” is interpreted as “earthly” or “blood-descended.”

I say that tribulations are inflicted upon us by the sons of Edom because of our remembrance of Jerusalem. And you, Lord, although you may now seem to have forgotten us here, remember us on the day of Jerusalem—that is, on the day of judgment, on which you will establish fully the heavenly Jerusalem of the sons of Edom.

That is, remember the tribulations inflicted upon us for our remembrance of Jerusalem by the sons of Edom, that is, by persecutors, the sons of this earthly or blood-descended world, so that you may eventually reward them, namely, on the day of Jerusalem.

Or this may be understood as a concession concerning the condemnation of the sons of Edom, in order to deter them from their wickedness: Remember, Lord, on the day of Jerusalem—that is, on the day of judgment—the sons of Edom who persecute us because of our remembrance of Jerusalem, so that you may justly punish them.

Those sons of Edom indeed speak to one another: “Empty, empty out what is in her,” that is, in the citizens of Jerusalem, “down to the foundation.” It is as though they were saying: Because they see us striving toward Jerusalem, moved by envy they persecute us with tribulations, saying: Let us persecute them with continual tribulations and thus empty out—that is, evacuate—the virtues and good works by which they are striving toward the heavenly Jerusalem.

Let us empty them so completely that we reach the emptying of the foundation itself: let us persecute them to such an extent that we even wrest their faith from them, since faith is the foundation of all their virtues and good works.

They also grieve over the misery of the sons of Edom, whom they call the daughter of Babylon, in order to show that by the feminine designation they are effeminate in virtues, as follows: You sons of Edom, who are also the daughter of Babylon—that is, of this world—you say, “Empty them,” and you consider us wretched while you consider yourselves blessed.

But, on the contrary, you, daughter of Babylon, are wretched, even if you flourish in worldly things. Blessed, both here and in the future, is anyone among the faithful who will repay you with the repayment that you made to us.

He therefore explains what repayment he will make when he adds: Blessed, both here and in the future, is the faithful person who will seize your little ones so that they do not grow—that is, those members of yours who have not yet come to mature wickedness but are still small in evil. Through preaching he will restrain them from their wickedness, lest they grow in it.

He will restrain them in such a way that he will dash your little ones against the rock of strength, namely Christ. He will destroy them insofar as they are evil by joining them through faith to Christ, the rock of strength, after the manner of little ones who are killed when dashed against a stone.

It is as though he were saying: Blessed, both here and in the future, is any faithful person who incorporates your little ones through faith, joining them to Christ the head, just as you incorporated some of our little ones—that is, simple people who fell away from the faith because of blandishments or tribulations—into yourself.

For it is evident that the impious have incorporated some of the simple faithful into themselves.

And behold the repayment that the sons of Jerusalem, who are blessed, make to the daughter of Babylon: they incorporate her little ones through faith just as she attempts to incorporate their little ones.

Or “the little ones of the daughter of Babylon” are those whom he calls impious people, who are incorporated here in part by the faithful. They are called little ones because, although they are exceedingly wicked, they grow in their wickedness after the manner of little ones, just as the unjust continually increase in their wickedness.

In the future, however, the just will be perfectly mature in charity, so that they will have no desire except for good things; whereas the impious will be so mature in wickedness that, out of envy of the glory of the good and of their own torments, they will have no desire except for evil, although they will have no power to perform evil.

## ON PSALM 137

**Title of Psalm 137.** “A Psalm directed to David himself,” that is, to Christ. This does not mean that Christ speaks here, but that the body of the perfect faithful, acting in this psalm, directs its words to Christ in thanksgiving, showing the good affection it has for giving thanks to the Lord Christ and for singing psalms.

It does this for the instruction of its hearers, in order to instruct them to have the same affection. It also prays for an increase of virtues, thereby instructing them to pray, and it wishes that the kings of the earth give thanks to the Lord and sing in his ways. It then adds the reasons why they ought to give thanks to him and sing in his ways.

I shall give thanks to you, Lord Christ, with my whole heart, that is, I shall praise you with the whole affection of my heart, although you were reviled by the Jews. And rightly shall I give thanks, because you heard me in such a way that I obtained all the words of my mouth.

It is as though he were saying: I did not pray to you only with the words of the heart, that is, with thoughts, but also with the words of the external mouth. And you heard all those words—namely, all those that were worthy of being granted. Hence the same is said in the Gospel: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John XV, 16).

I shall give thanks, I say, with my whole heart. And not only this, but I shall sing psalms to you, that is, I shall perform good works to your honor, in the presence, that is, in the contemplation, of the angels.

I shall not perform good works for human approval, but solely out of love for you, just as the angels perform the ministries entrusted to them solely out of love. Or “I shall sing psalms to you in the presence of the angels,” meaning that I shall be placed in that same special contemplation of your divinity in which they are placed; I shall sing with the intention of being worthy to attain that same presence which the angels enjoy.

And coming to your holy temple—that is, coming to this by living well, so that I may be worthy to be your holy temple, in which you dwell spiritually—I shall worship you in that temple. That is, I shall venerate you with a certain singular worship of supreme veneration, regarding you as God and Lord and myself as a creature and servant, and making myself your holy temple by my good life.

This worshiping God in such a temple was prefigured in the old law, in which it was established that after the temple had been built no one should worship God except in the temple.

Properly speaking, we call it worshiping God when we honor him with a uniquely worthy and singular worship, recognizing him alone as God and Lord and regarding ourselves as his servants and creatures. Hence in the Apocalypse we read that the angel prohibited John from worshiping him as follows: “See that you do not do it. I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers. Worship God” (Rev. XIX, 10).

I shall worship, I say, and give thanks to your name because of your mercy and your truth—that is, I shall praise you in consideration of your name, which is “Lord.” And this thanksgiving will arise from your mercy and your truth: I shall give thanks to you because of your mercy and the fulfillment of the truth of your promise.

That is, I shall give thanks to you on this account: because you saved us through mercy and in order to verify your promise; for you had promised to save the human race.

I shall also give thanks because you have magnified your holy name above every name, that is, you have shown by the evident reality itself that your holy name, which is “God and Lord,” is greater and more glorious than every name.

Hence the Apostle says: “And he gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. II, 9). For although the names “angel,” “archangel,” “virtues,” and other such names are glorious and signify great things, the name of the Lord Jesus—God, namely, and Lord of all and almighty—is more glorious and signifies something far greater.

Having shown the good affection he has for giving thanks and singing psalms, he proceeds to prayer, which is as follows: I shall give thanks, sing psalms, and worship. Therefore, on whatever day I call upon you—that is, whenever I pray to you inwardly with good affection, not merely outwardly with my voice, asking you to increase virtue in my soul—hear me, so that you may multiply virtue in my soul.

This you will certainly do; truly, you will increase every virtue in my soul from day to day. He promises this to himself with great certainty in order thereby to urge his hearers more strongly to pray for it, through the hope of obtaining it.

Having prayed for himself, he also prays for the other faithful, so that they too, being kings of themselves, may give thanks to the Lord and, following his example, sing in his ways, which is most beneficial for them. He does this with the intention of instructing his hearers to pray for the benefit of others.

I say: I shall give thanks and sing psalms; and following my example, let all the kings of the earth give every kind of praise to you, Lord—that is, all the faithful who have become kings of their own earth, that is, of their sensuality, so that they may rule it well and make their earth fruitful for God through good works.

Let them give thanks for this reason: because they have now heard all the words of your mouth through your preachers, namely, all those words of your teaching that pertain to the instruction of faith and morals, without knowledge of which no one is saved, and which you yourself spoke with your mouth to your disciples.

The Lord spoke many mystical and hidden things, which were not all heard by all the kings of the earth. Therefore, when he says “all the words of your mouth,” this must be determined as referring to those words pertaining to faith and morals, which it is not permissible to ignore.

Hence it is written in the Apostle: “The one who is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Cor. XIV, 38).

Let them give thanks, I say, and let them sing while existing in the ways of the Lord—that is, in the fulfillment of his commandments, which are the ways leading to life. Let them sing, that is, delight in those ways, after the manner of singers who delight in their singing.

For they could indeed be in the Lord’s ways by fulfilling them unwillingly, without singing; and that would not be so beneficial. Let them give thanks, I say, and sing.

Let them do this because the glory of the Lord is great, which in the future he will give to those who give thanks to him and sing in his ways. [Col. 1362A] Let them give thanks and sing also in consideration of this: that the Lord is exalted, that is, omnipotent, and therefore thanks are due to him.

And because he regards the lowly in consideration of his mercy—that is, he has mercy here upon all the lowly who give thanks to him—and because, while he regards the lowly, he also knows the proud in order to punish them, being far away—not spatially, but in mercy—he provides vengeance for the proud, so that he keeps his mercy far from them because of their evil merits.

He explains how he regards the lowly as follows: Truly you regard them with merciful regard, both me, who am lowly, and others like me. For although I am in the midst, that is, in the fullness of tribulation, if I walk—that is, if I persevere in my steadfastness so that I do not fail because of tribulation, as I truly walk—this kind of walking happens to me because you will enliven me inwardly in my soul by grace, while outwardly I am put to death in the body because of tribulation.

It is as though he were saying: It is proved that you regard me, who am lowly, because through your grace, which enlivens me inwardly, you make me steadfast in the midst of tribulation.

And you will so enliven me that you will stretch out your hand—that is, you will extend to me the aid of your grace—over the anger of my enemies, that is, above the wrathful assault of my enemies. This means: Although their assault is great, the aid of your grace in me is greater.

You will stretch out your hand to me here, I say, and finally, after the death of the body, your right hand—that is, your mercy—made me safe, that is, will make me safe, rescuing me from every torment and placing me at the right hand of the Father.

After showing his salvation, he shows the just retribution of his enemies, turning to the hearers in order to withdraw them from conformity with those enemies, as follows: O hearers, I say that the Lord will save me. But, on the contrary, the Lord will in the future repay my enemies with just condemnation for me—that is, because they unjustly inflict tribulation upon me.

Or “for me” means “in my place,” namely, because here I do not wish to repay evil for evil. Hence the Apostle says: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord” (Rom. XII, 19).

He also prays to attain what he has counted upon, as follows: I say that, Lord, you will enliven me inwardly through grace in virtues and will save me. And thus I pray that it may happen, O Lord, because your mercy, which you possess by nature, will endure forever; do not despise the works of your hands.

That is, do not appear to despise your worthy works, which you began to work in me—namely, the enlivening of my soul in virtues. You would seem to despise those works if you did not complete that enlivening in me. It is as though he were saying: Complete in me the works of enlivening which you have already begun.

## ON PSALM 138

**Title of Psalm 138.** “A Psalm of David, looking toward the end,” that is, toward his perfect completion; and this is what he discusses here.
