In this psalm the Lord’s human nature, speaking to God the Father in thanksgiving, demonstrates the perfect consummation of its innocence, justice, knowledge, and entire goodness, in order to render its hearers inexcusable. He shows himself to be so worthy because he has been perfectly consummated, so that they too may be consummated, insofar as possible, according to his example, and thus be drawn into conformity with him.

Lord Father, you have tested me, that is, you have made me approve and experience your commandments, so that they did not seem harsh and unpleasant to me, but approved, praiseworthy, and delightful. This prayer is condensed, equivalent to saying: “Lord Father, you have placed me in the approval and experience of your commandments, so that I might fulfill them.” And when I was led into this experience, you knew me, that is, you loved me. For God is said to know what he loves, and what he hates he is said not to know. Accordingly, in the Gospel it is read concerning the impious and foolish: “Truly I say to you, I do not know you” (Luke 13:25; Matthew 25:12).

But since he had affirmed that he was tested and known by God, unbelievers might object: “Since you have been tested and known in this way, it is strange that God the Father allows you to be humbled; surely he would not endure this concerning you unless your evil merits deserved it.” To remove this objection, he therefore adds: “Although you have tested and known me, you nevertheless, who have known nothing evil, that is, who have willed and ordained from eternity, have known my session, that is, my humiliation unto death; and thus through my session you have known my resurrection.” It is as though he said: “It will not be on account of evil merits of mine that I shall be humbled unto death, but solely on account of your will and ordinance.”

Nor have you merely tested and known me; rather, to say something greater, you have understood my thoughts, that is, you have made my thoughts so holy and suitable that they were worthy of your understanding. For God is said to understand only what is suitable. It is as though he said: “You loved my thoughts as worthy and suitable.” You understood them, I say, and not from recent time, but from afar; that is, you understood everything I thought from the beginning of my humanity.

And you understood my path, that is, you loved the completion of all the arduous and chief commandments that are in me. It is called a path because, after the manner of a narrow track, it is confined, that is, shared by few. And through the path and the thoughts you investigated—that is, you made me investigate and seek out—my measuring-cord, that is, the measure of my inheritance, which is signified by a cord because an inheritance is measured with a cord. This means: “Through the completion of your arduous commandments, you made me seek from you an inheritance, namely, the human race, which I shall measure, taking one part for salvation and leaving another part behind.” Hence, in the second psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm 2:8).

Where “cord” occurs here, the Hebrew translation has “reclining place.” This word equivalently signifies here the same thing as “cord,” namely, the portion of those to be saved, which is called God’s reclining place, that is, God’s rest, because God delighted in it, just as anyone delights in a reclining place.

Nor have you merely understood my thoughts, and so forth; rather, to speak universally, you also foresaw all my ways, that is, from eternity you ordained—that is, willed—all my actions by which I proceed. This certainly would not be so unless they were suitable. Or: “You foresaw all my ways,” that is, you made me foresee them, so that I would do nothing rashly or unexpectedly, but everything with reason and foresight. For what is done wisely is foreseen rationally.

But since he had commended himself for the instruction of his followers, lest he seem to have done this out of arrogance—for we call it arrogance when someone boastfully attributes to himself what he does not possess—he removes this charge as follows: “I say, you have tested me,” and so forth. Let no one think that this commendation of myself was spoken arrogantly, because this speech by which I have commended myself is not merely on my tongue but also exists in reality. This means: “I do not speak in such a way that these are empty words; for what I say is true in reality.”

And this is present and known to you—behold, that is, it is before you and recognized by you—because the speech is not merely on my tongue. For you, Lord, have known all things, both the latest and the ancient, that is, past and future; and since you know everything, you know this also. I say this because you understood my thoughts, foresaw all my ways, and tested me.

And so you, who are able to form me, formed me, that is, you made me beautiful inwardly in my character, although through tribulations I may appear outwardly deformed. Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44:4). You, I say, formed me.

And upon the one whom you formed you placed your hand, that is, the help of your grace, namely, so that I might not in any way fall away from that beauty. You placed upon me the assistance of your grace, which makes me persevere, after the likeness of one who helps another by placing his hand upon him to keep him from falling.

It should be noted that all this has been said with reference solely to his humanity.

I say that you formed me, and so forth. And you not only made me beautiful in character, but also knowing, so that I might know you uniquely and more secretly than others. And this knowledge of you—that is, knowledge given to me by you—was not made contemptible through me, as it was through Adam, who, although he possessed knowledge of you, made it appear contemptible by departing from it through evil conduct. For what is contemptible is usually cast aside as something worthless.

It was not, I say, made contemptible through me; rather, because I acted well and thus persisted in it, your knowledge was made wondrous through me, worthy of admiration by others and desirable. For when they saw me preaching wisely and acting well, they judged the knowledge given to me by you to be precious in a wondrous way. Hence, in the Gospel: “All who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers” (Luke 2:47).

And it was not only made wondrous, but also strengthened in the portion of those to be saved, which through Adam had been weakened in the whole human race. It is as though he said: “The knowledge by which the human race would know you, had Adam not sinned, was so weakened in everyone by his sin that they scarcely possessed any spark of knowledge of you, and saw you as if in a dream.” Hence Paul also says: “Now we see through a mirror in a riddle” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

But through the obedience of my death this knowledge will be strengthened—that is, reinforced—in the faithful, so that they may know you more fully than usual. Although in this life they will not possess this knowledge perfectly, they will possess it in the future.

But since he had been speaking of knowledge, which is especially wont to be a cause of pride, as the Apostle says: “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Corinthians 8:1), he prescribes in himself an example of humility for those who are to possess this knowledge, as follows: “Your knowledge, I say, has been made wondrous and has been strengthened through me.” And although I possess this knowledge fully, nevertheless I cannot attain to it, that is, I shall not judge myself capable of possessing it by myself, without your help. Thus, although I am knowing, I shall never ascribe this to myself, but always to you.

Through this he plainly instructs his hearers that no one should glory in his knowledge in himself, but in the Lord. Hence the Apostle: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

“Your knowledge, I say, has been made wondrous.” And when you have enlightened me with such great spiritual knowledge, where shall I go from your Spirit? This means: “If I depart from your Spirit, which enlightens me with this knowledge according to my humanity, by living badly, where shall I go—that is, to what other person shall I turn in devotion, according to my humanity, who might enlighten me?” I shall be able to go to no one.

And since I would deservedly experience your vengeance if I departed from your Spirit, where shall I flee from your face—that is, to what place could I flee from your presence in order to escape this vengeance? Nowhere. For if, wishing to flee, I should ascend locally into heaven, you are there—not locally, but in power. And if I should descend into hell in order to escape your presence—which nevertheless will never happen—it would be in vain, because you are there; that is, you are present there in power, and you will punish me.

Therefore one must not depart from you, since nowhere can a place of refuge be found. Nor are you present only in heaven and in hell, but also in this world, which is between heaven and hell. This is shown as follows.

For if, existing in this middle place, I should take my wings—that is, the virtues that are wings for those who rightly take them, by which one flies to paradise—and if I should take them at dawn, that is, in the illumination of good will, and if, in anticipation of flight through hope and through the conduct of a good life, I should dwell at the ends, that is, in the harbor of this sea—which is the other life, the final state after this life, called “sea” because of its changeability, and which is also a harbor of rest for the faithful escaping the storm of this life—you are present; that is, you show yourself to be present in this middle place through me, who take the wings and dwell at the ends of the sea.

It should be noted that when he says, “If I should take them,” and so forth, he does not mean that he had these wings only from that point onward. Rather, for the sake of demonstration, he makes a concession concerning something that will not happen. It is as though he said: “Let it be granted that I take wings at dawn, and that I take them in order to dwell at the ends; through this it will be evident that you are present in this middle place.”

Someone might ask: How will it be established that you are present in the middle, if you take wings? To indicate this, he adds: “Truly it will be evident that you are present in this middle place if I take wings. For your hand—that is, the operation of your power—will lead me there, so that I may take wings and dwell at the ends of the sea.”

But even if this occurs, so that I take wings and dwell at the ends of the sea, there your right hand—that is, your mercy—will hold me; that is, it will make me persevere. For after I have attained these things, I shall not be able to persevere in them unless your mercy holds me.

It should be noted that when the Lord’s human nature says in his own person, “Where shall I go from your Spirit?” and so forth, up to “And I said, perhaps,” he does not do this in his own person because it will ever happen to him that he goes away from God’s Spirit or flees from his face. For how could he depart from God’s Spirit, who is personally united to the Word of God? Rather, he is transfigured in his own person for this reason: to instruct his members in himself, lest any of them presume to depart from God’s Spirit, showing in himself that no one who departs can flee from his face.

Thus it has the same force as if he had said: “When you have made me so wondrous in knowledge and have strengthened that same knowledge in the human race, it is clear from this that no one should depart from your Spirit. For where will mine go if they depart from your face, and where will they flee from your face? Nowhere. For if they ascend into heaven, you are there; if they descend into hell, you are present. If in this middle place they take their wings at dawn and dwell at the ends of the sea, you are present. For your hand will lead them there, and your right hand will hold them.”

Having shown the perfection of his justice, character, and knowledge, he also shows that he must nevertheless be trampled underfoot by the Jews unto death, although he is so perfect. He subsequently shows the fruit of his passion, thereby making those for whom his passion is salutary subject to him, drawing them to conformity with his justice and holiness and to suffering for him, while showing the unbelieving Jews, who neglect to repent, to be without excuse concerning his death, since they trampled him, perfect in every respect, unto death.

He therefore speaks as follows: “I say that you formed me. And when you had formed me in this way, I said”—that is, I conceived within myself—“darkness will trample me unto death because of envy of my beauty and knowledge.” He calls the Jews “darkness” emphatically, because they were deeply enveloped in the darkness of ignorance when, out of envy, they handed their Creator and Savior over to death.

“Darkness,” I say, “will trample me.” And from my trampling it will happen that night, emphatically so called, will be my illumination, that is, the portion to be saved from the Jewish people, which is called “night” emphatically because it is enveloped in the night of ignorance; it will be enlightened by faith and knowledge of God through me.

I say that night is to be placed among my delights, that is, among my delights, namely, in the fellowship and conformity of my disciples, who are my delights and in whose holiness I take pleasure as in supreme delights.

It is certain from this that those who are called night and darkness will be enlightened through trampling, because, although they are now darkness, they will not be darkened by you; that is, they will not be blinded by your just judgment, as they are now justly darkened on account of their evil merits. When he says “they will not be darkened,” it is understood by litotes that they will be enlightened by God the Father; and through this it is evident that they will also be enlightened by the Son. For whatever the Father does, the Son also does, and conversely: they are one.

“They will not be darkened,” I say, “by you.” And that same people, while being night, will be so enlightened by you through faith and knowledge of you that it may be called day, on account of the extraordinary brightness of its faith and knowledge.

Or it may be understood as follows: “Night will be illuminated as day,” that is, in comparison with the apostles, who are called “day” emphatically. Night, I say, will be illuminated. And it will be illuminated in such a way that, just as its darkness is, so also will its light be; that is, however great the knowledge of the darkness of its ignorance is, so great will be its illumination in faith and knowledge. In other words, if its confession of ignorance and sins is great, its illumination will be great.

Through this he invites his hearers to a vehement confession of their sins, so that they may deserve a more vehement pardon.

Someone might ask: Why will night be illuminated through you rather than through any of the preceding saints, when it was unable to be illuminated through them? To show this, he replies as follows: “For this reason night will be my illumination”—that is, for this reason I am worthy to be the one through whom those who are night are illuminated—“because you possessed my reins,” that is, my delights, which are signified by the reins because delight ordinarily proceeds from the reins.

The word “you” is appropriately placed here for the sake of distinction. It is as though he said: “The delights of others are possessed in part by the devil, since at times an illicit thought arises in them. But you alone possess my delights, and from my beginning you have possessed them, so that there is no delight in me except what pleases you and has been ordained by you. Therefore, alone among all, I am worthy to be the one through whom unbelievers are illuminated.”

And you also received me from my mother’s womb; that is, you were my receiver and patron from the time when I was in my mother’s womb. You were my receiver in such a way that you alone made me free from original sin. For this reason also I am worthy that night be illuminated through me, because I shall confess to you perseveringly; that is, I shall never cease confessing your praise.

This means: “Whatever good there is in me, I shall ascribe to your praise.” And for this further reason: you have been magnified through me, that is, through my preaching and good life you have been magnified and glorified among my disciples. Hence he says in the Gospel: “Father, I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me” (John 17:6).

You have been magnified, I say, through me, and this in a terrifying manner; that is, in such a way that I have brought upon others the terror of just condemnation unless they too strive to magnify you by my example.

For this reason also I am worthy, because through me your works have been shown to be wondrous; that is, by conducting myself rationally I have shown that the things you have worked in me are wondrous and most worthy—namely, rationality and virtues, whose worth I have shown through the effect of good works.

It is as though he said: “Your works have been made wondrous through me. Adam, in whom you worked rationality and virtues, did not show them to be wondrous and worthy, since he fell away from them. But I have shown them to be wondrous by persevering in them and manifesting them outwardly through good works.”

“Your works have been made wondrous through me,” I say, “and my soul will know them exceedingly”; that is, it will regard them as exceedingly worthy and wondrous. It is as though he said: “Just as I have already regarded them as wondrous, so I shall continually regard them as wondrous and shall manifest to others that they are wondrous.” Adam certainly did not regard them as wondrous, since he neglected to persevere in them.

When he says, “My soul will know,” it has the same force as saying, “I shall know.” For he places the part for the whole.

But since he had said that the Father was magnified through him, he intends to show how he was magnified through him, as follows: “I say that you have been magnified through me, and I have magnified you through this: my bone, which you gave me, has not been hidden from me.” That bone, namely, you made in secret, that is, in my interior, namely, in the soul, which is hidden.

Here “bone” is used for “osseous structure,” not for “mouth.” He says that rationality is the bone of the soul, because it is the stronger part of the soul, just as bone is stronger in the body.

What he says—“it has not been hidden”—has the same force as saying: “My bone given by you, which you made in secret, has not been hidden from me”; that is, the power of my reason has not been hidden by me, but has been manifested outwardly, while by living well and preaching to others I have shown you to be glorious and great.

This power of reason was hidden by Adam, since, when he ceased obeying God, he did not strive to glorify him and show him to be magnificent. The statement is made by comparison with an inactive soldier who hides his sword when he ought to fight bravely.

When he says that the bone was not hidden, it is understood by litotes that he manifested that bone through good works and thereby magnified God. Free will is also called the bone of the soul. Its power is certainly hidden when it is not used rightly and is bent toward the exercise of an evil work. For since it was given by the Lord for exercise in good, and thus for merit, the person who turns instead toward evil action denies by the very experience of the matter that it was given for this purpose.

But since he had said that his bone was not hidden, someone might say: “It is no wonder that you did not hide the bone, since perhaps you were not in this passibility in which we are.” In response to this, he shows that he was passible, so that he might thereby commend even more strongly the perseverance of his good action. For it was a great thing that he persevered in his purpose of goodness when, on account of the weakness of passibility, he had the power to fail.

[Col. 1369A] He says this as follows: “I say that my bone has not been hidden, and my substance”—that is, my nature, which above I called bone—“has not been hidden.” That is, the power of my rationality and free will has not been hidden, although it exists in the lower parts of the earth, that is, in the parts of this world that are called the lower parts of the earth.

They are called the lower parts of the earth, that is, the less worthy parts of the earth, in comparison with the earthly paradise, in which Adam was first placed. That paradise is called more worthy and higher because there is no harshness or immoderation of the air, nor any excess of heat or cold, but everything is serene and temperate. In the valley of this world, by contrast, there is the greatest disturbance of the air, from which manifold suffering arises.

Therefore this world is lower than paradise, not according to the position of the place, but according to the unworthiness of the thing.

What he says—“my substance in the lower parts of the earth”—is adapted as follows: “My substance,” that is, the power of my nature, “has not been hidden, but has been manifested through perseverance in good action, although it has been placed in the lower parts of the earth,” that is, in the troubled valley of this world, where there could be an occasion for hiding it because of the pressure of manifold anxiety.

Adam certainly did this: he hid the power of his nature by not persisting in obedience, although he had not yet been placed in the lower parts of the earth, but in paradise, where there was no anxiety of suffering and no necessity of failing.

“My substance has not been hidden” has the same meaning as “my bone has not been hidden”; it is repeated in order to add “in the lower parts of the earth.”

Since, then, I am perfect because you possessed my reins and received me from my mother’s womb, and my bone has not been hidden, it is unquestionably clear that your eyes saw my imperfection; that is, the eyes of your ordinance foresaw and willed my imperfection, namely, my death, which is the greatest weakness and imperfection.

Although I am so consummated in every perfection of holiness, and therefore worthy that the faithful be saved through me, it pleased your ordinance that I should be imperfect and weak according to mortality, and that I should die for the salvation of those who would be mine in the future.

Through this imperfection of my death, days will be written in your book—that is, in me, who am your book, whom you established as an exemplar of justice in all things. Days will be written, that is, those who are to become days will be perfected: my disciples, who will be bright and enlightened in knowledge.

He calls himself a book and asserts that days are to be written according to his example by comparison with an excellent book, according to whose example other books are written.

He explains how they will be written according to his example by adding: “I say that in me, the book, days will be written,” that is, they will be formed according to my example; inwardly they will become beautiful in virtues. And no one will be formed while remaining in them. It is as though he said: “Although many will be made beautiful according to their example, no one will place his hope of beauty in them, imagining that he becomes beautiful through their gift.”

Hence Paul: “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Corinthians 1:13).

No one, I say, will place his hope of beauty in them. But to me—that is, for my honor—your friends, O God, have been greatly honored; that is, the faithful who will become your friends by living well will be honored in the beauty of virtues.

It is as though he said: “To me alone must be ascribed the fact that all the faithful who will be beautiful in virtues will become beautiful through me.”

And what is greater still: to me—that is, for my honor—their principate has been greatly strengthened; that is, it will be strengthened in the beauty of virtues. It is as though he said: “It must be ascribed to me that my disciples, who are rulers and more worthy among those friends, will be strengthened and made robust in this beauty.”

For I shall number them among friends; that is, I shall choose them, removed from the mass of those to be lost, by a definite number for the beauty of salvation. It is as though he said: “Their number will be so certain to me that it can neither increase nor decrease.” Through this he makes them well disposed, since he says that they have been numbered for salvation.

But because he had said, “I shall number them,” lest they appear to be countable among human beings, he adds: “Although I say that I shall number them, they will nevertheless multiply so greatly that they will be above the sand”—not so that they will be more numerous in number than the grains of sand, but they will be above the sand, that is, more uncountable than sand, so that the number of the sand could be known more quickly than their number.

That your friends will thus be honored will occur not only through my imperfection, that is, through my death, but also through this: that I have risen, that is, that I shall rise from death and become immortal and impassible.

And although I have not yet risen, nevertheless, while I still exist as mortal and passible, I am coeternal and consubstantial with you according to my divinity, and therefore I am able to honor your friends.

From this it is evident that I am also one with you in essence. For if you, God the Father, kill sinners—that is, it is established that you have already killed sinners by blinding them in soul through your just judgment, those unwilling to repent—saying to them by the hidden and inaudible word of your ordinance: “O men who pour out blood,” that is, “O men who kill your neighbors,” sometimes by punishing them in the body, sometimes by deceiving them in soul through flatteries, “depart from me,” that is, “withdraw and distance yourselves from knowledge of me and voluntary submission to me.”

And you rightly say, “Depart,” because in their most wicked thought they say: “Let the faithful receive their cities in vanity,” that is, the collections of people that they form for themselves, when they gather many to themselves and promise them certain invisible goods, from which they themselves also expect a reward.

Let them do this in vanity, that is, uselessly, so that neither they themselves may ever derive any benefit from it nor those whom they receive by conforming them to themselves.

“Do I not hate those sinners who hate you by doing evil”—that is, have I not hated them by killing them together with you, blinding them in soul? I certainly hated them; therefore it is established that I am the same as you in nature.

This has the same force as if he had said: “It is evident that I am with you because I likewise killed those sinners whom you killed, hating them for this reason: they said in their thought, ‘Let the faithful receive their cities in vanity.’”

And although I hated them, nevertheless I wasted away from compassionate mercy; that is, I was anxious for them in soul, by comparison with one who wastes away from excessive anxiety.

I wasted away, I say, extending myself in contemplation over those who were my enemies and who were justly to be punished; that is, I was anxious out of compassion for the damnation that I foresaw for them.

In this he prescribes an example for us in himself, so that we ought to be anxious out of compassion concerning the damnation of our enemies, even if we hate them insofar as they are evil. Hence Prosper: “In the wicked we rightly hate wickedness and love the creature.”

But since he had said that he hated sinners, and since a certain hatred is evil, he specifies which hatred he means when he says: “I hated them, I say, and I hated them not with an unjust hatred, but certainly with hatred”; that is, with a hatred that is good and belongs to perfect men.

I hated them insofar as they were evil, not insofar as they were creatures of God. “I say that I wasted away over my enemies.” And although I wasted away out of compassion for their damnation, nevertheless they became my enemies by living badly, which they should by no means have done; therefore I rightly hated them.

After showing, for the instruction of his hearers, that his perfection had been consummated, he prays for perseverance in that same perfection, so that he may instruct those same hearers to pray concerning that same perfection.

I said, O Lord Father, that you tested me, knew me, and knew my path. This I ask you to do perseveringly: test me perseveringly, God the Father; that is, lead me perseveringly into the approval and experience of your commandments. And I say this with respect to thoughts.

This means: “Make me think about your commandments carefully and diligently.” And thus know my heart; that is, make the thoughts of my heart so approved that my heart may be worthy for you to know it—that is, to love it. For God is said to know what he loves.

Nor do I ask you merely to test me with respect to thoughts; I also ask you to question me with respect to works; that is, make me experience and approve your commandments with respect to works. Make me act well by fulfilling your commandments.

“Question” is used for “experience” or “investigate,” because experience and investigation are ordinarily carried out by questioning.

“Question me,” I say, “according to works, and thus know my paths”; that is, make me experience your commandments so fully that you may know my paths, that is, love my purposes. They are called paths because they are arduous and singular.

“Test me,” I say, “and question me, and look upon me mercifully”; that is, I do not ask this solely on the basis of my merits, but I ask that you do this with regard to your mercy. For God is said to see and regard those on whom he has mercy.

“Look upon me,” I say, “if there is nevertheless in me any way of iniquity,” that is, any operation of iniquity, which is a way to condemnation in the heights; then may you never look upon me. It is as though he said: “Look upon me when there is no way of iniquity in me.”

And lead me in the way made eternal; that is, make me persevere in the way of your commandments, so that it may be eternal for me, that is, continual and leading to eternity. Make me persevere in it in such a way that I never cease from it and through it attain eternity.

For many persevere for a time and later fail, and thus do not attain eternity.

## ON PSALM 139

**The title of the one-hundred-thirty-ninth psalm:** “A Psalm of David,” that is, of every faithful person, looking toward the end, that is, toward Christ, who is the end and has been perfectly consummated in all justice and holiness, as was shown in the preceding psalm.

In order that they may be able to share in this perfection, they pray that God, through grace, may rescue them from evil men, that is, from those who act evilly, and from the iniquitous, that is, from heretics, who strive to conform them to themselves.

They make this prayer with the intention of giving others an example of praying for the same thing. They also show that the assault of those heretics is both hidden and manifest, so that they may teach their hearers to beware of it.

“Rescue me, Lord,” through the help of your grace, “from the evil man,” that is, from the mass of men who do evil, lest they be able to conform me to themselves.

“And rescue me from the iniquitous man,” that is, from the mass of heretical men, iniquitous by antonomasia, lest they be able to conform me to themselves.

It is fitting that at first “from the evil man” and “from the iniquitous man” are put in the singular; afterward “they who have devised” is put in the plural, because they are both one thing in the mass and many persons.

But when the faithful, acting in this psalm, have prayed to be rescued both from those who do evil and from iniquitous men, he dwells especially on the prayer for rescue from heretics, since the greatest danger lies in them.

He shows the assault of these heretics as follows: “Rescue me, I say, from the mass of iniquitous men. The iniquitous men have devised iniquities,” that is, iniquitous and heretical thoughts, invented in the heart and not found in the Scriptures.

It is as though he said: “It is necessary for me to pray to be rescued from iniquitous men because they have devised, and still devise, iniquities which they invented in their hearts and did not receive from the Scriptures.”

And they not only devised them, but “all day,” that is, continually, they prepared battles; that is, through the loquacity of their manifold arguments they contrived conflicts against Catholics.

Nor did they prepare battles in just any manner, but in such a way that “they sharpened their tongue”; that is, they made their words sharp and subtle, so that they might wound more severely and be more dangerous.

“They sharpened,” I say, “being like serpents,” that is, comparable to serpents. For just as serpents, proceeding crookedly, creep stealthily and thus strike secretly, so they, proceeding crookedly through various errors of heresies, strike the unwary secretly and unexpectedly.

“And under their lips is the venom of asps”; that is, an incurable error lies hidden in their words, just as the venom of asps is incurable. For once someone has been imbued with that error, he can scarcely free himself from it, just as someone imbued with the venom of asps is freed from it only with difficulty or never.

He appropriately says “under their lips,” since their words appear smooth and good, while an inextricable error lies hidden in them.

He rightly says “they hid [it].” For they prepare the snare of error in secret when, mixing in certain flattering words that seem holy, they strive by their insinuations to draw the faithful into error—after the likeness of a hunter who stretches a snare in hiding to deceive a wild animal or bird. But they not only hid the snare; they also openly stretched cords into the snare, that is, they made their arguments extended and methodically arranged, so that they might become a snare for me, that is, a capture and destruction. They are called “cords” because they are difficult to break, like snares made from cords—after the likeness of a hunter who stretches out snares made of cords to entrap wild animals.

But they not only stretched out cords; although they themselves were not on the road but beside the road, that is, although they appeared to hold the authority of the saints—which is the straight road of faith for the faithful, though they themselves interpret it perversely—and thus were not on the road itself but beside it, in this way they placed a stumbling block before me, that is, a most dangerous obstacle of error. For someone is more readily deceived when an authority, perversely interpreted by them, is put forward.

Since, then, they stretched out cords and placed a stumbling block beside the road, I said to the Lord, both inwardly with a good disposition and outwardly with my mouth: “You are my God,” that is, my Creator. I regard you as the Creator and myself as a creature. And since I regard you as my God, “Hear, Lord, the voice of my supplication”: since you are the omnipotent Lord, hear my voice, by which I beseech you to bring about what I ask.

This voice of supplication is as follows: “O Lord—truly Lord—who already grant me this benefit, that you are the strength and cause of my salvation,” that is, you are my steadfastness in every good, through which I shall attain eternal salvation, “you have overshadowed my head placed in the day of battle,” that is, you have granted the shade, or refreshment, of your mercy over my mind, placed in the heat of battle. The “day” signifies this because the sun’s heat is present by day. This means: You have already bestowed on me the benefit that, when I was placed in the heat of the battle with the heretics, you refreshed my mind with the spiritual and invisible refreshment of your grace, so that it would not fail beneath the excessive heat of that battle—after the likeness of combatants who are shaded so that they do not collapse from the heat.

[Col. 1374B] You, then, Lord, “do not hand me over to the sinner,” that is, do not permit me to be handed over to the heretic, who is, by antonomasia, the sinner, so that I become conformed to him. It is necessary that I pray for this. For the sinners have thought against me: they have devised things contrary to me, namely, how they might deceive me. I say that I am separated from my desire. For I desire to persevere in the integrity of faith. I would be removed from that desire if I were conformed to the sinner.

And because they have thought against me, I pray: “Do not abandon me without help,” while I, insofar as I can, resist the sinners by free choice. “Do not abandon me” means the same as what was stated above, “Do not hand me over to the sinner,” except that it indicates free choice and is repeated out of excessive feeling. For the person who accomplishes something by himself appropriately prays to be helped.

I say, “Do not abandon me, lest sinners be exalted,” that is, lest they boast arrogantly if I am abandoned. “Lest they be exalted,” I say, “and this perhaps”—that is, unhappily, to their misfortune. What he says, “lest perhaps they be exalted,” is a prayer for the sinners, instructing his hearers to pray for their enemies. It is as though he said: I therefore pray not to be abandoned, because, if I were abandoned and should fail, the sinners would thereby be exalted to their own misfortune and condemnation.

Or, “lest perhaps they be exalted,” that is, rashly. It is as though he said: I therefore pray that they not be exalted, since such an exaltation would be rash and consequently harmful to them.

“Do not abandon me,” I say. And it is necessary that I pray for this. For “their circuit surrounds and will continually cover their head,” and therefore it is dangerous to have dealings with them. By “their head” he means the summit of their heresy, since all their opinions are directed toward it, just as the head is chief over all the limbs. By “circuit” he means the manifold windings of their arguments and opinions, by which they conceal and fortify the summit of their heresy so that it may not be destroyed by Catholics—after the likeness of a serpent that covers its head with the coil of its tail, since its chief vitality is in its head, lest it be struck there.

He explains the statement “their circuit will cover their head” in this way: “Their circuit,” I say, “will cover their head,” that is, the manifold winding of their opinions and arguments will conceal and pre-fortify the summit of their heresy so that it cannot be extinguished. This means: “The labor of their lips will cover them,” that is, the multiplicity of their words, in finding which they themselves will labor greatly, will protect them.

Because he had prayed for the heretics, saying “lest perhaps they be exalted,” he shows that they will not be exalted. Rather, some of them will be converted and thus saved, while others, persisting in their loquacity, will be condemned. He says this with the intention of withdrawing all his hearers from heresy.

“I pray that perhaps they may not be exalted.” And truly they will not be exalted, for “coals will fall upon them,” that is, spiritual men who are desolating coals, kindled with the fire of charity and knowledge of God, will fall upon them. That is, with the great weight of their authoritative judgments they will crush and overcome them, after the likeness of a heavy object falling from above and crushing someone.

But the coals will not merely fall upon them in order to overcome them. Moreover, Lord, “by those same coals you will cast them into the fire,” that is, you will make them humble, afterward sending them into the fire, that is, into the illumination of the Holy Spirit. Once sent into the fire, they will no longer remain, that is, they will not continue in the miseries of heresies.

This is said of only a portion of them. Upon some of them, I say, the coals will fall; they will be cast into the fire and will not remain in their miseries. But “every loquacious man,” that is, anyone among them who, unwilling to recover his senses, perseveres in the loquacity of his heresy, “will not be set right by the Lord in this land,” where there is an opportunity for being set right—that is, as long as he lives in this land, he will not walk rightly with the Lord along the straight road of faith.

But at death, when the soul is separated from the body, evils of eternal condemnation will seize that unjust man, that is, the loquacious man, because he is unjust, so that he may not escape any further.

Since the loquacious man will thus be condemned, I learned this by contrast. I learned it from the fact that I learned that the Lord will in the future execute a just judgment for the poor, that is, will justly reward each of his faithful who suffers poverty here for his sake. It is as though he said: Since he is going to reward his own with inward blessedness, it is certain to me from this that he will also justly condemn the loquacious men.

And he will not only execute judgment for the poor; he will also “take vengeance for the poor upon the loquacious men.” From this, namely, it is certain to me that he will condemn the loquacious men, because I am certain that he will avenge his poor upon those loquacious men. This vengeance, certainly, will be nothing other than eternal condemnation. When he says that he will take vengeance for the poor upon the loquacious men, it is understood that those poor are persecuted by them.

To what is understood outside the book, the following words are joined in this way: I say that he will take vengeance for the poor upon the loquacious men because they persecute them. Nevertheless, although they persecute them, through fear of them “the righteous will not fail from your confession, O God,” but the righteous will continually confess your name, that is, praise you in consideration of your name, which is “Lord.”

Or the passage may be read as follows: I say that evils will seize the unjust man at death. I learned this from the fact that the Lord will execute judgment for the poor: he will here execute judgment concerning every good person who suffers poverty for his sake, according to what is written: “Let judgment begin from the house of God” (1 Pet. 4:17).

He explains what judgment he will execute concerning the poor when he adds: “And”—that is, he will “take vengeance for the poor,” that is, by his just judgment he will take vengeance concerning his poor when they sin, correcting them here through passing scourges. In this way he demonstrates that, if he does not spare his own, he will spare the unjust still less in the future.

He will, I say, take vengeance for the poor. Nevertheless, although here he corrects his righteous poor through scourges, the righteous will not therefore cease from your praise, but the righteous will confess your name. This is explained as above. Here, I say, they will confess your name.

And in the future “the upright will dwell,” existing in eternal glory, O Christ, “with your countenance,” that is, with the sight of you face to face.

Or, if this is said of the Father: “And in the future, O God the Father, the upright will dwell,” that is, they will remain in eternal glory, “with your countenance,” that is, with Christ your Son, who is called your countenance, as was shown in the fourth psalm, where it says: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4:7).

## ON PSALM 140

The title of the one hundred and fortieth. A psalm of David, that is, of the faithful, for the instruction of the hearers, showing that they cried out to the Lord and prayed to him to make them worthy to pray and to act well, and to guard them so that they would not sin criminally in mouth or heart, and so that they would not associate with people who practice iniquity.

They also show that, if they have sinned, they will be rebuked by the righteous, so that he may instruct the hearers not to flee from correction by the righteous whenever they sin. They also foretell the conversion of certain sinners, so that they may give the hearers an example of converting sinners. Moreover, they show that they will suffer tribulations from certain sinners who will not be converted, and they pray concerning those tribulations, so that they may give the hearers an example both of enduring and of praying in tribulations. They also speak of the failure of certain Christians in tribulations—those whom God permits to fail because of the desert of their iniquity—in order thereby to deter the hearers from iniquity, lest they fail and thus perish eternally.

[559] “Lord God, looking toward you, merciful and omnipotent, I cried out,” that is, I sent forth a cry of intense feeling, so that I might be wholly devoted to you with a good will. Since, therefore, I cried out, “hear me,” so that I may obtain what I cried for.

But I have not only cried out; I will also cry out perseveringly. And when I cry out to you, “attend to my voice,” that is, make yourself attentive to the inner voice of my cry, so that you may bestow intensely what I ask intensely.

I have cried out, I say, and I will cry out. And behold what I have cried out and will cry out: “Let my prayer be directed by you,” that is, make my prayer direct and just.

Because the prayer of certain hypocrites appears directed toward human beings, although it is rather unjust, he adds, for clarification, “in your sight.” It is as though he said: I do not pray that it be directed in the sight of human beings, but in your sight, that is, let it be directed in such a way that it is pleasing to you—namely, that I ask for what pleases you and what ought to be asked.

Since some pray for things that ought to be prayed for and that please God, but nevertheless do so with no good intention—as those who pray to acquire wisdom, not so that by living wisely they may seek heavenly goods, but so that, having obtained it, they may set themselves above others—he adds, “like incense.”

It is as though he said: I pray that my prayer be directed in your sight in such a way that it is like incense: that is, that you may direct your attention toward heavenly goods with the same intention with which the smoke of incense rises toward higher things.

All this means: Make me pray for what ought to be prayed for, and do so with the intention of heavenly goods.

“And let the lifting of my hands,” that is, of my works, “be an evening sacrifice,” that is, the fulfillment of the New Law, which is the sweetest sacrifice to God. Hence Prosper:

> No greater offering can be presented  
> than when a man offers libations of chaste conduct  
> and sacrifices from the gift of the virtues.

The New Law is called an evening sacrifice either because it is the latest, after the Old Law, so that no other follows it, just as when evening has come, being the final part, no further part of the day follows; or because it was consecrated in Christ’s death, which is called an evening sacrifice because, around evening, at the ninth hour, he offered himself to God as a sacrifice of praise by dying.

This offering of death was prefigured in the Old Law by the lamb, through whose evening sacrifice the Israelite people were freed from Egyptian slavery.

“Let the lifting of my hands,” I say, “be an evening sacrifice,” namely, permit me to lift up and magnify my good works with a good intention, so that I may fulfill not only the Old Law but also the New. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20).

But I did not pray only with an intense cry that my prayer be directed and that the lifting of my hands be an evening sacrifice. I also prayed concerning the guarding of my mouth:

“Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth,” that is, guard my mouth by the power of your will. But lest he seem to be praying that it be guarded so that it might say nothing, he adds for clarification: “And,” that is, namely, “place a door over my lips,” that is, a guard comparable to a door.

A door is placed in a house so that it may be opened to those worthy to enter the house, but closed to those who ought not to enter. In the same way, let the guard of your mercy preside over my mouth, so that I may say what ought to be said, but remain silent about what is empty and harmful.

“For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12:36).

“Place,” I say, “a door over my lips.” I call it a door of circumspection: place such a guard over my mouth that it not only guard my mouth simply from illicit speech, but also surround all the bodily senses and protect them from illicit movements—my sight, so that it may not look illicitly; my hearing, so that it may not hear illicitly; and the other senses likewise.

But I pray not only that a guard be placed over my mouth. I pray for something greater: “Do not let my heart decline,” that is, do not permit my heart to decline and be humbled from the dignity of its holiness, “into words of wickedness,” that is, toward thinking those words that wicked people speak when excusing themselves for their sins, whether by the weakness of nature or by the necessity of the deed.

It is as though he said: I pray not only that I may not speak words of wickedness; I also pray, as the lesser matter, that I may not conceive words of wickedness in my heart in order to excuse myself for my sins.

But I pray not only for this. I also pray: “Do not permit my heart to decline toward making excuses for myself while I am in sins,” namely, so that, if it should happen in some way that I foolishly excuse myself for my sins, you may at least not cast me down into this blindness, that I should excuse those very excuses, that is, conceive in my heart that those excuses were justly made. For excusing the excuse is worse than excusing the sins.

He shows what benefit will come to him if the prayer stated above is granted, so that by this he may become more worthy to obtain what he prays for:

“I pray: place a guard over my mouth and do not let my heart decline.” If I obtain this, I shall be blessed, because I will not associate with people who practice criminal iniquity, that is, I will not be a participant in or collaborator with their iniquity.

This must be determined in view of what follows, because the statement was made concerning those who practice the lesser forms of iniquity. “I will not associate,” I say, “with people who practice iniquity”; nor will I associate with “their chosen ones,” that is, with the leaders and superiors of those who practice iniquity.

But lest he seem to justify himself entirely out of arrogance, he shows, as an example of humility, that he needs correction, as follows:

“I will not associate,” I say, “with those who practice iniquity,” so as to sin criminally. Nevertheless, when I have sinned venially, ecclesiastical discipline will correct me: any righteous prelate of the Church will rebuke me, and this will not be done in anger but in mercy. He will reprimand me with severe words, and even that will be done in mercy.

“I will be rebuked by the righteous, but the oil of the sinner will not fatten my head,” that is, my mind. Thus I pray that the oil of the sinner—namely, the flattery of any sinner, called “oil” because it is sweet and smooth like oil—will not fatten my head, that is, will not soothe my mind and delight it so as to draw me toward illicit consent, after the manner of oil, which soothes those whom it fattens.

It will not fatten me, I say, so as to conform me to him. And truly it will not fatten me; rather, I will conform the sinner’s portion to myself.

Since a little space still remains, and afterward my prayer stated above will be among their good pleasures—that is, it will be included among what pleases them, namely, they will be pleased to pray for the same thing I prayed for above—and by this my prayer will be among their good pleasures, “they who have been swallowed up will be joined to the rock,” that is, they will be swallowed up by us, meaning that they will be incorporated with those who are joined to the rock of firmness, Christ, through a good life.

They will be swallowed up, I say, not only the lesser men; but, more wonderfully, their judges also—their prelates, namely, through whose judgment and example the lesser men sin. They will be swallowed up, I say, through the words of my preaching.

For they will hear my words with the ears of their hearts, and rightly, since those words have been able—that is, will be powerful and effective—for instructing them. Some, I say, will hear my words and will be swallowed up, to be joined to the rock.

But some, who will not listen, will be called “hell,” by emphasis, because by living badly and drawing others toward hell through their evil example they will do so. And beside this hell, that is, beside the judgment of this hell, “our bones have been scattered,” that is, will be scattered: the stronger among us according to the body will be destroyed through various torments.

I call them bones scattered as “the thickness of the earth broken up is spread over the earth,” that is, just as dung, although something filthy and vile, when broken up—that is, scattered—over the earth makes the thick earth rich and fertile, so we, as vile and filthy people to be torn apart through various punishments, will make the children of the Church rich in virtues by the example of our constancy, and thus make them fertile in good works.

We will be scattered, I say, according to the body. Therefore I pray, Lord, “do not take away my soul,” that is, do not permit my soul to be taken away by these destroyers, so that fear of bodily destruction may cause me to yield to them.

“Do not take away,” I say, and neither should you take it away, because, O Lord—truly Lord—my inward eyes, that is, my affections, look toward you, and I have hoped in the things that are in you, namely, eternal goods, not worldly ones.

Do not take away my soul, I say, but guard me from the snare of flatteries that sinners have set, that is, will set, for me, for my harm, so that by entangling me in it they may withdraw me from my purpose of holiness.

Guard me, I say, so that I may not be entangled in that snare. And I pray not only to be guarded from the snare of flatteries; guard me also so that I may not be overcome by the scandals of those who practice iniquity, that is, by evident tribulations which will inflict upon me the works of iniquity. I call them “scandals” because, when inflicted, they cause many to stumble.

Guard me, I say, and truly you will guard me so that I do not fall. But many sinful Christians, placed in the net of his iniquity, will fall, that is, will fail in the purpose of their confession, either through the snare or through the scandals.

It is as though he said: You will guard me so that I fall in no way, but you will permit many sinful Christians to fail because of the desert of their iniquity, in which they have become entangled.

The sinners, I say, are placed in the net of his iniquity; therefore they will fall.

But I, who pray to be guarded by you, am singular, that is, I possess a singular condition: I have a singular hope and desire for heavenly goods, not a manifold desire for earthly things, and I shall remain singular until I pass from this life through bodily death.

And because I am and shall be singular, do not permit me to fall. Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek” (Ps. 26:4), and so forth.

## ON PSALM 141

The title of the one hundred and forty-first. “Understanding of David, when he was in the cave.”

This psalm is rightly called “Understanding,” because it contains the understanding of Christ, the true David, which he possessed in his Passion.

The title is explained as follows: “This understanding,” that is, this psalm, is “of David,” namely, of Christ, and was possessed by that David “when he was in the cave,” that is, in the mortal humanity he assumed. In relation to his divinity, this humanity was humble, like a cave, and in it he lay hidden as in a cave.

Or it may be read as follows: In this psalm the understanding of David, Christ, is signified, which he possessed when he was in the cave, as explained above.

Or it was possessed when he was in the cave of the tomb—not yet in reality, but already in contemplation, namely, when he was already considering that he would die and be placed in the tomb. He uttered these words, or possessed this understanding which is conceived in this psalm.

Or he possessed it when he was still in the cave before the Passion, that is, while dwelling bodily in this world. This world is called a cave because of its lowliness in relation to the heavenly homeland, which is called a lofty mountain. Christ lay hidden in this world as in a cave when, having become incarnate, he appeared mortal and capable of suffering.

This title, however, is placed according to the historical account, which is as follows: When David was being pursued by Saul, he entered a cave and hid there. It happened that his persecutor Saul came to the place of that same cave. Not knowing that David was hiding there, he entered it to relieve his bowels. While he was doing so, David secretly approached him and cut off the edge of his cloak, that is, of his garment, in order to prove by this sign that he had had the opportunity to kill him (1 Sam. 24:4, 15).

The allegory of this history is not to be pursued in every detail, but is as follows: Through David, who hid in the cave because of Saul’s persecution, Christ is represented as having remained hidden humanly in this world for much of his life, persecuted by the Jews, members of the devil.

Through Saul, who entered the cave in order to discharge the filth of his belly, the devil is represented. He entered this world through the sin of the first parent in order to place here filthy and illicit thoughts and works.

David, Christ, cut off the edge of his garment with a sword when, by the sword of spiritual teaching, he separated for salvation from the devil’s domination a part of the human race that had been joined to him as a garment.

Thus, in this psalm the voice of the Head is heard, showing how, in contemplation of his Passion, he cried out to the Lord and entreated him, so that he might prescribe in himself an example for his members of praying in tribulations. He also indicates his Passion, so that he may make those for whose salvation he suffered indebted to him and give them an example of suffering for him.

“With my voice,” that is, with a voice suitable to me—namely, holy and pure, expressing intense devotion—“I cried out to the Lord the Father,” O hearers.

This means: I had an intense devotion and affection toward him, and this was an intense cry.

But I did not merely cry out while directing myself affectionately toward him; with my inward voice I also entreated him, that is, I made supplication, looking toward the Lord, who is merciful and omnipotent.

I did not merely cry out to the Lord and entreat him; even now I “pour out,” that is, pour forth completely, “my prayer in his sight,” namely, I make my prayer manifest in his sight, that is, in his knowledge, after the likeness of something enclosed which, when poured out—that is, poured outside—is made manifest.

This means: I make my prayer manifest and known to him, that is, I ask for something which, because it is suitable, is worthy of his knowledge. For things that are suitable for God are, by antonomasia, called known and manifest.

I pour out, I say, my prayer, and, “being before him,” that is, in his intimacy and favor, I declare, that is, inwardly recount, my tribulation, which I continually suffer and shall continue to suffer in fulfilling obedience to him.

I declare it not out of boastfulness, but in order to obtain a reward for it, after the likeness of a brave soldier who, being dear to his lord, does not speak to him through messengers but, standing before him, faithfully recounts the labor he has endured for him, so that he may receive from his lord a reward for that labor.

I declare my tribulation, I say, “in the failing of my spirit,” that is, in the destruction of my soul’s will. I call the spirit that proceeds from me—that is, from the frailty of my humanity—“spirit.”

It is as though he said: I declare my tribulation in such a way that, although in the frailty of the flesh I have an unwillingness to suffer, I set this will before you and am ready to obey your will, namely, to suffer, according to what he likewise says in the Gospel: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. 26:39; Luke 22:42).

[Col. 1381C] Where we have here “in failing,” the Hebrew translation has: “when my heart was distressed.” Hence it is clear that in this translation “in failing” may be read for “in being distressed.” It was not placed there because any distress of the Passion generated failure in him, but to show the intensity of his Passion, which could generate failure in another.

According to this interpretation, the passage is read as follows: I declare my tribulation, which I have and shall have, “in the failing of my spirit,” that is, in the distressing of my soul. This tribulation is now the cause, since it is now being experienced, and will be the cause when it is experienced, of my soul’s distress.

But lest this distress seem to come upon him against his will, he adds, “from me.” This means: I shall be distressed, I say, and the fact that my soul will be distressed will arise from me, that is, from my disposition and will.

After showing that he had cried out and made supplication, he also shows that he had acted well and that his works had pleased God, so that by his example he might encourage his hearers to act well, as follows:

“I cried out,” I say, “and made supplication, and I also performed good works. And you, who are a just judge, knew my paths,” that is, my difficult and singular good works pleased you.

Although I am so worthy that you should know my paths, nevertheless, while I was placed on this way of good works, in which I walked—that is, in which I continually advanced—they hid a snare for me, that is, secretly, for the sake of their reputation, they prepared death for me, by which they might entangle and hold me.

What is stated in the past tense must be read as referring to the future. It is as though he said: On this way on which I walk, they will hide for me a snare of death.

But when they prepare to hand me over to death, I will “look to the right,” that is, I will look toward those superior to me, namely, toward the disciples, who are represented by the right because it is the more worthy member, just as in the Church there are more worthy members. Hence the Gospel says: “The Lord turned and looked upon Peter” (Luke 22:61).

I will look, I say, and I will see, that is, I will test whether any of my own recognize me. “And there was no one who knew me,” that is, there will be none of my own who, by steadfastly confessing me, proves that he knows me to be both true God and man.

For when they deny me, they will make it appear that they do not know me.

When he says, “I looked and saw,” he speaks in human fashion, as though he were briefly saying: By the evidence of the event I will experience that no one will know me.

And although, with no one knowing me, there could be an opportunity for flight, “flight has perished from me,” that is, will perish from me: I will in no way flee death.

And when flight from me has perished, “there is not”—that is, there will not be—anyone among my own “who seeks my soul,” that is, who seeks the cause of my life, why it should be taken away from them. There will be none of my own who dares to pronounce judgment on my behalf that I am unworthy of death, after the likeness of an advocate attempting to free an innocent person, who investigates the cause of his condemnation in order to prove it unjust.

Or, “who seeks my soul,” that is, the innocence of my soul, and thus pronounces judgment for me.

It is as though he said: Let it be supposed that they do not know me to be God; nevertheless, even if I appear to be a mere man, since I am innocent, it would be just for them to seek my soul by pronouncing judgment on my behalf. Yet they will neither know me nor seek my soul.

Therefore, since I have no helper, looking toward you, my Lord, I cried out, that is, I will act with an intense cry. I said—that is, I will say, both with my inward and outward voice:

“O Lord, you are my hope,” and no one else. Through you I hope to be delivered and rewarded. “And my portion is in the land of the living,” that is, my chosen portion is among those who will be in the land of the living. Through my death I will choose that portion of humanity which will be in the land of the living in the future.

It is as though he said: This is what I hope from you: that you will give me as a portion and inheritance those who will be in the land of the living.

Therefore, since you are my hope and since my portion is in the land of the living, “attend to my supplication,” that is, pay close attention to my supplication; or make yourself attentive to my supplication, so that you may bestow intensely what I ask intensely.

And it is necessary that I pray for this, because “I have been humbled exceedingly,” that is, I have been and shall be greatly humbled and cast down in tribulations.

“Attend,” I say, “to my supplication.” My supplication is as follows: “Deliver me from my persecuting Jews, lest I become conformed to them.”

It is necessary that I pray to be delivered from my persecutors, because “they have grown strong against me to oppress me,” that is, they will consider themselves strong enough to oppress and overcome me.

And I pray not only, “Deliver me, so that I may not yield,” but also, after my death, when I am guarded by the Jews in the tomb, so that I may be held in perpetual death, “bring my soul out,” that is, raise me from the custody of the Jews by resurrecting me.

It should be noted that he says, “bring out my soul.” If he had said, “bring me out,” it could be understood that his body, not resurrected, was brought out of their custody either by force or in some other way. But when he says, “bring out my soul,” it is understood that he prays to be brought out in such a way that his soul is raised, which they suppose they are holding in death.

“Bring out,” I say, “my soul. And do this in order that I may confess your name,” that is, praise you in consideration of your name, which is “Lord.” Bring me out, namely, so that my righteous disciples, considering my deliverance, may confess you.

And truly, through my deliverance the righteous will confess you. For “the righteous await me”—will await me—until you reward me with deliverance, in completion of my obedience. On this account they will confess you.

That is, the righteous await—and will perseveringly await—you to give me this reward for my completed obedience: that you bring me out of death. They will wait until you grant me this reward. And thus, at last, on this account they will continually confess you. Therefore it is fitting that you bring me out of custody.

## ON PSALM 142

The title of the one hundred and forty-second. “A psalm of David, when his son persecuted him.”

This is explained as follows: This psalm is of David, that is, of the faithful penitent who is now acting manfully. Although previously he did not act manfully while he was in sin, it is nevertheless the psalm of the penitent David, composed “when,” that is, because, “his son persecuted him.”

His son is the wicked suggestion arising from the habit of a sin already abandoned. It is called his son because it proceeds from the frailty of his corrupted nature, just as every son proceeds from his father according to the origin of the flesh.

It is as though he said: These are the words of anyone who has now become penitent and ceased from sin. He utters them for this reason: although he has already abandoned his sin, nevertheless, from the very habit of the sin that has been abandoned, a wicked suggestion arises, which persecutes him and strives to drive him back to the same sin.

The penitent, considering himself placed in the distress of this persecution, reflects on how lofty he had been in virtues after baptism and before he sinned, and to what great abasement he descended through sin. He also observes what vast and most grievous condemnation his first parents incurred for their sin. Fearing that, since he sins in the same way, he may undergo a severe punishment, he prays both for the remission of sin and for the attainment of virtues, showing his own abasement and the persecution of his suggestion.

And because his spirit suffers distress from this, he also prays for perseverance in good works, for deliverance from enemies, and to hear mercy in the morning, putting forward several reasons why he should be heard.

He says all this with the intention of obtaining through prayer what he desires. Finally, out of excessive confidence, he promises that he will attain what he prays for, so that he may draw other penitents to pray through the hope of attainment.

Lord, hear my prayer; as if he were saying: Since I, now repentant, regard you as my God, and do not make myself my own free man but subject myself to you, O Lord, hear my prayer, so that I may obtain what I ask of you. And with the ears of your power receive my supplication—that is, hear my supplication effectually—after the likeness of hearers who carefully attend to words they willingly hear, so that they may grasp them and, having grasped them, fulfill them. He calls the Lord’s ears the capacity of his power to accomplish what is asked of the Lord. He calls that prayer a petition which is made without any adjuration, but a supplication one which is made as though with an adjuration, namely, one that is ordinarily prompted by more vehement desire. Yet it must not be said that an adjuration can be made to God; rather, when we pray to him through the merits of the Lord Jesus, we deal with him in the manner of those who adjure. What he states here in an undetermined way—“hear my prayer and supplication”—he determines below, where he says: “Do not turn away,” and so forth, up to “your spirit.” Since he had said “supplication,” he indicates that he is supplicating, that is, praying as though with an adjuration, when he adds “in truth.” This is what he means: “With the ears of your power receive my supplication.” And this, I beg, do not do in consideration of my merits, since they are nothing, but in your truth—that is, in consideration of the merits of your truth, namely, your Son, through whom you proved all your promises true by fulfilling them.

[Col. 1384C] I say, “Hear my prayer”; and, since there are no merits of mine in consideration of which you should hear me praying, hear me in your righteousness—that is, in consideration of your righteousness, namely, your Son, through whose death you justify sinners. Therefore your righteousness is named emphatically, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Who was made for us righteousness and redemption and sanctification” (1 Cor. 1:30). Here “truth” and “righteousness” designate the same thing, namely Christ. But because the word “truth” is more general—for it denotes the justification of sinners, the just recompense of good and evil people, and the fulfillment of all the Father’s promises—he introduces another word that more specifically denotes what pertains to his prayer, when he calls him “righteousness.” For by this word “righteousness,” as we said above, it is signified that he himself justifies sinners. The penitent now praying intends once more to obtain this justification, since he has already lost it by sinning. When, however, he calls him “righteousness,” he more effectively moves the Lord and Father to grant through him what he prays for. The equivalent meaning is as though he were saying: “Through the merits of him by whom you made the promise of your justification truthful, I pray to be heard. Since he is the justification of all who truly repent, may he mercifully grant justification to me also. I pray: hear me.”

And I also pray: Do not enter into judgment with me, your servant—that is, with me, now making myself your servant by repenting and desiring to make satisfaction to you for the sin I have committed. Do not enter into judgment with me—that is, do not charge my sins to me so as to punish them by a just judgment—after the likeness of judges who enter into judgment with any accused person in order to condemn him justly. “Do not enter,” I say, “into judgment with me, your servant.”

It is necessary for me to pray this, because no living person will be justified in your sight—that is, no living person will be found perfectly just in your consideration, even if he appears perfectly just in his own sight and in the sight of human beings. Hence the Apostle says: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4:4). As if he were saying: To say nothing of me, who am dead in sins, if you take all those who are truly living in virtues and wish to examine all their evil deeds justly, no one will be found so just in the scrutiny of your investigation that many stains of sin will not be found in him. Therefore I, dead in sins, must fear all the more that you might enter into judgment with me. For if you entered into judgment, you would punish me forever by a just judgment. “Do not enter,” I say.

I pray this because the enemy, the devil—that is, an evil suggestion—has persecuted my soul by urging it toward sins. And he has not persecuted it ineffectually, but in such a way that he humbled, that is, cast down, the dignity of its holiness: he humbled my life, that is, my soul, which previously ought emphatically to have been called “life.” He humbled, I say, my soul by evil consent and action. I speak of a soul existing on earth—that is, in the desire for earthly things—whereas previously, through the virtues, it desired only heavenly things. By taking away its virtues, he cast it down from the sublimity of that desire and brought it to desire earthly things alone. This is certainly no slight danger, after the likeness of a captured bird whose feathers are removed, so that, held on the ground, it no longer has the ability to fly upward.

Nor did he merely humble my soul by consent and evil action; he also placed me, that is, firmly established me through evil habit, in darkness—that is, in the darknesses of sins—whereas previously I had been in an abundance of the brightness of virtues. This means: He made me habitually commit sins, and through those sins I came into an excessive darkening of ignorance. “He placed me,” I say, “in darkness”—me, I mean, made like the dead of the world: that is, so dead in soul as those in the world who are already dead in soul. He placed me in sins in such a way that I was dead like the other lovers of this world, who have already incurred in their souls the death of blindness and the loss of virtues, and who in the future will be cast into outer darkness.

And because I have been humbled and placed in darkness, my spirit became anxious on this account—that is, the reasoning faculty of my spirit was troubled—and it was distressed over me, that is, over me who had been humbled and placed in darkness. This means: By reasoning I considered myself so humbled and placed in darkness, and because of this I had excessive anxiety in my soul.

Or it may be understood in this way, while the meaning remains the same: “My spirit became anxious,” that is, the reasoning faculty of my soul, considering that I had been humbled and placed in darkness, became anxious over me; after the likeness of a friend who, bending over a dead friend, is exceedingly distressed because of his death.

But because the spirit could become anxious not from the will of free choice—which would be fruitless—as someone is sometimes necessarily anxious over the loss of temporal things, he adds: “My heart was troubled,” that is, the reasoning faculty of my heart was troubled by anxiety, not from necessity but “in me,” that is, in the will of my free choice. I am anxious over this voluntarily, and therefore I merit forgiveness more greatly. “My spirit became anxious, and my heart was troubled” is a repetition of the same thought, so that he might add “in me” as a qualification.

“My spirit became anxious,” I say, because I had been placed in darkness. And my spirit became anxious not only because of this placement, but also because, when I had been so humbled and placed in darkness, I remembered ancient days—that is, my former virtues, which I had possessed before I sinned and lost by sinning. Because of their great brightness, they ought to be called “days.”

Or I became anxious because I remembered ancient days—that is, I remembered what happened in ancient days: namely, how severely our first parents were condemned on account of their sin. And since I was doing something similar, I feared being condemned severely.

Nor did I merely remember ancient days; on account of this remembrance I also meditated on all your works—that is, I meditated on fulfilling all your works. I meditated on how I might fulfill all your works. And not only did I meditate, but I will also continually meditate on completing the works of your hands—that is, your operations. I will meditate as though I were now performing works that could not in fact be performed except through the operations of your grace. Therefore, I beg, do not enter into judgment with me.

Nor did I merely meditate and continue to meditate; I also spread out my hands—that is, I enlarged and extended my affections—in order to embrace and love you, not in order to obtain earthly things. This means: I prepared myself intensely to love you, after the likeness of one who spreads out his hands to embrace someone whom he greatly loves. “I spread out my hands,” I say, “toward you.”

And still my soul longs for you and desires to attain you, as vehemently as dry land longs for water and greatly desires to be satisfied by it. This means: I love you exceedingly; I desire to cling to you alone.

Since, therefore, I have meditated on your works and spread out my hands toward you, hear me, O Lord, so that you may grant what I ask—and do so quickly, that is, without delay. And it is fitting that you hear me, for now my spirit has failed within me—that is, the will of my spirit, namely, the will that arose in me from the weakness of the flesh. This means: I have set aside the will of my weakness, reduced it to nothing, and clung to the fulfillment of your will.
