It should be noted that “Hear me quickly” is the same as what he said above: “Lord, hear my prayer.” But it is repeated after a lengthy intervening passage so that he might finally explain his prayer in parts, as follows: “Hear me,” I say, “quickly,” me, that is, praying in this way: “Do not turn your face away”—that is, your beauty—from me, namely the virtues that are the beauty of the soul. “Face” is used for “beauty,” because beauty is observed in the face. It is as though he were saying: “Because of the merits of my sins you have turned your face away from me,” that is, the beauty of the virtues that is given through you. But since I now practice repentance, I pray that you may not turn your face away from me any longer.

Here, by means of litotes, “Give me back your face” is understood: the face that you turned away from me because of the multitude of my sins.

“Do not turn your face away from me,” I say. And if you turn it away, I shall be like those who descend into the pit—that is, into the depths of hell—so that I may descend together with them. As if he were saying: If you turn your face away from me forever, I shall descend locally into the depths of hell with sinners, where there is no redemption. Therefore I pray: Do not turn your face away from me.

I pray that here you may not turn your face away; I also pray that in the morning of the day of judgment—that is, at the morning resurrection, which will occur at the dawn of the eighth day—you may cause your mercy to be heard: namely, that most gracious word which you will mercifully speak to those who are to be saved, and which is called “mercy.” It will be this: “Come, you blessed” (Matt. 25:34), and so forth.

But because many of those who are to be condemned will hear this to no advantage of their own, he adds: “Cause it to be heard,” I say, “for me,” that is, for my benefit, so that I may be one of those to whom this word of mercy will be spoken.

Therefore cause it to be heard, because I have hoped in you, not in myself—that is, I have placed all my hope of salvation in you, not in my merits.

I pray: Do not turn your face away from me—that is, I pray that you grant me the beauty of virtues. And I do not pray only that the beauty of virtues be given to me; I also pray that you make known to me the way of good works.

And lest it be thought that he prays only for this way to be made known to him according to knowledge, he determines how he asks that it be made known: “Make known to me,” I say, “the way of good works in which I may walk”—that is, in which I may advance from good to better. Make this way known to me according to the experience of advancement; that is, make me frequent this way, after the likeness of a traveler to whom the road he frequents is well known.

For this reason make known to me the way in which I may walk: because I previously depressed my soul by sinning, but now at last I have lifted it up—that is, exalted it—by repenting, thinking rightly, and loving virtues and good works. “I have lifted up my soul,” I say, “in order to love and attain you”; that is, I lifted up my soul with the intention of being able to attain you.

I pray: Make known to me the way in which I may walk. I also pray: Rescue me from my enemies—that is, from suggestions and evil spirits, and also from external enemies who strive to turn me back from my good purpose—so that they may not prevail against me.

Or: Rescue me from my enemies, namely, rescue me from the sins I have already committed by forgiving them.

And you ought to rescue me, O Lord, for I have fled to you by repenting and praying.

But since it would not be enough to be rescued from enemies unless good action also followed, teach me, by the illumination of your grace, to do your will—that is, to fulfill your commandments.

And I therefore pray that you teach me because you are my God. Since you are my Creator, without whom I could not exist, I know that without you I cannot act well. Therefore I pray: Teach me, and so forth.

It should be noted that “Teach me to do your will” means the same as what was stated above: “Make known to me the way in which I may walk.” But it is repeated for another purpose: namely, to indicate that it is not enough to be rescued from enemies unless good action follows, and that no one can act well unless the Lord teaches him.

After making his prayer, through the excessive certainty of a good conscience he promises himself that he will obtain what he prayed for. This serves to console other penitents, so that, relying on the hope of obtaining their requests, they may not despair of mercy but may pray by his example in order to attain mercy.

He therefore speaks as follows: I prayed that you would not turn your face away from me—that is, the beauty of virtues—and that you would make known to me the way in which I may walk, and that you would rescue me from enemies; and I will truly obtain what I prayed for.

For your good spirit will lead me into a level land. Although I had made myself a crooked and barren land, yielding no fruit of good works but producing thorns of evil works, your Holy Spirit, who is good by nature and can also make me good, will lead me from what I am—a crooked land—to become a good and level land, fertile in virtues and good works.

And by placing me through your Holy Spirit in the equity of virtues and good works—an equity that is yours, that is, given by you—you will make me alive in soul through this equity, since I have died through sin.

“You will make me alive,” I say; and you will do this for the sake of your name—that is, for the increase of your glory—or for the sake of your name, that is, because of your mercy, not because of my merits.

And by making me alive you will lead my soul out of distress: namely, when I am exceedingly anxious because I am dead in soul through sin and have lost the beauty of virtues, you will rescue my soul from this anxiety by making me alive in virtues.

And through this you will destroy, in your mercy—that is, in consideration of your mercy, not in consideration of my merits—my enemies. That is, by the mercy of forgiveness you will destroy the sins I have committed, which make war against me by deforming my soul.

And you will not only destroy the sins I have committed through forgiveness; you will also destroy all the enemies who afflict my soul—namely, evil suggestions and wicked people who distress my soul by wishing to drive it toward its accustomed sins. You will destroy them, that is, render them ineffectual.

And when you have done all this through mercy, you will do this also: although I previously resisted you by sinning, I am nevertheless your servant—that is, I have made myself your servant by repenting and desiring to make satisfaction.

## ON PSALM 143

The title of the one hundred forty-third: “A Psalm of David,” that is, of the mass of the faithful fighting against Goliath—namely, fighting by living well—against the devil and his members, and against the vices that incite him to evil action and thus intend to overcome him.

This battle was therefore prefigured by the battle of David, who fought against Goliath and struck him down with a stone. For just as Goliath, David’s persecutor, was struck down by the blow of a stone, so also the devil, who occupies the place of Goliath, and his members—namely, wicked people and the vices introduced by him—are overcome by each faithful person. The faithful person is David, strong of hand, acting courageously with the help of Christ, who is the rock of strength.

In this psalm, therefore, the mass of the perfect blesses God for the instruction of the lesser, and so God has mercifully delivered it from enemies, teaching it to fight courageously against them and continually protecting it. It blesses him also because he has already become known to faithful people. It prays as well that he may become known to those to whom he is not yet known.

It further prays to be liberated and rescued from heretics, lest they be able to make it like themselves either by their words, by the imitation of their works, or by tribulations. Through this it teaches the lesser to pray.

It also shows how dangerous their assault is: first, because their error is manifold; second, because they speak in a polished and dialectical manner; and third, because they are praised by many. In this way it teaches the lesser to beware of their deceptions.

“Blessed is the Lord my God by me,” and so forth; as if he were saying: O you hearers, bless the Lord by following my example. For I bless—that is, I exalt, both with my mouth, affection, and action—the Lord and Father, because he is both Lord, the Almighty, and my God, that is, my Creator.

“Blessed is he,” I say—that is, exalted by me—because the Lord God teaches, that is, has made my hands learned, for battle: for battle against the devil and his members, the vices.

And he who teaches my fingers for war teaches them to do the same thing. “Battle” and “war” here designate the same thing: namely, the struggle against the devil, his members, and the vices.

Hands and fingers, however, signify different things. Since battle is conducted at close quarters with swords by the whole hand, whereas the fingers act at a distance with arrows and other missiles—and this battle is less dangerous than one conducted at close quarters—“battle of the hands” here signifies battle against greater temptations, which press upon one with the utmost severity and as though at close quarters.

“War of the fingers” signifies the war against lesser suggestions, which assail less gravely and as though from a distance.

What he presents by this double likeness is equivalent to saying: I exalt the Lord for this reason: although he is Lord and my God, by enlightening me with spiritual understanding and making me learned and equipped in virtues, he has enabled me to fight courageously against greater and lesser suggestions.

The Lord God, I say, exists as my mercy emphatically—not because of my merits, but solely because of his mercy—and has made me learned for battle. He exists as my refuge, that is, my security, relying on whose help I persist securely in this battle.

“Refuge” is used for “security,” because those who are afraid frequently flee for refuge to a secure place.

He exists, I say, as my refuge, and also as my supporter, that is, my healer and restorer. Through the death of his Only-Begotten he restored and strengthened my reason and free choice, which had been weakened by original sin.

He also exists as my deliverer, because through the forgiveness of his grace he liberated me from the slavery of the sins I had committed. He exists as my protector, that is, my defender, so that I may not yield to the attacks of inner enemies—namely, evil suggestions—and external enemies, namely heretics and wicked men.

And I have hoped in him—that is, I have hoped that through him I shall obtain the good things that are in him, namely immortality and freedom from suffering. This means: He himself is my hope, through whom I have hope of reaching eternal goods.

For this consideration also he is blessed by me.

In him, I say, I have hoped; and by the help of his grace he subjects beneath me—that is, to me—the people of my enemies, made mine by conformity. He has subjected to me the immense multitude of wicked people who previously opposed me, so that it became conformed to me.

Or it may be understood in this way: He subjects my people beneath me—that is, the multitude of suggestions arising from my weakness. Since they are many, they are called a “people.” He subjected them to me not only so that he might protect me from them, lest they prevail against me, but also so that I might have the ability, whenever they arise, easily to trample them down and drive them entirely away from me.

After showing that he blesses the Lord in view of the benefits bestowed upon him, in order to arouse his hearers more strongly to bless him, he shows that he blesses him in consideration of those benefits that he has commonly bestowed on every person destined for salvation.

He says this as follows: I said, O Lord, that you are blessed by me because, by making me learned for battle, you are my mercy and refuge, and so forth.

You are also blessed by me for this reason: although humanity had been made vile and rejected through Adam, O Lord, what is a human being—that is, how great and precious has every person destined for salvation become? This has happened because you have become known to him, that is, because you have manifested yourself to him through faith and understanding, whereas previously he had been separated from knowledge of you through original sin.

Or: How great is the son of man—that is, the son of Adam—because you regard him as such? Each faithful person destined for salvation, although previously he was a son of the first man Adam not only according to the origin of the flesh but also according to the condemnation of original guilt, has become something great through this: you regard him, that is, you magnify him and hold him to be of great worth, forming an estimation of him by taking away from him the stain of original guilt and restoring in him the beauty of virtues.

Or you regard him as worthy to be placed among the angels, so that the order of angels that fell may be completed from him.

This verse is equivalent to saying briefly: I bless you for this reason: I consider that, although a human being was a child of perdition, something vile and rejected, you made him something great by enlightening him with knowledge of you, reforming virtues in him, and thus regarding him as being of great worth.

One might ask: You say that a human being was made something great because you became known to him and because you regard him in this way. Was he not something great in himself?

To this he adds the following: “Humanity is like vanity,” and so forth; as if he were saying: A human being was made something great because you became known to him and because you regard him in this way.

Although this human being had been made in the likeness of truth, in the likeness of God, by sinning in Adam he became like vanity—that is, he made himself like vanity, like nothingness.

It is as though he were saying: I do not mean that he became nothing, but that he made himself like nothing, so that he already appeared almost reduced to nothing, since he was tending from true being, in whose likeness he had been made, toward non-being, both through original sin and through actual sins.

He further shows in this respect that he made himself like vanity: his days quickly pass away like a shadow. As if he were saying: He still retains punishment for having departed from true being and tended toward non-being. From this comes the fact that his passing days are like a shadow. For he passes from youth into old age and thus ultimately dies. Hence he still appears like vanity.

For by what reasoning can that which is transient be denied to be vain? Hence Solomon says: “Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes; vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. 1:1).

Having shown that he blesses God because God has become known to the faithful, he prays that God may become known to those destined for salvation to whom he is not yet known.

I said: O Lord, faithful people have become something great because you have become known to them. But in order that the other human beings destined for salvation may become something great by your making yourself known to them, and in order that you may become known to them, O Lord, incline your heavens—that is, humble your preachers, who are exalted in knowledge.

“Humble” them, I say, either so that they do not shrink from suffering persecution for their teaching, or so that, although they are supreme in wisdom, they may adapt their teaching to the capacity of their hearers, giving them milk to drink, not solid food (1 Cor. 3:2), and thus making you known to them.

Hence the Apostle says: “Not in the wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power” (1 Cor. 1:17). And elsewhere: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2).

“Incline the heavens,” I say, “and descend through the heavens into the knowledge of your hearers.”

And he rightly says “descend.” Since they, being still weak in understanding, cannot ascend to the sublimity of divine contemplation, divine mercy descends to them when it illuminates them somewhat with the rays of its knowledge.

“Descend,” I say, “to them through knowledge; and by descending touch not only the lesser but also the mountains,” that is, the greater and the prelates. Touch them inwardly with fear of their sins, and when touched they will smoke—that is, they will emit smoke from themselves, namely, tearful compunction, which troubles the eyes of the body like smoke.

But so that your mountains may receive more fully the knowledge of you through the heavens that have been inclined, and may be touched and smoke, through those same heavens make lightning flash—that is, cause flashes to shine forth: namely, miracles, which are called flashes because they make those who see them astonished, in the manner of flashes of lightning.

“Flashes,” I say, “and lightning”; and thus you will divide—that is, separate—those who are to be saved from conformity with those who are to be destroyed.

And because miracles would not be sufficient, send forth through the heavens your arrows as well—that is, send your teachings openly. These are the elementary teachings, which, once they have acquired some knowledge of God, are suggested by preachers to the unlearned. Like arrows, they pierce as far as the heart and kill them in the respect that they are evil.

Or it may be understood in this way: After you have descended somewhat through the heavens into their knowledge, and they have already received something of elementary teaching so that they are not wholly uneducated, then through those same heavens send your arrows into them—that is, your commandments and institutions, which pierce the heart like arrows. These are the great institutions for living that are administered by teachers after the imparting of elementary doctrine.

“Send forth,” I say, “your arrows”; and thus you will trouble them. After you have instructed them how worthy and how holy your commandments are, they will be troubled—that is, they will grieve because they have not devoted themselves to your commandments.

Having made his prayer for others, he also prays for himself, that he may be delivered from heretics, saying:

I prayed for others when I said, “O Lord, incline,” and so forth. I also pray for myself, since I am attacked by heretics: Send forth your hand from on high—that is, send me your help openly from the height of your power.

“Hand” is used for “help,” because we assist someone who is about to fall with a hand.

“Send forth,” I say, “the help of your power to me.” And thus rescue me from many waters.

Do not rescue me only slightly; free me from many waters—that is, rescue me from the various and manifold doctrines of heretics in such a way that you free me from them entirely, so that I may contradict them freely and not be deceived in any respect.

He calls the doctrines of heretics “many waters” because, after the likeness of muddy water, they are filthy, and because they are manifold and varied, not agreeing in the simplicity of faith.

Nor only from many waters, but also rescue me from the hand of alien sons—that is, from the works of alien sons. Let me not be deceived by the feigned works of heretics, who, although they had been sons through participation in the Church’s sacraments, became alien through their error.

All of this is equivalent to saying briefly: Free me from heretics in such a way that I am not deceived either by their doctrine or by the imitation of their works, which appear good but are perverse.

Since he had prayed to be delivered both from the doctrines and from the works of heretics, he assigns separate reasons for each:

“Free me,” I say, “from the many waters of heretics, whose mouth has spoken vanity.” As if he were saying: It is necessary for me to pray to be freed from the doctrines of heretics, who speak nothing except things that are vain and full of error.

And for this reason I pray to be delivered from the works of heretics who are alien sons: because their right hand—that is, their work, which appears to be a right hand, namely, good—is a right hand of iniquity, that is, an evil work.

Therefore it is necessary for me to pray to be freed from both, lest I be deceived in any respect.

But if you deliver me from many waters, which pertain to the oldness of Adam, O God, I will sing a new song to you—that is, I will praise you with a new song, namely with the undivided faith that was given through the new human being.

And if you deliver me from the hand of alien sons, I will sing psalms to you—that is, I will act well to your praise. I will not do this unwillingly, but on a ten-stringed psaltery—that is, in a soul instructed by the ten commandments of the Law, in the will of a soul fulfilling the ten commandments of the Law.

It is called a psaltery because, as has often been said, it resounds with praise from above, after the likeness of a psaltery. The strings are called the commandments of the Law because, through their fulfillment, they produce sweet melody for God, after the likeness of strings that produce sweet song from themselves.

Or it may be understood in this way: “Free me,” I say, “from many waters and from the hand of alien sons.” If you do this, O God, I will sing a new song to you—that is, I will praise you with a new song, namely by fulfilling those sublime commandments which, since they were not given in the Old Testament, were given in the New Testament, such as loving one’s enemy, setting aside worldly things, and other commandments of this kind.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20).

“I will sing,” I say, “a new song to you”; and I will also sing psalms to you on a ten-stringed psaltery—that is, I will praise you by good action, in the will of a soul adorned with the ten commandments of the old Law.

This means: I will praise you through the fulfillment of the New and Old Testaments.

He repeats the prayer he had made concerning deliverance from heretics out of his intense desire to obtain it, and also to show how dangerous their assault is:

“I will sing,” I say, “to you, and I will sing psalms to you.” And so that this may happen, rescue me from the sword.

And because “sword” can refer to the sword of the Holy Spirit, which is good and useful, he determines which sword he means when he adds “malignant.” As if he were saying: Deliver me from the doctrine of heretics, which is a malignant sword, killing virtues in the soul that consents to it.

This is the same thing he said above: “Free me from many waters.”

“Rescue me,” I say, “from the malignant sword, and also deliver me from the hand of alien sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity,” as explained above.

“Rescue me,” I say, and “deliver me,” for you are powerful enough to do this, since you give salvation to kings—that is, to all the faithful, whom you have made their own kings. You give them salvation, namely virtues, which are the soul’s salvation.

And through the death of your Son you redeemed from original and actual sins David—that is, each faithful person acting courageously, strong of hand.

I speak of David made your servant, willingly obedient to you.

“Deliver me,” I say, “from the hand and work of alien sons.”

This is greatly necessary for me, since their sons—that is, their thoughts—are not established in the ancient authority of the Scriptures but in youth, that is, in erroneous novelty. I call it their own youth, that is, invented by them. Their thoughts are like young plants—that is, comparable to trees or herbs newly planted—and they continually increase from day to day for the worse, just as young plants continually grow while they are young.

Or it may be understood in this way: Their sons, that is, their thoughts, are like young plants; they are comparable to young plants in this respect: they are always young, always new, so that they may not in any way rely on ancient authorities.

I say that their sons are like young plants, but their daughters—that is, their utterances—are composed, that is, adorned, in such a way that they speak dialectically, rhetorically, and elegantly, so as to deceive more effectively.

Therefore, since it is exceedingly dangerous to deal with them, I pray: Rescue me from them.

They are composed, I say—that is, adorned—and not merely adorned, but adorned all around, that is, adorned in every respect, so that they are like the likeness of a temple. They are like a temple because faith is called a temple, since in it all sacrifices of good works and virtues are offered to God, just as sacrifices were offered to God in the temple.

By this same likeness faith is also called the Church, according to Prosper’s saying: “There is no place of a true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church.”

What he says—“like the likeness of a temple”—is equivalent to saying: Their utterances are adorned all around because they resemble the words of faith.

For they speak in such a way that they utter certain words which appear to pertain to the faith, so that they may deceive more quickly, secretly mingling their error with them.

Indeed, the thoughts are appropriately called “sons,” and the utterances “daughters,” because, although both proceed from them as sons and daughters proceed from fathers, thoughts are nevertheless more worthy than utterances, since utterances are signs of thoughts. Therefore, by the designation of the worthier sex—namely, “sons”—thoughts are expressed; whereas utterances are expressed by the name of the less worthy sex, namely, “daughters.”

Utterances are also called “daughters” because they are adorned and, by their adornment, attract their hearers, just as the daughters of the Midianites, when adorned by their parents and presented to the sons of Israel in the time of Moses, deceived them by the appearance of their adornment and caused them to offend God by driving them to fornication; on that account they were also defeated by the Midianites (Num. XXV).

Therefore I also pray, “Lord, deliver me from the evil sword of the verbosity of foreign sons,” because their storehouses—that is, their intellectual faculties, in which depraved thoughts are contained, just as wine and grain are contained in storehouses—are full, that is, crammed with those depraved thoughts, and “eructating,” that is, fully revealing those thoughts in words, passing from this to that, that is, from one argument to another, in the likeness of a very full storehouse in which wine or grain is transferred from one vessel to another. This is as though he said: Since their intellectual faculties are filled with depraved thoughts, they bring them forth through many arguments. By the force of these arguments they compel many to agree with them; therefore, it is exceedingly dangerous to act against them.

For that reason, too, it is dangerous to speak with them, and I pray to be delivered from them, because “their sheep are fertile”—namely, those who are called “sheep” as their leaders, because they beget inferiors in error, like sheep giving birth to lambs. They are fertile, that is, they have many offspring, producing many sons, by whose example many are attracted. Fertile, I say, they are, and they do not beget sons in the doctrine of faith, but are abundant in sons “in their goings-out,” not in the goings-out of faith. That is to say: Since they go out from the Catholic faith, in such departures they acquire many sons conforming to themselves, whom they likewise cause to go out with them.

Therefore they are also deceptive and dangerous, and I pray to be delivered from them, because “their oxen are fat”—namely, their teachers, called above “sheep,” who are also called “oxen” because they attract their inferiors to themselves by nursing them with the flatteries of their words, and cultivate those whom they have enticed with perverse doctrines, in the manner of cows nursing calves and cultivating fields. They are fat, that is, made prosperous and enriched by earthly riches, through whose generosity they attach many to themselves—people whom they cannot overcome by the inducements or arguments of their words.

And for that reason they are, moreover, to be feared, and it is necessary that I be delivered from them, because, when they build a “wall”—that is, a heap of arguments, which is called a wall because it is made from many arguments just as a wall is made from many stones—their wall does not easily collapse, namely, their heap of arguments cannot easily be thrown down and destroyed.

[Note: [Col. 1395D] Tertullian treats this beautifully in *On Prescription Against Heretics*.]

For there is great force in their arguments. He calls heretics “sheep” and “oxen” in the feminine gender because, after the manner of the feminine sex, they are effeminate in virtues.

“There is no collapse,” I say, “of their wall, nor is there a passage through that wall”—namely, when they enclose certain ignorant people, destined for destruction, within the very chain of their arguments, those people cannot pass out from it or escape, after the likeness of a captive who, placed in prison and enclosed on every side by walls, cannot escape from it.

“There is no passage,” I say, “through the wall, nor is there a cry,” that is, neither subtlety nor intensity of understanding, “in their streets,” that is, in the breadth of their error. For they do not stand in the truth, which is something definite and confined, but in error, which is broad and boundless; and because of its breadth it is called a “street.” In discovering error they consider themselves subtle and intense, yet there is no subtlety or intensity in them. For no intensity or subtlety of understanding can be said to exist where there is nothing but error and imprudence.

A “cry” is called subtlety and intensity because, just as the body cries out through a loud external voice, so the mind, in its own manner, cries out through intensity and subtlety of understanding. Hence, the Lord Jesus is often read to have cried out in the Gospel—not because he cried with an external voice, but because he cried out through subtlety of understanding and intensity.

Or: “There is no cry in their streets,” that is, there is no manifest utterance in the breadth of their error. In other words, they do not dare to dispute their great errors openly in councils where Catholics are assembled, but act secretly in chambers, where there is opportunity to deceive, and there they deal with the ignorant. “Cry” is used for manifest utterance because the voice of those who cry out is more evident than the voice of those who speak softly.

Therefore I also pray to be delivered from conformity with them, because foolish and ignorant people have called the people of the heretics blessed—the people to whom the things stated above belong: their sons are like young plantings; their daughters are adorned; their storehouses are full; their sheep are fertile; their oxen are fat; and there is neither collapse nor passage through their wall. They loudly proclaim that these people are truly blessed, and many, deceived by this praise, are added to them. Hence it is necessary for me to pray that I, too, may not be deceived in the same way.

Foolish, I say, are those who call this people blessed. But that is certainly false. Rather, without doubt, blessed is the people whose God is the Lord—namely, the people over whom no error rules, but whose God is its Lord, that is, the people that regards its God as its Lord.

## ON PSALM CXLIV

**Title of the one hundred forty-fourth:** “A praise of David.”

This is explained as follows: This praise, namely this psalm, is attributed to David himself, that is, to Christ. It is not that Christ speaks here, but that the assembly of the more perfect faithful, in order to instruct the lesser in praising God, promises that it will praise God through both the active and the contemplative life. It also commends him in many ways by recounting his greatness, justice, sweetness, and many other glorious things concerning him.

**I will exalt you, my God and king**, as though he said: Although, Lord Jesus, unbelieving Jews despise you and regard you as merely human, since you are nevertheless my God and my king—that is, my creator and ruler, who continually orders and governs whatever good exists in me—I will exalt you, that is, raise you up and glorify you, through my active life.

And I will bless your name, that is, I will praise you in contemplation of your name, which is “Lord.” I will bless you, I say, with a blessing lasting forever and throughout the age of the age—that is, I will praise you with the praise of the contemplative life, which will last both in this age and in the future, according to the Gospel saying: “Mary chose the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke X, 42). The active life, however, will last only in this age.

I will bless your name, I say. And this not only in prosperity or only in adversity, but I will bless you, that is, praise you, throughout every day, both of prosperity and of adversity. Or: I will bless you throughout every day, that is, through each ascent in virtue. I will praise you by ascending from virtue to virtue, which are called “days” because, in the likeness of day, they spiritually illuminate the soul.

I say that I will bless you and praise your name, that is, I will praise you in contemplation of your name forever and throughout the age of the age. Since this is the same as what was said above, “I will bless the name,” and so forth, it is repeated in order to add the reasons why he will praise him in this way.

I will praise the Lord, I say, O hearers, forever and throughout the age of the age. And this because the Lord is great in nature, that is, powerful, and worthy of praise, that is, deserving of praise. And this exceedingly, that is, beyond human understanding. Great, I say, he is, so much so that there is no end to his greatness, that is, no limit: it cannot be bounded or measured, either by place or by understanding, how great he is; for he is uncircumscribed.

Or: “There is no end to his greatness,” that is, it is eternal. I say that I will praise the Lord because he is great in nature.

**Generation and generation**, which is not sufficient to contemplate this, will at least praise your works, O Lord, and in praising your works they will declare your power among themselves with praise. This means: Those who are ignorant and simple in generation and generation—that is, in the various generations of the faithful—who will not be capable of seeing that you are great in nature, will nevertheless contemplate your wondrous visible works, namely the sun, the moon, and other such things. They will praise them because they are excellent, and in praising them they will ascend from them to you, their Creator; by their contemplation they will declare you powerful and will thus praise you among themselves.

When he says “generation” twice, all the generations of the faithful are understood. It is also noted that this praise arises only from the generation of works, which is not altogether perfect; it will be possessed only in this life, where there are various generations. In the other life, the generation of the saints will be simple, and the knowledge and praise of God will be perfect in every respect, according to the prophet’s saying: “No one shall say to his neighbor, ‘Know God,’ because all shall know me, from the least even to the greatest” (Jer. XXXI, 34).

But they will not only declare your power in contemplation of your works; they will also speak of the magnificence of the glory of your holiness, that is, of the magnificence of your glorious holiness. They will praise you by speaking among themselves of the magnificent and glorious holiness of conduct and virtues that you grant your saints in this life.

And they will recount your wonders, that is, they will praise you by recounting among themselves the wonders—the miracles—that you perform through your saints. All this is as though he said: They will praise you in contemplation of the conduct, virtues, and miracles of your saints.

They will also speak, to your praise, of the power of your terrible deeds—that is, of the powerful force of your terrible punishments, by which you punish the wicked here in many ways. This is as though he said: They will praise you because of your power, by which you also punish the wicked here.

And to your praise they will recount your greatness among themselves, that is, they will praise you by recounting your greatness, namely, the great advancement of your faithful in conduct and virtues. This means: They will praise you because you advance your people in virtues and conduct.

And not only this, but also they will “eructate,” that is, fully recount among themselves the memory of the abundance of your sweetness—that is, the memory of your abundant sweetness, namely your mercy. They will praise you by fully recounting the memory of your abundant mercy.

This means: They will praise you because they will recall that you magnify your saints in holiness of conduct and virtues, not on account of their merits, but because of the memory of your abundant mercy—because in your mercy you remember how to sanctify your own, whom you seemed, through Adam, to have consigned to oblivion.

They will also rejoice in your justice, that is, to your praise they will joyfully recount your justice. They will say among themselves that, when you punish the wicked here, you do so by just judgment, and on this account they will praise you.

He does not say “they will rejoice” because they rejoice in the punishment of the wicked, but because, in recounting their punishment, they will rejoice that they themselves were not such.

Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “The just man shall rejoice when he sees vengeance” (Ps. LVII, 11), and so forth.

I say, O hearers, that they will eructate the memory of the abundance of the Lord’s sweetness. And rightly so, for the Lord is compassionate according to the benefits of mercy bestowed, merciful in nature, and, even if he benefited no one, patient in awaiting sinners, whom he does not immediately punish justly.

Merciful, I say, he is, and not a little, but greatly merciful, more than anyone is capable of explaining. He shows that he is very sweet, that is, compassionate, by adding this: Compassionate, I say, is the Lord.

And not toward a few, but the Lord is sweet—that is, compassionate—toward all, that is, toward people of every kind, both Jews and Gentiles. He bestows the many benefits of his mercy upon people of every kind.

And his compassions, that is, the benefits of his mercy, are over all his works, that is, they preside over all his works. This is as though he said: When he works faith, charity, and the other virtues in his people, he does so out of compassion. When he presides over those same works in them, so that they may advance more and more, his compassions are also signified in those very advances.

Since he had said that the works of the Lord would be the cause and subject for which he himself would be praised by the faithful, he prays and desires that this may be as he had declared above.

I said, Lord, that generation and generation will praise your works, and so forth—that is, because your works, when considered excellent, will be the reason why you are praised by the faithful in every generation.

And so let it be: Let all your works confess to you, Lord, that is, let all your works, when contemplated, be the subject for which you are praised by the faithful. And whatever may be the case with the other works, at least let your saints, whom you make perfect in conduct and virtues, bless you, that is, praise you.

This means: Let the holiness of your saints be the subject of your praise.

What follows, however, when he says “the glory of your kingdom,” and so forth, is not a prayer or a wish, but a narrative directed to the praise of God, which is joined to the preceding words as follows:

I said that the faithful, in generation and generation, would speak of the magnificence of the glorious holiness that you, God, grant your saints here, and that they would praise you in contemplation of this. And not only this, but also, to your praise, they will speak among themselves of the glory of your kingdom, that is, they will praise you by speaking of and recounting the glory that in the future you will give your saints in your kingdom.

And I said that they would speak of the power of your terrible deeds—that is, to your praise they would speak among themselves of the powerful force of your terrible punishments, by which you punish the wicked here.

And not only this, but they will also speak of your power, by which you will punish the wicked in the future, and in contemplation of this they will praise you. They will speak, I say, among themselves of your power, yet in such a way that they will make this power of yours known to other sons of men—that is, to people who are ignorant of it—and thus cause them, by a good life, to beware of this power, lest it punish them.

And I said that they would speak among themselves of the glory of your kingdom, yet in such a way that they would make known to the ignorant the glory of its magnificence—that is, the magnificent glory of your kingdom—and, by making it known, draw them toward desire for this kingdom.

Your kingdom, I say, is the kingdom of all ages, that is, enduring through every age; it is eternal. Therefore it is to be desired with an immeasurable longing.

I also said that they would make your power known so that people would beware of it. And this dominion, that is, your power, endures through every generation of this life and even into the generation after this life, which is to come. Therefore it is greatly to be feared and avoided.

When he says “in every generation,” he indicates several generations and thereby suggests this entire life, in which generation is multiple. When he says “in the generation,” he indicates the other life, in which there will not be a multiplicity of generations, but one simple generation.

But the power of the Lord will not punish the wicked only after this life, in hell; while this entire life lasts, it also punishes many of them, already placed there.

I say that the kingdom and dominion of the Lord are eternal: the kingdom that he promised to the good, and the dominion with which he threatened the wicked.

And the Lord is faithful, that is, truthful in all his words, both in the promise of the kingdom and in the threat of just [dominion]—not like certain people who, presuming excessively upon the mercy of the Lord, say that he is truthful only in the promise of the kingdom and not in the threat of death. It is wicked even to think this. For unless he justly condemned the wicked eternally, he would not be faithful in all his words.

By asserting that he is truthful in all things, he consoles and assures the good concerning the promise of the kingdom, and terrifies the wicked concerning the threat of condemnation.

Faithful, I say, he is, and also holy, that is, just in all his works: he justly works the salvation of the good, and he justly works the condemnation of the wicked. This appropriately contributes to the praise of God, lest, when he appears gentle in the salvation of the just, he should appear harsh in the condemnation of the wicked.

The Lord is proved faithful—that is, truthful—in all his words because, although he promised his kingdom to human beings who have fallen from it through original and actual sins and cannot ascend to it by themselves, the Lord, by the reception of grace, lifts up all who fall from it—that is, people of every kind who fall from it through original and actual sin.

He lifts them up after the death of the body, giving them perfect blessedness in that kingdom, in the likeness of a good shepherd who, when a sheep falls from the pastures or from the sheepfold of some mountain and cannot ascend by itself, lifts it onto his shoulders and carries it back to the pastures or the sheepfold.

And he appropriately says “all,” not because he lifts up everyone who falls from it, but because from every kind of those who fall he lifts up many—both those who sin less gravely and those who sin more gravely.

He lifts them up, I say, after death. And because they could not be lifted up to this kingdom after death unless they had first been raised up in this life through the remission of sins, he first raises up all—that is, people of every kind who have been cast down, both more gravely and less gravely cast down. When they have been utterly cast down, that is, when their virtues and free will have been broken in them because of the excessive weight of their sins, and they cannot raise themselves from this broken condition, he raises them by remitting their sins and restoring innocence in them, in the likeness of someone who has fallen from a high place and, being seriously injured, cannot rise by himself but is raised by another.

Because of his intense affection, he turns directly to God in thanksgiving, saying:

I say, Lord, that you raise up those cast down in every way. And the interior eyes of all who have been raised—that is, the minds of all who have been raised—look and attend to you, O Lord, as merciful and powerful, and hope that you will give them food, salvation, protection, and finally elevation.

And you give food, that is, spiritual food of doctrine and understanding—their food, I say, suitable for them, giving milk to some and solid food to others (Hebr. V, 12).

You give them, I say, their food, and this at the appropriate time, that is, in this life, where there is an appropriate time. In the other life there will be no time for instruction.

I say that you give them food, and not sparingly, but you open your hand, that is, you make the activity of your generosity open and abundant, in the likeness of a generous dispenser who, when he gives something, does not contract his hand but opens it in order to give generously.

You open your hand, I say, and thus fill every animal with blessing, that is, all those who are animals—namely, gentle creatures ready to bear the yoke of the Lord, like oxen, which we commonly call “animals.” Or those who are animals are those who are not yet spiritual but are still animal, that is, carnal.

This means: You give them their food in full.

But the Lord, O hearers, not only gives food to his own, but is also just in all his ways—that is, in his commandments by which one comes to him, since he commands nothing except what is just—and holy, that is, merciful in all his works, that is, in works of every kind. For although he is just in prescribing commandments, he is likewise merciful in working and fulfilling those same commandments in his people by the help of his grace.

He is near to all who call upon him, that is, he is ready to do the will of those who call upon him. He is near, I say, as the Lord; and since he is Lord, he ought to be near to his servants who call upon him.

He specifies to whom he is near when he adds: He is near, namely, to all who call upon him, that is, who pray to him in truth, not indeed in vanity. A person is said to call upon him in truth when he asks for what ought to be requested—namely, good things—and asks for them as they ought to be requested, with intense affection.

Since he calls the Lord just and holy, this seems properly to pertain to his praise.

The Lord, I say, is near, and he is not merely ready to do the will of those who fear him, but will actually do it—that is, fulfill the will of those who fear him with chaste fear, that is, those who love him—and he will hear their prayer in order to bring it to completion.

It should be known that the saints desire and pray for this same thing. But when he says that the saints rightly desire and pray for what they desire, he instructs us by their example: when we rightly desire something, we should pray to God that this same thing may come to pass.

He explains what they desire and pray for as follows: He will hear their prayer, I say, and that is, he will save them, causing them here to perform good works, which is most salutary.

And when they have attained this salvation, the Lord preserves them in perseverance, so that they do not lose this salvation. He preserves them, I say, as those who love him; and because those who love him are worthy to be preserved.

He will save his own here, I say, so that at last they may be lifted into his kingdom. Conversely, he will destroy all unrepentant sinners, blinding them here and condemning them without end in the future.

Having shown the many reasons why God is worthy of praise, just as at the beginning of the psalm he promised that he would praise him, so at the end, for greater confirmation, he likewise promises to praise him.

I have shown, O hearers, that the Lord is sweet, great, and just, that he does the will of those who fear him, and that he preserves them. Since, then, he is such and such, my mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord, that is, I will praise him with my mouth.

By this he indicates that he will also praise him with affection and deed. I say that I will praise him with my mouth.

And following my example, everyone who still remains flesh—everyone, namely, who is still carnal and not yet spiritual, but who has been made spiritual—let that person bless his holy name, that is, praise him in contemplation of his holy name, because he is called just, sweet, God, and Lord, and is designated by many other holy names.

Let that person bless, I say, his holy name with a blessing directed toward the age and the age of the age—that is, let him praise him throughout this entire life and in the future. Here they shall bless him with affection, mouth, and deed; in the future, with affection alone.

## ON PSALM CXLV

**Title of the one hundred forty-fifth:** “Alleluia.”

The voice of the Prophet recalling all the faithful, so that, in contemplation of temporal things, they may not trust in princes, in whom their salvation does not lie; so that, by trusting in them, they may not flatteringly praise them; and also the voice of the Prophet drawing the faithful toward the praise of God on account of the many reasons that he sets forth.

To make his exhortation more authoritative, at the beginning of the psalm he introduces his rational faculty inviting his sensual faculty to praise God, and afterward introduces the sensual faculty promising that it will praise him. Neither of these utterances is spoken aloud, but both occur in thought.

**Praise the Lord, my soul**, as though he said: Many praise secular princes, trusting in them flatteringly and agreeing with them in an evil life. But you, the sensual faculty of my soul, praise the Lord alone by establishing a good life.

After the exhortation of rationality has been written, the responding sensual faculty is introduced, promising continually that it will praise the Lord in this way:

You say, O rational faculty, that I should praise God; and I will truly do so. I will praise the Lord in my life, that is, I will establish a good life, and thus praise him. And this not merely for an hour, but I will sing praise to my God as long as I exist, that is, as long as I am in this life; through my good activity I will praise God.

The sensual faculty is said to act well because, by its animating the body, the body acts well.

After the Prophet has shown that he will praise God, he turns to the hearers and attempts to remove them from trust in human beings and draw them toward the praise of God as follows:

I will praise the Lord, I say. Therefore you, O hearers, praising God by my example, trust in God himself, and do not trust in secular princes, as though they could do anything for you from themselves. Nothing visible or perceptible occurs that is not either commanded or permitted by that invisible and intelligible court of the supreme Emperor.

I speak of princes who are sons of men, that is, human beings who are not superior to you in nature; therefore it is sufficiently unworthy for you to place your trust in them. “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jer. XVII, 5).

I speak of the sons of men, in whom your salvation does not depend—those who cannot save you any more than you can save them—and therefore you must not trust in them.

In this respect, since your salvation depends on no prince, no one is to be trusted, because “his spirit will go forth,” that is, he will be separated from his body, “and then his body will return to the earth,” so that it becomes earth—earth, I say, which was its material.

For we read that man was made from the clay of the earth (Gen. II, 7). Therefore, on the day when the spirits of the princes go forth, all their thoughts will perish, that is, what they thought they would do—depressing some and raising others to wealth—will be rendered futile.

Hence it is clear that those are wretched who place their hope of assistance in them.

Conversely, blessed is the one whose God is his helper—namely, the person who desires and seeks to have his God as his helper in every good thing, not some earthly prince.

I speak of the God of Jacob, who is the God and helper of all who struggle manfully against vices. By this he urges his hearers to strive to be Jacob.

I say: Blessed is the one whose God is his helper, and whose hope of reward is in the Lord his God, not in princes.

In the Lord, I say, who is so powerful that he made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them—both the heavenly spirits, human beings, fish, and the other creatures. Since he is so great, hope must be placed in him.

Nor is hope placed in vain in one who is not truthful in his promise merely for a time, but “keeps truth forever,” that is, eternally. He never abandons truth, but always loves it, in the likeness of a man who carefully guards what he loves.

Since, then, he is truthful forever and has promised salvation to those who hope in him, hope must certainly be placed in him. And if persecutions of injuries arise for his sake, one must not flee. For he himself executes just judgment for those who suffer injury for his sake. He does so by rewarding them worthily and punishing their persecutors justly.

Since he had said that one must trust in God and not in princes, someone might object: It is true that one must hope in God for heavenly goods, but one must nevertheless trust in princes for secular goods.

To remove this objection, the text adds:

I say that he executes judgment for those who suffer injury. And he does not bestow only this benefit; he also gives bodily food to the hungry.

Although food is sometimes given by princes, it is not given without God’s command or permission. By “food” he indicates that he also grants all secular goods.

But the Lord does not confer only this benefit, giving food to the hungry; he also confers the benefits that follow, whose consideration should lead one to trust in him:

The Lord loosens those in fetters, that is, those who are bound and tied by the evil habit of sin, which wishes to drag them toward sins and leaves them without the ability to act well. He loosens them from the bond of that evil habit, so that it no longer presses upon them so heavily, and grants them the ability to act well, in the likeness of a man in fetters who, having no freedom of his own, is restored to his freedom when someone releases him from the fetters.

But he does not merely loosen those in fetters. The Lord also illuminates with the light of spiritual understanding the blind, namely those who are blind and deprived of understanding.

Nor does he perform only these benefits; moreover—and this is greater—the Lord raises up those who have been cast down, namely those who have been utterly cast down through sins, in whom virtues and free will have been completely broken and weakened. He raises them from this state of being cast down by forgiving their sins through confession and restoring virtues and free will in them.

After they have been raised, the Lord directs those who have been made just, that is, advances them from virtue to virtue. Or, if “he loves” is found there, the meaning is the same.

And he does not merely direct them by advancing them; the Lord also preserves the sojourners by his grace, so that they do not fall away from this advancement. That is to say: He makes those persevere in this advancement who do not regard themselves as citizens of this homeland but as sojourners—that is, as citizens of the heavenly homeland.

But if it should happen to some that they fall away from this advancement and become orphans and widows—orphans because they lack God as Father, widows because they have departed from God and clung to the despised world—nevertheless, when they have become orphans and widows through sin and have thereby been rejected from his grace, he will receive them into participation in grace if they wish to return through repentance, in the likeness of a merciful bridegroom who, out of mercy, receives back the bride whom he had rejected because of fornication, if she wishes to cease from fornication.

He will receive them, I say, although they are sinners. And by receiving them, he will destroy through forgiveness the way of sinners, that is, the multitude of sins by which, while they were sinners, they were previously proceeding toward death.

He will receive them, I say. And in those whom he has received, the Lord will reign forever, that is, throughout all these present ages; they will be the Lord’s kingdom and possession as long as these ages endure.

The Lord, I say, will reign—the Lord who is your God, O Zion, that is, the one whom you regard as your God, O Zion, the assembly of the faithful contemplating future things and not attending to the present.

And he will not reign only as long as these ages endure, but also in this present generation, lasting into the future generation. That is to say: He will reign in them both here and in the future—here by advancing them in goodness, and in the future by making them blessed without end.

## ON PSALM CXLVI

**Title of the one hundred forty-sixth:** “Alleluia.”

The voice of the Prophet inviting all the faithful to the praise of God, in contemplation of the fact that in the future he will build the heavenly Jerusalem and here gather the dispersions of Israel, as well as in contemplation of the other benefits that he sets forth in this psalm.

Praise the Lord, the Father, O faithful, in the future time of grace, with the psalm, for the psalm is good—that is, the psalm is useful for you. And because it is useful and salutary for you to praise God with the psalm, let this praise—being a psalm—be pleasing, that is, delightful to God, and seemly, that is, honorable, when offered by you to our God; as though he were saying: Since it is useful for you, and pleasing and seemly for him, that you praise him with the psalm, render him such praise.

Since, however, a psalm is made on the psalter, and thus involves both voice and the work of the hands, “psalm” is understood to mean both praise of God in good works, and praise in the external voice, namely, in the mouth, and praise in the interior voice, namely, in the affection. Praise, I say, the Lord, the Father. And do this in consideration of the fact that in the future the Lord will be building the heavenly Jerusalem, supplying from the human race whatever fell away through the pride of the angels. And so that the heavenly Jerusalem may be built from human beings, here he will gather into the unity of faith the scattered ones of Israel, namely, the scattered human beings who are destined to become Israel. This is to say: Those who are to be saved, from whom Jerusalem will be built, though previously scattered into various errors of idolatry, he will gather into the unity of faith, and thus here he will make them Israel.

He will gather them, I say. And after they have been gathered, he heals—that is, he will heal—those who have become brokenhearted. This is to say: After receiving the faith, when they are still weak through their habitual sins and feeble in doing good, he will heal this weakness in them with the medicine of his grace, so that he grants them facility for doing good. This is analogous to a sick person who, after escaping an illness, still retains weakness from the disease itself, but is gradually healed of that weakness while, with the help of physicians, he is restored to his former bodily strength. And he will therefore heal them because they will be brokenhearted through compunction: “For a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Psalm 50:19).

And before he heals them of this weakness, he binds up—that is, he will bind up—their contritions, namely, he will consolidate through baptism and the other ecclesiastical sacraments the powers of the soul and free will which, by sinning, they had broken and destroyed. This is to say: He will restore their powers and free will, which they themselves had squandered by sinning, by analogy with a physician who heals by binding up someone’s crushed bones or wounds.

Praise, I say, the Lord. After he has healed the brokenhearted, making from them through the illumination of grace a multitude of stars, he counts—that is, he will count—the multitude of those stars; namely, he will preserve them so that they do not fail, since they will be many stars, shining “in the midst of a crooked nation” (Philippians 2:15) through doctrine and good conduct, after the likeness of stars shining at night in the firmament. “To count” is used for “to preserve,” because a thing is ordinarily counted so that, once counted, it may be kept safe. He counts, I say, the many stars. And he gives names to all of them—that is, he will assign them names. This is to say: He will grant them diverse charisms, on account of which diverse names will be assigned to them, so that some will be called martyrs, others confessors, and still others monks or hermits, or they will be designated by many other honorable names.

Since he had shown the unity of the divine nature when he said, “Praise the Lord,” he also shows the plurality of persons in this way: Praise, I say, the Lord, and do so because our God, the Father, is great in nature—that is, he is powerful, whom we men, the authoritative prophets, regard as God. And great is his power, that is, the Son, who is called the power of the Father because the Father orders and governs all things through him. By affirming these two persons to be great, he implies that the Holy Spirit is great.

But lest, because of the different names, there seem to be diversity in the nature, he removes this possibility when he adds: Although the Son is another person from the Father, yet there is no number of his wisdom—that is, there is no diversity, multiplicity, or variety in the nature of the Father’s Son. For one essence of the Father and another of the Son are not counted; rather, their nature is perfectly the same and unchanging. He uses “number” for diversity and multiplicity because we are accustomed to count different and numerous things.

Since he had shown both unity in nature and multiplicity in persons, and since the understanding of this mystery is not apparent to all the faithful, although all must nevertheless derive their faith from it, there are many heretics who, lacking knowledge of so great a matter, do not inquire into it with gentleness. Rather, being ungentle, they disdain to have faith. He commends the gentleness of faith, showing that the gentle are received by the Lord, while, conversely, the ungentle sinners are humbled, in order that, withdrawing us from harshness, he may invite us to gentleness.

I say that the Lord—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is great. The Lord, I say, receives the gentle, who, if they do not immediately understand, do not reject the faith; rather, in order to understand how he is one and three, they strive to investigate it gently. He receives the gentle, that is, he heals them, removing the weakness of ignorance and granting the capacity for understanding. But he humbles sinners, antonomastically—that is, the ungentle—by withdrawing his grace; that is, he casts them down from understanding to the earth, that is, to an earthly understanding. This is to say: Because they are ungentle, the Lord humbles them by withdrawing the light of his grace, so that they not only fail to understand but, what is most serious, think of God in earthly terms and treat him as they would any human being.

Since, therefore, he receives the gentle and humbles sinners who conduct themselves proudly and harshly, all you faithful, so that you may be received if you have not yet been received, and so that, if you have already been received, you may be received more and more by remaining gentle, sing beforehand to the Lord in confession of your sins. This is to say: First of all, confess your sins humbly; this confession will be a sweet and primary song to God. And after confession, sing psalms to our God, that is, do good works to the honor of the Lord. Sing psalms, I say, while existing in the lyre, that is, in the mortification of the flesh.

And truly God must be sung to and praised. For he is the one who covers the heavens with clouds, that is, conceals his mystical secrets in preachers, who, on account of their sublimity, are called “heavens”; yet he prepares this heaven—that is, he makes rain, an open and irrigating doctrine—for his earth, the Church. It is as though he were saying: While he conceals the mystical understanding of his secrets in the apostles and prophets, lest that understanding be held cheap, he nevertheless at times reveals the same understanding to the faithful, who are his earth, through the illumination of his grace, so that it may take the place of rain for them—that is, so that it may instruct them and make them fruitful, after the likeness of rain, which waters the earth and makes it fertile. Such secrets are also called “heaven” because, like heavenly things, they are hidden.

He explains how this heaven makes rain as follows: God prepares rain for the earth from heaven. That heaven, existing in the mountains—that is, in the apostles and prophets, whom he earlier called clouds—produces, that is, opens and manifests to his faithful, heaven which consists of grass and herb. He uses “grass” for grain because, while it is green, it is called grass. Grain signifies the mystical understanding, which is suited only to spiritual and properly rational beings, just as grain is food for rational animals, namely, human beings. Hay, however, which is suitable only for irrational beings, signifies the literal understanding. Only the unlearned and simple faithful use this understanding; they appear almost irrational, and he also calls them beasts in comparison with those who understand mystically.

He explains for whom he produces hay and for whom herb in this way: He produces, I say, hay and herb. Herb, he says, is given to the service of human beings, that is, to more perfect believers, who are called “the service of human beings” because they serve less perfect people in doctrine, such as Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, Gregory, and others of this kind. He produces, I say, herb for the service of human beings, that is, for the perfect. He also gives the beasts—that is, the less perfect and the unlearned—their food, namely, food suited to them: hay.

[Column 1407B] Lest it seem that he gives this hay and herb only to the faithful descended from the Jews, he shows that he will also give them to faithful people from the nations, as follows: He gives, I say, food consisting of hay and herb. And not only to the faithful from the Jewish people, but also to the young of ravens, that is, to the children of Gentile idolaters, who resemble ravens in the blackness of their sins. He gives it, I say, not to all their young, but to those who call upon him, that is, who pray to him in purity of faith—namely, to the faithful from the nations, who are fittingly compared with young ravens.

For just as, according to the natural philosophers, young ravens, while they are still unlike their parents in blackness, are not fed by them but are said to live from dew, so also the faithful person from the nations, who through baptism is already unlike his parents in the blackness of sins, is not filled with the errors of those parents, but is refreshed by the dew of spiritual doctrine.

I have said that he will receive the gentle, who sing beforehand and sing psalms, and will give them hay and herb. But in the strength of a horse—that is, in a strong horse, namely, in a proud man, who is represented by the strong horse because it is an exceedingly proud animal—he will have no pleasure. This is to say: He will not love the proud or receive them. Nor will he take pleasure in the legs of a man, that is, he will not love the worldly pleasures of any human being, which are signified by legs, since legs are musical instruments associated with pleasure-seekers. Or by “the legs of a man” he means the lower parts of the human being, which are also called legs, by which lustful people are signified, because lust chiefly dominates in the loins, which are adjacent to the legs.

When, therefore, he says that he will take no pleasure in the legs of a man, the meaning is the same as if he said that he will take no pleasure in lustful people: he will not love or receive the lustful, but will justly destroy them. This was plainly prefigured in a vision shown to the prophet Ezekiel, to whom the Lord is read to have appeared from the waist upward in the form of electrum, and from the waist downward in the form of fire (Ezekiel 8:7). When he appeared in this way, he took upon himself the form of all Christians, both those to be saved and those to be destroyed. For by the upper part, which displayed the bright appearance of electrum, are understood those who are to be saved and who aspire to the heavenly homeland; they are bright and conspicuous in virtues and works. By the lower part, however, which appeared fiery, were signified the proud and those devoted to worldly pleasures, who, on account of their sins, are to be handed over to Tartarean fire.

He will not, I say, take pleasure in the proud or in the lustful, but the Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him with chaste fear. This is to say: The Lord is pleased with those who fear him, whom he regards with the regard of mercy so that he may make them fear him. He is pleased with those who hope not proudly in themselves, but in mercy—that is, in his mercy. For it is not enough to fear unless there is also hope, and conversely. This is to say: The Lord loves those who fear him and hope for salvation in him, not those who arrogantly presume upon their own merits.

## IN PSALM 147

The title of the one hundred forty-seventh psalm. Alleluia. The voice of the Prophet, who, since in the preceding psalm he had invited the faithful to praise God in consideration of the building of the heavenly Jerusalem and the gathering of idolaters made into Israel, also exhorts the faithful in this psalm to praise God, because he has strengthened the bars of the Church’s gates, so that they cannot be broken by heretics. He also does so in consideration of the conversion of certain heretics, which he likewise displays in this psalm.

Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion—as though he were saying: You, Church, praise the Lord, the Father, with this in view: that the Lord is God. Praise him, I say, in such a way that you are Jerusalem, that is, made peaceful, possessing peace with God and with your neighbor; and this peace is her highest praise. And praise him with this in view: that he is your God, your Creator. Praise him, I say, in such a way that you are Zion, gazing upon heavenly things; and this contemplation is her praise, in which he himself takes great delight.

I say: Praise the Lord your God. And therefore praise him, because he has strengthened the bars of your gates—that is, he will make your leaders strong and unconquerable against heretics. They will be the bars of your gates, that is, the guardians of the writings of the prophets, so that these writings cannot be scattered by heretics, who intend to reduce their authority to nothing, like the Manichaeans and many others, who assert that they must be entirely abolished.

This is said by analogy with bars, which are fastened to gates in order to fortify them, so that no robber may enter the house to devastate it. The prophets are called the gates of the Church because through their teachings they were the entrance into the faith, just as gates are the entrance to a house.

By strengthening the bars so that they do not yield to the attacks of heretics, he blessed—that is, he will bless—the children who remain in you, and who do not depart through the deception of heretics from the fellowship of your faith. He will indeed bless your children both by increasing their number and by exalting them in virtues. They would certainly be scattered by heretics unless the bars were strengthened.

I say: Praise the Lord, who will not only strengthen the bars of your gates, namely Augustine, Jerome, Hilary, and the others, and will not only bless your children, but also is the one who has established your boundaries as peace. With emphasis, this means that he will make your neighbors peaceful—namely, the heretics. This is to say: He will cause the heretics who attack you to have peace and concord with you, converting them so that they no longer press their false arguments against you.

He calls the heretics the neighbors of the Church because they appear to be close to her in this respect: they use the same ecclesiastical sacraments and seem to accept the same authorities, which they pervert by interpreting them wrongly.

He will establish, I say, your boundaries as peace, and he will also satisfy you with the fat of grain, not merely with bran—that is, with the mystical understanding of the Law, not merely with its literal meaning. He calls the inner part of grain its fat, which is also commonly called flour. By the fat of grain, therefore, which is inward and precious and sweeter in taste than bran, the mystical understanding of the Law is signified: it is interior, subtle, precious, and far sweeter than the literal understanding, with which the faithful of the Church are satisfied when Christ reveals it.

By bran, however, which is external and coarse and not so precious, the literal understanding is meant. It is, as it were, external and, in comparison with the mystical understanding, something coarse and not entirely precious; the ancient children of the Synagogue are nourished by it alone. Hence the Lord testified to the disciples: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand” (Luke 8:10).

He explains how he will make the boundaries of the Church peaceful, as follows: Praise, I say, the Lord, who sends—that is, who will send—his word to the earth, that is, his doctrine to earthly people, namely, to heretics. It is as though he were saying: He will reconcile the heretics, the neighbors of the Church, with the Church in this way: through the faithful of the Church, who have been satisfied with the fat of grain, he will send the doctrine of the faith to heretics who cling to earthly opinions.

His word of doctrine, however, will not be ineffective; rather, it runs swiftly—that is, his word of doctrine will run swiftly. This means that it will penetrate the hearts of earthly people most rapidly. Or, “his word will run swiftly” means that it will advance quickly and flow with the greatest force of eloquence, so that it cannot be hindered by the false objections of heretics, in accordance with what is said of Stephen: “They could not resist the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke” (Acts 6:10).

It will run swiftly, I say, his word. Through the efficacy of this word, he gives—that is, he will give—snow like wool, namely, those very heretics who will be snow, that is, frozen exceedingly like snow and cold in charity. He will make them so fervent in charity that they will even give themselves as wool to others who are cold, namely, so that they may warm those who are cold in charity and make them fervent in charity, after the likeness of wool, from which a garment is made to warm and heat the body.

He gives, I say, snow like wool, and he scatters— that is, he will scatter—mist like ashes. This means that those heretics who were previously misty and darkened in understanding he will illuminate with the understanding of the faith; once illuminated, he will scatter them like ashes, that is, distribute them for preaching to other misty people, so that they may take the place of ashes, making those people fruitful in understanding and good works. These people the heretics themselves had previously rendered sterile by their deceptions, after removing them from the Church.

He says this by analogy with ashes, which farmers spread over the earth in place of manure, so that by enriching it they may make it fertile.

Not only will he give snow like wool and scatter mist like ashes, but he also sends—that is, he will send—to others his crystallum as morsels, that is, something comparable to morsels. This is to say: He will not only convert those heretics who are snow, that is, readily capable of dissolving from the hardness of unbelief, just as snow can quickly dissolve, but also those who will be so hardened in unbelief that they can scarcely be dissolved. For this reason they are also called “crystal,” on account of the extreme hardness of their obstinacy.

For, as the natural philosophers assert, crystal is formed from ice hardened over a long period of time; and the hardness of crystal is so great that it can scarcely be broken or cut. God dissolves this crystal—that is, these heretics—despite such hardness of obstinacy, when, converted through the preaching of the faithful, he restores them to the fellowship of the Church and makes their formerly hardened hearts soft and receptive to the faith.

He renders this crystal, once melted, so perfect in knowledge and holiness of conduct that he also makes it retain the place of morsels for others who had previously been deceived by it and separated from the faith, so that they may refresh them with the sweetness of their preaching, after the manner of morsels by which a hungry person is refreshed.

[Column 1410C] He rightly says that they are not whole loaves but morsels, thereby indicating that no one is so perfect as to possess all knowledge or doctrine; rather, each person possesses some portion, just as a morsel is a part of bread. He also fittingly says not simply “crystal” but “his crystal,” to specify by this word that he will not make every crystal into morsels, but only that which will be his, namely, that which has already been predestined for salvation.
