He gives, I say, snow like wool, and sends crystal like morsels. And then who, standing before the face of his cold, will endure that face? No one. It is as though he were saying: When he sends those who, by emphasis, can be called “cold,” because they will be entirely cold in charity, to destroy and attack the other cold people—after that cold has been changed into the heat of charity and has become the possession of God himself—which heretic, standing before their face, that is, before their present assault, will be able to endure and resist such force of their words and eloquence, so as to be overcome and have nothing left to say in reply? No one.

What he presents under the form of a question, with greater weight of praise, is equivalent to saying this: When he sends those who were previously so cold that they could be called snow and crystal, but who have been made fervent, to attack heretics, such will be their wisdom and such their eloquence that no heretical eloquence will be able to resist them.

Since he had dealt with the conversion of heretics, he wishes to show that this conversion will be the work of the cooperation of the whole Trinity, as follows: God the Father gives, I say, snow like wool and crystal like morsels. But in order that these things may happen, he sends—that is, he will send—his Word, that is, from himself he sends his Son to accomplish this. He will send him not locally or visibly, but spiritually and ineffably.

Or, “he will send his Word” means that he will send his Son openly, with respect to knowledge. This is to say: He will give them knowledge of his Son, namely, faith, so that they may believe him to be truly God and man, coeternal with the Father and consubstantial with him. And through the sending of the Word he will melt these things, namely, the snow and the crystal. This is to say: Although they had previously been greatly hardened, so that they could be called snow and crystal, he, with the cooperation of the Son, will release them from their hardness and make them fluid and soft, and ready to believe.

Nor will he accomplish this only through the Son, but also through the Holy Spirit. For his Holy Spirit will blow—that is, will breathe inwardly upon the snow and crystal—and thus they will flow, having become water. They will flow, that is, they will become inclined and pliable toward faith and charity.

But they will become water for others: they will irrigate other hardened people by their doctrine, dissolve them from their hardness, and make them fertile. This is said by analogy with the south wind, whose blowing melts snow and ice, and, once turned into water, causes them to flow.

He explains how the snow and crystal, once dissolved and melted, become water for others, as follows: I say that the Lord will melt the snow and crystal and will make flowing waters. Through these waters the Lord announces—that is, will announce—to others who are to be hardened, Jacob, that is, his word to those who wrestle manfully, namely, the knowledge of his Son. Or, “his word” means the preaching of the faith.

After announcing the word of faith, he will announce to those same people who are to be made Israel—that is, to those who see God in contemplation—his righteousnesses and judgments, namely, his just judgments: his commandments, which are called “righteousnesses” by emphasis because they are just and justify those who fulfill them; and they are called “judgments” because he himself judges that they must be performed. Since they are both righteousnesses and judgments, they are worthy to be proclaimed.

He says that he will not bestow these benefits just mentioned upon all heretics, but upon some, so that in this way he may make those to whom they are granted more favorably disposed and not ungrateful. I say that he will dissolve heretics who exist as snow and crystal, and will also make them water for others. But he did not—that is, he will not—do this for every nation, that is, for the entire multitude of heretics. He will not dissolve all heretics in this way and make them water, nor will he reveal his just judgments to all. That is, he will not make it clear to all how, by a just judgment, he decides to dissolve and illuminate some through mercy, while, by withdrawing grace, he hardens and blinds others. Or, “he will not reveal his judgments to all” means that he will not reveal his commandments to all, nor make clear to all how his commandments must be fulfilled.

## IN PSALM 148

The one hundred forty-eighth psalm. Title. Alleluia. The voice of the Prophet exhorting all the faithful to praise God in consideration of all his creatures and in view of the future exaltation of his people.

Praise the Lord, all you faithful, with every kind of praise, from the heavens, that is, in consideration of the heavens which he created. Here by “heavens” we understand the material heavens themselves and all the creatures that are in them, both rational, such as the heavenly spirits, and irrational, such as the sun, moon, and stars. By material heavens we mean the air, the ether, the firmament itself, and also the seven circles of the seven planets.

Since, when he simply said, “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” he understood by “heavens,” as we have said, both the heavens themselves and the creatures that are in them, he now intends, for the heightening of divine praise, to designate those creatures individually, as follows: Praise, I say, the Lord from the heavens; namely, praise him in the heights, that is, in consideration of those creatures that are exalted in heaven, meaning that they are of more excellent nature.

He explains those exalted creatures individually when he adds: Praise him, all his angels—that is, all you angels, who, existing in such great dignity, were created by him, be for the faithful a reason to praise him. This is as though he were saying: Praise him, O faithful, in consideration of the angels, whom he created so worthy.

Nor should you angels alone be a reason for the faithful to praise him; rather, praise him, all his powers—that is, all you orders of heavenly spirits, created by him as most excellent in nature, be for the faithful a reason to praise him. By the powers, which are one order of heavenly spirits, he designates all the orders except the angels. This is evident from the Hebrew translation, which has: “Praise him, all his hosts.”

It should be noted that he appropriately says “his angels” and “his powers,” although afterward he does not say “his sun” and “his moon.” This is not because these creatures are not also his, but when he affirms that the heavenly spirits, who are more excellent, are his creatures, the rest are certainly included.

Having indicated individually the exalted and more excellent creatures of the heavens, he then deals with the less excellent heavenly creatures, which nevertheless, in view of their nature, are sufficiently splendid, when he adds: Not only should the angels and powers praise him, but also praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars. This is to say: You sun, moon, and stars, wondrously fashioned by him, be for the faithful a reason to praise him.

Nor should the sun, moon, and stars be a reason to praise him only inasmuch as they exist; let the light proceeding from them also praise him—that is, let it be a reason for praising the Lord. For it is one consideration to praise the Lord because these things exist, and another to praise him because they emit light.

Having shown the creatures of the heavens individually, he also deals with the heavens themselves when he adds: Not only should the sun, moon, stars, and light praise him, but also praise him—that is, be a reason for praising him—you higher heavens, embracing the lower heavens. By the higher heavens he means the firmament and the ether, which surround the lower heavens; by the lower, the circles of the planets and the air.

And not only should the heavens praise the Lord, but also the waters that are above the heavens should praise the name of the Lord—that is, they should be causes for the faithful to praise the name of the Lord, meaning that the Lord should be praised in consideration of his great name, since he is Lord and Creator. He appears exceedingly powerful and wondrous in this respect: he created waters not only beneath the firmament but also above the firmament, in accordance with what is read in Genesis: “God divided the waters that were under the firmament from those that were above the firmament” (Genesis 1:7). Why they were created there, even if it is hidden from us, must nevertheless be thought to have been done neither without reason nor without the greatest usefulness.

It may be asked: Why should we praise God in consideration of the sun, moon, stars, heavens, and waters? He answers as follows: For this reason, O faithful, praise him in view of all these things, because he spoke—that is, decreed, willed, and ordered—and the four elements, which were the material of all these things, came into being from nothing. Afterward, within that same ordering, he commanded, and all these things were created, that is, formed from the four elements. Once they had been created, by that same ordering he established that they should endure forever and ever, that is, he made them stable so that they would last eternally. And he placed his commandment—that is, his ordinance—in them, determining how each one should exist; and that ordinance will not pass away, that is, it will not be destroyed, but will always remain firm and stable.

[Column 1413C] After inviting the faithful to praise God in consideration of the heavens and the things that are in them, he invites them to the same praise in consideration of the earth and the creatures that are in it, adding as follows: I have said, “Praise the Lord from the heavens.” But do not praise him only in consideration of the heavens; also praise the Lord from the earth, that is, in consideration of the earth created by him. Just as above he understood by “heavens” both the heavens themselves and the things in them, so here by “earth” he signifies both the earth itself and the creatures contained in it.

He designates these individually for the accumulation of divine praise when he adds: Namely, let all the dragons of the abyss praise him, and fire, hail, snow, ice, and the spirit that raises storms, namely, the wind that stirs up storms on the sea. This is to say: Let all these things, which he has powerfully and wondrously made, be reasons why he is praised by the faithful.

When he deals with earthly creatures in relation to the praise of God, he seems not without reason to have placed these first. For although all these things are harmful to human beings, the very fact that they sometimes cause harm nevertheless occurs by the just judgment of God, who, through the service of these creatures, exacts vengeance from those who offend him. And because it was less clear whether these things belong to the praise of God, he deals with them first. Here is how they cause harm.

Since dragons are fiery by nature and are foremost among earthly animals—so much so that they are said even to be able to break elephants by the tightening of their tails—by God’s just judgment they sometimes stir up the air for the correction of sinners and corrupt it with their breath, so that a deadly pestilence arises from it. At times they devour human beings and their cattle, or set them ablaze with their breath. In the abysses, moreover, people are often submerged and perish, as in the excessive depths of rivers.

Since it is well known how fire, hail, snow, ice, and the spirit of storms harm human beings, it is not necessary to demonstrate this with examples. And although all these things cause harm by God’s just judgment, they nevertheless all pertain to the praise of his justice. That these things pertain to God’s justice is clearly indicated when he adds: All these things—the dragons, the abysses, and so forth—do his word, that is, his commandment, by harming those whom God’s just judgment compels them to harm.

[Column 1414B] Not only should these harmful creatures be a reason for divine praise, but useful earthly creatures should also praise God, that is, be a reason for the faithful to praise God. Let the mountains praise God, and all the hills, which are necessary for human beings because they contain fields and vineyards, from which human beings are fed and given drink; their herds also graze on them.

Let the fruitful trees that grow on the mountains praise God, whose fruits refresh human beings. Not only the fruitful trees, but also all cedars should praise God. By cedars, which are barren trees, he understands the other barren trees, which, although fruitless, are nevertheless suitable for building houses and for other human uses.

Let the wild beasts also praise God, some of which are harmful by God’s just judgment, such as lions and wolves, while others are useful through God’s mercy, such as hares and deer. Let all cattle also praise him, namely, domesticated animals such as oxen and beasts of burden, which are useful for human purposes. Let serpents also praise him, since they cause harm by God’s just judgment, and winged birds, which are beneficial. “Winged” is not added by way of distinction, but for the greater praise of God’s power. For it is one thing to praise God’s power in view of the fact that birds exist, and another in view of the fact that, being winged, they are capable of flying.

Let the kings of the earth and all subject peoples also be a reason for praising God, as well as the other rulers below kings, such as dukes and counts; and not only rulers, but all judges of the earth, both those who are rulers and those who are not. For there are many lesser judges who, although they are in a certain sense rulers, are not ordinarily called rulers.

All this is as though he were saying: In this also, O faithful, have a reason for praising God: that he arranged the human race so beautifully and orderly that some are kings, some rulers, some judges, and others subjects. Among these kings and rulers, some, by a just permission of God, oppress their subjects in many ways through tyranny, while others rule them well through the mercy of God.

Let young men and virgins also be a reason for praising God, namely, the male and female sexes. By young men he designates the male sex, and by virgins the female sex. Let old men together with the young praise the name of the Lord, that is, let old and young be reasons why the Lord is praised, in consideration of his name, which is that of Creator and Almighty.

This is to say: Let the faithful praise the Lord in consideration of the fact that he established diverse ages among human beings, both male and female—namely, youth, old age, and the other ages.

When he says, “let the old men praise with the young,” he similarly makes known that this applies to the other ages as well, and that God is to be praised in consideration of all of them. This too is a reason for praising the Lord: that, according to his humanity, his name alone has been exalted; that is, among all creatures he alone has a name that has been exalted above every name. For no creature—neither human being nor any heavenly spirit—is called “Lord of all” and “Almighty”; but he, although according to his humanity he is a creature, is called Lord and Almighty. At his name every knee bows, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. II, 10).

He explains in what respect his name has been exalted as follows: “His name alone has been exalted,” I say, and it has been exalted so greatly that his confession—that is, his praise—is [Col. 1415B] above heaven and earth; that is, among rational creatures who are above heaven and earth, namely, among the heavenly spirits and human beings. This is to say: Since he is Almighty and Lord of all, he is praised by human beings and angels.

After showing, from consideration of all creatures, that God is to be praised, he also shows that he is worthy of praise because in the future he will exalt his own. He says this as follows: “Not only, O faithful, should you praise the Lord in consideration of the heavens and the earth and the creatures that are in them, but also take from this an occasion for praise, because in the future he will exalt the horn of his people,” that is, he will exalt his people in eternal blessedness because of their horn—that is, because of the eminence they possess here in morals and virtues, which is understood by “horn,” since in an animal this is considered the higher part. This is to say: Because of the eminence of virtues and morals that the people of the faithful possess here, he will raise them up in the future through eternal glory; and therefore it is fitting that the faithful should praise him in consideration of this.

“He will exalt,” I say, “the horn of his people in the future.” Then there will be a hymn—that is, a cause for a hymn—for all his saints, namely, all his saints will praise him then with the eternal praise of love.

He explains who those saints are, section by section, as follows: “I speak of his saints, namely, the children of Israel,” that is, the faithful from the Jewish people, “and also of the people drawing near to him,” that is, drawing near to those children of Israel—namely, the people of the faithful from the nations, who will draw near to the faithful from the Jews through Christ, the cornerstone, that is, will be joined to them, so that from these two walls one city, namely the eternal Jerusalem, may be established.

Or it may be understood this way, with the qualification attached differently: “A hymn, I say, will belong to all his saints.” I speak of saints who are the children of Israel, that is, spiritual children who see God in contemplation. It is as though he were saying: In that state they will praise him in which, being spiritual children, they will see him in contemplation, as they do now, namely, seeing him from afar. But lest they should thus be understood to see Israel then as though through a mirror, he adds: “I speak of the children of Israel, namely, the people drawing near to him in knowledge.” This is to say: At that time the people of the children of Israel will be Israel in such a way that it will draw near to him according to knowledge; that is, they will no longer see and know God as through a mirror, but face to face, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “Now I know in part; then I shall know even as I am known” (I Cor. XIII, 12).

## IN PSALM CXLIX

**Title of the one hundred forty-ninth Psalm.** Alleluia. The voice of the Prophet inviting all the faithful to sing a new song to the Lord and explaining what it is to sing a new song, while also showing what benefit comes to those who sing in this way.

Sing a new song to the Lord Christ, O faithful—that is, praise the Lord with a new song. The old song is clinging to the actions of the old human being. The new song, however, is to possess, insofar as possible, conformity to Christ, the new human being, in the newness of life, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new human being, who was created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth” (Ephes. IV, 23).

I say: Praise the Lord with a new song, and praise him in the newness of life in such a way that you remain in the common fellowship of the faith of the Church of the saints. For his praise is found only in the Church of the saints. It is as though he were saying: Since you possess newness of life in virtues and good works, you ought therefore to persevere in the faith of the Church of the saints, because God is not worthily praised except by those who are in the Church of the saints. “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Eccl. XV, 9). He says “Church of the saints” in distinction from the Church of the wicked, which is called a church only improperly.

“Sing,” I say, [Col. 1416B] “O faithful, a new song to the Lord.” And whoever among those singing rises to such a dignity that he already becomes Israel here—that is, one who sees God in contemplation—should not rejoice in himself by ascribing this to himself; rather, let Israel rejoice, whoever in him has been made Israel by grace—namely, let him rejoice in the Lord, ascribing to him the fact that he is Israel.

And let the holy souls who already exist as daughters of Sion—that is, spiritual daughters of God through the adoption of grace—rejoice. I speak of daughters of Sion, that is, of those contemplating eternal things. Let them not proudly exult in themselves because of this, but let them exult in their King, namely, let them exult in the Lord with thanksgiving for the fact that he so governs them, advancing them from good to better, that they may be Sion.

For it is one thing to praise God because he makes his own Israel, and another to praise him because, by governing them in this contemplation, he makes them persevere in it. He calls holy souls “daughters” because of the extraordinary beauty of their virtues, since greater elegance and beauty are found in daughters than in sons.

[Col. 1416C] He explains section by section what he means by the new song, as follows: “Let the faithful sing,” I say, “a new song to you, O Lord,” namely, let them praise his name; that is, let them praise him in consideration of his name. “Let them praise,” I say, “and let them remain in the choir,” that is, in the harmony of love to be maintained toward God and neighbor. This is understood by “choir,” since properly speaking we call a choir a gathering of people singing in harmony.

And let them praise him “with the tambourine,” that is, in the mortification of the flesh through fasts and vigils and by removing carnal desires from themselves. Both of these are signified by the tambourine, since it is covered with the hide of dead animals, separated from the flesh and dried of all excess moisture.

“And let them sing psalms to him,” that is, let them do good works for his honor, laboring “with the psalter,” that is, in the enlivening of the spirit through virtues, which is the worthier and higher part of the human being. For this reason the psalter is appropriately understood as that which sounds from above.

They should praise the Lord in the choir, with the tambourine, and with the psalter because it is pleasing to the Lord that these praises should be present among his people. This alone ought to be a sufficient reason for doing so, even if no other reason existed.

There is also this other reason: Praise him in this way because he will exalt the meek—that is, he will greatly exalt those who praise him meekly, both here and in the future. He explains this section by section as follows: In the future he will exalt them, leading them into the salvation of eternal glory. And that glory will be so great that the saints—that is, the meek—will exult with eternal rejoicing in glory, that is, in the reception of that glory.

But lest they be thought to share in glory equally, he shows that they will share in it unequally, some more and others less. Through this he more strongly exhorts his hearers to live well, so that they may share in that glory more intensely. He says this as follows:

They will exult, I say, in glory. And yet they will rejoice “in their beds,” that is, in those suited to each of them—namely, in different shares of that glorious rest, which is signified by “beds,” since beds are suitable for the use of rest. It is as though he were saying: They will rejoice in that glory in such a way that each person will share in it in a different manner, according as it is fitting and according as he has deserved—one more, another less—in accordance with the Lord’s statement: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John XIV, 2). The Apostle also bears witness to this: “As star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV, 41).

I say that in the future he will exalt the meek into salvation. Here, however, he will exalt those same people in this way: “The exultations of God will be in their throat,” that is, the words of God’s preaching will be spoken exultantly in their throat. This is to say: They will proclaim God’s teaching exultantly to others with the external voice, which is formed in the throat. To preach this is indeed a great exultation and a great dignity, as the Lord testifies in the Gospel: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I too will confess him before my Father” (Matt. X, 32).

But because they could preach about God exultantly in such a way that it would nevertheless not be easy or straightforward for them to adapt the word of preaching according to their will and according to the capacity of their hearers, and their preaching might therefore not be effective, he specifies how they will preach when he adds: “The exultations of God will be in their throat, and in their hands”—that is, in their powers—“there will be two-edged swords,” that is, words of teaching that kill human beings according to what is evil in them, and for this reason they are called swords.

They are called two-edged because, after the likeness of two-edged swords, they cut away vices on both sides: through the old law and through the new. Or because for two reasons they destroy unbelief in human beings: by promising believers both bodily safety and eternal happiness.

This is as though he were saying: They will announce the word of teaching exultantly in such a way that they will have the power to arrange it as opportunity requires, after the manner of vigorous soldiers who, having swords in their hands, have the power to turn them in every direction as they please.

He shows for what useful effect the two-edged swords will be in their hands when he adds: “The swords,” I say, “will be in their hands, and this for great usefulness, namely, to execute vengeance upon the nations.” That is, the swords will be in their hands for the purpose of exercising God’s vengeance upon the multitudes of heretics, who are called “nations” because they have arisen in diverse heresies.

Preachers execute vengeance upon them for God either when they reconcile some of them, after their conversion, to the Church, or when they condemn others who refuse to convert by ecclesiastical anathema.

But because he had simply said “to execute vengeance,” lest it appear that they would thereby receive some secular vengeance, he indicates what vengeance they will execute when he adds: “And to administer reproofs among the peoples,” that is, among the multitudes of heretics. It is as though he were saying: For this they will have the two-edged swords of preaching in their hands: so that by this preaching they may rebuke the multitudes of heretics by refuting them, and thus execute vengeance upon them—reconciling some, as I have said, to the faith, but anathematizing others.

They will not have swords in their hands only to overcome lesser heretics; they will also have them “to bind their kings in the fetters of disputation,” that is, their principal heretics, who are kings and leaders of their faithlessness. This is to say:

For this purpose the swords of knowledge will be given to them: that they may overcome by their disputations those who are leaders of errors and bind them, as it were, with fetters, so that they have no power to resist.

And they have swords in their hands not only to bind lesser leaders, but also “to bind their nobles in iron shackles,” that is, in many strong bonds of argumentation from which they cannot escape, just as no bound person can escape from iron shackles.

Their nobles among the heretics [Col. 1418A]—that is, those heretics who are considered noble and more distinguished than the others, so that they even seem capable of performing miracles by displaying a certain appearance of false religion.

This is to say: The two-edged swords will be given to them for the purpose of binding those heretics who appear to be noble with many strong chains of argumentation, so that they have no power to resist.

And the two-edged swords will also be in their hands for this purpose: that, after they have bound and overcome the kings and nobles, they may “execute upon those kings and leaders a written judgment,” that is, the judgment of ecclesiastical discipline, which is written—that is, set down in many authoritative texts. Upon those who repent they should impose the burden of penance according to what is just; but those who do not repent they should condemn with a just anathema.

This is the glory of all his saints: namely, his saints regard this as glory—the faithful, whoever they may be—so that they praise him in the choir, with the tambourine, and with the psalter; be exalted unto salvation; bind kings and nobles in shackles and fetters; and execute upon them the written judgment.

He says this in order to invite his hearers more strongly to all the things that he has urged in the psalm.

The statement, “He will exalt the meek,” and so forth, is also read in another way. “He will exalt,” I say, as explained above, “the meek,” leading them into the salvation of eternal glory. In that glory the saints—that is, the meek themselves—will exult and rejoice in their beds, as explained above. In order that they may exult in glory, meanwhile “the exultations of God” will be in their throat here. Otherwise they would not be exalted in the future into salvation. The same applies to the other statements that follow, as they have been explained above.

## IN PSALM CL

**Title of the one hundred fiftieth Psalm.** Alleluia. The voice of the Prophet exhorting all the faithful to praise God in contemplation of the blessedness that the saints will possess in the future, which he also sets forth section by section in order to incite his hearers more strongly to such praise.

Praise the Lord Christ with mouth, heart, and deed, O faithful, “in his saints,” that is, in consideration of his saints.

He specifies according to what state of the saints he exhorts the faithful to praise God when he adds: Praise him, namely, “in his firmament,” that is, in consideration of the firmament of his virtue. It is as though he were saying: Praise the Lord because in the future he will strengthen his saints in virtue in such a way that there will no longer be any place in them for failure. Although they are strong here and, so to speak, spiritually virtuous, nevertheless, because of the weakness of the flesh, there remains in them a place for falling.

To increase God’s praise, he shows that there are several virtues in which they will be established, lest anyone suppose there is only one because he had said in the singular, “in the firmament of his virtue.” Praise him, I say, in the firmament of virtue; and this virtue will not be simple, but manifold. Therefore praise him “in his virtues,” that is, in consideration of the virtues in which he will strengthen the saints in the future.

Although they will not then exercise the effects of the virtues, they will nevertheless possess the dispositions themselves that we call virtues. For although there will no longer be an occasion for doing good works or suffering for Christ, patience and charity will nevertheless remain in them by nature. The same will be true of the other virtues, except for hope and faith, which will be brought to an end.

And do not praise him only in the virtues; praise him also “according to the multitude of his greatness,” that is, according to consideration of the manifold greatness by which he will magnify the saints in the future. Just as he will greatly magnify them, so praise him greatly.

He explains this greatness section by section when he adds: Praise him “with the sound of the trumpet,” that is, in consideration of the sound of the trumpet—namely, in consideration of the victory that he will give his own in the future, when neither death, nor the devil, nor unlawful suggestion will any longer be able to prevail against them. This is understood through the sound of the trumpet, since, when battle has ended and the enemies have been put to flight, victors customarily sound the trumpet.

Praise him also “with the psalter and the lyre,” that is, in consideration of the glorification of the soul, which is called the psalter, and of the body, which is called the lyre. The soul is signified by the psalter because it is the higher part of the human being, and the psalter sounds from above. Through the lyre, because it sounds from below, the body—which is lower in the human being—is expressed.

He also explains the glorification of the body section by section when he adds: Praise him “with the tambourine,” that is, in consideration of the tambourine—namely, in consideration of the removal of carnal pleasures, which is signified by the tambourine, because it is covered with hide separated from the flesh and dried of all excess moisture. It is as though he were saying: Praise him in consideration of this, because he will purify the body so completely that every carnal pleasure leading to sin will be removed from it.

Do not praise him only with the tambourine, but also “in the choir,” that is, in consideration of the choir—namely, in consideration of the harmony that will be possessed with the angels, which is expressed through the choir, since properly speaking we call a choir an assembly of people singing in harmony.

It is as though he were saying: He will glorify the body, which is so fragile, so weak, and of such heavy nature, making it immortal and of an agile nature, so that it will approach, to some degree, conformity with the nature of angels.

He specifies by what means they will attain this dignity when he adds: Praise him “with strings,” that is, in consideration of strings—namely, in consideration of the way by which he will make his own like strings. Just as the intestines of rams, although initially greasy and thick and then useless for producing any sound, are separated from their fat, dried, and reduced to slenderness, and thus become strings that produce a sweet sound, so also the saints, when here they become slender and lean in the flesh through the excessive affliction of fasts and vigils, will thereby attain in the future such dignity that, like strings, they will produce the sweetest melody of a pure conscience and bodily glorification.

Not only with strings, but also “with the organ,” praise him—that is, in consideration of the diverse merits of the saints, which are rightly understood through the organ. For just as in an organ, which is a musical instrument, there are many different pipes, some larger and others smaller, which nevertheless emit a harmonious symphony, so also the merits of the saints, although diverse—some greater and others lesser—will nevertheless be pleasing to God after the manner of a harmonious and sweetest symphony.

And do not praise him only with the organ; praise him also “with cymbals,” that is, in consideration of cymbals—namely, in consideration of the saints, who will become like cymbals in their bodies: that is, they will be so bright in the flesh, after the likeness of cymbals, which, being made of selected brass, have a shining color.

I speak of “well-sounding cymbals,” namely, because the saints will offer God the sweet song of a rightly ordered conscience and good devotion, in comparison with well-sounding cymbals.

He shows that they will sing to God not moderately when he adds: Praise him, I say, “with cymbals of jubilation,” that is, in consideration of the saints, who will sing to God without end with the jubilation of intense affection.

To speak universally, O faithful: “Let every spirit praise the Lord,” that is, let everything spiritual be for you an occasion of praising the Lord. It is as though he were saying: Let the bodies and souls of the faithful, which he himself will make glorious and spiritual, be for you, O faithful, an occasion of praising God.

He calls the bodies of the saints “spirits,” not because on the day of judgment they will not truly be bodies, as they are now, but because in immortality and agility they will in some way be made like spirits. Hence the Apostle says: “It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body” (I Cor. XV, 44). And shortly afterward: “But not first what is spiritual, but what is animal, and afterward what is spiritual” (ibid., 40).

Or it may be understood this way: Because he had invited the faithful to the praise of the Lord on the occasion of bodily glorification, he also exhorts them to the same praise on the occasion of the glorification of the spirit when he adds: Not only, O faithful, should you praise God with strings, organ, and cymbals, but also “let every spirit of the saints praise the Lord,” that is, let all the souls of the saints, which will be glorified in every respect in the future, be for you, O faithful, an occasion of praising the Lord.

To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1419] **End of the first volume of the Works of Blessed Bruno containing an exposition of the Davidic Psalms**

# ORDER OF THE MATERIALS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

**SAINT BRUNO, FOUNDER OF THE CARTHUSIAN ORDER.**
[Col. 1419C] **Acts of St. Bruno.** 9

**Preliminary Commentary.** 9

§ I.—Which life or acts should be published; the various sources from which these were either compiled or will be elucidated—whether aids or documents—and one of these documents, which is also to be published at the end of the Acts. *Same page.*

§ II.—The saint’s noble lineage, homeland, and time of birth. 23

§ XIII.—Whether Theodoric, abbot of Trudon, may rightly be counted among the writers who testified in favor of the resurrection of the Parisian doctor and its accompanying details. 132

§ XIV.—The testimony of Caesarius of Heisterbach is examined, and a judgment is established concerning it. 141

§ XV.—Whether anything contrary to the resurrection in which the doctor publicly declared that he had been condemned can be inferred from the silence either of St. Bruno, Guigo, or Guibert of Nogent. 151

§ XVI.—What judgment should be formed concerning the silence of the Carthusian order—as Launoy calls it—and of Peter the Venerable. 165

§ XVII.—What should be concluded from the silence of the other ancient writers whom Launoy also praises. 176

§ XX.—Whether tradition nevertheless cannot render certain, or at least probable, the miracle in which the doctor publicly declared before those present that he had been condemned, despite the universal silence of the writers mentioned above. 201

§ XXI.—National records favorable to the miracle in which the Parisian doctor publicly declared from his coffin before the assembled multitude that he had been condemned are brought forward; and it is examined whether, in the end, they make the event in any measure probable. 215

§ XXII.—The opinion that the condemned man’s miracle occurred within the deceased man’s private house, in the presence of only a few people, is proposed; and it is examined whether it should not be rejected as foolish and recently fabricated. 224

**Earlier Life of St. Bruno.** 481

**Single Chapter.**—The occasion of St. Bruno’s conversion; his decision to seek solitude; his drawing others to the same purpose; his journey to Grenoble; his withdrawal into the wilderness of Chartreuse; his journey to the pontiff after being summoned from there; his obtaining from him permission to return to solitude; his hiding himself in the Turritan wilderness of Calabria; and his death there. *Same page.*

**Second Life.** 491

**Prologue.** *Same page.*

**Chapter I.**—On the occasion of a dead man’s proclaiming from his coffin, during the solemn funeral rites, that he had been condemned, Bruno resolves to withdraw into solitude; draws others to the same purpose; and undertakes the journey with them to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble. 492

**Chapter II.**—Bruno comes with his companions to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble; obtains from him the wilderness of Chartreuse; lives there with great austerity; and, after approximately six years, is summoned by the pontiff and resolves to obey the one who calls him. 504

**Chapter III.**—The saint travels from Chartreuse to Rome; urges the disciples who followed him there to return to Chartreuse; and, after obtaining from the pontiff permission to withdraw and refusing the archbishopric of Reggio, hides himself in the wilderness of Calabria. There he enjoys the goodwill of Count Roger, founds new churches, and lives and dies in great holiness. 513

**Third Life.** 525

**Chapter I.**—A dead man publicly proclaims from his coffin that he has been condemned; on the occasion of this spectacle the saint resolves to withdraw into solitude to do penance, together with several others whom he moved to do the same; he sets out for Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and is kindly received by him. 526

[Col. 1423] **Chapter II.**—The saint enters the wilderness of Chartreuse; from there, where he lives in great holiness, he is summoned by Pope Urban II. His disciples follow him to Rome, and he urges them to return to Chartreuse; he refuses the archbishopric of Reggio and afterward obtains from the pontiff permission to return to solitude. 535

**Chapter III.**—He is found in the Turritan wilderness by Count Roger; saves him from the most imminent danger; builds two monasteries there through Roger’s generosity; lives until his death in great holiness in one of them; shines forth through miracles after his death; and finally, with the pontiff’s permission, is honored by the Carthusians with the honors due to the saints. 544

**Appendix**, or Supplement to the saint’s posthumous glory. 605

§ I.—The veneration shown in Calabria to the saint, already numbered among the blessed and transferred to the church of St. Stephen, and the miracles frequently performed at his invocation, some of which occurred before the year 1600, are related. *Same page.*

§ II.—Several miracles performed in the seventeenth century, though before its twenty-fourth year, are related; and it is explained how the saint’s cult was finally extended to the universal Church and his feast celebrated at Cologne. 615

§ III.—It is examined whether the saint was canonized in 1623 by Gregory XV, or only later by Clement X; and the remaining matters contributing to his posthumous glory, especially those that seem more worthy of notice, are brought forward. 624
